### Series title page

**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY—ENTIRE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL—OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIMES OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL THE EXTANT MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, MOST CAREFULLY CORRECTED BY COMPARISON WITH THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED BY THE DISCOVERY OF ALL WORKS COMPLETED AFTER THE MOST EXTENSIVE EDITIONS PRODUCED DURING THE LAST THREE CENTURIES; PROVIDED WITH SPECIAL ANALYTICAL INDEXES FOLLOWING THE INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ARRANGED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY DISTRIBUTED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AND WITH TITLES DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING ITS SUBJECT MATTER; EXPANDED WITH WORKS BOTH DUBIOUS AND APOCRYPHAL WHICH YET POSSESS SOME AUTHORITY IN RELATION TO ECCLESIASTICAL TRADITION; ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDEXES: ONE, NAMELY, OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH WHATEVER EACH Father has written upon any topic may be seen at a glance; THE OTHER OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH THE READER MAY READILY DISCOVER WHICH FATHERS HAVE COMMENTED ON THE INDIVIDUAL TEXTS OF THE INDIVIDUAL BOOKS OF SCRIPTURE, AND IN WHAT PLACES OF THEIR WORKS.**

**A MOST ACCURATE EDITION, EASILY TO BE PREFERRED TO ALL OTHERS, if one considers: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient form of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the whole series, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and small works hitherto scattered here and there, now for the first time assembled in our Library from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.**

**SECOND SERIES, IN WHICH ARE PUBLISHED THE FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND WRITERS OF THE LATIN CHURCH FROM GREGORY THE GREAT TO INNOCENT III.**

Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Library of the Entire Clergy, or of Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. # [THE DECREE OF GRATIAN]

[Col. 0007]

## NOTICE CONCERNING GRATIAN

(Fabricius, *Library of Medieval and Later Latin*, vol. III, p. 82.)

[Col. 0007] Gratian of Clusium [Note: [Col. 0007] At about the same time were Peter Lombard of Novara and Peter Comestor, a Gaul of Troyes; those who say that they were full brothers are mistaken. See [Col. 0008] Pagi on A.D. 1164, no. 19; and, on Gratian, add A.D. 1151, no. 10.], a city of Tuscany, monk of St. Felix at Bologna, of the Order of St. Benedict, completed in that monastery, in A.D. 1151, during the pontificate of Pope Eugenius III, a work which he had begun as early as 1127. Innocent III calls it the *Corpus of Decrees*; its author himself entitled it *The Concordance of Discordant Canons*. It is divided into 101 Distinctions, each again divided into its own chapters; and 36 Causes, subdivided into questions, and the questions into chapters; together with a treatment *On Consecration*, completed in five distinctions. In Cause XXXIII there further occurs a treatment *On Penance*, completed in seven distinctions.

This work was composed by Gratian on private initiative, making vigorous use of the collections of Burchard, Anselm, and Ivo; he eclipsed the renown of them all. As Pancirollus notes, it subsequently attained such authority that he was commonly called **THE MASTER**, and carried the greatest weight in deciding cases, even though, as a private individual, his pronouncements did not have the force of law. Compare what John Chiflet wrote in his praise and defence in *On the Architects of Both Laws*, chapter 5, Antwerp, 1651, quarto; and in vol. I of Everhard Otho’s *Treasury of Law*, p. 186 ff. Many have already observed how frequently Gratian erred: either in following the errors of Burchard and others, or in excerpting things which he had not read accurately, or in lending an ear to mistaken interpreters—he himself not even knowing the rudiments of Greek, as Baluze observed in his notes on Antonio Agustín’s *On the Correction of Gratian*, p. 536.

Cotta Palea, his disciple, is said to have added certain chapters to this collection of Gratian which are not found in the older manuscripts. The name *Paleae* has been attached to these. Some suppose it to be *παλαιόν*, “ancient,” referring to an old interpreter; others, *palea*, “chaff,” as though a matter of lesser importance. Neither explanation is satisfactory.

The first edition of Gratian, at Strasbourg, in large paper, 1471, folio, by Heinrich Eggestein, is mentioned by Jean Caillie in his *History of Printing*, published in French at Paris in 1689, quarto, p. 19; and thence by Michael Maittaire in the *Annals of Printing*, vol. I, p. 92. On p. 94 he also cites the *Authorities of the Decrees* by John Caldrini, from the Cologne edition of 1471, folio, printed by Peter de Olpe.

[Col. 0008] Baluze regarded the Mainz edition as the first, at the end of which these words are read:

> In the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1472, on the Ides of August, under the most holy Father and Lord in Christ, Sixtus IV, Supreme Pontiff; under the most illustrious Frederick, most glorious King of the Romans, lord of affairs, of the most noble House of Austria; while the noble and well-born Adolf of Nassau held the archbishopric of Mainz: in the noble city of Mainz, called “Golden” by our forefathers, which divine clemency has also deigned graciously to distinguish above the other nations of the earth by the art of printing, Peter Schoeffer of Gernsheim, with the aid of Almighty God, happily completed this present *Decree* of Gratian with its rubrics, not by pen and ink or reed, but by a certain ingenious art of printing, marking it with his own devices.

There follows a double shield or emblem: on one is the cross of St. Andrew with four looped and pointed projections; on the other, a figure resembling a capital Greek lambda, between three stars.

This was followed by Venetian editions of 1474 and 1479, folio, with the preface of Peter Albignano of Troyes; that of 1480, quarto, by Adam of Rotwil; and editions with the gloss at Venice in 1478 and 1486, folio, and 1493, folio; Basel, 1476, folio, with glosses; Paris, 1500, quarto; 1508 and 1517, octavo; 1522 and 1528, quarto.

*Gratian’s Decree corrected and enlarged with notes by Paul Constable, of the Order of Preachers, by command of Gregory XIII*, Venice, 1584, octavo, etc.

[The meaning of the *Palea* material in Gratian—or, rather, what that name prefixed to certain canons signifies—is determined by Fabricius, who supposes that it identifies the author of those canons as Cotta Palea, who judged them fit to be added to Gratian’s *Decree*. But the authority of the older manuscripts prevents me from accepting this. In them these *Paleae* are absent in such a way that the name *Palea* is never found, whereas the canons themselves are sometimes found. Therefore the *Paleae* are not Cotta’s addition; otherwise both the name and the canons would be absent from these old codices. Thus, for example, old codices read: “Palea of the canon *Magnus episcopus* [‘A great bishop’], Distinction LIV,” and “Palea of chapter *De servorum ordinatione* [‘On the ordination of slaves’], ibid., canon 6.” —Mansi.]

[Col. 0009]

# GREGORY XIII, POPE, TO ALL CHRIST’S FAITHFUL WHO SHALL EXAMINE THESE PRESENT LETTERS: GREETING AND APOSTOLIC BLESSING

The correction of the decrees and passages collected by Gratian—for that book was most full of errors and corruptions of testimonies—had been wisely undertaken by certain Roman Pontiffs, our predecessors, and entrusted to selected cardinals of the Holy Roman Church and other most learned men for that task. It had, however, hitherto been delayed by many and various impediments. Now at last, after the oldest codices had everywhere been sought out, the very authors whose testimonies Gratian had used had been read through, and matters wrongly placed had been restored to their proper places, we have ordered it to be published as completed and perfected with great diligence.

In this matter great regard has been had for the dignity of the work itself and for public usefulness, especially for those engaged in this field of study. We therefore command that everything corrected and restored be retained with the greatest care, so that nothing may be added, altered, or diminished.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, under the Ring of the Fisherman, on the second day of June 1582, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

Ant. Buccapadulius.

[Col. 0009]

# GREGORY XIII, POPE, FOR PERPETUAL REMEMBRANCE

Since, by reason of the pastoral office laid upon our shoulders, we have especially set before ourselves the task of ensuring, with every zeal and diligence, that all Christ’s faithful—especially in these so grave and calamitous times—remain in the true and Catholic faith; and since for this reason we must above all act and provide so as to remove from everyone every occasion of straying from it: some time ago, for carrying this purpose into effect, we entrusted to certain of our brethren, the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, assisted by the efforts of certain men distinguished for learning and piety, the task of revising, correcting, and purging the work called Gratian’s *Decree* without glosses, as well as that same *Decree* together with the *Decretals* of our predecessor Pope Gregory IX, the *Sixth Book*, the *Clementines*, and the *Extravagants*: not only of the old glossators—who, since they were pious and Catholic men, seem deserving of pardon if they spoke too freely in any respect through error, or because most matters had not yet been defined by sacred councils—but also of the material hostile to Catholic truth which had been scattered over them by impious writers, both in the outer margins and within the text.

Now, since the said *Decree* without glosses has already been wholly emended and corrected by those whom we appointed, and illustrated with certain annotations; and since the greater part of it has been reviewed and approved by our beloved son Paul Constable, then Master of our Apostolic Palace, together with the already printed *Decretals* of our predecessor Gregory IX of happy memory; and since we have ordered the remainder of the same *Decree*, together with the aforesaid annotations, both without glosses and in its entirety with glosses, and also the *Sixth Book*, the *Clementines*, and the *Extravagants*, to be reviewed and approved by our beloved son Sixtus Fabri, Master of our Apostolic Palace, and to be printed and, once printed, published in the printing-house of the Roman People—which was established especially in order that sacred books might be printed there faithfully and without corruption—and since, for the greater convenience of Christ’s faithful everywhere dwelling both within and outside Italy, on this and the other side of the Alps, this body of Canon Law may be faithfully and incorruptly printed from the exemplar printed here at Rome by Catholic printers chosen by the Roman People or by persons appointed or to be appointed by it for the time being:

We, wishing suitably to provide that this Canon Law, thus purged, may reach all Christ’s faithful everywhere whole and unimpaired, and that no one may be permitted to add anything to, alter, or pervert the same work, or to append any interpretations to it, but that, as [Col. 0011] it has now been printed in our City of Rome, it may always and perpetually be preserved entire and incorrupt: of our own motion, with certain knowledge and from the fullness of Apostolic power, do by these present letters prohibit and forbid, under holy obedience, all and each printer, publisher of books, bookseller, and any other person, of either sex, of whatsoever dignity, status, rank, order, or condition, whether dwelling in our dominions or in the dominions of the Holy Roman Church, immediately or mediately subject to us or to that Roman Church, or entering them under any pretext, and likewise those existing anywhere outside the said dominion, under sentence of major excommunication *latae sententiae*; and, as regards those now or hereafter dwelling in the dominion immediately or mediately subject to us and to the Roman Church, also under the penalty of forfeiture of the books and of one thousand gold ducats of the Apostolic Camera—one third, namely, to the office of the Inquisition into heretical depravity, another third to the accuser, and the remaining third to the enforcing judge, to be applied irrevocably—together with such other penalties at our discretion as shall be incurred automatically, whenever the prohibition is violated, by each offender:

They shall not, for ten years from the date of these presents, under any title, retain, sell, give, donate, otherwise possess, or transfer Gratian’s *Decree* with annotations, or the same with glosses, the *Decretals* of our predecessor Gregory IX, the *Sixth Book*, the *Clementines*, and the *Extravagants*, as aforesaid, whether printed or to be printed, anywhere other than in our City and in the said printing-house of the Roman People, and by those to whom the Roman People or its appointees for this purpose have granted faculty and permission for that period, anywhere in Italy or outside Italy. We grant to the Roman People and its appointees that they may freely and lawfully give such licence and faculty, in Italy and beyond Italy, to any persons whatsoever whom the Roman People or those appointed by it for the time being shall judge and choose; provided that the person is first notified to and approved by us; and that they may freely and lawfully revoke a licence thus granted, whenever and as they please.

Nor may such persons, without the express written licence of the Roman People and its appointees, print the said *Decree* of Gratian with the annotations, or the same with glosses, the *Decretals* of our predecessor Gregory IX, the *Sixth Book*, the *Clementines*, and the *Extravagants;* nor during the said ten years may they otherwise possess, retain, sell, donate, or cause to be printed, retained, sold, donated, or otherwise transferred, either themselves or through another or others, publicly or secretly, directly or indirectly, by any contrived pretext or device, any such work printed or to be printed by persons other than the said Roman People and its appointees, or without their licence as aforesaid.

Thus we decree, enact, and ordain that absolutely no person, whether in the City and throughout Italy or anywhere beyond, in whatsoever lands, kingdoms, regions, or provinces of the whole world, may add to, remove from, alter, or pervert anything in these books of the said Canon Law, reviewed, corrected, and purged by our command as aforesaid, or append interpretations to them; but that this work, as now printed at Rome, be always and perpetually preserved entire and incorrupt.

We command all and each venerable brethren, patriarchs, archbishops, and bishops, the other Ordinaries of places and their vicars in spiritual and temporal matters, and, in the temporal state of the Holy Roman Church, also the legates and vice-legates of the Apostolic See, and the governors, magistrates, and lieutenants of that state: whenever they, or any of them, are requested on behalf of the said Roman People and its appointees, or those who at the time hold licence and authority from them as aforesaid, they shall assist that People, its appointees, and persons holding such licence and authority with the protection of effective defence; and, at the request of the Roman People, its appointees, or persons holding their licence or authority, shall enforce the foregoing against the disobedient as rebels by Apostolic authority, including by ecclesiastical censures, to be repeatedly aggravated if necessary, and by other remedies of law, invoking, should there be need, the aid of the secular arm.

Moreover, because it would be exceedingly difficult for these present letters to be conveyed to every place, we will and decree by the same Apostolic authority that authenticated copies and exemplars thereof, signed by the hand of a public notary and sealed with the seal of a court or of a person established in ecclesiastical dignity, and also those printed in the works themselves, shall everywhere receive full and exactly the same credit, both in court and out of court, as these present letters would receive. Notwithstanding Apostolic constitutions and ordinances; statutes and customs of whatever places, academies, and universities, including general universities, reinforced by oath, Apostolic confirmation, or any other form of firmness; privileges likewise granted; and Apostolic letters granted and approved, or hereafter to be granted and approved, to those persons or to any others, under whatsoever tenor and form, even by like motion, knowledge, and fullness of power, or otherwise in any manner contrary to this.

With respect to all these, even if special mention of them ought to be made, we regard their tenors as expressly set forth in these presents; while they are otherwise to remain in force, we derogate from them on this occasion only, specially and expressly, notwithstanding anything to the contrary. Or notwithstanding any indult granted, jointly or severally, by the same See to certain persons, that they cannot be interdicted, suspended, or excommunicated through Apostolic letters not making full, express, and word-for-word [Col. 0013] mention of such indult.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, under the Ring of the Fisherman, on 1 July 1580, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

Caes. Glorierius.

[Col. 0013]

# [TO THE READER]

The matters concerning which it seemed proper at the outset to warn the reader are these.

[Col. 0013A] It is plainly established that, in the Roman Church, the teacher of all Churches, the canons of councils and decrees of pontiffs have customarily been preserved and communicated to the other Churches.

The collection which Nicholas the Pope calls, in chapter *Si Romanorum*, Distinction 19, the *Code of Canons*, appears especially to have been in use. It contained the canons and rules enumerated by Leo IV, chapter *De libellis*, Distinction 20. Three manuscript exemplars of this code are held at Rome in the Vatican Library. It was also printed at Mainz in the year of salvation 1525.

There has also been found in a very old codex of Cardinal Vercelli’s collection of Cresconius addressed to Bishop Liberinus a sort of *nomocanon*, or code of ecclesiastical and civil law. After several headings of cases have been proposed, it sets forth the places in synodal texts and decretal letters in which those cases are treated. Its chapters correspond very well with the chapters of the Mainz code, and its numbers with the numbers of that code. The diligence employed by Cresconius [Col. 0013B] sufficiently shows that this collection was in extremely frequent use. It is this collection that, in the annotations now published, is called simply the *Code of Canons*.

Among private collectors, however, who endeavoured to gather far more material, Isidore is very ancient. His collection extends from the canons of the apostles to the Second Council of Seville. It is preserved in two codices of the Vatican Library and in one of the Dominican monastery of St. Mary above Minerva; and it is printed in editions of the councils—more pure in the earlier editions, but mixed in the later editions with many other councils and writings. Archbishop Hincmar of Rheims, in his book *On Synods*, declares that this Isidore was the celebrated man of Seville. Trithemius likewise testifies that a book of decrees was compiled by him; and certainly many words found in the preface of this collection occur in the fifth book of the *Etymologies*. [Col. 0013C] In the codex of the Dominican library, the beginning of the preface reads: “Isidore Mercator, servant of Christ, to his fellow-servant the reader,” etc.; and not much differently in the Vatican codices. In the printed copies the reading at this place is: “Isidore the sinner, servant of Christ,” etc.

Afterwards followed—as we may first speak of those whose works have been printed—Burchard, bishop of Worms, in the age of the emperors Otto III and Henry II of Bavaria. He thought that he should follow not the order of times and provinces, as Isidore did, but that of subjects and cases.

Not much later Ivo, bishop of Chartres, followed in the same tracks. But, in the meantime, the heresy of Berengar had arisen; therefore he added much relevant to its refutation, and much besides from the *Pandects* and the *Code*, since he believed that he must also treat the duties of laymen, something Burchard had considered less necessary.

There are two volumes bearing Ivo’s name [Col. 0013D] and containing the same preface. One is entitled *Panormia*; the other, simply *Decree*, is a kind of epitome of the former. Yet other most distinguished men also worked admirably in this field and proved their worth: Cresconius, Anselm, Cardinal Deusdedit, Gregory the Priest, who entitled his volume *Polycarpus*, and several others. The latest of all these, apart from [Col. 0014A] the author of the *Panormia*—for he may be later—was Gratian, a Benedictine monk. He devoted himself not only to collecting decrees, as his predecessors had done, but, perhaps stirred by Ivo’s preface, applied himself especially to setting forth definite questions, and to bringing forward and explaining what could be said from the canons on either side, where they sometimes seemed to conflict with one another. In short, he sought to bring into harmony their diversity, which had the appearance of disagreement. Yet in a long and very difficult work much was attacked by unfair-minded people, and even pious and modest persons sometimes found certain things wanting.

Accordingly, lest the authority of this most useful and weighty code should be shaken, it pleased Pius IV, and subsequently Pius V and Gregory XIII—under whom belongs the credit for this completed work, as also for other very great achievements—that the utmost effort should be devoted to its correction: that scribal errors [Col. 0014B] should be removed; that, if Gratian as a man had seen less clearly in any matter, this should be noted with restraint; and that the chapters themselves should be restored with the greatest care to their authors.

Thus the Vatican Library at Rome, the Dominican monastery above Minerva, and several other collections were examined. The most learned men were invited from other cities and regions to do the same and, if they found anything relevant to this matter, willingly to communicate it in accordance with their piety and send it to the pontiff. By this diligence it came about that a source is now assigned to a great part of the material. Consequently, one can usually understand which decrees and opinions are those of general synods, which of supreme pontiffs, which of provincial councils, and which of the Fathers; and, among these, which have been approved by the Holy Roman See and which have not. Thereafter scarcely anyone can err by following uncertain things as certain, or by holding established things to be doubtful and suspect.

[Col. 0014C]

**On citations.**—With respect to citations of authors, where an error was obvious, or where certain copies of Gratian agreed with a truer citation produced by other collectors, false attributions were removed and true ones restored. But where, although a chapter was found in another author, it was nevertheless possible that it also belonged to the author cited by Gratian—for decrees transmitted from one source to another and similar opinions are not uncommon among sound authors—Gratian’s citation was retained, and it was judged sufficient to indicate the place where the material is found today.

And because sometimes one part of a chapter belongs to the cited author while another part does not, or because the words have been substantially changed, this too is indicated. Furthermore, the margin records where the same chapter occurs in the Ordinary Gloss on the Bible, the books of the *Sentences*, and the other collectors, especially those who were of great assistance in correcting this work. It was observed, moreover, that in former times there were many volumes of homilies collected from various authors—some of which are still extant [Col. 0014D] today—in which either the author’s name had not been prefixed to a homily or had even been changed. This sometimes gave occasion for error to collectors of decrees, who, in that scarcity of books, were generally unable to consult the sources.

Gratian also frequently gathers several opinions of the Fathers together and encloses them in a single chapter—though in the commonly circulated codices they are generally divided into different chapters, but almost without headings. When he does this, he does not cite the authors’ exact words; rather, at his discretion, he changes, adds, diminishes, and summarizes them. [Col. 0015A] Burchard and Ivo do the same when they cite in this manner: “from the sayings of Augustine,” “from the sayings of Jerome.”

**On corrections.**—In correcting the text, the beginnings of chapters were first left unchanged because of the customary citations of scholars; but where they differed from the original, the genuine reading was indicated in the margin or in an annotation. Next, regard was had for the gloss itself in this way: nothing was altered in the text where the alteration itself would have obstructed recognition of the glossator’s intended meaning; rather, the error was indicated in the margin or in an annotation. But where these considerations did not stand in the way, the following method of correction was generally observed.

If Gratian appeared to have intended to report the exact words of the authors whom he cited, the text was corrected from the original source; at times, where no slight advantage was thereby proposed, something was also added—unless the common reading seemed preferable. In that case it was retained, [Col. 0015B] with a note stating how the original itself reads. But if Gratian had not intended to reproduce the very words, but either to make a summary himself or to report a summary made by others, such as the author of the Ordinary Gloss, Ivo, or other collectors, then almost nothing was corrected or added, unless restoration of the reading of the Father from whom the collector had drawn it seemed likely to produce considerable benefit. In many places this was noted, and the words of the original itself were supplied, so that the reader might repeatedly be reminded of this precaution and relieved of the labour of consulting the originals.

If the same chapter was formed from several neighbouring passages of a Father—for passages far apart, it was generally enough to indicate them in the margin—those passages above and below were added to the text, where they would not obstruct the sequence and connection of the compilation. But where Gratian himself speaks, a pure and genuine reading was restored from manuscript exemplars of this book.

[Col. 0015C]

**On translations.**—In the *Code of Canons*, the chapters cited from Greek synods were translated into Latin by Dionysius Exiguus, whose preface is found prefixed to manuscript exemplars of the code itself. Isidore, however, used partly this very translation of Dionysius, although rarely; partly perhaps that ancient translation mentioned by Dionysius in his preface, whether whole or somewhat altered; and partly others which then existed, as Isidore himself testifies, but which today survive nowhere except among these collectors of decrees.

Therefore it is by no means surprising if the other collectors, and Gratian, nearly the last of them all, who possessed both that *Code of Canons* and Isidore’s collection as well as others, did not always cite the same canon from the same translation. Readers are often warned of this in the annotations; and where it seemed necessary, the Greek words of the canon were given with a new translation. The same has been done with the other opinions of Greek Fathers.

[Col. 0015D] **On the Paleae.**—There are various opinions among learned men concerning the name *Palea*. Many have thought that chapters containing empty and trivial matters were called by this name; others that it was as though *τὰ παλαιά*, that is, “the ancient things”; others that it denoted certain additions, deriving—or rather corrupting—the word from the adverb *πάλιν*, “again,” which Latin writers also used in Gratian’s time.

But John Andreae, in his additions to the *Speculator*, under the title *On Disputations and Allegations*, near the end—a view followed by Imola in the rubric *On Obligations of Words*, by Alexander in the preface to the *Decretals*, by Jason in the rubric of the title *On Actions*, and by others—believes that a certain Protopalea, whom Jason adds was a cardinal, appended these chapters to Gratian’s collection.

In order that some inference may be drawn from conjecture in a matter so uncertain, [Col. 0016A] the following observations from the collated exemplars will be set forth. In the three that are most ancient and appear to have been written shortly after Gratian’s time, very few chapters of this sort occur. In one, which is very carefully corrected, they have been placed in the margin without any indication, but not all those occurring in the printed editions—although, conversely, that manuscript has some additions not found in the printed editions. In another, written in very ancient letters, the *Paleae* themselves, in a later hand, are prefixed to the whole volume. In the rest, either all or most are found, partly under the name *Paleae* and partly without any distinction from the other chapters.

From this observation it appears possible to infer that these *Paleae* are additions, made at different times, first written in the margin of Gratian’s original collection, and that perhaps some were made by Gratian himself, as happens during composition or revision. Certain scribes then omitted them; others placed them in the text, sometimes [Col. 0016B] joined with preceding chapters and sometimes with some distinction. The opinion of those who think them contemptible is false. For many occur both in the *Decretals* and among Gratian’s older collectors, as will be indicated in their proper places.

### On the Title

In most ancient copies of this collection, the following is written in red letters as its heading: *Concordance of Discordant Canons*, with the word *Begins* added in some, but with no mention of Gratian. In that very ancient Vatican manuscript, however—the one in which, as was said, the *Paleae* are prefixed to the beginning of the volume itself in a later hand—this title precedes the *Paleae*:

> The Decree of Gratian, monk of Saint Felix at Bologna, of the Order of Saint Benedict, compiled in the said monastery in the year of the Lord 1151, in the time of Pope Eugenius III.

But in two other manuscripts, the following occurs at the end:

> Here ends the Decree compiled by Gratian, monk of the monastery of Saint Felix of Bologna.

In the Chronicle entitled *The Orchard of the Church of Ravenna*, a book preserved in the Vatican Library, the following is written concerning Gratian:

> In the year of Christ 1151, Gratian, a monk, born in the city of Classa [Note: [Col. 0015D] alternatively, Clusium; alternatively, Ginsa.] in Tuscany, composed the Decree at Bologna, in the monastery of Saint Felix.

The same is attested by Huguccio, the most ancient interpreter of this book, in Cause 2, Question 6, chapter *Post appellationem*; by Vincent of Beauvais twice in his *Mirror of History*, once in Book 23, chapter 31, when speaking of Isidore, and again in Book 25, chapter 84, when treating Ivo and other collectors of decrees; and by Saint Antoninus, Part Three of the *History*, title 18, chapter 6. Trithemius, moreover, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, recognizes Gratian as the author of this collection, as he also does in Book Two of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*. Yet there he adds—perhaps considering the actual beginning of the work—that it was composed by him in the year of the Lord 1127 [Col. 0016D]. Innocent III, in his letter to the Archbishop of Compostela, calls this collection the *body of decrees*. Therefore, on account of these authorities and the opinion universally received, the title bearing Gratian’s name has been prefixed to the first page of this volume.

### On the Annotations in the Gloss

As regards glosses that have catholic and pious authors, errors of somewhat greater consequence that have crept into them through the weakness of human understanding have been noted in the margin, and what ought to be held in a catholic sense has been shown. These notes, marked with an asterisk, must henceforth necessarily be added in all editions.

[Col. 0017]

## PREFACE TO THE READER BY AEMILIUS LUDOVICUS RICHTER

Since canon law, long despised and rejected as though useless, began once again to be studied more diligently, a new and more corrected edition of the body of canons was demanded more and more each day. Copies of earlier editions were available only rather rarely, and even in the better editions there was an abundance of material that appeared still to require correction. This being so, we undertook the work with the purpose of preparing an edition as free as possible from printers’ errors, one which would include everything that could be gathered from the writings of various learned men concerning the correction of individual canons. We should now briefly inform the kindly reader how we have conducted our undertaking.

To speak first of the text which we have followed: reason itself advised that we ought not depart from the edition formerly published at Rome by command of Gregory XIII. At first, indeed, the text of Boehmer’s edition seemed sufficient, since it too bore Gregory’s name and was justly praised by all as outstanding. But on closer examination we discovered that the two texts differ from one another more than once.

[Note: [Col. 0021] Let the following serve as examples: D. I, c. 5, § 1, *quoniam* (“because”): Boehmer = *quando* (“when”): Roman edition.—c. 6, *susceptio* (“receiving; begetting”): Boehmer = *successio* (“succession”): Roman edition.—*commodatae* (“lent”) : Boehmer = *commendatae* (“entrusted”): Roman edition.—D. IV, c. 1, *refrenetur audacia et nocendi facultas* (“let boldness and the ability to harm be restrained”): Boehmer = *refrenetur nocendi facultas* (“let the ability to harm be restrained”): Roman edition.—D. V, c. 4, § 1, *debet* (“ought”): Boehmer = *valet* (“is valid”): Roman edition.—at the end of the section, *esuriamus* (“we may hunger”): Boehmer = *esurerimus* (“we shall have hungered”): Roman edition.—Distinction VI, c. 1, § 3, *etsi dormienti* (“although [to one] sleeping”): Boehmer = *etsi dormienti corpore* (“although with the body sleeping”): Roman edition.—Distinction VII, c. 3, *quantumvis vulgata, quantumvis vetusta* (“however common, however ancient”): Roman edition.—Distinction X, c. 1, § 2, *quibus ecclesia* (“to whom the Church”): Boehmer = *quibus saepe ecclesia* (“to whom the Church often”): Roman edition.—Distinction XI, c. 5, *successores* (“successors”): Boehmer = *successiones* (“successions”): Roman edition.—c. 11, § 1, *convenisse non dubium est* (“there is no doubt that [they] agreed”): Boehmer = *convenisse* (“to have agreed”): Roman edition.—*arbitrarer* (“I might judge”): Boehmer = *arbitraremur* (“we might judge”): Roman edition.—Distinction XIII, c. 2, § 4, *declinaret* (“he/she/it might decline”): Boehmer = *declinarent* (“they might decline”): Roman edition.—D. XV, c. 6, *alia concilia* (“other councils”): Boehmer = *concilia* (“councils”): Roman edition.—D. XVI, c. 4, *Primus* (“First”): Boehmer = *Primo* (“Firstly”): Roman edition.—*canones* (“canons”): Boehmer = *canonum* (“of canons”): Roman edition.—*est interpolatum* (“has been interpolated”): Boehmer = *interpolatur* (“is interpolated”): Roman edition.—c. 6, *utpote* (“namely; since”): Boehmer = *ut* (“as; that”): Roman edition.—c. 7, *suo* (“his own”): Boehmer = *tuo* (“your own”): Roman edition.—Distinction XVII, Part 2, § 3, *subscripsit* (“he signed”): Boehmer = *subscripsi* (“I signed”): Roman edition.—*episcopum* (“bishop,” accusative): Boehmer = *episcopus* (“bishop,” nominative): Roman edition.—D. XIX, c. 17, *agitur* (“is dealt with”): Boehmer = *agitatur* (“is discussed”): Roman edition.—*referet* (“will report”): Boehmer = *reseret* (“will unlock”): Roman edition.—*ad resistendum potius, quam ad obediendum* (“rather for resisting than for obeying”): Boehmer = *non ad obediendum potius, quam ad resistendum* (“not rather for obeying than for resisting”): Roman edition.—D. XX, c. 1, *judicant* (“they judge”): Boehmer = *judicantur* (“they are judged”): Roman edition.—Distinction XXI, c. 1, § 15, *tam clara* (“so clear”): Boehmer = *tam clara erit* (“it will be so clear”): Roman edition.—c. 6, at the end: *judicandi coercendique sunt, si his* (“they are to be judged and restrained, if by these”): Boehmer = *judicandis coercendi sunt, si his* (“they are to be restrained by judging, if by these”): Roman edition.—D. XXII, c. 5, at the end, *qui* (“who,” masculine): Boehmer = *quae* (“which; who,” feminine): Roman edition.—D. XXIII, c. 3, at the beginning, *Hic igitur* (“Therefore this”): Boehmer = *His igitur* (“Therefore by these”): Roman edition.—c. 10, *Sed qui ita* (“But he who thus”): Boehmer = *Sed quia ita* (“But because thus”): Roman edition.—c. 13, 14, *presbyterum quendam* (“a certain presbyter,” accusative): Boehmer = *presbyter quidam* (“a certain presbyter,” nominative): Roman edition.—D. XXIV, c. 3, *supradicta* (“the aforesaid things,” neuter plural): Boehmer = *supradictae* (“the aforesaid,” feminine): Roman edition.—Distinction XXV, c. 1, § 7, *aures habere* (“to have ears”): Boehmer = *aures haberi* (“ears to be had”).—§ 11, *epistolam* (“a letter”): Boehmer = *Apostolum* (“the Apostle”): Roman edition.—Thus far these examples. Very many others are indicated in the notes. Moreover, in Boehmer’s edition, in the Correctors’ warning, p. LI; Distinction XLVII, p. 3; p. 139; Distinction L, c. 41; Cause 1, Question 1, c. 41, nearly entire lines dropped out through the carelessness of the typesetters.]

For Boehmer, a man of immortal memory, relying on the authority of manuscripts and Torquemada, sometimes altered the text, and did not use the Roman edition itself. Hence it came about that he did not sufficiently avoid errors found in common editions through typographical fault. It was therefore a fortunate day when the most distinguished Gustav Haenel kindly shared with us that Roman copy itself; by its assistance we have at last been able to restore the text to the original condition in which Gregory intended it always to remain unimpaired.

There is no need to speak of its character and quality, since all agree that the Roman Correctors emended the text not by returning to ancient manuscripts of Gratian, but to the sources themselves and to passages of authors—and sometimes also, though more rarely, to the canon collections of Ivo, Burchard, and Anselm—in such a way that it could almost seem to have been made anew. Since they usually refrained from indicating what they had changed, we labored especially to show what had been altered by them and what they had either removed or added.

We therefore collated the most ancient editions of the Decree:

[Note: [Col. 0021] 1. *Decree, by the venerable Heinrich Eggestein*. Strasbourg, 1471.—2. *Decree, by Michael Wenssler*. Basel, 1481.—3. *Decree, printed by the art of Johann Herbort of Seligenstadt, a German*. Venice, 1482.—4. *Decree, by Giorgio Arrivabene*. 1490.—5. *Decree, by Koberger*. Nuremberg, 1493.—6. *Decree, by Jean Chappuis*. Paris, 1506, quarto.—7. *Decree*. Lyons, 1515.—8. *Decree*. Lyons, at the press of Hugues de la Porte, 1559.—9. *Decree*. Lyons, 1554, quarto.]

These were the Strasbourg, Basel, two Venetian, Nuremberg, Paris, and three Lyons editions. Among them the Basel edition appeared especially excellent, because it often differs very little from the readings of Ivo, Anselm, and the other authors whom Gratian followed in compiling the Decree. We therefore rightly suspect that it was printed from very ancient manuscripts of Gratian [Col. 0023]. Accordingly, we recorded variant readings in the annotations placed below the text; additions—which occur very frequently—we carefully marked with an asterisk.

Yet the Correctors, despite all their diligence, left not a few matters that still required correction. The chief cause of this was that they adhered too closely to the glosses, and, in revising the canons of councils, used almost exclusively Merlin’s collection of councils, which, as no one is unaware, presents pseudo-Isidorian wares. Since circumstances prevented us from correcting the text ourselves, we considered it in the public interest to indicate in annotations the genuine reading both of the canons and of the remaining fragments.

Accordingly, we used the best editions of the sources: for the canons of councils, González’s Spanish collection;

[Note: [Col. 0023] I. *Collection of Canons of the Spanish Church, now first published from the most approved and ancient codices by the public library at Madrid*. Madrid, Royal Press, A.D. 1808. It contains: 1. A preface by the editor, Francisco Antonio González, nine folios; 2. the index of canons, as it is called, contained in ten books, p. LX; 3. the preface of the compiler, one folio; 4. canons of councils, col. DCLXXX. II. *Decretal Letters and Rescripts of the Roman Pontiffs*. Madrid, press of the heirs of Don Joaquín de Ibarra, A.D. 1821, folio, pp. CLXVII; index of subjects and arguments, pp. 169–196.]

this too was provided to us by the distinguished Haenel; Justellus’s Dionysian codex and Eusebius Amort;

[Note: [Col. 0023] *Library of Ancient Canon Law*, by the work and study of G. Voellus and H. Justellus. Paris, 1661, two folio volumes.—Eusebius Amort, *Ancient and Modern Canon Law*, vol. II. Ulm, 1757, quarto.]

the Quesnel codex of the Ballerini brothers;

[Note: [Col. 0023] In the Appendix to the works of Saint Leo the Great. Venice, 1757, folio.]

together with the *Statutes of the Ancient Church* published by them, which commonly circulate under the name of the Fourth Council of Carthage; the collection of councils of Gaul published by Dom Labat;

[Note: [Col. 0023] *Collection of the Councils of Gaul, Both Published and Unpublished*, by the work and study of the monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, vol. I, folio. In the copy preserved by the Pauline Library at Leipzig, Henri Grégoire, formerly Bishop of Blois, wrote the following in the margin: “Dom Labat, a Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint Maur, published a first volume of a new edition of the councils of France. Printing of the second volume had begun, but the events of the Revolution interrupted this work. The entire work in manuscript, which would make about eight folio volumes, exists in the hands of Dom Brial, member of the National Institute and fellow Benedictine of Dom Labat. The latter died about three years ago, and Dom Brial printed the biographical notice. H. Grégoire, at Helmstedt, August 1803.”]

and Mansi’s collection.

For revising fragments of decretal letters, we had at hand Coustant’s excellent edition of the letters of the Roman Pontiffs;

[Note: [Col. 0023] Vol. I. Paris, 1721, folio.]

the Maurist edition of Gregory the Great;

[Note: [Col. 0023] *Volume II of the Complete Works of Gregory the Great*. Paris, 1705, folio.]

the Ballerini edition of Leo the Great; Mabillon’s *Ancient Analects*;

[Note: [Col. 0023] Paris, 1723, folio.]

Baluze’s *Miscellanies*;

[Note: [Col. 0023] Paris, 1678–1715, vols. 7–8.]

d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*;

[Note: [Col. 0023] Paris, new edition, 1723, three folio volumes.]

Lucas Holstenius’s Roman collection;

[Note: [Col. 0023] Rome, 1662.]

and the collections of Ivo;

[Note: [Col. 0023] *Works of Ivo*, Paris, 1647, two folio volumes. We used Brandt’s edition of the *Panormia* (Basel, 1499). Theiner recently observed that the Louvain edition of 1557 is nothing but a reprint of Brandt’s edition: *On Ivo’s Alleged Decree*, Mainz, 1832.—We have not yet obtained Burchard’s great volume of decrees. Therefore, we borrowed the numbers of books and chapters from the Roman edition, which is most correct; nor did we omit to report what Berardus copied from Burchard.]

and Anselm’s collection, in which the true reading is often concealed. The distinguished Haenel supplied us with a copy of Anselm, which exists only in manuscript. Among other treasures (*κειμήλια*, “precious possessions”), he brought home a copy of Anselm transcribed from the Paris manuscript: Codex Chartaceus folio, Royal Library, Supplement Latin no. 1665; Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Congregation of Saint Maur, no. 939, 2–3.

[Note: [Col. 0023] See what the Ballerini brothers observed concerning Anselm of Lucca’s collection in *Works of Leo the Great*, vol. 3, p. CCXCVII. The copy that we have recently collated contains a considerable number of decretals pertaining to a later period, added—as Augustine would say—after Anselm’s death by some diligent man. It consequently happened that the numbers produced by the Correctors from what appear to have been their older manuscripts did not adequately correspond with ours. We therefore thought it proper to give both sets.]

To the variant readings indicated in the remaining chapters, besides the canons of councils and fragments of decretals, we added the book and chapter numbers under which the individual canons are cited by the collectors; and we mentioned Regino as well,

[Note: [Col. 0023] His collection is available in Harzheim, volume two of the collection of German councils, published at Cologne in 1760.]

together with the collection in three parts, whose description Theiner recently published.

[Note: [Col. 0023] *On Ivo’s Alleged Decree*. Mainz, 1832.]

We then took particular pains to identify the true headings of the chapters, which everyone knows have been astonishingly corrupted, and to supply whatever the Correctors had not seen, or had seen insufficiently. In this undertaking we received notable assistance from the editions of the Pithou brothers and of Boehmer; Augustine’s immortal work,

[Note: [Col. 0023] Antonio Agustín, *On the Correction of Gratian*, 2 books. Duisburg on the Rhine, 1677, octavo.]

illustrated by Baluze’s most learned observations; and Berard’s excellent book,

[Note: [Col. 0023] *The Genuine Canons of Gratian Distinguished from the Spurious*, by the work and study of Carlo Sebastiano Berardi, priest of Unelli. Second Venetian edition, vol. 4. Venice, 1783, quarto.]

in which one scarcely knows whether to admire its learning or its diligence more. Sometimes we ourselves, chiefly through Anselm and the penitential books, were able either to trace the origins of chapters or at least to approach the truth more closely. Accordingly, some chapters have been restored to authors from whom Berard had taken them away; we have found that in these matters he was sometimes less exact than was fair.

We assigned some passages to Gratian himself (cf. D. 45, c. 4), and others to the author of the *Paleae* [Col. 0025].

[Note: [Col. 0025] We have followed the recension of the *Paleae* published by J. Bickell, *An Inquiry into the Paleae Found in Gratian’s Decree* (Marburg, 1827, quarto). We may add that c. 3, D. XV, from § 17 onwards, must itself be regarded as a *Palea*; see the Correctors’ note at this place, and what we have observed from the three Leipzig manuscripts of Gratian: no. 956, Leipzig manuscript A; no. 957, Leipzig manuscript B; no. 958, Leipzig manuscript C.]

Where the word *Palea* was first assigned to a chapter, we enclosed it in brackets.

In fragments drawn from Pseudo-Isidore, we carefully identified the sources from which whoever composed those letters drew, using above all the work of Knust,

[Note: [Col. 0025] *On the Sources and Design of the Pseudo-Isidorian Collection*. Göttingen, 1852.—The copy of Merlin’s collection of councils which we used was published at Cologne in 1530.]

which the venerable faculty of theologians of the University of Georgia Augusta recently honored with a prize. Finally, in the canons of councils we noted which material was derived from Dionysius and which from the so-called ancient translation, so that the errors committed in this matter by the Correctors now seem at last to have been eliminated. Chapters in which no mention of the translator is made are to be understood as belonging to Isidore.

As for chronological determinations, we recorded in the notes everything certain that could be drawn either from the headings of the chapters themselves or from the writings of learned men, especially the Ballerini brothers. Yet we did not think that the Pithou brothers, in whose footsteps Boehmer followed, ought to be followed: indulging their ingenuity too freely, they added chronological determinations nearly everywhere, even when a chapter was highly uncertain. Since this is so, and since these very uncertain chronological determinations, resting only on conjecture, ought now at last to be discarded, we have omitted chronological data in nearly all passages drawn from the Fathers, intending at a later point, in the index of chapters, to give for all such chapters the very year in which their authors died.

We have revised throughout the punctuation, which was in the greatest need of correction. We have moved the Correctors’ annotations to the margin of the text with the purpose that the latter might be presented as pure as possible and not intermixed with extraneous matter by which readers are very frequently confused.

[Note: [Col. 0025] This happened to Pelleterius, who published the Pithou brothers’ edition: he gave Gratian’s name to a small part of an annotation by the Correctors, on c. 4, D. 91; Boehmer did not notice it either.]

If these things do not wholly displease you, kind reader, we shall consider ourselves very fortunate. But if we have done anything less correctly, we shall not take it ill if you warn us; for in a work so difficult, we are not such men as to suppose that human error is foreign to us.

Moreover, we consider it a most sacred duty to declare our gratitude to the most learned men to whom we owe whatever we have achieved: the illustrious Biener and the illustrious Bickell, who did not disdain to assist us with counsel and dissuasion; and the most distinguished Haenel, who has deserved exceptionally well of us by generously supplying us with many most precious books. We shall say more in a preface when, with God’s help, we have brought the edition of the Decree to completion.

Given at Leipzig, on the very day of Saint John the Baptist, A.D. 1833.

[CONCORDANCE OF DISCORDANT CANONS.]

[Col. 0027]

[CONCORDANCE OF DISCORDANT CANONS.]

The books cited in the annotations and mentioned in the preface are these:

Ans.: Collection of Anselm of Lucca.  
Baller.: Edition of the works of Leo the Great by the Ballerini brothers.  
Burch.: Burchard of Worms’s great volume of decrees.  
Boehm.: Edition of the *Corpus Juris Canonici* prepared by Boehmer. Halle, 1747.  
Capit.: Capitularies of the Frankish kings.  
Cap. Mart. Brac.: Chapters of Martin of Braga, available in González.  
Cap. Theodori: Chapters of Theodore of Canterbury, ed. Petit, Paris, 1676, quarto.  
Coll. tr. p.: Collection in Three Parts.  
Coll. Hisp.: González’s Spanish Collection.  
Cap. Mart. Brac.: Chapters of Martin of Braga.  
Coustant: Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, from Coustant’s edition.  
Deusd.: Collection of Cardinal Deusdedit cited by the Correctors.  
Ed. Ant.: Antwerp edition of Contius.  
Ed. Arg.: Strasbourg edition, 1471.  
Ed. Bas.: Basel edition, 1481.  
Ed. Lugd. I: Lyons edition, 1515.  
Ed. Lugd. II: Lyons edition, 1548.  
Ed. Lugd. III: Lyons edition, 1564.  
Ed. Nor.: Nuremberg edition, 1493.  
Ed. Par.: Paris edition, 1506.  
Ed. Ven. I: Venetian edition, 1482.  
Ed. Ven. II: Venetian edition, 1490.  
Interpr. Dionys.: Latin translation of Greek canons made by Dionysius Exiguus.  
Iv. Pan.: Ivo’s *Panormia*.  
Iv. Decr.: Ivo’s *Decree*.  
Isid. Merl.: Merlin’s collection of councils.  
Ed. Maur.: Edition of the works of Gregory the Great by monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur.  
Poen. Rom.: Roman Penitential.  
Mansi: Mansi’s *Greatest and Most Comprehensive Collection of Councils*.  
Polyc.: The collection of canons of Gregory the Priest, called *Polycarpus*.  
Rab. poen.: Penitential of Rabanus Maurus.  
Reg.: Regino’s two books *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*.  
Statutt. eccl. ant.: Statutes of the Ancient Church, commonly cited under the name of the Fourth Council of Carthage.

## CONCORDANCE OF DISCORDANT CANONS, AND FIRST

[Note: [Col. 0029B] *And first*: At this point there is great variation in manuscript codices. In some there is no heading here; in others one reads: “On written and unwritten law, and which is to be preferred to which, and on the authors of laws and the choice of two evils, or dispensation” [Col. 0029C]. Or: “And first, concerning the law of the constitution of divine and human nature” [“on the law of the constitution of nature and of man”: Basel edition; “on the law of the constitution of nature and of humanity”: Venetian editions I and II, Nuremberg edition; “on the law of the constitution of nature [and] humanity”: Strasbourg edition]. Or: “On the law of nature and human constitution,” which Dominic of Geminiano acknowledges and which occurs in certain earlier editions. Or: “On the law of nature and constitution,” a heading which seems best to suit Gratian’s discussion, since he often returns to these chapters, as at the beginning of Distinctions 5, 7, 8, and 15; and in 11, Question 1, c. *Si quae causae*, where, indicating this entire passage, he writes: “Look at the beginning, where the distinction between natural law and the law of constitution is marked.” Nevertheless, amid such great variation—which, apart from other conjectures, can be evidence that no rubric was placed here by Gratian himself—it has seemed sufficient to retain the common reading and indicate the others.]

## ON THE LAW OF DIVINE AND HUMAN CONSTITUTION

[Col. 0029]

## DISTINCTION I

[Col. 0029A] GRATIAN

The human race is governed by two things: namely, natural law and customs. Natural law is that which is contained in the Law and the Gospel, by which each person is commanded to do to another what he wishes done to himself, and is forbidden to inflict upon another what he does not wish inflicted upon himself. Hence Christ says in the Gospel:

[Note: [Col. 0029] Matthew 7:12.]

> Therefore, whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them; for this is the Law and the Prophets.

Thus Isidore says in Book V of the *Etymologies*, chapter 2:

### C. I. Divine laws rest upon nature; human laws upon customs.

All laws are either divine or human. Divine laws rest upon nature; human laws upon customs. Therefore they differ, because different laws please different nations.

§ 1. *Fas* is divine law; *jus* is human law. To pass through another person’s field is permitted by divine law, but it is not permitted by human law.

[Note: [Col. 0029] “To pass through another’s property”: Isidore.]

[Col. 0029B] Gratian. From the words of this authority it is clearly understood in what divine and human law differ from one another: everything that is *fas* is understood under the name of divine or natural law, whereas under the name of human law are understood customs set down and handed on in law.

§ 1. Now *jus* is a general name, containing many species under itself.

[Col. 0030A] Hence Isidore says in the same book of the *Etymologies*, chapter 3:

### C. II. Law is a genus; statute is a species.

*Jus* is a general name; a statute (*lex*) is a species of law. *Jus* is so called because it is just. All law consists of statutes and customs.

### C. III. What a statute is.  
[Isidore, same work, chapter 3.]

A statute is a written enactment.

### C. IV. What custom is.  
[Isidore, same work, chapter 3, and Book II, chapter 10.]

Custom is a long-established practice derived solely from conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0030C] “Custom is”: In Isidore the following precedes: “Custom is a practice approved by age, or unwritten law. A statute is not called *lex* from reading because it is written. But custom is a long practice,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0029] *tantundem* (“just as much”): Isidore.]

### C. V. What usage is.  
[Isidore, same work, chapter 3, and Book II, chapter 10.]

Usage is a kind of law established by customs, [Col. 0030B] which is accepted in place of statute when statute is lacking.

§ 1. It makes no difference whether it rests upon writing or reason, since reason also commends a statute.

[Note: [Col. 0029] “Since”: Boehmer.]

§ 2. Further, if statute rests upon reason, then everything that rests upon reason will now be statute, provided only that it accords with religion, agrees with discipline, and promotes salvation.

§ 3. It is called *consuetudo* (“usage; custom”) because it is in common use.

[Col. 0031A] Gratian. Therefore, when it is said that it makes no difference whether usage rests upon writing or reason, it is apparent that usage is partly reduced to writing and partly preserved only in the customs of those who employ it. What has been reduced to writing is called a constitution or *jus*; but what has not been reduced to writing is called by the general name “usage,” that is, *consuetudo*.

§ 1. There is also another division of law, as Isidore attests in the same Book V, chapter 4, saying:

### C. VI. What the species of law are.  
[Isidore, same work, chapter 4.]

Law is either natural law, civil law, or the law of nations.

[Note: [Col. 0031] “Law is either natural law”: Isidore.]

### C. VII. What natural law is.  
[Isidore, same work, chapter 4.]

[Col. 0031B] Natural law is common to all nations, because it exists everywhere by natural instinct, not by any enactment: for example, the union of man and woman, the succession [Note: [Col. 0031C] Succession: In three manuscript codices of Isidore and several of Gratian, the reading is: “the begetting and upbringing of children,” a reading which agrees with Institutes, I, title “On justice and law,” at the words “hence follows.”] [Note: [Col. 0031] Begetting: Isidore; editions of Grial, Madrid 1591, and Areval, Rome 1797.—Böhm.] and upbringing of children, the common possession of all things and the single liberty of all, the acquisition of things taken from heaven, earth, and sea; likewise, restoration of a thing deposited or of money entrusted [Note: [Col. 0031] “Lent”: Isidore, cited editions.—Böhm.], and the repelling of force by force. § 1. For this, or anything similar to it, is never regarded as unjust, but as natural and equitable.

### C. VIII. What civil law is. [Isidore, same book, c. 5.]

Civil law is that which each people or city establishes for itself, with divine and human grounds in view [Note: [Col. 0031] That is, having regard to the cause: Böhm.].

[Col. 0032A]

### C. IX. What the law of nations is. [Isidore, same book, c. 6.]

The law of nations comprises the occupation of sites, building, fortification, wars, captivities, slavery, rights of return after captivity, treaties, peace treaties [Note: [Col. 0031] “Treaties of peace”: all the older collated editions.], truces, the sacred inviolability of ambassadors, and marriages with foreigners being forbidden. § 1. It is called the law of nations for this reason [Note: [Col. 0031] “And for this reason,” i.e. because: Isidore.]: because nearly all nations employ that law.

### C. X. What military law is. [Isidore, same book, c. 7.]

Military law is the formal declaration of war; the binding conclusion of a treaty; advancing against the enemy or joining battle when the signal has been given; likewise retreating at the signal; likewise the discipline imposed for military disgrace if one abandons one’s post; likewise the scale of pay, ranks of dignity, and the honour of rewards, as when crowns or torques are bestowed; likewise the apportionment of booty, its just division according to the rank and labours of persons, and the sovereign’s share.

### C. XI. What public law is. [Isidore, same book, c. 8.]

Public law concerns sacred matters, priests, and magistrates. [Note: [Col. 0031] From Digest, fr. 1–2, “On justice and law.”]

### C. XII. What the law of the Quirites is. [Isidore, same book, c. 9.]

The law of the Quirites belongs properly to the Romans, and is possessed by none except Quirites—that is, Romans. § 1. It treats of lawful inheritances, formal acceptances of inheritances [Note: [Col. 0031C] Formal acceptances: Earlier the text read: “or guardianships, [Col. 0032C] or contracts.” It was corrected from both printed and manuscript codices of Isidore. Ulpian explains what *cretio* is in his Titles, c. 22, as does Isidore himself in the same book V of the *Etymologies*, c. 24.], guardianships, and acquisitive prescriptions—laws found among no other people, but peculiar to the Romans and established for them alone.

## DISTINCTION II

[Col. 0031]

[Col. 0031B] **GRATIAN**

**Part I.** The law of the Quirites consists of statutes, plebiscites, decrees of the senate, enactments of emperors, and edicts [Note: [Col. 0031] “Edicts of senators”: editions published before the correction of the *Decretum*, except the Basel edition.] or opinions of jurists.

### C. I. What a statute is. [Isidore, *Etymologies*, book V, c. 10, and I. II, c. 10.]

A statute is an enactment of the people, by which the elders together with the commons established something.

### C. II. What a plebiscite is. [Isidore, same book, c. 11.]

Plebiscites [Note: [Col. 0031] “Enactments are”: Isidore.] are those measures established by the commons alone; [Col. 0031C] and they are called plebiscites [Note: [Col. 0031] “Called enactments”: ibid.] because the commons know them, or because they deliberate and petition that they be made [Note: [Col. 0031] “Or because it deliberates as it was petitioned”: ibid.].

[Col. 0032B]

### C. III. What a decree of the senate is. [Isidore, same book, c. 12.]

A decree of the senate is that which senators alone determine by advising the people.

### C. IV. What an enactment or edict is. [Isidore, same book, c. 13.]

An enactment or edict is that which a king [Note: [Col. 0031] “Which a king alone”: earlier Roman editions except Basel.—Böhm.] or emperor enacts or proclaims [Note: [Col. 0031] Before correction the reading was: “proclaimed.”].

### C. V. What the opinions of jurists are. [Isidore, same book, c. 14.]

The opinions of jurists are the answers which legal experts are said to give to those seeking advice; hence they are called the opinions of Paul. For there were certain learned men and arbiters [Col. 0033A] of equity who issued compilations of the institutions [Note: [Col. 0033] “Constitutions”: Basel edition, Böhm.—Isidore himself preserves the received reading.] of civil law, by which they might settle the lawsuits and disputes of those in disagreement.

### C. VI. What consular or tribunician statutes are. [Isidore, same book, c. 15.]

**Part II.** Certain statutes are also named from those who enacted them: consular, tribunician, Julian, and Cornelian statutes. Thus under Caesar Augustus the suffect consuls Papius [Note: [Col. 0033C] Papius: The earlier reading was “Papius and Pompeius,” and shortly afterward, “Papia and Pompeia.” It was corrected from manuscript copies of Isidore. Alciatus had noted the error in printed copies, book III, *Dispunct.*, c. 3. In the Capitoline tables, in the 761st year of the city, according to the Julian Calendar, the suffect consuls are recorded as M. Papius and Q. Poppaeus.] and Poppaeus enacted a statute called, from their names, the Papian-Poppaean law, containing rewards for fathers who begot children. Under the same emperor, Falcidius, tribune of the commons, enacted a statute forbidding anyone to leave to strangers [Note: [Col. 0033C] Strangers: This expression is not found in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, translated into Latin and enlarged by St Jerome [Col. 0033D] (from which Isidore seems to have taken this passage), nor in law 1, § 2, *ad legem Falcidiam*, where the statute’s own words are reported. Yet it occurs in Isidore, even in the manuscript codices.] [Note: [Col. 0033] The expression “to strangers” is absent from Isidore’s Areval edition.—“At the end of the will”: Venice edition I.] by will more than would leave one quarter to the heirs. From his name it is called the Falcidian law.

### C. VII. What a composite statute is. [Isidore, same book, c. 16.]

A composite statute [Note: [Col. 0033D] Composite statute: In several manuscript codices of Gratian and one of Isidore the reading is *satura*. Festus explains it thus: “A *satura* is a kind of dish seasoned from various ingredients; and it is a statute packed with many other statutes.” Therefore statutory enactments include the words: “nor shall it be repealed or derogated from by a composite enactment,” and other phrases to the same effect.] is one that speaks of several matters at the same time [Note: [Col. 0033] “Sets forth”: Isidore and the Basel edition.]. It is named from the abundance of things, as though from fullness; hence to write satire is to compose varied poems, as did Horace, Juvenal, and Persius.

### C. VIII. What Rhodian laws are. [Isidore, same book, c. 17.]

Rhodian laws are laws concerning maritime commerce, named after the island of Rhodes, where merchant activity existed in ancient times.

## DISTINCTION III

[Col. 0033]

[Col. 0033B] **GRATIAN**

**Part I.** All these kinds are parts of secular laws. But because one constitution is civil and another ecclesiastical, and civil law is called forensic or civil law, let us see by what name an ecclesiastical constitution is called. § 1. An ecclesiastical constitution is designated by the name *canon*. Isidore, in book VI of the *Etymologies*, c. 16, explains what a canon is, saying [Note: [Col. 0033] Anselm, in the prologue.]:

### C. I. What a canon is.

*Canon* is Greek; in Latin it is called a rule.

### C. II. Whence the name “rule” is derived. [Isidore, [Note: [Col. 0033] Anselm, ibid.] same book, c. 16.]

A rule is so called because it guides aright and never draws anyone [Note: [Col. 0033] “Anything”: Lyons editions I and II, Paris, Antwerp.] elsewhere. Others have said that it is called a rule either because it governs, because it provides a norm for right [Col. 0033C] living, or because it corrects what is warped and depraved [Note: [Col. 0033] “What is warped and depraved”: Isidore.—“Whatever is depraved”: Anselm.].

**Part II. Gratian.** Further, some canons are decrees of popes, others statutes of councils. Of councils, some are universal and others provincial. Some provincial councils are held by the authority of the Roman pontiff, namely with a legate of the holy Roman Church present; others by the authority of patriarchs, primates, or metropolitans [Col. 0034B] of the same province. This is to be understood as concerning general rules.

§ 1. There are also certain private laws, both ecclesiastical and secular, called privileges. Concerning them Isidore says in book V of the *Etymologies*, c. 18:

### C. III. What a privilege is.

Privileges are laws for private persons, as it were private laws. For a privilege is so called [Note: [Col. 0034C] Privilege: Cicero, book III *On the Laws*, says: “Our ancestors did not wish laws to be passed concerning private persons; that is a privilege.” But Budaeus and others have observed that this word has not always been used in the same sense.] because it is enacted concerning a private person.

**Part III. Gratian.** The function of secular and ecclesiastical laws is to command what must be done [Note: [Col. 0034C] Done: In certain old codices the following words read: “To forbid what is evil to do; to permit either lawful things, such as seeking a reward, or even certain things,” etc.], to forbid what is evil to do, or to permit what is lawful, such as seeking a reward, or even certain unlawful things, such as issuing a bill of divorce, lest graver things occur. Hence in the same book, c. 19, Isidore writes:

[Col. 0034C]

### C. IV. What the function of law is.

Every law either permits something—for example, “let a brave man seek a reward”—or forbids it—for example, “let no one be permitted to seek marriage with consecrated virgins”—or punishes it—for example, “let one who has committed murder suffer capital punishment.” For human life is regulated by its reward or punishment. But divine law commands [Note: [Col. 0034D] Divine: From this point to the end these words are absent from Isidore’s codices and from certain Vatican copies of Gratian. In others, omitting “divine,” the reading is: “or commands, as: You shall love the Lord your God.”] [Note: [Col. 0033] Deuteronomy 6:5], for example: “You shall love the Lord your God.”

[Note: [Col. 0035] The Benedictine editors of St Ambrose’s works, Congregation of St Maur, Paris 1686, reject this canon as Ambrose’s.—Anselm, book 7, c. 184.]

## DISTINCTION IV

[Col. 0035]

[Col. 0035A] **GRATIAN**

**Part I.** The purpose of establishing laws is to restrain human audacity and curb the capacity for doing harm, as Isidore testifies in the same book V, c. 20 [Note: [Col. 0035] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 142; *Decretum*, part 4, c. 168. “Audacity and capacity for doing harm”: from Turrecremata, Fontanini edition, Böhm.]:

### C. I. Why laws were made.

Laws were made so that human audacity might be restrained by fear of them; that innocence might be safe among the wicked; and that, even in the wicked themselves, the capacity for doing harm might be curbed through dread of punishment.

**Part II. Gratian.** Moreover, in the very establishment of laws, the character of the laws to be established must especially be considered: they should contain uprightness, justice, possibility, suitability, and the other qualities which Isidore enumerates in the same book [c. 21], saying:

### C. II. What kind of law a law ought to be.

[Col. 0035B] A law ought to be honourable, just, possible, in accordance with nature and the custom of the country, suited to place and time, necessary, useful, and also clear, so that it contain nothing which, through obscurity, may entrap [Note: [Col. 0035D] “May entrap”: Earlier the text read: “in a precautionary entrapment.” The true reading has been restored from manuscript codices of Isidore, book 5, c. 21, and from printed copies also of book 2, c. 10, where the same material is written; partly also from old copies of Gratian, which lack the word “precautionary.” Paul uses a similar expression in *Sentences*, book 5, title 33, c. 2: “Let no one,” he says, “in taking precautions fall into the entrapment of words.”] [Note: [Col. 0035] “In entrapment”: Basel edition.—“In precaution”: Ivo, *Decretum*, cited passage.] anyone; it must be written for the common benefit of citizens, not for any private advantage.

**Part III. Gratian.** These things must be considered in the very establishment of laws because, once laws have been established, it will not be permissible to judge them; rather, judgment must be given according to them. Hence Augustine says in *On True Religion*, c. 31 [Note: [Col. 0035] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 143; *Decretum*, part 4, c. 169.]:

### III. Laws are to be judged when they are established, not when they have been established.

Although men judge these temporal laws when they establish them, yet once [Col. 0035C] they have been established and confirmed, it is not permitted to a judge to judge them, but only according to them.

**Gratian.** Laws are established when they are promulgated; they are confirmed when approved by the practices of those who use them. For just as certain laws have now been repealed by contrary practice, so laws themselves are confirmed by the practices of those who use them. Thus the decree of Pope Telesphorus—that clerics should fast from meat and delicacies from Quinquagesima [Note: [Col. 0035D] Quinquagesima: After this word printed codices continued: “should undertake a purpose of fasting [Col. 0036D] and abstain from meat and delicacies.” But almost all manuscripts read as restored here.]—does not make those who act otherwise guilty of transgression, because it has not been approved by common practice.

[Col. 0036A]

### C. IV. Let clerics abstain from meat and delicacies for seven weeks before Easter. Telesphorus, Bishop of the City of Rome, to all bishops, Epistle I. [Note: [Col. 0035] Pseudo-Isidorian Epistle.—Anselm, book 7, c. 183; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 174; *Decretum*, part 4, c. 25.]

We decree that for seven full weeks [Note: [Col. 0035] From the *Liber Pontificalis*.] before holy Easter all clerics called to the Lord’s lot shall fast from meat. For just as the life of clerics ought to be distinct from the conduct of laypersons, so too there ought to be distinction in fasting. And below: Therefore, throughout these seven weeks, all clerics shall fast from meat and delicacies and strive day and night to cleave to the *Lord* by hymns, vigils, and prayers.

### C. V. Telesphorus adds the seventh week to Lent. Likewise Ambrose, in the book of sermons. [Note: [Col. 0036D] Sermons: Several manuscript sermons bearing Ambrose’s name were found in the Vatican Library in Rome and in the library of the monastery of St Ambrose in Milan. Among them is a sermon on Sexagesima beginning, “The time is at hand,” from which this chapter is taken.]

Lent has six weeks. Pope Telesphorus added a seventh week, and [Col. 0036B] this period was called Quinquagesima.

**Gratian.** The same must be understood concerning the chapter in which Blessed Gregory [I] [Note: [Col. 0035] The Maurist brothers deny that St Gregory is the author of this canon: Paris edition, 1705.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, c. 29.] writes to Augustine, bishop of the English, as follows:

### C. VI. Those whom the dignity of ecclesiastical rank adorns shall undertake the intention of fasting from Quinquagesima.

Accordingly, priests, deacons, and all others whom the dignity of ecclesiastical rank adorns shall undertake the purpose of fasting from Quinquagesima, so that they may add something to the measure of holy observance and excel in religious observance, just as they do in rank, those who stand in the lay order. § 1. Yet concerning that Sunday itself we are uncertain what ought to be said, since on that day all lay and secular persons seek meat dishes more eagerly and elaborately than usual on other days; and unless, in a kind of new greed, they gorge themselves until midnight, they think they cannot otherwise begin the observance of this holy season. This is surely to be ascribed not to reason but to pleasure—indeed, to a certain blindness of mind. Therefore they cannot be turned from such a custom and must be left, with pardon, to their own disposition, lest they become worse if forbidden it. For, as Solomon says [Note: [Col. 0035] Proverbs 30:33], “He who squeezes hard draws out blood.” And a little later: § 2. It is likewise fitting that on the days when we abstain from the flesh of animals, we fast also from all things deriving their origin from the seed [Col. 0037A] of flesh—namely milk, cheese, and eggs. And a little later: § 3. The eating of fish is left to the Christian in such a way that it may furnish relief for weakness, not kindle the fire of luxury. Accordingly, one who abstains from meat should by no means prepare more costly feasts of sea-creatures. § 4. Wine too is permitted [Note: [Col. 0037] “We are permitted”: Ivo.] to be drunk only in such a way that we wholly avoid drunkenness; otherwise it remains for us to do likewise everything that pleases the body.

[Col. 0038A]

**Part IV. Gratian.** Although these matters have been established by laws, they do not accuse those who fail to observe them of transgression, because they have not been approved by common use. Otherwise [Note: [Col. 0037] Words of St Gregory below, Causa 25, question 1, c. 13.] those who disobeyed them would be deprived of their own rank, since those who do not know how to obey the sacred canons are commanded utterly to lose the office they have undertaken—unless perhaps one says that these were written not as binding decrees but as exhortations. A decree imposes necessity; exhortation stirs free will.

## DISTINCTION V

[Col. 0037]

[Col. 0037A] **GRATIAN**

**Part I.** These matters written concerning privileges and the other matters set below apply to both secular and ecclesiastical laws. Let us now return to the distinction between natural law and the others. [Note: [Col. 0037D] “Now to the distinction”: The received editions read, “But now to instruction.” The text has been corrected from old codices and from the beginning of Distinction 15, where this occurs.] § 1. Natural law [Col. 0037B] holds primacy over all things in time and dignity. For it began with the origin of the rational creature; it is not changed by time, but remains immutable. § 2. Yet since natural law is said above to be contained in the Law and the Gospel, while certain things contrary to what was established in the Law are now found to be permitted, natural law does not seem to remain immutable. For the Law commanded [Note: [Col. 0037] Leviticus 12:5] that a woman who bore a male child should refrain from entering the temple for forty days, but if she bore a female, for eighty days; now, however, she is not forbidden to enter church immediately after childbirth. Likewise [Note: [Col. 0037] Leviticus 15:20], a menstruating woman was deemed unclean under the Law; now neither she is forbidden immediately to enter church or receive the mysteries of holy communion, nor is a woman who gives birth, or that which is born, forbidden to be baptized immediately [Col. 0037C] after birth.

Hence Gregory [I] writes to the same Augustine, bishop of the English [Note: [Col. 0037] Epistle 64, book 11, indiction IV, A.D. 601; in response to Augustine’s tenth question; Paris edition, 1705. The epistle, of highly doubtful authenticity, is given complete in Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, book 1, c. 22.]:

### C. I. PALEA. [Note: [Col. 0037D] *Palea*: The general discussion of *Paleae* appears in the preface. This passage, to which the name *Palea* is first prefixed, also occurs in manuscript copies [Col. 0038D], except two Vatican manuscripts; in four it is joined to the following chapter, “If a woman,” with the word “For” added at the beginning, as in Gregory.]

“When a woman has given birth, after how many days she ought to enter church, you have learned from the precept of the Old Testament: namely, that she should abstain for thirty-three days after a male child, and sixty-six after a female. Yet you should understand that this is received mystically.”

### C. II. A woman who has given birth is not forbidden to enter church at the same hour to give thanks. [Gregory, immediately following, in the same place.
