[Note: [Col. 0037] Pope Nicholas, in response to the consultations of the Bulgarians, c. 65, in Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, vol. XV; Bede, cited passage. Gratian, however, took this canon from the Collection in Three Parts, part 1, title 55, c. 70.]]

If a woman enters church in the very hour in which she has given birth in order to give thanks, she is not burdened by any weight of sin. For pleasure of the flesh, not pain, is at fault. In sexual union there is pleasure; but in [Note: [Col. 0037] “For in the bringing forth of offspring there is groaning”: Gregory’s codices, with Bede agreeing.] the birth of offspring there is pain and groaning. Hence it is said to the first mother of all [Note: [Col. 0037] Genesis 3:6], “In pains you shall give birth.” Therefore, if we forbid a woman who has given birth to enter church, [Col. 0038B] we turn her very punishment into a fault [Note: [Col. 0037] “Turn”: all earlier editions.].

### C. III. Nothing forbids baptizing, at the same hour, a woman who has given birth or what has been born from her. The same to the same. [Note: [Col. 0037] Collection in Three Parts, part 1, title 55, c. 71; Burchard, book 4, c. 32; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 1, c. 62.]

But neither a woman who has given birth, nor what she has borne, is in any way forbidden to be baptized, if the danger of death presses—whether the woman in the very hour in which she gives birth, or the child in the hour in which it is born. *For [Note: [Col. 0038D] “For as”: From here to the words “lest while” has been added from St Gregory.], just as the grace of the holy mystery must be provided for the living and discerning with great discrimination, so it must be offered without any delay to those threatened by death, lest, while time is still being sought in which to administer the mystery of redemption, a slight intervening delay mean that no one can be found to be redeemed.*

[Col. 0038C]

### C. IV. Before a child is weaned or its mother purified, her husband shall not have intercourse with her. Likewise. [Note: [Col. 0037] Pope Nicholas, book …; Bede, cited passage; Collection in Three Parts, part 1, title 55, c. 72; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, c. 88.] [Gregory, immediately following, in the same place.]

Her husband, however, ought not to have intercourse with her until the child that is born has been weaned.

[PALEA.]

“But an evil custom has arisen among married persons: women disdain to nurse the children they bear and hand them over to other women to be nursed. This appears to have been devised solely because of [Note: [Col. 0037] “Incontinence of the flesh”: all the collated editions.] incontinence: since they refuse to restrain themselves, they scorn to suckle those whom they bear.”

Therefore women who, through an evil custom, hand their children over to others to be nursed ought not to have intercourse with their husbands until the period of purification [Col. 0038D] has first passed. [Col. 0039A] Indeed, even apart from childbirth, when they are subject to their customary menstruation, they are forbidden to have intercourse with their husbands, so that the sacred law [Note: [Col. 0039] Leviticus 15.] strikes with death any man who approaches a menstruating woman. § 1. Yet while a woman undergoes her customary menstruation, she should not be forbidden to enter church, because the superfluity of nature cannot be imputed to her as sin; and since she suffers it unwillingly, it is not just that she be deprived of entering church. For we know [Note: [Col. 0039] Matthew 9] that the woman suffering from an issue of blood came behind the Lord [Note: [Col. 0039] “Came humbly”: Gregory; Argentinian and first Venetian editions.] and touched the fringe of his garment, and her infirmity immediately departed from her. If, therefore, a woman afflicted with a flow of blood could laudably touch the Lord’s garment, why should a woman who suffers menstrual blood [Col. 0040A] not be permitted to enter the Lord’s church? And below: If the woman sick with an ailment rightly presumed to touch the Lord’s garment, why should what is granted to one sick person not be granted to all women who are troubled by the defect of their nature? § 2. Nor should she be forbidden to receive the mystery of holy communion on those same days. If, from great reverence, she does not presume to receive it, she is to be praised; but if she receives it, she is not to be judged. For it belongs to good minds to recognize their sins, even in some manner, where there is no sin; because often that which comes from sin is done without sin. Thus, when we hunger, we eat without sin, although it came about through the fault of the first human being that we should hunger [Note: [Col. 0039] “That we hunger”: Böhm.].

## DISTINCTION VI

[Col. 0039]

[Col. 0039B] **GRATIAN**

Since discussion has begun concerning the superfluity of nature, the question is raised whether, after an emission which commonly occurs in sleep, anyone may receive the body of the Lord, or, if he is a priest, celebrate the sacred mysteries.

Blessed Gregory [I] writes on these matters to Augustine, bishop of the English, in his answer to question 11 [Note: [Col. 0039] In response to Augustine’s eleventh question, A.D. 601; Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, book 1, c. 27; Collection in Three Parts, part 1, title 35, c. 76; Burchard, book 5, c. 43; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, c. 160; *Decretum*, part 2, c. 52; Polycarp, book 3, title 16.]:

### C. I. On the several kinds of nocturnal emission.

The Testament of the old law calls such a person unclean before the Lord and does not allow him, unless washed with water, even to enter church until evening. But the spiritual people understand this differently: they regard as having been deceived as though in a dream the person who, when tempted by unclean true [Note: [Col. 0039D] True: In most codices of St Gregory, in Bede, and in the 1530 Cologne printed collection of councils, the reading is “vain”; in some of Gregory’s codices, “various.” But the text has not been changed because of the gloss.] images [Note: [Col. 0039] The Maurist editors of Gregory affirm that the reading “true” is found in most manuscript codices of Gregory and Bede, differing from the Roman correction.], is polluted in thought. But he must be washed with water, so that he may wash away by tears the fault of thought; and, unless the fire of temptation has first receded, he should acknowledge himself guilty, as it were, until evening. § 1. Yet in this same emission a distinction is very necessary: it must be carefully weighed from what cause it comes to the mind of the sleeper. For it may arise [Note: [Col. 0039] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 9, c. 111.] from overindulgence, from a superfluity or weakness of nature, or from thought. § 2. When it results from a superfluity [Col. 0040B] or weakness of nature, this emission is not at all to be feared, because the mind, without knowing it, has suffered it; it ought rather to be grieved than considered to have done it. § 3. But when the appetite of gluttony is carried beyond measure in taking food, and the reservoirs of bodily fluids are consequently burdened, the mind thereby incurs some guilt—yet not so far as to be forbidden to receive the sacred mystery or celebrate the solemnities of Mass, when perhaps a feast day requires it, or necessity itself compels the priest to administer [Note: [Col. 0039] “Be administered”: Gregory.] the mystery because no other priest is present. But if others are present who can perform the mystery, an emission caused by overindulgence ought not to prohibit receiving the sacred mystery; rather, one ought, I think, humbly to abstain from offering the sacred mystery [Note: [Col. 0039] “To abstain”: Gregory.], if [Note: [Col. 0039D] “If nevertheless”: Gregory’s codices and Bede read: “if nevertheless a shameful image has not shaken the mind of the sleeper.” But the collection of Isidore, also in manuscript, reads: “if nevertheless shameful images have shaken the sleeping mind”; the reading of the *Panormia* preserves this sense [Col. 0040D]. Burchard and Ivo differ little from the original.] the emission has nevertheless not shaken the sleeper with a shameful image. For there are people in whom this emission often occurs in such a way that their mind, even when the body is asleep, is not defiled by shameful images. In this matter one thing is shown: that the mind itself is not then guilty, but is wholly free in its own judgment [Note: [Col. 0040D] “Not then, but in its own”: Nearly all manuscript copies of Gratian read “or in its own” [Col. 0039]—nevertheless all the older collated editions read “but in its own.” There is considerable variation here among other compilers, Bede, and Gregory’s codices. The manuscript collection of Isidore reads: “In this matter one thing is shown: the mind itself is not guilty, and yet is not free in its own judgment.” But because of the variety of codices, nothing has been changed in the text.] [Note: [Col. 0039] “The mind itself is shown to be guilty, not then or free in its own judgment”: Maurist edition of Gregory’s works, following Bede.], when, although it remembers seeing nothing while its body was asleep [Note: [Col. 0039] Absent from Böhm.], it nevertheless remembers, while its body was awake, that it had fallen into gluttony. § 4. [Col. 0041A] But if the emission in the sleeper’s mind arises from shameful thought while awake, the mind’s guilt is evident. For it sees from what root that pollution proceeded: what it knowingly thought, it unknowingly suffered [Note: [Col. 0041] “Who, what”: Gregory.]; and [Note: [Col. 0041D] From “and because” to the end these words occur neither in Gregory’s codices, nor in Bede, nor in three old copies of Gratian. They do occur, however, in Burchard, Ivo, the *Panormia*, and Polycarp.] because of such pollution it ought to abstain from the sacred mystery on that day.

**PALEA** [Note: [Col. 0041D] *Palea*: This *Palea* is absent not only from the first and tenth Vatican manuscripts, but also from other manuscripts containing several *Paleae*. Its rubric is absent from all. In those where the chapter occurs, it is joined with the preceding one, as also in Burchard and Ivo.] [Note: [Col. 0041] Gregory, cited passage; Bede, cited passage; Burchard, book 5, c. 43; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, c. 12.]

### C. II. Sin is not said to be committed by thought alone, but by delight and consent.

“But one must consider whether the thought itself occurred as suggestion, delight, or—what is greater—consent to sin. For every sin is completed in three ways: by suggestion, delight, and consent. Suggestion is made by the devil, delight by the flesh, and consent by the spirit. For [Col. 0041B] the serpent first suggested sin [Note: [Col. 0041] “For the first”: Gregory, “who, when he first…”; Ivo.]; Eve, as flesh, was delighted; Adam, as spirit, consented. § 1. Great discrimination is necessary, so that the mind, presiding as judge over itself, may distinguish between suggestion [Note: [Col. 0041D] Suggestion: Corrected from the original, from which Ivo differs little. Earlier it read: “And great discrimination is necessary between suggestion and delight, [Col. 0042D] and between delight and consent; let the mind set itself as judge over itself.” Burchard: “let the mind preside as judge over itself.” The remainder is almost as in Gratian. But Bede has: “let the mind itself preside as judge between suggestion and delight, and between delight and consent.” The collection of Isidore: “and it is necessary by great discrimination to bring forth the mind as judge between suggestion, delight, and consent.”] [Note: [Col. 0041] The Maurist edition of Gregory’s works preserves the reading cited by the corrector from Bede.], delight, and consent. When the evil spirit suggests sin in the mind, if no delight in sin follows, the sin has not at all been committed. But when the flesh begins to take delight, sin then begins to be born; and if it descends by deliberation even to consent, the sin is recognized as complete. Thus the seed of sin is in suggestion; in delight it receives nourishment; in consent it reaches completion. § 2. It often happens that what the evil spirit sows in thought is drawn by the flesh into delight, and yet the mind does not consent to that delight. And although the flesh cannot delight without the soul, the mind itself, resisting the pleasures of the flesh, is in some manner involuntarily bound in fleshly delight: it resists by reason and does not consent, yet is bound by delight and deeply groans that it is bound. Therefore that foremost soldier of the heavenly host also groaned, saying [Note: [Col. 0041] Romans 7:23], “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and making me captive in the law [Note: [Col. 0041] “Into the law”: Argentinian and first Venetian editions.] of sin which is in my members.” But if he were captive, he would not be fighting; yet he was fighting, and therefore he was both captive and fighting [Note: [Col. 0042D] There is considerable variation among the codices here also. The shortest and fairly complete reading is in the former Paris edition of St Gregory’s epistles: “But if he was captive, he was not fighting; but he was fighting; therefore he was not captive. Behold then,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0041] The Maurist edition of Gregory’s works follows the reading indicated by the corrector.—The Chifflet manuscript has Gratian’s reading.]. Therefore the law in his members was warring against the law of his mind; but if it was warring, he was not captive. Behold, then, a human being is, so to speak, both captive and free: free by the righteousness that he loves, captive by the delight that he bears unwillingly.”

### C. III. When it is sin to be deceived by nocturnal images. Likewise Isidore, book III of the *Sentences*, *On the Supreme Good*, c. 6. [Note: [Col. 0041] Ivo, *Decretum*, book 9, c. 112.]

It is not sin when we are unwillingly deceived by nocturnal images; but it is sin if, before we are deceived, we have been forestalled by the affections of thought. Images of lust which we have experienced in reality often appear in the minds of sleepers, but they are harmless if they are not met with desire. § 1. A person polluted by a nocturnal emission, although he feels himself defiled apart from any recollection of shameful thoughts, should nevertheless attribute the fact that he was tempted to his own fault, and immediately wipe away his impurity with tears.

Gratian. The reply to these points is as follows. Natural law is contained in the Law and in the Gospel; nevertheless, not everything found in the Law and Gospel is shown to belong to natural law. For in the Law there are certain moral precepts, such as “You shall not kill”; and certain mystical precepts, such as the commands concerning sacrifices—for example, that concerning the lamb—and others like them. The moral commands pertain to natural law and therefore are shown to admit no change. The mystical commands, so far as their outward surface is concerned, are shown to be alien to natural law; but so far as their moral meaning is concerned, they are found joined to it. Accordingly, although they may appear to have been changed in their outward form, yet [Col. 0042C] in their moral meaning they are shown to know no change.

§ 1. Natural law, therefore, beginning with the origin of rational creation, as stated above, remains unalterable. But customary law had its beginning after natural law, when people gathering together began to live in one place. This is believed to have occurred from the time when Cain is read to have built a city [Note: [Col. 0041] Gen. 4:17.]. Since this seems to have been virtually extinguished by the Flood [Note: [Col. 0041] Gen. 7.] because of the scarcity of people, it is thought subsequently to have been restored—or rather altered—from the time of Nimrod, when he, together with others, began to oppress others; and others, through their own weakness, began to be subject to his rule. [Col. 0043A] Hence Genesis says of him [Note: [Col. 0043] Gen. 10:9.]: “Nimrod began to be a mighty hunter before the Lord,” that is, [Note: [Col. 0043C] That is: the ordinary gloss on this passage, from Alcuin, reads: “that is, an oppressor and destroyer of men; whom he enticed to build a tower against God.”] an [Col. 0044A] oppressor and destroyer of men, whom he also enticed to build the tower.

## DISTINCTION VII

[Col. 0043]

[Col. 0043A] GRATIAN.

Part I. Constitutional law began with the ordinances which the Lord gave to Moses, saying [Note: [Col. 0043] Exod. 21:1.], “If you buy a Hebrew slave,” etc.

Accordingly Isidore says in Book V of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1:

### C. I. On the makers of laws

Moses was the first of all to expound divine laws to the Hebrew people in sacred writings. Phoroneus, king of the Greeks, [Col. 0043B] was the first to establish laws and judicial decisions for them. Mercury Trismegistus first delivered laws to the Egyptians. Solon first gave laws to the Athenians. Lycurgus first devised laws for the Lacedaemonians by Apollo’s authority. Numa Pompilius, who succeeded Romulus in the kingship, first promulgated Roman laws. Then, when the people could not endure seditious magistrates [Note: [Col. 0043] So it is also read in Aurelius Victor, *On Illustrious Men*, whom Isidore followed.], they created ten men to write laws; these men set forth in twelve tables laws translated into Latin from the books of Solon.

[Col. 0044A]

### C. II. The names of those who set forth the laws of the Twelve Tables

[Isidore, continuing in the same place.]

These were Appius Claudius, Titus Genucius, Publius Sextius, Spurius Veturius, Gaius Julius, Aulus Manlius, Servius Sulpicius, Publius Curiatius, Titus Romilius, and Spurius Posthumius. These ten were elected to draft the laws. Pompey, when consul, first wished to arrange the laws in books, but did not persist [Col. 0044B] because he feared his detractors. Caesar then began to do this, but was killed before he could complete it. Gradually, however, the ancient laws became obsolete through age and neglect [Note: [Col. 0043] “became obsolete”: Isidore.]; and although they are now of no use, knowledge of them nevertheless appears necessary. New laws began with Emperor Constantine and his successors; they were intermingled and unorganized. Later [Note: [Col. 0043] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 144; *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 170.], the younger Emperor Theodosius, after the model of the Gregorian and Hermogenian Codes, arranged the code of constitutions enacted since Constantine under the title of each respective emperor, and called it the Theodosian Code after his own name.

## DISTINCTION VIII

[Col. 0043]

[Col. 0043B] GRATIAN.

Part I. Natural law [Note: [Col. 0043] “law of nature”: Basel ed.] differs from custom and constitution. For by natural law all things are common to everyone. This is believed to have been observed not only among those of whom it is written [Note: [Col. 0043] Acts 4:32.], “The multitude of believers [Col. 0043C] had one heart and one soul,” etc., but is also found to have been taught by philosophers in an earlier age. Thus, in Plato, that city is described as most justly ordered in which no one knows private affections. But by customary or constitutional law, this is mine and that belongs to another.

Accordingly Augustine says, in Tractate VI on John 1, §25 [Note: [Col. 0043] Anselm, bk. 12, ch. 62 [56]; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 63; *Decree*, pt. 3, ch. 194.]:

### C. I. By divine law all things are common to all; but by constitutional law this is mine and that another’s

[Col. 0044B] By what law do you defend the estates of the Church [Note: [Col. 0043D] “Of the Church”: This phrase is not found in St Augustine. For there he argues against the Donatists, who complained that imperial laws had taken estates from them and assigned them to the Catholic Church. Thus, when the Donatists said, “They have taken away our estates; they have taken away our lands,” he inserts certain preliminary remarks in order to prove that they had, and have, no right in them, adding: “By what law do you defend the estates? By divine law,” etc. And below, 11, question 1, ch. *Si quae causae*, where Gratian cites the beginning of this chapter, the phrase “of the Church” is absent. It is nevertheless found in Anselm, Ivo, and the *Panormia* at the places indicated.] [Note: [Col. 0043] The word “of the Church,” which the Correctors assert is found in Anselm, was certainly not found in the Anselm manuscript collated], by divine law or by human law? We have divine law in the Scriptures; human law in the laws of kings. Whence does anyone possess [Col. 0044C] what he possesses? Is it not by human law? For by divine law “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 24:1.]. God made poor and rich alike from [Note: [Col. 0043] Gen. 2.] one clay, and one earth supports both poor and rich. Yet by human law it is said: “This estate is mine; this house is mine; this slave is mine.” Human laws, however, are the laws of emperors. Why? Because God himself distributes these human laws to humankind through emperors and kings of the world.

Again, a little further on:

§ 1. Take away [Note: [Col. 0043D] “Take away”: Since the gloss prevented all the things that seemed to require correction or addition from being corrected or added, it was thought best to append the complete passage of St Augustine. In Augustine, therefore, after the word “human” in the preceding paragraph, the following occurs: “Do you wish us to read [Col. 0044D] the laws of the jurists [ [Col. 0045] “emperors”: Augustine, Anselm, Boehmer], and to deal with estates according to them? If you wish to possess by human law, let us recite the laws of the emperors; let us see whether they wished anything to be possessed by heretics. But what is an emperor to me? You possess land according to his law. Or take away the laws of emperors, and who dares say: ‘That estate is mine,’ or ‘That slave is mine,’ or ‘This house is mine’? But if people received the laws of kings in order that such things might be held by them, do you wish us to recite the laws, so that you may rejoice that you have even one of these things, and not attribute it except to the gentleness of the dove that you are even there allowed to remain? For clear laws are read, in which the emperors commanded,” etc.] the laws of emperors, [Col. 0045A] and who dares say: “That estate is mine,” or “That slave is mine,” or “This house is mine”? But if kings made laws in order that people might hold these things, do you wish us to keep silent [Note: [Col. 0045] “let us recite”: Augustine, Ivo.] about the laws, so that you may rejoice? Etc.

Again, in the same place, after a few intervening words:

§ 2. Let the laws be read [Note: [Col. 0045] “Let the laws be reread”: all collated older editions.] [Note: [Col. 0045] Theodosian Code, bk. 16, tit. 5, constitutions 43, 51, 54; Justinian Code, bk. 1, tit. 5, constitution 4.], in which the emperors clearly commanded that those who, apart from communion with the Catholic Church, usurp for themselves the Christian name and do not wish peacefully to worship the author of peace, should dare to possess nothing in the name of the Church.

§ 3. “But what have we to do with the emperor?” But I have already said: the question concerns human law. And yet the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0045] 1 Pet. 2:17.] wished kings to be served and honored, and said: “Fear the king.” Do not say, “What have I to do with the king?” What then have you to do with property? Possessions are possessed by the laws of kings. [Col. 0045B] You have said, “What have I to do with the king?” Do not call them your possessions, because you have renounced those very [Note: [Col. 0045] “those very”: Augustine, Ivo.] human laws by which possessions are possessed.

Part II. Gratian. In rank, natural law simply prevails over custom and constitution. For whatever has been received by custom or comprised in rescripts is to be held void and invalid if it is contrary to natural law.

Accordingly Augustine says in Book III of the *Confessions*, chapter 8 [Note: [Col. 0045] Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 178.]:

### C. II. No one may do anything against natural law

The disgraceful acts which are contrary to human customs must be avoided according to the diversity of customs, so that no citizen’s or stranger’s lust may violate an agreement, established by custom or law, among the members of a city or nation. For every part is ugly when it does not fit its whole. [Col. 0045C]

§ 1. But when God commands something contrary to the custom or agreement of any persons, even if it has never been done there, it must be done; if it has been omitted, it must be restored; and if it had not been instituted, it must be instituted.

§ 2. For if a king is permitted to command something in the city over which he rules, which neither anyone before him nor he himself had ever commanded, and obedience is not contrary to the fellowship of his city—indeed, disobedience is contrary to that fellowship, for obedience to one’s kings is the general compact of human society—how much more [Col. 0045D] must service without hesitation be rendered to God, ruler of all his creation, in those things which he has [Col. 0046A] commanded? For just as, among the powers of human society, the greater authority is set above the lesser for obedience, so God is above all.

### C. III. A harmful custom must be uprooted

Likewise Pope Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0045D] This chapter is from Nicholas’s letter beginning, “The letter of Your Beatitude”; it survives, together with other letters of the same and other popes, in manuscript at Rome in the library of the Dominican monastery, from which this chapter was corrected.] [Note: [Col. 0045] Dated 868, among the acts of the Synod of Soissons. Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, vol. 15, p. 752; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 165; *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 203.] to Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims:

An evil custom, which must be avoided no less than a destructive corruption [Note: [Col. 0045] “must be rejected and avoided”: Venetian eds. I and II; Paris and Lyons eds. I and II.], unless it is quickly uprooted altogether, is appropriated by the wicked [Note: [Col. 0045] “the impious”: all collated older editions; Ivo.] as a right of privilege. Then transgressions and various presumptions, if not checked very swiftly, begin to be revered as laws and perpetually observed in the manner of privileges.

### C. IV. Custom must yield to truth and reason

Likewise Augustine, Book III *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 6 [Note: [Col. 0045] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 165; *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 208; among the same, ch. 6.]:

[Col. 0046B] “‘Once truth has been made manifest, let custom yield to truth’ [Note: [Col. 0045] Words of Libosus of Vaga at Cyprian’s Council of Carthage, ch. 30, A.D. 256.].” I answer without qualification: who doubts that custom ought to yield to manifest truth? Again: “Let no one place custom before reason and truth, because reason and truth always exclude custom [Note: [Col. 0045] Words of Felix of Buslacena, ibid., ch. 63.].”

### C. V. Every custom must yield to truth

Likewise Gregory [Note: [Col. 0046D] “To Guitmund”: In several manuscripts and in Ivo it reads, “Gregory VII.” During this pope’s pontificate, Guitmund, bishop of Aversa, wrote *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* against Berengar; the work survives.] [Note: [Col. 0045] A canon of plainly uncertain date; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 166; *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 213; “Gregory VII to Guitmund, bishop of Aversa”: Ivo; “Gregory VII to Guillimund, bishop of Aversa”: Basel ed.; “Gregory to Guillimund, bishop of Aversa”: all collated older editions with the *Panormia*; “Gregory VII to Gilmund, adversary bishop”: Durand, preface to bk. 2, *On the Manner of Celebrating General Councils*; Baluze noted, in his edition of Antonio Agustín, *On the Emendation of Gratian*, that Gregory IV is cited in an old manuscript of the *Panormia*.] to Guitmund, Bishop of Aversa:

If perhaps you invoke custom, you must note what the Lord says [Note: [Col. 0045] John 14:6.]: “I am truth and life. He did not say, ‘I am custom,’ but ‘truth’ [Note: [Col. 0045] Words of Libosus of Vaga at the Council of Carthage, ch. 30.].”

§ 1. And certainly, to employ the judgment of blessed Cyprian [Note: [Col. 0045] At the Council of Carthage just cited.], every custom, however ancient and however widespread, must absolutely be subordinated to truth; [Col. 0046C] and a practice contrary to truth must be abolished.

### C. VI. When truth is revealed, custom must yield to it

Likewise Augustine, Book III *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 5:

Whoever [Note: [Col. 0045] Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 234; from the beginning these are words of Castus of Sicca, in the same work, bk. 1, ch. 28.] presumes to follow custom in contempt of truth is either envious and malicious toward brethren to whom truth is revealed, or ungrateful toward God, by whose inspiration his Church is instructed; and [Col. 0046D] below: In the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0045] Cf. the preceding notes 15 and 16.] the Lord says, “I am [Col. 0047A] truth”; he did not say, “I am custom.” Therefore, once truth has been made manifest, let custom yield to truth. And below: Once truth has been revealed [Note: [Col. 0047] Words of Zosimus of Tharassa, bk. I.], let custom yield [Note: [Col. 0047D] “Let custom yield”: In St Augustine, Ivo, and the *Panormia*, the reading is “let error yield.” But St Augustine rightly infers from Zosimus’s own words that what he called error was custom. For he replies: “This man indeed did not wish to say ‘custom,’ but ‘error.’ Yet when he says that Peter, who formerly circumcised, yielded to Paul preaching truth, he sufficiently indicates that something else was also customarily done concerning baptism.”] to truth, because Peter [Note: [Col. 0047] Gal. 2:7.], who formerly circumcised, yielded to Paul preaching truth. And below: Since Christ [Note: [Col. 0047] Words of Honoratus of Tucca, bk. I, ch. 77.] is truth, we ought to follow truth rather than custom, because [Note: [Col. 0047D] “Because custom”: These words through the end are fittingly connected here in Ivo and Gratian, repeated from the words of Felix reported above, chapter “Truth.”] reason and truth always exclude custom [Note: [Col. 0047] Above in the same distinction, ch. 4.].

### C. VII. Custom is vainly opposed to reason

The same author in Book IV *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 0047] Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 2, ch. 94; cf. pt. 4, ch. 235.]:

“Vainly,” he says, “do some who are overcome by reason object custom to us, as though custom were greater than truth, or as though in spiritual matters we ought not to follow what has been revealed for the better by the Holy [Col. 0047B] Spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0047] Words of Cyprian in his letter to Jubaianus.] This [Note: [Col. 0047] Words of Augustine himself.] is plainly true, because reason and truth must be preferred to custom. But when truth supports custom, nothing ought to be retained more firmly.

### C. VIII. Custom must not hinder reason

Likewise Cyprian, in his letter [Note: [Col. 0047] Letter 74 [written ca. A.D. 256] in the Oxford edition of his works.] to Pompey, against Stephen’s letter:

A custom which had stealthily arisen among some persons must not prevent truth from prevailing and conquering. For custom without truth is the antiquity of error. [Col. 0048A] Therefore, leaving error behind, let us follow truth, knowing that in Ezra also [Note: [Col. 0047] 3 Esdras 4:38.] truth conquered, as it is written: “Truth remains and grows strong forever, and lives and prevails for ages of ages.”

The same author, in the middle of his letter [Note: [Col. 0047] Letter 73, ibid.] to Jubaianus:

Pardon [Note: [Col. 0047D] “Pardon”: In St Cyprian the reading is “For pardon may be granted,” preceded by the words printed above under chapter “Vainly,” through the word “revealed.”] may be granted to one who simply errs, as the Apostle Paul says of himself [Note: [Col. 0047] 1 Tim. 1:13.]: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an injurious man; but I received mercy, because I acted in ignorance.” But after inspiration and revelation have occurred, one who perseveres in the error in which he had been is knowingly and deliberately sinning without the pardon of ignorance. For he persists through a kind of presumption and obstinacy, although overcome by reason.

### C. IX. We must follow God’s truth, not human custom

The same author, Book II, Letter 3, to Caecilius [Note: [Col. 0047] Letter 63, A.D. 253, Oxford ed.; Anselm, bk. 9, ch. 8 [5].]:

[Col. 0048B] If Christ alone is to be heard, we ought not to attend to what someone before us thought should be done, but to what Christ, who is before all, first did. For we ought not to follow human custom but God’s truth, since God speaks and says through the prophet Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0047] Isa. 29:13.]: “In vain do they worship me, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men.”

Gratian. Thus it clearly appears that custom is subordinated to natural law.

## DISTINCTION IX

[Col. 0047]

[Col. 0047C] GRATIAN.

Part I. That constitution too yields to natural law is proved by many authorities.

For Augustine says in Letter 50 to Count Boniface [Note: [Col. 0047] Letter 185, written ca. A.D. 417, Maurist edition.]:

### C. I. The laws of princes must not prevail over natural law

PALEA [Note: [Col. 0048D] *Palea*: In old copies of Gratian in which there are either no *Paleae* or only a few, this place contains only the passage from “Whoever” through “For also in the times.” In other copies, in which they occur, this whole chapter is present without the designation *Palea*. It is all found in the same passage of St Augustine.].

“When emperors establish bad laws for falsehood against truth, believers are tested and those who persevere are crowned; but when they establish good laws for truth against falsehood, the violent are frightened and the thoughtful corrected.” [Col. 0048C]

§ 1. Whoever [Note: [Col. 0048D] “Whoever”: In Ivo and the *Panormia* as well, Augustine’s word order has been changed; in Augustine, the person deserving reward comes first and the person deserving punishment second.] [Note: [Col. 0047] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 145; *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 148.] therefore refuses to obey imperial laws issued for God’s truth incurs a great punishment. But whoever refuses to obey imperial laws issued against God’s truth gains a great reward.

“§ 2. For in the times of the prophets, all kings [Col. 0049A] who did not forbid or overthrow what had been established against God’s commands among the people of God are blamed; and those who forbade and overthrew it are praised above the merits of others. And King Nebuchadnezzar [Note: [Col. 0049] Dan. 3:5.], when he was a servant of idols, enacted a sacrilegious law that the image should be worshipped; but those who refused to obey his impious enactment acted piously and faithfully. Yet the same king, corrected by a divine miracle, enacted a pious and praiseworthy law for truth: that whoever uttered blasphemy against the God [Note: [Col. 0049] “the true God”: Augustine.] of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego should utterly perish together with his household.”

[Col. 0049B]

PALEA.

### C. II. Princes are themselves bound to live by their own laws

Likewise, from Isidore’s words in Book III of the *Sentences*, *On the Supreme Good*, chapter 53 [Note: [Col. 0049D] This chapter is absent from certain old copies; in others it is joined to the preceding chapter and has no rubric.] [Note: [Col. 0049] Burchard, bk. 15, ch. 42; Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 16, ch. 43.]:

“It is just that a ruler obey his own laws. For then he should judge that his laws ought to be observed by all, when he himself renders them reverence. It is fitting that rulers be bound by their own laws; nor may they annul [Note: [Col. 0049] “annul laws”: Isidore. Arevalo’s edition of Isidore preserves Gratian’s text; Breul’s edition of Isidore preserves Isidore’s text.] in their own case the laws which they establish for their subjects. For their command has just authority if they do not permit themselves what they prohibit to the people.”

### C. III. The writings of commentators serve the canonical Scriptures

Likewise Augustine, in the prologue to Book III *On the Trinity* [Note: [Col. 0049] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 120; *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 71.]:

Part II. Do not devote yourself to my writings as though they were canonical Scriptures. But in the latter, when you find something you did not believe, believe it without hesitation; in the former, [Col. 0049C] when you have not understood something to be certain [Note: [Col. 0049] “which you had held certain”: Argentinian, Basel, Venetian I editions.], do not hold it as firmly established [Note: [Col. 0049] “hold firmly”: Augustine, Ivo; “hold securely”: Basel edition.].

### C. IV. Many things are found in the works of commentators which need correction

The same author, to Vincentius Victor, Book IV *On the Soul and Its Origin*, chapter 1 [Note: [Col. 0049] Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 73.]:

I cannot and ought not deny that, just as in my own greater works [Note: [Col. 0049] “character”: Augustine, Ivo.], so in my many lesser works there are many things which may rightly be condemned without any rashness.

### C. V. Falsehoods are not admitted in canonical writings

The same author, to Jerome, Letter 19 [Note: [Col. 0049] Letter 82, §3, written A.D. 405, Maurist edition; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 119; *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 74.]:

[Col. 0049D] I have learned to render this reverence and honor to those books of Scripture [Note: [Col. 0049] “books of Scriptures”: Augustine, Ivo, *Panormia*.] alone which are now called canonical: [Col. 0050A] I most firmly dare not believe that any one of them [Note: [Col. 0049] “that their authors erred in writing anything”: ibid.] erred in writing. If I encounter anything in them that appears contrary to truth, I do not doubt that either the manuscript is faulty, or the translator has not understood what was said, or I have not understood it at all. But I read other authors in such a way that, however eminent they may be in holiness and learning [Note: [Col. 0049] “preeminent”: Augustine.], I do not regard something as true because they thought it so, but because they have been able to persuade me [Note: [Col. 0049D] “To me through others”: So also in the manuscripts and the gloss. In St Augustine the reading is: “to me either through those canonical authors or by probable reasoning”; and Ivo is not much different. It was thought sufficient to indicate certain other variants in the margin.] through other authors, either canonical authorities or probable reasons, that it does not depart from truth.

### C. VI. Hebrew books confer authority on the old books, Greek on the new

The same author [Note: [Col. 0050D] The words of this chapter are Jerome’s, from Letter 28 to Lucinius of Baetica, but the attribution was not changed because of the gloss on the word “Greek.”]:

[Col. 0050B] Just as the trustworthiness of Old Testament books must be tested against Hebrew volumes, so that of New Testament books requires the standard of the Greek language.

### C. VII. Nothing of authority will remain to canonical Scriptures if falsehoods are admitted into them

Likewise Augustine, to Jerome, Letter 9 [Note: [Col. 0049] Letter 40, ch. 3, written ca. A.D. 397, Maurist ed.; Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 215.]:

If even useful [Note: [Col. 0049] “or as it were useful”: Augustine; “have been useful”: Lyons I edition.] falsehoods are admitted into the holy Scriptures, what authority will remain in them? What judgment, finally, will be pronounced from those Scriptures, by whose weight the perversity of contentious falsehood may be [Note: [Col. 0049] “be barred”: Argentinian, Venetian I and II, Nuremberg, Lyons I and II editions.] crushed?

### C. VIII. Sacred Scripture is preferred to the writings of all bishops

Likewise, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, Book II, chapter 3 [Note: [Col. 0049] Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 227; Polycarpus, bk. 3, tit. 21.]:

[Col. 0050C] Who does not know that holy canonical Scripture, of both the Old and New Testaments, is contained within its own fixed limits, and is so preferred to all later writings of bishops that it is altogether beyond doubt or dispute whether whatever is established to have been written in it is true or right? But letters of bishops, written or to be written after the canon was confirmed, may be criticized if they have perhaps departed [Col. 0050D] from truth: by the perhaps wiser discourse of someone more learned in that matter, by the weightier authority and more instructed judgment of other bishops, and by councils.

[Col. 0051A]

### C. IX. Calumnies against divine commands must not be collected from the statements of any bishops

The same author, to Vincentius, Letter 48 [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 93, ch. 10, A.D. 408; Anselm, bk. 4, ch. 56 [59]; Deusdedit, pt. 2; Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 236.], against the Donatists:

Brother, do not seek to assemble calumnies from the writings of bishops against such numerous, clear, and indubitable divine testimonies—whether they are bishops of our own side, such as Hilary, or of that very unity, [Note: [Col. 0051D] “Or before”: Formerly the reading was: “or Cyprian and Agrippinus, before the party of Donatus separated.” The true reading has been restored from St Augustine, several copies of Gratian, and Ivo. For Cyprian and Agrippinus died within the unity of the Church long before Donatus’s schism; in this matter the author of the gloss erred.] [Note: [Col. 0051] Anselm reads as restored by Corrector R.] before Donatus’s party was separated—such as Cyprian and Agrippinus. First, because this kind of writing must be distinguished from the authority [Note: [Col. 0051] “from canonical authority”: Augustine manuscripts.] of the canon. For they are not read in the same way as if testimony were to be produced from them such that one may not think otherwise, should they perhaps have held a view other than truth demands. For we belong to the number of those who do not disdain to accept even the Apostle’s words as addressed to us [Note: [Col. 0051] Phil. 3:15.]: “And if in anything you think otherwise, God [Col. 0051B] has revealed [Note: [Col. 0051D] “Has revealed”: So read the original, Ivo, and certain editions of the New Testament. But St Augustine in his Tractates on John 5, 45, 53, and 98, and almost everywhere else, reads “will reveal,” and explains it. The Greek is ἀποκαλύψει, ‘will reveal.’] [Note: [Col. 0051] “will reveal”: Argentinian and Basel editions.] this also to you.”

### C. X. Canonical Scriptures and their expositions are not owed equal authority

Likewise, to Fortunatianus, Letter 3 [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 148, §15, written before A.D. 413; Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 237.]:

We ought not to treat the disputations of any persons, however Catholic and praiseworthy, as canonical Scriptures, so that, while preserving the honor due to those persons, we may not criticize or reject something in their writings [Col. 0052A] if we happen to find that they held otherwise than truth has it—truth understood, with divine help, either by others or by ourselves. In reading others’ writings, I am such a reader as I wish readers of mine to be [Note: [Col. 0051] “such”: Augustine.].

### C. XI. Sound reason is preferred to examples

The same author, to Marcellinus, *The City of God*, Book I, chapter 23 [Note: [Col. 0051] *Collectio trium partium*, pt. 2, tit. 50, ch. 27; Polycarpus, bk. 1, tit. 26.] [ch. 22, §2]:

Sound reason must indeed be preferred even to examples. Examples agree with it, but those are the more worthy of imitation insofar as they excel in piety.

Gratian. Therefore, since natural law commands nothing other than what God wills to be done, and forbids nothing other than what God forbids to be done; and since canonical Scripture contains nothing other than what is found in divine [Col. 0052B] laws, while divine laws consist in nature: it is clear that whatever is shown contrary to the divine will, or to canonical Scripture, is likewise contrary to natural law. Thus whatever is judged subordinate to the divine will, canonical Scripture, or divine laws, must have natural law preferred to it. Therefore ecclesiastical or secular constitutions, if shown to be contrary to natural law, must be wholly rejected.

## DISTINCTION X

[Col. 0051]

[Col. 0051C] GRATIAN.

Constitutions of princes do not take precedence over ecclesiastical constitutions, but obey them.

Accordingly Pope Nicholas writes to the bishops assembled in council at Convicinum [Note: [Col. 0051] Letter 32, written A.D. 863; Anselm, bk. 12, ch. 34; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 138; *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 86; Polycarpus, bk. 1, tit. 27.]:

### C. I. The law of emperors cannot dissolve ecclesiastical rights

The law [Note: [Col. 0051D] “The law”: This chapter was taken from Nicholas’s letter surviving in the Dominican library manuscript mentioned above, Distinction 8, chapter “Evil Custom.” The letter’s heading there reads: “Nicholas, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy fellow-brothers, the metropolitans, bishops, and other prelates of various provinces and cities, who have assembled at the public estate of Convicinum near the city of Senlis.” The letter was recently printed in the appendix to the *Library of the Holy Fathers*.] of emperors must not be used in all ecclesiastical controversies, especially since it is found at times to conflict with evangelical and canonical enactments [Col. 0052C] [Note: [Col. 0052D] “To conflict”: Nicholas continues directly: “to demonstrate which,” etc. But the material inserted by Gratian is not in that place in the letter, nor in Polycarpus or Anselm. The words “The law of emperors is not above God’s law but beneath it” are cited by Burchard and Ivo from the decrees of Pope Pius, chapter 3; they are found in the appended capitularies, chapter 17; the rest occurs below in this same chapter, § “Behold how.”]. Again [Note: [Col. 0051] “the same”: Basel ed.]: The law of emperors is not above God’s law but beneath it. Ecclesiastical rights cannot be dissolved by imperial judgment.

§ 1. To demonstrate this, the testimonies of these two men [Note: [Col. 0051] “heroes”: original and Anselm; “men”: Basel ed.], namely Innocent and Gregory, sufficiently serve. Holy Innocent indeed says in his decretal letter to Alexander, bishop of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0051] Innocent, Letter 24, written ca. A.D. 415, Coustant ed.; Burchard, bk. 15, ch. 10; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 139; *Decree*, pt. 16, ch. 11.]:

“As to your inquiry whether, when provinces are divided by imperial judgment so that there are two metropolitan sees, two metropolitan bishops ought likewise to be named: it has not seemed [Note: [Col. 0051] “it has not seemed expedient”: Innocent.] right that the Church of God should be changed at the shifting [Col. 0053A] demands of worldly affairs and should undergo honors or divisions which the emperor thinks must be made for his own reasons.”

Blessed Gregory, writing to the patrician Theoctista, says among other things [Note: [Col. 0053] Letter 44, bk. 1, 1; cf. below, C. 27, question 2, ch. 1.]:

“If marriages are said to have to be dissolved for religious reasons, it must be known that, even if human law has permitted this, divine law has nevertheless forbidden it.”

Behold how ecclesiastical rights cannot be dissolved by imperial judgment. Behold how what human law has permitted has been forbidden by divine law.

§ 2. We do not say that the laws of emperors—by which the Church is often defended against heretics, against tyrants, and against all manner of wicked persons—must be entirely rejected. Rather, we assert that no prejudice can be introduced by them against evangelical, apostolic, and canonical decrees, to which they [Col. 0053B] must be subordinated.

### C. II. It is not lawful for an emperor to do anything contrary to evangelical rules

Likewise Pope Symmachus, in the sixth Roman Synod held in the time of King Theodoric [Note: [Col. 0053] The synod commonly said to have been held in A.D. 502 is spurious. The very words of this canon are found in the letters of Pseudo-Isidore’s Callistus I and Marcellinus II. They are cited from Hadrian’s capitularies in Burchard, bk. 15, ch. 8; Anselm at the end of bk. 3; Deusdedit, pt. 1, ch. 3; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 141; *Decree*, pt. 4, ch. 231, pt. 16, ch. 9.]:

It is not lawful for an emperor—or for anyone who maintains piety—to presume anything against divine commands, or to do anything contrary to evangelical, prophetic, or apostolic rules.

### C. III. In ecclesiastical affairs the royal will must be subordinated to priests

Likewise Pope Felix [III] [Note: [Col. 0053] From the letter to Emperor Zeno, written A.D. 484; Anselm, bk. 4, ch. 11; Polycarpus, bk. 1, tit. 18.]:

It is certain that it is salutary for your affairs that, [Col. 0053C] when God’s causes are under consideration, in accordance with his own ordinance you strive to subordinate royal will to Christ’s priests rather than to set it above them; that you learn holy matters through their bishops rather than teach them; that you follow the ecclesiastical form rather than set before it humanly devised laws to be followed; and that you do not wish to exercise dominion over its enactments, to whose clemency God has willed the necks of your pious devotion to submit—lest, by exceeding the measure of the heavenly dispensation [Note: [Col. 0053] “dispensation”: Anselm.], offense be given to the One who orders all things.

[Col. 0054A] C. IV. Constitutions cannot conflict with good morals and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs. Likewise [Note: [Col. 0053] “the same”: editions of the old collection. This canon is taken from Hadrian’s Capitularies, c. 39; it is also cited by Anselm at the end of bk. 3, together with Deusdedit, pt. 1, c. 3; Ivo, Decretum, pt. 5, c. 38; and Polycarpus, bk. 1, final chapter. Burchard, on the contrary, in bk. 15, c. 9, cites c. 1 of the Council of Tribur, and in this he found Ivo, pt. 16, c. 11, as an imitator. The very words, however, may be found in bk. 7, c. 346 of the Capitularies, Baluzian edition.] 

Constitutions against the canons and decrees of the Roman bishops, or against good morals, have no force whatever.

C. V. Kings may not usurp what belongs to priests. Likewise Pope Nicholas I, in the letter [Note: [Col. 0053] Letter VIII in Mansi, written A.D. 865.—Collection in three parts, pt. 1, tit. 62, c. 70.] to Emperor Michael, which begins: “We had proposed.”

Your Empire ought to be content with its daily administrations of public affairs and not usurp what belongs solely to the priests of the Lord.

[Col. 0054B] C. VI. The tribunals of kings are subject to priestly authority. Likewise Gregory Nazianzen, in his address to the citizens of Nazianzus, full of anguish, and to the angry magistrate [Note: [Col. 0053] Collection in three parts, pt. 2, tit. 14, c. 6; Gregory Nazianzen, *To the Emperors at Constantinople*: editions of the old collection.] 

Do you accept freedom of speech? Do you gladly accept that the law of Christ subjects you to priestly authority and makes you subject to these tribunals? For he has given authority to us also; he has given us a rule far more perfect than your rules. Or does it seem just to you that spirit should yield to flesh, heavenly things be overcome by earthly things, and human things be preferred to divine?

Part II. Gratian. Behold that the constitutions of princes are to be subordinated to ecclesiastical laws. But where they do not conflict with evangelical and canonical decrees, they are to be held worthy of every reverence.

[Col. 0054C] Hence Augustine says in the *Dialogue*, that is, book II *Against the Letters of Petilian*, c. 58 [Note: [Col. 0053] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 153; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 153.]: C. VII. It is permissible to invoke imperial laws in aid of the Church [Note: [Col. 0053C] “Church”: The author of this rubric understood the chapter as though it concerned laws enacted by emperors in favor of the Church; whereas Blessed Augustine there grants Petilian and the Donatist heretics that they may use imperial laws in their own aid, [Col. 0053D] provided they did not do so deceitfully—which, he proves, they did.] 

If you think that the laws even of an earthly empire should be invoked in your aid, we do not blame you. Paul did this [Note: [Col. 0053] Acts, c. 22.] when, against violent men, he declared that he was a Roman citizen.

C. VIII. Kings need pontiffs for eternal matters, and pontiffs need kings for temporal matters. Likewise [Note: [Col. 0053D] In printed codices this heading was prefixed to the chapter: “Cyprian to Emperor Julian,” which is contrary to every chronological consideration. [Col. 0054C] In all manuscripts except Vatican MS 11, the word “Emperor” is absent, as also in Ivo. MS 9, however, has “to Bishop Julian.” Another very ancient manuscript has “to Jubian.” In fact this whole chapter occurs in Nicholas’s letter to Emperor Michael [Col. 0054D] which begins “We had proposed”; it is cited below, Distinction 96, c. *When in truth*, with other words from the same letter upon which these words depend. It is taken from Gelasius’s treatise *On the Bond of Anathema*.] Pope Nicholas I, in Letter VII [Note: [Col. 0053] Letter written A.D. 865; below, Distinction 96, c. 6.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 188.—The chapter is attributed to Bishop Julian: editions of Arg., Ven., Nor.—To Julian Lupus: Venice II, Lyons I–II, Antwerp.—To Julian: Basel edition.] to Emperor Michael.

Because the same mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, [Col. 0055A] by distinct proper spheres of action and dignities, separated the proper functions of each of the two powers [Note: [Col. 0055B] “Proper”: the original reads: “wishing his own to be raised up by healing humility.” Ivo has the reading of Gratian here in most manuscripts. [Col. 0055C] In some, however, it reads: “wishing his own to be raised up by healing humility,” as also below, Distinction 96, c. *When in truth*. In Gelasius, at the cited place, it reads: “thus, by distinct actions and dignities, he separated the functions of each power, wishing his own to be saved by healing humility and not again ensnared by human pride, so that Christians,” etc.], wishing human hearts to be raised upward by healing humility [Note: [Col. 0055] “raised upward by humility”: Argentinian edition.], rather than plunged again into the depths by human pride: so that Christian emperors might need pontiffs for eternal life, and pontiffs might use imperial laws solely for the course of temporal affairs; in order that spiritual action might be distinct from carnal incursions, and therefore [Note: [Col. 0055] “and serving God”: editions of the old collection.] “one serving God might not entangle himself in secular affairs” [Note: [Col. 0055] 2 Tim. 2:4.]; and conversely [Note: [Col. 0055] “lest”: editions of the old collection; Ivo.] that he who was involved in secular affairs might not seem to preside over divine things.

C. IX. The laws of emperors ought to be observed. Likewise Leo IV to Augustus Lothair [Note: [Col. 0055] Fragment of a lost letter, written about A.D. 847.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 149; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 176.] 

Concerning the inviolable observance and preservation of the capitularies or commands of Your Imperial Majesty and of your [Col. 0055B] [Note: [Col. 0055C] “And of your”: This letter has not been discovered; and there seems to be an error in these words, from which the author of the gloss took occasion for error, attributing to Christian emperors, such as Lothair’s predecessors, what Isidore says of pagans: namely, that emperors were customarily called pontiffs. On this matter Gelasius is excellent in his treatise *On the Bond of Anathema*, and below, Distinction 21, c. *The clergy*. In Ivo one reads: “your own and also of the pontifical predecessors of ours”; in the *Panormia*: “of ours and of our pontiffs and predecessors.” But perhaps the rest is correctly given in Gratian [Col. 0055D] and only the conjunction *and* should be added before “predecessors,” as in the *Panormia*. For the meaning will then be that those emperors customarily issued capitularies after taking the pontiffs of the realm into counsel, which is very true. These words written by Leo seem in every respect to concern the capitularies of Charles and Louis, which Lothair had commanded to be observed throughout Italy. For in Lombard laws, bk. III, tit. 35, Lothair [Col. 0056B] is reported to have decreed thus: “It has pleased us that the capitularies which we have excerpted from the capitulary of the glorious lord Charles, of good memory, and of our father Louis, [Col. 0056C] most invincible emperor, shall be held and observed as law by all these, both our faithful subjects and those established in the holy Church in the kingdom of Italy; and whoever proves contemptuous of these capitularies shall pay sixty solidi.” This was very displeasing to the Roman people, who were prevented from using the ancient law of the Romans, as may be inferred from the final chapter below in this same distinction; and a rumor was even spread that the Pope and people held the same view. Leo seems to have wished to clear himself by this letter; nevertheless, afterwards he dealt again more carefully with the same Lothair to preserve Roman civil law, as appears from the said final chapter.] pontifical predecessors, we profess that, insofar as we have been able and are able, with Christ’s favor, we shall preserve them by every means now and forever. And if perhaps anyone has told or shall tell you otherwise, know with certainty that he is lying.

C. X. What is done contrary to law is undone by the authority of law. Likewise John VIII [Note: [Col. 0055] John VII: editions of the old collection except Basel.—A chapter of uncertain date.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 230; cf. pt. 6, c. 115.] to Emperor Louis.

You see, dearest son, that what is acquired contrary to laws deserves to be dissolved through laws.

[Col. 0056A] C. XI. The laws of princes or the rules of the Fathers may not be despised. Likewise Gelasius to Bishops Rufinus and Aprilius [Note: [Col. 0055] Fragment of a letter written at the end of the fifth century; below, Distinction 54, c. 11.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 150; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 179.] 

Who indeed [Note: [Col. 0055] “who or”: Ivo.] would say that the laws of princes, the rules of the Fathers, or paternal admonitions [Note: [Col. 0055] “modern”: Ivo.] ought to be despised, except one who judges that he may pass over so grave an offense with impunity?

C. XII. The laws of Roman princes are to be observed by all. Likewise to King Theodoric [Note: [Col. 0055] Fragment of a letter of uncertain date.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 180.] 

It is certain that Your Magnificence wishes the laws of Roman princes—which it has commanded to be observed in human affairs—to be observed much more, for the sake of increasing your prosperity, in reverence for blessed Peter the apostle. [Col. 0056B]

C. XIII. Roman law must not be corrupted by anyone’s rashness. Likewise Leo IV to Augustus Lothair [Note: [Col. 0055] Fragment of a lost letter, which learned scholars conjecture to have been written about A.D. 847.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 151; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 181.] 

Your [Note: [Col. 0056C] “Your”: Lothair appears to have granted the Roman people what Leo here sought. For in Lombard laws, bk. II, tit. 57, it reads: “Let the Roman people be asked by what law they wish to live”; and the following constitution follows [Note: [Col. 0055] The Capitularies, whose Lombard recension is given here—for a Roman recension also exists, published from the collection of Cardinal Deusdedit by Holstenius, *Collection of Roman Monuments*, Rome, 1662—was written before Leo’s time, in A.D. 824, as Baluzius long ago observed, *Capitularies*, preface §24.]:

[Col. 0056D] Emperor Lothair.

We wish the entire Roman people to be asked by what law it wishes to live, so that they may live by the law by which they have professed to live. And let this be declared to them, so that every person—judges, dukes, and the remaining people alike—may know it. If they commit an offense against that law, they shall be subject to the same law by which they profess to live, by dispensation [variant: *disposition*] of the Pope and of us.] 

We beseech your clemency that, just as Roman law has hitherto prevailed free from all storms and is not remembered to have been corrupted for the sake of any person, so now it may retain its own strength and proper vigor.

## DISTINCTION XI

[Col. 0057]

[Col. 0057A] GRATIAN.

Part I. That custom yields to laws, Isidore testifies, saying in the *Synonyms*, bk. II [c. 16] [Note: [Col. 0057] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 165; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 207.]:

C. I. A bad practice is overcome by reason and law.

Let practice yield to authority; let law and reason overcome bad practice.

C. II. No one’s custom can oppose the enactments of pontiffs. Likewise Pope Nicholas I to Emperor Michael [Note: [Col. 0057] The words of the chapter occur in Nicholas I’s letter to Photius, written A.D. 862; Mansi, vol. 15, p. 175.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 211; Collection in three parts, pt. 1, tit. 62, c. 14.] 

It follows that what is enacted by the rulers of this see with full authority must not be set aside, on the pretext of any custom, by persons merely following their own wishes; rather, it must be firmly and unshakably maintained.

[Col. 0057B] C. III. Members may not dissent from the custom of the Roman Church. Likewise Pope Julius I to the Eastern bishops, Letter I [Note: [Col. 0057] Pseudo-Isidorian letter. Anselm, bk. 1, c. 8; Polycarpus, bk. 1, tit. 17.] 

Do not err, my dearest brothers; do not be carried away by diverse [Note: [Col. 0057] Heb. 13:9.] and strange [Note: [Col. 0057] “foreign”: Vulgate.] teachings. Behold, you have the institutions of the apostles and apostolic men, and the canons: enjoy these, be enclosed by these [Note: [Col. 0057B] “Be enclosed by these”: This passage has been enlarged from the original and Anselm. [Note: [Col. 0057] Yet the words enclosed by asterisks are absent from the Anselm codex.]], delight in these, arm yourselves with these, *that, relying on these,* enclosed, [Col. 0058A] delighted, and armed, you may be able to stand firm against every dart of the enemies. For it is sufficiently unworthy that any bishop or member of the subsequent orders should reject this rule which he sees the see of blessed Peter both follow and teach. For it is greatly fitting that the entire body of the Church should agree with itself in this observance, which has its authority from that place where the Lord established the primacy of the whole Church.

C. IV. Practice and custom cannot overcome law and reason. Likewise Emperor Constantine Augustus to Proculus, Code, bk. VIII, title *What Constitutes Long Custom* [tit. 53, constitution 2] [Note: [Col. 0057] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 163; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 202.] 

Long-standing custom and practice are not of slight authority; but their force is not so great that they overcome either reason or law.

[Col. 0058B] Part II. Gratian. But since custom is shown to conflict neither with sacred canons nor with human laws, it must be observed unshakably.

Hence from the sayings [Note: [Col. 0057B] “From the sayings”: This chapter was formerly cited as Augustine, in a book *From the Sayings of Basil*. In the Vercelli codex it reads: “Hence Augustine says,” or “from the sayings of Basil”; and the latter half of this alternative was retained because [Col. 0057C] Burchard and the author of the *Panormia* cite it thus. Ivo, however, cites it from Basil’s book *On the Holy Spirit*, c. 27, as indicated in the margin. Moreover, because the gloss prevented correction in many places, it seemed necessary to adduce the complete passage of Blessed Basil in both Greek and Latin:

“Of the doctrines and proclamations preserved in the Church, some we possess from written teaching, while others, handed down to us from apostolic tradition, we have received in mystery. Both have the same force for piety, and no one will contradict these who has even the slightest experience of ecclesiastical ordinances. For if we should undertake to reject the unwritten customs as though they did not possess great force, we would unknowingly injure the Gospel in its very vital parts—or rather reduce the proclamation to a bare name. For example, to mention first the primary and most common practice: who taught us in writing that those who have hoped in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ should be marked with the sign of the cross? What writing taught us to turn toward the east in prayer? Who among the saints left us in writing the words of invocation at the presentation of the bread of the Eucharist and the cup of blessing? For we are certainly not content with those things mentioned by the Apostle or the Gospel; rather, we also say other things before and after, [Col. 0058B] having received them from unwritten teaching as possessing great force for the mystery. We bless the water of baptism and the oil of anointing, and moreover the very person being baptized: from what written sources? Is it not from the silent and mystical tradition? And what written discourse taught the anointing with oil itself? Whence comes the threefold baptism of a person? And the other things concerning baptism—the renunciation of Satan and his angels—from what Scripture are they? Are they not from this unpublished and secret teaching, which our Fathers guarded in undistracted and uncurious silence? They had rightly been taught that the venerable things of the mysteries are preserved in silence.”

That is: Of the doctrines and ordinances preserved in the Church, some we have from teaching committed to writing; others we have received in mystery from the tradition of the apostles transmitted to us. Both have the same force for piety, and surely no one who possesses even a little knowledge of ecclesiastical laws will contradict them. For if we should undertake to reject things that rest not on writing but only on custom [as though they had no great force], we should unknowingly injure the Gospel, indeed in its chief parts; or rather, reduce the institutions themselves to some empty name. For example—to mention first what is primary and especially common [Col. 0058D]—who taught in writing that those who have placed their hope in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ are to be marked with the sign of the cross? What writings taught us to turn toward the rising sun while praying? Who among the holy Fathers left us in writing the words of invocation when the bread of the Eucharist and the cup of blessing [Col. 0059C] are offered? For we are not content with those things mentioned by the Apostle and the Gospel; rather, both before and afterwards we say other things, as having great weight for the mystery itself, taught by doctrine not written but handed down. We bless the water of baptism and the oil of anointing, and besides, the person himself who is baptized: from what Scripture? Is it not from secret and mystical tradition? What written discourse taught the anointing with oil itself? Whence have we received that a person is to be immersed three times? The renunciation of Satan and his angels, and all the other things whatsoever [Col. 0059D] that we observe in baptism—which Scripture commanded them? Is it not this very little-publicized but secret teaching that our Fathers guarded in quiet and wholly uncurious silence? They rightly understood that the majesty of mysteries is preserved by silence.] of Basil [Note: [Col. 0057] Regino, Appendix, bk. 1, c. 53; Burchard, bk. 3, c. 127; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 159; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 69.]:

C. V. Custom is inviolable when it is shown to conflict neither with human laws nor sacred canons.

Of ecclesiastical ordinances, we have received some from writings [Col. 0059A] [Note: [Col. 0059] “in writings”: all the old editions of the collection.], others as confirmed by apostolic tradition through successive generations [Note: [Col. 0059] “successors”: the same editions; Böhm.], and still others have been approved and strengthened by established custom. Equal observance and the same devotion of piety are due to both; and who that has even some experience of sacred Scriptures would hesitate over this? For if we should attempt [Note: [Col. 0059] “consider”: editions and old codex.] to regard as worthless the customs of the Church handed down by the Fathers apart from writings, those who examine carefully will plainly see how great a loss religion would suffer. §1. For what Scripture, to begin there, taught that the faithful should be marked with the sign of the saving cross? Or what Scripture commended the words of the lengthy prayer or consecration, arranged in three parts, over bread and the cup? For in the secret rites [Col. 0059B] we say not only what is contained in the Gospel or added by any Apostle [Note: [Col. 0059] “by whichever Apostle”: Argentinian, Venetian I, Nuremberg editions; “by the Apostle which”: remaining editions.], but add many other things that lend, as it were, great force [Note: [Col. 0059] “suited to effecting”: Burchard.] to the mysteries. What written form taught us to pray toward the east? We bless the font of baptism with the oil [Note: [Col. 0059] “the oil”: the same source.] of anointing. To this is added the fact that we anoint with oil three times [Note: [Col. 0059] “we immerse three times those whom we baptize, [and] anoint with oil”: the same source.] those whom we baptize and instruct them with words to renounce Satan and his angels. Whence come these and many other things of this sort, unless because, in silent and mystical tradition, the Fathers have observed them in the mysteries [Note: [Col. 0059] “in the ministries”; Ivo: “observed more”: same source; editions of the old collection; Böhm.] with more reverent care according to ecclesiastical custom in silence than they have published them in writing?

C. VI. A custom which adopts nothing contrary to faith is praiseworthy. Likewise Pope Pius I [Note: [Col. 0060C] The words of this chapter, formerly attributed to Blessed Augustine, are found among the decrees of Pius, decree VII, in the Cologne edition of the councils in three volumes, and in a letter of the same Pius from the codex of sixteen books, bk. 3, c. 19; Burchard, Ivo, and the author of the *Panormia* also cite it. Yet nearly all the words of that letter occur in bk. 1 of the register of Blessed Gregory, cited in Polycarpus, Letter 75; and those relevant to this chapter are reported below, Distinction 12, c. *We permit the custom*.] in the decrees, decree VII [Note: [Col. 0059] The words of the canon wrongly ascribed to Pius are taken from Gregory the Great’s letter to the bishops of Numidia, written in the ninth indiction (Letter 77, bk. I, Maurist edition). The old editions of the collection cite Augustine to the priest Casulanus as author.—Burchard, bk. 3, c. 124; Anselm, bk. 4, c. 42; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 157; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 66; Polycarpus, bk. 3, tit. 27.] 

We commend a custom that is known to adopt nothing contrary to the Catholic faith.

[Col. 0059C] C. VII. Where authority is lacking, the custom of God’s people and the institutions of the elders are observed as law. Likewise Blessed Augustine to Casulanus, Letter LXXXVI [Note: [Col. 0059] Letter 36, written A.D. 396, Maurist edition.—Anselm, bk. 4, c. 43; Burchard, bk. 3, c. 126; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 158; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 68; Polycarpus, bk. 3, tit. 23, final chapter.] 

In matters concerning which divine Scripture has laid down nothing certain, the custom of the people of God and the institutions of the elders are to be held as law. And just as [Note: [Col. 0060C] “And just as”: From here to the end the words are not in the cited letter, but are also transmitted by Burchard, Ivo, [Col. 0060D] and the *Panormia* [Note: [Col. 0059] These words also occur in Anselm at the cited place.]] transgressors of divine laws are to be restrained, so also despisers of ecclesiastical customs are to be restrained.

C. VIII. The Church is governed by authority and by general or particular tradition. The same author, in the book *On the Christian Faith* [Note: [Col. 0060D] Today no work bearing this title survives among the works of Blessed Augustine. The same thought, however, is expounded at length in Letter 118 to Januarius, cc. 1–2.] 

The Catholic Church, spread throughout the world, is shown to exist in three ways. For whatever is maintained in it is either the authority of Scripture, universal tradition, or a proper and particular institution. But the whole Church is bound by authority; likewise, the whole Church is bound by the universal tradition of the elders; while each Church, according to variety of places and as seems good to it, stands and is governed by private enactments and particular regulations.

[Col. 0060B] C. IX. The authority of the Catholic Church has force in matters of faith. The same author, in the book *Against the Manichaeans* [Note: [Col. 0060D] In Blessed Augustine, bk. 11 *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, c. 2, one reads: “And you see in this matter”—he speaks of the authority of copies—“what force the authority of the Catholic Church has, which from the very firmly founded apostolic sees,” etc. Augustine considered this succession of bishops, especially in Peter’s see, rightly to be a most certain mark of the Catholic Church also in the book *Against the Letter of the Foundation* and in Letter 165, *On the Donatist Schism*.] [Note: [Col. 0059] *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, bk. 11, c. 2.] 

It is evident that, in a doubtful matter, the authority of the Catholic Church has force for faith: it is established from the most firmly founded sees of the apostles down to the present day by the succession of bishops succeeding one another and by the agreement of so many peoples.

C. X. One may not depart from apostolic institutions. Likewise Pope Leo to the bishops established throughout Sicily, Letter IV, c. 6 [Note: [Col. 0059] Letter 16, c. 6, written A.D. 447, Ballerini edition.—Anselm, bk. 1, c. 45; Polycarpus, bk. 1, tit. 17.] 

We enjoin this upon your charity: that no further departure whatsoever be made from apostolic institutions, because henceforth it cannot go unpunished if anyone believes apostolic rules may be neglected in any respect.

[Col. 0060C] C. XI. What the Roman Church observes must be observed by all. Likewise Innocent I to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio, Letter I [Note: [Col. 0059] Letter 25, written A.D. 416, in Coustant.—Burchard, bk. 3, c. 125; Anselm, bk. 1, c. 41; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 67; Polycarpus, bk. 1, tit. 17; bk. 3, tit. 24.] 

Who does not know or recognize that what was handed down to the Roman Church by Peter, prince of the apostles, [Note: [Col. 0061] In these and the following words the author of the canon imitated Leo the Great, Letter 14, c. 6, and Letter 16, c. 1; Ballerini edition.] [Col. 0061A] and is still observed, ought to be observed by all? Nothing should be added or introduced that either lacks authority [Note: [Col. 0061] “general authority, or ought to receive precedent from elsewhere?” all editions of the collection, including Basel, omitting “general.” In Ivo the reading is as restored by the Correctors from Innocent himself.] or seems to derive its precedent from elsewhere. Especially because it is evident that throughout all Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one founded churches except those whom the venerable apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests. Or let them read whether any other of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0061] “apostle”: all editions of the collection.] is found in these provinces, or is read to have taught there. But if they do not read this, because it is nowhere found, they must follow what the Roman Church observes, from which they unquestionably received their beginning; lest, while pursuing foreign statements [Note: [Col. 0061] “assertions”: Dionysian and Hispanic collections; Ivo.], they seem to omit the head of institutions [Note: [Col. 0061] “lose”: all old editions.].

1. Your Beloved has often come to the City [Col. 0062A] and met with us in the Church, and has learned [Note: [Col. 0061C] “Has learned”: In the original passage as inserted in the four-volume collection of councils, it reads: “has undoubtedly learned. I should have considered that this was sufficient for the instruction or correction of your Church, if your predecessors had observed anything insufficiently or differently, unless you had judged that we should be consulted about certain matters.” But because of the gloss, especially on the word “custom,” it was not altered.] [Note: [Col. 0061] “has recognized”: the same editions.] what custom it maintains both in considering the mysteries and in conducting the other secret rites. We should have thought [Note: [Col. 0061] “I should have thought”: Hispanic Collection; Ivo; Böhm.] this sufficient for the instruction or correction of your Church, if your predecessors had observed anything insufficiently or differently; and we should have held it quite certain [Note: [Col. 0061] “I should have held”: Hispanic Collection; Ivo; Basel edition.], unless you had judged [Note: [Col. 0061] “you had judged”: same source; Ivo; Argentinian, Basel, Venetian I–II editions.] that we ought to be consulted about some matters. We therefore answer these questions, not because we believe you ignorant of *anything*, but so that by greater authority you may instruct your people [Note: [Col. 0061] “or your people”: Dionysian and Hispanic collections; Ivo; Böhm.], or, if any stray from the institutions of the Roman Church, either admonish them or do not delay to report them to us [Note: [Col. 0061] Absent in the Dionysian and Hispanic collections and in Ivo.], so that we may know who they are that either introduce innovations or think that the custom of some Church other than the Roman is to be observed.

## DISTINCTION XII

[Col. 0061]

[Col. 0061B] GRATIAN.

Part I. That no one may act without the discernment of justice.

Hence Pope Callixtus I says to all bishops in Letter I [Note: [Col. 0061] Pseudo-Isidorian letter.] to Bishop Benedict:

C. I. No one may act, without the discernment of justice, against the discipline of the Roman Church.

It is not fitting [Note: [Col. 0061] Anselm, bk. 1, c. 12 (13); Polycarpus, bk. 1, tit. 17.] [Note: [Col. 0061] “permitted”: Lyons II–III editions.] for the members to depart from the head; rather, according to the testimony of sacred Scripture, all members should follow the head. No one indeed doubts that the Apostolic Church is the mother of all churches, and it is in no way proper for you to depart from its rules. And as the Son of God came to do the Father’s will, so you too should fulfill the will of your mother, which is the Church, whose head, as has been said, is the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0061] “stands”: all editions of the collection except Basel.]. Therefore reason permits nothing done, without the discernment [Col. 0061C] of justice, against its discipline to be considered valid.

[Col. 0062B] C. II. Let no one proudly resist apostolic commands.
