Likewise Pope Gregory IV [Note: [Col. 0062C] Gregory: This entire chapter is found in Gregory IV’s letter, “To all bishops established throughout Gaul, Germany, Europe, and all provinces,” which is in the previously cited codex of the library of the Dominican monastery. Its opening, however, is also found in Anastasius II’s letter to Emperor Anastasius, c. 6.] [Note: [Col. 0061] The entire letter *Of Unoffending Faith* is found in Mabillon, *Veteran Analects*, p. 298, with the added subscription: “Given on the eighth day before the Ides of July, in the eleventh indiction, A.D. 832.”—Anselm, bk. 1, c. 20 (21); Polycarpus, bk. 1, tit. 17.] 

Let apostolic commands not be resisted with harsh pride, but let those things commanded by the holy Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0061] Absent from the original.] and by apostolic authority be salutarily fulfilled through obedience, if you desire to have communion with the same holy Church of God, which is your head. And after much else:

§1. By this present command we prescribe nothing new, but confirm things that appear to have been granted long ago. For no one doubts that not only an episcopal cause, but every matter of holy [Note: [Col. 0062C] “Holy religion”: Thus corrected from the letter itself and several manuscript codices of Gratian, by inserting the words: “hope of the Roman Church.”] religion [Note: [Col. 0061] The reading marked by the Correctors is preserved by Venetian I–II, Nuremberg, Lyons I–II editions.—“Of the Holy Roman Church and religion”: Argentinian and Lyons III editions; Basel alone has the restored reading.] ought to be referred to the Apostolic See as to the head of the churches, and receive its norm [Note: [Col. 0061] “receive,” and a little later “received”: editions of the old collection except Basel.] from the place whence it received its beginning, lest it seem to omit the head of institution [Note: [Col. 0061] “be omitted”: editions of the old collection.]. Let all priests uphold the ordinance of that authority, if they do not wish to be torn away from the firmness of the apostolic rock upon which Christ [Col. 0063A] founded the universal Church [Note: [Col. 0063] “shaken”: the same editions except Basel.]. If anyone does not observe these commands of the Apostolic See, let him not be doubted to be an enemy of the honor he has received.

C. III. A custom to which canonical authority does not object must not be resisted. Likewise Leo IX [Note: [Col. 0063C] This chapter has been composed from two very different passages. For up to the words “if canonical authority,” it is taken from the first letter or treatise of Leo IX against the unheard-of presumption of Michael of Constantinople and Leo, bishop of Acrida, c. 29. Speaking of the Roman Church, he says: “For it knows that customs differing according to place and time do not harm the salvation of believers, when one faith working through love commends to the one God all the good it can.” These words are reported almost verbatim by Ivo and in the *Panormia*. The second part is taken from Nicholas’s [Col. 0063D] second letter to Photius, beginning: “After blessed Peter.” There one finds: “Concerning the customs which you seemed to set against us, writing that customs differ in different churches: where canonical authority does not stand in their way, so that we ought to oppose them, we make no judgment and do not resist them.”] to Michael, bishop [Note: [Col. 0063] “to Emperor Michael”: editions of the old collection together with Ivo.—Letter 2 in Mansi’s collection of councils, A.D. 862.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 155; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 223 and pt. 5, c. 44.] of Constantinople, Letter I, c. 29; and Nicholas I, Letter II to Photius.

The holy Roman Church knows that customs differing according to place and time do no harm to the salvation of believers, if canonical authority does not oppose them, requiring us to withstand them. Therefore we judge that they ought not, nor can, be resisted [Note: [Col. 0063] “be resisted”: editions of the old collection.].

[Col. 0063B] C. IV. Customs that do not injure faith are to be observed as handed down by the elders. Likewise Jerome to Lucinius, Letter XXXVIII [Note: [Col. 0063] Anselm, bk. 4, c. 44.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 156; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 212.] 

I think I should briefly admonish you of this: ecclesiastical traditions, especially those which do not injure faith, should be observed as they have been handed down by the elders; nor should one group’s custom be overthrown by another group’s contrary practice.

C. V. Traditions instituted by the Fathers are not to be broken. Likewise Nicholas to Archbishop Hincmar [Note: [Col. 0063D] It occurs in the letter written to Hincmar and [Col. 0064C] the other archbishops and bishops governing churches in Charles’s realm, found in the already mentioned codex of the Dominican library; this chapter has been enlarged from it. Formerly it was shorter, as it also is in Ivo and the *Panormia*.] [Note: [Col. 0063] Letter 70, written A.D. 867.] 

It is ridiculous and a sufficiently abominable disgrace that *in our times we should permit the holy Church of God either to be falsely accused, or should suffer those* traditions which we received of old from the Fathers to be broken at the whim of those who are always erring.

C. VI. Long-established customs are to be treated as law. Likewise Justinian, *Institutes*, bk. I, tit. 2 [*On Natural Law*, §9] [Note: [Col. 0063] Anselm’s Collection, bk. 7, c. 2; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 160; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 194.] 

Long-established customs, approved by the consent of those who use them, imitate law.

[Col. 0064A] C. VII. Whatever is done contrary to long custom must be recalled. Likewise Code, bk. VIII, tit. [53], *What Constitutes Long Custom*, law 1 [Note: [Col. 0063] Anselm’s Collection, bk. 7, c. 68; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 162; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 201.] 

The existing custom and the reason that prompted the custom must be maintained. And whatever [Note: [Col. 0064C] “Whatever”: The original reads: “and lest anything be done contrary to long custom”; but because the rubric seems better suited to Gratian’s reading, which also occurs in Ivo and the *Panormia*, it was not altered.] is done contrary to long custom shall be referred back by the provincial governor for his consideration.

C. VIII. Let custom remain unaltered when it is known to adopt nothing contrary to the Catholic faith. Likewise Gregory to all the bishops of Numidia, bk. I, Letter LXXV [Note: [Col. 0063] Bk. 1, Letter 77, written A.D. 591, Maurist edition; cf. above, Distinction 11, c. 6.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 204.] 

We permit the custom which is known, *however*, to adopt nothing contrary to the Catholic faith, to remain unaltered, whether concerning the appointment of primates or other chapters, except in the case of those who [Col. 0064B] have come from the Donatists to the episcopate. We absolutely forbid these to be promoted to the dignity of a primacy, even when the order of clergy [Note: [Col. 0064C] “Order of clergy”: Thus it is also read in [Col. 0064D] several ancient manuscripts of Gratian and in some codices of Blessed Gregory. But the author of the gloss does not appear to have had the word “clergy,” any more than Ivo, most manuscript copies of Gratian, or some editions of the works of Blessed Gregory.] brings them to that same rank. It is enough for them to care for the people entrusted to them; they must not *also* precede, in attaining the summit of primacy, those bishops whom the Catholic faith has both taught and begotten in the bosom of the Church.

C. IX. Things that belong to custom are not denied. Likewise Gregory to Maximus, Bishop of Salona, Book VII of the Register, Epistle 81. [Note: [Col. 0063] Ep. 81, bk. 9 (written A.D. 599), Maurist edition.]

Just as we do not permit unlawful acts to be committed, so neither do we deny what belongs to custom.

[Col. 0064C] C. X. It is not place that commends custom, but custom that commends place. Likewise Gregory to Augustine, Bishop of the English, Response [to the Interrogations], 3. [Note: [Col. 0063] Ep. 64, bk. 14 (written A.D. 601; cf. Distinction 5, c. 1), Maurist edition.]

Your brotherhood knows the custom of the Roman Church, in which it remembers having been nurtured. But it pleases me that, whether in the Roman Church, or in the Gallican [Note: [Col. 0063] “Of Gaul”: Gregory; “Gallican”: Ivo.], or in any other church, you find something that may please almighty [Col. 0065A] God more, you should carefully choose it; and you should introduce into the Church of the English, which is still new in the faith, by a principal institution, whatever you are able to gather from many churches [Note: [Col. 0065] “Were able”: Gregory.]. For things are not to be loved for the sake of places, but places for the sake of things [Note: [Col. 0065] “Things for us”: same source.]. Therefore choose from each of the churches whatever is devout, religious, and right; and, having gathered these together as it were into one bundle, establish them as a custom among the minds of the English.

C. XI. What is proved to be neither against faith nor against good morals is to be held indifferently. Likewise Augustine to Januarius, Epistle CXVIII, chapter 1 [and 2]. [Note: [Col. 0065] Book 1, *On Januarius’s Inquiries*, that is, Epistle 54 (written about A.D. 400), Maurist edition.]

Those things which we keep not as written but as handed down, and which are observed throughout the whole world, are understood to have been recommended and established either by the Apostles themselves or by plenary councils (whose authority in the Church is most salutary): for example, that the Lord’s Passion, Resurrection, Ascension into heaven, and the coming *from heaven* of the Holy Spirit are celebrated by annual solemnity; and anything else of this kind that is observed by the universal Church wherever it extends. § 1. But other things, which vary according to places and regions of the earth—for instance, some fast on Saturday, while others do not; some receive communion daily in the Lord’s Body and Blood, while others receive it on specified days; *in one place no day is omitted on which the offering is not made, in another it is made only on Saturday and Sunday*—and any other such matters that may be observed, the whole class of these things has free observances. *Nor [Col. 0065C] is there any better discipline in these matters for a grave and prudent Christian than to act in the way in which he sees the Church act to which he may happen to come.* What is enjoined that is proved to be neither against faith nor against good morals [Note: [Col. 0065] “Is proved to be”: collected editions and Augustine, Maurist edition.] must be regarded indifferently and observed for the sake of the society among whom one lives.

My mother [Note: [Col. 0065D] “My mother”: in this chapter, as also in the following one, many matters have been corrected from Blessed Augustine, and some have also been added. From this point to the end, however, because Blessed Augustine’s words had been suitably reduced to an epitome, nothing has been added.] followed me to Milan [Note: [Col. 0065] Before correction it read: “having followed.”] and found the Church there not fasting on Saturday; she began to be uncertain what she should do. Then I consulted on this matter the man of most blessed memory, Ambrose. He said: “When I come to Rome, I fast on Saturday; when I am at Milan, I do not fast. You likewise, whenever you come to a church, observe its custom, if you do not wish either to be a scandal to anyone or to have anyone be one to you.” When I reported this to my mother, [Col. 0065D] she gladly embraced it.

[Col. 0066A] Second Part. Gratian. This, however, must be understood concerning that custom which is strengthened either by the usage of the universal Church or by the nearness of time. But if diverse customs are introduced according to the variety of times, dispositions, or places, then, when an opportunity is found, they ought rather to be cut away than observed.

Accordingly Augustine writes to Januarius’s inquiries, Epistle CXIX, chapter 19. [Note: [Col. 0065] Ep. 55 (written near the beginning of the fifth century), Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 168; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 206.] C. XII. Things not approved either by authority or by the customs of the whole Church are to be cut away.

All such things as are neither contained in the authority of the holy Scriptures, nor found established in councils of bishops, nor strengthened by the custom of the universal [Note: [Col. 0065] “Of the whole”: Ivo.] Church, but are varied innumerably according to the differing practices of differing [Col. 0066B] places—so that the reasons which people followed in instituting them can scarcely, or never at all, be found—I judge ought, whenever the power is granted, to be cut away without any hesitation. For although it may not even be discovered how they are contrary to faith, nevertheless they oppress religion itself—which the mercy of God intended to be free by means of very few and very manifest sacramental celebrations—with slavish burdens [Note: [Col. 0065] “Oppress it so greatly”: collected editions.], so that the condition of the Jews is more tolerable. For they, although they have not recognized the time of freedom, are nevertheless subjected to legal sacraments [Note: [Col. 0065] “Burdens”: Augustine.], not to human presumptions.

C. XIII. Let all provinces [Note: [Col. 0065] “Provincials”: collected editions.] maintain in chanting the same manner which they have learned the metropolitan see to possess. Likewise from the Eleventh Council of Toledo, chapter 3. [Note: [Col. 0065] Held A.D. 675.—Collection, third part, pt. 2, title 42, c. 2.]

[Col. 0066C] Third Part. Concerning those who, contrary to the Apostle’s [Note: [Col. 0065] Eph. 4:14—“apostolic”: older collected editions, all except Basle.] will, are carried about with every wind of doctrine, *this* holy council has decreed that the citizens of each province [Note: [Col. 0065D] “Citizens of the province”: in a very ancient Lucchese manuscript in the library of the Catholic King, and in the printed councils, the margin reads: “the bishops of the province”; this expression, repeated at the end of this chapter, shows that it is the true reading. Yet in the text of all editions of the councils, and in two Vatican manuscripts, “citizens” is read.] and the rulers of churches, compelled by the authority of the metropolitan see, shall maintain one and the same manner of chanting which they have learned to be instituted in [Note: [Col. 0065] “At”: same editions, except Basle.] the metropolitan see; nor shall they permit themselves to be separated from the metropolitan see by any diversity in any order or office. For it is right that each should take the rules of instruction from the place whence he receives the consecration of honor [Note: [Col. 0065] “Received”: Hispana collection; all older collected editions also use the past tense.], so that, according to the decrees of the elders, the see which is the mother of each one’s priestly dignity may be the teacher of ecclesiastical [Note: [Col. 0065] “Of ecclesiastical dignity or of right instruction”: collected editions except Basle.] reason.

But, with the offices granted to abbots which they are regularly to perform according to the will of their bishop, they may not celebrate the other public offices—that is, Vespers, Matins, or Mass—otherwise than in the principal church. § 1. Whoever violates these decrees shall be deprived of communion for six months and remain under penitential discipline with the metropolitan, to be corrected; so that with him he may both wash away with tears the guilt of his past transgression and diligently learn the necessary instruction concerning the offices. § 2. Under this rule of discipline, therefore, not only shall the metropolitan bind the bishops or [Col. 0068A] priests of his entire province, but the other bishops also shall compel the rulers of churches subject to them to obey these [Note: [Col. 0067] Omitted in the Basle edition—“their”: collected editions.] institutions.

C. XIV. One and the same order is to be observed in morning and evening offices. Likewise from the First Council of Braga, chapter 1. [Note: [Col. 0067] First Council of Braga (Second in Mansi, vol. 9, p. 774), held A.D. 561.]

It pleased [Note: [Col. 0067] Cf. Fourth Council of Toledo, c. 2.] all by common consent that one and the same order of chanting should be maintained in morning and evening offices, and that diverse and private [Note: [Col. 0067] “Diverse and private”: Hispana collection.] customs of monasteries should not be mixed with the ecclesiastical rule [Note: [Col. 0067D] “Nor the monastery”: in the council itself, in the latest Cologne edition, the word “nor” is absent. But in the other editions it reads: “private customs of monasteries shall be mixed with ecclesiastical rules” [Col. 0068D] (i.e., with “nor” omitted).].

## DISTINCTION XIII

[Col. 0067]

[Col. 0067A] GRATIAN.

First Part. No dispensation is allowed against natural law, unless perhaps two evils press so urgently that one of them must necessarily be chosen.

[Col. 0067B] Hence in the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 2, we read. [Note: [Col. 0067] Eighth Council of Toledo, held A.D. 653. Burchard, bk. 12, cc. 29 and 84.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 119; *Decretum*, pt. 12, c. 16.] C. I. Of two evils the lesser is to be chosen.

Although two evils must be avoided with the utmost caution, nevertheless, if the necessity of danger compels one to commit one of them, we ought to decide upon that which is known to bind us with the lesser bond [Note: [Col. 0067] “Return”: in the council in Mansi—“violate rashly”: Hispana collection—“moderate”: Ivo, *Decretum*.—“To be bound”: older collected editions, all with the *Panormia*.]. Let us investigate by the sharpness of pure [Note: [Col. 0067] “Pious”: Hispana collection—“by”: in the council in Mansi.] reason which of these is lighter and which more serious. For when we are compelled to swear falsely, we indeed offend the Creator, but we defile only ourselves. But when we fulfill harmful promises and *proudly* despise God’s commands, we injure our neighbors with impious cruelty and slaughter ourselves with a more cruel sword [Note: [Col. 0067] “With the sword of death”: Hispana collection—the council in Mansi—Ivo—older collected editions.]. There [Note: [Col. 0067] “From there”: collected editions except Basle.] we are destroyed by a double weapon of sins [Note: [Col. 0067] “Are struck”: Hispana collection—in the council in Mansi—“we perish from here”: collected editions except Basle.]; here we are cut down threefold.

[Col. 0067C] C. II. On the same subject. Likewise Gregory in the *Morals*, on Job 40, Book XXXII, chapters 17, 18, 19, and 20.

“The sinews of Leviathan’s testicles are intertwined,” because the arguments of his suggestions are bound together by intricate devices [Note: [Col. 0067] “Devices”: Gregory.], so that they make many people sin in such a way that, if perhaps they desire to flee sin, they cannot escape it without some other snare of sin, and they commit a fault while avoiding [Note: [Col. 0067] “While avoiding some fault”: collected editions except the first Basle, Lyons II–III, and Antwerp.] it; nor can they free themselves from one bond unless they consent to be [Col. 0068A] bound by another [Note: [Col. 0067] “Absolve”: Argentinian, Venetian II, Paris, Lyons I editions.]. We shall show this more clearly if we bring forward examples of this entanglement from human life [Note: [Col. 0067] “Compare”: Gregory.]. And after several intervening passages:

§ 1. Behold, a certain man, while seeking the friendships of this world, binds himself by oath to another man living a life like his own, that he will cover all in silence the secret [Note: [Col. 0067] “Secret crimes”: all collected editions.] deeds of that [Col. 0068B] man. But the man to whom the oath was sworn is discovered to be committing adultery, so that he even attempts to kill the adulteress’s husband. The person who gave the oath comes to his senses and is assailed by conflicting thoughts. He fears to keep the matter silent, lest by silence [Note: [Col. 0067] “By keeping silent”: Lyons II–III and Antwerp editions.] he become an accomplice in both adultery and homicide; and he is afraid to reveal it, lest he bind himself by the guilt of perjury. Thus he is bound by the intertwined sinews of the testicles, because whichever way he turns, he fears that he will not be free from the contamination of transgression.

§ 2. Another man, abandoning everything that belongs to the world and seeking in every respect to break his own will, desires to subject himself to another’s governance. But by an insufficiently careful inquiry he distinguishes poorly the person who ought to preside over him before [Note: [Col. 0067] “Before God”: all editions except those cited.] God. Perhaps the person chosen without judgment, once he has begun to rule, forbids him to do what belongs to God and commands what belongs to the world. The subordinate, therefore, considering both what the sin of disobedience is and what contamination belongs to secular life, fears to obey and fears not to obey: lest, in obeying, he forsake God in God’s commands, or, conversely, in not obeying, despise God in the chosen superior. And below:

§ 3. Another, neglecting to weigh the burden [Note: [Col. 0067] “Honor”: Basle edition.] of ecclesiastical office, ascends to a place of governance by bribes [Col. 0069A]. But because everything eminent in this world is afflicted more by sorrows than it rejoices in honors, while his heart is oppressed by tribulations [Note: [Col. 0069] “Tribulation”: collected editions except Lyons II–III and Antwerp.], he recalls his sin [Note: [Col. 0069] “The sin”: Venetian I–II, new Paris, Lyons I editions.] to mind. He grieves that he came to labor through sin, and, broken by the very difficulty, recognizes how wicked was what he committed [Note: [Col. 0069] The text is undoubtedly corrupt here: Basle edition.]. Therefore, recognizing himself guilty with respect to the bribes expended, he wishes to abandon the place of eminence he has obtained; but he fears that it would be a more serious sin to abandon the care of the flock he has undertaken. He wishes to care for the flock he has undertaken, but fears that it would be a worse sin to possess, by purchase, the offices of pastoral grace [Note: [Col. 0069] “Of the flock”: all collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 0069] “To relinquish than to possess what was purchased”: collected editions except Basle.]. Thus, through ambition for office, he sees himself bound by guilt on either side. For he sees that neither course is without the guilt of sin: whether a flock once undertaken is abandoned, or a sacred office bought in a worldly manner is retained. He fears on every side and dreads every exposed flank: lest, by remaining in the purchased office, he mourn unworthily that he does not amend the matter even by abandoning it [Note: [Col. 0069] “Amend”: at this point the construction of the words in the original seems confused and must be restored from Gratian.], or, indeed, by abandoning the office while striving to bewail one wrong, he again commits another through the very abandonment of the flock. And below:

Second Part. § 4. Yet this is usefully done [Note: [Col. 0069] “Usefully”: Gregory.] to overthrow Behemoth’s wiles: when the mind [Col. 0070A] is hemmed in between lesser and greater sins, if no way of *escaping* altogether without sin lies open, the lesser sins should always be chosen. For one who is shut in on every side by the circuit of walls so that he cannot flee throws himself into flight where he finds the wall lower [Note: [Col. 0069] “Is entered upon”: collected editions except Lyons II–III and Antwerp.]. Thus Paul [Note: [Col. 0069] 1 Cor. 7:2], seeing certain incontinent persons in the Church, allowed lesser things so that they might avoid greater, saying: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife.” And because spouses are then alone without fault in intercourse when they come together not to satisfy lust but to receive offspring, he immediately added, in order to show that even what he had permitted was not without fault, though it was the least fault: “But I say this by way of concession [Note: [Col. 0069] “Understanding”: Basle edition.], not by way of command” [Note: [Col. 0069] 1 Cor. 7:6]. For what is forgiven, not commanded, is not without defect [Col. 0070B]. He plainly saw a sin which he foresaw could [Note: [Col. 0069] “May”: Lyons II–III, Basle; “could”: remaining collected editions.] be forgiven. But when we are constrained in doubtful situations, we usefully submit to the least evils, lest we sin gravely without pardon. § 5. Thus the entanglement of the sinews of this Behemoth is often loosened when one passes to the greatest virtues through lesser faults committed.

## DISTINCTION XIV

[Col. 0069]

[Col. 0069B] GRATIAN.

First Part. But this is to be understood in one and the same person. [Col. 0069C] Whether the same dispensation has a place in different persons—namely, whether we may commit lesser wrongs lest others be entangled in more serious ones—is rightly questioned.

Augustine writes thus on these matters in Book *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 42. [Note: [Col. 0069] Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 9, c. 117.] C. I. We must not commit sins in order that others may not commit more serious ones.

Lot says to the Sodomites [Note: [Col. 0069] Gen. 19:7]: “I have two daughters who have not yet known men; I will bring them out to you. Use them as seems good to you; only do no wrong to these men.” Since he wished to prostitute his daughters by this exchange, so that his male guests might suffer no such thing from the Sodomites, it is rightly asked whether an exchange of shameful acts, or of any sins whatever, is to be admitted—so that we do something evil lest another commit a more serious evil—or whether it should rather be ascribed to Lot’s agitation, not to his deliberation, that he [Col. 0070B] said this. And certainly this exchange is admitted most dangerously. But if it is attributed to human agitation and to a mind disturbed by so great an evil, [Col. 0070C] it is by no means to be imitated.

Second Part. Gratian. The strictness of custom or constitution is sometimes relaxed.

Therefore Pope Leo says to Rusticus, Bishop of Narbonne, Epistle XC, before chapter 1. [Note: [Col. 0069] Ep. 167 (written A.D. 458 or 459), Ballerini edition. Collection, third part, pt. 1, title 43, c. 46. Anselm, bk. 2, c. 73. Ivo, prologue, c. 12.] C. II. Which constitutions may be moderated, and which may not.

Just as there are certain things which cannot be overturned for any reason, so there are many which ought to be moderated either because of the necessity of the times [Note: [Col. 0069] “Circumstances”: Leo; Anselm.] or because of consideration for ages; provided that this principle [Note: [Col. 0069] “Condition”: Leo.] is always observed: in matters which are doubtful or obscure, we must know that what is to be followed is that which is found neither contrary to evangelical commands [Col. 0070D] nor opposed to the decrees of the holy Fathers.

## DISTINCTION XV

[Col. 0071]

[Col. 0071A] GRATIAN.

First Part. Since we have thus far discussed natural law and constitution or custom, setting forth the distinction by which they are mutually distinguished, let us now turn our pen to ecclesiastical constitutions, briefly setting forth their origin and authority insofar as we can gather it from the books of the holy Fathers.

C. I. At what time the canons of general councils began.

The canons [Note: [Col. 0071] Anselm, in the prologue; Ivo, *Panormia*, 1.2, c. 104. In Boehmer, contrary to the evidence of manuscripts and editions, the heading reads: “Pope Leo.”] of general councils (as Isidore says in Book 6 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 16 [Note: [Col. 0071C] This chapter is also found in Isidore’s collection of councils before his preface, but not in the manuscript of the Dominican library; nevertheless, in that manuscript, down to the words “among other things,” it is likewise placed, as in others, before the beginning of the Council of Nicaea.]) began in the time of Constantine. For in the preceding years, while persecution raged, there was no opportunity at all for instructing the peoples. Hence Christianity was divided into diverse heresies [Col. 0071B], because bishops were not permitted to assemble together [Note: [Col. 0071] “To assemble”: Isidore.] until the time of the aforesaid emperor. For he gave Christians the opportunity to gather freely. Under him also the holy Fathers, assembling from the whole world in the Council of Nicaea, handed down a creed, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic faith, as the second creed after the Apostles’.

§ 1. Among the other councils, we know four venerable synods [Note: [Col. 0071] “There are four venerable synods”: older collected editions.] which chiefly encompass the whole faith, like the four Gospels or the same number of rivers of Paradise. § 2. The first [Note: [Col. 0071] “Earlier”: same editions with Anselm.] of these, the Synod of Nicaea, was held under the Emperor Constantine Augustus, with 318 bishops. In it was condemned the blasphemy of Arian perfidy, by which Arius himself asserted the inequality of the holy Trinity; and the same holy synod, through its creed, defined God the Son as consubstantial with God [Col. 0071C] the Father [Note: [Col. 0071] “Of God”: collected editions.]. § 3. The second synod, of 150 Fathers, was assembled at Constantinople under the elder Theodosius. Condemning Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God, it declared the Holy Spirit consubstantial with the Father and the Son, giving the form of the creed which the entire Greek and Latin confession proclaims in the churches.

§ 4. The third synod, the first Ephesian Synod, consisting of 200 bishops, was held under the younger Emperor Theodosius. It condemned Nestorius by a just anathema for asserting two persons in Christ, showing that the one person of our Lord Jesus Christ remains in two natures [Note: [Col. 0071D] “Remains”: in most ancient copies of Gratian and in the printed manuscript of Isidore, the text reads as corrected. But other manuscript and printed copies of Gratian read: “that two natures and one person of our Lord Jesus Christ remain in Christ” [ [Col. 0071] Yet Basle reads as restored by the correctors from Isidore.].]

§ 5. The fourth synod, the Council of Chalcedon, of 630 priests, was held under Emperor Marcian. In it Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, who declared that the Word of God and the flesh were of one nature, was condemned; so also were his defender Dioscorus, formerly bishop of Alexandria, and Nestorius himself again with the remaining heretics, by the single sentence of the Fathers. The same synod proclaimed that Christ the Lord was so born of the Virgin that we confess in him the substance of divine and human nature.

§ 6. These are the four principal synods, proclaiming most fully the doctrine of faith. But any other [Col. 0072B] councils [Note: [Col. 0071] “If there are any other councils”: collected editions; Boehmer.] established by holy Fathers filled with the Spirit of God remain confirmed in all force after the authority of these four; their acts, set down in this work, are contained herein [Note: [Col. 0071] The words “their acts,” etc., are taken from Isidore’s preface to the collection of canons and are absent from Anselm.].

§ 7. *Synod* is interpreted from Greek as “company” or “assembly.” The name *council* [Note: [Col. 0071D] “But the name council”: this passage is corruptly read in Isidore’s *Etymologies*. But in the preface of the same Isidore, prefixed to the Paris edition of the councils and compared with several ancient manuscripts, it reads: “The name council is derived from a common intention, because all direct the gaze of the mind to one point. For the eyelashes are the *cilia* of the eyes; hence those who disagree with one another do not hold a council, because they do not think one thing. An assembly is a meeting or gathering, from *coeundo*, that is, coming together into one; hence it is called a *conventus*, because people come together there. Just as a meeting, assembly, or council is named from the association of many into one.” In Gratian’s manuscripts there are many variations, from which the reading retained was judged better, although perhaps something is still wanting.] is derived from Roman usage. For at the time when cases were argued, all assembled in one place and deliberated with a common purpose. Hence *concilium* (“council”) is said to derive from *communis intentio* (“common intention”), as though *consilium* (“deliberation”); and *consilium* as though *considium*, with the letter *d* changing into *l*. Or *concilium* is said to derive from common intention, because they direct the entire gaze of the mind toward one object. For *cilia* [Note: [Col. 0071] “Eyebrows”: collected editions except Lyons II–III and Antwerp.] are parts of the eyes; hence those who disagree among themselves do not hold a council, because they do not agree in one thing. [Col. 0072C] An assembly (*coetus*) is a meeting or gathering, from *coeundo*, that is, from coming together into one. Hence a meeting (*conventus*) is so called because people gather there into one; and just as an assembly is named from a meeting, so a council is named from the association of many into one [Note: [Col. 0071] “Just as an assembly is called a meeting into one, so also a council.”—“Is called”: Basle.—“Just as a meeting or assembly is called, so it is also named”: Argentinian, Venetian I–II, Nuremberg, Paris, Lyons I.—Lyons II–III and Antwerp read as in the text.—“Just as a meeting, an assembly,” etc.: Anselm.].

Concerning the four councils, Blessed Gregory writes as follows in Book I of the *Register*, Epistle 24. [Note: [Col. 0071] Bk. 1, ep. 25 (written to John, Bishop of Constantinople, and the other Fathers, A.D. 591), Maurist edition—the former canon.] C. II. On the authority of the four councils.

I confess that I receive and venerate the four councils just as I do the four books of the holy Gospel: namely, Nicaea, in which the perverse doctrine of Arius is destroyed; Constantinople, in which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius is refuted; the first Ephesian Council, in which Nestorius’s impiety is judged; and Chalcedon, in which the depravity of Eutyches and Dioscorus is rejected. I embrace them with entire devotion and preserve them with most complete approval, because in them, as upon a square stone, the structure of the holy faith rises, and the rule of every [Col. 0073A] life [Note: [Col. 0073C] In Blessed Gregory the reading is: “And whoever he may be in life and action, if he does not hold their firmness, even if he seems to be a stone, he nevertheless lies outside the building. The fifth,” etc.; and the following passages refer to those Three Chapters on account of which some did not receive the Fifth Synod.] [Note: [Col. 0073] “Common life”: collected editions except Basle.] and action stands.

§ 1. I likewise venerate *equally* the Fifth Council, in which the letter called that of Ibas [Note: [Col. 0073] “There”: same editions except Lyons I–III and Antwerp.] is condemned as full of error; in which Theodore, by separating the person of the mediator of God and men into two substances, is proved to have fallen into the perfidy of impiety; and in which the writings of Theodoret, produced in mad audacity and criticizing the faith of blessed Cyril, are also refuted [Col. 0073B]. I reject all persons whom the aforesaid venerable councils reject, and embrace those whom they venerate. Since they were established by universal consent, whoever presumes either to release those whom they bind [Note: [Col. 0073] “Absolve”: collected editions.] or to bind those whom they release [Note: [Col. 0073] “Bind”: same editions.—“Bind again”: same editions except first Basle.—“Absolve”: collected editions.] destroys himself, not them.

Gelasius likewise writes concerning the same matters in a council held at Rome with seventy bishops, saying: [Note: [Col. 0073] This decree, commonly attributed to Gelasius presiding over the Roman Council (A.D. 494 or 496)—though some consider the whole work apocryphal—is found in Burchard, bk. 3, c. 220 ff.; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, cc. 94 and 123; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 64 ff.; in the capitulary of Atto of Vercelli in D’Achery, c. 100; and partly (§§ 15–18) in Anselm, bk. 2, c. 193 (208). In González’s Hispana collection (at the end of vol. 2), its heading is: “A decretal issued in the city of Rome by Pope Hormisdas concerning the divine Scriptures: what the Catholic Church universally receives, and thereafter what it ought to avoid.” The recension printed in Gratian indeed appears to be Hormisdas’s (cf. Ballerini, edition of the works of Leo the Great, vol. 3, p. CLI). Three recensions are printed in Mansi’s collection of councils. The last, taken from Chifflet’s Jura manuscript, agrees almost with the Hispana collection, except that several items have been corrected in the latter, as will be noted below.—In certain collected editions (Venetian I–II, Basle, Nuremberg), the passage is presented so that after the words *subdenda* (“to be appended”), which conclude the chapter in Ivo, there follows: “Seventieth [Distinction]: concerning the books of the apocrypha, with a new preface prefixed: ‘Likewise, which treatises or books are to be reckoned among the apocrypha, Gelasius himself shows, saying.’” In precisely the same manner, except that *subdenda* is changed to *damnanda* (“to be condemned”), it appears in Leipzig manuscript A.—In the Argentinian edition, the same preface being retained, the words “of which a few,” etc., are transferred to the end of the entire decree, and there follows: “Fiftieth [Distinction].”—In Leipzig manuscript C these words are absent, though the preface is retained; finally, in Leipzig manuscript B everything from §17 onward is absent.] C. III. Which councils the holy Roman Church receives.

The holy Roman Church, after those Scriptures of the Old and New Testament which we receive as canonical, does not forbid these also to be received: the holy Synod of Nicaea, of 318 Fathers, held through the agency of Constantine the Great Augustus, in which the heretic Arius was condemned; the holy Synod of Constantinople, [Col. 0074A] held through the agency of the elder Emperor Theodosius, in which the heretic Macedonius received his deserved condemnation; the holy Ephesian Synod [Note: [Col. 0073] “The first Ephesian [Synod]”: collected editions.], in which Nestorius was condemned with the agreement of Pope Celestine of most blessed memory, through Cyril, bishop of the Alexandrian see, and Arcadius, a bishop sent from Italy; the holy Synod of Chalcedon, held through the agency of Emperor Marcian and Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, in which the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies, together with Dioscorus and his accomplices, were condemned. We also decree and command that any councils established hitherto by holy Fathers, after the authority of these four, are both to be kept and received [Note: [Col. 0073C] “We command”: immediately after this word the Decree of Gelasius continues: “Likewise the treatises of Cyprian,” etc. But Burchard, Ivo, and the *Panormia* have the reading found in Gratian. Certainly throughout this chapter the collections differ from the original in so many ways that it cannot be determined with sufficient certainty what is Gelasius’s true and uncorrupted reading. Nor is it especially surprising if there are some points which cause difficulty. Therefore readings that could safely be corrected with the aid of manuscripts have been corrected; at other places variants have partly been indicated, and partly—because it would have been endless to indicate them all—the task of consulting the books has been left to the careful reader.].

§ 1. It must now be set forth concerning the works of the holy Fathers which are received in the Catholic Church. [Col. 0074B] § 2. The works of blessed Cyprian, martyr and bishop of Carthage. § 3. Likewise, the works of blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. § 4. Likewise, the works of blessed Gregory Nazianzen, bishop. § 5. Likewise, the works of blessed Basil, bishop of Cappadocia. § 6. Likewise, the works of blessed John, bishop of Constantinople. * § 7. Likewise, the works of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria. § 8. Likewise, the works of blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria. * § 9. Likewise, the works of blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers. § 10. Likewise, the works of blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan. § 11. Likewise, the works of blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo. § 12. Likewise, the works of blessed Jerome, presbyter. § 13. Likewise, the works of Prosper, a most devout man. § 14. Likewise, the letter of blessed Pope Leo addressed to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, the text of which [Note: [Col. 0073] “the text of which, or even one iota, if any ignorant person”: the same editions, except Basle.]—if anyone disputes it even to a single iota and does not reverently receive it in every respect—let him be anathema. [Col. 0074C]

§ 15. Likewise, we decree that the works and treatises of all orthodox Fathers who in no respect departed from communion with the holy Roman Church, nor were separated from its faithful [Note: [Col. 0075] “faith or”: Hispana Collection—Burchard.] preaching, but remained, by the grace of God, participants in its communion until the last day of their lives, are to be read [Note: [Col. 0075] “chosen”: Lyons edition III.]. [Col. 0075A] § 16. Likewise, decretal letters which the most blessed Popes at various times issued from the city of Rome in response to consultations of various Fathers are to be received with reverence.

§ 17. Likewise, the acts [Note: [Col. 0075C] “Likewise, the acts”: From here to the end of the chapter, everything is absent from most old manuscripts of Gratian; the Archdeacon also noted this. Yet the material is of the same Gelasius as far as the words “But which books,” and is also reported by Burchard and Ivo immediately after the foregoing.] of holy martyrs, who shine forth through manifold sufferings of torments and wondrous triumphs of confession. Who among Catholics could doubt that they endured very great things in their contests, and bore all things not by their own strength but by God’s grace and help? Yet, according to ancient custom [Note: [Col. 0075] “authority and custom”: editions generally collated.], they are not read in the holy Roman Church with special caution, because the names of those who wrote them are entirely unknown, and because they are thought to have been written by unbelievers or ignorant persons [Note: [Col. 0075] “sayings”: the same editions, with Anselm and Ivo.] with superfluous material, or with matters less suitable than the order of the subject required: as are the passions of a certain Quiricus and Julitta [Note: [Col. 0075] “Julitta, his mother”: Venetian editions I, II, III; Antwerp.], and of Gregory [Note: [Col. 0075] “George”: editions generally collated, except Antwerp.], and others of that kind, which are said to have been written by heretics [Note: [Col. 0075] “are approved”: Paris, Lyons I, II, III, Antwerp.]. Therefore, as has been said, lest even a slight occasion for mockery should arise [Note: [Col. 0075] “a slighter”: editions generally collated.], they are not read in the holy Roman Church. Nevertheless, together with the aforesaid Church, we venerate with every devotion all martyrs and their glorious contests, which are better known to God than to human beings. [Col. 0075B]

§ 18. Likewise, we receive with every honor the Lives of the Fathers—Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits—which, however, the most blessed Jerome wrote. [Col. 0075C] § 19. Likewise, the Acts of blessed Sylvester, bishop of the Apostolic See: although we do not know the name of the person who wrote them, we know that they are read by many Catholics in the city of Rome, and that many churches follow this practice because of its antiquity.

§ 20. Likewise, writings concerning the discovery of the holy cross of the Lord, and other writings concerning the discovery of the head of blessed John the Baptist, are indeed recent revelations [Note: [Col. 0075] “accounts”: Hispana Collection.], and some Catholics read them; but when these have come into Catholic hands [Note: [Col. 0075] “arrived”: Hispana Collection—Basle edition.], the judgment of the blessed Apostle Paul must first be observed: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good” [1 Thess. 5]. [Col. 0076A]

§ 21. Likewise, Rufinus, a devout man, published very many books of ecclesiastical work and also interpreted certain writings; but because blessed Jerome criticized him in some matters concerning freedom of the will, we hold what we know the aforesaid blessed Jerome held; and this applies not only to Rufinus but also to all those whom the man so often mentioned rebuked out of zeal for God and religious concern for the faith.

§ 22. Likewise, we receive for reading certain works of Origen which the most blessed Jerome does not reject; but all the rest, together with their author, we say are to be rejected.

§ 23. Likewise, the Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea and the books of his Ecclesiastical History: although in the first book of his narrative he grew lukewarm, and afterward [Note: [Col. 0075] omitted in Venetian I, II; Lyons I, II, III; Paris; Antwerp.] wrote one book in praise and defense of the schismatic Origen, nevertheless, because of the exceptional knowledge of events which contributes to instruction, we do not say that they are to be rejected altogether. [Col. 0076B]

§ 24. Likewise, we commend Orosius, a most learned man, because he composed for us a history very necessary [Note: [Col. 0075] “necessary”: editions generally collated.] against the calumnies of pagans, and wove it together with remarkable brevity.

§ 25. Likewise, we praise with distinguished commendation [Note: [Col. 0075] “prefer”: original text.] the Paschal work of the venerable Sedulius, which he composed in heroic [Note: [Col. 0075] “heretical”: Venetian editions I, II.] verse.

§ 26. Likewise, we do not despise the no less laborious work of Juvencus [Note: [Col. 0076C] “Juvencus”: Earlier the text read, “Vincent.” The true reading has been restored from Gelasius, Burchard, and Ivo. Blessed Jerome mentions this Juvencus in his catalogue.], but admire it [Note: [Col. 0075] “imitate it”: editions generally collated.].

§ 27. But [Note: [Col. 0075] “the rest”: Hispana Collection.] whatever has been written or preached by heretics or schismatics the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church in no way receives. We believe that a few examples which have come to mind, and which Catholics must avoid, ought to be appended [Note: [Col. 0075] Earlier it read: “we have decreed”—“we decree”: Basle edition.] below. [Col. 0076C]

§ 28. First [Note: [Col. 0075] Burchard, book 3, ch. 121; Ivo, Panormia, book 2, ch. 123; Decree, part 4, ch. 65.], we confess that the Synod of Rimini, convened by the Emperor Constantius, son of Constantine, through the agency of Taurus the prefect, has from that time, now, and for eternity been condemned.

§ 29. Likewise, the itinerary in the name of the Apostle Peter, called that of Saint Clement, in eight books [Note: [Col. 0075] “nine”: Hispana Collection.], is apocryphal.

§ 30. The Acts in the name of the Apostle Andrew are apocryphal.

§ 31. The Acts in the name of the Apostle Philip are apocryphal.

§ 32. The Acts in the name of the Apostle Peter are apocryphal.

§ 33. The Acts in the name of the Apostle Thomas are apocryphal. [Note: [Col. 0075] The Hispana Collection adds: “The Gospel in the name of Matthias, apocryphal; the Gospel in the name of Barnabas, apocryphal; the Gospel in the name of James the Less, apocryphal;” and, with Basle: “the Gospel in the name of Peter, apocryphal.”]

§ 34. The Gospel in the name of Thaddaeus is apocryphal.

§ 35. The Gospel in the name of the Apostle Thomas, which the Manichaeans use, is apocryphal.

§ 36. The Gospel in the name of [Col. 0077A] Barnabas is apocryphal.

§ 37. The Gospel in the name of the Apostle Bartholomew is apocryphal.

§ 38. The Gospel in the name of the Apostle Andrew is apocryphal.

§ 39. The Gospels falsified by Lucian are apocryphal.

§ 40. The Gospels falsified by Hyrcius [Note: [Col. 0077] “Hesychius”: Hispana Collection—“Ysicius”: Burchard—“Ysius”: Ivo—“Ylius,” and later § repeated in error: “Ithicius”: Basle—“Iricius”: Argentinensis.] are apocryphal.

§ 41. The book On the Infancy of the Savior is apocryphal.

§ 42. The book on the Nativity of the Savior, and on Saint [Note: [Col. 0077C] “On Saint Mary”: the Isidorian collection reads: “and on Mary and the midwife.” In Burchard: “and on Mary, or the midwife.” In Ivo: “and on Saint Mary, or on the Savior’s midwife.”] Mary, and [Note: [Col. 0077] “or”: Hispana Collection—editions generally collated, except Lyons.] on the Savior’s midwife, is apocryphal.

§ 43. The book called *The Shepherd* is apocryphal.

§ 44. All books made by Lenticius [Note: [Col. 0077] “Leucius”: Hispana Collection, Burchard, Ivo—“Lucius”: Mansi—“Euticius”: Basle edition.], disciple of the devil, are apocryphal.

§ 45. The book called *The Foundation* is apocryphal.

§ 46. The book called *The Treasure* is apocryphal.

§ 47. The book called *On the Daughters of Adam*, or [Note: [Col. 0077] “leptogenesis”: Mansi—“added to Genesis”: Hispana Collection—“Adam’s Genesis”: Burchard—“or Genesis”: editions generally collated.] *Genesis*, is apocryphal.

§ 48. The cento [Note: [Col. 0077] “Cento”: Hispana Collection—“Pentameter”: editions generally collated.] concerning Christ, put together from Virgilian verses, is apocryphal. [Col. 0077B]

§ 49. The book called *The Acts of Thecla and the Apostle Paul* is apocryphal.

§ 50. The book called *Nepos* [Note: [Col. 0077] Earlier it read: “Lepotius”—“Netipous”: Basle.] is apocryphal.

§ 51. The Book of Proverbs written [Note: [Col. 0077] “copied”: editions generally collated.] by heretics and marked with the name of Saint Xystus is apocryphal.

§ 52. The Revelation called that of the Apostle Paul is apocryphal.

§ 53. The Revelation called that of the Apostle Thomas is apocryphal.

§ 54. The Revelation called that of Stephen is apocryphal.

§ 55. The book called the *Passing* [Note: [Col. 0077] *Transitus*, that is, assumption: Hispana Collection—Antwerp edition.] of Saint Mary is apocryphal.

§ 56. The book called the *Penitence of Adam* is apocryphal.

§ 57. The book in the name of Ogias [Note: [Col. 0077] “Ugias”: Hispana Collection—older editions and Burchard give the name “Diogenes”—“Diogias”: Basle—“Diogenias”: Ivo.], the giant who, according to heretics, fought with a dragon after the flood, is apocryphal.

§ 58. The book called the *Testament of Jacob* [Note: [Col. 0077] “Job”: Hispana Collection—Burchard, Ivo—editions generally collated, Paris and Antwerp, add from a gloss: “otherwise, Jacob.”] is apocryphal.

§ 59. The book called the [Col. 0077C] *Penitence of Origen* is apocryphal.

§ 60. The book called the *Penitence of Saint Cyprian* is apocryphal.

§ 61. The book called the *Penitence of Jamnis* [Note: [Col. 0077] “Jamna”: editions generally collated.] and Mambres is apocryphal.

§ 62. The book called the *Lots* [Note: [Col. 0077] “Lot”: the same editions.] of the Apostles is apocryphal.

§ 63. The book [Col. 0078A] of Lusana [Note: [Col. 0077] “Praise of the Apostles”: Mansi—“Lusa of the Apostles”: Burchard—“Law of the Apostles”: Hispana Collection, so that the authors of the canon seem to have had in mind the Constitutions of the Apostles, themselves apocryphal.] is apocryphal.

§ 64. The book of the Canons of the Apostles is apocryphal.

§ 65. The book *Physiologus*, written by heretics and falsely marked with the name of blessed Ambrose, is apocryphal.

§ 66. The History of Eusebius Pamphilus is apocryphal.

§ 67. The works of Tertullian [Note: [Col. 0077] “The works of Tertullian are apocryphal. The works of Lactantius, or Africanus, are apocryphal”: Hispana Collection.] or Africanus are apocryphal.

§ 68. The works of Postumianus [Note: [Col. 0077] “Geminianus”: Argentinensis edition—“Jovinianus”: the remaining earlier editions, Basle.] and Gallus are apocryphal.

§ 69. The works of Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla are apocryphal.

§ 70. All works of Faustus the Manichaean are apocryphal. [Note: [Col. 0077] The Hispana Collection adds: “The works of Commodian are apocryphal”; and after § 71: “the works of Tasc[?] Cyprian, Arnobius, and Ticonius are apocryphal.”]

§ 71. The works of the other Clement of Alexandria are apocryphal.

§ 72. The works of Cassian, presbyter of Gaul, are apocryphal.

§ 73. The works of Victorinus [Note: [Col. 0077] Earlier the text read “Victor,” and later, in § 74, “Faustinus of Riez.” Yet the identity of Victorinus of Poitiers is not sufficiently certain; the reading apparently ought to be *Pitabiensis* (or *Petabionensis*), a view also accepted by Mansi. Thus it is also read in the expanded Dionysian collection, in Amort, *Elem.*, vol. 2. Petavium is situated on the River Drava in Moravia.] of Poitiers are apocryphal.

§ 74. The works of Faustus of Riez in Gaul are apocryphal.

§ 75. The works of Frumentius [Note: [Col. 0077] “Frumentius the blind”: Hispana Collection—“Frumenticius”: editions generally collated, except Basle.] are apocryphal.

§ 76. The letter of Jesus to King Abgar [Col. 0078B] [Note: [Col. 0077] “Abagar”: editions generally collated—the word “king” is also absent in the Hispana Collection, though it occurs in Ivo and Burchard.] is apocryphal. [Note: [Col. 0077] The Hispana Collection continues: “The letter of Abgar to Jesus, apocryphal.”]

§ 77. The Passion of George [Note: [Col. 0077] “Gregory”: Paris edition.] is apocryphal.

§ 78. The Passion of Cyricus and Julitta [Note: [Col. 0077] “Vilicta”: Basle edition.] is apocryphal.

§ 79. The writing called the *Contradiction* [Note: [Col. 0077] “Prohibition”: Hispana Collection.] of Solomon is apocryphal.

§ 80. All phylacteries which are written not by the craft of angels [Note: [Col. 0077] “by an angel, as they invent, but rather by a demon”: editions generally collated.] but rather of demons are apocryphal.

§ 81. These and all things similar to them, which Simon Magus, Nicolaus, Cerinthus [Note: [Col. 0077] “Cherindus”: Basle edition—“Thervidus”: remaining editions. The name of Photinus, absent from editions generally collated, occurs in Burchard.], Marcion, Basilides, Ebion, Paul of Samosata, Photinus, Bonosus, and those who fell away through like error; likewise Montanus with his most obscene followers; Apollinaris [Note: [Col. 0077] “Apollinaris Valentinus”: Hispana Collection.], Valentinus or Manichaeus, Faustus [Note: [Col. 0077] “Faustus Africanus”: the same collection.], Sabellius, Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, Novatus, Sabbatius, Coelestius [Note: [Col. 0077] “Callixtus”: the same collection—editions generally collated, in which a little later Eustachius and Jubianus are named.], Donatus, Eustathius, Jovinianus, Pelagius, Julianus and [Note: [Col. 0077] “Julianus of Edessa”: Burchard—“of Celaenae”: Hispana Collection.] Latiensis, Coelestinus, [Col. 0078C] Maximinus, Priscianus [Note: [Col. 0077] “Priscillianus”: the same collection and editions generally collated, in which shortly afterward one reads “Lampedius”—in the former text follows: “Nestorius of Constantinople, Maximus the Cynic,” etc.] from Spain, Lampedius, Dioscorus, Eutyches, Peter and another Peter—one of whom stained Alexandria, the other Antioch—Acacius of Constantinople with his associates, and also all heresies [Note: [Col. 0077] “heresiarchs”: Hispana Collection.] which [Note: [Col. 0080C] “On Psalm LIV”: Thus also in Ivo. In the Roman Order, in the chapter on the divine offices from the Lord’s Supper until the octave of Pentecost, and in Burchard, one reads: “on Psalm 63,” namely, “Hear my prayer, O God, when I make supplication.” Likewise, in the chapter on the order for the night of Preparation: “Three [readings] from Saint Augustine’s treatise on Psalm 63.”] they and their disciples or schismatics taught or wrote, whose names are by no means retained [Note: [Col. 0079] “we have retained”: Hispana Collection—“we revere”: Argentinensis—“we retain”: remaining editions generally collated.], we confess to have been not only repudiated but even removed from every Roman and Apostolic Church, and, together with their authors and the followers of those authors, condemned for eternity under the indissoluble bond of anathema. [Col. 0079A]

§ 82. Furthermore [Note: [Col. 0079C] “Furthermore”: From here to the end this material is found neither in the Isidorian collection nor in any old manuscript of Gratian that has been collated. Yet from the words “In Septuagesima they appoint” onward, it is reported by Burchard and Ivo without an author’s name, and in the Panormia as from Gelasius himself together with seventy bishops. Nearly all of it, however, is found scattered through the book called the *Roman Order*.], we have judged it worthy of notice which books some read in ecclesiastical offices throughout the yearly [Note: [Col. 0079] The entire § 82 is absent both from Burchard and Ivo and from the Argentinensis, Venetian I and II, and Nuremberg editions, and from Leipzig manuscripts A, B, and C. The author of this portion of the canon is uncertain, although Antonio Agustín testified that he had found it in a book of Amalarius. Similar material, however, is read in the *Micrologus on the Office of the Mass*, a manuscript preserved in the Pauline Library at Leipzig (no. 608), and in a certain treatise found at the end of a manuscript codex of Ivo’s abridged Decree: *Order of Readings in the Matins Office through the Cycle [of the Year], and Their Reasons* (Pauline Library 955), apparently excerpted from the *Micrologus*, but closely distinct from Gratian’s words.] cycle, because the Apostolic Church does not disapprove that rite but follows it, for the edification of the faithful.

Some [Note: [Col. 0079] Burchard, book 3, ch. 222; Ivo, Panormia, book 2, ch. 90; Decree, part 4, ch. 63.] appoint the Pentateuch [Note: [Col. 0079C] “Pentateuch”: In Ivo one reads “Heptateuch,” so as to include beyond the five books also the books of Joshua and Judges; blessed Jerome uses this word and grouping of books in writing to Lucinius. Others call it the *Heptaticum*, as Saint Gregory does in book 7, indiction 2, letter 48, and book 10, letter 22, and elsewhere; likewise Rabanus in his preface to Jeremiah, and the *Roman Order*, chapter on Septuagesima.] in Septuagesima until the fifteenth [Note: [Col. 0079] “tenth”: Basle—“eleventh”: remaining editions generally collated.] day before Easter; on the fifteenth day they appoint Jeremiah until the Lord’s Supper. At the Lord’s Supper they read three lessons from the Lamentation of Jeremiah [Lam. 1]: “How does the city sit solitary,” etc.; and [Col. 0079B] three from Saint Augustine’s treatise on Psalm LIV: “Hear my prayer, O God, and do not despise” [Note: [Col. 0079] “supplication”: editions generally collated, except the earlier Basle and Lyons I.]; and three from the Apostle, where he says in the letter to the Corinthians [1 Cor. 11:10]: “When you come together in one place.” The second lesson begins thus [Luke 22:20]: “Likewise also the cup after he had supped,” etc. The third [1 Cor. 12:1]: “Now concerning spiritual matters, we do not wish [Note: [Col. 0079] “I do not wish”: editions generally collated, with the Vulgate—except the earlier Basle.] you to be ignorant, brethren.”

On Preparation Day, there are three lessons from the Lamentation of Jeremiah; and three from Saint Augustine’s treatise on Psalm LXIII: “Hear my prayer, O God, when I make supplication” [Note: [Col. 0079] “supplication”: editions generally collated.]; and three from the Apostle, where he says in the letter to the Hebrews [Heb. 4:11]: “Let us hasten to enter into that rest,” etc. The second lesson [Heb. 5:1]: “For every high priest.” The third [ibid., v. 11]: “Of whom we have much to say.”

On Holy Saturday there are three lessons from the Lamentation of Jeremiah the prophet [Col. 0079C] and three from Saint Augustine’s treatise on the same Psalm LXIII: “Hear my prayer, O God, when I make supplication”; and three from the Apostle, where he says in the letter to the Hebrews [Heb. 9:11]: “Christ, having appeared as high priest of the good things to come.” [Col. 0080A] The second lesson [ibid., v. 16]: “For where there is a testament.” The third [ibid., 10:1]: “For the law, having a shadow of the good things to come.”

At the Lord’s Easter, homilies appropriate to that day; during the week, homilies. In the octaves [Note: [Col. 0080C] “In the octaves”: That the eighth day itself was customarily designated by the plural expression, that is, “octaves,” will be noted below, *On Consecration*, distinction 3, chapter *pronunciandum*.] of Easter they appoint the Acts of the Apostles, the Catholic Epistles, and the Apocalypse, until the octave of Pentecost. In the octave of Pentecost they appoint the books of Kings and Chronicles until the Kalends of August. On the first Sunday of August they appoint Solomon until the Kalends of September. On the first Sunday of September they appoint Job, Tobit [Note: [Col. 0079] “to Judith”: Ivo.], Esther, and Ezra until the Kalends of October. On the first Sunday of October they appoint the book [Note: [Col. 0079] “books”: Ivo.] of Maccabees until the Kalends of November. On the first Sunday of November they appoint Ezekiel [Col. 0080B] and Daniel and the minor prophets until the Kalends of December. On the first Sunday of December they appoint the prophet Isaiah until the Nativity of the Lord.

At the Nativity [Note: [Col. 0080C] “At the Nativity of the Lord”: Burchard and Ivo read, “on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord,” and so does the *Roman Order*, in the chapter entitled: “In the name of Christ begins the order of the Catholic books which are appointed in the Roman Church.” The Panormia, however, agrees with Gratian.] of the Lord, they first read three lessons from Isaiah. The first lesson [Isa. 9:1]: “At the first time the land of Zebulun was lightened,” etc. The second [ibid., 40:1]: “Comfort, comfort.” The third [ibid., 52:1]: “Arise, arise” [Note: [Col. 0079] adds “Jerusalem”: Venetian I, Paris, Lyons I, II, III, Antwerp.]. Then sermons or homilies appropriate to that day are read. On the feast of Saint Stephen, a homily on that day; likewise on the feast of Saint John; likewise on the feast of the Innocents; likewise on the feast of Saint Sylvester. On the octave of the Nativity of the Lord, a homily on that day. On the first Sunday after the Nativity of the Lord, they appoint the letters of Paul until Septuagesima.

At Epiphany, three lessons from Isaiah. The first lesson begins [Col. 0080C]: “All [Note: [Col. 0079] Isa. 55:1.] who thirst.” The second [ibid., 60:1]: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem.” The third [ibid., 61:10]: “Rejoicing, I will rejoice in the Lord.” Then sermons or homilies appropriate to that day are read.

## DISTINCTION XVI

[Col. 0081]

[Col. 0081A] **GRATIAN**

**Part I.** The Canons of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0081] The same things are read in the prologue to Anselm’s Collection; similar material also occurs in Berthold of Constance’s treatise *On the Authority of the Canons*, § 28 (ed. 1792).], said by some to have been translated by Clement, bishop of Rome [Note: [Col. 0081C] “Translated”: In the heading prefixed to the Canons of the Apostles in the Isidorian collection and in the council of Pope Stephen IV—of which Cardinal Deusdedit reports a large part in his collection of canons—the word “promulgated” occurs instead of “translated.” Dionysius Exiguus certainly makes no mention of this translation; and some writers customarily cite the letters of Clement in this manner: “From the sayings of the Apostle Peter, promulgated through Clement,” as does the author of Polycarpus and others.], number fifty.

Isidore writes that these are not to be received but reckoned among the apocrypha, saying:

### C. I. The Canons of the Apostles are rejected by apostolic authority.

The canons [Note: [Col. 0081C] This chapter occurs in Isidore’s preface to the collection of councils which was copied from the library of the Church of Toledo and sent to Rome. For in the preface to the common Isidorian collection, discussed at the beginning, the opposite rather seems to be said; it is cited below, chapter *Placuit*, in this same distinction, if indeed the author is the same Isidore.] which are called those of the Apostles, because neither the Apostolic See received them nor the holy Fathers gave them assent [Note: [Col. 0081] “consent”: Hispana Collection.], are known to have been composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles. Although useful things are found in them, nevertheless it is clear that by canonical and apostolic authority their acts have been removed and reckoned among the apocrypha. [Col. 0081B] [Note: [Col. 0081] “reckoned”: Hispana Collection.]

But Zephyrinus writes otherwise to the bishops established throughout Sicily, Letter I [Note: [Col. 0081] Pseudo-Isidorian Letter— Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, ch. 105; *Decree*, part 4, ch. 107; Polycarpus, book 3, title 10.]:

### C. II. The Canons of the Apostles are to be received.

The Apostles prescribed [Note: [Col. 0081] “set before”: original—Ivo.] sixty [Note: [Col. 0081C] “Sixty”: Ivo and the author of the Panormia also have “sixty”; likewise the original in the margin. But in the text: “seventy.” Polycarpus: “fifty.”] decisions, with many [Note: [Col. 0081] “very many”: original—Ivo—editions generally collated.] other bishops, and judged that they were to be observed.

### C. III. Except for fifty chapters, the Canons of the Apostles are reckoned among the apocrypha. Likewise, Pope Leo IX against the letter of Abbot Nicetas. [Note: [Col. 0081D] “Likewise Leo”: This chapter was taken from Humbert, legate of Leo IX, in his response [dated A.D. 1054; Note: [Col. 0081]] to the booklet [Col. 0082C] issued by Nicetas, presbyter and monk, against the Latins. It survives in manuscript at Rome in the monastery of Santa Maria Nuova and in many private libraries. Leo IX could properly be cited, since Humbert, legate of the Apostolic See, wrote these things by his authority and command. Note: [Col. 0081] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, ch. 124; *Decree*, part 4, ch. 105.]

The Fathers number Clement’s book—that is, the itinerary of the Apostle Peter—and the Canons of the Apostles among the [Col. 0082A] apocrypha, except for fifty chapters, which they decreed ought to be added to the rules [Note: [Col. 0081] “to orthodox rules”: Ivo.] of orthodox faith [Note: [Col. 0081] adds “expounders”: Lyons edition I; “expounders”: II, III.].

### C. IV. Likewise, the Sixth Synod, chapter 2. [Note: [Col. 0081] From canon 2 of the Quinisext Synod, held A.D. 692, though with some alteration of meaning—cf. below in this same distinction, c. 7. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, ch. 125; *Decree*, part 4, ch. 106.]

It pleased this holy synod that from this time the eighty-five chapters of the Canons of the Apostles should be confirmed and valid.

**A letter of Isidore at the head of the Canons.** [Note: [Col. 0082C] “Letter”: Ivo calls this letter the preface to the work of canons; it is the one prefixed under Isidore’s name to the volumes of councils, although certain words are lacking in the older edition, in which the earlier Isidorian collection occurs. This chapter was made up from two passages of that preface. The words “Because of their authority,” etc., through the word “constitutions,” occur not far from the beginning; the remainder occurs at the end. Note: [Col. 0081] From the preface to the Pseudo-Isidorian collection, whose wording the author altered from the prefaces of both Dionysius and Isidore of Spain—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, ch. 125; *Decree*, part 4, ch. 107.]

Isidore [Note: [Col. 0082C] “Isidore, servant”: In the Panormia it stands in the same way as in Gratian. § 1. Likewise, below:

§ 2. First, indeed, as has been said, an order for holding a council [Col. 0082B] is inserted; and afterward a compendium is interwoven [Note: [Col. 0081] “has been interwoven”: editions generally collated—Böhmer.] in its proper order of the Canons of the Apostles, the decrees of the early Apostolic [Note: [Col. 0081] omitted in editions generally collated, except the earlier Basle.] [Fathers]—that is, from Saint Clement to Saint Sylvester—and of various councils.

**Gratian.** Moreover, since Pope Hadrian receives the Sixth Synod with all its canons, and since the holy eight universal councils have been confirmed by the profession of the Roman Pontiff, while in the Sixth Synod [Note: [Col. 0081] “the seventh synod, or in the sixth council”: Argentinensis edition.]—or in the Seventh Council—the Canons of the Apostles were received and approved, it is evident that they are not to be reckoned among the apocrypha.

### C. V. The Sixth Synod is strengthened by Hadrian’s authority.

I receive the holy Sixth Synod with all its canons.

[Note: [Col. 0083B] “The Sixth”: This occurs in the second session of the Seventh Synod, in Hadrian’s letter to Tarasius. But in that passage Hadrian reports the words of the synodal letter Tarasius had sent to him. Gratian here does not report the actual words of Hadrian’s letter; for in the translation of Anastasius the Librarian it reads thus: “We find, moreover, in the aforesaid synodal letter of your Holiness, after the fullness of faith and confession of the sacred creed, a miracle most worthy of praise and veneration concerning all six holy synods and concerning sacred and venerable images. Therefore I also receive those same six holy synods with all the rules which they rightly and divinely promulgated.” These final words indeed also occur in that very letter of Tarasius, as is plainly evident from the Greek council and the new translation.]

**Gratian.** But there is doubt whether it composed canons; this is readily resolved from the fourth session of the Sixth [Note: [Col. 0083C] “Sixth”: In the second and third Vatican manuscripts: “sixth,” elsewhere “seventh.” It is in fact the seventh, but nothing has been changed because of the gloss. Note: [Col. 0083] The Basle edition adds from the gloss: “or, it is the seventh.”] Synod.

For Peter [Note: [Col. 0083] Ivo, *Decree*, part 4, ch. 121.], bishop [Note: [Col. 0083] “to the bishop”: older editions generally collated, except Basle.] of Nicomedia, says:

### C. VI. The Sixth Synod composed canons.

I have a book [Note: [Col. 0083C] “I have a book”: These are the words of Peter, bishop of Nicomedia, and Tarasius, patriarch of Constantinople, in the fourth session of the Seventh Synod. They spoke of the one hundred and two canons issued in the Trullo under Justinian Rhinotmetus in the second year of his restoration to the empire. Yet Tarasius’s very words show that these canons are not proper to the Sixth Synod, because he acknowledges that they were issued four or five years after that synod had ended; and at that time it is most certain that neither the same Roman Pontiff nor the same bishops were present. Nevertheless, in this chronological matter one should rather believe the most diligent chronologists—Theophanes, whose words relevant to this place, translated fairly faithfully from the original Greek preserved in the Vatican Library, are read in Franciscus Turrianus, *On the Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Synod*; Anastasius; and George Cedrenus—than Tarasius. For they state that not four or five years, as Tarasius says, but twenty-seven [Col. 0084B] years intervened from the end of the Sixth Synod held in the time of Agatho to the issue of these decrees.

The address of those bishops to the emperor itself testifies that the bishops who issued these canons did not wish to issue them as canons of the Sixth Synod, but wished to supply what seemed to be wanting in the Fifth and Sixth Synods. Therefore this assembly of bishops must be called a new one; consequently, as Balsamon writes, the Greeks call it πενθ᾽ ἕκτην, that is, the “fifth-sixth” synod. Moreover, that not all those [Col. 0084C] canons were received by the Roman Church is plainly testified by two men highly learned in ecclesiastical matters: Anastasius the Librarian and Humbert, legate of Leo IX.

Humbert indeed says in these words: “I am not surprised that you attribute to Pope Agatho and to the holy Fathers of the Sixth Synod your absurdities and the chapters which you have either corrupted or fabricated, when you even attribute fabrications to the Lord Jesus himself and his Apostles. Therefore, knowing that the Sixth Synod was convened to destroy the heresy of the Greek Monothelites, and not to hand down new constitutions to the Romans, we wholly reject the chapters which you append to us under its authority, because the first and Apostolic See has neither ever accepted them nor observes them to this day.”

Anastasius, moreover, wrote thus in the preface to the Seventh Synod, addressed to John VIII, Roman Pontiff: “Therefore the principal See admits the rules which the Greeks maintain were issued in the Sixth Synod only so far that none of those rules are received which are found contrary to earlier canons, to decrees of the holy pontiffs of this See, [Col. 0084D] or indeed to good morals; although all these rules remain entirely unknown among the Latins to this day because they have not been translated. Nor are they found in the archives of the other patriarchal sees, although they use the Greek language; evidently because when they were issued, none of those sees was found either promulgating, assenting, or even present, although the Greeks maintain that they were promulgated by the same Fathers who were present at the Sixth Synod. Yet they can prove this by no evidence.”]

I have a book containing the canons of the holy Sixth Synod. The Patriarch said:

§ 1. Some are scandalized through ignorance concerning these canons, saying: “Did the Sixth Synod make canons?” Let them therefore know that the holy Sixth Synod was convened under Constantine against those who said that there was one operation and one will in Christ; in it the holy Fathers anathematized them as heretics [Note: [Col. 0083] “as being”: editions generally collated—Böhmer.] and expounded the orthodox faith.

[Col. 0084A] Part II, §2. The synod was dissolved in the fourteenth year of Constantine. But four or five years later the same holy Fathers assembled under Justinian, Constantine’s son, and promulgated the aforesaid canons, concerning which no one should doubt. For the bishops who had been present in the synod under Constantine were the very same men who subscribed these canons under Justinian. It was fitting that an ecumenical synod should promulgate ecclesiastical canons. Likewise [Note: [Col. 0083] From Act 6 of the Second Council of Nicaea]: §3. After the holy Sixth Synod had promulgated its definition against the Monothelites, the Emperor Constantine, who had convened it, died not long afterward, and his son Justinian reigned in his place. §4. The same holy synod, inspired by God, assembled again at Constantinople in the fourth or fifth year and promulgated 102 canons [Note: [Col. 0083] 202, editions cited in the margin.] for the correction of the Church.

Gratian. From these things, therefore, it is inferred that the Sixth Synod met twice: first under Constantine and enacted no canons; secondly under Justinian his son and promulgated the aforementioned canons.

[Col. 0085A] Hence the holy Fathers, assembled for the second time in the same synod, said:

C. IX. On the dates of the councils.

The Sixth Ecumenical Synod was held at Constantinople and composed in the Greek language, in the time of Pope Agatho, under the direction *and presidency* of the most devout Emperor Constantine within his palace, with the legates of the Apostolic See and 150 bishops sitting together.

§1. For the First Ecumenical [Note: [Col. 0085] “probable”: Lyons editions I and II.] Synod was assembled at Nicaea against Arius, consisting of 318 Fathers, in the time of Pope Julius [Note: [Col. 0085] “Silverius”: Basel edition.] and under the Emperor Constantine.

[Note: [Col. 0086D] “Julius”: It is certain that the First Nicene Synod was held in the time of Sylvester. But amid that obscurity of chronology it is not surprising that Bede and others erred.]

§2. The Second, of 150 Fathers, was held at Constantinople against Macedonius and Eudoxius, in the time of [Col. 0087A] Pope Damasus and the Emperor Gratian, when Nectarius was ordained bishop of that city [Note: [Col. 0087] “of the same city”: editions cited in the margin.].

§4. The Fourth was at Chalcedon, of 630 Fathers, under Pope Leo, in the time of the Emperor Marcian, against Eutyches, head of the most wicked monks.

§5. The Fifth [Note: [Col. 0087] *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 111.] was likewise at Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0087] “in the Constantinopolitan [synod]”: Argentinensis edition; “in the city of Constantinople”: the remaining cited editions.], in the time of Pope Vigilius [Note: [Col. 0087] “Julius”: editions cited in the margin; Panormia.], under the Emperor Justinian, against Theodore and all heretics.

C. X. [Note: [Col. 0087] In Merlin’s collection of councils, an enlarged recension of the Pseudo-Isidorian collection, this chapter bears the following title: “On the principal synods: in what places, for what causes, at what times, and under what authorities they were held.”—In Anselm’s preface, after the words “Of the Apostles,” etc. (which appear under Gratian’s name at the beginning of this distinction), occurs the heading: “Likewise, an account of the canons of the Apostles and of the six principal synods.”]

§2. The Seventh [Note: [Col. 0090C] “The Seventh”: Here only the one Carthaginian synod contained in the codex of canons is counted, of which Distinction 20, chapter *De libellis*, will speak below.] was the Carthaginian, in which 217 Fathers established thirty-three canons, whose chief author was Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, is also said to have been present in that synod, in the time of the Emperor Honorius.

§7. The Eighth was the African council under the Emperor Theodosius the Younger, in which 217 Fathers [Note: [Col. 0089] “214”: D’Achery and Merlin.] recited and confirmed 105 canons, said to have been written in various councils of the African province in the time of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage.

§8. The Ninth was the Council of Arles, in [Col. 0090B] which 200 Fathers [Note: [Col. 0089] Both numbers are absent from Merlin’s Isidore.] established four canons, whose chief authors were Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, and Saint Marinus [Note: [Col. 0089] “Maurinus”: editions cited in the margin.] bishop of Arles, in the time of the Emperor Constantine, as some maintain.

§9. The Tenth was likewise at Arles, in which nineteen Fathers established canons, whose chief author was Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles [Note: [Col. 0089] Added: “in the time of the Emperor Constantine”: same source.].

§10. The Eleventh was likewise at Arles, in which [Col. 0091A] sixteen Fathers [Note: [Col. 0091] “Eighteen”: D’Achery.] established canons.
