§11. The Twelfth was likewise at Arles, at the Vicus Hortensius [Note: [Col. 0091] “Hortensicus”: Basel edition; “Hortensius”: remaining cited editions.], in which eleven Fathers established canons, whose chief author was Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles.

§12. The Thirteenth was likewise at Arles, in which nineteen Fathers established canons, whose chief author was Sarpidius [Note: [Col. 0091] “Sapardus”: Merlin and D’Achery; “Larpedius”: Argentinensis edition; “Lapidius”: Norimberga edition.] bishop of Arles.

§13. The Fourteenth was the Council of Orange, in which sixteen Fathers [Note: [Col. 0091] “Seventeen”: Berthold.] established canons, whose chief author was Bishop Hilary.

§14. The Fifteenth was the Council of Epaone [Note: [Col. 0091C] “Epaone”: Thus corrected from several manuscripts and the Vatican collection of Isidore. It previously read “Empanensis.” Nevertheless, no Caesarius is named in the printed Council of Epaone; Avitus is mentioned first.] [Note: [Col. 0091] “Hyponensis”: Basel edition; “Empanensis”: remaining editions; the whole section is absent from Merlin.], in which twenty-six Fathers [Note: [Col. 0091] “Twenty-seven,” and afterward “sixty”: D’Achery.] established thirty-nine canons, whose chief author was Bishop Caesarius.

§15. The Sixteenth was the Council of Agde, in which twenty-nine Fathers [Note: [Col. 0091] “Thirty-four”: Merlin and D’Achery; “twenty-four”: Berthold.] established canons, whose chief author was Bishop Caesarius [Note: [Col. 0091] “of Arles”: editions cited in the margin; “Gozasius”: Berthold.].

§16. The Seventeenth [Col. 0091B] [Note: [Col. 0091C] “The Seventeenth”: Here three councils of Orléans are counted, for which the following indications occur in the printed councils. At the Fifth Council of Orléans, Aurelius of Arles signs in the first place. At the First, among others, the name of Melanius of Rennes is read. At the Third, Albinus, bishop [Col. 0091D] of Angers, signs in fourth place.] was the Council of Orléans, in which seventy-two Fathers established canons, whose chief author was Aurelius [Note: [Col. 0091] “Aurelianus”: editions cited in the margin; Argentinensis edition: “Melanius of Rennes,” otherwise “Aurelius of Arles.”] bishop of Arles, *in the time of King Clovis.*

§17. The Eighteenth was likewise at Orléans, in which thirty-one Fathers established canons, whose chief author was Melanius [Note: [Col. 0091] “Melianus”: same editions.] bishop of Rennes.

§18. The Nineteenth was likewise at Orléans, in which thirty Fathers [Note: [Col. 0091] “Twenty-five”: D’Achery.] established canons, whose chief author was Saint Albinus, bishop of Angers.

§19. The Twentieth was the Council of Clermont, in which fifteen Fathers established canons, whose chief author was Honoratus, bishop of Breutes [Note: [Col. 0091] “Brevitensis”: D’Achery; “Brelitensis”: cited editions, first Paris.].

§20. The Twenty-first was the Council of Mâcon, in which twenty-one Fathers established canons, whose chief author was Priscus, bishop of Lyons.

§21. The Twenty-second [Col. 0091C] was likewise at Mâcon, in which eighty-six Fathers [Note: [Col. 0091] “Sixty-four”: D’Achery.] established canons, whose chief author was the same Priscus, bishop of Lyons.

§22. The Twenty-third was the Council of Lyons, in which eighteen Fathers [Note: [Col. 0091] “Fourteen”: same source.] [Col. 0092A] established canons, whose chief author was Philippus, bishop of Vienne [Note: [Col. 0091] “of Menes”: Argentinensis and Paris editions.].

§23. The Twenty-fourth was likewise at Lyons, in which twenty Fathers established canons, whose chief author was the same Priscus, bishop of Lyons.

But that the Nicene Synod is said above to have established twenty canons seems contrary to what is found in Athanasius’s letter. For Athanasius [Note: [Col. 0091] Pseudo-Isidorian letter of Anastasius and the bishops of Egypt to Pope Mark—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 106; *Decree*, part 4, ch. 108; Anselm, bk. 1, chs. 59–60; Polycarpus, bk. 3, tit. 20.], bishop of Alexandria, writes to Pope Mark as follows:

C. XII. Letter of Athanasius requesting the chapters of the Nicene Council.

We desire to receive, through these present legates, by the authority of your holy see, the seventy chapters of the Nicene Council—those which, by command of my lord Alexander and by decree [Note: [Col. 0091] “Decrees”: editions cited in the margin.] of all the bishops, I brought from the aforesaid synod—which were burned by fire.

§1. In our presence, eighty [Note: [Col. 0091] “Seventy,” and shortly afterward “thirty”: same editions.] chapters were discussed in the aforementioned synod: forty issued by Greeks in the Greek language, and forty by Latins likewise issued in the Latin language. But it seemed good to the 318 bishops [Note: [Col. 0091] “Fathers”: original.] filled with the Holy Spirit—especially to the already mentioned Alexander and to the envoys of the Apostolic See—that ten chapters should be combined, while the others should be inserted in suitable places; and that, after the pattern of the seventy disciples, or of the languages of the entire world, there should be seventy chapters of so great and excellent a council, to instruct the whole Christian world.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] “Seventy”: These words of Athanasius establish that not all the canons of the Nicene Synod are now extant, either in Greek or Latin. Pope Julius, in writing to the Easterners, Innocent to Victricius, and others cite many canons from it which are not among the twenty in general circulation. Isidore writes on this matter [Col. 0092C] in the preface inserted in the volumes of councils. A certain letter of Gregory X to the king of Armenia, when he had summoned the Council of Lyons—preserved in manuscript by Cardinal Sirleto—indicates that the entire Nicene Council existed at that time in Armenian. Thus he writes: “Since it is in many ways advantageous that, during the celebration of the same council, we should have a collection of the ancient councils, we earnestly request and exhort Your Royal Highness to send to us, as quickly as you can, the complete Nicene Council and the other councils which you say you possess, in Armenian script, [Col. 0092D] together with some skilled interpreters.” Eighty canons written in Arabic under the name of this council have also been found at Tunis and Alexandria; they are held at Rome by the same Cardinal Sirleto in Arabic and Armenian and have recently been translated and printed in Latin.]

Gratian. How, then, is it said that only twenty chapters were established in the Nicene Synod, when seventy chapters, as Athanasius writes, are shown to have been established there? The answer is this: some chapters of the Nicene Synod have fallen into disuse; only twenty are held in the Roman Church.

[Note: [Col. 0093] “said”: editions cited in the margin, together with Panormia.]

[Col. 0093A] Hence Pope Stephen writes to Luythobius, bishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0093] The author of this chapter—sought in vain with Boehmer among the acts of the Roman council of A.D. 765—appears to be Stephen V. For in his time Luitbert of Mainz (thus, rather than the name Humbert found in manuscripts, it seems one should read) presided over the Council of Mainz in A.D. 888.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 107; *Decree*, part 4, ch. 232.]:

C. XIII. Only twenty chapters of the Nicene Council are extant.

Only twenty [Note: [Col. 0093C] In Ivo, part 4, ch. 232, this chapter occurs in a fuller form: “We do not doubt that the chapters of the Nicene Council, seventy in number according to the testimony of Athanasius, were written in the figure of the seventy disciples; of these only twenty are in the holy Roman Church,” and what follows.] chapters of the Nicene Synod are held in the holy Roman Church; but through what neglect the others have disappeared is uncertain. Very many think that they were inserted into the Council of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0093] “uncertain”: Lyons I.].

The Sardican Council also is received by authority of Pope Nicholas. Thus he writes to the clergy [Note: [Col. 0093] Rather, to Photius of Constantinople, A.D. 862, whom Ivo correctly cites: *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 117; *Decree*, part 4, ch. 135.] of Constantinople:

C. XIV. The Sardican Council is received by apostolic authority.

[Col. 0094A] Your statement that you possess neither the Sardican Council nor other decretals [Note: [Col. 0093] “decretal letters”: Ivo.] of the holy pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0093] “holy Fathers, nor receive”: editions cited in the margin; “pontiffs and priests, nor receive”: Panormia; “sacred pontiffs, nor receive”: Decree.] is not readily believed by us, especially since the Sardican Council was held among you in your regions and is received by the whole Church: how can it be appropriate [Note: [Col. 0093] “is appropriate”: editions cited in the margin.] that the holy Church of Constantinople should reject it and fail to retain it as is fitting [Note: [Col. 0093] “receive it”: editions cited in the margin.]?

## DISTINCTION XVII

[Col. 0093]

[Col. 0093A] GRATIAN.

Part I. It has been shown above at what times the general councils were held, and whose authority prevails over the authorities of the other saints. But the authority to convene councils belongs to the Apostolic See.

Hence Pope Marcellus writes to Maxentius [Note: [Col. 0093C] “Maxentius”: It formerly read “to Maxentius, bishop”; but in the volumes of councils the letter’s superscription is “to Maxentius the tyrant,” while at the beginning of the letter itself stands “Marcellus to Maxentius,” a reading thought worth retaining.] [Note: [Col. 0093] Pseudo-Isidorian Letter II to Maxentius the tyrant, whose source in this chapter is the *Tripartite History*, bk. 4, ch. 9; bk. 5, ch. 34. Compare Council of Sardica, ch. 5; Anselm, bk. 2, ch. 60; Ivo, *Decree*, part 4, ch. 240; Polycarpus, bk. 1, tit. 13.]:

C. I. A synod ought not to be assembled without the authority of the Roman Pontiff.

You cannot lawfully hold a synod of bishops without the authority of this holy see, although you may be able to gather certain bishops.

[PALEA.]

“Nor [Note: [Col. 0093C] “Nor”: From here to the end these words are absent from [Col. 0094C] certain manuscript copies of Gratian.] may you condemn any bishop who has appealed to this Apostolic See before a definitive judgment has issued from here. For if laypersons use written appeals in public courts, how much more is it permitted to priests to do the same, since they are above those persons? Of them it has been said: ‘I said, you are gods’ [Note: [Col. 0093] Psalm 81.]?”

[Col. 0094A] C. II. A council not supported by the authority of the Roman Church is not valid. Likewise Pope Julius I, in his reply against the Easterners on behalf of Athanasius. C. XXIX [Note: [Col. 0093] Pseudo-Isidorian letter. Compare Ennodius, Letter 20, bk. 1; *Tripartite History*, bk. 10, ch. 17; bk. 4, chs. 9 and 19.—Anselm, bk. 2, ch. 47 (46); Polycarpus, bk. 1, tit. 13.].

Your rule has no force and cannot have any, because this council was neither conducted by orthodox bishops [Col. 0094B] nor attended by a legate [Note: [Col. 0093] “delegation”: original; Anselm; Basel edition.] of the Roman Church; for the canons command that councils must not be held without its authority. Nor is, nor ever shall be, any council valid which has not been supported by its authority.

C. III. Let no one usurp what has been granted to the Roman Church. Likewise Pope Damasus I, Letter IV to Stephen [Note: [Col. 0093] A spurious letter, nevertheless composed before the time of Pseudo-Isidore.—Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 55; Polycarpus, bk. 1, tit. 17.].

Let no one presume, without consulting it, to usurp what has been granted to this see alone, if he does not wish to be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honour as a despiser [Note: [Col. 0093] Absent from Anselm’s collection and from the Argentinensis and Basel editions.] [Note: [Col. 0093] “or”: editions cited in the margin, except Basel.].

### C. IV. Without the authority of the Apostolic See, no one may convene a particular synod against a universal one. Likewise Gregory.

[Note: Gregory: This is undoubtedly Pelagius’s, as it is cited by Anselm and Ivo. In Gratian there are many chapters from Pelagius concerning this subject: that recourse must be had to the apostolic sees when lower bishops or any others desire to ascertain what has been established in some universal synod; and that those who do not communicate with the apostolic sees are very severely to be condemned—such as Causa 23, question 5, chapter *Non vos*, and the chapter *De Liguribus*. From the present chapter comes “nor was it permitted,” and from the chapter *Istud*, Causa 11, question 1. There is preserved there the complete letter of Pelagius, as Anselm reports it.

But Polycarpus cites it under Gregory’s name, with the marginal addition: “To the bishops of Mauritania.” Moreover, among the chapter summaries in the Pope’s own Dictatus, found in Book II of the Register of Gregory VII, occurs this proposition among others: that no general synod ought to be called without the command of the supreme pontiff.]

[Note: Rather, Pelagius I, Letter to Narses; the same material is found in the fragment of Pelagius’s letter to the patrician Valerian, from Holstenius’s collection, printed in Mansi, vol. IX, p. 732. This is also the heading of the chapter in Ivo, *Decree*, part 4, chapter 239.—In Anselm, book 12, chapter 43, it is cited as Pelagius’s; in Polycarpus, book 1, title 14, as Gregory’s.—In the Basel edition it reads: “Pope Gregory to Constantinople.”]

It was never permitted to anyone, nor will it be permitted, to convene a particular [Col. 0095A] synod [Note: *Synod*: In Anselm, Ivo, and Polycarpus the following is added: “to judge a universal synod.” This is what Pelagius prohibits here. At that time many people, either through ignorance or perversity of mind, refused to accept the Fifth Council—on which matter St. Gregory often speaks, especially in Book VII, Letter 53 [Col. 0096C]—and preferred a particular synod to a universal one and to the authority of the apostolic sees. Thus in this chapter Pelagius, or Gregory, does not prohibit bishops from convening diocesan synods or metropolitans from convening provincial synods; rather, he prohibits their assembling such synods in order to judge a universal synod. [Col. 0096D] The rubric has accordingly been corrected.] But whenever any doubt concerning a universal synod arises for anyone, then, in order to receive an explanation of what they do not understand, either those who desire the salvation of their souls should voluntarily approach the Apostolic [Note: *apostolic sees*: Ivo; Holstenius.] See to obtain an explanation; or, if perhaps—as it is written concerning such persons: “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises” [Note: Proverbs 12:2.]—they prove so obstinate and contumacious that they refuse to be taught, they must by all means be drawn toward salvation by those same apostolic sees, or else—lest they become the ruin of others—be restrained, in accordance with the canons, by secular [Note: *oppressed*: Anselm.—“must be oppressed”: the other collected editions.] powers.

[Col. 0095B] ### C. V. It is not a council but a conventicle that is held without the authority of the Apostolic See. Likewise Pope Pelagius II, to the bishops who had assembled at the unlawful summons of John of Constantinople, Letter I, chapter 1.

[Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian letter.—Anselm, book 2, chapter 36. Polycarpus, book 1, title 14.]

We are repeatedly instructed by many [Note: Added: “ways,” Basel edition.] apostolic, canonical, and ecclesiastical rules that councils ought not to be held without the judgment of the Roman pontiff. [Note: The same words occur in the decretals of Julius, chapter 9, Causa 3, question 6; in these matters the author seems to have followed what is read in the *Tripartite History*, book 4, chapters 9 and 19, translated from Socrates’s Greek.]

§ 1. Therefore, as has already been said, your assembly or little conventicle is rightly annulled—not a council—and whatever was done in it is regarded as void and without force. Henceforth, you yourselves should see that, at no one’s urging, you presume to do such things, if you do not wish to lack communion with the Apostolic See. And below [Note: Chapter 3; cf. Council of Antioch, canon 14; Chalcedon, canons 9 and 17; and Innocent I, Letter 2.]:

§ 2. But if questions arise in any province, and disagreement begins among the bishops of that province itself, and the dissentients cannot agree among themselves, the matters should then be referred to a higher see. If they cannot there be readily and justly decided, they are to be judged canonically and justly wherever a synod has been regularly convened. Greater and more difficult questions, however—as the holy synod has decreed and blessed custom requires—are always to be referred to the Apostolic See.

### C. VI. Provincial councils have no weight without the presence of the Roman pontiff. Likewise Pope Symmachus.

[Note: *will lack*: the other collected editions.]

[Note: Rather, from Ennodius’s apologetic tract on behalf of the Fourth Roman Synod, held in 501.—Anselm, book 2, chapter 56 [55].—Ivo, *Decree*, part 4, chapter 242. Polycarpus, book 1, title 7.]

Councils of priests, decreed annually [Col. 0096A] throughout the provinces by ecclesiastical laws, have lost their efficacy because they do not have the Pope’s presence. [Note: *They have lost*: In Ennodius’s tract, recent editions here have a question mark. For these are the words of Symmachus’s enemies, raising this as though it were an absurdity. Ennodius answers them in the following words: “Read,” etc.] Have you read, you utterly mad persons, that anything was ever established in them apart from the sanction of the apostolic summit, and that, if anything concerning more important matters occurred, it was not reserved for consultation [Note: *conference*: the original.] to the judgment of the aforesaid See?

## Part II. Gratian

[Note: These materials, presented by Isidore Merlin among the acts of the Fourth Roman Synod—his third, held in 501—are found complete in Anselm’s collection, book 3, chapter 105.]

Accordingly, when the authority of King Theodoric had ordered priests from various provinces to assemble in the city of Rome, so that the holy council might judge concerning the accusations said to have been brought by his adversaries against the venerable Pope Symmachus, bishop of the Apostolic See, the bishops of Liguria, Aemilia, and Venetia declared that the man said to have been [Note: *was being judged*: Merlin.] attacked ought himself to convene the synod. They knew that [Col. 0096B] to his See the merit of Peter, the first Apostle, and thereafter the Lord’s command, had granted, by the authority of venerable councils, a unique power in the churches; and that the bishop of the aforesaid See was not subject to the judgment of inferiors. And below:

§ 1. To this the most serene king, with God inspiring him, replied that it was for synodal judgment to prescribe what course should be followed in so important a matter; that nothing in ecclesiastical affairs belonged to him except reverence; and he entrusted the decision to the authority of the pontiffs, that, whether they wished to hear the proposed case or not, they should determine what they thought more useful—provided that, through the care of the venerable council, peace should be given in the city of Rome [Note: Added: “to all Christians,” in Merlin and Mansi.]

But the bishops sitting in synod, assembled by the authority of that same Symmachus, said: “Pope Symmachus, bishop of the Apostolic See, having been attacked by accusations of this sort [Note: *propositions*: those editions.], is, so far as human beings are concerned, immune and free; his entire case we reserve to the judgment of God.” And below:

§ 2. “Concerning the clergy of the aforesaid Pope, who departed from their bishop before the proper time contrary to the rules and made a schism, we decree that this be done: those who make satisfaction to their bishop are to obtain mercy and are to rejoice in being restored to ecclesiastical offices.” [Note: In those editions: “that mercy may follow those who make satisfaction to him.”]

There also follows:

§ 3. “I, Laurentius, [Note: Held in 332 [commonly 341].—Burchard, book 1, chapter 44.—Ivo, from Dionysius’s version, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 15; *Decree*, part 5, chapter 154.—Polycarpus, book 3, title 19.] [Col. 0097A] bishop of the church of Milan, subscribed to this our decree, in which we have committed the entire case to God’s judgment.” [Note: *subscribed*: Böhm.] Peter, bishop of the church of Ravenna, subscribed under the same words, and after him seventy-five bishops.

That determination concerning the clergy is recognized as having been made mercifully and by dispensation, in order to restore peace in the City. § 4. This too should be noted: in this council and in another synod of Pope Symmachus, the bishop of Milan is recorded as having subscribed and answered before the bishop of Ravenna; from this it is inferred that he had precedence of rank over him.

[Col. 0098A] ### C. VII. For Gregory I says, Book VII of the Register, Letter 112, to Syagrius, bishop of Autun:

[Note: Letter 108, book 9, written in 599, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 134 [131].]

We decree that bishops, whether in taking their seats in council, in subscribing, or in any other matter, shall observe their places according to the time of their ordination and claim for themselves the prerogative of their respective ranks.

Gratian: But the time of ordination relates not to churches but to persons, as is clearly apparent from the practice of the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church and of the bishops of every province.

# DISTINCTION XVIII

[Col. 0097]

[Col. 0097B] ## GRATIAN

Thus bishops’ councils, as appears from the foregoing, are invalid for defining and establishing matters, but not for correcting them. Bishops’ councils are necessary for exhortation and correction; although they do not possess the force of legislation, they nevertheless possess authority to impose and enjoin what has otherwise been established and commanded to be observed, either generally or specially.

### C. I. PALEA. From the Council of Chalon, chapter 6.

[Note: In a very ancient manuscript of Gratian this *Palea* occurs at the end of the preceding distinction, where it agrees with that distinction’s final chapter, “Bishops.” The other collectors also cite it from Chalon; but it is found in the First Council of Braga, canon 24, and agrees with canon 13 of the Council of Milevis and canon 53 of the African Council.]

[Note: Rather, from the First Council of Braga, held in 561, canon 6.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 55. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 20; *Decree*, part 5, chapter 165.]

“It has pleased us that, while preserving the primacy of the metropolitan, the other bishops, according to the time of their ordination, shall yield place to one another [Note: Added: “in sitting,” Spanish Collection and Ivo.—“to one sitting”: Basel edition, where, more correctly it seems, this chapter is placed at the end of the preceding distinction.].”

[Col. 0097C] Hence Leo I, Letter LXXXII, chapter 7, to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica [Note: Letter 14, chapter 7, written in 446, Ballerini edition.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 43. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 13; *Decree*, part 4, chapter 241. Polycarpus, book 3, title 15.]:

### C. II. Two assemblies shall be held by bishops each year.

Concerning episcopal councils, we prescribe nothing other than what the holy Fathers have beneficially ordained: namely, that two assemblies be held in each year, in which judgment is given concerning all complaints that ordinarily arise among the various ranks of the Church. But [Note: *and*: Spanish Collection, Ivo, and the other collected editions.] if a case concerning more serious sins should arise among those who themselves preside—which may it never happen—and it cannot be decided by provincial examination, the metropolitan shall take care to inform Your Fraternity of the entire nature of the affair; and, if after the parties have been brought before you the matter has not been settled by your [Note: *your*, and shortly afterward, *recognition*: Basel edition.] judgment, whatever it may be shall be transferred to our cognizance.

### C. III. At what time councils of bishops are to be held. Likewise from the Council of Nicaea, chapter 5.

[Note: Held in 325.—Polycarpus, book 3, title 19.]

Let a council be held once before the days of Lent, so that, with every resentment removed, the pure [Note: *Pure*: This chapter follows the version used by Isidore. Yet at this point it reads: “a pure and solemn gift to God,” as it does in Polycarpus and some manuscripts of Gratian: “a pure and solemn gift to God.” The Greek is: Ἵνα πάσης μικροψυχίας ἀναιρουμένης τὸ δῶρον καθαρὸν προσφέρηται τῷ θεῷ, that is, “that, every narrowness of spirit having been removed, a pure gift may be offered to God.”] fast and solemn offering to God may be made; the second is to be held about the time of autumn.

[Col. 0098C] ### C. IV. For the correction of morals and the settlement of disputes, an episcopal council shall be held twice yearly. Likewise from the Council of Antioch, canon 20.

For ecclesiastical causes and the settlement of disputes that arise, it has seemed sufficient that a council of bishops be held twice a year in every province: once, indeed, after the third week of the Paschal feast [Note: *solemnity*: the other collected editions.], so that the council may be completed in the fourth week following—that is, in the middle [Note: *That is, in the middle*: Formerly it was read: “and in the middle of the time between Easter and Pentecost” [though in the Basel edition it is read as restored here]; and not much differently in Ivo: “that is, in the middle of the time,” etc. But this reading has been restored from most manuscripts of Gratian and from Isidore’s collection, which has this same version. The other collectors seem rather to have followed Dionysius’s version found in the code of canons. Yet Burchard and the *Panormia* here have “that is, in the middle of Pentecost,” or “in mid-Pentecost,” where Dionysius’s version reads: “so that [the council be held] in the fourth week of Pentecost,” word for word. For the Greek is: Ὥστε τῇ τετάρτῃ ἑβδομάδι τῆς πεντηκοστῆς, “so that in the fourth week of Pentecost.”] of Pentecost. [Note: *May be completed*: Dionysius translates ἐπιτελεῖσθαι as “may assemble.”] Those bishops who live in the larger—that is, metropolitan—cities shall summon their fellow-provincial [Col. 0099A] bishops.

§ 1. The second council shall be held on the Ides of October; this day is found to be the tenth day of the month Hyperberetaeus among the Greeks. [Note: *Hyperbericus*: Basel edition; *Hyperberiti*: Venice editions I and II; *Hyperberiti*: Norimberga edition.]

[Note: *Tenth*: Precisely from the Greek. Dionysius, however, whom Burchard and Ivo follow, reads: “on the Ides of October,” that is, the fifteenth day of October, which the Greeks call Hyperberetaeus. Yet in Apostolic Canon 37 it is read that the second synod of the year is to be held ὑπερβερεταίου δωδεκάτῃ, that is, “on the twelfth day of Hyperberetaeus.” That the Latin months do not entirely correspond to the Greek ones is sufficiently certain. Suidas indeed writes that among the Macedonians Hyperberetaeus is the same as October; Galen of Pergamum, however, says it is the same as September.]

At these councils, presbyters and deacons also ought to be present, together with all who consider themselves injured, and they should await the synodal judgment. Nor may anyone hold councils privately, without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishops [Note: Added: “and consent,” in the other collected editions, first Basel edition, and Böhm.], to whom judgment in all causes is known to be entrusted.

### C. V. Those summoned to a synod who scorn to attend accuse themselves. Likewise from the Council of Laodicea, chapter 40.

[Note: Council of Laodicea, held between 347 and 381.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 47. Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 157, from Dionysius’s version.]

[Col. 0099B] Bishops summoned to a synod must not disdain [Note: Added: “to come,” in the other collected editions and first Basel edition.] to attend, but ought to go [Note: *depart*: Spanish Collection.] and either teach or be taught what is useful for correcting the Church and the rest. If they despise this, they appear to accuse themselves—unless perhaps they cannot go because of *illness*.

### C. VI. Bishops summoned to a council who scorn to come are to be reproved. Likewise from the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 19.

[Note: Council of Chalcedon, held in 451.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 199. Ivo, *Decree*, part 4, chapter 243.]

It has reached our ears that the appointed [Note: *established*: Spanish Collection.] councils of bishops are not being held in the provinces. This [Note: *This is proved from the fact*: In Isidore’s collection, which otherwise seems to have the same version, it reads: “it is proved from this fact that many …” [thus indeed in Isidore Merlin; but the Spanish Collection reads “are held, and that,” etc.]. Ivo likewise adds the particle “and.” The Greek is: Καὶ ἐκ τούτου πολλὰ παραμελεῖται τῶν διορθώσεως δεομένων ἐκκλησιαστικῶν πραγμάτων, that is, “and consequently many ecclesiastical matters requiring correction are neglected.”] is shown by the fact that many ecclesiastical matters requiring correction are neglected.

Therefore this holy synod decrees, according to the rules of the Fathers, that bishops in every province assemble twice yearly in one place, where each matter [Note: *Where each matter*: Thus in Isidore’s collection, and in Ivo and Anselm. The Greek is: Ἔνθα ἂν ὁ τῆς μητροπόλεως ἐπίσκοπος δοκιμάσῃ, καὶ διορθοῦν ἕκαστα τὰ ἀνακύπτοντα, which Dionysius translates: “where the metropolitan bishop shall judge fit, and [there] correct each matter, should any perhaps arise.”] that arises may be corrected.

§ 1. Those bishops appointed in their cities who refuse to assemble, especially while enjoying bodily health [Note: *are in health*: Spanish Collection.—“are enjoying health”: the other collected editions.] and free from every other pressing necessity [Note: Absent from the Spanish Collection, Isidore Merlin, and Ivo.] and unavoidable [Col. 0100A] business, may be reproved by admonitions of brotherly love.

### C. VII. A metropolitan who neglects to hold a council at least once yearly is subject to canonical penalties. Likewise from the Seventh Synod, chapter 6.

[Note: Second Council of Nicaea, held in 787.—Version of Anastasius the Librarian.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 373.]

## Part II

Since there is a rule stating that regular inquiries ought to be made twice yearly through a gathering of bishops in every province [Note: Cf. above, this distinction, chapter 4; below, chapter 15.], the holy Fathers of the Sixth Synod, on account of fatigue [Note: *fatigues*: the other collected editions.] and so that those who must assemble might be suitably [Note: *And suitably*: The Greek is καὶ τὸ ἐνδεῶς ἔχειν πρὸς ὁδοιπορίαν, that is, “and because they are not well equipped for making a journey.”] prepared to travel, determined—removing every excuse—that it should by all means be done once a year, and that what is corrupt be corrected. We too renew this canon. If any ruler is found to hinder this, let him be deprived of communion. But if any [Col. 0100B] metropolitan neglects to do this without necessity, compulsion, or some reasonable cause, let him be subject to canonical penalties.

While the synod is engaged upon canonical and evangelical matters, the assembled bishops ought to devote themselves to meditation and careful concern for keeping the divine and life-giving commandments of the Lord. And after a few words:

§ 1. Further, a metropolitan shall not have permission to demand from the things which a bishop brings with him either a beast of burden or any other [Note: *some other*: those editions.] kind of property. Whoever [Note: *Who*: Basel edition.] is convicted of having done this shall pay fourfold.

### C. VIII. Presbyters are not to be compelled to bring *eulogiae* to holy councils. Likewise Leo IV to the bishops of Britain, chapter 3.

[Note: This letter is preserved in manuscript at Rome, as stated in the index.]

[Note: Letter written about 850.—Three-Part Collection, part 1, title 60, chapter 5.]

We find that our predecessors determined nothing concerning the bringing of *eulogiae*—blessed gifts—to holy councils; rather, it is left as each presbyter sees fit. For if it were decreed that gifts of blessing be brought at that time [Note: The other collected editions, except the first Basel edition: “that something be brought to him at the time of blessing.”], perhaps they would come less willingly to synods and would be more reluctant to attend. In my judgment, such things should not be demanded as a matter of right, nor should they be rejected when freely offered.

[Col. 0101A] ### C. IX. Without serious necessity, a bishop is not to delay going to a synod. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 21.

[Note: The canons contained under the name of the Fourth Council of Carthage, held in 398, in Isidore’s collection cannot in any way be attributed to that council; indeed, the Ballerini have observed that they are nothing but certain summaries of ancient canons. Our chapter is found as no. 9 among the *Ancient Statutes of the Church* published by them.—Three-Part Collection, part 2, title 18, chapter 70. Anselm, book 7, chapter 170.]

A bishop must not delay going to a synod unless prevented by a sufficiently serious necessity; yet he must send a representative in his stead, who is to accept, without prejudice to the truth of the faith, whatever the synod decrees. [Note: Burchard, book 1, chapter 51, and Polycarpus, book 2, title 16, from Felix, report a similar opinion in nearly the same words.]

### C. X. Those burdened by impediments and unable to attend a synod must send letters of excuse. Likewise from the Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 10.

[Note: Fifth Council of Carthage, held in 401.—Three-Part Collection, part 2, title 19, chapter 10. Anselm, book 7, chapter 188.]

It has pleased us that whenever a council must be assembled, bishops who are hindered neither by age [Note: The words “neither by age” are absent from the Spanish Collection, but occur in Isidore Merlin.] nor illness nor any other more serious necessity should attend in due course. And below:

§ 1. If they cannot attend, they shall set down their excuses in writing [Note: *In writing*: In the printed councils this reads: “in a *tractoria*” [though in the Spanish Collection *tractoria* occurs as a variant reading].

There has been doubt whether it ought to read “in a *tractoria*.” The letters by which emperors or [Col. 0101C] kings summoned their governors, or granted a travel authorization, were called *tractoriae*. Thus Book 8, title 6, of the Theodosian Code is entitled “Concerning *tractoriae* and stationing-orders”; and so it seems that Book 12 of the Code should be corrected, although the printed editions read “concerning *tractatoria*.” Charlemagne used the word *tractoria*, with the same meaning, in his Capitularies, book 4, chapters 30 and 69, and it has the same sense in the Council of Meaux, chapter 71. St. Augustine likewise uses *tractoria* for a summons-letter in his book *After the Conference against the Donatists*, chapter 24: “Thus they were summoned by their primate through a *tractoria*.” In this canon, where the subject is the summoning of bishops to a council, the term would be especially apt.

For in the African Council inserted in the Code of Canons, canon 43, where the same matter occurs, and canon 57, § “Lucianus,” and § “Alypius,” the ancient manuscripts always read *tractoria*, where the printed editions have *tractatoria*; and in the Greek Carthaginian Council, canon 91, the word is ἡ συνοδική, “the synodal letter.” Yet the same Blessed Augustine [Col. 0101D] uses the term *tractatoria* in the statement that follows. Speaking in Letter 162 of bishops who, when summoned, had refused to come to a council and clear themselves there of accusations, he says: “If they do not do this, their wickedness and perversity will become known there also; and when a *tractatoria* concerning their names has been sent throughout the whole world, wherever the Church of Christ has now spread [Col. 0102B], their communion will be cut off by all churches.” The same word also occurs four times in his second sermon on Psalm 36; and the letter of Siricius read in the Council of Telepte is there called a *tractatoria*. Mentioning it, Innocent says in his letter to Exsuperius of Toulouse, chapter 1: “The clear admonitions of Bishop Siricius, a man of blessed memory, have reached us concerning these matters.” By these words he seems to indicate that Siricius’s *tractatoria* was sent not to African bishops alone but to all provinces. Thus Pope Leo II, after the Sixth Ecumenical Council had ended, sent to the bishops of Spain a short summary of that council for their subscription, calling it a *tractatoria*. Manuscript letters of Leo II were sent from Spain to Rome.] [Col. 0101B] unless, however, [Note: *Unless, however*: The original reads: “or if, after the arrival of the *tractatoria*, certain necessities should perhaps suddenly arise, unless they give their primate an account of the hindrance, they ought to be excluded from the Church’s communion” [“content” in the Spanish Collection]. The remainder is the same in African Council, canon 43; but its ending is nearly as in Gratian: “they ought to be content with the communion of their own church.” Likewise in the Greek Council of Carthage: Ὀφείλειν τοὺς τοιούτους τῇ κοινωνίᾳ τῆς ἰδίας αὐτῶν ἀρκεῖσθαι ἐκκλησίας, “such persons ought to be content with the communion of their own church.” A somewhat similar penalty is imposed in the same council below, Distinction 58, final chapter.] they give their primate an account of their impediment, they must be content with communion in their own church.

### C. XI. PALEA. Likewise from the Council of Tours, chapter 2.

[Note: This *Palea* is absent only from those manuscripts in which very few *Paleae* are found. Gratian repeats it below, Causa 18, question 2, after the final canon, from the same Council of Tours; as do Burchard and Ivo.]

[Note: Burchard, book 8, chapter 73. Ivo, *Decree*, part 7, chapter 91. This chapter is not found among the canons of the councils of Tours, and it seems that Burchard, whose custom this is, borrowed it from Theodore’s Penitential, chapter 2.]

“A bishop must not compel an abbot to go to a synod unless some reasonable cause exists.”

[Col. 0102A] ### C. XII. One who has scorned to attend a synod is to be excluded from communion. Likewise from the Council of Arles, chapter 19.

[Note: Held no later than 460, unless it is some private collection of ancient canons, as the Ballerini maintain.—Three-Part Collection, part 1, title 47, chapters 1–2. Burchard, book 1, chapter 50. Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 160, from the Council of Seville, chapter 10. Polycarpus, book 2, title 15.]

If anyone neglects to attend a synod, or thinks that the assembly of brethren ought to be abandoned before the council is dissolved, let him know that he is excluded [Note: *alienated*: original and Basel edition.] from the communion of the brethren. He may not be received back unless he has been absolved at the following synod.

### C. XIII. Until the next synod, one summoned by the metropolitan who, without serious necessity, neglects to attend the synod is to abstain from communion. Likewise from the Council of Agde, chapter 35.

[Note: Held in 506.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 49. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 17; *Decree*, part 5, chapter 159.]

If a metropolitan bishop sends letters to his fellow-provincial bishops, inviting them to a synod by order of the supreme pontiff, they must, setting aside everything else—except serious bodily illness or a royal command—not delay to be present on the appointed day. If they are absent, then, as the ancient authority of the canons has decreed [Note: Cf. chapter 12 of this distinction.], they shall until the next synod be deprived of the charity of their brethren and of ecclesiastical communion.

[Col. 0103A] ### C. XIV. A bishop summoned to a synod by the metropolitan who scorns to come is to be deprived of communion. Likewise from the Council of Tarragona, chapter 6.

[Note: Held in 516.]

If any bishop, warned by the metropolitan to attend a synod, scorns to come when no serious bodily necessity intervenes, he shall, as the enactments of the Fathers have decreed, be deprived of the communion of charity with all the bishops until the future council.

### C. XV. Presbyters, deacons, and all who believe themselves injured are to attend the metropolitan synod. Likewise from the Council of Pope Martin.

[Note: *Martin*: Gratian first cites this under the name of Pope Martin, and thereafter will cite under the same name many things all taken from the book of chapters of Greek synods by Martin, bishop of Braga. For bishops were formerly called *popes*. Since he was Greek, Martin rendered these chapters into Latin for the benefit of the churches of Spain, where he held the episcopate. In some instances he added certain material and in others omitted some, as in this chapter, taken from the Council of Antioch, canon 20, above in this distinction under “For ecclesiastical causes.” He also included in that booklet some materials from the Councils of Toledo.]

[Note: Chapters of Martin of Braga, chapter 18, from the Synod of Antioch.—Polycarpus, book 3, title 17.]

For ecclesiastical causes and the settlement of disputes [Col. 0103B], it has been thought good that a council be held twice yearly in every province, the metropolitan bishop summoning all the provincial bishops, so that all presbyters and deacons, or those [Note: *let them proceed in these matters*: Spanish Collection.] [Note: *Or those*: In several editions of the councils it reads: “so that the cases of those who believe themselves injured may be … in the council.”] [Note: “or those whose cases in their council …”: apparently corrupt in the Spanish Collection.] who consider themselves injured, may come to the council, in order that the cases may be examined in council and brought to a just judgment. If any bishops, presbyters, or deacons are clearly found guilty of an offence, they are to be excommunicated according to the judgment which it is agreed by common consent to pronounce concerning them. No bishop [Col. 0104A] may hold councils privately on his own, except those entrusted with metropolitan sees.

### C. XVI. PALEA.

[Note: *Palea*: It is found in none of the collated manuscripts, but the phrase “each individual” is joined to the preceding chapter, “For ecclesiastical causes.” These are Gratian’s words.]

[Likewise from the Council of Bylon.]

[Note: The Council of Bylon plainly does not exist; rather, Berardus conjectures that the canon belongs to the Council of Hippo, held in 393, a summary of which is found in Quesnel’s manuscript Code of Canons, in the works of Leo the Great edited by the Ballerini, vol. 3.—Furthermore, this *Palea* is absent from the Basel edition.]

“Each year a bishop shall hold a synod in his diocese concerning his clergy, as well as abbots, and shall examine the other clergy and monks.”

Gratian: Let each bishop diligently make known to his churches what is decreed in councils.

Hence in the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, chapter 6 [Note: Chapter 7, held in 691.]:

### C. XVII. Each bishop shall make known to his churches what is decreed in councils.

We decree that, while a council is being held in any province, every bishop shall not delay, within six months, to summon by his admonitions all abbots, [Col. 0104B] presbyters, deacons, and clerics, as well as the entire assembly of the city over which he is known to preside, and also all the people of his diocese, so that [Note: *So that*: In two manuscripts [and in the Spanish Collection] of this Sixteenth Council of Toledo, this passage is read thus: “so that, with everything publicly disclosed before them, they may be made most fully aware of those things which in that year have been done or determined in the council.”] he may fully disclose before them everything [Note: *report*: the same.] known to have been done or determined in the council that year. And below:

§ 1. If anyone considers these matters to be negligible, he shall in every respect remain punished by a sentence of excommunication for a period of two months.

# DISTINCTION XIX

[Col. 0103]

[Col. 0103C] ## GRATIAN

## Part I

Concerning decretal letters, however, the question is raised whether they possess authoritative force, since they are not found in the body of canons.

Pope Nicholas writes as follows concerning them to the archbishops and bishops established throughout Gaul [Note: This letter is found among the acts of the Roman Council held in 865.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 33.]:

### C. I. Decretal letters possess authoritative force.

If the writings of other commentators are approved or rejected by decree of the Roman Pontiffs, so that what the apostolic see has approved [Note: [Col. 0103] Added: “truly”: the collected old editions.] is today held accepted, and what it has rejected is hitherto considered without effect [Col. 0104C], how much more ought those things which it itself has written at different times for the Catholic faith, for sound doctrine, for the various and manifold needs of the Church and the conduct of the faithful, to be preferred with every honor, and reverently adopted by all, on every occasion, with discretion or dispensation as teacher? Although some of you have written that those decretal letters of the ancient Pontiffs are not copied in the entire body of the code of canons [Note: [Col. 0103] Addition in the collected old editions: “and therefore are not to be received among the canons”; these words are absent, however, from the original.] [Note: [Col. 0104D] “Whereas they themselves”: the passage was emended from the very letter of Nicholas, preserved in manuscript at Rome and recently printed in the appendix to the *Library of the Holy Fathers*, as stated above, Distinction 10, chapter “Laws.” That letter contains many other matters relevant even to the most ancient decretal letters.], whereas they themselves, when they see these letters support their intention, use them indiscriminately, and only now, to diminish the power of the apostolic see and increase their own privileges, declare them less acceptable.

Likewise below:

§ 1. If they say that decretal letters of the ancient Roman Pontiffs are not to be admitted because they are not entered in the code of canons, then no enactment or writing of St. Gregory, nor of anyone else who was before or after him, is to be received, because it is not entered in the code of canons. Therefore let them erase from their books his teaching and enactments, which are revered by every tongue, because they are not entered in the code of canons. Why, then, do they occupy parchment with them, once they are not accepted? But why do we linger long over this, when we shall not even receive the divine Scriptures of the Old and New Testament [Col. 0105B], if we listen to these men? For neither of them is included in the code of ecclesiastical canons.

But these men, who are always readier to resist than to obey [Note: [Col. 0105] The collected old editions read: “readier to resist than to obey.”], will answer, saying [Note: [Col. 0105] Basel edition: “asserting”; Ivo: “acting.”], that among the canons there is found a chapter of Pope St. Innocent [Note: [Col. 0105] In the letter to Exsuperius of Toulouse, final chapter.], by whose authority we are taught that both Testaments must be received, although neither is wholly included in those same paternal canons. To this it must be answered [Note: [Col. 0105] Collected old editions: “answered”; Ivo: “referred.”]: since the Old and New Testaments are to be received, not because they are wholly appended to the code of canons, but because Pope St. Innocent’s judgment concerning their reception appears to have been issued, it necessarily follows that the decretal letters of the Roman Pontiffs must be received [Col. 0105C], even if they are not incorporated into the code of canons. For among the canons themselves there is admittedly interwoven one chapter of Blessed Leo, which commands that all decretal enactments of the apostolic see be observed in such a way that anyone who offends against them is to know that pardon will thereafter be denied him.

[PALEA. [Note: [Col. 0105] Absent from the Basel edition.]]

“For he says in chapter 10 [Note: [Col. 0105] The original and Ivo read “fifth.” This passage is taken from the letter to the bishops of Campania, written in the consulship of 443, letter 4, Ballerini edition.] of his decretal letters: ‘And lest anything perhaps be thought to have been omitted by us, we command that all decretal enactments, both those of Innocent of blessed memory and of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the discipline of the canons, be observed by your charity in such a way that anyone who offends against them shall know that pardon [Col. 0105D] will henceforth be denied him.’”

In saying, “all decretal enactments,” he omitted none of the decretal enactments which he did not command to be observed. And again, by declaring, “of all our predecessors,” [Col. 0106A] he excepted none of the Roman Pontiffs before him whose decretal enactments he did not command all to observe in such a way that anyone who offended against them should know that pardon would thereafter be denied him. Therefore it makes no difference [Note: [Col. 0105] The original, Ivo, and the collected old editions read: “is of no concern.”] whether all the decretal enactments of the apostolic see are or are not interwoven among the canons of councils. They cannot all be incorporated in one body; and among those canons are included those which give firmness to those that are absent and confer their force upon them. This is especially so since the synodal proceedings, among which the canons themselves were established [Note: [Col. 0105] Ivo: “constituted”; Basel edition: “instituted.”], are not contained in the code of canons, yet are venerated by us with every due honor.

The holy and most eloquent Pope Gelasius concurs with this most blessed Pope Leo in his decretals [Note: [Col. 0105] Compare above, Distinction 15, chapter 3.], saying: “We decree that decretal letters, which the most blessed Popes at various times have issued from the city of Rome in response to the consultations of various Fathers, are to be received with reverence.” Here it should be noted that he did not say, “The decretal letters which are contained among the canons,” nor merely [Note: [Col. 0105] Collected old editions add: “or.”] “those which modern Pontiffs have issued,” but: “which the most blessed Popes at various times have issued from the city of Rome.” In saying [Note: [Col. 0105] Argentinensis edition: “you say from”; other collected editions: “saying.”] “at various times,” the holy man also included those times in which the increasing persecutions of pagans made it exceedingly difficult for cases of bishops to be brought to the apostolic see.

Having thus, by divine grace, set out these points beforehand, we have shown that there is no difference between those decrees of the bishops of the apostolic see which are contained in the code of canons, and those which, because of their multitude [Col. 0106C], can scarcely be found separately throughout volumes. For we have proved that the eminent bishops Leo and Gelasius commanded that all decretal enactments of all their predecessors, and decretal letters which the most blessed Popes at various times issued from the city of Rome, be received and observed with reverence.

## II. All enactments of the apostolic see must be observed without challenge.

Likewise Pope Agatho, to all bishops [Note: [Col. 0105] These appear to be excerpts from Agatho’s allocution to the bishops assembled at the Roman council of 680. — Deusdedit, part 3; Ivo, *Decree*, part 4, chapter 238; *Polycarpus*, book 1, title 17.]:

Thus all enactments of the apostolic see must be received as though they had been confirmed by the voice of the divine Peter himself.

[Col. 0106D]

### Chapter III. The yoke imposed by the holy see must be borne, even if it seems unbearable.

Likewise from the Capitularies [Note: [Col. 0105D] “Capitularies”: thus corrected from several manuscripts and Ivo. Nauclerus, volume 2, generation 28, relates that this was one of twenty-three chapters of laws [Col. 0106D] which Charlemagne sent to all his provinces. Burchard cites it from the Council of Tribur, chapter 30, where it is also found.] of Emperor Charles [Note: [Col. 0105] Compare Baluze, *Capitularia of the Kings of the Franks*, under the year 891, vol. 1, p. 367; and the Council of Tribur, held 895, chapter 30. — Burchard, book 1, chapter 220; Ivo, part 5, chapter 50.]:

In memory of the blessed apostle Peter, let us honor the holy [Col. 0107A] Roman and apostolic see, so that, since it is for us the mother of priestly dignity, it ought also to be the teacher of ecclesiastical order. Therefore humility is to be maintained with gentleness [Note: [Col. 0107] Ivo reads “humanity.”], so that [Note: [Col. 0107] Collected old editions read “and.”], although a yoke scarcely bearable may be imposed by that holy see, we may nevertheless bear it and endure it in devout devotion.

§ 1. But if—something unfitting—anyone, whether priest or deacon, is convicted of plotting some disturbance, laying snares against our ministry, and bringing from the apostolic [Note: [Col. 0107] Council of Tribur: “from the Apostolic [See].”] see a false letter, or anything else which did not come from there [Note: [Col. 0107] “Came together”: in the same source and in Baluze’s *Capitularies*.], then, with faith intact [Note: [Col. 0107C] Burchard reads: “with false and imperfect faith.”] and humility toward the Apostolic [See], the bishop has authority to commit him to prison or some other custody, until he petitions the apostolic majesty by letter or through suitable envoys of his party. Then that majesty may especially deign, by its holy legation, to decree what the Roman law lays down should justly be determined concerning such persons, so that he may be corrected and a limit imposed upon the rest.

### Chapter IV. Whatever the Roman Church establishes or ordains must be observed by all.

Likewise Pope Stephen [Note: [Col. 0107] These words are read at the end of Stephen V’s letter to the eastern bishops, published by Mansi at the end of the Fourth Council of Constantinople, the twelfth general council, vol. 16. The Argentinensis, Basel, Venice I, and Nuremberg editions also cite Stephen V.]:

Indeed, because the holy Roman Church, over which Christ willed us to preside, has been set before all as a mirror and example [Note: [Col. 0107] Basel edition: “has been set before all”; Nuremberg, Venice I and II, Paris, Lyons I: “has been placed over.”], everything which it establishes and everything which it ordains must be observed by all perpetually [Note: [Col. 0107] Collected old editions and the first Basel edition add “indeed.”] and without challenge.

### Chapter V. Whoever refuses obedience to apostolic commands must be excluded from pontifical offices.

Likewise Gregory IV [Note: [Col. 0107D] This chapter occurs in the same letter of Gregory IV from which the chapter “By our decree,” below, Causa 2, Question 6, is taken. It is found in the frequently mentioned manuscript of the Dominican library.] [Note: [Col. 0107] From a letter dated 832; compare Distinction 12, chapter 2. Anselm, book 2, chapter 21; Ivo, part 5, chapters 11 and 349; *Polycarpus*, book 1, title 17.]:

[Col. 0107C] It is lawful for no one either to wish or to be able to transgress the commands of the apostolic see and the ministry of our ordinance, which your charity ought to follow.

### Part II

§ 1. Therefore let whoever wishes to oppose apostolic decrees lie cast down in grief at his own ruin, and let him thereafter have no place among priests, but be made an exile [Note: [Col. 0107] Collected old editions and the first Basel edition read “deprived.”] from the holy ministry. Let no one afterward concern himself with his judgment, since he is undoubtedly already condemned by the holy and apostolic Church *and by its authority* [Note: [Col. 0107] Omitted in the collected old editions; the original reads, with an uncertain construction: “by this authority and his disobedience”; Ivo: “for his disobedience.”] for disobedience and presumption. For one to whom the discipline of the holy Church has been entrusted, who [Note: [Col. 0107] Collected old editions read “because”; Anselm, “to obey.”] ought not only to have obeyed the commands of the aforesaid holy Church but also to have warned others not to disregard them, must be cast out by the penalty of greater excommunication. Let him be excluded from divine and pontifical offices who refused to obey apostolic commands [Note: [Col. 0107] Below, Part I, distinction 6, chapter 212 [209]: “Let him hold,” etc.].

### Chapter VI. Decretal letters are counted among the canonical Scriptures.

Likewise Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book II, chapter 8 [Note: [Col. 0107D] The passage in Blessed Augustine at the cited place reads as follows: “But among the canonical Scriptures let him follow, as fully as possible, the authority of the Catholic churches; among these, certainly, are those which have deserved to possess apostolic sees and receive letters.” He will therefore observe this rule in canonical Scriptures: those which are received by all [Catholic] churches he should prefer to those which some do not receive. Among those not received by all, he should prefer those received by the more numerous and more weighty churches to those held by fewer churches and churches of lesser authority. But if he finds some held by more churches and others by weightier churches—although he could scarcely find this [easily]—I think they should nevertheless be regarded as of equal authority.” This judgment of Blessed Augustine concerns canonical and sacred Scriptures, not decretal letters of the Roman Pontiffs.] [Note: [Col. 0107] Anselm, book 3, final chapter [123]; *Polycarpus*, book 1, title 25.]:

Among the canonical Scriptures, the most diligent investigator of the divine Scriptures should follow, as fully as possible, the authority of the Catholic churches, among which certainly are those that have deserved to possess apostolic sees [Col. 0108B], and others to receive letters from it [Note: [Col. 0107] “And others from it” is absent in Anselm.].

§ 1. Therefore he shall observe this rule in canonical Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0107] Basel and Lyons II–III editions add “the investigator.”]: those which are received by all churches [Note: [Col. 0107] Anselm adds “canonical.”] he shall prefer to those which some do not receive. Among those not received by all, he shall prefer those received by the more numerous and weightier churches to those held by fewer churches and churches of lesser authority.

§ 2. But if he finds some held by more churches and others by weightier churches—although [Note: [Col. 0107] Argentinensis edition: “when.”] this [Note: [Col. 0107] Venice I and II: “these.”] can scarcely be found—yet I think that they are to be regarded as of equal authority.

[Col. 0108C]

### Chapter VII. Whoever departs from Peter’s firmness should understand himself to be excluded from the divine ministry.

Likewise Pope Leo I, to the bishops of Vienne, letter LXXXVII [Note: [Col. 0107] Letter 10 in the Ballerini edition, written about 445; Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 6.]:

Thus our Lord Jesus Christ, savior of the human race, instituted matters so that the truth formerly contained in the proclamation of the Law and Prophets should go forth through the apostolic trumpet for the salvation of the whole world, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0107] Psalm 18:5.]: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” But the Lord willed the mystery of this office to belong to the ministry of all the apostles [Col. 0109A], while placing it principally in the most blessed Peter, chief of all the apostles [Note: [Col. 0109] Original: “placed.”], so that from him as from a kind of head he might diffuse his gifts through the whole body [Note: [Col. 0109] The Hispanic Collection: “wished [them] to flow into the whole body.”], and so that anyone who dared to depart from Peter’s firmness might understand himself excluded [Note: [Col. 0109] Basel edition: “an exile.”] from the divine mystery [Note: [Col. 0109] Collected old editions, except the first Basel and Nuremberg editions: “ministry.”].

For, having taken him into partnership in indivisible unity, he willed him to be named what he himself was [Note: [Col. 0109] Basel and Nuremberg: “the Lord”; other collected editions: “the Lord himself.”], saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” [Note: [Col. 0109] Matthew 16:18.], so that the building of the eternal temple might, by the marvelous gift of God’s grace, stand upon Peter’s firmness. By this firmness [Note: [Col. 0109] Basel: “this”; other collected editions: “this also.”] he strengthened his Church, so that neither human rashness could attack it nor the gates of hell prevail against it. But anyone who attempts to break its authority, favoring his own desires and not following what he received from the ancients, seeks with utterly impious presumption to violate this most sacred firmness of the rock, built, as we have said, by the Lord’s construction [Col. 0109B].

Gratian. This must, however, be understood of those enactments or decretal letters in which nothing contrary to the decrees of preceding Fathers or to evangelical commands is found. For Anastasius II, with the support of Emperor Anastasius, decreed that those whom Acacius had ordained priests or Levites after the judgment pronounced against him ought to exercise rightly the offices they had received, saying as follows:

[Col. 0109C]

### Chapter VIII. No share of injury touches one ordained by heretics already condemned.

Anastasius II, to Emperor Anastasius, letter I, chapters 7 and 8 [Note: [Col. 0109] Letter 1, written about 497; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 1, title 47, chapters 1–2; Anselm, book 9, chapter 62; book 13, chapter 31; Ivo, *Decree*, part 1, chapter 151; *Polycarpus*, book 3, title 10.]:

According to the custom of the Catholic Church, may the most sacred heart of Your Serenity recognize that no share of injury arising from Acacius’s name touches any of those whom Acacius baptized or whom he ordained, according to the canons, as priests or Levites; lest perhaps the grace of the sacrament conferred through one who is unjust might appear less secure.

§ 1. For even baptism—which may it be far [Note: [Col. 0109] Original and collected old editions, except Venice II and Lyons II–III: “be far.”] from the Church—if it has been administered by an adulterer or thief, reaches the recipient as an unimpaired gift. For that voice which sounded through the dove [Col. 0110A] excluded every stain of human defilement, when it declares and says [Note: [Col. 0109] Collected old editions: “which declares when it is said.”]: “This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit and fire” [Note: [Col. 0109] Luke 3:16.]. For if the rays of this visible sun, when they pass through the foulest places, are not stained by any defilement of contact, much more is the power of him who made this visible sun not constrained by any unworthiness of the minister [Note: [Col. 0109] Hispanic Collection: “touched.”].

For Judas, though sacrilegious and a thief, nevertheless conferred through the office entrusted to him among the apostles gifts which suffered no loss because they were given through one unworthy. The Lord himself declares this in the clearest voice: “The scribes [Note: [Col. 0109] Matthew 23:2.],” he says, “and the Pharisees sit upon Moses’ seat. Do what they say; but do not do what they do, for they speak and do not act.”

§ 2. Therefore whatever any minister in the Church appears [Note: [Col. 0109] Collected old editions: “appear.”] to do by virtue of his office for human benefit [Col. 0110B] is wholly sustained by the effective operation of divinity. Thus Paul, through whom Christ speaks, affirms: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. Therefore neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase” [Note: [Col. 0109] 1 Corinthians 2:6.].

§ 3. Indeed, the question is not who preaches or what sort of person he is, but what [Note: [Col. 0109] Basel: “which.”] he preaches; so much so that Paul affirms [Note: [Col. 0109] Original and collected old editions: “confirms.”] that even the envious preach Christ well. The devil was cast down by this evil [Note: [Col. 0109] Hispanic Collection: “deceived, and he does not cease to hasten this very thing.”], yet he himself does not cease to preach this. Therefore this man also [Note: [Col. 0109] Basel edition adds from the gloss: “namely, Acacius.”], whose name we say is to be passed over in silence [Note: [Col. 0109] Basel: “is said to be rejected”; other collected editions: “is said to be passed over in silence.”], injured only himself by administering good things badly. For the inviolable sacrament which was given by him to others [Note: [Col. 0109] Collected old editions, first Basel and Venice I: “in others”; Basel: “unto perfection.”] obtained the perfection of its own power.

§ 4. This [Note: [Col. 0109] The original printed by Mansi reads: “Since this is so, the suspicion of some extends so far,” etc.; the Hispanic Collection: “But if the suspicion of some extends so far,” etc.] is generally true, unless the inquisitive suspicion of some extends so far [Col. 0110C] that, after Pope Felix’s judgment had been issued, they imagine that Acacius acted without effect in the sacraments which he administered; and therefore they fear, for those who received the mysteries conferred in consecrations or baptism, that the divine gifts may appear void [Note: [Col. 0109] Omitted in the Basel edition.].

Gratian. Since, therefore, he issued these rescripts unlawfully and uncanonically, contrary to the decrees of his predecessors and successors—as Felix and Gelasius prove, who excommunicated Acacius before Anastasius, and Hormisdas, third after Anastasius, who afterward condemned that same Acacius [Col. 0111A]—he is therefore rejected by the Roman Church and is recorded to have been struck by God in the following manner:

### Chapter IX. Anastasius, rejected by God, was struck by the divine will.

Anastasius [Note: [Col. 0111C] This chapter is indeed found in volume two of the councils, in the *Life of Anastasius*. But it is plainly shown to be wholly fabricated, not only by many other arguments but also by this: Acacius—as Nicephorus, book 16, chapter 12; Evagrius, book 3, chapter 18 and following; and, most clearly, Anastasius the Librarian in the *Chronology* testify—died in the time of Felix III, who was succeeded by Gelasius, and Gelasius by Anastasius. At the beginning of his letter and in chapter 1 to Emperor Anastasius, he wrote that Acacius was already dead and stood with Felix before Christ the Judge, as Gelasius had also written before him; this is found below, Causa 24, Question 2, chapter “Nor Anyone.” How, then, could Anastasius discuss restoring one who had already died?] II, a Roman by birth, lived in the time of King Theodoric. At that time many clerics and priests withdrew themselves from his communion [Note: [Col. 0111] Ivo: “cast out”; original: “raised up.”], because, without a council of the bishops, priests, and clerics [Note: [Col. 0111] Collected old editions: “of the clerics”; Ivo: “or of them.”] of the whole Catholic Church, he had communicated with a deacon of Thessalonica named Photinus, who had communicated with Acacius; and because he wished secretly to restore Acacius [Col. 0112A], and could not do so, he was struck by the divine will.

Concerning Maximus also [Note: [Col. 0111D] From the words of this canon, especially the Greek and Balsamon’s translation, the *Life of Gregory the Theologian* written by Gregory the Presbyter, and other passages—although Theodoret appears to have handled this rather carelessly—it appears that this Maximus was never a bishop. It was therefore rightly decided that he could imprint no character of orders, which could not be asserted of Acacius. The Greek words of this canon are: “Περὶ Μαξίμου τοῦ κυνικοῦ καὶ τῆς κατ᾽ αὐτὸν ἀταξίας τῆς ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει γενομένης. Ὥστε μήτε Μάξιμον ἐπίσκοπον ἢ γενέσθαι, ἢ εἶναι, μήτε τοὺς παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ χειροτονηθέντας ἐν ὁιῷ δήποτε βαθμῷ κλήρου, πάντων καὶ τῶν περὶ αὐτὸν καὶ τῶν παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ γενομένων ἀκυρωθέντων,” that is: “Concerning Maximus the Cynic, and the disorderly acts done in connection with him at Constantinople: neither that Maximus ever became or is a bishop, nor that those ordained by him are to be reckoned in any rank of the clergy, since all things done concerning him and by him are annulled.” The most ample testimony that this same Maximus was never a bishop occurs in Pope Hadrian’s letter to Emperor Basil, found in the first session of the manuscript Eighth Synod in Cardinal Sirleto’s possession. Citing Leo I, he says: “For the loud-sounding trumpet, the holy Pope Leo of the apostolic see, whose judgment everything Catholic everywhere celebrates and venerates as a heavenly miracle and oracle, says: ‘Since a question often arises concerning an honor wrongly received, who can doubt that what is not shown to have been conferred ought by no means to be granted to such persons?’ Nor have we established that there is any distinction between Photius the adulterer and Maximus the Cynic, condemned by the Second Synod, or between the ordinations of this one and that one.”] it was decreed at the Synod of Constantinople, under Pope Damasus, chapter 6 [Note: [Col. 0111] First Council of Constantinople, held 381. In the Hispanic Collection the chapter begins: “Concerning Maximus the Cynic philosopher and the whole …”]:

### Chapter X. Acts performed concerning disorderly prelates, or by them, are to be annulled.

Because of the teaching of his entire disorderliness, which arose at Constantinople, it was decreed that Maximus should not be thought either to have been or to be a bishop, nor should those ordained by him hold any degree whatever of the clergy; that is, all things done concerning him or by him are annulled.

# DISTINCTION XX

[Col. 0111]

[Col. 0111B] GRATIAN.

### Part I

Decretal letters, therefore, are equal in law to the canons of councils. The question now concerns expositions [Note: [Col. 0111] Basel edition: “expositors.” Part II.] of sacred Scripture: are they equal to these, or subject to them? For the more anyone relies upon reason, the greater authority his words seem to possess. Now many commentators, as they excelled others in fuller grace of the Holy Spirit, so also in ampler knowledge, and are shown to have adhered more closely to reason. Hence the sayings of Augustine, Jerome, and other commentators seem to be preferred to the enactments of certain Pontiffs.

### Part II

§ 1. But it is one thing to impose an end upon cases and another to expound the sacred Scriptures diligently. In deciding matters, not knowledge alone [Col. 0111C] but authority also is necessary. Thus Christ, when about to say to Peter, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0111] Matthew 16:18.], first gave him the keys of the kingdom of heaven: in the one giving him knowledge for distinguishing leprosy from leprosy; in the other giving him authority to expel persons from the Church or receive them. Since all matters reach their conclusion either in the acquittal of the innocent or in the condemnation of offenders, and acquittal or condemnation requires not knowledge only but also the authority of those presiding, it is clear that interpreters of the divine Scriptures, even if they surpass Pontiffs in knowledge, nevertheless, because they have not attained the summit of their rank, are placed above them in expositions of sacred Scripture, but in determining cases deserve the second place after them.

Therefore Pope Leo IV writes to the bishops of Britain [Note: [Col. 0111] Letter II, section 6, written 850; Anselm, book 1, chapter 123; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 118; *Decree*, part 4, chapter 72; Deusdedit, part 2; *Polycarpus*, part 3, title 20.]:

### Chapter I. The writings of others are not to be preferred to the decrees of Roman Pontiffs.

It is not fitting for anyone [Note: [Col. 0113] Collected old editions: “any persons.”] to judge from the pamphlets and commentaries of others while abandoning the canons of holy councils or the rules of decretals—that is, those which we possess together with the canons [Note: [Col. 0113] Original in Mansi, vol. 14, p. 884, Anselm, and Ivo: “with those in the canon.”]. The canons by which we make use of judgment in all ecclesiastical cases are [Note: [Col. 0113C] “The canons”: this indicates the canons and rules making up the body or code of canons mentioned in the preface, which the Roman Pontiffs used especially in judicial cases. This code contains only canons, not synodal proceedings, as Nicholas wrote above in Distinction 19, chapter “Of the Romans.”] the canons of the Apostles, of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Constantinople, Ephesus, Chalcedon, Sardica, Africa, and Carthage [Note: [Col. 0113C] In the code of canons there is one Carthaginian synod containing thirty-three canons [Col. 0113D] collected from various councils held at Carthage. The apostolic see seems to have approved those canons and used them when it arranged for their inclusion in the code of canons. The Greeks also translated these same canons, in the order in which the Latins have them, into their own language, together with many other African synodal canons. These are the very canons which Anselm, Burchard, and Ivo cite by the same numbers. Yet Gratian sometimes uses these and at other times draws canons from individual Carthaginian councils, as will be indicated in their respective places. The statement in the first note to chapter “First,” above, Distinction 16, seventh passage, must be understood of this single Carthaginian synod; its explanation was postponed until this place.], and together with these the rules of the Roman bishops Sylvester, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, Hilary, Symmachus, Hormisdas, Simplicius, and the younger Gregory [Note: [Col. 0113] The name is absent from the original; nevertheless, several passages from Gregory’s decretal letters are read in the same letter, chapter 5, from which his name appears to have been transferred here.].

These, without exception, are the authorities through whom bishops judge, and through whom bishops and clerics are themselves judged [Note: [Col. 0113] Böhm reads “judge.”]. But if some unusual matter should arise or occur [Col. 0113B] which cannot possibly be decided by these, then, if sayings of Jerome, Augustine, Isidore, or other similar holy doctors whom you recall are found, they are to be boldly retained and promulgated; or such matters are to be referred [Note: [Col. 0113] Ivo and the collected old editions: “be referred.”] to the apostolic see.

§ 1. For this reason I do not fear to declare more clearly and in a loud voice: whoever—whether bishop, cleric, or layperson—is shown not to receive without reservation the enactments of the holy Fathers which we have mentioned, and which among us are entitled by the name of canons [Note: [Col. 0113] Ivo: “canons.”], is shown neither to retain nor to believe, profitably and effectively unto his salvation, the Catholic and apostolic faith or even the holy four Gospels [Note: [Col. 0114C] Anselm, Deusdedit, and Gregory the Presbyter in *Polycarpus* read: “whoever does not receive these same things without distinction convicts himself of not retaining the Catholic and apostolic faith unto the effect of his salvation.”].

### Chapter II. Those who do not possess or observe the decrees of Roman Pontiffs are to be reproved.

Likewise Nicholas I, to Photius, in the letter beginning, “After Blessed Peter” [Note: [Col. 0113] Written 862. In the collected old editions the chapter is entitled “To the clergy of Constantinople.” — *Collection in Three Parts*, part 1, title 62, chapter 16.]:

If you do not possess the decrees of Roman Pontiffs, you must be accused of neglect and carelessness. But if you possess them and do not observe them, you must be reproved and rebuked for rashness.

### Chapter III. To whom recourse should be had when the authority of sacred Scripture is unavailable.

Likewise Pope Innocent [Note: [Col. 0114D] This chapter is not among the many extant letters of Innocent I; nor can it be by Innocent II, since Burchard and Ivo, who cite this passage, wrote before him.] [Note: [Col. 0113] A fragment of uncertain author and date. — Burchard, book 3, chapter 128; Ivo, *Decree*, part 4, chapter 70; *Polycarpus*, book 1, title 7.]:

For cases in which no authority for loosing or binding appears in the books of the Old Testament, the four Gospels [Col. 0114B], or all the writings of the apostles, have recourse to the Greek texts of the divine writings. If not even in these, consult the canons of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0114D] These words, absent in Gratian, occur in Burchard, Ivo, and *Polycarpus*, where they stand in this very place, to which they have been restored.]. If not even in these, turn to the Catholic histories of the Catholic Church, written by Catholic doctors. If not even in these, carefully recall the examples of the saints. But if, after examining all these, the nature of this question is not clearly discovered, assemble the elders of the province and consult them. For what is sought by several elders is found more easily. For the true Promiser, the Lord, says [Note: [Col. 0113] Matthew 18:19.]: “If two or three of you agree on earth in my name, whatever matter they ask concerning shall be done for them by my Father.”

# DISTINCTION XXI

[Col. 0113]

[Col. 0113C] GRATIAN.

I. Part. Ecclesiastical affairs, therefore, are determined by the decrees of the Roman Pontiffs and the sacred canons of ecclesiastical councils, as has been shown above. The ministers [Col. 0114C] of the sacred canons and papal decrees are the supreme pontiffs, the bishops beneath them, and the remaining priests, whose institution was begun in the Old Testament and more fully completed in the New.

§ 1. For supreme pontiffs [Col. 0115A] and lesser priests were instituted by God through Moses [Note: Exod. ch. 28; 1 Chron. ch. 25 and 2 Chron. ch. 23], who, by the Lord’s command, anointed Aaron as supreme pontiff and his sons as lesser priests. Afterwards David, when he enlarged the ministries of the house of the Lord, established gatekeepers and singers.
