Moreover, Solomon discovered a certain method of exorcism by which demons, when adjured, were expelled from possessed bodies; those assigned to this office were called exorcists. Concerning them the Lord says in the Gospel [Note: Luke ch. 11, v. 19]: “If I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons”—that is, the exorcists—“cast them out?”

The Church has imitated all these things in the New Testament: it has its gatekeepers, whom we call doorkeepers. In place of singers it has established readers, who are also singers. It has retained exorcists, with the ancient name and office remaining. In place of the sons of Aaron, all who administer the priesthood beneath [Col. 0115B] the supreme pontiff have been consecrated.

§ 2. Among these a certain distinction has been maintained: some are called simply priests, others archpriests, others chorepiscopi, others bishops, others archbishops or metropolitans, others primates, others patriarchs, and others supreme pontiffs.

§ 3. This distinction among them was introduced chiefly from the Gentiles, who called some of their flamens simply flamens, others archflamens, and others protoflamens. But the basic distinction between greater and lesser priests in the New Testament took its beginning from Christ himself, who instituted the Twelve Apostles as greater priests and the seventy-two disciples as lesser priests. He chose Peter as, so to speak, supreme priest, when before and for all the others he gave him the keys of the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0115C], gave him the name Peter from himself, the Rock, testified that he had prayed especially for his faith, and commanded him to strengthen the others, saying [Note: Luke ch. 22, v. 32]: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when you have at last turned back, strengthen your brethren.”

Following this same pattern, the Apostles ordained bishops and presbyters in individual cities. We also read that Levites were ordained by the Apostles; the greatest among them was blessed Stephen [Note: Acts ch. 6]. In the course of time the Church established subdeacons and acolytes for itself.

Blessed Isidore writes as follows concerning these matters in book VII of the *Etymologies* [Note: compare Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book 2 = ch. I of Rabanus, *On the Institution of Clerics*, book 1, ch. 2], chapter 12, explaining their names and the reasons for the names:

### C. I. Whence the names of ecclesiastical ranks are derived

[Col. 0115D] We believe that the terms *clerus* and *clerici* are so called because Matthias [Note: Acts ch. 1] was chosen by lot, and he is the first whom we read to have been ordained through the Apostles. For κλῆρος (*klēros*) in Greek is called *sors*, “lot,” or *hereditas*, “inheritance,” in Latin. Clerics are therefore so named either because they belong to the Lord’s lot, or because they have the Lord as their portion. Generally, however, all who serve in the Church of Christ are called clerics; their ranks and names are these: doorkeeper, psalmist, reader, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, presbyter, bishop.

§ 1. The order of bishops is fourfold [Note: “threefold”: Rabanus], namely, patriarchs, archbishops, metropolitans, and bishops.

§ 2. *Patriarch* is interpreted in the Greek language as “chief of the Fathers,” because he holds the first—that is, the apostolic—place [Note: “Apostolic”: formerly it was read “after the apostolic.” The true reading has been restored not only on the authority of Isidore and old manuscripts of Gratian, but from Isidore’s own reason, since he calls the Roman, Antiochene, and Alexandrian patriarchs such because they hold an apostolic place. Blessed Gregory likewise explains this in book 6, epistle 37, writing to Eulogius of Alexandria: “Accordingly, although there are many apostles, nevertheless, because of the primacy itself, only the see of the Prince of the Apostles has prevailed in authority; and it is one see in three places. For he himself exalted the see in which he deigned both to rest and to end his present life. He adorned the see to which he sent his disciple the Evangelist. He established the see in which he sat for seven years, though destined to depart.” Anacletus says the same in the chapter *Sacrosancta*, below, Distinction 22], and therefore, because he exercises the highest honor, he is designated by such a name, as are the Roman, Antiochene [Col. 0116B], and Alexandrian patriarchs.

§ 3. *Archbishop* is called by a Greek term [Note: “is interpreted”: collected editions], because he is the chief of bishops; for he holds apostolic office and presides over both metropolitans and the other bishops.

§ 4. Metropolitans are so called from the measure or status of cities; for they preside over individual provinces, and the other priests are subject to their authority and teaching. Without them the remaining bishops are permitted to do nothing, for the care of the whole province has been entrusted to them.

§ 5. All the orders designated above are called bishops by one and the same name; but certain persons use a particular designation because of the distinction of powers which they have received individually.

§ 6. A patriarch is the chief of Fathers. For ἄρχων (*archōn*) means “chief” in Greek; hence an archbishop is the chief of bishops [Col. 0116C], just as a metropolitan is so called from the measure of cities.

§ 7. The term *episcopate* is derived from the fact that one who becomes [Note: “is made over”: Isidore] bishop oversees [Note: from Augustine, *City of God*, 19, ch. 19], that is, takes care of those subject to him; for σκοπεῖν (*skopein*) is called *intendere*, “to direct one’s attention,” in Latin. Bishops are called in Greek, and interpreted in Latin, as “watchers”; for the overseer set over the Church is called a watcher because he watches and observes the conduct and life of the peoples placed beneath him.

§ 8. A pontiff is the chief of priests, as though the way of those who follow. He is also called high priest and supreme pontiff. For he makes priests and Levites; he arranges all ecclesiastical orders; he shows what each person ought to do. In former times those who were kings [Col. 0116D] were also pontiffs [Note: “were pontiffs and kings”: collected editions]. For it was the custom of the ancients that the king should also be priest and pontiff. Hence Roman emperors too were called pontiffs.

§ 9. A *vates*, “seer,” is so called from the strength of the mind [Note: “is called”: Basel edition]; and the word has several meanings, for it sometimes signifies a priest, sometimes a prophet, sometimes a poet.

§ 10. A priest is called an *antistes*, “one standing before,” because he stands before others: he is first in the order of the Church and has no one above him [Note: Basel edition adds from the gloss: “or, in Latin, sacred leader”].

§ 11. The name *sacerdos*, “priest,” is compounded from Greek and Latin, as though meaning “one giving the sacred.” For just as a king is so called from ruling, so a priest is called from sacrificing [Note: “sanctifying”: Isidore]; for he consecrates and sacrifices [Note: “sanctifies”: ibid.]. The priests of the Gentiles were called flamens. They wore a cap on the head, with a short rod upon it and some wool above. When they could not bear this because of the heat, they began merely to bind their heads with a thread [Note: “a thread on the head”: collected editions]; for it was forbidden for them to go with heads entirely uncovered [Col. 0117B]. Hence they were called *flamines* from the thread which they used, as though *filamines*, “thread-men.” Yet on feast days, having set aside the thread, they put on the cap as a mark of the eminence of the priesthood.

§ 12. *Presbyter* is interpreted from Greek into Latin as “elder.” They are called presbyters not only by reason of age or decrepit old age, but also on account of the honor and dignity which they have received. Hence [Note: “Hence also among…” These words have been restored to their proper place, where they occur in Isidore] [Note: In the collected editions these words are read at the end of the section.] among the ancients bishops and presbyters were the same persons, because that name denotes dignity and not age [Note: “And not age.” The original reads, “this is of age,” and thus also Jerome in epistle 83 to Oceanus; but it has not been changed because of the gloss]. Presbyters are also called priests because they administer sacred things, just as bishops do. Although presbyters are priests [Note: from Innocent I, epistle to Decentius, ch. 3], nevertheless they do not possess the summit of pontifical office, because they neither sign the forehead with chrism nor confer the Spirit, the Paraclete; the reading in the Acts of the Apostles [Note: Acts ch. 8] shows that these things belong to bishops alone.

§ 13. Levites are called from the name of their founder. For the Levites sprang from Levi, and through them the ministries of the mystical sacraments were performed in the temple of God. They are called *diaconi* in Greek and *ministri*, “ministers,” in Latin, because just as consecration belongs to the priest, so the administration of ministry [Note: “mystery”: Isidore] belongs to the deacon.

§ 14. Those called *hypodiacones* in Greek, whom we call subdeacons, are so named because they are subject to the commands and offices of the Levites. They themselves receive in the temple of God the offerings from the faithful and hand them over to the Levites to be placed upon the altars. Among the Hebrews they are called Nathinaeans [Note: “Anathaneans”: Basel edition; “Nathaneans”: the remaining editions].

§ 15. Readers are so called from reading and psalmists from singing psalms. The former proclaim to the people what they should follow; the latter sing in order to stir the minds of their hearers to compunction [Col. 0117D]. Yet some readers pronounce words so mournfully that they drive some hearers to weeping and lamentation. They are also called pronouncers because they announce publicly [Note: “to the people”: collected editions, first Argentinian, Basel, and Nuremberg editions]. Their voice will be so powerful and clear [Note: omitted by Boehmer] that it fills the ears even of those who are far away.

§ 16. A singer is so called because he modulates the voice in song. In the art of music there are two kinds of singer, so far as learned persons have been able to name them in Latin: the *praecentor*, “precentor,” and the *succentor*, “responding singer.” The precentor is the one who begins the melody in song; the responding singer answers by singing afterwards. A *concentor* is so called because he sings in harmony. But one who neither harmonizes nor sings together will be neither a singer nor a harmonizing singer.

§ 17. Acolytes [Note: Ivo, *Decrees*, part 6, ch. 8] are called in Greek, and in Latin *ceroferarii*, “candle-bearers,” because they carry candles when the Gospel is to be read [Col. 0118B] or the sacrifice offered. At that time lights are kindled and carried by them, not to drive away darkness while the sun shines at that very time, but to display a sign of joy, so that under the figure of bodily light that light may be shown of which it is read in the Gospel [Note: add “of Christ”: Basel edition] [Note: John ch. 1, v. 9]: “There was the true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world.”

§ 18. Exorcists are called, from Greek into Latin, “those who adjure” or “those who rebuke.” For over catechumens, or over those who have an unclean spirit, they invoke the name of the Lord Jesus, adjuring through him that the spirit may depart from them.

§ 19. Doorkeepers, also called gatekeepers, were chosen in the Old Testament to guard the temple, so that no one unclean in any respect might enter it [Note: add “spirit”: Basel edition]. They are called doorkeepers [Note: “are” is added and “but” omitted in the collected editions.] because they are set over the doors of the temple [Col. 0118C]. Holding the key, they guard everything inside and outside; and, exercising judgment between good and bad, they receive the faithful and reject the unbelieving.

### C. II. The Roman Church received primacy from Christ. Likewise Anacletus, to the bishops of Italy, epistle II

[Note: An epistle of Pseudo-Isidore; in this chapter the author chiefly imitated Isidore, book 2, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, ch. 5. — Anselm, book 1, chs. 1 and 7; Burchard, book 1, ch. 1; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, ch. 82; *Decrees*, part 5, ch. 1.]

In the New Testament, after Christ the Lord, the priestly order began with Peter, because pontifical office in the Church of Christ was first given to him, the Lord saying to him [Note: Matthew ch. 16, v. 18]: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” Therefore he first received from the Lord the power of binding and loosing [Col. 0118D], and he was the first who, by the force of his preaching, brought the people to faith.

The other Apostles, indeed, received honor and power with him in equal fellowship, and they wished him to be their chief; at the Lord’s command they were scattered through the whole world and preached the Gospel.

§ 1. When they too died, bishops succeeded in their places. Their ordination ought to take place in the aforesaid [Note: “previously touched upon”: original] order and manner. Whoever receives them and their words receives God; but whoever despises [Note: “rejects”: collected editions, first Basel and Lyons II–III editions] them despises him by whom they were sent and whose embassy they discharge, and he himself will without doubt be despised by the Lord.

§ 2. Seeing [Note: Luke ch. 10; Matthew ch. 9] that the harvest was great and the laborers few, the Apostles asked the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest. Therefore seventy-two disciples [Note: “seventy”: Ivo] were chosen by them; presbyters bear their type and have been appointed in their place in the Church.

### C. III. No synod, but Christ, instituted the primacy of the Roman Church. The same, Gelasius, bishop of the city of Rome, to all orthodox Christians

[Note: This chapter belongs to the decree of Gelasius—Pelagius is cited in the collected editions—dated A.D. 494 or 496; several matters concerning it have been noted above at Distinction 15, ch. 2. — Anselm, book 1, ch. 69; Burchard, book 3, ch. 220; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, ch. 8; Polycarpus, book 1, title 2. Moreover, Pseudo-Isidore adapted the words “to whom was given,” etc., to his own purpose; below, Distinction 22, ch. 2, Anacletus.]

Although all the Catholic Churches throughout the world are one bridal chamber of Christ, nevertheless the holy Roman, Catholic, and Apostolic Church was not set above the other churches by any synodical enactments; rather, it obtained primacy by the Gospel declaration of our Lord and Savior: “You are Peter,” he says, “and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.”

To it was also given the fellowship of the most blessed Paul, the chosen vessel [Col. 0119C], who, not at a different time—as heretics babble—but at one and the same time, on one and the same day, struggling unto death with Peter in the city of Rome under Caesar Nero, was crowned with a glorious death. Together they consecrated the aforesaid holy Roman Church to Christ the Lord, and by their presence and venerable triumph set it above all cities throughout the world. Therefore the Roman Church is the first see of the Apostle Peter, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of the kind.

III. Part. Gratian. In all these ranks, the higher the rank, the greater the authority found. For the greater possess the power of governing and commanding; the lesser have the obligation of obeying.

Thus Pope Nicholas I writes to Emperor Michael in the epistle beginning, “We had proposed” [Note: dated A.D. 865. In the collected editions it is addressed: “Nicholas to the bishop of Constantinople.” — Collection in three parts, part 1, title 62, ch. 68]:

### C. IV. The acts of inferiors are subject to the judgments of superiors

An inferior see cannot absolve a superior one [Note: “a more powerful one”: collected editions]. Therefore only the superior can fittingly absolve the inferior [Col. 0120A]. From this it is clearly understood that an inferior cannot bind by judicial decision one whom it cannot absolve. And below: Hence the Prophet [Note: Isaiah ch. 10] says: “Shall the axe boast against him who cuts with it? Or shall the saw exalt itself against him who draws it?” Having recalled these matters from divine Scripture and the teaching of approved Fathers, we have shown more clearly than the sun that no person of lesser authority can subject to his judgments, or subjugate by his own determinations, one who possesses greater power.

### C. V. On the same matter. The same, in the same epistle

[Note: Collection in three parts, part 1, title 62, ch. 69.]

Do not suppose that we wish to defend the blameworthy actions of any of our neighbors; rather, we desire children to be so devoted and sober toward their spiritual father, and disciples toward their master, that they may not, with any rashness whatsoever, rush forward to judge their life—or, I will not say [Note: “we will not say”: collected editions], even lightly to rebuke it.

### C. VI. Inferiors can neither bless nor curse their superiors. The same Pope Nicholas, in the same epistle

[Note: Anselm, book 7, ch. 154; Ivo, *Decrees*, part 5, ch. 17, and part 6, ch. 355.]

Finally, if we read in the Epistle to the Hebrews that the lesser is blessed by the greater, it necessarily follows that, as reason requires, he is also cursed by the greater. Foreknowing these dangerous times, those who were before us handed down a prudent custom in the churches, and it is still observed without omission [Note: “without omitting”: original; Anselm’s version in the Basel edition] in the Roman Church, which is the teacher of all churches. No priest is to attempt to impart a blessing upon any matter without the assent of his greater fellow-priest. Likewise, one standing before the people to pronounce a reading asks for a blessing; yet no inferior at all dares to bless him [Col. 0120C]. Why is this? Is blessing a sin? Far from it. For the Apostle says concerning those who curse, not those who bless [Note: Galatians ch. 5], that they shall not possess the kingdom of God. But this indicates how firmly every inferior must be restrained from judging his superiors, if they possess absolutely no right even of blessing them.

### C. VII. On the same matter. The same, in the same epistle

[Note: Anselm, book 2, ch. 65; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, ch. 6; *Decrees*, part 5, ch. 8; Polycarpus, book 1, title 20. In the collected editions it is only at this point entitled, “To Emperor Michael.”]

[Col. 0120D] Now, by divine inspiration, we shall not hesitate, nor will it be impossible for us to show you—if only you are willing to listen—that no one can rightly be subjected to judicial determinations by persons of inferior dignity or rank.

For in the time of the emperors Diocletian [Col. 0121A] and Maximian, Marcellinus, bishop of the city of Rome, who afterwards became an illustrious martyr, was so compelled by pagans that, having entered their temple, he placed grains of incense upon coals. On account of this act a council of many bishops was assembled and an investigation made; the pontiff himself confessed that he had done this. Yet none of them dared to pronounce sentence against him, while all repeatedly declared to him [Note: “said”: collected editions]: “Judge your cause by your own mouth, not by our judgment.” And again: “Do not,” they say, “be heard in our judgment, but gather your case into your own bosom.” And again: “For by your own words,” they say, “you will be justified, or by your own mouth you will be condemned.” And again they say: “The first see shall be judged by no one” [Note: “shall be justified”: Basel and Nuremberg editions].

The same, in the same work.

§ 1. Likewise, when at one time certain people attempted to bring some evil report [Note: “not good”: original; Anselm] against Pope Sixtus, and it was said in a council attended also by Emperor Valentinian that it was not lawful to pronounce judgment against the Pontiff, the emperor at once rose and granted the aforesaid Pontiff authority to judge his own case. Indeed, no pontiff of lesser or inferior cities is found to have been compelled by judicial proceedings [Note: “by judgment”: Basel edition].

### C. VIII. Greater persons cannot be judged by lesser. The same Nicholas, in the same epistle

[Note: Collection in three parts, part 1, title 62, ch. 72.]

Ignatius is subjected to the deliberations of lesser, inferior, and subordinate persons, whereas the sacred canons command, and the examples of the holy Fathers show, that one must always go where greater authority is found [Note: “that one must go”: collected editions, first Argentinian, Paris, Antwerp, and Lyons II–III editions; some read “to the same person”], and that in every controversy the proceeding is directed to the judgments of the more powerful see [Col. 0121C] [Note: “proceeding” is absent from the original and from the first collected editions, first Argentinian, and Lyons II–III and Antwerp editions]. This is known to have been observed not only by Catholics but even by heretics themselves.

Otherwise it is evident that a council is headless when a matter concerning so great a person is under consideration and the judgment of the greater authorities is not awaited, whereas even in the case of clerics of lower rank, the judgment of their bishop alone is not to be sought merely [Note: “awaited”: Basel edition].

### C. IX. Judgments of lesser persons cannot condemn greater persons. The same Nicholas, in the same epistle

[Note: Anselm, book 2, ch. 65; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chs. 6–7; *Decrees*, part 5, ch. 8; Polycarpus, book 1, title 20.]

The holy Fathers at Chalcedon so detested this presumption that, among other grounds, they condemned Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, above all and without any restoration, because, persisting in obstinacy [Note: From this point to the word “setting” the text has been added from the original; it is also absent from Anselm and Ivo. The words “setting,” etc., are taken from Psalm 72 [73], v. 9] against the privilege of the first Roman see, he would not repent of his superstitions, so as to be preserved by the first Apostolic See; and, setting [Col. 0122B] his mouth in heaven and his tongue passing over the earth, he pronounced excommunication against Pope Saint Leo. Thus in the sentence pronounced against him they appear chiefly to mention this, saying: “For by his second offenses he greatly exceeded his former iniquity; for he presumed even to pronounce excommunication against the most holy and most blessed Archbishop Leo of great Rome.”

Is it read there that an investigation was made whether Dioscorus had pronounced that excommunication justly or unjustly [Note: “against him”: same editions]? Certainly not. Rather, without any controversy they punished this in him: because he was inferior, he had attempted to assail a superior with insults of every kind. Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, bears witness, saying [Note: Act V of the Council of Chalcedon]: “Dioscorus was not condemned on account of the faith, but because he excommunicated Lord Archbishop Leo.”

## DISTINCTION XXII

[Col. 0121]

[Col. 0121C] GRATIAN.

I. Part. Since, therefore, a greater person ought not to be judged by a lesser, we must consider which church holds the first place among the other churches, and which the second or third. The Roman Church, as was said above, holds the first place among the others; the Alexandrian Church holds the second, and the Church of Antioch received the third place from it.

Hence Pope Nicholas II writes to the Milanese through Peter Damian, his legate [Note: These words, which in Anselm, book 1, ch. 64, bear the name of the younger Nicholas, occur in Peter Damian’s letter to Hildebrand, found among the acts of the Council of Milan, A.D. 1058, in Mansi, vol. 19]:

### C. I. The Roman Church holds primacy over the others

The Roman Church instituted all the supreme dignities of every patriarchate, the primacies of metropolitan sees [Col. 0122C], the episcopal cathedras, and the dignities of churches of every rank. But he alone founded it and raised it upon the rock of newly born faith, who entrusted to blessed Peter [Note: add “Peter”: collected editions], the keeper of the keys of eternal life, the rights of earthly and heavenly rule alike [Col. 0122D]. Therefore it was not any earthly decree, but the Word through whom heaven and earth were made, through whom indeed all the elements were created, that founded the Roman Church. It exercises the privilege of that Word and is supported by his authority. Hence there is no doubt that whoever takes away its right from any church commits an injustice.

§ 1. But whoever attempts to take away the privilege of the Roman Church, handed down by the supreme head of all churches himself, undoubtedly falls into heresy. And whereas the former is called unjust, the latter must beyond doubt be called a heretic. For he violates the faith who acts against her who is the mother of faith; and he is found disobedient to her who is known to have been set above all churches. And below:

§ 2. Thus Saint Ambrose himself professes that in all things he follows the holy Roman Church as his teacher.

### C. II. The Roman Church received primacy not from the Apostles but from the Lord himself. Likewise Anacletus, servant of Christ Jesus, to all bishops, epistle III, ch. 3

[Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian epistle. — Anselm, book 1, ch. 67, where the words marked with asterisks are likewise absent; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, ch. 2, where the beginning and end of the chapter occur; *Decrees*, part 5, ch. 26, from the preface of the Nicene Council in the Quesnel manuscript; Polycarpus, book 1, title 2.]

The most holy Roman and Apostolic Church received primacy not from the Apostles but from our Lord and Savior himself [Col. 0123B], and attained preeminence of power over all churches and over the entire flock of the Christian people. For he himself said to the blessed Apostle Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed in heaven.”

§ 1. The fellowship of the most blessed Apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, was also added in the same city of Rome. On one day and at one time, struggling unto death with Peter under Prince Nero, he was crowned with a glorious death; and both consecrated the holy Roman Church [Col. 0123C] and set it above all other cities throughout the world by their presence and venerable triumph.

And although the continual prayer of all the saints is offered to God for all persons, nevertheless the most blessed Apostle Paul promises this to the Romans in these words in his own handwriting, saying [Note: Romans ch. 1, v. 9]: “For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I always make remembrance of you in my prayers.”

§ 2. Therefore the first see is, by heavenly favor, the Roman Church [Note: “the Roman Church”: collected editions], which, as has been mentioned, the most blessed Peter and Paul consecrated by their martyrdom.

§ 3. The second see at Alexandria was consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and Evangelist, because Mark himself, sent by Peter, first preached the word of truth in Egypt and received glorious martyrdom; the venerable Abilius succeeded him [Note: From “because” to “third” these words have been added from the original, as have several other passages].

§ 4. The third honored see at Antioch is held in the name of that same—that is, blessed Peter the Apostle—because he lived there before coming to Rome and appointed Ignatius bishop there; and there the name of Christians first arose for the new people.

And a little later:

§ 5. Among the blessed Apostles there was a certain distinction of power [Note: absent from Ivo]. Although they were all Apostles [Col. 0124B], it was nevertheless granted to Peter by the Lord—and they themselves also wished this among themselves—that he should preside over all the other Apostles and that Cephas [Note: “Cephas.” In the Gospel of John, ch. 1, Cephas, a Syriac word, is explained as πέτρος (*petros*), which in Greek means “rock.” Blessed Jerome teaches the same in his commentary on Galatians, ch. 2. It should not be believed that Anacletus was ignorant of this, but that he intended to refer the word to the Greek language, in which it was then very well known. Cyril of Jerusalem did this in Catechesis 10 concerning the name Jesus, attributing to it not only a Hebrew but also a Greek etymology. Moreover, Optatus of Africa, an ancient and approved author highly valued by Jerome and Augustine, understood the very name Cephas in the same way as Anacletus, using these words in book 2: “Therefore you cannot deny that you know that in the city of Rome the episcopal chair was first conferred upon Peter, in which Peter, head of all the Apostles, sat; whence he was also called Cephas.” And Isidore, book 7 of the *Etymologies*, ch. 9, speaks thus of Peter: “He was called Cephas because he was appointed at the head of the Apostles. For κεφαλή (*kephalē*) means ‘head’ in Greek.” But Burchard and Ivo read thus: “that he should preside over all the other Apostles, Cephas, that is, that Peter should hold the primacy of the apostolate”] should hold the head and beginning of the apostolate. The Apostles also handed down this same pattern to be observed by his successors and the other bishops [Note: “and the other bishops”: the original reads, “and the Apostles to the other bishops”].

Nor was this established only in the New Testament; it also existed in the Old. Hence it is written [Note: Psalm 98 [99], v. 6]: “Moses and Aaron were among his priests,” that is, they were first among them.

And a little later:

§ 6. This Apostolic See is the hinge and head, as was said before, of all churches [Note: these words are also absent from Ivo], established by the Lord and by no other. And as a door is governed by its hinge, so, by the authority of this holy see, all churches are governed, the Lord so disposing.

Gratian. By this authority the Alexandrian Church is judged to hold the second place after the first [Col. 0124C]. But later, at the Council of Constantinople, the Church of Constantinople received the second place after the Apostolic See.

Hence at the same synod—that is, Constantinople I [Note: The Roman Correctors assert in the margin that this canon of the Council of Constantinople, A.D. 381, which belongs to the Hispana translation, was taken from an ancient source. In that council, however, canon 28 of the Council of Chalcedon is read in its place; on this matter see Ballerini, in the works of Leo, vol. 3, p. 555. — Polycarpus, book 2, title 22]—chapter 5, it was thus decreed:

### C. III. The bishop of Constantinople holds the second place after the Roman Pontiff

The bishop of the city of Constantinople ought to possess the honor of primacy after the bishop of Rome [Col. 0125A], because it is New Rome.

[Note: This canon is among those which the Apostolic Roman See did not receive from the beginning and for a long time thereafter. This may readily be known from epistle 51, otherwise 53, of Pope Leo I to Anatolius of Constantinople and other letters of the same pope; likewise from two letters of Leo IX, one against the presumptions of Michael and Leo, ch. 28, and the other to that same Michael. But it appears far more clearly from Blessed Gregory’s epistle 31, book 6, to Eulogius of Alexandria and Anastasius of Antioch, and from the epistle of Nicholas I to Emperor Michael beginning “We had proposed.” Although the bishops of Constantinople, relying on the power of the emperors, usurped for themselves the second place among patriarchal sees, this was at last conceded to them for the sake of peace and tranquility, as Pope Innocent III declared in the chapter *Antiqua*, on privileges.]

### C. IV. The Church of Constantinople Is Known to Be Subject to the Apostolic See

Item: Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse, book VII, epistle 63.  
[Note: [Col. 0125D] This chapter is taken from two letters written to the same John, bishop of Syracuse. But in epistle 63, from which the first part was taken, Gregory treats of the Church of Constantinople; whereas in the following epistle, 64, he treats of the primate of Byzacena, a province of Africa—not of the patriarch of Constantinople. Yet Gratian and Anselm, in whose work it is read in the same manner, seem to have intended otherwise, perhaps misled by the brief summary prefixed to Gregory’s letter. The author of the gloss plainly set forth what he thought Gratian had meant.]  
[Note: [Col. 0125] Epistle 12, book 9 (written A.D. 599), Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 2, chapter 65.]

As to what they say concerning the Church of Constantinople, who can doubt that it is subject to the Apostolic See? *This is continually professed both by our most pious lord the emperor and by our brother Eusebius,* bishop of that city.  
[Note: [Col. 0125] There is a scribal error in this name. Eusebius was not then bishop of Constantinople; consequently this name is absent from the better manuscripts of Gregory and from Anselm.]

Yet, if either that church itself or any other church possesses anything good, I am ready to imitate it in what is good, together with those inferior to me whom I restrain from unlawful conduct. For he is foolish who thinks himself first in such a way that he disdains to learn the good things he sees.

The same writer to the same person, epistle 64.  
[Note: [Col. 0125] Epistle 59, Maurist edition, written in the same year.]

[Col. 0125B] For as to the primate of Byzacena saying that he is subject to the Apostolic See: if any fault is found in bishops, I do not know what bishop is not subject to it;  
[Note: [Col. 0125] Addition in the original: “bishop.”]  
but when no fault requires it,  
[Note: [Col. 0125] *exigitur*, “is required”: Basle edition.]  
we are all equal according to the principle of humility.

### C. V. The Bishop of Constantinople Is Deposed by the Authority of the Roman Pontiff

Item: Pope Gelasius I to Faustus, master of the embassy.  
[Note: [Col. 0125] Written A.D. 493.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 9.]

By what tradition of the Fathers do they summon the Apostolic See to judgment? Were the bishops of the second and third sees, and other priests conscious of their own good standing, to have been expelled, while one who proved an enemy of religion was not to be expelled? Let them see, then,  
[Note: [Col. 0125] “Let them see”: collected editions.]  
whether they possess other canons by which to carry out their absurdities. But those canons that are called sacred, ecclesiastical, and lawful cannot summon the Apostolic See to judgment; and was the bishop of the city of Constantinople—who in any event received no rank among the sees through the canons,  
[Note: [Col. 0125] “which”: Bohmer.]  
and who had fallen back into communion with the faithless—not to have been removed?  
[Note: [Col. 0125] “But the bishop of Constantinople”: same editions.]

### C. VI. The Church of Constantinople Holds Second Place after Rome

Item: from the Sixth Synod assembled under Justinian, chapter 36.  
[Note: [Col. 0125] From the Quinisext Synod, held A.D. 692.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 11, chapter 17.]

Renewing  
[Note: [Col. 0126C–D] “Renewing”: this concerns that fifth canon of the Constantinopolitan Synod, mentioned above in the present distinction, chapter *Constantinopolitanae*. As to all these canons attributed to the Sixth Synod, see the note on chapter *sextam*, above, Distinction 16.]  
the decrees of the holy Council of Constantinople, we request  
[Note: [Col. 0125] The original has: ὁρίζομεν, that is, “we decree.”]  
that the see of Constantinople receive privileges similar to those possessed by higher Rome,  
[Note: [Col. 0126D] “Higher”: this is found in several ancient copies; the common editions read “lower.” The Greek is τῆς πρεσβυτέρας Ῥώμης, that is, “of the more ancient” or “elder Rome,” as in the following chapter. In any event, this chapter is much shorter in this translation than in the Greek copy, except that it is fuller in one point, since it numbers the see of Antioch, of which there is no mention in the common Greek text.]  
and that it likewise be magnified in ecclesiastical affairs as Rome is;  
[Note: [Col. 0126D] “And likewise”: corrected from several manuscripts and from the Greek; formerly the text read, “not however.”]  
yet it is to stand second after Rome, before the see of Alexandria is numbered; then comes Antioch, and after it Jerusalem.  
[Note: [Col. 0125] “As”: Basle edition.]

[Col. 0126B] Gratian. From this it is understood that the Alexandrian Church was changed from second to third place, and the Antiochene from third to fourth—unless perhaps someone should contend that there are two second places, so that Constantinople and Alexandria may be held to possess an equal rank of dignity.

Therefore, in the Eighth Synod, held under Pope Hadrian II, canon 21:  
[Note: [Col. 0125] Held A.D. 869.—This is Anastasius the Librarian’s translation of the canon.—Anselm, book 2, chapter 72 (70); Deusdedit, part 3.]

### C. VII. Which Patriarchal See Holds First Place, and Which Subsequently

We decree that no worldly ruler whatever may dishonor any of those who preside over the patriarchal sees, or attempt to remove him from his own throne; rather, they are to be judged worthy of every reverence and honor: above all, indeed, the most holy Pope of elder Rome; then the patriarch of Constantinople; [Col. 0126C] then those of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem.

# DISTINCTION XXIII

[Col. 0127]

[Col. 0127A] **GRATIAN**

## Part I

We have briefly shown the difference among ecclesiastical offices. Now, beginning with the highest and descending to the lowest rank, let us show by the authorities of the saints how each is to be ordained.

Accordingly Pope Nicholas II, at the Lateran Council,  
[Note: [Col. 0127] At the Roman council held A.D. 1059. Yet there are those who consider this decree, as found in Gratian, corrupt; on this matter see Baronius under A.D. 1059.—The *Chronicle of Farfa*, in which the Roman Correctors discovered it, is printed in Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum*, vol. II, part 2, p. 645.]  
issued the following:

[Note: [Col. 0127D–0128D] A complete copy of this decree is found in a very ancient book of the abbey of Farfa, written in Lombardic letters nearly five hundred years ago, and elsewhere.]

### C. I. Decree of Pope Nicholas concerning the Election of the Supreme Pontiff

In the name of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. In the year of his Incarnation 1059, in the month of April, in the twelfth indiction, with the most holy Gospels set forth, and with the most reverend and blessed Nicholas, *Apostolic* Pope, presiding in the basilica of the Lateran Patriarchate, called the Constantinian Basilica, while the most reverend bishops, abbots, presbyters, and deacons were also seated, this venerable Pontiff, decreeing by apostolic authority concerning the election of the supreme Pontiff, said:

§ 1. Your blessedness knows, most beloved brothers and fellow bishops—and these things have not escaped even the lower members of *Christ*  
[Note: [Col. 0127] “Lower” (*inferiora*); Panormia reads *anteriora*, “former.”]  
—what adversities this Apostolic See, which I serve by God’s appointment, endured after the death of our predecessor, Lord Stephen of pious memory; and how it was subjected to repeated hammer-blows and frequent beatings by the money-changers of simoniacal heresy,  
[Note: [Col. 0127] *Tonsionibus*, “shavings,” in Venetian editions I and Lyons I; the text reads *tunsionibus*, “beatings.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0127] “Was subjected” (*subjacuit*): collected editions.]  
so that the pillar of the living God seemed almost already shaken and ready to totter,  
[Note: [Col. 0127] “Already”: collected editions and Panormia; in these the following word, *concussa*, is also absent.]  
and the net of the supreme Fisherman was compelled, amid swelling storms, to sink into the depths of shipwreck.  
[Note: [Col. 0127] “To be submerged”: original in Mansi.]

Therefore, if it pleases your brotherhood, with God’s help we ought prudently to provide against future misfortunes [Col. 0127C] and safeguard the ecclesiastical condition, lest recurrent evils—God forbid—prevail in the future.  
[Note: [Col. 0127] “Recurring”: *Chronicle of Farfa.*]  
[Note: [Col. 0127] Addition: “in the future”: ibid.]

§ 2. Accordingly, instructed by the authority of our predecessors and of other holy Fathers, we decree and establish that, when the Pontiff of this Roman universal Church dies, the cardinal bishops shall first discuss the election together with the greatest care,  
[Note: [Col. 0127] *Diligentissima*, “with the greatest care”: Basle edition; the text has *diligentissime*, “most carefully.”]  
and then immediately call in the cardinal clerics of Christ;  
[Note: [Col. 0127] “Themselves” (*ipsi*): the original.] and thus the remaining clergy and people shall approach in order to consent to the new election, taking care, of course, that the disease of venality does not creep in under any pretext. Therefore the most religious men are to lead in advancing the election of the Pontiff, while the rest follow.  
[Note: [Col. 0127] This sentence is absent from the same source.]

§ 3. This certain and lawful order of election [Col. 0127D–0128A] is discerned if, after considering the rules and acts of the various Fathers, the following judgment of our predecessor, Blessed Leo, is also recalled:  
[Note: [Col. 0127] “This” (*hic*) is absent from the Basle edition.]

> “No principle permits persons to be counted among bishops who have neither been elected by the clergy, nor sought by the people, nor consecrated by the bishops of the province with the judgment of the metropolitan.”

[Note: [Col. 0127] Compare below, Distinction 62, chapter 1.]

But since the Apostolic See is set before all churches throughout the world, and therefore cannot have a metropolitan over itself,  
[Note: [Col. 0127] Some collected editions and the first Basle edition read “but since” (*sed quia*); in the latter the preceding words are absent.] the cardinal bishops undoubtedly perform the office of a metropolitan, since they raise the elected bishop to the summit of the Apostolic office.

§ 4. Let him be elected from the bosom of that Church itself, if a suitable man is found; but, if one is not found within it, let him be taken from another church. The due honor [Col. 0128B] and reverence of our beloved son Henry, who at present is regarded as king and, God granting, is hoped to become emperor, are preserved—just as we have already granted this to him and to his successors who have personally obtained this right from this Apostolic See.

§ 5. But if the perversity of wicked and unjust men should become so strong that a pure, sincere, and gratuitous election cannot be held in the City, the cardinal bishops, together with religious clerics and Catholic laymen, even though few, shall possess the right and authority to elect the Pontiff of the Apostolic See wherever they judge it suitable.  
[Note: [Col. 0127] “Of electing”: collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0127] “Where they judge more suitable”: Panormia and the *Chronicle of Farfa*; “where it may be suitable”: collected editions and first Basle edition. These words, though differently expressed, appear in Ivo’s *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 80.]

§ 6. Clearly, after the election has been made, if a storm of war or any effort of men motivated by malice resists, so that the one elected cannot be enthroned in the Apostolic See according to custom,  
[Note: [Col. 0127] “Authorized”: original in Mansi.]  
the elect shall nevertheless, as true Pope, possess the authority to govern the Roman Church and dispose of all its resources—as we know Blessed Gregory did before his consecration.

§ 7. If anyone, contrary to this decree of ours promulgated by synodal judgment, has been elected, ordained, or enthroned by sedition, presumption, or any contrivance whatsoever, let him, together with his authors, supporters, and followers, be cast out and separated by perpetual anathema, through the authority of God and of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, from the threshold of God’s holy Church, as an antichrist, an invader, and a destroyer [Col. 0128D–0129A] of all Christendom. Let no hearing on his behalf ever be reserved;  
[Note: [Col. 0129] Addition: “at any time”: ibid., Panormia, and Basle edition.]  
rather, without reconsideration, let him be deposed from every ecclesiastical rank he held before. Whoever adheres to him, renders him any reverence as though to a Pontiff, or presumes in any way to defend him, shall be bound by the same sentence.  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “Sentence”: Basle and Lyons II–III and Antwerp editions.]

§ 8. Whoever is a violator of this decretal sentence of ours  
[Note: [Col. 0129] Addition: “holy”: collected editions, except Basle.]  
and attempts, by his presumption, to confuse and disturb the Roman Church contrary to this statute,  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “Decree”: Basle and Nuremberg editions.]  
let him be condemned by perpetual anathema and excommunication; let him be reckoned with the ungodly, who shall not rise in judgment;  
[Note: [Col. 0129] Psalm 1:5.]  
let him feel the wrath of the Almighty against himself, and in this life and in the life to come feel the anger of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, whose Church he presumes to throw into confusion. Let his dwelling be desolate, [Col. 0129B] and let there be none to inhabit his tents;  
[Note: [Col. 0129] Psalm 68:26.]  
let his children become orphans and his wife a widow;  
[Note: [Col. 0129] Psalm 108:9.]  
let him and his children be driven away in agitation; let them beg and be cast out from their dwellings; let the usurer search out all his substance, and strangers plunder the fruits of his labor;  
[Note: [Col. 0129] Addition: “all”: Basle edition.]  
let the whole world fight against him,  
[Note: [Col. 0129] Wisdom 5:21.]  
and let all the elements be opposed to him; let the merits of all the saints at rest confound him, and in this life openly display vengeance upon him.

§ 9. But may the grace of almighty God protect those who observe this decree of ours, and may the authority of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul absolve them from the bonds of all sins.

## Part II. Gratian

Let us show, from the authority [Col. 0129C] of the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 1—at which Augustine was present in the reign of the Emperor Honorius—how bishops and the other orders below them ought to be ordained, beginning with their examination.

### C. II. When a Person Chosen as Bishop Is to Be Examined

A man who is to be ordained bishop  
[Note: [Col. 0129] Chapter 1 of the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*, in Ballerini; concerning which see above on chapter 9, Distinction 18.—Regino, book 1, chapter 448; Burchard, book 1, chapter 8; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 62; Polycarpus, book 2, title 9.]  
must first be examined to determine whether he is prudent by nature, teachable,  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “Tractable”: Basle edition and Ivo. The collected editions add: “whether he is watchful.”]  
moderate in character, chaste in life, sober, always attentive to his duties,  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “Free from duties”: *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*; “always attentive to his duties, gracious toward people”: Hispanic Collection.]  
humble, gracious, merciful, learned, instructed in the law of the Lord, careful in understanding the Scriptures,  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “Careful or acute”: collected editions.]  
and trained in ecclesiastical doctrine.

[Note: [Col. 0129D–0130D] This entire chapter appears in the Roman Order, with these words added at the beginning: “Ecclesiastical statutes.” Those who edited the volumes of councils testify that a similar title was prefixed to the whole Fourth Council of Carthage in certain ancient codices.]

And above all, he must be examined as to whether he affirms the articles of faith in simple words: namely, confessing that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, and preaching the whole divinity of the Trinity as coessential, consubstantial, coeternal,  
[Note: [Col. 0129] Ivo and Ballerini read “the unity in the Trinity” (*unitatem in trinitate*); the collected editions add “unity.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “Coeternal”: Ivo and collected editions except Basle.]  
and co-omnipotent; whether he believes each person of the Trinity to be fully God, and all three persons to be one God;  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “Each individual person”: Regino; Ivo according to the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua* and Hispanic Collection.]  
whether he believes that the incarnation of the Godhead was accomplished not in the Father nor in the Holy Spirit, but in the Son alone,  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “Divinity” (*divinitatis*): Basle edition.]  
so that he who was, in the Godhead, the Son of God the Father, *might himself become, in humanity, the son of a human mother*: true God from the Father, true man from his mother, having flesh from his mother’s womb and a rational human soul, and in him the truth of both natures—[Col. 0130B] the same God and man, one person, one Son, one Christ, one Lord,  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “Both” (*ambae*): Ballerini.]  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “God”: collected editions.]  
creator and author of all things that are, Lord and ruler, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, of all creatures;  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “Of creatures” (*creaturarum*): Hispanic Collection and Regino.] whether he suffered a true suffering of the flesh,  
[Note: [Col. 0129] Addition: “for our salvation”: collected editions.]  
died a true death of his body, rose by a true resurrection of his flesh  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “Reception”: collected editions.]  
and a true resumption of his soul, and whether he will come in that same reality to judge the living and the dead.

§ 1. He must also be questioned whether he believes that the author and God of the New and Old Testaments—that is, of the Law, Prophets, and Apostles—is one and the same;  
[Note: [Col. 0129] The collected editions and first Basle edition add: “and God, who will judge the living and the dead”; Lyons II and III read “finally” for “God.”]  
and whether the devil became evil not through creation but through his own choice.  
[Note: [Col. 0129] Addition: “his own”: Ivo.]

§ 2. He must also be questioned whether he believes in the resurrection of this flesh which we bear, and not of another;  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “Of this kind” (*hujusmodi*): the editions.] whether he believes that judgment is to come and that each person will receive, for deeds done in the flesh, either punishments or rewards;  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “Glory”: Ballerini.]  
whether he does not forbid marriage,  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “Disapprove”: Regino, Ivo—where the word “not” is absent—the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*, and Hispanic Collection.]  
does not condemn second marriages, does not censure the eating of flesh, communicates with penitents who have been reconciled, believes that in baptism all sins are forgiven—that is, both the original sin contracted and sins voluntarily committed—  
[Note: [Col. 0129] “Sin”: Basle edition; the original and other collected editions read “contracted sin.”]  
and believes that no one is saved outside the Catholic Church.

§ 3. When he has been examined in all these matters and found fully instructed, then, with the consent of clergy and laity and with the assembly of the bishops of the whole province—and especially with the authority or presence of the metropolitan—[Col. 0131A] let him be ordained bishop.  
[Note: [Col. 0129] In Regino, Burchard, and Ivo this section is reduced to an epitome. The Hispanic Collection reads “with” (*ex*) before “the consent.”] Having received the episcopate in Christ’s name, he is to comply not with his own pleasure nor his own impulses,  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Character”: Hispanic Collection and collected editions.]  
but with these determinations of the Fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0131D–0132D] “Comply”: after this word, both in the council and in the Roman Order, follows the following passage, apparently added from outside: “In his ordination, the age also is to be required which the holy Fathers established for bishops to be chosen beforehand.”]

### C. III. What the Conduct of Clerics Ought to Be

Item: Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book 2, chapter 2.  
[Note: [Col. 0131] The same material is found in the Council of Mainz, book 1, chapter 10. In the collected editions it is entitled: “Isidore on the life of clerics.”]

## Part III

Thus the law of the Fathers provides  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Here”: Bohmer.]  
that, separated from common life, they abstain from worldly pleasures; that they take part neither in spectacles nor in public displays; that they avoid public banquets and keep private ones not merely decent but sober; that they do not engage at all in usury, nor seek the pursuit of disgraceful gain and anyone’s fraudulent schemes;  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Frauds”: collected editions.]  
that they flee love of money as the source of all crimes; and that they reject worldly offices and business affairs.  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Decline”: Basle, Lyons I–III, Antwerp, and Paris editions.]

They are not to seek degrees of honor through ambition;  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Undertake”: collected editions.]  
they are not to accept gifts in return for the benefits of God’s healing; they are to beware of deceits and conspiracies; to flee hatred, rivalry, detraction, and envy; to walk neither with roaming eyes,  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Roaming”: same editions.]  
nor with an unbridled tongue, nor with a wanton  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Wantonness”: Basle edition.]  
and loose bearing,  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “With a swollen gait”: original.]  
but to show the modesty and restraint of their minds in simple dress and manner of walking. They are to detest utterly the obscenity of words just as much as that of deeds;  
[Note: [Col. 0131] Addition: “of bodily members”: collected editions.]  
to avoid frequent association with widows and virgins;  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Very frequent visits”: collected editions.]  
never to seek cohabitation with women who are strangers; to strive continually to preserve the chastity of an inviolate body, or at least to be bound by the bond of one marriage; to render due obedience to their elders and never exalt themselves through any desire for self-display. Finally, they are to apply themselves unceasingly to the reading of doctrine, to psalms, hymns, and songs.  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Unceasing”: original and Basle edition.]

For such ought those to be who seek to *present themselves* as devoted to divine worship, so that, while they devote themselves to learning, they may administer the grace of teaching to the people.

### C. IV. Those Unable Worthily to Administer the Sacraments Must Not Be Chosen for Divine Ministry

Item: Clement to James, the brother of the Lord, epistle II.  
[Note: [Col. 0131] A spurious epistle. The Ballerini argued, but did not prove, that Rufinus himself had given it Latin form.—Polycarpus, book 4, title 31.]

Let such clerics be chosen for ministry as can worthily administer the Lord’s sacraments. For it is better [Col. 0131D–0132A] for a priest of the Lord to have few ministers who can worthily perform God’s work than many useless ones who impose a heavy burden on their ordainer.

### C. V. If Objections Are Raised against a Man Chosen as Bishop, Five or Six Bishops Shall Meet for His Vindication

Item: from the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 40.  
[Note: [Col. 0131] Held A.D. 397. The collected editions and first Argentinensis edition cite the Fourth Council of Carthage.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 17, chapter 28; Anselm, book 6, chapter 65; Burchard, book 1, chapter 6; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 60; Polycarpus, book 2, title 8.]

The following is to be established: whenever we meet to elect a bishop, if any objection arises  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Has arisen”: collected editions and first Basle edition.]  
—for such things have often happened among us—not merely three bishops are to presume to come forward for the vindication of the man to be ordained;  
[Note: [Col. 0131] Addition: “to come forward”: collected editions; “three already”: Hispanic Collection.]  
rather, two or three are to be requested in addition to the number mentioned above.  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “The number mentioned above”: Basle edition.]

In the same people for whom he is to be ordained, the persons making the objections shall first be examined; then the charges themselves shall also be considered. When he has been vindicated in public view, [Col. 0132B] only then shall he be ordained. If this agrees with the mind of your holiness, let it be confirmed by the reply of your dignity.

All the bishops said: “It is entirely agreeable.”

### C. VI. Those Whom Ecclesiastical Discipline Promotes Shall Pledge the Vows of Their Promise

Item: from the Eleventh Council of Toledo, chapter 10.  
[Note: [Col. 0131] Held A.D. 675.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 42, chapter 5.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 88.]

Although all who are devoted to sacred orders are bound by canonical rules, it is nevertheless expedient that those whom ecclesiastical discipline approves for ranks of promotion should pledge the vows of their promise under guarantee.  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Promotes”: Hispanic Collection.]  
For what is individually promised is customarily feared more than what is contained in a general undertaking.  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Bond”: Hispanic Collection.]

§ 1. Therefore this holy council decreed  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Holy synod”: Basle edition.]  
that everyone who is about to ascend to ecclesiastical ranks  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Approach”: ibid. and Hispanic Collection.]  
shall not receive the consecration of office [Col. 0132C] until, by a written record of his agreement,  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Binding”: Hispanic Collection.]  
he promises that, preserving the Catholic faith with sincere devotion of heart, he will live justly and piously; that in none of his acts will he oppose the canonical rules; and that each shall render in every respect due honor and reverent obedience to his superior, according to that decree of Blessed Pope Leo:

> “He who knows that he is placed over some persons should not take it badly that another is set over him; rather, he should himself render the obedience which he demands.”

[Note: [Col. 0131] Leo, epistle to Anastasius of Thessalonica.]

Moreover, in accordance with the practice of ecclesiastical custom, punishment is to be imposed in respect of such agreements  
[Note: [Col. 0131] “Yet”: collected editions; “inserted”: Hispanic Collection.]  
and paid by those who have transgressed them.

[Col. 0133A] There follows an ordinance concerning how ecclesiastical offices are ordained, in the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 2.  
[Note: [Col. 0133] These and the following chapters appear under the title “Summary of the ordination of ecclesiastical officers,” from chapter 90 among the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*; concerning these, see above, Distinction 18, chapter 9. They also appear in part in the Gelasian Sacramentary, book 1, no. 95; Anselm, book 6, chapter 53; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 18; *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 124; Polycarpus, book 2, title 9.]

### C. VII. How a Bishop Is Ordained

When a bishop is ordained, two bishops shall place and hold the book of the Gospels over his head and neck; and while one of them pours the blessing over him,  
[Note: [Col. 0133] “Pours”: Hispanic Collection, *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*, Anselm, and Ivo.]  
all the other bishops present shall touch his head with their hands.

### C. VIII. How a Presbyter Is Ordained

From the same source, chapter 3.  
[Note: [Col. 0133] Chapter 91 of the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*; Anselm, book 7, chapter 53 [98]; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 33; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 12; Polycarpus, book 2, title 32.]

When a presbyter is ordained, while the bishop blesses him and holds his hand upon his head, all the presbyters present shall also hold their hands upon his head, next to the hand [Col. 0133B] of the bishop.  
[Note: [Col. 0133] “Hands”: collected editions and *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua.*]

But just as, on the day of his ordination, a priest is encircled by the *orarium* upon both shoulders, so during the time of consecration he ought continually to use that same *orarium*.  
[Note: [Col. 0133] These words are absent from the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*, Anselm, and Ivo, and therefore appear to be Gratian’s own. Almost all the collected editions support this view.]

Accordingly, in the Third Council of Braga, chapter 3, we read:  
[Note: [Col. 0133] Held A.D. 675.—Collection in three parts, part 1, title 48, chapter 1.]

### C. IX. What Each Receives at Consecration He Shall Wear at the Time of Offering

By ecclesiastical *and ancient* institution we know it has been established that every priest, when ordained, is encircled by the *orarium* on both shoulders: so that one who is commanded to stand undisturbed amid prosperity and adversity, ever adorned with virtue, may appear surrounded on both shoulders.  
[Note: [Col. 0133] “On both sides”: Hispanic Collection.]  
[Note: [Col. 0133] This phrase is absent from the same source.]

Why, then, at the time of sacrifice does he not put on what he does not doubt he received in the sacrament? Therefore it is fitting in every way [Col. 0133C] that each retain at the offering, or at the receiving of his salvation, what he received in the consecration of his office. That is, when a priest approaches the solemnities of the Mass, whether to offer sacrifice to God himself or to receive the sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, he is not to *approach* otherwise than encircled by the *orarium* upon both shoulders, just as he is known to have been consecrated at the time of his ordination; so that, pressing neck and both shoulders alike with one and the same *orarium*, he may form upon his breast the sign of the cross.

§ 1. But if anyone acts otherwise, he shall be subject to the due excommunication.  
[Note: [Col. 0133] “Shall be subject”: collected editions.]

## Part V. Gratian

Neither bishops nor deacons are permitted to use dalmatics without apostolic permission.

[Col. 0134A] Accordingly Gregory, to Aregius, bishop among the Franks, book VII, epistle 111:  
[Note: [Col. 0133] Epistle 107, book 9, written A.D. 599, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 93.]

### C. X. Without Apostolic Permission Neither Bishops nor Deacons May Use Dalmatics

Our common son, the deacon Peter, informed us that your brotherhood, while he was here, requested us to grant you and your archdeacon permission to use dalmatics. But because he departed in haste, compelled by the infirmity of his people, in such a way that neither the sorrow pressing upon him permitted him to remain longer—as was fitting and as the requested matter required—  
[Note: [Col. 0133] “Threatening”: Anselm.]  
nor did prudent consideration of ecclesiastical order allow us, burdened as we were with many matters, to grant this new privilege rashly and suddenly, the fulfillment of the request was delayed.

Now, however, recalling the good qualities of your charity, [Col. 0134B] by this written instrument of our authority we grant what was sought,  
[Note: [Col. 0133] “The thing requested”: Basle edition.]  
and allow you and your archdeacon to be adorned by the use of dalmatics. We have sent the same dalmatics through our most beloved son Cyriacus, abbot.

### C. XI. How a Deacon Is Ordained

From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 4.  
[Note: [Col. 0133] Chapter 92 of the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*; Anselm, book 7, chapter 52 [60]; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 31; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 13; Polycarpus, book 2, title 32.]

When a deacon is ordained, only the bishop who blesses him shall lay a hand upon his head, because he is consecrated not to the priesthood but to ministry.  
[Note: [Col. 0133] “When”: *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*, Hispanic Collection, and Basle edition.]

## Part V. Gratian

The question is raised whether, after the blessing, the hands of presbyters and deacons ought to be anointed with the liquid of chrism.

[Col. 0134C] Pope Nicholas [I] writes as follows on this subject to Ralph, Archbishop of Bourges:  
[Note: [Col. 0133] Written A.D. 864.—Collection in three parts, part 1, title 62, chapter 51; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 121.]

### C. XII. Neither Presbyters nor Deacons May Have Their Hands Anointed with Chrism at Consecration

You further inquire whether, when they are ordained, the hands are to be anointed with the liquid of chrism for presbyters alone or also for deacons. This is done for neither order in this holy Roman Church, which, by God’s appointment, we serve.  
[Note: [Col. 0133] “Concerning neither”: collected editions.]

Nor do we read anywhere—unless memory deceives us—that it has been done by ministers of the New Law. Therefore we direct your holiness to the canonical decrees of Blessed Pope Innocent; and the opening pages of the letter sent to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio, will fully instruct you [Col. 0134D] concerning what you must observe in consecrations and orders.  
[Note: [Col. 0133] “Ordinations”: original in Mansi.]

[Col. 0135A]

### C. XIII. PALEA

[Note: [Col. 0135] This *Palea* is absent from the Basle edition.]

From the Second Council of Seville, chapter 5.  
[Note: [Col. 0135] Held A.D. 619.—Burchard, book 3, chapter 3; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 213, and part 6, chapter 102.]

> From a letter of Pope Simplicius addressed to Bishops Severus and Florentinus.  
> [Note: [Col. 0135D–0136D] “From a letter”: this *Palea* has not been found in any manuscript copy. Before this chapter, which begins “To the knowledge,” Burchard and Ivo report another chapter beginning “Report,” from a letter of Simplicius sent to Equitius, Florentius—or Florentinus—and Severus, bishops. The title may therefore have been transferred here from that source. Moreover, Burchard cites this chapter from the Council of Braga; Ivo, in part 5, chapter 213, cites it as from Carthage, and in part 6, chapter 102, as from the Second Council of Seville, chapter 5, where it also occurs. The following canon, *Quorundam*, is, as it were, a summary of this one.]
>
> Through the report of the deacon of Gabrum,  
> [Note: [Col. 0135] “Egabrum”: Hispanic Collection.]  
> information has come to the attention of our examination concerning certain clerics of that church. When one of them was being consecrated to the presbyterate and two to the ministry of Levites,  
> [Note: [Col. 0135] “Being made sacred”: ibid.]  
> their bishop, hindered by an illness of the eyes, is said merely to have laid his hand upon them, while a certain presbyter gave them the blessing contrary to ecclesiastical order.  
> [Note: [Col. 0135] “A certain presbyter”: collected editions and Bohmer.]
>
> Because of the audacity of so great a presumption, he might have been condemned when accused before the present tribunal, had he not, while still in the body, been forestalled by the summons of death. But because he has now been left to divine judgment and cannot be accused before a human court, those who survive—who received from him not the title of consecration but rather a badge of disgrace  
> [Note: [Col. 0135] “Blessing”: collected editions; “received a pronouncement”: Hispanic Collection.]  
>—are to be removed, by an equitable judgment, after deposition from the rank of priestly or Levitical order which they perversely acquired, lest such an unlawful usurpation grant itself further license.  
> [Note: [Col. 0135] “Admitted”: Lyons editions; “they judge”: other editions.]
>
> For such men have rightly been judged to deserve removal, because they were found to have been improperly appointed.

Gratian. The question is likewise raised whether the ordination should be held valid for those upon whom a bishop, hindered by illness of the eyes, lays hands while a presbyter says the prayer over them.

[Col. 0135C] The Council of Toledo has determined the following concerning this:

### C. XIV. Both Ordainer and Ordained Shall Undergo the Penalty of Condemnation When a Bishop Lays on Hands and Another Says the Prayer

When certain clerics—one to the presbyterate and two to the ministry of Levites—were being consecrated, their bishop, hindered by illness of the eyes, is said only to have laid his hand upon them,  
[Note: [Col. 0135] “Placed”: Basle edition.]  
while a certain presbyter gave them the blessing contrary to ecclesiastical order. But because he has now been left to divine judgment and cannot be accused in a human court, those who survive shall lose the rank of priesthood or Levitical order which they perversely acquired.

[Col. 0136A]

### C. XV. How a Subdeacon Is Ordained

Item: from the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 5.  
[Note: [Col. 0135] Chapter 93 of the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*, in Ballerini; Anselm, book 7, chapter 59; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 3; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 14; Polycarpus, book 2, title 32.]

## Part VI

When a subdeacon is ordained, because he does not receive the laying on of hands, he shall receive from the bishop’s hand an empty paten and an empty chalice; but from the hand of the archdeacon he shall receive a pitcher with water,  
[Note: [Col. 0135] “Water and a water-vessel”: Hispanic Collection and Gelasian Sacramentary.]  
a hand-basin,  
[Note: [Col. 0135] “Hand-basin”: collected editions, first Basle edition, and Lyons editions.]  
and a towel.

### C. XVI. How an acolyte is to be ordained. Likewise from the same Council, c. 6.  
[Note: [Col. 0135] c. 94, *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*.—Anselm, book 10, c. 58. Ivo, *Panormia*, same place. *Decretum*, same place, c. 15. *Polycarpus*, same place.]

When an acolyte is ordained, he is to be instructed by the bishop how he ought to perform his office; but from the archdeacon he is to receive a candlestick [Note: [Col. 0135] *cereoforalium*: *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*.] with a candle [Note: [Col. 0135] “candles”: Hispana Collection.], so that he may know that he is assigned to light the lamps of the church. He is also to receive an empty cruet for presenting wine for the Eucharist of Christ’s blood.

[Col. 0136B] ### C. XVII. How an exorcist is to be ordained. Likewise from the same source, c. 7.  
[Note: [Col. 0135] c. 95, *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*.—Anselm, book 7, c. 57. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 37. *Decretum*, part 6, c. 16. *Polycarpus*, book 2, title 32.]

When an exorcist is ordained, he is to receive from the bishop’s hand a little book in which the exorcisms are written, the bishop saying to him: “Receive it, commit it to memory [Note: [Col. 0135] omitted in the Gelasian Sacramentary.], and have authority to lay hands upon one possessed, whether baptized or a catechumen.”

### C. XVIII. How a reader is to be ordained. Likewise from the same Council, c. 8.  
[Note: [Col. 0135] c. 96, *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*.—Anselm, same place, c. 55. Ivo, same place, c. 38. *Decretum*, same place, c. 17.—*Polycarpus*, same place.]

When a reader is ordained, the bishop shall speak to the people concerning him, indicating his faith, life, and abilities. After this [Note: [Col. 0135] “this”: collected editions other than Basel.], with the people looking on, he shall hand him the book from which he is to read, saying *to him*: “Receive it, and be a reciter [Note: [Col. 0135] “reader”: Basel edition.] of the word of God; if you faithfully and profitably fulfill your office [Col. 0136C] [Note: [Col. 0135] added: “your”: collected editions other than Basel.], you shall have a share with those who have ministered the word of God [Note: [Col. 0135] added: “well”: Roman Ordinal.].”

### C. XIX. How a doorkeeper is to be ordained. Likewise from the same source, c. 9.  
[Note: [Col. 0135] c. 97, *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*.—Anselm, same place, c. 54. Ivo, *Panormia*, same place, c. 39. *Decretum*, same place, c. 18. *Polycarpus*, same place.]

When a doorkeeper is ordained, after he has been instructed by the archdeacon how he ought to conduct himself in the house of God, at the archdeacon’s prompting the bishop shall hand him the keys of the church from the altar, saying [Note: [Col. 0135] added: “thus”: Basel edition; “to him”: the other editions.]: “Act thus, as one who is to render an account to God for those things which are opened by these keys.”

[Col. 0137A] ### C. XX. How a psalmist is to be ordained. Likewise from the same Council, c. 10.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] Anselm, book 7, c. 53. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 40. *Decretum*, part 6, c. 19. *Polycarpus*, same place.]

A psalmist, that is, a singer, may undertake the office of singing without the bishop’s permission, by the command of a priest alone, the priest saying to him: “See that what you sing with your mouth you believe with your heart, and what you believe with your heart you confirm by your works.”

Gratian. Clerics are forbidden to let their hair grow; the top of their head ought to be shaved in the shape of a sphere.

Accordingly Pope Anicetus, to the bishops of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0137] Pseudo-Isidorian epistle. This chapter itself is derived from the *Liber pontificalis*.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, c. 46.]:

### C. XXI. Clerics are forbidden to let their hair grow.

Forbid, brothers, throughout all the churches of your regions, clerics, in accordance with the Apostle, to let their hair grow; rather, let them shave the top of their head in the shape [Col. 0137B] of a sphere.

### C. XXII. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Agde, c. 20.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] held in A.D. 506.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 28, c. 18.]

Clerics who let their hair grow are to be shorn by the archdeacon, even against their will if they refuse. Nor may they use or possess clothing [Note: [Col. 0137] “but clothing, or even footwear”: Basel edition.] or footwear except such as befits the religious life.

### C. XXIII. On the same matter. Likewise Gregory II, in the Council held at Rome in the Basilica of St Peter, c. 17.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] held in A.D. 731.—Anselm, book 10, c. 53.—Compare the Compilatio I, *Decretals*, title “On the life and conduct of clerics,” c. 3, and X, same title, c. 4. Nearly the same provisions are found in the Roman council held in A.D. 743, c. 8.]

If any cleric lets his hair hang loose [Note: [Col. 0137] “lets it hang loose”: Basel edition.], let him be anathema.

### C. XXIV. In what garments a nun is to be clothed when she is consecrated. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 11.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] c. 99, *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*.—Burchard, book 8, c. 23. Ivo, part 7, c. 43. *Polycarpus*, book 4, title 35.]

[Col. 0137C] When a consecrated virgin is presented to her bishop for consecration, she is to be dressed in such garments as she is always to use, appropriate to her profession and consecrated life.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] “her”: *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*.]

Gratian. Women dedicated to God are also forbidden to touch consecrated vessels and altar cloths, or to carry incense about the altars.

Accordingly Pope Soter, in his second letter to all the bishops of Italy [Note: [Col. 0137] A Pseudo-Isidorian epistle, whose source in this chapter is the *Liber pontificalis*.—Anselm, book 7, c. 240. Burchard, book 3, c. 215. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, c. 72, and part 3, c. 265. *Polycarpus*, book 3, title 9.]:

### C. XXV. Women are forbidden to touch altar vestments and consecrated vessels.

It has been reported to the Apostolic See that consecrated women or nuns among you touch sacred vessels [Col. 0138A] or consecrated altar cloths and carry incense about the altars. No sound-minded person can doubt that all these practices are wholly deserving of rebuke and condemnation. Therefore, by the authority of this holy see, we decree that you cut off all these practices utterly as soon as you can. And lest this pestilence [Note: [Col. 0137] “of this kind”: Basel edition.] spread more widely, we command that it be speedily wiped out through all the provinces.

### C. XXVI. Subdeacons may not enter the sanctuary. Likewise from the Council of Laodicea, c. 21.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] held between A.D. 347 and 381.—Anselm, book 7, c. 89, from Dionysius’s translation. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 105.]

Subdeacons [Note: [Col. 0137] “ministers”: Hispana Collection.] ought not to be permitted to enter the sanctuary or *secretarium*—which the Greeks call the *diaconium*—or to touch the Lord’s vessels.

[Col. 0138B] ### C. XXVII. On the same matter. Likewise from the same source, c. 22.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] Anselm, same place, c. 88.]

A minister ought not to wear an *orarium* [stole], nor to leave the doors [Note: [Col. 0137] “*Hostias*”: the genuine reading, found also in several manuscripts, is *ostia* (“doors”), but it has not been restored because of the gloss.] [Note: [Col. 0137] “doors”: Hispana Collection—“victims”: Lyons editions II and III.].

### C. XXVIII. On the same matter. Likewise from the same source, c. 23.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] Anselm, same place.]

Readers or psalmists ought not to wear *oraria* [stoles] and read or chant in that manner.

### C. XXIX. A woman is not permitted to teach men in an assembly. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Carthage, cc. 99 and 98.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] cc. 36 and 37, *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*.—Burchard, book 8, c. 83. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, c. 101 and part 8, c. 324.—Below, *De consecratione*, Distinction 4, c. 20.]

A woman, even if learned and holy, must not presume to teach men in an assembly. Nor may a layman dare to teach in the presence of clerics, unless they request it [Note: [Col. 0137] “approve it”: *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*.].

[Col. 0138C] ### C. XXX. Unconsecrated ministers may not touch the Lord’s vessels. Likewise from the Council of Agde, c. 66.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] This chapter, which is indeed very similar to cc. 25 and 26 of the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*, does not belong to the Council of Agde; it is an addition, as are all its canons after the forty-seventh.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 28, c. 64.]

Unconsecrated ministers ought not to be permitted to enter the sanctuary—which the Greeks call the *diaconium*—or to touch the Lord’s vessels.

### C. XXXI. Not every reader may carry the sacred vessels of the altar. Likewise from the First Council of Braga, c. 10.  
[Note: [Col. 0137] held in A.D. 561.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 45, c. 1.]

No reader may be permitted to carry the sacred vessels of the altar, nor may anyone else [Note: [Col. 0137] omitted in the Hispana Collection.], except those who have been ordained subdeacons by the bishop.
