[Col. 0139A] ### C. XXXII. On the same matter: that clerics are not to let their hair grow. Likewise from the Council of Pope Martin, c. 41.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] c. 41 among the chapters of Martin of Braga.—Compare c. 31 of this Distinction.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, c. 377.]

No one may touch the Lord’s vessels in the *secretarium* [Note: [Col. 0139] “sanctuary”: Basel edition.], except a subdeacon or acolyte. § 1. Nor [Note: [Col. 0139] c. 66 of Martin.—Ivo, part 6, c. 378.—Compare cc. 25 and 26 of the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*, that is, Fourth Council of Carthage, cc. 44–45.] ought clerics to let their hair grow and [Note: [Col. 0139] added: “thus”: collected editions other than Basel.] minister; rather, with shorn heads and uncovered ears, and wearing, according to Aaron [Note: [Col. 0139] Exodus, c. 41.], a robe reaching to the ankles, they are to be dressed in becoming attire.

[Col. 0140A] ### C. XXXIII. How bridegroom and bride are to be blessed. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 13.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] c. 101, *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 18, c. 12. Burchard, book 9, c. 5. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, c. 20; *Decretum*, part 8, cc. 6 and 143—the latter here in fact taken from the Council of Valence.—Compare below, c. 5, Cause 30, question 5.]

When the bridegroom and bride are to be blessed by the priest, they are to be presented by their parents or by their attendants; and, having received the blessing, they are to remain virgins that same night, out of reverence for the blessing itself.

## DISTINCTION XXIV

[Col. 0139]

[Col. 0139A] **GRATIAN**

**Part I.** It has been briefly shown how a bishop is to be examined and how he, together with those placed beneath him, is to be ordained. We must now consider whether priests and the rest are to be promoted without [Col. 0139B] examination. Paul writes thus concerning them to Timothy [Note: [Col. 0139] Epistle, c. 5.]: “Do not lay hands hastily upon anyone, and do nothing with prejudice, inclining to one side.”

### C. I. On the same matter. [PALEA.] From the decrees of Pope Sylvester, in the Roman Synod, c. 9.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] From the apocryphal constitution of Sylvester.—Anselm, book 7, c. 56. Burchard, book 5, c. 34. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, c. 43.]

“No acolyte or subdeacon [Note: [Col. 0139C] “Or subdeacon”: these words are not in the Roman synod under Sylvester, but occur in Burchard and Ivo, and in those Vatican manuscripts of Gratian which contain this [Col. 0139D] chapter. In the older copies it is absent; after the phrase “inclining to one side,” there follows immediately: “Let no one be ordained.”] may hand to others a thing consecrated by a priest [Note: [Col. 0139] added: “already”: Basel edition.]—for a minister is one thing, an assistant another—unless he merely supports that which the priest has placed upon him, blessed by the priest’s own word.”

### C. II. No cleric is to be ordained before probation. Likewise from the Third Council of Carthage, c. 22.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] held in A.D. 397.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 17, c. 14. Anselm, book 7, c. 88.]

[Col. 0139C] No one is to be ordained a cleric unless he has been tested either by examination of the bishops or by the testimony of the people [Note: [Col. 0139] “popular”: collected editions other than the first Basel edition.].

### C. III. Clerics of a church are to be promoted to the ministry of that same church. Likewise Pope Gelasius to Bishop Celestinus.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] The year of this letter of Gelasius is uncertain. It is read in Anselm, book 7, c. 92, and, though abbreviated, in the collection of Deusdedit, book 1, c. 141, from which Holstenius published it.]

The priests, deacons, and all the clerics of the city of Stomensis [Note: [Col. 0139] “Stoniensis”: Anselm.—“Histoniensis”: Deusdedit.] have presented us with a petition, reporting that in the church of the blessed martyr Bishop Eleutherius—which is shown to have been built in the parish [Note: [Col. 0140C] “Parish”: thus it is read in all ancient copies, printed as well as manuscript; in more recent printed editions *paroecia* had been substituted for this word. But it seemed necessary to retain the ancient reading, [Col. 0140D] especially since this word also has a most fitting Greek etymology.] of the aforesaid city—the priest who had been appointed has died, [Col. 0140A] and that Julian, deacon of that same church [Note: [Col. 0139] “basilica”: Anselm.], ought to be ordained in his place as soon as possible, for the sake of the solemnity of that place.

And therefore, dearest brother, if there is nothing in his life or conduct contrary to the provisions of the canons, you shall invest the aforesaid man with the [Note: [Col. 0139] “aforesaid”: Basel edition.] honor of the priesthood, knowing that you have made him a visitor in your own name, not a cardinal of the pontiff. Likewise you shall appoint the deacon Felicissimus to the ministry of that church, if his manner of life permits it, so that this place, most celebrated for its processions, may lack neither priest nor minister for the consecration of the mysteries [Note: [Col. 0139] “ministries”: collected editions other than Basel.].

### C. IV. Bishops are to be promoted upon examination by metropolitans and bishops. Likewise from the Council of Laodicea, c. 12.  
[Note: [Col. 0139] held between A.D. 347 and 381.—The Dionysian translation.—Burchard, book 1, c. 9. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 63.]

Those are to be raised to ecclesiastical rank by the judgment of the metropolitans and of the bishops who are nearby, namely those who have long been tested both in the word of faith and in the example of upright conduct.

[Col. 0140C] **Part II. Gratian.** Since, therefore, no one is to be ordained without examination, it must be considered in what manner and at what time the examination of priests and others in subordinate positions ought to take place.

On this subject, the following is read in the Council of Nantes [Note: [Col. 0139] The date of this council—called “Manetense” in the Basel edition and “Navatense” in the others—is uncertain. It is commonly said to have been held in A.D. 895, during the time of Pope Formosus; but since chapters 3 and 11 occur in book 7 of the *Capitularies*, it must be maintained that it is older than Benedict the Levite. Nor are there lacking historians who speak of a Council of Nantes held about A.D. 660.—Regino, book 1, c. 441. Burchard, book 2, c. 1. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 21. *Decretum*, part 6, c. 21. *Polycarpus*, book 2, title 29.], c. 11:

### C. V. Those to be ordained are to assemble on Wednesday for examination.

Whenever a bishop intends to conduct ordinations, all who wish to enter the sacred ministry are to be summoned to the city on the Wednesday before the ordination itself, [Col. 0141A] together with the archpriests [Note: [Col. 0141] “priests”: collected editions other than Basel.] who ought to present them. The bishop should then choose from among those at his side priests and other prudent men [Note: [Col. 0141] “appoint”: the original.], knowledgeable in divine law and trained in ecclesiastical enactments, to investigate diligently the life, family, homeland, age, education, and place where those to be ordained were brought up; whether they are well educated [Note: [Col. 0141] these are the very words of canon 2, Distinction 23.], whether they are instructed in the law of the Lord, and, before all else, whether they hold the Catholic faith firmly and can affirm it in simple words.

§ 1. Those to whom this is entrusted must take care not to depart from the truth through favor or because they have been enticed by desire for any gift, so as to present to the bishop’s hands for reception into sacred orders one who is unworthy or less fit. If they do so, both he who approached unworthily will be removed from [Col. 0141B] the altar, and those who attempted to sell the gift of the Holy Spirit, already condemned before God, will lose ecclesiastical rank.

§ 2. Therefore let them be examined carefully for three consecutive days; and on Saturday let those found approved be presented to the bishop.

[Col. 0142A] Gratian. Moreover, a bishop must not presume to ordain anyone without the counsel of the clergy and the testimony of the people.

Accordingly, in the Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 22, we read [Note: [Col. 0141] c. 10, *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 18, c. 21.]:

### C. VI. A bishop is not to ordain clerics without the counsel of his clergy.

A bishop is not to ordain clerics without the counsel [Note: [Col. 0141] “council”: Basel and Lyons editions II and III; “of his fellow priests”: Ballerini.] of his clergy, so that he may seek the concurrence and testimony of the citizens.

**Part III. Gratian.** The question is what ought to be done about those who have been promoted without examination.

On this matter the following is read in the Council of Pope Martin [Note: [Col. 0141] In Martin of Braga, among the chapters, c. 24.—Canon 9 of the Council of Nicaea—for Martin translated it—is read below, Distinction 81, c. 4, and in Dionysius’s translation in Anselm, book 8, c. 13.]:

### C. VII. Concerning those ordained without examination who later confess their sins.

If any priests or deacons have been ordained without any examination, [Col. 0142B] or, when examined, have confessed their criminal sins [Note: [Col. 0141] “have concealed”: Hispana Collection.], or have after ordination been exposed by others, they are to be cast out of the clergy.  
[Note: [Col. 0141D] “Have confessed”: in the original the reading is “have not confessed,” followed by “and after ordination,” etc. But in the Council of Nicaea, c. 9, from which this chapter seems to have been taken, the text stands without the negation, as it does here and below [Col. 0142D] in Distinction 81, c. “If anyone without.”]

§ 1. The same rule is to be observed concerning the entire order of clerics; for the holy Catholic Church safeguards for itself that which is irreproachable [Note: [Col. 0141] “will safeguard”: same source—“may safeguard”: collected editions other than Basel.].

## DISTINCTION XXV

[Col. 0141]

[Col. 0141B] **GRATIAN**

**Part I.** It has been briefly shown that no one is to be ordained without examination. But what pertains to a bishop, and what to each person below him, Isidore, bishop of Seville, writes in a letter to Ludifred [Note: [Col. 0142D] This entire letter is found in a codex of the library of the Dominican monastery.] [Note: [Col. 0141] This letter to Ludifred—or Leofred, Leudefred, or Laudefred—is attributed principally to Isidore because it is generally transmitted in Pseudo-Isidorian manuscripts and its copies differ greatly from one another. Saint Leudefred—also, but incorrectly, called Leudeficus—subscribed the Fourth Council of Toledo. The letter itself, apparently added by a later hand, is read at the end of book 7 of Anselm under the title “Isidore of Seville to Laudefred, bishop of Corduba, concerning all ecclesiastical orders”; then in Burchard, book 3, c. 50; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 41; *Decretum*, part 6, c. 20; and, mutilated, in Gregory’s *Polycarpus*.]—as follows:

### C. I. What is the office of bishops and of the others in the Church.

Having read Your Holiness’s letter, I rejoiced that I learned from its report of your desired welfare. As to the matters which the language of your discourse has endeavored to set forth in what follows, I give thanks to God [Note: [Col. 0141] added: “my”: Basel edition.] that you devote concern to the pastoral office and inquire how ecclesiastical duties are to be ordered. Although all these things are known to your prudence, nevertheless, because you consult me in brotherly affection, I shall explain them as far as I am able, and shall state what pertains to each of all the ranks of the Church.

§ 1. The keys of the church pertain to the doorkeeper, so that he may close and open God’s temple, and guard everything within and without; receive the faithful, and exclude [Note: [Col. 0141] “cast out”: Anselm.] the excommunicated and unbelieving.

§ 2. It pertains to the exorcist to retain the exorcisms by memory and to lay hands upon the possessed and catechumens in exorcizing them.

§ 3. It pertains to the acolyte to prepare the lights in the sanctuary; he carries the candle, and he prepares the requisites for the Eucharist and the chalices [Note: [Col. 0141] “of the chalice”: Anselm and Ivo.] for the subdeacons.

§ 4. It pertains to the psalmist to perform the office of singing: to say blessings, praises, the sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0141] “sacrifice”: same sources.], responsories, and whatever belongs to the skill of singing.

§ 5. It pertains to the reader to pronounce the lessons and preach to the people those things which the prophets foretold.

§ 6. It pertains to the subdeacon to carry the chalice and paten to Christ’s altar and hand them to the Levites, and to minister to them; likewise, to hold the cruet and [Col. 0143A] water [Note: [Col. 0143] “with water”: Ivo.—In the following phrase, “priests”: collected editions other than Basel.], the hand-basin and the hand-towel, and to provide water for the bishop, priest, and Levites to wash their hands before the altar.

§ 7. It pertains to the deacon to assist the priests and minister in all that is done in Christ’s sacraments: namely in baptism, in chrism, and with paten and chalice; likewise to bring and arrange the offerings upon the altar; also to set and cover the Lord’s table, carry the cross, and preach the Gospel and the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0143] added: “to the people”: collected editions other than the first Basel edition.]. For just as readers are commanded to proclaim the Old Testament, so deacons are commanded to proclaim the New. The office of prayers and the recitation [Col. 0143B] of names also pertain to him. He gives the warning that ears be attentive to God [Note: [Col. 0143] Anselm: “he prepares ears for God,” and the rest as in Ivo; compare the corrections.—“clearly”: Roman edition, by printer’s error.]; he urges them to cry out [Note: [Col. 0143C] “To cry out”: in the letter of Blessed Isidore and in Ivo it reads: “he urges prayer, he cries out, and he announces peace.”]; he bestows peace and himself announces [Note: [Col. 0143] added: “festivals”: Basel edition—“may announce”: Argentinian and first Venetian editions.].

§ 8. It pertains to the priest to consecrate the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood upon God’s altar, to say prayers, and to bless God’s gifts.

§ 9. It pertains to the bishop to consecrate basilicas, anoint the altar, and make chrism. He distributes the aforesaid offices and ecclesiastical orders, blesses consecrated virgins, and, although each person takes precedence in particular matters, he nevertheless is the chief director in all.

§ 10. These are the orders and ministries of clerics; yet by pontifical authority they are apportioned under the care of the archdeacon and the diligence of the primicerius and treasurer [Note: [Col. 0143] “treasurer”: Basel edition.].

§ 11. For the archdeacon commands the subdeacons and Levites; the following ministries pertain to him: directing the Levites’ vesting of the altar, the care of incense [Note: [Col. 0143] Anselm adds: “and of carrying the sacrifice to the altar; the care of the subdeacons in bringing things to the altar.”], and necessary oversight of the sacrifice; determining which Levite is to read the Apostle and the Gospel, which is to say the prayers, or chant the responsories [Note: [Col. 0143] “the responsory, and afterward the solemnity”: Ivo.] on Sundays or feast days. The care, ordering, and disputes of parishioners [Note: [Col. 0143C] “Parishioners”: the letter reads *parochitanorum*, as it does slightly below; this term is frequent in ancient copies of the Councils of Toledo.] [Note: [Col. 0143] “parishioners”: Anselm.] also fall under his charge. For repairing the diocesan basilicas, he makes recommendations to the priest; by the bishop’s command he inspects the parishes and the ornaments or [Note: [Col. 0143] “and”: collected editions other than Basel.] property of the parish basilicas. He reports to the bishop the records of the churches’ liberties; receives the money collected from communion and brings it to the bishop; and distributes to the clerics their respective shares.

The archdeacon reports to the bishop the offenses of deacons. He announces to the priest in the sanctuary the days of fasts and festivals, and they are publicly proclaimed in church by him [Note: [Col. 0143D] “Are proclaimed”: corrected thus from a Gratian manuscript and from the original. Previously the text read “are proclaimed” in the plural.]. When the archdeacon is absent, the next deacon performs his duties.

§ 12. The archpriest [Note: [Col. 0143D] From this point through the phrase “To the primicerius” [Col. 0144C] these words are not in Isidore’s letter itself, nor in the *Panormia*, nor in Burchard [Note: [Col. 0143] nor in Anselm.]; and X, title 1, chapter “On the office of an archpriest,” cites them from the Council of Toledo.] must know that he is subject to the archdeacon and must obey his commands as those of his own bishop [Note: [Col. 0143] added: “himself”: the same editions.]. His particular ministry is to exercise oversight above all priests placed in the order, to remain constantly in church, and, when his bishop is absent, to celebrate the solemnities of Mass in his stead [Col. 0144B] and say the collects, or appoint someone else to do so [Note: [Col. 0143] Basel edition: “that man.”].

§ 13. Acolytes, exorcists, psalmists, and readers pertain to the primicerius; also, giving the signal for the clerics’ office, ensuring uprightness of life, and diligently directing and performing the office [Note: [Col. 0143] “singing”: Ivo.—Collected editions other than Basel.], determining which cleric ought to say the lessons, blessings, psalm, praises, offertory [Note: [Col. 0143] The word “offertory” is absent from the collected editions other than the first Basel. In the Venetian I and II, Lyons, and Paris editions, it reads: “the responsory of the offices.”], and responsories. Also his responsibility are the order and manner of chanting [Note: [Col. 0143] “singing”: editions other than Basel.] in choir according to the solemnity of the seasons [Note: [Col. 0143] “and season”: Anselm, Ivo, and the collected editions other than Basel.], and the arrangements for carrying the lamps.

If anything is needed [Note: [Col. 0143] “is needed”: collected editions other than Basel.] for repairing basilicas in the city, he reports it to the priest [Note: [Col. 0143] “may report”: Basel edition—Ivo.]. He sends the bishop’s letters concerning fast days to the parishioners [Note: [Col. 0143] “parishioners”: collected editions other than Basel.] through the doorkeepers. He disciplines clerics whom he knows to be offending; and concerning those whom he cannot correct [Col. 0144C] he reports their offenses to the bishop’s attention. He appoints basilica clerics [Note: [Col. 0143] “basilicarii”: Anselm and Ivo—Basel edition.] and organizes the register [Note: [Col. 0143] “registers”: Ivo—Basel edition.].

When the primicerius is absent, the person next to him either by law or by learning is to inquire into [Note: [Col. 0143] “carry out”: Basel edition.] the aforesaid duties [Note: [Col. 0143] “stated”: collected editions other than Basel.] [Note: [Col. 0144D] “By learning”: in the original [Note: [Col. 0143] and in Anselm.] the reading is: “certain in learning for carrying these things out.”].  
[Note: [Col. 0144C] In the first Vatican manuscript the reading is “the clerics of the city”; and after “report” there is added: “for the rest who are outside the city pertain to the archdeacon’s care,” as likewise in several other copies [Note: [Col. 0143] and in the Basel edition.].]

§ 14. It pertains to the treasurer to arrange the basilicas and [Note: [Col. 0143] “and” is absent in the collected editions other than Basel.] doorkeepers, prepare incense, oversee the making of chrism, arrange the baptistery, and prepare lights in the sanctuary and at sacrifices [Note: [Col. 0143] “prepare the sacrifice”: Anselm.].

[Col. 0145A] **Part II. Gratian.** From this letter it is clear what belongs to each office. There is also another distinction of bishops, priests, and deacons, made by Clement in his third letter [Note: [Col. 0145] An apocryphal epistle. Anselm, book 7, c. 81. The words of this chapter are drawn from Clement’s *Recognitions*, themselves also spurious.], as follows:

### C. II. What ought to be heard from bishops, priests, and deacons.

One ought to listen most attentively to the bishop and receive from him instruction in the faith; seek counsels for life from priests; and from deacons, the order of discipline.

Gratian. A priest also wears the *orarium* around both shoulders; but a deacon wears it around the left alone, so that he may move about more freely in service.

[Col. 0145B] Accordingly, in the Fourth Council of Toledo, c. 40 [Note: [Col. 0145] held in A.D. 633.—Anselm, book 7, c. 86.]:

### C. III. Why a Levite wears the *orarium* over one shoulder only.

A Levite ought to wear one *orarium* over his left shoulder, because he prays—that is, preaches; but he ought to keep the right side free, so that he may move more readily [Note: [Col. 0145] “being free”: Hispana Collection—Anselm.] to perform priestly service.

## III. Part

**Gratian.** Now, proceeding through the individual grades in order, let us briefly consider who may ascend from which orders to which grade; who may be restored after a fall and who may not; for what faults they deserve to be deposed from their own grade; by whose accusation and on whose testimony they may be convicted; and by whose judgment they are to be acquitted or condemned.

§ 1. First, beginning with the pontifical grade, let us diligently investigate what sort of man ought to be ordained bishop [col. 0145C], following the Apostle’s rule, which he writes concerning this matter to Timothy and Titus, saying: “A bishop must be blameless” [1 Tim. 3:2]—that is, not liable to reproach [from the interlinear gloss on this passage]. This is addressed to Timothy. But to Titus [Titus 1:7]: “A bishop must be without crime,” which, as Jerome writes to Oceanus [and below, in the same distinction, C. VI], is the same thing.

§ 2. By the name “crime,” however, any sin is understood [col. 0146A]. Hence Jerome says in the same epistle:

> It is almost contrary to nature that anyone should be without sin; but such a man should be chosen that, in comparison with him, the others may be called a flock.

[Editorial note, col. 0145C: “It is contrary”: approximately thus in the ordinary gloss at the word *irreprehensibilem* (“blameless”); it is a kind of epitome of Blessed Jerome’s words in his letter to Oceanus, explaining the Apostle’s passages to Timothy and Titus.]

In the epistle to Titus [and in the ordinary gloss at the corresponding passage in the epistle to Timothy], “crime” is called a criminal sin or criminal infamy. Hence it is read there:

> A crime is a charge—that is, a sin worthy of accusation and condemnation.

[Editorial note, col. 0145D: “Hence”: that is, not in Blessed Paul, but in the ordinary gloss on Blessed Paul’s passage. The statement is taken from Blessed Augustine, *Tractate 41 on John*; his words are also found in Bede on the same passage of Blessed Paul and below, Distinction 81, C. I, “The Apostle.”]

§ 3. The command that the man chosen as bishop be without accusation is to be understood not of the time before baptism, but after baptism: namely, so that from the time of baptism onward the consciousness of no crime may gnaw at his mind.

[Variant: *crimine* (“crime”) in the editions collated by O.; Böhm.]

[Editorial note, col. 0145D: “May gnaw”: the common editions continued, “Hence Jerome writes in the same letter to Titus.” These words were inserted, since they are found in no manuscript; they occur below in the same distinction before C. I.]

§ 4. The designation “crime,” however, sometimes has a broad scope, embracing every sin that proceeds from deliberation. Hence Bede, commenting on the Epistle of James, says [col. 0146B]:

> The sins committed through ignorance or human weakness, he says and commands us to confess to one another, because they are easily forgiven; but whatever is done through deliberation is forgiven only through repentance.

[Editorial note, cols. 0146C–D: “Hence Bede”: in his commentary on James 5, at the words “Confess to one another,” it reads: “In this saying there must be such discrimination that we confess our daily and lighter sins to one another among our equals, and believe that they are saved through their daily prayer; but let us disclose the uncleanness of more serious leprosy to the priest according to the law and, according to his judgment, take care to be purified in the manner and for the length of time he commands.”]

Hence Augustine also says:

> No sin is so venial that it does not become criminal while it is pleasing.

[Editorial note, col. 0146D: “No sin”: in the ordinary gloss on 1 Corinthians 11, at the words “he will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord,” this statement is cited from Blessed Augustine, *Homily 24 on John*, in these words: “No sin is venial while it pleases, however small; just as no mortal sin is judged such if it truly displeases.”]

At other times, however, it signifies only those offenses which, once committed, are sufficient for condemnation.

§ 5. For many acts proceed from deliberation which, unless they are repeated frequently and developed into a habit, although they weigh upon a person after death, nevertheless do not destroy him eternally; for even if they are called crimes in some sense, they are not deadly or capital.

Hence Augustine, in a homily on purgatorial fire [*Sermon 41 on the Saints, or on the Souls of the Dead*], explaining the Apostle’s words, “If anyone builds upon this foundation wood, hay, and stubble,” and so forth, says [col. 0146C]:

> Many people, misunderstanding this passage, are deceived by false security, believing that, if they build capital crimes upon the foundation of Christ, those sins themselves can be cleansed through transitory fire and that they may afterward attain eternal life. This interpretation, dearest brothers, must be corrected, because those who flatter themselves in this way deceive themselves. By that transitory fire of which the Apostle says [1 Cor. 3], “He himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire,” not capital sins but slight sins are cleansed. Some of these should be mentioned, if not all, lest anyone try vainly to excuse himself and say that he does not know which are the lesser sins or which are capital crimes.

[Variant: *sic* (“thus”) in the editions collated by O.]

[Variant: the Basel edition adds *quasi* (“as it were”) before *minuta* (“slight sins”).]

[Variant: *minuta* (“slight”) for *minora* (“lesser”) in the editions collated by O.]

§ 6. Although the Apostle has mentioned many capital sins, nevertheless, lest we seem to cause despair, we briefly state what they are: sacrilege, homicide, adultery, fornication [absent from the original], false witness, theft, robbery, pride, envy, avarice; and anger, if retained for a long time, and drunkenness, if habitual, are counted among them.

[Variants: *computabitur* (“will be counted”), Basel edition; *computatur* (“is counted”), editions collated by O. and the original.]

For whoever recognizes that any one of these sins rules within him [col. 0147B], unless he has amended himself worthily, and, if he has had time, has done penance for a long period, given abundant alms, and abstained from those sins, cannot be cleansed by that transitory fire of which the Apostle speaks; rather, eternal flame will torment him without any remedy.

[Variant: *aliqua* (“any sins”) for *aliquod* (“any one sin”) in the original.]

[Variant: the editions collated by O. add *non* (“not”) before “given abundant alms.”]

[Variant: *trucidabit* (“will slaughter”) for *cruciabit* (“will torment”) in the Basel edition.]

§ 7. Although the slight sins are known to everyone, nevertheless, since it would take too long to enumerate them all, we must name at least some of them.

Whenever anyone takes more food or drink than is necessary, let him know that this belongs among slight sins; whenever he speaks more than he ought, or keeps silent more than is expedient; whenever he irritates poor people who beg importunately; whenever, though physically healthy, he wishes to dine while others are fasting, or, given over to sleep, rises too late for church; whenever, except for the desire for children, he has intercourse with his wife; whenever he has been slow to seek out prisoners shut up in prison or placed in chains; whenever he has been slow to visit the sick; if he has neglected to recall those at discord to harmony; if he has irritated a neighbor, wife, son, or servant more than he ought; if he has been more flattering than is expedient; if, from choice or necessity, he has wished to flatter any person of higher rank; if, while the poor are hungry, he has prepared excessively luxurious or costly banquets for himself; if in church or outside church he has occupied himself with idle tales, for which an account must be rendered on the day of judgment; if, when we swear carelessly and then cannot fulfill this because of some necessity, we certainly commit perjury; and if with complete ease or rashness we utter curses, although it is written [1 Cor. 6:10]: “Nor shall revilers possess the kingdom of God.”

[Editorial and variant notes: The Basel edition reads *et* (“and”) for *aut* (“or”) in “food or drink.” The editions collated by O. read *est* (“is”) for *sit* (“may be”) in “than is necessary.” The Basel edition and Böhm read *pauperem petentem* (“a poor person begging”) for *pauperes importune petentes* (“poor people begging importunately”). *Clausos, aut in vinculis* (“shut up, or in chains”) is an editorial restoration. The editions collated by O. omit *et* (“and”) before “the sick.” The same editions read *oportet* (“is fitting”) for *expedit* (“is expedient”) after “more flattering.” The Basel edition reads *pro aliqua necessitate* (“because of some necessity”) for *per aliquam necessitatem* (“through some necessity”).]

## C. IV. What the venial sins are that are cleansed after this life

Also Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 39.

[Editorial note: A work not of unimpeached faith. Compare Anselm, book 11, chapter 159.]

As each person departs from this life, so is he presented at judgment. Yet concerning certain light faults it must be believed that there is a purgatorial fire before judgment, because Truth says [Matt. 12:32]: “If anyone has spoken blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him either in this age or in the age to come.”

[Variant: *blasphemias* (“blasphemies”) for *blasphemiam* (“blasphemy”) in the editions collated by O.]

In this saying it is understood that certain faults can be forgiven in this age and certain others in the future. For when something is denied of one thing, the consequent meaning is clear: that it is granted concerning certain others.

Yet, as I have said, this must be believed possible only concerning small and very slight sins, such as habitual idle speech, immoderate laughter, or the sin involved in household care—which is scarcely conducted without fault even by those who know how they ought to avoid fault—or an error of ignorance in matters that are not serious. All these weigh upon a person even after death if they have not been remitted while he was still in this life.

[Variant: the Basel edition and Böhm add *rei* (“of the matter”) after *curae* (“care”).]

[Variant: *etsi* (“although”) for *si* (“if”) in the Strasbourg edition.]

[Variant: the editions collated by O., except the Basel edition, add *in morte* (“at death”) after “not at all.”]

## C. V. On the same subject. PALEA

[Also Augustine, *On True and False Penance*, chapter 18.]

[Editorial note: Learned men long ago warned that the book *On True and False Penance* is not Augustine’s. In the Basel edition this Palea has no inscription.]

He who postpones the fruit of conversion to another age will first be cleansed by the fire of purification. Although this fire is not eternal, it is nevertheless grievous in a wonderful manner. For it surpasses every punishment that anyone has ever suffered in this life, or can suffer.

[Variant: *purgandus est* (“must be cleansed”) for *purgabitur* (“will be cleansed”), Böhm.]

[Variant: *superat* (“surpasses”) for *excellit* (“exceeds”), the same.]

[Editorial note: “Or can suffer”: these words are not in the original, nor below in *On Penance*, Distinction 7, final chapter, concluding section, where the same passage is repeated.]

[Variant: “can suffer” is absent from the Basel edition.]

**Gratian.** At other times, however, it signifies only those offenses whose infamy is perpetual.

Hence Jerome writes in the same epistle to Titus, chapter 1:

[Editorial note: In his commentary on Titus 1:6.]

## C. VI. From the day of baptism, one who is to be ordained bishop must be found without crime

First, therefore, a bishop is commanded to be without crime, which I think is expressed in other words to Timothy as “blameless”: not that he must be without any crime only at the time when he is to be ordained and have washed away former stains by a new manner of life, but that from the time when he was reborn in Christ no consciousness of sin may gnaw at him.

[Variant: *conversione* (“conversion”) for *conversatione* (“manner of life”) in the Basel edition.]

[Variant: *mordeatur* (“bite him”) for *remordeatur* (“gnaw at him”) in the editions collated by O.]

For how can the ruler of a church remove evil from its midst when he himself has fallen into a similar offense? Or with what freedom can he rebuke a sinner when he silently answers himself that he has committed the same things which he rebukes?

[Variant: *delictum simile* (“a similar offense”) for *dilecto simili*—an evident corruption—in the editions collated by O.]

**Gratian.** Behold: one who is to be ordained bishop [col. 0150A] must be free from crime not only at the time of his ordination, but throughout all the time after baptism.

# DISTINCTION XXVI

[Col. 0149]

## GRATIAN

### I. Part

In both epistles there follows: “the husband of one wife” [1 Tim. 3:2; Titus 1:6]—namely, after baptism, not before baptism.

Hence Jerome writes to Oceanus, Letter 83:

[Editorial note, col. 0149C: The opinions of this chapter and the following one are indeed those of the Fathers cited, namely Jerome and Augustine; the actual words, however, appear rather to have been taken from Bede’s collections and from the ordinary gloss—this chapter from 1 Timothy 3 and the following one from Titus 1.]

## C. I. After baptism, the man to be ordained bishop must be monogamous

“The husband of one wife,” that is, monogamous after baptism. For if before baptism he also had a wife who died, this is not imputed to him, since neither fornications nor any other things that occurred previously now harm a man who has become wholly new.

[Variants: *imputabitur* (“will be imputed”), Basel edition; *imputetur* (“let it be imputed”), the other collated editions.]

[Editorial note: “To a wholly new man” is absent from the ordinary gloss on this passage of Timothy and from the Basel edition.]

## C. II. He who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism is not to be ordained

Augustine, however, testifies to the contrary, writing on the Epistle to Titus.

[Editorial note: From the ordinary gloss on Titus 1, though the opinion is taken from Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 18. Anselm, book 9, chapter 59; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 66; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 294; Polycarp, book 2, title 31; below, Causa 28, question 3, chapter 2.]

They understand more acutely who have judged that even a man who, while a catechumen or pagan, had one wife and after baptism another, is not to be ordained, because the matter concerns a sacrament, not a sin.

[Variant: the editions collated by O. read: “a pagan who before baptism had one wife and after baptism another.”]

[Editorial note, cols. 0149C–D: After “sin” there followed, “because of the sanctity of the sacrament, just as if a woman,” and so forth. This entire passage has been restored from the ordinary gloss, for in Blessed Augustine and the other collectors it is still fuller.]

For in baptism all sins are forgiven, and the man who said, “If a virgin marries, she does not sin” [1 Cor. 7:32], sufficiently made clear that marriage is not a sin. But because of the sanctity of the sacrament, just as a woman who was defiled while a catechumen cannot after baptism be consecrated among God’s virgins, so it has not unreasonably seemed that a twice-married man did not sin, but lost the norm of the sacrament necessary not for the merit of life but for the sign of ecclesiastical ordination.

And as the many wives of the ancient Fathers signified the churches that were to come from all nations, subject to one husband, that is, Christ, so our prelate—that is, a bishop who is the husband of one wife—signifies the unity drawn from all nations and subject to the one husband, Christ.

[Variant: the same editions read *Sicut episcopus* (“Just as a bishop”) for “our prelate, that is, bishop.”]

### II. Part

§ 1. Therefore, just as it is not lawful to serve two masters [Matt. 6:24], so it is not lawful to apostatize from the one God and go over into another’s superstition.

## C. III. A man is proved twice-married if he had one wife before baptism and another after baptism

Also Innocent I, to Rufus and Eusebius and the other bishops of Macedonia, Letter XXII, chapter 2.

[Editorial note: Written A.D. 414. Burchard, book 4, chapter 98; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 1, chapter 292, and part 8, chapter 303; Polycarp, book 6, title 4.]

It is then proposed that a man ought not to be called twice-married who, while a catechumen, had and lost a wife, if after baptism he obtained another; and that she who was joined to the new man should be regarded as the first, because that marriage was washed away with the other crimes by the sacrament of baptism.

[Variant: *opponitur* (“it is objected”) for *ponitur* (“it is proposed”) in the editions collated by O.]

[Variant: the Basel edition adds *unam* (“one”) after “wife.”]

[Variant: *per* (“through”) also in Merlin’s Isidore.]

[Variant: *ablatum* (“taken away”) for *ablutum* (“washed away”) in the editions collated by O.]

But when this is said of one wife, certainly, if he had three wives while still in the old man, she who is fourth after baptism will, by this interpretation, be the first, and she who was taken in the fourth place will likewise receive the name of virgin.

[Editorial note, col. 0150C: “In the old man, wives”: thus in all the manuscripts and in Burchard and Ivo, part 1, chapter 292, although the original and the same Ivo, part 8, chapter 303, read somewhat differently and more obscurely.]

[Variant: *virginisque* (“and of a virgin”) in the original as printed by Coustant.]

Who, I ask, does not see that this is contrary to the Apostle’s command [Titus 1:6], who says that a priest ought to be made “the husband of one wife”?

But it is objected that in baptism everything whatsoever that was done in the old man is dissolved.

[Editorial note: “Everything” is absent from the *Collectio Hispana*.]

[Variant: *lotum* (“washed”) for *solutum* (“dissolved”) in the *Collectio Hispana* and Merlin’s Isidore.]

Tell me—with your leave I speak—are only crimes forgiven in baptism, or also those things which are accomplished according to the Lord’s commands and God’s institutions?

[Variants: the editions collated by O. read *ut loquar* (“that I may speak”); Ivo reads *loquar* (“I may speak”); in Böhm *an* (“whether”) follows, although it is absent from the original.]

[Variant: *legis* (“the law’s”) for *Domini* (“the Lord’s”) in the original as printed by Coustant.]

Is taking a wife a crime, or is it not a crime? If it is a crime, then—with the foregoing pardon for my words—the one who commanded in Paradise that crimes be committed, when he himself blessed them, will be the author of guilt.

[Variant: the editions collated by O. add *ut cum* (“so that with”) before the parenthesis.]

[Editorial note, col. 0150D: In the original and the other collectors it reads: “in Paradise, when he himself joined them, he blessed them.”]

But if it is not a crime, because it would be wicked to call criminal what God instituted, and Solomon added [Prov. 19:14], “Indeed, a wife is prepared for a man by God,” how can what is read to have been brought to completion by God as author be believed to have been forgiven among crimes?

[Variant: *junxit* (“joined”) for *instituit* (“instituted”) in the original.]

[Variant: *est* (“is”) for *sit* (“would be”) in the editions collated by O.]

[Variant: *commissum* (“committed”) for *dimissum* (“forgiven”) in the Basel edition.]

What is determined concerning the children of such persons? Will they not be admitted to a share in the inheritance [compare below, Causa 28, question 1, chapter 1] because they were born from her who was a wife before baptism? Will they be called either natural children or bastards because no marriage is legitimate except that which, as you think, is undertaken after baptism?

[Variants: *fuerit* (“has been”), Basel editions; *fuerat* (“had been”), the other collated editions, for *fuit* (“was”).]

When the Lord himself was questioned by the Jews whether it was lawful to dismiss a wife, and explained that it ought not to be done, he added [Matt. 19:6]: “Therefore what God has joined, let no human being separate.”

[Editorial note: The editions collated by O. read “those whom God has joined,” omitting *ergo* (“therefore”), which is found only in the Basel edition.]

[Variants: *At* (“But”), Böhm; *an* (“whether”), Strasbourg, Venice I, Nuremberg, Lyon, and Antwerp editions, for *Ac* (“And”).]

And lest he be thought to have spoken of those who obtain wives after baptism, let him remember that this was both asked by Jews and answered to Jews.

[Editorial note, cols. 0151C–D: Burchard and Ivo, part 1, read the feminine: “those women who obtain husbands after baptism.” The original, Ivo, part 8, the *Panormia*, and below, Causa 28, question 1, chapter “Whether,” read the masculine: “those who obtain wives after baptism.” Nothing has been changed because of the gloss.]

[Variant: *quae* (“women who”) in the original as printed by Coustant and in the Strasbourg, Paris, and Basel editions; the Basel edition then adds *uxorem* (“a wife”).]

§ 2. I ask—and I ask with concern—if the wife of a man who was first a catechumen and later a believer is one and the same woman, and he had children by her while he was a catechumen and then other children while he was a believer, are they to be called brothers, or are they to have no share in the division of the inheritance after their father’s death, because spiritual regeneration is thought to have taken away from them the name of children?

[Variant: the editions collated by O. add *filios* (“children”) after “other.”]

Since it is absurd to think and judge so, what—an evil thing—is the reason for defending this and vaunting it by empty opinion rather than strengthening it by any authority, when what the law commanded and God joined cannot be counted among sins?

[Variant: Ivo reads: “what reason is there for defending this evil and approving an empty opinion?” The *Collectio Hispana* reads: “what reason is there for defending this evil and approving an empty opinion?”]

[Variants after “God”: Merlin’s Isidore adds *et lex junxit* (“and the law joined”); Ivo reads *conjunxit* (“joined together”); the Basel edition *subjunxit* (“subjoined”); the other editions *adjunxit* (“added”); Böhm *injunxit* (“enjoined”).]

§ 3. Or if a catechumen pursued virtues, followed humility, maintained patience, gave alms, rescued persons destined for death by any means, abhorred adulteries, and maintained chastity, I ask whether he loses these things when he becomes a believer because baptism is thought to remove everything the old man had done.

[Variants: *qui* (“who”), Strasbourg, Basel, Venice I, and Nuremberg editions; *quis* (“anyone”) is absent from the other collated editions. In what follows, all use the past tense: “pursued,” and so forth.]

Let us consider the Gentile Cornelius [Acts 10], devoted to prayers and alms, hearing an angel through revelation and seeing Peter himself. Were these things taken away from him through baptism, on account of which baptism appears to have been granted him?

[Editorial note, cols. 0151D–0152C: “And Peter himself”: in Innocent’s *Codex canonum* and in Burchard it reads, “and to have seen alms, the revelation, and Peter himself.” In Innocent himself as printed in the conciliar volumes: “to have seen through revelation the angel and Peter himself.” In Ivo: “to have seen Peter himself by revelation.”]

[Variant: *ei* (“from him”) for *illi* (“from that man”) in the Basel edition.]

If this is believed, believe me, there is no slight error, for whatever has been done well and observed according to legal commands cannot perish for those who do it.

§ 4. Therefore the union of marriage, since it is effected by God’s command, cannot be called a sin; and what is not a sin must not at all be believed to be dissolved among sins. It will therefore be sound to judge that the designation “former wife” cannot be abolished, since what was fulfilled by God’s will was not forgiven as sin.

[Editorial and variant notes: The words “be believed” are absent from the original; conversely, *solvi* (“to be dissolved”) is absent from Ivo. Ivo adds *dimissum* (“forgiven”), at which point his chapter ends. The Basel edition reads *abolere* (“to abolish”) for *aboleri* (“to be abolished”). The original reads *quia* (“because”) for *quod* (“what”).]

## C. IV. In baptism guilt is forgiven; the law of marriage is not abolished

Also Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I, final chapter [chapter 80].

[Editorial note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 64; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 291.]

Only one union, and not a repeated one, is permitted us; and even in marriage there is a law: not to repeat marriage and not to obtain union with a second spouse.

It seems strange to many why even marriages repeated before baptism create impediments to the choice for office and the prerogative of ordination, when even offenses ordinarily cease to be an obstacle if they have been remitted through the sacrament of washing.

[Variant: *quum* (“although/when”) for *cur* (“why”) in the editions collated by O.]

[Editorial note, cols. 0152C–D: “Repeated”: in Blessed Ambrose this passage is read in different ways. The old editions have *iterato conjugio* (“by a repeated marriage”); the more recent have *iterati conjugii* (“of a repeated marriage”), as do the *Panormia* and Ivo. They agree, however, in what follows, reading: “generate impediments to the choice for office and the prerogative of ordination.”]

[Variant: *electionis* (“of the choice”) for *electioni* (“to the choice”) in the Basel editions.]

But we must understand that in baptism guilt can be forgiven, while law cannot be abolished.

[Variant: the same editions add *conjungi* (“to be joined”) after “law.”]

In marriage there is not guilt but law. Therefore what belongs to guilt is relaxed in baptism; what belongs to law is not dissolved in marriage. How, moreover, can one be an exhorter to widowhood who has himself entered marriages repeatedly?

**Gratian.** John the Baptist also, when he forbade Herod an incestuous union, saying [Matt. 14:4], “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife,” clearly showed that marriages exist among unbelievers. Hence it is understood that those called twice-married are not only persons who enter repeated marriages after baptism, but also those proved to have had one wife before baptism and another afterward.

§ 1. A twice-married man, moreover, should not be ordained priest, not because he sinned by taking a second wife, but because he has been deprived of the priestly prerogative.

Hence Ambrose, writing to the people of Vercelli, book X, Letter 82, says:

[Editorial note: Written after the death of Limenius, bishop of Vercelli, A.D. 371. In the inscriptions the editions collated by O. add “in a letter.” Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 63; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 290.]

## C. V. A twice-married man does not sin, but is deprived of the priestly prerogative

He who is without crime and is the husband of one wife is bound to undertake the law of the priesthood. But he who has repeated marriage does not bear the guilt of defilement, yet is deprived of the priestly prerogative.

# DISTINCTION XXVII

[Col. 0153]

## GRATIAN

### I. Part

Since a bishop is commanded to be the husband of one wife, the question is asked whether this should be understood of the time of ordination, so that during his administration he may make use of union with the one virgin whom he betrothed.

Pope Martin prohibits this, saying:

[Editorial note: Chapter 10 of the Council of Ancyra, from Martin of Braga’s version, among the chapters, chapter 39. Compare Distinction 28, chapter 8; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 97; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 376.]

## C. I. A deacon is not to be ordained unless he has professed chastity

If a chosen deacon declares, with a view to entering marriage, that he cannot remain chaste, he is not to be ordained.

[Variant: Ivo adds *se* (“himself”).]

But if he keeps silent at ordination and is ordained, and afterward desires marriage, he is to be excluded from the ministry and must leave the clergy.

**Gratian.** This authority makes it understood that those who have wives or wish to take them can become neither deacons nor priests unless they profess continence.

§ 1. But if a deacon wishes to withdraw from the ministry, he may lawfully make use of a marriage he has contracted. For although he offered a vow of chastity at his ordination, nevertheless the power of the sacrament of marriage is so great that the marriage itself cannot be dissolved even because of the violation of the vow.

Hence Augustine, in his book *On the Good of Widowhood*, addressed to the widow Juliana, chapter 10, says:

[Editorial note, col. 0153C: The actual words of this chapter have not been found in Blessed Augustine. The opinion is nevertheless found in the treatise *On the Good of Widowhood*. This must be understood entirely of a simple vow, as Gratian explains at the end of this distinction.]

## C. II. Those who marry after a vow are not to be separated from one another

[Editorial note: Some do not fail to deny Augustine’s authorship of *On the Good of Widowhood*. The actual words of this canon are not found in it; something similar is nevertheless read there and is cited below, Causa 27, question 1, chapter 41. The canon is also transmitted under Augustine’s name in the *Antonian Penitential*, title 8, chapter 11.]

### II. Part

Some assert that those who marry after a vow are adulterers. But I say that those who separate such persons sin gravely.

## C. III. On the same subject

Also Theodore in the *Penitential*.

[Editorial note: Chapter 32 in D’Achery; *Roman Penitential*, title 8, chapter 11; compare below, Causa 27, question 1, final chapter. The Basel edition reads “Theodosius.”]

If a man who has a simple vow of virginity joins himself to a wife, he is not afterward to dismiss his wife, but is to do penance for three years.

[Editorial note, cols. 0153C–0154C: “Simple”: this word is absent from all the manuscripts and, below, Causa 27, question 1, chapter “If anyone has a vow,” also from the printed editions. In some very ancient manuscripts, however, it is an interlinear gloss.]

[Variant: “simple” is absent from Theodore and the Basel edition.]

Jerome, however, writes to the contrary:

[Editorial note, col. 0154C: Gratian here and below, Causa 17, question 1, chapter “Those who vow,” and the Master of the Sentences attribute this to Jerome, in whom it has not been found. In the ordinary gloss on 1 Timothy 5, at the words “having condemnation,” it is cited from Blessed Augustine, whose actual words occur below, Causa 27, question 1, chapter “Of marriages,” after the beginning.]

[Editorial note: These words, which in the *Roman Penitential*, title 8, Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*, book 4, Distinction 38, and below, Causa 17, question 1, chapter 2, bear Jerome’s name, appear rather to belong to chapter 9 of the book *On the Good of Widowhood*, commonly attributed to Augustine.]

## C. IV. For those who have vowed virginity, to wish to marry is damnable

For those who have vowed virginity, not only to marry but even to wish to marry is damnable.

## C. V. She who has vowed virginity will incur condemnation if she marries

The same author, *Against Jovinian*, book I.

[Editorial note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 192; *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 124; *Roman Penitential*, title 8, chapter 10. The Strasbourg, Nuremberg, and Venice I editions read “Against Lucian.”]

“If a virgin marries, she does not sin”—not that virgin who has dedicated herself to God’s service. For if any of these marries, she will incur condemnation, because “she has made void her first faith” [1 Tim. 5:12].

[Variant: *peccavit* (“she sinned”) for *peccat* (“she sins”) in the original and Ivo.]

[Variant: *se semel* (“herself once”) for *semet* (“herself”) in the same sources.]

[Variant: *divino* (“divine”) for *Dei* (“God’s”) in the editions collated by O.]

## C. VI. A woman who pretended to be a nun is not free to marry

Also Pope Nicholas I, to Albinus, Archbishop of the Church of Vienne.

[Editorial note: The collectors differ greatly among themselves in this inscription. Burchard, book 8, chapter 47, and Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 65, attribute it to Nicholas, writing to Adalwin, Archbishop of Vienne. The *Panormia* has “Adalwin, bishop of the church of Viviers.” By contrast, in the same Ivo, the same part, chapter 152, it reads “Aluminus, bishop of Juvigny.” The Basel edition has “the bishop of Alduinom.” With Regino, however, in the appendix, book 1, chapter 57, it should be read: “Adalwin, Archbishop of Juvavum,” that is, Salzburg, who attended the Council of Cologne in A.D. 870.]

Concerning the woman about whom you inquired, who, after her husband’s death, placed a sacred veil over her head and pretended under that veil to be a nun, but afterward returned to marriage: it seems good to me that, because through hypocrisy she wished to disturb the ecclesiastical rule and did not lawfully remain in her vow, she should do penance for her wicked deception, return to what she promised, and remain in the sacred ministry which she began.

[Variant: *mortem* (“death”) for *obitum* (“demise”) in the Basel edition.]

[Variant: Regino adds *feminam* (“a woman”) after “nun.”]

[Variant: “to me” is absent from the same source.]

[Variant: Regino and Ivo read *ministerio inchoavit* (“she began in the ministry”) for “remain in the sacred ministry which she began.”]

## C. VII. PALEA

[Editorial note: Burchard and Ivo, *Decretum*, at the same place; *Panormia*, at the same place, chapter 206. The designation “Palea” is absent from the Basel edition.]

[The same author, in the same place.]

[Editorial note, col. 0155D: In many manuscripts of Gratian this chapter, in which it occurs without the designation “Palea,” is joined to the preceding chapter, as it is also in Burchard and Ivo. In the *Panormia*, however, it is separate.]

> For if we agree that everyone may, as he wishes, pretend to perform all the ecclesiastical sacraments without truly performing them, the whole ecclesiastical order will be thrown into confusion; neither will the laws of the catholic faith stand firm, nor will the sacred canons be rightly observed.
>
> [Variant: Regino reads *fiat* (“be done”) for *faciat* (“perform them”).]
>
> [Variants: Regino reads *conturbatur* (“is thrown into confusion”); Ivo reads *conturbabitur* (“will be thrown into confusion”), followed by *consistent* (“will stand firm”) and *observabuntur* (“will be observed”).]
>
> For what profit was it to Simon Magus falsely to receive holy baptism and pretend that he would remain in Christianity, when, after his fraud had been exposed by the Apostle, what was to happen to him was pronounced?
>
> [Variant: *fraus* (“fraud”) for *fraude ejus* (“his fraud”) in Regino.]
>
> [Variant: *praenunciatum est* (“was foretold”) for *pronunciatum fuit* (“was pronounced”) in Ivo.]
>
> For he says [Acts 8]: “May your money perish with you, for your heart is not right before God. Therefore repent of this your wickedness and pray to God, if perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you; for I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity.”
>
> [Variant: “before God” is absent from the Basel edition.]
>
> [Variant: the editions collated by O., except the Basel edition, read *ab hac iniquitate tua* (“of this your iniquity”) for *ab hac nequitia tua* (“of this your wickedness”); the words are omitted in the Basel edition.]
>
> [Variants: the Basel edition reads *ut remittantur cogitatus* (“that the thoughts may be forgiven”); the other collated editions read *cogitationes* (“thoughts”).]
>
> Therefore we judge that such persons, unless they come to their senses, should be struck with the spiritual sword. For it is not lawful to lie to the Holy Spirit, as Ananias and Sapphira lied and immediately perished [Acts 5:3].

## C. VIII. Those established in sacred orders are not to take wives; and, if they do so, they are to be separated

Also Pope Calixtus II.

[Editorial note: At the Council of Reims, A.D. 1119, chapter 5, and the First Lateran Council, A.D. 1123, chapter 21.]

[Editorial note, cols. 0155D–0156D: “Priests”: this canon was found in a Vatican Library manuscript, in a fragment of a council held by Urban II, chapter 2. From the same council also come the canons “Alienations,” Causa 12, question 2, and “Paternal,” Causa 24, question 3.]

We absolutely forbid priests, deacons, subdeacons, and monks to have concubines or contract marriages. We judge that marriages contracted by persons of this kind are to be dissolved and that the persons are to be brought to penance, in accordance with the determinations of the sacred canons.

**Gratian.** Here a distinction must be made: some who vow are persons who make a simple vow, of whom Augustine and Theodore spoke; others are persons to whose vow a blessing of consecration is added, or a profession of religious life, of whom Jerome, Nicholas, and Calixtus wrote.

Hence Jerome himself, writing against the same Jovinian, book I, says:

[Editorial note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 193; *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 124.]

## C. IX. Virgins who marry after consecration are incestuous

Virgins who have married after consecration are not so much adulteresses as incestuous women.

# DISTINCTION XXVIIII

[Col. 0155]

## GRATIAN

### I. Part

It has now been shown that those unwilling to vow continence cannot ascend either to the subdiaconate or to higher grades. Hence those approaching the subdiaconate are commanded not to be admitted without a vow of chastity, by the authority of Blessed Gregory, who, writing to Peter the subdeacon [book I, Letter 42, at the end], says:

[Editorial note: Letter 44, written A.D. 591, book 1 in the Maurist edition. Compare below, Distinction 31, chapter 1; *Collection of Tracts*, part 1, book 55, chapter 60.]

## C. I. A man who has not promised to live chastely is not to be made a subdeacon

Bishops should presume to make no one a subdeacon unless he has promised to live chastely. And—after some intervening matter—because no one ought to approach the ministry of the altar unless his chastity has been approved before he undertakes the ministry.

C. II. Subdeacons and those constituted above them who are incontinent and take a wife or concubine shall be deprived of ecclesiastical benefice and office. Likewise Innocent II, in the Roman Council [Note: [Col. 0155] held in A.D. 1139. You will find nearly the same provisions in the Council of Reims, held in A.D. 1131, c. 4.—Ivo, Panormia, bk. 8, c. 142.], c. 6.

[Col. 0155D] We decree that those who, being in the order of subdiaconate [Note: [Col. 0155] diaconate: Ivo.] [Col. 0156B] or above, have taken wives or kept concubines shall be deprived of office and ecclesiastical benefice. For since they ought to be, and to be called, the temple, vessels of the Lord, and sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, it is unworthy that they [Col. 0156C] should serve beds and impurities.

C. III. Those to be ordained deacons or priests shall promise to live chastely. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Toledo [Note: [Col. 0155] held in A.D. 633.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 143; Burchard, bk. 2, c. 153; Ivo, Panormia, bk. 3, c. 22; Decree, pt. 3, c. 130; pt. 6, c. 248.], c. 27.

Part II. When priests or [Note: [Col. 0155] and: collected editions.] deacons are appointed throughout parishes, they must *first* [Note: [Col. 0155] absent from the Hispanic Collection and Ivo.] make a profession to their bishop that they will live chastely and purely in the fear of God, so that, once such a profession has bound them [Note: [Col. 0155] binds: Hispanic Collection; obligates: collected editions.], they may retain the discipline of holy life [Note: [Col. 0155] “may retain discipline”: Hispanic Collection.].

C. IV. One who does not possess long-standing continence of his body ought not to be chosen bishop. Likewise Gregory to the *clergy and* noble citizens of Naples, bk. VIII, epistle 40 [Note: [Col. 0155] Ep. 62, written A.D. 600, bk. 10, Maurist edition.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 13.].

Part III. Before your letters reached us, we learned, from the report of certain persons, that John the deacon, who [Col. 0156D] was elected by the other party, [Col. 0157A] has a very young daughter. Therefore, had they wished to heed reason, neither should the others [Note: [Col. 0157] “those”: Basel edition.] have elected him, nor should he himself have consented. For with what presumption does [Note: [Col. 0157] may he dare: same edition; dared: other collected editions.] he dare approach the episcopate, when, his little daughter bearing witness, he is shown not to have maintained long-standing continence of his body? [Note: [Col. 0157C] “Little daughter”: Thus corrected from the original, Anselm, and Polycarp, whereas it had formerly read “daughter.” Above he had likewise said “a very young daughter,” words which plainly express recent incontinence.]

C. V. Those about to enter the subdiaconate shall profess continence. Likewise from the Second Council of Toledo, c. 1 [Note: [Col. 0157] held in A.D. 527.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 42 (50).].

Part IV. Concerning those whom the will of their parents, from the earliest years of infancy, devoted to the office of the clergy [Note: [Col. 0157C] “Of the clergy”: In all editions and in two Vatican manuscripts of the councils, the reading is: “placed in the office of the clergy, or of a monk [alternatively, monks].” But in the royal Lucchese codex it stands in the same manner [Col. 0157D] as in Gratian.] [Note: [Col. 0157] “shall have devoted”: same source; collected editions.] [Col. 0158C], we decree that the following be observed: once they have been tonsured or handed over to the ministry of readers [Note: [Col. 0158C] “Ministry of readers”: In all previously cited manuscripts of the councils, including the Lucchese one, the reading is “ministry of the chosen.” Yet in Siricius’s first letter to Himerius, c. 9, and Innocent’s twenty-fourth letter, c. 5, where nearly the same matter is treated, it is “the ministry or office of readers.”] [Note: [Col. 0157] “of the chosen”: Hispanic Collection.] [Note: [Col. 0157] “when they have been handed over”: same source; Anselm.], they are to be educated in the house of the church under the bishop’s presence by the superior set over them. [Col. 0157B] But when they have completed the eighteenth year of their age, the bishop shall inquire, in the sight of all the clergy and people, whether they wish to seek marriage. If, by God’s inspiration, the grace of chastity pleases them, and they have promised [Note: [Col. 0157] “by a promise”: collected editions.] to preserve their own chastity without the necessity of marriage [Note: [Col. 0157] adds “themselves”: Hispanic Collection.], they shall, as seekers of the most narrow way [Note: [Col. 0157] “life, by the gentlest”: Hispanic Collection.], be subjected to the Lord’s very light yoke; and, after proof of their profession has been given, they shall undertake the ministry of the subdiaconate at the age of twenty. [Note: [Col. 0157] “subdiaconium”: Basel edition; “subdeacon”: other collected editions.] If they have passed their twenty-fifth year [Note: [Col. 0157] “twenty-five years”: Basel edition.] of age [Note: [Col. 0157] absent from the Hispanic Collection.] blamelessly and without offense, they ought to be promoted to the office of the diaconate [Note: [Col. 0157] “diaconium”: editions of Argentinensis, Basel, and Nuremberg; “deacon”: other collected editions.], if the bishop finds that they can knowingly [Note: [Col. 0157] adds “this”: collected editions.] fulfill it. Yet they must beware lest, ever forgetful of their pledge, they resort [Note: [Col. 0157] “or resort”: collected editions.] to earthly marriages or secret concubinage [Col. 0157C] thereafter [Note: [Col. 0157] willingly: collected editions.]. If they should do so, they are to be considered outsiders from the Church and guilty of sacrilege [Note: [Col. 0157] “that they be condemned guilty, and [be separated] from”: Hispanic Collection.]. But we cannot take away the permission granted by the Apostle from those whose own will, at the time of inquiry, has persuaded them to desire marriage; provided that, once established in marriage at a mature age, they promise by mutual consent to renounce works of the flesh, they may aspire to sacred orders.

C. VI. A man established in marriage ought not to be admitted to the priesthood. Likewise from the Second Council of Arles [Note: [Col. 0157] held no later than A.D. 460; nevertheless see what we have noted on c. 12, Distinction 18.—Collection in three parts, pt. 2, tit. 24, c. 2. In the collected editions, first Basel edition, the Council of Arles III is cited; and in the following chapter, IV.], c. 2.

Part V. It is not fitting that anyone established in the bond of marriage be admitted to the priesthood [Note: [Col. 0157] “cannot be admitted”: Hispanic Collection.], unless conversion has first been promised [Note: [Col. 0157] “premised”: same source.].

C. VII. Deacons who do not profess chastity shall not be ordained. Likewise from the same Third [Council of Arles]. [Note: [Col. 0157] This chapter belongs to c. 43 of the Second Council of Arles, from which the preceding canon was taken, and corresponds exactly to c. 22 of the First Council of Orange.]

Furthermore [Note: [Col. 0158C] “Furthermore”: In the extant Arles collections this canon itself is not found at all. But the sense occurs at the end of c. 2 of the Third [Council of Arles]. [Col. 0158D]], it was resolved that henceforth deacons should not be ordained [Note: [Col. 0157] adds “married”: original and collected editions; “sworn together”: Basel edition.] unless they have first professed chastity under a purpose of conversion.

Gratian. Yet by that earlier authority marriage seems to be allowed to deacons, since only married men are forbidden to be admitted to the priesthood. Moreover, by the following authority it seems to be allowed to subdeacons, since it is specifically commanded concerning deacons that they not be ordained without proof of chastity.

The same seems to have been allowed in the Synod of Ancyra [Note: [Col. 0157] held in A.D. 314.—Panormia, bk. 3, c. 87; Polycarp, bk. 4, tit. 31.], where c. 10 decreed as follows:

C. VIII. Deacons shall not be forbidden the ministry if, at their ordination, they say that they cannot remain continent.

Whatever deacons, when they are ordained, have declared in the very ordination itself, saying that they wish to have wives and cannot remain continent—if they later enter into marriage [Note: [Col. 0157] “come together”: Hispanic Collection; “arrive”: collected editions except Basel. The immediately following words, which agree exactly with the Hispanic Collection, have been corrected by Ballerini in the Quesnel canon collection as follows: “let them remain only in the clergy, and be removed from the ministry.”]—shall remain in the ministry, [Col. 0158C] because the bishop gave them permission. But all who kept silent and received the laying on of hands after professing continence, if they later enter into marriage [Note: [Col. 0157] “come together”: original and Basel edition; “arrive”: other collected editions.], must cease from the ministry [Note: [Col. 0157] Quesnel adds “or from the clergy.”].

[Col. 0159A] C. IX. A priest who takes a wife shall be deposed from his order. Likewise from the Council of Neocaesarea [Note: [Col. 0159] held in A.D. 314. Regino, bk. 1, c. 84; Burchard, bk. 2, c. 108; Ivo, Panormia, bk. 3, c. 91; Decree, pt. 6, c. 185, from the version of Dionysius.], c. 1.

Part VI. If a priest takes a wife, he ought to be deposed from his own order. But if he commits fornication or adultery, he ought to be cast out of the Church and reduced to penance among the laity [Note: [Col. 0159C] “Among the laity”: The Greek reads: Ἐξωθεῖσθαι τέλεον, καὶ ἄγεσθαι αὐτὸν εἰς μετάνοιαν, “He must be expelled completely and led into repentance,” which Dionysius Exiguus translates: “he must be driven out further and reduced to penance.” There is no mention there of penance to be performed among the laity; that matter will be discussed more fully below, Distinction 30, final chapter.].

C. X. Concerning one who took the wife left by a certain deacon. Likewise Gregory, bk. XI, epistle 59 [Note: [Col. 0159] Ep. 5, written A.D. 604, bk. 14, Maurist edition.—Collection in three parts, pt. 1, tit. 55, c. 68.—Ivo, Decree, pt. 9, c. 126; pt. 6, c. 184.].

Part VII. Since there are faults in which it is a fault to relax punishment, the truth must always be sought, so that inquiry should determine whether wrongdoing proves the accused guilty [Note: [Col. 0159] adds “due”: Basel edition.], or whether innocence, having been shown, withdraws him from punishment [Note: [Col. 0159] “of punishment”: same edition.]. Thus it has come to us that Fantinus [Note: [Col. 0159] Fautinus: collected editions.] the defender [Col. 0159B] wished to exact punishment upon Peter, the bearer of this letter, because, it is said, while he was a tenant, he gave in marriage [Note: [Col. 0159] adds “in”: same edition.] the woman left by a certain deacon to a husband. But since this man asserts that she was not the deacon’s wife, saying that she did not come to him a virgin [Note: [Col. 0159] “that woman”: original and Ivo.], nor, indeed [Note: [Col. 0159] “indeed, so that she did not presume to change into religious dress”: original.], did she change into religious dress after he was promoted to sacred order, and further alleging that before he became a deacon [Note: [Col. 0159] “had come”: Basel edition; “had arrived”: other collected editions.] and afterwards she lived under an evil reputation: therefore we urge your brotherhood in these words to investigate this case with the fear of God, as is fitting, by a wholly careful inquiry [Note: [Col. 0159] “mind”: Nuremberg edition; “to investigate”: editions of Argentinensis, Venice I, and Nuremberg; “you investigate”: the other collected editions. In all copies, the following “so that” is read “and.”], so that, if it is established that the woman in question was the deacon’s wife, the aforementioned bearer may by all means be handed over to the aforesaid defender and steward of the patrimony for punishment, and [Col. 0159C] those who have been improperly joined may be separated with suitable reparation. But if she was not his wife, we wish you, by our command, to warn the said Fantinus not to presume to do anything against him, and that no false accusation weigh him down before Fantinus in any respect [Note: [Col. 0159] absent from the earlier Maurist editions of Gregory.].

[Col. 0160A] C. XI. Concerning the wife of a priest or deacon if she joins herself to another. Likewise from the First Council of Orléans [Note: [Col. 0159] held in A.D. 511.—In the Hispanic Collection this is canon 9.—Collection in three parts, pt. 2, tit. 29, c. 12.], c. 13.

If a woman left by a priest or deacon in a double marriage joins herself to anyone [Note: [Col. 0159] “whomever”: original.], let them separate; or certainly, if they persist in the intention of their crime [Note: [Col. 0159] “crimes”: original.], let them be punished by equal excommunication [Note: [Col. 0159] “either let them enjoy chastity, or let them separate”: collected editions; “let them separate after being corrected”: original.].

C. XII. On the same matter. Likewise from the council of Pope Martin [Note: [Col. 0159] Chapter of Martin of Braga, c. 29, taken from the First Council of Toledo, c. 18, from which it was copied in Anselm, bk. 10, c. 6.].

If any woman who is the widow of a bishop, priest, or deacon takes a husband, let no cleric and no religious person [Note: [Col. 0159] absent from the Hispanic Collection and Anselm.] share a meal with her or ever communicate with her; nevertheless, in her dying hour let the sacraments assist her [Note: [Col. 0159] “only”: Hispanic Collection; “let assistance be given by the sacrament”: Anselm.].

[Col. 0160B] C. XIII. The ordination of a certain bishop is deferred because he has a wife and children. Likewise Pelagius to the patrician Cethegus [Note: [Col. 0159D] “Likewise Pelagius”: Anselm and the author of Polycarp, from the same letter, report these words preceding this chapter: “We learned of your wish that a salutary election of judgment should be made for the bishop to be ordained for the church of Catania; immediately, examining him on the following day according to custom, we consecrated him bishop on the third day, on which he came”; and similarly concerning the church of Syracuse, and what follows. Yet Polycarp has the heading: “Pope Gelasius to Cethegus.” But Ivo, in his letter to Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, beginning “The case of Beauvais,” etc., writes: “For if Pope Gelasius formerly [deferred] the elect of the city of Syracuse, who had a wife and children, at the intervention of the patrician Cethegus,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0159] A fragment of a letter of Pelagius I, published by Holstenius from the collection of Deusdedit in the *Monuments*.—Collection in three parts, pt. 1, tit. 54, c. 12.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 48; Polycarp, bk. 2, tit. 1.].

Part VIII. At the very beginning of your illustrious administration, we wished to comply with your desires concerning the bishop of the city of Syracuse; but many considerations compelled us to defer his priestly ordination for no short time, because either the quality of the person—as you yourselves know better—or his surviving wife or children, through whom ecclesiastical property is accustomed to be endangered [Note: [Col. 0159] Compare Justinian, Novella 6, c. 1, §§3–4, and Novella 123, c. 1.], kept our minds in suspense concerning his ordination for a long time [Note: [Col. 0159] singular “kept”: collected editions, first Venice edition.]. And, so far as human caution was concerned, we deferred it for almost a full year, thinking that a better election might result for the Syracusans. But because they persisted irrevocably in their intended course, and no other person was found in that church, unless it were deferred for still longer periods of time [Col. 0160C]—lest they should grow somewhat more frantic, as we learned from the testimony of our sons, the distinguished men of the praetorium—we judged it more prudent, amid such uncertainties, to do the following: by suitable provision, we would, while preserving the disposition of the plan [Note: [Col. 0161] “council”: Holstenius from Deusdedit; Anselm; collected editions except Basel.], secure the case on account of which an imperial constitution forbids a man having children and [Col. 0161A] a wife to be promoted to the episcopal order. Therefore, before the bishop of the city of Syracuse could be ordained by us, we required from him with the utmost care the following guarantee: that he should acknowledge what property, however small, he possessed at the present time, after an inventory of his goods had been made; that he would never appropriate anything belonging to the Church, either personally or through his children or wife, or through any relative, member of his household, or perhaps outside person; and that he would join to the ownership of his church all acquisitions made during his episcopate, leaving to his children or heirs nothing beyond what has now been inventoried.

Gratian. Behold, by this authority one elected to the episcopate is not forbidden [Note: [Col. 0161C] “Is not forbidden”: In many ancient copies [Col. 0161]—Argentinensis; Venice I and II; Nuremberg; Paris; Lyons I—the word “not” is absent. It has nevertheless been retained, because Gratian here, arguing for the other side from the previously cited canons, appears to prove that subdeacons, deacons, and even priests were not forbidden the use of marriage. Yet he himself later explains how this must be understood, from “But what” to “That, however.” This matter will also be treated below in the note at the beginning of Distinction 31.] to have a wife and children. But no one should be chosen to the episcopate unless he is either a priest or a deacon; a subdeacon only when necessity compels. Therefore, whether he was priest, deacon, or subdeacon, it appears that persons constituted in the aforesaid orders may lawfully use marriage.

§1. Therefore, because by Gregory’s authority one who gave the woman left by a deacon to a husband is to be punished; likewise, in the Council of Neocaesarea, a priest who takes a wife—not a deacon—is ordered deposed; likewise, in the Synod of Ancyra, deacons who declare at their ordination that they wish to have wives are not forbidden the ministry if they later enter marriage: it is clear that neither deacons nor subdeacons are to be forbidden marriage. But the objection drawn from election is indeed true: one ought not to be elected bishop unless established in sacred orders. Yet that he has a wife [Col. 0161C] and children is not inconsistent with the foregoing authorities concerning clerical continence.

§2. For while established in lay dress or in the minor orders, he could have had a wife and children; and if afterwards, with his wife’s consent, he professed continence and attained the rank of subdeacon, deacon, or priest, he nevertheless had to provide necessities for his wife and children.

§3.
