But Gregory’s statement is resolved in two ways: either because the church in which that deacon had served [Note: [Col. 0161] “had been enrolled in military service”: collected editions except Basel and Nuremberg.] had not yet adopted the vow of continence for deacons and the other ministers; or because, as was written earlier concerning the bishop-elect, that deacon had married her before becoming a subdeacon.

§4. But the decrees of the Synods of Neocaesarea and Ancyra are understood either with respect to time or place: with respect to time, because continence for ministers of the altar had not yet been introduced; with respect to place, because both synods are Eastern, and the Eastern Church does not adopt a general vow of chastity. It nevertheless observes this with diligent care: after attaining the priesthood, if his first wife, with whom he became a priest, has died, and he takes another wife, he is to be deposed.

The following is also objected, which is read in the Canon of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0161] Burchard, bk. 1, c. 78.—Ivo, Panormia, bk. 3, c. 113; Decree, pt. 5, c. 184.], c. 6, alternatively 5:

C. XIV. A priest shall not despise his own wife on grounds of religion.

[Col. 0162B] Part IX. If [Note: [Col. 0161D] Gratian reports the sense of the canon; the other compilers give almost the actual words as well.] anyone teaches that a priest should despise his own wife under the pretext of religion, let him be anathema.

C. XV. Let him be anathema who separates himself from communion with a married priest on account of marriage. Likewise from the Council of Gangra [Note: [Col. 0161] held about A.D. 355.—Burchard, bk. 3, c. 75.—Ivo, Decree, pt. 2, c. 128; pt. 3, c. 158.], c. 4.

If [Note: [Col. 0162C] The Greek is: Εἴ τις διακρίνοιτο παρὰ πρεσβυτέρου γεγαμηκότος, ὡς μὴ χρῆναι, λειτουργήσαντος αὐτοῦ, προσφορᾶς μεταλαμβάνειν, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω: “If anyone separates himself from a priest who has taken a wife, as though, when that priest performs the liturgy, one ought not to receive the offering, let him be anathema.” This version does not differ greatly from that of Dionysius Exiguus.] anyone separates himself from a married priest, as though that priest ought not, on account of marriage, to offer, and for that reason abstains from his offering [Note: [Col. 0161] absent from collected editions.], let him be anathema.

C. XVI. A priest bound by an unlawful marriage shall abstain from office. Likewise from the Sixth Synod in Trullo [Note: [Col. 0161] held in A.D. 692.—The Fathers borrowed the words of this canon from St. Basil’s canons to Amphilochius, c. 27.], c. 26.

Part X. We decree that a priest bound, *through ignorance*, by an unlawful marriage may retain his seat, but must abstain from office [Note: [Col. 0162D] “From office”: The Greek is: Τῶν δὲ λοιπῶν ἐνεργειῶν, “from the other functions.”]. For such indulgence is sufficient for him, because it is not fitting that one who ought to heal his own wounds should bless others. For blessing is the imparting of sanctification. How, then, can one who does not possess it because of an offense of ignorance impart it to others? Therefore, he shall not bless publicly or privately [Note: [Col. 0161] “for”: collected editions.], nor distribute the body of the Lord to others, nor minister in any other manner. It is enough for him that he presides and implores God that the iniquity of his ignorance may be forgiven him. It is evident, moreover, that such an unlawful marriage shall be dissolved, and that [Col. 0163A] the man shall have no access whatever [Note: [Col. 0163] “in no way”: same source.] to the woman on whose account he has been deprived of sacred ministry.

C. XVII. Laymen are not to judge priests. Likewise Nicholas, in response to the consultations of the Bulgarians [Note: [Col. 0163] Letter written A.D. 866.—Ivo, Panormia, bk. 5, c. 12; Decree, pt. 2, c. 82.], c. 70.

Part XI. You decree that counsel should be sought as to whether you ought to support and honor a priest [Note: [Col. 0163C] “A priest”: In the final chapter of these responses are reported the Bulgarians’ words, saying that many Greeks, Armenians, and [Col. 0163D] others were among them who taught diverse things. For they had not yet received a bishop or priest from the Roman See. There is therefore nothing surprising if the priest dealt with in this chapter was married.] who has a wife, or cast him out from among you. To this we reply: although they are indeed very blameworthy, it is nevertheless fitting that you imitate God, who [Note: [Col. 0163] Matthew 5:15.] makes his sun rise [Col. 0164A] upon good and evil. You ought not, however [Note: [Col. 0163] “for”: collected editions.], to cast him out from among you for this reason, because the Lord did not expel Judas from the number of the apostles when he was a lying disciple. But [Note: [Col. 0163] adds “and”: same editions; “and thus”: Basel edition.] you who are laymen must neither judge priests nor investigate anything concerning their life [Note: [Col. 0163] “anything whatever”: collected editions.]; rather, everything [Note: [Col. 0163] adds “that”: same editions; “that matter”: Basel edition.] must in all respects be reserved for the judgment of bishops.

## DISTINCTION XXIX

[Col. 0163]

[Col. 0163A] GRATIAN.

But it should be noted that, according to Isidore, very many chapters must be considered with regard to cause, place, time, and person.

[Col. 0163B] For Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0163] The author of this canon is not sufficiently certain. For in Isidore of Seville’s book *On the Rule of Life*—which some consider spurious—only similar words are found. The notation of the Correctors, which appears in the Roman edition itself and thence in the editions of Pelleterius and Boehmer, was removed, for the Correctors themselves so directed in their index of errors.]:

C. I. The rules of canons are understood from time, place, person, and cause.

It should be known that very many chapters must be considered with respect to cause, person, place, and time. Because their modes are not investigated to the marrow, some, becoming entangled, stumble into the labyrinth of error: they judge before they understand, and condemn before they examine what they have repeatedly read.

Gregory likewise says [Note: [Col. 0163] Canon equally uncertain. Anselm, bk. 4, c. 52.]:

C. II. The rules of the saints are tempered according to the diversity of circumstances.

The rules of the holy Fathers were handed down according to time, place, person, and the necessity of the matter at hand [Col. 0164A].

[Col. 0164B] C. III. Scriptures must be understood according to the diversity of places, times, and persons. Likewise Jerome, in the preface to his letter to the Ephesians.

It is necessary that, according to the diversities of places, times, and persons to whom [Note: [Col. 0163D] “To whom they were written”: Earlier the reading was, “for whom diverse writings were made.” This has been corrected from the manuscripts and the original, as have several other readings.] they were written, they should have different causes, arguments, and origins. And just as Blessed John, writing in his Apocalypse to seven churches [Note: [Col. 0163] “to seven churches”: collected editions.], rebukes particular vices or approves virtues in each one of them, so too the Holy Apostle [Note: [Col. 0163] adds “Paul”: Boehmer.] treats the wounds inflicted upon the individual churches; he does not, like an unskilled physician, wish to cure every eye with one salve.

## DISTINCTION XXX

[Col. 0163]

[Col. 0163C] GRATIAN.

Part. But what is read in the Canon of the Apostles, in the Council of Gangra, and in the Sixth Synod is to be considered in light of cause and time. The cause was the heresy of the Manichaeans [Note: [Col. 0164C] “Of the Manichaeans”: Strictly speaking, the Council of Gangra decreed against the Eustathians, as noted above at Distinction 16, first note. But the Eustathians had drawn this error from the Manichaeans.], because they detested marriage, just as the superstition of certain others is found to have introduced many things in detestation of Catholics. Against them it is recorded that sixteen chapters were decreed in the Council of Gangra [Note: [Col. 0164D] In some ancient copies all the material here cited from the Council of Gangra is read as one chapter in continuous discourse. It is from the ancient version [Col. 0163]—indeed, from the Hispanic version. But Dionysius Exiguus’s version corresponds much more closely to the Greek original, though not wholly.].

[Col. 0164C] C. I. Concerning the manifold superstition of heretics whom the Council of Gangra anathematized. Council of Gangra, c. 16 [Note: [Col. 0163] held about A.D. 355. Ivo, Decree, pt. 8, c. 319.].

If any children abandon their parents, especially believing parents, on the pretext of the worship of God, maintaining that this is the case, and do not rather render the due honor to their parents, so as to reverence in them this very thing—that they are believers—let them be anathema [Note: [Col. 0163] “let him be”: original.].

[Col. 0165A] C. II. On the same matter. Likewise from the same source, c. 17 [Note: [Col. 0165] Burchard, bk. 8, c. 62; Ivo, Decree, pt. 8, c. 320, and, from Dionysius’s version, pt. 7, c. 80.].

Whatever woman, judging it fitting for religion [Note: [Col. 0165B] “For religion”: The Greek is: Διὰ νομιζομένην ἄσκησιν, “because of what is regarded as an exercise of piety,” which Dionysius translates, “because of divine worship, as she supposes.” The Greeks properly called the life of those whom we call religious persons ἄσκησις, “ascetic exercise.” Burchard and Ivo in part 6 followed Dionysius’s version, but Ivo in part 8 the ancient one.] to cut off her hair, which God gave her as a covering [Note: [Col. 0165C] “As a covering”: These words are absent from the Greek original and Dionysius’s version. They seem to be taken from 1 Corinthians 11.] and as a reminder of her subjection, as though dissolving the law of subjection, let her be anathema.

C. III. On the same matter. Likewise from the same source, c. 14 [Note: [Col. 0165] Ivo, Decree, pt. 8, c. 229, from Dionysius’s version, and the same work, c. 317.].

If any woman, leaving [Note: [Col. 0165] “having left”: Basel edition.] her husband, wishes to depart after dissolving the marriage bond, condemning marriage [Note: [Col. 0165] “despising”: Ivo, c. 317; collected editions, first Basel edition.], let her be anathema.

C. IV. On the same matter. Likewise from the same source, c. 10 [Note: [Col. 0165] Burchard, bk. 8, c. 64; Ivo, Decree, pt. 8, c. 316 and pt. 7, c. 82; here from Dionysius’s version, which is read in Distinction 31, c. 9.].

If anyone who has professed virginity for God [Note: [Col. 0165] “his own virginity or continence, and has …”: Basel edition.] disparages those established in marriage through arrogance, let him be anathema [Note: [Col. 0165] “shall disparage”: Hispanic Collection; Ivo.].

C. V. On the same matter. Likewise from the same source, c. 9 [Note: [Col. 0165] Burchard, bk. 8, c. 61; Ivo, Decree, pt. 7, c. 79, from Dionysius’s version.].

If anyone, having professed either [Note: [Col. 0165] absent from the Basel edition.] virginity or continence [Note: [Col. 0165C] “Having professed”: Here there had been added “in marriage,” which appears neither in the Greek canon nor in the Latin one cited below at Distinction 31, “Whoever,” nor in many manuscript copies of Gratian.], judges marriages abominable, and not on this ground alone—that a holy and good purpose of continence [Note: [Col. 0165] “because continence and virginity are a good and holy …”: Hispanic Collection; “a good and holy [thing]”: Basel edition.] and virginity has been proposed, let him be anathema.

C. VI. On the same matter. Likewise from the same source, c. 13 [Note: [Col. 0165] Burchard, bk. 8, c. 60; Ivo, Decree, pt. 7, c. 78, from Dionysius’s version.].

If any woman, judging it useful to her own purpose [Note: [Col. 0165] “this”: Hispanic Collection.] to use male dress [Note: [Col. 0165] absent there.], for this reason affects male attire [Note: [Col. 0165] “for this purpose”: same source; “and for”: collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 0165C] “Imitate”: The Greek reads: Καὶ ἀντὶ τοῦ εἰωθότος γυναικείου ἀμφιάσματος ἀνδρεῖον ἀναλάβοι, “and instead of the customary woman’s garment takes up a man’s.” Dionysius Exiguus aptly translates: “and in place of the customary feminine clothing takes on male clothing”; thus Burchard has it, and nearly also Ivo.], let her be anathema.

[Col. 0166A] C. VII. On the same matter. Likewise from the same source, c. 18 [Note: [Col. 0165] Burchard, bk. 13, c. 219; Ivo, Decree, pt. 4, c. 51, Dionysius’s version.].

If anyone, judging this fitting to continence, fasts on the Lord’s Day in contempt of that day [Note: [Col. 0166C] “Of that day”: The ancient [Col. 0165] version—in which, as noted, “or” does not occur, any more than in the ancient version—has: “or in contempt of that day.” This seems to be expressed in Dionysius’s version, which Burchard and Ivo cite, by the words “or through obstinacy” [alternatively, “because of obstinacy”]; but in the commonly received Greek there is nothing corresponding to those words.], let him be anathema.

C. VIII. On the same matter. Likewise from the same Council of Gangra, c. 19 [Note: [Col. 0165] Regino, bk. 1, c. 280; Burchard, bk. 13, c. 5; Ivo, Decree, pt. 4, c. 38, Dionysius’s version.—Moreover, the Hispanic version differs in some respects from Gratian’s canon, as appears from the Correctors’ note, to whom it was known as the ancient version.].

If anyone among those who have undertaken continence becomes proud on account of bodily necessity and considers the common fasts of the whole Church contemptible, judging that he has perfect understanding in his own conscience, let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0166B] “Beyond bodily necessity”: Nothing has been altered because of the glosses; but the text differs in many ways from both the ancient version and Dionysius’s version, which Burchard and Ivo followed. The ancient version reads: “If anyone among those who have undertaken continence, apart from bodily necessity, and proudly considers the common fasts of the whole Church contemptible, claiming perfect understanding in his own knowledge, let him be anathema.” Dionysius’s version reads: “If anyone among those devoted to continence, without bodily necessity, proudly breaks the fasts handed down in common and observed by the Church, driven by the spur of his own thought, let him be anathema.” This version agrees sufficiently with the Greek original, even the received Greek, in its other parts; but its final portion varies notably. For where Dionysius has “driven by the spur of his own thought,” the received Greek has: ἀποκυροῦντος ἐν αὐτῷ τελείου λογισμοῦ, “a perfect reasoning within him, as it were, annulling them.” But in manuscript copies of this canon some read ὑποικουροῦντος, “with perfect reasoning dwelling within him”; others ἐπικουροῦντος, “with the perfect reasoning within him bringing him aid.” The Eustathians are marked out—later imitated by the Bogomils—who maintained that, after completing some definite fast, they had attained such a condition of perfect life that thereafter all things were indifferent to them; they were bound by no commands, were wholly free, and could not even sin. On this point see Balsamon in his interpretation of this chapter.]

C. IX. On the same matter. Likewise from the same source, c. 20 [Note: [Col. 0165] Ivo, Panormia, bk. 2, c. 8.].

If anyone, through pride and considering himself perfect [Note: [Col. 0165] “considering”: Hispanic Collection; Paris edition.], either condemns the gatherings held in places and basilicas of the holy martyrs, or believes that the offerings celebrated there ought to be despised, and that the memorials of the saints ought to be scorned, let him be anathema.

C. X. On the same matter. Likewise from the same source, c. 5 [Note: [Col. 0165] Burchard, bk. 3, c. 94; Ivo, Decree, pt. 3, c. 84, Dionysius’s version.].

If anyone teaches that the house of God and the assemblies held in it [Note: [Col. 0165] “were held”: Argentinensis edition.] ought to be despised, let him be anathema.

C. XI. On the same matter. Likewise from the same source, c. 6 [Note: [Col. 0165] Burchard, bk. 3, c. 95.].

If anyone, gathering people privately outside the Church, despises [Note: [Col. 0167] “condemns”: Basel edition.] ecclesiastical ordinances [Note: [Col. 0167B] “Ordinances”: After this word the ancient version inserts: “and wishes otherwise to appropriate what belongs to the Church, without a priest being present [Col. 0167C] according to the bishop’s decree,” followed by the words that follow here. Dionysius’s version, which corresponds very well to the Greek words and is reported by Burchard, is: “If anyone, holding separate assemblies outside the Church and despising the Church, wishes to appropriate what belongs to the Church without a priest being present according to the bishop’s decree, let him be anathema.”], and conducts the Church itself at his own place without the counsel [Note: [Col. 0167] “council”: original; Basel, Venice II, Lyons I editions.—The Greek is: μὴ συνόντος τοῦ πρεσβυτέρου κατὰ γνώμὴν τοῦ ἐπισκόπου, “without a priest being present according to the judgment of the bishop.”] of the bishop, together with a priest, let him be anathema.

C. XII. On the same matter. Likewise from the same source, c. 1 [Note: [Col. 0167] Burchard, bk. 8, c. 61; Ivo, Decree, pt. 7, c. 79.—Below, Distinction 31, c. 8, from Dionysius’s version.].

If anyone brings marriage into accusation [Note: [Col. 0167] “leads into accusation”: Hispanic Collection.] and believes a faithful and religious woman sleeping with her husband to be abominable or even blameworthy, as though married persons cannot enter the kingdom of God, let him be anathema.

C. XIII. On the same matter. Likewise from the same source, c. 2 [Note: [Col. 0167] Ivo, Decree, pt. 4, c. 30.].

If anyone believes that a person who eats flesh with faith and reverence—apart from blood and what has been sacrificed to idols and strangled—is to be condemned, as though the eater had no hope, let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0167] *flesh*: “fleshes,” Hispana Collection. — “sacrificed to idols”: “to idols,” Ivo. — “sacrificed to idols and strangled,” Basil edition.]

[Col. 0167B] C. XIV. On the same subject.—Likewise from the same source, ch. 15.

[Note: [Col. 0167] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 318.]

If anyone abandons his own children and does not support them or provide what is necessary for them—as is required by filial duty—but, under the pretext of continence, thinks that they should be neglected, let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0167] “abandons”: “leaves,” collected editions other than the first Basil edition. — “his own”: absent from the Hispana Collection. — “and”: “and according to what,” ibid. — “under”: absent there.]

[Note: [Col. 0167C] “What is required by filial duty”: Dionysius much more faithfully renders: “and does not direct, so far as lies in his power, toward the fitting worship of God.” For the Greek is: καὶ τὸ ὅσον ἐπ’ αὐτῷ [variant: ἑαυτῷ] πρὸς θεοσέβειαν τὴν προσήκουσαν ἀνάγῃ, “and, insofar as it depends on him [or on himself], does not lead toward the fitting reverence for God.” The negative particle, that is, “not,” is understood from the preceding clause.]

C. XV. On the same subject.—Likewise from the same source, ch. 12.

[Note: [Col. 0167] Burchard, book 8, ch. 63; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, ch. 81 (from Dionysius’s version).]

If any man thinks that it accords with a holy undertaking—that is, continence—to wear a cloak, as though he will thereby acquire righteousness, and reproves or judges others who reverently wear coarse cloaks and other ordinary clothing in common use, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0168A] C. XVI. On the same subject.—Likewise from the same source, final chapter.

[Note: [Col. 0167] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 321.]

Part II. We have written these things not to exclude those in the Church of God who, according to the Scriptures, choose the holy purpose of continence, but [to exclude] those who adopt its profession and are lifted up in pride against those who live more simply. Yet we also condemn those who exalt themselves against the Scriptures and ecclesiastical canons and introduce new precepts. We, however, admire virginity joined with humility; we declare continence joined with chastity and godliness to be most acceptable to God; we commend and praise, when joined with humility, renunciation of secular business and occupations; we honor the honorable bond of marriage that endures in chastity; and we do not reject the rich when they possess justice and good works.

[Note: [Col. 0167C] “Those who”: the Greek reads: Τοὺς λαμβάνοντας τὴν ὑπόθεσιν τῆς ἀσκήσεως εἰς ὑπερηφανίαν κατὰ τῶν ἀφελέστερον βιοῦντων ἐπαιρουμένους τε καὶ παρὰ τὰς γραφὰς καὶ τοὺς ἐκκλησιαστικοὺς κανόνας καινισμοὺς εἰσάγοντας: “those who take the purpose of this discipline as an occasion for self-exaltation, raise themselves against those who live more simply, and introduce innovations contrary to the Scriptures and ecclesiastical canons.”]

[Note: [Col. 0167] “more simply”: “simply,” Basil edition. — “introduce” (*introducunt*): “may introduce” (*introducant*), collected editions other than the first. — “godliness”: “religion,” the same editions. — “renunciation of secular business and occupations”: the Hispana Collection adds “departure.”]

[Note: [Col. 0167D] “And the bond of marriage”: Greek, Καὶ γάμου συνοίκησιν σεμνήν, which Dionysius renders, “and the chaste bond of marriage.”]

[Note: [Col. 0167] “that endures in chastity”: Hispana adds “with itself.”]

[Note: [Col. 0168B] “We do not reject”: Immediately after these words, the council itself continues with material found below, *On Parsimony*, Distinction 41.]

C. XVII. He who follows Manichaean superstitions is anathematized. Likewise from the Council of Pope Martin.

[Note: [Col. 0167] Chapters of Martin of Braga, chs. 57 and 58; Burchard, book 13, ch. 20; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, ch. 52 (from the Council of Tours, ch. 57).]

If any priest, because of public penance received from a priest, without any necessity fasts on the Lord’s Day on account of some religious observance, as the Manichaeans do, let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0168B–D] “Priest”: there followed “or deacon.” These words have been removed because they are absent from most manuscripts and from the original. Burchard and Ivo, however, cite a similar canon from the Council of Tours, reading: “If anyone, because of public penance received from a priest, or because of some necessity,” etc. In some manuscripts of Gratian the reading is: “If anyone, apart from public penance received from a priest, without any necessity,” etc.; this seems the best reading. For in ch. 18 of the Council of Gangra, from which Martin seems to have taken this, no mention is made of a priest; rather, it is pronounced universally, as above in the same distinction, “If anyone, under the pretext of an exercise of piety, as it is thought, fasts on the Lord’s Day, let him be anathema.” The words “without any necessity” also seem imported here from ch. 19 of that council. Nor were priests subjected to penances of this kind in the manner of laymen; see ch. *Illud*, with the following chapter, Distinction 50, and final ch., verse *Nec enim*, Distinction 82. But when they publicly incurred very grave crimes, they were deposed and ordered to travel as penitents; ch. *Si quis sacerdos*, 39, question 1; ch. *Sacerdos*, *On Penance*, Distinction 6.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] “or deacon”: added in collected editions and the first Basil edition. — “without”: “or,” Hispana Collection.]

§ 1. Likewise, because the ancient canon handed down by the apostles maintains that it is fitting that on every Lord’s Day and throughout all the days of Pascha until Pentecost they should not prostrate themselves in prayer as an act of humility, but perform the office of prayer with faces raised toward the Lord—for on these days we celebrate the joy of the Lord’s resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0168D] “Likewise, because”: this is taken from the final canon of the Council of Nicaea.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] Hispana Collection and collected editions read: “and that which has been handed down by the apostles, the canon”; Basil has “handed down.” — “it is fitting that”: “so that,” Hispana. — “and”: “as well as,” ibid.]

[Note: [Col. 0169C] “They should not prostrate themselves”: In the royal Lucca manuscript one reads: “not prostrate, but with faces raised toward the Lord, let them perform the office of prayer.”]

[Note: [Col. 0169] Hispana: “not prostrate or humbled, but with faces raised toward the Lord let us perform the office of prayers.” — “the Lord’s”: “of the Lord,” collected editions.]

If anyone abstains from flesh, not for the discipline of abstinence but from abhorrence of foods, the holy council decreed that he should first taste it and then, if he wishes to abstain, abstain. But if he despises it so as not even to taste vegetables cooked with meat, then, being disobedient and failing to remove suspicion of heresy from himself, he shall be deposed from clerical rank.

[Note: [Col. 0169C] “If anyone also”: this is taken from the Council of Ancyra, ch. 13 [or 14], where priest and deacon are mentioned.]

[Note: [Col. 0169] “the discipline of abstinence,” Hispana. — “from abhorrence of foods”: “from food of flesh,” ibid. — “abstains”: “abstains himself,” ibid; collected editions: “abstains.”]

[Note: [Col. 0169] “taste”: “eat,” Basil edition.]

## DISTINCTION XXXI

[Col. 0169]

[Col. 0169A] GRATIAN.

Part I. There was also a time when it had not yet been established that priests should observe continence.

[Note: [Col. 0169C–0170D] Gratian’s assertion here—that there was a time when priests had not yet been required to observe continence—can apply to subdeacons, who are sometimes included under the designation “priests.” For “priest” can have the same force as “one constituted in holy orders,” as is noted below at the beginning of Distinction 33 and in the gloss on ch. 1, question 1, *Qui per pecuniam*. There was indeed a time when subdeacons in certain provinces, such as Sicily, were not bound by laws of continence. The passage of Gregory, which Gratian will cite immediately as the sole confirmation of this point, clearly proves it. But that deacons and priests in the Latin Church were never permitted to make use of wives whom they had married before sacred orders is clearly demonstrated by the canons cited later in this distinction and many others, especially Siricius’s second letter to Himerius of Tarragona.]

Accordingly, Gregory writes to Peter, subdeacon of Sicily, book I, letter 42:

[Note: [Col. 0169] Letter 44, written A.D. 591, book 1, Maurist edition; *Panormia*, book 3, ch. 89; Polycarpus, book 4, title 31.]

C. I. He who has not promised chastity is not to be compelled to separate from his wife.

[Col. 0169B] Three years ago the subdeacons of all the churches of Sicily had been forbidden to have intercourse with their wives in the manner of the Roman Church. This seems to me harsh and improper: that a man who has not embraced the practice of such continence and has not previously promised chastity should be compelled to separate from his wife and thereby—which God forbid—fall more grievously. Therefore it seems to me that, from the present day, all bishops should be told not to presume to make anyone a subdeacon unless he promises to live chastely, so that past evils, which were not sought by a purpose of the mind, may not be violently exacted, and future ones may prudently be prevented.

[Note: [Col. 0169] “had been”: “were,” Basil edition. — “have intercourse”: “may have intercourse,” Ivo and collected editions except Basil. — Ivo and collected editions add “in” before “thereby.”]

[Note: [Col. 0170D] “Evils”: This word is absent from Polycarpus and from some old manuscripts of Gratian.]

[Note: [Col. 0169] The words “which … exacted” are absent from the Basil edition; compare Distinction 28, ch. 1.]

§ 1. Those, however, who after the prohibition made three years ago have lived continently with their wives are to be praised and rewarded, and encouraged to remain in their good course.

[Note: [Col. 0169] “in their good course”: absent from Ivo.]

§ 2. But we do not wish those who, after the prohibition was made, refused to refrain from their wives to be promoted to sacred order, because no one ought to approach the ministry of the altar unless his chastity has been proved before he undertakes the ministry.

Part II. Gratian. The reason for this establishment was priestly purity, so that they might freely devote themselves to prayer on all days. For if, as Paul says, one must abstain from wives in order that we may devote ourselves to prayer more readily, then surely ministers of the altar, upon whom the daily necessity of prayer rests, are never permitted to engage in conjugal intercourse.

[Note: [Col. 0169] 1 Corinthians 7.]

Accordingly Bede, in his commentary on Luke, ch. 1, says:

[Note: [Col. 0169] *Panormia*, book 3, ch. 92.]

C. II. Priests are commanded always to observe chastity.

Priests, in order that they may always be able to stand at the altar, are commanded always to abstain from wives and always to observe chastity.

[Note: [Col. 0169] “may be able”: “may prevail,” collected editions. — “always”: not found in IV.]

C. III. Those who serve the divine sacraments ought to be continent. Likewise in the Second Council of Carthage, ch. 2.

[Note: [Col. 0169] Held A.D. 390; compare below, Distinction 84, ch. 4; *Panormia*, book 3, ch. 95; Rabanus, *On Penance*, ch. 29.]

It was decreed concerning bishops, priests, and deacons, as befits holy prelates and priests of God, and likewise Levites, or those who serve the divine sacraments, that they ought in every respect to be continent.

[Note: [Col. 0169] “thus”: absent from Böhm. Collected editions read: “as was decreed and is fitting, holy prelates or priests or Levites.” — Ivo and the Basil, Lyons II–III, and Antwerp editions add “ought”; other editions read “must.”]

C. IV. Priests and Levites must not have intercourse with their wives. Likewise Innocent I, letter II to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, ch. 9.

[Note: [Col. 0169] Written A.D. 404; *Register*, book 1, ch. 88; Anselm, book 7, ch. 134 [144]; Burchard, book 2, ch. 118; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, ch. 94; *Decretum*, part 6, chs. 94 and 194. Nearly the same words occur in Innocent’s letter to Exsuperius, ch. 1; compare below, Distinction 82, ch. 2.]

The Church must altogether maintain that priests and Levites do not have intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied with the daily necessities of ministry. For it is written: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy.” For if in ancient times priests did not depart from the temple of God during the year of their turn—as we read of Zechariah—nor entered their own houses at all, though the use of a wife had been permitted to them for the succession of offspring, because no one was commanded to approach the priesthood from another tribe or apart from the seed of Aaron, how much more ought these priests and Levites to preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, since their priesthood or ministry is without succession and no day passes on which they are free either from divine sacrifices or from the office of baptism?

[Note: [Col. 0169] Collected editions add “in every way.”]

[Note: [Col. 0171] “have intercourse”: the original in Coustant reads “come together.” — Leviticus 11:14. — “if”: absent from collected editions. — “during the year of their turn”: Luke’s account of Zechariah is intended; the printed reference is Leviticus 21:12. — “wife’s”: “marital,” original in Coustant; absent from Basil. — Numbers 18:7. — “apart from”: “besides,” Coustant’s original and Merlin; Hispana and others: “had been commanded”; Coustant: “had been commanded to no one”; collected editions except Basil: “was permitted.” — “preserve”: “keep,” Basil.]

C. V. PALEA. [The same, in the same place.]

“For, as Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying, ‘Abstain for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer’—and he certainly commanded this to laypersons—how much more must priests, for whom prayer and sacrifice are a continual duty, always abstain from such intercourse.”

[Note: [Col. 0171C] This *Palea*, found only in two Vatican manuscripts and the Basil edition, is joined to the preceding chapter, as also in Innocent’s letter, and reads: “For as Paul ….” But it has not been altered because it begins a chapter.]

[Note: [Col. 0171] “For”: original; “as,” Basil edition. — “Paul to the Corinthians”: 1 Corinthians 7:5. — “duty”: “office,” original.]

C. VI. Those who abstain from their wives are to be admitted to the sacrifices. The same, letter III to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse, ch. 1.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Written A.D. 405; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, ch. 95; below, Distinction 82, ch. 3.]

It is lawful to admit to the sacrifices those who do not engage in carnal intercourse even with a wife.

[Note: [Col. 0171C–D] In Innocent and below, Distinction 82, ch. *Proposuisti*, where this is repeated, the reading is: “nor is it lawful to admit to the sacrifices those who engage in carnal intercourse even with a wife.”]

[Note: [Col. 0171] “is”: editions of Nuremberg, Paris, Lyons II–III, and Antwerp. — “even”: added in editions of Strasbourg, Venice I–II, Nuremberg, Paris, and Lyons I. — “engage”: “engage,” collected editions.]

[Col. 0171C] C. VII. A priest, who must always pray, must always refrain from marriage. Likewise Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book I.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, ch. 96.]

If a layman, indeed any believer, cannot pray unless he refrains from conjugal intercourse, then a priest, for whom sacrifices must always be offered for the people, must always pray; and if he must always pray, then he must always refrain from marriage.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Collected editions add “therefore”; others read “indeed.” — “for the people”: emphasized in the source. — “therefore”: absent from Basil.]

[Col. 0172A] Gratian. That the foregoing statement concerning marriage was made on account of the Manichaeans and concerning priests is clear from the Council of Gangra, in which ch. 1 is recorded as decreeing thus:

[Note: [Col. 0171D–0172D] Gratian restricts the following canon to priests’ marriages, although it condemns those who disparaged marriage altogether and were unwilling that any Christian, even a layman, should have children. Nor was it issued strictly against the Manichaeans but against a certain Eustathius, who had disseminated this error together with many others in Armenia. This chapter is the same as ch. *Si quis nuptias*, above, Distinction 30, but from another translation.]

[Note: [Col. 0171] Held about A.D. 355; Dionysius’s version, also used in the following passage; compare above, Distinction 30, ch. 12, from the Hispana version.]

C. VIII. Let him who disparages marriage be anathema.

If anyone disparages marriage and detests, or considers blameworthy, a faithful and religious woman sleeping with her husband, as though she could not enter the kingdom of God, let him be anathema.

C. IX. On the same subject. Likewise from the same source, ch. 9.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Above, Distinction 30, ch. 5, from the Hispana version; Burchard, book 8, ch. 61; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, ch. 79.]

Whoever guards virginity or pursues continence as though abhorring marriage, and does not for this reason assume the name of virginity because it is good and holy, let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0171] Original and Ivo add “defiles.”]

[Col. 0172B] Part III. Gratian. The statement read in the Canons of the Apostles can also be understood otherwise. The sense of the chapter may be this: if anyone teaches a priest to despise his wife—not a wife whom he took while already a priest, but one whom he married while still a layman or established in minor orders, and with whom he professed continence when he ascended to sacred orders—no one ought to despise her; that is, no one should cast her out of his mind and affection, without providing her necessities. This interpretation is proved by the authority of Pope Leo, who, writing to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, in letter 90, ch. 3, says:

[Note: [Col. 0171] Letter 167, written A.D. 458 or 459, Ballerini edition; *Register*, book 1, ch. 96; Anselm, book 6, ch. 201; Burchard, book 2, ch. 114; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, ch. 106; *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 68; Polycarpus, book 4, title 31.]

C. X. Ministers of the altar are subject to the same law of continence as bishops and priests.

The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and priests. While they were laymen or readers, they could lawfully marry wives and beget children; but when they reached the aforesaid ranks, what had been lawful for them ceased to be lawful. Therefore, so that a carnal marriage may become spiritual, they must neither dismiss their wives nor possess them except as though they did not possess them, so that affection may remain secure while the works of marriage cease.

[Note: [Col. 0171] “reached”: “reach,” Hispana. — Collected editions add “now”; Hispana reads “so that this.”]

[Note: [Col. 0173] Strasbourg, Basil, Venice I–II, and Nuremberg editions read: “but those who have them should be seen to have them as though they had them not”; other editions: “although those who ….” — “affection”: the following word should read “cease,” not “ceases.”]

C. XI. A bishop or priest must not cast his own wife out of his care. Likewise Leo IX, against the letter of Abbot Nicetas.

[Note: [Col. 0173C] “Leo IX”: This occurs in Humbert’s response to the tract of Nicetas, priest and monk, written against the Latins. Since Humbert wrote the response in the name of Leo IX, whose legate he was, it may rightly be cited under Leo’s name, just as many things from the book of Ennodius are cited under Symmachus’s name above, Distinction 17, ch. *Concilia*, and below, Distinction 40, ch. *Non nos*; Distinction 81, ch. *Nemo*; question 8, ch. 4, *Nonne*; and question 9, ch. 3, *Aliorum*. Likewise above, Distinction 22, the chapter *Omnes*, which occurs in Peter Damian’s discourse, is cited under Nicholas’s name.]

[Note: [Col. 0173] Written A.D. 1054; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, ch. 115.]

We entirely confess that it is not lawful for a bishop, priest, deacon, or subdeacon to cast his own wife out of his care on account of religion; that is, he must furnish her food and clothing, but not lie with her carnally according to the customary manner. We read that the holy apostles acted thus. The blessed apostle Paul says: “Do we not have the right to take about with us a woman, a sister, as do the brothers of the Lord and Cephas?” See, foolish man: he did not say, “Do we not have the right to embrace a sister-woman?” but “to take about with us”—that is, so that she might be supported from the reward of preaching—yet there would thereafter be no carnal marriage between them.

[Note: [Col. 0173] Collected editions read “but.” — “furnish”: collected editions add “but.” — “thus”: “as also,” ibid.; Basil, “as.” — 1 Corinthians 9.]

[Note: [Col. 0173D] “Do we not have …?” There are various interpretations of this passage, as among others Jerome shows in book 1 of *Against Jovinian*.]

[Note: [Col. 0173] Basil reads “James, the brother of the Lord”; other collected editions, “as also the brother of the Lord.” — “a sister-woman”: Basil has “of a woman.”]

Gratian. The same point is confirmed by Gregory’s statement, “A certain priest,” which you should seek below in the following distinction, next-to-last chapter, § 1. Therefore, as is clear from these authorities, priests may supply necessities to wives whom, while in lay status or constituted in minor orders, they lawfully married; but they may not render the marital due.

Part IV. § 2. But an objection is made from book II, ch. 14 of the *Tripartite History*.

[Note: [Col. 0173] Compare Socrates, book 1, ch. 11; Sozomen, book 1, ch. 23; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, ch. 85.]

C. XII. At Paphnutius’s persuasion, the Nicene Synod did not decree that priests should not sleep with their wives.

The Nicene Synod, wishing to reform the lives of those dwelling in the churches, issued laws which we call canons. During their discussion, some seemed inclined to introduce a law that bishops, priests, deacons, and subdeacons should not sleep with wives whom they had married before consecration. But Paphnutius the confessor rose in their midst and objected, declaring marriage honorable and intercourse with one’s own wife to be chastity. He persuaded the council not to enact such a law, asserting that it would be burdensome and might become an occasion of fornication for the men themselves or their wives. Paphnutius—although himself inexperienced in marriage—set forth this view; the synod approved his opinion and decreed nothing on this matter, but left it to each person’s will rather than necessity.

[Note: [Col. 0173D–0174C] “And subdeacons”: These two words are absent from some old manuscripts and from the original of Socrates. Sozomen, however, book 1, ch. 22, has them in Greek and in both the old and new Latin translations, as does Nicephorus.]

[Note: [Col. 0173] “Paphnutius”: collected editions other than the first Basil have “Pannutius”; that Basil edition has “Phanutius.” — “in their midst”: emphasized in the source. — Basil adds “was.” — “persuaded”: collected editions except Basil read “persuaded therefore.” — “law”: Basil. — “themselves”: collected editions read “or themselves”; original, “marital.” — “these things”: “this,” collected editions.]

C. XIII. Priests are to abstain from the embrace of their wives not permanently, but at the time of offering. Likewise the Sixth Synod, ch. 13.

[Note: [Col. 0173] Rather, ch. 13 of the Quinisext Synod, held A.D. 692; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, ch. 86.]

[Col. 0174B] Since we have learned that it has been handed down as a canon in the Church of Rome that those who are to be ordained deacons or priests ought to declare that they will no longer have intercourse with their wives, we, following the ancient canon and apostolic diligence and constitutions, will that the lawful marriages of sacred men shall henceforth remain valid. We in no way dissolve their unions with their wives or deprive them of mutual association at a suitable time. Therefore, whoever is found worthy at subdiaconal, diaconal, or priestly ordination is by no means to be prohibited from ascending to such a rank because of lawful cohabitation with his wife; nor is he to be compelled at his ordination to profess that he must abstain from association with his lawful own wife.

[Note: [Col. 0174C–D] Greek: Ἐπειδὴ ἐν τῇ Ῥωμαίων ἐκκλησίᾳ ἐν τάξει κανόνος παραδεδόσθαι διέγνωμεν, “Since we have learned that it has been handed down as a canon in the Church of the Romans,” etc. This Roman ecclesiastical tradition is defended not only by Jerome in *Against Jovinian*, the Humbert cited above, and other Latin writers, but also quite plainly by Balsamon in his explanation of this canon. What should be thought of all canons attributed to the Sixth Synod has been sufficiently explained at ch. *Habeo librum*, Distinction 16.]

[Note: [Col. 0173] “are to be ordained”: original Greek, μέλλοντας ἀξιοῦσθαι, “those about to be judged worthy.” — “ought”: absent from Basil. — “constitutions”: “constitution,” Ivo. — “worthy”: original and Ivo, ἄξιος. — Collected editions other than the first Basil, Lyons II–III, and Antwerp read “they … are prohibited.” — “lawful”: emphasized in the source. — Basil omits “nor even.” — Basil, Lyons II–III, and Antwerp add “chastity.” — “lawful”: Basil and Böhm read “lawful”; “own”: emphasized in the source.]

Likewise below:

§ 1. Those who minister at the altar ought in every respect to be continent at the time of offering the holy things, so that they may obtain from God what they ask simply.

§ 2. Therefore, if anyone presumes, contrary to the apostolic canons, to deprive any priests or deacons of intercourse and communion with a lawful wife, let him be deposed.

§ 3. Likewise, a priest or deacon who expels his wife on account of religion shall be excommunicated; but if he persists in this, he shall be deposed.

[Note: [Col. 0173] “simply”: collected editions read “suppliantly.” — The original, Anselm, Ivo’s *Decretum*, and Basil read “of marriages”; other editions, “chastity of marriages”; Ivo’s *Panormia* has a variant in the original. — “therefore”: “then,” Basil. — “intercourse”: some editions read “contract.” — Collected editions add “his.”]

Gratian. This must be understood in relation to place. For the Eastern Church, for which the Sixth Synod prescribed a rule of life, did not adopt a vow of chastity for ministers of the altar.

Accordingly Pope Stephen IV says in the first session of the synod which he convened in the Lateran basilica:

[Note: [Col. 0175] These words are not found in the Lateran council held A.D. 769, though Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, ch. 84, also cites them from ch. 4, act 1. We think rather that Stephen IX is meant, since Peter Damian—and, after him, Berthold of Constance’s chronicle—testifies that he enacted certain provisions concerning the celibacy of priests in the Roman Church, perhaps at the Roman council held A.D. 1058, of which a fragment appears in Mansi.]

C. XIV. The Western Church, not the Eastern, has offered a vow of chastity.

Part V. The tradition of the Eastern churches is one thing, and that of this holy Roman Church another. Their priests, deacons, and subdeacons are joined in marriage; but in this Church, or in the Western churches, no priest from subdeacon up to bishop has permission to contract marriage.

[Note: [Col. 0175C] “Marriage”: that is, they may at the same time be in sacred orders and joined in marriage. For even they were not permitted to contract marriage after ascending to sacred orders.]

[Col. 0176A] Part VI. Gratian. Nicholas’s chapter is likewise to be understood with reference to place, because the Bulgarian people, newly converted to the faith, had not yet learned fully to undertake the purpose of sacred religion.

§ 1. But the priest punished in ch. 16 of the Sixth Synod for being bound in unlawful marriage is not to be understood as being in a lawful second marriage, from which every priest ought to be exempt by canonical authority. The statement of the Council of Gangra, “If anyone distinguishes a married priest,” etc., must likewise be understood either as a local enactment or as calling a man married to the woman whom he had married before the time of his ordination.

§ 2. The statement of Pope Martin, “If a subdeacon takes a second wife,” is likewise to be understood in this way. A man is permitted to have a first wife before becoming a subdeacon; when she has died or professed chastity, he is promoted to the subdiaconate. But if, after promotion, he should desire a second marriage, he will be subject to Pope Martin’s judgment.

## DISTINCTION XXXII

[Col. 0175]

[Col. 0175B] GRATIAN.

Part I. Therefore continence must be observed by all who are constituted in sacred orders.

Accordingly Pope Leo says to Anastasius in letter 82, chs. 3 and 4:

[Note: [Col. 0175] Letter 14, written A.D. 446, Ballerini edition; Anselm, book 7, ch. 147; Burchard, book 1, ch. 5 and book 2, ch. 148; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, ch. 100; *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 59, and part 6, chs. 98 and 221.]

C. I. Marriage is not permitted even to subdeacons.

The election of all priests is so exalted that things which in other members of the Church are free from fault are nevertheless held unlawful in them. For although those outside clerical orders are free to pursue the union of marriage and the procreation of children, nevertheless, in order to display the purity of perfect continence, not even subdeacons are permitted carnal marriage: so that those who have wives may be as though they had none, and those who have none may remain unmarried. If this is fittingly observed in this order, which is fourth from the head, how much more must it be observed in the first, second, and third, so that no one may be judged suitable for Levitical ministry, priestly honor, or episcopal excellence if he is discovered not yet to have restrained the pleasure of a wife.

[Note: [Col. 0175] “all”: absent from the original. — “although”: collected editions read “for although.” — Hispana, Anselm, and Ivo add “choice.” — Collected editions except Nuremberg add “and unmarried.” — “is”: “exists,” collected editions. — “Levitical ministry”: absent from the original, Anselm, and Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 0175C–0176D] “Of a wife”: thus corrected from Leo’s letter and the other collectors, except Ivo in part 6, ch. 98, where “luxury” occurs, as previously in Gratian. This passage from the letter shows that at that time it was also the custom in many churches for subdeacons to abstain from their own wives. Before blessed Gregory, however, this was not enjoined generally upon all churches, since Sicily observed differently; see ch. *Nullum*, above, Distinction 28, and ch. *Ante triennium*, Distinction 31.]

[Note: [Col. 0175] “restrained”: “refrained,” the same editions.]

[Col. 0176C] C. II. PALEA. Likewise Gregory to Leo, bishop of Catania, book III, letter 34.

[Note: [Col. 0175] Letter 36, written A.D. 594, book 4, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 7, ch. 148; Polycarpus, book 4, title 31; compare below, Cause 27, question 2, ch. 20.]

“From the report of many we have learned that this custom formerly prevailed among you, that subdeacons might lawfully have intercourse with their wives. To prevent anyone from presuming this again, Servodei, deacon of our see, by the authority of our predecessor, forbade it in this manner: those who were already joined to wives were then to choose one of two alternatives, namely, either to abstain from their wives or certainly not to presume, on any account, to perform ministry. And, as is said, Speciosus, then a subdeacon, withdrew himself from the office of administration on this account and, until the time of his death, performed the office of notary; he ceased from the ministry which a subdeacon ought to perform.

“And after some things:

§ 1. Henceforth, however, let your brotherhood be altogether diligent to examine most carefully those whom it happens to promote to this office, lest, if they have wives, they obtain permission to have intercourse with them; rather, in the likeness of the Apostolic See, let it establish by its own strict authority that they observe all these requirements.”

[Note: [Col. 0175] “learned”: “have come to know,” Basil. — “have intercourse”: “may have intercourse,” collected editions. — “wives”: “spouses,” original and Anselm. — “presume”: “presumes,” Basil. — “or certainly”: the next column begins here. — “time of his death”: collected editions except Basil read “the death of his times,” although Basil itself has *tempora* for *tempus*. — Basil reads “remove from this office.” — “have”: “have,” Basil. — “strictness”: “distinction,” Basil.]

[Col. 0177B] C. III. Those constituted outside sacred orders should marry wives and receive stipends from the Church. Likewise Gregory to Augustine, bishop of the English, ch. 2, in answer to the second question.

[Note: [Col. 0177] Letter 64, written A.D. 601, book 11, Maurist edition; compare the note to ch. 1, Distinction 5; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, ch. 108; *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 86.]

But if there are clerics constituted outside sacred orders who cannot remain continent, they should take wives and receive their stipends from outside, because concerning the very Fathers of whom we have spoken, we know that it is written: “It was distributed to each according to whatever anyone needed.” Therefore provision and care must be taken for their stipends; they must be kept under ecclesiastical rule, so that they may live with good morals, diligently sing psalms, and, by God’s help, keep heart, tongue, and body from all unlawful things.

[Note: [Col. 0177] Acts 2. — “was distributed”: collected editions read “they distributed to each.” — “also”: Ivo. — Collected editions add “and” after “unlawful.”]

C. IV. A subdeacon is not permitted to take a wife. Likewise Pope Nicholas [I] to Odo, archbishop of Vienne.

[Note: [Col. 0177] Letter 1 to Ado of Vienne, written A.D. 864; Ivo, part 6, ch. 119.]

Concerning that cleric named Alveric, whom you say lived chastely through the ecclesiastical orders up to the subdiaconate, we are surprised that he took a wife by your authority, since we never grant anyone permission to take a wife, except those to whom the ecclesiastical rule permits it.

[Note: [Col. 0177] “Alveric”: the original in Mansi, vol. 15, Ivo, and editions of Strasbourg, Venice I–II, and Nuremberg read “Alvic”; Böhm has “Alvero.” — “to take”: “to have,” collected editions other than the first Basil.]

C. V. The Mass of a priest who has a concubine is not to be heard. Likewise Pope Nicholas [II] to all bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0177] At the Roman council, held A.D. 1059, ch. 3; Anselm, book 8, ch. 40. In Ivo’s *Panormia*, book 3, ch. 135, this chapter is entitled: “Decrees of the younger Nicholas and Alexander.”]

II Part. Let no one hear the Mass of a priest whom he certainly knows to have a concubine or a woman living with him. [Col. 0178A] Therefore the holy synod itself established this chapter under penalty of excommunication, saying: “Whoever among priests and deacons,” etc., as is contained in the following chapter of Alexander II. [Note: “As in the following.” This is Gratian’s clause, omitting to report from Nicholas’s chapter those matters which he was immediately to report from Alexander. For the words are the same. Nicholas II, in the extant letter written to all Catholic bishops, stated that in the council which he held at Rome, of 113 bishops, he issued this canon; Alexander II afterwards repeated it in the same words in a council held by himself, as he likewise testifies in a manuscript letter. Hence in the Panormia it is called the decree of the younger Nicholas and Alexander.] [Note: add., “saying to all bishops,” Basel edition.]

C. VI. The Mass of a priest who has a concubine is not to be heard. Likewise Alexander II. [Note: In the Roman council held A.D. 1063, cc. 3, 4, 5.—Ivo, Panormia 1.3.135; 8.142.]

Moreover, we command by precept that no one hear the Mass of a priest whom he certainly knows to have a concubine or a woman living with him. Therefore the holy synod also established this chapter under penalty of excommunication, saying: §1. Whoever is a priest, deacon, or subdeacon, after the enactment of our predecessors of blessed memory, the most holy Popes Leo and Nicholas, concerning the chastity of clerics, has openly taken a concubine or has not put away one already taken, in the name of almighty God and by the authority of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul we command and absolutely forbid him to sing Mass, to read the Gospel or Epistle at Mass, to remain in the sanctuary for the divine offices with those who have obeyed the aforesaid enactment, or to receive a share from the church.

[Note: “From the beginning,” in the original at Mansi.] [Note: “Established,” Basel edition.] [Note: “Priests,” collected editions.] [Note: “Subdeacon” absent from the original.] [Note: “Holy,” collected editions. The author of the canon alludes to the enactments of Leo IX in the Roman council.] [Note: “Or,” original and Basel edition.] [Note: “Of the blessed” absent from the original; “chief Apostles,” collected editions.] [Note: add., “read,” Basel edition.] [Note: “Say,” ibid.]

§2. We also enact by command that those of the aforesaid orders who, obedient to these same predecessors of ours, have preserved chastity shall, beside the churches to which they were ordained, eat and sleep together, as religious clerics ought, and hold in common whatever is due them from the churches.

And, entreating them, we urge them to strive earnestly to attain the apostolic—that is, communal—life, so that, having attained perfection with those who are enriched by the hundredfold fruit, they may deserve to be enrolled in the heavenly homeland. Then, that tithes, first-fruits, and the offerings of the living and the dead be faithfully rendered by laypeople to the churches of God, and that they be under the bishops’ administration; those who withhold them are to be separated from communion with holy Church.

[Note: add., “this,” collected editions.] [Note: “And, entreating.” These words down to “Then” were added from Alexander’s manuscript letter; some of them also occur in Nicholas’s council, which further contains the following sentence beginning “Then,” absent from Alexander’s letter.] [Note: “Communal” absent from the original.] [Note: Matthew 13.] [Note: add., “they,” collected editions.] [Note: “If,” Basel edition.]

III Part. Gratian. Yet these principles seem, by their authority, to conflict with Jerome, Augustine, and the others who show that Christ’s sacraments are not to be avoided whether administered by a good or an evil person, as the following cause concerning simoniacs demonstrates more fully. But Urban II, in a letter addressed to the provost of Saint Iventius, resolves this apparent contradiction, saying:

[Note: “Demonstrate,” collected editions.] [Note: Urban’s letter (17 in Mansi) to Lucius, provost of Saint Juventius near Ticinum.] [Note: “Vincentius,” Basel, Strasbourg, and Lyons editions; “Innocentius,” collected editions.]

§1. Concerning what is further asked in the same letter—namely, whether ordinations and the other sacraments administered by criminals, such as adulterers, violators of consecrated virgins, or persons of that sort, are to be used—we answer as follows. If they are not separated from the Church by schism or heresy, we do not deny that their ordinations and other sacraments are holy and venerable, following blessed Augustine, who discusses such matters concerning John as copiously as he does truthfully. For he says: “A good servant baptizes, and so does a bad servant; the person baptized should not know that he is baptized except by him who has retained for himself the power of baptizing.” And shortly afterwards: “Let not the dove shrink from the ministry of the evil; let it look to the Lord’s authority.”

[Note: “On this point.” Everything from here to the end of the chapter is taken from Urban II’s letter to L[ucius], provost of Saint Iventius at Ticinum, found in an old Vatican Library manuscript. The beginning and a large part of this letter occur below, Causa 1, quaestio 3, chapter *Salvator*, and in several old Gratian manuscripts it forms a separate chapter entitled “On the same subject.”] [Note: Tractate 5 on John 1.]

§2. Nevertheless, our predecessors Nicholas and Gregory decreed that the faithful should abstain from the Masses of priests known truly to be such, both to remove from others the license to sin and to call such persons back to the lamentations of worthy repentance. Our predecessor Gregory writes this, among other things, to Rudolf, duke of Swabia, and Bertulf, duke of the Carentanians: “Knowingly receive in no way the ministry of simoniacs and those lying in fornication; and, as far as you can, forbid such persons from the holy ministries, where it is necessary,” etc.

[Note: Gregory, *Register*, book 2, epistle 45. The words enclosed by asterisks are absent from the original in Mansi.] [Note: “Mysteries,” original.] [Note: “Where,” collected editions; “if,” original.]

§4. Furthermore, concerning the objections syllogistically raised against you in the same letter—namely, if the body and blood of Christ are not, and if the other things mentioned above do not possess the efficacy proper to their dignity, how do they harm those who perform them? But if they do possess it, why are they despised if they are presumptuously undertaken by an unworthy person?—we answer as follows. They do indeed possess the efficacy proper to their dignity, as the aforesaid Augustine says concerning John against the Donatists. But for those who administer or receive these sacraments contrary to the enactments of the aforesaid pontiffs—unless death alone intervenes, so that no one may depart this life without baptism or communion—they harm them so greatly that they are truly idolaters; for both the conferring of ordinations and sacraments by such persons, and their knowing reception otherwise than as set forth above, are most vehemently forbidden by the holy canons. For the prophet Samuel says: “To resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse obedience like the crime of idolatry.” This concerns evil Catholics who are within the Church.

[Note: “Do not possess the efficacy of their own power,” collected editions.] [Note: “If anywhere,” original.] [Note: “Powers and,” collected editions.] [Note: “True,” original and Basel edition.] [Note: 1 Kings 15.]

§4. But the sacraments of schismatics and heretics, because they are outside the Church, we profess, according to the traditions of the holy Fathers—Pelagius, Gregory, Cyprian, Augustine, and Jerome—to possess the form of the sacraments indeed, but not the effect of their efficacy, unless they themselves, or those initiated by their sacraments, return to Catholic unity through the laying on of hands. It should be known, however, that the canons of the Apostles, by whose authority the Eastern Church and, in part, the Roman Church make use of them, and the distinguished martyr Cyprian, together with eighty bishops, call the baptism of heretics “the washing of the devil.” But the martyrs Stephen and Cornelius, Roman pontiffs, and the venerable Augustine in his book *On Baptism*, sharply rebuke Cyprian himself and the aforesaid bishops for this reason, maintaining that baptism celebrated according to ecclesiastical custom, whether by a heretic or a schismatic, is valid. And rightly so, because baptism requires a different consideration from the other sacraments, since it is both prior in rank and more necessary. For a person about to die suddenly is first provided with baptism, before communion of the Lord’s body or other sacraments; and when perhaps no Catholic can be found, it is better to receive the sacrament of baptism from a heretic than to perish eternally. Innocent, Siricius, Leo, Anastasius, Gregory the Great, and the whole Catholic Church followed this judgment of the aforesaid pontiffs Cornelius, Stephen, and Augustine.

[Note: Apostolic Canons 45, 46, 47.] [Note: “More holy,” collected editions.] [Note: Innocent, letter to Victricius, c. 15.] [Note: Siricius, letter to Himerius, c. 1.] [Note: Leo, letter to Rusticus of Narbonne, c. 16.] [Note: Anastasius, letter to Anastasius Augustine, cc. 7–8.] [Note: Gregory, *Dialogues* 1.2.13.]

IV Part. Therefore, receiving sacraments from the hands of such priests is forbidden, not because they are not true in form and effect, but because, when priests of this kind see themselves despised by the people, the shame of embarrassment may more easily spur them to repentance.

C. VII. Whoever wishes to marry must do so before the order of subdeacon. Likewise from the Sixth Synod, chapter 6. [Note: From the Quinisext Synod, A.D. 692; Panormia 3.102. Compare X 1.14.9 (Innocent III).]

If any of those entering the clergy wishes to be joined to a woman by marital right, he must do so before the order of subdeacon.

[Note: “Ordination,” collected editions.]

C. VIII. Readers must either marry or profess continence. Likewise, from the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 19. [Note: Held A.D. 397.—Anselm 7.61 and 152; Panormia 3.111.]

When readers reach the years of puberty, they must be compelled either to marry or to profess continence.

[Note: “Reach,” collected editions.]

C. IX. Subdeacons must preserve continence. Likewise Gregory to Boniface, bishop of Reggio, book III, epistle 5. [Note: Epistle 5, written A.D. 594, book 4, Maurist edition.—Panormia 3.99.]

We decree that your subdeacons observe what we have enacted concerning the Sicilians; nor are you to permit our ruling to be undermined by anyone’s obstinacy or rashness.

[Note: “Individual persons,” Ivo and collected editions.]

C. X. Those who devote themselves to wives after the subdiaconate are to lose benefice and office. Likewise Urban II, in the synod at Melfi, chapter 12. [Note: Held A.D. 1089.—Panormia 3.101. The words “except nevertheless” occur in the Strasbourg edition.]

We remove from every sacred order, and decree that they shall lose office and ecclesiastical benefice, those who wish after the subdiaconate to devote themselves to wives. If, when admonished by their bishop, they do not reform, we grant princes permission to reduce their women to servitude. But if bishops consent to their wrongdoing, they themselves shall be punished by suspension from office.

[Note: “Subdiaconate.” Formerly “diaconate” was read here, marked with an asterisk. It has been corrected from several old manuscripts of Gratian and from the council itself, one copy of which is in the Vatican Library and another was sent from France. For in the Latin Church deacons are never found to have been permitted marriage or its use; Siricius and Innocent always joined them to bishops and priests under the same law of continence. After blessed Gregory and the prohibition contained above, Distinction 31, chapter *Ante triennium*, the same law was established for subdeacons; Urban II here decrees that it be renewed.] [Note: “Of the same man,” collected editions.]

C. XI. Subdeacons and those in higher orders must be excluded from the dignity of their ranks if they refuse continence. Likewise, to Dominic, Patriarch of Grado. [Note: “Likewise,” Böhm. More correctly, however, as seems likely from the collectors of councils after Labbe, these words are attributed to Alexander II, in whose time Dominic lived.—Ivo, Panormia 3.103. Compare X 1.14.9, where the same words are offered under Urban II’s name.] [Note: “Gradensis,” Böhm; “Gangrensis,” Basel edition.]

Let the ungodly be ashamed and plainly understand that, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, those set in the sacred orders of priesthood, diaconate, and subdiaconate, unless they put away women and live chastely, must be excluded from all dignity of those ranks. We speak of manifest cases; of hidden matters God is both knower and judge.

[Note: “The three sacred grades,” Ivo and collected editions.]

The same man, presiding at the Synod of Melfi, said, chapter 3. [Note: Held A.D. 1089.—Panormia 3.104.—X 1.14.9. In Ivo and the collected editions the Council of Meaux is cited.]

C. XII. No one may approach sacred orders unless he is a virgin or of proven chastity.

No one may be permitted to approach a sacred order unless he is either a virgin or of proven chastity, and has had, down to the subdiaconate, one wife who was a virgin.

[Note: “Had,” Basel edition.]

C. XIII. Those established in the three ranks must abstain even from wives. Likewise in the Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 3. [Note: Held A.D. 401.—Panormia 3.105.]

It was decided that bishops, priests, and deacons, in accordance with the prior enactments, must also abstain from their wives; if they do not, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office. Other clerics, however, are not to be compelled to this, but the custom of each church is to be observed.

[Note: “Deacons.” The word “subdeacons” followed, but was removed because it is absent from the original, from the African canon 37, from the Greek Carthaginian canon 71, and from Distinction 84, chapter *Cum de quorundam*, though it occurs in the Carthaginian *Code of Canons*, chapter 5.] [Note: add., “subdeacons,” collected editions.] [Note: “According to the prior enactments”: in Greek, Κατὰ τοὺς ἰδίους ὅρους, “according to their own terms”; Balsamon interprets this as “at the time of his turn,” which departs from the original sense.] [Note: Absent from the Hispanic collection.]

C. XIV. Those in minor orders may marry unless prohibited by a vow or religious habit. Likewise Leo IX against the letter of Abbot Nicetas. [Note: Rather, from the reply of Humbert, legate of Leo IX, against Nicetas, written A.D. 1054.—Panormia 3.107.]

We shall set forth in order and openly what the holy Roman Church does concerning the ranks of clerics. It permits clerics who are only doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, or acolytes—if they are found outside a monk’s vow and habit and do not wish to profess continence—to marry a virgin with priestly blessing; but it does not permit them to marry a widow or divorced woman. For because of this they cannot afterwards be advanced even to the subdiaconate, since neither a layman who takes a non-virgin as wife nor a bigamist can ascend to the clergy. If any of the aforesaid orders wishes to ascend to the subdiaconate, he cannot do this without his wife’s consent: thereafter their carnal marriage must become spiritual, with no one compelling them to this. Nor is the wife afterwards permitted to be joined carnally to the same husband, or to marry anyone during his life or after his death.

[Note: “In,” collected editions; “says,” collected editions.] [Note: “Only.”] [Note: “We permit,” Basel edition; “they are permitted,” other collected editions and Ivo.] [Note: “Unless,” Ivo and collected editions.] [Note: “Or,” the same editions.] [Note: “Cannot,” the same editions.] [Note: “For this.”]

C. XV. Clerics may not take a wife of another sect. Likewise from the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 14. [Note: Held A.D. 431.—Dionysius’s translation.—Ivo, Panormia 3.110.]

Since in certain provinces readers and psalm-singers have been permitted to marry, the holy synod decrees that none of them may take a wife of another sect.

C. XVI. Women may not live with clerics unless their natural relationship excludes every suspicion. Likewise in the Council of Nicaea, chapter 3. [Note: Held A.D. 325.—Dionysius’s translation.—Regino 1.9; Burchard 2.109; Anselm 6.202 (199); Ivo, Panormia 3.112; Decretum, part 6, c. 186.]

V Part. The holy synod absolutely forbade any bishop, priest, deacon, or indeed any person in the clergy to have a woman living with him, except perhaps his mother, sister, aunt, or those suitable persons who escape every suspicion.

[Note: “Great,” original and Ivo’s *Decretum*, Burchard.] [Note: add., “subdeacon,” collected editions except Strasbourg.] [Note: Absent from the original and cited collections.] [Note: “Or also”: Greek, Ἢ ἃ μόνα πρόσωπα πάσαν ὑποψίαν διαπέφευγεν, that is, “or only those persons who have escaped every suspicion.”] [Note: “Or only those,” original and cited collections; in the first Panormia the reading is as in Gratian.] [Note: “Escape,” original; “take refuge from,” Regino.]

C. XVII. PALEA. Likewise Jerome, in his letter to Nepotian on the life of clerics, and elsewhere.

“Let women’s feet tread your lodging either rarely or never. §1. For one who is joined to women’s visits cannot dwell with God with his whole heart. §2. A woman burns the conscience of one living with her. §3. Never discuss women’s appearances. §4. Let women know your name, but not your face. §5. Love in mind, not by bodily familiarity, a woman whom you see living well. §6. If it is good not to touch a woman, then it is evil to touch one.”

[Note: “Lodging.” This chapter occurs in many manuscripts without the name *Palea*. It is collected from several passages of blessed Jerome concerning the avoidance of association with women.] [Note: “Cannot.” In the letter to Oceanus, not thought to be Jerome’s, one reads: “Believe me, [one cannot] dwell with the Lord with his whole heart,” etc.] [Note: “A woman.” In the same place, somewhat earlier: “A woman strikes the conscience of one living with her with fiery fire and burns up the foundations of minds.”] [Note: “Know.” Earlier the text read: “Let women not know your name.” Corrected from several manuscripts and Jerome’s letter to the monk Rusticus.] [Note: “Familiarity.” The letter to Oceanus reads: “frequent in adornment.”]

C. XVIII. A priest must love his wife as a sister and flee her as an enemy. Likewise Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 2. [Note: Ivo, Panormia 5.114.]

A certain priest governed the church entrusted to him with great fear of the Lord. From the time he received his order, he loved his presbytera as a sister but guarded against her as against an enemy. He did not allow her to come nearer to him, nor permitted her under any circumstance to approach him; he utterly cut off from her all intercourse of familiarity.

[Note: “Permitted,” collected editions except Basel.] [Note: “Had cut off,” Ivo.]

Gratian. The Council of Laodicea, chapter 11, shows what kind of woman we ought to understand by “presbytera,” saying:

[Note: Held between A.D. 347 and 381.]

C. XIX. Widows or elder women are called presbyterae.

Women who among the Greeks are called *presbyterae* are called among us widows, elder women, women married only once, and *matricuriae*; they ought not to be established in the Church as though ordained.

[Note: “Women.” Thus reads the ancient—indeed Hispanic—translation. Greek: Περὶ τοῦ μὴ δεῖν τὰς λεγομένας πρεσβύτιδας, ἤτοι προκαθημένας ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ καθίστασθαι: “That those called *presbyterae*, that is, female presidents, ought not to be appointed in the church.” This is Dionysius’s translation except in its final words; for he has “be ordained in churches.” Balsamon on this passage should be consulted.] [Note: add., “however,” collected editions.] [Note: “Matriculariae,” Hispanic collection and Böhm.]

## DISTINCTION XXXIII

[Col. 0183]

[Col. 0183B] GRATIAN.

I Part. Thus it is clear that those established in sacred orders cannot have wives, or, if any are found to be bigamists, cannot ascend to sacred orders. But it is asked whether a man who has had a concubine in addition to a wife may be promoted to the priesthood. Such a man is forbidden sacred orders by the authority of the canons of the Apostles, in which chapter 17 is enacted as follows:

[Note: Anselm 6.148; Ivo, *Decretum* 8.287.]

C. I. A man joined in a second marriage after baptism, or having a concubine, cannot ascend to sacred order.

If anyone after receiving baptism has been joined in a second marriage or has had a concubine, he cannot become bishop, priest, deacon, or indeed any of those who serve in the sacred ministry.

[Note: add., “holy,” Basel edition; “sacred,” other collected editions.] [Note: “Be,” Dionysius.] [Note: add., “from the number,” collected editions.] [Note: “Ministry.” Greek: Τοῦ καταλόγου τοῦ ἱερατικοῦ, “those who are in the priestly catalogue.”]

Gratian. Those serving in the sacred ministry are understood to be subdeacons, who offer the chalice to the deacon, and acolytes, who precede the deacons with candles and are therefore called candle-bearers; they also minister wine and water to the chalice in preparing it. “Concubine” must be understood as in addition to a wife, so that the sense of this chapter is: if anyone, after receiving holy baptism, has been joined in a second marriage or has taken a concubine—whether before he took a wife or after his wife’s death.

Therefore blessed Gregory says:

[Note: “Gregory.” This chapter is taken from chapter 72 of the booklet *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, published among the works of blessed Augustine and frequently cited elsewhere by Gratian himself. Trithemius attributes it to Alcuin, others to Isidore; but more and weightier authorities assign it to Gennadius, including Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Regulations*, book 20; Peter Lombard, *Sentences* 2, distinction 8; Thomas Aquinas, *Quodlibets* 12, article 10; Platina on Symmachus; and others.] [Note: These words appear under Augustine’s name in Anselm 7.26, Ivo’s *Decretum* 8.295, and Polycarpus 2.31.]

C. II. A man who, after baptism, has been husband of two married women is not to be ordained a cleric.

We have determined that a man who, after baptism, has been husband of two married women is not to be ordained a cleric; nor one who had one woman indeed, but a concubine and not a married woman; nor one who has taken in marriage a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute; nor one who, overcome by some anger or by just or unjust fear, has mutilated himself in any member of his body; nor one proved to have taken usury or known to have performed on the stage; nor one who has bewailed mortal crimes in public penance; nor one who at any time became insane in a frenzy or was afflicted by diabolic oppression; nor one who, through ambition, offered money in imitation of Simon Magus.

[Note: add., “we have determined,” Basel edition; “we determine,” other collected editions.] [Note: The collected editions read: “nor indeed one who has taken one concubine or prostitute in marriage.”] [Note: The words “not a married woman; nor one who has taken a widow or a divorced woman” are marked with asterisks.] [Note: “By cutting off any member,” from Anselm, collected editions.] [Note: “Of his body.”] [Note: “Them,” and thenceforth the plural throughout, collected editions.] [Note: “Bewails,” original, Anselm, and Ivo.] [Note: “Purchase,” collected editions.] [Note: “And,” Basel edition.] [Note: “Offers,” original, Anselm, and Ivo; Ivo adds at the end, “seeking office.”]

C. III. Those possessed or epileptic must not minister at sacred altars. Likewise Pope Pius. [Note: add., “to Bishop Felix, chapter 3,” Basel edition. Yet the chapter is taken from the Eleventh Council of Toledo, chapter 13; the error is due to Burchard, 3.72.—Ivo, *Decretum* 2.125; Polycarpus 4.31.]

II Part. We decree generally that none of those who are cast to the ground by demons, or who are driven into frenzy by assaults of affliction of whatever kind, may dare to minister at the sacred altars or rashly thrust themselves into the divine sacraments. Those are excepted who, suffering bodily ailments but free of such attacks, are found cast down to the ground; yet even they are to be suspended from the rank and place of their office until, over the period of a year and at the bishop’s discernment, they are found free from attacks of demons.

[Note: “Ground,” cited collections and collected editions.] [Note: “By any assaults of affliction,” Basel edition.] [Note: “Dare … thrust himself,” ibid.] [Note: “Bodily infirmity,” collected editions; add., “various,” Hispanic collection.] [Note: “Ground,” collected editions.] [Note: “From his office,” Basel edition.] [Note: “Free,” original, Ivo, and Burchard.]

C. IV. On the same subject. Likewise Pope Nicholas. [Note: Something similar occurs in the First Council of Orange, chapter 16. Ivo cites Nicholas to “Aluvinus, archbishop of Jovanensis”; perhaps the reading should be Adalwin, bishop of Juvavum, mentioned above at Distinction 27, chapter 6, and perhaps also the recipient of chapter *Quorundam*, below, Distinction 34.] [Note: Ivo, *Decretum* 11.104.]

Clerics known to have been possessed by demons in youth cannot ascend to the higher rank of sacred government.

[Note: “Approach,” Basel edition.]

C. V. On the same subject. Likewise Pope Gelasius I, letter to all bishops established throughout Lucania, chapter 19. [Note: Written A.D. 494.—Burchard 2.20; Ivo, *Decretum* 2.88 and 6.40; Polycarpus 3.9.]

We have learned that unlawful practices have broken out there to such an extent that the handling of most sacred ministries is granted to persons entangled in demonic and similar afflictions.
