If, while engaged in this work, they encounter some personal necessity, which of the faithful can be confident of his own salvation when he sees the ministers themselves of human healing afflicted by so great a calamity? Therefore they must necessarily be removed, lest a scandal be produced for the weak among those for whom Christ died. Finally, if the divine law did not permit one wounded or perhaps infirm in body to touch holy things, how much more unfitting is it that those struck in mind—which is worse—should be dispensers of the heavenly gift?

[Note: “In that,” Basel edition.] [Note: “Demon-possessed,” original in Mansi.] [Note: “Are granted,” Basel and Paris editions.] [Note: “Of his own and of the faithful,” Ivo; “of his own and of the faithful also,” collected editions.] [Note: Leviticus 21.]

C. VI. Those who had wives at the time of baptism are not forbidden to become clerics if they afterwards live religiously. Likewise Pope Innocent I to Felix, bishop of Nuceria, letter IV, chapter 4. [Note: Letter of uncertain date.—Anselm 7.34; Ivo, Panormia 3.45; *Decretum* 6.95. In the Basel, Lyons, and Antwerp editions it is addressed to Felix, bishop of Capua; this appears to have arisen because manuscripts of Gratian and the Panormia read, “To Bishop Felix, chapter IV.” In Ivo’s *Decretum* it is given from the letter to Exsuperius.]

III Part. Laymen who were baptized while having wives, and who have so ordered their lives that their reputation is in no respect wavering—whether they have joined themselves to clerics or, since their baptism, have attached themselves to monasteries—if they have known neither concubine nor mistress, and have been vigilant in every good work, are not forbidden to be admitted to the clerical state.

[Note: “Are” / “have attached themselves,” collected editions.] [Note: “Have adhered,” Hispanic collection and Ivo, Panormia.] [Note: “If they have not,” collected editions.]

[Col. 0187A] IV Part. Gratian. We nevertheless read that some had a concubine before receiving sacred order, whom the sacred canons do not reject if, after sacred order, they keep themselves unstained from intercourse with her.

Therefore Gregory to Andrew, bishop of Taranto, book II, epistle 44:

[Note: Epistle 45, written A.D. 593, book 3, Maurist edition.—Burchard 1.195; Anselm 8.12; Ivo, *Decretum* 5.310; Polycarpus 4.39.]

C. VII. Concerning a bishop who had a concubine before attaining the summit of his episcopacy.

We have learned with manifest certainty that you had a concubine, concerning whom an unfavorable suspicion has also arisen among some people. But because judgment ought not to be absolute in doubtful matters, we choose to commit this matter to your conscience. Therefore, if, while established in sacred order, you remember that you have been defiled by intercourse with her, after laying aside the honor of the priesthood you must in no way presume to approach ministry. Know that you minister at peril to your soul and will undoubtedly render an account to our God, if, conscious of this crime, you wish to remain in the order you hold while concealing the truth.

[Note: “We have learned.” The words “and we have learned that you share in that crime,” which also occur in the Froben edition of blessed Gregory’s works, followed here. They have been removed because they are absent from other editions, from the other collectors, and from John the Deacon, book 3, no. 43, of Gregory’s life, and utterly disrupt the sense.] [Note: “Chose,” Böhm.] [Note: “To be.”] [Note: “Such,” Basel edition.]

## DISTINCTION XXXIV

[Col. 0187]

[Col. 0187B] GRATIAN.

I Part. A bishop must also avoid excessive familiarity with members of his household.

Therefore Pope Nicholas to Albinus, archbishop:

[Note: “Alduinus,” Basel edition; “Alvinus,” other collected editions and Ivo. Yet it seems it should be read “Adalwin, bishop of Juvavum”; compare Distinction 27, chapter 6.—Ivo, *Decretum* 5.353.]

C. I. A bishop must avoid excessive familiarity even with female relatives.

We have been informed by the report of certain faithful persons that Bishop Lanfred, who is also said to be young, is devoted to hunting—a vice which disgracefully entangles many of the clerical register, namely Germans and Gauls by birth. But this man, if matters are as we have heard, is rightly called young, since, occupied with youthful desires, he is restrained by no gravity. And below: “For, as blessed Jerome says, we never read of a hunter who was holy.” And below: Furthermore, it has been reported to our apostolic office concerning this bishop that he maintains excessive familiarity with a certain daughter of his, and that for this reason an evil reputation has arisen against him. On that account he was admonished and rebuked by your holiness and his fellow bishops, but was in no way reformed. This matter is particularly displeasing, and causes an ever worse opinion of him, because he does not obey the judgments of your blessedness and of his fellow bishops, and through disobedience falls back into the fault of the first-created man.

§1. Therefore your fraternity ought to summon a synodal council with your bishops and suffragans, confront this bishop with salutary words, and command him by pastoral authority to abstain entirely from hunting all beasts and birds and to restrain himself altogether from excessive familiarity with his daughter. If he scorns to obey and, despite your admonitions, delays obedience both in abandoning hunting and in avoiding excessive association with his daughter, let him depart excommunicated from your fellowship. But if he still appears obstinate in this, he must cease from ministry.

[Note: “Leufred,” Basel edition.] [Note: “Is” absent from the collected editions except Basel.] [Note: “Also” absent from Basel edition.] [Note: add., “or,” Basel edition.] [Note: “Irreverently,” collected editions except Basel read *irreveremes*, an apparent error.] [Note: add., “of elders,” Ivo.] [Note: On Micah 5 and Psalm 90.] [Note: add., “to be,” Basel edition.] [Note: “Admonished,” collected editions.] [Note: “To your blessedness,” Basel edition.] [Note: “His fellow bishops,” Basel edition.] [Note: “His,” ibid.] [Note: add., “or dignity,” ibid.]

[Col. 0188C] C. II. PALEA. [From the Fourth Council of Orléans.]

[Note: “Orléans.” This *Palea* is also cited in the Decretals, title *On Hunting Clerics*, chapter 1, from the Council of Orléans, and in the Panormia from chapter 8; but it has not been found in the extant Orléans councils. Burchard and Ivo, part 6, chapter 288, cite it from Meaux. The same ruling occurs in Agde, chapter 55, also cited by Ivo, part 5, chapter 366 and part 13, chapter 30, and in Epaone, chapter 3.] [Note: From the Council of Epaone, held A.D. 517.—Regino 1.176; Burchard 2.213; Ivo, Panormia 3.167; *Decretum* 5.366, 6.288, 13.30; chapter 1, *Compilatio I*, *On Hunting Clerics*; X 1.21.1.]

“An episcop, presbyter, or deacon may not keep dogs for hunting, hawks, or things of that sort. But if any person of these ranks is repeatedly found occupied in this pleasure [Note: [Col. 0187] *voluntate*, “inclination”: original—Ivo.] [Note: [Col. 0187] *detectus*, “detected”: ibid.—Comp. I, bk. 1—Ivo, who nevertheless, pt. 5, c. 366, has *repertus*, “found.”], if he is a bishop, let him be suspended from communion for three months [Note: [Col. 0188C] *From communion*: The Decretals read: “from communion [Col. 0188D] if a presbyter, for two [months]; if a deacon, let him be suspended from every office.” Burchard has: “let the presbyter suspend himself from communion for two [months]; but let the deacon be suspended from every office and communion”; nor is it much otherwise in Ivo, part 6, and in the Council of Epaone. But in Agde and in Ivo, part 5: “Let him suspend himself from communion; let the presbyter abstain for two months; but the deacon [ [Col. 0189] for one [month] ] shall cease from every office and communion.” Yet in the same Ivo, part 13, likewise from the Council of Agde, it is read thus: “let him abstain from communion; let the presbyter abstain for two months [ [Col. 0189] *abstineatur*, “be kept from,” and at the end *cessabit*, “shall cease”: Hispanic Collection], the deacon for one [ [Col. 0189] *vero*, “indeed”: Böhm.] shall cease from every office or communion.”] [Note: [Col. 0187] addition: “if a presbyter, for two [months]”: Basel edition]; but let the deacon be suspended from every office and communion.”

[Col. 0189A] C. III. PALEA [Note: [Col. 0189B] This Palea also occurs under the same title, *On the Hunting of Clerics*, c. 2, where it is cited from the same Council of Orléans, as also in Burchard and Ivo. A ruling in nearly the same words occurs in the Frankish synod under Pope Zachary, which is included in the collections of councils, appears in book 5 of the *Capitularies*, c. 2, and is also found in manuscript among Zachary’s letters, [Col. 0189C] in the frequently mentioned codex of the Dominican monastery.] [Note: [Col. 0189] From the Synod under Boniface, A.D. 742.—Burchard, bk. 2, c. 214. Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 289.—c. 2, Comp. I, *On the Hunting of Clerics*, c. 2, X, same title, bk. 1.]  

“We forbid all servants of God to hunt or wander in the woods with dogs, and to keep hawks or falcons.”

II. Part. Gratian. Here a concubine means a woman united without the legal instruments and taken into a marital relationship by conjugal affection; affection makes her a wife, but the law calls her a concubine. Of her it is said in the First Council of Toledo, c. 17 [Note: [Col. 0189] held A.D. 400.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 6, c. 49; *Decretum*, pt. 8, c. 64.]:

C. IV. He who has no wife but has a concubine in her place is not excluded from communion.

He who [Note: [Col. 0189C] The complete canon of the council, also reported by Ivo and in the *Panormia*, is this: “If anyone, having a believing wife, keeps a concubine, let him not communicate. But he who has no wife and has a concubine in place of a wife [ [Col. 0189] *habeat*, “has”: Hispanic Collection] is not to be excluded from communion; provided, however, that he is content with union to one woman only, whether wife or concubine, as he chooses. Otherwise [ [Col. 0189] addition: *vero*, “indeed”: ibid.] let him be excluded while he remains so, until he ceases and returns to penance.” Nor was every kind of concubinage permitted even at that time. There is no need to report what may be read concerning it in the laws of pagan emperors. Certainly Justinian, Novel 18, c. 5—as it stands in Julian the Antecessor—compares in some manner to wives certain concubines taken without the solemnity of dotal documents. To this class of concubines [Col. 0189D] must be referred what Blessed Augustine wrote in *On the Good of Marriage* and what is cited below, C. 32, q. 2, c. *Solet*. Three things were necessary in such cases: first, that both parties were unmarried; then, their mutual pledge not to join themselves to another, [Col. 0190B] and not to shrink from the procreation of children; third, that they proposed to remain in that union of life until death. Blessed Augustine writes that in these cases it may in some way be called marriage and wedlock, though he does not venture to call a woman thus kept a wife, because dotal documents and other things required by civil and canon law for a lawful wife had not intervened. This appears in the said Novel 18 and below, C. 30, q. 5, c. *Aliter*. Thus women of this kind, since they were not wives, were called concubines; yet because of those three conditions, and especially because they had resolved to remain in marital affection, they were allowed to communicate and were regarded as wives taken with less solemnity. This is what is meant here and in the following chapter by having a concubine “in place of” or “as” a wife; Gratian himself [Col. 0190C] indicated this at the end of the preceding chapter, § *Concubina*. But concubinage with women taken only temporarily, even if they were kept for begetting children, was plainly illicit, as the same Blessed Augustine maintains in c. *Audite*, below in the same question, and in the same *On the Good of Marriage*, c. *Concubina*, below, C. 32, q. 2.] has no wife and has a concubine in place of a wife [is] not excluded from communion; provided, however, that he is content with union to one woman only, whether [Note: [Col. 0189] addition: “namely”: Basel edition] wife or concubine.

[Col. 0189B] C. V. On the same. Likewise Isidore, *On the Difference between the New and Old Testament* [Note: [Col. 0189] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 6, c. 50; *Decretum*, pt. 8, c. 66—from the book *On the Harmony of the New and Old Testament*. However, no book of this kind is extant among Isidore’s works; comparable material occurs in bk. 2, *On Spiritual Differences*, no. 28; *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, bk. 2, c. 19; and bk. 1 of the *Sentences*, c. 20, entitled “On the Difference of the Testaments.”].

For a Christian it is lawful, I shall not say to have many, but not even two at once [Col. 0190A]: only one, either a wife or, certainly, in place of a wife—if a spouse is lacking—a concubine.

C. VI. PALEA. [From statements of Augustine in book VII of the *Homilies*, homily 49 [Note: [Col. 0189] Sermon 392, Maurist edition; compiled from various Augustinian passages and apparently spurious.—Burchard, bk. 9, c. 15; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 6, c. 43; *Decretum*, pt. 8, c. 153; Polycarpus, bk. 6, title 8.]]

“Hear, dearest brethren, members of Christ and children of the mother Catholic Church! What I say to the candidates [Note: [Col. 0190C] *Competentibus*, “to the candidates”: At this point the words have been restored from the original to their proper order. Who were called *competentes* is explained by Blessed Augustine in his sermon to the candidates; this may also be understood from Augustine elsewhere and from other writers.] [Note: [Col. 0189] “what I say to the candidates, let the faithful hear; what I say to the faithful, let the candidates also hear; what I say to the faithful, candidates, and penitents” (these two words are absent from the Basel editions), “let the catechumens hear, and all,” etc.: editions compared with the original council.] and the faithful, let the penitents hear. What I say to the faithful, I say also to the candidates and penitents. Let the catechumens hear; let all hear; let all fear; let no one despise [this]. Let your hearing be a consolation to me, lest my grief be evidence against you. To the candidates I say: it is not lawful for you to commit fornication; let wives suffice you [Note: [Col. 0190C] *Wives*: In this particular section Augustine’s own words have not been reproduced; some things have been omitted and altered. For he writes thus: “Let wives suffice you—or no wives at all; it is not lawful for you to keep concubines. Let God hear, if you are deaf; let his angels hear, if you despise: it is not lawful for you to keep concubines. If *the candidates hear what I say to the faithful*: you do not have wives; it is not lawful for you to keep concubines whom later you [dismiss, so that you] may take wives. How much greater will your condemnation be if you wish to keep both concubines and wives [whom you] dismiss?”]; let God hear, if you are deaf; let angels hear, if you despise. It is not lawful for you to keep concubines; and if you do not have [Note: [Col. 0189] *habeatis*, “you have”: Basel edition] wives, nevertheless [Col. 0191A] it will not be lawful for you to keep concubines whom you later [Note: [Col. 0191] *propterea*, “therefore”: ibid.] dismiss and take wives; your condemnation [Note: [Col. 0191] *damnum*, “loss”: ibid. + The words enclosed by asterisks are not found in the Maurist editions.] will be all the greater if you wish to have wives and concubines.”

III. Part. Gratian. But if the concubine was not of such a kind, and the age of the man in question is recognized as removing suspicion of future incontinence, he may, by apostolic concession, be promoted to the order of deacon.

Accordingly Pope Pelagius writes to Bishop Florentinus [Note: [Col. 0191] This letter, apparently by Pelagius II, is printed in full in Anselm; Baluze published it in almost precisely the same words from the Colbert manuscript, bk. 5 of the *Miscellanea*.—Polycarpus, bk. 2, title 1.]:

C. VII. He who after his wife’s death has children by a female servant is permitted to become a deacon.

Having received your Fraternity’s report, we have learned that its bearer did not in fact contract a second marriage; yet you have stated that he did not preserve chastity [Note: [Col. 0191] *cum*, “with”: Paris, Lyons, Antwerp editions—Böhm.] after his first [Col. 0191B] marriage. And although there are many things which the authority of canonical exactness [Note: [Col. 0191] *subtilitatis*, “subtlety”: Anselm.] commands to be observed in cases of this kind, nevertheless, because the deficiency of our [Note: [Col. 0191] “of our time”: editions compared with the original.] times—in which not only human merits but human bodies themselves have declined—does not permit the rule of that strictness to remain *in every respect*, and because the age of the man in question is recognized as removing suspicion of future incontinence, you are to know that we have granted that he may be promoted to the diaconate [Note: [Col. 0191] “to the order of the diaconate”: same editions], *yielding, as stated, to the deficiency of the times*. And below:

§ 1. But Micena [Note: [Col. 0191] *Nicena*: Basel edition.], his female servant, by whom he confessed that he had children after his wife’s death, we order to be entrusted, under your direction, to a monastery of whatever kind [Note: [Col. 0191] *cujuscunque*, “of whatsoever”: ibid.], where she is to profess continence [Note: [Col. 0191D] *Entrusted*: Anselm continues: “so that, being of better standing, he may be able to minister in the office to which he is promoted with the merit of a good reputation, and no opportunity may remain for tarnishing his repute”; not much otherwise in Polycarpus.].

Gratian. This is by a dispensation of mercy; but the following decree of the Council of Orléans [Note: [Col. 0192D] *Of Orléans*: These words occur verbatim in the Council of Gerona [ [Col. 0191] held A.D. 517.—Burchard, bk. 2, c. 38; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 139.], c. 8.] is understood according to the strictness of discipline:

C. VIII. A man who has known another woman besides his wife is not to be admitted to the clergy.

If any layman, after [his] wife, has known a woman of any condition whatsoever, he is in no way to be admitted into the clergy [Note: [Col. 0191] *clero*, “in the clergy”: original—*clerum*, “into the clergy”: editions compared with the original.].

IV. Part. Gratian. Therefore, what is written by Gregory and Innocent concerning a concubine and a prostitute is believed to have been enacted because of the expectation of future incontinence: for one who is not afraid to defile himself by unlawful intercourse finds it difficult to preserve continence. Or a man who has known a concubine or prostitute with marital affection is forbidden ordination [Col. 0192A] either because a defiled woman has lost the flower of virginity, or because she does not cease to prostitute herself even if she is taken as a wife. Each circumstance is an impediment sufficient to prevent a person from attaining sacred orders.

Accordingly Pope Hilary, in the Roman Synod, c. 2, writes as follows [Note: [Col. 0191] held A.D. 465.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 15; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, c. 50.]:

C. IX. He who has not taken a virgin as wife is not to approach sacred orders.

Care [Note: [Col. 0191] *cavendum*, “care must be taken”: original—Ivo.] must therefore first be taken that, as was prescribed above in the earlier enactments, no one may aspire to sacred orders [Note: [Col. 0191] *gradus*, “ranks”: original—Anselm—Ivo.] who has taken as wife a woman who was not a virgin [Note: [Col. 0191] *quisquis*, “whoever”: original.] [Note: [Col. 0191] *duxerit*, “has taken”: Basel edition.].

C. X. A bigamist, a penitent, a bodily impaired person, one ignorant of letters, or one subject to public office or any condition is not to become a cleric. Likewise Gregory, bishop of the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0191] Epistle 37, written A.D. 592, bk. 2, Maurist edition.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 35 [42]; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 8, c. 288.—Polycarpus, bk. 2, title 31.], to the Bishop of Squillace [Note: [Col. 0191] “of Salerno”: Basel edition—“of Silitum”: other editions compared.] in book II, epistle 25.

[Col. 0192B] We command that you never perform unlawful ordinations, nor permit a bigamist, one who has not obtained a virgin as wife, one ignorant of letters, one impaired in any part of the body, one under penance [Note: [Col. 0191] *poenitentem*, “a penitent”: Gregory—Anselm—Ivo; from whom the two immediately following words are likewise absent.], or one subject to public office or to any condition, to approach sacred orders. If you find any such persons [Note: [Col. 0191] *reperis*, “you find”: Paris edition], do not dare to promote them.

C. XI. A man whose wife is clearly established to have committed adultery is not to become a priest. Likewise in the Council of Neocaesarea [Note: [Col. 0191] held A.D. 314.—The interpretation of this chapter in Anselm, bk. 7, c. 19, agrees neither with the old version, nor the Hispanic, nor the Dionysian version.], c. 8.

If it has been clearly proven that the wife of any man committed adultery while he was a layman, that man cannot be admitted to ecclesiastical ministry. But if, after he has already been established in the clerical state, she commits adultery, he must dismiss her after giving her a divorce. If, however, he wishes to retain her companionship, he cannot exercise the ministry he has received.

C. XII. On the same. Likewise from the council of Pope Martin [Note: [Col. 0191] c. 28. Capitula of Martin of Braga, from c. 8 of the Council of Neocaesarea.].

If the wife of any layman [Note: [Col. 0191] “of any man”: Hispanic Collection.] is caught in adultery, such a man is in no way to be brought into ecclesiastical ministry. But if, after the ordination of any cleric, his wife has committed adultery, let him dismiss her [Note: [Col. 0191] addition: “from his charge”: Basel edition.]. But if he wishes to remain with her, let him be excluded from ministry.

[Col. 0193A] Gratian. By the authorities set forth above, bigamists and those who have not obtained virgins as wives are prohibited from sacred orders. But it is asked whether a man who took a widow as wife before baptism is for that reason prohibited from sacred orders.

Pope Innocent writes as follows on these matters to Victricius [Note: [Col. 0193] written A.D. 404.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 11; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 55.] [Note: [Col. 0193] *Victori*, “Victor”: editions compared with the original.] bishop of Rouen, epistle II, c. 5 [and 6]:

C. XIII. He who has taken a widow as wife before baptism or after baptism is not to be admitted to the clergy.

If anyone, even as a layman, has taken a widow as wife, whether before baptism [Note: [Col. 0193] absent from the Basel edition.] or after baptism, he is not to be admitted to the clergy, because he appears to be excluded by the same defect. For in baptism sins are forgiven; the bond of a wife already taken is not dissolved. And below:

§ 1. But if a wife taken before baptism is thought not to be counted as a wife, then neither are children begotten before baptism to be regarded as children.

Gratian. Bigamists are also prohibited from every clerical rank, according to the statement of Ambrose, Epistle LXXXII [Note: [Col. 0193] circa A.D. 396.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 6, c. 63; *Decretum*, pt. 8, c. 290.], to the church of Vercelli [Note: [Col. 0193] “to the Vercellians”: editions compared with the original.]:

C. XIV. He who contracts a second marriage is not to become a cleric.

Let us recognize [Note: [Col. 0193] *cognoscimus*, “we recognize”: Basel edition.] that the Apostle established this not only concerning a bishop and presbyter, but that the Fathers also added in the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea [Note: [Col. 0193] *concilio Nic. tractatus*, “proceedings of the Council of Nicaea”: original.] that no one should be a cleric who has contracted a second marriage.

V. Part. Gratian. Similarly, husbands of widows, female servants, or prostitutes cannot become clerics.

[Col. 0193C] Hence one reads in the Canons of the Apostles, c. 18 [Note: [Col. 0193] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 6, c. 68; *Decretum*, pt. 8, c. 297.]:

C. XV. He who takes as wife a woman devoted to public spectacles, a repudiated woman, or a female servant is not to become a deacon.

If anyone takes a widow or [Note: [Col. 0193] “or a rejected woman”: Basel edition—“and her”: other editions compared.] a repudiated woman, a prostitute, a female servant, or any woman devoted to public spectacles, he cannot be a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or one of those who serve in sacred ministry.

VI. Part. Gratian. What a widow, repudiated woman, or prostitute is, Jerome shows in Epistle CXXVIII, to Fabiola, *On the Priestly Garment*, saying:

C. XVI. What a widow, repudiated woman, or prostitute is.

A widow is one whose husband has died. A repudiated woman is one cast off by her husband while he lives. A prostitute is one open to the lust of many.

[Col. 0194A] VII. Part. Gratian. But afterward Pope Martin, yielding to the deficiency of the times, permitted such men to be placed in minor orders, without laying down a rule [Note: [Col. 0193] these three words are absent from the Argentinensis and Norimbergensis editions.], saying:

C. XVII. A subdeacon who takes a second wife is to be assigned among readers or doorkeepers.

If a subdeacon takes a second wife [Note: [Col. 0193] c. 44, Capitula of Martin of Braga, from the Council of Toledo, c. 4.], let him be counted among readers or doorkeepers, provided that he does not read the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0193] “the epistle”: Lyons II and III editions.].

Gratian. Yet where necessity requires, a bigamist may be promoted as far as the subdiaconate.

Accordingly Pope Martin says [Note: [Col. 0193] c. 43, Capitula of Martin of Braga, from the same Council of Toledo, c. 3.]:

C. XVIII. A man who takes a widow as wife may become a subdeacon if necessity requires.

If a reader takes as wife another man’s widow, let him remain a reader; or, if necessity perhaps arises [Note: [Col. 0193] *fuerit*, “shall arise”: editions compared with the original.], let him become a subdeacon, but nothing higher. The same applies if he is a bigamist.

VIII. Part. Gratian. Those forbidden their own marriages are also forbidden to attend wedding banquets.

Thus one reads in the Council of Agde, c. 39 [Note: [Col. 0193] held A.D. 506.—Regino, bk. 1, c. 325; Burchard, bk. 2, c. 134; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 208; Polycarpus, bk. 4, c. 31.]:

C. XIX. Presbyters ought not to attend wedding banquets.

Presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and those thereafter, who are not permitted to take wives [Note: [Col. 0193] *licitum*, “lawful”: Ivo.] [Note: [Col. 0193D] *They are not permitted*: Printed codices read, “they are not permitted at present.” The word “at present” was expunged, since it occurs neither in the original nor in old copies of Gratian, Burchard, Ivo, or the Council of Vannes, c. 11, where this same provision is repeated. Presbyters, indeed, were never permitted to take wives, not even among the Greeks.], should also avoid the banquets of others’ weddings and should not mix with gatherings [Note: [Col. 0193] *admisceantur*, “be mingled”: Hispanic Collection—Ivo.] where love-songs and indecencies are sung, or obscene movements of the body are displayed in choruses and dances [Note: [Col. 0193] *choris*, “choruses/dances”: ibid.] [Note: [Col. 0193] *offeruntur*, “are offered”: Basel edition.], lest the hearing or [Note: [Col. 0193] “and”: editions compared with the original—Ivo.] sight of persons assigned to sacred mysteries [Col. 0194C] [Note: [Col. 0193] *ministeriis*, “ministries”: editions compared with the original, first Basel, Argentinensis.] be polluted by the contagion of shameful spectacles and words [Note: [Col. 0193] singular *deputatus—polluatur*: Hispanic Collection, except Basel edition.].

IX. Part. Gratian. A widow, however, is to be understood as one separated from her husband by his death after the solemn bond of marriage has been made. But if before they come together they have been separated by fatal necessity through the death of either party, then—even though she has been called a wife from the betrothal—after her betrothed’s death she is not called a widow, even if she has been led into his house and veiled with him; nor is anyone prohibited from sacred orders because of union with her.

Accordingly Pope Pelagius writes [Note: [Col. 0193] Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 113, gives this letter under Pelagius’s name, writing to Marcellus, bishop of Atonium (“bishop of Sens”: Baluze, *Miscellanea*, bk. 5). Yet some scholars consider it spurious.]:

C. XX. He who takes as wife a woman veiled with another but not married to him is not forbidden to become a priest.

Since the woman joined in marital union to the cleric Valentinus had earlier been veiled with another, [Col. 0195A] though not married to him, but had remained a virgin, and after the death of the man to whom she had been betrothed and veiled [Note: [Col. 0195] *sponso*, “betrothed”: Baluze, bk. 1—Basel edition—*fuerat sponsa*, “had been betrothed”: editions compared.] she received the veil again [Note: [Col. 0195] *interim*, “meanwhile”: Ivo—Baluze.], no obstacle is thereby created to his promotion [Note: [Col. 0195] *generatur*, “is created”: Böhm.], because, so far as this issue is concerned, there is nothing that conflicts with the canonical enactments [Note: [Col. 0195] *constitutis*, “enactments”: Baluze, bk. 1—editions compared, first Basel, Lyons, Antwerp.].

# DISTINCTION XXXV

[Col. 0195]

[Col. 0195A] GRATIAN.

I. Part. It has been shown briefly by many authorities from what orders bigamists are prohibited; whether those who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism are accounted bigamists; and whether persons established in sacred orders may take wives. § 1. The apostolic description continues [Note: [Col. 0195] 1 Tim. 3:2.]: the person to be ordained is to be sober, not given to wine. This requirement [Col. 0195B] was introduced on the authority of the Old Testament. For ministers [Note: [Col. 0195] below, same distinction, c. 6.] of the Temple are forbidden to drink wine and *sicera*, lest their hearts be weighed down by drunkenness, so that their senses may always remain alert and keen; or because a belly heated with unmixed wine easily boils over into lust. Thus Noah, in drunkenness, exposed his thighs; and Lot, whom Sodom did not overcome, was overcome by wine. § 2. Yet the prohibition against being given to wine is to be understood not of a single occasion but of being frequently filled with wine.

Thus it is also read in Canons 43 and 42 of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0195] Regino, bk. 1, c. 144; Burchard, bk. 14, c. 5; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, c. 179; *Decretum*, pt. 13, c. 73; Polycarpus, bk. 6, title 17; Rabanus, *On Penance*, c. 28.]:

C. I. A deacon, presbyter, or bishop devoted to drunkenness and gambling is to be deposed unless he desists [Note: [Col. 0195] “be deprived of communion”: editions compared with the original.].

A bishop, presbyter, or deacon devoted to gambling and [Note: [Col. 0195] “or”: Basel edition.] drunkenness must either cease or certainly be condemned [Note: [Col. 0195] *deponatur*, “be deposed”: original.]. A subdeacon, reader, or cantor [Col. 0195C] who does the same must either cease or be deprived of communion. The same applies also to a layperson.

C. II. The eating of meat and drinking of wine are read to have been granted after the Flood and prohibited after Christ’s coming. Likewise Jerome, book I *Against Jovinian*.

From the beginning of the human creation, we neither ate meat, nor gave repudiation, nor had our foreskins removed as a sign. In this course we came as far as the Flood. But after the Flood, with the giving of the Law—which no one could fulfill—meat was introduced for eating, repudiations [Note: [Col. 0195] “repudiation—hardness”: editions compared with the original.] were permitted because of hardness, and the knife of circumcision was imposed, as though God’s hand [Note: [Col. 0195] *munus*, “gift”: same editions.] had created more in us than was necessary [Col. 0195D]. But after Christ came at the end of the ages [Note: [Col. 0195] “of the world”: Basel edition.] and turned back Ω to Α [Note: [Col. 0195] “also flies back”: editions compared with the original, first Basel.]—that is, drew the end back to the beginning [Note: [Col. 0195] “that is”: editions compared with the original.]—we are neither permitted to give repudiation, nor circumcised, nor do we eat [Col. 0196A] meat, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0195] Rom. 14:21.]: “It is good not to drink wine and not to eat meat.” For wine too was instituted together with meat after the Flood.

C. III. It is alien to a wise person to devote himself to drinking bouts and drunkenness. The same, book II *Against Jovinian*.

Wine is a luxurious thing [Note: [Col. 0195] Prov. 20:1.], and drunkenness is tumultuous [Note: [Col. 0195] *contumeliosa*, “insulting”: editions compared with the original.]; everyone [Note: [Col. 0195] addition: “for”: Basel edition.] who mixes with these will not be wise.

[Col. 0196B] C. IV. It is shameful for a priest to abound in luxuries, feasts, and wantonness. The same, on Micah, chapter 2.

The prophetic utterance describes the leaders of the Church, who abound in luxuries and believe that they preserve chastity amid banquets and wantonness, as people who must be cast from spacious houses, lavish feasts, and meals acquired with much labour; they are to be cast out because of [Note: [Col. 0195] In the editions compared with the original these words occur in the next sentence after “are to be cast out.”] their evil thoughts and deeds. And if you wish to know where they are to be cast out, read the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0195] Matt. 22:13.]: namely, into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Is it not confusion and disgrace to preach Jesus crucified, a poor and hungry *teacher*, with bodies stuffed full, and to utter the teaching of fasts with flushed [Note: [Col. 0195] addition: “kind and”: Basel edition.] cheeks and swollen mouths? If we are in the place of the apostles, let us imitate not only their teaching [Col. 0196C] but also embrace their manner of life [Note: [Col. 0195] absent from the Basel edition.] and abstinence.

C. V. On the same. PALEA. The same, to Oceanus, Epistle 83.

“A belly heated with unmixed wine quickly boils over [Note: [Col. 0195] *spumat*, “foams”: editions compared with the original, except Basel.] into lusts. Where drunkenness is, there lust and frenzy rule.”

C. VI. On the same. PALEA. [The same, to Nepotian, *On the Life of Clerics*.]

“A wine-loving priest is condemned by the Apostle and forbidden by the old [Note: [Col. 0195] Lev. 10:9; Num. 6:3.] Law. Priests who minister [Note: [Col. 0195] “serve the altar”: original.] in God’s Temple are forbidden to drink wine and *sicera*, lest their hearts be weighed down [Note: [Col. 0195] “in”: Basel edition.] in revelry and drunkenness [Note: [Col. 0195] *graventur*, “be weighed down”: ibid.] [Col. 0196D]. In the Hebrew language, *sicera* [Note: [Col. 0195] “Greek”: ibid.] denotes every drink capable of causing intoxication [Note: [Col. 0195] “by which someone can become drunk”: editions compared with the original.]. And below: Flee every intoxicant and every thing [Note: [Col. 0195] absent from the editions compared with the original.] that overturns the state of the mind, just as [Note: [Col. 0195] “and a man in whom there is light”: ibid.] wine. The Apostle says, “Do not become drunk [Note: [Col. 0195] “It is not lawful”: Basel edition—Eph. 5:18.] with wine, in which there is dissipation.” And above: “Those who serve [Col. 0197A] the altar [Note: [Col. 0197] Compare Jerome, commentary on Galatians 5, and Epistle to Eustochium.] must not drink wine and *sicera*.” Let the bride of Christ [Note: [Col. 0197C] *Bride of Christ*: In the letter to [Col. 0197D] Eustochium it reads: “This first I admonish, this I entreat: let the bride of Christ flee wine as poison.” And shortly afterward: “Wine and youth are a double fire of pleasure.”] flee wine as poison. Wine and drunkenness are a fire.”

C. VII. On the same. [PALEA.] Likewise Prosper [Note: [Col. 0197] Rather, Julianus Pomerius, whose book this is.], *On the Contemplative Life*, book II, c. 22.

“Excessive consumption of wine, not its nature, produces and nourishes luxury.”

C. VIII. In paradise there was abstinence; after paradise, the indulgence of eating began. Likewise Ambrose, *On Elijah and Fasting*, chapters 4 and 5.

On the sixth day beasts were created, and with beasts arose the power of eating and the use of food. Where food began, there the end of the world was made; there [Note: [Col. 0197] “where—there”: original.] it began not to know its own increase, where the divine works [Note: [Col. 0197] *tempora*, “times”: Basel edition.] [Col. 0197B] around it began to rest. By this indication [Note: [Col. 0197] *judicio*, “judgment”: editions compared with the original.] it was declared that the world would be diminished through the foods by which it ceased to increase. And below:

§ 1. And so that we may know fasting not to be new [Note: [Col. 0197] *novellum*, “recent”: same editions.], God the Lord established there the first law concerning fasting. And below: No one yet knew how to transgress, because that which is the first transgression had not yet arisen [Note: [Col. 0197] *quum*, “when”: same editions, first Argentinensis.]. A fast was imposed: the law of abstinence by the Lord God; transgression of the law by the devil; fault through food, concealment after food; awareness of weakness in food, the strength of firmness in fasting. And below: The serpent persuades [Note: [Col. 0197] *suasit*, “persuaded”: editions compared with the original.] toward gluttony; the Lord decrees fasting. Therefore gluttony expelled the ruler [Note: [Col. 0197] “from”: same editions.] from paradise; abstinence recalled the wanderer to paradise. And below:

§ 2. At the beginning of humankind drunkenness was unknown. Noah first planted a vineyard: he provided its nature but did not know its power. Thus wine did not spare even its own discoverer. And below: But his drunkenness urges sobriety upon us. Noah was drunk only once [Col. 0198A]. Once he recognized the evil of drunkenness, he tempered his beast [Note: [Col. 0197] *inventum*, “discovery”: original.] for a remedy, rather than pouring it out for vice.

§ 3. Before wine was discovered, unshaken freedom remained for all [Note: [Col. 0197] addition: “however”: editions compared with the original.]; no one knew how to exact the services of slavery from a partner in his own nature. There would be no slavery today if there had been no drunkenness. Envy of fraternal precedence had indeed already crept in, but reverence for paternal affection still remained. Affection was wounded when drunkenness was laughed at [Note: [Col. 0197] *deridetur*, “is mocked”: Basel edition—*irridetur*, “is ridiculed”: other editions compared.]. Therefore wines do not harm only those whom they tempt, but even more those before whose eyes the drunken limbs of drunkards are exposed.

§ 4. We also read that Lot’s daughters made their father drunk on the mountain to which they had fled, fearing the burning of the Sodomites, and where they lived in a cave. And below:

§ 5. Drunkenness was thus the origin of incest [Note: [Col. 0197] addition: “of intercourse”: editions compared with the original, except Argentinensis and Norimbergensis.], a birth worse than the worst kind of reproduction [Note: [Col. 0197] *regeneratricis*, “regenerative”: editions compared with the original, first Basel.].

§ 6. But Abraham did not serve wine at his banquet; rather, he sacrificed a calf and offered butter and milk even to his angelic guests. *He recognized the Lord of heaven as the maker of the world. He therefore could not offer wine.* Yet rightly [Note: [Col. 0197] “For rightly”: editions compared with the original.] the material of sin was absent where there was forgiveness of sins. Finally John announced him [Note: [Col. 0197] “the Lord”: same editions—compare Matt. 11:18.] without eating bread or drinking wine. Whoever announces Christ [Note: [Col. 0197] *annuntiavit*, “announced”: Basel edition.] ought to keep himself free from every incitement of vices.

C. IX. A cleric who is proved to have been drunk is to abstain from communion for thirty days. Likewise from the Council of Agde [Note: [Col. 0197] held A.D. 506.—Burchard, bk. 14, c. 11; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 13, c. 79.], c. 41.

Above all, drunkenness, the tinder and nurse of every vice, is to be avoided by clerics [Note: [Col. 0197] *vetetur*, “is to be forbidden”: Hispanic Collection—editions compared—In the collection of Gallican councils edited by Dom Labat: “let drunkenness be avoided by clerics.”]. Therefore we decree that anyone who is established to have been drunk is, as rank permits, [Col. 0198C] either to be excluded from communion for thirty days [Note: [Col. 0197] “is to be excluded—is to be subjected”: editions compared with the original.] or subjected to corporal punishment.

# DISTINCTION XXXVI

[Col. 0197]

GRATIAN.

[Col. 0197C] I. Part. The person to be ordained must also be prudent. This should be noted against those who excuse the foolishness of priests under the name of simplicity. A prudent bishop [Note: [Col. 0197] Interlinear gloss on 1 Tim. 3:2.] is to be understood as possessing not merely knowledge of letters, but also competence in the management of secular affairs [Note: [Col. 0197] *dispensatione*, “administration”: editions compared with the original.].

[Col. 0198C] Hence in the letter of Pope Gelasius to the bishops throughout Lucania, c. 18 [Note: [Col. 0197] written A.D. 494.—This is the numbering of Merlin’s canon; in the other collections of councils it is c. 16.—Regino, bk. 1, c. 411; Burchard, bk. 2, c. 18; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, c. 46; *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 37.]:

C. I. The unlettered and bodily impaired are not to be promoted to the clergy.

Let no one presume to promote to the clerical order [Note: [Col. 0197] “of clerics”: Basel edition.] the unlettered, or persons impaired [Note: [Col. 0198C] *Impaired, or*: These two words [Col. 0198D] are absent from most old copies of Gratian and from the original [ [Col. 0197] as also from Regino and Ivo.], whose sense rather than exact words is reported.] in any part of the body, or mutilated [Note: [Col. 0197] *provehere*, “advance”: Regino—Ivo.]. For one lacking sacred learning cannot [Col. 0199A] be suited to ecclesiastical offices, and legal precepts decree that no defective thing at all is to be offered to God [Note: [Col. 0199] *offerre*, “to offer”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0199] Lev. 22.]. § 1. Likewise, those who castrate themselves [Note: [Col. 0199] this is the substance of c. 17 [19 in Merlin] in Gelasius.].

C. II. He who has not been trained in divine service and disciplines is not to aspire to the supreme priesthood. Likewise Pope Zosimus, in a letter to Hesychius, bishop of Salona [Note: [Col. 0199] written A.D. 418.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 28; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, c. 102.].

He who has not been instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines in due sequence, and trained by testing over time in divine service, must in no way presume to aspire to the supreme priesthood of the Church. Not only is his ambition to be held ineffective, but his ordainers also are to lose that rank which they believed they could presume to confer *without due order* [Note: [Col. 0199] These words are likewise absent from Anselm and Ivo, but are found in the original. Here, both in the original and in Anselm, the preceding words read: “but also in his ordination, so that they should lose,” etc.], contrary to the injunctions of the Fathers.

Gratian. See how necessary it is for a bishop to possess knowledge of the sacred writings [Col. 0199B]. Hence, in the Old Testament [Note: [Col. 0199] Exodus, chapter 28, from the interpretation of the Septuagint], among the other ornaments the high priest carried the breastpiece upon his breast, on which “manifestation and truth” were written, because knowledge of the truth ought to be manifest in the breast of the high priest.

§ 1. Hence also the poles [Note: [Col. 0199] Exodus, chapter 25] by which the ark was carried were continually inserted in the rings, so that, whenever the ark had to be carried, no delay would occur in inserting the poles; for preachers, through whom the Church is carried about, ought always to apply themselves to the sacred writings, lest they seek to learn only when their office requires them to teach others.

§ 2. Hence also David [Note: [Col. 0199] 2 Samuel, chapter 5] first received the gift of knowledge through the grace of the Holy Spirit and afterward obtained the administration of the kingdom.

§ 3. Solomon [Note: [Col. 0199] 2 Samuel, chapter 3; 1 Chronicles, chapter 1] likewise asked and obtained from God not riches or a long span of this life, but wisdom.

§ 4. Hence also the Lord first puts his words into the mouth of the prophet and afterward appoints him over nations and kingdoms, saying to Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0199] Jeremiah, chapter 1, verse 9]: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and over kingdoms.”

§ 5. Hence also Malachi [Note: [Col. 0199] Malachi, chapter 2, verse 7] says: “The lips of the priest shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.”

§ 6. Hence also our Savior [Note: [Col. 0199] Luke, chapter 2] first sat in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them, and afterward began to preach, because each person ought first to learn and afterward to undertake the office of preaching.

§ 7. Hence also Solomon first says [Note: [Col. 0199] Ecclesiastes, chapter 3, verse 7], “a time for silence,” and afterward, “a time for speaking,” because truth is first learned in silence and afterward preached in speech [Col. 0200A].

§ 8. Hence the same Lord says [Note: [Col. 0199] Revelation, chapter 22, verse 17]: “Let him who hears say, ‘Come.’”

§ 9. Hence also he first taught the apostles and then sent them to preach, saying [Note: [Col. 0199] Matthew, chapter 10, verse 16]: “Therefore be prudent as serpents and simple as doves.” Likewise, after the resurrection, he first opened their understanding and explained the Scriptures to them, and afterward said to them [Note: [Col. 0199] Mark, chapter 16, verse 15]: “Go into all the world,” and so forth.

Therefore, when he wished to feed five thousand people with five loaves [Note: [Col. 0199] Matthew, chapter 14], he first took the loaves and broke them, then gave them to the disciples, and finally set them before the crowds through them; for he first expounded the mysteries of the Law and the Prophets by discussion, afterward gave their knowledge to the disciples, and finally dispensed it through them to the faithful.

§ 10. Hence Peter too, writing to the rulers of the Church, says [Note: [Col. 0199] 1 Peter, chapter 3, verse 15]: “You ought to be ready to give an account to everyone who asks you for a justification concerning the faith and hope that are in you” [Col. 0200B].

§ 11. Hence Paul too, writing to Timothy, says [Note: [Col. 0199] 1 Timothy, chapter 4, verse 13]: “Attend to reading, exhortation, and doctrine.”

§ 12. From all these things it is plainly gathered that good conduct and moral integrity do not suffice for prelates unless knowledge of doctrine is added.

§ 13. Therefore the priests [Note: [Col. 0199] Exodus, chapter 38], before entering the tabernacle, first washed in the bronze basin which Moses had made from the mirrors of the women.

§ 14. Hence also, in the Song of Songs [Note: [Col. 0199] chapter 5, verse 12], the eyes—by which the prelates of the Church are understood—are compared to doves that rest beside very full streams.

Hence also Jerome [Col. 0199D] [Note: It is cited as from Blessed Jerome and is found in Origen’s sixth homily on Leviticus. Jerome rendered these homilies, along with many others, into Latin, but in such a way that he cut away everything harmful and translated what was useful; he himself declared this in Epistle 62 to Theophilus, Epistle 75 to Vigilantius, and in the prologue to book II on Micah [Col. 0200D]. Gratian frequently cites Origen’s material under Jerome’s name, either because the authority of the Church’s foremost doctor carries greater weight or because Jerome had, by translating it in the manner stated, almost made it his own.] on Leviticus [chapter 8] [Note: Rather, from Origen’s Homily 6 on Leviticus, translated by Rufinus]:

### C. III. It belongs to a priest to possess knowledge of the Law and to devote himself not to wars but to prayers.

[Col. 0200C] If anyone wishes to be a high priest not so much in title as in merit, let him imitate Moses; let him imitate Aaron. For what is said of them? That they do not depart from the tabernacle of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0199] This is absent from the Basel edition]. Moses, therefore, was continually in the tabernacle of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0199] The reading is *orat*, “he prays,” in the Argentinian edition]. And what was his work? Either to learn something from God or himself to teach the people. These are the two tasks of the high priest: either to learn from God by reading the divine Scriptures and meditating on them frequently, or to teach the people. But let him teach those things which he himself has learned from God [Note: [Col. 0199] Absent from the Basel edition] [Note: [Col. 0199] The older editions read *didicerat*, “had learned,” rather than *didicerit*, “has learned”], not from his own heart or human opinion, but those which the Holy Spirit teaches.

§ 1. Moses also performs another task: he does not go to war; he does not fight against enemies. But what does he do? He prays, and while *he* prays, his people conquer. If he relaxes and lets down his hands [Note: [Col. 0201] The other editions read *dimiserit*, “has let go,” rather than *demiserit*, “has let down”], his people are conquered and put to flight. Therefore the priest of the Church too should pray without ceasing, so that the people who are his own may overcome the invisible Amalekite enemies [Note: [Col. 0201] The Basel edition adds “and”], that is, the demons who attack those who wish to live devoutly in Christ [Note: [Col. 0201] The same edition adds “Jesus”].

# DISTINCTION XXXVII

[Col. 0201]

## GRATIAN

### Part I

But it is asked whether they ought to be educated in secular letters. The following is written concerning this in the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 16 [Note: [Col. 0201] Chapter 5 of the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*, in Ballerini; see above at Distinction 18, canon 9. Burchard, book 1, chapter 95; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 130; *Decretum*, part 4, chapter 160, and part 5, chapter 197; Polycarpus, book 4, title 7]:

### C. I. A bishop shall not read books of the gentiles.

A bishop shall not read books of the gentiles; but, when necessity or circumstance requires, he may read those of heretics [Note: [Col. 0201] The editions add “read them through”; the original has “according to the necessity of the time”].

### C. II. Priests who neglect the Gospels and read comedies are reproved.

Likewise Jerome, to Pope Damasus, on the prodigal son, Epistle 146 [Note: [Col. 0201] Written about A.D. 398; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 131; *Decretum*, part 4, chapter 162].

We see priests of God, neglecting the Gospels and the Prophets, reading comedies, singing the amorous words of bucolic verses, holding Virgil [Note: [Col. 0201] Ivo adds “in their hands”; this is also found in the other editions except Basel], and turning into a crime of pleasure in themselves what is a matter of necessity in boys [Note: [Col. 0201] The Basel and Argentinian editions read “is a cause”; the other editions read “is present as a cause”].

### C. III. Those occupied with secular disciplines walk in vanity and darkness of understanding.

The same author, commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, book II, on chapter 4.

Does it not seem to you that the person who is tortured day and night by the art of dialectic walks in vanity of understanding and darkness of mind [Note: [Col. 0201] The Basel edition adds “that”?]? Or the investigator of nature, who raises his eyes beyond heaven and plunges beyond the depths of earth and the abyss into a certain void [Col. 0201D]? Or the person who strikes an iamb—“constructs an iamb” (*iambum struit*) in the printed original, while earlier editions read *iambum fervet*—who diligently distinguishes and heaps up in his heart such a forest of metres [Col. 0201C]? And—to turn to the other side—the one who seeks riches by right and wrong; who flatters kings, hunts after others’ inheritances, and gathers wealth which he does not know to whom he will leave in a moment?

[Note: *Ferit*, “strikes,” was formerly read as *fervet*, “boils.” In the original printed text one finds *iambum struit*, “constructs an iamb.” The reading was corrected from an ancient exemplar of Gratian. Terentianus writes of the iamb:

> The iamb itself remains in six positions,
>
> And from this the name “senarius” was given;
>
> But it is struck three times, and hence is called “trimeter,”
>
> Because in scanning we join two feet together.

Of these same senarii Isidore says in book 1 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 38: “The Greeks call these trimeters because they strike them in pairs.”]

### C. IV. One who misunderstands Holy Scripture or misuses secular wisdom is intoxicated with wine and strong drink.

The same Jerome, book IX, on Isaiah, chapter 28.

[Col. 0202A] They are intoxicated with wine when they misunderstand and corrupt the holy Scriptures; with strong drink when they misuse secular wisdom and the snares of dialecticians, which ought to be called not so much bonds as phantoms [Note: [Col. 0201] The other editions and Böhm read “phantasms”], that is, certain shadows and images which swiftly perish and dissolve [Note: [Col. 0201] The other editions read “are dissolved again”].

The same author [Note: [Col. 0201] From Jerome’s commentary on Jeremiah, book 5, chapter 29, volume 8]:

§ 1. In a tropological sense, we ought to understand as false prophets those who take the words of Scripture otherwise than the Holy Spirit signifies, and as diviners those who, by the conjecture of their own mind, pronounce uncertain future events as though true, without the authority of divine words.

The same author [Note: [Col. 0201] In the same work, book 6, on chapter 31, verse 29]:

§ 2. Whoever does not understand the Scriptures as the truth of the matter requires [Note: [Col. 0201] Absent from the Basel edition; the other editions read “whoever does not understand them … eats”] eats a sour grape.

### C. V. Bishops who educate their sons in secular letters are reproved.

The same Jerome, commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, book III, on chapter 6 [Note: [Col. 0201] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, chapter 166].

Let bishops and presbyters who educate their sons in secular letters read this: they make them read comedies and sing the shameful writings of mimes, perhaps educated at the expense of the Church. What a virgin or widow, or any poor person who poured out all his substance, had offered into the treasury for sin, the grammarian and orator convert into a New-Year’s gift, a Saturnalian dole, and a Minervalian present; or they convert it into household expenses [Note: [Col. 0201] Ivo and the other editions read “the expenses of the temple”] or into filthy prostitutes [Note: [Col. 0201] The other editions read “filthy profit”]. Eli [Note: [Col. 0201] 1 Samuel, chapter 2] the priest was himself holy; but because he did not educate his sons in all discipline and correction [Note: [Col. 0201] Böhm and the other editions read “reproof”], he fell backward and died.

### C. VI. PALEA.

Likewise from the reply of Pope Hadrian to Charlemagne, chapter 49 [Note: [Col. 0202D] This chapter was formerly attributed to Urban. It is found in Hadrian’s writing on images addressed to Charlemagne, chapter 49, and was corrected from there. The same material is found in Blessed Ambrose, book 1, *On the Faith*, addressed to Emperor Gratian, chapter 3.] [Note: [Col. 0201] Written A.D. 787; Ivo, part 4, chapter 229. In the other editions it is cited from the replies of Pope Urban].

“Heretics place all the force of their poisons in dialectical disputation [Col. 0203A], which the opinion of philosophers defines as having force not for establishing, but for the pursuit of destroying [Note: [Col. 0203] The other editions, except Basel, read *disputantes*, “disputing,” for *disputatione*, “disputation”; Ivo reads *ponunt*, “place,” for *constituunt*, “set/place”]. But it did not please God to save his people by dialectic [Note: [Col. 0203] The other editions, except Basel, omit the following words and read “it pleased God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit”]. For the kingdom of God is in the simplicity of faith, not in contention of speech.”

### C. VII. Blessed Jerome is beaten by an angel because he read Cicero’s books.

Likewise Rabanus, *On the Afflictions of the Church* [Note: [Col. 0203] The book is actually by Atto of Vercelli, not Rabanus, and was published by D’Achery in the *Spicilegium*. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 132; *Decretum*, part 4, chapter 164; the latter citation is partly from Rabanus, *On the Afflictions of the Church].

We read of Blessed Jerome that, when he was reading a book of Cicero [Note: [Col. 0203] Ivo reads “the book”], he was rebuked by an angel because he, a Christian man [Note: [Col. 0203] The Basel edition reads *vix*, “hardly,” rather than *vir*, “man”], gave his attention to the fictions of pagans.

Gratian. Hence also that prodigal son in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0203] Luke, chapter 15] is reproved who wished to fill his belly with the husks which the swine ate.

§ 1. Hence also Origenes [Col. 0203D] understands the gnats and frogs by which the Egyptians were struck as the empty chatter of dialecticians and sophistical arguments [Note: Origen, in Homily 4 on Exodus, chapter 7, compares frogs with poets and gnats with dialecticians]. From all these things it is gathered that ecclesiastics should not seek proficiency in secular letters.

§ 2. But, on the contrary, we read that Moses and Daniel [Note: [Col. 0203] Daniel, chapter 1] were educated in every branch of Egyptian and Chaldean knowledge. We also read [Note: [Col. 0203] Exodus, chapter 3, verse 22] that the Lord commanded the children of Israel to despoil the Egyptians of gold and silver, morally instructing us that, if we find among poets either the gold of wisdom or the silver of eloquence, we should turn it to the use of salutary instruction.

§ 3. In Leviticus [Note: [Col. 0203] Leviticus, chapter 2, verse 14] too we are commanded to offer to the Lord the firstfruits [Col. 0203D] of honey—that is, the sweetness of human eloquence.

[Note: Leviticus 2 forbids leaven and honey to be burned in the sacrifice of the Lord, yet commands their firstfruits to be offered, though not placed on the altar. In the ordinary gloss honey is understood as Gentile eloquence; Hesychius interprets it as pagan teaching, whose firstfruits may be offered to God in imitation of Blessed Paul the Apostle.]

§ 4. The Magi [Note: [Col. 0203] Matthew, chapter 2; Rabanus, on this passage] likewise offered three gifts to the Lord, in which some wish to understand the three parts of philosophy.

§ 5. Finally, as Cassiodorus [Col. 0203D] attests in his exposition of the Psalter, every splendor of rhetorical eloquence, every mode of poetic diction, and every variety of graceful delivery derives its origin from the divine Scriptures.

[Note: Cassiodorus, in the prologue to the Psalter, chapters 15 and following, explains and commends the eloquence of divine Scripture at length [Col. 0204D]. What he says at the beginning of his exposition of Psalm 6, however, seems especially to correspond to the words cited here.]

§ 6. Hence Ambrose [Col. 0204D] too says on the Epistle to the Colossians: “Every principle of knowledge of the heavenly or earthly creature is in him who is their head and author; thus whoever knows him should seek nothing further, because he is perfect power and wisdom. Whatever is sought elsewhere is found here perfectly. In Daniel and Solomon he showed unbelievers that he is the author of all wisdom. Unbelievers do not think so because they do not read in the Gospels and Prophets astrology, geometry, and similar disciplines. These have therefore been despised by our people, because they avail nothing for salvation but lead into error; while people study them, they take no care for the soul. But one who knows Christ has found the treasure of wisdom and knowledge, because he knows what is useful.”

[Note: These words are collected in summary from Blessed Ambrose’s exposition of chapter 2 of the Epistle to the Colossians and are also reported in the ordinary gloss and by Anselm on the same chapter 2. Gratian’s words closely resemble Anselm’s.]

Hence also Bede, book II of Kings, chapter 9, in his allegorical expositions of Samuel [Note: [Col. 0203] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 133; *Decretum*, part 4, chapter 85]:

### C. VIII. Clerics should not be forbidden to read secular letters.

He disturbs the understanding of the needy and forces it to fail who thinks that they ought altogether to be forbidden to read secular books [Note: [Col. 0203] The other editions read “letters” rather than “books”]. For, if any useful things are found in them [Col. 0204B], it is permissible to take them as one’s own [Note: [Col. 0203] The Basel edition reads “things found”; Ivo reads “useful things found anywhere in them”]. Otherwise Moses and Daniel too would not have allowed themselves to be educated in the wisdom or letters of the Egyptians [Note: [Col. 0203] The other editions add “and of the Chaldeans”], though they abhorred their superstitions and luxuries alike. Nor would the teacher of the nations himself have inserted several verses of poets into either his writings [Note: [Col. 0203] The other editions read “Scriptures”] or his sayings.

### Part II

Gratian. Why, then, are those things forbidden to be read which are so reasonably approved for reading? Some read secular letters for pleasure, delighted by the fictions of poets and the ornament of words; others learn them for instruction, so that by reading they may detest the errors of the gentiles and devoutly turn whatever useful things they find in them to the use of sacred learning. Such persons laudably study secular letters.

Hence Blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 0203] Below, Distinction 86, canon 5] does not reprove a certain bishop because he had learned them, but because, contrary to episcopal duty, he expounded grammar to the people in place of Gospel reading.

Hence Ambrose also writes on Luke, in his explanation of the prologue [Note: [Col. 0203] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 134]:

### C. IX. Secular letters should be read so that they are not unknown.

We read some things lest they be neglected; we read lest we be ignorant; we read not in order to retain them, but in order to reject them [Col. 0204D].

[Note: The *Panormia* likewise reads “lest they be neglected”; but the original and one manuscript of Gratian read “lest they be read.” There the discussion concerns pseudo-gospels. The text was not altered because of the gloss.]

### C. X. Grammar should be read so that the sacred Scriptures may be understood.

Likewise Jerome, on chapter 1 of the Epistle to Titus [Note: [Col. 0205] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 135].

If anyone knows grammatical art or dialectic, so as to have the method of speaking correctly and to distinguish false things from true [Note: [Col. 0205] Böhm reads “judge” rather than “distinguish”], we do not disapprove [Note: [Col. 0205C] These two words, “we do not disapprove,” are absent from the original. Explaining the words at the beginning of the Epistle to Titus, “and the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness,” Blessed Jerome wrote: “There is indeed a truth which does not possess godliness, if someone knows grammar,” and so forth].

§ 1. Geometry too [Note: [Col. 0205] Absent from the other editions, except the older Basel edition, which reads “but”], arithmetic, and music possess truth in their own science; but that science is not the science of godliness. The science of godliness is to know the Law [Note: [Col. 0205] The other editions read “to read the Scriptures”], understand the Prophets, believe the Gospel, and not be ignorant of the Apostles.

§ 2. The teaching of grammarians [Note: [Col. 0205D] This is not by Blessed Jerome but by Isidore, book 3, *On the Highest Good*, chapter 13] may also contribute to life, provided it is taken up for better uses.

### C. XI. Daniel’s example proves that it is not a sin to be educated in secular letters.

Likewise Jerome, on chapter 1 of Daniel [Note: [Col. 0205] Polycarpus, book 4, title 7].

Those who refuse to eat from the king’s table and drink his wine [Note: [Col. 0205] The original reads “who does not wish,” in the singular, and continues in the singular] lest they be defiled—certainly, if they knew that Babylonian wisdom and learning themselves were sinful, they would never consent to learn what it was not lawful to learn. But they learn them not in order to follow them, but in order to judge and refute them; just as someone wishing to write against astrologers, if unskilled in astrology [Note: [Col. 0205] The other editions read *matheseos*, “of astrology,” rather than *mathematis*, “of mathematics”], would expose himself to ridicule [Note: [Col. 0205] The other editions add “not”], as would someone disputing against philosophers if he did not know the doctrines of philosophers.

Therefore they learn the teaching of the Chaldeans with the intention [Note: [Col. 0205] The Basel edition adds “the doctrines and”] with which Moses too learned all the wisdom of the Egyptians. The same author [Note: [Col. 0205] In the prologue to Daniel]:

§ 1. Whenever we are compelled to recall secular literature and to learn from it certain things which we formerly neglected [Note: [Col. 0205] The Roman edition reads “to say” rather than “to learn”; this is an error of the printers], this is not of our own will but, so to speak, of the gravest necessity: so that we may prove that those things predicted many ages earlier by the holy prophets are contained in the writings of Greeks, Latins, and other peoples [Note: [Col. 0205] The Basel edition reads “contain”].

### C. XII. Bishops shall appoint teachers and instructors in suitable places.

Likewise from the Synod of Pope Eugenius II, chapter 34 [Note: [Col. 0205] Held A.D. 826; Anselm, book 7, chapter 2; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, chapter 214; Polycarpus, book 4, title 32].

[Note: Anselm cites this as from a synod held at Rome in the Lateran consistory by Blessed ***. Polycarpus does likewise and adds the name Eugenius, from whom Ivo also cites it. It has been found in the synod of Pope Eugenius II and in the synod of Leo IV; copies of these synods, as stated elsewhere, are in the Vatican Library [Col. 0206D]. The index of a synod held at Rome by Gregory VII also gives the following summary of such a chapter: “That all bishops shall cause the arts of letters to be taught in their churches.”]

It is reported to us concerning certain places that neither teachers nor care for the study of letters are to be found [Col. 0206A]. Therefore, in all bishoprics and subject parishes [Note: [Col. 0205] The other editions read “throughout all the bishoprics and subject parishes”; Böhm has the same], and in other places where need arises, care and diligence must altogether be employed [Note: [Col. 0205] The original, Anselm, and the other editions read “be held” rather than “be employed”], so that teachers and instructors may be appointed [Note: [Col. 0205] The Basel edition reads “instituted”] who continually teach literary studies and the doctrines of the liberal arts, because in these the divine commands are especially made manifest and explained.

### C. XIII. By the authorities of the gentiles their vanity is checked and refuted.

Likewise Augustine, *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, book XIII, chapter 15 [Note: [Col. 0205] The passage is fuller there].

If the Sibyl, Orpheus, or other Gentile seers or philosophers are said to have foretold anything true concerning God, it indeed has some value for refuting the vanity of pagans [Col. 0206B], but not for embracing the authority of such persons. For as great as is the difference concerning Christ’s coming between the preaching of angels and the confession of demons [Note: [Col. 0205] The other editions read “demons” rather than “devils”], so great is that between the authority of prophets and the inquisitiveness of sacrilegious persons.

### C. XIV. Proficiency in secular learning is shown to be necessary for understanding the sacred Scriptures.

Likewise Pope Clement I, Epistle V, to his disciples [Note: [Col. 0205] A Pseudo-Isidorian epistle. Nearly the same words, attributed to the Apostle Peter, are found in book 10 of Clement’s *Recognitions*. Collection of Treatises, part 1, title 1, chapter 25].

### Part III

It has been reported to us that certain people dwelling in your regions oppose sacred teachings [Note: [Col. 0205] Isidore of Seville reads “sound teachings”] and appear to teach, as seems right to them, not according to the tradition of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0205] The other editions read “of the fathers”], but according to their own understanding. For, as we have heard, certain ingenious people of your regions [Note: [Col. 0205] Isidore of Seville reads “according to human ingenuity”] draw many plausible arguments from what they read.

Therefore one must carefully observe that, when the law of God is read, it is not to be read or taught according to one’s own intellectual capacity [Note: [Col. 0205] The other editions add “or ability”]. For there are many words in the divine Scriptures which can be drawn into that sense which each person has rashly presumed for himself [Note: [Col. 0205] The other editions read “has presumed”], but this ought not to be done.

You must not seek an alien and extraneous meaning which you falsify from outside (*adulteretis*) [Note: [Col. 0205] Isidore reads *attuleritis*, “which you have brought in”; the other editions read “a meaning foreign from outside”], or in any manner confirm it by the authority of the Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0205] The other editions and Böhm read “so that you may in some way confirm it by the authority of the Scriptures”], but must draw the meaning of truth from the Scriptures themselves [Note: [Col. 0205] The Basel edition reads “from the written texts”] [Col. 0207A] [Note: [Col. 0207] The other editions add “as one ought”].

Therefore one must learn the understanding of the Scriptures from him who has preserved it as handed down to him by his elders according to truth [Note: [Col. 0207] Isidore and the other editions read “preserves”; the Basel edition adds “and learn the knowledge from him”], so that he may competently uphold what he has rightly received.

For when someone has received from the divine Scriptures a complete and firm rule of truth [Note: [Col. 0207] The other editions add “which is required”], it will not be absurd if he also contributes something from common learning and liberal studies, perhaps acquired in childhood, to the defense of true doctrine—provided that, once he has learned what is true [Note: [Col. 0207] Isidore reads “has learned”], he rejects what is false and fictitious.

### C. XV. Why Christians are forbidden to read poetic fictions.

Likewise Isidore, book III of the *Sentences*, *On the Highest Good*, chapter 13 [Note: [Col. 0207] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 137; *Decretum*, part 4, chapter 167].

### Part IV

A Christian is forbidden to read the fictions of poets because, through the delight of empty tales [Note: [Col. 0207] The other editions read “excessive” rather than “empty”], they stir the mind toward incentives to lust. For one sacrifices to demons not only by offering incense, but also by receiving their sayings with pleasure.

### Part V

Gratian. Thus, as appears from the foregoing, ignorance must always be adverse to priests; for when, blinded through ignorance, they begin to lead others, both fall into the pit [Col. 0208A]. Hence it is said in the Psalm [Note: [Col. 0207] Psalm 68, verse 24]: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bend their back always.”

For when those who lead are darkened, their followers easily bend down to bear the burdens of sins. Priests must therefore labor to cast ignorance away from themselves as though it were a kind of plague.

For although the servant who does not know his master’s will and does not do it is said to be beaten with few stripes [Note: [Col. 0207] From Gregory the Great, *Pastoral Rule*, book 1, chapter 1], this is nevertheless not to be understood universally of all persons. For the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0207] 1 Corinthians, chapter 14, verse 38]: “Whoever is ignorant shall be ignored.” This must be understood of one who refused to understand in order to act rightly [Note: [Col. 0207] Psalm 35, verse 4].

Hence Augustine says in the book *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, question 67 [Note: [Col. 0207] An apocryphal book; Anselm, book 8, final chapter]:

### C. XVI.

[Col. 0208B] Not every ignorant person is immune from punishment. That ignorant person can be excused from punishment who found no one from whom he might learn. But forgiveness is sought for those who, though they had someone from whom they could learn, gave no effort to learning [Note: [Col. 0207] The other editions read “they cannot be forgiven”]. *Such things may not be unknown; therefore they will receive pardon if they are converted.*

[Note: In most ancient manuscripts of Gratian this chapter is joined to the preceding one. It is an answer to a question introduced under Augustine’s name in these words: “What is the meaning of the Savior’s saying while on the cross [Note: [Col. 0207] Luke, chapter 23, verse 34], ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’? For if they do not know, why is forgiveness granted? Especially when King Abimelech says to God [Note: [Col. 0207] Genesis, chapter 20, verse 4], ‘Will you destroy an ignorant nation?’ Not every ignorant person is immune,” and so forth. At the end, certain material from Blessed Augustine himself has been added in order to make the statement more complete.]

Since voluntary ignorance is harmful to all, it is dangerous for priests.

Hence the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 24, reads as follows [Note: [Col. 0207] Held A.D. 633; Collection of Treatises, part 2, title 37, chapter 6; Burchard, book 1, chapter 100; Anselm, book 7, chapter 114 (118); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 202]:

Ignorance, the mother of all errors, is especially to be avoided by the priests of God, who have undertaken the office of teaching among the people [Note: [Col. 0207] The other editions read “among the people of God”]. Priests, therefore, should know the holy Scriptures and the canons [Note: [Col. 0207] Compare the Council of Arles IV, canon 3], so that all their work may consist in preaching and teaching, and that they may build everyone up both by knowledge of the faith and by discipline of works.

[Col. 0208B]

Likewise Leo, bishop, to the clergy and people of the city of Constantinople, Epistle XXII [Note: [Col. 0207] Epistle 59, written A.D. 450, Ballerini edition; Anselm, book 7, chapter 119; Polycarpus, book 4, title 4].

If ignorance seems scarcely tolerable in laypersons [Note: [Col. 0207] Anselm and the other editions read “intolerable”], how much more in those who preside is it worthy neither of excuse nor of pardon [Col. 0209A]?

For how can anything be duly observed by us [Note: [Col. 0209] The original reads “worthily preserved”] if the norm of decretal enactments is broken, at the whim of some persons, by permission granted to the people?

Likewise from sayings of Augustine [Note: [Col. 0209] These words are found in Bede, whom the Roman Correctors wished to regard as the author of the canon; only similar material is found there. Burchard, book 2, chapter 2, and book 19, chapter 8; Anselm, book 7, chapter 109 (121); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 24; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 22; Polycarpus, book 4, title 31].

If even one of these is lacking, the designation “priest” will scarcely stand in him [Note: [Col. 0209] The Argentinian and Basel editions read “in the name”; the Basel edition also reads “will be able to stand”], because the Gospel’s threats are very grave, where it says [Note: [Col. 0209] Matthew, chapter 15, verse 14]: “If a blind man leads a blind man, both fall into the pit.”

[Note: Other collectors also cite Augustine. Almost all these things occur in Bede’s penitential, in the book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, and elsewhere.]

### C. VI. What one who is to be ordained bishop ought to know.

Likewise from the Seventh Synod, chapter 2 [Note: [Col. 0209] Held A.D. 787; translation of Anastasius the Librarian; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 372].

[Source ends here.]

All who chant the psalms promise God: “I will meditate on your ordinances; I will not forget your words” [Note: [Col. 0209] Psalm 118:16]. This is indeed most salutary for all Christians to observe, but especially for those who have attained ecclesiastical [Note: [Col. 0209] “hierarchical”: Ivo.—Collected editions, comparison.] dignity. Therefore we decree that everyone who is to be advanced to the rank of bishop must know the Psalter in every respect [Col. 0209C], so that from it all the clergy under him may likewise be admonished and instructed. The metropolitan is to inquire diligently whether he is ready [Note: [Col. 0209] “This law”: Basel edition.—“Has the law”: Ivo.] to read carefully and not superficially both the sacred canons and the holy Gospel, as well as the book of the divine Apostle and all divine Scripture, and to conduct himself [Note: [Col. 0209] “To be preserved”: Basel edition.—“To conduct oneself or to be preserved”: Argentan edition.—“To be preserved”: the remaining collected editions.] according to God’s commandments [Note: [Col. 0209] This is absent from the collected editions.—“According to their commandments”: Basel edition], and to teach the people entrusted to him. For the substance of our supreme priesthood consists in divinely delivered utterances—that is, in the true discipline of the divine Scriptures [Col. 0210A]—as the great Dionysius testifies [Note: [Col. 0209] Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, book 1, chapter 1]. But if he disputes this and does not promise that he will gladly do and teach these things, he must by no means be consecrated. For God says prophetically [Note: [Col. 0209] Hosea 4:6]: “You have rejected knowledge, and I will reject you, so that you shall not exercise priesthood for me.”
