[Note: [Col. 0209] Held A.D. 397.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 61. Collection in Three Parts, part 2, title 17, chapter 1.—“In their ears”: Basel edition.—“They repent”: Hispanic Collection; collected editions, comparison.]

[Note: [Col. 0209] The collected editions read “in the *Moralia*.”]

[Note: [Col. 0209] Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book 3, distinction 38.]

#### Part II

[Note: [Col. 0209] The original reads *error—cavendus* (“error—must be avoided”).]

Although error ought to be avoided with as much care as we can, not only in greater but also in lesser matters, and although one cannot err except through ignorance of things, it does not follow that everyone who does not know something immediately errs [Col. 0211A], but rather everyone who thinks that he knows what he does not know [Note: [Col. 0211] “If anyone”: collected editions, comparison]. For he approves as true what is false; and that is characteristic of error. Nevertheless, it matters very greatly in what matter each person errs. For in one and the same matter, the person who knows is rightly preferred to one who does not know, and the person who does not err to one who errs. But in different matters—that is, when one knows some things and another knows others, and the first knows more useful things while the other knows less useful or even harmful things—who would not, in the matters the latter knows, prefer that person to one who does not know? For there are some things which it is better not to know than to know.

#### Part III. Gratian

Yet even if bishops or presbyters utter something faulty through ignorance of grammar, they are not therefore to be despised by scholars, because faults of conduct must be guarded against more than faults of speech.

[Col. 0211B] Hence Augustine, in *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, chapter 9 [Note: [Col. 0211] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 383].

### Chapter XII. Scholars must not despise ecclesiastical simplicity

Scholars are to be diligently admonished [Note: [Col. 0211D] “Scholars” is absent from the original. Instead, the following precedes this passage there: “There are also certain persons coming from the most familiar schools of grammarians and rhetoricians, whom you would not dare count among the uneducated, nor among those most learned persons whose minds have been exercised by questions of great matters. And below [Note: [Col. 0211] “For these”: Basel edition; this sentence is absent from the collected editions, comparison.]: It is especially useful for them also to know that meanings are to be preferred to words, just as the mind is preferred to the body. From this it follows that they should prefer hearing truer rather than more eloquent speeches [Note: [Col. 0211] “More discerning”: Basel edition], just as they should prefer having wiser rather than more beautiful friends. They should also know that there is no voice reaching [Col. 0211C] God’s ears except the affection of the mind. Thus they will not mock if they happen to observe some bishops and ministers of the Church invoking God with barbarisms and solecisms, or failing to understand the very words which they pronounce, and separating them confusedly—not because these things ought not to be corrected, so that the people may say “Amen” to what they plainly understand [Col. 0212A], but because they are to be borne devoutly by those who have learned that, as blessing is given by sound in the marketplace, so it is by intention in church [Note: [Col. 0211] “Yet”: original.—“They may have learned”: Basel edition]. ## DISTINCTION XXXIX

[Col. 0211]

### GRATIAN

[Col. 0211C]

Behold, it has been fully shown that priests ought to be skilled in letters, both sacred and secular. The question now arises whether they ought also to possess knowledge of secular affairs. That this is necessary for prelates is demonstrated by many arguments. For prelates ought to provide their subjects not only with spiritual but also with bodily aid [Col. 0211D], after the example of Christ, who taught the crowds following him not only by word but also healed them by power and refreshed them with bodily food. But in order that prelates may fully accomplish all these things, they ought to have practical skill in secular affairs [Col. 0213A], so that through their prudence the churches may be kept unharmed and necessities may be supplied to each person according to his condition. Hence a certain man elected bishop was rejected by Blessed Gregory because of his simplicity, lest the property of the Church be squandered through him.

For Gregory writes thus to the clergy and nobles of Naples, book VIII, letter 40 [Note: [Col. 0213] Letter 62, written A.D. 600, book I, number 10, Maurist edition.—Anselm, I.6.13, “To the noble citizens of Naples.”—*Polycarpus*, 1.2.1]:

### Chapter I. Those unskilled in secular affairs are not to be ordained bishops

[Col. 0214A] Peter the deacon, whom you assert has been elected by you [Note: [Col. 0213] Basel edition: “by all of you”], is altogether, as is said, simple; and you know that at this time a person should be placed upon the height of government who knows how to be concerned not only for the salvation of souls but also for the outward welfare and protection of those subject to him.

## DISTINCTION XL

[Col. 0213]

### GRATIAN

[Col. 0213B]

#### Part I

A bishop ought also to be adorned and hospitable [Note: [Col. 0213] 1 Timothy 3:2]. Episcopal ornaments should be understood as virtues, which are promised them by the Lord when he says: “I will clothe his priests with salvation” [Note: [Col. 0213] Psalm 131:16]. Hence in the Old Testament [Note: [Col. 0213] Exodus 28] priests are said to have been adorned, by the Lord’s command, in various garments, because the life of a pontiff ought to shine with virtues of many kinds, so that he may bring to his rank the beauty which he did not receive from it. For it is not places but life and conduct that make a priest holy. Therefore they should know that they have acquired from the office undertaken not permission to sin, but the necessity of living well.

Hence Pope Symmachus says [Note: [Col. 0213D] This chapter, cited as from Symmachus, occurs in the book which Deacon Ennodius wrote on Symmachus’s behalf. It is rightly cited under Symmachus’s name, because Symmachus and the entire Fifth Synod held concerning Symmachus approved that book in such a way as to grant it authority equal to that of synods and apostolic decrees.—From Ennodius’s apologetic book for the Fourth Synod, held A.D. 501.—*Polycarpus*, book 3, title 7]:

### Chapter I. The priestly office does not confer, but removes, permission to sin

[Col. 0213C] We do not judge that Blessed Peter, as you say, received from the Lord, together with the privileges of his see, permission to sin, nor did his successors. He transmitted to posterity an enduring endowment of merits together with an inheritance of innocence [Note: [Col. 0213] “Transmitted”: collected editions, comparison]. What was granted to him because of the brightness of his deeds [Note: [Col. 0213] “Through the light”: the same editions] belongs to those whom an equal splendour of conduct illumines. For who would doubt that the one whom the summit of so great a dignity raises up is holy? If goods acquired by merit are lacking in him, those supplied by the predecessor of the place [Note: [Col. 0213] “Predecessor”: the same editions] are sufficient [Note: [Col. 0213] “Testify”: the same editions, principally the second and third Lyons editions and Antwerp]. For this dignity either raises persons already distinguished to these heights, or makes those who are raised distinguished.

[Note: [Col. 0213] Burchard, I.1.207; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 321; *Polycarpus*, I.3.8.—Below, Causa 2, question 7, chapter 29.]

It is not easy to stand in Paul’s place and hold the rank [Col. 0214B] of Peter, now reigning with Christ, because this is said: the children of saints are not those who hold the places of saints, but those who perform their works.

[Note: [Col. 0213] The collected editions and Ivo read “to stand in the place of Paul and Peter, and to hold the chair.” [Col. 0213D] The words “because this” through the end are not found in Blessed Jerome, although the other collectors also cite them from him or from his sayings.]

We who preside ought to be known not by the dignity of places or of birth, but by nobility of character; not by the splendour of cities, but by purity of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0213] Letter 32, written A.D. 597, book I, number 7, Maurist edition.—Collection in Three Parts, part 1, title 55, chapter 109.]

Likewise, John Chrysostom [that is, the author of the *Imperfect Work on Matthew*, Homily 40 on chapter 21] [Note: [Col. 0213] *Polycarpus*, in the same place.]

#### Part II

A Christian man falls heavily into sin for two reasons: either because of the magnitude of the sin [Note: [Col. 0213] “Sin”: collected editions, comparison], or because of the height of the dignity.

### Chapter VI. The Apostolic one is condemned if he neglects his own salvation and that of his brethren. Likewise, from the sayings of Boniface the martyr

[Note: [Col. 0214D] “From the sayings of Boniface”: Nauclerus, *Generations*, book 26, testifies that this was said by Boniface the martyr. But Deusdedit, cardinal priest of the title of the Apostles in Eudoxia, in the time of Pope Victor III, composed four books *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, which are preserved in the Vatican Library. In book I, chapter 231, he reports these words concerning the Roman pontiff and the apostolic see of that most holy man, from the acts—as do many manuscripts of Gratian and Ivo—of Boniface, martyr and archbishop of Mainz, but apostolic legate. This chapter occurs among them and is greatly elucidated by what precedes and follows.]

The holy Roman Church, made after Christ Jesus the head of all churches by a privilege of special authority, both divine and human, affects all the members of Christendom according to the quality and condition of its bishop or ruler: they correspond to its safety with their own safety and rejoice with it, and likewise share its infirmities with their own infirmity; and just as they are glorified with its glory, according to the Apostle [2 Corinthians 1; [Col. 0215C]], so they are cast down by its downfall. Thus that prophetic saying is seen to be fulfilled especially in it: “The whole head is sick, and the whole heart sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in it” [Isaiah 1:5].

And indeed all receive the summit of the aforesaid apostolic see with such reverence that they seek a certain discipline of the holy canons and the ancient institution of Christian religion more from the mouth of its ruler than from sacred pages and paternal traditions. They inquire only what he wills and what he does not will, so that they themselves relax or apply their way of life according to his judgment [Col. 0215D].

But if, as is most expedient both for himself and for all, he wastes away without intermission in zeal for the house of God, proves a faithful and prudent steward, and strives to preserve himself irreproachable before God and men in work and word, then, to speak truly, he causes almost the whole world, astonished and anxious with him, to run after God; he leads to the Lord, to be set over all his goods, crowds of people of both sexes and of diverse profession, condition, and age. But if he is found negligent of his own salvation and that of his brethren, useless and slack in his works, and furthermore silent regarding good [Col. 0216C]—which harms both himself and all others more—he nevertheless draws countless peoples with him in crowds, as the first slave of Gehenna, to be beaten with many stripes together with him forever.

No mortal presumes here to rebuke his faults, because he who is to judge all is judged by no one, unless he is found to have departed from the faith. For his enduring stability the whole body of believers prays all the more earnestly, since they perceive that their own salvation, after God, depends more directly upon his safety.

Without prejudice to the mystery of divine omnipotence, in the place rightly held by the Roman Church second after God, the saying of Blessed Job may not inappropriately be applied to the holy Roman Church: “If he destroys, there is no one who builds; and if he shuts a man in, no one opens for him; if he restrains the waters, all things will dry up; and if he lets them loose, they will overturn the earth” [Job 12:14]. Nor without reason, since it holds more especially in Peter the reins of heaven and earth.

Since this Church is the spiritual mother in Christ of all believers, no one ought to refuse to be struck by her discipline [Col. 0216D] or corrected by her censure, according to those proverbs of Solomon [Proverbs 1:8 and 6:21]: “Do not forsake the law of your mother; bind it continually upon your heart”; for whoever rejects discipline is unhappy, and the foolish man despises his mother. And again [Deuteronomy 29:16]: “He is cursed by God who angers his mother, and a mother’s curse uproots foundations.” That is, those who are arrogantly divided [Note: [Col. 0215] Perhaps the reading should be “arrogantly divided”] from that see to which it was said, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” [Matthew 16:18], are proved to be established upon the sand of carnal desire or human presumption; the course of a stream cannot prosper if it is divided from its source.

[Note: [Col. 0213] “The chapter is not of unoffending faith”: Deusdedit, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, book 1, chapter 231; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 23, “from the acts of Boniface.” Inserted in the same way in the Basel edition.]

#### Part III

If the Pope is found negligent of his own salvation and that of his brethren, useless and slack in his works, and furthermore silent concerning good—which harms both himself and all others more [Col. 0215A]—he nevertheless draws innumerable peoples with him in crowds, as the first slave of Gehenna, to be beaten with many stripes together with him forever [Note: [Col. 0215] “To be beaten”: Ivo]. No mortal presumes here to rebuke this man’s faults, because he who is to judge all is judged by no one, unless he is found to have departed from the faith [Note: [Col. 0215] The same formula appears in Clement I’s letter to James; compare also Isidore of Seville, *Sentences*, 1.3.39]. For his enduring stability the whole body of believers prays all the more earnestly, since it perceives that its own salvation, after God, depends more directly upon his safety [Note: [Col. 0215] “They perceive”: Ivo].

### Chapter VII. It is not ranks but merits of life that commend us to God. Likewise, Augustine to Valerius, Letter CXLVIII

[Note: [Col. 0215] Letter 21, written A.D. 391, Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 389.]

#### Part IV

Before all things I ask that your religious prudence consider that there is nothing in this life, and especially at this [Col. 0215B] time, easier, more cheerful [Note: [Col. 0215] Ivo: “lighter”; collected editions, comparison], or more acceptable to men than the office of bishop, presbyter, or deacon, if it is carried out perfunctorily and flatteringly; but before God nothing is more wretched, sorrowful, or damnable.

§ 1. Likewise [Note: [Col. 0215] “The same”: the collected editions, principally Basel.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 193.], there is nothing in this life, and especially at this time [Note: [Col. 0215] The collected editions read “and even at this time”; they also read *est* (“is”) for *esse* (“to be”).], more difficult, laborious, or dangerous than the office of bishop, presbyter, or deacon; but before God nothing is more blessed, if one serves in it in the manner commanded by our Emperor. But what that manner is, I learned neither in childhood nor in my youth; and at the time when I began to learn it [Note: [Col. 0215] Basel adds *tempore* (“at the time”)], violence was done to me because of my sins. For I know not what else to think of it: the second place at the helm was entrusted to me [Note: [Col. 0215] The collected editions, principally Basel and the second and third Lyons editions and Antwerp, read “was entrusted.”] [Col. 0216A], though I did not know how to hold an oar [Note: [Col. 0215] Anselm and C. Vilt read “the last oar.”].

### Chapter VIII. The priesthood is corrupted and dragged down to earth unless it is preserved lawfully and justly. Likewise, Isidore

[Note: [Col. 0215] An entirely uncertain fragment.]

Just as the fitting union of man and woman makes one marriage, and just as the joining of two makes one body [Note: [Col. 0215] “Makes”: Basel edition], so clerical status and priesthood make one presbyter, and election and consecration make one bishop. All these make one body, which is more quickly corrupted and dragged down to earth unless it is preserved lawfully, unless it is commended by just living.

### Chapter IX. Grace, not place, saves the soul. Likewise, Ambrose, *On Paradise*, chapter 4

#### Part V

Observe this [Note: [Col. 0215] Basel edition: “observe.”]: man was made outside Paradise, and woman within Paradise, so that you may observe that each person obtains grace not by nobility of place or birth but by virtue. Finally, the man made outside Paradise, that is, in the lower place, is found better; while she who was made in the better place, that is, in Paradise, is found inferior [Note: [Col. 0215] “Is found”: collected editions, comparison].

### Chapter X. On the same matter. Likewise, Gregory, book VI of the *Register*, letter 5

[Note: [Col. 0217] Letter to Cyriacus, bishop of Constantinople, letter 4, written A.D. 597, book I, number 7, Maurist edition.—Collection in Three Parts, part 1, title 55, chapter 4.]

[Col. 0217A] No hidden places can save the soul without the grace of God; this we sometimes observe even in the errors of the elect themselves. For Lot [Note: [Col. 0217] Genesis 19] was righteous in that very perverse city; on the mountain he sinned. But why do we say these things, when we know greater examples? For what is more delightful than Paradise? What more secure than heaven? Yet man fell from Paradise, and an angel from heaven [Note: [Col. 0217] “From”: Basel edition], by sinning.

### Chapter XI. On the same matter. The same author

[Note: [Col. 0217] Burchard, I.1.206; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 320.]

Adam [Note: [Col. 0217C] In Blessed Gregory’s first book on Ezekiel, Homily 9, the following words occur, which seem to bear somewhat upon this matter [Col. 0217D]: “But that places do not fortify the mind is testified by the first parent of the human race himself, who fell even in Paradise.”], the first man, was cast out of Paradise because of sin: that is, because he cast down from himself the nobility given by God [Note: [Col. 0217] “Cast out”: Basel edition], he was deprived of the nobility of place [Note: [Col. 0217] “May be deprived”: Ivo.—“Is deprived”: Argentan, Basel editions].

### Chapter XII. Not everyone called a priest is a true priest. Likewise, John Chrysostom

[That is, the author of the *Imperfect Work on Matthew*, Homily 43 on chapter 23.] [Note: [Col. 0217] Apocryphal fragment.]

#### Part VI

Many are priests, and few are priests: many in name, few in deed. See therefore how [Col. 0218A] you sit [Note: [Col. 0217] The original reads “may sit”; Argentan, Basel, and Nuremberg editions read “sit”; Böhm] upon the chair, because the chair does not make the priest, but the priest the chair; the place does not sanctify the man, but the man the place; not every priest is holy, but every holy person is a priest. Whoever sits well upon the chair receives honour from it [Note: [Col. 0217] “From the chair”: collected editions, comparison]; whoever sits badly does injury to the chair. Therefore the bad priest acquires from his priesthood an accusation, not dignity.

For if, seated in judgment, you live well and teach well [Note: [Col. 0217] “You teach the people”: collected editions, comparison], you are the judge of all; but if you teach well and live badly, you will be the condemner of yourself alone. For by living well and teaching well you instruct the people how they ought to live; but by teaching well and living badly you instruct God how he ought to condemn you.

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0217] In the same work, Homily 35 on chapter 20]:

§ 1. Whoever desires primacy on earth [Col. 0218B] will find confusion in heaven, nor will he who plots for primacy be numbered among Christ’s servants [Note: [Col. 0217D] “Nor among”: in the indicated passage it reads: “so that there may be no contest for primacy among Christ’s servants, nor let any one,” etc. But the gloss prevented alteration]. Let none of them hasten to appear greater than others, but rather to appear lower than all, because the person greater in honour is not thereby more just; rather, the more just person is the greater. *Therefore a better way of life is to be desired, not a higher rank.*

## DISTINCTION XLI

[Col. 0217]

### GRATIAN

[Col. 0217B]

#### Part I

Behold the moral qualities with which a priest ought to be adorned. But besides these he ought to be adorned outwardly, namely in dress and bearing: in dress, so that he may adorn himself neither in shining nor in filthy garments [Col. 0217C]. For, as Jerome says [Note: [Col. 0217D] Jerome writes to Eustochium, *On the Guarding of Virginity*: “Neither affected shabbiness nor elaborate finery suits a Christian.” He writes to Nepotian also in nearly the same sense: “Avoid dark garments just as much as white ones; finery and shabbiness are equally to be fled, because the one reeks of luxury, the other of glory.”], neither affected shabbiness nor elaborate luxury produces praise; this must be understood of food as well as garments.

Hence Augustine says in book III of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 12 [Note: [Col. 0217] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 195; *Decretum*, part 4, chapter 24]:

### Chapter I. In accordance with the habits of those among whom we live, we ought also to use food

Whoever uses transitory things more restrictively than the habits of those among whom he lives allow [Note: [Col. 0217] Basel reads “allow” (*habeant*)], is either intemperate [Note: [Col. 0218D] In Augustine and Ivo the reading is “temperate.” But because of the gloss it has not been changed] or superstitious. But whoever uses them so as to exceed the bounds of the good custom of those among whom he lives either signifies something or is morally shameful. For in all such matters it is not the use of things but the desire of the user that is at fault.

And below:

§ 1. Therefore we must carefully consider what is fitting to places, times, and persons, lest we rashly condemn things as shameful. For it can happen that, without any fault of desire [Col. 0218C] or gluttony [Note: [Col. 0217] “Of delicacy”: Augustine], a wise person uses very costly food, while a foolish person burns with the foul flame of gluttony even for the cheapest vegetable [Note: [Col. 0217] The words “to the food” are absent from Augustine and Ivo.—Basel: “food”]. And a person might more soundly prefer, following the Lord’s example, to eat fish [Note: [Col. 0217] Luke 24] rather than lentils after the example of Esau [Note: [Col. 0217] Genesis 25], Abraham’s grandson, or barley after the manner of beasts of burden. For most beasts are not more self-controlled than we are merely because they are fed on cheaper foods. In all matters of this kind, what we do is to be approved or disapproved not from the nature of the things we use, but from the reason for using them and the manner of desiring them.

### Chapter II. It is not food but appetite that is at fault. Likewise, on the Epistle of John

Any luxuries, if received without desire, do no harm; and cheap foods, accepted eagerly, hinder progress in abstinence. For David poured out water that he had desired wrongly [Note: [Col. 0219] 2 Samuel 23], and Elijah ate meat [Note: [Col. 0219] 2 Samuel 17.] [Note: [Col. 0219C] These words have not been found in the printed or manuscript works of Blessed Augustine that have hitherto come to hand. Yet nearly the same words occur in Prosper, *On the Contemplative Life*, book 2, chapter 22: “Nor do any luxuries, if received without desire, cause harm; and cheap foods often hinder the progress of abstinence, if they are received eagerly. Hence Saint David punished in himself a desire for water and poured it out when it was offered him by his men, lest he seem to satisfy his desire from it; and the unbidden reception of meat did Saint Elijah no harm.”].

### Chapter III. Wealthy persons should not be compelled to use certain foods contrary to the custom required by their weakness. Likewise, on the Words of the Lord according to Matthew, chapter 7, Sermon V

[Note: [Col. 0219] Sermon 61, Maurist edition.]

Let not the rich be compelled to eat the food of the poor; let them follow the custom required by their weakness, but grieve that they cannot otherwise sustain themselves [Note: [Col. 0219] “To be sustained”: Basel, second and third Lyons, and Antwerp editions.—“To sustain themselves”: the remaining collected editions]. If they change their custom, they fall ill. Let them use superfluities, but give necessities to the needy; let them use costly things, but give cheap things to the poor.

### Chapter IV. Equanimity in enduring, not the use or abstinence from food, constitutes righteousness. Likewise, book II of *Questions on the Gospels*, chapter 11

[Note: [Col. 0219] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, chapter 23.]

What the Lord says in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0219] Matthew 11; Luke 7], “Wisdom has been justified by all her children,” shows that the children of wisdom understand that righteousness lies neither in abstaining nor in eating, but in equanimity in enduring want, in temperance so as not to be corrupted by abundance, and in taking or not taking at the proper time those things whose use is not reprehensible but whose desire is.

For it makes no difference at all what kind of food you take to meet the body’s necessity, provided that you conform [Note: [Col. 0219] The collected editions read the singular “conforms” (*congruat*).], in kinds of food [Col. 0219C], to those among whom you must live. Nor does it matter greatly how much you take, since we see that some people’s stomachs are satisfied more quickly [Note: [Col. 0219] The collected editions add “by foods,” except Argentan], yet they greedily, intolerably, and utterly shamefully crave the very little by which they are satisfied; while others are indeed satisfied with somewhat more [Note: [Col. 0219] The collected editions: “with a little more drink”], but endure want more tolerably [Note: [Col. 0219] “Tolerably”: collected editions, comparison], and, if necessity requires it at the time, look calmly upon dishes set before them and do not touch them [Note: [Col. 0219] “Before the hour”: Augustine’s manuscripts; Ivo; collected editions, comparison].

Therefore it matters more not what or how much food a person takes in accordance with the circumstances of other people and his own person, and with the necessity of his health, but with what ease and serenity of mind he goes without it when he ought [Note: [Col. 0219] “Ought”: Basel edition] or is compelled to do so [Note: [Col. 0219] The source adds “also”: Böhm]. Thus may be fulfilled in the Christian mind what the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0219] Philippians 4:12]: “I know how to have little; I know also how to abound. Everywhere and in all things [Note: [Col. 0219] Basel adds *inaequalitatem* (“inequality” or “change of condition”).] I have been instructed: both to be satisfied and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things in him who strengthens me.”

### Chapter V. Moderation in food and clothing, not their excess, is commended. Likewise, from the Council of Gangra, last chapter

[Note: [Col. 0219] Held about A.D. 355.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 321.]

[The supplied source ends here.]

[Col. 0220B] We do not condemn frugality combined with humble dress; likewise, we commend unostentatious adornment for no purpose beyond bodily care. [Note: [Col. 0220C] “Beyond bodily”: this is from the ancient version. [ [Col. 0219] Rather, from the version found in Isidore Mercator. In the Spanish Collection and in the Quesnel manuscript published by the Ballerini, it reads: “for the sake of.” In the following note even greater confusion appears. For Gratian here too, following Ivo, used the received text of Isidore. Dionysius’s translation, however, is quite different; for it reads: “with extraordinary liberality” (καθ᾽ ὑπερβολήν, “beyond measure”). By contrast, the Spanish Collection reads: “according to,” as Corrector has indicated.] The Greek is: Δι᾽ ἐπιμέλειαν μόνον τοῦ σώματος ἀπερίεργος, that is, “for the sake of bodily care alone, neither superfluous nor laborious”; but it has not been altered because of the gloss.] But we do not admit slovenly and disordered dress and bearing; [Note: [Col. 0219] “and bearing”: Ivo.—Collected editions.] we honor the houses of God, and we accept as holy and beneficial the assemblies held in them, without confining piety to private houses, but honoring every place built in the name of God; [Note: [Col. 0219] “we honor”: Collected editions.—Spanish Collection.] and we accept an assembly held in church for the common benefit; and we bless the good works which are performed beyond one’s means for poor brethren, according to ecclesiastical traditions; [Note: [Col. 0220C] “Beyond one’s means”: in that ancient version it is “according to [Col. 0220D] one’s means.” Dionysius has the reading found in Gratian. But the Greek is: Τὰς καθ᾽ ὑπερβολὴν εὐποιΐας τῶν ἀδελφῶν τὰς κατὰ τὰς παραδόσεις διὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας εἰς τοὺς πτωχοὺς γινομένας, that is, “the brothers’ exceptional and outstanding acts of beneficence, which according to the traditions are carried out through the Church toward the poor.”] [Note: [Col. 0219] Absent from the Basel edition.] and we desire that everything which accords with apostolic traditions and the precepts of the holy Scriptures be done in the Church.

[Col. 0220C] C. VI. Vices often insinuate themselves under the appearance of virtue. Likewise, Gregory to John of Constantinople, Book I of the Register, Epistle 24. [Note: [Col. 0219] Epistle 25, written A.D. 591, Book I, Maurist edition.—Collection in three parts, part 1, tome 55, chapter 3.]

Vices often pretend that they are virtues: stinginess wishes to appear frugality, prodigality generosity, cruelty zeal for justice, and laxity mercy. [Note: [Col. 0219] Added: “insinuate themselves and”: Collected editions.—“Avarice”: same editions—original.]

[Col. 0221A] C. VII. Episcopal authority is to be sought through merits of faith and life, not riches. Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 15. [Note: [Col. 0221] Ancient Church Statutes, chapter 4; cf. chapter 9, Distinction 18.—Collection in three parts, part 2, tome 18, chapter 14.]

Let a bishop have humble furnishings, table, and food, and seek the authority of his rank through the merits of faith and life. § 1. Let him also have a lodging-house [Note: [Col. 0221] Chapter 14, received council text—chapter 1, Ancient Church Statutes—Regino, Book I, chapter 82. In all these, and in the Basel edition, it reads *hospitiolum*, “small lodging-house.”] not far from the church.

C. VIII. On the same matter. Likewise, from the same source, chapter 45. [Note: [Col. 0221] Ancient Church Statutes, chapter 26.—Burchard, Book 2, chapter 209; Anselm, Book 7, chapter 202; Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chapter 284.]

A cleric should demonstrate his profession both by dress and bearing, and therefore should seek elegance neither in garments nor in shoes.

Gratian. Therefore, just as we are admonished in food to observe the customs of those among [Col. 0222A] whom we live, so the same must be understood concerning clothing. For, as is said elsewhere, [Note: [Col. 0221] Above, in this same distinction, chapter 1.] “Whoever, despising those among whom he lives, seeks for himself finer or harsher clothing or food than others, is either self-indulgent or superstitious.” But a priest ought to be orderly in his bearing, so that by the gravity of his walk he may show the maturity of his mind. For disorderliness of body, as Augustine [Note: [Col. 0221] Epistle 109, to nuns.] says, indicates instability of mind. Hence that historian, [Note: [Col. 0221] Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 15.] when describing the inconstancy of a man whose conscience, aroused by anxieties, ravaged his mind, judged this also notable among other things, saying: “Now swift, now slow, was the manner of his gait.” [Note: [Col. 0221] Thus Sallust.—“Arisen”: Collected edition.—Böhm.]

## DISTINCTION XLII

[Col. 0221]

[Col. 0221B] GRATIAN.

Part I. A priest ought also to be hospitable, lest he be among those to whom it will be said at the judgment: “I was a stranger, and you did not receive me.” [Note: [Col. 0221] Matthew 25:35.] For how can one who, following the Apostle, ought to invite others to hospitality be an exhorter to hospitality if he shuts his own house against guests? For if a priest must first require of himself and of his household church what he is afterward to command the people; if, by imitating Christ, he must first do what he afterward teaches the people: it is necessary that he receive the poor as guests, so that by his own example he may more easily draw his subjects to hospitality. § 1. Therefore, a priest about to be ordained should call to mind how Abraham [Note: [Col. 0221] Genesis 18 and 19.] and Lot pleased God by works of hospitality and deserved to receive angels [Col. 0221C] as guests; how the angels, entering the hospitable house at Sodom, delivered Lot with his family; how fire, entering houses shut against guests, destroyed them; and how, according to Jerome, [Note: [Col. 0221] In a Rule of Monks wrongly ascribed to him.] one is convicted of taking what belongs to another if he is proved to retain for himself more than is necessary. Thus let him be trained by works of piety, so that he may receive from God both the supports of this present life and the rewards of eternal glory; for both are promised to piety. § 2. Hence the Apostle, writing to Timothy, [Note: [Col. 0221] 1 Timothy 4:8.] says: “Exercise yourself in piety. For bodily exercise is useful for a little, but piety is useful for all things, having the promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come.” Whoever is a stranger to this cannot be ordained priest. § 3. For if a widow [Note: [Col. 0221] There, chapter 5.] is forbidden to be admitted into the Church when she has not received the poor as guests, has not washed the saints’ feet, and has not performed every good work, then much more must those be forbidden the priesthood who are proved strangers to works of piety. § 4. Hence [Note: [Col. 0221] Added: “some”: Collected editions and first Basel edition.] those who despise works of hospitality are excommunicated by the Council of Gangra. [Note: [Col. 0221] Held about A.D. 355.—Dionysius’s translation.—Burchard, Book 19, chapter 124; Anselm, Book 5, chapter 76; Ivo, *Decree*, part 15, chapter 77.] For this is decreed in it, chapter 11.

### C. I. Those who provide meals for the poor are not to be despised

If anyone despises those who faithfully provide *agapae*, that is, meals, for the poor, and who invite brethren for the honor of God, [Note: [Col. 0221] “The Lord”: Collected editions.] and refuses to share in such invitations, thinking lightly of what is done, let him be anathema.

Gratian. Hence John the Evangelist also excommunicates in his epistle a certain Diotrephes, who neither received the poor nor allowed those who did receive them to remain in the Church. In hospitality, however, there must be no choosing of persons; rather, we must show ourselves hospitable without distinction to all whom we are able to support.

[Col. 0222C] Hence John Chrysostom, in his Epistle to the Hebrews, Homily XI on chapter 6, near the end:

### C. II. No distinction should be made in receiving guests

Part II. Let us rest from this absurd, devilish, and destructive curiosity. [Note: [Col. 0221] “Pernicious”: original.] For if someone says that he is elect among the clergy, if he calls himself a priest, investigate him; for in such cases indiscriminate fellowship is not without danger: the danger concerns matters of greater consequence, for you are not giving but receiving. But if he asks for food, examine nothing in such persons. [Note: [Col. 0221] “Not even in these”: Basel edition.—“Nor in these”: the other collected editions.] Consider how Abraham showed himself hospitable toward all. If he had investigated [Note: [Col. 0221] “Were”: Collected editions.] those who fled to him, he would never have received angels as guests. Perhaps, not thinking [Note: [Col. 0221] “Had thought”: same editions.] that they were angels, he would have repelled them too along with the rest; [Note: [Col. 0221] “But he would have repelled”: same editions. *Rather, the Spanish text.*] but because he received everyone, [Col. 0222D] he received angels also. For God will repay you not according to the life of those whom you receive, but according to your own will, your generosity, abundant honor, mercy, and goodness.

[Col. 0223A] Part III. Gratian. But although meals themselves are not to be despised, they should nevertheless not be celebrated in churches, nor should clerics who are invited to them take portions away for themselves.

Hence, in the Council of Laodicea [Note: [Col. 0223] Held between A.D. 347 and 381.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 128; and from Dionysius’s translation, Anselm, Book 5, chapter 77.], chapter 27:

### C. III. Clerics invited to an *agape* are not to take portions for themselves

Ministers of the altar or any clerics [Note: [Col. 0223D] “Clerics”: in the Greek council and likewise in the ancient version there is added: “or laypeople.”] invited to an *agape* ought not to take portions, because of the insult [Note: [Col. 0223D] “Because of the insult”: the Greek is Διὰ τὸ τὴν ὕβριν τῇ τάξει προστρίβεσθαι τῇ ἐκκλησιαστικῇ, that is, “because reproach is attached to the ecclesiastical order.”] which may on this account be imputed to the ecclesiastical order. [Note: [Col. 0223] “May be”: Spanish Collection—Collected editions—Ivo.]

### C. IV. In places consecrated to God, neither eating nor spreading couches is permitted. Likewise, from the same source, chapter 28

[Note: [Col. 0223] Regino, Book I, chapter 57.—From Dionysius’s translation: Burchard, Book 3, chapter 82; Anselm, Book 5, chapter 77; Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 73.]

[Col. 0223B] Part IV. It is not proper to hold an *agape* in basilicas [Note: [Col. 0223] “In the Lord’s churches”: Spanish Collection.—“In divine dwellings, or churches”: Regino.] or churches, or to eat within them [Note: [Col. 0223D] “And within”: the Greek is Καὶ ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ τοῦ [Col. 0224D] θεοῦ, “and in the house of God”; Dionysius translates it “nor within the house of God,” but in Balsamon the word “God” is absent.], or to spread couches.

[Col. 0224A] C. V. Unless constrained by necessity, clerics are not to dine in church. Likewise, from the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 30. [Note: [Col. 0223] Held A.D. 397.—Regino, Book I, chapter 56; Burchard, Book 3, chapter 83; Collection in three parts, part 2, tome 17, chapter 20; Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 74.]

No bishops or clerics may dine in church, unless perhaps, while traveling, they are refreshed there because lodging is necessary. [Note: [Col. 0223] “May refresh themselves”: Spanish Collection.—“May stay”: Regino.] The people also, so far as possible, are to be prohibited from such meals.

### C. VI. On the same matter. PALEA

[Note: [Col. 0223] Rule of Saint Benedict, A.D. 515, chapter 52.—Regino, Book I, chapter 55; Burchard, Book 3, chapter 81; Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 71.]

Likewise, from the sayings of the blessed Abbot Benedict.

Let this be what the oratory is called: and let nothing else whatsoever be done or stored there except what [Note: [Col. 0223] These final words are absent from the original and Regino.] is fitting for divine [Note: [Col. 0223] Absent from Ivo.] services. [Note: [Col. 0223] “Praises”: Argentinensis edition.—“Mysteries”: Venetian editions I and II, Nuremberg, Lyons I, Paris.]

### C. VII. On the same matter [PALEA]. Augustine, Epistle CIX, on the Rule of Monks

[Note: [Col. 0223] Certain similar matters occur in Augustine’s Epistle 211 to consecrated women, written A.D. 413. Baluze attests that he found the same in the Rule of the monastery of Tarnat.—Regino, Book I, chapter 54; Burchard, Book 3, chapter 80; Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 72.]

[Col. 0224B] In the oratory, absolutely nothing is to be done except the worship of prayer and psalmody, so that the name and the works continually performed there may agree.

## DISTINCTION XLIII

[Col. 0223]

[Col. 0223B] GRATIAN.

Part I. A priest must likewise be chaste, so that he may continually display modesty both in conduct and speech. Hence, in the Song of Songs, [Note: [Col. 0223] Song of Songs 5; interlinear gloss there.] the bride’s cheeks, that is, [Col. 0223C] preachers, are compared to the turtledove. § 1. He must also possess the grace of teaching, because, as Jerome [Note: [Col. 0223] Epistle to Oceanus, and the ordinary gloss on 1 Timothy 3.] says: “An innocent life without speech harms by silence as much as it benefits by example.” For wolves must be driven away by the barking of dogs and the staffs of shepherds. [Note: [Col. 0224D] “Staff”: in Blessed Jerome’s epistle it reads, “The frenzy of wolves must be deterred by the shepherd’s staff also.” But the ordinary gloss agrees with Gratian.] In teaching itself, however, a ruler must be discerning, lest he utter what ought to be concealed or conceal what ought to be uttered.

Hence Gregory, Part II of his *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 4, says:

### C. I. On discernment in preaching and silence

Let a ruler be discerning in silence and useful [Note: [Col. 0223] Added: “and cautious”: Venetian editions I and II, Basel, Lyons, Antwerp.] in speech, lest he utter what should be concealed or remain silent about what should be uttered. For just as careless speech draws into error, so indiscreet silence leaves in error those who could have been instructed. Often, indeed, imprudent rulers, fearing to lose human favor, are afraid to speak freely what is right; and, in accordance with the voice of truth, [Note: [Col. 0223] John 10.] they no longer serve the guardianship of the flock with a shepherd’s zeal, but act as hirelings, because when the wolf comes [Col. 0224C] they flee by hiding themselves in silence. Hence the Lord rebukes them through the Prophet, [Note: [Col. 0223] Isaiah 56:10.] saying: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark.” Hence again he complains, saying: [Note: [Col. 0223] Ezekiel 13:5.] “You have not gone up into the breach, nor set yourselves as a wall for the house of Israel, that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0223] “Set”: Collected editions except the first Basel; all add “yourselves.”] To go up into the breach is to oppose the powers of this world with free speech in defense of the flock. [Note: [Col. 0223] “Of this kind”: Collected editions except Basel.] And to stand in battle on the day of the Lord is to resist, from love of justice, those who contend wickedly. [Note: [Col. 0223] “Combatants”: Basel edition.] For a shepherd to fear to speak what is right—what else is that but to offer his back by keeping silent? [Note: [Col. 0223] “For the shepherd”: original.] Yet if he sets himself before the flock, [Col. 0225A] he places a wall before the enemies on behalf of the house of Israel. Hence again it is said to the sinful people: [Note: [Col. 0225] Jeremiah 2:8.] “Your prophets [Note: [Col. 0225] Added: “indeed”: Basel edition.] saw false and foolish things for you and did not uncover [Note: [Col. 0225] Added: “for you”: Collected editions.] your iniquity, to call you to repentance.” For in sacred speech teachers are sometimes called prophets: since they declare present things fleeting and make known things to come, [Note: [Col. 0225] “Judge”: Basel edition.] divine speech reproves them for seeing false things because, while they fear to rebuke faults, they vainly flatter sinners with promised security. They do not uncover the iniquity of sinners because they keep silence instead of speaking rebuke. For the key of opening is the word of correction, [Note: [Col. 0225] “Reproof”: Böhm edition.] since rebuke reveals a fault which often even the person who committed it does not know. Hence Paul says: [Note: [Col. 0225] Titus 1:9.—“Hence also”: Collected editions.] “That he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and [Col. 0225B] refute those who contradict.” Hence it is said through Malachi: [Note: [Col. 0225] Malachi 2:7.] “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.” Hence the Lord exhorts through Isaiah, saying: [Note: [Col. 0225] Isaiah 58:1.] “Cry aloud; do not cease; lift up your voice like [Note: [Col. 0225] “As”: Basel edition.] a trumpet.” Whoever approaches the priesthood assumes the office of a herald, [Note: [Col. 0225] “Assumed”: Böhm.] so that before the terrible coming of the Judge who follows, he himself may go forward crying aloud. [Note: [Col. 0225] “Proclaiming”: same editions except Basel.] Therefore, if a priest is ignorant of preaching, what cry of proclamation is a dumb herald to utter? Hence the Holy Spirit sat upon the first shepherds in the form of tongues, because those whom he has filled he immediately makes speak of him. Hence Moses is commanded [Col. 0225C] [Note: [Col. 0225] Exodus 28:35.] that the priest entering the tabernacle be surrounded with bells, so that he may have the voices of preaching and not offend the judgment of the heavenly Inspector by silence. For it is written: “That the sound may be heard when he enters [Note: [Col. 0225] Absent from the Basel edition.—“And goes out”: the other collected editions.] or leaves the sanctuary in the sight of the Lord, and that he may not die.” A priest entering or leaving dies [Note: [Col. 0225] “May die”: Nuremberg edition.] if no sound is heard from him, because he draws [Note: [Col. 0225] “Raises”: Nuremberg and Paris editions.] upon himself the wrath of the hidden Judge if he proceeds without the sound of preaching. Appropriately, moreover, the bells are described as attached to his garments. For what else are the priest’s garments to be understood as but upright works? This is attested by the Prophet, who says: [Note: [Col. 0225] Psalm 131:9.] “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness.” Bells, therefore, cling to his garments, so that the priest’s good [Col. 0225D] works themselves may cry out the way of life together with the sound of his tongue. But when a ruler prepares himself to speak, let him consider with what carefulness he should speak, lest, if he is swept into speaking without order, the hearts of hearers be wounded by the blow of error, and lest, while perhaps he desires to appear wise, [Note: [Col. 0225] “To appear wise in virtue”: Collected editions.] he foolishly sever the fabric of unity. Therefore truth says: [Note: [Col. 0225] Mark 9:50.] “Have salt [Note: [Col. 0225] “Salt”: Collected editions except Argentinensis.] in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves.” By salt, indeed, the wisdom of speech is signified. Therefore, whoever strives to speak wisely must take great care lest the unity of the hearers be thrown into confusion by his speech. Hence Paul says: [Note: [Col. 0225] Romans 12:3.] “Do not be wise beyond what it is fitting to be wise, but be wise unto sobriety.” Hence, by the divine command, [Note: [Col. 0225] Exodus 28.] pomegranates are joined to bells on the priest’s garment. For what is signified by pomegranates but the unity of faith? For just as many seeds are enclosed within the one outer rind of a pomegranate, [Note: [Col. 0225] “Are united”: Basel edition.] so the unity of faith covers the countless peoples of the holy Church, though diversity of merits possesses them within. Therefore, lest a heedless ruler rush into speech, truth itself cries to the disciples what we have already stated: [Col. 0226B] [Note: [Col. 0225] Mark 9:50.] “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves”; as though, figuratively through the priest’s apparel, it said: “Join pomegranates to bells, so that through everything you say you may preserve unity of faith by careful observance.” § 1. Rulers must also carefully take heed that they utter from themselves not only nothing wicked, but not even what is right excessively or without order. For often the force of spoken words is lost when it is made cheap in the hearts of hearers by the heedless intrusiveness of talkativeness, [Note: [Col. 0225] “Talkativeness”: Collected editions.] and this same talkativeness defiles its author when it does not know how to serve hearers for their spiritual profit. Hence it is well said through Moses: [Note: [Col. 0225] Leviticus 15:2.] “The man who suffers an issue of semen is unclean.” In the minds of hearers, the seed of a subsequent thought is the quality [Note: [Col. 0225] “Equality”: Collected editions.] of the speech that is heard, [Col. 0226C] since when a word is conceived through the ear, a thought is generated in the mind. Hence, even by the wise men of this world, the outstanding preacher was called a “seed-word babbler.” [Note: [Col. 0225] Acts 17:18.—“Half-word babbler”: Collected editions except Paris, Lyons, and Antwerp.] Therefore, one who suffers an issue of semen is said to be unclean, because, being subject to much speech, he defiles himself by that which, if he had brought it forth in due order, could have produced offspring of right thought in the hearts of hearers. [Note: [Col. 0225] “Heart”: same editions.] And while he heedlessly flows out through talkativeness, he pours forth seed not for the use of generation [Note: [Col. 0225] “Of the race”: Collected editions.] but for uncleanness. Hence Paul also, when exhorting his disciple concerning persistence in preaching, said: [Note: [Col. 0225] 2 Timothy 4:1.] “I charge you before God and Christ Jesus, who shall judge the living and the dead, by his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word; be urgent in season, [Col. 0226D] out of season.” When he was about to say “out of season,” he first said “in season,” because speech destroys itself in the hearer’s mind by its very usefulness [Note: [Col. 0225] “Senility”: Basel edition.—“Cheapness”: Argentinensis and Venetian editions I and II.—Original.] if its intrusiveness does not know how to have timeliness.

[Col. 0227A] C. II. Sacred things are not to be entrusted to swine and dogs. Likewise, Clement, Epistle III, at the end. [Note: [Col. 0227] A Pseudo-Isidorian epistle. Nearly the same words occur in Clement’s *Recognitions*, Books 1 and 2. In the collected editions they are presented under Origen’s name.]

Part II. We have been commanded that, on coming to a city, we should first learn who in it is worthy, so that we may eat food at his house. [Note: [Col. 0227] Matthew 10:11.] How much more fitting is it to know [Note: [Col. 0227] “Necessary”: Collected editions.] what sort of person he is to whom words of immortality are to be entrusted! We must be anxious, and very anxious, not to cast our pearls before swine. [Note: [Col. 0227] Matthew 7:6.] But for other reasons also it is useful for me to have knowledge of such a man. [Note: [Col. 0227] “Of this kind”: Collected editions.] For if I know that he is reformed and blameless in matters in which there can be no doubt that they are good—that is, if he is sober, merciful, just, gentle, and humane, things which no one doubts to be good—then it will seem consequent that to him who possesses the goods of virtues [Col. 0227B] there should also be given what is lacking of faith and knowledge, and that those things in which his life, otherwise commendable, seems stained should be corrected. [Note: [Col. 0227] “Seemed”: Collected editions.] But if he remains entangled and defiled in sins which are openly evident, I ought not to speak to him anything concerning the more secret [Note: [Col. 0227] Added: “mysteries”: Basel edition.] and remote matters of divine judgment; rather, I should testify and admonish him to cease sinning and amend his deeds from vices. But if he presses himself upon us and provokes us [Note: [Col. 0227] “Will provoke”: Argentinensis, Basel, Nuremberg, Venetian editions I and II.] to say things which he, while acting wrongly, ought not to hear, [Note: [Col. 0227] “Ought”: Collected editions.] we must prudently evade him. For it does not seem useful to give no answer at all for the sake of the hearers, lest they perhaps think that we decline the contest through lack of an answer and the faith of those who do not understand our purpose be harmed.

[Col. 0227C] C. III. Prelates are not to withhold words of preaching from their persecutors. Likewise, Anacletus, Epistle I, to all bishops. [Note: [Col. 0227] A Pseudo-Isidorian epistle.—Collection in three parts, part 2, tome 11, chapter 4; Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 237.]

Part III. We know, however, that many harass teachers [Note: [Col. 0227] Added: “their own”: Collected editions.] in order to destroy them and fulfill the desires of their own will. Yet teachers ought not, insofar as their strength permits, to withdraw from righteous zeal and good intention, [Note: [Col. 0227] These three words are absent from the Basel edition.] knowing that [Col. 0228A] blessed are those [Note: [Col. 0227] Matthew 5:10.] who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.

### C. IV. He is not clean from the blood of his subjects who does not proclaim God’s counsel to them. Likewise, Gregory to Venantius, Book I, Epistle 33

[Note: [Col. 0227] Epistle 34, written A.D. 591, Book I, Maurist edition. Collection in three parts, part 1, tome 55, chapter 59.]

Paul says to the Ephesians: [Note: [Col. 0227] Acts 20:26.] “My hands are clean from the blood of all of you; for I did not shrink from proclaiming to you the whole counsel of God.” Therefore he would not have been clean from their blood had he refused to announce God’s counsel to them, [Note: [Col. 0227] “Pronounce”: Basel edition.] because, when he refuses to rebuke sinners, the shepherd undoubtedly kills them by his silence.

[Col. 0228B] C. V. The preacher who does not scatter the seed of the divine word incurs the punishment of eternal damnation. Likewise, Nicholas to the Emperor Michael, in the epistle beginning, “We had proposed.” [Note: [Col. 0227] Dated A.D. 865.—Anselm, Book 1, chapter 75. In these matters Nicholas imitated Gelasius’s epistle to the Emperor Anastasius.]

The dispensation of heavenly seed has been entrusted to us: woe [Note: [Col. 0227] 1 Corinthians 9:16.] if we do not scatter it; woe if we keep silent. Since the vessel of election fears and cries out this, how much more must every insignificant person fear! Accordingly, just as no light danger rests upon pontiffs if they keep silent concerning what is fitting for the worship of God and correction of the Church, so no slight danger—God forbid—rests upon those who, though they ought to obey, despise.

Part IV. Gratian. A priest must likewise take care not to begin to unveil the secret mysteries in his preaching to the unworthy and uncomprehending. For one who teaches things which his hearers cannot understand does so not for their benefit but for his own display. Hence, in the exposition of “Blessed are the undefiled,” it is said: [Note: [Col. 0227] Ordinary gloss from Ambrose, Sermon 2 on Psalm 118, on the words “I have hidden your words.”] [Col. 0228C] “It is a fault to make secret mysteries public to the unworthy. This happens either through careless talkativeness, when an irrevocable word flies out without judgment; or through flattery, that one may please the person to whom one reveals secrets; or through boasting of knowledge, that one may seem to know more.” In all these things it is surely made clear how great must be the discernment in a priest’s preaching; if he lacks it, he is judged unworthy of the priestly office, like a man with a crooked nose.

## DISTINCTION XLIV

[Col. 0227]

[Col. 0227C] GRATIAN.

Part I. When, moreover, he is forbidden to be given to wine, he is by no means permitted to have intemperance of appetite; for drunkenness is not forbidden while gluttony is permitted. The Apostle counts both among the works of darkness, writing to the Romans: [Note: [Col. 0227] Romans 13:13.] “Not in revelries and drunkenness.” For the greediness of the belly readily incites lust and destroys every good work. Hence [Note: [Col. 0227] Compare Jerome, Epistle to Amandus; Augustine, Sermon on the Seasons 65; and Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, Part 3, chapter 20.] the belly and the genitals are close to one another, so that from the proximity of the members the alliance of vices may be understood. Hence it is also read that Nebuzaradan, [Note: [Col. 0227] 2 Kings 25, according to the Septuagint.] the chief [Col. 0228D] of the cooks, destroyed the walls of Jerusalem, because the belly, served by a multitude of cooks, levels the structures of virtues to the ground. Therefore a priest should seek to live from the altar, not to indulge himself, as Jerome says: [Note: [Col. 0227] On Micah 3, at the end.] “To you, O priest, it is permitted to live from the altar, not to indulge in luxury.” [Col. 0229A] § 1. Revelries are harmful not only to priests but also to laypersons, who think that they cannot celebrate feast days and solemn days worthily in any other manner [Note: [Col. 0229] Compare Gregory to Augustine, above, Distinction 4, chapter 6.] unless they devote themselves to revelries.

Hence Augustine writes to Bishop Aurelius, Epistle LXIV: [Note: [Col. 0229] Epistle 22, written A.D. 391, Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decree*, part 13, chapter 68.]

### C. I. One must not devote oneself to revelries and drunkenness

Revelries and drunkenness are considered so permitted and lawful that they are celebrated in honor even of the most blessed martyrs, not only on feast days—which, who would not see to be lamentable if he does not view these things with fleshly eyes? [Note: [Col. 0229] “Which each person [sees] to be lamentable”: Collected editions.—Added “not”: Basel edition.]—but even every day. And after a few words: Therefore these practices are not removed harshly, in my judgment, [Note: [Col. 0229] “Esteem”: Venetian editions I and II, Nuremberg, Lyons I.—In place of the following words, through a printer’s error the Argentinensis edition reads: “did not lead.”] not roughly, and not in an imperious manner; [Note: [Col. 0229] “Imperiously”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.] rather by teaching than commanding, rather by warning than threatening. For thus must one act with a multitude of sinners. [Note: [Col. 0229] Absent from the original and Ivo.] Severity, however, [Note: [Col. 0229] “Also”: Basel edition.] is to be exercised against the sins of the few. And if we threaten anything, let it be done with grief, by threatening from the Scriptures the vengeance to come, so that we ourselves may not be feared in our own power, [Note: [Col. 0229] Added: “be feared”: Basel edition.] but God in our speech. Thus those who are spiritual, or near to being spiritual, will first be moved, and by their authority and most gentle [Note: [Col. 0229] “Lightest”: Collected editions.] but most insistent warnings the remaining multitude will be subdued.

### C. II. No cleric or person pledged to continence may enter taverns. Likewise, from the Council of Laodicea, chapter 24

[Note: [Col. 0229] Held between A.D. 347 and 381.—Regino, Book I, chapter 178; Burchard, Book 2, title 131; Anselm, Book 7, chapter 91; Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chapter 205, cite Dionysius’s version.—Compare the Council of Aachen, chapter 60.]

Clerics [Note: [Col. 0229] Absent from the Spanish Collection.] engaged in sacred ministry [Note: [Col. 0229D] “Clerics engaged in sacred ministry”: the Greek is ἱερατικούς, which Dionysius translates “those devoted to sacred ministry”; this translation is given by the Council of Aachen, Burchard, and Ivo.] [Note: [Col. 0229] Added: “of the altar”: there.]—from presbyters to deacons [Note: [Col. 0229] “Subdeacons”: Council of Aachen.] and thereafter all of the ecclesiastical order, [Col. 0229C] down to ministers, readers, exorcists, doorkeepers, psalmists, and even those who have undertaken continence—ought not to enter taverns. [Note: [Col. 0229D] “Taverns”: the printed editions continued, “unless for a necessary cause”; these words have been deleted because they occur neither in most manuscripts nor in Burchard and Ivo, [Col. 0230D] nor in the Council of Laodicea itself or that of Aachen, where this same provision is repeated in chapter 60. They nevertheless seem to have been taken from Apostolic Canon 54.]

### C. III. A cleric who wishes to have a tavern or workshop is to be deposed. Likewise, from the Sixth Synod, chapter 9

[Note: [Col. 0229] Rather, from the Quinisext Synod, held A.D. 698.—Translation of Anastasius the Librarian.]

No cleric may have a tavern [Note: [Col. 0230D] “A tavern or workshop”: the Greek is Καπηλικὸν ἐργαστήριον, that is, “a tavern-keeper’s shop.”] or workshop. For if he is forbidden to enter such a tavern, [Col. 0230A] how much more to serve others in it! But if anyone does such a thing, let him either cease or be deposed.

### C. IV. Unless compelled by necessity, clerics are not to enter taverns. Likewise, from the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 27

[Note: [Col. 0229] Held A.D. 397.—Regino, Book I, chapter 177.—Collection in three parts, part 2, tome 17, chapter 17; Burchard, Book 2, chapter 130; Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chapter 204.]

Clerics are not to enter taverns for the sake of eating or drinking, unless compelled by the necessity of travel.

### C. V. A bishop occupied with banquets must be rebuked. Likewise, Gregory to Bishop Natalis, Book II of the Register, Indiction X, Epistle 14

[Note: [Col. 0229] Epistle 18, written A.D. 592, Book II, Maurist edition.—Collection in three parts, part 1, tome 55, chapter 97.]

Part II. From many persons coming from your city, dearest brother, I have learned that, abandoning pastoral care, you occupy yourself solely with banquets. I would not believe this report unless I confirmed it by the evidence of your actions. For that you apply yourself in no way to reading, in no way give attention to exhortation, and indeed are ignorant even of the practice of ecclesiastical order, is attested by the fact that you do not know how to preserve reverence toward those under whom you are placed.

### C. VI. On the same matter. The same author to the same recipient, Book II, Epistle 37

[Note: [Col. 0229] Epistle 52, written in the same year, Book II.—Collection in three parts, part 1, tome 55, chapter 98.]

The banquets [Note: [Col. 0229] “Common”: added against manuscript authority in later editions of Gregory, except the Maurist; read in the same way in the collected editions, except the first Basel, and in Böhm.] which are provided with the intention of showing charity are rightly praised by your brotherhood [Note: [Col. 0229] “Holiness”: original.] in its letters. But it must nevertheless be known that they then truly proceed from charity when no absent person’s life is maligned in them, no one is reproached in mockery, and no empty tales of secular affairs are heard in them, but words from sacred reading; when the body is not [Col. 0230C] served more than necessity requires, but its weakness alone is refreshed, so that it may be kept fit for the exercise [Note: [Col. 0229] “Use”: Collected editions.] of virtue. Therefore, if you act thus in your banquets, I confess that you are teachers of the abstinent.

### C. VII. PALEA

[Note: [Col. 0229] These matters do not belong to the Council of Nantes (Mâcon: Basel edition), concerning whose date some remarks were made above at chapter 5, Distinction 24. Rather, they are taken from chapter 14 of the Capitularies of Hincmar of Reims, A.D. 852, under whose name they appear in Regino, Book I, chapter 213. Here too you will recognize the author of the error: Burchard, Book 2, chapter 161.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chapter 252. Compare below, *On Consecration*, Distinction 5, chapter 35.]

[Likewise, from the Council of Nantes.]

“No presbyter, when presbyters have assembled for the anniversary day, the thirtieth, or the seventh, or the third day of any deceased person [Col. 0231A], or upon any occasion for a gathering, may in any way presume to become drunk [Note: *inebriari*, “to become drunk”: Basel edition.—“not at all”: Ivo.—Collected editions, except Paris, Lyons, Antwerp], nor, at the entreaty made out of love for the saints or for the soul itself, drink, compel others to drink, or gorge himself at another’s entreaty [Note: “at the entreaty”: original.—Regino, Ivo.—“to transgress through affection”: Basel edition] [Note: “preaching”: Basel edition]; nor may he presume there to make unseemly applause and laughter, or tell empty tales, or sing, or allow shameful jokes to be performed before him by a bear [Note: “seen”: Basel edition] or by female tumblers [Note: “presume to perform”: original.—perhaps “permit”: Regino, Ivo—with the original and Regino]; nor may he consent to masks of demons being carried before him, because this is diabolical and forbidden by the sacred canons.” [Note: Burchard adds: “which the common people call *talamascas*.]

### Chapter VIII. On the same matter. PALEA. Likewise from the same source.

[Note: Chapter of Hincmar in the same place.—Regino, book 1, chapter 215; Burchard, book 2, chapter 162; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 253.]

“When presbyters assemble [Note: “assemble”: Lyons II, III, Antwerp editions.—“come”: Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, Paris, Venice I and II editions] for some banquet, one of them [Note: “a dean or one”: original.—Regino, Burchard] who is senior should begin a verse before the table and bless the food. Then [Col. 0231B] they should sit according to rank, each rendering honour to the other [Note: “of the other … bearing”: original.—“bearing”: Regino], and in turn [Note: “successively”: original] bless food and drink; and one of their clerics should read something from Holy Scripture. After the meal they should likewise recite a holy hymn, *following the example* of the Lord, as he is read to have done at the supper; and *thus* all presbyters should conduct themselves, especially in such places, so that their ministry may not be reproached.” [Note: “our”: original.—Regino.]

### Chapter IX. On the same matter. PALEA. Likewise from the same source.

[Note: Hincmar, chapter 15.—Regino, book 1, chapter 216; Burchard, book 2, chapter 164; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 255.]

“When presbyters come together on the Kalends [Note: “in one place”: Basel edition] after the divine mystery has been performed [Note: “ministry”: Regino, Ivo; collected editions], for [Note: “and”: Basel edition] a necessary conference [Note: “collection”: collected editions], they should sit down at table not as though for a full meal but as though for a luncheon [Note: Basel adds “for themselves”], lest by such dishonourable banquets they burden one another [Col. 0231C], since this is unbecoming and burdensome. Often also, when they return late to church, they incur greater harm through reproach from the drunkenness they contract together [Note: Regino also reads this.—“so that”: Basel edition] than they obtain profit there from food [Note: “food”: same edition]. For Paul [Note: 1 Corinthians 11] rebukes the Corinthians for gathering to eat the Lord’s Supper improperly. So too, those who meet under a pretext for the Lord’s Supper—that is, for a conference [Note: “collection”: Argentinensis, Basel, Norimbergensis, Venice I and II editions] on the word—but in reality [Note: “age”: Regino; “gluttony”: Ivo; collected editions except Basel, which reads “gorging”] join together on account of their bellies, are regarded as blameworthy before God and human beings. Therefore, when everything has been completed, those who wish should break bread in charity in their brother’s house together with their brothers; each should give each other drink, and above all they should not touch the cup beyond the third round [Note: “should touch”: Basel edition], and thus return to the churches.”

### Chapter X. Christians are not to celebrate banquets from mutual contributions. Likewise, from the Council of Laodicea, chapter 55.

[Note: Held between A.D. 347 and 381.—The same provisions occur in the Council of Aachen, chapter 83; Rabanus, *Penitential*, chapter 27.]

**Part III.** Ministers of the altar, or any clerics, or even Christian laypeople, ought not to celebrate banquets from contributions, which the populace calls *comessalia* [Note: “commissalia”: Spanish Collection].

### Chapter XI. Reading of the sacred Scriptures should always be combined with priestly banquets. Likewise, from the Third Council of Toledo, chapter 7.

[Note: Held A.D. 589.—Burchard, book 2, chapter 169; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 260; Rabanus, *Penitential*, chapter 28.]

[Col. 0232B] Out of reverence for God and for priests [Note: “for God and priests”: Spanish Collection], the entire holy synod decreed this: because idle tales are frequently introduced at meals [Note: “at meals”: Basel edition], the reading of the divine Scriptures should be combined with every priestly banquet. For by this souls are built up toward good, and unnecessary tales are prohibited.

### Chapter XII. Clerics may neither give banquets from collective contributions nor eat before the third hour of the day. Likewise, from the Council of Pope Martin, chapters 61 and 66.

[Note: Chapters of Martin of Braga, chapters 61 and 66. Burchard, book 2, chapter 165.—The first chapter is an interpretation of chapter 55 of the Council of Laodicea; the latter is said in Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 256, to have been drawn from chapter 12 of the Council of Carthage, where, so far as we know, one would seek it in vain. It was also found in the Regino Collection, book 1, chapter 187, and in Burchard, book 2, chapter 185.]

Priests or clerics—and likewise religious laypeople—may not hold banquets from collective contributions. § 1. Nor ought clerics or religious laypeople to begin banquets before the sacred third hour of the day, nor should clerics ever eat bread unless a hymn has been sung [Note: “eat”: Spanish Collection]; and after [Col. 0232C] eating, they should give thanks to God their Creator.

**Gratian.** If disgraceful revelries are condemned in laypeople, they are charged all the more heavily against priests, unto Gehenna. For, as Jerome says [Note: Letter to Nepotian], “a fat belly produces a gross understanding,” whereas priestly understanding ought, on the contrary, to be watchful and subtle. Therefore those liable to the vice of gluttony ought not to be anointed as priests. For, as Gregory says in the *Morals* [Note: Book 23, chapter 12], those who are still subject to the warfare of vices ought in no way to preside over the teaching of others through the practice of preaching.

## DISTINCTION XLV

[Col. 0233]

[Col. 0233A] **GRATIAN.**

**Part I.** It follows: “not a striker” [Note: 1 Timothy 3:2]. For a bishop ought not to be so prone to anger and so disturbed in mind that he strikes, when he ought to be patient; rather, he should follow him who gave his back to the scourges.

Hence Gregory writes to John, Bishop of Constantinople, book I, letter 52 [Note: Letter 53, written A.D. 594, book 3 of the Maurist edition; *Polycarpus*, book 4, title 9]:

### Chapter I. A bishop should be feared through correction by words, not by blows.

Your Fraternity knows well what the canons say about bishops who wish to be feared through blows. For we have been made shepherds, not strikers [Note: “persecutors”: Gregory]; and the outstanding preacher says [Note: 2 Timothy 4:2]: “Reprove, entreat [Note: “obscure”: Basel edition], rebuke with [Note: “in”: same edition] all patience and teaching.” But this is a new and unheard-of preaching, which demands faith by blows.

[Col. 0233B]

### Chapter II. On the same matter. Likewise, in the Roman Council under Sylvester, chapter 17.

[Note: From the apocryphal *Constitutum Silvestri*. Collected editions: “Likewise, in a certain council.”]

No one at all may lay hands in violence [Note: “blows”: Basel edition] upon an offending cleric: neither may a presbyter [Note: “a presbyter [upon] a deacon”: collected editions] nor a deacon nor a bishop bring a cleric or servant of the church to a beating. But if the case so requires, let the cleric be deprived of his rank for three days, so that, penitent, he may return to mother Church.

### Chapter III. Some are to be called to the faith by gentle, not harsh, words. Likewise, Gregory to Paschasius, Bishop of Naples, book XI, letter 15.

[Note: Letter 12, written A.D. 603, book 13 of the Maurist edition.—*Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 55, chapter 16.]

Those who with sincere intention desire to bring strangers to the Christian religion and to the right faith [Note: “lead”: original and Basel edition] ought to strive to do so by gentleness, not harshness, lest adversity drive far away [Col. 0233C] those whose mind reasonable explanation, plainly presented [Note: “from the plain”: collected editions except Lyons II, III, Antwerp], might have recalled [Note: “called forth”: Basel edition]. For whoever acts otherwise, and under this pretext wishes to suspend them from the customary observance of their rite [Note: “remove”: collected editions], is shown to be attending more to his own interests than to God’s [Note: “to them”: same editions].

§ 1. The Jews dwelling at Naples [Note: “inhabiting Naples”: collected editions, from Ivo] have complained to us, asserting that certain persons are unreasonably trying to exclude them from some of the solemnities of their festivals, so that they may not be permitted to observe the solemn celebrations of their feasts as they themselves have been permitted to do until now, and as their parents were permitted to do in times long past. If this is indeed true, these persons appear to be devoting effort to a superfluous matter [Note: “applying effort”: original and Ivo]. For what benefit is there [Col. 0234A], when, even if the Jews are forbidden contrary to their long-standing practice, this contributes nothing to their faith and conversion [Note: “to conversion to that faith”: collected editions]? Or why do we lay down rules for Jews concerning how they must observe their ceremonies, if we cannot gain them by this? Therefore it must be done so that, summoned rather by reason and gentleness, they may wish to follow us, not flee us; and so that, by showing them from their own books what we say, we may, with God’s help, convert them to the bosom of mother Church.

Therefore, your Fraternity should indeed, as far as possible, with God’s help kindle them toward conversion by admonitions; and should not permit them again to be disturbed concerning their solemnities. Rather, they should have free permission to observe and celebrate [Col. 0234B] all their feasts and holy days, just as they and their parents have hitherto maintained them through long periods of time past.

### Chapter IV. Prelates should correct their subjects not with severity but with goodwill. Likewise, Gregory IV, in a letter to bishops established throughout Gaul and Germany.

[Note: A.D. 832; compare chapter 2, Distinction 12.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 368.—Most of the words of this chapter are Leo the Great’s, below, in this same distinction, chapter 6.]

Although matters deserving rebuke often occur among priests, yet toward those to be corrected goodwill should accomplish more than severity, exhortation more than threat [Note: “disturbance”: Ivo and Basel edition], charity more than power, since none of us lives without blame or sin. For if the Lord [Note: Matthew 26] had judged the blessed Apostle Peter, our teacher, immediately after his threefold denial, he would not have received from him so much fruit as he did. Therefore rulers of the Church are more to be waited for and corrected than immediately judged [Note: Ivo adds: “without our counsel”], [Col. 0234C] *since the canons of the holy Fathers—established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world—command that greater matters and more difficult outcomes of cases be held in suspense pending our judgment and brought to an end by our moderation.* Hence it is necessary that *these and all other ecclesiastical* matters, after the experience of many cases, be examined more carefully [Note: “provided for”: original] and guarded against more diligently, so that by the spirit of charity and peace every source of scandals, the presumption of the envious [Note: In the letter of Gregory IV [in the original in Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 298, the reading apparently correct is “of the envious”] (which is in the often-mentioned manuscript of the Dominican Library), and in several old copies of Gratian, “of the Jews” is read], and the oppression of simple brothers may be removed from the churches of the Lord. And just as none of the brothers wishes to be burdened by the judgment of others, so he should not dare to inflict upon another what he does not wish done to himself.

[Col. 0235A] **Gratian.** [Note: These are Gratian’s words; they are distinguished from the rest by different type.] Jews are not to be compelled to the faith; yet, if they have received it unwillingly, they are to be compelled to retain it. Hence it was decreed in the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 56 [Note: Held A.D. 633.—Burchard, book 4, chapter 89; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 72; *Decretum*, part 1, chapter 276, and part 13, chapter 94]:

### Chapter V. Just as Jews are not to be compelled to the faith, so converts are not permitted to depart from it.

Concerning the Jews, the holy synod decrees [Note: “decreed this”: Spanish Collection] that henceforth violence is to be inflicted upon no one in order to make him believe [Note: “to inflict”: same source; collected editions except Lyons II, III]. “For God has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” [Note: Romans 9:18]. Such persons are not to be saved unwillingly, but willingly, so that the form of justice may remain whole. For just as a human being perished by obeying the serpent through the choice of his own will, so each person is saved by believing, through the conversion of his own mind, when summoned by the grace of God [Note: “by”: absent from the Spanish Collection]. Therefore they are to be persuaded to convert not by force but by the capacity [Note: Collected editions add: “and will”] of free choice; they are not to be driven.
