But those who long ago were compelled to come to Christianity (as happened in the times of the most religious prince Sisebut), since it is now clear that they have been joined to the divine sacraments [Note: “associated”: same editions with the Spanish Collection], have received the grace of baptism, have been anointed with chrism, and have become partakers of the body *and blood* of the Lord, ought to be compelled to retain the faith which they received even by force or necessity, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed and the faith which they received be held cheap and contemptible.

### Chapter VI. Goodwill should accomplish more than severity toward those to be corrected. Likewise, Pope Leo, letter LXXXII, to Anastasius, Bishop of Thessalonica, chapter 1.

[Note: Letter 14, written A.D. 446, Ballerini edition.—*Polycarpus*, book 4, title 29.]

Although matters deserving rebuke sometimes occur in priestly [Col. 0235C] persons, yet toward those to be corrected goodwill should accomplish more than severity, exhortation [Note: “exhortation”: collected editions except Basel] more than threat [Note: “disturbance”: original], charity more than power. But those [Note: “from these … one departs”: original and collected editions] who seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ, easily depart from this rule; and while they seek rather to lord it over their subjects than to care for them, *honour pleases* [Note: Original and collected editions read: “honour inflates pride,” though the latter, except Basel, add “it”], pride inflates, and what was provided for concord turns toward harm.

### Chapter VII. A presbyter, deacon, or bishop who seeks to be feared by blows is to be deposed from office. Likewise, from the Canons of the Apostles, canon 28, according to the ancient version.

[Note: Rather, from the translation of Dionysius Exiguus.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 159; *Polycarpus*, title 4, chapter 9.]

We command that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who strikes delinquent believers or unbelievers acting unjustly, and wishes through this to be feared [Note: “wishing”: Paris edition], be deposed from his office, because the Lord nowhere [Note: “never”: collected editions] taught us this. On the contrary, he himself [Note: 1 Peter 2:23], when struck, did not strike back; when cursed, did not return curses [Note: “cursed”: collected editions]; when suffering, did not threaten.

### Chapter VIII. Bishops should correct their subjects not by blows but by words. Likewise, from the Third Council of Braga, chapter 7.

[Note: Held A.D. 675.—*Collectio tripartita*, part 2, title 48, chapter 2.]

Although the blessed Apostle [Note: Collected editions add “Paul” (2 Timothy 4:2)] commands that one reprove, entreat, or rebuke with all patience [Note: Paris, Norimbergensis, Lyons II and III, Antwerp add “and goodness”; the Spanish Collection reads “patience … and teaching”], we know that, contrary to this teaching, some of our brothers rage with such beatings against honoured [Note: “dishonourers”: Basel edition; “dishonoured”: the other collected editions] *subjects* as the persons of robbers might deserve. Therefore those who have already attained ecclesiastical ranks—that is, presbyters, abbots, and [Note: “or”: Spanish Collection and collected editions] levites—who, except for graver and mortal faults, ought to be subject to no beatings [Col. 0236B], ought not to have each prelate indiscriminately subject his more honourable [Note: “honourable”: Spanish Collection] members to blows and pain as he chooses and sees fit. Otherwise, while he rashly strikes subject members [Note: “strike”: collected editions except Basel], he himself [Note: “they”: same editions except Basel, Lyons II, III, Antwerp] may also deprive himself of the reverence owed to him by his subjects, according to the saying of a certain wise man: “One lightly chastised shows reverence to the one chastising him; but the rebuke of excessive harshness [Note: Spanish Collection: “but the excessively harsh rebuke”] receives neither correction [Note: “rebuke”: Spanish Collection and collected editions] nor salvation.”

And therefore, if anyone, puffed up by the licence of authority received, believes in malice of heart [Note: Absent from the Spanish Collection] that the aforesaid honourable subjects should be beaten otherwise than has been said, he shall incur, according to the measure of the blows he inflicted, a sentence both of excommunication and exile.

**Part II. Gratian.** Solomon, however, gives the contrary admonition [Note: Proverbs 23:14], saying: “Strike your son with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from death.” Hence the blessed Gregory also writes in the *Dialogues* [Note: Book 2, chapter 4] that the blessed Benedict healed a certain monk by striking him with a rod, whom he could not cure by frequent admonition. Hence too the Lord [Note: John 2], having made a whip of cords, scourged those behaving wrongly in the temple and cast them out of the house of prayer. Hence too the Apostle [Note: 1 Corinthians 5] delivered that fornicator to Satan for bodily affliction, and condemned that magician [Note: Acts 13] to bodily blindness. Hence too in the canons [Note: Pope Siricius, letter 1, chapter 6], boys who behave irrationally before the years of reason are ordered to be chastised with blows. Likewise virgins, if they have laid aside the garment of religion and joined themselves to others, are ordered to be confined in workhouses.

[Col. 0237A] Hence Gregory also says in the *Morals*, book XX, part 4, chapter 6 [Note: On Job 29; compare *Pastoral Rule*, part 2, chapter 6]:

### Chapter IX. Discipline must not be maintained without mercy, nor mercy without discipline.

Discipline or mercy is greatly deficient if either is maintained without the other. But among their subjects, rulers ought to have both mercy that consoles justly [Note: “advises”: collected editions] and discipline that rages piously [Note: “serves”: Antwerp edition]. Thus wine and oil were both applied to the wounds of the half-dead man whom the Samaritan [Note: Luke 10] brought to the inn: so that by the wine the wounds might be bitten [Note: Basel edition: “moderated … cherished”], and by the oil cherished. Thus everyone set over healing wounds should apply in wine the bite of strictness, and in oil the softness of piety: by wine corrupt matter should be cleansed [Note: Collected editions: “is cleansed … is cherished”], and by oil what is to be healed [Col. 0237B] should be cherished.

Gentleness must therefore be mingled with severity, and a certain balance made out of both [Note: “therefore do”: same editions, especially Lyons II, III, Antwerp], so that subjects may neither be ulcerated by excessive harshness nor weakened by excessive kindness. This is, indeed, what the ark of the tabernacle [Note: Hebrews 9] signifies: within it, together with the tablets, are both the rod and manna, because in the breast of a good ruler, together with knowledge of sacred Scripture, if there is a rod of strictness, there should also be manna of sweetness [Note: Collected editions add “there is”].

Thus David also says [Note: Psalm 22:4]: “Your rod and your staff, they have consoled me.” For we are struck with the rod and supported with the staff. Therefore, if there is the strictness of the rod that strikes [Note: Collected editions: “if therefore there be the strictness [Norimbergensis: discernment] of justice”], there should also be the consolation of the staff that supports. Let there then be love, but not softening; rigour, but not embittering; zeal, but not raging without moderation; piety, but not sparing beyond what is expedient.

[Col. 0237C] It is pleasing to observe mercy joined with severity in the breast of Moses [Note: Collected editions add “together”]. Let us see one who loves piously and rages strictly. Certainly, when the Israelite people had incurred before God’s eyes an offence almost beyond pardon, so that their ruler heard [Note: “had heard”: same editions; compare Exodus 32:7]: “Go down; your people has sinned,” as though the divine voice said to him: “He who has fallen into such a sin is *now* no longer mine”; and then added: “Let me alone, that my wrath may be angry against them and I may destroy them, and make you into a great nation”—he, once and again, placing himself as a barrier against the onset of God’s anger for the people over whom he presided [Note: Absent from Venice I, II, and Paris], said: “Either forgive them this offence, or, if you do not, blot me out of your book which you have written.”

Let us consider, therefore, with what deep affection he loved that same people, for whose life he asked that he himself be blotted from the book of life. [Col. 0238A] Yet let us consider with what zeal for righteousness this man, bound by such love for that people, was kindled against their faults. For as soon as, by his first petition, he had obtained pardon for their guilt so that they might not be destroyed [Note: Collected editions: “as soon as he had obtained pardon for their guilt so that they might not be destroyed [Basel: condemned]”], he came to that same people and said [Note: In the same passage]: “Let every man put his sword upon his thigh; go to and fro from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each kill his brother [Note: Venice I, II, Paris, Lyons II, III, Antwerp add “wife”], friend, and neighbour.” And on that day about twenty-three thousand persons fell [Note: “Twenty-three.” This is also read in manuscripts of Gregory; but the Hebrew text, the Chaldean paraphrase, the Septuagint version, and the Vulgate read “three thousand”].

Behold: he who sought the life of all people, even at the cost of his own death [Note: Collected editions read “of people”], extinguished the lives of a few by the sword. Within, he burned with the fires [Note: “fire”: same editions with the original] of love; without, he was inflamed with zeal for severity. His piety was so great that he did not hesitate to offer himself to death before the Lord for them; his severity so great that he himself struck with the sword of judgment those whom he had feared might be struck by God [Note: “divinity”: Basel edition; “had feared”: Argentinensis reads “has feared”]. [Col. 0238B] He so loved those over whom he presided that he did not spare even himself for them; yet he so pursued in their sin those whom he loved that, even while the Lord spared, he cast them down.

A mighty envoy in both respects, an admirable mediator in both, he pleaded the cause of the people before God by prayers, and the cause of God before the people by swords. Within, loving, he resisted divine wrath by supplication; without, raging, he consumed sin by striking. *He brings help more quickly to all by displaying the death of a few. And therefore almighty God more quickly heard his faithful servant acting for the people, because he saw what Moses himself would do over the people for God.*

Thus, in governing the *people*, Moses combined both, so that neither discipline might be absent from mercy nor mercy from discipline. Hence he too is described in relation to both virtues [Note: Collected editions: “Hence in Job [29:25], according to both”]: “When I sat as a king surrounded by an army, I was nevertheless a comforter of the sorrowful.” To sit surrounded by an army is the strength [Note: Collected editions: “the strength of discipline” (Basel adds “greater”)] and discipline of governance; to console the hearts of the sorrowful is the ministry of piety.

[Col. 0238C]

### Chapter X. One who judges justly preserves mercy together with justice. Likewise, Isidore, *Sentences on the Supreme Good*, book III, chapter 54.

[Note: Burchard, book 16, chapter 25.]

Everyone who judges justly holds a balance in his hand and bears justice and mercy in each pan. By justice he gives sentence to the sinner [Note: “sins”: Basel edition; “of sin”: the other editions], and by mercy he moderates the punishment of sin [Note: “to the sinner”: Bohm edition], so that by a just weighing he may correct some things through equity [Col. 0239A], but pardon others through compassion [Note: “mercy”: Bohm edition]. Whoever sets the judgments of God before his eyes [Note: “places before”: Basel edition], always fears and trembles in every matter, lest he stray from the path of justice, fall, and be condemned precisely where he is not justified.

### Chapter XI. Both one who forgives and one who corrects show mercy. Likewise, Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 72.

[Note: Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book 4, Distinction 15.]

One who corrects by a blow someone over whom authority has been given him, or restrains him by some discipline, and yet from his heart forgives the sin by which he himself was injured or offended, or prays that it may be forgiven that person, gives alms—not only in forgiving and praying, but also in correcting and punishing with some corrective [Note: “more corrective”: Basel edition] penalty—because he extends mercy. For many benefits are conferred on unwilling persons when consideration is given to their benefit rather than to their will, because they are found to be enemies to themselves.

[Col. 0239B] **Gratian.** There are many kinds of almsgiving, concerning which Albinus says [Note: In Alcuin, *On Virtues and Vices*, chapter 17]:

### Chapter XII. On the manifold kinds of almsgiving.

There are three kinds of almsgiving: one bodily—to give to a needy person whatever you can; another spiritual—to forgive one by whom you have been injured; the third—to correct offenders [Note: “an offender”: Basel edition] and lead those in error back into the way of truth.

### Chapter XIII. Almsgiving of the heart is preferred to almsgiving of money. Likewise, Augustine, book L of *Homilies*, homily 6.

[Note: An apocryphal sermon.—*Panormia*, book 2, chapter 193.]

There are two kinds of almsgiving, one of the heart and the other [Note: “another”: original and collected editions] of money. Almsgiving of the heart is to forgive the person by whom you have been injured [Col. 0239C]. For you may wish to give something to a needy person and not possess it; but the ability to forgive an offender is abundant for you as much as you wish. And below:

§ 1. Almsgiving of the heart is much greater than almsgiving of the body.

And below:

§ 2. The almsgiving of charity is sufficient in itself without earthly substance; but that which is given bodily, if it is not bestowed with a kind heart, is wholly insufficient.

**Part III. Gratian.** From all these things it is apparent that neither the gentleness of meekness without the uprightness of severity, nor zeal for uprightness without meekness, ought to be found in prelates. Therefore the “strikers” who, under the foregoing authorities, are removed from episcopal office are to be understood not as all persons who inflict corporal blows, but as those who, setting meekness aside, are always ready [Col. 0239D] with blows, who seek by beatings not to correct vices but to be feared. To them Peter writes [Note: 1 Peter 5:3]: “Do not lord it over the clergy, but become examples to the flock from the heart.”

[Col. 0240A] Hence Gregory also writes in the *Morals*, book XIX, part 4, chapter 23 [Note: Chapter 12, section 16, on Job 29]:

### Chapter XIV. Meekness and strictness are not to be separated from one another.

For there are some so strict that they lose all gentleness of kindness; and there are some so gentle that they lose the rights of strict governance. Therefore both must be held most firmly by all rulers: so that in the vigour of discipline they may not abandon the kindness of meekness, nor again, through meekness, the strictness of discipline. Thus they should neither become hardened against the compassion of piety [Note: “toward compassion”: Basel edition] while correcting the obstinate, nor weaken the vigour of discipline while consoling the minds of the weak. Let the vigour of discipline, therefore, regulate meekness, and let meekness adorn [Col. 0240B] [Note: Collected editions add “speech”] vigour; and so let each be commended by the other, that vigour may not be rigid nor meekness lax.

### Chapter XV. True justice sympathizes with the wretched and is indignant with offenders. The same author, Homily XXXIV on the Gospels, near the beginning.

[Note: On Luke 13.]

True justice has compassion, but false justice has disdain, although the just also rightly tend to be indignant with sinners [Note: “be indignant”: original]. But one thing is done by the swelling [Note: “pride”: collected editions] of pride, another by the zeal [Note: Basel adds “is carried on”] of discipline. For they are indignant [Note: “are indignant”: collected editions], but they are not disdainful [Note: Same editions, except Basel, add “are”].

And shortly afterward:

§ 1. By contrast, those who are accustomed to pride themselves on false justice despise all others, do not condescend in any mercy to the weak, and become worse [Col. 0240C] sinners precisely because they do not believe themselves sinners [Note: Basel adds “indeed”].

### Chapter XVI. Sinners are to be summoned by meekness, not cast away through austerity. Likewise, Jerome on chapter 4 of *Lamentations*.

[Note: These seem rather to be Rabanus’s words, among whose works they circulate.]

“Depart,” they say, “you defiled; depart, go away; do not touch us; do not *in any respect* have fellowship with us” [Note: “with us”: collected editions]. Such speech does not enlighten the blind, heal the sick, or cure the infirm; rather, it kills and sends one in peril into despair [Note: “allows [him] to fall”: same edition]. Good rulers, indeed, reckoning the infirmities of others by their own weakness, strive rather through the aid of humility and meekness to draw sinners from the snare of error than through austerity to thrust into the pit of perdition those wavering toward it. Hence the teacher of the nations says [Note: Basel adds “says”; compare 1 Corinthians 9:22]: “I became weak to the weak.”

[Col. 0240D]

### Chapter XVII. God’s anger rages against the people when a preacher flatters offenders rather than corrects them. Likewise, from Origen, Homily VII on Joshua.

[Note: From Rufinus’s translation.]

But this must not be passed over without attention [Note: “passed over”: original and collected editions]: that when one person sins, the anger of God comes upon the whole people. [Col. 0241A] When does this happen? When priests who preside over the people wish to appear kindly disposed [Note: “benevolent”: same editions] toward offenders, and, fearing the tongues of sinners lest perhaps they speak ill of them, forget priestly severity and refuse to fulfil what is written [Note: 1 Timothy 5:20]: “Reprove the sinner before all, that the rest also may have fear” [Note: Original and collected editions: “that the rest may have fear”]; and again [Note: 1 Corinthians 5:13]: “Remove the evil from among yourselves.”

Nor, kindled with zeal for God, do they imitate the Apostle who says [Note: In the same passage]: “I have delivered such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved.” Nor do they endeavour to fulfil that Gospel instruction: if they see someone sinning, they should first approach him privately [Note: Collected editions add “him”], then with two or three persons brought in [Note: Original adds “arbiters”; collected editions add “witnesses”]; if he scorns this and after [Note: Collected editions: “after correction by the Church”; original: “correction”] correction by the Church is not amended, they should regard him, expelled from the Church, as a Gentile and a publican. [Col. 0241B] While they spare one person, they bring destruction upon the whole Church. What kind of goodness, what kind of mercy [Note: Collected editions add “is this”] is it to spare one person and bring all into danger? For the people are defiled by one sinner. [Col. 0242A] Just as a whole flock is infected by one diseased animal, so too the entire people is defiled by one [Note: Basel adds “or”] fornicator or one committing any other crime whatsoever.

**Gratian.** Hence it is also said elsewhere [Note: Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part 2, chapter 9]: “Let piety make a ruler a mother to his subjects, but discipline a father.”

**Part IV.** A “striker” is also one who wounds the consciences of the weak by useless speech.

Hence Pope Anacletus, Letter II to the Bishops of Italy [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian letter.—*Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 2, chapter 18]:

### Chapter XVIII. One who strikes the consciences of the weak by careless speech is called a striker.

That teacher is rightly called a striker who wounds the conscience of the weak with useless speech. [Note: Col. 0241, from Jerome on Titus 1.] Therefore you and all the faithful ought to hold fast to the faithful word which accords with doctrine, so that he may be able to console by holy teaching, refute those who contradict it, and strengthen those who live uprightly and uphold the right faith. [Note: Col. 0241: Paris and Venice I–II read “faithful in speech”; Nuremberg, “faithful and the word”; Argentinensis, “the word which accords with doctrine”; Basel reads “exhort” for “console,” “sacred” for “holy,” and “maintaining” for “uphold”; Bohm reads “sound.”]

## DISTINCTION XLVI

[Col. 0241]

[Col. 0241B] GRATIAN.

### Part I

It follows [Note: 1 Tim. 3:3]: “Not quarrelsome.” For nothing is more shameless than the arrogance of the uneducated, who consider loquacity to be authority and, puffed up and ready for disputes, thunder against their subjects; and it is evident that this arises from arrogance and pride.

[Col. 0241C] Hence Gregory writes in the *Moralia*, book XXIII, part 5, chapter 12 [chapter 13, §§23–24], on Job 33:

### Chapter I. The arrogant do not know how to impart humbly what they teach.

This is characteristic of the teaching of the arrogant [Note: “arrogance”: Basel]: they do not know how humbly to impart what they teach, and they cannot rightly administer the sound things which they understand. [Note: “which they teach”: the collected editions and the first Basel edition read “which”; the same, except Basel, read “also rightly.”] For their speech reveals that, when they teach, they seem to themselves to be seated as it were upon a lofty summit [Note: The original and the collected editions read “summit”], and they look upon those whom they teach as placed far beneath them, as though in the depths; they do not deign to speak to them in counsel, but scarcely otherwise than in domination. Rightly, therefore, the Lord says to them through the prophet [Ezek. 34:4]: “But you ruled them with harshness and with power.” For those rule with harshness and power [Col. 0241D] who hasten not to correct their subjects by calm reasoning [Note: The collected editions read “with calmness”], but to bend them harshly through domination.

On the contrary, true teaching flees this fault of self-exaltation in thought all the more vigorously [Col. 0242B] as it more ardently pursues, with the darts of its words, the very master of exaltation. [Note: The collected editions read “knowledge” rather than “thought.”] For it takes care not to preach with more exalted manners the one whom it attacks in the hearts of its hearers by sacred discourses.

### Part II

Gratian. Behold why quarrelsome persons are forbidden to be ordained bishops. There is also another reason for this prohibition. [Col. 0242C] For contentious persons either win over the minds of rulers by flattery, or cast the stain of infamy upon their brethren by slandering them, or never cease to stir up sedition by sowing discord among brethren. All these things are shown to be blameworthy in prelates.

Hence Gregory writes in the *Moralia*, book XVIII, part 4, chapter 3, on Job 27:

### Chapter II. Concerning those who flatter sinners.

There are some who, while extolling men’s evil deeds with praise, increase what they ought to have reproved. [Note: “ought to have reproved”: the collected editions read “ought.”] Hence it is said through the prophet [Ezek. 13:18]: “Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow of the hand, and make pillows beneath the head of every age.” [Note: The collected editions, except Basel, read “Woe to them.”] A cushion is placed beneath the elbow, or a pillow beneath the head, of one lying down so that he may rest more softly. [Note: A cushion beneath the elbow or a pillow beneath the head of one lying down is placed so that he may rest softly; the collected editions give this explanation and, except Argentinensis, read “he may rest.”] Whoever, therefore, flatters those who act wickedly places a cushion beneath the elbow or a pillow [Col. 0242D] beneath the head of the one lying down, so that he who ought to have been rebuked for his fault may rest softly in it, supported by praises. [Note: Basel adds “or a pillow”; the collected editions read “a cushion beneath the elbow or a pillow beneath the head.”]

§ 1. Hence again it is written [Ezek. 13:10]: “He was building a wall, but they were plastering it.” By the name “wall” the hardness of sin is signified. To build a wall, therefore, is for someone to construct against himself the obstacles of sin. But those flatterers plaster the wall who flatter persons committing sins, so that what the latter build by acting perversely, the former make, as it were, shining.

§ 2. But the holy man, just as he does not esteem evil things to be good, so he refuses to judge good things from evil, saying [Job 27:5]: “Far be it from me” [Note: The collected editions, except Basel, add “this”] “that I should judge you righteous; until I fail, I shall not depart from my innocence.”

Hence also one reads in the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 56 [Note: *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*, chapter 43; cf. Distinction 18, chapter 9; Burchard, book 2, chapter 176; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 173; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 267]:

### Chapter III. A flattering or treacherous cleric is to be removed from office.

[Col. 0243B] A cleric discovered to devote himself to flattery and treachery is to be removed from office.

### Chapter IV. Those who bring unprovable charges against brethren are to be excommunicated by the bishop.

Likewise, from the same council, chapter 55 [Note: The same, chapter 17].

Let the bishop excommunicate accusers of brethren who bring unprovable charges against their brethren; and, if they amend their fault, let him receive them into communion, but not into the clergy. [Note: The words “who bring unprovable charges against their brethren” are found neither in the original nor in many ancient manuscripts of Gratian.]

### Chapter V. A slanderous cleric is to be removed from office; a buffoon and one envious of the advancement of brethren is not to be promoted.

[Note: This rubric applies also to the present chapter and to the following two chapters.]

Likewise, from the same council, chapter 57 [Note: The same, chapter 44; *Regino*, book 1, chapter 153; Burchard, book 10, chapter 66; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 11, chapter 11, and part 13, chapter 66].

A slanderous cleric, especially among priests [Note: The Hispanic Collection and Basel read “and especially”], is to be compelled to ask pardon. If he refuses, he is to be deposed and never restored to office without satisfaction. [Col. 0243C]

[Col. 0244A]

### Chapter VI. On the same matter.

Likewise, from the same council, chapter 60 [Note: The same, chapter 73; cf. Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 23, and Agde, chapter 70; *Regino*, book 1, chapter 152; Burchard, book 2, chapter 172; Anselm, book 7, chapter 163 (177, from Agde, chapter 70); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 172; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 263, part 11, chapter 79].

We decree that a scurrilous cleric, one who jokes with obscene words [Note: The Hispanic Collection reads “one who jokes”], is to be withdrawn from office. [Note: This clause is absent from the collected editions, except Basel, and from Lyon II–III and Antwerp.]

### Chapter VII. On the same matter.

Likewise, from the same council, chapter 54 [Note: The same, chapter 42; Burchard, book 2, chapter 16; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 35].

A cleric who envies the advancement of his brethren [Note: Ivo reads “their promotions”] is not to be promoted so long as he remains in that fault.

### Chapter VIII. Those given to sedition are not to be ordained.

Likewise, from the same council, chapter 67 [Note: The same, chapter 55; Council of Agde, chapter 69; *Regino*, book 1, chapter 171; Burchard, book 2, chapter 17; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 36].

We decree that seditious persons are never to be ordained clerics, just as neither are usurers nor persons who avenge injuries done to themselves. [Note: The Hispanic Collection reads “or” rather than “nor.”]

[Col. 0244B]

### Chapter IX. Clerics are by no means permitted to exact interest.

Likewise, from the Council of Laodicea, chapter 5 [Note: Held between A.D. 347 and 381; *Chapters of Atto of Vercelli*, chapter 17; *Regino*, book 1, chapter 223, from Dionysius’s translation].

### Part III

Ministers of the altar, or those established in priestly rank, may not engage in lending at interest or receive either interest or gains called *sescupla*.

### Chapter X. A cleric is not to be a moneylender either in his own name or another’s.

Likewise, Pope Leo, to the bishops throughout Campania, letter I, chapter 4 [Note: Written A.D. 443; Burchard, book 2, chapter 121; Anselm, book 7, chapter 150 (160); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 66].

Just as no cleric may venture to practice usury in his own name, so neither may he do so in another’s name. For it is an unseemly crime to devote one’s own wrongdoing to another’s profit. [Note: The collected editions, except Argentinensis, add “to devote.”] But we ought to seek and practice only that kind of lending at interest by which what we mercifully give here, we may be able to receive from *that* Lord, [Col. 0244C] who gives manifoldly gifts that endure forever.

## DISTINCTION XLVII

[Col. 0243]

[Col. 0243C] GRATIAN.

### Part I

The reason why usurers are forbidden to be ordained at the end of the preceding chapter is that those who practice usury are shown to be serving greed; and the greedy are forbidden by the Apostle [1 Tim. 3:3] to be ordained, because such persons would easily depart from justice.

[Col. 0244C] Hence in the *Canons of the Apostles*, chapter 44, one reads [Note: *Regino*, book 1, chapter 221; Burchard, book 2, chapter 119; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 157; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 195 and part 13, chapter 15]:

### Chapter I. A deacon, presbyter, or bishop who exacts interest is to be deposed unless he ceases.

A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who exacts interest from debtors must either cease or certainly be deposed. [Note: The original and the cited collections read “condemned” rather than “deposed.”]

[Col. 0245A]

### Chapter II. Anyone exacting interest, whether cleric or subject to a rule, is to be cast out.

Likewise, from the Council of Nicaea, chapter 17 [Note: Held A.D. 325; Dionysius’s translation; *Regino*, book 1, chapter 222; Burchard, book 2, chapter 120; Anselm, book 7, chapter 163; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 196 and part 13, chapter 8; Rabanus, *Penitential*, chapter 32; below, Causa 14, question 4, chapter 8, from the Hispanic version].

Because many persons subject to the rule pursue avarice and shameful gain, forgetting the divine Scripture, which says [Ps. 14:5]: “He has not given his money at interest,” they lend and demand one-hundredth interest. Therefore the holy and great synod has rightly decreed that, if anyone is found after this ordinance to be receiving interest, or transacting business by some contrivance or in any manner whatsoever, or exacting *hemiolia*, that is, *sescupla*, or devising anything of this kind at all for the sake of shameful gain, he is to be cast out of the clergy and become alien to the rule. [Note: The collected editions add “any contrivance”; they also add “doing” after “some contrivance.” The words “or transacting” through “in any manner” are absent from the Regino collection.]

[Col. 0245C] *Sescupla* is the form of interest called *sesquialtera*, one-and-a-half-fold interest. Although it was extremely burdensome, Constantine permitted it by law in wet or dry crops; that law is now found in the Theodosian Code, book 2, final title, “On Usury,” law 1. The same matter is addressed by Blessed Jerome in his commentary on Ezekiel, book 6, chapter 18, in these words: “In fields, interest is customarily exacted in wheat and millet, wine and oil, and other kinds of produce; or, as divine speech calls it, ‘excess.’ For example, we give ten measures in winter and receive fifteen at harvest, that is, an additional half.” Therefore, by this canon, in which those Fathers forbid all monetary interest to clerics, they intended expressly to forbid these same persons also the *sescupla* of crops. Later, however, in other councils and by Roman pontiffs, every kind of usury, as contrary to natural and divine law, was forbidden both to clerics and to laypersons, as appears in the *Decretals*, under the title “On Usury.”

[Col. 0245B] Hence Gregory also writes in book XIX of the *Moralia*, chapter 16, section 25, on Job 29:

### Chapter III. Those who serve temporal profits are not shown to serve God.

All lovers of this world are strong in earthly things and weak in heavenly things. For the sake of temporal glory they desire to toil until death, yet for the hope of eternity they do not persevere even a little in labor. For earthly gain they endure any injuries, but for a heavenly reward they refuse to bear even the insults of the slightest word. They are strong enough to stand before an earthly judge even for a whole day [Note: Basel reads “before the judgment”], yet in prayer before the Lord they grow weary within the space of a single hour. They often endure nakedness, humiliation, and hunger in order to acquire wealth and honors; they torture themselves by abstinence for the sake of things which they hasten to attain [Note: The collected editions add “in the hope of those things”]. But they are all the more negligent in laboriously seeking heavenly things because they think their recompense will come more slowly. [Note: The collected editions add “more.”]

§ 1. Such persons are, as it were, like other [Note: The collected editions, except Lyon II–III and Antwerp, add “evil”] trees: broad below and narrow above, because they remain strong for lower things but fail in reaching upward. On the contrary, the advancing life of the righteous is signified by the character of palm trees. Such persons are not strong in earthly pursuits [Note: The collected editions read “desires”] and weak in heavenly ones; [Col. 0246A] rather, they show themselves more earnestly devoted to God, farther and more consistently, than they remember having been to the world. [Note: The collected editions read “remember” rather than “have remembered.”]

§ 2. For when our preacher says to certain persons [Rom. 6:19], “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification,” he undoubtedly condescends to their weakness of heart [Note: Basel adds “of heart”], as though saying to them more plainly: “If you cannot do more, at least be such in the fruit of good works as you formerly were in the practice of vices, lest the holy freedom of *aeris* (“air”) find you weaker, whom the practice of earthly pleasure found strong in the flesh.”

[Note: For *aeris*, Gregory reads either “holy freedom [find] heirs” or “the holy freedom of charity [find] you weaker than it found you in the flesh.” One Vatican manuscript of Gratian reads “of heavenly conduct”; the gloss adduces this reading to explain *aeris*. In Gregory the readings are “holy freedom, heirs” or “holy freedom of charity”; one manuscript of Gratian reads “of heavenly conduct.”]

[Col. 0246B]

### Chapter IV. Usurers ought not to be promoted to holy orders.

Likewise, Gregory, to the clergy and citizens of Naples, book VIII, letter 40 [Note: Letter 62, written A.D. 600, book 10, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 6, chapter 9 (13: “To the noble citizens of Naples,” which is likewise read in the collected editions); *Polycarpus*, book 2, title 1].

You should know that the report has reached us concerning Peter that he lent solidi at interest. You ought to investigate this with all diligence; and if it is established to be so, choose another and without delay refrain from choosing this man. For we lay hands upon lovers of usury for no reason whatever. But if, after a careful inquiry, this proves false [Note: Anselm reads “if you should think this”], since his person is unknown to us, and we do not know whether what has been reported to us accords with his character, then it is necessary for you to come to us with the decree made by you, so that, by more carefully examining his life and conduct [Col. 0246C] [Note: Basel reads “inquiring” rather than “examining”], we may also learn his understanding, and, if he is found suitable for this judgment, may fulfill your wishes concerning him [Note: Basel reads “him” rather than “concerning him”], with the Lord’s help.

### Chapter V. A cleric found to receive interest is to be deposed.

Likewise, from the Council of Elvira, chapter 20 [Note: Held no later than A.D. 310; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 156; *Decretum*, part 13, chapter 12].

If any cleric is discovered to receive interest, it has been decreed [Note: The original adds “with”] that he is to be deposed and required to abstain.

[Col. 0247A]

### Chapter VI. A priest ought neither to be entangled in error nor corrupted by greed.

Likewise, Leo, to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, letter LI [Note: Letter 106, written A.D. 452, Ballerini edition; Anselm, book 7, chapter 140 (159)].

### Part II

A catholic man, and especially a priest of the Lord, ought neither to be entangled in any error nor corrupted by any greed, as holy Scripture says [Ecclus. 18:30]: “Do not follow after your desires.” For a mind greedy for power knows neither how to abstain from forbidden things, nor to rejoice in things permitted, nor to give assent to piety. [Note: This final clause is absent from the original, but is also found in Anselm.]

### Chapter VII. One who does not cut greed away from himself cannot cling to the Author of good things.

Likewise, Gregory, book VII, letter 100 [Note: Letter 106, written A.D. 599, to Syagrius and others, book 9, Maurist edition; *Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 55, chapter 5].

We cannot cling otherwise to the Author of good things unless we cut away from ourselves greed [Note: Basel adds “of possessions”], which is the root [Col. 0247B] of all evils [1 Tim. 6:10].

### Chapter VIII. It is characteristic of the greedy to seize the goods of persons whose needs they are able to relieve.

Likewise, Ambrose, Sermon LXXXI, on what is written in the Gospel: “The field of a certain rich man yielded abundant crops” [Note: From Basil’s homily on Luke 12:16].

Just as those who have been driven mad and removed from their right mind see no longer the things themselves but the phantasms of their own disorder, so too the mind of the greedy person, once bound by the chains of desire, always sees gold, always silver, always calculates revenues, and looks more gladly upon gold than upon the sun [Note: The original adds “he sees”]. Even his prayer and supplication to the Lord [Note: The collected editions read “to God”] seek gold.

And shortly afterward:

§ 1. Sometimes, by the utterly wicked art of usury, gold is born from gold itself. But what are you doing? There will never be either satiety [Col. 0247C] or an end to greed.

And below:

§ 2. But you say [Note: Basel reads “the greedy man says”; the other collected editions read “someone says”]: “What is unjust if, while I do not seize another’s goods, I guard my own more carefully?” O shameless assertion [Note: The collected editions, except the first Lyon edition, read “shameless thing to say”]! You call them “your own” [Note: The collected editions, except Basel, read “What do you call your own”?] Which things? From what storehouses did you bring them into this world? When you entered this light, when you came forth from your mother’s womb, with what resources, I ask, and with what means did you enter, equipped as you were?

And shortly afterward:

§ 3. Let no one call his own what is common, what has been taken in greater quantity than would suffice and even violently retained. [Note: In Blessed Ambrose the reading is: “Let no one call his own what has been taken from the common stock in a quantity greater than would suffice and violently retained.” It has not been changed because of the gloss. The collected editions read “what has been taken for use” rather than “what has been taken.”]

And below:

§ 4. Is God unjust, that he does not distribute the means of life equally among us, so that you should be wealthy and abounding while others should lack and be needy? Or is it rather for this reason: that he wished both to confer upon you proofs of his kindness [Col. 0248A] and to crown another through the virtue of patience? Yet you, having received God’s gifts and gathered them into your own bosom [Note: The collected editions read “and” rather than “even if”], do you think that you do nothing unjust if you alone retain the means of life for so many? For who is so unjust, so eager, so avaricious [Note: The collected editions add “so” before “eager”], as the person who makes the sustenance of many people not his use, but his surplus and luxury? For it is no lesser crime to take away from one who has than, when you are able and abound [Note: The collected editions read “when you are abundant”], to refuse to those in need. The bread which you keep back belongs to the hungry; the clothing which you lock away belongs to the naked; and the money which you bury in the earth [Note: The collected editions read “in the earth”] is the redemption and release of the wretched. Know, therefore, that you seize the goods of as many persons as those to whom you could provide whatever you wished. [Note: The first Lyon edition reads “of so many” rather than “of as many,” and “to as many as” rather than “as those to whom.”]

### Part III

Gratian. It is also necessary that the person [Col. 0248B] who is to be ordained should govern his own household well; that is, if while in lay dress he had a wife or children, he should summon them from vices to the pursuit of virtues by word and example, so that he may first require from his own household what he will afterward command the people. Hence the Apostle writes to the Ephesians [Eph. 5:28] that they should love their wives as their own bodies, and should not provoke their children to anger but nourish them in every discipline and correction of the Lord.

Thus, when Paul wrote to Timothy [1 Tim. 3:2] and had said, “one who governs his own household well,” he immediately added: “having children subject to him in all chastity,” not “under accusation of debauchery” [Tit. 1:6]. For a cohabitant of such people has no face to rebuke others. Hence one reads of blessed Job [Job 1] that he offered daily sacrifices to God for his sons, offering burnt offerings for each of them. He bound them together in such perfection of charity [Col. 0248C] that each in turn prepared a banquet for his brethren on his own day and invited his three sisters likewise to feast with him.

Because Eli neglected to do this, and, overcome by false piety, refused to strike his offending sons—as is recorded in the book of Kings—he brought upon himself with his sons a cruel sentence from the strict Judge. Hence the divine voice says to him [1 Sam. 2:29]: “You have honored your sons more than me.”

David likewise, exercising kindness toward his sons rather than the severity of discipline, discovered by experience that their youth was pernicious, since in their childhood he had allowed wandering license to be pleasurable. [Note: This final part of the sentence is absent from the Bohm edition.]

For one of them, after defiling his own sister by rape, was slain by her brother—namely Absalom [Note: 2 Sam. 13–18]—at a banquet which he had deceitfully prepared for his brethren. [Col. 0249A] Absalom, moreover, after obtaining pardon from his father, expelled him from the kingdom and went in to his concubines; finally, pursuing his father through the pathless wilderness, he became entangled in an oak tree and so died hanging.

Paul likewise writes to Timothy [1 Tim. 5:8]: “Whoever does not provide for his own, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.” Rightly, then, the person who does not know how to govern his own household is forbidden to be ordained a bishop. For if he is not faithful in the smallest matter, concerning which he ought to have a more intimate care, how will he exercise diligent solicitude in the church of God, where there are so many persons not his own?

Hence Jerome says [Commentary on Titus 1]: “For a righteous man is not defiled by the vices of his children; rather, freedom is reserved by the Apostle for the head of the church, so that he may be such a person [Col. 0249B] as does not fear to rebuke outsiders because of the faults of his children.” [Note: The original reads “therefore” rather than “for.”]

### Part IV

§ 1. This will happen when there is nothing that can be charged against him. For although the steps of a man are directed by the Lord [Ps. 36:5], and his ways are not in man’s own power [Jer. 10:23], he can rebuke but cannot correct; he can knock but cannot open; he can restrain the hand but cannot change the mind.

Hence Augustine, to the clergy and people of Hippo, letter CXXXVII [Note: Written A.D. 404; *Collectio tripartita*, part 2, title 53, chapters 37–38]:

### Chapter IX. The discipline of good people cannot change character.

However watchful the discipline of my household may be, I am a man [Col. 0249C] and live among men. Nor do I dare arrogate to myself [Col. 0250A] that my household is better than Noah’s ark, where nevertheless among eight people one reprobate was found [Note: The collected editions read “only”]; or better than Abraham’s household, where it was said [cf. Gen. 21], “Cast out the slave woman and her son”; or better than Isaac’s household, of whose two twins it was said [Note: The collected editions add “in Malachi 1”], “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

And below:

§ 1. I frankly confess to your charity before the Lord our God, who is witness over my soul [Note: The collected editions, including the first Basel edition, add “to me”]: from the time I began to serve God, just as I have found with difficulty persons better than those who have made progress in monasteries, so I have found none worse than those who have fallen in monasteries. [Note: The collected editions, except Basel, read “worse” as “more inferior”; all the collected editions read “fallen” as “failed”; Basel reads “thus” as “whence.” They read “in a monastery” rather than “in monasteries” here and below. They also read “since” for “from the time,” and, except Basel, add “just as.”] Thus I think that this is why it is written in the Apocalypse [Rev. 22:11]: “Let the righteous become more righteous, and let the filthy become filthier still.” [Note: The collected editions read “let the righteous be justified, and let the filthy become filthier.”]

[Col. 0250B]

### Chapter X. The insults of the lost ought not to move us from the way of uprightness.

Likewise, Cyprian, book I, letter 3, to Pope Cornelius [Note: Written about A.D. 252].

As far as we are concerned, brother [Note: The collected editions add “always”], it accords with our conscience to take care that no one should perish from the church through our fault. But if anyone perishes of his own accord and by his own crime, and refuses to do penance and return to the church, we believe that on the day of judgment we shall be without blame, since we counsel them for their healing [Note: The collected editions add “their health”]; while only those will remain in punishments who refused to be healed by the wholesome character of our counsel [Note: Basel adds “or consoled”].

Nor ought the insults of the lost move us to depart from the straight way and certain rule, since the Apostle also teaches [Note: Some editions read “taught”], saying [Gal. 1]: “If I were pleasing men, I would not be [Col. 0250C] a servant of Christ.” [Note: The collected editions read *quam* (“than”) for *quando* (“since/when”); the intervening conjunction is absent from the Basel, Venice I–II, Lyon II–III, and Antwerp editions.]

## DISTINCTION XLVIII

[Col. 0249]

[Col. 0249C] GRATIAN.

### Part I

Neophytes also are forbidden to be ordained bishops [Note: 1 Tim. 3:2, the ordinary gloss there, and Jerome to Oceanus], so that one who yesterday was a catechumen may not today become a bishop; one who yesterday was in the theater may not today sit in the church; one who in the evening was at the circus may not today minister at the altar; one who formerly was a supporter of actors may not today be a guardian of virgins. [Note: From Leo, in Anselm, book 6, chapter 34 (35).]

The reason for this prohibition, according to the Apostle, is lest, puffed up with pride as if the Christian religion had greatly needed him, he should fall into the downfall of the devil. For a priest made in a moment does not know how to possess humility, to observe the proper measures toward persons, or to despise himself. He has not fasted, not wept, not corrected himself, and not distributed to the poor. Those who, in an instant of time, become teachers while not yet disciples fall into arrogance—which is the devil’s downfall. As Innocent says [Letter to Aurelius], it is a miserable thing for a man to become a teacher before he has learned to be a disciple.

Hence one reads in the Council of Nicaea, chapter 2 [Note: Held A.D. 325]:

### Chapter I. A neophyte is not to be ordained bishop.

Because many things have been done contrary to the rule, whether through necessity or through some other cause—Greek: *ἢ ἄλλως ἐπειγομένων τῶν ἀνθρώπων*, “or when people are otherwise pressing,” as Dionysius translates it [Note: “Through some other cause”: the Greek is *ἢ ἄλλως ἐπειγομένων τῶν ἀνθρώπων*, which Dionysius renders *aut alias cogentibus hominibus*, “or when people otherwise compel”—so that persons newly catechized or instructed from the life of the Gentiles [Note: The collected editions read “of the Gentiles”] came immediately to spiritual baptism, and, as soon as they had been baptized [Note: The collected editions add “they were”], were promptly advanced even to the episcopate or presbyterate—it has rightly seemed good that nothing of this sort *ought* henceforth to be done. For time is needed for someone to be a catechumen, and after baptism he needs much testing. For the apostolic injunction is evident, saying [1 Tim. 3:6]: “Not a neophyte, lest perhaps, being puffed up, he fall into judgment and the snare of the devil.”

But if, as time proceeds—Greek *προϊόντος*, that is, “proceeding” [Note: The wording has not been altered because of the gloss]—he commits some mortal sin [Note: “Mortal” is absent from the ancient, indeed Hispanic, version. The Greek is *ψυχικόν τι ἁμάρτημα*, “some sin of the soul,” which Dionysius translates *delictum animae*, “an offence of the soul”] and is convicted by two or three witnesses, let such a person cease from the clergy [Note: The Hispanic Collection reads “he shall cease”]. But if anyone acts otherwise than these provisions [Note: The collected editions read “this”], as doing things contrary to the decrees of the holy council [Note: The collected editions read “contrary to the statutes”], he himself will be cast down from the rank of his clergy [Note: The Hispanic Collection reads “he himself will also suffer loss.”]

Gratian. Today, however, persons newly undertaking the profession of the sacred religious life are called neophytes.

[Col. 0252A] Hence blessed Gregory writes to Syagrius the bishop and other bishops, book VII, letter 110 [Note: Letter 106, written A.D. 599, book 9, Maurist edition; cf. the letter to Virgilius of Arles, book 5, letter 53; Anselm, book 6, chapter 26 (30); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 131, from the letter to Virgilius; *Polycarpus*, book 2, title 1]:

### Chapter II. Who is called a neophyte.

Just as a neophyte was then called one who at the beginning was planted in the instruction of the holy faith, so now he is to be considered a neophyte who, having been suddenly planted in the religious habit, has crept in to seek sacred honors. [Note: In book 7, letter 110, where the first portion of this chapter is found down to the words “But we know,” the reading is “was planted in the way of life of the holy faith.” But in book 5, letter 51, or chapter 95, where nearly the same words are found and, in addition, the following portion through the end, the reading here is: “who was still newly planted by instruction in the faith.” The original reads “at the beginning”; the collected editions read “in the beginning.” Basel reads “to seek” as “to deliberate about seeking.”]

§ 1. Therefore one must approach the orders in due sequence [Note: The original and Anselm read “ascend” rather than “approach”; the collected editions likewise read “ascend”]. For the person who seeks an ascent to the heights of the highest place [Note: The original reads “of the highest place”] by steep paths, setting aside the steps, seeks a fall. We know, moreover, that walls which have been built do not receive the weight of beams until they have dried from the moisture of their newness [Note: The original omits “from”], lest, if they receive weights before they are made firm, they bring down the entire structure together to the ground.

## DISTINCTION XLIX

[Col. 0251]

[Col. 0251B] GRATIAN.

Behold from what vices those who are ordained bishops ought to be free. For those prepared as intercessors for the people before God must needs deserve his grace by living well. Hence Gregory says in the *Pastoral Rule* [part 1, chapter 10]:

§ 1. One must carefully fear lest he who is believed able to appease God’s wrath should himself deserve it by his own guilt. For we all know clearly that, when a person who is displeasing is sent to intercede, the mind of the angry person is provoked to worse things. Therefore, let one who is still bound by earthly desires take care lest, by more gravely kindling the wrath of the strict Judge while taking delight in a position of glory, he become for his subjects an author of ruin.

Therefore [Note: *Pastoral Rule*, part 1, chapter 11] let each person diligently measure himself, and let him not dare to assume the place of government if a vice still reigns damnably within him. Nor let one corrupted by his own crime desire to become an intercessor for the faults of others.

### Chapter I. Let one stained by vices not offer sacrifice to God.

The same author, in the same *Pastoral Rule*, immediately following, in the same chapter.

Hence by a heavenly voice it is said to Moses [Note: [Col. 0251] Leviticus 21:1. — In all the collected editions except Lyons II and III and Antwerp, here and in the following passages the books of Sacred Scripture are cited in the text itself.]: “Speak to Aaron: No man of your seed throughout their families who has a blemish shall offer bread to *the Lord* his God, nor shall he approach His ministry.” Thereupon [Col. 0252B] it is immediately added: “If he is blind, if lame, if he has either a small or a large and [Note: [Col. 0251] “Or”: the collected editions.] crooked nose, if his foot or hand is broken [Note: [Col. 0251] “If maimed, if hunchbacked”: the same editions.], if hunchbacked, if bleary-eyed, if he has a white spot in his eye, if continual scabies, if [Note: [Col. 0251] “If also”: Basel edition.] an eruption on his body, or if he is heavy.”

§ 1. A blind man is one who does not know the light of heavenly contemplation: oppressed by the darkness of this present life, because he does not behold the light to come by loving it, he does not know where to direct the steps of his action [Note: [Col. 0251] “Direct”: Lyons II and III and Antwerp editions.]. Hence, when Hannah prophesied [Note: [Col. 0251] 1 Samuel 2:9.], it was said: “He will guard the feet of His saints, and the wicked shall be silent in darkness.”

§ 2. The lame man, however, is one who indeed sees where he ought to go, but through weakness of mind cannot hold to the path of perfect life [Note: [Col. 0251] The original reads “perfectly”; the collected editions read “of perfect life.”] which he sees; because [Note: [Col. 0251] The collected editions read “because, namely, someone.”], since he is not raised from his wavering habit to a state of virtue, the steps of action do not effectively follow to the place upon which he leans *by* desire [Note: [Col. 0251] *Per* (“by”) is absent even from the original. The original reads *nititur* (“strives” or “leans”); the collected editions, except Basel, likewise read *nititur* in place of *innititur* (“leans upon”).]. Hence Paul says [Note: [Col. 0251] Hebrews 12:12.]: “Lift up the slack hands and the feeble knees, and make straight paths [Note: [Col. 0251] Basel reads “outgoings.”] for your feet, so that no lame person may go astray, but rather [Note: [Col. 0251] The original and the collected editions read “but rather.”] be healed.”

§ 3. A man with a small nose is one unfit to maintain the measure of discernment. For by the nose we distinguish odors from stenches. Discernment is therefore rightly expressed by the nose, by which we choose virtues and reject faults. Hence, in praise [Note: [Col. 0251] “In praises”: the same editions except Basel.] [Col. 0253A] of the bride, it is said [Note: [Col. 0253] Song of Songs 7:4.]: “Your nose is like the tower which is in Lebanon,” because the holy Church, through discernment, perceives from each circumstance what temptations arise and detects from on high the coming battles of the vices. But there are some who, unwilling to be thought [Note: [Col. 0253] “To be considered”: all the collected editions; the same editions except Basel add “themselves.”] dull, often [Note: [Col. 0253] “Themselves” is absent from the collected editions except Lyons II and III and Antwerp.] mislead themselves through excessive subtlety by applying themselves to inquiries more than is necessary. Hence it is also added here: “or with a large and [Note: [Col. 0253] “Or”: the collected editions.] crooked nose.” A large and crooked nose is an immoderate subtlety of discernment which, when it grows beyond what is fitting, itself confounds the rectitude of its action.

§ 4. A man with a broken foot or hand is one entirely unable to proceed in the way of God [Note: [Col. 0253] “The Lord”: the same editions.] and wholly devoid of good works; he does not even retain these things, like a lame man, with infirmity, but is in every respect [Note: [Col. 0253] Basel reads “entirely.”] [Col. 0253B] alien to them.

§ 5. The hunchbacked man [Note: [Col. 0253] “A hunchback”: all the collected editions except Basel.] is one oppressed by the weight of earthly care, so that he never looks toward things above, but attends only to things trodden underfoot in the lowest places. Even if he should at times hear something concerning the good of the heavenly homeland, he does not lift up the face of his heart toward it [Note: [Col. 0253] Basel reads “toward these things.”], being weighed down, of course, by the burden of his perverse habit; for he cannot raise the state of his thought [Note: [Col. 0253] “Understanding”: all the collected editions except Basel.], which the practice of earthly care keeps bent. Representing such people, the Psalmist says [Note: [Col. 0253] Psalm 118:107; Luke 8:14.]: “I am bowed down and humbled exceedingly.” Truth itself likewise rebukes their fault: “The seed which fell among thorns [Note: [Col. 0253] Basel reads “into thorns”]—these are they who hear [Note: [Col. 0253] The original and the collected editions read “who heard.”] the word and, going forth, are choked by the cares, riches, and pleasures of life, and bring forth no [Col. 0253C] fruit.”

§ 6. A bleary-eyed man [Note: [Col. 0253] Basel reads “indeed.”] is one whose natural intelligence shines out toward the knowledge of truth, but whose carnal works nevertheless obscure it [Note: [Col. 0253] The editions of Nuremberg, Venice I and II, and Paris read “these things” rather than “this.”]. In bleary eyes the pupils are sound, but the eyelids, weakened by the running discharge [Note: [Col. 0253] The editions of Argentan and Böhmer read “by infirmity”; the other collected editions read “weakening.”], become swollen [Note: [Col. 0253] Argentan reads “become diseased.”]; and because they are worn away by continual flux, even the sharpness of the pupil is impaired [Note: [Col. 0253] The original and Basel read “because of which”; the other collected editions, except Lyons II and III and Antwerp, read “because of which indeed”; some of these read *quidam* (“some”) for *quidem* (“indeed”).]. So there are some whose understanding is wounded by the activity of a carnal life. By natural ability they could keenly perceive what is right [Note: [Col. 0253] Basel adds “and strive.”], but through the practice of depraved deeds they grow dark [Note: [Col. 0253] The collected editions read “are darkened.”]. Thus he is bleary-eyed whose nature has sharpened his understanding but whose wicked manner of life confounds it. To him the Angel fittingly says [Note: [Col. 0253] Revelation 3:18.]: “Anoint your eyes with eye-salve [Note: [Col. 0253] Basel reads “join.”], that [Note: [Col. 0253] Basel reads “and.”] you may see.” We anoint our eyes with eye-salve in order to see [Note: [Col. 0253] The editions of Argentan, Nuremberg, and Venice I and II read “join”; Basel reads “enjoin.”], when, for the purpose of knowing the brightness of the true light, we aid the sight of our understanding [Col. 0253D] with the medicine of good action.

§ 7. He has a white spot in his eye who is prevented from seeing the light of truth because he is blinded by the arrogance of wisdom [Col. 0254A] or righteousness. The pupil of the eye sees because it is black; when afflicted by a white spot, it sees nothing. Thus the faculty of human thought, if it understands itself to be foolish and sinful, attains knowledge of inward brightness. But if it ascribes to itself the whiteness of righteousness or wisdom, it excludes itself from the light of heavenly knowledge; and it does not penetrate the brightness of the true light precisely because it exalts itself in its own estimation through arrogance. As it is said of some [Note: [Col. 0253] Romans 1:22.]: “Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools.”

§ 8. He has continual scabies whose fleshly wantonness rules without ceasing. In scabies the heat of the inward parts is drawn to the skin; by it lust is rightly signified, because [Note: [Col. 0253] The collected editions, following Basel, read “because even if”; the printed reading is *quia si* (“because if”).] if the temptation of the heart springs forth into action, the inward heat surely bursts out into the scabies of the skin [Col. 0254B] and now wounds the body outwardly, because when pleasure is not restrained in thought, it also rules in action. Paul seemed to be wiping away the itching of the skin when he said [Note: [Col. 0253] 1 Corinthians 10:13.]: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human,” as if he were plainly saying: It is human indeed to suffer temptation in the heart, but demonic to be overcome in [Note: [Col. 0253] “In” is absent from all the collected editions.] action in [Note: [Col. 0253] The same editions and the original read “and” for this second “in.”] the contest of temptation.

§ 9. Whoever is ravaged in mind by avarice also has an eruption upon his body; if avarice is not checked in small matters, it is surely extended without measure [Note: [Col. 0253] The editions of Argentan and Venice I and II read “excessively.”]. An eruption takes hold of the body without pain; growing without distress to the afflicted person, it disfigures the beauty of the limbs. So avarice ulcerates the captive soul while seeming to delight it; setting before its thought every object to be acquired [Note: [Col. 0253] All the collected editions except Lyons II and III and Antwerp add “transactions.”; some read “each person” for “each thing.”], it inflames it toward enmities, and it causes no pain in the wound, because through fault it promises abundance to the fevered mind. But the beauty of the limbs is lost, because through it the beauty of the other virtues also is corrupted; and it roughens, as it were, the whole body, because through every vice it trips the mind. Paul testifies to this when he says [Note: [Col. 0253] 1 Timothy 6:10.]: “Covetousness is the root of all evils.”

§ 10. The one heavy in the genitals is he who does not commit shameful acts but whose mind is continually and without restraint burdened by the thought of them. He is not indeed carried as far as a wicked deed, but his soul takes delight in the pleasure of lust without any obstacle of resistance [Note: [Col. 0253] All the collected editions except Lyons II and III and Antwerp read “stimulus.”]. The defect called “heaviness” occurs when the moisture of the inward parts flows down to [Col. 0254D] the sexual organs, which then swell with the immodesty of shame. Therefore, the one heavy in the genitals is he who, wholly giving way in thought to lasciviousness, bears the burden of shamefulness [Col. 0255A] in his heart. Although he does not perform wicked deeds [Note: [Col. 0255] The collected editions read “works.”], he is nevertheless not torn away from them in mind [Note: [Col. 0255] Basel reads “raised”; the other editions read “torn away.”], nor can he rise openly to the practice of good works, because a shameful weight oppresses him in secret.

§ 11. Whoever is subdued by any one [Note: [Col. 0255] The collected editions read: “whoever is subjected to any one of these vices.”] of these vices is forbidden to offer bread to the Lord, lest indeed [Note: [Col. 0255D] “Lest indeed”: this is also found in the printed original and in all the collected editions except Basel. In some manuscripts of Gratian it reads: “Nor indeed can one whom his own sins still ravage cleanse the sins of others.”] one whom his own sins still ravage should be unable to cleanse the sins of others [Note: [Col. 0255] Argentan reads “these” for “one.”].

§ 12. Since, then, we have shown briefly how one worthy of pastoral office ought to come to it and how one unworthy ought to fear it, let us now show how the man who has worthily attained it ought to live in it.

## C. II. An unlearned man, one pursuing earthly gain, or a vicious man ought not to be ordained

Likewise Jerome on Malachi, chapter 1 [vv. 7–8]. [Note: [Col. 0255] These matters are treated much more fully in Jerome.]

[Col. 0255B] Priests despise the name of the Lord and, so far as they are concerned, offer defiled bread: those who approach the altar unworthily [Col. 0256A] and those who presume to take up the priesthood by giving a gift. He too defiles the bread who distributes the Lord’s teaching badly among the people, and who honors the powerful and despises the poor. And below:

§ 1. “If you offer a blind [Note: [Col. 0255] The collected editions add “animal.”] animal for sacrifice, is it not evil?” etc. Having above been accused concerning bread, they are now [Note: [Col. 0255] Basel adds “however.”] accused concerning victims. He offers a blind animal who ordains an unlearned man in the place of a learned one [Note: [Col. 0255] The collected editions add “in.”] and makes a master of one who could scarcely have been a disciple. He offers a lame animal who installs one seeking earthly gain, as one who places a foot in two different directions—one in divine matters, the other in carnal matters—to whom may be applied that saying from the Book of Kings [Note: [Col. 0255] 1 Kings 18:21.]: “How long do you limp between two sides?” [Note: [Col. 0255] All the collected editions except Basel read the singular, “How long do you limp?”] He offers a sickly animal who regards a vicious man as religious, and who approves as patient one who is slow and lazy [Note: [Col. 0255] Basel reads “as patient.”], calling him [Col. 0256B] patient when he ought to be rebuked for negligence [Note: [Col. 0256D] The manuscripts and the gloss also punctuate the sentence in this way, “and approves the patient,” although it could also be divided thus: “and approves one who is slow and lazy, calling him patient,” etc.]. For it is unworthy to give God what a human being disdains.

## DISTINCTION L

[Col. 0255]

[Col. 0255B] GRATIAN

### Part I

From the authorities set forth above it has been clearly shown that those entangled in various crimes cannot be ordained priests. But now the question is raised concerning these same persons: after completing penance, can they remain in their own orders or ascend to higher ranks? By many authorities, persons entangled in various crimes are deposed from their own orders and forbidden access to higher ones.

[Col. 0255C] Thus Gregory says to Constantius, bishop of Milan, book IV, letter 17 [Note: [Col. 0255] Letter 4, written A.D. 595, book 5, Maurist edition. — Anselm, book 8, chapter 25 (35); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 145; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 80. — “To Constantine”: all the collected editions.]:

### C. I. The fallen cannot be restored to their order

If those who have fallen are granted permission to return to their order, the vigor of canonical discipline is undoubtedly broken, since, because of [Note: [Col. 0255] The original reads *per … spem* (“through … hope”).] hope of returning, no one [Note: [Col. 0255] The collected editions read “anyone.”] fears to conceive desires for grave misconduct. And after a few words:

§ 1. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0255] The same editions read “however.”] strive above all that no petition of anyone may in any way seek [Note: [Col. 0255] The same editions retain “seek.”] to recall to sacred order those who have fallen, lest punishment for such persons be thought not to have been imposed, but merely delayed for a time.

### C. II. He who falls after his ordination shall remain deposed

Likewise Pope Martin I, to Bishop Amandus [Note: [Col. 0255] Letter to Amandus of Tongeren, written A.D. 649. — Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 141.]:

[Col. 0255D] Whoever, once after his ordination, has fallen into sin shall thereafter remain deposed and shall be able to attain no rank of priesthood.

### C. III. After a fall, a presbyter cannot on any ground be restored to sacred order

Likewise Pope Gregory, to Bishop Sabinianus, book VII, letter 25 [Note: [Col. 0255] Letter to Sabinianus (Sabinus: Basel edition; Fabianus: the other collected editions) of Zadar, letter 24, written A.D. 598, book 8, Maurist edition. — Anselm, book 8, chapter 26; *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 146.]:

Know that the presbyter concerning whom your brotherhood has consulted us through the mission of the bearer of this letter [Note: [Col. 0255] The original and Anselm read *relatione* (“report”) rather than *legatione* (“mission”).] can neither remain nor be recalled in sacred order after his fall, on any ground whatsoever [Col. 0256C] [Note: [Col. 0255] The collected editions read *cognoscat* (“let him know”) for *cognoscas* (“know”).]. Yet he must be dealt with more gently, because he is said to have readily confessed the crime he committed.

### C. IV. After committing homicide, one cannot perform priestly office

Likewise John VIII, to the bishop of Le Mans, Uticensis [Note: [Col. 0255] Fragment of a lost letter. — Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 153; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 114; part 10, chapter 51: “to Caenomocus, bishop of Venice.”]:

I am astonished that your poorly instructed understanding [Note: [Col. 0255] Basel and Ivo, part 10, chapter 51, read “judgment.”] should think that, after committing homicide, a priest can minister in the priesthood; indeed—what is more absurd—that you should wish to persuade us to assent to such presumption. Who could be so mad and of such perverse judgment as to think that anything of this kind should be allowed even after however great a penance, when it is altogether [Note: [Col. 0255] Ivo reads “entirely.”] contrary to canonical discipline? Therefore, deprived of the priesthood, he ought with a fountain of tears to wash away so enormous an offense [Col. 0256D] [Col. 0257A], so that, healed at least by such remedies, he may find the aid of salvation.

### C. V. A cleric who has killed a pagan cannot be promoted to a higher rank

Likewise Pope Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0255] Fragment of a lost letter to Wilfred (or Humifred, Huntfred, or Guifred), bishop of Thérouanne. — Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 120.]:

A cleric who has killed a pagan ought not to be promoted to a higher rank; he ought even to lack what he has acquired [the reading *acquisitio* is materially uncertain], for he is a homicide. Since the soldiers of the world are distinct from the soldiers of the Church, it is not fitting for soldiers of the Church to serve as soldiers for the world, through which they must necessarily come to the shedding of blood.

### C. VI. He who kills a pagan in self-defense must relinquish priestly office

The same, to Osbald, chorepiscopus of Quadrantum [Note: [Col. 0257] Fragment of a lost letter. — Collection in Three Parts, part 1, title 62, chapter 64.]:

Concerning those clerics about whom you have sought advice—namely, those who killed a pagan while defending themselves—whether, having afterward amended their lives through penance, they can return to their former rank or rise to a higher one: know that we give them no occasion and grant them no permission to kill any person in any manner. But if it happens that a cleric of priestly order kills even a pagan, he takes great care for himself if he withdraws from priestly office; it is better for him in this life to serve the Lord blamelessly in a lower station than, by unlawfully seeking high things, to be plunged damnably into the depths [Note: [Col. 0257] The collected editions add “of hell.”].

### C. VII. Let a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who commits a capital crime fall from office

Likewise from the Council of Agde, chapter 50 [Note: [Col. 0257] Held A.D. 506; compare, however, the observations attached to chapter 30, Distinction 23. — Collection in Three Parts, part 2, title 28, chapter 48.]:

[Col. 0257C] If a bishop, presbyter, or deacon commits a capital crime, falsifies a document [Note: [Col. 0257] The Hispanic Collection reads “if they falsify,” continuing thereafter in the plural.], or gives false testimony, having been deposed from the honor of office, he shall be shut up in a monastery [Note: [Col. 0257] All the collected editions except Lyons II and III and Antwerp read “into a monastery”; Böhmer reads “be thrust down.”]; and there, as long as he lives, he shall receive lay communion only.

### C. VIII. One conscious after baptism of homicide by deed, command, or counsel shall not be ordained a cleric

Likewise from the council of Pope Martin, chapter 26 [Note: [Col. 0257] Martin of Braga’s translation of Apostolic Canon 17 and Canon 21 of the Council of Ancyra.]:

If anyone has taken a widow or a woman dismissed by another man [Note: [Col. 0257] The collected editions read “left behind.”], [Col. 0258A] he shall not be admitted to clerical status [Note: [Col. 0257] Thus in Merlin; the Hispanic Collection and all the collected editions read “to the clergy.”]. If he has slipped in [Note: [Col. 0257] The Hispanic Collection reads “or if he has crept in.”], he shall be deposed. Likewise, if after baptism he has been implicated in homicide by deed, command, counsel, or defense [Note: [Col. 0257D] “Defense”: in the royal Lucca manuscript—in which these chapters collected by Martin, bishop of Braga, also occur—and in Anselm and the three-volume edition of the councils, the margin reads “assent”; the Hispanic Collection preserves the same reading. This agrees with what is read near the end of chapter 11 of the Council of Tribur.], and has come into the clergy by some deception, he shall be deposed; and at the end of his life he shall receive lay communion only [Note: [Col. 0257] “Lay” is absent from the Hispanic Collection and Isidore-Merlin, as is the following word *tantummodo* (“only”). The collected editions read “receive” rather than “take.”].

### C. IX. Those who have fallen from sacred orders cannot be restored

Likewise Gregory, to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, book III, letter 26 [Note: [Col. 0257] Letter 26, written A.D. 594, book 4, Maurist edition. — Anselm, book 8, chapter 20; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 133; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 78; Polycarpus, book 4, title 39.]:

It has come to us that certain persons fallen from sacred orders are being recalled to the office of their ministry, either after penance or even beforehand. We altogether forbid this, and the most sacred canons also oppose it in this matter. Therefore, whoever, after receiving sacred order, falls [Col. 0258B] into the sin of the flesh shall be deprived of sacred order *in such a way* that he shall not *thereafter* approach the ministry of the altar.

### C. X. On the same matter

The same, to Venantius, bishop of Luni, book IV, letter 5 [Note: [Col. 0257] Letter 7, written A.D. 595, book 5, Maurist edition. — Anselm, book 8, chapter 21; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 83; Polycarpus, in the same place.]:

When you arrive at the island of Gorgona, let your brotherhood investigate what has been reported to us concerning Saturninus, a presbyter [Note: [Col. 0257D] “Presbyter”: in an old manuscript of the letters of St Gregory and in some ancient copies [Col. 0258D] of Gratian, as also in Anselm, it reads “former presbyter” (*expresbyter*); likewise below in this chapter: “Saturninus, former presbyter,” or, as in the printed editions of St Gregory, “concerning a former presbyter.” Deposed presbyters were called *expresbyteri*, and those who had abandoned monasteries *exmonachi*, just as men who had held the consulship or quaestorship were customarily called former consuls (*exconsules*) or former quaestors (*exquaestores*).] [Note: [Col. 0257] The collected editions read “related” rather than “reported.”]. It has reached us that, after being deposed from priestly rank because of the crime of his fall, he presumed to approach the performance of priestly ministry [Note: [Col. 0257] The original, Anselm, Ivo, and all the collected editions read “the ministry of the presbyter.”] and to offer sacrifices to almighty God. If your brotherhood finds that this was so done, let it reduce him to penance, deprived of participation in the sacred body and blood of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0257] The collected editions read *Domini* (“of the Lord”) for *dominici* (“the Lord’s”).], [Col. 0258C] so that he remains in the same excommunication until the day [Note: [Col. 0257] The same editions add “last.”] of his death and receives only viaticum at the time of his departure.
