But if your brotherhood finds that he has performed such penance that mercy ought justly to be shown him, even before death, by receiving communion among the laity, we place this in the power of your brotherhood.

And below:

§ 1. Furthermore [Note: [Col. 0257] From letter 3 to the same Venantius, written in the same year. — Anselm, book 8, chapter 22; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 132.], replying to the inquiries of your brotherhood, we decree that the deacon and abbot of Portus Veneris, whom you state has fallen [Note: [Col. 0257] The collected editions add “into crime.”], ought neither to be nor can be restored to sacred order in any [Note: [Col. 0259] The same editions read “in some.”] way [Col. 0259A]. You ought to assign him to penance, deprived of sacred order; if his conduct and manner of life later deserve it, he may hold the place of prior among the other monks, wherever you decide, though not an order [Note: [Col. 0259] The same editions add “not an order.”]. Likewise, subdeacons bound by a similar fault, having been irrevocably deposed from their office, shall receive communion among the laity. In the place of the fallen deacon at Portus Veneris, however, you shall ordain another to fulfill this office. Concerning Saturninus, the presbyter [Note: [Col. 0259] The original and Anselm read “former presbyter.”], we have decreed that he shall give written assurance never to presume to approach the ministry of sacred order; yet we permit him to supervise the monasteries on the islands of Gorgona and Capraria, and to remain in his present status without molestation by anyone [Col. 0259B] [Note: [Col. 0259] Basel reads “we permitted.”].

### C. XI. Another is to be ordained in place of one who has fallen

The same, to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna, book VI, letter 39 [Note: [Col. 0259] Letter 42, written A.D. 597, book 7, Maurist edition. — “Marianus”: Böhmer edition. — In all the collected editions the superscription is simply “The same.” — Anselm, book 8, chapter 25.]:

Since no rule permits a person who has criminally departed to be recalled to the position *from* which he fell, and since the decrees of the sacred canons do not permit a Church to be without a bishop for more than three months, lest, when the shepherd has fallen [Note: [Col. 0259] Anselm and the collected editions read “the falling shepherd.”], the ancient enemy—God forbid—tear apart the Lord’s flock by his snares, your brotherhood ought to assent to their petition and ordain a bishop in place of the fallen man.

### C. XII. He who falls after his ordination ought not to handle the sacred mysteries

Likewise Pope Martin I, in a letter to Amandus [Note: [Col. 0259] Written A.D. 649 to Amandus, bishop of Tongeren. — “In the council of Pope Martin”: Basel edition.]:

[Col. 0259C] If anyone after his ordination falls and is found guilty of the sin of transgression, he must by every means be forbidden [Note: [Col. 0259] All the collected editions read: “he must be forbidden … with,” and mark this as the beginning of Part II.] to handle the mysteries of our salvation with filthy and defiled hands.

### Part II

Gratian. On the contrary, examples and authorities prove that after penance has been performed, one may lawfully exercise one’s own rank and ascend to higher ranks. For Miriam [Note: [Col. 0259] Numbers 12; compare Cause 33, question 2, chapter 11.], Aaron’s sister, after she was struck with leprosy because she had murmured against Moses, was cleansed from sin and healed after doing penance, and received again her former grace of prophecy. Aaron [Note: [Col. 0259] Exodus 32.], after fashioning the calf, was nevertheless consecrated high priest. David [Note: [Col. 0259] 2 Samuel 1 and 12.], after adultery and homicide, received the spirit of prophecy and remained in his own rank. Ahab also [Note: [Col. 0259] 1 Kings 21.], after the death of the most holy man Naboth, humbled himself through penance and remained upon the royal throne. And, to pass over many examples from the Old Testament, Peter [Note: [Col. 0259] Matthew 26; John 21.] denied Christ and yet afterward became prince of the apostles; Paul [Note: [Col. 0259] Acts 7 and 9.] stoned Stephen and yet was chosen by God as an apostle. Many also who returned from heresy to the unity of the Catholic faith were received in their orders, while others were even promoted to episcopal rank [Col. 0260B], such as Augustine and many others.

### C. XIII. On the same matter. PALEA

[Note: [Col. 0259C] *Palea*: This chapter is absent from the older manuscripts. In the commonly printed editions it was headed, “Likewise from the letter of Cyril to John of Antioch”; this heading was removed because the matters treated in this chapter were collected from various histories, and some occurred long after Cyril of Jerusalem and Cyril of Alexandria [Col. 0259D]. Nor is any such heading found in Burchard or Ivo, but only in the *Panormia*.]

[Note: [Col. 0259] Among the sources of this chapter, the Roman Pontifical seems to hold the primary place; indeed, below, Cause 35, question 9, chapter 8, the words “Misenus,” etc., are said to have been excerpted from the Pontifical, although the words themselves do not occur there. — Burchard, book 1, chapter 233; Ivo, in the prologue to the *Panormia* and the *Decretum*.]

“John Chrysostom was judged *by* two synods of orthodox bishops, but was restored again. Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, was deposed but later recovered his own episcopate. Asclepius, judged by a synod, later recovered his Church. Lucius [Note: [Col. 0259] The collected editions read “Marcianus.”], bishop of Adrianople [Note: [Col. 0259] Lyons II and III and Antwerp read “Andronopolites”; the other collected editions read “Andrinopolites.”], condemned by Pope Julius, recovered the church of his bishopric. Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, was deposed and afterward reconciled to his Church. In the same way Pope Sixtus condemned Polychronius [Note: [Col. 0259] Basel and Lyons II and III read *Polocronius*; Antwerp reads *Polycromius*; the other collected editions read *Polocromius*.], bishop of that same Church of Jerusalem, and himself again reconciled him. [Col. 0260C] Pope Innocent condemned Bishop Photinus [Note: [Col. 0259] The collected editions read “Fortunatus.”] but later restored him to his own place in his Church. Misenus [Note: [Col. 0260C] The earlier reading [Col. 0259]—thus in the Paris, Lyons, and Antwerp editions—was “Nicaenus.” It was corrected from Burchard, Ivo, and the chapter *Gregorius*, Cause 35, question 9. In a manuscript Roman Pontifical, in the Life of Nicholas I, these words occur: “Just as the blessed Pope Felix deprived Vitalis and Misenus, bishops who had been compelled to assent in the case of Peter of Alexandria, defiled with heretical dregs, of priestly rank—indeed, of ecclesiastical communion.” [Col. 0260D]] a bishop condemned by Pope Felix, was reconciled and restored to his Church by Pope Gelasius, Felix’s successor [Note: [Col. 0259] Ivo adds “and admitted him to communion.”]. Leontius [Note: [Col. 0259] Argentan and Venice I read “Leucius”; Nuremberg, Venice II, and Lyons I read “Leuncius.”], while a presbyter, was deposed but later became patriarch at Antioch. Pope Gregory IV consecrated as bishop of the holy Church of Segni [Col. 0261A] [Note: [Col. 0261] All the collected editions except Basel read “of Seguina.”] Theodosius, whom Eugenius, his predecessor, had deprived of the honor of the presbyterate. Ibas [Note: [Col. 0261] The collected editions read “Abbas.”], a bishop, was judged, but the holy canonical synod restored his Church to him. Pope Nicholas reconciled both Rothad [Note: [Col. 0261] Nuremberg reads “Bocardus”; Argentan, Venice I and II, and Lyons I read “Rocardus.”], bishop of the holy Church of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0261] Nuremberg reads “of the Sueovian Church”; Argentan, Venice I and II, Paris, and Lyons I read “of the Suesovian Church.”], condemned by the synod at which Charles was present, and Sophronius [Note: [Col. 0261] Ivo reads “Sofrenus”; all the collected editions except Basel read “Sophidinus.”], bishop of Piacenza, rightly reproved.”

Moreover Pope Callixtus I writes thus concerning such persons, in his second letter to the bishops of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0261] Pseudo-Isidorian letter.]:

### C. XIV. Clerics can be restored to their orders after a fall

Let everyone weigh his own words, and let him not say to another what he would not wish said to himself. Hence Sacred Scripture rightly says [Note: [Col. 0261] Tobit 4:46.]: “Do not do to another what you do not wish done to yourself.” For we [Note: [Col. 0261] From Ambrose, Letter 39.] need time in order to act with greater maturity [Col. 0261B], and should not [Note: [Col. 0261] Basel reads “lest”; the other collected editions read “not.”] rush our counsels [Note: [Col. 0261] All the collected editions except Nuremberg, Venice I and II, Lyons II and III, and Antwerp read “councils.”] and deeds, or disturb their order [Note: [Col. 0261] The collected editions add “of them.”].

§ 1. But [Note: [Col. 0261] Burchard, book 19, chapter 42; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 48.] if anyone has fallen in whatever [Note: [Col. 0261] Ivo reads “in any”; the collected editions read “in whatever.”] manner, let us bear him [Note: [Col. 0261] The original reads “let us not lose him … but.”] and correct him with brotherly affection, as the blessed Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0261] Galatians 6:1–2.]: “If a person is caught in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself lest you too be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ.”

§ 2. Moreover [Note: [Col. 0261] From Augustine, Letter 50.], St David did penance for deadly crimes and nevertheless remained in honor.

§ 3. Blessed Peter also shed most bitter tears when he repented of having denied the Lord, and yet remained an apostle. And the Lord promises *sinners* through the Prophet, saying [Note: [Col. 0261] Ezekiel 18:22.]: “On whatever day a sinner is converted and groans [Note: [Col. 0261] The collected editions read: “at whatever hour he is converted and groans.”], [Col. 0261C] I shall remember none of his iniquities any more.” Those therefore err [Note: [Col. 0261] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 148; Polycarpus, book 4, title 38. From Augustine, Letter 50.] who think that *the Lord’s* priests, after a fall, cannot minister to the Lord and enjoy their honors if they have performed worthy penance, subsequently led a good life, and guarded their priesthood worthily [Note: [Col. 0261] The same editions read “worthily.”]. Those who think this not only err, but also appear to dispute and act against the keys given to the Church [Note: [Col. 0261] Ivo and all the collected editions read “to despise the keys given to the Church.”], concerning which it was said [Note: [Col. 0261] Matthew 16:19.]: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.” Otherwise this saying either is not the Lord’s, or it is true.

§ 4. We, however, unquestionably believe that both priests of the Lord and the rest of the faithful can return to honors after worthy satisfaction, as the Lord testifies through the Prophet [Note: [Col. 0261] Compare Gregory, book 9, letter 52, the supposititious fragment concerning the fallen inserted into the letter to Secundinus. Psalm 40:9.]: “Shall not he who sleeps rise again?” [Note: [Col. 0261D] The letter of Callixtus and the indicated collectors read: “Shall he who falls not proceed to rise again, and shall he who has turned away not return?” And elsewhere: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, says the Lord, but that he be converted and live.” [Col. 0262D] These two sayings occur in Jeremiah 8 and Ezekiel 33. Nothing has been changed because of the gloss.] And the prophet [Note: [Col. 0261] Psalm 50:14.] David, doing penance, said: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a sovereign spirit.” After his penance, he both taught others and offered sacrifice to God, giving an example to the teachers of holy Church that, if they have fallen and have rendered worthy penance to God, they can do both. For he taught when he said: “I shall teach transgressors your ways, and the wicked shall turn to you.” *And* he offered sacrifice to God *for himself* when he said: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God.” Seeing that his crimes had been cleansed by penance, the Prophet did not hesitate, by preaching and offering sacrifice to the Lord, to heal [Col. 0262B] the faults of others as well [Note: [Col. 0261] The collected editions add “also.”].

And below:

§ 5. Therefore a person is cleansed from sin and, having fallen, rises again by the grace of God [Note: [Col. 0261] The collected editions read “from the fall.”], and he remains in his former office according to the authorities stated above. Let him see that he sins no more [Note: [Col. 0261] The editions of Argentan, Venice I and II, and Nuremberg read “that he does not lie”; the other collected editions read “that he does not fall.”], so that the Gospel saying may remain in him [Note: [Col. 0261] The collected editions read: “but the evangelical saying remains, which says”; compare John 8:11.]: “Go, and sin no more.” Hence the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0261] Romans 6:12.]: “Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires.”

And below:

§ 6. Brothers, reject an opinion that forbids mercy—not only refuse to hold it, but refuse even to hear it [Note: [Col. 0261] The collected editions read “flee” for “reject.”]—because mercy is greater than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.

### C. XV. Priests can be recalled to their former rank after penance

Likewise Jerome on chapter 3 of Malachi.

[Col. 0262C] “And he shall cleanse the sons of Levi” [Note: [Col. 0261] Mal. 3:3.]; for “the time has come for judgment to begin with the household of God” [Note: [Col. 0261] 1 Pet. 4:17.], and elsewhere it is written: “Begin with my holy ones” [Note: [Col. 0261] Ezek. 9:6.]. By the sons of Levi understand every priestly dignity [Note: [Col. 0261] *understanding*: collective editions, except Lyons II, III, and Antwerp, which have *understands*; add *to be*, except Basle.]. But if priests must be cleansed and refined, so that pure gold and silver may remain, what is to be said of the rest? When they have been cleansed and refined, then they shall offer just sacrifices to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0261] *to God*: collective editions.], and their sacrifice shall be pleasing, which they offer [Note: [Col. 0261] *offer*: Basle edition; *is offered*: the remaining collective editions.] for Judah and Jerusalem [Col. 0263A]—that is, for those who confess the Lord and behold his peace with the mind [Note: [Col. 0263] *rightly*: Basle edition; *conceive*: Lyons II and III.]—as in the days of old and as in former years [Note: [Col. 0263] *so*: Basle edition; collective editions add: *that is*.], so that, just as they pleased God in the beginning, so after sin and repentance they may begin to please him, when they have been cleansed of every defilement of all sins [Note: [Col. 0263] *of all*: same editions, except Basle.].

### C. XVI. Those who have fallen may be restored. Likewise Gregory, to Secundinus, Book VII, Letter 53.

[Note: [Col. 0263] This fragment, inserted within Gregory’s letter to Secundinus (Letter 52, written A.D. 599, Book 9), has long been judged apocryphal by learned scholars; nevertheless, it seems to have been composed before the time of Pseudo-Isidore.—Rabanus, *On Penance*, ch. 1. Burchard, Book 19, ch. 43. Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 3, ch. 147. *Decretum*, Part 6, ch. 85.]

Because your Holiness requested this of us, that we should write to you [Note: [Col. 0263] *to you*: Ivo and the other collective editions.] authorities concerning the restoration after a fall to priestly office, since you say [Note: [Col. 0263] *you say*: Ivo and the other collective editions.] that you have read different canons on this matter and found differing opinions [Note: [Col. 0263] Absent from Ivo; the collective editions read: “that you have read differing opinions of different canons.”]: some holding that restoration is possible, others that it is not at all possible. Therefore we [Note: [Col. 0263C] *Therefore we*: In two editions of the letters of Blessed Gregory it reads: “therefore we find that the most general councils, beginning with the Nicene Council, agree with the other four. For we too follow those who went before,” etc. One manuscript has *most generally*; the rest agree in the same way. In Burchard, Ivo, and the *Panormia*: [Col. 0264C] “For we generally”; otherwise they differ little from Gratian.] venerate the general [Note: [Col. 0263] The original adds: *holy*.] synods, beginning with Nicaea, this one [Note: [Col. 0263] Absent from the original.] together with the other four [Note: [Col. 0263] The original adds: *made afterward*.], because the rest, following it, agree unanimously with it in all canonical determinations. We, however, ought to follow the Fathers who preceded us [Note: [Col. 0263] Ivo and the collective editions read: “we follow, because.”], since, with God as author, we do not depart from their sacred teaching.

Beginning, therefore, with the head and proceeding down to [Note: [Col. 0263] *in*: there.] the fourth minister of the altar [Note: [Col. 0263] *ministry*: original and Basle edition.], we recognize that this rule must be observed [Note: [Col. 0263] *have recognized*: collective editions.]: just as the greater precedes the lesser in honor, so also in crime; and he who is followed by the greater fault is punished with the greater penalty [Note: [Col. 0263] *is involved*: Collection of Paul the Deacon; Argentinian and Basle editions.], so that afterward repentance may be believed fruitful.

§ 1. For what profit is it to sow wheat and not gather its fruit [Note: [Col. 0263] The collective editions read: “and not reap its fruit” (*its*: Basle edition, *that*: the others).]? Or to build a house and not dwell in it? Therefore, after worthy satisfaction, we believe that one may return [Note: [Col. 0263] *return*: collective editions and Ivo; Ivo adds: *one who has fallen*.] to honor.

And below:

§ 2. Let us have recourse to the fountain of mercy and bring forth the evangelical saying [Note: [Col. 0263] *evangelical*: Ivo and the collective editions; cf. Luke 15:7.]: “I rejoice,” he says, “over one sinner doing penance more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance.” And the Lord himself testifies that the lost sheep, leaving the ninety-nine that had not gone astray in the wilderness, was carried back to the fold upon the shoulders of the loving shepherd [Note: [Col. 0263] These two words are absent from Ivo and the Basle edition.]. If the lost sheep, wandering, after it has been found is carried back to the fold on his shoulder [Note: [Col. 0263] The collective editions read: “is borne back, the aforesaid ninety-nine that did not stray having been left in the wilderness.”], why should the fallen man [Note: [Col. 0263] The original and the collective editions, except Argentinian, add: *this man*.] [Col. 0264A] not be recalled after repentance to the ministry of the Church?

[Note: [Col. 0264C] From here through the phrase “For what is” the passage is absent from some printed and two manuscript copies of the letters, as well as from Burchard, Ivo, and Rabanus.]

As it is said in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0263] Rev. 2:4.] concerning a minister [Note: [Col. 0263] *ministry*: Basle edition.] of the Church: “Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do the first works.” For what is more serious: to commit a carnal offence, without which few are found, or to deny the Son of God with an oath? Yet we know that Blessed Peter himself, prince of the apostles, at whose sacred body we unworthy men sit, fell in this latter respect [Note: [Col. 0263] The original and collective editions add: *word*.]. But repentance followed his denial, and mercy was given after repentance, because he who had foretold that Peter would deny him did not afterward expel him from the apostolate [Note: [Col. 0263] *deferred*: Basle edition; *cast down*: Ivo.], though he had previously foretold that he would deny him [Note: [Col. 0263] Ivo reads: “whom … would deny”; *previously* is absent from Basle.].

[Col. 0264B] ### C. XVII. After the most severe repentance, those who have fallen are restored. The same author, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, Homily IX, on chapter 2.

What is this, that the prophet, while lying down, is told: “Stand upon your feet, and I will speak with you”? Why does he who spoke with him while he lay down promise that he will speak only when he stands [Note: [Col. 0263] *immediately*: Argentinian, Venice I and II, Nuremberg, Lyons II.]? But we must understand that some things ought to be heard while we lie down, others while we stand [Note: [Col. 0263] *we ought*: collective editions.]. To one lying down it is said that he should rise; but one standing is commanded to go forth to preach. For while we still lie in the confusion of weakness, the authority of preaching ought not to be granted to us. But when we now rise in good work, when we have begun to stand upright, it is fitting that we should be sent into preaching in order to win others.

The prophet, therefore, standing, saw a spiritual vision and fell; but having fallen, he received the word of admonition [Note: [Col. 0263] *words of admonition*: same editions.] that he should rise; and having risen, he heard the command that he should preach. For when we still stand on the height of pride, once we have begun to perceive something of the fear of eternity, it is fitting that we should fall into repentance [Note: [Col. 0263] *through*: Basle, Lyons II and III, Antwerp; *approach*: the collective editions, except Argentinian, Lyons II and III, and Antwerp.]. And when, discerning our weakness closely [Note: [Col. 0263] The collective editions read: “while we humbly lie down, acknowledging our weaknesses”; *acknowledging*: Basle.], we lie humbly down, we are commanded by the consolation of the divine word to rise [Note: [Col. 0263] *let us rise*: Argentinian and Basle; *let us rise again*: the remaining collective editions.] to stronger works.

[Col. 0265A] ### C. XVIII. On the same subject. The same author, *Morals*, Book XVIII, ch. 16, on Job 28.

“Iron is taken from the earth” when a strong defender of the Church is separated from the earthly activity in which he was formerly engaged. Therefore he ought not to be despised for what he was, because he now begins to be what he was not [Note: [Col. 0265] *who*: original.].

### C. XIX. After fitting repentance, former offices are to be restored. Likewise Jerome, on Micah chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 0265] In Anselm’s collection this is attributed to Augustine, whom the collective editions have followed.]

“When I hear them, I shall give them the power of my Spirit, and I shall fill them with my judgment and strength.” Observe [Note: [Col. 0265] *Observe ye*: collective editions.] that in the present passage someone may teach after sin, provided that he has washed away his former vices by worthy repentance. Thus David, after adultery and homicide, says in the Psalm [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 50:9.]: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, [Col. 0265B] and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall become whiter than snow.” Nor is he content merely with his own cleansing, but adds: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit”; and when you have done this, he says, “I shall teach transgressors your ways, and the ungodly shall be converted to you.”

### C. XX. On the same subject. Likewise Jerome, Book II Against Jovinian.

Jesus, son of Jozadak, the high priest—although he preceded the Savior in type [Note: [Col. 0265] The collective editions add: *the coming*.], the Savior who bore our sins and joined to himself the foreign Church from the Gentiles—nevertheless, according to the letter, is represented as defiled after his priesthood. The devil stands at his right hand, and afterward white garments are restored to him [Note: [Col. 0265] *stands beside*: collective editions, except Basle.].

[Col. 0265C] ### C. XXI. Clerics corrected through repentance recover their rank and dignity. Likewise from the Council of Agde, chapter 2.

[Note: [Col. 0265] Held A.D. 506.—Ivo, *Decretum*, Part 6, ch. 366.—*Capitularies*, Book 7, ch. 311.]

Rebellious clerics are to be corrected by bishops [Note: [Col. 0265] *by the bishop*: collective editions, except Basle and Argentinian.] according as the order of their rank permits [Note: [Col. 0265] *rebuked*: Basle edition.]. If any, puffed up by the pride of a former rank, perhaps despise communion [Note: [Col. 0265] Basle has the singular, *despises*, and continues thereafter in the singular.] or neglect to attend church or fulfil their office, they are to be assigned communion as strangers; so that, when repentance has corrected them, they may be re-entered in the register and recover their rank and dignity.

[Col. 0266A] ### C. XXII. On the same subject. Likewise from the Council of Pope Martin, chapter 17.

[Note: [Col. 0265] Chapter 21 of the Council of Ancyra, in the translation of Martin of Braga; *Capitularies*, ch. 17.—Regino, Book 1, ch. 342. Burchard, Book 3, ch. 179. Ivo, *Decretum*, Part 3, ch. 240, from the Second Council of Braga.—Ivo, same work, ch. 173: from Martin.]

If any presbyter or deacon [Note: [Col. 0265D] *Deacon*: There followed [Col. 0265]—though not in the Argentinian and Basle editions—“or subdeacon.” These two words have been struck out, because they occur neither in Martin, Burchard, or Ivo, nor in the old manuscripts of Gratian.] is found to have sold anything belonging to the ministries of the Church, since he has committed sacrilege, it has been decreed that he shall not be retained in ecclesiastical ordination. Yet it must be left to the bishop’s judgment [Note: [Col. 0265] *must be left*: Ivo and the collective editions.] whether he is worthy or unworthy to be received back in his rank [Note: [Col. 0265] The collective editions, following Ivo, read: “whether he ought to be received in his rank, because,” etc.; the words “whether he ought” are absent from the Hispanic Collection.], because this very matter—that something pertaining to the most holy altar has been defiled—has often been left to the bishop’s authority [Note: [Col. 0265] The Hispanic Collection reads: “in this very matter, namely that they have defiled something belonging to the sacred altar, this has been left to the bishops.”].

### C. XXIII. PALEA

[Note: [Col. 0265D] *Palea*: In some old copies of Gratian these two paleae do not occur; rather, after the end of the chapter “If any presbyter,” the text continues directly: [Col. 0266D] “How, then.” Yet they occur in many copies, including ones from which paleae are generally absent. They seem to be summaries partly of the preceding chapters—“Let him weigh,” and “Because your Holiness”—and partly of the following chapter, “That it might be established,” quoted from Augustine to Boniface. From this source the same citation may have slipped into these paleae.]

[Note: [Col. 0265] Letter 185, written A.D. 417, Maurist edition.]

Likewise Augustine, to Boniface.

“It is right that a priest be restored to his honor after repentance has been completed, although on this matter different persons [Col. 0266B] think differently, saying that he cannot be restored to honor. But this was said because of the feigned repentances of some, and because of their ambitious pursuit of dignities of honor.”

### C. XXIV. PALEA

[Note: [Col. 0265] Compare Pseudo-Callistus I, and the spurious fragment on the fallen in Gregory to Secundinus, above, ch. 16, from which these are excerpted.—In the collective editions they circulate under Augustine’s name.]

“A priest, indeed, if he falls, is able and has a place for restoration to his honor after worthy repentance has been completed [Note: [Col. 0265] Basle adds: *and*.], as the Prophet testifies, saying: ‘Will not one who falls add, so that he may rise?’ [Note: [Col. 0265] Jerome, ch. 8; *sleeps*: Basle edition.] And Blessed Gregory says this in the enclosed letter to his friend Secundinus: ‘We also have the Prophet himself on this point, who, although after committing adultery and homicide he transgressed [Note: [Col. 0265] *transgresses*: there.], nevertheless afterward, when worthy repentance had been completed, was restored by God’s grace to his former office.’”

[Col. 0266C] **Part III. Gratian.** Let us briefly consider, then, how the discord of authorities of this kind may be brought into harmony. There are some whom repentance is compelled not by hatred of crime, but by fear of humiliation, loss of their own rank, and ambition for a higher one. The sacred canons depose these without possibility of restoration [Note: [Col. 0265] *without possibility of repair*: Basle edition.], because one who does not obtain pardon from God through feigned repentance or the pursuit of honor does not deserve restoration from the Church either.

[Col. 0267A] Hence Augustine writes to Boniface, Letter L [Note: [Col. 0267] Letter 185, written A.D. 417, Maurist edition.—Anselm, Book 8, ch. 3. Ivo, *Decretum*, Part 6, ch. 386, and in the prologue. *Polycarpus*, Book 6, title 20.—Supplementary Chapter 132. C. XXV.]:

### C. XXV. Why it has been established in the Church that no one return to clerical office after repentance.

That it should be established in the Church that no one, after repentance for any crime, receive clerical office, return to clerical office, or remain in clerical office, was done not in despair of forgiveness but through the rigor of discipline. Otherwise there would be an argument against the keys given to the Church, concerning which it was said: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.” But lest anyone’s mind, swelling with hope of ecclesiastical honor, should perform repentance proudly even for other crimes [Note: [Col. 0267] *discovered*: original.], it was most severely decreed that, after repentance had been performed for a condemnable crime, no one should be a cleric; so that by despair of temporal eminence there might be a greater and truer medicine [Col. 0267B] of humility [Note: [Col. 0267] *humility*: Böhm.].

For Saint David also repented of deadly crimes, and nevertheless remained in his honor; and Blessed Peter [Note: [Col. 0267] *Peter*: Basle edition.], when he shed most bitter tears, certainly repented that he had denied the Lord, and nevertheless remained an apostle. But for that reason the diligence of later generations ought not to be regarded as superfluous [Note: [Col. 0267] *thought*: collective editions, except Basle.]; for, where nothing was taken away from salvation, they added something to humility, so that salvation might be more safely secured for all [Note: [Col. 0267] The collective editions read: *more safely*.], having learned, I believe, through experience of some persons’ feigned repentances, pursued under the guise of ambitious claims to honor [Note: [Col. 0267] The same editions, except Basle, read: “might be found, having learned by experience.”]. For experience of many diseases compels the discovery of many remedies.

But in cases of this kind, where through grave divisions of dissension the danger is not that of this or that man but the ruin of peoples [Note: [Col. 0267] *very many*: Basle; *very many peoples*: the other collective editions.] lies at stake [Note: [Col. 0267] *lies*: collective editions.], [Col. 0267C] something must be deducted from severity, so that sincere charity may come to the aid of healing greater evils.

### C. XXVI. The benefit of restoration cannot be granted except after repentance. Likewise from the letter of the Roman clergy, sent to Pope Cyprian.

[Note: [Col. 0267C] This chapter has been enlarged from the original.]

[Note: [Col. 0267] Letter 30, written A.D. 250, Fell edition.—Anselm, Book 8, ch. 20 [30].]

Far be it from the Roman Church to abandon its vigor through such profane indulgence and to loosen the sinews of severity once the majesty of faith has been overthrown, so that, while the ruins of fallen brethren not only still lie low but continue to fall, remedies of communion offered too hastily [Col. 0268A] should certainly prove unprofitable, and new wounds should be inflicted by false mercy upon the old wounds of transgression, so that repentance itself may be taken away from the wretched, to their greater ruin. For where can the medicine of pardon [Note: [Col. 0267] *repentance*: Anselm.] be effective [Note: [Col. 0267] *go before*: Lyons II and III; *proceed*: the remaining collective editions.] if the physician himself, cutting repentance short, indulges dangers? If he merely covers the wound and does not permit the remedies required by time to bring about a scar? This is not healing but, if we wish to speak the truth, killing.

### C. XXVII. Forgiveness cannot be granted to the unrepentant. Likewise Cyprian, in the sermon *On the Lapsed*.

[Note: [Col. 0267] Anselm, Book 8, ch. 32.]

If anyone, with rash and premature haste [Note: [Col. 0267] *misplaced*: collective editions.], thinks that he can give remission of sins to everyone, or dares to annul the Lord’s commands, he not only does no good but harms the fallen. It is to provoke wrath, not to observe the judgment; not to think that the mercy of God must first be implored [Note: [Col. 0267] The collective editions read: “to implore the most merciful God.”], but, despising the Lord, to presume upon one’s own indulgence.

And below:

§ 1. The martyrs command certain things to be done. If these are just, lawful, and not contrary to the Lord himself, they are to be done by the priest of God [Note: [Col. 0267] The collective editions read: “and by God’s priests, they are to be done.”]; let the consent of the one obeying be ready and willing [Note: [Col. 0267] *if*: same editions.], if the moderation of the petitioner has been devout. The martyrs command something [Note: [Col. 0267] *certain things*: same editions.] to be done; but if what they command is not written in the Lord’s law, we must first know that they have obtained from God what they request, and then do what they command. For it cannot immediately appear that what human promise has pledged has been granted by the divine majesty [Note: [Col. 0267] Absent from the collective editions, except Argentinian.]. Moses also prayed for the sins of the people, yet when he had prayed, he did not receive pardon for the sinners [Col. 0268C] from God [Note: [Col. 0267] The collective editions add: *from God*.].

### C. XXVIII. Who are to be restored after a fall, and who are not. Likewise Isidore, to Bishop Massanus.

[Note: [Col. 0267] There are those who consider this letter of Isidore, written to Massona—for that is the correct reading—bishop of Toledo, to be spurious. Against them, the most recent editor of Isidore’s works, Arevalo, has defended its authenticity. Most manuscript codices assign it to A.D. 606.—Rabanus, *On Penance*, Book 1, ch. 1. Burchard, Book 19, chs. 43 and 73. Anselm, Book 8, ch. 37. Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 3, ch. 149; *Decretum*, Part 6, ch. 397, Part 15, chs. 57 and 86.—See also Alger’s preface to the book *On Mercy and Justice* in Mabillon’s *Analecta*.]

To the holy lord and brother Massanus, blessed for his merits, bishop: greetings [Note: [Col. 0267] The collective editions add: “Isidore, bishop.”].

What your venerable Fraternity made known in its letters [Note: [Col. 0267] *indicated*: Böhm.]—namely, that in Canon XIX of Ancyra [Note: [Col. 0267C] *Of Ancyra*: This chapter occurs in the letter recently printed at Paris together with the other works of Isidore, under the title: “Letter of Isidore, Archbishop of Seville, to Bishop Massanus.” [Col. 0268C] “To the holy lord, blessed for his merits,” etc. But in the longer letter on the same subject and in almost the same words—printed both there and previously at Antwerp with the books *On the Highest Good*—there is no mention at this point of the Council of Ancyra. Nevertheless, the Paris edition bears the title: “Letter of Isidore, Archbishop [Col. 0269C] of Seville, concerning the restoration to their former dignity of penitent clerics,” or: “Explanation of certain canons of the Council of Ancyra.” Yet in Canon 19 of Dionysius’s translation—Canon 20 among the Greeks and in other translations—where it reads “to attain perfection according to the former ranks,” the Greek is: κατὰ τοὺς βαθμοὺς τοὺς προάγοντας, that is, “according to the ranks which lead thereto.” And Balsamon draws a wholly different conclusion from it than Isidore does.] it is read that after a carnal fall a rank of honor is to be restored after repentance, whereas elsewhere it is read that, after such an offence, the merit of the former order is by no means to be restored [Col. 0269A]—is resolved in this way [Note: [Col. 0269] *distinguished*: original, Anselm, and Ivo; *speaks*: Basle edition.].

For the canons command those to return to their former ranks [Note: [Col. 0269] Ivo adds: *of office*; Basle reads: *former state*.] whose repentance has been preceded by satisfaction or a worthy confession of sins. On the other hand, those who are not corrected from the vice of corruption [Note: [Col. 0269] *seized*: original; *of the body*: Ivo, Part 15.], and who strive with superstitious recklessness in some way to defend the very carnal offence they commit, receive neither a rank of honor nor the grace of communion.

Therefore the ruling must be determined thus: those who deserve, through repentance, to have received reconciliation from divine mercy must necessarily be restored to a place of honor [Note: [Col. 0269] Absent from the original, Ivo, and Basle.]. For not without reason do those attain the state of dignity taken away from them [Note: [Col. 0269] *attained*: Ivo and the collective editions, except Lyons II, III, and Antwerp.] who are known, through amendment of repentance, to have received the remedy of life. And lest this perhaps remain ambiguous, let it be confirmed by the declaration of divine authority [Col. 0269B] [Note: [Col. 0269] *is confirmed*: Basle.].

The prophet Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0269] Ezek. 16:52.], under the figure of faithless Jerusalem, shows that after the satisfaction of repentance former honor can be restored [Note: [Col. 0269] Absent from the original and Basle.]: “Be ashamed,” he says, “O Judah, and bear your disgrace.” And a little later: “You and your daughters,” he says, “shall return to your former condition.”

§ 1. By saying “Be ashamed,” he shows that everyone ought to blush after committing sin, and after confession of the crimes committed [Note: [Col. 0269] *defilements*: Basle.] sink to the ground a shamefaced countenance cast down, because he has committed a deed deserving confusion [Note: [Col. 0269] *committed*: Basle.]. Then he commanded that after disgrace and the casting down [Note: [Col. 0269] *that is*: there.] of his name or dignity, he should return to his former condition. Therefore, while anyone is ashamed after the act of his confession, and, bearing disgrace, mourns his deposition with humility [Col. 0269C], he may, according to the Prophet, be recalled to his former state.

Likewise John the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 0269] Rev. 2:4.] writes among other similar things to the angel of the Church of Ephesus: “Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do the first works [Col. 0270A]; otherwise I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place” [Note: [Col. 0269] Basle adds: “unless you repent.”].

§ 2. Behold, insofar as I have been able, I have explained the ancient, clear, and complete authority [Note: [Col. 0269] Basle adds: *judgment*, and in place of *rank* in the following verse reads *order*.] of the Council of Ancyra by sacred testimonies, showing that he can be restored in his own rank who, through the satisfaction of repentance, has known how to lament his own offences. But you should know that the one who neglects and does not mourn what he has done, and commits shameful acts without any shame of religion or fear of divine judgment, can in no way be restored to his former rank.

§ 3. At the end [Note: [Col. 0269D] *At the end*: These words are now found in the longer letter [Col. 0270C], but not in the other letter, which otherwise Gratian appears to have followed.] [Note: [Col. 0269] See below, C. 33, q. 2, ch. 11.] of this letter I thought it necessary to add that whenever a conflicting judgment is found in the acts of councils, the judgment of that council whose authority is either older or greater should be preferred [Note: [Col. 0269] *exists*: Basle.].

**Gratian.** Therefore, all who have worthily offered repentance to God for their crimes may, by the authority of Gregory, Augustine, Jerome, and Isidore, recover the rank of their former dignity [Col. 0270B]. But those who offer false repentances to God, not from hatred of crime but from fear of losing advantage or ambition for honor, can by no means be restored to the rank of their former honor.

But the statement of Pope Hormisdas is objected, who writes to all bishops throughout the provinces:

[Note: [Col. 0269] The first part of this canon belongs to Canon 23 of the First Council of Orange, held A.D. 441. The author of the other and longer part is not certainly known. It must, however, be assigned to Hormisdas because both the original and Anselm, as well as the canonical collection of Jacques Petit (Paris, 1677), mention Pope John II. Sirmond, editor of the Gallican councils, reasonably conjectured that Caesarius of Arles was the author of the canon; the Ballerini brothers also approved this view.—Anselm, Book 11, ch. 87. Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 3, ch. 98.]

### C. XXIX. A deacon or presbyter found in adultery cannot be restored.

If any deacon or presbyter, after receiving the Levitical blessing, is found incontinent with his wife [Note: [Col. 0269] *is found*: collective editions, except Basle.], he shall be deposed from his office [Note: [Col. 0269] *cast out*: collective editions.].

§ 1. Behold, it is plainly established that, according to the enactments of the ancient Fathers, written at the prompting of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0270D] *At the prompting of the Holy Spirit*: Anselm reads: “sent by Saint Pope John”; and “the determinations of 318 bishops,” which seems to agree with what follows below: “Is there greater mercy in them than in Saint John, the apostolic Pope?”], and according to the determinations of 318 bishops—which the Gallican canons also seem to contain—clerics found in adultery, whether confessing it themselves or convicted by others [Note: [Col. 0269] *re-convicted*: original.], cannot return to honor.

But since perhaps there are not lacking [Note: [Col. 0269] *will not be lacking*: there.] persons to whom the foregoing severity of the holy Fathers seems unacceptable because of excessive piety, let them know that they are censuring or condemning the determinations of the 318 bishops [Col. 0271A] gathered in the Council of Nicaea, who established the remaining canons [Note: [Col. 0271] The original reads: “the commands of the bishops, and the authority of Saint Pope”—that is, John II—“and of those pontiffs who, with the 318 bishops establishing the rest,” etc.]. But perhaps there is greater piety in them than in the aforesaid 318 bishops? Greater mercy in them than in Saint John, the apostolic Pope? Greater charity than in the other holy priests who, by their definitions, devised remedies for the churches from this example [Note: [Col. 0271] The original reads: “as an example and remedy.”]? Therefore let them either assent with ready [Note: [Col. 0271] *full*: original; *good*: Lyons II; *inclined*: the remaining collective editions.] will to those precepts, or, if they do not, recognize that they have made themselves opponents and enemies of them all.

What is this kindness, hostile to justice [Note: [Col. 0271] *goodness*: collective editions.], that strokes criminals and preserves their wounds untreated until the day of judgment?

§ 2. If we saw them performing the most severe repentance for many years, then we could both provide for their salvation and ought to temper the decrees of the canons [Note: [Col. 0271] *observe*: original.]. But when in some there appears neither the contrition of humility nor diligence in praying and lamenting; when they do not imitate blessed David, who says: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will drench my couch with my tears” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 6:7.]; and, “I ate ashes as bread and mingled my drink with weeping” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 101:10.]; and when we do not see them devoting themselves to fasts or readings [Note: [Col. 0271] *nor*: Basle; *reading*: original.], we can recognize with how much negligence, torpor [Note: [Col. 0271] *lukewarmness*: original; *body*: Argentinian.], and soul-destroying security they would remain if they returned to their former honors [Note: [Col. 0271] The collective editions add: *ranks and*.], believing that God has forgiven them without worthy repentance having been performed [Note: [Col. 0271] *worthily*: original.] just as priests appear to have forgiven them.

Truly I say that those very persons toward whom we appear to act indulgently with a dangerous and false mercy, when they come before Christ’s tribunal to be condemned for such great sins, will bring an accusation against us, saying that, because we feared either the harshness [Col. 0272A] of their tongue or gladly accepted their false flatteries and dangerous adulations, we uselessly indulge them in continuing in the same sins, or allow the sins themselves to increase; not remembering [Note: [Col. 0271] *recalling*: original and collective editions.] what is written in the Old Testament [Note: [Col. 0271] Num. 16:22.]: that when one sinned, the wrath of God raged against all [Note: [Col. 0271] *rages*: original and collective editions, except Lyons II, III, and Antwerp.].

### C. XXX. It is difficult to return to one’s former rank after a fall. Likewise Jerome.

[Note: [Col. 0271C] Something similar to the first part of this chapter occurs in Canon 27 of Basil to Amphilochius and Canon 26 of the Synod in Trullo.]

[Note: [Col. 0271] A chapter by an uncertain author.—Burchard, Book 19, ch. 78. Ivo, *Decretum*, Part 15, ch. 91, “from the sayings of Jerome.”—*Polycarpus*, Book 4, title 39.]

Whoever does not preserve the dignity of his divine rank should be content to save his soul. For it is difficult to return to one’s former rank after a fall [Note: [Col. 0271] These two words are absent in Ivo and the Argentinian, Basle, and Nuremberg editions.].

### C. XXXI. After repentance, one who has fallen is to minister only at the altar. Likewise Basil.

[Note: [Col. 0271C] *Basil*: Ivo cites this as from the sayings of Augustine. Something bearing on this subject occurs in Basil’s letter to Amphilochius, ch. 27. But Canon 14 of the First Council of Orléans and Canon 9 of the Council of Neocaesarea—found below, 15, question 8, ch. “He who committed”—come closer to this ruling, especially if the text is read, as in most manuscripts of Gratian [Col. 0271D] and the Argentinian and Basle editions: “to give communion to the sick, but not to offer sacrifice and minister at the altar.” Balsamon reports a similar ruling from a novella of Leo on Canon 21 [Col. 0272C] of the Synod in Trullo.]

[Note: [Col. 0271] Burchard, Book 19, ch. 80. Ivo, *Decretum*, Part 15, ch. 19.]

[Col. 0272B] Let him who has fallen from his rank, after repentance, be content to baptize, give communion to the sick, and minister only at the altar.

### C. XXXII. Concerning priests, deacons, and laypersons who burn incense to idols. Likewise from the Council of Ancyra, chapter 1 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0271] Held A.D. 314.—The first part of the chapter, through § 2, is from the Hispanic translation; the second is from the translation of Dionysius. § 6 is Canon 11 of the Council of Nicaea, also in Dionysius’s translation.—Burchard, Book 5, chs. 40–41. Ivo, *Decretum*, Part 2, chs. 49–50. *Polycarpus*, Book 6, title 12, ch. 2; these too use the same translation for the first part.]

Priests who sacrificed [to idols] and afterwards again entered the contest, if they struggled in good faith, and did not deliberately make a display in order that they might be seized, are to retain the honor of their own seat; but they are not permitted to make offerings, to address the people, or to discharge any priestly functions.  

§ 1. Likewise deacons who sacrificed and afterwards again resisted: they ought indeed to retain their honor, but they must cease from every sacred ministry, so that they neither offer bread nor the cup, nor proclaim the Gospel—unless perhaps certain bishops, aware of their labor, humility, and gentleness, should wish to grant them or take away from them something more. The authority concerning these matters will therefore rest with the bishops.

[Note: “If in good faith”: here the words of the council have been condensed; but the version of Dionysius, which Burchard and Ivo cited, comes closer throughout to the Greek wording. Nevertheless, certain matters in this chapter have been corrected and expanded from versions which Gratian seems to have followed.]

[Note: “By agreement”: Basel edition.]

[Note: “That they might be seized”: the original reads “that they might be offered up”; collected editions read “that they might offer themselves.”]

[Note: “Nor proclaim the Gospel”: in the older version—that is, in Merlin’s—the reading is “nor proclaim”; in another version, cited by Burchard, it is “or by preaching,” Greek κηρύττειν, which properly means to preach the Gospel and the doctrine of faith. In the Spanish Collection, however, these three words are omitted, although there too there is a variation of reading.]

[Note: “Are”: the Spanish Collection reads “add”; the collected editions likewise. The word “take away” is found in Dionysius and Isidore in Merlin’s edition. The ancient version reads “diminish.”]

§ 2. But those who, while fleeing, were seized, or betrayed by members of their household, or after the seizure of their property endured tortures, or, thrown into prison, proclaimed themselves Christians and were constrained so far that, their hands being seized, they were forcibly dragged to deadly sacrifices, or were compelled by necessity to consume some polluted food—continually confessing themselves Christians and unceasingly displaying, by every abasement, manner, and humility of life, their grief over what had happened—we decree that these, being regarded as outside the guilt, are not to be excluded from the grace of communion.

[Note: “Who”: Anselm, book 8, chapter 31.]

[Note: Basel adds “confidently”; the remaining collected editions read “confessing the faith of life.”]

[Note: The collected editions, the first Basel edition, Lyons II–III, and Antwerp add “indeed.”]

[Note: The original, followed by Anselm, reads “we decree that they are not forbidden,” omitting the word “decree.”]

§ 3. If, however, they have been excluded by some persons through excessive caution or through the ignorance of certain people, let them be received at once.

§ 4. The same rule ought likewise to be observed concerning clerics and all other laypersons.

[Note: The collected editions read “it is fitting to observe.”]

§ 5. It was also asked whether laypersons who had fallen into these straits of necessity could be promoted to clerical rank. It was therefore decided that these too, as persons who had committed no sin, should be advanced to this office, provided their previous life is approved.

[Note: Basel reads “will be approved”; the remaining collected editions read “has approved.”]

§ 6. Concerning those, however, who denied [the faith] apart from necessity, or apart from confiscation of property, or apart from danger, or anything of this kind—which occurred under the tyranny of Licinius—the holy synod decided that, although they are proved unworthy of humane consideration, benevolence should nevertheless be extended to them.

[Note: Anselm, book 11, chapter 134.]

[Note: Basel adds “voluntarily.”]

Gratian. But the statement of Pope Hormisdas prohibits the restoration of those who are idle and negligent, rather than truly penitent. § 1. Jerome’s statement, however, acknowledges that this is difficult, not impossible. § 2. Basil shows that the rigor of justice must be maintained toward offenders, whereas others mercifully maintain that it should be relaxed toward penitents. § 3. The foregoing authorities may also be distinguished differently. Those whose crimes are public before or after ordination must be deposed from sacred orders; but those whose sins are secret and have been cleansed by secret satisfaction according to the priest’s injunction may remain in their own orders.

[Note: Rabanus, *On Penance*, chapter 1.]

[Col. 0274A] Therefore Pope Nicholas [writes] to Archbishop Charles and his suffragans:

[Note: Rather, chapter 11 of the Council of Worms, held in 868.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 136; *Decree*, part 10, chapter 180.]

### C. XXXIII. A priest whose crime has been public cannot be restored.

If priests fall into the snare of fornication and the commission of the crime has been public or revealed, they cannot retain priestly honor by the authority of canonical institution.

Likewise Archbishop Rabanus writes to Heribald:

[Note: Letter to Heribald, bishop of Auxerre, written in 853; compare Rabanus, *On Penance*, chapter 10. The same words occur in chapter 49 of Theodore of Canterbury, from which they were drawn. Burchard, book 19, chapter 150; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 152; *Decree*, part 6, chapter 400.]

### C. XXXIV. Who may be restored after a fall, and who may not.

We have thought it necessary to write concerning those who hold sacred orders and confess that they have defiled themselves, before or after ordination, by capital crimes.

[Note: The original, Ivo, and the Basel edition read “have and”; the remaining collected editions read “having and.”]

[Note: Basel, following the original and Ivo, reads “profess.”]

In their case, as it seems to me, this distinction must be made: those who have been publicly detected or apprehended in perjury, theft, fornication, and other crimes of this kind must fall from their proper rank according to the ordinances of the sacred canons. For it is a scandal to the people of God to have placed over them persons known to be excessively vicious. Indeed, people are thereby drawn away from the sacrifice of God—as is recorded of old concerning Eli’s sons when they sinned—and, becoming rebellious and opposed on this account, they grow daily worse through such persons’ depraved examples.

[Note: I Samuel, chapter 2.]

But those who, concerning the aforesaid sins secretly committed by themselves, make secret confession before the eyes of God, also in the presence of the priest who is to impose penance upon them, and lament that they have sinned grievously, if they strive to cleanse themselves through fasts, almsgiving, vigils, and holy prayers, are to be promised hope of pardon through God’s mercy while retaining their rank.

[Note: The collected editions read “secretly.”]

[Note: The collected editions read “angels.”]

[Note: The same editions add “their sins.”]

[Note: The original reads “accuse themselves.”]

[Note: “If they [cleanse themselves] through fasts”: thus also in the manuscripts and in Ivo and the *Panormia*. But the original reads: “if they have truly repented, and cleanse themselves through fasts.” Burchard also cites this chapter from the Council of Lleida.]

## Part IV

Gratian. Concerning those who have also fallen into heresy, this too must be observed: before the judgment of a council, no one is to communicate with them.

Therefore Pope Cyprian says among other things to Antonianus, book IV, letter 2:

[Note: Written about 254.—Anselm, book 8, chapter 28.]

### C. XXXV. Those who communicate with the fallen before their restoration must abstain from communion.

As to what ought to be determined concerning the case of the fallen, I deferred the matter, so that, when peace and tranquillity had been granted and divine indulgence permitted the bishops to assemble, we might then, after consultation and careful deliberation upon the common counsel of all, decide what ought to be done. But if anyone before our counsel and before the judgment established by the common counsel of all should rashly wish to communicate with the fallen, he himself must be excluded from communion.

[Note: The Argentinian edition omits “however”; Basel, Venice I–II, and Nuremberg read “however.”]

[Note: The collected editions read “bishops.”]

[Note: Anselm reads “deliberated.”]

[Note: Basel, Venice I, Paris, Lyons I, and Antwerp read “council.”]

[Note: The collected editions read “I might decide.”]

[Note: Basel, Venice II, Paris, Lyons I, and Antwerp read “council.”]

[Note: The same editions, together with Lyons II–III, read “council.”]

[Note: The collected editions read “let him abstain”; Böhm reads “would abstain.”]

## Part V

Gratian. What is read above concerning killers must be understood where an opportunity for escape is available and persons are not shut in by the necessity of siege. But when they are pressed by necessity and cannot escape, if they then commit homicide, after being purified by penance they shall be restored both to office and to communion.

[Col. 0275B] Therefore the Council of Lleida, chapter 1, reads:

[Note: Held in 546.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 34, chapter 1.]

### C. XXXVI. Clerics who, placed under the necessity of a siege, have shed blood are to be restored to office and communion after two years’ penance.

Concerning those clerics who have been placed in the necessity of a siege, it has been decreed that those who minister at the altar, distribute Christ’s body and blood, or handle vessels assigned to sacred use must abstain from all human blood, even that of an enemy. But if they fall into this offense, for two years they are to be deprived both of their office and of communion in the body of the Lord. During these two years they are to expiate their offense, according to the means which the Lord grants them, by vigils, fasts, prayers, and almsgiving; and only then are they to be restored to office or communion, on the condition nevertheless that they are not afterwards promoted to higher offices. If, within the prescribed period, they prove more negligent concerning their salvation, the extension of the time of their penance is to remain in the priest’s power.

[Note: “Siege”: the Argentinian, Basel, Venice I–II, and Nuremberg editions read “sieges”; the remaining collected editions read “siege.”]

[Note: These two words, “and blood,” are absent from the Spanish Collection.]

[Note: The collected editions, except Lyons II–III and Antwerp, read “that they abstain from.”]

[Note: The cited editions read “fall.”]

[Note: The Spanish Collection and Isidore in Merlin read “be deprived of communion.”]

[Note: The collected editions except Basel read “during these two [years].”]

[Note: “Promoted”: Spanish Collection and collected editions.]

[Note: The Spanish Collection reads “within the prescribed time”; Isidore in Merlin reads “within an unlimited time.”]

Gratian. Likewise, if a cleric commits homicide by accident, he is permitted by dispensation to remain in his own rank.

Therefore Urban II writes to Guernerius, bishop of Narbonne:

[Note: It seems that, with Baluze, one should read: “Guarnerius, bishop of Merseburg” (died 1093), supported by the *Panormia* (book 3, chapter 154) and several manuscripts.]

### C. XXXVII. One who commits homicide by accident is to remain in his order by dispensation.

A boy is said to have been killed when a cleric threw a stone. Out of regard for you, we permit him to remain in his order, provided that he always remains in penance and fear.

[Col. 0276A]

### C. XXXVIII. On the same matter. Likewise Stephen V to Sichibert, bishop of Corsica.

[Note: Fragment of uncertain date; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 155.]

Because you judge yourself liable because, having been captured by Saracens, you appear to have killed people, you do well. But since it is recognized that you did not do it of your own will, you are in no way subject to canonical judgment for that reason.

[Note: Basel reads “a person,” rather than “persons.”]

Gratian. But if a priest, stirred by anger, kills someone, even if he has not had the intention of killing, he shall nevertheless be deposed permanently.

Therefore Pope Nicholas writes to Osbald, chorepiscopus of Quadrantinus:

[Note: “Chorepiscopus”: previously “co-bishop” was read, though not in the Argentinian edition. It has been corrected from all the collated old copies of Gratian, and it agrees extremely well with Nicholas’s words.]

[Note: Fragment of uncertain origin.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, chapter 24.]

### C. XXXIX. A priest who, stirred by anger, kills someone, even without intending it, is to be deprived of office permanently.

[Col. 0276B] Let your holiness endeavor to persuade your bishop to associate with himself the canonical number of fellow bishops—that is, six brothers and fellow bishops from neighboring provinces. Joined with you, they should carefully investigate and exert every effort to determine whether that deacon, as is reported, died from the blow of the aforesaid priest or from a broken neck. If indeed he was not struck to death by the frequently mentioned priest, but fell from his horse and died with a broken neck, then, at your discretion, impose an appropriate penance for the blow upon the priest who acted incautiously, and suspend him from the solemnities of the Mass for some time, after which he is to return to priestly office. But if the deacon truly died from any blow inflicted by that priest, we decree that he is in no circumstances to minister as a priest; for although he did not have the intention to kill, the rage and anger from which that fatal motion proceeded are forbidden in every person, but especially in ministers of God, in many ways and everywhere condemned. Yet if the priest has perhaps been so deserving of your concern, we command that such a benefice be granted to him in his own church that both he and his household may have sufficient means of support.

[Note: The collected editions read “associate.”]

[Note: The same editions read “joined.”]

[Note: Ivo reads “endeavor.”]

[Note: Basel reads “from the blow”; the remaining collected editions read “for the blow.”]

[Note: Basel adds “acting incautiously.”]

[Note: Böhm reads “and”; Venice II, Paris, Lyons, and Antwerp read “who.”]

[Note: The collected editions read “are forbidden—and condemned.”]

[Note: Ivo reads “harmful.”]

[Note: Böhm reads “to him and.”]

### C. XL. On the same matter. *Palea.* Likewise from the Council of Mâcon, chapter 6.

[Note: Burchard and Ivo cite this from the Council of Mainz; yet it occurs in none of the surviving acts of that council. Something similar is read in the Council of Worms, chapter 27. In the Council of Worms, held in 868, chapter 27 makes no ruling about Jews; but in Regino, book 2, chapter 95, where that chapter is presented as from Mainz, the killings of Jews as well as pagans are prohibited.]

[Note: Burchard, book 6, chapter 33; Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, chapter 162.]

> “But whoever, with deliberate hatred or from greed, kills a Jew or a pagan, because he destroys the image of God and the hope of future conversion, shall do penance for forty days on bread and water.”

[Note: Basel reads “conduct of life”; Ivo reads “had destroyed.”]

### C. XLI. On the same matter. *Palea.*

[Note: Compare the Roman Penitential, book 1, chapter 16; Anselm, book 11, chapter 34.]

> “If anyone commits homicide: if he is a bishop, let him do penance for fifteen years and be deposed; moreover, let him end all the days of his life in pilgrimage. Let a priest do penance for twelve years, three of them on bread and water, and be deposed by the judgment of his superior. Let a deacon do penance for ten years, three of them on bread and water. Let a cleric or layperson do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water, and let him not presume to approach any rank of priesthood.”

[Note: The Argentinian and Basel editions omit “moreover.”]

[Note: The Roman Penitential reads “four.”]

[Note: Basel reads “of a superior.”]

[Note: The words “Let a cleric … bread and water” were inserted by Böhm, contrary to the authority both of the source itself and of Gratian’s manuscripts.]

### C. XLII. Those who commit homicide by accident are to abstain from communion for five years. Likewise from the Council of Ancyra, chapter 22, § “But those.”

[Note: Held in 314.—Compare the Council of Tribur, chapter 52; Burchard, book 6, chapter 15; Anselm, book 11, chapters 45–46; Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, chapters 25 and 144; Polycarpus, book 6, title 10.]

But those who have committed homicide not intentionally but by accident: the earlier rule admitted them to communion after seven years’ penance, according to the established stages; but this more humane rule grants a period of five years.

[Note: The collected editions add “only.”]

[Note: Basel adds “of penance.”]

[Note: “But this”: in Greek, Ὁ δὲ δεύτερος τὸν πενταετῆ χρόνον πληρώσει, that is, “But the second [rule] shall complete the period of five years.” Burchard and Ivo likewise, from Dionysius’s version, and below in the same chapter, “If anyone intentionally.”]

[Note: The Spanish Collection and Isidore in Merlin read “more humane”; Isidore in Merlin and the collected editions add “decision.”]

### C. XLIII. For what periods of time she who intentionally or accidentally kills her maidservant must abstain from communion. Likewise from the Council of Elvira, chapter 4.

[Note: Held no later than 310.—Compare the Council of Worms, held in 868, chapter 39; Rabanus, *On Penance*, chapter 14; Burchard, book 6, chapter 19; Anselm, book 11, chapter 36; Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, chapters 22 and 148.]

If any woman, inflamed by jealous rage, beats her maidservant with whips so that within the third day she expires in agony, then—because it is uncertain whether she killed intentionally or accidentally—it was decided that she is to be admitted to communion after seven years if intentionally, but after five years if accidentally, once lawful penance has been performed. If she becomes ill within the prescribed periods, let her receive communion.

[Note: Ivo reads “mistress.”]

[Note: The original and Anselm read “scourges.”]

[Note: The collected editions, except Basel, Lyons II–III, and Antwerp, read “within.”]

[Note: The collected editions read “gives up.”]

[Note: Spanish Collection reads “a five-year period.”]

[Note: Basel reads “periods.”]

[Note: Spanish Collection and the collected editions except the first Basel, Lyons II–III, and Antwerp read “within.”]

### C. XLIV. On those who commit homicide intentionally or accidentally. Likewise from the chapters of Martin, bishop of Braga, chapter 78.

[Note: Chapter 22 of the Council of Ancyra, in Martin of Braga’s translation.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, chapter 39.]

If anyone commits homicide intentionally, let him always lie at the door of the Catholic church, and receive communion at the end of his life. But if he commits homicide not intentionally but by accident, the first canon ordered him to do penance for seven years; the second commanded five.

[Note: The Spanish Collection and the collected editions except Basel read “intentionally.”]

[Note: The collected editions read “lie.”]

[Note: The same editions read “intentionally.”]

[Note: Spanish Collection reads “to be done.”]

### C. XLV. On the same matter. Likewise, *Digest*, title *On Thefts*, law *He Who [Steals] a Bag*, fragment 77, title 2, book 4.

One who steals a bag containing money is liable in an action of theft also on account of the bag, even though he had no intention of stealing the bag.

[Note: The original reads “steals”; the collected editions read “stole.”]

[Note: “In an action of theft” is absent from the original and from the collected editions except the Argentinian edition.—Chapter XLVI.]

From the example of the sacred writings of Diocletian and Maximian, book IX of the Code, title *On the Lex Cornelia concerning Assassins*, law 5, it is inferred that an intention, not an act, is punished:

[Note: Given in 290.—Chapter XLVII.]

### C. XLVI. On the same matter.

[Col. 0278B] We desire that a person who asserts that he committed homicide not intentionally but by an accidental event, when the occasion of death appears to have been supplied by a kick, should be released from every fear and suspicion which he incurs from the danger of the deed committed, in accordance with what has been set forth in our annotation, if this is so and cannot be doubted.

### C. XLVII. *Palea.* Likewise Emperor Antoninus, *Code*, title *On the Lex Cornelia concerning Assassins*, law 1.

[Note: Given in 216.—This *Palea* is absent from the Argentinian, Basel, Venice I–II, and Nuremberg editions.—Paris edition: “Likewise Antoninus in the council.”]

> “Your brother would do better if he presented himself to the governor of the province. If he proves that he struck the man without an intention to kill, the penalty for homicide having been remitted, the governor will pronounce judgment according to military discipline. For a crime is incurred when an intention to harm is also present. But occurrences arising from an unforeseen accident rather than from malice are generally imputed to fate, not to wrongdoing.”

[Note: Lyons II–III and Antwerp read “that.”]

[Note: Paris, Lyons, and Antwerp read “to be pronounced”; Böhm reads “let him pronounce.”]

[Note: The same editions read “are to be imputed.”]

Hence also Pope Gelasius:

[Note: The Argentinian, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice I–II editions read “Pelagius”; nevertheless, the very style of composition shows that this chapter belongs to neither.]

### C. XLVIII. On the same matter.

As this Placidus states, last year it was said concerning that man’s wife that she was found suddenly among horses; and while the horses were being driven, she was struck, and miscarried. If this is so, perhaps, if he took another’s horses, he is culpable on that account. For concerning the woman who was accidentally crushed among the horses, when no harmful intention on his part is known, he cannot and ought not to be held liable under the laws.

[Note: The words “and, like swine, have lain in wallows of mud” are absent from the old Cologne and Paris editions of the councils, from two Vatican manuscripts, from the royal Lucchese manuscript, and from the Spanish Collection, and also from below, Causa 15, question 8, chapter “Those Who.” They are nevertheless found in Ivo and in the fourth Cologne edition.]

[Note: The collected editions except Basel add “stolen.”]

[Note: Basel reads “is recognized.”]

### C. XLIX. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Nicholas.

[Note: A fragment equally uncertain. Collection in three parts, part 1, title 62, chapter 21.]

Those who appear to be cutting down trees, if it happens that a falling tree kills a person, are without blame and innocent, because the homicide was committed neither by their will nor by their desire. But if it is found that the death of the person arose through some fault or negligence on their part, they are to be removed from rank and are in no way to be admitted to sacred order.

[Note: Basel reads “a tree.”]

### C. L. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Worms, chapter 29.

[Note: Held in 868.—Regino, book 2, chapter 17; Burchard, book 6, chapter 21; Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, chapter 150.—Compare Saxon Law, chapter 11, and Lombard Law, book 1, title 9, chapter 5.]

[Col. 0279B] It often happens, when someone is engaged in necessary work and cuts down a tree, that another person coming beneath it is crushed. Therefore, if this happened through the intention or negligence of the tree-cutter, he must altogether submit to penance as a homicide offender. But if it occurred neither by his wish, nor negligence, nor indeed knowledge—if, while he was perhaps attending to necessary work, the other unexpectedly came beneath the tree unawares and was crushed beneath it—the tree-cutter is not liable as a homicide offender.

[Note: The collected editions read: “but through his carelessness [adding Basel: ‘who’] he died, this does not occur with this judgment”; Argentinian, Venice I–II, and Nuremberg read “occurred.” They further read: “For if while … he comes under the tree, and beneath it,” etc.]

### C. LI. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Tribur, chapter 36.

[Note: Held in 895.—Regino, book 2, chapter 19; Burchard, book 6, chapter 22; Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, chapter 151. But there it is fuller.]

If two brothers are felling trees in a forest, and, as one tree is about to fall, one brother says to the other, “Take care!” and the other, while fleeing, runs into+ the crushing fall of the tree and dies, the surviving brother is to be judged innocent of his brother’s blood.

[Note: Regino reads “by chance”; Regino and Ivo read “one”; the Basel edition also reads “one”; the collected editions read “fell.”]

Gratian. From the foregoing authorities, the fallen are permitted, after penance, to be restored in their own orders; but no authority permits them to rise to a higher rank after their fall—indeed, this is altogether prohibited.

Therefore in the Council of Lleida, chapter 5, it is read:

[Note: Held in 546.—Rabanus, *On Penance*, chapter 1; Burchard, book 19, chapter 74; Ivo, *Decree*, part 15, chapter 87.—Below, Causa 15, question 8, chapter 2.]

### C. LII. The fallen may be restored in their own orders, but may not rise to higher ones.

Those who serve at the altar of God, if they suddenly fall into a lamentable weakness of the flesh, and, under the Lord’s regard, duly repent so that, having mortified the body, they offer God the sacrifice of a contrite heart, it remains in the bishop’s power either not to suspend for long those truly afflicted or to separate the idle for a longer time from the body of the Church. Yet they are to recover the places of their offices in such a way that they cannot afterwards be promoted to higher offices.

[Note: Nuremberg and Venice I read “If any.”]

[Note: The collected editions add “holy.”]

[Note: Basel, Nuremberg, Paris, and the Spanish Collection omit “into.”]

### *Palea.*

§ 1. “But if they return repeatedly like dogs to their vomit and lie like swine in wallows of mud, let them not only be deprived of the dignity of office, but also receive holy communion only at the point of death.”

[Note: From “But if repeatedly” to the end, this passage is absent from those manuscripts of Gratian in which *Paleae* are usually absent. In another manuscript the name *Palea* is placed here before it.]

[Note: Paris, Lyons, and Antwerp read “overturned”; the remaining editions and Ivo read “immersed.”]

Gratian. But by the example of blessed Peter—who, after washing away by a confession of love the stains of his threefold denial, not only remained in the rank of his apostleship but also deserved to be appointed by Christ shepherd of the whole Church—it is proved that, after worthy penance, the fallen may not only retain their own offices but may also ascend to higher ones. That blessed Peter was appointed shepherd of the Church by the Lord after his denial is proved by the authority of blessed Gregory, who writes concerning the same prince of the apostles in his homily on the Lord’s resurrection:

[Note: Homily 21 on the Gospel, Mark chapter 16.]

### C. LIII. Peter, after the fault of denial, was appointed prince of the Apostles by the Lord.

We must consider why almighty God permitted the man whom he intended to set over the whole Church to fear a maidservant’s voice and deny himself. We recognize, surely, that this was done by a dispensation of great mercy, so that he who was to be shepherd of the Church might learn from his own fault how he ought to have mercy on others. Thus God first showed him to himself and then set him over others, so that from his own weakness he might know how mercifully to bear the weakness of others.

[Note: Basel reads “another’s weakness”; the remaining collected editions read “others’ weaknesses.”]

### C. LIV. After the denial, Peter advanced in faith and rank. Likewise Ambrose, in Sermon XLVII on Peter’s faith.

[Note: This sermon is elsewhere attributed to Maximus of Turin, *Library of the Fathers*, volume 6. It is also ascribed to Augustine, in the appendix to the Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 1, chapter 71.]

Peter became more faithful after he had wept that he had lost his faith; and therefore he found a greater grace than he had lost. For as a good shepherd he received the flock to guard, so that he who had previously been weak in himself might become a support to all, and he who had wavered under the trial of questioning might establish others by the steadfastness of faith. Finally, because of the firmness of his devotion he is called the rock of the churches, as the Lord says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” He is called a rock because he was the first among the nations to lay the foundations of faith and, like an immovable stone, sustains the structure and mass of the whole body of Christianity.

[Note: Matthew, chapter 16, verse 18.]

[Note: The original and Anselm read “of the Christian work”; Basel, Paris VI read “Christian.”]

## Part VI

Gratian. It is likewise objected that penitents ought not to be promoted to sacred orders; therefore the fallen cannot attain higher rank after penance.

Therefore in the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapters 68 and 69, it is read:

[Note: *Statutes of the Ancient Church*, chapters 84–85; compare distinction 18, chapter 9. Burchard, book 2, chapter 35; Anselm, book 7, chapter 20; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 160; *Decree*, part 6, chapter 136 and part 15, chapter 23; Polycarpus, book 2, title 31.]

### C. LV. A cleric is not to be ordained from among penitents.

No cleric is to be ordained from among penitents, even if he is a good man. If this occurs through the bishop’s ignorance, he is to be removed from the clergy, because at the time of ordination he did not disclose that he had been a penitent. But if the bishop knowingly ordains such a person, he himself is to be deprived, so far as ordination is concerned, of the power of his episcopal office. The bishop will be subject to a similar judgment if he knowingly ordains as a cleric a man who has had a widow, a divorced woman, or a second wife.

[Note: The collected editions add “nevertheless.”]

[Note: In the original the reading is: “He himself is to be deprived only of the power of ordaining belonging to his episcopal office.” Another reading: “he himself [is to be deprived] of his episcopal office,” as also in Ivo, part 15, chapter 5.]

### C. LVI. A bigamist, a penitent, or the husband of a widow who enters sacred service is to remain permanently in his order without hope of promotion. Likewise Pope Siricius to Bishop Himerius, Letter I, chapter 15.

[Note: Written in 385.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 21.]
