Whoever, being a penitent, a bigamist, or the husband of a widow, improperly and incompetently intrudes into sacred service, is to understand that we have granted him pardon on this condition: he must consider it a great favor if, every hope of promotion having been taken away from him, he remains with permanent stability in the order in which he is found.

[Note: The Spanish Collection reads “this”; the original in Coustant reads “advancement.”]

### C. LVII. One who, oppressed by illness, received the blessing of penance through communion is not to be barred from the clergy. Likewise from the Council of Gerona, chapter 9.

[Note: Held in 517.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 32, chapter 4.]

But if a person, overwhelmed by the weakness of sickness, receives through communion the blessing of penance—which we designate as viaticum—and afterwards recovers, yet has not publicly submitted himself in the Church to the formal state of penance, he is to be admitted to the clergy, provided that he is not held guilty of prohibited vices.

[Note: The Spanish Collection and collected editions read “But if he.”]

[Note: The collected editions read “we call [it].”]

[Note: The same editions read “if [his] head.”]

### C. LVIII. One confined in a monastery to perform penance is not to be ordained priest. Likewise Pope Hormisdas to all bishops established throughout the provinces.

[Note: This does not belong to Hormisdas; compare above, chapter 39 of the same [Causa].—Anselm, book 7, chapter 22 and book 11, chapter 87; Polycarpus, book 2, title 31.]

If a person who voluntarily seeks penance, even though he performs it perfectly, cannot be ordained bishop or priest, such that even if he is ordained through ignorance and is afterwards convicted of having received penance, he is to be deposed, then with what conscience is one who is sent unwillingly into a monastery to perform penance—who is surely to be called nothing other than a penitent—permitted to come to the priesthood? Let no one raise against me any constitutions whatsoever contrary to the authority of the Apostolic See, or of the 318 bishops, or of the other canons. For I do not doubt that it is not only rash but dangerous to accept whatever may be said contrary to their determination, in which we believe that the Holy Spirit has spoken.

[Note: Anselm and the collected editions read “in a monastery.”]

[Note: The collected editions read “attain.”]

[Note: The same editions read “and.”]

### C. LIX. A bigamist, or anyone after penance, is not to be assigned to sacred ministries. Likewise Gelasius, bishop of the city of Rome, to all bishops throughout Lucania, etc., chapter 5.

[Note: Written in 494.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 18.]

No bishop should presume to assign to divine ministries bigamists, persons who marry women abandoned by others, any persons after penance, persons without letters, those physically impaired, persons of servile condition, persons bound by obligations to the municipal council or public service, or persons indiscriminately examined without waiting for a suitable period of time.

[Note: Anselm and the collected editions add “that it is lawful.”]

[Note: The same editions read “abandoned.”]

### C. LX. Penitents cannot even become clerics. Likewise Innocent to Agapitus and the others, Letter VI.

[Note: A letter of uncertain date.]

The canons established at Nicaea exclude penitents even from the lowest clerical offices.

[Note: Compare the Council of Nicaea, chapter 9.]

Gratian. This is not to be understood of penitents of every kind, but only of those who, after completing penance, take up the belt of secular military service. Concerning them Bishop Innocent writes to Bishop Victricius of Rouen, Letter II, chapter 2:

[Note: Written in 404.—Collection in three parts, part 1, title 38, chapter 19; Anselm, book 7, chapter 13.]

### C. LXI. One who has held the belt of military service after remission of sins ought not to become a cleric.

If anyone has held the belt of secular military service after remission of sins, he must by no means be admitted to the clergy.

Gratian. It may also be understood otherwise. There is a kind of penance called solemn penance, which is granted only once in the Church. Of it Ambrose says: “As baptism is one, so penance is single.” Likewise: “There is no second place of penance.” Those who think that penance must be performed repeatedly are rightly reproved, because they indulge themselves in Christ. For if they truly performed penance, they would not think it must later be repeated.

[Note: Book 2, *On Penance*, chapter 10; compare distinction 3, *On Penance*, chapters 2 and 49.]

[Note: “Are reproved”: the reading was “are found.” It has here been corrected from the original; this could not be done below, at chapter “Are Found,” distinction 3, *On Penance*, because there the word “are found” begins the chapter.]

### C. LXII. On the same matter. Likewise Augustine to Macedonius, Letter LIV.

[Note: Written in 414.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 15, chapter 24; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 14, chapter 3.—Below, distinction 3, *On Penance*, chapter 22.]

Although it has been prudently and salutarily provided that the place of that most humble repentance be granted only once in the Church, lest a remedy exceedingly useful be held cheap, nevertheless forgiveness is never denied through repentance to those who sin daily.

[Note: “Lest the remedy”: In some very old copies of Gratian this chapter is joined to the preceding one. For he adapts Augustine’s passage in his own way. In Augustine it reads here as follows: “Lest a remedy be cheap and less useful to the sick—a remedy which is the more salutary the less contemptible it is considered. Yet who would dare to say to God, ‘Why do you still spare this man, who after his first repentance again binds himself in the snares of wickedness?’” etc.]  
[Note: “be held exceedingly cheap”: Basel edition: “be held too cheap.”]

Gratian. How this repentance is to be imposed is found in the Council of Agde, where the following was decreed in chapter 15:

[Note: held in A.D. 506.—Capitularies, book 5, ch. 58; book 7, ch. 310. Regino, book 1, ch. 290. Burchard, book 19, ch. 27. Ivo, Decree, part 15, ch. 17.]

### Chapter LXIII. How penitents enter upon penance

At the time when penitents seek penance, they shall receive from the priest the laying on of hands and sackcloth upon their heads, as has been established everywhere. But if they have not cut off their hair or changed their clothing, they shall be rejected; and unless they repent worthily, they shall not be received. Penance is not to be entrusted readily even to young people, because of the frailty of their age. Yet viaticum is not to be denied to any who are at the point of death.

[Note: “heads”: Regino and Ivo: “head.”—“established”: those editions read “decreed.”]  
[Note: Basel edition: “they receive.”]  
[Note: Basel edition: “indeed.”]

### Chapter LXIV. What must be observed in solemn penance. From the same source

[Note: “From the same source”: Burchard, Ivo, and Cardinal Rhebald—who flourished in the time of Pope Paschal—in his book *On Public Penance Not to Be Repeated*, also cite this as from Agde. In one manuscript copy of Burchard, however, it is cited from the Roman Penitential. Most of the substance of this chapter occurs in the Pontifical and the Roman Order, pp. 24–30.]  
[Note: It has been found among Theodore’s Capitula, ch. 40, whence it passed into Regino’s collection, book 1, title 291, under the heading “From above.” Consequently Burchard, book 19, ch. 26, and after him Ivo, Decree, part 15, ch. 45, understanding the matter less correctly, cited the Council of Agde as the source of the chapter.]

At the beginning of Lent all penitents who undertake or have undertaken public penance shall present themselves before the doors of the church to the bishop of the city, clothed in sackcloth, barefoot, with their faces cast down to the ground, declaring themselves guilty by their very dress and expression. There the deans—that is, the archpriests of the parishes—and the priests of the penitents must be present. They must carefully examine the penitents’ conduct and impose penance according to the measure of the offense, through the aforesaid grades.

After this, they shall bring them into the church; and, with all the clergy, the bishop, prostrate on the ground, shall chant with tears the seven penitential psalms for their absolution. Then, rising from prayer, he shall, as the canons command, lay hands upon them, sprinkle holy water over them, first put ashes upon them, then cover their heads with sackcloth, and, with groaning and repeated sighs, declare to them that, just as Adam was cast out of Paradise, so they too are cast out of the Church because of their sins. After this he shall order the ministers to drive them out through the doors of the church, while the clergy follow them with the responsory: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread,” etc. [Genesis 3:19], so that, seeing holy Church shaken and disturbed on account of their crimes, they may not make light of penance. But at the sacred Supper of the Lord they shall again be presented at the threshold of the church by their deans and priests.

[Note: “barefoot”: absent from Theodore.]  
[Note: “with their faces cast down”: Theodore, Regino, Burchard, and Ivo: “prostrate.”]  
[Note: Theodore: “The archpriests of the parishes—that is, the priests of the penitents—must be present.”]  
[Note: Regino adds: “with witnesses, that is.” In the collected editions, except Basel, the text reads: “deans, that is, archpriests, parish priests, and the priest [priests, Antwerp edition] of the penitents.”]  
[Note: “and the priests”: Burchard reads: “that is, the priests.”]  
[Note: The collected editions except Basel add: “their penance and.”]  
[Note: “aforesaid”: Theodore and the cited collections: “prescribed.”]  
[Note: “bring them”: Theodore, the cited collections, and Basel: “bring him.”]  
[Note: “penitential psalms”: cited collections and Basel: “psalms of penance.”]  
[Note: “on the ground”: Theodore, cited collections, and Basel: “to the ground.”]  
[Note: Regino: “rising.”]  
[Note: Theodore, cited collections, and Basel: “and they too.”]  
[Note: Regino: “are cast down.”]  
[Note: Theodore and Basel: “through the door.”]  
[Note: Regino: “because of”; Lugdunum II and III: “before.”]  
[Note: Theodore omits “by their deans and”; Regino reads: “they shall again present themselves at the threshold of the church.”]

Gratian. No cleric is ever permitted to undergo this penance; therefore penitents of this sort are forbidden admission to the clergy.

Accordingly it was decreed in the Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 11:

[Note: held in A.D. 401.—Regino, book 1, ch. 310. Collection in three parts, part 2, title 19, ch. 11. Burchard, book 19, ch. 72. Ivo, Decree, part 15, ch. 85.—Capitularies, book 5, ch. 66.]

### Chapter LXV. Hands are not to be laid upon clerics as upon penitents

It has been confirmed that, if priests or deacons are at any time convicted of some more serious fault for which it is necessary that they be removed from ministry, hands are not to be laid upon them either as penitents or as lay believers; nor is it ever to be permitted that rebaptized persons be promoted to a clerical grade.

[Note: The original reads “confirmed.”]

Accordingly Pope Siricius, in Letter I to Himerius, chapter 14:

[Note: written A.D. 385.—Collection in three parts, part 1, title 36, ch. 9. Burchard, book 19, ch. 49. Anselm, book 7, ch. 20. Ivo, Decree, part 6, ch. 54; part 15, ch. 65.]

### Chapter LXVI. Neither may a cleric perform penance, nor may a penitent enter the clergy

It was also fitting for us to provide that, just as no cleric is permitted to perform penance, so after penance and reconciliation no layman whatever may be allowed to attain clerical rank. For although they have been cleansed from the contagion of all sins, nevertheless those who were formerly vessels of vices ought not to receive the instruments for administering the sacraments.

[Note: The collected editions read “no one whatever.”]  
[Note: The same editions read “to anyone no.”]  
[Note: The same editions and the first Basel edition: “receive.”]  
[Note: Basel: “had been.”]

### Chapter LXVII. Hands ought not to be laid upon priests and deacons as upon penitents. Likewise Pope Leo, Letter XC to Rusticus of Narbonne, chapter 2

[Note: Letter 167, written A.D. 458 or 459, Ballerini edition.—Anselm, book 11, ch. 28. Burchard, book 19, ch. 71. Ivo, Decree, part 6, ch. 67. Polycarpus, title 4, ch. 39.]

It is foreign to ecclesiastical custom that those consecrated in priestly honor or in the rank of the diaconate should receive, for some crime of their own, the remedy of repentance through the laying on of hands. This undoubtedly descends from apostolic tradition, according to what is written: “If a priest sins, who shall pray for him?” Hence persons fallen in this way must seek a private withdrawal in order to obtain God’s mercy, where their satisfaction, if worthy, may also be fruitful.

[Note: “Priest”: this passage is often customarily indicated in the margin as from 1 Samuel 2, as below, *On Penance*, distinction 1, chapter “If a priest.” Yet in that scriptural place the Vulgate reads: “But if he sins against God, who shall pray for him?” Gregory the Great likewise derives this sense in his moral interpretation of that place: “What intercessor remains for him when he, who was ordained to intercede for others, casts himself down by transgression?”]  
[Note: “withdrawal”: this has been corrected from ancient codices and from the letter itself; the author of the gloss also had this reading, as manuscript glosses show, and it should therefore be corrected there as well. Previously the reading was “succession is nevertheless to be sought.”]

Gratian. Such penitents are also proved by the authority of the First Council of Toledo not to be admitted to the clergy. In chapter 2 it was decreed as follows:

[Note: held in A.D. 400.—Burchard, book 2, ch. 37. Anselm, book 7, ch. 31. Ivo, Panormia 1.3.61; Decree, part 6, ch. 138. Polycarpus, book 2, title 31.—Compare the Capitula of Martin of Braga, ch. 23.]

### Chapter LXVIII. In a case of necessity penitents may be admitted to the clergy

It was resolved that penitents are not to be admitted to the clergy, except only where necessity or usefulness demands it; and then they shall be assigned among the doorkeepers or readers, so that they do not read the Gospels or the Epistle. But if any were ordained deacons before this, they shall be counted among the subdeacons, so that they do not lay on hands or touch the sacred things. By “penitent” we mean one who, after baptism, because of homicide or various crimes and most grievous sins, has performed public penance under sackcloth and has been reconciled to the divine altar.

[Note: Basel adds “solemnly”; the Hispana Collection reads “concerning a penitent.”]  
[Note: “they are assigned”: Hispana Collection.]  
[Note: The original and cited collections read “the Apostle” instead of “the Epistle.”]  
[Note: Hispana Collection: “subdeacons”; collected editions: “into deacons.”]  
[Note: Hispana Collection: “the penitent.”]  
[Note: Anselm reads “council” for “sackcloth.”]

## Part VII

Gratian. Apostates also ought not to be admitted to a clerical office.

Accordingly, in the Second Council of Arles, chapter 25:

[Note: held no later than A.D. 460.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 24, ch. 8. Burchard, book 19, ch. 67. Ivo, Decree, part 15, ch. 81.]

### Chapter LXIX. Apostates are not to be admitted to a clerical office

Those who, after the holy profession of religion, apostatize and return to secular life, and afterward do not seek the remedies of penance, are not to receive communion at all without penance. We also command that they not be admitted to a clerical office. And whoever he may be, after penance he must not presume to assume secular dress. If he does presume it, let him be regarded as cut off from the Church.

[Note: The original, Ivo, and Basel read: “return to the world.”]  
[Note: The collected editions except Basel read “of penitents.”]  
[Note: Basel: “who.”]

## Distinction LI

### Gratian

## Part I

Here we see that persons guilty of crimes, persons not truly penitent, and persons undergoing public penance are forbidden sacred orders. Holy Mother Church has added that municipal officeholders, persons serving in the army after baptism, and persons litigating in court are to be forbidden sacred orders.

Accordingly Pope Innocent says to the bishops assembled in the Synod of Toledo, Letter XXIV, chapter 2:

[Note: The Hispana Collection and Isidore Mercator read “Toulousain.”]  
[Note: written about A.D. 404. Chapter I.]

### Chapter I. Those serving in the army after baptism, or litigating in court, are forbidden sacred orders

We have discovered that certain persons who, after receiving the grace of baptism, were engaged in forensic practice and undertook the obstinacy of litigation, have been summoned to the priesthood; Rufinus and Gregory are said to belong to their number. We have found certain persons from military service who, while obeying authorities, necessarily carried out cruel commands; certain municipal officeholders who, while obeying authorities, did what was commanded them; and certain persons who celebrated entertainments and public shows for the people, to have attained the honor of the high priesthood. None of all these ought even to have attained membership in the clerical order.

If we ordered each case to be examined separately, we would introduce no small disturbances or scandals into the Spanish provinces, whose restoration we desire. Therefore we think these matters should rather be remitted. But lest similar acts be committed hereafter, the prudence of your charity must provide that an indispensable end at least now be imposed upon so great an usurpation, by this provision: whoever shall be ordained in such circumstances shall be deposed together with his ordainers.

[Note: The original has “how many?” and thereafter similarly, as an exclamation.]  
[Note: Basel: “some persons from their number are forbidden to be received into ministry.”]  
[Note: Hispana Collection and Isidore Mercator: “severe” for “cruel”; the word is lacking in Constantius.]  
[Note: Collected editions: “obeyed.”]  
[Note: “games and mimes”; Constantius and the Hispana Collection read “offices”; Basel, “lesser persons.”]  
[Note: The collected editions read “attain.”]  
[Note: Collected editions: “if we ordered.”]  
[Note: Collected editions, first Basel, Lugdunum II and III, and Antwerp: “reforms.”]  
[Note: Lugdunum I: “we would proclaim”; other collected editions: “we would introduce”; Hispana Collection: “we introduce”; Isidore Mercator: “let us proclaim.”]  
[Note: The following words slipped from the margin into the text of Isidore Mercator.]

### Chapter II. From which laypersons some cannot attain the clergy. The same pope, to Felix, bishop of Nocera, Letter IV, chapter 3

[Note: A letter of uncertain date.—Anselm, book 7, ch. 10. Ivo, Decree, part 6, ch. 95. Polycarpus, book 2, title 31.—The collected editions read “to the bishop of Miceria.”]

The classes of laypersons from whom some cannot attain the clergy have been specified: that is, if a believer has served as a soldier; if a believer has pleaded causes—that is, acted as an advocate; if a believer has administered public affairs. The reason concerning municipal officeholders is evident: even if men of this kind are found who ought to become clerics, nevertheless, because they are often reclaimed by the municipal council, they must be avoided because of the distress that often comes to the Church from them.

[Note: The collected editions read “some may come.”]  
[Note: The words “if a believer has served as a soldier … if a believer has pleaded causes … if a believer has administered” are absent from the Hispana Collection.]  
[Note: Hispana Collection, Isidore Mercator, Anselm, Ivo, and the Argentinensis and Basel editions read “to the council” rather than “from the council.”]

### Chapter III. Municipal officeholders are not to be admitted to clerical office. The same pope, to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, Letter II, chapter 11

[Note: written A.D. 404.—Ivo, Decree, part 6, ch. 349.]

Furthermore, certain of our brothers frequently endeavor to make clerics of municipal officeholders or persons occupied with any public functions. Yet afterward there arises greater grief than favor from their admission, when the emperor orders something concerning their recall. For it is certain that in those offices they also provide entertainments, which there is no doubt were invented by the devil, and either preside over or perhaps take part in the displays of games and mimes. Let the concern and sorrow of the brethren, which we often endured when the emperor was present, be an example; as you yourself learned when you were with us, when we repeatedly petitioned on behalf of such persons, against whom there pressed a grave demand that they be returned—not only lower clerics drawn from municipal officeholders, but even men established in the priesthood.

[Note: The collected editions read “for whom.”]  
[Note: The same editions add “there is.”]  
[Note: The same editions read “then, when already,” while the Argentinensis and Norimbergensis editions omit “then.”]  
[Note: The words “from their admission” are absent from the Hispana Collection.]  
[Note: Constantius and the Hispana Collection read “offices”; Basel, “of lesser persons.”]

### Chapter IV. One who after baptism armed himself to kill a believer is not to be promoted to the diaconate. Likewise from the First Council of Toledo, chapter 8

[Note: held in A.D. 400.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 35, ch. 4.]

If anyone has served as a soldier after baptism and has assumed the military cloak or belt for killing believers, even if he has committed no grave offense, if he is admitted to the clergy, he shall not receive the dignity of the diaconate.

[Note: The collected editions add “received.”]  
[Note: The same editions read “or.”]  
[Note: The same editions read “to kill.”]  
[Note: “for killing believers”: these words are absent from the royal Lucchese codex and the Hispana Collection, though they occur in Merlin.]

### Chapter V. From what a person to be ordained bishop must be free. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 19

[Note: The Argentinensis and Basel editions read “is to be ordained.”]  
[Note: held in A.D. 633.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 37, ch. 3.]

Those who have been detected in any crime; those stained by the mark of infamy; those who have confessed through public penance that they committed certain crimes; those who have fallen into heresy, or are known to have been baptized or rebaptized in heresy; those who have mutilated themselves, or are known through a natural defect of limbs or through cutting to lack something; those who have entered a union with a second wife or contracted many marriages; those who have married a widow or a woman deserted by her husband, or have been husbands of defiled women; those who have had concubines or prostitutes; those subject to servile status; those unknown; neophytes or laymen; those devoted to secular military service; those bound by the obligations of the municipal council; those ignorant of letters; those who have not yet reached thirty years; those who have not advanced through the ecclesiastical grades; those who seek office through canvassing; those who strive to obtain office by gifts; and those chosen to the priesthood by their predecessors—none of these shall be ordained.

Moreover, hereafter no one shall be a priest whom neither the clergy nor the people of his own city elected, or for whom the authority of the metropolitan or the consent of the bishops of the province was not sought. Therefore, whenever anyone hereafter is proposed for the priestly order, examined regarding the matters stated above and found guilty of none of them, and has been found, upon examination, to have an approved life and teaching, then, according to synodal or decretal enactments, he shall be consecrated priest on Sunday, with the will of all the clergy or citizens, by all the bishops of the province, or at least by three, the others who are absent concurring by letter, and especially with the authority or presence of him established in the metropolis. A bishop of the province is to be consecrated where the metropolitan chooses; but a metropolitan only in the metropolitan city, with the bishops of the province assembled there. If anyone hereafter, contrary to the aforesaid canonical prohibitions, strives unworthily to attain the rank of priesthood, he and his ordainers shall be liable to the loss of the honor attained.

[Note: The collected editions read “detained.”]  
[Note: “or through cutting”: these words have been added from the old Cologne and Paris editions. In the newest Cologne edition, however, “or through deficiency” is read in place of “or through cutting.”]  
[Note: “something”: absent from the collected editions except the Argentinensis and Basel editions.]  
[Note: “or prostitutes”: the royal Lucchese codex and the Hispana Collection read “for fornications,” apparently to be understood of concubines kept temporarily, as is noted above, distinction 34, chapter “He who.”]  
[Note: Hispana Collection: “approached” for “advanced.”]  
[Note: Basel: “predecessors.”]  
[Note: Hispana Collection: “is proposed.”]  
[Note: Hispana Collection: “approved.”]  
[Note: Hispana Collection and Böhm: “consenting.”]  
[Note: The collected editions except Basel read “by the bishops of the province”; Basel adds “truly.”]

## Distinction LII

### Gratian

But one who has passed over certain grades and has ascended to a higher one not from pride but negligence must abstain from the higher offices until, at a suitable time, he receives the grades he omitted.

Accordingly Alexander II writes to Grimald, bishop of Constance:

[Note: In a very ancient book there is a letter of the same Alexander to Gervasius, archbishop of Rheims, in which he gives the same counsel that he says he had given to Rumald, bishop of Constance.]  
[Note: Letter to Rumold, bishop of Constance, written A.D. 1065.—Ivo, Decree, part 6, ch. 409.]

### Chapter I. Concerning one ordained deacon and priest after passing over the order of subdeacon

Your charity’s concern has sought advice whether the bearer of this letter is fit or unfit to perform the office of deacon and priest, since he is known to have ascended to it by an improper course, passing over the order of subdeacon through negligence rather than pride. Therefore, in advising your charity, we direct you to prohibit him from priestly office until, at the next Ember fast, you duly impose upon him the ministry of the subdiaconate; then you may permit him thereafter to return to the higher offices.

[Note: Ivo and Basel: “too hasty” for “improper.”]

## Distinction LIII

### Gratian

As written above, municipal officeholders are prohibited from ordination because, when they are frequently reclaimed from the Church, the Church suffers many inconveniences; or because these same officeholders transfer themselves to the Church not by a vow of religion, but in order to escape the rendering of accounts for their offices.

Accordingly Pope Gregory writes in Book VII of the Register, Indiction I, Letter 11, to all the bishops of Sicily concerning the law of the Emperor Maurice:

[Note: Letter 5, written A.D. 598, book 8 of the Maurist edition.—Ivo, Decree, part 10, ch. 124.]

### Chapter I. Why it has been established that municipal officeholders are not to be ordained

I have taken care to send to your brotherhood the law issued by the most pious emperor, lest perhaps those bound to military service or public accounts should, while fleeing the danger of their legal affairs, assume ecclesiastical dress or enter monasteries. Above all, I exhort you for this reason: those entangled in secular business are not to be received hastily into the clergy of the Church, because, when they live in ecclesiastical dress no differently from the way they lived before, they are in no way trying to flee the world, but to change it. If persons of this kind also seek a monastery, they are by no means to be received unless they have first been released from public accounts.

But if any military men hasten to convert in monasteries, they are not to be received rashly unless their life has been carefully investigated. According to the rule they must be tested in their own dress for three years, and then, with God as author, receive the monastic habit.

[Note: The collected editions read “for this reason above all”; Ivo: “this chiefly urges.”]  
[Note: The collected editions add “before.”]  
[Note: The same editions read “each one.”]  
[Note: The original reads “public accounts.”]  
[Note: “men”: in some old copies of Gratian and in Ivo, “numbers,” signifying soldiers enrolled on a short roll or register.]  
[Note: Basel: “enter”; other collected editions: “be enrolled.”]  
[Note: The collected editions read “having been tested … let them be received.”]

## Distinction LIV

### Gratian

## Part I

Servants are forbidden to be ordained unless they obtain lawful freedom from their own masters.

Accordingly Bishop Leo writes in Letter I to all bishops throughout Campania, etc.:

[Note: written A.D. 443.—Anselm, book 7, title 28. Polycarpus, book 2, title 31.]

### Chapter I. A slave is not to be promoted to a clerical office

No bishop shall presume to promote another’s slave to a clerical office unless perhaps the request or consent of those who claim some authority over him has been secured. For the person to be enrolled in divine warfare must be free from other persons, so that he may not be drawn away by any bonds of necessity from the camp of the Lord, in which his name is enrolled.

[Note: This chapter seems to have been made up from the heading prefixed in the code of canons to Leo I’s first decree and from the latter part of the decree itself, which contains the exception to what he had earlier established. The preceding part, omitted here, occurs below in this distinction, chapter “They are admitted.”]  
[Note: Burchard, book 2, ch. 22; Ivo, Decree, part 6, ch. 64.]  
[Note: Anselm: “drawn away by no bonds of necessities.”]

### Chapter II. No one of servile status shall attain sacred orders. Likewise from the Council of Tribur

[Note: The substance rather than the words of this chapter occurs in the Council of Tribur, ch. 29. The wording appears in part to agree with the passage in Capitularies, book 1, ch. 88, on the ordination of slaves, beginning “And whenever.”]  
[Note: held in A.D. 895. Regino, book 1, ch. 407. Burchard, book 2, ch. 21. Ivo, Panormia, book 3, ch. 48; Decree, part 6, ch. 41.]

No one of servile status shall be promoted to sacred orders unless he first obtains lawful freedom from his own masters. The charter of that freedom shall be publicly read from the ambo before ordination; and, if no one objects, they shall be duly consecrated. But a slave not canonically consecrated, once he has fallen from his rank, shall be of the condition in which he was before the rank.

[Note: Regino and Basel read the singular “shall be consecrated.”]

### Chapter III. PALEA. From the First Council of Carthage, chapter 8

[Note: Printed codices cite this from Mainz. It has been corrected from Burchard, Ivo, and the Decretals, in the sole chapter *On the Obligation to Render Accounts*.]  
[Note: held in A.D. 348 or 349.—Burchard, book 2, ch. 36. Ivo, Decree, part 6, ch. 137.—Compare Decretals, Compilation I, ch. 1, and *X*, book 1, title 19, ch. 1, *On the Obligation to Render Accounts*.]

“Magnus, bishop of Astia, said: ‘What seems right to your charity concerning procurators, agents, executors, and guardians of wards: should they be ordained?’ Gratus, bishop, said: ‘If, after they have relinquished everything and rendered their accounts, the conduct of their lives has been found approved in every respect, they ought, if proposed, to be honored with a place among the clergy, and with commendation. For if, before they are free from business or offices, they are ordained by anyone without consideration, the Church is dishonored.’ All said: ‘Your holiness has rightly established everything; therefore this is also our judgment.’”

[Note: Hispana Collection and Ivo: “Astuagensis”; Decretals at the cited place and Basel: “Augustensis”; other collected editions: “Augustodinensis”; Mansi: “Aptongensis.”]  
[Note: The collected editions read “of your charity.”]  
[Note: Hispana Collection adds “guardians also”; Argentinensis: “defenders.”]  
[Note: The words “or guardians” are absent in Ivo.]  
[Note: The collected editions read “ought.”]  
[Note: Basel: “be counted.”]  
[Note: The collected editions, first Basel, Lugdunum editions, and Antwerp read “and from.”]  
[Note: “The Church is dishonored”: corrected from the council, the Decretals, Burchard, and Ivo. Previously it read: “let them be weakened by the Church.”]  
[Note: Hispana Collection: “and therefore what is your judgment is ours also.”]

### Chapter IV. After the gift of freedom, servants of the Church are to be recalled into the clergy. Likewise from the Ninth Council of Toledo, chapter 11

[Note: held in A.D. 655.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 35, ch. 4. Ivo, Decree, part 6, ch. 373.]

Those drawn from the households of the Church by their bishops for service in the clergy must receive the gift of freedom; and if they have become distinguished by the merits of an honorable life, only then may they perform the higher offices. But those whom the incorrigible stain of wrongdoing has defiled shall be bound in the permanent chain of servile condition.

[Note: The collected editions read “servants.”]  
[Note: The same editions add “assisted.”]  
[Note: Basel: “chain.”]

Gratian. Those who are to be ordained and obtain freedom from their masters must be wholly free of their masters’ patronage, so that in nothing may they be found subject to their service.

Accordingly, in the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 73, we read:

[Note: held in A.D. 633. Regino, book 1, ch. 394. Burchard, book 2, ch. 25. Collection in three parts, part 2, title 37, ch. 3. Ivo, Panormia, book 3, ch. 46; Decree, part 6, ch. 126. Polycarpus, book 2, title 31.]

### Chapter V. Those are admitted to the clergy who receive freedom from their masters with no service retained

All who receive freedom from their masters in such a way that the patron retains no service from them may, if they are free from crime, be admitted freely to clerical rank, because they are known to have been released by direct manumission. But those manumitted with service retained are not to be promoted to ecclesiastical rank in any way, because they remain bound in servitude to their patron, lest, whenever their masters wish, slaves be made out of clerics.

[Note: Basel: “retains.”]  
[Note: Ivo adds “capital.”]  
[Note: Hispana Collection: “freely.”]  
[Note: Hispana Collection: “to a patron”; Basel: “to patrons.”]

### Chapter VI. PALEA. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 82

[Note: Burchard and Ivo likewise cite this as from Toledo. In the Panormia, however, beginning with “if any slave,” it is cited from Book I of the Capitularies, where this chapter is found entire, together with the following chapter, “On Property.”]  
[Note: Rather, from the Capitularies of the Kings of the Franks, book 1, ch. 82, whence Regino, book 1, ch. 396, cites it correctly.—Burchard, book 2, ch. 31. Ivo, book 6, ch. 132.—Compare Decretals, Compilation I, ch. 2, and *X*, book 1, title 18, ch. 2, *On Slaves Not to Be Ordained*.]

“Concerning the ordination of slaves, who are everywhere indiscriminately promoted to ecclesiastical grades, all resolved that agreement with the sacred canons was necessary; and it was decreed that no bishop hereafter should presume to promote them to sacred orders unless they had first obtained freedom from their own masters.

“If any slave, fleeing his master, or by letters, or through witnesses hired or corrupted by payment, or by any stratagem or fraud, reaches ecclesiastical grades, it is decreed that he shall be deposed and his master shall receive him back.

“But if a grandfather or father migrating from one country to another has begotten a son in that province, and that son, having been brought up there, has been promoted to ecclesiastical grades, and it is unknown whether he is a slave, and afterward his master comes and legally claims him, it is decreed that, if his master wishes to give him freedom, he shall remain in his rank. But if he wishes to draw him away from the camp of the Lord by the chain of servitude, he shall lose his rank, because, according to the sacred canons, a person remaining in a servile condition cannot exercise the dignity of priesthood.”

[Note: The Capitularies and cited collections add “indiscriminately.”]  
[Note: The Capitularies read “were promoted.”]  
[Note: Ivo, Panormia, book 3, ch. 163.]  
[Note: The word is “his.”]  
[Note: The Capitularies and cited collections read “or in hiding” for “by letters.”]  
[Note: The collected editions add “is.”]  
[Note: The Capitularies read “does not know” for “is unknown.”]

### Chapter VII. Without the patron’s consent, one bound by anyone’s patronage is not to be ordained. Likewise from the Council of Pope Martin

[Note: Chapter 46 among the Capitula of Martin of Braga, from the Council of Toledo I, held in A.D. 400, chapter 10.]

If anyone is bound by a servile tax, by some condition, or by the patronage of any household, he is not to be ordained cleric unless he has an approved life and the patron’s consent has been obtained.

[Note: Basel: “master.”]  
[Note: Hispana Collection: “permission.”]

### Chapter VIII. PALEA. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 2

[Note: This Palea occurs in the Capitularies joined to the preceding Palea, “On the Ordination of Slaves”; but in Burchard and Ivo they are separately reported as from the same Council of Toledo.]  
[Note: Regino, book 1, ch. 397. Burchard, book 2, ch. 23. Ivo, Decree, part 6, ch. 38.]

“But concerning the property or peculium of those who are granted freedom by their own masters in order that they may lawfully be promoted to ecclesiastical grades, it is decreed that it shall remain in the masters’ power whether they wish to grant them what they possessed before their freedom or retain it for themselves.”

[Note: Basel reads “freedom” in the dative.]  
[Note: The collected editions, following Ivo, read “ought to be promoted.”]

Gratian. If, however, they have not obtained freedom from their masters and have somehow slipped into ecclesiastical orders, a priest shall be punished by the loss of his peculium; a deacon shall either furnish a substitute for himself or be recalled into slavery. The remaining grades, however, cannot free anyone from the bond of slavery.

Accordingly Gelasius writes to Martin and Justus, bishops:

[Note: There is no reason to doubt the authenticity of this letter. Martyrius—for this is how it should be read with Anselm, book 7, ch. 29—was bishop of Tarracina; and Justus is recorded as having presided over the Church of Acerenza in Lucania. Its date is uncertain, but it seems to have been written shortly after the letter to the bishops of Lucania, etc. (A.D. 494), whose opening calls it a “new synodal explanation.”]

### Chapter IX. If a slave has secretly slipped into the priesthood, he shall be punished by the loss of his peculium
From the ancient rules and from the recent synodal exposition, it has been established that persons bound to servitude are not to be girded with the belt of the heavenly soldiery. But I do not know whether you are carried away by ignorance or by willfulness, so that scarcely any bishop seems free from blame on this account [Note: [Col. 0293] *fault*: Anselm.]. For frequent complaints from many persons ring about us, as though nothing whatever had been laid down in this matter.

§ 1. The agents of our son, the illustrious man Amandus [Note: [Col. 0293] *Amandianus*: Anselm; Ivo.], indeed, complain grievously that men still owing service by right to his authority [Note: [Col. 0293] add: *still*: ibid.] have been ordained, some already clerics and others already deacons [Col. 0294A]; although, not only after the recent council—which is known to have been completed by the gathering of so many bishops with the unanimous assent of a most salutary provision [Note: [Col. 0293] *profession*: Basel edition.]—ought persons of this sort not to have been admitted [Note: [Col. 0293] *ought not*: ibid.], but even if any had previously been admitted into the service of the divine soldiery through ignorance, they ought altogether to have been removed, stripped of religious privilege, and compelled by due admonition to return to the possessions of their masters [Note: [Col. 0293] *ought*: Basel edition; *ought to have*: the other editions.].

Therefore, dearest brothers, investigate those whom the agents of the aforesaid man show to be retained in clerical office; and, once they have been examined and proved subject to servitude, restore them without delay, observing the course of the laws [Note: [Col. 0293] *having been kept*: ibid.]. Thus, if any one of them is found already to be a priest, he is to remain in that rank [Col. 0294B], punished by the forfeiture of his peculium [Note: [Col. 0293] *alone*: Anselm; Ivo; Basel edition.], [Note: [Col. 0293] omitted by Anselm and Ivo.] A deacon, however, shall either provide a substitute or, if he has none, shall himself be returned. Let the remaining offices [Note: [Col. 0293] *residual*: Anselm; Ivo.] understand that no one convicted can be released from this state of subjection [Note: [Col. 0293] *harmfulness*: the same; the collected editions except Basel.], so that, by observing this order, neither the rights of masters nor ecclesiastical privileges may be disturbed on any ground.

### C. X. A slave made a cleric remains subject to servitude.

The same, to Herculentus, Stephen, and Justus, bishops. [Note: [Col. 0293] Dated not long after A.D. 494; cf. chapter 9 of this distinction. Anselm, book 7, c. 30; Polycarpus, book 2, title 31.]

Frequent and continual complaint indeed rings about us concerning those bishops who, mindful neither of the ancient rules nor of our newly issued decrees, do not reject persons subject to estates [Note: [Col. 0293] *owners*: Anselm; Basel edition.] and bound in obligation [Col. 0294C] when they come to the belt of clerical office [Note: [Col. 0293] *to the clerical belt*: Anselm; the collected editions.].

§ 1. Recently the agents of the illustrious woman Placida [Note: [Col. 0293] *Placidias*: Anselm; Ivo; Basel edition.] complained in a formal petition that Sabinus, bishop of the city of Marcellanian [Note: [Col. 0293] *Marcellianian*: the same; the collected editions.] or of Clusium [Note: [Col. 0293] *Cusilinate*: Anselm; Ivo; “or of Clusium” is absent from the Argentinian edition.], had taken advantage of the absence of their mistress and brought Antiochus, a slave belonging by right [Note: [Col. 0293] *by right*: Basel edition.] to his patroness, as far as the honor of the priesthood [Note: [Col. 0293] *having been brought*: Anselm; Ivo; the collected editions except Lyons II–III and Antwerp.], and had adorned his brother Leontius with the privilege of clerical office.

Therefore, dearest brothers, by our authority we commit to you the hearing between the aforesaid agents and those claimed on the ground of their lowly status [Note: [Col. 0293] *are claimed, the charge having been made*: Ivo.], so that, after every truth has been investigated, if they cannot in fact remove by just reasoning the blemish objected against them [Note: [Col. 0293] *cannot*: Anselm; Ivo.] through lawful objection [Col. 0295A], you are to order Leontius the cleric—whom his assigned rank does not protect under the laws—to be returned in every way to the necessity of his condition. [Note: [Col. 0295D] *You are to order him returned.* In most ancient copies of Gratian, and in Anselm, Ivo, and Polycarpus, one reads *redhibete*, “restore”; but it has not been altered because of the gloss.] [Note: [Col. 0295] *Order*: the collected editions except Lyons II–III and Antwerp.]

Antiochus, however, because he cannot be restored to his former status on account of the priesthood [Note: [Col. 0295] *be raised up through the priesthood*: Anselm; Ivo.], if his mistress desires to retain him in his church in the rank he now holds [Note: [Col. 0295] omitted by Anselm and Ivo.], is not to be regarded as restored to her, but as received for the celebration of the mysteries [Note: [Col. 0295] *ministries*: Anselm; Ivo.].

### C. XI. On the same subject.

The same, to Rufinus and Aprilis, bishops. [Note: [Col. 0295] An epistle of not entirely certain date, but apparently genuine. Cf. D. 10, c. 11; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 150; *Decretum*, part 4, c. 179, part 6, c. 194; Deusdedit, part 4.]

Who would say that the laws of princes, the rules of the Fathers, or recent admonitions ought to be despised, except one who thinks that such a transgression may pass unpunished? The agents of our daughter, the illustrious and magnificent woman Maxima, have complained to us in a formal petition [Col. 0295B] that her dependants by birth, Silvester and Candidus, were ordained deacons by the bishop of Nuceria [Note: [Col. 0295] read: *Nucerian*.] contrary to the constitutions mentioned above, although objection had first been raised [Note: [Col. 0295] add: *not lawfully*: the collected editions.].

Therefore [Note: [Col. 0295] *And therefore*: Ivo; Basel edition.], dearest brothers, you are to know that the excess of so great a violation must be investigated with the greatest care; and, if the complaint is established as supported by truth, those who were unlawfully created despite a prior objection are immediately to be excluded from sacred offices.

### C. XII. Slaves are not to be admitted either to the religious life or to clerical office without their masters’ consent.

The same, to the bishops throughout Lucania, etc., epistle I, c. 16. [Note: [Col. 0295] Written A.D. 494; Anselm, book 7, c. 196 (198); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, c. 100; Polycarpus, book 4, c. 34.]

The presumption which gives rise to a general complaint must also be avoided [Col. 0295C]: almost everyone complains that slaves and serfs by birth, fleeing the rights and possession of their masters [Note: [Col. 0295D] *and of estates*: thus emended from Gelasius’s decree, whereas formerly the text read “and possession.” For serfs by birth were attached not only to masters but also to lands and estates: law *Quemadmodum*, law *Originarios*, Code book XI, title *On cultivators*. Therefore the word *possessionibus*, “estates,” was not changed above in the chapter “Frequent,” although most ancient manuscripts read *possessoribus*, “owners.”], are everywhere received indiscriminately, under the pretext of religious conversion, either into monasteries or into ecclesiastical service, with bishops conniving as well [Note: [Col. 0295] *indeed*: Böhm.].

This evil must in every way be removed, lest through the institution of the Christian name either another’s rights appear to be invaded [Note: [Col. 0295] add: *rights*: the collected editions except Argentinian.] or public discipline be overthrown; especially since it is unfitting that the dignity of clerical ministry itself should be stained by such an obligation, and that it should be compelled to dispute over the status and condition of those serving it [Col. 0296A] [Note: [Col. 0295] *condition*: Basel edition.], or appear—far be it—to be subject to obligation.

Once such persons have been duly prohibited by a vigilant interdiction, any bishop, priest, or deacon, or any of those known to preside over monasteries, who retains persons of this kind and believes that they are not to be restored to their patrons, or henceforth to be assigned either to ecclesiastical service [Note: [Col. 0295] *service of the church*: the collected editions.] or to religious communities, unless they have first been released by their masters’ will, under documentary testimony [Note: [Col. 0295] *subscription*: the same.] or granted by a lawful settlement, must not doubt that he will incur danger to his own rank and to communion [Note: [Col. 0295] add: *our*: Anselm.] if a truthful complaint by anyone reaches us on this matter.

§ 1. For, according to the blessed Apostle [Note: [Col. 0295] add: *Peter*: the collected editions; cf. 1 Timothy 6; 2 Peter 2.], the greatest care must be taken lest the faith and discipline of the Lord be blasphemed. The same [Note: [Col. 0296D] *The same*: These words are not found in Gelasius [the Pithoei testify that they found them in Gelasius’s letter to Maximus and the clergy; Col. 0295], nor are they found in the other collectors.]: § 2. We believe that ecclesiastical interests lose nothing if what belongs to others is returned [Col. 0296B].

## Part II

Gratian. This must be observed when master and slave are found to belong to the same religious profession. But if a Jew purchases a Christian slave, the slave must be brought to freedom by the authority of a judge or bishop, even against the Jew’s will.

Accordingly, Gregory, to Libertinus, prefect of Sicily, book II, epistle 37 [Note: [Col. 0295] Epistle 38, written A.D. 593, book 3 of the Maurist edition; *Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 54, c. 64.]:

### C. XIII. Christian slaves purchased by Jews are to be brought to freedom.

Bring whatever Christian slaves it becomes evident that a Jew has purchased to freedom, according to the precepts of the laws and without any ambiguity [Note: [Col. 0295] omitted by the Basel edition.], lest—God forbid—the Christian religion, made subject to Jews [Note: [Col. 0295] *subjected*: the collected editions.], be defiled [Col. 0296C].

### C. XIV. Public offices are not to be entrusted to Jews.

Likewise, from the Third Council of Toledo, c. 14. [Note: [Col. 0295] Held A.D. 589; *Collectio trium partium*, part 2, title 36, c. 7.]

No public offices are to be imposed upon Jews [Note: [Col. 0295] *them*—that is, Jews—“must perform”: the Hispanic Collection.], by which an opportunity may be given them to inflict punishment upon Christians. But if any Christians [Note: [Col. 0295] omitted by the collected editions except Basel.] have been stained by them with the rite of Judaism [Note: [Col. 0295] *in Judaism*: Basel edition.] or even circumcised, they are to return to freedom and to the Christian religion without payment of the price.

Gratian. But concerning those who, having been bought while in unbelief, desire to come to the grace of baptism [Col. 0297A], Pope Gregory writes as follows to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples, book V, epistle 31. [Note: [Col. 0297] Epistle 32, written A.D. 596, book 6 of the Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, c. 106; Polycarpus, book 7, title 14.]

### C. XV. Slaves who pass from unbelief to faith are to be claimed for freedom.

Your Fraternity ought *to be solicitous about these matters* [Note: [Col. 0297] add: *first*: the collected editions except Basel.], *and* if from Jewish servitude not only a Jew but also any pagan wishes to become a Christian, once his will has been made known, no Jew may have the power to sell him to anyone by any device or pretext [Note: [Col. 0297] *by a cunning device*: Basel edition.]. Rather, one who desires to be converted to the Christian faith is to be claimed in every way for freedom under your protection.

§ 1. Yet you must take careful account of those who have to lose slaves of this sort, lest perhaps they consider their own interests [Col. 0297B] unreasonably impeded [Note: [Col. 0297] *suppose*: Ivo; the collected editions.]. Thus, if pagans whom they purchased from foreign regions [Note: [Col. 0297] *outside regions*: the collected editions.] for purposes of trade flee, by chance, to a church within [Note: [Col. 0297] *below*: the same.] three months while no purchaser is found to whom they may be sold [Note: [Col. 0297] *to whom they ought to be sold*: the original.], and say that they wish to become Christians, or even declare such a wish outside a church, let their owners receive their price there [Note: [Col. 0297] add: *there*: the collected editions except Basel; Böhm.] from a Christian purchaser [Note: [Col. 0297] omitted by the collected editions except Basel.] [Note: [Col. 0297] *let it be received*: Basel edition.].

But if, after the prescribed three months, any slave of this sort [Note: [Col. 0297] add: *of Jews*: the collected editions.] declares his wish [Note: [Col. 0297] *says*: the same.] and wishes to become a Christian, and no one afterward purchases him [Note: [Col. 0297] *to purchase*: the original.], his master may not dare to sell him on the pretext of any circumstance. Rather, he is without doubt to be brought to the rewards of freedom, because he is understood to have been purchased not in order to be sold, but in order to serve his master [Note: [Col. 0297] *is understood to have reserved*: ibid.] [Col. 0297C].

### C. XVI. PALEA.

[The same, to Januarius, bishop of Caralis, book III, epistle 9. [Note: [Col. 0297] Epistle 9, written A.D. 594, book 4 of the Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, c. 102.]]

“If any slave of the Jews flees to the venerable places on account of the faith, do not allow him in any way to suffer prejudice. Rather, whether he has long been a Christian or has now been baptized, let him be defended in every way for freedom under the religious protection of ecclesiastical mercy, without any loss to Christian [Col. 0298A] poor persons.” [Note: [Col. 0297C] *Christian*: John the Deacon, in his *Life of St. Gregory*, book 4, no. 46, when reporting this letter, and Ivo, part 13, c. 102, have this word [Col. 0297D]; yet it is absent from the printed and manuscript codices of St. Gregory’s letters which have been collated.]

### C. XVII. PALEA.

[Likewise, from the Twelfth Council of Toledo, c. 9. [Note: [Col. 0297] Held A.D. 681; Burchard, book 4, c. 86; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 1, c. 280.]]

“And [Note: [Col. 0297] *That*: original.] if slaves of Jews, not yet converted [Note: [Col. 0297] *in churches*: the collected editions.], should hasten to Christ’s grace, let them be granted freedom [Note: [Col. 0297] *freedom*: original; the collected editions.].”

### C. XVIII. PALEA.

[Likewise, from the First Council of Mâcon, c. 16. [Note: [Col. 0297] Held A.D. 581; Burchard, book 4, c. 88; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 1, c. 282.]]

“By this present council, under God’s authority, we decree that [Note: [Col. 0297] Original: “No Christian slave … ought to serve.”] no Christian slave shall henceforth serve a Jew. Rather, upon payment of twelve solidi for each sound slave, any Christian [Note: [Col. 0297] *of Christians*: the collected editions.] may have permission to redeem the slave either into free status or into service. And [Note: [Col. 0297] From this point through the word *do* is absent from the original.] if he desires to become a Christian and is not permitted, let him do likewise; for it is wicked to keep in chains, as a blasphemer of the Christian religion, one whom Christ the Lord redeemed by the shedding of his blood [Note: [Col. 0297] Original: *remain ensnared in the bonds of blasphemous persecutors*.].

“But if any Jew refuses to comply with what we decree [Note: [Col. 0297] *our enactments*: the collected editions.], then, for as long as he delays receiving the fixed sum, the slave himself [Note: [Col. 0297] *to the slave himself*: original.] may live wherever he wishes with Christians.”

[Note: [Col. 0297D] *Present*: This chapter is reported in the same manner by Burchard and Ivo; in the council itself [Col. 0298C] it is given somewhat differently, and certain material is lacking.]

### C. XIX. On the same subject.

Likewise, from the First Council of Orléans, c. 5. [Note: [Col. 0297] Held A.D. 511; Regino, book 1, c. 392; Burchard, book 2, c. 24; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, c. 125; Polycarpus, book 2, title 31.]

## Part III

If a slave, while his master is absent or unaware, is ordained deacon or priest, though the bishop knows that he is a slave, the cleric is to remain in his clerical office, and the bishop shall compensate his master [Note: [Col. 0297] add: *his*: the collected editions.] with double satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0297] *recompense*: the same.]. But if the bishop did not know that he was a slave, those who gave testimony [Col. 0298C] [Note: [Col. 0297] *gave testimony*: Basel edition.] or requested his ordination shall be liable to the same restitution [Note: [Col. 0297] *restitution*: the collected editions.].

### C. XX. On the same subject.

Likewise, a New Constitution. [Note: [Col. 0298C] This chapter occurs word for word in Irnerius’s epitomes of the Novels, which are customarily placed after the *Code*, and also in Novel 123, c. 26, through Julian the antecessor. The words added in the title, “Emperor Leo to all bishops,” seem to have intruded there from the following title.]

If [Note: [Col. 0297] Justinian, Novel Constitution 123, c. 17, and *Auth. Si servus*, Code *On Bishops and Clerics* (1.3).] a slave is ordained among the clergy with his master’s knowledge and without his objection, he shall by that very fact—*because he has been appointed*—be free and freeborn. But if his master is unaware [Note: [Col. 0297] add: *his*: the collected editions.], he is allowed, within the space of one year, both to prove the slave status and to recover his slave [Col. 0299A].

Moreover [Note: [Col. 0299] Justinian, Novel 5, c. 2; *Auth. Verum*, Code *On Bishops and Clerics* (1.3).], even if a person of servile status is lawfully proved [Note: [Col. 0299] *proved*: original; Argentinian, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice I and II editions.], if he becomes a monk, he escapes the yoke of slavery. For they must remain in a monastery for three years before becoming monks; but afterward, if they have become monks, they become free.

For episcopal rank [Note: [Col. 0299] Justinian, Novel 123, c. 4; *Auth. Episcopalis*, Code *On Bishops and Clerics* (book 3).] frees one from servile or adscriptitious status, but not from curial or official status, for this continues even after ordination. Episcopal dignity also releases a person from the law of paternal power [Note: [Col. 0299] Justinian, Novel 81; *Auth. Sed episc.*, Code, same title.]. But we allow adscriptitii [Note: [Col. 0299] Justinian, Novel 123, c. 17; *Auth. Adscriptitios*, Code I, c.] to become clerics on the estates themselves even against their masters’ will, provided that, once made clerics, they fulfill the agricultural work imposed upon them.

### C. XXI. On the same subject.

Likewise, Pope Leo, to all bishops, epistle I, c. 1. [Note: [Col. 0299] Epistle 4, written A.D. 443, Ballerini edition; Regino, book 1, c. 391; Burchard, book 2, c. 22; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, c. 64.]

Persons are everywhere admitted to sacred rank who have neither the standing of birth nor the standing of morals to recommend them, and who have by no means been able to obtain freedom from their masters, yet are advanced to the height of the priesthood—as though servile baseness could rightly obtain this honor. And below: Therefore, dearest brothers, let all the priests of your province abstain from these persons; and we wish them to refrain not only from these, but also [Note: [Col. 0299] Original: “but also from other persons who are bound by birth or by some…”] from other serfs by birth, or from those bound by any condition, unless the petition or will of those who claim some power over them has been obtained.

## Part IV

Gratian. A question is raised concerning slaves of a monastery: whether they can be attached to ecclesiastical offices or not. But servants of churches are not to be ordained, as was said above [Col. 0299C], unless they obtain freedom from their own bishops. Moreover, a slave of a monastery cannot obtain freedom [Note: [Col. 0299D] *Cannot*: In the first Vatican manuscript, after these words follows: “for those who belong to a monastery cannot pass into anyone’s legal ownership. Thus not even an abbot can say, ‘This is mine; therefore …’” The chapter now cited by Gratian is found nowhere else than in Isidore of Seville, *Rule for Monks*, chapter *On family life*.]; therefore he is not permitted to enter the clerical state. That he cannot become free is proved by the authority of the Eighth Synod, in which the following enactment is read.

### C. XXII. It is not lawful for an abbot or monk to set free a slave of a monastery.

An abbot [Note: [Col. 0299] Isidore, *Rule for Monks*, c. 19; *Collectio trium partium*, part 2, title 14, c. 29.] or monk may not set a slave of a monastery free. For one who has nothing of his own cannot grant freedom in another’s property; for [Note: [Col. 0299] add: *also*: the collected editions.], as the secular laws likewise enact, a possession cannot be alienated except by its own master.

Gratian. By this authority slaves are prohibited from obtaining freedom to withdraw from service to the monastery; they are not prohibited, however, from obtaining freedom for advancement to sacred orders. For one established in sacred orders can serve the monastery perpetually; and thus a slave of a monastery can both obtain freedom and be joined to sacred offices [Col. 0300A]. Accordingly, in another chapter of the aforesaid constitution this reason is given: “For it is unjust that, while monks perform rural work, their slaves should languish in idleness and abound in luxuries.” [Note: [Col. 0300D] *Unjust*: This very text is cited below, 17, question 4, c. *In venditionibus*, gloss on *unjust*, from the Council of Agde, where it also appears, c. 56.]

## Part V

Gratian. That slaves of churches—by which term we understand slaves of monasteries also to be indicated—ought to be admitted to the religious vocation is proved by the authority of Gregory, who, sitting in a general synod [Note: [Col. 0299] A.D. 595; Anselm, book 7, c. 184 (193); Polycarpus, book 6, title 16; cf. Council of Tribur, c. 29.], said:

### C. XXIII. If a servant of the church has demonstrated a religious way of life, he may be ordained.

We know that many from the ecclesiastical household *or secular military service* [Note: [Col. 0299] These words are absent from Anselm; original: “ecclesiastical or secular household.”] hasten to the service of almighty God, so that, freed from human servitude, they may live more intimately [Note: [Col. 0299] omitted by Anselm.] in monasteries in divine service. If we dismiss them indiscriminately [Note: [Col. 0299] *dismiss*: Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I and II editions.], we provide everyone an opportunity to flee the lordship of ecclesiastical right. But if we incautiously retain those hastening to the service of almighty God, we are found to deny something to him who gave all things.

Therefore it is necessary that anyone who desires to turn from the service of ecclesiastical right or secular military service to God’s service [Note: [Col. 0299] The collected editions: “from ecclesiastical men or …”] should first be tested while in lay dress [Note: [Col. 0299] *lay*: the same.]. And if his character and manner of life bear witness to his good desire [Col. 0300C], he is to be allowed without any hesitation to serve almighty God in a monastery [Note: [Col. 0299] *the Lord*: the same.], so that he may withdraw free from human service, since he desires, constrained by divine love, to undertake a stricter servitude.

But if [Note: [Col. 0299] What follows is not read in the synod itself, but is found in Anselm.] he has also lived blamelessly in monastic dress [Note: [Col. 0299] *monastic*: the collected editions except Basel, where it reads *monachico*.] according to the rules of the Fathers, after the periods fixed [Note: [Col. 0299] *fixed*: Anselm.] by the sacred canons [Note: [Col. 0299] *from the sacred*: the collected editions.], he may then lawfully [Note: [Col. 0299] *lawfully*: Anselm.] be advanced to any ecclesiastical office, provided he has not been stained by those crimes which are punished with death in the Old Testament.

Gratian. Behold how slaves may be admitted to the clergy, and how they are not admitted. Freedpersons also [Note: [Col. 0301] Original: *their own*; Ivo; the collected editions except Argentinian and Basel, where it is omitted.] are not to be promoted to the clergy unless they have been released from the service owed to their patron [Col. 0301A].

Accordingly, in the Council of Elvira, c. 80 [Note: [Col. 0301] Held no later than A.D. 310; *Collectio trium partium*, part 2, title 30, c. 16.]:

### C. XXIV. Freedpersons are not to be promoted to the clergy without their patron’s consent.

It must be prohibited that freedpersons whose patrons remain in secular life be promoted to the clergy.

# DISTINCTION LV

[Col. 0301]

[Col. 0301A] **GRATIAN**

## Part I

Persons physically impaired are likewise prohibited from sacred offices.

Accordingly Pope Gelasius, writing to the bishops established throughout Lucania and Bruttium, epistle I, cc. 2 and 3, says [Note: [Col. 0301] Written A.D. 494; Anselm, book 7, c. 46; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, cc. 142–143; Polycarpus, book 2, title 31.]:

### C. I. One who comes from monastic disciplines to a clerical office—and also a layman—must have his previous life examined.

Therefore, while the ancient enactments remain in force because of the reverence due them [Col. 0301B] [Note: [Col. 0301] *institutions*: the collected editions from Ivo; *enactments*: Böhm.]—which ought regularly to be observed wherever no scarcity either of circumstances or of time presses [Note: [Col. 0301] add: *indeed*: the collected editions.]—we grant churches that are deprived of all ministers, or so stripped even of sufficient service [Note: [Col. 0301D] *To such an extent to churches*: This passage has been restored from Gelasius’s letter and Ivo.] that they cannot supply the divine offices to the peoples belonging to them, a measured latitude both for appointing and for promoting clerical service [Note: [Col. 0301] Original: *providing*; the collected editions: “the intervals for clerical service are thus to be dispensed.”]. Thus, if anyone trained in monastic discipline comes to clerical office, his prior life is to be investigated even in the case of laymen [Note: [Col. 0301D] *Trained in monastic disciplines*: Here Gelasius’s words seem deliberately to have been altered and abridged; the complete words are given below, Distinction 77, c. *Si quis*, where they are to be read.],

§ 1. lest he be tainted by some crime, illiterate, a bigamist, stained from adolescence, physically impaired, of servile or serf-by-birth condition, entangled in the bonds of the curia or public obligations, marked by public penance [Col. 0301C], or examined without the waiting period appropriate to his case.

### C. II. Whoever ordains someone contrary to the form of the canons is subject to a year’s suspension.

Likewise, from the Third Council of Arles, c. 3. [Note: [Col. 0301] Rather the Fourth, according to Sirmond; held A.D. 524; *Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 25, c. 1.]

No one shall dare to ordain to the aforesaid ranks a penitent, a bigamist, or a husband of widows [Note: [Col. 0301] *of women remarried after widowhood*: the Hispanic Collection.]. And although the enactments of nearly all the canons already contain this, still, lest the importunity or [Col. 0302A] wicked suggestion of petitioners should creep up on any priest, as we have already said [Note: [Col. 0301] *creep in*: ibid.], it has been necessary for the Lord’s priests now to wish to impose a stricter rule upon themselves.

Therefore, whoever from this day presumes to ordain a cleric contrary to what has been set out above shall, from the day on which this can be proved against him, not presume for a whole year to celebrate Mass [Note: [Col. 0301] *celebrate*: the collected editions.]. If anyone refuses to observe this and, acting contrary to the enactment [Note: [Col. 0301] *enactments*: the same.] of the brethren, presumes to celebrate Mass, he shall be deprived of communion with the church [Note: [Col. 0302D] *He shall be deprived of communion with the church*: These words are not in the council itself and seem to mean the same as the following words; nevertheless they occur also in ancient manuscripts of Gratian.], and shall know himself to be excluded from the communion of all the brethren [Col. 0302B], because it is fitting that one who despises to observe the salutary enactments so often [Note: [Col. 0301] omitted by the Hispanic Collection and Isidore Mercator.] established by the holy Fathers should feel the severity of ecclesiastical discipline.

### C. III. Penitents and illiterate persons are not to be ordained.

Likewise, Hilary, from the Roman Council held by him, c. 3. [Note: [Col. 0301] Held A.D. 465; Anselm, book 7, c. 16.]

Penitents [Note: [Col. 0301] The words “Penitents or” are absent in Anselm’s collection and seem to have intruded from the rubric of Isidore’s collection.] or persons ignorant of letters, or those who have suffered some loss of limbs [Note: [Col. 0301] add: “or those who are among the penitents”: the Hispanic Collection.], may not dare to aspire to sacred orders. Whoever has been the consecrator of such persons shall himself undo what he has done.

Gratian. By those physically impaired are meant not persons mutilated by accident, but those cut off by their own will.

Accordingly, it is read in the Canons of the Apostles [cc. 22 and 23] [Note: [Col. 0301] Anselm, book 7, cc. 37–38.]:

### C. IV. Whoever has castrated himself is not to be ordained.

If anyone has castrated himself—that is, if anyone has cut off his genitals—he is not to become a cleric, because he is his own murderer [Note: [Col. 0301] *his own*: original; Anselm.] and an enemy of God’s creation [Note: [Col. 0301] *creation*: the collected editions.].

§ 1. If anyone, while he is a cleric, castrates himself, he is to be condemned altogether, because he is his own murderer [Note: [Col. 0301] *his own*: original; Anselm.].

### C. V. Those who castrate themselves are not to be admitted to the clergy.

Likewise, from the Second Council of Arles, c. 7. [Note: [Col. 0301] Held no later than A.D. 460; cf. D. 18, c. 12; *Collectio trium partium*, part 2, title 24, c. 4.]

Those [Note: [Col. 0301] The Hispanic Collection: “Those who … cannot.”] who, not knowing that they ought [Note: [Col. 0301] add: *ought*: Basel edition.] to resist carnal vice [Col. 0303A], castrate themselves cannot enter the clergy.

Likewise, Innocent writes to Felix, bishop of Nuceria, epistle IV, c. 1. [Note: [Col. 0303] An epistle of uncertain date; Regino, book 1, c. 410—from Felix’s letter; Burchard, book 2, c. 14; Anselm, book 7, c. 35; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 43; *Decretum*, part 6, c. 58; Polycarpus, book 2, title 31.]

### C. VI. One who deliberately cut off part of a finger is not to be ordained.

The canons do not admit to the clergy one who deliberately cut off part of any finger of his own. But if this happened to someone by accident [Note: [Col. 0303] *happens*: the collected editions.], while he was attending to rural work or, while doing something, struck himself unintentionally [Note: [Col. 0303] *strikes*: the collected editions.], the canons command that such persons both become clerics and, if they are found already in the clergy, not be expelled.

For in the former cases the will has been condemned [Note: [Col. 0303] *is to be punished*: the collected editions.] because it dared [Note: [Col. 0303] *cause*: Hispanic Collection; Anselm.] to apply the blade to itself [Note: [Col. 0303C] *Apply*: The original continues, “so that there can be no doubt that others too might do this”; the Hispanic Collection reads: “to cut with iron.”]; in the latter cases, however, accident has deserved pardon [Col. 0303B].

Gratian. The same is to be understood concerning those whom physicians cut because of illness, whom barbarians mutilate, or whom masters castrate.

Accordingly, it is read in the Council of Nicaea, c. 1 [Note: [Col. 0303] Held A.D. 325; Dionysian translation; Anselm, book 7, c. 36; Polycarpus, same place.]:

### C. VII. One cut by physicians because of illness may be admitted to the clergy.

If anyone has been cut by physicians because of illness, or mutilated by barbarians [Note: [Col. 0303] *cut off*: original; Anselm; the collected editions.], let him remain in the clergy. But if anyone, while healthy, castrates himself [Note: [Col. 0303] add: *while healthy*: the collected editions.], it is fitting that he, even if established in the clergy, abstain, and that henceforth [Note: [Col. 0303D] *And henceforth*: These words have no counterpart in the common Greek text, but occur very well in Balsamon, as also in the Sixth Council of Carthage, in the chapters of the Nicene Synod translated by Theilo and Thearistus.] no one of this kind be promoted.

Just as it is clear that these provisions have been said of those who seek this thing [Note: [Col. 0303] *have sought this thing*: Nuremberg, Venice I–II, Argentinian, and Basel editions, omitting *thing*.] and dare to castrate themselves [Note: [Col. 0303] *the enactments which have been stated*: the collected editions except the Argentinian and Basel editions, where it reads *has been decreed*.], so the rule receives into the clergy [Col. 0303C] [Note: [Col. 0303] *may receive*: Böhm.] those whom barbarians or masters have castrated, if they are otherwise found entirely worthy [Note: [Col. 0303] *church*: Anselm; *ecclesiastical rule*: the collected editions.].

### C. VIII. A man made a eunuch through the malice of others may lawfully be ordained bishop.

Likewise, from Canon 21 of the Apostles.

If a eunuch has been made so through the malice of men [Note: [Col. 0304C] *Through malice*: ἐξ ἐπηρείας (*ex epēreias*), that is, “from assault and injury” [Col. 0304D].], or if his genitals have been cut off in persecution, or if he was born so, and he is worthy, let him become a bishop [Note: [Col. 0304D] *Bishop*: This word is not found in the Greek copies and seems to have *cleric* (κληρικός) understood.].

### C. IX. Those castrated by physicians, barbarians, or their masters are not excluded from the clergy.

Likewise, from Martin, bishop of Braga, in the chapters of the Greek synods, c. 21. [Note: [Col. 0303] “From the chapter of Pope Martin”: the collected editions; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 56; *Decretum*, part 6, c. 374.]

If anyone has had his genitals cut by physicians because of illness [Note: [Col. 0303] *for the cause of illness*: Hispanic Collection.], and likewise those who have been castrated by barbarians or their masters [Note: [Col. 0303] *foolish men*: ibid.]—provided they have appeared worthy in character [Note: [Col. 0303] *are found*: the collected editions.]—the canon permits [Note: [Col. 0303] *the canons permit*: Basel edition.] them to be advanced to the office of the clergy [Note: [Col. 0303] *the clergy*: the collected editions.].

But if anyone while healthy, not through the discipline of religion and abstinence but by cutting off the body formed by God, supposing [Note: [Col. 0303] *supposes, and therefore*: the collected editions.] that he can cut away from himself carnal desires, castrates himself, we decree that he is not to be admitted to any clerical office. If he has already been advanced to the clergy, he is to be removed from his ministry and deposed [Col. 0304B].

### C. X. One made lame by a physician’s incision is not barred from sacred orders.

Likewise, from the Council of Lleida. [Note: [Col. 0303] This belongs to the Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895; Burchard, book 2, c. 15; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 42; *Decretum*, part 6, c. 34.]

If a cleric, while ill, is made lame by a physician’s incision, we do not deny him advancement to sacred orders [Note: [Col. 0303] *do not deny*: Basel edition.].

### C. XI. One who accidentally cuts off his finger is not barred from the clergy.

Likewise, Stephen [V], to Robert, bishop of Metz. [Note: [Col. 0303] Written about A.D. 887; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 44; *Decretum*, part 6, c. 118. The collected editions except Basel read *Marensis*.]

The bearer of this letter, namely the cleric Flavius [Note: Flavinus: Ivo], having come to the holy apostolic see, delivered to us a letter sent by you. In it you sought to ascertain whether, since he had recently been captured by the Normans and had had a finger of his left hand cut off, he could on that account be advanced to ecclesiastical rank or not. [Note: “you inquire”: collected editions.] [Col. 0304C] Finding this to be true [Note: added: “to be true”: Basel, Lyons II and III, Antwerp editions], and since your diligence, especially solicitous on this point and always wishing to follow the rule of justice [Note: “desiring”: collected editions], requests instruction from the apostolic see, we deservedly commend the zeal of your holiness. We wish your reverence to know that, if it is indeed so that the said finger was cut off by the Normans, this will not hinder his advancement, if he is otherwise worthy; for we do not believe that your charity is unaware what the sacred canons determine concerning those who suffer such a thing involuntarily at the hands of masters, physicians, or pagans. [Col. 0305A]

### C. XII. A rank received while one is sound is not lost when disability follows.

Likewise, Pope Gelasius to Bishop Palladius. [Note: The date of this letter is not sufficiently certain. It was written to Palladius (Palladinus: Paris edition), bishop of the church of Sulmona in the Abruzzi.—Anselm, book 7, c. 39. Ivo, Panormia, book 3, c. 55. Decretum, part 6, c. 107. Polycarpus, book 2, title 31.]

The prescriptions of the canons by which ecclesiastical discipline is governed do not allow those physically disabled to come to the priesthood; but if anyone has already been established in it and is then wounded, he cannot lose what he received while sound. [Note: added, “in office”: Ivo.] §1. For the priest Stephen, in a petition presented to us, tearfully declared what is contained below [Note: “what is contained”: thus corrected from Anselm and ancient manuscripts of Gratian. This is the customary form in letters of Roman pontiffs where they append the petitioners’ own words. Formerly it read: “that he had”], namely that many years before he had received the dignity of the priesthood, which he had indeed received while his body was unimpaired; [Note: “and before”: collected editions] but recently, because of the devastation of the province—which the savage cruelty of barbarians of diverse sects and their unsettled minds had brought upon Tuscany more than upon all other provinces [Note: added, “provinces”: collected editions]—while he was striving to escape threatening swords by the aid of flight, he reported that, leaping over barriers that met him and were furnished with sharp stakes, he had impaled the lower parts of his body, which could scarcely have been cleansed by treatment within two years. Therefore, dearest brother, restore to the aforesaid man his place and dignity, so that he may administer the most holy mysteries as he was accustomed to do.
