For it is not fitting that he be deprived, on this account, of an order already received, in which he is afterwards shown, by an accidental occurrence, to have fallen into bodily infirmity. [Note: “into health”: Ivo.]

[Col. 0305C] **Part II. Gratian.** This, however, is not to be understood of all limbs. For one who loses an eye by accident, although voluntary intent is lacking, nevertheless cannot attain the priesthood.

[Col. 0306A] Therefore Gelasius writes to Bishop Rufinus [Note: In Anselm, book 11, c. 169, and Ivo, Decretum, part 6, c. 111, this chapter is given under the name of Pelagius; nor does it seem able to be attributed to Gelasius, since in his time it was not yet customary for clerics to be confined in monasteries]:

### C. XIII. The rights of the priesthood are not to be granted to one whose eye has been torn out.

If the Gospel admonition does not allow anger to break out even so far as an enraged word, lest one who says “Raca” to his brother be liable to the fire of Gehenna, what punishment do we think should be inflicted on one who not only impiously struck with his fist a man serving in the ministry of Levitical office, but, as though his hand were not enough for the assault, was so carried away by anger—at the devil’s instigation—that with a stick he not only struck but even tore out his brother’s eye [Note: added, “his own”: Basel edition]? Although an offence of this kind deserved a graver punishment, your brotherhood nevertheless did well in removing him from the office of the priesthood. [Note: “to be removed”: collected editions.] Yet let this be your concern: appoint for him a place of penance and confine him in some monastery, granting him only lay communion. You must ordain another priest in his place, for the rights of the priesthood cannot, according to the canons, be granted to one whose eye has been torn out. [Note: “according to”: Ivo; Basel edition.] It does him no good that he lost his eye unwillingly [Note: “who”: collected editions; “may have lost”: Basel edition], since no one is to be thought to have willingly lost an eye, nor do we find that the most sacred canons have made an exception in their rules for any accidental loss of an eye that would not obstruct the attainment of the priesthood. [Note: added, “his”: Basel; “to him”: other collected editions.] Rather, we see that the Fathers regarded this alone as sufficient for prohibition: one who lacks an eye cannot attain the office of the priesthood. Nor can sacred ordination be granted, as it were in compensation for the injury, to the man who was able to provoke his own priest to such great anger that the one lost the office he held and the other lost the possibility of his own advancement. [Note: “advantage”: Basel edition.]

## DISTINCTION LVI

[Col. 0305]

[Col. 0305C] **GRATIAN.**

**Part.** Even the sons of priests are not to be admitted to sacred offices.

Thus Pope Urban II says [Note: From the Council of Melfi, held in 1089; nearly the same words occur in Urban’s letter to Pibo of Toul, epistle 17 in Mansi, apparently written in the same year.—Anselm, book 6, c. 150 (147). Ivo, Panormia, book 3, c. 51. Decretum, part 6, c. 410, from the decrees of Gregory II and Urban II]:

### C. I. Sons of priests are barred from sacred offices.

We exclude the sons of priests from the sacred ministries of the altar, unless they have proved themselves by religious life in monasteries or in communities of canons. [Note: “canonical communities”: collected editions except Lyons II and III, Antwerp; “regular canons”: Ivo, Decretum; “regular monasteries”: Panormia.] [Note: “to live”: Anselm.]

**Part II. Gratian.** But this must be understood of those who have been imitators of their fathers’ incontinence. If, however, uprightness of character has made them commendable, examples and authorities show that they may become not only priests but even high priests.

[Thus Pope Damasus writes [Note: In no ancient manuscript of Gratian is the name “Palea” attached here. In Vatican manuscript 10 and certain others, this is joined to Gratian’s preceding words, from “For Felix III” to the end. In another, also quite well corrected, these same matters are connected with the preceding passage; but after the words “was descended from the priest Gordian,” it continues: “Thus Pope Damasus writes: Pope Deusdedit was the son of the subdeacon Stephen; Pope Boniface, the son of the priest Jucundus; Pope Felix, the son of the priest Felix of the title of Fasciola; Pope Agapetus, the son of the priest Gordian; Pope Theodore, the son of Theodore, bishop of the city of Jerusalem; Pope Silverius, the son of Hormisdas, bishop of Rome. Very many others also,” etc. Nor is it especially surprising that all these things are cited from Damasus, who lived before those listed here. For the book called the *Pontifical Book*, in which these statements occur in their respective places, was begun by Damasus; hence, although much was afterwards added by others, it retained the name of its first author. Ivo indeed reports nearly the same things from the deeds of the Roman pontiffs. It is certain from Gratian’s words at the end of the preceding chapter and in the penultimate chapter of this distinction that at least some part of this chapter, namely that found in Vatican manuscript 10, was written by Gratian himself. But the author of the Palea, wishing to make a single chapter on his own, disturbed the order, especially by repeating Felix III and rashly adding the statement about Osius, which was the name of no Roman pontiff.] [Note: The collected editions add, “to Jerome the priest,” owing to the fact that a spurious letter of Damasus to Jerome is prefixed to the *Pontifical Book*, which some wrongly ascribed to Damasus. What follows after “Felix,” etc., is drawn from the prologue and chapter 52 of book 3 of Parnomia, and does not appear to have formed a distinct chapter before the time of the author of the Paleae.]:

### C. II. PALEA.

“Osius, Pope, was the son of Stephen the subdeacon. Boniface, Pope, was the son of the priest Jucundus. Felix [Note: the words “Felix—priest” are absent in the collected editions, first Basel edition, Lyons II and III] Pope was the son of Felix, priest of the title of Fasciola. Agapetus, Pope, was the son of the priest Gordian. Theodore, Pope, was the son of Theodore, bishop of the city of Jerusalem. Silverius, Pope, was the son of Silverius [Note: Hormisdas: Panormia], bishop of Rome. Deusdedit, Pope, was the son of Stephen [Note: “the priest Jucundus”: collected editions] the subdeacon.”

“For Felix III, a Roman by nation, was the son of Felix [Col. 0307B] the priest. Likewise Gelasius, an African by nation, was born of Valerius, a bishop, as his father. Likewise Agapetus, a Roman by nation, was descended from Gordian the priest as his father. Very many other persons are found who, born of priests, presided over the apostolic see.”

Hence Augustine says in book *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 16 [Note: Ivo, in the prologue to the Panormia, and Decretum, part 6, c. 415]:

### C. III. The vices of parents are not imputed to children.

Wherever people are born, if they do not follow their parents’ vices and worship God rightly, they will be honorable and saved. [Note: “follow”: collected editions.] For human seed, from whatever human being it comes, is God’s creature; and it will go badly for those who use it badly, but it will never itself become evil. Just as the good children of adulterers do not defend adultery, [Note: “of adulterers”: original] so the bad children of married persons do not make marriage guilty.

[Col. 0307C]

### C. IV. On the same matter.

Likewise John Chrysostom, Homily III on Matthew [chapter 1]. [Note: Ivo, Decretum, part 6, c. 414.]

[Col. 0308A] Let us never be ashamed of our parents’ vices, but let us seek and embrace this one thing: virtue. [Note: “Let us seek”: the version now current reads, “and let us strive with every effort to be ennobled by the honor of our own virtues.” The complete Greek passage reads: “Thus he also teaches us through these things never to be ashamed because of the wickedness of our ancestors, but to seek only virtue.” — Παιδεύων καὶ ἡμᾶς διὰ τούτων μηδέποτε ἐγκαλύπτεσθαι ἐπὶ τῇ τῶν προγόνων κακίᾳ· ἀλλ’ ἓν μόνον ἐπιζητεῖν τὴν ἀρετήν.] [Note: added, “always”: collected editions, from Ivo.] A person of this kind, even if he has [Note: this word is absent from Ivo and the collected editions except Lyons II and III and Antwerp; “has”: those editions] a foreign-born mother, even if she has been defiled by fornication or stained by any similar disgrace, is nevertheless not darkened by her low status or polluted by her crime. If a fornicator himself, once converted to better things, is in no way defiled by his former life, much more is one born of a prostitute and an adulteress, if adorned by his own virtue, not disgraced by the reproaches of his parents. [Note: “discolored”: Ivo.] Likewise below:

§1. No one is at all to be praised or blamed on account either of the virtue or the vice of parents; no one is thereby truly obscure or illustrious. Indeed, if it is necessary to say something at variance with common opinion [Note: “If it is necessary to say something at variance with common opinion”: thus corrected from the Greek: *Ei de chrē ti kai paradoxon eipein*—“But if one must say something even paradoxical.” Formerly it read, roughly as in the current translation and in Ivo: “that we may speak something more carefully or more precisely.”; “if”: added in the Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I and II editions], I do not know how, but the man shines more brightly who, though born of parents utterly estranged from virtue, is himself remarkable for virtue.

### C. V. It is one’s own fault, not one’s parents’, that condemns each person.

Likewise Jerome, in the letter to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem. [Note: Written in 393.—“Jerome’s letter against Rufinus”: collected editions and Ivo, Decretum, part 6, c. 413.]

To be born of adultery is not the fault of the one born, but of the one who begets. As, among seeds, the earth that nurtures them does not sin, [Note: “cherishes”: Ivo and collected editions] nor does the seed cast into furrows, nor the moisture and [Note: “or”: same editions] warmth by which duly proportioned grain springs into a shoot; but, for example, the thief and robber sins who takes the seeds away by deceit and force. So in the generation of human beings the earth—that is, the womb—receives what belongs to it, cherishes what it has received, gives bodily form to what it has cherished, differentiates into limbs what has been formed, and God’s hand is always at work among those secret narrow spaces of the womb. [Note: “sacred”: same source.] He is the creator both of body and [Col. 0309A] soul. Do not despise the goodness of your potter [Note: added, “that is, God”: collected editions except Basel], who fashioned you and made you as he willed. He is the power of God and the wisdom of God, who built a house for himself in the womb of the Virgin. [Note: added, “Mary”: collected editions.] Jephthah [Note: Judges 11:1; Hebrews 11:32], numbered by the Apostle among holy men, was the son of a prostitute. But hear this: Esau, born of Rebecca and Isaac, hairy in mind as well as body, degenerates like good wheat into darnel and wild oats, because the cause of vices and virtues lies not in seeds but in the will of the one born. [Note: “among”: collected editions.]

### C. VI. The iniquities of parents cannot harm their children.

Likewise Augustine against Faustus, book XXII, chapter 64. [Note: In blessed Augustine, book 22 against Faustus, c. 64, it reads: “For believers to come from all nations should also learn, even from the example of his flesh, that their parents’ iniquities cannot harm them. Accordingly, that bridegroom, suited to the guests whom he would call to the wedding—both good and bad—also willed to be born from good and bad persons.” This chapter is composed from those words.]

That bridegroom [Note: compare Matthew 22] who would call both good and bad persons to the wedding, fitting the guests he was to invite, also willed to be born of good and bad persons, so that believers might learn by this example that their parents’ iniquities cannot harm them. [Note: “children”: collected editions.]

### C. VII. Not another’s fault but one’s own removes a person from the rank in which he serves.

Likewise Gregory to Columbus, Bishop of Numidia, book X, letter 8. [Note: Letter 8, written in 602; book 12, Maurist edition.]

It is shown to be quite perverse and contrary to ecclesiastical discipline that a person should needlessly be deprived of his offices because of certain persons’ desires, [Note: “because of the pleasures of certain parents a person is deprived of his offices”: collected editions; “pleasures”: Böhm] when he is not removed from the rank of the office he exercises by his own fault or crime.

### C. VIII. Those born of adulterous unions are not barred from the priesthood.

Likewise Jerome. [Note: At Jerome, on Matthew chapter 1 and in the preface to his commentary on Hosea, there are some similar passages. These exact words from the exposition of the genealogy of Jesus Christ occur in the letter of the clergy of Noyon to those of Cambrai, printed in Mabillon, *Museum Italicum*, vol. 1, part 2, p. 128.—Anselm, book 6, c. 149. Polycarpus, book 2, title 31.]

Our Lord Jesus Christ willed to be born not only from foreigners but also from adulterous unions, [Col. 0309C] providing us with great confidence: however we may be born, provided only that we imitate his footsteps, we are not separated from his body, of which we have become members through faith. [Note: “provided only”: Basel edition.] And just as he is the true high priest, born of adulterous unions, [Note: “and of”: collected editions except Lyons II and III and Antwerp] so anyone, of whatever rank he may have been born, is not at all excluded from the priesthood, provided that he has perfect faith, fulfills in works what he holds by faith, is literate, and is the husband of one wife. [Note: “nevertheless”: collected editions.] For the patriarch Judah lay with Tamar, his daughter-in-law, and from that union Pharez and Zerah were born; then Salmon, who was leader in the wilderness; then Obed [Note: “Then Obed”: in the first chapter of the Gospel of Saint Matthew, Boaz is said to have begotten Obed]; and then Boaz [Note: Ruth 4]; and then Jesse, who was the father of David. From that lineage, therefore, the origin of Christ is drawn, who is the true priest; and therefore, if we are his children, we ought to imitate what he did. [Note: “however”: Basel edition.]

### C. IX. A person is not separated from God’s people by his mother’s condition, but by his own fault.

Likewise Augustine, *On the One Baptism against the Donatists*, book I, chapter 15. [Note: Ivo, Panormia, book 6, c. 47; Decretum, part 8, c. 61.]

For Ishmael to be separated from God’s people, his mother’s being a slave did not harm him, [Note: added, “Hagar”: Basel, Lyons II and III] but brotherly discord harmed him. Nor did the status of the wife, whose son he was more properly, benefit him, because through her marital rights he was both conceived in the slave woman and born from the slave woman. [Note: added, “was”: collected editions.]

**Part III. Gratian.** In opposition, Boniface the Martyr, writing to Ethelbald, king of the English [Note: Written about 750.—Ivo, Decretum, part 8, c. 224: “Boniface to Hillribald, king of the English”]:

### C. X. The vices of parents are transmitted even to descendants.

If the English people—as has been spread abroad through these provinces, is reproached to us in France and Italy, and is made a reproach by the pagans themselves [Note: “the reproach is brought”: Basel, Lyons II and III, Antwerp; the word *improperium*, “reproach,” is absent from the other collected editions; “was reproached”: Böhm]—have led a foul life, despising lawful marriages and committing adultery and lusting after the manner of the Sodomite people, then from such intercourse with prostitutes we must expect degenerate, ignoble peoples, frenzied by lust, to be begotten; and at last the whole people, [Col. 0310C] declining into worse and more ignoble conditions, will eventually be neither strong in secular war, nor steadfast in faith, nor honorable among human beings, nor beloved by God. This happened to other peoples of Spain, Provence, and Burgundy, [Note: “Burgundians”: Böhm] who, departing from God, committed fornication in this way until the almighty judge [Note: “avenger”: Basel, Lyons II and III, Antwerp] permitted the avenging punishments of such crimes to come and rage through those ignorant of God’s law—that is, [Note: “also”: collected editions except Basel, Lyons II and III, Antwerp] through the Saracens. [Note: “Through those ignorant”: In the letter of blessed Boniface the Martyr, preserved in manuscript with many others in the often-mentioned codex of the Dominican library, it reads: “through ignorance of God’s law and through the Saracens,” etc. Several ancient manuscripts of Gratian [and the Basel edition], and almost Ivo as well, agree with this reading.]

[Col. 0311A] Therefore Urban [Note: compare above, in the same distinction, c. 1], making a distinction at the end of the preceding chapter, added:

### C. XI. If sons of priests are found religious, they are to be ordained.

Unless they have proved themselves by religious life in monasteries or communities of canons. [Note: “canonical communities”: collected editions except Lyons II and III, Antwerp.] [Note: “to live”: Argentinensis and Basel; “the sons of priests are not admitted to the clergy”: collected editions except Nuremberg.]

### C. XII. On the same matter.

Likewise Alexander II. [Note: Berard doubted greatly, but without reason, about the authenticity of this chapter. For we read that Alexander II, when a question arose concerning the election of Arnold of Le Mans, graciously answered in this manner; compare the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans* in Mabillon, *Annals*, p. 307. In Anselm, book 6, c. 19, the words found at the end of the following chapter are read at the end.]

By apostolic authority we command you: if you find that the man elected by the church is worthier than the other and that his election is canonical, then, supported by our authority, consecrate him. For although he is said to be the son of a priest, if other virtues are present in him, we do not reject him; rather, yielding to his merits, we admit him.

[Col. 0311B] **Gratian.** But this rule concerning the sons of priests appears to have been introduced by ecclesiastical dispensation; and what is introduced by dispensation cannot be made into a consequential rule.

Thus Pope Urban II writes to Bartholomew, Archbishop of Tours [Note: This fragment would more correctly be assigned to Alexander than to Urban, for Bartholomew had long been dead in Urban’s time. Moreover, it seems to have been compiled from Alexander II’s letter as given by Anselm.—Ivo, Panormia, book 3, c. 53]:

### C. XIII. Sons of priests are not barred from the episcopate if other virtues are found in them.

We do not reject the elect of Le Mans because he is said to be the son of a priest, if other virtues are present in him; rather, supported by his merits, we patiently receive him. [Note: added, “him”: collected editions.] Yet this is not to be adopted as a rule for the future; rather, provision is being made temporarily for the peril of the church.

[Col. 0312A] **Gratian.** Since, therefore, those born of priests are read above to have been advanced to the supreme pontificate, they are to be understood as born not from fornication but from lawful marriages, which were everywhere permitted to priests before the prohibition and are shown to be permitted to them in the Eastern church even to this day. [Note: “To priests before”: Here Gratian openly shows that he held the opinion that at one time presbyters in the Latin church too were permitted to use marriage, as it was permitted both formerly and presently in the Greek church. That this was by no means so has been noted above at the beginning of Distinction 31. Concerning those whom he previously reported to have become supreme pontiffs, it must be said that they were begotten before their fathers had been invested with any sacred order.] §1. The assertion that the vice of one’s origin is not imputed to offspring seems contrary to the saying: “The children of adulterers are an abomination to the Lord.” [Note: Wisdom 3.] But, as was said above concerning sons of priests, so this also appears to be understood concerning the children of adulterers: those are called an abomination to the Lord upon whom their fathers’ wicked acts descend by hereditary succession. Urban’s statement, which he himself writes to Petronius [Note: It seems one should read “Peter, bishop of León,” as in the collected editions except Basel, Lyons II and III, Antwerp. Peter of León is mentioned among the acts of the Council of Fusel, held in 1088 in Spain.—In Ivo, Panormia, book 3, c. 54, the name itself is absent] bishop of León, is to be understood similarly:

[Col. 0312B]

### C. XIV. On the same matter.

Because, having come simply to the apostolic see, you humbly confessed the sin which seemed to obstruct the exercise of your pontifical office—namely, that you were begotten by an illegitimate mother, whom your father is known to have known while his own wife was living [Note: “is known”: Ivo; Basel edition]—we, prompted by the grace of apostolic gentleness, recognize from your own profession and the testimony of the brothers who are with you [Note: “with himself”: Argentinensis edition] that you are free from the other crimes which impede the priesthood; and, hearing of your religious life, we absolve you from the bond of this sin [Note: added, “kind”: Basel edition] and confirm you in the priestly office you have received.

## DISTINCTION LVII

[Col. 0311]

[Col. 0311C] **GRATIAN.** Likewise, one baptized while afflicted by illness ought not to be ordained priest. Thus it is read in the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 12. [Note: Held in 314.—Burchard, book 4, c. 43. Decretum, part 1, c. 227; part 6, c. 101. Polycarpus, book 2, c. 31.]

### C. I. One baptized while ill is not to be ordained priest.

If anyone has been baptized while ill, he ought not to be ordained priest, [Col. 0312C] for his faith is not voluntary but arises from necessity—unless perhaps his subsequent zeal and faith prove commendable, or a scarcity of persons requires it. [Note: “compels”: original and Ivo.]

[Note: Held in 398.—Collection in Three Parts, part 2, title 19, c. 3.]

[Note: What this canon establishes seems to have been observed much earlier in the Roman church, as appears from Pope Cornelius’s letter concerning Novatian. The relevant words, reported by Eusebius in *Ecclesiastical History*, book 6, c. 35, are these: “When, indeed, he had been delivered from that evil spirit by the help of exorcists, and afterwards fell into such a serious illness that he was thought to be nearly dying, he received baptism by water poured around him on the bed in which he lay.” A little later, when discussing his ordination, Cornelius adds: “The bishop, though forbidden not only by all the clergy but also by many laypersons, since it was by no means lawful to admit to the clergy one baptized on a bed because of illness, as had happened to this man, urgently requested that he be allowed to lay hands on this man alone for the share of the priesthood.”]

## DISTINCTION LVIII

[Col. 0313]

[Col. 0313A] **GRATIAN.** Likewise, no one is taken from the monastic habit for ecclesiastical office unless he has been offered by the will of his own abbot. Thus Gregory writes to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna, book VII, letter 18. [Note: Letter 15, written in 598; book 8, Maurist edition.]

### C. I. A monk is not to be ordained cleric unless his abbot offers him to the bishop of his own will.

No monk is to be brought out of a monastery for ecclesiastical office [Note: absent from the original, together with the word “bishop” at the end], unless the abbot of that place, having been informed, offers him to the bishop of his own will.

[Col. 0314A]

### C. II. On the same matter.

Likewise from the Fifth Council of Carthage.

If anyone receives someone from another monastery [Note: “from the community of another monastery”: collected editions; Greek: *Ean tis ap’ allotriou monastēriou hypodexētai tina*, that is, “if anyone receives someone from another monastery”], whether he wishes to advance him to clerical rank or appoint him a superior of the monastery in his own monastery, the bishop who does so is to be separated from communion with the others and content only with communion with his own people; and that person is to remain neither a cleric [Note: The words “nor a canon” followed, though not in the Argentinensis edition; they were removed for the same reasons] nor a superior. [Note: “appoint”: formerly followed, “without the permission of the abbot and his monks”; these words have been deleted because they are absent from the Councils of Carthage and Africa and from most ancient manuscripts of Gratian. Added, “a person”: same editions.] [Note: “only”: collected editions.]

## DISTINCTION LIX

[Col. 0313]

[Col. 0313A] **GRATIAN.** Likewise, those who have not been trained in ecclesiastical disciplines and tested by the approval of time are not to aspire to the supreme priesthood. Thus Pope Zosimus says to Hesychius, bishop of Salona, letter I. [Note: Written in 418.—Anselm, book 6, c. 28. Ivo, Decretum, part 5, c. 102.—Above, Distinction 36, c. 2.—In the Basel edition this chapter is moved to the end of the Distinction.]

### C. I. One not trained in ecclesiastical disciplines is not to aspire to the supreme priesthood.

[Col. 0313B] One who has not been trained through the sequence of ecclesiastical disciplines and educated for divine service through the testing of time is by no means to presume to aspire to the church’s supreme priesthood. [Note: “nor”: collected editions.] Not only is his ambition to be held ineffective, but his ordainers also are to be deprived of the order which they believed they could presumptuously confer without observing the sequence, contrary to the precepts of the Fathers. [Note: “so that”: Collection of Hispana.]

[Col. 0313C]

### C. II. No one is to enter the priestly office unless tested through each individual grade.

The same, in the same letter. [Note: This chapter was formerly attributed to Urban. The attribution has been corrected from most ancient copies of Gratian, for it is found in the same letter.] [Note: Anselm, same place.]

If secular offices grant the principal position not to persons who have merely entered the threshold of public service, but to those tested through individual grades [Note: “principal”: collected editions, from the original and Anselm; “many”: original and Anselm], who is so arrogant and so shameless as to desire at once to be commander in the heavenly militia—which ought to be weighed more carefully and tested like gold by repeated fires—when he has not first been a recruit, and to wish to teach before learning? Let him become accustomed in the Lord’s camp, first in the grade of reader, to the rudiments of divine service; [Note: “chosen”: Basel edition; “rudiments”: Isidore, Merida] nor let him consider it lowly to become successively an exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, and deacon—not by a leap, but at the prescribed times established by the ordination of the elders. Then let such a person approach the summit of the priesthood that both his age fulfills the title and the periods of service already performed attest his merit of uprightness. Thereafter he will rightly have to hope for the position of supreme pontiff.

This is brought about by the excessive laxity of our fellow priests, [Note: “priests”: Basel edition] who seek the display of a multitude and think that some dignity is gained for themselves from this crowd. Hence a numerous populace of such persons is found everywhere, even in places where there is solitude, [Note: “multiplicity”: collected editions] while they desire to extend themselves through parishes, [Note: added, “in”: same editions] or lavish holy orders upon those to whom they can offer nothing else. [Note: added, “through”: same editions.] This must always be judged strictly. For everything great is rare. [Note: added, “always”: Basel edition.]

[Col. 0315A]

### C. III. No layman, whatever his merit, is to aspire immediately to the supreme priesthood.

Likewise Gregory, book VII of the Register, letter 110. [Note: Letter 106, written to Syagrius of Autun in 599; book 9, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 6, c. 32. Polycarpus, book 2, title 1.]

We receive with no less worthy detestation the report which has reached us: certain men, inflated by desire for honor, [Note: “inflamed”: collected editions] are tonsured when bishops die, suddenly become priests from laymen, and shamelessly assume leadership of the religious profession before they have even learned to be soldiers. [Note: added, “and suddenly”: same editions.] What do we think such men will offer to those subject to them, when before they have reached the threshold of discipleship they are not afraid to hold the position of masters? It is therefore necessary that, however blameless a person’s merit may be, he first be exercised in ecclesiastical offices through the distinct ecclesiastical orders. [Note: “be exercised through the distinct offices of ecclesiastical order”: Anselm; “exercise himself”: collected editions.]

[Col. 0315B]

### C. IV. One not trained in ecclesiastical disciplines is not to aspire to the supreme priesthood.

Likewise Celestine to the bishops of Gaul, letter II, chapter 3. [Note: Written in 428.—Burchard, book 1, c. 18. Ivo, Decretum, part 5, c. 72.]

We have learned, dearest brothers, that certain bishops have been ordained and raised to the summit of so great a dignity without having been established in any ecclesiastical orders, [Note: “appointed”: collected editions] in contravention of the decrees of the Fathers, by the usurpation of one who acknowledges that he did this. Yet the episcopate ought to be reached through those grades concerning which very frequent safeguards have been established, [Note: “to be reached”: same editions] so that persons initiated in lesser offices may be strengthened for greater ones. [Note: “in lesser”: collected editions; “from lesser”: Hispana Collection.] For whoever desires to be a teacher must first be a disciple, so that he may teach what he has learned. Every course of life confirms itself by this reasoning in relation to the goal toward which it tends. [Note: “this” is absent from the Paris and Lyons editions; “which”: collected editions except the first Basel edition.] One who has given no attention to letters cannot be a teacher of letters. One who has not advanced through every period of service to merit cannot reach the rank merited by service. Is the priesthood alone, I ask, more worthless than these things because it is granted more easily, when it is fulfilled with greater difficulty? [Note: “to whom”: Basel; “why”: other collected editions.]

## DISTINCTION LX

[Col. 0315]

[Col. 0315B] **GRATIAN.**

Behold, it has been shown in part who can be advanced to the order of the priesthood and who cannot. Now it must be considered from which orders persons ought to be chosen as archpriest, provost, bishop, or archbishop. [Col. 0315C]

It was decreed concerning these matters in the council of Pope Urban, held in Auvergne:

> [Note: In the manuscript chapters of the Council of Clermont held by Urban II (which are not decrees of the council itself, but certain summaries of them), the following is read in the third chapter, relevant to the present canon: “No one is to be made dean in a church unless he is a priest; no one archdeacon unless he is a Levite [i.e., deacon].” The canons of the Council of Clermont were published entire from the manuscript volume of Cencius Camerarius in Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, vol. 20.]
>
> [Col. 0315] The Council of Clermont was held in 1095.

### C. I. An archpriest, dean, or archdeacon is not to be ordained unless he is a deacon or priest.

No bishop shall presume to appoint an archdeacon in his church unless he is a deacon, nor to ordain an archpriest or dean unless they are priests. In order that this may be observed more strictly, we prohibit and forbid it by apostolic authority.

### C. II. No one is to be ordained provost or archpriest unless a priest; no one archdeacon unless a deacon. Likewise Pope Calixtus [II].

> [Note: Both rubric and chapter have been corrected from manuscript codices.]
>
> [Col. 0316D] codices.
>
> [Note: At the First Lateran Council, held in 1123.]

No one is to be ordained provost

> [Note: Added: “no one archbishop”: the collective editions.]

no one archpriest,

[Col. 0316B] no one dean unless a priest

> [Note: Added: “or deacon”: the same editions.]

and no one archdeacon unless a deacon.

### C. III. On the same matter. Likewise Innocent II, at the Roman Council, c. 10.

> [Note: The Second Lateran Council was held in 1139. It agrees with c. 8 of the Council of Rheims in Ivo’s *Panormia*, book 8, c. 140. C. III.]

Moreover, we renew and command that no one be ordained archdeacon

[Col. 0316C] or dean unless he is a deacon or priest. But archdeacons, deans, or provosts who stand below the aforesaid orders, if they disdain to be ordained through disobedience, are to be deprived of the honor which they have received. Moreover, we forbid those offices to be granted to young men, or to persons below the sacred orders, unless they are distinguished by prudence and merit of life.

**Gratian.** One of these provisions was enacted because of the insolence of certain persons who, having obtained the name of provost, despise the office, unwilling to become priests. Otherwise it would be pointless, since even persons in the subdiaconate may be chosen bishops, according to this statement of Pope Urban:

> [Note: Urban: In c. *A multis*, X, *On age and qualification* [Col. 0315: and c. 3, Comp. III, on the same title], this is cited as a decree of Urban I. But in Ivo and the *Panormia* it is from the Synod of Benevento, held in the time of Victor III, whom Urban II succeeded. For Urban I preceded the Nicene synod by approximately a hundred years.]

[Col. 0317A]

### C. IV. No one is to be chosen bishop unless he stands in sacred orders.

No one

> [Note: C. 1 of the Council of Benevento, held under Urban II in 1091. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 5; *Decree*, part 5, c. 72.]

is to be chosen bishop unless he has been found to be living religiously in sacred orders. By sacred orders we mean the diaconate and priesthood. For the primitive Church is recorded to have possessed these alone. But, since subdeacons also minister at the altars,

[Col. 0318A] we permit them when necessity requires, provided that they are of proven

> [Note: Added: “life”: the collective editions.]

religious character and learning. Yet we permit this only with the authorization

> [Note: “Authorization”: Thus altered from the cited chapter *A multis*, Ivo, and the *Panormia*, although in old manuscripts of Gratian [Col. 0317: and in the collective editions] one also reads: “learning.”]

of the Roman Pontiff

> [Note: Added: “care”: Basel edition. “Pontiff, or with”: the remaining collective editions.]

or metropolitan.

> [Note: Added: “firmly”: the collective editions.]

**Gratian.** The other provision—that no one be chosen bishop or archbishop unless established in sacred orders—was enacted for the dignity of the order.

## DISTINCTION LXI

[Col. 0317]

[Col. 0317A] **GRATIAN.**

**Part I.** Likewise, laymen are not to be chosen bishops, but must first be tested through the individual orders.

Accordingly Gregory, to Brunhild, Queen of the Franks, book VII of the *Register*, letter 113:

> [Note: Letter 109, written in 599, book 9, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 6, c. 77 (75); *Polycarpus*, book 2, title 1.]

### C. I. Priests are not to be ordained from laymen.

The priestly office in your regions has, as we have learned, been brought to such

> [Note: “Such ambition”: collective editions except Lyons II, III, and Antwerp.]

ambition that priests are suddenly—an exceedingly grave matter—ordained from laymen.

### C. II. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Hormisdas to bishops established throughout Spain, letter III, c. 1.

> [Note: Written in 517; Anselm, book 6, c. 22; *Polycarpus*, same place.]

In choosing

> [Note: Added: “or consecrating”: collective editions.]

priests, care must be manifest. For those who must preside over persons needing correction ought to be blameless. And below:

§ 1. He to whom the helm of the Church is entrusted ought to demonstrate his life by a long testing.

> [Note: “Ought”: *Coll. Hisp.*]

### C. III. On the same matter. The same, continuously in the same place.

> [Note: In most old manuscripts of Gratian, this chapter is joined to the preceding one, as it is in Hormisdas’s letter itself.]
>
> [Note: Anselm and *Polycarpus*, same place.]

[Col. 0317C] We do not deny that among laymen there are dispositions pleasing to God; but the institutions of the faithful seek for themselves tested soldiers.

> [Note: “Faithful”: *Coll. Hisp.*; Anselm.]
>
> [Note: “First”: absent from the same sources.]

Each person must learn before teaching, and should offer others, rather than receive from others, an example of religious conduct in his own person. The one who must pray for the people ought to be more upright than the people. Religious worship must be handed down through long observance, so that he may shine forth and,

> [Note: Added: “for a long time”: *Coll. Hisp.*]

while being trained by service in clerical duties, may minister; thus, when brought to the summit of a venerable rank, he may show what fruit humility bears. And below:

[Col. 0318A] § 1. We forbid not only anyone to be consecrated from among laymen,

> [Note: “To consecrate”: collective editions.]

but neither may any profane and reckless offender, even from among penitents, aspire to a rank of this kind.

> [Note: “Nor”: *Coll. Hisp.*; Anselm.]

Let pardon granted be enough for one who asks it.

> [Note: “That pardon be granted”: collective editions; Böhm.]

With what conscience can a man absolve an accused person when he knows that he himself has confessed his sins publicly, with the people as witnesses?

> [Note: “His own sins”: Basel edition; “his sins”: the remaining collective editions.]

[Col. 0318B] For who would venerate as a bishop one whom he saw lying prostrate only a little before?

> [Note: “Sees”: Paris and Lyons editions; “had seen”: remaining collective editions.]

A man bearing the stain of a memorable

> [Note: “Bearing”: collective editions.]
>
> [Note: “Memorable”: *Coll. Hisp.*; Anselm reads “lamentable.”]

crime does not possess the bright dignity of the priesthood.

### C. IV. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Innocent to Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage, letter XII.

> [Note: Written in 416; Anselm, book 6, c. 34; *Polycarpus*, same place. In the Basel edition, § 4 of the following chapter has been inserted as the fourth chapter.]

It is pitiable for one to become a teacher who was never a disciple; for one to become high priest who has never served a priest in any rank.

> [Note: “Had served”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.]

### C. V. On the same matter. Likewise Bishop Leo to the African bishops, letter LXXXV, otherwise LXXVII, c. 1.

> [Note: Letter 12, written in 446, Ballerini edition; *Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 43, c. 34; Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, c. 105.]

We are amazed that among you, through the occasion of unsettled times,

[Col. 0318C] either the presumption of aspirants or popular tumult has prevailed so greatly that the pastoral eminence and government of the Church have been entrusted to any unworthy persons

> [Note: “To any persons”: collective editions.]

who stand far outside priestly merit. This is not to provide for peoples,

> [Note: “For the people”: the same editions with Ivo.]

but to injure them; not to furnish governance, but to increase danger.

> [Note: “Increase”: Basel reads “carry on.”]

For the integrity of rulers is the safety of subjects; and where obedience is secure, there is a sound form of teaching.

§ 1. But the authority

> [Note: “Authority”: Most manuscript codices of Gratian read “Authority is” [Col. 0318D: Col. 0317: hence in the Basel edition this section is marked as a *Palea*]. And below: “But if,” etc. This seems to have occurred because below, Causa 1, question 1, c. *Principatus*, this sentence is cited, as is noted in the gloss, which is found also in those old copies in which no other glosses occur.]
>
> [Note: Anselm, book 6, c. 20; cf. Causa 1, question 1, c. 25.]

which either sedition has extorted or ambition has seized, even if it does not offend in morals and actions,

[Col. 0319A]

> [Note: “Does not show”: Basel edition.]

is nevertheless pernicious in the example of its own beginning. And it is difficult for things which have been begun from an evil beginning to be carried through to a good end.

But if in every rank of the Church provision and informed care must be taken that in the Lord’s house nothing may be disordered or perverse, how much more must effort be made that no error occur in the choice of the person who is set above every rank? For the condition and order of the whole household of the Lord

> [Note: Absent from *Coll. Hisp.*]

> [Note: “Is found”: collective editions from Ivo; Anselm reads “is.”]

in the head. Where

> [Note: Anselm, book 6, c. 35.]

is that command of the blessed Apostle Paul, uttered through the Spirit of God, by which, in the person of Timothy, the whole body of Christ’s priests is instructed, and therefore

> [Note: “Therefore”: collective editions; absent from Anselm and the original in Ballerini.]

said to each one of us:

> [Note: 1 Timothy 5:22.]

“Lay hands suddenly on no one, nor share

[Col. 0319B]

> [Note: “Share”: collective editions.]

in another’s sins”? What

> [Note: This same manuscript reading has: “What is it to lay hands quickly,” etc. And below, “For just as”; in the margin is cited below, Distinction 78, c. *Quid est manus*.]
>
> [Note: Cf. Distinction 78, c. 3.]

is it to lay hands quickly, except to confer priestly honor on persons not yet proved—before the maturity

> [Note: “Age of maturity”: the original; Ivo.]

of age, before the time of examination, before the merit

> [Note: “Time of obedience”: Basel; “the deserved time of obedience”: remaining collective editions; “merit of obedience”: original.]

of labor, before experience in discipline? And what is it to share in another’s sins except to make the ordainer such as that person

> [Note: The source marks *ille*, “that person.”]

§ 3. For just as

> [Note: Anselm, book 6, c. 21.]

the man who maintains sound judgment in choosing a priest gains for himself the fruit of a good work,

> [Note: “Examines”: *Coll. Hisp.*]
>
> [Note: “A priest”: collective editions.]

so he who raises an unworthy person to the fellowship of his own rank inflicts grave harm upon himself. For in no person may what is contained in general enactments be disregarded, nor may that honor be thought lawful which has been conferred contrary to the commands of divine law.

> [Note: *Coll. Hisp.* reads: “conferred by transgression.”]

[Col. 0319C] And below:

§ 4. Rightly, when the venerable enactments of the holy

> [Note: “Blessed”: same source; Ivo; collective editions.]

Fathers spoke concerning the election of priests,

> [Note: “Of a priest”: Basel.]

they judged fit for sacred administrations only those whose entire age, from boyhood onward to more mature

> [Note: “More advanced”: *Coll. Hisp.*]

years, had passed through the stages of ecclesiastical discipline. Thus a prior life might provide testimony for each person, and there could be no doubt about the advancement of one to whom the reward of a higher place was due for many labors, chaste morals, and vigorous actions.

> [Note: “Actions”: collective editions.]

§ 5. For if it is unworthy to attain worldly honors without the support of time and without merit of labor, and those whom proofs of uprightness do not support are usually branded as ambitious, how careful and prudent must the administration of divine gifts and heavenly dignities be?

[Col. 0320A]

### C. VI. None are to be chosen to the episcopate except those commended by a proven life. Likewise from the Council of Laodicea, c. 12.

> [Note: Held between 347 and 381; above, Distinction 24, c. 4, from Dionysius’s translation.]

A bishop ought not to be appointed to the leadership of a church apart from the judgment of metropolitan and neighboring bishops. Nor are any to be chosen except those commended long beforehand by a well-known and proven life,

> [Note: “Long beforehand by a proven”: *Coll. Hisp.*]

and likewise proved, by their own manner of life, in speech of faith and right conduct.

> [Note: “Reason”: same source and collective editions.]
>
> [Note: “For their manner of life”: collective editions.]

[Col. 0320B]

### C. VII. On the same matter. Likewise Celestine to the bishops of Apulia and Calabria, letter III, c. 2.

> [Note: Written in 429; Anselm, book 7, c. 33; *Polycarpus*, book 2, title 1.]

What advantage will it be that clerics have served through every stage and spent their whole lives in the Lord’s camp, if those who are to preside

> [Note: “Those who are to become priests”: collective editions; the original reads: “if those who are to preside over them.”]

are sought from among laymen? They, being idle in secular life and ignorant of the whole ecclesiastical order, ambitiously seek, with excessive desire, to leap by a precipitate

> [Note: “Perverse”: collective editions except Argentinensis and Basel.]

bound into another’s honor and, trampling underfoot reverence for ecclesiastical discipline, to pass into another kind of life. Therefore, dearest brethren, we, who guard the helm of our law—that is, of the canons—must oppose such persons,

> [Note: “We shall oppose”: Lyons II.]

and by these letters admonish your brotherhood not to admit a layman to clerical rank

[Col. 0320C] and thereby allow something to happen which both deceives him and gives him grounds by which he becomes guilty of the established decretals.

> [Note: The original reads: “guilty of the established decretals.”]

### C. VIII. The helm of the Church is not to be entrusted to the inexperienced and unskilled. Likewise Leo I, letter LXXXV, otherwise LXXXVII, c. 1, to the African bishops.

> [Note: Letter 12, written about 446, Ballerini edition; *Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 43, c. 35; Anselm, book 6, c. 138 (136); Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, c. 105.]

We decree

> [Note: “We decree”: In the letter itself, the words of this chapter are joined to the final words of the preceding chapter *We are amazed*, above, as follows: “how careful and prudent must the administration of divine gifts and heavenly dignities be, lest apostolic and canonical decrees be violated in any respect, and lest the Church of the Lord,” etc.; the whole sentence is expressed as a question.]

that apostolic and canonical decrees be violated in no respect, and that the Church of the Lord not be entrusted for governance to persons ignorant of lawful institutions and of all

[Col. 0321A] humility, who wish to take their beginning from the highest places, not to receive advancement from the lowest.

> [Note: “From the weak”: Böhm.]

**Gratian.** By all these authorities laymen are forbidden to be chosen to the episcopate.

**Part II.** § 1. On the other hand, Saint Nicholas was chosen from a layman as bishop; Saint Severus was taken from the wool trade and made archbishop; Saint Ambrose, though not yet baptized, was chosen archbishop. § 2. But it must be understood that ecclesiastical prohibitions have their own causes; when those causes cease, the prohibitions themselves cease. For the reason why a layman was not to be chosen bishop was that lay life, not trained in ecclesiastical disciplines

[Col. 0321B] in due sequence, does not know how to offer others examples of religious life which it has not itself learned by experience. Therefore, when any layman surpasses clerical life by the merit of his perfection, his election may be held valid by the example of Saints Nicholas, Severus, and Ambrose.

### C. IX. Accordingly Ambrose himself, in letter LXXXII to the people of Vercelli, says of himself:

> [Note: In several old copies this chapter is joined to the preceding one. For Gratian, as he often does, intended to give the sense rather than report all Saint Ambrose’s exact words in the same order. The complete passage is as follows:
>
> [Col. 0321D] “How I resisted being ordained! Finally, when I was compelled, I at least sought that my ordination be delayed. But resistance did not prevail; compulsion prevailed. Yet the western bishops approved my ordination by their judgment, and the eastern bishops even by their example. And yet a neophyte is forbidden to be ordained, lest he be puffed up by pride. If delay was lacking in the ordination, that is due to the force of the one compelling; if the humility fitting for priesthood is not lacking, then, where the cause does not adhere, the fault is not imputed.”]
>
> [Note: Written about 396.]

A neophyte is forbidden to be ordained lest he be puffed up with pride. But if the humility fitting for priesthood is not lacking, where the cause does not adhere,

> [Note: “Adheres”: collective editions.]

the fault is not imputed. Thus the western bishops approved my ordination by their judgment, and the eastern bishops also by their example.

[Col. 0321C]

### C. X. A learned man from the forum or from public administration may be requested as bishop. Likewise, the following from the Council of Sardica, c. 13, is raised as an objection.

> [Note: Held in 344; Burchard, book 1, c. 27; Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, c. 71.]

Bishop Hosius said: “I judge that this too must be considered with the greatest care: if perhaps a wealthy layman

> [Note: “Layman”: This word is absent from the council, but has not been removed because of the gloss.]

or a learned man from the forum

> [Note: “From the forum or from public administration”: in Greek there is only ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγορᾶς, “from the marketplace/forum.”]

or from public administration

> [Note: “From an administrator”: original.]

is requested as bishop, he is not to be ordained until he has first discharged the office of reader and the service of deacon

> [Note: “Diaconate”: Argentinensis and Basel.]

or priest,

> [Note: “Priesthood”: Argentinensis, Basel, Paris, and Lyons I.]

and then rises through the individual grades, if worthy, to the summit of the episcopate.”

**Part III. Gratian.** But to be requested is one thing, to be

[Col. 0322A] chosen another. One bound by the obligations of a civic office is requested from the emperor; a cleric of another city, from his bishop. But no one is chosen unless he is established in sacred orders. For an election is made with the solemnity of a decree confirmed by the subscriptions of all; a request, however, by a simple petition. Saint Gregory indicates this distinction in the *Register*, book II, letter 19, writing to Bishop Benenatus:

> [Note: Letter 28, written in 592, book 2, Maurist edition.]

### C. XI. The election of a bishop must be made with the solemnity of a decree confirmed by the subscriptions of all.

When a bishop has been requested, let him come to us to be consecrated with the solemnity of a decree confirmed by everyone’s subscriptions, and with the testimony of your charitable letters.

> [Note: “To be consecrated”: collective editions.]

**Gratian.** Thus Saint Ambrose, before receiving baptism,

[Col. 0322B] was requested by the emperor, not chosen.

> [Note: Ambrose: That the synod, rather than the emperor, chose Ambrose is shown in c. *Valentinianus*, below, Distinction 63. Ambrose himself recounts aspects of his election in *On Duties*, book 1, c. 1; *On Penance*, book 2, c. 8; and in the letter to the Vercellians.]

**Part IV. Gratian.** Likewise, clerics of another church are not to be preferred in an election to those who serve well in their own church.

Accordingly Pope Celestine, to the bishops of Gaul, letter II, c. 4:

> [Note: Written in 428; Anselm, book 6, c. 11; Deusdedit, part 1; *Polycarpus*, book 2, title 1.]

### C. XII. Strangers are not to be preferred to those who have earned their rank in their own churches.

Foreigners and strangers, and persons previously unknown, are not to be preferred to clerics

> [Note: “Clerics” is also missing in the collection of Anselm.]

who have earned their rank in their own churches, to the exclusion of those who are well commended by the testimony of their fellow citizens.

> [Note: “Unknown”: collective editions.]
>
> [Note: “Testimony”: the same editions.]

### C. XIII. On the same matter. The same, in the same letter, c. 5.

> [Note: Burchard, book 1, c. 7; Anselm, book 6, c. 25; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 7; *Decree*, part 5, c. 61; Deusdedit; *Polycarpus*, same place.]

No bishop is to be imposed upon unwilling people. The consent and desire of clergy, people, and order are to be sought.

> [Note: From “clergy” through “Then” these words have been added from the original and are cited below, Distinction 63, c. *Cleri*.]

Then someone from another church is to be chosen only if no worthy person can be found among the clergy

> [Note: “Clerics”: original.]

of the very city whose bishop is to be ordained—a situation which we do not believe can occur.

> [Note: “Whose”: collective editions.]

For the local candidates must first be rejected before anyone from another church may deservedly be preferred. Let every person have the fruit of his own service in the church in which he has spent his life through every office.

> [Note: “Spends”: Argentinensis; “will have spent”: Basel.]

Let no one intrude into another’s service in a foreign church, nor dare to claim for himself the reward due to another. Let clerics have the freedom to resist

[Col. 0323A]

> [Note: The original in Coustant and Isidore Mercator, Ivo, collective editions except Lyons II and III, and Böhm reads “to resist”; *Coll. Hisp.* reads “to oppose.”]

if they see themselves burdened, and let them not fear to reject those whom they recognize are being thrust upon them indirectly.

> [Note: “Whom they see”: collective editions from Anselm.]
>
> [Note: “Of strangers”: *Coll. Hisp.*]

For although they ought not to have either the reward due to them

> [Note: Added: “of the episcopate”: collective editions.]

or unrestricted judgment concerning the man who is to govern them.

### C. XIV. PALEA

> [Note: This *Palea* is absent from all collated old copies of Gratian. It appears in the Rule of Saint Benedict, from which some readings have been corrected.]
>
> [Note: From the Rule of Benedict, c. 64. This *Palea* is not found in the Basel edition.]

“In the appointment of a provost

> [Note: “Abbot”: original.]

the following principle must always be observed: the person appointed should be the one whom the entire harmonious community, in the fear of God, or even a part of the community, however small, with sounder counsel, has chosen for itself. The person to be appointed is to be chosen for merit of life and wisdom, even if he is last

> [Note: “Last in the order of the community”: collective editions.]

in the order of the community. But if the entire community, by an equal counsel, chooses a person who consents to its vices—which God forbid—and if the vices themselves in some way come to the knowledge of the bishop,

[Col. 0323B] to whose diocese that place belongs, or to neighboring provosts or Christians,

> [Note: The original reads: “or becomes known to abbots or neighboring Christians.”]

let them prevent the evil men’s consent from prevailing, and appoint

> [Note: Added: “and let the bishop appoint with others”: collective editions.]

a worthy steward for the house of God.”

### C. XV. On the same matter. Likewise Gregory to the clergy and noble citizens of Naples, book VIII of the *Register*, letter 40.

> [Note: Letter, written in 600, book 10, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 6, c. 13.]

Let it be the concern of your zeal to provide also another suitable person, so that, if perhaps Peter, whom you assert has been chosen by you, does not seem fit for this rank, there may be someone

> [Note: Added: “someone”: Basel.]

to whom your choice can turn.

> [Note: “To whom your … turn,” etc.: collective editions except Lyons II, III, and Antwerp.]

For it will be a grave disgrace to that clergy if, should this man perhaps not be approved, they say that they have no other person who ought to be chosen.

[Col. 0323C]

### C. XVI. On the same matter. Likewise Gregory to Bishop Barbarus, book XI, letter 16.

> [Note: Written in 603, book 3, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 6, c. 26; Deusdedit, part 1.]

A report sent to us has made known the death of Victor, bishop of the city of Panormus.

> [Note: “Makes known”: Argentinensis.]

Therefore we formally entrust to your brotherhood the task of visiting that church, now deprived of visitation.

> [Note: “To you”: Basel.]

You must perform it in such a way that no one presumes anything from the advancement of the clerics,

> [Note: “Revenues”: Böhm.]

income, furnishings, ministries, or anything whatever belonging to the patrimony of that church.

> [Note: “Your brotherhood … hasten”: collective editions.]

Therefore your charity shall hasten to the aforesaid church

[Col. 0324A]

> [Note: Added: Anselm.]

and, through constant exhortations, urgently admonish the clergy and people of that church to seek, laying aside partisan zeal and with one and the same consent, a priest to be set over them who can be found worthy of so great a ministry and in no way rejected by the venerable canons. When he has been requested, let him come to us to be consecrated with the solemnity of a decree confirmed by the subscriptions of all, and with the testimony of your charitable letters.

§ 1. We also admonish

> [Note: “Admonishing”: original; Anselm.]

your brotherhood not to permit anyone to be chosen from another church, unless perhaps no person worthy of the episcopate can be found among the clergy of that city in which you are carrying out the office of visitation—which we do not believe can occur.

> [Note: “Can”: collective editions.]

Above all, you shall ensure that no lay person, whatever his manner of life or merit, presumes to aspire to this office.

> [Note: “To this”: collective editions from Anselm.]
>
> [Col. 0323D] “That no one aspire to this”: A similar clause occurs also in the immediately following letter 17 of the same book; in book 2, indiction 10, letter 19, to Bishop Benenatus; in letter 26, to Bishop John of Squillace; and in book 7, indiction 2, letter 25, to Bishop Fortunatus of Naples. By comparison with old manuscripts of these letters, this passage has been corrected so that it does not differ greatly from Gratian’s ancient reading. Yet in more recent editions of Saint Gregory’s letters, the cited letter here reads: “that you permit no lay person, of whatever manner of life or merit, to aspire to it.”]

[Col. 0324B] lest their effort prove ineffective

> [Note: The collective editions from Anselm read: “lest those persons also fail to attain the object [Basel: effect] of their desire.”]

and you incur, God forbid, danger to your rank.

> [Note: “You”: original, Anselm, collective editions, and Böhm.]

But we permit any monasteries situated within its parish to remain under your care and administration until a proper bishop has been ordained there.

### C. XVII. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Pelagius [II] to Eucarpos, Bishop of Messana.

> [Note: This letter, written between 580 and 590, was published by Baluze among the *Miscellanea*, vol. 5, p. 467; Anselm, book 6, c. 44 (41).]

We entrust to you the visitation of the Church of Catania, whose bishop, we have learned from the report of its clergy, has passed from this life. For it is impossible for us, in that province, namely in the region of Syracuse, to commit matters pertaining to God

> [Note: “The Lord”: Basel.]

to anyone else, unless perhaps God should now choose through you in the Church of Catania such a person in whose conscience we can be secure, so that we may remove these labors a little from you. Therefore let your charity go at once to the aforesaid Church of Catania, and, with God’s help, urge and persuade the election of a man from the clergy who has neither wife nor children, nor any crime contrary to the canons; then send him at once to the city of Rome with a decree and an attestation in your report.

[Col. 0325A]

### C. XVIII. He who is chosen bishop must not be guilty of crimes which the sacred law punishes by death. Likewise Gregory to Bishop Passivus, book X, letter 13.

> [Note: Letter 12, written in 602, to Passivus [the collective editions read Passinus], Bishop of Fermo, book 12, Maurist edition.]

Your brotherhood knows well

> [Note: “Your”: collective editions.]

how long Abruzzo has been deprived of pastoral care. There we long sought someone who ought to be ordained and could by no means find him. But because Opportunus is highly commended to me for his character, devotion to psalmody, and love of prayer,

> [Note: The original reads: “commended, religious”; collective editions read “commended, and is said to lead a religious life.”]

and is said in every respect to lead a religious life, we wish your brotherhood to have him come to it and admonish him concerning his soul, so that he may grow in good pursuits. And if no crimes stand against him which, according to the rule of sacred law, are to be punished by death,

> [Note: “Stand”: collective editions except Argentinensis, Basel, and Nuremberg.]

then he is to be exhorted to become either a monk or a subdeacon under you; and after some time, if it pleases God, he ought himself to be promoted to pastoral care.

[Col. 0325B]

**Gratian.** The person to whom visitation is entrusted must not allow anyone to presume anything concerning the goods of the same church.

Accordingly Gregory to Bishop Gaudentius, book IV, letter 12:

> [Note: Letter 13, written in 595, book 5, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 5, c. 12 (13).]

### C. XIX. A visitor entrusted with the visitation of a church must allow no one to presume anything concerning its goods.

Since Festus,

> [Note: “Fuscus”: original.]

bishop of the Church of Capua, died in the city of Rome, it was our concern—such care as we extend to all churches—to send these letters to your brotherhood,

> [Note: “To your brotherhood”: collective editions from Anselm.]

that you should come as visitor of the aforesaid church. Yet you must not allow anyone to presume anything from the clerics’ revenues,

> [Note: “Advancements”: the same editions.]

income, furnishings, ministries, or whatever may be found to belong to that place;

> [Note: “May be able”: the same editions from Anselm.]

[Col. 0326B] rather, it is fitting that you display every vigilance and precaution concerning the clergy and people of that church, so that they may diligently and devoutly serve in vigils and ecclesiastical worship.

## DISTINCTION LXII

[Col. 0325]

[Col. 0325B] **GRATIAN.**

**Part I.** It has been briefly shown from which orders persons are to be chosen for which grades. Now it must be considered by whom they are to be chosen and consecrated. The election of clerics is the petition of the people.

> [Note: “Is”: In the commonly circulated codices there followed “the consent of the prince.” In manuscripts [Col. 0326D] there is partly “the consent of the people” [Col. 0325: Basel edition], partly “the petition of the people”; the text has therefore been corrected accordingly.]

Accordingly Pope Leo to Rusticus, Bishop of Narbonne, letter XC, otherwise XCII, c. 1:

> [Note: Letter 167, written in 458 or 459, Ballerini edition; Burchard, book 1, c. 11; Anselm, book 6, c. 75 (73); Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, c. 65; *Polycarpus*, book 2, title 1.]

### C. I. Those are not to be counted among bishops who are neither chosen by clerics nor sought by the people.

No reason permits those to be counted among bishops

[Col. 0325C] who have neither been chosen by clerics nor sought by the people nor consecrated, with the metropolitan’s judgment, by the bishops of the province.

> [Note: “Fellow-provincial”: collective editions.]

And since a question often arises concerning improperly received honor,

> [Note: “Arises”: the same editions.]

who can doubt that what is not shown to have been conferred should not be granted to these persons?

> [Note: “By these”: the same editions.]
>
> [Note: *Coll. Hisp.* reads: “nor is shown to have been conferred.”]

But if any clerics have been ordained by these pseudo-bishops in those churches, etc., as below in the case concerning simoniacs. [Causa 1, question 1, c. 40.]

### C. II. The people ought not to lead but to follow. Likewise Pope Celestine to the bishops of Apulia and Calabria, letter III, c. 3.

> [Note: Written in 429; Burchard, book 15, c. 13; Ivo, *Decree*, part 16, c. 14; Deusdedit, part 1; *Polycarpus*, book 6, title 1.]

The people must be taught, not followed; and we too,

> [Note: “We too”: collective editions.]

if they do not know, ought to remind them what is lawful and what is not lawful, rather than give our consent to them. But whoever attempts to try what has been forbidden will find that the censure of the Apostolic See is by no means lacking.

> [Note: “Failing”: Basel.]

For what we do not correct by the authority of admonition alone, we must punish by severity appropriate to the rules. Therefore we wish this to become known throughout all churches

> [Note: “Here”: Basel.]

which lack their own rulers,

> [Note: “To become known”: Basel and Lyons II.]

so that no one, perhaps flattering himself with some hope,

[Col. 0326C]

> [Note: “Flatteries”: collective editions.]

may deceive himself.

**Gratian.** But unless a person has been canonically chosen, he ought not to be consecrated.

Accordingly Pope Calixtus II:

> [Note: C. 10 of the First Lateran Council, held in 1123.]

### C. III. No one is to be consecrated bishop unless canonically chosen.

Let no one consecrate as bishop anyone who has not been canonically chosen. If this is presumed, both consecrator and consecrated person are to be deposed without hope of restoration.

> [Note: “And”: absent from the collective editions except the first Lyons, Lyons II, III, and Antwerp editions.]

## DISTINCTION LXIII

[Col. 0327]

[Col. 0327A] **GRATIAN.**

**Part I.** Laymen, however, must in no way insert themselves into an election.

Accordingly, Pope Hadrian, in the Eighth Synod held at Constantinople under him [c. 22] [Note: [Col. 0327D] Here are cited certain portions of canon 22 of the Eighth Synod, held under Pope Hadrian II and rendered into Latin by Anastasius the Librarian.] [Note: [Col. 0327] Held in 870.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 23; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, c. 8; *Decretum*, pt. 5, c. 222; Deusdedit, pt. 2.]:

### C. I. Laymen are not to involve themselves in the election of pontiffs.

No lay ruler or magnate is to involve himself [Note: [Col. 0327] Basel adds: “himself”] in the election or promotion of a patriarch, metropolitan, or any bishop, lest disorderly and inappropriate confusion or contention arise *from this* [Note: [Col. 0327] Added: “election or”: collected editions and *Panormia*]. This is especially so since it is not fitting that any person in authority, or any other layman, should possess any power in such matters. And below [Note: [Col. 0327] Compare the following chapter.—Polycarpus, bk. 2, tit. 1.]:

Whoever *however* among secular rulers and magnates, or any layman of another rank, attempts to act against the common, harmonious, and canonical election of the ecclesiastical order [Col. 0327B] is to be anathema until he obeys and assents to whatever the Church shows itself to will concerning the election and ordination of its own prelate.

### C. II. On the same matter. Likewise from the Eighth Synod, first session [Note: [Col. 0327] Compare *Collectio tripartita*, pt. 2, tit. 23, c. 2, and the collection cited, bk. 1.].

Pope Hadrian II—following the arrangement made by his predecessor Nicholas—sent his legates, namely Donatus, bishop of Ostia; Stephen, bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, deacon of the holy Roman Church, to the emperor Basil and to his sons Constantine and Leo, Augusti, at Constantinople. With them also went Anastasius, librarian of the Roman see, skilled in both languages, Greek and Latin. When the synod had assembled [Col. 0327C]—which those attending called the eighth universal synod—they settled the schism arising from the deposition of Ignatius and the ordination of Photius [Note: [Col. 0327] “Photinus,” and below “Photinus”: collected editions], anathematizing Photius and restoring Ignatius. There it was decreed as follows:

In agreement with the earlier councils, this holy and universal synod defines that the consecrations and promotions of bishops are to be carried out by the election of the clergy [Note: [Col. 0327] “Of the clergy” is absent from the original and from Anselm] and by the decree of the college of bishops [Note: [Col. 0327] “And of the college of bishops”: Ivo and the collected editions], and establishes and lawfully promulgates this [Note: [Col. 0327] “Defined—promulgated”: in the same place]. It decrees [Note: [Col. 0327] The word “and” is absent from the Argenteus edition] that no lay ruler or magnate is to involve himself in the election or promotion of a patriarch, metropolitan, [Col. 0328A] or any bishop, lest disorderly and inappropriate confusion or contention arise from this [Note: [Col. 0327] Added: “election or”: collected editions and *Panormia*] [Note: [Col. 0327] “Contempt” (*contemptio*): the same editions, except Basel and Lyon III]. This is especially so since no person in authority or other layman ought to have any power in such matters. Rather, he should remain silent and attend to himself until the election of the future pontiff has regularly received its completion from the college of the Church.

But if some layman is invited by the Church to confer and cooperate, such a person [Note: [Col. 0327] The collected editions and *Panormia* add “layman”] may, if he wishes, respectfully comply with those who invite him. For in this way it regularly promotes for itself a worthy pastor for the salvation of its Church [Note: [Col. 0327] *Ecclesiae* (“of the Church”): *Panormia*; “and the Church”: collected editions] [Note: [Col. 0327D] “Promotes”: if the clause “Whoever,” from the preceding chapter, is added here, canon 22 of the Eighth Synod will be complete. In the printed editions the word *clerus* (“clergy”) followed, but in older copies it is an interlinear gloss.] [Note: [Col. 0327] Added: “clergy”: collected editions].

### C. III. The emperor ought not to take part in the election of bishops. Likewise from the *Tripartite History*, book VII, ch. [7.] 8.

[Col. 0328B] The emperor Valentinian, coming from the East to the western regions—as ecclesiastical history relates—after the death of Auxentius, master of Arian perfidy, who had ravaged the Church of Milan like a wolf, wished [Note: [Col. 0327] The collected editions add “the emperor”], by God’s appointment, to have a Catholic bishop consecrated there [Note: [Col. 0327] The same editions read “be consecrated”]. Summoning the bishops, he addressed them thus:

“You know plainly, *being indeed* instructed by the divine utterances, what kind of man a pontiff ought to be; and that [Note: [Col. 0327] The same editions read “because”] it is not fitting for him to govern those subject to him by word alone, but also by conduct, to show himself an imitator of every virtue, and to have good conduct as the witness of his teaching. Therefore appoint to the episcopal see such a man that we also, who govern the empire, may sincerely submit our heads to him, and, whenever as human beings we have sinned [Note: [Col. 0327] The collected editions read “whenever we sin”], may necessarily receive his admonitions as remedies from a physician who heals” [Note: [Col. 0327] *Tanquam* (“as”): Lyon II and III read *tamen* (“nevertheless”)].

When the emperor had said this [Note: [Col. 0327] The Argenteus edition reads “here”; the collected editions add “however”], the synod asked that he himself, being considered wise and devout, should decide instead. But he said: “Such an election is above you” [Note: [Col. 0328D] “Above you”: the true reading is “above us,” Greek μεῖζον ἢ καθ’ ἡμᾶς (*meizon ē kath’ hēmas*), “greater than what pertains to us.” It has not been restored because of the gloss.]. “For you, having received divine grace and shining with that splendor, will be better able to choose.” Then the priests withdrew from the episcopal seat and deliberated.

And below, § 1: When Ambrose, not yet baptized, had been chosen by divine appointment, the rejoicing emperor said: “I give thanks to you, Lord God almighty and our Savior, because I had entrusted bodies to this man [Note: [Col. 0327] Basel adds “to whom”], but you have entrusted souls to him, and you have shown that my judgment accords with your justice.”

And when Saint Ambrose was distressed by what had occurred, as he himself writes in his letters [Note: [Col. 0329] In the letter to the people of Vercelli], the emperor encouraged him, saying: “Do not fear, because [Note: [Col. 0329] Basel adds “and”] God, who chose you, will always help you; and I shall always be your helper and defender, as befits my station.”

### C. IV. A bishop is to be chosen by apostolic authority, not royal favor. Likewise Pope Nicholas I to King Lothair [Note: [Col. 0329] The complete letter, of which this is a fragment, is not extant.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, c. 37.].

Moreover, know [Note: [Col. 0329] This is absent from Ivo] that it has been reported to us that you permit no one to be chosen for promotion to a bishopric in your kingdom unless he is favorable to you. Therefore, by apostolic authority and under adjuration before the divine judgment, [Col. 0329B] we command you that in the city of Trier and in Cologne of Agrippina you allow no one to be chosen before a report on this matter has been made to our apostolic office.

### C. V. A man who has obtained episcopal rank through royal appointment is not to be received by his fellow-provincial bishops. Likewise from the Council of Paris, book I, ch. 8 [Note: [Col. 0329] Held in 557.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, c. 9; *Decretum*, pt. 5, c. 123.].

If anyone, with excessive rashness, presumes to seize the lofty summit of honor through royal appointment, he is in no way to deserve reception by the bishops of that place who are fellow-provincials [Note: [Col. 0329] The original has “bishop”], since they know that he has been improperly ordained [Note: [Col. 0329] The Argenteus edition adds *vere* (“truly”); the remaining collected editions read *vero* (“however”)] [Note: [Col. 0329] The collected editions read “recognize”]. If any fellow-provincial presumes to receive him contrary to this prohibition [Note: [Col. 0329] Basel reads “prohibition” in the singular], he is to be separated from all the brethren and removed from the charity of them all [Note: [Col. 0329] The collected editions read “all” in the singular; Basel reads “removed”].

[Col. 0329C]

### C. VI. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Laodicea, ch. 13 [Note: [Col. 0329] Held between 347 and 381.—Burchard, bk. 2, c. 8; Anselm, bk. 6, c. 38 (43); Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 28; Deusdedit, pt. 1, 4.].

It must not be permitted that crowds conduct the election of those who are to be promoted to the priesthood.

### C. VII. The election of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon made by rulers is to be void. Likewise from the Seventh Synod, that is, the Second Council of Nicaea, of 350 bishops, ch. 3 [Note: [Col. 0329C] “From the Seventh”: it had previously been cited from the second session of the Sixth Synod. [Col. 0329] The same chapter heading is found in Anselm. Yet in some of his manuscripts one reads: “From the Seventh Universal Synod, held by five patriarchs with 150 bishops under the first Hadrian, ch. 3.” The passage has been restored from Ivo.] [Note: [Col. 0329] Held in 787.—Burchard, bk. 3, c. 109; Anselm, bk. 6, c. 8; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, c. 120; Deusdedit, in the same place.].

Every election of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon made by rulers is to remain void, according to the rule which says [Note: [Col. 0329] Apostolic Canon 31; compare C. 16, q. 7, c. 14.]:

“If any bishop, making use of secular [Col. 0330A] powers, obtains a church [Note: [Col. 0329] The collected editions read “churches”] through them, let him be deposed, and let all who communicate with him be separated from the Church [Note: [Col. 0329] The words “from the Church” are absent from the original, Anselm, Ivo, and the editions of Argenteus, Basel, and Nuremberg].”

[Note: [Col. 0329C] “And let them be separated”: in some old copies of Gratian the reading is *segregetur* (“let him be separated”), but most agree with the common reading. In Apostolic Canon 31 the Greek reads: Καθαιρεῖσθω, καὶ ἀφοριζέσθω, καὶ κοινωνοῦντες αὐτῷ πάντες (*Kathaireisthō, kai aphorizesthō, kai koinōnountes autō pantes*), “Let him be deposed and separated, and all who communicate with him as well.” And below, in C. 16, q. 7, chapter *Si quis episcopus*, where this same canon is cited in another translation, the reading is: “and let him be separated, together with all who communicate with him”; the same form appears in Anselm. But Anastasius the Librarian’s version reads as in Gratian and agrees with the ancient and Dionysian translation.]

### C. VIII. Those who are to be promoted to the clergy are not to be chosen by the people. Likewise from the Council of Pope Martin, ch. 1 [Note: [Col. 0329] Chapters 12–13 of the Council of Laodicea, in the translation of Martin of Braga.—Burchard, bk. 1, c. 10; Anselm, bk. 6, c. 12; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, c. 64.].

It is not lawful for the people to conduct the election of those who are promoted to the priesthood [Note: [Col. 0329] The original and Anselm read *provocantur* (“are called forth”); Ivo reads *provebantur* (“were being advanced”)], but the matter is to rest in the judgment of the bishops [Note: [Col. 0329] The original has the singular “judgment”; the collected editions read “bishops”], so that they themselves may examine the man [Note: [Col. 0329] The original, Anselm, and Ivo add “who is to be ordained”] to determine whether he has been instructed in speech, faith, and spiritual life [Note: [Col. 0329] The original, in the Spanish Collection, reads “is instructed”; Anselm reads “has been instructed”].

**Gratian.** By all these authorities laymen are excluded from the election of priests, and the necessity of obedience, not the freedom to command, is imposed upon them.

## Part II

On the other hand, Saint Gregory writes to John, [Col. 0330B] bishop of Prima Justiniana in Illyricum, book IV, letter 15 [Note: [Col. 0329] Letter 23, written in 592, bk. 2, Maurist edition.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 95 (96).]:

### C. IX. The will of the ruler is sought in the ordination of a pontiff.
