Since, therefore, the report received from our fathers and *our fellow-bishops* declares that, by the united agreement [Note: [Col. 0329] Basel reads “sole agreement”] of the entire council and the will of the most serene ruler, you are being summoned to the place of the priesthood, we have offered great thanks with rejoicing to *almighty God*, our Creator [Note: [Col. 0329] The collected editions read “our Savior”], *who has made your former life and conduct so approved that he has caused you, most commendably, to please the judgment of all. With these judgments* we too assent in every respect concerning your brotherhood’s person; and we pray almighty God that, as his grace chose your charity [Note: [Col. 0329] The same editions, except Lyon II and III and Antwerp, add “you”], [Col. 0330C] so he may guard it in all things by his protection.

### C. X. Clergy and people are to take part in the election of a pontiff. Likewise Gregory to John the subdeacon, book II, eleventh indiction, letter 30 [Note: [Col. 0329] Letter 30, written in 593, bk. 3, Maurist edition.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 26 (27); Polycarpus, bk. 1, tit. 5.].

The more it is established that the apostolic see, God being its author [Note: [Col. 0329] The collected editions read “by its own authority”], is set over all churches, the more, amid our many concerns, we are greatly troubled where our judgment is awaited [Note: [Col. 0329] Venice I and II and Lyon I read “is hoped for”; the editions of Argenteus, Basel, and Nuremberg read “is considered”] for the consecration of a bishop.

Therefore, after Lawrence [Note: [Col. 0331] The collected editions add “the bishop”]—bishop of the Church of Milan [Col. 0331A] [Note: [Col. 0331] The collected editions read “archbishop”]—had died, the clergy informed us by their report that they had unanimously agreed in the election of our son Constantius, their deacon. But because that report was not subscribed, lest we omit anything required for caution, it is necessary that you, fortified by the authority of this command, proceed to Genoa [Note: [Col. 0331] *Januam*, which is the same place: the same editions except Lyon II and III and Antwerp].

And because many Milanese are gathered there under barbarian violence, you must investigate their wishes when they have been summoned together [Note: [Col. 0331] The collected editions, especially Argenteus and Basel, read “the clergy” in place of “them”; Böhm] [Note: [Col. 0331] The collected editions, except Lyon II and III and Antwerp, read “in an assembly” rather than “together”]. If no division separates them from unity in the election, and if you ascertain that the will and consent of all remain firm in our aforementioned son Constantius, then have him consecrated by his own bishops, with the assent of our authority, as the custom of antiquity requires, the Lord supporting [Col. 0331B] and helping [Note: [Col. 0331] These two words are absent from Gregory, Anselm, and the editions of Argenteus, Basel, and Nuremberg]. Thus, while this custom is preserved, both the apostolic see retains its proper force and does not diminish the rights it has granted to others.

### C. XI. The people ought to be present in the election of a bishop. Likewise Pope Gelasius to Bishops Philip and Geruntinus [Note: [Col. 0331] Neither the date of this letter nor the bishops to whom it was addressed is known.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 48.] [Note: [Col. 0331] The collected editions, except Basel and Lyon II and III, read “Gerentinus”; Anselm reads “Gerontius.”].

The people of Diotrensis [Note: [Col. 0331] Böhm judged from Royal manuscript I that one should read “Diestrensis,” the name of a town in Moesia Secunda, otherwise called Durostorum. In Anselm one reads “Clientensis.”] lamented to us in a petition that for a long time they had been scattered without the governance of their own ruler. And, as is alleged, the man whom you are said already to have approved is thought to have been chosen by a few and insignificant persons [Note: [Col. 0331] Basel adds “already”], whereas it belongs to you to compel all by continual admonition to agree upon one man whom they see to be worthy of the priesthood and free from any reproach.

Therefore, dearest brethren, you must repeatedly summon together presbyters [Note: [Col. 0331] The collected editions read “and presbyters, and” (*et presb., et*)], deacons, and the whole body of people from the several parishes of the aforesaid place [Col. 0331C], so that they may seek for themselves—not as each happens to prefer, but with harmonious minds and under your admonition [Note: [Col. 0331] Anselm reads “with you pressing upon them”]—a person chosen solely with regard to God, whom no opposition can recall from the established prescriptions [Note: [Col. 0331] Anselm reads “precepts”; the collected editions read “rescripts”].

[Col. 0332A]

### C. XXII. On the same matter. Likewise Stephen, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Romanus, archbishop of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0331] There seems to be an error concealed in this heading. For Romanus of Ravenna died while John VIII was still alive; compare John, Ep. 304, in Mansi. Yet the authenticity of the letter itself—which survives only in Anselm, bk. 6, c. 36—need not be doubted. If conjecture is permitted, it seems to us that one should read “Dom.,” that is, Dominic, who is known to have been Romanus’s successor.].

We wish your brotherhood to know that word has reached our ears that the bishop of Imola has departed this life, and that a division among the people has arisen in the election of his successor. Since this often happens, because each seeks what is his own and not what belongs to Jesus Christ, we are not greatly surprised. Nevertheless, you must exercise the greatest care in this matter, so that, when clergy and people have been called together, through God’s mercy such a person may be chosen there [Note: [Col. 0331] Anselm reads “therein”] as is not opposed by the sacred canons. For election belongs to the priests [Note: [Col. 0331] The collected editions add “consent”], and the consent of the faithful people must be obtained; for the people are to be taught, not followed.

[Col. 0332B]

### C. XIII. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Nicholas to John, archbishop of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0331C] In an old Modenese manuscript are recorded six chapters of a Roman council, the second of which is this. Much on this same matter is also found in a manuscript *Pontifical* in the acts of Nicholas I.] [Note: [Col. 0331] Rather, from the Roman council held in 861, in the case of John of Ravenna.].

Do not consecrate bishops throughout Emilia unless after the election of clergy and people.

### C. XIV. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Pelagius to Julian, bishop of Grumentum [Note: [Col. 0331] Letter of uncertain date; compare Distinction 76, final chapter.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 60 (58); Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 112; Polycarpus, bk. 2, tit. 29.] [Note: [Col. 0331] Anselm reads “Jullinus”; Ivo reads “Tullianus.”].

We have received your charity’s letter, in which you state that Latinus, your deacon, is being requested for the bishopric of the Church of Marcelliana by the clergy and all who gather there. And below: But [Note: [Col. 0331] Anselm and the collected editions read “Therefore”] now we say this also: if all choose him and you wish to grant him, know that it is pleasing to us; and, if possible, let him hasten to come before the holy day [Note: [Col. 0331] Basel adds “of Easter”], so that on the Saturday itself of the Great Night, after baptism, he may by God’s grace be ordained [Col. 0332C].

### C. XV. A man is ordained at the imperial command. Likewise the same to Lawrence, bishop of Centumcellae [Note: [Col. 0332C] “At the imperial command”: this heading has been corrected so as to indicate that the person in question was ordained at the emperor’s request. For *sacra* means an imperial letter. [Col. 0332D] Previously it read: “The sacred authority of the ruler is necessary for those to be ordained.”] [Note: [Col. 0331] Letter of uncertain date.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 94.].

A report from the commander of the most devoted soldiers stationed there in the city of Centumcellae has been sent to us, declaring that they have obtained a sacred letter [Note: [Col. 0331] The collected editions add “letter”] from the most clement ruler, which commands that a presbyter, deacon, and [Col. 0333A] subdeacon are to be made for them. Therefore we exhort your charity to see the persons themselves and inquire diligently [Note: [Col. 0333] The same editions, following Anselm, read “investigate”] whether they have committed anything contrary to the canons. If you find them blameless and see commendable testimony to their lives, then, when the middle week of Easter comes [Note: [Col. 0333] Basel reads *hebdomada* (“week”) for *septimana* (“week”)]—if the Lord wills and we live—do not delay promoting each of them through the orders we have specified.

### C. XVI. The pope asks the Augusti graciously to grant the Church of Rieti to a certain chosen man. Likewise Leo IV to the Augusti Lothair and Louis [Note: [Col. 0333] Written before 853, in which year Colus of Rieti subscribed to the Roman council.—*Collectio tripartita*, pt. 1, tit. 62, c. 10.].

The Church of Rieti, which has remained deprived of pastoral care through so long a span of time [Note: [Col. 0333] The collected editions read “has stood”], ought to be supported by the arm of your greatness and protected by the covering of governance [Note: [Col. 0333] The collected editions and Böhm read “rule”]. Therefore, after offering the customary greeting [Col. 0333B], we beseech your gentleness graciously to grant that same Church to the humble deacon Colonus for his governance, so that, having received your permission, we may there consecrate him bishop with God’s help.

But if you do not wish a bishop to be set over the aforesaid Church, may your serenity [Note: [Col. 0333] The same editions read “severity”] graciously grant him the Church of Tusculum, which stands bereft, so that, consecrated by our episcopal office, he may give thanks to almighty God and to your empire.

### C. XVII. At the king’s command Colonus is ordained bishop of the Church of Rieti by the Apostolic See. Likewise to Countess Rita [Note: [Col. 0333] A letter written, apparently, shortly after the preceding one.—*Collectio tripartita*, in the same place.].

The lord emperor and empress told us by their letters that we ought to make Colonus bishop in the Church of Rieti, [Col. 0333C] which for a long time had appeared destitute of a pastor’s office; and we have done so.

### C. XVIII. The emperor’s letter is required for confirmation of an election. Likewise Stephen to Count Guido [Note: [Col. 0333] Letter to Guido, or Wido, count of Spoleto.—*Collectio tripartita*, pt. 1, tit. 64, c. 7.].

Having read the letter of your sagacity—which stated that, after the death of the bishop of the Church of Rieti, the clergy and people of that Church had chosen a future bishop for themselves and had sent him to us, to be consecrated through your efforts [Note: [Col. 0333] The collected editions read “and by us to be consecrated”], lest that Church remain long without its own pastor—we, grieving over the death of the former bishop, did not ordain with the utmost speed [Note: [Col. 0333] Basel reads “with the utmost certainty”] this man who had now been chosen by the unanimous and canonical election of that Church, as you instructed. We omitted to do so because he did not bring us the imperial letter of authorization, as custom requires [Col. 0333D] [Note: [Col. 0333] Basel reads “they did not bring”; the remaining collected editions read “he did not bring”].

For this reason, being uncertain [Note: [Col. 0333] Basel reads “in God”], we delayed complying with your wish in this matter, lest the imperial mind should take it very harshly in some way. But knowing that the Church of God ought not long to remain without its own pastor, we command your glory—since we ought not to have acted otherwise—to obtain, by your diligence, imperial permission, as ancient custom dictates, and to have the emperor’s letter sent to us, as we believe you understand. Then we shall comply with your wish in this matter and, with the Lord’s help, consecrate the same chosen man. Dearest son, do not take this amiss in any way [Note: [Col. 0333] Basel addresses the plural “you”].

### C. XIX. A metropolitan is to be ordained with the will of clergy and citizens. Likewise Pope Leo I to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, letter 82, otherwise 84, ch. 6 [Note: [Col. 0333] Letter 14, written in 446, Ballerini edition.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 19; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, c. 348; Deusdedit, pt. 1.].

When a metropolitan has died and another is to be substituted in his place, the provincial bishops ought to gather [Note: [Col. 0333] The collected editions read “ought”] in the metropolitan city [Col. 0334B], so that, after the will of all the clergy and citizens has been considered, the best man among the presbyters or deacons of that Church may be ordained [Note: [Col. 0333] The original, Anselm, and Ivo read “chosen”].

### C. XX. The election of an archpresbyter is to be made with clergy and people. Likewise Isidore in the book *On Ecclesiastical Offices* [Note: [Col. 0333] The author of this chapter has not been identified.].

If archpresbyters in the communities die or are removed from office because of some offense, the archdeacon is to proceed there as quickly as possible and conduct the election with the clergy and people of that community, so that a worthy pastor may be appointed for the household of God and, while he is being ordained, that community may be protected by his oversight.

[Col. 0334C]

### C. XXI. A man chosen Roman pontiff is not to be ordained unless his decree is first presented to the emperor. Likewise from the acts of the Roman pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0333] From Anastasius the Librarian’s *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*.].

Agatho, a Sicilian by nation, during whose embassy John, bishop of Porto, on the Sunday of the octave of Easter [Note: [Col. 0333] The collected editions read “on the eighth day”] publicly celebrated Latin Mass before the emperor and patriarch in the Church of Saint Sophia, received from him, at his own request, an imperial letter [Note: [Col. 0333] The collected editions add “that is, a royal letter”; Böhm reads “revealed”] by which the amount customarily paid for the ordination of a pontiff was reduced+. Yet it was provided that, if an election should occur after his death, the man chosen must not be ordained unless the general decree is first brought into the imperial city according to ancient custom, so that the ordination may take place with the emperor’s knowledge [Note: [Col. 0333] The collected editions read “conscience”] and command [Note: [Col. 0333] The same editions read “prosper”].

§ 1. Likewise Vitalian, a native of Segni, [Col. 0334D] sent his representatives with a synodical letter, according to custom, to the imperial city, to [Note: [Col. 0333] The same editions read “among”] the most pious rulers, reporting his ordination.

[Col. 0335A]

### C. XXII. The emperor has the right of choosing the pontiff. Likewise in the *Ecclesiastical History* [Note: [Col. 0335] The author of this chapter has been identified as Sigebert of Gembloux, under the year 774; he died in 1112. Its reliability has been vigorously disputed among learned men; its most recent defender was A. C. Ernesti, *Dissertation on the Authority of the Lateran Council of 774*, Leipzig, 1761, quarto. In Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, c. 134, this heading reads: “From the Eighth Synod, Ecclesiastical History.” Theodoric of Niem produced the passage from a very ancient Florentine book in his *Treatise on the Privileges and Rights of the Empire*, in Schard’s collection of works on imperial jurisdiction, etc., Basel, 1566, folio.].

Pope Hadrian asked King Charles to come to Rome to defend the possessions of the Church. Charles came to Rome, besieged Pavia, and, leaving his army there, was honorably received at Rome by Pope Hadrian at the holy Resurrection. After the holy Resurrection he returned to Pavia and captured King Desiderius. Then, returning to Rome, he convened a synod there with Pope Hadrian in the Lateran patriarchal residence [Note: [Col. 0335] Ivo and the collected editions read “patriarchate”], in the Church of Saint Saviour. This synod was attended by 153 religious bishops and abbots.

Pope Hadrian and the entire synod granted [Note: [Col. 0335] Basel has the singular “granted”] Charles the right and power to choose the pontiff and to appoint the apostolic see. They also granted [Note: [Col. 0335] Basel has the singular “granted”] him the dignity of patrician [Col. 0335B]. Moreover, the synod decreed that archbishops and bishops in each province should receive investiture from him; that no bishop should be consecrated unless approved and invested by the king; and that whoever acted against this decree should be bound by the bond of anathema and, unless he repented [Note: [Col. 0335] Basel reads “unless he looked back”], should have his goods confiscated.

### C. XXIII. The election of the Roman pontiff belongs by right to the emperor. Likewise Pope Leo [Note: [Col. 0335] So far as we know, Theodoric of Niem was the first to publish, in book I, the complete constitution of Leo VIII, assigned to 963, from which these passages are excerpted, taking it from a Florentine book nearly consumed by excessive age. Its authenticity is likewise not agreed upon among historians. Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 135.].

Pope Leo in a synod assembled at Rome in the Church of Saint Saviour [Note: [Col. 0335D] The beginning of this chapter appears to be “Following the example,” etc.; and the preceding words likewise belong to the heading, so that the complete heading reads: “Pope Leo in a synod assembled at Rome in the Church of Saint Saviour.” This is Leo VIII, concerning whom Liutprand writes much at the end of book 6, and Saint Antoninus, pt. 2, tit. 16, c. 16.]:

Following the example of the blessed Hadrian, prelate of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0335] Ivo reads “bishop”], who granted to Lord Charles, most victorious king of the Franks and Lombards, the dignity of patrician, the appointment of the apostolic see, and the investiture [Col. 0335C] of bishops, I too, Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, together with the whole clergy and Roman people [Note: [Col. 0335] Ivo reads “all the clergy”], establish, confirm, and strengthen, and by our apostolic authority grant and bestow upon Lord Otto I, king of the Germans, and his successors in this kingdom of Italy, in perpetuity, the power to choose a successor [Note: [Col. 0335] Basel, following Ivo, adds “for himself”] and to appoint the pontiff of the supreme apostolic see; and thereby [authority over] archbishops and bishops, so that they may receive investiture from him and consecration from the proper source, except for those whom the emperor has granted to pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0335] Ivo and the collected editions read the singular “pontiff”] and archbishops.

Further, no one henceforth, of whatever rank or religious status [Note: [Col. 0335] The collected editions read “religion”], is to have the power, without the consent of that emperor—and this is to be done without any payment—to choose either a patrician or the pontiff of the supreme apostolic see, or to ordain any bishop whatever; and he himself is to be patrician and king. If any bishop is chosen by clergy and people, he is not to be consecrated unless approved and invested by the aforesaid king. If anyone attempts anything against this *rule and* apostolic authority, we decree that he is subject to excommunication and, unless he repents, is to be punished by irrevocable exile or subjected to the ultimate penalties [Note: [Col. 0335] Ivo reads “struck by the ultimate penalties”].

### C. XXIV. At the rulers’ command, pardon is granted to Maximus, who was ordained without apostolic authorization. Likewise Gregory, book IV of the *Register*, letter 34, to the Empress Constantia [Note: [Col. 0335] Letter 21, written in 595, bk. 5, Maurist edition.—Polycarpus, bk. 1, tit. 5.].

[Col. 0336B] The bishop of the city of Salona was ordained without the knowledge of me or my representative, and an act occurred such as had happened under none of the earlier rulers. When I heard this, I immediately sent to that transgressor, who had been irregularly ordained, ordering him not under any circumstances to presume to celebrate the solemnities of Mass until I had learned from our most serene lords whether they themselves [Note: [Col. 0335] “Themselves” is absent from the Basel edition] had commanded this to be done. I gave him this order under threat of excommunication.

But he, despising and disregarding me, even now presumes to celebrate Mass through the bold support of certain secular men, to whom, it is said, he gives many rewards from the resources stripped from his Church; and he refused to come to me in accordance with the command of our lords. Yet, obeying the command of their piety [Note: [Col. 0335] Basel adds “cause”], I have so heartily forgiven Maximus—who was ordained [Col. 0336C] without my knowledge—for presuming in his ordination to pass over me or my representative, as though he had been ordained with my authorization [Note: [Col. 0335] The collected editions read “had been ordained”].

But I cannot, for God’s sake, leave unexamined his other perversions: namely, the bodily evils which I have learned of; that he was chosen with money [Note: [Col. 0335] The same editions have the singular “money”]; and that, though excommunicated, he presumed to celebrate Mass. And below: If he delays long [Note: [Col. 0335] “Long” is absent from the Basel edition] in coming to me, I shall in no way cease to exercise canonical severity against him.

### C. XXV. The ruler’s assent is required in the election of bishops. Likewise from the Twelfth Council of Toledo, ch. 6 [Note: [Col. 0335] Held in 681.].

Since [Note: [Col. 0335] The original reads “while”], over a territory spread far and wide, the speed of messengers is impeded, so that either the death of a departing bishop cannot become known to the king’s ears [Note: [Col. 0337] The original reads “to the king’s ears”; the collected editions read “with the kings hearing”], or the free choice of the ruler concerning the successor of a dying bishop cannot be awaited [Note: [Col. 0337] The collected editions read “awaited”], there often arises both difficulty for our order in making such reports and a countless burden for royal power while it awaits our counsel concerning the substitution of pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0337] The Spanish Collection reads “injurious” rather than “countless”; the collected editions read “either—or” rather than “and”].

Therefore all the pontiffs of Spain and Gaul [Note: [Col. 0337] The Spanish Collection reads “Gaul”] determined, without prejudice to the privilege of each province, that henceforth it should remain lawful for the bishop of Toledo to place as bishops, in any provinces and in the sees of preceding bishops, those whom royal power has chosen and whom the judgment of the aforesaid bishop of Toledo has found worthy, and, when bishops die, to choose successors. Yet this is subject to the condition [Note: [Col. 0337] The Spanish Collection and the collected editions read “so”] that [Col. 0337B] whoever is ordained must, within three months after his ordination, come to appear before his own metropolitan.

**Gratian.** Elections of the supreme pontiffs and of other lesser prelates were also formerly reported to emperors, as is read concerning the election of Saint Ambrose and Saint Gregory. From these examples and the foregoing authorities it is plainly inferred that laymen are not to be excluded from election, nor rulers rejected from the ordination of churches. But the fact that the people [Note: [Col. 0337] Venice I and II, Paris, the Lyon editions, and Böhm read “the people or ruler”] are commanded to take part in the election does not mean that they are commanded to be summoned to conduct the election, but rather to give consent to the election.

For election belongs to priests, as is stated at the end of Pope Stephen’s preceding chapter, and it belongs to the faithful people humbly to consent. Therefore the desire of the people is required in order that it may agree with the election of the clergy [Col. 0337C]. For then a bishop will properly be set over the Church of God, when the people likewise acclaim the man whom the whole clergy have chosen in common.

Accordingly Pope Celestine says to the Bishops of Gaul, Epistle II, ch. 5. [Note: [Col. 0337] cf. above, D. 61, ch. 13.]:

C. XXVI. It is not for the people to choose, but to consent to the election.

The agreement and desire of the clergy, people, *and order* are to be sought.

C. XXVII. On the same matter. Likewise Leo I, to the Bishops of the province of Vienne, Epistle LXXXVII, alternatively LXXXIX. [Note: [Col. 0337] Ep. 10, written A.D. 445. Ballerini edition, but there somewhat differently and more fully.]

The votes of the citizens, the testimony of the people, the judgment of the persons of rank, and the election of the clergy are awaited in the ordinations of priests. [Col. 0337D] [Note: [Col. 0337] *constituantur*, “are appointed”: editions cited above.] And below: Let those who are to preside as priests be sought in peace and quiet; let the subscription of the clergy, the testimony of the persons of rank, the agreement of the order [Note: [Col. 0337] *conventus*, “assembly”: editions cited above.] and of the people be maintained. [Note: [Col. 0337] *futuri*, “about to be”: same editions; *postulantur*, “are sought”: Arg., Nor., Ven. I and II editions.]

[Col. 0338A] III. Part. Gratian. Custom and constitutional provision established that the elections of Roman pontiffs and other bishops should be reported to princes and emperors, because of the dissensions of schismatics and heretics, by which the Church of God was sometimes shaken and endangered; against them the Church is frequently recorded as having been fortified by the laws of most faithful emperors. The election of Catholic pontiffs was therefore communicated to princes, so that, strengthened by their authority, no heretic or schismatic might dare to oppose it; and so that the princes themselves, as most devoted sons, might consent to him whom they saw chosen as their father, and might support him in all things. Thus Valentinian is read above to have said to Saint Ambrose: “Do not be afraid, because God, who chose you, will always help you, and I too shall always be your helper and defender, as befits my rank.” [Col. 0338B]

Accordingly Pope Stephen decreed as follows. [Note: [Col. 0337] Baronius, Papebrochius, Natalis Alexander, and other writers of this sort attacked the authenticity of this chapter fiercely. Pagius, in opposition to Baronius, judged that it should be attributed to Stephen VI, alternatively VII; Muratori, however, attributes it to Stephen IV, in A.D. 816, a view which we also adopt. That it is certainly not fabricated is apparent even from the fact that John IX, in A.D. 898, repeated and confirmed it word for word in the Roman council. — Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 1, § “Stephen.”]

C. XXVIII. The Roman Pontiff is to be ordained in the presence of the emperor’s legates.

Because the holy Roman Church, over which we preside by God’s appointment, suffers many acts of violence when a pontiff dies—acts inflicted for this reason, that the consecration of a pontiff takes place without imperial knowledge [Note: [Col. 0337] Addition: “the election and”: editions cited above; Böhm.] and without the attendance, according to canonical rite and custom, of envoys sent by the emperor to prevent scandals [Note: [Col. 0337] *sunt*, “are [present]”: editions cited above.]—we will that, when a pontiff is to be appointed, the man to be ordained shall be chosen by the assembled bishops and the whole clergy, in the presence of the senate and people; and, having thus been chosen by all, he shall be consecrated in the presence of imperial legates. [Col. 0338C] Nor may anyone, at peril to himself, dare by some newly invented device to extort oaths or promises, except those demanded by ancient custom, [Note: [Col. 0337] *exegit*, “demanded”: Basel edition.] lest either the Church be scandalized or the imperial dignity diminished.

IV. Part. Gratian. But because emperors, sometimes ignorant of their proper measure, wished to be not among those who consented but foremost among those who bestowed—indeed, who destroyed—and frequently, having fallen into the treachery of heretics, attempted to assail the unity of the Catholic mother Church, statutes of the holy Fathers were therefore issued against them. These provided that they should not insert themselves into the election, and that whoever obtained a church by their support should be bound by the bond of anathema. For divine Scripture also says that Hezekiah [Note: [Col. 0337] 4 Kings, ch. 18.] [Col. 0338D] “destroyed the high places, broke the statues, cut down the sacred groves, and shattered the bronze serpent which Moses had made.” That is: because God had commanded that serpent to be made, lest the people perish by a serpentine death, the people themselves [Col. 0339A] began to worship and venerate it; and therefore this man destroyed what that other had made at God’s command.

Thus this is a weighty principle in the Church: if some of our predecessors and elders did things which in their own time could be without fault, but which later turn into error and superstition, they must be destroyed by their successors without delay and with great authority. Finally, elections of Roman pontiffs are found to have been celebrated in the presence of, and without consulting, the emperors’ legates; and at last those same emperors, with devout disposition, renounced the aforesaid privileges, while also bestowing many gifts upon the Church.

Accordingly Gregory writes. [Note: [Col. 0339C] “Gregory”: this was formerly cited as from Gregory IV, to whom it cannot belong, since Hadrian II, mentioned here, was later than Gregory IV. But it occurs in the pontifical manuscripts among the acts of Hadrian II [Col. 0339D] and likewise in a manuscript collection of the decrees of Roman pontiffs, among the decrees of that same Hadrian II.] [Note: [Col. 0339] From additions to Anastasius’s *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, customarily but wrongly attributed to William the Librarian. — Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 16.]

C. XXIX. Hadrian II is elected to the pontificate without consultation of the emperor’s legates.

[Col. 0339B] When Hadrian II was being brought to the Roman pontificate from the Church of God’s Mother, our Lady, called *Ad praesepe* (“At the Manger”), to the Lateran patriarchal palace, he was borne eagerly by clergy, nobles, and people. [Note: [Col. 0339] “people”: editions cited above.] On hearing this, the envoys of Emperor Louis took it badly and were indignant, namely because, though present, they had not been invited and had not been permitted to take part in the election of the future bishop which they desired. [Note: [Col. 0339] “and were indignant”: same editions; “had been”: Basel edition.]

When they received the explanation that this had been omitted [Note: [Col. 0339] “had been done”: editions cited above.] not out of contempt for the Augustus, but in foresight of the future—namely, lest through such an opening there should become established a practice of waiting for the princes’ legates in the election of Roman bishops—they completely calmed their indignation and themselves approached the elect humbly to greet him. [Note: [Col. 0339D] “They approached”: In the same pontifical manuscripts the following immediately occurs: “On hearing this, Louis, the most Christian emperor, at once wrote an imperial letter [Col. 0340C] praising all the Romans who had performed the office of choosing a bishop worthy of so great a task. By that letter he made known, namely, that no reward of any kind was to be promised to anyone for the consecration of a Roman pontiff, [Col. 0340D] since he himself most ardently desired that it should arise not at the prompting of his own men, but rather from the unanimity of the Romans; especially since he declared that he longed for the restoration of what had been taken away, not for anything to be taken from, or lost by, the Roman Church.”]

[Col. 0339C] C. XXX. The election of Roman pontiffs is granted to the Romans by Louis. Likewise, the constitutional compact of Emperor Louis I with the Roman pontiffs. [Note: [Col. 0339] The complete constitution—apparently forged in the eleventh century and compiled from Otto’s constitution below, ch. 32—is available in Baluze, *Capitularia*, vol. I, p. 591. — Anselm, bk. 4, ch. 35; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 51.]

I, Louis, Emperor Augustus, decree and grant by this pact of our confirmation to you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and through you to your vicar, Lord Paschal, supreme pontiff *and universal pope*, and to his successors forever, [Note: [Col. 0339] “your successors”: Basel edition.] the city of Rome with its duchy, all its suburbs and villages, [Note: [Col. 0339] *villiculis*, “small estates”: Lugdd. and Antwerp editions.] its mountain territories, seacoasts and ports, and all cities, castles, towns, and villages in the regions of Tuscany, just as [Col. 0340A] you have held and administered them in your power and jurisdiction down to the present from our predecessors. [Note: [Col. 0339] “your predecessors”: Ivo; editions cited above.]

Likewise below, § 1. When, by divine calling, the pontiff of this most sacred see departs this world, no man under our authority—whether Frank, Lombard, or of any nation—from our kingdom shall have leave to come against the Romans, publicly or privately, or to conduct an election; nor shall anyone presume, on this account, to do any harm in cities or territories belonging to the authority of the Church of blessed Peter the apostle. Rather, the Romans may, with all reverence and without any disturbance, render an honorable burial to their pontiff, and may consecrate, without any doubt or contradiction and according to canonical custom, the man whom all the Romans, by divine inspiration and Saint Peter’s intercession, have chosen with one counsel [Note: [Col. 0339] *concilio*, “council”: Arg. and Basel editions.] and agreement, [Note: [Col. 0339] Addition: “as one”: same editions.] without any promise, [Note: [Col. 0339] *aliqua*, “any”: same editions.] to the order of pontiff. [Note: [Col. 0339] “and”: same editions; “canonically”: Anselm.] When he has been consecrated, legates shall be sent to us or to our successors, the kings of the Franks, who shall unite friendship, charity, and peace between us and [Note: [Col. 0339] “between”: same editions.] him. [Col. 0340B]

C. XXXI. The election and consecration of the Roman pontiff shall take place only justly and canonically. [Likewise Leo IV, to the Augusti Lothair and Louis.] PALEA. [Note: [Col. 0339] These words have not been found among the letters of Leo IV, but nevertheless appear altogether genuine. — Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 14.]

“By the tenor of a pact between us and you it has been established and [Col. 0340C] confirmed that the election and consecration of the future Roman pontiff ought to take place only justly and canonically.”

C. XXXII. No hindrance to the election of the Roman pontiff shall be created by the emperor or his envoys. [Likewise the Constitution [Note: [Col. 0340D] “Constitution”: this title was restored in Gratian from an old exemplar. In that exemplar [Col. 0341C] after this title, with a rubric inserted, the chapter begins: “That no one,” etc., as also in Ivo. But since it has become customary for this chapter to begin with the word “Constitution,” these words have been retained at the beginning of the chapter itself. This chapter also occurs in [Col. 0342C] old exemplars in which Paleae [Col. 0342D] are not usually found.] of Henry I and Otto I with the Roman pontiffs. [Note: [Col. 0339] An authentic and genuine diploma, dated 13 February A.D. 962. In Anselm, bk. 4, ch. 37, this subscription is added: “Both emperors subscribed, each in his own time.” Under Otto, indeed, ten bishops, five counts, and eight magnates subscribed. Year of the Lord’s Incarnation 962, indiction 5. Under Henry—where an error seems to lie—thirteen bishops, three abbots, three dukes, nine counts, and eight magnates subscribed. — Anselm, bk. 6, tit. 37; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 52.] PALEA.

“The Constitution of Henry I and Otto I with [Col. 0341A] the Roman pontiffs. We absolutely forbid any of our envoys, whoever they may be, to dare to devise any pretext of obstruction in the election of the Roman pontiff. Likewise, § 1. In [Note: [Col. 0341] In Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 7, these are rightly cited from Lothair’s capitulary. Cf. *Leges Langobardorum*, bk. 3, tit. 11, no. 3.] the election of Roman pontiffs, neither free person nor slave may presume to intervene in order to create any hindrance for those Romans whom ancient custom, through the constitution of the holy Fathers, has admitted to this election. If anyone presumes to act against this our constitution, [Note: [Col. 0341] Omitted in Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 37, and in the editions cited above except Basel.] let him be handed over to exile.”

C. XXXIII. Otto’s oath which he made to Lord Pope John. Likewise, Otto’s Constitution. [Note: [Col. 0341] Liutprand mentions this oath for A.D. 961. By contrast, an anonymous writer’s fragment—printed in *Notices et extraits*, vol. VII, p. 45—asserts, apparently incorrectly, that Otto personally gave it at Rome. — Anselm, bk. 1, tit. 90.]

To you, Lord Pope John, I, King Otto, promise and swear [Note: [Col. 0341] “I promise and swear”: *Notices*; “I promise”: Basel edition.] by the Father, Son, and Holy [Col. 0341B] Spirit, by this wood of the life-giving cross, and by these relics of the saints, that, if—with the Lord’s permission—[Note: [Col. 0341] “God”: Anselm, Vatican manuscript; Basel edition.] I come to Rome, I shall exalt the holy Roman Church and you, its ruler, according to my ability. I shall never, by my will, counsel, consent, or urging, cause you to lose life, limb, or the very honor which you possess. In the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0341] “in Rome”: original, II. cc.; editions cited above.] I shall make no arrangement or ordinance concerning anything belonging to you or the Romans without your counsel. Whatever of Saint Peter’s land comes into our power, I shall restore to you; and whoever I entrust with the Italian kingdom, I shall make swear that he will be your helper in defending [Note: [Col. 0341] “to defend”: editions cited above.] Saint Peter’s land according to his ability. *So may God [Note: [Col. 0342D] “So may God”: these words were added from Cencius Camerarius, [Col. 0341] wrongly, in our opinion, since they are found neither in the original nor in the two chapters,] in whose book are many forms of oaths and which survives in manuscript at Rome.] help me, and these holy [Col. 0341C] Gospels of God.*

C. XXXIV. Let the clergy and people be free to choose a bishop from their own diocese. Likewise from the first book of the Capitularies of the Emperors Charles and Louis, ch. 84. [Note: [Col. 0341] Dated A.D. 803. — Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 6.]

Not ignorant of the sacred canons, and in order that the holy Church of God might more freely enjoy its own honor, [Note: [Col. 0341] *potiatur*, “may enjoy”: Anselm and editions cited above.] we have given our assent to the ecclesiastical order, [Note: [Col. 0341] *praebemus*, “we give”: there.] namely, that bishops be chosen from their own diocese by election of clergy and people, in accordance with the statutes of the canons and without respect of persons or gifts, for merit of life [Col. 0342A] and the gift of wisdom, so that by example and words [Note: [Col. 0341] “word”: editions cited above.] they may in every respect benefit those subject to them.

Gratian. From these constitutions and the compact of Emperor Louis it is perceived that emperors renounced the privileges concerning the election of the supreme pontiff which Pope Hadrian had granted to Emperor Charles, and Pope Leo, following his example, to Otto I, king of the Germans. Since, therefore, all the authorities set forth above plainly establish that election belongs to clergy alone, the question arises: whose election is it—only that of the clergy of the greater church, or also of other religious persons in the same city?

But, as is found in the abridgment of canons by Fulgentius, deacon of the Church of Carthage, it was decreed in the seventh chapter of the Council of Nicaea and in [Col. 0342B] the Council of Gangra that the judgment of the mother church suffices for choosing a bishop. [Note: [Col. 0341] “the seventh Nicene council”: Arg. edition; “seventh Nicene chapter”: remaining editions. Yet, with Ferrandus himself, ch. 11, one should read “the Council of Septimunicia,” and, in place of “Gangra,” “Macriana.”] Now, however, just as the election of the supreme pontiff is to be made not by cardinals alone but also by other religious clergy by authority of Pope Nicholas, [Note: [Col. 0341] Nicholas II, Roman council, A.D. 1059; cf. Distinction 23, ch. 1.] so too the election of bishops is to be made not by canons alone but also by other most religious clergy, as was decreed in the general synod held at Rome by Pope Innocent. [Note: [Col. 0341] Second Lateran Council, held A.D. 1139, ch. 28.] For he says:

C. XXXV. Let the canons of the greater church not choose a bishop without the counsel of religious men.

When bishops die, since the enactments of the holy Fathers forbid a church to remain vacant for more than three months, we prohibit under bond of anathema the canons of the episcopal see from excluding from the election [Col. 0342C] of bishops the most religious men. Rather, a worthy and suitable person shall be chosen bishop with their counsel. [Note: [Col. 0341] “religious”: editions cited above; “worthy … choose”: Basel edition.] If an election has been held with those same religious persons excluded, [Note: [Col. 0341] “made”: editions cited above.] whatever has been done without their assent [Note: [Col. 0341] “consent”: same editions.] and concurrence shall be held invalid and void.

Gratian. The question now arises: if the votes of the electors divide into two parties, which party’s candidate is to be preferred? Leo the bishop writes as follows on this subject to Anastasius, Bishop of Thessalonica, Epistle LXXXII, alternatively LXXXIV, ch. 5. [Note: [Col. 0341] Ep. 14, written A.D. 446, Ballerini edition. — Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 19; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 6; *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 347; *Polycarpus*, bk. 2, tit. 1.]

[Col. 0343A] C. XXXVI. When the votes of the electors have divided into two parties, which is to be preferred to the other?

If [Note: [Col. 0343] In the original and the cited collections the opening is: “If the votes of the parties have perhaps divided toward one person or another”: Ivo, *Panormia.] perhaps—[what [Note: [Col. 0343C] “What we judge neither blameworthy nor irreligious”: these words, not reported by the other collectors, are not found in Leo but in Gregory, from whom they are cited below, 8, question 1, ch. *Nec novum*.] we judge neither blameworthy nor irreligious]—the votes of the electors divide into two parties, the metropolitan’s judgment shall prefer [Col. 0344A] to the other the man who is aided by greater support and merits; provided only that no one be ordained against the will of persons who do not seek it, [Note: [Col. 0343] “penitent persons”: Arg. edition; “be given”: editions cited above.] lest the city [Note: [Col. 0343] “people”: editions cited above.] despise or hate an unwanted bishop.

## DISTINCTION LXIV

[Col. 0343]

[Col. 0343A] GRATIAN.

I. Part. Here it must be considered by whom, or at what time, sacred orders are to be conferred, and in what places patriarchs, primates, archbishops, bishops, chorepiscopi, and the remaining priests are to be ordained. By whom bishops are to be ordained was determined in the First Council of Nicaea, where ch. 4 reads as follows. [Note: [Col. 0343] Held A.D. 325. — Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 27; Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 59, and, from Dionysius’s translation, same work, ch. 52; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 117.]

[Col. 0343B] C. I. Bishops are to be ordained by all their fellow-provincial bishops.

Bishops ought to be ordained by all who are in their province. But if this is difficult, either because of pressing necessity or the length of the journey, then certainly three bishops should gather in one place, provided that they hold in letters the consent of the others who are absent, and thus perform the ordination. Authority, indeed, or confirmation shall belong in each province to the metropolitan bishop.

C. II. On the same matter. Likewise Anacletus, to the bishops of Italy, Epistle II. [Note: [Col. 0343] Pseudo-Isidorian epistle. — Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 15; Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 52 [51]; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, chs. 12 and 17; *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 69; *Polycarpus*, bk. 2, tit. 16. — Cf. below, Cause 75, ch. 1.]

By apostolic authority, ordinations of bishops are to be celebrated by all the bishops who are in the same province. [Note: [Col. 0343] “are”: editions cited above.] And below, § 1. But if they cannot all meet at the same time, they should nevertheless give their consent in their [Col. 0343C] letters, [Note: [Col. 0343] “his”: Basel edition. “Letters”: the epistle reads “prayers”; Ivo and Burchard read “prayers and writings.”] so that they may not be absent in spirit from the ordination itself.

C. III. PALEA. [From the First Council of Orange, ch. 21. [Note: [Col. 0343] Held A.D. 441. — Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 30; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 20; *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 141. This Palea is absent in the Basel edition.]]

“Concerning [Note: [Col. 0343D] In the council itself [Col. 0343] according to Merlin’s edition—in the Hispanic Collection its opening is: “In our provinces,” etc.—the beginning of this [Col. 0344C] chapter is: “If two presume to ordain a bishop,” etc.; then the whole matter is more fully stated. But among the other collectors it appears almost in the form given here, while it is absent from many old manuscripts of Gratian.] the rejection [Note: [Col. 0343] Addition: “and ambition”: editions of the collections cited above.] of one whom two bishops in our [Note: [Col. 0343] “your”: those editions.] provinces have presumed to ordain, it has been decided concerning the presumptuous persons [Note: [Col. 0343] “presumptuous acts”: those editions.] that, wherever it happens that two bishops ordain [Note: [Col. 0343] “consecrate”: Ivo.] a third, both he himself and his authors [Note: [Col. 0344C] “And he himself”: thus corrected from the original and the other [Col. 0344D] collectors; formerly it read “and the bishops and authors.”] [Note: [Col. 0343] “agents”: editions cited above, except Lugdd. and Antwerp.] shall be condemned, so that the more cautiously those things established [Note: [Col. 0343] “decreed”: editions cited above.] of old may be preserved.”

C. IV. With the others consenting, a bishop may be ordained by three provincial bishops. Likewise Anicetus, in an epistle to the bishops of Gaul. [Note: [Col. 0343] Pseudo-Isidorian epistle. — Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 28; Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 39; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 10; *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 139; *Polycarpus*, bk. 2, tit. 8.]

If necessary, fellow-provincial bishops may, with the consent of the others, be consecrated by three bishops at the command of the archbishop. [Col. 0344B]

C. V. A bishop is not to be ordained without the knowledge of the metropolitan. Likewise Pope Innocent, to Bishop Victricius of Rouen, Epistle II, ch. 1. [Note: [Col. 0343] Written A.D. 404. — Anselm, bk. 6, 56 [54]; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 113; *Polycarpus*, same place.]

No one may dare to ordain a bishop without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop. A judgment confirmed by the opinions of many is sound. Nor should a single bishop presume to ordain a bishop, lest a benefit secretly bestowed appear to be involved. For the Synod of Nicaea likewise established and determined this. [Note: [Col. 0343] Addition: “by establishing”: editions cited above.]

[Col. 0344C] C. VI. Bishops are to be consecrated by their metropolitan, and he by those same bishops. Likewise Gelasius, to all persons established throughout Dardania. [Note: [Col. 0343] You will seek this in vain among Gelasius’s letters to the bishops of Dardania. The words cited by Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 41, from Gelasius’s letter to Natalis the presbyter in the *Corrector*, agree only with the first part. Hence Gratian appears to have followed the Tripartite Collection, part 1, tit. 46, ch. 35.]

II. Part. Since some are not ashamed, through unlawful ambitions, to disturb the rights of churches and rashly invade the privileges which antiquity decreed for metropolitan or provincial bishops, the brethren in apostolic communion, whether throughout Dardania or wherever else, desire to maintain schism, so that, divided from its authority, they may exercise their own usurpations with impunity. [Col. 0345A] [Note: [Col. 0345] Addition: “because”: editions cited above, first Lugdd. and Antwerp.] They do not consider that they will render account to the eternal Judge, not without the ruin of everlasting condemnation, both for injury to Catholic sincerity and for prejudice to paternal traditions, if they persist in this obstinacy.

We have therefore thought it right to instruct your charity that all of you brethren jointly, whether established throughout Dardania or in any neighboring province, who remember that you are subject to your metropolitans and decree that you are to be appointed by them, [Note: [Col. 0345] The reading appears to require *decedentes*, “when [they] die.”] should unanimously appoint bishops, as ancient custom requires. Conversely, if the metropolitan dies by the lot of the human condition, you should in every way judge that he is to be consecrated by [Col. 0345B] the fellow-provincial bishops, as the received form has transmitted; and you should allow no one to claim for himself what ancient disposition has granted to you. Thus, even amid the storms of hostile wills, you must never cease to observe the ancient rules, [Col. 0346A] as there is no doubt that our Fathers did steadfastly in times of various persecutions.

C. VII. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Pope Martin. [Note: [Col. 0345] Ch. 2; Martin of Braga, from the Council of Nicaea, ch. 4.]

III. Part. A bishop should, indeed, be appointed above all by the whole council. But if this is difficult because of necessity or distance of journey, [Note: [Col. 0345] Addition: “or”: original and editions cited above.] three are to be selected from all, [Note: [Col. 0345] “assembled”: original and Arg. and Basel editions.] and the subscriptions of all, present and absent, are to be secured; then the ordination shall take place. § 1. Authority in this matter throughout every province belongs to the metropolitan bishop. [Note: [Col. 0345] “belongs”: editions cited above.]

[Col. 0346B] C. VIII. He who has been ordained contrary to the metropolitan’s judgment shall not be bishop. Likewise from the First Council of Nicaea, ch. 6. [Note: [Col. 0345] Held A.D. 325. Dionysius Exiguus’s translation. — Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 42; Deusdedit, part 1.]

This is generally clear: if anyone has been made bishop contrary to the judgment [Note: [Col. 0345] Addition: “or knowledge”: editions cited above.] of the metropolitan, the great synod has determined that he ought not to be bishop.

## DISTINCTION LXV

[Col. 0345]

GRATIAN.

I. Part. The consent of fellow-provincial bishops is universally required in the ordination of a bishop. But if some, prompted by hostility, wish to oppose, the judgment of the majority shall prevail.

[Col. 0345C] Accordingly, in the Council of Nicaea, ch. 7, [Note: [Col. 0345] Held A.D. 325.] we read:

C. I. If, while the others consent to the ordination of bishops, two or three object, the judgment of the majority shall prevail.

If, indeed, with the common consent of all, reasonably approved according to ecclesiastical rule, [Note: [Col. 0345D] “Consent”: the Greek reads: **Ψήφῳ εὐλόγῳ οὔσῃ, καὶ κατὰ κανόνα ἐκκλησιαστικόν**, “by a vote that is well-grounded and in accordance with the ecclesiastical canon,” which Dionysius translates: *decreto rationabili et secundum ecclesiasticam regulam comprobato*, “by a decree reasonably approved and in conformity with ecclesiastical rule.”] two or three, driven by hostility, object through contention, the judgment of the majority of priests shall prevail.

C. II. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Pope Martin. [Note: [Col. 0345] Ch. 3; Martin of Braga, from the Council of Antioch, ch. 19.]

A bishop should not be ordained without the counsel [Note: [Col. 0345] “council”: Paris edition.] and presence of the metropolitan bishop. All the priests in the province, whom the metropolitan ought to summon by his letter, should be present. [Col. 0345D] If all come, that is good; [Note: [Col. 0345] “come”: Basel and Arg. editions; “may come”: remaining editions; “better”: Hispanic Collection.] but [Col. 0346B] if this is difficult, several ought to come together. [Note: [Col. 0345] “assemble”: editions cited above except first Arg.] Those who do not attend should make their presence known by letters [Note: [Col. 0345] Addition: “their own”: editions cited above.]; and, once all have given consent, the bishop’s ordination ought to take place. But if it is done otherwise than we have determined, we decree that such an ordination has no force. [Col. 0346C] [Note: [Col. 0345] “prevail”: Hispanic Collection and Isidore-Merlin; P III.]

II. Part, § 1. But if a bishop’s ordination has been conducted in accordance with the canons and someone maliciously objects to something, [Note: [Col. 0345] “against his own malice”: there; “with his own malice”: editions cited above.] the agreement of the majority shall prevail.

C. III. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Antioch, ch. 19. [Note: [Col. 0346D] A second translation, that of Dionysius, corresponds much better to the Greek wording and should therefore be consulted.] [Note: [Col. 0345] Held A.D. 332, commonly dated A.D. 341.]

A bishop is not to be ordained without the counsel [Note: [Col. 0345] “apart from council and presence”: Hispanic Collection. Yet the Greek words **δίχα συνόδου** show that “council” should be read.] and presence of the metropolitan bishop. It is better that bishops from the entire province should gather. If that cannot be done, those unable to be present should indicate their consent concerning him in their own letters; and only then, after the consent of the majority [Note: [Col. 0345] Addition: *episcoporum*, “of bishops”: editions cited above.], whether by [Note: [Col. 0345] *sive per*, “whether by”: absent from the Hispanic Collection.] [Col. 0346D] presence or by letters, [Note: [Col. 0345] “a consonant judgment by letters”: Hispanic Collection and Isidore-Merlin.] he shall be ordained by a concordant judgment. [Col. 0347A] If it is done otherwise than has been established, let him know that such an ordination has no force. [Note: [Col. 0347] Addition: “let him know”: editions cited above.] § 1. But if an ordination is celebrated even according to the prescribed rules, and some object because of their private and domestic quarrels, disregarding them, the judgment of the majority concerning him shall prevail. [Note: [Col. 0347] “ordained”: Arg. and Basel editions.]

Gratian. But if a province is known to have a primate, even the metropolitan may not consecrate a bishop without his knowledge.

Accordingly Pope Leo, to Bishop Anastasius, Epistle LXXXII, alternatively LXXXIV, ch. 6. [Note: [Col. 0347] Ep. 14, written A.D. 446, Ballerini edition. — Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 348; Deusdedit, part 1.]

C. IV. A metropolitan shall not ordain a bishop without the primate’s consent.

Concerning the person to be consecrated bishop and the consent of clergy and people, the metropolitan bishop should report to your brotherhood, and should make known to you what has been approved in the province, so that your authority too may confirm the ordination to be duly celebrated. [Col. 0347B] This ought to cause no delay or difficulty to proper arrangements, [Note: [Col. 0347] “ought”: original, Ivo, and editions cited above.] lest the Lord’s flocks lack pastoral care.

C. V. On the same matter. Likewise from the Second Council of Carthage, ch. 12. [Note: [Col. 0347] Held A.D. 390.]

It pleased all that no one should so readily presume, without consulting the primate of any province, even with many bishops, [Note: [Col. 0347] Omitted in the original.] to ordain a bishop in any place without his command, as stated. § 1. But if necessity arises, three bishops, wherever they may be, ought to ordain a bishop at the primate’s command. [Note: [Col. 0347] “will be obliged to”: Basel edition; “ought to”: remaining editions. “A bishop” omitted in the original.]

[Col. 0347C] C. VI. Let each church retain its own honor. Likewise from the Council of Nicaea, ch. 6. [Note: [Col. 0347] Held A.D. 325. Anselm, bk. 4, ch. 46; *Polycarpus*, bk. 2, tit. 22.]

Let the ancient custom continue in Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis: the Bishop of Alexandria is to have authority over all these, since the Roman bishop has a like custom. [Note: [Col. 0347] “may continue”: original; “since indeed”: editions cited above. “Like”: The Greek reads **ἐπειδὴ καὶ τῷ ἐν τῇ Ῥώμῃ ἐπισκόπῳ τοῦτο συνηθές ἐστιν**, that is, “because this is customary also for the bishop in Rome.” These words introduce no equality between the Roman and Alexandrian patriarchates, as some have wrongly interpreted. On this subject Nicholas I wrote most aptly in his letter to Emperor Michael, beginning *Proposueramus*: “The Nicene synod recognized that every privilege had been granted to the Roman Church by the Lord’s word. If everything, then nothing was lacking which He had not granted to her. Finally, if the enactments of the Nicene synod are carefully examined, it is certainly found that that synod conferred no increase upon the Roman Church; but rather, in granting something to the Alexandrian Church, it took a particular example from the Roman model.” Thus far Nicholas. Therefore it was decreed that this should be observed in the Alexandrian Church [Col. 0348D] because it was done so in the Roman Church.] [Note: [Col. 0347] These words appear to have entered Isidore’s collection from Dionysius’s translation, as it was current in Gaul. In the Hispanic Collection it reads: “since indeed the Bishop of Rome has this same custom.”] § 1. Likewise at Antioch and in the other provinces, let each church retain its own honor.

[Col. 0348A] C. VII. On the same matter. Likewise from the same council, ch. 7.

Since ancient custom and old tradition have prevailed that honor should be accorded to the Bishop of Aelia, that is, Jerusalem, he shall accordingly possess honor, while the metropolitan city retains its own dignity. [Note: [Col. 0347] “city”: editions cited above; “its own honor”: editions cited above except first Basel.]

Gratian. Whoever has been ordained by his fellow-provincial bishops with the metropolitan’s permission must present himself before him within the appointed time.

Accordingly, in the Council of Tarragona, ch. 5, we read: [Note: [Col. 0347] Held A.D. 516. — Tripartite Collection, part 2, tit. 31, ch. 4.]

C. VIII. A newly made bishop shall present himself to the metropolitan.

If a bishop has not been ordained in the metropolitan city, after receiving consecration [Col. 0348B] and attaining the episcopal honor by the metropolitan’s letters, we have decreed it best that, subsequently, at the appointed time—that is, after two months have been completed—he should present himself before his metropolitan, so that, instructed by him in ecclesiastical admonitions, he may learn more fully what he ought to observe. [Note: [Col. 0347] “we decree”: editions cited above; Böhm. “present”: editions cited above.] If he neglects to do this, he shall be corrected by his brethren after being rebuked in synod. But if he has been prevented by some illness from doing this, [Note: [Col. 0347] “hindered”: same editions.] he should take care to notify the metropolitan by letter.

### Part III

Gratian. From these authorities it is understood that bishops ought to be ordained by their fellow-provincial bishops. But the question is asked: if there are very many bishops in a province [Note: “there are not”: Basel ed.], and it should happen that only one bishop remains, what ought to be done? Since he is alone, he cannot ordain a bishop [Col. 0348C]; for he has no fellow-provincial bishops with whom he may consecrate a bishop. Therefore, when such necessity arises, what is to be done is determined in the Council of Sardica [Note: held A.D. 347.—Burchard, bk. 1, c. 26; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, c. 137.], in which, in chapter 6, the following decree is read.

#### C. IX. If only one bishop remains in a province, bishops from a neighboring province are to be summoned for the consecration of a bishop.

If [Note: This chapter, as Gratian reports it—especially its first part—agrees neither with the Latin version, of which there are two in the collections of councils, nor, still less, with the Greek canon; indeed, it is read differently in Burchard and Ivo. That the canons of this council were originally written in Latin by the Latins and in Greek by the Greeks is indicated by Pope Nicholas, writing to Photius in the letter beginning *Innumerabilium*, in these words: “How can you alone maintain that the Sardican canons are not among you, when they were enacted and promulgated not only by men of the Latin tongue but also together with men of the Greek tongue?” Hence it is not credible that each group did not transmit what was determined there in its own language. Dionysius Exiguus also, in the letter to Bishop Stephen in which he offered him his translation of the Greek canons, indicates that the Council of Sardica was published from the beginning in Latin among the Latins: “Then, adding the decrees of the holy Council of Chalcedon, we declare that the Greek canons end here, lest we seem to wish to withhold anything further from your knowledge. The decrees also of the Council of Sardica and of the African Council, which were issued in Latin, are seen to be distinguished by their own numbering.”] it should happen that only one bishop remains in a province [Col. 0349A], the surviving bishop shall summon bishops of a neighboring province and, with them, ordain fellow-provincial bishops for himself. But if he neglects to do this, the people shall approach the bishops of the neighboring province; and they shall first admonish the bishop residing in that province and show that [Col. 0350A] the people seek a bishop as their ruler, and shall teach that it is right that he himself come [Note: “That he himself come”: both in the council contained in the code of canons and in the collection of Isidore [in the Hispana collection, nevertheless, the reading is: “that they too come,” to which the Greek text corresponds], and in Burchard and Ivo, the reading is: “that they too come, and with him ordain a bishop.” But the Greek canon reads as follows:

> “Bishop Osius said: If it should happen in a province in which there are many bishops that one bishop remains, and he, through some negligence, is unwilling to assemble and consent to the appointment of bishops, while the assembled populace request that the bishop whom they seek be appointed, then that remaining bishop must first be reminded by letters of the primate of the province—that is, the bishop of the metropolitan see—that the people are worthy to have a shepherd given to them. I think it right also to wait for him to be present. But if, when requested by letters, he does not come, nor even reply, the will of the populace must be satisfied. Bishops from the neighboring province must also be summoned for the appointment of the metropolitan bishop.”

That is:

> Osius the bishop said: If in some province in which there are many bishops it should happen that one bishop remains absent, and through some negligence he is unwilling either to meet with them or to consent to the creation of bishops, while the assembled people request that the bishop whom they desire be appointed, that bishop who remains absent must first be admonished by letters from the primate of the province—that is, the metropolitan bishop—concerning the petition of the people, who ask that a shepherd be given to them. I think it right that he too should be awaited, so that he may be present. But if, though requested by letter, he does not appear and does not even reply, the people’s wish must be satisfied. Bishops from a neighboring province must also be summoned for the creation of the metropolitan bishop.

—and with them he shall ordain a bishop. But if, having been summoned by letters, he is silent and dissimulates, and sends no reply, then the people’s wishes must be satisfied: bishops from a neighboring province shall assemble and ordain a bishop.

## DISTINCTION LXVI

[Col. 0349]

### GRATIAN

#### Part I

An archbishop, however, ought to be ordained by all the bishops of his province.

Therefore Pope Anicetus, in a letter to the bishops of Gaul [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian epistle, whose source here may be recognized as the Council of Carthage, A.D. 409, c. 12; Nicaea, c. 4; Antioch, c. 19.—Burchard, bk. 1, c. 28; Anselm, bk. 6, c. 39; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, c. 10; *Decretum*, pt. 5, c. 139.—Cf. c. 9, *Compilatio I*, *De electione*, and c. 5, *X*, *De tempore ordinationum* (1.11). C. I.]:

#### C. I. An archbishop is to be ordained by all his suffragans.

An archbishop shall be ordained by all the bishops of his province. And below [Note: Here in the epistle, besides much else, occurs the chapter *Comprovinciales*, above, Distinction 64.]: §1. Yet that which was prescribed and commanded concerning the consecration of an archbishop—namely, that all the suffragans ordain him—may by no means be altered; because he who presides over them must be appointed by all the bishops over whom he presides. But if another course has been presumptuously taken, it undoubtedly has no force [Col. 0350A], because his ordination, performed otherwise, will be invalid.

#### Part II

Gratian. Concerning bishops not being ordained by fewer than three bishops, Anacletus, in his second epistle [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian epistle, this passage compiled from the preface to the Council of Nicaea in Quesnel and from Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, bk. 2, c. 5.—Burchard, bk. 1, c. 15; Anselm, bk. 6, c. 53 [51]; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, c. 17; *Decretum*, pt. 5, c. 139; *Polycarpus*, bk. 2, title 8.], writing to the bishops of Italy, says:

#### C. II. A bishop is to be ordained by no fewer than three bishops.

Moreover, the first archbishop of the Jerusalemites, blessed James, who was called the Just and was styled the Lord’s brother according to the flesh, was ordained by the apostles Peter, James, and John, thus giving a model to their successors: that a bishop should in no case be ordained by fewer than three bishops, all the rest giving their assent, and that the ordination should be celebrated by common vote.

## DISTINCTION LXVII

[Col. 0351]

### GRATIAN

#### Part I

Priests and chorepiscopi may be ordained by one bishop.

Therefore Anacletus, in his second epistle to the bishops of Italy [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, composed from Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, bk. 2, c. 6.—Anselm; *Polycarpus*, II. cc. C. I.]:

#### C. I. Priests may be ordained by one bishop.

The remaining priests shall be ordained by their own bishop, with citizens and the other priests giving their assent, and they shall celebrate the ordination fasting [Col. 0352A]. Deacons likewise shall be ordained. For the conferral of the remaining grades, the testimony of three trustworthy persons, together with the bishop’s approval, may suffice.

Likewise, in the Second Council of Seville [Note: held A.D. 619.—Cf. C. 15, q. 7 = C. II, Part II, c. 7.], c. 6, one reads:

#### C. II. On the same matter.

#### Part II

A bishop alone can confer rank upon priests and ministers; he cannot alone remove it.

## DISTINCTION LXVIII

[Col. 0351]

### GRATIAN

#### Part I

The question is asked about those who are ordained by persons who are not known to have been bishops: must they be consecrated again [Col. 0351B], or not? That they ought not to be consecrated is proved by the authority of Gregory, who, writing to John, bishop of Ravenna, in book II, epistle 32 [Note: Epistle 46, written A.D. 592, Maurist edition.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 104; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, c. 76; *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 82; *Polycarpus*, bk. 2, title 36; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, bk. 4, Distinction 25, c. 1.], says:

#### C. I. One consecrated once ought not be consecrated again.

Just as one baptized once ought not to be baptized again, so one consecrated once ought not to be consecrated again in the same order. But if anyone perhaps comes to the priesthood with a minor fault, penance should be imposed for the fault, and yet the order should be retained.

Against this, Gregory III [Note: written A.D. 740.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 110, from Gelasius; Ivo, pt. 6, c. 117.], writing in his second epistle to Bishop Boniface, attests:

#### C. II. Concerning priests ordained by those who are known not to have been bishops.

The priests [Col. 0351C] whom you found there: if the persons who ordained them are unknown, and it is uncertain whether or not they were bishops, then, if those priests are men of good conduct and Catholic, instructed in Christ’s ministry and in all holy law, let them receive the priestly blessing from their bishop and be consecrated; and thus let them perform the sacred ministry.

Gratian. Therefore, the prohibition against a person consecrated in the same order being consecrated again must be understood of one consecrated by a person certainly known to have had the right to consecrate. But one consecrated by a person not known to have possessed the right to consecrate must be consecrated again; for if that person did not have the right of consecration [Col. 0351D], this one received no consecration from the pouring out of the oil. And because he had not been consecrated in that order, he now receives from the bishop the priestly blessing and consecration as though coming to consecration for the first time [Col. 0352A]. But if the former had the right to consecrate, he received consecration in the first anointing; in the second, however, consecration is not repeated, but only the anointing—as one concerning whom it is uncertain whether he has been baptized or not ought to be baptized. If he had not previously been baptized, he receives the grace of baptism; but if he had been baptized, he receives nothing in the second anointing. This does not amount to repetition of baptism, but to a precaution for salvation. The same is likewise to be observed concerning the consecration of churches.

Therefore it is read in the Nicene Council [Note: The author of this chapter, wrongly attributed to the Council of Nicaea, has not been found.—Cf. below, D. 1, *De consecratione*, c. 20.]:

#### C. III. A church once consecrated must not be consecrated again.

No further consecration ought to be applied to churches once consecrated to God, unless they have been burned by fire, polluted by the shedding of blood [Col. 0352C], or by the emission of anyone’s semen. For just as an infant baptized once by any priest in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit ought not to be baptized again, so neither ought a place dedicated to God to be consecrated again, except for the causes named above—provided that those who consecrated it held the faith of the Holy Trinity.

#### Part II

Gratian. The difference between bishops and chorepiscopi is this: bishops may be ordained only in cities, whereas chorepiscopi may also be ordained in villages. Bishops issue *formatae*; chorepiscopi can issue only letters of recommendation and peace. Bishops possess the right of consecration; chorepiscopi confer only the minor orders [Col. 0352D], and cannot confer Levitical or priestly blessing.

Leo I [Note: A spurious epistle.—Almost the whole passage is taken from the Second Council of Seville, c. 6.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 123 [125]; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 72; *Polycarpus*, bk. 4, title 26.], writing to the bishops of Germany and Gaul in epistle 86, or 88, says the following:

#### C. IV. In what respects chorepiscopi differ from bishops.

Although chorepiscopi and priests share with bishops much of the administration of ministries, they should know that certain things are forbidden to them by the authority of the old law, and certain things by new and ecclesiastical rules: namely, the consecration of priests, deacons, or virgins; likewise the establishment of an altar, and blessing or anointing. For they are not permitted to erect altars or consecrate churches or altars; nor, by laying on of hands, to impart the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, to baptized believers or converts from heresy; nor to make chrism; nor to mark the foreheads of the baptized with chrism [Col. 0353B]; nor even publicly reconcile any penitent at Mass; nor send *formatae* letters to anyone.

**[PALEA.]**

> “For all these things are unlawful for chorepiscopi, who are known to exist after the example and pattern of the seventy-two disciples, or for priests, who bear the same figure; because, although they have consecration, they do not possess the summit of the pontificate.”

#### Part III

Gratian. But because of their presumption, by which they usurped for themselves the offices of bishops, they are now prohibited by the Church.

Therefore Pope Damasus says to the bishops of Africa, in epistle V [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian epistle.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 123 [126]; *Polycarpus*, bk. 4, title 26.]:

#### C. V. The order of chorepiscopi is rejected by the Apostolic See.

Chorepiscopi have been prohibited both by this Holy See and by the bishops of the whole world [Col. 0353C]. Their institution, therefore, is exceedingly wicked and exceedingly perverse, because, if they presume anything belonging to the ministry of the high priest, it lacks all authority [Col. 0354A]. And below: §1. For we have known that there are no more than two orders among the disciples of the Lord, namely, those of the twelve apostles and of the seventy disciples. Whence this third order arose, we are utterly ignorant. And what lacks rational basis must be uprooted.

#### Part IV

§2. That those ordained by fewer than three bishops are not bishops is evident to all; for, as you well know, the holy Fathers have forbidden those ordained by one or two bishops even to be called bishops. If they do not have the name, how can they have the office?

Therefore Pope Urban II [Note: Chapter of uncertain origin.] says:

#### C. VI. Bishops hold the place of the apostles in the Church.

Whose place bishops hold in the Church, and who ought to confer this dignity upon them, Saint Augustine shows, saying: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you.” What does “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you” mean? The apostles sent forth were fathers; in place of the apostles sons were born to you—they were appointed bishops. For whence were the bishops who today exist throughout the whole world born? The Church herself calls those men fathers; she herself gave them birth, and she herself appointed them to the seats of the fathers. Therefore do not think yourself abandoned because you do not see Peter, because you do not see Paul, because you do not see those through whom you were born: from your offspring fatherhood has grown for you. “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them rulers over all [Col. 0354C] the earth.” And below: “The Church gave birth to sons and appointed them rulers over all the earth in place of her fathers.”

## DISTINCTION LXIX

[Col. 0353]

### GRATIAN

#### Part I

A cleric may receive tonsure from the hand of an abbot, if it is known that the laying on of hands was performed upon that abbot by a bishop.

Therefore, in the Seventh Synod, c. 14 [Note: Second Council of Nicaea, A.D. 787, from Anastasius’s translation.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, c. 376. C. I.], it is read:

#### C. I. Abbots upon whom a bishop lays hands may tonsure certain persons.

Since we see that certain persons, receiving clerical tonsure from childhood without the laying on of hands, and before receiving the laying on of hands from a bishop [Col. 0353D], irregularly read from the ambo in the assembly, we command that this no longer be done. The same is to be observed among monks as well.

#### Part II

§1. An abbot alone has permission to impose hands upon a reader in his own monastery, provided that the same abbot is known to have received the laying on of hands from a bishop [according to the custom for appointing abbots], and provided that he is known to be a priest. §2. Likewise, according to ancient custom, chorepiscopi ought, by the bishop’s command, to appoint readers.

[Col. 0355A]

#### C. II. Those not appointed by a bishop must not perform exorcisms.

Likewise from the Council of Laodicea, c. 26 [Note: held between A.D. 347 and 381.]:

Those who have not yet been appointed by bishops [Col. 0356A] ought not to perform exorcisms, whether in churches or in houses.

## DISTINCTION LXX

[Col. 0355]

### GRATIAN

A cleric may not be ordained by the bishop of another city, nor may he be ordained without assignment even by his own bishop. For ordination without assignment is forbidden by the Council of Chalcedon, which commands that the laying on of hands be void [Col. 0355B]. There the following is decreed, canon 6 [Note: held A.D. 451.—In Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, c. 27, only the first part of this canon, from the Hispanic version—that found in Gratian—is used; in the second part and in the *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 26, with Regino, bk. 1, c. 386; Burchard, bk. 2, c. 6; Anselm, bk. 7, c. 105, Dionysius is followed.]:

#### C. I. No one is to be ordained without assignment.

No one, whether presbyter, deacon, or any person established in an ecclesiastical order, is to be ordained without assignment, unless he receives the publicly proclaimed designation of ordination specifically in the church of a city, estate, martyr-shrine, or monastery [Note: In Greek: *Ei mē idiōs en ekklēsia poleōs ē kōmēs ē martyrio ē monastēriō ho cheirotonoumenos epikēryttēto*, “unless the person ordained is named specifically in the church of a city, village, martyr-shrine, or monastery.” The Roman Ordinal mentions such a proclamation, made by the archdeacon in the bishop’s name: “For the title of St Stephen we elect Peter as reader for that same title.”]. But the holy synod decreed that those ordained without assignment have a void laying on of hands and that such an act can nowhere have effect, to the injury of the person who ordained him [Note: Greek: *Mēdamou dynasthai energein*, “to be unable to function anywhere.”].

#### C. II. Ordination performed without a title is void.
