Likewise, from the Council of Urban II held at Piacenza, c. 15 [Note: held A.D. 1095.]:

By a decree consonant with the statutes of the holy canons [Col. 0355C], we determine that an ordination made without a title is to be considered void, and that each person assigned to a church shall remain in it permanently. §1. No one may in any way be assigned to two churches; rather, each shall be considered a canon only in that church to which he has been assigned. For although, by the bishop’s disposition, one person may preside over several churches [Col. 0356B], nevertheless a canon holding a prebend ought to belong only to the one church in which he is enrolled. §2. If, however, there are chapels that cannot support clerics from their own revenues, their care and administration shall devolve upon the provost of the greater church to which the chapels appear subject; and he shall provide both from the estates and from the ecclesiastical offices of the chapels.

Gratian. In the same council, a tenth preface was added to the previous nine, reading as follows: “It is fitting and salutary to praise, bless, and proclaim you in the veneration or assumption of the Blessed Mary, who both conceived your Only-Begotten by the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit and, with the glory of virginity remaining, poured forth upon the world the eternal light, Jesus Christ [Col. 0356C] our Lord.”

## DISTINCTION LXXI

[Col. 0355]

### GRATIAN

Concerning clerics not being ordained by a bishop of another city, the Council of Sardica [Note: held A.D. 347; Regino, bk. 1, cc. 432–433.], c. 18 and 19, decreed as follows. Bishop Januarius is recorded as having said:

#### C. I. Clerics are not to be ordained by a bishop of another city.

Let your holiness also decree that no bishop may solicit an ecclesiastical person from another city [Col. 0355D] and ordain him as a cleric in his own diocese. [Note: “Ecclesiastical person”: the Latin council reads, “solicit an ecclesiastical minister and make him a cleric in his own parishes,” etc. Below, in the same chapter, *Primatus*, where the sense of this canon seems to be reported, one reads: “that no one usurp a person belonging to another people.” This chapter, which is the eighteenth in the Latin text, is absent from the Greek.] All said: It is agreeable, because disputes commonly arise from such acts; and therefore, by unanimous judgment, it is prohibited that anyone dare do this. §1. Bishop Osius said: We all have also decreed this: whoever wishes to ordain a minister belonging to another parish without the consent and will of that bishop shall have an invalid ordination [Col. 0356D].

[Col. 0357A]

#### C. II. On the same matter.

Likewise, Innocent, in his second epistle to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, c. 7 [Note: written A.D. 404.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, c. 64.]:

No one may presume to ordain a cleric from another church unless his bishop, prevailed upon by entreaties, chooses to grant permission.

#### C. III. The ordination of one ordained without his bishop’s consent is void.

Likewise, from the Council of Nicaea, c. 16, at the end [Note: held A.D. 325.—From Dionysius in Regino, bk. 1, c. 384; Burchard, bk. 1, c. 109.]:

If anyone dares to ordain in his own church someone who belongs to another, without the consent of the bishop from whom the cleric departed, such ordination shall be void.

#### C. IV. A cleric of one church is not to be ordained in another.

Likewise, from the Council of Chalcedon, c. 20 [Note: held A.D. 451.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 361.—From Dionysius: Anselm, bk. 7, c. 109.]:

Clerics appointed in their own churches [Col. 0357B], as we have already determined, may not be ordained in the churches of another city; rather, they shall remain in that church in which they first received appointment to minister, except those who have lost their own cities and from necessity migrated to other churches. But if any bishop, after this decree, receives a cleric belonging to another bishop, the holy synod decreed that both the receiver and the one received shall remain excommunicated until that cleric returns to his own church.

#### C. V. By apostolic permission, a cleric of one church may be ordained in another.

Likewise, Gregory, in book V, epistle 11, to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples [Note: Epistle 11, written A.D. 596, book 6 of the Maurist edition.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 80; *Polycarpus*, bk. 1, title 7.]:

We remember that your brotherhood requested us to grant to your church Gratian, deacon of the church of Venafro, to be incardinated in it [Note: “To be incardinated”: previously the text read “to be ordained.” It has been corrected from the epistle itself. Saint Gregory seems to use *cardinare*, or “make cardinal”—as at the end of this chapter—to mean a canonical transfer. Since in Saint Gregory’s time canon 6 of the Council of Chalcedon was carefully observed, so that a place in a church—now called a title—was never given to anyone unless he was ordained to that place at the same time, when someone already ordained was transferred to another church by some necessity in order to serve there in the same grade in which he had been ordained in the first, he was said to be incardinated in the second. This is clear from the passage just cited, from bk. 3, epistle 14, and elsewhere. Saint Gregory did the same with bishops, bk. 2, indiction 10, epistles 6 and 25—the latter quoted below, 7, q. 1, c. *Pastoralis*—and indiction 11, epistle 13 and the following letter, found below, 21, q. 1, c. *Relatio*. On this matter, John the Deacon, bk. 3, chapters 8, 11, and 16. John VIII also imitated Gregory, both in practice and in using the term in this sense, as appears from several manuscripts of his letters.]. And since he has neither a bishop whom he ought to obey nor a church of his own in which to exercise his ministry, the enemy preventing this, we did not think your petition should be deferred [Col. 0358A]. Therefore, by these present writings, we have judged that he must be granted to you, so that, God willing, you may have authority through our intervention to establish that deacon as a cardinal cleric of your church.

#### C. VI. No cleric is to be received in any church without letters from his own bishop.

Likewise, from the First Council of Carthage, c. 5 [Note: held A.D. 348.—Burchard, bk. 2, c. 43; Anselm, bk. 6, c. 124; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 144.]:

Bishop Primatus of Vegesela said: “I submit to your holiness that you decree that no one may receive a cleric belonging to another without letters from his own bishop, or retain him; nor may anyone take for himself a layman from another people, so as to obtain him without the knowledge of the bishop whose people he belongs to.” Bishop Gratus said: “This observance preserves peace [Col. 0358B]. For I remember that it was decreed in the most holy Council of Sardica that no one should usurp a person belonging to another people. But if he should perhaps be necessary, let him ask his colleague and receive him by consent.”

#### C. VII. Without letters of recommendation, a cleric is not to minister outside his own church.

Likewise, from the Council of Chalcedon, c. 13 [Note: held A.D. 451.—From Dionysius: Burchard, bk. 2, c. 139; Anselm, bk. 7, c. 162 [176]; *Polycarpus*, bk. 4, title 31.]:

No foreign cleric or reader may anywhere at all minister outside his own city without letters of recommendation from his own bishop.

#### C. VIII. On the same matter.

Likewise, from a sermon of Saint Augustine to the people [Note: Not found among Augustine’s sermons.—Burchard, bk. 15, c. 30; Anselm, bk. 7, c. 181; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 16, c. 31: from Augustine’s sayings.]:

We exhort your Christian body, in accordance with the ordinances of the holy canons, that in churches founded by you no priest coming from elsewhere be received unless he has been consecrated by the bishop of your church [Col. 0358C], or is received by him through letters of recommendation.

#### C. IX. Traveling clerics are not to be received without a *formata*.

Likewise, from the Council of Antioch, c. 7 [Note: held A.D. 332, commonly dated 341.]:

No traveling cleric ought to be received without a *formata*, which the Greeks call a letter [Note: Greek: *Mēdena aneu eirēnikōn dechētai tōn xenōn*, rendered by Dionysius: “No traveling person is to be received without letters of peace,” that is, letters of recommendation. Burchard and Ivo read it in this manner.].

## DISTINCTION LXXII

[Col. 0359]

### GRATIAN

A bishop, however, should not give letters dimissory unless requested, as was decreed in a synod held at Rome.

Therefore Pope Leo says [Note: From the synod of Eugenius II, held A.D. 826, c. 18, confirmed by Leo IV.]:

#### C. I. No letters dimissory are to be given unless requested by the applicant.

A bishop shall not issue letters dimissory to a priest or other cleric subject to him unless requested by that person, lest the sheep be found as though lost or straying.

#### C. II. On the same matter.

Likewise, from the Third Council of Carthage, c. 21 [Note: held A.D. 397.—Burchard, bk. 2, c. 42; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 143.]:

No one may dare either retain or promote in the church entrusted to him a cleric belonging to another, unless that cleric’s bishop grants permission [Col. 0360A]. The designation “clerics” includes readers, psalmists, and doorkeepers as well.

It was resolved that whoever is elected even once in one church [Note: “Is elected”: the Council of Milevis reads *vel semel legerit*, “or has read even once” [the Hispana collection: “or has read even once”]; likewise the Greek Council of Carthage, c. 91: *Kan hapax anagnō*, “even if he has read once”; while the African Council, c. 57, reads: “or has read after undertaking office once.”] shall not be retained for clerical service by another church.

### Apparatus and editorial notes omitted above

- Part III, opening: The Basel edition reads “are not” (*non fuerint*) for “there are [many]” (*fuerint*).
- Part III, C. IX: The preceding editorial note is located at [Col. 0347]; the cited Sardican council was held in A.D. 347.
- Part III, C. IX, after “he himself come”: The Hispana collection nevertheless reads “that they too come” (*veniat et ipse*), corresponding to the Greek; Burchard and Ivo read “that they too come, and with him ordain a bishop.” The editions collectively read “And if” (*Et si*) for “But if.”
- Distinction LXVI, C. I: The opening sentence of the Anicetan epistle and the versions of other collectors set out this first passage more fully. At §1, the collective editions read “But this” (*Hoc autem*) for “Yet that which”; the Basel edition has “all” (*omnibus*) at “he who presides over them”; the collective editions add *autem* after *sin*; and they read “the archbishop’s” (*archiepiscopi*) for “his” ordination.
- Distinction LXVI, C. II: The Basel edition has *Hierosolymitanorum*, and the other editions *Hierosolymitanus*, for *Hierosolymitarum*. The Argentinensis and Basel editions add *autem* after “successors”; the Basel edition reads *scilicet* for *videlicet*; and the phrase “by” (*ab*) before “three bishops” is absent from the Argentinensis and Basel editions.
- Distinction LXVII, C. I: The Basel edition omits *cum* in “together with the bishop’s approval.” The source describes the Second Council of Seville as held in A.D. 619. In C. II the Basel edition adds *autem* after “alone.”
- Distinction LXVIII, C. I: The collective editions read “so also one ordained once cannot be consecrated again” for the present wording; Anselm reads *valet* (“is valid”) for *debet* (“ought”); *forsitan* (“perhaps”) is absent from Anselm; the collective editions read *venerit* (“comes/will have come”) for *venit*; and they read *servetur* (“let the order be preserved”) for *servari*.
- Distinction LXVIII, C. II: The Roman edition originally reads *Presbyteris*, corrected to *Presbyteri* in its errata. The collective editions add *viri* (“men”) after “those”; the original reads “by whom they were ordained” for “who ordained them”; the Basel edition has *aut* for *an*; and the negative *non* is absent in the collective editions, the first Basel edition, and the second and third Lyons and Antwerp editions. The Bohmer edition omits “and thus let them perform the sacred ministry.”
- Distinction LXVIII, Gratian’s discussion: The source’s “consecrated in that order” means that, if the first minister lacked the right to consecrate, the recipient had not in fact received ordination in the order in question.
- Distinction LXVIII, C. III: The collective editions read *dedicatus* (“dedicated”) for *dicatus*. The transmitted ending varies: *tenuerit* (“has held”) and, in the Basel edition, *consecraverit* (“has consecrated”), for *tenuerunt* (“they held”).
- Distinction LXVIII, C. IV: The letter attributed to Leo I is spurious; almost the whole passage is taken from the Second Council of Seville, c. 6. The words marked by asterisks are absent from Anselm. Ivo reads *permittimus* (“we permit”) and Anselm *licitum est* (“it is permitted”) for *licet* (“they are permitted”). The original and Ivo read “those to be baptized,” rather than “baptized believers”; the original and Anselm read “from heresy,” and Ivo “concerning heresy,” for “converts from heresy”; and the Basel edition adds *clerico* (“cleric”) after “to anyone.”
- Distinction LXVIII, [Palea]: The same words occur in an epistle of Damasus, of which the following canon is a portion (Part III).
- Distinction LXVIII, C. V: The collective editions read “are” (*sunt*) and Bohmer “were” (*fuerunt*) for *fuerant*. The collective editions read the sentence from “For their institution” through “perverse” as one continuous clause. They read *et si* for *ut*; and *carent* (“they lack”) for *caret* (“it lacks”). They read seventy-two disciples, while Anselm reads seventy. The collective editions add *funditus* (“utterly”), and the Basel edition reads *exstirpandum est* (“must be uprooted”) for *exstirpari*.
- Distinction LXVIII, §2: The collective editions add *enim* after “forbidden” and after “name.”
- Distinction LXVIII, C. VI: This is a chapter of uncertain origin; the collective editions introduce it “Likewise, Urban.” Its source is Augustine’s commentary on Psalm 44, at the end. The collective editions read “the whole universe” for “the whole world.”
- Distinction LXIX, C. I: The original, Ivo, and the collective editions read *clerici* for *cleri*; the collective editions read “many” for “certain persons.” In §1 the second Council of Nicaea’s Greek canon does not contain the bracketed phrase “according to the custom for appointing abbots”; the original, Ivo, and the collective editions add *unicuique* (“to each”) after “abbot.” In §2 Ivo and the collective editions have the singular *chorepiscopum* for *chorepiscopos*.
- Distinction LXIX, C. II: The Council of Laodicea was held between A.D. 347 and 381. The collective editions add *suis* (“their own”) after “bishops”; the original and Basel edition read *provecti* for *promoti*; and the Hispana collection reads “among houses” for “in houses.”
- Distinction LXX, C. I: The collective editions read “neither … nor” in place of “or … or.” The Greek says: “Unless the person being ordained is specifically proclaimed in the church of a city, village, martyr-shrine, or monastery.” The Roman Ordinal records the analogous proclamation by an archdeacon in the bishop’s name: “For the title of Saint Stephen we choose Peter as reader for that same title.” The collective editions, following Ivo, add “his own” after “city” and “here” after “monastery,” and read *publicae* for *publicatae*. The Greek for “such an act can nowhere have effect” is *Mēdamou dynasthai energein*, “to be unable to act anywhere.”
- Distinction LXX, C. II: The collective editions, except the first Argentinensis, Basel, and first and second Venice editions, read *intitulari* and later *intitulatus* for *titulari* and *titulatus*. The Basel, second and third Lyons, and Antwerp editions read *earum* (“of them”) for *ea* (“their”).
- Distinction LXXI, C. I: The eighteenth canon is absent from the Greek text. The Latin council reads “solicit an ecclesiastical minister and make him a cleric in his own parishes,” rather than “solicit an ecclesiastical person from another city”; below, in the chapter *Primatus*, the same sense is expressed as “that no one usurp a person of another people.” The words marked by asterisks are absent from the Hispanic translation, although present in Dionysius, from whom Gratian’s correctors inserted them. The Argentinensis and Basel editions read *prohibetur*, and the remaining editions *prohibeatur*, for *prohibet*; the collective editions read *omni* for *omnium*; and they read *sui* for *ipsius* after “bishop.”
- Distinction LXXI, C. II: The original reads *usurpet* (“usurp”) for *praesumat* (“presume”).
- Distinction LXXI, C. IV: The Hispana collection, Ivo, and the collective editions read *singulis* (“several/individual”) for *suis*; the Hispana reads *decrevimus* for *diffinivimus*. The reading “in which he first received appointment to minister” appears to have entered the printed collection of Isidore from Dionysius; the genuine Hispana reading is “in which he began to minister.” The Hispana, Isidore-Merlin, Ivo, and the collective editions read *hunc* for *eum*; the Hispana and Isidore-Merlin also have variant forms for “may not” and “acquiesce.”
- Distinction LXXI, C. V: The original and the Basel, Lyons, and Antwerp editions read *Venefranae* for *Benafranae*. The earlier printed reading was *ordinandum* (“to be ordained”); *cardinandum* (“to be incardinated”) is restored from Gregory’s epistle itself. In Gregory, *cardinare* or “make cardinal” denotes canonical transfer: a cleric already ordained and transferred to serve in another church in the same grade was said to be incardinated in the second church. Compare book 3, epistle 14 and other passages; for bishops, book 2, indiction 10, epistles 6 and 25, indiction 11, epistle 13 and the following epistle; John the Deacon, book 3, chapters 8, 11, and 16; and John VIII’s letters. Anselm and the collective editions instead read “he has his own church, to whose bishop he ought to submit.” The source says that he has neither a bishop whom he ought to obey nor his own church, because an enemy prevents him from exercising his ministry there. It reads *habiturus* (“being about to have”) for *habituro* (“having”).
- Distinction LXXI, C. VI: The Hispana identifies the speaker as “Privatus, bishop of Vegesela,” rather than “Primatus, bishop of Vegesela.” The collective editions add *episcopo* after “from another”; the Hispana and Isidore-Merlin read *ordinet* (“ordain him”) for *obtineat* (“obtain him”); the Basel edition reads “holy” for “most holy”; the Hispana, Basel, second and third Lyons, and Antwerp editions add *sibi* (“for himself”) after “usurp”; and the collective editions and Bohmer add “of his bishop” after “by consent.”
- Distinction LXXI, C. IX: The Greek is *Mēdena aneu eirēnikōn dechētai tōn xenōn*: “Let no one receive any of the strangers without letters of peace.” Dionysius renders it “No traveler is to be received without peaceful—that is, commendatory—letters”; Burchard and Ivo have that form.
- Distinction LXXII, C. II: Ivo reads *retineant* (“let them include”) for *retinent* (“include”).
- Distinction LXXII, C. III: The Council of Milevis actually reads *vel semel legerit* (“or has read even once”), not *vel semel eligitur* (“is elected even once”); the Hispana likewise reads “or has read even once.” The Greek Council of Carthage, c. 91, has *Kan hapax anagnō*, “even if he has read once”; the African Council, c. 57, has “or has read once after receiving office.”

## DISTINCTION LXXIII

[Col. 0359]

### GRATIAN
The manner in which a letter of recommendation, dismissal, or *formata* is to be made must be considered. Greek letters must be inserted in such a letter, and not without reason. For no one with even a slight acquaintance with the Greek language is unaware that the letters of the Greek alphabet also express numbers. Therefore, lest some fraudulent falsification should rashly be attempted in making canonical letters—which Latin custom calls *formatae*—the Fathers, 318 in number, assembled at Nicaea, most beneficially devised and established that letters *formatae* should employ the following system of calculation or reckoning: namely, that the first Greek letters of “Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit” should be included in the calculation—that is, Π, Υ, Α—which letters signify the numbers eighty, four hundred, and one. The first letter also of the Apostle Peter, namely Π, which signifies the number eighty.[Note: [Col. 0359] “Which number”: original text; Regino; Anselm.] The first letter of the bishop who writes; the second letter of the person to whom he writes; the third letter of the recipient; the fourth letter of the city from which the letter is written; and the number of the indiction, whatever it may be at that time,[Note: [Col. 0359] “The same”: original text; Anselm, chapter I.] are to be included. Thus, with all these Greek letters—which, as we have said, express numbers—added together into one total, the letter is to contain whatever sum has been collected; and the person receiving it is to require this sum to be stated expressly,[Note: [Col. 0359] “Expressed”: same source.] with every precaution. Moreover, he shall separately add to the letter the number ninety-nine, which according to Greek letters signifies Ἀμήν, “Amen.”

[Note: [Col. 0359] This is the rule for *formatae*, which is customarily and consistently attributed to Atticus of Constantinople. It is printed in full in Regino, book 1, chapter 438; Anselm, book 6, chapter 121 (122); and Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 433.]

[Col. 0359D] CHAPTER I. Example of a *formata* letter, established at the Nicene Synod by the 318 Fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0359] Burchard, book 2, chapter 227.]

[Col. 0360B] In the name of the Father Π, and of the Son Υ, and of the Holy Spirit Α. Π. To Walter, bishop of Speyer: I, Burchard, devoted servant of Christ’s flock in the holy Church of Worms, wish you in God indeed the blessedness of highest happiness.

Although the holy catholic Church is ready to follow the teachings of the Gospel, which say: “He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and he who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward,” etc.; and although the Apostle commands us to pursue hospitality and share in the necessities of holy persons—nevertheless, because of those who have their own conscience seared, who call themselves simple while filled with diabolical cunning, and who say that they travel from place to place for a work of piety while in fact their own malice makes them fugitives; and who say that they are attached to sacred ministry when they are not—it has been established by the holy Fathers that no bishop shall receive an unknown cleric from another jurisdiction and enthrone him in his own church unless he has a letter from his own bishop, called in the canons a *formata*.

[Note: [Col. 0359] Matthew, chapter 10.]

We therefore make known to your brotherhood that our present brother, the bearer of this letter, named Hermann—

[Note: [Col. 0359] Ecmanus: Burchard.]

—has not been expelled by us on account of his wrongdoing. Rather, at the request of the brethren, because he belonged to our household and was baptized among us, we canonically granted him freedom, received at the horn of the altar, and ordained him to the rank of priest. We also make for him these letters of dismissal or recommendation, and direct him to your beloved brotherhood, so that within your diocese, under your sacred rule and protection, he may be able to remain.

[Note: [Col. 0359] “from”: Basel edition.]

I, Burchard, humble bishop, I say, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and in the unity of the holy Church—in which Peter was given the authority of binding and loosing—release Hermann, priest of the city of Worms, in the tenth indiction; and I give you permission to enthrone him in whatever church of your diocese you wish.

[Note: [Col. 0361] “Father Π, and Son Υ, and Holy Spirit Α”: collected editions.]

We have therefore resolved to secure this letter on every side with Greek letters and have judged it proper to validate it with the seal of our church. May Christ preserve your brotherhood safe for us. Π. Υ. Α. Π. Β. Ε. Ζ. Ξ. ἀμήν.

[Note: [Col. 0361D] “May preserve”: In this and the following chapter only those readings have been corrected which could be restored with the help of manuscripts. The material that follows here is corrupted even in Burchard. It can, however, readily be restored from the rules set forth at the beginning of this distinction. The example supplied by Ivo, part 6, chapter 435, corresponds especially well to those rules, if the letters placed at the end of chapter 434 are put in place of those given in chapter 455 itself. For when the word Ἀμήν, “Amen,” is added to them, the number stated there results, namely 1,378. The example in chapter 434 will also work properly if, where the total now is 1,539, it is made 1,439. It is enough to have indicated the passage.]

Given at Worms on the Ides of March, in the year 1012 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the tenth indiction.

[Note: [Col. 0361] “1002, month 12”: collected editions.]

[Col. 0361B] CHAPTER II. Here begins the *formata* letter issued by the 318 bishops and by Atticus, bishop of the city of Constantinople.

[Note: [Col. 0362D] “By Atticus”: formerly the reading was “by abbots.” The passage has been restored by conjecture—something done very rarely—because the reasoning for it was compelling.]

To A., most holy brother in Christ, to be embraced with the utmost sweetness of charity, bishop of that city: Y., prelate of that church, wishes you everlasting blessedness and salvation in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0361] Added: “service”: Basel edition.]

Ω Y. A. Ω.

Henceforth let your holy brotherhood know that this cleric, named Hermann—

[Note: [Col. 0361] “B.”: Argentinian and Basel editions; “Ber.”: Nuremberg and Venice II editions; “Her.”: Venice I.]

—was trained and tonsured in our diocese, and requested our lowliness to write him letters of recommendation, by which, commended to your eminence, he might live under the protection of your government. Assenting to his wish in accordance with canonical authority, we gave him letters of dismissal, through which we both permit him, by persevering in divine service under your instruction, to serve his own welfare, and grant you leave, if you judge him worthy, to promote him to sacred orders. Receive him therefore, commended to your care, and preserve him, released on our side, among the number of your sheep.

In order that these letters, confirmed in the strength of truth, may be received by you without doubt, we endeavor to authenticate them with Greek letters, as canonical authority teaches. May the Holy Trinity grant your blessedness perpetual well-being for the governance of His holy Church. Ἀμήν, “Amen.”

[Note: [Col. 0362D] “Ἀμήν,” or alternatively: “Et. Θ.” These have been added from several ancient manuscripts, and each of these two signs signifies the same number, ninety-nine. In printed copies there was either nothing, or the word *Amen* written in Latin, which has no numerical significance.]

[Or alternatively: Et. Θ.

[Note: [Col. 0361] “YE”: collected editions.]

(They express the same total.)] In the tenth indiction. This *formata* letter contains a sum of 1,315. We put Greek Υ first in his name, because Greeks in some places use it for consonantal Y, as in Δαυίδ, “David,” and εὐαγγέλιον, “Gospel.”

[Note: [Col. 0361] That this passage is astonishingly corrupted in the printed editions will be shown by these examples: read in the Basel edition: “a. jj. yo. id.”; in the Argentinian edition: “a. n. y. s. id.” From this, however, seems to have arisen the reading in the Paris and Lyons editions, ἀπουσία, that is, “absence,” which is entirely without sense.]

## DISTINCTION LXXIV

[Col. 0361]

GRATIAN.

[Col. 0361B]

Part I. The question concerns those who disdain to be promoted by their bishops: whether they ought to be elevated unwillingly or not.

The following determination is found concerning them in the Third Council of Orléans, chapter 7:

[Note: [Col. 0361] Held in A.D. 538.]

CHAPTER I. A bishop who presumes to ordain an unwilling person shall be subject to suspension for a year.

A bishop who presumes to ordain someone unwilling or protesting shall be subjected to a year’s penance and shall not presume to celebrate Mass.

[Col. 0362B] CHAPTER II. No one is to be promoted unwillingly. Gregory likewise, to Natalis, bishop of Salona, in book I of the *Register*, letter 19.

[Note: [Col. 0361] Letter 19, written A.D. 591, book 1, Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 379; Polycarpus, book 2, title 33.]

[Col. 0362C] We have learned that the acts which you sent us, drawn up in the record-office of your council, in which Archdeacon Honoratus is arraigned, are full of seeds of quarrels. For at one and the same time a single person, unwillingly, is promoted to the order of priesthood, while, as though unworthy, he is removed from the office of deacon. And just as it is right that no one should be compelled to advance unwillingly, so likewise, in my judgment, no innocent person should be unjustly removed from the ministry of his order.

[Note: [Col. 0361] “Council”: Basel edition. “In which”: “wherein,” ibid. “Is arraigned”: “is brought,” collected editions and first Basel edition. “Is promoted”: “may be promoted,” Basel edition. “Is removed”: “may be removed,” collected editions.]

[Col. 0363A] The contrary is found in the Council of Carthage, chapter 31:

[Note: [Col. 0363] From the Synod of Carthage, held A.D. 419, in Dionysius; Burchard, book 2, chapter 178; Anselm, book 7, chapter 103; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 42.]

CHAPTER III. Those who disdain promotion by their bishops are to be removed from their positions.

If any clerics disdain promotion by their bishops, they are not to remain in the positions from which they refused to depart.

[Note: [Col. 0363D] “If any”: the words of this chapter are the heading of the following chapter, “It pleased [the council],” which is the actual canon 31 of the Council of Carthage in the collection of canons and among the Greeks.]

CHAPTER IV. On the same subject.

It pleased [the council] that any clerics or deacons who, because of the necessities of ecclesiastical affairs, do not obey their bishops when those bishops wish to promote them to a higher dignity in their own church, shall not minister in the rank from which they refused to depart.

[Note: [Col. 0363D] “Because of the necessities”: in Greek, Διὰ τίνας ἀναγκαστικὰς αἰτίας τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν αὐτῶν, that is, “because of certain compelling causes concerning their churches.”]

[Note: [Col. 0363] “Churches”: original text; Anselm; Burchard.]

CHAPTER V. Bishops shall not set later persons before earlier ones. From the Council of Agde, chapter 23.

[Note: [Col. 0363] Held A.D. 506; Collection in three parts, part 2, title 28, chapter 21.]

No one shall set a later bishop before an earlier one whose life is beyond reproach, unless perhaps the latter, puffed up with pride, disdains to carry out what the bishop has commanded for the necessity of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0363] “Bishop”: original text.]

Part II, §1. But if, because of a simpler disposition, he cannot perform or manage the office of archdeacon, the man whom the bishop chooses to set over the administration of the church shall retain the title and rank of his own place.

[Note: [Col. 0363] “Archdeacon”: Venice I, II, and Lyons editions. “Simple”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0364D] “And the administration”: although the more recent Cologne editions of the councils read, “and the man whom the bishop chooses shall be set over the administration of the church,” and the same reading occurs in the Hispana Collection, while the Basel edition has “for the administration,” nevertheless the old Cologne edition, two Paris manuscripts, and two Vatican manuscripts of the councils agree with Gratian’s text.]

CHAPTER VI. No one should be kept unwillingly in the place in which he was ordained. Gregory likewise, to John, bishop of Syracuse, book XI, letter 34.

[Note: [Col. 0363] Letter 28, written A.D. 603, book 13, Maurist edition.]

It has come to us by report of certain persons that Cosmas, who was made subdeacon in the church of Syracuse by your predecessor Maximianus, of revered memory, after having been a monk of the monastery of St. Lucy, and was subsequently ordained priest by you in the estate called Juliana, is so severely distressed by excessive sadness and by the character of the place that he regards life as a punishment and seeks escape as a remedy for his affliction. Therefore, because we ought to be toward our subjects such persons as we ourselves, if we were subjects, would wish our superiors to be toward us, it would be an act of great kindness if your holiness wished to bring him back to the church in which he served as subdeacon and establish him there as a cardinal priest.

[Note: [Col. 0363] “Your,” and thus the singular number thereafter: collected editions. “Revered”: “venerable,” original text and collected editions. “Affliction”: “for affliction,” Basel edition. “Would wish”: “should wish,” collected editions. “Church”: “in the church,” same editions. “Wished”: “endeavored,” same editions.]

[Col. 0364A] We think you ought to do this, provided there is nothing that justly provokes your minds against him. But if there is some fault, let your brotherhood inform us of it by letter, so that we may know.

[Note: [Col. 0363] “Your minds”: “your mind,” collected editions.]

Part III. Gratian. Gregory’s statement, however, must be understood of those who complain of promotion by their bishops, not from necessity, but cunningly from resentment. The ruling of the Council of Carthage, on the other hand, is to be understood of those who refuse to obey their bishops when, because of the Church’s necessity, they wish to promote them to higher office. Anyone may confirm this distinction from the decree of Pope Simplicius, who, writing to John, bishop of Ravenna, in letter II, says among other things:

[Note: [Col. 0363] Written A.D. 482; Burchard, book 1, chapter 29; Anselm, book 6, chapters 66–67 [64–65]; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 140; Polycarpus, book 2, title 33.]

[Col. 0364B] CHAPTER VII. No one is to be dragged unwillingly to the episcopate.

Where did you learn these things that you carried out against our brother and fellow bishop Gregory, not from love but from envy? You allowed him to be dragged to you and harassed by inexcusable violence, so that you might impose upon him such an honor, almost not through tranquillity of mind, but—as it must be said—through madness. Such things could not have been done with sound judgment. We do not wish to magnify what was done, lest we be compelled to pronounce the judgment it deserves; for he deserves to lose the privilege of office who abuses the power entrusted to him.

[Note: [Col. 0363] “Brother”: “fellow brother,” Basel edition. “Fellow bishop”: “bishop,” collected editions. “To”: “from,” same editions. “Mind”: “year,” Basel edition. “Must be said”: “was said,” collected editions. Added: “of dignity,” same editions.]

And below:

[Note: [Col. 0363] Compare Cause 25, question 2, chapter 23.]

We declare that, if hereafter you presume anything of this kind and think you can make any person—whether bishop, priest, or deacon—unwillingly [do so], you are to know that the ordinations of the churches of Ravenna and Aemilia will be taken from you.

[Note: [Col. 0363] “Anything”: “something,” collected editions. Added: “such,” same editions. Added: “to be able,” same editions.]

[Col. 0364C] CHAPTER VIII. On the same subject. Gregory likewise, to Antoninus the subdeacon, book II, letter 16, indiction 10.

[Note: [Col. 0363] Letter 20, written A.D. 592, book 2, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 7, chapter 75.]

Honoratus, archdeacon of the church of Salona, had requested by a petition sent to my predecessor of holy memory that he should by no means be forced, against custom, to be promoted unwillingly by his bishop to the order of a more eminent rank. He maintained that this was done to him not for the sake of promoting him, but from resentment. For this reason, our predecessor of holy memory had already then forbidden by his letters our brother and fellow bishop Natalis to promote the said Archdeacon Honoratus unwillingly, or to retain longer in his heart the pain of resentment conceived.

[Note: [Col. 0363] “By no means”: “in no way,” collected editions. “For the sake”: “on account,” same editions. “Already then”: “also,” same editions. “Predecessor”: same editions. “By us”: “by me,” same editions, from Anselm. “Had been”: “had been,” same editions. “Letters”: “letter,” same editions. “Our”: “my,” same editions, first Basel edition.]

Although we too had most emphatically forbidden these things to him, disregarding not only God’s commands but also despising our letters, he attempted, by crafty artifice, to demote the aforesaid archdeacon under the appearance of promoting him to a higher honor. It followed that, after removing him from the office of archdeacon, he selected another who could comply with his wishes in every matter. We judge that the bishop could have had no other reason for disliking Archdeacon Honoratus than that Honoratus forbade him to give sacred vessels to his relatives.

[Note: [Col. 0365] “Had forbidden”: “forbade,” collected editions, from Anselm. “Crafty artifice”: “craftily,” same editions from Anselm. “From the office”: “from the same [office],” same editions. Added: “in all matters,” Basel edition. “Could have”: “could,” collected editions from Anselm. “Forbade”: “had forbidden,” same editions, first Argentinian and Nuremberg editions.]

[Col. 0365B] My predecessor of holy memory then, and I now, wished to investigate this matter by close inquiry; but he, conscious of his own deeds and those of his associates, neglected to send a representative to judgment. Accordingly, we have judged that your competence should be supported by the authority of this present command, so that, when you come to Salona, [an uncertain subject] may endeavor to urge Natalis, our brother and fellow bishop, warned at least by so many letters, to receive without delay the above-mentioned archdeacon back into his own position. If, as is his custom, he perhaps stubbornly delays doing this, you shall prohibit him, by authority of the Apostolic See, from using the pallium granted him by this See. If, even after losing the pallium, you see that the same bishop persists in that obstinacy, you shall deprive him also of participation in the Lord’s body and blood.

[Note: [Col. 0365] “Investigate”: “inquire into,” collected editions. “His own deeds and those of his associates”: “his own and his people’s,” same editions from Anselm. “Accordingly”: “therefore,” same editions from the same source. “When you come to Salona”: “when you come into Salonia,” same editions. “May endeavor”: “you may endeavor,” same editions. “In his own position”: “in the position in which he was,” same editions. “Granted”: “had been granted to him,” same editions. “You shall prohibit”: “prohibit,” original text and Anselm.]

[Col. 0366A] Gratian. Discipline must also be applied, by which those unwilling to be promoted to sacred orders are brought to obey their bishops. For those established in minor orders should gradually be promoted through the individual grades, so that those who disdain obedience to their bishops may regret that those whom they previously had as subjects are set over them.

Thus Gelasius writes to Victor, bishop:

[Note: [Col. 0365] An uncertain chapter; from Pelagius: Anselm, book 7, chapter 102; from Gelasius: Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 106; Polycarpus, book 2, title 31.]

CHAPTER IX. When they disdain to be ordained to higher orders, persons from lower orders are to be promoted.

Your belovedness has consulted us concerning the promotion of your clerics, reporting that the deacons refuse to advance to the rank of priesthood, which you say your church needs. Therefore, because ecclesiastical moderation and gravity do not permit unwilling persons to be compelled, that ordination can make the unwilling willing if you have among the acolytes or subdeacons persons of more mature age and approved life: endeavor to promote these to the priesthood. Then those who refused advancement in their own orders will be made junior to their inferiors after those of lower rank, and will obtain the advantages of a priest more eagerly than those of a deacon; so that, constrained at least by this consideration, they may try to seek both the honor and the gain which they had shunned.

[Note: [Col. 0365] Added: “us,” Basel edition. “May make [the unwilling] willing”: “may profit,” Ivo. “Or”: Ivo, book 1, chapter 43. “In their own orders”: absent from Anselm. “After those of lower rank”: “after later persons,” Ivo.]

## DISTINCTION LXXV

[Col. 0365]

[Col. 0365C] GRATIAN.

Part I. The time of consecration, as contained in the Roman Order, is not selected for the blessing of a bishop. For they may be blessed at any time, provided that they fast and receive the blessing at the third hour.

Therefore Pope Anacletus writes to the bishops of Italy, letter II, at the beginning:

[Note: [Col. 0365] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Burchard, book 1, chapter 15; Anselm, book 6, chapter 53 [51]; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 12; *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 69; Polycarpus, book 2, title 6; compare above, Distinction 64, chapter 2.]

CHAPTER I. At what hour bishops’ ordinations ought to take place.

By apostolic authority, ordinations of bishops are to be celebrated by all bishops who are within the same province. When they have assembled together, they are carefully to conduct an examination and celebrate a fast with prayers involving everyone; and, while laying their hands upon the holy Gospels which they are to preach, they are to pray on Sunday at the third hour and solemnly celebrate the ordination with sacred anointing, anointing their heads in the manner of the apostles and Moses, following the example of prophets and kings who anointed heads. For every sanctification consists in the Holy Spirit, whose invisible power is mingled with the holy chrism.

[Note: [Col. 0365] “From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 4.” “Carefully conduct an examination and celebrate a fast with prayers involving everyone”: from the ancient ecclesiastical statutes, chapter 96, Ballerini edition. “Upon”: “with,” original text; Anselm; Ivo; collected editions. “Which they are to preach”: supplied wording. “Kings who anointed heads”: collected editions. Added: “to be,” same editions.]

Part II. Gratian. The time of consecration, however, is confined within a period of three months, beyond which consecrations of bishops may not be deferred after election, unless necessity compels.

Therefore, in the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 25, one reads:

[Note: [Col. 0365] Held A.D. 451; from Dionysius: Burchard, book 1, chapter 24; Anselm, book 6, chapter 40; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 135.]

CHAPTER II. The ordination of bishops is not to be delayed beyond three months.

Since, as has been reported to us, certain metropolitans neglect the flocks entrusted to them and delay the ordination of bishops, the holy synod has resolved that bishops’ ordinations shall take place within three months, unless perhaps an inexcusable necessity has compelled the time of ordination to be further prolonged. But if any bishop does not observe this, he ought to be subject to ecclesiastical condemnation; and the revenues of the same vacant church are to be kept intact with the steward of that church.

[Note: [Col. 0365] “Within”: “below,” Basel and Paris editions. “Prolonged”: “extended,” Hispana Collection.]

[Note: [Col. 0367D] “But if any”: this is likewise the wording in the ancient—indeed, the Hispana—translation. The Greek is: Εἰ δὲ μὴ τοῦτο ποιήσοι, ὑποκεῖσθαι αὐτὸν (or αὐτῷ) ἐκκλησιαστικῷ ἐπιτιμίῳ, “But if he should not do this, he is to be subject to ecclesiastical punishment.” Another translator rendered it: “But if he does not do this at all, he shall be subject to ecclesiastical correction.” For it speaks of the metropolitan.]

[Note: [Col. 0367] “These”: “this,” collected editions. “We resolve”: same editions.]

Part III. Gratian. Other ordinations, especially those of priests and Levites, ought to take place only at specified times and days: namely, on the evening of Saturday or on Sunday morning, with the fast continued.

Therefore Pope Zephyrinus writes to the bishops of Egypt, letter II:

[Note: [Col. 0367] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, drawn from the *Liber Pontificalis*; Burchard, book 2, chapter 3; Anselm, book 7, chapter 43; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapters 23 and 47; Polycarpus, book 2, title 28.]

CHAPTER III. At what hour the ordinations of priests or Levites ought to be performed.

[Col. 0367B] Solemnly conduct the ordinations of priests and Levites at a suitable time, before many persons who stand present; and promote proven and learned men to this task, so that you may take great joy in their fellowship and assistance.

CHAPTER IV. At what hour priests and Levites are to be ordained. Leo, bishop, likewise, to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, letter LXXIX, chapter 1.

[Note: [Col. 0367] Letter 9, written A.D. 445, Ballerini edition; Anselm, book 7, chapter 44; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 31; Polycarpus, book 1.]

We wish you also to preserve what we know our Fathers observed with more attentive care: namely, that priestly or levitical ordination should not be celebrated indiscriminately on every day, but that the beginnings of that night which dawns on the first day of the week, after Saturday, should be chosen for consecration. On that occasion the sacred blessing is bestowed on those to be consecrated while they fast, and by persons who are fasting. The same observance is kept if ordination is celebrated on Sunday morning itself, with Saturday’s fast continued; for that time does not depart from the beginning of the preceding night, which undoubtedly belongs to the day of the resurrection, as is also made clear in the Lord’s Passover.

[Note: [Col. 0367] “By us”: “by you,” collected editions. “For consecration”: absent from the original. Added: “ordination,” collected editions. “Which”: “than,” original text.]

CHAPTER V. Why priests’ ordinations are celebrated on Sunday. The same, in the same chapter.

[Note: [Col. 0367] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 13; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 70.]

Part IV. That ordinations of priests should be celebrated on Sunday is known by us to derive not only from custom but also from apostolic teaching. Scripture shows this, because, when the Apostles sent Paul and Barnabas, by command of the Holy Spirit, to preach the Gospel to the Gentiles, they fasted and prayed and laid hands upon them. Thus we may understand with what devotion, both of those giving and those receiving, care must be taken that the sacrament of so great a blessing may not appear to have been performed negligently.

[Note: [Col. 0367] “On the day”: Basel edition.]

Therefore you will piously and laudably follow apostolic institutions if you yourself observe in the churches over which the Lord has willed you to preside this form of ordaining priests: that blessing is never bestowed on those to be consecrated except on the day of the Lord’s resurrection, the beginning of which is known to be reckoned from Saturday evening. That day has been consecrated by such great mysteries of divine dispensations that whatever the Lord has established as more eminent has been accomplished in the dignity of this day. On this day the world received its beginning; on this day, through Christ’s resurrection, death received destruction and life received its beginning. On this day, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0367D] “That [on] Sunday”: this chapter is taken from the same passage as the preceding one, though with the order of words altered and some material added at the beginning. In the letter itself, immediately after the final words of the preceding chapter, there follows continuously: “For, besides the authority of custom, which we know derives from apostolic teaching, sacred Scripture also shows that, when the Apostles,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0367] Added: “all,” ibid. “And”: the original and collected editions read “which, consecrated by so great…”; the Hispana Collection reads “and … consecrated.” “Dispensations”: “arrangements,” original text. “More eminent”: “eminent,” collected editions. “Christ”: supplied wording. “Beginning”: “origin,” same editions.]

CHAPTER VI. On the same subject. PALEA. Likewise, in the Roman Order, in the chapter on the ranks of the Church:

[Note: [Col. 0367] This chapter is found in the Roman Order—see on chapter 2, Distinction 23—which Mabillon published as no. IX in the *Museum Italicum*; Anselm, book 7, chapter 61 [51].]

> “Clerics may be ordained up to the office of subdeacon whenever and wherever it pleases; but deacons and priests, never except at a public ordination.”

[Col. 0368C] CHAPTER VII. On times of ordination. Gelasius likewise, to the bishops throughout Lucania, letter I, chapter 13.

[Note: [Col. 0367] Written A.D. 494; Anselm, book 7, chapter 45; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 25; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 74; Polycarpus, book 2, title 28.]

Part V. Ordinations of priests and deacons should be performed only at specified times and days: namely, at the fast of the fourth month, of the seventh, and of the tenth; also at the beginning of Lent, in the middle week, and at the Saturday fast near evening. Nor should they, for the sake of anyone’s advantage, prefer either a priest or a deacon to those who were ordained before them.

[Note: [Col. 0367] “On the day in the middle of Lent”: original text; Anselm; Ivo. Added: “they are to know that the ordinations themselves are to be celebrated,” collected editions from Anselm. Added: “dare,” same editions.]

## DISTINCTION LXXVI

[Col. 0369]

[Col. 0369A] GRATIAN.

Part I. Pope Calixtus determines the times at which fasts are to be celebrated, writing to Bishop Benedict in letter I:

[Note: [Col. 0369] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, drawn from the *Liber Pontificalis*; compare the Roman Order in Hittorp, p. 83; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 175; *Decretum*, part 4, chapter 27; Polycarpus, book 3, title 25.]

CHAPTER I. At what times fasts are to be celebrated.

The fast which you learned that we celebrate three times in the year, we now decree should more suitably be observed at four times, so that, just as the year revolves through four seasons, we too may perform a solemn fast four times through the year’s four seasons.

CHAPTER II. On the same subject. From the First Council of Mainz, chapter 34.

[Note: [Col. 0369C] The author of the *Micrologus*, discussing in chapters 24 and 25 this very canon of the Council of Mainz, openly says that it arose from ignorance of ecclesiastical tradition. Hence Pope Leo says, “Of this observance,” etc., as reported below in this same distinction, chapter 6. And lest anyone should be deceived on the occasion of these German councils, Gregory VII—as is recounted in the same *Micrologus*—renewed the ancient custom of the Roman Church. On this subject the following is established in chapter 1 of Urban II’s Council of Clermont: “The first fast of the four seasons shall always occur in the first week of Lent; the second in the week of Pentecost, without bending of knees, with Alleluia and Gloria in excelsis Deo, and in solemn vestments; the third in the full week before the autumnal equinox; the fourth in the full week before the Lord’s Nativity, with its vigil included.” The same is repeated in the later second Council of Piacenza, preserved in the Vatican Library, and cited below in this same distinction, chapter *Statuimus*.]

[Note: [Col. 0369] Chapter 34, Council of Mainz, held A.D. 813, reduced to an epitome; *Capitularies*, book 5, chapter 86; Regino, book 1, chapter 277; Burchard, book 13, chapter 2; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 180; *Decretum*, part 4, chapter 35.]

We establish that the four seasons of the year are to be observed by all in a common fast: namely, in March, the first week; in June, the second; in September, the third; and in December, the fourth.

[Note: [Col. 0369] “We establish”: “We decree,” Basel edition. Added: “people,” collected editions.]

CHAPTER III. On the same subject. From the Council held at Seligenstadt, chapter 2.

[Note: [Col. 0369] Held A.D. 1022; Burchard at the end; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 181; *Decretum*, part 4, chapter 33.]

Concerning the uncertain fast of the four seasons, we establish this certainty: if the Kalends of March fall on Wednesday or earlier, the fast shall be celebrated in that same week. §1. But if the Kalends of March extend into Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, the fast shall be postponed until the following week. Likewise, if the Kalends of June fall on Wednesday or earlier, the fast shall be celebrated in the following week; but if they occur on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, the fast shall be reserved for the third week.

[Note: [Col. 0369] “Following week”: collected editions. “Occur”: “occurs,” same editions. “Third [week]”: “third week,” same editions, first Lyons II and III editions.]

§2. It must also be known that if, according to the aforesaid rule, the June fast should fall on the vigil of Pentecost, it is not to be celebrated then, but in the solemn week of Pentecost itself, [because the vigil and the fast ought not to be celebrated together]; and then, because of the solemnity of the Holy Spirit, deacons are to wear dalmatics, Alleluia is to be sung, and *Let us bend the knee* is not to be said.

[Note: [Col. 0370D] “Because the vigil”: the words from here through “ought not [to be celebrated]” are not in the council itself as printed from Burchard; nevertheless, the same sense is repeated at the end of the chapter.]

§3. The same rule has been established concerning the September fast: if the Kalends of September fall on Wednesday or earlier, the fast is to be celebrated in the third week; but if they occur on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, the fast must be observed in the fourth week.

[Note: [Col. 0369] “September”: “the seventh month,” collected editions; “month of September,” Basel edition. “Occur”: “occurs,” same editions.]

§4. In December this is to be observed: the fast is to be celebrated on the Saturday immediately before the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, because if the vigil falls on Saturday, it is not fitting to celebrate vigil and fast together.

[Note: [Col. 0369] “To be celebrated”: “to be celebrated [passively],” collected editions.]

Against this, Urban II, in the Council of Piacenza, chapter 14:

[Note: [Col. 0369] Held A.D. 1095; Polycarpus, book 3, title 25.]

CHAPTER IV. On the same subject.

We likewise establish that the fasts of the four seasons shall be celebrated in this order: the first at the beginning of Lent, the second in the week of Pentecost, the third in September, and the fourth in December, according to the customary practice.

CHAPTER V. On the same subject. Pope Leo I likewise, in Sermon I on the fast of Pentecost.

[Note: [Col. 0369] Sermon 78, Ballerini edition; Polycarpus, in the same place.]

Accordingly, after the days of holy rejoicing which we have spent in honour of the Lord rising from the dead and then ascending into the heavens [Note: [Col. 0369] “ascending into the heavens” is absent from the Lyon editions; “ascending into heaven”: the other collected editions], and after receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, the custom of fasting has rightly and necessarily been established: so that, if negligent freedom and unrestrained licence have perhaps presumed anything disorderly amid the very joys of the festivals [Note: *of the festival*: the collected editions], the discipline of religious abstinence may correct it [Note: *have presumed immoderately*: the same editions].

C. VI. On the same matter. The same author, Sermon VIII on the fast of the tenth month. [Note: Sermon 19, Ballerini edition; Polycarpus, ibid.]

[Col. 0370C] The benefit of this observance, most beloved [Note: add “brothers”: the collected editions], is especially established in the Church’s fasts. These, through the teaching of the Holy Spirit, are distributed throughout the course of the entire year in such a way that the law of abstinence is assigned to every season. Thus we observe the spring fast in Lent, the summer fast at Pentecost, the autumn fast in the seventh month [Col. 0371A; Note: September: Basel edition], and the winter fast in this, the tenth month [Note: “but”: emphasis in the text; “we observe”: collected editions], understanding that nothing in the divine commands is without purpose, and that by the Word of God all the elements serve our instruction; while, through the four quarters of the world itself, as though through four Gospels, we learn by an unceasing trumpet-call both what we are to preach and what we are to do [Note: *unceasingly*: original text; nevertheless, the reading “unceasing” appears in the homilies of Paul the Deacon and in the first edition of the works of Leo the Great, as in Gratian].

II. Part. Gratian. But we must understand the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth months not according to the reckoning of the Hebrews, but according to ours. For among them the first month is April, the fourth July, the seventh October, and the tenth January. What reason they had for fasting in these months, and also in the fifth month, which is August, Jerome explains in his commentaries on Zechariah, chapter 8, saying [Note: Polycarpus, ibid.]:

[Col. 0371B] C. VII. Why the Law commanded fasts in the months stated above.

“The fast of the fourth, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth [for *of the month* is understood in common after each] [Note: absent from the first Basel and other collected editions] shall be turned for the house of Judah and Jerusalem into feast-days and joy: God seeks only truth and peace.”

In this passage many of our people [Note: “your people”: Argentinensis and Basel editions] have said many things, and things at variance with one another. And, after a few intervening words:

§ 1. “We are therefore compelled to have recourse to the Hebrews and to seek the truth of knowledge from the fountain rather than from the streams.”

And a little later:

§ 2. “The fast of the fourth month, which among Latins is called July, they suppose [Note: “we suppose”: collected editions except Louvain II, III, and Antwerp] to be on the seventh and tenth days of that same month, when Moses, coming down from Mount Sinai [Note: Exodus, ch. 32], threw down and shattered the tablets of the Law, and when, according to Jeremiah [Col. 0371C; Note: Jeremiah, ch. 52], the walls of the city were first breached. In the fifth month [Note: add “indeed”: collected editions], which among Latins [Note: “among us”: the same editions] is called August, when a rebellion had arisen among the people because of the scouts of the Holy Land, they were commanded not to go up the mountain, but to wander for forty years at prolonged cost [Note: “at greater cost”: the same editions except Louvain II, III, and Antwerp], away from the Holy Land [Note: “toward the Holy Land”: original text], so that, except for the two Caleb [Note: Numbers, ch. 14] and Joshua, all might fall in the wilderness. In this month, both by Nebuchadnezzar [Note: 4 Kings, ch. 25; Jeremiah, chs. 39 and 41] and, many centuries later, by Titus and Vespasian, the Temple at Jerusalem was burned and destroyed; the city of Bethel was captured [Note: “when the city of Bethel was captured”: collected editions except Louvain II and Antwerp], to which many thousands of Jews had fled; [Col. 0372A] the Temple was ploughed up, to the disgrace of the nation subdued by Titus Annius Rufus [Note: the following words are absent from the collected editions except Louvain II, III, and Antwerp]. But in the seventh month, which among us is called October, as we said above, Gedaliah was killed, and the tribe of Judah and the remnant of Jerusalem were scattered. Let us read Jeremiah [Note: ch. 52]. In the tenth month, which among us is called January, because it is the gate and beginning of the year, Ezekiel, placed in captivity [Note: Ezekiel, ch. 33], heard—as did the whole people of the captives—that in the fifth month the Temple had been overthrown, as we learn most fully in that prophet himself. This, then, is the whole meaning of the words: Know that the days of mourning and fasts which hitherto you have had for grief shall be turned for you—for I have determined to do good to Jerusalem [Note: “Israel”: collected editions except Louvain II, III, and Antwerp] and to the house of Judah—into gladness, joy, and festivals; provided only that you love truth [Col. 0372B] and peace. In the anagogical sense, because we fast when the bridegroom is taken away from us [Note: John, ch. 16] and we do not deserve to have his presence, when the Lord has returned to us and has determined to do us good, all sorrow shall be turned into joy, and the former hunger shall be recompensed by the presence of the Word of God, by the teachings of him, and by the abundance of heavenly bread” [Note: “compensated”: collected editions].

III. Part. Gratian. But the fasts of the fourth month do not appear able to be celebrated before the day of Pentecost. For from the day of the Lord’s resurrection until the day of Pentecost fasts are not prescribed for observance.

Therefore Ambrose, in Sermon LXI on the same day, which begins as follows [Note: This sermon is attributed to Maximus of Turin, *Bibliotheca Patrum* (Lyon edition), vol. 6, p. 29]:

C. VIII. On the same matter.

“Your holiness ought to know” [Note: *Your holiness ought to know*: In many manuscript copies, from the beginning “The Fast” to the chapter “After Easter,” and in some even to the end, there is no division into chapters. Many authorities cited by Gratian are contained, as it were, in one continuous context. Therefore these words, “Your holiness ought to know,” are connected with Gratian’s final words at the end of the preceding chapter [Col. 0372D], and should be read thus: “Therefore Ambrose, in Sermon LXI on the same day, which begins: ‘Your holiness ought to know’;” then one should add, “During these fifty days,” etc. Gratian adapted this passage in his own way; for it is somewhat otherwise in St Ambrose.] “During these fifty [Col. 0372C] days there is for us a continuous and unbroken festival, so that throughout this whole period we neither proclaim fasts to be observed nor bend our knees in prayer to God [Note: “the Lord”: collected editions]” [Note: “there is”: collected editions except Louvain II, III, and Antwerp; “bend”: the original reads *succidamus*, and Louvain II, III, and Antwerp likewise].

And below:

§ 1. “Therefore the whole course of the fifty days is celebrated after the pattern of the Lord’s Day [Note: add “of the resurrection”: the same editions], and all these days are counted as Sundays. For the Lord’s Day is the Resurrection [Note: add “day”: ibid.]. For on Sunday the Saviour, rising again, returned to humankind, and after the Resurrection he remained with humankind throughout the entire fifty days. Therefore it was necessary that the festival of those days should be equal [Note: “equal to them; therefore”: Nuremberg, Venice I–II, Paris, Lyon I], whose holiness was likewise equal [Note: add “days”: Lyon II–III] [Col. 0373A; Note: “is”: collected editions]. For the Lord so ordered it that, as we grieved at his Passion in the fasts of Lent, so we might rejoice at his Resurrection during the fifty festival days. Therefore we do not fast during [Note: add “this”: Basel, Lyon II–III] the fifty days, because during these days the Lord remains with us” [Note: “remained with us”: collected editions].

Likewise, in the *Apology of David* [Note: ch. 8]:

“We celebrate this number, namely the fiftieth, joyfully after the Lord’s Passion, since the whole debt of guilt has been forgiven, the bond [Note: “and the bond”: collected editions; cf. Colossians, ch. 2] has been cancelled, and we are free from every obligation. We receive the grace of the Holy Spirit coming upon us; on the day of Pentecost, fasting being absent [Note: “fasts are absent”: collected editions], praise is offered to God [Note: add “and prayer”: the same editions except Argentinensis], and Alleluia is sung.”

Gratian. Therefore the Church necessarily established that fasts should be celebrated after the day of Pentecost. But the denial that one should fast during those fifty days is to be understood as arising from the obligation of observance.

Therefore the same Ambrose, in Sermon LX on the same day, which begins as follows [Note: Ambrose’s name is omitted in the collected editions]:

C. IX. On the same matter.

“I believe you know, brothers” [Note: *I believe you know*: The same thing occurs in this chapter as was noted to have occurred in the preceding one. It is connected with what precedes, its first period being, as it were, a summary of them.] “that we celebrate the day of Pentecost with no less joy than we have taken care to celebrate holy Easter [Note: “that we celebrate holy Easter”: collected editions]. For then, as we have just done now, we fasted on Saturday, kept vigils, and persevered all night in prayers [Note: “all-nightly”: Basel edition with the original]. It is therefore necessary that a similar observance [Note: original: “a similar observance, a similar joy follows”] should be followed by similar joy.”

Gratian. But “similar observance” is said with regard to the act, not with regard to necessity.

Therefore Isidore, Book I, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 42:

C. X. On the same matter.

After Easter until Pentecost, although the tradition [Col. 0374A] of the Churches has relaxed the rigor of abstinence at meals, nevertheless, if any [Note: “if anyone … desires”: collected editions] monks, clerics [Note: add “or laymen”: ibid.], desire to fast, they are not to be forbidden; for Antony and Paul and the other ancient Fathers are read to have practised abstinence even during these days in the desert, and not to have relaxed their abstinence except on Sunday alone.

C. XI. On the same matter.

Likewise Jerome to Lucinius [Note: written A.D. 385; Anselm, Book 4, ch. 44; Polycarpus, Book 3, title 23], Letter XXVIII [Note: “Lucianus”: Böhm]:

Would that we were able to fast at every season—as we read in the Acts of the Apostles that the Apostle Paul and the believers with him did on the days [Note: “day”: Basel edition] of Pentecost and on the Lord’s Day.

And below:

I do not say this because I think that fasting should be kept on Sundays [Note: “festival days”: collected editions], or because I would abolish the continuous fifty festival days [Note: “sixty”: original text; add “and solemnities”: collected editions]; but let each province abound in its own judgment, and regard the commands [Col. 0374B] of its elders [Note: add “and”: Basel edition] as apostolic laws [Note: “regard”: Nuremberg edition; “let us regard”: Venice I–II, Lyon, Paris].

C. XII. On Holy Saturday, after the hour of baptism, a bishop may be ordained. Likewise Pope Pelagius to Peter, Bishop of Potenza [Note: Letter of uncertain date; Anselm, Book 6, ch. 59 (61); Polycarpus, Book 2, title 25; cf. Distinction 63, chapter 14; “Pontino”: Lyon II edition; Böhm].

We have received the letter of your affection, in which you report that Latinus, deacon of the Church of Grumentum, has been elected by all to the episcopate of the Church of Marcellianum or Clusium [Note: “Clusitanum”: Argentinensis edition; “Cassilitanae”: Basel edition; “Cusilinatium”: Anselm], as you had previously reported. We ordered him to come, believing that they had received from his bishop letters dimissory concerning that same person. If they have now done so, have him come quickly to the city of Rome, so that, if God so commands, he may be ordained on Holy Saturday after the hour of baptism. But if he does not arrive before the day mentioned, he will be obliged to wait until the fasts of the fourth month [Note: “remain”: collected editions except Paris and Lyon; Böhm].

## DISTINCTION LXXVII

[Col. 0373]

[Col. 0373B] GRATIAN.

[Col. 0373C] At these times, according to Anacletus, Zephyrinus, Gelasius, and Pelagius, bishops, presbyters, and deacons are to be ordained. But, according to Leo, a metropolitan is to be ordained from among the presbyters of the same Church, or from its most worthy deacons. No one from among monks or laymen, however, ought to attain to the supreme priesthood except through the grades of the Church.

Therefore Pope Caius, to Bishop Felix, one letter, at the end [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, composed according to the *Liber Pontificalis*; *Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 26, ch. 2]:

[Col. 0374C] C. I. No one is to aspire to the priesthood except through the distinct grades.

We decree and command you and all to observe this: those who deserve to be ordained are to ascend to ecclesiastical orders in the Church in the following manner. That is, if anyone deserves to be a bishop, he shall first be a doorkeeper, then a reader, afterwards an exorcist; thereafter he shall be consecrated acolyte, then subdeacon, [Col. 0375A] then deacon, and afterwards presbyter; and thence, if he deserves it, he shall be ordained bishop.

Therefore Zosimus, Bishop of the city of Rome, says to Hesychius, Letter I, chapter 3 [Note: written A.D. 418; Anselm, Book 7, ch. 49]:

C. II. What intervals of time are to be observed in the individual grades.

In the individual grades the following times are to be observed: if from childhood [Note: *If from childhood*: This first part of the chapter is summarized. The full passage reads: “If from childhood he has enrolled himself in ecclesiastical ministries, he shall remain among the readers in uninterrupted observance until his twentieth year of age. If he comes when already older and advanced in years, yet desires immediately after baptism to devote himself to the divine militia, he shall remain either among readers or among exorcists for five years; thereafter, as acolyte or subdeacon, for four years, and then to the blessing,” etc. Indeed, in one very ancient manuscript of Gratian and in Rabanus, Book I, chapter 13, *On the Institution of Clerics*, one reads “four years,” not “fourteen.” But because of the gloss, nothing has been changed or added.] he has enrolled himself in ecclesiastical ministries, he is to remain among readers and exorcists for five years; thereafter he is to become an acolyte or subdeacon for fourteen [Note: “four”: original text; Anselm] years, and then, if worthy, he is to approach the blessing of the diaconate. In that order he must remain for five years, if he has conducted himself blamelessly [Note: “adhere”: collected editions]. Thereafter, with the successive stages supporting him, having supplied proofs of his own faith through so many grades, he may merit the priesthood of the presbyterate; and from that position, if a more exacting life brings him to good morals, he ought to hope for the supreme pontificate.

And below:

§ 1. Defenders of the Church also, who are made from laymen, are to be bound by the aforesaid observance, if they deserve [Note: “shall deserve?”: collected editions] to be in clerical order.

C. III. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Siricius to Himerius of Tarragona, Letter I, chapter 9 [Note: written A.D. 385; *Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 36, chs. 10–11; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 91 ff.]:

Whoever from childhood has devoted himself [Note: “has vowed”: original text, Ivo, Basel edition; “shall wish”: Paris and Lyon editions] to the services of the Church ought, before the years of puberty, to be baptized and associated with the ministry [Note: “office”: Basel edition] of readers. If he has lived commendably from the onset of adolescence until his twentieth [Note: *twentieth*: in most old copies both of Gratian and of the letter, and in Ivo, “thirtieth” is read; but in the letter of Zosimus cited in the preceding note, “twentieth”] [Note: “thirtieth”: original text and Ivo; add “of his”: collected editions] year of age, he must be content with one wife only—one whom he received as a virgin through the common blessing of a priest—and serve as acolyte and subdeacon. Afterwards he may advance to the grade of deacon, if, with continence preceding, he has first proved himself worthy. If there he has ministered commendably for more than [Note: *more than*: thus in all manuscripts and in the original itself; the printed editions had “within”] five years, he shall fittingly receive the presbyterate. Thereafter, after ten years, he may attain the episcopal chair, provided that during these periods his integrity of life [Note: add “his”: the same editions] and faith have been approved.

But one already advanced [Col. 0376A] in age, moved by a manner of life of better purpose and hastening to pass from the laity into the sacred militia, shall not obtain the fruit of his desire otherwise than by being immediately associated, at the time when he is baptized, with the number of readers or exorcists, provided it is established that he has had, or has, one wife and that he received her as a virgin. When he has been initiated, after two years are completed, he shall serve as acolyte and subdeacon for another five years, and thus be promoted to the diaconate [Note: “to the office of the diaconate … be promoted”: Spanish Collection], if during those periods he is judged worthy. Thereafter, as time advances, he may deservedly be associated with the presbyterate or episcopate, if the election of clergy and people has called him [Note: “or”: collected editions; “or of clergy”: Lyon II; *edecumaverit*: Constantine from the Pithoean manuscript and an old Colbert manuscript written in Lombardic characters].

C. IV. On the same matter. Likewise from the Sixth Synod, chapter 15 [Note: from the Synod *Penthekte* (the Quinisext Council), held A.D. 692; *Collectio trium partium*, part 2, title 11, ch. 6].

[Col. 0376B] A subdeacon shall not be ordained under twenty years of age.

§ 1. But if anyone has been ordained to any sacred [Note: add “sacred”: collected editions] priestly order apart from the appointed ages, let him be deposed.

C. V. On the same matter. Likewise from the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 4 [Note: held A.D. 397; Burchard, Book 2, ch. 11; Anselm, Book 7, ch. 95; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 3, ch. 30; *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 31; Polycarpus, Book 2, title 27].

It was decided that neither deacons be ordained nor virgins consecrated before twenty-five years of age, and that readers shall not greet the people.

C. VI. The Levitical blessing is not to be conferred on persons under twenty-five years. Likewise from the Council of Agde, chapters 16 and 17 [Note: held A.D. 506; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 365].

A bishop shall in no case confer the blessing of the diaconate on persons under twenty-five years of age.

[Col. 0376C] § 1. Certainly, if married young men consent [Note: add “themselves”: collected editions] to be ordained, the consent of their wives must also be required, so that, after their marital bedroom has been set apart and religious commitment has been promised, they may be ordained once they have together adopted the religious life.

§ 2. No metropolitan shall presume to ordain a presbyter or bishop before thirty years, that is, before he has reached the age of a perfect man [Note: plural “they reach”: Spanish Collection and collected editions], nor deacons before twenty-five, lest through youth they be blamed for some error—as has sometimes happened.

C. VII. On the same matter. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 20 [Note: held A.D. 633; Burchard, Book 2, ch. 12; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 3, ch. 31; *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 32; Polycarpus, Book 2, title 27].

In the old Law Levites are commanded [Note: “are prescribed”: Ivo; “are ordered”: collected editions] to serve in the tabernacle from their twenty-fifth year. The holy Fathers followed this authority in the canons. We, forgetful of the command of both the divine Law and the councils [Note: “the canonical precepts”: the same editions], make infants and boys Levites before the lawful age and before experience of life. Therefore, lest this be done further by us, we are admonished both by the divine [Note: “divine Law”: original text and Ivo] Law and by canonical judgments that Levites be consecrated at twenty-five years of age [Note: add “their”: collected editions], and presbyters ordained at thirty.

[Col. 0377B] C. VIII. At what intervals of time one chosen from monks into the clergy is to be ordained. Likewise Pope Gelasius to the bishops throughout Lucania, Letter I, chapter 3 [Note: written A.D. 494; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, ch. 143].

If anyone trained in a religious purpose and [Note: add “from”: collected editions] monastic discipline comes [Note: “comes”: the same editions; “comes after the proceedings”: Lyon II and Antwerp; “proceedings at the times”: the remaining collected editions] to a clerical office, first let his life as lived in former times [Note: “past”: emphasis in the text] be investigated: whether he is found tainted by no grave crime; whether he has perhaps not had [Note: “has not had”: collected editions] a second wife or is shown to have taken a woman left by a husband; whether perhaps he has not undergone public penance; whether he appears maimed in no part of his body; whether he is not subject to servile or native condition; whether he is shown to have been released from the bonds of the curia; whether he has acquired letters, without which he could scarcely perhaps fulfil even the ministry of doorkeeper.

[Col. 0377C] C. IX. On the same matter. Likewise in the same and following chapter [Note: *Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 46, ch. 12].

A novice monk, however, if supported by moral integrity [Col. 0378A; Note: “if … supported”: Böhm], shall immediately be made reader, notary, or at least defender; after three months he shall become [Note: “be made”: Basel edition] an acolyte, especially if age also [Note: emphasis in the text] supports him. In the sixth month he shall receive the title of subdeacon; and if he proves to be of modest conduct and honourable intention [Note: “prove”: collected editions], in the ninth month he shall be deacon, and after a year is complete he shall be presbyter. Yet the voluntary devotion of his holy purpose must be shown to have supplied what the intervals of years would have conferred upon him.

§ 1. But if any layman is to be admitted to ecclesiastical offices, such a person ought to be examined in each of the matters set forth above with proportionately greater care [Note: “to examine”: the same editions], since there is plainly a difference between worldly and religious life. For the suitable ministries of the Church must be restored [Note: “assigned”: the same editions], not imposed upon unsuitable merits [Col. 0378B].
