And, in proportion as the time within which these things were to be attained [Note: “will be attained”: the same editions] is reduced, so much more must what may be fit for sacred service be sought in their formation, so that uprightness of character may be shown to possess what a longer habituation has not supplied. Otherwise, through the opportunity of making up a clerical shortage [Note: “of the clergy”: the same editions], we may be reckoned to have introduced vices into divine worship rather than to have provided lawful economies for the household of the Lord [Note: “may be reckoned”: Argentinensis and Basel editions]. For their promotions we nonetheless add six months beyond the yearly limits, since, as has been said, there ought to be a distinction [Note: “we believe”: Basel; “there must be”: the remaining collected editions] between a person devoted [Note: “dedicated”: collected editions] to divine worship and one coming from the life of laymen. Yet we have thought this indulgence should be granted only so far that, where Churches are exempt from this occasion [Note: *Churches*: Gelasius explains this much more fully: “That the ministries may be restored in those Churches in which, through the ravages of war, either none at all or only a few remain, so that, when by God’s favour they are restored, the old form of the canons of the Fathers may be preserved in appointing ecclesiastical grades. Nor may what is provided as a remedy for an accidental deficiency prevail against them on any pretext, nor be proposed by a new law contrary to the ordinances of the elders; other Churches being exempt from this occasion, since those which have not been laid waste by a like disaster ought to maintain the former rule in making ordinations.], the ancient form of the canons of the Fathers be preserved [Col. 0378C].

## DISTINCTION LXXVIII

[Col. 0377]

[Col. 0377C] GRATIAN. Pope Boniface [Note: *Boniface*: Other collectors cite the decrees of Fabian. It occurs in Martin, Bishop of Braga, *Capitula of Greek Synods*, ch. 20, from Neocaesarea, ch. 11] determined the age at which priests ought to be ordained, saying [Note: Regino, Appendix 1, ch. 39, “from the ancient canons of the Eastern Fathers”; Burchard, Book 2, title 10; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 3, ch. 29; *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 30; Polycarpus, Book 2, title 20, “from the decrees of Fabian”]:

C. I. A presbyter is not to be ordained before thirty years.

If anyone has not completed thirty years of age [Col. 0378C], he is in no way to be ordained presbyter, even if he is very worthy.

C. II. On the same matter. PALEA. Likewise in the *Novels*, in the Authenticum *On the Most Holy Bishops*, § “Clerics,” in Julian the Antecessor, Constitution CXV, chapter 19 [Note: Polycarpus, Book 2, title 27]:

“No one shall be consecrated presbyter who is under thirty [Col. 0379A] years; no one shall become deacon or subdeacon who is under twenty-five years; no one shall be enrolled among readers who is under eighteen years; no woman shall be consecrated among the deaconesses of the most holy Church who is under forty years or has entered a second marriage” [Note: “has entered”: original text; Basel edition; C. III].

C. III. A priest is not to be ordained unless he has been tested by a long examination. Likewise Pope Leo to the African bishops, Letter LXXXV, chapter 1 [Note: Letter 12, written A.D. 446, Ballerini edition; Anselm, Book 6, ch. 34 (35); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 105; cf. Distinction 61, ch. 5]:

What is it to lay hands hastily, except to confer the priestly honour upon persons not proved—before the maturity of age [Note: “before maturity of age”: collected editions], before the time of examination, before the merit of obedience [Note: “labour”: original text and Ivo; C. IV], before experience of discipline? And what is it to share in another’s sins, except to make the ordainer [Col. 0379B] such as is the person who did not deserve to be ordained?

C. IV. A presbyter is not to be ordained before thirty years of age. Likewise from the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 11 [Note: held A.D. 314; from the translation of Dionysius: Anselm, Book 7, title 95, and Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 3, ch. 29, “from the decrees of Pope Fabian, Eastern Fathers sent to the Council of Neocaesarea”; Polycarpus, Book 2, title 27].

A presbyter shall not be ordained before thirty years of age, even though his life is commendable; but let him wait [Note: “let it be observed”: collected editions] until the fixed [Note: “former”: Argentinensis and Basel editions] time. For our Lord Jesus Christ was baptized in his thirtieth [Col. 0380A] year, and then preached.

Gratian. This is the regular rule; accordingly, Christ, John the Baptist, Ezekiel, and certain of the prophets are not read to have prophesied or preached before this time. But since Jeremiah [Note: Jeremiah, ch. 1] and Daniel [Note: Daniel, ch. 1] are read to have received the spirit of prophecy before youthful age, David and Solomon are found to have been anointed in adolescence, John the Evangelist likewise [Note: Matthew, ch. 4], while still an adolescent, is found to have been chosen by the Lord as an apostle and sent with the others to preach; and Paul the Apostle [Note: Acts, ch. 7] is also said to have been chosen by the Lord in adolescence and sent to preach: the Church likewise, when necessity requires, has customarily ordained some persons before thirty years.

[Col. 0380B] Therefore Pope Zacharias, to Bishop Boniface, Letter VI, beginning “Blessed be God” [Note: written A.D. 751]:

C. V. When necessity requires, presbyters of twenty-five years may be ordained.

If persons thirty years old are not found and necessity demands it, Levites and priests of twenty-five years and above may be ordained.

## DISTINCTION LXXIX

[Col. 0379]

[Col. 0379B] GRATIAN.

I. Part. But the Apostolic [i.e. the Pope] is to be enthroned only by cardinals and religious clerics.

[Col. 0379C] Therefore Pope Nicholas II says in the letter in which he reports the synod held by him at Rome, chapter 1 [Note: A.D. 1059; Anselm, Book 6, ch. 15; Polycarpus, Book 1, title 4]:

C. I. On one enthroned without the concordant election of the Cardinals.

If anyone [Note: *If anyone*: The words of Nicholas in the letter printed in the volumes of councils after the decrees of Nicholas I are these: “First, with God as inspector, it was decreed that the election of the Roman Pontiff shall be in the power of the cardinal bishops, so that if anyone is enthroned to the apostolic see without their prior concordant and canonical election, and then the consent of the religious clerics and laymen of the following orders,” etc. Nearly the same appears at the end of that synod and is cited below in the chapter “If anyone by money.”] is enthroned to the apostolic see without the concordant [Note: “concord”: Argentinensis and Basel editions] and canonical election of the Cardinals of that Church, and thereafter of the following religious [Note: add “and”: the same editions] clerics, he is to be regarded not as Pope or Apostolic, but as an apostate.

[Col. 0380B] C. II. While the Pope lives, no one may dare, without consulting him, to speak concerning the election of a future Pontiff. Likewise Pope Symmachus, in the First Roman Synod, chapters 3 and 5 [Note: held A.D. 499; Burchard, Book 1, ch. 223; Anselm, Book 6, ch. 1; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 336; Polycarpus, Book 1, title 4].

If anyone, while a Pope [Note: *If anyone, while a Pope*: This beginning, down to the clause “If any presbyter,” is chapter 2 of the petition of Fulgentius, archdeacon of the Roman Church. Together with three other chapters it precedes the First or Second Synod under Symmachus in the volumes of councils, under the heading: “Chapters of the First Roman Synod under Pope Symmachus.” In the code of canons it is headed: “Four titles of the decrees of Pope Symmachus.”] is alive, is convicted of giving support in any way to anyone for the Roman pontificate, shall be deprived of the honour of his position or of communion [Note: “shall be deprived of the rank of his position”: Anselm].

If any presbyter [Note: *If any presbyter*: These are the proper words of chapter 3 of that synod itself, which is second in the code of canons], deacon, or cleric, while the Pope is alive and without consulting him, attempts to give a subscription in support of the Roman Pontiff, promise written pledges (*pittacia*), make an oath, promise any support whatever, or, after arranging private meetings for this purpose, deliberate [Note: add “anything”: collected editions] and decide, he shall be deprived of the dignity of his position and of communion [Col. 0381A; Note: “or”: the same editions].

And below:

Because of hidden frauds and the secret snares of conspiracies, which are subject to this strict sentence, if anyone brings to the Church’s knowledge [Note: add “or”: the same editions] the plans of those who have acted against this synod by canvassing for the pontificate, and proves them by reasonable evidence, that participant in such an action shall not only be cleared of all guilt, but also be supported by a reward that is not unworthy. “The whole synod,” etc.

C. III. No one is to be promoted to the height of the apostolate except from among the Cardinals. Likewise from the Council [Note: held A.D. 769; Polycarpus, Book 1, title 4; Deusdedit, part 1, adds: “held in the Constantinian basilica, act 3”] of Pope Stephen III [Note: In Anselm, Book 6, ch. 25 ff., from which the Correctors cite it, neither this chapter nor those following have been found].

It was fitting that this our most holy lady, the Roman Church, should be rightly ordered—as had been established by Blessed Peter and his successors [Col. 0381B]—and that one of the cardinal presbyters or deacons should be consecrated to the height of the apostolate.

C. IV. On the same matter. Likewise from the same source [Note: In two manuscript *Pontificals*, one Vatican and the other of Cardinal Sirleto, under the Life of Pope Stephen III and in reporting the synod held in his time, the following relevant material is read: “Then, after the most sacred canons had been brought forward and carefully examined, a judgment was issued by the same priestly council, forbidding under anathema that any layman should ever presume, nor anyone from another order, unless he had ascended through the distinct grades and had been made a cardinal deacon or presbyter, to be promoted to the honour of the sacred pontificate; and they decreed that many other matters needing canonical correction should be amended in the same council.”] [Note: held A.D. 769; cited collections].

No layman, nor anyone from another order, may ever presume to be promoted to the honor of the sacred pontificate unless, ascending through the distinct grades, he has become a cardinal deacon or priest.

C. V. Let anathema be pronounced upon a bishop, monk, or layman who invades the Roman Church and breaks into the rank of her sons. Likewise from the same source. [Note: [Col. 0382C] Deusdedit, cardinal priest of the title of the Apostles in Eudoxia, part 2, chapter 131, reports many matters from the synod held by Stephen III, among which this entire chapter is contained.] [Note: [Col. 0381] held in A.D. 769.—Deusdedit, book 1.]

If any bishop, priest, monk, or layman, breaking through the decrees of the canons and holy Fathers [Note: [Col. 0381] “institutions”: the collected editions], shall presume to enter the rank of the sons of the holy Roman Church—that is, of the cardinal priests and deacons—and if any of the aforesaid should attempt to invade this Apostolic See and wish to ascend to the supreme pontifical honor, let perpetual anathema fall upon him and those who support him. And below:

§ 1. If anyone should presume to oppose the priests and chief men of the Church, or the whole clergy, in their election of a Roman Pontiff for themselves according to canonical tradition, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0382A] C. VI. Let him be anathema who presumes to oppose the canonical election of the Roman Pontiff. Likewise from the Council of Pope Leo IV. [Note: [Col. 0381] These words are not found among the acts of Leo IV’s council.]

If any of the priests, noble chief men, or the whole clergy [Note: [Col. 0381] add “of this”: collected editions] of the holy Roman Church should presume to oppose the election of the Roman Pontiff, as is recorded to have been decreed in the council of the blessed [Note: [Col. 0381] add “most blessed”: same editions] Popes Boniface and Stephen, let him be anathema.

C. VII. No election of a bishop is to take place until the third day after another’s deposition. Likewise from the Council of Pope Boniface III. [Note: [Col. 0381] From the Roman Pontifical.—Deusdedit, part 1.]

II. Part. While the Roman Pontiff or the bishop of his city is alive, no one may presume to speak or form a party for himself; only on the third day after his deposition, when the clergy and sons of the Church have assembled, may the election take place.

[Col. 0382B] III. Part. Gratian. But it is asked: if two persons have been elected through the rashness of rival factions, which of them is to be preferred to the other? On this matter the Emperor Honorius writes thus to Pope Boniface. [Note: [Col. 0381] dated A.D. 420.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 17.—cf. Distinction 97, chapter 2.]

C. VIII. If two have been ordained through the rashness of rival parties.

If, perhaps, two persons have been ordained contrary to right through the rashness of rival factions [Note: [Col. 0381] Thus in Dionysius; “contending”: Hispanic Collection], neither of them shall at all be a priest; rather, that man alone shall remain in the Apostolic See whom divine judgment and the agreement of the whole body, by a new ordination, have chosen from the number of the clergy.

IV. Part. Gratian. This chapter, however, must not be understood of the case where, after one has been ordained through apostasy, another is enthroned in the Apostolic See by the cardinals and religious clergy, even if that apostate has held the chair of Blessed Peter so violently that a canonical election cannot be held within the City.

Accordingly Pope Nicholas II decreed in the Roman Council, saying: [Note: [Col. 0381] held A.D. 1059.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 16 (Nicholas in the thirteenth council of the bishops). Ivo, Decree, part 5, chapter 80. Polycarpus, book 1, title 4.]

C. IX. Concerning one ordained through money or popular tumult rather than canonical election.

If anyone, through money, human favor, popular or military tumult, without the unanimous and canonical election and blessing of the cardinal bishops, and then of the religious clergy of the following orders, is enthroned in the Apostolic See, he is to be regarded not as Apostolic but as apostate. The cardinal bishops, together with religious and God-fearing clergy and laity, may repel the invader from the Apostolic See by anathema and by human aid and exertion, and may set over it whomever they judge worthy. [Note: [Col. 0383] Anselm reads: “anathematize that man and expel him from the Apostolic See by human aid.”] But if they cannot accomplish this within the City, let them, assembled by our Apostolic authority in a place outside the City [Note: [Col. 0383] added by Anselm and the collected editions] which pleases them, elect [Note: [Col. 0383] Anselm: “carry out the election, granting to the person elected”] the person whom they perceive to be worthier and more useful to the Apostolic See, granting him authority to govern and administer the affairs and welfare of the holy Roman Church, as shall seem best to him according to the circumstances of the time, as though he had already been fully enthroned.

[Note: [Col. 0381] “of cardinal bishops” is absent from Anselm.]
[Note: [Col. 0383] “of cardinal bishops” is lacking in Anselm.]
[Note: [Col. 0383] “with other God-fearing persons”: Anselm and the collected editions.]
[Note: [Col. 0383] “set over”: Anselm reads “restore.”]
[Note: [Col. 0383] “our” is absent from Anselm.]
[Note: [Col. 0383] “in a place”: add “outside the City”: Anselm and the collected editions.]
[Note: [Col. 0383] “which”: Anselm reads “where.”]

V. Part. Gratian. The election of the Roman Pontiff, however, ought to be made with the deliberation of his predecessor.

[Col. 0383B] Accordingly Pope Symmachus says in the Roman Synod, chapter 4. [Note: [Col. 0383] held A.D. 499.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 1. Ivo, Panormia, book 3, chapter 2. Deusdedit, part 1. Polycarpus, book 1, title 4.]

C. X. If the Pope has been unable to decide beforehand concerning the election of his successor.

If the Pope’s death—may it not happen!—should occur unexpectedly, so that he cannot decide beforehand, as was determined above, concerning the election of his successor: if the election of the entire ecclesiastical order has indeed united in one body [Note: [Col. 0383] “has assembled”: Ivo and the collected editions], the elected person shall be consecrated bishop. But if, as usually happens, their inclinations begin to differ, and a dispute arises concerning the candidates, the judgment of the greater number shall prevail [Note: [Col. 0383] “shall prove”: same source and Anselm]; provided, however, that the man who has decided concerning the election when induced by a promise rather than right judgment shall be deprived of priesthood. The Synod said: It is pleasing, etc.

VI. Part. Gratian. As has been shown above, the election of the high priests ought to be made by cardinals and religious clergy; their removal is reserved to divine judgment.

[Col. 0384B] Accordingly Pope Anacletus says to the bishops of Italy, letter 2. [Note: [Col. 0383] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Ivo, Decree, part 5, chapter 238.]

The Lord has reserved to himself the removal of high priests, although he granted their election to good priests and spiritually minded peoples.

[Note: [Col. 0383] “removal” is absent from the Basel edition.]
[Note: [Col. 0383D] “High”: this was followed by “Pontiffs or priests.” The first two words were removed because they occur neither in the original nor in Ivo nor in old manuscripts of Gratian.]

## DISTINCTION LXXX

[Col. 0383]

[Col. 0383B] GRATIAN.

I. Part. The places in which primates, patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, and priests are to be ordained are these, according to Popes Lucius, Clement, and Anacletus.

[Col. 0383C] For Pope Lucius says: [Note: [Col. 0383] The same material occurs in the second Pseudo-Isidorian letter of Stephen.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 115.]

C. I. In what places primates or patriarchs ought to be ordained.

The cities and places over which primates ought to preside were established not by modern men, but even many ages before the coming of Christ; the Gentiles also called their primates upon for their greater affairs. After Christ’s coming, the Apostles and their successors placed patriarchs or primates in those cities; matters concerning bishops and major causes, while the Apostolic authority is preserved in all things, are to be referred to them after the Apostolic See.

[Note: [Col. 0383] From the letter of Sixtus III to the Synod of Thessalonica.]

C. II. On the same subject. Likewise Pope Clement to James, letter 1. [Note: [Col. 0383] This chapter is drawn from material which Pseudo-Isidore is known to have added to Clement’s letter translated into Latin by Rufinus.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 155. Anselm, book 6, chapter 110. Polycarpus, book 2, title 22.]

In those cities where formerly among the pagans their chief flamines and chief doctors of the law were found, Blessed Peter commanded that primates or patriarchs of bishops be established, to handle in the faith the causes of the other bishops and major affairs whenever necessary. And a little later:

§ 1. But in those cities in which there had formerly been archflamines among the aforesaid pagans [Note: [Col. 0383] add “pagans”: collected editions], who nevertheless occupied ranks lower than the aforementioned primates, he commanded archbishops to be established. And below:

§ 2. In every remaining city [Note: [Col. 0383] cf. Council of Nicaea, chapter 8] he commanded that one bishop, and not two, three, or more, be appointed; they were to bear only the title of bishop, not the name of primate, archbishop, or metropolitan, because they do not hold mother-cities. For even among the Apostles themselves there was not equal rank, but one presided over all.

[Note: [Col. 0383] The words enclosed in asterisks are likewise absent from Anselm.]
[Note: [Col. 0383] According to Isidore of Seville, in the spurious letter to Eugenius of Toulouse.]

C. III. On the same subject. Likewise Anacletus, letter 3, chapter 2. [Note: [Col. 0383] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, whose source has been found in Pope Zacharias’s letter to Boniface.—cf. Council of Nicaea, chapter 4.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 4. Ivo, Decree, part 5, chapters 58–59.]

Bishops ought not to be established in castles or small towns; rather, priests are to be ordained and appointed by bishops throughout castles, small towns, and villages, each nevertheless in his own individual title. A bishop ought to be ordained not by one bishop but by several bishops and, as has been said, is to receive title and designation not for a small town, lest the name of bishop be cheapened, but for an honorable city. A priest, however, is to be set over any place whatever or a church established in it.

[Note: [Col. 0385] The collected editions read “but bishops.”]
[Note: [Col. 0385] Add “of the church established there”: collected editions.]

C. IV. On the same subject. Likewise Pope Leo to the bishops of Africa, letter LXXXV, chapter 2. [Note: [Col. 0385] Letter 12, written A.D. 446, Ballerini edition.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 32. Ivo, Decree, part 5, chapters 107 and 143. Polycarpus, book 2, title 23.]

We especially wish that, among all the statutes of the canons, that which concerns priestly dignity should be observed: bishops are not to be consecrated in any places whatever, nor in any castles, nor where there were none before. For where the congregations are smaller and the assemblies less numerous, the care of priests is sufficient; episcopal governance, however, ought to preside only over larger peoples and more populous cities, lest the priestly eminence which the divinely inspired decrees of the holy Fathers prohibited be assigned to hamlets and estates, or obscure and isolated municipalities.

[Col. 0386A] C. V. On the same subject. Likewise from the Council of Laodicea, chapter 57. [Note: [Col. 0385] held between A.D. 347 and 381.]

Bishops ought not to be ordained in villages and rural districts, but visitors—that is, those who travel about—should be appointed. [Note: [Col. 0385] “But visitors”: the printed Greek text reads *ē periodeutas* (ἢ περιοδευτάς), “or visitors”; but three manuscripts read *alla periodeutas* (ἀλλὰ περιοδευτάς), “but visitors.”] We judge that those ordained previously should do nothing without the knowledge of the bishop of the city. Likewise priests also should do nothing without the command and counsel of the bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0385] “previously”: “before this” in the collected editions.]
[Note: [Col. 0385] “also”: “however” in the same editions.]

II. Part. Gratian. Episcopal sees should not be separated by a long distance, so that bishops may readily come to the consecration of a colleague from their own province.

[Col. 0386B] Accordingly Gregory says to Augustine, bishop of the English, Response 8. [Note: [Col. 0385] Letter 64, written A.D. 601, book 11, Maurist edition.—cf. chapter 1, Distinction 5.—Panormia, book 3, chapter 16.]

C. VI. Episcopal sees ought not to be separated from one another by a long distance.

We wish you to ordain bishops in England in such a manner that the bishops themselves are not separated from one another by a long distance, so that there may be no necessity preventing them from assembling for the ordination of any bishop. For an episcopal ordination must by no means take place without three or four bishops assembled.

[Note: [Col. 0385] “by no means”: the collected editions.]

## DISTINCTION LXXXI

[Col. 0385]

[Col. 0385B] GRATIAN.

I. Part. Let what we have said concerning those to be ordained and those who ordain, and concerning the distinctions and offices of the individual ranks, suffice. But because we have lingered somewhat more fully over these matters, let us set before the memory, by way of summary, certain points connected with what preceded.

A man to be ordained bishop, as the Apostle writes, must be without crime—that is, without mortal sin. This must be understood not only of a bishop but also of anyone elected to any office of governance in the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0385] Titus 1:7.]

Accordingly Augustine writes in Treatise XLI on John, chapter 8: [Note: [Col. 0385] Bede on Titus, book 1.]

C. I. He who is ordained bishop must be without crime and grave sin.

When the Apostle Paul chose persons to be ordained priests or deacons, and whoever is to be ordained to an office of governance in the Church, he did not say, “If anyone is without sin.” For if he had said this, every human being would be rejected and no one ordained. Rather, he says, “If anyone is without crime,” such as homicide, adultery, some impurity of fornication, theft, fraud, sacrilege, and other things of that kind.

§ 1. A crime, however, is a grave sin, most deserving of accusation and condemnation.

[Note: [Col. 0385] Add “or”: Basel edition.]
[Note: [Col. 0385] Cf. above, Distinction 25, Part III.]

II. Part. Gratian. Therefore, anyone implicated in any of these offenses ought not to be ordained. If, however, he has already been ordained and is proved to have committed any of them before or after the time of his ordination, he shall be deprived of the office of the rank he received.

Accordingly Pope Symmachus says: [Note: [Col. 0385] From Ennodius’s apologetic tract for the fourth Roman Synod, held A.D. 501.—Collection in three parts, part 1, title 48, chapter 6.]

C. II. He does not rightly take on the role of admonisher who teaches by words and not by deeds.

No one rightly takes on the role of admonisher except one who condemns faults by his own actions and shows love of innocence through his conduct.

C. III. Let him who does not fear to elevate an unworthy person be deprived of the rank which he confers. Likewise Celestine to the bishops of Gaul, letter II, chapter 3. [Note: [Col. 0385] From a letter written to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne, A.D. 428.—Collection in three parts, part 1, title 41, chapter 6.]

Daniel, burdened by so many testimonies and assailed by so serious an accusation of crimes, allegedly defiled by incest with consecrated virgins, is said to have been ordained bishop. As is contained in the records of our archive, copies of which we have also sent to you, he stealthily obtained pontifical dignity at the very time when, by letters sent from us, he was being summoned to plead his case. Far be injury from the sacred name! It is easier that the ordaining bishop himself has lost this dignity by conferring it upon such a man than that the ordained man should obtain it; the person who believed him worthy to be associated with himself by granting him the episcopate will be associated with the convicted man. For whoever ordains such men reveals what kind of man he himself is.

[Note: [Col. 0385] “and as”: absent from the original.]
[Note: [Col. 0385] “will be summoned”: Argentinensis edition.]
[Note: [Col. 0387] “for it is”: collected editions.]

C. IV. Ecclesiastical order does not receive one ordained without examination or who later confesses. Likewise from the Council of Nicaea, chapter 9. [Note: [Col. 0387] held A.D. 325.—Burchard, book 2, chapter 13. Ivo, Decree, part 6, chapter 33. Anselm, book 8, chapter 13, from Dionysius’s translation.]

If any have been promoted to the priesthood without examination and, when subsequently examined, have confessed their sins, and after their confession men, acting contrary to the rule, have laid hands upon them, ecclesiastical order does not receive such persons. In all matters the holy Church upholds what is irreproachable.

[Note: [Col. 0387] Add “rashly”: original.]
[Note: [Col. 0387] “received”: editions of Strasbourg, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice I and II.]
[Note: [Col. 0387] “holy” is absent from the original.]

[Col. 0387B] C. V. Let those fallen away who were ordained through ignorance or the contempt of their ordainers be deposed. Likewise from the same council, chapter 10. [Note: [Col. 0387] held A.D. 325.]

Whoever among those who have fallen away was ordained through ignorance, or through the disregard of those who ordained them, this does not prejudice the ecclesiastical rule. For when the fact has been discovered, they are deposed.

[Note: [Col. 0387] Add “already”: collected editions.]
[Note: [Col. 0387D] “or through the contempt”: in the commonly printed Greek of the council it is *ē kai proeidotōn tōn procheirisamenōn* (ἢ καὶ προειδότων τῶν προχειρισαμένων), that is, “or even with the prior knowledge of those who ordained them.”]
[Note: [Col. 0387] “shall be deposed”: same editions, with the original.]

C. VI. Let him who unlawfully defiles his ministry by his manner of life be removed from it. Likewise Innocent to Maximus and Severus, letter V. [Note: [Col. 0387] Letter of uncertain date.—Anselm, book 8, chapter 15 [14]. Ivo, Decree, part 6, chapter 96. Polycarpus, book 4, title 39.]

Our son Maximianus [Note: [Col. 0387] “Maximilianus”: original, Anselm, and editions of Strasbourg and Basel], an official in civil administration, has lodged the complaint whose substance is set out in the attached petition. Moved by zeal for faith and discipline, he does not permit the Church to be defiled by unworthy priests, whom he alleges to have begotten children while serving in the priesthood. I would not need to explain that this is unlawful, unless I knew that your prudence possesses knowledge of the whole law. Therefore, dearest brothers, having examined the tenor of the attached petition, you shall order those said to have perpetrated such acts to be brought forward; and, after investigating the charges made against those priests, if they are convicted, they are to be removed from the priestly office—for those who are not holy cannot handle holy things—and made strangers to the ministry which they have unlawfully defiled by their lives.

[Note: [Col. 0387] The original reads: “our son Maximilianus, an official in civil administration, the kind of complaint…”]
[Note: [Col. 0387] Anselm reads: “it was lawful to explain.”]
[Note: [Col. 0387] “dearest” is absent from the original.]
[Note: [Col. 0387] The collected editions read “you ought to place.”]
[Note: [Col. 0387] The collected editions with the original read “if they can be convicted.”]

[Col. 0388A] C. VII. For anyone deposed from orders, the bishop’s care should assign a place for penance. Likewise Pope Eugenius II. [Note: [Col. 0387] In the Roman council held A.D. 826, chapter 14.]

A priest, or anyone else advanced in ecclesiastical order, if he is found guilty of a crime proved to require his removal, once deposed is to be placed, by the bishop’s care, in a suitably provided place, where he may lament his sins and commit them no further.

[Note: [Col. 0387] “sin”: Basel edition.]

C. VIII. Priests who disdain to do penance are to be confined in a monastery. Likewise from the Council of Mainz. [Note: [Col. 0387] Chapter 40, Council of Chalon held A.D. 813. Burchard, book 2, chapter 191. Ivo, Decree, part 6, chapter 236.]

It has been reported to us that priests canonically degraded because of their negligence, after losing their rank, live as laymen and neglect the good work of doing penance. We therefore decree that, after losing their rank, they be sent for the purpose of doing penance to a monastery or to a regular community of canons. If some cause should prevent this, wherever they are, they are not to cease doing penance. But if, after losing their rank, they wish to live as laymen and neglect to do penance, they are to be separated from the communion of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0387D] “To a monastery”: at the Council of Chalon, where this canon is found—although Burchard and Ivo also cite Mainz—and in the other collectors, the text reads: “in a monastery, either canonical or regular”; one very ancient manuscript of Gratian reads: “in a monastery according to the canonical rule.”]
[Note: [Col. 0387] “a canonical community”: collected editions and the first Lyons editions II and III.]

C. IX. Change of place sometimes benefits those converted to penance. Likewise Isidore, *Sentences on the Supreme Good*, book II, chapter 10.

For those converted, change of place is sometimes beneficial for the salvation of their souls. For often, when the place is changed, the disposition of the mind is changed also. It is fitting, therefore, to be torn away bodily from the very place where one has served allurements. For the place where one has lived wickedly brings before the mind’s sight that which one often thought or did there.

[Note: [Col. 0387] Add “their”: collected editions.]
[Note: [Col. 0387] “therefore”: same editions.]
[Note: [Col. 0387] “uprooted”: same editions and the first Basel edition.]
[Note: [Col. 0387] Add “lived wickedly and”: Basel edition.]
[Note: [Col. 0387] “always”: original.]
[Note: [Col. 0387] Add “each person”: collected editions.]

C. X. A clerk convicted or confessing adultery is to be confined in a monastery. Likewise from the Third Synod of Orléans, chapter 7. [Note: [Col. 0387] held A.D. 538; in the Hispanic Collection it is Orléans II. The collected editions cite Orléans V; the first Lyons editions II and III cite Orléans VI.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 143; *Decree*, part 8, chapter 285.]

If any cleric is found to have committed adultery, whether confessing it or convicted, he is to be deposed from office, granted communion, and confined in a monastery for the whole of his life.

[Note: [Col. 0387] “confined again”: original.]

C. XI. On the same subject. Likewise Pope Pelagius [Note: [Col. 0387] Whether this belongs to Pelagius I or II is by no means clear.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 144.] to Constantine the Defender.

Romanus, a cleric of the Church of Thaeana [Note: [Col. 0387] “Thianensis”: collected editions; nevertheless the correction by the editors appears right, since the Church of Thaeana was situated in Apulia], has been deposed from clerical order for the crime of adultery which he is reported to have committed, and has by our command been confined here in the city of Rome in a monastery to do penance.

[Note: [Col. 0389] Add “for the whole period”: Basel edition.]

C. XII. A priest or deacon caught in a crime is to be deposed, but not deprived of communion. Likewise from Apostolic Canon 25. [Note: [Col. 0389] Regino, book 1, chapter 86. Burchard, book 2, chapter 189. Anselm, book 11, chapter 29. Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chapter 234. Polycarpus, book 4, title 31.—cf. Council of Tribur, chapter 11; Rabanus, *Penitential*, chapter 1.]

A priest or deacon caught in fornication, perjury, theft, or homicide is to be deposed, but not deprived of communion. For Scripture says: “The Lord will not punish twice for the same thing.”

[Note: [Col. 0389C] “Or homicide”: this phrase is not in Apostolic Canon 25, nor in Anselm, but is in the Council of Tribur. When the Fathers there had said: “We read in the Apostolic Canons that a bishop, priest, or deacon caught in fornication, perjury, or theft is to be deposed,” they infer that the same should be decreed all the more concerning a murderer. This perhaps was the reason why Gratian and other collectors added the phrase to this canon. In Canon 32 of Basil, the same is decreed concerning clerics who commit a sin unto death; this had also been explained concerning fornicators in Canon 3.]
[Note: [Col. 0389C] “Deprived”: the printed codices continued, except for the Basel edition, “if he obeys the sentence”; these words have been deleted because they occur neither in the original nor in old manuscripts of Gratian.]
[Note: [Col. 0389] “God judges”: collected editions.]

C. XIII. On the same subject. Likewise. [Note: [Col. 0389C] The proper author of this chapter has not been found; but something similar occurs in the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 1, and in the chapters of Martin of Braga, chapter 27.] [Note: [Col. 0389] Chapter 1 of the Council of Neocaesarea, held A.D. 314. Anselm, book 11, chapter 31, produced it from Martin of Braga’s translation.]

If any bishop, priest, or deacon, after receiving the rank of deacon, has committed fornication or adultery, let him be deposed, expelled from the Church, and do penance among the laity.

[Note: [Col. 0389D] “Among the laity”: these two words do not occur in chapter 1 of the Council of Neocaesarea; they are not found there in Dionysius, though they occur in Isidore. Nor do they occur in the chapter of Martin of Braga.]

C. XIV. On the same subject. Likewise from the First Council of Orléans, chapters 9 and 12. [Note: [Col. 0389] held A.D. 511.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 368, and part 15, chapter 18.]

If a deacon or priest commits a capital crime, he is to be expelled both from office and from communion. But if, on account of their offense, they have removed themselves from communion at the altar under a profession of penitence, these likewise, if others are unavailable and a clear case of necessity arises, may baptize one asking for baptism.

[Note: [Col. 0389] Thus in the original; “they”: editions of Strasbourg and Basel.]
[Note: [Col. 0389] “certainly”: editions of Nuremberg, Venice I and II, Lyons I, and Paris.]

[Col. 0390A] C. XV. Priests, deacons, and subdeacons living in the crime of fornication are not to enter a church. Likewise Gregory VII to all who render the obedience due to St Peter throughout the kingdom of Italy and the Germans. [Note: [Col. 0390C] This letter, containing exactly all the words of this chapter, has not been found in the register of Gregory VII’s letters. It nevertheless contains much that mentions this decree: book 1, letter 30, to the bishop of Salzburg; book 2, letter 61, to the bishop of Liège, and the following letter to Sicard of Aquileia. Concerning this decree, urging its full execution, he writes with especial care in book 2, letter 66, to Burchard, bishop of Halberstadt, and in the following letter to Anno, archbishop of Cologne; he gives the same command in book 3, letter 4, to Sigifred, archbishop of Mainz; and in book 4, letter 10, he writes to the countess of Flanders, and in the following letter to the count, on the same matter. The decree is also more correctly mentioned among Innocent II’s decrees. Marianus Scotus reports the very wording of this chapter up to the sentence “But whoever [disobeys] this most health-giving…” at the end of his chronicles. The following words, however, are very characteristic of Gregory VII.]
[Note: [Col. 0389] Mansi published this as a fragment of the Roman council held A.D. 1074, from Gerhoh of Reichersberg.—Berthold of Constance, in his chronicle, records it under the same title now found in Gratian, but dated A.D. 1079.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 134.]

If there are any priests, deacons, or subdeacons living in the crime of fornication, we forbid them, in the name of God Almighty and by the authority of St Peter, to enter church until they repent and amend their lives. But if any prefer to persevere in their sin, let none of you presume to hear their office, because their blessing is turned into a curse and their prayer into sin, as the Lord testifies through the Prophet: “I will curse your blessings.” But whoever refuses to obey this most health-giving command incurs the sin of idolatry, as Samuel testifies and Blessed Gregory confirms: “Disobedience is the sin of divination, and refusal to comply is like the crime of idolatry.” Therefore whoever, while professing himself a Christian, scorns to obey the Apostolic See incurs the sin of paganism.

[Note: [Col. 0389] Add “the Father”: collected editions.]
[Note: [Col. 0389] Malachi 2:2.]
[Note: [Col. 0389] Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 36.]
[Note: [Col. 0389] “refuse … incur”: collected editions.]
[Note: [Col. 0389] 1 Samuel 15:23.]
[Note: [Col. 0389] Cf. Cause 11, question 1, chapter 10.]
[Note: [Col. 0389] “instructing”: collected editions.]
[Note: [Col. 0389] “as”: absent from the same editions and the first Basel edition.]

C. XVI. Let a bishop, priest, or deacon who takes a woman or keeps one already taken be deprived of office and benefice. Likewise Alexander II to the bishops and king of the Dalmatians. [Note: [Col. 0389] Although the letter itself must everywhere be regarded as genuine, an error seems to lie in its address: Baronius testifies that the dukes of Dalmatia were not called kings until Gregory VII.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 138.]

If henceforth any bishop, priest, or deacon takes a woman or retains one already taken, let him fall from his own rank until he comes to satisfaction; let him not remain in the choir of psalm-singers, nor have any share in ecclesiastical property.

[Note: [Col. 0389] “from his own”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0391C] “Nor serve drink”: Clement’s letter reads: “nor offer water to priests for their hands; let her close the doors from outside; let her perform lesser services; let her not carry a pitcher or chalice to the altar.” But Ivo reads: “But let her offer water only to the hands of priests; let her close the doors from outside; let her perform lesser services; but let her bring a pitcher to the altar.”]

[Col. 0391A] C. XVII. On the same subject. The same to the clergy of Milan. [Note: [Col. 0391] This chapter may perhaps have been taken from the regulations prescribed for Milan by Maynard and John, legates of the Apostolic See.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 139.—The Basel edition cites the Council of Milan; the Strasbourg edition, the Council of Meaux.]

If any priest, deacon, or subdeacon, stubbornly abandoning his office, chooses a woman for himself, then, just as he voluntarily abandons office because of fornication, so he shall be compelled, even unwillingly, to abandon his benefice because of transgression.

[Note: [Col. 0391] “shall choose”: Basel edition; “chooses”: Lyons editions II and III, and Böhm.]

C. XVIII. On the same subject. The same to the people of Milan. [Note: [Col. 0391] Cf. preceding chapter.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 140.]

We judge that those also who, so that fornication may be permitted them, abandon the divine office and, departing from God, serve the devil and his works, ought, just as they most justly make themselves strangers to office, to be deprived of the benefices of churches.

[Note: [Col. 0391] “judge”: collected editions.]

C. XIX. On the same subject. Likewise Pope Lucius. [Note: [Col. 0391] From the second apocryphal letter of Clement.—Anselm, book 8, chapter 3. Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 87. Polycarpus, book 4, title 41.]

Let such priests or deacons be chosen as ministers of the altar for the Lord’s offices as preserve continence.

§ 1. But if, after their ordination, ministers should happen to enter the bed of their own wife, they are not to enter the thresholds of the sanctuary, nor become bearers of sacred things, nor touch the altars, nor receive from offerers the oblation of holocaust and victim, nor approach the portion of the Lord’s body, nor serve drink, nor perform lesser offices without the authority of an elder. Nor indeed are they to bring a pitcher or chalice to the altar.

[Note: [Col. 0391C] “Sanctuary”: in Clement’s second letter, from which this chapter may seem to have been taken and from which Ivo cites it, the reading is “sacrifice.” In one ancient manuscript of Gratian: “sacred.”]
[Note: [Col. 0391] Add “and victim”: Basel edition.]
[Note: [Col. 0391] “carrying”: original.]
[Note: [Col. 0391] “they shall offer”: Basel edition.]
[Note: [Col. 0391] “perform”: same edition.]
[Note: [Col. 0391] “not”: collected editions; absent from the original, published by the Ballerini under the title *Precepts of St Peter on Preserving the Sacraments*. = C. XX.]

[Col. 0391C] C. XX. Let a cleric who frequents the homes of married women be deposed. The same. [Note: [Col. 0391] In the same place, a little below.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 147 [149], book 8, chapter 42. Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chapter 89. Polycarpus, book 4, title 31.]

III. Part. A cleric is not to visit a woman’s dwelling alone, nor go there without the command of an elder priest; nor is a priest alone to engage in conversation with a woman alone. Nor may an archdeacon, under the pretext of humility or office, frequently enter the homes of married women; nor may he perhaps secretly convey anything to a married woman through clerics or household servants. If this becomes known, let him be deposed and let her be barred from the thresholds of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0391] Add “frequently”: Basel edition.]
[Note: [Col. 0391] “priest” is absent from Ivo; Anselm, book 7, and the Basel edition read “and priest”; Anselm, book 8, reads “prince.”]
[Note: [Col. 0391C] “Command”: Clement’s letter continues: “Nor may a priest be alone with a woman alone; rather, let him visit a sick woman after bringing two witnesses. Nor may he alone converse with a woman alone, nor may an archdeacon or deacon, under the pretext of humble office, visit frequently,” etc.]
[Note: [Col. 0391] This seems to have been inserted by Pseudo-Isidore into a letter composed before him.—cf. Isidore of Seville, *On Offices*, book 2, chapter 2; Third Council of Tours, chapter 29.]
[Note: [Col. 0391] “secretly”: Anselm, book 7 reads “of a secret matter.”]

C. XXI. On the same subject. PALEA. The same. [Note: [Col. 0392C] This *palea* is joined to the preceding chapter in most ancient manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 0391] There continuously.—Anselm and Polycarpus, in the same place.]

“But if some intervention should be necessary, it should be reported to the bishop. And if it concerns a person to whom he ought to go by a charitable intervention, let him go himself; otherwise, let him send someone from his household with two or three witnesses. Yet no one may live with a woman not of his family, unless she is a close relative or sister. And let this be done with great care. For we are not ignorant of Satan’s malice.”

[Note: [Col. 0392C] “Let him send”: Clement’s letter continues: “with two or three persons who should remedy this. Certainly no cleric may enter to visit a sick woman unless accompanied by two or three. Nevertheless, no one,” etc.]
[Note: [Col. 0391] “snares”: Basel edition.]

C. XXII. On the same subject. PALEA. [From the decree of Pope Eugenius.] [Note: [Col. 0392C] “From the decree”: this canon was first issued in a Roman council by Eugenius II and was afterward repeated by Leo IV in a council; it is cited in the Decretals, title *On the Cohabitation of Clerics and Women*. In most ancient manuscripts it appears without a name.] [Note: [Col. 0391] Chapter 15, Roman council held A.D. 826.—Anselm, book 8, chapter 9. Polycarpus, book 4, title 31.—cf. chapter 3, *On the Cohabitation of Clerics and Women*, in the Common Book.]

“If any priest—that is, presbyter, deacon, or subdeacon—after a first, second, and third admonition [Note: [Col. 0392C] *Admonition:* In the same canon there follows: “of the metropolitan or another bishop, or of him to whom he appears to be subject.”] is found to be conversing or in any way associating with any woman with whom he is suspected of the crime of fornication, let him be excommunicated; but let the woman be judged according to the canons.”

### C. XXIII. Priests may not live together with women. Likewise Gregory.

[Note: [Col. 0391] The author of the canon has been identified as Pope Zacharias, in the Roman council held in A.D. 743.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 7, c. 76 (“Gregory to the citizens of Rome”). *Polycarpus*, book 4, title 31.]

**Part IV.** Priests, to whom the Lord’s people have been entrusted, ought with great firmness of spirit to keep watch over the Lord’s sheep, lest they be torn by wolfish bites—that is, by the goads of the devil.

§ 1. Nor should I be silent about this, which I say with great sorrow of heart [Col. 0393A] [Note: [Col. 0393] Added: “and bitterness”: collected editions]: I see priests living with women. It is wicked even to say or hear this, and contrary to the enactments of the holy canons. For where persons dwelling together have such cohabitation, the goads of the ancient enemy are not absent. They must therefore be admonished not to be deceived by the fraud of the ancient enemy, so that, in accordance with the Apostle’s words [Note: [Col. 0393] 2 Cor. 6:3], our ministry may not be reproached. For, brothers, we ought to beware of unlawful things, so that we may be able to raise clean hands to the Lord. For it is written [Note: [Col. 0393] Lev. 20:7]: “Be holy, for I, the Lord your God, am holy.” But if anyone presumes to act otherwise, let him be deprived of the honor of his priesthood.

Therefore, brothers, we must by every means beware lest we deceive the people and the saying of the Prophet [Note: [Col. 0393] Zeph. 3:4.—“prophetic”: Basel edition] be fulfilled in us: “My priests defile holy things and reject the law”; [Col. 0393B] and another prophet rebukes them also, saying [Note: [Col. 0393] Mal. 1:6]: “O priests, who deceive my name, and say, ‘In what respect do we deceive your name?’” They are answered: “By offering defiled bread upon my altar.” “I have no pleasure in you,” says the Lord, “and I will not accept a sacrifice from your hands, because you are defiled.” [Note: [Col. 0393] ibid.]

### C. XXIV. On the same matter. The same, to Symmachus the Defender, Book I of the Register, Indiction IX, Epistle 50.

[Note: [Col. 0393] Epistle 62 (written A.D. 591), book 1, Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, c. 81.]

We desire that priests be forbidden to associate with women, except only with a mother, sister, or wife, who must be governed chastely. [Note: [Col. 0393] “must be governed”: “must be governed [plural]”: Basel edition.]

[Col. 0393C]

### C. XXV. On the same matter. The same, Book VII, Epistle 39.

[Note: [Col. 0393] From the letter to the Roman defender, written A.D. 599; book 9, epistle 60, Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, c. 77.—“The same in the Register”: collected editions.]

We read that blessed Augustine did not consent even to live with his sister, saying: “The women who are with my sister are not my sisters.” Learned men’s caution, therefore, ought to be a great instruction to us.

[Note: [Col. 0393] From Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, c. 26: not in the same words, but in the same sense. It was also cited by Regino, book 1, c. 98.]

### C. XXVI. On the same matter. Likewise from the Seventh Synod.

[Note: [Col. 0393D] This chapter is also cited in several manuscripts as from the Seventh Synod, in the final chapter of which some relevant matters indeed occur. Yet in most it is cited as from the Eighth, and the statement appears to be taken from c. 83 of the *Ascetical Rules* of St Basil. It has often been observed elsewhere that his rules are cited under the name of the Eighth Synod.]  
[Note: [Col. 0393] *Collectio tripartita*, part 2, book 14, c. 15.—“an asterisk”; also Basel edition.]

In all things it is fitting to observe that a cleric should appear to, or speak with, women only with certainty as to the person, at a fixed time, in a fixed place, and in the presence of specified persons, so that every disgraceful suspicion may be excluded. Certainly no rule of religion permits a man, when alone himself, to approach a woman who is alone. [Col. 0394A] For it is better [Note: [Col. 0393] Eccles. 4:9] for two to be together than for one. [Note: [Col. 0393] “two rather than one”: collected editions, first Lyons edition, II and III.] For a matter is conducted both more faithfully and more safely when they are together. “Woe to one alone, because, if he falls, there is no one to raise him up.”

### C. XXVII. On the same matter. Likewise from the Third Council of Carthage, c. 17.

[Note: [Col. 0393] Held A.D. 397.—*Collectio tripartita*, part 2, title 17, c. 10.]

No unrelated women whatsoever are to live with clerics; only mothers, grandmothers, maternal aunts, paternal aunts, sisters, and daughters of brothers or sisters may do so; and likewise any women who, through domestic necessity, were already living with them even before they were ordained; or if their sons, after their parents had been ordained, took wives; or if it became necessary to bring in from elsewhere wives for servants who have none in the household whom they may marry.

[Note: [Col. 0393] “whoever”: Lyons editions II and III.]  
[Note: [Col. 0393] “even”: absent from the collected editions, first Basel edition.]

[Col. 0394B]

### C. XXVIII. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Laodicea, c. 30.

[Note: [Col. 0393] Held between A.D. 347 and 381.]

Ministers of the altar, or indeed any clerics, or persons professing continence, or absolutely any Christian, ought not to have baths in common with women. For this is the first reproach among the Gentiles.

### C. XXIX. On the same matter. Likewise Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, Book III, Epistle 26.

[Note: [Col. 0393] Epistle 26, written A.D. 594; book 4, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 7, c. 146.]

I hear that you forbade your archdeacon to live with women, and that until now you have been disregarded in that prohibition. Unless he obeys your command, we desire that he be deprived of sacred orders.

[Col. 0394C]

### C. XXX. Women who seek unlawful companionship with clerics are to be sold by the bishop. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Toledo, c. 42.

[Note: [Col. 0393] Held A.D. 633.—Anselm, book 7, c. 148 (150). *Polycarpus*, book 4, title 39.]

Certain clerics, having no lawful marriage, seek the forbidden companionship of unrelated women or of their own female servants. Therefore, those women who are thus joined with clerics are to be removed by the bishop and sold; the clerics whom their lust has corrupted are to be relegated for a time to penance.

[Note: [Col. 0393] “which are forbidden”: collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0393] “whatever”: the Hispana collection—Anselm.]  
[Note: [Col. 0393] “attached”: Hispana collection.]  
[Note: [Col. 0393] “bound”: Hispana collection and Isidore Mercator—Anselm.]

### C. XXXI. Women may not live with clerics except those excused by kinship. Likewise Pope Siricius to Himerius, bishop, Epistle I, c. 12.

[Note: [Col. 0393] Written A.D. 385. Burchard, book 2, c. 110. Anselm, book 7, c. 149 (151). Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, cc. 52 and 187; *Polycarpus*, book 4, title 31.]

We do not permit any women other than those alone whom the Synod of Nicaea allowed to live with clerics solely because of ties of kinship to be in clerics’ houses. [Col. 0395A]

[Note: [Col. 0393] “house”: collected editions.]

### C. XXXII. Clerics are not to visit women’s homes except by command of their superiors. Likewise from the African Council, c. 5.

[Note: [Col. 0395] C. 25, Third Council of Carthage, held A.D. 397, from Dionysius.—Anselm, book 7, c. 151 (153).]

Clerics, or persons professing continence, are not to visit widows or virgins except by the order or permission of bishops or presbyters. Nor are they to do this alone, but with fellow clerics, or with those whom the bishop or presbyter has directed. Nor are bishops and presbyters themselves to have access to women of this kind alone, but only where clerics or some reputable Christians are present.

[Note: [Col. 0395] “or”: absent from the collected editions, first Basel edition, Lyons II and III.]

[Col. 0396A]

### C. XXXIII. Bishops must ensure that, under pretext of temporal support, women are not assigned to clerics’ households. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 102.

[Note: [Col. 0395] C. 68, *Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua*; see c. 9, Distinction 18. Burchard, book 8, c. 55. Ivo, *Decree*, part 7, c. 73. *Polycarpus*, book 4, title 37.]

It is chargeable to the bishop or presbyter who presides over a parish if younger widows or consecrated women are placed in the households of clerics for the support of their present life.

### C. XXXIV. On the same matter. Likewise from the same source, c. 103.

[Note: [Col. 0395] C. 103, *Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua*.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 8, c. 327. *Polycarpus*, ibid.]

Widows who are supported at the expense of the Church ought to be so constant in God’s work that they assist the Church both by their merits and by their prayers.

## DISTINCTION LXXXII

[Col. 0395]

[Col. 0395B] **GRATIAN**

**Part I.** In general, a bishop must also provide necessities for the poor and for those who cannot work with their own hands.

Accordingly, in the First Council of Orléans, c. 18, we read [Note: [Col. 0395] Held A.D. 511.—*Collectio tripartita*, part 2, title 29, c. 11]:

### C. I. On the same matter.

Let the bishop bestow food and clothing, insofar as he is able, upon poor or infirm persons who, because of weakness, cannot work with their own hands.

[Note: [Col. 0395] “clothing”: collected editions, first Basel edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395] “possible”: “means”; Basel edition—“has the means”: original.]

### C. II. He who has preferred pleasure to duty must be removed by every means. Likewise Innocent to Exsuperius of Toulouse, Epistle III, c. 1.

[Note: [Col. 0395] Written A.D. 405.—Anselm, book 8, c. 8. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 137; *Decree*, part 6, c. 57. *Polycarpus*, book 4, title 31.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395] “of Toledo”: Argentinensis, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice I and II editions.]

**Part II.** You have asked what must be observed concerning those who, having been placed in the ministry of the diaconate or in the office of the presbyterate, are reported by children begotten to be or to have been incontinent. [Col. 0395C] Regarding these, both the discipline of the divine laws is manifest and the warnings of Siricius, bishop of blessed memory, have plainly been conveyed: those placed in such offices who are incontinent must be deprived of every ecclesiastical honor and must not be admitted to a ministry which ought to be fulfilled by continence alone.

For the authority of the sacred law, very ancient and observed from the beginning, is that priests were commanded to reside in the temple during the year of their assigned turn, so that, in serving the sacred offerings, they might claim the divine ministries for themselves as pure and cleansed from every stain, [Col. 0396B] and that those who engage in carnal intercourse even with a wife might not lawfully be admitted to sacred offices. For it is written [Note: [Col. 0395] Lev. 11:44; 20:7]: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy.”

For them, indeed, the use of a wife had been permitted for the sake of the succession of offspring, because no one from another tribe, and none except one descended from Aaron, had been commanded to approach the priesthood. How much more, then, ought these priests or Levites to preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, since their priesthood or ministry does not pass by succession, and no day passes on which they are free either from divine sacrifices or from the office of baptism.

[Note: [Col. 0395] “cleansed”: Hispana collection and Isidore Mercator.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395] “sacrifices”: ibid.—Anselm.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395] “also”: collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395] “intercourse”: Basel edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395] Added: “therefore”: collected editions with the original.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395] “wife”: absent from the collected editions, first Basel edition, Lyons II and III.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395] “had been”: “would have been”: the same editions, first Lyons II and III.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395] These words are not in the original.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395] “permitted”: Basel edition—“dared”: the remaining collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395] “How”: “How much”: Anselm from the original.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395] “these”: “bishops”: Argentinensis edition—“themselves”: remaining collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395] “or”: collected editions.]

For if the blessed Apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying [Note: [Col. 0395] 1 Cor. 7:5], “Abstain for a time, that you may be free for prayer”—and he of course commanded this to laypeople—how much more ought priests, whose duty of prayer and sacrifice is continual, always to abstain from such intercourse. If one of them has been defiled by carnal desire, with what shame will he presume to sacrifice, or with what conscience and by what merit does he believe that he will be heard? For it is said [Col. 0397A] [Note: [Col. 0397] Titus 1:15]: “All things are clean to the clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean.”

[Note: [Col. 0395] Added: “more readily”: collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395] Added: “therefore”: the same editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395] “who”: “because”: the same editions, first Basel.]  
[Note: [Col. 0395C] *Carnal desire:* This passage has been corrected and expanded from Innocent’s own letter, as have many others in this chapter wherever the gloss allowed it. But in the letter of Siricius cited in the Council of Telepte—thus it seems should be read instead of “Tellense,” though, in the opinion of the Ballerini, “Telense,” or rather “Zellense,” should be read—it reads thus: “What will he do? Will he make an excuse? With what shame? With what disposition will he presume? By what merit does he believe that he will be heard?”]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] Added: “but their mind and conscience are defiled”: collected editions.]

But perhaps he believes this to be allowed because it is written [Note: [Col. 0397] 1 Tim. 3:2], “the husband of one wife.” He did not say this so that a man might persist in the desire to beget children, but because of future incontinence. [Note: [Col. 0397C] *He did not say this:* The original reads: “He did not say this for one persisting in the desire to beget.”] Nor did he exclude those sound in body, he who said [Note: [Col. 0397] 1 Cor. 7:7], “I would that all were as I myself am.” He explains this still more clearly, saying [Note: [Col. 0397] Rom. 8:9]: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are no longer in the flesh, but in the Spirit.” And he said, “having children,” not “begetting them.” [Note: [Col. 0397] 1 Tim. 3:4.—“to one having”: Hispana collection.]

But that is plainly a different and distinct judgment. For if this form and discipline of ecclesiastical life, which was sent by Bishop Siricius to all the provinces, [Note: [Col. 0397] Added: “all”: collected editions.] is not shown to have reached some persons, pardon will not be denied to them in their ignorance; provided that henceforth they begin wholly to abstain, and retain the rank in which they were found, without being allowed to rise to higher positions. It should count as a favor to them that they do not lose even the position which they retain.

[Note: [Col. 0397] “is not shown”: “will not be shown”: Anselm from the original.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397B] “ignorance”: “failure to know”: ibid.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] “will not be denied”: “will not be remitted”: original.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] “rise”: Basel edition.]

§ 1. But if any are discovered to have known the rule of life sent by Siricius and yet not immediately cast away the desires of lust, they must by every means be removed, because, after the admonition became known to them, they judged their own will to be preferable.

[Note: [Col. 0397] “to have known”: “to know”: Hispana collection.]

### C. III. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Siricius to Himerius, Bishop of Tarragona, Epistle I, c. 7.

[Note: [Col. 0397] Written A.D. 385.—*Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 26, c. 3. Ivo, *Decree*, part 60, c. 50. *Polycarpus*, book 4, title 31.]

We have learned that many priests of Christ and Levites, after long periods following their consecration, have begotten children both by their own wives [Col. 0397C] and by shameful intercourse; and that they defend their crime by this pretext, that in the Old Testament priests and ministers are said to have been granted permission to beget children.

Let whoever he may be who is a follower of lust and teacher of vices tell me now: if he thinks that in the Law of Moses the reins of lust were indiscriminately loosened by our God for sacred orders, why does He forewarn those to whom the Holy of Holies was entrusted, saying [Note: [Col. 0397] Lev. 11:44], [Col. 0398A] “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy”? Why, too, were priests commanded to reside in the temple, far from their homes, during the year of their assigned turn? Clearly for this reason: that they might be unable to have carnal intercourse even with their wives, so that, shining in the integrity of their consciences, they might offer an acceptable gift to God.

When their period of service was complete, the use of a wife was permitted to them only for the sake of succession, because no one except from the tribe of Levi had been commanded to be admitted to God’s ministry.

[Note: [Col. 0397] “marriages”: collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] “thinks”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] Added: “their”: collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] “also”: absent from the original.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] “of a wife”: “of a wife”: original and collected editions; added “his” in the latter.]

### C. IV. On the same matter. The same, a little further on.

[Note: [Col. 0397C] This chapter is joined to the preceding one in several manuscript copies of Gratian.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] *Collectio tripartita*, *Polycarpus*, and Ivo, ibid.]

Since some of those of whom we speak, as your holiness has reported, bewail that they have fallen through ignorance, we say that mercy ought not to be denied them on this condition: [Col. 0398B] that, without any increase of rank, they remain for as long as they live in the office to which they have been reduced, provided that henceforth they endeavor to show themselves continent.

But those who rely upon the excuse of an unlawful privilege and maintain that this has been permitted them by the old law are to know that, by the authority of the Apostolic See, they have been removed from every ecclesiastical honor which they have used unworthily. Nor can they ever handle the venerable mysteries, from which they themselves have deprived themselves while greedily pursuing obscene desires.

And because present examples forewarn us to take care for the future, if any bishop, presbyter, or deacon should hereafter—what we do not desire—be found to be such, let him understand already that every avenue of indulgence through us has been barred to him: wounds which have not felt the remedy of poultices must necessarily be cut away with the knife. [Col. 0398C]

[Note: [Col. 0397] “through ignorance”: Hispana collection—“ignorantly”: Isidore Mercator.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] “to which”: Böhm.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] “reduced”: “discovered”: original.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] “and maintain”: Hispana collection.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] “handle”: collected editions, first Basel.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] “ministries”: Basel edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] “from which”: collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] “themselves”: Basel edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] “or”: collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0397] “do not feel”: the same editions.]

**Part III. Gratian.** Those who are ordered to be deposed because of sins may, after worthy penance, be restored to their rank.

Accordingly, in the Irish Council [Note: [Col. 0397D] *Irish:* This chapter used to be cited from the Council of Gangra, where it is found. It has been corrected from *Polycarpus* and another very ancient manuscript book containing many penitential canons, in which this is cited from Theodore, archbishop of Ireland.] [Note: [Col. 0397] It is quite certain that these matters do not belong to the Irish Synod. Anselm appears to have given Gregory, author of the *Polycarpus* (book 4, title 39), the occasion for the error. For at the end of his book 8, after c. 2 of Causa 9, Question 2, and the final chapter of Distinction 6, *On Penance*, which are alleged from the Irish Council, he introduces the following preface: “Among other enactments made concerning the order of the holy churches, the holy Irish Synod, over which Leo, bishop of the Holy Roman Church, presided in the time of Charles, king of the Franks, together with Theodore, bishop of the English and Irish, and many other bishops of those regions, said thus concerning the fall of priests.” There follow the words: “But also this in every penance,” etc. Accordingly, in view of human frailty, if a priest, at the devil’s prompting, falls into fornication and, by God’s mercy, has recourse to the remedy of penance, he will be purified over four years in this manner, etc. When these are completed, under the heading “Likewise,” the chapter now in question is finally produced. Yet at the time of the Irish Synod the Pseudo-Isidorian collection employed by the author of this chapter had not yet appeared, and it is not plausible that the same synod proposed different modes of penitence for the same crime to priests—that is, presbyters. Therefore it seems to us, and to them, that this chapter was taken from some penitential book.] we read:

### C. V. What penance is to be imposed upon a priest convicted of fornication.

If a presbyter has committed fornication, although according to the canons of the Apostles he ought to be deposed, nevertheless, by the authority of blessed Pope Silvester, if he does not persist in the vice but has voluntarily confessed it and added the desire to rise again, he is to do penance for ten years in the following manner.

For three months he is to remain apart from the others in a private place, using bread and water from evening to evening; only on Sundays and principal feasts is he to be refreshed with a little wine, small fish, and vegetables, without meat, the fat of sheep, or cheese. Clothed in sackcloth, he is to remain on the ground and continually implore, day and night, the mercy of almighty God.

[Col. 0399A]

[Note: [Col. 0399] “but if by his own [impulse]”: collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0399] “in a private place”: absent from the Basel edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 0399] “only”: absent from the Basel edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 0399] “blood”: collected editions, first Paris and Lyons II–III editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0399C] *And cheese:* In the printed editions there followed, except in the Argentinensis and Basel editions, the word “use.” It has been removed on the authority of almost all manuscript copies of Gratian, of *Polycarpus*, and of the manuscript book identified in the preceding note.]

When the three continuous months have ended, he may leave; nevertheless, he is not to appear in public, lest the flock of the faithful suffer scandal because of him. For a priest ought not to perform penance publicly as a layperson does.

Afterward, when he has recovered his strength somewhat, he is to complete one year and a half on bread and water, except Sundays [Col. 0399B] and principal feasts, on which he may use wine, the fat of sheep, and cheese in accordance with the canonical measure. When the first year and a half has ended, he is to partake of the body and blood of the Lord, lest he become hardened; he is to be restored to peace; he is to sing the psalms last in the choir with the brothers; he is not to approach the corner of the altar; and, in accordance with the words of blessed Clement, he is to perform lesser offices.

[Note: [Col. 0399] Added: “prison”: Basel edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 0399] Added: “days”: collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0399] “feasts”: the same editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0399] “blood”: Argentinensis, Venice I–II, Nuremberg, Lyons I editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0399] Cf. Distinction 81, c. 19.]

Then, until the completion of the seventh year, he is to fast throughout the year, except during Eastertide, on three lawful weekdays of every week, with bread and water. When the seven-year cycle has been completed, if his fellow brothers, among whom he has done penance, approve his worthy penance, the bishop may restore him to his former honor by the authority of blessed Pope Callixtus.

[Col. 0400A]

[Note: [Col. 0399] “his brothers”: collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0399] “have praised”: the same editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0399] Epistle 2.]

It should certainly be known that he may redeem the second weekday, if necessary, by singing one psalter or giving one denarius to the poor. But after the seven years are finished, until the end of the tenth year he is to observe the sixth weekday on bread and water, with no redemption intervening.

[Note: [Col. 0399] “if necessary”: “a laborer”: *Polycarpus*—Argentinensis edition.]

[Col. 0400B]

§ 1. The same penance is also to apply to a priest for all other sins and crimes that lead to his deposition. Nor should this seem burdensome to anyone, if a priest who has fallen, after doing worthy penance as stated above, is restored to his former honors.

## DISTINCTION LXXXIII

[Col. 0399]

[Col. 0399B] **GRATIAN**

**Part I.** Care must also be taken that a man chosen for ordination, even though he appears free from his own vice, is not defiled by consenting to the vices of others. For as Pope Symmachus says: “There is no great difference whether you inflict death or permit it. For one is proved to inflict death upon the sick who does not prevent it when he can.” [Col. 0399C]

[Note: [Col. 0399] From Ennodius’s pamphlet in defense of Symmachus.]

Hence Gregory VII says in the Register, book VI, c. 12, of the Roman Synod celebrated in the year of the Lord 1080 [Note: [Col. 0399] Berthold of Constance reports this council in full under A.D. 1078.—Anselm, book 6, c. 177 (174).], or 1078:

### C. I. A bishop who consents to the fornication of his clerics is to be suspended from office.

If any bishop, for a price or through entreaties, consents to the fornication of presbyters, [Col. 0400B] deacons, or subdeacons, or to the crime of incest in his parish; or if, once it has been committed and made known to him, he does not oppose it by the authority of his office, he is to be suspended from office.

[Note: [Col. 0399] “fornication … crime”: original text—Böhm.]  
[Note: [Col. 0399C] *Subdeacons:* This has been added from the original and from Anselm, as have, a little later, the words “and made known to him.” It is known that from the time of Gregory I subdeacons were bound by the same law of continence as presbyters.]  
[Note: [Col. 0399] These words are absent from Berthold.]

[Col. 0400C]

### C. II. He who sins under the name of holiness does the greatest harm to the Church. Likewise Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, Part I, c. 2.

[Note: [Col. 0399] In the collected editions these words are cited from Augustine. Burchard, book 1, c. 209. Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, c. 323. *Polycarpus*, book 4, title 31.]

No one in the Church does more harm than one who acts perversely while bearing the name or rank of holiness. No one dares to rebuke such a delinquent, and the fault spreads vigorously as an example when the sinner is honored out of reverence for his rank.

A bishop, therefore, who does not correct the crimes of such men [Col. 0401A] is more properly called an impudent dog than a bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0399] Added: “of God”: collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0399] Added: “and priesthoods”: the same editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0400C] *A bishop:* These words are not found there in blessed Gregory. Similar statements are cited below, Causa 2, Question 7, c. *Qui nec regiminis*, from Augustine, to whom the remainder of this chapter was formerly attributed; Burchard and Ivo also cite them from Augustine. However, those same collectors—Burchard in book 1, c. 13, and Ivo in part 5, c. 67—report some passages from Origen that agree to some extent with these.]  
[Note: [Col. 0399] Burchard, book 1, c. 203. Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, c. 317 (from Gregory). The complete canon is also found in Alger, *On Mercy and Justice*, Martène, *Thesaurus*, vol. V, c. 20.]

### C. III. He who does not resist errors consents to them. Likewise Innocent.

[Note: [Col. 0401] Nearly the same words occur at the end of the Pseudo-Isidorian letter of Eleutherius; cf. c. 55, Causa 2, Question 7, taken from Felix III, Epistle 1.]

An error which is not resisted is approved, and truth, when it is not defended, is oppressed. To neglect to overthrow wicked men when you can do so is nothing other than to encourage them. Nor is one free of the guilt of secret complicity who ceases to oppose a manifest crime.

[Note: [Col. 0401] “overthrow”: “disturb”: collected editions.]

### C. IV. It does not help one not to be stained by one’s own error if one consents to another’s. Likewise Pius, Epistle I, to all Christ’s faithful.

[Note: [Col. 0401] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, repeated from Hormisdas, Epistle 25.]

For what does it profit a person not to be stained by his own error if he gives his consent to one who errs?

[Col. 0401B]

### C. V. He who does not intervene consents to the one who errs. Likewise Gregory.

[Note: [Col. 0401D] *Gregory:* These words are not found in the printed letters of blessed Gregory. But in book 7, epistle 117, to Syagrius, bishop of Autun, after the words “whoever has not resisted,” the following occurs in a very ancient manuscript Register and in *Polycarpus*, where the whole letter is reported: “For he seems to consent to the one who errs who does not intervene so that things requiring correction may be cut away.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0401] From the letter to Syagrius, written A.D. 549, epistle 113, book 9, Maurist edition.—*Polycarpus*, book 4, title 31.]

He seems to consent to the one who errs who does not intervene to cut away what ought to be corrected.

[Note: [Col. 0402C] “intervene”: “run together”: Maurist edition.]

**Gratian.** But just as he ought not to flatter the faults of others, neither should he delight in the praise of evil men. Hence Pope Anacletus, Epistle I, to all bishops [Note: [Col. 0401] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, whose sources have been identified as the letter of the bishops of Tours (Mansi, vol. 9, p. 808), Epistle 73 of Boniface, from the Wurdwein edition, and Ennodius, *Dicta*, book 8, c. 11.—Anselm, book 6, c. 154 (151). Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, c. 237]:

### C. VI. The most wretched bishop is one who glories in the praise of evil men.

[Col. 0402A] Nothing is more wretched than the shepherd who glories in the praise of wolves. If he wishes to please them and chooses to be loved by them, great destruction will thereby come upon the sheep. Therefore no shepherd can please both wolves and flocks of sheep. For a mind bound in the prisons of earthly things loses remembrance of lips (*labiorum*). Just as diligence is found to be the mother of the arts in each work, so negligence is the stepmother of learning.

[Note: [Col. 0402D] *Of lips:* The letter of Anacletus reads “of labor”; Anselm and one old manuscript of Gratian read “of labors.” Thus the corruption may have entered, although it has not been removed because of the gloss.]  
[Note: [Col. 0401] Added: “however”: collected editions.]

**Part II. Gratian.** Although a priest ought to be free both from his own crimes and from those of others, nevertheless, if he has behaved otherwise, the words of his preaching ought not for that reason to be despised. For as Jerome says [Note: [Col. 0401] Cf. Burchard, book 1, c. 204.
