Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, c. 318]: just as lye flowing through damp ashes washes but is not washed, so sound teaching through an evil teacher washes the souls of believers from the filth of sins.

## DISTINCTION LXXXIV

[Col. 0401]

[Col. 0401B] **GRATIAN**

**Part I.** A bishop must also be diligent and watchful in defending the poor, relieving the oppressed, and protecting monasteries. If he neglects to do this, he must be severely rebuked.

[Col. 0401C]

Accordingly, Gregory, to Anthemius, subdeacon of Campania, Book XI, Epistle 29 [Note: [Col. 0401] Epistle 26, written A.D. 603, book 13, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 6, c. 188]:

### C. I. A bishop negligent in his office is to be rebuked.

It has come to us that our brother and fellow bishop Paschasius is so slothful and negligent in everything that in no respect is he recognized as a bishop. Thus neither his church nor the monasteries, nor the children of the Church, nor oppressed poor persons experience his loving care toward them. Nor does he give the just aid of defense to persons petitioning him against injustice. And, what is still more serious to say, he permits himself for no reason to accept the counsels of the wise and of those who urge what is right, so that what he cannot attend to by himself he may at least learn from another. [Col. 0401D]

And below: If this is so, know that you too are not without fault, since you have delayed to rebuke and restrain him as is fitting. Because, then, all this not only disgraces him but is also shown to bring reproach upon the priestly office, [Col. 0402C] we desire that you should summon him before the other priests and certain noble members of his flock, formally charge him on this matter, and exhort him. But if, after this our exhortation—which we do not believe—he should still attempt to be negligent after his accustomed manner, he must by every means be sent to us, so that, being here, he may learn what and how a priest ought to act according to the fear of God.

[Note: [Col. 0401] “children of the Church”: absent from Anselm and from the better manuscripts of Gregory.]  
[Note: [Col. 0401] “or oppressed poor”: “or poor”: collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0401] “to him”: “to them”: original.]  
[Note: [Col. 0401] “still”: absent from the collected editions, first Basel edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 0401] The words enclosed in asterisks are likewise absent from Anselm.]  
[Note: [Col. 0401] Added: “therefore”: collected editions from Anselm.]  
[Note: [Col. 0401] “our”: “your”: collected editions.]

### C. II. On the same matter. The same to the same person, same book, Epistle 33.

[Note: [Col. 0401] Epistle 27, written A.D. 603, book 13, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 6, c. 189.]

We have been informed that the bishops of Campania are so negligent that, forgetful of their rank, they show no care of fatherly vigilance toward either the churches or their children, nor do they take thought for monasteries or devote themselves to the protection of oppressed and poor persons. Therefore, by this authority, we command you, after summoning them, strictly to admonish them in our name that they must no longer be negligent, but must show by their deeds that they possess priestly zeal and diligence; and that they must be so watchful in those things which it is right for them to do according to God that no fresh complaint concerning them may provoke us.

If, after this, you find any of them to be negligent, send him to us without any excuse, so that he may experience in the discipline applied to himself how serious it is to refuse correction in matters that are blameworthy and highly deserving of reproach.

[Note: [Col. 0403] “or”: collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0403] Added: “them”: the same editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0403] “negligent”: absent also from the Anselm collection.]

**Part II. Gratian.** What is commanded to priests concerning the purity of chastity must also be understood concerning all who serve at the altar.

Accordingly, in the Second Council of Carthage, c. 2, Bishop Aurelius is recorded as having said [Note: [Col. 0403] Held A.D. 390.—The canon is taken from Dionysius, among whose canons it is presented as one established under Aurelius in A.D. 419.—*Collectio tripartita*, part 2, title 19, c. 3]:

### C. III. Those who serve the divine sacraments must preserve continence in all things.

When, at the previous council, the rule of continence and chastity was under discussion, these three ranks—bishops, that is, presbyters, and deacons—were by a certain enactment bound to chastity through their consecrations. It was resolved that, as befits holy bishops and priests of God, and likewise Levites, or those who serve the divine sacraments, they should be continent in all things, so that they may simply obtain what they ask from God, and that we too may preserve what the apostles taught and antiquity itself observed.

All the bishops said: “It pleases everyone that bishops, presbyters, and deacons, or those who handle the sacraments, should be guardians of chastity and abstain even from their wives.” All said: “It pleases us that chastity be observed in all things and by all who serve at the altar.”

[Note: Col. 0403: *sanctos*, “holy”: the older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0403: Compare Distinction 31, canon 3.]

[Note: Col. 0403: *Domino*, “the Lord”: the older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0403C: *Docuerunt*, “taught”: in the commonly printed codices there followed—except in the Basel edition—“by example”; this has been removed because it occurs neither in the Second Council of Carthage, printed or manuscript, nor in the sole codex of canons which agrees with the Greek canon, nor in old exemplars of Gratian; it seems to have been transferred from the gloss into the text.]

[Note: Col. 0403: “or”: the older collected editions.—Canon IV.]

When the incontinence of certain clerics, even toward their own wives, was reported, it was resolved that bishops, presbyters, and deacons should, in accordance with the earlier decrees, also abstain from their wives. If they do not do so, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office. Other clerics, however, are not to be compelled to this, but the custom of each church is to be observed.

[Note: Col. 0403: *priorum*, “of the earlier [decrees]”: Hispana Collection.]

[Note: Col. 0403: Omitted in the same.]

### Gratian, Part III

Likewise, since a bishop is commanded to be the husband of one wife, this requirement must also be extended to the remaining ecclesiastical orders.

[Col. 0404B] Hence Pope Siricius, in his first letter to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, chapter 11:

## Canon V. A cleric who takes a widow or a second wife is to be content with lay communion alone.

Whoever among the clergy takes a widow, or indeed a second wife, is immediately to be stripped of every privilege of ecclesiastical rank, with lay communion alone granted to him. He can retain even this only if thereafter he commits nothing for which he ought to lose it.

[Note: Col. 0403: Written A.D. 385.—Anselm, book 8, canon 5; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, canon 51.]

[Note: Col. 0403: *uxorem*, “wife”: the older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0403: *denudetur*, “be stripped”: the same editions, from Anselm.]

[Note: Col. 0403: “for which he ought to be deprived of it”: the same editions.]

### Gratian, Part IV

Although the name “presbyter” is derived from old age, it signifies maturity of wisdom rather than grayness of body.

Hence Anacletus, in his second letter to the bishops of Italy:

## Canon VI. Presbyters are called elders not so much because of age as because of wisdom.

[Col. 0404C] Moreover, Moses is commanded to choose presbyters, that is, elders. Hence it is said in Proverbs: “Gray hair is the glory of old men.” But this grayness signifies wisdom, of which it is written: “Prudence is the gray hair of humankind.” Since we read that human beings lived nine hundred years and more from Adam to Abraham, no one before Abraham was called presbyter—that is, elder—although Abraham is shown to have lived far fewer years. Therefore presbyters are so called not because of decrepit old age, but because of wisdom.

[Note: Col. 0403: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter derived from Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book 2, chapter 5.—Burchard, book 2, canon 5; Anselm, book 7, canon 96 (100); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, canon 25.]

[Note: Col. 0403: “that is”: these words are not in the original.]

[Note: Col. 0403: Proverbs 20:29.]

[Note: Col. 0403: *hic*, “this”: older collected editions, before Venice II and Norimberga.]

[Note: Col. 0403: Wisdom 4:8.]

[Note: Col. 0403: *nongentis … annis*, “nine hundred … years”: the older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0403: *legamus*, “we read”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0405: *aetatem*, “age”: the same editions.]

# DISTINCTION LXXXV

[Col. 0405A] **GRATIAN**

Hospitality is so necessary for bishops that, if they are found lacking it, they are rightly forbidden to be ordained.

Hence Gregory writes to John, bishop, book XII, letter 6:

## Canon I. One ignorant of hospitality is not to become a bishop.

We have learned that the archdeacon of the church of Ancona, who was elected to the episcopate, possesses knowledge of Holy Scripture, but is already so worn out by old age that he cannot rise to the duty of government. We have also learned that he is so miserly that no friend ever enters his house for the sake of fellowship. Rustic, a deacon of the same church who was likewise elected, is said to be an alert man, but, as is asserted, he does not know the psalms. We know that Florentius, a deacon of the church of Ravenna who is said to have been elected by all, is conscientious; but we do not know at all what he is inwardly like.

Therefore let your fraternity hasten to go there with our brother and fellow-bishop Armenius, visitor of the aforesaid church of Ancona, and carefully inquire into the character of each: whether they are conscious of no crime that bars them from assuming this office. You must also inquire whether the report concerning the aforesaid archdeacon—that no friend has ever entered his house—is true, and whether he is such from necessity or from miserliness; whether he is so old that he cannot rise to govern; or whether, as has been reported to us, after touching the holy Gospels he has sworn never to undertake the episcopate.

You must also investigate how many psalms Deacon Rustic fails to know. As for Florentius, the deacon of Ravenna, if there is, as we have said, no crime to impede him, it is necessary to deal with his bishop so that he may permit him to depart—though not by our command or direction, lest he seem to grant the departure against his own will.

[Note: Col. 0405: Letter 11, written A.D. 604, book 14, Maurist edition.]

[Note: Col. 0405: *contractum*, “contracted/weakened”: the original.]

[Note: Col. 0405: *Florentinum*, “Florentine”: the original and older collected editions.]

# DISTINCTION LXXXVI

[Col. 0405C] **GRATIAN**

### Part I

A bishop ought to be a teacher, lest the faults of those below be charged against him who has received the office of teaching but does not know how, or neglects, to carry it out.

Hence Bishop Leo writes to the bishop of Aquileia, letters III and LXXXIV, or LXXXVI:

## Canon I. The faults of those below are imputed to negligent rulers.

The faults of lower orders are to be attributed to none more than to idle and negligent rulers, who often nourish a great plague while they neglect to apply a harsher remedy.

[Note: Col. 0405: Letter to Septimus of Aquileia, written A.D. 442; Ballerini edition, letter 1.—Anselm, book 6, canon 155 (152). The same words occur in the letter to Januarius, letter 18, Ballerini edition.]

[Note: Col. 0405D: *Austeriorem*, “harsher”: this is the reading in letter 84. But in Leo’s letter 3 the reading is *necessariam*, “necessary.” The rest is the same in both.]

## Canon II. Human beings are to be loved; sin is to be hated.

Likewise Bishop Leo, to Rustic, bishop of Narbonne, letter XC, or XCII, at the beginning:

Sins are to be hated, not human beings. The proud are to be rebuked; the weak are to be endured. Whatever in sins must be punished more severely is to be punished not with the mind of one raging, but of one healing.

[Note: Col. 0405: Letter 167, written A.D. 458 or 459, Ballerini edition.]

## Canon III. Whoever neglects to correct what he can bears the guilt of the doer.

Likewise John VIII:

Beyond doubt, one who neglects to amend what he is able to correct bears the guilt of the doer. For it is written: “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are judged participants.” § 1. One offers good things to the Lord who drives adversities away from the afflicted. To neglect, when you can cast down the perverse, is nothing other than to encourage them. Nor is one free from the scruple of secret consent when he ceases to oppose an open crime. One proves that he hates vices by condemning those who err. One who does not spare the transgressor leaves him no room to stray. The first degree of innocence is to hate abominable things. One who joins consent to wickedness opens a wide entrance to offenders. And it profits no one not to be punished for his own sin if he must be punished for another’s.

[Note: Col. 0405D–0406D: This chapter was compiled from various sayings gathered from different places. The first, down to the word “amend,” is taken from Blessed Gregory’s letter 114, book VII, indiction 2, to Theuderic and Theudebert, kings of the Franks.]

[Note: Col. 0405: An uncertain fragment.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, canon 115.—Compare Distinction 83, canons 3, 4, 5.]

[Note: Col. 0405: Romans 1:32.]

[Note: Col. 0405: *libet*, “is pleasing”: Basel edition.]

### Gratian, Part II

But if anyone exceeds the proper measure in rebuking, he should seek pardon not from his subjects but from the Lord.

Hence Augustine, *On the Life of Clerics*:

## Canon IV. One who has exceeded the proper measure in rebuking should not seek pardon from his subjects.

When the necessity of discipline compels you to speak harsh words in restraining those under you, even if you yourselves perceive that you have exceeded the proper measure, you are not required to seek pardon from them, lest, among those who ought to be subject to you, the authority of governing be broken by the observance of excessive humility. Yet pardon must be sought from the Lord of all, who knows with how much goodwill you love even those whom perhaps you rebuke more severely than is just.

[Note: Col. 0407D–0408D: *On the Life*: among the minor works of Blessed Augustine printed at Parma in A.D. 1481 are three sermons on the common life of clerics. Two of these appear in the commonly printed volumes of Augustine’s works, volume 10, as sermons 52 and 53, *To the Brethren in the Desert*. The third agrees entirely with letter 109, except that in the letter it is addressed to monks, while in the sermon it is addressed to men. Gratian took many chapters from these three sermons on the common life of clerics, as will be noted in their places; this one is from the third.]

[Note: Col. 0407: Rather, from Augustine’s letter to Seleucianus.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, canon 384.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *in moribus*, “in conduct”: older collected editions, from Ivo.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *in ipsis*, “in them”: original and Ivo.]

[Note: Col. 0407: “that you seek pardon from your subjects”: older collected editions; “that you from your subjects”: Ivo.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *subditos*, “subject”: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *nimium*, “excessively”: older collected editions, from Ivo.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *et tamen*, “and yet”: older collected editions.]

### Gratian, Part III

In teaching Sacred Scripture, however, a bishop should give priority to its authority, not display expertise in secular letters. For it is not the office of a bishop to expound grammar, lest praises of Jupiter resound from a pontiff’s mouth.

Hence Gregory writes to Bishop Desiderius, book IX, letter 48:

## Canon V. A bishop ought to expound Sacred Scripture, not grammar.

When many good things had been reported to us concerning your studies, such joy arose in our heart that we were by no means able to refuse what your fraternity requested should be granted. But afterwards there reached us a report—which we cannot mention without shame—that you expound grammar to certain persons. We received this matter so painfully and rejected it so vehemently that we turned what had formerly been said into groaning and sorrow, because the praises of Christ cannot be contained in one mouth together with the praises of Jupiter. Consider for yourself how grave and wicked it is for bishops to sing what is not fitting even for a religious layman.

[Note: Col. 0407: Letter 54, written A.D. 601, book 11, Maurist edition.—Burchard, book 1, canon 97; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, canon 161, and part 6, canon 199.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *innata*, “inborn”: older collected editions, before Basel.]

[Note: Col. 0407C: *deposcit*, “demands”: older collected editions; *poposcerat*, “had requested”: Ivo with the original.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *fuerant*, “had been”: the same editions, with the original and Ivo.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *vestram*, “your [plural]”: older collected editions.]

### Gratian, Part IV

A priest must also be liberal toward those suffering need; otherwise he bears the empty name of bishop.

[Col. 0408A] Hence Gregory writes in book V, letter 29, among other things to Secundinus, servant of God:

## Canon VI. Without liberality the name of bishop is borne in vain.

Rouse our brother Marinianus, bishop, by whatever words you can, for I suspect that he has fallen asleep. And below: Tell him, then, that he should change both place and mind. Let him not believe that reading and prayer alone suffice, so that he may strive to sit apart and bring forth no fruit from his hand. Rather, let him have a generous hand; let him come to the aid of those suffering need; let him regard another’s poverty as his own. For if he does not have these things, he bears the empty name of bishop.

[Note: Col. 0407: Letter 30, written A.D. 596, book 6, Maurist edition.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *Maurianum*: Basel edition; *Marianum*: the remaining collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0407: “Tell him, that when”: older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *nec*, “nor”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0407: “that he strive to sit apart and bear no fruit from his hand”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *hoc*, “this”: the same editions.]

### Gratian, Part V

In liberality itself, moreover, regard must be had for things and persons: for things, so that not everything is given to one person, but something to each, in order that we may benefit more people, according to the Prophet’s saying: “He has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor”; for persons, so that gifts are given first to the righteous and then to sinners—though we are forbidden to give to the latter not because they are human beings, but because they are sinners.

Hence Augustine, tractate C on John, chapter 16:

## Canon VII. It is an enormous sin to give one’s property to actors.

To give one’s property to actors is an enormous vice, not a virtue. And you know how frequently such people are publicly praised, because, as it is written, “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the worker of iniquity is blessed.”

[Note: Col. 0407: Ivo, *Decretum*, part 11, canon 84.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *sed*, “but”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.]

[Note: Col. 0407: Psalm 9:3.]

[Col. 0408C]

## Canon VIII. Those who give anything to a hunter sin grievously.

The same, on Psalm CII, at the verse “Who performs mercies”:

Those who give to hunters—why do they give? Tell me: why do they give to a hunter? They love in him that by which he is most wicked; they nourish in him that; they clothe in him that; they display that very wickedness publicly in spectacles before all. Those who give to actors, charioteers, and prostitutes—why do they give? Do they not also give to human beings? Yet in this they do not consider the nature of God’s work, but the wickedness of human work.

[Note: Col. 0407: Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, canon 31.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *publicant*, “publicly display”: older collected editions, before Basel.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *hominum*, “of human beings”: older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *ipsa*, “the things themselves”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0407: *donantur*, “are given”: Lyons II and III editions.]

[Col. 0409A]

## Canon IX. On the same subject.

The same, in the same place a little further on:

Those who give to hunters do not give to a human being, but to a most wicked trade. For if he were merely a human being and not a hunter, you would not give to him; in him you honor vice, not nature.

[Note: Col. 0409: Ivo, same place.]

[Note: Col. 0409: *tribuit … donat*, “bestows … gives”: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 0409: Add *ei*, “to him”: older collected editions.]

## Canon X. On the same subject.

The same, on Psalm CXLVI:

People see a hunter and delight in him. Woe to the wretched, if they do not correct themselves. For those who see a hunter and delight in him will see the Savior and grieve.

[Note: Col. 0409: Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, canon 34.]

[Note: Col. 0409: *venatores*, “hunters”: older collected editions.]

## Canon XI. On the same subject.

Likewise Jerome, on Psalm XC, at the verse “I shall hope in the Lord”:

Esau was a hunter because he was a sinner. And nowhere do we find in the Holy Scriptures any holy hunter; we find holy fishermen.

[Note: Col. 0409: These words do not belong to Jerome.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, canon 33.]

[Col. 0409B]

## Canon XII. On the same subject.

Likewise Ambrose, homily XXXIII, on Lent:

What does it profit to fast in one’s belly and revel in hunting? To abstain from food and to wander in sins?

[Note: Col. 0409: The Maurist Fathers attribute this canon and the next to Caesarius of Arles in their edition of Augustine’s works.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, canon 31.]

[Note: Col. 0409: *luxuriari*, “to revel”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0409: “from foods and”: the same editions.]

## Canon XIII. On the same subject.

The same, in the same place a little further on:

Do you think, brothers, that the man fasts who, at first light, does not keep vigil at church and does not seek out the holy places of the blessed martyrs, but rises, assembles his servants, sets out nets, brings forth dogs, and ranges through glades and forests? He drags along with him, I say, servants perhaps more eager to hasten to church, and by his pleasures heaps upon himself others’ sins, not knowing that he will be guilty both of his own fault and of the destruction of his servants.

[Note: Col. 0409: Ivo, same place.]

[Col. 0409C]

## Canon XIV. What must be observed in liberality.

Likewise Ambrose, book I, *On Duties*, chapter 30:

It is not enough to wish well; one must also act well. Nor, again, is it enough to act well unless this proceeds from a good source—that is, from a good will. And below: § 1. Perfect liberality is commended by faith, cause, place, and time, so that you act first toward members of the household of faith. It is a grave fault if, with your knowledge, a believer is in need; if you know that he lacks means, endures hunger, suffers distress—especially if he is ashamed to be needy—if he has fallen into a case involving captivity of his own or of his children, or a false accusation, and you do not help him; if he is in prison and, though righteous, is tormented with punishments and tortures on account of some debt. For although mercy is owed to all, it is owed more abundantly to the righteous. If in the time of his affliction he obtains nothing from you; if, at the time of peril, when he is being carried away to death, your money is worth more to you than the life of one dying—this is no light sin.

[Note: Col. 0409: Anselm, book 13, canon 28; Polycarpus, book 6, title 20.]

[Note: Col. 0409D: From “It is not enough” down to the chapter beginning “But if anything,” certain old exemplars of Gratian and Anselm have a single chapter.]

[Note: Col. 0409: Add *procedat*, “proceeds”: older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0409: *operetur*, “may he act”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0409: “and endure hunger”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0409: *erubescit*, “is ashamed”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0409: “his own captivity or that of his children”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0409: Add *positus*, “placed”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0409: Add *sui*, “his own”: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 0409D: “This is no light sin”: these words are not found there in Ambrose, but are found in Anselm and Polycarpus.]

## Canon XV. On the same subject.

The same, in the same place a little further on:

The Lord does not wish wealth to be poured out all at once, but to be distributed, unless perhaps one is like Elisha, who killed his oxen and fed the poor from what he possessed, so that he might be held by no domestic concern, but, leaving all things, devote himself to prophetic discipline.

[Note: Col. 0409: Anselm and Polycarpus, same place.]

[Note: Col. 0409: Compare 3 Kings 19.]

## Canon XVI. On the same subject.

The same, continuously in the same place:

That liberality too is to be approved by which you do not despise those close to you by blood when you know them to be in need. For it is better that you yourself assist your own people, who are ashamed to ask support from others or to request aid for necessity from anyone else. Yet this should not be so that they want to become richer from what you could contribute to the needy; for natural obligation takes precedence over favor. You have not dedicated yourself to the Lord in order to make your own people rich, but in order to acquire everlasting life for yourself through the fruit of good work and redeem your sins by the price of compassion. Do they think they ask too little? They seek your reward; they strive to take away the fruit of your life, and accuse you because you have not made them rich, although they wish to defraud you of the recompense of eternal life.

[Note: Col. 0409: Anselm and Polycarpus, same place.]

[Note: Col. 0409: *et alia*, “and another”: older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0409: *ne*, “lest”: the same editions, before Lyons II and III.]

[Note: Col. 0409: *petere*, “to seek”: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 0409: *necessitatis*, “of necessity”: older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0409: *ex eo*, “from it”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0409: *potes*, “are able”: Böhmer.]

[Note: Col. 0410D: At Ambrose the reading is “for the cause takes precedence, not favor,” and the same is found in Anselm and Polycarpus. But old codices of Gratian and the gloss agree with the printed editions. Some other passages have been corrected from Ambrose himself.]

[Note: Col. 0409: “you have dedicated yourself to God”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0409: *illos*, “them”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0409: *praemium*, “reward”: the same editions, before Basel.]

[Note: Col. 0409: Böhmer adds, against manuscript and printed codices: “and they think they act justly.”]

## Canon XVII. On the same subject.

The same, in the same place a little further on:

In giving, age and weakness must also be considered, and sometimes modesty, which shows an honorable birth; so that you may give more generously to old people, who can no longer obtain sustenance for themselves by labor. Bodily weakness likewise should be helped more promptly; and so also if someone has fallen from wealth into poverty, especially if he has lost what he had not through his own fault, but through robbery, proscription, or false accusations.

[Note: Col. 0409: Anselm and Polycarpus, same place.]

[Note: Col. 0409: “promptly to be helped”: older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0409: *quum*, “when”: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 0411: “if not without”: older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0411: *praescriptione*, “prescription”: older collected editions.]

## Canon XVIII. On the same subject.

The same, book II of *On Duties*, chapter 21:

It is also a fine liberality to keep measure even in what is given to the poor, so that you may have enough for more people and not overflow beyond measure for the sake of gaining favor. Whatever is promised from pure and sincere affection is honorable. Do not undertake superfluous buildings, nor neglect necessary ones. This especially befits a priest: to adorn God’s temple with fitting honor, so that by this worship too the Lord’s hall may shine; to make fitting expenditures of mercy; to give to strangers as much as ought to be given—not superfluous things, but appropriate ones, and so forth.

The same: § 1. Let us have compassion on others’ calamities; let us help others’ necessities as much as we can, and sometimes more than we can. For it is better, for the sake of mercy, to lend one’s support to causes or endure envy than to put forward cruelty as an excuse. Thus we ourselves at times incurred envy when we broke up sacred vessels in order to ransom captives.

[Note: Col. 0411: Anselm and Polycarpus, same place.]

[Note: Col. 0411D: At Ambrose the reading is: “It is a fine liberality to keep measure even toward the poor themselves.” But Anselm and Polycarpus read as Gratian does, and there is a gloss on the word *dato*, “gift.”]

[Note: Col. 0411: *nec*, “nor”: older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0411: Add *enim*, “for”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0411: *promittitur*, “is promised”: the same editions, before Lyons II and III.]

[Note: Col. 0411: *sacerdotibus*, “priests”: older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0411: “superfluous … appropriate”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0411: Add *itaque*, “therefore”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0411: *ut* is absent from the Basel edition; the remaining collected editions read “and we.”]

[Note: Col. 0411: “we” is absent from the Argentinensis edition.]

## Canon XIX. On the same subject.

The same, on Luke chapter 3, at the verse “Brood of vipers”:

Saint John the Baptist gave an answer suited to each class of people: to tax collectors, that they should exact nothing beyond what was prescribed; to soldiers, that they should commit no extortion and seek no plunder. Thus he taught that military pay is fixed in order that, while provisions are sought, the robber may not rage abroad. But these and other precepts of duty belong severally to particular persons; mercy has a common use. Therefore it is a common precept, necessary to all occupations and all ages, and to be observed by all. Neither tax collector nor soldier is excluded; neither farmer nor townsman, rich or poor: all are jointly admonished to give to one who has not. For mercy is the fullness of virtues, and therefore a model of perfect virtue is set before all, so that they do not spare their clothing and food. Yet a measure of mercy itself must be observed according to the capacity of the human condition, so that no one strips everything from himself, but shares what he has with the poor.

[Note: Col. 0411: *calumnias*, “extortions”: older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0411: Add *sunt*, “are”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0411: *misericordiae*, “of mercy”: the same editions.]

[Col. 0412A]

## Canon XX. On the same subject.

The same, on Luke chapter 18:

Moreover, it is God’s ordinance that you first feed your parents. For if, according to the divine oracle, dishonoring a parent is punished by death, how much more [serious is] hunger, which is worse than death? At this point the Lord restrains insolent boasting, and so forth.

[Note: Col. 0411: Leviticus 20; Exodus 21; Matthew 15.]

## Canon XXI. On the same subject.

The same, in the book *On Duties*:

Feed the person dying of hunger. For whoever could save a human being by feeding him and did not feed him, has killed him.

[Note: Col. 0412D–0413C: This chapter is not found in Blessed Ambrose, but it is cited from him in Anselm and Polycarpus. [Note: Col. 0411: Anselm, book 13, canon 28.]

[Note: Col. 0411: *poteris*, “will be able”: older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0411: *paveris*, “will have fed”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 0411: Add *fame*, “by hunger”: the same editions, before Basel.]

## Canon XXII. On the same subject.

Likewise Jerome, in his commentary on Galatians, chapter 6, at the verse “Bear one another’s [burdens]”:

One who does not have compassion and is not clothed with bowels of mercy and tears, even though spiritual, does not fulfill the law of Christ.

[Note: Col. 0411: *adimplebit*, “will fulfill”: the original.]

### Gratian, Part VI

Likewise, a bishop must not be a striker—that is, one readily given to vengeance.

Hence Gregory writes to John, bishop of Palermo, book XI, letter 49:

## Canon XXIII. A bishop ought not to be ready for vengeance.

If anything concerning any cleric reaches your ears that may justly offend you, do not readily believe it, nor let an unknown matter inflame you to vengeance. Rather, in the presence of the elders of your church, the truth must be carefully investigated; and then, if the character of the matter demands it, canonical severity should strike the fault of the offender.

[Note: Col. 0411: Letter 44, written A.D. 603, book 13, Maurist edition.—*Collectio Tripartita*, part 1, title 55, canon 15.—Compare Causa 15, question 7, canon 2.]

[Note: Col. 0411: *Corinthiorum*, “of the Corinthians”: older collected editions.]

## Canon XXIV. Concerning a bishop who, before celebrating the solemnities of Mass, went out on Sunday to plough up a certain person’s crop.

The same, to Januarius, bishop, book VII, indiction 2, letter 1:

Such great wickedness concerning your old age has reached my ears that, unless we still took human frailty into account, we would already have struck you with a definitive curse. For I have been told that on Sunday, before you celebrated the solemnities of Mass, you went to plough up the crop of the bearer of this letter; and after ploughing it up you celebrated the solemnities of Mass. After the Mass solemnities you did not fear to uproot the boundary markers of that estate. All who hear of it know what punishment ought to follow this deed.

We had been uncertain concerning such perversity; but when our son Cyriacus, abbot, was questioned by us, while he was at Cagliari, he declared that he knew it to be so. Since we still spare your gray hairs, we urge you: repent at last, wretched old man, and restrain yourself from such levity of conduct and perversity of deeds. The nearer you come to death, the more careful and fearful you ought to become. Indeed, a sentence of punishment ought to have been launched against you; but because we know your simplicity along with your old age, we are silent for the present.

But we decree that those by whose counsel you did these things are excommunicated for two months, provided that, should anything requiring human compassion befall them during that two-month period, they are not deprived of the blessing of viaticum. Henceforth be on your guard against their counsels. Guard yourself also carefully, lest, if you are their disciple in evil when you ought to have been their teacher in good, we spare neither your simplicity nor your old age any longer.

[Note: Col. 0411: Letter 1, written A.D. 599, book 9, Maurist edition.—Burchard, book 1, canon 197; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, canon 78, and part 8, canon 312.]

[Note: Col. 0413: *sequi*, “follow”: older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0413: *dum esset Caralis*, “while he was at Cagliari”; *choralis*, i.e. “regional officer”: Ivo.]

[Note: Col. 0413: “we urge: repent”: Ivo and Burchard, from the original.]

[Note: Col. 0413: *compescos*: original; *compescere*, “to restrain”: Ivo, Burchard, and the older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0413: *esse*, “to be”: older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0413: *decrevimus*, “we have decreed”: the older collected editions, before Lyons II and III.]

[Note: Col. 0413: *humanitatis*, “of humanity”: the older collected editions, before Basel.]

[Note: Col. 0413: The words which follow are omitted in the Argentinensis, Norimberga, and Venice II editions.]

### Gratian, Part VII

He is also forbidden to be a striker, namely, so that he does not beat anyone with his own hands.

Hence it is read in the Council of Agde:

## Canon XXV. A bishop may not beat anyone with his own hands.

It is not permitted for a bishop to strike anyone with his own hands. For this ought to be foreign to a priest.

[Note: Col. 0413C–0414C: This chapter is not found in the extant Council of Agde. Burchard and Ivo cite it from the decretals of Pope Boniface. It is found, however, in Novel 123, chapter 16, in Julian the Antecessor. Canon 28 of the Apostles is also similar; it is interpreted by the Constantinopolitan synod called the First-and-Second, chapter 9.]

[Note: Col. 0413: From Justinian, Novel 123, chapter 11.—Burchard, book 1, canon 202; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, canon 316.]

[Note: Col. 0413: *liceat*, “may be permitted”: older collected editions.]

[Col. 0414A]

### Gratian, Part VIII

A bishop is also forbidden to be desirous of shameful gain, so that he does not seek his livelihood or other necessities through any dishonorable business. This must be understood generally of all persons devoted to divine worship—that is, clerics and monks.

Hence it is read in the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 3:

## Canon XXVI. Those enrolled among the clergy are not to engage in shameful gains.

It has come to the holy synod that, among those enrolled in the clergy, some, for the sake of shameful gain, take leases of other persons’ estates and undertake secular cases; they separate themselves from sacred duties through negligence, but run to the houses of laypersons and, for the sake of greed, undertake administration of their property. Therefore the holy and great synod decreed that from now on none of these—that is, bishop, cleric, or monk—may lease estates or involve himself in secular administrations, unless he is unavoidably drawn by law into guardianships or curatorships for minors; or unless the bishop of that city entrusts him with the administration of ecclesiastical property, or with the care of orphans and widows who are defenseless, and of those persons who, for fear of God, especially need the Church’s assistance. But if anyone transgresses these decrees, he shall be subject to ecclesiastical correction.

[Note: Col. 0413: Held A.D. 451.—Burchard, book 2, canon 148; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, canon 218, from Dionysius.]

[Note: Col. 0413: *in*, “in”: Hispana Collection and Isidore Mercator.]

[Note: Col. 0413: *aliorum*, “of others”: Hispana Collection and older collected editions; *majorum*, “of superiors”: Isidore Mercator.]

[Note: Col. 0413: *saecularium*, “secular”: older collected editions; add *negotiorum*, “businesses”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]

[Note: Col. 0413: *sanctis ministeriis*, “holy ministries”: Hispana Collection and Isidore Mercator.]

[Note: Col. 0413: Add “and ecumenical”: older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0413: *miscere … posse*, “to involve … be able”: Hispana Collection; *misceri … posse*, “to be involved … be able”: older collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 0413: *possessionibus*, “estates”: Lyons II and III editions.]

# DISTINCTION LXXIX

[Col. 0421]

[Col. 0421C] **GRATIAN**

**I. Part.** A bishop ought also to preside well over his own household [Note: [Col. 0421] 1 Timothy 3:2], so that certain indications, as it were, of his future administration may be drawn from it. In administering the Church, moreover, he should know that this rule is to be observed: he is not to entrust two offices at once to any person, however experienced, nor entrust ecclesiastical affairs to secular men.

Hence Gregory writes to all bishops. [Note: [Col. 0421D–0422D] “Gregory”: collectors cite this chapter as though these were words from some letter of St Gregory. But John the Deacon, book 2 of the life of the same holy pontiff, no. 54, reports them thus: “He used to say that the individual offices of ecclesiastical law ought each to be entrusted separately to individual persons, affirming that, just as in one,” etc. Some matters have therefore been corrected from that source.] [Note: [Col. 0421] From John the Deacon’s *Life of Gregory the Great*, c. 54.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 108 (111); Ivo, *Decr.*, p. 6, c. 344; Polycarp, bk. 4, title 23.]

### C. I. Two offices are not to be entrusted to one person

We order that every office of ecclesiastical law be entrusted separately to individual persons. For as we have many members in one body, yet all the members do not have the same function, so in the body of the Church [Note: [Col. 0421] Anselm reads “in the Church.”], according to Paul’s truthful statement [Note: [Col. 0421] Romans 12], in one and the same spirit [Note: [Col. 0421] The collected editions read “spiritual body.”] one office is to be assigned to one person [Note: [Col. 0421] The same editions add “to one.”], another entrusted to another; nor [Note: [Col. 0421] The same editions add “for.”] should the offices of two matters be entrusted at one time to a single person, however experienced. For if the whole body is an eye, where is the hearing?

Just as variety among the members, through their different offices, both preserves the body’s strength and displays its beauty, so likewise variety among persons, distributed among different offices, manifests both the strength and loveliness of God’s holy Church. [Note: [Col. 0421] The Basel edition reads “established” instead of “distributed.”] And just as it is improper in a human body for one member to perform another’s office, so it is surely harmful and at the same time most disgraceful if the individual ministries of affairs have not been distributed among an equal number of persons.

### C. II. Every bishop is to have a *vicedominus* and an *oeconomus*. Likewise Gregory to Anthemius, subdeacon, book IX, letter 66

[Note: [Col. 0421] Letter 77, written A.D. 601, book 11, Maurist edition.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 145 (142); Polycarp, bk. 4, title 22.]

**II. Part.** We wish our brother Paschasius to appoint for himself both a *vicedominus* and a chief steward of the household, so that he may be capable and prepared both for guests who arrive and for cases that arise. But if you perceive him to be negligent and delaying the fulfilment of what we have said, the whole clergy must be called in, so that by common counsel they may choose for him [Note: [Col. 0421] The collected editions read “may choose bishops.”] persons who can be appointed to the matters aforesaid. [Note: [Col. 0423] Böhm reads “are able” instead of “may be able.”]

**Gratian.** From this [Note: [Col. 0423C] The words from “From this” as far as the sentence beginning “The office” are absent from most ancient copies and from the Basel edition.] it may be inferred that the election of an archdeacon can canonically be made by the whole clergy if the bishop has been negligent or dilatory. The office of the *vicedominus* is to administer the bishopric.

Hence Gregory, to Clementina the patrician, book I, letter 11, among other matters. [Note: [Col. 0423] Letter 11, written A.D. 591, book 1, Maurist edition.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 77.]

### C. III. What the office of the *vicedominus* is

As for the deacon Anatolius, whom you asked to be sent to you [Note: [Col. 0423] The collected editions, except the second and third Lyon editions, read “whom you asked us to send.”], it is the circumstances of the case, rather than the severity of strictness [Note: [Col. 0423] The collected editions read “authority” instead of “severity.”], that make us unable to do this. For we have appointed him *vicedominus* and entrusted the episcopal household to his judgment for administration. [Note: [Col. 0423] The Strasbourg, Nuremberg, first and second Venice, and Lyon editions, followed by Böhm, read “bishop” instead of “episcopal household.”]

### C. IV. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Chalcedon, canon 26

[Note: [Col. 0423C] The same canon is reported below, C. 16, q. 7, c. *Because in certain churches*, from Dionysius’s version. Here it is from the ancient—or rather Spanish—version, extant in Isidore’s collection.]

[Note: [Col. 0423] Held A.D. 451.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 143 (140), from the ancient version; Deusdedit, p. 4; Polycarp, bk. 4, title 22.—Cf. C. 16, q. 7, c. 21.]

Since, as has come to our attention, bishops in certain churches administer ecclesiastical property without an *oeconomus*, it has seemed good that all churches having bishops should also have an *oeconomus* from their own clergy, who is to administer the Church’s property at his bishop’s discretion. [Note: [Col. 0423] The collected editions, from the original, read “*oeconomi*, who are to govern.”] Thus the administration of ecclesiastical property may not be without testimony, and the property of that Church may not consequently be scattered and reproach brought upon priestly dignity. [Note: [Col. 0423] The same editions read “nor as a result of this”; the Basel edition adds “for.”] If anyone does not observe this, let him be subject to the divine rules. [Note: [Col. 0423] The same editions read “he shall be subject.”]

### C. V. Ecclesiastical property is not to be entrusted to laymen. Likewise Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, book VII, letter 66

[Note: [Col. 0423] Letter 65, written A.D. 599, book 9, Maurist edition.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 146 (143).]

[Col. 0423C] It has been reported to us that you have entrusted the care of your patrimony [Note: [Col. 0423] The collected editions, except the second Lyon edition, read “patronage.”] to certain laymen, who were afterwards found engaged in despoiling and harassing your peasants. [Note: [Col. 0423D–0424C] “And harassing”: most manuscripts read “and from harassments” [Anselm: “and through this, from harassments”]; the editions of St Gregory’s letters read “and through this, also by harassments”; one old codex of those letters reads “and through this, by expulsions.”] *They put off restoring the property which they improperly retain as though it belonged to their own jurisdiction, since they are not subject to your administration, and disdain to render you an account of their actions.* [Note: [Col. 0423] The words enclosed in asterisks, and likewise the words “in them” below, are absent from Anselm.]

If this is so, you must investigate it strictly and examine the case more carefully between them and the peasants of your Church. Whatever fraud is found *in them* must be restored by them together with the penalty prescribed by law. In future, however, Your Fraternity must take care that ecclesiastical property [Note: [Col. 0423] The collected editions read “the property of any Church”; Böhm reads “private property.”] not be entrusted to secular men who do not live under our rule, but to approved clerics of your own office, so that, if any *wickedness* can be found in them, you may be able, as they are your subordinates, to correct whatever has been done unlawfully: so that, in your presence, the duty imposed by their habit may cause them to administer more fittingly than to furnish grounds for accusation. [Note: [Col. 0424C] “So that”: in St Gregory the text reads: “whose office, commended among you more by their conduct, may excuse them.”] [Note: [Col. 0423] Anselm reads: “so that their conduct may be more fitting than accusatory.”]

**III. Part. Gratian.** A bishop must not dare to entrust ecclesiastical offices even to relatives or persons connected with him by favour.

[Col. 0424B] Hence it is read in the Tenth Council of Toledo, canon 3. [Note: [Col. 0423] Held A.D. 656.—*Coll. tr.*, p. p. 2, t. 41, c. 1.]

### C. VI. A bishop is not to entrust ecclesiastical offices to relatives or persons connected by favour

It seems fitting to all both to rescind such an act in the present instance and to prevent its being done in the future. Therefore, if any bishop henceforth attempts to entrust such gains to blood-relatives or to any persons [Note: [Col. 0423] The collected editions, except the second and third Lyon editions, read the singular “person.”] connected with him by favour [Note: [Col. 0423] The original reads “bound.”], let what has been commanded be revoked as null, to the ruin brought upon him by his impious presumption [Note: [Col. 0423] The Spanish collection reads “by the audacity of impious presumption.”], and let the person who made the appointment be subject to excommunication for a year. Whatever may perhaps have been taken away shall be restored twofold by the person who took it. [Note: [Col. 0423] Ibid., and the Strasbourg and Basel editions, read “has taken.”]

**Gratian.** Further, why these offices ought to be distinguished in this manner and why all should not be entrusted to one person is made clear by the authority of Popes Gregory and Boniface [Note: [Col. 0423] Boniface II’s letter to Eulalius is attributable to Pseudo-Isidore; the very words cited by Gratian are found in Gregory the Great’s letter to the bishops of Gaul, letter 54, written A.D. 595, Maurist edition.], who say as follows:

### C. VII. The distribution of ranks and orders preserves ecclesiastical unity

[Note: [Col. 0424C–D] This chapter is found in almost the same words in the letter of Boniface II to Eulalius and in that of Gregory I to the bishops of Gaul, book 4, letter 52. Likewise, many things found in other letters of St Gregory occur in writings of earlier pontiffs.]

For this purpose the provision of divine dispensation established different grades and distinct orders, so that, while inferiors showed reverence to superiors and superiors extended love to inferiors, a true concord might be woven from diversity, and the administration of each individual office be rightly produced. [Note: [Col. 0423] The original reads: “one fabric of concord might be woven from diversity.”] For the whole could not subsist by any other arrangement unless such a great order of differentiation preserved it. Since no creature can be governed or live in one and the same quality [Note: [Col. 0425] Ibid. reads “equality.”], the example of the heavenly hosts instructs us: since there are angels and [Note: [Col. 0425] “And” is absent from the collected editions except the second and third Lyon editions.] there are archangels, it is clear that they are not equal, but one differs from another in power and order, as you know. [Note: [Col. 0425] The collected editions read the plural “they differ.”]

# DISTINCTION XC

[Col. 0425]

[Col. 0425A] **GRATIAN**

**I. Part.** A contentious person is likewise forbidden to be ordained, because one who ought by his authority to draw those in discord into concord, and who is forbidden to receive the offerings of those at variance, ought by no means to provoke others to dissension through readiness for litigation.

Hence it is read in the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 59. [Note: [Col. 0425] Canon 48, *Statutes of the Ancient Church*.—Cf. c. 9, Dist. 18.—Burchard, bk. 2, c. 215; Ivo, *Decr.*, p. 6, c. 290.]

### C. I. Discordant clerics are to be deposed or recalled to concord

A bishop shall draw discordant clerics to concord either by reason or by authority; let the synod condemn the disobedient [Note: [Col. 0425] The Basel edition adds “them.”] after a hearing.

### C. II. Gifts offered by brothers at variance are not to be received in church. Likewise from the same, canons 93 and 94

[Note: [Col. 0425] Canons 49 and 69, *Statutes of the Ancient Church*.—Burchard, bk. 4, cc. 38–39; Ivo, *Decr.*, p. 2, cc. 47–48.]

The offerings of brethren at variance are to be received neither in the sanctuary nor in the treasury.

Likewise:

§ 1. The gifts of those who oppress the poor are to be rejected by priests. [Note: [Col. 0425] Cf. below, c. 8.]

### C. III. One who has no peace with his neighbour is shown to be outside the Church. Likewise Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*

God did not look upon Cain’s gifts [Note: [Col. 0425] The collected editions read “He did not look upon Cain or his gifts.”]; for he could not have God at peace with him [Note: [Col. 0425] The same editions, except the Basel edition, read “pleased”; the Basel edition reads “for he could not have peace with God.”] when he did not have peace with his brother because of the discord of jealousy. [Note: [Col. 0425] The collected editions read “not peace, but the discord of jealousy.”] What peace, then, do enemies of the brethren promise themselves? What sacrifices do rivals of priests believe that they celebrate? Do they suppose that Christ is with them when they have assembled, though they assemble outside Christ’s Church? Even if such persons are killed [Note: [Col. 0425] The Basel edition reads “idle.”] in confession of the Name [Note: [Col. 0425] The collected editions add “of Christ.”], this stain is not washed away even by blood. [Note: [Col. 0425] The Strasbourg and Basel editions read “not” instead of “not even.”] The grave and inexpiable guilt of discord [Note: [Col. 0425] The collected editions add “for.”] is not purified even by suffering.

### C. IV. Those who murmur are to be made strangers to the unity of the brethren. Likewise, from the Eighth Synod.[^c0040-1][^c0040-2]

Let him who murmurs be a stranger to the unity of the brethren, and let the work of one who has been found murmuring be rejected, lest he incur the punishment of murmurers, of which the Apostle says: “Neither murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer.”[^c0040-3] Therefore, in proportion to the deed, let the sinner do penance, at the priest’s judgment, for his sin—something more fully explained in this apostolic pronouncement.

[^c0040-1]: [Col. 0425C] In the booklet of St Basil, *On the Institutes of Monks*, translated by Rufinus (recently printed at Cologne together with the Rule of St Benedict), ch. 42, the final answer contains the first part of this chapter down to the words “let it be rejected.”
[^c0040-2]: [Col. 0425] These passages are taken from the booklet *On the Institutes of Monks*, attributed to Basil, chs. 71 and 93. The latter part of the canon, however, belongs to the first discourse of the same Basil on the institution of monks. Regino, bk. 1, chs. 164–165. Roman Penitential, title 6, ch. 9; Burchard, bk. 10, ch. 54; and Ivo, *Decree*, part 13, ch. 53, cite them from the Council of Mainz.
[^c0040-3]: [Col. 0425C] “One who murmurs”: ch. 50 of the same booklet, penultimate question, reads thus: “But if someone should murmur on account of food, what sentence is to be observed toward him?” Answer: “The sentence applied to those who murmured in the wilderness; for the Apostle says: ‘Neither murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer.’” [Col. 0425] 1 Corinthians, ch. 10.

[Col. 0425C] “In proportion”: this part is not found in that passage of Basil. [Col. 0426C] But in Burchard and Ivo, who cite it from the Council of Mainz, it reads: “in proportion to the measure and deed of the sin, because in this sentence,” etc.

[Col. 0425] “And deed of sin”: the cited collections.

### C. V. Those who love quarrels and disputes are to be corrected. Likewise, from the same source.[^c0040-4]

If any monk[^c0040-5] loves disputes or quarrels, or directs a public insult against a brother, let him expiate it by prolonged penance, according to the judgment of the superior and the measure of the sin.

Likewise:[^c0040-6]

§ 1. Let one who has proved contentious or murmuring do penance for as long as the gravity of his fault persists, according to the judgment of his superior.

[^c0040-4]: [Col. 0425] In the Council of Agde, from which Burchard, bk. 10, ch. 62, and Ivo, *Decree*, part 15, ch. 63, cite it, only similar provisions occur. The complete first part, taken from Isidore of Seville’s Rule of Monks, is found in the Roman Penitential, title 6, ch. 10.
[^c0040-5]: [Col. 0426C] “If any monk”: Burchard and Ivo cite this first part from the Council of Agde, where it is also found in the codex of the Sixteen Books, bk. 5, ch. 22. But the word “monk” is almost everywhere absent, even in many copies of Gratian. [Col. 0425] Regino, bk. 1, ch. 159; Collection in Three Parts, part 2, title 13, chs. 23–24.
[^c0040-6]: [Col. 0425] Regino, bk. 1, ch. 160; Burchard, bk. 10, ch. 53; Ivo, *Decree*, part 13, ch. 54. [Col. 0426C] “For as long”: in Burchard and Ivo, who cite this latter part from Mainz—it occurs in the *Book of Sayings of the Fathers*, ch. 96, from the Statutes of the Elders—it reads: “let him do penance in such a manner as the character of the fault requires.” [Col. 0425] “Persists”: “may persist,” Basel edition.

[Col. 0427A]

### C. VI. Dissenting bishops are to be compelled to return to concord. Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 25.[^c0040-7]

If the fear of God does not reconcile dissenting bishops, let the synod reconcile them.

[^c0040-7]: [Col. 0427] Ch. 47 of the *Statutes of the Ancient Church*. Compare above, Distinction 18, ch. 9. Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 62; Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 172.

### C. VII. On the same subject. Likewise, from the same source, ch. 26.[^c0040-8]

Bishops must endeavor to compel dissenting brethren, whether clerics or laypeople, toward peace rather than toward judgment.

[^c0040-8]: [Col. 0427] Ch. 54 of the *Statutes of the Ancient Church*. Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 101; Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 203. “Compel”: “exhort,” the correct reading.

### C. VIII. The gifts of those who oppress the poor are not to be accepted. Likewise, from the same source, ch. 94.[^c0040-9]

The gifts of those who oppress the poor are to be refused by priests.

[^c0040-9]: [Col. 0427] Compare above, ch. 2.

[Col. 0427B]

### C. IX. Those who disdain to return to concord are to be excluded from the assembly of the faithful. Likewise, from the Council of Agde, ch. 31.[^c0040-10]

It has also been decreed that, if—as often happens—any persons have fallen into disagreement with one another through hatred or a prolonged dispute, and cannot be recalled to peace because of obstinacy long maintained, they are first to be rebuked by the priests of the city. If, with ruinous persistence, they refuse to lay aside their enmities, they are to be driven from the communion of the Church by a most just excommunication.

[^c0040-10]: [Col. 0427] Held in A.D. 506. Burchard, bk. 10, ch. 61; Ivo, *Decree*, part 13, ch. 62. “Long maintained obstinacy”: “persistent intention,” original.

### C. X. Let one who refuses reconciliation with his brother be severely disciplined by fasting. Likewise, Pope Fabian.[^c0040-11]

If anyone who has been offended refuses to be reconciled with his brother when the person who caused the offense makes satisfaction, let him be chastened by most severe fasts until he receives the satisfaction with a grateful spirit.

[^c0040-11]: [Col. 0427] The author of this chapter has been sought in vain; only its opening words have been found among the Sayings of Basil, ch. 4. Burchard, bk. 10, ch. 59; Ivo, *Decree*, part 13, ch. 68.

### C. XI. Bishops are to afford each other counsel and assistance for steadfast maintenance of peace. Likewise, Innocent II.[^c0040-12]

**Second Part.** We command that bishops, having regard only to God and to the salvation of the people, putting aside all lukewarmness, give one another mutual counsel and help for firmly preserving peace, and do not neglect this from love or hatred toward anyone. If anyone is found lukewarm in this work of God, let him incur the loss of his own rank.

[^c0040-12]: [Col. 0427] Held in A.D. 1139. Compare Council of Reims, ch. 11; *Compilatio I*, “On Truce and Peace,” ch. 1; and *X*, under the same title, ch. 1. Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, ch. 147. “For we command”: “we command,” with “for” added in the cited editions. “Putting aside”: “setting aside,” those editions.

[Col. 0428B]

### C. XII. Those who refuse mutual reconciliation are to be expelled from the communion of the faithful. Likewise, Pope Victor to the Africans, Letter II.[^c0040-13]

It has been reported to the Apostolic See that some among you wish to harm brethren and strive for their downfall; that likewise you differ in the sacraments; and that on this account disputes and rivalries arise among you. We command you to turn away from these dissensions, to be at concord in all these matters, and to render mutual assistance. For if you quickly neglect to do this and do not strive to be reconciled with one another, do not doubt that you will be expelled from the communion of the Apostolic See and of the whole Church.

[^c0040-13]: [Col. 0427] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter. *Polycarpus*, bk. 4, title 13.

## DISTINCTION XCI

[Col. 0427]

[Col. 0427C] **GRATIAN.**

**First Part.** Those who are forbidden to seek their livelihood by shameful gain or dishonest trade are to receive support from the offerings of the Church. But if the Church cannot provide enough for them, let them procure their necessities by their own handicraft or farming—following the example of the Apostle,[^c0040-14] who lived by the labor of his hands—provided, however, that through the occasion of their work they do not fail in the Church’s vigils. This is permitted to no one with impunity unless it can be done without injury to his body.

Whence Pope Pelagius:[^c0040-15]

### C. I. Clerics who withdraw from the morning or evening offices are to be rebuked.

Our brother and fellow bishop Eleutherius complains that his clerics insolently oppose him contrary to the canons. Although, when we commanded it and a formal undertaking had been entered in the register, he promised that vigils would be celebrated every day in his church, he cannot enforce this because they disregard it. Rather, each one busies himself with his own affairs, setting aside the service of the Church. Therefore let your experience restrain by fitting rebuke those whom you find rebellious, and compel them by every means to attend to the vigils.

[^c0040-14]: [Col. 0427] Acts, ch. 2.
[^c0040-15]: [Col. 0427] An uncertain fragment. Anselm, bk. 7, ch. 165 (169).

### C. II. On the same subject. *Palea.* Likewise, from the Council of Nantes.[^c0040-16]

“A priest, in the morning, after the completion of the morning office, shall discharge by singing Prime, Terce, Sext, and None the allotted obligation of his service.[^c0040-17] Yet afterward, at the appropriate hours and at the indicated signals, they are to be publicly completed, according to ability, either by himself or by the pupils.[^c0040-18] Then, after the hours have been performed and the sick visited, if he wishes, he may go out fasting to rural work, so that until the appointed hour, according to the nature and convenience of the season, he may again be able to assist the needs of pilgrims, guests, and various travelers, and also of the sick and the dead.”

Likewise, from the sayings of St Benedict:[^c0040-19]

§ 1. “The Prophet says: ‘Seven times a day I have given praise to you.’[^c0040-20] This sacred number of seven will be fulfilled by us if at the time of Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline we discharge the offices of our service; for concerning these the Prophet said: ‘Seven times a day I have given praise to you.’ But concerning the night vigils the same Prophet says: ‘At midnight I rose to give praise to you.’ Therefore at these times let us render praises to our Creator for the judgments of his righteousness.”

[^c0040-16]: [Col. 0427] The author of this chapter has been identified as Hincmar of Reims, among the capitula, ch. 9. Regino, bk. 1, ch. 208; Burchard, bk. 2, ch. 104; Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, ch. 181. *X*, “On the Celebration of Mass,” ch. 1, cites it from Agde.
[^c0040-17]: [Col. 0427] “And Vespers”: added in the cited editions.
[^c0040-18]: [Col. 0427] “And at the indicated signals”: absent from Regino and the Argentinian edition; in the Basel edition the word “signals” is omitted.
[^c0040-19]: [Col. 0429] Ch. 16. Burchard, bk. 2, ch. 105; Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, ch. 182.
[^c0040-20]: [Col. 0429] Psalm 118 [119], v. 164. “Will be fulfilled”: “is fulfilled,” cited editions. “Of Matins”: “of the morning office,” those editions.

[Col. 0429B]

### C. III. Without detriment to his office, a cleric is to procure his necessities by handicraft. Likewise, in the Fourth Council of Carthage, chs. 52 and 49.[^c0040-21]

A cleric shall provide himself food and clothing by handicraft or farming, provided only that this causes no detriment to his office.

Likewise:

§ 1. A cleric who fails to attend the vigils without bodily incapacity is to be deprived of his stipend and excommunicated.[^c0040-22]

[^c0040-21]: [Col. 0429] Chs. 29 and 35 of the *Statutes of the Ancient Church*. See Distinction 18, ch. 9. Burchard, bk. 2, ch. 103; Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chs. 179–180. “Clothing”: “garment,” cited editions. “Provide”: “prepare,” original; cited collections and editions.
[^c0040-22]: [Col. 0429] “For a cleric”: “a cleric,” with “for” added in the cited editions. [Col. 0429C] “Deprived”: the most recent Cologne edition of the councils reads “let him be deprived.” But the older Cologne editions, two Paris editions, two Vatican manuscript copies of this council, and one royal manuscript at Soria read as in Gratian. [Col. 0429D]

### C. IV. On the same subject.[^c0040-23] Likewise, from the same source, chs. 51, 53, 48, and 50.[^c0040-24]

A cleric, however learned in the word of God, shall seek his livelihood by handicraft.

Likewise:

§ 1. All clerics who are capable of working shall learn both crafts and letters.[^c0040-25] But those who walk about marketplaces or forums not to buy something are to be degraded from their office. Clerics who depart from their office in times of trial, or discharge it negligently, are likewise to be removed from their office.[^c0040-26]

[^c0040-23]: [Col. 0429D] This chapter has been assembled from many chapters of the Fourth Council of Carthage, not arranged in their original order.
[^c0040-24]: [Col. 0429] Chs. 79, 45, 34, 72 of the *Statutes of the Ancient Church*. Burchard, bk. 2, chs. 51, 102, 210; Ivo, in the same places and ch. 285, from Dionysius.
[^c0040-25]: [Col. 0429] “Any cleric”: “every cleric,” Argentinian and Basel editions. “By handicraft”: “by a craft,” those editions. “Who are capable”: it appears that “incapable” should be read.
[^c0040-26]: [Col. 0429D] “Those who depart”: in manuscript copies of the council it is also read: “A cleric who departs from his office in times of trial or performs it negligently is to be removed from his office.” On the other hand, canon 42 commands: “A cleric who applies himself to his office in times of trial is to be elevated in rank.” But the text has not been altered on account of the gloss. [Col. 0430C] St Ambrose, Letter 17, treats of the trials on account of which some clerics, apart from persecution by tyrants, abandoned their office. [Col. 0429] These words are wrongly presented in the editions of Pelleterius, Freiesleben, and Boehmer as a saying of Gratian.

### C. V. On the same subject. Likewise, from the First Council of Orléans, ch. 28.[^c0040-27]

[Col. 0430B] Clerics who disdain to be present for the holy work are to undergo ecclesiastical discipline according to the judgment of the bishop.

[^c0040-27]: [Col. 0429] Held in A.D. 511.

## DISTINCTION XCII

[Col. 0429]

[Col. 0429B] **GRATIAN.**[^c0040-28]

**First Part.** When they come to church, moreover, they should remember that God is to be sung to more with the heart than with the voice.

Whence Jerome, book III of his commentary on ch. 5 of the Epistle to the Ephesians, v. 19:

### C. I. We ought to praise God with the heart, not merely with the voice.

“Sing and make melody in your hearts to the Lord.” Let young men hear this;[^c0040-29] let those hear it whose duty is to sing psalms in church: God is to be sung to not with the voice but with the heart. Their throats and jaws are not to be anointed with sweet medicine in the manner of tragic actors,[^c0040-30] so that theatrical tunes and songs may be heard in church, but rather in fear, in works, and in knowledge of the Scriptures.

Gratian. Deacons, however, are found exempted from the office of singing and chanting psalms, lest, while they devote themselves to the modulation of their voices, they neglect the ministries of the altar.

[^c0040-28]: [Col. 0429] Anselm, bk. 7, ch. 70 (71).
[^c0040-29]: [Col. 0429] “Young men”: “adolescents,” Basel edition.
[^c0040-30]: [Col. 0429] “Tragic actors”: “tragedies,” cited editions. [Col. 0429C] “Sweet” is absent in the first Lyons editions, II and III. “Are to be anointed”: “are to be smeared over,” Lyons editions II and III.

[Col. 0430B]

Whence Gregory (book IV, Letter 44, and book XII after the end of the letters, in the council held by him):[^c0040-31]

### C. II. Deacons are not to usurp the office of singing.

A very reprehensible custom has for some time arisen in the holy Roman Church: certain persons are chosen as singers for the ministry of the sacred altar, and, being established in the order of deacon, devote themselves to vocal modulation, though it was fitting for them to apply themselves to the office of preaching and to the care of alms. It therefore often happens that, while a pleasant voice is sought for the sacred ministry, an appropriate life is neglected; and the singer, who delights the people by his voice, provokes God by his conduct. Therefore, by this present decree I establish that in this See ministers of the sacred altar must not sing, but only perform the office of reading the Gospel in the solemnities of Mass; psalms and the other readings, however, I order to be performed by subdeacons, or, if necessity requires it, by the lesser orders. If anyone attempts to contravene this decree of mine, let him be anathema.

[^c0040-31]: [Col. 0429] Held in A.D. 603. Anselm, bk. 7, ch. 70, headed: “Gregory, presiding over a general synod, said”; Ivo, *Decree*, part 2, ch. 79; *Polycarpus*, bk. 4, title 31. “Sacred”: “the sacred,” Basel edition. [Col. 0430D] “Ministry”: the printed editions, except Basel, continued: “having been appointed,” but this phrase has been deleted, since it appears neither in old copies of Gratian nor in St Gregory nor in the other collectors, and seems to be a gloss added to the word “ministry”; that gloss itself is absent from the older copies. [Col. 0429] “For the sacred ministry”: “in the sacred ministry,” cited editions. “Is sought”: “may be sought,” cited editions. “In this matter”: “concerning this matter,” those editions. “I establish”: “by this present decree I establish,” Basel edition. [Col. 0431] Held in A.D. 332; a Dionysian translation. Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 141; Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 152; *Polycarpus*, there.

**Second Part.** Gratian. It has briefly been shown from whom candidates for ordination ought to be free. From whose hands, however, they ought to receive orders is readily apparent. For a priest and all those established below him must be ordained by their bishops.

Whence it is read in the Council of Pope Martin:[^c0040-32]

### C. III. Those not ordained by a bishop are not to chant or read from the pulpit.

It is not permitted to chant or read from the pulpit except to those ordained as readers by the bishop.

[^c0040-32]: [Col. 0431] Ch. 15 of the Council of Laodicea, from the translation of Martin of Braga, ch. 45.

Gratian. It has above been determined concerning bishops by whom, or in what places, they ought to be ordained.

**Third Part.** § 1. The question now arises concerning those who, though ordained, are not received by their own dioceses, or who for some reason refuse to go to them: may they exercise episcopal office in another’s diocese? Concerning them, the Council of Pope Martin established as follows:[^c0040-33]

### C. IV. A bishop whom his own diocese does not receive is to exercise only priestly office.

If an ordained bishop, through the contention of the people or for some reason, and not through his own fault, does not go to the diocese assigned to him, he ought to retain only the honor of the priesthood, provided that he presumes nothing for himself from the property of the church to which he comes; rather, he must await whatever the holy council determines concerning him.

[^c0040-33]: [Col. 0431] Ch. 18 of the Council of Antioch, held in A.D. 332, from the translation of Martin of Braga, ch. 10. Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 40; Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, ch. 151, citing the Council of Orléans; *Polycarpus*, bk. 2, title 13. [Col. 0431C] “Bishop”: the vulgate editions continued, “to the diocese to which he was elected”; these words have been introduced on the authority of the manuscripts, the original, and the other collectors. [Col. 0431] “Through”: “by,” Ivo. [Col. 0431C] “Contention”: two old copies of Gratian and one copy of the councils of the Catholic king read “contempt.” [Col. 0431] “Is not received”: “has not been received,” Ivo. “And”: Hispanic Collection. “Comes”: “assembles,” Basel edition. “For himself”: omitted in the cited editions. “Whatever”: “what,” Hispanic Collection and cited editions. “Determines”: “has determined,” Ivo.

[Col. 0431C]

### C. V. Concerning an ordained bishop whom his own diocese does not receive. Likewise, from the Council of Antioch, ch. 18.

If an ordained bishop does not at all go to the diocese to which he has been elected, not through his own fault, but because either the people refuse him, or for some other cause not caused by his own fault, he shall share in both honor and ministry, provided that he causes no disturbance whatsoever in the affairs of the church where he is known to minister. He ought also to await whatever the complete synod of the province may decide by judgment.

[Col. 0431] “To which”: “to whom,” original and Ivo. [Col. 0431D] “Refuse”: διὰ τὴν τοῦ λαοῦ παραίτησιν, “because of the people’s refusal.” [Col. 0432A] “Causes no disturbance”: “is troublesome in nothing,” Ivo. [Col. 0431D] “Await”: ἐκδέχεσθαι, that is, “to await and receive.” [Col. 0431] “Ought”: “will ought,” Basel edition. [Col. 0431D] “Complete”: formerly “of a complete synod” was read. The correct reading has been restored from the original, Burchard, and Ivo. What is meant by the synod called here “complete,” and in the chapters shortly following “entire,” is explained below in the same distinction, ch. *If Any Bishop*, § 3. [Col. 0431] “Completely”: Lyons editions II and III.

### C. VI. Those not received by their own diocese are not to cause trouble to others. Likewise, from the Council of Ancyra, ch. 28.[^c0040-34]

If bishops who have been ordained but have not been received by the diocese in which they had been designated wish to seize other dioceses and use force against their bishops by stirring up seditions against them, it has been decreed that they are to be deposed. But if they wish to remain, in the rank of presbyter, where they had formerly been as presbyters, they are not to be deprived of their proper rank. If, however, they stir up seditions against the bishops established there, even the honor of the presbyterate is to be taken away from such persons, and they are to be marked as liable to condemnation.

[^c0040-34]: [Col. 0431] Held in A.D. 314; from the Dionysian translation. Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 36; Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, ch. 147; *Polycarpus*, there. “Had been”: “were,” Boehmer. [Col. 0432B] “Stir up”: “have stirred up,” there.

### C. VII. A bishop who neglects to go to the church entrusted to him is to be deprived of communion. Likewise, from the Council of Antioch, ch. 17.[^c0040-35]

If any bishop has received a bishopric through the laying on of hands and neglects to assume the ministry entrusted to him, and does not consent to go to the church committed to him, he ought to be deprived of communion until, under compulsion, he undertakes the office, or until at least the synod of priests of the same province has made some entire determination concerning him.

[^c0040-35]: [Col. 0431] Held in A.D. 332; from the translation of Dionysius Exiguus. Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 37; Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 148; *Polycarpus*, bk. 2, title 12. [Col. 0432C] “And [the] ministry entrusted to him”: Burchard and Ivo likewise have this. But in the version of Dionysius, which they reproduce in the other parts, it reads: “and, having been appointed to preside over the people, [he neglects] to undertake the ministry,” etc.; this is translated word for word from the Greek. [Col. 0431] “Undertakes”: “receives,” Ivo.

### C. VIII. Without a council of the full order, a bishop without a see is not to enter a vacant church. Likewise, from the same source, ch. 16.[^c0040-36]

If a bishop without a see bursts, without a council of the full order, into a church having no bishop, seizing its people, even though the people whom he has led astray desire him, he must nevertheless be held alien from the Church. By a full and complete council we mean one at which the metropolitan bishop was present.

[^c0040-36]: [Col. 0432D] This translation, followed by Gratian, Burchard, and Ivo, is almost the same as that of Martin of Braga. The Dionysian version comes much closer to the Greek wording. [Col. 0431] From the translation of Martin of Braga, ch. 9; Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 39; Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 150. [Col. 0431] “Nevertheless”: added in the cited editions. [Col. 0432D] “Metropolitan”: “also [the metropolitan] must be added.” For the Greek reads: Καὶ ὁ τῆς μητροπόλεως, “and the [bishop] of the metropolis.” [Col. 0431] “Was present”: “has been present,” Basel edition, Burchard, and Ivo.

[Col. 0433A]

**Fourth Part.** Gratian. The preceding command that clerics who withdraw from vigils be excommunicated must be understood of those who, after frequent admonition by the bishop, disdain to correct their negligence.

Whence it is read in the Council of Pope Martin:[^c0040-37]

### C. IX. A cleric who, after admonition by the bishop, neglects to attend at morning or evening hours is to be excommunicated.

If any presbyter, deacon, or other cleric assigned to a church is within a city or in any place where there is a church, and does not come to church for the daily office of psalmody at the morning or evening hours, let him be deposed from the clergy—provided that, when corrected, he refuses to obtain pardon from the bishop by making satisfaction.

[^c0040-37]: [Col. 0433] From the First Council of Toledo, held in A.D. 400. “Office of psalmody”: “sacrifice,” original. “Does not come”: “does not come together,” there.

## DISTINCTION XCIII

[Col. 0433]

[Col. 0433A] **GRATIAN.**

**First Part.** The lower orders owe obedience to the higher. For obedience is owed by all to the supreme pontiff in such a way that no one may communicate with a person with whom he himself has become hostile on account of that person’s deeds; nor can one remain in the Church who abandons his chair.

Whence the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, addressing the people at Clement’s ordination, said among other things:[^c0040-38]

### C. I. We must not communicate with one to whom the Apostolic See is hostile on account of his deeds.

If this Clement is hostile to anyone because of his deeds, do not wait for him to tell you, “Do not be friends with that man.” Rather, you ought prudently to observe and obey his will without admonition, and turn away from him against whom you perceive Clement himself to be opposed.
