Nor should you even speak to those with whom he does not speak, so that everyone who is at fault, desiring to retain the friendship of you all, may hasten quickly to be reconciled with him who presides over all, and through this return to salvation when he begins to obey the admonitions of the presiding bishop.

But if anyone is friendly with those with whom he himself is not friendly, and speaks with those with whom he does not speak, that person too is one of those who seek to destroy God’s Church. Though he may appear to be with you in body, in mind and spirit he is against you. He is a far more wicked enemy than those who are outside and openly hostile; for, under the appearance of friendship, he does hostile things and scatters and devastates the Church. Therefore, beloved, instructing and warning you by these apostolic ordinances, we urge you, now that your charity has been made more certain, to strive henceforth to act more diligently and cautiously, so that perverse and faithless men may not have the opportunity to harm the faithful and well-disposed.

[^c0040-38]: [Col. 0433] This chapter is taken from that apocryphal part of Clement’s letter which Rufinus translated from Greek into Latin. Collection in Three Parts, part 1, title 18, ch. 2; Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 6; Ivo, *Decree*, part 14, ch. 22; *Polycarpus*, bk. 1, title 6. “Without admonition”: “with admonition,” Basel edition. “But”: absent from the cited editions except Basel. “So that”: “whence,” cited editions. “Retain”: “have,” those editions. [Col. 0433C] “Therefore”: from here to the end, the words occur only in Fabian’s letter. It consequently seems that Gratian chiefly took the rest from it. [Col. 0433] “Beloved”: “such persons,” cited editions. “So that they may not”: “lest,” those editions.

### C. II. No one ought to receive a person whom the Roman Church rejects. Likewise, Gregory, book V, Letter 26.[^c0040-39]

I was greatly astonished that among so large a clergy and people of the Church of Salona scarcely two persons in holy orders were found—namely, our brother and fellow bishop Paulinus, and my most beloved son Honoratus, archdeacon of the same church—who did not consent to communicate with Maximus as he usurped the priesthood, and who recognized themselves as Christians. For, dearest sons, you ought to have considered your orders and recognized as rejected the man whom the Apostolic See rejected, so that he might first, if possible, be cleansed from the charges brought against him, and then receive communion from your charity, lest you become participants in his liability.

[^c0040-39]: [Col. 0433] Letter 26, written A.D. 596; bk. 6 in the Maurist edition. Anselm, bk. 12, ch. 11. “Among”: “in,” cited editions.

[Col. 0434C]

### C. III. One who does not follow Peter’s chair is not in the Church. Likewise, Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*.[^c0040-40]

Let one who abandons Peter’s chair, upon which the Church is founded, not trust that he is in the Church.

[^c0040-40]: [Col. 0433D] In the edition of Cyprian printed at Rome, the following words are read: “Does one who does not hold the unity of the Church believe that he holds the faith? Does one who rebels and resists the Church trust that he is in the Church?” But in the Vatican Library, besides eight complete copies of Cyprian, there is another containing only certain smaller works, among them this treatise. In that codex, as also in another complete copy from the monastery of St Saviour at Bologna, the words here cited by Gratian and Ivo are found. And indeed, a little earlier Cyprian had shown that this very chair of Peter was that upon which the Church’s unity depended. [Col. 0433] Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 361.

Gratian. Bishops subject to apostolic ordination owe also this reverence: that every year they present themselves at the thresholds of the apostles.

Whence Popes Anacletus and Zacharias:[^c0040-41]

### C. IV. Bishops subject to apostolic ordinations are to visit the thresholds of the apostles every year.

In accordance with the ordinances of the holy Fathers and the canons, all bishops subject to the jurisdiction of this Apostolic See who are nearby shall, setting aside every excuse, present themselves each year about the Ides of May at the thresholds of the holy chief apostles Peter and Paul. Those who are far away shall fulfill this according to their written undertaking. Whoever disregards this ordinance, unless prevented by illness, should know that he is subject to canonical penalties.

[^c0040-41]: [Col. 0433] From the Roman Council held in A.D. 743. Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 164 (161); *Polycarpus*, bk. 4, title 25. [Col. 0434D] This is canon 4 of the Roman synod held under Pope Zacharias, preserved in the Vatican Library; from it certain points in this chapter have been corrected. [Col. 0435] “About the Ides”: “on the Ides,” original. “Holy chief apostles”: “holy chief fathers,” Argentinian and Basel editions. “Who are far away”: “who are far away,” with “are” added in the cited editions. “This”: “such,” those editions.

**Second Part.** Gratian. The remaining lesser persons in the Church must always be subject to their superiors, as is read in the Roman Synod of St Silvester, ch. 7:[^c0040-42]

### C. V. Inferiors are to render obedience to superiors.

From the subdeacon down to the readers, all are to be subject to the cardinal deacon of the city of Rome, rendering him honor in the church. Further, the presbyter is to render service to the pontiff; the deacon to the presbyter; the subdeacon to the deacon; the acolyte to the subdeacon; the exorcist to the acolyte; the reader to the exorcist; the doorkeeper to the reader; the abbot to the doorkeeper; and the monk to the abbot, in every place, whether in public or within the precinct of the church.

[^c0040-42]: [Col. 0435C] This chapter appears very corrupt both in Gratian and in editions of the synod itself. Burchard, Ivo, and Anselm have as follows: “From the subdeacon down to the reader, all are to be subject to the cardinal deacon of the city of Rome, rendering honor only in church. But presbyter, deacon, subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, reader, abbot, and monk are to render service to the pontiff in every place, whether in public or within the precinct of the church.” Yet, because of the great variety of manuscripts, and because of glosses and sayings of doctors, almost nothing has been changed in the text. [Col. 0435] From the apocryphal *Constitution of Silvester*, ch. 7. Burchard, bk. 2, ch. 224; Anselm, bk. 7, ch. 65 (67); Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, ch. 299. “Most reverend man”: added in the cited editions from Anselm; “most reverend and religious man,” Argentinian edition. [Col. 0436C] “Abbot”: in editions of the synod there is no mention of abbot or monk.

### C. VI. What the office of deacons is. Likewise, from the First Letter of Clement to James, brother of the Lord.[^c0040-43]

Let the deacons of the Church be, as it were, the eyes of the bishop, going about and surveying with modesty the affairs of the whole Church, and carefully searching whether they see anyone approaching ruin and near to sin, so that they may report these things to the bishop.

And below:[^c0040-44]

§ 1. They are likewise to report to the bishop concerning the relief of strangers, and other similar matters. Let those matters which pertain to the worship and discipline of the Church be the concern of the deacons.

[^c0040-43]: [Col. 0435] From the first part, rendered into Latin by Rufinus. Anselm, bk. 7, ch. 68.
[^c0040-44]: [Col. 0436C] “And below”: so it is read in most manuscripts. The vulgate editions read “and thus”; certain other words have been restored from the original. [Col. 0435] “And thus report to the bishop those things pertaining to worship,” etc.: cited editions.

### C. VII. On the same subject. Likewise, from the same letter.[^c0040-45]

The blessed Peter, teaching that priests are the salt of the earth and the light of the world, commanded them to glorify God the Father in the splendor of good works. Of them the Lord says:[^c0040-46] “Blessed are you when people revile you,” etc.; and again: “You are the salt of the earth.”

[^c0040-45]: [Col. 0435] From Pseudo-Isidore’s additions to Clement’s letter; according to Gregory the Great, Letter 18, bk. 5. Anselm, there.
[^c0040-46]: [Col. 0435] “Said”: added in the cited editions. “Them”: added in those editions. Matthew, ch. 5.

### C. VIII. Those clerics who are not governed under episcopal oversight are not to be regarded as clerics. Likewise, from the Council of Paris.[^c0040-47]

For no reason are clerics or priests to be considered such if they are governed under the discipline and oversight of no bishop. Ancient custom of the Church called such persons *acephali*, that is, “without a head.”

[^c0040-47]: [Col. 0435] From the Synod of Pavia—that is, Ticinum—held in A.D. 850, ch. 18. Similar provisions occur in the Council of Mainz, held A.D. 813, ch. 22. Burchard, bk. 2, ch. 226; Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, ch. 301.

### C. IX. On the same subject. Likewise, from the Third Letter of Clement.[^c0040-48]

Those who do not obey their bishops are unquestionably guilty and reprobate. But they receive from God the gift of the highest office who, walking in the paths of his justice and commandments, willingly obey their teachers, who are rightly understood to be bishops.

[^c0040-48]: [Col. 0435] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, taken from the *Recognitions of Clement*, bk. 2, ch. 20.

### C. X. Those who do not obey their own bishop take offense against God. Likewise, Anacletus, Letter I.[^c0040-49]

Without doubt, he takes offense against God who does not teach rightly and who causes offense to his bishop or priest.

[^c0040-49]: [Col. 0435] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter. Compare Ambrose, *On the Dignity of the Priesthood*, and Boniface of Mainz, Letter 73, from Würdtwein’s edition. Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, ch. 245.

### C. XI. There ought to be seven deacons in each city. Likewise, Evaristus to the African bishops, Letter I.[^c0040-50]

Deacons—who seem to be, as it were, the bishop’s eyes—ought, in each city, according to the ordinances of the apostles, to be seven. They are to guard the bishop while he preaches, lest either the bishop himself be assailed in any way by plotters, or be harmed by his own people, or the divine words be defiled or despised through disparagement or plotting. Rather, let truth breathe spiritual fervor, and let the peace preached by the lips agree with the will of the heart.

[^c0040-50]: [Col. 0435] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter. The words “who … bishop” derive from First Clement; the impostor borrowed the remainder from the *Pontifical*. Anselm, bk. 7, ch. 69; *Polycarpus*, bk. 2, title 38. “Evaristus to all bishops”: cited editions.

### C. XII. On the same subject. Likewise, from the Council of Neocaesarea, ch. 14.[^c0040-51]

There ought to be seven deacons according to the rule, even if the city is large. The authority of this rule is that the book of the Acts of the Apostles indicates the same thing.

[^c0040-51]: [Col. 0435] Held in A.D. 314. This chapter has been compiled from the translations of Isidore and Dionysius. Burchard, bk. 2, ch. 119; Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chs. 294–295. [Col. 0436C] “Even if [the city is] large”: formerly it read “even if [it is] not large.” It has been corrected from the Greek canon—which is also cited in the Sixth Synod, ch. 16—and from the vulgate translations. In the canons of the First Nicene Synod recently published in an Arabic-to-Latin translation, ch. 62 contains much relevant material; perhaps this was the canon signified by Andrew of Colossae in session 7 of the Council of Florence.

### Part III. Gratian

Therefore, as appears from the foregoing, deacons owe obedience to presbyters, just as presbyters owe obedience to bishops. But deacons, swelling with pride, sought to be made equal to priests—or rather, to be preferred to them. Against their insolence many authorities were issued, restraining their arrogance and decreeing that they should render due obedience to priests.

Accordingly Pope Gelasius [Note: **[Col. 0437C] Gelasius:** So it stands in most manuscripts, and in Burchard and Ivo. For the printed editions read: *Pelagius*.], in his letter to the bishops throughout Lucania, chapters 9 and 10, says [Note: **[Col. 0437]** written A.D. 404.—Burchard, book 4, ch. 57. Anselm, book 7, ch. 63. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 1, ch. 252, and part 6, ch. 99. Polycarpus, book 3, title 10.]:

#### C. XIII. Deacons are not to claim anything belonging to the first orders.

We decree that deacons keep their proper measure [Note: **[Col. 0437]** *observe*: editions compared, or from Ivo.], and we do not permit them to attempt anything beyond the limit assigned by the canons of the Fathers [Col. 0437B], nor to appropriate in any way to their own ministry anything which antiquity has specifically decreed for the first orders. They must not dare to baptize without a bishop or presbyter, unless perhaps extreme necessity compels it when the aforesaid orders are established at a distance [Note: **[Col. 0437]** *offices*: original.]. This is often permitted even to Christian laypersons. And below, §1: They have no right to exercise the prerogative of distributing the sacred body [Note: **[Col. 0437]** *prolongation*: Ivo; Basel edition.—*dispensation*: the other editions compared.] in the sight of a bishop [Note: **[Col. 0437]** *bishop*: editions compared, or] or presbyter, unless these are absent.

#### C. XIV. Let deacons recognize themselves as inferior to presbyters. Likewise from the Council of Nicaea, canon 14 or 18.

[Note: **[Col. 0437C]** The first part of this chapter, down to the words “let them be cut off,” is from the ancient [**[Col. 0437]** indeed, Spanish] translation, in canon 14. The remaining part is from Dionysius’s translation in canon [Col. 0437D] 18; the whole of it is cited by the *Code of Canons*, Burchard, and Ivo.]

[Note: **[Col. 0437]** held A.D. 325.—Burchard, book 5, ch. 26. Anselm, book 7, ch. 64. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, ch. 36 (from Dionysius).]

It has come to the holy council’s attention that, in certain places and cities, deacons distribute the sacraments [Col. 0437C] to presbyters. Neither rule nor custom [Col. 0438A] has handed down that those who have no authority to offer sacrifice should give Christ’s body to those who offer it. It has also become known that certain deacons receive the sacraments even before bishops. [Note: **[Col. 0437D] Sacramenta sumunt, “receive the sacraments”:** The Greek is *Τῆς εὐχαριστίας ἅπτονται*, “they touch the Eucharist,” which Dionysius translates as *oblata contingant*, “they touch the offerings.” Burchard and Ivo, differing almost only at this point, read respectively: *sacra oblata contingant*, “they touch the sacred offerings,” and *sacram oblationem contingant*, “they touch the sacred offering.”] Therefore let all these things be cut off [Note: **[Col. 0437]** added: “and removed”: editions compared, or], and let deacons remain within their own measure, knowing that they are ministers of bishops but are regarded as inferior to presbyters [Note: **[Col. 0437]** added: “to”: editions compared, or]. Thus, in order, let them receive the grace of holy communion after the presbyters, with either bishop or presbyter distributing it. Nor may deacons sit among the presbyters [Note: **[Col. 0437]** *the deacon*: editions compared, or], because, if this occurs, it is shown to be contrary to rule *and order* [Note: **[Col. 0437]** the words enclosed in asterisks are absent in Anselm.]. But if anyone, *even* after these determinations, refuses obedience, he must cease from ministry.

[Col. 0438B]

#### C. XV. Let the deacon show honor to the presbyter, and himself be honored by inferiors. Likewise from the Council of Laodicea, canon 20.

[Note: **[Col. 0437]** held between A.D. 347 and 381.—from Dionysius’s interpretation.—Burchard, book 2, ch. 221. Anselm, book 7, ch. 65. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 296.]

A deacon ought not to sit in the presence of a presbyter, but should sit by the presbyter’s command. Likewise, a deacon should receive honor from those who follow him—that is, from subdeacons and all clerics. [Note: **[Col. 0437]** The original reads: “Honor is to be shown to deacons by those who obey them.”—Burchard; Ivo.]

#### C. XVI. Deacons may not bless the cup or give the bread. Likewise from the same source, canon 25.

[Note: **[Col. 0437]** from Isidore’s version.—Anselm, book 7, ch. 90, from Dionysius.]

Deacons [Note: **[Col. 0438C] Diaconos, “deacons”:** In older editions of the ancient translation, the reading is *diaconum*, “a deacon.” The Greek is *ὑπηρέτας*, “attendants,” which Dionysius translates *subdiaconos*, “subdeacons”; this is also the reading in the Council of Aachen.] [Note: **[Col. 0437]** *a deacon*: Isidore; Merlin.—*ministers*: Spanish Collection.] ought not to give the bread or bless the cup.

#### C. XVII. As to bishops, so also let deacons minister to presbyters. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 37.

[Note: **[Col. 0438C] Fourth:** This chapter and the following two occur in the Fourth Council of Carthage and in manuscript copies of Gratian [**[Col. 0437]** and editions compared, or]; likewise, in Anselm the title of this chapter had added: “Fourth Council of Carthage, at which Pope Zosimus was present through vicars.” But the acts of the Sixth Council of Carthage show this to be quite impossible. To that council Zosimus sent as legates Faustinus, bishop of the church of Potentia, Philip, [Col. 0438D] and Asellus. For the fourth council was held under the consulship of Honorius IV and Eutychianus, whereas the sixth was held under Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII—that is, twenty years later. In that year, as is evident from canon 76 and following of the African council, Pelagius and Caelestius appealed to Pope Zosimus. This is shown by certain manuscripts of letters of Zosimus and of the African bishops to him, preserved in the Vatican Library [Col. 0439C]. Since Zosimus lived in the pontificate for only two years and some months, it necessarily follows [Col. 0439D] that the Fourth Council of Carthage was held long before his pontificate.]

[Note: **[Col. 0437]** canon 57 of the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*.—cf. canon 9, Distinction 18.—Anselm, book 7, ch. 63 (66). Polycarpus, book 2, title 39.]

Let deacons recognize themselves to be ministers of presbyters just as they are ministers of bishops. [Note: **[Col. 0437]** *The deacon*—*as … minister*: Spanish Collection and Ballerini.] [Col. 0438C]

[Col. 0439A]

#### C. XVIII. On the same subject. Likewise from the same source, canon 38.

[Note: **[Col. 0439]** canon 55 of the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*.—Burchard, book 5, ch. 13. Anselm, book 7, ch. 66. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, ch. 23. Polycarpus, same place.]

When a presbyter is present, a deacon, if necessity requires and when commanded, may distribute the Eucharist of Christ’s body to the people.

#### C. XIX. On the same subject. Likewise from the same source, canons 39, 40, and 41.

[Note: **[Col. 0439]** canons 59, 60, 61, same work.—Anselm, same place.]

A deacon shall sit in whatever place the presbyter commands [Note: **[Col. 0439]** added: “in”: editions compared, or]. Likewise, when questioned in a gathering of presbyters, a deacon shall speak. He shall use the alb [Note: **[Col. 0439]** *orarium*, “stole”: Ballerini.] only at the time of the offering or reading [Note: **[Col. 0439]** *and*: editions compared, or; *be clothed*: Isidore; Merlin.].

#### C. XX. Let deacons not regard themselves as superior to presbyters. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 39.

[Note: **[Col. 0439]** held A.D. 633.—Burchard, book 2, ch. 222. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 297.]

Some deacons break out into such pride [Col. 0439B] that they place themselves before presbyters and presume to stand first in the first choir, while presbyters are placed in the second choir. Therefore, that they may acknowledge presbyters to be their superiors, both the one and the other shall stand in both [Note: **[Col. 0439D] In utroque, “in both”:** Although printed copies of Gratian [**[Col. 0439]** and the Basel and Lyons II–III editions] read “in both orders,” and printed volumes of the councils [**[Col. 0439]** and Ivo and Burchard] read “in both choirs,” nevertheless neither word occurs in the old codex of councils of the Catholic King, nor in most old copies of Gratian, including printed ones [Col. 0440C].].

### Part IV. Gratian

Deacons are not permitted to wear *campagi*—a type of shoe—without the authorization of the Apostolic See; just as no clerics whatsoever are allowed to use *mappulae* without the authority of that same see.

Accordingly Gregory, in book VII, letter 28, indiction I, to John, bishop of Syracuse, says [Note: **[Col. 0439]** Letter 27, written A.D. 598, book 8 of the Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 7, ch. 74.]:

#### C. XXI. Without apostolic permission deacons must not presume to use *campagi*.

It has come to us that the deacons [Note: **[Col. 0439]** editions compared, or read: “that a deacon … had presumed.”] of the church of Catania have presumed to go out shod in *campagi* [Note: **[Col. 0439]** The correct reading is *campagis*, a kind of footwear deriving its name from Greek *καμπή*, “a bend, curve.”]. You well remember that [Col. 0439C], throughout all Sicily, this had hitherto been permitted to no one except the deacons alone of the church of Messina, to whom it is beyond doubt that it was granted long ago by our predecessors. Therefore, because an act of such rashness must not be treated lightly, let your Fraternity investigate this matter with every care [Note: **[Col. 0439]** *requirat*, “inquire”: Basel edition.], *and, if it finds that it is true [Note: **[Col. 0440C] And if it is true:** Here and somewhat below several words have been added from the original.] as has reached us [Note: **[Col. 0439]** editions compared, or: “whether it be true in itself.”],* let us be carefully informed whether they presumed this on their own authority or by someone else’s authority [Col. 0440A], *so that, once the truth is known, we may determine what must be done.* For if we negligently overlook things that are wrongly usurped, we open a way for transgression to others.

#### C. XXII. Clerics must not use *mappulae* without apostolic permission. The same pope to John, bishop of Ravenna, book II, letter 54, near the end.

[Note: **[Col. 0439]** Letter 57, written A.D. 593, book 3 of the Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 7, ch. 168 (174).]

But concerning what you wrote about the use of *mappulae* by your clergy, our clerics strongly objected, saying that this had never been granted to any other church; that the clergy of Ravenna had not, there or in the city of Rome, presumed with a clear conscience to do anything of the kind [Note: **[Col. 0439]** *other*: Argentinensis and Basel editions]; and that, even if it had been attempted, no prejudice could arise for them from a furtive usurpation. Rather [Col. 0440B], they maintain that, even if this has been presumed in any church, it must be corrected, because it is presumed not by concession of the Roman Pontiff but by mere [Note: **[Col. 0439]** added: “usurpation or”: editions compared, or] stealth.

#### C. XXIII. As in ministry, so in administration let a bishop not live without a deacon. Likewise Jerome, *On the Seven Orders of the Church*, chapter 5.

[Note: **[Col. 0439]** The letter of Jerome to Rusticus, or booklet *On the Seven Grades of the Church*, is known to be spurious.—Anselm, book 7, ch. 72. Polycarpus, book 2, title 39.]

### Part V. Gratian

The deacons are those whom we read of in the Apocalypse [Note: **[Col. 0439]** Revelation 1.] as the seven angels of the churches; they are the seven golden lampstands; they are the voices of the thunders. And below, §1: Distinguished by the working of virtues, endowed with humility, peaceable, humble, proclaiming peace, announcing good things, cutting off dissensions, quarrels, and scandals; teaching [Note: **[Col. 0439]** absent from the original and Anselm.]; conversing with God alone; thinking in the temple [Col. 0440C] of nothing whatever belonging to the world; saying to father and mother, “I have not known [Note: **[Col. 0439]** *we have known*: Basel edition.] you,” and not recognizing their own children.

And a little later, §2: Without this person the priest has no name [Note: **[Col. 0440D] Nomen non habet, “has no name”:** So also in the original; but many manuscripts of Gratian [**[Col. 0439]** and editions compared, or, Lyons II–III], and Anselm, read: “he has a name, but does not have an office.”], no origin, no office. This man is called God’s minister, because it is written: “Who is greater: he who ministers, or he to whom ministry is rendered?” And as there is ministry in the priesthood [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *consecration*: the true reading.], so in the minister there is the distribution of the sacrament [Note: **[Col. 0439]** added: “of administration”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.].

And a little later, §3: Priests too, because of presumption, may not take the cup from the Lord’s table unless it has been handed to them by a deacon [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *deacons*: editions compared, or.]. And after a few intervening words, §4: For our almighty God has so arranged all things that he who thinks himself greater should be lesser [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *was*: those editions.], and he who seemed lesser should become greater. Finally, consider for yourself how true this is. *Levites bring the offerings to the altar; Levites prepare the Lord’s table; Levites stand with the priests when they bless the sacraments; Levites pray before the priests,* so that [Note: **[Col. 0441]** “And if it be believed”: those editions, Lyons II–III.] if distinction of places is believed [Note: **[Col. 0441]** added: “in the world”: those editions, from Anselm.], bishops may see even at God’s altar, if they are proud, that deacons are placed before them. If they love humility, let them recognize that they are greater in being humble [Note: **[Col. 0441]** added: “and deacons”: those editions; *recognize again*: those editions.].

Then at last, that we may have ears for the Lord, the deacon gives the acclamation [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *cries out*: editions compared, or, Lyons II–III.]; he preaches, he exhorts, he admonishes while the priests stand by, lest you lightly regard this voice which speaks these things and announces peace, or think it contemptible [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *nor*: Anselm; editions compared, or, Lyons II–III; *by which*: editions compared, or.]. It is enough for this order that so much has been granted to it by the Lord: that the priest alone may not appear to perform and fulfill everything in the temple [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *the temple of God*: editions compared, or, from Anselm.].

And below, §5: But now, since avarice has increased in the churches as in the Roman Empire, the law has perished from [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *from*: Basel edition.] the priest and vision from the prophet. Each person, by virtue of the episcopal [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *co-episcopal*: editions compared, or, Lyons II–III.] title which he has unlawfully claimed for himself apart from the church, reduces to his own uses everything belonging to the Levites. Nor does he claim merely for himself what is written as allotted to him [Note: **[Col. 0441]** “not merely this, which has been assigned to him”: those editions.]; he takes everything away from all. The unhappy cleric begs in the streets and, enslaved to civil [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *servile*: those editions.] labor [Col. 0441C], requests public sustenance from anyone at all [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *asks*: those editions; *alms*: those editions.]. And indeed, because of this the priestly office is despised by all [Note: **[Col. 0441]** “which for that reason is more despised”: those editions, from Anselm.], while one desolated by misery [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *wretched and desolate*: editions compared, or; *desolated by misery*: Anselm.] is thought justly to have come to this disgrace.

And below, §6: He alone broods over goods [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *riches*: original; *gifts*: Anselm.]; he alone uses ministry [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *ministries*: Basel edition.]; he alone claims everything for himself; he alone seizes the portions of others; he alone destroys everyone.

And a little later, §7: Hence, because of priests’ avarice, hatreds arise [Note: **[Col. 0441]** added: “always”: Anselm; “often”: editions compared, or.]; hence bishops are accused by clerics; hence lawsuits of princes [Note: **[Col. 0441]** “the beginning of litigation”: Anselm; editions compared, or, Lyons II–III.]; hence the cause of disparagement [Note: **[Col. 0441]** “causes of desolations”: original.]; hence [Note: **[Col. 0441]** added: “comes”: editions compared, or.] the origin of crime. For if each person in this visible world is commanded to possess something so as to be content only with his own possession and not invade another’s goods—not take the poor person’s field [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *of the poor person*: those editions.], nor [Col. 0442A] vineyard, nor any beast of burden, nor servants, nor produce [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *produce*, singular: those editions.]—how much more must one who presides over God’s church keep justice in all things: claiming only for himself what he knows belongs to him by right; not plundering or touching what belongs to another; making himself equal to the others; and, just as he does not live without them in ministry [Note: **[Col. 0441]** Anselm reads: “just as the church did not exist without them, so neither should he live without them in the administration of ministry.”], so also not living without them in administration?

§8. Certainly, as you yourself know, one who visibly invades another’s right in this world is accused by the poor person and condemned by the judge. So too, in God’s church, when each loses his own stipends [Note: **[Col. 0441]** absent from editions compared, or, Basel.], he cries to God and is heard by Christ; and the sentence of vengeance is not delayed *in this matter* [Note: **[Col. 0441]** these words are absent in the collections and Anselm.] if everything is not restored [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *pacified*: Anselm; Argentinensis and Basel editions.]. For God’s moderation and mercy seek only our return and desire us to be saved by his long [Note: **[Col. 0441]** absent from the original.] kindness. But if [Col. 0442B] we are not converted, if we are hard [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *stiff-necked*: editions compared, or, from Anselm.] of heart, if we unlawfully persist in sins unto death, God does not have mercy on one who sins continually [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *of sinners*: editions compared, or; Böhm.], *as it is written.*

### Part VI. Gratian

In this chapter priests’ avarice is reproved, and deacons’ dignity or office commended. But because, as stated above, insolent deacons considered themselves to be preferred even to presbyters, Jerome writes against their arrogance, to Bishop Evagrius [Note: **[Col. 0441]** Anselm, book 7, ch. 87 (92).], in Letter 85:

#### C. XXIV. Deacons ought to be subject to presbyters.

We read in Isaiah: “The fool will speak folly” [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *speaks*: same source; editions compared, or.—cf. Isaiah 32:6.]. I hear that someone has broken out into such madness as to prefer deacons to presbyters—that is, to bishops. [Col. 0442C] For when the Apostle clearly teaches that presbyters and bishops are the same persons, how can a minister of tables and widows endure to puff himself up above those at whose prayers Christ’s body and blood are consecrated?

Do you ask for authority? Hear the testimony [Note: **[Col. 0441]** Philippians 1:1.]: “Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, to all the saints *in Christ Jesus* who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons.” Do you want another example? In the Acts of the Apostles Paul speaks thus to the priests of a single church [Note: **[Col. 0441]** Acts 20:28.]: “Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you [Note: **[Col. 0441]** added: “brothers”: editions compared, or.] as bishops, to govern the church of the Lord, which he acquired by his own blood.”

And lest anyone should contentiousy maintain that there were several bishops in one church, hear [Note: **[Col. 0441]** *let him hear*: those editions.] another [Col. 0443A] testimony, in which it is most clearly proved [Note: **[Col. 0443]** added: “is declared” or: those editions.] that bishop and presbyter are the same: “For this reason I left you in Crete [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *in Crete*: editions compared, or, Lyons II–III.], that you might correct what was lacking and appoint presbyters in every city, as *I also* commanded you: if anyone is without reproach, the husband of one wife, having [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *have*: Böhm.] believing children, not under accusation of debauchery or insubordination. For a bishop must be without reproach, as God’s steward.” And to Timothy [Note: **[Col. 0443]** 1 Timothy 4:14.]: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given you through prophecy [Note: **[Col. 0443C] Through prophecy:** So in the Vulgate edition and in Greek, *Διὰ προφητείας*, “through prophecy.” But here in St Jerome [**[Col. 0443]** and Anselm]: *prophetiae*, “of prophecy.”], through the laying on of the hands of the presbyterate.”

Peter also says in his first epistle [Note: **[Col. 0443]** 1 Peter 5:1.]: “I exhort the presbyters among [Note: **[Col. 0443]** “who are among you”: editions compared, or.] you [Note: **[Col. 0443]** added: “I”: those editions.], a fellow-presbyter and witness of Christ’s sufferings, and partaker of the glory that is to be revealed: shepherd [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *to shepherd … to oversee*: Anselm.] Christ’s flock and oversee it, not [Col. 0443B] under compulsion but willingly [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *by will*: Basel edition.] according to God.” The Greek expresses this more pointedly: *ἐπισκοποῦντες*, “exercising oversight” [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *Epichius*: Basel edition; *Epitius*: other editions compared, or, Paris and Lyons II–III.], from which the name *bishop* (*episcopus*) is derived.

Do the testimonies of such great men seem insignificant to you? Let the evangelical trumpet sound—the Son of Thunder, whom Jesus loved exceedingly, who drank streams of doctrine from the Savior’s breast: “The Presbyter to the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth” [Note: **[Col. 0443]** 2 John 1.]. And in another letter [Note: **[Col. 0443]** 3 John 1.—The words “And … in truth” are omitted by Anselm.]: “The Presbyter to beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth.”

§1. That later one person was chosen and placed over the others was done as a remedy for schism, lest each person, drawing Christ’s church to himself, should tear it apart. For even at Alexandria, from Mark the Evangelist down to Bishops Heraclas [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *Esdras*: editions compared, or, Lyons II–III.] [Col. 0443C] and Dionysius, the presbyters always chose one of themselves [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *used to choose … place … whom*: those editions, Lyons II–III.], placed him in a higher rank, and called him bishop; just as if an army were to make an emperor [Note: **[Col. 0443]** added: “for itself”: those editions, Lyons II–III.], or deacons [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *But deacons*: those editions.] were to choose from among themselves one whom they knew to be capable and call him archdeacon [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *designate*: editions compared, or.]. For what does a bishop do, apart from ordination, that a presbyter does not do [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *does*: those editions.]?

Nor should the church of the city of Rome be thought one thing and that of the whole world another. Gaul, Britain, Africa, Persia, the East, India, and all barbarian peoples worship one Christ and observe one rule of truth. [Note: **[Col. 0443]** “and the East and India” are absent in Anselm.] If authority is sought [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *were sought*: those editions, Basel and Lyons II–III.], the world is greater than a city [Col. 0444A]. Wherever a bishop may be—at Rome, Eugubium [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *Eugubio*: Argentinensis and Basel editions.], Constantinople [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *Constantinopolim*: those editions.], Rhegium [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *Regio*: those editions.], Alexandria, or Tanais [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *Thebans*: Argentinensis edition; *Thebes*: other editions compared, or, Basel; added: “or Worms”: editions compared, or, Argentinensis.], he is of the same merit and the same priesthood. The power of wealth and the lowliness of poverty do not make one bishop higher and another lower; all alike are successors of the apostles.

§2. But you say [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *you will say*: editions compared, or.], “How is it that at Rome a presbyter is ordained at the recommendation of a deacon?” Why do you set before me the custom of one city? Why do you claim for church laws a scarcity from which arrogance has arisen? Everything rare is more desired. Pennyroyal among the Indians is more precious than pepper. The small number of deacons makes them honorable; the crowd of presbyters makes them contemptible. Yet even in the church of Rome presbyters [Col. 0444B] sit and deacons stand. Although, as abuses have gradually increased, I have seen a deacon sit among presbyters in the absence of the bishop, and at domestic banquets give blessings [Note: **[Col. 0443]** “the blessing in the presence of presbyters”: those editions.] before presbyters. Let those who do this learn that they do not act rightly, and hear the Apostles [Note: **[Col. 0443]** Acts 6:2.]: “It is not fitting that we should leave the word of God and minister to tables.” Let them know why deacons were established. Let them read the Acts of the Apostles and remember their condition. Presbyter and bishop are names, one of age, the other of dignity. Thus, in the letters to Titus and Timothy, there is discussion of the ordination of bishop and deacon; presbyters are entirely passed over in silence, because the presbyter is included in the bishop.

One who is promoted is promoted from lesser to greater. Therefore either let a deacon be ordained from a presbyter, so that the presbyter may be proved inferior to the deacon [Note: **[Col. 0443]** “greater than a presbyter”: editions compared, or.] into whom he grows from a lower rank [Note: **[Col. 0443]** *grows together*: those editions, Basel.]; or, if a presbyter is ordained from a deacon, let him know himself [Col. 0444C] [Note: **[Col. 0443C] Noverit se, “let him know himself”:** The original [**[Col. 0443]** and Anselm] reads: “let him know himself to be lesser in material gains, but greater in priesthood.”] to be greater than laypersons but lesser than priests.

This also bears on what the same Jerome writes on the final chapter of Ezekiel: that the multitude of Levites should understand itself to be distinct from the priestly rank; and that this serves to crush the arrogance of ministers, who, unaware of the lowliness of their own rank, swell beyond priests—that is, presbyters—and evaluate dignity not by merit but by wealth. But this has not been changed because of the gloss [Col. 0444C].

#### C. XXV. On the same subject. Likewise Cyprian, book III, letter 9.

[Note: **[Col. 0443]** Letter to Rogatianus, written about A.D. 266.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 355.]

Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, our king, judge, and God, preserved honor for high priests and priests until the day of his passion, although they preserved neither fear of God nor acknowledgment of Christ. [Col. 0445A] For when he had cleansed the leper, he said to him [Note: **[Col. 0445]** Luke 5:14.]: “Go and show yourself to the priest [Note: **[Col. 0445]** *show yourself to the priests*: editions compared, or.], and offer the gift.” By the humility with which he taught us also to be humble, he still called priest one whom he knew to be sacrilegious. Likewise, under the blow of his passion [Note: **[Col. 0445]** *subjected to the passion*: those editions.], when he had received a slap and was told [Note: **[Col. 0445]** John 18:23.], “Do you answer the high priest in this way?”, he said nothing insulting about the person of the high priest, but rather defended his innocence, saying [Note: **[Col. 0445]** John 18:23.], “If I have spoken wrongly, testify to the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?” He did all these things humbly and patiently so that we might have an example of humility and patience. For he taught that true priests are to be honored lawfully and fully, since he himself acted thus even toward false priests.

§1. Deacons, moreover, ought to remember that [Col. 0445B] the Lord chose apostles—that is, bishops and rulers [Note: **[Col. 0445]** *presbyters*: editions compared, or.]—whereas, after the Lord’s ascension into heaven, the apostles established deacons for themselves as ministers of their episcopate and [Col. 0446A] of the church. If we can dare anything against God, who makes bishops, then deacons, by whom bishops are made, can also dare against us.

### Part VII. Gratian

What is said here concerning the inferiority of deacons must be observed everywhere, except when a deacon holds the place either of his own patriarch or of his metropolitan.

Accordingly, in the Sixth Synod, canon 7, we read [Note: **[Col. 0445]** rather, the Quinisext Synod, *πενθέκτη*; held A.D. 692. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 123.]:

#### C. XXVI. A deacon is not to be preferred to priests unless he occupies the place of his metropolitan.

We decree that a deacon—even though he may hold a dignity, that is, any ecclesiastical office—shall not sit before a presbyter, unless he holds the place of his own patriarch or metropolitan [Note: **[Col. 0445]** *metropolitan*: Argentinensis and Basel editions.] on some occasion; for then, as holding that person’s place, he will be honored [Col. 0446B]. But if anyone tyrannically presumes to do this, having been removed from his own rank, let him become last of all in his order.

## DISTINCTION XCIV

[Col. 0445]

[Col. 0445B] **GRATIAN**

### Part I. Even the supreme patriarch may entrust his functions to a subdeacon.

Accordingly Gregory [Note: **[Col. 0445C] Gregory:** The heading has been restored from Polycarpus; formerly it read “Pope Symmachus” [**[Col. 0445]**—an error apparently arising because in Anselm a fragment concerning Symmachus precedes it.]], in book I, letter 1, to the bishops of Sicily, says [Note: **[Col. 0445]** Letter 1, written A.D. 591, book 1 of the Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 1, ch. 26. Polycarpus, book 1, title 14.]:

#### C. I. The Apostolic Church entrusts its functions even to subdeacons.

We have perceived it to be very necessary that, as was the judgment of our predecessors, we should entrust everything to one and the same person, so that [Note: **[Col. 0445]** *and because*: editions compared, or.] where we cannot be present, our authority may be represented through the person to whom we give orders. Therefore, with God’s help [Col. 0445C], we have entrusted our functions within the province of Sicily to Peter, subdeacon of our see. For we cannot doubt his conduct, since, with God’s help, we know that we have entrusted to him the entire patronage [Note: **[Col. 0445]** *patrimony*: original; Argentinensis, Basel, and Norimberg editions.] of our church.

### Part II. Gratian

Whoever impedes a legate of the Apostolic See is to be excommunicated until he makes satisfaction.

Accordingly Pope Alexander I, in Letter II to all bishops, says [Note: **[Col. 0445]** A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Burchard, book 15, ch. 37.]:

#### C. II. Let one who attempts to impede a legate of the Apostolic See be excommunicated.

If anyone impedes a legation [Note: **[Col. 0445C] Legationem, “a legation”:** In the letter itself, in the Council [Col. 0446C] of Tribur (canon 9), and in Burchard, *vestram*, “your,” is added. The legation apparently meant is that in which St Paul taught apostles and bishops to act as ambassadors for Christ: 2 Corinthians 5.], he turns aside the advancement not of one person but of many. And just as he harms many, so he must be rebuked by many and deprived of the fellowship of the good [Note: **[Col. 0445]** *kept away*: original.]. And because he obstructs God’s cause and disturbs the church’s order, he must be excluded from its thresholds. Therefore everyone must beware of such a person [Note: **[Col. 0445]** *also*: same source.], and he must not be received into the communion of the faithful until he has made satisfaction.

### Part III. Gratian

Although an archdeacon, by virtue of his office, ought to investigate clerics’ lives with careful scrutiny and report to the bishop whatever he finds needing correction, he is nevertheless forbidden to exercise dominion over them or exact a tax from them.

[Col. 0446C] Accordingly, in the Council of Chalon, canon 15, we read [Note: **[Col. 0445]** held A.D. 813.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, ch. 134.]:

#### C. III. Archdeacons shall not exercise jurisdiction over presbyters.

It has been reported that in very many places archdeacons exercise a certain dominion over parish presbyters and exact a tax from them. This pertains more to tyranny than to the order of uprightness [Note: **[Col. 0445]** *fortitude*: Ivo.—*order*: editions compared, or.].

§1. For if, according to the Apostle’s statement [Note: **[Col. 0445]** 1 Peter 5:3.], bishops ought not to lord it over the clergy but to be examples to the flock from the heart, much less should these persons do so. Rather, let them be content with regular discipline [Note: **[Col. 0445]** editions compared, or: “Let them therefore be content.”], keep their proper measure, and endeavor to carry out in their parishes what is enjoined upon them by the bishops, presuming nothing through greed or avarice.

## DISTINCTION XCV

[Col. 0447]

[Col. 0447A] **GRATIAN**

### Part I

That priests are commanded above to obey bishops as subjects is not to be understood as though, when bishops are present, they may not celebrate the sacred mysteries—as some, in episcopal arrogance, wished to forbid presbyters to do—but that presbyters ought to obey pontiffs as sons obey parents. They are also permitted to anoint the baptized with chrism.

Accordingly Gregory writes to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, in book III, letter 26, indiction XII [Note: **[Col. 0447]** Letter 28, written A.D. 59[?], book 4 of the Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 7, ch. 129. Polycarpus, book 3, title 10.—Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book 4, Distinction 7, ch. 1.]:

#### C. I. Where bishops are absent, presbyters may anoint the foreheads of the baptized with chrism.

It has also come to us that certain persons have been scandalized because we prohibited presbyters from touching with chrism *on [Col. 0447B] the forehead* those who have been baptized [Note: **[Col. 0447]** *are to be baptized*: original.]. We indeed acted according to the ancient custom of our church. But if anyone is deeply troubled on this matter, we allow that, where bishops are absent, presbyters also should touch the baptized [Note: **[Col. 0447]** *those to be baptized*: same source.] on the forehead with chrism.

Gratian. Above, Pope Leo says the contrary: “Although concerning chorepiscopi,” etc. [Distinction LXVIII.]

#### C. II. Presbyters must not presume to exceed their proper measure. Likewise Pope Gelasius to the bishops throughout Lucania, etc., Letter V, chapter 8.

[Note: **[Col. 0447]** written A.D. 494. Anselm, book 7, ch. 127.]

We forbid presbyters to extend themselves beyond their proper measure [Note: **[Col. 0447]** *strive*: editions compared, or.], or rashly to assume for themselves what is due to episcopal eminence: they are not to claim for themselves authority either to make chrism or to administer episcopal confirmation [Col. 0447C] [Note: **[Col. 0447]** *receive*: Böhm; Part II.].

Gratian. But this concession of Gregory is read as having been made once, in order to allay scandal. The ruling of Pope Leo and Gelasius, however, has prevailed with usage approving it—unless perhaps the custom of some places has admitted this: that, in the bishop’s absence, when extreme necessity compels, priests, by Gregory’s concession, may anoint the baptized on the forehead. But the prohibition of Leo and Gelasius is to be understood in the case where bishops are present, or where extreme necessity does not compel. Priests are permitted, however, to anoint the sick with consecrated oil [Col. 0448A]. Hence James says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call in the presbyters of the Church, that they may pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person.”

II. Part. § 1. But the question is asked whether bishops may anoint the sick with the same oil, and whether an anointing of this kind ought to be granted to the impenitent.

On these matters Pope Innocent writes as follows to Decentius, Bishop of Eugubium, Epistle I, final chapter [Note: [Col. 0447] written A.D. 416.—Collection in three parts, part 1, title 38, chapter 5. Ivo, Decree, part 12, chapter 75.]:

C. III. A bishop is not forbidden to touch the sick with consecrated oil.

We consider it superfluous to add a question concerning the bishop, when there is no doubt that it is lawful for presbyters. For this reason presbyters were mentioned [Note: [Col. 0447] “of” is absent from the original and Ivo.], because bishops, hindered by other occupations [Note: [Col. 0447] “preoccupations”: collected editions.], cannot go to all the sick [Col. 0448B]. But if a bishop either can, or considers someone worthy of his personal visit, he may without delay both bless and touch him with chrism—he whose office it is to prepare the chrism itself. For it cannot be poured upon the impenitent [Note: [Col. 0447C] “To the impenitent”: In Innocent’s printed and manuscript letters (although the author of the gloss testifies otherwise), in the Council of Worms, where this same passage is found, in Alcuin and Ivo, and in several manuscripts of Gratian, it is read without the negation. The gloss, as found in ancient exemplars, explains both readings.] [Note: [Col. 0447] “poured”: the same editions.], because it is a kind of sacrament. For to those to whom the other sacraments are denied, how can one kind be thought capable of being granted? Thus, dearest brother, we have taken care to answer, as far as we could, all the matters which your affection wished us to explain [Note: [Col. 0447] “to explain”: Basel edition.—Part III.].

III. Part. Gratian. Priests should obtain chrism from their own bishops for the consecration of baptism.

Hence, in the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 36 [Note: [Col. 0447] Statutes of the Ancient Church, chapter 87.—Compare chapter 9, Distinction 18.—Burchard, book 4, chapter 76; Ivo, Panormia, book 1, chapter 101; Decree, part 1, chapter 270, from the council at Valence.]:

C. IV. Chrism is to be requested annually from one’s own bishop.

[Col. 0448C] Priests who govern churches throughout dioceses must request chrism not from just any bishops but from their own; nor through a junior [Note: [Col. 0447] “inferior”: collected editions.] cleric, but every year [Note: [Col. 0448C] “Every year”: These words are absent from the two Cologne editions of the councils and from the edition printed in four volumes, and also below, On Consecration, Distinction 4, where the same passage is cited from the council at Valence. Yet they occur in the old Cologne edition and the three-volume edition, in two Paris editions, and in two Vatican manuscripts. In chapter *Literis*, On Consecration, Distinction 3, Pope Fabian directs that new chrism be made every year.] before the solemnity of Easter, either personally or through the person who keeps the sacristy [Note: [Col. 0447] “who is of the same order”: Burchard, Ivo.].

C. V. A presbyter is the same as a bishop; bishops preside over presbyters only by custom. Likewise Jerome, on chapter 1 of the Epistle to Titus, on the words “And appoint.” [Note: [Col. 0447] Anselm, book 7, chapter 129 (130).]

Formerly a presbyter and a bishop were the same; and before factions arose in religion through the devil’s instigation [Col. 0449A], and people said [Note: [Col. 0449] 1 Corinthians 1:12.], “I belong to Paul; I to Apollos; I, however, to Cephas,” churches were governed by the common counsel of presbyters. But after each person began to regard those whom he had baptized as his own rather than Christ’s, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the presbyters, *chosen*, should be set over the rest [Note: [Col. 0449] “all”: collected editions.], to whom the care of the whole Church should belong, and that the seeds of schisms might be removed.

And a little later:

§ 1. Therefore, just as presbyters know that, by the custom of the Church, they are subject to the one set over them, so bishops should know that they are greater than presbyters more by custom than by the truth of the Lord’s ordinance [Note: [Col. 0449] “arrangement”: original.—Anselm.], and that they ought to govern the Church jointly.

[Col. 0449B]

C. VI. It is lawful for presbyters to teach in the presence of bishops [Note: [Col. 0449] “not lawful”: Basel edition.]. The same author, to Rusticus, Bishop of Narbonne, on the seven grades of the Church [Note: [Col. 0449] We have noted above that Jerome’s Epistle to Rusticus is not genuine.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 128 (131).].

Behold, I say that presbyters, with their bishops present and standing at the altar, may perform the sacraments. And below:

§ 1. But because it is written [Note: [Col. 0449] 1 Timothy 5:17.], “Let presbyters be honored with double honor, especially those who labor in the word of the Lord,” it is fitting that they preach; it is useful to bless [Note: [Col. 0449] “For it is useful”: collected editions.]; it is appropriate to confirm; it is proper to give communion; it is necessary to visit the sick, pray for the infirm, and perform all the sacraments of God.

And below:

§ 2. Let none of the bishops, puffed up by the devilish temptation of envy [Note: [Col. 0449] “be puffed up”: Anselm; Basel edition.], be angry in church if presbyters sometimes exhort the people, preach in churches, or, as it is written, bless the congregations [Note: [Col. 0449] “the congregation”: Anselm; collected editions.]. Indeed, to one refusing me these things I would say: whoever does not wish presbyters to do what God commands, let him say: who is greater than Christ? Or what can be set before His body or [Note: [Col. 0449] “and”: the same editions, first Basel.] blood? If the presbyter consecrates Christ when he blesses the sacraments of God at the altar [Note: [Col. 0449] adds “of Christ”: Argentinian and Basel editions.], ought he not to bless the people [Note: [Col. 0449] “bless the people”: collected editions.] who has *also* merited [Note: [Col. 0449] “does not fear”: the same editions.] to consecrate Christ?

And a little later:

§ 3. Concerning laypeople [Note: [Col. 0450C] In the tract it reads: “Nevertheless, the judgment of the high priest must be believed, and what he commands concerning laypeople and women must be done. At your command, most unjust priests, the presbyter of God does not rightly [exercise] the blessing …”] and women: at your command, O most unjust priests, the presbyter loses the office of God’s blessing [Note: [Col. 0449] “offices”: the same editions.], loses the work of his tongue, has no confidence to preach, and is mutilated in every part of his powers [Col. 0450A]. He has only the name of presbyter; he does not retain the fullness and [Note: [Col. 0449] “to”: Lyons II edition.] perfection belonging to his consecration.

§ 4. What, I ask, O priests, is this honor of yours, that you inflict harm upon the flocks? [Note: [Col. 0449] “flocks”: the true reading.] For when, through your power, care worthy of God is taken away from pastors, a kind of contagion and calamity grows among the flocks, and you seek losses to the Lord’s inheritance [Note: [Col. 0450C] In the same place it reads: “and do you not seek losses to the inheritance of our God, while you alone desire to exercise power in the churches?”], while you wish alone to wield power in the Church.

After a few intervening words:

§ 5. Presbyters, from the beginning, *as we read,* were commanded to be judges in disputes; presbyters ought to take part in the counsel of priests [Note: [Col. 0449] “council”: original; adds “ought”: collected editions.], because presbyters themselves, as we read, are called bishops, according to what is written to the bishop [Note: [Col. 0450C] At this point the reasoning in the tract is much fuller [Col. 0451C], and many other passages from the Apostle to Timothy are adduced for this authority.] [Note: [Col. 0449] 1 Timothy 4:14.]: “Do not neglect the grace given you through the laying on [Col. 0450B] of the hands of the presbyterate” [Note: [Col. 0449] “presbysteri”: collected editions.—Böhm.]; and elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0449] Acts of the Apostles 20:28.] to the elders: “He made you bishops to govern the Church of God” [Note: [Col. 0449] “his own”: collected editions.].

And below:

§ 6. But proud priests hate this title in presbyters [Note: [Col. 0449] “in the name of presbyter”: collected editions, from Anselm.], since they do not wish to be what Christ was—Christ who washed His disciples’ feet, who was baptized by John, although John proclaimed that he himself [Note: [Col. 0449] “he”: Lyons II and III editions; absent from the other collected editions.] ought to be baptized by the Lord. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0449] “For this reason I write these things to you”: collected editions.] I write these things, so that, if the error of past times can no longer be recalled, humility may at least now be preserved in the churches [Note: [Col. 0449] The words enclosed by asterisks are not found in Anselm.]: so that presbyters may do in their churches what is done at Rome; or in the East; in Italy; *in Crete, in Cyprus*; in Africa; *in Illyricum*; in Spain; in Britain; and *also in part* throughout [Note: [Col. 0449] “in Gaul”: collected editions, from Anselm.] Gaul [Note: [Col. 0449] adds “in Gascony”: Basel edition.]; what is done in all places where humility endures; what is also [Note: [Col. 0449] adds “also”: collected editions.] done in heaven [Col. 0450C]—which is greater—where you read that the seats of the angels [Note: [Col. 0449] “their”: original.—Anselm.] are arranged [Note: [Col. 0449] “are read to have been arranged”: collected editions.].

C. VII. Bishops and clerics should render honor to one another. Likewise, to Nepotian, Epistle II [Note: [Col. 0449] written A.D. 392.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 121 (131).].

Be subject to your pontiff, and receive him as a parent of your soul [Note: [Col. 0449] “love”: the same editions, from Anselm.].

And a little later:

§ 1. But bishops should know that they are priests [Note: [Col. 0449] “know”: the same editions, from the same source.], not lords; let them honor clerics as clerics, so that *they also* [Note: [Col. 0449] adds “bishops”: the same editions, from the same source.] may receive honor from clerics [Note: [Col. 0449] “from clerics” absent from the Argentinian and Basel editions.] as bishops.

§ 2. That saying of the orator Domitius is apt [Col. 0451A]: “Why,” he says, “should I regard you as a leading man, when you do not regard me as a senator?”

§ 3. Let us recognize Aaron and his sons as representing the bishop and presbyters.

§ 4. One Lord, one temple [Note: [Col. 0451] adds “one baptism”: the same editions.], and one *also* ministry.

§ 5. Let us always remember what the apostle Peter commands [Note: [Col. 0451] 1 Peter 5:2.] priests [Note: [Col. 0451] “commands”: Lyons and Paris editions; “commanded”: other collected editions.]: “Feed the Lord’s flock which is among you, exercising oversight not under compulsion [Note: [Col. 0451] “compulsorily”: collected editions.], but willingly according to God [Note: [Col. 0451] “according to the Lord’s command”: the same editions.]; not *for* shameful gain, but willingly; nor as lording it over the clergy, but as examples to the flock [Note: [Col. 0451] “flock”: the same editions.] from the heart, so that when the chief Shepherd appears you may receive the unfading crown of glory.”

§ 6. It is a very bad custom in certain churches for presbyters to remain silent and not speak when bishops are present, as though [Col. 0451B] the bishops either envied them or did not [Note: [Col. 0451] “disdained”: the same editions.] deign to hear them. “And if something is revealed to another,” says [Note: [Col. 0451] “as the apostle Paul says”: the same editions; compare 1 Corinthians 14:30.] the apostle Paul, “who is seated, let the first be silent.” And a little later: “A wise son is the glory of his father” [Note: [Col. 0451] Proverbs 10:1.]. Let the bishop rejoice in his judgment [Note: [Col. 0451] “in his judgment”: collected edition.—Böhm.] when he has chosen such priests for Christ.

C. VIII. Presbyters should not precede bishops, but accompany or follow them. Likewise, from the Council of Laodicea, chapter 56 [Note: [Col. 0451] held between A.D. 347 and 381. *More precisely, the received version of Isidore.—In the Spanish Collection: “if he is away.”].

Presbyters ought not to enter before the bishop enters and sit upon the benches of judgment, but ought to enter with the bishop, unless perhaps the bishop is ill or [Col. 0452A] is known to be absent because of the necessities of travel [Note: [Col. 0451C] “Because of the necessities of travel”: thus the old version; but Dionysius is much closer to the Greek wording: “unless perhaps the bishop is detained by illness or is away” (πλὴν εἰ μὴ ἀνωμαλοίη, ἢ ἀποδημεῖ).] [Note: [Col. 0451] “inconvenience”: Argentinian edition.].

C. IX. A bishop should recognize himself as not the lord but the colleague of presbyters. Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 34 [Note: [Col. 0451] chapter 12, Statutes of the Ancient Church.—Compare chapter 9, Distinction 18.].

A bishop, sitting anywhere, should not allow a presbyter to remain standing [Note: [Col. 0451] adds “for a long time”: original in Ballerini.].

C. X. On the same matter. Likewise, from the same council, chapter 35 [Note: [Col. 0451] chapter 2 there.—Ivo, Decree, part 5, chapter 337.].

In church *also* [Note: [Col. 0451] absent from the original in Ballerini.—“in the assembly of the Church”: Spanish Collection.] and in the assembly of presbyters, the bishop should sit in a higher place. But within his house he should recognize himself as the colleague of presbyters.

C. XI. Without the bishop’s command a presbyter should not sign infants. Likewise, from the Council of Pope Martin [Note: [Col. 0451] chapter 57, among the chapters of Martin of Braga, from the First Council of Toledo, held A.D. 400.—Compare On Consecration, Distinction 4, chapter 124.].

[Col. 0452B] A presbyter, when the bishop is present, shall not sign infants unless the bishop has commanded him to do so.

C. XII. On the same matter. PALEA. [Likewise, from the Council of Neocaesarea [Note: [Col. 0451D] “Neocaesarea”: previously it was cited as from Genoa [ [Col. 0451] “Genitensis”: Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice I editions; “Januensis”: the other collected editions, and Lyons II and III.]. The heading has been restored from the other collectors. [Col. 0452C] This is substantially Dionysius’s version.], chapter 13 [Note: [Col. 0451] held A.D. 314.—Burchard, book 5, title 4; Ivo, Decree, part 2, chapter 53.]:

“Country presbyters cannot, in a city church, when the bishop or the presbyters of that city are present, offer, give the sacrificial bread [Note: [Col. 0452C] “Consecrated”: everywhere else the reading is “sanctified.” In the printed council the Greek is ἄρτον διδόναι ἐν εὐχῇ, ‘to give bread in prayer’; but in Balsamon it is ἄρτον εὐχῆς, that is, ‘bread of mystical prayer.’], or present the chalice. But if these are absent, and they alone are called upon to give the prayer [Note: [Col. 0452D] “To give the prayer”: καὶ εἰς εὐχὴν κληθῇ μόνος, δίδωσιν, that is, ‘and if he alone is called to the mystical prayer, he gives.’], they ought to give it [Note: [Col. 0451] “ought”: collected editions.].”

## DISTINCTION XCVI

[Col. 0451]

[Col. 0451C] GRATIAN.

That decree of the Emperor Honorius which, as stated above, concerns the election of the supreme pontiff, is proved to be of no force, since laypersons are never found to have been granted authority to make dispositions not only concerning orders but even concerning ecclesiastical property. Hence whatever decrees made by rulers concerning orders or ecclesiastical affairs are found to exist are shown to possess no authority.

Therefore Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, presiding over a synod, said [Note: [Col. 0451] Third Roman Synod, held A.D. 502.]:

C. I. Laypersons retain no authority to dispose of ecclesiastical affairs.

Your brotherhood, indeed, obedient to ecclesiastical laws [Note: [Col. 0451] “accustomed”: collected editions.], has, under fear of the divine judgment, determined what had to be established, and has reached the full measure of justice by embracing all matters sufficiently [Note: [Col. 0451] “when it embraces everything”: the same editions.]. A complete determination needs no addition, especially concerning clerics whom the love of domination has seized, causing them to reject the yoke of ecclesiastical discipline [Col. 0453A].

And a little later:

§ 1. It is difficult to recount their offenses; yet I shall not delay in reporting to your venerable order one matter which has occurred. Among other things, they said that a certain Basil of illustrious memory had composed a document, ostensibly out of love for ecclesiastical property, in which no bishop of the Roman Church was present *nor* subscribed [Note: [Col. 0453] “or”: the same editions.], through whom it might have acquired legal validity. But lest I myself *indeed* argue about a matter on which your council should be asked to judge, let it be produced and brought forward [Note: [Col. 0453] “reported”: collected editions.], that from its reading you may know [Note: [Col. 0453] “recognize”: original; Basel edition.] what substance it may have.

The holy synod replied: “Let it be brought forward, that its nature may be recognized.”

And while this was being said, Hormisdas the deacon read:

“When Basil, the most exalted and eminent man, prefect of the praetorium and patrician, also acting as deputy of the most excellent King Odoacer, was seated in the Mausoleum [Note: [Col. 0453C] “When [he was seated] in the Mausoleum”: In the volumes of the councils and the code of canons, the beginning of Basil’s document reads: “When the eminent … had assembled together at [the shrine of] the blessed Apostle Peter.” [ [Col. 0453] In the collection edited by Eusebius Amort, known to be Dionysian, it is read as in the text.]. [Col. 0453B] which is at the blessed Apostle Peter’s [Note: [Col. 0453] “Paul”: collected editions.], he said:

“Although it concerns your zeal and religion that concord be especially preserved in the Church in the election of a bishop, nevertheless, lest the condition of the city be called [Note: [Col. 0453] “recalled”: the same editions.] into question through an occasion of sedition [Note: [Col. 0453] “election”: collected editions.], you remember that, by the admonition of the most blessed man, our Pope Symmachus [Note: [Col. 0453] The former name is absent from the original in Mansi; the latter is lacking in Amort’s collection.], Simplicius [Note: [Col. 0453] “whom”: Argentinian and Basel editions.], which we ought always to keep before our eyes, this was entrusted to us under solemn charge: on account of that disturbance and harm to the venerable Church, if it should happen that he passes from this life, no election of anyone is to be held without our consultation.”

When this was read, Cresconius, bishop of the Church of the city of *Tuder*, rose from the assembly [Note: [Col. 0453] “meeting”: collected editions except Basel.] and said: “Let the holy synod consider here whether, with religious persons passed over—persons to whom concern for so great a pontiff chiefly belongs—laypersons have brought the election into their own power [Note: [Col. 0453] “can bring”: the same editions.], which is plainly contrary to the canons.”

Likewise Hormisdas the deacon read [Note: [Col. 0453] “is read to have said”: the same editions.]:

“For, when we observe what confusion and loss the venerable Church sustained, we are astonished that, with us passed over, anything concerning ecclesiastical property was attempted [Note: [Col. 0453] “ecclesiastical property” is missing from the original.], although, while our bishop was still alive, nothing ought to have been undertaken without us. Therefore [Col. 0454A], if it pleases your highness or holiness, let us preserve with religious reverence all things concerning the election of the future bishop, setting forth especially this law, which we establish for ourselves and our heirs in the devotion of Christian purpose: that no rural or urban estate, nor ornaments or equipment of churches, whether now existing or hereafter coming by any title into the rights of churches, may ever be alienated, by whatever title or contrivance, by the person now to be ordained bishop by common election, or by those who will follow in future ages [Note: [Col. 0453] “follow”: collected editions.]. If anyone should wish to alienate any of these things, the act shall be judged ineffective and void, and let the one acting, consenting [Note: [Col. 0453] adds “giving”: the same editions.], or receiving be anathema.”

§ 2. Maximus, bishop of the Church of Blera [Col. 0454B], said: “Let the holy synod now deign to declare whether it was lawful for a layperson to pronounce an anathema in an ecclesiastical order, or whether a layperson could pronounce an anathema upon a priest and establish, contrary to the canons, something which did not belong to him. Tell me: what does it seem to you? Was it lawful for a layperson to enact a law concerning me?”

The holy synod said: “It was not lawful,” and added: “Read what follows.”

Hormisdas the deacon read:

“And whoever has acquired a rural or urban estate belonging to ecclesiastical right should know that he is protected by no law or prescription. But whether the person who alienated it, or the one succeeding him [Note: [Col. 0453] “the one following him”: collected editions; “who follows in sequence”: original in Mansi and Amort; “who frequently”: original in Merlin.], wishes [Note: [Col. 0454C] “To revoke”: thus corrected from all printed and manuscript copies of the council; previously it read “to retain.”] [Note: [Col. 0453] “attempts”: Basel edition, from the original.] to revoke such an alienated estate, he shall restore it with the fruits which he has received from it [Note: [Col. 0453] “which that [estate]”: original.].”

§ 3. When this was read, Stephen, bishop of the Church of Venosa [Col. 0454C], rose from the assembly [Note: [Col. 0453] “consent”: Argentinian and Lyons I–II editions.] and said: “Let it be read through.”

Hormisdas the deacon read:

“By what penalty it was resolved that even the heirs of the recipient should be bound [Note: [Col. 0454C] In all editions of the councils it reads: “What penalty it pleased [the synod] to impose upon the heirs and successors of the recipient.” In the manuscript code of canons, the word *proheredes* (‘successors’) is absent.]. In this matter every cleric is to have freedom to object [Note: [Col. 0453] adds “none”: collected editions.]. For it is unjust, and akin to sacrilege, that things which anyone has given or at least bequeathed to the venerable Church for the salvation or *for* the repose of their souls, for the sake of the poor, should be transferred to another by those to whom it most especially belonged to preserve them. Certainly, whatever appears in gems, gold, silver, or garments less suitable for the use or adornment of the Church [Col. 0455A], and which cannot be preserved and last long, should be sold at a just valuation and should benefit religious distribution [Note: [Col. 0455] “religious distribution”: the same editions.].”

§ 4. When this had been read, Laurentius, bishop of the Church of Milan, said: “This document could bind no pontiff of the Roman city, because laypersons were not permitted to possess any authority for establishing matters in the Church apart from the Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. 0455] “pope”: Argentinian and Basel editions, with the original.]. Their necessity is to obey, not authority to command—especially since neither the Roman pope subscribed nor the assent of any metropolitan, as required by the canons, is recorded.”

§ 5. Peter, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, said: “It is manifest that the document published in our assembly has no force [Note: [Col. 0455] “has no force”: collected editions.], because it neither agrees with the canons nor appears to have been composed by anyone but a layperson [Note: [Col. 0455] “lay”: collected editions.]; above all because no bishop of the apostolic see is shown to have been present at it or to have confirmed it by his own subscription [Note: [Col. 0455] adds “it”: the same editions.].”

§ 6. Eulalius, bishop of the Church of Syracuse, said: “It is established by most evident proofs that the document read in the priestly council is invalid: first, because it appears to have been made contrary to the rules of the Fathers by laypersons, even if religious—persons to whom no authority ever has been granted to make any disposition concerning ecclesiastical resources [Note: [Col. 0455] “anything else”: Argentinian and Basel editions.]; secondly, because it is shown to have been confirmed by the subscription of no bishop of the apostolic see. If the holy Fathers decreed that whatever priests of any province attempt [Note: [Col. 0455] “conduct”: collected editions; “establish”: original in Amort.] within their own borders, without their metropolitan’s authority, must be void, how much more plainly is that known to lack force which was undertaken at the apostolic see when no bishop was present [Note: [Col. 0455] “now being present”: collected editions.]—the bishop who, by the merit [Note: [Col. 0455] “by the prerogative of the merits”: original in Mansi; “by the prerogative of merit”: original in Amort.] of the blessed Apostle Peter, holds primacy of the priesthood throughout the whole world and customarily gives validity to synodal enactments—by laypersons, even though some bishops consented, who nevertheless could not prejudice the pontiff by whom they are known to have been consecrated?”

§ 7. The holy synod said: “Although, according to the presentation of our venerable brothers [Note: [Col. 0455] absent from the Argentinian and Basel editions.], Laurentius, Peter, Eulalius, Cresconius, Maximus, and Stephen, it is not uncertain to us that this document itself has no force, nevertheless [Note: [Col. 0455] “although even”: original.] even if it could have stood on any ground [Col. 0456A], it was altogether fitting that it should be invalidated and annulled in a synodal assembly by the prudent judgment of your blessedness, lest it remain as a precedent for any laypersons, however religious or powerful, in any city, in any manner, to decree anything concerning ecclesiastical resources, whose administration is taught to have been entrusted by God without dispute to priests alone [Note: [Col. 0455] “if only”: Basel edition.].”

Therefore, in the sixth session of the Council of Chalcedon, Emperor Marcian said among other things [Note: [Col. 0455] held A.D. 451.—Anselm, book 3, chapter 107.]:

C. II. Emperors ought to attend a synod in order to confirm the faith, not to display power.

Following the example of the most religious ruler Constantine, we have wished to attend the synod in order to confirm the faith, not to display power, so that once truth has been discovered [Col. 0456B], the multitude may no longer be drawn into discord by corrupt doctrines.

C. III. On the same matter. Likewise, from the same sixth session, at the end [Note: [Col. 0455] held A.D. 451.—Anselm, there.—Deusdedit, part 3.].

There are certain chapters which, in honor of your reverence, we have reserved for you [Note: [Col. 0455] “observed”: collected editions, especially Lyons II and III.], judging it more fitting that they should regularly be confirmed by you through a synod than enacted by our law.

C. IV. It is not fitting for emperors to attend a synodal assembly except when faith is at issue. Likewise, Pope Nicholas, in his letter to Emperor Michael beginning, “We had proposed.” [Note: [Col. 0455] written A.D. 865.—Collection in three parts, part 1, title 62, chapter 6 and following.]

Where have you read that your predecessor emperors [Note: [Col. 0455] “our”: Argentinian and Basel editions.] attended synodal assemblies, except perhaps those in which [Note: [Col. 0455] “certain ones where”: collected editions.] the faith was treated—a faith which is universal, [Col. 0456C] which *is* common to all, which pertains not only to clerics but also to laypeople and indeed to all Christians whatsoever?

C. V. Those set over divine matters cannot be judged by those who are set over human matters. The same, in the same letter [Note: [Col. 0455] Collection in three parts, there.].

Finally, we are wholly unable to understand how those who have been permitted to preside only over human, not divine, affairs dare to judge those through whom divine things are administered.

C. VI. Neither should the emperor usurp the rights of the pontiff, nor the pontiff royal rights. The same, a little below [Note: [Col. 0455] The actual words, however, are taken from Gelasius’s treatise on the bond of anathema.—Collection in three parts, there.—Compare above, Distinction 10, chapter 8.].

When the truth was reached [Note: [Col. 0455C] “When the truth was reached”: Immediately after the final words of the preceding chapter, Nicholas’s letter continues: “These things existed before Christ’s advent, so that certain persons might typologically be both kings and priests. Holy history relates that Saint Melchizedek was such; and the devil imitated this in his members—for he always strives, in a tyrannical spirit, to claim for himself what belongs to divine worship—so that pagan emperors might be called likewise supreme pontiffs. But when the truth was reached, no emperor or pontiff henceforth …” Nothing has been changed, both because of the gloss and because this is the beginning of the chapter. Several other relevant points are noted above, Distinction 10, chapter *Quoniam*.], neither did the emperor seize for himself the rights of the pontificate, nor did the pontiff usurp the imperial title [Note: [Col. 0457] “usurp”: Basel edition.].
