For the one mediator between God and humankind, the man Christ Jesus, *thus*, by distinct acts and distinct dignities, separated the offices of the two powers, intending that His own people should be exalted upward by healing humility, not again cast down into hell by human pride [Note: [Col. 0457] “hell”: collected editions.], so that Christian emperors might need pontiffs for eternal life, and pontiffs might employ imperial laws only for the course of temporal affairs; in order that spiritual action might remain separate from carnal incursions [Note: [Col. 0457] “from carnal”: the same editions.], and *therefore* one serving God might not involve himself in secular affairs, while conversely the person involved in secular affairs might not appear to preside over divine things.

[Col. 0457B]

C. VII. A pontiff can neither be bound nor released at all by secular power. The same, in the same letter, after a few intervening words [Note: [Col. 0457] Collection in three parts, there.—Anselm, book 1, chapter 71 (75).].

It is shown clearly enough that a pontiff *can* in no way be bound or released by secular power, since Constantine, that pious ruler, is known to have called him God—as we recalled much earlier [Note: [Col. 0457] “whom”: collected editions.]—and it is manifest that God cannot be judged by human beings [Note: [Col. 0457] adds “all”: Basel edition.]. But Theodosius the Younger, writing to the First Holy Synod of Ephesus, said [Note: [Col. 0457D] These words are taken from the letter of the Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian sent through Candidianus to the Ephesian Synod, found at the end of that synod’s first session. In the old version preserved in the Vatican Library and in the version published at Paris, these very words occur here together with those quoted by Nicholas [Col. 0458D], and they agree very well with the Greek.]:

“Accordingly, Candidianus, the most distinguished count of the corps of imperial bodyguards, has been appointed to go to your most holy synod and in no respect to participate in *those* inquiries—or rather expositions—which are to be made concerning pious doctrines [Note: [Col. 0457] “these”: Lyons II and III editions.]. For it is unlawful for one who is not of the order of the most holy bishops to interfere in ecclesiastical deliberations” [Col. 0457C].

And after a few words:

§ 1. Since these things have thus been clearly established, it is evident that our fellow minister Ignatius could in no way whatsoever have been expelled merely by an imperial judgment. Since the assent of bishops also followed in his condemnation, it is evident that this was done from flattery, not by lawful enactment.

C. VIII. The emperor ought not judge the acts of pontiffs. The same, to Emperor Louis [Note: [Col. 0457] Rather, from the same letter of Pope Nicholas to Michael.—Collection in three parts, there.].

In the Scriptures it is related that the Emperor Constantine said: “Truly, if I had seen with my own eyes a priest of God, or any of those clothed in the monastic habit, committing sin, I would strip off my cloak [Note: [Col. 0457] “I would unwrap [it] and cover [him]”: the original.] and cover him, lest he be seen by anyone.” [Note: [Col. 0457] “in the monastic habit”: the editions collectively, especially Lugdd. II and III.] Therefore [Note: [Col. 0457] added: *igitur* (“therefore”): the editions collectively.], most beloved (*desideratissime*) son [Note: [Col. 0457] *desiderantissime*: Bas.], you are necessarily admonished that, just as you appear equal to him in faith, religion, and equality of honour, so you should likewise strive to equal him in humility and devotion, so that, following the example of him who showed himself such before all other examples, you may be found in no respect inferior to him but rather superior. [Note: [Col. 0457] “such”: the editions collectively; “such examples”: the editions collectively.] We have said this because we wish to make you cautious: if you should hear anything concerning the priests of the Lord, who are rightly called fathers [Note: [Col. 0457] “of souls”: the editions collectively.] that brings confusion to devout minds, then, imitating Noah’s modest sons, do not remain unbridled, but henceforth cover your father’s shame, so that, under the Lord’s governance, you may deserve, as they did, to be filled with abundant blessing. [Note: [Col. 0457] “of the Lord”: the editions of Arg. and Bas.; “of lords”: other editions.]

### C. IX. Priests are considered the fathers and teachers of kings and princes.

Likewise, from the letter of Gregory VII to Hermann, bishop of Metz, book VIII, letter 21. [Note: [Col. 0457] Written A.D. 1080.—Anselm, book 1, c. 84; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, c. 108; *Decretum*, part 5, c. 378.]

Who can doubt that the priests of Christ are regarded as the fathers and teachers of kings, princes, and all the faithful? Is it not recognized as wretched madness if a son should endeavour to subject his father, or a pupil his teacher, to himself, and by unjust bonds submit to his own power the one by whom he believes that he may be bound and loosed not only on earth but also in heaven?

### C. X. The sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power govern the helm of this world.

Likewise, Pope Gelasius to the Emperor Anastasius. [Note: [Col. 0457] More probably from the same letter of Gregory VII.—Anselm, book 1, c. 73 (84); *Panormia*, book 5, c. 109; *Polycraticus*, book 1, title 27.]

There are indeed two things, most august Emperor, by which this world is principally ruled: the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power. Of these, the burden borne by priests is so much the graver because they must render an account at the divine judgment even for the kings themselves. [Note: [Col. 0457] *regiminibus* (“governments”): Lugdd. II and III; *regibus vel legibus* (“kings or laws”): the remaining editions collectively.] [Note: [Col. 0458D] This chapter is taken from the same letter of Gregory VII as the preceding one; from this beginning down to the word “will,” the words are Gelasius’s own, from the letter printed and cited by Gregory VII.] And shortly afterwards:

§ 1. You know, therefore, that in these matters you depend on their judgment, not that they are to be reduced to your will. [Note: [Col. 0457] “wish”: Anselm.]

§ 2. Supported by such ordinances and authorities, many pontiffs excommunicated some kings and others emperors. For, if a particular example concerning rulers is required, Blessed Pope Innocent excommunicated the Emperor Arcadius because he consented to the expulsion of St John Chrysostom from his see. [Note: [Col. 0459C] “He excommunicated”: if the following chapter—“Likewise, below, 15, question 6”—is inserted here, this portion of the letter will be complete.]

Blessed Ambrose also, though holy, was not the bishop of the universal Church; nevertheless, for an offence that did not appear so grave to other priests, he excommunicated and excluded the Emperor Theodosius the Great from the Church. [Note: [Col. 0459] “by other priests”: the editions collectively, especially Lugdd. II and III.] In his writings he also showed that the priestly dignity is higher than royal power to a greater degree than gold is more precious than lead. [Note: [Col. 0459] “order”: the editions collectively.] At the beginning of his *Pastoral* he writes as follows:

> “Honour, brethren, and the sublimity of the episcopate cannot be equalled by any comparisons. If you compare it with the splendour of kings and the diadem of princes, it will be far lower than lead is when compared with the brilliance of gold; for you see the necks of kings and princes bowed at the knees of priests, and, after kissing their right hands, they believe themselves strengthened by their prayers.” [Note: [Col. 0459] “to receive communion or to be fortified”: Lugdd. II and III; “to receive communion or to be protected”: the other editions.]

### C. XI. Emperors ought to be subject to pontiffs, not set over them.

Likewise, Pope John. [Note: [Col. 0459] The author of this chapter has not been discovered, nor does it appear possible to attribute it to John VIII.—Anselm, book 4, c. 12; *Polycraticus*, book 1, title 19.]

If the emperor is Catholic—though we say this with due regard for him—he is a son, not a prelate, of the Church. In matters pertaining to religion, it befits him to learn, not to teach. He possesses the prerogatives of his power, divinely granted to him for administering public laws, so that, not ungrateful for those benefits, he may usurp nothing contrary to the ordering of the heavenly hierarchy.

For God wished matters that are to be arranged in the Church to belong to priests, not to the powers of the world; and, if those powers are faithful, he wished them to be subject to the priests of their Church. Let him not claim another’s right or ministry, which has been entrusted to another, lest he strive against him by whom all things have been established, and seem to fight against the benefits of him from whom he received his own power. [Note: [Col. 0459] “contend”: the editions collectively; “and not”: the same editions, especially Lugdd. II and III.]

Almighty God willed that the clergy and priests of the Christian religion should be ordained, and that those returning from error should be examined and received, by pontiffs and priests—not by public laws or secular powers. Christian emperors ought to submit their enactments to ecclesiastical prelates, not set them above them.

### C. XII. On the same subject. [PALEA.]

Likewise, Gelasius to the Eastern bishops. [Note: [Col. 0459] Written about A.D. 494.—Anselm, book 6, title 157 (155); *Polycraticus*, book 1, title 19.]

> “No one has ever judged pontiffs except the Church; human laws have no authority to pronounce judgment on such persons without the pontiffs principally appointed by the Church. Christian rulers are accustomed to obey the decrees of the Church, not to place their own authority above them; a prince is accustomed to bow his head to bishops, not to judge their heads.” [Note: [Col. 0459] “ought to judge”: the editions collectively, from Anselm.]

### C. XIII. On the same subject. PALEA.

[Note: [Col. 0459C] In Anselm, book 4, in place of the heading of chapter 32, these words occur: “That the Emperor Constantine granted to the Pope the crown and all royal dignity in the city of Rome, in Italy, and in the western regions.” At the beginning of the same chapter 32 one reads: “In the Acts of Blessed Sylvester,” etc., down to the end of this and the following *Palea*, as also in the collection of Deusdedit.]

> “The Emperor Constantine granted the crown and all royal dignity in the city of Rome, in Italy, and in the western regions to the Apostolic See. For in the Acts of Blessed Sylvester—which Blessed Pope Gelasius recalls as having been read by Catholics in a council of seventy bishops, and says that many churches imitate according to ancient usage—one reads as follows.”

### C. XIV. On the same subject. PALEA

[Note: [Col. 0459D] This *Palea* is found in many manuscripts in which other *Paleae* are not usually found.]

[Note: [Col. 0459] It is not sufficiently certain whether the author of this chapter was Greek or Roman. Yet it appears to have been composed long before Pseudo-Isidore, in whose collection it occurs, from the Acts of Blessed Sylvester, which were translated from the Greek book of Eusebius. Gratian took this canon from Anselm, book 4, c. 32; hence the Correctors acted wrongly in reducing it to the text of Isidore, which is most thoroughly corrupted.—Deusdedit, book 4, c. 1.]

> “On the fourth day after his baptism, the Emperor Constantine conferred a privilege upon the pontiff of the Roman Church, so that throughout the whole Roman world priests should have him as their head, just as judges have the king. [Note: [Col. 0459D] “Constantine”: these words down to “In that privilege” occur not only in Anselm and Deusdedit, but also in the Acts of Blessed Sylvester, among the acts attributed to Constantine during the eight days after his baptism.]
>
> “In that privilege, among other things, the following is read: ‘We have judged it useful, together with all our satraps, the whole senate, and our nobles [Note: [Col. 0459] “also our nobles”: Anselm.], and likewise all the people subject to the rule of Roman glory [Note: [Col. 0461] “of the Church”: the editions collectively.], that, just as Blessed Peter is seen to have been appointed on earth as vicar of the Son of God, so also the pontiffs who perform the office of that prince of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0461] “on earth”: the editions collectively, especially Bas.; “in the place of that prince of the apostles”: Anselm.] may obtain from us and our empire a power of primacy greater than the clemency of our earthly imperial serenity appears to possess, choosing that the prince of the apostles himself, or his vicars, should be steadfast patrons for us before God.
>
> “And just as our earthly imperial power is honoured, so we have decreed that his most holy Roman Church be reverently honoured, and that the most sacred see of Blessed Peter be gloriously exalted above our empire and earthly throne, granting to it power, dignity and glory, strength, and imperial honour. [Note: [Col. 0461] “and glory”: the editions collectively.] And by our decree we establish that it shall hold primacy both over the four principal sees—Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem, and Constantinople—and over all the churches of God throughout the whole world; and that the pontiff who, in his time, shall preside over that most holy Roman Church shall stand higher than, and be prince of, all the priests of the whole world; and that by his judgment whatever must be arranged for the worship of God or for the stability of Christian faith shall be ordered.
>
> “And below:
>
> “§ 1. We have bestowed estates upon the churches of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul for the maintenance of their lights [Note: [Col. 0461] “for their arrangement”: Isidore Mercator and Anselm.], and have enriched them with various resources. [Note: [Col. 0461] In Anselm the passage reads: “And by our imperial command we enriched them in the West with various resources, and also from the northern region,” etc.] By our sacred imperial command, we have granted them from our bounty possessions in the East and West, and also in the northern and southern regions, namely in Judaea, Greece, Asia, Thrace, Africa, and Italy, and in various islands, upon this express condition: that all things be disposed of through the hands of our most blessed father Sylvester, supreme pontiff, and his successors.
>
> “And below:
>
> “§ 2. To Blessed Sylvester, our father, supreme pontiff and Pope of the universal city of Rome, and to all his successor-pontiffs who shall sit in the see of Blessed Peter until the end of the world, we herewith hand over [Note: [Col. 0461] “we have handed over”: the Venetian editions I and II and Lugd. I; “we hand over”: the remaining editions.] our imperial Lateran palace [Note: [Col. 0461] “our”: absent from the editions of Arg. and Bas.]; then the diadem, that is, the crown of our head; likewise the *phrygium*; also the *superhumeral*, that is, the *lorum* customarily worn around the imperial neck; further, the purple cloak, scarlet tunic, and all imperial garments; also the dignity of the imperial equestrian officials [Note: [Col. 0463] “of the imperial presiding officials, and also the horse”: Ivo, *Decretum*; “of the imperial presiding officials and preceding horsemen”: the editions of Arg. and Bas.]. We confer likewise the imperial sceptres, all the standards, the *banda* [Note: [Col. 0463] “banners”: Anselm and the editions collectively.], various imperial ornaments, the entire ceremonial procession of imperial eminence, and the glory of our power. [Note: [Col. 0463C] “Imperial equestrian officials”: in Greek Balsamon has: *Καὶ ἀξιώματα τῶν βασιλικῶν ἀλόγων*, that is, “and the dignities of the imperial horses.”
>
> “§ 3. We establish that the most reverend clergy serving the same most holy Roman Church in its various orders [Note: [Col. 0463] “in various orders”: the editions collectively.] shall possess that singular height, power, and pre-eminence with which our most illustrious senate appears adorned [Note: [Col. 0463C] “height of singular power and pre-eminence”: the editions collectively, Anselm, and Ivo.], namely, that they shall be made patricians and consuls, and that we proclaim them decorated with the other imperial dignities. [Note: [Col. 0463C] The Greek reads: *Καὶ ἔχειν ἐκείνην τὴν ὑψηλότητα καὶ μεγαλοσύνην, ἣν κεκόσμηται ἡ μεγάλη σύγκλητος ἡμῶν, ἤτοι οἱ πατρίκιοι, καὶ οἱ κόνσουλοι, ἤτοι οἱ ὕπατοι, καὶ λοιπὰ ἀξιώματα*—that is, “And that they should possess that height and magnificence with which our great senate is adorned, namely the patricians and consuls, that is, the *hypati*, and the remaining dignities.”]
>
> “And just as the imperial service is adorned [Note: [Col. 0463] “with imperial dignities”: the editions collectively.], so we decree that the clergy of the holy Roman Church be adorned. [Note: [Col. 0463] “stands decorated”: the same editions, with Anselm and Ivo.] And just as the imperial power is arrayed with various offices—namely chamberlains, doorkeepers, and all guards [Note: [Col. 0463] “chamberlains”: the same editions.]—so we wish the holy Roman Church also to be adorned.
>
> “And, that pontifical dignity may shine forth most splendidly, we decree also that the clergy of this holy Roman Church shall decorate horses with *manipuli* [Note: [Col. 0463] “*mappulae*”: the editions collectively, from Anselm.] and linens, that is, with the brightest white, and ride them thus. [Note: [Col. 0463] “that they ride decorated horses”: the same editions, from the same source.]
>
> “And just as our senate uses footwear with *udones*, that is, footwear brightened with white linen [Note: [Col. 0463D] The Greek wording differs somewhat throughout this passage: *Καὶ ὡς ἡ ἡμετέρα σύγκλητος φέρει ὑποδήματα, ἤτοι σανδάλια λευκὰ διὰ ὀθονίων, οὕτως καὶ τὰ οὐράνια, ὡς καὶ τά γήϊνα πρὸς αἴνεσιν τοῦ Θεοῦ*—that is, “And as our senate wears shoes, or white sandals with linen, so also may heavenly things, like earthly things, be for the praise of God.”], so let the clergy use them, so that, as heavenly things, so also earthly things may be adorned to the praise of God.
>
> “§ 4. Before all else, by our decree we grant to our most holy father Sylvester himself and his successors permission to make a cleric, at their own discretion, whomever they choose and to enrol him among the number of religious clerics; no one whatsoever may dare arrogantly to oppose this. [Note: [Col. 0464C] The Greek reads: *Ἵνα ἐάν τις τῆς συγκλήτου βουληθῇ μετὰ ἰδίου θελήματος, καὶ εὐαρήστου, γενέσθαι κληρικὸς, καὶ ἐν τῷ ἀριθμῷ τῶν ἁγίων κληρικῶν συναριθμεῖσθαι, μήτις τολμᾷ ἀπὸ πάντων ἐμποδίζειν τούτῳ*—that is, “If anyone from the senate should, of his own will and as pleases him, desire to become a cleric and to be enrolled among the number of holy clerics, let no one among all persons dare to hinder him.”]
>
> “§ 5. We have therefore decreed this also: that he and his successors should use the diadem—that is, the crown which we granted him from our own head—of purest gold and precious gems, and wear it on the head, to the praise of God and in honour of Blessed Peter. [Note: [Col. 0463] “We decree”: the editions of Bas. and Lugdd. II and III.] Yet the most blessed Pope, because he wears the crown of the clerical office for the glory of Blessed Peter, did not at all permit himself to use that golden crown. [Note: [Col. 0463] This is absent from Anselm, Ivo, and the editions collectively.] We therefore placed with our own hands upon his most sacred head a *phrygium* shining with white brilliance, signifying the Lord’s resurrection [Note: [Col. 0463] “but we”: there.], and, holding the bridle of his horse in reverence for Blessed Peter, we performed for him the office of groom. We established that all his successors should use the same *phrygium* in processions as a special privilege, in imitation of our empire.
>
> “§ 6. Therefore, lest the summit of pontifical dignity be debased, but rather be adorned in glory and power more than the dignity of an earthly empire, behold: we hand over and leave both our palace, as stated above [Note: [Col. 0463] “as aforesaid”: Anselm and Ivo.], and the city of Rome, and all provinces, places, and cities of Italy and the western regions [Note: [Col. 0463] “accidental regions”: the Venetian editions I and II.], to our aforesaid most blessed father Sylvester, universal pope. [Note: [Col. 0463] “we grant”: Isidore Mercator and the editions collectively.] We decree that they shall be administered by him and his successors under this sacred and pragmatic constitution of ours, and we grant them to remain under the right of the holy Roman Church. [Note: [Col. 0463] “to remain”: the same editions, from Anselm.]
>
> “§ 7. We have therefore judged it fitting that our empire and royal power should be transferred to the eastern regions [Note: [Col. 0463] Absent from the editions collectively, especially Lugdd. II and III, which read: “from the eastern regions.”], that a city bearing our name should be built in the best place of the province of Byzantium, and that our empire should be established there; because where the primacy of priests and the head of the Christian religion has been established by the heavenly Emperor, it is not just that an earthly emperor should have power there.
>
> “§ 8. We decree that all these things which we have established and confirmed by this sacred imperial decree of ours and by other divine decrees [Note: [Col. 0464D] “All these things”: there is also considerable variation in the wording here, though the sense is nearly the same.] shall remain inviolate and unshaken until the end of the world. [Note: [Col. 0463] “we have decreed”: the editions collectively, especially Lugdd. II and III.] Therefore, before the living God [Note: [Col. 0463] “before you, God”: the editions of Arg. and Bas.], who commanded us to reign, and before his dreadful judgment, we adjure [Col. 0465A] by this imperial constitution of ours [Note: [Col. 0465] The words marked by asterisks are absent from Anselm.] all our successors who shall be emperors, and all nobles, satraps, the most illustrious senate, and the entire people, now and in future times and in all times past, throughout the whole world subject to our empire, that none of them may in any way be permitted to infringe [Note: [Col. 0465] “break”: the editions collectively, from Anselm.] or overthrow [Note: [Col. 0465] “be overthrown”: the same editions, especially Lugdd. II and III.] these provisions.
>
> “But should anyone—which we do not believe—prove a violator or despiser in this matter, let him be bound under eternal condemnations; let him find God’s holy ones, Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, opposed to him in this present life and in the life to come; and let him, consumed in the lowest hell with the devil, perish together with all the ungodly.
>
> “We have confirmed the document of this imperial decree of ours with our own hands and placed it upon the venerable body of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Given at Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the fourth consulship [Note: [Col. 0465] “in his fourth consulship”: the editions collectively.] of our lord Flavius Constantine Augustus and the consulship of Gallicanus, *V. C.* [vir clarissimus].” [Note: [Col. 0465] “fourth council”: the same editions, especially Lugdd. II and III.]

[Note: [Col. 0459D] From “Useful” to the end is taken from the Acts or Deeds of St Sylvester, in which much precedes and much is later narrated more fully. Here, however, only what appears in the collections of Anselm and Deusdedit seems to be cited. The proper title of this section in the Acts is: “The privilege of the holy Roman Church, established by the Lord Constantine Augustus for St Sylvester, bishop of the city of Rome, and all his successors for ever, and offered upon the body of Blessed Peter the apostle.” Concerning this privilege Leo IX, in Letter I, or the treatise against the unheard-of presumptions of Michael of Constantinople and Leo, bishop of Acrida, chapter 13, says: “We shall produce publicly a few passages from the privilege of Constantine himself, laid with a golden cross by his hand upon the venerable body of the heavenly key-bearer.” Gelasius, in the council of seventy bishops, also speaks of the same Acts or Deeds as though approving them; they are cited above in Distinction 15, chapter *Sancta Romana*. The Roman Martyrology and Usuard, on the feast of St Sylvester, read: “His illustrious Acts are extant.” They are still found, written in very ancient script, in the Vatican Library and in the Abbey of Nonantola. Their translator says in his preface:

> “Our historian Eusebius, bishop of the Palestinian city of Caesarea, when writing ecclesiastical history, omitted matters contained in other short works, or which he remembers having related. For he caused twenty books to be compiled containing the passions of martyrs, bishops, confessors, holy virgins, and women from almost all provinces. Then he followed the succession from the Apostle Peter and recorded the names and deeds of all bishops, and of those cities known to hold the summit of the pontificate through apostolic sees, namely Rome, Antioch, Jerusalem, Ephesus, and Alexandria. In Greek he recorded the names and deeds, down to his own time, of all former bishops of these cities. From this number you have commanded me, holy and blessed lord father, to translate from Greek into Latin the life of St Sylvester, one of the bishops of Rome.”

By these words, whoever the author of this preface may be, he plainly professes that the same Acts were written in Greek by Eusebius. They are also related in the Life of Blessed Sylvester in very ancient pontificals and manuscripts containing lives of the saints. Pope Hadrian, in his letter to the Emperor Constantine and his mother Irene, reproduced the part of these Acts concerning Constantine’s baptism and the images of Saints Peter and Paul; the letter is found in Actio 2 of the Seventh Ecumenical Synod. Leo IX, in the place indicated above, gives the privilege itself almost entire, as does Theodore Balsamon in his commentary on Photius’s *Nomocanon*, title 9, chapter 1, although in other matters he is not sufficiently fair to the Roman Church, as Greeks generally are accustomed to be. Before Gratian, Anselm, Deusdedit, and Ivo had cited this same donation in the places noted.

To this belong the words written by Peter Damian in the synodal disputation between the royal advocate and the defender of the Roman Church:

> “Read,” he says, “the edict of the Emperor Constantine, in which he established the primacy of the apostolic see over all churches throughout the world. For after he had erected a basilica over the body of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and after he had built the Lateran patriarchal palace in honour of the Blessed Saviour, he immediately established by the course of an imperial rescript the dignity of the Roman Church. There, indeed, he offered to Blessed Sylvester and his successors that they should bind their heads in royal fashion with a golden crown and employ the other insignia of royal splendour. But Blessed Sylvester adopted for his own use the ornaments which he judged suitable to the priestly office; he declined the crown and the other things that appeared more ambitious than mystical.
>
> “Constantine also granted him in perpetual right the Lateran Palace, which until then had been a royal residence, and entrusted to him the rule of Italy. For these are the words of the emperor himself: ‘Therefore we have judged it fitting that our empire and royal power should be transferred and changed to the eastern regions, that a city bearing our name be built in the best place in the province of Byzantium, and that our empire be established there; because where the primacy of priests and the head of the Christian religion has been established by the heavenly Emperor, it is not just that an earthly emperor should have power there.’”

Ado of Vienne writes of this same matter in his commentary on the sixth age, and Gottfried of Viterbo in his *Chronicles*, part 6, chapter 2.]

### C. XV. Imperial authority does not alter the measure of religious administration.

Likewise, Gelasius to the bishops of Dardania. [Note: [Col. 0465] Written A.D. 495.—Anselm, book 12, c. 68.]

Just as even a small city does not diminish the prerogative of the present kingdom, so the presence of an emperor does not alter the measure of religious administration. And below:

§ 1. It has always been the case that judgments concerning priests issue from a priestly council. [Note: [Col. 0465D] “Always”: the compiler altered the structure of the sentence so that the preceding words would not have to be cited.] For whatever kind of pontiffs they may be, even if human error should occur, provided that they do not in any way transgress against religion, they cannot in any way be struck down by secular power. [Note: [Col. 0465] “they appear”: the editions collectively.]

### C. XVI. It belongs to a good ruler to restore ruined churches, not to persecute pontiffs.

Likewise, Pope Marcellus to Maxentius. [Note: [Col. 0465D] “To Maxentius”: the printed editions, except Bas., added “bishop”; the word is absent from all manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 0465] Pseudo-Isidorian letter.—Anselm, book 6, c. 192 (194).]

It belongs to a good and religious ruler to restore churches that have been ruined and torn apart [Note: [Col. 0465] “and shaken”: Bas.; absent from Arg.], to build new ones, and to honour and protect God’s priests. Hence we read that the holy apostles and their successors, under divine attestation, ordained and commanded [Note: [Col. 0465] “appointed and commanded”: the editions collectively, from Anselm.] that persecutions ought not to occur, disturbances ought not to be inflicted, those labouring in the Lord’s field ought not to be begrudged, nor ought the stewards of the eternal King to be expelled. [Note: [Col. 0465] “to be expelled”: the editions collectively.]

## DISTINCTION XCVII

[Col. 0465]

[Col. 0465B] **GRATIAN.**

**Part I.** This chapter plainly shows that neither the emperor nor any layperson is permitted to decree anything either concerning the election of a pontiff or concerning ecclesiastical affairs. Whatever they establish must be held void unless strengthened by the subscription of the Roman Pontiff. Hence that decree of the Emperor Honorius, mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0465] Chapter 8 of Distinction 97.], appears vain, since he attempted to determine the election of the supreme pontiff contrary to the authority of the sacred canons.

Yet, as is stated in the same chapter, at the Church’s request an emperor has power to issue decrees against those who act presumptuously, just as they are recorded as having decreed long ago, in defence of the faith, that heretics should possess nothing in the name of the Church. But unless invited by her, they have no authority to arrange anything concerning ecclesiastical affairs.

The Emperor Honorius, however, took care not by his own authority, but at the entreaty of Blessed Boniface, to provide for ecclesiastical tranquillity and punish the ambition of rival claimants.

Therefore the same bishop Boniface sent a petitionary letter to the Emperor Honorius, saying [Note: [Col. 0465] Written A.D. 420.]:

### C. I. Letter of Boniface to the Emperor Honorius.

Concern for my Church, to which our God assigned my priesthood while you govern human affairs, obliges me—although I am still confined by bodily illness—not to be absent from her causes before the ears of the most Christian prince, on account of the assemblies that are agitated by the disturbances of all priests, clerics, and the Christian people. [Note: [Col. 0465] “and laypeople”: Bas.] For if anything happens otherwise than it ought, it will appear that not you, who settle everything with equitable moderation, but I, through my silent negligence [Note: [Col. 0465] “while we are silent”: the original in Dionysius.], have allowed something capable of overturning the city’s tranquillity and the Church’s peace.

Since, by the Lord’s favour, you provide for human affairs as one who worships the divine religion [Note: [Col. 0465] “preside”: the same source and Bas.], it will be my fault if, beneath your glory—which has certainly always supported divine matters with a more ready mind—that which has been maintained through the course of so many years, and even under rulers who were bound by no concern for our religion, is not preserved by firm and stable law: namely, that lawful things may be maintained and that under the rule of your merciful empire unlawful things need not be feared. [Note: [Col. 0466D] The letter itself reads: “that I may confidently make use of lawful things.” “That is, pagan things”: Coustantius’s conjecture; “that is, lawful things”: Dionysius in Amort; against Gratian, Voellus has the reading. The Spanish collection reads as noted by the Correctors.]

§ 1. For the Church itself addresses your devotion, most Christian Emperor, not indeed in my words but in her own venerable affection. [Note: [Col. 0465] “not in my words”: the editions collectively.] Christ our God, the faithful ruler and governor of your empire, preserves her, pledged to himself alone, as an untouched virgin. Do not permit the waves of storms raised by any plotters to strike against her, nor her tranquil countenance to be disturbed by the swelling of an unfamiliar tempest, most glorious and most tranquil Augustus. [Note: [Col. 0467] “your true faith”: the editions collectively; “always Augustus”: Bas.]

Therefore this Church—which is pledged to one, yet is nevertheless our mother [Note: [Col. 0467] “your mother”: Bas., together with the original.]—appeals to your piety through this embassy, entrusted to her priests; she recalls past and present assistance. “While you rule religiously [Note: [Col. 0467] “most religiously”: the editions collectively.],” she says, “my people, which is now yours, has increased, as faithful to God as to you, who are a Christian prince.” [Note: [Col. 0467D] This passage has been corrected by adding several words from the letter: “My people, which is now safe, has increased.” The original in Dionysius reads: “my people, now mine, now yours.”]

For behold, amid the very mysteries, amid the prayers which she offers for the prosperity of your empire [Note: [Col. 0467] “the Church”: the editions collectively.], with holy Peter as witness—before whom, and concerning whose see, the dispute is conducted—the Church cries out in anxious words for observance of religion. Prayer is joined to an anxious petition that discord, secretly prompted by the tempter, may not, once it has torn us away from our accustomed worship, draw us into different human affairs. [Note: [Col. 0467D] In most ancient copies the reading is: “lest discord, once it has torn these persons away from their customary worship, secretly prompted by the tempter, draw them into diverse matters.” In the original: “lest discord, once it has torn us away, draw us elsewhere”; “you” appears in place of “us.”]

Mother Church would increase for many more, most Christian prince, if she were secure with you concerning her causes [Note: [Col. 0467] “secure”: the original; “would act”: Dionysius, though the word is absent from the original.], and if, amid the suppression of idols and correction of heretics, your faith had prevailed, while divine worship flourished always together with our empire. [Note: [Col. 0467] “our”: the editions collectively.]

§ 2. She has as a pious refuge the disposition of your clemency, joined with reverence for her religion, since whatever advances her good you do, and you entrust it to my brethren and fellow priests, men of proven character, delegates from me and from all who constitute the Church [Note: [Col. 0467] “of this kind”: Dionysius in Voellus; “the things which this embassy commands”: Dionysius.]. We pray that, while they pursue the cause of sacred religion, you may, in the city of your clemency, provide permanently for the settled order of the universal Church in the same disposition by which you assent to their requests. [Note: [Col. 0467] “and assent”: the editions collectively; “assembled”: the Spanish collection.]

### C. II. Rescript of Honorius to Pope Boniface.

Victor Honorius, renowned, triumphant, ever Augustus, to the holy and venerable Boniface, Pope of the eternal city [Note: [Col. 0467] of Rome: editions compared with the original.]. We have received the writings of your Blessedness with the fitting gladness of reverence [Note: [Col. 0467] “congratulation”: Basel and Lyons editions II, III.]; and, after reading them, we gave the greatest thanks to almighty God because we learned that, after a long indisposition, your Holiness had been restored to the health for which we hoped [Col. 0468A]. Therefore, through the return of the venerable men, we attest our joy by the authority of our sacred letters [Note: [Col. 0467] “holy”: editions compared with the original; “our”: Dionysius in Amort.], and ask that your Apostleship may deign to devote, in its daily prayers, its zeal and petition to our safety and empire [Note: [Col. 0467] “your”: Böhm.]. Know, moreover, that this has greatly pleased our Piety [Note: [Col. 0467] “your”: Argentinian and Basel editions.]: that your Holiness is concerned for any disturbance of the churches or the people [Note: [Col. 0467] “and”: same source.]. Our Clemency has judged that sufficient provision has been made lest this occur in any way. Finally, while your Blessedness proclaims it, we wish it to come to the knowledge of all the clergy that, should anything happen to your religious person through the common lot of humanity—which we do not desire [Note: [Col. 0467] “happens”: Argentinian edition.]—all may know that they must refrain from ambitions [Col. 0468B]. And if two [Note: [Col. 0467] cf. Distinction 79, chapter 8.], as above.—And below:

§ 1. It must therefore be observed [Note: [Col. 0467] “kept”: editions compared with the original.] that all preserve tranquil minds and peaceful spirits in response to the admonition of our Serenity, and do not attempt anything by seditious [Note: [Col. 0467] “sedition”: same editions; “by seditions and conspiracies”: Dionysius in Amort.] conspiracies, since it is certain that no party will profit from its own efforts.

**Part II. Gratian.** It is not the custom of the Roman Church to receive an embassy from any quarter without authenticated letters [Note: [Col. 0468D] “Receive”: in the vulgate editions there followed “nor to send,” which is absent from the old copies and does not agree with what is cited in the following chapter.].

Whence Pope Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0467] Cochlaeus, in his collection of the decrees of Nicholas I, cited as the source of this chapter an epistle of Nicholas to Emperor Louis, in Mansi, vol. 15; it has not, however, been possible to find it. Collection in three parts, part 1, title 62, chapter 31.]: Chapter III. The Roman Church is not accustomed to receive an embassy from any quarter without authenticated letters.

Your Sublimity’s most noble and vigorous envoy [Col. 0468C], although he had brought no letter from you to our Pontificate in accordance with custom, and although it has never been the practice [Note: [Col. 0467] “custom”: editions compared with the original.] of the Apostolic See to receive an embassy from any quarter without authenticated letters, nevertheless, honoring you in him, and recognizing his dignity and the truthful assertions of his words, we received him as was fitting and believed him as was proper.

# DISTINCTION XCIX

[Col. 0469]

[Col. 0469B] **GRATIAN.**

**Part I.** Concerning primates—of whom we have spoken above—the question is asked: what rank do they hold in the Church [Col. 0469C]? Do they differ in any respect from patriarchs? What obedience do archbishops owe them? Primates and patriarchs have different names but the same office. Bishops appeal from archbishops to primates whenever necessary; but it is not permitted to appeal from primates to archbishops. Therefore archbishops owe obedience to primates in all matters that are justly commanded them by the latter.

Whence Pope Anacletus said to the bishops of Italy, Epistle II [Note: [Col. 0470C] This entire chapter is repeated [Col. 0470D] by Gregory VII, book 6 of the register, epistle 35, written to the archbishops of Rouen, Tours, and Sens; some readings have been restored from it and from the original.] [Note: [Col. 0469] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore; Anselm 6, chapter 111; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 23; *Decrees*, part 5, chapter 52; Chapter I.]:

## Chapter I. What obedience is to be rendered to primates and patriarchs

For the most part, provinces were divided long before Christ’s advent; and afterward this division was renewed by the apostles and by our predecessor, Blessed Clement. In the chief cities of the provinces [Note: [Col. 0469] add “of all”: Basel and Lyons editions II, III.], where in former times were the primates of secular law [Note: [Col. 0469] “laws”: Ivo.] and the highest judicial power—to whom those dwelling throughout the remaining cities used to have recourse when necessary, when they could not, or were not permitted to, flee to the court [Col. 0470C] of the emperor [Note: [Col. 0469] “emperors”: editions compared with the original, from Ivo.] or kings because of their oppressions [Note: [Col. 0469] add “their”: same editions.] or injustices, and whom they appealed to whenever necessary, as was prescribed [Note: [Col. 0469] “written”: same editions, first Basel edition.] in their law—in these same cities or places the divine and ecclesiastical laws commanded that our patriarchs or primates be appointed and exist. They maintain one form, although their names differ; bishops were to have recourse to and appeal to them if need arose; and they alone were to enjoy the title of primate, *and no others*. The remaining metropolitan cities, however, which had lesser judges—although greater than counts [Note: [Col. 0469] add “or counties”: Argentinian and Basel editions.]—were to have their own metropolitans, who should justly obey their aforesaid [Note: [Col. 0469] add “own”: Basel edition.] primates, as had formerly been ordered in secular law [Col. 0471A]. These were not to enjoy the title of primate, but that either of metropolitan or archbishop.

## Chapter II. None are to be called primates except those who hold the primary sees. Likewise Anicetus to the bishops of Gaul

[Note: [Col. 0471] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore; Anselm, book 2, chapter 13; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 25; *Decrees*, part 5, chapter 51; Polycarpus, book 2, title 21.]

**Part II.** No archbishops are to be called primates except those who hold the chief cities [Note: [Col. 0471] “sees”: editions compared with the original.], the bishops of which the apostles and the successors of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0471] “their”: same editions.] have regularly established as patriarchs and [Note: [Col. 0471] “or”: same editions.] primates—unless thereafter some people is converted to the faith for whom, because of the multitude [Note: [Col. 0471] “because of the great multitude”: same editions.] of them, it is necessary that a primate be appointed. The rest [Note: [Col. 0471] “The remaining men who hold other metropolitan sees are to be called metropolitans”: same editions.] who have acquired other metropolitan sees are not to be called primates but metropolitans.

[Note: [Col. 0471] Chapter 26 of the Third Council of Carthage, held A.D. 397; chapter 37 in Dionysius Exiguus; Burchard, book 1, chapter 3; Ivo, *Decrees*, part 5, chapter 57; Polycarpus, book 2, title 26.]

The bishop of the first see is not to be called prince of priests, high priest, or anything of the kind, but only “bishop of the first see.”

**Part II.** Nor is even the Roman Pontiff to be called universal.

[Col. 0472A] Whence Pelagius II, in an epistle to all bishops unlawfully convoked by John of Constantinople, etc. [Note: [Col. 0471] A Pseudo-Isidorian epistle. Almost the same words are found in Gregory the Great, book 4, epistle 36; Anselm, book 6, chapter 130 (128); Polycarpus, book 2, title 25.]:

## Chapter IV. Not even the Roman Pontiff is to be called universal

Let none of the patriarchs ever use the title of universality [Note: [Col. 0471] “university”: Basel edition; “universal”: Argentinian edition.], because, if one patriarch is called universal, the title of patriarch is derogated from the rest. But far be this [Note: [Col. 0471] “far be this from the faithful”: editions compared with the original, from Anselm.], far be it from the mind of any believer that anyone should wish to seize this title for himself [Note: [Col. 0471] “is absent from Anselm.”], whereby he might seem to diminish, even in the slightest degree, the honor of his brothers. Therefore let your Charity never call anyone universal in its letters, lest, in conferring an undue honor on another, it take away what is due to itself [Note: [Col. 0471] “offers”: Basel edition; “inflicts”: the remaining editions except Argentinian.].

[Col. 0472B] ## Chapter V. On the same matter. Likewise Gregory to Eulogius, Patriarch of Alexandria, book VII, epistle 30, indiction 1

[Note: [Col. 0471B] In St. Gregory the following occurs: “And indeed your Holiness knows that at the holy Synod of Chalcedon, and afterward, this title was offered to my predecessors by the fathers who followed; yet none of them ever wished to use this title, so that, while they loved in this world the honor of all priests, they might preserve their own honor with almighty God.” He explains the matter more fully in book 4, epistle 32. St. Thomas also reports in his tract *Against the Errors of the Greeks* that the entire synod acclaimed St. Leo thus: “May Leo, most holy, apostolic, and ecumenical—that is, universal—patriarch live for many years.” Leo IX, writing to Michael, Archbishop of Constantinople, concerning this same title, says: “Although the holy Synod of Chalcedon decreed this for our predecessor, the great Leo, and his successors.” In many documents contained in the third session of that same synod is the heading: “To Leo, most holy and blessed universal patriarch of great Rome.” In manuscripts of many letters to Roman pontiffs preserved in the Vatican Library—of which private persons possess many copies—more than three hundred archimandrites and monks of Second Syria write thus to Pope Hormisdas: “To Hormisdas, most holy and blessed patriarch of the whole world, who holds the see of the chief apostle Peter: the prayer and petition of the least of the archimandrites and of the other monks of Second Syria.” And about the middle of the letter: “Since Christ our God has made you, our holy angel, chief shepherd, teacher, and physician of souls, it is fitting to set forth the sufferings that have befallen us,” etc. Avitus, bishop in Gaul, likewise writes to Hormisdas: “Since you perceive that it accords with the condition of religion and the full rules of the Catholic faith, your watchful care instructs me by exhortation to tend the flock committed to you throughout all the members of the universal Church.” John, bishop of Nicopolis, writes to the same pope: “I fittingly have recourse to your prayers, that according to the custom of your Apostolic See you may deign to have care of the church of Nicopolis also, as of all churches, in accordance with your ancient special authority.” In chapter 22 of the *Breviary* of Liberatus, the bishop of Patara says to the emperor concerning Pope Silverius: “There are many kings in this world, and not one alone, as that pope is over the Church of the entire world.” Regino the German, book 11 of the *Chronicles*, speaking of Nicholas I, often calls him universal pontiff. But the expression “universal” has two meanings, which Innocent III explains in book 2, epistle 206—beginning *Apostolicae sedis*—writing to the patriarch of Constantinople: “For the universal Church is called that which consists of all churches, which in Greek is called Catholic; and in this sense of the term the Roman Church is not the universal Church, but a part of the universal Church, namely the first and chief part, like the head in a body, because in it resides the fullness of power, while some share of that fullness is derived to the others [Col. 0472D]. And the one Church that contains all churches under itself is called universal. In this sense of the name, the Roman Church alone is called universal, because by the unique privilege of its dignity it has been set above the others, just as God is called universal Lord—not as though he were divided into genera, most specific species, or even subordinate species—because all things are contained under his dominion. For there is one general Church, of which Truth says to Peter: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church.’”] [Note: [Col. 0471] Epistle 30, written A.D. 598, book 8, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 6, chapter 131 (129); Polycarpus, book 2, title 26.]

Behold: in the preface of the letter which you addressed to me—though I forbade it—you took care to insert the word of a proud title, calling me “universal Pope.” I ask that your Holiness, most dear to me, do this no longer, because what is granted to another beyond what reason demands is taken away from you. For I seek to prosper not in words [Col. 0473A] but in conduct; and I do not count as honor that in which I recognize that my brothers lose their own honor. For my honor is the honor of the universal Church; my honor is the firm strength of my brothers. Then I am truly [Note: [Col. 0473] “indeed”: Böhm.] honored [Col. 0474A], when the honor due to each individual is not denied. For if your Holiness calls me universal Pope, it denies that it is what it acknowledges me to be universally. But far be this; let words withdraw that inflate vanity [Note: [Col. 0473] “unity”: Basel edition; “truth”: the remaining editions except Argentinian.] and wound charity.

Earlier it was read: “contrary to the welfare of the Church and the course of custom, which alone—as you well know—is the deprivation of priestly office.”], which alone—as you well know—is the elevation of priestly office [Note: [Col. 0475] “deprivation”: editions compared with the original.]. Had your wisdom received these reports gently [Note: [Col. 0475] “or gently”: same editions.] or with episcopal diligence, it ought not to have been inflamed against those men; rather, you ought yourself to have corrected these very matters with thanksgiving.”

## Chapter VIII. On the same matter. Likewise to John, Bishop of Ravenna, in the same epistle

[Note: [Col. 0475] Anselm, book 9, chapter 95 (92); Polycarpus, book 2, title 20.]

For it is contrary to ecclesiastical custom if even an unjust correction is not borne with the greatest patience—which be far from you [Note: [Col. 0475] “us”: original and editions compared with the original.]. And below:

§ 1. We do not think, dearest brother, that you are unaware that scarcely any metropolitan in any part of the world [Col. 0476A] has been heard of claiming for himself the use of the pallium outside the time of Mass. You have shown us most plainly in your letters that you know this to be the good custom of the universal Church [Note: [Col. 0475] “most plain”: same editions.]. In those letters you transmitted to us, appended below, the decree of our predecessor Pope John of blessed memory, which provides that all the customs granted to you and to your Church by the privilege of our predecessors must be observed. Thus you confess that the custom of the universal Church is otherwise, since you claim what you do by privilege. Therefore, as we think, no doubt can remain for you in this matter. Either the custom of all metropolitans must also be observed by your Brotherhood, or, if you say that something was specially granted to your Church [Col. 0476B], or commanded [Note: [Col. 0475] “granted, commanded”: original.] by former pontiffs of the city of Rome, whereby these things were granted to the Church of Ravenna, this must be shown by you. But if it is not shown, then, since you claim no right to act thus either from the general custom or from a privilege, it remains for you to acknowledge that you have usurped [Note: [Col. 0475] “to usurp”: the editions, first Basel and Lyons II, III.] what you have done. And below:

§ 2. Perhaps we wish [Note: [Col. 0475] “we do not wish”: editions compared with the original.] one who is unbecoming in conduct to be adorned with the pallium, when nothing shines more brightly upon an episcopal neck than humility. Therefore, if your Brotherhood has resolved in mind to defend its honors by whatever arguments, it must either follow the unwritten usage of the whole Church or defend itself by written privileges [Note: [Col. 0475] “written privilege”: original.]. But if neither of these is finally the case, we do not wish you to furnish the other metropolitans with an example of this presumption.

[Col. 0476C] **Part V. Gratian.** Privileges also ought always to be granted together with the use of the pallium.

Whence the same Gregory, to Syagrius, bishop of Autun, book VII, epistle 112 [Note: [Col. 0475] Epistle 108, written A.D. 599, book 9, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 6, chapter 86 (91); Polycarpus, book 2, title 21.]:

## Chapter IX. Certain privileges ought to be granted with the use of the pallium

The order of reason wholly admonishes us that, together with the use of the pallium, we ought to grant certain privileges *at the same time, as we have said*. But since with an increase of honor the burden of solicitude ought likewise to increase [Note: [Col. 0475] “grow”: original and editions compared with the original.], so that the ornaments of conduct may correspond to the adornment of garments, it is necessary that your Brotherhood apply itself more earnestly in every endeavor and keep vigilant care concerning the actions of its subjects [Note: [Col. 0476D] “And concerning”: this passage has been enriched from the original.] [Note: [Col. 0475] absent from Anselm.], *so that your example may be their instruction [Col. 0476D], and your life their teacher* [Note: [Col. 0475] the words marked by asterisks are absent from Anselm.].

[Col. 0477A] ## Chapter X. The use of the pallium is granted and ancient privileges are renewed. Likewise to John, Bishop of First Justiniana in Illyricum, book IV, epistle 15

[Note: [Col. 0477] Epistle 23, written A.D. 592, book 2, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 6, chapter 99 (96).]

We have sent you the pallium according to custom, and by renewed confirmation we decree [Note: [Col. 0477] “we have decreed”: editions compared with the original.] that you exercise the functions of the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0478A] ## Chapter XI. On the same matter. Likewise to the bishops of Epirus, book IV, epistle 7, indiction 14

[Note: [Col. 0477] Epistle 8, written A.D. 596, book 8, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 6, chapter 100 (97).]

The report in your letters, dearest brothers, disclosed that Andrew, *our brother*, bishop of the city of Nicomedia, had, by God’s favor, been solemnly ordained [Note: [Col. 0477] “ordained, to whom the pallium”: Anselm and editions compared with the original.]. And below: Know that we have sent the pallium to the aforesaid Andrew, *our brother and fellow bishop* [Note: [Col. 0477] “know”: original and same editions.], and have granted the privileges *and* all things that our predecessors bestowed upon his predecessors.

# DISTINCTION CI

[Col. 0477]

[Col. 0477A] **GRATIAN.**

There ought not to be two metropolitans in one province, as was decreed by chapter 12 of the Council of Chalcedon [Note: [Col. 0477] held A.D. 451; Burchard, book 1, chapter 35; Ivo, *Decrees*, part 5, chapter 146, from Dionysius; indeed, Isidore’s translation.].

[Col. 0477B] ## Chapter I. There ought not to be two metropolitans in one and the same province

It has come to our attention that certain persons, in defiance of ecclesiastical regulations and desirous of power, divide one province into two by an imperial pragmatic sanction [Note: [Col. 0477B] “Imperial pragmatic sanction”: the ancient translations and the Dionysian version read “by a pragmatic form.” The Greek is: *Dià pragmatikôn* (Διὰ πραγματικῶν), which a little later in the same chapter is said as *Dià grammátōn basilikôn* (Διὰ γραμμάτων βασιλικῶν), that is, “by imperial letters.”], so [Note: [Col. 0477] “and thereby”: editions compared with the original.] that two metropolitan bishops are found in one and the same province. Therefore the holy synod decrees [Col. 0478A] that nothing of this kind shall henceforth be attempted by any bishop; those who attempt anything of this kind [Note: [Col. 0477] “attempt”: Hispanic Collection.] are to fall from their own rank.

**Gratian.** Thus far we have treated the election and ordination of clerics. Let us now proceed to simoniacal ordinations [Col. 0478B], and, so that what the authority of the holy Fathers has decreed concerning this heresy may become clear, let a case be put forward whose subject includes those knowingly ordained by simoniacs, those unknowingly consecrated by simoniacs, and ordinations performed for money.

# SECOND PART OF THE DECREE

[Col. 0477]

# CAUSE I

[Col. 0477C] **GRATIAN.**

[Col. 0477D] A certain man, having a son, offered him to a very wealthy monastery. When ten pounds were demanded by the abbot and brothers, he paid them so that his son might be received, although the son himself was unaware of this benefit because of his age. The boy grew and, through the progress of time and offices, reached manhood and the rank of priesthood. Thereafter, supported by his merits, he was elected bishop; and, through the intervention of service and paternal entreaties, with money also given to one of the archbishop’s advisers, he was consecrated bishop, unaware of his father’s service and the money offered. As time passed, he ordained some persons for money, while to others he gave priestly blessing freely. At last, accused and convicted before his metropolitan, he received upon himself [Col. 0478C] a sentence of condemnation.

[Col. 0478D] **Question I.** First it is asked whether it is a sin to buy spiritual things.

**Question II.** Secondly, whether money ought to be demanded for admission into a church; or, if demanded, whether it ought to be paid.

**Question III.** Thirdly, whether buying admission or prebends in a church is simoniacal.

**Question IV.** Fourthly, whether this man is guilty of the crime committed by his father without his knowledge.

**Question V.** Fifthly, whether he may remain in the Church or exercise the office which he obtained through his father’s money.

**Question VI.** Sixthly, whether those who were unknowingly ordained by him when he was already a simoniac are to be deposed or not.

**Question VII.** Seventhly, whether, if he renounces his heresy, he is to be restored to episcopal rank or not.

# QUESTION I

[Col. 0479A]

**GRATIAN.**

**Part I.** That buying spiritual things is a sin is proved by the authority of many writers [Note: [Col. 0479] “authorities”: editions compared with the original.].

For Pope Leo says:

## Chapter I. Simoniacs do not confer the grace which they seek to sell

Grace [Note: [Col. 0479C] The opening words of this chapter are very similar to words in epistle 84 of Leo I, written to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia. Speaking of grace, he says: “unless it is given freely, it is not grace but payment.” The remainder has not been found in Leo himself.] is not grace if it is not given or received freely. But simoniacs do not receive freely [Note: [Col. 0479] This chapter is taken from chapter 4 of Cardinal Humbert’s response concerning simoniacs, in Martène, *Thesaurus*, vol. IV.]; therefore they do not receive the grace that works especially in ecclesiastical orders. But if they do not receive it, they do not possess it; and if they do not possess it, they can give it to no one, either freely or otherwise. What then do they give? Certainly what they possess. And what do they possess? Surely, the spirit of falsehood. How do we prove this? [Col. 0479B] Because, if the Spirit of truth—as Truth itself testifies [Note: [Col. 0479] Matthew, chapter 10.], from whom it proceeds—is received freely, then without doubt that spirit which is not received freely is proved to be the spirit of falsehood [Note: [Col. 0479] add “or given”: editions compared with the original.].

## Chapter II. Whoever is simoniacally ordained is called a priest in vain. Likewise Gregory to Syagrius, Bishop of Autun, book VII, epistle 110

[Note: [Col. 0479C] This chapter has been corrected and expanded from the original.] [Note: [Col. 0479] Epistle 106, written A.D. 599, book 9, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 6, chapter 77 (79).]

Whoever strives to purchase holy orders by the giving of a price [Note: [Col. 0479] “through giving”: editions compared with the original, first Argentinian and Basel editions—the latter reading “gift”—Venice I, Nuremberg.], *attending not to the office but to the name*, desires not to be a priest, but only vainly to be called one.

### C. III. He who obtains a church by money is to be stripped of his office. Likewise, from the Register.

[Note: [Col. 0479C] This is not found in the Register of Blessed Gregory from which it appears to be cited. Similar material occurs in Gregory VII, book 6 of the Register, in the index of the council held in that year; in the Council of Tours under Charlemagne, c. 15; the Council of Rheims, c. 21; the Council of Mainz under Rabanus, c. 12; another Council of Mainz under Arnulf, c. 5; and below, the same question, c. 3, chapter *Altare*, which is there cited [Col. 0479D] from Paschal.]

[Note: [Col. 0479] Berthold of Constance, in his Apologeticus for Gregory VII, cites these words from a letter of Gregory the Great to Clement of Bizacena (book 4, ep. 13), although they occur there somewhat differently. The latter part of this chapter is cited below, question 3, c. 14, from Paschal I, in whom it has not been found.]

[Col. 0479C] If a presbyter has obtained a church by money, [Col. 0480A] he must not only be deprived of the church, but also stripped of the honour of the priesthood; for no believer is ignorant that buying or selling an altar, tithes, or the Holy Spirit is the Simoniacal heresy.

### C. IV. On the same matter. Likewise, Gregory I, in the aforementioned letter 110, book VII.

[Note: [Col. 0479D] In certain old copies this chapter is joined to the preceding one. Besides the indicated letter 110, the same opinion occurs in book 4, ep. [Col. 0480C] 55, and book 5, ep. 107, addressed to the bishops of Epirus.]

[Note: [Col. 0479] Compare c. 2 above.—Burchard, book 1, c. 21; Anselm, book 6, c. 80. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, cc. 75 and 112.—Compare Council of Meaux, c. 42.]

His blessing is turned into a curse who is promoted for the purpose of becoming a heretic.

[Note: [Col. 0479] *vertitur*, “is turned”: Basel edition.]

### C. V. He who does not burn vehemently against Simoniacs will have a share with Simon. The same, in the same place.

[Note: [Col. 0480C] The exact words of this chapter have not been found in the letters of Blessed Gregory. Yet Pope Paschal II, as found in Ivo and Polycarpus, cites them from Blessed Gregory himself. The first part of this chapter is very similar to book 4, letters 55 and 56, and the latter part to book 10, letter 33, to Bishop Victor. John the Deacon, book 3, c. 4, writes that Blessed Gregory’s general judgment against the heresy of simony and neophytes is contained in the letter written to Victor. Chapter 42 of the Council of Meaux, cited by Ivo, part 5, c. 75, partly agrees with the letter to Victor itself, partly with the material which Ivo and Polycarpus cite from Paschal, and with that reported here by Gratian. Concerning the expulsion of this heresy [Col. 0480D] from Gaul, Gregory writes to Virgilius of Arles in book 4, letter 51, and to Syagrius and the other bishops of Gaul in book 7, letter 110.]

[Note: [Col. 0479] We have found the source of this chapter to be the letter to the Church of Milan which a certain Guido the musician—perhaps Guido of Arezzo, the Camaldolese monk—falsely attributed to Paschal I. On this matter see Berthold of Constance (ed. Martin Gerbert, 1792), p. 204.—In Anselm, book 6, c. 77 (81), Gregory to Victor is cited (Ep. 29, book 12, Maurist edition), whose words the author of the letter imitated.—Burchard, book 1, c. 21; Deusdedit, part 2; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, c. 84 and part 5, c. 75; Polycarpus, book 2, title 1.]

Whoever is ordained by money is promoted for the purpose of becoming a heretic. Therefore whoever, in accordance with the demands of his office, does not burn vehemently against the Simoniacal heresy and the heresy of neophytes should not doubt that he will [Col. 0480B] have a share with him who first committed this accursed crime.

### C. VI. Simon’s condemnation equally encompasses giver and receiver. Likewise, Pope Gelasius to the bishops established throughout Lucania, letter I, c. 26.

[Note: [Col. 0479] Written A.D. 494.—Deusdedit, part 2; Burchard, book 1, c. 22; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 76.]

Those who are found unworthy by their merits and convicted of having purchased sacred dignity at a price must be excluded, since, in perpetrating such a crime, they do so not without peril; for the condemnation of Simon, as sacred Scripture attests, encompasses alike both giver and receiver.

[Note: [Col. 0479] *sacramenta*, “sacraments”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0479] Add *illos*, “those persons”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0479] The words “not … perpetrating” are absent from Ivo.—C. VII.]

### C. VII. He who is ordained simoniacally is condemned by a sentence of anathema. Likewise, Ambrose, in the *Pastoral Book*.

[Note: [Col. 0480D] This chapter is not found in the *Pastoral Book* of Blessed Ambrose, from which it is cited. It does, however, occur in the Eighth Council of Toledo, c. 3. Anselm, book 6, c. 85, cites that canon in full, while Ivo, part 5, c. 83, cites a portion of it, both from the said council.]

[Note: [Col. 0479] Rather, Council of Toledo VIII, c. 3, held A.D. 653, which Anselm correctly cites at book 6, c. 85.]

Very many are found who, through the business of a gift, are to perish, [Col. 0480C] wishing to purchase the grace of the Holy Spirit. They offer [Col. 0481A] a paltry price in order to receive the lofty summit of pontifical rank, forgetting Peter’s words to Simon: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed by money” [Acts 8:20]. Therefore, because this great evil is both customary and demonstrably often cut down by the sword of our forebears, we too apply to this cancerous wound the glowing iron which still remains, decreeing absolutely that whoever henceforth is discovered to have offered any reward in order to receive the dignity of the priesthood shall know himself, from that moment, condemned to the disgrace of anathema and excluded from participation in Christ’s body and blood, since he is known to have committed this abominable crime against Christ.

But if anyone should arise [Col. 0481B] who accuses him, the person who had acquired this rank by giving gifts shall be deprived of the rank of honour he received and confined in a monastery under perpetual penance. Those who have been receivers of gifts for this purpose, if clerics, shall be punished by loss of their rank; but if laymen, they shall be condemned by perpetual anathema.

[Note: [Col. 0479] *negotiatione*, “commerce”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] “they”: the same editions from Anselm.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] *illi*, “they,” for *vile*, “paltry”: the same editions from Anselm.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] Acts 8:20.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] *perceptione*, “reception,” for *participatione*, “participation”: Spanish Collection.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] *sublimitatem*, “sublimity”: the same editions from the same source.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] *possess it can be possessed*: Lyons editions II and III.—*possess*: the other editions and the original.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] *exstat*, “is found”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] “to receive the dignity of the divine gift”: the same editions from Anselm.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] “the accuser of him”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] *fuerit*, “shall have been”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] *acceptione*, “receiving”: Spanish Collection and Anselm.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] *suscepti*, “of the rank received”: Spanish Collection and Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] *religetur*, “be bound/confined”: Spanish Collection.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] Add *de*, “concerning”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] Add *sui*, “their own”: collected editions.]

### C. VIII. A bishop who performs an ordination for money is condemned. Likewise, from the Council of Chalcedon, c. 2.

[Note: [Col. 0481] Held A.D. 451.—Dionysius’s translation.—Abbo of Fleury, c. 13; Burchard, book 1, c. 112; Anselm, book 6, c. 88 (85); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 118; *Decretum*, part 5, c. 118; Polycarpus, book 2, title 37.]

If any bishop performs an ordination for money and reduces to a price the grace which cannot be sold; if he ordains for money a bishop, chorepiscopus, presbyter, or deacon, or anyone among those counted [Col. 0481C] in the clergy; or promotes for money a steward, defender, or *mansionarius* [an official responsible for church lodgings], or absolutely anyone subject to a rule, for the sake of his own shameful profit: the man proved to have attempted this shall be liable to loss of his own rank. The person ordained shall gain nothing from an ordination or promotion effected through trafficking, but shall be excluded from the dignity or office which he acquired by money. If anyone has served as intermediary in such shameful and impious giving or receiving, he too, if he is a cleric, shall fall from his own rank; if a layman or monk, he shall be anathematized.

[Note: [Col. 0481] Add “of the Holy Spirit”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] “and promotes”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] *Et ipse*, “he too,” is absent from the original cited and from Anselm.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] These words are read neither in Dionysius’s version from the Amort edition nor in Anselm and Burchard.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] Anselm: “he whose attempt has been proved”; Basel edition.]

### C. IX. He who ordains or is ordained for money is excluded from the priesthood. Likewise, from the Eighth Synod.

[Note: [Col. 0481C] “Eighth”: In some old copies this chapter is cited from the Seventh Synod, in which, c. 5, [Col. 0481D] Canon 30 of the Apostles is reported as relevant to this matter. But in Tarasius’s letter to Pope Hadrian—which in the copies of the Vatican Library and others stands at the end of the Seventh Synod—Canon 22 of the Synod in Trullo is reported in these words: “We decree that those ordained for money, whether bishops or any clerics, and not according to examination and choice of life, be deposed; and likewise those who are known to have ordained them.” There is also a letter of Basil on this subject to the bishops subject to him.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] These belong to Basil, c. 91, in Beveridge’s *Pandect of Canons*.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 121.]

Whoever consecrates anyone for money, or has been consecrated by another, is to be excluded from the priesthood.

[Col. 0482B]

### C. X. No one may be ordained or promoted in the Church of God for money. Likewise, Pope Calixtus II.

[Note: [Col. 0482C] This is Calixtus II, who lived shortly before Gratian. In several councils held by him against simony and the investitures of churches, which the German emperors had usurped, he issued many decrees. Abbot of Ursberg writes carefully concerning these matters [Col. 0482D] from A.D. 1118, when he was elected pope, to A.D. 1124.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] From the First Lateran Council, held A.D. 1123.]

Following the examples of the holy Fathers and renewing what is required by our office, by the authority of the Apostolic See we absolutely forbid anyone to be ordained or promoted by money in the Church of God. If anyone has acquired ordination or promotion in the Church in this manner, let him be utterly deprived of the dignity acquired.

### C. XI. On the same matter. Likewise, Gregory Nazianzen.

[Note: [Col. 0482D] Nothing of this kind has been found in the extant Greek and Latin works of Blessed Gregory Nazianzen. Similar material, however, occurs in Tarasius’s letter to Hadrian.]

[Note: [Col. 0481] The letter of Tarasius, which the Correctors wished to regard as the source of this chapter, is printed in full among the acts of the Second Council of Nicaea, held in 787. Nearly the same material occurs in Alger of Liège, *On Mercy and Justice*, in Martène’s *Thesaurus*, vol. V, c. 32, part 3; and indeed it seems there to have been composed by Alger himself from the section beginning “Gehazi.”]

Whoever endeavours to purchase the gift of God for a price cannot, beyond any doubt, remain or be restored in sacred orders by any means. Such a person must in every way be cut off from communion. For what else is buying the gift of the Holy Spirit for a price but a capital [Col. 0482C] crime and the Simoniacal heresy? How detestably it was punished in both Testaments is readily apparent from many examples.

Gehazi sold Naaman the Syrian the grace of healing; rebuked by Elisha, he became leprous and lost that same grace of healing. [Col. 0483A] Judas, who sold the Redeemer of all, was soon hanged by a noose and did not obtain that same grace of the Redeemer—and deservedly, because no one can retain what he has sold. Simon the magician likewise, when he wished to buy the same grace of the Holy Spirit, heard from Peter the sentence of condemnation: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed by money.”

[Note: [Col. 0481] 4 Kings [2 Kings] 5.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] Acts 8.]

The Lord also, in order to show that sellers and buyers are devoid of this grace, dismissed all sinners in the Temple through grace, but rebuked and scourged only the sellers and buyers, casting them out of the Temple. It is clear that sellers and buyers are deprived and empty of the grace of the Holy Spirit. For will the Spirit of Christ make his temple out of those whom Christ expelled from the Temple?

[Note: [Col. 0481] *domum*, “house”: Argentinensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] Add “who”: Lyons editions II and III.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] Add “his own”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “possess”: collected editions except Lyons II and III.]

### C. XII. Simoniacal persons cannot be priests. Likewise, Gregory.

[Note: [Col. 0483C] Deusdedit, in his treatise against the Simoniacs, reports this from a letter of Pope Paschal II to the Milanese.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] These words are thought formerly to have belonged to the letter to the Milanese falsely attributed to Paschal I, which we have noted to be spurious; see above at c. 5. They cannot belong to Paschal II, whom Deusdedit, part 4, cited, as the very words of Urban—who lived before Paschal II—in his letter to Lucius clearly show; see C. 1, q. 3, c. 8.]

Whoever sells or buys sacred orders cannot be priests. Hence it is written: “Anathema to the giver, anathema to the receiver: this is the Simoniacal heresy.” How then, if they are under anathema and are not holy, can they sanctify others? And since they are not in Christ’s body, how can they give or receive Christ’s body? How can one who is cursed bless?

[Note: [Col. 0483] “of giving … of receiving”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “are anathematized”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]

### C. XIII. On the same matter. Likewise, Gregory to Syagrius and the other bishops, book VII, letter 110.

[Note: [Col. 0483] Letter 106, written A.D. 599, book 9, Maurist edition.—Burchard, book 1, c. 121; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 75; Deusdedit, part 2; Polycarpus, book 2, c. 1.]

[Col. 0483C] Since it is clear that this heresy has crept in before all others through a pestilential root, and that in its very origin it was condemned by apostolic detestation, why is it not avoided? Why is it not considered that his blessing is turned into a curse who is promoted for the purpose of becoming a heretic?

[Note: [Col. 0483] Compare c. 4 above.]

[Note: [Col. 0483D] “All”: formerly the reading was *omnia*, “all things,” but the gloss seems better suited to the restored reading, which occurs in certain manuscripts and in the original itself.]

### C. XIV. He who ordains for a price confers leprosy, not office. Likewise, Ambrose, *On Ministries*, or *On Priestly Dignity*, c. 5.

[Note: [Col. 0483] This book is demonstrably apocryphal.—Deusdedit, part 2; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 95.]

[Col. 0484A] When he was ordained bishop, what he gave was gold and what he lost was his soul; when he ordained another, what he received was money and what he gave was leprosy.

### C. XV. On the same matter. The same, in the same place.

[Note: [Col. 0483] Compare c. 14.]

You did not receive grace when you were ordained, because you did not merit it freely.

### C. XVI. On the same matter. The same, book IV, on Luke, chapter 4 [v. 27].

[Note: [Col. 0483] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 132; Deusdedit, part 2.]

Leprosy swiftly follows shameful payment, and money [Col. 0484B] wickedly acquired stains body and soul. And a little later:

§ 1. You see that by the deed of the originator the succession of the heir is condemned. The guilt of a mystery sold is inexpiable, and heaven’s vengeance for grace passes to descendants. Thus the Moabites and others shall not enter the Church until the third and fourth generation—that is, to give the simpler interpretation, until the manifold succession of generations had effaced the guilt of the originators.

But although those who sinned against God through the error of idolatry seem to have been punished to the fourth generation, the judgment by which Gehazi’s seed is condemned forever by prophetic authority for the greed of possession seems clearly harsher, especially since our Lord Jesus Christ, through the washing of regeneration, has granted [Col. 0484C] forgiveness of sins to all—unless you understand “seed” as the offspring of vices rather than of lineage. For just as those who are children of promise are reckoned as good seed, so also those who are children of error are reckoned as evil seed. For the Jews are from their father the devil, certainly not by descent of flesh but by descent of crime.

Therefore all the covetous, all the greedy, possess Gehazi’s leprosy together with their riches; and by their wickedly acquired [Col. 0485A] reward they have amassed not so much a patrimony of resources as a treasure of crimes, for eternal punishment and fleeting gain.

[Note: [Col. 0483] *acquisita*, “acquired”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] *ministerii*, “ministry”: collected editions except Argentinensis and Venice I–II.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “into”: collected editions from Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “in”: the same editions from the same source.]
