[Note: [Col. 0483D] “To the fourth”: formerly the reading was “to the third and fourth.” But the word “third” is absent both from Blessed Ambrose and from one old Gratian manuscript. In Deuteronomy 23, the children of Edomites and Egyptians are permitted to enter the Church of the Lord in the third generation; but of the Moabites it is written: “Ammonites and Moabites, even after the tenth generation, [Col. 0484D] shall not enter the Church of the Lord forever.”]

[Note: [Col. 0483] *prophetiae*, “of prophecy”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0484D] After “sins” followed “why then is Gehazi’s seed condemned forever?” These words do not occur in Blessed Ambrose.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] “unless that”: Ivo and collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] *promissionum*, “of promises”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] Add “are”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] Add “spiritual”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0485] *facultatem patrimonii*, “the estate’s resources”: collected editions.]

## Part II. Gratian

Therefore, since by the authority of Pope Leo Simoniacs receive nothing but the spirit of falsehood; since, according to Gregory, priesthood does not subsist among Simoniacs; since their blessing is turned into a curse; since among them anathema remains upon giver and receiver; since they are not holy and are not constituted in Christ’s body; since they are cursed and cannot sanctify others, give or receive Christ’s body, or bless others; since, according to Ambrose, they are condemned to the disgrace of anathema and excluded from participation in Christ’s body and blood; since gold is received and leprosy given, and the guilt of a mystery sold is [Col. 0485B] inexpiable; since, according to the Council of Chalcedon, they are judged to gain nothing from such ordination; since, according to Gelasius, they are encompassed by Simon’s condemnation; since, according to Gregory Nazianzen, they cannot by any means remain or be restored in sacred orders, are smitten with leprosy by Elisha, condemned to perdition by Peter, and cast out of the Temple by Christ: what else can one Simoniac confer upon another in his ordination, except what Innocent testifies of other heretics, saying in letter XVIII to Alexander, c. 3?

[Note: [Col. 0485] Written A.D. 415.—Anselm, book 6, c. 73 (78).]

### C. XVII. Those who do not possess the Spirit’s perfection cannot give it.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] This chapter does not report Innocent’s words exactly, though they occur partly below in the same question, c. *Arianos*, and partly in the next chapter, in the section “But conversely.”]

Those who have lost the perfection of the Spirit which they had received cannot give its fullness, [Col. 0485C] which is especially effective in ordinations and which they lost through their own faithlessness. And again:

§ 1. He who did not possess honour could not give honour; nor did the other receive anything, because there was nothing in the giver, but through a wicked laying-on of hands he gave the condemnation which he possessed.

[Note: [Col. 0485] From the letter to Rufus; compare the next chapter.]

[Note: [Col. 0485] Compare cc. 73, 97, and 98 below in the same question.]

### C. XVIII. By a wicked laying-on of hands, a Simoniac confers not blessing but condemnation. The same, to Rufus and the other bishops, letter XII, c. 3.

[Note: [Col. 0485] Written A.D. 414.—Collection in three parts, part 1, title 38, cc. 12–13; Anselm, book 1; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 130; *Decretum*, part 6, c. 59 (60); Polycarpus, book 2, title 31, and book 7, title 7.]

We have come to the third question, which because of its [Col. 0486A] difficulty requires a longer discussion. Since we say that those ordained by heretics have their head wounded through that laying-on of hands, a remedy must be applied where the wound has been inflicted, so that they may recover health. But health following a wound cannot exist without a scar; and where the remedy of penance is necessary, we decree that there can be no place for the honour of ordination.

For if, as it is written, “whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean,” how can that be bestowed upon him which purity and cleanness are accustomed to receive?

§ 1. But conversely it is asserted that a person who has lost his office cannot give office, and that the other received nothing because there was nothing in the giver which he could receive. We agree, and it is certainly true that he could not give what [Col. 0486B] he did not possess. Yet he gave the condemnation which he possessed by his wicked laying-on of hands; and I cannot discover how one who has become a participant in a condemned person ought to receive office.

§ 2. But it is said that the true and just blessing of a lawful priest removes every defect which had been introduced by one who was defective. If that is so, let the sacrilegious, adulterers, and persons guilty of every crime be brought forward for ordination, because crimes and defects are thought to be removed by the blessing of ordination. Let there be no place for penance, because ordination can accomplish what prolonged satisfaction ordinarily accomplishes.

But the law of our Church is that those coming from heretics who were nevertheless baptized there are admitted to communion only through lay laying-on of hands, lest anyone from among them be [Col. 0486C] appointed to even the least honour in the clergy.

[Note: [Col. 0485] *dicimus*, “we say”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0485] *quo*, “by which”: Spanish Collection.—*ut*, “so that”: Coustant.]

[Note: [Col. 0485] Absent from Coustant.—“is certainly possible”: Anselm.]

[Note: [Col. 0485] “For if, just as”: Lyons II–III editions.—“For just as”: other collected editions, Spanish Collection, and Anselm.]

[Note: [Col. 0485] Numbers 19:22.]

[Note: [Col. 0485] “He who touches an unclean thing shall be unclean”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0485] *agi*, uncertain in context: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0485] *econtra*, “on the contrary”: collected editions, original, Anselm, and Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 0485] *honores*, “honours”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0485] *factus est*, “has become”: Basel edition.—*factus sit*, “may have become”: other collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0485] *damnati*, “of the condemned person”: Basel edition.—*damnationis*, “of condemnation”: other collected editions, Böhm, and Coustant.]

[Note: [Col. 0485] *per benedictionem*, “through the blessing”: original.]

## Part III. Gratian

But this objection is raised: other heretics depart from the faith, whereas Simoniacs, although they regard the grace of the Holy Spirit as saleable, are nevertheless not alien from the faith; therefore what Innocent decrees about other heretics cannot consequently be understood to apply to them. The reply is this: although Simoniacs seem to retain the faith, they are nevertheless subject to the perdition of unbelief.

Accordingly, Blessed Ambrose writes against the Novatians in book II, *On Penance*, c. 4:

[Col. 0487A]

### C. XIX. Simoniacs do not possess integrity of faith.

Peter said to Simon, who had been corrupted by his practice of magical art and thought that he could purchase with money the grace of Christ through the laying-on of hands and the infusion of the Holy Spirit: “You have no part or lot in this faith, because your heart is not right before God,” etc. You see that apostolic authority condemns this man, who through the vanity of magic blasphemed against the Holy Spirit, all the more because he did not possess the pure conscience of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0487] “when Simon”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0487] Acts 8.]

[Note: [Col. 0487] Add “any”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0487B] “In this faith”: the Vulgate edition reads “in this matter.” The Greek is: *en tō logō toutō*, “in this word/matter.”]

[Note: [Col. 0487] *arte*, “art”: in the same source.]

[Note: [Col. 0487] “the Holy Spirit”: collected editions except Lyons II–III.]

[Col. 0488A]

### C. XX. A Simoniac is proved to be an unbeliever. Likewise, Gregory, book IX, letter 53, to King Theodoric.

[Note: [Col. 0487] Letter 59, written A.D. 601, book 11, Maurist edition.]

Since all avarice is service of idols, whoever does not vigilantly guard against it—especially in conferring ecclesiastical honours—is subject to the perdition of unbelief, even though he may seem to hold the faith which he neglects.

[Note: [Col. 0487B] “Which he neglects”: this has been corrected from manuscript copies and the original. The printed editions read: “may seem to hold the faith in words which he denies in deed.” [Col. 0487] The collected editions except Basel, in which the restored reading is found.]

### C. XXI. The Simoniacal heresy is proved more condemnable than others. Likewise, from the letter of Tarasius, Bishop of Constantinople, sent to Pope Hadrian.

[Note: [Col. 0487B] This chapter is part of Tarasius’s letter to Hadrian. But the sequence of words has been altered in several places, and an abridgment has been made, as also in Anselm. The complete letter survives in manuscript after the Seventh Synod in the Vatican Library, in Greek codices of that synod, and in Latin in the translation of Anastasius the Librarian. It is also printed in Latin in Balsamon. But that translation contains a shameful error, whether from the translator or from the copy he followed. For where Tarasius greatly praises Hadrian, the translator represents him as reproving Hadrian in these words: “Therefore your fraternal priestly holiness, which administers the pontifical office neither lawfully nor according to God’s will, labours under great disgrace.” [Col. 0487C] This is plainly contradicted both by much else and especially by the immediately following words, in which he calls him “a man of the Spirit’s desires” and adorns him with other splendid titles. The Vatican Greek copies, those of the Seventh Synod, and Balsamon’s own copy all read excellently. It therefore seemed necessary to provide the earlier part of the letter both in Greek and in a new translation; the remainder may be consulted in the printed Balsamon.]

**To the altogether most holy and most blessed brother and fellow-minister, Lord Hadrian, Pope of elder Rome: Tarasius, unworthy Bishop of Constantinople, greetings in the Lord.**

In many portions and in many ways, by evangelical, apostolic, and patristic teaching, we are instructed to maintain a manner of life free from avarice in the consecration of the priesthood, and neither to receive gold or silver nor to appropriate anything for ourselves at the ordination of any priestly man, as we shall show in the passages set below from scriptural divine utterances and patristic teachings.

For those who lay hands on others are ministers [Col. 0487D] of the Spirit, not sellers of the Spirit. Having received the grace of the Spirit freely, they have been appointed, in accordance with the Lord’s command, to give it freely to those who receive it from them, having received this freedom. But if anyone is convicted of having bought it with gold, they pronounce such a person excluded from priestly rank. Even if he has been allotted the priesthood in name, yet the designation is falsified in the actual case. For, as we have learned from the Gospel, no one can serve God and Mammon.

And since we have heard God crying through the prophet, “Priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem,” and again threatening and saying: “If [Col. 0488B] the watchman sees the sword coming and does not sound the trumpet, and the people do not guard themselves, and the sword comes and takes a life from among them, I will require its blood from the watchman’s hand,” we announce to all the leaders of the churches among us, from fear of condemnation for silence, so that we may say boldly with the divine Apostle: “We are clean from the blood of those who transgress the canonical ordinances,” and especially from the blood of those who ordained or were ordained for money. For Peter the divine Apostle—whose see your fraternal holiness has inherited—deposes them as Simon the magician.

For this reason we do not shrink from proclaiming the truth, preserving and maintaining what has been canonically handed down by the holy and all-praised Apostles and by our ever-memorable Fathers. If any of these things has been transgressed by anyone, we abhor it. Therefore your fraternal, archiepiscopal holiness, administering the priestly consecration ardently and according to God’s will, possesses renowned glory. For [Col. 0488C] Christ our God, the first and great High Priest, said through the prophet: “As I live, I will glorify those who glorify me.”

For you know, O man of the Spirit’s desires, that the impious heresy of Macedonius and those around him who oppose the Holy Spirit is more tolerable. For they foolishly declare that the Holy Spirit is a creature and servant of God the Father; but these persons make him, as they suppose, their own servant. For every master, if he wishes, sells whatever he possesses, whether a household slave or anything else that he owns. Likewise, the buyer, wishing to be master of what he has bought, acquires it by a price in silver.

Thus those who perform this unlawful act degrade the Holy Spirit, sinning equally with those who blasphemed by saying that Christ casts out demons by Beelzebul; or, to say what is truer, they resemble Judas the betrayer, who sold the Lord to the God-killing Jews for a price in silver. Therefore, since the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with Christ our God, they shall manifestly be of precisely the same portion, as has been shown.

But if the priestly dignity is not sold—and plainly it is not—then undoubtedly the grace of the Holy Spirit, or the consecration of the priesthood, is not in them; and what they have not received they do not possess. Let them remember Saint Peter, speaking thus to the man who attempted this: “You have neither part nor lot in this matter.” If priestly dignity is sold, then a reverent way of life and conduct in purity and virtue are superfluous among them. Superfluous to them also is the divine Apostle Paul, teaching that a bishop must be irreproachable, self-controlled, orderly, apt to teach, continent, sober, holding firmly to the trustworthy word according to the teaching, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound [Col. 0489B] doctrine and to refute those who contradict it.

All these things, therefore, disappear because the priesthood is sold and bought. The following sacred passages accordingly declare wholly alien from the priesthood anyone who has ever given or received, at any time whatever, whether before ordination, during ordination, or after ordination. For “to receive” means to receive at any time. They also reject all ecclesiastical promotions on account of the giving of money.

[Greek textual variants: *ἀξίας*, “dignity,” for *τάξεως*, “rank”; *εἴτ᾽ οὖν*, “or then,” for *ἤτοι*, “that is”; *ἄρα* for *ἆρα*, “then”; and *ἀφαιροῦσιν*, “remove,” for *ἀφορίζουσιν*, “exclude.”]

**To the altogether most holy and most blessed brother and fellow-minister, Lord Hadrian, Pope of old Rome: Tarasius, unworthy bishop of Constantinople, new Rome, greetings in the Lord.**

We are taught in many ways and by many means, from the Gospel and the commandments of the Apostles and Fathers, to maintain conduct wholly remote from avarice in the consecration of the priesthood, and not to receive gold or silver, or claim anything else for ourselves, at the ordination of any priestly man. The statements below, from the divine Scriptures and the teachings of the Fathers, [Col. 0489C] will demonstrate this.

For those who impose hands are ministers of the Spirit, not sellers of the Spirit. Since they received the grace of the Spirit freely, they were likewise commanded by the Lord’s word to give it freely to those who receive from them, receiving this very freedom and authority. If anyone is convicted of having bought it with gold, they pronounce that he has fallen from the priestly order, although he has received the priesthood in name; yet it is shown by the reality that this name is falsely conferred on him. For no one can serve God and Mammon, as we have learned from the Gospel.

And because we have heard God crying through the mouth of the prophet, “Priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem,” and again threatening and saying: “If the watchman sees the sword coming and does not sound the trumpet, and the people do not protect themselves, and the sword comes and takes a life from among them, that person indeed is taken in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from the watchman’s hand,” we therefore announce to all [Col. 0489D] the leaders of the churches among us, so that, confidently imitating the divine Apostle, we may say: “We are clean from the blood of those who ordained or were ordained for money.” For Peter, that divine Apostle whose see your fraternal holiness has inherited, deposed them like Simon the magician.

Therefore we do not refuse to preach the truth, preserving and retaining what has been canonically handed down by the holy and altogether blessed Apostles and by our illustrious Fathers. If anything of these things has been violated by anyone, we reject it. Therefore your fraternal holiness, befitting the highest priesthood, lawfully and suitably administering the priestly consecration according to God’s will, has attained renowned glory. For Christ, the first and great high priest, said through the prophet: “As I live, unless I glorify those who glorify me.”

For you know, O man of the desires that belong to the Spirit, that the heresy of Macedonius and those who, with him, oppose the Holy Spirit is far more tolerable. For while they foolishly say that the Holy Spirit of God and the Father is a creature and servant, these make him, so far as they think, their own servant. Every master sells, when he chooses, whatever he has, whether a servant or anything else among his possessions. Likewise, a buyer, wishing to become master of the thing bought, acquires it by the price of silver.

Thus those who commit this impious crime debase the Holy Spirit, sinning equally with those who blasphemously said that Christ cast out demons by Beelzebul; or, to speak more truly, they are like Judas the betrayer, who sold the Lord for a price in silver to the Jews, slayers of God. Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with Christ our God, it is altogether clear that they are to be reckoned in the same portion and lot, as we have shown.

But if he is not sold—as certainly he is not—it is likewise most certain that the grace of the Holy Spirit, or the consecration of the priesthood, is not in these people; and what they have not received they do not possess. Let them remember Saint Peter speaking in this way to the man who had attempted this: “You have neither part nor lot in this matter.” For if priestly dignity is sold, then among them an honourable manner of life and the cultivation of purity and virtue are superfluous. Superfluous among them also is the divine Apostle Paul, teaching that a bishop must be blameless, temperate, modest, fit to teach, continent, sober, adhering to the faithful word according to doctrine, so that he may be capable both of exhorting in sound [Col. 0490D] doctrine and refuting opponents.

All these things perish, therefore, because priesthood is sold and bought. The following statements collected from the saints pronounce wholly excluded from the priesthood anyone who has given or received at any time whatsoever, whether before ordination, at ordination, or after ordination. For receiving means receiving at any time. They also decree void all ecclesiastical promotions in which money intervenes.

[Note: [Col. 0487] Written A.D. 787.—Anselm, book 6, c. 86 (83); Deusdedit, part 2.]

Peter, the divine Apostle—whose see your Holiness has inherited—casts down, like Simon Magus, those who have laid on hands, or do lay them on, for money. [Col. 0489A] And below:

§ 1. For the impious heresy of Macedonius and those associated with him, who attack the Holy Spirit, is more tolerable. In their delirium they confess that the Holy Spirit is a creature and servant of God the Father and the Son; but these men make that same Spirit their servant. [Note: [Col. 0489] Added: “Holy”: editions collated with the original.] For every master, if he wishes, sells what he possesses, whether a slave or anything else among his possessions. Likewise, whoever buys something acquires it for a money price, wishing to be master of what he has bought. Thus those who commit this wicked act demean the Holy Spirit, sinning equally with those who blasphemed by saying that Christ cast out demons by Beelzebub [Note: [Col. 0489] Matt. ch. 12.] [Note: [Col. 0489] “demon”: Basel edition]; or rather, to speak more truly, they are compared with Judas the betrayer, who sold Christ to the Jews, the killers of God. [Col. 0490A] [Note: [Col. 0489] “of God” absent from the editions collated with the first Basel edition.] Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with Christ, they too will altogether share the same lot. And undoubtedly the grace of the Holy Spirit—that is, the holiness of priesthood—is not in them. For they do not possess what they have not received. For Peter says to Simon [Note: [Col. 0489] Acts ch. 8]: “You have neither part nor lot in this matter, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money.” And above:

§ 2. For the twenty-ninth canon of the holy Apostles, their Acts, and the Third and Fourth Books of Kings pronounce wholly alien from the priesthood anyone who has ever given or received money at any time, whether before the laying on of hands, *in the laying on of hands itself*, or afterward. [Note: [Col. 0489] Added: “the laying on of hands”: Basel editions, from Anselm.] For to receive is to receive at whatever time.

[Col. 0491A] **C. XXII. Let both giver and receiver, in order that holy orders may be conferred, be anathema. Likewise from the Second Council of Braga, ch. 3.** [Note: [Col. 0491] Held A.D. 572.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 128.]

It has seemed good that bishops receive no gifts for the ordination of clerics, but that, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0491] Matt. ch. 10, v. 8], what they receive from God’s free gift they give freely. Let neither the grace of God [Note: [Col. 0491] “of God” absent from Ivo.] nor the laying on of hands be sold for any price, because the ancient determination of the Fathers established concerning ecclesiastical ordinations: “Let the giver and receiver be anathema.” [Note: [Col. 0491] Above, ch. 2.] Therefore, because certain men, overwhelmed by many crimes and unworthily ministering at the holy altar, obtain office not through the testimony of good deeds [Note: [Col. 0491] “works”: editions collated with the original.] but through lavish gifts, clerics must be ordained not through the favour of gifts, but first by careful examination and then by the testimony of many persons. [Col. 0491B]

[Note: [Col. 0491] “not by this testimony”: Ivo.]  
[Note: [Col. 0491] Added: “therefore”: Hispanic Collection—Ivo.]

Gratian. From that authority of Blessed Ambrose and Gregory it is clear that simoniacs, like other heretics, depart from the faith; and consequently what is decreed concerning others is understood to apply to them.

**Part IV.** § 1. The following objection is raised: prophecy is a gift of the Holy Spirit, yet in the Old Testament it was customarily sold by holy prophets. Thus Saul did not presume to go to Samuel to seek an oracle unless he brought a gift. Likewise Jeroboam’s wife approached the man of God only with a gift. Again, Christ, though sold by Judas, healed the servant’s ear. Thus the examples of Saul and Jeroboam’s wife show that buying or selling the gift of the Holy Spirit is not sinful. Christ’s example makes clear that the Holy Spirit, even if simoniacs wrongly suppose him saleable, nevertheless does not forget his power and does not cease, even when sold, to grant the effect of his grace. But on prophecy Blessed Jerome gives an apt answer in Micah chapter 3, declaring that only evil prophets, not good ones, received payment:

**C. XXIII. Evil prophets, not good prophets, sold prophecy.** [Note: [Col. 0491C] This chapter is joined to the preceding one in an old copy; and in place of the first word, “Judges,” it reads “Leaders,” as in Blessed Jerome’s version of the Septuagint.]

“‘Her judges,’” he says, “‘gave judgment for gifts; *and* her priests gave answers for payment; [Col. 0492A] and her prophets practised divination for money [Note: [Col. 0491] “moneys”: editions collated with the original, first Basel edition.], while resting upon the Lord, saying, “Is not the Lord among us? Evils will not come upon us.” Therefore, because of you, Zion shall be ploughed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become a watchman’s hut in an orchard.’” [Note: [Col. 0491] “you”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0491] “us”: Argentinian edition.] [Note: [Col. 0491] “orchard”: editions collated with the original, except Lyons II and III.] No one doubts [Note: [Col. 0491] “should doubt”: editions collated with the original.] that Jerusalem was overthrown because of the crimes described in this chapter. [Note: [Col. 0491] “read”: same editions.] And below:

§ 1. Peter could certainly have sold Simon Magus what he sought; indeed, he could have pretended to sell it [Note: [Col. 0491] “pretend to sell”: Basel, Venice II, Paris, Lyons I; Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice I editions] (for the Holy Spirit can neither be sold [Note: [Col. 0491] “be vendible”: editions collated with the original.] nor bought). But he condemned both the money offered and its offerer. And a little later:

§ 2. Nor should anyone be troubled by what we read in the First Book of Kings [Note: [Col. 0491] “Books of Kings”: Argentinian and Basel editions; cf. 1 Kings ch. 9]: that Saul, wishing to go to Samuel, said to his servant that he could not go to him because he had no price to offer for the oracle; [Col. 0492B] [Note: [Col. 0491] “because there is no price in my hand; and he added, ‘A quarter-part is in my hand; I shall give it,’ etc.”: editions collated with the original, except Lyons II and III.] and the servant replied: “Behold, a quarter of a shekel of silver has been found in my hand; I shall give it to the man of God, and he will tell us our way.” For it is not written that Samuel received it, or that they offered it to him; rather, they were fed by the prophet and invited to dinner. *But suppose that he did receive it:* the offerings of the tabernacle are to be valued more highly than gifts for prophecy. [Note: [Col. 0491] “of the prophet”: editions collated with the original.] For a shekel has twenty obols, and a quarter-shekel is five obols. [Note: [Col. 0491] “therefore a quarter”: same editions, except Lyons II and III.] And [Note: [Col. 0491] Absent from the same editions.] so, if our priests wish to sell prophecy and display doves in their chairs—the doves which the Lord overturned with a whip—let them be content with the payment of only five obols; would that they received not the prices of estates but five obols. [Note: [Col. 0491D] “Let them be content with the payment of only five obols, who”: all this is absent from more recent editions of Blessed Jerome and from older ones as well, except the word “who”; but it has not been deleted because it does not conflict with the sense.]

§ 3. The same meaning is found in the Third Book of Kings [Note: [Col. 0491] 3 Kings ch. 14—“Kings”: editions collated with the original, first Basel edition]: Jeroboam’s wife, when her son was ill, went to Ahijah, the man of God, and brought him ten loaves, [Col. 0492C] [Note: [Col. 0491] Concerning Jeroboam’s wife going to the man of God, who offered only ten loaves, a cake, and a jar of honey: editions collated with the original, except Lyons II and III.] a cake, and a jar of honey. [Note: [Col. 0491D] “Ten loaves”: Blessed Jerome has in the Latin Vulgate: “loaves, raisins, and a little vessel of honey.” But the common Greek version also mentions cakes and raisins: “Ἄρτους … καὶ κολλύρια τοῖς τέκνοις αὐτοῦ, καὶ σταφύλας”—“loaves … and cakes for his children, and raisins.”] These are to be reckoned rather as provisions for the prophet than as a gift for prophecy, although those accustomed to go to diviners—*for there were many prophets and diviners in Israel*—may through evil custom have thought the same thing of prophets and wished to offer holy men what they customarily offered diviners. [Note: [Col. 0492D] From “because these are rather” to “although” these words are not found here in Blessed Jerome; instead: “For it is stated what she carried with her, yet the prophet is not written to have received it, especially since he rebuked her and foretold the coming mourning; although,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0491] “as gifts”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0491] “could”: editions collated with the original, first Basel edition and Lyons II–III.] [Note: [Col. 0491] “from their evil [custom]”: editions collated with the original.] [Note: [Col. 0491] “thought”: same editions.] [Note: [Col. 0491] “not wished”: Basel edition.]

§ 4. Hence [Note: [Col. 0493] These appear to be Gratian’s words.] we read in the Fourth Book of Kings [Note: [Col. 0493D] “Hence, in the Fourth [Book]”: these words through the end are not found in Blessed Jerome.] [Note: [Col. 0493] 4 Kings ch. 5] that Elisha came to Damascus, and Ben-hadad king of Syria was sick. They announced to him, saying, “The man of God has come here.” *And* the king said to Hazael, “Take gifts with you, go to meet the man of God, and consult the Lord through him, saying, ‘May I recover from this illness?’” Hazael therefore went to meet him, taking gifts with him—every good thing of Damascus, loads of forty camels. But one should not believe that Elisha accepted them, since we read of the same Elisha that Naaman, cleansed of leprosy, offered him gifts, saying, “I beg you, accept a blessing from your servant.” But he replied, “As the Lord lives, before whom I stand, I shall not accept.” And although Naaman pressed him strongly, he absolutely refused.

[Col. 0493B] **C. XXIV. That “divination” is taken in a good sense. In the same chapter.** [Note: [Col. 0493D] This chapter also is joined to the preceding in several old copies and reads, as in the original: “For divination is never …”]

“Divination” is never taken in a good sense *in the Scriptures*. “There is no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel.” [Note: [Col. 0493] Num. ch. 23, v. 23.] They thought themselves prophets, but because they received money, their prophecy became divination.

Gratian. Since, therefore, according to Jerome, good prophets did not receive gifts for prophecy but offerings for the tabernacle, whereas for the evil men who did receive them prophecy—which was God’s gift—was turned into divination, which is demonic, what else follows except that no spiritual grace cooperates with simoniacs, as was said above? For since in the sacraments “neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, [Col. 0493C] but God who gives the increase,” [Note: [Col. 0493] 1 Cor. ch. 3, v. 7.] who works in them if the Lord who gives increase does not shine in them but remains inactive?

Likewise, the assertion about Christ—that as Christ when sold restored Malchus’s ear and performed miracles, so the Holy Spirit can be sold and can work his grace in that very sale—does not establish the comparison. The Holy Spirit does not work spiritually in the faithless commercial dealings of avarice what Christ did bodily, for the sake of a definite mystery and as an example of patience. For if the analogy holds in every respect, then, since he is thought able to be sold as Christ was, the Holy Spirit must also be thought able to be crucified, which is impossible. Or it may be understood, lest we depart from the analogy, that as Christ when sold granted the gifts of his grace not to the seller or buyer, but to those who were present in ignorance, [Col. 0493D] and for whom he also prayed on the cross, so the Holy Spirit is shown to grant the effect of his grace not to seller or buyer, but to those who, led by ignorance, receive the Lord’s sacraments from their hands. [Col. 0494A]

§ 1. Again, it is objected that, even if buying ecclesiastical office is evil, evil beginnings often reach happy ends: Jacob attained a blessing through supplanting; grain sown by a leprous hand is nevertheless harvested clean; beautiful offspring is born from adulterous intercourse. Thus money acquired through simony has a happy outcome when it is distributed for the benefit of the poor. But none of these considerations supports simoniacs.

[Col. 0494B] For Leo, bishop, says to the bishops of Mauretania, Epistle LXXXV, otherwise LXXXVII [Note: [Col. 0493] Written about A.D. 446.—Anselm, book 6, ch. 20]:

**C. XXV. What is begun from an evil principle is not completed with a good outcome.**

A position of authority which either sedition has extorted or ambition has seized, even if it gives no offence in morals and acts [Note: [Col. 0493] “will give offence”: Basel edition], is nevertheless ruinous by the example of its very beginning. And it is difficult for things begun from an evil principle to be completed with a good outcome.

**C. XXVI. No good work is built up where Christ is not the foundation. Likewise Gregory, to [Anastasius], bishop of Antioch, Book VII, Epistle 47, Indiction 2.** [Note: [Col. 0493] Epistle 49 (written A.D. 599), book 9, Maurist edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0493D] In Blessed Gregory it reads: “But the outstanding preacher says: ‘Foundation,’ etc. Whoever therefore, with love of God and neighbour, holds fast the firmness of the faith which is in Christ, has set the same Jesus Christ, Son of God and man, as his foundation. Therefore it is to be hoped that where Christ is the foundation, the building of good works will also follow.”]

Since Paul says, “No one can lay another foundation besides that which is Christ Jesus,” [Note: [Col. 0493] 1 Cor. ch. 3, v. 11.] it is consequently proved that where Christ is not the foundation, no building of good work exists.

[Col. 0494C] **C. XXVII. Alms cannot be made from money acquired through simony. The same, to Syagrius and other bishops, Book VII, Epistle 110.** [Note: [Col. 0493] Epistle 106, written A.D. 599, book 9, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 5, ch. 30 (31). Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, ch. 194; *Decree*, part 5, ch. 112. Polycarp, book 2, title 1.]

It must not be considered almsgiving if something received from unlawful sources is distributed to the poor, because one who receives evil with the intention of distributing it *as though* well is burdened rather than helped. [Note: [Col. 0494D] “Helped”: if the chapter “Almsgiving,” below, 14, question 5, is inserted here, this passage will be complete.] [Note: [Col. 0493] “may be helped”: editions collated with the original.] And shortly afterward:

§ 1. Hence it is certain also that, even if monasteries, hostels for strangers, or anything else are built from money given for holy orders, it does not contribute to one’s reward. [Note: [Col. 0493] “from”: editions collated with the original.] And shortly afterward:

§ 2. Therefore, lest under the pretext of almsgiving we should endeavour to receive anything sinfully, Sacred Scripture plainly forbids us, saying: “The sacrifices of the impious, offered from wickedness, are abominable.” [Col. 0494D] [Note: [Col. 0493] Added: “to the Lord”: editions collated with the original, first Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0493] Prov. ch. 21, v. 27.] Whatever is offered from wickedness in God’s sacrifice does not appease the anger of almighty God but provokes it. Hence it is also written: “Honour the Lord from your righteous labours.” [Col. 0495A] [Note: [Col. 0495] Prov. ch. 3, v. 9.] Whoever, then, takes wickedly in order to give *as though* well, plainly does not honour the Lord. Likewise Solomon says: “He who offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is as one sacrificing a son in his father’s presence.” [Note: [Col. 0495] Ecclus. ch. 34, v. 24.] *Let us consider how great is a father’s pain if his son is sacrificed before his eyes,* and from this we readily recognize how greatly God’s pain is inflamed when a sacrifice from robbery is offered to him. [Note: [Col. 0495] “is recognized”: editions collated with the original.] [Note: [Col. 0495] “how great”: editions collated with the original, from the original text.] Therefore, dearest brethren, one must most carefully avoid committing the sins of the simoniacal heresy under the pretext of almsgiving. For it is one thing to give alms because of sins, and another to commit sins because of alms. [Col. 0495B] [Note: [Col. 0495D] “Commit”: here Blessed Gregory inserts the chapters “This also” (Distinction 59) and “Like Neophyte” (Distinction 48).] [Note: [Col. 0495] “perpetrate”: same editions.]

And a few lines later:

§ 3. Whoever desires to obtain priesthood, not for the pomp of self-exaltation but for usefulness, should first measure his strength against the burden he is about to undertake, so that, if unequal to it, he may abstain; and that he may approach even what he considers himself sufficient for with fear. [Note: [Col. 0495] “who”: original.]

**C. XXVIII. A simoniacal shepherd provides no remedy for the sheep. The same, to Theuderic and Theudebert, kings of the Franks, Book VII, Epistle 114.** [Note: [Col. 0495] Epistle 110, written A.D. 599, book 9, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 6, ch. 78 (76). Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 111. Polycarp, same place.] [Note: [Col. 0495] “Theudebert”: original.]

The simoniacal heresy—which first crept against God’s Church through a diabolical planting [Note: [Col. 0495] “supplanting”: editions collated with the original—Ivo.] and was struck down and condemned at its very birth by the zeal of apostolic vengeance—is said to reign within the borders of your kingdom, although in priests faith must be chosen together with life. [Note: [Col. 0495] The words placed in parentheses are lacking in Anselm.] For if life is lacking, faith has no merit, as Blessed James testifies when he says: “Faith without works is dead.” [Note: [Col. 0495] Jas. ch. 2, v. 17.] What works can a priest have who is proved to have obtained the honour of so great a sacrament by payment? [Note: [Col. 0495] “honours”: Basel edition—Ivo.]

And a few lines later:

§ 1. Thus not only is a deadly wound inflicted upon the soul of the ordainer and the ordained; the rule of your Majesty is also heavily burdened by the fault of the bishops, by whose intercessions it ought rather to have been aided. [Note: [Col. 0495] “your government”: editions collated with the original—“your royal excellence”: Anselm.] For if a man is believed worthy of priesthood when not merits of conduct [Note: [Col. 0495] “accusation”: Basel edition.] but abundance of payments speaks on his behalf, it remains that in ecclesiastical honours neither seriousness nor diligence accomplishes anything, but that the profane love of gold gains everything. [Col. 0496A] And while vices are rewarded with honour, one who perhaps ought to have been punished is brought into the place of avenger; hence priests are judged not to advance but rather to perish. For when the shepherd is wounded, who can apply medicine to cure the sheep? Or how can one defend the people with the shield of prayer who exposes himself to be struck by enemy missiles? Or what fruit will be produced by one whose root is infected with a grave pestilence? Therefore a greater calamity is to be feared in those places where such intercessors are brought to the place of government: men who provoke God’s anger in themselves more than they ought to appease it through themselves. [Note: [Col. 0495] “are honoured”: original—“honour rewards”: Ivo; Basel and Lyons II–III editions—“rewards with honour”: Lyons I—“endows with honour”: remaining editions.] [Note: [Col. 0495] “enemies”: Ivo; editions collated with the original.] [Note: [Col. 0495] Added: “indeed”: Basel edition.]

Gratian. Therefore, since according to Leo simony is not completed with a good outcome; since, according to Gregory, no structure of good work follows; since that which is distributed to the poor from the price of simony is not to be considered almsgiving; since no medicine is applied to heal sheep when the shepherd is wounded; since no fruit is produced from an infected root; and since a greater future calamity is feared—from so sinister a beginning, what happy outcome can be hoped for? [Col. 0496B]

Augustine also says [Note: [Col. 0495] Chapter of uncertain origin; the same words are cited under Augustine’s name in Alger, book 3, ch. 47]:

**C. XXIX. The sacraments of simoniacs lack the effect of grace.**

Just as the eunuch who bought Joseph had no living seed because his genitals were dry, so he who purchases grace has no living seed. Likewise the fire of sacrifice, which had lived under water during the seventy years of Babylonian captivity, was extinguished when Antiochus sold the priesthood to Jason. [Note: [Col. 0495] Gen. ch. 39.] [Note: [Col. 0495] 2 Macc. chs. 1 and 4.] This signified that the fire of the Holy Spirit does not shine in simoniacal sacraments. [Col. 0496C]

Gratian. What did Blessed Augustine intend to mark by these comparisons except that the sacraments of simoniacs, like those of other heretics, though true as to their form, are nevertheless empty and false as to their effect, since they cannot generate or kindle heavenly grace in human hearts?

**Part V.** § 1. But the following statement of Augustine, in his fifth tractate on the Gospel of John against the heretics, is raised as an objection: [Note: [Col. 0495] Anselm, book 9, ch. 30 (42). Polycarp, book 3, title 10.—Cf. below, *On Consecration*, Distinction 4, ch. 39, § 4.]

**C. XXX. Whether the minister is good or bad, the effect of grace is conferred through either.** [Note: [Col. 0495D] From the beginning of this chapter to “gift of Christ,” [Col. 0496D] Alger, book 3, cites it from Blessed Augustine, whose actual words, however, occur below, *On Consecration*, Distinction 4, ch. “Another,” § “If he shall be.”]

If the minister is righteous, I count him with Paul, who does not seek his own glory, saying: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase.” [Col. 0497A] [Note: [Col. 0497] 1 Cor. ch. 3, v. 7.] But if the minister is proud, he is counted with the devil; [Note: [Col. 0497] “Zabulus”: editions collated with the original.] [Note: [Col. 0497] “will be counted”: Venice I–II, Nuremberg, Lyons editions, and Anselm.] yet Christ’s gift is not defiled, because a pure stream passes through him and comes to fertile ground. I know that a stone cannot bear fruit from water; and if water passes through stone channels into garden beds, nothing is produced in the stone channel; yet the garden bears abundant fruit. [Note: [Col. 0497] “garden”: Argentinian, Basel, Nuremberg, Lyons II–III editions—“gardens”: Böhm.] For the spiritual power of the sacrament, like light, is received pure by those being illuminated; but although it passes through the unclean, it is not defiled.

[Note: [Col. 0497D] In Blessed Augustine’s fifth tractate it reads: “What flows through him is pure; what passes through him comes clear to fertile ground—for example, because he is stony, because he cannot bear fruit from the water. Water passes through a stone channel to the garden beds: it produces nothing in the stone channel, but it bears much fruit in the gardens. For the spiritual power of the sacrament is like light: it is received pure by those being illuminated, and if it passes through the unclean, it is not defiled.”]

**C. XXXI. On the same. The same, to Vincentius the Donatist, Epistle XLVIII.** [Note: [Col. 0497] Written about A.D. 408. Polycarp, book 3, title 10.]

All the Lord’s sacraments belong to the Catholic Church, [Col. 0497B] and you possess and administer them [Note: [Col. 0497] “as”: editions collated with the original, first Basel edition], just as [Note: [Col. 0497] “as”: Basel edition—“so”: editions collated with the original] they were possessed and administered even before you left it.

**C. XXXII. On the same. The same, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, Book V, ch. 19.** [Note: [Col. 0497] Anselm, book 9, ch. 49. Ivo, *Decree*, part 1, ch. 117.]

God is present to his sacraments and words, however they are administered; and God’s sacraments are everywhere right, just as evil men, to whom they do no good, are everywhere perverse. [Note: [Col. 0497] “if”: original—Ivo, Anselm.] [Note: [Col. 0497] “by whomever”: editions collated with the original.] [Note: [Col. 0497] “whose sacraments and words”: same editions.] [Note: [Col. 0497] Added: that is, outside and inside: same editions.]

**C. XXXIII. On the same. The same, Book IV, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, ch. 12.** [Note: [Col. 0497] Anselm, book 9, ch. 48. Polycarp, same place.]

Thus neither outside nor inside can anyone who belongs to the devil’s party [Note: [Col. 0497] “whose father is the devil”: original.] defile, either in himself or in anyone else, the sacrament which belongs to Christ.

[Col. 0497C] **C. XXXIV. Sacraments that have not been changed are shown to be common to Catholics and heretics. The same Augustine, to Emeritus, Epistle CLXIV.** [Note: [Col. 0497] Written A.D. 405; Epistle 57, Maurist edition.—Polycarp, book 7, title 10.]

The sacraments which you have not changed are approved by us as you possess them, lest, while seeking to correct your perversity, we commit sacrilegious injury against those mysteries of Christ which have not been corrupted by your perversity. For not even Saul had corrupted the anointing he had received; [Note: [Col. 0497] 1 Kings ch. 24.] and King David, God’s servant, showed great—indeed more than once—honour to that anointing. [Col. 0498A] [Note: [Col. 0497] “earlier”: Lyons II edition; added: “often”: Basel edition—“more often”: remaining editions.]

**C. XXXV. On the same. The same, to the Donatists.** [Note: [Col. 0497D] The words in the first part of this chapter through “is rejected” [Col. 0498D] have not been found in Blessed Augustine, though its sense occurs in *On Baptism against the Donatists*, Book I, ch. 12. The remainder occurs in the same book, ch. 13.]

Just as pretenders truly receive, and do not receive falsely, nor is their baptism rejected, so also those things which schismatics or heretics possess and perform—*if* they do not possess or perform them differently from the true Church—are not corrected but rather approved when they come to us. [Note: [Col. 0497] “and do not”: Basel edition.]

**C. XXXVI. God’s sacraments, whoever administers them, are not to be avoided.**

The same, *Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book III, ch. 9. [Note: [Col. 0498D] In Book 3 of *Against the Letters of Petilian*, from which this chapter appears to have been taken, it reads: “Let no one glory even in a good man; let no one flee God’s good things even in an evil man.” This chapter is indicated above, Distinction 32, ch. “Besides,” § “But the principles.”] [Note: [Col. 0497] Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, ch. 75.]

Let no one avoid God’s sacraments in a good person, nor in an evil person.

[Col. 0498B] **C. XXXVII. Human wickedness does not profane the sacraments. The same, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, Book VI, ch. 44.**

Were not the Sodomites pagans—that is, Gentiles? [Note: [Col. 0497] “and pagans”: Basel edition.] The Jews, therefore, were worse, to whom the Lord says: “It will be more tolerable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for you”; [Note: [Col. 0497] Matt. ch. 10, v. 15.] and to whom the Prophet says: “You have justified Sodom,” that is, Sodom has been made just *in comparison with you*. [Note: [Col. 0497] Ezek. ch. 16, v. 51.] [Note: [Col. 0497] “your”: editions collated with the original, first Basel edition and Lyons II–III.] But were the divine sacraments among the Jews therefore such as they themselves were? The Lord himself commanded those sacraments and sent lepers whom he had cleansed to celebrate them; [Note: [Col. 0497] Zech. ch. 1.] and an angel stood beside Zechariah as he ministered them and announced that he had been heard while sacrificing in the Temple. [Note: [Col. 0497] Luke ch. 17.] The same sacraments existed in the good people of that time and in evil people worse [Col. 0498C] than pagans, since they surpassed the Sodomites in wickedness; nevertheless those sacraments were whole and divine in both groups. For even the Gentiles, if they could possess anything divine and right in their teachings, were not condemned for that by our holy men, [Note: [Col. 0497] “men”: editions collated with the original, first Basel edition.] although through their superstitions, idolatry, pride, and other ruinous practices they deserved to be detested and, unless corrected, punished by divine judgment.

[Col. 0499A] **C. XXXVIII. The wicked may possess sacraments, although they cannot possess the power of the Holy Spirit. The same, Book III, ch. 16.** [Note: [Col. 0499] Anselm, book 9, ch. 39 (41). Polycarp, book 3, title 10.]

There are many operations of the Holy Spirit, which the Apostle, having listed in one passage as much as he considered sufficient, concluded thus: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each severally as he wills.” [Note: [Col. 0499] 1 Cor. ch. 12, v. 11.] Since, then, one thing is a sacrament, which even Simon Magus could possess; another is prophecy, which is also wont to occur in evil men, as in Saul; another is the operation of the same Spirit, which only good people can possess, such as “the end of the commandment,” namely love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith—[Note: [Col. 0499] Cf. 1 Tim. ch. 1, v. 5.] whatever heretics and schismatics may receive, love, [Col. 0499B] which covers a multitude of sins, [Note: [Col. 0499] 1 Pet. ch. 4, v. 8.] is the particular gift of Catholic unity and peace, and is not in all of them, because not all belong to it.

[Note: [Col. 0499] Added: “the same”: Basel edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 0499] “as much as he considered sufficient”: absent from Anselm.]  
[Note: [Col. 0499] “to each his own”: same place.]  
[Note: [Col. 0499] “as Saul possessed it”: original.]  
[Note: [Col. 0499] “that is”: Anselm—editions collated with the original; the following words are lacking in Anselm.]  
[Note: [Col. 0499] “whichever”: Argentinian edition—“any of these”: remaining editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0499] “receive”: editions collated with the original, except Argentinian, Venice I–II, and Nuremberg.]  
[Note: [Col. 0499] “covers”: editions collated with the original, from Anselm.]  
[Note: [Col. 0499] Added: “of his house”: same editions.]

**C. XXXIX. Although the wicked administer sacraments, they do not confer remission of sins. The same, same book, ch. 18.** [Note: [Col. 0499] Anselm, book 9, ch. 33 (45).]

The avaricious did not confer the remission of sins, which is given through the prayers of the saints—that is, through the groanings of the dove—whoever baptizes, provided that those to whom it is given belong to its peace. [Note: [Col. 0499] “Remitted”: original—Anselm.] [Note: [Col. 0499] “confer”: editions collated with the original.] [Note: [Col. 0499] “prayer”: same editions.] [Note: [Col. 0499] “baptizes”: same editions, first Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0499] Added: “nevertheless”: editions collated with the original.] For the Lord would not say to robbers and usurers: “If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven; if you retain anyone’s sins, they are retained.” [Note: [Col. 0499] John ch. 20, v. 23.] Outside, indeed, nothing can be bound or loosed where there is no one able either to bind or to loose; but the person who makes peace with the dove is loosed, [Col. 0499C] and the person who has no peace with the dove is bound, whether openly outside or apparently inside. [Note: [Col. 0499] “someone”: same editions.] [Note: [Col. 0499] Added: “another”: same editions.] [Note: [Col. 0499] “absolve”: same editions, first Basel edition and Lyons II–III.]

Gratian. Therefore, if sacraments cannot be defiled by the unclean, like light; if, like a pure stream, they reach fertile garden beds through stone channels; it is clear that simoniacs possess the sacrament of anointing to their own harm and ruin, but administer that same anointing to others beneficially and savingly. Thus, as the sacraments of heretics are true in form, so they are true and not empty in effect.

[Col. 0500A] **Part VI.** But it must be noted that some sacraments are of necessity and others of dignity. Since necessity has no law but makes law for itself, sacraments necessary for salvation, because they cannot be repeated, must not be taken away or lost when they are valid, but are permitted to stand with penance. But sacraments of dignity, unless they have been administered worthily—so that worthy persons are promoted worthily by worthy persons—cease to be dignities. This does not diminish the truth of the sacrament, but causes the office of administering to cease, whether by place, time, or promotion.

By place, as Leo says to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, Epistle XC, otherwise XCII, ch. 1: [Note: [Col. 0499D] This chapter has been corrected and enlarged from the Epistle itself, and is reported above, Distinction 62, ch. 1, § “If any.”] [Note: [Col. 0499] Epistle 167, written A.D. 458 or 459, Ballerini edition—Burchard, book 1, ch. 11. Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 65.—Cf. above, Distinction 62, ch. 1.]

[Col. 0500B] **C. XL. Concerning those ordained by pseudo-bishops.**

If any *clerics* have been ordained by *these* pseudo-bishops in churches belonging to their proper bishops, and their ordination was performed with the consent and judgment of the presiding bishops, it may be held valid, provided that they remain in those churches. Otherwise the ordination is to be considered void, because it is neither established by place nor secured by authority. [Note: [Col. 0499] “shall have been”: editions collated with the original.] [Note: [Col. 0499] The words from “which” to “was performed” are lacking from the editions collated with the original, first Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0499] The following words to the end are absent from the editions collated with the original, first Basel edition.]

Gratian. Behold: if someone ordained by pseudo-bishops changes the place of his ordination, that ordination will be void and without administrative function.

By time, as Innocent says in Epistle XXII, ch. 5, concerning those ordained by Bonosus: [Note: [Col. 0499] Written A.D. 414—Ivo, in the prologue.—Cf. below, question 7, ch. 7.]

**C. XLI. What is granted from necessity will cease when the necessity ceases.**

What has been established by the necessity of the time ought, when necessity has ceased, likewise to cease, because legitimate order is one thing, and usurpation another—the usurpation which present necessity compels. [Col. 0500C] [Note: [Col. 0499] “that”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0499D] “which present necessity compels”: these words are added from Innocent, whose words, summarized in this chapter, are set out more fully below, question 7, ch. “What for remedy.”]

Gratian. Therefore someone ordained at another time by a man like Bonosus will cease from the administration which had been allowed by the necessity of that time.

Likewise by promotion, as Leo says in Epistle III to Julian, bishop of Aquileia: [Note: [Col. 0499] Epistle 17, written A.D. 447, Ballerini edition.—Thus in Merlin; but “Januarius” should be read.—Cf. Causa 1, question 1, ch. 112; Causa 1, question 7, ch. 21.]

[Col. 0501A] **C. XLII. Those returning from heretics may be received in their orders without hope of promotion.**

If anyone has stained himself by the contagion of heretical communion, let him count it a great benefit if, when every hope of promotion has been taken away from him, he remains in the order in which he is found. [Note: [Col. 0501D] “Has stained himself”: here in Blessed Leo other words are inserted, as also the chapter “Most salutary,” below, question 7. For this chapter is a kind of summary, as is the chapter “Every,” below in the same question, though that one is somewhat fuller.]

Gratian. Behold: if a cleric communicates with heretics, whether in ordination or in any sacrament, he scarcely remains in his own order when barred from promotion. For this sacrament is not like the others. The others are given either to wash away sins, as baptism and penance, or are denied for sins not eternally but temporarily, as the Eucharist, which at the point of death is granted to a penitent even for heinous sins. This one alone is forbidden not only on account of fault but also on account of disgrace [Col. 0501B], and because the prerogative of purity—whether external or internal—and of perfection has been diminished: thus it is denied to bigamists, to men married to widows, to the unlearned, or to those impaired in any bodily part; yet baptism or the Eucharist is not denied to them. Such a person may also administer the other sacraments priestly, though he is unable to confer this one alone.

Therefore Leo says to the bishops of Africa, Epistle LXXXV, alternatively LXXXVII, chapter 2 [Note: These words are not found in the epistle itself (Ep. 12, written A.D. 448, Ballerini edition), nor do they appear to belong to Leo; for they occur in the epistle concerning chorepiscopi, which is known to have been falsely attributed to Leo before the time of Pseudo-Isidore.—Anselm, book 6, chapters 35 and 74 (72). Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 107.—Cf. C. 25, q. 2, c. 24.]:

### C. XLIII. Concerning bishops who consecrate someone whom it is unlawful to consecrate.

If any bishops have consecrated as a priest a man such as it is unlawful [Note: Add: “to be”: editions compared, old collection] to be, even if in some manner they escape loss of their own rank, they shall nevertheless thereafter have no right of ordination; nor shall they ever participate in that sacrament [Col. 0501C] which, *disregarding divine judgment,* they improperly conferred.

Gratian. Behold: although they escape danger to their rank, so that they are permitted to administer the other sacraments priestly, they are excluded from this one alone—not only for heresy or any greater fault, but even for negligence. In all these matters it must be carefully observed that the sacrament of priestly promotion must be given or received more carefully and worthily than all the rest, because unless it has been conferred in this manner, it ceases to be valid insofar as it has not been duly performed. For the other sacraments are given to each person for that person's own sake, and become such for each recipient as the heart or conscience with which they are received. This one alone is given not merely for its recipient's own sake, but [Col. 0501D] for others; and therefore it must be received, so far as concerns oneself, with a true heart and pure conscience, but so far as concerns others, not only without every fault but also without every disgrace, because of the scandal [Col. 0502A] of the brethren, for whose benefit the priesthood is given—not merely that its holders may preside, but that they may also be of service.

Therefore Jerome, on Micah chapter 3:

### C. XLIV. Simoniacs are guilty of the unbelief of those scandalized by them.

Those who ordain as *clerics* [Note: “While ordaining”: editions compared, old collection; add “bishops”: Basel edition] whomever they choose from among their own followers, and expose their lives as a scandal to the people, are guilty of the unbelief of those who are scandalized.

Gratian. For indeed those who are chosen to preside over others ought, just as they are set before them in dignity, likewise to surpass them in holiness. Otherwise, why are men preferred to others who are elevated above them by no excellence of merit? Hence Symmachus also wrote to Laurence, bishop of Milan [Col. 0502B], after the sixth Roman Synod [Note: Written circa A.D. 500]:

### C. XLV. As each person is pre-eminent in rank, so he ought also to excel in learning.

He who is higher in rank must be judged most contemptible unless he excels in learning and holiness.  
[Note: The original reads: “He must be compared with the most contemptible.”]

## Part VII

Gratian. Thus Augustine's statement—that sacraments of Christ administered through heretics do not lack their effect—is evidently not to be understood universally of all sacraments, but of the sacrament of baptism.

Therefore the same Augustine says in Tractate V on John:

### C. XLVI. Baptism, whether administered by a good person or an evil one, ought not to be repeated.

Judas gave baptism, and no one was baptized after Judas; John gave baptism, and people were baptized after [Col. 0502C] John, because the baptism given by Judas was Christ's baptism [Note: The editions compared read: “is”], whereas that *given* by John was John's. We rightly prefer, not Judas to John, but Christ's baptism, even when given through Judas's hands, to John's baptism, *even when given through John's hands.* And a little later:

§ 1. Those whom John *baptized, John baptized; but those whom Judas baptized,* Christ baptized. Thus those baptized by a drunkard [Note: “Drunkard”: several additions, omissions, and corrections have been made in this chapter from the original; this word, however, was not altered because of the gloss. The reading should be *ebriosus*, “a habitual drunkard.”], those *baptized* by a murderer, those *baptized* by an adulterer—*if it was Christ's baptism*—were baptized by Christ. Again, after a few intervening words:

§ 2. *That* sacrament is so holy that it is not defiled even when a murderer administers it.

### C. XLVII. On the same subject. The same author, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, book IV, chapter 4.

[Note: Anselm, book 9, chapter 35 (47). Ivo, *Decretum*, part 1, chapter 165; part 2, chapter 94. Polycarp, book 3, title 10.]

[Col. 0502D]

Just as I seem to be pressed when someone says to me, “Then does a heretic forgive sins?” so I in turn press him when I say: “Then does one *who does not keep the heavenly commandments*—[Col. 0503A] a covetous man [Note: Add: “a pretender to religion”: editions compared, from Anselm], *a robber, a usurer, an envious man, one who renounces the world in words rather than deeds*—forgive sins?” If it is by the power of God's sacrament, then, as with the former, so with the latter [Note: In Böhm, through a printer's error, almost a whole line has dropped out.—The source has been identified as Alger the Scholastic, in *On Mercy and Justice*, part 3.]; if by his own merit, then neither the former nor the latter does. For that sacrament is recognized as Christ's even among evil persons; but in the body of the one dove, incorrupt, *holy, chaste, having neither spot nor wrinkle,* neither the former nor the latter is found. [“Just as, if someone's hand were withered, it would indeed be a true member, though bloodless, ineffective, and dead, so faith also, though true, is nevertheless dead without works.”] [Note: From “Just as, if someone's hand” through the word “Again” in [Col. 0503D], these words are not found at this point in the standard manuscripts of Augustine, nor among the other collectors.] Again, a little later:

§ 1. Thus one baptized in heresy in the name of the holy [Note: Add: “and undivided”: Basel edition] Trinity nevertheless does not become a temple of God if he does not withdraw from heresy; just as one baptized in the same name amid covetousness [Col. 0503B] does not become a temple of God if he does not withdraw from covetousness, which is the service of idols.

## Part VIII

Gratian. From these words, therefore, it appears that baptism administered by heretics confers remission of sins by its own power.

But Augustine himself states the contrary in book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 1, saying:

### C. XLVIII. Christ's baptism, although violated by no perversity, nevertheless lacks effect among heretics.

Even those slower of heart, *so far as I think,* understand that Christ's baptism cannot be violated by any perversity *of a person,* whether giver or recipient. But because the sacrament is one thing and the effect of the sacrament another, and because it is established that those who live ruinously even within the unity of the Church can neither [Col. 0503C] give nor possess forgiveness of sins—since it was said not to evil but to good children [Note: John 20:23], “If you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven [Note: The Basel edition reads: “shall be forgiven”] *him; if* you retain anyone's sins, they are retained”—it is clear that heretics only give or receive the sacrament of baptism and do not give remission of sins.

### C. XLIX. On the same subject. The same author, in Sermon XI on the Words of the Lord, concerning blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.

[Note: In several very old manuscripts, this and the following chapter are joined to the preceding chapter.]  
[Note: Sermon 71, chapter 19, Maurist edition.]

The bodily sacraments, which even those separated from the unity of Christ's body bear and celebrate, can display [Note: The editions compared read: “possess”] the form of godliness. But the invisible and spiritual power *of godliness* [Col. 0504A] cannot be in them, just as sensation does not remain with a *human* limb when it is cut off from the body.

### C. L. On the same subject. Likewise Ambrose, in the book *On Initiating Beginners*.

[Note: Alger, *On Mercy and Justice*, book 3, chapter 17.]

The baptism of the faithless does not heal, does not cleanse, but defiles [Note: Thus far Ambrose. But Alger, book 3, chapter 1, while reporting this passage, adds material through the word “approaches” in [Col. 0504C]; then, in chapter 13, while also citing the same book of blessed Ambrose, he joins the remainder of this chapter through the end.], because amid the flood of many waters it does not approach the Lord [Note: Editions compared read: “they shall approach”]; because, as the Apostle says [Note: Romans 14:23], whatever is not from faith is sin, and it not only benefits neither those who do it nor those for whom they do it, but is also unto judgment.

### C. LI. Those who receive baptism from heretics are to be confirmed through the laying on of hands. Likewise Leo to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, Epistle LXXVII, alternatively LXXIX, chapter 7.

[Note: Epistle 195, written A.D. 458, Ballerini edition.—Collection in three parts, part 1, title 43, chapter 33. Anselm, book 9, chapter 36. Polycarp, book 3, title 10.]

[Col. 0504B] Those who received baptism from heretics, when they had not previously been baptized, are to be confirmed solely by the invocation of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands [Note: The editions compared read: “hand”; Hispanic Collection], because they received only the form of baptism without the power of sanctification. And [Note: Cf. below, chapter 57.] we preach that this rule, as you know, must be observed in all [Note: Add “in”: editions compared; Hispanic Collection] churches: that the washing once received should be violated by no repetition. For the Apostle says [Note: Ephesians 4:6], “One Lord [Note: The editions compared read: “God”], one faith, one baptism.” Its washing must not be rashly repeated; rather, as we have said, the sanctification of the Holy Spirit alone is to be invoked, so that a person may obtain from Catholic priests what no one receives from heretics.

## Part IX

Gratian. But it should be noted that heretics such as Arians and Sabellians—some of whom professed inequality, [Col. 0504C] others an indistinction, of the persons—administered baptism not in the form of the Church but in that of their own perversity.

§ 1. Ambrose spoke specifically of these when he said, “The baptism of the faithless does not heal,” and so forth. Moreover, it was decreed at the Council of Nicaea [Note: Held A.D. 325], chapter 19, that they should be rebaptized and reordained:

### C. LII. Those who return to the Church from Paulianists and Cataphrygians are to be rebaptized and reordained.

If anyone flees to the Catholic Church from the Paulianists and Cataphrygians [Note: “Cataphrygians”: this term occurs in the ancient translation found in various printed and manuscript copies of Isidore's collection, but not in the Greek canon, Dionysius's translation, or other later versions. That these too must be baptized was handed down in the Council of Laodicea, chapter 8; the Seventh Synod, or Nicaea II, chapter 7; and below, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter *Hi vero*, which is Gregory's.], it has been decreed [Note: The Hispanic Collection reads: “be decreed”] that they must certainly be rebaptized. If any among them were clerics [Col. 0505A], then, if they are blameless and beyond reproach, they are to be rebaptized [Note: The text requires: “and”] and then also ordained anew by the bishop [Note: Add: “Catholic”: Basel edition] of the Catholic Church. But if, upon examination, they are found less suitable, they must be deposed. The same rule shall likewise be observed concerning deacons [Note: Greek: *Peri tōn diakonissōn, kai holōs peri tōn en tō kanoni exetazomenōn*: “Concerning deaconesses, and in general concerning those examined among the canonical clergy.”], and all others found in the same clergy.

### C. LIII. On the same subject. Likewise Innocent to the bishops of Macedonia, Epistle XXII, chapter 5.

[Note: Written A.D. 414.]

The Paulianists did not baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and [Note: The words “and … baptized” are absent from the Hispanic Collection] the Novatians baptized with these same dread *and venerable* names, and among the latter no question was ever raised concerning the unity of the divine power—that is, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit [Col. 0505B].

Gratian. Others preserve the Church's form in baptizing. Yet, while persons are baptized by those with whom they share communion in heresy or schism, they do indeed receive from them the sacrament of baptism, but do not obtain its power, which no one can obtain without faith. Hence it is said of the Lord that in his native country he could perform no sign because of their unbelief.

Therefore Augustine, Tractate LXXX on John chapter 15, and in the sermon on the cataclysm, chapter 3 at the beginning:

### C. LIV. When the word is added to the element, a sacrament comes into being.

Take away the word [Note: Add: “from the water”: editions compared, first Argentinian and Nuremberg editions], and what is *water* [Note: The editions compared read: “will be”] but water? The word is added to the element, and a sacrament comes into being. And below:

§ 1. Whence comes this great power [Col. 0505C] of water, that it touches the body and washes the heart, except by the working of the word? Not because it is spoken, but because it is believed. For even in the word itself, one thing is the passing sound, another the abiding power.

Gratian. Augustine also writes concerning those baptized in heresy or schism in the book *On Faith*, to Deacon Peter, chapter 36, saying [Note: The Maurists observed that this book is not Augustine's, but belongs to Fulgentius.]:

### C. LV. Those baptized outside the Church heap destruction upon themselves if they do not return to the Church.

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that those baptized outside the Church, if they do not return to the Church, heap destruction upon themselves through baptism. For membership in ecclesiastical society has such power [Note: The original reads: “unity”] for salvation that a person is not saved by baptism unless it is given there where it ought to be given.

### C. LVI. Gifts possessed outside the unity of the Church are powerless. The same author, Tractate XIII on John chapter 3.

[Col. 0506A] Let us hold fast to unity, my brethren. Outside unity, even one who performs miracles is nothing; within unity [Note: The original reads: “for within unity”] was the people Israel, and it did not perform miracles; outside unity were Pharaoh's magicians [Note: Exodus 7], and they performed things like those of Moses. The people Israel, as I have said, performed no miracles. Who were saved [Note: Editions compared read: “to be saved”] before God: those who performed miracles or those who did not? The apostle Peter [Note: Acts 8:9] raised a dead person. Simon Magus performed many things. There were *there* many [Note: Editions compared read: “certain”] Christians who could do neither what Peter did nor what Simon did. Yet why [Note: Basel edition reads: “nevertheless”; the other editions compared, “therefore”] did they rejoice? Because [Note: Luke 10:20] their names were written in heaven.

### C. LVII. Baptism once administered is not to be repeated. Likewise Leo to Nicetas, bishop, Epistle LXXVII, alternatively LXXIX, chapter 7.

[Note: Epistle 159, written A.D. 458, Maurist edition.]

[Col. 0506B] We preach that this rule, *as you know,* is to be observed [Note: Editions compared read: “preserved”] in all churches: that the washing once received should be violated by no repetition. For the Apostle says [Note: Ephesians 4:5], “One Lord [Note: Editions compared read: “God”; P. X], one faith, one baptism.” Its washing must not be rashly repeated; but, *as we have said,* the sanctification of the Holy Spirit alone must be invoked, so that a person may obtain from Catholic priests what no one receives from heretics.

## Part X

Gratian. No one established in heresy or schism is to be understood in this way. But if someone, with integrity of faith and purity of mind, receives baptism from the hand of heretics in [Col. 0506C] the Church's form, then Augustine's statement is fulfilled [Note: Cf. above, chapter 30]: “Water passes through a stone channel to the flowerbeds.” And again: “The spiritual power of the sacrament,” and so forth.

### C. LVIII. The good are gathered even through the wicked. The same [Augustine], Sermon XI on the Words of the Lord, concerning blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.

[Note: Sermon 71, Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 104.—Cf. below, chapter 81.]

The Holy Spirit works in the holy Church even in this time, when, as grain [Note: The original reads: “a threshing floor”] is threshed [Note: Editions compared read: “ground down”] with chaff, in such a way that he despises no one's true confession, is deceived by no one's pretence, and flees the reprobate in such a way that he nevertheless gathers the approved even through their ministry.

Gratian. Behold when baptism is received from heretics together with its power—its administration is so necessary [Col. 0506D] that even when given by pagans it cannot be repeated. [Col. 0507A] Thus it is read in ecclesiastical history [Note: Book 10, chapter 14] that Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, while celebrating the solemnities of Peter the Martyr, after the mysteries of the Mass had been completed, saw at the seashore a game of boys imitating, as commonly happens, a bishop and performing those things customarily done in the Church. He immediately ordered them brought to him and asked what they had done. They explained the course of events, confessing that certain catechumens had been baptized by them through the boy Athanasius, who had acted as their bishop. When he saw from their answers that everything accorded with the rite of our religion, he decided that baptism ought not to be repeated for those upon whom water had been poured with the requisite questions and answers complete, but that those things customary for priests should be supplied.

Isidore also says [Note: Burchard and Ivo cite this chapter as from the sayings of Isidore; from this formula of citation it is usually judged not to be the author's own words. In its first part it seems either to propose a question or to relate someone's false opinion, to which the true answer is then opposed in the latter part: “But the Roman …,” etc. This passage is also cited below, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter *Romanus*, as from Isidore. This is explained more clearly in book 5 of the *Capitularies*, chapter 4, in these words: “If anyone has been baptized by a priest who was not baptized, and the Holy Trinity was invoked in that baptism, he has been baptized, as Pope Sergius said; but he needs the laying on of hands. Gregory, bishop of Rome, and John the Sacellarius thought so.”]  
[Note: The author of the chapter has been identified as Egbert of York, or whoever was the author of the penitential book printed in Mansi, volume 12, page 435.—Burchard, book 4, chapter 100. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 97; *Decretum*, part 1, chapter 294. Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 5, preface. Alger, book 1, chapter 52.]:

### C. LIX. Concerning those who are ordained through ignorance before being baptized.

If anyone is ordained through ignorance before being baptized, those baptized by him must be baptized again, and he himself must not thereafter be ordained. But the Roman Pontiff judges not the man who baptizes, but that the Spirit of God supplies [Note: Add: “is believed to supply”: editions compared] the grace of baptism, even though the baptizer is a pagan.

### C. LX. PALEA

[Note: This *Palea* is cited both in the indicated places and in the collection in volume 3 of the *Councils*, after the decrees of Alexander III, and in chapter 1, *On a Priest Not Baptized*, as from a council held at Compiègne.]  
[Note: This whole chapter is absent from the Basel edition.]  
[From a council at Compiègne [Note: Rather, from Theodore of Canterbury's *Capitula*.—Cf. *Capitularies*, book 6, chapter 93. Burchard, book 4, chapter 74. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 96; *Decretum*, part 1, chapter 268.—Chapter 1, *Compilatio*, book *On a Priest Not Baptized*—chapter 1, X, on this title.]]

> “If an ordained priest discovers that he has not been baptized, let him be baptized and ordained again.”  
> [Note: “Again”: this was followed by “and all whom he had previously baptized,” which words have been deleted because they are not found in the said chapter 1, *On a Priest Not Baptized*, nor in chapter *Veniens*, under the same title where it is reported, although they occur in the other places indicated [and in the original in Theodore].]

Gratian. That the other sacraments cannot be administered by heretics is attested by Jerome on Haggai the Prophet, chapter 2:

### C. LXI. Things offered by heretics do not please God.

Thus this people of all heretics is before me, says the Lord; everything they do, whatever they offer me—vows [Note: The original reads: “or vows for salvation,” but this was not altered because of the gloss], whether for salvation, peace offerings, sin offerings, *for the beloved one,* or burnt offering [Note: Argentinian edition: “or burnt offering”; the other editions compared: “or burnt offerings”]; or [Note: Argentinian edition: “through almsgiving or through fasting”] alms, fasts, *abstinence from food,* and [Note: “or”: editions compared] bodily chastity—[Col. 0508A] shall be defiled before me. For although what is offered *by such persons* appears holy in outward appearance, yet because it has been handled [Note: Editions compared read: “treated”] by one polluted in soul, all things are defiled.

### C. LXIII. On the same subject. The same Jerome on Amos the Prophet, chapter 5.

[Note: Anselm, book 9, chapter 48 (60). Alger, book 3, chapter 12. Deusdedit, part 2.]
