God hates the sacrifices of heretics and casts them away from himself; and whenever they have assembled under [Note: Editions compared read: “in his name”] the name of the Lord, he detests their stench and closes his nostrils.

### C. LXII. On the same subject. The same author on Hosea, chapter 6.

They offer sacrilegious bread, give alms, and seem to pursue humility. If these things are truly done, I interpret them as burnt offerings. But when they have abandoned the knowledge of God, they boast in vain that they possess the other [Col. 0508B] members after cutting off the head of faith.

### C. LXIV. Without faith and charity, the Gospel is not possessed, nor do any good works profit. The same author on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 1 [verse 11].

Marcion, Basilides, and the other plagues of heretics do not possess God's Gospel, because they do not possess the Holy Spirit, without whom the Gospel that is taught becomes human. Nor should we suppose that the Gospel lies in the words of Scripture, but in its meaning; not on the surface, but in the marrow; not in the leaves of expressions, but in the root of reason.

### C. LXV. On the same subject. The same author on chapter 5 of the same epistle [verse 14].

See how great a good charity is [Note: Editions compared read: “charity is”]. If we endure martyrdom in such a way that we wish our remains to be honored by people [Col. 0508C] [Note: Editions compared, first Basel edition: “by all people”]; if, pursuing popular esteem, we have fearlessly shed our blood, and given our substance even to our own impoverishment, this work deserves not so much reward as punishment; and these are torments of faithlessness rather than the crown of victory.

### C. LXVI. The blessing of heretics is a curse. Likewise from the Council of Laodicea, chapter 32.

[Note: Held between A.D. 347 and 381.—Burchard, book 3, chapter 259. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 260.]

One ought not [Note: Lugdunum II edition: “ought”] to accept the blessings of heretics, for they are curses rather than blessings.

### C. LXVII. It is lawful to pray neither with heretics nor with schismatics. Likewise from the Council of Pope Martin, chapter 70.

[Note: Chapters 32 and 38 of the Council of Laodicea, from the translation of Martin of Braga.]

It is not lawful for clerics or laypersons [Note: Add: “Catholic”: original] to receive blessings (*eulogiae*) from heretics, because they are curses rather than blessings; nor is it lawful to pray either with heretics or with schismatics.

### C. LXVIII. There are no true sacrifices outside the Church. Likewise Leo to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, Epistle XLVIII, chapter 2.

[Note: Epistle 81, written A.D. 451, Ballerini edition.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 9, from Lanfranc's book *On the Eucharist*.]

[Col. 0509B] In the Church of God, which is Christ's body, neither priesthoods are valid nor sacrifices true otherwise than when the true high priest reconciles us in the proper reality of our nature, *and the true blood of the spotless Lamb cleanses us.*  
[Note: The editions compared read: “his own” for “our.”]

### C. LXIX. The divine sacraments withdraw themselves from the hands of the impious. The same author to the Emperor Leo, Epistle LXXIII.

[Note: Epistle 156, written A.D. 457, Ballerini edition.—Anselm, book 9, chapter 40 (52).]

It is evident that through the most cruel and insane violence [Note: Anselm reads: “madness”], in the Alexandrian see every light of the heavenly sacraments has been extinguished. The offering of sacrifice has been interrupted, the consecration of chrism has failed, and all mysteries have withdrawn themselves from the parricidal hands of the impious.

### C. LXX. Sacraments may be administered outside the Church, but they cannot confer salvation. Likewise blessed martyr Cyprian, in his epistle against heretics.

[Note: This chapter has been compiled, sometimes with alterations and condensation, from various passages in Cyprian's letters and from the council held by him; the sources are indicated in the margin.]

If anyone, he says [Note: The first part of the chapter is excerpted from Cyprian's epistle to Magnus], has gone out from the Church through heretical presumption, he is condemned by himself. With such people, according to the Apostle, we ought not even to eat. This is shown in the Book of Kingdoms [Note: Editions compared, first Basel: “Kings”; cf. 3 Kings 13], where, when a man of God had been sent to Jeroboam to reproach *him* [Note: Editions Lugdunum II and III read: “which”] with his sins and foretell future punishment, he was forbidden to eat bread *also* with him and drink water [Note: Editions compared read: “was prohibited”]. Since he did not observe this, while returning from there [Col. 0510A] he perished on the road by a lion's bite, through the divine judgment.

§ 1. And does anyone dare to say that the saving water [Note: Editions compared read: “the saving sacrament”] of baptism and heavenly grace can be common with heretics, with whom neither earthly food nor worldly drink ought to be held in common? It is established [Note: From the epistle to Januarius, Epistle 70 in Baluze's edition. Nearly the same things occur in the Council of Carthage held A.D. 256.] that oil by which the baptized are anointed cannot at all be sanctified among them, nor can the Eucharist be made, where there is no hope and faith is false, where everything is conducted through falsehood. For a heretic, after the manner of apes—who, though not human, nevertheless imitate human things [Note: The editions compared read: “human form”]—wishes [Note: The editions compared read: “the face … and he claims for himself the authority and truth of the Catholic Church, although …”] to claim for himself the authority and truth of the Catholic Church, although he himself is not in the Church. Accursed by God [Note: Editions compared read: “although he is accursed”], he blesses; dead, he promises life; blasphemous, he invokes God; profane, he administers priesthood; sacrilegious, he sets up [Col. 0510B] an altar [Note: Basel edition: “constructs an altar”; other editions: “places an offering before the altar”]. To all this evil is added that an overseer of the devil dares to make the Eucharist, although [Note: Editions compared read: “although neither sacrifice nor …”] the offering cannot there be sacrificed or sanctified where the Holy Spirit is absent; nor does the Lord benefit anyone through his prayers and supplications, when he himself has violated the Lord [Note: Editions compared read: “God”].

For if those who despise the Church [Note: Editions compared read: “violate”] are regarded as both Gentiles and publicans, then much more surely those who are rebels and enemies, who fabricate false altars, unlawful priesthoods, sacrilegious sacrifices, and adulterated [Note: Editions compared read: “all”; “spurious”: editions compared and Böhm] names, must be counted among Gentiles and publicans; for all of them have plainly departed from the charity and *from* the unity of the Church [Note: Add: “Catholic”: editions compared]. Therefore [Note: Words of Nemesianus from the same council] everything heretics do is carnal, empty, and false, so [Note: From the said epistle to Januarius] that none of what they have performed [Col. 0510C] ought to be approved by us. Things vaunted in Christ's name [Note: From the epistle to Jubaianus] are not immediately to be received and accepted, but those performed in Christ's truth. For how can those who attempt against God what they are not permitted to attempt accomplish what they do [Note: Basel edition: “accomplish anything that is done”] or obtain anything from God by unlawful endeavors?

§ 2. Therefore, unless they separate themselves from communion with evildoers, those who support heretics and schismatics are shown, by the divine judgment in their deed, to be appointed to punishments together with not only the leaders and authors but also their accomplices [Note: In the epistle itself the text reads: “They contend in vain that anyone can be baptized and sanctified there by saving baptism, where it is clear that the baptizer has no authority to baptize; and, that the nature of the divine judgment against such audacity might be better understood, we find that in such an offence not only leaders and authors, but also participants, are appointed to punishments,” etc.]. For the Lord commanded through [Col. 0511A] Moses, *saying* [Note: Numbers 16:26]: “Separate yourselves from the tents of these most hardened men, and touch nothing [Note: Editions compared read: “of”] that belongs to them [Note: Editions compared read: “is in them”], lest you perish with them in their sins.” What the Lord had threatened through Moses he fulfilled: whoever [Note: Editions compared read: “whoever”] did not separate himself from Korah, Dathan, and Abiram immediately paid the penalty for impious communion [Note: Editions compared read: “paid”]. Likewise the Holy Spirit testifies and says through the prophet Hosea [Note: Editions compared read: “testifies, saying”; cf. Hosea 9:4]: “Their sacrifices are like bread of mourning; all who eat them shall be defiled,” thereby teaching and showing that absolutely all who have been contaminated by their sin are joined in punishment with their authors [Note: Add: “supporters”: editions compared].

### C. LXXI. True sacrifices are celebrated only in the faith of the Church. Likewise Augustine, book of *Sentences Collected by Prosper of Aquitaine, Bishop of Regium*, chapter 15.

[Note: This book is apocryphal.]

Outside the Catholic Church there is no place of true sacrifice.

Likewise Gregory in book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 31, says concerning Hermenegild [Note: Read: “Hermenegild,” and later “Leovigild”], son of King Leovigild:

### C. LXXII. Communion is not to be received from the hand of heretics.

When the day of the Paschal feast came, in the silence of the deep night his faithless father sent an Arian bishop to him, so that he might receive from his hand the communion of sacrilegious consecration and thereby deserve to return to his father's favor. But the man devoted to God reproached the coming Arian bishop as he ought, and repelled his faithlessness from himself with fitting rebukes [Col. 0511C].

### C. LXXIII. Priests of heretics are not considered worthy of Christ's honors. Likewise Innocent to Alexander, bishop, Epistle XVIII, chapter 3.

[Note: Written circa A.D. 415.—Anselm, book 9, chapter 18 (17). Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 129.]

Arians, moreover, and the other plagues of this kind [Note: [Col. 0511D] “Plagues”: Previously there followed “we detest,” which was removed because it occurs neither in the ancient codices nor in the letter itself, nor in Anselm or the *Panormia*], because we receive their laypeople when converted to the Lord under the appearance of penance and through the sanctification of the Holy Spirit by the laying on of hands, ought not, it seems, to have their clerics received with the dignity of priesthood or of any ministry. [Note: [Col. 0511] Variant: “they seem—ought to be received”; collected editions.] For those whose baptism alone we allow to be valid—which is certainly performed in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0512A] [Note: [Col. 0511] Variant: “is received,” for “is performed”; collected editions]—we do not judge to possess the Holy Spirit through that baptism and those mysteries [Note: [Col. 0511] Variant: “ministries”; same editions], since, when their authors departed from the Catholic faith, they lost the perfection of the Spirit which they [Note: [Col. 0511] Variant: “who”; same editions] had received; nor can they give its fullness, which works especially in ordinations, and which they lost through the perfidy of their impiety rather than through faith, I would say [Note: [Col. 0511] Addition: “of the Lord”; same editions]. Therefore it cannot be that we should consider their profane priests worthy of Christ’s honors, when, as I have said, we receive their imperfect laypeople to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit under the appearance of penance.

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0511] Compare above, ch. 18]: §1. If, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0511] Num. 19:22], “Whoever touches an unclean thing shall be unclean” [Note: [Col. 0511D] The letter has, “Whatever an unclean person touches”; but this was not altered because of the gloss, and the sense of this reading is also found in the same indicated passages of Scripture], how can that be bestowed upon him which purity [Note: [Col. 0511] “Who is accustomed to receive uncleannesses and defilements”; collected editions] and cleanness are accustomed to receive? And below: §2. How one who has become a participant in one condemned [Note: [Col. 0511] Variant: “has become”; same editions] ought to receive honor, I cannot discover [Note: [Col. 0511] Variant: “we cannot discover”; same editions].

Gratian. But from the fact that the laying on of hands is commanded to be repeated, it is shown not to be a sacrament.

Whence Augustine, Book III *On Baptism against the Donatists*, ch. 18 [Note: [Col. 0511] Anselm, bk. 9, ch. 24 (34); Polycarpus, bk. 3, bk. 10]:

### C. LXXIV. The laying on of hands is not a repetition of a sacrament

Unlike baptism, the laying on of hands can be repeated. For what else is it but prayer over a person?

Gratian. Therefore, since Innocent allows only baptism among the sacraments of heretics to be valid; since Gregory calls the consecration of the Arians sacrilegious; since Cyprian judges everything done by heretics to be carnal, empty, and false; since Jerome asserts that everything offered by them is defiled in God’s sight; and since Leo declares that outside the Church there are neither valid priesthoods nor true sacrifices, it is clear that ecclesiastical sacraments, apart from baptism, as was said above, cannot be administered by heretics.

Likewise, that passage of Jerome *Against the Luciferians* is objected to [Note: [Col. 0512D] The beginning of this chapter down to the words “I beg you” is not found in that place in Blessed Jerome. It is, however, found in Alger, Book III, ch. 10; there, too, certain words from what follows occur in the same form as in Gratian, although they are read differently in Blessed Jerome] [Note: [Col. 0511] Alger, Book III, ch. 23]:

### C. LXXV. He who is holy in baptism will not be a sinner at the altar

As Christ is the one who baptizes, so Christ [Note: [Col. 0511] “He himself”; collected editions—“he” here; Alger] is the one who sanctifies. Therefore, I beg you, either grant permission to sacrifice to him whose baptism you approve [Note: [Col. 0511] Variant: “approve”; collected editions], or reject the baptism of him whom you do not think to be a priest. For it cannot be that one who is holy in baptism should be a sinner at the altar. [Note: [Col. 0511] Variants: “Christ himself” in the collected editions, “he” in Alger; “approve” for *approbas* in the collected editions.]

Gratian. But [Note: [Col. 0513] This statement of Gratian is read word for word in Alger.] this must be understood only of a Catholic sinner, not of a heretic. [Note: [Col. 0513C] “A sinner”: at that place Blessed Jerome argues, as dialecticians say, *ad hominem*; he does not seek to establish or decree anything, but only to make his opponent moderate. Once he has brought him to profess himself no longer an opponent but a disciple, he then explains to him the very true reason why the Church receives bishops who had unwittingly agreed with heretics at the Council of Rimini.] For whatever he does in the exercise of his office with Catholic faith, though unworthy, is nevertheless believed valid through the cooperation of divine grace. Otherwise, if this statement were understood of heretics, he would contradict himself, since he says on Amos, chapter 5: “The Lord hates their sacrifices.” And elsewhere, in the person of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0513] Alger, Book I]:

### C. LXXVI. God curses the blessings of heretics

“I will curse your blessings” [Note: [Col. 0513C] These words occur in the interlinear gloss on that passage of Malachi, derived from Jerome] [Note: [Col. 0513] Malachi 2:2], that is, whatever is blessed by you will be cursed by me [Note: [Col. 0513] Variant: “through me,” for “by me”; collected editions].

[Col. 0513B]

### Part XI

Gratian. Thus, the former statement must be understood of the heretic, but the statement *Against the Luciferians* of an ecclesiastical sinner. Of him Augustine says in the book *On the Body of the Lord* [Note: [Col. 0513C] This chapter is also cited by Alger, Book III, ch. 8, as Augustine’s, from a book *On the Body of the Lord*. But Possidius, in his index of Blessed Augustine’s works, makes no mention of such a book; and these words occur verbatim, except for the final sentence, in Paschasius the abbot’s *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, ch. 12. The chapter “It Is Repeated,” and those following, below, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, also come from that book] [Note: [Col. 0513] Alger, Book I, ch. 56]:

### C. LXXVII. Good and bad priests alike make the body of Christ

Within the Catholic Church, in the mystery [Note: [Col. 0513] Variant: “ministry”; editions of Arg., Bas.] of the body and blood of the Lord, nothing greater is accomplished by a good priest and nothing less by a bad one, because it is accomplished not by the merit of the consecrator [Note: [Col. 0513] Addition: “is”; Basel edition and Alger] but by the word of the Creator and the power of the Holy Spirit. And below: For if it were in the priest’s merit, it would not belong to Christ. But now, just as he himself [Note: [Col. 0513] Addition: “Christ”; collected editions] is the one who baptizes, so he himself, through the Holy Spirit, makes this his flesh and changes it into blood. For it must be believed that the sacraments are effected in Christ’s words. By whose command they were first created, by his word they are surely recreated for the better. [Note: [Col. 0513D] “It must be believed”: these words occur in the same form in Alger. Paschasius’s wording in ch. 15 is: “By whose power, therefore, they were first created, by his word they are surely recreated for the better, because no one is taught in the Catholic faith to be the creator or re-creator of anything except the one God. Therefore one must come to Christ’s words and believe that they are effected in accordance with those same words.”]

### C. LXXVIII. On the same subject

Likewise Augustine, Book II *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, ch. 10 [Note: [Col. 0513] Alger, Book I, ch. 73]:

Although all sacraments harm those who handle them unworthily, they nevertheless benefit those who receive them worthily through such persons, as the word of God also testifies [Note: [Col. 0513] Addition: “testifies”; original]. Hence it was said [Note: [Col. 0513] Matthew 25]: “Do whatever they say, but do not do what they do.”

### C. LXXIX. On those who use holy things wrongly

[Note: [Col. 0514C] In Tractate VII on the Epistle of John there are some passages that can be referred to the sense of this chapter, and it was formerly cited from there. But the exact words occur in the indicated place.]

The same, on Psalm 103, at the verse “Who coverest” [Note: [Col. 0513] These words are cited from Augustine’s tractate on the Epistle of John by Alger, Book I, ch. 58, and in the collected editions, first Lyon edition III]:

Even Saul, the wicked king, prophesied; and he prophesied when he was persecuting holy David [Note: [Col. 0513] Addition: “also”; Alger and collected editions]. And below: Let not those, therefore, who perhaps have had [Note: [Col. 0513] Variant: “have”; same source] this holy gift of God without charity boast; rather, let them consider what account they will have to render to God, who use holy things in an unholy manner. Among them will be those who will say: “In your name we prophesied.” They will not be told, “You are lying,” but will be told, “I never knew you,” and so forth. [Note: [Col. 0513] Variant: “They will not be told”; collected editions: “They will not be told by them.”]

Gratian. Therefore, they must be said to have possessed the spirit of prophecy, not merit.

### C. LXXX. No one is so much sanctified by offerings as defiled on account of sin

Likewise Jerome on Haggai, chapter 2 [Note: [Col. 0514C] Blessed Jerome reads as follows: “O people, who, though only the altar has been built and my house lies in ruins, offer me sacrifices on the altar and suppose that you are sanctified by its victims and flesh: know that you are not so much sanctified by the sacrifices—which cannot benefit you while the Temple lies in ruins—as all your works and everything you do are defiled because you neglect to build my house and have rather sought to build your own. What is offered on the altar is indeed holy; but you are not so much sanctified by the sacrifices as you are defiled because you dwell in valleys and are involved in dead works.” In two ancient Gratian manuscripts “O people” is also read; yet Jerome immediately applies these same matters allegorically to an ecclesiastical man] [Note: [Col. 0513] Alger, Book I, ch. 59]:

O prophet [Note: [Col. 0513] “O people” is absent from the collected editions, first Lyon and Paris editions] [Note: [Col. 0513] “People”: Alger, from the original], who, although only the altar has been built and my house lies in ruins, offer me sacrifices on the altar and think yourself sanctified by its victims, know that what is offered on the altar is indeed holy, but that you are not so much sanctified by the sacrifices as defiled by dead works [Note: [Col. 0513] Variant: “defiled by the fact that you are involved in dead works”; same source].

[Col. 0515A]

### C. LXXXI. A word is spoken against the Holy Spirit when one never returns from dispersion

Likewise Augustine, in the book *On the Words of the Lord*, sermon XI, near the end [Note: [Col. 0515] Ivo, *Decrees*, pt. 2, ch. 104]:

Thus a word is spoken against the Holy Spirit when one never comes from dispersion to the assembly which has received [Note: [Col. 0515] Original: “receives”] the Holy Spirit for the remission of sins. Even if someone comes to that assembly through a bad cleric, yet a Catholic minister—reprobate and hypocritical—if he himself comes with a sincere heart, the Holy Spirit works in that person the remission of sins. [Note: [Col. 0515C] “The Holy Spirit”: this passage concisely reports Blessed Augustine’s opinion; it is stated more fully above, in the same chapter, “The Holy Spirit”] [Note: [Col. 0515] Compare above, ch. 58.] For he works in the holy Church so as to flee the reprobate, yet through their ministry to gather the approved.

[Col. 0515B]

### C. LXXXII. Sins are remitted not by human merits, but by the power of the Holy Spirit

The same, in the sermon *On the Remission of Sins* [Note: [Col. 0515] Sermon 49, Maurist edition; Alger, Book I, ch. 66]:

In order to show clearly that sins are forgiven by the Holy Spirit, whom the Lord gave to his faithful, and not by human merits, he said in one place [Note: [Col. 0515] John 20:22], rising from the dead: “Receive the Holy Spirit”; and immediately added: “If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven him.” That is, the Spirit forgives, not you. Therefore, just as one whom a priest tolerates in the Church is nevertheless outside the Church and outside the body whose head is Christ, if the doorkeeper does not open to him [Note: [Col. 0515D] “Does not open”: some ancient manuscripts read “has not opened”; others, “may open”; one lacks the negative], so someone is not thereby outside the Church, nor is he or she not of the body, if someone is compelled by the unjust judgment of a shepherd to remain outside [Note: [Col. 0515] Variant: “opens”; Basel edition] [Note: [Col. 0515] The words “not thereby” are absent from the Basel edition].

[Col. 0515C]

### C. LXXXIII. The Lord considers not the merits of persons, but the offices of priests

Likewise Ambrose, *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*, ch. 5 [Note: [Col. 0515] Alger, Book I, ch. 67. In the collected editions this is cited from Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*]:

Since Scripture testifies to you that fire descended from heaven at Jeroboam’s prayers [Note: [Col. 0515] Variant: “descended”; collected editions], and again, at Elijah’s prayer, fire was sent to consume the sacrifices, it is to be understood [Note: [Col. 0515D] The words “it is to be understood” are not in the original. Since what precedes depends on what came before, a new period begins here: “Do not consider the merits of persons, but the offices of priests.” Several other variants, some of considerable importance, are indicated in the margin] that God considers not the merits of persons but the offices of priests. And a little later: §1. Visible fire was sent to them so that they might believe; an invisible fire works in us who believe [Note: [Col. 0515] Variant: “which”; same source, except Arg.]. And after a few intervening words: §2. Believe, therefore, that the Lord Jesus is present when invoked by the prayers of priests, he who said [Note: [Col. 0515] Matthew 18:20]: “Where two or three are gathered, there I am in their midst” [Note: [Col. 0515] “Where two or three are gathered, there I am in their midst”: collected editions, chiefly Basel, have this reading; in that edition the word “gathered” is absent].

### C. LXXXIV. It is not the merits of priests, but divine power, that sanctifies the sacraments

Likewise Gregory [Note: [Col. 0516D] This chapter has been assembled partly from the opinions of Blessed Gregory and partly from the actual words of Blessed Isidore and Blessed Jerome] [Note: [Col. 0515] The author of the chapter, who has not been identified, imitated Gregory the Great, *Pastoral Rule*, pt. 3, admonition 5, and *Morals*, bk. 15, ch. 16, in the first part down to §2]:

Many laypeople, when they scrutinize the lives of priests more than their own, incur the grave crime of contempt for the divine sacraments. For, having their eyes injured by a great beam and disregarding it, they see in the eyes of others the slender speck which, while they hasten heedlessly to pluck it out [Note: [Col. 0515] Variant: “to pluck it out”; Basel edition], causes them to fall into the pit of error. They consider too little that the life of priests would not injure them if they themselves humbly lent an ear to the good admonitions of priests. But while, after the fashion of hypocrites, they judge the reputation of others more than their own life or their own neglect of life [Note: [Col. 0515] Variant: “neglect”; same source], they despise holy admonitions and spiritual gifts. Hence it comes about that they not only reject what such men say but, what is worse, even despise the divine mysteries, so that they do not receive the communion of the body or blood of our Lord Jesus Christ consecrated through their ministry, thinking it less sanctified if it is performed through the office of those whose life seems dishonorable in their eyes.

§1. Alas, into what a great snare they fall when they believe that divine and hidden mysteries can be made more holy by some persons than by others, whereas the one and same Holy Spirit, diffused throughout the Church over the whole world [Note: [Col. 0515] Variant: “diffused”; same source], incomprehensibly and secretly, invisibly [Note: [Col. 0515] Variant: “works and by working”; same source], sanctifies those mysteries by his operation and blesses them by blessing.

§2. A mystery, brothers, is so called because it has a secret and hidden dispensation; but a sacrifice is, as it were, a sacred act, because it is consecrated for us by mystical prayer in remembrance of the Lord’s passion. [Note: [Col. 0516D] These words down to “This concerning the body” occur in Isidore, though not in precisely the same order] [Note: [Col. 0515] Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book VI, ch. 19.] And below:

§3. A sacrament, moreover, is present in some celebration when an act has occurred in such a way that something is understood to be signified [Note: [Col. 0515] Variant: “the signified thing”; Basel edition—“signified”; other editions—addition: “or symbolically”; Arg. edition] which must be received reverently. The sacraments are baptism, chrism, and the body and blood of Christ. They are called sacraments because, beneath the covering of bodily things, divine power works in secret the salvation of those same sacraments. Therefore they are called sacraments from secret powers or sacred things. They are fruitfully performed in the Church because the Holy Spirit, remaining in her, secretly works the effect of those sacraments. The sacrament of this bread and cup is called in Greek *eucharistia*, and in Latin is interpreted as “good grace.” And what is better than the body and blood of Christ?

§4. Therefore, whether it is administered through good or bad ministers within God’s Church [Note: [Col. 0517] Variant: “whether, therefore”; collected editions], it is nevertheless a sacrament, because the Holy Spirit mystically gives it life—he who once appeared in visible works in apostolic times. It is neither increased by the merits [Note: [Col. 0517] Variant: “neither by the merits of the good nor by the works of the good”; Basel edition] of good dispensers nor diminished by those of bad ones [Note: [Col. 0517] Basel edition reads “are diminished”; other editions, “is diminished”], because “neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” [Note: [Col. 0517] 1 Corinthians 3:7]. [Note: [Col. 0517] Thus far Isidore.] This must be thought and maintained concerning the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and likewise concerning baptism and chrism, because divine power works more secretly in them, and this power or authority is divine alone, not an efficacy belonging to human beings [Note: [Col. 0517] Variant: “and also divine”; same source].

We therefore defile the bread—that is, Christ’s body—when we approach the altar unworthily [Note: [Col. 0517] Variant: “unworthily”; collected editions] and, being filthy, drink the pure blood. And below:

§5. “I will curse,” he says, “your blessings” [Note: [Col. 0517D] In the same author, on chapter 2, it reads: “‘And I will curse,’ he says, ‘your blessings,’ that is, those things which you now possess through my blessings; or whatever is blessed by you will be cursed by me. And I will curse them”—understand, “your blessings”—“because you did not wish to understand what is said”; this is what is meant by “you did not lay it upon your heart”], that is, those things which you now possess through my blessings, or whatever is blessed by you I will curse, or because they do not bless the holy from a true heart, or because those who act wickedly are blessed by them and they flatter sinners, provided only that they are rich [Note: [Col. 0518C] Taken from the same passage somewhat below, where the following is read: “Or certainly, because the command is specifically directed to priests, their blessings are turned into a curse when they do not bless the holy from a true affection of heart, as Isaac blessed Jacob, Jacob the patriarchs, and Moses the twelve tribes; but by sweet speeches and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent. Those who act wickedly are blessed by them, and they flatter sinners, provided only that they are rich, and they indulge their vices.”].

### C. LXXXV. We should consider not the life of priests, but what they teach and administer

Likewise Pope Fabian, to the Eastern bishops, Letter II [Note: [Col. 0517] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled from Augustine, Book 50, final homily]:

You have further reported that many observe that many persons in ecclesiastical offices do not live in a manner consistent with the sermons and sacraments administered through them to the people. O wretched people, who, while looking at these men, forget Christ! He had long before foretold that the law of God should rather be obeyed than that those who say what they do not do should seem fit for imitation; and, tolerating his betrayer to the end, he sent him with the others even to preach [Note: [Col. 0517] Variant: “to evangelize him”; Basel edition—“to have him evangelize”; collected editions] the Gospel. For the apostles neither had such a custom nor taught that it should be had.

### C. LXXXVI. On the same subject

Likewise Pope Nicholas, to the Emperor Michael, in the letter beginning, “We had proposed” [Note: [Col. 0517] Letter 8 in Mansi, written A.D. 865; Anselm, Book I, ch. 75; Ivo, *Decrees*, pt. 5, ch. 18]:

You must take the greatest care to consider not what the Lord’s priests are like, but what they say concerning the Lord. In the vicars of Blessed Peter the Apostle, you must attend not to who they are [Note: [Col. 0517] Variant: “what”; collected editions], but to what they diligently undertake for the correction of the churches and for your salvation [Note: [Col. 0517] Variant: “our salvation”; Basel edition]. For you will not call them inferior to the scribes and Pharisees sitting on Moses’ seat, concerning whom the Lord gave command, saying [Note: [Col. 0517] Matthew 23:3]: “Observe and do whatever they tell you, but do not do according to their works.” Therefore, Emperor, consider attentively [Note: [Col. 0517] Addition: “attentively”; Basel edition]: if he said that those seated on Moses’ seat should be heard, how much more ought you to judge that those seated on Peter’s seat should be obeyed [Note: [Col. 0517] Variant: “you judge—or may judge—that they ought to be obeyed”; second and third Lyon editions; collected editions].

### C. LXXXVII. The uncleanness of priests does not defile the sacraments

Likewise Augustine, *Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book II, ch. 22 [Note: [Col. 0517] Ivo, *Decrees*, pt. 2, chs. 98–99]:

The Lord declared that, in a single assembly of persons receiving the same sacraments, the uncleanness of some cannot harm the clean [Note: [Col. 0517] Variant: “does not harm”; collected editions]. And below [Note: [Col. 0517] Ibid., ch. 30]:

§1. Petilian said: “But if anyone knows by heart a priest’s chants [*carmina sacerdotis*], is he thereby a priest because with a sacrilegious mouth he makes public a priest’s flesh?”

Augustine replied: You say this as though we were now asking who is a true priest, rather than what is true baptism. For in order for anyone to be a true priest, he must be clothed not only with the sacrament but also with justice, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0517] Psalm 131:9]: “Let your priests be clothed with justice.” But one who is a priest only by the sacrament, as was the high priest Caiaphas, persecutor of the one and most true Priest, although he himself is not truthful, nevertheless gives what is true, if he gives not his own but God’s.

Likewise, a little below:

§2. “One of their own prophets said” [Note: [Col. 0519] These words down to “This testimony is true” are absent in Ivo] [Note: [Col. 0519] Titus 1]: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies” [Note: [Col. 0519] Collected editions read: “sluggish in heart.”] “This testimony is true.” If, therefore, the Apostle himself bore witness to the testimony of some foreigner because he found it true, why do we not distinguish, whenever we find what belongs to Christ and is true in anyone—even if the person in whom it is found is perverse and deceitful—between the fault which the person has [Note: [Col. 0519] Variant: “because of the fault”; same source] and the truth which he has not as his own but as God’s [Note: [Col. 0519] Variant: “Christ’s”; same source]? Why do we say, “This sacrament is true,” just as he said, “This testimony is true”? Do we therefore say that the man himself is truthful because we say, “This sacrament is true”?

And a little later:

§3. But you must necessarily always err so long as, because of human faults, you violate God’s sacraments, or think that we must assume the sacrilege of your schism because, on account of God’s sacraments which are in us [Note: [Col. 0519] Variant: “in you”; Basel, Venice I and II, and second and third Lyon editions], we are unwilling to violate them.

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0519] Ibid., ch. 35]:

§4. The purity of baptism is wholly distinct from the purity or uncleanness of the conscience, either of the giver or of the recipient [Note: [Col. 0519] Variant: “receiver”; Basel edition].

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0519] Ibid., ch. 47]:

§5. Remember, therefore, that the morals of bad people do no harm to God’s sacraments, so that they either are not sacraments at all or are less holy [Note: [Col. 0519] Addition: “at all”; collected editions].

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0519] Ibid., ch. 48]:

§6. I ask: if Saul did not possess the holiness of the sacrament, what did David venerate in him? But if he possessed innocence, why did he persecute the innocent? For David both honored him while alive and avenged him when slain, on account of his most sacred anointing [Note: [Col. 0519] Collected editions read: “the sacrament of anointing”]; and because he cut off even a small piece from Saul’s garment [Note: [Col. 0519] Variant: “cut off”; same source], he trembled, stricken in heart. Behold, Saul did not possess innocence, yet he possessed holiness, not from the merit of his life [Note: [Col. 0519] There followed “but from anointing”; these words are absent from all ancient Gratian manuscripts, although they occur in printed editions of Blessed Augustine]—for no one can possess this without innocence—but from God’s sacrament, which is holy even in bad persons [Note: [Col. 0519] Addition: “but from anointing”; collected editions] [Note: [Col. 0519] Variant: “the sacrament”; first Basel edition].

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0519] Ibid., ch. 52]:

§7. We say that for each person the sacrifice becomes such as the person who approaches to offer is, and such as the person who approaches to receive is; and that those who approach such sacrifices in such a manner as those persons are eat of their sacrifices. Thus, if a bad person offers to God and a good person receives from it, it is such for each as each person is [Note: [Col. 0519] Variant: “it is”; same source], because it is also written [Note: [Col. 0519] Titus 1:15]: “All things are pure to the pure.” By this true and Catholic judgment, you too were not defiled by Optatus’ sacrifice, if his deeds displeased you. For his bread was surely bread of mourning, under whose iniquities all Africa mourned; but your evil of schism makes the bread of mourning common to all of you [Note: [Col. 0519] Variant: “not”; collected editions, chiefly Basel].

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0519] Ibid., ch. 54]:

§8. Thanks be to God, because at last you have confessed that the invoked name of Christ can avail for the salvation of others, even if it is invoked by sinners. From this, then, understand that when Christ’s name is invoked, the sins of another do not harm another’s salvation [Note: [Col. 0519] Variant: “understand”; Arg., Basel, and first and second Venice editions].

### C. LXXXVIII. Even through a bad minister, God’s gifts reach those who receive in faith

The same, on Psalm 10, at the verse “But what has the righteous man done?” [Note: [Col. 0519] Ivo, *Decrees*, pt. 2, ch. 105]:

What has Christ done to you [Note: [Col. 0519] Variant: “to us”; collected editions], he who bore his betrayer with such patience that he gave him, as to the other apostles, the first Eucharist consecrated by his own hands and entrusted by his own mouth? What has Christ done to you [Note: [Col. 0519] Variant: “to us”], Christ [Note: [Col. 0519] Variant: “God”; first Basel and second and third Lyon editions], who sent that same betrayer—whom he called a devil, who before betraying the Lord could not keep faith even with the Lord’s money-box—with the other disciples [Note: [Col. 0519] Matthew 10] to preach the kingdom of heaven, in order to show [Note: [Col. 0519] Variant: “to show”; collected editions] that the gifts of God reach those who receive in faith, even if the person through whom they receive is such as Judas was?

### C. LXXXIX. A bishop’s wickedness does not harm the sacraments

Likewise Gregory [Note: [Col. 0519] Chapter of uncertain origin]:

A bishop’s wickedness does not harm either the baptism of an infant or the consecration of a church, because baptism is given by God and does not come from man; so also the Eucharist and everything [Note: [Col. 0519] Addition: “else”; Basel edition] placed upon the altar receive sanctification not from man but from God.

Gratian. But that statement of Jerome on Zephaniah, chapter 3, is objected to [Note: [Col. 0519] Ivo, *Decrees*, pt. 2, ch. 110]:

### C. XC. It is not words but the merits of priests that make the Eucharist

Priests who serve the Eucharist and distribute the Lord’s blood to his people act impiously against Christ’s law when they suppose that the words of the one making the invocation, rather than his life, make the Eucharist, and that solemn prayer alone is necessary rather than the merits of priests—of whom it is said: “And the priest in whom there is a blemish shall not approach to offer oblations to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0519] “In whomsoever”; collected editions from Ivo. Addition: “who is found”; Basel edition. Compare Leviticus 21:21].

[Col. 0521A]

### C. XCI. The more worthy priests are before God, the more readily they are heard

Likewise Alexander, Letter II [Note: [Col. 0521] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Ivo, *Decrees*, pt. 2, ch. 69, and pt. 6, ch. 45]:

The priests themselves intercede for the people and consume the sins of the people, because by their prayers and offerings they wipe them out and consume them; and the more worthy they are, the more readily they are heard concerning the needs for which they cry out [Note: [Col. 0521] Variant: “in,” for “concerning”; collected editions from Ivo].

### C. XCII. The Holy Spirit is not present in sacraments administered by criminal persons

Likewise Gelasius, to Bishop Elpidius [Note: [Col. 0521] The date of this letter is uncertain; Elpidius was bishop of Volaterrae. Ivo, *Decrees*, pt. 2, ch. 90, and pt. 6, ch. 110]:

The most holy religion, which contains Catholic discipline, claims such reverence for itself that no one should dare approach it except with a pure conscience. For how will the heavenly Spirit, when invoked, come to the consecration of the divine mystery if the priest, and the one who prays for his presence, is condemned as full of criminal acts?

### C. XCIII. An unclean hand defiles what it touches; it does not cleanse it

Likewise Gregory, *Register*, Book I, Letter 24 [Note: [Col. 0521] Letter 26, written A.D. 591, to John, bishop of Constantinople, and the other patriarchs, Book I, Maurist edition; compare *Pastoral Rule*, pt. 2, ch. 2]:

The hand that undertakes to wash away filth must strive to be clean, lest what it touches be defiled all the more if it itself holds the muddy mire of dung [Note: [Col. 0521] Variant: “the dirty mud which follows”; collected editions—“the mud which follows it”; original]. For it is written [Note: [Col. 0521] Isaiah 52:11]: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord.” Those bear the Lord’s vessels [Note: [Col. 0521] Variant: “bore”; Basel edition] who undertake to bring their neighbors’ souls into the inner sanctuaries [Note: [Col. 0521] Original: “inner sanctuaries”] by the example of their own conduct.

[Col. 0521C]

### C. XCIV. The word of Christ and the body of Christ must be guarded equally

Likewise Augustine, Book L of Homilies, Homily 26 [Note: [Col. 0521] The sermon from which these words are taken is spurious. The Pithou brothers cite the canon from Origen’s Homily XIII on Exodus. Ivo, *Decrees*, pt. 2, ch. 106]:

I ask you, brothers or sisters: tell me, which seems greater to you, the word of God [Note: [Col. 0521] “Christ”; collected editions from Ivo] or the body of Christ? If you wish to answer truthfully, you must surely say that the word of God is not less than the body of Christ [Note: [Col. 0521] “The word of the Lord”; collected editions, chiefly Basel]. Therefore, with as much care as we take when Christ’s body is administered to us, so that none of it falls from our hands onto the ground, let us take equal care lest the word of God that is distributed to us [Note: [Col. 0521] “Imparted”; Basel edition] perish from our hearts while we think or speak of something else. For the person who has heedlessly heard God’s word will be no less guilty than the one who through negligence has allowed Christ’s body to fall to the ground [Note: [Col. 0521] Collected editions add “from a pure heart”].

[Col. 0522A]

### C. XCV. On the same subject

The same, Book IV *On the Trinity*, ch. 14 [Note: [Col. 0521] Ivo, *Decrees*, pt. 2, ch. 107]:

Nor can it be duly offered except through a just and holy priest, nor can that which is offered be received except by those for whom it is offered [Note: [Col. 0521] Basel edition: “for whom you offer”], and it must be without blemish, so that it may be offered for cleansing those who are blemished. This, certainly, all desire who wish that sacrifice be offered to God for themselves.

Gratian. When the life of priests is said to be necessary for the Eucharist, this must be understood not of consecration but of its effect. For it does not confer the effect of salvation upon one whom his merits render unworthy; rather, the Apostle’s statement is fulfilled in him [Note: [Col. 0521] 1 Corinthians 11:27]: “Whoever eats the body of the Lord and drinks his blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” Thus Jerome’s statement above [Note: [Col. 0521] Above, ch. 90] must be understood against those who believe themselves able to be cleansed by frequent offering of sacrifice while not ceasing to act impiously against God’s law. But that a priest, even if bad, nevertheless pours grace upon people by virtue of the dignity of his office, Augustine attests in Book [Note: [Col. 0521] The book is apocryphal. Ivo, *Panormia*, Book III, ch. 79; *Decrees*, pt. 2, ch. 100] 11 of *Questions on the Old Testament*.

### C. XCVI. Priests invoke the name of the Lord, but the Lord bestows the blessing.

God said in Numbers to *Moses and* Aaron, *the priests* [Note: [Col. 0521] ch. 6]: “You shall place my name upon the children of Israel, and I, the Lord, will bless them,” so that tradition may convey grace to human beings through the ministry of the ordainer [Note: [Col. 0521] *traditam*: “the grace handed down”; all collated editions] [Note: [Col. 0521] *ordinati*: “of the ordained”; the same editions with Ivo], and the priest’s will may neither harm nor benefit, but rather the merit of the person requesting the blessing.

§ 1. Let us observe from this how great is the dignity of the priestly order [Col. 0522C] [Note: [Col. 0521] add: “or office”; the same editions]. For it was said [Note: [Col. 0521] *autem*: “however”; the same editions, from Ivo] concerning the utterly wicked Caiaphas, the murderer of the Savior, among other things [Note: [Col. 0521] John 11:51]: “He did not say this from himself; but, since he was chief [Note: [Col. 0521] *pontifex*: “high priest”; Basel edition—*pontifex et princeps*: “high priest and chief”; the remaining editions] of the priests that year, he prophesied.”

This shows that the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0521] add: “Holy”; all collated editions, from Ivo] of graces does not follow the person *either* of the worthy or of the unworthy, but the ordination handed down; so that, although someone may be of good merit, he nevertheless cannot bless unless he has been ordained, in order that [Note: [Col. 0521] *vel*: “or”; Lyons editions; compare Distinction 19, ch. 9] he may perform the office of ministry. But it belongs to God to grant the effect of the blessing.

Gratian. The assertion that sacraments of rank administered by heretics lack effect is disproved [Col. 0522D] by the authority of Pope Anastasius, who approves the ordination performed by Acacius, although Acacius was a heretic, as valid to such an extent that he asserts that Acacius’s culpable person harmed in no respect even those whom he baptized or ordained after his own condemnation [Col. 0523A]. [Note: [Col. 0523D] “But this he”: Above, Distinction 19, chapter *Anastasius*. It has been shown that Anastasius was undeservedly reproached and that what he himself wrote and decreed concerning Acacius is entirely true.]

But Felix and Gelasius, who excommunicated Acacius before Anastasius, and Hormisdas, who was the third after Anastasius to condemn that same Acacius, prove that Anastasius did this unlawfully and uncanonically—indeed, contrary to the decrees of his predecessors. Therefore he is also rejected by the Roman Church; and in the Acts of the Roman Pontiffs he is said to have been struck by God, as follows: “Anastasius + the Second, a Roman by nation,” etc. Look back in the treatise on decretal letters.

Likewise, the following passage from Augustine, Book II *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, ch. 13, is raised as an objection [Note: [Col. 0523] Algerus, bk. 3, ch. 83]:

### C. XCVII. One who withdraws from the Church loses neither baptism nor the right to confer it.

What some say—that one who withdraws from the Church does not lose the baptism he has received [Note: [Col. 0523D] “Which he has received”: so also Algerus, although the original reads somewhat differently], *but* does lose the right to confer it which he has received—is shown in many ways to be said vainly and without foundation [Col. 0523B].

§ 1. First, because no reason is shown why one who cannot lose baptism itself could lose the right of conferring it. For both are sacraments [Note: [Col. 0523] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 77; *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 97], and each is given to a person by a kind of consecration: the former when he is baptized, the latter when he is ordained. Therefore neither may be repeated in the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0523] *a catholica*: “from the Catholic Church”; Algerus, from the original].

§ 2. For if at any time [Note: [Col. 0523] *quando*, “at any time,” is absent from all collated editions except the first Basel edition and Lyons II and III] even leaders [Note: [Col. 0523] *propositi*: “those set over”; Basel edition] coming from that party are received for the sake of peace, after the error of schism [Note: [Col. 0523] *schismaticorum*: “of the schismatics”; all collated editions] has been corrected, and it has seemed necessary that they should exercise the same offices which they exercised [Note: [Col. 0523] *agebant*: “they performed”; the same editions], they are not to be ordained again [Note: [Col. 0523] *ordinati*: “ordained”; the original—Algerus]. Rather, just as baptism remained whole in them, so too ordination remained whole, because the defect lay in the separation [Col. 0523C]—which was corrected by the unity of peace—not in the sacraments, which, wherever they are, are themselves true.

And when this seems expedient to the Church [Note: [Col. 0523] *videtur ipsa eccl.*: “the Church itself deems it expedient”; Basel edition—*vid. ipsi eccl.*: “it seems expedient to the Church itself”; the remaining editions], so that their leaders, upon coming into Catholic fellowship, should not exercise their honors there, the sacraments of ordination themselves are nevertheless not taken away from them, but remain [Note: [Col. 0523] *ibi remanent*: “remain there”; Argentan and Nuremberg editions—add: “even”; all collated editions except the Argentan edition] upon them. Therefore hands are not imposed upon them among the people, lest injury be done not to the person but to the sacrament itself.

And below:

§ 3. Just as they possess in baptism [Note: [Col. 0523] *est*: “there is”; all collated editions, from Algerus] that which can be conferred through them, so in ordination they possess the right of conferring it; both indeed to their own destruction [Col. 0524A], so long as they lack the charity of unity. Yet it is altogether one thing not to possess, another to possess destructively, and another to possess beneficially.

Whatever is not possessed must be given when there is need for it to be given; but what is possessed destructively must, after the destructiveness has been removed by correction [Note: [Col. 0523] *correptionem*: “rebuke”; the same editions except Basel and Lyons], be so treated that it may be possessed beneficially.

Although, if a layman, compelled by the necessity of someone perishing, has given something [Note: [Col. 0523] *aliquid pereunti*: “something to a person who is perishing”; Algerus—*alicui pereunti baptisma*: “baptism to someone who is perishing”; all collated editions] which, when he himself received it [Note: [Col. 0523] *acceperit*: “has received”; the same editions except the first Basel edition and Lyons II and III], he learned ought to be given [Note: [Col. 0523] add: “to someone”; Basel and Lyons II and III; *addiscit*: “learns”; Paris edition], I do not know whether anyone could piously say that it must be repeated. If it is done when no necessity compels, it is the usurpation of another’s office. But if necessity presses, it is either no sin or a venial sin.

Yet [Note: [Col. 0523] *Sed si*: “But if”; all collated editions] even if it is usurped under no necessity [Note: [Col. 0523] *in nulla necessitate*: “in no necessity”; Venice II, Lyons, and Paris editions], and is given by anyone to anyone, what has been given cannot be said not to have been given, although it may rightly be said to have been unlawfully given [Col. 0524B]. The disposition of one who remembers and repents therefore corrects the unlawful usurpation. But if he has not corrected it, what was given will remain for the punishment of the usurper [Note: [Col. 0523] *usurpationis*: “of the usurpation”; all collated editions], or of the one who unlawfully gave it, or of the one who unlawfully received it; nevertheless, it will not be considered not to have been given.

*Nor in any way shall the royal mark be violated by a devoted soldier because it was usurped by private persons.* [Note: [Col. 0524D] “Nor in any way”: these words through “violated” have been added from the original, from which this chapter has also been enlarged elsewhere.]

§ 4. For if certain persons, secretly and irregularly, outside the public mints, have stamped gold or silver [Note: [Col. 0524D] “Or silver”: in the printed codices of St. Augustine there follows “but bronze”; in two Vatican manuscripts, however, “or bronze”] by striking it, when this has been discovered, would not the recognized royal stamp, after those persons had been punished or freed by pardon, be ordered to be brought into the royal treasuries? [Note: [Col. 0523] *cogeretur*: “would be compelled”; the original—*congregetur*: “is to be gathered”; all collated editions.]

And a little later:

§ 5. If perhaps *that* military mark upon his body had caused a man not serving as a soldier, in cowardice, to shudder, and he had fled to the emperor’s clemency, *and, after a prayer had been poured forth* [Col. 0524C] and pardon obtained, had then begun to serve as a soldier, would that mark be repeated when the man had been freed and corrected? Would it not rather be acknowledged and approved?

Or do Christian sacraments adhere less firmly [Note: [Col. 0523] *habent*: “have”; Algerus and Lyons II and III—*haberet*: “would have”; Basel edition—*haberent*: “would have”; the remaining editions] than this bodily mark, when we see that not even apostates lack baptism? When they return through repentance, it is certainly not restored to them, and therefore is judged incapable of being lost.

And a little later:

§ 6. Concerning [Note: [Col. 0523] add: “indeed”; Basel edition] those who have separated from the unity of the [Note: [Col. 0523] add: “Catholic”; all collated editions] Church, there is now no question that they both possess *and* can confer [Note: [Col. 0523] add: “the sacraments”; the same editions except Basel], and that they possess and confer them destructively [Note: [Col. 0523] “but they possess them destructively, because they are outside,” etc.; all collated editions] outside the bond of peace [Col. 0525A].

And below:

§ 7. Injury must be done to neither sacrament.

And below:

§ 8. Just as those who depart from unity do not possess them rightly [Note: [Col. 0525] *habet qui … recedit*: “the one who withdraws possesses”; the same editions], but nevertheless possess them, and therefore they are not given back to the person returning, so likewise one who departs from unity does not confer them rightly, but nevertheless confers them; and therefore what someone received from him is not repeated when that person comes to unity [Note: [Col. 0525] *item iteratur*: “is repeated again”; Lyons II].

And below:

§ 1. Just as what the returning person possessed outside is not given back to him, so what the person coming in possessed outside is not to be repeated; so what the person coming in received *even* outside is not to be repeated [Note: [Col. 0525] *acceperat*: “had received”; all collated editions]. From this it follows that human perversity must be corrected, but the holiness of the sacraments must not be violated in any perverse person.

For it is evident that this holiness remains unstained and inviolable in perverse and wicked persons, whether they are inside or outside [Col. 0525B]. Although evil persons are said to defile it [Note: [Col. 0525] *eam*: “it”; the same editions except Basel], they are said to do so only insofar as lies in them, while it remains unstained [Note: [Col. 0525] *permaneat*: “may remain”; the same editions except the first Argentan and Basel editions]. But in the good it remains [Note: [Col. 0525] *permaneret*: “would remain”; Nuremberg edition—*permanet*: “remains”; the remaining editions except Basel] unto reward; in the wicked it remains [Note: [Col. 0525] *permanet*: “remains”; in the same place] unto judgment.

And below:

§ 10. How do Catholics not glorify God [Note: [Col. 0525] “the Lord”; all collated editions], *who trust that his promises cannot be prevented from being fulfilled by any crimes of human beings,* and who treat his sacraments with such due veneration that, *even if they* have been handled by unworthy persons, those persons being condemned by their own perversity, the sacraments are shown to remain in uncorrupted holiness [Note: [Col. 0525] *demonstrantur*: “are shown”; the same editions]?

### Part XII. Gratian.

[Note: [Col. 0525] These words down to § 2 are read verbatim in Algerus.]

From these words of Augustine it is clear that Christ’s sacraments remain true in themselves and holy in all persons—apostates, heretics, and the condemned alike—and, unless aid is supplied through repentance or pardon [Col. 0525C], they lead to the condemnation of the usurper, whether the one possessing, conferring, or receiving them.

What benefit, then, is there in their being true and holy, when they destroy their usurpers just as much as though they were evil and harmful? Crassus thirsted for gold and drank gold: he perished from real gold just as he would have perished from real poison.

§ 1. Likewise, gold is just as genuine in a thief’s chest as in the king’s treasury. But it is possessed, given, or received unlawfully by the thief; whereas it is possessed, given, and received lawfully by the king. Therefore the thief himself and the participant in his theft—unless perhaps they have cleared themselves in conscience of the theft—will each, as Gelasius testifies to Emperor Anastasius, be justly and deservedly condemned.

§ 2. But the following is raised as an objection to Augustine’s view: the authority to confer baptism, the right to consecrate the Lord’s body, and the right to bestow holy orders differ greatly from one another [Col. 0525D].

When a priest is suspended or deposed, no authority to offer sacrifice remains to him. Yet the sacrament of baptism, if administered not only by a deposed priest or a Catholic layman but even by a heretic or pagan, is not to be violated by any repetition [Col. 0526A]. But no reason permits those to be counted among priests who receive the oil of sacred—indeed, execrable—anointing from the hands of a layman or pagan.

It therefore does not follow that, if those withdrawing from the faith retain the right of baptizing, they also retain the authority to distribute holy orders, although both arise from consecration. For a degraded bishop has no authority to bestow holy orders, although he has not lost the capacity to baptize.

§ 3. But lest we wholly reject Augustine in this opinion [Note: [Col. 0525D] Here Gratian seems to speak of St. Augustine as though Augustine’s opinion in this matter were doubtful or uncertain, although no one has explained the matter better or more fully than he did in his book against the Donatists, and he agrees entirely with the Council of Chalcedon and Innocent], let us understand that the power of distributing holy orders is one thing, and the exercise of that power another.

Those established within the unity of the Catholic Church who receive priestly or episcopal anointing acquire, through consecration, both office and the exercise of their office [Col. 0526B]. But those who withdraw from the integrity of the faith retain the power received insofar as the sacrament is concerned, while they are entirely deprived of the effect of their power—just as married persons who separate from one another do not dissolve a marriage once contracted, although they are excluded from marital intercourse.

§ 4. Augustine therefore speaks of those who, after receiving priestly power, withdraw from the unity of the Catholic Church, not of those who receive priestly anointing while situated in schism or heresy. Otherwise he would contradict the Council of Chalcedon [Note: [Col. 0525] compare above, ch. 8], in which those ordained by simoniacs are judged to gain no benefit from it, and Innocent [Note: [Col. 0525] above, ch. 17], who testifies that those ordained by other heretics through a perverse laying-on of hands obtained only condemnation and a wound upon the head.

§ 5. Nevertheless, it may generally be said that sacraments celebrated among heretics in no different manner than in the Church of God are true and valid in themselves, but false and ineffectual in their effect, both in those by whom they are wrongly handled and in those by whom they are wrongly received [Col. 0526C].

Nor is this surprising. Our Salvation himself gave a morsel to Judas [Note: [Col. 0525] John 13]; immediately with the morsel, not a good but an evil spirit entered him. Why? Not because the Good One did not give a good thing, but because the evil man received the good thing evilly. Thus the good thing did not have a good effect, because it found no place in which to produce it.

§ 6. Likewise, the Lord [Note: [Col. 0525] Matthew 13] was truly and actually present in his own country; he could accomplish nothing, not through an evil minister but through himself, because he did not find faith. Because of others’ faithlessness, he did not lack his own truth, but the effect [Col. 0526D] lacked the power of goodness.

§ 7. To show this plainly in all sacraments, while he was in the flesh he was transfigured twice. In one transfiguration [Note: [Col. 0525] Matthew 17] he appeared wondrous as the sun, so that believers’ faith might be increased to contemplate the heavenly glory raised above them.

In the other, as a traveler [Note: [Col. 0527] Luke 24] unrecognizable to those who doubted about him, he pretended that he was going farther and, so that he should not be recognized, held their eyes. To what other end, except to show that, because he was not in their hearts through faith, he was withdrawing farther from them, and that, because they did not believe him to be what he was, they should see him as other than he was?

Behold, in both appearances there were his presence and truth. But in one faith was exercised, so that they might believe more than they had believed; in the other unbelief was held fast, so that they did not even recognize what they saw.

Therefore the sacrament of his body and blood is salvation to some and judgment to others. Faith also, although true, is dead without works [Note: [Col. 0527] James 2]. So all ten virgins alike were virgins [Note: [Col. 0527] Matthew 25], but five of them were foolish and five prudent. The reality of virginity was equal [Col. 0527B], but because of the intention accompanying that same virginity, identity of merit was not equal in all.

So too martyrdom or almsgiving unacquainted with charity is sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal [Note: [Col. 0527] 1 Corinthians 13]. If a blind person ministers the truth of a lamp to a blind person, neither thereby illuminates his own blindness any more. Thus an evil person ministers true sacraments to an evil person, but not thereby spiritual gifts, because the Holy Spirit is prevented by their evil merits from working in them what is his own.

Therefore Innocent [Note: [Col. 0527] above, ch. 73], while allowing that the baptism of heretics is valid, does not allow that the Holy Spirit is possessed through that baptism. And Leo [Note: [Col. 0527] above, ch. 51] does not permit those who have received the form of baptism to be rebaptized, but commands that they obtain from Catholic priests [Col. 0527C], through invocation and the laying-on of hands, the Holy Spirit, whom no one receives from heretics.

It must be understood that heretics’ sacraments are called invalid, or even condemnable, false, and empty, not in themselves—for they are holy and true even when celebrated by heretics—but because, while they are unto judgment for faithless persons who confer them unlawfully, they do not confer the Holy Spirit upon those who receive them unlawfully from such persons.

They are called invalid and untrue because they do not give what they promise and are believed to confer, and they are therefore called condemnable so that their conferral or reception from heretics may not be approved but forbidden. For they are not polluted in themselves, although they are said to be polluted by heretics.

Thus Gregory [Note: [Col. 0527] above, ch. 72] calls Arius’s communion [Col. 0528A] an execration, and Innocent [Note: [Col. 0527] above, chs. 17 and 18] calls Bonosus’s ordination a condemnation—not because they are such in themselves, but because they produce that result in those who confer or receive them wrongly.

Likewise Jerome, in Hosea [Note: [Col. 0527] ch. 9], calls their sacrifices “bread of mourning,” not with respect to themselves but with respect to their effect, as he himself shows when he adds: “Whoever eats from it shall be defiled,” because he takes it unto judgment for himself.

Accordingly, Augustine, Book II *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, ch. 5 [Note: [Col. 0527] Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 97]:

### C. XCVIII. Although sacraments harm those who handle them unworthily, they benefit those who receive them worthily.

Through Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0527] ch. 66:3] the Lord says: “The criminal who sacrifices a calf to me is like one who kills a dog [Note: [Col. 0527] add: “alive”; Basel edition], and one who cooks fine flour as though it were swine’s blood [Col. 0528B], and one who offers incense as a memorial, like a blasphemer.”

[Note: [Col. 0527D] “And one who cooks”: In St. Augustine the text reads: “and one who offers fine flour, as swine’s blood, and one who offers incense, as though he blesses an idol.” Ivo has the same, except that he reads “and one who places fine flour,” as does St. Augustine in *Against the Letters of Petilian*, bk. 2, ch. 52. Jerome’s translation according to the Septuagint corresponds very well to the commonly received Greek reading: “But the wicked man who sacrifices a calf is like one striking a man; one who sacrifices from the flock, like one killing a dog; [Col. 0528D] one who offers fine flour, like one offering swine’s blood; one who gives incense as a memorial, like a blasphemer.” But the Latin Vulgate from Jerome according to the Hebrew text reads: “He who sacrifices an ox is like one who kills a man; he who slaughters a beast is like one who breaks a dog’s neck; he who offers an oblation is like one who offers swine’s blood; he who makes memorial of incense is like one who blesses an idol.”]

And after a few intervening words:

§ 1. Whoever, wherever he may be, offers sacrifice with such a heart or such deeds [Note: [Col. 0527] *tale*: “such a thing”; Ivo] that he deserves to hear this brings destruction upon himself, not upon those good persons who receive from such persons the same sacraments, who, according to the prophet Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0527] Ezekiel 9], groan and mourn over the sins [Note: [Col. 0527] add: “and iniquities”; all collated editions] committed in their midst, although they do not separate themselves bodily from them.

And below [Note: [Col. 0527] in the same book, ch. 6]:

§ 2. The sacrifices of the ungodly harm those persons *themselves* who offer them ungodly. For one and the same sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0527] add: “is”; all collated editions], because of the name of the Lord which is invoked upon it [Note: [Col. 0527] add: “there”; the same editions], is always holy, and becomes such for each person as is the heart with which he approaches to receive it.

“For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment for himself” [Note: [Col. 0527] 1 Corinthians 11:27]; he does not *say*, “for others,” but “for himself.”

And below [Note: [Col. 0527] in the same book, ch. 10]:

§ 3. We admonish that this should be understood in almost all questions of this kind [Col. 0528C], namely, that [Note: [Col. 0527] compare above, ch. 78] although all sacraments harm those who handle them unworthily, they nevertheless benefit those who receive them worthily through such persons.

And below [Note: [Col. 0527] in the same book, ch. 11]:

§ 4. The Holy Spirit is present in a ruler or minister of the Church in such a way that, if he is not false, *the Holy Spirit* works through him, both *toward* that minister’s reward unto eternal salvation and toward the begetting or edification of those who are either consecrated or evangelized through him.

But if he is false, since it is most truly written [Note: [Col. 0527] Wisdom 1:5], “*For* the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from a false person,” he is indeed absent [Note: [Col. 0527] *desit*: “may be absent”; all collated editions] as regards that person’s salvation, so as to withdraw himself [Note: [Col. 0527] *et auferet*: “and he will withdraw”; Lyons II and III—*et auferat*: “and may withdraw”; Argentan and Basel editions] from thoughts [Col. 0529A] lacking understanding; yet he does not abandon [Note: [Col. 0529] *deserat*: “may abandon”; Basel edition] that person’s ministry, through which he works salvation for others.

Gratian. It is therefore clear, as Innocent says [Note: [Col. 0529] above, ch. 17], concerning the other heretics, that those ordained by simoniacs through the perverse imposition of a simoniacal hand have a wounded head.

§ 1. But it is objected that in the ordination of simoniacs the only thing found reprehensible is that the grace of the Holy Spirit is thought to be reduced to a price, whereas in every other respect the complete form of the sacraments is preserved.

Therefore, once the unlawful usurpation of a sacrament has been corrected through repentance, so that the grace of the Holy Spirit is considered gratuitous and not saleable, the full effect of anointing should be present. Indeed, even if repentance does not follow, the person should nevertheless be held to have been truly consecrated, albeit simoniacally [Col. 0529B], just as those who formerly were admitted neither to the regeneration of holy baptism nor to participation in holy communion except upon payment of a price were nevertheless accounted baptized or participants in holy communion, although simoniacally.

The sacred canons have established only this: that henceforth Christ’s sacraments are not to be distributed simoniacally.

Accordingly, Gelasius, to the bishops throughout Lucania, Letter I, ch. 7 [Note: [Col. 0529] written A.D. 494—*Register*, bk. 1, ch. 121; Burchard, bk. 4, ch. 71; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 1, chs. 72 and 265]:

### C. XCIX. No payment is to be demanded from persons being baptized or confirmed.

Priests are to set no charges for believers being baptized or confirmed, nor seek to harass those being reborn by imposing any exactions, because we are commanded to give freely what we receive [Note: [Col. 0529] *accepimus*: “we have received”; the original and the cited collections] freely [Note: [Col. 0529] Matthew 10:8].

Therefore they must attempt to demand absolutely nothing from the aforesaid persons, lest, driven away by poverty or repelled by indignation, they disdain to approach [Note: [Col. 0529] *jure*: “by right”; all collated editions] the means of their redemption [Col. 0529C]. They must know for certain that those found to have committed prohibited acts, or who do not instead correct their offenses voluntarily, are to incur [Note: [Col. 0529] *subeant*: “let them incur”; the same editions] danger to their own rank.

### C. C. A price must not be required from one receiving the grace of communion.

Likewise, from the Sixth Synod, ch. 23 [Note: [Col. 0529] held A.D. 692—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 92]:

No bishop, presbyter, or deacon who dispenses holy communion is to exact any payment from one receiving the grace of communion.

[Note: [Col. 0529C] “Grace”: so also Ivo. One old Gratian manuscript reads *gratia communionis*, “for the sake of communion,” which agrees better with the Greek reading: *παρὰ τοῦ μετέχοντος εἰς πράττειν τῆς τοιαύτης μεταλήψεως χάριν ὀβολοὺς ἢ εἶδος τὸ οἱονοῦν*, that is: “to exact from one who receives communion, for the sake of such participation, obols or any other kind [Col. 0529D] whatsoever.” There are also several other variants of no great importance.]

For grace is not sold, nor do we give the grace of the Holy Spirit for a price; rather, without defrauding them, we permit worthy persons to share in the gift [Note: [Col. 0529] *muneribus*: “gifts”; all collated editions—*participamus*: “we cause to participate”; Ivo]. But if any of those mentioned among the clergy exacts any payment from the person to whom he dispenses holy communion, let him be deposed as an imitator of simoniacal deceit.

### C. CI. The gifts of invisible grace are not to be acquired for profit.

Likewise, from the Eleventh Council of Toledo, ch. 8 [Note: [Col. 0529] held A.D. 675—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 1, ch. 37, and pt. 5, ch. 126]:

Whatever is bestowed through the consolation of invisible grace [Note: [Col. 0529D] “Consolation”: in councils formerly printed at Cologne and Paris, in two Vatican codices, in one codex of the Catholic king [Col. 0529] and the Hispanic Collection, and in Ivo, the reading is *collatione*, “bestowal”; but the text has not been emended because of the gloss] must never be sold outright for profits [Note: [Col. 0529D] “Never for profits”: in the same royal codex [Col. 0529] and the Hispanic Collection the reading is: “must absolutely never be sold for monetary gain or any rewards whatever”; in the other sources cited above: [Col. 0530C] “never for gain”] or for any rewards whatever, as the Lord says: “What you have received freely, give freely.”

Therefore, if anyone henceforth established in ecclesiastical order receives any price or reward for baptizing or confirming believers, for the conferral [Note: [Col. 0529] “for chrism”; all collated editions] of chrism, or for advancement through ranks—unless voluntarily offered [Note: [Col. 0529] *ornata*: “adorned”; Basel edition]—[Note: [Col. 0530C] “Unless”: this word is absent from the same royal codex [Col. 0529] and the Hispanic Collection, so that in these cases even voluntary offerings are forbidden, as was established concerning baptism in the Council of Elvira, below in the same *causa*, chapter *Emendari*, and concerning sacred ordinations at the Council of Trent, session 21, ch. 1. The word “unless,” however, occurs in the other manuscripts], then, if such an act has been committed by subordinates with the local bishop’s knowledge, that bishop shall be subject to excommunication for two months, because he countenanced known evil and did not apply the necessary rebuke [Note: [Col. 0529] *correctionem*: “correction”; Hispanic Collection—Ivo—Böhmer].

[Note: [Col. 0530D] “Because he countenanced known”: Earlier the reading was “in evil conscience.” It has been emended from the royal codex and Ivo; the printed councils vary: *quod et scita mala*, “because also known evil”; Hispanic Collection—*in consequentia*, “in consequence”; Lyons I—*in conscientia*, “in conscience”; Lyons II and III—*in scientia*, “in knowledge”; the remaining editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0529] *acquisiverit*: “has acquired”; Basel edition—*acquisivit*: “acquired”; the remaining editions.]

But if any subordinate, without that bishop’s knowledge, considers that he may receive something for any of the aforesaid matters [Col. 0530C] [Note: [Col. 0529] “anything concerning the matters mentioned above”; all collated editions], then, if he is a presbyter, he shall be punished by four months’ excommunication [Note: [Col. 0529] “three”; Hispanic Collection]; if a deacon, by three months [Note: [Col. 0529] “four”; the same source]; but a subdeacon or cleric serving these covetous desires shall be punished by an appropriate penalty [Note: [Col. 0529] *verbere*: “beating”; the same source] and by due excommunication.

[Note: [Col. 0530D] “And appropriate”: In the commonly received editions the text read “by a penalty appropriate at discretion”; the words “at discretion” have been removed, since they do not occur in the old exemplars, in printed or manuscript councils, or in Ivo, nor does the author of the gloss recognize them.]

### C. CII. Nothing is to be demanded by priests for the balsam placed in chrism.

Likewise, from the Second Council of Braga [Note: [Col. 0531] “of Braga”: the heading has been corrected from several old codices. In the commonly received editions it read “from Carthage IV,” in which this text is not found], ch. 4 [Note: [Col. 0531] held A.D. 572—*Collection in Three Parts*, pt. 2, tit. 46, ch. 4. In all collated editions except Basel, it is cited as Council of Carthage IV]:

It was resolved [Note: [Col. 0531] “It was resolved that for the small amount of balsam,” etc.; Hispanic Collection] that no bishop should demand anything further [Note: [Col. 0531] *aliquid*: “something”; all collated editions] for the small amount of balsam blessed and distributed through the churches for the sacrament of baptism, since [Note: [Col. 0531] *qui*: “who”; Böhmer] they customarily exact one *tremissis* apiece for it [Note: [Col. 0531] “because they customarily exact one *tremissis* apiece for it”; Hispanic Collection] [Note: [Col. 0531] *exigatur*: “is to be exacted”; Roman edition, erroneously], lest what is consecrated for the salvation of souls through the invocation of the Holy Spirit be damnably sold by us—and we ourselves thereby be sold—just as Simon Magus wished to buy the gift of God with money [Note: [Col. 0531] “lest we seem to be selling it”; Hispanic Collection].

### C. CIII. Nothing is to be exacted from those who bring their infants for baptism.

Likewise, from the same council, ch. 7 [Note: [Col. 0531] *Collection in Three Parts*, same place, ch. 7]:
