It was resolved that every bishop should command [Note: [Col. 0531] *faciat*: “should cause”; all collated editions] throughout his churches [Col. 0531B] that, if those who present their infants for baptism voluntarily offer something in fulfillment of their own vow, it may be received from them. But if, through the constraint of poverty [Note: [Col. 0531] “because of necessity”; Basel and Lyons II and III], they have nothing to offer, no pledge is to be forcibly taken from them by clerics.

For many poor persons, fearing this, keep their children from baptism [Note: [Col. 0531] *retraherent*: “would keep back”; Basel edition]; and if, while the children are delayed [Note: [Col. 0531] *differunt*: “they postpone”; Hispanic Collection], they should perhaps depart this life without the grace of baptism, their loss must necessarily be required of those whose spoiling [Note: [Col. 0531] *expolia*: “spoils”; the same source] they feared and on that account withdrew themselves from the grace of baptism [Note: [Col. 0531] *subtraxerunt*: “withdrew”; all collated editions].

### C. CIV. One being baptized is not to put coins into the basin.

Likewise, from the Council of Elvira, ch. 48 [Note: [Col. 0531] held no later than A.D. 310—*Collection in Three Parts*, pt. 2, tit. 30, ch. 9]:

It was resolved that this practice be corrected: those being baptized are not to put coins into the basin, as used to be done [Col. 0531C], lest the priest appear to sell for a price what he received freely. Nor are their feet to be washed by priests or clerics [Note: [Col. 0531] add: “indeed”; all collated editions].

### C. CV. Nothing is to be exacted for receiving baptism or chrism.

Likewise, from the Council of Tribur [Note: [Col. 0531] These words are not found in the Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895, from which Regino, bk. 1, ch. 147; Burchard, bk. 4, ch. 101; and Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 1, ch. 295, cite them.—Berthold of Constance mentioned this decree in his treatise *On the Purchase of Churches* (ed. 1792, p. 377)]:

It was reported that in certain places coins are customarily given for receiving chrism, and likewise for baptism and communion. The holy synod denounced and anathematized this *seed* of simoniacal heresy [Note: [Col. 0531] “to be heresy”; all collated editions except Basel and Lyons II and III], and decreed that henceforth nothing whatever should be exacted for ordination, chrism, baptism, balsam, burial, or communion; rather, Christ’s free gifts should be given through free dispensation [Col. 0531D].

### C. CVI. Nothing is to be exacted for dedicating churches or administering the other sacraments of the Church.

Likewise, from the Council of Chalon, in the time of Charlemagne, ch. 16 [Note: [Col. 0531] held A.D. 813—Burchard, bk. 4, ch. 93; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 98; *Decretum*, pt. 1, ch. 287]:

We decree that, just as nothing is to be received for dedicating churches or conferring orders, so priests who are to receive chrism are to give nothing for buying balsam or lights. Bishops, therefore, are to purchase balsam from the resources of the Church, and each is to *provide for the preparation of lights* in his own churches.

### Part XIII. Gratian.

Therefore, just as these sacraments, although administered simoniacally, nevertheless confer the effect of blessing upon the recipient, so the priest’s anointing, although administered simoniacally, ought not to lack its effect [Col. 0532B].

But, as was said above [Note: [Col. 0531] compare above, ch. 39], those sacraments are sacraments of necessity, whereas this is one of dignity; therefore the privileges of the former cannot generate a general rule for the latter.

Those ordained by simoniacs, therefore, have a wounded head through the perverse imposition of a simoniacal hand. But this is to be understood of persons whom neither ignorance nor the force of inducement excuses: those ordained by persons whom they know beyond doubt to be simoniacs, whether they are ordained simoniacally or non-simoniacally by them.

For, as Pope Nicholas distinguishes, some are ordained simoniacally by simoniacs; others simoniacally by non-simoniacs; and others non-simoniacally by simoniacs. Pope Nicholas II indicates this distinction in writing to all bishops [Note: [Col. 0531] From Nicholas’s letter reporting the council he held in A.D. 1059.—Gratian, however, has reported its sense rather than its exact words.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 127].

### C. CVII. On the threefold class of simoniacs.

[Col. 0532C] We decree *concerning the threefold heresy of simoniacs, that is,* concerning simoniacs who ordain simoniacally or are ordained simoniacally; concerning simoniacs ordained simoniacally by non-simoniacs; and concerning simoniacs ordained non-simoniacally by simoniacs.

§ 1. Simoniacs ordained simoniacally, or simoniacal ordainers, shall fall from their own rank according to the ecclesiastical canons. Likewise, simoniacs ordained simoniacally by non-simoniacs shall be removed from the office wrongly received.

§ 2. But simoniacs ordained non-simoniacally by simoniacs we mercifully permit, through the laying-on of hands and because of the need of the time, to remain in office.

Gratian. But this must be understood of those who were ordained by simoniacs whom they did not know to be simoniacs. They are made simoniacs not by guilt for the crime, but by the ordination of a simoniac [Col. 0532D].

[Col. 0533A] Concerning these, Pope Urban II, in the Council of Piacenza, chapters 3 and 4, says [Note: [Col. 0533] held A.D. 1095.]:

### C. CVIII. Concerning those who are ordained by simoniacs, but not simoniacally.

If any have been ordained by simoniacs without simony, provided that they can prove that, when they were ordained, they did not know those persons to be simoniacs, and that they were then [Note: [Col. 0533D] *And that they were then*: formerly the reading was “and that at that time,” as though the burden of proving this rested on one wishing to clear himself. It was corrected, however, from two manuscript copies of this council.] [Note: [Col. 0533] “and then”: Basel edition.] regarded in the Church as Catholics, we mercifully uphold the ordinations of such persons, provided nevertheless that a praiseworthy life commends them. But concerning those who knowingly allowed themselves to be consecrated—indeed, execrated—by simoniacs, we decree that their consecration is altogether void.

### C. CIX. Concerning one who is ordained by someone whom he knows to be a simoniac.

The same, the younger Nicholas. The same ruling is found in Alexander II. [Note: [Col. 0533D] The words of this and the following chapter, “Therefore, simoniacs,” occur in the letter of Nicholas II in which he reports the council held by himself; Alexander II repeated them in a letter addressed to all Catholic bishops, preserved in Rome in three very ancient manuscript codices.] [Note: [Col. 0533] See on c. CVII.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 126; *Decretum*, part 5, c. 79.]

[Col. 0533B] Henceforth we decree that, if anyone hereafter permits himself to be consecrated by one whom he does not doubt to be a simoniac, both consecrator and consecrated shall undergo an equal sentence of condemnation. but each of them, once deposed, shall do penance and remain deprived of his own rank.

### C. CX. No mercy is to be extended to simoniacs for preserving their rank.

The same, a little below. [Note: [Col. 0533] See on c. CVII.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 125; *Decretum*, part 5, c. 79; Deusdedit, part 2.]

We decree that no mercy is to be shown toward simoniacs in allowing them to retain their rank [Note: [Col. 0533] “we have decreed”: editions compared; first Basel, Lyons II and III.], but, according to the enactments [Note: [Col. 0533] “enactment”: editions compared.] of the canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers, we utterly condemn them and, by apostolic authority, ordain that they must be deposed.

Gratian. It must be understood: unless they were forcibly dragged in. For Innocent says concerning these persons, and concerning those forcibly ordained by heretics of any kind, in Letter XXII to the bishops of Macedonia, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 0533] written A.D. 414.—Here too the very words of the source are not reproduced.]:

### C. CXI. Concerning those who are dragged unwillingly into ordination by heretics.

It is certain that many have suffered violence and have been dragged away against their will, and, resisting, ordained by heretics. But if such a person, after such ordination, did not take part when they performed the sacraments, did not share in their communion, and, as soon as they departed, renounced their [Note: [Col. 0534D] “Their”: in the three-volume edition the reading is “departing from his most evil ….” But the four-volume edition and the code of canons read as Gratian does; moreover, in this chapter the compiler adapted much according to his own judgment.] wicked assembly and returned to the Church, such a person may have some appearance of excuse. But those who returned after a month or more, when they recognized that they had been [Col. 0534A] ordained by heretics, although [Note: [Col. 0533] “certainly although”: Basel edition.] they received nothing from them [Note: [Col. 0533] “accepted”: ibid.], are nevertheless [Note: [Col. 0533] added: “nevertheless”: ibid.] guilty of usurped rank.

Gratian. Such persons are commonly restored, out of regard for mercy, by a Catholic laying-on of hands, with satisfaction and the remedy of penance. But we read of the condemnation of simoniacs and of those who agreed with them; we do not read of an authoritative remedy expressly named for this heresy, except that, as was customary with Novatians or Donatists—certainly lesser heretics—not canonically but out of regard for mercy, we infer that persons may likewise be made from these. This is so also because in every other respect they have an orthodox faith, except that they believe the Holy Spirit to be purchasable. And, as Blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0533] above, c. 97.], when heretics return, they are healed in the respect in which they cut themselves off from the Church, while in the respect in which they adhered to it they are acknowledged.

[Col. 0534B] Hence Leo, to Januarius [Note: [Col. 0534D] “To Januarius”: it is likewise cited below, the same question 7, c. *Saluberrimum*, and is so found in manuscript codices of Leo, although printed editions read “Julian.” The actual words of the letter are quoted in the dictum of c. *Saluberrimum*, and partly above in the same c. *Si quis haereticae*. Here the sense rather than the words is given.] of Aquileia, Letter III [Note: [Col. 0533] Letter 12, written A.D. 446, Ballerini edition.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 131; *Polycarpus*, book 7, title 5; Anselm, book 5, c. 19.—See above c. 42 and below question 7, c. 21.]:

### C. CXII. Those who return from heresy to the Church are, as a favor, to remain in the rank in which they are found.

Every cleric of whatever rank who, having abandoned Catholic unity, has defiled himself with the contagion of a heretical or schismatic association, if he returns to the Church with lawful satisfaction and condemnation of his error, shall regard it as a great favor if, all hope of promotion having been removed from him [Note: [Col. 0533] “all”: editions compared.], he remains in the rank in which he is found.

Gratian. Concerning those who are ordained simoniacally by non-simoniacs—for example, persons who, without the bishop’s knowledge, give money to an archdeacon or to the bishop’s advisers in order to obtain holy orders from his hand—[Col. 0534C] Gregory VII writes as follows [book 6 of the *Register*, in the Roman Synod held on 19 November A.D. 1078, c. 5. [Note: [Col. 0533] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 81; *Polycarpus*, book 2, title 38.]]:

### C. CXIII. Ordinations carried out simoniacally are judged false.

We judge false those ordinations which take place through the intervention of payment [Note: [Col. 0533] “sin”: Basel edition.], or prayers, or service rendered to some person with that intention; and those which are not made by the common agreement of clergy and people in accordance with canonical enactments, and are not approved by those to whom the consecration belongs. [Note: [Col. 0533] “invalid and void”: original.] For those who are ordained in this manner do not enter by the door—that is, through Christ—but, as Truth itself attests [Note: [Col. 0533] John 10.], are thieves and robbers.

[Col. 0535A]

## Part XIV. Gratian.

Since, therefore, simony is noted in the chapter in three ways, it must be considered in how many ways payment is given in this heresy.

Blessed Gregory explains this at the end of Homily 4 in his exposition of the Gospels, saying [Note: [Col. 0535] *Register*, book 1, c. 239; Burchard, book 1, c. 113; Anselm, book 6, c. 83 (80); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 121; *Decretum*, part 5, c. 86.]:

### C. CXIV. Concerning the several kinds of simoniacs.

There are some who receive no monetary payments for ordination, yet grant holy orders for human favor [Note: [Col. 0535] added: “or praise”: editions compared, first Basel.] and seek from that very granting [Note: [Col. 0535] “from that same granting itself”: editions compared.] only the recompense of praise. Such persons plainly do not freely give what they have received freely [Note: [Col. 0535] “receive”: same editions; “received”: Anselm.], because from an office of holiness which they have conferred they demand the coin of favor. Therefore, when the Prophet described a righteous man, he well said [Note: [Col. 0535] Isaiah 33.]: “He [Note: [Col. 0535] “Blessed is he who”: editions compared.] shakes his hands free from every gift.” He does not merely say, [Note: [Col. 0535] “he said only”: same editions.] “who [Col. 0535B] shakes his hands free from a gift,” but adds: “from every,” because one kind of gift is from service, another gift from the hand, and another gift from the tongue. A gift from service is undue subjection [Note: [Col. 0535] “servitude”: same editions.]; a gift from the hand is money; a gift from the tongue is favor. Therefore one who confers holy orders then shakes his hands free from every gift when, in divine matters, he seeks not only no money but also no human favor.

### C. CXV. Whoever approaches holy orders through any kind of gift will find eternal condemnation.

The same, in the *Register*. [Note: [Col. 0535] These words have not been found either in Gregory the Great or in the letters of Gregory VII.]

If anyone, neither distinguished by holy morals nor called by clergy and people nor compelled by insistence, presumptuously receives Christ’s priesthood—already defiled by any crime—out of the unjust desire of his heart, or by the filthy prayers of his mouth, or by attendance, or by manual service, or by a deceitful little gift; if, supported not by concern for souls but by greed for vain glory, he receives episcopal or priestly rank, and does not voluntarily abandon it in his lifetime, and if unexpected [Note: [Col. 0535] “Unexpected”: in several ancient manuscripts of Gratian [and the Basel edition] the reading is: “a harsh death found him penitent.”] death does not find him penitent, he will without doubt perish eternally.

Hence the same Gregory writes to John, bishop of the Corinthians, book IV, Letter 55 [Note: [Col. 0535] Letter 57, written A.D. 595, book 5, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 6, c. 90 (87); *Polycarpus*, book 2, title 1.—See Distinction 100, c. 3.]:

### C. CXVI. Nothing whatever is to be accepted for ordinations.

Under strict prohibition we have forbidden the acceptance of anything for ordinations [Note: [Col. 0535] “we decree”: Norimberg edition; “we have decreed”: other editions, first Lyons II and III.]. Therefore you ought neither [Col. 0535D] through a benefit [Note: [Col. 0535] “gift”: editions compared.], nor through favor or the entreaty of certain persons, to consent or permit [Col. 0536A] anyone to be brought to holy orders. [Note: [Col. 0535] “consent”—“permit”: same editions.]

### C. CXVII. Let no one approach holy orders through payment, prayer, favor, or entreaty.

The same, to all bishops established throughout the province of Hellas [Note: [Col. 0535] “Helladia”: original—Ivo; “Elendam”: Argentinensis edition; “Iterdam”: other editions.], in the same book, Letter 56. [Note: [Col. 0535] Letter 58, written A.D. 595, book 5, Maurist edition.—The same is read in Letter 53, book 5, and Letter 8, book 6.—Burchard, book 1, c. 21; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 108.]

I have learned from the reports of certain persons that in those regions no one attains sacred order without giving a benefit. If this is so, I say it weeping, I declare it groaning: when the priestly order has fallen within, it cannot long remain standing without. For we know from the Gospel what our Redeemer himself did: entering the temple, he overturned the seats of those selling doves. To sell doves is to receive temporal gain from the Holy Spirit—whom Almighty God, consubstantial with himself, grants to human beings through the laying-on of hands. From this, as I have said, it is indicated what follows: those who presumed to sell doves in God’s temple had their seats cast down by God’s judgment. [Note: [Col. 0535] “From which … it is now believed that evil results”; “evil is now indicated”: original, book 6, Letter 8—Ivo.]

§ 1. This error, moreover, spreads among subjects with increase. For the very person [Note: [Col. 0535] “for by the very fact that anyone is brought to sacred order [added: ‘or honor’: editions compared, first Basel]”: original, book 6, Letter 8; editions compared.] who is brought to holy orders, already corrupted at the root of his advancement, is more ready to sell [Note: [Col. 0535] “vend”: editions compared.] to others what he bought. And where is what is written [Note: [Col. 0535] Matthew 10:8.]: “Freely you received; freely give”? And since the simoniacal heresy first arose against the holy Church, why is it not considered—why is it not seen [Note: [Col. 0535] “guarded against”: Basel edition.]—that the person whom one ordains for payment is, by being advanced, made into a heretic? Therefore we exhort you that none of you hereafter [Col. 0536C] permit this to happen, and that no one dare promote anyone to holy orders either through someone’s favor or through entreaty, unless the quality of his life [Note: [Col. 0535] added: “merit”: editions compared, first Basel.] and conduct shows him worthy of it. For if we learn that it has been done otherwise again, know that it will be checked by strict and canonical punishment.

### C. CXVIII. Let no one attain episcopal honor through canvassing.

Likewise Symmachus to Caesarius, Letter I, c. 5. [Note: [Col. 0535] written A.D. 502.]

Accordingly, let no one be permitted to attain episcopal honor through canvassing. For if this excess is blamed in secular life, who doubts that it brings reproach upon those who are religious and serve God? [Note: [Col. 0535] “brings upon” or “inflicts”: editions compared, first Basel; “brands”: Collection II.]

[Col. 0537A]

### C. CXIX. On the same subject.

Likewise Gregory to Adeodatus, bishop, book II, Indiction XI, Letter 48. [Note: [Col. 0537D] This chapter has been supplemented from the original in two places where it seemed expedient.] [Note: [Col. 0537] Letter 49, written A.D. 593, book 3, Maurist edition.]

Be especially careful, therefore, in ordination, and admit no one at all to holy orders [Note: [Col. 0537] “to aspire to holy orders, unless”: original.] unless he is advanced in age and pure in conduct, “lest perhaps they cease ever to be what they hasten prematurely to become.” First examine the life and morals of those who are to be placed in sacred office. So that you may be able to employ persons worthy of this office, do not let the influence or entreaty of any persons steal in upon you. “Above all, however, you must be watchful, and let no venality occur in ordination, lest—God forbid—a greater danger threaten both those ordained and those ordaining.” Whenever, therefore, it is necessary to deliberate concerning these matters, associate serious and experienced men with your counsels [Note: [Col. 0537] “with your counsel”: editions compared.] [Col. 0537B] and weigh the question with them in common deliberation.

### C. CXX. Let no one be promoted to holy orders either through favor or through venality.

The same to Columba, bishop, book II, Indiction XI, Letter 47. [Note: [Col. 0537] Letter 48, written A.D. 593, book 3, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 7, c. 46.]

Let boys by no means be admitted to holy orders, lest they fall [Note: [Col. 0537] “withdraw”: Basel edition.] more dangerously in proportion as they hasten more quickly to climb to higher things. Let there be no venality in ordination; let the influence or entreaty of persons obtain nothing against these prohibitions of ours. For God is undoubtedly offended if anyone is promoted to holy orders not by merit but through favor—God forbid—or through venality.

Gratian. On the other hand, the same Gregory is read to have ordained, at the entreaty of certain persons, [Col. 0537C] one acolyte and another deacon, as he himself writes in book VII, Indiction I, Letter 2, to Peter [Note: [Col. 0537D] “To Peter”: in the printed codices, the letter from which this chapter was taken is addressed to Chrysanthus, bishop. But in a very ancient Vatican codex of the same letters it is addressed: “To Peter, bishop, through Corsica.” Anselm likewise reads as Gratian does. Another letter to Peter, bishop of Alexandria in Corsica, is found in book V, c. 122, though “Alexandria” may perhaps be an error and “Aleria” should apparently be written.] bishop of Corsica, among other things [Note: [Col. 0537] Letter 1, written A.D. 598, book 8, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 7, c. 76.]:

### C. CXXI. At a bishop’s intervention, the Pope ordained a certain acolyte.

Through [Note: [Col. 0537] “for the intercession”: original.] the intercession of your holiness we have made the bearer of this letter an acolyte, and have sent him [Note: [Col. 0537] “sent him back”: editions compared.] to your service [Note: [Col. 0537] “your”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.], so that, if he serves more fully in gaining souls, he may be able to advance further.

### C. CXXII. Whoever receives sacred order in the Roman Church may not thereafter leave it.

The same to Elias, priest and abbot, book IV, Letter 30. [Note: [Col. 0537] Letter 38, written A.D. 595, book 5, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 7, c. 78.]

You directed us to promote and send back to you your son Epiphanius to sacred [Col. 0538A] order. [Note: [Col. 0537] “send back”: original.] We have complied with you in one matter, but in the other we could by no means comply. He has indeed been made a deacon; but whoever has once received rank [Note: [Col. 0537] added: “sacred”: ibid.; editions compared.] in this Church has no further permission to leave it. If, therefore [Note: [Col. 0537] “indeed”: editions compared.], I could not see you, I have this consolation: that I rest in your son.

Gratian. Therefore, ordinations are not judged false on account of just anyone’s prayers, but only those which are made because of requests submitted by the person to be ordained or by his friend through a carnal rather than a spiritual affection, though they would otherwise not have taken place; these are extorted not by charity intervening but by ambition pleading. Moreover, the supreme pontiff may ordain in the Roman Church not only the clerics of any bishop, but, when need requires, may also summon and invite monks and any clerics.

[Col. 0538B] Hence Pope Nicholas, in the letter to Emperor Michael beginning “We had proposed” [Note: [Col. 0537] written A.D. 865.—Anselm, book 1, c. 75; book 2, c. 14.—below C. 9, q. 3, c. 21.]:

### C. CXXIII. On the same subject.

By the principal authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we have the right [Note: [Col. 0537] “and the right”: original; Basel edition.] to summon to ourselves and invite, when necessary and when ecclesiastical needs require it, not only monks [Note: [Col. 0537] “into monks”—“into clerics”: editions compared.] but also any clerics from whatever diocese.

## Part XV. Gratian.

Therefore, when any kind of gift intervenes, an ordination is judged false. But just as holy orders must not be conferred when payment intervenes, so neither may they be restored thereby. For, as Blessed Ambrose says, holy orders [Col. 0538C] are neither to be bought for money nor redeemed for money.

Hence Gregory VII likewise says [book VI of the *Register*, at the council held A.D. 1078, in the sixth year of his pontificate, c. 9. [Note: [Col. 0537] Fifth Roman Council—*Polycarpus*, book 4, title 21.]]:

### C. CXXIV. A priestly office under interdict is not to be restored for payment.

No bishop shall impose upon his abbots or clerics a burden or servile service arising from custom contrary to the ecclesiastical rule, nor shall he restore an interdicted priestly office for payment. If he does so, he shall incur peril to his office.

Gratian. But those who receive money in order not to confer holy orders upon candidates for ordination, or not to give their assent to a canonical election, or to withhold a blessed stone or consecration from churches which are to be built [Col. 0539A] or consecrated, are shown by many arguments to be guilty and infamous because of the money received.

For Paschal II says [Note: [Col. 0539] The exact words have not been found in the letters of Pope Paschal.]:

### C. CXXV. Those who do not permit the Church of God to be regularly ordered are to be judged sacrilegious.

There are some who, either by violence or by favor, do not permit churches to be regularly ordered. We have likewise decreed [Note: [Col. 0539] “we decree”: Basel edition.] that they are to be judged sacrilegious.

### C. CXXVI. On the same subject.

Code, book IX, under the Julian law concerning extortion; the Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius. [Note: [Col. 0539] c. 4, law 27—issued A.D. 386.]

We command and exhort that, if any one of the honorable class, decurions, landholders, or finally even tenant farmers, has been shaken down on any pretext by a judge of whatever rank; if anyone knows that a judicial decision has been sold; if anyone can establish that a penalty was either remitted for payment or imposed through the fault of greed; if, finally, anyone can prove a corrupt judge for any cause whatever—then, whether that judge is still in office or has laid down his administration, let him come forward publicly, lodge the charge, and prove the charge he has lodged. When he has proved it, he will obtain both [Col. 0539B] victory and glory.

### C. CXXVII. On the same subject.

The same, in the *Digest*, book III, title “On Calumniators,” law 1. [Note: [Col. 0539D] In this and the following laws cited from the *Digest*, the titles have been restored from ancient copies of Gratian, which agree closely with the Florentine Pandects.] [Ulpian, book X, *On the Edict*.]

Against a person alleged to have accepted money in order, for purposes of vexatious litigation, to conduct or not conduct a proceeding [Note: [Col. 0539] “is alleged”: Argentinensis and Basel editions; “is discovered”: other editions.], an action in factum lies, within the useful year, for four times the money alleged to have been received; after a year, for the single amount. [Note: [Col. 0539D] “Useful”: this word is absent from ancient codices of Gratian and from the Pandects, but has not been removed because of the gloss.] [Note: [Col. 0539] “for the single amount”: editions compared.]

### C. CXXVIII. In the same place, book XLVII, title 13, law 2, “On Extortion.”

[Macer. [Note: [Col. 0539] “Marcellus”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.] Book I, *Public Prosecutions*.]

The proceeding for extortion is not public. But if someone accepted money because he threatened an accusation, there can be a public proceeding under the senatorial decrees by which those are ordered to be liable to the punishment of the Cornelian law who have conspired to accuse innocent persons, or who accepted money for making or not making an accusation, denunciation or non-denunciation, or testimony.

### C. CXXIX. In the same place, book XLVIII, title 11, under the Julian law concerning extortion, law 3.

[Macer. [Note: [Col. 0539] “Marcellus”: Argentinensis, Basel, Norimberg, Lyons II and III editions.] Book I, *Public Prosecutions*.]

[Col. 0540A] A person is liable under the Julian law concerning extortion if, while holding any public power, he accepted money to adjudicate or not adjudicate [Note: [Col. 0539D] “Or not adjudicate”: these words are likewise found in the common printed *Digest*, but are absent from the Florentine Pandects. This *Palea* occurs in nearly all ancient copies of Gratian, and from the chapter *Sunt quidam* to the end of the question there is no division into chapters.] or to decree, [Venuleius Saturninus, law *Vel quo*, same title.] or so that he might do something more or less fully in the exercise of his office.

### C. CXXX. On the same subject.

The same, in the same title, law 6.

Under the same law is liable [Note: [Col. 0539] “are liable”—“have accepted”: Böhm.] anyone who accepts money for giving or not giving testimony [Note: [Col. 0540D] “Has accepted”: the Pandects continue with a clause, “A person condemned under this law,” which is placed at the end of this chapter.]. And after a few words:

§ 1. The Julian law concerning extortion provides that no one shall accept money for enrolling or dispatching a soldier, nor for delivering an opinion in the senate or public council, nor for prosecuting or not prosecuting.

§ 2. Macer [Note: [Col. 0539] “Marcellus”: editions compared.] [Col. 0540B], Book I, *Public Prosecutions*, law 7: The Julian law concerning extortion commands that no one accept anything for appointing, changing, or ordering a judge or arbitrator to adjudicate [Note: [Col. 0539] omitted in editions compared, first Lyons II and III.], nor for not appointing, not changing, or not ordering him, etc.; nor for evaluating a lawsuit, or conducting or not conducting a capital or pecuniary trial. [Note: [Col. 0539] “has accepted”: editions compared, first Lyons II and III.]

And below:

§ 3. Today persons are punished extra ordinem under the Julian law concerning extortion [Note: [Col. 0539] absent from the Basel edition.], and are commonly punished either by exile or even more severely, according to the offense committed.

§ 4. *Venuleius, same title, law 6.* A person condemned under this law is forbidden to give public testimony [Note: [Col. 0539] “give”: editions compared.], to be a judge, or to seek judicial office.

# QUESTION II

[Col. 0540C]

## GRATIAN

### Part I.

The second question follows: whether money may be demanded for entering a monastery, or, if demanded, paid. That both may lawfully be done is proved by the course of both Testaments. For it is read [Note: [Col. 0539] 1 Samuel 1.] in the first book of Kings that Hannah brought Samuel with her, after he was weaned, with three calves, three measures of flour, and an amphora of wine, to the house of the Lord at Shiloh.

§ 1. In the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0539] Acts 4:32.] it is read that the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul; none said that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them. Each sold his estates and laid their prices at the feet of the apostles. One of them, [Col. 0541A] named Ananias [Note: [Col. 0541] Acts 5.], having kept back part for himself, fell dead at the apostle’s feet with his wife Sapphira, after receiving a sentence of curse.

§ 2. From this it clearly appears that those about to enter a monastery ought to offer their property to its rulers, and are not otherwise to be received unless they have offered their property. But it is one thing to offer voluntarily and another to pay what has been demanded. Hannah, Samuel’s mother, offered gifts to the priests voluntarily, not because they were demanded or requested. The believers too voluntarily offered their possessions to the apostles for service to the needs of the indigent; under the pressing persecution of unbelievers, they were not permitted to retain those possessions. Ananias likewise was condemned not because he was unwilling to offer his goods, but because, having lied to the Holy Spirit, he fraudulently withheld part of the price of what he had offered to the apostles. Therefore these authorities do not permit [Col. 0541B] rulers to demand anything from entrants, but permit them to accept what is voluntarily offered, because the former is blameworthy while the latter is not.

Hence it is read in the Second Council of Braga, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 0541] held A.D. 572.—Burchard, book 3, c. 37, and Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 42, from the Council of Worms, where nearly the same words occur.]:

### C. I. Nothing is to be demanded for dedicating churches.

It has pleased us that whenever bishops are invited by any of the faithful to consecrate churches, they shall not demand any gift from the founder as though it were owed [Note: [Col. 0541] “from”: Hispanic Collection.] [Note: [Col. 0541] “let it be demanded”: Basel edition.]. But if he himself offers something from his own vow, it shall not be rejected; if poverty or necessity restrains him, nothing shall be demanded of him. Nevertheless, each bishop must remember this: he must not dedicate a church [Note: [Col. 0541] added: “or basilica”: ibid.] until he has first received confirmation, by a charter of donation, of the endowment of the basilica and provision for its service. [Note: [Col. 0541] “confirmed”: Basel, Lyons II and III editions.] For this rashness is no slight fault [Note: [Col. 0541] absent from the Hispanic Collection.], if a church is consecrated like a private house [Col. 0541C] without lamps or without substantial support for those who are to serve there. [Note: [Col. 0541] absent from the same collection.]

Likewise Boniface [Note: [Col. 0541] The manner of writing itself and the silence of Dionysius Exiguus show that this chapter does not belong to Boniface.], bishop of the city of Rome, writes to all the cenobites of the Church of Cagliari [Note: [Col. 0541] “to all”: Basel edition.]:

### C. II. Nothing is to be demanded from those who come to conversion, nor is anyone to be invited to conversion for payment.

With what pious affection of mind the Roman Church sympathizes with your abandonment, dearest brothers, is perhaps unknown to you [Note: [Col. 0541] “your”: ibid.], but it is not unknown to the Knower of all things. I call God to witness that, as to what adequate answer we should give to your doubt, that doubt itself renders me anxious and unequal to the task. For nowhere [Note: [Col. 0541] “Never”: editions compared, first Lyons II and III.] do we read that the Lord’s disciples, or persons converted through their ministry, induced anyone to God’s worship through the intervention of any gift—unless perhaps someone inaptly raises the matter of food for the poor, to whom provisions were denied to none, of whatever profession they were. We certainly know [Note: [Col. 0541] James 1:17.] that every good thing given and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights; and one who resolves, by the holy freedom of deliberation, to serve God freely receives from him the gift of good will. [Note: [Col. 0541] “with whom and from whom”: editions compared, first Basel.] It follows, therefore, that one who takes a gift for some ecclesiastical [Note: [Col. 0541] “of the Church”: editions compared.] reception sells God’s gift, which ought to descend from the Father of lights; and the person giving the gift buys importunately. What follows for sellers or buyers of a divine [Col. 0542B] gift need not be spelled out.

§ 1. Take care, then, brothers, how doubtful is the counsel you have sought [Note: [Col. 0541] “seek”: Basel edition.], which we find no basis whatever for confirming according to the purpose of your will. Yet if the person whom you have found [Note: [Col. 0541] “requested”: ibid.] is so suitable to your need [Note: [Col. 0541] “will”: ibid.], provided that every bargain is absent, every agreement ceases, and no alienation of your church occurs, let him come, begin to serve God freely, and devoutly render the service of his government. Afterwards, the Roman Church permits you, as though by way of assistance, to bestow certain gifts upon his church for the relief of the brothers. [Note: [Col. 0541] “devout”: ibid.]

[Col. 0542C] Hence Pope Urban, in the council at Melfi, c. 12 [Note: [Col. 0541] held A.D. 1089.]:

### C. III. On the same subject. PALEA.

[Note: [Col. 0541D] In certain ancient copies, which contain few *Paleae*, this chapter is found through the word “rule.” The remainder consists of passages of Blessed Gregory judged to be interpolated.]

“No abbot shall presume to receive or demand payment from persons coming to conversion, under any pretext of an agreement [Note: [Col. 0541] “arrangement”: original.] [Note: [Col. 0541] added: “or entreaty, or”: Basel edition; “or manner of life, or”: other editions.]. Following the ancient rule, I decree that absolutely nothing is ever to be accepted for ordinations: neither for giving the pallium, nor for handing over [Note: [Col. 0541] “donation”: editions compared.] charters, nor under the name of *pastellus*, a designation that a new simulation [Note: [Col. 0541] “through a new”: Basel edition.] discovered through ambition. [Note: [Col. 0541] These passages are taken from the council held under Gregory the Great at Rome, A.D. 595.—Anselm, book 6, c. 91 (88); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 109; *Polycarpus*, book 2, title 1.] For when [Note: [Col. 0541D] “For when”: in most copies containing this *Palea*, these two words are absent. Yet they occur in Blessed Gregory, since the sentence is still dependent and is joined with the material presented in the following chapter as follows: “For when the pontiff lays his hand upon a bishop being ordained, a minister reads the Gospel lesson, and a notary writes the letter of his confirmation; just as it is not fitting for the pontiff ….”] a bishop is being ordained, the pontiff lays on his hand, a minister reads the Gospel lesson, and a notary writes the letter of his confirmation. [Note: [Col. 0541] “when ordaining”: editions compared.]

[Col. 0543A]

### C. IV. Nothing should be demanded from one being ordained; yet voluntarily offered gifts should not be refused.

Likewise Gregory, *Register*, book IV, Letter 44, or c. 88, in the Roman Synod. [Note: [Col. 0543] Gregory, continuously in the same place.—Anselm and Ivo, in the same place.—See c. 1, X, *On Simony*.]

Just as it is unfitting for a bishop to sell the hand that he lays on, so a minister or notary ought not to sell his voice or pen at that person’s ordination. And a little later:

§ 1. If the person ordained wishes, after receiving the charters and pallium, to give something to any member of the clergy solely as a token of favor—not by agreement [Note: [Col. 0543] “pact”: editions compared.], not under compulsion, and not because it has been requested—then we in no way forbid its acceptance. His offering entails no stain of guilt, because it did not proceed from the solicitation of one seeking office. [Note: [Col. 0543] “hesitating”: Basel edition; “which did not proceed from the recipient’s canvassing”: original—Anselm.]

Gratian. Boniface’s authority plainly shows that, just as no one is to be invited to conversion for payment, [Col. 0543B] so entrance into the Church ought not to be granted to anyone through the intervention of money. Gregory’s authority, however, makes it understood that it is not lawful to demand money for entrance into the Church, but that it is lawful to accept what is voluntarily offered.

### Part II.

Likewise, the following saying of the Apostle is objected from 1 Timothy, chapter 5 [v. 2.]:

### C. V.

[Note: [Col. 0543D] In many ancient codices this chapter is joined to the preceding one.] [Note: [Col. 0543] These words occur somewhat differently in Holy Scripture.]

Honor widows who are truly widows. But those who are not truly widows—that is, those who can be supported by their own resources or those of their parents—are not to be received, so that the Church may suffice for those who are truly widows.

### C. VI. A person who can be supported from his own resources is not to receive maintenance from the Church.

Likewise Jerome to Pope Damasus. [Note: [Col. 0543D] Below also, Question 16, c. 1, final chapter, this is cited from Jerome. Similar material occurs in the Rule of Monks, in *On Poverty*, and in the ordinary gloss on 1 Timothy 5, from Jerome.] [Note: [Col. 0543] Chapter of uncertain origin.—See C. 16, q. 1, c. 68.]

Those clerics ought to be supported at the Church’s expense [Col. 0543C] for whom no property of parents or relatives provides assistance. But those who can be supported by their parents’ goods and their own resources, if they take what belongs to the poor, unquestionably commit sacrilege and, through such misuse, eat and drink judgment upon themselves.

### C. VII. Those who have resources sufficient for themselves are not to be maintained from the Church’s provisions.

Likewise Prosper, *On the Contemplative Life*, book II, chapters 9 and 10. [Note: [Col. 0543] Rather, Julianus Pomerius, whose book this is.—See the Council of Aachen, c. 107.]

A pastor of the Church ought not to distribute anything to those whose own resources suffice, since [Note: [Col. 0543] *quandoquidem*, “since”: editions compared with the original.] to give to persons who possess means is nothing other than to waste. Nor do those who possess property and wish something to be given them take without grave sin that from which a poor person would have lived. Indeed, the Holy Spirit says of clerics through the Prophet [Note: [Col. 0543] Hosea 4:8.]: “They feed upon the sins of my people.” But just as those who possess nothing of their own [Note: [Col. 0543] *proprii*, “of their own”: Basel edition.], receive—not sins—but the provisions that they appear to need, so possessors receive—not the provisions in which they abound—but the sins of others.

Gratian. Yet by these authorities, those are forbidden to receive support from the Church not who were once rich but later left everything, as [Note: [Col. 0543] Cf. Matthew 5; Luke 19; Acts 4.] Peter, Matthew, and Paul did; or distributed it to the poor, as Zacchaeus did; or added it to the Church’s resources, as did those who sold their estates and laid the prices at the apostles’ feet, so that all things might be common to them. Rather, those are forbidden who live in their parents’ houses, or refuse to leave their own possessions [Col. 0544B] and yet desire to be maintained from ecclesiastical resources.

Concerning them, the following is added in chapter 10 of the same book of Prosper [Note: [Col. 0543] Council of Aachen, in the same place.]:

### C. VIII. He who is unwilling to leave his own possessions ought not to be maintained at the expense of the Church.

If someone is unwilling to leave his own possessions for the reason that he may have something from which to live, why does he receive that for which he must render an account? Why does he increase his own possessions by others’ sins? The same author, a little earlier in the same place:

§ 1. It is not for me to say by what sin [Note: [Col. 0543] “what sin they commit”: Basel edition.—“what sin it is for them”: Lyons editions II and III.—“what sin it is”: the remaining editions.] they presumptuously receive the food of the poor—those who, when they ought to assist the Church from their own resources, further burden it with their own expenses. Perhaps they live in the community for this reason: that they may not feed any poor persons, receive visitors, or diminish their own income by daily expenditure.

§ 2. But if they contribute something from their revenues to the Church, as though for their own maintenance, let them not set themselves above, in empty boasting, those whom the Church feeds and clothes although they possess nothing. For more perfect [Note: [Col. 0543] Added: “indeed”: editions compared with the original.] is the person who strips himself of the things of the world, or who, having had nothing, does not desire to possess anything, than the person who gives the Church something from the many things he possesses [Note: [Col. 0543] “has given”: the same editions except Argenteuil.], and perhaps boasts of what he has given.

Gratian. Behold those who are forbidden to receive support from the Church. But those who leave all their possessions, distribute them to the poor, or add them to the Church’s resources ought both laudably to receive support from the Church and to be maintained from its resources.

[Col. 0545A] Hence chapter 11 of the same book reads [Note: [Col. 0545] Cf. Council of Aachen, chapters 108 and 111.]:

### C. IX. Those who leave their possessions, distribute them to the poor, or add them to the Church’s resources laudably administer ecclesiastical goods.

A priest entrusted with the duty of administration receives from the people, not only without greed but also with the praise of piety, goods to be administered; and he faithfully administers what he receives, because [Note: [Col. 0545] “who”: editions compared with the original, first Lyons II and III, Venice I and II.] he has either left all his possessions to his parents [Note: [Col. 0545D] “To his parents”: In certain manuscripts of Gratian it reads, “or left [them] to the poor.” But in an old manuscript of Prosper and in the Council of Aachen it reads: “because he either left all his possessions, or added them to the Church’s resources.” Yet, because many manuscripts of Gratian and Prosper have the received reading, nothing has been altered.], distributed them to the poor, or added them to the Church’s resources; and, out of love for poverty, he has placed himself among the poor, *so* that he himself lives as a voluntary poor man from that from which he supplies the poor.

Likewise, clerics whom either *will* or birth has made poor should receive, with perfection of virtue, the necessities of life, whether they live in their own homes or in a community [Col. 0545B]; for it is not the desire *to possess* that leads them to receive these things, but the necessity of living that compels them. And below, in chapter 14:

§ 1. The Apostle seems to speak of such persons when he says: “Those who serve in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary, and those who minister *at* the altar share with [Note: [Col. 0545] “from”: the same editions except Basel.] the altar” [Note: [Col. 0545] “may be shared”: Basel edition.—“may share”: the remaining editions.—Cf. 1 Corinthians 9:13.]. Unless he had wished this to be understood of those who despise their own property, he would never have added immediately afterward: “So also God ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel.”

Those live by the Gospel who wish to have nothing of their own; who neither have nor desire to have anything, being possessors not of private goods but of common goods. What else is it to live by the Gospel than for the worker to receive the necessities of life from the work in which he labours? Yet the Apostle, who preached the Gospel in such a way that *he did not live by the Gospel, but* supplied his own necessities with his hands [Col. 0545C], confidently says of himself: “But I have used none of these things.” And afterward he explained why he had said *this*, saying: “It would be better for me to die than for anyone to make my glory void.” He calls his glory made void if he had wished to receive the expense of temporal life from those to whom he preached. For he did not wish to receive in the present life the fruit of his labour, but in the future.

### C. X. Priests shall distribute ecclesiastical stipends according to the merit of labour. Likewise, from the Council of Agde, chapter 36 [Note: [Col. 0545] Held A.D. 506.].

All clerics who faithfully and diligently serve a church shall receive from priests, according to the merit of their service, through the ordinance of the canons, stipends due to their holy labours [Col. 0546A] [Note: [Col. 0545] “or”: Hispanic Collection.].

Gratian. It is clearer than light from the authorities of many [Note: [Col. 0546D] “Of many”: In the common manuscripts [Col. 0545] and editions compared with the original, except Basel, this heading preceded the present §, “Of many”: “Likewise, from the council of Pope Urban held in Auvergne.” It has been removed because it is absent from all the old copies compared, and in most copies this § is the beginning of the following third question.] that it is not lawful to demand money from those about to enter a monastery, lest both the one who demands it and the one who pays it incur the crime of simony.

## QUESTION III

## GRATIAN

But the objection is still raised that those who give money in order to enter a monastery buy not the religious profession but a share in the Church’s stipends. Therefore, since they buy temporal things, not spiritual things, they are by no means to be regarded as simoniacs.

§ 1. The answer to this is: Not only those who receive or give spiritual things for a price, but also those who receive or give for a price the temporal things attached to them [Col. 0546B], are judged simoniacs. Hence Malachi [Note: [Col. 0545] Malachi 1:16.] speaks in the person of the Lord: “Who among you,” he says, “will shut the doors and kindle my altar without payment? I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not receive an offering from your hand.” To shut doors is not an office of sacred ministry, but merely something attached to it.

Likewise Gregory writes to all the bishops of Spain [Note: [Col. 0545] Chapter of uncertain identification.]:

### C. I. Concerning those who dispense sacred orders through the receipt of gifts.

We have heard, beloved, what we ought indeed to have heard [Note: [Col. 0545] “to hear”: editions compared with the original, except Basel.], but certainly had no wish to hear: namely, that there are certain professed ministers of sacred orders who, by giving or receiving gifts, appropriate to themselves churches of God or [Col. 0546C] their benefices. We are greatly astonished that you have not already long ago severely corrected this crime; for both parties ought justly to be corrected and removed from the thresholds of the holy Church: both the person who bestows gifts in pursuit of a church [Note: [Col. 0545] “bestow,” and so thereafter: Argenteuil, Norbertine, Venice I editions.], and the person who presumes to receive anything in order that another may obtain a church. The former presumes to buy God’s gift; the latter to sell it. Nor would I say that this deed differs from sacrilege, since what ought freely to have been done voluntarily and by the sacred discretion of deliberation is made conditional upon a monetary agreement. Therefore, dearest brothers, carefully refute [Note: [Col. 0545] “reveal”: Basel edition.] acts so done, prevent their completion, and do not hesitate to strike those who resist your commands with the fitting bond of anathema.

[Col. 0547A]

### C. II. Concerning those who sell churches or ecclesiastical benefices. The same, to the bishop of Rouen and to all the Gallic bishops [Note: [Col. 0547] The authorship of this chapter is uncertain; yet, like the preceding chapter, it seems to belong to the time of Gregory VII.—Polycarpus, book 2, title 4.].

If anyone, whether giver or receiver, acquires churches of God or ecclesiastical benefices (which some [Note: [Col. 0547] “indeed”: Basel and Venice II editions.] call prebends) through the intervention of money—whether buying by giving or selling by receiving—he is not excluded from Simon’s [Note: [Col. 0547] “simoniacal”: Basel edition.] perdition. But if he persists, let him be punished with everlasting damnation. For anyone who wishes, under the pretence of religion, to serve God, if he receives anything [Note: [Col. 0547] “has received”: Basel edition.], both loses his merit and is deprived of the benefit he has received. Consequently, the force of reason compels him to restore what he has unjustly received [Note: [Col. 0547] “received”: Argenteuil and Basel editions.], and not to retain anything that he received [Note: [Col. 0547] “accepted”: Basel edition.] for the sake of shameful gain.

[Col. 0547B]

### C. III. A bishop who sells benefices or ecclesiastical offices shall be suspended from office. Likewise Pope Gregory VII, *Register*, book VI, in the Synod, chapter 4 [Note: [Col. 0547] Fifth Council of Rome, held A.D. 1078.].

If any bishop sells prebends, archdeaconries, provostships, or any ecclesiastical offices, or ordains otherwise than the enactments of the holy Fathers prescribe, let him be suspended from ecclesiastical office. For it is fitting that, just as he received [Note: [Col. 0547] “receives”: Basel edition.] the episcopate freely, so he should distribute freely the members of that same episcopate.

### C. IV. Bishops may sell neither altars nor prebends. Likewise, from the council of Pope Urban II held in Auvergne [Note: [Col. 0547C] In the summaries of the chapters of the Council of Clermont held in Auvergne—concerning which see the statement above on chapter 1, Distinction 60—chapter 6 contains the following, apparently relevant to this chapter: “That altars given through persons to communities of canons or monks shall, upon the death of those persons, return free into the hands of the bishops, unless they have been confirmed to those communities by the bishops’ writings or privileges.”] [Note: [Col. 0547] Held A.D. 1095. The same provisions occur in the Council of Nîmes held under Urban.].

A question was raised concerning bishops who frequently compelled monasteries to redeem with money altars that had been given to them, because [Col. 0547C] a certain [Note: [Col. 0547] “indeed”: Basel edition.] practice of simoniacal depravity has for a long time become entrenched in regions of Gaul: churches or tithes—called “altars” among them in the common idiom—given to monasteries are often sold by bishops under a cloak of avarice [Note: [Col. 0547] “are sold”: editions compared with the original, first Lyons II and III.], whenever the clerics whom they call “persons” die or are replaced. We, by God’s authority, repelling every form of venality from both ecclesiastical property and ministries, forbid by apostolic authority that this be done further; likewise [Note: [Col. 0547] “thus”: Basel edition.] we also forbid all prebends to be put up for sale [Col. 0548A]. Moreover, whatever altars or tithes monasteries are known to have possessed for thirty years or more under such a redemption, we establish that they shall henceforth possess them peaceably and without any molestation.

§ 1. The bishops’ annual due, which they have been accustomed to receive from the same altars, is of course reserved.

### C. V. Whatever is acquired in sacred orders through money given or promised shall be deemed void. Likewise [Note: [Col. 0547D] “Likewise”: Formerly the reading was “Likewise Gregory.” But in several old copies it correctly reads “Likewise,” namely Urban II, in whose synod these provisions occur.] at the Council of Piacenza, chapters 1 and 2 [Note: [Col. 0547] Held A.D. 1095.].

We likewise confirm, by the judgment of the *Holy Spirit* and by apostolic authority, the enactments of the holy Fathers concerning simoniacs. Therefore, whatever has been acquired, *whether* in sacred orders or in ecclesiastical property, through money given or promised, we decree to be void and never to have any force [Col. 0548B] [Note: [Col. 0547] “to obtain”: Basel edition.].

### C. VI. Whatever is possessed is understood under the name “money.” Likewise Augustine, *On Christian Discipline*, or *On the Gift of Discipline*, chapter 1 [Note: [Col. 0547] “Augustine, On Christian Doctrine”: editions compared with the original.—The correct title is *On Christian Discipline*; for the book *On the Gift of Discipline* is apocryphal.].

Everything that people possess [Note: [Col. 0547] “have”: editions compared with the original.] on earth—all things of which they are owners—is called money: whether a slave *be*, a vessel, a field, a tree, or livestock; whatever belongs among these is called money. And below:

§ 1. It is called money because the ancients had *all* that they possessed in livestock.

### C. VII. He who buys ecclesiastical benefices is shown to buy churches also. Likewise Pope Paschal [Note: [Col. 0547] An apocryphal chapter; cf. on C. 1, q. 1, c. 12.—Anselm, book 13, chapter 33; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 123; *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 84; Deusdedit, part 2; Polycarpus, book 7, title 6.—The same material occurs in Berthold of Constance, in his work *On the Condemnation of Schismatics*.].

[Col. 0548C] If anyone objects that consecrations are not bought [Note: [Col. 0547] “sold”: Anselm and Berthold.], but only the things themselves which result from consecration, he is shown to be wholly [Note: [Col. 0548C] “Wholly”: Deusdedit and Anselm, as well as Berthold, read: “he indeed seems to say something, but wholly understands nothing.”] foolish. For since a material church, or a bishop, an abbot, or anything of that sort cannot in any respect exist without material goods, just as the soul does not live bodily without the body, whoever sells either of the two, without which the other does not exist, leaves neither unsold. Therefore let no one [Note: [Col. 0548D] “Therefore let no one”: Deusdedit, Polycarpus, Ivo, and a manuscript codex of papal decretals—in which nearly the whole letter of Paschal from which this chapter was taken is reproduced—do not contain these words, but immediately after “leaves neither unsold” continue: “Yet the sacred canon of Chalcedon wholly destroys that objection,” etc. The author of this chapter and of the entire letter is Paschal I. For in that codex of decretals this letter of Paschal occurs after the decrees of Hadrian II, whereas the decrees of Paschal II occur after Urban II, in precisely the order in which they succeeded one another; this is also indicated by the following chapter.] [Note: [Col. 0547] These words seem rather to belong to the Council of Poitiers held under Pope Urban. They likewise do not occur in Anselm’s collection, though they are found in Alger, book 3, chapter 39.] buy a church, prebend, or anything ecclesiastical, nor pay for such a thing, before or afterward, either a little cake or a meal [Col. 0549A] [Note: [Col. 0549] Added: “by agreement”: Argenteuil edition.].

### C. VIII. On the same matter. Likewise Urban II, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son L., provost of the church of Saint Juventius at Pavia, greeting and apostolic blessing [Note: [Col. 0549D] Deusdedit reproduces the entire letter of Urban II to his beloved son L., provost of the church of Blessed Juventius at Pavia, in his collection.] [Note: [Col. 0549] Letter to Lucius, provost of Saint Juventius (Vincentius: editions compared with the original), written A.D. 1089.—Deusdedit, part 2.].

The Saviour foretells [Note: [Col. 0549] “foretold”: original.—Cf. Matthew 24.] in the Gospel that, near the end of the age, false Christs [Note: [Col. 0549] “false apostles”: Basel, Paris, Lyons II and III editions.] and false prophets will arise and deceive many, and that his faithful will suffer many afflictions in the world; yet the gates of hell will not prevail *against the Church*. Therefore, *because*, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0549] 1 Corinthians 11:19.], “there must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest,” we must rise in opposition with the Prophet [Note: [Col. 0549] Ezekiel 13.], set a wall before the house of Israel, and with the *same* Apostle [Note: [Col. 0549] Acts 14.] enter the kingdom of God through many [Col. 0549B] tribulations, because [Note: [Col. 0549] Romans 8.] the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us.

§ 1. Therefore, since you have informed us that the question has been raised against you whether selling an ecclesiastical thing is simoniacal, it is plainly inferred that it is simoniacal from what the blessed Apostle Peter said [Note: [Col. 0549] Acts 8:20.] to Simon: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money.” For the Holy Spirit is God’s gift, and a thing offered to the Church itself is God’s gift. And, if you consider carefully, Simon Magus, who deceitfully came to the faith, did not wish to buy the Holy Spirit *for the sake of the Holy Spirit* [Note: [Col. 0549D] “For the sake of the Holy Spirit”: these two words have been added, and this whole passage corrected from the letter itself, as have several other passages.]—of which he was himself unworthy, since, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0549] Wisdom 1:5.], “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from deceit” [Col. 0549C]—but [Note: [Col. 0549] “but wished to buy the gift of God [‘his’: Argenteuil, Basel, Norbertine editions]”: editions compared with the original.] wished to buy it in order that, as far as lay in his power, he might gain multiplied money by selling the signs performed through that Spirit. Nor did the Apostle condemn the purchase of the Holy Spirit—which he knew could not be rightly accomplished—but he abhorred and struck with the dart of a curse the ambition for such profit and the avarice, which is idolatry, in Simon [Note: [Col. 0549] “struck him”: editions compared with the original, except Basel.].

Therefore, whoever sells or buys ecclesiastical things—which are gifts of God [Note: [Col. 0549] “and gifts of God”: editions compared with the original, except Basel.] [Col. 0550A], because they are given by God to the faithful and by the faithful to God; are received freely from him; and therefore ought to be given freely—for his own gain, thinks with Simon that God’s gift is possessed with money. Thus one who bestows or acquires those same things not for the purpose for which they were instituted but for his own profit, by a gift of speech, undue service, or money, is a simoniac; for Simon’s primary purpose was avarice for money alone [Note: [Col. 0549] “namely the cause of money, that is”: editions compared with the original.—Colossians 3:5.], that is, idolatry, as the Apostle Paul says.

Otherwise, why does the holy Synod of Chalcedon prohibit the appointment by money of an administrator or advocate of a church, or anyone subject to rule, so strictly that it anathematizes even the intermediaries in so great a crime, unless it judges them to be simoniacs [Col. 0550B]? If the aforesaid soldiers of the Church are thus struck down for such a crime, no wise person will deny that persons not serving in the Church ought to be punished much more severely for this cause, namely buying or selling.

But our blessed predecessor Paschal [Note: [Col. 0550C] “Paschal”: Formerly the reading was “Paschasius, in the book *On Consecration*.” The passage has been restored from old manuscripts and the original. For the citation here is of the statement in the preceding chapter from Pope Paschal’s letter.] [Note: [Col. 0549] “predecessor Paschasius affirmed in the book *On Consecration*”: editions compared with the original, except Basel.—Cf. preceding chapter.] affirms concerning consecration that whoever sells either of two things without which the other does not exist leaves neither unsold; and therefore it is understood that one who sells or buys a Church’s property is a simoniac [Note: [Col. 0549] “we understand”: Argenteuil edition.—“understands”: remaining editions with the original.].

§ 2. By the name *procurator* the aforesaid synod means any administrator of ecclesiastical goods, for example, a provost, steward (*oeconomus*), or deputy lord (*vicedominus*); by the name *defender*, an advocate or *castaldus*, and a judge; and under those subject to a rule, an archpriest, archdeacon [Note: [Col. 0549] Added: “deacon”: the same editions except Basel.], canon, monk, or anyone bound to an ecclesiastical office [Col. 0550C].

§ 3. But that one who sells or buys a provostship or anything of that sort sells or buys the Holy Spirit, so far as lies in him, hear Augustine on John: “O how many *praepositurae* [provostships] they have made [Note: [Col. 0550D] “O how many *praeposituras*”: In Saint Augustine, whose many old manuscripts were collated here, the reading is: “O how many purposes [*proposita*] they have made! One purpose, etc.” But throughout Urban’s letter it is *proposta* and *propostum*.] [Note: [Col. 0549] “separate”: Basel edition.—“separate or follow”: the remaining editions except Lyons II and III.]! Primianus has one provost [Note: [Col. 0549] “another”: editions compared with the original, except Basel and Lyons II and III.] at Carthage [Note: [Col. 0549] *Carthagini*: Basel edition.—*Carthaginem*: Lyons I.—*Carthaginensis*: Ard., Norbertine, Venice I and II, Paris editions.] [Note: [Col. 0549] “principate”: editions compared with the original, except Lyons II and III.]; *Maximianus has another* [Col. 0551A]; Rogatus has another *in* Mauretania; and those people, whom we are now unable even to name, have another in Numidia [Note: [Col. 0551] “that man or [‘and’: Lyons II and III] that man has”: editions compared with the original.].” Therefore someone goes about to buy a dove [Note: [Col. 0551] John 2.]; each praises his own provost, what he sells [Note: [Col. 0551D] “His own provost”: In Saint Augustine the reading is: “each, for his own purpose, praises what he sells.” But in Urban’s letter: “each praises his own purpose, what he sells.” The term *propositum* is sometimes known to signify a sect in Augustine, from book 2 *Against Cresconius*, chapter 56.], etc.

See: the venerable Augustine, discussing the sale of a provostship, understands by the name of the dove the sale or purchase of the Holy Spirit, as do all interpreters of this Gospel chapter.

§ 4. We must consider what punishment is due to those who sell or buy things already offered to God and his Church, if those who sold or bought things which were to be offered to God were driven from God’s temple with whips. If it was said of sellers or buyers of things to be offered [Note: [Col. 0551] Matthew 21.], “You have made my Father’s house a house of trade and a den of robbers,” what will be said [Col. 0551B] of sellers or buyers of things already offered to the Church?

§ 5. And lest any madman object that the Lord rightly punished this so harshly because those things were then sold in God’s temple, whereas ecclesiastical property is now sold outside the temple [Note: [Col. 0551] “is sold”: Argenteuil, Norbertine, Venice I editions, with the original.], consider Augustine above: he does not specify the place of the sale or purchase of provostships, but simply says without qualification, “Someone goes about to buy a dove; each praises his own provost, what he sells,” adding neither “in the temple” nor “outside the temple.” Let this suffice concerning sellers or buyers of sacred things [Note: [Col. 0551] Absent from the original.].

[Col. 0551C]

### C. IX. Ministers and servants of the Church are to be ordained by bishops without any venality. Likewise Alexander II [Note: [Col. 0551] This letter, written A.D. 1068, exists in two forms: one shorter, produced in Gratian; the other much longer, published by Mansi.]. Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the Church of Lucca: everlasting greeting [Note: [Col. 0552D] The complete letter occurs in the Vatican Library after the book of Anselm of Lucca.] [Note: [Col. 0551] “To the clergy of the Church of Lucca, for ever”: Basel edition.].

We have learned that for a long time this detestable evil has become entrenched in your Church: no cleric, however religious, however endowed with learning and morals, was ever granted an ecclesiastical benefice unless he endeavoured to buy it with the profane gift of money. Thus the Church and its property became as saleable as some earthly and worthless merchandise [Note: [Col. 0551] “wares”: Basel edition.] set out for sale by traders. How detestable this evil is, how contrary to God and his saints [Note: [Col. 0551] Added: “his”: Lyons II and III editions.—“its”: Basel edition.], the sacred canons teach, and it is evident to almost everyone.

§ 1. For the Council of Chalcedon [Note: [Col. 0551] Cf. above, question 1, chapter 8.—In the editions compared with the original, this is prefaced from the Gloss: “This ruling [‘learning’: Lyons II and III editions] is found in the second canon of the Council of Chalcedon.”], one of the principal councils, condemns with a like penalty those who acquire a Church benefice through the intervention of money [Col. 0552A] and those who are known to traffic in sacred laying-on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is conferred. For with invincible authority it commands both to be expelled: the former from their benefice, the latter from sacred order. Hence the Redeemer of humankind, casting all buyers and sellers out of the temple, overturned the seats of those selling doves and poured out the money of the moneychangers, declaring and saying by the authority of his command [Note: [Col. 0551] John 2:16.]: “Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.”

§ 2. Consider carefully also in the same act that nowhere in the whole text of the holy Gospel is the Lord found to have reproved sinners with such severity and such strict judgment of justice. Not only did he rebuke them by speech, but by action, whipping them with a scourge of cords, he cast them all [Col. 0552B] out of the temple. He thereby openly demonstrated that such traders are not to be rebuked as other sinners are, but must be cast far away from the temple of God, that is, from the holy Church. For just as the sellers of doves signify those who try to sell sacred laying-on of hands, so the moneychangers signify sellers of ecclesiastical benefices, who, as the Gospel testifies, make God’s house a den of robbers.

§ 3. Therefore I, Alexander, bishop—or rather, unworthy minister—of the holy Roman Church and Apostolic See, seeing so many and such great evils arise from unrighteous desire in many churches, especially in the Church of Lucca, have decreed to uproot and utterly eradicate them, lest the blood of the wicked be required from our hand by the strict Judge. We therefore establish [Col. 0552C] and confirm by this present decree—as our predecessors [Note: [Col. 0551] “predecessors”: Böhm.] are known to have done of old—that no bishop hereafter shall ever dare to confer upon clerics, for any price or gift, a Church benefice—which some call a canonry [Note: [Col. 0551] “canonicate”: Argenteuil and Norbertine editions.], prebends, or even orders. Rather, let them endeavour to ordain all ministers and servants of the Church freely and without any [Note: [Col. 0551] Absent from Basel edition.] venality in the holy Church. Let them not choose for the house of the Lord those who offer larger bags of money, but those who, rich in morals, discipline, and learning, are able worthily to sustain the Church itself in their office.

We likewise establish and confirm that no cleric of any rank shall dare to contribute anything for a Church benefice—whether to the building works of churches, to church offerings, or [Col. 0553A] even to that which is to be distributed to the poor—because, as Scripture testifies [Note: [Col. 0553C] “As Scripture testifies”: Here are cited words of blessed Gregory from his letter to Syagrius, found above in the same question, chapter *Non est putanda*.], one who receives something wrongly in order that he may *as though* dispense it rightly is burdened rather than helped [Note: [Col. 0553] “helped”: editions compared with the original.]. But if anyone, forgetful of divine commands and the salvation of souls, led by unrighteous greed, should presumptuously dare to sell or buy the aforesaid Church benefice, we decree that he shall be liable to loss of his rank, as determined at the Council of Chalcedon. He may not minister to the Church which he desired to make saleable for money [Note: [Col. 0553] “money”: Basel edition.]; moreover, pierced by the terrible sword of anathema, unless he repents, he shall in every way be cut off from the Church of God which he injured.

[Col. 0553B]

### C. X. Those who sell or buy God’s gifts are alike condemned by God. Likewise Gregory, Homily XXXIX [Note: [Col. 0553] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 119; *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 88.].

Christ casts sellers and buyers out of the temple [Note: [Col. 0553] “from”: editions compared with the original, following Ivo.], because he condemns both those who confer the laying-on of hands for a gift and those who strive to buy the gift [Note: [Col. 0553] “house”: Basel edition.] of the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0553] “of God”: editions compared with the original, following Ivo.]. Likewise below:

§ 1. Sellers in the temple are those who bestow for reward what is by right due to certain persons. For to sell justice is to preserve it in return for receiving a reward [Note: [Col. 0553] “price”: original.]. But buyers in the temple are those who, while unwilling to render to their neighbour what is just, and scorning to do what is lawfully due, buy sin by giving a price [Note: [Col. 0553] “reward”: original.] to patrons [Note: [Col. 0553] “is bought”: editions compared with the original, except Basel.].

[Col. 0553C]

### C. XI. Those who do not exercise freely the grace received from God are sellers of doves. Likewise Bede on John, chapter 2 [Note: [Col. 0553] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 124; *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 97.].

Not only are those sellers of doves, and makers of God’s house into a house of trade, who seek sacred orders by offering the price of money, praise, or even honour. So too are those who exercise a spiritual rank or grace in the Church, which they received through the Lord’s bounty, not with a single-minded intention but for the sake of some human recompense, contrary to the words of the Apostle Peter [Note: [Col. 0553] 1 Peter 4:11.]: “Whoever speaks, as [Col. 0554A] the utterances of God; whoever ministers, as from the strength which God supplies, so that in all things God may be glorified *through Jesus Christ*.” Therefore, whoever are such, if they do not wish to be removed from the Church when the Lord comes, let them remove these things from their conduct, lest they make God’s house a house of trade.

### C. XII. Let no one appropriate by force or payment things which result from consecration. Likewise from a letter of Pope Urban [Note: [Col. 0553] Cf. above, chapter 8.].

Teaching that no one ought to convert to his own right, whether by force or by any payment, Church property that results from consecration, Saint Urban says: “Whoever [Note: [Col. 0553C] “Whoever”: These words are from the letter of Urban II reproduced above under chapter *Salvator*. The preceding words are found nowhere [Col. 0553] and appear to us to be Gratian’s words, although certain similar words, with a different meaning, occur in a letter of Blessed Urban I. In several old copies of Gratian this chapter is cited as follows: “Likewise Bede, from a letter of Pope Urban,” which does not cohere.] sells or buys ecclesiastical things—which are gifts of God, because they are given by God to the faithful and by the faithful to God, are received freely from him, and [Col. 0554B] therefore ought to be given freely—for his own gain, thinks with Simon that God’s gift is possessed with money.”

### C. XIII. A bishop who distributes tithes and offerings to laymen rather than clerics is a simoniac. Likewise Gregory VII [Note: [Col. 0553D] Below also, C. 16, q. 7, c. *Pervenit*, this chapter is cited from Gregory. Lambert of Schafnaburg indeed recounts that a certain bishop of Bamberg retained that church for some time, contrary to Gregory VII’s excommunication, through the favour of soldiers to whom he gave many gifts; and in Gregory’s *Register*, book 6, letter 5, a similar matter is reproved in Hermann, bishop of Metz.] [Note: [Col. 0553] A similar ruling occurs in the Fifth Council of Rome, held A.D. 1078, chapters 1 and 6.—Polycarpus, book 3, title 11.—Cf. below, C. 16, q. 7, c. 3.—In Lyons edition II it is cited under the name of Paschal II.].

An evil report has reached us that certain bishops are conferring tithes and the offerings of Christians not upon the priests of their own diocese but rather upon lay persons—namely soldiers or retainers, or, what is more serious, relatives. Therefore, if henceforth any bishop is found to be a transgressor of this divine command, let him be reckoned among the greatest heretics and as no insignificant antichrist; and, as the Nicene synod ruled concerning simoniacs, both the bishop who gives and the laypersons who receive from him, whether for payment or favor, are to be consigned to the fires of eternal burning.

[Col. 0554C]

### C. XIV. He sells the Holy Spirit who grants tithes for money. Paschal II.

[Note: [Col. 0554D] Above, the same Question 1, chapter *Presbyter* [Col. 0553; and Alger, book 1, chapter 49], attributes this same statement to Gregory which is here attributed to Paschal II. Perhaps Paschal received this, as many other things, from Gregory VII, who himself renewed them. In Polycarpus, book 3, title 11, it is cited from the Council of Toledo.]

[Note: We think that this canon was drawn from the Council of Poitiers, held in the year 1100.]

No member of the faithful is ignorant that to give an altar and tithes for money, and to sell the Holy Spirit, is the Simoniacal heresy.

[Col. 0555A]

### C. XV. Let him forfeit the honor wickedly acquired who has attempted to obtain ecclesiastical benefices for money. Innocent II, in the Roman Synod, chapter 2.

[Note: Held in the year 1139. The same things are read in the Council of Reims, held in 1131.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 138: “from a council of the Roman see.”]

If anyone, through the abominable ardor of avarice, acquires for money prebends, a priory, a deanery, any ecclesiastical honor or promotion, or any ecclesiastical sacrament—for example chrism, holy oil, or the consecrations of altars or churches—let him forfeit the honor wickedly acquired. Buyer, seller, and intermediary are to be struck with the mark of infamy. Nothing at all is to be demanded from *anyone*, either before or afterward, whether for maintenance or under the pretext of any custom; nor may anyone presume to give it, since this is simoniacal. Rather, let him freely *and* without any diminution enjoy the dignity and benefice conferred upon him.

[Note: *utputa* (“for example”): corrected editions.]

[Note: “sanctified”: Basel edition.]

[Note: “acquired”: Basel edition; “he acquired”: the other editions, with the original; “he purchased”: Böhm.]

[Note: “Benefice”: in one of two manuscript copies of this council it is read thus; in the other, “office.”]

Gratian. What the sacred canons determine concerning the second and third questions has been made clear by authorities brought forward from both sides.

## QUESTION IV

## GRATIAN

### Part I
