We must now consider the fourth question: whether his father’s crime is imputed to this person, when it is established that it was committed without his knowledge. That ignorance excuses him is proved by many authorities.

For Augustine says in Letter XLVIII to Vincentius:

[Note: Letter 93, written in 408; Maurist edition.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 2, tome 50, chapters 31–32.]

### C. I. Another’s crime does not stain one who is unaware of it.

The crime of no one stains a person who does not know of it.

### II. On the same subject. The same, in the same letter.

[Note: Augustine’s words are: “What place is left for innocence, if it is itself a crime not to know another’s crime?”]

[Note: Letter 93, written in 408; Maurist edition.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 2, tome 50, chapters 31–32.]

What place is left for innocence if another’s crime stains one who does not know of it?

### C. III. Concerning children baptized by heretics. Likewise, it is read in the African Council, chapter 14.

[Note: Chapter 48 of the Third Council of Carthage, held in 397, in Isidore; chapter 14 in Dionysius.—Alger, book 3, chapter 27.]

It was decided concerning children baptized by heretics that, when they have been converted to the Church of God with a saving purpose, their parents’ error should not prevent them from being advanced to the ministry of the sacred altar, on account of something they did not do by their own judgment.

[Note: “And it was decided”: corrected editions, first Basel edition, Lyons II and III.]

[Note: “nor by their own”: corrected editions.]

[Note: “returned”: corrected editions; Alger.]

[Note: “ministry”: Basel edition and Alger; “to the ministry”: the other corrected editions.]

[Col. 0556A]

### C. IV. On the same subject. Likewise, in the same council, chapter 24.

[Note: From the Fifth Council of Carthage, held in 401, chapter 2. Its decrees survive complete in Dionysius and incomplete in Isidore.—Deusdedit, part 2; Alger, book 3, chapter 27.]

Those baptized as little children among the Donatists, not yet able to know the ruinous character of their error, and who afterward, upon reaching an age capable of reason, recognize the truth, abhor their falsehood, and are received by the ancient rite through imposition of hands into the Catholic Church of God spread throughout the whole world—such persons ought not to be prevented from undertaking the office of cleric on account of the name of error.

[Note: “their own”: corrected editions, first Basel edition.]

[Note: “have reached”: Basel edition; “come forth”: Lyons II; “arrive”: the other editions.]

[Note: “from the Church”: corrected editions.]

[Note: The words marked with asterisks are not found in Alger either.]

### C. V. The misdeeds of relatives do not harm clerics in any respect unless they were aware of them. Leo IV to Bishops Ebrunius and Adelfred.

[Note: Berardus conjectures that this letter of Leo IV was addressed to Erpuinus, bishop of Senlis, and Hermenfridus, bishop of Beauvais.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 1, tome 60, chapter 18.]

Because the ministry of our episcopal office, as you well know, must be concerned not only for the welfare of priests but also for that of secular persons, we wish your brotherhood to know that this priest before us has come to the apostolic see and has duly reported to us the violence done to him and his excommunication. He likewise stated that his church had been taken from him without a just process of law, and that another priest, having given a bribe and led by envious zeal, had presumed to usurp it. Thereupon his relatives, compelled by great grief, immediately seized the priest who held his church and tore out his eyes. Yet the oft-mentioned priest says that this was done without his will and without his counsel. If this is so, as he himself testified to us with his own mouth, you must take the greatest care that, if he was not canonically excommunicated, canonical remission be granted him.

[Note: “his”: corrected editions, first Basel edition.]

[Note: “to us”: Böhm.]

### C. VI. PALEA. In the Digest, title “On Punishments,” law *Crimen*.

[Note: Digest, book 48, title 19, fragment 26.—The Basel edition adds: “The Emperors Gratian and Theodosius Augustus.”]

A father’s crime or punishment can inflict no stain upon his son. For each person is subjected to his lot on account of his own act, and is not made heir to another’s crime. The divine brothers also so replied by rescript to the people of Hierapolis.

[Note: The corrected editions add “also.”]

### C. VII. The perfidy of parents ought not to harm their children. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 60.

[Note: Held in 633.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 1, tome 37, chapter 20.]

Baptized Jews, if afterward they become transgressors and are condemned to any punishment for offenses against Christ, ought not to have their faithful children excluded from their property, because it is written: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.”

[Note: The words “against Christ … condemned” are lacking in the Basel edition.]

[Note: Ezekiel 18.]

[Note: The corrected editions and first Argentinensis edition add: “and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son.”]

### C. VIII. The sins of parents are not imputed to those shown to be personally separated from them. Augustine to Boniface, Letter XXIII.

[Note: Letter 98, written about 408; Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 417.]

Therefore, once a human being exists in himself, having become distinct from the one who begot him, he is not held liable for another’s sin without his own consent. He did draw guilt because he was one with, and in, the one from whom he drew it, when the act from which he drew it was committed. But one person does not draw from another once each is living his own proper life, so that it may truly be said: “The soul that sins shall itself die.” But when one offered for consecration can be regenerated through the ministry of another’s will, the one Spirit by whom the offered person is regenerated accomplishes this.

[Note: “contracted”: corrected editions.]

[Note: The same editions read “so that it may truly.”]

[Note: Ezekiel 18:4.]

Hence Gregory also, in book XXVI of the *Morals*, chapter 8, on Job chapter 35:

### C. IX. Another’s impiety harms the person who imitates it.

“Your impiety will harm a man like yourself, and your righteousness will help a son of man.” Human impiety harms the person whom it stains by perverting him; conversely, our righteousness helps the person whom it changes from wicked deeds. For things that cannot corrupt a person from good or transform him from evil do not know how to harm or help.

[Note: Job 35:8.]

[Note: “defiles”: corrected editions.]

[Note: “changes”: the same editions.]

[Note: “help”: the same editions.]

Gratian. On the other hand, the Lord says to Moses: “I am a jealous God, visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation.” Yet Augustine maintains that this was said not from inequality of judgment but from greatness of mercy, as follows: “In the Law the Lord threatens that he will repay to children in the third and fourth generation the sin of their fathers, not by inequality of judgment, so that some sin and others are punished, but by greatness of mercy: since he always waits for repentance and does not correct and amend what is sinned in the first generation until the third and fourth generation has also come.”

Since Innocent writes concerning those baptized by heretics: “It is the law of the Church to grant only lay communion, through imposition of hands, to those baptized by heretics, and to appoint none of them even to the lowest honor of clerical office,” it is clear that children baptized by heretics are excused only by ignorance, so that, according to the African Council, the name of error does not prevent them from receiving clerical office.

[Note: Exodus 20:5.]

[Note: Above, Question 1, chapter 18.]

[Col. 0558A]

Likewise Augustine writes to Bishop Auxilius in Letter 75:

[Note: In several ancient copies, both this chapter and those following it to the end of the question are joined to the preceding chapter. For Gratian here adduces, almost in his own words—as he often does—statements drawn from various places. The substance of this part is indeed found in Augustine at the cited place. But the actual words are reported below, C. 24, q. 3, c. *Si habes*.]

[Note: Letter 250, Maurist edition.]

[Note: “Auxentius”: Böhm.]

### C. X. On the same subject.

The sins of parents committed after the birth of their children are not imputed to the children; nor are children to be punished with a spiritual penalty for their parents’ sins.

Gratian. But deprivation of an ecclesiastical office or benefice is a spiritual penalty; therefore a son does not deserve this penalty because of his father’s sin. Likewise, if one who is unknowingly ordained by a simoniac is excused, as is read above in Urban’s chapter, then he too is to be excused who is simoniacally ordained through ignorance.

### Part II

But the following statement of Gregory is objected:

[Note: “Gregory”: several ancient codices read “Augustine.” Anselm, however, cites it from Alexander II.]

[Note: In Anselm, book 5, chapter 20 [21], and Gerhoh of Reichersberg, in the treatise *On Simony* in Martène, tome V, these words are presented as from Alexander II: “A church which is clearly consecrated by bargain—or rather, to speak more truly, execrated—is by no means regarded as a church.”]

### C. XI. Concerning a church consecrated by bargain.

A church consecrated by bargain ought rather to be called execrated than consecrated.

Gratian. Likewise, the treasures of Jericho are read to have been anathematized because of the sin of its citizens. Hence Achan, who stole a gold bar and certain other precious objects, is said to have taken from what was under the anathema. § 1. Likewise, because of the sin of the Amalekites, their animals were ordered to be killed; because Saul spared them, he heard from Samuel: “Do you not know that to resist is the sin of divination, and that refusal to obey is like the crime of idolatry?” § 2. Likewise, because of the sin of the Egyptians, their possessions were given over to hail, and their cattle and firstborn were consumed by death. § 3. Likewise, because of the sin of the Israelites, the ark of the Lord was delivered to the Philistines.

Therefore, if insensible things—such as a church, an altar, the ark of the Lord, and the stones of Jericho—are either execrated, delivered to sinners, anathematized, or devastated by hail; if things without the power of understanding—such as the animals of Egypt and the Amalekites—perish by death on account of human sins: it is clear that ignorance of a crime excuses no one, especially when gain from it comes to the ignorant person. For example, if someone amasses wealth for his unsuspecting son by theft and robbery, the son’s ignorance does not excuse him from being compelled, after his father’s death, to restore what was wrongly acquired. § 4. Likewise, because of Achan’s sin, the people of Israel were delivered into the hands of enemies. § 5. Likewise, because of the sin of Eli’s sons, the people fell into the hand of the Philistines. § 6. Likewise, because of the people’s sin, their chosen ones were often hindered, and finally the prophets were taken captive with them.

[Note: Joshua 6.]

[Note: 1 Samuel 15:23.]

[Note: Exodus 9.]

[Note: 1 Samuel 4.]

[Note: Joshua 7.]

[Note: 1 Samuel 4.]

[Note: Psalm 77.]

### Part III

§ 7. The response to these arguments is this. Insensible and irrational things are execrated, anathematized, or destroyed by death because of human sin, not through participation in sin, but for the sake of sacramental signification, the detestation of sin, or the chastisement of offenders. They are so treated for the sake of sacramental signification, as in the case of the treasures of Jericho and the animals of the Amalekites. For Jericho is interpreted as “moon” and signifies this world. Amalekites is interpreted as “those who lick blood,” and they signify the covetous, the avaricious, and demons. Israelites is interpreted as “men seeing God,” and they signify the multitude of saints. Therefore the stones and treasures of Jericho are anathematized, and the animals of the Amalekites are ordered to be killed, in order to test the covetousness of the Israelite people and to signify that the walls of vices, the treasures of this world—represented by the stones and treasures of Jericho—and even the irrational impulses of vice, understood through the animals of the Amalekites, ought not to pass into the inheritance of the saints.

But the animals, possessions, and firstborn of the Egyptians were consumed by hail and death, so that those who rejoiced in their prosperity might be punished in them, and so that it might be understood that the world and its lust will perish. The land of the Israelites, too, was turned into salt marsh; adverse rains fell upon their crops, and their animals were destroyed by barrenness and disease, so that they might at least perceive amid punishments the author whom they had refused to know through benefits.

[Note: Psalm 106.]

But Simon’s money was condemned in detestation of sin, when it was said to him: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed for money.” Likewise, in detestation of the same crime, an altar and a church consecrated through simony are said not so much to be consecrated as execrated, because one who pours out the oil of consecration through the intervention of money must be said not to consecrate but to execrate. Thus Saint Gregory ordered churches consecrated by Arians to be consecrated again, because those lacking faith could not confer the sanctification of consecration, which is accomplished only in faith in the Trinity.

[Note: Acts 8:20.]

[Note: Distinction 1, *On Consecration*, chapter 21.]

But the ark and the prophets were delivered to enemies because of the sin of their fellow citizens. The chosen ones, too, hindered by the people’s murmuring, suffered these things not as punishment for sin but as a trial and example of patience.

§ 8. Likewise, the people delivered into the hands of enemies because of the sin of Achan and Eli’s sons signifies that subjects are corporally chastised so that, amid those very chastisements, the sins of prelates may be struck down, just as Achan, exposed by the lot, was crushed beneath stones.

§ 9. Likewise Jonah’s little ship is endangered, so that the fugitive, exposed by the lot, might be plunged into the waves. Sometimes the life of subjects is corrupted because of the merits of their prelates, so that subjects who favor their prelates in evil may fall together with them—just as the children of Israel, long bearing the sins of their priests, finally fell with them into the hands of enemies. Likewise David numbered the people, and because of this sin the sword of the Lord raged against the people. But “in a numerous people is a king’s glory; in the diminution of the people is a prince’s ruin.” Therefore he who took pride in the multitude of his people was justly punished by its diminution.

[Note: Jonah 1.]

[Note: 1 Samuel, final chapter.]

[Note: Proverbs 14:28.]

§ 10. Ignorance did not excuse the little children of the Sodomites from being consumed by heavenly fire because of their fathers’ crime. Yet by this fire their punishment was reduced, since succession in their fathers’ crime was taken away from them. It is likewise shown that children are sometimes corporally chastised for their parents’ sins. The same should be understood of the children who, because of the sin of Dathan and Abiram, went down alive into hell.

[Note: Genesis 19.]

[Note: Numbers 16.]

§ 11. When Ham sinned, his son Canaan was cursed; when Gehazi sinned, leprosy was transmitted to his descendants. When the Jews cried, “His blood be upon us and upon our children,” even their remnant was subjected to the punishment for Christ’s death. Likewise, when Ahab sinned, his descendants lost the throne of the kingdom; and those of his seed born in the kingdom of Judah were excluded from the genealogy of the Lord until the stain of that family was cleansed. Esau’s hatred also, as Malachi testifies, passed to the Edomites. From all these things it is concluded that ignorance of sin excuses no one.

[Note: Genesis 9.]

[Note: 4 Kings 5.]

[Note: Matthew 27:25.]

[Note: 3 Kings 21.]

[Note: Malachi 1.]

§ 12. But these examples do not prove that persons are bound by the sins of others except when they imitate their wickedness. For all who, from the seed of Esau and of the others, turned to God and detested their fathers’ evil experienced not hatred but God’s mercy.

Likewise, as Ambrose says in Sermon XI:

[Note: The substance of this chapter too is drawn from Ambrose’s Sermon 11 and book 5, chapter 1, of his commentary on Luke chapter 5. The actual words appear below, C. 24, q. 1, c. *Non turbatur*.]

[Note: Compare C. 24, q. 7, c. 7.]

### C. XII.

Peter’s little ship, in which Judas was, is troubled, because he who was firm by his own merits was troubled by another’s.

Gratian. Peter was unaware of Judas’s sin. Therefore ignorance did not excuse him; rather, this disturbance is understood not as contamination by sin but as bodily persecution, because the good are sometimes so heavily oppressed by the merits of the wicked that their firmness is shaken. Thus the simoniacs on whose behalf money was given without their knowledge are not proved guilty by these authorities. Therefore this man cannot be proved guilty of a crime of which he had no awareness.

### Part IV

§ 1. It must also be observed that not every kind of ignorance excuses someone. There is ignorance of fact and ignorance of law. Ignorance of fact is of one kind when it concerns something a person ought to know, and of another when it concerns something he ought not to know. Something he ought not to know is illustrated by the Apostle’s saying: “If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no question. But if someone tells you, ‘This has been sacrificed to idols,’ do not eat it.” Thus a person invited to dinner need not know that the meat placed before him has been sacrificed to idols. But something he ought to know is illustrated by the ignorance of the Jews and other unbelievers, who still do not know that the things foretold by the prophets concerning Christ have been fulfilled, whence the Jews still expect him to come. Such ignorance excuses no one.

[Note: 1 Corinthians 10:27.]

§ 2. Likewise, ignorance of law is either natural or civil. Ignorance of natural law is blameworthy in all adults; ignorance of civil law is permitted to some and not to others. Ignorance of civil law harms no one in avoiding loss if a transaction has thereby occurred; for example, if a minor gives money to a son under paternal power, he may recover it. But in the case of a person of full age, it is as though a delict.

§ 3. Likewise, if you, though of full age, divide with another without a judge an inheritance which has come to you, thinking the will legally valid when it was not, you will retain the entire inheritance. Or if you pay or promise, as though under a written acknowledgment of debt, something which you did not owe under any law, or which you did not owe by natural law but only by civil law, you may recover it; not so if it is a delict. For if he thinks it lawful under the law to seize his own property, he incurs that constitution of the Code, book VIII, under the title *Whence by Force*.

[Note: “Constitution”: most ancient codices read, “he incurs the constitution *If anyone has reached such a pitch …*” The rest is absent.]

[Col. 0561C]

### C. XIII. PALEA.

[Note: Title 4, chapter 7.—Absent from the Basel edition.]

[Emperor Valentinian Augustus.]

[Note: “Valerius”: corrected editions.]

“If anyone has reached such a pitch of frenzied audacity that, before the outcome of judicial decision, he violently seizes possession of property held by the treasury or by any persons whatsoever, then, if he is the owner, he shall restore to the possessor the possession which he took away and lose ownership of that property. But if he seized possession of another’s property, he shall not only restore it to the possessors, but shall also be compelled to repay the value of the same property.”

[Note: “arrival”: original.]

[Note: “of the same”: there.]

Gratian. But in this case there was ignorance not of law but of fact, and of a fact which he ought not to have known. Therefore ignorance excuses him from liability for the crime of his father’s offense—a fact which, even if he ought to have known it, he could not discover because of the weakness of his age.

## QUESTION V

[Col. 0562A]

## GRATIAN

### Part I

The fifth question, then, is whether one whose father’s money obtained it may lawfully remain in the church or exercise the ordination. Urban’s authority determines the matter. Writing concerning simoniacs, he says among other things in the Council of Piacenza, chapter 5 and following, and likewise in the Roman Council:

[Note: Held in 1095.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 109.]

### C. I. Concerning children who purchase churches through their parents’ covetousness.

All who, through the covetousness of their parents, while still children, obtained churches or parts of churches by money, after they have entirely relinquished them, are permitted by us, out of great mercy, to remain there if they wish to live canonically in them; and we do not remove them from sacred orders because of this act, if they are otherwise found worthy.

§ 1. But those who, on their own account, once they were already of mature age, purchased them under the prompting of wicked covetousness, are permitted, if they wish to live canonically in other churches, to minister there in their own orders, out of great mercy. But if perhaps they cannot be transferred to other churches and promise to live canonically in them, let them be content with lower orders and not proceed to sacred orders, while the authority of the apostolic see is in every respect preserved.

§ 2. If any were canonically ordained before the purchase, after relinquishing what they purchased and living a canonical life, let them remain in their ranks—unless perhaps the church is such that they would be bound to hold first place there. For we do not permit them to hold in purchased churches the first, sole, provost’s, or official’s position.

[Note: “Parts”: the council itself reads “benefices,” but it has not been corrected because of the gloss.]

[Note: The Basel edition adds “churches.”]

[Note: The corrected editions add “them.”]

[Note: “have purchased”: Basel edition.]

[Note: The same edition adds “churches.”]

[Note: “Provost’s”: the council adds, “or official’s.”]

### Part II

Gratian. That he said this not to the prejudice of the canons, but as a dispensation of mercy, is gathered from a letter of the same author sent to Vitalis, a priest:

[Note: In a manuscript book of papal decrees this canon is cited as from Nicholas to Vitalis, priest of Pruvia.]

[Note: Fragment of the letter to Vitalis, priest of Brescia, which Baluzius testified that he had found entire in the Rivipullensis codex.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 2, tome 50, chapter 24.]

### C. II. Mercy may be extended to simoniacs in preserving their rank if their life commends them.

Those who have purchased a church, if they are persons whose life commends them—namely, if they live regularly in communities of canons or monasteries—we allow, yielding mercifully, to minister in the office of their rank, but without prejudice to the holy canons.

[Col. 0562D]

### Part III

Gratian. From this authority it is therefore gathered that ignorance excuses such persons from liability for the crime, as stated above, but not from the benefit of the purchase. For they are permitted to remain in churches obtained by their parents’ money only after they have entirely relinquished them, and then only through mercy. This makes clear that, although the sin of simony was committed without their knowledge, they cannot receive the benefit of their fathers’ purchase. That they are excused from the crime is clear from this: they are not removed from sacred orders because of that act. For if they were participants, they could not ascend to sacred orders. The same must be understood of one who obtained priestly rank by money paid not to the bishop but to one of his leading men, both ordainer and ordained being unaware of it.

Urban II therefore writes to Albert, Bishop of Metz:

[Note: Although this letter may seem to be Urban II’s, its address is erroneous. For Adalbero, whom the emperor intruded into the churches of Metz, Toul, and Verdun, was rejected by the people of Metz; after this they canonically elected Poppo, who was consecrated by Gebehard, bishop of Constance—as Berthold testifies in his Chronicle for 1093—or by Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, as Hugh of Flavigny reports.]

[Col. 0563B]

### C. III. Concerning one for whom his parents, through negligence, paid money not to the bishop but to one of his leading men.

You have stated that the bearer of this letter obtained priestly rank unwillingly, because of his parents’ negligence, through money paid not to the bishop but to one of his leading men. Although the holy canons declare that he ought to be deposed, nevertheless, because he committed this fault unknowingly and under compulsion, and because he voluntarily asked to be deposed from that order, we advise your brotherhood, applying the bowels of mercy, that he remain in the same order, on grounds of prudent discernment—discernment being the mother of all virtues—rather than by the rigor of the canons. Yet if the church in which he serves does not suffer from a shortage of priests, let him remain suspended from priestly office. But if the church’s usefulness perhaps requires that he undertake the care of governance, he may, by permission of his bishop and obedience to the brethren, exercise priestly office.

[Note: “and unwillingly”: corrected editions, first Basel edition.]

[Note: The Basel edition adds “discernment.”]

[Note: “suffers”: there.]

### QUESTION VI

## GRATIAN

What ought to be done concerning those unknowingly ordained by simoniacs—the sixth question—should be sought above, namely in Urban’s chapter beginning, “If any from simoniacs,” etc.

[Note: Above, Question 1, chapter 108.]

But now the question concerns those who offer money not for ordination but for election: who distribute rewards in order that a decree of election may be issued, ratified by subscription, or not resisted. Is their election to be judged defective? For they do not seem to buy the gift of the Holy Spirit who give gifts not for consecration but for election, since an election makes no one a participant in any spiritual grace. Yet just as purchasers of ecclesiastical property are judged simoniacs, because it is so joined to ecclesiastical office that neither can accrue to anyone without the other, so too, since consecration is attained through election, one who gives rewards for an election is deemed a simoniac just as though he had given gifts for consecration.

Symmachus therefore writes to Bishop Caesarius, Letter I, chapter 5:

[Note: Written in 502. Anselm, book 6, chapter 69 [74]. Polycarpus, book 2, title 1.]

### C. I. Concerning those who procure ordination by gifts.

If anyone desires the episcopate, he must not employ powerful persons as advocates for himself by giving money; he must not compel clerics or citizens, by fear of any kind, to issue a decree for him or to subscribe to it; nor must he induce them by any rewards.

[Note: The corrected editions add “for himself.”]

[Note: “to subscribe”: *Collectio Hispana*; Anselm.]

### C. II. A person who distributes rewards in order to be elected is a simoniac. Gregory to those resident at Salona, book V, Letter 26.

[Note: Letter 26, written in 596, book 6 of the Maurist edition. Polycarpus, book 2, title 3.]

But I, having regard both for your beloved selves and, in fear of Almighty God’s judgment, for my own soul, wish Maximus’s case to be carefully investigated: whether, burdened by none of the crimes which bar one from sacred order, he is striving to attain the priestly office not through the Simoniacal heresy—that is, by offering rewards to certain persons who elect him. For only then will he come to the place of intercession as a free intercessor for you before the Lord, if he has not come there bound by his own deeds.

[Note: “cases”: original; corrected editions.]

[Note: “among them”: Basel edition.]

[Note: “for us”: there.]

### C. III. As ordination, so election or consent must be preferred without venality. Gregory to Syagrius, Bishop of Autun, and other bishops, book VII, Letter 110.

[Note: Letter 106, written in 599, book 9 of the Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 79 [77]. Polycarpus, book 2, title 1.]

Just as the person who refuses when invited and flees when sought should be brought to the sacred altars, so he who seeks office unprompted or thrusts himself forward importunately must undoubtedly be rejected. For one who thus strives to climb to higher things does what else but diminish by rising, and by ascending outwardly descend inwardly to the depths? Therefore, dearest brothers, let sincerity prevail in ordaining priests; let consent be simple and free from venality; let election be preferred in purity, so that advancement to the highest priesthood may be believed to proceed not from the support of sellers but from God’s judgment.

[Note: The corrected editions read “anything else.”]

[Note: “into the depths”: Basel and Lyons editions; “in the depths”: the other editions.]

[Note: “dearest brother”: corrected editions.]

[Note: “and without”: the same editions.]

[Note: “Highest things”: printed codices read “to the highest of priesthood or pontificate.” This passage has been corrected from the original, Anselm, Polycarpus, and most ancient copies of Gratian.]

[Note: “highest”: original and Basel edition; “highest point”: other editions.]

[Note: Chapter 9 of the Council of Neocaesarea; compare C. 15, q. 8, c. 1.]

[Col. 0565A]

Gratian. But if money was promised or paid while the person elected or ordained was wholly unaware of it, and he did not attain election or ordination by that means, it seems in no way to harm him. It pertains neither to liability for a crime of which he had no awareness nor to annulment of the election or ordination, which he is otherwise shown to have attained not through their depraved greed.

## QUESTION VII

## GRATIAN

### Part I

We must now treat the seventh question: whether one renouncing his heresy is to be received in episcopal rank.

Cyprian writes concerning these matters in book II, Letter 1:

[Note: Written in 256.—Anselm, book 8, chapter 39.]

### C. I. Those returning from heresy are to be received in their orders.

If any priests or deacons, previously ordained in the Catholic Church, afterward stood as faithless and rebellious persons against the Church; or if, among heretics, they were promoted by pseudo-bishops and antichrists through a profane ordination contrary to Christ’s ordinance, and attempted outside the Church to offer false and sacrilegious sacrifices against the one divine altar: when they return, they ought to be received on this condition also, that they communicate as laypersons and consider it enough that they are admitted to peace, having been enemies of peace. Nor ought they, on returning, retain among us the weapons of ordination and honor by which they rebelled against us.

[Note: “were”: Anselm; corrected editions.]

[Note: “and indivisible”: Cyprian manuscripts; “and the divine word”: corrected editions.]

[Note: “It is fitting”: the original does not contain this word. Instead it has before this chapter: “Moreover, dearest brother, we add and join, by common consent and authority, that if any priests,” etc. Much in this chapter has also been corrected from Saint Cyprian himself.]

[Note: “as laypersons”: the same editions.]

[Note: “were,” and at the end, “rebelled”: the same editions.]

## C. II. Concerning those who confer ordination for gifts, and those who, returning from heresy, are received in their orders. Likewise from the Seventh Synod.

If [Note: [Col. 0565] these are words of Basil in the first session of the Second Council of Nicaea, held A.D. 787. — Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, ch. 198. Deusdedit, part 2.] anyone [Note: [Col. 0565D] *If anyone*: This chapter has for the most part been compiled from various passages of the Seventh Synod, but not from the translation of Anastasius the Librarian, although Gratian often otherwise uses it. Its beginning is indeed in Session 1, Anathema 7.] violates every written or unwritten ecclesiastical tradition [Col. 0566A], let him be anathema.

§ 1. Every [Note: [Col. 0565] from the letter of Tarasius to John, priest and anchorite, written in that same year. — Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 87. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 121, come closer to the words of Anastasius the translator.] bishop [Note: [Col. 0565D] *Every bishop*: From here as far as the words “Tarasius the patriarch” the material is taken from the letter of Tarasius to John the priest [Col. 0566C]—though at times some words are omitted. This letter occurs in Anastasius’s translation after the acts and canons of the Seventh Synod; but in the new translation printed in the volumes of councils it stands before the synod itself.] or priest or deacon who is convicted of having given or received ordination for gifts shall fall from the priesthood.

§ 2. But perhaps some say: “We do penance for sin, and God forgives it.” I too say that God accepts every repentance and through repentance forgives sins already committed. For I know that God received David, an adulterer and murderer, through repentance, and said concerning [Note: [Col. 0565] Acts 13:22.] him: “I have found a man after my own heart, *who will do all my wills*.” Again, I know that the same man heard from God [Note: [Col. 0565] 1 Chronicles 22:8.]: “You shall not build me a house, because you are a man of blood.” I know that Manasseh [Note: [Col. 0565] 2 Chronicles 33.] had his impiety forgiven through confession. I know that prostitutes [Note: [Col. 0565] Matthew 21.] and tax-collectors were received through repentance [Col. 0566B]; yet I know none of those who sinned before baptism [Note: [Col. 0566D] *Before baptism*: There is plainly an error here which troubled the author of the gloss: Οὐδένα δὲ τούτων εἰς ἱερωσύνην ἀριθμηθέντα, εἰ μήπω πρὸ τοῦ βαπτίσματος τοῦτο πεπράχεν, that is: “Yet none of these was numbered among the priesthood, unless perhaps he committed this before baptism.”] to have been numbered among the priests.

I know that some, while they were in the world, remained in much fornication, but after becoming monks shone like lights of the world; yet none ascended to the priesthood. Even if this occurred rarely [Note: [Col. 0566D] *Even if rarely*: Much more fully in the new translation: “But if this has happened once or twice, it nevertheless does not at once prescribe a law in the Church.” The Greek is: Εἰ δὲ καὶ σπανίως γέγονε, οὐ νόμος ἐκκλησίας τοῦτο.], it was nevertheless no law of the Church. We know Mary, previously a sinner [Note: [Col. 0565] “first”: Basel edition.]; after her conversion, although holy and chaste, she was nevertheless not numbered among deaconesses.

But why do I say this [Note: [Col. 0566] “here”: Basel edition.]? Following the holy apostles and venerable Fathers, I proclaim with complete confidence [Note: [Col. 0565] Apostolic Canon 28.]: Whoever has been ordained through simony, whether bishop, priest, or deacon, is excluded from the priesthood. For the grace of the Holy Spirit is not for sale [Col. 0566C]; the tradition of Caiaphas [Note: [Col. 0565] John 11.] and Simon’s invention [Note: [Col. 0565] Acts 8.] are alien to the holy priesthood.

§ 3. And [Note: [Col. 0565] Apostolic Canons 16 and 24.] if anyone falls into fornication after baptism, he is not admitted to the priesthood; for the canons forbid this. But if anyone has advanced to the priesthood while guilty of this sin, once discovered he shall be deposed.

Likewise, shortly afterward:

§ 4. I confess that a bishop ordained through money is received through repentance [Col. 0567A] [Note: [Col. 0567] “God receives”: editions of Argentoratum, Basel, and Nuremberg.]. For God is good to all, and his compassion is open to every person [Note: [Col. 0567] absent from the Basel edition.] who repents. But since, according to the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0567] 1 Timothy 3.], a bishop must be blameless, whoever either has ordained someone through money or has himself been ordained through money shall be excluded from every priestly office.

§ 5. Tarasius [Note: [Col. 0567C] *Tarasius*: These appear to be taken from Tarasius’s letter to Hadrian—mentioned above, question 1, at the chapter “Those who”—or from chapter 5 of the Seventh Synod, where Apostolic Canon 30 is cited.] the patriarch [Note: [Col. 0567] from Tarasius’s letter to Hadrian; cf. ch. 21, Causa 1, question 1; and ch. 5, Second Council of Nicaea.] said: Whoever, for money, ordains, has ordained [Note: [Col. 0567] added: “or are ordained”: editions of Argentoratum and Basel.], or has been ordained as a bishop, priest, deacon, or any other member of the priestly rank [Note: [Col. 0567] “of priests”: Basel edition.], through money, shall be wholly expelled from priestly [Note: [Col. 0567] “from the priesthood”: ibid.] honor, as Simon Magus was by Peter.

Whoever has obtained, through money [Note: [Col. 0567C] *If, however, a religious*: These words are not in the Apostolic Canon [Col. 0567D].] [Note: [Col. 0567] cf. Council of Chalcedon, ch. 2; Novella 123, ch. 24.], administration or charge of monasteries, churches, religious houses, homes for the aged (*gerontocomia*) [Note: [Col. 0567] “homes for the sick”: Basel edition; “homes for the holy”: the remaining early editions of Lyons.], hostels for strangers, or orphanages, shall be expelled from that administration and charge together with deposition.

He who, after baptism, having fallen into fornication, is ordained, shall cease from ministry if he afterward confesses it; but if convicted by someone else, he shall be wholly deposed. [Note: [Col. 0567] Council of Neocaesarea, canon 9.]

§ 6. Likewise [Note: [Col. 0567] Apostolic Canon 28; the word “likewise” is absent from the Basel edition.], a bishop, priest, or deacon who strikes someone, whether personally or through another person, as though wishing by this to inspire fear, shall be deposed.

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0567] Second Council of Nicaea, canon 3, from Apostolic Canon 31; cf. ch. 7, Distinction 63.]:

§ 7. Whoever has been ordained or has obtained a church through secular powers shall be deposed; but if he has obtained a religious [Note: [Col. 0567C] *If, however, a religious*: These words are not in the Apostolic Canon [Col. 0567D].] house, he shall be expelled.

## C. III. On the same matter. PALEA. [Likewise from the Council of Meaux, ch. 43] [Note: [Col. 0567] held A.D. 845. — Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 21. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 75.]

“It must be guarded against and most diligently prevented, and through the power of Christ’s blood forbidden, both to bishops and kings, to all higher powers [Col. 0567C], and to all supporters and electors whatsoever, and to all consenting parties and ordainers in ecclesiastical rank, that no one obtain a position of *government* through the heresy of simony, by any [Col. 0568A] intrigue [Note: [Col. 0567] “favor”: Ivo; “function”: the other collected editions.], cunning, promise, advantage, or gift, either personally or through a subordinate [Note: [Col. 0567] “a person sent out”: the original, Burchard, Basel edition, and C. IV.] person.”

## C. IV. Whether those returning from heretics may be received or not. Likewise in the same Seventh Synod, Session 1. [Note: [Col. 0567D] This chapter too has been compiled from various passages of the first session of the same Seventh Synod; it is altogether worth the trouble to read that entire session. Some points, however, will be noted.] [Note: [Col. 0567] held A.D. 787.]

### Part II

When they had assembled at Nicaea in Bithynia, and Peter the archpriest [Note: [Col. 0567] “archbishop”: the other collected editions.] and Peter, priest and abbot of the monastery of Saint Sabas, representatives of Pope Hadrian, were seated with Tarasius, archbishop of Constantinople, John and Thomas, apocrisiaries of the apostolic eastern sees, and the other bishops, the bishops of Sicily said: “It is fitting [Note: [Col. 0567D] *It is fitting*: This passage occurs after the reading of the names of the bishops who had assembled; but it is reported very briefly, as also happens elsewhere in this chapter.] that we inquire concerning the future.”

§ 1. Likewise Basil, bishop of Ancyra, said: The ecclesiastical ordinance [Note: [Col. 0567D] *Ordinance*: The words immediately preceding this part are: Ἀπὸ λιβέλλου ἀνέγνω οὕτως, that is, as Anastasius translates it, “he read thus from a written statement.” Basil is not now delivering an opinion, but abjuring the heresy into which he had fallen with others. He had to recite this abjuration together with a profession of the Catholic faith from a written statement, as is even now customary. This statement begins: “The ecclesiastical ordinance,” etc.] handed down canonically from ancient times by the holy apostles and their successors, our holy Fathers [Col. 0568B] and teachers, by the holy six universal synods and the orthodox local synods, is that those who return from any heresy to the orthodox faith and the tradition of the Catholic Church must in writing renounce their heresy and confess the Catholic faith.

§ 2. Likewise Tarasius the patriarch said: “Does it seem right to you that those returning from heresy should receive their sees?”

§ 3. The most devout monks said: “As the six universal synods received those returning from heresy, so we too receive them.” [Note: [Col. 0567] “we received”: Basel edition.]

§ 4. The holy synod said: “It pleases us all.” And Basil, bishop of Ancyra, Theodore, bishop of the city of Myra [Note: [Col. 0567] “Emira”: Basel edition; “Mirea”: the remaining editions.], and Theodosius, bishop of *Amorium*, were commanded to sit [Col. 0568C] in their ranks and their seats.

§ 5. Likewise Constantine [Note: [Col. 0568C] *Constantine*: After the reception of Basil, Theodore, and Theodosius, other bishops came forward who had fallen into the same heresy and requested that they too be admitted by the holy synod. When one of them excused himself by saying that he had been led astray by evil teachers, Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, reproached him with these words. The Greek reproach is: Ἔδει ὑμᾶς ἐπισκόπους ὄντας μὴ διδασκαλίας δεῖσθαι, ἀλλὰ διδασκάλους εἷναι ἑτέρων, which Anastasius translates thus: “You ought, since you were bishops, to have no need of instruction, but rather to be teachers of others.”] bishop of Cyprus said: “It is not fitting that we who are bishops should need instruction; we should be teachers of others.”

§ 6. Likewise Tarasius the bishop said: “The doctrine [Col. 0569A] [Note: [Col. 0569C] *Evil*: When Hypatius and other bishops, who were requesting admission by the holy synod, said that they had received evil teachings from evil teachers, Tarasius the patriarch answered them: Ἐπειδήπερ εἴπατε, κακῶν διδασκάλων κακὰ τὰ μαθήματα, ἡ ἐκκλησία ἐκ κακῶν διδασκάλων ἱερεῖς δέχεσθαι οὐ προστίεται. That is: “Since you have said, ‘Evil teachings come from evil teachers,’ the Church is not readily induced to admit priests who come from evil teachers.” From this it is apparent [Col. 0569D] that Tarasius does not contradict Constantine, as the author of the gloss thought.] of evil teachers is evil. The Church has not received priests from evil teachers.”

§ 7. Likewise John [Note: [Col. 0569D] *Likewise John*: After Tarasius’s words had been read, the synod debated whether these men too ought immediately to be received, as the first three had been. John, apocrisiary of the patriarch of Antioch, and Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, asked that the pertinent canons and books of the holy Fathers be read, so that it might be settled more carefully how those returning from heresy to the Catholic Church should be received. While Canon 8 of the First Council of Nicaea, concerning the reception of Cathari, was under discussion, John made this intervention.] the apocrisiary of the eastern sees said: “Heresy separates every human being from the Church.”

§ 8. Likewise Tarasius the bishop said: “Behold, many canonical, synodal, and patristic books have been read; they have taught us to receive those returning from heresy, if there is no other cause [Note: [Col. 0569D] *If there is no other cause*: The Greek is: Καὶ ἐάν τις αἰτία πονηρὰ οὔκ ἐστιν ἐν αὐτοῖς, which Anastasius translates: “unless perhaps some harmful fault is found in them”; and shortly afterward: “if there is no wicked cause in them.”] in them.”

§ 9. Likewise Peter [Note: [Col. 0570C] *Peter*: After many canons had been read and many authorities of the holy Fathers cited, Tarasius concluded from them that those returning from heresy ought to be received in the Catholic Church. Peter, Hadrian’s legate, confirms this by the example of Pope Benedict.] the Pope’s apocrisiary said: “At Rome the heretic Macarius was exiled by the holy Sixth Synod; our father Pope Benedict gave him a period of forty days, and every day sent his adviser Boniface to him, instructing him with admonitory words from divine Scripture. But he was entirely unwilling to be corrected. This was done [Note: [Col. 0569] “was being done”: Basel edition.] so that the pope might receive him [Col. 0569B] in his rank.”

§ 10. Likewise Tarasius the bishop [Note: [Col. 0569] “patriarch”: the other collected editions.] said: “What do you say about Anatolius? Did he not become a leader even in the Fourth Synod? Yet behold, he was ordained by Dioscorus himself. Therefore let us likewise [Note: [Col. 0569] absent from the Basel edition.] receive those ordained by heretics, as Anatolius was received.”

§ 11. Likewise: “It is truly the voice of God [Note: [Col. 0569] Ezekiel 18.] that sons do not die for their fathers, but each person shall die [Note: [Col. 0569] “dies”: editions of Argentoratum and Basel.] in his own sin”; *let this be added*: “for ordination is from God.”

§ 12. Likewise Tarasius the patriarch said: “We have heard the commands of the Fathers. What then? Must we receive those ordained by heretics?”

§ 13. The holy synod said: “We have heard, lord, and we must receive them.”

§ 14. Tarasius the patriarch said: “Many of those who gathered in the Sixth Synod were ordained [Col. 0569C] by Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter, leaders of the heresy of the Monothelites [Note: [Col. 0569] “Monozelites”: editions of Argentoratum, Venice, and Nuremberg; “Monoscelites”: the remaining editions.], because these sat successively in the see of Constantinople. From the last of them, namely Peter, to the Sixth [Note: [Col. 0570D] *To the Sixth*: The Greek is: Ἕως τῆς ἕκτης συνόδου ἔτη πλέον οὐ διῆλθον ἢ δεκαπέντε, that is: “No more than fifteen years elapsed before the Sixth Synod.”] Synod, no more than twelve years elapsed. Yet Thomas, John, and Constantine were made archbishops by those heretics [Col. 0570A], and were nevertheless not rejected for that reason.”

§ 15. The holy synod said: “This is clear.”

§ 16. Constantine, bishop of Cyprus, said: “It has been sufficiently shown that those coming from heretics must be received. But if anyone voluntarily goes to a heretic and receives ordination, he shall not be received.”

§ 17. Likewise Tarasius the patriarch said: “I too reject those who for such a reason were ordained for the overthrow of the faith—especially when orthodox bishops were present, from whom they could have been ordained. Such is [Note: [Col. 0569] “and”: Basel edition.] indeed the understanding of the Fathers. But if there has been synodal [Note: [Col. 0570D] *But if synodal*: The Greek reads: Ἐὰν δὲ συνοδικὴ ἐκφώνησις γένηται καὶ ὀμόνοια τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν ἐπ᾽ ὀρθοδοξίᾳ, ὁ τολμῶν ἀπὸ τῶν βεβήλων αἱρετικῶν χειροτονεῖσθαι τῇ καθαιρέσει ὑποπεσεῖται, which Anastasius translates: “But if a synodal proclamation and agreement of the churches has been made for the sake of orthodoxy, whoever presumes to be ordained by profane heretics shall incur deposition.”] agreement and unity of the churches concerning orthodoxy, those who presume to be ordained by impure heretics shall be subject to deposition.” The holy synod [Col. 0570B] said: “This is a just judgment.”

### Part III. Gratian

From this authority it is understood that one who has passed from the unity of the Catholic faith into the society of heretics in order to receive from their hands the sacraments of ecclesiastical dignity, or who, despising orthodox bishops, has desired to be ordained by heretics, cannot exercise the office he has received, even if he afterward renounces his heresy and returns to the Church.

By Cyprian’s authority [Note: [Col. 0569] above, ch. 1.], however, those who, ordained within the Catholic Church, fall away to attack the faith are forbidden ecclesiastical administration. Simoniacs, moreover, are not ordained by heretics for the subversion of the faith, nor, when ordained within the Catholic Church, do they take up arms against the faith. Although they ordain some persons for money, they do not attack the faith [Col. 0570C] or proclaim the grace of the Holy Spirit saleable. Therefore, when through true repentance they have repudiated their heresy, the authorities set forth above do not forbid their reception in their ranks.

Nevertheless, by that chapter of the Nicene Synod [Note: [Col. 0569] above, question 1, ch. 9, and the same question, ch. 7, ch. 2.], “If anyone through money,” etc.; by that other chapter of the Seventh [Col. 0571A] Synod, “If anyone violates every tradition,” etc.; and by the authorities of Innocent [Note: [Col. 0571] above, question 1, ch. 73.] and many others, they are commanded to be condemned irreparably.

Accordingly Leo IV also wrote to the bishops of Britain [Note: [Col. 0571C] A large part of this letter of Leo IV to the bishops of Britain, including this chapter, is found in a very ancient manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0571] written A.D. 850. — Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 115.]:

## C. V. Simoniacs cannot perform penance in an improperly acquired order.

You ask concerning those who do not fear to sell doves in the temple of the Lord for shameful gain, and who join their deeds [Note: [Col. 0571] “actions”: original, Ivo, and the other collected editions.] to the heresy of Simon through wicked recklessness: whether they can perform penance while remaining in their order, or only outside their order and priestly [Note: [Col. 0571] absent from the Basel edition.] rank.

We can offer no remedy of penance to those convicted and known to have committed so detestable a crime—already condemned by many councils—nor can we oppose so many spiritual [Col. 0571B] Fathers. Let it be certain that I agree with all those Fathers in their judgment.

### Part IV. Gratian

Unless at times the rigor of discipline is relaxed through a dispensation of mercy. For many crimes are condemnable which the Church nevertheless tolerates, according to time, person, consideration of piety, necessity, or utility, and the outcome of the matter.

According to time: as Gelasius, when through the incursions of war and famine he saw that the Italian Church was deprived of the service of nearly all its clerics, so that many peoples lacked help for the government of souls, permitted clerics to be taken from monks or laymen. Thus he said to the bishops throughout Lucania, Letter I, chapter 1 [Note: [Col. 0571] written A.D. 494. — Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 75. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, ch. 141. Polycarpus, bk. 7, title 15. Alger, bk. 1, ch. 10.]:

[Col. 0571C]

## C. VI. By the necessity of the times, decrees of the Apostolic See are moderated.

We are constrained by the necessary dispensation [Note: [Col. 0571] “arrangement”: Hispana Collection; Anselm, Ivo, Alger.] of affairs, and are bound by the governance of the Apostolic See to weigh the decrees of the canons of the Fathers and measure the commands of our predecessors and former bishops in such a way that, with careful consideration, we temper—so far as possible—those things which the necessity of present times requires to be relaxed in restoring churches.

[Col. 0572A] Gratian. Likewise: “Therefore, in ancient times,” etc. [See above in the treatise on those to be ordained.]

Likewise Pope Innocent, when, because of the necessity of the times and to prevent excessive scandal in the Church, he received those ordained by the heretic Bonosus, says in his decrees, Letter XXII to the bishops of Macedonia, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 0571] written A.D. 414. — cf. above, question 1, ch. 41. Alger, bk. 1, ch. 9.]:

## C. VII. When the necessity ceases, that which it compelled ought also to cease.

What has been established as a remedy because of the necessity of the times is plainly not original. And below: Therefore, what necessity has devised as a remedy must certainly cease when the necessity has ceased, together with that which compelled it, because one thing [Note: [Col. 0571C] *Because one thing*: In the original, in Ivo, and in many manuscripts of Gratian, the reading is: “one thing is [Col. 0571D] the lawful order; another, the usurpation which the present time compels to be done.”] is the lawful order, another that which usurpation compels to be done for the present time.

Gratian. Likewise, by dispensation the Nicene [Col. 0572B] Council, canon 8 [Note: [Col. 0571] held A.D. 325.], decreed concerning the Novatians that those returning to the Church should be ordained:

## C. VIII. Those who return from the Novatians to the Church shall be ordained again.

If any from the Novatians wish to come to the Catholic *and [Note: [Col. 0571] the words “and apostolic” are not found in Isidore. They do occur, however, in Dionysius’s translation.] apostolic* Church, the holy council decreed that they should be ordained [Note: [Col. 0571D] *That they should be ordained*: The Greek is: Ὥστε χειροθετουμένους αὐτοὺς μένειν οὕτως ἐν τῷ κλήρῳ, which Dionysius translates: “so that, receiving the laying on of hands, they may thus remain in the clergy.” But Tarasius, patriarch [Col. 0572C] of Constantinople, in Session 1 of the Seventh Synod, after this canon had been read, interprets the word χειροθεσία as “blessing,” not “ordination.”] and thus remain in the clergy. But before all else, a written confession must be required of them: that they confess themselves bound to observe, with the common consent of the Catholic *and [Note: [Col. 0571] cf. preceding note.] apostolic* Church, its decrees.

## C. IX. Oath of those returning from schism. Likewise Gregory, *Register*, book X, letter 31. [Note: [Col. 0571] This oath seems to have been made in A.D. 602 by Bishop Firminus, to whom Letter 33 is addressed; ch. 12 in the Mansian edition. — Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 161 (158). Polycarpus, ch. 7, bk. 6.]

Whenever the eye of the heart, covered by the cloud of error, is made clear by the light of heavenly illumination, one must take great care lest the author of schism secretly attack and again cut away from the root of unity by the weapon of error those who had returned [Note: [Col. 0571] “have returned”: editions of Basel and Lyons II and III.] to it.

And therefore, after I, [Note: [Col. 0571] Here and below, for the word *ille* (“that same”), N is printed in editions corrected from the original.] that same [Note: [Col. 0572D] *I, that same*: The old designation *ille* has been restored from printed and manuscript copies of the letters of Blessed Gregory; this designation recurs many times in this chapter. In the commonly printed copies of Gratian, N stood in its place. Some other readings that differed little from the original were judged not worth changing.] [Note: [Col. 0571] “such”: Basel edition.] bishop of that city, learned of the snare of division by which I was held, and after long reflection [Note: [Col. 0571] “deliberation”: the other collected editions.], have, by humble and spontaneous will and with divine grace as guide, returned to the unity of the Apostolic See; and lest I be thought to have returned with an insincere rather than a genuine mind [Note: [Col. 0571] “insincerely”: original, Anselm, and the other collected editions, except the first Paris and Lyons editions.], I pledge and promise, under penalty of loss [Col. 0573A] of my order and the bond of anathema, to you, and through you to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and to his vicar, the most blessed Gregory, or his successors, that I shall never, by anyone’s persuasion or by any other means, return to the schism from which, through the merciful deliverance of our Redeemer [Note: [Col. 0573] “grace”: Anselm and the other collected editions.], I have been rescued; but that I shall always remain in every respect in the unity of the holy Catholic Church and the communion of the Roman Pontiff [Note: [Col. 0573] “to remain”: Anselm.].

Therefore, swearing [Note: [Col. 0573] “having sworn”: the other collected editions.] by almighty God, these holy four Gospels which I hold in my hands, and the welfare [Note: [Col. 0573] “the welfare of the peoples and of the illustrious lords”: corrected from Anselm; “the welfare and genius of that man and of the lords”: Anselm, newly collated; “the welfare and genius of the illustrious lords”: original.] of our lords governing the commonwealth, I declare that I shall always and without hesitation remain, as I have said, in the unity of the *Catholic* Church and [Note: [Col. 0573] added: “to which, God being favorable, I have returned”: the other collected editions, from the original and Anselm.] communion of the Roman Pontiff.

If, God forbid, I separate myself from this unity by any excuse or pretext, may I, having incurred the guilt of perjury, be found bound to eternal punishment and have my portion in the world to come with the author of schism.

I dictated for writing this little document of my profession [Note: [Col. 0573] “confession”: original and Basel edition.] and promise to that notary [Note: [Col. 0573] “my notary”: original, Anselm, and the other collected editions.], with the consent of the priests, deacons, and clerics who, binding themselves with me in this unity in [Note: [Col. 0573] “themselves”—with “also” added in the Basel edition—in place of “in the aforesaid”: the other collected editions.] all the aforesaid matters, have followed with equally humble [Note: [Col. 0573] “likewise”: the same editions.] will and are to subscribe with their own hands [Note: [Col. 0573] “subscribed”: Basel edition.]. I subscribed it with my own hand and delivered it to you. Done in that place, on that day, under the aforesaid consuls.

Subscription [Note: [Col. 0573] absent from Anselm and the other collected editions except the first editions of Argentoratum and Basel; it appears to be a rubric.] of that bishop: “I, that same bishop of that city, have subscribed to this confession and promise of mine, after taking an oath to preserve all the aforesaid [Col. 0573C] matters.”

Gratian. Yet Pope Felix III writes to the contrary, according to the rigor of the canons, to all bishops, Letter I, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 0573] written A.D. 488. — Anselm, bk. 7, ch. 17. Burchard, bk. 4, ch. 99. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 1, ch. 293.]:

## C. X. Those baptized outside the Church or rebaptized shall not be admitted to ecclesiastical service.

Those who at any age have been baptized or rebaptized anywhere other than in the Catholic Church shall by no means [Note: [Col. 0573] “shall never”: original and the cited collections.] be permitted to enter ecclesiastical service. It must suffice for them that they have been received among the number of Catholics. For judgment concerning his order and communion shall be rendered against anyone who violates this institution [Note: [Col. 0573] “of bishops”: ibid.], or who fails to remove someone whom he has learned has crept from [Note: [Col. 0573] “from these”: ibid.] his community into clerical ministry [Col. 0573D].

[Col. 0574A] Gratian. According to the person: as Blessed Gregory, writing to Bishop Januarius, book VII, indiction 2, letter 1, says [Note: [Col. 0573] Letter 1, written A.D. 599, book 9 of the Maurist edition. — Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 197. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, ch. 78, and part 5, ch. 312. Alger, bk. 1, ch. 8.]:

## C. XI. The rigor of the canons is sometimes relaxed on account of the person.

Such wickedness concerning your old age has reached my ears that, unless we still made allowance for it on human grounds, we would already strike it with a fixed sentence of condemnation. And below:

§ 1. Indeed, a sentence of punishment [Note: [Col. 0573] “almost”: editions of Lyons II and III.] should have been pronounced against you; but because we know [Note: [Col. 0573] “have known”: the other collected editions.] your simplicity together with your old age, we are silent for the present.

Gratian. On account of piety: as Gelasius says concerning the unlettered and physically impaired to the bishops throughout Lucania, Letter I, chapter 18 [Note: [Col. 0573] written A.D. 494. — Alger, bk. 1, ch. 11.]:

[Col. 0574B]

## C. XII. The decrees of the canons are sometimes relaxed on account of piety.

If [Note: [Col. 0573] “Those who”: editions of Argentoratum, Basel, and Nuremberg.] any such persons have previously been admitted through their own rashness or through the negligence of their superiors, let them remain, to that extent, in the places in which they have been established, so that [Note: [Col. 0573] “promotion”: editions of Venice I, Paris, and Lyons.] they may never receive any promotion [Note: [Col. 0573] “seize”: Hispana Collection.], and let it suffice them that this very thing has been granted [Note: [Col. 0573] “permitted”: ibid.] to them through extraordinary mercy.

Gratian. On account of necessity: as Pope Hilary, speaking of a certain bishop ordained without the knowledge and consent of his metropolitan, said in his letter to Ascanius and all the bishops of the province of Tarragona, so that grave scandal should not arise on both sides [Note: [Col. 0573] written A.D. 465. — Alger, bk. 1, ch. 12.]:

[Col. 0574C]

## C. XIII. Certain things are tolerated in the Church because of necessity.

Since we see that whatever has been asserted [Note: [Col. 0573] “judged”: the other collected editions.] by either party is confused by every [Note: [Col. 0573] “every”: Hispana Collection.] perversity, taking account of the necessity of the times, we decree that what has been done deserves pardon, provided that henceforth no bishop [Note: [Col. 0573] *No bishop*: Hilary’s words are here reported summarily.] is ordained without the knowledge and [Note: [Col. 0573] “or”: the other collected editions.] consent of the metropolitan.

## C. XIV. On the same matter. Likewise Innocent to the bishops of Macedonia, Letter XXII, chapter 6. [Note: [Col. 0573] written A.D. 414. — Alger, bk. 1, ch. 15.]

Whenever sin is committed by peoples or a crowd, because punishment cannot be inflicted on all on account of their multitude, it is customarily allowed to pass unpunished. I therefore say that former matters must be left to God’s judgment, while for the future the greatest care must be exercised [Col. 0574D] [Note: [Col. 0573] “to be prevented”: the other collected editions and Alger.].

[Col. 0575A]

## C. XV. By dispensation, certain things are tolerated which the rigor of the canons condemns. Likewise from a letter of Cyril sent to Maximus, deacon of Antioch. [Note: [Col. 0575B]

This letter of Blessed Cyril is cited in Session 1 of the Seventh Synod. Since it treats an argument of great importance and is written most wisely, while many things in this translation required correction, it was thought proper to provide the Greek letter itself with a new translation.

“Memorandum of our holy father Cyril, archbishop of Alexandria, to Maximus, deacon of Antioch. I learned from the beloved monk Paul that your Reverence has until this day declined communion with the most devout Bishop John, because there are some in the Church of Antioch who either still hold the views of Nestorius [Col. 0575C], or did hold them but perhaps now refrain from them.

“Let your moderation therefore determine whether those said to assemble openly and shamelessly still think Nestorian thoughts and speak them to others, or whether they once had their consciences seared but now assemble because they have repented of the errors into which they had been swept together, though perhaps ashamed to confess their failure. For such things happen to those who have been deceived. And if you see them now joining the true faith, put out of mind the evils of the past. For we would rather see them denying those errors than shamelessly defending Nestorius’s wickedness.

“And lest we seem to honor contentiousness, let us embrace communion with the most reverent Bishop John, granting him indulgence and, for the sake of economy (*oikonomia*), not scrutinizing too severely those who repent. For the matter, as I have said, requires much economy.”

— “Admonition of our holy father Cyril, archbishop of Alexandria, to Maximus, deacon of Antioch: I learned from the beloved monk Paul [Col. 0575D] that your piety has to this day refused communion with the most devout Bishop John, because some in the Antiochene Church either still think with Nestorius, or did indeed formerly think with him but perhaps now abstain from him. Let your equity therefore consider whether those said to meet openly and shamelessly both think Nestorian thoughts and speak them also to others, or whether they once had a seared conscience but now meet because they have repented of the errors into which they were swept together, though perhaps ashamed to confess their lapse. For something of this kind commonly happens to those who have been deceived. But if you see them now converted to the right faith [Col. 0576B], put away remembrance of past evils. For we prefer to see them denying rather than defending Nestorius’s errors. But lest we appear lovers of contention, let us embrace communion with the most devout John, granting him indulgence and, in order that suitable moderation may be maintained in these matters, not investigating too diligently those who return to their senses. For the matter, as I said, requires great moderation.

“To the same effect he writes to John, patriarch of Antioch, in the letter found in volume 5, act of the Council of Ephesus, recently printed at Ingolstadt, in these words: [Col. 0576C] ‘We desire that all should attend to their own affairs and not again stir up disturbances in the churches—now in some measure settled through Christ’s grace and the prudence of teachers wherever they are active—nor cause trouble either for themselves or for others. But if there are people who at one time stood with Nestorius but now sincerely repent, withdraw from those trifles, change their mind, and begin to embrace the true and blameless faith, they ought to be received gently. No one should reproach any of them with the past, lest in some way an occasion be given to certain people to hasten more hesitantly toward better things.’”

[Note: [Col. 0575] In the first session of the Seventh Synod, held A.D. 787. — Ivo, in the prologue. *Collectio tripartita*, part 2, title 24, ch. 3.]

I learned from the monk Paul, dear to me, that your piety declines, even to this day, to embrace communion with the most reverend Bishop John, because certain persons in the Antiochene Church either still think wrongly with Nestorius or indeed formerly thought so [Note: [Col. 0575] “certain persons”: editions of Argentoratum, Basel, Paris, and Lyons I.], but perhaps have come to their senses.

Let your moderation therefore test whether at any time those [Note: [Col. 0575] These words are not found in Ivo either.] said to assemble openly and irreverently think with Nestorius and confer with one another; although they may at one time have had a seared conscience, they now assemble after doing penance [Col. 0575B] for the matters in which they were ensnared, though perhaps ashamed to confess their transgression.

And below:

§ 1. But lest we be thought [Note: [Col. 0575] “think”: editions of Argentoratum and Basel.] to love contention, let us embrace communion with the most reverend Bishop John [Col. 0576A], granting him indulgence; and, for the sake of dispensation, let his matter not be examined more subtly, strictly, or harshly in relation to him. For the matter, as I have said, greatly requires the grace of dispensation [Note: [Col. 0575] “without punishment”: Basel edition.].

## C. XVI. On the same matter. The same author [Note: [Col. 0575] from the same first session of the Seventh Synod, in Anastasius’s translation. — Ivo, in the prologue. *Collectio tripartita*, same place.] to Gennadius [Note: [Col. 0575] “Januarius”: the other collected editions.], priest and archimandrite.

The exigencies of circumstances sometimes compel certain persons to depart slightly from what is due, in order to secure some greater advantage. For just as those who sail the sea, when a storm presses and the ship is endangered, anxiously throw certain things overboard so that the rest may remain safe, so we too, when we do not have complete certainty of preserving all affairs, disregard some of them, lest we suffer the loss of all.

> [Note: Col. 0576C] **Affairs:** In Greek: “Thus we too, in matters of business, when it is not possible to preserve the utmost exactness, overlook certain things” (*Οὕτω καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐν τοῖς πράγμασιν, ὅταν μὴ ἐξῇ τὸ λίαν ἀκριβὲς περισώζειν, παρορῶμέν τινα*).

> [Note: Col. 0576C] **Losses:** Here Gratian omitted from this letter the material most pertinent to the question proposed. Ivo also cites it: “And I write this because I know that Your Piety is distressed with our most holy and God-worshipping brother and fellow-minister, Bishop Proclus, because he admitted to communion the *hegumen* of the Aelians, whom the laws of the Church do not recognize as head of Palestine.” And below, §1: “Therefore let not Your Piety refuse communion with the most holy and God-beloved Bishop Proclus. For he and I had one concern, and the method of dispensation displeased none of the wise.” Anastasius seems to have supplied the word *hegumenon*, that is, “head” or “superior,” in order to express the Greek phrase *Τὸν τῶν Αἰλιενσίων* (“the one of the Aelians”); or perhaps he had it in his manuscript.

Gratian. On grounds of expediency: as is stated in the Council of Meaux, chapter 64, concerning the children of virgins violently abducted and thus forced into marriage:

> [Note: Col. 0575] Held in A.D. 845.—Alger, book 1, chapter 16.

[Col. 0577A]

### C. XVII. For the sake of expediency, certain things are tolerated in the Church.

Those born from such a marriage are not to be admitted to ecclesiastical orders, unless perhaps either a very great benefit or necessity of the Church requires them, or an evident distinction of merits commends them.

Gratian. In agreement with this, Peter says: “In truth I have found that God is no respecter of persons,” etc. §1. Certain things are also tolerated in the Church because of the outcome of the matter. Thus Leo, in his decrees concerning laymen suddenly ordained bishops contrary to the decrees of the canons, says in Letter LXXXV, alternatively LXXXVII, chapter 1, to the bishops of Africa:

> [Note: Col. 0577] Letter 12, written A.D. 446, Maurist edition.—Alger, book 1, chapter 7.

[Col. 0577B]

### C. XVIII. Laymen promoted to the episcopate contrary to the decrees of the canons are mercifully allowed to retain the office they have assumed.

The circumstances require that fitting punishment be pronounced not only against such bishops but also against their ordainers. Yet on the one side the gentleness of mercy surrounds us, and on the other the strictness of justice, so that we judge some offenses to be tolerable in some fashion, but others to be cut away altogether. Therefore, those whose promotion incurs only this reproach—that they were chosen from the laity for the episcopal office—we permit to retain their position. This does not prejudice the enactments of the Apostolic See or dissolve the rules of the blessed Fathers; for remission of sin does not grant permission to sin, nor may what could be conceded for some reason be lawfully committed again without punishment, lest what we have granted temporarily in pious leniency be afterward punished by just retribution.

> [Note: Col. 0577C] **The circumstances require:** In Leo’s letter the following precedes: “Since, therefore, among you either the zeal of the populace or the ambition of the proud has prevailed so greatly that we learn that not only laymen but also men with second wives”—for this is the correct reading in the letters printed at Cologne with other works of St Leo, rather than “men with secular wives,” as in the volumes of councils—“or husbands of widows have been elevated to the pastoral office, do not apostolic concerns require that the churches in which these things have been done be cleansed by a stricter judgment, and not only such bishops,” etc. This chapter has in fact been reduced to a summary in many places, omitting the narrative of those offenses which that most holy pontiff by no means pardons.

> [Note: Col. 0577] **Afterward:** “Thereafter”: collected editions; Alger.

> [Note: Col. 0577] **Of Salicinum:** “Salacinum”: Hispanic Collection; “Seminacensem”: Lyons editions; “Seiacensem”: other collected editions.

### C. XXI. Those returning from heresy after a public profession may be received in their orders.

The same to Januarius, Bishop of Aquileia, Letter III.

> [Note: Col. 0577] Letter 18, written A.D. 447, Ballerini edition.—Anselm, book 12, chapter 39; Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chapter 97.—Compare above, question 1, chapter 112.

For it is most salutary and most full of the benefit of spiritual medicine that priests, deacons, or clerics of whatever order, who wish to appear corrected and desire to return again to the Catholic faith which they had long ago lost, should first unequivocally confess that their errors and the very authors of those errors are condemned by them. Thus, when corrupt opinions too have been destroyed, no opportunity for hope remains, lest any member of such persons be able to be violated by fellowship, since in every respect their own confession has begun to oppose them. We also direct that the canonical provision concerning them be observed: they should count it a great benefit if, with every hope of promotion removed from them, they remain with permanent stability in the order in which they are found, provided that they have not been defiled by repeated baptism.

> [Note: Col. 0577] **Or clerics:** The original, Ivo, and the collected editions add: “or subdeacons.”

### Part V

Gratian. Behold the reasons why certain things are tolerated in the Church and, once those reasons cease, are punished with pious severity. But when they are to be tolerated and when cut away, Pope Gelasius distinguishes, saying to the bishops throughout Lucania, Letter I, chapter 11:

### C. XXIII. When certain things are to be tolerated in the Church.

Although certain things must sometimes be allowed which, if the integrity of the rest remains intact, cannot by themselves cause harm, those things must nevertheless be especially guarded against which cannot be accepted without manifest disgrace. And if the consideration of circumstances and times, or regard for prompt provision, compels or excuses the indulgence occasionally granted to things thought to involve no loss, how much more must those things never be impaired which neither any necessity nor any ecclesiastical advantage whatever compels?

Gratian. For the necessity or advantage of the Church sometimes limits and relaxes canonical precepts.

### Part VI

§1. We have briefly shown which persons returning from heresy can be received in their orders, and which cannot. Now, however, the question is raised concerning those ordained by heretics: if they return to the unity of the Catholic mother Church, can they be ordained again in the same order? For one who has been consecrated once, as St Gregory says, ought not to be consecrated again.

> [Note: Col. 0579] Above, Distinction 68, chapter 1.

§2. Likewise, the sacraments administered by heretics in the form of the Church, as Augustine testifies, ought not to be repeated, lest injury seem to be done not to the human being but to the sacrament.

> [Note: Col. 0579] Above, question 1, chapter 97.

[Col. 0579C]

§3. But Gregory’s statement is understood of those who have received priestly or episcopal consecration: when they return to the Church, they either receive, through the laying on of hands, the effect of their anointing, or are ordered to cease permanently from its administration. Likewise Augustine’s statement is understood of that same mystical anointing and of the sacrament of baptism.

§4. But there are other orders in the Church which are conferred without sacramental anointing, by the bishop’s blessing alone together with a certain distribution of vessels or vestments: such are the Levites and those established below them. Although these are ordained by heretics, when they return to the Church they are to be ordained in the same order, if otherwise worthy; nor will this constitute a repetition of the office in them, since heretics are understood to have conferred nothing upon them.

[Col. 0580A]

Therefore Urban II writes to Peter, Bishop of Pistoia, and Rusticus, Abbot of Vallombrosa:

### C. XXIV. Those coming back from heretics are to be ordained.

We have found that Daibert was ordained deacon by Nezelon, although the latter was simoniacal, yet not simoniacally according to Daibert’s own confession. The judgment of Blessed Pope Innocent has declared that Nezelon—whom we know to have been ordained by heretics—because he had nothing, could give nothing to the man on whom he laid hands. Therefore, strengthened by the authority of so great a pontiff and confirmed by the testimony of Pope Damasus, who says, “What has been wrongly done must be done again,” we have appointed afresh as deacon Daibert, who has withdrawn body and spirit from heretics and labors to the best of his ability for the benefit of the Church, since the necessity of the Church had become pressing. We judge this not to be a repetition, but only the complete bestowal of the diaconate; for, as we have said, he who had nothing could give nothing.
