### Part VII

We decree that men of this kind shall proceed to govern provinces: men who are customarily advanced to marks of honor not through ambition or price, but through testimony to a life proved worthy and to your high standing. Those to whom such offices are entrusted through your election or ours shall, under oath and in the official records, declare that for obtaining administrative posts they have given nothing, nor will ever afterward give anything, whether personally or through an intermediary, in evasion of the law and oath; whether under the name of a gift or sale, or under any other guise of any contract. And on this account they shall receive absolutely nothing, except salaries, whether while in office or after leaving office, for any benefit rendered during their term of administration which they had deserved gratuitously. And although we suppose that no one mindful of divine fear will, by disregarding an oath, place any advantage before his own salvation, nevertheless, so that the necessity of danger may be added to the fear for salvation, if anyone dares to disregard the oaths given, we grant to all the right to accuse not only the recipient but also the giver, as for a public crime, and to punish in every way with a fourfold penalty the person convicted.

Gratian. Having briefly set these matters forth, let us proceed to those offenses which the Church is prepared to punish by the severity of discipline. We shall show by whose accusations or testimony any persons are to be convicted; by what judge each person ought to be condemned or acquitted; by what remedy a case, if vitiated, can be remedied; and whether, if the accusers fail, the accused person must be compelled to undergo purgation. And so that what we are about to say may become clearer, let an example be set before our eyes, in which the authorities disputing on either side may be distinguished and the judgment of the authority of the holy Fathers may be clearly indicated.

## CASE II

[Col. 0581]

[Col. 0581B]

## GRATIAN

A certain bishop is accused by a layman of a fall of the flesh; two monks, one a subdeacon, and two Levites give testimony against him. He considers himself oppressed by his metropolitan. During the very hearing of the case, three of the witnesses fail, either deceived by a promise or rejected by canonical examination. Yet the bishop is despoiled, because his crime was notorious.

(Question I.) First, the question is whether judicial procedure must be required in manifest cases.  
(Question II.) Second, whether one who has been despoiled may be judged by anyone.  
(Question III.) Third, by what penalty those who fail in accusation or testimony are to be punished.  
(Question IV.) Fourth, whether he is to be condemned on the testimony of two persons.  
(Question V.) Fifth, whether, when the accusers fail, he must be compelled to undergo purgation.  
(Question VI.) Sixth, whether a remedy must be afforded to one who, because of delay in the case, has entered an appeal.  
(Question VII.) Seventh, whether laymen, monks, or persons of any lower orders are to be heard in accusations against superiors.  
(Question VIII.) Eighth, how accusation ought to be made: in writing or without writing.

## QUESTION I

[Col. 0582B]

## GRATIAN

§ 1. Concerning the person of the *aforesaid* bishop, this is to be determined [Note: [Col. 0583] “done”: the collected editions other than the first Basel edition.]: if no criminal charge worthy of exile or deposition has been brought or proved against him, then the man who, while he was still alive, presumed perversely and contrary to the canons to be ordained bishop in his church [Note: [Col. 0583] “shall have presumed”: ibid.] is to be deprived of the priesthood and excluded from every ecclesiastical ministry. But if the bishops, to the prejudice [Note: [Col. 0585D] “But if the bishops, to the prejudice”: this passage through the words “But if perhaps” has been added from the letter [ [Col. 0585] it is also found in Anselm], as likewise somewhat below, from the word “delay” [Col. 0586D] through the words “But if the bishop,” so that the course of the discourse may be more coherent. For Gratian referred to the preceding passages, in which similar matters occur, in this manner: “etc., as above concerning the case of Bishop Januarius.” But the openings of those chapters that are cited from the passages below were left as they had previously stood, so that Gratian’s customary method of citation may be recognized.] of the condemnation [Note: [Col. 0583] “damnation”: the collected editions other than the first Basel edition.] or deposition of the said bishop confess that, through fear of the judge, they consented and did such things not [Note: [Col. 0583] absent from Anselm and the Basel edition.] of their own accord [Note: [Col. 0583] “confessed”: Anselm—the collected editions.], both their term is to be shortened and the manner of their penance moderated. But if the man who invaded his place has perhaps departed from this life [Note: [Col. 0583] “shall have departed”: the collected editions and the original.] and another has been ordained, since he seems guilty of a lighter fault [Note: [Col. 0583] “a lighter fault”: Anselm with the original.] (since [Note: [Col. 0583] the words “since” and “seems” in the following verse are absent from Anselm and the Basel edition.] he seems to have succeeded a deceased man, not, as in the former case, supplanted one still living), he is to be forbidden the episcopal office only in that church, so that in another church lacking a bishop he may be bishop if elected, yet never under any circumstances to return to the church of Málaga. [Col. 0584C]

§ 2. The glorious little count is to be compelled to restore to the aforesaid bishop whatever the bishop, upon oath, affirms that he expended or lost through that man’s violence and persecution. [Note: [Col. 0583] “is to be condemned”: original—Anselm—the collected editions, except Arg.] But if it is perhaps reported that matters occurred otherwise than the petition of the aforesaid bishop states, careful inquiry is to be made; and, once the truth is known, judgment is to be rendered in the fear of God as the order of justice advises.

§ 3. Therefore, since Bishop Stephen asserts that, through hatred [Note: [Col. 0583] “through his hatred”: original—Anselm—editions Arg., Ven. I–II, Nor., Lugd. I.] directed against him, certain matters were fabricated, that he was accused on false counts, that nothing was done in due order, and that he was condemned unjustly, [Col. 0585A] it must first be carefully investigated [Note: [Col. 0585] “inquired into”: Basel edition.] whether the judgment was conducted in due order—that is [Note: [Col. 0585] “or whether”: original.], whether the accusers were different persons from the witnesses [Note: [Col. 0585] “were”: Basel edition.]. Then the nature of the charges must be examined: whether it was worthy of exile or deposition [Note: [Col. 0585D] “Exile”: in the vulgate editions there followed [ [Col. 0583] and in the collected editions other than the first Basel edition]: “or deportation”—words removed because they occur neither in the old copies of Gratian nor in St. Gregory [ [Col. 0583] nor in Anselm].]; whether testimony against him was given under oath in the presence of the accused [Note: [Col. 0585] “who was accused” is absent in Anselm.]; whether proceedings were put in writing, *or* whether he himself had leave to answer and defend himself [Note: [Col. 0585] “had”: the collected editions.].

Careful inquiry must also be made into the persons of the accusers and witnesses [Note: [Col. 0585] adds: “what manner of life”: Bohmer.]: what their social standing was, what their reputation, whether they were impoverished [Note: [Col. 0585] adds: “in property”: the collected editions—Bohmer.], *or* whether they perhaps had some enmities against the aforesaid bishop [Note: [Col. 0585] “pastor”: the collected editions.], *and* whether they gave testimony from hearsay [Note: [Col. 0585] “gave”: the collected editions.] or rather testified that they knew the matter specifically; whether, if judgment was given in writing, the sentence was read out in the presence of the parties. [Col. 0585B] [Note: [Col. 0585] “was”: ibid., except Basel.]

But if perhaps these things were not performed solemnly, and no charge worthy of exile or deposition was proved, he is in every way to be restored to his church. Those, however, who condemned him contrary to the fear of God and the statutes of the canons are to be excommunicated and sent to a monastery [Note: [Col. 0585] “in a monastery”: ibid.] to do penance for six [Note: [Col. 0585] “seven”: Basel edition.] months; provided, however, that if danger of death should threaten any of them [Note: [Col. 0585] “peril”: the collected editions.], the blessing of viaticum is not to be denied. But the man who, while he was living, rashly sought his place is to be deprived of priesthood and excluded from every ecclesiastical ministry, and handed over to the same most beloved brother and fellow bishop of ours, so that he may either send him to us or hold him in custody with himself. The bishops who presumed to ordain him, or gave their consent [Note: [Col. 0585] “assent”: ibid.] to his perverse [Col. 0585C] ordination, *likewise* being deprived of communion, are to be assigned to do penance in a monastery for six months.

*But if the bishops, to the prejudice [Note: [Col. 0585D] “But if the bishops, to the prejudice”: this passage through the words “But if perhaps” has been added from the letter [ [Col. 0585] it is also found in Anselm], as likewise somewhat below, from the word “delay” [Col. 0586D] through the words “But if the bishop,” so that the course of the discourse may be more coherent. For Gratian referred to the preceding passages, in which similar matters occur, in this manner: “etc., as above concerning the case of Bishop Januarius.” But the openings of those chapters that are cited from the passages below were left as they had previously stood, so that Gratian’s customary method of citation may be recognized.] of the condemnation or deposition of the said Stephen, declare that through fear of the judge they consented and did such things not [Note: [Col. 0585] absent from Anselm.] of their own accord, their term is to be shortened and the manner of their penance moderated. If, therefore, the man who invaded the place of the aforesaid Stephen has perhaps died, and another bishop has been ordained in his church, the same determination concerning him is to be made as we stated above in the case of our brother and fellow bishop Januarius.*

§ 4. But if [Col. 0586A] some of the charges brought against the said Bishop Stephen have been proved, whereas others could not at all be demonstrated, it must be weighed with every careful consideration whether the lighter counts or the graver ones have been proved, so that from them you may know how to frame your decision.

§ 5. But if it becomes clear that the aforesaid bishop is innocent, the glorious little count is to restore to him without any delay whatever he took from his goods or from those of his church. *And whatever the same bishop shall swear that he expended in consequence of that man’s persecution and violence, or suffered as loss, the same aforementioned glorious little count shall repay and make satisfaction for.* [Note: [Col. 0585] “whatever”: the collected editions—Anselm.] But if the *aforesaid* bishop is found to have *committed* such a fault (which God forbid!), etc., as below [C. XVI, q. 6, c. 3], in the case concerning monks. [Col. 0586B] “Concerning the person of the presbyter,” etc., as below [C. XI, q. 1, c. 38], in the case: “A cleric against a cleric.” And below in the same letter, Book XI, Epistle 54.

§ 6. Concerning the person of Bishop Januarius, it must be understood that it was altogether a grave act and contrary to the laws that he was forcibly dragged from his church; since, if a bishop has suffered in a church any *other* injury from anyone [Note: [Col. 0585] “by a bishop”: Bohmer, wrongly.], the law strikes the offender with capital punishment and, treating him as guilty of treason, grants everyone leave to accuse him, as the text of this law says in Code, Book I, title III, constitution 10 [Note: [Col. 0585] Theodosian Code, Book 16, title 2, c. 31—Justinian Code, Book 1, title 3, c. 10.]:

§ 7. “If anyone should break out into this kind of sacrilege [Note: [Col. 0585] “rush into”: the collected editions.] so as, by rushing into Catholic churches [Note: [Col. 0585] “the Catholic church”: certain editions, first Lugd. II–III.], to inflict some injury upon priests and ministers [Note: [Col. 0585] adds: “or upon the worshippers themselves”: Bohmer.], or upon worship itself or the place,” etc. And below in the same letter.

§ 8. Concerning the person of Bishop Stephen, it must *for this purpose* [Col. 0586C] be observed that he ought neither to have been dragged unwillingly to trial nor judged by bishops of a foreign council. And below:

§ 9. If against these things it is said that he had neither metropolitan nor patriarch, the reply must be that this case ought to have been heard and decided by the Apostolic See, which is the head of all churches, as the aforesaid bishop is known to have requested, since he held the bishops of a foreign council to be judges altogether suspect. [Note: [Col. 0585] “Therefore, because bishops . . . sentence, etc.”: Anselm—the collected editions.] *Therefore, because a sentence pronounced by a judge not his own possesses no force, the tenor of this reading in Book VII of the Code, etc., demonstrates.* And below:

§ 10. As for the statement that he was accused by his servants, it must [Col. 0587A] be known that they ought by no means to have been heard. [Note: [Col. 0587] “ought to have heard”: Basel edition.] And below:

§ 11. But if [Note: [Col. 0587] “But if it is said that he is accused of this, namely of something amounting to the crime of treason”: original.] he is said to be accused of the crime of treason, even this ought not to have been believed of him [Note: [Col. 0587] “not even they”: the collected editions other than the first Basel edition.] if his prior life or reputation was not such. And below:

§ 12. As for the statement of the same bishop that, in his absence, some most worthless witnesses were produced: if this is true, it must *be* known *in law* to be of no weight. [Note: [Col. 0587] “is of no weight”: also found in Anselm.] And below:

§ 13. Very many laws show what sort of witnesses, or witnesses of what reputation, are to be admitted to testimony; these laws are scarcely unknown to anyone. They also enact [Note: [Col. 0587] “know”: Basel edition; “make”: Paris edition.] that the testimony of the most worthless witnesses ought not to be believed without bodily examination.

§ 14. As for the assertion that nothing was judged in writing [Note: [Col. 0587] “judged in writing”: Arg. edition; “judged without writing”: Basel edition; “to be judged in writing”: Ven. I; “to be judged without writing”: the remaining editions.], title XLIV of Book VII of the Code must be read [Note: [Col. 0587] adds: “the final constitution”: the collected editions.], because the case ought to have been judged in writing. For there, among other things, it *is said [Col. 0587B] and* commanded that a sentence pronounced without a written record should not deserve *even* the name of a sentence.

### C. VIII. A final sentence must be delivered from a written text. Likewise from Book VII of the Code

[Note: [Col. 0587C] In two old codices neither this nor the following chapter is found, and St. Gregory plainly indicated this law of the Code in the preceding chapter.] [Note: [Col. 0587] Given in A.D. 374, Book 7, Code title 44, constitution 3; cf. Gregory the Great, Book 3, Epistle 45.], under the title “On Sentences to Be Read from a Brief,” [Note: [Col. 0587] “peril”: the collected editions other than the first Lugd. II–III editions.] the Emperors Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian Augusti. [PALEA.]

> “By general enactments we have commanded that all judges to whom we have granted authority to administer justice in the provinces, after cases have been heard, shall pronounce their final decisions by reading from a written text. To this enactment we add [Note: [Col. 0587] “we add”: Basel edition; “we adjudge”: Arg. edition.] that a sentence pronounced when it has not been written shall not deserve even the name of a sentence, nor need the formalities of appeal be sought in order to rescind decrees wrongly made. [Col. 0587C]”

Likewise, from the council at Saint-Médard. Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims, said [Note: [Col. 0587] held A.D. 853. Burchard, Book 2, c. 197. Ivo, Decree, part 6, c. 269.]:

### C. IX. On the same matter. [PALEA.]

> “The custom *and* authority of ecclesiastical laws are such that in judicial proceedings they always require a written record, [Note: [Col. 0587] “a written record is required”: the collected editions.] so much so that one approaching the sacred font is commanded to give his name. One advanced to the supreme priesthood is chosen by a decree confirmed by the hands of all. [Note: [Col. 0587] “is chosen”: ibid.] One who has been ordained is commanded to receive letters from his ordainers. One also who is severed from [Col. 0588A] ecclesiastical fellowship by any transgression is either received or expelled by the registration of a written petition. [Note: [Col. 0587] “by the written form of a petition”: original—Burchard—Basel edition; “by the inscription of a petition”: Ivo—Lugd. III; “by the description of a petition”: the other collected editions.] And one who [Note: [Col. 0587C] “And one who”: the original reads: “But one who is accused, [Col. 0587D] or who is excommunicated, having been reconciled, is commanded to be accused by writing or, having been reconciled, to be commended by writing. And thus, etc.”] is accused or excommunicated or reconciled is commanded to be accused or reconciled by writing. Thus, in other matters of this sort, writing is so necessary that, as St. Gregory, drawing from Roman law, writes in his memorandum to the defender John [Note: [Col. 0587] cf. the end of the preceding chapter.]: ‘A sentence pronounced without a written record [Note: [Col. 0587] “writing”: Burchard—Ivo—Basel; “written records”: the other editions.] does not deserve even the name of a sentence.’ [Note: [Col. 0587] “deserves”: Ivo—editions Arg., Bas., Nor., Ven. I.]”

### C. X. He whose expulsion is established to have occurred without either conviction or confession must be restored. Likewise, Pope Nicholas to Girard [Note: [Col. 0587] It should be read “Herard,” who was bishop of Tours in the time of Nicholas I. In the Basel edition the heading reads “Artald”; in Ivo (part 6, c. 429), “Airard.” The date of the letter is uncertain.] Archbishop of Tours.

Let it be known to your fraternal charity that this poor presbyter, named Christopher, has tearfully complained to our clemency [Col. 0588B] of his distress, saying that he was attacked with false accusations and was irrationally expelled from his church without either conviction or confession. For, as he himself relates, after your diligence had conducted an inquiry on three occasions, no fault could be found in him, either concerning the crime of fornication or complicity in homicide [Note: [Col. 0588C] “Complicity”: this has been corrected from most old copies. Previously the reading was “confession.” Ivo, however, has “consent.”] [Note: [Col. 0587] “confession”: the collected editions other than the first Arg. and Basel editions.]—the matters of which he was accused—except that, because of his poverty, he either refused to consent to what was demanded or was unable to fulfill it. [Note: [Col. 0587] “fulfill completely”: the collected editions.] Yet his rival voluntarily did this, unjustly seizing his church beforehand. Therefore we strongly exhort your reverence that whatever seems to have been done in Gehazi-like greed, perhaps without your knowledge, be corrected by the prompt amendment of your brotherhood’s discipline: namely, by restoring the aforesaid priest to [Col. 0588C] his own church and, in your kindness, returning to him the former honor which he lost. Do not permit canonical institutions to be despised through anyone’s rashness, because equal punishment binds the doer and the consenting party.

### C. XI. No one ought to be excommunicated before the charge is proved. Likewise from the book of constitutions

[Note: [Col. 0587] Julian, Epitome Novels 115, c. 15—Anselm, Collection of Canons dedicated, Book 2, c. 300—Abbo of Fleury (in Mabillon, *Analecta*), c. 36—Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 5, c. 124; *Decree*, part 5, c. 371; part 14, c. 42; cf. below, C. 24, q. 3, c. 6.]

No bishop and no presbyter may excommunicate anyone before the charge for which [Col. 0589A] the ecclesiastical canons command this to be done has been proved. But if anyone excommunicates someone contrary to this [Note: [Col. 0589] adds: “constitution”: the collected editions other than the first Basel edition.], then indeed *the person excommunicated shall, by the authority of the higher priest, return to the grace of holy communion; but the person who has excommunicated him unlawfully [Note: [Col. 0589] adds: “him”: the same editions, first Arg. and Basel.] shall abstain from the most holy communion for such a time* as the higher priest judges proper, so that what he did unjustly [Note: [Col. 0589] “has done”: ibid.; adds: “by excommunicating him”: the collected editions.] he himself may suffer justly.

### C. XII. Uncertain and doubtful matters cannot be judged. Likewise, Augustine in Epistle CXXXVII, to the clergy and all the people of Hippo

[Note: [Col. 0589] Written A.D. 404—Anselm, Book 5, c. 80—Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, c. 358.]

For this reason I did not venture either to suppress or erase the name of the presbyter from the number of his colleagues, lest I seem to do an injury to the divine power [Note: [Col. 0589] “mercy”: Basel edition; “the power of mercy”: the other collected editions except Arg.], before whose tribunal the case is still pending, if I wished to anticipate his judgment [Col. 0589B] with my own; something that even judges do not do in secular affairs when the uncertainty of a *case* is referred [Note: [Col. 0589] “deferred”: ibid.] to a higher authority, lest, while the reference is pending, they dare to alter anything. And it has been determined [Note: [Col. 0589] “ordained”: Basel edition.] in a council of bishops [Note: [Col. 0589] “also in [a council] of bishops”: the collected editions; Augustine is understood to refer to the Third Council of Carthage, held A.D. 397.] that no cleric who has not yet been convicted ought to be suspended from communion, unless he fails to present himself for examination of his case.

### C. XIII. No one is to be condemned either at the discretion of suspicion or before a true and just judgment. Likewise, Pope Melchiades to the bishops of Spain

[Note: [Col. 0589] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore. Collection of Councils, third part, part 1, tome 31, c. 1.]

Before all else, always inquire carefully, so that you may decide with justice and truth [Note: [Col. 0589] “charity”: the collected editions.]. Condemn no one before a true and just judgment. Judge no one at the discretion of suspicion. Rather, first prove the matter, [Col. 0589C] and afterward pronounce a charitable sentence; and do not do to another what you do not wish done to yourselves.

### C. XIV. Who are prohibited from accusation, and who are to be admitted. Likewise, Digest, Book XLVIII, title “On Accusations and Registrations,” law *Qui accusare*

[Note: [Col. 0589] Macer, Book 2, “On Public Judgments.”]

Some are prohibited from accusing because of sex or age, such as a woman or a minor. Others because of an oath, such as those receiving military pay. Others because of the office or power in which they are acting, since they cannot be summoned to court without impropriety. [Note: [Col. 0589] “called out”: original.] Others because of their own offense, such as persons of bad repute. Others because of shameful gain, such as those who have registered two prosecutions against two defendants, or have received money to accuse or not [Col. 0590A] accuse. [Note: [Col. 0589] “received”: Basel edition.] Others because of their condition, such as [Note: [Col. 0589] adds: “children against parents and”: Lugd. II–III editions.] freedmen [Note: [Col. 0589] “freedpersons”: Basel edition.] against their patrons. [Note: [Col. 0589] Fragment 9, from Paulus, Book 5, *Sentences*.] Others because they are suspected of malicious prosecution, such as those who have given false testimony after being suborned. [Note: [Col. 0589] Fragment 10, from Hermogenianus, Book 6, *Epistles*.] Some because of poverty, such as those possessing less than fifty gold pieces. Yet all these [Note: [Col. 0589] Fragment 11, from Macer, Book 2, *On Public Judgments*.], if they pursue a wrong done to themselves or defend the death of relatives, are not excluded from accusation. [Note: [Col. 0589] “shall be excluded”: Basel edition.]

Freeborn persons and freedpersons are not to be prohibited, for the protection of their own interests, from complaining of an act committed by their parents or patrons [Note: [Col. 0589] “from defending”: ibid.]—for example [Note: [Col. 0589] “as if”: the collected editions following the original.] if they say they were forcibly expelled by them from possession—not in order to bring against them a charge of violence, [Note: [Col. 0589] “against them”: Basel; “in them”: the other editions except Lugd. II–III.] but merely [Note: [Col. 0589] adds: “only”: Basel.] to recover possession. A son, indeed, is not prohibited from complaining about an act of his mother [Note: [Col. 0589] “complaining”: the collected editions.], if he says that she falsely passed off a child as hers, in order that she might have [Col. 0590B] an additional co-heir; but he is not permitted to prosecute her under the Cornelian law.

§ 1. One person cannot bring an accusation already brought by another; but another person is not prohibited from accusing one who has been removed from the list of accused persons owing to a public or private abolition, or because the accuser has withdrawn. [Note: [Col. 0589] “others”: Basel edition.]

§ 2. The divine Verus [Note: [Col. 0589] “Severus”: the collected editions.] and Antoninus rescripted that a woman bringing an accusation concerning the public interest in the grain supply is to be heard by the prefect of the grain supply. Persons of bad repute who bring accusations are likewise admitted without any doubt. Soldiers also—*who cannot bring cases belonging to others, who keep watch for peace, or rather*—are to be admitted to this accusation. Slaves bringing accusations are likewise heard.

## Part II. Gratian

From all these authorities it is understood that no one is to be condemned unless, after judgment has been conducted in due order, he is either convicted or himself confesses guilt. Yet these provisions are to be understood of those whose crimes are hidden; matters that are manifest, on the other hand, do not require judicial procedure.

Hence Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0589D] Ivo, in the letter to Hugh beginning “Literas V. P.,” speaks thus: “St. Ambrose, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Corinthians, testifies that a manifest charge does not require [Col. 0590D] [an accuser], saying as follows concerning the man with his stepmother: ‘It is not the judge’s task,’ etc., as below, chapter “On a Manifest [Case].”] [Note: [Col. 0589] The sentence is taken from the commentary on First Corinthians falsely attributed to Ambrose.]:

### C. XV. They are to be judged without a manifest accusation.

They do not require a manifest accusation.

### C. XVI. On the same matter. Likewise, Pope Nicholas, in a letter to King Louis [Note: [Col. 0589] “Charles”: the collected editions.] beginning “Syllabarum”

[Note: [Col. 0590D] This is taken from a letter preserved in the frequently mentioned manuscript of the Dominican monastery, in which the following precedes it: “We have certainly learned that King Lothair has no accuser except the one called in the Apocalypse the accuser of the brethren, and his works, which are likewise perpetrated at the prompting of that same ancient enemy; but what King Lothair, etc.”]

The actions of King Lothair, your nephew, require no accuser. For the works of the flesh are manifest [Note: [Col. 0589] “for his works are manifest”: Arg. edition, with the rest omitted; “his works are manifest, as the Apostle testifies—the works of the flesh, which are”: Basel; cf. Galatians 5:19.]: fornication, impurity, etc.

[Col. 0591A] Gratian. For in manifest matters the accused is not oppressed by the cunning of accusers, nor is one’s own crime concealed through evasion, since the fault voluntarily presents itself to everyone’s eyes. Therefore judicial procedure is not required in such cases; it was instituted so that neither innocence might be exposed to the snares of opponents nor the guilt of offenders escape the sentence of a just examination.

Hence Pope Stephen V to Leo, Bishop of Theano [Note: [Col. 0591] Fragment of a lost letter, written A.D. 887—Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 4, c. 117; *Decree*, part 6, c. 431—the same material occurs in Gerhoh, *On the Building of God*, in Pez, *Anecdota*, vol. 2, part 2, p. 374.] [Note: [Col. 0592D] This complete letter survives in an anonymous collection of canons in the Vatican Library.] [Note: [Col. 0591] “of Tours”: Basel edition; “Leonitanus”: Ivo, *Panormia*.]:

### C. XVII. A manifest case does not require judicial procedure.

In a manifest and well-known case to many, witnesses need not be sought, as St. Ambrose said in his commentary on the Epistle to the Corinthians [Note: [Col. 0591] “says”: the same editions, first Paris and Lugd.; cf. Corinthians, c. 4.], explaining the Apostle’s sentence concerning fornication [Note: [Col. 0591] “the fornicator”: the collected editions following Ivo.]:

> “It is not the judge’s task to condemn without an accuser, because *even* the Lord, when Judas was a thief [Note: [Col. 0591] “had been”: the same editions, from the same source.], *knew [Note: [Col. 0591] these words are found neither in Ivo nor in Gerhoh.]: but* because he was not accused, he did not cast him out.” [Note: [Col. 0591] “expel”: the collected editions other than the first Arg. and Basel editions.]

> *“Let the one who committed this deed be removed from your midst.”* Once this deed was known [Note: [Col. 0591] adds: “however”: Ivo, Gerhoh, and the collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 0591] “his”: Basel and Lugd. II–III editions.], the Apostle judged that he *was to have been* expelled from the fellowship of the brethren. [Note: [Col. 0591] adds: “apostolic”: Basel edition.] For everyone knew his crime and did not accuse him. Publicly, he had his stepmother in the place of a wife; in that affair neither were witnesses needed nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion.

And shortly afterward:

> “Absent in body but present in the authority of the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0591] adds: “Holy”: Arg. and P. III editions.], who is absent nowhere, I have already judged, as though present, that the man who committed this should be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.”

## Part III. Gratian

But it must be known that among manifest matters, some are known to the judge and unknown to others; others are manifest to others and hidden from the judge; [Col. 0591C] while some are known both to the judge and to others. Matters known only to the judge cannot be struck down without examination, because when the judge assumes the role of accuser, judicial authority is lost. In one and the same case, no one can at once be both accuser and judge.

Hence Augustine, in Homily L on Penance, chapter 12 [Note: [Col. 0591] Sermon 351, Maurist edition—Anselm, Book 3, c. 70—Polycarpus, Book 7, title 7.]:

### C. XVIII. When some persons are to be corrected and when they are to be tolerated.

Many are corrected, like Peter; many are tolerated, like Judas; many are unknown until [Note: [Col. 0591] 1 Corinthians 4:5.] the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness. And below:

§ 1. We, however, cannot prohibit anyone from communion—although this prohibition is not yet deadly but medicinal—unless he has either confessed voluntarily, [Col. 0592A] or been named and convicted in some secular or ecclesiastical judgment. [Note: [Col. 0591] “or”: the collected editions.] For who would dare [Note: [Col. 0591] “would have dared”: the collected editions.] take both roles upon himself, so that he himself might be both accuser and judge of anyone? This rule, too, the Apostle Paul is understood briefly to have indicated in the *same* Epistle to the Corinthians [Note: [Col. 0591] adds: “his”: the collected editions other than the first Basel edition.], when, after recalling certain crimes, he gave from particular instances the form of ecclesiastical *judgment* for all similar cases. For he says [Note: [Col. 0591] 1 Corinthians 5:8.]:

> “I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with fornicators. [Note: [Col. 0591] “not to associate”: the collected editions.] Not at all with the fornicators of this world, or the greedy, or robbers, or idolaters; otherwise you would have had to leave [Note: [Col. 0591] “to leave”: the same editions, first Basel.] this world.”

For people living in this world cannot help living among such people, nor can they win them for Christ if they avoid their company [Note: [Col. 0591] “company, fellowship, and table-companionship”: Basel edition.] and association. [Col. 0592B] Hence the Lord too, eating with tax collectors and sinners [Note: [Col. 0591] absent from the collected editions other than the first Basel edition.], says: “The healthy do not need [Note: [Col. 0591] “necessary”: the collected editions.] a physician, but the sick do. For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” [Note: [Col. 0591] adds: “to repentance”: the collected editions other than the first Arg. edition.]

And therefore the Apostle continues [Note: [Col. 0591] “those that follow”: the collected editions.] and adds [Note: [Col. 0591] 1 Corinthians 5:11.]:

> “But now I have written to you not to associate [Note: [Col. 0591] “not to associate”: the collected editions other than the first Basel edition; adds: “with fornicators”: the collected editions.] if anyone called a brother *among you* is a fornicator, or an idolater, or greedy, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber; with such a person do not *even* eat *together*. What have I to do with judging those outside? Do you not judge those within? But God will judge those outside. Remove the evil person from among yourselves.”

By these words he sufficiently shows that evil persons are to be removed from the communion of the Church not rashly or in any arbitrary fashion, but through judgment; so that, if they cannot be removed through judgment, they should rather be tolerated, lest *anyone* perversely avoid the wicked and, by himself departing from the Church, bind those whom he seems to flee [Col. 0592C] to Gehenna. [Note: [Col. 0591] “conquer”: Basel; “or conquer”: Nor. and Ven. I; “or join or send”: Arg.; “send”: Paris and Lugd.]

For examples are also set before us in the *holy* Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0591] absent from the collected editions other than the first Basel edition.]: as in the harvest, where chaff is endured until the final winnowing; or inside the nets, where good fish are patiently endured with bad ones until the separation [Note: [Col. 0591] “division”: the collected editions other than the first Basel edition.] that will occur on the shore—that is, at the end of the age.

§ 2. For this is not contrary to the passage in which the Apostle says *elsewhere* [Note: [Col. 0591] Romans 14:4.]: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own master he stands or falls.” He did not wish one human being to be judged by another on the basis of mere suspicion or by an extraordinary judgment usurped without authority, but rather according to the law of God and the order of the Church—whether the person had voluntarily confessed or was accused and convicted. Otherwise, why did he say: “If anyone called a brother is a fornicator or an idolater,” etc., unless he intended [Note: [Col. 0593] “intends”: Basel edition.] that “being called” should mean a designation made against someone when a sentence is pronounced in judicial order and integrity? For if the designation *alone* suffices, many innocent people must be condemned, because crimes are often falsely alleged against someone.

§ 3. Therefore those whom we exhort to do penance should not seek companions for punishment [Note: [Col. 0593] “punishments”: the collected editions.], nor rejoice because they have found [Note: [Col. 0593] “find persons like themselves”: the same editions.] more people. For they will not burn any less because they burn with many.

[Col. 0593B]

### C. XIX. A sin known only to the judge cannot be condemned by him.

[Note: [Col. 0593] Sermon 82, Maurist edition—Anselm, Book 11, c. 26.]

Likewise, in Sermon XVI, *On the Words of the Lord*.

“If your brother sins against you,” he says, “rebuke him between yourself and him alone.” Why? Because he has sinned against you. What does “He has sinned against you” mean? You know that he has sinned [Note: [Col. 0593] add.: against you: Ed. Bas.]. Since it was secret when he sinned against you, seek secrecy when you correct what he has done against you. For if you alone know that he has sinned against you, and you wish to accuse him before everyone, you are not [Note: [Col. 0593] no longer: ib.] a reprover [Note: [Col. 0593] you will be: Edd. coll. o.], but a betrayer [Note: [Col. 0593] corrector: same editions.—add.: of the error: same editions; first Bas.].

Consider how the righteous man Joseph treated with such kindness so great an offence which he suspected concerning his wife, before he knew by whom she had conceived, although he perceived that she was pregnant and knew that he himself had not approached her. Thus a certain suspicion of adultery remained; and yet, because he alone had perceived it, he alone knew it. What does the Gospel say of him? [Col. 0593C] “Joseph, however, being a just man and unwilling to expose her publicly” [Note: [Col. 0593] to disgrace her: Edd. Lugdd. II, III.—to expose and disgrace her: other editions].

“The husband’s grief did not seek vengeance: he wished to benefit the sinner, not to punish the sinner. Since,” it says, “he was unwilling to expose her publicly,” he wished to send her away secretly. And below:

§ 1. Therefore those very offences which are committed publicly should be rebuked publicly; but those committed more secretly should themselves be rebuked more secretly. Distinguish [Note: [Col. 0593] distinguish: Edd. Ven. I, Par., Lugdd.] the occasions, and Scripture agrees [Note: [Col. 0593] will agree: Ed. Bas.—will agree: later editions]. Let us act thus, and thus ought we to act, not only when a sin is committed against us, but also when someone sins in such a way that another does not know of it: we ought to rebuke him in private [Note: [Col. 0593] and: Edd. Par., Lugd. I.—the following words, “that another … in private,” are lacking in the collected editions and Lugdd. II, III].

And a little later:

§ 2. A bishop knows, for example, some murderer [Note: [Col. 0593] “I do not know whom he may know”: Edd. coll. o., Lugdd. II, III], and no one else knows him [Col. 0594A]. I do not wish to rebuke him publicly, and do you demand that I denounce him in writing? Certainly I neither betray nor neglect him: I rebuke him privately; I set before his eyes [Note: [Col. 0593] before him: Ed. Bas.] God’s judgment; I frighten his blood-stained conscience; I urge him to repentance. We ought to be endowed with this charity. Hence people sometimes blame us because we seem not to rebuke, or they suppose that we know what we do not know, or suppose that we keep silent about what [Note: [Col. 0593] add.: if anything: Ed. Arg.] we do know. But perhaps what you know, I also know; yet I do not rebuke him before you, because I wish to heal, not to accuse.

§ 3. There are adulterers in their own homes; they sin secretly [Note: [Col. 0593] sinning: Edd. coll. o.]. Sometimes they are disclosed to us by their wives—often out of jealousy, sometimes because they seek their husbands’ salvation. We do not reveal them openly [Col. 0594B] [Note: [Col. 0593] lacking in Edd. coll. o., Lugdd. II, III], but rebuke them in private [Note: [Col. 0593] correct: Ed. Bas.]. Let the evil die where [Note: [Col. 0593] so that where: Edd. coll. o.] it occurred. Yet we do not neglect that wound, but above all show the person involved in such a sin, who bears a wounded conscience, that the wound is deadly.

**Part IV. Gratian.** When, however, a crime is known to others but not to the judge, even then it must not be punished without examination, because a judge ought not pronounce sentence upon a charge unknown to himself.

Hence Pope Evaristus says in Epistle II [Note: [Col. 0593] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, drawn from Gregory, *Morals*, book 19, ch. 14.—The same occurs in the Council of Tribur, ch. 22.—Burchard, book 11, ch. 9; Anselm, book 3, ch. 67; Ivo Panormia, book 4, ch. 116; Decretum, part 5, ch. 240; Polycarpus, book 7, title 1]:

### C. XX. A sentence must not be pronounced precipitately.

Almighty God, in order to restrain us from pronouncing hasty judgment, although all things are naked and open to His eyes [Note: [Col. 0593] Heb. 4], nevertheless did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom merely upon report before He openly ascertained [Col. 0594C] [Note: [Col. 0593] came to know: same editions] the things said. Thus He Himself said [Note: [Col. 0593] Gen. 18]: “I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.”

Almighty God, to whom nothing is hidden, but to whom all things are manifest even before they come to pass, deigned personally to investigate these and many other things—not because He was ignorant of them, but in order [Note: [Col. 0593] not because He was ignorant of them, but so that: same editions] to give us an example, lest we be hasty in examining and judging cases, and lest anyone presume to believe the evils of others [Note: [Col. 0593] neighbours: same editions] before proving them. These matters, omitted here to avoid prolixity [Note: [Col. 0593] which we have not inserted here to avoid prolixity: Edd. coll. o.], serve no other purpose.

By His example we are warned never to be hasty in pronouncing sentence, nor rashly and carelessly to judge matters not examined and proved [Note: [Col. 0593] add.: proved: Edd. Bas., Par., Lugdd.—disproved: later editions, from Ivo Panormia] in whatever manner [Col. 0595A], as the voice of Truth says: “Do not judge, that you may not be judged; for with what judgment you judge, you shall be judged,” and the rest [Note: [Col. 0595] “and you shall not be judged”: Ivo and Edd. coll. o., except Arg.—cf. Matt. 7:1].

Therefore, reports of evil should move no one, and no one should ever believe things commonly said without certain proof; rather, he should carefully investigate reports before acting, lest anyone do anything precipitately [Note: [Col. 0595] nor precipitately: Edd. coll. o.]. For if the Lord, the Knower [Note: [Col. 0595] add.: Knower: same editions, from Ivo] of all things, although He knew all the evils of the Sodomites—whose outcry had reached heaven—was unwilling either to believe or to judge before He Himself, diligently investigating with trustworthy witnesses, had truly established in deed what He had heard [Note: [Col. 0595] proved: same editions], much more ought we, frail and sinful human beings [Note: [Col. 0595] we who are human and sinful: same editions], to guard against this and to judge or condemn no one before true and just proof. The hidden judgments of God are unknown to us; and the Apostle Paul plainly says [Note: [Col. 0595] Rom. 14:4]: “Who are you, to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls to his own master.”

**Part V. Gratian.** But when a crime is known to the judge and to others, sometimes the accused denies the act—for example, if someone denies having killed a man whom he killed before the judge’s eyes in the sight of many. In that case, because he denies guilt, he cannot be punished without examination. At other times the very evidence of the act testifies that he is guilty, when by a public act he confesses his crime. Then, after the second and third correction, he is to be condemned or punished without examination if he proves incorrigible.

It is in this final case that the authority of Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0595] above, chs. 15, 16] and Nicholas is to be understood: “Manifest cases need no accusation.” For that fornicator against whom apostolic sentence proceeded without examination publicly had his stepmother as his wife before everyone [Col. 0595C]. Lothair also, concerning whom Nicholas writes, had similarly dismissed his wife publicly and brought in another.

Hence Pope Nicholas writes to the archbishops and bishops established throughout Gaul, Italy, and Germany [Note: [Col. 0595] written A.D. 863. Ivo, Decretum, part 8, ch. 226]:

### C. XXI. Those guilty of manifest offences are to be punished without accusation.

The crime which King Lothair—if indeed one can truly call him king, who restrains the desires of the body by no wholesome government, but rather yields through slippery weakness to their unlawful motions—committed with two women, namely Thietberga [Note: [Col. 0595] Teberga: Edd. coll. o.—Theiberga: Ivo] and Waldrada, is manifest to all [Col. 0596A]. And almost the whole world, flocking from every quarter to the thresholds or see of the Apostolic See, had long reported to us that in this affair he had Bishops Theutgaud [Note: [Col. 0595] Teuguald: Ed. Bas.—Teugald: later editions with Ivo] and Gunther as his defenders and supporters.

And below: Therefore, the holy synod decreeing with us [Note: [Col. 0595] with you: Ed. Bas.], they unquestionably stand deposed in our presence, excommunicated from the priestly office, and removed from the governance of the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0595] may stand: ib.].

## QUESTION II

**GRATIAN**

That a person despoiled cannot stand before a judge is proved by many authorities.

[Col. 0596B] For Pope John I says to Zacharias, Archbishop [Note: [Col. 0595] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter drawn from Theodosian Code, book 9, title 10, ch. 3; cf. Breviary of Alaric, book 8, title 1, ch. 2.—Anselm, book 3, ch. 44, and at end of book 7; Ivo Panormia, book 4, ch. 47]:

### C. I. Before joinder of issue, everything must be restored to the possessor.

It was decreed long ago that the bishop or primate should restore to the possessor all possessions, everything taken from him, and all fruits received before joinder of issue [Note: [Col. 0595D] “Received”: in old copies, and in the epistle of John as also of Eusebius, and in Anselm and Ivo at the cited places, it is *perceptor* (“receiver”) or *primas* (“primate”) should restore to the possessor.] [Note: [Col. 0595] receiver, or bishop, or primate: Ed. Bas.]. [Note: [Col. 0595] It seems one should read *primo* (“first”).]

### C. II. On the same subject. Pope Nicholas likewise [Note: [Col. 0595] From the preface of Pseudo-Isidore.—Cf. C. 33, q. 2, ch. 3].

All laws, ecclesiastical as well as common and public, command that everything taken from a person be restored to him who has been despoiled of his goods.

### C. III. No one ought to be accused while despoiled of his goods. Pope Stephen likewise, Epistle II [Note: [Col. 0596D] This chapter has been restored to its integrity from the original.] [Note: [Col. 0595] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter composed from *Tripartite History*, book 8, ch. 12, and the third synod under Symmachus; Collectio tripartita, part 1, title 21, ch. 3.—Burchard, book 1, ch. 142; Anselm, book 3, ch. 52; Ivo, Decretum, part 5, ch. 255].

No bishop, while he has been despoiled of his goods or driven from his own see on any pretext, ought to be accused [Col. 0596C], nor may any charge be brought against him by anyone, until he has been restored most fully and everything which had been taken from him by whatever contrivance [Note: [Col. 0595] has been: Ivo; Edd. coll. o.] has been restored according to law, and he himself has been regularly returned to his own see and former condition. Thus the primates and synod must completely restore to the bishop in question all possessions, all estates [Note: [Col. 0595] add.: estates: Ivo] unjustly taken from him, and all their fruits [Note: [Col. 0595] add.: its: Ed. Bas.] received before the accusation was begun [Note: [Col. 0595] begun: Edd. Bas., Lugdd.—received: later editions—conceived: Ivo].

### C. IV. A despoiled person should neither be summoned to a synod nor judged in any matter. Eusebius likewise, to the brethren dwelling throughout Alexandria and Egypt, Epistle II [Note: [Col. 0595] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. the spurious fifth synod of Symmachus.—Anselm, book 3, ch. 44; Ivo Panormia, book 4, ch. 45; Decretum, part 5, ch. 249].

In your letters we have found that certain bishops [Col. 0597A] in your regions have been accused by their own flocks—some, indeed, on suspicion and some upon certain grounds—and that for this reason some have been despoiled of their goods, while others have been driven from their own see [Note: [Col. 0597] expelled: Ed. Bas.—driven away: later editions]. You should know that they can be summoned neither to a provincial synod nor to a general one [Note: [Col. 0597] convened: Edd. coll. o.; Ivo], nor judged in any matter, until everything taken from them [Note: [Col. 0597] offered to them: Ed. Par.—taken from them: later editions except Bas.] has been restored to their control according to law.

### C. V. On the same subject. Pope Julius likewise, in his letter to the Orientals, chs. 35 and 8 [Note: [Col. 0597C] This chapter was composed from the thirty-fifth and eighth decrees of Julius, though with altered wording and a different arrangement.] [Note: [Col. 0597] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter composed after Ennodius’ apology for Symmachus.—Burchard, book 1, ch. 144; Ivo Panormia, book 4, ch. 46; Decretum, part 5, ch. 257].

No one can be summoned [Note: [Col. 0597] called: Ed. Bas.] or judged before everything taken from him and all his rights have been restored to him in full, because one already stripped has no privilege by which he can be stripped further.

[Col. 0597B]

### C. VI. On the same subject. Pope Zephyrinus likewise, to the bishops of Egypt, Epistle II [Note: [Col. 0597] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore, drawn from *Tripartite History*, book 7, ch. 12.—Ivo Panormia, book 4, ch. 43; Decretum, part 5, ch. 246].

It is therefore prescribed in the ancient statutes that bishops who have been expelled and despoiled of their goods should recover their own churches; that all their property should first be restored to them; and then, if anyone wishes justly to accuse them, he should do so at equal risk. Bishops of sound judgment are to be appointed judges and meet in the church where the witnesses for each of those who appeared oppressed are present; nor ought they to be required to answer before everything belonging to them and to their churches has been restored most fully according to law.

## QUESTION III

[Col. 0597C]

**GRATIAN**

**Part I.** The censure of the canons determines what penalty those who fail in an accusation are to suffer. They shall receive the punishment for the charge brought, together with loss of reputation.

Hence Pope Caius [Note: [Col. 0597C] “Caius”: so in most ancient copies, and this chapter occurs in his sole epistle, in which the words of the chapter “If any bishop,” below in the same question, ch. 7, occur immediately before these. In the printed editions Gelasius was cited here.] says [Note: [Col. 0597] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter whose source is Theodosian Code, book 16, title 2, ch. 41.—Anselm, book 3, ch. 46; Alger, part 2, ch. 37]:

### C. I. Concerning those who bring unprovable charges.

If anyone brings against such persons charges which cannot be proved, let him understand by the authority of this enactment that he will suffer the loss of good repute, so that through loss of honour and reputation [Note: [Col. 0597] valuation: Edd. coll. o., except Bas., Lugdd. II, III] he may learn that, at least in future, he is not permitted with impunity to plot against another’s good name.

### C. II. If an accuser fails in his accusation, let him receive retaliation. Pope Damasus likewise, to Archbishop Stephen, Epistle III [Note: [Col. 0597C] These very words of Damasus are cited below, 4, q. 4, ch. *Nullus introducatur*.] [Note: [Col. 0597] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter repeated from Theodosian Code, book 9, title 1].

A false accuser, if he fails in his accusation, shall receive the penalty of retaliation.

[Col. 0598B]

### C. III. On the same subject. From the decree of Pope Hadrian, in the chapters collected by him, ch. 52, in the middle [Note: [Col. 0597] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Pope Fabian, Epistle 3; cf. C. 3, q. 6, ch. 1.—The source is the interpretation of ch. 10, Theodosian Code, book 9, title 1.—Alger, book 2, ch. 47].

Whoever does not prove what he has alleged [Note: [Col. 0597] alleged: Edd. coll. o.] shall himself suffer the punishment which he intended to inflict.

### C. IV. Concerning those who attack someone with false charges. Likewise [Note: [Col. 0597D] “Likewise”: so in most old manuscripts. In the printed editions it read “Pope Damasus likewise.” Yet this chapter occurs in Hadrian’s chapters, ch. 62, and in the Council of Elvira, ch. 75. Ivo cites it from Carthage. In the collections of councils it is joined to Carthage III.] [Note: [Col. 0597] From the Council of Elvira, held no later than A.D. 319, ch. 75; cf. Council of Arles II, ch. 24, and Hadrian’s chapters, ch. 62.—Regino, book 2, ch. 338; Burchard, book 2, ch. 195; from Carthage, Anselm at end of book 3; Ivo, Decretum, part 6, ch. 240].

If anyone attacks [Note: [Col. 0597] brings a charge against: Edd. coll. o.—add.: or accused: same editions except Bas.] a bishop, presbyter, or deacon with false accusations and cannot prove them [Note: [Col. 0597] cannot prove: same editions], we decree that communion is not to be given him even at the end [Note: [Col. 0598C] “Not even at the end”: this is read in the Council of Elvira, not only in this canon but in others also; for that reason, and also because of the gloss, nothing has been altered. Hadrian, however, reads: “unless communion is not to be given him at the end.” Ivo reads: “communion is to be given him only at the end.”] [Note: [Col. 0597] end: Hispana Collection] [Note: [Col. 0597] lacking in the Hispana Collection, Anselm, Ivo, and Burchard].

**Part II. Gratian.** It is one thing not to complete an accusation and another not to prove an insult. The former is permitted to no one without abolition; the latter is permitted to all.

[Col. 0598C] Hence Pope Fabian, to Bishop Hilary, Epistle III [Note: [Col. 0597] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter drawn from the interpretation of Theodosian Code, book 9, title 1, ch. 15; cf. Hadrian’s Chapters, ch. 54.—Anselm, book 3, ch. 89 [87]; Ivo Panormia, book 4, ch. 74; Decretum, part 6, ch. 324]:

### C. V. An insult is not to be regarded as an accusation.

If anyone, in anger, rashly alleges some charge against another [Col. 0599A], the insult is not to be regarded as an accusation. He should be allowed time for consideration and confess in writing that he will prove what he said while angry, so that if, perhaps coming to his senses, he does not wish to repeat or put in writing [Note: [Col. 0599] formally enter in writing: same editions] what he said in anger [Note: [Col. 0599] through anger: Edd. coll. o.] [Note: [Col. 0599] said: same editions except Bas.], he is not held liable as guilty of the charge.

**Part III. Gratian.** But it is one thing to be unable to prove a charge brought [Note: [Col. 0599C] “Prove”: in most copies follows, “because it is false, another …”; but in better copies those words are either absent or added in another hand]; another to abandon an accusation because of some promise. Forgiveness is given to the person who, deceived by a promise, abandons his accusation; but infamy is imposed on one unable to prove the charge brought.

[Note: [Col. 0599C] “Because of a promise”: it must not simply be said that persons who abandon an accusation for some promise are always to be forgiven. In the case of Paul, of whom Blessed Gregory speaks in the chapter below, there were other circumstances explained in the letter itself: “Nevertheless, because it is fitting that we be more merciful than strict, we forgive him this fault and judge that he should be received in his rank and place. For we believe that the affliction he suffered from the time sentence was pronounced has sufficed as punishment for this fault.” Later in the same letter he reports certain acts by the aforementioned Paul for the benefit of the Church which may also have moved Blessed Gregory to greater clemency toward him. Many words of Blessed Gregory had been omitted from the chapter itself; some of them seemed fit to be added.]

Hence Blessed Gregory writes to John, Bishop of Corinth, book IV, Epistle 50 [Note: [Col. 0599] Ep. 52, written A.D. 505, book 5, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 3, ch. 113; Polycarpus, book 1, title 6]:

### C. VI. Concerning one who, enticed by a promise, abandons an accusation.

[Col. 0599B] Although the deacon Paul is greatly shamed [Note: [Col. 0599] add.: and reproved: original; Anselm] by his own fault, because, deceived by a promise, he withdrew from the accusation of his bishop, recently deposed though formerly his bishop, nevertheless we forgive him this fault.

**[PALEA.]**

“Therefore everyone [Note: [Col. 0600C] From “Therefore everyone” to the end, these words are not found in the older and better manuscripts of Gratian; nor are they Gregory’s, but those of Popes Fabian and Hadrian, cited below in q. 8, ch. *Qui crimen*, and 3, q. 6, ch. 1, from Fabian, and in the final chapter from Hadrian’s chapters.] [Note: [Col. 0599] Ivo, Decretum, part 6, ch. 524; cf. C. 3, q. 6, chs. 1 and 18, and C. 6, q. 1, ch. 6] who brings a charge should state in writing that he will prove it. Indeed, a case is always tried where a charge is admitted [Note: [Col. 0599] is tried: Edd. coll. o.]; and whoever does not prove what he has alleged [Note: [Col. 0599] alleged: Edd. coll. o.] shall himself suffer the punishment which he intended to inflict.”

### C. VII. Concerning those who abandon an accusation in order to receive ecclesiastical orders. Gregory likewise, in the same letter [Note: [Col. 0599] Anselm, book 8, ch. 36].

Euphemius and Thomas, who received holy orders in order to abandon the accusation of their bishop [Note: [Col. 0600D] “Of their bishop”: these words are not at this point in the letter, but preceding material indicates that the bishop by whom Euphemius and Thomas were ordained in order to cease accusing him was their own bishop.] [Note: [Col. 0599] of their bishop: lacking in Anselm], we judge to have been deprived of those holy orders [Col. 0599C], and we wish them to remain deposed as they are.

Gratian. From this it is inferred that the infamy of clerics can be removed by the Roman Pontiff, contrary to the statement of Gelasius [Note: [Col. 0599] rather, Calixtus, Epistle 2 [Pseudo-Isidore].—Ivo, Decretum, part 9, ch. 23]: “Although we can save souls through repentance, we cannot remove infamy”; and contrary to Stephen, who, after enumerating causes from which infamy arises, says: “We admit all these to repentance under the mark of perpetual infamy.”

Or else, not all whom secular laws pronounce infamous become infamous by the law of the canons. For the deacon Paul, who withdrew from his accusation without having obtained abolition, recovered the dignity of his office by this authority, although the senatus consultum Turpillianum declares him infamous. We must acknowledge the same concerning a woman who marries within the period of mourning: marriages today are regulated by the law of heaven, not the law of the court; and under the law of heaven a woman, after her husband’s death, is free from the law of her husband: let her marry whom she wishes.

§ 1. But Stephen, on the other hand, writes: “We call infamous all whom secular laws pronounce infamous.” Yet the statement of Gelasius and Stephen [Note: [Col. 0599] C. 6, q. 1, ch. 17], “Although [we can save] souls,” and “Under the mark of perpetual infamy,” is understood of persons on whom infamy is imposed by a civil judge. As their examination and punishment belong to the civil judge, so also does their restoration to full legal status. But in the case of a woman who marries during mourning, this does not conflict with Stephen’s statement, “We call infamous,” etc. Since secular laws, especially in marriage, do not disdain to follow sacred canons, they do not appear to pronounce infamous a woman whose marriage is not unlawful by apostolic and canonical authority.

**Part IV. § 2.** It should also be noted that it is one thing when someone repents of having made a criminal accusation and entered it in writing, if he has been acquitted by the innocent person; another when he has received money from a guilty person in order to desist from proving what he alleged.

[Col. 0600C] Hence one reads in the *Book of Capitularies*, ch. 175 [Note: [Col. 0599] Rather, in the interpretation of Theodosian Code, book 9, title 37, ch. 1. Ivo, Decretum, part 16, ch. 251]:

### C. VIII. Concerning one who repents of having made a criminal accusation.

If anyone repents of having made a criminal accusation and entered in writing something which he could not prove, and if he reaches an agreement with the accused person who is innocent [Note: [Col. 0599] lacking in Edd. coll. o., except Bas.], let them mutually absolve one another. But if the judge finds that the accused person is guilty, and an agreement has been made between the defendant [Col. 0601A] and the accuser by corrupt collusion [Note: [Col. 0601D] “By corrupt collusion”: Ivo reads: “If a corrupt agreement is made concerning collusion, he shall receive the penalty established by law.” But the interpretation of Law 1 in the Theodosian Code reads: “If an agreement is made through corruption concerning release from liability, the person proved guilty, collusion set aside, shall receive the penalty established by law.”], let him receive the penalty established by law [Note: [Col. 0601] receive: Edd. Arg., Bas.].

**Part V. Gratian.** It should also be noted, as is read in Digest, book XLVIII, title *On the Abolition of Crimes*, law I [Note: [Col. 0601] fr. 1 ff., *On the Senatus Consultum Turpillianum and the Abolition of Crimes*, 48.16]: “The rashness of accusers is exposed in three ways and subjected to three penalties. For they either calumniate, prevaricate, or withdraw. To calumniate is to bring false charges; to prevaricate is to conceal true charges; to withdraw is to desist altogether from the accusation.”

§ 1. The penalty is lawfully imposed upon calumniators [Note: [Col. 0601] by the lex Remmia: original]. Yet anyone who fails to prove what he alleges is not thereby immediately considered a calumniator. Inquiry into that matter is entrusted to the discretion of the cognizant judge, who, after acquitting the accused, begins to inquire into the accuser’s purpose: with what intention he proceeded to the accusation. If he finds an honest error, he acquits him; but if he finds him guilty of manifest calumny, he imposes the legal penalty. Either result is made clear in the very words of the judgment. If he pronounces, “You have not proved it,” he has spared him; but if he pronounces, “You have calumniated,” he has condemned him. Even if he has added nothing concerning the penalty, the authority of the law will nevertheless be exercised against him. For, as Papinian answered, the question of fact lies in the judge’s discretion, but prosecution of the penalty is entrusted not to his will but reserved to the authority of the law.

But if, in an interlocutory ruling [Note: [Col. 0602D] Up to this point Gratian had reported the words of the jurist. From here until the words “It is necessary,” he reports only the sense.], he says, “Titius appears to have accused rashly,” he has not pronounced him a calumniator. Rashness admits pardon as a matter of easy credulity [Note: [Col. 0601] good fortune: Ed. Bas.], and unconsidered heat is free from the fault of calumny [Col. 0601C]; therefore no penalty ought to be inflicted upon him.

Ulpian, book XLVII, title *On Prevaricators*, law 1 [Note: [Col. 0601] book 47, title 18, fr. 1 ff.]:

§ 2. A prevaricator is, as it were, a “straddler,” one who assists the opposing side after betraying his own case. Labeo says that the name is taken from a shifting contest [Note: [Col. 0601] contest: Edd. coll. o., Lugdd. II, III]. For one who prevaricates takes his stand on both sides—indeed, on the other side. Properly speaking, however, he is called a prevaricator who has accused in a public proceeding. An advocate, on the other hand, is not properly called a prevaricator. What then shall be done with him? Whether he has prevaricated in a private or a public proceeding—that is, betrayed his case—he is customarily punished extra ordinem.

§ 3. It should be known that today an extraordinary penalty is imposed upon those who have prevaricated.

And below:

§ 4. An accuser convicted of prevarication may not thereafter accuse under the law.

§ 5. In all cases, except capital ones, anyone who corrupts an informer is considered defeated [Note: [Col. 0601] add.: by senatorial decree: Ed. Arg.—by the senatus consultum Turpillianum: later editions].

And below, in book XLVIII, title *On Abolitions of Crimes*:

§ 6. We have shown that he is a prevaricator who colludes with the accused and performs the office of accuser merely as a formality, because he suppresses his own proofs while admitting the accused’s false defences [Note: [Col. 0601] accusations: Ed. Bas.].

§ 7. If anyone withdraws from an accusation without abolition, he is punished. Abolition is customarily requested and obtained privately from governors; likewise before the tribunal, not summarily; nor may a governor delegate this cognizance to another. If the same person has brought several charges against the same person, he must request abolition for each one; otherwise [Col. 0602B], according to what he has committed [Note: [Col. 0601] omitted: Edd. coll. o., Lugdd. II, III], he shall suffer, under the name of that charge, the penalty of the senatorial decree.

Under the same title: We understand him to have withdrawn [Note: [Col. 0601] fr. 13, *On the Senatus Consultum Turpillianum*] who has wholly abandoned his intention to proceed, not one who has postponed [Note: [Col. 0601] has postponed: Edd. coll. o., except Bas.] the accusation. But one who withdrew from the accusation by the emperor’s permission goes unpunished [Note: [Col. 0601] withdrew: Ed. Bas.].

§ 8. For abolition remits the penalty but does not remove infamy. Hence the Emperors Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian, Augusti, are read to have said in book IX of the Code, under the same title *On General Abolition* [Note: [Col. 0601] ch. 3, title 43]: “Indulgence, conscript fathers, marks those whom it frees from punishment [Note: [Col. 0601] add.: from punishment: Edd. coll. o., except Bas.]; it does not remove the infamy of the crime, but grants remission of the penalty.” But if the emperor says, “I restore you to full legal status,” he removes infamy.

Hence, in the same book, under the title *On Those Who Have Received Sentence and Been Restored*, the Emperor Antoninus is read to have said to a person deported to an island [Note: [Col. 0601] ch. 1, title 51]: “I restore you to full legal status in your province,” [Col. 0602C] and he added: “But that you may know what it is to restore someone to full legal status, I restore you to your honours, your order, and all else besides.”

## QUESTION V [Note: [Col. 0602D] He places the fifth after the third because the subject of these questions is very similar.]

**GRATIAN**

**Part I.** When accusers fail, the accused does not appear to be compellable to clear himself. For just as a possessor who is sued is not compelled, when the plaintiff fails, to prove his title to possession, so the person attacked is not believed to be compellable to prove his innocence. By the authority also of Pope Cornelius and the Council of Tribur, priests are forbidden to swear except for the right faith.

[Col. 0603A] For Cornelius says in Epistle II to Rufus, bishop of the East [Note: [Col. 0603D] In old manuscripts this chapter is joined with the following two, which are from the same epistle of Pope Cornelius.] [Note: [Col. 0603] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter drawn from act 1 of the Council of Constantinople, held A.D. 448; Collectio tripartita, part 1, title 19, ch. 1; Burchard, book 1, ch. 193; Ivo, Decretum, part 5, ch. 308 and part 12, ch. 77]:

### C. I. An oath is not to be demanded of priests.

We have never known an oath to be demanded of the highest priests [Note: [Col. 0603D] “Highest”: this is the original reading. But Burchard and Ivo, in part 5, have “from bishops and the remaining orders”; Ivo, in part 12, has “from the highest priests or other ministers of God.”] [Note: [Col. 0603] from priests or other ministers of God: Edd. coll. o.], or of ministers of God, except for the right faith; nor do we find that they have sworn voluntarily.

### C. II. On the same subject. The same, a little below [Note: [Col. 0603] Collectio tripartita, same place; Burchard, same place; Ivo, part 12, ch. 77].

Following the examples of the saints, we uphold the laws of the holy apostles and their successors, and forbid the taking of imprudent oaths.

### C. III. On the same subject. The same, in the same place [Note: [Col. 0603] Collections cited].

We do not know of an oath having been imposed upon bishops, nor ought it ever to be done [Note: [Col. 0603D] “Ought”: the following words, “except for the right faith,” have been removed because they occur neither in the best manuscripts nor at this place in the epistle itself, but above in the same ch. 1].

[Col. 0603B]

### C. IV. If a presbyter has a complaint against a layman, or a layman against a presbyter, it is to be settled at the bishop’s command. From the Council of Tribur, ch. 21 [Note: [Col. 0603] held A.D. 895; Burchard, book 2, ch. 182; Ivo Panormia, book 5, ch. 10; Decretum, part 6, ch. 227].

If a presbyter has any disputed complaint against a layman, or a layman against a presbyter, it shall be settled at the bishop’s command without respect of persons. The layman shall clear himself by an oath, if necessary; but the presbyter shall be examined through his holy consecration in place of an oath [Note: [Col. 0603] instead of an oath: original], because priests ought not to swear for a trivial cause. For shall the hand through which Christ’s body and blood are consecrated be defiled by an oath? Far be it! For the Lord says in the Gospel to His disciples—whose place we unworthy men hold in the holy Church—[Note: [Col. 0603] Matt. 5:34]: “Do not swear at all. But let your speech be: Yes, yes; No, no.” Whatever exceeds these is from evil [Col. 0603C] [Note: [Col. 0603] from: Burchard; Edd. coll. o., except Bas., Lugdd. II, III].

**Part II. Gratian.** Yet these authorities do not prohibit priests from taking every sort of oath, but only imprudent oaths and those offered before a temporal court for any kind of cause. But when priests are oppressed by popular infamy, they ought to offer oaths in affirmation of their innocence.

[Col. 0604A] Hence Pope Gregory III [Note: [Col. 0603] Rather Gregory II, A.D. 726; Burchard, book 1, title 2, ch. 186; Anselm, book 3, ch. 79; Ivo Panormia, book 5, ch. 9; Decretum, part 6, ch. 231] writes to Boniface, Epistle I:

### C. V. A priest accused by the people is to affirm his innocence by oath.

If a presbyter, or any priest whatever, has been accused by the people, and reliable witnesses are not found who can establish the truth of the charge brought, an oath shall be made publicly, and he shall produce as witness to the purity of his innocence Him to whom all things are naked and open.

[Note: Other collected editions add “found.”]

[Note: The cited collections read “who declare the truth concerning the charge brought”; other collected editions, “of the charge brought.”]

[Note: Ivo reads “he shall make [the oath] publicly”; other collected editions, “he shall make [it] in public.”]

### C. VI. Concerning Bishop Leo, whom Blessed Gregory caused to furnish a purgation

Likewise from the *Register* of Gregory, book II, indiction 10, epistle 23 [Note: Epistle 33 (written A.D. 592), book 2, Maurist edition.—Burchard, book 1, ch. 194. Anselm, book 6, ch. 162. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, ch. 5. *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 309. *Polycarpus*, book 6, title 11.], to Justin the Praetor [Note: “Praetor”: In Gratian manuscripts it is “the Emperor.” In the printed epistle one reads “to Justin the Presbyter”; but this was corrected from two old manuscripts of the letters and from Polycarpus. This is the same Justin to whom epistle 2 of book I was written; in printed books the address of that letter is uncorrupted.] [Note: “the Emperor”: cited collections—other collected editions.]

It is a particular trait of the envy of the ancient enemy that those whom it cannot cast down into the commission of wicked deeds—God resisting it—it tears to pieces in their reputations by inventing falsehoods for the occasion. Therefore, since an adverse report had spread certain allegations against the priestly character of Leo, our brother and fellow bishop, we caused the question whether they were true to be investigated for a long time and with strictness, and found in him no fault concerning the matters alleged. But lest anything should seem to have been omitted which might leave doubt in our hearts, we caused him, beyond what was required, to take solemn oaths at the most sacred body of Blessed Peter the Apostle. When these had been given, we rejoiced with great exultation that by such a test his innocence shone forth plainly. Therefore let Your Glory receive the aforesaid man with every charity, and show him the reverence appropriate to a priest, lest any doubt concerning matters now purged remain in hearts. Rather, you ought in every respect to adhere most devotedly to the bishop named above, so that in his person, whose minister he is, you may seem fittingly and becomingly to honour God.

[Note: “wicked”: other collected editions.]

[Note: “had spread”: original text; cited collections and other collected editions read differently.]

[Note: “omitted”: other collected editions read “ambiguous.”]

[Note: “him”: Böhm, against the source, reads “them.”]

[Note: “a priest”: some editions and Ivo’s *Panormia* read “the priest.”]

[Note: “lest any”: Böhm reads “nor any”; the original reads “nor a certain [doubt].”]

[Note: “But”: other collected editions read “And.”]

### C. VII. How Blessed Gregory caused Bishop Menna to be purged by oath

Likewise from the same author, to Brunhild, Queen of the Franks, book XI, epistle 8 [Note: Epistle 7 (written A.D. 603), book 3, Maurist edition.—Burchard, book 1, ch. 196. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, ch. 6. *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 311. *Polycarpus*, book 1.]

But after investigating the allegations that had been made against Menna, our most reverend brother and fellow bishop, and finding him guilty in no respect, we permitted him to return there cleansed and absolved. For, having moreover given satisfaction under oath at the most sacred body of Blessed Peter the Apostle, he showed himself free from the charges made against his reputation. As it was right that, if he had persisted guilty in any matter, we should punish his fault canonically, so it was not right that, his innocence assisting him, we should retain or afflict him any longer in any respect.

[Note: “had been made”: other collected editions read “are”; Ivo reads “will have been.”]

[Note: “are”: Basel edition.]

### §1

Nevertheless, we entrust to your discretion that he himself furnish before you a purgation, joined by two priests of his own order, if the accuser withdraws.

[Note: “Purgation”: Here there was a very serious error. For these words were read together with the preceding passage addressed to Brunhild, as though Blessed Gregory had entrusted the purgation of a presbyter to a woman. But nothing of the kind is found in Blessed Gregory’s letter from which the first part of this chapter was taken. Rather, Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, ch. 15, and *Panormia*, book 5, ch. 8, cite this from a letter of Alexander II to Raynald, bishop of Como; that letter begins below in the same question, “Concerning the case.” This sentence, “We entrust the purgation,” must be read continuously after the final words of that chapter. The learned men’s citations did not prompt a correction here; rather, the name of Alexander II was added in the margin. Thus no ground remains for the glossator’s astonishment, since Roman pontiffs are nowhere found to have entrusted cases of this kind to women.]

[Note: From the letter of Alexander II to Raynald of Como; compare ch. 11 of this question.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, ch. 8. *Decretum*, part 10, ch. 15.]

[Note: Basel edition adds “here.”]

[Note: Other collected editions, except Basel, read “we entrusted.”]

Finally, we neither permit him to undergo, nor in any way wish you to demand, the popular law which is supported by no canonical sanction—namely, the ordeal of boiling or cold water, the touching of red-hot iron, or any other popular contrivance (since these are wholly invented by the fabricating of envy). Indeed, by apostolic authority we most firmly prohibit it.

[Note: “all”: Basel edition.]

### C. VIII. Concerning Maximus, Bishop of Salona, who purged himself by oath

Likewise Gregory to Castorius, notary of Ravenna, book VII, indiction 2, epistle 80 [Note: Epistle 80 (written A.D. 599), book 9, Maurist edition.—Collection in three parts, part 1, title 35, ch. 10.]

The more confidence is placed in you by us, and the more necessary the causes which you see laid upon you, the more energetic and diligent you ought to show yourself. Therefore, if Maximus of Salona, after taking an oath, has affirmed that he is not infected with the Simoniacal heresy, and, when questioned only about the other charges before the body of Saint Apollinaris, has answered that he is innocent, and has done penance for his disobedience, as we directed, we wish your experience to give him, for his consolation, the letter which we wrote to him, in which we indicated that we had restored to him our favour and communion. For as it is fitting that we be severe toward those who persist in contumacy, so we ought not to deny room for pardon to those who have been humbled and repent.

[Note: Other collected editions read “trust is placed [in you].”]

[Note: The same editions read “you ought to show yourself.”]

[Note: “most holy”: Basel edition.]

[Note: “for consoling”: Basel, Venice I and II, and Nuremberg read “for consulting.”]
