[Note: Other collected editions read “by which we also indicated to him…”]

[Note: “humiliated”: Lyons II reads “humility.”]

### C. IX. Concerning the same

The same author to Marinianus, Bishop of Ravenna, book VII, epistle 79 [Note: Epistle 81 (written A.D. 599), book 9, Maurist edition.—Collection in three parts, same place, ch. 11.—*Polycarpus*, book 1, title 2, ch. 37.]

You have learned from the letters which we previously sent you what is to be done in Maximus’s case. But because we learned, from the report of Castorius, our chartulary who bears this letter, what the will and especially the request of your Fraternity is in this matter, therefore, if Maximus himself before you and our aforesaid chartulary has purged himself by oath of the Simoniacal heresy, and, when questioned only about the other matters before the body of Saint Apollinaris, as we wrote, has answered that he is free, we commit to the judgment of your Fraternity his case concerning the fact that, while excommunicated, he presumed to celebrate the solemnities of Mass: namely, what penance ought to purge such a fault. Therefore dispose securely whatever seems good to you according to God, and have no doubt concerning us. For whatever you shall determine in this matter, we receive gratefully and willingly admit.

[Note: “are”: other collected editions.]

[Note: “most holy”: Basel edition.]

[Note: “gratefully”: Strasbourg reads “freely”; the remaining editions read “gladly.”]

### C. X. How Sixtus purged himself

Likewise Sixtus, Pope III, letter to the Eastern bishops, ch. 1 [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled for the *Liber Pontificalis*.—Collection in three parts, part 3, book 10, ch. 10.]

You directed me to write to you how the present dispute against me arose, and by whom, so that it might be repelled by your assistance and my case established. Know that I am accused by one Bassus and unjustly persecuted. On hearing this, the Emperor Valentinian ordered a synod to be assembled by our authority. When the council had been held, I gave satisfaction to all after a thorough examination and, although I could sufficiently have escaped by another means, I nevertheless avoided suspicion and purified myself before all; that is, I freed myself from suspicion and hostile rivalry. Yet I did not thereby give others who are unwilling, or who do not freely choose this, a rule or an example for doing so.

[Note: Basel adds “here.”]

[Note: Other collected editions read “of doing.”]

### C. XI. Concerning the case of the presbyter Guilland

Likewise Alexander [Note: Letter of uncertain date.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, ch. 8. *Decretum*, part 10, ch. 15.] to Raynald [Note: Ivo reads “Ramaldo”; Basel, “Runaldo”; the remaining editions, “Rimaldo”], Bishop of Como.

Concerning the case of your presbyter Guilland, who has been defamed in connection with the death of his bishop, your predecessor, we have taken counsel publicly. Therefore, with the unanimous agreement of the brethren present, we write to Your Belovedness that the aforesaid presbyter Guilland is to appear before you. There, if reliable accusers are lacking, then, justice so dictating, the presbyter shall without any controversy recover both the priesthood and the whole benefices which he unjustly lost on that account.

[Note: Other collected editions read “Gilland.”]

[Note: Other editions read “we report.”]

[Note: Other editions read “be presented again.”]

[Note: Other editions read “shall have lost.”]

[Note: “Benefices”: In the letter, this is followed by the sentence “We entrust the purgation,” above under the same question, chapter “Menna,” as noted there.]

### C. XII. Concerning the purgation of clerics if they cannot be convicted

Likewise from the Council of Agde [Note: This clearly does not belong to the Council of Agde. In the penitential published by Canisius, *Lectiones antiquae*, vol. 2, it is cited as from a great council under King Louis. This chapter was taken from the Council of Mainz held in A.D. 851, edited among the *Monumenta Germaniae Historica* of Pertz, vol. III, p. 413.—Compare *Capitularies*, book 5, ch. 34.—Burchard, book 2, ch. 181. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, ch. 1. *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 226.—Ch. 1, Compilation I, “On canonical purgation,” and ch. 2, *X*, same title.]

If lawful accusers cannot prove the crimes of a priest and he denies them, then he shall purge himself of the charge with seven companions of his own order, if he is able. But if a deacon is accused of the same crime, he shall exculpate himself with three.

[Note: “Crimes”: Other collectors read: “But if there are no lawful accusers who undertake to prove his crimes by manifest judgments, and he himself,” etc.]

[Note: Canisius, in the cited place, reads “six.” This agrees remarkably with the Council of Carthage, ch. 20 in Dionysius, which the authors of this chapter followed.]

### C. XIII. Concerning the same

Likewise from the Council of Lleida [Note: This chapter is likewise of uncertain origin. Compare, however, *Capitularies*, book 5, ch. 36, and the capitula of Isaac of Langres in Baluze, vol. 2, ch. 3.—Burchard, book 2, ch. 184. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, ch. 9. *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 229.]

If a presbyter has been defamed by an evil reputation among the people entrusted to him, and the bishop cannot establish the matter by lawful witnesses, he shall be suspended until adequate satisfaction is made, lest the people of the faithful suffer scandal through him. Adequate satisfaction is, as the elders are said to have established, when, whether according to the canons or at the bishop’s discretion, he joins to himself seven colleagues and swears upon the most holy Gospel set before him that he did not commit the crime charged against him. Once purified by this satisfaction, let him thereafter discharge his office without fear.

[Note: Basel reads “and if.”]

[Note: “As established by the elders”: Here, as also somewhat below, other collectors contain more words.]

[Note: “Most holy”: In the same sources one reads: “upon the holy Gospel placed before him,” as in the chapter *Testimony*, in the sentence *No one [shall accuse] a cleric*, below, 11, question 1.]

### C. XIV. Concerning the same. PALEA

[Likewise Pope Sylvester [Note: It is cited here from Sylvester. Almost the same passage occurs in the decretal title “On simony,” ch. *The accused*, where it is attributed to Pope Deusdedit. But nothing of this kind has been found in extant writings of either of these two pontiffs. In the register of Blessed Gregory, book 5, epistle 3, to Maximus, presumptuous officer of the Church of Salona, are these words: “It has therefore come to us that you were ordained through the Simoniacal heresy. Many other allegations against you have also been made here, one in particular being the reason why we found it necessary most emphatically to forbid you in writing to celebrate the solemnities of Mass until we could discover what the truth was.” This *Palea*, ch. *The accused*, and ch. *Whenever*, *X*, “On simony,” appear to have been taken from this letter. Its opening is: “Whenever against…”] [Note: Rather, from Gregory the Great’s letter to Maximus, book 6, epistle 13, written A.D. 596.]]

> “We found it necessary most emphatically to forbid in writing one accused of Simony to celebrate the solemnities of Mass until we could learn more truly what the matter was.”

[Note: “more truly” is absent from the Strasbourg edition.]

### C. XV. PALEA

[Likewise from the Council of Tribur [Note: Burchard also cites Council of Tribur, ch. 10; and the printed Council of Tribur contains several matters relevant to this question.] [Note: In the Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895, which Burchard, book 16, ch. 19 cites, only the sense occurs. Regino, book 2, ch. 43, and Burchard, book 6, ch. 7, cite certain similar matters from the Council of Mainz held under Rabanus. Yet Theodore of Canterbury seems to be the author of the chapter, since it has been found among his capitula.—Compare ch. 1, “On popular purgation,” Compilation I; ch. 1, *X*, “On canonical purgation.”—This *Palea* is absent from the Basel edition.]]

> “If a nobleman or freeborn man is accused in a synod and denies the charge, and if he is known to be a believer, let him purge himself with twelve freeborn men. If he has previously been caught in theft, perjury, or false testimony, he shall not be admitted to an oath, but, like one who is not freeborn, shall purge himself by boiling water or red-hot iron.”

[Note: Strasbourg reads “shall purge himself.”]

### C. XVI. Concerning the same

Likewise Hincmar, Bishop of Reims [Note: This chapter is reported in the ninth canon of the Council of Trosly at Reims as from a synod held by Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims.] [Note: Ch. 24, capitula of Hincmar of Reims, Mansi, vol. 15. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 420.]

If an evil report concerning a presbyter has arisen and lawful accusers and witnesses are lacking, then, lest the hearts of the weak be struck by the presbyter’s evil reputation contrary to the Apostle, lest our ministry be disparaged, and lest presbyters, becoming too secure, fall more freely into sin, he shall clear his reputation by oath, according to the decrees of the elders, with neighbouring presbyters named for this purpose, whom we know to be unwilling to commit perjury.

[Note: Basel reads “have failed.”]

[Note: “According to the decrees”: The synod reads: “according to the decree of Gregory the Younger, an oath shall be made publicly, and the presbyter of evil reputation shall have, in the oath for his purgation, Him as witness whom he will also have as judge.”]

### C. XVII. Concerning the same. [PALEA]

Likewise Innocent to the Patriarch of Aquileia and the Bishop of Mantua [Note: This chapter occurs in the decretal title “On canonical purgation” and is attributed to Innocent III. But it seemed that there was an error there, III being put for II. For the compiler of the decretals ordinarily observes this order among pontiffs, citing first those who preceded; thus, since this chapter occurs there before several canons of Alexander and Lucius III, who preceded Innocent III, it does not seem attributable to him, although it is also ascribed to him among his works after the sermons and in the councils divided into four volumes, vol. 3. Moreover, this entire chapter is absent from most manuscript codices of Gratian, even those in which *Paleae* usually occur. From the sentence “We therefore” to the end it is absent from all.] [Note: Letter of Innocent II, of uncertain date.—Compare ch. 4, Compilation I; ch. 5, *X*, “On canonical purgation.”—Omitted in the Basel edition.]

> “We do not think Your Prudence unaware how often our brother, the Bishop of Trent, has been accused of Simony in our presence and in yours. When his cause was at length examined in our presence, accusers were brought forward against him, asserting orally and in writing that he had given the church of Saint Peter of Pado to the presbyter Paul for four modii of grain which he had received from the laymen of that church. But since neither accusers nor witnesses could proceed in the case according to the form of the canons and the enactments of the holy Fathers, by the common counsel of our brethren we judge that he must purge himself in your presence of the aforesaid Simony with the third hand (*tertia manu*) of his own order and four abbots and religious priests.

> “The form of the purgation shall be as follows. First, the bishop himself shall swear upon the holy Gospels that neither he himself personally, nor through a subordinate person, nor anyone else acting for him with his knowledge, received a price for giving the church of Saint Peter of Pado to the presbyter Paul. Then the purgators shall swear upon the holy Gospels that, as they believe, he has sworn truthfully. Entrusting the course of this case to your prudence, we command you to take care to assemble in one suitable place and there restore the case itself, by the Lord’s help, according to the present tenor, so that henceforth every scruple concerning this question may be removed and each party’s justice preserved. If any of you cannot attend because a definite cause prevents him, those of you who can be present shall conclude the same judgment. But if our aforesaid brother A. has made the prescribed purgation, restore to him by our authority the aforesaid office and the Church of Trent. We command that this purgation be completed before the coming Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary.”

[Note: “in our”: other collected editions and Compilation I read “in ours and yours.”]

[Note: “orally”: Compilation I reads “by one voice.”]

[Note: Other collected editions read “in writing.”]

[Note: Compilation I reads “of Pasorum.”]

[Note: Strasbourg and Lyons read “counsel”; Compilation I likewise.]

[Note: “third hand”: the Decretals read “fourth.”]

[Note: “purgation”: other collected editions read “exculpation.”]

[Note: “purgators”: the same editions read “exculpators.”]

[Note: Strasbourg adds “likewise”; the remaining editions add “that is.”]

[Note: Strasbourg reads “has sworn”; the text reads “swore.”]

[Note: Other collected editions, except Lyons II and III, read “into the case.”]

[Note: Rome reads “and you,” through a printer’s error.]

[Note: Strasbourg reads “business.”]

Gratian. In the authorities set out above, it is understood that the accused must wish to purge himself: thus the sacred canons impose upon the accused a manner, not a necessity, of purgation. This appears from the conclusion of the chapter of Pope Sixtus and from the authority of Leo, who, having performed a purgation, says of himself:

### C. XVIII. Concerning Leo: how he purified himself

[Note: This chapter is of Leo III. The whole history of the false accusation against him and his purgation is recounted in old pontificals, from which Saint Antoninus took a large part in part 2 of his history, title 14, ch. 1, §8. Marianus Scotus and Aimoin, book 4, ch. 90, also mention it. In Burchard and Ivo this chapter is fuller, and the following seemed worthy of note: “Therefore I, Leo, Pontiff of the Holy Roman Church, judged by no one and compelled by no one, but by my own free will, purify myself in your presence, before God and His angels, who know my conscience, and before Blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, in whose presence we stand, because I neither committed nor ordered to be committed those criminal and wicked acts which they charge against me. God is my witness, before whose judgment we are to come and in whose presence we stand. I do this of my own free will in order to remove evil suspicions, not as though it were found in the canons, or as though I were imposing this custom or decree in the holy Church upon my successors, or upon our brethren and fellow bishops, but so that you may better cut off rebellious thoughts.”]

It has been heard, dearest brothers, how wicked men have fabricated serious crimes against me. Therefore I, Leo, Pontiff of the Holy Roman Church, purify myself in your presence before God and His angels, because I neither committed nor ordered to be committed those criminal and wicked acts which they charge against me. But in doing this I prescribe no law for others requiring them to do the same.

[Note: A fabricated chapter from the book of the Roman Order.—Burchard, book 1, ch. 198; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, ch. 4; *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 313.]

[Note: Other collected editions read “to commit.”]

Gratian. See how the supreme pontiff purges himself, yet does not prescribe to others a necessity of purgation. Hence it is understood that the satisfaction of purgation rests in the will of the accused, not in the discretion of the judge. But since at the Council of Lleida a presbyter is ordered to be suspended until adequate satisfaction, and since in Leo’s decree the number of associates with whom a priest must purge himself is placed in the bishop’s discretion, it is clear that he must be compelled to purgation, and that it does not rest in his own will but in the discretion of the judge.

Accordingly Pope Leo, writing to King Charles, says [Note: Among the collectors this chapter is reported as though taken from a decretal letter of Leo to Charles. But from book 5 of the *Capitularies*, where this is ch. 34 itself, and from the very form of the wording, it is sufficiently clear that this capitulary was issued in the name of Charlemagne after consultation with Leo III and with the counsel of many bishops. Yet the pious prince, because he appeared to have arrogated jurisdiction over presbyters to himself, corrected it in book 7 of the *Capitularies*, ch. 281, writing as follows: “We wish all of you, both present and future, to know that, after consultation with the Apostolic See, all our bishops and other priests, and especially all our faithful, we dealt with the case of the purgation of accused priests and decreed that it be carried out with witnesses, as contained in our earlier capitulary, because we did not know that the same matter had been determined by Blessed Pope Gregory. For when we held a general assembly at Worms, a letter of Blessed Pope Gregory was brought to us by Riculf, metropolitan of Mainz, containing among other things the following: ‘But concerning a presbyter, or any priest accused by the people, if reliable witnesses are not found who can establish the truth of the charge brought, an oath shall be made publicly, and he shall produce as witness to the purity of his innocence Him to whom all things are naked and open; and thus he shall remain in his own rank.’ Since all these matters exceed our powers, we leave them to be decided by the judgment of bishops according to canonical sanction, so that, when such matters arise, they may strive to decide them in such a way as to incur neither just reproach according to the world nor—God forbid—condemnation before the Lord, but, with the help of Him who gives all things without deceit, may obtain the rewards of eternal blessedness.”] [Note: From Charlemagne’s Capitularies, A.D. 803; compare *Capitularies of the Kings of the Franks*, book 5, ch. 36.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, ch. 3, “Decretal and response of Leo to Charles.” *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 419, “Decree and response of Pope Leo to Emperor Charles.”]

### C. XIX. How priests ought to purge themselves

We do not doubt that it is known to all of you by sight or hearing that, very often through the persuasion of the ancient enemy, diverse crimes are charged against priests. But although, in the time of your lord father Pippin of blessed memory, or in earlier times, the question of what reasonable examination and satisfaction should be made concerning such charges was often discussed by holy Fathers and other men of good devotion, we have nevertheless been unable to find it fully and clearly determined. In our times the same matter has often been discussed by holy bishops, other priests, and ministers of every ecclesiastical rank dwelling in your kingdoms or elsewhere for God, and by us acting with them, because of the many and excessive complaints which have reached us from different regions.

But we wish you to know all this: by the counsel of our lord and father Leo, the Apostolic [Pope], the other bishops of the Roman Church, the remaining priests, the eastern and Greek patriarchs, many holy bishops and priests, our bishops, all other priests and Levites, and all our faithful and counsellors, it has been determined by their authority, agreement, counsel, reason, and necessity that, whenever a crime is charged against any priest, if the accuser is a person who ought to be received—for the canons set forth fully what persons may be admitted to accuse priests—then, if that canonically admissible accuser can prove the charge before the bishops with the lawful number of true and worthy witnesses, the priest shall be judged canonically and, if found guilty, condemned canonically. But if the accuser cannot prove him upon the grounds stated above, this too shall be determined canonically.

Therefore, if that priest is under suspicion or is not believed by his bishop, his fellow priests, or good and just men from his people or congregation, then, lest he remain under the charge or the aforesaid suspicion, he shall restore himself to the Church as purged by an oath made before the people upon the four Gospels. He shall do this with three, five, or seven good neighbouring priests, following the example of Pope Leo, who had twelve bishops at his purgation, or with more if his bishop judges it appropriate or sees that necessity requires it because of popular tumult; and with other good and just men. Whoever wishes to know what witnesses should be received for accusing priests, and what is to be done concerning an accuser, will be able to find it fully in the canons.

[Note: “are charged”: other collected editions read “are being charged.”]

[Note: The original and Ivo read “because how.”]

[Note: Other editions read “reasonably.”]

[Note: Basel reads “blessed.”]

[Note: The original reads “our lord father”; other editions add “of faith and.”]

[Note: Other editions read “fully something concerning it.”]

[Note: The original reads “your”; Basel reads “our.”]

[Note: The original reads “us”; Basel reads “you.”]

[Note: Other collected editions read “from” in place of “out of.”]

[Note: “our bishops”: Printed editions had “our Roman bishops.” But “Roman” is absent not only from the capitulary but also from older Gratian manuscripts and from Ivo. The *Panormia* reads: “our bishops and all Roman priests.”]

[Note: The original reads “you all.”]

[Note: “true”: Ivo and other collected editions read “living.”]

[Note: Other sources read “shall be judged.”]

[Note: The following words through “had” also occur in the other collectors, but not in the capitulary.]

[Note: Ivo omits “be present”; other editions read “be.”]

[Note: The original and Ivo read “what”; other editions read “whatever.”]

[Note: Ivo and other editions read “be found.”]

### Part III. Gratian

But purgation by an oath involving red-hot iron or boiling water is not to be added.

Accordingly Stephen V, to Humbert [Note: The name ought apparently to read “Luitpert”; compare ch. 13, Distinction 16. Basel reads “Lampert”; other collected editions, “Hubert.”], Bishop of Mainz [Note: Letter of not entirely certain date.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, ch. 27.]:

### C. XX. The ordeal of red-hot iron and boiling water is forbidden to be carried out in the Church

You have consulted us concerning infants found dead while sleeping in one bed with their parents: whether the parents ought to purify themselves by red-hot iron, boiling water, or any other ordeal, in proof that they did not crush them. Parents must be warned and admonished not to place such tender children in one bed with themselves, lest through any negligence they be suffocated or crushed and their parents thus be found guilty of homicide. For the sacred canons do not judge that a confession may be extorted from anyone by the test of red-hot iron or boiling water; and what has not been sanctioned by the teaching of the holy Fathers must not be presumed through superstitious invention.

Offences made public by voluntary confession or by the proof of witnesses are to be judged by our governance with the fear of God before our eyes. But hidden and unknown matters are to be left to Him who alone knows the hearts of the children of men. Those, however, who are proved or confess themselves guilty of such an offence are to be punished by your moderation. For if one who destroys a conceived child in the womb by abortion is a murderer, how much more will one who kills an infant even one day old be unable to excuse himself from being a murderer?

[Note: The phrase “are entrusted to our governance” is absent from Ivo.]

[Note: Basel reads “of such a charge.”]

[Note: Basel reads “accuse” instead of “excuse.”]

Gratian. Whether this applies to every kind of purgation, or only to these two kinds which seem prohibited here, is not without reason doubtful because of the sacrifice of jealousy and Gregory’s statement [Note: Compare Causa 33, question 1, ch. 1.]: “If a man who is said to be of a frigid nature can establish by a true judgment that he has never known his wife, let him be separated from her.”

### C. XXI

[Note: In printed editions this chapter had the name *Palea* placed before it; but in all manuscripts collated it occurs without the name *Palea*, and indeed joined to the preceding chapter. Certainly the sentence “But every such…” seems to show that this passage from Numbers was cited by Gratian himself.]

[Note: These are Gratian’s own words.]

For in the Book of Numbers [Note: Other collected editions, except Strasbourg and Basel, read “Numbers”; compare Numbers ch. 5.] one reads that the Lord commanded Moses to speak to the children of Israel and say to them:

> “If a man’s wife has gone astray and, despising her husband, has slept with another man, and the husband cannot discover it because the adultery is hidden and cannot be proved by witnesses, since she was not found in the act of fornication; if the spirit of jealousy stirs the man against his wife, whether she has been defiled or is assailed by false suspicion, he shall bring her to the priest and offer for her a tenth part of a *satum* [a measure] of barley flour. He shall not pour oil upon it or put frankincense upon it, because it is a sacrifice of jealousy and an offering investigating adultery.

> “The priest shall present her and set her before the Lord. He shall take holy water in an earthen vessel and put into it a little dust from the floor of the tabernacle. When the woman stands in the Lord’s presence, he shall uncover her head and place in her hands the sacrifice of memorial and the offering of jealousy. But he himself shall hold the most bitter waters, into which he has put the curse with its imprecation. He shall adjure her and say: ‘If no strange man has slept with you and you have not been defiled by abandoning your husband’s bed, these most bitter waters, into which I have put curses, shall not harm you. But if you have turned aside from your husband, have been defiled, and have lain with another man, you shall be subject to these curses: may the Lord make you a curse and an example among all His people; may He cause your thigh to waste away and your swollen womb to burst; may the cursed waters enter your belly, and, as your womb swells, may your thigh waste away.’ And the woman shall answer: ‘Amen, amen.’

> “The priest shall write these curses in a scroll and wash them away in the bitter waters into which he put the curses, and shall give them to her to drink. When she has drained them, the priest shall take from her hand the sacrifice of jealousy, elevate it before the Lord, and lay it upon the altar. Yet he shall first take a handful from what is offered as the sacrifice and burn it upon the altar, and then give the woman the bitter waters to drink. When she has drunk them, if she has been defiled and is guilty of adultery through despising her husband, the waters of the curse shall pass through her; her belly shall swell, her thigh shall rot away, and the woman shall become a curse and an example to all the people.

> “But the husband shall be without guilt, and she shall bear her own iniquity. But if she has not been defiled, she shall be innocent and shall bear children.”

[Note: Basel reads “here.”]

[Note: Basel reads “can.”]

[Note: “*satum*, that is, a measure”: Strasbourg edition; other collected editions read “sack.”]

[Note: Other collected editions, except Basel, read “shall hold you.”]

[Note: Basel reads “shall lift.”]

[Note: From “But the husband” through “But if” these words have been transferred here from the end of the same fifth chapter of Numbers.]

### Part IV. Gratian

But every purgation of this kind seems to be prohibited, since in the preceding authority of Pope Stephen it is said: “By voluntary confession,” etc.

### C. XXII. Single combat is not accepted under the New Testament. Likewise from the decrees of Pope Nicholas.

[Note: [Col. 0613D] The letter written to King Charles, uncle of Lothair (from which this chapter is taken), exists at Rome in the often-cited manuscript of the Dominican monastery. Among other things, it reports that Lothair, wishing to know whether Theuperga—or Thietperga, as Regino calls her—his wife, had committed adultery, wished two men to undertake single combat, so that, if [Col. 0614D] the man defending Theuperga’s cause should fall, she would plainly be judged convicted of adultery. Nicholas strongly rebukes this, teaching that it is not a lawful method of proving crimes—although found in Lombard constitutions and in the Capitularies—but is nothing other than tempting God. He adds that Lothair had denied Theuperga a just purgation, in these words: “But concerning adultery she wished to clear herself in the presence of our envoys, but he did not consent.” Regino recounts this entire history in Book 2 of the Chronicle. These facts show that Gratian’s heading for this chapter is overly general, since Nicholas seeks only to establish that single combat must not be used for purgation.] [Note: [Col. 0613] written A.D. 867.—Regino 1.2, c. 77. Burchard 1.9, c. 15. Ivo, Decree, part 8, c. 187.]

We do not, however, admit single combat into the law, [Col. 0614C] since we do not find that it was commanded [Note: [Col. 0613] “commanded”: the cited collections—the collected editions—Böhm] [Note: [Col. 0613] “which”: the cited collections—the collected editions]; for, although we read [Note: [Col. 0613] “let us read”: Ivo, Burchard—the collected editions] that certain persons entered into it, as sacred history records concerning holy David and Goliath [Note: [Col. 0613] 1 Samuel, c. 17], nevertheless divine authority has nowhere ordained that it should anywhere be held as law [Note: [Col. 0613] “for anyone”: Argentinensis and Basel editions], since those pursuing this and similar practices seem only to tempt God.

### Part V. Gratian.

But, on the contrary, in the Council of Worms, c. 15 [Note: [Col. 0613] held A.D. 868.—Regino, book 2, c. 276. Burchard, book 11, c. 66]:

[Col. 0615A] ### C. XXIII. If thefts occur in a monastery, let the monks clear themselves by judgment.

It often happens that thefts are committed in monasteries, and that those who commit them are unknown. Therefore we decree that, when the brothers themselves must clear themselves of such matters [Note: [Col. 0615] “must”: original—“ought”: Regino—the collected editions], Mass shall be celebrated by the abbot, or by someone whom the abbot has ordered; and, in the presence of the brothers [Note: [Col. 0615] “in the presence”: the collected editions], when Mass has thus been completed, all shall communicate with these words: “May the Body of the Lord be to me [Note: [Col. 0615] “to you”: the same editions—Regino] today for proof.”

[Note: [Col. 0615C] “When Mass has thus been completed”: this chapter adds certain words from the council which the collectors seemed to have omitted; but here it was thought sufficient to indicate the variation. For in the council itself the text reads: “and thus, at the final celebration of Mass, let them receive for their purgation the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0615D] so that thereby they may show themselves innocent.”]

### C. XXIV. Whoever is accused of adultery shall clear himself by a credible judgment. Likewise in the Council of Salzburg, c. 7.

[Note: [Col. 0615] held A.D. 1122.—Burchard, at the end of the work. Ivo, Decree, part 15, c. 173.]

It was asked: if two persons are charged with adultery [Note: [Col. 0615] “in”: original—Burchard—Ivo], and one confesses while the other denies it, what is to be done [Col. 0615B] in consequence? [Note: [Col. 0615] “was”: there—original.] The holy council decreed that the one who denies it shall clear himself by a credible judgment, while the one who has confessed shall perform worthy [Note: [Col. 0615] “worthily”: there] penance.

### C. XXV. When several are accused of adultery and one wishes to clear the others, all are to be held guilty if he fails in the judgment. Likewise in the same council, c. 14.

[Note: [Col. 0615] Burchard, there—Ivo, there, c. 180.]

The holy synod likewise decreed that, if two persons have been accused of adultery, both deny it, and ask that one of them be permitted to clear both by divine judgment, then, if that one fails [Note: [Col. 0615] “falls”: original—the cited collections], both are to be held guilty.

### C. XXVI. Let Mass be celebrated separately for each person accused of any crime. Likewise in the Council of Worms, c. 10.

[Note: [Col. 0615] held A.D. 868.—Regino, book 2, c. 277. Burchard, book 2, c. 199. Ivo, Decree, part 6, c. 273.]

[Col. 0615C] If a criminal charge—that is, homicide, adultery, theft, or maleficium (wrongdoing) [Note: [Col. 0615] “some maleficium”: the collected editions]—has been laid [Note: [Col. 0615] “reckoned”: Regino] against a bishop or priest, then for each charge he must celebrate [Note: [Col. 0615] “in”: original—Regino, Burchard] Mass [Note: [Col. 0615] “perform”: the cited collections], communicate, and demonstrate himself innocent of each allegation made against him [Note: [Col. 0615] “render”: original]. If he does not do this, he is to be kept outside the threshold of the church for five years.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] “Celebrate”: in the council and in Burchard and Ivo [Col. 0615] and in Regino] there follows: “and publicly say the secret prayer.”]

[Col. 0616A] **Gratian.** What Sixtus and Leo added at the end of their purgation must be understood as an example from them. By the example of their own satisfaction, they did not wish to prescribe to others a law for purgation.

# QUESTION IV

## GRATIAN

### Part I.

What was asked fourth—whether a bishop may be condemned on the testimony of two persons—is established by many authorities. For, as is read in the Gospel of John [Note: [Col. 0615] John 8:17], Christ said to the Jews: “In your law [Note: [Col. 0615] Deuteronomy 17:6] it is written that the testimony of two human beings is true.” He then argues from this against them, saying: “If the testimony of two human beings is true, why do you not receive the testimony of myself and [Col. 0616B] the Father?” Likewise Paul, in the Epistle to the Corinthians [Note: [Col. 0615] 2 Corinthians 13:1]: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand.” Likewise, in the Epistle to the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0615] Hebrews 10:28]: “Whoever violates the law of Moses, having been convicted by two or three witnesses, shall be stoned without mercy.”

### C. I. By how many witnesses each cleric ought to be convicted. Likewise from the Second Council of Braga, c. 8.

[Note: [Col. 0615] held A.D. 572.—Three-Part Collection, part 2, title 46, c. 8.—Burchard, book 2, c. 202. Ivo, Panormia, book 4, c. 97; Decree, part 6, c. 276.—cf. Capitularies, book 5, c. 240.]

It pleased the council that, if anyone charges a cleric with the accusation [Note: [Col. 0615] “defilement”: Basel edition—“stain”: the remaining editions] of fornication, two or three testimonies shall be required of that accuser, according to the command of the Apostle Paul. If he cannot establish by the testimony offered what he has said [Note: [Col. 0615] “what”: Hispanic Collection; “says”: Lyons editions II and III], the accuser shall receive the excommunication incurred by the accused [Note: [Col. 0615] “shall incur”: Hispanic Collection].

### Part II. Gratian.

From the foregoing it is therefore gathered [Col. 0616C] that a bishop can be convicted and condemned on the testimony of two or three witnesses. But Pope Sylvester, sitting in a general synod, said the contrary [Note: [Col. 0615] from the apocryphal canon of Sylvester, c. 3.—cf. Capitularies of Hadrian, c. 72.—Council of Mainz, held A.D. 888, c. 12. Deusdedit, part 3. Ivo, Panormia, book 4, c. 91; Decree, part 6, c. 334. Polycarpus, book 6, title 1.—In the Argentinensis edition a certain canon, under the name “Deusdedit P. Laudatus,” is prefixed to this chapter.]:

### C. II. By how many witnesses a bishop, priest, or other cleric is to be convicted.

A bishop shall not be condemned [Note: [Col. 0615] “be condemned”: Basel and Lyons editions II and III—“is condemned”: the remaining editions] except with seventy-two witnesses; nor shall the supreme bishop be judged by anyone, [Col. 0617A] because it is written [Note: [Col. 0617] Matthew, c. 10]: “The disciple is not above the master.” A cardinal priest [Note: [Col. 0617] absent from the original], however, shall not be condemned except with forty-four witnesses [Note: [Col. 0617] “sixty-four”: the collected editions] [Note: [Col. 0617] “be deposed”: there]; nor shall a cardinal deacon of the city of Rome be condemned except with twenty-seven witnesses. A subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, reader, or porter shall not be condemned except with seven witnesses [Note: [Col. 0617] the second “not” is absent from the collected editions, first Basel edition, and Böhm]. Witnesses and accusers must be free from every infamy.

[Note: [Col. 0616C] “Nor shall the supreme bishop”: these words through the term “priest” were added from the Roman council under Sylvester and from the other cited places, except the Panormia. It is remarkable that the author of the gloss thought that the supreme pontiff could be condemned by fewer witnesses [Col. 0616D] than a cardinal deacon or a porter, although the pontiff himself could by no means be excluded from the general designation “bishop.”]

### C. III. Bishops are not to be condemned except by seventy-two witnesses. Likewise Leo IV, in a letter to the bishops of Britain.

[Note: [Col. 0617] written about A.D. 850. Ivo, Decree, part 5, c. 116.]

We judge that no condemnation of bishops is ever valid unless it occurs either before a lawful number of bishops—which is constituted by twelve bishops—or, assuredly, upon a judgment established by seventy-two suitable witnesses, [Col. 0617B] who must be persons able also to accuse. § 1. And first they shall take oaths upon the four sacred Gospels of Christ that they will utter nothing false, as blessed Sylvester handed down to us [Note: [Col. 0617C] “As blessed Sylvester handed down to us”: from here through the word “Church” these words are not read in the manuscripts of Leo’s letter; nevertheless they are found in Ivo [Col. 0617] and in Nicholas, in the letter to Salmon, king of the Britons, where Leo’s letter is reported.] and as the holy Roman Church appears to maintain. And if among the persons whom people declare ought to be condemned there is a bishop who asks that his case be heard in the presence of the bishop of the Roman See, no one shall presume to pronounce a definitive judgment against him; rather, we decree that he must be heard in every respect.

**Gratian.** But this must be understood either as a special privilege concerning clerics of the Roman Church, or because of the wickedness of certain persons who, lacking approved life and learning, suddenly rush into accusations against ministers of God. Yet those whose life is so praiseworthy that it appears worthy of imitation by all, and whose assertions can raise no doubt, may lawfully be convicted and condemned on the testimony of any two or three such witnesses.

# QUESTION VI

## GRATIAN

### Part I.

The sixth question follows, asking by what remedy a defective case may be remedied, and whether that remedy ought to be granted to one who has raised the voice of appeal merely for the sake of delay. A defective case may indeed be remedied by appeal.

Accordingly Pope Fabian says to Bishop Hilary, Letter III, c. 3 [Note: [Col. 0617] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, taken from Anianus’ interpretation of Theodosian Code, book 11, title 30, c. 20.—Capitularies, book 7, c. 333. Burchard, book 1, c. 148. Anselm, book 2, c. 11, and among Hadrian’s capitularies at the end of book 3. Ivo, Panormia, book 4, c. 121.]:

### C. I. Let the remedy of appeal aid a defective case.

An appellant may remedy a defective case by the remedy of appeal.

### C. II. On the same subject. PALEA.

[The same, a little earlier. Note: [Col. 0617] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, drawn from Anianus’ interpretation of Theodosian Code, book 11, title 30, cc. 2 and 15.—Burchard, there. Anselm, there. Ivo, there.]

> “No affliction, whether of imprisonment [Note: [Col. 0617] added: “or of prison”: Anselm—Capitularies, book 1—the collected editions—Böhm] or of detention in custody, ought to harm an appellant.”

### C. III. On the same subject. Likewise Pope Anacletus, Letter I, at the end.

[Note: [Col. 0617] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled from Innocent’s letter to Victricius, c. 3, and Leo the Great’s Letter 5 (Ballerini edition), c. 6.—Three-Part Collection, part 1, title 2, c. 5. Anselm, book 3, c. 21.]

Every oppressed person may freely appeal, if he wishes, to the judgment of priests, and shall be prohibited by no one; rather, he shall be supported, freed [Col. 0618B] and heard [Note: [Col. 0617] “and heard”: the collected editions] by them. If difficult cases or greater matters arise, they shall be referred to a higher see. And if they cannot readily be decided [Note: [Col. 0617] “determined”: Lyons editions II and III] or justly settled there, then, where an assembly of the highest authorities has convened—which customarily ought to take place twice each year—the ecclesiastical affairs shall be judged justly and in a manner pleasing to God before the patriarch or primate, and secular affairs before the patrician, in common.

[Note: [Col. 0617C] “Assembly”: in the printed editions [Col. 0617] the words “under the metropolitan” followed, but they have been removed because they occur in no manuscript or original and are explained by the following words, which indicate before whom the council is to be held.]

[Note: [Col. 0618C] “Ecclesiastical affairs”: the letter reads, “before the ecclesiastical primate, and secular affairs before the patrician,” etc.]

Likewise Pope Sixtus, in Letter II, writes to all rulers of the Church, saying [Note: [Col. 0617] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Anselm, book 2, c. 8. Ivo, Decree, part 5, c. 3.]:

### C. IV. Whoever is attacked shall appeal to the Apostolic See.

If any of you is assailed in any adversity, [Col. 0618C] he may freely appeal to this holy and Apostolic See and have refuge [Note: [Col. 0617] “support”: the collected editions] in it as to a head, so that he may not be condemned while innocent or his church suffer loss.

### C. V. In more serious cases, those attacked shall appeal to the Apostolic See. Likewise Gratus, Letter I.

[Note: [Col. 0618C] “Gratus”: this is restored from most old copies—for the printed editions read, “Likewise Gregory”—although in the volumes of councils this letter is attributed to [Col. 0618D] Sixtus II, while the letter from which the preceding chapter is drawn is attributed to Sixtus I.]

[Note: [Col. 0617] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, belonging to Letter 1 of Sixtus II.—Burchard, book 1, c. 144. Ivo, Panormia, book 4, c. 124, attributed to Gregory; Decree, part 5, c. 257, attributed to Julius, as is also read in the collected editions, first Basel edition, and the manuscripts themselves.—Anselm, book 2, c. 12.]

All bishops who are accused or charged in certain more serious cases [Note: [Col. 0617] “some”: the collected editions] may, whenever necessary, freely [Col. 0619A] appeal to the Apostolic See and flee to it as to a mother.

### C. VI. Appeal may be made to the Roman Church by all. Likewise Pope Marcellus, Letter I, to the bishops of the province of Antioch.

[Note: [Col. 0619] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled from Innocent I, Letter 4, cc. 1–2.—Anselm, book 2, c. 7. Polycarpus, book 1, title 7.]

All bishops who wish, or for whom it is necessary, ought to flee to the Roman Church as to a head and appeal to it, so that they may receive protection and consecration from it.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] “And consecration”: in the original the reading is [Col. 0619] “so that they may receive protection and deliverance from that source from which they received instruction and consecration.” The same words occur in a collated manuscript of Anselm; but a certain Vatican manuscript reads as Gratian, as we find indicated in the margin. The text has not been altered because of the gloss.]

This must by no means be denied to all bishops; rather, they shall be permitted to go freely, without any detention, excommunication, condemnation, or despoiling.

### C. VII. Whoever believes himself oppressed by his own metropolitan shall appeal to a higher see. Likewise Victor to Theophilus of Alexandria, Letter I, c. 3.

[Note: [Col. 0619] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled from Council of Chalcedon, c. 17.—Anselm, among Hadrian’s capitularies at the end of book 3, c. 5; Burchard, book 1, c. 144. Ivo, Decree, part 5, c. 257, attributed to Julius; Panormia, book 4, c. 126.]

[Col. 0619B] If anyone believes himself oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him be judged before the patriarch or primate of the diocese, or before the See of the universal Apostolic Church.

### C. VIII. All shall appeal to the Roman Church as to a mother. Likewise Zephyrinus, bishop of the city of Rome, Letter I.

[Note: [Col. 0619] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Anselm, book 2, c. 6.]

All persons, but especially the oppressed, ought to appeal and have recourse to the Roman Church as to a mother, that they may be nourished at her breasts, defended by her authority, and relieved from their oppressions; for a mother cannot and ought not to forget her son.

[Col. 0619C] ### C. IX. Whenever anyone appeals, a hearing shall not be denied him. Likewise Pope Julius in the decrees, or in the rescript to the Eastern bishops, c. 22.

[Note: [Col. 0619] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled from Third Council of Carthage, c. 10.—Three-Part Collection, part 1, title 32, c. 6. Anselm, book 2, c. 9, and under Julius, book 3, c. 123; and among Hadrian’s capitularies, c. 43, at the end of book 3. Ivo, Decree, part 6, c. 326.]

It pleased the council that, whenever an appeal is made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges, where authority is greater, a hearing shall not be denied.

### C. X. The unjustly condemned ought to obtain restoration, and the oppressed assistance, from the Roman Church. Likewise c. 30.

[Note: [Col. 0619] Anselm, book 2, c. 47.]

For this reason the aforesaid privileges were specially granted to this holy See, both concerning the convocation of councils and judgments and restorations of bishops, and concerning the highest [Col. 0620A] affairs of churches: that all oppressed persons may receive assistance from it, the unjustly condemned restoration, and that such acts may not be presumed by wicked persons without vengeance, nor performed without their condemnation.

[Note: [Col. 0619] “not”: the collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0619] added: “their own”: there.]

### Part II. Gratian.

Since, therefore, Zephyrinus says that all are to appeal, but especially the oppressed, and Marcellus writes, “All bishops who wish, or for whom it is necessary, ought to appeal,” it is clear that the voice of appeal must not be denied to an accused person, whether oppressed or not. Some, however, distinguish the passage thus: they refer “those who wish” to persons seeking consecration, and “those suffering necessity” to the oppressed. The sense would then be: all who wish to receive consecration from the Roman Church and are prevented by certain persons ought to appeal to it; likewise, all for whom it is necessary to flee to it in their oppressions ought to raise the voice of appeal, so that the former may receive protection and the latter consecration from it.

Zephyrinus’s statement is similarly distinguished: “All are to appeal to the Roman Church” means those who wish to receive consecration from it, or who have suffered some injury from their prelates—especially the oppressed. According to the first interpretation, the oppressed are persons subjected to some injury; according to the second, the oppressed are persons unjustly condemned by a judge. According to this distinction, those who raise the voice of appeal in certain matters not for relief but for delay have no authority to appeal.

But Gregory writes to all throughout the provinces [Note: [Col. 0619] written A.D. 832.—cf. D. 12, c. 2. Ivo, Decree, part 5, c. 340. Anselm, book 2, c. 19 [22]. Polycarpus, book 1, title 7]:

[Col. 0620C] ### C. XI. No one may hear a case on appeal except the person to whom the appeal is made.

By our decree, requesting your charity, we command that if anyone—though we do not wish it—should wickedly attempt to accuse Aldric, bishop of the Church of Le Mans, one of his rivals, then, in honour of the memory of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, of the privilege of the Roman Church over which he presided, and of the authority of our name, he may, after a hearing before the primate of the diocese, appeal to us if necessary, and by our authority conduct and determine his actions either before us [Note: [Col. 0619] “them”: Böhm] or before legates [Col. 0621A] sent from our side [Note: [Col. 0621] “our”: original—Ivo—the collected editions, except the Basel edition], according to the decrees of the Fathers. No one shall judge him, or presume to judge him, before these proceedings. But if anything grave and intolerable should be alleged against him—which God forbid—our judgment must be awaited, so that nothing may first be decreed concerning one who has fled to the bosom of the holy Roman Church and implores its aid, before it has been directed by the authority of that same Church. For it has so imparted its offices to the other churches that they are called to share in its solicitude, not in the fullness of its power.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] “In honour of … authority”: from here through the phrase “our authority” these words have been added from the letter itself, which exists in the Dominican library and appears to be Gregory IV’s. From it was also taken the chapter *Nulli fas*, Distinction 19; in Ivo both chapters are found together. Aldric—so it is inferred from the catalogue of bishops of Le Mans—is mentioned in the council at Saint-Médard, held shortly after Gregory IV. Thus the defence afforded him by Gregory was useful.]

And below:

§ 1. But if—something we do not suppose—anyone has presumed otherwise, let him be removed from clerical office and judged by all to be guilty of violating apostolic authority, lest wolves who have entered under the appearance of sheep dare, with bestial savagery, to tear apart anyone [Col. 0621B] and presume to inflict upon others what they do not wish inflicted upon themselves.

[Note: [Col. 0621] “guilty of injuries”: original—C. XII.]

Likewise, Pope Vigilius says in his letter to Eleutherius, last chapter [Note: [Col. 0621C] This chapter has been restored to Vigilius on the authority of old exemplars. Formerly it was attributed to [Col. 0621D] Julius [Col. 0621] in the collected editions, first Basel edition. Its earlier portion through “For the Church itself” occurs in Julius’s first letter—as likewise in Leo, Letter 84, quoted above in Distinction 23, c. *Quanquam*, and in the following chapter, *Qui sunt*—as does the sense of the remaining portions.]

[Note: [Col. 0621] From c. 7 of Vigilius’s letter to Profuturus, which, like the sixth, is Pseudo-Isidorian.—Three-Part Collection, part 1, title 52, c. 2. Anselm, book 2, c. 22 [20], with the subscription: “Given on the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Belisarius and John.”—The beginning of the chapter is taken from Leo the Great’s letter to Anastasius, below, c. 4.]:

### C. XII. The cases of appellants must be heard by those to whom they appeal.

Whoever knows that he is set over others should not take it ill that someone is set over him. For the Church itself which is first has entrusted its offices to the other churches in such a way that they are called to share in its solicitude, not in the fullness of its power. Hence it is clear that the judgments of all bishops appealing to the Apostolic See, and all matters of greater cases, are reserved to that holy See; particularly since in all these matters its counsel must always be awaited. If any priest attempts to oppose its course, he should know that he will have to render account of his cases before that same holy See, not without peril to his honour.

[Note: [Col. 0621] “all”: the collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 0621] absent from the same, first Basel edition.]

**Gratian.** Likewise, Pope Nicholas, addressing Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, is found to rebuke him because he dared to condemn Bishop Rhotad while Rhotad was appealing to the Apostolic See, saying [Note: [Col. 0621] written A.D. 865.—Anselm, book 2, c. 67 [64].]:

### C. XIII. Concerning the archbishop of Reims, who dared to judge one appealing to the Roman See.

Would that your subtle wisdom, directed toward good, had taken up the incitement to judgment and the material for deposition against Rhotad, removed him from the path to the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0621] “recalled”: original], condemned without interruption one appealing to the Apostolic See, and committed him to prison custody. And below [Note: [Col. 0621] Anselm, at the end of book 2]:

§ 1. Yet you ought by no means to have consigned to oblivion the privileges of the Apostolic See, by which the venerable canons command that the judgments of the whole Church be referred to this See. And below:

§ 2. You should know that we acted in Rhotad’s case for this reason: that the privileges of the Apostolic See, which appeared to have been improperly violated by you and which, despite our great expenditure of effort, could not be recovered because of your resisting obstinacy, might at last, through apostolic authority and the venerable deliberation of the Fathers, be adorned with their former character [*genius*] [Note: [Col. 0621] absent from the original—“ingenuity”: the collected editions] and proper honour.

[Note: [Col. 0622C] “Venerable”: whereas the earlier reading was *canonica* (“canonical”) [Col. 0621] and the original in Anselm reads *canonica*, it has been corrected thus from the letter itself, which survives in manuscript and was recently printed in the appendix to the library. In Ennodius’s work for Symmachus occurs *cana miracula et canum genium* (“venerable miracles and the spirit of the grey-haired”), following Virgil:

> “Venerable Faith and Vesta, Quirinus with his brother Remus,  
> dispensed laws …”]

[Col. 0622B] ### C. XIV. Let each person render to superiors the obedience that he desires from inferiors. Likewise Pope Leo to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, Letter LXXXII, alternatively LXXXIV.

[Note: [Col. 0621] written A.D. 446; Letter 14 in the Ballerini edition.—Three-Part Collection, part 1, title 43, c. 17.]

Whoever knows himself to be set over certain persons should not take it ill that someone is set over him. Rather, he himself should render the obedience he demands [Note: [Col. 0621] “will demand”: the collected editions, first Basel edition]; and just as he does not wish to bear the burden of a heavy load, so he should not dare impose an unbearable weight upon another [Note: [Col. 0621] “others”: the collected editions]. For we are disciples of the humble and gentle [Note: [Col. 0621] “most gentle”: Basel edition] Master, who says [Note: [Col. 0621] Matthew 23:4]: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart.”

**Gratian.** It is therefore clear that no appellant must be denied a stay. But if he appeals for the sake of frivolous delay, he shall be condemned by the judge to whom the appeal has been made. The time for appeal is both before and after judgment has been given. For whenever someone feels himself oppressed, he may freely appeal.

Accordingly Pope Sixtus II says in Letter I to Bishop Gratus [Note: [Col. 0621] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled from Council of Chalcedon, cc. 9 and 17.—Anselm, book 2, c. 9. Ivo, Panormia, book 4, c. 126. Polycarpus, book 1, title 6.]:

### C. XV. Whoever is oppressed by his own metropolitan shall appeal to the primate or the See of the universal Church.

If anyone believes himself oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him be judged before the primate of the diocese or before the pope of the universal Apostolic Church.

[Col. 0623A] ### C. XVI. Let one who considers the judge suspect appeal to the Roman See. Likewise Felix II, to the bishops assembled in the Alexandrian synod, c. 19.

[Note: [Col. 0623] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, composed from Council of Sardica, cc. 4 and 7.—Anselm, book 2, c. 60 [58].]

Whenever bishops believe themselves oppressed by their fellow-provincial bishops or by the metropolitan, or regard them as suspect, they shall immediately appeal to the Roman See. They may freely go there [Note: [Col. 0623] “and to them”: the collected editions] without any detention or seizure of their property. Once they have appealed to the aforesaid Roman mother Church [Note: [Col. 0623] “See”: Basel edition], or requested to be heard by it [Note: [Col. 0623] “earnestly requested”: original—Anselm], no one shall presume, before their case has been concluded by the authority of the Roman pontiff, to excommunicate them, seize their sees, take away their property, or inflict any force upon them. If anyone presumes otherwise, it shall be null and without force.

### C. XVII. On the same subject. Likewise Pope Julius, in the rescript to the Eastern bishops, c. 30.

[Note: [Col. 0623C] This is a summary of the chapter quoted above, in the same question, c. *Ideo*, and it occurs in old copies in which *Paleae* are not usually found.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Anselm, book 2, c. 47.]

> “For this reason the aforesaid privileges were specially granted to this holy See, so that all the oppressed may receive assistance from it, and the unjustly condemned restoration.”

**Gratian.** “The oppressed” and those who believe themselves oppressed are understood to be persons before judgment has been given; “the unjustly condemned,” persons after judgment has been given.

Accordingly Eutychianus, bishop of the city of Rome, writes to the bishops throughout Sicily, Letter II, c. 1 [Note: [Col. 0623] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—cf. Extracts of Egbert’s Canons (Mansi, vol. 12), c. 3, where these words are quoted from Gregory.—Anselm, book 3, c. 73. Ivo, Panormia, book 4, c. 100; Decree, part 6, c. 336. Polycarpus, book 5, title 1.]:

### C. XVIII. One may withdraw by appeal before the conclusion of a case.

Ecclesiastical cases must not be conducted as secular cases are. In secular law [Note: [Col. 0623] “for in secular law, after”: the collected editions], once someone has appeared when summoned and begun to litigate in court, he may not withdraw before the case has been completed. In ecclesiastical matters, however, one may withdraw after stating his case, if necessary or if he perceives himself to be oppressed.

### Part III. Gratian.

But whoever, out of contumacy, refuses to obey the judges shall be deprived of communion.

Accordingly, in the Council of Milevis, c. 24 [Note: [Col. 0623] held after A.D. 416.—Three-Part Collection, part 2, fol. 22, c. 11.—Ivo, Panormia, book 4, c. 182, attributed to the Council of Split]:

### C. XIX. Let one who will not obey his judges be excommunicated.

Whoever is proved through contumacy to be unwilling [Col. 0624A] to obey his judges, when this has been established before the bishop of the first See [Note: [Col. 0623] “brought forward”: Hispanic Collection], shall be given letters directing that none of the bishops communicate with him until he obeys.

**Gratian.** Pope Fabian also testifies that an appeal may be made after judgment has been rendered, saying to Bishop Hilary, Letter III, c. 2 [Note: [Col. 0623] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, taken from the interpretation of the Theodosian Code, book 11, title 30, c. 20.—Burchard, book 1, c. 148. Anselm, book 2, c. 11. Ivo, Panormia, book 4, c. 122; Decree, part 5, c. 261.]:

### C. XX. Appeal shall not be denied to one whom a judgment has designated for punishment.

It is permissible also to appeal in criminal cases, and the voice of appeal must not be denied to one whom a judgment has designated for punishment [Note: [Col. 0623] “for punishment”: Burchard, Ivo, Decree—Lyons editions II and III; “in punishment”: Ivo, Panormia—the remaining collected editions].

**Gratian.** The same pope affirms this a little earlier in the same chapter [Note: [Col. 0623] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Burchard, Anselm, there. Frankish Collection, part 1, title 18, c. 9. Ivo, Panormia, book 4, c. 120; Decree, part 5, c. 248.]:

### C. XXI. It is permissible for someone to appeal before judgment has been rendered.

If anyone perceives the judge to be hostile to him, let him raise the voice [Col. 0624B] of appeal.

### Part IV. Gratian.

But whoever wishes to appeal after judgment has been given must appeal within five days; within the same period he must receive from the judge against whom he has appealed letters of referral, and within the same period set out for the judge to whom he has appealed.

Accordingly, in the Theodosian laws [Note: [Col. 0623D] “Theodosian”: this and the four following chapters cited from the Theodosian laws occur in Book 5 of the *Sentences* of Julius Paulus, with an interpretation. From this it appears that, even in Gratian’s time, these *Sentences* were joined with the Theodosian Code or the Breviary of Alaric. In his preface Alaric declares that he compiled that volume not from the Theodosian Code alone, but from [Col. 0624C] various books, and that he made particular use of the work of bishops in compiling and interpreting the collection of laws.] the following enactment is found [Note: [Col. 0623] From the interpretation of Paulus, *Sentences*, book 5, title 33, §1.—Ivo, Panormia, book 4, c. 127; Decree, part 5, c. 281.]:

### C. XXII. Within what time one must appeal after judgment has been pronounced.

Because of the excessive freedom of appellants, lest they seem to have unrestricted discretion in reopening or revoking judgments, both periods for appeal and penalties have been established. Thus, whoever wishes to appeal before the judge who heard his case and to appeal [Col. 0624C] to another judge [Note: [Col. 0623] “make an appeal”: original—Ivo—the collected edition] must appeal within five days; and within those same five days he must arrive, without any evasion [Note: [Col. 0623] “pretence”: Ivo, Panormia], before the judge to whom he has appealed. The day on which he received the letters is specifically to be counted among those five days. If the journey is longer, the number of days required for travelling may be counted in addition to the five days.

### C. XXIII. PALEA.

[Note: [Col. 0624D] This chapter is absent from the older manuscripts of Gratian, from the original, Ivo, and the Panormia. In one very carefully corrected manuscript of Gratian it appears in the margin of the preceding chapter as a kind of gloss.]

[Note: [Col. 0623] From fragment 1, *Digest*, “If anyone concerning sureties,” 2.11.—absent from the Basel edition.]

> “After calculating twenty thousand paces, one day shall be reckoned for each such distance.”

[Col. 0625A] ### C. XXIV. Letters of referral shall be sent from the judge against whom an appeal is made to the judge to whom it has been made. Likewise there, title XXXIV.

[Note: [Col. 0625] From Paulus, *Sentences*, book 5, title 34.—Ivo, Panormia, book 4, c. 128; Decree, part 5, c. 282.]

From the person from whom the appeal has been made [Note: “from whom”: original—Ivo], letters of referral shall be sent to the person who is to hear the appeal; these are commonly called *apostoli* (“apostolic letters”). Their request and receipt must be completed officially within five days. [Note: “epistle”: Ivo, Panormia. “Of which”: original. “To be completed”: Ivo—the original.] This has already been interpreted above under the title “On securities and penalties of appeals.” [Note: This is the interpretation of Paul in the same place.] § 1. Whoever has not requested, received, or returned the letters of referral within the prescribed times is barred from proceeding by prescription and compelled to bear the penalty for the appeal. [Note: “have requested,” and so thereafter: Ivo—collected editions from the original. “They shall be barred—shall be compelled”: ibid. “Inflict”: original.]

C. XXV. On those who appeal in order to obtain delay. Likewise in the same place, title XXXV, chapter 2. [Note: From the interpretation of Paul, *Sentences*, recension, book 5, title 35—Ivo, Panormia, book 4, chapter 129—Decree, part 5, chapter 283.]

[Col. 0625B] Whoever appeals, not in confidence of a just cause but for the purpose of causing delay, so that judgment may not be pronounced against him; or whoever, having confessed his own act, wishes to appeal in order not to be adjudged liable—such appeals are not admitted. [Note: “of postponing”: Ivo, Panormia, collected editions. “Be dismissed”: Ivo, Panormia—“be cast out”: collected editions. “Be admitted”: same editions.]

C. XXVI. When a possessor appeals, while the outcome of the case is uncertain the fruits of the possession shall be sequestrated. Likewise in the same place, title XXXVI, chapter 1. [Note: From the interpretation of Paul, *Sentences*, recension, book 5, title 36—Ivo, Panormia, book 4, chapter 130—Decree, part 5, chapter 284.]

Whenever, after the case has been heard before the judge, the possessor appeals, the fruits of the possession in dispute are rightly placed in sequestration while the outcome of the second hearing remains uncertain. For if the claimant has appealed, this cannot be demanded of him, because what he does not possess cannot be sequestrated. § 1. If an appeal concerns urban estates or slaves, their rents or hire-payments are customarily deposited; likewise freight charges, if the matter concerns a ship. [Note: “Judge”: Ivo, Panormia, collected editions; absent from the Basel edition. “Following”: Basel edition—“to be followed”: the other collected editions from Ivo and Panormia. Added: “or beasts of burden”: Ivo, Panormia, collected editions, Basel edition. “Possessions”: collected editions from Ivo and Panormia. “Of freight charges”: Ivo, *Decree*—“freight”: collected editions. “If it concerns a ship’s freight-charge”: same editions from Ivo and Panormia.]

C. XXVII. One who appeals unjustly must be punished in every case. Likewise in the same place, title XXXVII, chapter 1. [Note: Paul, book 1, title 37—Ivo, Panormia, book 4, chapter 131—Decree, part 5, chapter 285.]

He must in every case be punished, so that whenever an unjust appeal is pronounced, he is compelled to repay fourfold, not merely singly, the expenses which his adversary incurred in pursuing the case. [Note: “Must in every case be punished”: In Paul’s *Sentences* the reading is, “It must in every way be proved,” etc. But because this is the beginning of the chapter, and doctors have made many annotations concerning such punishment, it was not altered; only the course of the sentence was corrected by adding the particle “so that.” “To be punished”: original, Arndts edition.]

Gratian. By the authorities set forth above, everyone is permitted to appeal within five days after judgment has been rendered. Later Justinian corrected this in his constitutions and decreed that the remedy of appeal must be granted to everyone within ten days, saying:

C. XXVIII. The remedy of appeal is granted within ten days. Emperor Justinian Augustus. [Note: This is the complete Novella 23, issued in A.D. 536.]

In applying very many remedies to the severity of earlier laws, and especially in making these provisions concerning appeals, we have judged it necessary at the present time to extend this benefit. For antiquity had provided that, if anyone conducted his case personally and was condemned, he should have permission to appeal only within two days; but if the case had been argued through an advocate, the period was extended to the following third day. Yet experience has shown this to be quite harmful: many persons, ignorant of the subtleties of the law and thinking that appeals might be extended to the third day, have fallen into immediate danger and, after the two days had elapsed, lost their cases. Therefore we have judged it necessary to remedy this matter appropriately.

And we enact that all appeals, whether cases are conducted personally, through advocates, or through defenders, curators, or guardians, may be submitted to the judges by the interested parties within ten days, reckoned from the reading of the judgment, whether the parties are adults or minors—excepting, of course, the most exalted prefecture of the praetorium. Thus a person may deliberate fully during that period whether he ought to appeal or remain quiet; appeals are not to be made in the pressure of immediate fear, but everyone is to have an opportunity for examination, which may restrain even people’s unconsidered passions. [Note: “Interposing”: collected editions. “To be made”: same editions, Basel and Lyons II–III editions. The phrase “and at the present time …” is absent from the collected editions and Basel. “To antiquity”: original, collected editions, Böhm. “Of days to be reckoned”: collected editions, Basel.]

§ 1. We further enact that, whenever a case is expected to be brought before our consistory, if imperial majesty should happen to be occupied with public affairs and, because of worldly business, unable to summon the Fathers for the case to be argued, the litigation shall not thereby be endangered. What fault of litigants is it if the imperial eminence is occupied? Or who has such authority that he can compel an unwilling prince to summon the Fathers and the other great men? But if anything of this kind occurs, the case shall remain untouched until the emperor, moved of his own accord, orders the great men to be summoned, permits the case to be brought forward, and allows all things to proceed according to custom. [Note: “The emperor’s”: same editions, Basel, Nuremberg. “Be agitated”: Basel. Added: “and the other great men”: collected editions, Basel, Lyons II–III.]

§ 2. In the third chapter there must also be provided what antiquity wisely established but novelty neglected. For venerable antiquity so arranged the magistracies that some were greater, some intermediate, and some lesser; and appeals from lesser judges were referred not only to the highest judges but also to the tribunal of the *spectabiles* judges, so that they too, with the sacred court in attendance, might hear the case. But novelty abandoned this arrangement. The result was that our greatest judges were troubled over the smallest cases, and men were burdened with great expense on account of trivial matters, so that perhaps the value of the entire litigation would not suffice for the legal costs.

Therefore we enact that, whenever an appeal is expected from the Egyptian district or the two Libyas joined to it, involving an amount up to ten pounds of gold, it shall not come to this imperial city but to the Augustal Prefect, who shall hear and decide the case in the capacity of a sacred judge; after his definitive judgment, no appeal at all shall be submitted. Similarly, whenever such a matter arises in the Asian or Pontic diocese, appeals up to the aforesaid amount of ten pounds of gold shall be referred to *spectabiles* men—perhaps counts, proconsuls, praetors, or governors—whom we have specially appointed to conduct such litigation. They too shall act in the manner of the Augustal Prefect, in the capacity of a sacred judge, and shall undertake to decide the cases without hope of appeal, yet in the fear of God and of the laws.

We enact that cases suspended by appeal in the Eastern district, limited to an amount of ten pounds of gold, shall be sent to the *vir spectabilis*, Count of the East, who shall similarly conduct the hearing and impose a final determination. This shall be observed: *spectabiles* dukes or other *spectabiles* judges shall not transfer their appeals in cases, whatever the amount, to other judges adorned with the same rank of *spectabilis*—for appeals ought not to be referred to judges of equal standing, but must rise from a lower tribunal to a higher one. Rather, their appeals, of whatever dignity or amount, shall be directed to their most illustrious prefecture, which, together with the *vir excellens* serving at the time as quaestor, shall determine them, with both offices supplying assistance: that is, both the sacred archives in the customary way and the prefectural office.

Yet we enact this in such a way that no appeal from dukes or other *spectabiles* judges—upon whom imperial majesty may perhaps have imposed cases even though they are private persons—shall go to the aforesaid *spectabiles* judges, lest the case appear to proceed not by grades but improperly. Appeals within the stated amount shall instead be referred from provincial governors and judges appointed by us, if they are not *spectabiles* judges. But if the judges appointed by us are *illustres*—whose dignitary titles are higher than the rank of *spectabilis*—or if they are dukes, who are in every case adorned with the rank of *spectabilis*, or persons delegated by the prince who hold *spectabilis* rank, their appeals, whatever the amount, shall be referred to the appropriate judges in this imperial city according to the ancient custom. All other provisions established concerning appeals by ancient tradition, by the authority of earlier constitutions, or by our own humanity shall remain untouched and unimpaired. [Note: “Arranged”: Lyons II–III. “Greater”: collected editions, Basel, Lyons II–III. “Are referred”: same editions. “May hear”: same editions. “Abandoned”: same editions, Lyons II–III. “They”: same editions. “Wholly”: absent from the same editions. “Eastern districts”: Argentinensis and Lyons I editions—“Eastern district”: the remaining editions, Lyons II–III. Added: “we enact”: collected editions, Basel. “Observed”: same editions. The Argentinensis edition reads: “so that *spectabiles* men not …”; Venice II: “so that *spectabiles* judges not ….” “Dukes” is absent from the collected editions and Lyons II–III. Added: “of dignity or”: same editions. Added: “his”: Basel, Venice II, Paris, Lyons I. “Are referred”: original, collected editions, Basel, Böhm.]

C. XXIX. When appeal must be made, on the first or second day. Likewise, Digest book XLIX, title “When Appeal Must Be Made,” law I, § “Two days.” [Note: From Digest 49, title 1, fragment 1, § 5 ff. The rubric placed over the chapter is absent from the Argentinensis and Basel editions.]

The two-day or three-day period for appeal must be reckoned from the day judgment was rendered. § 1. What then if a judgment has been pronounced conditionally? Do we reckon the time for appealing from the day when the judgment was *pronounced*, or from the day when the condition of the judgment took effect? Strictly speaking, a judgment ought not to be called conditional; but if it has been pronounced in this way, what is to happen? It is useful that the times for appeal should be reckoned immediately.

§ 2. The rule accepted in judgments—that appeal may be made on the second or third day—must also be observed in other proceedings from which no judgment is pronounced, but in which, *as stated above*, it is nevertheless proper and possible to appeal; for example, when someone is nominated to a guardianship or to other civil duties and his excuse is not accepted. [Note: “Has taken effect”: collected editions. Added: “however”: collected editions, Basel. “Prescribed”: original, collected editions, Lyons II–III. “Another”: Basel. “Is proper and possible”: collected editions. The reference is to §§ 1–2 of the same fragment. “For example, when someone …”: this passage through “is not accepted” is not in the Pandects; but because the opinion concerning it is expressed above in the same law, it was not deleted but printed in different characters.]

§ 3. The speech of the deified Marcus determined that these days in which appeal must be made are of use if the person from whom appeal is made is not available, so that petitions may be given to *him*. For he says: “The day shall be preserved on which there is first an opportunity of approaching him.” Therefore, if after judgment has been immediately pronounced, the person who pronounced it does not make himself available—as commonly happens—it must be said that this does not harm the appellant. For as soon as he has an opportunity to approach him, he may appeal. Thus, if the judge immediately withdraws, relief must likewise be given.

§ 5. What then if the time of day caused him to retire? If judgment happened to be pronounced already at the final hour, he will certainly not be thought to have withdrawn. § 3. We always understand there to be an opportunity of approach if he has made himself available in public. But if he has not, should anyone be blamed for not having come to his house, or for not having gone to his gardens, and further, to his suburban estate? It is more reasonable that this should not be imputed to him. Therefore, if there was no opportunity to approach him in public, it is better said that there was no opportunity of approach. [Note: “Withdraws”: collected editions. “Likewise”: same editions from the original. “Causes”: same editions, Lyons II–III. “Was thought”: Basel. “Has made”: collected editions, Basel. “Has made” for “has not made”: Basel. Added: “to him”: Basel.]

§ 6. If someone has had no opportunity to approach the judge from whom he appealed, in order to give him petitions, but has had an opportunity to approach the person to whom he appealed, it must be considered whether he may be barred because he did not approach the former. Under this law we follow the rule that, if there was an opportunity to approach either of the two, prescription takes effect. [Note: Added: “judge”: Basel. “Had”: collected editions from the original. “In order to give him petitions”: these words are not in the Pandects, but were not removed because of the gloss. “To whom”: collected editions. “Whether”: original, collected editions.]

§ 7. “*In one’s own case, two days are allowed. How do we distinguish one’s own case from another person’s?*” It is clear that a case is one’s own when its gain or loss pertains to a person in his own name.

And below:

§ 8. If judgment has been pronounced against an absent person, the two or three days are reckoned from the time when he learns of it, not from the time when it was pronounced. The statement that an absent person may appeal from the time when he knows is understood in this way: if he was not defended in the case through an advocate. For if that advocate did not appeal, it is difficult for this appeal to be heard. [Note: “Is understood”: Basel—“we understand”: the other editions.]

§ 9. If a provincial governor has marked someone for deportation to an island and has written to the emperor that he is to be deported, let us consider when an appeal must be made: when the emperor has rescripted that he is to be deported, or when the governor writes concerning him.
