I think that the appeal must be made when the governor orders him to be taken into custody, *having pronounced judgment and written to the emperor that he is to be deported.* But it must be feared that it is too late if appeal is then made when the emperor has assigned him an island; for when the governor’s or praetor’s judgment has been confirmed, the emperor customarily assigns an island to him. Conversely, it must be feared that, if the governor has burdened before the prince with lies the man whose deportation he was seeking, the way of appeal may be cut off from him. What then? It will rightly be said, on grounds of humanity, that appeal may usefully be made at both that time and the earlier time, because the appeal is not against the prince but against the judge’s cunning.

And below: [Note: Fragment 3 of the same title.]

§ 10. Let us also consider this: if, when the writing was sent to the emperor, a copy of the letter was issued to the litigant and he did not appeal, but afterwards a rescript was issued against him, may he appeal against the letter previously issued to him? [Note: “Previously” (*pridem*): Böhm reads “indeed” (*quidem*).] Since he who did not appeal then seems to have agreed that the matters written were true, he is not to be heard if he says that he awaited the outcome of the *sacred rescript*. [Note: At the beginning of the same fragment. “Someone” (*quidem*): original, collected editions, Argentinensis, Lyons II–III. “The emperor has written”: this is corrected from the Pandects. Earlier the reading was: “The emperor has rescripted.” “Rescripted”: same editions, Basel. “I think”: collected editions. “Judgment pronounced”: these words through “But” have been added from the Pandects. Added: “after ten days”: Argentinensis. Added: “or praetor”: collected editions, Basel. Added: “to them”: Basel—“to him”: Lyons II–III. “Was seeking”: collected editions. “Cuts off”: Basel. “May he?” In the common codices and collected editions, Basel, the words “Certainly he cannot” followed; they occur neither in the ancient manuscripts nor in the Pandects.]

C. XXX. Likewise Ulpian, book XLIX, in the title “On Receiving or Not Receiving Appeals,” law 1. [Note: Fragment 1, title 5, book 49.]

Part V. Appellants are not customarily heard except those whose interest is involved, those to whom authority has been given, or those who manage another’s business, which the defendant subsequently ratifies. But even if a mother, *when she observes that her son’s affair has been overturned by a judgment*, appeals in the exercise of maternal devotion, it must be said that she too ought to be heard. If she prefers to make arrangements for conducting the litigation, she is not considered an interloper, although she could not defend him from the beginning. [Note: “Which the defendant subsequently ratifies”: collected editions. “Mother”: formerly the shorter reading was: “But if a mother appeals from devotion, it must be said,” etc. Many other passages in this and the following chapter have been corrected from the Pandects. “Overturned”: original, Böhm.]

§ 1. Scaevola, book IV of *Rules*. [Note: Fragment 2 in the same title.] Appeal may be made before judgment if the judge has made an interlocutory order that an inquiry be held in a civil matter, or in a criminal matter if he does so contrary to the laws. [Note: Added: “given”: Basel.]

§ 2. Macer, book I *On Appeals*, law 4. [Note: Fragment 4 in the same title.] The request of one who delays conducting his case because he says that he has submitted a petition to the prince and awaits a sacred rescript is forbidden to be heard; and if he appeals for that reason, his appeal is forbidden by sacred constitutions to be received.

C. XXXI. On letters of referral. Likewise Marcian, book 2, *On Appeals*, title “On Letters of Referral,” sole law. [Note: Digest, book 49, title 6.]

After an appeal has been lodged, letters must be given by the person from whom the appeal is made to the person who is to hear it, whether the prince or anyone else; these letters are called letters of referral or *apostoli*. The purport of the letters is this: that Lucius Titius, for example, has appealed from the judgment of that judge which was pronounced between them. It is enough to have requested letters of referral urgently and repeatedly within the allotted time, *so that*, even if he does not receive them, he may attest that very fact. For the constitutions require persistence in one who requests letters of referral. It is therefore equitable that, if the failure to give the letters was due to the person who ought to have given them, this should not injure the person who was to receive them. [Note: “Anyone whatsoever”: collected editions. “That judge N.”: Basel—“such a judge”: remaining editions. “Between him and Maevius”: collected editions. “Requester”: same editions. “Was due”: same editions, Basel. “Ought”: collected editions, Argentinensis, Böhm.]

§ 1. Ulpian, book IV *On Appeals*, title “Nothing Is to Be Altered Once an Appeal Has Been Lodged,” sole law. [Note: Digest, book 49, title 7, beginning.] Once an appeal has been lodged, whether it has been received or not, nothing ought to be altered in the meantime. And below: [Note: Fragment 5 in the same title.]

§ 2. If someone condemned for several crimes appeals concerning some of them and not concerning others, the question is whether his punishment must be deferred. If the crimes concerning which the appeal was lodged are more serious, while the matter concerning which he did not appeal is less serious, the appeal must certainly be received and the punishment deferred. But if he deserved a heavier sentence from the charge concerning which no appeal was made, punishment must in every case be imposed. [Note: “Has been”: original, Basel. “In every case”: collected editions.]

Gratian. This is the form of letters of referral: “I, N., bishop of the holy church of Bologna,” [Note: The collected editions and Basel read “I, N.”; the Argentinensis edition reads “I, Henry.”] release you, Roland, priest and chaplain of St Apollinaris, from observance of my judgment, by these apostolic letters, to the Apostolic See to which you have appealed.” The form for one appealing before judgment is: “I, Adelinus, minister—though unworthy—of the church of Holy Regina, perceiving that I am oppressed by Lord Gualterius, archbishop of the holy church of Ravenna, appeal to the Roman See and request apostolic letters.”

§ 1. But if he wishes to appeal after judgment has been delivered, this shall be his form of appeal: “I, A., minister—though unworthy—of the holy church of Regina, appeal to the Roman See against the judgment of Lord G., archbishop of the holy church of Ravenna, unjustly rendered against me on the day before the Kalends of May, in the year 1141 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the fourth indiction; and I request apostolic letters.” [Note: The common editions read 1161, a number which, as the gloss correctly says, cannot stand. This is confirmed because the fourth indiction mentioned here does not correspond to that year. Since the manuscripts differ, this reading was judged preferable: it can be restored merely by transposing the numeral signs, and the fourth indiction coincides with this year. The Basel and Lyons editions read 1161; the others read 1105.]

§ 2. If one or two persons wish to appeal on behalf of many, they shall appeal as follows: “We, P. and G., syndics of the canons of the holy church of B., perceiving that we are oppressed,” or, “against the judgment,” etc., “appeal to the Roman See and request apostolic letters.” Appeals of this kind must be made in writing.

It is not lawful to appeal to the judgment of one of another faith.

Therefore, in the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 7: [Note: Chapter 30 of the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua* in Ballerini; compare the note on chapter 9, Distinction 18.]

C. XXXII. A Catholic who entrusts his case to the judgment of one of another faith shall be excommunicated.

A Catholic who refers his case, whether just or unjust, to the judgment of a judge of another faith shall be excommunicated. [Note: The phrase “of a judge” is absent from the original.]

[Col. 0632B] Part VI. Gratian. It should be noted that there are certain judges from whom appeal ought not to be made.

Thus in the Council of Milevis, chapter 24, it is read: [Note: Held after A.D. 416—Ivo, Panormia, book 19, chapter 132, from the Council of Split—Decree, part 6, chapter 365.]

C. XXXIII. From which judges appeal is not permitted.

It is not lawful to appeal from judges chosen by common agreement. [Note: “Chose”: Nuremberg and Venice II editions. “To be appealed from”: collected editions.]

Gratian. This must be understood of arbitrators. For some judges are ordinary and others arbitral. Ordinary judges are those who receive lawful authority from the Apostolic See, if they are ecclesiastical, or from the emperor, if they are secular. Arbitral judges are those who, having no authority, are chosen as judges by the agreement of litigants, who submit to them on the condition that their judgment shall stand. Of these, some are both ordinary and arbitral, while others are arbitral only. Both ordinary and arbitral are those who possess lawful authority and are chosen as arbitrators by persons not subject to their jurisdiction. From such persons, even though they sit as arbitral judges rather than ordinary judges, an aggrieved party may appeal by virtue of the privilege of their ordinary rank.

Therefore, in the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 10: [Note: Held A.D. 397—Anselm, book 3, chapter 123—Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chapter 363.]

C. XXXIV. It is lawful to appeal from judges chosen by common agreement.

Certainly, if judges have been chosen by agreement of the parties, appeal is permitted even from a number smaller than that prescribed. [Note: “Appeal is permitted”: Gratian cites this canon, as he himself explicitly acknowledges, to show that appeal is permitted from such judges. Yet in the printed and manuscript Council of Carthage, compared with various copies; in the one printed and manuscript codex of canons; in the Greek text, which agrees with it; in the African text, where this passage is repeated; and in Ivo, the reading is “appeal is not permitted.” The preceding material in the canon itself, cited below in the same chapter, also shows conclusively that it must be read with the negation.]

[Col. 0633A] C. XXXV. Those who complain of bishops’ judgments shall be heard by neighboring bishops, or by others brought in with their consent. Likewise from the Council of Milevis, chapter 22. [Note: Held after A.D. 416—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 22, chapter 10—compare below, Causa 11, question 3, chapter 34.]

It was resolved that, if presbyters, deacons, or other inferior clergy complain of the judgments of their bishops in cases they have, neighboring bishops shall hear them and settle whatever dispute exists between them, with persons brought in by them with the consent of their bishops. But if they think an appeal must be made from these judges *as well*, they shall appeal only to African councils or to the primates of their own provinces. Whoever thinks that an appeal should be made overseas shall not be received into communion by anyone within Africa. [Note: “Determine”: collected editions. “Appeal shall be made”: Basel. “Primacies”: Hispanic Collection. “Thinks”—“shall be received”: same source and collected editions.]

Gratian. Unless perhaps they have appealed to the Roman See. But one who has appealed must not be remitted to the person from whom he appealed.

Therefore, in the Council of Sardica, chapter 7: [Note: Held A.D. 347—Anselm, books 1–2, chapter 78—Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 27.]

C. XXXVI. On the same matter.

If a bishop has been accused and the assembled bishops of his region have judged him and deposed him from his rank, and if the deposed man appeals and takes refuge with the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church and wishes to be heard, then, if the Roman bishop judges it right that the examination be recalled or renewed, he shall deign to write to the bishops in the neighboring and adjacent province, that they may investigate everything diligently and determine it according to the faith of truth. [Note: Added: “all”: Isidore Mercator—Ivo—collected editions. “When”: same editions, Basel. “Appears”: original, cited collections, Basel. “Wishes to be heard”: Greek: *καὶ βουληθείη αὐτοῦ διακοῦσαι*, that is, “and if the Roman bishop should wish to hear him.” “That it be renewed, or”: these words are absent from both the printed and manuscript council, compared with various copies, and from Anselm, Ivo, and the Basel edition. It reads only “that the examination be renewed,” as in Greek, *ἀνανεώσασθαι*; Nicholas and Ivo so report it. The words were not introduced because of the gloss. Added: “the Roman bishop”: original, cited collections, collected editions. Added: “other”: original, collected editions. “There”: Anselm. “Investigate thoroughly”: Basel.]

But if the man who requests that his case be heard again moves the Roman bishop by his entreaty, so that he sends presbyters from his own side, it shall be within his power *both* to decide what he wishes and what he judges appropriate. And if he decrees that persons should be sent to sit in judgment together with the bishops, so that they may also possess the authority of the person by whom they were dispatched, this shall be at his discretion. But if he thinks the bishops sufficient to put an end to the affair, let him do what he judges best according to his most prudent counsel. [Note: “If someone requests that his case be heard again”: the Greek is *Εἰ δέ τις ἀξιῶν καὶ πάλιν αὐτοῦ τὸ πρᾶγμα ἀκουσθῆναι*, that is, “But if someone requests that his case be heard again,” so that there is a second appeal, also indicated in the chapter “Gaudentius,” which in the Greek precedes this chapter immediately. “Moved”: collected editions from Ivo. “From”: Hispanic Collection—“of”: Anselm. The word “and” is absent from the original and cited collections. “Decrees”: Böhm. “Bishops”: The Gratian manuscripts, as also Ivo, continued with “fellow-provincial bishops,” a word absent from the council and from Nicholas; it occurs, however, in Isidore Mercator and Ivo. The Hispanic Collection and Anselm read “provincial bishops.” The Greek reads *καὶ ἀπόφασιν τοῦ ἐπισκόπου*, “and the judgment of the bishop himself.” Balsamon, however, appears to have read *τῶν ἐπισκόπων*, “of the bishops,” and first interprets it of provincial bishops, then of others. “Let them do”: Lyons II–III—“he shall do”: remaining editions, Basel, Ivo, Isidore Mercator. “Counsel”: Basel, Venice II, Nuremberg, Paris, Lyons I.]

Gratian. Purely arbitral judges are those who have received no lawful authority. Appeal is not permitted from them, because litigants must blame themselves for choosing such persons. But if the judgment of those from whom appeal is made is set aside, this will not harm them unless they are proved to have rendered an unjust judgment through hostility or corruption by money. [Note: The common editions and collected editions, Basel, continued: “by the person to whom appeal was made”; these words were deleted because they are absent from the ancient codices.]

Therefore, in the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 10, it is read: [Note: Held A.D. 397—Ivo, Panormia, book 4, chapter 133—Decree, part 6, chapter 363.]

C. XXXVII. When a judgment is set aside through appeal, it ought not harm one who did not judge with an unjust disposition.

[Col. 0634B] Part VII. It was further resolved that, whenever appeal is made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges of higher authority, the setting aside of their judgment shall not harm those judges, if they cannot be convicted either of judging with an unjust disposition or of having been corrupted by some greed or favor. [Note: “Hostile” for “unjust”: original—Ivo—Argentinensis edition.]

Gratian. A question is raised whether the person from whom appeal is made ought to be summoned as a witness before the person to whom appeal is made concerning the affair of which he first assumed cognizance.

Concerning this, the Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 1, decreed as follows: [Note: Held A.D. 401—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 19, chapter 1—Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chapter 230, from Dionysius.]

C. XXXVIII. A cleric shall not be summoned as witness in the case of which he first assumed cognizance.

[Col. 0634C] It was decreed that if someone *perhaps* wishes to conduct in a church any case by apostolic law imposed upon churches, and if perhaps the clerics’ decision displeases one party, it is not lawful to summon for testimony in court the cleric who was president or cognizant in the matter; and no person of any ecclesiastical order shall be summoned to give testimony. [Note: “To be decreed”: original—Argentinensis and Basel editions. “Perhaps”: the source reads *forte*. “Present”: original—Basel. Added: “order”: same edition.]

Gratian. Nor is it lawful to appeal further from those to whom appeal has been made, as is read in the African Council, chapter 63: [Note: Chapter 5 of the Fifth Council of Carthage—chapter 61 in Dionysius.]

C. XXXIX. It is not lawful to appeal from those to whom appeal has been made.

But if appeal has been made, the appellant shall choose judges, *and* the person against whom he has appealed shall choose with him, so that from them it shall thereafter be lawful for no one to appeal.

Gratian. This must be understood after the second appeal: for in one and the same case it is not lawful to appeal a third time on the same points. Therefore, in book VII of the Code, under the title “That It Is Not Lawful to Appeal a Third Time in One and the Same Case,” sole law, Emperor Justinian writes:

If anyone has appealed a second time in any litigation, he may not use an appeal a third time in the same litigation on the same points, nor reopen judgments of the most excellent prefects of the praetorium. Litigants may, however, before joinder of issue and with an arbitrator having been appointed, invoke the hearing of the person who appointed him; such a petition shall in no way have the force of an appeal. § 1. But when an accusation has been brought in a capital case or a case concerning status, the appellants must conduct their own case in person, not through advocates. [Note: Code of Justinian, book 7, title 70. “Given”: collected editions, Argentinensis. “Petition”—“obtain”: Basel.]

[Col. 0635C] Therefore Pope Hadrian says in the chapters collected by him, chapter 44: [Note: From the interpretation of Paul, *Sentences*, book 5, title 35—Anselm, at the end of book 3, chapter 42.]

C. XL. It is not lawful to prosecute through an advocate an appeal lodged in a capital case or a case concerning status.

If at any time a person has been summoned in a capital case or a case concerning status, the matter must be conducted not through a procurator [Note: [Col. 0635] *procuratore* (“by a procurator”): original], but by the persons themselves [Note: [Col. 0635] *ipsis praesentibus* (“with them present”): original].

Gratian. The period for pursuing an appeal is one year, or, if a just cause intervenes, two years. Thus in the *Authentics*, constitution 11, collation V, we read:

### C. XLI. On the same matter

[Note: [Col. 0635] From Novella 47, *Auth. Ei, qui*, Code, title 63, law 7.]

A year is granted to one who appeals, within which he is to pursue the suit jointly in person with his adversary [Note: [Col. 0635] *comm.* or: ed. Bas.; *communiterve* (“or jointly”): the other editions, from the original]; or, if a just [Note: [Col. 0635] *unjust*: ed. Bas.] cause intervenes, another year is granted [Note: [Col. 0635] *indulgetur* (“is granted”): editions of the collection], after which, if the suit has not been completed, the judgment remains valid.

§ 1. If the appellant defaults, when one month remains of the two-year period, the victor may proceed in order that the defendant may be sought; and, whether found [Col. 0635D] or not found, he may bring forward his allegations, and [Note: [Col. 0635] *ut* (“that”): the same editions] the judgment may either [Col. 0636A] be confirmed or rescinded, the absent party [Note: [Col. 0635] *absentem* (“the absent person”): the same editions, first Paris and Lyons II–III] in every event being condemned in costs [Note: [Col. 0635] *in expensis* (“in costs”): original; editions of the collection], according to the periods of the fatal days. But if neither party appears [Note: [Col. 0635] *curanti*: ed. Arg.; *occurrente* (“appearing”): ed. Bas.], after the second [Note: [Col. 0635] *annum* (“year”) added: editions of the collection, except Bas.] fatal term the judgment shall remain [Note: [Col. 0635] *permanet* (“remains”): six editions of the collection] valid.

In constitution 2, collation IV [Note: [Col. 0635] From Novella 23, *Auth. Sed et ei*, Code, book 7, title 63]:

§ 2. But a suit which is expected to be brought before the emperor’s consistory remains untouched, without prejudice from delay, until he causes it to be introduced and decided by the great officers according to custom.

Gratian. But if the person who appealed, moved by repentance, wishes to withdraw from the appeal, he is not forbidden. For in book 7 of the Code, title *On Appeals*, law 28, the emperors Arcadius and Honorius are recorded as having decreed:

[Note: [Col. 0635D] From “If anyone has submitted petitions” to the end of this chapter Gratian cites various laws of the Code, not reproducing their exact words, but those which he judged relevant to his question.]

If anyone has submitted petitions of appeal, let him know that he has permission to change his mind and recover his petitions [Col. 0636B], lest humane regard for justified repentance be cut off.

§ 1. There are also cases in which it is unnecessary to lodge an appeal. In the same book and title, law 27, the same emperors decreed:

Appointments made by petitions or edicts are invalid without public deliberation; and, where the required formality is absent, there is no need to appeal concerning them.

### Part VIII

§ 2. A definitive judgment which contains neither condemnation nor acquittal is held null. [Note: [Col. 0635] Chapter 3, Code, book 7, title 45.]

§ 3. Likewise, a judgment pronounced by a governor outside the customary judicial procedure does not acquire the authority of a thing adjudged. [Note: [Col. 0635] Chapter 4, there.]

§ 4. Likewise, if a judgment has been delivered against matters previously adjudicated, from which no appeal was made, it will have no authority as a judgment; and therefore [Col. 0636C] there is no need to appeal. [Note: [Col. 0635] Chapter 1, Code, book 7, title 64.]

§ 5. Likewise, if judgment is delivered contrary to written law—for example, by asserting that a deceased person was under fourteen years old and nevertheless validly made a will—it has no force, and the remedy of appeal is unnecessary against it. [Note: [Col. 0635] Chapter 2, there.]

§ 6. But if judgment is said contrary to the litigant’s right—for example, when a person under fourteen is declared to have completed his fourteenth year and thus to have made a will lawfully—recourse must be had to the remedy of appeal.

§ 7. Likewise, if several judges have been appointed and only one of them is said to have pronounced judgment, there appears to have been no need to appeal, since the judgment has no legal validity. [Note: [Col. 0635] Chapter 4, there.]

§ 8. Likewise, since judges may impose fines only for a defined reason and purpose [Note: [Col. 0635] *sententia* (“judgment”): ed. Bas.; *fine certo* (“a definite purpose”): the other editions; Böhm], if they impose a fine otherwise than according to the amount prescribed by statute, what was done contrary to law has no binding force [Col. 0636D] and may be rescinded without appeal. [Note: [Col. 0635] Chapter 5, there.]

[Col. 0637A] § 9. It has likewise been decreed that venal judgments, delivered by corrupt judges for payment, are invalid even without the aid of an appeal having been lodged. [Note: [Col. 0637] Chapter 7, there.]

§ 10. Likewise, if, because of the incapacity of your age, you prove yourself unfit for the office to which you have been appointed, the unjust appointment shall be removed without an appeal. [Note: [Col. 0637] Chapter 8, there.]

§ 11. There are also persons whose appeals are not admitted. For the appeal of one who is absent through contumacy, when summoned to conduct the case, cannot be received, if, after a summary examination of the matter, he is to be condemned. [Note: [Col. 0637] Chapter 1, Code, book 7, title 65.]

§ 12. No murderer, poisoner, evildoer, adulterer, or person who has committed manifest violence, once convicted by evidence, overcome by witnesses, or having confessed the vice and crime in his own voice, shall be heard appealing. [Col. 0637B] This applies in notorious cases. [Note: [Col. 0637] Chapter 2, there.]

§ 13. But in hidden cases: if, after witnesses have been produced, documents brought forward, and other proofs supplied, judgment has been delivered against him, and the condemned person [Note: [Col. 0637] *condemnandus* (“the person to be condemned”): Böhm] has either not confessed in his own voice at all, or has said something against himself through fear of torture, he is not denied leave to appeal. [Note: [Col. 0637] The same constitution.]

§ 14. No official is granted an appeal from the judgment of his own judge, except in that case alone which he may happen to have instituted before his own judge by civil procedure concerning property. [Note: [Col. 0637] Chapter 3, there.]

§ 15. Whenever payment of a fiscal assessment is demanded, a tax is exacted, or repayment of a manifest and established public or private debt is required, appeal being excluded, judicial coercion is necessarily exercised against the contumacious party. [Note: [Col. 0637] Chapter 4, there.]

§ 16. No appeal may be made from execution of judgment, unless perhaps the executor of the judgment exceeds the limits of the adjudication. [Note: [Col. 0637] Chapter 5, there.]

§ 17. If anyone has dared to appeal in order that the will of a deceased person, written in a testament, might not be opened, or that those shown to have been named heirs might not be put into possession, and the person having jurisdiction in the matter has admitted the appeal, both the judge who has shown such cowardly connivance and the litigant who has appealed so importunately shall be fined twenty pounds of silver. [Note: [Col. 0637] Chapter 6, there.]

§ 18. If a case is heard concerning possession and its immediate enjoyment, the judgment called interlocutory takes effect when delivered, even though an appeal has been lodged. [Note: [Col. 0637] Sole chapter, Code, book 7, title 69.]

§ 19. Sometimes several persons jointly incur one and the same condemnation, and diversity of acts does not admit of separation. [Col. 0637D] In that case, if all appeal, and, with one of them conducting the case, their appeal is pronounced just, the benefit of victory will extend also to the others. But if only one appealed and his appeal is pronounced just, it also benefits the person who did not appeal. [Note: [Col. 0637] Chapters 1–2, Code, book 7, title 68.]

[Col. 0638A] § 20. But if one person obtains restitution against the judgment by reason of the privilege of age, this rescript does not benefit an adult who did not appeal in his own right.

§ 21. Judges are charged not only with the duty of receiving an appeal; they are also assigned a period of thirty days from the day of judgment, within which the record, together with the report, must be furnished to the litigants. [Note: [Col. 0637] Chapter 24, Code, book 7, title 62.]

§ 22. Likewise, an arbitrator is compelled to receive an appeal and provide a report, if he has been delegated. [Note: [Col. 0637] Chapter 31, there, at the end.]

§ 23. Litigants are also permitted to appeal immediately by word of mouth, without written petitions, when the judicial matter requires it, in civil as well as criminal cases. [Note: [Col. 0637] Chapter 14, there.]

§ 24. From the person who hears an appeal, no recourse may be made to the judge from whom the appeal was taken. Therefore those who seek to have litigants remitted to the provinces should understand that this opportunity is remote from them and entirely excluded, since upon every matter under appeal it is lawful only to pronounce the appeal either unjust or just. [Col. 0638B] [Note: [Col. 0637] Chapter 6, there.]

§ 25. You will find all these matters in book VII of the Code, from the title *On Appeals* to the title *That It Is Not Permitted to Appeal a Third Time in One and the Same Case*.

# QUESTION VII

## GRATIAN

### Part I

That laymen are not to be heard in accusations against bishops is testified by Pope Evaristus, who says in his second letter to the bishops throughout Egypt [Note: [Col. 0637] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, taken from Isidore of Spain, *Sentences*, book 3, chapter 39; Anselm, book 3, chapter 11; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, title 37.]:

### C. I. Laymen are not to be admitted to accuse bishops.

[Col. 0638C] A bishop is not to be reproved or accused by the common people or by ordinary persons, even if he is irregular, because the life of rulers is ordered by God according to the deserts of their subjects. And below: “I say these things because the tempter very often turns good into evil and places a stain upon the elect.” [Note: [Col. 0637] *ponere* (“to place”): editions of the collection.]

### C. II. A layman is not to accuse a cleric.

Likewise, Pope Silvester, in the epilogue to the Roman Council:

No layman may dare bring a charge against a cleric. [Note: [Col. 0637] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, composed from the *Liber Pontificalis*; Burchard, book 1, chapter 151; Anselm, book 3, chapter 23; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 264.]

### C. III. On the same matter.

Likewise Pope Marcellinus, in his second letter to the Eastern bishops:

A layman is not permitted to accuse any cleric. [Note: [Col. 0637] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, taken from the Life of Silvester in the *Liber Pontificalis*; Anselm, book 3, chapter 22; cf. C. 11, q. 1, c. 3.]

[Col. 0638D] ### C. IV. An excommunicated person cannot accuse priests.

Likewise Pope Julius, in his decrees, chapter 36 [Note: [Col. 0637] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled from the Seventh Council of Carthage, chapter 1; the constitution of Silvester, letter 1; and letters 1 of Zosimus and Siricius; *Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 32, chapter 7.]:

It was ordained in the holy Nicene synod that no one under anathema [Note: [Col. 0637] *anathema*: original] be admitted in an accusation brought against us [Note: [Col. 0637] *nostram accusationem* (“our accusation”): editions of the collection, including the first Basle edition], nor those who are unwilling to admit us in their complaint or accusation [Note: [Col. 0637] *suam accusationem* (“their accusation”): editions of the collection], since we know that we have been appointed by the Lord over them, [Col. 0639A] not they over us. And just as a greater person cannot be judged by a lesser, so neither can he be bound [Note: [Col. 0639] *colligari* (“be bound”): original], because everything great is rare. We bear the burdens of all who are burdened; indeed, blessed Peter the apostle bears them in us, whose office we discharge as legates and by whose rule we are instructed, so that, supported by his help, we may be defended against all adversities now and forever.

[Note: [Col. 0639] *Portemus* (“let us bear”): the same editions, first Basle; *hominum* (“of human beings”): ed. Basle. The text reads “all who are burdened”; the Basle edition has “all human beings.”]

### C. V. On the same matter.

Likewise Eusebius, in his first letter to the bishops of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0639] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled from the constitution of Silvester; Anselm, book 3, chapter 25.]:

It has hitherto been observed and decreed that laymen should not accuse bishops, because they are not of the same manner of life, and some are exceedingly hostile to them. For their life and conduct ought to be private and removed from the activities of laypeople; nor ought they to be attacked by those [Col. 0639B] who are unwilling to imitate their chastity and seriousness [Note: [Col. 0639] *quorum* (“whose”): Anselm], especially since these latter are unwilling to admit them in accusations of their own [Note: [Col. 0639] *noluerint* (“were unwilling”): ed. Basle; *quum eos nolunt* (“since they are unwilling concerning them”): editions of the collection].

### C. VI. Neither clerics in accusations against laymen, nor laymen in accusations against clerics, are to be admitted.

Likewise Pope Fabian, in his second letter to the Eastern bishops [Note: [Col. 0639] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled from the Life of Silvester in the *Liber Pontificalis* and the constitution of Silvester; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 61; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 320.]:

Just as priests and the remaining clerics are excluded from accusation by secular laypersons, so laypersons are to be excluded and kept apart from accusations brought by clerics. And just as these are not admitted by those, so those are not admitted by these, because, just as the manner of life of the Lord’s priests ought to be separate from their manner of life, so ought litigation also to be separate; for a servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel [Note: [Col. 0639] Added: “but be gentle toward all,” Ivo, *Panormia*; editions of the collection, including the first Argenteus; cf. 2 Timothy 2].

[Col. 0639C] ### C. VII. On the same matter. [PALEA.]

Likewise, from the Council of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0639C] This chapter is absent from most ancient manuscripts of Gratian and is not correctly placed here; it occurs in Burchard, who has *plebesanos* in place of *plebeios*.] [Note: [Col. 0639] These words are not found in the extant councils of Mainz; Burchard, book 16, chapter 7. This *Palea* is absent from the Argenteus, Venetian I–II, Nuremberg, and Paris editions.]

“It has been decreed that presbyters may both accuse and bear witness against their own plebeians. But if they neglect to do so, they shall be liable to the peril of their rank.”

### C. VIII. Laymen ought not accuse clerics.

Likewise Clement, in his first letter to James [Note: [Col. 0639C] In this and the following chapter the exact words of Saint Clement are not reported.] [Note: [Col. 0639] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, drawn from Benedict’s Rule, chapters 4 and 5.]

Priests, the other ministers of the Church, and all congregations ought to love their bishops and obey their commands, [Col. 0640A] even if they themselves act otherwise [Note: [Col. 0639] Added: “than they should”: editions of the collection, including the first Argenteus, Nuremberg, and Venetian I]—which God forbid—unless they have departed from the faith.

### C. IX. On the same matter.

Likewise, in the second letter to the same person [Note: [Col. 0639] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, taken from Justinian’s confession against the Three Chapters, Mansi, volume 9, page 576.]:

Divine Scripture shows what sort of condemnation threatens those who sin against fathers. For if Ham was cursed because he did not cover his father’s nakedness, much greater condemnation is deserved by those who insult fathers discharging God’s embassy.

Gratian. Persons of lower ranks are not to be admitted in accusations against those of higher rank.

Therefore Pope Silvester, in the epilogue to the Roman Council [Note: [Col. 0639] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, drawn from the constitution of Silvester; Burchard, book 1, chapter 151; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 262]:

### C. X. Inferiors ought not accuse superiors.

A cleric against an exorcist, an exorcist against an acolyte, an acolyte against a subdeacon, a subdeacon [Col. 0640B] against a deacon, a deacon against a presbyter, and a presbyter against a bishop cannot lodge an accusation or give testimony [Note: [Col. 0639D] “Or give testimony” is not in the original or in the other places cited; moreover, the entire order in the enumeration has been changed. For in the council and in the other sources it is: “He established these ranks in the bosom of the synod, so that a presbyter [may not proceed] against a bishop,” etc.].

[Note: [Col. 0639] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, drawn from the constitution of Silvester; Burchard, book 1, chapter 151; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 262.]

### C. XI. On the same matter.

Likewise Pope Zephyrinus, in his first letter to the bishops of Sicily:

No superior is to be attacked by accusations from inferiors.

[Note: [Col. 0640C] In the original, as also in Ivo [and Anselm], it reads: “Nor shall any of the highest be attacked or destroyed by accusations of the lower.”]

[Note: [Col. 0639] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter drawn from the same source; Anselm, book 3, chapter 62; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 245.]

### C. XII. On the same matter.

Likewise Pope Anacletus, in his third letter [Note: [Col. 0639] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled from Isidore of Spain, *Sentences*, book 3, title 39; Anselm, book 3, chapter 37; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 239; Deusdedit, part 3.]:

Those who betray the faults of their teachers or superiors are condemned by the judgment upon Ham, son of Noah: like Ham, who did not cover his father’s nakedness [Note: [Col. 0639] *verenda* (“shameful parts”): editions of the collection], but instead displayed it for ridicule [Note: [Col. 0639] *irridenda* (“for mockery”): editions of the collection].

[Col. 0640C] ### C. XIII. Sheep cannot accuse their shepherd unless he has departed from the faith.

Likewise Pope Eusebius, in his second letter to the bishops of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0639] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, taken from Isidore, book 1, and Gregory the Great, *Pastoral Rule*, book 3, chapter 5; Anselm, book 3, chapter 44; Burchard, book 1, chapter 139; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 139; *Polycarpus*, book 5, title 1.]:

Sheep committed to their shepherd ought neither to reprove him—unless he has departed from the right faith—nor can they accuse him in any way, because the deeds of shepherds are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, although they may seem rightly deserving of reproof.

[Note: [Col. 0639] *oris vel ovis* (“of the mouth or of a sheep”): ed. Argenteus; *ovis* (“of a sheep”): ed. Basle; *eorum* (“of them”): Burchard.]

### Part II

Gratian. These authorities prove that subjects, whether lay or clerical, cannot accuse their prelates. But this must be understood of criminal and disreputable persons, who are ready to criticize the lives of their prelates rather than imitate them. This is apparent from the words of Anacletus, who says [Note: [Col. 0641] The passage does not occur in Anacletus, from whom it is cited. Nearly the same words are nevertheless found in the letter of Eusebius above, under the chapter “Laymen”]:

### C. XIV. Why laymen are not heard in accusations against bishops.

Laymen [Note: [Col. 0641] Compare above, chapter 5.] are not to be heard in accusations against bishops, because some are exceedingly hostile to them, and it is unworthy that those should accuse them who are unwilling to imitate their seriousness.

### C. XV. Priests can be accused only by suitable and approved men.

Likewise Anacletus, in his second letter to the bishops of Italy [Note: [Col. 0641] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Anselm, book 3, chapter 31; in part Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 58, and *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 238.]:

The accusation concerning them, on which you wished to consult us, [Col. 0641B] ought to be made only by suitable and most approved men, who are free from both suspicions and crimes [Note: [Col. 0641] These are words of Constantine the Great in his letter to Ablavius, and of the Council of Carthage held in 421, chapter 6, and Isidore of Spain, *Sentences*, book 3, chapter 39]. For the Lord did not wish the ministers of his sacred body to be defamed or calumniated by low, rejected, and unsuitable persons, nor did he permit them to be calumniated; rather, he himself drove sinful priests from the temple with his own scourge. Hence it is clear that the chief priests—that is, bishops—are to be judged by God, not torn to pieces by human beings or persons of depraved life, but rather borne by all the faithful. The Lord himself gave the example when he expelled those selling and buying from the temple in person and not through another.

And shortly afterward:

§ 1. For, I think, no one among us is found who wishes his own servant to be judged by anyone other than himself. And if this has been presumed, he himself either becomes angry with great indignation or rather seeks vengeance [Note: [Col. 0641] *vindictam* (“vengeance”): Ivo; the editions of the collection] upon that person.

And below:

§ 2. Therefore the Lord also says through the Prophet [Note: [Col. 0641] Zechariah, chapter 2, verse 8]: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye.”

And shortly afterward:

§ 3. If detractors of any persons are severely judged and fall into the snare of destruction, much more are the slanderers, detractors, and accusers of the aforesaid servants of God, and their persecutors, condemned; and unless they amend themselves and perform worthy penance through satisfaction to them, they undoubtedly fall into the abyss [Note: [Col. 0641] *vadunt* (“they go”): original; Ivo] and are burned in avenging flames [Note: [Col. 0641] *flaminis* (“of a flame”): ed. Basle].

And below:

§ 4. Considering these and other dangers, the apostles decreed that the pillars of the holy Church of God—that is, the apostles [Col. 0642A] and their successors, as they are not undeservedly called—should not easily be stirred up against, torn to pieces, or accused. But if anyone is stirred up against them or their churches, or has causes against them [Note: [Col. 0641] *causam* (“a cause”): editions of the collection], let him first have recourse to them in the spirit of charity, so that, being admonished in a familiar conversation, they may heal what needs healing and correct charitably what they recognize ought justly to be corrected. But if any persons presume, before doing this, to tear them to pieces, accuse them, or harass them, let them be excommunicated and by no means absolved before they have performed worthy penance by satisfaction, as has already been said; for injury done to them pertains to Christ [Note: [Col. 0641] From the first letter of Anastasius II; cf. the Council of Aachen, held in 836, chapters 3 and 7], whose embassy they discharge.

[Note: [Col. 0641] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter. The phrases derive from the words of Constantine the Great in his letter to Ablavius, the Council of Carthage held in 421, chapter 6, and Isidore of Seville, *Sentences*, book 3, chapter 39. “They are the pillars”: phrasing from the Council of Paris, held in 829, chapter 3. The following material is compiled according to the Council of Orléans V, chapter 17. “Pertains to Christ”: from Anastasius II, letter 1; compare the Council of Aachen, held in 836, chapters 3 and 7.]

[Col. 0642B] ### C. XVI. Let him be deprived of communion who complains publicly against a bishop before meeting him privately.

Likewise Alexander, in his first letter, chapter 3 [Note: [Col. 0641] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, taken from the Council of Orléans V, chapter 17; Burchard, book 1, chapter 132; Anselm, book 3, chapter 85 (36); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 35, and *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 244; Alger, book 2, chapter 31.]:

If anyone believes that he has any just complaint against a bishop or the agents of a church, he should not first approach primates or other judges, but should meet privately with those by whom he considers himself injured [Note: [Col. 0641] *existimat* (“considers”): Ivo, *Decretum*; editions of the collection]—not once only, but very often—so that he may receive from them either his due justice or a just excuse. And below: But if he acts otherwise, let him be deprived of communion by them and by others, as a despiser of the apostles and the other Fathers.

### C. XVII. Accusers of bishops are not to be heard until their reputation has been examined.

Likewise Pope Evaristus, in his second letter to the bishops throughout Egypt [Note: [Col. 0641] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. the Council of Carthage III, chapter 8; Anselm, book 3, chapter 51; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 59.]:

If there are any detractors or accusers of bishops [Col. 0642C] or other priests, they ought not be heard by the judges of the Church before the suspicion or reputation attached to their standing has been examined [Note: [Col. 0641] *existimationis* (“of reputation”): editions Argenteus, Basle, Lyons II–III; *Alger].—with what intention, faith, rashness, life, conscience, and merit they have undertaken these things; whether for God, vain glory, enmity, hatred, or greed—or not.

### C. XVIII. Persons older in rank are not to be accused except by those of right faith and conduct.

Likewise Pope Calixtus, in his second letter to the bishops of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0641] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled from chapter 53 of the *Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua*; Anselm, book 3, chapter 8; *Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 14, chapter 13; Burchard, book 1, chapter 171; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 57, and *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 289.]:

In judgment one must inquire what manner of conduct and faith belong to the accuser and to the accused. For those who are not of upright conduct and faith, whose lives are blameworthy [Note: [Col. 0641] *culpabilis* (“blameworthy”): editions of the collection except Argenteus and Basle], and whose faith, [Col. 0643A] life [Note: [Col. 0643] “life” is absent from the editions of the collection, including the first Basle and Lyons II–III], and freedom are unknown, are not permitted to accuse persons older in rank. Nor are low persons to be admitted in accusations against them.

### C. XIX. Accusations against bishops are not to be received without two or three witnesses.

Likewise Pope Sixtus II, in his second letter to the bishops of Spain [Note: [Col. 0643] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.]:

An accusation against bishops is not readily to be received, the Lord saying [Note: [Col. 0643] Exodus, chapter 50, verse 1]: “You shall not receive [Note: [Col. 0643] *suscipias* (“you shall receive”): ed. Basle; *accipias* (“you shall accept”): the other editions] a false report.” And the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0643] 1 Timothy 5:19] that an accusation against a presbyter is not to be received without two or three suitable witnesses. If such precautions are necessary concerning presbyters or the other faithful, how much more concerning bishops?

[Col. 0643B] ### C. XX. No one is to be removed from communion merely for bringing an action against a bishop.

Likewise, from the First Council of Orléans, chapter 8 [Note: [Col. 0643] Held in 511; *Collectio tripartita*, part 2, title 29, chapter 4.]:

If anyone believes that he must reclaim anything from his own bishop, from the church, or from his own right, and makes no accusation of insult or crime, he may not be removed from communion with the Church merely for bringing the action.

### C. XXI. Why subjects cannot reprove their prelates.

Likewise Pope Evaristus, in his second letter [Note: [Col. 0643] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Anselm, book 3, chapter 11.]:

There are some who perversely criticize their superiors if they have been even slightly troublesome to them.

Gratian. From all these passages it is understood that those are excluded from accusation who seek, not from charitable affection but through the depravity of their own conduct, to defame and criticize the lives of their superiors.

§ 1. That criminal persons are prohibited by the foregoing authorities from accusing prelates is testified by Augustine in the book *Soliloquies*, as follows:

[Col. 0643C] ### C. XXII. Not all subjects, but only criminal persons, are prohibited from accusing prelates.

Prelates presume that they ought not to be criticized or accused, because the canons do not establish that accusations against them may be made indiscriminately. Yet this is denied only to criminal persons, since Truth himself decrees concerning reproof [Note: [Col. 0643] A chapter of uncertain origin; Alger, book 2, chapter 16]: “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness concerning the wrong,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0643] John 18:23.]

Gratian. An objection is made to this distinction: the sacred canons themselves distinguish the case in which shepherds are to be accused by their subjects, saying: “Sheep [Note: [Col. 0643] Above, chapter 13.] are not to accuse [Col. 0644A] or reprove their shepherds unless they depart from the faith.” Thus, this is the case in which they are to be accused by subjects; in other cases, not at all.

### Part III

§ 1. The answer to this objection is as follows. That distinction of the canons is to be understood concerning criminal and disreputable persons. For criminal and disreputable sheep cannot accuse or reprove their shepherd unless he has departed from the faith. But if he has departed from the faith, the stain of that crime is so great that both slaves against masters and any criminal or disreputable persons against anyone are admitted to accuse him.

Therefore Pope Dionysius, in his second letter to Bishop Severus [Note: [Col. 0643D] In many ancient manuscripts the rubric of this chapter reads: “Disreputable persons may accuse heretics.” The Basle edition has the same reading; in contrast, the Venetian I–II, Paris, and Lyons I editions read: “Disreputable persons cannot accuse heretics”; the Nuremberg edition reads: “Disreputable persons cannot accuse.” In some other manuscripts it reads: “Disreputable persons cannot accuse Catholics.”] [Note: [Col. 0643] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. C. 3, q. 4, c. 1; Anselm, book 3, chapter 65.]:

### C. XXIII. Disreputable and heretical persons cannot accuse persons of good repute.

[Col. 0644B] We cannot and ought not receive one who shares another’s error, who voluntarily departs from the path of his own professed purpose, or who does not obey the sacred rules and constitutions of the Fathers; nor do we permit them to attack those who rightly believe or obey the enactments of the holy Fathers. For we judge all to be disreputable who betray either their own faith [Note: [Col. 0643] “their faith” added by the editions of the collection] or the Christian law, or willingly put aside apostolic or regular authority.

### C. XXIV. Those who have abandoned the faith they received cannot accuse Christians or testify against them.

Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 63 [Note: [Col. 0643] Held in 633; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, chapter 96.]:

No one can be faithful toward human beings who has proved faithless toward God [Note: [Col. 0643] *infidelis* (“faithless”): editions of the collection, including the first Basle]. Therefore Jews who formerly became Christians but have now betrayed Christ’s faith [Col. 0644C] [Note: [Col. 0643] *in fide* (“in the faith”): editions of the collection] are not to be admitted to give testimony, even though they proclaim themselves Christians [Note: [Col. 0643] *quamvis sese Christianos* (“although they themselves [proclaim themselves] Christians”): *Collectio Hispana*]. For as they are suspect in the faith of Christ, so they are held doubtful in human testimony. Therefore the testimony of those shown false in faith must be rejected, and no credence is to be given to those who have cast away from themselves fidelity to truth [Note: [Col. 0643] *abjiciunt* (“cast away”): *Collectio Hispana*].

### C. XXV. Heretics, Jews, or pagans cannot accuse Christians.

Likewise Pope Caius to Bishop Felix [Note: [Col. 0644D] The words of the letter are: “First you should know that pagans and heretics cannot accuse Christians,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0643] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, taken from the Seventh Council of Carthage, chapter 2; Anselm, book 3, chapter 46; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 63.]:

Pagans, heretics, and Jews cannot accuse Christians or bring against them a defamatory accusation.

[Col. 0645A] Gratian. This chapter decrees that heretics may not attack those who rightly believe. Hence, conversely, it is understood that heretics may be attacked by heretics. Likewise, those who voluntarily depart from the course of their professed purpose cannot attack those who keep the bounds of their profession. From this it is understood that persons departing from their profession may accuse others who likewise depart from it. Likewise, those who do not obey the enactments of the holy Fathers cannot accuse persons obedient to sacred constitutions. In this it is similarly understood that disobedient persons may accuse the disobedient. Hence, in general, it is inferred that equality of faith and conduct between accuser and accused must always be considered in an accusation, so that the accuser is found either equal or superior.

[Col. 0645B] ### C. XXVI. A heretic may accuse and testify against a heretic.

Likewise, Novella 45 of the *Novellae Constitutiones*, at the end [Note: [Col. 0645] Julian, Novella 41, chapter 2; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 28; *Decretum*, part 16, chapter 131.]:

If a heretic litigates against a heretic, either may bring a heretic as witness. But if an orthodox person litigates against a heretic, the testimony even of a heretic is valid for the orthodox person; whereas against an orthodox person only the testimony of an orthodox person is valid.

§ 1. But when orthodox persons litigate, no heretic may have access to give testimony.

Gratian. But it is asked whether a most wicked Catholic can sue a heretic concerning a crime other than heresy. The response to this question is as follows: in that in which the heretic is inferior—namely, in the rule of faith—he can be accused by an evil Catholic. But in that in which he is superior—namely, in conduct of life—he cannot be sued by one who is most wicked [Col. 0645C].

§ 1. Likewise, the statement that shepherds are to be tolerated rather than rebuked for their acts is understood in two ways: either because they are to be tolerated rather than corrected by criminal persons; hence it is added there that the lives of rulers are often corrupted because of the deserts of subjects. Therefore those through whose fault, God permitting it, the lives of rulers are corrupted ought rather to tolerate them than correct them. Or because there are some who often lack public proofs and cannot establish before judges the crime which they allege.

Of these Augustine says in his homily on penance, chapter 12 [Note: [Col. 0645] Sermon 351, Maurist edition; Bede on 1 Corinthians, chapter 5]:

### C. XXVII. Matters which cannot be proved by public evidence must be tolerated.

Often [Note: [Col. 0645D] In certain ancient manuscripts it reads *plerique* (“many persons”), as in Bede and in the original; nevertheless the exact words of the original are not reproduced here.] good men endure the sins of others [Col. 0645D] and remain silent, because they frequently lack public proofs by which they can demonstrate to judges the things that they themselves know,
IV. Part. Gratian. The statement of Anacletus is also to be understood of such persons [Note: [Col. 0645] above, same distinction, c. 12]: Those are condemned by the sentence concerning Ham, son of Noah, who disclose the fault of their teachers or superiors, like Ham, who did not cover his father’s nakedness but displayed it for ridicule. By this authority, subjects are not forbidden to make an accusation, but to betray. For betrayal is one thing, accusation another. A betrayer reports what cannot be proved; an accuser, with the defendant present, brings the charge before the judge, intending to prove what he alleges. Ham alone saw his father’s nakedness; therefore he signifies those who, since they alone know of their prelates’ crimes and consequently cannot accuse them, nevertheless offer their lives to others for ridicule by defaming them.

§ 1. Again it is objected that subjects, even religious persons, cannot accuse their prelates. For it is read in Exodus [Note: [Col. 0645] Exod. c. 15] that Miriam, Aaron’s sister, who first after the crossing of the Red Sea deserved, taking up a tambourine, to sing a hymn [Col. 0646B], afterward murmured against Moses [Note: [Col. 0645] Num. c. 12] because he had taken an Ethiopian woman as his wife, and was struck with leprosy by the Lord.

§ 2. Again, it is read in the Book of Kings [Note: [Col. 0645] 1 Kings c. 24] that, when David was fleeing from Saul, he hid in a cave. When Saul turned aside into it to relieve himself, David cut off the edge of his cloak—a deed which he afterward deeply regretted and bitterly repented. Saul [Note: [Col. 0645] ibid., c. 16] had been rejected by the Lord and, out of envy, persecuted David in order to deliver him to death. David was humble and gentle, appointed by the Lord in Saul’s place and anointed king through Samuel; yet because he cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak, he wept bitterly, although Saul surpassed him only in the administration of anointing. Hence it is understood that subjects, even though religious, cannot accuse their criminal prelates [Col. 0646C]. For [Note: [Col. 0645] Ordinary Gloss on 1 Kings c. 24], by Saul relieving himself are understood prelates who bring into deed the malice conceived in their hearts.

Again, it is read in the Book of Kings [Note: [Col. 0645] 2 Kings c. 6] that, when the ark of the Lord was being brought back from Gabaa to Jerusalem, the ark tilted when the oxen kicked. When Uzzah the Levite put out his hand to raise it, he was struck by the Lord and died. By the ark prelates are understood; by Uzzah, subjects; by the tilting of the ark, the falls of prelates; and by the man who put forth his hand, those are understood who rebuke or accuse the lives of teachers, and who perish when struck by the Lord.

§ 3. The reply is as follows. It is true that prelates are signified by the ark, and subjects by Uzzah. But it is false that the fall of prelates is signified by the ark’s tilting. To tilt or descend is one thing; to fall is another [Col. 0646D]. For we read [Note: [Col. 0645] John c. 8] that our Savior bent down, as when he wrote with his finger upon the ground; and that he often descended from mountains which he had ascended, whether to spend the night in prayer, to teach his disciples higher precepts on the mountain, or, fleeing the crowds, to look upon them from the mountain height and teach them freely [Col. 0647A].

Tilting or descent signifies humility, by which spiritual persons sometimes condescend to carnal persons and sympathize with their weakness, according to the Apostle’s saying [Note: [Col. 0647] 2 Cor. c. 11]: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” The angels whom Jacob saw [Note: [Col. 0647] Gen. c. 28] descending upon the ladder likewise signified such persons. Of them it is also said through the Prophet [Note: [Col. 0647] Ps. 17]: “He bowed the heavens and came down.”

Accordingly, by the tilted ark are understood prelates who mercifully bear the fault of their subjects and humbly sympathize with their weakness. Thus it is rightly said that the ark tilted when the oxen kicked. For the kicking oxen signify subjects who do not obey their teachers; when prelates sympathize with them, the ark, as it were, tilts at the kicking of the oxen. The Levite who put out his hand signifies those who criticize the compassionate mercy of their prelates and wish to raise them up into the bitterness of severity. Therefore this Levite is rightly called Uzzah; for *Uzzah* means “strong.” Those are called strong who, presuming upon their own righteousness, think mercy ought to be denied to sinners and criticize those who grant it. Therefore they perish when struck by the Lord, because [Note: [Col. 0647] Jas. c. 2] “judgment without mercy shall be for those who are unwilling to show mercy to offenders.” To such a person Solomon says [Note: [Col. 0647] Eccles. c. 7, v. 16]: “Do not be overly righteous”; for there is a righteous man who perishes in his own righteousness.

The same is the meaning of the passage concerning Moses. By Moses prelates are understood; by the Ethiopian woman sinners are denoted. Moses took an Ethiopian woman as his wife when any preacher joins a sinner to himself [Col. 0647C], so that he may be able to beget from that person for God an offspring of good works. When Miriam—that is, subjects—criticizes this union, she is infected with the leprosy of sin. Or, by Miriam is understood the synagogue, which murmured against Moses—that is, Christ—because he joined to himself the Ethiopian woman, that is, the Church from among the Gentiles, whom the leprosy of unbelief and error had made unclean. Therefore, by these authorities [Note: [Col. 0647] Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, pt. 3, c. 5], subjects are not forbidden to accuse their prelates, but are warned not to criticize their merciful compassion.

§ 4. Again, prelates are understood by Saul, and subjects by David. Saul relieving himself signifies those who bring into external deed the malice conceived in the heart. But by the cutting off of the cloak is signified only the rebuke of sin [Note: [Col. 0647D] “Is not signified”: In some old copies one reads, “the rebuke of sin is not signified”; but in certain others, “the rebuke of sin is signified.”]. For the cloak signifies royal power [Col. 0648A]. He cuts it off who strikes a prelate with a sentence of condemnation, something permitted to none of the subjects. For the deeds of a pastor are not to be struck by subjects with the sword of the mouth—that is, with a sentence of condemnation [Note: [Col. 0647] above, c. 13]. Hence Jerome says on Mark [Note: [Col. 0647] on c. 14] concerning the high priest who tore his garments: “The tearing of the garment signifies the tearing of the priesthood, which was soon to be torn apart and taken away from the Jews.”

Or David signifies those who, seeing the wickedness of their prelates, overlook their greater sins but strive to criticize and expose the smallest and lightest ones, as though cutting off the outermost edge of the cloak. Or this may be because Saul alone turned aside into the cave in which David alone was hiding [Note: [Col. 0647D] “David alone”: In 1 Kings c. 21 it is read: “But David and his men were hiding in the inner part of the cave.”].

§ 5. Again, this may be understood in light of what was said above [Note: [Col. 0647] above, c. 12] concerning Ham, who alone saw his father’s nakedness [Col. 0648B], did not cover it, and displayed it for ridicule. Therefore this authority does not prohibit subjects from accusing prelates, if they are liable to accusation.

§ 6. Again, it is proved that subjects cannot accuse their prelates, even if they are religious. For they become infamous by the very fact that they attempt to criticize their teachers’ lives. Likewise, by the authority of the canons, all who take up arms against their fathers, and who criticize or accuse the lives of their teachers, become infamous. But no infamous person is to be heard in an accusation against prelates, unless perhaps the latter has departed from the faith, as was said above. Therefore, since subjects become infamous by the very fact that they launch into accusations against prelates, and since infamous persons are denied the opportunity to accuse, it is plain that subjects cannot accuse their prelates.

§ 7. The reply is as follows. Not all prelates are regarded as prelates; for it is not the name but the life that makes a bishop [Col. 0648C].

Hence Gregory writes to Bishop Januarius, Book VII, Indiction 2, Epistle 1:

### C. XXVIII. He whom age, not life, makes an elder is to be sharply rebuked.

Paul says [Note: [Col. 0647] Ep. 1, written A.D. 599, bk. 9, Maurist edition; Alger, bk. 2, c. 18; cf. 1 Tim. c. 5, v. 1]: “Do not rebuke an elder.” But this rule of his is to be observed in the case of an elder only when that elder’s fault does not by his example draw the hearts of younger people to destruction [Note: [Col. 0647] “then in his case is to be observed”: Basel edition; “now in his case is to be observed”: other editions]. But where an elder offers the young an example leading to destruction, there he must be struck with stern rebuke [Note: [Col. 0647] “stern”: Basel edition]. For it is written [Note: [Col. 0647] Isa. c. 42]: “All of you are a snare to the young”; and again the Prophet says [Note: [Col. 0647] Isa. c. 65]: “Accursed is the child of a hundred years.”

[Note: [Col. 0647D] “Accursed is the child”: In Gregory’s manuscripts it is read in some copies approximately in this form, but in others: “and the sinner of a hundred years is accursed,” as also in John the Deacon and the Vulgate, except that the latter has not “is” but “shall be.” The Septuagint, as found in St. Jerome, had: “and the sinner who dies at a hundred years shall be accursed.”]

[Col. 0649A]

### C. XXIX. Dignity does not make a bishop, but life does.

Again, Jerome to Heliodorus, Epistle I, *In Praise of the Solitary Life* +:

Not all bishops are bishops. You look to Peter, but consider Judas also [Note: [Col. 0649] “Look”: editions collated with the first Lyons edition, II and III; “but” absent from the Basel edition; “also” absent from Alger and editions collated with the first Basel edition]. You admire Stephen, but look at Nicholas also [Note: [Col. 0649] “receive”: editions collated with the first Argentinian and Lyons II–III editions; “also” absent from editions collated with Lyons II–III; “reject”: Basel edition]. And below:

§ 1. Ecclesiastical dignity does not make one a Christian. Cornelius the centurion [Note: [Col. 0649] Acts c. 10], though still a Gentile, is cleansed by the gift of the Holy Spirit; Daniel, a boy [Note: [Col. 0649] Dan. c. 13; “still a boy”: Basel edition], judges elders. And below:

§ 2. It is not easy to stand in Paul’s place [Note: [Col. 0649] “of Peter and Paul”: Alger; editions collated with Lyons II–III], or to hold the rank of Peter [Note: [Col. 0649] “place”: same editions], who now reign with Christ. And below:

§ 3. Salt that has lost its savor [Note: [Col. 0649] Luke c. 14, v. 34] is good for nothing except to be thrown out and trampled by swine.

[Col. 0649B]

### C. XXX. Not the name bishop, but life, merits reverence.

Again, Augustine, Tractate VI on John, c. 1 [Note: [Col. 0649] Alger, same place]:

Not everyone who says, “Peace be with you” [Note: [Col. 0649] “with you [plural]”: editions collated with the original], is to be heard as though he were a dove. And below: Ravens feed upon death. The dove does not do this; it lives upon the fruits of the earth, and its food is innocent.

### C. XXXI. The learned are sometimes rightly rebuked by the unlearned, clergy by laymen.

The same Bede, on c. 2 of the Second Epistle of Peter [Note: [Col. 0649] Collected Treatises, pt. 2, vol. 50, cc. 15–16]:

They followed the way of Balaam of Bosor, who loved the reward of iniquity, but received a rebuke for his madness. A dumb beast of burden, speaking in a human voice, restrained [Note: [Col. 0649] “proved”: original] the prophet’s folly. Often heretics put forward doctrines so foolish and sacraments so abominable that even persons of dull understanding, pagans [Col. 0649C] [Note: [Col. 0649] added: “Jews”: Basel edition], and those wholly lacking the rational capacity for divine knowledge, detest [Note: [Col. 0649] “detest”: Basel edition; “detest”: other collated editions and original] their insanity and, with sounder judgment, rebuke [Note: [Col. 0649] “rebuke”: original and editions collated with the original] their distorted paths that are contrary to God.

And—what is worse, because more frequent—sometimes many Catholics love the reward of iniquity so greatly that the learned are rightly rebuked by the unlearned, clergy by laymen [Note: [Col. 0649] “are torn to pieces”: original], who are rightly [Note: [Col. 0649] “truly and rightly”: Paris and Lyons I editions; “truly and rightly”: other editions before Basel and Lyons II–III] compared to the prophet rebuked by the words of an ass speaking contrary to nature, and yet not diverted from the purpose of his wicked path. The name of the city from which Balaam is said to have come also fits them very aptly [Note: [Col. 0649] “most plainly”: editions collated with the original]. For *Bosor* is interpreted “fleshly” or “in tribulation” [Note: [Col. 0649D] “In tribulation”: This was followed by “placed” [in the column and editions collated with the original]; the word has been removed because it is found neither in Bede nor in St. Jerome’s interpretation of Hebrew names.].

For there is no greater cause for the licentious to adulterate the word of truth through love of money or desire for temporal things [Col. 0650A] [Note: [Col. 0649] “desires”: original] than that they have enslaved themselves to the lust of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0649] “who”: Basel, Venice II, Paris editions]. And below: The very name Balaam, which is interpreted “vain people” or “casting them down,” is also suited to such people. For those who of their own will themselves abandon the way of truth that they have known [Note: [Col. 0649] absent from Basel], what are they but a vain people? What do they do [Note: [Col. 0649] “who also cast down”: editions collated with the original] but plunge their hearers into ruin [Note: [Col. 0649] “send”: original], when they preach not wholesome things that correct them but erroneous things that delight them? Of these it is fittingly said [Note: [Col. 0649] “plainly”: editions collated with the original]: “These are springs without water and mists driven by whirlwinds, for whom the blackness of darkness is reserved.”

Gratian. Therefore, since not all bishops are bishops, elders are judged by the boy Daniel, salt that has lost its savor [Col. 0650B] is trampled by swine, and one who says, “Peace be with you,” is often regarded not as a dove but as a raven, it is plain that an accusation is not always to be withheld out of regard for the office and authority of the person. Rather, action must be taken against the wicked, since every person who sins criminally is made other than he was and, so to speak, is reckoned as less than a head in the eyes of the law. For one who commits sin is the slave of sin, both in penalty and in fault.

Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0649D] This chapter has not been found in Augustine, from whom it is cited. Burchard and Ivo cite it from Gregory; Gratian himself also appends almost the same words above, Distinction 83, to the chapter *For No One*, which is Gregory’s. Burchard, bk. 1, c. 13, and Ivo, pt. 5, c. 67, offer something similar from Origen.] [Note: [Col. 0649] cf. on Dist. 83, c. 2; Burchard, bk. 1, c. 203; Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 5, c. 317; Alger, bk. 2, c. 20]:

### C. XXXII. One who does not administer the office he has undertaken is not a bishop, but a shameless dog.

He who neither has undertaken the responsibility of governance, nor wiped away his own offenses, nor corrected the crime of his children, should be called an shameless dog rather than a bishop.

Gratian. Therefore, when Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory take away from certain persons the name of dove, bishop, and elder, must not the privilege of their dignity also be taken away, so that they may be rebuked by subjects? Hence Scripture, disregarding the privilege of a wicked old age, says: “Accursed is,” not “an elder,” but “a child of a hundred years” [Note: [Col. 0649] cf. above, c. 28]. It is therefore apparent that those become infamous through accusing prelates who attempt to criticize and attack the lives of persons holding the place of their government not merely by name, but in life and morals. But others become praiseworthy rather than infamous through accusing their prelates.

Again, the statement that no greater person [Note: [Col. 0649] cf. above, c. 11] is to be attacked by accusations from lesser persons [Col. 0651A] is to be understood of persons lesser not in dignity but in life.

Hence Jerome says concerning Paul, on the Epistle to the Galatians [Note: [Col. 0651D] This chapter, cited in most copies from St. Jerome and in some from St. Augustine, has been found in neither author’s works. But at the words in the Epistle to the Galatians, “I withstood him to his face,” the Ordinary Gloss adds this interlinear explanation: “which he would not have dared unless he felt himself not unequal.” And in the commentaries of St. Ambrose at that same passage are found these words: “For which of them would have dared resist Peter, the first apostle, to whom the Lord gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven, unless another such man, who, through confidence in his own election, knew himself not unequal, steadfastly disapproved what Peter had done without counsel?”]:

### C. XXXIII. “Greater” and “lesser” must be understood not in dignity but in life.

Paul rebuked Peter [Note: [Col. 0651] Gal. c. 2], which he would not have dared unless he knew himself not unequal.

Gratian. This is understood not of the office of ecclesiastical dignity but of purity of life and holiness of conduct. For Peter alone held primacy among the apostles.

[Col. 0651B]

Hence Augustine says to Jerome, Epistle XIX, near the end [Note: [Col. 0651] Ep. 40, Maurist edition, written A.D. 397; Alger, same place, c. 21]:

### C. XXXIV. Not the name bishop, but life, makes one greater.

Although, according to the terms of honors which the usage of the Church has now established, the episcopate is greater than the presbyterate, yet Augustine is inferior to Jerome in many respects.

### C. XXXV. Although bishops may be equal in merits, they differ in rank of dignity.

The same, Book II *On Baptism against the Donatists*, c. 1 [Note: [Col. 0651] Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 5, c. 24]:

I think that, without any insult to himself, Bishop Cyprian may be compared with the Apostle Peter as regards the crown of martyrdom. Yet I should be more afraid of being insulting toward Peter. For who does not know that the primacy of his apostleship is to be preferred to any episcopate whatever [Col. 0651C]? But although the grace of their chairs differs, the glory of the martyrs is one. And below: When Peter is corrected by Paul, who came later, and, preserving the bond of peace and unity [Note: [Col. 0651] “truth”: Basel edition], advances to martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0651] “is advanced”: original], how much more readily and firmly ought what has been confirmed by the statutes of the universal Church to be preferred over either the authority of one bishop or the council of one province?

### C. XXXVI. A son is made equal or preferred to his father not in honor but in truth.

The same, Tractate XXX on John, at the end:

A father complains about a bad son, or a son complains about a harsh father. We preserve the honor due from son to father [Col. 0652A], which the son fails to render. We do not make the son equal to the father in honor, but prefer him if he has a good case. We make the son equal to the father in truth; and so we render due honor that equality does not destroy merit [Note: [Col. 0651] “fairness”: editions collated with the original].

### C. XXXVII. Peter and Paul were equal in merits, although differing in rank.

Again, Ambrose, Sermon LXVI on the birthday of Peter and Paul [Note: [Col. 0652D] The sermon from which this chapter is taken is Sermon 66 among the sermons of St. Ambrose, Sermon 27 among Augustine’s sermons *On the Saints*, and Sermon 5, on the same feast, among those of Maximus of Turin, where it is numbered 54.] [Note: [Col. 0651] Some attribute this sermon either to Augustine or to Maximus of Turin; Anselm, bk. 1, c. 71]:

Blessed Peter and Paul stand out among all the apostles and excel by a certain special prerogative; yet it is uncertain which of the two ought to be preferred to the other. For I think that they are equal in merits because they are equal in suffering, and that they lived with like devotion of faith [Col. 0652B], since we see them arrive together at the glory of martyrdom.

§ 1. For we should not think without reason [Note: [Col. 0651] “we think”: editions collated with the original, from Anselm] that they endured the sentence of one tyrant on one day in one place [Note: [Col. 0651] “suffered under one persecutor”: same editions, from the same source]. They suffered on one day [Note: [Col. 0651] omitted in the same editions before Basel], that they might come together to Christ; in one place, so that Rome might not lack either one; under one persecutor, so that equal cruelty might bind them both. Thus the day was appointed for their merit, the place for their glory, and the persecutor for their courage. And in what place did they suffer martyrdom? In the city of Rome, which holds the primacy [Note: [Col. 0651] added: “alone”: Basel edition] and headship among the nations: namely, so that where the head of superstition was, there the head of holiness might rest; and where the leaders of the Gentiles lived, there the leaders of the churches might dwell [Note: [Col. 0651] “might die”: editions collated with the original; Böhm.].

V. Part. Gratian. Again, penitents, bigamists, and priests [Col. 0652C] cannot accuse priests. Hence it is gathered generally that whoever are not priests or cannot be priests cannot bring an accusation or testimony against priests.

Hence Fabian says in Epistle II to the Eastern bishops [Note: [Col. 0651] This chapter is from Pseudo-Isidore and is worded somewhat differently in the original; Anselm, bk. 3, c. 47 (14); *Polycarpus*, bk. 5, title 1]:

### C. XXXVIII. Those who cannot be priests cannot accuse priests.

The apostles themselves and their successors formerly ordained that those who are not of their order, and cannot be, should neither accuse the Lord’s priests nor give testimony against them.

[Col. 0653A]

### C. XXXIX. Those barred from election to the priesthood cannot accuse priests or testify against them.

Again, Pope Damasus to Archbishop Stephen, Epistle III, c. 3 [Note: [Col. 0653] A chapter fabricated from Pseudo-Isidore for the Seventh Council of Carthage, c. 2; Burchard, bk. 1, c. 172; Anselm, bk. 3, c. 41 (47); Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 4, c. 186; *Polycarpus*, same place]:

Witnesses [Note: [Col. 0653D] “Witnesses”: Damasus’s words are: “But the accusers and witnesses of bishops, concerning whom you asked, must be without all infamy or suspicion,” etc.; Burchard and Ivo cite them thus, while the *Panormia* has the text as Gratian gives it.] must be free from every infamy, suspicion, or manifest stain, and instructed in the fullness of the true faith [Note: [Col. 0653D] “Fullness”: In the letter itself one reads *pleniter* (“fully”); Burchard and Ivo [in the *Decree*, though not the *Panormia*] have: *vera fide pleniter* (“fully in the true faith”).], and must be such as divine authority commands to be chosen for the priesthood. For priests, as ancient authority teaches [Note: [Col. 0653] “of the ancients”: cited collections and editions collated with the original], cannot be accused [Note: [Col. 0653] cf. c. 38] or testified against by those who ought not, and cannot, be advanced to that same honor.
