Gratian. The statement of Silvester is understood in the same manner: “A layman shall not accuse a cleric,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0653] cf. above, c. 2]; that is, those established in a lower rank, who cannot ascend to a higher one [Col. 0653B], ought not accuse persons acting in the higher ranks.

§ 1. Behold, it has been shown how to answer the authorities and arguments by which subjects seemed to be excluded from accusations against prelates. It must now be shown by what reasons they are proved admissible, and what answer prelates make in reply.

Christ, who was the shepherd of shepherds, said to his sheep—of whom he said [Note: [Col. 0653] Matt. c. 15, v. 24], “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,” etc.—amid the insults and blows which he suffered from them [Note: [Col. 0653] John c. 18, v. 23]: “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness concerning the wrong,” etc. Again [Note: [Col. 0653] John c. 8, v. 46]: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” But whoever are admitted to give testimony against someone or to rebuke that person may be admitted to accuse that same person. Therefore, since sheep are admitted to testify against their shepherd and to rebuke him, if they can [Col. 0653C], it is plain that subjects can accuse their prelates.

§ 2. The reply is as follows. Although Christ was the shepherd of his sheep, whom he fed by word and example, nevertheless, as regards the distribution of offices—from which, today in the Church, some preside over others, so that some are called prelates and others subjects—he did not exercise the pastoral office among his people. For he was anointed neither king nor priest by a mystical and visible anointing; yet these were the only two persons among that people who claimed for themselves the name of prelate. Therefore this authority does not prove that subjects are to be admitted to accuse prelates; it only shows that hearers may rebuke and testify against those who, though holding no ecclesiastical offices [Col. 0654A], nevertheless strive by word and example to win to God whomever they can.

§ 3. There is another answer: one thing is what we are compelled to observe by the rigor of discipline, another what is permitted in view of perfection. Christ admitted the Jews to accuse him out of the perfection of humility, not by the severity of law. For if they had been admitted by legal rigor, this authority would establish that criminal and infamous persons are to be received in accusations against religious persons, since those people were most wicked, seeking Christ’s death and wishing to condemn one who was innocent. Therefore prelates are not compelled by this example to receive their subjects in accusations against themselves, but are permitted to do so.

§ 4. Again, Paul [Note: [Col. 0653] Gal. c. 2] rebuked Peter, who was the chief of the apostles. Hence it is understood that subjects may rebuke their prelates if they are liable to rebuke. But this is easily refuted [Col. 0654B] if one considers the reason for which Peter was rebuked. Peter compelled Gentiles to Judaize and to depart from the truth of the Gospel, joining the flock with the Jews and secretly withdrawing himself from Gentile food. But it is equivalent in itself to depart from the faith and to cast others down from the faith by example or word. Therefore this example does not prove that prelates may be accused by subjects, unless perhaps they have departed from the faith or compelled others to depart from it.

§ 5. Again, when Peter [Note: [Col. 0653] Acts c. 11] entered Cornelius’s house, the brethren who were in Judaea complained and rebuked him because he had gone in to a Gentile. Behold: prelates may rightly be rebuked by subjects.

[Col. 0654C]

But Blessed Gregory answered this objection in writing to the patrician Theoctista, Book IX, Epistle 39 [Note: [Col. 0654D] It will be worth consulting Gregory himself; for he expounds at length what Gratian here relates briefly.] [Note: [Col. 0653] Ep. 45, written A.D. 601, bk. 11, Maurist edition]:

### C. XL. When the faithful asked Peter why he had gone in to the Gentiles, he did not answer by authority but humbly gave a reason.

Peter had received the power of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0653] “of governing”: Basel edition], and yet this same first of the apostles answered the complaint made against him by the faithful, asking why he had gone in to the Gentiles, not by the authority of his office—by which he could have said, “Sheep must not accuse or rebuke their shepherd”—but by an account of the divine power by which the Gentiles had received the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0653] “authority”: editions collated with the original].

Gratian. Therefore, since Peter could have rejected the complaints by virtue of his office but did not wish to do so, prelates are not compelled by this example to receive the rebukes of subjects. From this same exercise of humility is understood the statement of Leo IV [Note: [Col. 0654D] In Ivo the heading of this chapter is: “That Pope Leo wished his case to be examined in the presence of the emperor’s legates.” Nicholas likewise, to the Emperor.] addressed to Emperor Louis [Note: [Col. 0653] It appears that “Leo III” should be read; for it is known that disputes occurred between him and Louis the Pious. Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 5, c. 22]:

[Col. 0655A]

### C. XLI. The Apostolic pontiff promises to correct himself by the emperor’s judgment if he has acted unjustly toward his subjects.

If we have acted improperly in any respect and have not maintained toward our subjects the path of just law, we wish all things to be corrected by your judgment and that of your envoys. For if we, who ought to correct the sins of others, commit worse offenses, then certainly we shall be, not disciples of truth, but—as we say with sorrow—above all others teachers of error. Therefore we earnestly implore the clemency of Your Greatness to send into these regions persons who fear God in all things, to investigate everything diligently—as though your imperial majesty itself were present—and to inquire not only into those matters alone of which we have spoken above. Rather, whether lesser or even greater charges against us are brought to their attention, let all be concluded by their lawful examination, so that henceforth nothing may remain among them unexamined or undecided [Col. 0655B].

### Part VI

Gratian. Again, when Balaam the diviner was going to curse the people, the angel of the Lord stood in the road against the she-ass on which he was riding, and, with sword drawn, turned her back from the way. When Balaam afflicted her with blows, she broke out into speech and rebuked the madness of the prophet. If, therefore, a dumb animal, through angelic power, rebuked a prophet’s folly, much more may subjects accuse their prelates.

§ 1. The answer to this is as follows: It is true that subjects are signified by the she-ass, and prelates by Balaam. Yet this example does not prove that prelates are to be accused by subjects; rather, it merely provides subjects with a model for humbly resisting prelates if perhaps they should wish to compel them to evil. For Balaam, pressing the she-ass in order that she might carry him to curse the people of God, signifies those who demand by beatings and torments that their subjects become their supporters and helpers in evil. But because the angel—that is, any preacher—with drawn sword, namely by openly preaching the fear and terror of future vengeance, recalls them from consent to another’s wickedness, they are permitted in such a case to break out in a voice of complaint and say to their prelates: “Why do you afflict us with blows? Why are you unjustly angry with us? Have we ever been disobedient to you, except now, when we are compelled to evil? Look at him who forbids what you have undertaken.” Therefore prelates are not, on this ground, shown to be subject to accusation by their subjects.

§ 2. Again, when David had committed adultery and homicide, Nathan the prophet was sent by God to rebuke him. Behold: prelates are to be reproved and censured by subjects.

§ 3. But it must be noted that there are two persons by whom this world is governed: the royal and the priestly. As kings preside in secular causes, so priests preside in the causes of God. It belongs to kings to impose bodily punishment; to priests, to inflict spiritual vengeance. David, therefore, although through royal anointing he stood above priests and prophets in secular affairs, was nevertheless subject to them in the causes of God. Hence kings were anointed by prophets and priests, and the sins of kings were expiated by their offering.

§ 4. Therefore, just as Uzziah was struck with leprosy by the Lord because he wished to usurp the offices of the priests, so priests and prophets were not permitted to usurp the offices of kings. When Nathan the prophet rebuked the king, he performed his own office, in which he was superior to the king; he did not usurp the king’s office, in which he was inferior to the king. He admonished him to expiate his sins through repentance; he did not pronounce upon him the sentence by which, as an adulterer and murderer, he would be condemned to death.

§ 5. Thus also Blessed Ambrose excommunicated Theodosius, and Blessed Innocent excommunicated the Emperor Arcadius and prohibited him from entering the church.

§ 6. For just as a judge does not bear the sword without reason, so priests do not receive the keys of the Church without reason. The former bears the sword for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good; the latter have the keys for excluding those to be excommunicated and reconciling penitents. Therefore, by this example subjects are shown to be subject to reproof by prelates, not prelates by subjects.

§ 7. Again, Daniel, exercising no lawful authority, convicted judges appointed by the people of false testimony and, having convicted them, condemned them. It is therefore clear that persons possessing no authority may rebuke those raised to dignities.

§ 8. The answer to this is as follows. Miracles—and especially those of the Old Testament—are to be admired, not drawn into an example for our conduct. For many things were then allowed which are now utterly prohibited. At that time Samuel cut Agag, the exceedingly fat king of Amalek, to pieces; now no ecclesiastic is permitted to exercise judgment involving bloodshed. At that time Phinehas killed a Jew having intercourse with a Midianite woman, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness; today such an action would result in the ruin of a priest’s office. Thus, by Daniel’s example, subjects would claim for themselves not only the power of accusing or rebuking, but even that of judging their prelates, if it were lawful to adopt as an argument for our conduct that which is never permitted by any authority.

Rather, this deed gives us to understand that in the last times God would raise up the spirit of a younger boy: namely, of him of whom it is said through the Prophet: “A child is born to us”; and again, “Behold my servant,” who would convict and condemn the judges of iniquity—that is, the scribes and Pharisees—who accused Susanna, that is, the Church, with false charges and pronounced her guilty of adultery because she followed Christ.

§ 9. Again, Jerome reports in the *Book of Illustrious Men* that Pope Damasus, accused of adultery by his subjects, cleared himself with forty-two bishops.

§ 10. Again, Pope Symmachus, deprived of his dignity in the Roman synod, was first decreed to be restored to his status, so that he might then come to trial and, if this should rightly seem fitting, answer the accusations of his accusers. This appeared a matter worthy of effect to the very large number of priests; and when afterward arrangements were made for the aforesaid Pope to answer the charge and for how he should be accused, he was prevented by his enemies.

[Note: [Col. 0655] Num. c. 22.]

[Note: [Col. 0655] 2 Reg. c. 12.]

[Note: [Col. 0655] 2 Reg. c. 8.]

[Note: [Col. 0655] 2 Paral. c. 26.]

[Note: [Col. 0655] 1 Petr. c. 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0655] Dan. c. 13.]

[Note: [Col. 0655] 1 Reg. c. 15.]

[Note: [Col. 0655] Num. c. 25.]

[Note: [Col. 0655] Es. c. 9, v. 6.]

#### Chapter XLIV. Paulus, bishop of the city of Dyacline, is deposed upon the accusation of his subjects and conviction.

The bearer Nemesion, coming to us, reported that Paulus, bishop of the city of Dyacline, having among other evils fallen into a bodily crime, was accused and convicted by his clerics and deposed by episcopal sentence. Afterwards, coming with the assistance of secular persons, he entered the bishopric as a robber; and, after taking away the goods of the church, he expelled from that bishopric our most beloved Nemesion, the bearer of this letter, who had been appointed in his place, and brought him almost to extreme injury and death.

Therefore let your Fraternity take care to ascertain all these matters, and compel him, without delay or excuse, to restore whatever he has taken from the church. But if he says that he took nothing belonging to the church but his own property—although it was grave and unjust that he did not request this from you or from his metropolitan, but presumed to act with rash boldness—nevertheless, if he took anything of his own, it must be established under your Fraternity’s examination whether this is true. Moreover, it must be diligently investigated whether he has squandered anything improperly from the church’s property, so that he may in every way be compelled, from what he has now taken, to make restoration and satisfaction for it.

[Note: [Col. 0657] *Declanenae*: Ivo.—*Doclavenae*: Burchard.—Yet the reading should be *Docleatinae*, for Doclea is a city in Illyricum, commonly called Antivari.]

[Note: [Col. 0657] “From us”: Argentinensis and Basel editions read “from you.”]

Gratian. By this edict he does not take vengeance upon the accusers or those who deposed him, but further proceeds against the deposed bishop, so that, if he attempts again to aspire to the bishopric, he may be repelled in every way and forced into a monastery to perform perpetual penance. Since Gregory repels in every way one aspiring to the bishopric and subjects him to severe penance, it is clear that he was accused and convicted by subjects, not through Gregory’s dispensation, but by the censure of the canons.

§ 1. ### Part II

§ 1. But Paul, in the *Digest*, book 48, title 3, “On Public Judgments,” title “On Accusations and Formal Inscriptions,” law 3, shows what the form of accusation is and what method is used for drawing up formal bills, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0663] Digest, book 48, title 3, fragment 3.]

§ 2. The formulation of a formal bill of accusation is as follows: “The consul and the day. Before such-and-such praetor or proconsul, Lucius Titius declared that he charges Maeviam under the Julian law on adulteries, alleging that she committed adultery with Gaius Seius in such-and-such city, in his house, in such-and-such month, under such-and-such consuls.” Certainly the place where the adultery was committed, the person with whom it is said to have been committed, and the month must be specified. For this is provided by the Julian law on public judgments, and is generally commanded of all who denounce someone as guilty. He is not obliged to include either the day or the hour. But if bills of formal accusation have not been lawfully drawn up, the name of the accused is erased, and the power to bring the accusation anew is granted.

§ 3. Again, the person who presents the bill must sign that he has made the declaration, or another person for him if he does not know letters. But if he alleges another crime—for example, that she made her house available so that a married woman might suffer sexual violation; that he released an adulterer caught in the act; that he accepted a price for adultery discovered; or anything similar—that particular matter must also be included in the bill. If the accuser dies, or another cause prevents him from being able to accuse, or anything similar occurs, the name of the accused is erased at the accused’s request; this is provided both by the Julian law on violence and by senatorial decrees, so that another may be allowed to accuse the defendant anew. But we shall see within what time this may occur; and in any case thirty available days must be observed.

[Note: [Col. 0665] Absent from the original.]

[Note: [Col. 0665] “Bill”: original reads the plural, “bills.”]

## Causa III

[Col. 0665B] **GRATIAN**

A certain bishop has been driven from his own see and seeks restoration. After restoration he is brought to trial; he requests a postponement; at last a person not lawfully joined, two infamous persons, and three religious persons proceed to accuse him. The accusers produce witnesses from their own household and other persons hostile to him from outside his province. The accused is presented to a judge tainted by crime, to be heard and judged by one person alone. Some of the accusers and witnesses, being absent, seek to accuse him and testify against him by letter. When many counts were alleged against him, the accusers fail on the first; finally, the accusation is turned against the accuser.

(Question I.) The first question is whether restoration must be granted to all persons who have been despoiled.

(Question II.) Second, concerning postponements: whether they must be granted to all persons only after restoration, or also after a summons to trial.

(Question III.) Third, for what number of months must they be granted to each side?

(Question IV.) Fourth, whether infamous persons and persons not lawfully joined are to be admitted to accusation.

(Question V.) Fifth, whether witnesses from the households of accusers are to be produced, or the testimony of enemies heard.

(Question VI.) Sixth, whether the accused is to be brought outside his province.

(Question VII.) Seventh, whether the sentence of a person whose malice equally taints him along with the accused is to be heard.

(Question VIII.) Eighth, whether a bishop is to be heard or judged by one person alone.

(Question IX.) Ninth, whether accusers or witnesses may present a voice of accusation or testimony against an absent person.

(Question X.) Tenth, whether those who fail on the first count are to be admitted to subsequent counts.

(Question IX.) Eleventh, whether the accused may turn the accusation against the accuser.

## Question I

[Col. 0666B] **GRATIAN**

That restoration must be granted to all persons whatsoever is proved by many authorities.

For Pope Caius says, in his sole letter to Bishop Felix, chapter 3:

[Note: [Col. 0665] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore.—Anselm, book 3, chapter 46.—“From Hyginus”: Basel edition.]

#### Chapter I. All things must be restored to those despoiled or expelled.

To bishops who have been despoiled of their property or expelled from their own sees, all things taken from them must be restored according to the laws, because before this is done no crime can be alleged against them.

### C. II. On the Same. Likewise Pope Fabian, Letter II to the Eastern Bishops

[Note: [Col. 0665] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, composed after *Tripartite History*, book 7, chapter 12.—Anselm, book 3, chapter 50.]

[Col. 0666C] If bishops have been expelled from their own sees or churches [Note: [Col. 0665] “church”: Basel edition.] without the authority of the Roman Pontiff [Note: [Col. 0665D] “Without the authority of the Roman Pontiff”: these words also occur in Anselm, although they are not expressly present in the original, [Col. 0666D] whose sense rather than its actual wording is reported here, down to the words “None.”], [Note: [Col. 0665] Addition: “or ejected”: ibid.] before they are summoned to a synod, their own place and all that is theirs must be restored to them. For no reasoning permits that, while their goods, churches, and property are for a time held by rivals or by anyone else, any charge should be brought against them. Nor can any person, whether of greater or lesser rank, bring anything whatever against them while they lack their churches, property, or powers.

Gratian. But it should be noted that a judgment ordering restitution alone is insufficient unless all things are actually restored through the judge’s office, so that the ejected or despoiled person recovers even natural possession, whether by his own intention and another’s bodily presence, as through an agent, or by his own intention and bodily presence. Likewise, all things that had been taken from him [Col. 0667A] under any condition must be restored in the same place from which they had been stolen.

Hence John, bishop of the city of Rome, writes to Zacharias, archbishop, in Letter I [Note: [Col. 0667] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, composed from *Theodosian Code*, book 9, title 10, chapter 3, and the *Breviary of Alaric*, book 8, title 1, chapter 2.—Anselm, book 3, chapter 44.]:

### C. III. On the Same

Everything must be restored in person to despoiled or ejected bishops by ordinance of the pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0667] “of the pontiff”: Basel edition.], and must be fully returned in the place [Note: [Col. 0667D] “In the place”: in John and Symmachus the text reads: “and they must be fully restored to their authority, from which they had departed.” But in Eusebius: “they must be fully restored to the places from which they had departed.”] from which they had departed, whenever they are known to have lost ecclesiastical or personal property, or their own possessions, through any circumstance of time, captivity, fraud, or the violence [Note: [Col. 0667] “force”: Anselm.] of greater persons, or [Note: [Col. 0667] “and”: collected editions.] through any unjust causes, *before their accusation [Note: [Col. 0668D] “Before their accusation”: the words from here to the end were added from the original, where the sentence is completed; Gratian repeats part of them at the end of this question.] or their regular summons to a synod, and so forth*.

### C. IV. On the Same. Likewise Eusebius, Bishop of the Apostolic See, Letter II to the Egyptians

[Note: [Col. 0667] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare preceding chapter.]

[Col. 0667B] Everything must be restored to despoiled [Note: [Col. 0667] “spoiled”: Basel edition.] or ejected bishops, etc., as far as “fully restored,” in the same manner as above.

### C. V. He Is Not a Priest but a Schismatic Who Withdraws Himself from Service to His Brethren. Likewise Pope Alexander, Letter II, at the Beginning

[Note: [Col. 0667] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.]

There is no doubt that the good are always persecuted and afflicted by the wicked. Therefore let us humble ourselves [Note: [Col. 0667] “it is necessary to humble oneself”: collected editions; compare 1 Peter 5:6.] beneath the mighty hand of God, that he may deliver [Note: [Col. 0667] “exalt”: Argentinian edition.] us in the time of tribulation. For, *as a roaring lion goes about seeking whom he may devour, so* the devil does not cease to go about [Col. 0667C] and seek whom among the faithful he may destroy—especially those whom he finds more fervent in the Savior’s service and intimate with him. By “intimate” I mean those whom he willed to be consecrated to himself and established in the apostolic order [Note: [Col. 0667] Addition: “God”: Basel and Lyons editions.]. For they intercede for the people and consume the people’s sins [Note: [Col. 0667] Compare Hosea 4:8.], because by their prayers and offerings they blot them out and consume them.

And below [Note: [Col. 0667] Burchard, book 1, chapter 129; Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 229.]:

But whoever is of your fellowship [Note: [Col. 0667] “has fled”: Ivo.] and withdraws himself from your aid will be shown to be more a schismatic than a priest. “Behold,” says the Prophet [Note: [Col. 0667] Psalm 132:1.], “how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.” But those do not dwell together in unity who withdraw themselves *from* the comfort of their brethren, or—what is worse—*prepare* plots against their brethren or lay snares for them.

And at the end of Letter III: Those who persecute the Lord in his priests crucify him, because [Note: [Col. 0667] A phrase taken from Gregory the Great, Homily 37 on the Gospels.] a cross (*crux*) is so called from torment (*cruciatus*). Great indeed is the torment endured by one who suffers violence.

### C. VI. Let Those Who Inflict Reproach and Calumny upon Priests Be Excommunicated. Likewise Pope Fabian, Letter II to the Eastern Bishops

[Note: [Col. 0667] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, taken from Proclus’s Letter to Domnus of Antioch; see Act 14 of the Council of Chalcedon.]

God, therefore, brothers, appointed beforehand you and all who exercise the supreme priesthood for this purpose: that you should remove injustices, cut off presumptuous acts, assist those laboring in the priesthood, give no occasion for their reproaches and calamities, but bring aid to one who suffers calumny and reproach [Col. 0668B]; cut off, however, the person who commits calumny or reproach; and bring assistance to the Lord and his priests.

Gratian. It is therefore clear that those despoiled must first be restored in person before being summoned to trial. But an objection is made: where there was no lawful institution, there can be no restitution. For one who was never first installed cannot be proved to have been removed, and consequently cannot demand restoration. Therefore those whose election is defective; those not elected by the clergy or sought by the people; and those who entered by simony, are not to be regarded as bishops. Thus, if they are expelled from sees which they appeared to hold, they cannot request restitution before being summoned to trial. Hence above [Note: [Col. 0667] Compare Distinction 79, chapter 9.] in the treatise on ordinations: [Col. 0668C] “If anyone by money, human favor, or a popular or military tumult,” etc.

But this is understood only in the case in which the Apostolic See is occupied by force: in that case no judge can be found through whose office that apostate may be excluded. In other cases it has no place, since violent possession cannot be taken from a violent holder except by a judge’s sentence. But if the true owner, not in a continuous war but in one renewed, ejects him by force from possession, he will restore possession to the robber by the judge’s authority. Therefore, if bishops have been violently ejected, not by a judge, from sees which they appeared to hold in whatever fashion, they must after their ejection be restored before a regular summons to a synod.

## QUESTION II

[Col. 0669A]

### GRATIAN

Part I. Concerning the respite to be granted after restoration and the period for which it should be allowed, Pope John writes in Letter I to Zacharias, archbishop [Note: [Col. 0669] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare below, chapter 6.—Anselm, book 3, chapter 44.], saying:

### C. I. The Period of Restitutionary Respite Is Granted According to the Time of Despoilment

For as long as they appear to have been despoiled or expelled [Note: [Col. 0669] “appeared”: collected editions.] before being summoned to a synod, respite shall be granted to them for the same length of time.

### C. II. While a Bishop’s Possessions or Property Are Held, No Charge Can Be Brought against Him. Likewise Pope Pelagius II, to the Bishops of Italy

[Note: [Col. 0669] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, composed from *Tripartite History*, book 7, chapter 12.—Anselm, book 3, chapter 63.]

When a bishop’s church, possessions [Col. 0669B], or property are held against his will by his rivals or anyone else, no charge ought or can be brought against him by anyone before all his property has been restored. Rather, everything must first be restored to him according to law, and afterward the stated matters must be heard at the time fixed by the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0669] “prefixed”: collected editions from the original.].

### C. III. Things Violently Taken Must Be Restored before the Joinder of Issue. Likewise Pope Stephen V, to Gerard of Liège

[Note: [Col. 0669D] “The Fifth”: this word was added from old codices, and the reading “of Liège” restored, where formerly “of Laodicea” was read. Mansi’s materials concerning the chapter below show that these words were written not to a Greek bishop but to a German or Gaul.]

[Note: [Col. 0669] Berardus suspects that the reading should be “Gerard of Lodi,” who was a suffragan of the Archbishop of Milan and subscribed to the councils of Pavia and Ravenna held under Stephen V.—*Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 64, chapter 2.]

It is necessary that you first cause yourselves to be reinvested, both in the cities, monasteries, and estates that have been invaded and in all your other goods generally, because we ought neither to contend naked nor to set ourselves unarmed against enemies.

### C. IV. Let Those Who Have Seized the Places of the Expelled in Adulterous Defilement Be Removed from the Clergy and Made Infamous. Likewise Pope Evaristus, Letter II

[Note: [Col. 0669] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, composed from Council of Sardica, chapters 4–6, and Fifth Council of Orléans, chapter 12.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 140; Anselm, book 3, chapter 45; Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 254; *Polycarpus*, book 2, title 11.]

[Col. 0669C] We have heard that certain bishops among you have been defamed, torn down, and driven from their own cities [Note: [Col. 0669] “expelled”: collected editions.]—for bishops cannot be appointed elsewhere except in cities of no small importance—and that others have been installed *in those very places* [Note: [Col. 0669] “bishops”: Basel edition.] while they are still living [Note: [Col. 0669] Addition: “there”: ibid.]. We therefore write this to you so that you may know that this may not be done, but that the rightful bishops must be recalled and restored in the fullest integrity.

But those who, in adulterous [Col. 0670A] defilement [Note: [Col. 0669] “ferocity”: ibid.], hold their own brides [Note: [Col. 0669] “brides,” that is, churches: Anselm.]—whom we understand, by the foregoing wording, to be also their wives [Note: [Col. 0669] Absent from collected editions except the first Basel edition.]—we command to be cast out as adulterers, made infamous, and excluded from ecclesiastical honors. But if you have any complaint against them, it shall be investigated after these matters have been carried out and settled by the authority of this holy see.

### C. V. A Respite of Six Months Shall Be Granted to Those Ejected or Despoiled. Likewise Caius, Letter I to Felix

[Note: [Col. 0669] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—In the collected editions, except Basel, it is cited under the name of Pope Gelasius.]

After full restoration, those ejected or despoiled must be granted a year’s respite or six months.

### C. VI. Respite Must Be Granted after Restoration. Likewise Pope Eusebius, Letter II

[Note: [Col. 0669] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, composed from *Tripartite History*, book 7, chapter 12.—Anselm, book 3, chapter 44; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 50; *Decree*, part 5, chapter 249.]

[Col. 0670B] First, therefore, all things must be restored by law to those despoiled, and the churches which have been taken from them [Note: [Col. 0669] “to themselves”: collected editions.] restored to them with every privilege belonging to them [Note: [Col. 0669] “his own”: ibid.; cited collections.]; and afterward, not within a short period [Note: [Col. 0669] “not within a short time, let a period be allowed them” (“was allowed”: Paris edition), but “as much”: collected editions.], but as much time must be allowed them as they appear to have been despoiled or expelled [Note: [Col. 0669] “appeared”: ibid.] before being summoned to a synod.

### C. VII. On the Same. Likewise Pope Felix II, in a Rescript to the Bishops of Egypt, Chapter 8

[Note: [Col. 0669] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Anselm, book 3, chapter 53; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 52.]

Let him reside peacefully and with full authority in his own see, disposing of all matters [Note: [Col. 0669] Addition: “acts”: collected editions.], for as long as he was seen to have lacked his property after being expelled [Note: [Col. 0669] “or driven back”: Basel edition.] or despoiled.

### C. VIII. No One Should Be Summoned to Trial before Restoration. Likewise Pope Felix I, Letter II to the Bishops of Gaul

[Note: [Col. 0669] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare *Tripartite History*, book 7, chapter 12.—Anselm, book 3, chapter 84, at the end of book 3 after chapter 123; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 44; *Decree*, part 5, chapter 248.]

[Col. 0670C] If a bishop has been despoiled of his own goods or of the goods of the church entrusted to him, or—may it not happen, since it ought to be foreign to all the faithful—has been ejected from his own see or separated from his flock by some detention [Note: [Col. 0669] “from”: Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venetian editions.], then he must first be restored canonically to his former state with every privilege of his office, and [Col. 0671A] all that was taken from him by the snares of all his enemies [Note: [Col. 0671] Addition: “all”: Basel edition.] must be restored to him by law.

[Note: [Col. 0669D] “Then canonically”: the original reads: [Col. 0670D] “then he must be restored canonically (before he is restored to his former condition [Note: [Col. 0669] “honor”: Anselm.]) with every privilege of his office, and all his goods which were taken from him by the snares of his enemies must be restored by law; nor can he be summoned or judged, unless he himself,” etc. Ivo and the *Panormia* are not much different, except that in place of “before” they read, like Gratian, “first.”]

For he cannot be summoned or prejudged, unless he chooses of his own accord to appear for his own need—yet by no means to be judged. Therefore he must by no means be compelled by anyone *to answer* before all that he had lost through the instigations of his enemies has been restored in due legal order to his authority by an honorable council.

§ 1. Moreover, let the prelate be restored to his former condition with every honor; and after he has freely and securely arranged and ordered his affairs for a considerable time, he shall then, and not before, be summoned to appear at the appointed time before a lawful and canonical council within four, five, six, or seven months, according to what is possible for him [Note: [Col. 0671] “assemble”: collected editions.], to answer the propositions of the accusers, if this seems just [Col. 0671B].

Part II. Gratian. But if a bishop, through evil living, has squandered the resources of the church, he must be removed from its patrimony until the question of the dissipation of ecclesiastical goods is determined, following the example of guardians and curators, who, when under suspicion, are removed from guardianship or administration until the suspicion is examined.

Hence Pope Pelagius to Peter the priest [Note: [Col. 0671] A letter of Pelagius I, of uncertain date, but apparently genuine; compare chapter 44, Cause 23, question 3.]:

### C. IX. Those Who Squander Church Property through Evil Living Must Be Removed from Administration

Because the allegations concerning the frauds of Maximilian [Note: [Col. 0671D] “Maximilian”: in the vulgate editions [Col. 0671] and collected editions except Basel, “the priest” followed, a word introduced because it occurs in none of the old manuscripts of Gratian that have been collated. Gratian, however, took this chapter as concerning a bishop, not a priest.] have reached our ears in a lamentable petition, and cannot easily be ascertained according to the truth unless the resources of the church which he squandered by improperly converting them to his own uses are removed from his control until the case [Note: [Col. 0671] “concerning the case”: Basel edition.] is determined [Col. 0671C], we therefore wish him meanwhile to be removed from the patrimony of the aforesaid church [Note: [Col. 0671] “to remove”: collected editions.], and that it be held under your supervision during the time of the inquiry [Note: [Col. 0671] “times”: Argentinian, Basel, Nuremberg, and first and second Venetian editions.].

## QUESTION III

### GRATIAN

Part I. That respite ought not be denied to one who comes to judgment after being summoned is attested by Pope Felix II, in his letter to the brethren of Egypt, chapter 8, who says [Note: [Col. 0671] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Anselm, book 3, chapter 55 [53]; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 98; *Decree*, part 6, chapter 335.]:

### C. I. Respite Must Not Be Denied to One Coming to Judgment

When the accused has come to judgment, if he wishes [Col. 0672A] and it is necessary [Note: [Col. 0671D] “And it is necessary”: these words have been added from the letter itself and are found in Ivo and the *Panormia*, and occur below in the same chapter, “Respite.”], the periods of respite established by the Fathers must be granted to him when he asks for them, without hindrance; and judges chosen by himself must be assigned to him [Note: [Col. 0671] “be attributed”: Basel edition.].

### C. II. That Periods of Respite Measured in Months Must Be Granted to Bishops. Likewise from the Same Letter to the Brethren of Egypt, Chapter 20

[Note: [Col. 0671] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Third Council of Carthage, chapter 7; *Tripartite History*, book 7, chapter 9; *Theodosian Code*, book 2, title 7, chapters 1–2.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 180; Anselm, book 3, chapters 118–119; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 102; *Decree*, part 5, chapter 296; Alger, book 1, chapter 52.]

Concerning the periods of respite for bishops, about which you have consulted us, we find diverse rules established by the Fathers. Some ordered that a year and six months be granted in order to repel the machinations of adversaries [Note: [Col. 0671] “obstacles”: Ivo; “enemies”: Basel edition; “emperors”: second Lyons edition; Alger; “the unskilled”: other editions; Burchard.], prepare their responses, confirm their witnesses, and seek the counsel of bishops and friends. Others ordered a year, and the majority agree on this. But I find no period shorter than six months; for this has been granted even to laypeople [Col. 0672B], how much more to the priests of the Lord?

And below:

§ 1. For periods of respite must not be granted within a short time but over a long interval, so that the accused may be able to prepare themselves, meet all their associates situated in the provinces, prepare witnesses, and arm themselves fully against plotters.

### C. III. On Granting Respite. Likewise Pope Eleutherius, in a Letter to the Provinces of Gaul

[Note: [Col. 0671] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Burchard, book 16, chapter 30; Anselm, book 3, chapter 56 [54]; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 103; *Decree*, part 6, chapter 317; Alger, book 2, chapter 60.]

A substantial period of respite must be given for investigation, lest anything seem to be done too hastily by either side, because [Note: [Col. 0671] A phrase derived from Apostolic Canon 34.] many things arise by stealth.

### C. IV. On the Same. PALEA. Likewise Pope Damasus, Letter III to Stephen, Archbishop

[Note: [Col. 0671] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Anselm, book 2, chapter 76; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 101; *Decree*, part 6, chapter 287.]

[Col. 0672C] “In criminal cases, an accused person must be granted six months’ respite, or more if necessary.”

Part II. Gratian. The duration of adjournments, as is found in book III of the Code, title 11, *On Adjournments* [Note: [Col. 0671] Chapter 1, *Code*, book 3, title 11.], must be regulated on this principle: if either a person or documents are sought from the province where the suit is being heard, no more than three months shall be allowed. But if they are sought from neighboring provinces, justice requires six months to be observed [Note: [Col. 0671] “justice”: collected editions except the Lyons editions.]. In an overseas adjournment, however, nine months must be reckoned.

Those judging must understand that, on this ground, discretion to grant adjournment is not conceded to them; rather, they must know that the same adjournment, if the most urgent reason of the matter demands it and the need for the requested evidence requires it, is not readily to be granted more than once, nor with any contrivance for delay [Col. 0673A].

§ 1. But adjournment must wholly be denied to one who has brought a rescript to an extraordinary judge [Note: [Col. 0673] “brought back”: Basel edition.]. It must, however, be granted to one summoned to judgment, to prove the falsehoods of petitions or to produce documents or witnesses, because one who is unexpectedly drawn before an unfamiliar tribunal could not have been prepared [Note: [Col. 0673] “to disprove”: original.].

§ 2. But when a rescript has been issued by the emperor concerning an appeal or consultation—whether an adjournment was sought at the first hearing and [Note: [Col. 0673] “and was not granted”: collected editions.] was not granted, or was not even sought—no one may be given one, for the same reason that adjournment is not customarily granted even in trials involving imperial cognitions.

§ 3. It is not fitting to request an adjournment from a judge who is proceeding [Note: [Col. 0673] ibid., chapter 4.] even if it is granted with both parties present, since it can be granted only after the case has been examined. The examination of the case is not lawfully established by a simple application [Note: [Col. 0673] “plenary”: Böhm.], but rather only after the judge has considered it [Note: [Col. 0673] “considering”: original; Gloss; collected editions.], so that, if perhaps the request for adjournment is rejected, the issue undertaken may be decided by the judge’s sentence.

In Constitution Seven, Collation Seven, § 4: A plaintiff may not submit a libellus except after first furnishing security both to the person whom he alleges to be liable and to the executor of the case, undertaking either to join issue within two months or to restore double all loss accruing to the defendant [Note: [Col. 0673] Absent from the collected editions except the Lyons editions.]. In Collation V, Constitution 6.

Part III. § 5. Let a libellus be offered [Note: [Col. 0673] Novel 53, chapter 3; Code, in the same title, *Authenticum*, “Let it be offered.”] to the person summoned to judgment. Then, after the fees have been paid and security furnished [Note: [Col. 0673] “when a surety has been given”: Basel edition.], let him enjoy twenty days’ respite [Col. 0673C], in which to deliberate whether he should yield or contest, and whether he should request that another judge be joined to the judge or should challenge him—unless he is the person whom he himself, having already challenged another, requested.

Finally, when present he shall be asked whether this time for the *litis contestatio* has elapsed. This must appear not only from his own answer but also from his endorsement of the libellus, which he ought to make at the beginning. Therefore a joinder of issue entered contrary to this concession [Note: [Col. 0673] “privilege”: original.] is null.

In the same place, § 6. This must not be done unless the plaintiff has given sufficient security, promising a definite sum that he will pay if he does not pursue the suit, or, having pursued it, does not prevail. If, therefore, after the time fixed *by himself* [Note: [Col. 0673] “pre-fixed”: collected editions.], he does not appear within ten days while the defendant is present, the defendant shall be dismissed after recovering what was promised [Col. 0674A], and also whatever additional expense he swears, with the judge’s assessment, that he incurred in the suit.

§ 7. The exception concerning forum [Note: [Col. 0673D] “Exception concerning forum”: this final section is absent from most ancient copies. In one it occurs in the margin under the title “Gloss of John.” The same words occur below, in the same question, chapter 6, “If Any Bishop,” § “Exception,” and there they are in all ancient codices.] is dilatory; therefore it must be raised and proved at the beginning of the suit. But peremptory exceptions, such as prescriptions of long time, need only be asserted at the beginning of joinder of issue.

## QUESTION IV

### GRATIAN

That persons of ill repute and those not lawfully joined in marriage ought not be admitted to accusation, and which persons generally must be excluded from accusation, is made clear by many authorities.

Thus Pope Hyginus says in Letter II [Note: [Col. 0673] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare above, Cause 2, question 7, chapter 23.—*Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 7, chapter 3; Anselm, book 2, chapter 16 [17]; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapters 70 and 88.]:

### C. I. Persons of Ill Repute Cannot Accuse Those of Good Reputation

[Col. 0674B] We cannot receive one who follows companionship in another’s error [Note: [Col. 0673] “a companion from the path of his own purpose”: original.], or departs from the course of his own purpose, or disobeys the commands [Note: [Col. 0673] “institutions”: Basel edition.] of the Apostolic See; nor do we permit such a person to assail those who rightly believe or obey the commands of the holy Fathers, because a great distinction must exist between faithful and unfaithful persons.

### C. II. One Who Voluntarily Transgresses His Own Law Cannot Accuse Those Acting Rightly before His Own Return. Likewise Pope Anacletus, in the First Decretal

[Note: [Col. 0673] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare the interpretation of *Theodosian Code*, book 16, title 1, chapter 7.—Anselm, book 3, chapter 9; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 60.]

Our blessed predecessor Clement, an apostolic man filled with God’s Spirit, together with his other holy colleagues, established as follows: Permission to accuse or [Col. 0674C] testify shall be denied to those who have neglected the dignity of the Christian religion and name, and the standard of their own law or profession, or things regularly forbidden. For voluntary transgressors and violators of their own law, *and those who depart from it*, are called apostates. Every apostate must be rejected before his return and must not be received in accusation or testimony against those acting rightly.

### C. III. Those Departing from Their Profession Are Infamous. Likewise Pope Pius, Letter I

[Note: [Col. 0673] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*, chapter 52.—*Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 8, chapter 2; Anselm, book 3, chapter 4.]

But if anyone turns backward from his profession [Note: [Col. 0673] “If anyone from the true profession”: collected editions except Basel.] and willingly transgresses the command [Note: [Col. 0673] “commands”: collected editions.] of the Apostolic See, he becomes infamous. Therefore the censures of those suspected in the true faith must be rejected. Their faith and conduct must first be examined [Note: [Col. 0673] “previously”: Basel edition.] [Col. 0675A], and only then are those who appear irreproachable to be received.

### C. IV. Incestuous Persons and Those Not Lawfully Joined Cannot Accuse Priests or Persons Lawfully Joined. Likewise Pope Callixtus, to the Bishops of Gaul, Letter II, Chapter 4

[Note: [Col. 0675] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Third Council of Orléans, chapter 10; Second Council of Tours, chapter 20; *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*, chapter 101; Seventh Council of Carthage, chapter 2.—Burchard, book 7, chapter 1; Ivo, *Decree*, part 9, chapter 23.]

Unions of blood relatives are neither lawful nor able to remain, but must be rejected. And below, chapter 5:

§ 1. Whoever is known to be unlawfully joined, or united without a dotal charter and a priest’s blessing, cannot in any way accuse priests or those lawfully joined, or testify against them, since everyone polluted by the stain of incest is infamous and is not permitted to accuse the aforesaid persons [Col. 0675B]. Therefore not only these persons must be rejected [Note: [Col. 0675] “repelled”: collected editions.] and made infamous, but also all who agree with them.

§ 2. We judge that the same must be done with abductors and those who attack their elders. Secular laws indeed put these persons to death; but we, mercy going before, receive such persons to penance under the mark of infamy.

### C. V. Those Not to Be Received in Accusation. The Same, in the Same Letter

[Note: [Col. 0675] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Council of Carthage held in 421, chapter 6.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chapter 346.]

Conspirators are not to be received in anyone’s accusation; nor can the voice of such persons or of those anathematized harm or accuse [Note: [Col. 0675] “injure”: collected editions.] anyone.

### C. VI. On the Same. Likewise Pope Stephen, Letter II

[Note: [Col. 0675] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Seventh Council of Carthage, chapter 1.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 71.]

No one among those anathematized [Note: [Col. 0675] “of anathema”: original; Ivo.] shall be received, nor should anyone believe what they say or write [Col. 0675C]. By “anathematized” I mean those whom bishops have anathematized in their writings, or whose enactments anathematize them.

### C. VII. Anathematized Faithful Persons Cannot Accuse. Likewise Pope Fabian, Letter I to the Ministers of the Church

[Note: [Col. 0675] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Anselm, book 3, chapter 16; *Polycarpus*, book 5, title 1.]

We exclude and remove from every accusation of the faithful all whom the enactments of the holy Fathers anathematize, both in times past and times to come.

### C. VIII. A Cleric Who Accuses His Bishop Becomes Infamous. Likewise Pope Stephen, Letter II, Chapter 8

[Note: [Col. 0675] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare *Theodosian Code*, book 16, title 2, chapter 39.]

[Col. 0676A] A cleric who accuses his bishop or proves to be his plotter is not to be received, because he has become infamous; he must withdraw from his rank and be handed over to the curia for service.

### C. IX. Let Those Who Persecute Bishops Become Infamous and Exiles. Likewise Pope Alexander, Letter I, Chapter 1

[Note: [Col. 0675] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Anselm, book 3, chapter 7.]

Those who persecute their bishops [Note: [Col. 0675D] “Their”: this word is absent from most manuscripts and from the original [Col. 0675] and from the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and first Venetian editions, but has not been removed because of the gloss.] and unjustly strive to remove them contrary to apostolic authority, although they are forbidden to be put to death, as the Lord says [Note: [Col. 0675] Ezekiel 33:11.], “I do not will the death of the sinner, but [Note: [Col. 0675] Addition: “rather”: Basel edition.] that he should turn and live,” are nevertheless marked with perpetual infamy [Note: [Col. 0675] Addition: “without doubt”: collected editions.] and judged worthy of exile in a neighboring place. Concerning them, from apostolic times and below, we maintain *these matters* and have decrees [Col. 0676B], *by which* we silence their voice in accusing bishops or testifying against them, since we know them to be dead not by human [Note: [Col. 0675] “from human”: same editions except the second and third Lyons editions.] but by divine acts.

### C. X. Let Detractors and Instigators of Enemies Not Accuse Bishops. Likewise Pope Zephyrinus, Letter I to the Bishops of Sicily

[Note: [Col. 0675] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*, chapter 46.—Anselm, book 3, chapter 35 [62]; Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 245.]

We remove from episcopal accusation and testimony detractors, whom divine authority commands to be rooted out, and instigators [Note: [Col. 0675] “actors”: Lyons editions.] of enemies.

### C. XI. A Person of Ill Repute or a Sacrilegious Person Cannot Accuse a Devout Christian. Likewise Pope Eutychian, Letter II to the Bishops of Sicily

[Note: [Col. 0675] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Paul, *Sentences*, book 1, title 2, § 1, with interpretation; Burchard, book 16, chapter 11; Anselm, book 3, chapter 25 [24]; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 92; *Decree*, part 6, chapter 333.]

No infamous or [Note: [Col. 0675] “or”: collected editions.] sacrilegious person may ever, in any matter [Col. 0676C], give testimony against a devout Christian, even though he be a lowly [Note: [Col. 0675] Addition: “objected”: same editions except the Argentinian edition.] and servile person; nor may such a person assail a Christian in any action, suit [Note: [Col. 0675] “ground”: collected editions.], or formal accusation.

Gratian. It should be noted, however, that excommunication is one thing and anathema another.

Hence Pope John VIII writes to a certain bishop [Note: [Col. 0675D] This letter of John VIII has not been found. Yet Nicholas I, at the last chapter of a council held by him at Rome for the complete abolition of the Synod of Metz, recounts that he had twice struck Engeltrude with anathema. Regino, book 2 of the *Chronicles*, recounts the wicked acts of this woman for which she most justly suffered this punishment. But she may have lived in the time of John VIII, since Hadrian II, who intervened between Nicholas I and John VIII, did not complete the fifth year of his pontificate.]

[Note: [Col. 0675] Fragment of a lost letter of John VIII to Liutbert, Archbishop of Mainz, who presided over the Council of Mainz held in 888; compare Ivo, *Decree*, part 14, chapter 51, and John’s Letter 108, in Mansi. The chapter heading was omitted by Böhm.]

### C. XII. Excommunication Is One Thing; Anathema Another

Know that Engeltrude, wife of Boso, has been repeatedly struck not only with excommunication [Col. 0677A], which separates one from fellowship with the brethren, but also with anathema, which cuts one off from Christ’s very body, which is the Church.

Gratian. From this it is understood that anathematized persons are to be regarded as separated not merely from the fellowship of the brethren but altogether from the body of Christ, which is the Church.

## QUESTION V

### GRATIAN

That witnesses from the household of accusers should not be produced, and that the testimony of enemies should not be heard, is established by many authorities.

Thus Pope Callixtus says in Letter II to the bishops of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0677] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, taken from the Council of Carthage held in 421, chapter 7.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 171; Anselm, book 3, chapter 55; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 85; *Decree*, part 5, chapter 289; *Polycarpus*, book 3, title 1.]:

### C. I. Blood Relatives and Household Members Shall Not Testify against Outsiders

[Col. 0677B] Blood relatives of an accuser [Note: [Col. 0677] “accusers”: original; cited collections.] shall not testify against outsiders, nor household members or those coming from his household. But if they wish and mutually consent, relatives may testify only among themselves, and not against others.

### C. II. Persons Recently Enemies Cannot Be Accusers or Witnesses. Likewise Pope Anacletus, Letter III, Chapter 5

[Note: [Col. 0677] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Ambrose, Letter 64.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 152; Anselm, book 3, chapter 13; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 85; *Decree*, part 5, chapter 239.]

Accusers and witnesses cannot be persons who were enemies the day before yesterday or three days ago, lest in anger they desire to harm [Note: [Col. 0677] “and lest”: Basel edition.], or, having suffered injury, wish to avenge themselves [Note: [Col. 0677] “or lest”: ibid.—“lest”: the remaining editions; Burchard, Ivo, *Panormia*.]. [Col. 0677C] Therefore the disposition of accusers and witnesses must be sought to be unoffended, not suspect.

### C. III. On the same matter

Likewise Pope Symmachus, in the Fifth Roman Synod held under him [Note: [Col. 0677] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, drawn from Paul, *Sentences*, bk. 5, tit. 15, § 1; Council of Chalcedon, c. 27; and the first Synod of Symmachus, c. 5.]:

No credence is to be given to hostile accusers, or to those coming from an enemy’s household, or living with enemies [Note: [Col. 0677] “living”: the collected editions.], or who are suspect, lest in anger they desire to harm, or, having suffered injury, wish to avenge themselves. And below:

§ 1. If anyone presumes to violate, or deliberately attempts to transgress, these provisions prohibited today in *this* holy synod, if he is a cleric, let him be wholly deprived of his rank; but if a monk or layman, let him be deprived of communion; and, if he does not correct the fault, [Col. 0678A] let him be struck with anathema. But if anyone brings to the Church’s notice either secret or open plots made against bishops by anyone whatsoever, or matters embraced by the decree of this holy synod, let him obtain honour; and let those who devise hostile measures against them, as was long ago established by the holy Fathers and is today confirmed by synodal and apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 0677] “confirmed”: ibid.], be entirely cast out and handed over to perpetual exile, with all their possessions confiscated [Note: [Col. 0677] “with all their possessions removed”: Basel edition; “with their own possessions removed”: ibid.].

### C. IV. Persons who cannot be accusers or witnesses

Likewise Pontianus, Bishop of the Holy and Universal Church, Letter II, to all Christians [Note: [Col. 0677] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, drawn from Paul, *Sentences*, bk. 5, tit. 15, § 1, and the Council of Carthage held in A.D. 421, c. 6.—Anselm, bk. 3, c. 16 (15).]:

Persons who are suspect, enemies, prone to litigation, not of good conduct, whose life is blameworthy, or who neither hold nor [Col. 0678B] teach the right faith—our predecessors, the apostles [Note: [Col. 0677] “our predecessors”: absent from the collected editions and the first Basel edition.]—prohibited them from being accusers and witnesses; and by their authority we exclude them and bar them for future times.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] “Apostles”: thus corrected from Vatican manuscripts. Earlier the reading was “apostolic.” In Böhm and the collected editions and first Basel edition it reads “apostolic.” In Anselm it reads: “our predecessors, the apostles, rejected [them] by authority; and we exclude [them].” The original printed text, however, reads: “and our predecessors rejected [them] by apostolic authority, and we exclude [them], and for future times,” etc.]

### C. V. Those whom secular laws do not admit are to be excluded from accusations against clerics

Likewise Eusebius, Letter I, to the bishops of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0677] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Carthage VII, c. 2, and Ennodius, *Apology for Symmachus*.—Anselm, bk. 3, c. 26 (25).—Cf. C. 6, q. 1, c. 19.]:

Concerning accusations against clerics, about which you have written: know that from the time of the apostles it has been observed in this holy City that accusers and accusations not recognized by the laws of foreign customs are excluded from accusing clerics. And below:

Therefore, following in the footsteps of the Fathers for the salvation of God’s servants, we also deny to all persons whom public laws do not admit to bring an accusation the licence to attack [Col. 0678C] another; and no accusations prohibited by secular laws are to be heard by ecclesiastical judges.

### C. VI. Foreigners and those whom divine utterances call dead cannot accuse bishops

Likewise Pope Pelagius II to the bishops of Italy [Note: [Col. 0677] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. the Council of Carthage held in A.D. 421, c. 6.—Anselm, bk. 3, c. 59 (63).]:

Following and strengthening the canonical decrees of the holy Fathers, lest the pillars of the holy Church should totter, we utterly exclude from every accusation against bishops all persons of ill repute, all suspects and enemies; those who are not of their people; those whose faith, life, and free status are unknown; those who are not of good conduct; and those whose life is blameworthy. [Col. 0679A] Likewise, we judge that all whom divine laws call dead must be excluded from this accusation and subjected to public penance.

### C. VII. Clerics reject accusations not recognized by secular laws

Likewise from a Roman Synod held under Pope Hadrian [Note: [Col. 0679D] This chapter and the others cited below in the same question, C. 6, as from a Roman synod, occur among Hadrian’s chapters; they are also expressly called synodal below, 5, q. 3, at the beginning.] [Note: [Col. 0679] C. 11 among Hadrian’s chapters; cf. *Capitularies*, bk. 7, c. 307, and Herard of Tours, c. 102.—Anselm, bk. 3, c. 20 (19), “from the Synod of Nicaea,” and at the end of bk. 3, c. 9.]:

We decree that accusations, accusers, and their proceedings [Note: [Col. 0679] “their proceedings”: original has “these”], which secular laws do not recognize, are wholly to be rejected by clerics under divine and synodal authority; for it is unworthy that superiors should suffer from inferiors what inferiors disdain to suffer from them.

[Col. 0679B]

### C. VIII. Neither slave, freedman, nor person of ill repute may presume to accuse bishops

Likewise Stephen, Bishop of the Roman Church, to all bishops, Letter II, on accusations against priests, c. 3 [Note: [Col. 0679] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, and Council of Carthage held in A.D. 421, c. 6; Theodosian Code, bk. 9, tit. 1, c. 10; Carthage VII, c. 1.—Anselm, bk. 3, c. 18 (17). Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 6, c. 327.]:

We exclude accusers and accusations whom the laws of the age do not receive [Note: [Col. 0679] “admit”: the collected editions.] and whom our predecessors prohibited. Let no foreigner become either their accuser or their judge. Hence it is written concerning Lot [Note: [Col. 0679] Genesis 19:9]: “You came in as an alien—are you to act as judge?” Let no slave or freedman be accuser of our people [Note: [Col. 0679] “your people”: original], nor any suspect or infamous person.

### C. IX. Persons of ill repute who resort to sorcerers and diviners can be neither accusers nor witnesses

Likewise Pope Eusebius, Letter III, to the bishops of Tuscany [Note: [Col. 0679] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, drawn from Carthage VII, c. 2.—Cf. Hadrian’s chapters, c. 67.—Anselm, bk. 3, c. 18, and at the end of bk. 3, c. 10.]:

We have decreed anew, confirming the canonical ordinances of the Fathers, together with all the bishops who are with us, [Col. 0679C] as we find it decreed of old, that murderers, evildoers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, robbers, adulterers, incestuous persons, poisoners, suspects, criminals, household dependants, perjurers, those who have committed abduction, given false testimony, or resorted to sorcerers [Note: [Col. 0679] The original reads “sacrilegious persons.”] and diviners [Note: [Col. 0679] The collected editions, except the first Argentinian edition, read “resort” in the present tense.], and persons like them, are in no way to be admitted either to accusation or testimony; for they are infamous and must rightly be rejected, because their voice is deadly [Note: [Col. 0679] Basel edition adds “in such persons”: “because their voice in such persons is deadly.”].

### C. X. Suspect or influential persons are not to be admitted to accusation

Likewise Pope Julius, in his rescript to the Easterners, c. 33 [Note: [Col. 0679] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. the Council of Carthage held in A.D. 421, c. 6.—Anselm, bk. 3, c. 21 (20).]:

Likewise, in the synod already mentioned it was decreed [Col. 0680A] that suspects, infamous persons, criminals, persons of influence, calumniators, relatives, wicked persons, and those prone to litigation are not to be received as accusers, but only persons entirely free from every suspicion [Note: [Col. 0679] Anselm reads “entirely”; the Basel edition adds “from every fault and.”].

### C. XI. He who pursues enmities or is prone to litigation can be neither accuser nor witness

Likewise Pope Felix II, Letter I, c. 14 [Note: [Col. 0679] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Carthage VII, cc. 1–2.—Anselm, bk. 3, c. 62 (66).]:

Let no slave, no freedman, no unbeliever [Note: [Col. 0679] The original reads “faithless”; Anselm likewise.], no person entangled in crimes, no calumniator, no one devoted to enmities, no one who frequently litigates [Note: [Col. 0679] Anselm reads “no one who frequently litigates.”] and is quick to accuse or disparage, no infamous person, nor any whom public laws do not admit to accuse public crimes, be permitted to accuse bishops.

[Col. 0680B]

### C. XII. Household associates, suspects, and persons coming from the house are not to be received in an accusation

Likewise Pope Calixtus, Letter II, to the bishops of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0679] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled from Paul, *Sentences*, bk. 5, tit. 15, § 1, with the interpretation, and Ambrose, Letter 44.—Burchard, bk. 1, c. 171. Anselm, bk. 3, c. 57 (55). Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 5, c. 289.—Cf. above, same question, c. 1.]:

Suspect accusers or witnesses are not to be received, nor household associates or persons coming from the house [Note: [Col. 0679] The Basel edition omits “nor.”]; nor may relatives of an accuser testify against outsiders. For the attachment arising from kinship, familiarity, and domination commonly obstructs truth. Carnal love, fear, and greed often dull human understanding and pervert judgments, so that people regard gain as piety and money as though it were the reward of prudence.

### C. XII. Those who are enemies or suspects, and who pursue anyone in hatred, are to be removed from accusation

Likewise Pope Pelagius II, Letter VIII, c. 4 [Note: [Col. 0679] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled from Proclus’s Letter to Domnus of Antioch in Act 14 of Chalcedon.—Anselm, bk. 3, c. 6, “from Gelasius.”]:

[Col. 0680C] We judge all who take up arms against the Fathers to be infamous as invaders and slaughterers of the Fathers. And below:

Accordingly, the authors or perpetrators of these offences are not to be received in accusations against bishops [Note: [Col. 0679] The collected editions, except the first Basel edition, read “into an accusation.”] [Note: [Col. 0679] The Basel edition reads “against a bishop.”], but wholly rejected, because the canonical decrees of the Fathers command that neither accusation nor testimony be received in any way from persons who pursue anyone in hatred [Note: [Col. 0679] The original reads “persecute”; Anselm reads “follow.”] or who are considered enemies or suspects.

### C. XIV. On the same matter. *PALEA.*

Likewise Pope Paschal [Note: [Col. 0680D] In one very ancient manuscript of Gratian, from which most *Paleae* are absent, this chapter appears not here but above, 2, q. 7, after c. *Blessed Peter and Paul*, where it is also cited as from Paschal II.] [Note: [Col. 0679] Chapter of uncertain origin.—Cf. c. 3, *Compilatio I*, on accusations, c. 5, *X* on this title.]:

“No bishop may exclude [Col. 0681A] from bringing an accusation against him those whom, before he is assailed by them, he has neglected to separate from his common familiarity.”

[Note: [Col. 0681C] The same manuscript reads: “those whom, before they attacked him, he neglected to separate from his common familiarity.” In some other manuscripts, where this *Palea* occurs here, it reads: “those whom, before they knew that they were to be attacked by them, he neglected to separate from his…” In the Decretals, however, the wording is not much different: “before he knew he was to be attacked by them, he neglected to separate [them] from his…”]

Gratian. The reason enemies are barred from accusation is that innocence is often oppressed by their cunning. But since Athanasius is ordered to be restored to his see because he complained of the hostility of his patriarch, it is clear that, even if someone’s crimes are manifest, he is nevertheless not to be condemned upon an enemy’s accusation.

Therefore Pope Nicholas writes to Emperor Michael in the letter beginning “We had proposed.” [Note: [Col. 0681] Written A.D. 865.]

### C. XV. Enemies cannot be judges

That suspects and enemies ought not to be judges is dictated by reason itself and proved by many examples.

§ 1. For what could anyone give an enemy that is more welcome and pleasing [Col. 0681B] than entrusting to him for attack the person whom he might wish to harm? The Synod of Constantinople is known to have prudently prohibited this in the sixth of its canonical chapters [Note: [Col. 0681C] “Sixth”: this is the sixth canon of the First Council of Constantinople among the Greeks. In editions of the councils gathered in four volumes—though absent from other editions—it is given twice in volume I: first in the Council of Constantinople itself, then in the collection of synodal constitutions. Concerning this chapter and other canons of that council, see the note above, Distinction 22, and below, 4, q. 1, c. *But*.].

§ 2. Let us then come to the holy Synod of Chalcedon, and hear what it relates to us concerning Athanasius, bishop of Paraeon. [Note: [Col. 0681] Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 5, c. 55.] This bishop, summoned a third time to the synod and failing to appear, had been canonically condemned by his patriarch; but solely because, when called to the synod, he cried out that the very person judging him was his enemy, he was reserved by the holy Synod of Chalcedon for examination of the charges brought against him; and unless he should again be convicted [Note: [Col. 0681] Ivo and the collected editions read “unless he were convicted again.”], he was judged entitled to receive his own church.

If Athanasius, [Col. 0681C] deposed by his patriarch because he complained of that patriarch’s hostility, [Col. 0682A] is sent back for a renewed trial, and, although manifest crimes stand against him, is nevertheless commanded to be restored to his church, how much more ought Ignatius—who was not deprived by a patriarch, but was himself patriarch—not to have been despoiled of his own church [Note: [Col. 0681] The collected editions add “and deprived of it.”] by the decision of hostile and suspect judges?

[Note: [Col. 0681C–0682D] The true reading is: “and unless manifest crimes stand against him, he is ordered to be restored to his church.” It is the same as the passage previously reported from the council: “and unless he is convicted anew, he is judged entitled to receive his own church.” The text was not corrected because of the gloss, and because Gratian plainly shows in the following words that he used the false reading, transferring what is said here of the judge’s hostility to an accuser’s hostility. Nor, as is readily clear from the entirety of Act 14, was Athanasius the plaintiff seeking restoration in that case: although deposed at the Council of Antioch, he had subsequently recovered the episcopate through Dioscorus and was then in possession. Rather, Savinianus, appointed by the metropolitan and fellow-provincial bishops in Athanasius’s place after Athanasius’s deposition, had been expelled by Dioscorus and therefore sought restoration of the episcopate for himself. At Chalcedon itself it was decreed that, since Athanasius said he had not attended the Council of Antioch when three times summoned because the then patriarch of Antioch, *domnus*, was his enemy, Savinianus should remain bishop in the meantime; Athanasius’s case, however, should be heard before Maximus, then patriarch of Antioch, and within eight months it should be determined whether Athanasius had committed an offence deserving deposition; and, unless it were established that he had committed one, his episcopate should be restored to him. From this entire affair Nicholas selected the part that best served his argument.]

And a little later:

§ 3. Let our most fruitful Pope Gelasius also come, the bravest assailant of heretics, and explain to us now what he said then about the bishops of Constantinople, who were at that time ill, as was their usual custom. “I ask,” he says [Note: [Col. 0681] In the *Commonitorium* to Faustus.], “from these persons, where can the judgment they allege be conducted? Before themselves, so that the same men are enemies, witnesses, and judges? But not even human affairs ought to be entrusted to such a judgment.” If human affairs ought not to be entrusted to a court where the same persons are enemies and [Col. 0682B] judges, how much less divine—that is, ecclesiastical—affairs? Let the wise understand [Note: [Col. 0681] The Basel edition adds “and not understand.”].

§ 4. And indeed, for this reason the pious Emperor Justinian [Note: [Col. 0681] “formerly”: the second and third Lyon editions.] is known to have promulgated in his laws [Note: [Col. 0681] “pious laws”: Ivo; Argentinian edition.], saying: “Anyone who considers a judge suspect [Note: [Col. 0681] The collected editions add “suspect to himself.”] may, before the suit begins, reject him [Note: [Col. 0681] Ivo reads “has him suspect”], so that recourse may be had to another.” For it is in some measure natural to avoid the snares of suspect judges and always to wish to flee the judgment of enemies.

§ 5. Hence Saint Athanasius often avoided the snares of enemies. Hence Saint John Chrysostom refused to enter the assembly of the council gathered against him.

Gratian. It is therefore clear that even when someone’s crimes are manifest, he is not to be condemned upon an enemy’s accusation.

# QUESTION VI

[Col. 0683A]

## GRATIAN

### Part I

An accused person is in no circumstance to be brought outside his province.

Therefore Pope Fabian writes to Bishop Hilary, Letter III, c. 4 [Note: [Col. 0683] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. C. 2, q. 3, c. 3; C. 2, q. 8, c. 4; and below, final chapter.—Anselm, bk. 11, c. 81.]

### C. I. Where the crime is committed, there the case is to be heard

A case must always be conducted where the crime was committed [Note: [Col. 0683] The collected editions, except the first Basel and the second and third Lyon editions, add “for.”], and whoever fails to prove what he alleged must himself suffer the penalty which he sought to inflict.

### C. II. The accused is to be heard only in his own forum

The same, in the same letter, c. 2 [Note: [Col. 0683] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Gregory the Great, Letter 8, bk. 3, Maurist edition.—Burchard, bk. 1, c. 147. Anselm, bk. 3, c. 77 (76). Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 5, c. 260. *Polycarpus*, bk. 5, tit. 1.]:

If any bishop is accused of particular crimes [Note: [Col. 0683] The collected editions read “is accused.”], let him be heard by all the bishops who are in his province, because an accused person ought not to be heard anywhere [Col. 0683B] but in his own forum.

Gratian. An objection to venue is dilatory and therefore must be raised and proved at the beginning of the suit. Peremptory objections, however—such as prescriptions based on long time—need only be asserted at the commencement of litigation.

### C. III. On the same matter

The same Fabian, in the same place [Note: [Col. 0683] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Theodosian Code, bk. 9, tit. 1, c. 10; bk. 9, tit. 10, c. 3; and the third synod under Symmachus.—Anselm, bk. 2, c. 11, and among Hadrian’s chapters at the end of bk. 3, c. 3. Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 4, c. 123; *Decree*, pt. 6, c. 323. *Polycarpus*, bk. 1, tit. 7.]:

Let the defendant plead his case before his own judge; but, if summoned before a judge who is not his own, he may remain silent if he wishes. Whenever defendants appeal, let them be granted a postponement.

Gratian. What was said concerning place must be understood to apply when the truth of the case can be discovered only in the place where the crime was committed, or unless one party seeks the judgment of a superior person, whether by declining the court or appealing a sentence.

[Col. 0683C] Therefore Stephen, Bishop of the Holy, Apostolic, and Universal Roman Church, writes to all bishops, Letter II, c. 7 [Note: [Col. 0683] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Theodosian Code, bk. 9, tit. 1, cc. 10 and 16.—Anselm, at the end of bk. 3, among Hadrian’s chapters, c. 9. Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 4, c. 33.]:

### C. IV. A case is to be heard only within the province and by fellow-provincials

The licence to accuse must not extend beyond provincial boundaries [Note: [Col. 0683] The original reads “the province’s boundaries.”]; every accusation must be heard within the province and concluded by fellow-provincials, unless an appeal has been made to the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0683] The Basel edition adds “nevertheless.”].

[Col. 0684A]

### C. V. A bishop accused or judged by fellow-provincials is to appeal to the Apostolic See

Likewise Pope Sixtus II, Letter I, to Bishop Gratus [Note: [Col. 0683] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Sardica, cc. 4, 5, 7.—*Collectio tripartita*, pt. 1, tit. 22, c. 2.—Burchard, bk. 1, cc. 144, 176. Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 4, c. 125; *Decree*, pt. 5, cc. 4, 257.]:

A bishop accused or judged by his fellow-provincials in any case may freely appeal and approach the pontiff of the Apostolic See, who shall arrange for the matter to be reconsidered either personally or through his vicars [Note: [Col. 0683] The collected editions read “to reconsider.”]. While the pontiff conducts the case upon renewed trial, no other bishop is to be installed or ordained in his place. For although provincial bishops may investigate the case of an accused bishop [Note: [Col. 0683] The collected editions read “of a bishop.”], they are not permitted to decide it [Note: [Col. 0683] The original reads “to be decided.”] without consulting the Roman Pontiff.

### C. VI. On the same matter. *PALEA.*

Likewise Pope Damasus, Letter II, to Archbishop Stephen, c. 2 [Note: [Col. 0683C–D] This chapter is absent from certain ancient manuscripts, and no gloss upon it exists.] [Note: [Col. 0683] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Innocent I, Letter 2, and Gregory the Great, bk. 3, Letter 8.—Anselm, bk. 2, c. 61 (59).]:

[Col. 0684B] A metropolitan, together with all his fellow-provincials, none being absent and all agreeing in each individual matter [Note: [Col. 0683] The collected editions, except the first Basel edition, read “agreeing together.”], may investigate bishops and the principal cases of ecclesiastical affairs; but he may by no means decide their principal complaints and cases, or condemn bishops, without the authority of this *holy* See [Note: [Col. 0683] The Basel edition omits “holy.”], which all must appeal if necessary [Note: [Col. 0683] The collected editions read “because all ought to appeal to it.”] and whose assistance they must seek.”

### C. VII. Fellow-provincials and metropolitans may hear a bishop’s case but cannot decide it

Likewise Pope Eleutherius, writing to the provinces of Gaul, c. 2 [Note: [Col. 0683] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled from Sardica, c. 4.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 4, cc. 134, 136; *Decree*, pt. 6, c. 316.]:

Although accusations and [Col. 0684C] criminal charges against bishops may be examined before fellow-provincials, metropolitans, and primates [Note: [Col. 0683] The collected editions read “and charges.”], they may not be decided without the authority of this holy See, as has already been decided by the apostles and their successors with the consent of many bishops. Nor are others to be set over or ordained in their churches before their affairs have here been justly concluded. The cases of other clerics, however, may both be examined and justly concluded before provincial bishops [Note: [Col. 0683] “fellow-provincials”: ibid.], metropolitans, and primates [Note: [Col. 0683] The Basel edition reads “decided.”].

[Col. 0685A]

### C. VIII. Before apostolic censure, no final sentence is to be issued in cases concerning bishops
