Likewise Leo, Bishop of the City of Rome, to Anastasius, Bishop of Thessalonica, Letters LXXXII–LXXXIV, c. 1 [Note: [Col. 0685] Written A.D. 446, Letter 14 in the Ballerini edition.—*Collectio tripartita*, pt. 1, tit. 43, c. 20.]:

I am greatly astonished, dearest brother, and deeply grieved that against a man concerning whom you had judged nothing more than that, when summoned, he delayed appearing and pleaded illness as an excuse, you could become so fierce and vehement, especially since—even if he had deserved something of the kind—you ought to have awaited my reply to your consultation.

And below:

Even if he had committed something grave and intolerable [Note: [Col. 0685] The original reads “if he were to commit”; the collected editions read “if he were to do something.”], our censure ought to have been awaited [Note: [Col. 0685] The Basel edition reads “your censure.”], so that you should decide nothing before learning what pleased us. For we entrusted our vicariate to your charity in such a way that you were called to share in our solicitude, not in the fullness of our power. Thus, as the matters you have managed piously greatly delight us, so those managed wrongly certainly grieve us [Note: [Col. 0685] The original reads “excessively”; the collected editions read “very much”; the second Venetian edition reads “very little.”].

### C. IX. Apart from the sentence of the Roman Pontiff, neither councils are to be held nor a bishop condemned

Likewise Pope Julius to the Eastern bishops, Letter I [Note: [Col. 0685] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. *Tripartite History*, bk. 4, c. 9; the Donation of Constantine; and Innocent I, Letter 2.—Anselm, bk. 2, c. 41.]:

It had long ago been decreed in the ancient ordinances [Note: [Col. 0685] The original adds “aforesaid”; Anselm omits it.] of the holy apostles and their successors—which the holy, universal, apostolic Church observes to this day—that councils ought not to be held nor a bishop condemned apart from the sentence [Note: [Col. 0685] The collected editions, except the first Basel edition, read “apart from the knowledge.”] of the Roman Pontiff [Note: [Col. 0685] The original reads “or.”], because they wished the holy Roman Church to be primate [Note: [Col. 0685] The collected editions read “to possess primacy.”] of all churches; and, just as the blessed Apostle Peter was first of all the apostles, so this Church, consecrated in his name by the Lord’s institution, is first and head of the rest. To it, as to a mother and summit, all greater ecclesiastical cases and judgments concerning bishops must have recourse and receive their final determination according to its sentence; and none of these things ought to be decided apart from the Roman Pontiff.

### Part II

Gratian. At times many bishops are found to have been condemned without consulting the Roman Pontiff, and others appointed in their places; the Church is recorded to have tolerated their condemnation and replacement by dispensation for the sake of peace.

[Col. 0686A] Therefore Pope John to Solomon, third and last King of the Britons [Note: [Col. 0685] Rather Nicholas I, A.D. 865, under whose name the letter is cited in the collected editions.—*Collectio tripartita*, pt. 1, tit. 62, c. 58.]:

### C. X. The Church tolerated for peace the deposition of certain bishops effected without the cognizance of the Roman Pontiff

For this is indeed the ordinance of God your father and the law of the Church your mother: you must not refuse to send all the bishops of your kingdom to the Archbishop of Tours, nor disdain to seek his judgment [Note: [Col. 0685] The Basel edition reads “his judgment also.”]. He is the metropolitan, and all bishops of your kingdom are his suffragans, as the records of my predecessors plainly show. Those predecessors sought to rebuke your predecessors with severe censure [Note: [Col. 0685] The original reads “with strong rebuke”; the collected editions read “to correct.”] because they had withdrawn those bishops from his jurisdiction; nor, it seems, are our own letters sent on this matter lacking.

And when, before the designated bishop of the Church of Tours and the full number of his colleagues—that is, twelve bishops—a council has been held and the expelled bishops have been duly examined, and it has appeared that they were canonically expelled [Note: [Col. 0685] The phrase “the bishops were expelled” was omitted through a typographical error in the Basel edition.], then, while they remain deposed, those consecrated in their places may indeed hold the honour of the episcopate. But if the expelled bishops are declared innocent, those substituted for them being removed, let the former recover their churches. For although my predecessors, the pontiffs, neither admitted nor approved the expulsion of those bishops who were driven from their churches, nor called legitimate bishops, while those bishops lived, the persons who had subsequently been substituted for them [Note: [Col. 0685] “Substituted afterward”: thus restored from several ancient and highly corrected manuscripts. Earlier it read: “may be substituted,” as in the collected editions, the first Basel edition, and the original as printed by Mansi, where it reads “have been substituted.”].

But if you disdain perhaps to send the aforesaid bishops to the Archbishop of Tours, take care to send two of the expelled bishops and two of those substituted, together with the legate of your Church, to the Apostolic See of blessed Peter; there, after due examination, it may appear who are the legitimate bishops, and they may not irregularly lose their churches. For I can determine nothing else in the present matter [Note: [Col. 0685] The collected editions read “For there is nothing else that can now be finally determined”; the original has this alternative wording.].

Since there is great controversy among the Britons over who is metropolitan, although no one remembers that you ever had a metropolitan church in your region, you will nevertheless be able easily to ascertain this if you wish, after almighty God has established peace between you and our beloved son Charles, the glorious king. But if you believe you should proceed so contentiously [Note: [Col. 0685] “More contentiously”: ibid.], strive to send [Col. 0687A] the matter to our apostolic see, so that by our judgment it may become clearer than light which church among you was formerly archiepiscopal, and thereafter, all ambiguity removed, your bishops may know without hesitation whom they ought to follow [Note: [Col. 0687] The Basel and first Venetian editions read “which one.”]. For the churches of God need not suffer any loss from division through the discord of kings, since, so far as lies within them, they ought to endeavour to preserve among themselves and toward all persons the peace which they preach.

### Part III

Gratian. In other cases, however, a bishop’s sentence will be void and must be reconsidered by a synod. Therefore Pope Felix I, Letter I, to Paternus [Note: [Col. 0687] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*, c. 51.—*Collectio tripartita*, pt. 1, tit. 24, c. 3.—Anselm, at the end of bk. 3, among Hadrian’s chapters.]:

### C. XI. An unjust condemnation is void and must be reconsidered by a synod

We judge the condemnation of bishops to be void and unjust [Note: [Col. 0687C] “And unjust”: this is the reading in the original, preceded by the word “otherwise.” In Julius’s *Decrees*, in the Fourth Council of Carthage—whence it is cited below, 11, q. 3, c. *Void*—in Hadrian’s chapters, and in Anselm, the reading is: “We judge an unjust condemnation of bishops to be void,” etc. This reading appears better suited to the heading of the chapter.], and therefore to be reconsidered by a synod, so that aid may be given in every case and in every respect by all to those oppressed.

Gratian. Pope Sixtus III attests, in his letter to the Eastern bishops, c. 3, that no one may disregard his own metropolitan and seek the judgment of others [Note: [Col. 0687] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Theodosian Code, bk. 9, tit. 1, c. 10.—*Collectio tripartita*, pt. 1, tit. 42, c. 2.—Burchard, bk. 1, c. 147. Anselm, bk. 3, c. 77 (76), and among Hadrian’s chapters at the end of bk. 3. Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 5, c. 260; pt. 6, c. 331.—*Polycarpus*, bk. 5, tit. 1.]:

### C. XII. Foreign tribunals are to be excluded

While preserving apostolic authority in all respects, we prohibit foreign tribunals by a general sanction, because it is unworthy that those who ought to have fellow-provincials and judges chosen by themselves should be judged by outsiders, unless an appeal has been made.

### C. XIII. On the same matter

Likewise Pope Anacletus, Letter I, c. 3 [Note: [Col. 0687] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—*Collectio tripartita*, pt. 1, tit. 2, c. 6.]:

[Col. 0687C] By apostolic authority we confirm the laws of the Church and exclude foreign tribunals [Note: [Col. 0687] The Basel edition adds “entirely.”]. Hence the Lord, making mention of Lot [Note: [Col. 0687] Genesis 19:9], speaks through Moses, saying: “He came in indeed,” they say [Note: [Col. 0687] “he says”: the same edition], “as an alien; is he to act as judge?” [Note: [Col. 0687] The collected editions read “concerning Lot.”]

[Col. 0688A]

### C. XIV. No one may seek the judgment of other provinces

Likewise Pope Innocent to Victricius, Bishop of Rouen, Letter II, c. 3 [Note: [Col. 0687] Written A.D. 404.—Anselm, bk. 2, c. 52.]:

Without prejudice, however [Note: [Col. 0687] The Basel edition omits “without prejudice.”], to the Roman Church, to which reverence and authority are due in all cases, no one may leave those bishops who, by God’s will, govern the churches in the same province [Note: [Col. 0687] The Hispanic Collection reads “in those same provinces.”] and flee to other provinces, or seek or submit to the judgment of bishops of other provinces [Note: [Col. 0687C] In the letter of Marcellus and in Innocent’s letter, in the Hispanic Collection, and in Anselm, the wording includes: “without prejudice, however, to the Roman Church, to which reverence must be preserved in all cases.” The final four-volume edition of the councils omits the words “without prejudice,” as well as, a little below, “or seek or submit to the judgment of bishops of other provinces”; these words are nevertheless found in the other indicated sources.]. If anyone presumes to do so, let him be removed from clerical office and judged by all as guilty of wrongs [Note: [Col. 0687] The collected editions read “guilty of the wrong.”].

Gratian. The reverence due to the Apostolic Church, and its authority, are to be understood when an appeal has been made to it, or when judges chosen by it are granted. Hence Pope Sixtus, when he said, “They ought to have judges who are fellow-provincials and chosen by themselves,” immediately adds: “unless an appeal has been made.”

## Chapter XV. Without a decree of the Apostolic See, we may not approach foreign judges. Likewise Pope Anacletus, Letter I, chapter 3

[Note: [Col. 0687] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore; cf. Council of Sardica, ch. 3.—Collection in Three Parts, part 1, treatise 2, ch. 7.—Anselm, book 3, ch. 21.]

Every province ought, both according to the laws of the Church and according to secular laws, to have its own judges, just and not unjust, and not foreign judges, unless the authority of this Apostolic See has so decreed.

[Note: [Col. 0687] The editions of the collections read *ecclesiasticas*, “ecclesiastical laws,” instead of *ecclesiae*, “of the Church.”]

## Chapter XVI. Judges of another province ought not to be approached except through an appeal. Likewise from the Roman Synod

[Note: [Col. 0687] Chapter 5. A chapter of Hadrian, taken from Letter I of Felix I (Pseudo-Isidore).—Cf. Novel 1, book 3, title 1, together with its interpretation.—Anselm, book 3, ch. 123. Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 218; part 6, ch. 331.]

No one ought to be brought from one province into another province or before the count's court, except upon referral to the judge *to whom an appeal has been made*, so that the plaintiff follows the defendant’s forum.

[Note: [Col. 0687] The editions of the collections, except the Basel edition, read *exire*, “to go out,” instead of *exhiberi*, “to be brought.”]

[Note: [Col. 0688C] *To whom an appeal has been made*: these words have been added from Hadrian, the synodical letter of Felix, and Ivo.]

And below:

[Note: [Col. 0687] Chapter 9. A chapter of Hadrian, taken from chapter 2 of the Council of Chalcedon.—Anselm, among the chapters of Hadrian at the end of book 3, ch. 8.]

§ 1. Matters belonging to each province are to be administered by the synod of that province, as is known to have been decreed at the Council of Nicaea.

[Note: [Col. 0688C] “Matters belonging to each province.” From here to the end these words are found only in the chapters of Hadrian.]

§ 2. Permission to accuse must not extend beyond the boundaries of a province. Every accusation is to be heard within the province and settled by fellow-provincials, unless the accused is a prelate.

[Note: [Col. 0687] Chapter 10. A chapter of Hadrian.—Cf. *Capitularies*, book 6, ch. 381.]

[Note: [Col. 0689] The Basel and earlier Lyon editions read “unless an appeal has been made to the Apostolic See.”]

[Note: [Col. 0689C] “Unless the accused is a prelate.” These words occur neither in the chapters of Hadrian nor in the older manuscripts of Gratian; in other copies they are replaced by: “unless an appeal has been made to the Apostolic See.”]

## Chapter XVII. On the same matter. Likewise Sixtus

[Note: [Col. 0689C] This chapter, cited as from Sixtus, is found in no letter of any pope bearing that name. In several old copies it reads only “Likewise,” apparently referring to the same Roman Synod as in the preceding chapter—that is, the synod contained in the chapters of Hadrian. Ivo, however, part 6, ch. 329, cites it from Felix I.]

[Note: [Col. 0689] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore; cf. the letter of Eleutherius to the provinces of Gaul and Letter I of Felix I.—Cf. the interpretation to Novel 1, book 3, title 1.—Anselm, book 3, ch. 27, and at the end of book 3 among the chapters of Hadrian, ch. 7.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chs. 318, 329.]

If any cleric has been accused of any crimes, his accuser is to pursue his actions in the province in which the accused person resides; nor should his accuser suppose that he may drag him elsewhere or farther away for judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0689] The editions of the collections read *pulsatus*, “the person accused,” instead of *accusatus*, “accused.”—The cited collections.]

[Note: [Col. 0689] Anselm and Ivo, part 6, ch. 329, read *exerat*, “bring forth,” instead of *exerceat*, “pursue.”]

[Note: [Col. 0689] The editions of the collections read *protrahendum*, “to be dragged forth,” instead of *pertrahendum*, “to be dragged away.”]

## Chapter XVIII. Where a crime is committed, there the case is to be examined. Likewise from the decree of Pope Hadrian

[Note: [Col. 0689] Chapter 52, Chapters of Hadrian.—Burchard, book 16, ch. 3, from the Council of Orange. Anselm, book 3, ch. 87. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, ch. 75; *Decree*, part 6, ch. 324.]

Let the person who alleges a crime know that he must prove it. The case should indeed be tried where the crime is committed.

[Note: [Col. 0689] Ivo reads *scribat*, “let him write,” instead of *sciat*, “let him know.”]

# QUESTION VII

[Col. 0689B]

# GRATIAN

**Part I. That a person whom a stain equal to or greater than the defendant’s infects cannot be a judge is proved by many authorities.**

For the holy Roman Synod says:

[Note: [Col. 0689D–0690C] The first part of this chapter, down to the word *cognitor*, is found in Letter II of Felix I, in which he reports a synod held by himself, recalling it at the beginning of the letter in these words: “For your support, brethren and our fellow bishops, we summoned more than seventy, with whom we decreed that the matters inserted below should be dealt with canonically.” The same part is found in the chapters of Hadrian, which—as noted above at the same Question 5, chapter *Accusations*—are sometimes cited under the name of the Roman Synod. The remainder of this chapter appears to be Gratian’s, though taken almost word for word from the law *When the praetor*, at the passage “For certain persons,” in the Digest, title *On Judgments*; similarly, many matters in the following chapter are collected from various laws of the Digest and Code. Therefore, in the older manuscripts all these passages through the chapter *He Who Is without Sin* occur together.]

[Note: [Col. 0689] Chapter 5, Chapters of Hadrian, taken from Letter II of Felix I (Pseudo-Isidore).—Cf. the interpretation to Paul’s *Sentences*, book 1, title 2.—Anselm, book 3, ch. 7 (123). Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, ch. 78; *Decree*, part 5, ch. 248; part 6, ch. 331. *Polycarpus*, book 5, title 1.]

## Chapter I. Infamous persons cannot be judges

An infamous person can be neither a procurator nor a *cognitor*.

Gratian. There are three grounds on which certain persons are prevented from becoming judges:

- nature, as in the case of a deaf-and-mute person, one who is permanently insane, and a minor, because they lack judgment;
- law, as in the case of one who has been removed from the Senate;
- custom, as in the case of women and slaves—not because they lack judgment, but because it has been established that they do not perform civil offices.

[Note: [Col. 0689] From fragment 12, book 5, title 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0689] The original and the Basel edition read *motus*, “removed,” instead of *amotus*, likewise “removed.”]

Nevertheless, if a slave, while believed to be free, rendered a judgment by delegation, then, even if he was afterward reduced to slavery, the judgment rendered by him retains the force of a matter adjudged.

## Chapter II. In the Digest, title *On Making Applications to Court*

[Note: [Col. 0690C–D] This chapter, as indicated in the preceding note, is not separated from the preceding chapter in older copies, and is a collection of various laws made by Gratian. But because most of the words are those of the authors themselves, and because it is distinguished as a separate chapter in the printed editions, it has been printed in the same type as the other chapters attributed to authors.]

Infamous persons cannot be procurators or advocates in causes. There are three classes of those who are forbidden to make applications to court.

[Note: [Col. 0689] From fragment 1, book 3, title 1, with its wording adapted differently.]

§ 1. To make an application is to set forth one’s own claim or that of one’s friend in court before the person who presides over jurisdiction, or to oppose another’s claim.

§ 2. As we have said, there are three classes of those who may not make applications. Some are forbidden altogether to do so, either because of age, as those under seventeen years, or because of incapacity, as a deaf person who hears nothing at all. Others are forbidden to apply on behalf of others, either because of sex, as women; because of incapacity, as those deprived of sight in both eyes; or because of the stigma of disgrace, as those who have suffered sexual acts upon their bodies in the female role—unless perhaps they can prove that they were violated by force of robbers or enemies.

Likewise, those who have been condemned in a public trial for a capital crime or for malicious prosecution, and those who hired out their services to fight beasts in the arena, are forbidden to apply for others.

[Note: [Col. 0689] “For malicious prosecution” is absent from the Strasbourg edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0689] The editions of the collections read *publici judicii*, “of a public trial,” instead of *publico judicio*, “in a public trial.”]

These persons are permitted to plead for themselves but are forbidden to apply for others, unless perhaps they administer the guardianship of minors or the curatorship of young persons, not because they sought it but because it was necessary. For they are permitted to apply on behalf of those whose care they undertake.

[Note: [Col. 0689] The Basel edition reads *alio*, “for another,” instead of *aliis*, “for others.”]

All others who are marked as infamous cannot apply except for themselves and certain specified persons, unless they have received restoration in full.

§ 3. They are, however, permitted to apply on behalf of a parent; a patron or patroness; the children and parents of a patron or patroness; their own children; brothers and sisters; a *wife*; father-in-law; mother-in-law; son-in-law; daughter-in-law; stepfather; stepmother; stepson; stepdaughter; a male or female ward; an insane man or woman; a foolish man or woman; a mute person; a deaf person; a spendthrift; and a young person.

[Note: [Col. 0691] The editions of the collections add “also their own” to “children.”]

[Note: [Col. 0691] The Strasbourg, Nuremberg, and Venetian I editions add “brothers and parents of the patron and patroness.”]

[Note: [Col. 0691] The Basel edition reads *fratre, sorore*, “a brother, a sister,” instead of *fratribus et sororibus*, “brothers and sisters.”]

[Note: [Col. 0691] From fragments 2 and 3 of the same title.]

§ 4. Likewise, they may apply on behalf of those for whom curators are usually appointed because of infirmity and those who cannot attend to their affairs because of some lasting disease.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Fragments 4 and 5 of the same title.]

§ 5. All who discharge an office not voluntarily but from necessity may apply without violating the *edict*, even if they are among those permitted to apply only for *themselves*.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Fragment 6 of the same title.]

§ 6. By relationships by marriage we must understand not former relationships but present ones.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Fragment 13 of the same title.]

§ 7. Under the designations daughter-in-law, son-in-law, father-in-law, and mother-in-law are also included the more remote relations to whose names the prefix *pro-* is customarily added.

[Note: [Col. 0691] The Basel edition reads *accidere*, “to occur,” instead of *accedere*, “to be added.”]

## Part II

§ 8. Those persons are also excluded from the profession of advocates—as is found in book II of the Code, title *On Making Applications to Court*—who, under the name of fees, are found to demand for themselves from the very cases they have undertaken to defend a fixed share of the proceeds, with grave injury to and spoliation of the litigant.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Chapter 5, Code, book 2, title 6.]

[Note: [Col. 0691] *Honorariorum*: “of fees”; the Strasbourg edition reads *honoratorum*, “of the honored.”]

[Note: [Col. 0691] *Certae partis*: “of a fixed share”; the Basel edition reads *certi temporis*, “of a fixed time.”]

[Note: [Col. 0691] The Basel edition reads *deprecatione*, “entreaty,” instead of *depraedatione*, “spoliation.”]

§ 9. Likewise, if anyone is so insolent as to think that litigation should be conducted not by reason but by insults, let him suffer diminution of his reputation.

[Note: [Col. 0691] The editions of the collections, except the Basel and Lyon II and III editions, add *verbis*, “words,” after “insults.”]

[Note: [Col. 0691] The original and the editions of the collections read *patietur*, “he will suffer,” instead of *patiatur*, “let him suffer.”]

§ 10. Moreover, an advocate is not permitted to enter into any contract or make any agreement with the litigant whom he receives under his personal protection, nor deliberately to prolong a dispute.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Chapter 6, § 2, of the same title.]

§ 11. At Rome, even persons of rank who have chosen this profession may plead for as long as they wish, provided that this opportunity is not seized for shameful profit and disgraceful gain. For if they are captivated by gain and money, they will be numbered, as degenerate persons, among the lowest.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Chapter 6, § 5, of the same title.]

[Note: [Col. 0691] The Basel and Venetian I editions read *stipendium deforme*, “a disgraceful fee,” instead of *stipemque deformem*, “and disgraceful gain.”]

[Note: [Col. 0691] The Basel edition adds “abject and” before “degenerate.”]

§ 12. But if in a single courtroom there are only two, or more, advocates whose reputation is more distinguished than that of the rest, it is the duty of the judge to ensure an equal distribution of advocates and to equalize the assistance of each among the parties.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Chapter 7 of the same title.]

[Note: [Col. 0691] The Strasbourg, Nuremberg, and Venetian II editions read *etenim aequetur*, “and indeed let it be equalized,” instead of *et exaequetur*, “and let it be equalized.”]

[Note: [Col. 0691] The editions of the collections read *pro partibus*, “for the parties,” instead of *partibus*, “among the parties.”]

§ 13. If anyone, after being warned by a judge, refuses advocacy to any party on an excuse that cannot be proved, he shall be barred from the forum; and he should know that permission to act will never be restored to him.

[Note: [Col. 0691] The editions of the collections read *agendi*, “of acting,” instead of *ad agendum*, “to act.”]

§ 14. But if any litigant is discovered to have dealt privately with several advocates and, *by such fraud*, to have deprived his opponent of an equal opportunity for defense, he will undoubtedly show that he is fostering an unjust suit and will find that he has evaded judicial authority.

[Note: [Col. 0691] The Basel edition reads *ostendit*, “he shows,” instead of *ostendet*, “he will show.”]

§ 15. Likewise, although those who have conducted the case of the treasury are forbidden to provide advocacy against the treasury, they may nevertheless now provide advocacy for private persons even against the treasury, provided that they decline to undertake the case which they handled while they were advocates of the treasury.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Chapter 1, Code, book 2, title 9.]

§ 16. Likewise, if you have pleaded a case against the father of a ward, you are not forbidden, if appointed guardian or curator, to defend the same case.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Fragment 10, Digest, book 3, title 1.]

§ 17. *Cognitores* are understood to act by office, not by personal choice. For it makes no difference whether the person who undertakes arbitration is of unimpaired reputation or infamous.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Cf. fragment 3, Digest, book 4, title 8.]

[Note: [Col. 0691] Fragment 7 of the same title.]

[Note: [Col. 0691D–0692D] “For it makes no difference.” The words of the law from which Gratian took this passage and the following sentence, “A slave cannot be an arbitrator,” are these: “Paedius in book nine and Pomponius in book thirty-three write that it makes little difference whether an arbitrator is freeborn or a freedman, of unimpaired reputation or infamous. Labeo writes in book eleven that an arbitration agreement cannot be made with a slave; and this is correct.”]

[Note: [Col. 0691] *Is*: “he”; the editions of the collections, except the Lyon II and III editions, read *eum*, “him.”]

§ 18. A son may also be an arbitrator in a matter involving his father. For most jurists hold that he may also be a judge.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Fragment 6 of the same title.]

§ 19. But if anyone is a judge, he is forbidden by the *Julian law* to undertake arbitration in the matter in which he is judge, or to order an arbitration agreement to be made with himself; and if he has rendered judgment, no action to recover the penalty is to be granted. A slave cannot be an arbitrator; a freedman can.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Fragment 9, § 2, of the same title.]

[Note: [Col. 0691] Fragment 9, opening section, of the same title.]

§ 20. Infamy is imposed in many ways. Sometimes it is incurred by the kind of offense declared in a judgment, as when the judge pronounces: “You have committed an injury; you have plundered an inheritance; you have brought a malicious accusation.”

[Note: [Col. 0691] Cf. chapters 5 and 12, Code, book 2, title 12.]

Sometimes it results from the kind of penalty, as with those who are condemned to public works: they retain their former status but remain subject to the harm of infamy even after the prescribed period has been completed.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Chapter 6, Code, same title.]

Sometimes it results from both the kind of penalty and the offense declared in the judgment, as when, after a man has been beaten with rods, the herald says: “You have acted as a malicious accuser” (*ἐσυκοφάντησας*), that is, “You have brought a malicious accusation.”

[Note: [Col. 0691] Chapters 16 and 17 of the same title.]

[Note: [Col. 0691] The Lyon II and III editions read *συκοφαντεῖς*, “you make a malicious accusation,” that is, “you accuse maliciously.” The remaining editions read *sycophantis*, glossed “a malicious accuser.”]

Sometimes it results from the very nature of the act: for example, those who practice improper moneylending and illegally exact compound interest; a woman who contracts marriage during the period in which it is customary to mourn her husband; and the man who knowingly marries her.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Chapter 20 of the same title.]

[Note: [Col. 0691] Chapter 15 of the same title.]

Gratian. Pope Felix attests the same, in the same words.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Above, Question 5, chapter 11.]

§ 1. Likewise, in the Gospel, the person who carries a beam in his own eye is shown unable to remove a speck from his brother’s eye.

[Note: [Col. 0691] Matthew 7:5.]

§ 2. Likewise David says in the Book of Psalms:

[Note: [Col. 0691] Psalm 49:16.]

“But God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my righteous ordinances and take up my covenant?” etc.

§ 3. Likewise Gregory says:

[Note: [Col. 0693] Homily 12 on the Gospels.]

“When a person’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching also is held in contempt.”

## Chapter III. Those who punish the faults of others should strive first to correct their own. Likewise Gregory, *Morals*, book XIV, on Job, chapter 15

## Part III

“Let him among you who is without sin cast the first stone at her.”

[Note: [Col. 0693] John 8:7.]

[Note: [Col. 0693] The Basel edition reads *prius*, “first,” instead of *primus*, “the first.”]

They were going to punish the sins of others and had left their own behind. They are therefore called back inwardly to their conscience, so that they may first correct their own faults and then rebuke those of others.

[Note: [Col. 0693] The editions of the collections read *revocentur*, “let them be called back,” instead of *revocantur*, “they are called back.”]

Thus, when the tribe of Benjamin had been overwhelmed by a crime of the flesh, all Israel assembled to avenge the wrong; yet once and again Israel itself was defeated in the contest of war.

[Note: [Col. 0693] Judges 20.]

For, having consulted the Lord whether it should go to exact vengeance, it was commanded that it should go. It proceeded in obedience to the command of the divine voice and was defeated once and a second time; only then, striking the sinful tribe severely, did it almost utterly destroy it.

[Note: [Col. 0693] The original reads *autem*, “but,” instead of *enim*, “for.”]

[Note: [Col. 0693] *Ut*, “that,” is lacking in the original.]

[Note: [Col. 0693] The original reads *cecidit*, “fell,” instead of *perdidit*, “lost” or “was defeated.”]

What does this mean—that it is inflamed to avenge wickedness and yet is itself first overthrown—except that those through whom the faults of others are to be struck must first themselves be cleansed, so that those who hasten to correct the faults of others may come to inflict punishment already purified?

[Note: [Col. 0693] “This” is added in the editions of the collections, except the Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0693] The editions of the collections read *ultione*, “in vengeance,” instead of *ultionem*, “vengeance.”]

[Note: [Col. 0693] “Themselves” is absent from the Basel edition; the remaining editions read *iste*, “that person,” instead of *ipse*, “he himself.”]

[Note: [Col. 0693] The Basel edition reads *qui et*, “who also,” instead of *qui*, “who.”]

## Chapter IV. Let him judge another’s life who has nothing in himself to punish. Likewise Ambrose on “Blessed are the undefiled,” Sermon XX, at the verse “Your mercies, O Lord”

[Note: [Col. 0693] From Ambrose’s commentary on Psalm 118.—Anselm, book 3, ch. 34.]

Let him judge another’s error who has nothing in himself that he must condemn. Let him judge who does not do the same things that he thinks should be punished in another, lest, while judging another, he himself pronounce sentence upon himself. Let him judge who is led to pronounce judgment by no hatred, no offense, and no fickleness.

[Note: [Col. 0693] The original reads *novitate*, “novelty,” instead of *levitate*, “fickleness.”]

And a little later:

§ 1. A good judge does nothing according to his own discretion or the design of his private will, but pronounces according to laws and rights; he obeys the established rules of law, does not indulge his own will, brings from home nothing prepared or premeditated, but judges as he hears and determines according to the nature of the *matter in dispute*. He obeys the laws and does not oppose them; he examines the merits of the case and does not alter them. Learn, judges of the world, what disposition, what sobriety, and what integrity you ought to maintain in judging.

[Note: [Col. 0693] The Basel edition reads *propriae*, “of his own,” instead of *domesticae*, “private” or “domestic.”]

[Note: [Col. 0693] The original and Anselm read *scitis*, “rules,” instead of *statutis*, “established rules”; the Basel edition reads *si quis scitis*, “if anyone by the rules.”]

[Note: [Col. 0693] The editions of the collections read *de domo*, “from home,” instead of *domo*, with the same sense.]

[Note: [Col. 0693] *Negotii*, “of the matter in dispute,” is absent from Anselm.]

And shortly afterward:

§ 2. He who judges ought not to obey his own will, but to maintain what belongs to the laws.

[Note: [Col. 0693] The Basel edition reads *legis*, “of the law,” instead of *legum*, “of the laws.”]

And a little later:

§ 3. In judging, let the preservation of truth matter more to the heart than obedience to one’s will.

[Note: [Col. 0693] The editions of the collections read *est*, “is,” instead of *sit*, “let it be.”]

## Chapter V. One burdened with crimes cannot judge. Likewise Gregory, Preface to Job, chapter 3, otherwise 6

[Note: [Col. 0693] Collection in Three Parts, part 1, treatise 55, chs. 41–43.]

A person placed in grave sins, while weighed down by his own, does not wash away those of others.

§ 1. For we all clearly know that, when the person sent to intercede is displeasing, the mind of the offended party is without doubt provoked to worse things.

[Note: [Col. 0693] From the *Pastoral Rule*, part 1, ch. 10.—Cf. Distinction 49, opening section.]

[Note: [Col. 0693] The editions of the collections read “It is clear to all” instead of “We all clearly know.”]

§ 2. For it is written: “The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable to God, but the vows of the righteous are pleasing.”

[Note: [Col. 0693] From the letter to Reccared, Letter 122, written A.D. 599, book 9, Maurist edition.—Cf. Causa 14, Question 5, ch. 11.]

[Note: [Col. 0693] Proverbs 15:8.]

For in the judgment of almighty God, attention is given not to what is offered, but by whom it is offered.

[Note: [Col. 0693] The original adds *datur*, “is given.”]

§ 3. Hence it is written: “The Lord looked upon Abel and upon his offerings, but upon Cain and his offerings he did not look.”

[Note: [Col. 0693] Genesis 4:4–5.]

For, when Scripture was about to say that the Lord looked upon the offerings, it carefully first stated that he looked upon Abel. From this it is clearly shown that it was not the offerer because of the offerings, but the offerings because of the offerer, that found acceptance.

§ 4. For the Most High does not approve the gifts of the unrighteous; he does not look upon their offerings, nor will he be propitiated for sins by the multitude of their sacrifices.

[Note: [Col. 0693] “Gifts.” These words are not found there in Blessed Gregory; nevertheless, they occur in Ecclesiasticus 34 and are repeated below, Causa 14, Question 5, chapter *It Is Written*.]

[Note: [Col. 0693] Ecclesiasticus 34:23.]

[Note: [Col. 0693] The editions of the collections, except the Basel edition, read *oblationibus*, “upon their offerings,” instead of *oblationes*, “offerings.”]

§ 5. Likewise: “The Lord is far from the wicked, but he will hear the prayers of the righteous.”

[Note: [Col. 0693] Proverbs 15:8.]

## Chapter VI. We ought first to correct ourselves, and then our neighbours. Likewise Bede on John, chapter 8, concerning the judgment of the adulterous woman

When the Lord was asked to judge the sinful woman, he did not immediately give judgment. Rather, first bending down, he wrote with his finger upon the ground, as though judging only after being earnestly entreated. By this symbolic act he instructs us that, whenever we see any faults of our neighbours, we should not judge them by rebuking them before humbly returning to our own conscience, diligently engraving it with the finger of discernment, and carefully examining what in it pleases the Creator and what displeases him, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Brothers, if a person is overtaken in any offense,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0693] In place of “as though judging only after being earnestly entreated,” the editions of the collections read “as though he judges whatever is asked.”]

[Note: [Col. 0693] The Basel edition adds “faults.”]

[Note: [Col. 0693] The Strasbourg edition reads *exsculpemus*, “we shall engrave”; the remaining editions, except the Lyon II and III editions, read *exculpemus*, “let us scrutinize,” instead of *exculpamus*, “we scrutinize.”]

[Note: [Col. 0693] Galatians 6:1.]

And below:

§ 1. “Let him among you who is without sin”: that is, first fulfil the righteousness of the law yourselves, and then, innocent in hands *and pure in heart*, come together to stone the guilty woman.

[Note: [Col. 0693] John 8:7.]

## Chapter VII. A priest must first cleanse his own sins, and then those of others. Likewise Augustine to a certain Count

[Note: [Col. 0695C–D] In an old edition of the letters of Blessed Augustine there is a very long letter to Count Julian; in more recent editions of all his works it appears in volume IV under the title *On Salutary Instructions*, chapter 52 of which work is this chapter.]

[Note: [Col. 0695] From the book *On Salutary Instructions*, which learned scholars consider spurious.—Anselm, book 7, ch. 101.]

A priest, like a wise and perfect physician, should first know how to cure his own sins, and afterward cleanse and heal the wounds of others, and not make them public.

[Note: [Col. 0695] The Strasbourg, Venetian I, and Nuremberg editions read *delere*, “to destroy”; the remaining editions read *diluere*, “to wash away,” instead of *curare*, “to cure.”]

Gratian. Likewise, in the Gospel salt that has lost its savor is said to be good for nothing except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by people. From all these things it is understood that a criminal person cannot be judge of another’s crime, and that he condemns himself when he pronounces sentence upon another’s crime.

[Note: [Col. 0695] Matthew 5:14.]

§ 1. But an objection is raised. Saul, though rejected by the Lord, judged the people of God, and the whole people sought his judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0695] 1 Samuel 15.]

Likewise David, though an adulterer and murderer, when questioned by the prophet passed sentence upon the rich man who seized the poor man’s sheep, saying: “This man deserves death.”

[Note: [Col. 0695] 2 Samuel 12.]

Likewise Solomon, although through love of women he worshiped the gods of the nations, was nevertheless approached by all the people of Israel for judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0695] 1 Kings 11.]

Ahab also, though he worshiped Baal, judged the ten tribes.

[Note: [Col. 0695] 1 Kings 16.]

Many others are found in both the Old and the New Testament whose life was blameworthy, but whose judgment was nevertheless upheld because it proceeded from their office with the integrity of judicial order preserved. Therefore the Lord also says in the Gospel: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0695] Matthew 23:2.]

Hence it is clear that evil pastors, when by a sentence of just examination they punish the crimes of others, harm themselves because they strive to correct others’ faults without offering the example of their own amendment; but they benefit their subjects if the latter, corrected by their rebuke or restrained by their sentence, learn to change their lives for the better. Therefore, while such pastors are tolerated by the Church, it is not permissible to evade their judgment.

# QUESTION VIII

# GRATIAN

That a bishop ought not to be heard or judged by one person alone is attested by Pope Zephyrinus in Letter I to the bishops of Sicily, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0695] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore.—Cf. *Ancient Ecclesiastical Statutes*, ch. 53; Council of Paris, held A.D. 829; and Theodosian Code, book 4, title 1.—Anselm, book 3, ch. 38 (41). Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 245.]

## Chapter I. A bishop is not to be heard and judged except by several persons

Let accusers of bishops be wholly free from suspicion, because the Lord willed his pillars to stand firm, not to be shaken by just anyone.

§ 1. Let no sentence rendered against any of them by one who is not his proper judge bind him, because even secular laws command that same rule to be observed:

[Note: [Col. 0695D] From here through the word “judges,” these words are found neither in Zephyrinus’s letter nor in the older manuscripts of Gratian.]

Thus in the Code, book VII, title *On the Judgments and Interlocutory Decisions of All Judges*, the next-to-last law:

§ 2. Whoever observes a person’s decision when bringing an action should not disdain to have that same person as judge against himself in the same matter.

§ 3. Any bishop who is accused shall, if necessary, choose twelve judges by whom his case may be justly judged. He is not to be heard, excommunicated, or judged before they have been chosen by himself and, after he has first been canonically summoned to the assembly of his own bishops, his case has been justly heard and reasonably determined by them.

[Note: [Col. 0695] Cf. Causa 5, Question 4, ch. 2.—Cf. Gregory the Great, Letters 53 and 54, book 5, Maurist edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0695] The editions of the collections read *vocatus*, “having been summoned,” instead of *vocato*, “after he has been summoned.”]

The final disposition of his case is to be referred to the Apostolic See, so that it may be concluded there. Nor is it to be concluded *until it is supported by that authority, as was formerly established by the apostles or their successors*.

[Note: [Col. 0695] The words enclosed in asterisks are absent from Anselm. In the Strasbourg and Venetian II editions the passage reads: “so that it may be concluded there, unless he has been absent through contumacy. But no absent person is to be judged, because,” etc.]

And a little above:

§ 4. No absent person is to be judged, unless he has been absent through contumacy, because both divine and human laws prohibit this.

[Note: [Col. 0695] Cf. the same Question 9, ch. 13.]

[Note: [Col. 0696C] “Unless he has been absent through contumacy.” These words are absent from most manuscripts, from the letter itself, and from Anselm and Ivo. Below, in the same Question 9, chapter *The Absent Person*, they occur as Gratian’s words.]

Likewise Bishop Felix said in the Second Council of Carthage, chapter 10:

[Note: [Col. 0695] Held A.D. 390; chapter 12 in Dionysius.—Burchard, book 1, ch. 149. Anselm, book 3, ch. 46 (121). Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 262.]

## Chapter II. By how many bishops a bishop who has incurred an accusation is to be heard

I propose, according to the statutes of the ancient councils, that if any bishop—which we do not wish—incurs some accusation, and if the necessity is so great that he cannot assemble many bishops, then, lest he remain under accusation, he should be heard by twelve bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0695] The editions of the collections read *inciderit*, “has fallen into,” instead of *incurrerit*, “has incurred.”]

[Note: [Col. 0695] The editions of the collections read *si*, “if,” instead of *et*, “and.”]

[Note: [Col. 0695] The editions of the collections add “bishops” after “many.”]

[Note: [Col. 0695] The editions of the collections read *maneat*, “remain,” instead of *remaneat*, likewise “remain.”]

[Note: [Col. 0696D] “By twelve bishops.” What is cited here from chapter 10 of the Second Council of Carthage is repeated below at Causa 15, Question 5, chapter *Felix*; the textual variation will be noted there.]

# QUESTION IX

# GRATIAN

**Part I. That accusers and witnesses cannot present an accusation or testimony against an absent person is clear from many authorities.**

For Pope Telesphorus says in his only letter:

[Note: [Col. 0697] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore, taken from the interpretation of the Theodosian Code, book 11, title 39, ch. 9.—Anselm, book 3, ch. 12.]

## Chapter I. Unless the defendant is present, the accuser is not to be heard

We decree that no credence at all is to be given to an accuser who presents a case while his opponent is absent, before the just hearing of both parties.

## Chapter II. It is unlawful to pronounce sentence in the absence of one’s opponent. Likewise Pope Eleutherius in his letter to the bishops of Gaul

[Note: [Col. 0697] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore; cf. *Ancient Ecclesiastical Statutes*, ch. 53.—Chapters of Hadrian, ch. 53. Burchard, book 16, ch. 14. Anselm, book 3, ch. 27. Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, ch. 319.—Cf. *Capitularies*, book 7, ch. 219.]

Let judges of the Church take care not to pronounce sentence when the person whose case is being examined is absent, because it will be invalid; indeed, they themselves will have to answer for the matter before the synod as for a deed committed. But neither the malicious accusation nor the voice of a traitor is to be heard.

## Chapter III. When the defendant is absent, the accuser is not to be heard. Likewise Pope Calixtus, Letter II to the bishops of Gaul

[Note: [Col. 0697] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore; cf. the interpretation of the Theodosian Code, book 9, title 1, ch. 15, and *Ancient Ecclesiastical Statutes*, ch. 53.—Burchard, book 1, ch. 171. Anselm, book 3, ch. 55. Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, ch. 289.—Cf. Causa 2, Question 8, ch. 1.]

When the person whom someone wishes to accuse is absent, no credence is to be given to the accuser, because without writing it is difficult, but by writing he is never to be received. For no one can *accuse or* be accused by a written document; rather, each person must pursue his accusation in his own voice and in the presence of the person whom he wishes to accuse.

[Note: [Col. 0697] The editions of the collections, except the earlier Lyon II and III editions, read *quicquam*, “anything,” instead of *quispiam*, “someone.”]

[Note: [Col. 0697] The Strasbourg and Basel editions read *qui*, “who,” instead of *quia*, “because.”]

[Note: [Col. 0697] “Is” is added in the editions of the collections, except the Strasbourg and Basel editions.]

## Chapter IV. Everything done against absent persons is to be wholly annulled. Likewise Pope Cornelius to Rufus, Letter II, chapter 2

[Note: [Col. 0697] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore, taken from the Council of Chalcedon, session 10.—Anselm, book 3, ch. 62 (61).]

Everything done or judged against absent persons, in every matter or place, is to be wholly annulled, because no one adjudges an absent person liable, nor does any law condemn one.

[Note: [Col. 0697] The Basel edition reads *in*, “against” or “in the case of,” instead of *adversus*, “against.”]

## Chapter V. A person is not to be judged unless he is personally accused or convicted. Likewise Pope Marcellus to Maxentius, Letter II

[Note: [Col. 0697] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore, drawn from Acts 25:16.—Collection in Three Parts, part 1, treatise 29, sole chapter.]

No one ought to be judged or condemned before he has legitimate accusers present and receives an opportunity to defend himself and clear himself of the accusations.

[Note: [Col. 0697] The Strasbourg, Nuremberg, and Venetian II editions read *judicare*, “to judge,” instead of *judicari*, “to be judged.”]

## Chapter VI. On the same matter. Likewise Damasus to Archbishop Stephen, Letter III, chapter 8

[Note: [Col. 0697] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore, taken from Acts 25:16.—Anselm, book 2, ch. 39. Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, ch. 347.]

It is likewise established in the decrees of the holy Fathers that it is not canonical to judge or condemn any priest before he has present accusers who have been canonically examined and receives an opportunity to defend himself—that is, ecclesiastical time to clear himself of the accusations.

## Chapter VII. *Palea*. The same Damasus, continuing in the same place

[Note: [Col. 0697] Anselm and Ivo, in the same place.]

No accusation for an initial examination is to be made outside one’s own province without an apostolic command, to which reverence must be preserved in all cases, because the ancient rule of the Fathers teaches this, and imperial enactments agree with it as well.

[Note: [Col. 0697C–0698C] “One’s own.” This reading has been corrected from the letter itself, Anselm, and Ivo. Previously the text read: “Nor is a province to be made outside one’s own fatherland” [the editions of the collections read “province”]. Some additional material has also been added from the letter.]

[Note: [Col. 0697] Cf. Innocent I, Letter 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0697] “And” is absent from the editions of the collections, except the Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0697] Anselm, Ivo, the editions of the collections, and Böhmer read *imperialia*, “imperial enactments,” instead of *imperialiter*, “imperially.”]

“The examination of crimes,” they say, “must take place where the crime was committed. For elsewhere a person charged with crimes is forbidden to be heard.”

[Note: [Col. 0697] From the interpretation of the Theodosian Code, book 9, title 1, final chapter.]

And elsewhere *it is prescribed in the canons*:

[Note: [Col. 0697] From the letter of the Africans to Pope Celestine.]

“Whatever matters arise in their own places are to be concluded in those places,” *and other matters of this kind and similar matters*, while apostolic authority is preserved in all things, *so that nothing in these matters is decided before it is known to please that authority by which all ought to be supported*.

[Note: [Col. 0697] The editions of the collections read *agitanda*, “to be examined,” instead of *agenda*, “to be conducted.”]

[Note: [Col. 0697] The Nuremberg and Lyon I editions read *absorpta*, “absorbed,” and the remaining editions, except the Lyon II and III editions, read *absorta*, likewise “absorbed,” instead of *orta*, “arisen”; the conjectured reading is *oborta*, “arisen.”]

## Chapter VIII. On the same matter. Likewise the same Damasus to the bishops of Italy, Letter VI

[Note: [Col. 0697] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore, composed from Acts 25:16.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, ch. 348.]

Whoever chooses to accuse another must accuse in person and not through another, with a formal written accusation first submitted. Nor is anyone ever to be judged before he has legitimate accusers present and receives an opportunity to defend himself and clear himself of the accusations.

## Chapter IX. On the same matter. Likewise from the Sixth Council of Toledo, chapter 11

[Note: [Col. 0697] Held A.D. 639.—Burchard, book 16, ch. 5, from the decrees of Pope Felix.]

It is fitting that the life of an innocent person should not be stained by any destructive action of accusers. Therefore, if anyone is accused by anyone else, the accused person is not to be handed over to punishment before the accuser is produced and the judgment of the laws and canons is sought. If the accuser is found to be a person unworthy to accuse, the accused person is not to be judged on that accusation, *unless a case concerning a capital charge against the royal majesty is at issue*.

[Note: [Col. 0697] The Spanish Collection reads *innocentum … non maculetur pernicie accusantum*, “the lives of the innocent should not be stained by the ruinous action of accusers.”]

[Note: [Col. 0697] Isidore Mercator and the Spanish Collection read *accusatoris*, “of the accuser,” instead of *accusatorum*, “of accusers.”]

[Note: [Col. 0697] Burchard reads *adeo*, “to such an extent,” instead of *ideo*, “therefore.”]

[Note: [Col. 0697] The Spanish Collection, Isidore Mercator, Burchard, and the Basel edition read *quisquis*, “whoever,” instead of *quis*, “anyone.”]

[Note: [Col. 0697] The Spanish Collection reads: “the judgments of the laws and canons are to be sought, so that.”]

[Note: [Col. 0698C] “Unless” and the clause following it have been added from the original.]

## Chapter X. Sentence is to be passed against one who neglects to be present in his own case. Likewise Pope Boniface to the Gauls, Letter II

[Note: [Col. 0697] Written A.D. 419.—Burchard, book 1, ch. 161. Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 271; part 6, ch. 338.]

We decree that your trial ought to take place within the province, and that a synod be assembled before the Kalends of November, so that, if he wishes to attend and is confident, he may answer the charges in person; but if he neglects to attend, he shall not gain a postponement of judgment on account of his absence. For it is clear that one confesses to the crime who, when granted and so often assigned an opportunity of clearing himself by trial, does not use it. For it makes no difference whether not all that has been alleged is proved in the hearing at hand, since his repeatedly contrived absence itself likewise amounts to a confession.

[Note: [Col. 0697] “We have decreed” (*decrevimus*): original—cited collections. “Your” (*vestrum*): original—Burchard IV, p. 5. [Col. 0699D] “Not all”: the original, the other collectors, and one very ancient Gratian manuscript read “all”; but, because the same sense results and a gloss is present, it has not been changed. [Col. 0699] “Contrived absence”: Lyons II reads “is contrived”; the remaining collected editions read “from contrived [absence].”]

### C. XI. Persons absent can neither be accused nor judged.

Likewise, Pope Felix to the bishops of Gaul, Epistle II. [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. *Pauli Sententiae*, book 5, title 5, §6, together with the interpretation.—Chapter of Hadrian, c. 4. Anselm, at the end of book 3. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, c. 54; *Decretum*, part 5, c. 248, part 6, c. 331.]

When the opposing party is absent, the accuser is not to be heard; nor shall a judgment pronounced by a judge while the other party is absent have any force.

[Col. 0699B]

### C. XII. A definitive sentence is not to be pronounced while the other party is absent.

Likewise, Pope Nicholas to Gallio, Archbishop of Siena. [Note: An uncertain chapter.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 62, c. 42.—Similar material in the first part occurs in Nicholas’s Epistle 32, in Mansi.]

Truly, he is not a just mediator who does not fear to decide disputes arising between two parties when one litigant is present and the other absent. These matters having been stated beforehand, we wish and, by apostolic authority, admonish that, if the priest in question wishes to approach the Apostolic See after his excommunication, no one shall presume to impede his journey.

### C. XIII. Sentence is not to be pronounced against an absentee.

Likewise, Pope Zephyrinus to the bishops of Sicily, Epistle I. [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*, c. 53.—Cf. above, question 6, c. 1.]

No one who is absent is to be judged, for both divine and human laws prohibit this.

Gratian. Unless he is absent through contumacy. For contumacy causes him to be treated as present.

### C. XIV. On the same matter.

Likewise, Pope Nicholas to Gallio, Archbishop of Siena. [Note: From the epistle to Wenilo, Bishop of Siena, written A.D. 862.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 62, c. 49.]

You report that Bishop Hermann has frequently been accused concerning certain matters. Since the person on his side is absent, we certainly cannot believe one party to the detriment of the other. Moreover, you have not yet stated what the offenses there were, nor have you clearly shown whether that same bishop was of sound mind or not when he committed those offenses. We judge it better to attribute any infirmity in the meantime to the penalty of sin than to sin itself; for he should rather be cared for and pitied than punished or struck in any manner whatsoever.

[Note: “showing”: Basel edition.—“more holy”: ibid.—“also”: collected editions.]

### C. XV. Witnesses are not to give testimony except about matters which they know personally and truthfully.

Likewise, Pope Calixtus to the bishops of Gaul, Epistle II. [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Burchard, book 1, c. 171. Anselm, book 3, c. 55. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, c. 93; *Decretum*, part 5, c. 289.]

Witnesses are not to offer testimony through any written document, but, being present, are truthfully to state testimony concerning the matters which they know and have seen. Nor are they to testify concerning other causes or business, except those matters known to have been transacted in their presence.

[Note: “offer”: collected editions except the first Basel edition.—“state”: collected editions.—“not known”: Basel edition.]

**Second Part. Gratian.** Those who heard something may also testify in a civil case, if they were summoned for that purpose, as is read in the *Authentics*, collection VII, title “Concerning Witnesses”:

§1. “If a debt has been put in writing, and proof of payment is offered by the litigants through witnesses without written documentation, we decree that it is admissible before the judge, provided that the witnesses were engaged for this very purpose: to give testimony for establishing payment, or for recalling a payment already made, and for the acknowledgment of the person who received the money. But we judge that idle testimony given incidentally and in passing—for example, if someone, arriving for another task, heard a person say that he had received gold from someone, or that he owed something to someone—has no validity whatever.”

**Third Part.**

§2. It is likewise necessary that they have seen the matter. But if one person has seen it at one time and another at another time, the difference in time prevents their testimony from being admitted.

Therefore Pope Leo says: [Note: An uncertain chapter, perhaps to be referred to Leo III.]

### C. XVI. Persons not proved to have been present at the affair at the same time are not to be admitted as witnesses.

Witnesses who testify anything maliciously are likewise to be punished; nor are the voices of persons to be admitted as though they were several witnesses, when difference of time prevented them from having been present together.

### C. XVII. A witness is to add nothing of his own to the sequence of events.

Likewise, Ambrose, *On Paradise*, c. 12. [Note: Anselm, book 3, c. 58.]

The sequence of testimony must be stated plainly and simply. Frequently a witness, while adding something of his own to the sequence of events, tarnishes the whole credibility of his testimony by a partial falsehood. Therefore nothing, even what seems good, is to be added.

[Note: The complete Ambrosian passage reads: “The plain and simple form of a command must be observed, or the sequence of testimony must be stated.”]

[Col. 0701A]

### C. XVIII. An absentee can neither accuse nor be accused through another.

Likewise, Pope Felix to the bishops of Gaul, Epistle II. [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 248, part 6, c. 331. *Policraticus*, book 5, title 1.]

An absentee cannot accuse or be accused through another, nor is a kinsman admitted as a witness.

[Note: “no one”: Basel edition.]

**Fourth Part. Gratian.** Except in an action for injuries, in which a person of illustrious rank may both bring and answer an action even through a representative, with the other formalities preserved; as in the Code, title “Concerning Injuries,” final law.

### C. XIX. When the defendant is absent, a bill of accusation is offered in vain.

Likewise, Pope Pelagius to Sindula, Master of Soldiers. [Note: Apparently an epistle of Pelagius I.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 54, c. 8.]

[Note: Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, c. 67, reports a chapter of an epistle written by Pelagius to Sindula, Master of Soldiers.]

The documents which Lucidius gave us would have been valid if his adversary had been present there at that time. But because the proceedings which he recounted to us are recorded as having been conducted while the adversary was absent, the laws do not accept such things.

### C. XX. Witnesses are to give testimony after taking an oath in person.

The same [Pope] to Decoratus, Patrician. [Note: *Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 54, c. 9.]

We urge you, preserving in this matter also, under the fear of the Lord, the customary integrity of your conscience, to remove all fear from the persons who can know the truth of this case and to have them brought before you, so that, after touching the most holy Gospels and lawfully taking an oath, they may disclose by their declared testimony what they know to be true about the facts. Thus, when everything has been made plain, you may determine what ought to be decided according to law and justice, and give an outcome appropriate to the laws and to the truth.

[Note: “from persons”: Basel and Lyons editions.—“so that they”: Basel and Lyons II–III; “which, so that”: Lyons I.—“suitable”: Basel edition.]

[Col. 0701C]

### C. XXI. Accuser and accused must be present together.

Likewise, Pope Nicholas to Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims. [Note: An uncertain chapter.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 62, c. 33.]

It is necessary, according to the teaching of the sacred Scriptures and according to the path of justice, that both accused and accuser be present together, and that one party, however great its authority and whatever its character, be heard only in such a way that no prejudice is inflicted upon the other party.

## QUESTION X

[Col. 0702A]

## GRATIAN

That persons who fail on the first count are not to be admitted to subsequent counts is confirmed by the Seventh Council of Carthage, [Note: Held A.D. 419.—Rabanus, *Poenitentiale*, c. 1. Burchard, book 2, c. 198. *Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 22, c. 3. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, c. 64; *Decretum*, part 6, c. 271.] in which the following is decreed in c. 3:

[Note: “Persons who fail”: In the commonly circulated manuscripts the reading was “witnesses who fail”; but the word “witnesses” has been deleted, since it is absent from most ancient manuscripts. For the authorities adduced in this question concern not witnesses but accusers; and at the beginning of the cause, in the proposition of this tenth question, no mention is made of witnesses.]

### C. I. Whoever fails on the first count is not to be admitted to the others.

It has been decided that whenever accusers bring many charges against clerics, and are unable to prove one of those charges which they pursued first, they are not thereafter to be admitted to the others.

[Note: “were unwilling”: Basel edition.]

Gratian. The same proposition is proved by the authority of the Second Council of Arles, where the following was decreed in c. 24: [Note: Held not later than A.D. 460.—Cf., however, what we said at Distinction 18, c. 12.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 2, title 24, c. 7. Burchard, book 16, c. 34.]

### C. II. Those who bring false accusations against brethren are not to communicate until death.

It has been decided that those convicted of having brought false capital charges against brethren are not to communicate until death—as the great synod previously decreed—unless they repent through worthy satisfaction.

[Note: “false”: original; absent from Burchard.—“capital”: original and Burchard.—The “great synod” is the First Council of Arles, c. 14.—“previously”: Basel edition.]

### C. III. Whoever cannot prove what he alleges is not thereafter admitted to make accusations, unless he wishes only to assert his own civil cause.

Likewise, Pope Felix in the second decretal, to the bishops of Gaul. [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. the Council of Carthage, held A.D. 409, c. 24.—Chapter of Hadrian, c. 4. *Capitularies*, book 5, c. 395. Anselm, at the end of book 3. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, c. 418.]

If the persons of accusers are found blameworthy in the judgment of bishops, they are not thereafter to be admitted to accuse bishops, unless they wish to assert their own causes—though not criminal or ecclesiastical causes.

[Note: “Bishops thereafter”: These words are absent from all ancient manuscripts, the Basel edition, and the other cited sources. The author of the *casus*, however, had and weighed them.—“are admitted”: Basel edition.]

Gratian. Therefore, since those who bring false charges against brethren are forbidden communion until the end of life, and those found blameworthy in the judgment of bishops are forbidden thereafter to bring accusations, it is apparent that persons failing on the first count, as bringers of false accusations, cannot proceed to the subsequent counts.

## QUESTION XI

## GRATIAN

**First Part.** That an accusation may not be turned by the accused against the accuser is prohibited by many authorities.

For Pope Stephen says, Epistle II, c. 7: [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, taken from the Theodosian Code, book 9, title 1, c. 12, with interpretation.—Burchard, book 1, c. 164. Anselm, book 3, c. 74. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, c. 67; *Decretum*, part 5, c. 274.]

### C. I. The accused cannot accuse others unless they have first cleared themselves.

Accused persons must be denied permission to make criminal accusations before they have freed themselves from the crime with which they are burdened, because the confession of persons entangled in crimes is not to be believed against others unless they have first proved themselves innocent; for the statement of a defendant against anyone is dangerous and must not be admitted.

### C. II. On the same matter. Code, book IX, title I, law 19. The Emperors Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian, Augusti.

Accused persons—unless they pursue injuries done to themselves or their own—must be denied permission to make criminal accusations in a crime equal or less serious than that with which they are burdened, until they have freed themselves from it according to the enactments of the ancient founders of law. Nevertheless, they themselves may lodge formal accusations against such persons even while the accusation against them is pending.

[Note: “unless”: collected editions.—“pursue”: ibid.—“unless first”: Basel edition.—“according to the enactments of the ancient founders”: missing in the collected editions except the first Venice and Lyons editions.]

### C. III. On the same matter.

Likewise, from Pope Hadrian’s decree, c. 33. [Note: Cf. c. 1 above.—Anselm, at the end of book 3.]

The confession of persons entangled in crimes is not to be believed against others unless they have first proved themselves innocent, because the statement of a defendant against anyone is dangerous and must not be admitted.

[Note: “confession”: Basel edition.]

Gratian. This, however, is to be understood concerning a crime equal or less serious. But if he wishes to accuse him of a more serious crime—for example, if a person accused of fornication wishes to charge his accuser with perjury, homicide, simony, or any other crime of this sort—he is not prohibited by these authorities. For sometimes a criminal action prejudices a civil action, and sometimes another criminal action. Hence one reads in Code, book III, title “On the Order of Judgments,” law 4: “A civil action being suspended, it often happens that judgment is first given concerning a crime, which, because it is greater, is rightly preferred to the lesser.”

[Note: “dispute”: original.—“Sometimes [a criminal action prejudices] another criminal action”: Earlier editions read, “sometimes a civil [action prejudices] a criminal action”; the word “civil” has been deleted on the authority of ancient manuscripts. For here the only issue is when a criminal cause takes precedence over a civil or criminal cause. The following section, “Sometimes a civil [action],” explains when a civil cause is preferred to both a civil and a criminal cause.]

[Col. 0704A]

### C. IV. Likewise, Code, book IX, title “On Those Who Cannot Accuse,” law 1.

First you must answer the charges of homicide and wounding which your adversary brings against you as more serious crimes; then, according to the outcome of the case, the judge shall decide whether you should be permitted to accuse that same person, although you were the first to lodge a formal accusation.

**Second Part. Gratian.** Sometimes a civil action takes precedence over a civil action, and sometimes over a criminal action. For, as one reads in Code, book VII, title “On the Order of Cognitions,” law “If [the dispute is] concerning an inheritance”:

“If there is a controversy over inheritance and freedom, the cause of freedom must be heard first.”

Likewise, in the following law:

§1. “If any crime is alleged against one said to be freeborn, the cause concerning freedom must first be heard in its proper order, with the governor furnishing his jurisdiction; for, if the offense is proved, it is first necessary to know whether judgment ought to be rendered against the person as free or as a slave.”

[Note: In the law itself the text reads, “whom you say is freeborn.” It addresses a woman. Thus, somewhat lower down, where Gratian reads, “whether [judgment should be rendered] against a freeborn free man or against a slave,” the law reads, “against a freeborn free woman or against a female slave.” Gratian also reduced the next two laws he cites to summaries of his own.]

**Third Part.**

§2. A person who admits that he is undergoing a dispute over status vainly seeks leave to accuse the person whom he acknowledges to be his master. Once the cause concerning freedom has been decided, if he is declared a slave, he cannot accuse his master.

Code, book IX, title 1, penultimate law:

§3. If any member of the household or slave of any house comes forward as an informer and accuser of any crime, seeking the reputation, life, and property of the person to whose household or dominion he belongs, he is to be struck by the avenging sword at the very presentation of the charges and at the opening of the accusation, before witnesses are produced and the case examined. For the deadly voice ought rather to be cut off than heard. We except, however, the crime of treason against majesty.

Likewise, the final law:

§4. If freedmen presume to accuse their manumitters or their heirs, they shall be subject to the same punishment as slaves, to pay the penalty before the beginning of their prohibited denunciation.

## CAUSE IV

[Col. 0704]

## GRATIAN

A man under excommunication intends to accuse a bishop. He brings forward a youth under fourteen years of age in support of his case. Forbidden to accuse, he makes the youth accuser and himself witness. The youth wishes to act as both accuser and witness. On the appointed day, the bishop does not appear before the tribunal of chosen judges; he is suspended from communion. At last, when the judgment is recalled, the accuser is found blameworthy in the accusation; finally he proceeds to assert his own cause.

(Question I.) The first question here is whether a person under excommunication can accuse another.

(Question II.) Second, whether a person under fourteen years of age can testify in a criminal case.

(Question III.) Third, whether one prohibited from accusing can assume the role of witness.

(Question IV.) Fourth, whether the same person can be both accuser and witness.

(Question V.) Fifth, whether one who does not appear on the appointed day is to be removed from communion.

(Question VI.) Sixth, if the person of an accuser is found blameworthy in the judgment of bishops, whether that person is thereafter to be admitted to assert his own cause.

## QUESTION I

[Col. 0705B]

## GRATIAN

Concerning the first question, the following is decreed in the first and second chapters of the Seventh Council of Carthage, attended by Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church: [Note: Held A.D. 419.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 2, title 21, c. 1. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, c. 72; *Decretum*, part 14, c. 69.]

### C. I. A person persisting in excommunication is not to be admitted to make an accusation.

We determine that a person is rightly not admitted to make an accusation if, after being excommunicated, he wishes to accuse while still under that excommunication, whether he is cleric or layperson.

§1. All persons stained with the marks of infamy—that is, actors and persons subject to disgraceful occupations—likewise heretics, pagans, and Jews, are prohibited from making accusations.

[Note: “rightly”: Ivo; “ritually”: collected editions.—“or”: Ivo and collected editions.—“suspect”: Basel edition.—“They are prohibited from accusation”: These words are absent from the council, being understood from the beginning of the chapter: “they are not to be admitted to accusation.”]

[Col. 0706A]

### C. II. Those who are separated from the Church by schism or excommunication are shown to be heretics.

Likewise, Pope Nicholas, in the epistle to Emperor Michael beginning, “We had proposed.” [Note: Written A.D. 865.—Anselm, book 1, c. 71 [75]. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, c. 70.]

That those who had been deposed, excommunicated, or anathematized by our already mentioned brother and fellow-minister Ignatius could not bring any condemnation against him is declared by the cited chapter of the Second Ecumenical Synod, where it is said:

“If the charge brought against the bishop is ecclesiastical, then the persons of the accusers must be examined, so that heretics may not, in the first place, be permitted to bring accusations against orthodox bishops in ecclesiastical matters.”

But lest you deny that these are heretics, hear what follows:

“By heretics,” they say, “we mean both those who were formerly cast out of the Church and those who have subsequently been anathematized by us.”

Moreover, if you still do not believe even this, hear what is added:

“Besides these, [we mean] those who pretend to confess the sound faith, yet are schismatics and hold separate assemblies apart from bishops in communion with us. Further, if certain persons have been censured by the Church in certain matters and have been cast out or excommunicated, whether from the clergy or the lay order, they too are not permitted to accuse a bishop before they have first cleared themselves of their own crime. Likewise, persons still under an earlier accusation are not acceptable as accusers of a bishop or other clerics until they have shown themselves innocent of the crimes charged against them.”

You do not fail to know what danger threatens those who despise this rule.

[Note: “already” is absent in the Argentinian, first Venice, and Nuremberg editions.—“aforementioned”: collected editions.—“or excommunicated”: same editions.—“cited”: Nicholas here cites a canon which among the Greeks belongs to the Sixth Canon of the First Council of Constantinople. Earlier in the same epistle he had quoted the first part of this canon; it is indicated above, 3, question 5, final chapter. At that point Nicholas had added concerning this chapter: “This, however, is not found among us, but is said to be held among you.” For this canon is found neither in Dionysius’s translation nor in the ancient translation; and St Gregory writes to Eulogius concerning all the canons of that council, book 6, epistle 31: “The Roman Church has not hitherto possessed or received the same canons or the acts of that synod.” It nevertheless accepted that synod insofar as it defined against Macedonius.—“has been”: Anselm and collected editions.—“deny”: collected editions.—“Formerly cast out of the Church”: In this part of the canon it is decreed that Macedonians and Eudoxians, condemned at this First Council of Constantinople, are to be considered heretics in the same way as the Paulianists and Arians whom the Nicene Synod had long before cut off from the Catholic Church. The proposition is therefore not pronounced concerning every excommunicated person, as the author of the gloss thought.—“cast out”: Basel edition.—“after this”: collected editions.—“indeed”: original and collected editions.—“sound”: original and collected editions, with “deny or” added.—“are”: collected editions.]

[Note: “Schismatics also”: Thus in Nicholas’s epistle and in Ivo. The Greek, however, is: **Πρὸς δὲ τούτοις καὶ τοὺς τὴν πίστιν μὲν τὴν ὑγιῆ προσποιουμένους ὁμολογεῖν, ἀποσχήσαντας δὲ καὶ ἀντισυνάγοντας τοῖς κανονικοῖς ἡμῶν ἐπισκόποις.** That is: “Furthermore, [we mean] those who pretend indeed to confess the sound faith, but have separated themselves and hold assemblies in opposition to our canonical bishops.” Thus it is no wonder that these too are considered heretics, as Balsamon interprets; for they pretend to uphold the faith which they attack.]

## QUESTIONS II AND III

[Col. 0707A]

## GRATIAN

**First Part.** The second and third questions are decided by one and the same fourth chapter of the Seventh Council of Carthage: [Note: Held A.D. 419.—Cf. Cap. 1, 7, c. 101. Burchard, book 16, c. 20. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, c. 83; *Decretum*, part 6, c. 364.]

### C. I. Persons excluded from accusation, or not yet fourteen years old, cannot be witnesses.

We determine that persons are not to be admitted as witnesses if they have been ordered not to be admitted to make accusations, or if the accuser himself has produced them from his household. Nor are persons under fourteen years of age to be admitted to give testimony.

[Note: “ordered”: collected editions.—“within”: *Collectio Hispana*, Ivo’s *Panormia*, Basel and Lyons II–III editions.—“being”: collected editions.]

### C. II. On the same matter. *Palea.*

Likewise, from the Council of Mâcon, c. 6. [Note: Rather, from the Frankish royal capitularies, book 3, c. 52.—*Regino*, book 2, c. 336. Burchard, book 16, c. 35.—c. 1, *Compilatio II* and X, “On Witnesses.”]

“It has pleased the holy assembly that witnesses are not to be hired for money to give testimony; that the best and most trustworthy persons are to be chosen as witnesses, so that the person against whom they must bear testimony cannot bring any accusation against them; and that no one is to testify unless fasting.”

[Note: “to bear testimony”: Burchard.—“take away”: Basel edition.]

**Second Part. Gratian.** Likewise, in a criminal case, a witness who has previously testified against that defendant cannot be produced, as is found in Digest, book 22, title “On Witnesses,” law 23. Likewise, in the same title, law *Ob carmen*, § *If [there are] witnesses*:

### C. III

[Note: In this chapter Gratian reports various laws of the Digest and Code in such a way that he sometimes gives precisely the same words, but sometimes changes, transposes, and reduces them to a summary.
