Many passages have indeed been corrected from the original, except where Gratian deliberately changed them.]

If all the witnesses are of the same honesty and reputation, and the nature of the matter and the judge’s disposition concur with them, all the testimony must be followed without qualification. But if some of them say otherwise, even in an equal number, what conforms to the nature of the matter and is free from suspicion of hostility or favor must be believed; and the judge shall confirm his own judgment from the arguments and testimony which he finds more suitable to the case and nearer to the truth. For attention should not be paid to numbers, but to the unblemished credibility of testimonies and to those testimonies upon which the light of truth rests more fully.

Likewise, law 2, Digest, same title:

§1. In witnesses, credibility, standing, character, and seriousness must be examined; and therefore witnesses who waver contrary to the trustworthiness of their testimony are not to be heard.

Likewise, law 3:

§2. The credibility of witnesses must be examined carefully; and therefore, first of all, the condition of each must be investigated: whether he is a town councillor or a commoner; whether of honorable and blameless life or instead marked and reprehensible; whether wealthy or needy, so that he might readily admit something for gain; whether an enemy of the person against whom he bears testimony or a friend of the person for whom he gives it. For if the testimony is free from suspicion either because of the person who gives it, who is honorable, or because of the cause, because it is given neither for gain, favor, nor hostility, it is to be admitted.

[Note: “all”: collected editions.—“unequal”: Argentinian, Basel, Lyons II–III editions; original.—“testimonies”: original.—“character”: Basel edition.—“or also”: Venice II, Paris, and Lyons editions.—“or”: Basel; “or else”: Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I, and Lyons editions.—“is given”: Argentinian; “be”: remaining editions.—“is admitted”: collected editions.]

Likewise, somewhat lower in the same law:

**Third Part.**

§3. The Julian Law on Violence provides that the following may not give testimony against a defendant under this law: a person who has freed himself from that defendant or from the defendant’s parent; one who is under age; one condemned in a public trial and not restored to full legal status; one held in chains or public custody; one who has hired himself out to fight with wild beasts; a woman who openly engages, or has engaged, in prostitution; or one adjudged or convicted of accepting money to give or withhold testimony.

Likewise, law 4:

§4. The Julian Law on Public Trials provides that no person be compelled unwillingly to testify in litigation against his father-in-law, son-in-law, stepfather, stepson, cousin, female cousin, a child of a cousin, or persons related in a nearer degree.

§5. Likewise, [no person is compelled to testify] against his own freedman, or against the freedman of his children, parents, husband, or wife.

§6. Likewise, neither patrons or patronesses against freedmen nor freedmen against a patron are to be compelled to testify.

§7. When it is excepted that a son-in-law or father-in-law is not to be compelled unwillingly to testify, the term “son-in-law” is understood also to include the fiancé of one’s daughter, and “father-in-law” the father of one’s fiancée.

Likewise, law 6:

§8. Those who can be ordered to become witnesses are not regarded as qualified witnesses.

Likewise, law 7:

§9. A slave’s answer is to be believed only when there is no other proof for discovering the truth.

Likewise, law 8:

§10. Elderly persons, persons in ill health, soldiers, persons absent on public business with a magistrate, and persons not permitted to come are not compelled unwillingly to give testimony.

Likewise, law 19:

§11. Tax-farmers likewise do not testify unwillingly.

§12. Likewise, a person who is absent not for the purpose of refusing testimony.

§13. Likewise, a person who has contracted to supply provisions to an army. But no summons to testify may be served on wards.

Likewise, law 20:

§14. An accuser must not summon as a witness one who is a defendant in a public trial, or who is under twenty years of age.

Likewise, law 21:

§15. A person condemned for a defamatory poem becomes incapable of giving testimony.

§16. If the matter requires it, not only private persons but even magistrates, if present, are to give testimony. A praetor also must give testimony in a trial concerning adultery.

§17. But if the condition of the case is such that we are compelled to admit an arena-fighter as witness, or a similar person, his testimony is not to be believed without torture.

Likewise, law 24:

§18. It has been decided that witnesses whom the accuser has produced from his own household are not to be questioned.

Likewise, law 25:

§19. Advocates likewise are not to testify in a cause in which they have provided advocacy; this is also to be observed regarding persons entrusted with the execution of business affairs.

Likewise, law 16:

In Question XI, C. I, compare below C. I, §1, see Ivo, *Decretum*, part 16, c. 64.

For C. “condemned” (*damnatus*) is “to be condemned” (*condemnandus*) in the Argentinian edition; “fight” (*depugnet*) is “fought” (*depugnaret*) in the collected editions and original; “a woman who” (*quaeve*) is “a man who” (*quive*) in the Argentinian, Basel, Venice I–II, and Lyons editions; “engages” (*faciat*) is “will engage” (*faciet*) in Basel and “engages” (*facit*) in the remaining editions; and “is” (*erit*) is “has been” (*fuerit*) in the collected editions. §4: “may give” (*liceat*) is “might give” (*liceret*) in the editions and original; “stepdaughter” (*privignam*) is added in the editions and first Basel; “female cousin” (*sobrinave*) is added in the collected editions, first Argentinian, Venice II, and Nuremberg; “nearer” (*priore*) is *propiore* or *propriore* in the listed Venice, Nuremberg, Paris, and Lyons editions, which also add “in … degree.” §13: the original reads, “one who has contracted to supply something to an army.” §14: “is a defendant” (*reus erit*) is “has been a defendant” (*fuerit*) in the collected editions and first Basel; the words “or who is under twenty years old” are absent from Argentinian. §15: “becomes” (*fit*) is “will become” (*erit*) in the collected editions. §16: the collected editions vary in the wording from “concerning” through “case.” §17: “such that” (*ut*) is “where” (*ubi*) in the collected editions; “we are compelled” (*cogamur*) is “we are compelled” (*cogimur*) in those editions and first Basel. §18: “his own household” (*sua*) is “a private household” (*propria*) in the remaining editions; “has produced” (*produxit*) is “has produced” (*produxerit*) in the collected editions. §19: “have provided” (*praestiterunt*) is “provide” (*praestant*) in the editions.]

IV. Part. § 20. Those who have given false [Note: [Col. 0709] *false*: Edd. Bas., Ven. II.] or inconsistent [Note: [Col. 0709] *inconsistent*: Ed. Ven. II.] testimony, or have betrayed both parties, are to be punished appropriately by the judges [Note: [Col. 0709] *are punished*: collected editions].

Likewise, law 17:

§ 21. A father and a son who is under his authority, likewise two brothers who are under the authority of the same father, may be witnesses for both parties in the same will [Note: [Col. 0709] add: “to be”: collected editions and first Basle edition], or in the same transaction [Note: [Col. 0709] “to be”: Basle edition], since no harm results from employing several witnesses from one household in another person’s affair.

Likewise, law 15:

§ 22. Whether a hermaphrodite may be admitted to give testimony is shown by the predominant character of the sex.

Likewise, law 9:

[Col. 0709C] § 23. A father is not a competent witness for his son, nor a son for his father.

Likewise, law 10:

§ 24. No one is regarded as a competent witness in his own case.

Likewise, law 11:

§ 25. Even a witness who has not been formally called is recognized as serving to establish the credibility of an act performed.

Likewise, law 12:

§ 26. Where no number of witnesses is specified, even two are sufficient [Note: [Col. 0709] *are sufficient*: collected editions and first Basle edition]. For the plural expression is satisfied by the number two.

Likewise, law 3:

§ 27. In the case of witnesses who appear to have testified straightforwardly [Note: [Col. 0709] “who give straightforward testimony”: editions], it must be considered whether they have offered one and the same prepared [Note: [Col. 0709] *prepared*: same editions] statement, or whether they have given plausible answers spontaneously to the questions asked [Note: [Col. 0709] *give answers*: same editions].

Likewise, a little below:

§ 28. Often the truth of a matter is discovered without public records [Note: [Col. 0709] *defences*: Basle edition; *documents*: other editions]; at one time the number of witnesses, at another their rank and authority, at another a reputation that seems to concur, confirms the credibility of the matter under inquiry. A judge, therefore, ought not immediately to bind his investigation to a single kind of proof [Note: [Col. 0709] “his own”: collected editions], but should judge according to his own conviction what he believes, or what he thinks insufficiently proved.

Likewise, a little below:

§ 29. The authority of witnesses who are present is one thing; that of testimonies which are customarily read aloud is another.

Likewise, Code, book IX, title *On Witnesses*, law 2 [Note: [Col. 0709] Code, book 4, title 20, chapter 2]:

§ 30. Witnesses alone are insufficient to prove free birth, unless they are supported by documents and evidence.

Likewise, law 3:

§ 31. Even under civil law, the credibility of domestic testimony is rejected.

Likewise, law 4:

§ 32. It is certain that a case produced by attestation alone, and not established by other lawful supports, has no force whatever.

Likewise, law 5:

§ 33. Those witnesses ought to be employed [Note: [Col. 0709] *regarded*: Böhm] to assist the truth [Col. 0710B] who are able to place the trust owed to judicial conscience above every favour and exercise of power [Note: [Col. 0709] *are able*: collected editions].

Likewise, law 6:

§ 34. Parents and children may not be admitted to testify against one another, even if willing.

Likewise, law 7:

§ 35. He who makes an allegation must bring proofs proper to his own allegation [Note: [Col. 0709] *allegation*: same editions], and must not demand that his opponent be compelled to produce those through whom [Note: [Col. 0709D] *Through whom*: in the vulgate text [Col. 0709] and the collected editions, the reading was *through which*. It has been corrected from the manuscripts and from the law itself, which deals with the production of witnesses, not the production of documents.] his case is made.

Likewise, law 8:

§ 36. Slaves may be questioned neither for their master nor against their master, but concerning their own deed.

Likewise, law 9:

§ 37. Before witnesses give testimony, let them be bound by the sanctity of an oath [Note: [Col. 0710D] *Let them be bound*: thus in certain manuscripts; this reading agrees better with the words of the law, “we order that they be strictly bound,” than does *let them be coerced*, which stood in the printed editions [Col. 0709] *they are coerced*: Basle edition; *let them be coerced*: other editions.], and let greater credence be given to more honourable witnesses.

§ 38. No judge should readily allow the testimony of one person to be admitted in any case whatsoever; indeed, the answer of a single witness is not to be heard at all, even if he shines with the honour of an illustrious [Note: [Col. 0709] *of a governor’s*: Norimberg, Venice I, Paris, Lyons editions; *of a governor’s court*: other editions] court.

Likewise, law 10:

§ 39. The laws have removed from everyone the right to give testimony in his own case [Note: [Col. 0709] *testimonies*: collected editions].

Likewise, law 11:

§ 40. Free persons [Note: [Col. 0709] *freedmen*: Lyons II and III] are to be called as witnesses in others’ cases [Note: [Col. 0709] *are called*: collected editions], provided that they are not said to be associates and accomplices in the crime, but that testimony concerning what they know is sought from them. Those coming to court at the accuser’s summons, or at the summons of those by whom they had been requested [Note: [Col. 0709] *will have been*: Basle and Lyons editions], are to be supplied with suitable expenses [Note: [Col. 0709] “let suitable expenses be supplied”: collected editions; Böhm], even if, in a financial case, witnesses are to be produced by either party.

Likewise, law 12:

§ 41. Freedmen must not dare to come forward voluntarily against their patrons [Note: [Col. 0709] *proceed*: collected editions]; nor, even when summoned, are they to be compelled to come to court [Note: [Col. 0709] *in court*: same editions].

Likewise, law 17:

§ 42. If someone has used witnesses, and those same witnesses are produced against him [Col. 0711A] in another suit, he may not object to their persons [Note: [Col. 0711] *against their persons*: Basle, Venice I, Lyons editions], unless he shows that hostilities arose afterward between himself and them [Note: [Col. 0711] *had arisen*: collected editions], of the kind for which the laws order witnesses to be rejected. This does not, of course, take away his freedom to challenge their testimony on the basis of their depositions themselves.

§ 43. But if he shows by clear proofs that they have been corrupted by the giving or promise of money, that allegation too ought to be fully preserved for him.

Gratian. But the case of blessed Brice is objected: he was proved innocent by the voice of a child thirty days old [Note: [Col. 0711] Sulpicius Severus, book 3 of the *Life of St Martin*]. But divine miracles are to be admired, not drawn into an example for human action.

## QUESTION IV

[Col. 0711B]

## GRATIAN

I. Part. Concerning the fourth question, Pope Fabian, in Epistle II [Note: [Col. 0711] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. *Capitularies*, A.D. 744, c. 18; *Capitularies*, book 7, c. 339; Burchard, book 16, c. 15; Anselm, book 3, c. 75; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, c. 81; *Decretum*, part 6, c. 321.], laid down the following for the eastern bishops:

### C. I. An accuser and a witness or judge cannot be the same person at once.

No one may ever presume to be accuser and judge or witness at the same time, since in every judgment four persons must always be present [Note: [Col. 0711] *be present*: collected editions]: chosen judges, competent accusers [Note: [Col. 0711C] *Competent*: In Fabian, Burchard, and Ivo this passage reads: “chosen judges, accusers, defenders, and witnesses.” But because the words *competent*, *suitable*, and *lawful* occur in all the old manuscripts of Gratian and the *Panormia*, nothing has been altered.], suitable defenders, and lawful witnesses. Judges [Note: [Col. 0711] These words are taken from *Capitularies*, A.D. 744, c. 18.] moreover [Note: [Col. 0711D] *Judges moreover*: these words occur neither in the epistle nor in the other collectors, except in the *Panormia*.] ought to employ equity; witnesses, truth; accusers, an intention to enlarge the case; and defenders, mitigation in order to reduce the case.

[Col. 0711C]

### C. II. No one ought to perform two roles in a case.

Likewise Pope Damasus, Epistle IV, chapter 7 [Note: [Col. 0711] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Theodosian Code, book 2, title 2, chapter 1, and book 9, title 1; Burchard, book 16, c. 51; Anselm, book 3, c. 47; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, c. 81; *Decretum*, part 6, c. 337.]:

No person is to be introduced personally [Note: [Col. 0711] add: “into a case”: collected editions], but accusers and accused are to be heard with equal fairness, as the order of the *proceedings* requires. Accusers and judges must not be the same persons, but accusers separately, judges separately, witnesses separately, accused separately—each person in his own proper order.

II. Part. § 1. For an inscription must always first be made, so that the calumniator may receive retaliation; because no one ought to be judged or condemned before the inscription, since the laws of the secular world also maintain these same requirements.

Gratian. Thus in Code, book IX, title *On Accusations and Inscriptions*, law 6; and in the Code, in the same book, *On Adulteries*, law 6; and under the title *On Cattle-Thieves*, sole law.

§ 1. At times an accusation may also be made without an inscription. For it is well known that matters reported to provincial governors by officials [Note: [Col. 0711] *office*: original text] may be examined without the formalities of accusations.

§ 2. Likewise, Code *On Adulteries*, law 6: If a husband wishes, by the husband’s right—that is, within sixty available days—to accuse his wife of adultery, whom he may render accused on suspicion alone, he is not bound by the requirement of inscription.

§ 3. Likewise, Code *On Cattle-Thieves*, sole law: An accusation concerning a driven-off animal may be brought not only with inscriptions, but also without the prescribed observance.

§ 4. Likewise, Code *On Accusations*, law 8: If anyone thinks that he has suffered an injury from someone and wishes to lodge a complaint, he should not run to the police officers, but approach the governor’s authority, either offering written petitions or depositing his complaints in the official records.

§ 5. In other criminal cases [Note: [Col. 0712C] *In other criminal cases*: Law 16 of the Code, *On Accusations*, reads: “In criminal cases”; the remainder follows exactly as introduced by Gratian.], however, it is proper that inscriptions be filed beforehand, indicating the gravity of the crime and its time, so that the worthy authority of the laws may intimidate either party [Note: [Col. 0712D] *Authority*: In the vulgate editions the little verse “Inscription,” from Damasus’s chapter, was repeated here; but it is absent from the older manuscripts and is repeated without purpose.].

III. Part. Gratian. Nor should an accuser or witness be produced from the judge’s household, lest the judge incur grounds for suspicion.

[Col. 0712C]

Therefore Pope Nicholas, in his epistle to Emperor Michael, beginning “We had proposed” [Note: [Col. 0712D] This chapter has been corrected from the original itself, printed at Rome.] [Note: [Col. 0711] written A.D. 865; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 1, title 62, c. 71]:

### C. III. A judge from whose household either accuser or witness is produced incurs the charge of suspicion.

An accuser is produced from the imperial household contrary to ecclesiastical rite and venerable laws; and one who may be commanded to give false testimony is employed [Note: [Col. 0711] “When someone is employed to give false testimony” (absent from the Argentinian, Norimberg, and Venice II editions): collected editions]. Judges become suspect and hirelings, and wolves become guardians—those who seemed to be shepherds.

## QUESTION V

[Col. 0713A]

## GRATIAN

Concerning the fifth question, the following definition is found in the Third Council of Carthage [Note: [Col. 0713] held A.D. 391; Burchard, book 1, c. 160; Anselm, book 3, c. 122 (121); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, c. 106; *Decretum*, part 5, c. 170.], chapter 7:

### C. I. One unable to appear in court on the appointed day is not to be suspended from communion.

Whoever accuses a bishop shall bring the case before the primate [Note: [Col. 0713] *primates*: collected editions, Hispanic Collection, Dionysius] of that province [Note: [Col. 0713] *of that very one*: Basle and Lyons editions; *he of that one*: other editions]. Nor is the person against whom a charge is brought to be suspended from communion unless, having been summoned by letters from the chosen judges [Note: [Col. 0713D] *Chosen judges*: these two words are absent from the Cologne four-volume edition of the councils [Col. 0713] though they are indeed read in Isidore Mercator and Dionysius, but not in the Hispanic Collection.] to state his case on an appointed day, he fails to appear—namely, within the space of a month, reckoned from the day on which it is established that he received the letters [Note: [Col. 0713] add: “of the first see”: Anselm, Hispanic Collection]. But if he proves some genuine [Note: [Col. 0713] *genuine*: Ivo] causes of necessity which clearly show that he could not appear, he is to retain an undiminished opportunity to state his case within a second month. Yet [Note: [Col. 0713] add: *nevertheless*: Basle edition] he is not to communicate after the second month until he has been cleared. But if he refuses even to appear at the general council [Note: [Col. 0713D] *General*: the council itself [Col. 0713] adds, in Dionysius, Isidore Mercator, and Anselm, *annual*; African Council c. 62 shows that the “general council” is to be understood as the general council of Africa.] [Note: [Col. 0713] add: “within the period of a year”: Burchard, Ivo], so that his case may at least be concluded there, he is to be judged to have pronounced a sentence of condemnation against himself. During the time when he does not communicate, he is not to communicate either in his own church [Note: [Col. 0713D] *Nor in his own church*: thus in the other editions of the councils, the code of canons, and the other collectors. But the four-volume edition reads, “nor shall he communicate among his own people.” In Greek, c. 19, reads: **μηδὲ ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐκκλησίᾳ, μηδὲ ἐν παροικίᾳ κοινωνήσῃ**, that is, “he shall communicate neither in his own church nor in the parish.”] nor [Note: [Col. 0713] *nor either*: collected editions and first Basle edition] in a parish. But if his accuser has never been absent on the days appointed for the hearing of the case [Note: [Col. 0713] add: “withdrawing himself”: Ivo, *Panormia*, collected editions], he is not to be removed from communion. But if he has at some time been absent by withdrawing himself, then, when the bishop has been restored to communion, the accuser is to be removed from communion—provided, however, that he is not deprived of the right to pursue the case if he proves that he did not refuse [Col. 0713C] to appear by [Note: [Col. 0713] *before*: Argentinian, Norimberg, Venice II editions] the appointed day [Note: [Col. 0713] add: “appointed”: Ivo; “fixed”: collected editions], but was unable to do so.

## QUESTION VI

[Col. 0714A]

## GRATIAN

The sixth question is decided in the same seventh chapter of the Third Council of Carthage [Note: [Col. 0713] held A.D. 397; Burchard, Anselm, Ivo, same place.], which continues as follows:

### C. I. A person found blameworthy in the accusation of a bishop is admitted to prosecute only a civil and personal matter.

It was further decided that, when proceedings have begun in the judgment of bishops, if the person of the accuser is found blameworthy [Note: [Col. 0713] *liable to condemnation*: collected editions], he is not to be admitted to prosecute [Note: [Col. 0713] add: “thereafter”: same editions], unless he wishes to assert his own cases, though not ecclesiastical or criminal ones [Note: [Col. 0714D] *Or criminal*: this is absent from the council and the other collectors, but has been retained because of the case, and occurs in the chapter *If the Accusers*.].

### C. II. A person who may not accuse may conduct his own case.

[Col. 0714B] Likewise, from the Seventh Council of Carthage, chapter 2, near the end [Note: [Col. 0713] held A.D. 419; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 2, title 21, c. 2; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 16, c. 64.]:

All those to whom the right to accuse is denied are not to be denied the right of prosecuting in their own cases [Note: [Col. 0713] *denied*: original, Ivo, Basle edition].

### C. III. A person who fails in the accusation of bishops may proceed only civilly.

Likewise Pope Felix, in Epistle II to all bishops established throughout the provinces of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0713] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. c. 1 of the same material; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, c. 418; cf. C. 3, q. 10, final chapter.]:

If the persons of accusers appear blameworthy in the judgment of bishops, they are not to be admitted to prosecute, unless they wish to assert their own cases, but not criminal or ecclesiastical cases.

### C. IV. On the same matter.

Likewise Pope Hadrian, in the *Capitularies*, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 0713] cf. chapters 1 and 3 of the same material; Anselm, at the end of book 3.]:

If the persons of accusers appear blameworthy in the judgment of bishops [Col. 0714C], they are not to be admitted to prosecute unless they have personal cases, but not criminal or ecclesiastical ones.

## CAUSE V

[Col. 0713]

[Col. 0713C] GRATIAN

To defame a certain bishop, a document of accusation is secretly drawn up [Col. 0714C]; at last the accuser comes forward publicly. The bishop, having once been summoned by letters, is unable to be present on the appointed day for his case and presents himself to the judge through an agent; he is condemned without a synodal hearing. Later, when the judgment is renewed through an appeal, the bishop complains of the accuser’s hostility; finally, in the proof itself the accuser fails.

(Question I.) First, the question is asked: by what punishment should one be struck who, secretly writing a defamatory libel, neglects to prove what he committed to writing?

(Question II.) Second: how many times must he be summoned to the case before receiving a sentence of condemnation?

(Question III.) Third: may one who cannot himself attend his own case conduct it through an agent?

(Question IV.) Fourth: may he be condemned without a synodal hearing?

(Question V.) Fifth: is a person to be regarded as an enemy merely because he judges another’s crime?

(Question VI.) Sixth, [Col. 0715B] by what punishment should one be punished who cannot prove what he alleged?

## QUESTION I

## GRATIAN

On the first question Pope Hadrian writes in the *Capitularies*, chapter 49, otherwise 50, as follows [Note: [Col. 0715] *Capitularies*, book 7, c. 361; Anselm, at the end of book 3, c. 42; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, c. 156, part 16, c. 235.]:

### C. I. Let one who has neglected to prove writings defaming another be flogged.

Whoever publicly [Note: [Col. 0715D] *Publicly*: Hadrian, the Capitularies of Charles, and Ivo read *in public*.] fabricates a writing or insulting words against another’s reputation, and is found not to have proved the writings, is to be flogged; and whoever first finds them is to destroy them, if he does not wish to incur liability as the author of the act [Note: [Col. 0715] *reputation*: Basle edition].

[Col. 0715C]

### C. II. On the same matter.

Likewise Gregory, book V, epistle 30 [Note: [Col. 0715] Epistle 31, written A.D. 596 to Marinianus of Ravenna, book 6, Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, c. 381.]:

A certain man, filled with the counsel of a malicious spirit, posted during the silence of night, in a public [Note: [Col. 0715D] *Public*: this word is absent from the manuscripts [Col. 0715] and the collected editions except Lyons II and III, as well as from the original and Ivo; but it has been retained because of the case, and in certain old copies it is an interlinear gloss.] place in the city a denunciation speaking against Castorius, our notary and representative, alleging a crime against him [Note: [Col. 0715] “speaking to me, and also, etc.”: Argentinian, Norimberg, Venice II editions], and also craftily opposing me concerning the making of peace [Note: [Col. 0715D] *Opposing*: what follows down to “But if” has been added from the epistle itself and is also reported [Col. 0716D] by Ivo.] [Note: [Col. 0715] add: “they alleged”: collected editions].

And because whoever speaks truthfully ought not to fear to make himself known, he must come forward publicly and show whatever he presumed to say in his denunciation [Col. 0716A]. But [Note: [Col. 0715] *Who*: same editions] if he does not come forward and make public confession, whoever he may be who presumed to do this [Note: [Col. 0715] *has presumed*: same editions], or who gave consent *to* so great a scheme of wickedness, we decree by the Spirit of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ that he be deprived of participation in His holy body and blood. But if, because he is concealed and unknown, he cannot be subjected to discipline [Note: [Col. 0715] *from discipline*: original], and if, being conscious of so great an evil, even after prohibition [Note: [Col. 0715] *and now*: original], he presumes to receive the body and blood of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0715] *presume*: Basle edition; *has presumed*: other editions], he is struck by the penalty of anathema [Note: [Col. 0716D] *He is struck*: previously the reading was “let him be struck” [Col. 0715] thus the collected editions; but because what precedes binds by the act itself, since it concerns a hidden offence, this has been corrected, like many other readings, from the epistle itself. Ivo, however, reads: “struck by the punishment of anathema as a deceiver,” etc.], and is separated from the body of the holy Church as a deceiver and a pest.

And below: But if, having come out publicly in the same city [Note: [Col. 0715] *in the same city*: Lyons II and III editions], he can show what he said [Note: [Col. 0715] *having entered*: collected editions; *will be able*: same editions; *has said*: Basle, Venice I, Lyons editions], or if, knowing that he cannot prove what he wrote, he has openly confessed his error, he is not to be deprived of participation in the Lord’s body and blood [Col. 0716B], nor regarded as excluded from the body of the holy Church.

### C. III. Let those who place defamatory libels in a church be anathematized.

Likewise, in the Council of Elvira, chapter 52 [Note: [Col. 0715] held no later than A.D. 310; *Capitularies*, book 6, c. 316; Burchard, book 3, c. 199; Anselm, at the end of book 3; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 201, part 4, c. 154; Polycarpus, book 3, title 21.]:

If any persons are found [Note: [Col. 0715] *Those*: Hispanic Collection; Argentinian and Basle editions] placing defamatory libels [Note: [Col. 0715] add: “or unknown ones”: Burchard; “and unknown ones”: Ivo, part 3] in a church [Note: [Col. 0715] *reading*: Anselm, Ivo, part 4; *reading or singing*: Burchard, Ivo, part 3], let them be anathematized.

Gratian. Likewise, Code, book IX, title *On Defamatory Libels*, sole law. Emperors Valentinian and Valens, Augusti:

If anyone finds a defamatory libel, whether at home [Note: [Col. 0715] *or at home*: collected editions] or in public, or in any place whatsoever, without knowing its author, he must either destroy it before another finds it, or confess its discovery to no one [Note: [Col. 0715] *declare*: Basle edition]. But if he does not immediately either destroy the same sheets or consume them by fire [Note: [Col. 0715] *burn*: collected editions and first Basle edition], but reveals their contents [Note: [Col. 0715] add: *deceitfully*: collected editions], let him know that, as though author [Col. 0716C] of such an offence, he is subject to capital sentence. And below: But a libel of this kind must not injure another person’s reputation.

## QUESTION II

## GRATIAN

The summons of a person against whom proceedings are brought ought not to be made once only, but twice and a third time, at suitable intervals and by reasonable written notices.

[Col. 0717A]

Therefore Pope Damasus writes to Archbishop Stephen in Epistle III [Note: [Col. 0717] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Fourth Council of Carthage, held A.D. 419, c. 24; Burchard, book 1, c. 156; Anselm, book 3, c. 50 (47); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 266; Polycarpus, book 5, title 1.]:

### C. I. The summons to a synod of one against whom proceedings are brought must be in writing and allow a suitable interval.

According to the canonical decrees of the Fathers, the summons to the synod of the person against whom proceedings are brought must be made by reasonable written notices [Note: [Col. 0717D] *By reasonable written notices*: Damasus’s epistle reads in place of these words: “both by their personal presence and by writings and envoys.” Yet Anselm, Burchard, the author of Polycarpus, and Ivo agree with the vulgate reading.] over a suitable and canonical period. For unless he has been canonically summoned at the appropriate time and in canonical manner, even if he comes to the assembly through some necessity, he is in no way to answer his assailants unless he wishes to do so voluntarily.

### C. II. At what intervals the accused person is to be summoned to the case.

Likewise Pope Silvester [Note: [Col. 0717] An uncertain chapter; Anselm, book 3, c. 120; Polycarpus, book 5, title 3.]:

By the present decree we ordain that they are first summoned paternally [Col. 0717B] [Note: [Col. 0717] *personally*: Anselm] and awaited for seven days, without any prohibition of access to any ecclesiastical matter. To this waiting period another seven days are then added, with access to church and the hearing of all divine offices prohibited. Then two days are added [Note: [Col. 0717] *be added*: same source; Basle edition], during which they are suspended from the peace and communion of the holy Church. Thereafter they are again kept under the same waiting period for another two days [Note: [Col. 0718D] *They are kept*: previously the reading was “they are awaited” [Col. 0717] as in all collected editions except the Argentinian. It has been corrected from Polycarpus, Anselm, and old copies of Gratian, in some of which occurs the interlinear gloss: “that is, they are awaited.”]. When one day has been added to these, all further waiting being regarded as now hopeless, let the accused immediately be struck with the sword of anathema.

### C. III. No accusation is to be received through writings.

Likewise Pope Damasus, to the bishops of Italy, Epistle VI [Note: [Col. 0717] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Anselm, book 3, c. 48; Polycarpus, book 5, title 1.]:

It has been reported to the apostolic see that you receive accusations against brethren by written documents, without a lawful accuser. By apostolic authority we forbid this henceforth throughout the entire world [Col. 0717C]; and we take care that what has recently been done be corrected without any delay [Note: [Col. 0717] *we ask that it be corrected*: original]. Nor may it ever be permitted to examine by writings the case [Note: [Col. 0717] *cases*: collected editions] of those who are accused before they have been canonically summoned to the synod through the formal complaint of those making the accusation, so that a present person may truly know and understand from one who is present [Note: [Col. 0717] add: “these things”: same source] what is objected to him.

And below, § 1: For secular laws require accusers to be present, not absent through writings. Hence the canonical enactments of the Fathers proclaim, not once but very often, that neither accusations nor any testimony [Note: [Col. 0717] *testimonies*: original] may be presented through writings, and that no one may testify concerning matters other than those [Col. 0718A] known to have been done in his presence. Likewise, whoever chooses to accuse another must accuse in person and by himself, not through another, after first filing an inscription. Nor may anyone ever be judged before he has lawful accusers present and has received an opportunity to defend himself and clear away the charges. Care must also be taken [Note: [Col. 0717] *also*: collected editions] that anger not seize anyone unawares [Note: [Col. 0717] *steal upon anyone*: same editions] and make him quickly do everything that is unlawful [Note: [Col. 0717] *may be lawful*: Basle edition].

### C. IV. Those driven out by force or fear, or stripped of their possessions, are not to be summoned to a synod.

Likewise Pope Felix II, to Athanasius and all eastern bishops, Epistle I, chapter 3 [Note: [Col. 0717] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Council of Carthage, held A.D. 419, c. 24; Burchard, book 1, c. 221; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 335.]:

If the primates cannot amicably reconcile with them the accusers of bishops, then at a lawful time they are to summon them canonically to a synod [Note: [Col. 0717] add: *before*: Basle edition; *previously*: collected editions] convened [Col. 0718B] not within [Note: [Col. 0717] *within*: cited collections and collected editions] narrow periods; and they must first notify them in writing what [Note: [Col. 0717] *whatever*: Basle edition] is alleged against them, so that they may come prepared to answer. For if they have been driven out by force or fear, or stripped of their possessions [Note: [Col. 0717] *by their own people*: same source], they can neither be canonically summoned to a synod nor ought to answer their adversaries before they have been canonically restored and all their property has legally been returned to them.

Gratian. These authorities make it entirely clear that unless someone has been canonically summoned, even if he comes to a synod on some occasion, he is by no means compelled to answer his assailants. A canonical summons is one in which, after the prescribed intervals of days have been observed according to the authority of blessed Silvester, he is ordered by letters to attend his case; and those letters, according to the authority [Col. 0718C] of Pope Felix, must state what is alleged against him.

## QUESTION III

## GRATIAN

That one who is prevented from attending his case may conduct it through his agent seems proved by the authority of the Roman synod held in the time of Pope Hadrian, in which chapter 5 is recorded as follows [Note: [Col. 0717] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. C. 4, q. 5, sole chapter; Burchard, book 1, c. 51; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, c. 19; *Decretum*, part 5, c. 161; Polycarpus, book 5, title 1.]:

### C. I. Let the person burdened by grave necessity send a representative to the synod in his place.

If a bishop is ill, or some grave necessity detains him, he is to send a representative to the synod in his place. Nor is the person against whom a charge is brought to be suspended from communion unless, having been summoned by letters from the chosen judges to state his case on the appointed day, he fails to appear—namely, unless some extraneous necessity has intervened, within [Note: [Col. 0719] *within*: Lyons II and III editions] a period of two or three months, or longer [Note: [Col. 0719] *or*: collected editions], as the case requires.

Gratian. Code, book IX, title *On Accusations and Inscriptions*, law 3:

Emperor Alexander Augustus: The laws governing public trials permit persons accused of capital crimes, even when absent, to be defended through an agent.

§ 1. Here it is stated that a bishop who is prevented and unable to attend his case is ordered to send a representative to the synod in his place. But this representative is sent not to conduct the case, but to explain to the synod the necessity [Col. 0719B] that prevented the bishop from appearing before it. No one is permitted to conduct a case, especially a criminal case, except in person.

Therefore Pope Hadrian says in the *Capitularies*, chapter 38 [Note: [Col. 0719] Anselm, at the end of book 3; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, c. 36.]:

### C. II. One accusing or accused criminally must proceed in person.

In criminal cases, an accuser may accuse no one except in person, nor is an accused person permitted to defend himself through another person.

### C. III. In every case except criminal cases, bishops and priests may have an advocate in their place.

Likewise Pope Anacletus [Note: [Col. 0719D] This chapter attributed to Anacletus occurs in the council of Pope Eugene II, held under Emperors Louis and Lothair, chapter 19. It was also repeated by Leo IV. From this canon Lothair, in book II of the Lombard laws [Col. 0720D], title *On Advocates and Vice-Domini*, composed the eighth capitulary.] [Note: [Col. 0719] from the Roman Council held A.D. 826.]:

Because a bishop and all priests are appointed solely for [Col. 0719C] the praise of God and the performance of good works [Note: [Col. 0719] *performance*: original and Basle edition], each of them ought, both for ecclesiastical affairs and for his own cases—except, that is, for a public crime—to have an advocate, not a person suspected of ill repute, but one found to have good standing and an honourable profession, lest, while they attend to human gain, they lose eternal rewards.

## QUESTION IV

## GRATIAN

That a bishop ought not be condemned without a synodal hearing is proved by the authority of Pope Julius [Note: [Col. 0719] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 1, title 32, c. 1; Anselm, book 3, c. 86; cf. Hadrian’s *Capitularies*, c. 3; *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, book 6, c. 287.], who says in Epistle I:

### C. I. A bishop may not be judged, heard, or condemned except in a lawful synod.

No bishop who is accused of certain charges may be heard, judged, or condemned except in a lawful synod, convened at the appropriate time by apostolic authority [Col. 0720A]. If certain persons have presumed otherwise, what they have done is to be declared void and in no way counted among ecclesiastical enactments [Note: [Col. 0720D] *Enactments*: this word is absent from the original and the other cited passages.].

### C. II. An accused bishop is to be heard by twelve; the conclusion of the case is to be referred to the apostolic see.

Likewise Zephyrinus, Archbishop of the City of Rome, in Epistle I to the bishops of Sicily [Note: [Col. 0719] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Gregory the Great, book 5, epistles 53 and 54; Anselm, book 3, c. 45 (41); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 245; Polycarpus, book 5, title 4.]:

Every accused bishop, if necessary, is to choose twelve judges, by whom his case may be judged justly. He is not to be heard, excommunicated, or judged before those judges have been chosen by him personally, and, having been regularly summoned [Note: [Col. 0719] *summoned* in the feminine: original and Ivo], his case is first justly heard and reasonably decided by them in the assembly of his own bishops [Col. 0720B]. But the conclusion of his case is to be referred to the apostolic see, that it may be completed there; nor is it to be concluded before then [Note: [Col. 0719] the words enclosed in asterisks do not occur in Anselm.]—as was formerly established by the apostles or their successors—until it is confirmed by that see’s authority.

Gratian. The prohibition against condemning a bishop without a synodal hearing must be understood without prejudice to the Roman see, which by its authority can condemn anyone or absolve those condemned. Hence Pope Gelasius [Note: [Col. 0719] C. 9, q. 3, c. 16]: “These are the canons,” etc. Below, in Cause IX: “Marked by a sentence of excommunication.”

§ 1. Likewise Hadrian, chapter 8: Saving in all things the primacy of the Roman Church, it is clear that the synod of each province administers those matters which concern that province, as is shown to have been decreed in the Council of Nicaea. But when the accused comes before the council, whatever is done in the deliberations of those sitting [Col. 0720C], or proposed by the accusers, must be set forth not in contentious voices but with the gentlest presentation of words.

Therefore in the Eleventh Council of Toledo, chapter 1, we read [Note: [Col. 0719] held A.D. 675; Anselm, at the beginning; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, c. 245]:

### C. III. Contentious persons have no place in the hearing of cases.

The priests of the Lord, seated in the place of blessing, ought neither to make a din with unrestrained voices [Note: [Col. 0719] “no one ought”: editions compared with the original], nor be disturbed by any tumults [Note: [Col. 0719] “to disturb”: editions compared with the original], nor engage in idle tales or laughter; nor—what is worse—pour forth tumultuous voices in obstinate disputes [Note: [Col. 0719] “contentions”: Spanish Collection; Anselm]. For if anyone, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0719] Jas. 1:26], thinks himself religious while not restraining his tongue [Col. 0721A], but deceiving his heart, that person’s religion is vain. For justice loses its worship when a noisy crowd of interrupters [Note: [Col. 0721] “whirlwind”: editions compared with the original] confounds the silence of judgment, as the Prophet says [Note: [Col. 0721] Isa. 32:17]: “The worship of justice shall be silence.” Therefore whatever is done in the deliberations [Note: [Col. 0721] “conferences”: Spanish Collection] of those sitting in judgment, or is proposed by the accusers [Note: [Col. 0721] *ab* absent in the Spanish Collection and Ivo; “or by the litigants”: Isidore, Merlin edition], ought to be presented in so calm a manner of speech that it neither disturbs the understanding [Note: [Col. 0721] “the hearing”: Spanish Collection; “the ears of the hearers”: Anselm] of those hearing it with contentious voices, nor weakens the force of judgment by tumult [Note: [Col. 0721] “of those judging”: Spanish Collection, Anselm; “of judges”: Ivo; “of just judgment”: Argentinian edition; “of judgments”: remaining editions]. Therefore whoever, in an assembly of a council, believes that the foregoing provisions may be violated, and contrary to these prohibitions disturbs the council by tumult, insults, or laughter [Note: [Col. 0721] “disturbs”: cited Collections and editions compared with the original], in accordance with the decree of divine law, which commands [Note: [Col. 0721] “which commanded”: Basel edition] [Note: [Col. 0721] Prov. 22:10]: “Cast out the scoffer, and contention will depart with him,” shall be removed from the session [Col. 0721B] [Note: [Col. 0721] “confession”: Ivo; Basel and Lyons I editions] from the common assembly with every disgrace [Note: [Col. 0721] “with every shameful disgrace of confusion”: Spanish Collection; “with confusion and disgrace”: Anselm], and shall undergo a sentence of excommunication for three days [Note: [Col. 0721] “shall bear”: editions compared with the original].

## QUESTION V

## GRATIAN

The question now is whether a person is to be judged malevolent because he reports another’s crime. On this point Blessed Augustine writes in Sermon III on the common life of clerics, or Rule 3, saying [Note: [Col. 0721] The book *On the Common Life of Clerics* is not Augustine’s, but was compiled by an unknown author from Augustine’s letter to Seleucianus]:

### Chapter I. He who conceals a crime does more harm than one who reports it in friendship.

Do not judge yourselves malevolent when you report another’s crime. For you are not more innocent [Note: [Col. 0721] “you are guilty”: editions compared with the original] if, by keeping silent, you allow your brothers to perish when you can correct them by reporting them [Col. 0721C]. If your brother has a bodily wound which he wishes concealed because he fears being cut, do you not cruelly keep silent about it and mercifully reveal it? How much more, then, ought you to disclose a crime [Note: [Col. 0721] *est* absent in the Basel edition; “him”: original], lest it rot more grievously in the heart?

### Chapter II. One who spares is not necessarily a friend, nor one who strikes an enemy.

The same, to Vincentius the Donatist and Rogatist, Letter XLVIII [Note: [Col. 0721] Written A.D. 408, Letter 103, Maurist edition; cf. C. 23, q. 4, c. 37]:

Not everyone who spares is a friend, nor everyone who strikes is an enemy. The wounds of a friend are better [Note: [Col. 0721] Added: “for”: editions compared with the original; cf. Prov. 27:6] [Col. 0722A] than the willing kisses of an enemy. It is better to love with severity than to deceive with gentleness.

§ 1. It is more useful for bread to be taken from a hungry person, if, secure in food, he was neglecting justice, than for bread to be broken for a hungry person so that, led astray, he may assent to injustice [Note: [Col. 0721] “unjustly”: Basel edition].

§ 2. Both the one who binds a madman and the one who awakens a lethargic person are troublesome to them both [Note: [Col. 0721] Added: “is, and yet”: Basel edition], yet each loves both.

§ 3. Who can love us more than God? Yet he never ceases not only gently to teach us, but also beneficially to terrify us. Along with the gentle fomentations by which he consoles [Note: [Col. 0721] Added: “God”: editions compared with the original; “all”: Lyons II, III, Venice I, II, Nuremberg, and Paris editions], he often also adds the most biting medicine of tribulation [Note: [Col. 0721] “adds”: editions compared with the original]. He exercises the patriarchs, even the devout and religious, by hunger [Note: [Col. 0721] Gen. 42]; he chastens a rebellious people with harsher punishments; when asked three times, he does not remove from the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0721] 2 Cor. 12] the thorn of the flesh, so that power may be perfected in weakness [Col. 0722B].

And below, § 4: Know [Note: [Col. 0721D] In Blessed Augustine the reading is “and know,” and this clause depends upon the preceding part of the sentence: “and you think that no force ought to be applied to a man,” etc.] that sometimes a thief scatters fodder to draw away livestock [Note: [Col. 0721] “in drawing away”: Basel edition], and sometimes a shepherd recalls wandering livestock to the flock with a whip.

### Chapter III. One who is chastised and rebuked is not hated, but loved.

Likewise, from Ambrose’s Sermon LXXXIV, which begins, “Perhaps more bitter”:

A father does not always kiss his son, but sometimes chastises him. Therefore, when one who is loved is chastised, care is being exercised toward him. For love too has its wounds, which are sweeter when inflicted most bitterly [Note: [Col. 0721] “more bitterly”: original; “you love most bitterly”: Basel and Lyons editions]. Religious chastisement is sweeter than indulgent remission. Hence the Prophet says [Col. 0722C] [Note: [Col. 0721] Prov. 27:6]: “The wounds [Note: [Col. 0721] “stripes”: Basel edition] of a friend are sweeter than the willing kisses of an enemy.”

Gratian. From these words it is understood that the person who pursues a crime by accusation or report contributes more to a brother’s welfare than one who endeavors to encourage it by concealment. But Pope Eusebius appears to decree the contrary when, in accusations against bishops, he forbids the admission of persons who voluntarily confess others’ crimes. He says in Letter I to the Bishops of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0721] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, compiled from the Council of Carthage held A.D. 421, c. 6; Ambrose, Letter 64; Anianus on Paul, book 5, title 15, § 2; Theodosian Code, book 9, title 1, c. 18; and Ennodius’s *Apology*; Anselm, book 3, c. 25]:

### Chapter IV. Those voluntarily confessing the crimes of others are not to be admitted to make an accusation.

Those suspected either in the Catholic faith or through enmity [Col. 0723A] are not to be admitted to impeach bishops [Note: [Col. 0723] “the aforesaid”: Anselm], because unbelief and enmity commonly obstruct truthfulness of profession. Nor are those to be believed or admitted who voluntarily confess the crimes of others. Therefore the truth which a voice spontaneously brought forth cannot possess in them [Note: [Col. 0723] Added: “of anyone”: Basel edition] must be examined carefully anew. A religious torturer [Note: [Col. 0723] “rigorous”: original] ought to extract it from its hiding places by various tortures, so that, while bodies are subjected to bodily punishments [Note: [Col. 0723] “bodies”: Basel edition], what was done may be investigated faithfully and truthfully.

### Chapter V. On the same matter.

Likewise in Proverbs, chapter 11 [Note: [Col. 0723] Prov. 11:13; 25:8]:

“He who walks deceitfully reveals secrets; but he who is faithful conceals what has been entrusted by a friend.” Likewise below, chapter 25, § 1: “What your eyes have seen, do not quickly bring forth [Col. 0723B] in a quarrel, lest afterward you be unable to make amends when you have dishonored your friend.”

Gratian. But it is one thing, from charity, to bring forward others’ crimes, so that those whom we cannot correct by secret admonition may, once convicted, be rebuked by a judge’s sentence; and another thing to bring false charges by plotting, or easily to reproach true charges in insult. The former is the office of charity; the latter, of impiety.

§ 1. Hence in the same Proverbs, chapter 12, it is said [Note: [Col. 0723] Prov. 12:6]: “The words of the wicked lie in wait for blood; the mouth of the righteous shall deliver them.” And below: “He who speaks what he knows is a judge [Note: [Col. 0723D] “Judge”: so also in Bibles printed at Complutum and Antwerp. But some manuscripts have *index*, ‘informer.’ In Greek: ἐπιδεικνυμένην πίστιν ἀναγγέλει δίκαιος, ὁ δὲ μάρτυρ τῶν ἀδίκων δόλιος—that is: “The righteous person gives clear testimony, but the witness of the unjust is deceitful.”] of justice; but he who lies is a deceitful witness” [Note: [Col. 0723] Prov. 12:17]. Likewise [Note: [Col. 0723] ibid., v. 19]: “A truthful lip shall be firm forever; but a hasty witness fashions a tongue of lying.” Likewise [Col. 0723C] in chapter 13 [Note: [Col. 0723] Prov. 13:3]: “He who guards his mouth guards his soul; but he who speaks rashly [Note: [Col. 0723] “is rash in speaking”: Vulgate; Argentinian edition] shall suffer evils.” And below [Note: [Col. 0723] ibid., v. 5]: “The righteous shall detest a lying word; but the wicked man brings shame and shall be put to shame.”

§ 2. Likewise Augustine on Psalm 37: If at any time through human weakness our feet move toward some sin, the tongues of most wicked enemies rise up [Note: [Col. 0723] “most wicked”: Argentinian and Basel editions]; when pity was called for, the wicked mock at what causes the godly grief.

## QUESTION VI

[Col. 0724A]

## GRATIAN

### First Part. He who cannot prove what he alleges ought to be punished.

Hence Pope Hadrian says in the Capitularies, chapter 41 [Note: [Col. 0723] Anselm, at the end of book 3, among Hadrian’s chapters; Capitularies, book 7, c. 348]:

### Chapter I. Let one who brings false charges against others be punished.

Everyone who brings false charges against others shall be punished, and for his falsehood shall bear infamy.

### Chapter II. On the same matter.

Likewise Pope Gregory:

He who does not prove a charge which he has brought ought to incur the penalty which the accused would certainly have suffered had he proved it.

### Chapter III. By what penalty one who does not prove a charge brought is punished.

Likewise in the Register [Note: [Col. 0724D] These words have not been found in the Register of Blessed Gregory, but all occur in his *Life* written by John the Deacon, book 4, c. 31. After citing Letter 66, book IX, written to the subdeacon Anthemius, John draws these statements from it: “Therefore Gregory orders the subdeacon, who had not proved what he alleged, to be deprived of office, because according to the canonical judgments of the Fathers, one who [brings] a calumnious charge,” etc., to the end. As this chapter was taken from John the Deacon, so chapter 1, title *On Calumny*, in the Decretals, was taken from Gregory’s own letter to Anthemius] [Note: [Col. 0723] John the Deacon, *Life of Gregory the Great*, book 4, c. 31]:

[Col. 0724B] Since, according to the canonical judgments of the Fathers, one who does not prove a charge which he has brought must incur the penalty which the accused would certainly have suffered had he proved it; and since for this reason the subdeacon was unable to prove the crime against the deacon, because he did not possess imposition of hands—which he could not have lacked—he was deprived not only of priesthood but also of office, and, as truly infamous, deserved to be chastised with stripes. For where any crime is proved against a man with three witnesses, as against a layman, it is no wonder that, if he cannot prove what he alleged, he is subjected, as a layman, to bodily infamy by analogy of law. For what it was for a deacon to lose his rank, that was for a subdeacon to lose the fullness of his good name.

[Note: [Col. 0724D] “Only”: this word is absent from the original, but has not been removed on account of the gloss.]

Gratian. In Book I of the Code, under the title *On Bishops and Clerics*, law 8, Emperor Theodosius states:

### Second Part

§ 1. Presbyters shall give testimony without the indignity of interrogation [Note: [Col. 0723] “interrogations”: editions compared with the original], provided nevertheless that they do not feign falsehood. But other clerics, who next follow their [Note: [Col. 0723] “him”: original] rank or order, if asked to give testimony, shall be heard as the laws prescribe [Note: [Col. 0723] “shall wish”: Basel edition], provided that litigants retain an action for false testimony, should presbyters—who are commanded to give testimony concerning matters of higher rank in their own name without any bodily indignity [Col. 0725A] [Note: [Col. 0723] “against”: ibid.]—suppress the truth precisely because they fear nothing [Note: [Col. 0725] “fear”: editions compared with the original]. For those on whom so much honor has been conferred by our command are much more deserving of punishment if they are found secretly [Note: [Col. 0725] “secretly”: editions compared with the original] guilty of a crime.

Likewise, Constitution Three, Collation IX:

§ 2. Presbyters [Note: [Col. 0725] Novella 123, c. 20; Authentica *Presbyteri*, Code, ibid.] or [Note: [Col. 0725] absent in the Argentinian, Basel, Venice I, and Nuremberg editions] deacons, if they give false testimony in a pecuniary case, shall be separated from divine ministry for three [Note: [Col. 0725] “twelve”: Argentinian, Basel, Nuremberg, and Venice II editions] years only and consigned to a monastery; if in a criminal case, they shall be stripped of clerical honor and subjected to the lawful punishments. Other [Note: [Col. 0725] absent in the Argentinian, Basel, Nuremberg, and Venice II editions] clerics, expelled from ecclesiastical office by common law [Note: [Col. 0725C] These words, “expelled from ecclesiastical office by common law,” are absent from the manuscripts and from the editions compared with the original, except Venice I and Lyons; they nevertheless occur in the translation contained in the Code. Gratian did not reproduce precisely the words either of the old translation, or of Julian, or of Irnerius. It would therefore be worthwhile to consult the Greek Novella itself and the current translations, for some significant variants exist], shall, without distinction of case, be lawfully punished.

### Chapter IV. One who does not prove the charge brought shall not approach the ministry of holy communion.

Likewise Gregory, to Januarius, Bishop, book III, Letter 24 [Note: [Col. 0725] Letter 17, written A.D. 594, book 4, Maurist edition]:

[Col. 0725B] Third Part. Epiphanius [Note: [Col. 0725C] “Epiphanius”: the following precedes in the letter: “Moreover, you know Epiphanius, the presbyter, bearer of these letters, [who has been accused] by certain …”], a presbyter, was criminally accused in letters by certain priests [Note: [Col. 0725] “Sardinians”: original]. Having investigated his case as best we could and found none of the charges [Note: [Col. 0725] Added: “crimes”: Basel and Lyons I editions] alleged against him, we absolved him so that he might return to his own place. We therefore wish you to investigate the authors of this accusation against him [Note: [Col. 0725] “this”: Basel edition; wanting in the rest], and unless the person who sent those letters [Note: [Col. 0725] “that letter”: editions compared with the original] is prepared to demonstrate by canonical and most stringent proofs what he alleged [Note: [Col. 0725] “alleges”: Lyons II and III; “shall have alleged”: Basel], he shall by no means approach the ministry [Note: [Col. 0725] “mystery”: original] of holy communion.

### Chapter V. By what penalty an informer is to be punished.

Likewise from the decree of Pope Hadrian, chapter 49 [Note: [Col. 0725D] Found among Hadrian’s chapters, c. 49, apparently derived from secular laws. For nearly the same thing occurs in the Theodosian Code, book X, title 10, law 2; and precisely the same thing in Capitularies, book 7, c. 360] [Note: [Col. 0725] Anselm, among Hadrian’s chapters at the end of book 3; Capitularies, book 7, c. 360]:

The informer’s tongue shall be cut off [Note: [Col. 0725] “amputated”: Argentinian edition], or, if convicted, his [Col. 0726A] head shall be cut off.

§ 1. Informers are those who betray others through envy [Note: [Col. 0725] “from their own envy”: Basel edition].

### Chapter VI. On the same matter. PALEA.

[Likewise from the Council of Elvira [Note: [Col. 0725] Held no later than A.D. 310; Capitularies, book 6, c. 317, book 7, c. 205; Burchard, book 6, c. 27; Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, c. 156].]

“If any informer [Note: [Col. 0725] “Of informers”: Basel edition] is a member of the faithful, and through his information someone [Note: [Col. 0725] Added: “of the faithful”: Ivo, Burchard, and editions compared with the original] has been proscribed or killed, it has been decreed that he shall receive communion only at the end [Note: [Col. 0726C] “Only at the end”: in the council itself and the Capitularies the reading is “not even at the end,” repeatedly found in many decrees of that council. But the reading found here and in Burchard and Ivo accords with canon 13 of the Council of Nicaea, which decrees: “Concerning those who are approaching death, the ancient canonical law shall still be observed, so that if anyone departs from the body, he shall by no means be deprived of the last and necessary provision.” Innocent I, Letter 3, c. 2, to Exsuperius, Bishop of Toulouse, explains this controversy fully]. If the cause has been less serious [Note: [Col. 0725] “milder”: Nuremberg edition], he may receive communion within [Note: [Col. 0725] “i tra”: Burchard; Basel edition] five years. If he is a catechumen, after the period of five years [Note: [Col. 0725] “five-year period”: editions compared with the original] he shall be admitted [Note: [Col. 0725] “is admitted”: same, first Basel edition] to baptism.”

### Chapter VII. One who stains an innocent person with a false charge shall be cleansed by a long penance at the priest’s discretion.

Likewise from the Eighth Synod [Note: [Col. 0726C] In printed editions this chapter bore the heading *Palea*, which has been removed on the authority of all the ancient copies collated. It occurs in the Rule of Monks of Blessed Isidore, c. 17] [Note: [Col. 0725] Rather, from Isidore’s Rule of Monks, c. 17; Collection in three parts, part 2, title 14, c. 26; the name *Palea* is absent in the Argentinian, Basel, and Venice II editions]:

[Col. 0726B] If anyone tells a falsehood or stains an innocent person with a false charge, he shall be purified by a long penance, at the priest’s discretion.

### Chapter VIII. A secular person or layperson who harasses a church or cleric with a calumnious charge shall be restrained from communion.

Likewise from the Council of Agde, c. 32 [Note: [Col. 0725] Held A.D. 506; Burchard, book 15, c. 5; Anselm, book 3, c. 116; Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, c. 367, part 16, c. 6]:

But if any secular person [Note: [Col. 0725] absent in the Basel edition] attempts [Note: [Col. 0725] “presumes”: editions compared with the original] to harass a church or cleric through a calumnious accusation, and is convicted [Note: [Col. 0725] “proved guilty”: Ivo, part 16; Burchard], he shall be restrained from the thresholds of the church [Note: [Col. 0725] Added: “his own”: editions compared with the original, first Basel edition] and from communion with Catholics, unless he performs worthy penance.

## CAUSE VI

[Col. 0725]

[Col. 0725C] GRATIAN

Two fornicators, also branded with infamy, seek to accuse a certain religious bishop of simony. [Col. 0726C] The defendant requests the judgment of an archbishop of another province; finally the accuser fails in proof, and the defendant is compelled to establish his innocence. (Question I.) Here it is first asked [Col. 0727A] whether persons entangled in crime or branded with infamy are to be admitted to such an accusation. (Question II.) Second, if the bishop wishes to turn the accusation against them, whether his simple assertion is to be believed. (Question III.) Third, whether he may seek the judgment of an archbishop of another province. (Question IV.) Fourth, whose judgment he should seek if the bishops of his own province happen to disagree concerning their decision. (Question V.) Fifth, if the accuser fails in proof, whether the defendant is to be compelled to prove his innocence.

## QUESTION I

## GRATIAN

[Col. 0727B] First Part. Pope Anacletus attests that persons entangled in crime cannot accuse others, saying in Letter II to the Bishops of Italy [Note: [Col. 0727] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Council of Carthage II, c. 6]:

### Chapter I. A priest may not be accused by criminals.

Since a priest is commanded to be chosen without crime, he is by no means permitted to be accused or subjected to a calumnious charge by persons entangled in crimes [Note: [Col. 0727] “criminals”: editions compared with the original], nor by any other persons than those who are free from crime and are able to be ordained priests in accordance with election [Note: [Col. 0727D] “In accordance with election”: thus in all the collated manuscripts except one, which has “by a just election,” and the Basel edition likewise reads “which is just.” Printed editions read, “in accordance with canonical election.” But the letter itself reads: “and in accordance with election, if necessity requires or if they themselves choose to serve the Lord willingly, they may become and be ordained priests without crime, and may in all respects be such as priests are commanded to be chosen”], and who are found in all respects such as priests are commanded to be chosen.

### Chapter II. The infamous, and those who through culpability cannot be advanced to the priesthood, must not accuse priests.

Likewise Pope Hadrian, in the Capitularies, chapter 21 [Note: [Col. 0727] Anselm, at the end of book 3; Polycarpus, book 5, title 1; Capitularies, book 7, c. 437]:

We call infamous all those whom the laws of the secular world call infamous, and all those who through their culpability cannot be advanced [Col. 0727C] to the priesthood. For it is unworthy [Note: [Col. 0727] absent in the Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I, and Venice II editions] that those who cannot be what these persons are should accuse them; for, just as greater persons are not judged by lesser, so lesser persons cannot accuse them of crime.

### Chapter III. Those who cannot attain the kingdom of God are infamous.

Likewise Pope Fabian, Letter II to the Eastern bishops [Note: [Col. 0727] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Anselm, book 11, c. 33]:

Those who commit the sins of which the Apostle says [Col. 0728A] [Note: [Col. 0727] Gal. 5:21], “Those who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God,” must be carefully guarded against and, if they refuse to reform voluntarily, compelled to reform [Note: [Col. 0727] Added: “themselves”: Basel edition], because they are stained with the marks of infamy and are falling into the abyss [Note: [Col. 0727] “will be condemned,” alternatively “will fall”: Argentinian edition], unless help is given them by priestly authority.

§ 1. Likewise those of whom he himself says [Note: [Col. 0727] 1 Cor. 5:11], “With such persons [Note: [Col. 0727] “these”: Argentinian edition] do not even take food,” because they are marked by infamy, until they are healed by priestly authority [Note: [Col. 0727] “treated”: editions compared with the original, first Basel edition] and restored within the bosom of holy mother Church; for those who are outside us cannot communicate with us.

### Chapter IV. Before satisfaction, the excommunicated are not to be admitted to accusation.

Likewise Fabian, Letter II [Note: [Col. 0727] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter]:

[Col. 0728B] All those are to be barred from accusation whom the Apostle mentions when he says [Note: [Col. 0727] 1 Cor. 5:11], “With them do not even take food”; and before making satisfaction to the Church they are not to be received [Note: [Col. 0727] “accepted”: editions compared with the original, first Basel edition].

### Chapter V. Priests ought to be accused only by equals.

Likewise Pope Clement, Letter I to James, Bishop of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0728D] “Of Jerusalem”: previously “Metropolitan” [except the Argentinian, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice I, and Venice II editions]. The text has been corrected from most manuscripts, for Clement himself addresses James by this title in the letter] [Note: [Col. 0727] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. the Aachen Capitularies, A.D. 789, c. 34; Constitution of Sylvester, c. 3; Council of Carthage VII, c. 2; Capitularies of Pippin, A.D. 755, c. 9; and the *Life of Sylvester*; Anselm, book 3, c. 1]:

Blessed Peter prohibited murderers, adulterers, all those bound by criminal offenses, and persons not equal to them from harassing and accusing bishops, by the Lord’s teaching [Note: [Col. 0727] “saying”: original]; and he taught that no charge should be brought against them except by equals. And shortly afterward:

§ 1. He urged that all infamous persons, and those whom primates and the laws of the secular world do not receive [Note: [Col. 0727] “accept”: editions compared with the original, first Basel edition], as well as laypeople, should always be excluded from [Col. 0728C] accusation and harassment of bishops [Note: [Col. 0727] “should exclude”: editions compared with the original]; and he commanded that all should be subject to them [Note: [Col. 0727] Added: “to themselves”: Basel edition]. He taught [Note: [Col. 0727] “said”: Lyons I and Venice I editions] that the life of all priests is higher, holier, and distinct from that of secular and lay persons, and that all spiritual persons and priests must always be placed above carnal and lay persons [Note: [Col. 0727] “must establish and ought to be”: Anselm and editions compared with the original], since it ought to matter very little to us that we are accused and judged by such people or by a human day. He said that greater persons can by no means be accused or judged by lesser persons [Col. 0729A], because he taught that not only divine laws but also secular laws prohibit this.

### Chapter VI. A person guilty of crime cannot accuse priests.

Likewise Pope Hadrian, in the Capitularies, c. 68 [Note: [Col. 0729] Cf. above, C. 3, q. 11, c. 1, 3; Anselm, at the end of book 3]:

When someone brings a criminal charge, it must be known whether he himself was not first guilty of crime [Note: [Col. 0729] “is”: editions compared with the original; Böhm], because a criminal accusation by the defendant against anyone is dangerous [Note: [Col. 0729] “dangerous”: editions compared with the original] and must not be admitted. And below, c. 72:

§ 1. Witnesses must be free from every infamy, have wives and children, and wholly proclaim Christ.

Gratian. But not only criminals: all other persons too are excluded from accusing bishops.

[Col. 0729B] Hence Pope Anacletus says in Letter I [Note: [Col. 0729] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, taken from Ennodius, book 2, letters 19 and 22; Anselm, book 3, c. 38]:

### Chapter VII. God is not pleased by one who accuses his servants.

If everything were avenged in this world, divine judgments would have no place. He labors with superfluous expenditures for benefits, who strives to help the sun with torches. Therefore, if anyone thinks that he pleases God in this by accusing his servants, and says that he does it so that they may become better, he labors in vain and is driven more by the goads of envy than of charity; for the fullness of grace does not need addition, nor does it require any increase of commendation.

### Chapter VIII. The people cannot accuse or rebuke priests.

Likewise Telesphorus, in his only Letter, c. 3 [Note: [Col. 0729] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Jerome, Letter 1; Isidore, *Sentences*, book 3, c. 39; and the interpretation of the Theodosian Code, book 9, title 39, c. 9; Anselm, book 3, c. 12; Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, c. 314, 315]:

Priests, who with their own mouth confect the body of the Lord, must be heard [Note: [Col. 0729] “obeyed”: Anselm, Ivo, and editions compared with the original] and feared by all, not torn apart or disparaged. For the Lord’s people must by no means accuse those from whom they desire to be blessed, saved, and instructed [Note: [Col. 0729] “established”: Böhm]; nor is the crowd to be admitted to accuse them. For the people must be taught and rebuked [Note: [Col. 0729] “corrected”: Basel edition] by them, not they by the people, because [Note: [Col. 0729] Matt. 10:24] “a disciple is not above his teacher.” And below:

§ 1. Therefore, the person who accuses or desires the condemnation of priests whom God appoints accuses God’s ordinance [Note: [Col. 0729] “to accuse”: ibid.; “to condemn”: Anselm, Ivo, and editions compared with the original].

The same below:

§ 2. Those who are unsuitable must not be admitted to accusation. We judge infamous all who take up arms against the fathers—that is, priests [Note: [Col. 0729] Added: “i.e. priests”: editions compared with the original]. For all fathers [Col. 0730A] are to be revered, not rejected or plotted against [Note: [Col. 0729] “not accused or plotted against”: Basel edition; “or accused, plotted against, or defamed”: remaining editions].

### Chapter IX. On the same matter.

Likewise Pope Pius, Letter I [Note: [Col. 0729] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Isidore, *Sentences*, book 3, c. 39; Anselm, book 3, c. 32; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, c. 36; *Decree*, part 5, c. 243; Polycarpus, book 5, title 1]:

Let sheep not reproach their shepherd; let the people not accuse their bishop [Note: [Col. 0729] Added: “their”: Basel edition], nor let the crowd rebuke him, because [Note: [Col. 0729] Matt. 10:24] “a disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master.” But bishops [Note: [Col. 0729] “indeed”: Basel edition; “for”: remaining editions] are to be judged by God, who chose them as eyes for himself. They are not to be rebuked, accused, or torn apart by subjects or persons of corrupt life. And below:

§ 1. No one who does good wishes to harm another in word or deed. How much less ought a faithful person to come under suspicion of saying or doing what he does not wish to suffer? For every suspicion ought rather to be rejected [Col. 0730B] than approved or received.

Gratian. Yet this disparagement, although it arises from the vice of detractors, is nevertheless sometimes stirred up against good persons by God’s just judgment, in order that those whom either domestic presumption or others’ favor had lifted high may be humbled by disparagement.

Hence Ambrose, on Luke chapter 22:

### Chapter X. Let no one presume upon himself: by God’s command the tongues of the wicked are stirred against him.

[Note: [Col. 0729D] “Let no one”: this heading does not fit the chapter below very well and must be interpreted charitably; for David uses similar language in 2 Kings 16, speaking of Shimei.]

Imitate Peter, saying elsewhere for the third time [Note: [Col. 0729] John 21:15], “Lord, you know that I love you.” For, because he had denied three times, he confesses three times; but he denied at night and confesses by day. These things have been said so that you may know [Note: [Col. 0729] “we may know”: editions compared with the original] that no one ought to boast. For if Peter fell because he said [Note: [Col. 0729] Mark 14:29], “Even if others are scandalized in you, yet not I,” [Col. 0730C] who else can rightly presume upon himself? Finally, David too, because he had said [Note: [Col. 0729] Ps. 29:7], “I said in my abundance, ‘I shall never be moved,’” acknowledges that this boast had harmed him, saying: “You turned your face away from me, and I was troubled.”

### Chapter XI. So that good people may be beneficially humbled, the tongues of the wicked rise against them.

Likewise Gregory, book IX, Letter 39, to Theoctista the Patrician [Note: [Col. 0729] Letter 45, written A.D. 601, book 11, Maurist edition]:

There are many who praise the lives of honorable persons more [Note: [Col. 0729] Another reading: “perhaps”: editions compared with the original; original] than they ought; and lest some exaltation creep in through praise, almighty God permits evil persons to break out in detraction and rebuke, so that any fault born in the heart from the mouth of those praising may be choked by the mouth of those blaming [Col. 0731A]. Thus the Teacher of the Gentiles declares that in preaching he proceeds through [Note: [Col. 0731] “among”: editions compared with the original] infamy and good repute; he also says [Note: [Col. 0731] 2 Cor. 6:8], “As deceivers, and yet true.”

Gratian. But this authority forbids spiritual persons to be accused by carnal persons, not carnal persons by spiritual persons. This is understood from his own words, which he added in the same chapter [Note: [Col. 0731D] The statements Gratian adds—“when the head is sick,” etc.—occur in Anacletus’s third letter and in Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, book 3, c. 38], saying [Note: [Col. 0731] below, c. 13]:

“When the head is sick, the remaining limbs of the body are more easily infected,” as it is written [Note: [Col. 0731] Isa. 1], “Every head is sick, and every heart sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in it.” Therefore it is clear that the devil—who, like a roaring lion [Note: [Col. 0731] 1 Pet. 5], goes about seeking whom he may devour—persuades the hearts of peoples to bring slanders against their teachers and shepherds [Col. 0731B], or to accuse them, so that the sickly peoples, their shepherds no longer holding their reins, may run riot and fall into the depths, in order that they may at least thus be endangered. The losses of morals differ greatly from losses of temporal things, since the latter are outside us, but the former are within us. And below: “I do not think a worse evil exists [Note: [Col. 0731D] These words occur in the first letter of Alexander I] than for Christians to envy their own priests.”

Hence Felix II also says to the bishops assembled in the Alexandrian synod [Note: [Col. 0731] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter]:

### Chapter XII. It is not lawful to persecute those who rightly serve God.

The holy and great Council of Nicaea says: “Rest, and do not persecute those who rightly [Note: [Col. 0731] “perfectly minister”: original] serve God, who keep with sincere will the commands of the heavenly [Note: [Col. 0731] “heavenly”: editions compared with the original] God and are subject to our laws; [Col. 0731C] for it neither befits nor does order permit that wicked and carnal persons persecute spiritual persons.”

### Chapter XIII. Subjects ought not accuse their prelates.

Likewise Pope Anterus [Note: [Col. 0731D] “Anterus”: restored from most ancient copies. Previously the reading was “Gregory” [as in the editions compared with the original, first Basel and Nuremberg]. This chapter was compiled largely from the statements of Anacletus in Letter 3], in his only Letter [Note: [Col. 0731] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf.
