Isidore, *Sentences*, book 3, c. 38; Jerome, Letter 2 to Nepotianus and Letter 13 to Paulinus].

By reason of the people, bishops are sometimes corrupted, so that those who follow may fall more readily. When the head languishes, the other members of the body are infected. Worse [Note: [Col. 0731] Below, c. 15, and C. 9, q. 3, c. 15.] are those who corrupt the life and morals of good persons than those who plunder others’ possessions and estates. Let each person beware lest he have either an itching tongue or itching ears—that is, lest he himself malign others or listen to others maligning them. “Sitting,” says [Note: [Col. 0731] Psalm 49:20.] the Prophet [Note: [Col. 0731] Added: “the Prophet”: editions of Basle, Venice I, Lyons.], “you spoke slanderously against your brother, [Col. 0732A] and laid a stumbling-block against the son of your mother,” etc. Let each spare his tongue from slander, guard his words, and know that for all [Note: [Col. 0731] “all who”: editions Lyons II, III.] that they say about others they will be judged by their own sentence. No one willingly reports something to an unwilling hearer. Let it be the duty of each of you, beloved, to preserve not only chaste eyes but also a chaste tongue; and let no other household ever learn through them what takes place in anyone’s home. Let all have the simplicity of the dove; let them devise no deceits against anyone, nor the cunning of the serpent, lest they be overthrown by the snares of others.

Likewise Pope Lucius, in his only letter, writing to the bishops of Gaul and Spain [Note: [Col. 0731] Chapter of Pseudo-Isidore; cf. Sextus Pythagoras, Sentences 292; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 140.]:

### C. XIV. A wise person does not desire to harm.

Not everyone who harms is wise.

[Col. 0732B]

### C. XV. Slanderers of bishops are worse than robbers.

Likewise Pope Anacletus, Letter III [Note: [Col. 0731] Chapter of Pseudo-Isidore; cf. above, c. 13; Burchard, bk. 1, c. 138; Anselm, bk. 3, c. 11 (10); Deusdedit, part 3; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 239.]:

Worse are those who corrupt the life and morals of teachers than those who plunder other people’s possessions and estates. For the latter take away things outside ourselves, though they are ours; but our slanderers and corrupters of our morals, or those who take up arms against us, properly plunder us ourselves [Note: [Col. 0732D] “They plunder”: previously the reading was, “they deceive us ourselves.” It has been corrected from Isidore, book 3 *On the Highest Good*, c. 38, who, as may be inferred, reports Anacletus’s words; and it agrees very well with what precedes. Yet two ancient copies of Anacletus’s letters, one in the Vatican Library and the other in the Florentine Library, read: “they deceive not us, but properly themselves.”] [Note: [Col. 0731] “They deceive”: the cited collections and the old editions.], and therefore they are rightly infamous and deservedly are cast out from the Church. Therefore, because of the deserts of the people, the shepherds of the Church are often corrupted, so that those who follow fall more readily.

### C. XVI. On the same subject.

Likewise Pope Alexander, Letter III [Note: [Col. 0731] Chapter of Pseudo-Isidore; Anselm, bk. 11, c. 43.]:

It is the greatest iniquity to malign and accuse brethren. [Col. 0732C] Hence it is written [Note: [Col. 0731] 1 John 3:15.]: “Everyone who maligns his brother is a murderer; and no murderer has a share in the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0731] “of Christ and of God”: Basle edition.].

Gratian. It is therefore clear, as was stated above, that carnal persons are forbidden to accuse spiritual persons, but spiritual persons are not forbidden to accuse carnal persons.

## Part II

§ 1. Since, therefore, criminals and infamous persons are barred from accusations, we must consider whom the sacred authority of the canons calls infamous.

On this subject Stephen, bishop of the Roman Church, writes to Hilary, Letter I, c. 1, saying [Note: [Col. 0731] Chapter of Pseudo-Isidore; Burchard, bk. 1, c. 173; Anselm, bk. 3, c. 5; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 4, c. 66; *Decretum*, part 5, c. 291; Deusdedit, part 3; Polycarpus, bk. 5, title 1.]:

### C. XVII. Which persons are to be considered infamous.

We call infamous [Note: [Col. 0731] Cf. the interpretation on Paul, *Sentences*, bk. 1, title 2.] those persons who are marked by infamy on account of [Col. 0733A] some fault: namely, all who reject the rule of the Christian law and despise ecclesiastical ordinances; likewise thieves, sacrilegious persons, and all entangled in capital crimes; violators of tombs; *and those who willingly violate the ordinances of the Apostles, their successors, and the other Fathers*; and [Note: [Col. 0733] Cf. Proclus’s letter to Domnus of Antioch.] all who take arms against the Fathers, who are marked by infamy throughout the whole world; likewise [Note: [Col. 0733] Cf. Theodosian Code, bk. 9, title 38, c. 8, with interpretation.] incestuous persons, murderers, perjurers, robbers, evildoers, poisoners, adulterers, deserters from public wars [Note: [Col. 0733] Absent from the original; cf. Council of Arles I, c. 3.], those who seek to hold offices unworthy of them, or who unjustly seize [Note: [Col. 0733] “Take away”: Anselm, Ivo, and the old editions.] the Church’s resources; those who calumniate or accuse brethren [Note: [Col. 0733] Cf. c. 75, Council of Elvira.] without proving the charge; those [Note: [Col. 0733] Cf. the interpretation on Theodosian Code, bk. 9, title 39, c. 3.] who provoke the minds [Note: [Col. 0733] “Mind”: old editions.] of princes to anger against innocent persons; all who are anathematized or [Col. 0733B] expelled from the Church for their crimes [Note: [Col. 0733] “Rejected”: the same editions.]; and all whom either ecclesiastical or secular laws pronounce infamous. Certainly all these persons [Note: [Col. 0733] Cf. Gelasius, Letter 9.], as well as slaves before their lawful emancipation, penitents, bigamists, those who serve in the municipal curia, those not sound in body, those without a sound mind or understanding, those disobedient to the decrees of the holy [Note: [Col. 0733] Added: “Fathers”: old editions.] Fathers, and those manifestly insane—none of these, I say, ought to be advanced to holy orders; nor can these, nor freedmen [Note: [Col. 0733] Cf. Council of Carthage VII, c. 2.], nor persons under suspicion, nor persons lacking orthodox faith or worthy conduct, accuse high priests [Note: [Col. 0734] “Accuse”: in the printed [Col. 0733] and old-edition codices there followed: “nor can they in any way rightly be admitted either to accusation or to testimony.” These words have been deleted, because they are absent from the manuscripts (except one), the original, Burchard, and Ivo [though not Anselm]. In the *Panormia*, however, this final section, after the word “manifestly insane,” reads: “All these must nowhere be advanced to holy orders, nor may they in any way rightly be admitted either to accusation or to testimony.”].

### C. XVIII. A person becomes infamous who knowingly ventures to commit perjury.

Likewise Pope Fabian [Note: [Col. 0733] Rather from Halitgar of Cambrai’s penitential book, bk. 4, c. 28; cf. Rabanus’s letter to Heribald, c. 8; *Regino*, bk. 2, c. 324 (“from a penitential”); Burchard, bk. 12, c. 8; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 12, c. 65.]:

[Col. 0733C]

## Part III

Whoever knowingly [Note: [Col. 0733] Absent from *Regino*.] commits perjury shall do penance for forty days on bread and water, and for the next seven years; he shall never be without penance and shall never be admitted to give testimony. Yet after this [Note: [Col. 0733] “This”: old editions.] he shall receive communion.

### C. XIX. Ecclesiastical law also rejects accusers and persons whom secular laws do not admit.

Likewise Pope Eusebius, Letter I to the bishops of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0733] Chapter of Pseudo-Isidore; cf. C. 3, q. 5, c. 5; Anselm, bk. 3, c. 25.]:

Following the footsteps of the Fathers for the salvation of God’s servants, we also remove from such persons the permission to assail another by accusation—whatever persons the public laws do not admit to accusation; and ecclesiastical judges must hear no accusations prohibited by secular laws.

Gratian. But although infamous persons are barred from accusing bishops, they are nevertheless not to be barred from this kind of accusation. For infamous persons are not forbidden to accuse heretics, as was shown above in that [Note: [Col. 0733] “The same”: old editions; cf. C. 2, q. 7.] causa, where the accusation of superiors by inferiors was discussed.

### C. XX.

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0734] In most old copies this chapter is joined to the preceding one. It may therefore be inferred that these are Gratian’s words.] [Note: [Col. 0733] These are Gratian’s words.]:

Since inferiors are forbidden to accuse superiors in learning and morals, equals are not so forbidden by equals, nor inferiors by superiors. Therefore such persons are not to be barred from this accusation [Note: [Col. 0734] “Therefore … accusation”: this passage has been corrected from manuscripts. The printed editions read: “they are to be barred from accusations of this kind” [Basle edition: “they are not barred from accusations of this kind”]. From that reading a suitable sense can scarcely be drawn.], since a heretic is inferior to a Catholic [Col. 0734B].

But Augustine did not determine whether this should be understood generally. In book IV of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, c. 5, he says:

### C. XXI. It is uncertain whether a knowing miser or an unknowing heretic sins more gravely.

I ask, then, who sins more gravely: one who has fallen unknowingly *into* heresy, or one who knowingly has not withdrawn from avarice—that is, from idolatry? According to *that* rule by which the sins of those who know are ranked above the sins of those who are ignorant, the avaricious person who acts knowingly [Note: [Col. 0733] “The consciousness of the avaricious person”: old editions.] surpasses the other in wickedness. But lest [Note: [Col. 0733] “If”: there.] perhaps this *come about*, the very magnitude of the crime in heresy accomplishes [Note: [Col. 0733] “May accomplish”: the same editions, before Lyons II and III.] what the knowing commission accomplishes [Note: [Col. 0733] “May accomplish”: Basle edition.] in avarice, *so that* an unknowing heretic is made equal to a knowing miser [Note: [Col. 0733] “Is made equal”: old editions.]. Likewise, c. 20 of the same [Col. 0734C] book, § 1: Whether, moreover, we ought to rank a Catholic of the worst morals above some heretic in whose life people find nothing to blame [Note: [Col. 0733] “Are able to blame”: Basle edition.] apart from his being a heretic, I do not dare to give a hasty judgment.

## Part IV

Gratian. But this statement of Augustine, and that concerning the accusation of infamous persons, must be understood of those who are known to be heretics, not of those who deny that they have fallen into heresy. In the present case, however, a man who appears religious in every respect, while he denies ever having been infected with the stain of heretical communion, himself excludes infamous persons and others of this sort [Col. 0735A] from accusing him.

§ 1. Although these points seem supported by reason, they are shown to be void by the example of treason against majesty. In its accusation, when an accomplice in the conspiracy is admitted, the question is not whether merely to think against the emperor’s life is to violate majesty, but whether someone has plotted his death.

Hence the Emperors Arcadius and Honorius Augustus are recorded as having written in book IX of the Code, title *On the Julian Law of Majesty*, law 5 [Note: [Col. 0735D] This and the following chapter are joined to the preceding chapter in old copies and consequently have no headings.] [Note: [Col. 0735] Constitution 8, issued A.D. 397; Code, bk. 9, title 5.]:

### C. XXII.

If anyone [Note: [Col. 0735] “Whoever”: original.], whether with soldiers, private persons, or even barbarians, enters into a criminal conspiracy, receives or gives the oath of that conspiracy, or plots the death even of illustrious men who attend our councils [Note: [Col. 0735] “Councils”: Basle edition.] and our consistory, or of senators—for they too are part of our body—or, finally, of anyone who serves us (for the laws have willed the criminal intention to be punished with the same severity as its execution), he himself, as guilty of majesty, shall be struck by the sword [Note: [Col. 0735] “Shall strike”: old editions, before Lyons II.], all his property being assigned to our fisc. His sons, however, to whom we specially grant life through imperial clemency—for they ought [Note: [Col. 0735] “Ought to punish”: there.] to perish by their father’s punishment, since in them examples of their father’s, that is hereditary, crime are feared—shall be excluded from inheritance and succession from their mother, grandfather, and all their relatives [Note: [Col. 0735] “Excluded from their mother’s and from the succession of all”: editions of Strasbourg and Basle; “excluded from their mother’s and from the succession of all close relatives”: the other printed editions except Lyons II and III.]. They shall receive nothing under the wills of strangers; they shall remain perpetually needy and poor; their father’s infamy shall always attend them; they shall attain no offices whatsoever [Note: [Col. 0735] “Absolutely”: original, Strasbourg edition, and Böhmer.] and no sacraments whatsoever [Note: [Col. 0735] Added: “absolutely”: Basle edition; “utterly”: the remaining editions.] [Col. 0735C]; finally, let them be such that, stained by perpetual poverty, death is a consolation to them and life a punishment. We further order that those who ever attempt to intercede with us for such persons shall likewise be marked by infamy [Note: [Col. 0735] Added: “by infamy”: old editions.] without pardon. And below, § 1: Yet if any one of them, at the outset of the conspiracy, inflamed by zeal for true praise [Note: [Col. 0735] Added: “he himself”: the same editions.], reveals the conspiracy that has been entered into, he shall be rewarded and honored by us [Note: [Col. 0735] “And with a reward”: the same editions; original. “Adorned”: old editions, before Basle.]. But one who has participated in the conspiracy, even if [Note: [Col. 0735] Absent from the same editions, except Lyons and Paris.] late, nevertheless reveals its secrets while the counsels [Note: [Col. 0735] “Councils”: editions of Basle, Venice I and II, Nuremberg, Lyons I and II.] remain unknown, shall be deemed worthy only of acquittal and pardon.

Gratian. Furthermore, an accusation of simony must take precedence after the pattern of the crime of treason against majesty, as Emperor Leo is recorded to have decreed in book I of the Code, title *On Bishops [Col. 0736A] and Clerics*, law *If Anyone*. This must be understood of the accusation, not of the penalty.

Hence the Emperors Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian Augustus, in book IX of the Code, title *On the Julian Law of Majesty*, law *No One* [Note: [Col. 0735] Constitution 7; Code, bk. 9, title 5. Valens’s name is absent from the editions of Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Venice I and II; “Valerian,” on the other hand, from the Lyons editions.]:

### C. XXIII.

No one at all upon whom the torture of the rack is imposed [Note: [Col. 0735] “Offered”: old editions.] without our consultation and knowledge shall be forbidden to use the protection of military service, birth, or rank, except only in a case of majesty, in which alone all persons have equal standing.

Gratian. But since all those who may accuse of the crime of majesty are admitted in this accusation of simony, it is evident that, just as there the crime of majesty itself is not doubted but the accused is charged with having committed it, so here heresy is not denied, but the accused is challenged as to whether [Col. 0736B] he has committed heresy.

# QUESTION II

## GRATIAN

The question whether, if a bishop wishes to turn an accusation back upon his accuser, credit should be given to his bare assertion is easily resolved if the authority of the holy Fathers is carefully considered. For, as the holy Fathers determine, no credence is to be given to the confession of any person, however experienced, unless he provides suitable proofs.

Hence in the Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 29, one reads [Note: [Col. 0735] c. 89, *Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua*; cf. D. 18, c. 9.]:

### C. I. A bishop who charges someone with a crime must prove the charge in synod.

If a bishop brings a charge against a cleric or layperson, [Col. 0736C] he shall be brought before the synod for proof.

Gratian. But an objection is raised: if he knows himself alone to be aware of another’s crime, he cannot prove it by witnesses; what, then, is he to do? The First Council of Vaison, c. 8 [Note: [Col. 0735] Held A.D. 442; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 364.], determines this as follows:

### C. II. A bishop must not disclose what he cannot prove.

If a bishop knows himself alone to be aware of another’s crime [Note: [Col. 0735] “Knows”: old editions.], so long as he cannot prove it, let him disclose nothing; rather, let him work privately with the man by secret rebukes to bring him to compunction. But if the person rebuked [Note: [Col. 0735] “Corrected”: old editions, before Strasbourg.] should perhaps become more obstinate and thrust himself into public communion [Note: [Col. 0735] “Publicly”: Spanish Collection], even if the bishop lacks proof in reproving him [Note: [Col. 0735] “Him”: old editions.] whom he judges [Col. 0736D] guilty [Note: [Col. 0735] “Indicates”: the same editions, before Basle and Lyons.], he shall remain uncondemned [Note: [Col. 0735D] “Uncondemned”: the original reads: “Although he is ordered temporarily to withdraw, for the sake of a person of greater authority, from those who know nothing, so long as nothing can be proved, he shall remain in communion with all except the one who judges him guilty.”] (although [Col. 0737A] he may be ordered, by the authority of a person of higher rank, temporarily to withdraw from *those who know nothing [Note: [Col. 0737] “Who have known”: Strasbourg edition; “who has known”: Venice II and Nuremberg; “who knew”: Venice I, Lyons, Paris.], for the person’s sake [Note: [Col. 0737] “By the authority of a person of greater rank”: Spanish Collection.]), yet, so long as nothing can be proved, he shall remain in communion with everyone except the person who judges him guilty.

### C. III. Concerning a bishop who says that someone confessed his crime to him alone.

Likewise from the African Council, cc. 99 and 100 [Note: [Col. 0737] c. 5, Council of Carthage VII, held A.D. 419; Burchard, bk. 19, c. 127; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 363.]:

It was resolved that if a bishop ever says that someone confessed a personal crime to him alone, and that person denies it, the bishop must not think it an injury to himself that he is not believed on his word alone. And if, because of the scruple of his own conscience, he says that he does not wish to communicate with the person who denies it [Note: [Col. 0737D] “Communicate”: so in Carthage VII, c. 5, to which this chapter corresponds word for word. In the African Council, however, this follows: “Nevertheless, let him privately forbid him communion until he obeys,” as also in Burchard. The following words, “So long as,” etc., are the beginning of chapter 100.], then so long as his bishop does not communicate with the excommunicated person, the other [Col. 0737B] bishops shall not communicate with that bishop, so that a bishop may take greater care not to say against anyone what he cannot establish by other evidence.

# QUESTION III

## GRATIAN

It is not permitted to seek the judgment of an archbishop of another province.

Hence Gregory says in Response IX to Augustine, bishop of the English [Note: [Col. 0737] Letter 64, written A.D. 601, bk. 11, Maurist edition; cf. D. 5, c. 1.]:

### C. I. No one may judge another’s parishioner.

It is written in the law [Note: [Col. 0737] Deuteronomy 23:25.]: “When passing through another’s field of grain, you must not put a sickle [Note: [Col. 0737] “A sickle into it”: Basle edition.] into it; rather, gather and eat ears with your hand.” Therefore, you cannot [Note: [Col. 0737] “Must not”: old editions; “cannot and must not”: the remaining editions.] put the sickle of judgment into that crop [Note: [Col. 0737] “In that crop”: Strasbourg edition.] which appears [Col. 0737C] entrusted to another [Note: [Col. 0737] “To a stranger or another”: there.]. But by performing a good work, strip the Lord’s grain of the chaff of its vices [Note: [Col. 0737] “To strip”: editions of Basle, Venice I, Paris, Lyons; “stripped”: Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Venice II.], and by admonishing [Note: [Col. 0737] “Admonishing”: old editions; added: “convert”: Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Venice II.] and persuading [Note: [Col. 0737] “Commanding”: Basle and Lyons I; “eating”: Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Venice II.], convert it into the body of the Church [Note: [Col. 0737] “To crush”: Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Venice II; “to convert”: the remaining editions.].

### C. II. How many cities each province has.

Likewise Pope Pelagius II, Letter VIII, to all bishops [Note: [Col. 0737] Chapter of Pseudo-Isidore; cf. Gregory the Great, Letter 65, bk. 11; Council of Carthage III, c. 10; Theodosian Code, bk. 9, title 1, cc. 10, 16; Anselm, bk. 6, c. 107 (112); Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 4, c. 24; Polycarpus, bk. 5, title 1.]:

Know that a definite province is one that has ten [Col. 0738A] or eleven [Note: [Col. 0737] “Nine”: Basle edition.] cities, one king, and an equal number of lesser authorities under him; one metropolitan; and ten or eleven suffragan bishop-judges [Note: [Col. 0737] “Supporters”: original.], to whose judgment all cases of bishops [Note: [Col. 0737] The words “of bishops … cities” are missing in IV.], of the remaining clergy, and of cities are referred, so that they may be justly decided by them all with one voice [Note: [Col. 0737] “May be decided”: Strasbourg, Basle, Lyons I, Paris; “may be decreed”: *Panormia*, Lyons II and III.], unless the parties to be judged appeal to a higher authority. Therefore no province ought to be degraded or dishonored; but each should have within itself its judges, priests, and bishops, each according to his own rank. Whoever has a case shall be judged by the judges of his own province [Note: [Col. 0737] Added: “of the province”: Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Venice II.], not by outsiders—that is, by the just judges of his own province, not by strangers—unless, as has already been said, an appeal has been made by those to be judged.

[Col. 0738B]

### C. III. Every bishop is to submit himself to the judgment not of others, but of his primate.

Likewise Pope Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0737] This is not found among the letters of Nicholas I; Mansi therefore attributed it to the seventh council of Nicholas. Cf. D. 50, c. 13; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 1, title 62, c. 30.]:

Finally, if Suffredus knew himself guilty of such a crime that he could rightly be deprived of the episcopate, or if perhaps he felt himself burdened by an infirmity [Note: [Col. 0737] Absent from the Basle edition.] which prevented him from benefiting his neighbors at all through his office, he ought to have awaited the judgment of his own primate, not that of bishops from another diocese [Note: [Col. 0737] “To be requested”: Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Venice II.]. And if any uncertainty, or perhaps some dispute, had arisen regarding his examination [Note: [Col. 0737] Absent from the editions of Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Venice II.] or his resignation of the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0737] “Arisen”: Strasbourg, Basle, Nuremberg, Venice I and II, Lyons I.], the matter ought, according to custom, to have been referred to the Apostolic See, and all should have awaited our decrees in all these matters. Because this has been omitted [Col. 0738C] thus far, we regret it [Note: [Col. 0738D] “Omitted”: this passage was corrected from several old Gratian manuscripts. The readings were: “has been omitted—we grieve,” Basle edition; “has been omitted—we regret,” the remaining editions.], and I earnestly entreat your most beloved and glorious persons that the aforesaid Bishop Suffredus be restored to his own bishopric; and if he did anything deserving censure, the matter shall afterward be settled by correction or suitable punishment [Note: [Col. 0737] “May be settled”: Basle edition.].

Gratian. Yet there is a case in which a bishop may excommunicate another’s parishioner.

[Col. 0739A] Hence in the Council at Compiègne, c. 5 [Note: [Col. 0739] From Carloman’s capitulary, or from the council held in the palace at Verneuil, A.D. 882; Burchard, bk. 14, c. 12; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, c. 82.]:

### C. IV. When a bishop may excommunicate another’s parishioner.

It was resolved, for the common good *and because of urgent necessity*, that no bishop should take it badly if another bishop excommunicates his parishioner on account of [Note: [Col. 0739] Absent from the editions of Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Venice I and II.] plundering.

### C. V. On the same subject. PALEA.

[Likewise from the Council of Meaux, c. 2 [Note: [Col. 0739] Rather, from the same capitulary of Carloman, c. 6; *Regino*, bk. 2, c. 290; Burchard, bk. 11, c. 45; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, c. 109; cf. Compilations I and X, *On Robbery*, c. 1.]]:

> “Concerning those who have a benefice or inheritance within a parish but are parishioners of another bishop, who travel from place to place and commit robbery [Note: [Col. 0739] “Robberies”: the cited collections.] and plundering: it has been resolved that they are to be excommunicated and may not leave the parish before they have suitably made amends for what they committed [Note: [Col. 0739] “Performed”: old editions.]. Their [Col. 0739B] excommunication is to be reported to their lord and their own bishop, so that he may not receive them [Note: [Col. 0739] “Nor”: editions Lyons; “may receive them”: Basle edition.] before they return to the place where they committed robbery [Note: [Col. 0739] “Committed it”: Basle edition.] and there make full amends for everything.”

# QUESTION IV

## GRATIAN

Further, from whom judgment should be sought if the chosen judges begin to disagree among themselves is determined in the Council of Antioch, c. 14, as follows [Note: [Col. 0739C] This chapter is also cited from the Council of Laodicea in many old copies of Gratian. Yet one very ancient copy attributes it to the Council of Antioch, where it is indeed found, and it is the ancient translation.] [Note: [Col. 0739] Held A.D. 332; Burchard, bk. 1, c. 150; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 263, from Dionysius.]:

### C. I. By whom sentence is to be delivered when the bishops of the same province disagree.

If a bishop is criminally [Note: [Col. 0739] “Concerning certain criminal causes”: original.] accused before a judgment of bishops, and it happens that the bishops [Note: [Col. 0739] “Of the bishops”: there.] of the province who have assembled hold differing [Col. 0739C] opinions—some declaring him innocent and others guilty—then, in order to remove this controversy, the holy synod resolved that a metropolitan bishop from a neighboring province [Note: [Col. 0739C] “A metropolitan”: the Greek exemplar differs greatly here from this translation. From these words it may be inferred that the council of that province, at which its own metropolitan must be present, may summon the metropolitan of a neighboring province with several bishops. Martin of Braga also confirms this in the following chapter, which he took from the Council of Antioch. But the Greek passage reads: “The holy synod resolved that the bishop of the metropolis should summon from the neighboring province certain others who might adjudicate and dissolve the dispute, so that, together with the bishops of the province, they might confirm what is presented.” Dionysius, as also in the *Code of Canons*, translates it thus: “The holy synod resolved that the metropolitan bishop should summon from a neighboring province other judges, who should remove the controversy, so that through them together with the bishops of the province whatever appears just [Col. 0740D] may be approved.” And indeed, that one metropolitan should have to come at another metropolitan’s summons, and that two metropolitans would be present in the same council, scarcely seems fitting.] be summoned, together with several other bishops, who, sitting with them, shall settle whatever disputes [Note: [Col. 0739] “Whoever”: old editions; “the dispute”: the same editions and the Spanish Collection.] arise, so that the judgment pronounced by the bishops of one province may be firm.

### C. II. When chosen judges disagree among themselves concerning a sentence, an archbishop from a neighboring province is to be summoned.

Likewise from the Council of Pope Martin [that is, Bishop Martin of Braga], c. 13 [Note: [Col. 0739] The same chapter of the Council of Antioch, in Martin of Braga’s translation.]:

If a bishop is judged in certain *causes* and sees that the bishops in his own province [Note: [Col. 0739] Absent from the original.] disagree in judgment among themselves, so that [Note: [Col. 0739] Absent from the original.] some appear to acquit the man being judged and others condemn him, then, for the settlement of this disagreement, the holy [Note: [Col. 0739] “Holy synod”: old editions.] council resolved that another metropolitan bishop be summoned from a neighboring province [Col. 0740B], in order that through him what is approved according to the right canon may be confirmed.

Gratian. Unless the same province has a primate, to whom matters which cannot be settled by the metropolitan are to be referred.

Hence Pope Boniface, to the bishops [Note: [Col. 0740D] “To the bishops”: so corrected from several old codices, Burchard, Ivo, and Polycarpus. Previously it read “to the peoples.” Very similar to this chapter is Novella 123, c. 34, in Julian the Antecessor.] of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0739] Rather from Novella 123, c. 22; Burchard, bk. 1, c. 57; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 4, c. 22; *Decretum*, part 5, c. 167; Polycarpus, bk. 5, title 4.]:

### C. III. Matters which the metropolitan cannot settle are referred to the primate.

If uncertainty arises among the bishops of the same council [Note: [Col. 0739] “Counsel”: editions of Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Venice II.] about ecclesiastical law or other affairs, their metropolitan, considering the matter with others in council [Note: [Col. 0739] Added: “certain others”: cited collections and Basle edition.], shall first adjudicate it. If both parties do not [Note: [Col. 0739] “Not”: absent from the Basle edition.] accept what has been decided [Note: [Col. 0739] “What is to be decided”: Ivo, *Panormia*; “of those judging”: Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Venice I and II, Paris.], then the primate of the region shall hear them, and he shall determine whatever accords with ecclesiastical canons [Col. 0740C] and your laws [Note: [Col. 0739] “Our”: Basle edition and cited collections.], and neither party may oppose his judgment.

### C. IV. On the same subject. PALEA.

[Likewise Pope Alexander [Note: [Col. 0739] This chapter, whose origin neither Berardus nor Böhmer investigated, was taken from the Fifth Council of Orléans, held A.D. 549, c. 17; Burchard, bk. 1, c. 59; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 169.]]:

> “If a metropolitan, having been appealed to by any bishop of the same province in that bishop’s own case [Col. 0741A] [Note: [Col. 0741] “Bishop”: Burchard and Ivo add: “twice in the case,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0741] Added: “twice”: Burchard, though not Ivo in Fronto’s edition.], delays to hear him, the appellant shall be free to pursue his case at the next synod; and whatever has been established in justice by his fellow-provincial bishops must be observed [Note: [Col. 0741] “On account of”: Ivo, Burchard, and Basle edition.].”

Gratian. But if he has been condemned by the unanimous judgment of all his fellow-provincial bishops, the censure against him shall remain immovable.

Hence one reads in the Council of Antioch, c. 15 [Note: [Col. 0741] Held A.D. 332.]:

### C. V. A bishop against whom the bishops of his province have rendered a unanimous sentence cannot be judged by others.

If a bishop criminally accused receives [Note: [Col. 0741] “Excludes”: editions of Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Venice I and II, Lyons I, Paris.] one unanimous sentence from all the bishops within the province, he cannot afterward be judged by others [Col. 0741B]. Rather, the firm and ratified sentence delivered unanimously must remain against him as a concordant judgment [Note: [Col. 0741] “Against it”: old editions, before Basle.].

Gratian. It must nevertheless be understood as excepting a case in which an appeal has been made to a judge of greater authority. For then the sentence, being suspended by appeal, does not retain its force.

Hence Pope Nicholas says in the letter to King Charles which begins, “It never causes grief” [Note: [Col. 0741] Written about A.D. 868; Burchard, bk. 9, c. 49.]:

### C. VI. A decision once made may not be reconsidered, except where there is greater authority.

What has been properly decided once and deliberated with oaths having been administered must not be reconsidered by any repetition, unless perhaps there is [Note: [Col. 0741] “Is”: Basle edition.] greater authority.

[Col. 0741C]

### C. VII. In a renewal of judgment, the memory of Blessed Peter must be observed.

Likewise from the Council of Sardica, c. 4 [Note: [Col. 0741] Held A.D. 347; Anselm, bk. 2, c. 77.]:

Bishop Hosius said: “If any bishop has been adjudged in some case and thinks that he has a good case for a second [Note: [Col. 0741] “And”: Spanish Collection; yet *ut* occurs in the variant reading.] judgment to be renewed [Note: [Col. 0741] “Another judgment”: old editions; “removed”: Lyons II edition.], then, if it pleases you, let us honor the memory [Col. 0742A] of Saint Peter the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0741] Absent from the editions of Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Venice II.], by having either those who examined the matter or other bishops living in the neighboring province write to the bishop of Rome. If he judges [Note: [Col. 0741] “Adjudges”: Basle edition.] that the judgment should be renewed, let it be renewed, and let him appoint judges. But if he determines that the case is such that the proceedings ought not to be reopened [Note: [Col. 0741] “Repeated”: Spanish Collection; yet this is a variant reading.], then whatever the Roman bishop has decreed [Note: [Col. 0741] “Decreed”: Basle edition; “decrees”: Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Venice II.] shall be confirmed. If this pleases everyone, let it be established.” The synod [Note: [Col. 0741] “The whole synod”: Basle edition.] replied: “It pleases us.”

# QUESTION V

## GRATIAN

That, when an accuser is lacking, the accused is not to be compelled to furnish proof is demonstrated by Gregory’s authority. Writing to Maximus in book V, Letter 25, he says [Note: [Col. 0741] Letter 25, written A.D. 596, bk. 6, Maurist edition.]:

[Col. 0742B]

### C. I. The burden of proof does not rest on the accused.

What you request—namely, that we should send a person there in whose presence proof may be made concerning the allegations [Note: [Col. 0741] “In whose presence”: original.]—would be excusable in some fashion if reason ever imposed upon an accused person the necessity of proof. But since this burden rests not on you but on the accusers, do not fail, without delay, to come to us as we have stated.

Gratian. Likewise, the accused must prove not a denial but an exception. Code, book IV, title *On Proofs*, law *The Plaintiff* [Note: [Col. 0741] Constitution 23, issued A.D. 304; Code, bk. 4, title 19.]:

### C. II. On the same subject.

A plaintiff [Note: [Col. 0741] “Plaintiff”: original and Basle edition.] who acknowledges that he cannot prove what he asserts does not bind the defendant by necessity to show the contrary [Col. 0742C], since by the nature of things there can be no proof of a negative fact.

Gratian. This, however, must be observed when the accused person is not troubled by public repute. For then, by the authority of the same Gregory, in order to remove scandal, the accused must clear his own reputation. [Note: [Col. 0741] Cf. C. 2, q. 5, cc. 8, 9.]

# CAUSE VII

[Col. 0741]

[Col. 0741D] GRATIAN.

A certain bishop, weighed down by a long illness, asked that another be substituted for him. The supreme pontiff assented to his entreaties and granted what he had requested. Afterwards that same bishop recovered and wishes what he had formerly done to be rescinded; he brings an action against the man who had succeeded him and demands back his see as owed to him. (Question I.) Here the first question is asked: [Col. 0742D] whether, while a bishop lives, another can be ordained in the same church? (Question II.) Secondly, whether this man can reclaim the see which another received at his own intervention?

# QUESTION I

## GRATIAN

### Part I

That, while a bishop lives, another cannot be set over him [Col. 0743A] or ordained over him is determined by a council held at Auvergne, in which it is read: that, while a bishop lives, no other bishop is to be set over him or ordained over him, unless perhaps in the place of one whom a capital offence has deposed.

[Note: [Col. 0743D] Auvergne: Burchard and Ivo also cite this as from the Council of Auvergne, c. 13; but it is found in the Fifth Council of Orléans, c. 12.]

### C. I. A bishop is not to be deprived of his office on account of bodily illness.

Likewise, from the Register of Pope Gregory, Book IX, Epistle 41, to Anatolius, deacon of Constantinople.

[Note: [Col. 0743D] This chapter has been corrected and enlarged from the original.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] Ep. 43 (written A.D. 601), line 11, Maurist edition.—Burchard, Book 1, c. 188. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 304.]

Your Charity wrote to me that *our most pious lord* has directed my most reverend brother John, bishop of Prima Justiniana, to be succeeded because of the headache from which he suffers, lest perhaps, while that city does not have the rights of a bishop, it should perish at the hands of enemies—which may God forbid. Yet the canons nowhere prescribe [Col. 0743B] that a bishop should be replaced on account of illness; and it is altogether unjust that, if bodily affliction comes upon him, a sick man should be deprived of his office. *Accordingly, this cannot under any circumstances be done by us, lest through his deposition sin come upon my soul.* But it should be proposed that, if the man in charge is ill, a steward be found for him who can carry out all his care and fulfill his place in the government of the church—without his being deposed—and *in the safeguarding of the city*, so that neither almighty God may be offended nor the city found neglected.

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Our most pious lord”: these words are alike absent in Burchard and Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Has directed me”: Burchard.—The collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “To succeed”: the collected editions, except Arg., C. I.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Does not have”: original.—“May not have—perish at the hands of an enemy”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “A bishop should succeed a bishop”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “And therefore”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Comes upon”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Accordingly”: the words enclosed by asterisks are absent in Burchard and Anselm.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “If anyone is in charge”: in the Register; the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Preserve”: the same editions.]

### C. II. Affliction must not be added to those chastened by the Lord.

Likewise, Book II, Epistle 5, to Bishop Candidus.

[Note: [Col. 0743D] In the Decretals, title *On Sick Clerics*, c. 1, only the beginning of this chapter is cited, and from it what ought to be done is determined.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] Ep. 8 (written A.D. 592), line 2, Maurist edition.]

Since the judgment of God is unknown in this matter when bodily chastisement comes—whether it happens for purification or for punishment—affliction must not be added by us to those who are chastened, lest the offence of guilt, which God forbid, fall upon us.

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Happens”: original—the collected editions and first Basel edition.]

### C. III. No one ought to be deprived of his post because of illness.

The same Gregory, Book III, Epistle 13, to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse.

[Note: [Col. 0744D] “Maximianus”: thus corrected from both the printed and manuscript original; formerly it read: “to Clementinus, bishop, primate of Byzacena” [thus in the collected editions.—“To Clementius, primate of Byzacena”: Anselm].]

[Note: [Col. 0743] Ep. 13 (written A.D. 594), line 4, Maurist edition.—Anselm, Book 7, c. 124.]

Although the petition attached below explains the complaint of Adeodatus, the bearer of this letter, who says that he was improperly expelled *from* the post of his presbyterate, we have nevertheless judged that it should be set out a little more fully and clearly. For he asserts that our brother and fellow-bishop Quintianus, in order that certain of his own affairs might be arranged, granted him leave from his post, and that because of illness he was absent from his church for two months. Seizing this opportunity, our aforesaid brother ordained another presbyter there in his place. We therefore urge Your Fraternity carefully to investigate his case and strictly examine it; and, if you find that he was absent from his church, as is said, because of manifest illness, do not permit any prejudice to arise against him from the ordination of another presbyter, but have him restored to his post without any uncertainty whatsoever.

And below, § 1: We especially admonish Your Charity that, if this representation is true and he has been restored [Col. 0744B] to his order, you ought carefully and strictly to consider the case of the presbyter ordained in his place. If indeed he attained that order without any payment, so that he could not have fallen into the Simoniac heresy, we wish him to be ordained in any other vacant church. But if anything of that kind should be found in him—which may the Lord avert—let him too be deprived of the order of presbyterate, which is proved to have been assumed not to meet the church’s need but solely out of ambition.

[Note: [Col. 0743] “From”: absent in the original.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Nevertheless, a little more clearly”: collected editions—the original.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “More fully”: absent in the original and Anselm.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Examine”: absent in the original and Anselm.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “In his post”: Anselm—the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Of this kind”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “In his order”: Anselm—the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Any other vacant church whatsoever”: the same editions—Anselm.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Him”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Office or order”: Basel edition.]

### C. IV. Pontiffs are not to be removed because of infirmity or illness, nor are others to be substituted in their place.

Likewise, Pope Nicholas to Alwin, archbishop of Juvavum.

[Note: [Col. 0743] Epistle to Adalwin of Juvavum, date uncertain.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 352.—Cf. Dist. 34, c. 8.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Jovanensis”: Basel edition.—“Januanensis”: Arg. edition.]

Pontiffs afflicted by any infirmity or illness are not to be removed, nor ought others to be consecrated in their place, unless they have been taken from this life. If they complain concerning the ministry entrusted to them, let priests perform what is lawful. But in matters which they may not presume to undertake, let the assistance of neighbouring bishops be provided until health is recovered; and let this be carried out with careful caution, lest ambition for presumption spring up under the pretext of necessity. Bishops who have undertaken [Col. 0745A] the care and solicitude of the Lord’s flock ought not withdraw from its administration, so that the excellence of the talent received may not be effaced, but may be wholesomely increased through their struggle and yield fruit threefold.

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Recovered”: Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 0743] “Let them carry it out”: the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “Undertake”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “In struggle”: Basel edition.—“Struggle”: the remaining editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0745] Absent in Ivo.]

### C. V. While a bishop lives, another cannot succeed him.

Likewise, from Book IV, Epistle 2 of Cyprian, bishop and martyr, to Antonianus.

[Note: [Col. 0745] Written A.D. 252.—Anselm, Book 6, c. 58 (62). Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 359, with passages contracted here and there. Polycarpus, Book 7, title 4.]

Cornelius was made bishop by the judgment of God and of His Christ, by the testimony of almost all the clergy, by the vote of the people then present, and by the college of the ancient priests and worthy men, when no one had been made before him; when Fabian’s place—that is, the place of Peter and the rank [Col. 0745B] of the episcopal chair—was vacant. Once it had been occupied by God’s will and confirmed by the consent of us all, whoever should then wish to become bishop must necessarily be outside; nor does he have ecclesiastical ordination who does not hold the unity of the Church. Whoever he may be, however greatly he boasts of himself and however much he claims for himself, he is profane, a stranger, and outside. And since after the first there cannot be a *second*, whoever has been made after the one who alone ought to exist is no longer a second, but no bishop at all.

[Note: [Col. 0745D] “College”: this is the reading in printed and manuscript copies of Cyprian and in Polycarpus. A nearly similar expression occurs in the following chapter and at 23, q. 8, *Si quis membrorum*. Formerly it read: “consent.”]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “Consent”: Ivo—the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “Clergy and God”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “Has”: Arg., Basel, Nor., Venice I–II, Paris editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “Second”: absent in Anselm.]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “Ought”: the collected editions.]

### C. VI. He is no bishop who has intruded into a living bishop’s place.

Likewise, lower down in the same letter.

[Note: [Col. 0745] Anselm, Book 6, c. 59 (63).]

Novatian is not a bishop, since, after Cornelius had been made bishop in the Church by sixteen fellow bishops, he, an adulterer and outsider, strives through intrigue to become bishop by the agency of deserters. Since there is one Church of Christ throughout the whole world, divided into many members, and likewise one episcopate, spread abroad through the harmonious multitude of bishops, he, after God’s tradition and after the unity of the Catholic Church linked and joined together everywhere, attempts to create a merely human church and sends his new apostles through many cities in order to establish certain novel foundations [Col. 0745C] of his own institution. And whereas bishops have long since been ordained through all provinces and in every individual city—men advanced in years, sound in faith, tested in distress, proscribed in persecution—he dares [Col. 0746A] to create other pseudo-bishops over them, as though he could either traverse the whole world in the obstinacy of his novel undertaking or break apart the structure of the ecclesiastical body by sowing his discord. He does not know that schismatics always rage at their beginnings but cannot attain growth, nor enlarge what they have unlawfully begun; instead, they immediately fail together with their perverse rivalry.

And below, § 1: Therefore, one who neither keeps the unity of the Spirit nor the bond of peace, and separates himself from the Church’s bond and from the college of priests, can possess neither episcopal power nor honour, since he has refused to keep either the unity of the episcopate or peace.

[Note: [Col. 0745D] “Novatian”: the compilers rightly adapted this opening, so that the preceding material need not also be cited [Col. 0746D]. For Cyprian reads, after much intervening material: “unless perhaps he seems to you a bishop who, in the Church, [sets himself against] a bishop,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “Twelve”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “Attempts”: original.]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “Institution”: the collected editions, first Lyons II–III editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0746D] “Structure of the body”: thus corrected from several ancient copies, Anselm, and the original; formerly it read “structure of order” [thus the collected editions except Arg.].]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “Possess”: the collected editions.]

### C. VII. He who is not at peace with the bishop is not in the Church.

The same author, to Florentius Puppianus, Book IV, Epistle 9.

[Note: [Col. 0745] Written A.D. 251.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 360.]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “To Papinianus”: the collected editions.—“To Papianus”: Ivo.]

You ought to know that the bishop is in the Church and the Church in the bishop; and that, if anyone is not with the bishop, he is not in the Church. Those who have no peace with God’s priests deceive themselves in vain when they creep in and believe that they communicate secretly with certain persons, since the Church, which is one and catholic, is not rent or divided.

[Note: [Col. 0745] “Secretly”: Ivo—the collected editions.]

### C. VIII. No one ought to surrender his own right.

The same author, to Jubaianus.

[Note: [Col. 0745] Written A.D. 256.]

Holy Scripture declares how dangerous it is in divine matters for someone to yield his own right and authority: in Genesis Esau thereby lost his birthright and afterwards could not recover, or even ask for, what he had once surrendered.

[Note: [Col. 0745] “His own right and authority”: the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “Sacred”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “In Genesis”: “lost”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “Or ask for”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0745] “This”: “could”: the collected editions.]

### C. IX. Those who withdraw from bishops and divide the unity of the Church bring destruction upon themselves.

The same author, Book I, Epistle 6, to Magnus.

[Note: [Col. 0745] Written A.D. 255.]

Finally, how inseparable is the sacrament of unity, how devoid of hope such persons are, and how they acquire for themselves the greatest destruction through God’s indignation—those who make a schism and, abandoning their bishop, establish for themselves another pseudo-bishop outside—is declared by divine Scripture in the Books of Kings. There the ten tribes were divided from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, and, abandoning their king, established another for themselves outside. “And the Lord,” it says, “was angry with all the seed of Israel, and removed them, and gave them over to plunder, until He cast them away from His presence, [Col. 0747A] because Israel was divided from the house of David, and they made Jeroboam, son of Nabath, king for themselves.” It says that the Lord was angry and gave them over to destruction because, having been divided from unity, they established another king for themselves. The Lord’s indignation against those who had made a schism was so great that, when the man of God was sent to Jeroboam to rebuke him for his sins and predict the coming punishment, he was forbidden even to eat bread or drink water among them. Because he did not observe this and ate contrary to God’s command, he was immediately struck by the majesty of divine judgment, so that, on his return from there, he was killed on the road by the attack and bite of a lion.

And after a few intervening words, § 1: The Lord further satisfies in His Gospel and makes [Col. 0747B] the greater light of understanding manifest: those same persons who had then separated themselves from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, leaving Jerusalem and withdrawing to Samaria, were reckoned among the profane and Gentiles. For when He first sent *His own* disciples into the ministry of salvation, He commanded and said: “Do not go into the way of the nations, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans.” Sending them first to the Jews, He ordered the Gentiles still to be passed by. But by adding that a Samaritan city, where the schismatics were, should likewise be omitted, He showed that schismatics are equated with Gentiles.

And after a few words, § 2: Moreover, it cannot help such persons that they are said to know the same God the Father whom we know, the same Son, *Christ*, and the same Holy Spirit. For Korah, Dathan, and [Col. 0747C] Abiron, together with the priest Aaron and Moses, knew the same God; living under the same law and religion, they invoked the one true God who was to be worshipped and invoked. Yet because they transgressed the ministry proper to their station and claimed for themselves the right to sacrifice in opposition to the priest Aaron, who had received the lawful priesthood by God’s favour and ordination, they were struck by God and immediately paid the penalties for their unlawful attempts. Nor could sacrifices offered irreligiously and unlawfully against the right of the divine ordinance be valid or prosper.

The very censers in which incense had been unlawfully offered were, by the Lord’s command, melted down and purified by fire, drawn out into beaten sheets, and fastened to the altar, so that they might no longer be used by priests but might rather provide later generations with a reminder of divine indignation and vengeance directed toward their correction. As divine Scripture says: “A memorial for the children of Israel, that no foreigner who is not of Aaron’s seed may come near to offer incense before the Lord, lest he become like Korah.” Yet they had not made a schism, nor gone out and rebelliously and hostilely opposed God’s priests, as those now do who divide the Church and rebel against Christ’s peace and unity, seeking to set up a chair for themselves, assume primacy, and claim the right to baptize and to offer sacrifice.

### C. X. One who invades a living man’s place is not to be defended.

Likewise, Leo IV to Vernon, duke of Brittany.

[Note: [Col. 0747] “Gislardus”: Arg., Basel, Nor., Venice I–II editions.]

### C. XI. A bishop may not abandon his church.

Likewise, Pope Evaristus, Epistle II, to all bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0747] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore.—Burchard, Book 1, c. 76. Anselm, Book 6, c. 102 (107). Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 182.]

Just as a man ought not commit adultery against his wife, so neither ought a bishop against his church: that is, he must not abandon the church to which he has been consecrated, except through unavoidable necessity or an apostolic or canonical transfer, and join himself to another through ambition. And just as it is not lawful for a wife to leave her husband in order to unite herself in marriage with another while he lives, or commit adultery against him, even if her husband has committed fornication, but, according to the Apostle, must either be reconciled to her husband or remain unmarried; so it is not lawful for a church to abandon its bishop or separate itself from him in order to receive another while he lives. Rather, it must either retain him or remain unmarried—that is, it must not receive another bishop while its own lives—lest it incur the crime of fornication or adultery. But if it has committed adultery—that is, if it has joined itself to another bishop, brought another bishop over itself, caused one to exist, or desired one—it must either be reconciled to its own bishop through the strictest penance or remain unmarried.

And a little later, § 1: A bishop ought seasonably and unseasonably, [Col. 0749A] and without interruption, to teach his church, and prudently rule and love it, so that it may abstain from vices and be able to attain eternal salvation. And it ought to receive his teaching with such great reverence, and love and cherish him, as God’s envoy and herald of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0747] “Consecrated”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0747] 1 Corinthians 7.]

[Note: [Col. 0747] “Joined”: there.]

[Note: [Col. 0747] Cf. Clement I.]

Gratian. Behold, these authorities plainly show that, while a bishop lives, another cannot be ordained over him, not even because of his illness. But Gregory’s statement must be understood when the sick man does not ask that another be substituted for him. On the other hand, when someone, burdened either by old age or by infirmity, cannot administer the office he has undertaken, it may reasonably be done if he asks that another be substituted for him. Therefore the same chapter continues:

“If perhaps the same John, [Col. 0749B] because of his affliction, should ask to be relieved of episcopal office, then, upon his making this request in writing, it must be granted; otherwise, for fear of almighty God, we dare by no means to act.”

[Note: [Col. 0749] From the letter of Gregory the Great from which c. 1 above was taken.]

[Note: [Col. 0749D] “If perhaps the same John”: these words occur in the Register of Blessed Gregory, Book IX, Epistle 41, and follow c. *Scripsit* above.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “Are able”: the collected editions.]

Accordingly, blessed Augustine accepted the episcopal chair while his bishop had not yet died but was burdened by old age.

Therefore, in the sole letter of Paulinus to Romanianus, we read:

[Note: [Col. 0749] Written A.D. 596.]

### C. XII. Augustine did not so much succeed as join the episcopate.

We write this not merely to offer congratulations that Augustine has received the episcopate, but because, by God’s grace, the African Church deserved this care: that it might receive heavenly words from Augustine’s mouth. For, by a new custom and for the greater grace of the Lord’s gift, he was advanced and so consecrated that he did not succeed [Col. 0749C] a bishop in the chair but joined him. For while Valerius, bishop of the Church of Hippo, was still alive, Augustine was his fellow bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0749] “Wrote”: the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “Received”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “Deserved”: African Church, the same editions; first Arg. edition reads: “the African Church deserved.”]

Gratian. This same point is proved by the authority of Blessed Gregory, who substituted another for the bishop of Rimini, afflicted with head pain. Thus he writes in Book VII of his Register, Indiction 2, Epistle 49, to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna:

[Note: [Col. 0749] Ep. 19 (written A.D. 597), line 7, Maurist edition.—Burchard, Book 1, c. 189. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 305.]

### C. XIII. Another may be substituted for a bishop burdened by illness.

Your Fraternity has long known how the Church of Rimini has until now been deprived of pastoral governance because the bodily affliction of the priest ordained by us, as you know, has prevented him from exercising it. [Col. 0749D] Moved by the prayers of the inhabitants of that place, we repeatedly urged him that, if he felt himself improved from the same head pain by which he was afflicted, he should return with the Lord’s help to his church; he was allowed a delay and awaited for this purpose over these four years. [Col. 0750A] When, at the urging of clergy and citizens coming from there and pressing us with their petitions, we urged him more earnestly to return to them with the Lord’s help if he was able, he asked us in a written supplication to ordain a bishop for that church, since because of the affliction by which he is held he was utterly unable to undertake the governance of that church or the office he had accepted.

Therefore, since the charge of solicitude for all churches binds us, lest pastoral protection be lacking too long to the flock of believers, compelled by their prayers and by his renunciation grounded in his own incapacity, we judged that a bishop ought to be ordained for the Church of Rimini. Having issued the customary directions, we have not ceased to admonish the clergy and people of that church to unite in prudent agreement in electing a bishop for themselves. We therefore urge Your Fraternity to have summoned to yourself the man whom all have chosen by one consent, as they too are known to have requested of us. Examine him through careful investigation in every respect; and, if there is not found in him, with the Lord’s help, anything punishable by death according to the text of the Heptateuch, and if his life also commends itself to you through the testimony of trustworthy persons, [Col. 0750C] send him to us with the document of the decree and an accompanying letter of your own attestation, so that, by the Lord’s ordering, he may be consecrated by us as bishop of that church.

[Note: [Col. 0749] “As is known”: original.—“Because this is known”: Basel and Lyons editions.—“Because it is known”: Burchard, Ivo, remaining editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “Pastoral and sacerdotal”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “Long ago”: the same editions—Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “We urged”: the same editions—Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “By which he was held”: “held”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “Who, having been granted”: the same editions—Burchard and Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “Is awaited”: the same editions—Burchard and Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “At the urging”: “or citizens”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “There”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “Accusing”: Arg., Nor., Venice II editions—Burchard.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “God”: the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “Having given written”: the same editions—Burchard and Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “Was held”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “Of Christ”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0749D] “Heptateuch”: in this letter of Blessed Gregory and in many other places the reading is *Eptatici*, as also in Burchard, Ivo, and several old manuscripts of Gratian. This word was noted above at Dist. 15, c. *Sancta Romana*, under “Pentateuch.”]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “Contained in the Heptateuch”: the collected editions.]
