### C. XIV. On the same matter.

Likewise, from the same Register, Book XI, Epistle 7, to Bishop Etherius.

[Note: [Col. 0749] Ep. 5 (written A.D. 603), line 13, Maurist edition.—Burchard, Book 1, c. 191. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 307.]

[Note: [Col. 0749] “Eleutherius”: Böhm, less correctly.]

Although what we must say greatly saddens us, and brotherly compassion urges us rather to weep than permits us to determine anything from what we have heard, nevertheless the solicitude of the government entrusted to us pricks our heart with an urgent goad, compelling us to provide with great care for the churches*, and*, with God as author, to determine what must be done lest any of their welfare perish*.

It has therefore been reported to us by some persons [Col. 0750D] that a certain bishop [Col. 0751A] has incurred such an affliction of the head that he is accustomed, with his mind deranged, to utter groans and cries. Therefore, lest the flock, its shepherd being sick—which may God forbid—be exposed to be torn by the teeth of the assailant, or the interests of that church decay, we must make careful provision. And therefore, because necessity arising from illness, not crime, removes a living bishop from his office, no reason allows another to be ordained in his place unless he refuses it. But if he is accustomed to intervals of illness, let him, in a written petition, confess that the illness has overthrown his ability to exercise intellectual functions in this ministry and that he cannot undertake the other duties, and ask that another be ordained in his place. Once this has been done, let another who is worthy be solemnly elected by all and solemnly ordained bishop. [Col. 0751B] Yet this must be done so that, so long as life keeps that bishop in this world, his due maintenance is supplied from that same church.

But if he returns at no time to the function of a sound mind, a trustworthy person of approved life must be chosen who can be fit for governing the church, attend to the welfare of souls, restrain the unruly under the bond of discipline, administer ecclesiastical property, and show himself mature and effective in all things; he too, if he survives the bishop who is now ill, ought to be consecrated in his place.

[Note: [Col. 0749] “Had to be done”: Böhm.]

[Note: [Col. 0751] “For this ministry, namely intellectual duties, the illness having overthrown [his capacity]”: original.]

[Note: [Col. 0751] “Restrain tightly”: the collected editions.]

### Part II

Gratian. Lest priests suddenly seized by such ailments should leave their begun office unfinished, it has been instituted that a priest, whether chanting or offering sacrifice, should have others with him who, should such an occurrence intervene, may be able to complete the ministries that he began.

Therefore, in the Eleventh Council of Toledo, c. 14:

[Note: [Col. 0751] Held A.D. 675.—Burchard, Book 3, c. 73. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, c. 126, “from the decrees of Pope Soter.” *Collectio tripartita*, part 2, Book 42, c. 6.—Cf. Dist. 1, *On Consecration*, c. 58.]

### C. XV. Everyone offering sacrifice must have a priest beside him to complete the sacraments begun if some necessity should befall him.

Heeding individually that warning of the divine oracle which is written, “Woe to one alone, because when he falls he has no one to raise him up,” we must take the greatest care and precaution lest, in those hours and seasons in which psalms are sung or sacrifice is offered to the Lord, a harmful seizure or any bodily illness overtake someone who is individually engaged in divine offices, so as either suddenly to strike down the body or confuse the mind by derangement or terror. Therefore, taking precautions against such cases, we have judged it necessary to enact that, wherever circumstances of time, place, or abundance of clergy permit, whoever is there singing to God and offering sacrifice must have behind him [Col. 0752B] an assistant of neighbouring support, so that if, through some occurrence, the one who approaches to perform the offices is disturbed or struck to the ground, he may always have behind him one who fearlessly carries out his part. But if this frequently happens to one offering sacrifice, he is to be altogether forbidden to make the offering.

[Note: [Col. 0751C] “This”: the printed councils read “And this”; the royal Lucchese manuscript reads “Woe, this”; two Vatican manuscripts read “That this,” and so it stands below, *On Consecration*, Dist. 1, c. *Ut illud*, and in Burchard and Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 0751] “Mind”: the collected editions.—“At every moment”: *Collectio Hispana*.]

[Note: [Col. 0751] Ecclesiastes 4:10.]

[Note: [Col. 0751] “To be attended to”: *Collectio Hispana*.]

[Note: [Col. 0751] “Health”: *Collectio Hispana*.]

[Note: [Col. 0751] “Covered over”: the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0751] “For”: “against taking precautions”: *Collectio Hispana*.]

[Note: [Col. 0751] “Cleric”: Basel and Lyons editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0751] “Whoever he may be”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0751] “Had been”: there.]

[Note: [Col. 0751C] “But if this”: these words are printed in a different typeface because they are not in the Council of Toledo nor in most old copies of Gratian [nor in the Basel edition]. In a very ancient manuscript, glosses occur on the word “part,” and after the word “forbidden” there is added: “as below, in the same question, c. 2, *In literis tuis*.” But in Burchard and Ivo, who cite the decrees of Pope Soter, and below in *On Consecration* at the cited place, the following words stand in place of these: “and let him complete the office which has been begun.”]

### C. XVI. If a priest has been overcome by necessity, the sacraments begun are to be completed by another.

Likewise, from the Seventh Council of Toledo, c. 2.

[Note: [Col. 0751] Held A.D. 646.—Burchard, Book 3, c. 70. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, c. 124.]

Nothing contrary to the established order [Note: [Col. 0751] **orders**: Burchard.—**the established order**: Ivo.] is to be presumed upon through a rash venture; nor are those things which are held in the highest veneration to be relaxed by even the least act of presumption [Note: [Col. 0751] **or relaxed by any presumption**: collected editions.], when they have been commanded to be done only to such an extent that they are not recognized as interrupted, lest nature be deprived of the strength of health through the onset of illness [Note: [Col. 0752C] **Act**: thus corrected from the royal codex; for the printed codices of the councils, and Burchard and Ivo, read **touch**.]. [Note: [Col. 0751] **are relaxed, when those things commanded to be done are known to be interrupted only for this reason**: Hispanic Collection.] [Note: [Col. 0752C] **When only to such an extent**: there is great variation here. The royal codex reads: “when only to such an extent are the things commanded to be done, wherever they are, known to be interrupted, lest through illness,” etc. Burchard: “when still only so much has been commanded to be done, and they are not known to be interrupted, lest through illness,” etc. Ivo: “when for this reason, and not through illness,” with the remainder in the same manner.] [Note: [Col. 0751] **lest**: same source; Burchard; collected editions.—**nor**: Ivo.] [Note: [Col. 0751] adds: **or labour**: Basel edition.]

Therefore provision is made not only for human frailty [Col. 0752C], but also, by provident care, for the honour of the mysteries of God. [Note: [Col. 0752C] **But also for the sacred**: here likewise there is great variation. [Col. 0752D] In the royal codex [as in the Hispanic Collection; **care is taken, with concern, for the sacred ministries of God**: collected editions; **care is taken that the sacred mysteries of God be held with concern**: Isidore Mercator; **the sacred mysteries ... are provided to be held with concern**: Burchard; **care is taken that the sacred ministries be held with concern**: Ivo.] the sentence is fuller: “but abundant provision is also made for the honour of God’s mysteries, while careful precautions are also taken against the occurrence of offence.”] We have therefore judged [Note: [Col. 0751] **We judge**: Hispanic Collection; Ivo.] that it ought to be fitting [Note: [Col. 0751] adds: **ought**: collected editions.] that, when the holy mysteries are being consecrated by priests at the time of Mass [Col. 0753A], if any occurrence of sickness should arise [Note: [Col. 0753] **arises**: same editions; Burchard; Ivo.] by which the mystery of consecration once begun cannot be completed, another bishop or presbyter should be free to carry out the consecration of the office already begun. [Note: [Col. 0753] **of anyone whatsoever**: same editions; Hispanic Collection.] For nothing else is appropriate to supplement mysteries once initiated [Note: [Col. 0753] adds: **of themselves**: Hispanic Collection.] except the completed blessing either of the priest who began or of the one who follows him [Note: [Col. 0753D] **completed blessing**: thus restored from the royal codex [**may be completed by a blessing**: collected editions; **by a blessing to be completed**: Burchard, Ivo], with which several editions agree; and many other matters in this chapter have likewise been corrected.], because they cannot be regarded as completed unless they are completed in the order of completion.

For since we are all one in Christ, diversity of persons creates nothing contrary where the unity of faith exhibits the efficacy of prosperity. [Note: [Col. 0753] omitted in the Hispanic Collection, Isidore Mercator, Burchard, and Ivo.] Nor should the entire body of clergy doubt that this provision belongs to it as an indivisible grant [Note: [Col. 0753D] **indivisible**: the royal codex reads **granted** [as in the Hispanic Collection; **proclaimed** or **granted**: Burchard, Ivo].], but, as stated above, others should gladly succeed those preceding them in order to bring it to completion. [Note: [Col. 0753] **Not**: collected editions.]

Yet, lest that which is provided on account of the weakness of nature [Col. 0753B] be turned into the ruin of presumption, no one, after taking even the slightest amount of food or drink [Note: [Col. 0753] **any amount whatsoever**: Isidore Mercator; Böhm; collected editions.—**even the least intake of food and drink**: Hispanic Collection.—**food or drink, or any smallest intake whatever**: Burchard, Ivo.], is to celebrate Mass; and no minister or priest, unless an evident illness has arisen [Note: [Col. 0753] **evident**: Hispanic Collection.], once he has begun, is ever rashly to abandon the offices unfinished. Whoever has presumed rashly to violate these provisions [Note: [Col. 0753] **But whoever rashly**: collected editions.] shall undergo a sentence of excommunication.

### Part III. Gratian

Behold, it is plainly shown that, when a bishop asks and even the people petition, another may be substituted for one burdened by infirmity. But for one burdened by old age there must be given not a successor but a coadjutor, who, upon his death, succeeds him in the place of governance. Thus Augustine is said [Note: [Col. 0753] above, chapter 12.] to have joined, not succeeded, the bishop of Hippo.

[Col. 0753C] Accordingly Pope Zachary writes to Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0753D] The first part of this chapter, down to the paragraph “If the same man,” is taken from Pope Zachary’s letter beginning *At the sacred thresholds*. It survives in manuscript at Rome in the Dominican library and was also published by Brother Laurentius Surius in the *Life of St Boniface*, but from a poorly corrected codex. The remainder is contained in the last letter in the volumes of councils.] [Note: [Col. 0753] written A.D. 748.]:

### C. XVII. A coadjutor must be given to one burdened by old age, to succeed him at death.

You have asked that, with our advice, because old age and bodily weakness have overtaken you, if you can find another man in the same see over which you preside, you ought to place him there in your stead. [Note: [Col. 0753] **your**: collected editions.] With God’s help, however, we offer this counsel to your holiness: for the salvation of rational souls, with Christ as your supporter, you must by no means abandon the see of the church of Mainz which you hold. But if, according to your petition, the Lord grants you a perfect man, who can have concern and care for the salvation of souls [Note: [Col. 0753] adds: **your souls**: Basel edition.], you shall ordain him bishop in your stead [Col. 0754A]; and in the Gospel entrusted to you and in bearing the ministry of Christ he shall seek out and strengthen the Church of God everywhere.

Likewise, in the last letter to the same man [Note: [Col. 0753] written A.D. 743.], §1: If divine clemency should will that this same man survive the day of your departure, and if you find him suitable and it has been settled in your will, at the very hour when you know that you are about to depart from this present world, designate him as your successor in the presence of all, so that he may come here to be ordained. We allow this to no one else; but, constrained by charity, we have judged it right to grant it to you.

Likewise, a little earlier in the same place, §2: But concerning the man [Note: [Col. 0753] **whom**: collected editions.] whom you said you wished to appoint as your successor, so that while you live a bishop may be chosen in your place: we permit this on no account, because it is shown to be contrary to every ecclesiastical rule or ordinance [Note: [Col. 0753] **statutes**: same editions.] of the Fathers [Col. 0754B]. Rather, we wish him to minister to you and to be a helper in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0753] **Gospel**: same editions; original text.] of Christ. And below, §3: For it is plainly most blameworthy that, while you are alive, we should substitute another for you. Yet we admonish you that, *as long as divine clemency commands you to remain alive, without interruption*, you must not cease to pray that God may grant you that successor who can be pleasing to Him and can govern the people without reproach.

### C. XVIII. Not a successor but a coadjutor is given to a living bishop. Likewise Pope Pelagius to the clergy of Narni.

[Note: [Col. 0753] Chapter of uncertain source.—Collection in three parts, part 1, title 54, chapter 18.]

Because our brother and fellow bishop John, urged by zeal for ecclesiastical usefulness and after praiseworthy reflection upon his natural simplicity [Col. 0754C], acknowledges himself to be by no means suitable for managing the care of governing the patrimony or for preserving ecclesiastical discipline, he requests that the person of the presbyter Constitutus [Note: [Col. 0753] **presbyterate**: Basel edition.] be assigned to him for carrying these matters out, so that the things which are necessary may, through his suitable ordering [Note: [Col. 0753] adds: **by him**: Basel, Venice I, Lyons.], be *done* with appropriate care, and nothing improper or useless be allowed to occur.

Therefore by this present command we direct you that, preserving in the *first* place due reverence for the aforesaid bishop—which it is fitting for you to render without blame [Note: [Col. 0753] **will be fitting**: Basel edition.]—you shall render fitting obedience [Note: [Col. 0753] **reverence**: Böhm.—adds: **to him**: Basel edition.] to Constitutus [Col. 0755A] in all matters which pertain to the service of divine worship or which concern for ecclesiastical utility advises should be carried out. In no respect are you to resist his arrangements with a contumacious spirit [Note: [Col. 0755] **so that in no respect**: collected editions, first Lyons II and III and Venice I, in which the reading is: “to him, in no respect.”]; rather, with the diligent zeal of your appropriate vigilance, fulfill what Constitutus [Note: [Col. 0755] **that Constitutus**: collected editions.] has instructed for the conduct of ecclesiastical business, so that, once these things have been arranged, your customary stipends may be supplied and whatever is necessary concerning the patrimony of the aforesaid church, or for recovering the property belonging to it, may be completed.

Gratian: That statement of Cyprian concerning heretics must be understood of those who strive to usurp the churches of Catholics for themselves. §1. That statement of Pope Evaristus must be understood when neither unavoidable necessity (namely, that caused by persecutors) nor an apostolic or regular transfer, but ambition alone, compels a bishop to move from one church to another. §2. Hence, when at the beginning [Col. 0755B] of his chapter he said, “A bishop ought not to abandon his church,” he subsequently added: “Except for unavoidable necessity, or apostolic or regular transfer, and joining himself to another on account of ambition.”

### Part IV. §3

For whoever, from ambition, despising the modest status of his own church, wishes to move to a greater church, must be recalled to his own. If he disdains to return, he must lose both the other and his own.

Hence one reads in the Council of Nicaea, chapter 15 [Note: [Col. 0755D] In one better-corrected of two codices of Anselm’s collections, this chapter reads so that the words “That a bishop or the other orders ought not to move” are the rubric, and the chapter begins thus: “A bishop, presbyter, or deacon is not to pass from city to city.” In the other, however, the same rubric is written in black letters and is the beginning of the chapter. It therefore appears that this chapter was arranged as it stands in Gratian, while preserving the meaning of the canon itself.] [Note: [Col. 0755] held A.D. 325.—Dionysian translation.—Burchard, book 2, chapter 97; Anselm, book 6, chapter 112; Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chapter 374.]:

### C. XIX. A bishop or any cleric must not leave his own church in order to move to another.

A bishop or the other orders ought not to migrate from city to city: neither bishop, presbyter, nor deacon is to pass over. But if anyone, after the decision of the holy and great council, should attempt to do such a thing [Col. 0755C] and commit himself to such an undertaking, the act must be rendered wholly void [Note: [Col. 0755] **be brought**: Basel edition.], and he must be restored to the church of which he was ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon.

### C. XX. A bishop who refuses to reside in his own church is to be assigned to a monastery. Likewise Gregory to Anthemius the subdeacon, book V, letter 23.

[Note: [Col. 0755] Letter 23, written A.D. 596, book 6, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 178 (187).]

It has reached us that Pigmenius, bishop of the city of Amalfi, is not content to reside in *his own* church, but wanders abroad through different places. And below: Therefore by this authority we command you *not to cease to threaten the aforesaid bishop* [Note: [Col. 0755] **that ... cease**: lacking in Anselm.], so that he may not presume to do this hereafter, but may reside in his own church according to priestly custom. If, perhaps, after your warning, you find that he will not amend [Col. 0756A] [Note: [Col. 0755] **to amend**: collected editions except Lyons II and III.], assign him to a monastery [Note: [Col. 0755] **monastery**: collected editions.], and take every care to notify us, so that by our further command you may learn what you ought to do.

### C. XXI. No bishop is permitted to abandon his principal see and transfer himself to another church. Likewise from the Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 5.

[Note: [Col. 0755] held A.D. 401.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 176 (185). Collection in three parts, part 2, title 19, chapter 5.]

It has been resolved that no one may, having abandoned his principal see, transfer himself to some church situated within the diocese, or remain on his own property longer than is proper [Note: [Col. 0755] **is proper**: collected editions.], neglecting the appointed care or attendance due to his own see.

### C. XXII. An interim administrator may not retain the see to which he has been assigned. Likewise from the same Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 8.

[Note: [Col. 0755] Collection in three parts, part 2, title 19, chapter 8.]

[Col. 0756B] It has been established that no interim administrator may, through the efforts or factions of any people [Note: [Col. 0755] **of any one**: Basel edition.], retain the see for which he was appointed interim administrator; instead, he must take care to provide a bishop for them within a year. If he neglects this, once the year has elapsed [Note: [Col. 0755] **removed**: original text; Argentinian edition.], another interim administrator is to be assigned.

### C. XXIII. Clerics who leave their own church and refuse to return are to be excommunicated. Likewise from the Council of Nicaea, chapter 16.

[Note: [Col. 0755] held A.D. 325.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 107; Burchard, book 2, chapter 98; Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chapter 175, all from Dionysius.]

If any, acting without regard [Note: [Col. 0755] adds: **for God**: original text; collected editions.] and without the fear of God before their eyes, and not observing ecclesiastical ordinances, leave their own church—whether presbyter, deacon, or persons placed in any ecclesiastical order—they ought not to be received into *another* church; rather, with every necessity [Col. 0756C] they must be compelled to return to their own church. If they persist, they must be excommunicated.

### C. XXIV. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Antioch, chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 0755] held A.D. 332.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 170.]

If any presbyter, deacon, or other cleric, having deserted his own church, considers that he ought to move to another and attempts gradually to remain there permanently, where he has moved [Note: [Col. 0755] **has moved**: collected editions.], he must no longer minister, especially if his bishop has urged him to return. But if, after his bishop has summoned him, he does not obey but persists in disobedience, he must altogether be deposed from his office [Note: [Col. 0755] **must be deposed ... ought to have**: Basel edition.] and must never have hope of restoration [Note: [Col. 0755] adds: **we decree**: collected editions, first Basel; Böhm.]. If another bishop receives one deposed for this offence [Col. 0757A], he too shall incur from the common synod the penalty of reprimand [Note: [Col. 0757D] **reprimand**: in Greek, *epitimias tynchanēin* (ἐπιτιμίας τυγχάνειν), which in other translations is “be rebuked,” “be restrained,” or “be punished.”], as one who dissolves ecclesiastical laws.

### C. XXV. A bishop may not leave his own church and move to another. Likewise from the same Council of Antioch, chapter 21.

[Note: [Col. 0757] Burchard, book 1, chapter 72; Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 179, cite Dionysius.—Compare C. 9, question 2, chapter 6.]

We decree that a bishop ought not to move from one diocese to another: neither if he thrusts himself in, nor if he is forcibly drawn by the people, nor even if bishops urge this upon him [Note: [Col. 0757] **urged**: Basel edition.—**urge**: remaining editions.]; rather, he must remain in the Church of God which he received from the beginning, and must not migrate elsewhere from it, according to the rule long ago established concerning this by the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0757] adds: **we decree**: collected editions; Böhm.].

### C. XXVI. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 5.

[Note: [Col. 0757] held A.D. 451.]

[Col. 0757B] Concerning those bishops or clerics who move from city to city, it has been resolved that the definitions given by the holy Fathers [Note: [Col. 0757] compare above, chapter 19.] shall retain their proper force.

### C. XXVII. A bishop may not usurp another’s congregations. Likewise from the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 20.

[Note: [Col. 0757] held A.D. 397.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 64; Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 173.]

It has been resolved that another’s congregations are to be usurped by no bishop, and that no bishop is to encroach upon his colleague in the diocese [Note: [Col. 0757] **upon the diocese of his colleague**: Hispanic Collection.].

### C. XXVIII. A bishop may not ordain another’s clerics or consecrate altars. Likewise Anacletus.

[Note: [Col. 0757] Rather, from the Council of Orléans, held A.D. 538, chapter 15.]

A bishop ought not to intrude into another diocese [Note: [Col. 0757] **in another diocese**: collected editions.—**into foreign dioceses**: original text.] to ordain another’s clerics or consecrate altars. If he does so, those whom he ordained having been removed, while the consecration of the altar nevertheless remains [Note: [Col. 0757] **only**: collected editions.], the transgressor of the canons [Col. 0757C] shall abstain for one year [Note: [Col. 0757] **one**: absent from the original and the collected editions, first Paris and Lyons.] from celebrating Mass [Note: [Col. 0757] **celebration**: Argentinian, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice I and II editions.].

### C. XXIX. On solemn days a cleric must not be absent from his own church. Likewise from the Council of Agde, chapter 64.

[Note: [Col. 0757] held A.D. 506.—Compare, however, D. 23, chapter 30.—The same occurs in the Council of Clermont, chapter 15.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 28, chapter 62.]

If anyone enrolled among the clergy is absent from his church on solemn days—that is, the Nativity of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0757] adds: **holy**: Hispanic Collection.], Epiphany, Easter, or Pentecost—because he gives more attention to worldly [Note: [Col. 0757] **individual profit**: Isidore Mercator.] gains than to obeying the service of God, it is fitting that he be suspended from communion for three years. §1. Likewise, if a deacon or presbyter has been absent from his church for three weeks, he shall incur this condemnation.

### C. XXX. A bishop must be removed from the church into which he has intruded and compelled to return to his own. Likewise Pope Hilary to the bishops of Tarragona, chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 0757] written A.D. 465.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 109 (106).]

After Irenaeus, bishop of Barcelona, has been removed from that church and sent back to his own, and after the desires have been quieted by priestly moderation—desires which, through ignorance of ecclesiastical laws, seek to obtain what they may not lawfully obtain—let a bishop be promptly ordained for the people of Barcelona from their own clergy [Note: [Col. 0757] adds: **and**: collected editions.]. It is especially fitting, brother Ascanio [Note: [Col. 0757] **Asconi**: same editions, first Basel.], that you choose such a man, and becoming that you consecrate him [Note: [Col. 0757] **it may be fitting ... it may become**: same editions; original text.], lest, if perhaps something has been done otherwise, our command should rebuke especially the reputation of your name, not without reprimand [Note: [Col. 0757] **in**: collected editions.], because we have learned that something has been committed to the injury of God, from whom particularly comes the grace of priestly dignities.

### C. XXXI. Whoever seeks another’s see, once expelled from it, must also lose his own. Likewise Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, Letter LXXXII, otherwise LXXXIV, chapter 8.

[Note: [Col. 0757] Chapter 14, Ballerini edition; written A.D. 446.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 74; Anselm, book 6, chapter 104 (101); Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 103; Polycarp, book 1, title 9.]

If any bishop, despising the modest status of his own city, has coveted the administration of a more celebrated place and has, by whatever means, transferred himself to a larger people, he must not only be expelled from the other see but also lose his own [Note: [Col. 0757] **he shall also lose**: collected editions.], so that he may preside neither over those whom he coveted through avarice nor over those whom he despised through pride. Therefore let each be content with his own bounds, and let no one seek to be enlarged beyond the measure of his own right.

### C. XXXII. Whoever, in contempt of a lesser church, aspires to a greater loses both churches. Likewise from the Council of Meaux, chapter 30.

[Note: [Col. 0757] held A.D. 845.—Burchard, book 3, chapter 48; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 46; *Decree*, part 3, chapter 52.]

[Col. 0758C] If anyone of priestly rank, in contempt of a lesser church, has ambitiously and improperly aspired to a more important one, the canonical determination concerning him is to be maintained: that is, he is to lose both [Note: [Col. 0757] **both parties**: Burchard.] churches. [Note: [Col. 0758D] “That is, he is to lose both”: these words are not in the printed Council of Meaux, but occur nevertheless in the other collectors.]

Gratian: But whoever has entered a vacant church by payment must be deposed from his office, as is read in the Council of Rouen [Note: [Col. 0757] held about A.D. 650.—Regino, book 1, chapter 240; Burchard, book 3, chapter 114; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 49; *Decree*, part 3, chapter 90.—Capitularies, book 7, chapter 206.]:

### C. XXXIII. Let one who attempts to acquire a church by gifts be expelled from the clergy.

It has been decreed and in every way forbidden that, if any presbyter is found to give or to have given gifts, or to pay other money [Col. 0759A], to some cleric or layman, in order to *steal away* the church of another presbyter [Note: [Col. 0759D] **Steal away, or**: these two words have been added from Burchard. For a church cannot be said to be vacant while its presbyter-holder is alive. In book 7 of the *Capitularies*, chapter 206 [and in Regino], the word is **steal away**, but the second clause is absent: “or buy a vacant church for a price.” Ivo and the author of the *Panormia* read, as Gratian previously did: “buy a vacant church for a price.”], or to *buy a vacant church for a price*, let him, for this greed, robbery, or presumption for the sake of shameful gain, be expelled from the clergy and be excluded from the rule.

### Part V. Gratian

But that transfers of bishops may take place by common counsel and for the benefit of others, and that, while they live, others may be substituted for them in churches from which they have withdrawn, Pope Anterus demonstrates in Letter VII, writing to the bishops of the provinces of Baetica and Toledo [Note: [Col. 0759] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare *Ancient Ecclesiastical Statutes*, chapter 11; Council of Sardica, chapters 1–2; Cyprian, Letter 49.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 77; Anselm, book 6, chapter 94 (99); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 69; *Decree*, part 5, chapter 183.]:

### C. XXXIV. Transfers of bishops may be made for necessity or usefulness.

Know that transfers of bishops may lawfully be made for common usefulness and necessity, but not by anyone’s private will [Col. 0759B] or domination. Saint Peter, our teacher and chief of the apostles, was transferred from Antioch to Rome for the sake of usefulness, so that he might be more effective there. Eusebius also, by apostolic authority, was transferred from a certain small city to Alexandria. Likewise Felix was transferred to Ephesus from the city in which he had been ordained, by the choice of the citizens because of the teaching and good life which he possessed, [by the authority of this holy see and [Note: [Col. 0759D] **By the authority of this holy see and**: these words are not found in Anterus’s letter, the *Panormia*, Burchard, or Ivo. They do occur, however, in Anselm, Polycarp, and old copies of Gratian. The same is true of the words near the end of the chapter, “but not without the authority and permission of the most holy Roman see,” which for this reason are enclosed in brackets.]] by the common counsel of bishops and the remaining priests and peoples.

For he does not pass from city to city, nor is he transferred from a lesser to a greater, who acts not from ambition or private will but, having either been driven from his own see by force [Note: [Col. 0759] **expelled**: collected editions.] or compelled by necessity, is transferred by others for the usefulness of a place or people—not proudly [Col. 0759C], but humbly—and *enthroned*. [Note: [Col. 0759] absent in Anselm.] And below, §1: For just as bishops have authority regularly to ordain bishops and other priests, so, whenever usefulness or necessity compels it, they also have authority, in the manner stated above, to transfer and enthrone them, [but not without the authority and permission of the most holy Roman see]. And below, §2: For the cause of usefulness *and necessity* is one thing; the cause of avarice, presumption, or private will another.

### C. XXXV. Transfers of bishops may be made for necessity. Likewise Pope Pelagius II to Archbishop Benignus, Letter II.

[Note: [Col. 0759] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare chapter 34.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 97 (102); Polycarp, book 1, title 9.]

Know, most beloved brother, that the cause of necessity [Col. 0760A] and usefulness is one thing, and the *cause of presumption and private will* another. Therefore one does not change one’s see who does not change one’s mind; that is, one who moves from city to city not on account of avarice, domination, private will, or personal inclination [Note: [Col. 0759] **choice**: Anselm.—**affection**: Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice II editions.], but is transferred for necessity or [Note: [Col. 0759] **and**: collected editions.] usefulness. For the usefulness of many must be preferred to the usefulness or will of one. For it is one thing to transfer and another to be transferred. And below, §1: For it is one thing to go voluntarily, and another to come *by compulsion* or necessity. Hence such persons do not transfer cities [Note: [Col. 0759] **city**: same editions.], but are transferred, because they do this not voluntarily but under compulsion. And below, §2: Therefore those do not rightly understand ecclesiastical rules who deny that this can occur for necessity or usefulness whenever common usefulness or necessity has persuaded it.

### C. XXXVI. Whoever does not extend mercy to those suffering necessity is convicted of denying Christ. The same, in the same letter, a little below.

[Note: [Col. 0759] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.]

Everyone who was groaning and oppressed by Saul [Note: [Col. 0759] 1 Kings, chapter 22.] fled and came to David. Therefore, if the most devout and most just David had known it to be a sin to receive those fleeing persecution and moving from place to place and city to city, he would certainly not have received them, retained them with himself, or placed them in other cities. For those who persecute the Lord’s bishops and compel them to move from cities to other cities persecute not so much the bishops as our Lord Jesus Christ, whose embassy they discharge. Nor do the bishops themselves sin in this, because [Col. 0760C] they act not voluntarily but under compulsion; rather, those who persecute them sin. Nor can this be imputed to the bishops themselves, but to those who compel them to do it. And below, §1: But those who deny that mercy must be shown to persons fleeing and suffering necessity deny Christ Himself, who is mercy and truth. And below, §2: Whoever denies [Note: [Col. 0759] adds: **but**: Basel, Lyons II and III editions.] mercy to those suffering necessity—who does not permit peoples in need of divine ministries, and without their own bishop to instruct them, to receive, for usefulness and necessity, from another city, even a lesser one, into one which has no more learned [Note: [Col. 0759] adds: **or more eminent**: Basel, Lyons editions.] or more useful bishop, a man transferred by better counsel rather than voluntarily, but at the exhortation of superiors; or who does not permit a bishop who has been expelled [Note: [Col. 0759] **cast down**: collected editions.] [Col. 0761A] and is suffering persecution to be enthroned for usefulness or necessity [Note: [Col. 0761] **do not wish to enthrone**: same editions.]—denies mercy.

### C. XXXVII. A bishop is to move from church to church not by ambition but by synodal authority. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 27.

[Note: [Col. 0761] Chapter 11 of the *Ancient Ecclesiastical Statutes*.—Compare D. 18, chapter 9.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 70; *Decree*, part 5, chapter 125.]

A bishop is not to move through ambition from an obscure place to a distinguished one, nor is any cleric of an inferior order. But if the usefulness of the church demands that this *be done*, then, after a decree on his behalf has been submitted by clergy and laity to the bishops, he shall be transferred in the presence of the synod [Note: [Col. 0761] **synodal**: Böhm.], while another bishop is nevertheless substituted in his place [Note: [Col. 0761] **place**: collected editions, first Lyons II and III.]. Priests of a lower rank and other clerics may transfer to other churches with the permission of their bishops.

### C. XXXVIII. Bishops or presbyters are to be received in another church in their own rank. Likewise from the same Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 33.

[Note: [Col. 0761] Chapter 56 of the *Ancient Ecclesiastical Statutes*.]

If bishops or presbyters come to the church of another bishop for the purpose of visiting [Note: [Col. 0761] **to visit a church, they come to the church of another bishop**: Ballerini.—**to visit the church of another bishop, they come to a church**: Hispanic Collection.], they are to be received in their own rank and invited both to preach the word and to consecrate the offering.

### C. XXXIX. The church of one bishop ought not to be administered by another. Likewise Pope Callixtus to all the bishops of Gaul, Letter II, chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 0761] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Regino, book 1, chapter 250; Burchard, book 3, chapter 49; Anselm, book 6, chapter 103 (108); Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 53, part 5, chapter 101.]

Just as another man’s wife is not permitted to be adulterated, judged, or administered by anyone except her own husband while he lives, so neither is the bishop’s wife [Note: [Col. 0761] adds: **himself**: collected editions, first Basel.—**or presbyter**: Ivo, part 3; Burchard.—**and presbyter**: Regino.]—by which his church or parish is unquestionably understood—permitted, while he lives, without his judgment [Note: [Col. 0761] **counsel**: collected editions.] and will, to be judged [Col. 0761C], administered, or enjoyed in another’s intercourse, that is, ordination. Hence the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0761] 1 Corinthians 7:39.], “A wife is bound by the law [Note: [Col. 0761] adds: **of her husband**: collected editions.] as long as her husband lives; but when he has died, she is released from the law of her husband.” Likewise the bride of a bishop—for the church is called his bride and wife—is bound to him while he lives, but when he has died she is released. And [Note: [Col. 0761] 1 Corinthians 7:39.] “she may marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord,” that is, according to rule. For if she marries another while he lives, she will be judged an adulteress. Likewise he too, if he voluntarily takes another [Note: [Col. 0761] **another**: collected editions.], will be considered an adulterer [Note: [Col. 0761] **judged**: Argentinian, Basel, Venice I and II, Nuremberg editions.] and deprived of communion.

But if he is persecuted in his own church, he must flee to another [Note: [Col. 0761] adds: **church**: collected editions.], and be associated with it [Note: [Col. 0761] **joined**: same editions.], as the Lord says [Note: [Col. 0761] Matthew 10:23.], “If they persecute you [Col. 0762A] in one city, flee into another.” But if he must be transferred for usefulness, he is not to do this by himself [Note: [Col. 0761] adds: **nevertheless**: collected editions.], but must act at the invitation of his brethren and [Note: [Col. 0761] **with**: same editions.] with the authority of this holy see, not for the sake of ambition [Note: [Col. 0761] **as has been said**: same editions; Anselm.], but for usefulness or necessity [Note: [Col. 0761D] **Or necessity**: these words are not in the letter itself, but occur in Anselm. Necessity, however, provides a just cause for transfer; above, in the present question, chapter *Know*.] [Note: [Col. 0761] adds: **this must be done**: same editions except Basel.].

### Part VI. Gratian

This is to be understood not only of bishops but also of all ministers of the Church: namely, lest one person intrude into the place of another who is alive.

Hence St Gregory writes to Natalis, bishop of Salona, concerning a man who had consented to be promoted to another’s archdeaconry, book II, indiction 10, letters XIV and XVI [Note: [Col. 0761] From letters 18, written A.D. 592, and 20, written the same year to Antoninus the subdeacon, book 2, Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chapter 342.]:

### C. XL. Let one who does not fear to invade another’s place be deposed.

We depose from the honour of that archdeaconry one who consented, contrary to the rule of justice, to be promoted to another’s archdeaconry [Col. 0762B]. If he further presumes to minister in the same place, let him know that he is deprived of participation in sacred communion.

### C. XLI. There ought not to be two prelates in one church. Likewise Jerome to the monk Rusticus, Letter IV.

[Note: [Col. 0761] written about A.D. 400.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 356.]

Among bees there is one leader; cranes [Note: [Col. 0761] **and cranes**: collected editions.] follow one in a lettered formation [Note: [Col. 0761] **lettered**: same editions; Ivo.]; there is one emperor and one judge of a province. Rome, from its founding, could not have two brothers as kings at the same time, and is dedicated by fratricide. In Rebecca’s womb [Note: [Col. 0761] adds: **indeed**: collected editions.—Compare Genesis 25.] Esau and Jacob waged war. Each church has a single bishop, a single archpresbyter [Note: [Col. 0761] **archbishops**: same editions; Ivo.], a single archdeacon; and every ecclesiastical order [Col. 0762C] relies upon its own rulers.

### Part VII. Gratian

Behold the cases in which another may be substituted for a bishop while he is alive, although, in the truth of the matter, such a person is shown to succeed only when the bishop is not alive. For one transferred from one city to another ceases to be bishop of the city from which he is transferred; and therefore one who succeeds him is shown to be substituted not for a living bishop but, in a sense, for one who is dead. But the difference between one transferred by necessity arising from hostilities and one transferred for usefulness is this: the person who moves to another place through fear of hostilities must return to his former church if it should at some time be liberated from its enemies.

[Col. 0763A] Hence Pope Gregory writes to John, bishop of Squillace, book II, indiction 10, letter 25 [Note: [Col. 0763] Letter 37, written A.D. 592, book 2, Maurist edition.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 123: “from Gregory’s register, letter to Agnellus”; Anselm, book 6, chapter 99 (104); Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 223: “from Gregory’s register, letter to Angelus”; Polycarp, book 1, title 8, book 2, title 14.]:

### C. XLII. Whoever has moved to another place through fear of hostilities must afterwards return to his own church.

The care of our pastoral office admonishes us to appoint proper priests for churches that have been deprived, men who ought to govern the Lord’s flock with pastoral solicitude. Therefore we have judged it necessary to appoint you, John, bishop of the city of Lisbon, captured by enemies, as cardinal priest in the Church of Squillace, so that, with a view to future recompense, you may discharge the care of souls once undertaken. And although you have been driven from your own church by an imminent enemy, you ought to govern another church which lacks a pastor; provided, however, that if that city should be freed from its enemies and, by the Lord’s protection, restored to its former condition, you return to the church in which you were first ordained. But if the aforesaid city remains oppressed by the continuing calamity of captivity, you ought to remain in this church, in which you have been incardinated.

### Chapter XLIII. On priests who, having abandoned their own churches, migrated to others

We hold those priests who have migrated from churches to churches excluded from our communion until they return to the cities in which they were originally appointed. ### Chapter XLIV. Changes of episcopal sees may be made because of the necessity of the times

The character of the times admonishes us to transfer episcopal seats, established in ancient times in particular cities, to other places of the same diocese which we judge safer, so that their inhabitants may now live more securely and more easily avoid the danger of barbarian attack. Therefore we command you, brother John, our fellow bishop of the city of Velletri, to transfer your see from the place once called Arenata to St Andrew the Apostle; so that you may be more free from hostile assault and may there arrange the customary solemn festivals in due celebration.

VIII. Part. Gratian. Likewise, when someone, for the sake of humility and with apostolic permission, descends from an episcopal see to monastic subjection, another may be substituted in his place; but he will thereafter by no means be able to rise again to the episcopate.

Therefore, in the fifth session of the Synod of Constantinople, of 383 Fathers, under Pope John VIII, at which Peter, cardinal priest, Paul, bishop of Ancona, and Eugenius, bishop of Ostia, presided, the papal representatives said:

[Note: [Col. 0763C–0764C] In Ivo, part 7, chapter 149, the heading of this chapter reads: “From the proceedings of the fifth Synod of Constantinople, of 383 Fathers, under Pope John VIII, presided over by Peter cardinal priest, Paul bishop of Ancona, and Eugenius bishop of Ostia.” The beginning of the chapter itself is: “The papal representatives said: This by no means …”]

[Note: [Col. 0764C–0766D] This synod under John VIII exists in Greek in the Vatican Library. Only three canons of it, with Balsamon’s explanation, were published at Paris; there it is entitled the synod held in the Church of Holy Wisdom under Photius the patriarch. In the second chapter of those three is found the ruling of this chapter. In order that everything may be understood more clearly, the passage is set down here in Greek with a new translation.]

Photius the Patriarch said: “What do you think concerning those who transfer themselves from the rank of bishops into the condition of monks? Can those who have made themselves subject still retain authority over the same flock?”

The most holy representatives of elder Rome said: “This neither occurs among us nor is maintained as a custom. For whoever has been enrolled from the episcopal rank among the order of monks—that is, penitents—can no longer claim the dignity of a bishop for himself.”

Basil and Elias, representatives of the eastern thrones, said: “Nor has it ever been observed among us that this occurred. On the contrary, monks are promoted to become bishops; but those descending from bishops to monks cannot remain bishops.”

The holy synod said: “Let a canon also be established concerning this matter. For doubts often arise among us on this subject: some say that bishops who have become monks are not prevented from performing episcopal functions, while others do not concur in this opinion.”

The most holy representatives said: “Let a canon be promulgated.”

The holy synod said: “Moreover, we deem it right that canons be promulgated concerning laymen who have reached such madness and arrogance as to strike or imprison bishops or priests of God, and the rest.”

Photius the Patriarch said: “If your Holiness commands, let the canons be read.” Peter, the most God-beloved deacon and protonotary, took them and read:

“Although hitherto certain bishops, descending to the monastic habit, have sought to remain at the height of the episcopate, and though this practice was overlooked, this holy and ecumenical synod, correcting this negligence also and restoring this disorderly practice to the ordinances governing ecclesiastical order, has decreed that, if any bishop or other holder of episcopal dignity should wish to descend to the monastic life and fulfil the place of penitence, he shall no longer lay claim to episcopal dignity. For the compacts of monks concern subjection and discipleship, not teaching or presidency; they profess not to shepherd others, but to be shepherded. Therefore, as has been said, we decree that henceforth none of those enrolled among bishops and reckoned among shepherds shall transfer himself into the condition of those who are shepherded and do penance. But if anyone should dare to do this after the promulgation and knowledge of the judgment now pronounced, having himself deprived himself of episcopal rank, he shall not return to the former dignity which he has rejected by his actions.”

The Latin translation printed after the Greek reads:

Photius the Patriarch said: “What is your judgment about those who transfer themselves from the order of bishops into the place of monks? Can those who have chosen to make themselves subject still retain authority over the same flock?”

The most holy representatives of elder Rome said: “This does not occur among us at all, nor is it an established custom. For whoever is enrolled from the order of bishops among the order of monks—that is, penitents—can no longer claim for himself the dignity of a bishop.”

Basil and Elias, representatives of the eastern sees, said: “Nor has it ever been observed that this happened among us. On the contrary, monks are promoted to the order of bishops; but those who descend from bishops to monks cannot remain bishops.”

The holy synod said: “Let a canon also be established on this matter. For doubts often arise among us on this account: some indeed say that bishops are not forbidden, after becoming monks, to perform episcopal offices, while others do not approve this opinion at all.” The most holy representatives said: “Let a canon be enacted.” The holy synod said: “Moreover, we judge it fitting that canons be enacted concerning those laymen who have reached such madness and pride that they beat bishops or priests of God, or commit them to custody, and so forth.”

§ 1. Photius the Patriarch said: “If your Holiness commands, let the canons be read.” Peter, the most God-beloved deacon and protonotary, took them in hand and read: “Although until now certain bishops descending to the monastic habit have tried to remain at the summit of the episcopate, and although this was overlooked while they did it, nevertheless this holy and ecumenical synod, correcting this neglect too and recalling this disorderly practice to the laws concerning ecclesiastical order, has decreed that if any bishop, or anyone else holding episcopal dignity, should wish to descend to monastic life and fill the place of penitence, he is no longer to retain episcopal dignity. For monastic institutions pertain to obedience and discipline, not at all to teaching or presidency; they belong to those who profess not to shepherd others but to be shepherded. Therefore, as has been said, we decree that no one henceforth among those enrolled in the catalogue of bishops and reckoned in the number of shepherds transfer himself into the place of those who are shepherded and do penance. But if anyone, after the promulgation and knowledge of this judgment now pronounced, should dare to do this, since he has deprived himself of episcopal rank, he shall no longer recover his former dignity, which he has despised by his deeds.”

[Note: [Col. 0763] From the pseudo-synod of Photius, held A.D. 879.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 149.]

### Chapter XLVI. Because of the assaults of evildoers, a bishop may not abandon his flock

It has been reported to us that, on account of past labours and assaults, some among you have abandoned the peoples assigned to them and entrusted to them by God; and that in the future many wish to abandon the churches which they ought to protect, neglecting to labour for the sheep committed to them. They hasten to surrender themselves to the repose of monasteries; they choose freedom from episcopal labours and desire rather to pass their lives in silence and leisure than to remain in the duties entrusted to them. Yet the Lord says: “Blessed is he who perseveres to the end.” Whence comes blessed perseverance except from the virtue of patience? For according to the apostolic preaching, “all who desire to live piously in Christ Jesus suffer persecution.”

Therefore, dearest brothers, do not let the bitterness of afflictions force you to withdraw from the devout purpose of your minds. Consider how much our Creator, Lord, and Redeemer endured for our absolution and deliverance, and to what insults he surrendered himself, in order to free us from the bonds of the devil’s power. Therefore take heed to yourselves and to the entire flock in which the Holy Spirit appointed you bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood; so that there may be no one to deceive or seduce you by subtle argument, causing you to abandon the peoples entrusted to you and surrender yourselves, because of the reproach of wicked people, to some quiet life, saving yourselves alone and leaving your children orphaned.

### Chapter XLVII. In persecutions a bishop must not abandon his church

Likewise Pope Nicholas to Humfrid, bishop of the Church of Thérouanne.

You inquire through the priest Guldagarius whether, when you are driven from your bishopric by the Normans, you ought thereafter to live in a monastery. Know in this matter, dearest brother, that if it is ruinous for a helmsman to abandon a ship in calm weather, how much more so amid waves? We do not say that we must not flee persecutors—especially the snares of pagans, when for a time they rage and, because of the multitude of our sins, are divinely granted power to harm. Above all, we ought not voluntarily to go out to meet them; and it is clearer than daylight that many prophets and apostles, and the Lord himself, fled such pursuers. Rather, we say that we especially, who as rams lead the flocks—indeed, who are their shepherds—ought, by God’s help, to remain with them in dangers to the extent of our strength. And when tranquillity has been restored by divine mercy and the assault of the raging has been subdued, we ought immediately to seek out the flock, gather it into one, and raise its spirits upward by preaching the peace, and especially the security, of the heavenly homeland. We must remain so solicitous for their protection that, if by God’s judgment they perhaps lose the advantages of the present time, they may hope without doubt to receive the everlasting joys of the life to come.

[Note: [Col. 0767] “Humfred”: Argentinensis.—“Hunifred”: Basel.]

IX. Part. Gratian. This too is to be observed when among the subjects there are some whom the prelate’s life benefits, when the prelate is not being specifically sought and the Church’s safety cannot be secure through others, lest, if he begins to abandon those whom he can benefit, it be said of him: “The hireling, who is not a shepherd and whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees.”

But when he is specifically sought, he should flee after the example of Christ, who fled from Herod’s face into Egypt; he should flee after the example of Paul, who was lowered by the brethren through a wall in a basket. Therefore Augustine says:

[Note: [Col. 0767D–0768D] Gratian cites much in this discussion from Augustine. The thought is indeed found in Augustine, but the wording itself occurs in the Ordinary Gloss at the indicated places. On the question of when a bishop may withdraw from his church, however, blessed Augustine treats it in Letter 180, written to Bishop Honoratus.]

[Note: [Col. 0767] Ordinary Gloss on 2 Corinthians 11, at the end, from Augustine, Letter 180 to Honoratus.]

“Let the minister of Christ flee as Christ himself fled into Egypt; and let one who is specifically sought flee, while the Church’s safety is secured through others.” Hence the Lord also says to his disciples: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another.” Hence too he hid himself and went out of the Temple when the Jews took up stones to throw at him.

Hence Augustine also says concerning the same matter in Psalm 54: “‘Behold, I fled far away’ refers to Christ’s avoiding his persecutors in order to remove an occasion for wrath; and he remained in deserted places praying, thereby teaching us to pray and find rest in the secrecy of conscience when we are oppressed by evils.”

But when the safety not merely of prelates, but of the entire Church, is at issue, and the faith is attacked, they must rise up against the enemy and set themselves as a wall for the house of the Lord on the day of battle, and lay down their souls for their sheep, so that by the example of their suffering they may inflame those whom they cannot longer strengthen by the word of teaching. And this concerns open persecutions.

§ 1. There is another kind of persecution, under which the Apostle laboured when he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” Hence Augustine, on Psalm 101: “The bones, that is, the strong, are the griddle for those who are scandalized; for a good person is fried to the extent that he loves.” Hence the same writer, on Psalm 30: “The righteous man is angry at the sins of the chaff, yet does not hate, lest the eye be extinguished thereby; the belly signifies the inward parts, which are troubled when the wicked cannot even be corrected, when he does not cry out to them because his life fails in sorrow, seeing that what he preaches makes no progress.”

§ 2. Hence the same writer says in Psalm 69, distinguishing both kinds of persecution: “The voice of those afflicted is Christ’s voice, that is, the voice of martyrs endangered amid sufferings but trusting in the Head. With them is the voice of every righteous person for whom, through charity, even the overflowing iniquity of Christians is a suffering; thus Lot suffered no bodily persecution from anyone in Sodom, but suffered from the evil deeds of those among whom he lived. Therefore the righteous person’s persecution comes either from the lion in its attack or from the dragon in its snares; hence all cry out: ‘O God, attend to my help.’”

§ 3. When a prelate is distressed by the vices of his subjects, sometimes all share one insatiable obstinacy; sometimes evil persons are found mixed with the good. When good and evil live together, the good must not be abandoned because of the evil, lest, by perversely avoiding the wicked, we conquer unto Gehenna those from whom we flee. Rather, the evil ought to be tolerated for the sake of the good. Hence Gregory says: “He refuses to be Abel whom Cain’s malice does not exercise; for the iron of our mind cannot attain the sharpness of truth unless the file of another’s perversity has worn it down.”

Hence Augustine also says: “You who are good, endure evil,” etc., below, in the First Cause concerning the toleration of evils among heretics.

[Note: [Col. 0769] “In the First Cause”: this indicates Cause 23, where heretics are first considered expressly; this manner of citation is also found at 1, question 7, and elsewhere.]

The same writer says: “We commit a greater evil in separating the good than we avoid in association with the evil.” And below:

§ 4. “God does not impute his own sins to such a person, because he did not commit them; nor others’ sins, because he did not approve them; nor negligence, because he did not remain silent; nor pride, because he remained in unity.”

Hence the same writer, on Psalm 54: “‘Who will give me wings like a dove?’ He does not say, ‘like a raven.’ The dove seeks to fly away from troubles, but does not lose love and always groans. So the good person wishes to separate himself in body, not in love, from those whom he cannot benefit.”

And below:

§ 5. “But sometimes a person is bound, not by the birdlime of greed, but by care and office, so that he cannot depart unless released. If he is not released, then let him say: ‘I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ; but to remain in the flesh is necessary because of you’; and thus there is merit in the desire.”

§ 6. “‘Behold, I fled far away’: not in place, lest the love of the good be broken, lest the exercise of the evil be lost—those whom God mingles in, as Judas among the apostles. Though Christ knew him to be a thief, he nevertheless sent him to preach and gave him the Eucharist, teaching that the wicked are to be endured in the Church and that association with the wicked does not harm the good.”

But when all the subjects possess obstinate wickedness and the prelate’s presence benefits them nothing, then it is permissible even to depart from them bodily, lest their wickedness continually advance to worse things and the prelate lose the fruit which he might find from the progress of others. Thus blessed Benedict is recorded to have abandoned those whom he saw had unanimously conspired to kill him.

### Chapter XLIX. When prelates may, or may not, abandon their subjects

Evil persons are to be borne with equanimity where some good persons are found who may be helped. For where every fruit from the good is wholly absent, labour upon the evil sometimes becomes superfluous, especially if there are nearby opportunities capable of bearing better fruit for God.

§ 1. A circumstance often occurs in the minds of the perfect which must not be passed over in silence: when they see that their labour is fruitless, they transfer to another place in order to labour fruitfully. Hence that eminent preacher also, who desired to be dissolved and be with Christ, for whom “to live is Christ and to die is gain,” who not only sought contests of suffering for himself but also inflamed others to endure them, suffered persecution at Damascus; yet, in order that he might escape, he sought a wall, a rope, and a basket, and wished to be lowered secretly. Do we say that Paul feared the death which he himself testifies that he desired for the love of Jesus? Rather, when he perceived that there was less fruit for him in that place, he preserved himself elsewhere for arduous labour that would bear fruit. For the strong warrior of God refused to be held within an enclosure; he sought the field of battle.

### Chapter I. Concerning a certain priest suffering from epilepsy

Your letter contained the following: “This cleric holds the order of priesthood; but because he suffers from the falling sickness, and we have now personally ascertained this, we have not dared to permit him to offer or celebrate Mass. Yet since illness is not a fault, we have resolved to seek counsel on this matter by a decree of our authority.”

We advise, therefore, that if he is frequently afflicted by this illness, he should in every way be prohibited from offering and celebrating Masses. For it is indecent and dangerous that, while consecrating the Eucharist, overcome by epileptic illness, he should fall down. But if, by God’s mercy, he recovers, since illness and not fault is at issue, we no longer forbid him to sacrifice.

### Chapter II. One who is frequently dashed to the ground must be suspended from governing a church

Likewise Pope Gelasius to Rustic and Fortunatus, bishops.

The clerics of the Church of Foropopulensis recently disclosed in their own petition, together with Bishop Sabinus, Pelagius, and laymen, that their prelate was afflicted with a grave disorder, by the onset of which, they said, he was frequently dashed to the ground. Lest this appear to cause scandal to the faithful and disturb the Church of God everywhere by this offence—especially as they affirmed that he himself had willingly come here for this very reason—we sent letters to your charity, that you should make a suitable visitation of the church whose rector is held subject to such an affliction.

But because the same bishop has now come here and spreads abroad that all these allegations about him are false, after most diligently investigating the truth of the matter, in contemplation of divine judgment and out of regard for your conscience and reputation, inquire with the most searching examination possible whether he is ever proven suddenly to have collapsed—whether at home, in procession, or in any other place—and to have uttered confused cries and cast foam from his mouth. If this cannot be established by the testimony of anyone, or if it is said never to have occurred, that ought not to be thought sufficient; rather, clear and manifest proof is required, because a matter so grave must not be handled negligently. Brother Rustic, let your charity act according to its custom, and in a manner fitting for a great bishop: arrange that he remain with you for thirty days, and compel him to eat meat without restriction, as a necessary test.

[Note: [Col. 0771] *aestimationisque*, “and reputation”: Nuremberg, Venice I and II, Lyons, and Paris editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0771] “And when this cannot …”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0771] “Thirty”: in two old manuscripts one reads “eighty” [this, as we suppose, arose because the manuscripts followed by the collected editions, except Basel, read *l. XXX*, that is, “or thirty.”]]

# CAUSE VIII

[Col. 0771C] GRATIAN

A certain bishop, being at the point of death, appointed a successor for himself by testament. Thereupon, through the patronage of his friends, he is elected to the same episcopate. After his election, for the indemnity of the church, he gave an oath to the canons. He is accused of simony, on the ground that he rendered a gift in return for service. Before the time for judgment, he is abandoned by his clerics. Without apostolic letters, the bishop returns to his church.

(Question I.) Here the first question is whether it is lawful for a bishop to appoint his own successor.

(Question II.) Secondly, whether the patronage of friends ought to prevail in an election.

(Question III.) Thirdly, whether one is to be deemed a simoniac who, after election, gives the canons an oath of this kind.

(Question IV.) Fourthly, whether clerics may leave their bishop before the time for judgment.

(Question V.) Fifthly, whether he ought to return to his own church without apostolic letters.

## QUESTION I

## GRATIAN

I. Part. That it is lawful for a bishop to appoint a successor for himself is inferred from the words of Pope Zacharias, by which he permitted the Archbishop of Mainz to appoint himself an assistant who, after his death, would succeed to the fullness of authority.

§ 1. Likewise, from the words of Pope Symmachus, who says, “If the pope’s unexpected death should occur, so that he cannot determine beforehand concerning the election of his successor,” etc., it appears that bishops may appoint successors for themselves.

§ 2. Likewise, the same thing is proved by the example of blessed Peter, who appointed blessed Clement as his successor.

[Col. 0773A] Therefore John III writes to the bishops of Germany and Gaul, in his sole letter, chapter 2:

[Note: [Col. 0773] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Rufinus’s letter to Gaudentius.—Anselm, book 1, chapter 55 (56). Polycarpus, book 1, title 1.]

### Chapter I. Peter took Linus and Cletus as assistants, but Clement as successor

Although Peter, prince of the apostles, took Linus and Cletus as assistants, he did not hand over to them the authority of the pontificate or the rule of loosing and binding, but to his holy successor Clement, who deserved to hold, after Peter, the apostolic see and pontifical authority, these having been entrusted to him by blessed Peter. Linus and Cletus administered external matters, while Peter, prince of the apostles, devoted himself to preaching and prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0773] *instabat*, “was intent upon”: collected editions.]

[Col. 0773B]

### Chapter II. PALEA

“Therefore Clement himself writes, among other things, in a letter sent to James of Jerusalem, that Peter, while still living, chose Clement as bishop:

Simon Peter, in the very days when he foresaw the end of his life, grasped my hand and, suddenly rising, spoke these words in the hearing of the whole Church: ‘I ordain this Clement as your bishop. To him alone I entrust the chair of my preaching and teaching. I have found him, above all others, to be one who worships God, loves people, is chaste, devoted to the pursuit of learning, sober, kind, just, patient, and able to bear even the injuries of some of those who are instructed in the word of God.’”

[Note: [Col. 0773] An apocryphal chapter, drawn from the first part of Clement’s letter published by Rufinus.—Anselm, book 1, chapter 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0773] *discendis*, “learning/studies”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.]

Gratian. But the Council of Antioch absolutely forbids this practice. In its chapter 23 the following decree is read:

[Note: [Col. 0773] Held A.D. 332.—Dionysian translation.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 185. Anselm, book 6, chapter 57 (61). Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 301.]

### Chapter III. A bishop may not appoint a successor for himself

We decree that a bishop is not permitted to appoint another as his successor for himself, even though he has reached the end of life. If anything of this kind has been done, such an appointment shall be void. But ecclesiastical law is to be preserved, which provides that this must not be done otherwise than with a synod and the judgment of the bishops, who, after the death of the one who rests, have authority to promote the person found worthy.

[Note: [Col. 0773] “We decree that it is not permitted”: Basel edition.—*liceat*, “be permitted”: remaining editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0773D–0774D] In Gratian’s manuscripts the words “and the election of the clerics” followed *episcoporum*, “bishops” [thus in the collected editions], but they were deleted because they occur neither in the original nor in the other collectors.]

[Note: [Col. 0773] “to elect and promote”: the same editions.]

### Chapter IV. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Pope Martin, chapter 8

A bishop may not appoint another as successor in his own place before the end of his life. But if anyone attempts to usurp this, such an appointment shall be void. Therefore it ought not to be done otherwise than with the counsel and judgment of bishops, who, after the departure of the predecessor, have authority to elect a worthy person.

[Note: [Col. 0773] Adds *suae*, “his own”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0773] *concilio*, “council”: Basel, Venice I, Lyons I, and Paris editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0773] *judicio*, “judgment”: collected editions and cited collections.]

[Note: [Col. 0773] “to ordain the person whom they have elected as worthy”: Hispanic Collection.]

### Chapter V. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Hilary in the Roman Synod, chapter 5

Many priests, placed at the threshold of death, are reported to substitute others in their own place by designating names, so that lawful election is not awaited, but the favour bestowed by the deceased is regarded as the people’s assent. Consider how serious this is.

And therefore, if it please you, let us remove this permission generally from the churches, lest anyone think that what belongs to God is owed to a human being—shameful as it is to say so.

All cried out: “Let this presumption never occur. What belongs to God cannot be given by a human being.”

[Note: [Col. 0773] Held A.D. 465.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 56 (60). Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 104. Polycarpus, book 2, title 18.]

[Note: [Col. 0773] *gratificati populi*, “the favour of the gratified people”: Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: [Col. 0774D] From “And therefore” through the phrase “All cried out,” these words were added from the council itself, Anselm, Polycarpus, and Ivo.]

### C. VI. On the Same Subject. Likewise Jerome on Titus, ch. 1 [v. 5].

Moses, the friend of God, to whom God spoke face to face [Note: Exod. ch. 33], could certainly have made his own sons successors to his leadership and left his rank as a hereditary possession to his descendants. Yet Joshua, a stranger from another tribe, is chosen, so that we might know that authority over peoples is to be conferred not according to blood but according to life. But now we see very many people making this matter a favor: they do not seek to raise up in the Church as pillars those whom they recognize can benefit the Church more, but those whom they themselves love, or by whose services they have been won over, or those for whom some person of higher rank has made a request—and, not to mention worse cases, those who obtained clerical status through gifts.

[Note: “Jesus”: add, namely, Joshua, Basel edition; i.e. Joshua, the remaining editions. “Over peoples”: “over the people,” collected editions and first Lyons edition. “Very many”: “many,” collected editions. “Making this matter a favor”: “as a favor,” the same editions except Lyons II and III. The fuller original reads: “so that they do not seek those who can benefit the Church more, and in the Church, etc.” “Obtained”: “obtain,” collected editions, first Paris and Lyons editions.]

### C. VII. On the Same Subject. Likewise Pope Innocent II, in the Roman Council, ch. 16.

[Note: Held in A.D. 1139. The same provisions had already been issued by Innocent himself in the Council of Rheims, ch. 15. Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, ch. 152.]

By apostolic authority we forbid anyone to presume to claim or demand by hereditary right churches, prebends, provostships, chaplaincies, or any ecclesiastical offices. If any wicked person, or anyone guilty of ambition, should presume to attempt this, he shall be punished as he deserves and shall lose what he sought.

[Note: “Chaplaincies”: “chapels,” Ivo.]

Gratian. By all these authorities bishops are forbidden to appoint successors for themselves. But it is one thing to deliberate with their brethren concerning the election of a successor; it is another to seek a successor for oneself by testament, as though he were the heir of one’s rank. The former is permitted; the latter is altogether forbidden. Those who appoint such persons as successors for themselves may indeed take as an argument on their side the example of the blessed Apostle Peter, who sought for himself such a successor. But because office began to be conferred not according to life but according to blood, and because each began to seek as his successor in the episcopate persons either hateful to the people or found unsuitable to be taught by the populace, the sacred canons therefore established that no one should seek a successor to his own office, but that one should be sought by election of the people who would worthily serve their benefit: one who seeks their advantage, not his own gain; who wishes to raise up seed for Christ, not to gather riches for himself. Whoever scorns to do this is rightly rejected by the Church.

Hence Augustine, *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, bk. XXXII, ch. 10:

[Note: Here the words of blessed Augustine have both been reduced to a summary and at times altered, as has been observed elsewhere.]

### C. VIII. He Who Benefits Himself and the Church Is Understood to Be Shod on Both Feet.

Part II. Formerly a brother was commanded [Note: Deut. ch. 25] to take the wife of his deceased brother, so that he might raise offspring not for himself but for that brother, and that what was born from the union should be called by the dead man’s name. If he refused, he was customarily deprived of one sandal and spat upon in the face. Now every preacher of the Gospel ought to labor in the Church in such a way as to raise up seed for his deceased brother—that is, for Christ, who died for us—and that what is raised up may receive Christ’s name. But one elected by the Church who refuses the ministry of preaching the Gospel is deservedly and rightly despised by the Church itself. For one who benefits both himself and the Church is rightly understood to be shod on both feet. Hence that saying: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, of those who proclaim good things” [Note: Isa. ch. 52, v. 7]. But whoever avoids the care of gaining others will bear, not a figurative reproach of that barefoot man, but one fulfilled in himself.

[Note: “In the face”: “on the face,” Argentinian and Basel editions. “Now”: add “however,” Basel edition. After “preaching the Gospel,” the vulgate editions continued “and baptizing”; these words have been deleted because they are not found in the manuscripts or in the original. “Peace, proclaiming”: omitted in the Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I–II, and Paris editions.]

### C. IX. A Position of Government Is to Be Denied to Those Who Desire It, but Offered to Those Who Flee It. Likewise Pope Gregory in the *Register*, bk. VI, ep. 5, to Bishop Cyriacus.

[Note: Ep. 4, written A.D. 597, bk. 7, Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, ch. 350.]

In your letters you report that you have earnestly sought rest; but by this you show that you have fittingly come to pastoral responsibility, because, just as a position of government must be denied to those who desire it, so it must be offered to those who flee from it. And as it is written: “No one takes this honor upon himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” [Note: Heb. ch. 5, v. 4]. Again the same outstanding preacher says: “If one died for all, then all died; and Christ died for all, so that those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them” [Note: 2 Cor. ch. 5, vv. 14–15]. And the shepherd of the holy Church is told: “Simon, son of John, do you love me? Feed my sheep” [Note: John ch. 21, v. 17]. From these words it is gathered that, if one who is able refuses to feed the sheep of almighty God, he shows that he does not love the supreme Shepherd. For if the only-begotten Son of the Father came forth from the Father’s hidden dwelling into our public world in order to accomplish the benefit of all, what shall we say if we prefer our own seclusion to the benefit of our neighbors?

§ 1. Therefore rest is to be desired from the heart; yet for the profit of many it must sometimes be postponed. For just as we ought with all desire to flee occupations, so, if there is no one to preach, we must willingly take up the burden of occupation upon our shoulder. We are taught this by the conduct of two prophets, one of whom attempted to avoid the office of preaching and the other sought it. For Jeremiah answered the Lord who was sending him [Note: Jer. ch. 1, v. 6], saying: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, I do not know how to speak, because I am a child.” But when almighty God sought a person to preach, saying: “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” [Note: Isa. ch. 6, v. 8], Isaiah voluntarily offered himself, saying: “Here I am; send me.” See: from both came outwardly different words, yet they did not flow from a different fountain of love. For there are two commandments of charity: namely, love of God and love of neighbor. Thus Isaiah, desiring through the active life to benefit his neighbors, sought the office of preaching. Jeremiah, however, desiring through the contemplative life diligently to cleave to the love of his Creator, objected to being sent to preach.
