What one laudably sought, the other laudably feared: the latter, lest by speaking he lose the gains of silent contemplation; the former, lest by silence he suffer the losses of zealous work. But in both cases this must be carefully observed: the one who refused did not resist completely, and the one who wished to be sent first saw himself cleansed by a coal from the altar, lest anyone not cleansed dare approach the sacred ministries, or one whom heavenly grace has chosen proudly object under a guise of humility.

[Note: “Letters”: “writings,” original and Ivo. “Take”: “takes,” collected editions. The original continues: “It remains, therefore, that those who live…”; Basel: “It remains that those who live…”; other editions: “And if this is so, it remains that those who live….” “Shoulder”: “mind,” Ivo. “Sending”: “sending back,” Basel edition. “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God”: collected editions read “Behold.” “For us”: “from among you,” collected editions. “Flowed”: “flowed forth,” original, collected editions, and Böhm. “Sought”: “seeks,” original and Argentinian edition. “The other”: “another,” collected editions. “Anyone”: “whoever,” Basel edition. “Sacred ministries”: “sacred mysteries,” collected editions and first Basel edition. “Has chosen”: “chooses,” original, Argentinian, and Venice II editions.]

### C. X. A Lowly Position Is a Matter of Choice; a Dignified One Is Always Accepted from Necessity. The Same Author in the *Morals*, bk. XXXV, ch. 13, on Job ch. 42.

It must especially be known that obedience is sometimes no obedience if it has something of its own; at other times it is minimal if it has nothing of its own. For when success in this world is commanded, when a higher position is imposed, one who obeys in receiving these things empties for himself the virtue of obedience if he also longs for them from personal desire. For one does not govern himself under obedience if, in obtaining the prosperity of this life, he serves the appetite of his own ambition. Again, when contempt for the world is commanded, when one is ordered to undergo reproaches and insults, unless the mind itself seeks these things, obedience diminishes its own merit, because it descends unwillingly and reluctantly to what is despised in this life.

And a little earlier:

§ 1. Obedience is rightly preferred to sacrifices, because by sacrifices another’s flesh is slain, whereas by obedience one’s own will is slain. Therefore the more swiftly each person appeases God, the more he immolates himself before God’s eyes by the sword of the commandment, having repressed the pride of his own will. Thus disobedience is called the sin of divination, in order to show how great the virtue of obedience is. Therefore, by its opposite, what is thought of its praise is shown more clearly. For if resistance is like the sin of divination, and refusal to comply is like the crime of idolatry [Note: 1 Sam. ch. 15, v. 23], obedience alone possesses the merit of faith; without it anyone is proved unbelieving, even though he may seem to be faithful.

[Note: “Has”: “had,” Argentinian and Basel editions; “will have,” other editions. “Has”: “has,” original. “Obedience”: “of obedience,” Böhm. “Thus”: “which,” collected editions and first Nuremberg edition. “Is shown”: “is shown to be,” collected editions.]

### C. XI. He Who Desires to Preside and Not to Benefit Others Ought Not to Be a Bishop. Likewise Augustine, *City of God*, bk. XIX, ch. 19.

“He who desires the episcopate desires a good work.” He wished to explain what episcopacy is, because it is the name of a work, not of an honor. For it is a Greek word, drawn from this: the one set over others watches over those over whom he is set, namely, taking care of them. For *epi* (ἐπί) means “over,” while *skopos* (σκοπός) means “attention” or “aim.” Therefore *episcopi* may, if we wish, be called in Latin “overseers,” so that one may understand that he is not a bishop who has loved to preside rather than to benefit others.

Accordingly, no one is forbidden from the pursuit of knowledge of truth, which pertains to praiseworthy leisure. But a higher position, without which a people cannot be governed, even if it is held and administered as it ought to be, is nevertheless not rightly sought. Therefore holy leisure seeks the love of truth; the necessity of love undertakes just business. If no one imposes this burden, one should devote oneself to apprehending and contemplating the truth; but if it is imposed, it must be undertaken because love requires it. Yet even then the delight of truth must not be wholly abandoned, lest that sweetness be withdrawn and just necessity crush us.

[Note: “Name”: added in the Basel edition. “For *epi* means ‘over’”: absent in Anselm. Anselm and the collected editions read “indeed” after *skopos*. In Saint Augustine and Anselm the reading is: “ἐπισκοπεῖν, if we wish, may be called in Latin *superintendere*, ‘to oversee.’” “Abandoned”: Lyons editions read “desired.” “Crush us”: the original reads, “and this necessity crush [us],” but it has not been emended because of the gloss.]

### C. XII. A Teacher Should Adapt the Words of Instruction to the Capacity of the Learner. Likewise Peter.

[Note: From the apocryphal letter of Clement, published by Rufinus.]

Part III. He who teaches and instructs unformed souls ought to be such that he can accommodate himself to the ability of the learners and direct the order of his speech according to the hearer’s capacity. Therefore he himself ought especially to be thoroughly educated and learned, blameless, mature, fearful, as you yourselves have found this Clement will be after me.

### C. XIII. He Who Presides over All Should Endeavor to Relieve Each Person. Likewise the Same Author.

[Note: From the same source.]

Clement, since you know yourself to be one who is to preside over all, help each person as far as you can, and relieve each one, because you bear the burden and care of every individual.

[Note: “As though”: “if, as though,” collected editions and first Argentinian edition. “Since you know yourself”: “wishing,” Argentinian edition; “you will have wished,” remaining editions. “Can”: “will be able,” collected editions. “Because”: “that,” Basel edition.]

### C. XIV. Those Who Confer an Ecclesiastical Rank through Favor Rather Than Merit Act against Christ. Likewise Jerome on Titus, ch. 1.

“He who despises you despises me.” From this it is evident that those who, contrary to the Apostle’s law, wish to confer an ecclesiastical rank on someone not according to merit but through favor act against Christ, who through his Apostle has set forth in what follows what sort of person ought to be appointed presbyter in the Church.

[Note: “Those who”: “because those who,” collected editions except Lyons II and III. “Not according to merit”: “not according to merits,” collected editions. “On someone”: “of someone,” Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I–II editions. “Appear”: added in the collected editions and first Lyons II–III editions.]

### C. XV. No One Is to Be Chosen for the Priesthood Unless He Is Regarded as Holier and More Learned Than the Rest. Likewise Jerome in the Book of Leviticus.

[Note: In this and the following two chapters, blessed Jerome, the translator of these homilies, is cited in place of Origen. Why this may have occurred has been noted above, Distinction 36, ch. *Si quis*. From Origen’s Homily 6 on Leviticus ch. 8, translated by Rufinus.]

Although the Lord had commanded concerning the appointment of a leader, and the Lord had chosen him, nevertheless the synagogue also is assembled. For in ordaining a priest the presence of the people is required, so that all may know and be certain that the one chosen for the priesthood is he who is outstanding among all the people, more learned, holier, and more eminent in every virtue; and this is done with the people standing by, lest afterward there remain any reconsideration or any doubt in anyone’s mind. This is also what the Apostle commanded in the ordination of a priest, saying: “He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside” [Note: 1 Tim. ch. 3, v. 9].

Yet I see something further in the statement that Moses assembled the whole synagogue. I think that “assembling the synagogue” means gathering all the powers of the soul and bringing the virtues together into one, so that, when discourse is held concerning priestly mysteries, all the soul’s powers may be alert and attentive: so that there may lack in them neither wisdom nor diligence, but there may be present the whole multitude of perceptions and the whole assembly of holy thoughts, in order that one may, by reflecting within the sanctuary of one’s heart, understand what a high priest is, what anointing is, and what his garments are.

[Note: “Is required”: “let it be required,” Argentinian edition. “For”: “therefore,” collected editions. “Presence”: “judgment,” Basel edition. “Is chosen”: “be chosen,” Venice II edition. “Standing by”: “bearing witness,” collected editions. “Commanded”: “commands,” same editions. “But”: “also,” Basel edition. “And”: absent in the same editions. “Powers”: added in collected editions. “That … virtues”: omitted in Basel edition. “No wisdom”: collected editions add “of knowledge.”]

### C. XVI. The Government of the People Should Be Entrusted through Divine Election. The Same Author from the Book of Numbers.

[Note: From Origen, Homily 22 on Numbers ch. 27.]

If, therefore, that great and such a man as Moses does not allow judgment concerning the choice of a leader for the people, concerning the appointment of a successor, to rest with himself, who will dare—whether from the people, who are often accustomed to be moved by cries stirred up by favor or perhaps by money, or even from the priests themselves—who will judge himself fit for this, unless it is revealed by the Lord to one who prays and asks? Thus God says to Moses: “Take to yourself Joshua son of Nun, a man who has the Spirit of God within himself; lay your hands upon him; set him before Eleazar the priest; give him commands in the sight of the whole synagogue; command him concerning it before them; and give your splendor upon him, that the children of Israel may listen to him” [Note: Num. ch. 27, v. 18].

You hear the ordination of a leader of the people described so plainly that it scarcely needs explanation. Here there is no acclamation of the people, no consideration of blood relationship, no regard for kinship. Let inheritance of fields and estates be left to relatives. Government of the people should be entrusted to the man whom God has chosen: that is, to such a man as has within himself, as you have heard written, the Spirit of God; before whom God’s commands are set; and who is very well known and close to Moses—that is, one in whom there is the splendor and knowledge of the law, so that the children of Israel may be able to listen to him.

[Note: “Does not allow”: “is not allowed,” collected editions. “By favor or money stirred up”: collected editions read, “either by favor or by money … stirred up.” “For this”: added in the same editions. “Here”: “therefore,” Basel edition. “Has chosen”: “chooses,” Argentinian and Basel editions; “has chosen,” remaining editions. “Its”: added in collected editions.]

### C. XVII. Election Must Proceed Not from Favor but from Judgment. Likewise Gregory to the Clergy and Citizens of Naples, bk. VIII, ep. 40.

[Note: Ep. 62, written A.D. 600, bk. 10, Maurist edition; Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 9 [13]; Polycarpus, bk. 2, title 1.]

It is neither new nor blameworthy for the people’s votes to divide into two parties in choosing a bishop; but it is serious when, in such matters, election proceeds not from judgment but from favor alone.

Gratian. But when government of the people is commanded to be entrusted to the one whom God has chosen, it is thereby understood that it is sometimes entrusted to persons whom God has not chosen.

Hence Jerome, from Origen, Homily 4 on the Book of Judges, ch. 4:

### C. XVIII. At Times a Ruler of the Church Is Given Not by God’s Will.

Part IV. We perhaps say something bold, yet we say what is written. A ruler of the people and judge of the Church is not always given by God’s determination, but according as our merits demand. If our deeds are evil and we work wickedness in the sight of the Lord, rulers are given to us according to our heart. And I will prove this to you from the Scriptures. Hear what the Lord says: “They made a king for themselves, and not through me; a ruler, and not according to my counsel” [Note: Hos. ch. 8, v. 4].

This appears to have been said concerning Saul, whom indeed the Lord himself had chosen and commanded to be made king. But because he had been chosen not according to God’s will but according to the deserving of a sinful people, God denies that he was established by his own will or counsel. Let us therefore understand that something similar occurs in the churches: according to the merits of the people, either a ruler powerful in word and deed is granted by God to the Church, or, if the people do evil in the sight of the Lord, such a judge is given to the Church under whom the people suffer hunger and thirst—not hunger for bread or thirst for water, but hunger for hearing the word of the Lord.

[Note: “Work”: “work,” Argentinian edition; “work wicked things,” collected editions. “From the Holy Scriptures”: “holy” added in the same editions. “What”: “which … says,” same editions. “According to the merits of the people”: “namely” added in Basel edition. “Or”: “and,” collected editions and first Lyons II–III editions. The vulgate editions continued after “in the sight of the Lord”: “and such churches continue”; these words have been inserted on the authority of the manuscripts, the homily itself, and the ordinary gloss. In one manuscript they occur as an interlinear gloss. “Word of the Lord”: “of God,” collected editions.]

### C. XIX. Those Who Seek Honor from Men Are Not Sons but Hirelings. Likewise Augustine, Tractate XLVI on John ch. 10.

[Note: Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 146 [157].]

There are certain rulers in the Church of whom the Apostle Paul says: “Seeking their own things, not those of Jesus Christ” [Note: Phil. ch. 2, v. 21]. What does “seeking their own things” mean? It means not loving Christ freely, not seeking God for God’s sake, but pursuing temporal advantages, hungering after gains, and seeking honors from men. When these things are loved by a ruler and God is served for their sake, whoever he may be, he is a hireling; let him not count himself among the sons.

[Note: “Pursuing”: “obtaining,” Anselm; “following,” collected editions. “The sons”: “his sons,” added in the same editions.]

Gratian. Therefore those who are placed over others are not always understood to be better than the rest.

Hence Jerome on Titus, ch. 1:

### C. XX. Bishops Are Not Set over Others by Election but Approved by It.

This must be urged against those who are puffed up over the episcopate and think that they have received not Christ’s stewardship but an empire: they should understand that they are not thereby immediately better than all those who have not been ordained bishops, nor should they suppose themselves more approved because they themselves have been chosen. Rather, let them understand that some are excluded from the priesthood because the vices of their children have hindered them. But if the sins of children bar a just man from the episcopate, how much more should each person examine himself and, knowing that the powerful will suffer powerful torments, withdraw himself from this position—not so much an honor as a burden—and not covet to occupy the place of others who are more worthy.

[Note: “Bishops”: omitted in collected editions. “Themselves”: “they themselves,” Lyons II–III editions. “Suppose”: “judge,” collected editions and first Lyons II–III editions. The words “but … have hindered them” are absent from the collected editions and first Lyons II–III editions. “The powerful will suffer powerful torments”: the same editions, except Venice I, Paris, and Lyons, read “the powerful … will suffer.” “Withdraw”: “withdraws,” collected editions. “Covet”: “covets,” Nuremberg, Venice II, Lyons II–III editions; “doubts,” Argentinian, Basel, Venice I, Lyons I, and Paris editions.]

### C. XXI. Each Person Ought to Be Better in Proportion to the Rank of His Office. Likewise the Same Author on Titus, ch. 2.

For what sort of building will that of a disciple be if he knows himself to be greater than his master? Therefore not only bishops, presbyters, and deacons ought earnestly to provide that they surpass in conduct, speech, and knowledge all the people over whom they preside, but also the lower ranks—exorcists, readers, doorkeepers, acolytes, and indeed all who serve the house of God—for it greatly destroys Christ’s Church when laypeople are better than clerics.

[Note: “Knowledge”: “discipline,” Basel edition; “and knowledge” omitted in the collected editions and first Paris and Lyons editions. “Doorkeepers”: “keepers of the buildings,” collected editions. “Acolytes”: the word occurs in all ancient copies of Gratian, though it is not found in blessed Jerome. “Serve”: “serve devotedly,” same editions. “Christ’s Church”: “God’s Church,” same editions.]

### C. XXII. The People Will Judge a Bishop Who Does Not Perform His Duties. The Same Author on Titus, ch. 1.

I fear that, just as the queen of the South, coming from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, will judge the people of her own time, and the men of Nineveh, having done penance at Jonah’s preaching, will condemn those who scorned to hear the Savior greater even than Jonah, so very many among the people will judge bishops who withdraw themselves from their ecclesiastical rank and perform things not suitable to a bishop.

[Note: This passage is absent from the collected editions and first Lyons edition; compare Matt. ch. 10. “Greater even than Jonah”: “even” added in collected editions. “Things not suitable to a bishop”: the same editions read, “do not perform the things suitable to a bishop.”]

### C. XXIII. He Who Does Not Correct His Clerics Cannot Correct the People. Likewise Ambrose, in a Reproof to the People, Sermon 83.

[Note: There are some who deny that this sermon is by Ambrose.]

But why do I rebuke you, when you can convict me with one discourse? For I am convicted when in this respect I see the clerics more negligent than you. How can I correct sons when I cannot amend brothers? Or with what confidence can I be angry with laypeople when shame causes me to keep silent before my companions? Yet, brethren, I do not speak of all. There are certainly some who are devout, and there are others who are negligent. I name no one; let each person’s own conscience confront him.

[Note: “Certainly”: “however,” Basel edition.]

### C. XXIV. For a Bishop’s Salvation, It Is Not Enough to Equal the People in Conduct and Life. Likewise Bede on Matthew.

[Note: Collected tractates of the Fathers, pt. 2, vol. 50, ch. 18.]

Let us not suppose that it suffices for our salvation if we equal in faith or deeds the crowds of the negligent or of any unlearned persons, for whom the sacred Scriptures have laid down one and the same rule of believing and living.

[Note: “Unlearned”: “introduced,” Basel edition.]

Gratian. Therefore, lest, as was said above [Note: Compare above, ch. 7], anyone should seek such persons as successors to his own office, bishops are forbidden to appoint another as a successor in their place or, by designating names, to substitute another in their own place.

## QUESTION II

### GRATIAN

That the patronage of friends ought not to prevail in anyone’s election is proved by the authority of blessed Pope Gregory, who writes in the second book of the *Register*, Indiction 11, ep. 22, to Subdeacon Anthony:

[Note: Ep. 22, written A.D. 593, bk. 3, Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, ch. 129; Polycarpus, bk. 2, title 3.]

### C. I. In the Election of a Bishop, Neither the Giving of Gifts nor Anyone’s Patronage Is to Prevail.

Above all, let this be your concern: that in this election neither the giving of rewards in any form intervene nor the patronage of any persons prevail. For if anyone is elected through the patronage of certain people, once ordained he is compelled, out of the reverence due to them, to comply with their wishes; and thus both the property of that Church is diminished and ecclesiastical order is not maintained. Therefore, with your exhortation, they ought to choose for themselves such a person as may serve no unsuitable will of anyone, but may be found worthy of so great an order because he is adorned with life and character.

[Note: “Diminished”: “reduced,” collected editions. “With your exhortation”: “with your threatening,” original and Ivo. “But”: “if,” Argentinian and Basel editions.]

### C. II. In Choosing a Bishop, Each Person Should Look to the Common Good, Not His Own Gain. The Same Author to the Clergy of Milan, bk. II, Indiction 11, ep. 29.

[Note: Ep. 29, written in the same year, bk. 2, Maurist edition; Ivo, same place, ch. 130; Polycarpus, same place.]

Most beloved sons, warned by the discipline of our office, we urge that in this matter of receiving a bishop none of you, neglecting the common good, look to his own gain; lest anyone seeking private advantage deceive himself with a worthless judgment, since a mind bound by greed does not examine with free judgment the person to be preferred. Therefore, considering what is advantageous to all, always offer in all things most complete obedience to the one whom divine grace has set over you. For a person once set over you ought no longer to be judged by you; but he must now be judged with so much the greater care because afterward he is not to be judged.

[Note: “Look to his own gain”: “make progress,” Ivo.]

## QUESTION III

### GRATIAN

That a person who, after election, has taken an oath for the indemnity of the Church is not to be regarded as simoniacal is easily proved. For it is one thing to take an oath before election, or to bargain that one will do so in order to be elected; it is another, when no agreement has preceded, to offer such an oath after election. The former excludes a person from office as though it were a gift conferred; the latter creates no obstacle to the one being consecrated. Pope Pelagius writes concerning the former case to the clergy of Catania:

[Note: Epistle of Pelagius II; compare ch. 21, Distinction 61; Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 40 [45]; Polycarpus, bk. 2, title 3.]

### C. I. He Who Is Chosen Bishop Must Give No Security to Anyone Concerning Ecclesiastical Property.

We have already sent directions to our brother and fellow bishop Eucarpus concerning the visitation of the Church of Catania, so that you might have been able to recognize our judgment from them. Nevertheless, because we have learned also from your report that certain persons there are stirring up dissensions, not from a sound intention but through perverse schemes—persons who know that they cannot attain the episcopate by age, knowledge, or merits of life, and who wish to disturb the Church solely in order that the future bishop may promise them immunity concerning matters which have been unlawfully taken from that Church, and thus ambition for the episcopate may become security for plunder—we have thought it necessary to admonish you also that you should promptly bring to us, God willing, the decree made concerning Deacon Elpidius and subscribed by all those named in your report, together with the letter of the aforesaid visitor and with the deacon himself.

And after a few words: When our son Leo the praetor, a distinguished man, had come here, he reported to us individually on the matters raised there and how the votes of almost the entire city agreed upon Deacon Elpidius. Therefore, because we cannot at all doubt the testimony of this man, cause Deacon Elpidius, as has been said, to hasten to us; do not wait any longer for our admonition to have to be sent to him. Yet by your belovedness we expressly admonish him in this present command that he promise no one that he has given, or will give, anything; nor dare to make or promise any security to anyone concerning past ecclesiastical cases; nor, as though already made bishop, fail to recover what has been plundered, while freely allowing it to remain with those who plundered it. Let him know that if he has done or shall do anything of this sort, the promise itself will not be allowed validity by us in any respect, and, with the condemnation of our judgment upon him, he will be unable to obtain the rank of pastoral consecration.

[Note: “Not from a sound intention”: “not from a sound mind or intention,” Basel edition. “Wish”: “wished,” collected editions. “Bishop”: Anselm wrongly reads “bishop” for “deacon.” “Aforesaid”: “aforesaid [feminine],” Basel edition. The words “When, therefore … sent to him” are absent in Anselm. “Here”: “there,” Basel edition. “Sent”: “repeated,” Basel edition. “And”: “or,” Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice II editions; absent from the others. “In this present command”: “in this present [matter],” collected editions except first Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice II editions. “Past ecclesiastical cases”: absent in Anselm. “By us in any respect”: “by all,” Lyons II–III editions. “Upon him”: “upon himself,” collected editions.]

Gratian. Concerning the second case, however, it is read in the acts of Urban II:

[Note: Collected tractates of the Fathers, pt. 2, vol. 50, ch. 21.]

### C. II. After Election It Is Lawful for the Person Elected to Take an Oath for the Indemnity of the Church.

Bishop Artaldus of Arles, a suffragan of the Church of Narbonne, came to Rome to be consecrated by Lord Pope Urban. For his own archbishop refused to consecrate him because, after his election, he had sworn to the canons for the preservation of the Church’s property. He was therefore consecrated by Lord Pope Urban after he had first cleared himself concerning this oath:

> “Regarding the oath which I made to the canons of our Church after my election: I made no agreement before my election in order that I might be chosen. The archbishop of Narbonne omitted our consecration for no charge except this, so far as I know; nor am I conscious of any crime for which he might exclude me from sacred anointing.”

[Note: “Of Arles”: this is also the manuscript reading. But an error seems to underlie it, since this bishop is here called a suffragan of the archbishop of Narbonne, whereas in the Second Council of Arles that city is assigned to the Viennese province. Although William Durand cites this in the *Speculum de auctoritate et usu pallii* to show that the archbishop of Arles is subject to Narbonne, John Andreae explicitly writes in his notes on that passage that this chapter does not concern the archbishop of Arles. It is very probable that *Arelatensis* was corruptly written for *Electensis* or *Elatensis*; indeed, the correct reading will be *Helenensis*, for Helena—commonly Elne—is a city of Narbonese Gaul, from which the episcopal see, though retaining its name, was transferred to Perpignan by Clement VIII. “Their canons”: added in the Basel edition. “Sacred”: “priestly,” collected editions.]

## QUESTION IV

### GRATIAN

That clerics may not leave their bishop before the time of judgment is proved by the authority of Pope Symmachus, who says:

[Note: Under the name of Pope Symmachus is cited the treatise of Ennodius; the reason for this has been given above, Distinction 31, ch. *Omnino*, and Distinction 40, ch. *Non nos*. These passages are taken from Ennodius’s apology for the Fourth Roman Synod; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, chs. 340–341.]

### C. I. Clerics May Not Leave Their Bishop before the Time of Judgment.

Are not the words of the canons explicit? [Note: [Col. 0785C] “Canons”: thus corrected from ancient codices, Ennodius himself, and Ivo, whereas it had previously read [Col. 0785D] “decree” [Col. 0786C] [thus in the other collected editions and the first Basel edition]. Ennodius, however, intended to cite the canons issued before Symmachus on this matter. Those cited in the gloss are from letters of popes later than Symmachus. In the Carthaginian Council inserted in the code of canons there is indeed the eleventh canon, cited below at Cause 11, question 3, chapter *If Any Presbyter*; the nineteenth, reported above at Cause 4, question 6, chapter *Whoever of the Bishops*; and the twenty-fourth, cited there at chapter *It Pleased*. Ennodius appears to have referred to these, and especially to the first [Col. 0786D].] “Whoever of the clergy [Note: [Col. 0785] “If anyone”: the other collected editions.] departs from his bishop before the time of judgment because of a doubtful suspicion, it is evident that censure remains upon him [Note: [Col. 0785] “upon him” (*in eum*): the same editions.].” And below: § 1. “For [Note: [Col. 0785] “For” added: the same editions.] ecclesiastical law requires that a bishop accused by others not be abandoned before the charges brought against him have been established in the light.”

## QUESTION V

[Col. 0786A]

### GRATIAN

A bishop who has been accused and summoned by the Holy See must not return to his church without apostolic letters.

Accordingly Pope Sixtus I says in Letter II, chapter 2 [Note: [Col. 0785] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter, composed from the *Book of the Pontiffs* and Innocent I’s letter to Decentius of Gubbio.—Anselm, book 2, chapter 8.]:

**C. I. A bishop summoned by the Apostolic See must not return home unless he has been cleared and furnished with apostolic letters.**

Any one of the brethren against whom a charge has been made and who has been summoned by this Holy See, when he has appeared before us *, must nevertheless not return first to his own church * until he has been fully furnished with apostolic or formal letters and cleared, if there is cause for this [Note: [Col. 0785] “Hence” added: the other collected editions.], so that [Note: [Col. 0785] “and”: the same editions and the first Lyons editions II and III.], after he has returned home, his neighbors may know [Note: [Col. 0785] “recognize”: the other collected editions.] how [Col. 0786B] he concluded his own case and that of others here, so that he may report and proclaim it to everyone without any ambiguity [Note: [Col. 0785] “that case”: the same editions.]. For bishops have been commanded to be protected, defended, and delivered by this Holy See [Note: [Col. 0785] “and by”: Lyons editions II and III.—Böhm.] of the holy apostles, so that [Note: [Col. 0785] “and”: the other collected editions and the first Strasbourg edition.], just as they were first established by their ordering under the Lord, so in future times they may always remain free from every perversity through the protection of this Holy See, to whose ordering they reserved their cases and judgments. Hence those are blamed who have acted toward the brethren otherwise than they knew would please the rulers of this See.

## CAUSE IX

[Col. 0785]

[Col. 0785C]

### GRATIAN

A certain archbishop, marked by a sentence of excommunication, ordained several clerics belonging to another metropolitan; without consulting his suffragan, he deposed a certain chaplain of that suffragan and ordained another in his place. (Question I.) Here it is first asked whether an ordination performed by excommunicated persons can in any way be held valid. (Question II.) Second, whether it is lawful for a bishop, archbishop, primate, or patriarch to ordain another’s clerics without their own letters. (Question III.) Third, whether [Col. 0786C] an archbishop can condemn the clerics of his suffragan without consulting him, or absolve those already condemned.

## QUESTION I

### GRATIAN

That an ordination celebrated by excommunicated persons has absolutely no force, and ought not even to be called a consecration, is attested by Gregory, book III, letter 20, who says [Note: [Col. 0785] Letter 20, written A.D. 594, book 4, Maurist edition.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 55, chapter 93. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 134. *Polycarpus*, book 2, title 37.]:

[Col. 0787A]

**C. I. What is performed by excommunicated persons cannot be called a consecration.**

We can in no way call a consecration that which has been celebrated by excommunicated persons [Note: [Col. 0787] “Illicitly” added: the other collected editions.].

**C. II. PALEA** [Note: [Col. 0787D] This and the following *Palea* are absent from most ancient copies; nevertheless they occur in one very carefully corrected copy, in which few such additions are usually found. This first one appears to be a certain summary [Col. 0788D] of the following chapter.] [Note: [Col. 0787] “This is a summary of the following chapter.”]

“Excommunicated persons unlawfully impose hands because they do not possess the power of ordaining. But where the imposition of hands is unlawful, a wound is implanted [Note: [Col. 0787] “inflicted”: Böhm.]. Therefore what is shown not to have been conferred must necessarily be repeated.”

Accordingly Pope Damasus says in Letter IV [Note: [Col. 0787] Compare Cause 1, question 7, chapter 25.]:

**C. III. PALEA**

“Those who seemed to have received something had their heads wounded by an unlawful imposition of hands; and where a wound has been implanted, medicine [Col. 0787B] must be applied, by which the implanted [Note: [Col. 0787] “fixed”: there.] blemish may be healed. That is [Note: [Col. 0787] “Likewise”: there.], what is shown not to have been lawfully done or conferred must necessarily be repeated, *if it is to be complete.* For I cannot discover how one can retain an office who received [Note: [Col. 0787] “receives”: there.] it from one who did not lawfully have power to give it.”

Gratian. But the excommunicated persons here meant are those who incurred the penalty of excommunication in their very ordination and were never numbered among Catholics. On the other hand, if those who were formerly counted among Catholics are afterward marked by a sentence of excommunication, their ordinations are nevertheless mercifully tolerated by the Church.

[Col. 0787C]

Accordingly Pope Urban II writes as follows [Note: [Col. 0787] To Gebhard of Constance, A.D. 1089; compare Berthold of Constance’s chronicle for that year.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 456. Anselm, book 12, chapter 74.]:

**C. IV. Ordinations performed by excommunicated persons, when not simoniacal, are tolerated in mercy.**

Those ordained by excommunicated bishops who nevertheless were once Catholics, provided that they received these orders not simoniacally and that the bishops themselves are not proved to have been simoniacs—further [Note: [Col. 0787] “At this point” (*hoc*): the other collected editions.—Ivo.], if their more religious life and distinction in learning appear to deserve it [Note: [Col. 0787] “Appear to promise it”: Roman edition, through a printer’s error.]—you may permit them, after imposing such penance as you judge suitable, to remain in the orders they received. But we do not permit them to ascend to higher orders unless the greatest necessity or benefit demands it and their holy manner of life has deserved it.

Gratian. Gregory’s statement too is to be understood concerning those excommunicated by name, whose ordinations are [Col. 0788A] invalid if their condemnation was not unknown to those being ordained.

Accordingly Urban says in the Synod of Piacenza, chapter 9 and those following [Note: [Col. 0787] Held A.D. 1095.—*Polycarpus*, book 7, chapter 16; book 2, title 38.]:

**C. V. Those excommunicated by name, and those who invade the sees of others, cannot ordain others.**

We judge invalid the ordinations performed by heresiarchs excommunicated by name and by those who have invaded the sees of Catholic bishops still living, unless those ordained wish to prove that, when they were ordained, they did not know them to have been condemned.

§ 1. But those [Note: [Col. 0787] Chapter 10.] consecrated by bishops once [Note: [Col. 0787] “Indeed” added: the original and other collected editions.] ordained as Catholics but separated from the Roman Church in schism, we order to be mercifully received when they have returned to the unity of the Church [Col. 0788B], while retaining their own orders—provided, *however*, that their life and learning commend them [Note: [Col. 0787] “Commend”: the other collected editions, except the first Strasbourg, Basel, and Nuremberg editions.].

§ 2. Henceforth [Note: [Col. 0787] Chapter 11.], however, whoever permits himself to be ordained by the aforesaid schismatics and adversaries of the Holy Roman Church is by no means to be considered worthy of this indulgence.

§ 3. Although [Note: [Col. 0787] Chapter 12.], with mercy in view and under the compulsion of great necessity, we have established this dispensation in sacred orders, we do not wish any prejudice to be done to the sacred canons [Note: [Col. 0787] “We wished”: Böhm.]; rather, they are to retain [Note: [Col. 0787] “It is to retain”: Basel edition.] their proper force, and when necessity ceases, that too which was done because of necessity is to cease. For where the slaughter of many lies before us, something must be withdrawn from severity, *so that more may be added [Note: [Col. 0788D] “So that more may be added,” etc.: these words have been added from the council itself.] to charity.*

Gratian. An election too, unless it has been made by Catholics [Col. 0788C], is shown to be invalid.

Accordingly Gregory writes to the Milanese, book VIII, letter 65 [Note: [Col. 0787] Letter 4, written A.D. 601, book 11, Maurist edition.—*Polycarpus*, book 2, title 1. *Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 57, chapter 7.]:

**C. VI. An election not proved to have been made by Catholics is invalid.**

We in no way give our consent to a man who is not chosen by Catholics [Note: [Col. 0787] “And especially by Lombards” added: the original.]; nor, if he has been made [Note: [Col. 0787] “It has been made”: the original and other collected editions.] so by the usurpation of some *presumption*, do we receive him into that place or order of priesthood.

## QUESTION II

### GRATIAN

**Part I.** That a bishop, or any one of the superiors, ought not to ordain another’s clerics without their own letters [Col. 0789A] is written by Pope Callixtus in Letter II to the bishops of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0789] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Apostolic Canon 36 and Antioch, canon 3.—Regino, book 1, chapter 251. Anselm, book 6, chapter 120 (126). Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 236; part 14, chapter 72.]:

**C. I. No one may presume to judge a parishioner of another church.**

Let no one usurp another’s boundaries, nor presume to judge or ordain [Note: [Col. 0789] “Ordain” is absent from the original, Regino, and Ivo.], excommunicate, or condemn another’s parishioner, because such a judgment or [Note: [Col. 0789] “Or” is lacking there.] ordination, excommunication, or condemnation will neither be valid nor have any force, since no one will be bound or condemned by the sentence of any judge other than his own. Hence the Lord also says [Note: [Col. 0789] “In Deuteronomy” added: Lyons editions; “in the Gospel”: the remaining editions.—Compare Deuteronomy 19:14.]: “Do not transgress the ancient boundaries which your fathers established.”

[Accordingly [Note: [Col. 0789C] “Accordingly”: previously read “Likewise” [Col. 0789: “Likewise”: Strasbourg and Basel editions], that is, Callixtus; for when this *Palea* had not yet been inserted, chapter *No Primate*, which is Callixtus’s, followed. Gratian, however, cites this *Palea* from Urban II below, *On Penance*, distinction 6, final chapter.] Pope Urban [Note: [Col. 0789] Anselm at the end of book 8 cites it from the *Hibernensis*; Gratian’s error seems to have arisen because, in the same Anselm, a chapter of Urban (Cause 16, question 2, chapter 6) is placed before it.—Compare Distinction 4, *On Penance*, final chapter.]:

**C. II. PALEA**

[Col. 0789B]

“It has been decided that henceforth none of the priests may receive for penance anyone entrusted to another priest without the consent of the one to whom he had previously entrusted himself [Note: [Col. 0789] “To whom he had often confessed”: Strasbourg edition, with the remaining words omitted.], unless this happens through the ignorance of the one to whom the penitent had first confessed. But anyone who presumes to act against these enactments shall be liable to the peril of his rank.”

**C. III. In another’s parish, no one may do anything unless summoned by its bishop. Likewise Callixtus, Letter II.** [Note: [Col. 0789] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Antioch, canons 13 and 22.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 66. Anselm, book 6, chapter 119 (125). Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 28; *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 107.]

No primate, no metropolitan, and none of the other bishops may enter another’s city or approach a possession that does not belong to him [Col. 0789C] and *is* [Note: [Col. 0789] *Is* is absent from Ivo.] within another bishop’s parish [Note: [Col. 0789] *Parochiae*, “of the parish”: the text; *parochiam*, “parish” in the accusative: the other collected editions and Ivo; *parochia*, “parish” in the nominative or ablative: Böhm.], to make any disposition concerning anyone [Col. 0790A] [Note: [Col. 0789] “Concerning him” (*ejus*) rather than “concerning anyone” (*cujusquam*): the other collected editions.], unless summoned by the bishop [Note: [Col. 0789] “By that bishop”: Basel edition.] whose jurisdiction it is recognized [Note: [Col. 0789] “Known”: the other collected editions.] to be; nor may he arrange, ordain, or judge anything there, if he wishes to retain the honor of his rank. But if he presumes otherwise, he shall be condemned—not only he, but also his collaborators and those consenting to him—because, just as ordination is forbidden to them, so too are judgment and the administration of other affairs. For how [Note: [Col. 0789] “In what manner”: the same editions.] shall one who cannot ordain judge? Without doubt he cannot judge at all.

**C. IV. On the same matter. PALEA. Likewise from the Council of Nantes, chapter 1.** [Note: [Col. 0789C] This and the following chapter are absent from the six older and more carefully corrected copies of Gratian. In the others, however, they occur without the name *Palea*, as also in the printed editions. Both occur in the Council of Nantes; this first is cited from it in the Decretals, title *On Parishes*, chapter 2, and by Burchard and Ivo. It was thus corrected, whereas [Col. 0789D] it had previously been cited from the Council of Meaux.] [Note: [Col. 0789] Compare Distinction 24, chapter 5.—Regino, book 1, chapter 6 (“from Nantes, 419”). Burchard, book 2, chapter 93 (“from the same, chapter 419”). Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 122.—Compare the *Imperial Constitutions*, book 1, and the *Decretals*, title *On Parishes*, chapter 2.]

“On Sundays or feast days, before celebrating Masses, presbyters shall ask the people whether there is in the church a parishioner of another church who, having despised his own presbyter, wishes to hear Mass there. If they find such a person [Col. 0790B], they shall immediately expel him from the church and compel him to return to his own parish.”

**C. V. On the same matter. PALEA. Likewise from the same Council of Nantes, chapter 2.** [Note: [Col. 0789] Regino, book 1, chapters 61 and 255. Burchard, book 1, chapter 91.—*Capitularies*, book 1, chapter 149.—“Council of Natanensis”: Basel edition; “Council of Navatensis”: the remaining editions except the first Bartholomew edition.]

“No presbyter or deacon [Note: [Col. 0789D] “Or deacon”: these two words are read neither in the council nor in the *Capitularies*, nor in Burchard [Col. 0789: nor in Regino].] may dare receive another’s parishioner [Note: [Col. 0789] *Plebesanum*, “member of another congregation”: Burchard; *parochianum*, “parishioner”: Regino and the *Capitularies*; Burchard adds “against his will” (*eo nolente*).] at Mass, unless he is traveling or has a plea *there*.”

**C. VI. A bishop must not attend the ordination of clerics or churches belonging to another bishop unless invited by that bishop. Likewise from the Council of Antioch, canon 13.** [Note: [Col. 0789D] This is the old translation—indeed, from the Hispanic version. Dionysius’s translation, which is inserted in the volumes of councils and cited by Burchard and Ivo, expresses the sense of the Greek canon more aptly. Yet because even it does not correspond entirely at every point, it seemed advisable to append the Greek words with a new translation:

Μηδένα ἐπίσκοπον τολμᾷν ἀφ’ ἑτέρας ἐπαρχίας εἰς ἑτέραν μεταβαίνειν [Col. 0790C] καὶ χειροτονεῖν ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ τινὰς εἰς προαγωγὴν λειτουργίας, μηδὲ εἰ συνεπάγοιτο ἑαυτῷ ἑτέρους, εἰ μὴ παρακληθεὶς ἀφίκηται διὰ γραμμάτων τοῦ τε μητροπολίτου καὶ τῶν σὺν αὐτῷ ἐπισκόπων, ὧν εἰς τὴν χώραν παρέρχοιτο. Εἰ δὲ μηδενὸς καλοῦντος ἀπέλθοι ἀτάκτως ἐπὶ χειροθεσίᾳ τινῶν, καὶ καταστάσει τῶν ἐκκλησιαστικῶν πραγμάτων μὴ προσηκόντων αὐτῷ, ἄκυρα μὲν τὰ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ πεπραγμένα τυγχάνειν, καὶ αὐτὸν δὲ ὑπέχειν τῆς ἀταξίας αὐτοῦ, καὶ τῆς παραλόγου ἐπιχειρήσεως τὴν προσήκουσαν δίκην, καθῃρημένον ἐντεῦθεν ἤδη ὑπὸ τῆς ἁγίας συνόδου.

“No bishop may dare pass from one province to another and ordain persons in a church for advancement to the ministry, even if he brings others with him, unless he comes when summoned by letters of both the metropolitan and the bishops with him, into whose territory he is entering. But if, with no one calling him, he goes disorderly in order to ordain some persons and settle ecclesiastical affairs not belonging to him, what he has done shall indeed be invalid; and he himself shall undergo the fitting penalty for his disorder and unreasonable undertaking, being henceforth already deposed by the holy synod.”] [Note: [Col. 0789] Held A.D. 332.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 108. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 210, both from Dionysius.]

[Col. 0790C]

No bishop [Note: [Col. 0789] “Bishop” in the accusative singular rather than “of the bishops”: the other collected editions.] ought to dare to pass from [Note: [Col. 0789] “From one” (*ab una*): Basel edition.] another [Col. 0791A] province to another and to ordain persons [Note: [Col. 0791] “Clerics” added: Basel edition.] in churches or put them forward [Note: [Col. 0791] “Promote”: Hispanic Collection.] for sacred ministry. Nor may he be drawn there by others [Note: [Col. 0791] The Hispanic Collection and Isidore Mercator read: “Nor may a bishop draw others there with him”; “be drawn”: Basel, Lyons, and Paris editions.], unless perhaps he goes at the request, by letters, not only of the metropolitan but also of all the bishops of that province who are with him [Note: [Col. 0791] “All of that province” is lacking in the Hispanic Collection.]. But if, with no one inviting him, he arrives disorderly and presumes either to ordain persons or to usurp any *acts* belonging to that church which in no way concern him, everything he has done shall be empty and void; he himself, however, shall pay the fitting penalties for this undisciplined audacity and irrational undertaking, as one deposed by the holy synod and already condemned for such presumption.

[Col. 0791B]

**C. VII. A bishop must not attend to the ordination of a church not entrusted to him. Likewise from the same Council of Antioch, canon 22.** [Note: [Col. 0791] Burchard, book 1, chapter 71. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 178, from Dionysius.]

A bishop must not rush into a foreign city which is shown not to be subject to him, nor into a region known not to belong to his care, to ordain anyone [Note: [Col. 0791C] “To ordain anyone”: in this canon too Dionysius’s version is purer; this version has “concerning the ordination of anyone,” which in Greek is ἐπὶ χειροτονίᾳ τινος, that is, “in order to ordain someone.”], nor establish presbyters or deacons in places belonging to other bishops [Note: [Col. 0791C] “Belonging to other bishops”: Dionysius reads almost the same in Greek, εἰς τόπους ἑτέρῳ ἐπισκόπῳ ὑποκειμένους, that is, “in places subject to another bishop.”], unless perhaps with the will and testimony [Note: [Col. 0791C] “And testimony”: the Greek has only μετὰ γνώμης, “with consent,” which Dionysius renders “with counsel and will” [Col. 0791: “with counsel”: Hispanic Collection].] of the bishop of the proper region. If anyone should wish to do [Note: [Col. 0791] “Approach”: there.] any such thing, that ordination [Note: [Col. 0791] “Such an ordination”: the other collected editions.] shall indeed be invalid, and [Note: [Col. 0791] “And concerning even those things which … let him be censured”: the same editions; “and he who improperly … let him be censured”: Hispanic Collection.] the things which he has improperly [Note: [Col. 0791C] “And the things which he has improperly”: thus corrected from ancient copies and the other editions of the councils, except the latest four-volume edition. Dionysius [Col. 0791D] has: “and he himself is to be restrained by the synod,” which in Greek is καὶ αὐτὸν ἐπιτιμίας ὑπὸ τῆς συνόδου τυγχάνειν, that is, “and he himself is to be punished by the synod.”] usurped shall be censured by the synod. For if [Note: [Col. 0791C] “For if”: this entire clause is absent from the Greek canon [Col. 0791: and from the Hispanic Collection], against which three manuscript copies were collated [Col. 0792C], but both the old translation and Dionysius’s have it. A similar statement is read above in chapter *No Primate*.] he cannot ordain, he must by no means presume to judge those belonging to others.

[Col. 0791C]

**C. VIII. Bishops must not go to churches outside their diocese. Likewise from the First Synod of Constantinople, canon 2.** [Note: [Col. 0791] Held A.D. 381.]

Bishops who are outside their diocese [Note: [Col. 0791] “Their own” added: the other collected editions.] must not go to churches beyond their boundaries, nor throw churches into confusion and disorder. In accordance with [Note: [Col. 0792C] “In accordance with”: the punctuation has been altered to correspond more closely to the Greek canon, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τοὺς κανόνας τὸν μὲν Ἀλεξανδρείας, etc., which Dionysius renders: “but according to the canons, the bishop of Alexandria,” etc. In the three-volume edition of the councils these words were absent: “are to govern only what is in Egypt; but the bishops of the East.”] [Note: [Col. 0791] “But in accordance with”: Hispanic Collection.] the established rules [Note: [Col. 0791] This is lacking in the Hispanic Collection; “constituted rules”: Strasbourg and Basel editions.], the bishops of Alexandria [Col. 0792A] are to govern only what is in Egypt; the bishops of the East are to administer only the East, while preserving the honors of primacy of the church of Antioch contained in the rules of the Nicene Synod. The bishops of the Asian diocese are to govern what [Note: [Col. 0791] “And what”: the other collected editions.] is in Asia and belongs only to the Asian [Note: [Col. 0791] “Asia”: Basel edition.] diocese; the bishops of Pontus are to have charge only of the Pontic diocese; and those of Thrace, only of Thrace itself.

**C. IX. On the same matter. Likewise from the same synod, canon 3.**

Bishops who have not been invited must not go beyond their diocese for the ordination of anyone or for the administration of any ecclesiastical business, while preserving the rule [Note: [Col. 0792C] “While preserving the rule”: thus in all editions of this old—indeed, Hispanic—translation; but in the Greek canon [Col. 0792D] this begins a new period, and what follows depends upon it, as Dionysius renders: “But preserving the written rule concerning administrations, it is evident that the synod of each province administers the affairs of that province,” etc.] written above concerning each diocese. For it is evident [Col. 0792B] that the provincial synod must administer and govern everything in each individual province, according to what was decreed at Nicaea [Note: [Col. 0791] “At the Nicene Synod”: the other collected editions.].

**Part II. Gratian.** These authorities forbid any bishops whatsoever to ordain another’s clerics. But it is asked: if it happens that they confer sacred orders upon some of them, can those ordained be received by their own bishops in their proper orders?

Pope Urban writes on this question to Hugh, Archbishop of Lyons [Note: [Col. 0791] Written about A.D. 1095.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 412.]:

**C. X. Clerics ordained by the bishop of another parish may be received by their own bishop in their orders.**

Your religious prudence may receive with the honor of their ranks the clerics of the parish [Note: [Col. 0791] “Church”: Ivo.] of Lyons whom, as your letter has shown, bishops of another parish [Col. 0792C] ordained contrary to the statutes of the canons, if they are otherwise shown to have been ordained canonically and without any perversity, provided that you judge their commendable life to deserve this indulgence. For we read [Col. 0793A] [Note: [Col. 0793] Compare Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 6, chapters 12–13; *Tripartite History*, book 10, chapter 11.] that St. Epiphanius, bishop, ordained certain clerics from the diocese of St. John Chrysostom; that holy man would certainly not have done so if he had considered it likely to cause harm. Those, therefore, whom your moderation judges should be received, you shall receive, each in his own rank [Note: [Col. 0793] “When it has been ascertained” (*cognita*): the other collected editions.], in view of mercy, after imposing suitable penance by way of satisfaction for the church they offended, while preserving [Note: [Col. 0793] “Nevertheless” added: the same editions.] in every respect the discipline of the holy canons.

## QUESTION III

### GRATIAN

That an archbishop can condemn or absolve the clerics of his suffragan without consulting that suffragan seems capable of proof as follows. Just as the churches of the whole bishopric are within [Col. 0793B] the bishop’s power, so the churches of the whole archbishopric belong to the archbishop’s diocese. Bishops are called by the metropolitan to share his solicitude, not the fullness of his power. For he apportions his functions to them in such a way that he does not take his own authority away from himself. Thus they may do nothing without his counsel, as is read in the Council of Pope Martin, chapter 4 [Note: [Col. 0793] Chapter 9 of the Council of Antioch, in the translation of Martin of Braga.]:

**C. I. Bishops must not act without the metropolitan’s consent, nor he without theirs.**

In every province the bishops must acknowledge their metropolitan [Note: [Col. 0793] “The primacy of the metropolitan bishop”: Hispanic Collection.] and him as undertaking the care of primacy [Note: [Col. 0793] “Of primacy” is absent from the Hispanic Collection; “of his primacy” in the other collected editions.]; the remaining bishops, however, must do nothing [Note: [Col. 0793] “Ought” added: the same editions.] without him, in accordance with what is contained in the canon established of old by our fathers [Note: [Col. 0793] Apostolic Canon 34.]. Therefore the metropolitan [Note: [Col. 0793] “And the metropolitan”: the same editions.] bishop also must undertake nothing [Note: [Col. 0793] “For himself” added: Hispanic Collection.] [Col. 0793C] presumptuously without the counsel [Note: [Col. 0793] “Council”: Strasbourg edition.] of the others [Note: [Col. 0793] “Bishops” added: Strasbourg, Nuremberg, and Venetian I editions.].

[Col. 0794A]

**C. II. A bishop must do nothing outside his own diocese without the metropolitan’s knowledge. Likewise from the Council of Antioch, canon 9.** [Note: [Col. 0793] Held A.D. 332.]

In every province each bishop ought to know that the metropolitan of the bishops, who presides [Note: [Col. 0793] “Over them” added: Basel and Lyons editions II and III.], has undertaken the care and solicitude of the entire province. Therefore those who have cases are to resort [Note: [Col. 0793] “Are without doubt to resort”: Hispanic Collection.] to the metropolitan city. Hence it has been decided that he should also take precedence in honor [Note: [Col. 0793] “Go before”: there.], and that the remaining bishops should do nothing beyond this without him, according to the ancient canon of our fathers [Note: [Col. 0793] “Which has prevailed”: there.], except only what belongs to each church through its own diocese. For each bishop ought to have authority over his own diocese, so that [Note: [Col. 0793] The Hispanic Collection reads: “to govern it in accordance with the reverence entrusted to him, and to provide for the region which is subject,” etc.] he may direct and govern it with the reverence fitting in each case, and [Col. 0794B] exercise oversight over the whole territory subject to his city [Note: [Col. 0793] The words corresponding to “his … with” are lacking there.], so that he may *also* ordain presbyters and deacons by sound judgment and deliberate with moderation and discernment concerning each case of his own territory. But he is permitted [Note: [Col. 0793] “Will be permitted”: the other collected editions.] to do nothing further [Note: [Col. 0793] “Nothing further is to be done”: Hispanic Collection.] without the metropolitan bishop’s knowledge [Note: [Col. 0793C] “Knowledge”: the Greek is δίχα τοῦ μητροπόλεως ἐπισκόπου, μηδὲ αὐτὸν ἄνευ τῆς τῶν λοιπῶν γνώμης, “without the metropolitan bishop, nor he without the opinion of the rest.” Thus the canon uses the same word, γνώμης, for the consent both of the metropolitan and of the suffragans. Because of the many variant readings, it was thought proper to append the Greek words with a new translation:

Τοὺς καθ’ ἑκάστην ἐπαρχίαν ἐπισκόπους εἰδέναι χρὴ τὸν ἐν τῇ μητροπόλει προεστῶτα ἐπίσκοπον, καὶ τὴν φροντίδα ἀναδέχεσθαι πάσης τῆς ἐπαρχίας διὰ τὸ ἐν τῇ μητροπόλει πανταχόθεν συντρέχειν πάντας τοὺς τὰ πράγματα ἔχοντας. Ὅθεν ἔδοξε καὶ τῇ τιμῇ προηγεῖσθαι αὐτὸν, μηδέν τε πράττειν περιττὸν τοὺς λοιποὺς ἐπισκόπους ἄνευ αὐτοῦ, κατὰ τὸν ἀρχαῖον κρατήσαντα τῶν πατέρων ἡμῶν κανόνα, ἢ ταῦτα μόνα, ὅσα τῇ ἑκάστου ἐπιβάλλει παροικίᾳ, καὶ ταῖς ὑπ’ αὐτὴν χώραις· ἕκαστον γὰρ ἐπίσκοπον ἐξουσίαν ἔχειν τῆς ἑαυτοῦ παροικίας, διοικεῖν τε κατὰ τὴν ἑκάστῳ ἐπιβάλλουσαν εὐλάβειαν καὶ πρόνοιαν ποιεῖσθαι πάσης τῆς χώρας τῆς ὑπὸ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ πόλιν, ὡς καὶ χειροτονεῖν [Col. 0793D] πρεσβυτέρους καὶ διακόνους, καὶ μετὰ κρίσεως [Col. 0794C] ἕκαστα διαλαμβάνειν. Περαιτέρω δὲ μηδὲν πράττειν ἐπιχειρεῖν δίχα τοῦ τῆς μητροπόλεως ἐπισκόπου, μηδὲ αὐτὸν ἄνευ τῆς τῶν λοιπῶν γνώμης.

“The bishops in each province must recognize that the bishop presiding in the metropolis also undertakes the care of the entire province, because all who have business assemble in the metropolis from every direction. Therefore it has been decided that he shall take precedence in honor, and that the remaining bishops shall do nothing beyond, without him, according to the ancient canon of our fathers which has prevailed, except those things alone which belong to each one’s own parish and the territories subject to it. For every bishop is to have authority over his own parish: he is to administer it with the integrity appropriate to each and to provide and care for the whole territory subject to his city, so that he may ordain presbyters and deacons and decide every matter with judgment. Beyond this, however, they must undertake nothing without the bishop of the metropolis [Col. 0794D], nor may he act without the opinion of the rest.”], nor may the metropolitan do anything without the counsel of the other bishops.

Gratian. Unless perhaps the bishops themselves neglect to appoint stewards (*oeconomi*) in their own church.

Accordingly it is read in the Seventh Synod, chapter 11 [Note: [Col. 0793] Held A.D. 787.—Anastasius’s translation.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 374.]:

**C. III. A metropolitan is to appoint stewards whom a bishop has neglected to have.**

Since we are all bound to preserve the sacred rules [Note: [Col. 0793] Compare the Council of Chalcedon, canon 26.], and by every means must keep inviolable the rule which says that each church [Col. 0794C] ought to have stewards [Col. 0795A], if each metropolitan appoints a steward in his own church, that is certainly good. But if he does not, the bishops of Constantinople have authority on their own initiative to appoint stewards in his church. Likewise metropolitans have authority if the bishops under them have not taken care to appoint stewards in their churches. The same is also to be observed in monasteries. [Note: [Col. 0795] “Preserve”: Ivo and the other collected editions read “maintain.”]

Gratian. The same point is proved by the Apostle’s example: he delivered the unrepentant fornicator at Corinth to Satan, and afterward reconciled him, once repentant, to the Church; he merely wrote to the Corinthians in the first and second letters that they should not communicate with the excommunicated man and should join the reconciled man to themselves in shared love. But the contrary is proved by the authority of many.

[Col. 0795B]

For Pope Hyginus says in Letter I, chapter 2 [Note: [Col. 0795] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare the *Ancient Ecclesiastical Statutes*, chapter 14.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 65. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapters 99 and 174.—“Pope Eugenius”: Basel edition.]:

**C. IV. Without the consent or presence of the bishops, a metropolitan must not hear any of their cases.**

Saving in all matters the privilege of the Roman Church, no metropolitan may hear any cases without the active attendance of all the other bishops of his province [Note: [Col. 0795] Ivo, part 5, chapter 99, reads “the cases of the accused”; the Strasbourg and Basel editions read “their cases”; the original has “of the accused.”], because cases handled otherwise than after being discussed in the presence of them all shall be invalid, and he himself, if he does so, shall be restrained by his brethren.

**C. V. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Anicetus to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 1.** [Note: [Col. 0795] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Apostolic Canon [lacuna] 35.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 9, chapter 2.]

An archbishop may do nothing concerning the cases of bishops or other common matters, in accordance with the ordinances of the apostles, without the counsel of all of them; nor may they [Note: [Col. 0795] “Undertake” added: the other collected editions.] do anything beyond what belongs to their own parishes without his [Note: [Col. 0795] “Consent” added: the same editions.] [Col. 0795C], because the Most High delights in such concord and is glorified in his members.

**C. VI. On the same matter. Likewise in the same letter, chapter 3.** [Note: [Col. 0795] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 63. Anselm, book 2, chapter 23. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 26; *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 54. *Polycarpus*, book 2, title 24.]

But if any metropolitan has become puffed up and wishes, without the presence or counsel [Note: [Col. 0795] “Council”: Basel and Nuremberg editions.] of all the bishops of his province, to handle either them or [Note: [Col. 0795] “Their cases” added: the other collected editions and Ivo.] other cases—except only those belonging to his own parish—or to burden them, he is to be strictly corrected by all, lest he dare henceforth presume such things. But if [Note: [Col. 0795] Compare Isidore, *Sentences*, book 3, chapter 39.] he proves incorrigible and disobedient to them, his contumacy is to be reported to this Apostolic See, to which all bishops’ judgments have been commanded to be referred [Note: [Col. 0795] The original reads “to be concluded”; Burchard, Anselm, and Ivo likewise have “concluded.”—Compare Innocent I, Letter 2, chapter 3.], so that punishment may be inflicted upon him and the rest [Col. 0795D] [Note: [Col. 0795] “All”: Basel edition; “concerning him” added: the remaining editions.] may fear.

[Col. 0796A]

**C. VII. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Callixtus to the bishops of Gaul, Letter II, chapter 3.** [Note: [Col. 0795] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Apostolic Canon 35 and Antioch, canons 13, 20, and 9.—Burchard, book 1, chapter 60. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 27; *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 100; part 14, chapter 72. *Polycarpus*, chapter 26.]

No primate or [Note: [Col. 0795] “No”: the other collected editions.] metropolitan may presume, without the counsel or judgment of the diocesan bishop, to excommunicate or judge his church or parish, or anyone from his parish, or to do anything there. Rather, he shall observe what was established by the apostles, fathers, and [Note: [Col. 0795] “And” is lacking in the Strasbourg edition.] our predecessors and confirmed by us: namely, if a metropolitan bishop tries to do anything beyond what belongs solely to his own proper parish, without the counsel and will of all the bishops of his province, he shall be liable [Note: [Col. 0795] “Indeed” added: the other collected editions.] to the peril of his rank, and what he has done shall be regarded [Note: [Col. 0795] “Shall be”: the same editions.] as invalid and void. But [Col. 0796B] whatever must be done or arranged concerning the cases of provincial [Note: [Col. 0795] “Of the same province”: the same editions and Burchard.] fellow-bishops [Note: [Col. 0795] “Bishops”: the other collected editions.], their churches and clerics, and the needs of laypeople, is to be done with the common [Note: [Col. 0795] The original and Burchard read “with the consent of all.”] consent of the bishops of the province; and not with any proud display of domination, but in the humblest and harmonious administration, as the Lord says [Note: [Col. 0795] Matthew 20:28], “I came not [Note: [Col. 0795] “He came not”: Basel edition.] to be served but to serve,” and elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0795] Matthew 20:26], “Whoever is greater among you shall be your minister.” Likewise the fellow-bishops of the province themselves must do everything with his counsel, except what belongs to their own parishes, according to the enactments of the holy Fathers; and below: “so that with one mind and one voice the Holy Trinity may harmoniously be glorified for ever.”

[Col. 0796C]

**C. VIII. In a suffragan’s parish a metropolitan must do nothing without his counsel. Likewise Pope Nicholas to Rudolph, Archbishop of Bourges.** [Note: [Col. 0795] Written A.D. 864.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 29; *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 56.]

Our brother Sigedodus [Note: Sigebodus: original.—Sigegodus: Basel edition], archbishop of Narbonne, complained to our apostolic office that, against his will, you compel his clerics to come before your tribunal, and that, without consulting him, you dispose, as though by right of your patriarchate, of matters belonging to his church. Yet neither does antiquity—which the Fathers decreed should be revered—permit this, nor does the authority of the sacred canons allow it at all, unless perhaps they have appealed to you as to their patriarch in cases which cannot be settled locally [Note: “be settled”: collected editions], by appeals [Note: added in the original printed in Mansi, vol. 15; collected editions]; or if their bishop has died and they wish the goods of their church to be administered under your judgment [Col. 0796D] [Note: “and the goods”: Basel edition; “wish”: collected editions except Basel]. For we determine that primates or patriarchs possess no privilege above others except insofar as the sacred canons grant it and ancient custom has from of old conferred it upon them; thus, in accordance with the Nicene rules, churches are to retain their own privileges, unless the apostolic see has decreed to honor some church or its ruler with a particular special privilege.

### C. IX. On the same subject. Bede on the Apocalypse:

“And write to the angel of the church in Ephesus” [Note: In the Ordinary Gloss it is read thus: “And he writes to the angel, that is, the bishop, from whose hand he requires the sins of his subjects, and without whose consent John himself does not presume to judge the subjects.”] [Note: Ordinary Gloss on Revelation 2:1].

He writes to the bishop [Note: “John” added: collected editions except Basel], from whose hand he requires the sins of the subjects [Note: “of the people”: Basel edition], so that he ought not to judge the subjects without that bishop’s consent.

Gratian. For the Roman church alone has authority to judge concerning all; but no one is permitted to judge concerning it [Col. 0797B].

Therefore Pope Nicholas, in his letter to Emperor Michael, beginning, “We had proposed” [Note: This chapter has also been reduced by the other collectors to a kind of summary, with many words omitted.] [Note: written A.D. 865.—Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 75; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 4, ch. 11; *Decretum*, pt. 5, ch. 19]:

### C. X. The judgment of the apostolic see is not to be reconsidered by anyone.

It is certainly evident that the judgment of the apostolic see—than whose authority there is none greater [Note: “greater”: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions]—is not to be reconsidered by anyone, nor is anyone permitted to judge concerning its judgment [Note: “is permitted”: Ivo; collected editions]. This accords with what Pope Innocent [Note: In Nicholas’s letter and in the other collectors the name is Boniface. Yet what is cited here has not been found either in Boniface’s or Innocent’s letters. In that letter Nicholas also reports certain other matters from Boniface’s letter to the bishops throughout Thessaly.] wrote to Rufus and the other bishops established throughout Thessaly [Note: “Caesarea”: Basel edition], saying: “No one has ever boldly laid hostile hands upon the apostolic summit—whose judgment may not be reconsidered [Note: “reconsidered”: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions]—and no one has proved rebellious in this matter except one who wished judgment to be passed upon himself.” And blessed Pope Gelasius says [Note: compare below, ch. 16]: “Nor have the canons ever commanded that judgment be passed upon its judgment,” that is, upon the judgment of the Roman church [Col. 0797C]; “and they established that its sentence ought not to be annulled, whose decrees they rather commanded to be followed.”

### C. XI. Apostolic authority absolves those condemned or excommunicated by others. Athanasius, Patriarch, to Pope Felix II. [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; in the collected editions it is cited under the name Anastasius.—Collection in three parts, pt. 2, vol. 14, ch. 5; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, ch. 15.]

Your holy apostolic see has always been permitted [Note: “see”: collected editions] [Col. 0798A], by virtue of its sovereign authority, to restore those unjustly condemned or excommunicated, to restore all their possessions to them, and to punish with apostolic privilege those who condemned or excommunicated them, as we know this to have been done in our own times and those of our predecessors [Note: “we know it to have been done”: collected editions].

### C. XII. On the same subject. A little further on in the same place [Note: cited collections—there].

It has been established by ancient rules that whatever might be done—even in remote or far-distant provinces [Note: “regions” added: Basel edition]—concerning the complaints or accusations of bishops [Note: “their”: collected editions], ought not to be considered or accepted before it had been brought to the knowledge of your gracious see, so that by its authority the decision might be invalidated or confirmed [Col. 0798B] according to what ought to be done [Note: Ivo reads: “according to what the pronouncement had been, it should be invalidated or confirmed.” In the *Corpus of Councils*: “according to what had been pronounced justly,” etc. [“according to what had been pronounced”: Basel edition]].

### C. XIII. The first see is subject to no one’s judgment. Pope Innocent [Note: In all the old manuscripts of Gratian, this is cited from Innocent. But nearly the same words occur in the Roman council under Sylvester, ch. 20, and are cited from it by the indicated collectors.] [Note: rather, ch. 20 of the apocryphal Constitution of Sylvester.—Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 19 (20) (“Sylvester in the council of 272 bishops”); Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 4, ch. 5; Deusdedit, pt. 3; *Polycarpus*, bk. 1, title 16].

No one shall judge the first see, which desires to administer justice [Note: “which desires to administer justice”: so also in the *Panormia* under Sylvester. But in the common edition of the council it reads: “because all sees desire that justice be administered by the first see.”]. For it shall not be judged by the emperor, by all the clergy, by kings, or by the people.

### C. XIV. On the same subject. Pope Symmachus [Note: Rather, from Ennodius’s *Apologeticus* for the fourth Roman synod.—Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 24 (25); Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 4, ch. 8; *Decretum*, pt. 5, ch. 10; *Polycarpus*, there].

God willed that humans should settle the cases of other human beings; but He reserved the bishop of this see [Note: “the bishop”: collected editions] to His own judgment, without question. He willed that the successors of the blessed apostle Peter should owe their innocence to heaven alone and should present an inviolate conscience to the investigation of the most searching examiner [Col. 0798C] [Note: “have”: same editions]. Do not suppose that those souls lack fear of examination [Note: “examiner”: Basel edition; “of examiners”: Anselm] which God has reserved above others for His own scrutiny. Before Him the accused has no aid from the brilliance of an allegation, when he employs as witness and judge the very one who knows his deeds. You may perhaps say [Note: “You may say”: Basel, Paris, and Lyons editions] that in that judgment all souls will have such a condition. I shall reply: to one alone it was said [Note: Matthew 16:18], [Col. 0799A] “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my church; and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” Again, the testimony of the saints makes clear that the pontifical dignity of his see has been rendered venerable throughout the whole world, since all the faithful everywhere are subject to it and since it is designated the head of the whole body. It seems to me that the Prophet spoke of this [Note: Isaiah 10:3]: “If this is humbled [Note: “this one”: Basel edition], to whose help will you flee? And where will you leave your glory?”

### C. XV. On the same subject. Pope Anterus to the bishops of the provinces of Baetica and Toledo [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Isidore, *Sentences*, I.3, chs. 42, 38.—Collection in three parts, pt. 1, vol. 17, ch. 2; Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 53 (54); *Polycarpus*, there; compare Causa 6, question 1, ch. 15, 15. “Aurelius P.”: Basel edition.]

The acts of subjects are judged by us; our own acts are judged by God [Note: “are judged by the Lord”: collected editions]. And below: §1. Worse than those who plunder the property and estates of others [Col. 0799B] are those who corrupt the life and morals of the good.

### C. XVI. On the same subject. Pope Gelasius to the legate Faustus [Note: written A.D. 493.—Anselm, bk. 2, ch. 56 (54); Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, ch. 9.]

These are the canons themselves [Note: “Bishops”: Argentinensis editions], which decreed that appeals from the whole church should be brought to the examination of this see [Note: “to bring”: Basel edition]. But they established that no appeal whatsoever ought to be made from it [Note: “to make an appeal”: collected editions except Lyons II and III]; and consequently they decreed that it should judge the whole church, that it should proceed to the judgment of no one, and [Note: above, ch. 10] that judgment should never be passed upon its judgment; and they established that its sentence ought not to be annulled, whose decrees they rather commanded to be followed.

### C. XVII. On the same subject. The same, to all bishops [Note: Everything read in this chapter occurs in Gelasius’s letter to the bishops throughout Dardania, though not arranged in the same order. The following chapter, which contains many words from this very chapter, occurs in precisely the same form in that letter. It is therefore possible that this chapter was taken from another letter which no longer survives, or that Gratian reports these two as distinct chapters because he found them distinguished even among earlier collectors. In Nicholas’s letter to the bishops of Gaul, recently printed in the appendix to the library, this is cited from Gelasius.] [Note: in the letter to the bishops established throughout Dardania, written A.D. 498.—Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 47 (26), bk. 12, ch. 68; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 4, ch. 9.]

The church throughout the world knows that the most holy Roman church has the right to judge concerning all matters [Col. 0799C], and that no one is permitted to judge concerning its judgment. For appeal must be made to it from any part of the world; but no one is permitted to appeal from it. §1. Nor do we pass over the fact that the apostolic see, without any preceding synod, has had authority both to absolve those whom a synod had unjustly condemned [Note: “that”: Basel edition] and, with no synod present, to condemn those who ought to be condemned. And this, assuredly, belongs to its primacy, which the blessed apostle Peter both received by the Lord’s word and has always held and will hold.

[Col. 0800A] ### C. XVIII. On the same subject. The same, to the bishops established throughout Dardania [Note: compare the preceding chapter.]

The church throughout the world knows that the see of the blessed apostle Peter has the right to loose those bound by the sentences of any bishops whatsoever, since it has the right to judge concerning the whole church, etc.

### C. XIX. On the same subject. Pope Sixtus II to the bishops of Spain, Letter II, ch. 4 [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 192; Anselm, bk. 2, ch. 25; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, ch. 247; *Polycarpus*, bk. 1, title 8.]

Brothers, know that those whom you unjustly condemned through earthly fear have been justly restored by us; and we command that everything taken from them be restored to them in full by the authority of holy [Note: “blessed”: collected editions] Peter and apostolic authority [Note: “and” absent in Burchard and Ivo; “apostolic” absent in Basel edition], unless you wish both yourselves and your rulers to be separated from our fellowship and from the members of the church.

[Col. 0800B] ### C. XX. The Pope can ordain clerics of any church. Bishop Stephen to Patriarch Gualbert [Note: Apparently a letter of Stephen V.—Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 31 (36); Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, ch. 13.]

Now we write to you again, not wishing to infringe the privilege of any church, although by apostolic prerogative [Note: “authority”: Ivo; Basel edition] we can ordain a cleric from any church. Stop now, because of someone's jealousy, delaying the bishop of the Cumaean church [Cumensis] [Note: “Cumensis”: so also Anselm [it seems it should be read “of the church of Como,” which we know was subject to the patriarchate of Aquileia, held by Walbert. But Ivo gives more fully: “Stop now, because of someone's jealousy, delaying Lintuard, elected by the clergy and desired by the people, as bishop of the church of Como.”]], because if you delay and, though so often warned, do not promptly consecrate him, he will undoubtedly come to us and depart consecrated [Note: “will come”: Basel edition].
