### C. XXI. On the same subject. Pope Nicholas to Emperor Michael, in the letter beginning “We had proposed” [Note: written A.D. 865; compare Causa 1, question 1, ch. 123.]

Therefore, through the principal power of the blessed [Note: “therefore” added: collected editions] apostles Peter [Col. 0800C] and Paul [Note: “right hand” added: same editions], concerning which [Note: “which” accusative: same editions] we have explained in part above, we have authority [Note: “both authority and right”: collected editions] and right not only over monks [Note: “over monks”: same editions], but also, when necessity requires, over any clerics whatsoever [Note: “over any”: same editions] from whatever diocese, to summon them to us and to invite them when ecclesiastical needs require it.

Gratian. But one thing is assumed through the rashness of presumption, another is done through the necessity of charity. When the suffragans of archbishops begin to favor evil among their subjects and prove negligent concerning their correction [Col. 0801A], then metropolitan bishops may, even against their will, condemn those who must be bound and absolve those who must be reconciled. But when bishops, inflamed with zeal for divine charity, build up the good by word and example and rebuke the vices of the wicked with stern reproof, metropolitan bishops may not do or order anything in their dioceses without their counsel. Thus, at the end of the chapter of Pope Martin [Note: compare above, ch. 1], it was not simply said, “Let him do nothing,” but with the qualification, “Let him presumptuously undertake nothing [Col. 0802A] without their counsel,” so that the vice of presumption, not the office of charity, appears to be condemned. Likewise, because the Apostle saw that the Corinthians were negligent concerning the correction of the fornicator, he condemned him by his own authority. But because John saw that the bishop of Ephesus was ready to correct the vices of his subjects, he did not wish to correct them without that bishop’s authority [Note: above, ch. 9], but only admonished him concerning their correction.

# CAUSA X

[Col. 0801]

## GRATIAN

A certain layman seeks to separate from diocesan law a basilica built by himself; the bishop contends that the church together with its entire endowment belongs to his administration. In the end the bishop prevails, and cruelly rages through the parishes with the count’s soldiers; he seeks to usurp as though owed to himself those things which belong to the churches (Question I). The first question now is whether a basilica, together with its entire endowment, belongs to the bishop’s administration (Question II). Second, whether bishops may usurp the property of churches (Question III). Third, what they may exact from their priests under the name of *cathedraticum*.

# QUESTION I

## GRATIAN

### Part I

The first question is determined thus in the Council of Lleida, chapter 3 [Note: held A.D. 516.—Collection in three parts, pt. 2, vol. 43, ch. 3]:

### C. I. A consecrated basilica is not to be separated from diocesan law.

If any layman desires to have a basilica built by himself consecrated, he must by no means dare to separate it from diocesan law under the pretext of a monastery where no community is assembled [Note: “is assembled”: In the printed and manuscript council follows: “or a rule is not established by the bishop.”].

### C. II. Churches with their endowments are under the bishop’s authority. From the Third Council of Toledo, chapter 19 [Note: held A.D. 589.—Regino, bk. 1, ch. 32; Burchard, bk. 3, ch. 20; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 12; *Decretum*, pt. 3, ch. 23.—*Capitularies*, bk. 7, ch. 292.]

Thus certain persons, contrary to all authority, request to consecrate the churches which they have built [Col. 0802B] [Note: “be consecrated”: Hispana Collection; cited collections; collected editions], so that they may consider the endowment they conferred upon that church not to belong to the bishop’s administration. Let such a practice be corrected in the past [Note: “in this way”: Thus in the older editions and in two Vatican manuscripts of the councils; but in the Cologne four-volume edition, the royal Lucchese codex, the Councils of Worms and Mainz, and the *Panormia*: “Let this practice, both in the past [‘past’: Hispana Collection] be disapproved and in the future [‘future’: there] be prohibited.”], and prohibited in the future, so that all things may belong, in accordance with the ancient constitution, to the bishop’s administration and authority.

### C. III. Churches and all their rights belong to the bishop’s administration. From the Second Council of Chalon [Note: Rather, from the Frankish royal capitulary, bk. 7, ch. 468 (a capitulary of Charlemagne of uncertain year, III [Baluze, vol. 1, p. 529], ch. 11).—Burchard, bk. 3, ch. 146; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, ch. 211.]

It has been decreed that all churches, together with their endowments, tithes, and all their possessions [Note: “Their”: In the common editions there followed “rights” [thus collected editions except Nuremberg and Venice II], but this word is absent from all collated manuscripts. Ivo and Burchard have: “all their goods.”], shall be under the bishop’s authority and shall always belong to his administration.

[Col. 0802C] ### C. IV. Each parish is to be governed under the bishop’s oversight. Pope Leo IV, in a letter to the bishops of Britain, chapter 2 [Note: written about A.D. 850.—Collection in three parts, pt. 1, vol. 60, ch. 4.]

Each parish is to be governed under the bishop’s oversight and protection through priests or other clerics, whom he, in the fear of God, shall appoint to what seems by right to belong to them; and he ought [Note: “ought” added: Basel edition] to make a circuit as ecclesiastical utility [Note: “utility,” elsewhere “authority”: Argentinensis edition; “authority”: remaining editions] requires and as seems necessary to him.

### C. V. Ecclesiastical property is to be governed by the bishop’s judgment and authority. From the Council of Antioch, chapter 24 [Note: held A.D. 332.—Collection in three parts, pt. 2, vol. 6, ch. 18.]

Whatever things belong to the church [Note: “Whatever”: The Greek more clearly expresses: *τὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ φυλάττεσθαι δεῖν καλῶς ἔχει*, that is, “It is right that what belongs to the church should be preserved for the church itself.”] [Note: “ecclesiastical”: collected editions] ought to be governed and administered [Col. 0803A] with all diligence and with the good faith owed to God, who foresees and judges all things [Note: “and all”: collected editions], under the judgment and authority of the bishop, to whom the souls of the whole people appear to have been entrusted.

### C. VI. Let founders of basilicas recognize that they have no authority over church property. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 32 [Note: held A.D. 633.—Abbo of Fleury in Mabillon, *Vetera Analecta*, ch. 35.—Burchard, bk. 3, ch. 203; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 4; *Decretum*, pt. 3, ch. 255; *Polycarpus*, bk. 3, title 12.]

Let founders of basilicas recognize that they have no authority over the things which they bestow upon those churches [Note: absent from the Hispana Collection], but that, in accordance with the institutions of the canons [Note: “ordinances”: there, VII], as the church itself, so also its endowment belongs to the bishop’s administration.

### C. VII. On the same subject. From the Council of Orléans, book I, chapter 17 [Note: held A.D. 511.—Abbo of Fleury, there, ch. 27; Burchard, bk. 3, ch. 136; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 7; *Decretum*, pt. 3, ch. 202; *Polycarpus*, bk. 3, title 11.]

Let the decrees of the ancient canons be observed concerning those things which any faithful persons have offered to parishes in lands, vineyards, slaves, and peculium, so that all things may be under the bishop’s [Note: “bishops’”: collected editions] authority [Col. 0803B]. Yet from those things which come to the altar [Note: “into the altar”: Hispana Collection], a third part [Note: absent there] is faithfully to be conveyed to the bishops.

### C. VIII. Of things offered at the altar, the bishop is to claim half for himself. From the same source, chapter 16 [Note: Collection in three parts, pt. 2, vol. 29, ch. 9.]

Having reread the ancient canons, we believe that the earlier ordinances should be renewed: of those things which are offered at the altar by the oblation of the faithful [Note: “oblations”: Hispana Collection; “faith”: Argentinensis edition], the bishop is to claim half for himself, and the clergy are to receive half for administration according to their ranks [Note: “rank”: Hispana Collection; “of the second rank”: collected editions], both from their own estates and from every revenue remaining under the bishops’ authority [Note: “receive, from estates, from every revenue”: Hispana Collection].

[Col. 0803C] ### C. IX. Concerning bishops who neglect to visit their diocese and compel clerics to redeem the lodging dues owed to visiting bishops. From the Council of Toledo [Note: In a manuscript book of the privileges of the church of Toledo this is reported as chapter 15 of the fourth Council of Toledo, but it is not found in two copies of it sent from Spain. Burchard and Ivo cite it also from the Council of Tribur in the time of King Arnulf.] [Note: From the Council of Tribur, held in the time of King Arnulf (A.D. 895): Regino, bk. 1, ch. 14; Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 299; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, ch. 341.]

A complaint of the people was laid [Note: “brought”: Regino, Burchard] before the holy synod: certain bishops are unwilling to travel through their parishes during the year in order to preach or administer confirmation, yet demand that those who ought to have prepared lodgings for them redeem, at some price [Note: “another”: cited collections], the lodgings which the bishops should have used on their journey. This twofold disgrace, of negligence and avarice, was a great horror to the holy synod [Col. 0804A]. They therefore decreed that no one should any longer [Note: “at all”: Regino] exercise this device of greed, and that bishops should be more diligent in visiting their flocks.

### C. X. Churches are to be visited annually by bishops. From the Council of Tarragona, chapter 8 [Note: held A.D. 516.—Collection in three parts, pt. 2, vol. 31, ch. 6; Burchard, bk. 3, ch. 33; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, ch. 38.]

We have decreed that the order of ancient custom be observed and that dioceses be visited annually by the bishop. If perhaps some basilica is found neglected, it is to be ordered that it be repaired by its ordainer [Note: “by his administration”: In printed and manuscript copies of the council, and in Burchard and Ivo, it reads “let it be repaired by his administration” [“let it be repaired by his administration”: Hispana Collection], but it has not been changed because of the gloss. The remainder, however, has been corrected from the same sources. Burchard and Ivo further add at the end: “we know that it has been established among rulers.”], because we know it has been established by ancient tradition that a third part from all things is to be received by bishops [Note: “but let a third part be received by the bishops from all things, as we know ancient tradition has established”: collected editions].

### Part II

Gratian. But if a bishop is prevented by illness from visiting his dioceses in person, he should entrust the office of visitation to others.

Thus the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 35, reads [Note: held A.D. 633.—Regino, bk. 1, ch. 9; Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 87; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, ch. 193]:

### C. XI. A bishop burdened by illness should entrust the office of visitation to others.

A bishop ought to go each year through all his dioceses and parishes, in order to investigate what each basilica needs for its repair [Note: “repair”: Hispana Collection]. But if he cannot fulfill this duty because he is detained by sickness or involved in other occupations, he should send reliable priests or deacons to investigate the revenues and repairs of the basilicas and the life of their ministers.

### Part III

Gratian. But what visiting bishops ought to require from their clerics, and what they ought to teach them, is laid down as follows in chapter 1 of the Second Council of Braga [Note: held A.D. 572.—Regino, bk. 1, ch. 7; Collection in three parts, pt. 2, vol. 46, ch. 1; Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 85; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 1, ch. 75, pt. 5, ch. 191]:

[Col. 0804C] ### C. XII. What visiting bishops ought to require from their clerics.

It pleased all the bishops [Note: “us”: Burchard; Ivo, pt. 5, Part III] [Note: “and it was agreed” added: Hispana Collection; Regino, Burchard, Ivo, pt. 5] that bishops, travelling through individual churches and dioceses, should first examine the clerics as to how they observe the rite of baptism and of the masses, and [Note: “how all the offices are performed”: Hispana Collection] how they perform each office in the church. If they find that these are done properly, they should give thanks to God [Note: absent from Hispana Collection, Regino, Burchard IV; “give thanks”: Böhm]; but if not, they ought to teach [Note: “ought”: Hispana Collection] the ignorant and command this by every means, [Col. 0805A] as the ancient canons direct [Note: compare ch. 55, Distinction 4, *On Consecration*]: catechumens are to come for the cleansing of exorcism twenty days before baptism [Note: “come”: Hispana Collection], and throughout those twenty days the catechumens are to be specially taught the Creed, namely, “I believe in God the Father almighty.” After bishops have thus examined or instructed their clerics in these matters [Note: “these”: Hispana Collection; collected editions; absent from Regino], on another day, when the people of that church have been assembled, they should teach them to flee the errors of idols and various crimes—namely homicide, adultery, perjury, false witness, and the remaining deadly sins—and not to do to another what they do not wish done to themselves; and to believe in the resurrection of human beings and the day of judgment, on which each person will receive according to his deeds. Then the bishop should proceed from that church to another.

Thus Jerome, in a letter to Pope Damasus concerning altar offerings [Note: A supposititious letter.—*Polycarpus*, bk. 3, title 3]:

### C. XIII. Laypersons may not usurp the offerings of the church.

### Part IV

Since priests ought to pray for all [Note: “Ought”: In the common editions and the printed letter it reads “are accustomed”; but in most manuscript copies of Gratian and in *Polycarpus* it is “ought” [thus in the Basel edition]. Likewise Lupus, in his *Rule of Monks*, collected from Jerome’s writings, chapter “On contemplation, prayer, and reading”: “Priests too ought to pray for all, whose alms and offerings they receive.”], whose alms and offerings they receive, with what face do laypersons presume either to eat the offerings which Christians make for their sins, or [Note: “or themselves”: collected editions] to grant them to others, when they themselves ought not by virtue of their office [Note: “By virtue of their office”: These words are absent from most manuscripts of Gratian [Col. 0806C], and from the letter itself and *Polycarpus*] to pray to God for the people? Therefore, glorious Pope, you ought to put those presumptuous persons under perpetual excommunication, so that others too may have fear [Note: “desert”: Böhm] and these things may no longer occur in the church [Note: “not”: collected editions].

### C. XIV. Offerings made to altars or crosses are by no means to be taken away by laypersons. Pope Calixtus II [Note: chapter 14, First Lateran Council, held A.D. 1123.—*Polycarpus*, bk. 3, title 9.] [Note: “the Second”: This was added from most ancient copies. Yet he cannot be the First, in whose time the Pantheon was not yet called the church of Saint Mary Rotunda. For it was Boniface who, in the time of Emperor Phocas, dedicated it to the Blessed Virgin Mary and all the Saints.]

Confirming ordinances consonant with the canons of the holy Fathers, we absolutely forbid and prohibit under the strict penalty of anathema that offerings be taken away by laypersons from the most sacred and most venerable altar of blessed Peter [Note: “and Paul” added: Basel edition], and of the Savior, and of Saint Mary Rotunda, or from other altars or crosses of churches. By apostolic authority we also forbid churches to be made into fortresses by laypersons or reduced to servitude.

### C. XV. Church offerings are not to be held under lay control. Pope Damasus [Note: A supposititious chapter, whose author we judge to be the person who composed the spurious letter of Jerome to Damasus concerning offerings.—*Polycarpus*, there.]

We absolutely forbid this custom, which appears to be growing in opposition to the holy catholic church [Col. 0806A]: under no circumstances and at no time [Note: “at any time” added: collected editions] may offerings made within the holy church be held under lay control. Rather, priests alone, who are seen to serve the Lord daily, may eat and drink them. For in the Old Testament [Note: 1 Samuel 21] the Lord forbade the children of Israel to eat the holy loaves, except Aaron and his sons alone; those loaves [Note: absent from the collected editions except Lyons II and III] were far removed from those which are now offered in the holy church, because they were under the shadow of the Law, whereas those who now are [Note: “are” added: collected editions] under the grace of the Holy Spirit, while the Gospel shines throughout the whole world, appear more radiant. With what face or conscience do you wish to receive offerings when you can scarcely offer prayers to God for yourselves, much less for others? For it is wicked and contrary to the Lord’s command, and brings harm upon one’s soul, to attempt what is granted to one on no ground whatsoever. Since it pleased all the holy Fathers and our predecessors that this ordinance be made, we likewise [Note: “all” added: Basel edition] wish to persist in the same ordinances, so that no one may dare to render void what has been established, if he does not wish to remain in perpetual condemnation. But if anyone proves a rash presumptuous person against this our rule and against the rule of the 318 holy Fathers who established this in the Nicene council, and hereafter [Note: “further”: collected editions] attempts to take offerings from holy churches, let him be bound and condemned under the bond of anathema. All answered: “So be it, so be it.”

Gratian. By the foregoing authorities it is shown that churches with [Col. 0806C] all their property belong to the bishop’s administration, and that both churches and their offerings and resources are free from lay control.

# QUESTION II

## GRATIAN

### Part I

But when the resources of the church are said to be placed in bishops’ authority, this must be understood as authority to administer, not to alienate or squander.

Thus in the Council of Agde, chapter 7, we read [Note: held A.D. 506. C. I.]:

### C. I. Bishops may not alienate church property in any way.

As the ancient authority of the canons [Note: “of the holy canons”: collected editions] directs, bishops should possess cottages or small slaves of the church, or vessels for ministry [Note: “monastery”: same editions], as a faithful steward possesses goods entrusted to him, with the church’s right kept intact: that is, they should not presume either to sell or, through any contracts, to alienate property from which the poor live [Note: “presume”: In some better manuscripts of Gratian [and the Argentinensis and Basel editions], after this word follows § “But if necessity,” through the end—which is now found below, at the end of the Palea *Hujusmodi* in this same question—and the author of the *casus* read it thus].

Gratian. In Book I of the Code, under the title *On Most Sacred Churches*, in the law “We decree that no one…” [Note: Book 1, title 2, constitution 21], Emperor Justinian: except, of course, in the case of captivity.

### C. II. On the same subject. Emperors Leo and Anthemius [Note: constitution 14, Code, book 1, title 2.]

For those things which belong to the rights of the most blessed church, or may thereafter come to it [Note: “will come”: Basel edition; the words “or—come” are absent in the Argentinensis edition], ought to be kept reverently intact [Note: “inviolably”: collected editions] [Col. 0807B], just as the most sacred and religious church itself.

New Constitution [Note: *Authenticum*, “This right,” Code, book 1, title 2, constitution 14; Novella 7.]

This law extends to every venerable place and every association established by a pious act, so that its property may not be pledged. And this is to be observed perpetually with respect to immovable property which is assigned from the imperial household to the aforesaid places. In other matters an exception is made only where debt presses.

§ 1. Moreover, if it possesses superfluous vessels, *when it is in debt* and cannot pay from another source, then, so that no immovable thing may be alienated or sold, after proceedings have been held before the person responsible for administering the place, these vessels shall be given intact as offerings to other venerable places, or, once melted down, sold to some other person. But whoever receives them contrary to this rule shall be subject to the same penalties as have been prescribed concerning immovable property. If, however, the debt cannot be paid from movable goods, immovable property shall first be specially pledged, and the creditor shall credit its fruits toward both principal and interest, up to four per cent. If the *creditor is unwilling to accept it on these terms*, then the administrator of the house, after proceedings have been held without expense before the person by whom he is appointed, shall swear—with the consent of the majority of those serving there—that the debt is pressing and cannot be paid from movable goods. Once this has occurred, the church property shall be publicly known to be for sale for twenty days, so that it may be given to the highest bidder, the price in every case being applied to the debt. Otherwise the property is not granted to the purchaser; and this shall be entered in writing: that nothing has been done in this matter to the detriment of the house of God. If no purchaser is found, the property, strictly appraised, shall be given to the creditor in payment, with one tenth added to the price of the entire appraisal, and with the consent of the administrator and of the majority of those serving there. Yet the property must be of middling value among the others, having regard to its quality, quantity, and burden. And here that person is understood to be a creditor who proves that what he lent was used for the benefit of the house of God.

§ 2. Just as alienation of the church’s property is forbidden, so it is prohibited that any unproductive or otherwise burdensome possession be given to it, for example under the name or *burden* of fiscal obligations.

§ 3. Likewise, an estate rendered useless by a fiscal burden may be alienated, after the proceedings specified above have been drawn up and the same oath taken: namely, that it is alienated for no other reason than that the immunity of that venerable house may be preserved.

§ 4. But exchange with the emperor is permitted for a larger, *better*, or equal property, if the public interest requires it and an imperial rescript on the matter has preceded it.

§ 5. Likewise, they may rightly exchange with one another without loss to either party, provided that the consent of those mentioned above intervenes.

## Part II

§ 6. Perpetual emphyteusis is also permitted for these properties, if the transaction is conducted in the presence of those to whom this is assigned by law, and if those concerned swear that nothing detrimental to the house of God will result from the contract. The customary revenue of the property, such as it was when it was dedicated to divine ownership, is not to be reduced by more than one sixth; or, if it has been diminished by calamity, it may then be granted in emphyteusis for the pension now fixed. But if the property is valuable yet yields little or no rental income, it must be carefully appraised so that a fair pension may be established from it. Only such things as appear suitable for this purpose to the steward and the other administrators are to be granted in emphyteusis.

§ 7. Whoever makes such a leased or emphyteutic property worse, or fails for two years to pay the *emphyteutic* canon, may be expelled *under this law*, provided that he pays the rent for the whole period and makes good the damage he has done to the property. He shall not recover anything he has spent under the heading of improvements.

§ 8. If the aforesaid *houses of God* possess ruins which they cannot rebuild, *these too* may be granted in perpetual emphyteusis. The emphyteuta, having arranged the materials for the dwelling-house which he will use, shall receive a reduction of the pension by one third from that which was collected while the buildings still stood; or, if he first rebuilds it, one half of the rents added by appraisal shall be given to the religious house. For in the former case the pension must be paid from the beginning of the emphyteusis.

§ 9. Whoever has received the property already mentioned, not gratuitously under a title of alienation and apart from the legal form, shall restore the property indeed with all increase accrued during the intervening period. For what he paid, however, he has no action against the venerable place, but against the person who alienated it. The donee, moreover, shall restore both the property with all its appurtenances *and its fruits*, and also an equal additional amount. The creditor likewise, once the pledged property has been restored, shall have an action on the loan only against the giver of the pledge. The recipient in emphyteusis shall also forfeit it and shall not recover what he gave; indeed, he shall immediately pay what he would have had to pay *each year* had he contracted lawfully.

§ 10. But it is better said that actions of this kind should be wholly denied to the recipient. Emperor Leo:

§ 11. If the steward of a church judges it expedient that, at the request of anyone desiring it, temporary possession in usufruct of certain possessions and estates—*namely urban and rural*—belonging to ecclesiastical right should be granted, then the steward shall enter into and draw up an agreement with the person choosing this, whether the term agreed between the two parties be for a fixed period or requested by the applicant for the term of his life. The agreement shall establish the period during which this is to be granted and shall make clear what each party has received from the other.

## Chapter III. PALEA

[Note: In certain old copies, in which there are few Paleae, the words of this chapter follow continuously after the final words of the preceding chapter without any distinction, as also in the law of the Code itself. But in two very ancient copies, in which there are almost no Paleae, the first part of this chapter is missing down to the words “When the period has been completed”; the rest is read joined to the preceding material down to the words “But if necessity.” For this little clause, in those same copies, occurs not here but above, in the same chapter, “Casellas,” as noted there.]

> “The favour of such a benefit is to be granted by giving the usufruct of an ecclesiastical estate for a time; but after the appointed term, the ownership of the agreed revenues is firmly to revert to ecclesiastical dominion and right.”

That is, *namely*, that when either the period agreed between them has been completed, or at the time of death—if this too has been agreed—the person who, by intervening agreement, has undertaken possession of ecclesiastical property and usufruct of specified revenues must leave to the church the revenues of another property, of an amount no less than that which he had received, together with ownership of the estates themselves, the immovable property, and their coloni and slaves. Unless agreements have been made upon this condition, we decree that they too shall be invalid.

§ 1. This grant of use has place in every religious house. When it has ended, each property shall return in full right to the aforesaid house; and the property given in exchange shall not be burdened with greater taxes, *and its revenue shall be the same*.

§ 2. Although *this right* is permitted to others in whatever ways, certain persons are forbidden to receive such property: namely, the steward and his relatives. But if necessity compels that something be disposed of, whether in usufruct or by direct sale, for the church’s necessity or advantage, the reason why sale is necessary must first be demonstrated before two or three bishops of the same province or neighbouring bishops. Then, after priestly deliberation, the sale or transaction which has been made shall be confirmed by their subscription. A sale or transaction made otherwise shall not be valid. And below:

§ 3. We permit less useful possessions to be granted for use to strangers or clerics, with the church’s right preserved.

## Chapter IV. How grants at request (*precariae*) of ecclesiastical property ought to be made

Likewise, from the Council of Metz.

[Note: This canon is cited here as from the Council of Metz; but by Burchard and Ivo as from the Council of Beauvais, except for the final sentence, “Nor exchanges,” which they cite from the Council of Mâcon. It is also reported from the same Council of Beauvais in the Council of Meaux, c. 22. It appears in the Capitularies published under the fourth year of the reign of King Charles and his son Emperor Louis, at the royal estate of Cologne, c. 37. The title has not been changed, since the same matter may have been repeated in all those councils, as is known often to have occurred in surviving German and Gallican councils. Something concerning *precariae* is also found in the Council of Rheims, cc. 36–37, and the Council of Mainz under Arnulf, c. 20.]

[Note: From the Council of Meaux, held in A.D. 845, c. 22; Abbo of Fleury, in Mabillon, *Analecta veterum*, c. 7; Burchard, bk. 3, cc. 167–168; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, cc. 228–229; *Polycarpus*, bk. 3, tit. 14.]

No one shall presume to make a grant at request from ecclesiastical property, unless, for a fitting value given from his own property, he receives double the amount from the church’s property, in his own name alone, if he wishes to hold both his own property and ecclesiastical property in usufruct. But if he surrenders his own property at present, he may take from ecclesiastical property triple the amount in usufruct, in his own name alone. For each person ought to administer such things as a steward of ecclesiastical property, not as a lavish giver of his own.

§ 1. The holy synod also decreed, and imperial authority proclaimed, that no one should be compelled by any power to make a grant at request from things specifically dedicated to God and His saints, since reason and practice establish that no one may be forced, against advantage and reason, to confer a benefit from his own property upon someone whom he does not wish.

[Note: “Compelled”: so in all the old manuscripts of Gratian, and the gloss is present; but in the Council of Meaux, the Capitularies, Burchard, and Ivo, the reading is *praestitum*, “conferred.”]

§ 2. Nor shall any person presume to make exchanges of ecclesiastical property or slaves, even by royal licence and consent.

## Chapter V. On the same subject. PALEA

Likewise, from the Council of Beauvais.

[Note: Council of Meaux, c. 22; *Regino*, bk. 2, c. 365; Burchard, bk. 3, c. 169; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, c. 230; c. 1, *Compilatio I* and *X*, “On grants at request.”]

> “Grants at request shall be renewed from five-year period to five-year period, according to ancient custom *and authority*.”

## Chapter VI. On the same subject. PALEA

[Note: From the laws of Lothair I, c. 21; Lombard Laws, bk. 3, tit. 10, c. 2; *Compilatio I* and *X*, title cited.]

[Likewise, from the Council of Carthage.]

[Note: “Carthage”: It is also cited in the Decretals, under the title “On grants at request,” as from the Council of Carthage; but it has not been found in any of those councils. It may have belonged to a council of one of those provinces; it survives, however, in the Lombard Laws, book III, title 8, law 2.]

> “Concerning grants at request which were unreasonably made by rectors of churches and bound both themselves and their successors under a heavy penalty, so that their acts could not be dissolved: we command that no successor be bound under his predecessor’s penalty, but that it be entrusted to his own judgment that, if his predecessor has unreasonably distributed the church’s property, it be recalled by him to [lacuna] the use of that same church.”

## Chapter VII. The bishop shall have authority to administer the property of the church

Likewise, from the Council of Pope Martin, c. 16.

[Note: Council of Antioch, c. 25, in the translation of Martin of Braga.]

### Part III

The bishop shall have authority over the church’s property, so that he may distribute it with all reverence and fear of God to those in need. He ought also to receive what is necessary for himself. Yet if he himself, or the brethren who are with him, should need anything, they are not to suffer want in any way, according to the holy Apostle’s saying: “Having food and clothing, with these we are content” [1 Tim. 6:8].

But if a bishop should wish to appropriate ecclesiastical property for his own desires, and should not administer the church’s places and the fruits of its fields in consultation with the presbyters or deacons, or should grant authority to his brothers, sons, or any of his relatives so that through them the church’s property may be secretly harmed, then he must be held liable to a council. But if otherwise, the bishop, or the presbyters and deacons who are with him, are to be accused because they gather into their own bosoms things which come either from revenue or from any other ecclesiastical cause and occasion, and defraud and starve the poor. Such persons must be corrected in accordance with what has been ordained by the holy council.

[Note: “But if otherwise”: in the capitularies the reading is *similiter*, “likewise”; but the reading of two older manuscripts of Gratian, *sin aliter*, “but if otherwise,” seems better. It comes closer to the Greek of Antioch, c. 25, from which this is taken: *εἰ δὲ καὶ ἄλλως*, “but if in some other way also,” as below, 12, question 2, chapter “Episcopus.”]

[Note: “Act”: this word occurs in a similar matter below, 12, question 2, “The acts or patrimony of the Church of Volterra.” The Greek is *ἢ καὶ ἐξ ἑτέρας προφάσεως ἐκκλησιαστικῆς*, “or even from any other ecclesiastical cause and occasion.”]

### Part IV

Gratian. But if a bishop happens, contrary to this prohibition, to sell anything from the church’s property, it is decreed both that the property itself be restored to the church and that he be deposed from his rank.

Therefore, in the same Council of Pope Martin, c. 14, one reads:

## Chapter VIII. On a bishop who sells church property without necessity

If any bishop, compelled by no necessity grounded in ecclesiastical reasons, should presume, without the knowledge of his clergy—or, where there is no presbyter present—to sell anything of the church’s property, he shall be compelled to restore the property to the church itself; and, having been heard and convicted, he shall be deposed by judgment of the bishops and deprived of his office as one guilty of theft or robbery.

[Note: “Without the knowledge of his clergy”: the royal Lucchese manuscript reads *inscio clero*.]

[Note: “And convicted”: these two words occur neither in Martin’s chapter nor in the Hispanic Collection, Burchard, or Ivo, part 3. Moreover, in part 5 the word “having been heard” is absent. Nevertheless all the old manuscripts of Gratian agree with the printed editions.]

# QUESTION III

## GRATIAN

### Part I

What a bishop ought to exact under the name of *cathedraticum* is stated in the Second Council of Braga, c. 2.

## Chapter I. Apart from the honour of the cathedraticum, a bishop shall exact nothing through the dioceses

It has pleased us that no bishop, when travelling through his dioceses, shall take anything else from the churches beyond the honour due to his cathedra—that is, two solidi—nor demand the third part of any offering of the people in parish churches. Rather, *that third part shall be reserved for the church’s lights or* repair, and an accounting concerning it shall be rendered to the bishop each year. For if the bishop takes that third part, he has taken away the church’s light and its repair of roofs. Likewise, parish clergy shall not be compelled to perform servile labour for the bishop in any works, because it is written: “Nor as exercising lordship over the clergy” [1 Pet. 5:3].

## Chapter II. Let the third part, which the bishop had been accustomed to receive, be applied to repairing churches

Likewise, from the Council of Mérida, c. 16.

[Note: This chapter was cited corruptly in manuscripts of Gratian as from the Council of “Merech.” It is in the Council of Mérida, c. 16, two copies of which council were sent to Pope Gregory XIII. Innocent III mentions this council and chapter in the letters printed at Rome, bk. 2, in a letter to Peter of Compostela, in these words: “You were maintaining on many grounds that the Council of Mérida is authentic: first, because it is contained with other councils in the book called the *Corpus canonum*, which Pope Alexander authenticated through an authoritative interlocutory judgment; and second, because from that council was taken the chapter ‘Priscis quidem canonibus,’ which is contained in the corpus of decrees.”]

By ancient canons it had indeed been decreed that the bishop should receive a third from parish churches, though his own resources could fully suffice him.

[Note: “Could fully suffice”: the negation found in the printed editions has been removed, because it is absent both from the two copies of the council and from the old manuscripts of Gratian, and thus better accords with the rationale of the law.]

This holy council has decreed that no bishop of the province of Lusitania shall *exceed the limit of this ruling, nor* presume to take a third from any parish church. Rather, whatever could be obtained from it shall all be applied to repairing the churches themselves.

## Chapter III. Bishops shall not receive the third part unless they intend to repair ruined churches

Likewise, from the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, c. 5.

[Note: This chapter forms part of the fourth canon of the Sixteenth Council of Toledo. Two copies were sent from Spain, from which some points in this chapter have been corrected and added. This council was held in the Spanish Era 731 [A.D. 693], whereas the Council of Mérida was held in Era 704.]

The union of our assembly decrees and establishes that, if bishops consider that the thirds which ancient canons assigned them from their parishes ought to be exacted, the ruined churches shall be repaired by those bishops themselves. But if they prefer to relinquish them, repair must be provided for those churches by their custodians under the care and solicitude of their bishop. If all churches are either sound, or those which had been ruined have been repaired, then, according to the ordinances of the ancient canons, any bishop who wishes to obtain the thirds due to him shall have full authority to do so. This is subject to the provision that, apart from those thirds, no bishop shall demand anything from parish churches for royal requisitions, nor presume to give anyone anything from the estates of those churches as a stipend.

§ 1. We have also judged it necessary to establish that several churches must never be entrusted to one presbyter, because one man is unable throughout all the churches to perform the office, *or to meet the people’s needs by priestly right; nor* can he bestow the necessary care on their property. This is to be understood in the sense that a church possessing up to ten slaves shall have a priest over it, while a church possessing fewer *than ten slaves* shall be joined to other churches. If any bishop disregards this constitution of ours, let him know that he will be punished by excommunication for a period of two months.

[Note: “Punished”: the council continues: “So that, after returning from the prohibition of excommunication to the place of his rank, he may in every way endeavour to fulfil all the enactments of this canon.”]

## Chapter IV. On the same subject

Pelagius to the illustrious Cresconius.

We wish you by every means to observe this: that no bishop of Sicily presume to receive more than two solidi from the parishes belonging to him under the name of cathedraticum, nor compel the presbyters or clergy of their parishes to prepare banquets for them beyond their means.

## Chapter V. No numerical limit shall be imposed upon those to be baptized, nor shall cathedraticum be exacted beyond the ancient custom

Pope Gelasius to Bishop Fabian.

[Note: This chapter is of uncertain origin and cannot conveniently be attributed to Gelasius, since in his time it was not yet an ancient custom for cathedraticum to be exacted.]

No number is rightly thought to be imposed upon those to be baptized, since however many seek it or hasten to regeneration must not be turned away at another’s will. Therefore, dearest brother, you shall remove this superfluous regulation by every means, so that each person may be baptized either in a church near to him or in one chosen according to his own preference. You should also know that cathedraticum is to be demanded from the presbyter of that place only to the extent established by ancient custom; and, with regard to what has been offered through the devotion of donors on the day of dedication, you shall observe the custom prescribed generally for all churches.

### Part II

Gratian. The cathedraticum which bishops are permitted by these authorities to demand is to be understood apart from the half or third part of offerings which, according to the varying custom of churches, is also due to the bishop under the foregoing authorities. Nor is that share to be understood as a share of all offerings generally, but as a share either of the annual dedication or even of certain solemn days, according to what was agreed between bishop and priest at the time of dedication.

Concerning bishops who rage cruelly through their parishes, the following was established in the Third Council of Toledo, c. 20.

## Chapter VI. Bishops shall demand nothing from parish presbyters beyond the ancient custom

Because we have learned that bishops behave through their parishes not priestly but cruelly; and because it is written, “Be an example to the flock, not as exercising lordship over the clergy” [1 Pet. 5:3], while they impose exactions and losses upon their dioceses: therefore we decree—excepting what the ordinances of the ancients direct bishops to receive from parishes—that other things which have hitherto been presumptuously exacted from them shall be denied. That is, neither presbyters nor deacons shall be harassed in compulsory public services or *in* any levies, lest in the Church of God we seem to be called tax-collectors rather than bishops of God. Those clerics, both local and diocesan, who perceive that they are being burdened by their bishop must not delay in bringing their complaints to the metropolitan; and the metropolitan shall not delay to restrain such acts of presumption.

## Chapter VII. Bishops shall demand provisions from parishioners only with charity

Likewise, from the Second Council of Chalon, c. 4.

Care must indeed be taken that, when bishops travel through their parishes, they do not exercise some ruinous tyranny toward their subjects or companions, nor—God forbid—demand provisions from them with charity, but with a kind of judicial assault. They must also by every means observe this: if at any time the necessity of visiting their parishes rests upon them, they should devote their attention, in confirming persons, investigating matters needing correction, preaching the word of God, and gaining souls, rather to these things than to plundering and despoiling people and causing scandal to the brethren. And if at any time they must receive something from brethren or subjects for carrying out their ministry, they ought most carefully to ensure that they scandalize or burden no one. Such discernment must therefore be maintained in this matter that *the preacher of the word* of God may receive from the brethren where his own resources are lacking, while the brethren in turn are not burdened by his power, following the example of the Apostle Paul, who, so as not to burden anyone, sought his sustenance by craft and manual labour.

## Editorial and apparatus notes

The following source apparatus belongs to the preceding text.

- [Col. 0807] In the opening sentence, the Cologne editions and the first Louvain edition read: “so that they are not pledged and are kept in perpetuity.” The Argentinensis, Basle, Venice, and first Louvain editions omit “in these matters.” The source references the Authenticum, *Praeterea*, Code 1.2.21 and Novel 120, final chapter.
- [Col. 0807] For the disposal of superfluous vessels, the Cologne editions and Louvain II–III read: “or, having been melted down, let them be sold to anyone.” They read *citra* (“contrary to”) for *contra*; *speciali* for “specially”; *cujus* (“whose”) for “of which”; and *eadem* (“the same”) for “this.” The relevant Authenticum is *Hoc jus*, Code 1.2.14. The original reads *exsistere* (“to exist”) for “to be pressing.”
- [Cols. 0807–0808] The source’s marginal variants read: “religious house” for “house of God”; *alias* (“otherwise”) for *alioquin*; and *onere* (“burden”) for the preceding example of fiscal burdens. The references are Authenticum *Sicut*, Novel 7.12; *Idem praedium*, Novel 120.7; *Sed et permutare*, Novel 7.2; and *Item sibi*, Novel 54.2. The Argentinensis reads “may exchange with the emperor,” while the remaining editions read “emperors may exchange”; the other editions add “and above” after “those mentioned above.”
- [Cols. 0807–0809] The source cites Authenticum *Perpetua*, Code 1.2.14 and Novel 120.6. The Argentinensis, Basle, Nuremberg, and Venice II editions read “is conducted” for “may be conducted”; Basle reads “the customary revenues”; the other editions read *imminuendo* (“diminishing”) for “reducing”; and the Cologne editions and Louvain II–III omit “or, if it has been diminished by calamity.” They read singular “rental income” for “rental incomes.”
- [Col. 0809] The source cites Authenticum *Qui rem*, Novel 120.3. The Cologne editions read future *impenderit* (“he will have spent”) for “he has spent.” It cites Authenticum *Si quas*, Novel 120.1: the Argentinensis, Basle, Nuremberg, and Venice I editions read *usurae*; the other editions read “reduced” for “shall receive a reduction,” “dwellings” for “buildings,” and Basle omits from “For” through “pension.”
- [Cols. 0809–0810] The source cites Authenticum *Qui res*, Novel 120.11, and Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 185. Basle and Venice II read *circa* for *citra*; the editions read present “receives” for “has received,” “against the venerable house” for “against the venerable place,” and “has” for “he has.” Nuremberg omits from “against” through “giver of the pledge”; the Cologne editions and Nuremberg explicitly add “not against the church.” The reference for Emperor Leo is constitution 14, Code I, §5.
- [Cols. 0809–0810] In §11 the editions read “and rural” for “namely urban and rural,” and “if requested” for “or requested.” The chapter heading also has this apparatus: in some old copies with few Paleae the chapter follows continuously after the previous chapter, as in the Code; in two very ancient copies with almost no Paleae its first part is absent down to “When the period has been completed,” and the rest is joined to the preceding material down to “But if necessity.” In those copies that clause occurs above, in the same chapter, under “Casellas.” The Argentinensis omits the words from “Such” through “firmly.”
- [Cols. 0809–0810] In the usufruct passage the Argentinensis and Basle add “indeed” after “completed”; the other editions read “other” for “specified,” Basle has pluperfect “had undertaken,” the editions read *quantae* and Böhm *quantum* for *quantam*, and the Cologne editions read *ad invicem* (“in exchange”). The source cites Authenticum *Haec usus*, Novel 120.2, and explains that “For” is not in the Authenticum: old Gratian manuscripts have “N. C.,” meaning *novella constitutio* (“new constitution”). It also cites Authenticum *Quibuscunque*, Novel 120.5, and Agde, c. 7.
- [Cols. 0809–0811] The Chapter IV source citation is: Council of Metz; Regino 2.363. Burchard and Ivo attribute it to Beauvais, except for “Nor exchanges,” which they attribute to Mâcon; Meaux c. 22 also reports it from Beauvais. The extended bibliographical note is fully represented by: Abbo of Fleury in Mabillon’s *Analecta vetera*, c. 7; Burchard 3.167–168; Ivo, *Decretum* 3.228–229; and *Polycarpus* 3.14.
- [Cols. 0811–0812] For Chapter IV, the editions add “only” after “unless”; Louvain I reads future “shall receive,” and the remaining editions “let them receive,” for “he receives”; they read plural “gave” and “wish” for the singular; and they read “it is fitting” for “it is proper.” After “lavish giver,” the Council of Meaux and the Capitularies continue directly, “and let no one be compelled by any power,” without the intervening words printed here; comparable words occur in Burchard and Ivo under “Nor exchanges.” Basle reads present “proclaims” for “proclaimed”; Argentinensis, Nuremberg, and Venice II read “dedicated” for “specifically dedicated.” The old Gratian manuscripts read “compelled,” while Meaux, the Capitularies, Burchard, and Ivo read *praestitum* (“conferred”). Ivo reads “religion” for “royal.”
- [Cols. 0811–0812] Chapter V is cited from Meaux c. 22, Regino 2.365, Burchard 3.169, Ivo 3.230, and c. 1 of *Compilatio I* and the Decretals, “On grants at request.” Chapter VI is cited from Lothair I, c. 21; Lombard Laws 3.10.2; and the same titles. Although its heading attributes it to Carthage, the editor notes that it is cited as Carthaginian in the Decretals but is found in none of their councils; it may derive from a council of those provinces and survives in Lombard Laws 3.8.2.
- [Cols. 0811–0813] Chapter VII is from the Council of Pope Martin, c. 16, corresponding to Antioch c. 25 in Martin of Braga’s translation. Basle omits “holy”; the editions add “only” after “food”; the Hispanic Collection reads *lucra* (“profits”) for *loca* (“places”), and has both *contaminaverit* and *intaminaverit* (“shall have defiled” / “shall have kept undefiled”). The editions read “this man” for “then he,” while the better old reading is *sin aliter* (“but if otherwise”), rather than the capitularies’ *similiter* (“likewise”); it corresponds to Greek *εἰ δὲ καὶ ἄλλως*, “but if also otherwise.” The editions read *obveniunt* (“accrue”) or *venerunt* (“came”) for “come,” “uses” for “bosoms,” “the poor” in the dative, and variously “these indeed,” “for these,” or “for this,” for “such persons.” Greek *ἢ καὶ ἐξ ἑτέρας προφάσεως ἐκκλησιαστικῆς* means “or also from any other ecclesiastical cause and occasion.”
- [Cols. 0812–0813] The introductory judgment before Chapter VIII is followed in the source by references to Carthage V, c. 4; Burchard 1.215 and 3.181; and Ivo, *Decretum* 3.172, 242 and 5.329. Basle and Argentinensis read passive “be restored” for “restore.” The Lucchese royal manuscript reads *inscio clero* (“without the clergy’s knowledge”). “And convicted” is absent from Martin, the Hispanic Collection, Burchard, and Ivo part 3; in Ivo part 5 “having been heard” is also absent, though all old Gratian manuscripts agree with the printed text.
- [Cols. 0813–0816] The Question III introduction cites Braga II, c. 2, held A.D. 572; the *Collectio tripartita* 2.46.2; and Abbo in Mabillon, *Vet. anal.*, c. 33. Basle and Louvain read singular “his diocese”; Basle omits “travelling” and reads *cathedratici* for “of his cathedra.” The editions read “claimed for himself from parish churches” in place of the printed wording, “for repair” or “for restoration” for “for the church’s lights or repair,” present “takes,” “sacred” for “repair of roofs,” “of the bishop,” and omit “to perform servile labour.”
- [Cols. 0813–0815] Chapter II is Mérida c. 16, held A.D. 666. The editor says Gratian manuscripts corruptly cite “Merech”; two copies of the Mérida council were sent to Gregory XIII, and Innocent III discussed its authenticity in a letter to Peter of Compostela. The Hispanic Collection reads “By very ancient canons,” *parochitanis* for “parish,” *sequeretur* for “should receive,” and the Argentinensis “when” for “though.” The printed editions’ negation before “could fully suffice” is rightly removed: it is absent from both council copies and old Gratian manuscripts. The council copies read “and whatever could be obtained from it”; the Hispanic Collection reads “whatever,” while the editions have plural “let [these things] be applied to the repair of churches.”
- [Cols. 0813–0816] Chapter III is Toledo XVI, c. 5, held A.D. 693 (Spanish Era 731), while Mérida was held in Era 704. The Hispanic Collection reads “assembly,” and the editions “decreed,” “bishops to have,” add “church,” read “their,” and Basle reads “cause” for “as a stipend.” The editions read “necessary to establish”; *eadem* for “their”; add “we command”; read past “had”; and *spatio* for “a period.” The council continues after the two-month excommunication: on restoration to his office, the bishop must endeavour in every way to fulfil all the enactments of the canon.
- [Cols. 0815–0816] Chapter IV is an epistle of Pelagius II of uncertain date; Basle attributes it to Gregory, defender of Sicily; see Gregory the Great, Epistle 18, book 13, and Ivo 3.136. Chapter V is uncertain and cannot aptly be assigned to Gelasius, since cathedraticum was not yet ancient custom in his time; see *Collectio tripartita* 1.46.33. Basle reads “his own” for “near to him,” and the editions read *exstiterit* for “has been established.”
- [Cols. 0815–0816] The source cites Toledo III, c. 20, held A.D. 589; Ivo 3.137; and Abbo in Mabillon, *Vet. anal.*, c. 37. The Hispanic Collection omits “therefore we decree”; Basle and Louvain II–III omit “in”; it reads “presbyters or deacons … are harassed” for the printed construction; the editions read “avert” and the Hispanic Collection “strictly restrain” for “restrain.” Chapter VII is Chalon II, c. 4, held A.D. 813. The original adds “indeed” after “Care must”; editions read “through their parishes,” expand the phrase concerning ruinous tyranny, read *ne* for *nec*, and give the expanded contrast: “not with charity, but with a kind of boastful rashness; not with thanksgiving, but with a kind of judicial invention.” Basle reads “or” for “for,” and Böhm omits “the preacher of the word.”

## Chapter VIII. A bishop shall not presume to receive more than two solidi from parish churches

Likewise, from the Seventh Council of Toledo, c. 4.

Finally, among the other matters which it was fitting for us to address by common consent, it was necessary most diligently to consider also the complaints of the parish priests of the province of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0816D] “Gaul”: in the printed councils and in certain manuscripts of Gratian, “Galicia” is read; in the Hispana collection, “Gallaecia.” In other and more correct copies, and in the royal Lucchese manuscript of the councils, “the Gallican province” is found. For at that time the archbishop of Narbonne and the bishops of his province attended the synods of Toledo, as appears from the subscriptions to Toledo III. There Nigetius, metropolitan of Narbonne, Sergius, bishop of Carcassonne, Nebridius, bishop of Agde, and representatives of the bishops of Maguelonne and Nîmes subscribe. The subscriptions of the same metropolitan and of the bishops of that province are likewise printed in the Councils of Toledo IV and VI, leaving aside those preserved in manuscripts.], which, as we have learned, necessity at last compelled to be brought to public examination because of the rapacity of their bishops. For these bishops, as an evident investigation has disclosed, by burdening parish churches through indiscriminate administration, since they are frequently excessive in their exactions, are shown to have reduced certain basilicas almost to the exhaustion of their last resources. [Note: “Parish churches”: other editions read “parochial churches.” “Excessive”: other editions read “excesses.” “Frequently”: the Basel and Lyons editions read “frequent.”]

Therefore, lest what is known to have been hitherto rashly and disorderly undertaken happen henceforth, let none of the bishops of the aforesaid province demand that more than two solidi be paid to him annually from each basilica in his diocese, in accordance with the Synod of Braga [Note: Compare above, chapter 1. “Dioceses or basilicas”: the editions and the older collections.], the basilicas of monasteries, however, being exempted from this assessed payment [Note: “Expense”: the Venice I, Paris, and Lyons editions; “expression”: the Argentan, Nuremberg, and Venice II editions.]. [Note: “We decreed”: Basel edition.]

§ 1. When a bishop visits his diocese, moreover, he is not to be burdensome to anyone by reason of the size of his company, nor is he ever to exceed a retinue of fifty [Note: Various editions of this council read “five.” But the royal Lucchese manuscript, one Vatican manuscript, another manuscript in the Dominican library, old copies of Gratian, Burchard, and Ivo read “fifty.” Innocent III followed this reading in the Lateran Council, chapter *Cum apostolus*, X, *On dues and exactions*.] [Note: “Retinue”: other editions read “eviction.”], nor may he have leave to remain more than one day at each basilica [Note: Other editions read “to remain.”].

§ 2. But whichever of those bishops presumes to act otherwise than we decree shall without doubt be subject to canonical correction [Note: Other editions read “correction”], as a transgressor of synodal enactments and a corrupter of the decrees of the ancient Fathers [Note: The Hispana collection reads: “as transgressors of synodal constitutions, who ought to be corrected by the edicts of the ancient Fathers.” Other editions read “constitutions” for “enactments.”]

### Chapter IX. Priests are not to be burdened beyond measure by their bishops.

Likewise Gregory, to the bishops of Sicily, Book XI, Epistle 20 [Note: Epistle 18, written A.D. 603, Book 13 of the Maurist edition.]

It has been reported to us that in the time of my predecessor of holy memory, through the deacon Servusdei, who then administered the care of the ecclesiastical patrimony, it was arranged that priests established throughout all your dioceses should not be burdened beyond measure whenever you go out to confirm children. For a fixed sum had been established, with your consent, as I hear, which ought to be given by these priests for the work of the clergy. Yet what was then approved is now said not to be observed at all. I therefore admonish your brotherhood to take care not to be burdensome to those subject to you.

### Chapter X. Banquets are to be prepared for bishops in accordance with the modest means of the place.

Likewise Pelagius, to Cresconius the *Illustris* [Note: Epistle of Pelagius II; compare above, chapter 4; Anselm, Book 6, chapter 171 (168).]

We do not wish your Magnificence to be unaware that the bishop of the city of Syracuse, among the other matters which he promised in the document of his assurances, is also recorded as having specifically and lawfully promised, under provision for a penalty, never to demand from any priest of his diocese more than two solidi under the name of *cathedraticum*, nor under any other pretext to seek anything that would involve that priest’s loss. Your Magnificence should not cease to ensure, with fitting care, that this is observed not only by the aforesaid bishop but with respect to all bishops in Sicily; and likewise that the meals are not made excessive, but that a meal of hospitality is prepared, according to the means of each place, for a bishop arriving to administer confirmation [Note: Anselm reads “to prepare”], because we do not wish losses to be inflicted upon the poor under that pretext, nor do we permit it on any ground [Note: The Basel edition adds “we wish.”]

## CAUSE XI

### GRATIAN

A cleric brought an action against a cleric concerning estates. The defendant wished to bring him before a civil judge, but the latter was willing to stand only before an ecclesiastical judge. The plaintiff, however, by the power of a civil judge, dispossessed him of his property. When the bishop heard of this, he suspended him from office; but he, despising the bishop’s sentence, performed his office. Upon learning this, the bishop pronounced sentence against him without hope of restoration.

(Question I.) The first question here is whether a cleric is to be brought before a civil judge.

(Question II.) Second, if he is not to be brought before one, whether this fault merits suspension.

(Question III.) Third, if it does not merit suspension, whether one who despises the sentence of his bishop ought irreparably to be deposed.

## QUESTION I

### GRATIAN

**Part I.** That a cleric is not to be accused before secular judges, Pope Caius writes in a letter to Bishop Felix, chapter 2, saying [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare the Theodosian Code, Book 16, title 2, chapter 12, with the interpretation.]

### Chapter I. No cleric is to be summoned before a secular judge.

Let no one ever presume to accuse a bishop before a secular judge, or other clerics [Note: “The remaining”: the other collected editions.]

### Chapter II. PALEA

[Note: In Burchard, in certain manuscripts of Gratian among those containing this *Palea*, and in the Decretals, title *On competent jurisdiction*, chapter 2, this is cited from the Council of Paris, chapter 10. But it is reported in the Council of Reims at Trosly, chapter 6, from the Capitularies, where it occurs twice: Book 6, chapter 154, and Book 7, chapter 139. Something similar is read in the Fourth Council of Orléans, chapter 20, and in the Council of Auxerre, chapter 43.]

[Note: Chapter 6, Council of Paris, held A.D. 615; Capitularies, Book 6, chapter 156, Book 7, chapter 139; chapter 3, *Compilatio I*, chapter 2, X, *On competent jurisdiction*; Burchard, Book 16, chapter 22.]

> “No judge shall personally constrain or presume to condemn a priest, deacon, any cleric, or the junior clergy [Note: “Lesser clergy”: editions of Argentan and Venice II; the Basel edition adds “church attendants.”], without the bishop’s permission [Note: The original reads “knowledge.”] If he does so, he shall be excluded from the church to which he is known to have inflicted injury until he acknowledges and makes amends for his offense.”

### Chapter III. On the same matter.

Likewise Pope Marcellinus, Epistle II [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Third Council of Orléans, chapter 32; Anselm, Book 3, chapter 22; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 4, chapter 31.]

No one may presume to bring a cleric of any rank before a secular judge without the permission of his bishop; nor may a layperson accuse any cleric. [Note: In the second letter of Marcellinus, in the Third Council of Orléans where this is repeated, and in the *Panormia*, it reads: “A cleric of whatever rank, without his bishop’s permission, may presume no one,” etc. Nothing has been altered, however, because of the glosses and citations of the doctors.]

### Chapter IV. Every person is to be judged by those whom he has chosen as his judges.

Likewise from the Council of Nicaea [Note: This canon is no longer found in the Council of Nicaea; but it has been noted above, Distinction 16, chapter *Seventy*, that that council formerly had more canons. Julius recounts some of them in his rescript against the Orientals, where this chapter appears as number 34, and it is cited from there in Polycarp.] [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare the Theodosian Code, Book 4, title 16, chapter 2.]

But there ought to be no judges other than those whom the person accused himself has chosen, or those whom this holy see or its primates, *with* his consent, have delegated by the authority of this holy see. [Note: “Judges” is absent from the Basel edition; “other” is absent from the other collected editions except Basel; those editions read “unless” instead of “than.”]

### Chapter V. No cleric is to be dragged before secular courts.

Likewise the Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius Augusti [Note: Chapter 3, Theodosian Code, *On episcopal jurisdiction*; Anselm, Book 3, chapter 109; Polycarp, Book 1, title 19. Nearly all modern scholars, following Jacques Godefroy, editor of the Theodosian Code, rejected the title *On episcopal jurisdiction* as spurious. We can scarcely follow them, since we have learned from persons with more exact knowledge of these matters that this title is read in the most ancient manuscripts of the Theodosian Code; see Gustav Haenel, in Haubold’s *Works*, vol. II, p. XCII.]

By a perpetual law we enact that no bishop, nor any of those who serve the needs of the Church, shall be dragged before the tribunals of either ordinary or extraordinary judges. For they have their own judges, and have nothing in common with the public laws. [Note: The Venice I and II, Paris, and Lyons editions add “for” before “they have.”]

Likewise [Note: From Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 10, chapter 4; compare below, chapter 41]:

§ 1. When the Emperor Constantine presided over the holy synod assembled at Nicaea [Note: The words “Constantine the emperor” are absent from the Argentan and Basel editions.] and saw that a complaint of certain persons [Note: “Clerics”: added in the Basel and Lyons editions.] had been brought before him [Note: Other collected editions read “to be brought.”], he said: “You cannot be judged by anyone [Note: The Basel edition adds “by laypersons.”], because you are reserved for the judgment of God alone.” [Note: The humility with which Constantine conducted himself there is related by Eusebius, Book 2, *On His Life*, chapter 10; Socrates, Book 1, chapter 5; and Theodoret, Book 1, chapter 7.]

### Chapter VI. On the same matter. PALEA.

Likewise from the First Council of Mâcon, chapter 8 [Note: Held A.D. 583; Burchard, Book 16, chapter 21. The other collected editions read “from the Council of Matins.”]

> “No cleric may presume in any way to accuse another cleric before a secular judge or drag him to plead a cause. Rather, every affair of clerics is to be concluded in the presence of his bishop, or of priests together with the archdeacon. [Note: The Council of Mâcon reads: “or in the presence of his bishop, or priest, or archdeacon.” But in Bernard’s first collection of Decretals, title *On competent jurisdiction*, chapter 2, this chapter is reported in the same manner as in this *Palea*.] If any cleric delays to comply with this [Note: The Basel edition reads *implere*, “to fulfil,” for *adimplere*, “to carry out.”], if he is of lower rank, he shall receive one stroke fewer than forty [Note: Other collected editions read *ictibus*, “strokes,” for *ictus*, “a stroke.”]; but if he is of more distinguished rank, he shall be punished by thirty days’ confinement [Note: The same editions read *conclusione*, “confinement,” for *inclusione*, “imprisonment.”].”

### Chapter VII. On the same matter. PALEA.

Likewise Marcellinus, Epistle II, to the Eastern bishops [Note: In the Vulgate editions it was cited from Boniface to the bishops of Gaul, but certain old copies read “Marcel.” The Basel edition assigns it to Pope Mark. This chapter is in Marcellinus’s second letter and is attributed to him by Ivo; the following chapter, however, is that which old copies of Gratian, Burchard, and Ivo cite from Boniface to the bishops of Gaul, as will also be stated there.] [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Third Council of Carthage, chapter 9; Burchard, Book 3, chapter 139; Anselm, Book 3, chapter 22; Ivo, *Decree*, Part 3, chapter 205.]

> “Whatever disputes arise among Christians are to be brought before the Church and settled by ecclesiastical persons. And if they refuse obedience, they are to be excluded from the thresholds of the Church until they obey.”  
> [Note: The words from “And if they refuse obedience” to the end are not read in the letter itself, but occur in Burchard and Ivo.]

### Chapter VIII. A bishop is not to be brought before a civil judge either in a civil or a criminal cause.

Likewise Boniface, to the bishops of Gaul [Note: This was assigned to Marcellus, but, as stated in the preceding note, old manuscripts of Gratian, Burchard, and Ivo, Part 5, chapter 278, attribute it to Boniface, and it has accordingly been changed. Nearly the same provisions occur in Julian the Antecessor, Novella 123, chapter 10, as often happens in other texts cited under Boniface’s name. Ivo, in the same part, chapter 369, cites this chapter itself from the book of constitutions, adding some words found in Julian.] [Note: Chapter 10, Novella 115, in Julian; *Authenticum*, “No bishop,” Code, *On bishops and clerics*; Burchard, Book 1, chapter 168; Ivo, *Decree*, Part 5, chapters 278 and 369.]

No bishop is to be brought or produced before any judge, civil or military, either for a civil or for a criminal cause. For any magistrate who dares to command this [Note: The Basel edition reads “these things”] shall be punished by condemnation to the loss of his official belt [Note: Other editions read “by the loss of his property and belt.” Another reads “of his belt.”].

### Chapter IX. No cleric is to be examined in public.

Likewise Pope Silvester, in the Roman Synod, chapter 14 [Note: In the Roman synod under Silvester, chapter 14, and in the *Panormia*, the text is read as in Gratian, and therefore nothing has been changed. But in the epilogue of the same council it reads: “Let no one receive the testimony of a layman against a cleric.” It is read in the same way in the Capitularies of Hadrian, chapter 72, the Council of Tribur, chapter 4, and thence in Burchard and Ivo.] [Note: From the apocryphal constitution of Silvester; Anselm, Book 3, chapter 23; Burchard, Book 2, chapter 104; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 4, chapter 89; *Decree*, Part 6, chapter 278.]

Let no one receive the testimony of a cleric against a layperson; *for* let no one presume to examine any cleric in public, except in church. [Note: The Basel edition reads “receive” rather than “accept.”]

Gratian. Likewise, in Book I of the Code, title *On Bishops and Clerics*, the Emperor Theodosius says: “A bishop is not to be summoned to *give* testimony either by reason of his rank or by the laws.” [Note: Book I, title 3, chapter 7.]

§ 1. Likewise he said: “It is unfitting that a bishop be admitted to give testimony; for both the person is dishonored and the exceptional dignity of the priest is demeaned.” [Note: “Dishonored”: the Basel and Lyons editions read “honored”; other editions read “burdened.”]

### Novella Constitution

[Note: Julian, epitome of Novella 115, chapter 9; *Authenticum*, “But the judge,” Code, *On bishops and clerics*; Ivo, *Decree*, Part 5, chapter 369.]

A bishop is not to be summoned to testify on oath, but only with the Gospels set before him. [Note: “On oath”: this expression is not in the Novella. The Greek words bearing on this are: *Οὐδενὶ δὲ τῶν ἀρχόντων ἐξέσται τοὺς θεοφιλεστάτους ἐπισκοπους ἀναγκάζειν εἰς δικαστήριον παραγίνεσθαι ἐπὶ τῷ νεῖμαι μαρτυρίαν*, that is: “Moreover, no magistrate shall be permitted to compel the most God-loving bishops to appear in court for the purpose of giving testimony.”]

§ 1. Likewise: “But let the judge send some of his officials to him, so that, with the most holy Gospels set before him, he may state what he knows, as is proper for priests.” [Note: The Argentan edition reads *dicant quae noverint* (“let them state what they know”); the Basel edition reads *dicant quae noverunt* (“let them state what they know”).]

### Chapter X. A cleric who brings a cleric before a civil judge is to be anathema.

Likewise Silvester, in the epilogue of the Roman Council [Note: From excerpts from the decrees of St. Silvester; compare the apocryphal constitution of Silvester; Anselm, Book 7, chapter 170.]

If a cleric, accusing a cleric, enters the civil court, let him be anathema. [Note: The Basel edition reads: “If a cleric, accusing a cleric, enters the court, and whoever enters the court, let him be anathema.”]

Gratian. This must be understood if he has sought the hearing of public courts; for there is no objection to seeking episcopal judgment from the emperor.

Thus in the Eighth Council of Carthage it is read [Note: In ancient manuscripts the Eighth Council of Carthage is also cited, by which name the Council of Milevis seems to be meant, where this chapter is found as chapter 19.] [Note: Rather, from the Eleventh Council of Carthage, held A.D. 407; compare Ballerini, in the edition of the works of Leo the Great, vol. 3, p. XCV.]:

### Chapter XI. Whoever seeks from the emperor the hearing of public courts is to be deprived of his own rank.

It was resolved that whoever seeks from the emperor the hearing of public courts shall be deprived of his own rank. But if he seeks episcopal judgment from the emperor, this shall not harm him.

Gratian. The following authorities also must be understood in this way, by which causes of clerics are commanded to be heard only by clerics.

Thus Pope Gelasius writes to Count Ezechias [Note: A chapter of uncertain date; three-part collection, Part 1, title 46, chapter 42.]:

### Chapter XII. A cleric is not to be heard by a secular judge.

It should always be welcome to Christians to render what is requested from their dignity, because it is not fitting to deny a benefit to those serving God. Silvester and Faustinianus, who profess that they have been clerics from their cradles, complain that Theodora oppresses them by violence. They say that, although freeborn and, by God’s favor, released from the bonds of their former condition, they are again being assigned to the lot of most wretched servitude; and that, though bound by the clerical belt, they have been summoned by the archdeacon of the city of Grumentum under royal authority contrary to public laws. Yet it is evident that one who assails a soldier of heaven ought to pursue no tribunal but his own. Therefore, beloved son, after offering the greeting owed to you, I commend the aforesaid clerics to you, so that, if their adversaries disdain to appear before the judgment of delegates, they may be defended by your protection, lest either fraud or violence hostile to the laws impose any necessity upon them; for one who avoids judgment plainly shows that he mistrusts the justice of his cause. [Note: The Basel edition reads *eo, quod* (“on the ground that”) for *quia* (“because”); other Lyons editions retain *quia*. Other collected editions add *olim* (“formerly”) after “clerical belt”; the Basel edition reads “of the church” for “of the city [of Grumentum]”; “beloved son” is absent from the other collected editions except Lyons I; and they read *depensae* for *depenso*.]

### Chapter XIII. A cleric is to be summoned only to the judgment of bishops.

The same, to Bishops Crispinus and Sabinus [Note: A chapter likewise of uncertain date.]

Silvester and Faustinianus, clerics of the Church of Grumentum, have complained to us in a tearful petition that the freedom granted to them by the kindness of their master is being assailed by the oppression of his heirs. Though serving in the clerical office almost from their cradles, and continuing in that state even while their manumitter lived, they are not permitted to devote themselves to the service of divine ministries. Yet, if the truth supports their petition, the inheritance ought by law to be taken from those who act contrary to the deed of their father and benefactor, as unworthy persons; nor ought those who take the inheritance to be permitted to run counter to the judgment of their father and benefactor.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since they also complain that they are oppressed by the archdeacon of the said church—who, while they were absent, promised that they would follow the judgment of the governor, trampling upon all considerations, and thought that their own tribunal could be taken away in violation of divine and public laws—whoever he may be that assails a cleric must appear before your tribunal, so that the rights of the Church, which ancient emperors established by continual enactment, may not be denied to clerics who are attacked. [Note: The Basel edition omits “also”; it reads *securus* (“secure”) for *secuturos* (“would follow”), and *lacesserit* (“has assailed”) for *lacessit* (“assails”). The other collected editions except Basel and Lyons II–III omit “having trampled upon all considerations”; Basel and Lyons II–III omit “and,” while the remaining editions read “and in the same [judgment].”]

### Chapter XIV. Priests are not to be accused before a civil judge.

Likewise Alexander, to all orthodox persons serving Christ the Lord in various provinces, Epistle I, chapter 1 [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Innocent I, Epistle 4, and Third Council of Carthage, chapter 9; Anselm, Book 2, chapter 37; Polycarp, Book 1, title 2.]

It has been reported to the supreme authority of this holy and apostolic see—to which the disposition of the most important causes and the affairs of all churches have been entrusted by the Lord himself, as to a head, he himself saying to Peter, prince of the apostles, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” [Note: Compare Matthew 16:18.]—that enemies of Christ and plotters against his holy Church presume to accuse God’s priests before public judges, whereas the Apostle commands that Christians’ causes be brought before churches and settled there. By thus transgressing, they have transgressed against their God and do not obey his commands.

### Chapter XV. The plaintiff must follow the defendant’s forum.

Likewise Pope Pelagius, to Benegestus the Defender [Note: An epistle of uncertain date; three-part collection, Part 2, title 54, chapter 13; Holstenius from the collection of Deusdedit, chapter 113.]

By the present authority we command your Experience that, in causes in which any person holding ecclesiastical office acts as plaintiff and brings an action against a layperson, he must not fail to bring his claims before the judge of his own province [Note: Holstenius and the Basel edition read *desinat* (“cease”) for *deserat* (“abandon”); the resulting injunction remains negative.].
