But in matters in which a person holding ecclesiastical office is sued, with every obstacle of the accusation removed, an impartial hearing is to take place before the bishop or priests established in the place where the question is at issue [Note: The Basel edition reads “therefore” rather than “but.”]

### Chapter XVI. On the same matter.

Likewise to Sergius the Chancellor [Note: An epistle of uncertain date.]

If any cleric, whether of lower or higher rank, acts as plaintiff and brings his claims against a layperson, he must in every case come to plead his cause nowhere other than before the provincial judge [Note: The Basel edition reads “about to plead.”] But if any layperson thinks that a cleric of whatever rank should be sued, he must bring before the judgment of the bishops established in that city or territory the claims which he considers himself to have. That this order is in every respect fitting and consistent with the laws is made clear by the rule which commands the plaintiff always to follow the forum of the person sued. The authority of imperial enactments also establishes that the proper forum for clerics when sued is an episcopal court.

Likewise, in the Council of Agde, chapter 32, it is read [Note: The Council of Agde, chapter 32, begins: “Let no cleric presume to sue anyone,” etc. The latter part of the same chapter, found above, Cause 5, Question 6, final chapter, treats, as if conversely, of laypersons who harass the Church or clergy, and shows that the former passage concerns clerics who sued laypersons without their bishop’s permission. Ivo agrees with the original.] [Note: Held A.D. 506; Ivo, *Decree*, Part 6, chapter 367; compare below, chapter 47.]:

### Chapter XVII. A cleric ought not to be sued before a secular judge without the bishop’s permission.

Let no one presume to sue a cleric before a secular judge without the bishop’s permission; but if he is sued, he is not to answer or bring a claim, nor dare to bring a criminal action before a secular court. [Note: The Hispana collection reads *nequaquam* (“by no means”) for *nullus* (“no one”); it omits “but” and “not,” and reads *nec* (“and not”) for *vel* (“or”).]

### Chapter XVIII. A cleric disobedient to his bishop is to be deposed and handed over to the civil court.

Likewise Pope Pius, Epistle II [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Anselm, Book 8, chapter 17; Ivo, *Decree*, Part 5, chapter 243; Polycarp, Book 4, title 34.]

If any priest or other cleric is disobedient to his bishop, lays snares for him, or inflicts insult, false accusation, or abuse upon him, and can be convicted, he is immediately to be deposed and handed over to the civil court, and is to receive what he has unjustly done. [Note: “Deposed”: this word is absent from the original and from Ivo. “And is to receive”: the letter of Polycarp and Anselm read: “But he who does injury shall receive that which he has unjustly done.”]

### Chapter XIX. He who refuses to leave a people he has unlawfully seized is to be compelled by imperial authority.

Likewise from the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 38 [Note: Held A.D. 397; three-part collection, Part 2, title 17, chapter 27; Part 1, title 1, chapter 83.]

We ask that you deem it proper to give us authorization so that, necessity itself compelling, we may be free, in accordance with the statutes of the most glorious emperors, to approach the governor of the province against one who refuses to leave, even to this day despite admonition, the people whom he had seized, as had been decreed; so that one who would not yield to the admonition of your Holiness [Note: The Hispana collection reads “our Holiness.”] and correct what is unlawful may immediately be excluded by judicial authority. [Note: From “who refuses to leave the people” through “refuses” (*contemnit*), the compiler has transferred words from an earlier portion of the same canon, so as not to reproduce all of it. The Hispana collection reads *quoniam* (“because”) and the Basel edition *quatenus* (“so that”) for *qua* (“by which/so that”); the Basel edition adds “and governor.”]

Bishop Aurelius said: Provided the form of discipline is observed, it shall not be considered an act of aggression if, *by* your charity, he has been moderately admonished and refuses to withdraw, when he has *also* been summoned by judicial authority because of his own contempt and obstinacy.

Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: “This pleases everyone.”

*All the bishops said: “It is just; it pleases us.”* [Note: Some editions read “therefore” rather than “for”; other editions correctly retain the interrogative sense.]

### Chapter XX. Those whom the Church cannot correct are to be corrected by rulers.

Likewise Pope Gregory [Note: This chapter is reported in Polycarp without the author’s name; but in Book 7, title 5, something similar is reported from Gelasius to John, master of the soldiers. In that book Gelasius is often written in place of Pelagius. Anselm, however, reports the whole letter of Pelagius, of which this chapter is the first part, and the latter part is the chapter *Nec licuit*, above, Distinction 17.] [Note: From the same letter of Pelagius as chapter 4, Distinction 17; Anselm, Book 12, chapter 42 (43); Polycarp, Book 1, title 15.]

This is what we asked of you and now ask again: send Paulinus, the pseudo-bishop of Aquileia, and that bishop of Milan under proper guard to the most clement emperor, so that the former, who cannot in any way be a bishop because he was made one contrary to all canonical custom, may no longer destroy others; and so that the latter, who presumed contrary to ancient custom to ordain him, may be subject to the punishment of the canons. [Note: The Basel edition reads “Paul” rather than “Paulinus”; other editions read “may have presumed.”]

### Chapter XXI. Clerics who enter into sworn combinations or conspiracies are to lose their rank.

Likewise in the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 18 [Note: A.D. 451; compare below, chapter 18.]

The crime of sworn combinations and conspiracies, which among the Greeks is called *phratry* (*φρατρία*, a brotherhood or faction), is certainly altogether prohibited even by public laws. Therefore it is much more fitting that it be prohibited from occurring in the holy Church of God. But if any clerics or monks are found entering into sworn combinations or conspiracies, or forming *phratries* or factions against their bishops or other clerics, they shall altogether fall from their own rank. [Note: The Basel edition reads “but” rather than “therefore.”]

### Chapter XXII. Clerics who conspire, having lost their rank, are to be confined in prison; the rest are to be excommunicated.

Likewise Pope Calixtus, to the bishops of Gaul, Epistle II [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Council of Chalcedon, chapter 18; Burchard, Book 10, chapter 64; Ivo, *Decree*, Part 5, chapter 346 and Part 12, chapter 85; Polycarp, Book 4, title 39.]

We have heard that crimes of conspiracy prevail in your regions, and it has been reported to us that peoples are conspiring against their bishops. The craftiness of this crime is abominable not only among Christians but even among pagans, and is prohibited by foreign laws. Therefore those guilty of this crime are condemned both by ecclesiastical laws and by secular law—not only those who conspire, but also those who consent with them. Our predecessors, together with a very large company of bishops, decreed that all who hold the honor of priesthood or are clerics should lose the rank which they possess; but they ordered the rest to be deprived of communion and made exiles from the Church. They judged all men of both ranks alike to be infamous, not only those who commit such acts but also those who consent to them. [Note: The Basel edition reads “reported” rather than “announced”; other editions read “entrusted.” The Basel edition adds “publicans” after “pagans.” Some editions omit the final phrase “and those who consent to them.”]

### Chapter XXIII. Clerics or monks who form sworn combinations are to be deprived of their own honor.

Likewise from the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 18 [Note: This canon is part of canon 18 of the Council of Chalcedon, which shortly above, in the chapter *Conjurationum*, is reported in full from another translation.] [Note: Held A.D. 451; Dionysius’s translation; Anselm, Book 8, chapter 16; Burchard, Book 10, chapter 64; Ivo, *Decree*, Part 12, chapter 87; Polycarp, Book 4, title 34.]

If any clerics or monks are found forming sworn combinations or conspiracies, or laying snares for bishops or clerics, let them be altogether cast down from their own rank.

### Chapter XXIV. On the same matter.

Likewise from the Council of Toledo [Note: Ivo and the author of Polycarp, as well as Anselm, cite this from Toledo; but it has not been found in any such council. It is the same canon as the preceding one, with words merely changed.] [Note: The same chapter of the Council of Chalcedon, from the ancient translation; Burchard, Book 10, chapter 69; Anselm, Book 8, chapter 18 (17); Ivo, *Decree*, Part 12, chapter 88; Polycarp, same place.]

If clerics or monks are found conspiring, or devising accusations against bishops or clerics through a sworn combination, let them lose their own rank.

### Chapter XXV. On the same matter.

Likewise from the Third Council of Orléans, chapter 21 [Note: Held A.D. 538.]

If any clerics—as it has lately become clear that, in many places, this has been done through pride at the devil’s instigation—have gathered themselves into one body by a rebellious act, a conspiracy intervening, and if it is discovered either that oaths have been exchanged among them or that a written document has been drawn up, *this* presumption is not to escape under any excuses. But once the matter has been discovered and the synod convened, punishment is to be inflicted upon the offenders by the bishops then gathered together, according to the status of their persons and orders. For just as charity, by divine commands, is to be shown from the heart, not by a written document or conspiracies, so acts undertaken beyond the sacred Scriptures are to be restrained by episcopal authority and severity. [Note: The Hispana collection reads *interdicente* (“forbidding”) for *intercedente* (“intervening”), and *chartula conscripta* (“a written document drawn up”) for *chartulam conscriptam*; it also reads *res* (“things”) for *re* (“the matter”), *synodo* for *synodum*, and *praesumtoribus* for *praesumtores*. Its alternative conclusion is: *quod supra sacras scripturas admittitur auctoritate et districtione pontificali est reprimendum*—“what is undertaken beyond the sacred Scriptures is to be restrained by episcopal authority and severity.” Other editions read *conjuratione* (“a conspiracy”) for *conjurationibus* (“conspiracies”).]

### Chapter XXVI. Causes arising between clerics and laypersons are to be heard by bishops.

Likewise Pope Innocent, to Victricius of Rouen, Epistle II, chapter 3 [Note: Written A.D. 404; Anselm, Book 2, chapter 53 (52).]

*[The supplied source ends here, incomplete.]*
If disputes or controversies have arisen between clerics, or between laypersons and clerics, whether of higher or lower rank, it was decided that, in accordance with the Nicene synod, when all the bishops of the same province have assembled, the case is to be settled.

[Note: “or—clerics”: omitted in the Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: “or between”: Thus in the three-volume edition of the councils. In the four-volume edition, however, these words are absent: “or between laypersons and clerics.” In Gratian’s manuscripts the reading was: “controversies between clerics and laypersons” [editions cited; Anselm].]

[Note: “it was decided that”: omitted in the Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: See the Council of Nicaea, canon 5.]

[Note: “all”: omitted in the Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: “case”: In certain editions of the letter itself, in Anselm, the Capitularies, and in Nicholas’s letter to the bishops of Gaul, in the appendix to the *Library of the Holy Fathers*, where this chapter is reported, the reading is “dispute.”]

[Note: “are to be settled by judgment”: Basel edition.]

Gratian. Since, therefore, by all these authorities clerics are forbidden to be brought before a civil judge, and may not be presented to the court unless they have first been deposed or stripped of office, it is evident that clerics are not to be dragged before secular courts.

Part II, §1. The reply to this is as follows: Clerics are subject to the bishop by reason of their office; they are answerable to the emperor by reason of their landed possessions. From the bishop they receive anointing, tithes, and first-fruits; from the emperor, however, they obtain possession of estates. Hence Augustine says on John:

“By what right do you defend your country houses—by divine or by human right? Look to the beginning, where the distinction between natural law and constitutional law is marked.”

Therefore, since possession of estates has been established by imperial law, it is clear that clerics, by reason of their estates, are answerable to the emperor.

[Col. 0828A] C. XXVII. The Church ought not refuse tribute to the emperor. Likewise Ambrose, against Auxentius, in the discourse *On Handing Over the Basilicas*.

If the emperor demands tribute, we do not refuse it. The Church’s lands pay tribute. If the emperor desires the lands, he has authority to claim them. And, after a few intervening words: “Let him take them, if he wishes. I do not give them to the emperor, but neither do I refuse them.”

[Note: “we do not refuse it”: Basel and Lyons editions.]

[Note: “pay”: let them pay, editions cited.]

[Note: “to claim”: Basel edition reads “of claiming.”]

[Note: “Let him take them”: one reading, “let him take them for himself, if he wishes”; another, “let him take them,” etc.]

C. XXVIII. Tributes must not be refused to governing authorities. The same, in his commentary on Luke, book IV, chapter before the last, on chapter 5.

It is indeed a great and spiritual instruction, by which Christian men are taught that they ought to be subject to higher authorities, lest anyone suppose that a decree of an earthly king must be disregarded. For if the Son of God paid the tax, who are you, so great that you think it need not be paid?

[Note: “spiritual”: editions cited read “special.”]

[Note: Matthew 17.]

[Note: “think”: editions cited read “you think.” See Romans 13:1.]

Gratian. Likewise the Apostle says: “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities.” Likewise Peter the Apostle writes generally to all the faithful: “Be subject to your rulers, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good.”

[Note: 1 Peter 2:13.]

C. XXIX. A bishop ought not to take cognizance of secular affairs. Likewise from the first letter of Clement to James, the brother of the Lord.

You ought indeed to live blamelessly and strive with the utmost diligence to cast off all the occupations of this life, lest you become a surety, become an advocate in lawsuits, or be found entangled in any occupation whatsoever through involvement in worldly business. For Christ does not wish today to appoint you as judge or examiner of secular affairs, lest, choked by present human cares, you be unable to devote yourself to the word of God and, according to the rule of truth, distinguish good persons from bad. Let laypersons who have leisure attend to one another in those tasks which, as we have explained above, are less fitting for you; and let no one occupy you away from those pursuits through which salvation is given to all.

[Note: From Clement I’s letter, translated into Latin by Rufinus.]

[Note: “in any”: omitted in the Basel edition.]

[Note: “For neither”: editions cited read “Neither.”]

[Note: “These therefore”: Basel edition; “These indeed”: other editions.]

[Note: “which are less fitting for you”: “which are less fitting for you,” as above; editions cited read “which we have said.”]

[Note: “laypersons who have leisure”: Clement’s letter reads “learners, that is, laypersons”; but Gratian reads here, and again below after the *Palea*, “No one [shall bring] a cleric,” in the same manner.]

[Col. 0829A]

C. XXX. In matters pertaining to the use of common life, laypersons should render service to one another. Likewise, immediately following in the same place.

For just as it is a charge of impiety against you to undertake secular concerns while neglecting study of the word of God, so it is a sin for every layperson unless they faithfully render service to one another also in those matters pertaining to the use of common life. Let all work together to free you from matters to which you ought not attend. But if laypersons do not understand this for themselves, they must be instructed through the deacons, so that they may leave to you the concerns of the Church alone.

[Note: “for you”: Argentinensis edition reads “everywhere”; editions cited add “O Clement.”]

[Note: “attend”: the original reads “be free for.”]

[Note: “may leave”: Basel reads “may be left”; the other editions, “may leave.”]

[Col. 0829B] Gratian. From all this it is understood that, in a civil cause, a cleric is to be summoned before a civil judge. For just as an ecclesiastical judge is the administrator of ecclesiastical laws, so only a civil judge ought to be the executor of civil laws. Just as only he has the right to interpret canons who has the authority to make them, so only he ought to be interpreter of civil laws who gives them legal force and authority. In a criminal case, however, a cleric is to be examined only before a bishop. This is what has been defined above by laws and canons: namely, that in a criminal case no cleric is to be brought before a civil judge, except perhaps with the consent of his bishop; for example, when they are found incorrigible, then, after office has been taken from them, they are to be handed over to the court.

Hence Pope Fabian says, in Letter II to the Eastern bishops:

[Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; see Theodosian Code 16.2.39; Anselm, book 7, chapter 159 (173); *Polycarpus*, book 4, title 31.]

C. XXXI. One who plots against a bishop, having been removed from the clergy, is to be handed over to the court.

We decree that if any cleric is hostile to, or plots against, his bishop, and wishes to accuse him, or is a conspirator, he shall immediately, before the examination of the judgment, be removed from the clergy and handed over to the court, which he shall serve for the days of his life; and he shall remain infamous, with no hope whatsoever of restoration.

[Note: “has been”: editions cited read “has become.”]

Gratian. Therefore, because this man brought a cleric before a civil judge not in a criminal but in a civil case, he is not to be judged a transgressor of the canons, nor is he to be said to have dragged an accused person before a judge who was not his proper judge; for only a civil judge ought to take cognizance of a civil cause.

Part III, §1. On the contrary, the points stated in defense of the plaintiff seem plausible indeed, but lack weight. For both in civil and in criminal cases, sacred canons and civil laws forbid a cleric to be dragged before a civil judge.

Hence we read in Clement’s first letter to James:

[Note: See chapter 30 above; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 345; *Polycarpus*, book 5, title 1.]

C. XXXII. Brethren are to be judged before presbyters.

If any of the brethren have disputes among themselves, they are not to be judged before secular examiners, but whatever the matter may be is to be decided before the presbyters of the Church.

[Note: “have”: Basel reads “shall have.”]

C. XXXIII. No cleric may enter the court for any cause. Likewise Pope Sylvester, in the epilogue of the Roman Council.

No cleric, whether deacon or presbyter, may enter a court for any cause whatsoever, nor presume to plead a case before a civil judge.

[Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare chapter 16 of the apocryphal Constitution of Sylvester.]

[Note: “civil”: In the epilogue of the Roman synod under Sylvester, from which this appears to have been taken, the reading is “belted”; soldiers and magistrates received a belt from the emperor.]

[Note: Editions cited add “his own.”]

C. XXXIV. A penitent should seek ecclesiastical, not civil, judgment. Likewise Pope Leo, to Rusticus, Letter XC, or XCII, chapter 9.

It is one thing justly to demand what is owed; it is another, for love of perfection, to disregard one’s own claims. But a person seeking pardon for unlawful acts ought also to abstain from many lawful things, as the Apostle says: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient.” Therefore, if a penitent has a case which perhaps ought not to be neglected, it is better for him to seek ecclesiastical rather than civil judgment.

[Note: Letter 167, Ballerini edition; written A.D. 458 or 459. Compare below, *Distinction* 1, on Penance, chapter 65; Anselm, book 11, chapter 141.]

[Note: 1 Corinthians 6:12.]

[Note: Editions cited add “it is better for him that he.”]

[Note: “seek”: Basel and Lyons II–III read “should seek”; other editions, “should wait.”]

[Col. 0830C] Gratian. He does not say only “for a criminal matter,” but generally “for any cause,” understanding both civil and criminal cases.

Hence Emperor Theodosius:

[Note: Theodosian Code, *On Episcopal Jurisdiction*, law 1; compare note to chapter 5 above; Capitularies, book 6, chapter 366; Anselm, book 3, chapter 108; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 16, chapter 312.]

C. XXXV. Anyone may choose the judgment of the bishop of the most holy see.

Anyone who has a lawsuit, whether possessor or claimant, may, whether at the beginning of the suit, during the course of proceedings, when the case is argued, or even when sentence has already begun to be pronounced, choose the judgment of the bishop of the most holy see. Immediately and without any hesitation—even if the other party objects—he shall be directed, together with the statements of the litigants, to the judgment of the bishops.

[Note: “possessor or”: “possessor, or”: omitted in Anselm.]

[Note: “most holy see”: Anselm, Ivo, and the Capitularies read “law.”]

[Note: “shall be directed”: In the Theodosian Code, book 16, title *On Episcopal Judgment*, law 1, repeated in the Capitularies, book 6, chapter 281, and in the Third Council of Valence under Lothair, and in Ivo and Anselm, the following occurs: “For the authority of most holy religion investigates and brings forth many matters which do not suffer the snares of crafty prescription in judgment.” The following chapter is then immediately added: “Therefore all causes …”]

[Col. 0831A] C. XXXVI. Likewise in the same place.

Therefore, all causes which are conducted either under praetorian law or civil law, once settled by the judgments of bishops, shall be confirmed with perpetual legal stability; nor shall it thereafter be lawful to reopen a matter decided by episcopal sentence.

§1. Even testimony given by one bishop shall be accepted without hesitation by all judges; nor shall any other witness be heard when a bishop’s testimony has been offered by either party. For that is established by the authority of truth; that is to be regarded as uncorrupted which a most holy person has uttered from the conscience of an undefiled mind. We once decreed this by a salutary edict; we confirm it by perpetual law, repressing the malicious seeds of litigation.

[Note: “decided”: Basel reads “shall be decided”; other editions, “is decided.”]

[Note: Editions cited add “is to be regarded as.”]

[Note: “uttered”: editions cited read “has been uttered.”]

[Note: Editions cited, from Anselm, read: “We establish this by a salutary edict and judge that it must be observed by perpetual law.”]

Gratian. If anyone argues that these provisions have become obsolete because they are not included in this form in Justinian’s Code, let him recognize that they were renewed by Charles, who says among other things in his Capitularies, book VI, chapter 281:

C. XXXVII.

We will and command that all subject to our dominion, God helping us—Romans, Franks, Alemanni, Bavarians, Burgundians, Saxons, Thuringians, Frisians, Gauls, Britons, Lombards, Gascons, Beneventans, Goths, Spaniards, and all other persons subject to us—by whatever bond of law they seem to be bound or by whatever customary usage connected, shall all observe by perpetual law this decision which we have taken from the sixteenth book of Emperor Theodosius, namely chapter eleven, written in reply to the inquiries of Duke Ablavius and addressed to him and to all others; and which, by the counsel of all our faithful, both clerics and laypersons, we have placed among our capitularies to be held as law. That is:

“Anyone who has a lawsuit, whether possessor or claimant,” etc., as above.

[Note: “God helping us”: omitted in the cited editions.]

[Note: “bound”: Basel reads “restricted”; other editions, “bound fast.”]

[Note: “connected”: editions cited read “attached.”]

[Note: “sixteenth”: Basel reads “one hundred and twenty-seventh”; other editions, “seventeenth.”]

[Note: “which we have taken … written in reply”: Basel reads “which both to him and to all”; other editions, “which to them and to all.” “We have taken it as a rescript”: corrected from the Capitularies. Earlier the reading was “we have sent it in writing”; Norimberga and Venice II, “we have sent it as written”; Anselm.]

[Col. 0832A] Likewise Gregory, book XI, Letter 54, instructing John the defender as he was going to Spain, says:

[Note: Letter 45, written A.D. 603, book 13, Maurist edition; Collection of Canons of Anselm, dedicatory part 3, chapter 21; Anselm, book 3, chapter 95 (93).]

C. XXXVIII. A presbyter ought to be judged only before a bishop.

With respect to the person of a presbyter, this must be observed: if he had any case, he ought not to be summoned by another, but his own bishop ought to be approached, as the Novella constitution makes clear, which speaks concerning the most holy, God-beloved, and most reverend bishops, clerics, and monks:

“Emperor Justinian Augustus to Peter, most glorious prefect of the praetorium. If anyone has an action against any cleric, monk, deaconess, nun, or ascetic woman, he shall first inform the most holy bishop to whom each of these is subject. That bishop shall judge the case between them. And if indeed either party does not acquiesce in what has been adjudged, we command that these matters be fully carried into execution through the local judge,” etc.

[Note: “if”: Basel edition.]

[Note: “his own bishop ought to be approached”: Anselm reads “his bishop ought to hear [the case]”; Basel, “his own bishop ought to be approached”; Argentinensis, Norimberga, and Venice I, “the bishop himself ought to approach”; other editions, “his own bishop ought to approach.”]

[Note: “Novella”: Anselm and editions cited read “of the Novellae.”]

[Note: “thus”: added by editions cited.]

[Note: “Peter, most glorious prefect of the praetorium”: Argentinensis, Basel, Norimberga, and Venice I read “pope.”]

[Note: The Greek is: *magistrōi theiōn hēmōn offikiōn*, “master of our divine offices.”]

[Note: Anselm and editions cited add “chapter LIII”; compare Novella 123.]

[Note: “has”: Argentinensis, Basel, Norimberga, Venice I, and Anselm read “has”; editions cited read “may have.”]

[Note: “is subject”: editions cited, and Böhm, read “may be subject.”]

[Note: “does not acquiesce”: In the *Authentic* title *On the Most Holy Bishops*, and in Julian, the negation is absent.]

§1. But lest it be objected that this speaks of a cleric, not of a presbyter, it should be known that earlier in the same constitution, book I of the Code, it is said that the term “clerics” includes presbyters and deacons also. The words of the law are these:

“Presbyters and deacons, subdeacons, singers, and readers, all of whom we call clerics,” and the rest.

[Note: “this”: Basel reads “here.”]

[Note: Anselm: “chapter LI”; various editions give corrupt or abbreviated forms; compare Novella 123, chapter 19; *Authentic*, “Presbyters,” Code, *On Bishops and Clerics*.]

C. XXXIX. A cleric must not drag another cleric before public courts. Likewise Gregory, book IX, Letter 32, to Romanus, Defender of Sicily.

It has come to our notice that, when anyone has a case against any clerics, you cause those clerics to appear in your court, disregarding their bishops. If this is so, since it is plainly very improper, by this authority we command you not to presume to do this again. But if anyone has a case against any cleric, let him approach that cleric’s bishop, so that either the bishop himself may hear it, or judges may certainly be appointed by him; or, if it is perhaps necessary to proceed to arbitrators, let the enforcement officer appointed by him compel the parties to choose judges. But if any cleric or layperson has a case against a bishop, then you ought to intervene, so that you may either hear the matter yourself between them, or at least, upon your admonition, they may choose judges for themselves. For if the jurisdiction belonging to each bishop is not preserved, what else is being done except that ecclesiastical order, which ought to be preserved by us, is thrown into confusion through us?

[Note: Letter 37, written A.D. 601, book 11, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 3, chapter 29.]

[Note: “in”: omitted in Anselm.]

[Note: “since”: omitted in Anselm.]

[Note: Anselm and editions cited read “But by this authority.”]

[Note: The original reads “to choose a judge”; Anselm, “to choose judges”; Basel, “to choose a judge.”]

[Note: “enforcement officer”: the text prints *exsecutio*, perhaps an uncertain or defective reading.]

[Note: Anselm adds “there”; editions cited read “he.”]

C. XL. Clerics must not be oppressed by lay judges. The same, to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, book III, Letter 26.

We have learned from the report of our brother and fellow bishop Felix, and of Cyriacus the abbot, that priests are oppressed by lay judges on the island of Sardinia, and that the officials of your brotherhood despise you; and while you devote yourselves solely to simplicity, discipline, as far as we see, is neglected.

[Note: Letter 28, written A.D. 594, book 4, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 7, chapter 146.]

[Note: “your”: editions cited and Böhm read “of your brotherhood.”]

C. XLI. Priests are to be honored, not judged, by kings. Likewise Gregory, to Emperor Maurice, book IV, Letter 31.

Let not our lord more readily become angry with priests on the basis of earthly power; rather, with exalted consideration for the sake of him whose servants they are, let him exercise authority over them in such a way as also to render them due reverence. For in the divine utterances priests are sometimes called gods and angels. Thus through Moses it is said of one who is to be brought to an oath: “Bring him before the gods,” that is, before the priests. And again it is written: “You shall not speak evil of the gods,” namely, of priests. And the Prophet says: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.” What wonder, then, if your Piety deigns to honor those to whom God himself, conferring honor upon them in his word, also gives the names either of angels or of gods?

[Note: Letter 40, written A.D. 595, book 5, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 6, chapter 195.]

[Note: Editions cited read “through”; compare Exodus 22:8.]

[Note: Exodus 22:28.]

[Note: Editions cited add “namely”; Malachi 2:7.]

[Note: Basel adds “and righteousness”; other editions, “that is, righteousness.”]

§1. Ecclesiastical history also testifies that when written accusations against bishops had been presented to Emperor Constantine of pious memory, he received the written accusations; then, summoning the bishops who had been accused, he burned in their presence the documents he had received, saying: “You are gods, appointed by the true God. Go and examine your cases among yourselves, because it is not fitting that we judge gods.” Yet by this statement he granted more to himself out of humility than he bestowed upon them by honor rendered. For before him there were pagan rulers in the commonwealth, who, not knowing the true God, worshipped gods of wood and stone, and yet rendered the highest honor to their priests. What wonder, then, if a Christian emperor deigns to honor the priests of the true God, when pagan rulers, as we have said, knew how to render honor to priests who served gods of wood and stone?

[Note: See Sozomen, book 1, chapter 16.]

[Note: “documents of accusation”: omitted in Anselm.]

[Note: “You are … appointed”: omitted in the Basel edition.]

[Note: “examine”: the original, Anselm, and editions cited read “arrange.”]

[Note: “in the commonwealth”: editions cited read “by public law.”]

[Note: Basel adds “the pagans.”]

[Note: “deigns to”: editions cited read “honors.”]

[Note: Editions cited and Anselm add “to them.”]

§2. Therefore, we assert these things not so much particularly as generally on behalf of all priests, because we do not yet know what anyone will be in the dreadful judgment of God. For Paul, the eminent preacher, says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes,” and the rest. For there are many matters concerning his judgment which people do not know: perhaps he will condemn what you praise, and praise what you condemn.

[Note: This passage also occurs in Nicholas’s letter beginning “We had proposed”; but in the original it reads: “Therefore I suggest these things to the piety of my lords, not for myself but for all priests.” After many intervening words not reported here it adds: “For we do not yet know what anyone will be,” and “Paul, the eminent preacher,” etc. It is altogether preferable to read that entire passage, full of apostolic freedom.]

[Note: 1 Corinthians 4:5.]

[Note: “until”: Argentinensis, Norimberga, and Venice I read “as long as”; other editions, “up to the point that.”]

C. XLII. What penalty is imposed on a cleric who drags a cleric before secular courts. Likewise from the Council of Milevis.

An inveterate presumption has opened the way to unlawful audacities to such an extent that clerics drag their fellow clerics, abandoning their own bishop, before public courts. We therefore decree that this is not to be presumed in future. If anyone presumes to do this, having been summoned, he shall both lose his case and be made a stranger to communion.

[Note: Nothing of this kind occurs in the Council of Milevis as extant. Nevertheless it is also cited by Innocent III in chapter *Si diligenti*, *X*, *On Competent Forum*. It is found in the Third Council of Toledo, canon 13.]

[Note: Rather, from the Third Council of Toledo, held A.D. 589.]

[Note: “clerics”: editions cited read “fellow clerics.”]

[Note: Editions cited read: “We decree that this is not to be presumed hereafter.”]

[Note: “Having been summoned”: this word is found in no printed or manuscript copy of the council.]

C. XLIII. A cleric ought not to be judged before a civil judge. Likewise from the Third Council of Carthage, canon 9.

It was decided that if any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or cleric, when an accusation has been brought against him in the Church or a civil case has arisen, wishes, abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, to clear himself before public courts, even if sentence is pronounced in his favor, he shall lose his office. This applies in a criminal action. In a civil action, however, he shall lose what he has won if he has preferred to retain his office; for he judges unjustly concerning fellowship in the Church for the choosing of judges, and, thinking ill of the whole Church, seeks the aid of secular judgment, although the Apostle commands that the causes even of private Christians be brought before the Church and decided there.

[Note: Held A.D. 397; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 362.]

[Note: “brought”: Hispanic Collection reads “instituted.”]

[Note: “pronounced”: editions cited read “issued.”]

[Note: “For”: Other editions of the councils and one Vatican manuscript read: “For if he doubts about choosing judges from the fellowship of the Church, and judges the Church’s fellowship cheap, he who, thinking ill of the whole …” The more recent four-volume edition reads: “For to whom authority to choose judges is open on every side, that person judges himself unworthy of fraternal fellowship …” Much the same occurs in the royal Lucchese manuscript and in canon 18 of the council held at the Palace of Vernis.]

[Note: “private Christians”: 1 Corinthians 6.]

[Note: “decided”: Basel reads “terminated.”]

C. XLIV. A cleric is not to be accused except before an ecclesiastical judge. Likewise from the same source.

If anyone serving in the various orders of the Church incurs a criminal charge and refuses ecclesiastical judgment, he ought to be imperiled.

[Note: This is a summary of the preceding chapter. In councils formerly printed at Cologne and Paris, in two Vatican manuscripts, and in the canonical codex, it stands entirely as a summary; Ivo, part 6, chapter 362, is not much different.]

[Note: This is the rubric of the chapter in Dionysius, canon 15; Ivo, book 1.]

[Col. 0835B] C. XLV. Anyone who has litigation with a cleric should approach his bishop. Likewise Constitution LXXIV, chapter 1.

If anyone has a dispute with a cleric in a monetary matter, let him first approach the bishop under whose judgment the cleric is placed. For that bishop will impose a proper end upon the lawsuit without damage and without delay. But if the bishop is unwilling to settle the dispute, then the hearing of the case shall proceed to a civil judge. Where, however, the bishop wishes to settle the case, everything shall proceed without writing, and a definitive sentence shall be pronounced by him without written documents.

[Note: Julian’s *Epitome of the Novellae*, Constitution 77, chapter 1; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 427; part 16, chapter 150.]

[Note: “That bishop”: Basel reads “to him.”]

[Note: “For”: editions cited and Ivo read “however.”]

[Note: “is unwilling”: Thus also in Julian and Ivo, and so reads the author of the gloss; but Justinian’s Novella itself adds: “or is unable.”]

[Note: “wishes”: Basel reads “shall wish.”]

[Note: Basel adds “any.”]

[Note: “without written documents”: Basel reads “without writing”; Ivo, part 6, “without writings.”]

[Note: “shall be pronounced”: Justinian’s Novella itself continues: “unless perhaps the parties wish it to be entered in writing. But if …” In Ivo, in place of “shall be pronounced” stands “shall be entered,” which creates the suspicion that an intervening passage is lacking through a copyist’s fault.]

[Note: “shall be rendered”: editions cited; “shall be imposed,” Ivo, part 16; “shall be entered,” Ivo, part 6.]

§1. But if litigation arises concerning a criminal cause, the competent judges in that city or in the provinces, having been appealed to, shall impose a conclusion upon the case consistent with the laws, provided nevertheless that the hearing of the suit does not exceed a period of two months, counted from the joinder of issue. Likewise:

[Note: “concerning a criminal”: Justinian’s Novella adds “yet civil.”]

[Note: “in that city or in the provinces”: omitted in the Basel edition and in Ivo.]

[Note: “counted”: What follows as far as the words “Not otherwise” occurs neither in the Novella, nor in Julian or Ivo, nor in the old manuscripts of Gratian; but it has not been removed because of citations by the doctors.]

§2.

[PALEA.]

“In criminal causes, however, proceedings ought never to take place without writing.”

A cleric is not otherwise to be punished unless, having been found liable, he has been stripped by his bishop of the priesthood or of the honor of clerical rank. But if the offense is ecclesiastical, then the examination and punishment of the case shall proceed according to the canons through his bishop, other judges having no participation in such causes.

[Note: “In … ought”: omitted in the Basel edition.]

[Col. 0836B] C. XLVI. A cleric who has a dispute against a cleric must not resort to secular courts. Likewise from the Council of Chalcedon, canon 9.

If a cleric has a dispute against a cleric, he must not abandon his own bishop or resort to secular courts; rather, the matter is first to be heard before his proper bishop. Or certainly, if it is the decision of that bishop, the case is to be heard before arbitrators chosen by both parties. If anyone acts contrary to these provisions, he shall be subject to canonical corrections.

§1. If a cleric has a case against his own bishop or another bishop, it shall be investigated before the hearing of the synod of that province.

§2. But if a bishop or cleric has a controversy against the metropolitan bishop of the same province, he shall proceed to the primate of that diocese, or at least to the see of the imperial city of Constantinople, so that their case may there be investigated.

[Note: Held A.D. 451; Burchard, book 2, chapter 183; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 228, both from Dionysius; Anselm, book 3, chapter 78. In the first part of the canon Anselm follows the old translation, in the remainder the Hispanic translation.]

[Note: “resort”: omitted in the Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: “first”: Hispanic Collection reads “first of all.”]

[Note: “or indeed if it is the judgment of the bishop himself”: Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: “Or certainly if it is …”: The Greek reads: *ēgoun gnōmēi autou tou episkopou, par’ hois an ta amphotera merē bouloito, ta tēs dikēs synkrateisthai*, that is: “or certainly, by the decision of the bishop himself, before those whom both parties may wish, the matters belonging to the judgment are to be heard.” Dionysius translates it not very differently; Burchard, Ivo, and Innocent III, *X*, *On Competent Forum*, chapter 1, cite his translation. The sentence which is elicited here also from the old translation occurs a little later, in the clause “And if a cleric [has a cause] against his own …”; therefore it is not well repeated here, but has not been altered because of the gloss.]

[Note: “corrections”: editions cited read “reproofs.”]

[Note: “of that province”: Hispanic Collection and editions cited read “shall complain.”]

[Note: Hispanic Collection adds “and.”]

[Note: “he shall proceed”: editions cited read “they shall proceed.”]

[Note: “primate of that diocese”: Hispanic Collection and Anselm read “bishops.”]

[Note: “be investigated”: Hispanic Collection reads “be carried out”; editions cited, “be concluded.”]

[Note: Thus in the Basel edition.]

[Col. 0837A] C. XLVII. PALEA. Likewise from the Council of Agde, canon 32.

“No one may presume to summon a cleric before a secular judge without the bishop’s permission. But if he has been summoned, he shall neither answer nor make a claim, nor dare to bring a criminal matter before a secular court.”

[Note: It is absent from most old copies, and is repeated here pointlessly, since precisely the same material occurs above in this same question, chapter “No one [shall summon] a cleric.” The variation in the reading has been noted there.]

[Note: See chapter 17 above.]

[Note: “But”: omitted in the Basel edition.]

Gratian. From all this it is understood that a cleric is not to be brought before public courts either in a civil or in a criminal case, unless perhaps the bishop refuses to decide the civil case, or, in a criminal matter, strips him of the girdle of his rank. §1. But the statement made in Clement’s letter—“God does not wish you to be an examiner of secular affairs”—must be understood with reference to episcopal anointing. For a man is not anointed bishop in order to sit as examiner of secular affairs, but in order to be a guardian of souls and a distributor of spiritual things. Thus he is forbidden to occupy himself with secular affairs, not to remove himself for a time from public life. Or “secular courts” should be understood not as courts concerning secular things, but as courts of secular men. Courts concerning secular things are called secular, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “If therefore you have secular judgments, appoint those who are despised in the Church.” But the courts of secular persons are called secular according to the Apostle’s statement in Clement’s letter, as is understood from what follows when it says: “Let laypersons who have leisure perform for one another those tasks which we have said are less fitting for you.” Clerics, therefore, are prohibited from taking cognizance of the affairs of secular persons, not of secular causes. For the affairs of clerics, whether criminal or civil, are to be examined only before an ecclesiastical judge.

Hence Pope Hadrian, chapter 35:

[Note: Compare Pseudo-Isidorian Letter II of Julius, Letter III of Fabian, and the sole letter of Sixtus; Anselm among Hadrian’s chapters, book 3; Capitularies, book 7, chapter 332.]

C. XLVIII. A cleric is to be heard only in his own forum.

Whether cleric or layperson, if accused of a crime or sued, he shall be summoned and heard nowhere except in his own forum.

[Note: “of a crime”: Basel reads “concerning a crime.”]

C. XLIX. On the same matter. The same, in the same place, chapter 40.

In the case of clerics, this form is to be observed, so that none of them is bound by a judgment delivered by a judge who is not his own.

[Note: Compare Pseudo-Isidorian Letter II of Julius, Letter II of Zephyrinus, and Letter III of Eusebius; Anselm, same place; Capitularies, same place, chapter 347.]

[Note: “this”: Argentinensis, Basel, and Venice I read “of this kind.”]

[Note: “so that none”: editions cited read “that in no way”; [chapter] L.]

[Col. 0838A] Gratian. Moreover, a thing in litigation ought not be transferred to any person at all before the lawful outcome of the investigation.

Hence Pope Gelasius, to Bishop Quingesius:

[Note: “Quingesius”: In old copies this word appears variously as “Quingesius,” “Lucius,” “L.,” or “Quinquagesimus.”]

[Note: A chapter of uncertain date; Collection in Three Parts, part 1, title 46, chapter 24.]

C. L. A thing in litigation is not to be transferred to any person before the outcome of the investigation.

Because a thing in litigation cannot at all be transferred to any person until judicial inquiry has established to whom it is rather due, no one may be allowed to demand payments from that thing. Rather, while the thing remains in the same condition in which it appears to have been previously placed, as stated, whoever thinks that anything may be due to him shall seek a judicial examination, all prejudicial measures concerning it having been removed.

QUESTION II.

[Col. 0838B]

GRATIAN.

That fault is indeed deserving of suspension is plainly evident from that chapter of the Council of Milevis [Note: [Col. 0837] cf. above, epistle I, c. 42.]. For if one who considers that a cleric ought to be dragged before a civil judge is to be deprived of communion, much more is he deserving of suspension who did not hesitate to drag before a secular tribunal one appealing the judgment of his own bishop.

## QUESTION III.

GRATIAN.

Part I. But suppose that this fault was not deserving of suspension. The question is whether one who has dared to perform an office contrary to his bishop’s prohibition ought to be deposed. That a bishop’s sentence, whether just or unjust, must be feared is attested by Gregory in Homily XXVI on the Gospel, who says [Note: [Col. 0837D] The very words of Blessed Gregory are found [Col. 0838D] below in the same question, chapter “Not only,” at the words “whether justly.”] [Note: [Col. 0837] cf. below, c. 77.]:

### C. I. A pastor’s sentence must be feared.

A pastor’s sentence, whether just or unjust, must be feared.

### C. II. A person excommunicated by his own bishop is not to be received by another. Likewise from the Council of Antioch, c. 6 [Note: [Col. 0837] held A.D. 332.—Burchard, bk. 11, c. 37. Ivo, Panormia, bk. 5, c. 101. Decretum, pt. 14, cc. 27 and 101. Deusdedit, pt. 4, all from Dionysius.]

If anyone has been excommunicated by his own bishop, he ought not to be received beforehand by others, unless he has either been received by his own bishop, or, when a council of bishops has been held, he appears before it and answers; and, if he has satisfied the synod, he is to be received under another sentence, as it shall determine. [Note: [Col. 0838D] “Bishops”: In the authorities indicated, only the first part of this canon is reported, and it is from the version of Dionysius, which is also much better throughout this passage: “or certainly,” it says, “let him appear before the synod which is assembled, make satisfaction for himself, and, having persuaded the council, receive another decision.” For the Greek is: πείσας τε τὴν σύνοδον καταδέξοιτο ἑτέραν ἀπόφασιν, “and, having persuaded the synod, let him accept another judgment.”] [Note: [Col. 0837] Omitted in the Hispanic Collection.] This is likewise to be observed concerning laypersons, presbyters, deacons, and all who are in the clergy.

### C. III. One who communicates with excommunicated persons deserves a sentence of excommunication. Likewise Pope Nicholas to King Lothair, in the letter beginning “Having heard” [Note: [Col. 0839B] This chapter is taken from Nicholas’s letter beginning, “Having heard, upon the return of your messenger,” which survives at Rome in the monastery of the Dominicans. It has been reduced, as it were, to an epitome, with many words omitted. Regino, bk. 2 of the *Chronicles*, reports a considerable part of this letter.] [Note: [Col. 0839] written A.D. 867.—Anselm, bk. 3, c. 66 (bk. 12, c. 36).]

Above all, avoid communion with Gualdrada, your concubine, whom you have already long since repudiated; for she has been excommunicated and separated from every association of Christians until she comes into our presence. Therefore you must beware lest you be struck by the same sword of sentence with her and, bound and fettered by passion for one insignificant woman, be drawn into everlasting ruin. [Note: [Col. 0839] *now*: absent from the original.]

For prelates sin more grievously among the people, and are therefore punished more severely than others, as Blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0839] *Pastoral Rule*, pt. 3, c. 4.]: Prelates ought to know that, if they ever commit perverse acts, they deserve as many deaths as they transmit examples of destruction to their subjects. Hence they must guard themselves from fault with so much the greater caution because, through the wrongs they commit, they do not die alone. [Note: [Col. 0839] *more severely*: Basel edition.]

And below:

§ 1. Moreover, take heed lest at any time, according to the Lord’s command [Note: [Col. 0839] Matt. 18.], we bring two or three witnesses against you—or rather, lest we tell it to the holy Church—and lest thereafter, which we do not desire, you become to all as a heathen and a tax collector.

### C. IV. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Sardica, c. 17 [Note: [Col. 0839C] This canon is reported in nearly the same manner in the African Council, c. 101, as far as the words “Yet.” But the Greek Sardican canon, which is no. 14, is somewhat fuller and differs in sense in several places. It has therefore seemed proper to set down the Greek words with a new translation: Ὅσιος ἐπίσκοπος εἶπεν· τὸ δὲ παντοτέ με κινοῦν ἀποσιωπὴσαι οὐκ ὀφείλω. Εἴ τις ἐπίσκοπος ὀξύχολος εὑρίσκοιτο, ὅπερ οὐκ ὀφείλει ἐν τοιούτῳ ἀνδρὶ πολιτεύεσθαι, καὶ ταχέως ἀντικρὺ πρεσβυτέρου ἢ διακόνου κινηθεὶς ἐκβαλεῖν ἐκκλησίας τινὰ ἐθελήσοι, προνοητέον ἐστι μὴ ἀθρόον τὸν τοιοῦτον κατακρίνεσθαι, καὶ τῆς κοινωνίας ἀποστερῆσθαι. Πάντες εἰρήκασιν· Ὁ ἐκβαλλόμενος ἐχέτω ἐξουσίαν ἐπὶ τὸν ἐπίσκοπον τῆς μητροπόλεως τῆς αὐτῆς ἐπαρχίας καταφυγεῖν. Εἰ δὲ ὁ τῆς μητροπόλεως ἀπεστιν, ἐπὶ τὸν πλησιόχωρον κατατρέχειν, καὶ ἀξιοῦν, ἵνα μετὰ ἀκριβείας αὐτοῦ ἐξετάζηται τὸ πρᾶγμα. Οὐ χρὴ γὰρ μὴ ὑπέχειν τὰς ἀκοὰς τοῖς ἀξιοῦσιν. Κἀκεῖνος δὲ ὁ ἐπίσκοπος ὁ δικαίως ἢ ἀδίκως ἐκβαλὼν τὸν τοιοῦτον, γενναίως φέρειν ὀφείλει, ἵνα ἡ ἐξέτασις τοῦ πράγματος γένηται καὶ ἢ κυρωθῇ αὐτοῦ ἡ ἀπόφασις, ἢ διορθώσεως τύχῃ. Πρὶν δὲ ἐπιμελῶς καὶ μετὰ πίστεως ἕκαστα ἐξετασθῇ, ὁ μὴ ἔχων τὴν κοινωνίαν πρὸ τῆς διαγνώσεως τοῦ πράγματος ἑαυτῷ οὐκ ὀφείλει ἐκδικεῖν τὴν κοινωνίαν.

“Osius the bishop said: What continually moves me, I ought not to pass over in silence. If any bishop should prove prone to anger—which ought not to be found in such a man—and, being quickly stirred against a presbyter or deacon, should wish to expel someone from the Church, provision must be made that such a person is not suddenly condemned and deprived of communion. All said: Let the one expelled have authority to take refuge with the bishop of the metropolis of the same province. But if the metropolitan is absent, let him go to a neighboring bishop and request that his case be examined carefully. For it is not right to refuse a hearing to those who ask. And that bishop who has expelled such a person, whether justly or unjustly, ought to bear it generously that the case be examined, and that his decision either be confirmed or corrected. But before every point has been carefully and faithfully examined, the person who lacks communion ought not, before judgment of the case, claim communion for himself as his own right.”] [Note: [Col. 0839] held A.D. 347.—Anselm, bk. 3, c. 71. Ivo, Panormia, bk. 5, c. 127. Decretum, pt. 14, c. 15.]

If a bishop should perhaps be angry—which ought not to be—and should quickly and harshly be moved against his presbyter or deacon and wish to expel him from the Church, provision must be made that an innocent person is not condemned or loses communion. Therefore the person cast out has power to appeal to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard and more carefully considered; for a hearing ought not to be denied to one who asks. [Note: [Col. 0839] *If a bishop*: omitted in Anselm. *is moved*: “is moved” in Anselm and Ivo; the other collected editions agree. *his*: omitted in Anselm. *cast out*: “cast down” in the Hispanic Collection. *considered*: “thoroughly examined” in the collected editions and first Basel edition. *because … asks*: “because to one who asks”: omitted in Anselm. *That bishop*: “But that bishop” in the collected editions.]

And the bishop who cast him out, whether justly or unjustly, should patiently permit the matter to be examined, so that his sentence may either be approved by a majority or amended. Yet before the matter has been carefully and faithfully examined, no other person ought to presume to associate in communion the person separated from communion before the hearing of the case. [Note: [Col. 0839] *or*: omitted in Anselm. *so that*: omitted in the collected editions. *by a majority*: “by more persons” in the Basel edition. *faithfully*: “have been examined” in the Hispanic Collection. *has been*: “had been” in the collected editions. *separated*: “deprived” there. *before the hearing*: omitted in the Hispanic Collection. *other*: “receive and”: added in the Hispanic Collection.]

### C. V. On the same matter. Likewise from the Second Council of Carthage, c. 8 [Note: [Col. 0839] held A.D. 390.—Three-part Collection, pt. 2, title 16, c. 5. Burchard, bk. 2, c. 194. Anselm, bk. 12, c. 33. Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 239. Polycarpus, bk. 7, title 1.]

If any presbyter is rebuked by his bishop, he ought certainly to complain to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard by them and, through them, he may be reconciled to his bishop. [Note: [Col. 0840C] “By his bishop”: In Second Carthage, c. 8, when Alypius proposes the matter, it reads: “If some presbyter should be rebuked by his own bishop, or excommunicated,” etc. But when the canon is enacted by all the bishops, the term *bishop* is replaced by *superior*, and thus it reads in the Carthaginian code of canons, c. 11: “rebuked by his superior.” The Greek is: ἐν τῇ διαγωγῇ αὐτοῦ καταγνώσθῃ, that is, “he should be found blameworthy in his conduct of life.” But Burchard and Ivo agree with Gratian.] If he does not do this but, swollen with pride—which God forbid—decides to separate himself from the communion of his bishop and, creating a schism with certain others, offers sacrifice to God separately, let him be anathematized and lose his office. [Note: [Col. 0839] *rebuked*: “corrected” in the collected editions. [Col. 0841] *that is*: Basel edition. *let him be anathematized and nevertheless lose his office*: collected editions. *lose his office*: “with the office lost” in the Hispanic Collection.]

But if he has a just complaint against the bishop, it must be investigated. [Note: [Col. 0841C] “But if”: In the code of canons, the Greek Carthaginian text, and the collectors, nothing is inserted here. Yet in printed and manuscript copies of the council the following is inserted before this clause: “Nevertheless, let him also be removed farther from the city and congregation in which he was, lest he deceive either the ignorant or the simple-living by serpentine fraud; for, according to the Apostle, there is one Church, one faith, one baptism. And if he has a complaint,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0841] *and*: there.] [Note: [Col. 0841C] “But if he has a complaint”: Burchard and Ivo have the passage thus: “If he does not have a just complaint against the bishop, it must be investigated.” The Greek is: σκοπουμένου, μήποτε κατὰ τοῦ ἐπισκόπου μέμψιν ἔχοι δικαίαν, that is, “this being considered: whether perhaps he has a just complaint against the bishop.”]

### C. VI. On those condemned by a synod who perform sacred ministries. Likewise from the Council of Antioch, c. 4 [Note: [Col. 0841] held A.D. 332.—Dionysian translation.—Anselm, bk. 12, c. 26. Burchard, bk. 1, c. 199.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 8, c. 362, from Isidore.]

If any bishop condemned by a synod, or any presbyter or deacon by his own bishop, should dare to undertake anything of the sacred ministry—whether a bishop according to the preceding custom, or a presbyter or deacon—he must in no way be allowed either to have hope of restoration in another synod or to have an opportunity to make satisfaction. Moreover, all who communicate with him must be cast out of the Church, especially if, after learning that sentence had been pronounced against those mentioned, they attempt to communicate with them. [Note: [Col. 0841] *If any*: omitted in the Basel edition. *condemned*: Greek καθαιρεθείς, “deposed.” *is condemned*: collected editions. *or if*: same. *and daring*: same.]

### C. VII. Whoever presumes to communicate with excommunicated persons is without hope of reconciliation. Likewise from the Council of Pope Martin, c. 37 [Note: [Col. 0841] The same chapter, from the translation of Martin of Braga.]

If any bishop has been excommunicated in a council, or any presbyter or deacon by his own bishop, and after excommunication that bishop, presbyter, or deacon presumes to make an offering or to perform the morning or evening sacrifice, as though in his office, as before, he must not be allowed either to have hope of reconciliation in another council or ever to be restored. Moreover, all who communicate with him are to be rejected from the Church, especially those who knew that he had been deposed. [Note: [Col. 0841] *by his own bishop*: omitted in the Hispanic Collection. *restored*: “reconciled” in the collected editions.]

But if he persists in disturbing and stirring up the Church through external authority, he must be expelled from all the people as a seditious person. [Note: [Col. 0841C] “External”: in some manuscripts of Gratian and of the council, *forasticam*, “foreign.” In canon 5 of the Council of Antioch, from which this is taken, it reads: διὰ τῆς ἔξωθεν ἐξουσίας, “through outside authority,” which Dionysius translates *per potestates exteras*, “through foreign powers.”] [Note: [Col. 0841] *foreign*: Hispanic Collection.]

### C. VIII. On bishops who excommunicate innocent persons or persons guilty of very slight offenses. Likewise from the Council of Agde, c. 3 [Note: [Col. 0841] held A.D. 506.—Burchard, bk. 11, c. 11. Ivo, Panormia, bk. 5, c. 128; *Decretum*, pt. 14, cc. 16 and 81.]

If bishops, setting aside priestly moderation, presume to excommunicate innocent persons or persons guilty of very slight offenses, or perhaps refuse to receive those hastening to the grace of baptism, they are to be admonished by letters from neighboring bishops of the same province; and, if they refuse to comply, communion is to be denied them by the remaining bishops until the time of the synod, lest the excommunicated, because of the sin of the excommunicator, be overtaken by death after a long time. [Note: [Col. 0842C] “Baptism”: This is also found in the manuscripts, and scholars acknowledge the word. But in all editions of the councils [Col. 0841] and in the Hispanic Collection, as well as in two Vatican manuscripts, both in the Council of Agde and in the Council of Worms, c. 14, where this chapter is repeated, and in Burchard and Ivo, the expression is absent. Since the passage concerns excommunicated persons, it seems applicable only to those who have been baptized and hasten to “grace,” that is, reconciliation, with their bishop.] [Note: [Col. 0841] *neighboring*: “fellow-neighboring” in the Basel edition. *of any*: Hispanic Collection. *are to be admonished*: “are to be moved” in the Basel and second Venice editions. *comply*: “spare” in Burchard and Ivo, c. 81. *is to be denied*: Ivo, the *Panormia*, earlier editions of the councils, and two Vatican copies have this reading, and it seems similar to that above, 6, question 2, final chapter; but more recent editions read “is not to be denied” [Col. 0841] and the Hispanic Collection. The collected editions read “is to be denied.” *because of*: “through” in the collected editions. *of the excommunication*: “of the excommunicator” in the Hispanic Collection; “in that of the excommunicator” in Burchard and Ivo, c. 81. *be overtaken*: singular in those sources.]

### C. IX. On those who presume to communicate during their excommunication. Likewise from the African Council [Note: [Col. 0842C] This chapter is not found in the council now entitled African; but it is included in the Carthaginian council in the code of canons, and in the Greek as c. 29, and is reported in the Fifth Synod, session 7, in Vigilius’s letter.] [Note: [Col. 0841] c. 29, in Dionysius, from the Council of Carthage held A.D. 409.—Burchard, bk. 1, c. 200. Anselm, bk. 12, c. 27 (29). Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, c. 314. Polycarpus, bk. 7, title 1.]

It pleased the whole council that anyone excommunicated for his own negligence—whether bishop or any cleric—who presumes to communicate during the time of his excommunication before a hearing, is to be judged to have pronounced upon himself a sentence of condemnation. [Note: [Col. 0841] *to communicate*: “communion” in the original.]

### C. X. Bishops who communicate with excommunicated persons are to be deposed. Likewise Pope Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0842D] Ivo cites this chapter from Nicholas “to bishops and archbishops established throughout Gaul, Italy, Germany, and all the provinces.” In that letter Nicholas seems to have reported what had been decreed at a Roman council held by him: namely, that the Synod of Metz was to be wholly abolished and that Theutgaud and Gunther were to be deposed. Regino, bk. 4 of the *Chronicles*, writes accurately of that council and the deposition of these bishops: “Meanwhile, the archbishops Theutgaud and Gunther set out for Rome, intending to show that the king was innocent in the aforementioned affair and that they, together with their fellow bishops, had carried out ecclesiastical and apostolic decrees. They deserved indeed the epithet of folly, for they believed that they could deceive the see of Peter by some perverse doctrine—a see which neither deceived itself nor could ever be deceived by any heresy. When they had come into the presence of Pope Nicholas, they presented a document containing the synodal acts which they had established in the city of Metz and at Aachen. When it had been read by a notary before all, the pontiff asked whether they confirmed the writings by their words. They answered that it seemed improper for them to prefer to weaken by words what they had confirmed by their own hands. Thus, without their assertion either being rejected or admitted, they were ordered to go to their lodgings until recalled. A few days later they were summoned to the synod which the pope had convened. There their writings were condemned and anathematized, and they themselves were deposed by the judgment of all the bishops, presbyters, and deacons, and deprived of every ecclesiastical dignity.”] [Note: [Col. 0841] at the Roman synod held A.D. 863.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 8, c. 226.]

We judge Theutgaud, archbishop of Trier and primate of the Belgic province, and Gunther, archbishop of Cologne Agrippina, who now before us and the holy synod, under presentation of the records, have offered a writing concerning how they investigated and judged the cause of King Lothair and his two women, namely Theutberga and Gualdrada—a writing confirmed by their own hands—and have, before many persons present, affirmed in their own words that they did nothing more, less, or otherwise; and who have confessed publicly and orally that they violated the sentence which our most holy brother Thado, archbishop of Milan, and our other fellow bishops had requested the Apostolic See to pronounce against Engeltrude, wife of Boso, and which we, inflamed with divine zeal, had canonically pronounced under the attestation of anathema. In all these things we have found that they have transgressed apostolic and canonical sanctions in many respects and wickedly violated the rule of equity. We therefore judge them to remain wholly excluded from every priestly office, determining that they stand deprived of the governance of the episcopate by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and the authority of Blessed Peter exercised through us. [Note: [Col. 0841] *Teuguald*: “Theutgaud” in the original and Böhm. *and*: omitted in the original. *Theutberga*: “Theitberga” in the original and Böhm.] [Note: [Col. 0843] *records*: “representations” in the Basel edition. *nothing*: “and nothing” in Böhm. *before many persons present*: “witnesses” added in the collected editions, first Basel edition, and Böhm. *living*: “one” in Ivo. *holy*: “And therefore, holy” in the original and collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 0844C] “To remain”: In chapter 2 of the council the passage reads: “to remain; determining that if, according to the preceding custom, they should dare, as bishops, to undertake anything of the sacred ministry, they are in no way to be permitted either to have hope of restoration in another synod or an opportunity for satisfaction. Moreover, all who communicate with them are to be expelled from the Church, especially if, after learning that sentence had been pronounced against those mentioned, they attempt to communicate with them.” These words are taken from the chapter “If any bishop condemned,” above in the same question, from the Council of Antioch.] [Note: [Col. 0843] *defining*: “we define” in the original.]

To those deposed we grant leave to enter the church, communicate as laypersons, and state what is useful to them; but we do not grant them leave to stir up disturbances or provoke scandal. So far as the episcopal ministry specifically pertains, they are to have no permission to undertake it, as it is evident that we, with the holy synod, have already decreed. [Note: [Col. 0843] *specifically*: “special” in the Basel edition.]

### C. XI. Clerics and laypersons who do not obey bishops become infamous. Likewise Clement, Epistle III, to all fellow bishops [Note: [Col. 0843] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.]

But if all presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and other clerics, and all rulers both of the higher and lower rank, and the remaining people, do not obey you bishops, they shall be not only infamous but also exiled from the kingdom of God and the fellowship of the faithful, and alienated from the thresholds of the holy Church of God. [Note: [Col. 0843] *you*: “us” in the Basel edition. *deacons and subdeacons*: omitted in the Basel edition. *and the remaining people*: omitted there.]

### C. XII. One who grieves the teacher of truth sins against Christ. Likewise Peter, in the ordination of Clement [Note: [Col. 0843] From Clement I, translated into Latin by Rufinus.]

Whoever grieves the teacher of truth sins against Christ and provokes God, the Father of all; for this reason he shall also lose life.

### C. XIII. Obedience is not to be withheld from a bishop under a pretended zeal for virtues. Likewise Ambrose, bk. II, *On Duties*, c. 24:

But if anyone does not obey the bishop, desiring to exalt and elevate himself, and also seeking to overshadow the bishop’s merits by a pretended zeal for learning, humility, or mercy, such a person, wandering from truth, is proud. For this is the rule of truth: do nothing for the sake of commending yourself by which another person becomes less; nor, if you possess anything good, exercise it to the disfigurement and reproach of another. [Note: [Col. 0843] *nor*: “ne” in the Basel edition. *good*: “work” added in the collected editions. *and*: “or to” in the Basel edition.]

§ 1. Do not defend a wicked person, and do not think that holy things are to be entrusted to the unworthy. [Note: [Col. 0843] *or to*: Basel edition. *are to be*: omitted in the original.]

§ 2. Nor again accuse and attack one whose crime you have not discovered. [Note: [Col. 0843] *accuse*: “press” in the original.]

### C. XIV. One who does not obey a bishop is torn apart by the mouths of demons. Likewise Pope Anterus to the Bishops of Spain [Note: [Col. 0843] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Jerome’s letter to Heliodorus.]

Far be it from us to think anything sinister concerning those who, succeeding to the apostolic rank, make Christ’s body with their sacred mouth; through whom we too are Christians, and who, possessing the keys of the kingdom of heaven, judge before the day of judgment. Under the old law [Note: [Col. 0843] “In the old [law]”: collected editions; cf. Deut. 17.] anyone who did not obey the priests was either stoned by the people of God when placed outside the camp, or, with his neck submitted to the sword, expiated his contempt with blood. Now, however, the disobedient person is cut off by spiritual punishment and, cast out of the Church, is torn apart by the savage mouth of demons. [Note: [Col. 0843] *God*: added in the Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0845] *cast out*: “but cast out” in the second and third Lyons editions; “or cast out” in the rest. *from*: “out of” in the collected editions. *torn apart*: “plucked apart” in the collected editions and first Lyons, second and third Lyons editions.]

### C. XV. We must not even speak with those to whom the pope is hostile. Likewise Peter, in the ordination of Clement [Note: [Col. 0845] cf. Distinction 93, c. 1.]

If this Clement is hostile to anyone because of that person’s acts, do not wait for him to tell you, etc., as above in the treatise on ordinations, where the obedience of inferiors toward superiors is discussed.

### C. XVI. One who communicates with excommunicated persons is excommunicated. Likewise Bishop Fabian, Epistle I [Note: [Col. 0845] Cf. Apostolic Canon 11.—Regino, bk. 2, c. 398. Burchard, bk. 11, c. 35. Anselm, bk. 12, c. 19. Ivo, Panormia, bk. 5, c. 95.]

As the apostles decreed, saying: “There must be no communion with excommunicated persons.” And if anyone, knowingly disregarding the rules, merely speaks with or prays together with excommunicated persons in a house, he is to be deprived of communion. [Note: [Col. 0845] *disregarding*: “turning away from” in Anselm and the collected editions, first and second/third Lyons editions. *merely*: In Fabian’s letter it reads: “knowingly sings psalms in a house, or speaks together,” etc. But Gratian’s reading seems to agree better with the Apostolic Canon: εἴ τις ἀκοινωνήτῳ κἂν ἐν οἴκῳ συνεύξηται, οὗτος ἀφοριζέσθω, “If anyone so much as prays together in a house with an excommunicated person, let him be excluded.” Dionysius translates: “If anyone should pray together, even in a house, with an excommunicated person, that person is to be deprived of communion.”] [Note: [Col. 0845] *in*: “in one” added in Anselm.]

### C. XVII. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Calixtus, Epistle II, c. 2 [Note: [Col. 0845] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Apostolic Canon 11.—Burchard, bk. 11, c. 38. Anselm, bk. 12, c. 14 (13). Ivo, Panormia, bk. 5, c. 94; *Decretum*, pt. 14, cc. 23 and 102. Polycarpus, bk. 7, title 1.]

No one is to receive or reject any persons excommunicated by priests before the just examination of both parties; nor is anyone to communicate with them in prayer, food, drink, or a kiss, nor say “Hail” to them. For whoever knowingly communicates with excommunicated persons in these or other prohibited ways shall himself be subject to a like excommunication according to the institution of the apostles. [Note: [Col. 0845] *or reject*: supplied in the text. *or*: Basel edition. *communicate*: plural, and “shall be subject,” in the Nuremberg, first and second Venice, Lyons, and Paris editions. *shall be subject*: “be subject” in Ivo, c. 102, and Burchard.]

### C. XVIII. On the same matter. Likewise Isidore, *Rule for Monks*, c. 18 [Note: [Col. 0845C] The first part of this chapter, through the words “For if anyone,” is found in the Rule of St Isidore—which was sent from Spain—c. 18, from which Smaragdus cites it in his exposition of the Rule of St Benedict, c. 26, except for the clause “unless [matters] belonging to the same excommunication,” which is found neither in Blessed Isidore’s Rule nor in Smaragdus. It is, however, found in Burchard and Ivo.] [Note: [Col. 0845] Regino, bk. 2, cc. 392–393. Burchard, bk. 11, cc. 31–32. Three-part Collection, pt. 2, title 14, cc. 27–28. Anselm, bk. 12, c. 16. Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 14, cc. 95–96. Polycarpus, bk. 7, title 1.—For the second part of the chapter cf. below, the corrective note to c. 28, in the same question.]

It is not permitted to pray, speak—except concerning matters that pertain to that same excommunication—or eat with an excommunicated person. For if anyone has spoken with him openly or secretly, he immediately incurs with him the common penalty of excommunication. [Note: [Col. 0845] *is permitted*: “is permitted” in the collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 0845D] “For if anyone”: Smaragdus reports this to the end [Col. 0846C] from a certain teacher of monks, as will be noted below in the same question, chapter “If any brother.”]

### C. XIX. On the same matter. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 73 [Note: [Col. 0845] c. 40, *Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua*; cf. on c. 9, Distinction 18.—Burchard, bk. 11, c. 44. Anselm, bk. 12, c. 18. Ivo, Panormia, bk. 5, c. 99; *Decretum*, pt. 14, cc. 28 and 108. Polycarpus, same place.]

Whoever communicates or prays with an excommunicated person is, if a layperson, to be excommunicated; if a cleric, to be deposed. [Note: [Col. 0846C] “If a layperson”: Thus in Burchard [Col. 0845] and Anselm, and Ivo, pt. 14, c. 108, and in the *Panormia*. But in the council itself, collated with various manuscripts [Col. 0845] and the Hispanic Collection, and in Ivo in the same part, c. 28, it reads: “whether cleric or layperson, let him be excommunicated.”]

### C. XX. The names of excommunicated persons are to be announced openly and publicly to all neighboring persons. Likewise from the decree of Pope Honorius [Note: [Col. 0846C] Burchard, Anselm, and Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 14, c. 113, likewise cite this from the decrees of Honorius; but Ivo himself, in the same part, c. 65, attributes precisely this to John VIII at the Council of Ravenna.] [Note: [Col. 0845] c. 10, Council of Ravenna held A.D. 877.—Burchard, bk. 11, c. 49. Anselm, bk. 12, c. 32. Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 14, cc. 65 and 113.]

Let it be a concern to all bishops to make known the names of all excommunicated persons both to neighboring bishops and equally to their own parishioners, and, having placed those names in a conspicuous spot before the doors of the church, to impress them upon all who gather, so that by this twofold diligence ecclesiastical access may everywhere be denied to excommunicated persons, and every ground of excuse may be removed from all. [Note: [Col. 0845] *all*: omitted in Burchard. *access*: “hearing” in Burchard and the Nuremberg edition.]

Part II. Gratian. But this is to be understood of those excommunicated by name. For we undergo the penalty of excommunication in two ways: both when we incur guilt and when we are marked by a sentence.

Hence Jerome, in Homily II on the Book of Judges [Note: [Col. 0846C] Blessed Jerome is cited in this and the following chapter because he made these homilies of Origen into Latin, as has also been noted above, Distinction 36, c. “If anyone.”] [Note: [Col. 0845] Rather, Origen, Homily 2 on Judges, c. 2.]:

### C. XXI. A person is delivered to Satan in two ways.

Hear at last the Apostle speaking of one who had sinned: “I have delivered such a man,” he says, “to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved.” [Note: [Col. 0845] 1 Cor. 5:5.] You see, therefore, that God has delivered offenders into the hands of enemies not only through his apostles, but that sinners are also delivered through those who preside over the Church and possess power not only to loose but also to bind: when, on account of their offenses, they are separated from the body of Christ.

And, as it seems to me, people are even now delivered from the Church into the power of Zabul [the Devil] in two ways. In one way, as we said above, when their offense is manifest to the Church and they are expelled from the Church through priests, so that, marked out before all, they may be ashamed and may experience the converse of what follows: “that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0847] *not only now*: the collected editions. *are delivered*: “but are delivered” there. *Zabul*: “the Devil” in the Argentinensis, Nuremberg, first and second Venice editions. *In one*: “In this” in the collected editions. *through priests*: “through a priest” there. *conversely*: “in the converse” in the second Lyons edition. *may experience*: “may happen to him” in the collected editions. *that*: 1 Cor. 5:5.]

But in another way someone is delivered to Zabul when his sin is not manifest to human beings, but God, who sees in secret, perceives that his mind and soul serve vices and passions, and that in his heart God is not loved, but greed, lust, boastfulness, or other such things are loved. The Lord himself delivers such a man to Satan. [Note: [Col. 0847] *is delivered*: “has been delivered” in the collected editions. *Zabul*: “the Devil” in the second Venice edition. *is not*: “is” in the collected editions. *in secret*: “in the hidden place” there. *mind and soul*: “minds … serving” in the Basel edition; “mind” in the others. *delivers*: “has delivered” in the collected editions, first and second/third Lyons editions.]

How does he deliver him to Satan? He withdraws from that person’s mind, turns away, flees from his evil thoughts and unworthy desires, and leaves the house of his heart empty.
