[Note: [Col. 0847] *then*: added in the Basel and second Venice, Lyons, and Paris editions. *does deliver*: “has delivered” in the Argentinensis, Nuremberg, first and second Venice, first Lyons, and Paris editions.]

Gratian. Therefore, when anyone has been designated by a sentence, we ought not to communicate with him. But when, through guilt alone, he has secretly incurred the penalty of excommunication, we are not to withdraw from his communion. Thus the Lord [Note: [Col. 0847] cf. Matt. 18.] said in the Gospel that a sinner is to be regarded as a heathen and a tax collector only when he has despised hearing the Church. Likewise, the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0847] 1 Cor. 5.] does not say, “If any brother is a fornicator,” but “if any brother is named a fornicator,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0847] cf. c. 24 below.]—understanding designation by a sentence. Hence also Pope Urban II to Bishop Guitmund: “Indeed, concerning Richard …”; look under the case: “A certain bishop fell into heresy.” [Note: [Col. 0847] “Vilimund”: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, first Venice edition; “Guilimund”: the remaining editions.] Hence also Christ in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0847] Matt. 13.] said that tares must be tolerated until the harvest.

Hence also Jerome [Note: [Col. 0847] Rather, Origen, Homily 21 on Joshua, c. 15.]:

### C. XXII. The evil cannot be wholly separated from the good.

Do not depart from the Lord on this present day, that is, so long as the age endures. Let him show me, then, how the Jebusite dwells with the children of Judah in Jerusalem so long as the age endures, when not even the children of Judah themselves dwell in Jerusalem. [Col. 0848A] Therefore neither can this be true, that the Jebusites dwell with the Jews in Jerusalem, since they themselves do not dwell there. But let us understand these things spiritually, taking up the Gospel parable concerning the tares: “Let both grow together, lest perhaps, while you wish to root out the tares, you root up the wheat together with them.” And below:

§ 1. Hear, then, Scripture saying that the children of Judah were unable to destroy the Jebusites, but dwelt with them in Jerusalem unto this present day. Therefore I beseech you who are faithful to guard your life and conduct in such a way that you neither suffer scandal yourselves in any respect nor cause scandal to others. Let it be the object of your greatest concern and utmost caution that no defiled person enter this holy congregation of yours, and that no Jebusite dwell with you. You see, then, that Scripture says that the children of Judah could not cast the Jebusites out of Jerusalem. Now “Jebusite” is interpreted as “trampling.” Therefore, since we cannot cast out those who trample us, let us at least cast out those whom we can—those whose sins are manifest. For where sin is not evident, we cannot cast anyone out of the Church, lest perhaps, in rooting out the tares, we root up the wheat together with them. Yet I am struck by what it said: that they could not cast out the Jebusites, that is, those whose name is interpreted “trampling.” Let us therefore see who they are in the Church that trample. Without doubt, they are those of whom the Lord says in the Gospels: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine, lest perhaps they trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you to pieces.” This Jebusite, therefore—that is, “trampling”—is the person who hears the word of God unworthily and, having heard it, neither departs as an unbeliever nor remains as a believer; rather, having acquired knowledge of the mysteries and searched into the more secret matters of our faith, he subsequently turns and attacks us, tearing our hearts by his contradictions, trampling the pearls of the Lord’s word and defiling the ornaments of faith. Of these, therefore, it is said that the children of Judah could not cast the Jebusite out of Jerusalem unto this present day.

[Apparatus: *hodierno die* (“on the present day”) has *hodiernum diem* (“the present day”) in the collected editions. *Hiebusaeus* has *Hierusalem* in the Basel edition; *filii Juda* has *Israel et Juda* there; *ideo ergo* is absent there; *habitent* has *habitabant* (“were dwelling”) there; and *quandoquidem* has *quoniam* (“since”) there, while the other editions read *quando* (“when”). In the parable, *quum vultis* has *volentes* (“wishing”) in the collected editions; compare Matthew 13:29. *Potuerunt* has *poterant* (“were able”) in Basel and *poterunt* (“will be able”) in Lyons II. *Aliis* has *alii* in Basel. *Sanctam congregationem vestram* has *sanctorum* (“of saints”) in the collected editions, and *vobiscum* has *in vobis* (“within you”) there. *Vides ergo* has *enim* (“for”); *potuerunt* has *potuerint*; and *filii Juda* has *Israel vel Juda*, all in Basel. *Ergo* has *Esto ergo* (“Be it so, therefore”) in the collected editions; *qui sunt* has *sint*; *dicit* has *dicebat* (“was saying”) in the collected editions and in Argentinian, Norimbergian, and Venice I; compare Matthew 7. *Elidant* has *dirumpant* (“tear apart”). *Hiebusaeus* is supplemented by *id est* (“that is”). *Indigni* has *indigne* (“unworthily”); *mysteriorum* has *ministeriorum* (“ministries”) in Basel, Norimberg, and Venice II; and *scrutatis* has *perscrutatis* (“having thoroughly searched”) in the collected editions.]

[Col. 0849A]

### Chapter XXIII. Holy things are not to be entrusted to swine and dogs.

Likewise, the same author on the Twelve Prophets. [Commentary on Amos 5:12.]

Therefore, when an ecclesiastical man, prudent and discerning, learns that there are many impieties in that which is called the house of God—not merely many, but powerful ones, capable of oppressing justice—and that the frenzy of teachers has advanced so far that they receive a price in judgment, do everything for gifts, shun even the poor in the gates, and disdain to hear them, let him be silent at that time, lest he give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine, who, turning, may trample them. Let him imitate Jeremiah, who says: “I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness,” and that saying in the Psalm: “I am solitary, until I pass by.”

[Apparatus: The reference is Commentary on Amos 5:12. *Pretium* (“price”) has *praemium* (“reward”) in Basel; *ne det* lacks *det* in that edition. Compare Matthew 7. Jeremiah 15:17 has *eram* (“I was”) for *sum* (“I am”) in the collected editions. The Psalm reference is Psalm 49.]

### Chapter XXIV. One may eat with a pagan, but by no means with an excommunicated person.

Likewise John Chrysostom, Homily XXV on chapter 11 of the Epistle to the Hebrews.

If you wish to go to the table of pagans, we permit it without any prohibition. And below:

§ 1. “For if anyone,” he says, “is named among you as a brother.” Understand “brother” here simply as every believer, not merely a monk. What, moreover, produces brotherhood except the washing of regeneration, which makes it possible to call God Father?

And below:

§ 2. “If anyone,” he says, “who is named a brother, is a fornicator, or greedy, or a drunkard, do not even take food with such a person.” But when he spoke about pagans, he did not say this; rather: “If one of the unbelievers invites you”—meaning pagans—“and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you.” “If anyone who is named a brother is a drunkard,” and so forth. O what exactness! Yet we not only do not avoid drunkards, but even go to them and share with them.

[Editorial apparatus: *volueris* is the reading of the collected editions. The citation is 1 Corinthians 5:11; *non* is absent in Basel. *Facit* has *vocat* (“calls”) in the collected editions, and Basel adds *omnipotentem* (“almighty”) after “God.” The editions of Basel, Paris, and Lyons add *debetis* (“you ought”) after “do not even take food.” The following citation is 1 Corinthians 10:27.]

[Col. 0849C–0850C. Gratian thought that Chrysostom interpreted this expression in nearly the same manner as Augustine interpreted it above, 2, question 1, chapter *Multi*. The complete passage in Greek reads (the source then gives an editorial Latin translation—introduced “That is”—of the same passage):

“And are you not even afraid of Paul? He permits us, if we wish, to go without hindrance to the table of Greeks, but does not allow us, even if we wish, to go to the tables of the greedy and those who take what belongs to others. For, he says, ‘If anyone who is called a brother’—here calling every believer simply a brother, not merely a monk. For what makes brotherhood? The washing of rebirth, the ability to call God Father. Thus the catechumen, even if he is a monk, is not a brother; but the believer, even if he is a layman, is a brother. ‘If anyone,’ he says, ‘is called a brother.’ For at that time there was not even a trace of monasticism; this blessed man spoke wholly to laypeople: ‘If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or a drunkard, do not even eat with such a one.’ But he does not speak in this way concerning Greeks; rather, ‘If one of the unbelievers’—meaning Greeks—‘invites you, and you wish to go, eat everything set before you.’ ‘If anyone who is called a brother is a drunkard.’ What astonishing exactness! But we not only do not avoid drunkards; we even go to them, intending to partake of what comes from them.”]

Gratian. It is therefore clear from the foregoing that we are not compelled to avoid the communion of those who have not been marked by a sentence. But being marked by a sentence is understood in several ways.

§ 1. Sometimes someone is excluded from the thresholds of the Church and from communion in Christ’s body and blood either by the testimony of conscience, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup; for he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself”; likewise, according to Prosper: “They will more easily make God favorable to themselves,” etc.—look below, Cause XXXIII, question 1, concerning penance, “Prevented by magical arts”—or by an ecclesiastical sentence, as in the case of penitents, to whom the benefit of reconciliation is granted after a fixed time. This sentence is called excommunication because it forbids one marked by it communion in Christ’s body and blood, just as Adam was excommunicated from eating the tree of life, when the Lord said: “See lest perhaps they take from the tree of life.” By this sentence a person is not separated from the fellowship of the faithful.

There is also another sentence, called anathema, by which a person is separated from the fellowship of the faithful; concerning it it was said above: “Do not communicate with the excommunicated.”

§ 2. Anyone may observe this distinction from the authority of Pope John: “Engeltruda, wife of Boso,” etc.; look above, under the Cause: “A certain bishop deposed from his own see.” Likewise, from the authority of the same pope: “If anyone has violated the house of God,” etc.; look below, Cause XVII, “A certain priest burdened with infirmity.” Likewise, from the authority of Pope Sylvester: “By the present decree we determine,” etc.; look above, under the Cause: “Concerning the ill repute of a certain bishop.”

§ 3. Accordingly, in light of this distinction, the authority of Pope Innocent II—“If anyone, at the devil’s instigation,” etc.—is to be understood, as below in the Cause: “A certain priest”: namely, that, according to the etymology of the word *anathema*, that is, “separation,” the person who incurs that edict is subject to it—the person who makes himself alien to Christ’s body and blood and to entrance into the Church by daring to lay impious hands upon a cleric. Nor can he be absolved by any bishop, that is, reconciled in the manner of penitents, unless he first takes care to present himself before the Apostolic See.

§ 4. But Peter of Clement’s statement—“If this Clement is an enemy,” etc.—must be understood of persons marked by a sentence; likewise Urban’s statement, “Those with whom bishops do not communicate,” etc., as below in the same Cause. Otherwise the statement of the Second Council of Vaison would be false: “If a bishop knows himself conscious only of another’s crime.” Likewise also: “It has pleased us that, if at any time a bishop,” etc.; look above, under the Cause: “Two fornicators and persons marked by infamy.”

[References: Prosper, Distinction 1, chapter 32, on penance. For the examples, Cause 3, question 4, final chapter; Cause 17, question 4, chapter 21; Cause 5, question 2, chapter 2; Cause 17, question 4, chapter 29; Distinction 93, chapter 1; below, chapter 27; and Cause 6, question 2, chapters 2 and 3.]

### Chapter XXV. It is not lawful to communicate with those who communicate with excommunicated persons.

Likewise Gregory to the clergy and people of Salona.

[Editorial note: In the register of St. Gregory, book 5, chapter 148, these words occur in Epistle 48, written to the clergy, nobles, and people living at Jadera, alternatively called Jadertinum.]

[Epistle to the clergy and people of Jadera, Epistle 27, written A.D. 596, book 6, Maurist edition.]

I beg, exhort, and warn you that you wholly abstain from participation in forbidden communion, lest any one of you presume, against his own soul, to communicate with any priest who communicates with the aforementioned Maximus.

### Chapter XXVI. No cleric or layperson is to approach the house of an excommunicated person.

Likewise, from the First Council of Toledo, chapter 15.

[Held A.D. 400.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 30.]

If any layperson is barred from communion, no cleric or religious person shall approach him or his house. Likewise, if a cleric is barred, he is to be avoided by clerics. If anyone is discovered to have conversed or dined with him, he too shall be barred. But this applies to those clerics who belong to the same bishop and to all who have been warned concerning the person who is barred, whether he is any layperson or a cleric.

Part III. Gratian. But this applies especially to those who communicate with persons expressly named as excommunicated. Hence Urban: “Indeed, concerning Richard,” etc., below in the Cause: “A certain bishop who fell into heresy.” Likewise Pope Nicholas in the chapter “The most excellent King Charles,” etc., below, near the end of this Cause.

[Apparatus: *Si quis* has *Quisquis* (“whoever”) in the Spanish Collection; *devitetur* has *evitetur* (“let him be avoided”); and the collected editions add *vero* (“indeed”). The later cross-reference is below, chapter 102.]

### Chapter XXVII. The sentence of a pastor is to be feared, even if it binds unjustly.

Likewise Urban to all bishops, chapter 5.

[A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Clement I and Gregory the Great, Homily 26.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 145 (150), book 12, chapter 25; Burchard, book 11, chapter 1; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 74; *Polycarpus*, book 6, title 1.]

Do not communicate with those with whom bishops do not communicate, and do not receive those whom they have cast out. For the sentence of a bishop is greatly to be feared, even if it binds unjustly.

### Chapter XXVIII. Whoever communicates with excommunicated persons incurs the penalty of excommunication.

Likewise, from the Eighth Synod.

[Editorial note: This canon is found neither in the Eighth Synod held in the time of Nicholas I nor in the other synod also called the Eighth, celebrated under John VIII, both of which are preserved in the Vatican Library. Many passages cited by Gratian from the Eighth Synod are found in the rules of Basil, Isidore, and other writings concerning monks. This passage, above under the same heading, “With an excommunicated person,” was attributed to Isidore, as also by Burchard and Ivo. But Smaragdus, in his exposition of the Rule of St. Benedict, chapter 26, having previously discussed a monk excommunicated by his superior, writes words very similar to these: “Hence a certain teacher of monks says: If any brother, openly or secretly, has spoken with him or been joined to him, he incurs with him the common penalty of excommunication.” This reading agrees with that of Burchard and Ivo.]

[Compare above, chapter 18.]

If any brother has openly or secretly spoken with an excommunicated person, or joined him in communion, he immediately incurs with him the penalty of excommunication.

[Apparatus: *Junctus communione* has *conjunctus* (“joined”) in Basel.]

### Chapter XXIX. On the same matter.

Likewise, from the Second Council of Carthage, chapter 7.

[Held A.D. 390.—Burchard, book 11, chapter 43; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 98; *Decretum*, part 14, chapters 28 and 107; *Polycarpus*, book 7, title 1.]

Those who have been driven from the Church on account of their crimes, if they are received into communion by any bishop, priest, or cleric, the receiver himself shall likewise be held liable for the same offense together with them, as one fleeing the regular judgment of his own bishop.

[Apparatus: “Bishop, or priest” is absent from the Spanish Collection. The Basel edition reads *teneantur obnoxii refugientes*. The transmitted word is *refugientes* (“fleeing”); in Burchard and Ivo it is *refugientibus* (“for those fleeing”), agreeing with Greek canon 9. In recent editions of the councils, the words “fleeing the regular judgment of their own bishop” are placed after “received”; in the Soria manuscript of the Catholic King they are entirely absent.]

### Chapter XXX. Whoever judges the sentence of his bishop unjust is to appeal to a synod.

Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 66.

[*Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua*, chapter 68.]

A cleric who judges the severity exercised by his bishop against him to be unjust shall appeal to a synod.

[Col. 0853A]

### Chapter XXXI. Ecclesiastical bonds are not to be despised.

Likewise John Chrysostom, Homily IV on chapter 2 of the Epistle to the Hebrews.

[Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 88; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 48.]

Let no one despise ecclesiastical bonds. For it is not a human being who binds, but Christ, who gave us this power and made human beings masters of so great an honor.

[Apparatus: Ivo omits *nobis* (“to us”), and Basel adds *esse* (“to be”).]

### Chapter XXXII. Whoever is excommunicated from the Church is delivered to Satan.

Likewise Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*, Sermon LXVIII.

[A chapter of uncertain origin.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 94; part 14, chapter 50. Ivo also cites it in part 14, chapter 50; in part 2, chapter 94, together with many other words, he seems to cite it from the books *On the One Baptism*.]

Every Christian, beloved, who is excommunicated by priests is delivered to Satan. How? Clearly, because the devil is outside the Church, just as Christ is in the Church; and thus the person removed from ecclesiastical communion is, as it were, delivered to the devil. Hence the Apostle shows that those whom he declares to have been delivered to Satan were excommunicated by him.

[Apparatus: Ivo reads *tradi dicitur* (“is said to be delivered”) for the first *traditur*; Basel and Ivo have the same reading for the second. Basel reads *ecclesiae* (“of the Church”) for *ecclesiastica*.]

### Chapter XXXIII. On the same matter.

The same author, Tractate XXVII on chapter 6 of John.

Nothing should a Christian fear so much as being separated from Christ’s body. For if he is separated from Christ’s body, he is not a member of it. If he is not a member of it, he is not animated by its spirit. But “whoever,” says the Apostle, “does not have the Spirit of Christ, does not belong to him.”

Gratian. Likewise Jerome.

[Editorial note: These words are not found in St. Jerome, but in the second epistle of Eutychianus, cited by Ivo.]

“Whose sins you forgive,” etc., means: those to whom you have forbidden the Church—unless they are reconciled through satisfaction—the gate of the heavenly kingdom will be shut.

[Apparatus: Chapter XXXIII is Tractate 27 on John 6; the cited verse is Romans 8:9. Basel reads *Dominus* (“the Lord”) for *Hieronymus* (“Jerome”); the reference is Matthew 16:19.]

### Chapter XXXIV. Neighboring bishops are to hear those who complain of the judgments of their own bishops.

Likewise, from the Council of Milevis, chapter 22.

[In the common printed codices this chapter bore the name *Palea*, but it occurs in all ancient copies of Gratian. It is cited above, 2, question 6, chapter *Placuit. Held after A.D. 416.—Compare the African Council in Dionysius, chapter 92, and above, Cause 7, question 6, chapter 35.]

Presbyters, deacons, and other inferior clerics, if they complain in cases which they have about the judgments of their own bishops, shall be heard by neighboring bishops, summoned by them with the consent of their own bishops; and those bishops shall settle whatever lies between them. But if they judge that an appeal must also be made from these bishops, they shall appeal only to African councils or to the primates of their own provinces. Whoever judges that an appeal must be made overseas shall be received into communion by no one within Africa.

[Apparatus: *Questi* has *conquesti* (“having complained”) in the collected editions. The collected editions and the Spanish Collection read plural forms, *putaverint … suscipiantur*, for “if they judge … let them be received.”]

### Chapter XXXV. An unjust condemnation by bishops is deemed void.

Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 28.

[Chapter 51 of the *Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua*.—Compare the note on chapter 9, Distinction 18.]

We judge an unjust condemnation by bishops to be void and therefore to require reconsideration by a synod.

[Apparatus: The collected editions add *censemus* (“we judge”).]

### Chapter XXXVI. Whoever wishes to appear for his case and assert his innocence must do so within a year of excommunication.

Likewise, from the Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 12.

[Held A.D. 401.—Burchard, book 2, chapter 182; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 232; *Polycarpus*, book 7, title 1.]

It has again been decreed that, whenever clerics are convicted or confess to any crime, whether because consideration is shown for the modesty of those concerned, or because of disgrace to the Church, or the insolent mockery of heretics and pagans, should they wish to appear for their case and assert their innocence, they must do so within a year of excommunication. But if within a year they disdain to clear their case, no plea of theirs shall thereafter be heard at all.

[Apparatus: In all the indicated places the reading is *et* (“and”) rather than *vel* (“or”), including the Spanish Collection. Manuscript copies of Gratian, however, agree with the common editions. Some read *convicti clerici vel confessi* (“clerics convicted or confessing”). Ivo reads *ut aliquoties clerici convicti et confessi* (“that whenever clerics are convicted and confess”), and Burchard likewise has *aliquoties* (“whenever”).]

### Chapter XXXVII. Whoever delays presenting the cause of his excommunication for a year denies himself a hearing.

Likewise Gelasius.

[A chapter of uncertain date.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 46, chapter 21; Burchard, book 11, chapter 47; Anselm, book 12, chapter 24 (29); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 136; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 111; *Polycarpus*, same place.]

Whoever does not pursue his case before those who excommunicated him, whether civilly or publicly, within the space of a year, is to be regarded as having shut off for himself access to a hearing. But if, with a stubborn mind, they die without communion, then, reserving their cause to divine judgment in accordance with the sentence of our predecessor Blessed Leo, we ought not to communicate with them when dead, since we did not communicate with them when alive.

[Apparatus: Anselm omits *civiliter sive* (“civilly or”), reads *claudere* (“to shut”) for *clausisse* (“to have shut”), and Burchard, Anselm, and Ivo read *possumus* (“can”) for *debemus* (“ought”).]

### Chapter XXXVIII. PALEA.

[Burchard, book 11, chapter 48; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 142, from decrees of the same Gelasius. A chapter equally of uncertain origin; absent from the Basel edition.]

“Whoever knowingly communicates with an excommunicated person and henceforth even prays together in the same house, or provides him hiding places of protection so that he may not be brought to satisfaction, is to recognize that he is deprived of communion in the Lord’s body and blood until he receives penance from the bishop who excommunicated him.”

[Apparatus: Burchard and Ivo add *defensionis* (“of protection”) after *latebras* (“hiding places”); the collected editions add *episcopo* (“bishop”) after *excommunicatore*.]

### Chapter XXXIX. Whoever disdains to leave the Church at a priest’s command is to be received to pardon more slowly.

Likewise, from the Council of Lleida, chapter 10.

[Held A.D. 524.]

Whoever, at the command of a priest, disdains to leave the Church for any fault whatsoever shall, because of the offense of contumacy, be received to pardon more slowly.

Gratian. But the question is asked: if the bishop should happen to die before the condemned person is absolved, can the condemned person afterwards be absolved?

The following was decreed concerning this in the Council of Epaone, chapter 28.

[Held A.D. 517.—Burchard, book 11, chapter 50; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 121; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 114.]

### Chapter XL. The person who remains bound after the bishop’s death is to be released by his successor.

If a bishop is carried off by death before the condemned person’s absolution, his successor may absolve the corrected or penitent person.

[Apparatus: The Spanish Collection reads *quacunque* for *qualicunque*, uses the plural *contemserint … recipiantur*, and the collected editions read *contumeliae* (“insult”) for *contumaciae* (“contumacy”).]

Gratian. To the authorities set out above, by which we are commanded to obey unjust sentences until both parties have been examined, the following answer is made. Gregory does not say that a sentence unjustly pronounced must be observed, but that it must be feared, as Urban also says. It must be feared, therefore; that is, it must not be despised out of pride. The remaining authorities speak of excommunicated persons who either disdained to come when summoned to a synod, or, not knowing how to meet the stratagems of opponents, received an unjust sentence from a judge, or who, through neglect of their own lives, allowed an unfavorable opinion of themselves to arise and thus incurred a sentence against themselves. Only these persons, indeed, may lawfully be struck by a sentence of excommunication.

Hence in the Council of Meaux, chapter 56.

[Held A.D. 845.—Burchard, book 11, chapter 10; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 93; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 80; Abbo of Fleury in Mabillon, *Analecta Vetera*, chapter 36, from Cologne, chapter 56.]

### Chapter XLI. The offenses requiring someone to be deprived of communion.

No bishop shall deprive anyone of ecclesiastical communion without a certain and manifest cause of sin. But let no one presume, under anathema, to place anyone under it without the knowledge of the archbishop or fellow bishops, except where canonical authority teaches otherwise; for anathema is a condemnation to eternal death and ought to be imposed only for a mortal crime, and upon one who cannot otherwise be corrected.

[Apparatus: Basel reads *punire* (“punish”) for *ponere* (“place [under anathema]”). In the Council of Meaux and in the added Capitularies of Charles, son of Louis, the text reads: “But let him impose anathema upon no one without the consent of the archbishop or fellow bishops, after Gospel admonition has also been given.” The other compilers differ little from Gratian. The collected editions read *illis* (“upon those”) and preserve the variants *potuerint* / *potuerunt* (“may be able” / “were able”).]

### Chapter XLII. No one is to be deprived of communion for minor and slight causes.

Likewise, from the Council of Clermont.

[The passage is not found in the extant Council of Clermont, but in the Fifth Council of Orléans, chapter 2, and in the Council of Worms, chapter 13. Held about A.D. 550.—Compare the *Collection of Gallican Councils*, edited by Dom Labat, p. 1067 ff.]

No priest shall suspend from communion any person of right faith for small and slight causes, except for those offenses for which the ancient Fathers ordered offenders to be excluded from the Church.

### Chapter XLIII. Any person is to be deprived of communion for these three crimes.

Likewise, from the Council of Tribur.

[Not found in the printed Council of Tribur.—Burchard, book 11, chapter 74; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 112; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 122.]

It is certain that a person ought to be excommunicated for these three crimes: when, having been canonically summoned to a synod, he disdains to come; or when, after arriving there, he refuses to obey priestly commands; or when, before the examination of his case is concluded, he presumes to depart from the synod.

[Apparatus: Basel reads *contemserit* (“has disdained”) for *contemnit* (“disdains”), and the cited collections add *profugus* (“as a fugitive”) after “to depart.”]

Part IV. Gratian. The foregoing authorities speak, I say, of these and similar persons, not of persons unjustly suspended. That an unjust sentence is not to be obeyed is proved by many authorities. The first of these is Jerome’s statement in Book III of his commentary on Matthew.

[Editorial note: The passage is read variously by the compilers. In St. Jerome it reads: “We read in Leviticus concerning lepers, where they are commanded to show themselves to priests; and, if they have leprosy, they are then declared unclean by the priest—not because priests make lepers or render them unclean, but because they have knowledge of leper and non-leper and can discern who is clean and who unclean. Therefore, just as there the priest declares the leper clean or unclean, so here the bishop and priest bind or loose, not those who are innocent or guilty, but, in accordance with their office, when they have heard the varieties of sins, they know who ought to be bound and who ought to be loosed.”]

[Commentary on Matthew, chapter 16.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 130; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 86; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 7.]

### Chapter XLIV. The sentence of a pastor does not establish or make a person guilty or innocent.

Just as a priest does not make a leper clean, so a bishop or priest does not bind those who are innocent or loose the guilty; rather, in accordance with his office, when he has heard the varieties of sins, he knows who ought to be bound and who loosed.

### Chapter XLV. On the same matter. PALEA.

Likewise Augustine on Matthew.

[A chapter of uncertain origin.]

“It is absurd for us to say that a man bound by the bonds of his own sins is clean merely because the bishop is said to possess such power that those loosed by him are loosed in heaven and those bound on earth are bound in heaven. Let him, therefore, be blameless who binds or looses another.”

[Apparatus: The collected editions and the Paris and Lyons editions omit *mundum* (“clean”). Basel reads *episcopum* for *episcopus* and *absolvit* (“absolves”) for *solvit* (“looses”).]

### Chapter XLVI. Absolution is not to be sought when a sentence is pronounced unjustly.

Likewise Pope Gelasius to the eastern bishops concerning the condemnation of Dioscorus.

[Editorial note: “Concerning the condemnation of Dioscorus” is also the reading in the manuscripts. In Ivo it reads “concerning avoidance of communion with Acacius.” Dioscorus was condemned at the Council of Chalcedon and by St. Leo I; Acacius, however, was condemned by Felix III and Gelasius himself.]

[Rather Felix III, in the treatise against the followers of Acacius.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 8.]

Let the person against whom a sentence has been pronounced abandon his error, and it is void; but if it is unjust, he ought to care about it no more than an unjust sentence can burden anyone before God and his Church. Therefore he should not desire to be absolved from a sentence by which he clearly sees himself not bound in any way.

[Apparatus: Basel omits *sed* (“but”).]

### Chapter XLVII. God neither harms nor allows anyone to be harmed unjustly.

Likewise Augustine, *On the Highest Good*.

[From Book III of *On the Nature of the Good*, chapter 39.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 9.]

According to the Catholic faith, sound doctrine, and truth clear to the intelligent, no one can harm the nature of God, nor does God’s nature harm anyone unjustly or permit anyone to be harmed unjustly. For “he who does harm,” says the Apostle, “will receive what he has done harmfully.”

[Apparatus: Basel has *noceri* (“to be harmed”) for *nocere* (“to harm”); the original has *impune* (“with impunity”) for *injuste* (“unjustly”). The collected editions add *ut* before *ait* (“as he says”) and read *hoc* (“this”) for *illud* (“that”).]

### Chapter XLVIII. Justice breaks unjust bonds.

The same author, Sermon 16 on the words of the Lord.

[Sermon 82, Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 83; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 5.]

You have begun to regard your brother as a publican: you bind him on earth, but see that you bind him justly. For justice breaks unjust bonds. But when you have corrected and been reconciled with your brother, you have loosed him on earth; when you loose him on earth, he shall also be loosed in heaven.

[Apparatus: Basel reads *utrum* for *ut*. The collected editions substitute the wording “whom you loose, he says, in …” for the printed closing phrase. The restored sentence, from the original, Ivo, and the *Panormia*, is: “But when you have corrected and been reconciled with your brother, you have loosed him on earth.”]

### Chapter XLIX. Rashness in judging harms not the person judged, but the judge.

The same author, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, book II, chapter 29.

[Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 10.]

A rash judgment generally does no harm to the person rashly judged. But the rashness itself necessarily harms the person who judges rashly.

### Chapter L. An unjust sentence does not harm a person.

The same author, to the Clergy of Hippo, Epistle CXXXVII.

[Written A.D. 404.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 11; *Polycarpus*, book 7, title 1.]

What harm does it do a man if human ignorance refuses to have his name recited from that register, provided that an evil conscience does not erase him from the book of the living?

[Apparatus: The collected editions read *delere* (“to erase”) for *recitari* (“to be entered/recited”) and *deleat* (“may erase”) for *delet* (“erases”).]

### Chapter LI. On the same matter.

The same author, in the book against Secundinus the Manichaean, chapter 1.

[Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 12.]

Think of Augustine whatever you please: let conscience alone not accuse me in the eyes of God.

[Apparatus: Basel reads *accusat* (“accuses”) for *accuset* (“may accuse”).]

### Chapter LII. Those whom conscience justifies should not fear the slanders of others.

Likewise Gregory to Constantine, Bishop of Milan, book VI, Epistle 14.

[Epistle 14, written A.D. 597, book 7, Maurist edition.]

In all adversities that occur in this life, as you know, only the strict judgment of almighty God is to be weighed; and one must always return to one’s own heart, so that no person’s tongue may entangle us there where conscience does not accuse us. For the person defended by conscience is free even amid accusations; but he cannot be free, even without accusation, if conscience alone—by which he is inwardly convicted—accuses him. Therefore, with respect to your holiness, let it be far from Christian judgment that things which we believe to have been fabricated by the rumors of slanderous persons should be admitted to any degree of suspicion. For from the testimony of sacred utterance we maintain that grave evils, when perhaps alleged, ought not to be believed unless proved, but, once proved, ought to be avenged more promptly.

And below:

§ 1. I have said this in order to show how excessively frivolous a person is if he seeks to believe grave evils that cannot be proved. Therefore your holiness ought to detach your mind from the rumors and detraction of slanderous people, and to think only of those things that belong to eternal life and advance the welfare of those subject to you.

[Apparatus: The Argentinian, Norimbergian, and Venice I editions read *accuset* for *accusat*. Basel omits *liber* (“free”). Venice I, Venice II, and Norimberg read *adjicit* (“adds”) for *addicit* (“convicts”). The original and collected editions read *et … testimonium* rather than *ex … testimonio*. The original and Nicholas, Epistle 2 to Emperor Michael, support *mala gravia* (“grave evils”), repeatedly used in this letter; the earlier reading was *mala majorum* (“evils of elders”). Basel has *non* for *nisi*. The collected editions read *hoc* for *haec*, *qui … studeant* for *si quis … studeat*, and *obtrectationibus* (“slanders”) for *obtrectatione*.]

### Chapter LIII. A person whom God justifies is condemned by human beings in vain.

Likewise Augustine on Psalm XXXVI, third discourse, on the verse “Nor will he condemn him.”

[Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 13.]

And even if for a time you are condemned by a human being, and even if the proconsul has pronounced sentence against Cyprian, the earthly seat is one thing and the tribunal of heaven another. From the lower tribunal he received a sentence; from the higher, a crown.

[Editorial note: Augustine’s fuller printed context is: “When, therefore, that judgment has come, he will not condemn him; and even if for a time he seems to be condemned by a human being, and even if he has pronounced sentence …”]

[Apparatus: Argentinian reads *addixerit* (“has adjudged”) for *dixerit* (“has pronounced”). Ivo reads *proconsuli*, while Basel, Venice I–II, and Norimberg read *proconsulis*, for *proconsul*. The collected editions and Ivo read *aliud* (“another thing”) for *alia* (“one thing”); Ivo reads *coeleste* (“heavenly”) for *coelorum* (“of the heavens”).]

### Chapter LIV. The same author on Psalm XXXVII, on the verse “For I have hoped in you.”

[Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 14.]

[The supplied source ends here.]

Keep your innocence within, where no one can oppress your case. False testimony will prevail [Note: [Col. 0859] “has prevailed”: Ivo.] against you, but only among human beings. Will it prevail before God, where your case must be pleaded? When God is judge, you will have no witness other than your conscience. Between the just Judge and your conscience, fear nothing but your case.

### C. LV. We must attend not to human tongues but to consciences. Likewise Pope Gregory to the presbyter Palladius, Book VIII, Letter 45 [Note: [Col. 0859] Letter 2, written A.D. 601, line 11; Maurist edition.]

[Col. 0859B] Amid the words of those who praise or blame, one must always return to the mind; and if the good said of us [Note: [Col. 0859] “of you”: Argentinian edition.] is not found there, this ought to cause great sorrow [Note: [Col. 0859] Add “to you”: Basel edition.]; and again, if the evil which people say of us is not found there, we ought to leap into great joy. For what indeed [Note: [Col. 0859] “For what indeed”: several passages have been added from a letter of Blessed Gregory, and in part also from Sixtus III, in which nearly the same matter is repeated.] if people [Note: [Col. 0859] “not people”: Argentinian edition; “not all”: the remaining editions.] praise us, and conscience accuses us? Or what sorrow ought there to be if all accuse us and conscience alone shows that we are free? We have Paul saying [Note: [Col. 0859] 2 Corinthians 1:12.]: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience.” Job likewise says [Note: [Col. 0859] Job 16:20.]: “Behold, my witness is in heaven.” Therefore, if we have a witness in heaven and a witness in the heart, let us leave [Note: [Col. 0859] “dismiss”: the original.] fools outside to say what they wish.

[Col. 0859C] § 1. What else indeed [Note: [Col. 0859] Add “indeed”: the collected editions.] do detractors do, unless [Note: [Col. 0859] Add “that”: the collected editions; Böhm.] they blow dust about and stir up earth in their own eyes, so that from the very place whence [Note: [Col. 0859] “one”: Argentinian edition.] they scatter more dust [Note: [Col. 0859] “dust”: Basel edition.] of detraction, they see still less truth? Yet they themselves must also be summoned and gently admonished, and satisfaction must be given them in every way, remembering what Truth says concerning the Jews [Note: [Col. 0859] Matthew 17:26.]: “Lest perhaps we give them offence.” If they refuse to be satisfied by the truth, however, you have consolation which you may receive [Note: [Col. 0859] “look upon”: the remaining editions; “receive”: Basel edition.] in the holy Gospel. For because—when [Note: [Col. 0859] “because, when”: the original.] it had been said to the Lord, “Do you know [Note: [Col. 0859] Matthew 15:12.] that the Pharisees [Note: [Col. 0859] “Jews”: the collected editions.] were offended when they heard this saying?”—he answered [Note: [Col. 0859] Matthew 15:14.]: “Leave them alone; they are blind, and leaders of the blind.” The Apostle Paul likewise exhorts, saying [Note: [Col. 0859] Romans 12:18.]: “If it be possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people.”

[Col. 0859D] Since, indeed, he was about to say, “Let us have peace with all people” [Note: [Col. 0859] “Let us have”: the collected editions.], [Col. 0860A] and foresaw that this was difficult [Note: [Col. 0859] “perceiving”: the same editions.], he first said, “if it be possible.” But [Note: [Col. 0859] “and”: the same editions.] he nevertheless added what can [Note: [Col. 0859] “could”: the same editions.] be done when he says [Note: [Col. 0859] “said”: the same editions.], “so far as it depends on you”; because if we desire to preserve in our mind charity toward those who hate us, then—even though they have no peace with us [Note: [Col. 0859] “with you”: Basel edition.]—we nevertheless undoubtedly have peace with them [Note: [Col. 0859] “may have peace”: the same edition.].

Gratian. This must be observed among those who are ready to suspect what they do not see, always ready to criticize and never to imitate. With others, however, conscience is necessary for us, reputation for them.

Whence Augustine, *On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 22 [Note: [Col. 0859] Compare Distinction 27, chapter 2; Cause 12, question 1, chapter 10; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 1, title 55, chapter 108.]

### C. LVI. Conscience is necessary for us, and reputation for our neighbors.

Those holy men or women are not to be heeded [Col. 0860B] who, when reproved for some negligence of their own [Note: [Col. 0859] “who, when they are reproved for some negligence, etc.”: the collected editions.] through which they fall under an evil suspicion—though they know their life to be far removed from it—say that conscience before God is enough for them, contemptuously and indeed cruelly disregarding the esteem of human beings, since they kill [Note: [Col. 0859] “kill”: Basel edition.] the souls of others: either those who blaspheme the way of God, to whom, according to their suspicion, the chaste [Note: [Col. 0859] “just”: Basel edition.] life of the saints seems vile; or those who imitate, with an excuse, not what they see but what they suppose. Therefore, whoever preserves his life from the crimes of disgraceful and wicked deeds benefits himself; but whoever also [Note: [Col. 0859] “also” omitted in the Basel edition.] preserves his reputation is merciful toward others [Note: [Col. 0859] “toward others”: the collected editions.]. For our life is necessary for ourselves, but our reputation for others.

[Col. 0860C]

### C. LVII. Before God, one who delivers a judgment at variance with conduct is cursed. Likewise Jerome on Paul’s Epistle to Philemon [Note: [Col. 0859] On verse 4; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 5, chapter 84; *Decree*, part 14, chapter 6; compare Proverbs 17:15 according to the Septuagint.]

“If anyone calls the just unjust and the unjust just, both are abominable before God.” Likewise, one who says that a holy person is not holy, and conversely asserts that an unholy person is holy [Note: [Col. 0859] “if not”: Basel edition.], is abominable before God.

### C. LVIII. Whoever believes a holy person to be unholy, or an unholy person holy, violates Christ. The same author, in the same place a little earlier.

If anyone believes that a person who is not holy is holy, and joins him [Note: [Col. 0859] “has joined him”: Basel edition.] to the fellowship of God, [Col. 0860D] he violates Christ, [Col. 0861A] of whose body we are all members. And below:

§ 1. All believers, according to the Apostle, are made Christ’s body [Note: [Col. 0861] “we are made”: the collected editions and the first Basel edition; compare Romans 12:5.]. Whoever errs and stumbles concerning Christ’s body, maintaining that one of its members is holy when he is not, or is not holy when he is, see to what crime he makes himself liable: “Woe,” says Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0861] Isaiah 5:20.], “to those who call sweet bitter and bitter sweet, who make darkness light and light darkness.” I take holiness to be sweet, and bitter that which is contrary to holiness.

### C. LIX. Whoever calls good people evil and evil people good will find the eternal woe of a curse. Likewise Isaiah, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 0861] Isaiah 5:20.]

“Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness.” And a little earlier:

§ 1. “Therefore my people has been led captive [Col. 0861B] because it had no knowledge; its nobles have perished with hunger, and its multitude has dried up with thirst. Therefore hell has enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth without any limit; and its mighty ones, its people, and its lofty and glorious ones have gone down to it. Man shall be bowed down and the man humbled; the eyes of the lofty shall be brought low; and the Lord of hosts shall be exalted in judgment, and God the Holy One shall be sanctified in righteousness.”

### C. LX. Whoever exercises unjustly the power of binding and loosing deprives himself of that power. Likewise Gregory, Homily XXVI on the Gospels [Note: [Col. 0861] Compare below, chapter 88; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 5, chapter 79; *Decree*, part 14, chapter 3; Polycarp, Book 7, title 1.]

He deprives himself of the power of binding and loosing who exercises it according to his own wishes rather than according to the conduct of those subject to him [Note: [Col. 0861] “of those subordinate to him”: the collected editions.].

[Col. 0861C]

### C. LXI. On the same subject. The same author, in the same place a little below [Note: [Col. 0861] Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 5, chapter 80; *Decree*, ibid.]

Those who follow either their own hatreds or favor [Note: [Col. 0861] Basel omits “or hatred.”] in the cases of their subjects cannot judge their subjects worthily.

### C. LXII. A superior’s absolution is not true unless it follows the judgment of the inner Judge. The same author, in the same place a little below [Note: [Col. 0861] *Collection in Three Parts*, part 1, title 55, chapter 2; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 5, chapter 81; *Decree*, ibid.]

Then the absolution of the superior is true when it follows the judgment of the inner Judge. This is well signified by the resurrection of the man who had been dead four days: it plainly shows that the Lord first raised and gave life to the dead man, saying [Note: [Col. 0861] John 11:43.], “Lazarus, come forth”; and afterwards he who had been restored to life [Note: [Col. 0861] “living”: the collected editions.] came out and was loosed by the disciples, as is written.

### C. LXIII. Whoever abuses a privilege deserves to be stripped of it. The same author, in the *Register* [Note: [Col. 0861D] This passage has not been found in the *Register* of Blessed Gregory, from which it is cited. It is, however, found in Letter 2 of Pope Simplicius, to whom Nicholas I also attributes it in his letter to Hincmar, beginning, “The letter of your blessedness.” Burchard, Ivo, and certain old copies of Gratian likewise attribute it to him. Above also, Distinction 74, chapter *Ubi*, § “For a privilege,” it is cited from the same Simplicius. Similar is what Blessed Augustine writes in Sermon 247 *On Time*: “For by judgment of the laws, one who abuses a privilege granted him is rightly cast down from the dignity he has attained.”] [Note: [Col. 0861] Compare Distinction 74, chapter 7.]

Whoever abuses the authority granted to him altogether deserves to lose his privilege.

### C. LXIV. A person against whom no canonical sentence has been pronounced ought not to suffer a canonical penalty. Likewise Gregory to the subdeacon Anthony, Book II, Indiction XI, Letter 9 [Note: [Col. 0861] Letter 3, written A.D. 593, line 3; Maurist edition.]

A person in whose condemnation no canonical sentence has been pronounced ought not to suffer a canonical penalty.

Gratian. From these passages it is understood that an unjust sentence binds no one before God, nor is anyone burdened in God’s Church [Col. 0862B] by an iniquitous sentence, as is found in the chapter of Gelasius. Therefore one must neither abstain from communion with, nor suspend from office, a person against whom an iniquitous sentence is known to have been pronounced. Why, then, do the chapters of the councils of Carthage, Africa, and others forbid one unjustly condemned to be received into communion before an examination of the judgment? Why was the following also decreed in the Council of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0862D] This is found in the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 27, from which Ivo, part 5, chapter 367, and Polycarp, Book 2, title 36, cite it. Yet Ivo himself, part 6, chapter 237, and Burchard attribute it to the Council of Mainz; the author of the *Panormia* attributes it both to Mainz and Toledo.] [Note: [Col. 0861] Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 27, held A.D. 633; Burchard, Book 2, chapter 192; Anselm, Book 8, chapter 27; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 3, chapter 80; Polycarp, Book 2, title 36.]?

### C. LXV. How one condemned by a synod may be restored innocent at a second synod.

A bishop, presbyter, or deacon unjustly deposed from his rank, if he is found innocent [Note: [Col. 0861] “is discovered”: the collected editions.] at a second synod, cannot be what he was unless he receives, before the altar, the ranks he lost from the hands [Note: [Col. 0861] “hand”: Basel edition.] of the bishops: [Col. 0862C] if he is a bishop, the stole, ring, and staff; if a presbyter, the stole and chasuble [Note: [Col. 0861] “paten”: Basel edition.]; if a deacon, the stole and alb; if a subdeacon, the paten and chalice. So also the remaining ranks, at their restoration, shall receive the things which they had received when they were ordained.

Part V. Gratian. If, then, those unjustly deposed cannot even be restored through bishops unless they receive from their hands what they had lost, how may anyone, on his own authority, communicate with those unjustly bound, and, without requesting absolution, celebrate their offices—as Gelasius appears to think? The answer is that a sentence is sometimes unjust from the intention of the person pronouncing it, but just in procedure and cause; sometimes just in intention and cause, but not in procedure; sometimes just in intention and procedure, but not in cause. When it is unjust in cause, sometimes there is no offence at all in the accused person deserving condemnation; sometimes the offence is not that one for which the sentence is pronounced, but he is blameworthy for another.

It is unjust in intention when someone, while preserving the integrity of judicial procedure, pronounces sentence upon an adulterer or any criminal person—not from love of justice, but induced by the rancor of hatred, by payment, or by the favor of opponents. Hence Bede says on the Epistle of James [Note: [Col. 0863] The wording is altered but the sense preserved; James 1:20.]: “The anger of man does not work the righteousness of God,” because one who in anger pronounces sentence on another, even if that person receives a sentence just in relation to himself, nevertheless does not imitate the righteousness of God—in whom disturbance has no place—if he passed sentence upon him not from love of justice but from the rancor of hatred.

[Col. 0863B]

### C. LXVI. A sentence of justice must not be given for reward. Likewise Gregory [Note: [Col. 0863D] This is not found in Blessed Gregory, but in Isidore, Book 3, *On the Highest Good*, chapter 58, whom Burchard cites, and Bede in the *Scintillae*, chapter 71.] [Note: [Col. 0863] Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, Book 3, chapter 54; Burchard, Book 16, chapter 28.]

Whoever judges rightly and expects a reward from it commits fraud against God, because he sells for money the justice which he ought to dispense freely. Those use good things badly who judge justly for temporal profit. Such persons are moved to uphold the truth not by the defense of justice but by love of reward [Note: [Col. 0863] “price”: Basel edition.]; if hope of money is withdrawn from them, they immediately depart from the defense [Note: [Col. 0863] “confession”: Burchard and the collected editions.] of justice. The acceptance of money [Note: [Col. 0863] “gifts”: the original.] is a betrayal of truth. Hence it is said of the just person [Note: [Col. 0863] Isaiah 33:15.]: “He who shakes his hands [Note: [Col. 0863] “his hand”: Basel edition.] free from every gift, [Col. 0863C] he [Note: [Col. 0863] Omitted by Böhm.] shall dwell on high [Note: [Col. 0863] “dwells”: Argentinian edition.].”

### C. LXVII. In the actions of superiors, reason must claim all for itself. Likewise Gregory, Book VIII, Letter 12 to Guidiscalcus [Note: [Col. 0863] Letter 11, written A.D. 600, line 10; Maurist edition; Burchard, Book 15, chapter 29; Ivo, *Decree*, part 16, chapter 30.]

That concern of superiors is useful, that caution praiseworthy, in which reason does everything and anger claims nothing for itself. Authority must be restrained by reason, and nothing should be done before the mind, once agitated, returns to calm. For in a time of disturbance a person thinks everything [Note: [Col. 0863] “anger”: the original and the cited collections; “whole”: the collected editions.] he has done to be just [Note: [Col. 0863] Add “to be”: Basel edition.].

### C. LXVIII. Whoever pronounces sentence in anger sins grievously. Likewise Ambrose, *On Saint Joseph*, chapter 13.

Anger often brings even innocent persons into accusation, [Col. 0864A] because, while we are more angry than is just and wish to restrain another’s sin [Note: [Col. 0863] “another’s sins”: the collected editions.], we commit graver sins. Therefore the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0863] Romans 12:19.]: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to anger”; that is, let us turn aside from it, lest it seize us [Note: [Col. 0863] “corrupt”: Basel edition.]. Hence the Lord Jesus, sending [Note: [Col. 0863] “sending”: the collected editions.] his disciples to evangelize, sent them without gold, without silver, without money, without a staff: that is, in order to remove both the incentives [Note: [Col. 0863] “incentive”: the editions of Nuremberg and Venice I and II.] to litigation and the instruments of vengeance.

### C. LXIX. Reason must correct what anger has decreed. Likewise from Book XI of Rufinus’s *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 18.

When, at Thessalonica, a sedition having arisen [Note: [Col. 0863] The collected editions read: “a sedition having arisen, and.”], a certain military man had been killed by the onset of a raging crowd, Theodosius, inflamed by the atrocity of the sudden news, ordered the people to be invited to the Circus games; [Col. 0864B] soldiers were then to surround them unexpectedly and slaughter the people indiscriminately with the sword, as each person was encountered. Thus he ordered vengeance to be given [Note: [Col. 0863] “to give”: the collected editions.], not to the crime, but to anger. When he was rebuked [Note: [Col. 0863] “they rebuked”: the collected editions.] for this by the priests of Italy, he acknowledged his offence, confessed his fault with tears, performed public penance before the sight of the whole Church, and patiently completed the prescribed time without royal pomp. To all this [Note: [Col. 0863] Omitted in the Basel edition.] he also added the following in a remarkable way [Note: [Col. 0863] Böhm reads *miserabiliter*, “miserably,” instead of *mirabiliter*, “in a remarkable way.”]: by law [Note: [Col. 0863] “to the laws”: Basel edition; “laws”: the remaining editions.] he decreed for the future that sentences of rulers imposing punishment should be delayed by the executors until the twentieth day [Note: [Col. 0863] “thirtieth”: the collected editions.], so that room for mercy, or, should the matter require it, for repentance, might not be lost [Note: [Col. 0863] “perish”: Basel edition.].

[Col. 0864C]

### C. LXX. In pronouncing sentences, rulers must not be led by any anger. Likewise from the sayings of Gregory [Note: [Col. 0863D] Several passages concerning the need not to rush a judgment are read in Blessed Gregory, Book 19 of the *Morals*, chapter 23, on Job’s words, “I investigated most carefully the case which I did not know,” and in Book 12 of the *Register*, Letter 26, and elsewhere.] [Note: [Col. 0863] *Register*, Book 2, chapter 308; Burchard, Book 16, chapter 1; Anselm, Book 13, chapter 23.]

Rulers [Note: [Col. 0863] “lest rulers”: the editions of Nuremberg and Venice II; “that rulers”: the remaining editions.] of churches [Note: [Col. 0863] “of the Church”: the collected editions.] and those who exercise public judgments must take the greatest care [Note: [Col. 0863] “One must take care”: the collected editions.] that in pronouncing sentences they are in no way precipitate through fickleness or anger. Rather, after cases have first been carefully examined, when the matter that was unknown has fully come to knowledge, then divine and human law must be reviewed [Note: [Col. 0863] “law so that”: the Argentinian and Venice I and II editions; “revolved”: the *Register* and Anselm.]; and then, according to what has there been established, and with favoritism set aside, a definitive sentence must be pronounced. Hence Moses [Note: [Col. 0863] Exodus 33.], having entered the tabernacle of the Lord, always reported to him the complaints of the people [Col. 0865A] and set forth judgments according to the Lord’s command—plainly instructing us that we must pronounce a sentence of condemnation or justification not from our own heart but from the divine command.

### C. LXXI. A just judgment cannot be sold. Likewise Augustine to Macedonius, Letter LIV [Note: [Col. 0865C] The actual words of Blessed Augustine are quoted below, Cause 14, question 5, final chapter, at “But not for that reason.”] [Note: [Col. 0865] Compare below, Cause 14, question 5, final chapter.]

A judge may not sell a just judgment, although an advocate may sell a just defense and a jurist sound counsel.

### C. LXXII. On the same subject. Likewise Isidore, Book III, *On the Highest Good*, chapter 58 [Note: [Col. 0865] Chapter 54, Arevalo edition; Burchard, Book 16, chapter 28.]

Because a poor person has nothing to offer, he is not only despised when seeking a hearing but is also oppressed contrary to the truth. [Col. 0865B] Justice is quickly violated by gold, and an accused person fears no charge which he thinks he can redeem with money.

Gratian. Therefore, this sentence which is imposed upon anyone not from love of justice but from any other cause must be humbly obeyed.

Hence, in the Council of Nicaea, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 0865] Held A.D. 325; Burchard, Book 11, chapter 36; Ivo, *Decree*, part 14, chapter 100, both from Dionysius; Polycarp, Book 7, title 1.]:

### C. LXXIII. Those who incur the displeasure of their own bishops are not to be received by others.

Let this rule [Note: [Col. 0865] “and let this rule”: the Hispana collection; Basel edition.] be observed: those excommunicated by some are not to be received into communion by others. Inquiry must certainly be made lest any [Note: [Col. 0865] “whether perhaps”: the Hispana collection.] have been excluded by their bishop because of some indignation of mind, contention, or any such agitation [Note: [Col. 0865] Add “of temper”: the collected editions and the Hispana collection.] by excommunication [Note: [Col. 0865] Add “by excommunication”: the Hispana collection.]. And below: Thus, those who have deservedly incurred the displeasure of their own bishops [Col. 0865C] on account of their faults are to be held likewise as excommunicated by the rest, until it shall seem good to their own bishop to pronounce a more lenient sentence concerning them. [Note: [Col. 0865C] In the ancient translation contained in Isidore’s collection, which is very similar to this, one reads: “until it shall seem good in common, or to their own bishop” [Col. 0865: “in communion or to the bishop himself”: the Hispana collection]; and not much differently in the other common translation. The Greek is: *μέχρις ἂν τῷ κοινῷ τῶν ἐπισκόπων δόξῃ*, that is, “until it shall seem good to the common body of bishops.”]

Gratian. Again, a sentence is unjust in procedure when someone is condemned for his fault without judicial procedure having been observed.

[Col. 0866A] Hence Gregory writes to Constantine, bishop of Milan, Book VIII, Letter 30 [Note: [Col. 0865] Letter 29, written A.D. 600, line 10; Maurist edition; Anselm, Book 3, chapter 72.]:

### C. LXXIV. A doubtful matter must not be decided by a certain sentence.

It is sufficiently grave and unseemly for a certain sentence [Note: [Col. 0865] “to be pronounced”: the original.] to be given in a doubtful matter.

### C. LXXV. Things not demonstrated by certain proofs must not be believed. Likewise Augustine, in the book *On Penance*, chapter 3 [Note: [Col. 0865] Compare chapter 18, Cause 2, question 1; Anselm, Book 3, chapter 70; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 4, chapter 114; *Decree*, part 5, chapter 247.]

Although some things may be true, they must nevertheless not easily [Note: [Col. 0865] Add “easily”: the original.] be believed by a judge unless they are demonstrated by certain proofs.

### C. LXXVI. Some persons must not be judged before they have been examined. Likewise Pope Damasus, Letter VI [Note: [Col. 0865] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Anselm, Book 3, chapter 51 [48].]

It is not lawful to investigate the cases of those accused [Col. 0866B] before they come, having been canonically summoned, to the synod, and the accused person, being present, may truly recognize and understand through his accuser being present what is objected against him. This is also well said through the wisdom of Solomon [Note: [Col. 0865D] By “Solomon” he cites the wisdom book of Sirach, that is, *Ecclesiasticus*, under Solomon’s name. It is cited thus also by Blessed Gregory, Cause 1, question 1, chapter *Non est putanda*; by Cyprian, Book 3 to Quirinus, chapter 20; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book 7; Origen, Homily 18 on Numbers; Hilary on Psalm 67; and other Fathers. Blessed Augustine gave the reason for this in Book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 8, and elsewhere.] [Note: [Col. 0865] Ecclesiasticus 11:7 ff., according to the Septuagint.]: “Before you investigate, do not rebuke [Note: [Col. 0865] “do not”: the collected editions read “not.”]. Understand first, and then reprove. Before you have heard [Note: [Col. 0865] “hear”: the collected editions.], do not answer [Note: [Col. 0865] “do not reprove”: Basel edition; “do not rebuke”: the remaining editions.].” And although the reproof of opponents may be most evident, nevertheless those appointed [Note: [Col. 0865] “assigned”: the original.] to investigate them must observe procedure.

### C. LXXVII. Both one who makes a false statement about another and one who believes accusations are guilty. Likewise from the Eighth Synod [Note: [Col. 0866D] On this heading, “Eighth Synod,” see the note above in the same question, chapter 3, *If any brother*.] [Note: [Col. 0865] From Isidore of Spain, *Books of Sentences*, Book 3, chapter 55; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 2, title 14, chapter 25.]

Not only is the person guilty who makes a false statement about another, [Col. 0866C] but also [Note: [Col. 0865] Omitted in the Basel edition.] the person who readily lends an ear to accusations.

Part VI. Gratian. Therefore, when a sentence is unjust in procedure, one must not depart from it even then; indeed, before the sentence was pronounced against him, he was bound before God in accordance with the nature of his guilt. It sometimes happens that an adulterer receives a sentence for sacrilege, though he does not have that offence on his conscience. This sentence, although unjust because the crime for which it was pronounced is not in him, has nevertheless been justly received by him, because he had long before been excommunicated before God by reason of the guilt of adultery. In this case the authority of Gregory must be understood [Note: [Col. 0867] Above, in the same question, chapter 1.]: “The sentence of the shepherd,” etc.

§ 1. He calls a sentence just when the crime for which it is pronounced exists; unjust when that crime does not exist. Yet it must be feared or observed, because the person was already deserving of condemnation on another ground. Thus, after Gregory had said [Note: [Col. 0867] Homily 26 on the Gospels.], “Whether the shepherd binds justly or unjustly, the shepherd’s sentence must nevertheless be feared by the flock,” he continued: “Lest one who is subject to him, even when he is perhaps unjustly bound, deserve the sentence of his binding itself because of another fault.” Therefore, let the shepherd fear either to absolve indiscriminately or to bind indiscriminately. But let one under the shepherd’s [Col. 0867B] hand fear to be bound, even unjustly, and not rashly criticize his shepherd’s judgment, lest—even if he is unjustly bound—the fault which was not present come into being through the pride of his swollen criticism.

§ 2. Sometimes no crime exists, and yet a person receives upon himself a sentence of condemnation brought against him either through the judge’s hatred or through a conspiracy of enemies.

Hence Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0867D] This is not found in Gregory, but in Isidore, whom Burchard cites, and somewhat more fully; after several intervening passages it follows the chapter *Who judges rightly*, above in the same question.] [Note: [Col. 0867] From Isidore, Book 3, chapter 54; Burchard, Book 16, chapter 28.]:

### C. LXXVIII. In how many ways human judgment is perverted.

Human judgment is perverted in four ways: by fear, when we fear to speak the truth because of dread of someone’s power [Note: [Col. 0867] “are terrified”: the original.]; by greed, when we corrupt someone’s mind by a reward [Note: [Col. 0867] “we are corrupted by some gift”: the same source.]; by hatred, when we scheme against an adversary [Note: [Col. 0867] “against an opponent”: the same source.]; and by love, when we strive to please [Note: [Col. 0867] “to render assistance”: the collected editions and the original; add “assistance”: the collected editions except the first Basel edition.] a friend or relative.

Gratian. How grave it is to pervert judgment through hatred, friendship, fear, a gift, or in any manner whatever, Jerome testifies in his commentary on Amos, chapter 6, saying [Note: [Col. 0867] Jerome on Amos 6, at verse 23.]:

### C. LXXIX. Concerning those who pervert judgment in any way.

Whoever is guided in judging by either kinship or friendship, or conversely by hostile hatred or enmities, perverts the judgment of Christ, who is justice, and turns its fruit into bitterness [Note: [Col. 0867] Add “of condemnation”: the collected editions.].

[Col. 0868A]

### C. LXXX. Concerning those who conceal truth from fear of authority. Likewise Augustine to Casulanus [Note: [Col. 0868D] This chapter has not been found in Blessed Augustine; its latter part is also cited by Burchard as Augustine’s. Very similar words occur in the same Book 3 of Isidore, chapter 59.] [Note: [Col. 0867] From Isidore, Book 3, chapter 55; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 2, title 50, chapter 27; Deusdedit, part I; Burchard, Book 16, chapter 12.]

Whoever conceals the truth from fear of any authority provokes the wrath of God against himself, because he fears a human being more than God. And a little later:

§ 1. Both [Note: [Col. 0867] Compare chapter 1, X, *On the Crime of Forgery*.] are guilty: the one who conceals the truth and the one who tells a lie, because the former is unwilling to help and the latter desires to harm.

### C. LXXXI. On the same subject. Likewise [Note: [Col. 0867] Chapter of uncertain source.]

Let none of the learned or prudent suppose that there is less danger in lying with the words of the tongue than in shedding blood with the hands. It is better indeed [Note: [Col. 0867] “for”: Basel edition.] to suffer punishment for truth than to receive a benefit for flattery.

[Col. 0868B]

### C. LXXXII. On the same subject. Likewise Pope Pelagius II, Letter II, to Archbishop Benignus [Note: [Col. 0867] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.]

Everyone must take care not to persecute, judge, or punish [Note: [Col. 0867] “and”: Basel edition.] anyone unjustly, lest he persecute, judge, or punish Jesus [Note: [Col. 0867] The collected editions omit “judge or punish.”].

Gratian. Likewise, one who denies truth for money or gives false testimony against someone is shown to deny or sell God.

Hence Bede on Mark, chapter 14 [Note: [Col. 0867] *Collection in Three Parts*, part 2, title 50, chapter 19.]:

### C. LXXXIII. Those who give false testimony and deny truth for money become partners in Judas’s crime.

Judas went to the chief priests, and they agreed [Col. 0868C] to give him money. Many today recoil as though it were monstrous and wicked from Judas’s crime, because he sold the Lord, Master, and his God for money [Note: [Col. 0867] “for money”: Basel edition.], yet do not guard against it. For when they give false testimony against anyone in return for gifts, certainly, because they deny truth for money, they sell God for money. For he himself said [Note: [Col. 0867] John 14:6.], “I am the truth.” When they defile the fellowship of brotherhood with some plague of discord [Note: [Col. 0867] “of disagreement”: Basel edition.], they betray God, because God [Note: [Col. 0867] 1 John 4:7.] is charity. Therefore those who reject the commands of charity and truth betray God, who is charity and truth—especially when they sin not through weakness or ignorance but, in the likeness [Note: [Col. 0867] “through likeness”: Basel edition.] of Judas, seek [Note: [Col. 0867] Matthew 20.] an opportunity to change truth into falsehood and virtue into crime, when arbiters are absent [Col. 0869A].

### C. LXXXIV. Whoever makes himself a companion of the perverse denies Christ. Likewise Jerome on the Epistle to Titus, chapter 1, at the end.

Some suppose that Christ is denied only when a person, seized by pagans [Note: [Col. 0869] “by the nations”: the collected editions.] in persecution, refuses to be a Christian [Note: [Col. 0869] Add “to confess”: the same editions.]. But behold, the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0869] Titus 1.] declares that God is denied by all perverse deeds. Christ is wisdom, justice, truth, holiness, and strength. Wisdom is denied through folly, justice through iniquity, truth through falsehood, holiness through shameful conduct, strength through weakness of spirit. And as often as [Col. 0869B] we are overcome by [Note: [Col. 0869] Omitted in the Basel edition.] vices and sins, so often do we deny God; and conversely, as often as we do any good thing [Note: [Col. 0869] “the good”: the collected editions.], we confess God. Nor should it be thought that on the day of judgment [Note: [Col. 0869] Matthew 10.] only those who denied Christ in martyrdom will be denied by the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0869] Add “to be”: the Basel, Venice II, Lyons, and Paris editions.], but all those in whose deed, speech, or thought Christ, having been denied, denies, or, having been confessed, confesses [Note: [Col. 0869] The original reads: “Christ, denied, denies, or confessed, confesses through all deeds, words, and thoughts.”]. I think this is the confession about which he also commanded the disciples [Note: [Col. 0869] “from which the disciples learn”: the Lyons II and III editions; “from which they learn”: the remaining editions.] [Note: [Col. 0869] Compare Acts 1:8.], saying: “You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judaea, in Samaria, and unto the farthest end of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0869] “the last”: the collected editions.].

### C. LXXXV. Whoever denies that he is a Christian is proved to deny Christ. Likewise Augustine, Tractate CXIII on John, chapter 18.

[Col. 0869C] Not only does the person deny Christ who says that he is not the Christ, but also the person who, though he is one, denies that he is a Christian. For the Lord did not say to Peter [Note: [Col. 0869] Luke 22:34.], “You will deny that you are my disciple,” but, “You will deny me.” Therefore he denied Christ himself when he denied that he was Christ’s disciple. But what else did he deny in this way than that he was a Christian? Likewise [Note: [Col. 0869D] In two old copies of Gratian this is a separate chapter, with the rubric “On the same subject.” It is from Tractate 66 on John.] in Tractate LXVI:

§ 1. By fearing the death of your flesh, you will give death to your soul. For as great a life as confessing Christ is, so great a death is denying Christ. Did the Apostle Peter—as some endeavor to excuse him through perverse favor—[Col. 0870A] not deny Christ because, when questioned by a maidservant, he answered that he did not know the man?

### C. LXXXVI. A betrayer of truth is not only one who speaks falsehood for truth, but also one who does not freely preach truth. Likewise John Chrysostom [that is, the author of the *Imperfect Work* on Matthew, Homily 25.]

Do not fear those who kill the body [Note: [Col. 0869] Matt. 10:28], lest perhaps through fear of death you fail to state freely what you have heard, or fail confidently to preach to all what you alone heard in the ear. Thus [Note: [Col. 0869] “Therefore, just as”: ed. Bas.; “for just as”: the other editions] these words show that not only is the person a betrayer of truth who, transgressing truth, openly speaks a lie in place of truth, but also the person who does not freely proclaim the truth which ought to be freely proclaimed [Col. 0870B], or does not freely defend the truth which ought fittingly to be freely defended [Note: [Col. 0869] “ought”: original], is a betrayer of truth. For just as a priest is under obligation freely to preach the truth which he has heard from God, so a layperson is under obligation confidently to defend the truth which he has heard from priests and found confirmed in the Scriptures. If he does not do this, he is a betrayer [Note: [Col. 0869] “has betrayed”: eds. Arg. and Bas.; “betrays”: the other editions; “truth”: editions compared with the original] of truth. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation [Note: [Col. 0869] Rom. 10:10].

Gratian. This judgment harms the judge more than the person against whom it is rashly pronounced.

Accordingly Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0869] Algerus, book 1, ch. 67, correctly cites the first part of this chapter from Augustine, *To Classicianus*; the latter part is taken from book 3, *On Baptism*, ch. 18.—Anselm, book 12, ch. 67 (66); Polycarpus, book 7, title 1]:

C. LXXXVII. One who unjustly anathematizes someone harms himself, not others.

[Col. 0870C] I should certainly not say rashly that, if any one of the faithful has been unjustly anathematized, it harms rather the one who does it [Note: [Col. 0869] “did it”: ed. Bas.] than the person who suffers this injury. For the Holy Spirit dwelling in the saints, through whom each person is bound or loosed, imposes undeserved punishment upon no one. For through him charity is poured out in our hearts, and it does not act wrongly. The peace of the Church forgives sins [Note: [Col. 0869] “forgives sins, holds those estranged from the Church’s peace”: ed. Bas.; “forgives sins, and estrangement from the Church’s peace holds”: the other editions], and estrangement from the peace of the Church holds sins, not according to human judgment but according to the judgment [Note: [Col. 0869] omitted in ed. Bas.] of God. For the rock holds; the rock releases. The dove holds; the dove releases. Unity holds; unity releases.

[Col. 0871A] Gratian. Likewise Solomon [Note: [Col. 0871] Prov. 20:2]: “Like a bird flying uncertainly and a sparrow going wherever it will, so a curse uttered in vain comes upon the one who sent it.”

C. LXXXVIII. He whose life does not accord with his office, though himself bound, looses others. Likewise Pope Gregory, Homily XXVI on the Gospels [Note: [Col. 0871] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chs. 78–80; *Decretum*, part 14, ch. 3].

It often happens that one whose life least accords with the office holds the place of judge; and consequently it often happens that he either condemns the undeserving or, though himself bound, looses others. Often, in loosing and binding his subjects, he follows the impulses of his own will rather than the merits of their cases [Note: [Col. 0871] “follows”: editions compared with the original]. Hence it comes about that he deprives himself [Note: [Col. 0871] “by this very”: original; “itself”: Ivo, *Decretum*] [Col. 0871B] of the power of binding or loosing.

And below, § 1. It often happens that a pastor is moved toward some neighbour by hatred or favour. “To judge worthily concerning subjects,” etc. Hence the Prophet rightly says [Note: [Col. 0871] Ezek. 13:19]: “They were putting to death souls that did not die [Note: [Col. 0871] “die”: original, Ivo, *Decretum*, and editions compared with the original, except Bas.], and giving life to souls that do not live.” For he puts to death one who is not dying when he condemns the just man; and he attempts to give life to one who will not live when he seeks to absolve the guilty from punishment [Note: [Col. 0871] “loose”: editions compared with the original].

§ 2. Therefore cases must be weighed, and then the power of binding and loosing exercised. It must be seen what fault preceded, and what repentance followed after the fault, so that pastoral judgment may absolve those whom almighty God visits by the grace of compunction. For then absolution is true, etc. And below, § 3. From this consideration [Col. 0871C] it must be observed that, through pastoral authority, we ought to loose those whom we recognize that our Author gives life through awakening grace. And below, § 4. “Let the dead man therefore come forth”: that is, let the sinner confess his fault. But when he has come forth, let the disciples loose him, so that the pastors of the Church ought to remove the punishment from him which [Note: [Col. 0871] “because—ought”: editions compared with the original] he deserved, he who was not ashamed to confess what he had done. § 5.
