I have briefly spoken [Note: [Col. 0871] “we have spoken”: editions compared with the original] about the order of loosing, so that under great restraint [Note: [Col. 0871] “great moderation”: ed. Bas.] [Col. 0872A] the pastors of the Church may strive to loose or to bind [Note: [Col. 0871] “ought”: editions compared with the original].

C. LXXXIX. A judgment unjustly pronounced lacks force. Likewise Pope Calixtus, Epistle I to Bishop Benedict [Note: [Col. 0871] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Prosper of Aquitaine, *Sentences*, 179, 118.—Burchard, book 15, ch. 8; Anselm, book 3, ch. 84; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 235, part 16, ch. 9.—Cf. C. 25, q. 1, ch. 8].

An unjust judgment and an unjust decision, arranged or enacted by judges through fear or command of the king, or of any bishop or powerful person, shall have no force. § 1. For a religious person it ought to be too little merely not to pursue others’ hostilities, or not to increase them by speaking ill, unless he also strives to extinguish them by speaking well. § 2. Humble confession in evil deeds is better than proud boasting in good deeds.

[Col. 0872B] C. XC. The person unjustly cursed earns a reward. Likewise Augustine, on Psalm CXI, at the verse “The Lord performs acts of mercy.”

He who is just and is unjustly cursed receives a reward [Note: [Col. 0871] omitted in ed. Bas.].

Gratian. Although, as has been said, a person thus bound is not bound before God, he must nevertheless obey the sentence, lest one formerly held free by purity of conscience become bound through pride.

VII. Part. § 1. The same applies when a sentence is pronounced contrary to equity; for example, when subjects cannot be compelled to evil, knowing that obedience need not be rendered to superiors in unlawful matters.

Accordingly Pope Eutychianus [Note: [Col. 0871D] Burchard and Ivo attribute both this chapter and ch. *If Anyone*, C. 24, q. 1, to Eutychianus; Gratian, however, cites it from Julius] says [Note: [Col. 0871] From ch. 2 of the penitential work ascribed to Jerome.—Cf. C. 24, q. 1, ch. 41.—Burchard, book 19, ch. 105; Anselm, book 11, ch. 135; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, ch. 117]:

C. XCI. A bishop who orders Mass to be sung for heretics must not be obeyed.

[Col. 0872C] If any bishop or abbot orders his priest or monk to sing Masses for heretics [Note: [Col. 0871D] “For heretics”: the other collectors add “the dead,” a word here supplied by the author of the gloss], it is neither lawful nor expedient to obey them [Note: [Col. 0871] “for”: editions compared with the original].

C. XCII. It is often expedient not to obey commands. Likewise Augustine [Note: [Col. 0872D] The wording and, in part, the sense of this chapter are found in blessed Ambrose, *On Paradise*, ch. 6] [Note: [Col. 0871] Algerus, book 1, ch. 33, correctly cites it from Ambrose; see the correction].

It is not [Note: [Col. 0871] “for”: ed. Bas.] always evil not to obey a command [Note: [Col. 0871] “commands”: ibid.]; when the lord orders things contrary to God, then he must not be obeyed.

[Col. 0873A] C. XCIII. On the same matter. Likewise Jerome, in his letter to Titus [Note: [Col. 0873D] “Titus”: thus corrected from Polycarpus, whereas it was previously cited as *To the Ephesians*; the chapter itself was also corrected and somewhat enlarged from the original] on ch. 2, verse, “Servants subject to their masters” [Note: [Col. 0873] Anselm, book 13, ch. 26 (27); Polycarpus, book 1, final title].

If a master orders things that are not contrary to the Holy Scriptures, let the servant be subject to his master [Note: [Col. 0873] “contrary or adverse”: ed. Bas.; “his”: ibid.]. But if he commands things contrary to them [Note: [Col. 0873] “commanded”: ibid.], let him obey the master of the spirit rather than the master of the body. And below, ch. 3, § 1. If what the emperor and governor command is good, comply with the will of the one commanding [Note: [Col. 0873] “carry out the will”: ed. Bas.]; but if it is evil, answer [Note: [Col. 0873] “answers”: ed. Bohm] with that saying from the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0873] Acts 5:29]: “We must obey God rather than men.” Let us understand the same thing concerning servants under masters, wives under husbands, and children under parents [Note: [Col. 0873] “fathers”: editions compared with the original]: they ought to be subject to those masters, husbands, and parents only in matters that do not conflict with God’s commands [Col. 0873B] [Note: [Col. 0873] “are”: editions compared with the original].

C. XCIV. Those who command anything against God are not to be obeyed. Likewise Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0873D] This statement occurs below in the same cause, ch. *Emperors*, § *Julian* [Col. 0874D]; perhaps this chapter was composed from that passage with altered words] [Note: [Col. 0873] Cf. below, ch. 98].

Although the emperor Julian was an apostate, he nevertheless had Christian soldiers under him. When he told them, “Draw up the battle line for the defense of the state,” they obeyed him. But when he told them, “Take up arms against Christians,” then they recognized the Emperor of heaven.

C. XCV. One shown to fear God commands nothing unjust. Likewise Pope Fabian, Epistle II, to all bishops [Note: [Col. 0873] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Gregory the Great, book 5, epistle 43].

The person who fears almighty God consents in no way to do anything contrary to the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0873] “of Christ”: ed. Bas.] or [Note: [Col. 0873] “nor”: editions compared with the original] contrary to the Apostles, the Prophets, or the institutions of the holy Fathers [Col. 0873C].

C. XCVI. Both the sinner and the person consenting to the sinner are guilty. Likewise Pope Nicholas to King Lothair [Note: [Col. 0873] A chapter of uncertain date.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 227.—Cf. above, ch. 10].

You consented so to yield to the impulses of your body and, loosening the reins of pleasures, cast yourself, though forbidden, into the lake of misery and the mire of filth [Note: [Col. 0873] “at will”: Ivo], that you, who had been placed to govern peoples, became the ruin of many. The lawful downfall of Thietgaud [Note: [Col. 0873] “Theutgaud”: Bohm] and Gunthar, formerly bishops, proves this: because they did not properly instruct you [Col. 0874A] [Note: [Col. 0873] “had instructed”: ed. Bas.; “instructed”: the other editions except Lugd. II and III], indeed because they strove to cover up your transgression with their arguments and, under a certain appearance of justice and by contrived, ingenious devices, to overwhelm equity, they were deposed by our apostolic authority and canonically excluded from every administration of the episcopate.

C. XCVII. On the same matter. Likewise Augustine, Sermon VI, *On the Words of the Lord* [Note: [Col. 0874D] This chapter has been corrected and enlarged from the original] [Note: [Col. 0873] Sermon 68, Maurist edition; Polycarpus, book 1, title 27].

“Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” [Note: [Col. 0873] Rom. 13:2]. But what if it commands what you ought not to do? Then indeed disregard the authority by fearing authority. Observe the ranks of human laws themselves [Note: [Col. 0873] “observe”: editions compared with the original]. If an official commands something, must it not be done? Yet if the proconsul commands the contrary [Note: [Col. 0873] “the proconsul”: original, eds. Arg., Bas., and Lugd. I], you do not thereby disregard authority [Col. 0874B], but choose to serve the greater authority. Nor ought the lesser to be angry because the greater has been preferred [Note: [Col. 0873] “preferred”: editions compared with the original]. Again, if the proconsul himself [Note: [Col. 0873] “consul”: same editions] commands one thing and the emperor another, is there any doubt that, disregarding the former, one must serve the latter? Therefore, if the emperor commands one thing and God another, what do you judge? “Pay the tax; be obedient to me.” Rightly so—but not in the matter of an idol. He forbids it in the case of an idol. Who forbids it? A greater authority [Note: [Col. 0873] “God”: same editions]. Pardon me [Note: [Col. 0873] “O emperor”: same editions]: you threaten prison; he threatens Gehenna. Here you must take up your faith as a shield, by which you may extinguish all the fiery darts of the enemy.

C. XCVIII. On the same matter. The same, to the Donatists, Letter CLXVI [Note: [Col. 0873] Letter 105, Maurist edition, written A.D. 409].

If emperors were in error—which God forbid—and enacted laws for their error against truth, the just [Col. 0874C] would be tested [Note: [Col. 0873] “would be proved”: ed. Bas.] and crowned by not doing what they commanded, because God forbade it [Note: [Col. 0873] “forbids”: same editions]. Thus Nebuchadnezzar ordered that the golden statue be worshipped; those who refused to do so pleased God, who forbade such things [Note: [Col. 0873] “forbidding”: ed. Bas.]. But when emperors hold the truth, they command on its behalf against error. Whoever disregards this incurs judgment upon himself. For he both pays penalties among men and will have no lot before God [Note: [Col. 0873] “forehead”: original and editions compared with the original], because he refused to do what Truth itself commanded him through the heart of the king. Thus Nebuchadnezzar himself [Note: [Col. 0873] “and he himself”: eds. Bas., Ven. II, Lugd., and Par.; cf. Dan. 3], later moved and changed [Col. 0875A] [Note: [Col. 0875] “transformed”: ed. Bas.] by the miracle of the deliverance of the three youths, issued an edict for truth against error: whoever blasphemed the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego should perish, and their houses should be reduced to ruins [Note: [Col. 0875] “ruin”: same editions]. And do you not wish Christian emperors to command something similar against you, when they know that, in those whom you rebaptize, Christ is renounced by exsufflation?

The same, in the Psalms [Note: [Col. 0875] On Psalm 124; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 7]:

§ 1. Julian was an unbelieving emperor. Was he not an apostate, unrighteous, and idolater? Christian soldiers served the unbelieving emperor. When the matter of Christ was at issue, they recognized none but him who was in heaven. When he wished idols to be worshipped and incense offered to them, they put God before him. But when he said, “Draw up the battle line; go against that nation,” they immediately obeyed. They distinguished the eternal Lord [Col. 0875B] from the temporal lord, and yet, for the sake of the eternal Lord, they were subject even to the temporal lord.

C. XCIX. Through obedience it is permissible to abandon a good, but never to do evil. Likewise Gregory, ch. 12, book XXXV, on Job.

What wonder, then, if sinful man subjects himself to obedience during the brief span of this present life, when the mediator between God and men observed it and commanded it to be observed [Note: [Col. 0875C–D] “Observed it and commanded it to be observed”: these words are absent from most manuscripts and from the original. Something similar is read in blessed Augustine, Sermon 5, *To the Brethren in the Desert*: “Nor is it surprising that we sinners submit to obedience, when the mediator between God and men did not abandon it even in death and subjected himself to him who was equal to the Father in all things.”] [Note: [Col. 0875] omitted in ed. Bas.], and, when he rewards the obedient, does not abandon it? But it must be understood that evil is never to be done through obedience, whereas a good which is being done must sometimes be left undone through obedience. For the tree in Paradise, which God forbade man to touch, was not evil; rather, in order that man, created good, might grow better through the merit of obedience, it was fitting that he should be forbidden even a good [Col. 0875C] [Note: [Col. 0875] “this one”: omitted in the original; “be forbidden”: original and editions compared with the original], so that what he did might be a virtue all the more truly insofar as, by abstaining from a good, he showed himself more humbly subject to his Creator [Note: [Col. 0875] “and humble”: editions compared with the original].

C. C. Before God, the person who consents to sinners is cursed. Likewise Isidore [Note: [Col. 0875D–0876D] The first part of this chapter, down to the word “most severe,” is found in the Rule of St Pachomius, published at Rome. The whole occurs in Smaragdus’s exposition of the Rule of St Benedict, ch. 69 [Col. 0876C]. It cites Basil, as do Burchard, Ivo [and Anselm]; and the sense occurs in Basil’s *Shorter Rules*, rule 7.] [Note: [Col. 0875] *Collectio trium partium*, part 2, title 14, ch. 21; Burchard, book 11, ch. 46; Anselm, book 12, ch. 5; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, ch. 110].

One who consents to sinners and defends another’s wrongdoing shall be cursed before God and men [Col. 0876A], and shall be rebuked with a most severe rebuke. Hence a certain most holy Father also says: “If anyone defends a sinner, let him be restrained more harshly than the one who sinned.” Hence another Father says: “If anyone consents to another’s error [Note: [Col. 0875] “consents”: editions compared with the original], and gives him counsel to humble himself more slowly, let him know that he is liable to be judged guilty together with him in the same manner.”

C. CI. One must not obey what is commanded against God. Likewise Isidore [Note: [Col. 0876D] In Basil’s *Shorter Rules*, chs. 114 and 303, there are passages very similar to everything contained in this chapter].

If a superior does what the Lord has forbidden, or commands anyone to do it, or neglects what has been commanded or orders it to be neglected, the sentence of St Paul the Apostle must be applied to him, saying [Note: [Col. 0875] Gal. 1:8]: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven [Col. 0876B], should preach to you anything other than what we preached to you, let him be anathema.” Likewise, § 1. If anyone forbids you what the Lord has commanded, or again commands to be done what the Lord forbids, let him be accursed by all who love God. Likewise, § 2. If a superior either says or commands anything contrary to the will of God, or contrary to what is plainly commanded in the Holy Scriptures, let him be regarded as a false witness of God or as sacrilegious.

Gratian. Therefore, when subjects are excommunicated because they cannot be compelled to evil, the sentence must not be obeyed, because, according to that statement of Gelasius [Note: [Col. 0875] above, ch. 46 = C. CII], an unjust sentence burdens no one either before God or before his Church.

VIII. Part. § 1. But the instruction given above—that persons communicating with the excommunicated are to be cast out of the Church—must not be understood of every manner of communicating.

Accordingly Pope Nicholas, to Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims [Note: [Col. 0875] written A.D. 863; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, ch. 106; *Decretum*, part 14, ch. 46], says:

C. CII. Concerning those who communicate with the excommunicated.

The most excellent King Charles consulted our apostolic office as to what should be done concerning those who communicate with persons who communicate with Engeltrude, a woman repeatedly condemned, since it is established that she, together with her communicants [Col. 0877A] and supporters, is bound by an equal bond of anathema [Note: [Col. 0875] “them … bound”: original in Mansi]. Therefore we now enjoin upon your blessedness that, relying upon our authority, you strive to take charge of this matter. Since your holiness, divinely instructed, knows very well that one kind of wrongdoing arises from necessity, another from ignorance, and another from deliberate intent [Note: [Col. 0877] omitted in ed. Bas.; “from”: the other editions], and that this latter must be punished more strictly than the two former [Note: [Col. 0877] “and two”: ed. Bas.; “strictly”: original, Ivo, and editions compared with the original], let it diligently watch and, with cautious discernment [Note: [Col. 0877] “strictness”: editions compared with the original], judge the circumstances of each individual, so that those who offend through necessity or ignorance may be absolved through you by our authority [Note: [Col. 0877] “through you”: omitted in ed. Bas.], provided, however, that their ignorance or necessity is real and not feigned, and did not arise from their own will. For, as you well know [Note: [Col. 0877] “know”: ibid.], many are able but unwilling [Col. 0877B] to know what is right. Hence the Psalmist says of such people [Note: [Col. 0877] “they indeed did not wish … do good”: editions compared with the original, except Bas.], “He would not understand, that he might do good” [Note: [Col. 0877] same variant]. But those who bind themselves by their own deliberate act and, in contempt, set aside our prohibitions, we wish you by no means to absolve unless worthy satisfaction first intervenes.

C. CIII. Concerning those who communicate with the excommunicated without fault. Likewise Gregory VII, book V of the Register, at a council held at Rome [Note: [Col. 0877] At a Roman council held A.D. 1078; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, ch. 125; *Decretum*, part 14, ch. 43].

Since, because our sins so require, we see many persons perish daily on account of excommunication—overcome partly by ignorance, partly by excessive simplicity, partly by fear, and partly even by necessity [Note: [Col. 0877] “through necessity”: editions compared with the original]—we mercifully temper the sentence of anathema for a time, as we are able and as is opportune. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we withdraw from the bond of anathema wives, children [Note: [Col. 0877] “sons”: editions compared with the original; “children, sons”: Ivo, *Panormia*], male and female servants or dependents, as well as peasants in service [Note: [Col. 0877] “and servants”: editions compared with the original and Ivo], and [Note: [Col. 0877] “as well as”: omitted in eds. Arg. and Par.; “as well as and”: omitted in the other editions] all others who are not so much members of the curia that crimes are perpetrated through their counsel; also those who unknowingly communicate with the excommunicated, and those who communicate with persons who communicate with the excommunicated. If any petitioner, pilgrim, or traveller comes into the land of the excommunicated, where he cannot buy, or does not have the means to buy, we grant permission to receive things from the excommunicated. And if anyone wishes to give something to the excommunicated [Col. 0878A], not for the support of pride [Note: [Col. 0877] “for support”: omitted in editions compared with the original] but from humanity [Note: [Col. 0877] “humility”: ed. Bas.], we do not forbid it.

C. CIV. Concerning Boniface, who swore that he would not communicate with excommunicated persons and pseudo-bishops [Note: [Col. 0877D] “And pseudo-bishops”: in some old copies this previously read, “excommunicated by pseudo-bishops”]. Likewise Boniface the Martyr, to Pope Zacharias, in the letter beginning “Fatherly …” [Note: [Col. 0877D] The letter containing this chapter was published by Laurentius Surius in the life of St Boniface, legate to Germany and martyr. A more correct manuscript copy exists at Rome in the library of the Dominican monastery] [Note: [Col. 0877] written about A.D. 751; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, ch. 95].

When Gregory, the predecessor of your predecessor, of venerable memory, ordained me, though unworthy, and sent me to preach the word of God to the German peoples, he bound me by oath to be a supporter and helper of canonical and just bishops and priests in word, deed [Note: [Col. 0877] “and deed”: editions compared with the original], and consent [Note: [Col. 0877] “and consent”: eds. Bas., Lugd. II–III, and Ivo; “in consent”: ed. Arg.; “and in consent”: the other editions]—which, by divine grace, I have striven to fulfill [Note: [Col. 0877] “this, however”: original, Ivo, and editions compared with the original; “fulfill”: same editions]—but either to correct false priests, hypocrites, and deceivers of the people toward the way of salvation, or to avoid them [Col. 0878B] and refrain from their communion. This I have partly observed, and partly have been unable to observe and fulfill; yet I have fulfilled the oath spiritually, because my soul did not enter into their agreement [Note: [Col. 0877] “and into agreement”: ed. Bas.] or counsel, although bodily I was altogether unable to abstain from them. For, when I came to the prince of the Franks, compelled by the necessity of the Churches, I did not find there the sort of people I wished; yet I did not communicate with them in the holy communion of Christ’s body [Note: [Col. 0877] “them”: ed. Bas.].

C. CV. One who does not consent to them in mind does not communicate with the excommunicated. Likewise Pope Zacharias to Boniface the Martyr, in the letter beginning “Blessed be God” [Note: [Col. 0878D] The letter is preceded by these words: “Accordingly, your holy brotherhood represented in its letter that our predecessor, etc.”] [Note: [Col. 0877] written A.D. 751; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, ch. 96].

Our predecessor Gregory, of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0877] omitted in the editions compared with the original, except Bas.], bishop of this holy Apostolic See, when he sent your brotherhood [Col. 0878C] to preach the word of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0877] “of God”: ed. Bas.] in the regions of Germany and among those pagan peoples, wished it first to be fortified by a promise [Note: [Col. 0877] “and by word”: editions compared with the original; omitted in ed. Bas.; “instructed”: original], so that, if you found orthodox bishops, priests, or [Note: [Col. 0877] “and”: ed. Bas.] any others perfected in the word of exhortation, you would strengthen them further and communicate with them—which was done. But if you found deceptive bishops, pseudo-priests, or others likewise deviating from the straight path of faith, you were to have no communion with them. You have confessed that, with God’s assistance [Note: [Col. 0879] “helping”: ibid.], you have preserved this spiritually until the present; or, if, because of the princely and human favour of the Frankish people, when you came among them, you could not bodily abstain altogether, being compelled by the necessity of God’s Churches, yet your soul has not been defiled by sharing in their counsel and consenting to their communion [Col. 0879A] [Note: [Col. 0879] “nevertheless”: eds. Lugd. II–III and Bohm]. Therefore, because you associated with them without consenting to their wickedness, you suffer no loss before God.

IX. Part. Gratian. The form and manner of excommunication, and of reconciliation, are as follows.

C. CVI. The manner and form of excommunication [Note: [Col. 0879D] In Burchard and Ivo, the contents of this chapter and much else relevant to it are cited from the Council of Rouen [Note: [Col. 0879] thus in ed. Bas.]. But in a manuscript collection of canons by an unknown author it is reported in precisely these words as from Pope Zacharias].

Twelve priests must stand round the bishop [Note: [Col. 0879] A chapter of an unknown author, perhaps from Regino himself, book 2, ch. 409; Burchard, book 11, ch. 3; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, ch. 76], [Col. 0879B] holding lighted candles in their hands. At the conclusion of the anathema or excommunication, they must throw them to the ground and trample them underfoot. Then a letter is to be sent through the parishes containing the names of the excommunicated and the cause of their excommunication.

C. CVII. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Orange [Note: [Col. 0879] Cf. on the preceding chapter; Regino, book 2, ch. 413; Burchard, book 11, ch. 7; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, ch. 126].

Following canonical enactments and the examples of the holy Fathers, by the authority of God and judgment of the Holy Spirit, we expel violators of the Churches of God [Note: [Col. 0879D] “Violators”: in the same collection, in Burchard, and in two old manuscripts of Gratian, there follows the letter “N”; however, this mark is absent from other copies of Gratian and from Ivo] from the bosom of holy mother Church and from the fellowship of all Christendom, until they come to their senses and make satisfaction to the Church of God.

[Col. 0879C] C. CVIII. The manner of reconciling the excommunicated. Likewise from the same source [Note: [Col. 0879] Cf. on ch. 106; Regino, book 2, ch. 414; Burchard, book 11, ch. 8].

When someone who has been excommunicated or anathematized, moved by repentance, asks pardon and promises amendment, the bishop [Note: [Col. 0879] “to the bishop”: ed. Bas.] who excommunicated him must come before the doors of the church, together with twelve priests, who must stand around him on either side [Note: [Col. 0879D] “Must”: Burchard, who also cites this from the Council of Orange, continues: “Those also must be present to whom injury or loss has been done,” and much else that must be read in full]. If the person, prostrate upon the ground, asks pardon and pledges assurance for the future, then the bishop, taking his right hand, shall lead him into the church, restore him to Christian communion, and chant the seven penitential psalms [Col. 0880A] with these prayers: “Lord, have mercy”; “Our Father”; “Save your servant.” Prayer [Note: [Col. 0879] omitted in ed. Bas.]: “Grant, we beseech you, Lord, that this your servant may bring forth the worthy fruit of repentance, so that, having obtained pardon for his offences, he may be restored guiltless to your holy Church, from whose wholeness he had departed by sinning. Through, etc.”

X. Part. Gratian. John VIII, writing to the clergy and order of Salona, defines what penance is to be imposed upon priests who, though excommunicated, presume to handle the sacred ministry, saying [Note: [Col. 0879] In the collection of John VIII’s letters, epistle 311, in Mansi, vol. 17, and in Ivo, *Decretum*, part 14, ch. 35, it is said to have been addressed to the clergy and order of Salerno. In the *Panormia*, book 5, ch. 104, it reads as in Gratian]:

C. CIX. What penance is to be imposed upon priests who, though excommunicated, presume to handle the sacred ministry.

Those priests who, during the time of our most holy predecessor, Lord Pope Nicholas, presumed while excommunicated to handle the sacred ministry have incurred upon themselves the sentence of condemnation, as the sacred canons have decreed. Nevertheless, because apostolic compassion customarily grants pardon to the corrected, we extend this indulgence to them on account of the multitude of mercy: nourished by holy communion, they are to strive for three consecutive years to fast completely each week, on every Monday [Note: [Col. 0880D] “Every Monday”: Ivo and several old Gratian manuscripts read, “every Monday and Friday”; in the original, “every Wednesday and Friday”] and Wednesday and Friday, from wine [Note: [Col. 0880D] “From wine”: the *Panormia* reads, “either from wine or meat”; Ivo, “from wine or vinegar” [Note: [Col. 0879] “from food”: original]] and meat, and thereafter commit no further deeds requiring lamentation.

Gratian. Those who communicate with the excommunicated, however, are to receive penance according to the degree of their sin.

Accordingly Urban II, to Genebald, Bishop of Constance [Note: [Col. 0879] Berthold of Constance reports this letter as addressed to Gebehard of Constance, A.D. 1089, 14 Kalends of May; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, ch. 107; *Decretum*, part 14, ch. 45], says:

C. CX. Those who communicate with the excommunicated are to be punished according to the degree of their sin.

For the holy canons plainly provide that whoever communicates with an excommunicated person is to be excommunicated. Yet we determine the forms of that penance and absolution with such moderation [Note: [Col. 0879] “we have distinguished”: original; “we have decreed”: Ivo, *Decretum*] that whoever has contaminated himself by association, greeting, prayer, a kiss [Note: [Col. 0879] “or a kiss”: original, Ivo, and ed. Bas.], or conversation with them, whether through ignorance, fear, or the necessity of some very great and urgent business [Col. 0880C], may obtain participation in our fellowship through the remedy of a lesser penance [Note: [Col. 0879] “participation”: original and Ivo; “participated”: ed. Arg.]. But we wish those who have incurred this either voluntarily or negligently to be received under such disciplinary restraint that fear may be instilled in others.

CAUSA XII.

[Col. 0881]

[Col. 0881A] GRATIAN.

Certain clerics wish to leave property of their own; they make wills concerning their own goods and those of the Church; they bestow certain things from Church property. (Question I.) The first question, therefore, is whether clerics may lawfully possess private property. (Question II.) Second, whether Church property which they have given can be securely held by those who received it. (Question III.) Third, if persons who appeared to possess nothing before their ordination are known to have acquired something after ordination, whether they may leave it to whomever they wish, or not. (Question IV.) Fourth, if they are known to have acquired things from both their own resources and those of the Church, whether these belong jointly to both, or separately by right to the Church or to the priest. (Question V.) Fifth, whether they may make wills.

# QUESTION I

[Col. 0881B]

## GRATIAN

### Part I. Clerics are commanded by many authorities to possess nothing.

For the Fourth Council of Toledo says, chapter 23 [Note: [Col. 0881] Held in A.D. 633.—Collection in Three Parts, part 2, title 17, chapter 4; Anselm, book 7, chapter 1.]:

### C. I. Boys and adolescents living in one dormitory are to be assigned to a most approved elder.

Every age [Note: [Col. 0881] Add “also”: Argentinian edition.], from adolescence onward [Note: [Col. 0881] “Toward”: Basel edition.], is inclined toward evil. For nothing is more uncertain than the life of adolescents. For this reason it was necessary to establish [Note: [Col. 0881] “It was necessary to establish”: Hispanic Collection; Anselm.] that, if there are any boys [Note: [Col. 0881] “Adults”: Anselm.] or adolescents among the clergy, all should live together in one room of the atrium [Note: [Col. 0881] Omitted in all editions collated except Basel; “reside” (*commorentur*) for “live together” (*commaneant*): Hispanic Collection.], so that they may spend the years of their unstable age not in luxury but in ecclesiastical disciplines [Col. 0881C], assigned to a most approved elder whom they may have both as a teacher of discipline [Note: [Col. 0881] “Doctrine”: same source; Anselm; all editions collated.] and as a witness to their life.

§ 1. But if any among them are wards, they are to be cared for under priestly guardianship, so that both their lives may remain untouched by crimes and their property [Note: [Col. 0881] Add “their”: all editions collated.] unharmed by the injury of wicked [Note: [Col. 0881] “Impious”: the same editions.] persons. But those who resist these ordinances [Note: [Col. 0881] “Resist” (*reluctaverint*) for “rebel against” (*resultaverint*): Hispanic Collection.] are to be assigned to monasteries [Col. 0882A], so that wandering and proud minds [Note: [Col. 0881] “Souls … proud”: the same source.] may be restrained by a stricter rule.

### C. II. A common life must be maintained by all clerics. Likewise, Clement, Epistle V [Note: [Col. 0881] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare the *Recognitions of Clement*, book 10, chapter 5. It has not been found in Anselm, book 7, chapter 1, from which the Correctors cite it.]

Clement, bishop, to his most beloved brothers and fellow disciples living at Jerusalem with the most beloved brother James, fellow bishop [Note: [Col. 0881] “And fellow bishop”: all editions collated.]. A common life, brothers, is necessary for all, and especially for those who desire to serve God blamelessly and to imitate the life of the apostles and their disciples.

§ 1. For the common use of all things in this world ought to have belonged to all human beings. But through injustice one person said that this thing was his own, another that thing was his own [Note: [Col. 0881] “That”: the same editions], and thus division arose among mortals.

§ 2. Finally, one of the wisest Greeks [Col. 0882B], knowing that this was so, said: “All things ought to be common among friends.” [Note: [Col. 0881] Add “common”: Nore, Venice I and II, Lyons, and Paris editions.] [The words “Among all things, wives too are undoubtedly included” [Col. 0881C] are absent from the original as printed in recent editions of the councils, from two manuscripts of the work itself—one Vatican manuscript and another from the Library of St Mark at Florence—and from Anselm. Certain heretics wished to introduce this proposition, taken from Plato, into the Christian religion. Thus Epiphanius writes in Heresy 32: “First, Epiphanes himself, together with his father Carpocrates, leader of the sect, and his companions, decreed that wives should be held in common among men, taking occasion from Plato’s books *On the Republic* and fulfilling his own lust.” Yet Tertullian clearly attests in the *Apology* that this community of wives was also vigorously condemned among early Christians, in these words: “Among us all things are undiscriminated, except wives. In that one matter we dissolve partnership in which alone other people practise partnership: they not only appropriate the marriages of friends, but also most patiently provide their own wives to friends, following, I suppose, that teaching of their ancestors and wisest men, the Greek Socrates and the Roman Cato, who shared their wives with friends,” etc.]

And, he says, just as air and the brightness of the sun cannot be divided, so likewise the other things which have been given in this world for all to possess in common ought not to be divided, but ought to be held in common. Hence the Lord also speaks through the prophet [Note: [Col. 0881] Psalm 132:1.], saying: “Behold, how good and how pleasant,” etc.

§ 3. Retaining the custom of this practice, the apostles and their disciples, as has been said, led a common life together with us and with you. Hence, as you know well [Note: [Col. 0881] “For, as you know well”: all editions collated.], “the multitude of them had one heart and one soul; nor did any one of them or of us say that anything which he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them and to us,” and none among us was needy. [Col. 0882C]

§ 4. All [Note: [Col. 0881] “Indeed”: Basel edition; “but”: the remaining editions.] who possessed houses or lands sold them, and brought the prices of them and the other goods which they had [Note: [Col. 0881] “Offered” (*offerebant*) for “brought” (*afferebant*): all editions collated], laying them at the apostles’ feet—as some of you knew and saw among us—and they were distributed [Note: [Col. 0881] “They distributed”: Basel edition; “it was distributed”: the remaining editions; compare Acts 4.] to each person according to his need. [Col. 0883A]

§ 5. But Ananias, a stern man, and Sapphira his wife, who [Note: [Col. 0883] “Because”: all editions collated; compare Acts 5.] lied to the apostles concerning the price of their lands which they had sold, were both carried out dead [Note: [Col. 0883] “Carried away”: all editions collated.] before us, in the sight of all who stood around [Note: [Col. 0883] “Who were present”: Basel edition], from before the apostles [Note: [Col. 0883] Add “of all”: the same source], because of their sin and the lie which they committed. The other things which we have known and seen concerning such persons are worthy neither of recollection nor of demonstration. Therefore we command you to beware of these things and direct you to obey the teachings and examples of the apostles, because those who set aside their commands become not only guilty but also aliens from God [Note: [Col. 0883] The editions read “but also exiles from God.”]. These things are not only to be avoided by you, but also proclaimed to all.

And below:

§ 6. Therefore, giving counsel, we exhort your prudence not to depart from apostolic [Col. 0883B] rules, but to teach the common life and, rightly understanding the sacred Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0883] “Which you know well”: the same editions], to strive to fulfil what you have vowed to the Lord.

### C. III. Enclosures for clerics are to be established beside a church. Likewise, Pope Eugenius II and Leo IV, chapter 7 [Note: [Col. 0883D] This is chapter 7 of the Roman council first held by Eugenius II and later renewed by Leo IV. It was formerly cited as Leo IX.] [Note: [Col. 0883] In the Roman synod held in A.D. 826 and 853.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 5; folio 4, chapter 2; book 7, chapter 3; and at the end of that same book.]

For necessity requires [Note: [Col. 0883] “It arose” (*exstitit*): Nore edition; “exists” (*exsistit*): original and the remaining editions except Basel.] that enclosures be established beside a church, in which clerics may devote themselves to ecclesiastical disciplines. Thus there shall be one refectory and dormitory [Note: [Col. 0883] “Or” (*aut*) for “and” (*ac*): Basel edition.] for all, and the other workshops necessary for the use of clerics. After the bishop, ministers shall be chosen over them whose life and teaching may adorn them [Note: [Col. 0883] “May adorn them … may disgrace them”: original.] rather than disgrace them.

Gratian. No buildings other than those for clerics are to be placed in the church atrium. [Col. 0883C]

Accordingly Pope Nicholas says [Note: [Col. 0884D] Nearly the same things are read in chapter 12 of the Council of Seligenstadt, found at the end of Burchard’s collection and reported by Ivo, part 15.] [Note: [Col. 0883] Chapter 12, Council of Seligenstadt, held in A.D. 1022.—Burchard, at the end of his work; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, chapter 178.]:

### C. IV. No buildings except those of clerics are to be placed in the church atrium.

No buildings other than those of clerics alone [Note: [Col. 0883] Add “other”: Basel edition.] are to be erected in the church atrium.

### C. V. A cleric is to possess nothing secular. Likewise, Jerome to Nepotianus [Note: [Col. 0883] Anselm, book 7, chapter 2 (4); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 1.]

A cleric who serves the Church of Christ should first interpret his own name [Note: [Col. 0883] “First”: all editions collated.] and, having set forth its definition, strive to be what he is called. For if κλῆρος (*klēros*) in Greek is called *sors*, “lot,” in Latin, clerics are so named either because they belong to the Lord’s lot or because the Lord is the lot—that is, the portion—of clerics. [Col. 0884A] But one who is himself the Lord’s portion, or has the Lord as his portion [Note: [Col. 0883] “Of the Lord”: Ivo; “of the lord”: most editions], must present himself in such a way that he both possesses the Lord and is possessed by the Lord.

One who possesses the Lord and says with the Prophet, “The Lord is my portion” [Note: [Col. 0883] “May say”: Basel edition; Psalm 15:5.], can possess nothing outside the Lord. If he has anything else besides the Lord [Note: [Col. 0883] The passage from “If” through “Lord” is absent in Anselm.]—gold, for example, silver, estates, or various household goods—the Lord does not deign to become his portion together with those portions. But if I am the Lord’s portion and the cord of his inheritance, I receive no portion [Note: [Col. 0883] “Portions”: all editions.] among the other tribes; rather, like a Levite and priest [Col. 0884B], I live from tithes and, serving the altar [Note: [Col. 0883] “Serving” (*deserviens*): Basel edition.], am sustained by the altar’s offering. Having food and clothing [Note: [Col. 0883] 1 Timothy 6:8.], I shall be content with these, and naked I shall follow the naked cross [Note: [Col. 0883] “I follow”: Basel, Venice II, Paris, and Lyons editions.].

### C. VI. One chosen for God’s lot ought to care for nothing except God. Likewise, Ambrose, *On Flight from the World*, chapter 2.

He whose portion is God ought to care for nothing except God, lest he be hindered by the burden of another obligation. What is bestowed upon other duties is taken away from the worship of religion and from this duty of ours [Note: [Col. 0883] “From this” (*hinc*): Basel edition.]. For this is the true flight of a priest: renunciation of one’s household and a certain estrangement from those most dear, so that one who has chosen to serve God may deny himself to his own people [Note: [Col. 0883] The original reads “desires to serve.”].

### C. VII. Clerics and persons devoted to God may neither plead cases nor possess anything privately. Likewise, Jerome to one of his own Levites, *On the Two Kinds of Human Beings* [Note: [Col. 0883] Chapter of uncertain origin.]

There are two kinds of Christians. One kind is bound to divine service and devoted to contemplation and prayer; it ought to abstain from all the disturbance of temporal affairs [Note: [Col. 0883] Basel edition: “to be free from temporal affairs.”]. Such are clerics and persons devoted to God, namely converts. For κλῆρος (*klēros*) in Greek means “lot” in Latin. Hence such persons are called clerics, that is, persons chosen by lot. For God chooses all these as his own. These are kings—that is, ruling themselves and others in virtues [Note: [Col. 0883] “In their own virtues”: the same source.]—and thus they possess a kingdom in God; this is signified by the crown upon the head [Note: [Col. 0883] “Of the head”: the same source.]. [Col. 0885A] They have had this crown from the institution of the Roman Church, as a sign of the kingdom awaited in Christ. The shaving of the head, however, is the laying aside of all temporal things. Content with food and clothing, and possessing no private property among themselves, they ought to have all things in common.

§ 1. The other kind of Christians is that of laypeople. For λαός (*laos*) in Greek is *populus*, “people,” in Latin. They may possess temporal things, but only for use. For nothing is more wretched than to despise God for the sake of money. They are permitted to take a wife, cultivate land, judge between one person and another, plead cases, place offerings upon the altar [Note: [Col. 0885] “Altars”: all editions collated.], render tithes; and in this way they may be saved, provided nevertheless that by doing good they avoid vices.

### C. VIII. Clerics are to possess nothing privately. Likewise, Gregory to Augustine, bishop of the English, *Responses*, chapters 1 and 2 [Note: [Col. 0885] Epistle 65, written A.D. 601, book 14, Maurist edition.—Compare Distinction 5, chapter 1.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 3 (5).]

Because your brotherhood, trained in monastic rules, ought not to live separately [Note: [Col. 0885] Original: “to live.”] from its clerics in the Church of the English, which has recently been brought to the faith by God’s authorship, it ought to establish that manner of life which existed among our fathers at the beginning of the nascent Church. Among them no one said that anything he possessed was his own [Note: [Col. 0885] “Had anything as his own”: all editions collated.], but all things were common to them.

§ 1. But clerics who are outside sacred orders and cannot remain continent [Note: [Col. 0885] Compare Distinction 32, chapter 3.] ought to take wives and receive their stipends from outside. For concerning those same fathers of whom we have spoken, we know that it is written: “It was distributed to each according to his need” [Note: [Col. 0885] “They distributed”: all editions collated; compare Acts 4:35.]. Provision and care must therefore also be made for their stipend; and they must be kept under ecclesiastical rule, so that they may live with good morals, be diligent in singing psalms, and, with God’s help, keep heart, tongue, and body from every unlawful thing.

§ 2. But concerning those who live in common [Note: [Col. 0885] “A common … life”: original; Anselm.], what need be said by us about making distributions, offering hospitality, and carrying out mercy [Note: [Col. 0885] “By us”: all editions collated.], when everything left over [Note: [Col. 0885] Add “for necessities”: original and all editions collated.] must be expended on pious and religious causes? For the Lord and teacher of all says [Note: [Col. 0885] “Which you know well”: the same editions.]: “Give what remains as alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.”

### C. IX. All things ought to be common to clerics. Likewise, Pope Urban, to all Catholics, sole epistle, chapter 1 [Note: [Col. 0885] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 2 (6); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 139.]

We know that you are not unaware [Note: [Col. 0885] Add “brothers”: Basel edition.] that until now the common life has flourished among all Christians [Note: [Col. 0885] “Good Christians”: original; Anselm.], and still flourishes by the grace of God, especially among those chosen for the Lord’s lot, that is, clerics. Thus it is read in the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0885] Acts 4:32]: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul; nor did any one of them—or of us [Note: [Col. 0885] Add *aut nostrum*, “or of us”: Basel edition.]—say that anything of the things which he possessed [Note: [Col. 0885] Add *de his, quae*, “of the things which”: Basel edition.] was his own, and [Note: [Col. 0885] “And” (*et*) for “but” (*sed*): Basel edition.] all things were common to them.” [Col. 0886A]

And below:

§ 1. Whoever among you has undertaken the common life and vowed to possess nothing privately must see that he does not make his promise void, but faithfully keep what he has promised the Lord, so that he may acquire for himself not condemnation but reward. For it is better [Note: [Col. 0885] “Holier”: the same source; “better”: the remaining editions.] not to vow than, as far as one is able, not to fulfil a vow. For those who have made a vow or received the faith and have not fulfilled the vow, or have ended their life in evil, are punished more severely than those who ended life without a vow or died without faith, yet performed good works.

### C. X. On the same matter. Likewise, Augustine, in his sermon on the common life of clerics [Note: [Col. 0885D] The beginning of this chapter through the words “Whoever wishes to possess” is found in Sermon 2, *On the Common Life of Clerics*, or Sermon 52 *To the Brothers in the Desert*. The remainder is found partly in Sermon 55 *To the Brothers in the Desert*, or Sermon 3 *On the Common Life of Clerics*, and partly in the same Sermon 52 or 2; concerning these sermons, see the note above, Distinction 86. Part of this chapter is reported by Bede in his commentary on 2 Corinthians 8 under the title “From the sermon on the life and morals of clerics.”] [Note: [Col. 0885] Anselm, book 7, chapter 6 (8).—Compare the Council of Aachen, chapter 112.]

I do not want any of you [Note: [Col. 0885] “Of us”: Basel edition.] to find an occasion for living badly. For we provide good things, as the Apostle says, not only before God but also before all people [Note: [Col. 0885] The reference is lacking in the source; compare 2 Corinthians 8.] [Note: [Col. 0885] Omitted in the Venice II, Paris, and Lyons editions.]. For our own sake, our conscience is sufficient [Note: [Col. 0885] “Is necessary”: Anselm and the editions collated.] for us; for your sake, our reputation ought not to be stained but to be strong among you [Note: [Col. 0885] “Among us”: Basel edition.]. [Col. 0886C] Hold fast what I have said and distinguish it [Note: [Col. 0885] “Hold fast … distinguish”: omitted in Anselm.]: there are two things, conscience and reputation. Conscience is necessary for you; reputation, for your neighbour. One who, trusting in his own conscience [Note: [Col. 0885] Omitted in Anselm.], neglects his reputation [Note: [Col. 0885] Omitted in the editions collated except the first Basel edition.], is cruel.

And below:

§ 1. No one may [Note: [Col. 0885] “It is permitted” (*licet*) for “may” (*liceat*): Basel edition.] in our community possess anything privately; but [Note: [Col. 0885] Omitted in the Basel edition.] if perhaps some persons possess something [Note: [Col. 0885] Original: “anything”], this is permitted to no one; and those who possess it [Note: [Col. 0885] “But those who”: Basel edition; Anselm.] do what is not permitted.

And below:

§ 2. We may not have a treasury [Note: [Col. 0885] “For us” (*nobis*) is omitted in Anselm.]. For it is not the bishop’s [Note: [Col. 0885] “Of bishops”: Anselm and the editions collated.] task to preserve gold and to draw back from himself the hand of a beggar. Every day so many ask, so many lament, so many needy persons appeal to us, that we must leave more people sorrowful because we do not have enough to give to all. Therefore let us not have a treasury. [Col. 0887A]

And below:

§ 3. Whoever [Note: [Col. 0887] “Whoever has private property or wishes to possess it” (*Qui habuerit proprium vel habere voluerit*): all editions collated; compare Sermon 153.] wishes to possess private property, live from his own means, and act contrary to these precepts—it is too little for me to say that he shall not remain with me; he shall not even be a cleric. For I had said, and I know that I said, that if they did not wish to undertake the common life [Note: [Col. 0887] Add “also”: Nore and Venice I editions.] with me, I would not take away their clerical status [Note: [Col. 0887] Omitted in the Argentinian and Basel editions.], but they should remain apart and live apart—however they knew how, they should live for God—and yet I set before their eyes how great an evil [Note: [Col. 0887] “How great the evil”: all editions collated; Bohm.] it is to fall away from one’s purpose [Note: [Col. 0887] Omitted in the Basel edition.]. For I preferred to have blind or lame persons rather than mourn the dead. For every hypocrite is dead. How, then, could I fail to take clerical status from anyone who wished to remain outside and live from his own means? Yet now, because by God’s favour this common life has pleased them, whoever lives hypocritically, whoever is found possessing private property, I do not permit him to make a will from it [Note: [Col. 0887] “To make it”: Basel edition.], but I shall erase him from the register of clerics.

Likewise above:

§ 4. Whoever does not wish to remain with me and live in common may have freedom, but let him see whether he can possess the inheritance of blessedness [Note: [Col. 0887D] In the sermon itself chapter “Certainly I” precedes this passage below, and, after a few intervening words, there follows: “whoever does not wish this, let him have freedom,” etc.; [Col. 0887] “eternity”: original; C. XI.].

### C. XI. Those who renounce their own property and promise to live in common may not possess private property. The same author, Sermon III, *On the Common Life of Clerics* [Note: [Col. 0887D] This chapter is taken from Sermon 3, *On the Common Life of Clerics*, in which the Rule of St Augustine is contained and is repeated in Epistle 109. In that epistle, however, the address is directed to nuns.] [Note: [Col. 0887] From the epistle to Seleuciana concerning religious women.]

Do not call anything your own [Note: [Col. 0887] “That you have anything of your own”: all editions collated.], but let all things be common to you.

And below:

§ 1. If anyone has progressed [Note: [Col. 0887] “Entered”: Argentinian edition.] so far in evil as secretly to receive a letter or any gift from someone, if he voluntarily confesses this, he is to be spared and prayer is to be made for him. But if he is discovered and convicted, he is to be corrected more severely according to the judgment of the priest [Note: [Col. 0887] “Of the bishop or priest”: Basel edition.] or superior. [Col. 0887C]

And below:

§ 2. [Note: Similar things are read in the Rule to the Servants of God, wrongly attributed to Augustine.]

Since the brothers of this our congregation have renounced not only their own possessions but also their own wills at the very reception of their order [Note: [Col. 0887] “Of their order”: all editions collated], and through promised obedience have wholly subjected themselves to another’s authority [Note: [Col. 0887] “Will”: Basel edition] and commands in Christ and for Christ, it is certain that they ought neither to have, possess, give, nor receive anything without the superior’s permission.

[Note: [Col. 0888D] From “Since the brothers of this our congregation” through the words “It is certain,” these words have not been found in St Augustine.]

[Note: [Col. 0888D] “It is certain”: these words occur in the first Rule, chapter 4.]

§ 3. But if a relative, friend, or any brother wishes to offer something to anyone, it must first be reported to the prior, and then received if he commands it. Nothing else, however, is to be done with it except what pleases the prior. [Col. 0888A]

### C. XII. On the same matter. The same author, Tractate L on John 12.

Take the example of the Lord living on earth. Why did he have a money-box, when angels ministered to him [Note: [Col. 0887] “Ministered”: the editions collated], unless because his Church was to have its own money-box? Why did he admit a thief, unless so that his Church might patiently tolerate thieves when it suffers them [Note: [Col. 0887] “When it suffers”: the same editions]?

### C. XIII. Superiors of churches become stewards of their property. Likewise, Prosper, *On the Contemplative Life*, book II, chapter 9 [Note: [Col. 0887] Rather, Julianus Pomerius, whose book this is.—Compare the Council of Aachen, chapter 35.]

It is fitting that Church property be possessed, while one’s own property is despised for love of perfection. For the Church’s resources are not private but common; therefore, whoever, having left or sold everything which he possessed, becomes a despiser of his own property, when made superintendent of a church becomes the steward of all that the Church possesses. [Col. 0888B]

Finally, as you yourselves know better, St Paulinus sold the enormous estates which were his own and distributed them to the poor. But when he was made a bishop, he did not despise the Church’s resources, but administered them with the greatest fidelity. By this he sufficiently showed [Note: [Col. 0887] “Is shown” (*ostenditur*) for “he showed” (*ostendit*): Basel, Venice II, Paris, and Lyons editions.] both that one’s own property ought to be despised for the sake of perfection, and that Church resources—which are certainly common [Note: [Col. 0887] “Common”: Basel edition; original.]—may be possessed [Note: [Col. 0887] “May possess”: all editions collated except Lyons II and III.] without hindrance to perfection.

What of St Hilary? Did not he too [Note: [Col. 0887] Omitted in the editions collated except the first Basel edition.] leave all his goods [Col. 0888C] to his parents or, after selling them, distribute them to the poor? Yet when, by the merit of his perfection, he became bishop [Note: [Col. 0887] “Archbishop”: Basel edition.] of the Church of Arles, he not only possessed (*possedit*) what that Church then had [Note: [Col. 0887] “Was possessing” (*possidebat*) for “possessed” (*possedit*): all editions collated except the first Basel edition.], but even enlarged it through the numerous inheritances received from believers. Thus these most perfect bishops plainly proclaim by their deeds that what they did can and ought to be done. Since these men were without doubt most learned in both secular and divine matters [Note: [Col. 0887] “Scriptures”: Basel edition; “letters”: the remaining editions], if they had known that Church property ought to be despised, they who had left all their own possessions ought never to have retained it [Note: [Col. 0887] “Received it”: all editions collated.].

[Note: [Col. 0889] “Found”: Lyons I edition.]

### C. XIV. Deacons and all religious persons are to be compelled to lead a regular life. Likewise, Gregory to Felix, bishop of Acropolis, book II, epistle 29 [Note: [Col. 0889] Epistle 43, written A.D. 592, book 2, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 7 (9).]

Because the churches of Velina, Buxentina [Note: [Col. 0889] “Vicentina”: Lyons II and III editions; “Vixentina”: the remaining editions.] and Blandana [Note: [Col. 0889] “Blandina”: all editions collated]—which are situated near you and are known to lack the governance of a priest—we have formally imposed [Note: [Col. 0889] “We impose” (*injungimus*) for “we imposed” (*injunximus*): original and all editions collated.] upon your brotherhood the duty of visiting them [Note: [Col. 0889] “Work”: Argentinian, Nore, and Venice I editions.], especially charging you [Note: [Col. 0889] Omitted in the Argentinian, Nore, Venice I and II, Paris, and Lyons editions.] that wherever deacons or religious persons are found in the aforesaid churches or their dioceses [Note: [Col. 0889] “Dioceses”: all editions collated], they are to live strictly and canonically.

### C. XV. Why estates were sold in the primitive Church. Likewise, Pope Miltiades.

[Note: [Col. 0889C] Other collectors likewise cite Miltiades, but the author of the gloss rightly observes that this cannot stand. For this chapter mentions the Nicene synod, by whose time—as is clear from the synod itself, Eusebius, and other historians—Miltiades had already died. [Col. 0890C] It occurs in full in the writing *On the Primitive Church and Constantine’s Generosity*, which in the Isidorian collection, printed twice at Paris, follows immediately after the decrees of Miltiades, as was noted above at Distinction 88, chapter “He Decreed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0889] From the Pseudo-Isidorian decree *On the Primitive Church*.—Compare the *Acts of Sylvester* and Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 1, chapter 2.—Burchard, book 3, chapters 2 and 5; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 3; *Decretum*, part 3, chapters 4 and 7; Polycarpus, book 1, title 19.]

[Col. 0889B]

The apostles foresaw the future Church among the Gentiles; therefore they did not acquire estates in Judaea, but only money to support the needy. But when the Church grew amid the storms and adversities of the world, it reached the point [Note: [Col. 0889] “To this point”: all editions collated; “so far”: Burchard and Ivo, *Decretum*.] that not only the Gentiles but even Roman emperors, who held the monarchy of almost the whole world, flocked to the faith of Christ and the sacraments of baptism.

Among them Constantine, a most religious man, the first openly to embrace the faith of truth, granted that those living throughout the world under his empire [Note: [Col. 0889] “In”: Ivo, *Panormia*.] might not only become Christians but also build churches [Note: [Col. 0889] “To build”: all editions collated; “to be built”: Ivo, *Panormia*.], and he decreed that they might grant estates [Note: [Col. 0889] “To be granted”: the same editions; Ivo, *Panormia*.]. Finally, the same aforementioned prince bestowed immense gifts and established the construction of the church of the first see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles [Col. 0889C], so that he left the imperial seat which Roman emperors had possessed and granted it for the benefit of blessed Peter and his successors.

§ 1. The same ruler, presiding at the holy synod assembled at Nicaea, when he saw a complaint brought before him by certain persons [Note: [Col. 0889] “Examined”: Basel edition; “to be brought”: all editions collated.], said: “You cannot be judged by anyone, because you are reserved for the judgment of God alone. For you are called gods, and therefore you cannot be judged by human beings.”

From that time onward, most religious men [Note: [Col. 0889] “A religious man”: the same editions.] [Col. 0890A] consecrated to the Lord not only the possessions and estates which they owned [Note: [Col. 0889] “Had owned”: the same editions], but also themselves, building basilicas on their own lands in honour [Note: [Col. 0889] “In honour”: Lyons II and III editions.] of the holy martyrs in cities, and countless monasteries in which gatherings of those serving the Lord might assemble [Note: [Col. 0889] “Would have assembled”: Basel edition.].

### C. XVI. Why the estates of believers are not now to be alienated by the Church. Likewise, Pope Urban, sole epistle, chapter 1 [Note: [Col. 0889] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare the Council of Paris, held in A.D. 829, chapter 15.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 6; Burchard, book 3, chapter 3; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 5.]

But the high priests and others, the Levites, and the remaining faithful, seeing that greater benefit could be provided if they transferred to the churches governed by bishops the inheritances and lands which they sold, because from their revenues they could supply more and better things, both at present and in future times, to believers living the common life [Note: [Col. 0889] “The faith”: original.] than from their price, began to transfer to the mother churches the estates and lands which they had customarily sold, and to live from their revenues. [Col. 0890B]

§ 1. These same goods were, and are even now, and ought always in future times to be, under the authority of the bishops of the individual parishes, who hold the place of the apostles. From these goods bishops and their faithful stewards must supply every necessity [Note: [Col. 0889] “The common life”: all editions collated.] to all who wish to lead the common life, as best they can, so that none among them may be found needy.

§ 2. For these goods are called offerings of the faithful because they are offered to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0889] “Which are offered to the Lord by the faithful”: the same editions.].

And below, chapter 3:

§ 3. Through the aforesaid increases and religious observances the churches over which bishops preside have grown so greatly with the Lord’s help, and the greater part of them abounds in such extensive resources [Note: [Col. 0889] “In such resources”: the same editions.] that no one living the common life among them is needy [Note: [Col. 0889] Original: “leading”; Basel edition: “living the common life.”], but receives every necessity from the bishop and his ministers [Note: [Col. 0889] “May receive”: all editions collated.]. [Col. 0890C]

§ 4. Therefore, if anyone in present or future times attempts to tear these things away [Note: [Col. 0889] “This”: Basel edition.], let him be struck by the condemnation already stated.

### C. XVII. On the same matter. Likewise, Augustine, Tractate LXII on John [Note: [Col. 0889] Anselm, book 5, chapter 32; Polycarpus, book 3, title 24.]

The Lord had a money-box, preserving what was offered by the faithful [Col. 0891A], and giving from it both to meet the needs of his followers and to other needy persons. Then for the first time the pattern for ecclesiastical money was established, so that we might understand that his command not to be anxious about tomorrow was not given so that no money should be kept by the saints, but so that one should not serve God for the sake of money, or abandon justice through fear of poverty.

### Part II. Gratian.

From all these authorities it is clear that clerics may in no way possess anything privately; if they possess it, they will not be clerics. Nevertheless, clerical status is not to be taken from them.

Thus Augustine says in Sermon II, *On the Common Life of Clerics* [Note: [Col. 0891] Sermon 355, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 8.]:

### C. XVIII. Clerical status is not taken from those who wish to possess something privately.

Certainly, I am the one who had decreed, as you know, that I would ordain no one a cleric unless he wished to remain with me; or, if he wished to withdraw from the undertaking, that I would rightly take clerical status from him because he would abandon the promised and begun fellowship of holy community. Behold, in the presence of God and of you, I change my decision.

Those who wish to possess something privately, for whom God and his Church are not enough [Note: [Col. 0891] “His”: Anselm; the editions collated read “its.”], may remain where they wish and where they can. I do not take clerical status from them; I do not wish to have hypocrites. For who does not know that it is evil? [Note: [Col. 0891] Omitted in Anselm and the Argentinian and Basel editions.] It is evil to fall away from one’s undertaking, but worse to feign the undertaking.

And after a few words:

§ 1. If a person does not preserve holiness outwardly, he has fallen halfway; but if inwardly he harbours pretence, he has fallen entirely. I do not want him to have a need to pretend. I know how people love clerical status. I take it from no one who does not wish to live in common with me. [Col. 0891C]

Gratian. On the other hand, there are other authorities by which possession of private property is permitted not only to others but also to bishops.

Thus it is read in the Council of Agde, chapter 48 [Note: [Col. 0891] Held in A.D. 506.—Compare, however, Distinction 23, chapter 30.—Collection in Three Parts, part 2, title 25, chapter 46.]:

### C. XIX. Bishops may leave to their heirs property that is their own or that they have acquired.

Bishops may leave to their heirs, if they wish, property that is their own or that they have acquired, or whatever they possess from their own resources. [Note: [Col. 0891] “Whatever a bishop has from his own private property, to his heirs,” etc.: Hispanic Collection.] [Note: [Col. 0891] “Let them leave” or “let them bequeath”: Basel edition.] But whatever belongs to the endowment of their church—whether lands, produce, or offerings—we have decreed must all be kept in the right of the church. [Note: [Col. 0891] “Crops”: ibid.] [Note: [Col. 0891] “Keep”: collected editions, first Basel edition, Lyons II and III.]

[Col. 0892A] C. XX. On the same matter. Likewise, from the Council of Pope Martin, c. 15. [Note: [Col. 0891] c. 4 of the Council of Antioch, in the translation of Martin of Braga, with wording altered but the sense preserved.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 166, from the old translation.]

But the things belonging to the church ought to be known to those around them—that is, to the priests and deacons around the bishops—so that, should an unexpected death befall a bishop, the property of the church may in no way be diminished or lost; and so that the bishop’s private property may not suffer inconvenience on account of church property, with the result that neither the church incurs loss nor the bishop is deprived of his own property on account of church property. [Note: [Col. 0891] “Bishops”: Hispanic Collection; collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 0891] Omitted in the Hispanic Collection.] [Note: [Col. 0891] Adds “for”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0891] “Be prescribed”: Hispanic Collection.]

The same is laid down in canon 4 of the Apostolic Canons, where one reads: [Note: [Col. 0891] Anselm, bk. 6, c. 167 (166).]

C. XXI. On the same matter.

Let the private property of the bishop be known—if indeed he has private property—and let the Lord’s property be known, so that when the bishop dies he may have power to leave his own property as he wishes and to whom he wishes, and so that, under pretext of church property, things proved to belong to the bishop may not be lost. [Note: [Col. 0891] “May have”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions; “have”: the remaining editions.] [Note: [Col. 0891] “May be prohibited”: collected editions.] For perhaps he has a wife, children, relatives, or servants. And this is just before God and men: that neither the church suffer loss through ignorance of the pontiff’s property, nor the bishop or his relatives be dispossessed under pretext of the church and become involved in lawsuits, and that his death be subjected to the injuries of ill repute. [Note: [Col. 0891] “Ignorance”: the same editions; Anselm.] [Note: [Col. 0891D] “And [that] his death”: Previously it read, “and that, by the injuries of his death, they be disgraced” [thus in the collected editions]. The passage has been restored from the old version, with which the remainder of the chapter agrees. The Greek reads: Καὶ τὸν αὐτοῦ θάνατον δυσφημίαις περιβάλλεσθαι, that is, “and that his death be surrounded on all sides by calumnies.”]

C. XXII. If the bishop is in need, let him take from church property what is necessary for himself and his household. Likewise in the same canons, c. 41. [Note: [Col. 0891] Anselm, bk. 6, c. 164.]

From those things of which the bishop is in need—if indeed he is in need—let him himself receive for his necessities and for the use of travelling brethren, so that he may altogether lack nothing. [Col. 0892C] [Note: [Col. 0891] “In”: collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 0892D] “May lack”: It is also read as “they may lack” [thus in Anselm]. For in Greek manuscripts the reading is in part αὐτοῦ, “him,” and in part αὐτούς, “them.”] For the law of God commands that those who serve at the altar should be fed from it. [Note: [Col. 0891] 1 Cor. 9.] [Note: [Col. 0891] “From”: Basel edition.]

C. XXIII. Let the bishop administer ecclesiastical property. Likewise, from the Council of Antioch, c. 25. [Note: [Col. 0891] Held A.D. 332.—Dionysian translation.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 163 (167).]

Let the bishop have authority over ecclesiastical property in order to distribute it among all who are in need, with the utmost reverence and fear of God. Let him himself also share in those things he needs—if indeed he is in need—for the necessary uses both of his own household and of brethren received by him, so that in no circumstance they are defrauded, according to the holy Apostle, who says: “Having food and covering, let us be content with these.” [Col. 0893A] [Note: [Col. 0893] 1 Tim. 6:8.] [Note: [Col. 0891] Omitted in the Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0891] Omitted.] [Note: [Col. 0893] *nulla* (“no [occasion]”): Anselm; collected editions.] But if he is by no means content with these things, and turns church property to his domestic uses, and manages its revenues or the produce of its lands not with the knowledge of the priests and deacons but entrusts authority over them to his household servants, relatives, brothers, or sons, so that through such persons the affairs of the church may secretly be harmed, he shall pay the penalties imposed by the provincial synod. [Note: [Col. 0893D] “The affairs of the church may secretly be harmed”: In Dionysius’s translation it reads: “so that through such persons the other churches may secretly be harmed” [“the other churches are harmed”: Anselm; Dionysius]; and this agrees with another old translation, also found in the council volumes: “so that by their secret management ecclesiastical matters may appear to be harmed.” In the manuscripts consulted, the Greek reads: Εἰς τὸ διὰ τῶν τοιούτων λεληθότως βλάπτεσθαι τοὺς λόγους τῆς ἐκκλησίας, that is, “so that through such persons the accounts/affairs of the church may secretly be harmed.”]

But if a bishop, or the priests who are with him, is accused on another ground—namely, of appropriating to themselves things belonging to the church, whether from lands or from any other ecclesiastical resource—so that the poor are thereby afflicted and both the preaching of the word and those who administer these things are exposed to accusations and blasphemies, they must be corrected, with the approval of the holy synod as it determines. [Note: [Col. 0893] “Accusations”: collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 0893] “This”: the same editions.] [Note: [Col. 0893] “Approving”: the same editions with Anselm.]

C. XXIV. Church property is to be under the bishop’s authority. Likewise in the Apostolic Canons, c. 41. [Note: [Col. 0893] Anselm, bk. 6, c. 150 (164).]

We command that the bishop hold the church’s property under his own authority. For if the souls of men, which are more precious, have been entrusted to him, then much more must he administer money, so that under his authority everything may be distributed to those in need through priests and deacons, and may be administered with fear of God and every care. [Note: [Col. 0893] “Precious”: original.] [Note: [Col. 0893] “Concerning money”: Anselm; collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 0893] “Conduct”: collected editions.] But from these things, of which he is in need, etc., as above. [Note: [Col. 0893] Above, c. 22.]

Gratian. Therefore, since the Council of Agde, Martin’s council, and the Apostolic Canons say, “Let the bishop’s private property be known,” and since the Canons and the Council of Antioch direct that the bishop share in church property, if indeed he is in need, is it not plainly shown that the bishop may freely possess private property? For by saying, “if he needs church property,” the text indicates that he possesses private means which perhaps are insufficient for his needs. How, then, can a cleric cease to be one if he wishes to possess private property, while a bishop who possesses private property not only does not cease to be a bishop but is even commanded to keep all ecclesiastical resources under his authority?

§ 1. But it should be noted that Eastern bishops have wives and children; and that some in our regions, while they were laymen or in minor orders, had wives and children, and then, either after the death of their wives or after mutual observance of a vow of continence, proceeded to sacred orders. All such persons are permitted to possess private property for the use of themselves and their dependents. But those who from childhood have been committed to sacred service are in no way permitted to possess private property, because they have no excuse for ownership—unless perhaps they keep what is theirs and refrain from drawing upon the church’s resources. Prosper [Note: [Col. 0893] Rather, Julianus Pomerius.] testifies in *On the Contemplative Life*, book II, chapter 12, that this can be done, saying:

C. XXV. Concerning those so weak that they cannot renounce their property.

Those who are so weak that they cannot renounce their possessions, if they leave to the steward for distribution to those who have nothing the things they were going to receive, possess their own without sin. For they too in some sense abandon what is theirs, when, content with their own resources, they receive none of the things which they think are due to their labor or rank. [Col. 0894B]

Gratian. But concerning church property, the question is asked whether it may lawfully be divided by prebends, so that each person specially claims an annual revenue for himself. That this cannot be done is proved by argument and authority. Clerics are successors of those of whom it is said: “Now the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul.” [Note: [Col. 0893] Acts 4:32.] It is therefore necessary for them to follow the life of those whose rank they administer in the church. Thus they shall not claim anything as their own; rather, all things shall be common to them.

[Col. 0894C] Likewise Pope Urban says in his only epistle, c. 2. [Note: [Col. 0893] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Anselm, bk. 5, c. 35 (36); Polycarpus, bk. 6, tit. 15.]

C. XXVI. Let the bishop administer church property as though it were common.

Church property is not to be administered as though it were private property, but as common property offered to the Lord, and with the highest fear of God it must faithfully be distributed only for the aforesaid uses. [Note: [Col. 0893] “As though”: Basel edition.]

C. XXVII. A bishop may not convert church property to his own uses. Likewise, from the synod held at Rome under Pope Eugenius II, c. 16. [Note: [Col. 0893] Held A.D. 826.]

No bishop may keep for his own use movable or immovable property from subject congregations or other pious places, lest the more eminent be outrageously enriched and the lesser be found impoverished by such conduct. Whoever acts contrary to this shall be restrained by canonical authority. [Note: [Col. 0893] “Movable property or”: omitted in the original.] [Note: [Col. 0893] “For his own uses”: Basel and Lyons editions.]

[Col. 0895A] Gratian. Therefore, if church property must be held not as private but as common property, since no one says of common property, “This is mine,” no one can say of church property, “This is mine,” lest he seem not to imitate the charity of those among whom nothing was private to anyone but all things were common to them.

§ 1. The answer to this is as follows. While the perfection of charity remains, the ecclesiastical resources are distributed according to the discernment of the churches: possessions of a given church are entrusted to some persons for administration; and from these resources, although church property ought to be common to all, they must first provide what is necessary for themselves and for those serving their church, and then use what remains for the needs of the faithful. Likewise, while the same charity remains, the prebends of churches can be distributed piously and religiously. Then church property is not treated as private property but as serving common benefits: from the things assigned to him, a person first receives what he needs; but if anything remains beyond his needs, he spends it for the common uses of the church. [Col. 0895B]

Hence Augustine, in Letter L to Count Boniface: [Note: [Col. 0895] Letter 185 in the Maurist edition, written A.D. 417.—Cf. C. 23, q. 7, c. 3.]

C. XXVIII. On the same matter.

If we possess privately what is sufficient for us, those things are not ours but belong to the poor, whose administration we in some measure undertake; we do not claim ownership for ourselves by blameworthy usurpation. [Note: [Col. 0895] “If we privately possess what is sufficient for us”: original.]

Gratian. It has been shown how clerics may possess private property, and how they may not; likewise, how church property may be divided through prebends.

QUESTION II.

[Col. 0895C]

GRATIAN.

Part I. The question now is whether, if priests are known to have given away any church property, such gifts remain valid for those who received them. That church property may in no way be alienated, or possessed after alienation, is proved by many authorities.

For Pope Stephen says: [Note: [Col. 0895D] This chapter is not found in the extant letters of Stephen, but in the first letter of Anacletus, from which it is cited by Burchard and Ivo, and in the Council of Tribur, and below in the present question, “Whoever has taken away.” The same is also read under Pope Lucius.] [Note: [Col. 0895] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Boniface of Mainz, ep. 72.—Burchard, bk. 11, c. 18; Anselm, bk. 8, c. 43; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 14, c. 88.]

C. I. Whoever takes or steals the Church’s money is condemned as a murderer.

Whoever takes away, defrauds, or plunders Christ’s money and the Church’s money shall be reckoned as a murderer in the sight of the Judge.

[Col. 0896A] C. II. Whatever sacred vessels or implements have been appropriated by any cleric must be restored to the church. Likewise Pelagius to Bishop Hostilius. [Note: [Col. 0895] Chapter of uncertain date.—Tripartite Collection, pt. 1, tit. 52, c. 20.]

We have learned, through Augustine, notary of our see, who reported that your belovedness had informed him by letter, that certain members of your clergy—and especially of the parishes subject to you—had disposed of not a few sacred vessels or implements and had perpetrated certain deeds of this sort, alien to a religious profession. You desire that your charity be strengthened by the authority of our command, so that it may pursue or punish this with appropriate diligence.
