Therefore, by this present communication, we command that with fitting vigorous diligence you do not fail, without delay caused by anyone, to exact whatever you discover has been appropriated or alienated from sacred vessels or implements by any cleric, and to restore it to ecclesiastical use. [Note: [Col. 0895] “Augustus”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0895] “Your”: ibid.] [Note: [Col. 0895] “With fitting”: collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 0895] “Vessel”: printed text, probably an OCR error for *vasis*, “vessels.”] [Note: [Col. 0895] “To have been”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0895] “You should hesitate”: ibid.]

C. III. Whatever is consecrated to the Lord belongs by right to priests. Likewise Pope Boniface. [Note: [Col. 0895] From the Capitularies of the Frankish Kings, bk. 6, c. 405.—Burchard, bk. 11, c. 17; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 5, c. 113; *Decretum*, pt. 14, c. 37; Polycarpus, bk. 6, tit. 15.]

No one may be unaware that everything consecrated to the Lord—whether a human being, an animal, a field, or anything whatever once consecrated—shall be most holy to the Lord and shall belong by right to the priests. [Note: [Col. 0895] “Belongs”: original; Burchard; Ivo; collected editions.] Therefore everyone is without excuse who takes, devastates, invades, or seizes from the Lord and from the church to which these things belong; he shall be judged sacrilegious until restitution and satisfaction have been made to the church, and, if he refuses to make restitution, shall be excommunicated. [Note: [Col. 0895] Adds “person”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0895] “Belong”: ibid.]

[Col. 0896C] C. IV. Whoever invades church estates is subject to excommunication. Likewise Gregory VII, book VI of the Register, in a council, c. 1. [Note: [Col. 0895] c. 1 of the Roman council held A.D. 1078.—Polycarpus, bk. 6, tit. 15.]

Whoever among soldiers, or any person of whatever order or profession, receives or invades ecclesiastical estates from any king, secular prince, unwilling bishop or abbot, or any rector of a church; or holds them through the corrupt or vicious consent of their rulers, shall be subject to excommunication unless he restores those estates to the churches. [Note: [Col. 0895] “Receives, or has received or invaded, or even from,” etc.: original.]

C. V. Whoever harasses church estates incurs the crime of sacrilege. Likewise Pope Pius, Letter II. [Note: [Col. 0895] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Breviary of Alaric, bk. 16, tit. 4, c. 40.—Anselm, bk. 5, c. 36 (35); Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 13, c. 39; Polycarpus, ibid.]

Some apply estates handed over for divine uses to human uses, and withdraw them from the Lord to whom they were entrusted, so that they may serve themselves. Therefore the insult of such usurpation must be driven away by all, lest estates dedicated to the uses of the heavenly mysteries be harassed by certain aggressors. If anyone should dare to do this, let him be regarded as sacrilegious. [Col. 0897A] [Note: [Col. 0897] “Our God”: Anselm; collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 0897] “For their own uses”: original; Anselm; Ivo.] [Note: [Col. 0897] “Under secret [rites]”: Ivo.] [Note: [Col. 0897] “Dedicated”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0897] “Anyone”: Ivo; collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 0897] “Let him be judged”: original; Ivo; collected editions.]

C. VI. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Anacletus, Letter I. [Note: [Col. 0897] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. above, c. 1.]

“Whoever takes anything from father or mother and says, ‘This is not a sin,’ is an accomplice of a murderer.” [Note: [Col. 0897] “Will say”: collected editions.] Without doubt our Father is God, who created us; our mother is the Church, which regenerated us spiritually in baptism. Therefore whoever steals, takes away, or defrauds Christ’s money and the Church’s money is a murderer. [Note: [Col. 0897] “Murder”: Basel and Lyons editions.] [Note: [Col. 0897] Adds “for himself”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0897] Omitted in Venetian I–II, Lyons, and Paris editions.]

[Col. 0897B] C. VII. Whoever invades church property must restore fourfold. Likewise Pope John I, to Archbishop Zacharias. [Note: [Col. 0897] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. the fifth Roman synod of Symmachus.—Anselm, bk. 2, c. 45.]

In the ancient statutes of the Church it is decreed that one who invades another’s property shall not go unpunished, but shall restore everything with multiplication. Hence it is also written in the Gospel: “If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” [Note: [Col. 0897] Luke 19:8.] And the laws of the secular order likewise provide: “Whoever steals another’s property,” etc. (as appears below in the authority of Pope Eusebius). [Note: [Col. 0897] Cf. below, c. 10.]

C. VIII. Invaders of ecclesiastical property are to be punished according to the tenor of secular laws. Likewise Gregory to Queen Constance of Gaul, book IV, letter 33. [Note: [Col. 0897C] The beginning of this chapter, through the word “remain silent,” is taken from the indicated letter. The remainder has not been found.] [Note: [Col. 0897] Letter of Gregory V to Queen Constance of Gaul, written A.D. 998.—The beginning of the chapter attributed to Gregory V was altered from Letter 41, bk. 5, of Gregory the Great to Empress Constantina; hence it appears that the book and chapter number added to the heading by the Correctors should be deleted.—Burchard, bk. 11, c. 26; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 13, c. 36.]

Since I know that Your Most Devout Ladyship diligently considers the heavenly life and the remedy of her soul, I consider that I commit a grave fault if I keep silent concerning matters which ought to be urged out of fear of the almighty Lord, and do not diligently warn you, most holy lady, concerning the peace of the Church. The complaint recently brought by Julian, our brother and fellow bishop, has deeply grieved me, especially since the estates belonging to his church have been plundered by utterly wicked robbers and, like thieves, burned in nocturnal fires. [Col. 0898A] Since these same evil men, contrary to the decrees of our predecessor Boniface, have refused to make amends for the violated immunity, and since secular laws also have directed the same result, as the common law testifies, in which it is written:

[Note: [Col. 0897C] “Violated”: This word is absent from most old manuscripts—also from the original, Burchard, Ivo, and the Basel edition—both here and in the following chapter, where the common editions read “violated immunity.”]

“If anyone, armed and with as many as four men, comes into another’s village to do evil, the leader shall pay nine hundred solidi for his unlawful presumption, and each of his followers eighty solidi. But if they set a fire, they shall pay nine times as much; if they make plunder, they shall restore fourfold.” [Note: [Col. 0897] Lombard Law, bk. 1, tit. 18, c. 1.] [Note: [Col. 0897] “Makes a fire—shall pay, shall restore”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0897] “For himself ninefold”: Burchard; “the solidus ninefold”: Basel edition; “for himself ninefold”: remaining editions.] [Note: [Col. 0897] Adds “does”: Lyons II–III editions.]

C. IX. On the same matter. [Note: [Col. 0898C] In most old manuscripts, and in Burchard and Ivo, this chapter is joined to the preceding one.] [Note: [Col. 0897] From the same letter of Gregory V.—Burchard and Ivo, ibid.]

If secular laws have wished such justice to prevail, why should divine law be inferior, when in the presence of Truth himself Zacchaeus was praised for declaring that, if he should defraud anyone, he should restore fourfold? [Col. 0898B] [Note: [Col. 0897] Luke 19.] [Note: [Col. 0897] “Had been defrauded”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0897] “Would be restored”: ibid.; Ivo.] And because in affairs the highest good is to cultivate justice, preserve each person’s rights, and not permit in subjects what power can do but maintain what is equitable—which we trust that you too love and strive wholly to pursue—we shall therefore send Peter, our brother and fellow bishop, from the bosom of the holy Roman Church, to Your Excellency in November of this present year, in the second indiction, so that, when the brethren of that province are assembled together, violated immunity, presumption, and sacrilege may receive such an end through canonical authority and your royal dignity that henceforth the members of the devil, wicked sons, may not dare such things in the holy Church while you reign there also. [Note: [Col. 0897] “Kings”: original; cited collections.] [Note: [Col. 0897] “Therefore”: collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 0897] “We send”: original; Burchard; Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0897] Omitted in the original, cited collections, and Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0897] “After this”: Argentinian and Basel editions.]

[Col. 0898C] C. X. Whoever steals church property must restore tenfold what he has taken. Likewise Pope Eusebius, Letter II. [Note: [Col. 0897] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. the fifth Roman synod of Symmachus.—Anselm, bk. 5, c. 41 (42); Burchard, bk. 11, c. 27; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 4, c. 47; *Decretum*, pt. 13, c. 37, pt. 5, c. 249, pt. 3, c. 149; Polycarpus, bk. 8, tit. 15.]

The laws of the secular order provide: “Whoever steals another’s property shall restore to the one whose property was plundered what was taken, elevenfold.” [Note: [Col. 0897] “Tenfold”: collected editions and first Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0897] “Let them be restored to him”: Basel edition.] And in divine law it is written: “Cursed is everyone who moves his neighbor’s boundary markers, and all the people shall say, Amen.” [Col. 0899A] [Note: [Col. 0897] Deut. 27:17.] Such acts, therefore, must not be dared without punishment or committed without condemnation. Accordingly, if anyone seizes ecclesiastical offerings or what has been consecrated to God, or consents to those who do so, let him be judged sacrilegious, restore the damage fourfold, and do canonical penance. [Note: [Col. 0899D] From “Accordingly” to the end this is not in Eusebius’s letter, nor in John or Symmachus. It is found, however, in Burchard and Ivo, pt. 13, c. 37, and in Polycarpus, with several interpolated words, which occur in the letter after the word “condemnation”; also in Anselm at the cited place and in the Roman penitential, tit. 4, c. 1.]

Gratian. Against this, Gregory writes in chapter 4 of his answers to Augustine, bishop of the English, concerning those who secretly take something from a church. [Note: [Col. 0899] Letter 65, written A.D. 601, bk. 11, Maurist edition.—Cf. D. 5, c. 1.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 13, c. 5; Polycarpus, bk. 6, tit. 16.]

C. XI. The Church ought to recover what has been taken from it without an additional payment.

Your brotherhood can judge from the person of the thief how he may be corrected. Some commit theft while possessing resources; others offend in this matter out of poverty. Hence some must be corrected by financial penalties, others by beatings; some more severely, others more lightly. [Col. 0899B] And when proceedings are rather severe, they must be undertaken from charity, not from rage, because this is done for the benefit of the person corrected, lest he be consigned to the fires of Gehenna.

And below:

§ 1. You also ask with what additional amount those who took things by theft from churches ought to restore them. But far be it from the Church to receive with an additional payment what it seems to lose in temporal goods, or to seek gains from losses. [Note: [Col. 0899] “Had taken”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0899] “From losses”: ibid.]

Gratian. Eusebius’s statement concerning the severity of laws and Gregory’s statement concerning ecclesiastical gentleness must be understood accordingly.

[Col. 0899C] C. XII. Things acquired during a bishopric must not be alienated. The same Gregory, book X, letter 42, to Deusdedit, bishop of Milan. [Note: [Col. 0899] Letter 38, written A.D. 602, bk. 12, Maurist edition.—Cf. below, q. 5, c. 1.]

Priests have no permission to alienate property acquired during their episcopate.

C. XIII. Sacred vessels may not be alienated except for the ransom of captives. Likewise, from the Eighth Ecumenical Synod, c. 15. [Note: [Col. 0899D] “Eighth”: This has been corrected from Anselm; it previously read “Sixth.” It is canon 15 of the Eighth Synod, held in the time of Pope Hadrian II against Photius, in the translation of Anastasius the Librarian.] [Note: [Col. 0899] Held A.D. 869.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 171 (176).]

Renewing the apostolic and patristic canons, this holy and universal synod has decreed that no bishop whatsoever may sell or in any way alienate treasures and sacred vessels, except for the cause long established by ancient canons, namely the ransom of captives. [Col. 0900A] [Note: [Col. 0900D] “Namely, for the ransom”: In the council itself and in Anselm one reads, “which are received for the ransom of captives.”] Nor may he grant the revenues of churches on emphyteutic lease, nor sell other rural estates, and thus injure ecclesiastical revenues, which we decree exist for their proper purpose and for the sustenance of poor persons and travellers. [Note: [Col. 0899] “To be sold”: Argentinian, Basel, Venetian I–II, and Nuremberg editions.] [Note: [Col. 0900D] “We decree”: In the canon itself the following words occur: “But let everyone having authority over ecclesiastical property improve and extend, as need requires, those ecclesiastical places which produce revenues; and let him also distribute, entrust, or confer the disposition of property upon whomever he wishes and judges appropriate, according to his own authority and dominion.”]

And shortly afterwards:

§ 1. Whoever, after this decree of ours, is found to do anything contrary to this holy and universal synod shall be deposed as a transgressor of divine laws and commands. Any sale made in writing or without writing by a bishop, emphyteutic grant, or any other alienation of treasures and revenues of such places shall be wholly void. [Note: [Col. 0899] “Attempts”: collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 0899] “Things”: the same editions.] Whoever buys or receives anything from the aforesaid treasures or revenues and does not restore to the church the things belonging to the church, or does not provide for cancellation of the deed of sale or emphyteusis, shall be anathema until he does what this holy and universal synod has confirmed. [Col. 0900B] [Note: [Col. 0899] “Takes”: the same editions and first Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0899] “And”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0899] “And”: ibid.] [Note: [Col. 0899] “Restores”: collected editions.]

§ 2. But if a bishop is convicted of having built a monastery from ecclesiastical revenues, he shall hand over that monastery to the same church.

C. XIV. Sacred vessels are not forbidden to be alienated for the ransom of captives. Likewise Gregory, book VI, letter 35, to Donus, bishop of Messana. [Note: [Col. 0899] Letter 38, written A.D. 697, to Donus of Messana, bk. 7, Maurist edition.—Anselm, bk. 5, c. 48 (52).]

Both the sacred canons and legal enactments permit church implements to be sold for the ransom of captives. [Note: [Col. 0899] “Implements”: Böhm.]

C. XV. Church property may lawfully be expended for the ransom of captives. The same, to Demetrius and Valerian, clerics of Fermo, book VII, indiction 2, letter 14. [Note: [Col. 0899] Letter 17, written A.D. 599, bk. 9, Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, c. 145.]

The ordinances of the sacred canons and legal authority permit church property to be lawfully expended for the ransom of captives. [Note: [Col. 0899] Cf. *Code of Justinian*, bk. 1, tit. 2, c. 21.] Therefore, because you have informed us that about eighteen years ago a certain most reverend man, Fabius, bishop of the Church of Fermo, spent eleven pounds of silver from that church for the ransom of you, your father Passivus—our brother and fellow bishop, though then a cleric—and your mother, from enemies, and because you have consequently feared that what was given might at any time be demanded back from you, by the authority of this directive we have provided for the removal of your apprehension. We decree that neither you nor your heirs are ever to endure any claim for repayment in this matter, nor may anyone raise any question against you. [Col. 0901A] [Note: [Col. 0899] “Ransom”: collected editions and first Lyons II–III edition.] [Note: [Col. 0899] “A certain most reverend man”: supplied phrase.] [Note: [Col. 0899] “Fanius”: Basel and Lyons I editions; “Favius”: the remaining editions.] [Note: [Col. 0901] “Twelve”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0901] Adds “now”: ibid.] [Note: [Col. 0901] “And mother”: ibid.] [Note: [Col. 0901] Omitted in Basel edition.]

C. XVI. The property of a church in distress must not be preferred to captives. The same, book VI, letter 35, to Bishop Donus. [Note: [Col. 0901] From the same letter.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, c. 176.—C. XVII.]

Just as it is altogether serious to sell church implements needlessly, so likewise it is blameworthy, when such necessity presses, to prefer the property of a church—even a church in severe need—to its captives and to delay their ransom. [Col. 0901B]

Part II. Gratian. But what penance ought to be imposed upon such invaders and plunderers, who snatch sacred vessels and other things dedicated to divine worship and handle them as if they were profane, is determined by Pope Nicholas, writing to Frontarius, archbishop of Bordeaux. [Note: [Col. 0901D] This chapter has nowhere else been found except in a collection of canons by an uncertain author.] [Note: [Col. 0901] Chapter of uncertain date.—Tripartite Collection, pt. 1, tit. 62, c. 18.—Cf. Roman penitential, tit. 8, c. 19.]

C. XVII. What penance is to be imposed on invaders of ecclesiastical property.

Concerning the infamous man named Burgandus, who, stirred by mad rage, did not hesitate to entangle himself in the devil’s snares, and who, after the manner of pagans, lay in ambush along steep roads and crossroads: while you were staying on one of your church’s estates with your clerics, striving to instruct the people with wholesome admonitions of doctrine, refreshing empty human hearts with the bread of the spiritual word, and desiring commendably to visit the holy thresholds of the Apostles Peter and Paul for the salvation of your own souls, he gathered the followers of his malice and accomplices in wrongdoing. He then dared with demonic boldness to make criminal attacks and violent depredations; and, as the wording of your letter states, dared with polluted hands to seize the sacred altar, the sacred vessels of the Lord’s body and blood, and also holy chrism, as though these were cheap objects fit for common use. [Col. 0901C–0902A] [Note: [Col. 0901] “More wholesomely”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0901] “Dared”: collected editions, first Argentinian and Venetian I editions.] [Note: [Col. 0901] “Dared”: Venetian I–II editions; “dared”: remaining editions, first Argentinian edition.]

Your belovedness has consulted us whether, if he or those who joined him in such an impious and wicked crime should ever, touched by divine grace, wish to come to repentance, you ought to bind them with some discipline of penance, and you have sought the authoritative ruling of our instruction. [Note: [Col. 0901] “Drawn”: Basel edition; “touched”: remaining editions.] [Note: [Col. 0901] “Seek”: Basel edition.] Concerning them—if the report is true—we command that, when they hasten to return to repentance, they stand outside the Church of God for one year, since they did not hesitate, outside the rite of Christian faith, to despoil and carry off its most sacred vessels. In the second year they are to remain before the doors of the church without communion. In the third year they are to enter the Church of God and stand among the hearers without offering; they are not to eat meat or drink wine, except on the days of the Lord’s Nativity and Resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0901] “Enter”: ibid.] In the fourth year, if their labor of repentance has borne fruit during the preceding three years, they are to be restored to the communion of the faithful. Having pledged with their whole purpose of mind never again to do such things, they are to be allowed to receive the body and blood of the Lord; and until the seventh year they are to remain penitents, abstaining three days each week from eating meat and drinking wine. [Col. 0902B]

C. XVIII. A bishop may not presume to appropriate or alienate church property. Likewise, in the Council of Pope Leo IV. [Note: [Col. 0901] A summary of this chapter is found in the breviary of the synod of Leo IV, from an uncertain writer on the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, falsely attributed to Liutprand. (Mansi, vol. 14.)—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 170; Deusdedit, pt. 4; Polycarpus, bk. 4, tit. 19.]

Part III. We admonish and unanswerably affirm that no bishop or priest may presume to appropriate property belonging to his title; nor may he attempt, out of friendship, fear, or gift, to take away revenues offered by Christians to holy places, lest the Church of God be reduced to nothing. Whoever—a bishop or priest—presumes to do this shall without doubt undergo canonical punishment and be compelled to restore what has unjustly been taken from the church, so that thereafter he can have no standing to litigate or possess it. [Col. 0902C] [Note: [Col. 0901] “If”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 0901] Adds “that”: Anselm.]

C. XIX. A bishop or abbot may not alienate church property. Likewise, from the Seventh Synod, c. 12. [Note: [Col. 0901D] In Gratian, as also in Anselm, this was cited from the *History* of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea. Ivo cited the true author. The translation is that of Anastasius the Librarian, from whose manuscripts some readings have been corrected.] [Note: [Col. 0901] Held A.D. 787.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 184 (191); Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, c. 375; Polycarpus, bk. 6, tit. 15.]

Whoever, whether bishop or abbot, is found to have wished to transfer anything from the estates of a bishopric or monastery into the hands of rulers, or to confer it upon another person, whatever is established to have been given shall be void, according to the canon of the holy Apostles [Canon of the Apostles 39], which says:

“Let the bishop have care of all ecclesiastical property and administer it as under God’s inspection.”

But he may not defraud anything from those goods, or give to his own relatives what belongs to God. If they are poor, let him distribute to them as to poor persons; but under this pretext the Church’s goods must not be defrauded.

[Note: “Shall be found willing”: the collected editions read *shall have wished*.]

[Note: “Estates”: in Greek, ἐκ τῶν αὐσουργιων, in place of which the Paris edition of the Greek canons reads in the rubric ἐκ τῶν προαστείων, that is, “from the suburban estates”—as though *auturgia* were called suburban properties, because they are cultivated by the hands of their owner himself. Balsamon, however, interprets them as lands which can themselves bear fruit without extensive cultivation, such as forests and things of that sort.]

[Note: “Not permitted”: Anselm and Ivo.]

[Note: “Defraud”: Greek σφετερίδεσθαι, that is, “to claim for oneself and make one’s own.”]

[Note: “Own relatives”: the Basel edition reads “relatives.”]

§ 1. If he uses as an excuse that an estate or place produces a loss and yields no benefit, even then the estate or place shall not be assigned to the rulers who are in those regions, but to clerics or cultivators.

[Note: “If he puts forward an excuse”: the collected editions add “using a stratagem.”]

[Note: “To cause loss”: the collected editions add “the bishop.”]

[Note: “Estate or place”: the same editions, and the Argentinian edition, add “or place.”]

[Note: “Even then”: absent from the collected editions and the first Basel edition.]

§ 2. But if he has used a stratagem and a ruler has bought an estate from a tenant or a cleric, the sale shall be void, and it shall be restored to the bishopric or monastery. The bishop or abbot who does this shall be removed—the bishop indeed from the bishopric, the abbot from the monastery—as one who scatters what he has not gathered.

[Note: “Even so, the sale shall be void”: Anselm of Lucca and Ivo.]

[Note: “To the bishopric”: the collected editions read “to the bishop.”]

[Note: “And”: this conjunction is absent from some editions.]

[Note: “The bishop indeed from the bishopric, the abbot from the monastery”: these words were added from the canon itself to complete the sense; they are absent in Anselm.]

### C. XX. The Pope may not alienate the Church’s estates

Likewise, Pope Symmachus in the Third Synod, chapter 4 and following, down to chapter 9.

[Note: This chapter has been compiled from several chapters of the Third Roman Synod under Symmachus, though reduced to an epitome.]

[Note: Found in A.D. 502.—Three-Part Collection, part 1, title 48, chapters 15–17; Anselm, book 4, chapters 29–30.]

[Note: “Nor in”: absent from the Basel edition.]

The Pope may not alienate a Church estate in any way or for any necessity, nor give rural properties in usufruct, except only houses which in various cities are maintained at no small expense. By this law all custodians shall be bound, so that the donor, leaseholder, and seller lose their office. Whoever subscribes shall be anathema together with him who gave or received, unless restitution is made. Any ecclesiastical persons may also oppose the transaction and reclaim the alienated property together with its fruits. It is said that this is fitting for observance not only in the Apostolic Church but also in all the churches throughout the provinces.

[Note: “Gave”: the Basel edition reads “shall have given.” “Received”: it reads “shall have received”; the second Venetian edition has “receives.”]

[Note: “Nor in usufruct”: in editions of the councils one reads partly, “nor may it be permitted to give them to anyone under usufructuary right,” and partly, “nor may rights in usufruct be given to anyone,” as also in the printed code of canons. In an ancient manuscript, however, the reading is: “nor may usufruct be given to anyone.” Smaragdus, in his exposition of the Rule of Blessed Benedict, chapter 59, writes that *usufructuarium* and *usumfructum* signify the same thing, in these words: “He calls *usumfructum* what we call *usufructuarium*.”]

[Note: “In usufruct”: the editions of Argentan, Nuremberg, Venice I and II, and Paris read “in usufruct.”]

[Note: “That this is to be observed not only”: in the synod itself the wording is quite different: “But we wish the law of this constitution to be observed only in the Apostolic See; in all the churches throughout the provinces, let the custom be retained which their rulers, with consideration for souls, judge to accord with the purpose of religion.”]

### C. XXI. He who sells Church property must not dare approach the altar

Likewise, in the Sixth Synod.

[Note: Found in A.D. 504.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 182.]

He who dares to seize ecclesiastical property, or to possess it unjustly, or persists in maintaining it through an inequitable or unjust defence, is unworthy to be permitted to hasten to the altar of God.

[Note: “Or unjustly”: the synod reads, “or to possess it unjustly,” that is, without the bishop’s permission.]

[Note: “Persists”: the collected editions read *perdurare*, followed by “concerning which so great …”.]

And a little later:

§ 1. Provision must nevertheless be made that warning precede punishment, and that he who has unjustly taken property by usurpation, or retains property unjustly taken, restore it with equity assisting the laws.

[Note: “Warning”: the synod adds “manifest.”]

[Note: “Has taken”: the Basel edition reads “shall have taken.”]

[Note: “He who retains it”: the collected editions read “who retains it.”]

If he neglects this, and necessity compels, then at last let mature sacerdotal severity strike the robber.

And below:

§ 2. It is therefore exceedingly unjust and a great sacrilege that whatever anyone has bestowed upon, or certainly left to, a venerable church—whether for the remedy of sins, for the salvation, or for the repose of his soul—should be permitted to be transferred or converted to another use by those by whom such things ought most especially to be preserved, that is, by Christians and God-fearing men, and above all by rulers and leading men of the regions.

[Note: “Or for the salvation”: the collected editions read “or for the salvation and.”]

[Note: “Or for the repose”: this is absent in Ivo.]

[Note: “Men”: the words from this point through “to another use” have been added from the synod; they are absent from the Basel edition.]

[Note: “Preserved”: the Argentinian, Nuremberg, first Venetian, and first Lyons editions read “preserve.”]

Therefore, whoever has failed to foresee this and has sought, received, possessed, or unjustly defended or retained estates conveyed to churches otherwise than as written, unless he quickly corrects himself, shall be struck with anathema, by which an angry God strikes souls. Let there be anathema upon the receiver, the giver, and the possessor, and a continual association with the appointed punishment. Let no one who, contrary to right and without any consideration of piety, squanders what religious souls have left for the support of the poor fortify himself with any defence before Christ’s tribunal.

[Note: “Estates conveyed to churches”: the collected editions read *eccelsiae*, a misspelled singular form, instead of “to churches.”]

[Note: “Giver”: the same editions read “donor.”]

[Note: “Or unjustly defended or retained”: these words too have been added; thus all the circumstances which commonly arise in the usurpation of such property are set forth.]

[Note: “Who has received”: the same editions read “who has given.” The second Venetian edition reads “who receives.”]

### C. XXII. Those who seize Church property by the authority of rulers are to be excommunicated

Likewise, Pope Nicholas to Ado, Archbishop of Vienne, in the letter beginning: “Because of your holiness …”

[Note: This letter is found in the often-cited book of the Dominican Library, in which Nicholas answers certain questions submitted to him by Ado.]

[Note: Written about A.D. 865.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 152.]

Concerning things once contributed and dedicated to God, which afterward, under the pretext of a grant by rulers, are seized and plundered by certain persons, we decree that you should first consult the ruler, in order to cut short so presumptuous a faction and ascertain whether it was his grant or the invader’s presumption.

[Note: “After consulting the ruler”: the original reads “having consulted the ruler.” Ivo has the same.]

[Note: “And”: the Basel edition reads “and it is.”]

[Note: “The invader’s”: the same edition adds “was.”]

If the ruler’s grant was irregular, the ruler himself is to be rebuked for correction. But if the invader’s presumption is made clear, he is to be restrained by the punishment of excommunication until amendment.

### C. XXIII. Nothing of the Church’s goods is to be alienated

Likewise, Gelasius to Justin, Archdeacon, and Faustinus, *Defensor*.

[Note: Chapter of uncertain date.—Three-Part Collection, part 1, title 46, chapter 56; Deusdedit, part 3, chapter 93. The same letter, addressed to Justin and Faustus, is found in the collections of Anselm of Lucca, edited by Canisius, *Lectiones antiquae*, vol. 3.]

**Part IV.** For we have judged it expedient for you and for your reputation that someone be appointed in your bishop’s place by the same authority, to arrange all things jointly with you in his name, so that you may recall all estates to your supervision. You must not suppose that any plot of Church land ought to be assigned to any cleric as his portion, lest it be diminished through carelessness and neglect; rather, bring to the bishop the whole sum of rents collected from all rural and urban estates.

From this collection, however, provision is to be made for what appears necessary for the affairs or expenses of incidental necessities, so that it may be set aside from the common fund. Four portions are in every way to be made, either from the offerings of the faithful or from these rents: one for the bishop himself; another, to be distributed among the clerics according to his judgment and choice; a third, to be bestowed upon the poor with all conscientiousness; and the fourth for building works, which, as belonging to the bishop’s administration, we decree is to be paid out by you.

If anything remains after the annual expenditure, it shall be entrusted, under a suitable guardian chosen by both sides, to the chests, so that, if a major building project arises, what diligence has been able to preserve over different periods may serve as assistance; or else an estate may be purchased that looks to the common benefit.

[Note: “The whole”: the collected editions read “the whole sum.”]

[Note: “A suitable guardian chosen by both sides”: absent from the Basel edition.]

[Note: “Expenses of incidental necessities”: one edition has the erroneous reading “expenses of exceeding necessities.”]

[Note: “May be set aside”: the same editions read “may be set aside” with a different form.]

[Note: “Entrusted”: the Basel edition reads “believed.”]

[Note: “From different periods”: the Basel edition reads “from different times.”]

[Note: “Has been able”: the same edition reads “will be able.”]

### C. XXIV. He who tramples ecclesiastical privileges is to be deprived of participation in the divine gift

The same, to Majoricus, Serenus, and John, bishops.

[Note: Letter of uncertain date.—Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 150; part 4, chapter 185.—Holstenius published it from the collection of Deusdedit.]

Those who, having trampled both divine and human laws through uncivil condemnation and cast aside reverence for religion, strive either to trample ecclesiastical privileges or anywhere to rush to the injury of the poor, and who, even when warned and convicted, refuse to restrain such wickedness and repair the damage inflicted upon sacred things, are rightly to be deprived of participation in the divine gift, so that they may lack that reception which they held in contempt through sacrilegious acts.

[Note: The collected editions, together with the primary Basel and second and third Lyons editions, read “those who also, having trampled both divine and human laws.” Deusdedit and Ivo have “who both in divine and human laws.”]

[Note: “And”: the same editions read “so that.”]

[Note: “This”: the same editions, and the second and third Lyons editions, read “such.”]

[Note: “Repair”: the collected editions read “restore.”]

But the priest Coelestinus, of our brother and fellow bishop Serenus, who, breaking forth against episcopal judgment and against the commands of the Apostolic See, presumed to administer sacred communion to the aforesaid persons, though he could not have been ignorant of the sentence of his own priest, is immediately to be expelled from ecclesiastical office.

[Note: “Expelled”: the collected editions read “re-expelled.”]

Thus none of the Church’s ministers may seek to act contrary to episcopal enactments.

### C. XXV. On the same matter

The same, to the same Justin, Archdeacon, and Faustinus, *Defensor*.

[Note: “To Justin, etc.” Formerly it read: “The same, to the same.” It has been corrected, and the names of these men supplied from Ivo; the penultimate chapter above, beginning “For we have judged it expedient for you,” was also written to them. Moreover, that the matters now to be cited cannot concern the bishops to whom the immediately preceding chapter was addressed is indicated not only by the material here reported by Gratian, but even more plainly by the words which follow the end of this chapter in Ivo: “But if, to the detriment of your Church, or in those matters forbidden by our command, you see your bishop permit …”]

[Note: Chapter of uncertain date.—Three-Part Collection, part 1, title 46, chapter 57; Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 151.]

The acts or patrimony of the Church of Volterra, which we have learned has until now been left desolate after the condemnation of Eucharistus, by whose corrupting agency it had been dispersed, we have decreed should be entrusted to your care. By the diligence with which we believe you to be vigilant for the Church’s interests, restore its estates to their former cultivation and recover any slaves who have been sold or given away.

Possessions which you find held by the bishops Eumancius and Opilio, or by others under any title, are likewise to be reclaimed, since estates could not by any contrivance be alienated by bishops contrary to the decrees of the synod. Let purchasers have recourse against him who presumed to dispose of anything from Church property by an unlawful sale.

Bring the annual rents to the bishop, whose privileges ought in every respect to be kept intact, so that the customary portions may accrue under his administration. Let the bishop distribute the fourth portion belonging to them by his own direction, according as he knows each person’s rank and merit. The same is to be done from the offerings of the faithful: the bishop is to disburse a fourth part to the clerics according to his considered choice. The portion for building works is likewise to be paid out through your disbursement, with the bishop’s knowledge and direction, so that you may permit absolutely nothing to arise to the detriment of any property.

[Note: “Volterrane”: Ivo reads “Volaterrane.”]

[Note: “And afterward”: the collected editions read “and afterward”; Ivo reads “or afterward.”]

[Note: “Condemnation”: the text has “condemnation of Eucharistus,” but the wording is materially uncertain.]

[Note: “For the Church’s interests”: the Basel edition reads “for the Church’s interest.”]

[Note: “We believe”: the collected editions, together with the primary Lyons editions, read “we judge.”]

[Note: “Eumancius”: Ivo reads “Eumatius.”]

[Note: “In no way”: the Basel edition adds “in no way.”]

[Note: “Presumed”: the same edition reads “shall have presumed.”]

### C. XXVI. Two portions of revenues and offerings are to be entrusted to clerics

The same, to the clergy, order, and people of Brundisium.

[Note: The letter of Gelasius containing this chapter was sent, together with others, from Spain. The same letter appears as the third among the printed letters of Gregory II, addressed to the clergy and people of Thuringia. A somewhat similar but shorter letter is reported in the book entitled *Ordo Romanus*, and is called a formula to be given to a bishop.]

[Note: The same words, as a general formula, are found in Garnerius’s *Liber Diurnus*.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 43 (47).]

Since the bishop whom you requested has been granted to you—our brother and fellow bishop Julian—it was necessary, after he had soon been sent back to his Church, that our letters should also be sent to you, by which you might know that he had been commanded never to presume to make unlawful ordinations.

And below:

§ 1. Let him divide the revenues and offerings of the faithful into four portions: one he is to retain for himself; another he is to distribute among the clerics for their diligence in their offices; a third he is faithfully to disburse for building works; and a fourth for the poor and strangers, for all of which he will render an account at the divine judgment.

[Note: “My fellow bishop”: the Basel edition reads “our fellow bishop.”]

[Note: “He himself”: the collected editions read “to himself.”]

### C. XXVII. Concerning the offerings of the faithful: that portions are to be made, and what is to accrue to each

The same, in a letter to the bishops throughout Lucania and Bruttium, chapter 29.

[Note: Written A.D. 494.—Register, book 1, chapter 33; Three-Part Collection, part 1, title 46, chapter 19; Burchard, book 3, chapter 137; Anselm, book 5, chapter 68 (73); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 7, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 203; *Polycarpus*, book 3, title 11; Abbo of Fleury in Mabillon, *Vetera Analecta*, chapter 35.]

It is fitting that four portions be made, both from revenue and from the offerings of the faithful, according as the resources of each Church permit, as was reasonably decreed long ago: one for the bishop, another for the clerics, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be assigned to building works.

[Note: Ivo’s *Decree* and the collected editions add “is” after “building works.”]

Just as it is the bishop’s concern to pay the full stated amount to the Church’s ministers, so the clergy should know that they must not insolently demand anything beyond the sum allocated to them.

The restoration of the holy places must visibly show that what has been assigned to ecclesiastical buildings has genuinely been devoted to that work; for it is wicked, when sacred buildings are left destitute, for a bishop to divert to his own profit the expenditures assigned to them.

Although he will appear to show that he has administered the portion assigned to the poor according to divine accounting, nevertheless, as it is written [Matthew 5:16], “that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven,” it ought also to be proclaimed by present testimony and not left unspoken in the praises of a good reputation.

Therefore no cleric, etc.

[Note: “Is to be paid”: the collected editions read “is to be expended.”]

[Note: “Clergy”: the same editions read “cleric”; Ivo also has the singular.]

[Note: “To be restored”: the same editions add “for restoration.”]

[Note: “Restoration”: the Basel edition reads “repair.”]

[Note: “Sacred buildings”: the collected editions add these words.]

[Note: “Assigned”: the Spanish Collection, Burchard, Anselm, and Ivo read “designated.”]

[Note: Compare Causa 6, question 7, canon 47.]

### C. XXVIII. Four portions from the revenues of offerings and Church income are to be entrusted to the priest for administration

Likewise, Pope Simplicius to the bishops Florentius, Equitius, and Severus, Letter III.

[Note: Several words have been added in this chapter from the original, since they seemed relevant to the sense.]

[Note: Written A.D. 475.—Register, book 1, chapter 34; Anselm, book 5, chapter 66 (72).]

From the revenues of the Church or the offerings of the faithful, let nothing be permitted to one who does not know what is fitting; but let one portion alone of these be remitted to the bishop, while two portions, destined to benefit Church buildings and the distribution of aid to strangers and the poor, are administered by the priest Bonagros at the risk of his office. Let the last portion be divided among the clerics according to each one’s merits.

And below:

§ 1. We specially command Gaudentius—that is, the bishop—to restore the three portions which, it is said, he appropriated to himself alone for three years.

[Note: “What is fitting … but”: these words are absent in the Register and Anselm.]

[Note: “Strangers”: the source has “for and strangers”; the following words, and the name Bonagros, are absent in Anselm.]

[Note: “Among themselves”: this phrase is absent in the source tradition represented by Anselm.]

[Note: “That is”: the original adds “that is, Gaudentius”; the editions add “the bishop.”]

[Note: “We specially command”: the original reads “we specially command in this precept that it is incumbent”; Anselm has a similar wording.]

### C. XXIX. From Church revenues, including those newly acquired, a fourth part is to be disbursed to the clerics

Likewise, Gregory to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse, book III, letter 11.

[Note: Letter 11, written A.D. 594, book 4 of the Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 5, chapter 70 (71).]

We have learned that, from newly acquired revenues of the Church, the canonical arrangement of fourth parts has not been observed: local bishops distribute only a fourth of the old revenues, while retaining for their own use what has now been acquired.

Your Fraternity should hasten vigorously to correct this wicked and introduced custom, so that fourth portions may be disbursed according to canonical distribution, whether from earlier revenues or from those which will accrue or are accruing.

[Note: “Canonical arrangement”: the collected editions read “arrangement according to the canons.”]

[Note: “For this reason”: the original and Anselm read “wherefore.”]

For it is unfitting that one and the same Church property should in some fashion be reckoned under a double law, that is, the law of usurpation and the law of the canons.

[Note: The words “that is … and the law of the canons” are absent in Anselm.]

[Note: “Have accrued”: the original reads “have accrued”; other editions read “have accrued” or “have come in.”]

### C. XXX. Four portions must be made from the Church’s stipend

The same, to Augustine, bishop of the English, in reply to the first question.

[Note: Letter 64, written A.D. 601, book 11 of the Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 5, chapter 54 (70); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 8.]

It is the custom of the Apostolic See to give instructions to bishops when ordained: from every stipend that comes in, four portions must be made—one, namely, for the bishop and his household, for hospitality and the reception of guests; another for the clergy; a third for the poor; and a fourth for repairing churches.

[Note: The collected editions read “instructions are given to an ordained bishop,” rather than “instructions to bishops when ordained.”]

[Note: The original reading is “comes in”; Anselm reads “is received.” The collected editions, together with the primary and second and third Lyons editions, read “comes in.”]

### C. XXXI. On the same matter. PALEA

Likewise, from the Council of Toledo.

[Note: This chapter—which is found in all old copies except two, both without the name *Palea* and with a gloss—has been found in no Council of Toledo, whether printed or manuscript. In a collection of canons by an unknown author preserved in the Vatican Library, it is attributed to Sylvester, although in the Roman synod held under him, chapter 4, these portions are assigned somewhat differently, namely as in the preceding chapters.]

[Note: Chapter of uncertain origin.]

“We decree that all bishops shall be diligent in caring for lay persons, so that, if they find any in the faith of Christ, they may love them with great affection. Furthermore, we confirm that, if they receive any gifts from them, they shall immediately divide them into four portions: the first portion is diligently to be assigned, in accordance with the precepts of the Apostles, to the restoration of parish churches and cemeteries; the second to the clerics; the third to all poor persons; and the fourth to strangers.”

[Note: “Lay persons”: the collected editions, together with the primary and second and third Lyons editions, add “to them.”]

[Note: “Furthermore”: the collected editions read “and furthermore.”]

[Note: “The first”: the Basel edition has “first … assign,” “second …,” “third …,” and “fourth …,” with the repeated verbs supplied.]

[Note: “According to the precepts of the Apostles”: these words are absent from that collection. One old manuscript of Gratian has “according to the precepts of the Apostles.”]

### C. XXXII. All priests should endeavour to administer Church property according to the bishop’s command

Likewise, from the Council of Agde, chapter 22.

[Note: Held in A.D. 506.—Three-Part Collection, part 2, title 28, chapter 20; *Polycarpus*, book 3, title 12.]

**Part V.** We decree—as all the canons command—that priests or clerics of cities or dioceses shall hold Church property, saving the Church’s right, as the bishops have permitted; but they must by no means presume to sell or give it away. If they do so or have done so, the sale shall be invalid, and they shall restore the Church’s full indemnity from whatever private resources they possess, and shall be deprived of communion.

[Note: “Canons”: this word has been restored from the original. Formerly the reading was “bishops,” as in the collected editions. In *Polycarpus*, however, there is only: “as all command”; in the Spanish Collection: “as all enjoin.”]

[Note: “Shall have permitted”: the collected editions read “shall permit.”]

### C. XXXIII. Concerning clerics who suppress Church documents or hand them over to adversaries

Likewise, from the same council, chapter 26.

[Note: Register, book 1, chapter 353; Burchard, book 3, chapter 183; Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 156.—Compare below, chapter 40.]

If any cleric should presume, with culpable and punishable obstinacy, to suppress, deny, or perhaps hand over to adversaries the documents by which the Church’s possession is secured, he shall repay from his own resources whatever loss has been inflicted upon the Church through the absence of the documents, and shall be deprived of communion.

Those also who, wickedly solicited to the Church’s harm, have received anything from the betrayers shall be bound by the foregoing sentence.

[Note: “Culpable”: the collected editions read “deserving condemnation.”]

[Note: “Those also”: the same editions read “those, however.”]

[Note: The Spanish Collection reads: “Those who, having been wickedly solicited to the Church’s detriment, have received Church documents from betrayers.”]

[Note: “Have received”: Burchard, whose wording otherwise differs somewhat from the original, Ivo, and the collected editions read “shall have received.”]

### C. XXXIV. A bishop who has no heir shall appoint no heir for himself except the Church

Likewise, from the same council, chapter 33.

[Note: Three-Part Collection, part 2, title 28, chapter 31; *Polycarpus*, book 3, title 12.]

A bishop who has no children or grandchildren shall leave no heir other than the Church. If he has presumed to dispose of anything from the Church otherwise than for a Church cause or necessity, what he has sold or given away shall be held void. But if he has children, the Church shall be indemnified from the goods which he leaves by his heirs.

[Note: “Who has no children”: in the original, both printed and manuscript, and in *Polycarpus*, the reading is: “A bishop, having no children, left no heir other than the Church, if anything,” and so forth. The words of the First Council of Seville, chapter 1, come nearer to this reading, but it has not been altered because of the gloss.]

[Note: “Shall have presumed”: the Basel edition reads “has presumed.”]

[Note: “Leaves”: the Argentan and Basel editions read “shall leave.”]

### C. XXXV. Those established in the clergy must presume to alienate nothing of Church property

Likewise, from the same council, chapter 49.

[Note: Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 161.]

Deacons or priests appointed in a parish must not dare exchange, sell, or give away anything from the Church property entrusted to them, because such property is known to be consecrated to God. Likewise priests must not presume to alienate anything from the property of the Church entrusted to them, as set forth above.

If they do so, having been convicted in a council and deprived of office, they shall restore from their own resources twice as much as they are found to have presumed to dispose of.

[Note: “Entrusted”: the Spanish Collection reads “entrusted” in the plural.]

[Note: “Alienate”: the Spanish Collection has “diminish”; its variant reading is “exchange.”]

[Note: “If they do so”: the Spanish Collection reads “if they wish to do so.”]

[Note: “From their own”: the Spanish Collection, Ivo, and the collected editions add “own.”]

[Note: “Are found”: the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and first Venetian editions read “unless.”]

[Note: “To have presumed”: if here one inserts the chapter “If anyone in any way,” below in the same work, one will have the complete canon 49 of the Council of Agde.]

And below:

§ 1. We order, however, that freedmen whom priests or deacons wish to make from the Church entrusted to them shall perform the Church’s services. If they refuse to do so, it has been resolved that they shall return to their former servitude.

[Note: “Also”: the same editions read “even.”]

[Note: “From the Church”: the same editions add “of Christ.”]

[Note: “Wish to make”: the same editions read “wish to make” in the present tense.]

### C. XXXVI. Whatever is alienated by a priest from property under ecclesiastical right is to be held null and void

Likewise, from the same council, chapter 53.

[Note: Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 162.]

Whatever a parish priest has alienated from a possession under ecclesiastical right shall be held null and void, as regards the purchaser’s claim of ownership and the seller’s action.

[Note: “Alienated”: the Basel edition reads “alienated” in the past tense.]

[Note: “As regards the purchaser’s claim of ownership and the seller’s action”: the wording is likewise found in more recent editions of the councils. In others, and also in two Vatican manuscripts, the reading is “with the purchaser’s action turned against the seller.” Ivo has “by the purchaser’s purchase.” In the Council of Epaone, where this appears to be repeated: “with the purchaser’s action to be brought against the seller.”]

### C. XXXVII. Alienations made by intruders and ordinations without the clerics’ consent are void

Likewise, Pope Urban.

[Note: After Anselm’s collection, an extremely ancient manuscript contains a fragment of a certain council of Urban II. At its beginning are read these words: “We condemn the alienations made anywhere, especially by Otto, Guido, Jeremiah, or perhaps Philip, from the possessions of the Exarchate of Ravenna. But generally, [we condemn] the alienations made in any manner by all persons who have entered by intrusion or who have been canonically elected under the title of bishop or abbot … who is to be consecrated for his own Church”; and the text continues without any variation to the end of this chapter.]

[Note: Final canon of the First Lateran Council, held in A.D. 1123.]

We judge void the alienations of all those who, through intrusion or even though canonically elected under the name of bishop or abbot, are to be consecrated according to the usage of their Church—I mean alienations made by them in whatever manner—as also ordinations of persons made by the same persons without the common consent of the Church’s clerics, and likewise those made through simony.

§ 1. We also utterly forbid that any cleric presume in any manner to alienate his prebend or any ecclesiastical benefice. If this was presumed in the past or is ever presumed in future, it shall be void and subject to canonical punishment.

[Note: “Ecclesiastical”: the collected editions read “of the churches”; the original has the singular “ecclesiastical.”]

### C. XXXVIII. When a bishop has died, or is still at the point of death, nothing of Church property is to be appropriated

Likewise, from the Council of Lleida, chapter 16.

[Note: Held in A.D. 546.—Three-Part Collection, part 2, title 34, chapter 11.]

By the authority of this our agreement, we have resolved that the following be observed among us: when the bishop has died, or is still at the point of death, no cleric, whatever his order, office, or rank, shall presume to take anything from his house, or attempt to seize anything known to belong to the useful equipment of the house—that is, movable or immovable ecclesiastical property—concealing, removing, or hiding nothing by theft or fraud.

[Note: “Of his house”: the collected editions add “from his house.”]

[Note: “Or what is recognized as belonging to the useful equipment of the house”: the Spanish Collection and parallel editions read “or from what belongs to the useful equipment of the house”; the wording concerns the instruments and movable property of the house.]

[Note: “Nothing by theft”: in the royal manuscript of Lucca follows “nothing by force,” as also in the Spanish Collection.]

But he to whom the house has been entrusted, with one or two most faithful clerics placed under him, must preserve everything until the time when a bishop is appointed, and administer the customary maintenance to the clerics found in the house.

[Note: “With clerics placed under him”: editions of the councils continue “with the council,” while the royal manuscript adds “of clerics”; perhaps it should be read, “with the counsel of the clergy,” as in the Spanish Collection.]

The appointed bishop shall order the resources of the see which he has received as God commands, so that he may use them with those whom he knows faithfully to have obeyed his predecessor’s discipline and charity.

[Note: “The resources of the see which he has received”: the same royal manuscript reads, “having received the see, as his predecessor arranged, or as God commanded,” as in the Spanish Collection.]

If, after this, any cleric of any rank, as stated above, is proved on any pretext to have taken anything from the whole property, or perhaps fraudulently concealed it, he shall be condemned as guilty of sacrilege by a more extended anathema, and scarcely even communion among strangers shall be granted him.

[Note: “From the Church’s house”: the source adds “from the Church’s house” or “from the whole property.”]

[Note: “Even”: this word is absent from the collected editions.]

[Note: “Communion among strangers”: the source adds “of the soul.”]

For it is harsh that those who are known to have laboured in the Lord’s service with the bishop of the first see should be in any degree cruelly afflicted by those known to have been hoarders of their own goods or devoted and idle in pursuit of their own advantages.

[Note: “Despised”: the source has the noun “by acts of contempt.”]

### C. XXXIX. Bishops who contribute nothing to the Church may not grant freedom to its servants

Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 66.

[Note: Held in A.D. 633.—Burchard, book 3, chapter 189; Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 249.]

If those who distribute none of their own goods to Christ’s poor will be condemned by the word of the eternal Judge in the future, how much more those who take from the poor what they did not give?

Therefore bishops who have contributed nothing from their own property to the Church of Christ should fear this divine judgment and must not, to their own condemnation, make free persons from the household of the Church. For it is impious that one who has not contributed his own property to Christ’s Church should inflict loss and strive to alienate the Church’s right.

The successor bishop shall restore such freed persons to the Church’s jurisdiction without any objection, because it was not equity but wickedness that set them free.

[Note: The Register, book 1, chapter 356, contains this passage.]

[Note: “Such free persons”: the Spanish Collection reads “such freedmen.”]

[Note: “But”: the collected editions, together with the primary and second and third Lyons editions, add “even.”]

### C. XL. Concerning clerics who suppress or deny Church documents, or culpably hand them over to others

Likewise, from the Council of Orléans.

[Note: The same text is cited above under the same heading, “If any cleric,” from the Council of Agde, where it occurs. The title has not been changed, because it may also have been repeated in some Council of Orléans no longer extant.]

[Note: Compare above, chapter 33.]

If any cleric should presume, with culpable and punishable obstinacy, to suppress, deny, divert, or perhaps hand over to others the documents by which the Church’s possession is securely held, he shall repay from his own resources whatever loss has been inflicted upon the Church through the absence of the documents.

### C. XLI. Ministers of the Church may alienate nothing of its property without the bishop’s permission

Likewise, from the Third Council of Orléans, chapter 23.

[Note: Held in A.D. 538.—Three-Part Collection, part 2, title 44, chapter 1; *Polycarpus*, book 3, title 21; *Capitularies*, book 7, chapter 275.]

Abbots, priests, and other ministers may not alienate or pledge ecclesiastical property or property devoted to sacred ministry without the permission and signature of their own bishop.

Whoever presumes to do so shall be deposed, though communion is allowed him; and what has rashly been presumed or alienated shall be recovered by order of the bishop.

[Note: The collected editions read: “If they presume to do so, let them be deposed, with communion granted.”]

[Note: “Presumed or alienated”: the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and first and second Venetian editions read “ordained.”]

### C. XLII. Property of the church sold during the bishop’s absence is to be restored to ecclesiastical right. Likewise from the Synod of Ancyra, c. 15.  
[Note: [Col. 0913] held A.D. 314.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 172 (166).]

If the presbyters sell any of the church’s property while the bishop is not present [Note: [Col. 0913] “is present”: editions collected elsewhere], it has been decided that the transaction is to be annulled and the property restored to ecclesiastical right. It shall, however, rest with the bishop who has been appointed [Note: [Col. 0913] “Appointed”: Basel edition.] to decide whether the price should be repaid or not, because it often happens [Note: [Col. 0913] “Happened”: Böhm.] that the income from property sold has yielded a greater sum than the price received.

[Note: [Col. 0913C] “Yielded”: thus in certain copies of the ancient translation. In others it is “has yielded” [“has yielded”: Hispana Collection—Anselm]. The Greek reads: “Because the income from the things sold has often repaid those very persons a greater price,” that is: because the income from the things sold has often returned to those persons a greater price. But the text has not been altered on account of the gloss.]

[Col. 0913C] ### C. XLIII. Clerics are not to seize property belonging to a bishop after his death. Likewise from the Council of Chalcedon, c. 22.  
[Note: [Col. 0913] held A.D. 451.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 167.]

Clerics must not, after the death of their bishop, seize property belonging to him, as has already been established by the preceding [Col. 0914A] canons. If they do this, let them know that their own rank is endangered.

[Note: [Col. 0913] “from”: editions collected elsewhere.]

### C. XLIV. Precaria and exchanges made by usurpers are to be annulled. Likewise from the Council of Metz.  
[Note: [Col. 0913C] What is here cited from the Council of Metz [Col. 0913D] is reported in the Council of Meaux as taken from the Council of Beauvais; Burchard and Ivo also cite it from that council. But because the same matters are often repeated in Gallican and German councils, the heading has not been changed. Among the appended Capitularies originating in Gaul, there are, among other things, certain chapters excerpted by Lord King Charles and his princes from those chapters which bishops issued in synods in the year 846, etc. One of these chapters is this: that precaria and exchanges made during the vacancy of churches by persons who occupied bishops’ places are to be rescinded, and, if they are to be made afresh, are to be made with ecclesiastical or civil authority.]

[Note: [Col. 0913] c. 21 of the Council of Meaux, held A.D. 845.—Burchard, bk. 3, c. 166. Ivo, Decree, pt. 3, c. 227, from the Council of Beauvais.]

Precaria and exchanges made during the vacancy of churches by those who had occupied the places of bishops are to be annulled; and, if they are to be made, they are to be made with ecclesiastical or civil authority.

Hence Gregory, to Maximianus, Bishop of Syracuse, bk. III, epistle 11: [Note: [Col. 0913] Ep. 11, written A.D. 594, bk. 4, Maurist edition.]

### C. LXV. Stewards are to receive nothing from church property for the work of an inventory.

We have taken care to admonish your Charity that, if any bishop departs from this life, or [Col. 0914B]—which God forbid—is removed because of his own offences, when the stewards assemble [Note: [Col. 0914C] “Stewards”: so also in all ancient copies; but the printed and manuscript original reads “hierarchs.” John the Deacon, bk. 3, c. 23, has “sacred officials.”]

[Note: [Col. 0913] Perhaps read “hierarchs.”]

together with all the senior clergy [Note: [Col. 0913] “Clergy”: original.], and in their presence make an inventory of the church’s property, everything found is to be carefully entered in writing. Nothing—such as was formerly said to be done—whether a particular object or anything else belonging to the church, is to be taken as though for the labour of making the inventory.

And below, § 1: Let visitors of churches and their clerics, who travel with them through parishes outside their own city, receive, under your direction, some support for their labour. For it is just that those who are found for a time to lend their service should receive compensation.

[Note: [Col. 0913] “anything … support”: editions collected elsewhere. “There”: original. “who”: original.]

[Col. 0914C] ### C. XLVI. Laypersons who dare to plunder the goods of dying clerics are to be excommunicated. Likewise from the council held by Pope Urban in Auvergne.  
[Note: [Col. 0914C] In the headings of the chapters of the Council of Clermont [Col. 0914D]—which was held in Auvergne—the penultimate heading contains the following relevant words: “No cleric is to plunder or appropriate to his own uses the property of bishops or clerics, whether during their lives or after their death. If anyone does so, let him be anathema.” And all said: “Let it be so.”]

[Note: [Col. 0913] held A.D. 1095.]

A question was raised concerning laypersons who, when bishops [Col. 0915A] or other clerics are dying, seize the property of the deceased and steal it from the church and the poor. Against them the common anathema of the entire council was pronounced, the Pope himself promulgating the following sentence:

> “If anyone, after becoming aware of this present prohibition, seizes the property of bishops, presbyters, or other clerics, let him be excommunicated until he has made satisfaction.
>
> § 1. The goods of bishops who die are to be distributed in alms for their salvation, through the hands of archpresbyters or archdeacons, or according to the judgment of the deceased; or they are to be reserved for the successor who is to come. The same is to be done with the property of presbyters and other clerics, through the bishop, the aforementioned persons, or those to whom the dying persons have entrusted it. But if anyone ventures to act against these provisions, let him be anathema.”

### C. XLVII. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Innocent II, in the Lateran Council, c. 4.  
[Note: [Col. 0915] held A.D. 1139.—Cf. Council of Reims, held A.D. 1131, c. 3.—Panormia, bk. 8, c. 141.]

We command that what was established in the sacred Council of Chalcedon be observed inviolably: namely, that the goods of bishops who die are in no way to be plundered by anyone, but are to remain, for the use of the church and of its successor, under the free control of the steward and clerics. *Let that detestable and savage rapacity therefore cease henceforth.* But if anyone should henceforth presume to attempt this, he shall be subject to excommunication. Those who plunder the goods of dying presbyters or clerics shall be subject to the same sentence.

[Note: [Col. 0915] Cf. above, c. 43. “Established”: editions collected elsewhere. “Observed”: same.]

[Note: [Col. 0915C] “Of dying persons”: in the common editions “bishops” followed [thus in the editions collected elsewhere and the first Basel edition]. That word is absent both from the ancient copies and from the manuscript of the council itself, and would be a pointless repetition. Several words have been added somewhat above from the original.]

[Col. 0915C] Gratian. This is to be understood not only of laypersons, but also of metropolitans and any other clerics, as is read in the Sixth Synod, c. 35.

[Note: [Col. 0915] Rather, from the Quinisext Synod, held A.D. 692.—Collection in three parts, pt. 2, title 11, c. 6.]

### C. XLVIII. A metropolitan may not seize the property of a dying bishop.

A metropolitan may not, when a bishop subject to him has died, take either his property or that of his church; rather, these are to remain under the custody of the clergy of the church of the deceased bishop until another bishop is ordained. If there are no clerics in that church, the metropolitan is to restore everything intact to the bishop who is ordained there.

[Note: [Col. 0915] “May”: Böhm. “Dying”: editions collected elsewhere. “His own”: same. [Col. 0916A] “Clergy”: same.]

Gratian. Just as nobody may usurp the property of a church, so a church is not permitted to seize what belongs to another.

Hence Gregory, bk. II, epistle 43, to Bishop Boniface:

[Note: [Col. 0915] Ep. 44, written A.D. 593, bk. 3, Maurist edition.—Anselm, at the end of bk. 7.]

### C. XLIX. A church may not seize another’s property.

Just as a church ought not to lose its own property, so it ought not, in the passion of rapacity, to seize another’s property.

[Note: [Col. 0915] “Property” added in the Basel edition.]

Gratian. By all these authorities it is plainly shown that no priest may hand over ecclesiastical property to anyone; and anyone who has received church resources from a priest can assert no right to them, but must instead be compelled to restore what he received unlawfully.

§ 1. Yet it should be noted that, when certain grounds require it, church property may be alienated. Thus, when necessity requires, with the counsel of the clergy, or in order to provide for something better, church property may be alienated by priests.

Hence it is read in the African Council:

[Note: [Col. 0915C] Gratian cites this from an African council [Col. 0915D] and the following passage from a Carthaginian council. But in the single Council of Carthage included in the code of canons, this passage is the latter part and the following one the former part of the same final chapter, chapter 33. Burchard and Ivo report the whole chapter from the Council of Carthage.]

[Note: [Col. 0915] From the Council of Carthage, held A.D. 409; c. 33 in Dionysius.—Regino, bk. 1, c. 347. Burchard, bk. 3, c. 178. Anselm, bk. 7, c. 158. Ivo, Decree, pt. 3, c. 239.]

### C. L. Unless necessity requires it, not even a bishop may appropriate property of his church.

A bishop who has no necessity may not appropriate for the use of his own title-property anything belonging to the mother church.

[Note: [Col. 0915] “May”: Argentinensis, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice I and II.]

[Note: [Col. 0915D] “Church”: in the code of canons and in Burchard there follows “nor of the presbyters.” But in Ivo it reads: “Nor may a bishop appropriate property of the mother church for the use of his own title without the knowledge of the council or his presbyters.” The complete canon in Greek, with a new translation, will be set forth after the following chapter.]

[Note: [Col. 0915] “Seize or appropriate”: editions collected elsewhere and first Basel edition.]

[Col. 0916C] ### C. LI. Neither presbyters without the bishops’ knowledge, nor bishops without the council’s knowledge, may sell church property. Likewise from the single Council of Carthage, final chapter.  
[Note: [Col. 0915] Cf. the preceding chapter.—Burchard, Anselm, and Ivo, there.]

It has been decided that presbyters are not to sell property of the church in which they are established without the knowledge of their bishops; just as bishops may not sell church estates without consulting the council or all the presbyterate, unless there is necessity.

[Note: [Col. 0916C] “Or all”: in the canon of the single Council of Carthage it reads, “or their own presbyters.” It then continues: “A bishop who has no necessity,” etc., as in the immediately preceding chapter; likewise in Burchard and Ivo, although they read “one who has necessity.” The complete Greek canon reads:

> “Likewise it was decreed that presbyters should not, contrary to the judgment of their own bishops, sell a matter of the church in which they are consecrated; just as bishops are not permitted to sell church estates without the knowledge of the synod or their own presbyters. Therefore, unless necessity exists, not even a bishop may misuse anything from the title-property of the mother church.”

Likewise, it was decreed that presbyters should not, contrary to the judgment of their own bishops, sell church property in which they are consecrated, just as bishops are not permitted to sell church estates without the knowledge of the synod or their own presbyters. Therefore, unless necessity exists, not even a bishop may misuse any property from the title of the mother church.]

[Col. 0917A] ### C. LII. Except in order to provide something better, a bishop may not alienate church property. Likewise from an epistle of Pope Leo to all bishops established throughout Sicily.  
[Note: [Col. 0917] Ep. 17, written A.D. 447, Maurist edition.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 189 (177).]

Without exception we decree that no bishop may dare to give, exchange, or sell anything from the property of his church, unless perhaps he does one of these things in order to provide something better, and, after deliberation and with the consent of the whole clergy, chooses what unquestionably benefits the church.

And below, § 1: A bishop is to use church property as entrusted to him, not as his own. For a bishop’s sale or exchange of church property shall be void without the approval and subscription of the clergy.

[Note: [Col. 0917] These words are drawn from canons inserted into the Spanish collection under the name of the Fourth Council of Carthage, cc. 31–32; *Statutes of the Ancient Church*, cc. 15, 30.—Burchard, bk. 3, c. 170: from a council at Valencia, apparently derived from Anselm’s collection, pt. 10, cc. 17, 43, from which Burchard seems to have copied it. In that collection the *Statutes of the Ancient Church* are customarily cited under this title.—Ivo, Panormia, bk. 2, c. 86; Decree, pt. 3, c. 231.]

[Note: [Col. 0917D] “Approval”: formerly it read, “without the approval of all” [thus in the editions collected elsewhere]. The word “all” has been removed, because it is found neither in ancient copies nor in the Decretals, bk. 1, “On things done by prelates,” nor among other collectors. In Ivo, [Col. 0918C] who cites the Fourth Council of Carthage, and in the Panormia, which cites Leo from the council at Valencia, the word in place of “approval” is “commendation.”]

[Col. 0917B] Gratian. Likewise, houses in towns or castles which bring the church more inconvenience than benefit may be sold or exchanged by the governors of churches, as is contained in the preceding chapter of Symmachus, “A pope may not,” etc.

Likewise, as is read in the Council of Agde, c. 45:

[Note: [Col. 0918C] This chapter is joined to the preceding one in several ancient manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0917] held A.D. 506.—Regino, bk. 1, c. 351. Collection in three parts, pt. 2, title 28, c. 43. Ivo, Decree, pt. 6, c. 160.]

### C. LIII. On the same matter.

**Sixth Part.** Small plots of land or little vineyards, of little use to the church, or distant and small, the bishop may have authority to alienate without consultation of the brethren, if necessity requires.

[Note: [Col. 0917] “And” absent in Regino, bk. 5. “Council”: Ivo.]

Gratian. Likewise, bishops may alienate fugitive slaves who cannot be retained even when brought back.

[Col. 0917C] Hence in the same council, c. 46:

[Note: [Col. 0917] Regino, there, c. 352. Collection in three parts, there, c. 44.]

### C. LIV. Fugitives who cannot be retained are to be alienated.

Fugitives who abandon their homes or households, and who cannot be retained even if they are brought back, may likewise be alienated by the bishop, if he wishes, or if they have deserved this.

[Note: [Col. 0917] “Fugitives”: Hispana Collection. [Col. 0918A] “Bishops”: same and editions collected elsewhere. “If they do not wish”: Argentinensis, Basel, Venice I and II, Nuremberg; “if they wish”: remaining editions and Hispana Collection. “Thus” absent in the Paris and Lyons editions.]

### C. LV. PALEA.  
[Likewise from the Council at Tansiacum, c. 2.

[Note: [Col. 0918D] Burchard and Ivo [Col. 0917]—and Regino and Böhm—cite this from the Council at Carisiacum; but the Decretals, under the title “On exchange of property,” cite it from the Council at Senlis. This Palea occurs in most ancient copies of Gratian.]

[Note: [Col. 0917] Uncertain chapter.—Regino, bk. 1, c. 370. Burchard, bk. 3, c. 174. Ivo, Decree, pt. 3, c. 235.]]

> “It appears unjust and impious that slaves whom faithful men or women have consecrated to God and His saints for the redemption of their souls should again be reduced to secular slavery for the price of any payment or through commercial exchange, since canonical authority permits only fugitive slaves to be alienated. Therefore all governors of churches are most earnestly to beware lest one person’s almsgiving become another’s sin. It is absurd that a slave leaving ecclesiastical dignity should become subject to human [Col. 0918B] servitude.”

[Note: [Col. 0917] “Inappropriate”: editions collected elsewhere. “Consecrated”: cited collections; “consecrate”: Argentinensis and Basel editions. “From ecclesiastical”: editions collected elsewhere except Venice I and II.]

**Seventh Part.** Gratian. Likewise, if governors of churches wish to restore to the church an equal amount from their own property, they may freely transfer ecclesiastical resources, and the grants shall stand to those to whom they have been made with perpetual validity.

Hence it is read in the Council of Agde, c. 49:

[Note: [Col. 0917] held A.D. 506.—Nevertheless cf. Distinction 23, c. 30.—Ivo, Decree, pt. 3, c. 161.]

### C. LVI. How an alienation of church property can be valid.

If anyone presumes, under any condition, to alienate anything from church property, and contributes to the church from his own resources as much as he appears to have taken away, then, and only then, the act may stand.

[Note: [Col. 0917] “For any”: Hispana Collection and Ivo. “Wishes”: Hispana Collection.]

**Eighth Part.** Gratian. Likewise, if a bishop grants freedom to slaves of the church, they shall possess with perpetual validity the things given them at manumission, provided that the gifts do not exceed the amount fixed by the canons.

[Col. 0919A] Hence it is read in the same council, c. 7:

[Note: [Col. 0919] Ivo, Decree, pt. 16, c. 50.]

### C. LVII. On the same matter.

If a bishop grants freedom to any slaves of the church who have deserved well of him, it has been decided that the bishop’s successors shall preserve the freedom conferred, together with what the manumitter bestowed on them at manumission. Yet we direct that this be limited to the amount and measure of twenty solidi, in a small plot, little vineyard, or small dwelling. Whatever has been given beyond this shall, after the manumitter’s death, be restored to the church.

[Note: [Col. 0919D] “Of him”: so also in editions of the councils and in two Vatican manuscripts. But the word “of him” is absent in Ivo and in one ancient copy of Gratian [though not in the Hispana Collection].]

[Note: [Col. 0919] “To freedom”: editions collected elsewhere and the first Lyons editions II and III. “Had granted”: Argentinensis and Basel. “Number and”: absent in Ivo. “Or”: editions collected elsewhere. “The church shall restore”: Hispana Collection.]
