Gratian. But it should be noted that slaves of churches cannot be manumitted without ecclesiastical patronage being retained, unless the manumitter wishes to give the church two slaves of equal merit and equal peculium.

[Col. 0919B] Hence it is read in the Fourth Council of Toledo, c. 68:

[Note: [Col. 0919] held A.D. 633.—Regino, bk. 1, c. 357. Burchard, bk. 3, c. 176. Ivo, Decree, pt. 3, c. 237 and pt. 16, c. 65. Polycarpus, bk. 3, title 13.]

### C. LVIII. Concerning a bishop who manumits church slaves without retaining patronage.

A bishop who wishes to manumit a slave belonging by right to the church, without retaining ecclesiastical patronage, shall offer before the council of the church over which he presides, by exchange and with the subscribing priests, two slaves of equal merit and peculium, so that the decision of the person making the exchange may be found valid and just. He may then grant free manumission without the church’s patronage, because he has already acquired to his own right the person whom he intends to give to freedom.

§ 1. Such a freedman shall be denied permission to accuse or testify against the church to which he belonged by right. If he presumes to do so, it has been decided that, while the exchange remains valid, he is to be recalled to the servitude of his own church, which he attempts to harm.

[Note: [Col. 0919] “Two”: Basel edition. “Change”: same. “For”: Hispana Collection, cited collections, and editions collected elsewhere. “Who”: Hispana Collection. “Has decided”: editions collected elsewhere.]

Gratian. For a freedman is not permitted, unless leave has been obtained, to summon his patron into court. Hence in Digest, bk. 2, title *On Summoning into Court*, final law:

> If, without having obtained leave under the edict, a freedman summons his patron into court, then upon the patron’s complaint he either pays the above-mentioned penalty, namely fifty gold pieces, or, if he is found to suffer from poverty, he is punished by the prefect of the city as an undutiful person.

[Note: [Col. 0919] title 4, fragment 25.]

§ 1. But if someone has been manumitted by a corporate body or association, he owes respect not to the individual members but to the whole body. Hence in the same book, same title, law *But if in this case*:

> A person manumitted by some corporate body, association, [Col. 0920A] or city will summon the individual members into court. For he is not their freedman, but ought to show honour to the commonwealth. If he wishes to bring an action against the commonwealth or corporation, he must seek leave under the edict, even though he will be summoning their appointed representative into court.

[Note: [Col. 0919] fragment 10.]

§ 2. But if the emperor makes someone freeborn, he owes no respect to his patron.

§ 3. In a criminal case, however, if a freedman summons his patron into court with the intention of seeking his life and property, he is to be punished capitally before the action begins. The crime of treason is excepted; likewise, if he catches a female patron using her slave in an unlawful sexual relationship. In that case even a slave is permitted, with the reward of freedom, to accuse his master, as the Emperor Constantine is said to have ordained in Code, bk. 9, title *On Women Who Have Joined Themselves to Their Own Slaves*, sole law:

> If any woman is discovered to have a secret affair with her slave, she shall be subjected to capital punishment, the pimp being handed over to the flames. Let everyone have the right to prosecute this public crime; let the public office have the means of reporting it; and let the slave also have permission to inform against her. If the crime is proved, he shall be given freedom.

[Note: [Col. 0919] Compare Code, bk. 9, title 1, c. 20. Title 11, c. 1.]

§ 4. Nor may freedmen testify against their patrons, except in certain cases in which slaves also are ordered to be tortured against their masters.

Hence in the same book of the Code, title *On Examinations under Torture*, first law, Emperors Antoninus and Verus:

[Note: [Col. 0919D] In several ancient manuscripts this chapter is joined to the preceding one.]

[Note: [Col. 0919] title 41, c. 1; written A.D. 197.]

### C. LIX. On the same matter.

An examination under torture of slaves against their masters ought not to take place, except in accusations of adultery, charges concerning evasion of the census, and the crime of treason affecting the safety of the emperor.

§ 1. In other cases, although the judges ought not to frame their decision from what a slave has brought against his master, nevertheless, if faith in the truth is established by other proofs as well, the odium of the prohibition disappears.

§ 2. In financial cases it is clear that slaves may be questioned against their masters because of a lack of proofs.

[Note: [Col. 0919] “According to”: editions collected elsewhere. “Has said”: same.]

[Note: [Col. 0919D] “Because of a lack”: in ancient copies of Gratian the reading is “not because of a lack,” and the author of the gloss seems also to have read it thus. The older edition of Justinian’s Code likewise has the same reading in the law *An Examination*, title *On Examinations under Torture*; the author of those glosses followed it, and the same reading occurs in the Basilics, title 50, *On Examinations*. But because the edition of Haloander’s Code reads “because of a lack,” and because law *The Deified*, Digest, *On Examinations under Torture*, seems to establish that slaves may be tortured even in financial cases owing to a lack of proofs, the text has not been altered.]

### C. LX. On the same matter. Likewise there, second law.  
[Note: [Col. 0919] c. 2 there; written A.D. 205.]

It is unusual and a grave precedent for slaves to be heard against the guardians or mother of their masters, unless the guardianship itself is at issue.

[Note: [Col. 0919] “Where”: editions collected elsewhere.]

[Col. 0921A] Gratian. If a freedman withdraws from the church’s patronage on his own authority and, after warning, refuses to return, he shall be restored to slavery.

Hence it is read in the same Fourth Council of Toledo, c. 70:

[Note: [Col. 0921] held A.D. 633.—Burchard, bk. 3, c. 184. Ivo, Decree, pt. 3, c. 244.]

### C. LXI. Concerning freedmen of a church who depart from its patronage.

Freedmen of a church who depart from its patronage and attach themselves to any persons whatsoever shall, if warned, refuse to return, have their manumission declared void, because through contempt of obedience they are held liable by an action for ingratitude.

[Note: [Col. 0921] “Whatever”: editions collected elsewhere. “Attach themselves”: same. “Obedience”: Burchard.]

### C. LXII. Freedmen who rebel against the freedom of churches are to be recalled to slavery. Likewise from the Second Council of Seville, c. 8.  
[Note: [Col. 0921] held A.D. 619.—Collection in three parts, pt. 2, title 49, c. 5.]

[Col. 0921B] The eighth discussion concerned a certain Elisha, of the household of the church of Egabrum, who, having been granted freedom by his bishop, immediately passed from freedom into the disease of contumacy. Thus, in his pride, he wished not only to injure the health of that bishop by poisonous arts, but also, forgetful of his freedom, to condemn beforehand the church that was his patroness. Against him an action for ingratitude shall rightly be brought on the authority of the canons and laws: namely, that, punished by the loss of an undeserved freedom, he be recalled to the bond of slavery. For the condition of such people [Note: [Col. 0921] 66. c. 7, Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 16.]—who strive against their bishop or their patron church—ought rather to be cut down than preserved, so that slavery may be salutary for those whose freedom is harmful; and those who have learned to be proud upon attaining freedom, once exposed (*proditi*), may learn to obey as subjects.

[Note: [Col. 0921] “Elisept”: editions collected elsewhere. “Egabrian”: Hispana Collection. “Wicked or treacherous”: editions collected elsewhere. “Condemned”: Hispana Collection. “Be compelled to be recalled”: editions collected elsewhere. “Have learned”: Hispana Collection.]

[Note: [Col. 0921C] “After receiving freedom”: there is considerable variation at this point in ancient copies of Gratian. Some agree with this common edition; some have “having lost freedom, betrayed”; others, “endowed with freedom” [thus in the Hispana Collection], as in both the printed and manuscript council itself and also in the royal Lucca manuscript. But Ivo reads: “Puffed up by received freedom, let them, after losing it, learn to obey as subjects.”]

### C. LXIII. Freedmen promoted to holy orders are not to depart from the church’s patronage. Likewise from the Third Council of Toledo, c. 6.  
[Note: [Col. 0921] held A.D. 589.—Collection in three parts, pt. 2, title 36, c. 2.]

Concerning freedmen, the holy synod decrees this: if any have been made presbyters or deacons by bishops, according to the manner in which the ancient canons grant permission, they are to be free; yet neither they nor their descendants are to depart from the church’s patronage.

§ 1. Those likewise who have been handed over to freedom by others and entrusted to churches are to be gathered under the bishop’s patronage; and the bishop is to petition the ruler that they not be given to anyone.

[Note: [Col. 0921D] “Presbyters or deacons”: in the four-volume Cologne edition of the councils and in the royal Lucca manuscript [Col. 0922C] it reads: “Concerning freedmen, the priests of God decree this: if any have been made by bishops,” etc., with no mention of presbyters or deacons. Thus also in the Hispana Collection.]

[Note: [Col. 0921] “These”: editions collected elsewhere. “Episcopal”: Hispana Collection. [Col. 0922A] “Be gathered again”: Lyons editions II and III.]

Gratian. So that the condition of their origin may not be obscured by lapse of time, freedmen are, at the time of their manumission, to make a declaration professing that they belong to the church’s household and will never withdraw from its service.

Hence it is read in the Sixth Council of Toledo, c. 9:

[Note: [Col. 0921] held A.D. 638.—Collection in three parts, pt. 2, title 38, c. 4.]

### C. LXIV. Freedmen of a church are to make a declaration of their status.

It often happens through lapse of time that the condition of origin is not evident. Therefore it has already been decreed in a canon of the preceding universal council that freedmen of churches must make their declaration, professing [Col. 0922B] both that they are of the church’s households and that they will never abandon its service.

[Note: [Col. 0922C] “In the preceding”: this refers to c. 69 of the Fourth Council of Toledo, reported in the next chapter. That Fourth Council of Toledo, which was very comprehensive, is customarily called the universal council in subsequent councils of Toledo: in the Fifth, cc. 2 and 7; and in the Sixth, cc. 1, 3, 7, and 18. At the beginning of the Fourth Council itself the bishops say, “since we are holding a general council.”]

[Note: [Col. 0921] “Manumitted”: Hispana Collection. “Its”: same.]

We also add concerning these persons that, whenever a bishop completes the course of his life and departs this world, as soon as his successor arrives, all freedmen of the church and those descended from them must produce their documents before the bishop appointed in his place, in the sight of everyone, and renew their own declarations before the church, so that they may retain the force of their status and the church may not lack their obedience. But if, within a year of the ordination of the new bishop, they refuse to produce the written documents of their freedom or refuse to renew their declarations, those documents shall remain void and empty, and they shall be returned to their original status as perpetual slaves.

[Note: [Col. 0921] “Concerning these”: Basel edition. “Who is appointed”: editions collected elsewhere. “Declaration”: same; “his own declaration”: Basel edition. “Or”: absent in Nuremberg and Venice I–II; absent in editions collected elsewhere except the first Nuremberg and Venice I–II editions. “His own”: editions collected elsewhere.]

### C. LXV. Neither freedmen nor their descendants are to depart from the church’s patronage. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Toledo, c. 69.  
[Note: [Col. 0921] held A.D. 633.—Burchard, bk. 3, c. 185. Ivo, Decree, pt. 3, c. 245. Polycarpus, bk. 3, title 12.]

Freedmen of a church, because their patroness never dies, are never to depart from its patronage; nor indeed are their descendants, as earlier canons decreed. And lest their freedom perhaps not be evident in future descendants, and those descendants, *resisting by natural free birth*, withdraw themselves from the church’s patronage, it is necessary that both the freedmen and those born of them make to their bishop a declaration by which they acknowledge themselves to have been made freedmen from the church’s household, and neither abandon its patronage nor fail, according to their ability, to render it service or obedience.

[Note: [Col. 0921] “Of the church”: editions collected elsewhere. “The same”: Hispana Collection, Burchard, Ivo, and editions collected elsewhere. [Col. 0923A] “Descended”: Hispana Collection, Burchard, and Ivo.]

Gratian. Church property may also usefully be granted as compensation for service rendered.

Hence it is read in the Fourth Council of Toledo, c. 36:

[Note: [Col. 0923] Collection in three parts, pt. 2, title 37, c. 14. Abbo of Fleury in Mabillon, *Veteran Analects*, c. 33.]

### C. LXVI. What is provided from church property as recompense for service is to remain valid.

Whenever bishops, by the assistance of anyone, have provided for some ecclesiastical advantage, and in return have promised that person any benefit as recompense, they must fulfil what they promised, provided that the matter is brought before the provincial council so that it may be confirmed with their approval; because, as Paul says, “the labourer is worthy of his wages.”

[Note: [Col. 0923] “For ecclesiastical utility”: Hispana Collection and Abbo. “Small benefit”: same. “As recompense”: same and editions collected elsewhere. “Perform”: editions collected elsewhere. “Provincial”: same, Hispana Collection, and Abbo. [Col. 0923B] “Brought forward, by them”: Hispana Collection and Abbo. “Assembly”: Basel edition; “agreement” or “approval”: Argentinensis edition. 1 Timothy 5:19. “Hired labourer”: editions collected elsewhere. “To receive his wages”: Hispana Collection.]

### C. LXVII. Slaves of churches may be transferred into the ownership of those who serve ecclesiastical interests. Likewise Gregory, bk. II, indiction 11, epistle 18, to Theodore the Counsellor.  
[Note: [Col. 0923] Ep. 18, written A.D. 593, bk. 3, Maurist edition.—Polycarpus, bk. 3, title 13.]

It is fitting that those who labour hard for ecclesiastical interests should enjoy ecclesiastical recompense, so that those who voluntarily subject themselves to the voluntary necessities of service may fittingly be comforted by our provisions. Since, therefore, we have learned that you, Theodore, a most eloquent man and our counsellor, lack the service of slaves, we command that a boy named Acosimus, a Sicilian by birth, be given and transferred into your right and ownership. And since, by our will, you already possess him as transferred, it was necessary to support you by the authority of this written grant as testimony and confirmation for the future, so that, under the Lord’s protection, you may always possess him securely and without any suspicion of revocation, indeed as master.

[Note: [Col. 0923C] “You”: this word was added and the remaining text emended from the original, so that it may be understood that the recipient of the letter and the recipient of the gift are the same person.]

[Note: [Col. 0923] “His own”: editions collected elsewhere. “Transferred”: absent in editions collected elsewhere and the first Basel edition. “Authority”: editions collected elsewhere. “Possesses”: same. “You”: absent in the Basel edition. [Col. 0924A] “May possess”: editions collected elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 0923C] “Possess”: in St Gregory the following continues: “For we do not believe that anyone will desire or attempt in any way to revoke so small a grant, made to you for your devotion; since at one and the same time it is honourable not to undo good acts performed by predecessors, and honourable to teach others that they ought someday to pronounce a rescinding judgment upon their own grants.”]

Gratian. Slaves of churches may also be granted freedom out of compassion.

Hence Gregory, to Montana and Thomas, bk. 5, epistle 12:

[Note: [Col. 0923] Ep. 12, written A.D. 596, bk. 6, Maurist edition.]

### C. LXVIII. Slaves of churches may be manumitted from motives of compassion and piety.

When our Redeemer, the Creator of the whole creation, in his mercy willed to assume human flesh for this purpose—namely, that by the grace of his divinity, having broken the bond of slavery by which we were held captive, he might restore us to our former liberty—it is a salutary act when people, whom nature brought forth free in the beginning but the law of nations subjected to the yoke of servitude, are restored, through the favor of one who manumits them, to the liberty in which they were born. Therefore, moved by regard for piety and by consideration of this matter, we make you, Montana and Thomas, servants of the holy Roman Church, which, with God’s help, we serve, free from this day and Roman citizens; and we remit to you all your peculium of servitude. [Note: *voluerit*, “willed”: *voluit*, “willed,” in the collected editions and the first Lugdanese editions II and III. *permoti*, “moved”: *permotus*, “moved,” Basel edition. *vos*, “you”: *nos*, “us,” in the collected editions and first Basel edition. *adjutore*, “helping”: *auctore*, “authoring,” in the collected editions. “Of servitude” is absent in the original. *Peculium*: in an old Vatican manuscript of the letters of St Gregory, *periculum* (“danger”) is read.]

And below:

§ 1. We dictated that this document of manumission be written by Paterius the notary, and, for its fullest validity, signed it with our own hand together with three senior presbyters and three deacons; and we delivered it to you. Done in the city of Rome. [Note: “We delivered”: *tradimus*, “we deliver,” in the collected editions except the Argentinian edition.]

Gratian. Likewise, servants of churches ought not to be burdened with public compulsory services.

[Col. 0924C] Hence, in the Third Council of Toledo, canon 2, one reads: [Note: Held in A.D. 589.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 138.]

C. LXIX. Servants of churches are not to be burdened with public compulsory services.

We lament that servants of churches, and of bishops, or of all clerics, are burdened by judges or public officials with various compulsory services. Therefore the whole council petitioned the piety of our most glorious lord that he should henceforth prohibit such presumption; rather, let the servants of the aforementioned offices labor in their own employments or in that of the Church. But if any judge or official wishes to employ a cleric, or the servant of a cleric or of a church, in public or private business, let him be excluded from ecclesiastical communion, which he obstructs. [Note: In other printed and manuscript copies of this council that were collated, and in Ivo, the wording agrees with Gratian, except in the four-volume edition and the royal Lucca codex, in which the beginning of canon 21 reads: “Since we have learned that in many cities the servants of churches and bishops—or … [lacuna]—are burdened with various compulsory services, the whole council,” etc. No alteration was made here; but other readings, where all council manuscripts agree, have been corrected. “Of bishops”: the collected editions and Böhm add “or presbyters,” against the source. *actoribus*, “officials”: *exactoribus*, “tax-collectors,” in the collected editions. *ausus*, “presumption”: *usus*, “practice,” in those editions. *laborent*, “let them labor”: *elaborent*, “let them work out,” in the Hispanic Collection. *actorum*, “officials”: *auctorum*, “authors,” Basel edition.]

Gratian. Likewise, sacred property may be sold for the sustenance of the poor and the ransom of captives.

Hence Ambrose says in book II of *On Duties*, chapter 28: [Note: Anselm, book 13, c. 28; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 150; Polycarpus, book 6, title 20.]

C. LXX. For what reasons sacred property ought to be alienated.

The Church possesses gold, not in order to store it, but in order to distribute it and provide assistance in necessities. What use is it to keep what gives no help? Do we not know how much gold and silver the Assyrians carried away from the temple of the Lord? Is it not better for a priest to melt it down for the sustenance of the poor, if other resources are lacking, than for a sacrilegious enemy to carry it away after defiling it? Will not the Lord say: “Why did you allow so many needy people to die of hunger? And surely you had gold with which you might have supplied them with food. Why were so many captives carried off for sale and not ransomed, and killed by the enemy? It would have been better for you to preserve vessels of living persons than vessels of metal.”

No answer could be made to this. For what would you say? “I feared that the temple of God might lack ornament.” He would answer: “The sacraments do not seek gold; nor do things that are not bought with gold please by means of gold. The ornament of the sacraments is the ransom of captives; and those are truly precious vessels which ransom souls from death. That is the true treasury of the Lord which accomplishes what his blood accomplished.” [Note: “The priest melts down” is absent from the Argentinian edition. *alia*, “other”: *aliqua*, “some,” in the collected editions. “Defiles and carries away” in those editions; Ivo has “defiles and carries [it] away.” *mori*, “die,” Ivo and the collected editions. “And” is absent in the collected editions and first Basel edition. “Carried into captivity”: *in captivitatem ducti* in the collected editions. “And not ransomed? Why …”: original. *potes … referre*, “can … make,” in the collected editions. *dices*, “will you say,” in those editions. *Respondet*, “he answers,” in those editions. “Of sacred things” instead of “of the sacraments,” in those editions and Ivo.]

And a little later:

§ 1. No one can say, “Why does a poor person live?” No one can complain because captives have been ransomed. No one can accuse because a temple of God has been built. No one can be indignant because space has been enlarged for burying the remains of the faithful. No one can grieve because in Christians’ tombs there is rest for the dead. In these three kinds of case, it is permissible even to break up, melt down, and sell consecrated vessels of the Church. Care must be taken that the image of the mystical people does not depart from the Church, lest the ministry of a sacred chalice be diverted to wicked uses. Therefore vessels that had not been consecrated were first sought within the Church; then damaged ones; and finally they were melted down and, distributed to the needy in small disbursements, also served toward the prices for ransoming captives. But if new vessels, plainly not consecrated, are lacking, I think that everything may piously be converted to the uses mentioned above. [Note: *sepulcris*, “tombs”: *sepulturis*, “burials,” in the editions. *adversus*, “against,” Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venetian I and II, Paris editions. *denique*, “finally,” in the collected editions. *captivorumque*, “and of captives,” in those editions. *dixit*, “said,” in those editions.]

C. LXXI. The bishop’s glory lies not in adorning the walls of a temple, but in providing for the poor. Likewise Jerome, to Nepotian, *On the Life of Clerics*.

The glory of a bishop is to provide for the poverty of the poor; the disgrace of a priest is to pursue his own riches. Born in a poor house and a rustic hut, I who could scarcely satisfy a roaring belly with millet and coarse bread now disdain fine flour and honey.

Likewise, a little further below:

§ 1. Many build walls and withdraw the columns of a church; marbles gleam, gilded ceilings shine, the altar is distinguished with gems, and yet there is no selection of Christ’s ministers. Let no wealthy man in Judaea set before me the Temple: its table, lamps, censers, bowls, cups, mortars, and the other objects fashioned from gold. These things were approved by the Lord then, when priests offered sacrifices and the blood of beasts was remission of sins—although all these things came beforehand as a figure. But they were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. Now, however, when the poor Lord has dedicated the poverty of his own house, let us carry the cross and reckon riches as mud. [Note: *inopiae*, “poverty”: *opibus*, “resources,” in the collected editions. *subtrahunt*, “withdraw”: *substruunt*, “support from beneath,” original. *marmore*, “with marble,” Böhm edition. *dilectio*, “love,” Basel edition. *fabricata*, “fashioned,” in the collected editions. *probantur*, “are approved,” Argentinian edition. *redemptio*, “redemption,” original. *figuram*, “a figure,” Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venetian I–II, Lyons I, and Paris editions. *sint*, “may be,” Böhm; “it was written” in the collected editions and first Basel edition. *dedicavit*, “dedicated,” in those editions. *cogitemus*, “let us think,” original. *delicias*, “luxuries,” in the collected editions; *putemus*, “let us reckon,” in those editions and Böhm.]

Likewise, at the end of the same work:

§ 2. To steal anything from a friend is theft; to defraud the Church is sacrilege. To receive what ought to be distributed to the poor and hungry, and to wish to reserve it—whether from caution or timidity—or, what is a crime of the clearest kind, to take anything from it, surpasses the cruelty of all robbers. [Note: C. 13, question 2, c. 10. The collected editions read: “to reserve it, whether cautious or timid—or, as the Argentinian and Basel editions read, fearful—is …”; *exinde*, “from it,” in those editions.]

Likewise, in the same author’s letter to Paulinus, *On the Formation of a Monk*:

§ 3. Crates the Theban, once a very wealthy man, when he was going to Athens to study philosophy, threw away a great weight of gold; he did not think that he could possess virtues and riches at the same time. Yet we, laden with gold, follow the poor Christ; and, under the pretext of almsgiving, clinging to our former wealth, how can we faithfully distribute another’s goods when we timidly preserve our own? A full belly easily argues about fasting. It is praiseworthy not to have been in Jerusalem, but to have lived well in Jerusalem. [Note: *Crates*: *Socrates* in the collected editions except the first Nuremberg and Lyons II–III editions. *opibus*, “wealth”: *operibus*, “works,” Basel edition.]

Gratian. Likewise, a bishop may, as an act of generosity, give clerics a stipend from Church property; the recipient’s declaration must be made under the name of a precaria.

[Col. 0927A] Hence in the Sixth Council of Toledo, canon 5: [Note: Held in A.D. 638.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, c. 372.]

C. LXXII. Whoever receives a benefice from the Church shall make a declaration concerning it under the name of a precaria.

It often happens that long passage of time obstructs proof of original ownership. Therefore we prudently decree that if any cleric receives a stipend from the property of any bishop’s Church through generosity, he must write a declaration under the name of a precaria, so that he may not prejudice the Church through prolonged retention, and so that whatever he receives in use he may employ beneficially; thus things of divine right will not appear to be neglected on any pretext, and clerics may receive support from the Church which they serve. But if any of them refuses to do this, he will be deemed to deprive himself of his stipend. [Note: The royal Lucca codex continues: “or of any other persons,” as does the Hispanic Collection. *cujuscunque*, “of whatever [bishop]”: collected editions, Hispanic Collection, and Ivo. *percipiat*, “receives”: Hispanic Collection; *percipit*, “receives,” Ivo. *ne per retentionem*, “lest by retention”: collected editions; *nec per ret[entionem]*, Ivo. *usum*, “use”: Hispanic Collection. *percepit*, “received”: collected editions. *debet*, “must”: those editions. *videtur*, “is deemed”: Basel edition.]

[Col. 0927B] Gratian. Likewise, out of religious regard, things whose transfer does not injure the Church may be given to monasteries.

Hence in the Third Council of Toledo, canon 4, one reads: [Note: Held in A.D. 589.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 168.]

C. LXXIII. It is permitted to alienate Church property out of religious regard.

If a bishop wishes to dedicate one of the churches of his parish as a monastery, so that a community of monks may live there under rule, he has permission to do this with the consent of his council. If he also gives that place something from Church property for their support, provided that it causes no injury to the Church, the gift shall be secure. For the holy council gives its consent for the establishment of a good undertaking. [Note: *parochitanis*, “parish churches,” Hispanic Collection. *consilii*, “counsel,” Argentinian edition. *bene*, “well,” collected editions. *assensum*, “assent,” Hispanic Collection.]

[Col. 0927C] C. LXXIV. A bishop may not grant to a monastery he establishes more than a fiftieth part of Church property. Likewise from the Ninth Council of Toledo, canon 5. [Note: Held in A.D. 655.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 170.]

To provide for a good undertaking is held to be both an aid to the present life and an expectation of the reward of eternal recompense. Therefore, if any bishop wishes perhaps to build a monastery in his parish and decides to endow it from the property of the Church over which he presides, he must not give it more than a fiftieth part; thus, preserving this equitable moderation, he may provide suitable support to that to which he gives, while not inflicting grave loss upon that from which he takes. But to a church not to be organized under monastic rules, or one which he wishes to enlarge for his own burial, he may grant no more than a hundredth part of the revenues of the Church over which he presides—provided, however, that he takes only one of these two forms of endowment, whichever he chooses. [Note: *ex* is omitted in IV and the collected editions. *etiam cui*, “also to that to which”: Argentinian and Basel editions. “To enlarge”: *munificare*, “to enrich generously,” Hispanic Collection. *remunerandam*, “to be endowed,” ibid.]

C. LXXV. It is permitted to convey Church property by right of ownership for the building of monasteries. Likewise Gregory, book II, indiction 11, letter 17, to Gratiosus the subdeacon. [Note: Letter 17, written A.D. 593, book 3, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 5, c. 33.]

We ought to make suitable provision, with thoughtful consideration, for those choosing the religious life, lest any occasion of need make them idle or—God forbid—weaken the strength of their way of life. Therefore, by the present authority, we command you to convey to Abbess Flora, to be possessed by right of ownership without doubt, the house located in this city, in the fourth region, near the place called *ad gallinas albas* (“at the white hens”), and the garden belonging by right to the holy Roman Church over which, by God’s appointment, we preside. Campana, the former wife of Patricius, is known to have lived in this house; and you are likewise to convey the garden and lodgings which one doorway encloses within the same house. In that house Flora may, with Christ’s help, build a monastery of virgins, in which she can live with her community; and both she and whoever succeeds her in its place and dignity may possess, by peaceful and unchallenged right, the aforesaid house and garden with all their appurtenances, granted by us, as we have said, out of consideration for piety. [Note: *nec*, “and not”: Basel edition. “Wife”: the word is absent in several editions of the letters and some copies of Gratian; an old Vatican manuscript reads “the former patrician.” *clausit*, “enclosed”: Basel; *conclusit*, “shut in,” the remaining editions. “To the same [Flora]”: collected editions. “Flora the Abbess” is absent in Anselm. “Of virgins” is absent in Anselm. *ut*, “so that”: original and Anselm.]

Gratian. Behold, it has been shown how Church property may be given without fault and remain secure to those to whom it has been given.

## QUESTION III

## GRATIAN

Part I. It is now asked: if, before the time of their ordination, they appeared to possess nothing, what is to be done with things which they are known to have acquired after their ordination?

The following was decreed concerning them in the Third Council of Carthage, canon 49. [Note: Held in A.D. 397.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 17, c. 30; Burchard, book 3, c. 120; Anselm, book 7, c. 157; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 52; *Decretum*, part 3, c. 96.]

C. I. Concerning those who, possessing nothing at first, acquire something during their administration.

It was resolved that bishops, presbyters, deacons, and any clerics whatever who are ordained while possessing nothing, and who during their episcopate or clerical office purchase fields or any estates in their own name, are to be held guilty of the crime of invading the Lord’s property, unless, when admonished, they convey those very things to the Church. But if something properly comes to them through another’s generosity or through inheritance from relatives, let them do with it what accords with their profession. If they depart backward from their profession, they are to be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical rank, as reprobates. [Note: “Or presbyters or deacons”: Basel edition. *invasionis*, “of invasion”: *invasores*, “invaders,” ibid.; Burchard and Ivo add *obnoxii*, “liable.” *in ecclesiam*, “into the Church”: Hispanic Collection and Anselm; *ad ecclesiam*, “to the Church,” Burchard and Ivo. *venerit*, “came”: Hispanic Collection and Burchard; *evenerit*, “happened,” collected editions and Ivo. Burchard and Ivo add “what they wish.” *congruerit*, “will accord,” collected editions.]

C. II. Concerning ministers who acquire something through no Church occasion, but for their own advantage. Likewise from the Ninth Council of Toledo, canon 4. [Note: Held in A.D. 655.]

Whatever priests or ministers receive from anyone for their own advantage and friendship, or by remuneration, or in any manner, or by the tenor of a written instrument, cannot be counted among Church property; rather, whatever they wish to do with it shall lie within the discretion of their own will. But if after their death it perhaps remains undisposed of, the Church over which they presided or in which they served as minister shall claim it for itself forever. [Note: *sua*, “their own”: collected editions. “Or by remuneration, or” is absent in the Hispanic Collection. *meruit*, “received,” Venetian I–II and Nuremberg editions; *meruerit*, “may receive,” the remaining editions. *ab aliquo*, “from someone,” collected editions; Hispanic Collection adds *collata*, “bestowed.” “For itself” is absent in the Hispanic Collection. *perpetuo*, “forever,” ibid.]

Gratian. Thus, what a person has gained not through ecclesiastical office but through some remunerated service for his own benefit, he may give to whom he wishes.

Part II.

§ 1. But there is a question concerning things offered jointly to him and the Church, or separately, for the remedy of a soul; or concerning the third part which he receives as due to himself from the goods of parish churches: whether he can leave these to whom he wishes.

[Col. 0929C] The matter is decided thus in the Council of Agde, canon 6. [Note: Held in A.D. 506.—Burchard, book 1, c. 217; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 331.]

C. III. Concerning bishops to whom something is left by outsiders, either jointly with the Church or separately.

Bishops in the high priesthood, to whom outsiders leave or give something either jointly with the Church or separately—because the giver is shown to offer it for the redemption of his own soul, not for the priest’s personal advantage—shall count it among the Church’s resources, not as their own property but as property left to the Church. For it is just that, as the priest has what is left to the Church, so the Church should have what is left to the priest.

§ 1. But whatever is perhaps left under a trust either to the priest or to the Church, to benefit another person afterward, the Church shall not be able to count or retain among its own resources. [Note: The collections read: “something is given solely by outsiders.” Hispanic Collection adds *duntaxat*, “solely.” “By the priest”: collections.]

C. IV. A bishop may leave to the Church the third part due to himself. Likewise from the Ninth Council of Toledo, canon [4]. [Note: Held in A.D. 655.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 40, c. 3; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 171.]

If a bishop decides to confer either upon the Church whose property it is shown to be, or upon another Church which he has chosen, the third part which he knows is due to him from the goods of parish churches by paternal enactment, his decision shall remain lawful and possess irrevocable force. [Note: *pariter*, “equally,” Ivo. *patescit*, “is shown,” Hispanic Collection. “Which he has chosen”: “which he has elected” in the Hispanic Collection. *sententiam*, “decision,” Basel edition.]

## QUESTION IV

[Col. 0930B] GRATIAN

What is asked concerning those known to have acquired something from their own property and that of the Church—namely, to whom such acquisitions belong—is determined thus in the same Ninth Council of Toledo, canon 4. [Note: Held in A.D. 655.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 40, c. 1; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 169.]

C. I. Concerning those known to have acquired something from their own and the Church’s property.

Priests, or whoever else have been entrusted with the care of Church property, shall ensure that the documents for anything they purchase during their administration are drawn up in the name of the Church over which they preside, if they have had little or none from their own property [the transmitted wording is uncertain]. For it is not fitting that the Church should make rich in another’s property one whom it received as a stranger, while retaining as a defrauder one who wrongs it in its own property.

§ 1. But those known to have resources of their own, if the total amount of their own right and of Church property is equal, shall have every acquisition which they appear to have made after the day of their ordination—whether no documents or some documents have been drawn up—belong in equal right to the Church and to the proper heirs, after an accounting has been made of the proportion of their own resources and of Church resources. [Note: *vel quilibet*, “or anyone whatever,” collected editions. *parum*, “little,” Hispanic Collection and Ivo. *justum est*, “it is just,” collected editions. *quae*, “which”: Hispanic Collection, Ivo, and the collected editions except Lyons II–III. *conquisisse*, “acquired,” collected editions and Hispanic Collection. *compensata*, “after balancing”: Hispanic Collection. In the council itself, collated with old copies, the reading is: “after a balancing of the proportion both of his own right and of Church property.” The collected editions add *ambitione*, “by pursuit”; *habita*, “having been made,” is absent there.]

Gratian. But if anyone, for the gain of his own property, has caused loss to Church property, or if, by occasion of Church property, he has suffered loss in his own property, then in return those who receive the gain shall compensate those who suffer the loss.

[Col. 0931A] Hence in the Third Council of Braga, canon 8, one reads: [Note: Held in A.D. 675.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 48, c. 3.]

C. II. Losses suffered by either priest or Church through occasion of the other shall be compensated.

Whoever, through such neglect, has failed to cultivate divine property shall be bound by a special settlement: if he has increased his own profit through the property or increase of the Church and, thereby, has either neglected the labor due to Church property or caused its diminution or loss, he shall restore to that Church from his own property whatever diminution he caused in Church property—the Church from whose property and support he was able to enlarge his own undertakings. But if he has spent anything for the benefit or support of the Church, or suffered any expense or loss, and this can be proved, the whole shall be reimbursed to him from the property of that Church for whose benefit he is shown to have spent it. [Note: *argumentis*, “arguments,” Böhm edition. The Hispanic Collection reads: “or [if] the labors of his own property.” *minorationis exhibuit, totum de rebus propriis ecclesiae*, “he caused diminution: the whole [shall be restored] to the Church from his own property,” ibid. *ille*, “he,” collected editions. *convinctus*, “convicted,” Hispanic Collection. *pertulit*, “suffered,” ibid. *comprobare*, “to prove,” collected editions. *utilitatibus*, “benefits,” Hispanic Collection.]

Gratian. But if they are known to have acquired something solely from Church property, they must draw up documents in the Church’s name and cannot give such property to anyone.

Hence in the Council of Agde, canon 54, one reads: [Note: This chapter is also cited by Ivo and the author of the *Panormia* from the Council of Agde, where it occurs. But in the Decretals, under the title *On Clerics’ Peculium*, it is cited from the Council of Arles; and in Burchard and the first collection of decretals, from the Council of Orange. Held in A.D. 506.—Compare c. 30, Distinction 23.—Burchard, book 3, c. 119, “from the Council of Orange”; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 51; *Decretum*, part 3, c. 95; compare c. 2, X, *On Clerics’ Peculium*.]

C. III. Concerning things priests purchase: let them execute the document in the Church’s name.

While a presbyter holds a diocese, he shall draw up, in the name of the Church, the document for things he purchases; otherwise, let him leave the administration of the Church which he holds. [Note: *cum*, “when,” collected editions. “Has a church or diocese”: Argentinian edition. *tenuit*, “held,” Hispanic Collection.]

## QUESTION V

## GRATIAN

Part I. They may not make wills except concerning their own property.

Hence Gregory writes to Bishop Deusdedit, book X, letter 42: [Note: The heading formerly read “Lucidius.” It has been restored from the original; the complete heading is found above, in the same question, section 2, “Property during an episcopate.” That chapter is contained in this one. Letter 38, written A.D. 602, book 2, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 6, c. 175.]

C. I. How priests may make wills concerning Church property.

There is no doubt that, just as priests have no permission to alienate property acquired during an episcopate, so they are not forbidden to dispose as they wish of what they possessed beforehand. Thus we recall that, when you were with us, your fraternity complained that certain movable goods which your predecessor Constantius, having acquired them while already a bishop, had left by testamentary legacy to Luminosa, a handmaid of God and daughter of his brother; and we decreed that, if this were established, your Church should suffer no prejudice from it. You too ought to remember this, to cause no trouble to the aforesaid handmaid of God, and not to take anything from her, without investigation, from what she possesses. [Note: *habuerunt*, “had possessed,” collected editions. *vereantur*, “they may fear,” Nuremberg and Venetian I editions; *vetentur*, “they may be forbidden,” the remaining editions. *conquestam*, “having complained,” collected editions. The original printed and manuscript source reads *immobilia*, “immovable goods”; this was not altered because of the writings of learned persons, though certain other readings were corrected. “And to his brothers”: collected editions. *dereliquit*, “left behind,” those editions and the original. *constat*, “is established,” those editions except Lyons II–III.]

C. II. On the same matter. The same author, book IV, letter 22, to Cyprian the deacon. [Note: Letter 27, written A.D. 595, book 5, Maurist edition.]

We believe that your Beloved has now learned of the death of Bishop Theodore. But because he is said to have made a will, you ought carefully to investigate whether he consumed anything from the property of his Church. And if you learn that he improperly diminished anything from it, act so that the things themselves are restored by all means by the person concerned. [Note: “Of his Church” is absent in the Argentinian and Basel editions. *incongruum*, “improper,” Basel edition.]

C. III. Gifts made to monasteries by bishops ought not to be revoked. Likewise Gregory, to Marinianus, Bishop of Ravenna, book V, letter [1]. [Note: Letter 1, written A.D. 596, book 6, Maurist edition.]

Because John, formerly your predecessor, while living repeatedly requested us to confirm by our authority the things which he had granted to that monastery which he himself built beside the church of St Apollinaris, and because we promised that we would do this, we judged it necessary to exhort your fraternity not to allow in any way anything which he granted and established there to be diminished, but to endeavor that everything be maintained in firm stability. Since he is known to have mentioned this monastery and the property granted there in the will which he made, you should know that we confirmed these things not because we follow his last will, but because, as we said, we promised it to him while he was alive. Therefore let your fraternity hasten carefully to carry out all this, so that both the things he established in the aforesaid monastery and which we confirmed may be preserved, and those things which he decreed by will should be given or done to the detriment of his Church may acquire no validity, since the law plainly forbids it. [Note: “John, once your predecessor”: these words do not occur here in St Gregory, but were brought here from above. *illi*, “to that [monastery],” Basel edition. *huc*, “here,” collected editions. *tuam*, “your,” Basel edition. *praevidimus*, “we foresaw,” original and collected editions. *servare*, “to preserve,” collected editions. *collectarum*, “collected,” collected editions and Böhm. The collected editions and original add “all.” “In” is absent in Basel edition. *confirmata*, “confirmed,” collected editions. *damna*, “losses,” Lyons II–III; *damno*, “loss,” remaining editions. *nulla*, “no,” collected editions except Lyons II–III.]

C. IV. Whatever an episcopus acquired before his ordination, or afterward by hereditary succession, he may leave to whomever he wishes. Likewise from the Council of Seville. [Note: Burchard and Ivo likewise cite this as “from the Council of Seville,” and the first Hispanic collection contains several relevant passages. But the entire chapter occurs in the Council of Paris, book 1, canon 14, and is reported among the decrees of that council in the *Capitularies*, book 5, c. 175. Indeed, from the Council of Paris, held A.D. 829.—*Capitularies*, book 5, c. 327.—Burchard, book 1, c. 214; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 328.]

We decree that it shall be fixed and remain perpetual henceforth: a bishop may do whatever he wishes, in accordance with canonical authority, with property belonging to his own right which he acquired either before becoming bishop or, certainly, during his episcopate by hereditary succession, and may confer it upon whom he wishes. But whatever property he has purchased after becoming bishop, from the resources of the Church, whether in his own name or another’s and on any condition, we decree shall pass not into the rights of his relatives but into the rights of the Church over which he presides. [Note: *permansurum*, “to remain,” Basel edition. *rebus*, “property,” Böhm. The collected editions read: “may confer it upon whom he wishes and do whatever he wishes with it.”]

Gratian. A bishop may, however, make a will concerning Church property if he restores an equal amount from his own property.

Hence it was decreed in the Council of Agde, canon 51: [Note: Held A.D. 506.—Compare c. 30, Distinction 23.—Regino, book 1, c. 354; Burchard, book 1, c. 212; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 326.]

C. V. How provisions bequeathed by will from Church property can be valid.

If a bishop, having made a will, bequeaths something from property belonging to the Church, it shall be valid only if he makes up an equal amount from the resources of his own property. [Note: *tantum*, “only so much,” Hispanic and other collections. *facultatibus*, “resources,” those collections.]

Part II. Gratian. But if a bishop or anyone in ecclesiastical rank dies intestate, and no persons are found who succeed him by right of kinship, his Church shall succeed to him in full; nor may anyone presume to take anything from his property.

Hence it was decreed in the Council of Tarragona, canon 12: [Note: Held A.D. 516.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 31, c. 9.]

C. VI. The Church shall succeed in full to a bishop who dies intestate.

Wherever a bishop dies intestate, after his death an inventory of his property, from the least item to the greatest—that is, of utensils and all household goods—shall be faithfully drawn up by the presbyters and deacons. If anyone is convicted either of having appropriated anything from it or of having secretly taken anything, he shall restore everything according to the law of theft. [Note: Earlier editions read “this decision”; the collected editions read likewise, while the Hispanic Collection reads “after his deposition.” The wording has been corrected from various editions of the councils and two Vatican codices, as have some other readings. The royal Lucca codex reads “after his deposition.” *breve*, “inventory,” ibid.; the collected editions read “a brief written record shall be made,” with variants *brevis* / *brevi*.]

C. VII. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Tribur. [Note: Burchard and Ivo likewise cite this chapter from the Council of Tribur, presided over by Arnulf; but it does not occur in the extant text of that council. Very similar wording is found in Julian the Antecessor, Novella 131, chapter 18. From Novella 131, c. 18; Julian’s Epitome, Novella 119, c. 18.—Burchard, book 1, c. 207; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, c. 281.]

Whoever belonging to ecclesiastical rank dies without a will and without relatives, his inheritance shall devolve upon the Church where he served. Likewise concerning consecrated women. [Note: The collected editions add *assignatur*, “is assigned.” *evolvatur*, “be unfolded,” Argentinian and Basel editions.]

## CAUSE XIII

[Col. 0933C] GRATIAN

The diocesan parishioners of a certain baptismal church, oppressed by the calamities of war and compelled by fear of the enemy, transferred their homes into another diocese; nevertheless, they did not cease cultivating their former lands. They began to pay tithes to the Church into whose diocese they had moved, and chose burial places for themselves there. After fifty years had passed, the clerics to whom they had formerly paid tithes began to bring a claim against those who receive first-fruits and tithes from these persons. They come to litigation (Question I).

The first question now is whether those whose homes lie in the diocese of this baptismal church ought to pay tithes to that Church and conduct their funeral rites at the Church where these things were formerly done by their parents (Question II). Second, whether the right to receive tithes and perform burials is extinguished by prescription through lapse of time.

## QUESTION I

## GRATIAN

Part I. The claimants endeavor to prove by these arguments that all these things must rightly be rendered to the former Church. It is established that each baptismal church has a diocese lawfully assigned to it, just as parish churches have parishes allotted to them.

[Col. 0935A] Hence Pope Dionysius, in letter II to Bishop Severus: [Note: “Bishop Dionysius,” collected editions. A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare First Council of Tours, canon 9, and Leo the Great, letter 89.—Burchard, book 3, c. 43; Anselm, book 5, c. 73 [74]; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 42; *Decretum*, part 3, c. 47.]

C. I. Individual priests ought to have their own churches.

We assigned individual churches to individual priests; we apportioned parishes and cemeteries among them, and established that each should possess his own proper right. Thus no one is to invade another parish’s boundaries or rights; rather, each is to be content with his own boundaries and so guard the church and people entrusted to him that, before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, he may render an account of all entrusted to him and receive, not judgment, but glory for his deeds. [Note: [Col. 0935] “receive”: collected editions.]

Gratian. Within an assigned diocese, the tithing revenue from whatever estates are cultivated ought to be paid to the baptismal church. Therefore, since these estates [Col. 0935B] lie within the boundaries of our diocese, and the revenue of tithes has lawfully been assigned to us, it must be paid to our church.

II. Part. § 1. The reply to this is as follows. Tithes [Note: [Col. 0935] Num. 18.] were instituted by God through Moses, to be paid by the people to the sons of Levi for the ministry in which they served him in the tabernacle. The sons of Levi received tithes only from those for whom they offered prayers and sacrifices. Therefore, since we serve the Lord in the tabernacle by offering prayers and sacrifices for these persons, they too ought to pay us tithes and firstfruits.

§ 2. Likewise, when tithes were given to the sons of Levi, they were not paid at the donor’s choice, so that, disregarding the Levite who was with him, a person might himself choose to whom he wished to give tithes. For it is said [Note: [Col. 0935] Deut. 14; 27; 16:11.]: “The Levite who dwells with you and lives within your gates [Col. 0935C] shall eat them.” Accordingly, they received cities to inhabit from each tribe, so that every tribe might pay tithes to those who were with it. For Moses [Note: [Col. 0935] ibid., 12:5 ff.] commanded the children of Israel, as is read in Deuteronomy:

“To the place which the Lord your God shall choose, that his name may be there, you shall bring all that I command you: burnt offerings, sacrifices, tithes, the firstfruits of your hands, and whatever is foremost among the gifts that you have vowed to the Lord. There you shall feast before the Lord your God—you, your sons and daughters, male and female servants, and the Levite who dwells in your cities; for he has no other share or possession among you.”

And below:

§ 3. “The tithe of your grain, wine, and oil; the firstborn of your herds and flocks; everything [Col. 0935D] you have vowed; whatever you wish to offer voluntarily; and the firstfruits of your hands—you shall eat these before the Lord your God in the place which the Lord your God shall choose: you, your son and daughter, male and female servant, and the Levite who lives in your cities.”

§ 4. Therefore, since we reside within these people’s city walls and are joined to them by dwelling among them, we rightly receive tithes from them.

[Col. 0936A] The Prophet also says [Note: [Col. 0935] Ps. 103:14.]: “Bringing forth grass for cattle, and plants for the service of human beings.” Grass and plants spring from the earth—but for whom? For the cattle that water it, that is, for the people who cultivate it and thereby serve it.

Likewise the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0935] Gal. 6:6.]: “Let him who is instructed in the word share all good things with him who instructs him.” This he says to the Galatians. But to the Corinthians [Note: [Col. 0935] 1 Cor. 9:11.] he specifically proves that support is owed to himself, who ministered spiritual things to them, saying: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” Likewise [Note: [Col. 0935] ibid., v. 12.]: “If others share in authority over you, why not we rather?” Likewise: “Who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit?” We planted the vineyard, and you wish to eat its fruits?

Likewise the Lord commanded through Moses [Note: [Col. 0935] Deut. 23:25.] that no one put a sickle to another’s harvest. [Col. 0936B] This harvest is ours, and you wish to put a sickle to it? Likewise [Note: [Col. 0935] ibid., 25:4.]: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it treads out the grain.” We are the oxen treading out grain; you wish to muzzle us and seek your livelihood from our threshing floor?

Likewise the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0935] 1 Cor. 9:13.]: “Those who serve the altar should live from the altar.” But do they live from an altar which they do not serve? Likewise: “Those who work in the sanctuary share in the sanctuary.” But do they share in one in which they do not work? We serve the altar; you wish to share in it, while seeking to leave us empty and destitute.

Likewise the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0935] 2 Tim. 2:6.]: “The laboring farmer ought to be the first to receive of his fruits.” Yet you seek the opposite! We are laboring farmers, and you wish to be the first to receive our fruits—indeed, not merely first, since you do not wish to leave even the last portion for us. Beginning with the earlier portions, [Col. 0936C] you creep on little by little and strive to usurp the whole; so that the saying seems to have been made of you: “The wolf eats the lamb piece by piece.”

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0935] 1 Cor. 9:7.]: “Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who tends a flock and does not eat of its milk?” We serve as soldiers, and you seek the wages of our service for yourselves? We tend the flock, and you wish to take its milk and wool for yourselves? Wisdom consists in seeking livelihood from another’s labor—if wisdom consists in wishing for what one cannot have.

§ 5. Likewise the Lord said [Note: [Col. 0935] Luke 10:5.] to his disciples: “Into whatever house you enter, remain there, eating and drinking what they have. But when you enter, first say: ‘Peace to this house.’” We have entered this house and offered it peace; yet do you, as though idle, rejoice in being fed on another’s food? Take care lest that saying be turned against [Col. 0936D] you: “See [Note: [Col. 0935] Terence, *Eunuchus*, act 2, scene 2, v. 34.] what idleness and another’s food can do.”

§ 6. Likewise the Prophet says [Note: [Col. 0935] Ps. 80:13.]: “Take up the psalm and give the tambourine.” These people receive the psalm from us; and do you seek the tambourine from them?

§ 7. Likewise Leo IV says: “Concerning tithes, it has seemed right in due order not only to us but also to our predecessors that they ought to be given only to those congregations where the most holy baptisms are administered.” [Note: [Col. 0935] Below, C. 16, q. 1, c. 45.]

§ 8. [Col. 0937A] But to which congregations are they owed? To those from whom they receive baptism, or to others? We baptize them, and you take tithes from them? That is a handsome interpretation; would that you may find persons who interpret it so in your favor! Therefore, since we water this people by supplying it with the rain of teaching, and cultivate it with the ploughshare of preaching, opening its hearts to faith: if you do not wish to allow us this, at least allow it to bear fruit for us. And beware of doing to us what you would not have done to yourselves, lest, if you continue to say what you wish, you hear what you do not wish.

III. Part. § 9. To this they reply: You indeed strive cunningly and by manifold argument to take away our rights, so that, if words were believed, you would carry off not words for words but things for words. But, God willing, if you have given words, you shall receive words.

§ 10. You accuse us [Col. 0937B] of seeking to steal what is owed to you because we pursue what is ours. A maxim uttered, to be sure, by a wise and philosophical mouth! Is pursuing one’s own property the same as seizing another’s? How did this maxim come to you, unless because you desire our goods with such ardor that you imagine your own are being taken away when we obtain ours? Thus, when our case has reached its due conclusion, you will cry out [Note: [Col. 0937] Terence, *Heautontimorumenos*, act 4, scene 2, ch. 6.]: “Ah, wretch that I am, I am tormented that such a morsel has been snatched from my jaws.” But take care that you do not seek to compensate yourselves for the loss of spilt ointment.

You have made yourselves vine-dressers, diggers of fields, threshers of floors, irrigators of fields, and have assumed many other offices of this sort; and you complain that services owed to you are withheld by us. But we do not deny you what is yours. For the ox treading grain, [Col. 0937C] straw and coverings are reserved. Let these be yours, and leave the grain to us. Vineyard laborers, field diggers, irrigators of fields, and threshers of floors, having received their daily wage, leave the resulting fruits to their masters. Therefore, having received the wage of your work in the daily offerings and other services which those who receive spiritual things from you bring to you every day, leave to us the resulting fruits of tithes and firstfruits.

§ 11. Likewise the Lord commanded his disciples to eat and drink what was among their hearers, but he did not command them to cast householders out of their homes and strip them of their goods. You will not easily find people willing to receive such guests gladly. A mouse in a bag, fire in the lap, and a serpent in the bosom repay their hosts badly. Hence it is said in Proverbs: “He who nourishes a serpent in his bosom will be struck by it.” May you find for yourselves such hosts as you wish to be for us.

It does not suffice you to eat and drink what is in our house, while receiving the daily fruits of offerings from which you have food and clothing, with which you ought to be content, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0937] 1 Tim. 6:8.]; but you are unwilling, because you are not his imitators. Rather, you strive to cast us from our house and strip us entirely of our goods, since [Col. 0938A] you are unwilling to leave us even their tithes.

§ 12. To gather everything together universally: all the passages introduced in your favor, whether concerning the laboring farmer or one who does not serve at his own expense, we refer to this point: receive, in the offerings and daily services of these people, the fruit of your labor which you so eagerly seek to obtain; but leave untouched for us their tithes, which are owed to us. Otherwise, while seeking to usurp what is not yours, you may, by just judgment, be compelled to lose even that which seemed in some measure to belong to you.

§ 13. We can readily prove that these tithes are owed to you by no right whatever. For it is said in a certain council: “If [Note: [Col. 0937] Below, C. 16, q. 1, c. 42.] any layman or cleric, or person of either sex, [concerning] places of his property,” etc., [Col. 0938B] as is found noted in the same chapter in the case concerning monks. Therefore, if a layman, cleric, or any person selling or giving away places of his property cannot in any way withdraw their tithe revenue from the church to which it has lawfully been assigned, neither can these persons, by moving from diocese to diocese, take away from us the tithes of their estates which lie within the boundaries of our parish. For, as regards the right to receive tithes, a possessor’s moving from diocese to diocese is the same as transferring an estate from one diocesan jurisdiction to another.

## QUESTION II

[Col. 0938C] GRATIAN

I. Part. To this: Although these tithes are owed to you by right, as you assert, the objection of thirty years imposes silence upon you. For every possession is extinguished by prescription of thirty years, or forty years—as in the case of possessions of religious houses—or one hundred years, as in the aforesaid case of the holy Roman Church.

Accordingly Pope Gelasius says to the bishops of Sicily, epistle 2, chapter 2 [Note: [Col. 0937] Letter written A.D. 494; apocryphal in Berardi’s judgment.—Burchard, bk. 3, ch. 149. Anselm, bk. 5, ch. 19 (20). *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 65.—Cf. C. 16, q. 3, c. 2.]:

### C. I. What bishops have possessed for thirty years they may rightly claim.

The resources of a church, and likewise dioceses, if they are possessed by certain bishops, they may rightfully claim for themselves, since the law of thirty years has settled the matter; for the authority of our princely sons has also decreed [Col. 0938D] that after thirty years no one may bring an appeal concerning what the time fixed by law has excluded. [Note: [Col. 0937] “if”: omitted in Anselm.—“other certain [bishops]”: Burchard.—Cf. Codex, *On prescription of thirty or forty years*, ch. 4.—“excludes”: collected editions.]

Gratian. But they reply in turn: By the authority through which you impose silence on us, we close your mouths as well. For Gelasius himself says: “By no presumption may the established condition of parishes,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0937] Below, C. 16, q. 3, c. 5.] Therefore, if a temporal objection cannot tear apart a diocese once established, it is evident that it will not support you in changing the established order of our parish and claiming for yourselves, by actionable usurpation, tithes once lawfully assigned to us. [Col. 0939A] How these authorities are to be distinguished will be found in the case concerning monks. [Note: [Col. 0939] Below, C. 16, q. 4.]

II. Part. § 1. The question now concerns the right of burial: which of these churches has the right to bury these persons? As Jerome writes, married persons seem to be placed in one grave. For he says [Note: [Col. 0939] In *Questions on Genesis*.—Burchard, bk. 3, chs. 160, 161; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, chs. 223, 224; *Polycarpus*, bk. 8, title 5.]:

### C. II. Children are to be placed in the tomb of their parents.

Hebron is said to be the city of four men [Note: [Col. 0939D] “Four”: thus emended, whereas it was previously read as “three” [thus in the collected editions and in Burchard and Ivo]. For this is read in St Jerome, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, *On Hebrew Places*, and the *Epitaph of Paula*. The Hebrew word signifies “four,” and four patriarchs are counted as buried there: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Adam, with their wives.] because three patriarchs were buried there in the double cave with their three wives: Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, Jacob and Leah—besides Adam himself and Eve his wife.

Tobit says to his son [Note: [Col. 0939] Tob. 4:3; 14:12.]: “When God receives my soul, bury my body; honor your mother [Col. 0939B] all the days of her life [Note: “your life”: Basel edition.—Omitted in the Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, and first Venetian editions.]; and when she has completed her time, bury [Note: “you shall bury”: Basel edition.] her beside me in one grave.” In the same place:

§ 1. “Let one tomb unite those whom one marriage has united, because they are one flesh; and let not a human being separate those whom God has joined.” [Note: [Col. 0939] Matt. 19:6.]

### C. III. Likewise Augustine.

[Note: [Col. 0939D] In most ancient copies this chapter is joined to the preceding one, and the actual words of the authors are not fully quoted.]

[Note: [Col. 0939] The first part of the chapter, cited in Augustine by Burchard, bk. 3, ch. 100, and Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, ch. 225, has not been found. The second, cited from the same Augustine by Burchard, ibid., ch. 103, and Ivo, ibid., ch. 226, is read in Gregory, *Dialogues*, bk. 2, ch. 34.]

III. Part. Every woman should follow her husband, whether in life or in death. Likewise Gregory says:

§ 1. The sister of St Benedict was buried in the tomb which he had prepared for himself, so that burial might not separate the bodies of those whose minds had always been one in the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0939] “separate”: collected editions; first Norimbergensis and Lyons II–III editions.]

Gratian. Likewise Joseph [Note: [Col. 0939] Gen. 50.], dying in Egypt, begged his brothers that at the time of their visitation they should carry his bones [Col. 0939C] with them and place them in the tomb of his fathers.

§ 1. Likewise, it was said to the Prophet [Note: [Col. 0939] 3 Kings 13:22.] who had eaten in Bethel contrary to the Lord’s command: “Your corpse shall not be brought into the tomb of your fathers.”

§ 2. Likewise, of some persons it is read in the Book of Kings: “He died and was gathered to his fathers,” that is, into the tomb of his fathers.

§ 3. Likewise, in the New [Note: [Col. 0939] Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. 3, ch. 31.] Testament, St Philip is said to have built himself a tomb in which he and his daughters rested.

§ 4. Likewise, St Severus, archbishop of Ravenna, ordered a tomb to be made in which he placed himself, his wife, and his daughter.

§ 5. From all these examples it is inferred that the bodies of children should be placed in the tombs [Col. 0940A] of their parents. Therefore, because the parents of these persons were buried at the former churches, these persons too ought to be buried at the same churches.

§ 6. On the other hand, Adam [Note: [Col. 0939] Gen. 25.] was buried, as you assert, in the city of Arba. But were all his children buried there? So great a multitude of the human race cannot easily be contained in so small a grave.

§ 7. Likewise Abraham [Note: [Col. 0939] Ibid., chs. 33, 49, 50.] was buried there. But were Ishmael, Madai, and the others whom he begot by Keturah buried there?

§ 8. Likewise Isaac was buried there. But was Esau buried with him?

§ 9. Likewise Jacob was placed there. But was any of his sons except Joseph buried there? Rachel too is recorded as buried not at Hebron but beside Bethlehem. Therefore these examples make clear that children are free to be buried in the tombs of their fathers [Col. 0940B] and free, according to the circumstances of place and time, to find elsewhere a lodging for their bodies. Thus these persons are not compelled by this example to be buried in the tombs of their fathers.

§ 10. Likewise, it is not permitted to alter what has been determined by laws. But matters not specified by laws follow the judgment of human choice. Now the laws determine to whom tithes must be paid, and therefore the giver may not alter this. But the laws do not specify where each person must be buried, and therefore burial depends on the choice of the person arranging it.

Accordingly St Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0940D] The sense of this chapter is found in book 3, letter 9, in the words quoted below at 16, q. 1, “Admonere”; likewise in book 9, letter 20: “It is necessary,” he says, “that if this is fulfilled, the disposition of the deceased be preserved.” Thus the manuscripts, although the printed editions read “the burial be preserved.”] [Note: [Col. 0939] Cf. C. 16, q. 1, c. 14.]:

### C. IV. The last will of the deceased must be observed.

The last will of the deceased must be preserved in every way. [Note: [Col. 0939] “observed”: collected editions.]

IV. Part. Gratian. This must be understood of a free person, not a slave. For a slave cannot draw up the document of a will.

Accordingly Pope Gelasius writes to Bishop Honorius [Note: [Col. 0939] Chapter of uncertain date.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 16, ch. 111.]:

### C. V. A slave cannot make a will.

We also wish that it not escape your sincerity that it has been reported to us that Ampliatus, a leaseholder, who is known not merely to be a slave of the Church but to have been so entangled in its accounts for many years that, even if he were freeborn, he would necessarily remain liable until he had rendered all accounts, has presumptuously attempted to draw up a document of a will. All his peculium is undoubtedly bound by law to the Church’s right. [Col. 0941A] Therefore, in our stead, let your brotherhood oppose these presumptions and permit nothing whatever to be done by deceit. If anything human should happen to him—for he is said to be very old [Note: [Col. 0941] “is mentioned”: collected editions.]—let your humanity immediately, without delay, order [Note: [Col. 0941] Omitted in Ivo.] his property to be handed over, under a faithful inventory, only to his children, to whom this patrimony is shown to have been entrusted [Note: [Col. 0941] “unanimity”: Ivo.—“record”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.—“hand over”: Ivo.], until they are compelled to restore unimpaired the master’s shares for all the years in which he is known to have administered this patrimony.

V. Part. Gratian. Therefore, since according to Gregory the deceased’s last will must be observed, their bodies are to be buried according to their own will, not at the discretion of your arrangement.

[Col. 0941B] Likewise, it is read in the Council of Tribur [Note: [Col. 0941D] In the printed Council of Tribur, ch. 15, the same sense occurs, though not expressed in precisely the same words.] [Note: [Col. 0941] Held A.D. 895.—Burchard, bk. 3, ch. 237; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, ch. 278.—Cf. below, C. 16, q. 1, c. 16.]:

### C. VI. Where a person has paid tithes, there he ought to choose burial.

Wherever circumstances of time or place permit, burials are to be celebrated at the greater church, where the bishop has his seat. But if this seems difficult because of the harshness of time or place, the person is to be buried at a church in which [Note: [Col. 0941] “which”: collected editions; first Basel edition.] a religious community of regular canons, monks, or nuns lives together. But if this too seems unsuitable, where a person paid tithes while alive, there he is to be buried when dead.

Gratian. Therefore, because he paid tithes to us while alive, he is to be buried with us when dead. Likewise, if [Col. 0941C] someone moved from one province to another and established his residence there, being freed from the authority of the former judge, he would become subject to the jurisdiction of the judge in whose province he chose to settle. Therefore, because these persons have moved from your diocese into ours, they are free from your authority and subject to our right. The right to bury them is therefore ours.

But the following of Pope Miltiades is objected [Note: [Col. 0941] A chapter wholly uncertain.]:

### C. VII. It is not permitted, through one’s own rashness, to abandon the burial-place of one’s parents.

It has pleased the great council in every respect that no one should, through the rashness of his own judgment, arrange to go to another church for burial except that to which, by canonical institution, the practice of his ancient parents is said to be subject, [Col. 0941D] unless, prevented by illness, he has travelled to another region on some business. [Col. 0942A] If any prelate should endeavor to act against this, let him know that he subjects himself to ecclesiastical censure.

Gratian. But it is one thing, in the pride of rashness, not to follow the practice of one’s ancient parents; it is another, for a reasonable cause, to choose a new burial-place for oneself. He acts contrary to Pope Miltiades’s authority who, led by pride or hatred, or enticed by empty persuasions or various little gifts, scorns to follow the burial-place of his parents. [Note: [Col. 0941D] After “scorns to follow,” two Vatican copies of Gratian continue: “Bishop Leo says,” etc., and give in full the chapter *Relatum*, X, title *On Burial*, which is also reported by Ivo, pt. 7, ch. 150; Anselm, bk. 5, ch. 55; and *Polycarpus*, bk. 4, title 34, from Leo IX. But in two other ancient and very carefully corrected copies, this same chapter is placed after the sentence “He received the sacraments.” Certainly the words “and according to Leo,” etc., indicate that Gratian has cited this authority of Leo somewhere.]

According to Gregory, however, one who for a definite reason seeks a new lodging for his body has free choice.

§ 1. Or, as some distinguish, the last will of every person is free not in choosing a burial-place but in drawing up a will. It is called a “will” (*testamentum*) because by it each person freely declares what he wishes to be done with his own goods after death.

§ 2. Yet the will-maker’s choice does not seem free, since according to Augustine the testamentary distribution of property should be made in proportion [Col. 0942B] to the number of children: for example, if one has one child, one should consider Christ a second; if two, make Christ a third; and so in order. And according to Leo, each person is commanded to leave to the church where he received the sacraments of faith one half [Note: [Col. 0941] Cf. ch. 4, *Compilatio I*, and ch. 2, X, *On Burial*.] of what he bequeaths to Christ. But Augustine’s statement is not a command but an exhortation, lest someone in anger disinherit his son and leave everything to Christ.

[Col. 0942C] For he says in Sermon II, *On the Life of Clerics* [Note: [Col. 0941] Sermon 355, Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, ch. 178.]:

### C. VIII. A share of the inheritance should be offered to God in proportion to the number of children.

If someone is angry with his son and disinherits him when dying, would I not, if he were alive, placate him? Ought I not to reconcile his son to him? How then do I wish him to be at peace with his son, whose inheritance I seek? But let him certainly do as I have often urged. He has one [Note: “He who has one”: same editions.] son: let him regard Christ as a second; he has two [Note: “If he has two”: same editions.] sons: let him regard Christ as a third; he has ten: let him make Christ the eleventh, and I accept it.

Gratian. By this authority, plainly, a limit is set for the testator—not a measure which he is compelled to pay, but one which he is forbidden to exceed.

[Col. 0942D] VI. Part. § 1. Therefore, anyone unwilling to render the offerings of the deceased is to be excommunicated.

[Col. 0943A] Accordingly, in the Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 95 [Note: [Col. 0943] Ch. 86 of the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*; cf. on ch. 9, Dist. 18.—Burchard, bk. 3, ch. 142; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, ch. 208, both from a council at Valence; see on C. 12, q. 2, c. 52.]:

### C. IX. Those who deny churches the offerings of the deceased are to be excommunicated.

Those who deny the offerings of the deceased to churches, or render them with difficulty, are to be excommunicated as murderers of the needy. [Note: [Col. 0943] “with difficulty”: original text.]

### C. X. Unbelievers who withhold offerings of the deceased are to be expelled from churches.

Likewise from the First Council of Vaison, ch. 4. [Note: [Col. 0943] Held A.D. 442.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, ch. 155; Deusdedit, pt. 4.]

Those who withhold [Note: [Col. 0943] “detain”: original text.] offerings of the deceased and delay delivering them to churches are to be cast out of the Church as unbelievers.
