For this provocation of divine mercy is certainly seen to lead even to the emptying-out [Note: [Col. 0943] “utter emptying”: original text; Ivo; collected editions.] of faith, since believers departing from the body are defrauded of the fulfillment of their vows, while the poor are defrauded of the comfort of food [Col. 0943B] and necessary support. Such people [Note: [Col. 0943] “therefore”: collected editions.] are to be regarded as murderers of the needy and as persons who do not believe in the judgment of God. Hence one of the Fathers inserted in his writings this fitting statement [Note: [Col. 0943] C. 12, q. 2, c. 71.]: “To rob a friend of anything is theft; but to defraud the Church is sacrilege.”

### C. XI. Those who presume to retain offerings made to churches or property left by will are to be excommunicated.

Likewise from the Council of Agde, ch. 4. [Note: [Col. 0943] Held A.D. 506.—Burchard, bk. 3, ch. 140, from a council at Valence; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 5; *Decretum*, pt. 3, ch. 206.]

Clerics or laypersons who persist in retaining the offerings of parents, whether donated or left by will [Note: [Col. 0943] “wills”: original text and cited collections.], or who believe that what they themselves have given to churches [Note: [Col. 0943] “church”: Basel edition.] or monasteries ought to be taken away, are, as the holy synod has decreed, to be excluded from the churches as murderers of the poor until they restore it. [Note: [Col. 0943] “from the churches”: original text, cited collections, and collected editions.]

§ 1. But if any [Col. 0943C] cleric commits theft from the Church, he is to be granted communion only as a pilgrim.

VII. Part. Gratian. The question is also asked whether anything should be demanded for the burial of the dead.

Gregory writes as follows on this subject in book VII of the *Register*, indiction 2, letter 55, to Januarius, bishop of Sardinia [Note: [Col. 0943] Letter 3, written A.D. 599, book 9 in the Maurist edition.—*Regino*, bk. 1, ch. 122; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, ch. 101; *Polycarpus*, bk. 2, title 5.]:

### C. XII. No payment is to be demanded for burial.

The most noble woman Nereida complained to us that [Col. 0944A] your brotherhood wishes [Note: [Col. 0943] “is not ashamed”: original text.] to demand from her one hundred [Note: [Col. 0943C] “One hundred” is absent from some copies of Gratian and of St Gregory’s letters; but since it is read in other copies of those texts, including manuscripts, it has not been removed.] [Note: [Col. 0943] Omitted in the collected editions, first Lyons II–III editions.] solidi for the burial of her daughter. And below: We too, after God’s agency brought us to the dignity of the episcopate, wholly forbade this abuse in our church and did not permit that corrupt custom to be introduced again [Note: [Col. 0943] “through”: collected editions and Böhm.—“to introduce”: Böhm and the original text.], remembering that when Abraham [Note: [Col. 0943] Gen. 23.] asked from the sons of Ephron [Note: [Col. 0943C] “Ephron”: this passage is variously read. In the more accepted text of St Gregory’s letter it reads: “from the sons of Emor, that is, Ephron son of Seor”; and Gen. 23 has: “Intercede for me with Ephron, son of Seor.”], that is, from the sons of Seor, a burial plot [Note: [Col. 0943] “burial”: Basel edition; “tomb”: the other editions and original text.] for a price in which to bury his wife’s body, he refused to accept payment, lest he seem to have derived profit from a corpse. If, therefore, a pagan man showed such scruple, how much more ought we, who are called priests, refrain from doing this? I therefore admonish you lest this vice of avarice [Note: [Col. 0943] “here”: Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, and Venetian I–II editions.] be presumed to be attempted again either [lacuna] in other places.

§ 1. But whenever you allow anyone to be buried in your church, if the person’s parents, relatives, or heirs wish voluntarily to offer something for lights, we do not forbid its acceptance. [Col. 0944B] But we wholly forbid requesting or demanding anything, lest—as is very irreligious—the church perhaps [Note: [Col. 0943] Omitted in the same editions.] be called venal, or you appear to rejoice in human deaths, if you endeavor [Note: [Col. 0943] “endeavor”: Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, and Venetian I editions.] to gain profit in any fashion from their corpses. [Note: [Col. 0943D] After this chapter, two ancient copies contain two decrees of Urban II. They are included here lest they perish altogether, since they are not easily found elsewhere; one is cited in X, *On Burial*, ch. *Certificari*. Urban II to Godfrey, bishop of Maguelonne: “Of the deceased who desire to be buried in a monastery, we decree that either, in accordance with the decree of our predecessor Leo, half the alms be left to the parish churches, or, according to our dispensation promulgated at the Lateran Council, one third.” The same to the same: “We also wish the chaplains of monks, like the other clerics of your parish, to render you due obedience.”]

### C. XIII. Even when compelled, we ought not accept payment for burial.

Likewise Jerome, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, concerning Genesis 23. [Note: [Col. 0943] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 26.]

After Ephron was overcome by payment to sell a tomb for silver—although Abraham compelled him—the letter *waw*, which among them is read as *o*, was removed from his name; and instead of Ephron he was called Ephran. [Col. 0944C] Scripture thereby signifies that he was not of complete and perfect virtue, since he was able [Note: “was able”: Basel edition.] to sell the memorials [Note: “memorial”: collected editions, Ivo, and Böhm.] of the dead.

§ 1. Therefore let those who sell burial places know—those who are not compelled to receive payment, but extort something even from unwilling persons [Note: [Col. 0943] “anything”: collected editions.]—that their name is changed and that something of their merit perishes, [Col. 0945A] since even he who accepted payment unwillingly is reproved in secret. [Note: [Col. 0945] “accepts”: Lyons II edition; “accepted”: remaining editions.]

### C. XIV. On the same subject.

Likewise from the Council of Tribur, ch. 16. [Note: [Col. 0945] Held A.D. 895.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, ch. 215.]

For it is written in the ecclesiastical book [Note: [Col. 0945] Ecclus. 7:27.]: “Do not withhold kindness from the dead, knowing that we all shall die.” And likewise [Note: [Col. 0945] “Likewise”: original text, Ivo, and collected editions; cf. Ecclus. 41:13.]: “All things that are from the earth [Note: “sprung”: Ivo and collected editions.] return to the earth.” Why do you sell earth to earth? Remember that you are earth and shall go into earth [Note: [Col. 0945C] “You shall go”: the printed copies read “you shall return,” followed by: “and elsewhere it is said of a human being: ‘You tread earth, you bear earth, and you shall be turned into earth, for you are taken from earth.’” These words have been deleted because they are absent from most ancient copies [and from the Argentinensis edition and Ivo], as well as from the original text.]; and remember that death is to be yours: it draws near [Note: [Col. 0945] “hastens”: Pithoean and Böhm editions; “draws near”: collected editions, first Argentinensis and Basel editions.] and does not delay. Remember that the earth does not belong to a human being, but, as the Psalmist recalls [Note: [Col. 0945] Ps. 23:1.]: “The earth belongs to the Lord, and [Note: “and its fullness”: Ivo and collected editions.] those who dwell in it.” If you sell earth, you will be held guilty of invading another’s property. You received freely [Note: “received … give”: Basel edition.] from God; give freely for his sake.

Therefore [Col. 0945B] it is forbidden to all Christians without exception to sell earth to the dead and deny them due burial, unless perhaps the relatives and friends of the deceased wish freely to give something for the Lord’s name [Note: [Col. 0945] “of the Lord”: original text.] and for the redemption of the dead man’s soul. [Note: [Col. 0945] “of the deceased”: collected editions, first Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, and Venetian I editions.]

### C. XV. On the Same Subject. Likewise, from the Council of Vannes

[Note: [Col. 0945C] It appears in the Council of Nantes, c. 6, from which it is cited by Burchard and Ivo. But, since it may have been repeated in some Council of Vannes or Vaison, it has not been changed. In the epitome of councils, however, it is found in the Council of Vaison, c. 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0945] From the Council of Nantes.—cf. Dist. 24, c. 5.—Regino, book 1, c. 125; Burchard, book 3, c. 159; Ivo, Decree, part 3, c. 222.]

In accordance with the authority of the canons, it must be commanded that they demand no fee for graves and for the burial of persons, unless perhaps the person being buried, while alive, ordered that something of his possessions be given to the church in whose churchyard he is buried; or unless, after his death, those entrusted with making his almsgiving should wish voluntarily to give something from his possessions. Yet nothing at all is to be demanded by the priests of that church, either from them or from those who preside over estates and villages.

[Note: [Col. 0945] *tribui*, “to be given”: editions of Basel and Lyons II–III.]

[Note: [Col. 0945] Omitted in the original and the cited collections; *illis*, “to those persons”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0945] Original: “that something be demanded by those priests from his possessions”; Regino and Burchard: “that something else be demanded from his possessions”; Ivo: “yet let nothing be demanded from his possessions”; editions of Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I.]

[Note: [Col. 0945] *vicis*, “districts/villages”: original and cited collections.]

§ 1. In accordance with the institutions of the fathers, it must also be forbidden that anyone be buried inside a church; they are instead to be buried in the churchyard, portico, or side-chambers of the church. But inside the church, and near the altar where the body and blood of the Lord are consecrated, they are never to be buried.

[Note: [Col. 0945] *Infra*, “below/within”: original; Regino, Burchard, and the cited editions before Lyons II–III.]

[Note: [Col. 0945] *ecclesias*, “churches”: cited editions before Basel.]

### C. XVI. Those Whose Sins Have Not Been Forgiven Are Not Helped after Death by Holy Places. Likewise Augustine

[Note: [Col. 0945C] This chapter is also cited by Burchard and Ivo as Augustine’s, and something relevant to this matter occurs in the book *On Care for the Dead*, c. 1. But it appears to have been compiled from two passages in book 4 of the *Dialogues* of St Gregory: one in c. 51 and the other in c. 53, which is reported in the Council of Tribur, c. 17. For in c. 51, after recounting that a certain nun, buried in a church, had been seen being burned there, he draws this conclusion: “From this it is plainly made clear that those whose sins have not been forgiven cannot after death be helped by holy places so as to escape judgment.” In c. 53, after mentioning that the body of a certain Valentinus had been removed from its grave by demons and cast outside the church, he adds: “From this, Peter, conclude that for those oppressed by grave sins, if they arrange to be buried in a holy place, it remains that they are also judged for their own presumption; thus holy places do not free them, but even charge them with the fault of rashness.”]

[Note: [Col. 0945] Rather, Gregory.—cf. Correction.—Burchard, book 3, c. 152; Ivo, Decree, part 3, c. 214; Polycarpus, book 8, title 5.—cf. Council of Tribur, c. 17.]

**Part VIII.** Those whose sins have not been forgiven cannot after death be helped by holy places, because grave sins oppress us if we have ourselves buried in holy places; it remains that we be judged for our presumption, because holy places do not free us, but the fault of rashness accuses us.

[Note: [Col. 0945] *sepelire*, “to be buried”: cited editions before Lyons II–III; Ivo and Burchard.]

### C. XVII. Whom Burial in a Church Benefits. Likewise Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book IV, c. 50

[Note: [Col. 0945] Burchard, book 3, c. 153; Ivo, Decree, part 3, c. 216.]

When grave sins do not oppress them, burial in a church benefits the dead in this respect: their relatives, whenever they come to those sacred places, remember those whose graves they see and pour out prayers to the Lord for them. But the bodies of those oppressed by grave sins are placed in churches not so much for their absolution as for a greater accumulation of condemnation.

[Note: [Col. 0945] *Quos*, “those whom”: original; Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 0945] Added: “have been forgiven, and”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0945] *tunc*, “then”: cited editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0945] Ivo and cited editions: “their own burial.”]

[Note: [Col. 0945] *respiciunt*, “look back upon”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0945] Cited editions: “rather for the greater accumulation of their condemnation than for absolution”; Basel reads *absolutio*, “absolution.”]

### C. XVIII. Who Are to Be Buried in a Church. Likewise, from the First Council of Mainz, c. 52

[Note: [Col. 0945] Held A.D. 803.—Burchard, book 3, c. 233; Ivo, Decree, part 3, c. 274.]

No dead person is to be buried inside a church, except bishops, abbots, worthy priests, or faithful laypersons.

[Note: [Col. 0945] *infra*, “within”: Burchard, Ivo, and cited editions before Lyons II–III.]

[Note: [Col. 0945] *ecclesias*, “churches”: cited editions.]

Gratian. What benefit the dead receive from burial beside a church, and what reaches them thereby, Augustine shows in the last chapter of his book *On Care for the Dead*, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0947] Ivo, Decree, part 2, c. 113.]

### C. XIX. Why the Dead Are Buried beside a Church

Let us not suppose that anything reaches the dead for whom we care, except what we solemnly implore for them through sacrifices of the altar, prayers, or alms. These do not benefit all for whom they are offered, but only those who, while living, acquired the condition in which they may benefit them. But because we do not discern who they are, these things ought to be done for all the baptized, lest any of those to whom such benefits can and should reach be omitted. For it is better that these things be superfluous for those whom they neither harm nor benefit than that they be lacking to those whom they benefit.

[Note: [Col. 0947] Added: “indeed”: cited editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0947] *cooperantur*, “cooperate”: same editions.]

§ 1. Nevertheless, each person does this more diligently for his own close relations, so that the same may similarly be done for him by his own people.

[Note: [Col. 0947] *quod*, “which”: Ivo.]

§ 2. Whatever is expended upon burying a body is not an aid to salvation but an office of humanity, according to the affection by which no one ever hates his own flesh. Therefore a neighbor ought, insofar as he can, to care for the flesh after the person who cared for it has departed. And if those who do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh do these things, how much more ought those who do believe to do so? The service bestowed on a dead body, yet one that is to rise again and remain in eternity, is in some manner also a testimony to that same faith.

[Note: [Col. 0947] *effectum*, “effect”: cited editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0947] *habuit*, “has hated”: same editions and Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 0947] *quamdiu*, “as long as”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0947] Added: *inde*, “thence”: Ivo and cited editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0947] Added: *ut*, “that”: cited editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0947] *evidens*, “evident”: Basel edition.]

§ 3. But when anyone is buried near the memorial shrine of martyrs, this seems to me to benefit the deceased only in this respect: the affection which commends him also to the patronage of the martyrs increases the prayer of supplication on his behalf.

[Note: [Col. 0947] *quis*, “anyone”: editions of Nuremberg, Venice I–II, Lyons, and Paris.]

[Note: [Col. 0947] *memorias*, “memorial shrines”: Ivo and cited editions.]

Gratian. Conversely, Jerome, in his commentary on Galatians, c. 6, on the words, “Each shall bear his own burden,” says:

[Note: [Col. 0947D] These are the words of St Jerome: “Although we are taught obscurely by this brief saying of a new doctrine which lies hidden while we are in the present age, whether,” etc.]

### C. XX. After Death, the Prayers of the Living Do Not Benefit the Condemned Dead

In this present age we know that we can assist one another, whether by prayers or by counsel. But when we have come before the judgment-seat of Christ, neither Job nor Daniel nor Noah can pray for anyone; rather, each person will bear his own burden.

[Note: [Col. 0947] *adjuvari*, “be assisted”: cited editions.]

Gratian. But this must be understood of the impenitent, of whom the prophet says: “He shall not give God his propitiation, nor the price of the redemption of his soul; and therefore a brother shall not redeem him, but he shall labour for ever and live still unto the end.”

[Note: [Col. 0947] Psalm 48:8.]

It cannot be understood of others.

Therefore Pope Gregory II, in his last letter to Bishop Boniface:

[Note: [Col. 0947] In Anselm, book 7, c. 186, it is correctly entitled: Gregory III to Boniface, Bishop of Mainz.—Polycarpus, book 8, title 7.]

### C. XXI. The Good Works of the Living Benefit Those Who Die in Penance

You are known to have inquired concerning those who die, whether it is permitted to offer oblations for them. Holy Church holds thus: each person should offer oblations for his own truly Christian dead, and the priest should commemorate them. And although we are all subject to sins, it is fitting that a priest commemorate and intercede for deceased Catholics; yet it is not permitted to do such a thing for the impious, even though they may have been Christians.

[Note: [Col. 0947] *cognoveris*, “you have learned”: editions of Venice II, Lyons, and Paris; *cognosceris*, “you are known”: remaining editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0947] Added: “for them”: cited editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0947] *offerri*, “to be offered”: same editions; *offerre*, “to offer”: Böhm. The original reads: “You have also inquired concerning those who die, whether it is permitted to offer.”]

[Note: [Col. 0947] *subjacemus*, “we are subject”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0947] Original: *enim*, “indeed.”]

### C. XXII. The Souls of the Dead Are Released in Four Ways. Likewise

The souls of the departed are released in four ways: by the oblations of priests, by the prayers of saints, by the alms of loved ones, or by the fasting of relatives.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] No author has been found for the words from “The souls” as far as “Care.” Burchard cites them from the sayings of Origen; the same passage is praised in the penitential book in Mansi, vol. 12, p. 502.—Burchard, book 19, c. 112; Ivo, Decree, part 15, c. 124; Polycarpus, book 8, title 6. Ivo cites them from the sayings of Gregory.]

§ 1. But the care of the funeral, the condition of the burial, and the pomp of the obsequies are consolations of the living rather than aids to the dead. If an expensive burial benefits an impious person, then a cheap burial, or none at all, will harm a devout person. And below:

[Note: [Col. 0947] From Augustine, *On Care for the Dead*, addressed to Paulinus, cc. 1–2.]

§ 2. Yet the bodies of the dead, especially of the righteous and faithful, are not therefore to be despised and cast aside. And below:

[Note: [Col. 0947] *non*, “not”: cited editions.]

§ 3. Here too we beneficially learn how great may be the recompense for alms which we bestow upon the living and conscious, if not even that service and diligence which is rendered to the limbs of human beings in the office of burial perishes before God.

[Note: [Col. 0947] *diligentia*, “diligence”: same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0947] *persolvit*, “renders”: editions of Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I.]

### C. XXIII. Before the Day of Judgment, the Dead Are Helped by Sacrifices and Alms. Likewise Augustine, *Enchiridion*, cc. 109 and 110

[Note: [Col. 0947] Anselm, book 7, c. 170 [188]; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 45.]

The period between a person’s death and the final resurrection holds souls in hidden abodes, each according as it is worthy of rest or misery, according to what it obtained in the flesh while it lived. Nor must it be denied that the souls of the departed are relieved by the piety of their living friends, when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them or alms are given in the Church. But these things benefit those who, while they were living, merited that they could afterwards benefit them.

[Note: [Col. 0947] *quaeque*, “each”: cited editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0947] *ille*, “that person”: editions of Lyons II–III.]

[Note: [Col. 0947] *mediatori*, “to the Mediator”: editions of Basel and Lyons.]

§ 1. For there is a manner of life neither so good that it does not require these things after death, nor so bad that they do not benefit it after death. But there is a manner of life so good that it does not require them, and again one so evil that, when this life has passed, it cannot be helped even by these. Therefore all merit by which someone may be relieved or burdened after this life is acquired here. And shortly afterwards:

[Note: [Col. 0949] *haec*, “these things”: cited editions.]

§ 2. When sacrifices of the altar or alms of any kind are offered for all baptized persons who have died, they are thanksgivings for the very good, propitiations for those who are not very bad, and, for the very bad, although they are no aids to the dead, they are at least consolations of some kind for the living. But those whom they benefit are benefited either so that there is full remission, or at least so that the very condemnation may become more tolerable.

[Note: [Col. 0949] Added: *tamen*, “nevertheless”: same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0949] Anselm: “that the punishment of condemnation may be tolerable.”]

**Part IX.** Gratian. Concerning the observance of the third, seventh, thirtieth, or fortieth day, the question arises: from where did it originate?

Ambrose says, almost at the beginning of his book *On the Death of Emperor Theodosius*:

[Note: [Col. 0949] Anselm, book 7, c. 169 [187].]

### C. XXIV. Why Fixed Days Are Observed in Commemorating the Dead

Since some have been accustomed to observe the third day, others the thirtieth, others the seventh, and others the fortieth, let us consider what the reading teaches. “After Jacob died,” it says, “Joseph commanded his servant embalmers to bury him; and the embalmers buried Israel, and forty days were completed for him. For thus the days of burial were numbered. And Israel mourned him seven days.” Therefore the observance prescribed by the reading should be followed. Likewise in Deuteronomy it is written: “The children of Israel mourned Moses for thirty days, and the days of mourning were completed.” Thus each observance has authority by which the necessary office of piety is fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 0949D] At St Ambrose this reads: “Since some observe the third and thirtieth day, others the seventh and fortieth.” But in Roman missals, both ancient and recent, and in Ambrosian missals, there is no mention of the fortieth day; neither is there in c. *Nullus*, above, Distinction 44, nor below in *On Consecration*, Distinction 5, from the Council of Nantes. It is, however, frequent among the Greeks.]

[Note: [Col. 0949] Added: “in the office for the dead”: cited editions; Basel reads *pro*, “for,” in place of *in*.]

[Note: [Col. 0949] Genesis 50:3.]

[Note: [Col. 0949] Added: “Israel”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0949] Omitted in Anselm.]

[Note: [Col. 0949] *completi*, “completed”: cited editions before Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I.]

[Note: [Col. 0949] *dinumerabantur*, “were numbered”: cited editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0949D] The manuscripts of St Ambrose read: “And Egypt mourned him seventy days,” as in the Septuagint and Vulgate. Yet this reading, which is found also in all Gratian manuscripts, was thought sustainable because a little later in the same Genesis 50 the following is added concerning Joseph and the other sons of Israel: “They came to the threshing-floor of Atad, situated beyond the Jordan, where, celebrating the funeral rites, they filled seven days with great and vehement lamentation.”]

[Note: [Col. 0949] Deuteronomy 34:8.]

**Part X.** Gratian. Cyprian forbids mourning and sorrow for death, whether our own or that of others, saying in his sermon *On Mortality*:

### C. XXV. We Must Not Grieve Either for Our Own Death or for That of Others

How backward and perverse it is that, although we ask for God’s will to be done, when God calls and summons us from this world, we do not immediately obey the command of his will, but resist and struggle against it. Like stubborn slaves, we are brought into the presence of the Lord with sadness and grief, departing hence under the bond of necessity, not in obedience of the will; yet we wish to be honoured with heavenly rewards by him to whom we come unwillingly.

[Note: [Col. 0949] *postulamus*, “we ask”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0949] *vocat*, “calls”: cited editions before Lyons II–III.]

The same, a little below:

§ 1. Even to us, the least and lowest, how often has it been revealed, how frequently and plainly has it been commanded by God’s gracious favour, that I should continually and publicly testify and preach that our brethren, freed from this world by the Lord’s summons, are not to be mourned. For we know that they are not lost but sent on ahead: departing, they go before us, as those setting out on a journey or embarking by ship customarily do.

[Note: [Col. 0949] Added: *ut*, “that”: cited editions.]

### C. XXVI. Mourning the Dead Arises from Faint-Heartedness. Likewise John Chrysostom, Homily XXVI on Hebrews 11

[Note: [Col. 0949] Translator: Mutianus.]

Wherever we are buried, the earth and its fullness are the Lord’s. What must be done is wholly done. But mourning, bewailing, and lamenting those who depart from this life arise from faint-heartedness.

[Note: [Col. 0949] *sepeliamini*, “you are buried”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0949] Psalm 3:1.]

[Note: [Col. 0949] Basel: “provided that what ought to be done is accomplished”; Argentinensis: “that is, provided that what ought to be done is accomplished”; remaining editions: “according as what ought to be done is accomplished.”]

[Note: [Col. 0949] *ob*, “because of”: cited editions.]

Gratian. This, however, is to be understood as referring to despair of the future resurrection. Hence the Apostle does not simply say: “We do not wish you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, so that you do not grieve”; but he adds: “as do the others who have no hope.” We are not forbidden to mourn the dead out of an affection of piety and a regard for humanity, just as we read that certain saints shed devout tears at the funerals of others.

[Note: [Col. 0949] 1 Thessalonians 4:13.]

Therefore Pope Anastasius, Letter II to Nerianus:

[Note: [Col. 0949] An apocryphal letter, which agrees almost word for word with Gregory the Great, Letter 107, book 9, Maurist edition.—Burchard, book 19, c. 129; Anselm, book 7, c. 171 [189]; Ivo, Decree, part 15, c. 139.]

### C. XXVII. Those Who Have Hope of the Future Resurrection Ought Not to Grieve for the Dead

Perhaps those have a just excuse for prolonged sorrow who do not know another life and do not trust that there is a passage from this world to a better state. But we, who know, believe, and teach this, ought not to grieve excessively for those who die, lest what bears the appearance of piety among others should be a fault all the more serious in us. For it is in some sense a kind of unbelief to be tormented with sorrow against what one preaches, the Apostle saying: “We do not wish you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, lest you grieve as the others who have no hope.”

[Note: [Col. 0949] *tristari*, “to grieve”: cited editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0949] *culpae*, “of fault”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0951C] *Torqueri*, “to be tormented”: thus corrected from the letter of St Gregory in which the same passage occurs. In Anastasius’ letter it reads: “to complain against that which each person is preached, loving justice, saying,” etc. In Gratian’s manuscripts too, the reading appeared to be mixed from both versions as follows: “to seek against that which each person preaches, loving justice, saying,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0951] *quaerit*, “seeks”: cited collections.]

[Note: [Col. 0951] *quaere*, “seek”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0951] 1 Thessalonians 4:13.]

[Note: [Col. 0951] Added: *autem*, “however”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0951] Added: *fratres*, “brethren”: same edition.]

### C. XXVIII. On the Same Subject. Likewise, from the Third Council of Toledo, c. 22

[Note: [Col. 0951] Held A.D. 559.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 36, c. 12.]

Those who depart this life by the divine call ought to be carried to their graves only with psalms and the voices of those singing psalms. We wholly forbid the funeral song customarily sung for the dead among the common people, or striking oneself or one’s relatives or household upon the breast. It is sufficient that, in the hope of resurrection, the service of divine hymns be rendered to Christian bodies. For the Apostle forbids us to mourn our dead, saying: “Concerning those who sleep, I do not wish you to grieve as the others who have no hope.” And the Lord did not weep for Lazarus as dead, but wept over the miseries of this life to which he was to be restored. If the bishop can forbid all Christians to do this, let him not delay in acting. Yet we judge that it should by no means be done otherwise in the case of religious persons. For Christian bodies ought to be buried thus throughout the whole world.

[Note: [Col. 0951C] From “For the funeral song” to “It is sufficient” has been added from the original, so that it may be understood what things are forbidden in this canon.]

It must be admitted that the dead do not know what is happening here while it is happening. Afterwards, however, they hear from those who go hence to them by dying—not indeed everything, but what those who are allowed to communicate are allowed to remember, and what it is fitting for those to hear to whom they communicate it. The dead can also hear something from angels who are present at things done here, whatever the One to whom all things are subject judges that each of them ought to hear. And below:

[Note: [Col. 0951] *agitur*, “is done”: Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0951] *isti*, “these persons”: cited editions.]

**Part XII.** Gratian. A question is raised concerning those hanged on gallows: are they to be buried near churches? Concerning them the Second Council of Mainz under Rabanus, c. 27, held A.D. 847, and the Council of Worms, held A.D. 868, c. 80, decreed as follows:

### C. XXX. Communion Is Not to Be Denied to Those Hanged on Gallows

Certain brethren have asked concerning those who are hanged on gallows for their crimes after making confession to God: whether their bodies should be carried to churches, oblations offered for them, and masses celebrated, or not. We replied: if communion must be given at the end, according to canonical command, to all who make pure confession of their sins and do worthy penance, why should it not be given to those who pay the final penalty for their sins? For it is written: “God does not exact vengeance twice for the same thing.”

[Note: [Col. 0951] *respondemus*, “we reply”: cited collections and editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0951] *canonum*, “of the canons”: Ivo, *Panormia*, and cited editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0951] Cited editions, and Ivo and Burchard in nearly the same form: “Why do the canons forbid communion and burial to those who pay the final penalty for their sins and confess, or wish to confess?”]

[Note: [Col. 0951] Nahum 1:12, according to the Septuagint.]

[Note: [Col. 0951] *judicat*, “judges”: cited editions and collections.]

### C. XXXI. PALEA

[Note: [Col. 0951] Excerpt from c. 31 of the Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895.—Regino, book 2, c. 94; Burchard, book 11, c. 59; Ivo, Decree, part 13, c. 45.—cf. X, *On Thefts*, c. 2.]

“Thieves and robbers, if they are killed while stealing or plundering, are deemed not to be persons for whom prayer should be made. But if, when captured or wounded, they confess to a priest or deacon, we do not deny them communion.”

[Note: [Col. 0951] Cited editions: “that—there is no prayer”; this is not in the original.]

In the surviving text the decree of c. 31 is stated more fully, and makes no mention of a deacon, but says: “to God and the priest.”]

### C. XXXII. On the Same Subject. PALEA. Likewise, from the Council of Orléans

[Note: [Col. 0953D] Thus in all manuscripts containing this *Palea*, and in Burchard, Ivo, and the decretal, from which many corrections of great importance have been made.]

[Note: [Col. 0953] Rather, from the Roman Penitential, from which it is correctly cited in c. 2, X, *On Homicide*.—Regino, book 1, c. 44; Burchard, book 11, c. 60 and book 19, c. 5; Ivo, Decree, part 13, c. 46.]

“If a thief or robber, caught in the act of plunder, can be apprehended without being killed, and is nevertheless killed, then, because they were created in the image of God and baptized in his name, their killers shall not enter church for forty days. Clothed in woollen garments, they shall abstain from forbidden foods and drinks, from the marital bed, from carrying a sword, and from riding. On the third and fifth days of the week and on Saturday, they shall alternately and temperately use some kind of legumes or vegetables, fruit, and small fish, with a moderate quantity of beer. But if truthful witnesses establish that, without premeditated hatred, they killed members of the devil while freeing themselves and their own property, and that the latter could not have been captured, we do not impose on them penance for homicide, unless they themselves wish to do something humane. But if the killer is a priest, he is not to be deposed; nevertheless, all the days of his life he shall do penance.”

[Note: [Col. 0953] *et absque*, “and without”: editions of Nuremberg, Venice I–II, Lyons, and Paris; omitted in the Argentinensis edition.]
