[Note: [Col. 0953] *et*, “and”: cited editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0953] *comprobantur*, “are established”: editions of Argentinensis, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice I.]

[Note: [Col. 0953] “by the same persons” is absent in the Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0953D] “And they could not be captured”: in place of these words Gratian’s manuscripts had: “and let them do penance together,” which seems to conflict with the immediately following words: “we do not impose penance for homicide on them.” The passage has been restored from the other collectors.]

## CAUSE XIV

### GRATIAN

Certain canons of a church raise a question concerning estates. They produce witnesses from among their own brethren. They entrusted money to merchants in order to receive profits from their merchandise.

(Question I.) First, it is asked whether they may recover what is theirs.

(Question II.) Second, whether those witnesses ought to be heard.

(Question III.) Third, whether this is to exact usury.

(Question IV.) Fourth, whether clerics or laypeople may demand usury from anyone.

(Question V.) Fifth, whether alms may be made from usury.

(Question VI.) Sixth, whether usurers can do penance unless they restore what they have wickedly received.

## QUESTION I

### GRATIAN

That they cannot recover what is theirs seems easy to prove. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor.” Therefore, since these men undertake the way of perfection, it is not lawful for them to possess things of their own. Much less, then, is it lawful for them to recover them, because what may not lawfully be possessed ought not to be reclaimed.

[Note: [Col. 0953] Matthew 19:21.]

§ 1. Likewise: “If anyone wishes to take your tunic and contend with you in court, let him have your cloak also.”

[Note: [Col. 0953] Matthew 5:40.]

§ 2. Likewise, the Apostle in his letter to the Corinthians: “If you have secular lawsuits, it is altogether a sin among you.”

[Note: [Col. 0953] 1 Corinthians 6:4.]

§ 3. Likewise Gregory, explaining, “All things are lawful to me, but I shall be brought under the power of none,” says: “When the mind follows the desires it has conceived, it is proved to serve the things by whose love it is overcome.”

[Note: [Col. 0953] *Morals*, book 5, c. 3.]

### C. I. A Bishop, When Challenged over Temporal Things, Is Not to Litigate. Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 19

[Note: [Col. 0953] *Statutes of the Ancient Church*, c. 8.—cf. Distinction 12, c. 9.—Collection in Three Parts, part 2, title 18, c. 18.]

A bishop, even when challenged, is not to litigate over temporal things.

Gratian. Since, therefore, those who are perfect are generally forbidden to contend in court, it is clear that these men may not stand before a judge.

§ 1. The answer is this: the perfect person is forbidden to stand in court in pursuit of gain, but not to avoid loss. Or, alternatively: it is one thing to possess one’s own goods, another to be the administrator of common goods. Canons do not possess things of their own, because goods dedicated to God belong to no individual. For they use the property of the Church, not as their own, but as goods entrusted to them for administration. Hence Prosper, in his book *On the Contemplative Life*: “The priest to whom the care of administration is entrusted,” etc.; see the cause concerning the man from whom money was demanded for entrance into a monastery. Therefore, just as these men do not possess their own goods, so neither do they recover their own goods; rather, they recover the goods of the Church, whose administration they exercise. Similarly, the prohibition against their contending in court must be understood thus: they are not to stand before a judge on their own behalf, but on behalf of others. Yet we read that some saints stood before judges and petitioned judges on behalf of others. These men, however, do not stand for themselves but for the poor, for whose needs they reclaim goods that will be beneficial; thus they are not forbidden to stand before a judge.

[Note: [Col. 0953] Cf. Cause 1, Question 2, c. 9.]

§ 2. But the Gospel saying, “If anyone takes your tunic,” etc., is not a command but an exhortation.

Therefore Augustine says in book XIX *Against Faustus*, c. 25:

[Note: [Col. 0955D] In certain ancient copies this chapter is joined to the preceding one and has been compiled from words of St Augustine, book 19, *Against Faustus*, c. 25, taken from various places and sometimes altered. It is therefore preferable to read that chapter in its entirety.]

### C. II. The Person Who Demands More Than Is Owed Sins; Not the Person Who Reclaims What Is Owed to Him

What is owed, even if it is graciously forgiven, is not unjustly reclaimed. But the person who demands more than is owed sins; therefore the law, fixing a limit, instituted the punishment of retaliation. But you are as far from the sin of an unjust claimant as you do not demand what is owed at all. Therefore the good teacher says: “Whoever strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also,” especially lest we ourselves be compelled to repay a debt to someone who has no debt owing to him.

[Note: [Col. 0955] *remittitur*, “is forgiven”: cited editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0955] *fingens*, “fashioning”: Venice II and Lyons II–III editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0955] Matthew 5:39.]

Gratian. Understand the remaining passages in the same way.

### C. III. On the Same Subject. Likewise, in the Book *On Holy Virginity*, cc. 14 and 15

[Note: [Col. 0955D] *Virginity*: the citation has been restored from Polycarpus. Formerly it was cited as from the *Sermon on the Mount*. Likewise § “What is commanded” has been restored to Jerome.]

[Note: [Col. 0955] Polycarpus, book 1, title 24.]

Whoever does not obey commandments is guilty and liable to punishment. And shortly afterwards:

§ 1. Not to obey the Lord’s commandment is sin; if you choose not to use counsel, you attain less good, but commit no evil.

Likewise Jerome, book I *Against Jovinianus*:

[Note: [Col. 0955] “Gregory in the letter to Jovinian”: cited editions.]

§ 2. What is commanded is enjoined; what is enjoined must necessarily be done; if it is not done, it incurs punishment. And below:

[Note: [Col. 0955] *faciat*, “does”: Argentinensis edition.]

§ 3. Where counsel is given, the decision belongs to the person offering it; where there is a command, necessity belongs to the person serving.

[Note: [Col. 0956D] After “the person serving,” the following words appeared: “that he may obey, or of the one commanding, that he may be obeyed.” They have been deleted on the authority of ancient manuscripts and the original. In cited editions except Basel the text reads: “of the servant or of the co-operating person.”]

## QUESTION II

### GRATIAN

Concerning the question whether they can produce witnesses from among their brethren, this seems prohibited by many authorities. For the laws both of the sacred canons and of secular rulers forbid a witness from one’s own household to be produced against anyone. Each person can testify against himself, but by no means for himself. Since, therefore, these witnesses are produced to testify for the canons themselves—for they do not suppose that they will be wholly free from the advantage accruing to their church—it is clear that their voice should not be heard in such matters.

But this distinction and examination of witnesses must be observed in criminal cases, though not altogether in civil cases. For in an accused person’s case a witness from his own household may not be produced; but in a civil case it is permitted to prelates of the Church.

Therefore Paschal II, writing to Guy, Archbishop of Vienne and legate of the Apostolic See, says:

[Note: [Col. 0955] This letter, dated at Troyes, six days before the Kalends of September, Indiction VIII, is read among the acts of the Council of Tournai, held A.D. 1115.]

### C. I. Clerics May Bear Testimony for Their Own Church

We greatly marvel at your prudence, because in the affair of St Stephen you were unwilling to accept the testimony of the clerics themselves. For the kinds of cases differ, and crimes are not litigated in every case. In criminal cases, indeed, the strict distinction concerning accusers and witnesses contained in the canons must be observed, so that members of the household are not admitted as evidence. But in cases concerning possessions or matters of this kind, those persons ought above all to be admitted who handled the matters in question and concerning whose hearing and sight there can be no hesitation. Therefore, if these clerics are suitable to establish that case, they must not at all be excluded; rather, as has been determined by other letters, that dispute between the canons of St John and St Stephen is to be decided more fully.

[Note: [Col. 0955] Omitted in the Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0955] *distinctio*, “distinction”: cited editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0955] *repellantur*, “repelled/excluded”: original.]

Gratian. It may also be understood otherwise. Members of a household are not to be admitted to give proof, namely to bear testimony on behalf of those whose household members they are. But these persons (as was said above concerning plaintiffs) are not to testify on behalf of household members, but on behalf of the Church, which is the mother of all the poor. In drawing up instruments for secular business, moreover, priests are not to be summoned as witnesses; but, if by chance they happened to be present at the contract, they are to give testimony at the bishop’s command.

[Col. 0956C] Hence it was decreed in the Synod held at Rome by Pope Eugenius II, chapter 3 [Note: [Col. 0955] held in A.D. 826.]:

C. II. Priests are not to be summoned as witnesses in drawing up instruments.

Although the testimony of priests is regarded as credible [Note: [Col. 0955] *credibile*, “credible”: collected editions.], nevertheless they themselves are not to be asked, in [Note: [Col. 0955] *in ipsis*, “in these”: same editions.] secular affairs, either for testimony [Note: [Col. 0956D] *Pro testimonio*, “for testimony”: thus corrected from the councils of Eugenius II and Leo IV and from *Polycarpus*. Previously it read: *pro conficiendis instrumentis ad testimonium non rogentur*, “they are not to be asked for the drawing up of instruments as witnesses” [Col. 0955], thus in the collected editions.] or for drawing up instruments, because it is not fitting for them to be involved in such matters [Note: [Col. 0955] *talibus rebus interesse*, “to be involved in such matters”: other editions.]. But if, through some occurrence [Note: [Col. 0955] Original: “If, indeed, they have seen or heard anything in an arising case.”], they have been present in a case and have seen or heard something, where no suitable lay persons can be found, then, lest the truth be concealed and the bad be judged good, it shall be at the discretion of their own bishop that they establish the truth, either before him and competent judges or otherwise honorably [Note: [Col. 0955] *testificentur*, “bear witness”: collected editions.].

## QUESTION III

[Col. 0957A]

GRATIAN.

That to demand usury beyond the principal is to seek gain beyond what is due is proved by Augustine’s authority. Writing on Psalm XXXVI, at the verse “All day long,” he says [Note: [Col. 0957] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, ch. 17; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, bk. 3, dist. 37.]:

C. I. Whoever receives more than he gave demands usury.

If you lend to a person [Note: [Col. 0957] *hominem*, “a person”: collected editions; first Lyons editions II and III.], that is, if you have given your money as a loan [Note: [Col. 0957] *si mutuum*, “if [you give] a loan”: Ivo; *si mutuo*, “if [you lend] by loan”: collected editions.], and expect to receive *something* more than you gave—not money alone, but something more than you gave—whether it be wheat, wine, oil, or anything else whatsoever: if you expect to receive more than you gave, you are a usurer and, in this, blameworthy rather than praiseworthy.

[Col. 0957B] C. II. Whatever is demanded beyond what was given is usury. Likewise Jerome, on Ezekiel, book VI, on chapter 18 [Note: [Col. 0957] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 160; *Decretum*, part 13, ch. 18; Peter Lombard, ibid.].

Some think that usury exists only in money. Foreseeing this, divine Scripture removes every excess from a transaction, so that you may not receive more than you gave. Likewise in the same place, § 1: Others customarily accept gifts of various kinds in return for money lent, and do not understand that Scripture calls whatever it may be “usury” [Note: [Col. 0957] *scripturam appellare*, “Scripture calls it”: collected editions.] and “excess,” if they have received more from what they gave than they gave [Note: [Col. 0957] *reacceperint*, “received back”: same editions; Ivo, *Decretum*.].

C. III. Whatever is added to the principal is usury. Likewise Ambrose, in the book *On Tobit*, chapter 14 [Note: [Col. 0957] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, ch. 26.].

Many, evading the precepts of the law, when they have lent money to merchants, demand no monetary usury [Col. 0957C] but receive from their wares profits as though they were returns of usury. Therefore let them hear what the Law says [Note: [Col. 0957] Deut. 23:19.]: “You shall take neither usury of foodstuffs nor of any other thing.” Likewise, shortly afterward, § 1: *Food also is usury, clothing also is usury, and whatever is added to the principal* [Note: [Col. 0957] *accidit*, “is added”: Argentinensis edition.] is usury; whatever name you wish to give it, it is usury. Likewise, after a few intervening words, § 2: If someone thinks he must replenish a banquet [Note: [Col. 0957] *putet*, “should think”: collected editions and the first Lyons edition.], he sends to a merchant that a cup of absinthe wine be delivered to him gratis; he goes to an innkeeper to seek Picene or Tyrian wine [Col. 0958A]; to a butcher, that he may procure for himself a *hila* [Note: [Col. 0957] *vulvam*, “womb”: Ivo; Basel edition.]; to another, that he may prepare fruit for him.

[Note: [Col. 0957C–0958C] *Absynthiaci*: Dioscorides, book 5, chapter 49, mentions this wine, which hastens slow digestion and is therefore suitable for replenishing banquets. Lampridius, in *On Heliogabalus*, says: “He invited the populace to drink both rosé and absinthe wine.” Alciatus also discusses it, *Parerga*, book 7, final chapter.]

C. IV. Whenever more than is owed is demanded, it is usury. Likewise, from the Council of Agde [Note: [Col. 0957] Rather, from the Capitularies of the Frankish Kings, bk. 1, ch. 119; *Regino*, bk. 1, ch. 284; Burchard, bk. 2, ch. 126; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 161; *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 200.].

Usury exists where more is required than is given [Note: [Col. 0957] *quam quod*, “than that which”: collected editions.]. For example, if you give ten solidi and seek more, or give one measure of grain and demand something extra.

Gratian. Here it is plainly shown that whatever is demanded beyond the principal is usury.

## QUESTION IV

GRATIAN.

That neither clerics nor laypersons may demand usury [Col. 0958B] is proved by the authority of Gelasius and others.

For Pope Gelasius, writing to the bishops throughout Lucania and Sicily, chapter 17 [Note: [Col. 0957] written A.D. 494; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 17, ch. 28; cf. ch. 2, Distinction 88.], says:

C. I. Clerics are to abstain from the profits of trade.

Clerics must *either* [Note: [Col. 0957] *aut*, “either”: marked in the source.] know that they are to abstain from unworthy gains and to refrain from every contrivance or desire for any kind of trade; *or*, whatever rank they may indeed *hold* [Note: [Col. 0957] *vero*, “indeed”: collected editions.], if they refuse to desist [Note: [Col. 0958C] *Si cessare noluerint*: these words are neither in the letter [Col. 0957], nor in Ivo, nor are they cited above in Distinction 88, chapter *Consequens*; but they were not deleted because of the gloss.], they are immediately to be compelled to abstain from clerical offices [Note: [Col. 0957] *mox a clericalibus officiis*: “immediately from clerical offices”; this is absent from the Hispanic Collection and Ivo.].

C. II. Ministers who lend at usury are to be excommunicated. Likewise, from the First Council of Arles, confirmed by Pope Sylvester, chapter 12 [Note: [Col. 0957] held A.D. 314; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, ch. 10.].

It has been decided that ministers [Note: [Col. 0957] *De ministris*, “concerning ministers”: Hispanic Collection.] who lend at usury are to be excluded from communion in accordance with the divinely given rule.

[Col. 0958C] C. III. Those wishing to belong to the clergy are to abstain from the pursuit of trade. Likewise, from the Council of Tarragona, chapter 2 [Note: [Col. 0957] held A.D. 516; Regino, bk. 1, ch. 226; Burchard, bk. 2, ch. 122; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, ch. 13 and part 16, ch. 197.].

It has been established by the decrees of the canons that whoever wishes to be in the clergy shall not engage in the business of buying cheaply or selling dearly. If he *certainly* [Note: [Col. 0957] *certe*, “certainly”: marked in the source.] wishes to carry it on, he is to be restrained from the clergy.

C. IV. Whoever demands usury or an excess is to be removed from the clergy. Likewise, from the Council of Pope Martin, chapter 62 [Note: [Col. 0957] chapter 17 of the Council of Nicaea, in the translation of Martin of Braga.].

If anyone, forgetful of the fear of the Lord and of holy Scripture—which says [Note: [Col. 0957] *sanctarum scripturarum dicunt*, “the holy Scriptures say”: collected editions; Psalm 19:5.], “He has not given his money at usury” [Note: [Col. 0957] *Qui pecc.*: Hispanic Collection and collected editions.]—after this knowledge of the great council [Note: [Col. 0959C] “Great council”: Martin of Braga speaks thus because he took this sentence from chapter 17 of the Council of Nicaea, cited below in this same chapter at *Quoniam*; and in two old manuscripts of Gratian this is immediately appended after the present passage.], lends at usury and exacts a hundredth [Note: [Col. 0959] *vel centesimam*, “or a hundredth”: other editions.], or seeks shameful gain [Note: [Col. 0959] *turpia lucra*, “shameful gains”: Hispanic Collection; *turpi lucri*, “of shameful gain”: collected editions.] from any business [Note: [Col. 0959] *inhonesto*, “shameful”: Basel edition.], or receives increments by diverse kinds of wine, grain, or any other commodity through buying or selling, he is to be deposed from his rank and held outside the clergy [Note: [Col. 0959] *depositus*, “deposed”: Hispanic Collection.].

C. V. For money lent, a cleric may receive goods at a just price. Likewise, from the Council of Tarragona, chapter 3 [Note: [Col. 0959] held A.D. 516; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 159; *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 369 and part 13, ch. 14; the editions cite “from the same,” that is, from the Council of Martin.].

If any cleric lends a solidus in a time of need, he may receive for it wine or grain at the price at which it has been decreed that it should be sold at the appointed time for purposes of trade. But if he does not have the necessary commodity, he is to receive back, without any increase, the very thing he gave.

[Col. 0959B] C. VI. A cleric is not to receive more than he lent. Likewise, from the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 16 [Note: [Col. 0959] held A.D. 397; Regino, bk. 1, ch. 230; Burchard, bk. 2, ch. 124; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 158; *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 198 and part 13, ch. 9.].

No cleric is to receive more than he lent to anyone [Note: [Col. 0959] *accipiat*, “receive”: other editions; *commodavit*, “lent”: same editions.]: if money, he is to receive money; if goods [Note: [Col. 0959] *si speciem*, “if goods”: same editions, the Hispanic Collection, Ivo, and Burchard.], he is to receive the same kind [Note: [Col. 0959] *speciem*, “kind”: Argentinensis and Basel editions; cited collections.] and quantity of goods that he gave [Note: [Col. 0959] *dederit*, “gave”: collected editions.]; and whatever else it may be, he is to receive only as much as he gave [Note: [Col. 0959] *dedit*, “gave”: collected editions.]. [Note: [Col. 0959] The following words are omitted by Regino, Burchard, and Ivo’s *Decretum*.]

C. VII. Usury is reprehensible even for laypersons. Likewise, Pope Leo, letter, chapter 3 [Note: [Col. 0959] Letter 4, written A.D. 444, Ballerini edition; Burchard, bk. 2, ch. 123; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 65; Polycarpus, bk. 4, title 31.].

We have also judged that this must not be passed over: there are certain persons [Note: [Col. 0959] *esse quosdam, qui exercere volunt*, “there are certain persons who wish to practice”: collected editions; Basel has *exercent*, “practice.”] who, seized by the desire for shameful gain, practice usurious lending and wish to grow rich by interest. We [Note: [Col. 0959] *Quod nos, ut non*: collected editions read “which we, so that not”; *tantum*, “only,” is added by the first Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, and Venice I editions; *dicemus*, “we shall say,” is the reading of the collected editions.] grieve that this falls, I shall not say only upon those established in clerical office [Note: [Col. 0959] *ordine*, “rank”: same editions.], but also upon laypersons who wish to be called Christians [Note: [Col. 0959] *et qui*, “and who”: Basel edition.]. We decree that those convicted of it are to be punished more severely [Note: [Col. 0959] *fuerint*, “have been”: Basel, Venice II, Lyons, and Paris editions.], so that every opportunity for sinning may be taken away.

C. VIII. Those who pursue shameful gain are to be expelled from the clergy. Likewise, from the Council of Nicaea, chapter 17 [Note: [Col. 0959D] Above, Distinction 47, the same canon is given from Dionysius’s translation; here it is from the ancient translation found in Isidore’s collection [Col. 0960C].] [Note: [Col. 0959] held A.D. 325; above, Distinction 47, ch. 2, and in the cited collections it is reported from Dionysius.].

Because many clerics, pursuing shameful gains from avarice, have forgotten the divine precept which says [Col. 0960A] [Note: [Col. 0959] Psalm 14:5.], “He has not given his money at usury,” *and, lending at interest, exact hundredths*, this holy council decrees [Note: [Col. 0959] *statuit hoc*, “this council decrees,” is absent in the Basel edition.] that if anyone, after this definition, is found receiving usury, pursuing shameful gain from any such business, or even lending grain in kind at one and a half times its amount—that is, at fifty-percent interest [Note: [Col. 0959] In Greek: “half-hundredths in kinds of grain”; original in the Quesnel manuscript, published by Ballerini.]—every person who has attempted anything of this kind for profit [Note: [Col. 0959] *commentus*, “contrived”: Quesnel manuscript; the Hispanic Collection reads *conatus*, “attempted.”] is to be deposed from the clergy and held outside ecclesiastical rank.

C. IX. Whoever buys cheaply in order to sell dearly pursues shameful gain. Likewise, Pope Julius [Note: [Col. 0960C] This chapter is cited in Burchard, Ivo, part 6, ch. 201, and the *Panormia* as from the decrees sent by Pope Julius concerning usurers. But Ivo himself, part 13, ch. 21, cites it from the Capitularies, where it occurs in book 1, chapter 131 [Col. 0960D].] [Note: [Col. 0959] Rather, from the Capitularies of the Frankish Kings, bk. 1, ch. 125; Regino, bk. 1, ch. 287; Burchard, bk. 2, ch. 127; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 161; *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 201 and part 13, ch. 21.].

Whoever, at harvest or vintage time, buys grain or wine not from necessity but from greed—for example, buys a measure for two denarii and keeps it until it is sold [Col. 0960B] [Note: [Col. 0959] *venundetur*, “be sold”: cited collections; *venundare possit*, “can be sold”: original.] for four denarii [Note: [Col. 0959] *contra denarios*, “for denarii”: original.], *or six*, or more—this we call shameful gain.

C. X. Whoever receives usury commits robbery. Likewise, Ambrose, in the book *On the Good of Death*, chapter 12.

If anyone receives usury, he commits robbery; he does not live life.

C. XI. One who slaughters a poor person through usury is no less cruel than one who robs some rich person. Likewise, Augustine to Macedonius, letter LIV [Note: [Col. 0959] written A.D. 414; letter 153 in the Maurist edition; Anselm, bk. 11, ch. 112; Polycarpus, bk. 6, title 20.].

What shall I say about usuries, which even the laws and judges themselves order to be paid? Is one who takes away or snatches something from a rich person more cruel than one who slaughters a poor person by usury? These things and others like them are certainly possessed wrongly, and I would wish them to be restored; but there is no judge by whom they may be recovered. Moreover, *if* we consider wisely [Col. 0960C] what is written [Note: [Col. 0959] Prov. 17:6; Septuagint.]—“The whole world is wealth to the faithful person, but not even an obol to the faithless” [Note: [Col. 0959] *Fideli homini ... infideli*, “to the faithful person ... to the faithless”: collected editions.]—do we not prove that all who seem to rejoice in possessions acquired *lawfully*, yet do not know how to use them, possess what belongs to another [Note: [Col. 0959] *alienum*, “another’s”: collected editions.]? For certainly that is not another’s which is possessed by right; and it is possessed by right when it is possessed justly [Note: [Col. 0959] *possidetur*, “is possessed”: same editions, except Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, and Venice I.]; and justly when it is possessed well. Therefore everything possessed wrongly belongs to another; and one possesses wrongly who uses wrongly.

[Col. 0961A] Gratian. Furthermore, Ambrose declares from whom usury may be exacted, saying in the book *On Tobit*, chapter 15 [Note: [Col. 0961] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, ch. 27.]:

C. XII. We may exact usury from one whom we may rightly harm.

Exact usury from one whom you rightfully desire to harm; against one against whom arms may lawfully be borne, usuries may lawfully be levied [Note: [Col. 0961] *inferuntur*, “are brought”: Ivo; *auferuntur*, “are taken away”: collected editions.]. From one whom you cannot *easily* conquer in war, you can quickly exact the hundredth in vengeance. Exact usury from one whom it is no crime to kill. He who demands usury fights without iron; he who is a usurious collector from an enemy avenges himself without a sword. Therefore, where there is a right of war, there is *also* a right of usury.

## QUESTION V

[Col. 0961B]

GRATIAN.

Part I. That alms are not to be given from lending at interest or usury, nor from anything wrongly acquired, Augustine declares in the book *On the Words of the Lord*, sermon XXXV [Note: [Col. 0961] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, ch. 16.]:

C. I. Alms cannot be made from usuries.

Do not wish to give alms from lending at interest and usuries.

C. II. An offering from robbery is rejected by God. Likewise, Ecclesiasticus, chapter 34 [Note: [Col. 0961] Ecclus. 34:21, 23–27.].

The offering of one who sacrifices from what is unjust is defiled [Note: [Col. 0961] *immolantis*, “of one sacrificing”: original.]. And below: The Most High does not approve the gifts of the unjust, nor does he regard the offerings [Note: [Col. 0961] *oblationibus*, “offerings”: collected editions.] of the unjust, nor will he be propitiated for sins by the multitude of their sacrifices. Whoever offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor [Note: [Col. 0961] *pauperis*, “of the poor”: same editions.] is like one who sacrifices a son in the sight of his father [Note: [Col. 0961] *idem est quasi*, “is just as”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.]. The bread of the needy is the life of the poor. Whoever defrauds him is a man of blood. *Whoever takes away bread earned by sweat is like one who kills his neighbor.* Whoever sheds blood and whoever defrauds a wage-worker [Note: [Col. 0961] *necessario*, “a dependent person”: collected editions.] are brothers.

C. III. Nothing is to be taken from the rich in order to give it to the needy. Likewise, Augustine, in the book of Fifty Homilies, homily 7 [Note: [Col. 0961] Rather, an uncertain author who imitated Augustine’s sermon 178 in the Maurist edition.].

Perhaps someone thinks *to himself* and says: “There are many rich Christians, greedy and avaricious. I shall not sin if I take away what is theirs and give it to the poor. Since they do no good from it, I can have a reward *if I give alms. In this matter too, let everyone spare his own soul.*” For such a thought is suggested by the devil’s cunning [Note: [Col. 0961] Lyons II and III read *ei*, “to him”; the remaining editions read *a*, “from,” in place of *ex*, “from.”]. For *even* if he gives to the poor everything that he has taken away [Note: [Col. 0961] *abstulerat*, “had taken away”: collected editions.], he increases sins [Note: [Col. 0961] *peccatum*, “sin”: same editions.] rather than lessens them.

C. IV. On the same matter. PALEA [Note: [Col. 0961C–D] This and the following *Palea* are absent from most old manuscripts, even those in which the other *Paleae* are usually found. In one manuscript, however, they occur above, in the same Question 4, after chapter *Si quis usuram*.]. [Likewise Jerome [Note: [Col. 0961] An uncertain chapter.].]

“No one who dies after committing robbery is saved, if he has the means to make restitution. If he cannot find those to whom it belonged, let him give it to the Church or to the poor.”

C. V. On the same matter. PALEA. [Likewise Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0961] This chapter is likewise uncertain.].]

“It is not lawful to purchase stolen goods, except with that intention, that they be returned to the person from whom they were taken” [Note: [Col. 0961] *ea*, “that,” is absent from the Norimbergensis and Venice I and II editions.].

[Col. 0962B] C. VI. Whoever does not return what he finds commits theft. Likewise, Augustine, in the book of Fifty Homilies, homily 9 [Note: [Col. 0961] Cf. above, ch. 3; Polycarpus, bk. 3, title 16.].

If you have found something and have not returned it, you have robbed; you have done as much as you could. Because you did not find more, you did not rob more [Note: [Col. 0961] This clause is absent from the Argentinensis, Basel, and Norimbergensis editions.]. Whoever denies what belongs to another would also take it if he could. And after a few intervening words, § 1: God questions the heart, not the hand.

C. VII. Almsgiving from permitted and rightly acquired goods pleases God. Likewise, Gregory, book VII, letter 110, to Syagrius [Note: [Col. 0962C] In the letter of St Gregory, the words of this chapter are preceded by those of the chapter *Non est putanda*, above, 1, Question 1.] [Note: [Col. 0961] Letter 106, written A.D. 599, bk. 9 in the Maurist edition; Anselm, bk. 5, ch. 31; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 191; Polycarpus, bk. 2, title 1.].

That almsgiving is pleasing in the eyes of our Redeemer which is not amassed from unlawful *things* and injustice, but is bestowed from permitted and rightly acquired goods.

[Col. 0962C] C. VIII. Whoever does not return a found object sins. Likewise, Jerome, in the book of Leviticus [Note: [Col. 0961] Rather, from Origen, Homily 4 on Leviticus.].

Many think themselves without sin if they retain another’s property that they have found, and say: “God gave it to me; to whom am I to return it?” Let them learn, *therefore*, that this sin is like robbery, if someone does not return things found.

C. IX. Good use does not justify unjust acquisition. Likewise, Augustine, book *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 14.

For if someone uses lands unjustly and improperly seized [Note: [Col. 0961] *injuste*, “unjustly,” is added in the Basel edition.] in such a way that he gives abundant alms from their fruits, he does not thereby justify robbery. § 1. Nor, if another is greedily devoted to his paternal estate or to property justly acquired [Col. 0963A], is the rule of civil law blameworthy by which he was made the lawful possessor [Note: [Col. 0961] *quisquam*, “someone”: Lyons II and III; *aliquos*, “some”: Basel; *alias*, “other”: the remaining editions.]. § 2. Nor will the perversity of a tyrannical faction [Note: [Col. 0963] *tyrannide*, “tyranny”: Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, Venice I and II.] be praiseworthy if a tyrant [Note: [Col. 0963] *tyrannos*, “tyrants”: collected editions, first Paris and Lyons editions.] treats his subjects with royal clemency. § 3. Nor is the order of royal authority blameworthy [Note: [Col. 0963] *vituperetur*, “be blamed”: collected editions.] if a king rages with tyrannical cruelty. For it is one thing to wish to use unjust power justly, and another to wish to use just power unjustly [Note: [Col. 0963D] After these words Augustine’s chapter *Concubinae* follows, below, 32, Question 2.].

C. X. It is not lawful to help one person at another’s expense. Likewise, Ambrose, book III, *On Duties*, chapter 9.

Finally, if one person cannot be helped unless another is harmed, it is better that neither be assisted than that the other be burdened. Therefore it is not the office of a priest to intervene in monetary cases [Col. 0963B] [Note: [Col. 0963] *sacerdotale*, “priestly”: collected editions.], in which it cannot be avoided that the defeated party is often harmed, since he considers himself defeated through the intervener’s favor. The priest’s task, therefore, is to harm no one and to wish to benefit all; but to be able to do so belongs to God alone.

C. XI. Alms and sacrifices offered from wickedness do not please God. Likewise, Gregory, in the *Register*, book VII, indiction 2, letter 126, to King Reccared [Note: [Col. 0963] Letter 122, written A.D. 599, bk. 9 in the Maurist edition; cf. Causa 3, Question 7, chapter 5.].

It is written [Note: [Col. 0963] Prov. 15:8.]: “The sacrifices of the wicked are an abomination to God” [Note: [Col. 0963] *sunt*, “are,” is added in the collected editions.]; “the vows of the righteous are pleasing.” For in the judgment of almighty God, not what is given, but by whom it is given, is considered [Note: [Col. 0963] *quid*, “what”: collected editions.]. Thus it is written [Note: [Col. 0963] Gen. 4:4–5.]: “The Lord looked upon Abel [Note: [Col. 0963] *Deus*, “God”: collected editions.] and his gifts; but upon Cain and [Note: [Col. 0963] *et ad*, “and upon”: same editions.] his gifts he did not look.” For when he was going to say that the Lord looked upon the gifts, he first carefully stated that he looked upon Abel. From this it is plainly shown that it was not the offerer because of the gifts, but the gifts because of the offerer, that were pleasing [Note: [Col. 0963D] These are Gregory’s words up to this point, as noted above, 3, Question 7, chapter *In gravibus*.]. For the Most High does not approve the gifts of the unjust, nor does he regard their offerings [Note: [Col. 0963] *oblationibus*, “offerings”: collected editions.], nor will he be propitiated for their sins by the multitude of their sacrifices. Likewise: “The Lord is far from the wicked, but he will hear the prayers of the righteous” [Note: [Col. 0963] Prov. 15:8, Part II.].

Part II. Gratian. In Exodus, however, it is read that the children of Israel, when about to depart from Egypt, borrowed gold and silver vessels from their neighbors, from which they afterward built a tabernacle for the Lord. Augustine answers this in the book *Questions on Exodus*, question 39 [Note: [Col. 0963] Burchard, bk. 11, ch. 53; Anselm, bk. 11, ch. 107; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, ch. 2.]:

[Col. 0964A] C. XII. It is not lawful to seize another’s goods on the example of the Israelites despoiling the Egyptians.

The Lord said to Moses [Note: [Col. 0963] Exod. 11:2.]: “Let a man request from his neighbor, and a woman from her neighbor, vessels of gold and silver and clothing.” No one should think that he ought to take from this an example for despoiling his neighbor in this manner. For God commanded this, who knew what each person ought to suffer [Note: [Col. 0963] *oporteat*, “ought”: collected editions.]. Nor did the Israelites commit theft; rather, they performed service to God who commanded them.

Part III. Gratian. The following objection is also made: seizing another’s goods is not contrary to a commandment, since robbery appears nowhere to be prohibited by any command of God. But under the name of theft is understood every unlawful appropriation of another’s thing.

[Col. 0964B] Hence Augustine, in the same book, question 71, says [Note: [Col. 0963] Burchard, ibid., ch. 54; Ivo, ibid., ch. 3; Anselm, ibid., ch. 9; Polycarpus, bk. 6, title 16; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, bk. 3, dist. 37.]:

C. XIII. To snatch something by force merits a greater punishment than theft.

It is punishable to take secretly; it merits a much greater punishment to snatch visibly. Thus taking from an unwilling person, whether secretly or openly, has its own commandment. For under the name of theft every unlawful appropriation of another’s thing is properly understood. He who prohibited theft did not permit robbery; rather, he intended that robbery too should be understood under the name of theft in the law of the Old Testament. For by a part he signified the whole: whatever of a neighbor’s goods is unlawfully taken [Note: [Col. 0963D–0964D] *Furti enim*: these are words of St Augustine, although the phrasing has been altered; what precedes is not found in him. Augustine’s complete passage on theft and adultery occurs below, 32, Question 4, chapter *Meretrices*. *significatae quicquid aufertur*: Burchard’s reading; *rerum proximi*, “of a neighbor’s goods,” is absent from the Argentinensis and Basel editions; *auferatur*, “is taken,” is the reading of those editions.].

Gratian. These authorities prove that no one may give alms either from found goods or from ill-gotten goods.

Part IV. § 1. But Augustine says the contrary in sermon XXXV, *On the Words of the Lord* [Note: [Col. 0963] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, ch. 16.]:

[Col. 0964C] C. XIV. Good may be done from ill-gotten goods.

Whatever you have [Note: [Col. 0963] *aliquid*, “something”: collected editions.] from evil, make good from it. You who have nothing from evil, do not acquire from evil. Be yourself good, you who make good from evil; and when you have begun to make something good from evil, do not remain evil yourself. Are your coins converted into good while you remain evil?

Gratian. But this is to be understood in several ways. One makes good from evil who restores what he unlawfully took. The word “evil” also expresses the care and anxiety of mortals. Therefore one makes good from evil who dispenses to the poor what he has acquired with labor and anxiety [Col. 0964D], according to the Gospel saying [Note: [Col. 0963] Luke 16:9.]: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity.” Or something is acquired from evil when it is possessed through a disgraceful occupation, as when an astrologer gains something from the art he teaches or from the future events he foretells. Things thus acquired from evil can be converted to good. Things are also sometimes acquired from sin which may justly be distributed to the poor.

Hence Augustine, to Macedonius, letter LIV [Note: [Col. 0965] written A.D. 414; letter 153 in the Maurist edition; Anselm, bk. 11, ch. 111; Polycarpus, bk. 6, title 20.]:

C. XV. Things wrongly acquired can sometimes be rightly spent.

Certainly, not everything taken from an unwilling person is taken wrongfully. For many people do not wish to pay the honorarium due to a physician or the wages due to a worker; yet those who receive these things from an unwilling person receive them not by injury, since it would rather be an injury not to give them [Note: [Col. 0965] *accipiuntur*, “are received”: Basel and Lyons II and III editions.].

§ 1. But a judge must not therefore sell a just judgment, or a witness a true testimony, because an advocate sells just advocacy and a jurist true counsel. The former are employed between the two parties for examination; the latter stand on one side. But when judgments and testimonies, which ought not to be sold as either just or true, are sold as unjust and false, money is certainly taken much more wickedly, because it is wickedly given even though by willing persons. Yet the person who purchases a just judgment customarily seeks to recover the money *as though* it had been wrongly taken from him, because it ought not to have been for sale. But the person who paid for an unjust judgment would indeed wish to recover it, if he were not afraid or ashamed of having bought it.

§ 2. There are other persons of lower station who accept payments from both sides without insolence, such as an official, one removed from office, and one appointed to office. Things extorted from them by excessive dishonesty [Note: [Col. 0965] *probitatem*, “honesty”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.] are customarily recovered; things given through tolerable custom are not customarily recovered [Note: [Col. 0965D] These words have been added from the original, without which what follows was not sufficiently coherent.]. We condemn more those who recover such things in an unusual manner than those who receive them according to custom, because many persons necessary to human affairs are either invited or bound by such advantages.

§ 3. If these persons change their manner of life or ascend to a higher degree of holiness, they more readily give to the poor, as their own, what they acquired in this manner than restore it, as another’s, to those from whom it was received.

§ 4. But what anyone has taken contrary to the law of human society by thefts, robberies, false accusations, oppressions, or invasions [Note: [Col. 0965] *aliqua*, “some,” is added in the collected editions.], we judge should be restored rather than given away, following the Gospel example of Zacchaeus the publican [Note: [Col. 0965] Luke 19.].

## QUESTION VI

GRATIAN.

Part I. That penance cannot be done unless another’s property is restored is attested by Augustine to Macedonius, letter LIV [Note: [Col. 0965] written A.D. 414; letter 153 in the Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, ch. 4 and part 15, ch. 25.]:

C. I. Penance is not done if another’s property is not restored.

If another’s property, on account of which sin was committed, is not restored when it can be restored [Note: [Col. 0965] *reddi possit, et non redditur*, “can be restored and is not restored”: collected editions.], penance is not done but feigned [Note: [Col. 0965] *simulacro*, “as a pretence”: collected editions.]. But if penance is truly done, the sin is not forgiven unless what was taken is restored—*provided*, as I have said, that it can be restored. For often a person who takes loses it, whether by suffering *other* evil persons or by living badly himself, and has nothing else from which to make restitution.

§ 1. Certainly we cannot say to such a person, “Restore what you took,” except when we believe that he has it and is denying it. But [Note: [Col. 0965] *Verum*, “but”: collected editions.] indeed [Note: [Col. 0965] *quidam*, “someone”: Lyons II and III editions.] if he suffers torments from one seeking recovery [Note: [Col. 0965D] *repetente*, “from one seeking recovery”: thus corrected from the Vatican codex of the letters and the Antwerp edition; formerly it read *repente*, “suddenly,” as in the collected editions.], because he is believed to possess what he ought to restore, there is no injustice [Note: [Col. 0965] *non*, “not”: collected editions.]. For even if he has no means of repaying the money taken [Note: [Col. 0965] *luat*, “repay”: original.], still, when he is compelled to repay it by bodily sufferings [Note: [Col. 0965] *redhibere*, “repay”: original.], he deservedly [Note: [Col. 0965] *merito*, “deservedly”: marked in the source.] pays the penalties for the sin by which it was wrongly taken.

§ 2. But it is not inhumane to intercede even for such persons, *as for persons accused of crimes*—not in order that another’s goods may not be restored, but lest one human being rage fruitlessly against another.

And shortly afterward, § 3: I would say most confidently that whoever intervenes for a person in order that he may not restore what was wrongly taken, and whoever does not compel, so far as he honorably can, a person who has fled to him to make restitution, is a partner in fraud and crime. For we withdraw our aid from such persons more mercifully than we bestow it. One does not render aid by helping someone to sin; rather, one does not aid but opposes, overthrowing and restraining him [Note: [Col. 0966D] The following words have been corrected from printed and manuscript codices of the letters. Previously it read: “who helps him to sin, and ...”; Norimbergensis and Venice II read “but”; Venice I, “and if”; Argentinensis and Basel, “helps him to sin, but opposes him by overthrowing and restraining him.” The gloss fits very well with *adjuvat*, “helps,” as placed in its proper location.].

§ 4. But are we therefore either able or obliged to exact restitution ourselves, or to hand people over for its exaction? We act insofar as episcopal capacity allows [Note: [Col. 0965] *datur*, “is granted”: original.], threatening indeed at times human judgment, but above all and always divine judgment. Those whom we know both to have taken wrongly and to possess the means by which they may restore [Note: [Col. 0965] *reddantur*, “are restored”: Basel edition.], yet who refuse to restore, we rebuke, reprove, and entreat [Note: [Col. 0967] *detestamur*, “denounce”: original.]—some privately, some publicly—as the diversity of persons seems capable of receiving [Note: [Col. 0967] *et velle*, “and willing”: Argentinensis and Basel; *vel velle*, “or willing”: the other editions.] a different remedy.

Part II. Gratian. But if someone consecrates another’s property, he ought to restore not the same thing but its value.

Hence Gregory, book VII, indiction 2, letter 58, to Fantinus the *defensor* [Note: [Col. 0967] Letter 55, written A.D. 599, bk. 9 in the Maurist edition.]:

C. II. Whoever consecrates another’s property must restore its value.

We have learned that there was no reason why the property of the Jews could reasonably have been seized, and that it was consecrated rashly and recklessly [Note: [Col. 0967D] *Judaeorum*, “of the Jews”: this wording has been restored from St Gregory’s letter, where the collected editions read *eorum*, “their,” so that the referent of the contents of this chapter may be more easily understood; certain other readings have also been corrected. *consecrari*, “to be consecrated”: the same editions.]. Therefore we command your experience that, because what has once been consecrated cannot thereafter be restored to them [Note: [Col. 0967] *Judaeis*, “to the Jews”: original.], it shall be your concern that the bishop himself pay the price [Note: [Col. 0967] *praefatus frater et coepiscopus noster*, “the aforesaid brother and our fellow-bishop”: original.].

Part III. Gratian. For wrongdoers, however, the Church ought to intercede with rulers, not defend them with rash presumption.

Hence Gregory, to Romanus the *defensor*, book VII, indiction 2, letter 24 [Note: [Col. 0967D] Below, 23, Question 5, chapter *Reos*, gives the substance of this chapter, whereas here are Gregory’s own words.] [Note: [Col. 0967] Letter 27, written A.D. 599, bk. 9 in the Maurist edition; Polycarpus, bk. 6, title 16.]:

[Col. 0968A] C. III. The Church is to intercede for wrongdoers, not defend them with rash presumption.

Those implicated in public thefts must not appear to be defended unjustly by us, lest by the presumption of indiscriminate defence we in any way bring upon ourselves the reputation of evildoers. Rather, insofar as befits the Church, help them as far as you can by admonition and by employing a word of intercession, so that you may both bring aid to them and not stain the reputation of holy Church.

[Note: [Col. 0967] “others”: editions collated above.]

IV. Part. Gratian. Theft is assessed not so much by the quantity of the thing as by the intention of the thief.

Hence Jerome, in his Commentary on Titus, chapter 2.

[Note: [Col. 0968D] Jerome’s words are reported, though with some omissions and alterations, as also in Burchard and Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 0967] Regino, book 2, chapter 272. Burchard, book 11, chapter 55. Anselm, book 11, chapter 108. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 16, chapter 41. Polycarpus, same place.]

C. IV. Theft is committed not only in greater things, but also in lesser ones.

A thief is judged a thief not only in greater matters but also in lesser ones. For attention is paid not to the thing taken by theft, but to the mind of the thief. Just as, in fornication, fornication is not different because the woman is beautiful or ugly, enslaved or freeborn, poor or wealthy; whatever she may be, it is one and the same fornication: so also in theft, however much a person has taken, he incurs the crime of theft.

[Col. 0968B]

[Note: [Col. 0967] “poor”: editions of Argentinensis and Basle; Regino, Burchard, Ivo.]

CAUSE XV.

[Col. 0967]

[Col. 0967C] GRATIAN.

A certain priest is said to have fallen into a carnal offence before receiving priestly consecration. After he had obtained the priesthood, however, he became mad and killed someone. Having recovered his health, he is accused before the bishop by the woman with whom he is said to have fallen. The bishop examines the case on the Lord’s Day. The priest denies the charge brought against him and seeks the advocacy of certain clerics; but they do not support him without payment. At length the bishop extracts a confession by torture; finally, alone and without a synodal hearing, he pronounces sentence against him.

Question I: Are acts committed while the mind is deranged imputable?

Question II: May clerics demand payments for advocacy which they have provided?

[Col. 0967D]

Question III: Is this man to be condemned on the woman’s confession?

Question IV: Is his case to be heard on the Lord’s Day?

[Col. 0968C]

Question V: When he denies the charge, must an opportunity for purgation be granted him?

Question VI: Is his confession to be extracted by tortures?

Question VII: Can a bishop condemn a priest without a synodal hearing?

Question VIII: If he has voluntarily confessed, or has been convicted by others, of sinning before ordination, may he exercise the office of the order he has received?

## QUESTION I

GRATIAN.

I. Part. That acts done with a deranged mind are not imputable seems easy to prove. For some sins appear to rest upon the will of the mind, others upon the weakness of nature. Will, moreover, is—as Augustine says in book 1 of the *Retractions*, chapter 15—the movement of the mind, with no one compelling it, toward not losing or acquiring something.

[Note: [Col. 0967] Thus in the editions collated above, first Basle edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0968D] “With no one compelling”: these words have been added from St Augustine, so that the following words may be understood better.]

[Col. 0969A]

[Note: [Col. 0969D] “Imitandum”: in St Augustine, in *On Two Souls* and in book 1 of the *Retractions*, the reading is *amittendum*; because of the gloss, however, it has not been altered, but the earlier occurrence of *imitandum* has been removed. It is absent also from Gratian manuscripts. For the printed editions read: “toward imitating something, or toward not imitating it.”]

This was said so that, by this definition, the willing person might be distinguished from the unwilling.

§ 1. Sins therefore proceed from the will when they are committed by the free choice of the mind and the intention of the offender.

§ 2. Further, one kind of weakness belongs to the mind and another to the flesh. Weakness of mind is ignorance; weakness of flesh is concupiscence. But what proceeds from either weakness is imputed for punishment. Hence it is said of certain ignorant persons: “If anyone is ignorant, he shall be ignored.” Such were those of whom Christ said to the apostles: “They will put you out of the synagogue, because they will think that they are rendering service to God.”

[Note: [Col. 0969] John 16:2.]

The Apostle also writes concerning the same persons in the Epistle to the Romans: “I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.”

[Note: [Col. 0969] Romans 10:2.]

Yet this ignorance excuses none of them while persisting in his own unbelief.

From weakness of flesh proceed things done through the infirmity of nature. Unless these were imputed for punishment, the Apostle, burdened by the law of the flesh, would never have said: “Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from this body of death?” and so forth.

[Col. 0969B]

[Note: [Col. 0969] Romans 7:24.]

Therefore, whether sins rest upon the will or upon weakness, they are always imputed for punishment.

§ 3. The following saying of Augustine, *On True Religion*, chapter 14, seems contrary to this: “So greatly is sin a voluntary evil that it is not sin at all unless it is voluntary; and this is so manifest that neither a small number of learned persons nor a multitude of unlearned persons dissents from it. Therefore, either it must be denied that sin is committed, or it must be admitted that it is committed by the will.”

§ 4. But that this must not be understood universally of all sins, Augustine himself shows in book 1 of the *Retractions*, chapter 13, saying: “So greatly is sin a voluntary evil that it is not sin at all unless it is voluntary.”

§ 5. This definition may seem false; but if examined carefully, it will be found to be entirely true.

[Col. 0969C]

[Note: [Col. 0969] “is found”: editions collated above.]

For the sin to be considered is that which is sin only, not that which is also the punishment of sin. Although those things which are not without reason called involuntary sins, because they are perpetrated either by persons ignorant or compelled, cannot altogether be called involuntary. The same author, in the same book, chapter 15: “The definition of sin which we have given—‘Sin is the will to retain or acquire what justice forbids, and from which one is free to abstain’—is therefore true because what has been defined is that which is sin only, not that which is also the punishment of sin.”

[Note: [Col. 0969D] “Not without reason”: in printed books of St Augustine the reading is “without reason.”]

[Col. 0970A]

C. I. The sins of unwilling persons are only those of the ignorant. The same author, book IV of *Questions*, question 24, on Numbers 15.

[Note: [Col. 0969] Anselm, book 11, chapter 155.]

It is rightly asked what precisely are the sins of unwilling persons. Are they those committed by the ignorant? Or can what a person is compelled to do properly be called the sin of one unwilling? For this too is commonly called acting against one’s will; yet he certainly wills that for the sake of which he acts. For example, he may not wish to commit perjury, yet does so because he wishes to live, if someone threatens him with death unless he does it.

[Note: [Col. 0969] Addition: “the same”: Basle edition; “that”: other editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0970D] “For example, he may not wish to commit perjury, yet does so”: these words are not in the printed codices of St Augustine.]

[Note: [Col. 0969] Addition: “him”: editions collated above, first Basle, Paris, Lyons.]

He therefore wills to do it because he wills to live, and thus he does not seek to swear falsely for its own sake, but to live by swearing falsely.

[Col. 0970B]

[Note: [Col. 0969] “seeks”: editions collated above.]

If this is so, I do not know whether these may be called sins of unwilling persons, such as those said here to require expiation. For, if considered carefully, perhaps nobody wishes to sin itself; rather, the one who sins wills something else, and for its sake the act is done. For all who knowingly do what is unlawful would wish it to be lawful.

[Note: [Col. 0969] Addition: “sins”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0969] “is examined”: the same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0969] Addition: “to do it”: the same editions.]

So greatly does nobody seek sin itself for its own sake, but rather for the sake of that which follows from it. If these things are so, there are no sins of unwilling persons except those of the ignorant; and these are distinguished from the sins of the willing.

C. II. Digest, title *On Injuries*, law 3.

[Note: [Col. 0970D] In several ancient copies there is no division into chapters from the chapter “It Is Rightly Asked” to the chapter “No Woman.”]

[Note: [Col. 0969] Fragment 3, Digest 47.10.]

It is equally accepted that those who can suffer an injury can also inflict one. Yet there are some who cannot inflict an injury—for example, a madman and a child below puberty who is incapable of malice. Such persons usually suffer injury but do not inflict it. Since injury consists in the intention of the doer, it follows that, whether they strike someone or utter an insult, they are not deemed to have committed an injury.

[Col. 0970C]

Thus a person can suffer injury even if he does not perceive it; but nobody can inflict it unless he knows that he is inflicting injury, even though he does not know on whom he inflicts it. Therefore, if someone strikes another in jest or while competing, he is not liable for injury. If someone beats a free person while thinking him his own slave, he is in such a position that he is not liable for injury.

[Note: [Col. 0969] Addition: “indeed”: editions collated above.]

[Note: [Col. 0969] Addition: “another”: the same editions.]

Gratian. Thus, as appears from what has been stated, whether sins proceed from will or from weakness, it is plain that they are imputed. But weakness of the flesh is understood in two ways. There is the infirmity of nature called concupiscence of the flesh; more truly it may be called weakness of the soul, but it is called weakness of the flesh because it happens to the soul from its union with corrupt flesh.

[Col. 0971A]

There is, further, another weakness which is properly called weakness of the flesh: when the harmony of the elements or humours is disturbed, the flesh itself is afflicted and finally dissolved.

§ 1. Likewise, weakness of mind is twofold. One kind is called vice, by which the soul is separated from God, such as anger, hatred, and the like. Another weakness of the mind, which is not itself sin, is nevertheless both the punishment and the cause of sin, such as forgetfulness and ignorance. Madness, however, though it is not sin, is nevertheless the punishment of sin, just as fever and the other sufferings that we properly call sufferings of the flesh. Their impulses—that is, things done while they cause disturbance—are imputed to no one for punishment.

[Col. 0971B]

§ 2. But an objection is made concerning Lamech, who, although blind, killed Cain, and whose weakness of blindness did not excuse him. Hence it was said: “Vengeance shall be taken sevenfold for Cain, but seventy-sevenfold for Lamech.”

[Note: [Col. 0971] Genesis 4:15.]

But blindness resembles ignorance. § 3. For from each proceed certain things that are imputable and certain things that are not. But a mind deranged by madness, since it is not master of itself, does not incur the guilt of the acts it commits, because it has had no power of deliberation. Hence aid is given to a ward and a madman in wrongs committed, so that acts which have not proceeded from mental deliberation may not be imputed to them for punishment.

C. III.

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that, excepting those who are baptized in their own blood for Christ’s name, no human being will receive eternal life unless, while here, he has been converted from his evils through repentance and faith, and delivered through the sacrament of faith and repentance—that is, through baptism. For adults it is necessary both to repent of their evils, to hold the Catholic faith according to the rule of truth, and to receive the sacrament of baptism. But for little children, who cannot yet believe by their own will or repent for the sin which they derive originally, the sacrament of faith, which is holy baptism, suffices for salvation so long as their age is incapable of reason.

[Col. 0971D]

[Col. 0972A]

[Note: [Col. 0971] “not yet”: editions collated above.]

[Note: [Col. 0971] Addition: “their”: Basle edition.]

Hence Augustine, in the same book, chapter 3, gives the same reason regarding brute animals why their acts are not imputed to them: “Animals perform the course and adornment of this present world according to the incomprehensible will of the Creator; they will render no account of their deeds, because they are not rational. We know that some persons, suddenly made insane, have injured many with club, sword, stones, or bites, and that some have even killed. ## QUESTION III

GRATIAN.

[Col. 0976C] Third, it is asked whether this man is to be condemned upon the woman’s confession. In this matter one must first consider whether a woman can accuse a priest. Sacred canons seem entirely to prohibit it. For it is generally established by the decrees of Pope Fabian that priests of the Lord are not to be accused or testified against in a matter by persons who are not and cannot be of their order.

[Note: [Col. 0975] Cf. Cause 2, Question 7, chapter 6.]

But women can be promoted not only to no priesthood but not even to the diaconate; therefore they cannot accuse priests or give testimony against them. The laws also provide that, out of regard for the modesty of her sex, a woman may not appear before a praetor on another person’s behalf, unless perhaps she wishes to pursue injuries done to herself or her own people. But this woman, who is pursuing neither her own injuries nor those of her own people, ought not to be admitted to this accusation.

[Col. 0977A]

[Note: [Col. 0975] Cf. Digest, fragment 2, *On Rules of Law*, and the following chapter.]

§ 1. Conversely, a person capable of acting as judge is not excluded from the office of accuser. Whoever has read the Book of Judges cannot be ignorant that women judged the people in the Old Testament.

[Note: [Col. 0977] Judges 4.]

Therefore those who are known frequently to have exercised the office of judge cannot be excluded from accusation; nor are they prohibited from accusation by any sequence of the divine Scriptures.

§ 2. The response is as follows. In the old law many things were permitted which today have been abolished by the perfection of grace. For whereas women were allowed to judge the people, today, because of the sin introduced by woman, the Apostle directs them to be modest, subject to their husbands, and to have their heads veiled as a sign of subjection.

[Note: [Col. 0977] Ephesians 5.]

Therefore, a woman who is shown to be subject to a man in all these respects, and who is not permitted to plead for another, does not seem eligible to bring an accusation.

[Col. 0977B]

§ 3. Conversely, although a woman is not everywhere and without distinction admitted to bring an accusation, there are nevertheless certain crimes whose accusation she is not prohibited from undertaking.

Hence, in book IX of the *Code*, title 1, law 12, Emperor Diocletian writes:

[Note: [Col. 0977D] In several old copies there is no division into chapters from the beginning of this question to the chapter “Certainly.”]

[Note: [Col. 0977] “nevertheless”: editions of Basle, Venice II, Lyons I, Paris.]

C. I.

A woman is not permitted to accuse in a crime belonging to public prosecutions, except in specified cases: namely, if she pursues an injury to herself or her own people, and only according to the provisions of ancient law specially granted to them, without a formal subscription being required. Therefore, the governor of the province shall first examine whether the crime is one whose accusation a woman is not forbidden to undertake.

[Col. 0977C]

C. II. Likewise, in the Digest, Paul, book II *On Adulteries*, title *On Witnesses*, law 18.

From the fact that the Julian law on adultery prohibits a condemned woman from giving testimony, it follows that women also have the right to give testimony in court.

[Note: [Col. 0977] “of testimony”: original.]

Likewise, in the Digest, title *On Accusations and Enrolments*, law 2:

§ 1. A woman is not permitted to make anyone a defendant in a public prosecution, except, of course, when she pursues the death of her parents or children, of her patron or patroness, or of their son, daughter, grandson, or granddaughter.

C. III. Papinian, law 2, in the same title.

[Note: [Col. 0977] “Paul”: editions collated above.]

Public accusation is granted to women in specified cases, for example, when they pursue the death of those men and women against whom, under the law concerning public trials, they do not give testimony unwillingly.

[Col. 0977D]

[Note: [Col. 0977] “advocacy”: editions of Argentinensis and Basle.]

[Col. 0978A]

[Note: [Col. 0977] “give”: editions collated above.]

[Note: [Col. 0977] “in public”: Basle edition.]

§ 2. Under the testamentary law, wards have been permitted by decree of the senate to pursue the death of their father’s guardians; and a female ward, the death of her grandfather. [Note: [Col. 0977] “council”: editions of Argentinensis, Basle, Nuremberg, Venice I.]

In the Code, *On Those Who May or May Not Accuse*, law 4, Emperor Alexander to Dionysius:

§ 3. In proceedings concerning injured majesty, women too are heard.

Gratian. Any person admitted to accusation in public trials or for injured majesty is likewise not prohibited from bringing an accusation of simony.

Certainly, whoever is discovered to have assumed this holy and venerable episcopal see through the intervention of money, or to have received anything in order to ordain or elect another, shall, when an accusation has been brought after the manner of a public crime and injured majesty, be removed from the rank of priesthood.

[Col. 0978C]

[Note: [Col. 0977] “of priest”: editions collated above.]

We decree that he shall not only thereafter be deprived of this honour, but also condemned to perpetual infamy, so that both persons whom an equal crime defiles and makes equal may be followed by a like punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0977] “and equally”: editions of Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I.]

[Note: [Col. 0977] “together”: Argentinensis edition.]

Gratian. But although accusations which secular laws do not admit are altogether excluded by the sacred canons, it seems conversely that those which secular laws do not prohibit ought to be admitted. Yet this does not follow. For all clerics whom the sacred canons prohibit from contracting marriages are also prohibited by the laws of the emperors. But it does not follow that the laws admit the union of everyone whose union the sacred canons do not prohibit; for by the laws only cantors and readers, but by the canons even acolytes, may take wives.

[Note: **[Col. 0977D] “For by the laws”:** This discrepancy between laws and canons is not real. But perhaps Gratian adopted this view from certain words of Novel 22, which in the commonly printed *Authentics* occurs in collection 4, title *On Marriages*: “But if anyone enrolled among the most reverend clerics (we mean above the rank of reader or cantor) contracts marriage at all, we decree and will that he shall, under our constitution, fall from the priesthood.” Julian the antecessor, however, in the same Novel 22, no. 27, explains “above reader and cantor” as, for example, subdeacon and deacon. But the canons likewise prohibit these men from marriage. Leo, moreover, in the chapter *The Law of Continence*, above, Distinction 31, used almost the same words as Justinian in this Novel, and by the name “readers” denoted all the minor orders.]

[Col. 0979A] Therefore, although accusations which secular laws do not admit are excluded by the sacred canons, it does not consequently follow that all accusations which the laws of princes admit are received.

§ 1. But, as was set forth near the beginning of this work [Note: **[Col. 0979]** Distinction 10, chapter 1], imperial laws are to be used in ecclesiastical matters whenever they are not found contrary to the sacred canons. Therefore, either it must be shown specifically by the sacred canons that a woman is prohibited from an accusation of treason and simony, or she must be proved admissible to such an accusation by the reasons already stated.

§ 2. Nor should anyone seek to distinguish that women are to be admitted in this case of simony to accusations against others, but not against priests. For, since this is found generally permitted them by the laws, unless someone shows that it is specifically prohibited by some law, his distinction has no place. But since certain crimes are specially excepted from the general rules, in which a woman is permitted to accuse, and fornication is not reckoned among them, it is evident that this accusation is invalidated in two ways: both because she alleges the crime of fornication, and because, while she confesses concerning herself, she ought not to be believed concerning another’s crime.

Therefore Pope Julius writes in the Decrees, chapter 18, saying [Note: **[Col. 0979]** A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore; cf. interpretation on Theodosian Code, book 9, title 1, chapter 12.—Anselm, book 3, chapter 75 [65]. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 69. *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 288.]:

### C. V. A defendant’s confession must not be admitted against anyone.

No one—except in a charge of treason—may be believed against another’s crime on the basis of his confession concerning himself, because the confession of that person, and of every defendant, is dangerous and must not be admitted against anyone.

[Note: **[Col. 0979C] “Except in a charge of treason”:** This exception occurs in none of the cited passages except in Anselm [the words are not found in the collated Anselm manuscript].]

[Note: **[Col. 0979]** “May be believed”: *ought [to be believed]*: the collated editions.]

Gratian. Therefore, because this woman confesses concerning herself, she ought not to be believed concerning another’s crime; rather, her own confession is to be interpreted against her.

## QUESTION IV

### GRATIAN

That neither bishop nor presbyter may conduct any judicial proceeding on the Lord’s Day is forbidden in the Council of Tarragona, where the following was decreed, chapter 4 [Note: **[Col. 0979]** held A.D. 516.—Regino, book 1, chapter 376. Burchard, book 2, chapter 87 [from a council at Saint-Médard]. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, chapter 22.]:

[Col. 0980A]

### C. I. Ministers of the Church ought not to conduct cases on the Lord’s Day.

No bishop, presbyter, or cleric shall dare on the Lord’s Day to conduct proceedings in a matter of any case proposed, except only to perform the solemn observances appointed for God. On the other days, when the parties are assembled, they have leave to judge those matters which are just, except criminal cases.

[Note: **[Col. 0979]** “Conduct proceedings”: *judge*: the Hispanic Collection; *assert a claim*: the cited collections.]

[Note: **[Col. 0979]** “When the parties are assembled”: *when they consent*: the Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: **[Col. 0979]** “Except criminal cases”: *except criminal business*: there.]

### C. II. Secular courts shall not sit on solemn days or on days of lawful fasts. Likewise, from the Council at Erfurt, held in the presence of King Henry.

[Note: **[Col. 0979D] “Erphesfurt”:** The common editions read “Ephesus,” as though this were some decree of an Ephesian council held in the time of Pope Celestine and Theodosius the Younger. But it is a German council, held in the presence of King Henry, as is also said in Burchard and Ivo. Gratian manuscripts have the reading as restored. In this town Boniface requested that Pope Zachary establish a bishop, and obtained it. This appears from Boniface’s first letter to Zachary and Zachary’s last letter to Boniface.]

[Note: **[Col. 0979]** held A.D. 932.—Burchard, book 13, chapter 21. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, chapter 53.]

We decree that secular courts shall by no means be held on Sundays, on other principal feasts, or on those days on which lawful fasts are observed, in accordance with canonical constitution. Furthermore, the holy synod also decreed that no judicial authority may have leave, by its own authority, to summon Christians to court on the days mentioned above: namely, the seven days before the Nativity of the Lord through the octave of Epiphany; from Quinquagesima through the octave of Easter; and the seven days before the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist—so that people may have freer opportunity to go to church and devote themselves to prayer.

[Note: **[Col. 0979]** “On Sundays, or other feast days, or also on those days on which, etc.”: the original.]

[Note: **[Col. 0979]** “We decree”: *we will*: there.]

## QUESTION V

[Col. 0980C]

### GRATIAN

That one who denies an accusation must be allowed to clear himself is written by Stephen to Leo, bishop of Theano.

[Note: **[Col. 0980D]** The same heading occurs in chapter *Concerning the Manifest [Case]*, above, 2, question 1.]

[Note: **[Col. 0979]** Cf. 2, question 1, chapter 17.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 430.]

### C. I. If a deacon cannot be convicted of a crime, he shall secretly clear himself before the bishop.

Your deacon most truthfully declared that he was innocent of the crime alleged against him. Nevertheless, if there is suspicion, suitable accusers are found, and such witnesses as the sacred canons prescribe, let the accusers come with you before a fixed number of bishops; let Alderic the deacon himself also be summoned. If he denies it, let the case be heard canonically; and if he is either voluntarily confessing or proved guilty by lawful witnesses, let a canonical sentence be inflicted.

But if he neither confesses voluntarily, nor are lawful accusers and witnesses found, and evil report has become widespread, he shall clear himself not by a public examination, but secretly before you and several most reverend presbyters and deacons of your church, by oath. Thereafter, proclaim him to be of good repute; restrain and admonish the children of your church, lest they presume further to defame God’s priest, fearing that Ham was cursed because he mocked his father’s shameful parts.

[Note: **[Col. 0979]** “Let them be summoned”: Argentinensis edition.]

[Note: **[Col. 0981]** “Has become widespread”: *is becoming widespread*: Ivo; Argentinensis and Basiliensis editions; *will have become widespread*: the remaining editions.]

[Note: **[Col. 0981]** “Not by a public examination”: *in public*: the collated editions.]

[Note: **[Col. 0981]** “You”: omitted in the Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: **[Col. 0981]** Genesis 9.]

[Note: **[Col. 0981]** “Shameful parts”: *private parts*: Argentinensis and Basiliensis editions.]

### C. II. A presbyter or deacon must not be deprived [of office] unless he has voluntarily confessed or has been lawfully convicted. Likewise Nicholas to Solomon, bishop of Constance.

A presbyter or deacon whom you say refuses publicly to confess crimes, but wishes to defend himself by oath—even if the bishop nevertheless knows that a crime was committed by him—cannot hold a priestly or diaconal office through any penitence. But it is remarkable how, if he has not confessed, the crime committed by him can be known to the bishop, unless perhaps a suitable accuser establishes it through suitable witnesses.

Therefore, if, when the bishop investigates the case of a presbyter or deacon, the presbyter or deacon has not perhaps been convicted by testimony of witnesses, the crime is not lawfully known to the bishop unless he voluntarily confesses the crime himself. Unless he does so, meanwhile we do not see that the presbyter or deacon ought to be deprived of his office. Thus voluntary confession alone, and the canonical number and quality of witnesses—when the bishops decide and the accuser proves what he alleged—deprive a cleric of his proper rank.

[Note: **[Col. 0981]** A letter of uncertain date.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 122.]

[Note: **[Col. 0981]** “Committed by him”: *committed by himself*: the collated editions.]

[Note: **[Col. 0981]** “Unless”: *if*: the same editions before the second Lyons editions.]

[Note: **[Col. 0981]** “The presbyter or deacon”: *that presbyter*: Ivo.]

[Note: **[Col. 0981]** “The crime”: *the crime itself*: the collated editions.]

[Note: **[Col. 0981]** “And”: *or*: the same editions; Ivo; Böhm.]

## QUESTION VI

### GRATIAN

**Part I.** That a confession must not be extracted by torture is attested by Pope Alexander, writing to all the orthodox, first letter, chapter 2.

[Note: **[Col. 0981]** A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 118; *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 241.]

### C. I. The confession of ministers must not be extorted but voluntary.

If at any time any documents have been extorted from priests and administrators of the Church by fear, fraud, or force, or have been written or ratified by them through any device whatsoever so that they may free themselves, we decree that they shall avail for no prejudice or harm to them. Nor do we permit them ever to suffer, by God’s authority and that of the holy apostles and their successors, any infamy, calumny, or sequestration from their own property. In such matters confession must be voluntary, not compelled.

And below:

§ 1. For every confession made under necessity is not trustworthy.

And shortly afterward:

§ 2. Therefore, in such matters confession ought not to be extorted but rather made voluntarily; for it is most evil to judge anyone from suspicion or an extorted confession, since the Lord is more the inspector of the heart than of the deed.

After a few intervening words:

§ 3. A person whom the Lord has reserved for His own judgment cannot be condemned by human examination. For if all things were punished in this world, divine judgments would have no place.

Likewise, much earlier:

§ 4. It has also been brought to this holy see—something shameful to say and hostile not only to the priestly name but to every Christian name—that some compel bishops or priests by fear, force confessions from them by violence, or deceive them by fraud, to write letters of confession in a sense other than they ought; or to make documents, and ratify them with their own hands, concerning matters not brought against them, or, what is worse, in support of another’s erroneous sect; and to read and confess them before the people. They say that some are shut up in prisons and workhouses, so that, terrified at least by these snares, the Lord’s priests may depart from the way and favor their own wishes.

Likewise in the same place:

§ 5. In such matters confession must be voluntary, not compelled, as He Himself testifies who says: “For from the heart proceed murders, adulteries, fornications, blasphemies,” and the other things pertaining to this matter.

§ 6. Attention must be given not so much to what is done as to the intention with which it is done.

And shortly afterward:

§ 7. Moreover, God has greater regard for thoughts and spontaneous intentions than for acts done through simplicity or necessity.

[Note: **[Col. 0981]** “At any time”: absent from the Argentinensis, Basiliensis, Norimbergensis, and first Venetian editions.]
