But at this point the letter reads: “Likewise, if certain documents, etc., [have been extorted] from persons of this kind.” Before this passage there were many other matters, including those cited in this same chapter at the words “It has also been brought to this.” This chapter was composed from passages taken here and there from the letter, with the order not always preserved.]

### C. II. Apostolic authority renders utterly void unlawful oaths. Likewise Pope Nicholas to the bishops of Gaul.

Following the authority of our venerable predecessors, and specifically of the most blessed Pope and martyr Alexander, fifth from blessed Peter, we absolve from all oaths and obligations of whatever kind the archbishop of Trier, his provost, and all who, having then been captured, had bound themselves to those men in whatever way under compulsion from the violence of the wicked. We forbid those obligations to be kept, and we do not permit them ever to suffer on that account any infamy, calumny, or sequestration from their property, by the authority of God, the holy apostles, and our predecessors, as the Lord says through the Prophet: “Loose the bonds of wickedness.”

Moreover, we command our aforesaid brother and the children of the Church of Trier, together with its defenders, to pursue those wicked men and their supporters with both the spiritual and the material sword until, intact, the possessions—or whatever ecclesiastical property has been alienated or plundered through this deed or any agreement whatsoever—are restored.

## QUESTION VII

### GRATIAN

**Part I.** That a priest may not be condemned without a synodal hearing is prohibited as follows in the Council of Seville, in which Isidore participated, chapter 6:

[Note: **[Col. 0983]** held A.D. 619.—Abbo of Fleury, in Mabillon, *Veterum Analectorum*, chapter 12.]

### C. I. A presbyter or deacon shall not be deposed without examination by a council.

[Col. 0984C] In the sixth session we learned that Fragitanus, presbyter of the church of Cornubia, had long ago been unjustly deposed by his bishop and, though innocent, condemned to exile. Restoring him to his order, we have decreed anew, against our own presumption, that according to the synodal decision of the ancient Fathers none of us shall dare, without examination by a council, to depose any presbyter or deacon. For there are many who condemn persons without investigation by tyrannical power, not canonical authority. And just as they raise some up through the favor of partiality, so, moved by hatred and envy, they humiliate others and condemn on the light breath of rumor those whose crime they do not prove.

For a bishop can alone confer honor upon priests and ministers, but he cannot alone take it away. If those who in the secular sphere have received the honor of freedom from their masters are not returned to the bond of slavery unless they have publicly been accused before the tribunal of a praetor and governor in the forum, how much more is this true of those consecrated to the divine altars and adorned with ecclesiastical honor? Certainly they cannot be condemned by one person, nor, when one person is judging, stripped of the privileges of their rank. Rather, when brought before synodal judgment, what the canon prescribes concerning them must be determined.

[Note: **[Col. 0983]** “Fragitanus”: *Flagitanus*: the collated editions.]

[Note: **[Col. 0984C] “Restoring”:** Thus the text has been corrected from printed and manuscript copies of the councils. It more clearly declares that he was canonically restored by the council than does Gratian’s common reading, “we learned that he had been restored” [“we learned” is absent from the Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, and first Venetian editions].]

[Note: **[Col. 0984C] “Our”:** Earlier editions read “your” [thus the collated editions]. But more recent editions of the councils read “new.” The reading has been corrected from older editions, two Vatican manuscripts, and the royal manuscript of Lucca; likewise a little later, “none of us,” where the former reading was “none of you.” For modest and devout bishops are cautious even toward themselves. Some other readings have also been corrected from the same manuscripts.]

[Note: **[Col. 0983]** “To depose”: *to be deposed*: the Hispanic Collection; Abbo; the collated editions before the Basiliensis edition, where it reads “to be condemned.”]

## QUESTION VIII

### GRATIAN

Concerning the final question, the following was decreed in the Council of Neocaesarea, chapters 9 and 10:

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** held A.D. 314.—Burchard, book 2, chapter 49. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 151; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 150; all from Dionysius.]

### C. I. A presbyter who confesses that he fell into bodily sin before ordination shall not thereafter offer [the Eucharist].

One who has committed bodily sin and was afterward ordained presbyter, if he confesses that he sinned before his ordination, shall indeed not offer [the Eucharist], but shall remain in the other offices because of the usefulness of his diligence. For very many decreed that other sins also should deprive [a man] even of ordination. But if he has not confessed these things, nor can be openly convicted by anyone, authority concerning himself is entrusted to him. Likewise, if a deacon has been involved in the same kind of fault, he shall refrain from ministry.

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “Has committed”: *has committed [future perfect]*: the Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987C] “Because of the usefulness of his diligence”:** In Greek: *διὰ τὴν ἄλλην σπουδήν*, “because of the zeal and diligence which he otherwise displays.”]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “The other sins”: *and the other [sins]*: there; *but the other [sins]*: the collated editions.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987C] “Deprive”:** The Greek reads *τὴν χειροθεσίαν ἀφιέναι*, that is, “to dismiss by the laying on of hands,” approximately as Dionysius translates it, whose version the other collectors have supplied, though omitting this clause. The version cited by Gratian is ancient, found in Isidore’s collection. Thus a quite different conclusion is drawn from these words than the author of the gloss supposed.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “To deprive”: *to deprive [active]*: the Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “By anyone”: *by someone he can*: the Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “Is entrusted”: *is permitted*: there.]

### C. II. Those serving the altar, if they offend through weakness of the flesh, are subject to the bishop’s judgment. Likewise, from the Council of Lleida, chapter 5.

Those who serve at God’s altar, if they suddenly fall into lamentable weakness of the flesh and, under the Lord’s regard, worthily repent so that, having mortified the body, they offer God the sacrifice of a contrite heart, shall remain subject to the bishop’s discretion: either not to suspend for long those who are truly afflicted, or to separate the negligent from the body of the Church for a longer time. Yet they shall recover places in their offices in such a way that they cannot afterward be promoted to higher offices. But if, like dogs returning to their vomit, they relapse, and like swine lie in muddy wallows, they shall be deprived not only of the dignity of office but also of holy communion, which they shall not receive except at death.

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** held A.D. 546.—Burchard, book 19, chapter 74. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, chapter 87. Rabanus, *Penitential*, chapter 1.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “The Lord”: *God*: the collated editions.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “And like swine lie in muddy wallows”: absent from the Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “Not”: absent there.]

### C. III. Those born of ministers of the Church shall be assigned to the slavery of that Church. Likewise, from the Ninth Council of Toledo, chapter 10.

Since many decisions of the Fathers concerning the incontinence of the clerical order have hitherto been issued, and correction of their morals has in no way been able to reform them, the offences committed have carried the sentence of the judges so far that punishment is inflicted not only upon the authors of the crimes but also upon the offspring of the condemned. Therefore, henceforth, any man from bishop down to subdeacon who, while holding office, begets children by a detestable union either with a female slave or a free woman: the persons from whom they are proved to have been born shall be condemned by canonical censure; but the offspring, born from this unlawful defilement, shall never receive an inheritance and shall remain in perpetual legal servitude to that church from the disgrace of whose priest or minister they were born.

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** held A.D. 655.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 425.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “Incontinence”: *incontinence [accusative]*: Hispanic Collection; *innocence*: Basiliensis and first Lyons editions; *innocence [accusative]*: the remaining editions.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “Reform”: *confirm*: Ivo and collated editions.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “Sentence”: *by sentence*: Basiliensis edition.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “Punishment is inflicted”: *is inflicted*: collated editions; *is struck*: Ivo.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “Authors”: *agents*: Ivo; *actors*: collated editions before Basiliensis and the second and third Lyons editions; Böhm.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “Offspring”: *offspring [ablative]*: Ivo and Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “But the offspring”: *such offspring*: Hispanic Collection; *from this [defilement]*: Ivo.]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “Inheritance”: Hispanic Collection and Ivo add “of their parents.”]

[Note: **[Col. 0987]** “Servitude”: *in servitude [ablative]*: the collated editions before the first and second Venetian and first Lyons editions; Böhm.]

### C. IV. One who confesses that he sinned before ordination shall not sacrifice; but one convicted shall be deposed. Likewise, from the Council of Pope Martin, chapter 35.

If a presbyter has sinned before ordination and after ordination confesses that he had sinned beforehand, he shall not offer [the Eucharist], but only retain the name of presbyter for the sake of religion. But if he has not himself confessed and has publicly been convicted by another, he shall not even have the right to bear the name of presbyter. The same is to be observed concerning deacons: if they themselves have confessed, they shall receive the order of subdeacon.

[Note: **[Col. 0989]** Chapters 9 and 10 of the Council of Neocaesarea, from the translation of Martin of Braga.—Burchard, book 2, chapter 48. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 150; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 149.]

[Note: **[Col. 0989]** “Has sinned … had sinned beforehand”: *erred*: Hispanic Collection; *will have erred*: Burchard and Ivo’s *Decretum*; *had erred*: *Panormia*.]

[Note: **[Col. 0989]** “Shall not even have the right”: the Hispanic Collection reads, “shall have authority for this very thing.”]

[Note: **[Col. 0989]** “If they themselves have confessed … shall receive the order of subdeacon”: the Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: **[Col. 0989]** “Shall receive”: *shall retain*: Burchard and Ivo’s *Decretum*; *shall hold*: Ivo’s *Panormia*.

[Col. 0989B] C. V. The sacraments may lawfully be received from the hand of a priest whom the Church tolerates. Likewise, Nicholas, in his Answers to the Bulgarians, ch. 71. [Note: Written A.D. 866.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 5, ch. 13; *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 83.—Cf. X 4.3.7, *On cohabitation of clerics and women*.]

In answer to your inquiry whether you ought to receive communion from a priest who has either been caught in adultery or is merely tainted by a report of it, or not, we reply: no one, however defiled he may be, can defile the divine sacraments, [Col. 0990A] which are remedies cleansing every contamination; nor can a ray of sunlight, passing through sewers and latrines, draw any contamination from them. Therefore, whatever sort of priest he may be, he cannot pollute what is holy. Accordingly communion is to be received from him until he is rejected by the judgment of bishops, since evil persons, in administering good things, harm themselves alone; and a lighted wax torch causes loss to itself, but furnishes light to others in darkness, and from that by which it affords benefit to others it brings injury upon itself. § 1. Therefore receive Christ’s mysteries fearlessly from every priest, because all things are purified by the faith of Christ. For it is faith that conquers this world; and because it depends not on the giver but on the receiver, as Blessed Jerome says: “For believing, baptism is complete in every soul, and Christ’s body is complete in every priest.” In agreement with Holy Scripture he also says: “Before you have heard, do not judge anyone; and before an accusation brought has been tested, suspend no one from your communion, because one who is accused is not immediately guilty, but one who is convicted is criminal.”

[Note: “has been caught”: *has been apprehended*, Ivo, *Panormia*; printed editions generally.—“receive”: *accept*, printed editions generally.—“remedies” added in the original.—“Therefore”: supplied as *Consequently* in printed editions generally.—“cannot pollute what is holy”: “holy things cannot be polluted,” those editions and Ivo.—“And a wax torch”: Previously the text read “etc.” The wording has been restored from the original, from which other corrections and additions were also made.—“by faith”: “in the faith,” printed editions generally.—“depends”: *is*, Böhm.—“saying”: *teaching*, original.—Jerome: This is in the letter *On the Seven Grades*, as is what follows, “Before you have heard,” etc., which occurs earlier there.—“in every soul”: “for every soul,” printed editions generally.—Ecclesiasticus 11:7.]

# CAUSE XVI

[Col. 0989]

[Col. 0989B] GRATIAN.

A certain abbot possessed a parish church. He installed a monk there to perform the office for the people; [Col. 0989C] he possessed it for forty years without any challenge. At last the clerics of the baptismal church, in whose diocese that parish church stood, brought a complaint against the abbot. (Question I.) The first question here is whether monks may perform offices for the people, impose penance, and baptize. (Question II.) Second, if it happens that they possess chapels by episcopal benefice, must such chapels be assigned by them or by the bishops? (Question III.) Third, are the rights of churches extinguished by prescription? (Question IV.) Fourth, if one church may prescribe against another church, may a monastery likewise prescribe against a church? (Question V.) Fifth, [Col. 0989D] can it claim as its own, by right of territory, a chapel built within its territory? [Col. 0990B] (Question VI.) Sixth, if an archpriest or bishop has seized that chapel by his own authority and not by judicial sentence, does he lose his claim, so that the church over which he presides may no longer have a right to demand what its pastor unlawfully usurped? [Col. 0990C] (Question VII.) Seventh, the question is asked whether, if laymen held that chapel—as is customary with some people—and surrendered it into the abbot’s hands and handed it over to be assigned, the abbot may retain it with the consent of the bishop and clerics.

# QUESTION I

GRATIAN.

Part I. That monks cannot perform offices for the people is proved by many authorities. The first is that of the holy Synod of Nicaea, which says: [Note: This chapter is found today neither in the First nor in the Second Synod of Nicaea. Something similar, however, occurs in the Nicene canons translated from Arabic, canon 76. Whoever examines the cited canon will judge with us that this is not entirely true.] [Note: Chapter wholly uncertain.—Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 214, without the heading; Polycarpus, bk. 4, tit. 34.]

[Col. 0991A] C. I. The manner of life of monks ought to be distinct from that of all others.

It pleased all who were seated in the holy Synod of Nicaea that the conduct and life of monks should differ from that of all others, in accordance with the etymology of their name. For *monk* in Greek is called *singular* in Latin; hence a monk must act singularly in every respect. Therefore we firmly and irrevocably command everyone that no monk shall impose penance on anyone, except reciprocally upon his fellow monks, as is right; nor shall he bury a dead person, except a monk dwelling with him in the monastery, or if by chance one of the visiting brethren should die there.

[Note: “irrevocably”: *indissolubly*, printed editions generally.—“everyone”: *all*, Böhm.]

[Col. 0991B] C. II. No one can at the same time maintain monastic strictness and an ecclesiastical ministry. Likewise Gregory to John, bishop of Ravenna, bk. IV, ep. 1. [Note: Ep. 1, written A.D. 595, bk. 5 of the Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, ch. 18.]

No one can both serve in ecclesiastical duties and remain duly within the monastic rule, so as to maintain the strictness of a monastery, when he is compelled to remain daily in ecclesiastical ministry.

[Note: “and”: omitted in the cited variants.—“monastic”: *monastic*, printed editions generally.—“ministry”: *monastery*, editions of Arg., Nor., and Venice I–II.]

C. III. Monks promoted to the clergy ought not depart from their former purpose. Likewise Innocent to Victricius, ep. II, ch. 10. [Note: Written A.D. 404.—Anselm, bk. 5, ch. 67.]

Concerning monks who, after having lived long in monasteries, subsequently attain clerical rank, we decree that they ought not depart from their former purpose.

[Note: “depart”: *withdraw*, Basel edition; *deviate*, original.]

Gratian. If, therefore, as Innocent determines, they may not depart from their purpose, and if, as Gregory testifies, they cannot at once persevere devoutly in the monastic rule and serve in ecclesiastical [Col. 0991C] duties, it is evident that monks cannot be placed over parish churches.

C. IV. A monk has the office not of teaching but of mourning. Likewise Jerome to the presbyter Riparius, *Against Vigilantius*. [Note: Written A.D. 408.—Anselm, at the end, ch. 17; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 176; *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 3; Polycarpus, ibid.]

A monk has the office not of a teacher but of one who mourns: he mourns either himself or the world, and awaits the Lord’s coming in fear.

[Note: “teacher”: *doctor*, original, Ivo, and editions of Arg. and Basel.]

C. V. Monks ought not live amid popular crowds. The same author to Paulinus, *On the Training of a Monk*, ep. XIII. [Note: Written A.D. 394.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 175; *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 2.]

If you wish to be what you are called, a monk—that is, one who is alone—[Col. 0992A] what are you doing in cities, which are certainly not dwelling places for those who are alone but for many? And below: § 1. Keep the innocence of the dove, so that you devise deceit against no one; and the cunning of the serpent, so that you are not tripped up by the snares of others. There is little difference in fault between being able to deceive and being deceived. Regard as a trader rather than a monk a Christian whom you perceive always or frequently talking to you about money, except concerning almsgiving, which lies equally open to all. Beyond food, clothing, and evident necessities, give nothing to anyone, lest dogs eat the children’s bread.

[Note: “be deceived”: the original, Basel edition, and Ivo’s *Decretum* read “deceive a Christian. Regard as …”—“money”: *very small coins*, Basel edition.—“clothing”: *garment*, printed editions generally and Ivo.]

C. VI. The monk is fed; clerics feed. The same author to Heliodorus, *On the Praise of the Solitary Life*, ep. I. [Note: Written A.D. 372.—Anselm, bk. 7, ch. 123 (135).]

[Col. 0992B] The position of monks is one thing, that of clerics another. Clerics feed the sheep; I am fed. They live from the altar; but for me, as for an unfruitful tree, an axe is laid to the root if I do not bring an offering to the altar. And below: § 1. I may not sit before a presbyter. If I sin, he may hand me over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord [Note: “judgment,” edition of Arg.; cf. 1 Corinthians 12.] Jesus.

[Note: “monks”: “monk … clerics,” printed editions generally.—“tree”: *of a tree*, those editions.]

C. VII. Monks may do nothing without the counsel of presbyters. The same author to Rusticus. [Note: In Blessed Jerome’s commentary on Isaiah, ch. 3, from which this chapter appears to have been taken, the following is read: “Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, lost the kingdom because he would not listen to the elders.” A little lower: “Decrees of the senate are also called consultations; and Roman rulers of old were called consuls, either because they took counsel for the citizens or because they conducted everything by counsel. We too have in the Church our senate, the assembly of presbyters.”] [Note: In the commentary on Isaiah, ch. 3.—Deusdedit, pt. 5.]

The Church has its senate, the assembly of presbyters, without whose counsel monks may do nothing. Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, lost his kingdom because he would not listen to his presbyters. The Romans likewise had a senate, by whose counsel they conducted everything; and we have our senate, the assembly of presbyters.

[Note: “its own” added by the Basel edition.—“counsel”: *council*, Arg. edition.—“monks”: *a monk*, Basel edition.—3 Kings 14.—“whose”: *their*, Basel edition.]

C. VIII. In accordance with the etymology of his name, a monk should lead a solitary life. Likewise Pope Eugenius. [Note: Anselm also cites this from Eugenius’s decrees; it is likewise found in an old book of Decretals.] [Note: Chapter uncertain.—Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 213 (210).]

Our common council decreed that no monk should dare, by a most wicked presumption, to leave his monastery for earthly gain; nor to impose penance, receive a child from baptism, baptize, visit the sick, bury the dead, transfer to a secular church, or involve himself in any other business whatsoever. Let him be content with his cloister; for as a fish lacks life without [Col. 0993A] water, so a monk lacks it without a monastery. Let him therefore sit alone and be silent, because he is dead to the world but lives to God. § 1. Let him recognize his own name: for μόνος (*monos*) in Greek means “one” in Latin, while ἄχος (*achos*) in Greek signifies “sad.” Thus he is called *monachus*, that is, “one who is sad.” Let him therefore sit sad and attend to his own office.

[Note: “presence”: *penance*, Lugdunum II.—“lives”: *is alive*, Anselm.—The Greek phrase and the word *is* are absent from the Basel edition; the other editions read *is*.]

C. IX. Without the consent of bishops, monks are not to usurp episcopal rights. Likewise Paschal II to Victor, bishop of Bologna. [Note: Chapter uncertain.—Found in Anselm, bk. 5, final chapter, from which the Correctors cite it, but it has not been found.]

It has come to our attention, to our great astonishment, that certain monks and abbots in your diocese arrogantly claim for themselves episcopal rights and offices, contrary to the decrees of the holy Fathers—namely, penance, [Col. 0993B] remission of sins, reconciliation, tithes, and churches—although without leave of their own bishop or authority from the Apostolic See they ought in no way to presume such things. As the holy Fathers provided concerning such persons in the Council of Chalcedon, and prohibited them under the bond of anathema to all monks, so we command your charity to summon them and altogether forbid them to presume such things in future.

[Note: “of penitents” added by printed editions generally except Basel.—“although” is absent in the Basel edition.]

C. X. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Calixtus II. [Note: Ch. 17, First Lateran Council, held A.D. 1123.]

We also forbid abbots and monks to impose public penances, visit the sick, administer anointings, and sing public masses. They shall receive chrism and oil, consecrations of altars, and ordinations of clerics from the bishops in whose dioceses they live.

C. XI. Monks living within cloisters shall not exercise clerical offices outside. Likewise Alexander II. [Note: To the clergy and people of Florence.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 151.]

In accordance with the tenor of the excellent Council of Chalcedon, we command monks, however religious, to remain within the cloister according to the rule of Saint Benedict. We forbid them to range through villages, castles, and cities, and decree that they cease altogether from preaching to the people—unless perhaps someone, concerned for the salvation of his soul and wishing to adopt their habit, should seek their counsel within the cloister.

[Col. 0994A] C. XII. Monks who are in cities ought to be subject to the bishop. Likewise from the Council of Chalcedon, ch. 4. [Note: Held A.D. 451.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 174; *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 1.—From Dionysius: Anselm, bk. 5, ch. 54 (60).]

Those who truly and sincerely choose the solitary life are worthy of fitting honor. [Note: “Honor”: The chapter “Certain monks,” below, Causa 18, question 2, follows continuously; it is from the same ancient translation as this chapter.] And below: § 1. But concerning those who are in monasteries in the several cities or estates, it pleases us that they be subject to the bishop, devote themselves to quiet, observe fasts and prayers, and remain in the places in which they once vowed themselves to God; and that they neither disturb nor meddle in ecclesiastical or secular affairs, leaving their own monasteries, unless they are ordered by the bishop of that city because of urgent necessities. No slave is to be received into a monastery to become a monk with them except with his own master’s permission. But we have decreed that anyone transgressing these provisions be outside communion, lest the Lord’s name be blasphemed. § 2. It is fitting, moreover, that the bishop of the city show monasteries the necessary care and concern.

[Note: “subject to their own bishop,” Basel edition.—“quiet”: *quiet persons*, Hispanic Collection.—“vowed”: *have vowed*, that collection and printed editions generally.—“nor … meddle”: Greek: μήτε δὲ ἐκκλησιαστικοῖς, μήτε βιωτικοῖς παρενοχλεῖν πράγμασιν, ἢ ἐπικοινωνεῖν, “neither to disturb ecclesiastical nor secular affairs, nor to involve themselves in them.”—“meddle in”: *handle*, Basel edition.—“monastery”: *monasteries*, ibid.—“permission”: *knowledge*, Hispanic Collection.—“Anyone transgressing”: *Those transgressing*, Basel edition.]

Gratian. The answer to these points is as follows. The authority of the Nicene Synod forbids monks to leave monasteries and gather at chapels to conduct burials of the dead—that is, to come together after the manner of clerics to celebrate anyone’s funeral. But if someone wishes to be buried near a monastery, he is not to be forbidden.

[Col. 0994C] Thus Gregory writes to John, bishop of Old City, bk. I, ep. 12. [Note: Ep. 12, written A.D. 591, bk. 1 of the Maurist edition.]

C. XIII. The celebration of masses and the burial of the dead in a monastery are not forbidden.

Agapitus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Gregory, [Note: “George,” Arg. edition; original.] informed us that he suffers very many burdens from your holiness because you forbid masses to be celebrated in that monastery and also forbid the dead to be buried *there*. We urge you to refrain from such inhumanity and to permit the dead to be buried there and masses to be celebrated, without allowing any further objection.

[Note: “you forbid … you forbid”: *you forbid … you interdict*, original.—“there”: marked in the source.—“to be celebrated”: *to celebrate*, Basel edition.]

C. XIV. The pious wishes of the dead are not to be annulled. The same author to Januarius, [Note: Ep. 9, written A.D. 514, bk. 4 of the Maurist edition.] bishop of Cagliari, bk. III, ep. 9.

We wish to warn you that, God forbid, the pious wishes of the living or [Col. 0995A] the dead should be annulled through your remissness.

[Note: “of the living or” is lacking in the original.]

C. XV. The testator’s intention ought to be observed. Likewise Pope Gelasius. [Note: Chapter uncertain.—Tripartite Collection, pt. 1, tit. 46, ch. 45.]

Consideration for ecclesiastical utility requires that the intention of a testator be observed according to a just disposition.

[Note: “disposition”: Old copies read *dispensation*.—*dispensation*, Basel edition.—“testator”: *to the testator*, ibid.—“be” added in printed editions generally except Basel.]

C. XVI. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Tribur, ch. 15. [Note: In some old codices this chapter is joined to the preceding one.] [Note: Held A.D. 895.—Cf. Causa 13, question 2, ch. 6.]

“Wherever resources and opportunity of time are available, etc.,” [as is read above in the same chapter, in the cause concerning those who transferred from one diocese to another.]

Gratian. See: these authorities make clear that, if anyone wishes to choose burial at a monastery, he may freely be buried by the monks. Hence it is plainly inferred that the prohibition of the Nicene Synod was made because of the misconduct of wandering monks.

Thus we read in the Council of Chalcedon, ch. 23, [Note: Held A.D. 451:]

C. XVII. Wandering monks without their bishop’s permission are to be compelled to return to their own places.

Certain monks, to whom their own bishop has assigned nothing—and sometimes even those whom he has excommunicated—come to the imperial city of Constantinople and there disturb ecclesiastical peace and corrupt the houses of various persons. Therefore the holy synod decreed that these persons should first be warned to leave the imperial city; finally, that they should be expelled even unwillingly and compelled by the *defensor* to return thence to their own places.

[Note: “sometimes”: absent in the Basel edition.—“had been”: *have been*, Hispanic Collection.—“imperial”: marked in the source.—“the same”: Basel edition; “remaining for a long time,” Hispanic Collection.—“disturb … corrupt”: *may disturb … may corrupt*, ibid.—“these”: added by the Basel edition.—The Hispanic Collection reads: “These persons are first to be warned by the defensor of the Church of Constantinople, etc. But if they persist shamelessly in the same course, they are to be expelled even unwillingly by the same defensor, so that they may arrive at their own places.”—“warned”: In this final part especially, the ancient translation seems deliberately to have been reduced to an epitome. The complete canon is: “It came to the ears of the holy synod that certain clerics and monks, to whom nothing has been entrusted by their own bishop, and who sometimes have even been excluded from communion by him, come to the imperial city of Constantinople and remain there for a long time, creating disturbances and agitating the ecclesiastical order, and overturning the houses of certain persons. Therefore the holy synod decreed that such persons should first be admonished, through the defensor of the most holy Church at Constantinople, to leave the imperial city; but if they should shamelessly persist in the same practices, they should be expelled, even unwillingly, through the same defensor and return to their own places.” The Greek reads: Ἦλθεν εἰς ἀκοὰς τῆς ἁγίας συνόδου, ὠς κληρικοί τινες καὶ μονάζοντες μηδὲν ἐγκεχειρισμένοι ὑπὸ τοῦ ἰδίου ἐπισκόπου, ἔστι δὲ ὅτε καὶ ἀκοινώνητοι γενόμενοι παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ, καταλαμβάνοντες τὴν βασιλεύουσαν Κωνσταντινούπολιν, ἐπὶ πολὺ ἐν αὐτῇ διατρίβουσι, ταραχὰς ἐμποιοῦντες καὶ θορυβοῦντες τὴν ἐκκλησιαστικὴν κατάστασιν, ἀνατρέπουσί τε οἴκους τινῶν, ὥρισεν τοίνυν ἡ ἁγία σύνοδος, τοὺς τοιούτους ὑπομιμνήσκεσθαι μὲν πρότερον διὰ τοῦ ἐκδίκου τῆς κατὰ Κωνσταντινούπολιν ἀγιωτάτης ἐκκλησίας ἐπὶ τὸ ἐξελθεῖν τῆς βασιλευούσης πόλεως, εἰ δὲ τοῖς αὐτοῖς πράγμασιν ἐπιμένοιεν ἀναισχυντοῦντες καὶ ἄκοντας αὐτοὺς διὰ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἐκδίκου ἐκβάλλεσθαι, καὶ τοὺς ἰδίους καταλαμβάνειν τόπους.”—“from”: *out of*, Basel edition.—“thence”: absent in that edition.—“return”: *arrive*, printed editions generally except Paris and the Lugdunum editions.]

C. XVIII. Wandering monks are to be compelled by defensores. Likewise Pope Pelagius to Paulinus the Solitary. [Note: Chapter uncertain.—Anselm, bk. 7, ch. 193 (196); Polycarpus, bk. 4, tit. 34.] [Note: *Solatinus*, Anselm; *Solitano*, Basel edition; *Solatarius*, Arg. edition.]

[Col. 0996A] We command John the *defensor* to detain Probinus of Pharia, Milianus, Probinianus, and other false monks, so that, if they wish to learn the reason for their contention, they may be presented to us in order to be instructed. Certainly, if they have separated themselves from the ecclesiastical body by obstinacy alone, we have judged that the said *defensor* should be directed to exile them on the island of Reate, as you requested.

[Note: “Pharia”: Thus corrected from Anselm and Polycarpus; the former reading was *Samaria*; Basel reads *Sabaria*. Pharia is a city of Dalmatia.—“Probinianus”: *Probianus*, Anselm; *Probanus*, Basel edition.—“and”: *or*, Basel edition.]

C. XIX. No monk may dare to preach except the Lord’s priests. Likewise Pope Leo to Theodoret, bishop of Cyprus, ep. LXI, alternatively LXIII. [Note: Written A.D. 453. Ep. 120, Ballerini edition.—Burchard, bk. 2, ch. 158; Anselm, final section, ch. 7.]

We add also that which you communicated to us by word through our vicars concerning the misconduct of certain monks of your religious community, and establish in particular that, apart from the Lord’s priests, no one may dare to preach, whether he be monk or layman, though he glory in the name of any learning whatsoever.

[Note: “religious community”: *region*, original.—“by word”: *by words*, printed editions generally.—“through our vicars”: *your vicars*, those editions except Basel.—“and”: marked in the source.]

Gratian. See: in this chapter both the fault is expressly stated and it is removed by a general constitution. Their being forbidden to impose penance follows from the fact that no priest may bind or loose another’s parishioner. But monks, although at their consecration to the priesthood they duly receive—as do other priests—the power to baptize, preach, impose penance, remit sins, and enjoy ecclesiastical benefices, so that they may perform more fully and perfectly those acts which the constitutions of the holy Fathers establish as belonging to the priestly office, nevertheless do not have the exercise of their power [Col. 0996C] unless they have been elected by the people and ordained by the bishop with the abbot’s consent. They are forbidden to meddle in ecclesiastical and secular affairs so that they may not presume to undertake advocacy in lawsuits unless instructed by the bishop, and may not be occupied with secular cases by sitting as judges for deciding litigation.

Thus Pelagius writes to the patrician Antonina and Decia. [Note: Chapter of uncertain date.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 23.]

C. XX. A monk ought not become a *defensor*.

Do not be at all troubled in mind because the bearer of this letter was not made a *defensor*. For I consider it truly very bitter that men should be led from this purpose to that office, in which they can in no way fulfil what monks have promised to God. For the way of life of the one and the office of the other are wholly different. There are rest, prayer, and manual labor; here are the hearing of causes, agreements, proceedings, public disputes, and whatever either ecclesiastical institutions or the need of petitioners [Col. 0997B] demands. May God grant that those whom we nourish in this habit, or who grow up in monasteries, may be such that, when age has advanced and life has been proved, they may be promoted not to the offices of litigation but to the priesthood.

[Note: “there is no …”: lacking in Ivo.—“truly”: *very*, printed editions generally.—“that”: *another*, those editions except Basel and Lugdunum II–III.—“demands”: *compels*, Basel edition.]

Gratian. Yet Gelasius, as is found in the tract concerning the promotion of clerics, in that chapter, [Note: Distinction 77, final chapter.] “A novice monk,” etc., permits them by dispensation to become *defensores*.

Part II. That they possess power for priestly offices is attested by Ambrose, who says: [Note: Nothing of this kind has been found in Blessed Ambrose, and it seems to be the work of a much later author.] [Note: Chapter uncertain.]

C. XXI. Monk-priests are not to be forbidden to perform clerical offices.

We commend, with moderate dispensation, that learned and upright monks dedicated with the honor of the priesthood ought to baptize, preach, impose penance, remit what is owed to the wretched, and enjoy a just share of tithes, first-fruits, and the offerings of the living and dead; so that, in accordance with the Apostle, living from the altar which they serve, they may through service to the Lord’s people transform bread and wine by an unstained blessing into the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: “and upright”: *or upright*, editions of Nor., Venice I–II, Paris, and Lugdunum I.—“of the priesthood”: *of a priest*, Basel edition.—“remit”: *release*, printed editions generally.—“and”: marked in the source.—1 Corinthians 9.]

C. XXII. A monk who is a priest may freely enjoy ecclesiastical benefices. Likewise Pope Innocent. [Note: Chapter uncertain, perhaps of Innocent II.]

If a monk is promoted to the clergy, benefices, stipends, and tithes are to be granted him in full, without any diminution or delay, so that, as well as he can according to his means, whenever necessity arises, he may render assistance for ecclesiastical works and for restoring the church itself.

[Note: “can”: *may be able*, Rome edition, through a printer’s error.]

C. XXIII. On the same matter. Likewise Gregory. [Note: Chapter equally uncertain.]

By the moderation of apostolic authority we decree that monks, if they have been dedicated with the honor of the priesthood, may laudably claim for themselves, no less than other priests, through the merit of a more perfect righteousness and for their own benefit and that of their neighbors, the share of tithes, first-fruits, offerings, and donations made for the living and the dead, according to canon, together with the power of binding and loosing.

[Note: “for the dead”: absent in the Basel edition.—“according to canon”: *according to the just canon*, editions of Arg. and Basel.]

[Col. 0998B] C. XXIV. Monk-priests may freely administer clerical offices. The same author. [Note: This chapter appears to have been excerpted from ch. 24 of the Council of Nîmes, held A.D. 1096.]

By authority of this decree, which we have established by apostolic moderation and the office of piety, priests who are monks and bear the image of the apostles may preach, baptize, give communion, pray for sinners, impose penance, and absolve sins.

C. XXV. Monks adorned with priestly honor have the power of binding and loosing. Likewise from the decree of Pope Boniface. [Note: This chapter, with several others, was sent from Spain, copied from an old codex of the monastery of Poblet, whose title is: “From the council of Pope Boniface, who was fourth after Gregory: how monks may, with priestly office, minister wherever and whenever.”] [Note: Scholars agree that this decree, which Holstenius published in a form conforming to Gratian’s canon, does not belong to Boniface IV; it seems rather itself to have been composed from ch. 2 of the cited Council of Nîmes. Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 22, differs from Gratian in more than one place; Polycarpus, bk. 4, tit. 34.]

There are certain persons, unsupported by any doctrine, indeed very rashly inflamed by a zeal of bitterness rather than love, who assert that monks, because [Col. 0998C] they are dead to the world and live to God, are unworthy of the power of priestly office and cannot impose penance, confer Christianity, or absolve by the power divinely entrusted to them in priestly office. But they are wholly mistaken. And below: § 1. For Blessed Benedict, the gracious teacher of monks, was in no way an opponent of this matter; rather, he decreed only that they should be free from secular affairs. This is enjoined most emphatically by apostolic teachings and the institutions of all the holy Fathers, not only upon monks but also upon canons. For no one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in [Col. 0999A] secular affairs. § 2. We, however, instructed by the examples of so many Fathers—whom it is most dangerous to oppose—believe that the office of binding and loosing is worthily administered, God working through monk-priests, if they happen worthily to be elevated to this ministry. And below: § 3. Therefore we command in every way that those contending to exclude presbyters of monastic profession from the office of priestly power be restrained in future from such wicked presumptions, because the higher anyone is, the more powerful he is also in these matters.

[Note: “nevertheless” added in editions of Arg., Nor., and Venice I.—“very rashly”: *with a most rash [zeal]*, Basel and Lugdunum editions.—“impose penance”: “impose penance” added in Basel and Lugdunum II–III.—“this matter”: *a matter of this kind*, the original cited by Holstenius and Lugdunum II–III; *such a matter*, Basel.—“most emphatically”: *greatly*, printed editions generally.—2 Timothy 2:4.—The biblical sentence “For no one …” is absent from the Poblet codex, Polycarpus, and Ivo.—“so many”: *therefore so many*, Basel; *therefore*, cited original; printed editions otherwise.—“in every way”: *wholly*, Basel.—“higher”: *more exalted*, Basel and Lugdunum II–III.—“the more powerful”: “then he will be [more powerful] also for them,” printed editions generally; *then more powerful*, cited original.—“also”: absent in Böhm.]

Gratian. All these authorities clearly show that monks may lawfully impose penance, baptize, and administer the other priestly offices. But that they may exercise their power by election of the people, appointment of bishops, [Col. 0999B] and consent of the abbot is proved by the authority of Jerome, Gelasius, and Gregory.

For Jerome says to the monk Rusticus, ep. IV: [Note: Written about A.D. 400.]

C. XXVI. One who lives worthily in a monastery may be promoted to the clergy by election of the people.

Live in the monastery so that you may deserve to be a cleric. And below: § 1. Learn for a long time what you are afterward to teach, and among good men always follow the better. But if the people or the bishop elects you a cleric, do the things belonging to clerics.

[Note: “For a long time”: Blessed Jerome has a different and clearer sequence of words: “When you have reached mature age,” he says, “provided that your life has accompanied you, and either the people or the bishop of the city has chosen you for a cleric, perform the duties of clerics, and among them follow the better men.” And below: “Learn for a long time what you are to teach.”]

C. XXVII. Monks may be promoted to clerical rank. The same author to the same recipient, earlier in the same letter. [Note: Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 4.]

[Col. 0999C] If desire for the clergy tickles *you*, learn what you can teach, and offer Christ a rational sacrifice, lest you be a soldier before a recruit, or a master before a disciple. § 1. It does not belong to my humility or station to judge clerics and say anything unfavorable concerning ministers of churches. Let them have their order and rank. If you hold it, the book published to Nepotianus can teach you how you ought to live in it. § 2. Now we are discussing the first beginnings and habits of monks, and of that monk who, trained in liberal studies, placed Christ’s yoke upon his neck in youth. The first matter to be considered is whether you ought to live alone or with others in a monastery. It seems good to me that you should have the fellowship of saints, not teach yourself, and [Col. 1000A] not enter without a teacher upon a road you have never travelled.

[Note: “you”: marked in the source.—“can”: *could*, Basel edition.—“to Christ”: *to God*, Ivo and printed editions generally.—“lest”: “lest you be,” those editions.—“clerics”: *others*, printed editions generally and Ivo.—“first beginnings”: *cradles*, printed editions generally.—“and not”: *and*, Basel edition.]

C. XXVIII. A monk is to be chosen in the place judged fitting by the abbot and ordained priest by the bishop. Likewise Pope Gelasius. [Note: Chapter uncertain.]

If there is a monk who seems worthy of priesthood by the merit of a venerable life, and if the abbot under whose rule he serves Christ the King requests that he be made priest, he ought to be chosen by the bishop and ordained in the place which the bishop judges fitting, being prudently and justly to perform all that belongs to the priestly office by the election either of the people or of the bishop.

[Note: “seems worthy”: *is foreseen [as worthy]*, editions of Arg., Basel, and Lugdunum II–III.—“serves”: *ministers*, Basel; “by the bishop himself,” ibid.—“bishop”: Two old codices read *by him*; Ivo, *Panormia*, and editions of Venice I–II, Nor., Lugdunum, and Paris.—“priestly”: *of a priest*, editions of Arg., Basel, Nor., and Venice I–II.]

[Col. 1000B] C. XXIX. Monks are to be promoted to ecclesiastical orders at a mature age. Likewise Pope Siricius to Himerius, ep. I, ch. 13. [Note: Written A.D. 385.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, ch. 53; Polycarpus, bk. 2, tit. 31.]

We desire and decree that monks whom gravity of character and holy formation of life and faith commend should be admitted to clerical offices, provided that those who are worthy while under thirty years of age be promoted through the individual grades at increasing intervals of time to the minor orders, and thus attain, by consecration at mature age, the dignities of deacon or priest; and that they not immediately ascend by a leap to the summit of the episcopate, unless the same periods which we have laid down above for each dignity have been observed in their case.

[Note: “yet”: marked in the source.—“commend”: *commends*, Basel edition.—“desire”: *earnestly desire*, ibid.—“within the thirtieth year”: *thirty years*, ibid.—“at increasing intervals”: *increasing*, Hispanic Collection; “time” absent there.—“and that they not”: *so that they may not*, Basel and Lugdunum II–III.—“immediately”: absent in the Hispanic Collection.]

### C. XXX. Monks are neither to accept ecclesiastical offices through greedy ambition nor reject them through flattering indolence. Likewise Augustine to Eudoxius, Letter LXXXI.  
[Note: [Col. 0999] Letter 48 in the Maurist edition; written about A.D. 398.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 179.]

[Col. 1000C] But we exhort you, brothers, in the Lord, to keep your profession and persevere unto the end. And if mother Church should require any service from you, neither accept it in greedy self-exaltation nor reject it through seductive indolence; rather, obey God with a gentle heart, meekly bearing him who governs you—who guides the meek in judgment and teaches the meek his ways. Do not prefer your leisure to the necessities of the Church; for if, when she was in labour, no good persons had been willing to minister, you would have found no way in which to be born.

[Note: [Col. 0999] “unto the end”: the original reads “unto the end of life.”]
[Note: [Col. 0999] “any service from you”: “by what service of yours,” the collected editions and Ivo, *Panormia*.]
[Note: [Col. 0999] “God”: “the Lord,” Basel edition.]
[Note: [Col. 0999] “him who governs you”: “him who governs us,” collected editions.]
[Note: [Col. 0999] Adds “us,” Lyons I edition; compare Psalm 24:9.]

### C. XXXI. Gelasius directs that a certain monk, Ruffinus, be made a priest and ordained in a particular basilica. Likewise Pope Pelagius to Bono, bishop of Savinatum.  
[Note: [Col. 0999] A chapter of uncertain source.—Anselm, book 7, c. 96 (114), from Gelasius. *Polycarpus*, book 2, title 32.]

In your parish, in the basilica of St. Saurentius, founded on the [Col. 1001A] estate of Theodore, the distinguished man, son and counsellor of ours, we have learned that the office of presbyter is lacking. Since the aforesaid son of ours has reported to us that he has found a certain monk named Ruffinus, formerly proved to him by his life, religious devotion, and morals, and asks that he be consecrated priest there—something to which we did not consent should be done at once, the due observance having been deferred—therefore, upon receipt of this letter, let your belovedness make him deacon on the coming Saturday; and, if God wills and we live, we shall make him a presbyter in the middle of the week, so that, when the Paschal festival arrives, the sacred ministries may be duly performed in the said basilica by a suitable person.

[Note: [Col. 1001] *Theodosii*: edition of Basel.]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] “life, religious devotion”: omitted in the editions of Argentoratum, Basel, Norimberg, and in Anselm.]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] “and morals”: “and in all things,” editions of Argentoratum, Norimberg, and Venice I.]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] “Therefore”: “And therefore,” the collected editions and Lugdundunum II and III.]

### C. XXXII. A man who becomes a monk from being a cleric may be chosen and consecrated by the ordaining bishop proper to him. Likewise Gregory, book I of the *Register*, Letter 40.  
[Note: [Col. 1001D] The actual words of Blessed Gregory are these: “If any should happen to pass from the clerical state into monastic life, they must not be allowed of their own will to return again to the same or another church in which they had formerly served as soldiers, unless the monk is of such a life that the bishop under whom he had formerly served foresees him to be worthy of the priesthood, so that he ought to be chosen by him and ordained in the place [Col. 1002D] which he judges appropriate.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] Letter 42, written to Anthimus in A.D. 591, book 1, Maurist edition.]

If anyone should happen to enter monastic life from the clerical state, and is a monk of such a life that the bishop under whom he formerly served judges him worthy of the priesthood, he may be chosen and ordained in whatever place that bishop judges appropriate.

[Note: [Col. 1001] “If anyone”: “if any,” editions of Basel and Lyons II and III.]

### C. XXXIII. Monks are not to be chosen for clerical office without the testimony of their abbot. Likewise from the Council of Agde, c. 27.  
[Note: [Col. 1001] Held A.D. 506.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 157.]

Wandering monks are not to be ordained to clerical office, either in cities or in parishes, unless their own abbot has given them testimony. And below, §1: For if it is necessary to ordain a cleric from among monks, the bishop is to undertake this with the consent and will of the abbot.

[Note: [Col. 1001] “unless to them”: omitted in the Hispana collection.]  
[Note: [Col. 1002D] “They are to be ordained”: in the council itself there follows a final chapter, below, 20, question 4.]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] “from among monks”: “from a monk,” editions of Basel and Lyons II and III.]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] “let the bishop undertake this”: “let the bishop undertake it,” same editions.]

### C. XXXIV. With the abbot’s consent, monks whom the bishop wishes to ordain for the benefit of the Church are to be ordained. Likewise from the Council of Lleida, c. 3.  
[Note: [Col. 1001] Held A.D. 546.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 34, c. 3.]

When, for the benefit of the Church, a bishop has approved certain monks for advancement to clerical office, they must be ordained with the abbot’s consent. But offerings made from resources belonging by right to the monastery are not, on any pretext of diocesan law, to be touched by bishops.

[Note: [Col. 1001] “certain”: “those,” Hispana collection.]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] “to clerical office”: “to clerical office” in the singular, ibid.]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] “for advancement”: omitted there.]

### C. XXXV. Without the abbot’s command monks are not to presume to perform ecclesiastical ministries. Likewise from the Council of Tarragona, c. 11.  
[Note: [Col. 1002D] “Without the abbot”: this is the heading in most ancient copies. In the printed editions it read: “Without the abbot’s command, monks are not to be chosen for clerical office.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] Held A.D. 516.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 31, c. 8.]

We forbid monks who leave the monastery to presume to perform any ecclesiastical ministry, unless perhaps under the command of the abbot. Likewise, no one among them—that is, among the monks—is to become the undertaker or executor of secular business, except insofar as the welfare of the monastery requires, and then only under the abbot’s command.

[Note: [Col. 1001] “that which”: “the thing which,” Hispana collection and collected editions.]

### C. XXXVI. Deserters from monasteries are not to be chosen for the service of the clerical order. Likewise Augustine to Aurelius, Letter LXXVI.  
[Note: [Col. 1001] Letter 60, written about A.D. 401, Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, c. 7.]

I read your graciousness’s letter concerning Donatus and his brother, and for a long time I wavered over what answer to give. Yet, repeatedly considering what is beneficial for the salvation of those whom we serve by nurturing in Christ, I could think of nothing else except that this way must not be opened to servants of God: they must not suppose that they can more easily be chosen for something better if they have become worse.

For their own fall is made easier, and a most unworthy injury is done to the clerical order, if deserters from monasteries are chosen for clerical service, whereas from those who remain in the monastery we are accustomed to admit into the clergy only persons more tested and better. Unless perhaps, as ordinary people say, “a bad *choraula*—that is, a leader in the chorus—is a good accompanist”; so these same ordinary people will mock us by saying: “A bad monk is a good cleric.”

It is greatly to be lamented if we raise monks to such ruinous pride and judge clerics worthy of such a grave insult—we who are among their number—when even a good monk sometimes scarcely makes a good cleric, if he possesses sufficient continence but lacks the necessary training or the integrity appropriate to a regular religious person. But I believe that your blessedness judged concerning these men that they had left the monastery with our consent, so that they might be more useful to their fellow-countrymen. But this is false: they departed of their own accord; of their own accord they deserted, while we resisted, as far as we could, for their salvation.

[Note: [Col. 1001] “we served”: “we have served,” Basel edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] “their”: “those,” ibid.]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] “easy”: “easier,” collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, c. 180.]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] “from these”: “from those,” collected editions, first Lyons edition, Lyons II and III.]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] “that is, leader in the chorus”: added by the Basel edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] “raise”: “lift up,” editions of Basel and Lyons II and III; “raise up,” Ivo, *Decretum*; “lift somewhat,” editions of Argentoratum, Venice II, and Paris; “subject,” Venice I, Norimberg, and Ivo, *Panormia*.]  
[Note: [Col. 1001] The original, the collected editions, and Böhm read: “that our … had left …”; the wording continues through “had departed.”]

### Part III. Gratian

From all these authorities it is shown that monks elected by the people and ordained by the bishop with the consent of their abbot can lawfully exercise their authority. But Gregory’s statement above, c. 2—“No one can serve in ecclesiastical duties,” etc.—is to be understood of those who, having been ordained among the cardinals or bishops, strive to retain for themselves the administration of their monastery.

Accordingly, the same Gregory writes to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna, book VI, Letter 40:

### C. XXXVII. Monasteries are in no way to be burdened because of the promotion of an abbot or monk.  
[Note: [Col. 1003] Letter 53, written A.D. 597, book 7, Maurist edition.]

Lest monasteries perhaps bear any burden because of the promotion of any monk or abbot, you must take care that, if any abbot or monk from whatever monastery enters clerical office or sacred order, he is thereafter to have no authority there, as we have decided.

[Note: [Col. 1003] The original reads “through … promotion.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1003] “you”: “we,” collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 1003] “there”: “in that place,” same editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 1003] The marked words are “abbots or.”]

### C. XXXVIII. Those who serve churches in any manner cannot be abbots of monasteries. The same to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse, book III, Letter 11.  
[Note: [Col. 1003] Letter 11, written A.D. 594, book 4, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 7, c. 163 (191).]

Do not permit presbyters, deacons, or clerics of any order who serve churches in any manner to be abbots in monasteries. Rather, either, having entered clerical service, they are not to be advanced to monastic orders; or, if they have decided to remain in the position of abbot, they are in no way to be allowed clerical service. For it is quite incongruous that, when a person cannot diligently fulfil even one of these offices because of its greatness, he should be judged fit for both.

[Note: [Col. 1003D] “In any manner”: these words are absent from the printed and manuscript original.]  
[Note: [Col. 1003D] “Having entered clerical service”: so also in old manuscripts of Gratian, Gregory’s letters, and other editions of them, except the old Paris edition, in which, and in Anselm, one reads: “Or, having abandoned clerical service, let them be advanced to monastic orders.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1003] “advanced”: “promoted,” collected editions and Böhm.]  
[Note: [Col. 1003] “because of”: “for,” original and Basel edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 1003] “be judged”: “appear,” collected editions.]

Gratian. This may be understood either generally or as stated by a special privilege, as is recorded in Gregory’s register concerning a certain monastery in the following manner:

[Note: [Col. 1003] Chapter by an uncertain author: a decree of Gregory, reported in Letter 8, book 13, to Senator the abbot, who reports it.]

### C. XXXIX. Concerning a certain xenodochium, whose abbot is forbidden to be chosen as bishop.  
[Note: [Col. 1003D] The author of this chapter reports a constitution of Blessed Gregory concerning the abbot of a xenodochium in the city of Autun, found in book 11 of the *Register*, Letter 10.]

This is also why, because a xenodochium and monastery established in the same kingdom of the Franks was not being governed canonically through the ambitions and disputes of certain persons, Gregory, desiring to free it from the perversity of evildoers, ordered that no abbot should ever be introduced there by any act of surreption without royal provision and the election of the monks. He also ordered that the abbot of that monastery should never be chosen to the episcopate, lest perhaps the abbey should suffer some loss on account of the episcopate.

That privilege belongs so specifically to that church that it cannot establish a general law at all for kings or abbots. For what is granted separately to one person does not thereby apply to all.

[Note: [Col. 1003] “and”: “or,” collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 1003] “and”: “but,” Basel edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 1003] “provision”: “providence,” ibid.]

Gratian. The preceding authority does not prohibit abbots from becoming priests, since St. Benedict directs that an abbot give a blessing to brothers who go out and return, an act belonging only to priests. Likewise he assigns the reading of the Gospel to the abbot; and reading it with the following prayer is also an act of priestly office. But it prohibits those from becoming priests or [Col. 1004B] deacons who are obliged to remain continually in ecclesiastical service.

§1. Likewise, Jerome’s statement to the presbyter Riparius—“A monk has the office not of teaching but of mourning”—and to Heliodorus—“The cause of a monk is one thing, that of a cleric another”—and to Rusticus—“Monks may do nothing without the counsel of presbyters”—must not be understood so universally that no monk is allowed to undertake the office of teaching. Otherwise we should be compelled to deny that Blessed Gregory, Augustine bishop of the English, Blessed Martin, and countless others whom Scripture testifies were promoted from monastic life to the highest rank of priesthood possessed the office of teaching; or we should have to assert that, on the day of their consecration, they departed from their former profession—something which, as Innocent testifies, no one may do.

Jerome therefore wished to distinguish the person of a monk from that of a cleric, showing what belongs to each by his proper office.

§2. For one thing belongs to a person insofar as he is a monk, another insofar as he is a cleric. Insofar as he is a monk, he has the office of weeping over his own sins and those of others; insofar as he is a cleric, that of teaching and feeding the people.

§3. Ecclesiastical history testifies that until the time of Eusebius, Zosimus, and Siricius, monks were simply monks and not clerics. Jerome himself also reports that the monks of Scythia assembled together to find themselves a priest to celebrate for them the solemnities of the Mass.

[Note: [Col. 1003] “above, c. 4”; “above, c. 6”; “above, c. 7.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1004D] Johannes Andreae says that this passage of Jerome occurs in the letter *On the Works and Humility of Monks*. Yet in volume two of the works of Blessed Jerome, in Letter 60—Epiphanius’s letter to John of Jerusalem, translated into Latin by Jerome—one reads that Epiphanius ordained a presbyter at the request of monks, so that he might perform the Lord’s sacraments for them. The monastery was, however, in John’s diocese.]

### C. XL. All clerics and monks ought to possess exemption from guardianship. Likewise Leo Augustus, book I of the Code, *On Bishops and Clerics*, law 51.  
[Note: [Col. 1005D] In the Code of Justinian this law is attributed to Justinian himself, not Leo.]  
[Note: [Col. 1005] Indeed, Justinian, c. 51, *Code on Bishops and Clerics*. In the Basel and Venice I editions it is attributed to Pope Leo.]

We decree generally that all most reverend bishops, as well as presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and especially monks, even if they are not clerics, possess by law exemption from every guardianship—testamentary, appointed, or legal. They are to be free not only from guardianship but also from curatorship, not only of minors and adults but also of the insane, deaf, mute, and other persons for whom guardians or curators are provided by ancient laws.

§1. Yet we decree that clerics and monks possess this benefit only if they remain attached to the most holy churches or monasteries—not wandering about and not negligent in divine ministries—because we grant them this very privilege in order that, leaving all other things aside, they may devote themselves to the service of almighty God.

§2. We decree that this is to prevail not only in old Rome or in this imperial city, but throughout the whole earth wherever the Christian name is cultivated.

§3. They have also received exemption from new assessments and degrading public burdens. Hence Constantius writes to all clerics, under the same title, first law: “In accordance with the ordinance which you are reported long ago to have obtained, no one shall bind your lands and slaves to assessments, but you shall enjoy exemption.”

Likewise the Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the same book, under the title *On Most Holy Churches*, law 5:

§4. Having considered the tenor of a reasonable council, it pleases us to prescribe with strict moderation from what particular obligations the churches of individual cities are to be exempt. First, the outrage of that usurpation must be repelled, so that estates dedicated to the uses of heavenly mysteries may not be harassed by the dregs of degrading public services; that nothing extraordinary or additionally imposed may henceforth be demanded; that no obligation of transport be registered; and finally, that nothing beyond the ordinary canonical contribution be assigned to their services, except what the sudden burden of an unforeseen emergency may require. Whoever acts contrary to this shall, after the severity of the punishment due to sacrilegious persons has been imposed, be subjected to permanent deportation into exile.

[Note: [Col. 1005] “all”: “every,” collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 1005] “at”: “to,” same editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 1005] “we grant”: “we may grant,” original.]  
[Note: [Col. 1005] “is cultivated”: “is worshipped,” collected editions, original, and Böhm.]  
[Note: [Col. 1005] This was Constantius, A.D. 343; *Theodosian Code*, book 16, title 2, c. 8; Anselm, book 4, c. 13.]  
[Note: [Col. 1005D] “You are reported to have obtained”: Justinian’s Code reads, “you and your slaves have obtained”; the Theodosian Code, “you and your slaves are reported to have obtained.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1005] Written A.D. 412.—Anselm, book 4, c. 21.]  
[Note: [Col. 1005] “of a reasonable council”: “of reasonable counsel,” original and Lyons II and III.]  
[Note: [Col. 1005] “or additionally imposed”: “or additionally introduced,” editions of Argentoratum, Norimberg, Venice I and II.]  
[Note: [Col. 1005] “transport”: “transports,” original; the asterisk indicates its absence in Anselm.]  
[Note: [Col. 1005D] “Contribution”: the printed codices continued, “[Col. 1006D] unless it be that of an unforeseen emergency.” The common text of Justinian’s Code reads “and that of an unforeseen emergency”; the manuscript and Haloander’s edition omit the conjunction. The Theodosian Code reads “which is that of an unforeseen emergency.” Most old copies of Gratian read “except that of an unforeseen emergency.” The word *if* is absent from all and was therefore inserted.]  
[Note: [Col. 1005] “to be imposed”: “rightly to be imposed,” original, collected editions, and Böhm.]  
[Note: [Col. 1005] “permanent”: “perpetual,” collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 1005] “be subjected”: “be burned,” Anselm and Basel edition; “be fined,” the remaining editions.]

Gratian. The same is understood from the words of St. Silvester, who, assigning the obedience of inferiors toward superiors, says: “Let the abbot be subject to the doorkeeper, and the monk to the abbot,” above in the treatise on those to be ordained. Jerome therefore shows that monks simply may do nothing without the counsel of presbyters, nor may they take upon themselves the office of teaching without the authority of clerics, unless perhaps they are inwardly admonished by divine grace.

Thus Blessed Gregory relates in the *Dialogues* concerning St. Benedict that he brought the people of Mount Cassino to the faith and overturned the altar of Apollo erected there; and concerning a certain Equitius, to whom an angel appeared in sleep and sent him to preach. When he complained of an infirmity of speech, the angel touched his tongue with a lancet and cured the whole infirmity.

§1. Jerome’s including himself among such persons is like the Apostle’s statement to the Philippians: “Let all of us who are imperfect think this”; he thereby includes himself among the imperfect. Thus Jerome elsewhere says: “Born in a poor house and a rustic hut.” And below: “We, stuffed with gold, disdain honey while hungry”: he counts himself, though poor, among the rich, above where clerics who refuse to relinquish their own property are discussed, chapter *The Glory of a Bishop*.

§2. Behold, it has been sufficiently shown that monks honoured with the rank of presbyter, elected by the people and appointed by the bishop, may do the same things as other priests. This is also proved from the likeness of their consecration. For in their consecration nothing different is said from what is said in the consecration of others. For the bishop earnestly asks that the Lord’s blessing be poured out upon both alike. And when he consecrates, he says individually to every priest: “May these hands, O Lord, be consecrated and sanctified, so that whatever they consecrate may be consecrated, and whatever they bless may be blessed.” Behold: the blessing is common. Whence, then, the separation? Therefore, just as both receive a common power in the blessing, so in their appointment they likewise receive in common the exercise of that power.

§3. Besides, without the bishops’ permission, the exercise of authority is forbidden not only to monks but generally to all clerics.

[Note: [Col. 1005] Compare Distinction 93, c. 5.]  
[Note: [Col. 1005] Gregory, *Dialogues*, book 2, c. 8, and book 1, c. 4.]  
[Note: [Col. 1005] Philippians 3:15. The Apostle reads “perfect,” not “imperfect.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1005] C. 12, question 2, c. 71.]

[Col. 1007A] Hence Clement, Letter III:

### C. XLI. Presbyters are not to perform priestly acts without the bishops’ permission.  
[Note: [Col. 1007] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Burchard, book 2, c. 93; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, c. 123, and part 6, c. 90.]

All the faithful—and especially all presbyters, deacons, and other clerics—must take care to do nothing without the permission of their own bishop. No presbyter is to celebrate Mass in his parish without authorization; nor is he to baptize or do anything whatever without that bishop’s permission.

[Note: [Col. 1007] “anyone”: “any person,” Burchard, Ivo, part 2, and the collected editions; “each person,” Ivo, part 6.]

### Part IV. Gratian

Concerning those who remain within monastic enclosure, to whom the people are not entrusted for governance, the question is whether they ought to give or receive tithes. In this matter the following distinction must be observed: from fields and vineyards cultivated for their own support, they may retain tithes for themselves. For if tithes were paid by the people to the sons of Levi for the ministry by which they served the Lord in the tabernacle, offering sacrifices and burnt offerings for the people, it is clear that monks are no more obliged to pay tithes from their own estates than other priests are.

§1. But it is said that the estates of monks—whether purchased for a price or offered for the salvation of souls—before they came under the monks’ ownership paid firstfruits and tithes to baptismal churches or certain other churches, and that those churches cannot be deprived of their legal right.

Hence a statute is found in the Council of Mainz:

### C. XLII. A person who assigns his property to someone cannot take the income of tithes away from the former church.  
[Note: [Col. 1007] Rather, from the Council held at Koblenz, A.D. 922, c. 8.—Burchard, book 3, c. 241; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, final chapter.]

If any layman, cleric, or person of either sex assigns places or goods from his property to anyone as a gift, he has no authority to withdraw from that property the income of tithes lawfully assigned to the former church. If he attempts to do so, the transfer is to be judged wholly void, and he himself is to be compelled to make amends by ecclesiastical censure.

[Note: [Col. 1007] “to anyone”: “somewhere,” original, collected editions, and cited collections.]  
[Note: [Col. 1007] “give”: “donate,” original and cited collections.]  
[Note: [Col. 1007] “judged”: “declared,” collected editions and the first Argentoratum edition.]

### C. XLIII. Older churches are not to be deprived either of tithes or of any possession. Likewise from the Council of Chalon.  
[Note: [Col. 1007] Rather, from the Sixth Council of Arles, held A.D. 813. Compare *Capitularies*, book 2, c. 36; Regino, book 1, c. 29; Burchard, book 3, c. 9; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 12—both from the Council of Meaux; Anselm, at the end of book 7, “from the Council of Mainz, presided over by the Roman legate Boniface, martyr and bishop.” Compare the Council of Mainz, A.D. 813, c. 11.]

Churches established long ago are not to be deprived either of tithes or of any possession, in order that these may be granted to new oratories.

### C. XLIV. Older churches are not to lose their right because of new ones. Likewise from the Council of Worms.  
[Note: [Col. 1007C] Burchard and Ivo also cite c. 6 of the Council of Worms; in the extant text at that place there is something relevant to this matter.]  
[Note: [Col. 1007] Rather, from the capitulary at Salz, A.D. 804, c. 3.—Regino, book 1, c. 26; Burchard, book 3, c. 7; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 9.]

Whoever wishes to build a church on his own property may lawfully do so if he has the consent and approval of the bishop in whose parish it lies. Nevertheless, the bishop must take every precaution that older churches do not lose their right because of a new church, but that payment is always made to the older churches.

[Note: [Col. 1007] “because of a new [church]”: “because of new [churches],” Burchard and Ivo, Basel and Lyons I editions; “because of this occasion,” original and Regino.]  
[Note: [Col. 1007] “payment is made”: “payments are made,” collected editions.]

Gratian. Pope Leo IV affirms that tithes are to be paid to baptismal churches, saying:

### C. XLV. Tithes must be given to baptismal churches.  
[Note: [Col. 1007C] Ivo cites almost the same words from Gelasius; Anselm and Polycarpus cite Leo, as does Gratian.]  
[Note: [Col. 1007] Paschal II cites this from a letter of Leo IV to the Britons, in his letter to Baldric; Anselm, book 5, c. 53 (54), and, from the register of Leo VI, in the collections published by Canisius, vol. 3; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 151, from the letter to Justus and Faustus.]

Concerning tithes, it has seemed right in due order not only to us but also to our predecessors that they ought to be given only to the parish communities where the most holy baptisms are administered.

Gratian. Therefore, if no one may lawfully withdraw the income of tithes from the former church to which it was assigned; if the right of an older church must not be granted to newer ones; if tithes are to be given only to baptismal churches: it is clear that monks are obliged to pay tithes from their own estates. Yet the authority of the Council of Mainz speaks of a seller or donor, deciding that one who sells or gives may not take the tithe-income away from the church to which it had formerly been lawfully assigned. Monks, however, retain tithes and firstfruits not by the authority of the seller or donor, but by the authority of the same council and of Pope Paschal, by whom it has been decreed that monks need not pay tithes from their own estates.

For the Council of Mainz enacted as follows:

[Note: [Col. 1007C] This chapter occurs in no extant Council of Mainz, but in the Second Council of Chalon, from which Burchard and Ivo cite it. In a book of the Vatican Library containing the two councils of Urban II, Piacenza and Melfi, these words also occur: “It has been reported to the holy synod that there are certain bishops and abbots who do not allow peasants belonging to them to give tithes to the churches where they hear Mass and their children are baptized. Therefore this holy assembly decreed that bishops and abbots may retain for themselves the tithes from vineyards, fields, and crops which they cultivate for their own use or that of the brethren, for blessing or the reception of guests; but their household is to give its tithes where throughout the year it hears Mass and its children are baptized.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1007] Rather, from the Second Council of Chalon, held A.D. 813, c. 19.—Burchard, book 3, c. 132; Anselm, book 3, c. 57 (58); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 59; *Decretum*, part 3, c. 198.]

### C. XLVI. Abbots and bishops are not to pay tithes from their own estates.

Moreover, certain brethren complained that there were bishops and abbots who would not allow tithes to be given to the church where their peasants hear Mass. Therefore this holy assembly decreed that bishops and abbots are to have the tithes from fields and vineyards which they possess for their own support or that of the brethren brought to their churches; but their households are to give their tithes where their children are baptized and where throughout the course of the year they hear Mass.

[Note: [Col. 1009] “to be given”: “to give,” editions of Argentoratum, Norimberg, and Venice I.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “to the church”: “to churches,” original.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “their”: “they,” Anselm and Burchard.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “which they possess for their own support or that of the brethren”: “which they possess for the brethren’s use,” Argentoratum; “which they possess for use or support,” Ivo, *Panormia*.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009D] “their churches”: this word, “their,” is absent from the council itself and from the other collectors; there are also certain other variants indicated in the margin.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “give”: “bring,” Ivo.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “are baptized”: “may be baptized,” editions of Argentoratum, Norimberg, and Venice I.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “year”: “the year’s course,” Argentoratum edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “course”: adds “or circuit,” Basel edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “Mass”: “the Mass,” Lyons I edition.]

### C. XLVII. Monks and canons are in no way to be compelled to pay tithes from their own labour. Likewise Paschal II.  
[Note: [Col. 1009] A chapter of uncertain date.—Deusdedit, part 3.]

The authority of divine law has ordained that tithes be rendered by the people to priests and Levites. But no principle allows soldiers, bishops, or any persons whatsoever to exact tithes from monks or clerics living in common, upon their own labour or sustenance. Hence Blessed Gregory says:

“What are we to say concerning the division of portions, the provision of hospitality, and the performance of mercy for those who live the common life? For everything that remains must be expended on pious and religious causes, as the Lord says: ‘Give what remains as alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.’”

[Note: [Col. 1009] “by the people”: “by peoples,” Basel edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] Gregory, second reply to Augustine; compare C. 12, question 1, c. 8.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] Luke 11:41.]

### Part V. Gratian

But the statement that older churches are not to be deprived of tithes or any possession because of newer ones is not to be understood as though a bishop were in no circumstances permitted to grant for a time some portion of one church’s possessions or tithe-income to another. For just as the Pope can unite two bishoprics into one, so one bishopric, with the consent of its own bishop, can be divided into two; or any church can even be exempted by apostolic authority from a metropolitan’s jurisdiction against his will.

Accordingly Pope Gregory writes to Benenatus, bishop, book II, Letter 31:

### C. XLVIII. Apostolic authority can unite two bishoprics into one.  
[Note: [Col. 1009] Letter 45, written A.D. 592, book 1, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 6, c. 108 (105); *Polycarpus*, book 3, title 30.]

The circumstances of the times and the nearness of the places invite us to unite the churches of Cumae and Misenum, since they are neither separated from one another by a long distance of travel nor—because of sins—is there such a multitude of people that they ought to have separate priests, as they once did.
