Since, therefore, the priest of the fortress of Cumae has completed the course of this life, know that by this document of present authority we have united both churches and entrusted them to you, and know that you are the proper bishop of both churches.

Therefore, as their proper priest, you shall have free authority, with the consent and permission of our authority, to order and dispose of whatever concerning their patrimony or the ordering or promotion of the clergy appears proper to you according to the canons. Reside where you see it to be more convenient and useful, provided that you arrange with diligent and provident care for the other church, in which you are not bodily present, so that the divine mysteries may there be solemnly performed with the Lord’s help.

[Note: [Col. 1009D] “Misenum”: corrected from an old manuscript of Blessed Gregory, though the printed editions, as also Gratian, read “Musitanum.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “Musitanum”: Anselm and the collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “not long”: “not far,” collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “distance of travel”: “interval,” same editions and Anselm.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “separate”: “two,” ibid.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “know”: “you may know,” collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “clergy”: “cleric,” editions of Argentoratum and Basel, and Böhm.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “there”: omitted in Gregory himself, Anselm, and the Argentoratum edition.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] The original and Anselm read: “from which you are at present bodily absent.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “there”: “in those places,” Lyons II and III.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “with the Lord’s help”: “with the Lord presiding,” collected editions.]

### C. XLIX. Apostolic authority is able to unite two bishoprics into one. The same to John, bishop of Velletri, book II, Letter 35.  
[Note: [Col. 1009] Letter 50, written in the same year, in the same book.—Anselm, book 5, c. 24 (26); *Polycarpus*, book 1, title 9.]

After hostile impiety had, because of sins, so devastated the churches of various cities that no hope remained of restoring them when the people had failed, we are bound by a very great concern lest, when their priests have died, the remnant of the people, governed by no pastoral direction, be carried off—God forbid—into the snares of the crafty enemy of faith through trackless ways.

Frequently stirred by concern for this matter, we have resolved in our heart to entrust these churches to neighbouring bishops for governance. Therefore we have provided that the care and government of the church of the Three Taverns be entrusted to your brotherhood; it must be joined and united to your church, so that, with Christ’s help, you may rightly be bishop of both churches and, as their proper bishop, may have by our present permission free authority to dispose with vigilant and canonical care of whatever concerning its patrimony or the ordering and promotion of the clergy appears proper to you.

[Note: [Col. 1009] “no hope”: “no hope at all,” Anselm and collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “stirred”: “admonished,” original and collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 1010D] “of the Three Taverns”: the printed editions read “of Trier.” This has been corrected from several old copies, the original, and John the Deacon, book 3, c. 15. As he testifies, this letter was written to John, bishop of Velletri. The town of the Three Taverns is near Velletri.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “we have provided”: “we have foreseen,” editions of Argentoratum, Norimberg, Venice I and II, and the remaining editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “with Christ’s help”: “with Christ assisting,” collected editions.]  
[Note: [Col. 1009] “clergy”: “cleric,” editions of Argentoratum, Norimberg, Venice I and II.]  
[Note: [Col. 1011] “you may have”: “you will have,” Anselm.]

### C. L. Dioceses which have never had a bishop are not to have one. Likewise from the Second Council of Carthage, c. 5.  
[Note: [Col. 1011] Held A.D. 390.—Burchard, book 1, c. 33.]

Felix, bishop of Selemselita, said: “Even if this is agreeable, I submit to your Holiness that dioceses which have never had bishops should not have them, and that a diocese which has at some time had one should have its own [bishop].” [Note: [Col. 1011] *or*: Hisp. Collection.] [Note: [Col. 1011D] *Its own*: In the council itself the following words occur: “And if, as time goes on and faith in God increases, the people have multiplied and desire to have their own ruler, then, with the consent of him under whose authority the diocese has been established, they may have a bishop.”] “According to this course of proceedings, your Holiness should determine what ought to be done.” [Note: [Col. 1011D] *Course of proceedings*: This passage has been corrected from the printed and manuscript original. Previously it read [Col. 1012D] [ [Col. 1011] thus in the same edition]: “According to this persecution, it is for your Holiness to judge” [ [Col. 1011] *to judge*: Basle editions; Lyons II and III.—*to be judged*: the remaining editions.].] All said: “It is agreeable.”

C. LI. Dioceses held by a bishop are not to receive bishops of their own except with his consent. Likewise from the African Council, c. 20. [Note: [Col. 1011] c. 53 in Dionysius.—c. 42, Third Council of Carthage, held A.D. 397.—Burchard, same place.]

[Col. 1011B] It has been decreed by many councils of the assembly of priests that communities in dioceses retained by bishops, which have never had bishops, are not to receive rulers of their own except with the consent of the bishop by whom they are held. [Note: [Col. 1012D] *Rulers*: The African and Carthaginian council continues: “that is, bishops”; this is also added in the gloss.]

C. LII. Apostolic authority can exempt bishops from the jurisdiction of an archbishop. Likewise Gregory [Note: [Col. 1011] Epistle 7, written A.D. 593, Book III, Maurist edition.—Anselm, Book VI, c. 125 (130). Polyc. Book I, title 7.] to John, bishop of Larissa, [Note: [Col. 1011] *Lanseus*: Basle editions.—*Lauseus*: remaining editions.] Book II, Indiction 11, epistle 7.

Our brother Hadrian, bishop of the city of Thebes, having come to Rome, complained tearfully that in certain matters he had been condemned unlawfully and uncanonically by your Fraternity, and also by John, bishop of Prima Justiniana. [Note: [Col. 1011] “unjustly condemned by the bishop of the city of Justiniana”: collected editions.] And below: § 1. “Concerning his most wicked and condemnable judgment, we shall deal with the matter elsewhere, the Lord helping us. But we have found that Bishop Hadrian suffered from your hatred, contrary to priestly conduct, and that he was condemned by the sentence of your Fraternity in financial causes without any legal basis. § 2. Therefore, since he could not be deprived of his rank of honour by the aforesaid John, bishop of Prima Justiniana, contrary to law and the canons, we have decreed that he be restored to his church and recalled to the rank of his proper dignity. And although you ought to have been deprived of communion in the Lord’s body because, despite the admonition of our predecessor of holy memory—which exempted him and his church from the jurisdiction of your authority—you have again presumed to retain some jurisdiction over them; nevertheless, deciding more leniently and meanwhile preserving for you the sacrament of communion, we decree that your Fraternity abstain from all the jurisdictional authority formerly exercised over him and his church. In accordance with the writings of our predecessor, if any matter concerning faith, crime, or money should arise against the aforesaid Hadrian, our fellow-priest, it is to be examined through those who are or shall be our representatives in the imperial city, if the question is moderate; but if it is difficult, it is to be brought here to the Apostolic See, so that it may be decided by the judgment of our hearing. But if at any time, by any occasion or subterfuge, you attempt to act contrary to these provisions which we establish, know that you are deprived of holy communion; and we decree that, except at the final hour of your life, you may not receive it unless by an order granted by the Roman Pontiff.” [Note: [Col. 1011] *city*: added in the same editions.—[Col. 1011] *to his church*: Basle edition.—*after contempt of the admonition*: collected editions except the first Basle, in which *contempt* is absent, as in Anselm.—*predecessor*: Basle and Lyons II–III.—[Col. 1011] *after*: Basle.—*writing*: same.—*could arise*: same; Ivo, Decree, Part IV, c. 205.] [Note: [Col. 1012D] *Receive*: At this point the letter inserts the chapter *Hac consona*, below, 25, question 1.]

And shortly afterward: § 3. “Let your Fraternity restore to him without any delay the sacred property, as well as the other movable and immovable property, of his church which you are said hitherto to retain. We append to this letter the inventory of it submitted to us. If any dispute concerning these things is pending between you, we wish it to be argued before our representative in the imperial city.” [Note: [Col. 1011] *or immovable*: Basle edition.]

Gratian. But if those places have not yet been assigned within the diocese of any bishop, let them receive a bishop of their own by the authority of the Apostolic See.

Accordingly the younger Gregory writes to Bishop Boniface, in his final epistle: [Note: [Col. 1011] Rather, Gregory III, c. A.D. 738.]

C. LIII. Where the multitude of believers has increased, bishops are to be ordained.

We command that, according to the decrees of the sacred canons, where the multitude of believers has increased, you ought, by the authority of the Apostolic See, to ordain bishops; yet with pious consideration, so that the dignity of the episcopate may not be cheapened. [Note: [Col. 1011] *you ought*: “you ought [plural],” Pithou edition.]

Gratian. Just as two bishoprics can be reduced to one in the manner described above, and one can be divided into two, so also a bishop may establish baptismal and parish churches with the consent of his clergy. When this has been done, that part of the people which is placed under the new churches is released from the jurisdiction of the former church. Unless this could be done, a multitude of churches would be reduced to scarcity. But he cannot establish several baptismal churches within one territorial boundary.

Accordingly, the following is read in the Council of Toledo: [Note: [Col. 1013C] This chapter is found in no Council of Toledo. Burchard and Ivo cite it from the Council of Aachen.] [Note: [Col. 1013] Chapter of uncertain origin.—Burchard, Book III, c. 22. Ivo, Decree, Part III, c. 27.]

C. LIV. There cannot be several baptismal churches within one territorial boundary.

There cannot be several baptismal churches within one territorial boundary, but only one with its dependent chapels. And if there is a dispute concerning the boundary between two mother churches, let the congregations of both distinguish it; and if they do not agree, let the dispute be settled by the judgment of God. [Note: [Col. 1013] *subjects*: Burchard, Ivo.—*let it be distinguished*: Ivo.—*they agree*: Basle edition.—*let it be decreed*: same.]

[Col. 1013B] Part VI. Gratian. Therefore the right of churches must be interpreted thus: unless, by the bishop’s arrangement, something has been assigned to other churches, they are to suffer no diminution at all of their former revenues.

Accordingly Pope Anastasius [Note: [Col. 1013] Rather, Capitulary of the Kings of the Franks, Book VII, c. 7, from the Council of Gangra, canon 7; cited by Regino, Book II, c. 286; Burchard, Book III, c. 144 and Book XI, c. 21; Ivo, Decree, Part III, c. 209 and Part XIV, c. 91.—The heading itself is repeated from Anselm, Book V, c. 46 (45).]:

C. LV. Let him be deprived of communion who wishes to retain tithes or offerings without the bishop’s knowledge.

We decree that if anyone seeks to retain offerings to the church, or tithes which the people ought to give, or wishes to give them outside the baptismal church without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person entrusted with such duties, and refuses to act with their counsel, let him pay our ban and be deprived of communion. [Note: [Col. 1013] *ban—pay*: absent in Anselm.]

Gratian. When it adds, “without the bishop’s knowledge,” it leaves us to understand that, with the bishop’s consent, they may be given to other churches.

C. LVI. Tithes are to be distributed according to the bishop’s arrangement. Likewise. [Note: [Col. 1013] Rather, from the Council of Pavia, held A.D. 855.—Anselm, Book V, c. 46.]

It is laid down in the sacred canons that tithes are to be distributed according to the bishop’s arrangement. But certain laymen who have basilicas either on their own estates or as benefices, disregarding the bishop’s arrangement, give their tithes not to the churches in which they receive baptism, preaching, laying on of hands, and the other sacraments of Christ, but bestow them at their own discretion either upon their own basilicas or upon other churches. [Note: [Col. 1013D] *Other churches*: In the Council of Pavia, from which this chapter appears to have been taken, the reading is “their own clerics”; in Anselm, “their own churches.”] This is plainly contrary in every respect to divine law and the sacred canons. Therefore we request your authority to correct them. [Note: [Col. 1013D] *Therefore we request your*: These words are addressed to Emperor Louis II, who attended that synod. The council therefore continues: “The sacred [law] teaches,” etc.]

Gratian. Since they are reproved for doing this in disregard of the bishop’s arrangement, it is understood that, if they do it at the bishop’s direction, they are found blameless.

C. LVII. Let those who wish to distribute tithes and offerings without the bishop’s knowledge be anathema. Likewise Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said in the sixth Roman Synod. [Note: [Col. 1013] Held A.D. 504.—Anselm, Book V, c. 44 (48). Deusdedit, Part IV.]

In the canons established by apostolic authority in the Church of Gangra, it is written concerning offerings of produce owed to ministers of the Church, and those bestowed for the use of the poor: “If anyone wishes to receive or give offerings of the Church without the bishop’s knowledge, or without the knowledge of the person entrusted with such duties, and refuses to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.” [Note: [Col. 1013] Cf. the collections cited under c. 55.] [Note: [Col. 1014D] *Offerings of the Church*: In the Council of Gangra itself the reading is: “If anyone wishes to receive offerings of the Church outside the church,” etc.]

And again in the same Council of Gangra: “If anyone gives or receives things offered to God apart from the bishop, or apart from the one appointed by him to administer mercy to the poor, let both the giver and receiver be anathema.” [Note: [Col. 1013] Burchard, Book III, c. 145. Ivo, Decree, Part III, c. 210.—*offerings*: Anselm.—*of the bishop*: Lyons II–III.—“or with his consent”: Basle and Lyons II–III; “or with his counsel”: the remaining editions.]

§ 1. It is therefore utterly unjust and a great sacrilege that anything which anyone has contributed or certainly left to the venerable Church for the remission of sins, salvation, or the repose of their souls should be transferred or diverted to another purpose by those especially bound to preserve it—that is, Christians and God-fearing persons—and above all by rulers and the chief persons of the regions. [Note: [Col. 1013] *that is*: absent in the collected editions except the first Basle and Lyons II–III.]

And below: § 2. “In general, whoever presumes by dangerous assault to confiscate, claim, or seize the property of the Church, unless he most promptly corrects himself by making satisfaction to the church in question, let him be struck with perpetual anathema.” [Note: [Col. 1013] Ivo, Decree, Part III, c. 148.] [Note: [Col. 1014D] *Unless he*: These words through the phrase “Likewise” are added from the Synod of Symmachus [ [Col. 1013] absent in Anselm.].]

§ 3. Likewise, those who retain Church property by command or gift of rulers or certain powerful persons, or by some invasion or tyrannical power, and who leave it to their children or heirs as though hereditary—as we have heard has already been done by some—unless, having been admonished by the pontiff and having acknowledged the truth, they quickly restore God’s property, let them be struck with perpetual anathema. For we judge it unjust that we should be considered guardians of charters rather than defenders of entrusted property, as has been commanded. And below: § 4. “Wounds which do not respond to remedies must be cut away with the sword.” § 5. Likewise, those who are not corrected by priestly admonition ought to be excluded from the Church, as the Lord says: “Remove the evil from among you.” [Note: [Col. 1015] 1 Corinthians 5:13.]

The entire synod rose and cried out: “We ask that this be done.” This was said eight times. “We ask that these things be observed.” This was said ten times. “May they remain for ever and be confirmed by your authority.” This was said twelve times. [Note: [Col. 1015B] *We ask that these things be observed*: Likewise, these words through the phrase “Hear us” are supplied.] “Hear us, Christ; life to Pope Symmachus.” This was said twelve times. [Note: [Col. 1015] *may there be*: added in the collected editions.—Böhm.—C. LVIII.]

C. LVIII. Those who seize Church property and the goods of bishops are punished by the same penalty. Likewise in the same Synod. [Note: [Col. 1015] Ivo, Decree, Part III, c. 148.]

Likewise, we judge that this should, through the exhortation and judgment of you all, come to the notice of all churches and be firmly observed by everyone: since the property of bishops is unquestionably Church property, if anyone has ravaged their possessions with similar cruelty, let the invaders of the aforesaid property be struck by the punishment prescribed in the canons, so that those who are not corrected by their own morals and no rebuke of conscience may at least be pierced by the stings of ecclesiastical and canonical punishment. [Note: [Col. 1015] *these*: Basle edition.—*ecclesiastical*: added there.—“let them be struck by the aforesaid strictness of the canons”: Ivo; and the collected editions, omitting *canons*.—*may be corrected*: Basle.—C. LIX.]

C. LIX. Church property cannot be distributed by the authority of rulers. Likewise from Book I of the Capitularies of the Emperors Charles and Louis, c. 83. [Note: [Col. 1015] Capitulary I, A.D. 803, c. 1; Book I, c. 77.—Anselm, Book V, c. 43 (37).—Thus in the collected editions except the first Basle.]

Since, in accordance with the tradition of the holy Fathers, we know that Church property is the offering of the faithful, the price of sins, and the patrimony of the poor, we desire not only to preserve for each person what he possesses, but also, with God’s help, to confer much. [Note: [Col. 1015B] *Ecclesiastical*: The word “offices” followed [ [Col. 1015] and in Anselm], but it occurs neither in the ancient copies nor in the Capitular itself. For it refers to persons, not offices.]

But that we might remove from ecclesiastical persons the long-entertained suspicion concerning the division of Church property, we decree that during the times neither of ourselves nor of our children nor, by God’s dispensation, of our successors—who may wish to imitate our will or the example of our forebears—Church property shall suffer any division or loss whatever. [Note: [Col. 1015B] *division*: The printed Capitular reads “not [Col. 1015C] dividing [lacuna].” But the manuscript capitularies sent to King Louis by the bishops of the provinces of Rheims and Rouen contain the following relevant passage:

“Because Charles, prince and father of King Pippin, who first among all the kings and princes of the Franks separated and divided the property of churches, was above all eternally lost for this act alone. For Saint Eucherius, bishop of Orléans, who rests in the monastery of Saint Trudo, while at prayer was caught up into the other world; and among the other things which he saw, the Lord showing them to him, he saw Charles tormented in the lowest hell. When he asked the angel who was his guide, he was answered that by the judgment of the saints who shall judge with the Lord in the future judgment, because he had taken and divided the property of whomever he had despoiled, he was assigned, before that judgment, to everlasting punishments in soul and body; and together with his own sins he received punishments for the sins of all who, in honour and love of the Lord, had committed their property and possessions to holy places for the redemption of their souls, for the lights of divine worship and for the support of Christ’s servants and the poor.

“When he returned to himself, he summoned Saint Boniface and Fulrad, abbot of the monastery of Saint Denis and chief chaplain of King Pippin. Telling them these things, he gave them a sign: they were to go to Charles’s tomb, and, if they did not find his body there, they were to believe that what he said was true. They went to the aforesaid monastery, where Charles’s body had been buried; when they opened his tomb, a dragon was suddenly seen to come out, and the whole interior of the tomb was found blackened, as though it had been burned. We ourselves saw men who survived to our own age, who were present at this event and truthfully testified to us by living voice what they had heard and seen.

“When his son Pippin learned this, he caused a synod to be assembled at Liptinae, over which Gregory, legate of the Apostolic See, presided together with Saint Boniface. For we possess the synod itself, and Pippin arranged, insofar as he could, to restore to the churches the ecclesiastical property which your father had taken away. Since he could not restore the property to the churches from which it had been taken because of the conflict which he had with Waifar, prince of the Aquitanians, he asked the bishops to grant precarial leases from it. Until the property should return to the Church, he decreed that ninths and tithes for the restoration of the lands, and twelve denarii from every holding, should be paid to the church from which the property had been granted as a benefice, as is contained in the book of royal capitularies. Hence Lord Emperor Charles, while he still bore the royal title, issued an edict that neither he nor his sons nor his successors should attempt such acts. He confirmed it with his own hand; we possess the text in full, and anyone who has and wishes to read that book can find an excerpt of the chapter in his book of capitularies. We also have this account in writing, and some of us have heard your father, Lord Emperor Louis, relate it orally. Mention of this history is also made in the Life of Blessed Eucherius, bishop of Orléans, and of Blessed Rigobert, archbishop of Rheims.

“What such a division of ecclesiastical goods was like—the one introduced by Charles Martel but forbidden by Pippin and Emperor Charles—is explained thus in the same first book of Capitularies, before this chapter 83: ‘In the time of Pope Hadrian and Emperor Charles the Great, when Bishop Paulinus acted as representative of the Apostolic See, this chapter was enacted at Aachen, because laymen used to divide bishoprics and monasteries for their own benefit; and nothing would have remained to any bishop, abbot, or abbess except enough for them to live as canons and monks.’”] [Note: [Col. 1015] *entirely*: added in the original and collected editions.—*we may remove*: “we remove,” collected editions.—[Col. 1017] *shall suffer*: “shall suffer [plural],” original and collected editions.]

Gratian. Since, therefore, everyone is forbidden to distribute Church offerings without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person entrusted with such duties, it is plainly evident that they can be distributed to any churches with the bishop’s consent.

§ 1. That authority of the Fourth Council of Toledo, c. 32, seems contrary to this interpretation: [Note: [Col. 1017] Held A.D. 633.—Burchard, Book III, c. 203. Ivo, Decree, Part III, c. 255. Abbo of Fleury in Mabillon, *Vetera Analecta*, c. 35.]

C. LX. Let bishops presume to take nothing from the right of the diocese.

It has been decreed by the present council that bishops should govern their dioceses in such a way that they presume to take nothing from their legal right, but, in accordance with the authority of earlier councils, receive a third part from offerings, tributes, and produce. If they presume anything further, it is to be restored through a council, upon the appeal either of the founders themselves or certainly of their relatives, if the founders have already departed from this world. [Note: [Col. 1017] *from*: absent in Basle.—*earlier*: “former,” Norimberga edition.—*councils*: absent in the Argentinensis and Norimberga editions.—“tithes and tributes”: Burchard, Ivo.—*they shall receive*: Basle.—*anything further*: absent there.—*has been presumed*: “has been,” there; Ivo.—*departed*: collected editions.]

C. LXI. No one may alienate property left to the Church. Likewise Pope Symmachus to his brother Caesarius, c. 1. [Note: [Col. 1017] Written A.D. 502.—Anselm, Book V, c. 47 (51). Polyc. Book III, title 12.]

We do not permit possessions which anyone has given or left to a church by his own decision to be alienated under any titles or forms of sale, or under any pretext whatsoever, except perhaps to clerics in recognition of worthy merits, to monasteries for religious purposes, or indeed to strangers when necessity advises generosity—provided, however, that they enjoy these things not permanently but temporarily. [Note: [Col. 1017] *from his own*: Basle.—*to alienate*: Hisp. Collection and collected editions except Lyons II–III.—*or*: collected editions.—“honourable merits”: Hisp. Collection; “good in recognition of merits”: Argentinensis, Norimberga, Venice I–II.]

Gratian. But the provision of the Council of Toledo must be understood thus: bishops are to take nothing beyond the fourth or third part due to them according to the differing local customs.

Accordingly, it was decreed in the Council of Pope Leo IV, c. 26: [Note: [Col. 1017] In the Council of Eugenius II, held A.D. 826, and of Leo IV, held A.D. 853.—Anselm, Book VI, c. 166 (171). Polyc. Book IV, title 21.]

C. LXII. A bishop shall exact nothing from clerics and pious places beyond the statutes of the Fathers.

No bishop may exact from a priest subject to him, from any other cleric, or from pious places payments beyond the statutes of the Fathers, or impose additional compulsory services. But, since he ought to be an excellent provider, let him provide in such a way that all the sheep entrusted to him are especially fed and assisted by him in their necessities, and are not oppressed by unlawful exactions; for the Lord taught us to feed and instruct and minister to all, not to delight in earthly gains or avarice. [Note: [Col. 1017] *imposed*: “placed under,” collected editions except the first Basle.—*provider*: “overseer,” original.—*let him provide*: “let him perceive,” editions and collected editions except Lyons II–III.—“exacted payments”: original; Anselm.—*or*: “and,” collected editions.]

C. LXIII. A fourth part of Church revenues is to be distributed to clerics. Likewise Gregory to Leo, bishop of the Catanian people, [Note: [Col. 1017] Epistle 7, written A.D. 598, Book VIII, Maurist edition.—Anselm, Book V, c. 67 (68). Abbo of Fleury, c. 35.—“bishop of Carthage”: collected editions except the first Basle.] Book VII, epistle 8.

[Col. 1018B] The order of reason has distinguished ranks of places and established jurisdictions for this purpose: that superiors may not needlessly exert themselves to oppress their subjects, nor subjects in turn have unrestrained licence to resist their superiors. And below: § 1. Therefore we wish that whatever may perhaps accrue to your church from revenue or any other title, you should set aside from it a fourth portion without any diminution, and distribute it with discernment, as seems proper to you, among the priests, deacons, and clergy in the fear of God. [Note: [Col. 1017] *distinguished*: “distributed,” Basle.—*strive or exert themselves*: same.—*or from*: Basle and Lyons II–III.—“that a fourth”: same.]

C. LXIV. A bishop ought to exact nothing from his monks or clerics for the sake of shameful gain. Likewise from the Seventh Synod, c. 4. [Note: [Col. 1017C] This chapter was formerly cited from the Sixth Synod. It belongs, however, to the Seventh, in Anastasius’s translation; from that translation some things have here been added, removed, and corrected.] [Note: [Col. 1017] Held A.D. 787.—Anastasian translation.—Anselm, Book VI, c. 167 (173).—In the Basle edition it is cited from Synod IX; in the others, from VI.]

[Col. 1018C] Paul, the divine Apostle and preacher of truth, as though establishing a canon for the presbyters of Ephesus—indeed, for all the sacred multitude—declared with confidence: “I coveted no one’s silver or gold or clothing. I showed you all things: that by labouring thus we must support the weak, considering it more blessed to give than to receive.” [Note: [Col. 1017] *church*: collected editions; cf. Acts 20.—*fullness* (Greek: πληρώματι, “fullness”): Anselm; “multitude and sacred fullness”: collected editions.—“You yourselves know that this hand supplied what was necessary for me and those with me”: Venice I–II, Paris, Lyons.—*considering*: “considering [plural],” original.]

Therefore, instructed by him, we decree that a bishop must never, for the sake of shameful gain, devise excuses for sins in order to demand gold, silver, or another form of payment from bishops, clerics, or monks subject to him. [Note: [Col. 1017] *instructed*: “taught,” collected editions.—*we decree*: “we have decreed,” the same except Basle, Paris, and Lyons.] [Note: [Col. 1017C–1018C] *Devise*: The Greek words, ὁρίζομεν, μὴ ὅλως αἰσχροκερδῶς ἐπινοεῖσθαι ἐπίσκοπον προφασιζόμενον προφάσεις ἐν ἁμαρτίαις, ἀπαιτεῖν χρυσόν, would be translated more clearly: “We decree that it must never enter the mind of a bishop, for the sake of shameful gain, to demand gold while making excuses for sins,” etc.]

For the Apostle says: “The unrighteous shall not possess the kingdom of God”; and children ought not to lay up treasure for their parents, but parents for their children. [Note: [Col. 1019] *from priests*: absent in Anselm; “from presbyters,” collected editions.—1 Corinthians 6:10; 2 Corinthians 12:14.—*not*: Anselm, which also lacks the immediately preceding words; collected editions.]

And below: “For Peter, chief of the Apostles, also commanded: ‘Feed the flock of God which is among you, not under compulsion but willingly according to God; not for the sake of shameful gain, but voluntarily; nor as lording it over the allotted portions, but becoming an example to the flock. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you shall receive the unfading crown of glory.’” [Note: [Col. 1019] “And the Apostle Peter”: Anselm and collected editions; cf. 1 Peter 5:2.—*willingly*: “of one willing,” Basle; “of one’s own accord,” remaining editions.—*but voluntarily*: retained in the cited text.—*allotted portions*: “clergy,” collected editions and Anselm.—“from the heart”: Basle and Lyons.—*unfading*: “unfading [nominative],” collected editions.]

Gratian. But the clause placed at the end of Symmachus’s chapter—“provided that they enjoy these things not permanently but temporarily”—must be referred only to personal possessions, namely those of clerics and the poor, and not to monastic possessions.

Part VII. § 1. How serious it is before God not to pay tithes, offerings, and firstfruits to priests is evident from the authority of Jerome and Augustine.

For Jerome says in his commentary on Malachi, chapter 3:

C. LXV. One who does not pay tithes to priests is held guilty before God.

“‘Return to me, and I will return to you,’ says the Lord of hosts. ‘But you said, “In what shall we return?” Shall a man pierce God? For you pierce me. And you said, “In what do we pierce you?” In tithes and firstfruits. You are cursed with want, and you pierce me, the whole nation.’” [Note: [Col. 1019] Malachi 3:7 ff.—*I*: added in the collected editions.—*rob*: “afflict,” Basle and Böhm; “afflicts,” Paris and Lyons II–III; “would afflict,” the remaining editions.—*you rob*: “you afflict,” Basle; “you contend,” Lyons I–II; “you contend,” the remaining editions except Paris.—*we rob*: “we contend,” collected editions except Paris and Lyons III.—“and therefore in”: Argentinensis; “and so in”: remaining editions.—*you rob*: “you contend,” collected editions except Paris and Lyons III.]

Let us now follow the order of the prophecy: “Because you have not rendered tithes and firstfruits to me, therefore you are cursed with famine and want; and you supplant me, or defraud me, and deprive me—the whole nation.” [Note: [Col. 1019] *prophecy*: “prophet,” collected editions.—“you have supplanted, defrauded”: the same editions.] [Note: [Col. 1019C] *For nation*: These words through “Behold, a year” are added from Blessed Jerome to complete the sense.] In place of *nation*, which is written in Hebrew [the Hebrew word is omitted in the supplied text], the Septuagint translated *year*, ἔτος, for *nation*, ἔθνος; and this is the meaning:

“Behold, a year has passed, and you have carried nothing into my treasuries, but into your own storehouses. And in exchange for tithes and firstfruits, which would have been a small thing if you had given them, you have lost the abundance of your possessions and every plenty of crops. But so that you may know that this has happened through my anger, because you have defrauded me of my portion, I exhort and admonish you to bring tithes into the storehouses—that is, into the treasuries of the Temple—so that the priests and Levites who minister to me may have food. Test me, whether I shall not pour out such rains that the floodgates of heaven may seem opened, and pour out blessing upon you unto abundance.”

The term “pouring out” indicates generosity. Yet it may happen that, while rains irrigate the fields and there is indeed fertility, a locust, a beetle, blight, or caterpillar may destroy them, and human labour may perish. Therefore he adds and says: “And I shall rebuke for your sake the devourer”—that is, the locust and the other things we have mentioned—“and it shall not destroy the fruit of your land.” [Note: [Col. 1019] *year*: “has passed,” Basle.—*if*: “as,” collected editions.—*you*: “we,” Basle.—*this*: “that,” Basle and Lyons.—*you defrauded*: “you defraud,” Basle.—*my*: added in the collected editions.—*minister*: “may minister,” Argentinensis and Basle.—*may come*: Lyons II–III; “will come,” remaining editions.—*may destroy*: “will lay waste,” collected editions.—*adds*: “adds afterward,” Basle and Lyons II–III; “joins,” remaining editions.—“devouring locusts”: collected editions.]

(And below:) § 1. Whenever famine, want, and the scarcity of all things oppress the world, let us know that this descends from God’s wrath. In the poor, if they do not receive alms, he says that he is defrauded and deprived of his own portion; and we may interpret his possessions as tithes and firstfruits. [Note: [Col. 1019] *oppress*: “oppresses,” the same editions.] [Note: [Col. 1019C–1020C] *And his*: The original reads: “he says that he is defrauded and deprived of his own portion. We may also interpret tithes and firstfruits in this way.” It was not altered because of the gloss; some other matters, however, have been corrected.]

§ 2. If anyone learned and educated in the law of God is able to instruct others, he ought not to ascribe what he possesses to his own prudence and talent, but should first give thanks to God, who bestows all things, and then to his priests and teachers from whom he has learned. For if he does not give thanks but claims knowledge for himself, he shall be cursed with want. But if, understanding that God is the giver and giving thanks to those through whom he has been taught by God, he humbles himself and brings food into God’s storehouse—that is, ministers in the Church to the people the nourishment of Holy Scripture—then at once the floodgates of heaven shall be opened over him, spiritual rain shall be poured out, and God shall command his clouds to rain upon him; and he shall enjoy abundance in all things. [Note: [Col. 1019] *others*: “the rest,” the same editions.—*teachers*: “ministers,” the same editions.—*for himself*: “for God,” Basle.—*God’s*: “the Lord’s,” same.]

C. LXVI. That tithes are to be handed over to priests. Likewise Augustine, Sermon CCXIX, *On the Seasons*. [Note: [Col. 1020C–D] This chapter has been composed from passages of Blessed Augustine in Sermon 219—the first sermon for the twelfth Sunday after the feast of the Trinity—with the sequence and often the wording altered; it occurs in the same manner in Anselm.] [Note: [Col. 1019] A sermon whose authority is not sufficiently certain, in the judgment of the Maurists.—Anselm, Book V, c. 34.]

Tithes are the dues of needy souls. If [Col. 1021A] you give tithes [Note: “a tithe”: the editions compared with the original], you will receive not only an abundance of crops, but will also obtain health [Note: “salvation”: Basel edition] of body and soul. Therefore the Lord God asks not for a reward, but for honour. For our God, who deigned to give everything, has deigned to receive a tenth from us [Note: “accept”: Anselm], not for himself, but undoubtedly for our benefit. But if it is a sin to give slowly, how much [Note: “how much more grievous—a sin”: Anselm and the editions compared with the original Basel edition, in which the word “more grievous” is absent] worse is it not to have given at all? From military service, trade, and craft, pay tithes. For since by giving tithes you can merit both earthly and heavenly rewards, why [Note: omitted in Anselm and the Argentinian and Basel editions] are you, through avarice, deprived of a twofold [Note: “deprived of a double blessing”: Anselm; Basel edition] blessing? For this is the most just custom of God [Note: “the Lord”: Basel edition]: if you do not give him a tenth, you will be reduced to a tenth. You will give to an impious soldier what you refuse to give to a priest. God is always ready to do good [Col. 1021B], but is hindered by human wickedness. For tithes are demanded as a debt [Note: “sought out”: ibid.], and whoever refuses to give them [Note: “refuse … invade”: Anselm; editions compared with the original] has invaded another’s property. And however many poor people, in the places where he lives, have died of hunger because he did not give tithes, he will appear before the tribunal of the eternal Judge guilty of just so many murders, because he reserved for his own use property assigned by God to the poor. Therefore, whoever desires either to procure a reward for himself or to merit forgiveness of sins should pay a tenth; from the remaining nine parts he should also strive to give alms [Note: “perform”: Basel edition] to the poor.

### Chapter LXVII. He who withholds necessities from those preaching the Gospel condemns himself.

Likewise Jerome, in his Commentary on chapter 3 of the Epistle to Titus, at the end.

[Col. 1021C] To refuse to supply the apostolic men and preachers of Christ with necessities for their use is to condemn oneself to *sterility*.

That tithes may lawfully be granted to monks with the bishop’s consent, Blessed Jerome writes to Pope Damasus, saying [Note: Above also, 1, question 2, *Clericos*. A portion of this chapter is cited as from Blessed Jerome, in whose extant writings nothing of this kind has been found.] [Note: The chapter is uncertain.]

### Chapter LXVIII. Clerics are free to grant tithes to monks.

Since whatever clerics possess belongs to the poor, and their houses ought to be common to all, they must watch over the reception of travellers and guests. Above all, they must take care to expend from tithes and offerings upon monasteries and hostels whatever support they wish and are able to provide. For they are free to grant tithes, offerings, and every means of relief to monks and spiritual men who fear and worship God [Col. 1022A], and to transfer them from their own right into those men’s ownership and use, considering in the poor not so much poverty as religious devotion.

§ 1. But as to what Your Blessedness asked—whether the use of tithes and offerings may accrue to laypersons—your holiness knows that this is altogether unlawful [Note: “your”: Basel edition], as all [Note: added: “all”: Basel and Lyons editions II and III] divine authorities of the fathers’ canons attest. Therefore, if things known to belong to divine law have at some time been wrongly held by such persons, and have passed into the use of monks and servants of God, provided that the bishop of that place gives consent, all things shall remain with them, supported by perpetual firmness and stability.

§ 2. Those clerics [Note: C. 1, question 2, chapter 6] ought to be maintained from the revenues of the Church whose parents [Col. 1022B] and relatives [Note: “friends”: editions compared with the original Basel edition] provide no support [Note: added: “means of support”: editions compared with the original Argentinian edition]. But those who can be supported by their parents’ goods and resources, if they accept what belongs to the poor, undoubtedly commit [Note: “incur and commit”: editions compared with the original] sacrilege, and through the abuse of such things eat and drink judgment upon themselves.

Gratian. Concerning estates cultivated by their tenants, however, the Council of Mainz decreed as follows: “Moreover they complained,” etc., above in the same place.

## QUESTION II

## GRATIAN

**Part I.** Regarding chapels possessed by them, Pope John establishes that they are to be governed by priests through the monks’ appointment, writing to Isaac, [Col. 1022C] Bishop of Syracuse [Note: This chapter, together with others, was taken from an ancient codex of the monastery of Populetum; some passages of Gratian have been corrected from the example of this codex and from old copies.] [Note: By the judgment of nearly all interpreters, this chapter is apocryphal.]

### Chapter I. Priests are to be appointed in monastic churches by abbots.

Having seen the letters of your charity, from which it is sufficiently evident how earnestly you show reverence toward this holy see, we rejoiced greatly. Accordingly, concerning the matters on which you sought counsel, we give kindly and discerning advice to our dearest brother. For your pious gentleness has referred to us the question whether churches which, for the peace of the monks, were committed to them by holy councils and Catholic bishops should be established through priests appointed and invested by them [Note: “churches which … were committed”: Basel and Lyons editions II and III]. Your fraternity further added that from this cause no small dispute and sedition [Col. 1023A] had arisen between clerics and monks; and no one doubts that this was brought about [Note: “is brought about”: editions compared with the original] by the instigation of the crafty enemy. For he has a thousand ways of doing harm, and we are not ignorant of his wiles [Note: “wile”: the same editions]. From the beginning of his fall he strives to rend the unity of the Church, wound charity, infect the sweetness of holy works with the gall of envy, and by every means overthrow [Note: “pervert”: Basel edition] and disturb the human race. For he is greatly grieved and ashamed that steadfast human beings, made of clay, maintain on earth the charity which he could not possess in heaven. Therefore it is fitting, insofar as our frailty allows, that we fortify *most diligently* every avenue through which his cunning might harm us, lest death enter through our gates.

§ 1. Having diligently sought the counsel [Note: “council”: Basel and Lyons edition I] of many brethren, we have decreed [Note: “we decree”: editions compared with the original Argentinian and Basel editions] that henceforth churches entrusted to monks shall be established through their own priests [Col. 1023B]. For divine and secular laws provide that the appointment belongs to the person whose possession it is; and if charity was ready in giving what was greater, holy liberality should be readier in granting what is less. For it was a greater thing to give the possession than to grant the investiture. How would the owner’s rights be recognized [Note: “would be recognized … would be rendered”: Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice edition I], and the dues of his own property be rendered to him, where what is his is given through another and, whenever that other wishes, taken away? It is human nature to revere the person by whose judgment and will one is now raised up and now cast down. Hence the priest becomes readier to serve the bishop’s party, and thus the bishop draws to himself, under a kind of pretended authority, what he had given in a holy and religious manner. Thus he is deprived [Col. 1023C] of the reward he would have received [Note: “received”: editions compared with the original], both because, with feigned charity, he takes away what he had given, and because, made excessively credulous by the words of wicked priests who love quarrels and schisms and sow *lawsuits and dissensions among bishops*, he seeks, after the fraud has been exposed, to take away entirely by a kind of usurpation what he had first craftily laboured to gain [Note: “afterwards”: Basel edition]. Rejecting [Note: “perceiving”: editions compared with the original] these deceits and the crafty enemy’s persuasions, we henceforth grant all [Note: “entirely”: the same editions] monks leave to become the investitors of their own churches, provided, however, that [Col. 1024A] if they presume to act against the priesthood, they are punished by the judgment [Note: “in the judgment”: Basel edition] of a synod, and that the offences of priests are cut away by the blessed sword of the bishop [Note: omitted there].

**Part II. Gratian.** By this authority the investiture of their own churches is granted to monks. Yet Pope Urban II seems to say the contrary, declaring [Note: After these words, manuscripts in which the *Paleae* are absent continue with chapter *Sane*. In the four *Paleae* inserted here nothing concerns monks. This preceding material occurs in the Council of Mainz, book/chapter 38, and the ruling is repeated in book/chapter 10 and in III, chapter 17.] [Note: Chapter 38, Council of Mainz, held A.D. 813; *Capitularies*, book 5, chapter 154; Burchard, book 3, chapter 131; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 57; *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 197.]

### Chapter II. PALEA

“We admonish and command that the giving [Note: “to give”: Burchard, Ivo, *Decretum*; editions compared with the original] of tithes to God, which God himself ordained to be given [Note: “to give”: Ivo, *Panormia*; editions compared with the original Lyons editions II and III], must not be neglected [Note: “they neglect”: editions compared with the original]. For one must fear lest anyone [Note: “who”: editions compared with the original Basel edition] who withholds from God what is due to him [Note: “has not rendered”: Basel edition; “shall have withheld”: Ivo, *Panormia*], perhaps, because of his own sin [Note: “on account of what is due to him”: Basel and Lyons editions II and III; in the remaining editions simply: “lest he take from him his necessities”], God may take away his necessities.”

### Chapter III. On the same subject. PALEA.

Likewise Pope Nicholas II, sole epistle, chapter 5 [Note: Held A.D. 1059; Anselm, end of book 8; cf. D. 32, chapter 6, final section.]

[Col. 1024B] “We command that tithes [Note: “and tithes”: editions compared with the original Basel and Lyons editions II and III], firstfruits, and offerings [Note: added: “of whatever kind”: editions compared with the original] of the living and the dead be faithfully rendered by laypersons to the churches [Note: “and churches”: Basel edition] of God, and that [Note: “not”: ibid.] they be at the disposal of bishops [Note: added: “to be distributed according to the canons”: editions compared with the original]. Those who retain them [Note: “whoever retains [them], let him be deprived of, or separated from, holy communion”: editions compared with the original] shall be separated from communion with the holy *Church*.”

### Chapter IV. On the same subject. PALEA.

Likewise Pope Leo [Note: These words are found in the synodal admonition prefixed to Burchard, no. 45.]

“No one may receive tithes belonging to another.”

### Chapter V. PALEA.

Likewise Ambrose, Sermon I on Lent [Note: It occurs in Sermon I on Lent, which begins *Ecce nunc* (“Behold, now”), preserved together with other sermons not bearing the name of Blessed Ambrose in the Vatican Library and in the library of the Milanese monastery of that same Blessed Ambrose.] [Note: The Maurists judged this sermon not to be by St Ambrose.]

“For a person who refuses to render to God the tithes he has retained [Note: “held”: editions compared with the original], and does not endeavour to restore to another person what he has unjustly taken *from him*, still does not fear God and [Col. 1024C] does not know what true repentance and true confession are [Note: “what things”: the same editions]. Such a *person* cannot perform true [Note: “good”: original; Argentinian edition] almsgiving.”

### Chapter VI. Abbots are not to appoint priests in parish churches without the bishop’s counsel.

Likewise Urban II [Note: Chapter 4, Council of Clermont, held A.D. 1095; Anselm, end of book 8.]

Since certain monks strive to take away from bishops their right, we decree that they shall not install priests in parish churches which they hold without the counsel [Note: “council”: Basel edition] of bishops. Rather, bishops [Col. 1025A] shall entrust the care of the parish to a priest with the consent of the abbots, so that such priests may render account to bishops concerning the care of the people, while to the abbot they show due subjection regarding temporal matters belonging to the monastery; and thus the rights of each may be preserved. Likewise:

§ 1. In parish churches priests are to be appointed [Note: “constituted”: ibid.] by bishops, to answer to them regarding the care of souls and matters belonging to the bishop.

### Chapter VII. Churches of monks, of whatever sort, are subject to episcopal government.

Likewise from a council held at Faenza [Note: An uncertain chapter, perhaps to be referred to the Council of Piacenza under Urban II.]

We must decree [Note: omitted in the Basel edition] that the churches of monks of whatever kind, situated in individual parishes, be subject, as is fitting, to the divinely ordained government of bishops, [Col. 1025B] and render them the obedience due.

Gratian. See: Pope Urban prohibits monks from making investitures of parish churches, although Pope John granted this to them. But John’s ruling should be understood of those chapels which bishops grant to monks together with every right belonging to them. Urban’s ruling, however, is to be understood of those which abbots build on their own estates, in their villages or castles.

## QUESTION V

[Note: It appears contrary to the order of the work that the fifth question is placed between the second and third questions. In all ancient copies except two very old ones, all these canons which make up the fifth question occur in the second question; then the third and fourth questions follow with their chapters, as in the received codices; then Gratian’s words which in the received texts stand at the beginning of the sixth question, together with chapter *Consuetudo*, make up the fifth question, while the rest make up the sixth. Yet that the question now under discussion is the fifth is evident from the proposition made at the beginning of the cause. Gratian may have altered the order here because the argument of the fifth question [Col. 1026C] is very closely connected with matters brought forward at the end of the second. For this reason, and further because of the authority of those two codices and the accepted practice of citing these canons under the fifth question, it was thought that nothing should be changed.]

## GRATIAN

Such persons, even if they have territorial rights, nevertheless lack the authority to govern the people and administer spiritual matters. This is also to be understood concerning a bishop.

[Col. 1025C] Accordingly Pope Nicholas says [Note: Anselm cites from the Council of Orange, chapter 10, where nearly the same words occur.] [Note: Chapter 10, Council of Orange, held A.D. 441, abridged; in Anselm, book 5, chapter 9, from which the Correctors cite it, it was not found.]

### Chapter I. A bishop who builds a church in another’s diocese cannot claim its consecration for himself.

If any bishop, for any need of his own, proposes to build a church in the territory of another city, he must not presume to perform the dedication, [Col. 1026A] which belongs to the bishop in whose territory the church is erected. But to the bishop who builds it let this favour be reserved: the bishop whose territory it is shall ordain those clerics whom the builder wishes to be ordained on his property, or, if they have already been ordained, the building bishop shall be content to have them [Note: “bishops”: Basel edition]; and the whole governance of that church shall belong to him in whose city’s territory the church arose [Note: “shall arise”: ibid.].

### Chapter II. Newly founded basilicas belong to the bishop whose district they are shown to be.

Likewise from the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 34 [Note: Canon 34 of the Fourth Council of Toledo reads: “Just as thirty years’ possession removes another’s diocese, so it does not take away the district of a territory,” etc.; as below, same question, chapter 3.] [Note: Held A.D. 633; Burchard, book 3, chapter 147; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 212; cf. below, question 3, chapter 3.]

Possession of territory does not take away its district; therefore basilicas which are newly [Note: “new”: *Collectio Hispana*; the cited collections; editions compared with the original; Böhm] founded will undoubtedly belong to the bishop whose district they are shown to be.

[Col. 1026B] ### Chapter III. A bishop who builds a church in another’s diocese may not consecrate it.

Likewise Gregory, book XI, epistle 19, to John the Subdeacon [Note: Epistle 17, written A.D. 603, book 13, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 5, chapter 27 [28]; *Polycarpus*, book 1, title 13.]

John, the bearer of this letter, our brother and fellow bishop [Note: *Noster* (“our”): at this point many words are inserted in the epistle itself], has informed us that a certain Bishop Exsuperantius, in reckless presumption, built an oratory in his diocese and presumed, contrary to custom and without authorization from a mandate, to dedicate it [Note: “that [oratory]”; Basel edition; “the same [oratory]”: the other editions], and did not fear to celebrate *public* [Note: omitted in Anselm] masses there. You must correct this matter with the utmost [Note: omitted in editions compared with the original Venice edition II] promptness and strictness, and not permit any such attempt further.

Gratian. This is to be understood of the right of ordaining, not of possessing. From these authorities it may readily be perceived [Col. 1026C] that, whether abbots or bishops build churches in their castles or villages, this does not deprive the bishop in whose diocese they stand of the district; and therefore, according to the provisions of Urban and Nicholas, priests may be ordained in them only by bishops, although with the consent and election of those who built them.

## QUESTION III

[Col. 1027A]

## GRATIAN

**Part I.** That every right is extinguished by prescription of time is proved by the authority of the Council of Chalcedon, Pope Gelasius, and the Council of Toledo. The first is this [Note: This chapter is from the ancient translation contained in Isidore’s collection; it has been corrected from that translation by collation with two Vatican codices of the same collection.] [Note: Held A.D. 451; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 64; *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 106; Burchard, book 3, chapter 148, from Dionysius; *Polycarpus*, book 3, title 12.]

### Chapter I. Rural parishes are to remain undisturbed with bishops who have possessed them without violence for thirty years.

In each church [Note: *Ecclesias* (“churches”): in Balsamon’s manuscripts one reads καθ’ ἑκάστην ἐπαρχίαν, that is, “in every province.” But in the commonly received Greek canon: καθ’ ἑκάστην ἐκκλησίαν, “in each church.”] [Note: added: “of the provinces”: Argentinian and Nuremberg editions], we decree that rural parishes, *or those in possessions* [Note: “or those in possessions”: in Greek, ἀγροικικὰς παροικίας, ἢ τὰς ἐγχωρίους, that is, “parishes in the countryside, or those in villages and hamlets”], shall remain [Note: “remain permanently”: *Collectio Hispana*; editions compared with the original] undisturbed with the bishops who retain [Note: “hold”: the same collection and editions] them, especially if they have governed them, *already holding them*, without violence for thirty years. [Note: “have governed”: ibid.] But if within thirty years a dispute [Note: added: “also”: ibid.] has arisen or arises concerning them [Col. 1027B], those who say that they have been injured concerning them [Note: “therefore”: editions compared with the original] may bring the dispute before the synod of the province.

### Chapter II. Dioceses possessed by bishops for thirty years are to remain undisturbed.

Likewise Gelasius, Epistle II to the Sicilians, chapter 1 [Note: Written A.D. 494; cf., however, C. 13, question 2, chapter 1; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 147.]

The authority of our predecessors has laid down that bishops have the power to administer the resources of the Church, provided that they must distribute stipends to widows, orphans, and the poor, and also to clerics. We have also decreed [Note: omitted in the *Collectio Hispana*, Ivo’s *Decretum*, and the Basel edition] that this be given to them, as has hitherto been decreed; bishops shall claim the remainder for themselves, so that [Note: “so that not”: Basel edition], as we said before, they may be benefactors of strangers and captives.

[Col. 1027C] Likewise, ibid., chapter 2. [Note: “Gelasius II”: editions compared with the original Basel edition; cf. C. 13, question 2, chapter 1.]

§ It has also pleased us to add that, if—God forbid—the resources of the Church and also dioceses [Col. 1028A] [Note: “and dioceses which”: *Collectio Hispana*] are possessed by any bishops, they may claim as their right what the law of thirty years has settled; for the authority of our sons the princes has also issued to this effect [Note: added: “etc.”: Basel edition].

### Chapter III. Possession of territory does not take away its district.

Likewise from the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 34 [Note: Held A.D. 633; cf. above, question 5, chapter 2.]

Just as thirty years’ possession removes another’s diocese, so it does not take away the district of a territory [Note: “Possession” followed *territorii* in the received texts, but is absent from the old copies, Burchard, *Panormia*, and printed and manuscript council codices.] [Note: *Non adimit*, “does not take away”: thus in the Cologne editions of the councils, the royal codex, old copies of Gratian, and *Panormia*. But two Paris editions of the councils and Ivo read *non amittit*, “does not lose,” while two Vatican codices and Burchard read *non admittit*, “does not admit.”].

### Chapter IV. Thirty years’ possession must be observed within one province.

Likewise from the same council, chapter 33 [Note: Burchard, book 1, chapter 67; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 67; *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 131 and part 5, chapter 175; *Polycarpus*, book 3, title 12.]

Any bishop who has possessed the diocese of another bishop for thirty years without any challenge, although [Note: In the printed council collated with manuscripts one reads: “Because, according to the law, it appears to be his diocese, an action is not to be admitted,” etc. [Note: “is judged”: Ivo, part 5.] The *Collectio Hispana*: “because … it now appears.” Ivo, in part 3, states still more clearly after “possessed”: “let him hold it, because according to the law it appears [Note: “is judged”: Ivo, part 5] to be his diocese, and an action is not to be admitted,” etc. Burchard: “although according to the law it appears to be his diocese.” In *Panormia*, however, it is as in Gratian.] according to the law it does not appear to be his diocese, an action to reclaim it is not to be admitted against [Col. 1028B] him. But this applies within one province [Note: “Province”: the author of the Gloss interprets this as “diocese”; various editions of the councils and two Vatican codices read *parochiam*, “parish,” [Note: thus Burchard and Ivo] a word which often signifies “diocese,” as in Apostolic Canon 14: “A bishop may not, abandoning his own parish, invade another’s parish”; and in the Council of Antioch, chapter 21, some translate παροικίας as “parish,” others as “diocese.” Indeed, in the Toledan councils these terms are confused, as in Toledo III, chapter 20; Toledo IV, chapters 32 and 35; and Braga II, chapter 2. At the beginning of this chapter, too, *dioecesis* means a particular part, that is, a parish. But the royal Lucchese codex of the councils, old copies of Gratian, *Panormia*, and Ivo, part 5, have “province” in the margin.], but never outside it, lest, while a diocese is defended, the boundaries of provinces be confused.

**Part II. Gratian.** See: by these authorities it is proved that rights of possession and government are extinguished by prescription. But Gelasius himself testifies to the contrary, writing to Bishops Maximus and Eusebius [Note: An epistle of uncertain date. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 97; Anselm’s *Collectanea* in Canisius, vol. 3.]

### Chapter V. The status of parishes can be altered neither by presumption nor by prescription of time.

Although ancient rules contain the provision that parishes assigned by their original arrangement to each church can be overthrown for no reason, lest universal confusion arise through a most evil custom and the increasing recklessness of a bad example [Note: “everywhere universal”: the cited collections], nevertheless, in decrees sent by us not long ago, we ordered that all things which had been invaded in such a manner be restored. [Col. 1028C] But because the recklessness of invaders supposes that a law can arise in its favour if it adds persistent retention to its wrongdoing, we desire you to carry out what we decreed between our brother and fellow bishop Constantine, priest of the Church of Anusca [Note: *Anuscanae*: the old codices vary: *Canuscanae*, *Camuscanae*, *Tamiscanae*.] [Note: *Camiscanae*: ibid.; Basel edition; *Canustana*: Argentinian edition; *Camisanae*: Lyons edition I; *Canuscanae*: the remaining editions except the first Paris edition; according to Berardus, *Asculanae* seems the proper reading], and between the envoys [Note: “between the envoys”: omitted in the cited collections] sent by the bishop of Ancona [Note: “pontiff”: Basel edition]; and at that time we set down in writing the rule to be followed in other [Note: “certain”: ibid.] investigations.

Therefore, we do not permit the status of parishes, which has endured with the firmness of perpetual duration [Note: “perpetuity”: Basel edition] [Note: “has endured”: Basel and Lyons editions II and III], to be altered by any presumption; for neither a bishop’s negligence [Note: “bishops’”: the same editions], nor a temporal objection [Note: “abjection”: Anselm], which perhaps arises through carelessness, nor consent given through inaction, nor an order procured by a surreptitious [Note: “surreptitiously made”: Anselm; Basel edition] petition [Note: “reply”: Venice edition II] can tear apart a diocese once established, from which the devout people have always assembled [Col. 1029B] for regeneration and confirmation [Note: added: “of the bishop”: editions compared with the original] [Note: “devoutly”: Basel edition] [Note: “have assembled”: ibid.; “are established”: Anselm]. It is also long known to have been ordained that territory does not make a diocese [Note: These words are also reported by Anselm, though not by Ivo.].

Gratian. This is distinguished in several ways. Some dioceses are marked off by fixed boundaries; these can in no way be prescribed away. Others are not marked off by fixed boundaries, and no definite settlement concerning them has previously been made; these are extinguished by prescription.

Accordingly Pope Innocent says [Note: This chapter occurs in the Second Council of Seville, chapter 2, and Burchard cites it from there.] [Note: Chapter 2, Council of Seville, held A.D. 619; Burchard, book 1, chapter 69; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 99; *Polycarpus*, book 6, title 10.]

### Chapter VI. Possession of a boundary cannot be prescribed away.

A dispute was conducted between our aforementioned brethren, Bishops Fulgentius of Astigi [Note: “of Astigi”: Basel edition] and Honorius of Córdoba, concerning the parish of a certain basilica [Note: omitted in the *Collectio Hispana*]. One of them claimed it as Cellanensian [Note: *Cellanensem*: in the printed and manuscript council text one reads *Celticensem* [Note: thus in the *Collectio Hispana*; *Cellacens.*: Basel edition; *Callacens.*: Argentinian edition], and Pliny, book 3, chapter 1, lists Celtica among the towns of the conventus of Seville.], the other as Regian [Note: “Reginensian”: editions compared with the original; *Collectio Hispana*; Burchard; Ivo]. And because up to this point there had been litigation between the two [Col. 1029C] parties concerning the boundary [Note: “claimed”: *Collectio Hispana*; Burchard; Ivo], whose old retention, however long continued [Note: “although its … no”: editions compared with the original; Böhm], creates no prejudice to the right [Note: “will create”: Basel edition; Burchard; “would create”: Argentinian edition; *Collectio Hispana*; Ivo], therefore [Note: “and therefore”: *Collectio Hispana*; Burchard; Ivo; editions compared with the original], lest our judgment be further called [Note: “recalled”: Böhm] into doubt between them, the canons having been produced, synodal decrees were read. Their authority warns that covetousness must be restrained so that no one usurp another’s boundaries. Accordingly, it was decided that inspectors [Note: “inspection”: *Collectio Hispana*; Burchard; Ivo] should be sent between the opposing parties, so that the diocese of the possessing church—provided that a boundary fixed by genuine [Note: “ancient”: Burchard; “genuine”: Ivo] signs [Note: “seen beforehand”: Burchard, Ivo; editions compared with the original] shows the basilica to lie within it [Note: In editions of the councils and two Vatican codices: “so that, if a boundary seen by ancient signs shows the basilica to lie in the diocese of the possessor’s church,” etc. Likewise in the royal Lucchese codex, except that in place of *praevisus* it reads *praefixus* (“fixed”).]—to which belongs the right of retention [Note: “lawful retention”: *Collectio Hispana*], shall have perpetual ownership. But if a lawful boundary does not enclose that basilica [Note: “will enclose”: ibid.; “enclosed”: Argentinian edition], and a prescription by lapse of so long a time is alleged, the claim of the present [Note: “claiming”: ibid.] bishop will not prevail, because the objection of thirty years imposes silence upon him [Note: “places”: ibid.]. For the edicts of secular princes command this also, and the authority of Roman bishops has decreed it. But if, within the limits of the thirty-year period, unjust retention of a basilica outside another’s boundaries is found, it shall without delay be restored [Col. 1030B] to the right of the bishop reclaiming it [Note: “be restored”: Basel edition].

### Chapter VII. Spaces which have been defined cannot be prescribed by time.

Likewise Pope Gelasius to Bishop Justus [Note: An epistle of uncertain date; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 69; *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 135 and part 6, chapter 105.]

Your affection should take pains to ascertain faithfully the truth in every matter sought out, so that, if a definite settlement concerning the territories from which the dispute is said to have arisen was made long ago [Note: “very long ago”: Basel and Lyons editions II and III], it may be preserved inviolate. Otherwise, if nothing has ever been established as settled, then the party which relies [Note: “disputes”: Ivo, part 3; “trusts”: part 6; *Panormia*: “if any party offers the oath of faith”] upon prescription of time, if there is one, should offer an oath, so that [Note: “provided, however, that”: Basel and Lyons editions II and III; “so that, however, those things which”: the remaining editions] it may be permitted to swear concerning those things which it is proved to have possessed hitherto [Note: “is reported”: Ivo, *Panormia*, *Decretum*, part 3; “will be proved”: Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6; editions compared with the original].

**Part III. Gratian.** It may also be distinguished otherwise. What anyone usurps by his own authority cannot be prescribed, because he begins to possess with no title; and in this case Gelasius’s authority is to be understood: “A temporal objection, which perhaps arises through carelessness, cannot tear apart a diocese once established.” [Col. 1030C] [Col. 1031A] This must be understood if he began to possess it with no title, but by usurpation alone. But if he began to possess by a judge’s authority and long-established use of privileges, then a temporal objection imposes silence on the claimant.

Accordingly Pope Gelasius says [Note: What is here attributed to Gelasius occurs in the Eighth Synod, held under Hadrian II, chapter 18, and is cited from it by Anselm and Polycarp. But Gratian’s manuscript codices agree with the received texts.] [Note: Rather, from the Eighth Synod, held A.D. 869; *Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 46, chapter 23; Anselm, book 4, chapter 20 [31]; *Polycarpus*, book 3, title 12.]

### Chapter VIII. Privileges possessed for thirty years must be observed without alteration.

It pleased this holy and great synod that property and [Note: “or”: editions compared with the original] privileges which belong to the churches of God by long custom, and which have been granted in writing either by emperors of blessed memory or by other worshippers of God, and have been possessed by those churches for thirty years, must by no means be removed from the authority of their bishops by any secular [Note: “singular”: Basel edition] person acting through power [Note: omitted in the original], [Col. 1031B] nor taken away by any arguments whatsoever. Rather, all things known to have been possessed by churches within a period of thirty years shall remain under the authority and command [Note: “use”: Anselm] of the church’s bishop. Therefore, whoever among secular persons [Note: In the received texts this read: “Whoever among clerics or secular persons.” But the two words “among clerics or” are absent from several old copies and from the manuscript council text [Note: and Anselm]. The printed council reads: “Whoever acts contrary [Col. 1031D] shall be judged sacrilegious; and until he restores such privileges,” etc.] acts contrary to the present definition shall be judged sacrilegious; and until he corrects himself and restores the Church’s own privileges or property, let him be anathematized.

**The Same [Pope], to the Bishops of Dardania, among other things, says** [Note: [Col. 1031D] This chapter is not found in the extant letter of Gelasius to the bishops throughout Dardania. Nicholas I, in the letter to the bishops of Gaul beginning *Quamvis singularum*, recently printed, as stated above, in the appendix to the library, cites it from [Col. 1032C] a letter of Gelasius to the Easterners. Cardinal Deusdedit and Anselm cite Gelasius without qualification.] [Note: [Col. 1031] Rather, Felix III, in the treatise against Acacius.—Anselm, bk. 4, ch. 27. Deusdedit, pt. 1. +++ “Gelasius, Letters throughout Dardania”: Anselm manuscript collection.]:  

### C. IX. Things peacefully possessed for thirty years cannot be reclaimed.

I hear that certain persons wish to overthrow institutions established five hundred years after Christ, whereas a human law of thirty years cannot be broken.

**Part IV. Gratian.** Likewise, if a dispute has arisen concerning property of the Church and a judgment has followed, even if it is unjust, nevertheless, because the possessor began to possess not by his own authority but by that of the adjudicator, the thirty-year prescription imposes silence upon the claimant—provided, however, that the reckoning of prescription begins not from the time of the judgment but from the death of the adjudicator.

Accordingly, it was decreed in the Ninth Council of Toledo, ch. 8 [Note: [Col. 1031] held A.D. 655.]:

### C. X. The lifetime of one who invalidly disposes cannot count toward the thirty-year period.

If priests [Note: [Col. 1031] “priest or minister,” and so thereafter: Hispanic Collection.] or ministers, while they appear to administer the helm of the churches, are found to have made any dispositions concerning Church property contrary to the most holy enactments of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 1031] “rules”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1031] “to have made any [dispositions]”: omitted in the Hispanic Collection.], the period of reckoning shall run not from the day on which they decreed such things in writing, but from the time when, by dying, they left such things as settled. For the lifetime of one judging *this* [Note: [Col. 1031] omitted in the Hispanic Collection.] invalidly can never count toward a thirty-year period [Note: [Col. 1032C] “For never”: so also in ancient manuscripts of Gratian and in the royal Lucchese manuscript of the councils. In two Vatican manuscripts the word “thirty-year” is indeed present, but the remaining words vary somewhat. In printed councils, however, the reading is: “For the authority of one judging this invalidly shall never count toward a three-year period”; in some editions the word “authority” is absent.], because the standing of contracts did not take its beginning from the origin [Note: [Col. 1031] “beginning”: Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I, and Lyons editions.] [Col. 1032B] of equity [Note: [Col. 1031] “the beginning of iniquity”: Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice I editions.].

**Part V. Gratian.** Likewise, things possessed by benefice, or things possessed for a long period while fear of hostilities intervened, cannot be prescribed.

Accordingly, the Council of Agde, ch. 59, decreed [Note: [Col. 1031] held A.D. 506.—Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 3, ch. 166.]:

### C. XI. Things possessed by benefice cannot be acquired by prescription.

Whatever clerics may have possessed from some remuneration of the Church, however long the period, shall not be transferred by prescription of time into their own right [Note: [Col. 1031] “shall be transferred”: Hispanic Collection; “shall be transferred”: Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I and II editions.], provided it is evident that the property belonged to the Church. Thus bishops may not appear to have been obliged, during their tenure of administration [Note: [Col. 1031] omitted in the Hispanic Collection and Basel edition; add “their”: Basel edition.], to make prolonged or precarious grants [Note: [Col. 1031] “prolonged or precarious administrations”: Hispanic Collection], once they have been ordained; nor may they write over into the right [Note: [Col. 1031] “into the right”: omitted there.] of their own ownership [Note: [Col. 1031] “to ownership”: there.] resources held back for a long time. [Note: [Col. 1031] “any cleric whatsoever”: Hispanic Collection; “any [remuneration]”: omitted there; “shall be called”: there; “shall be called”: Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I and II editions; “not [to have] done”: omitted there. In the printed council and in Ivo the passage reads: “lest bishops appear to have been obliged, when ordained, to make prolonged or precarious administrations.” In the Council of Epaone the passage is manifestly corrupt.]

[Col. 1032C]

### C. XII. Things granted to some persons out of humane consideration cannot be acquired by prescription.

Likewise, from the First Council of Orléans, ch. 25 [Note: [Col. 1031] held A.D. 511.—Not found in Anselm, bk. 5, ch. 87, whence Corr. cite it.]:

If a bishop, out of humane consideration, grants little slaves, [Col. 1033A] vineyards, or small plots of land to clerics, monks, or anyone else [Note: [Col. 1033D] “Or anyone else”: these words are also in Anselm, but are absent from the printed and manuscript council.], to cultivate or to hold *for* a time, then, even if long stretches of years are proved to have passed, the Church shall suffer no prejudice; nor shall a prescription of secular law be invoked which impedes the Church [Note: [Col. 1033] “some Church”: collected editions, first Basel edition, in which “some” is omitted.].

### C. XIII. Prescription by time is not pleaded where fear of hostilities intervened.

Likewise, from the Second Council of Seville, at which Isidore was present, ch. 1 [Note: [Col. 1033] held A.D. 619.—Trullan Collection, pt. 2, tit. 49, ch. 1.]:

**Part VI.** The first petition presented to us by Theodulf, bishop of the Church of Málaga, asserted that the ancient parish of that city had once been divided by the danger of military hostility [Note: [Col. 1033] “torn apart”: Hispanic Collection], and that a certain part of it was retained by the churches of the cities of Écija, [Note: [Col. 1033] “Astrigita”: Basel edition; “Astiga”: other editions except Lyons II and III.] Elvira, [Col. 1033B] and Cabra [Note: [Col. 1033] “Egavensis”: Basel edition; “Egabensis”: Argentinian edition; “Egabiensis”: other editions.]. For this reason it pleased us that every parish which each church could prove it had held under its ancient jurisdiction before the military hostilities should be restored to its privilege [Note: [Col. 1033] “which, from”: there; “tradition”: Basel edition.]. For just as, under worldly law, those whom barbarian violence [Note: [Col. 1033] “severity”: collected editions.] has carried away into captive necessity receive back their former possession upon return by postliminium, so also a church shall recover the parish which it previously held with its possessions, whether it is possessed by other churches or has passed into anyone’s possession [Note: [Col. 1033] “possession”: Basel edition.]. For prescription of time is not to be objected where necessity of hostilities is involved [Note: [Col. 1033] “will be involved”: collected editions.].

[Col. 1033C]

### C. XIV. Prescription of time does not run while the fury of hostilities presses.

Likewise, Pope John VIII to Paul, bishop acting as legate in Germany and Pannonia [Note: [Col. 1033] A chapter of uncertain date.—Anselm, bk. 2, ch. 73 (71). Deusdedit, pt. 1. *Polycarpus*, bk. 1, tit. 11.]:
