Moreover, if anyone happens to complain concerning the number of years, let him know that among Christians and those of one faith a fixed number is prescribed. But where the fury of pagans and unbelievers is the cause, however long the periods that pass, they do not prejudice the rights of churches, which, knowing no bodily arms, patiently await the Lord alone and their defender, when it shall please Him to show mercy. But if length of years [Col. 1034A] hinders in such cases [Note: [Col. 1033] “hinders, therefore”: Anselm], God Himself must be reproved, who after four hundred and thirty years freed the children of Israel from Pharaoh’s harshest slavery and from the iron furnace. Yet He Himself [Note: [Col. 1033] “and He Himself”: there.] was our redeemer [Note: [Col. 1033] “our” omitted in the Basel edition; “was—who” omitted in Anselm and the Basel and Lyons II–III editions.], who [Note: [Col. 1033] omitted in the Argentinian edition.] rescued the human race after so many thousands of years from the prisons of hell.

**Part VII. Gratian.** Those dioceses are likewise lost by prescription which others have recalled from heresy to the integrity of the faith while their own bishops were negligent.

Accordingly, in the African Council, ch. 88, one reads [Note: [Col. 1033] In the Hadrianic codex, from the Council of Carthage, held A.D. 418.—Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 68. Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 5, ch. 176.]:

### C. XV. If bishops neglect to gain their dioceses for God, after three years they shall belong to the bishops through whose zeal they have been reconciled to the faith.

It pleased the council that any bishops [Note: [Col. 1033] “bishops” is absent from the original, Burchard, and the Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I–II, and Paris editions.] who neglect to gain for Catholic unity the places belonging to their see [Col. 1034B] [Note: [Col. 1033] “Catholic unity”: collected editions.] are to be summoned by neighboring bishops zealous for God [Note: [Col. 1033] add “God”: Ivo.], so that they may not delay to do this. If within six [Note: [Col. 1033] “within”: collected editions except Lyons II and III; “three”: Basel edition.] months from the day of summons [Note: [Col. 1033] “admonition”: Argentinian edition.] they have not accomplished it, the places shall belong to whoever is able to gain them [Note: [Col. 1033] “them”: original, Burchard, collected editions.], provided that, if he to whom they appeared to belong can prove that the heretics preferred his deliberate negligence—so that they might remain there without penalty—and that his own diligence had been forestalled, so that his more watchful care might thereby be avoided [Note: [Col. 1033] “forbidden”: Burchard and Ivo; “might appear”: Venice edition], then, when the episcopal judges have ascertained this [Note: [Col. 1033] “have known”: Basel edition], the places shall be restored to his see [Note: [Col. 1033] “shall restore”: original, cited collections, Argentinian edition.].

[Note: [Col. 1033D] The Greek canon in corrected manuscripts reads here: “Provided, however, that if he to whom such persons are shown to belong appeared deliberately to have acted negligently for some pastoral arrangement, this being established by the heretics, so that they might be received without disturbance, and meanwhile his care had been anticipated by another—though, had he employed it, he would have caused the same heretics greater harm—then, when the bishops judging the matter have ascertained this …”]

**Gratian.** That prescription of long time, by which Gelasius denies that the condition of parishes can be altered, may also be understood differently. For “long time,” as the laws provide, means ten or twenty years. [Col. 1034C] Therefore, by the authority of Gelasius and of secular laws, prescription for this long period cannot be raised against churches.

**Part VIII.** § 1. Some prescriptions were introduced from hostility toward the claimant and favor toward the possessor; others solely from hostility toward the claimant. For one who has held a thing in good faith and under a just title for ten years when the owner is present, or twenty when absent, shall be protected by a perpetual exception, not only against others but also against creditors to whom the thing itself had been pledged, and even against the true owner. [Col. 1035A] If he should for some reason lose possession, he may effectively claim the thing even against the true owner. But if, without any title but nevertheless in good faith, he has possessed someone’s property for thirty years, he will enjoy the like protection. Good faith, however, relates not to the course of the intervening period but to the beginning of possession. It suffices that one began possession in good faith, even if during the intervening time he learned that the thing belonged to another.

§ 2. These prescriptions were introduced in favor of the possessor and against the claimant, because the law favors those who possess in good faith and under a just title, or in good faith alone; but it detests and punishes those negligent and inactive concerning their own property.

§ 3. But if anyone began to possess another’s property in bad faith, after thirty years he shall be protected by an exception against every claimant. If, however, he should for some reason lose possession, he will have no action, because this prescription was introduced not in favor of a possessor in bad faith, but only against one who negligently fails to pursue his own property. If the property comes to his creditor or owner, he will have the advantage of retaining it; but if it comes to another, the creditor or another owner [Note: [Col. 1035D] “Or another owner”: in two ancient copies the word “another” is absent; in one, however, it reads “or another,” namely, owner.] may bring an action against him, and the exception of the intermediate possessor’s period [Note: [Col. 1035D] “Of the intermediate possessor’s period”: ancient manuscripts partly lack “period” and partly “possessor.”] will not benefit him, because he did not derive his ground of possession from that possessor. But if possession has come to them by force, the possessor in bad faith will recover the advantage of uninterrupted possession.

§ 4. These provisions concerning prescriptions of ten, twenty, or thirty years are to be understood where uninterrupted possession is proved. But if possession has been interrupted by natural detention, thirty new years shall be counted, from the day on which possession is recovered, in every [Col. 1035C] prescription [Note: [Col. 1035D] “In every prescription”: these words are absent in some manuscripts, but occur in the collected editions.]. If interrupted by joinder of issue, forty years shall be calculated from the last day of litigation. If someone acquires possession from one who was in the course of acquiring by prescription, he may join the preceding period to the period of his own possession. [Note: [Col. 1035] Compare the law, *Code on the Annual Exception*.]

§ 5. But if the person whose property is being prescribed cannot join issue, whether because of his opponent’s absence, infancy, or incapacity through madness, when he has no guardian or curator, or because he is under great authority, he should approach the governor within the prescribed period, present him a petition, and bring the matter forward as a complaint; thus he interrupts the running of time. If he cannot approach the governor, he should at least go to the local bishop or the defender [Col. 1036A] of the city and promptly declare his intention in writing. If the governor, bishop, or defender is absent, he may publicly post notice where the possessor has his domicile, either subscribed by the record-keepers or, if the city has no record-keepers, subscribed by three witnesses. This shall suffice for every temporal interruption, whether it concerns three years, long time, thirty years, or forty years.

§ 6. These things concern prescriptions between private persons. But against religious institutions no prescription runs except one of forty years. Thus in the *Authentics* [Note: [Col. 1035] Code, *On Holy Churches*, Authentic *Quas actiones*, Novel 131, ch. 6.]: “Actions which a thirty-year prescription excludes, if they belong to a religious institution, are excluded after forty years.” And in the *Novels* [Note: [Col. 1035] Novel 131, ch. 6; cf. below, Question 4, final chapter.]: “Neither a ten-year nor a twenty-year [prescription], etc.” In the canons, however, a church is allowed to prescribe against a church in thirty years; a monastery against a church only in forty years. But if a private person has possessed first-fruits and tithes, whether under title or without title, he can be protected by no prescription of time. For things which from the beginning cannot take legal effect do not become valid through passage of time [Note: [Col. 1035] Digest, *On Rules of Law*, fragment 29.].

§ 7. Therefore, if a free person is held as a slave for a long time, even if periods of forty years have passed, the rights of liberty shall by no means be impaired by length of time alone.

§ 8. Furthermore, to the Church, first-fruits and tithes hold the place of public civic obligations [Note: [Col. 1036D] “To the Church, [they are] public obligations”: emended from manuscripts. The earlier reading was “Church, public obligation.” Gratian sometimes omits and changes certain words of the laws he cites.].

§ 9. Public obligations cannot be acquired by prescription.

[Col. 1036C] Accordingly, in Book VII of the Code, title *On Prescription of Thirty or Forty Years*, Emperor Anastasius [Note: [Col. 1036D] In most ancient copies this chapter is joined to the preceding one.] [Note: [Col. 1035] ch. 6, Code bk. 7, tit. 39.]:

### C. XVI.

We command that those who have possessed any property continuously for forty years without any lawful interruption [Note: [Col. 1035] “have possessed”: collected editions and original.] shall by no means be removed from possession or ownership of the thing; but they shall be compelled to pay the public duties, the civil assessment, or any other public levy imposed upon them, and no prescription of whatever length of time shall be admitted as an objection to that part.

**Gratian.** Thus estates, whether belonging to a private person or to a church, can be acquired by prescription. The proceeds of first-fruits and tithes cannot be removed by prescription, even if any layman has obtained a rescript from the Roman pontiff concerning them. [Col. 1037A]

§ 1. For rescripts [Note: [Col. 1037] cf. Cause 25, question [illegible], chs. 2 and 15; Code, *On Offering Imperial Petitions*, ch. 7.] obtained contrary to written law are held to be of no force, unless they are such as benefit those to whom they are issued and harm no one.

§ 2. Likewise: tithes were set apart, by God’s command, for priests and Levites, so that those numbered in the Lord’s portion might live from His portion. Therefore they cannot be granted to laypersons by anyone’s privilege, lest human authority prejudice divine commands.

§ 3. Accordingly, Emperors Valentinian and Theodosius [Note: [Col. 1037] ch. 2, Code bk. 7, tit. 38; written A.D. 587.—Anselm, bk. 4, ch. 38 (40).] state: “We command that all lands which have been sold or alienated under any other agreement, in any province, by tenants or emphyteutic lessees [Note: [Col. 1037] “or emphyteutic lessees” omitted in Anselm.] belonging to the imperial domain, the commonwealth, or the *right of sacred temples*, be restored from those who hold them wrongfully [Note: [Col. 1037] add “and perversely”: Basel edition.] and contrary to the laws, without any obstacle from prescription of long time; [Col. 1037B] and unjust purchasers shall not even be permitted to demand back the price.”

**Part IX.** § 4. Concerning prescriptions of long time, however, the following is found in the *Authentics*, Collation VIII … Constitution VI [Note: [Col. 1037] Authentic *Quas actiones*, Code *On Holy Churches*; Novel 131, ch. 6.]:

“Actions which are otherwise barred by thirty-year, ten-year, or twenty-year prescription, if they belong to a religious institution, are barred after forty years, while usucaption and prescription of four years retain their proper place” [Note: [Col. 1037D] In most ancient copies there follows: “but only prescription of thirty years,” etc. In one copy follows: “Therefore, by the authority of Gelasius and secular laws, the prescription of this long time cannot be raised against churches; but only prescription of thirty years,” etc. The passage in the Code, *On Holy Churches*, final law, of the Authentic reads: “Actions which are otherwise barred by ten-, twenty-, or thirty-year prescription, if they belong to a religious institution, are barred after forty years, while usucaption and prescription of three or four years retain their force, the Roman Church alone enjoying the term or privilege of one hundred years.”].

**Part X. Gratian.** But only prescription of thirty years and thereafter applies; yet the privileges of the Roman Church are excluded from that prescription, since prescription can run against them only after one hundred years.

[Col. 1037C] Accordingly, John VIII writes to King Louis [Note: [Col. 1037] Chapter of uncertain date.—Anselm, bk. 4, ch. 45 (47). Trullan Collection, pt. 1, tit. 63, ch. 4.]:

### C. XVII. Privileges of the Roman Church are removed only by prescription of one hundred years.

Let no one take encouragement for resisting from the number of years, because the holy Roman Church [Note: [Col. 1037] “the holy Roman Church”: Böhm.]—which we serve by God’s providence—does not have its privileges, received upon the firm rock of Peter’s stability, restricted by any times or prejudiced by any divisions of kingdoms. And the venerable Roman laws, divinely promulgated through the lips of devout emperors, admit prescription against its property only after one hundred years.

## QUESTION IV

[Col. 1038A]

## GRATIAN

It has been shown when a church may prescribe against a church. Now it must be considered whether a monastery can prescribe against a church. Pope Urban II prohibited this, saying [Note: [Col. 1037] ch. 19, Second Lateran Council, held A.D. 1126.]:

### C. I. Abbots or monks cannot acquire anything by prescription of thirty years.

We absolutely forbid abbots or monks to possess for thirty years the possessions of churches and bishops.

**Gratian.** But although possession for thirty years is denied them, forty-year prescription is granted them by Blessed Gregory. For he says to Peter the subdeacon, bk. I, ch. 9 [Note: [Col. 1037] Epistle 9, written A.D. 591, bk. 1, Maurist edition.—Anselm, bk. 5, ch. 75 (67). Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 66; *Decree*, pt. 3, ch. 146.]: 

[Col. 1038B]

### C. II. Prescription of forty years is granted to religious houses.

We wish you, when you come [Note: [Col. 1037] “when you come”: collected editions.] to the city of Palermo, to decide the question itself on this basis—namely, that the ownership of the thing remains with the possessor as it has hitherto been possessed. If you find that the aforesaid monastery of St Theodore has possessed without disturbance for forty years the boundaries concerning which the dispute arose [Note: [Col. 1037] “for forty undisturbed years”: original and Ivo.], it is to endure thereafter no claim by the patriarch, even if something might belong to the holy Roman Church; rather, secure its undisturbed peace by every means. But if the claimants [Note: [Col. 1037] “authors”: collected editions except Lyons II and III.] of the Church show that it has not possessed them for forty years by an undisturbed right, but that some question concerning these boundaries has at some time been raised within this period, [Col. 1038C] let the matter be peacefully and lawfully settled by chosen arbitrators.

### C. III. On the same matter.

Likewise, from Justinian’s Novels, Novel CXXXI [Note: [Col. 1038D] Neither the Novels, nor Julian the antecessor, nor the Capitularies are quoted here in their own exact words.] [Note: [Col. 1037] Novel 131, ch. 6; Julian, Epitome of Novels 119, ch. 6; Capitularies, bk. 5, ch. 389.]:

Neither ten-year nor twenty-year nor thirty-year prescription, but only a period of forty years, shall be pleaded against religious houses, not only in other matters but also in legacies and inheritances.

**Gratian.** Therefore, just as under the law only a forty-year prescription may be pleaded against religious houses, so too, by Gregory’s authority, they can prescribe against other churches after the same period.

## QUESTION VI

[Col. 1039A]

## GRATIAN

**Part I.** Blessed Gregory testifies, bk. IV, ch. 88, that the governors of a church may not reclaim by their own authority, without judicial proceedings, things owed to the Church. He says [Note: [Col. 1039C] This chapter is taken from a council held by Blessed Gregory, which occurs twice in his register: once in bk. 4 after Epistle 43, and again after bk. 12 of the same register.] [Note: [Col. 1039] at the Roman Council held A.D. 595.—*Polycarpus*, bk. 4, tit. 8.]:

### C. I. Church property is to be defended by judgment, not by force.

A new and highly blameworthy custom has arisen in this Church: when its governors suspect that urban or rural estates belonging to its patrimony may be subject to its right, they affix official notices in the manner of the treasury and defend by force, rather than by judgment, that which they think belongs to the poor. And although truth says through its preachers, “Do nothing [Note: [Col. 1039] Philippians 2:3.] through contention,” [Note: [Col. 1039] The collected editions read: “and because, although the truth commands its preachers to do nothing through contention”; “because” is omitted in the Basel edition.] even the evil of contentious litigation itself is surpassed [Col. 1039B] [Note: [Col. 1039] “they surpass”: original.], and any property, when it is judged [Note: [Col. 1039] “is thought”: Basel edition.] possibly to belong to the Church, is seized by force [Note: [Col. 1039] “and if”: Argentinian edition.], [Note: [Col. 1039] “is seized”: Argentinian edition.]. Therefore, by this present decree, I establish that if any ecclesiastic ever presumes of his own accord to post notices on either a rural [Note: [Col. 1039] “rural”: collected editions except Argentinian.] or urban estate, he is anathema. And all answered: “Let him be anathema.”

§ 1. Moreover, if the one presiding over the Church either commands this to be done himself [Note: [Col. 1039] “here”: Basel edition.] or neglects to punish with fitting severity an act done without his command, he is anathema. And all answered: “Let him be anathema.”

**Part II. Gratian.** The authority of the Council of Milevis establishes that whoever, by his own authority, appropriates what he thinks is owed him and does not seek it through a judge forfeits his cause. It was decreed there as follows, ch. 21 [Note: [Col. 1039] Rather, from the Council of Carthage, held A.D. 418; whence Dionysius cites it, ch. 120, Hadrianic Code ch. 87.—Burchard, bk. 1, ch. 70. Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 5, ch. 177. *Polycarpus*, bk. 3, ch. 12. Trullan Collection, pt. 2, tit. 22, ch. 9.]:

[Col. 1039C]

### C. II. A bishop who seeks to enter churches held by another on his own authority shall suffer loss in his cause.

It pleased the council that any bishops who do not reclaim [Note: [Col. 1039] “reclaim”: Dionysius, Burchard, and Ivo.] the churches or congregations which they judge to belong to their see [Col. 1040A] [Note: [Col. 1039] “judge”: original in Dionysius, Burchard, Ivo.] by arguing their causes before bishops acting as judges, but invade while another holds them, whether the congregations are willing or unwilling, shall suffer loss in their cause. And if any have already done this [Note: [Col. 1039] “have done”: Dionysius, Hispanic Collection, Burchard, Ivo, Argentinian and Basel editions], then, if the dispute among the bishops has not yet been decided [Note: [Col. 1039] “defined”: Basel edition.] and they are still contending about it, let him withdraw from the matter who is shown to have invaded while bypassing ecclesiastical judges [Note: [Col. 1039] “judicial proceedings”: Dionysius, Burchard, Ivo.].

§ 1. Nor should anyone flatter himself if he has obtained letters from the primate [Note: [Col. 1039] “primacy”: Hispanic Collection.] permitting him to retain it. Rather, whether he has letters or not, let him meet with the one who holds it and receive his letters, so that it may appear that he has peacefully held the church belonging to him. But if that person raises any question, let the case be concluded through bishop-judges, either those appointed for them by the primate [Note: [Col. 1039] “primacy”: Hispanic Collection; “whom the primates appoint”: Dionysius and Burchard; in Ivo the words “either … appoint” are not read; “through them” is added in the Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] or those neighboring bishops [Note: [Col. 1039C] “Neighboring”: previously read *vicini*, “neighbors”; emended from older Cologne editions of the councils, one Vatican manuscript, the royal Soria manuscript, Burchard, and Ivo. In an old Greek copy of the Council of Carthage, ch. 121, the reading is *γειτνιῶντας*, “neighboring,” where the printed edition has *γεὶτ νιῶντες*, “neighbors.”] whom they choose [Col. 1040B] upon the advice of the primate [Note: [Col. 1040C] “Upon the advice of the primate”: this is also the reading in older editions of the councils, the royal Soria manuscript, and two Vatican manuscripts. But the later four-volume Cologne edition, Burchard, and Ivo read: “whom they choose from neighboring bishops by mutual agreement”; likewise the African Council in all editions.] [Note: [Col. 1039] “choose”: Argentinian and Basel editions.].

**Part III. Gratian.** Conversely, Gregory writes to John the Defender, going to Spain, bk. XI, Epistle 50, saying [Note: [Col. 1039] Epistle 45, written A.D. 603, bk. 13, Maurist edition; cf. Cause 2, question 1, ch. 7.]:

### C. III. The offense of a person cannot be turned into damage to the Church.

If it is established—may this not happen—that a bishop has committed such an offense [Note: [Col. 1039] “has committed”: original and collected editions.] that it is clear he was not deposed without reason [Note: [Col. 1039] “is”: collected editions.], let his deposition stand, and let all property of his church which is proved to have been taken away be restored to it, because the offense of a person must not be turned into damage to the Church. If, as they say, Comitiolus has died, let what was unjustly taken by him [Note: [Col. 1039] “by another”: Lyons II edition.] be restored by his heir without excuse.

[Col. 1040C]

### C. IV. Punishment should proceed against the offending person, not against his property.

The Same, to Peter the Subdeacon, bk. I, Epistle 42 [Note: [Col. 1039] Epistle 44, written A.D. 591, bk. 1, Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 16, ch. 81.]:

We have learned that, if anyone of the household commits an offense against the Church [Note: [Col. 1040D] “Church”: this word is absent from most ancient manuscripts of Gratian and from two copies of Blessed Gregory’s letters, although it occurs in printed editions and in John the Deacon and Ivo; it is nevertheless absent from Fronto’s edition.], punishment is inflicted not upon him but upon his substance [Col. 1041A] [Note: [Col. 1041] “substance”: original, Ivo, and collected editions except Lyons II and III.]. Concerning this, we command that whoever commits an offense shall indeed be punished in his own person as he deserves; but his estate [Note: [Col. 1041D] “From his estate”: this is also the reading in the Froben edition of Blessed Gregory’s works; but other editions, John the Deacon, and Ivo read “from his means,” a term repeatedly used in the letter to signify the assets themselves. Hence the words immediately following.] is to be entirely spared.

### C. V. The property of clergy who fall is to be committed with them to a monastery.

The Same, in the same letter [Note: [Col. 1041] Anselm, bk. 8, ch. 1. Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 6, ch. 380; pt. 15, ch. 20.]:

Concerning fallen priests, *or Levites* [Note: [Col. 1041] “or Levites”: omitted in the original and in Ivo, pt. 15.], or anyone from the clergy, we wish you to observe that you do not mingle yourself with their property to any corrupting end. Rather, seek out very poor regular monasteries [Note: [Col. 1041] “and regular”: Argentinian edition.] which are known to live according to God [Note: [Col. 1041] “know”: original, Ivo, pt. 15, and collected editions.], and commit the fallen persons to penance in those monasteries, so that the property of the fallen may benefit the same place [Note: [Col. 1041] “and”: there; “that place”: Ivo, pt. 15, and collected editions.] where they are committed to perform penance, in order that those responsible for their correction may have [Col. 1041B] assistance from their property. But if they have relatives, their property is to be given to their lawful relatives, provided that provision for those committed to penance is adequately made [Note: [Col. 1041] “they ought to provide for them”: collected editions, except Basel, which with Ivo reads “they ought to be provided for.”].

§ 1. But if any from the ecclesiastical household—priests, Levites, monks, clerics, or anyone else—have fallen, we wish them to be committed to penance, but their property is not to be withdrawn from ecclesiastical right. Yet let them receive for their own use enough to support themselves while performing penance [Note: [Col. 1041] “for penance”: collected editions and Ivo.], lest, if they are stripped bare, they become a burden on the places to which they have been assigned.

### C. VI. An unfit priest does not deprive his church of its dignity.

Likewise, Leo IV to King Charles [Note: [Col. 1041] Chapter of uncertain source.—Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 5, ch. 21.]:

If perhaps—as we do not believe—we are judged unfit among you, [Col. 1041C] the Church over which, by the Lord’s permission, we preside is nevertheless not unfit, but is deservedly called by all alike the head and beginning of all.

### C. VII. A bishop may not take away a monastery’s possessions because of an abbot’s sin.

The Same, in the Council of Mainz [Note: [Col. 1041] Chapter of uncertain source.—Burchard, bk. 8, ch. 88. Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 7, ch. 106.]:

A bishop may not take away a monastery’s possession, even though its abbot has sinned; rather, he should subject him to the authority of the abbot of another monastery [Note: [Col. 1042D] In Burchard and Ivo it reads: “he should send him to another monastery under the authority of another abbot.”].

[Col. 1042A]

### C. VIII. Subsequent pontiffs must by no means presume to take away what priests have given.

Likewise, Gelasius [Note: [Col. 1041] Rather, canon 17 of the Third Council of Orléans, held A.D. 538, reduced to an abridgment.—Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 172 (180).].

Whatever preceding priests have bestowed—whether from church property for the use of clerics or servants, or from their own property in ownership—subsequent bishops must by no means presume to take away. If, however, any fault has occurred, let punishment be imposed upon the person, according to the status of the persons involved or the rule of the preceding canons, not upon his property.

[Note: [Col. 1041] *dederunt* (“have bestowed”): Basel edition.]

Gratian. If, therefore, personal affection cannot be converted into injury to the church—for a steward can make the church’s condition better, not worse—and if a monastery’s possessions may not be taken away because of an abbot’s sin [Col. 1042B], how can an episcopal offence be turned into injury to the church, so that it suffers loss in its own legal cause? But “suffering loss in its cause” must not be understood as meaning that the church is deprived of its right; rather, it means that, while the clerics stand before their own judge, the bishop will remain silent, be fined for the injury inflicted, and retain his own property.

## QUESTION VII

## GRATIAN

### Part I

That churches may not be received from the hand of laymen, whether by an abbot or by anyone else, is attested by the authority of all the canons. For, generally, both churches and church property are under the authority of bishops. Laymen, however, cannot possess tithes or churches either by their own authority or by that of bishops [Col. 1042C]. Therefore bishops who give churches or tithes to laymen, whether as a favour or for a price, make the house of prayer a house of trade and a den of robbers. Accordingly, after their overthrow from the episcopal chair, being separated from the assembly of the faithful, they shall be scourged by the Lord with eternal punishment.

Therefore Gregory VII says in the Lateran Council, chapter 7, book VI of the Register:

[Note: [Col. 1042D] This is canon 7 of the council held by Gregory VII at Rome in the Lateran in A.D. 1078, found in book 6 of that Gregory’s Register. Innocent II repeated the same canon in the council which he held at Rome, chapter 9. Both councils are extant in the Vatican Library.]

[Note: [Col. 1041] Ch. 7, Roman council held A.D. 1078.—Anselm, book 5, ch. 55 (53); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, ch. 145; Polycarpus, book 3, title 11.]

### Chapter I. Tithes must not be possessed by laymen

By apostolic authority we forbid tithes—which canonical authority shows to have been granted for pious use—from being possessed by laymen. Whether they have received them from bishops, kings, or any other persons, unless they restore them to the church, let them know that they commit the crime of sacrilege and incur the danger of eternal condemnation.

[Note: [Col. 1041] *in usum* (“for use”): Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1043] “we decree”: Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, and Venetian editions I.]

§ 1. It is more fitting that we receive from all the people tithes and first-fruits—which we decree to belong by right to priests—which the faithful offer at the Lord’s command, in accordance with that prophecy of Malachi: “Bring the whole tithe into my storehouse, that there may be food in my house.”

[Note: [Col. 1043D] What follows through the end occurs in neither council, nor in Polycarpus, the *Panormia*, or Anselm; [Col. 1041] and it indeed appears to be by an author much older.—Deusdedit, part 3.]

[Note: [Col. 1043] Malachi 3:10.]

§ 2. We judge that these tithes are to be under the bishop’s hand, so that he who presides over all the others may distribute them justly to all, and may not grant anything more honourable to any person, so that others are troubled in conscience. Rather, let all things be common; for it seems shameful that some priests should possess wealth while others suffer want. But, just as there is one catholic faith, so it is necessary that he who is the overseer of the place, although there are many churches, distribute faithfully to all.

[Note: [Col. 1043] *cunctis* (“all”): Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1043] *ne* (“that not”): Argentinensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1043] *quicquam* (“anything”): editions collectively, except Argentinensis.]

[Note: [Col. 1043] “is absent in the Argentinensis edition.”]

Therefore Urban II:

[Note: [Col. 1043D] This chapter has not been found in Urban’s councils. It is found in the first collection of Bernardus Papiensis’s Decretals, under the title “On monks’ chapels,” cited there from the same Urban.]

[Note: [Col. 1043] Chapter of uncertain date, written after A.D. 1095, the year in which the Council of Clermont was held.]

### Chapter II. On the same matter. PALEA

“At a synodal assembly of many bishops convened in the city of Clermont, a question was put to us by some of them concerning churches or ecclesiastical possessions acquired up to the present time by clerics or monks without consulting bishops. Employing the sounder counsel of those same bishops, accommodating ourselves to the time and providing for ecclesiastical peace—because otherwise this question could not proceed without danger of unavoidable scandal—we have decreed by apostolic authority that those things which have been acquired up to this day by clerics, monks, or any persons whatever, insofar as they have been able, shall remain forever valid and undisturbed; provided, however, that in the future they do not presume to do such things without consulting bishops.”

[Note: [Col. 1043] *coepiscoporum* (“fellow bishops”): editions collectively.]

[Note: [Col. 1043] “and descending”: Argentinensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1043] *inevitabili* (“unavoidable”): editions collectively except Venetian II, Paris, and Lyons II–III.]

[Note: [Col. 1043] *vel usque* (“or up to”): editions collectively.]

[Note: [Col. 1043] *fuerunt* (“were acquired”): same editions.]

### Chapter III. On the same matter. PALEA. Likewise Gregory VII

[Note: [Col. 1043D] In the printed codices the name *Palea* was prefixed to this chapter, but it occurs in all manuscripts. It is also reported in precisely the same words at I, question 3, *Pervenit*, where it is discussed. In Polycarpus it is much fuller and is cited from an African council.]

[Note: [Col. 1043] Compare I, question 3, chapter 13.]

An unfavourable report has reached us that certain bishops bestow tithes and the offerings of Christians not upon priests of their own diocese, but rather upon lay persons—namely soldiers, servants, or, what is more serious, even relatives. Therefore, if henceforth any bishop is found to have transgressed this divine command, let him be regarded as no minor figure among the greatest heretics and antichrists; and, as the Nicene Synod decreed concerning Simoniacs, both the bishop who gives and the laymen who receive from him, whether for a price or as a favour, are to be consigned to the fires of eternal burning.

[Note: [Col. 1043] *nisi* (“except”): Basel edition.]

[Col. 1044B]

### Chapter IV. A person gives tithes faithfully who pays tithes of all that he possesses. Likewise Ambrose, in the Lenten sermon beginning “Behold, now is the time”

[Note: [Col. 1044D] This chapter is found in sermon I, “On Lent,” among sermons often cited which are ascribed to St Ambrose and preserved in the Vatican Library and the monastery of Milan.]

[Note: [Col. 1043] It does not appear to be Ambrose’s.]

Whoever recognizes in himself that he has not faithfully given his tithes should now amend what he has done inadequately. What does it mean to give tithes faithfully, except that he should never offer God anything inferior or less—whether from his grain, his wine, the fruit of trees, livestock, garden, trade, or even his hunting?

[Note: [Col. 1043] “God” is absent in the editions collectively except Basel.]

[Note: [Col. 1043] “or from his own hunting”: Basel edition.]

### Chapter V. Those unwilling to give tithes to priests are to be excommunicated. Likewise from the Council of Rouen

[Note: [Col. 1044D] Here too the name *Palea* has been inserted on the authority of ancient codices [Col. 1043] and is read in the editions collectively except Argentinensis and Basel.]

[Note: [Col. 1043] Held about A.D. 650.—Burchard, book 3, ch. 130; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, ch. 58; *Decretum*, part 3, ch. 196.—Compare Leviticus 27:28.]

All the tithes of the land, whether from crops or the fruit of trees, belong to the Lord and are consecrated to him: oxen, sheep, and goats that pass beneath the shepherd’s rod; whatever comes as the tenth shall be consecrated to the Lord. Neither good nor bad shall be chosen, nor shall one be exchanged for another. If anyone changes it, both what has been changed and that for which it has been changed shall be consecrated to the Lord, and shall not be redeemed. But because many are now found unwilling to give tithes, we decree that they be admonished once, a second time, and a third. If they do not amend themselves, they are to be struck with the bond of anathema [Col. 1045A], until due satisfaction and amendment.

[Note: [Col. 1044D] *Boves* (“oxen”): the words from here to “But because” are absent from some ancient codices. They nevertheless occur among the other collectors.]

[Note: [Col. 1045] It is not Augustine’s.]

Our forefathers abounded in every kind of wealth because they gave tithes to God and paid tribute to Caesar. But now, because devotion to God has departed, the fiscal levy has arrived. We were unwilling to share tithes with God; but now everything is taken away. The treasury takes what Christ does not receive.

[Note: [Col. 1045] *nolumus* (“we are unwilling”): editions collectively.]

And we have said this according to the literal sense. But according to the moral sense we shall say such things, first concerning the temple of which God said through the Prophet: “My house shall be called a house of prayer.” Therefore, according to the bodily circumcision of the flesh, and according to the bodily festivals and sacrifices of the law, the temple of God was consequently regarded as that which had been built from insensible stones: first by Solomon, then restored by Ezra, and afterwards, following Christ’s coming, destroyed by the Romans. That temple was regarded as a house of prayer; once it was destroyed, the Jews, as though no longer possessing a house of prayer, necessarily no longer possess the privilege of contemplating God [Col. 1046A], nor can they serve God according to the law.

§ 1. This having been done, Christ expelled all these things in the mystery of his spiritual acts, and then visibly did what he always does invisibly: he expelled those selling and buying from the temple, overturned the tables of the money-changers, and the seats of those selling doves, for the correction of the people, so that they might not celebrate festivals in God’s name for worldly festivals, nor engage in buying and selling in an unsuitable place—a place in which those who assemble as though in a house of prayer ought not to buy and sell, but devote themselves to prayers alone.

§ 2. But now I think that the temple of God built from living stones is Christ’s Church. Yet there are many within it who do not live spiritually as is fitting, but serve according to the flesh [Col. 1046B]. By actions unworthy of God’s Church, though fitting for a den of robbers, they make the house of prayer built from living stones into a den of robbers. For whoever observes in many churches the sins of Christians of this sort—who suppose gain to be godliness and, when they ought to live from the Gospel as God’s servants ought to live, do not do so but acquire wealth and many possessions—will he not say that under them the Church has become a den of robbers? Thus Christ rightly says to them on account of the dispersal of his Church: “What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption?” Likewise he speaks through Hosea in this manner: “Woe is me, for I have become like one gathering stubble at harvest, and like one [gathering] a cluster at vintage, when there are no clusters to eat, no first-ripe fruits. Woe to my soul, for the reverent person has perished from the earth, and there is no one among men to correct.”

[Note: [Col. 1045] *condecet* (“is becoming”): same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1045] *digni* (“worthy”): same editions except Argentinensis.]

[Note: [Col. 1045] *dices* (“you will say”): editions collectively.]

And when you understand Jesus speaking such things and grieving over our sins, consider also what is written in the Gospel: “When he saw Jerusalem, he wept over it and said: ‘If you too had known.’” If he reasonably wept over Jerusalem, he will with still greater reason weep over the Church, built indeed to be a house of prayer, but made into a den of robbers through shameful gains and through the luxury of certain leaders of the people—would that it were not so.

[Note: [Col. 1045] Luke 19:41.]

[Note: [Col. 1045] “he stood and wept”: editions collectively except Basel.]

[Note: [Col. 1045] *flevit* (“wept”): editions collectively.]

§ 3. I think the saying about those who sell doves applies to persons who hand churches over to greedy, tyrannical, undisciplined, and irreligious bishops or presbyters. For this reason the Evangelist said only that Jesus overturned their seats. Would that those who glory in the seats of Moses upon which they sit would hear these things with the admonition of Scripture—those who sell all the churches of the doves and hand them over to such rulers, to whom the Lord rightly says through the prophet Jeremiah: “The rulers of my people have not known me. For they are foolish and undiscerning children; they are wise to do evil, but do not know how to do good.”

### Chapter X. All basilicas belong to the bishop in whose territory they are situated

All basilicas constructed in various places, or constructed daily, shall, according to the rule of the earlier canons, be under the authority of the bishop in whose territory they are situated.

[Note: [Col. 1047] *constant* (“stand”): Basel edition; *consistunt* (“are under authority”): remaining editions.]

### Chapter XI. An archdeacon, archpriest, provost, or dean must not confer ecclesiastical offices or benefices without the bishop’s consent. Likewise Pope Calixtus

No archdeacon, archpriest, provost, or dean whatsoever may confer the care of souls or church prebends upon anyone without the bishop’s judgment or consent. Rather, as the holy canons have established, the care of souls and administration of ecclesiastical monies shall remain under the bishop’s judgment and authority. But if anyone presumes to act against this, or to claim for himself authority belonging to the bishop, let him be excluded from the thresholds of the church.

[Note: [Col. 1047] Chapter 7, First Lateran Council, held A.D. 1123.]

### Chapter XII. A bishopric or abbey must not be accepted from the hand of a layman

If anyone henceforth accepts a bishopric or abbey from the hand of any lay person, he is not to be regarded in any way as among bishops or abbots, nor is any hearing to be granted him as bishop or abbot. Moreover, we forbid him both the grace of blessed Peter and entrance into the church until, by repentance, he abandons the post which he undertook under the crime of ambition as well as disobedience—which is the crime of idolatry. We establish the same concerning lower ecclesiastical dignities.

[Note: [Col. 1047] *acceperit* (“has accepted”): Basel edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1047D] “Under the crime”: formerly the text read, “under the crime of both disobedience and ambition, from which the crime of idolatry began” [Col. 1047] in the editions collectively; “which he holds”: Basel edition. [Note: [Col. 1047] *deseruerit* (“shall abandon”): Basel, Venetian II, Lyons, and Paris editions.]

§ 1. If any emperor, king, duke, margrave, count, or any secular authority or person presumes to confer investiture of bishoprics or of any ecclesiastical dignity, let him know that he is bound by the bond of the same sentence.

[Note: [Col. 1047] “spiritual bishoprics”: Basel edition; *episcopatus* (“bishoprics”): remaining editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1047] *adstrictum* (“bound”): Basel edition.]

Because we have learned that, contrary to the statutes of the holy Fathers, investitures of churches are made by lay persons in many regions, and that from this arise very many disturbances in the Church—indeed, the ruin of holy religion, whereby Christian religion is trampled down—we decree that no cleric may receive investiture of a bishopric, abbey, or church from the hand of an emperor, king, or any lay person, male or female. If he presumes to do so, let him acknowledge that such investiture is void by apostolic authority and that he is subject to excommunication until fitting satisfaction has been made.

[Note: [Col. 1047] Polycarpus, book 2, title 4.—It has not been found in Anselm, from whose book 6, chapter 73, the Correctors cite it.]

[Note: [Col. 1049C] The sense of this chapter and the following one is found in a manuscript fragment of a council held by Paschal in A.D. 1116, preserved in the Vatican Library. Nauclerus, Generation 36, also relates that Paschal held a council at Troyes, where, among many other measures, he promulgated a decree concerning the free election of pastors and the restraint of lay presumption regarding ecclesiastical dignities, according to the decrees of his predecessors.]

[Note: [Col. 1049] Baluzius and Berardus, on the authority of chronicles, merely suspect that this chapter and the three following belong to the Council of Troyes, held A.D. 1107.]

[Note: [Col. 1049] “or canon”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1049C] “Antiochene”: the Council of Antioch makes no express decree against those who obtain ecclesiastical dignities through laymen. By these words laymen appear to be excluded. In the Second Council of Nicaea, chapter 3, the Apostolic Canon is repeated and confirmed.]

[Note: [Col. 1049] *laici* (“of a layman”): editions collectively.]

[Note: [Col. 1049] Compare chapter 16.—Polycarpus, book 2, title 4.]

[Note: [Col. 1049] *in sacris* (“in the sacred [canons]”): editions collectively.]

### Chapter XXII. Laymen are not to be appointed stewards, but are to be chosen from the bishop’s own clergy. Likewise from the Second Council of Seville, attended by Isidore, chapter 9

[Note: [Col. 1051] “but … and” is absent from the editions collectively except Argentinensis and Lyons II–III.]

[Note: [Col. 1051] Held A.D. 619.—Burchard, book 1, ch. 89; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 195.]

In the ninth session we learned that certain members of our body, contrary to ecclesiastical custom, have laymen appointed as stewards in divine affairs. Therefore, deliberating together, we determine that each of us, in accordance with the decrees of the Fathers of Chalcedon, shall appoint for himself a steward from his own clergy. For it is improper that a layman be the bishop’s vicar and that secular persons judge within the Church. In one and the same office there ought not to be a differing profession. This is also prohibited in the divine law, Moses saying: “You shall not plough with an ox and an ass together”—that is, you shall not associate persons of differing professions in one office. Hence we too must obey the divine books and the commands of the holy Fathers, establishing that those who are associated with bishops in church administrations ought not to differ either in profession or in dress. For persons whose pursuits and vows differ cannot cleave to and be united with one another.

[Note: [Col. 1051] Omitted in the Argentinensis and Basel editions, and in Burchard and Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 1051] “nor differ in profession or dress”: editions collectively.]

§ 1. But if any bishop henceforth chooses to have ecclesiastical property administered through lay management, or thinks it should be governed without the supervision of a steward, then, as a despiser of the canons and a defrauder of ecclesiastical property, he shall be judged guilty not only by Christ concerning the property of the poor, but shall also remain liable to the council.

[Note: [Col. 1051] *post haec* (“after these things”): Hispana Collection; Burchard; editions collectively; omitted in Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 1051] Omitted in the Argentinensis and Basel editions; “to lay administration”: Ivo and Burchard; “by lay arrangement”: Hispana Collection.]

[Note: [Col. 1051] “by Christ”: editions collectively.]

### Chapter XXIII. A layman has no authority to enact anything in the Church. Likewise in the Third Roman Synod of Pope Symmachus, chapter 3

[Note: [Col. 1051] Held A.D. 502.—Tripartite Collection, part 1, title 48, ch. 13; Anselm, book 5, ch. 9 (11).—Compare Distinction 96, chapter 1.]

It was not approved that a layman should have any authority to enact anything in the Church, apart from the Roman Pope, whom there remains a necessity to obey, not authority to command.

[Note: [Col. 1051] Original: “It was not permitted that laymen, etc.”]

[Note: [Col. 1051] Original: *quos* (“whom,” plural).]

Likewise, in the same place, Eulalius, bishop of the Church of Syracuse, said:

### Chapter XXIV. Laymen cannot administer ecclesiastical resources

No authority to administer anything of ecclesiastical resources is found to have been assigned to laymen, however religious they may be.

[Note: [Col. 1051] Compare Distinction 96, chapter 1.—Tripartite Collection, same place, ch. 14; Anselm, same place; Polycarpus, book 6, title 1; Deusdedit, part 4.]

[Note: [Col. 1051D] “Resources”: formerly the text read “dignities” [Col. 1051], as in the editions collectively. It has been corrected from the original—as above, Distinction 96, *Bene quidem*—the letter of Stephen I, and Paschal II’s manuscript decree, in which places this same ruling is repeated.]

### Chapter XXV. A layman who usurps the administration or lordship of ecclesiastical property is regarded as sacrilegious. Likewise Pope Calixtus II

If any ruler or other layman claims for himself the administration or lordship of ecclesiastical goods or possessions, let him be judged sacrilegious.

[Note: [Col. 1052C] It has not been found among the decrees of Calixtus from which it is cited. It is found in Paschal II’s manuscript decrees, chapter 5; but the name of Calixtus has not been changed, because these pontiffs, who lived at nearly the same period, frequently repeated the same decrees of their predecessors.]

[Note: [Col. 1051] Chapter 8, First Lateran Council, held A.D. 1123.]

[Note: [Col. 1051] *donationem* (“grant/donation”): original; Argentinensis, Basel, Venetian I, and Norimbergensis editions.]

### Chapter XXVI. In a church which one builds, one must claim nothing for oneself above others. Likewise Pope Gelasius to Bishop Senecio

[Note: [Col. 1051] Letter of uncertain date.—Anselm, book 5, ch. 9; Deusdedit, part 1, ch. 94, both adding the subscription: “Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August.”]

### Part III

The devotion of a pious mind is to be embraced, by which Julius is said to have founded, upon his own property at Juviana, a church which he wishes to be consecrated in his name in honour of Saint Vitus the Confessor. [Note: *Juviana*: Ballerini, by comparison with Deusdedit (Works of Leo the Great, vol. 3, p. CCCIV); *Viviana*: Anselm. — *is said*: editions of Argentoratum and Nuremberg, Venice I–II; *he says*: the remaining editions. — *honour*: the collected editions, except the first Lyons II–III editions. — *the matter*: added in the Basel edition.] Therefore, dearest brother, if you do not doubt that it belongs to your diocese, it is fitting that it be dedicated according to custom, after the solemn donation has first been made, which the donor of the aforesaid gift testifies that he has assigned to the ministers of the church; knowing without doubt that, apart from the right of entry in processions, which is due to every Christian, he will possess there nothing as his own by right.

### Chapter XXVII. On the same matter. The same authority.

[Note: A chapter of uncertain date. — Anselm, book 5, chapter 11; Polycarpus, book 3, title 12.]

Frigentius [Note: *Trigetius*: Anselm; *Frigerius*: Argentoratum edition.] informed us by a petition that, on his estate called Sextilianum, [Note: “which Sextilianum”: Basel edition.] he had founded a basilica of Saint Michael the Archangel and Saint Martin the Confessor for his protection. Therefore, dearest brother, if it belongs to your parish, perform the blessing of the aforesaid basilica with solemn veneration. [Note: “with devotion and veneration”: the collected editions.] Nevertheless, the founder is to understand that he may claim nothing for himself from this basilica except the right of entry in processions, which is due in common to all Christians. [Note: “in common”: same editions.]

[Col. 1053B]

### Chapter XXVIII. On the same matter. Likewise Clement, Epistle II, to James.

[Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter. Compare De consecratione, distinction 1, chapter 13.]

Build churches in suitable and useful places, which ought to be consecrated by divine prayers; and in each of them priests consecrated to God by divine prayers are to be appointed, whom all ought to venerate; and they are not to be burdened by anyone. [Note: “And in each”: these words through “whom” were added from the original.]

### Chapter XXIX. Laymen are not to expel priests from churches. Likewise Leo IV to King Charles.

[Note: Chapter of uncertain origin. — Ivo, Decree, part 3, chapter 102; Deusdedit, part 4.]

It seems contrary to the decrees of the holy Fathers if a secular person or layman attempts to expel priests from the churches in which they were designated or installed at the time of their ordination. [Note: *Designated*: in old copies and in Ivo, *denominated*, signifying the recitation of the name of the person being promoted and of the church to which he was ordained; concerning this see above, distinction 70, chapter *Neminem*. This was a canonical enrollment and establishment in that church, not a mere naming, as the author of the gloss understood it. — *strives*: Ivo.] But if founders of churches begin to fall into poverty, let them receive from those same churches assistance for their temporal life.

Therefore, in the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 37, one reads [Note: Held in A.D. 633. — Collection in three parts, part 2, title 37, chapter 15; Abbo of Fleury in Mabillon, *Veterum Analectorum*, chapter 34.]:

### Chapter XXX. If founders of churches begin to be poor, let them receive sustenance from those same churches.

Whoever of the faithful, out of personal devotion, has contributed anything from his own resources to a church, if he himself or his children should perhaps be reduced to poverty, shall receive from that church support for life according to the needs of the time.

Gratian. Therefore, if laymen do not have authority to administer ecclesiastical resources, still less can they entrust the churches themselves to anyone to govern, or take them away from others. § 1. Here, however, a distinction must be made: what right do founders of churches have in them, and what right do they not have? They have the right to provide for them, to advise, and to find a priest; but they do not have the right to sell, give away, or use them as their own.

Therefore, in the canons of the Ninth Council of Toledo, chapter 1, it is found [Note: Held in A.D. 655. — Abbo of Fleury, same work, chapter 32.]:

### Chapter XXXI. The heirs of one who built a church ought themselves to take care for it.

It shall be lawful for the sons, grandsons, and more respectable relatives of the person who built or endowed a church to exercise this diligence of good intention: if they see a priest or minister defrauding it of anything from the property contributed, they shall either restrain him through the proper procedure of honourable admonition, or report the matter to the bishop or judge for correction. [Note: *honourable*: Hispanic Collection; Abbo.] But if the bishop attempts to do such things, they shall see to it that these matters are reported to his metropolitan. [Note: *be reported*: the collected editions except Basel.] If the metropolitan does such things, they shall not delay in bringing them to the king’s attention.

§ 1. Yet it shall not be lawful for the heirs themselves to assert authority over these matters as though by their own right, to commit robbery or fraud, or to presume any violence whatever. Rather, they are to apply themselves solely to salutary care, so that harmful conduct either causes no injury or earns a great, or some, share of a salutary reward. [Note: *and*: collected editions. — *not*: same editions; Abbo. — “in no”: Hispanic Collection; Abbo. — *unwilling*: Basel; *fine*: remaining editions except Lyons II–III; *into a great*: Hispanic Collection; Abbo. — *recompense*: same source; Abbo.]

§ 2. But if anyone hereafter presumes to violate these provisions, [Note: *wishes*: same source; Basel edition.] he shall restore what he has wickedly seized with disgrace, and shall undergo a sentence of excommunication for a year.

[Col. 1054C]

### Chapter XXXII. Founders of churches are to present to the bishop persons to be ordained in them. Likewise from the Ninth Council of Toledo, chapter 2.

[Note: Held in A.D. 655. — Abbo of Fleury, chapter 32.]

We decree that, so long as founders of churches remain alive in this life, [Note: *are*: collected editions.] they shall be permitted to exercise diligent care for those places, [Note: *have*: same editions.] and they themselves shall present to the bishops suitable rectors to be ordained in those basilicas. [Note: *to the bishop*: same editions. — The following through “If, however, disregarding” was added from the council itself.] If perhaps such persons cannot be found by them, then those whom the bishop of the place judges pleasing to God shall be appointed, with their consent, to serve in sacred worship.

But if, disregarding the surviving founders, a bishop presumes to ordain rectors there, let him know that his ordination is invalid, [Note: *made*: Basel edition.] and that, to his own shame, others are to be ordained in their place—those whom the founders themselves have chosen as worthy.

[Note: *Disregarding*: this reading is also found in the royal Lucca manuscript; but editions of the councils and two Vatican manuscripts read: “If, while they are surviving.” — *those same*: same editions.]

### Chapter XXXIII. A monastery is not to be taken from the authority of its builder. Likewise from the Roman Synod of Eugenius II and Leo IV, chapter 21.

[Note: *Oratory*: editions of Argentoratum and Basel; *oratory or monastery*: Lyons II–III. — Held in A.D. 826 and 854. — Abbo of Fleury, same place, chapter 37.]

A monastery or oratory canonically constructed is not to be taken, against the builder’s will, from his authority. [Note: “from the builder’s authority”: lacking in Abbo. — *against his will*: original.] He may entrust it, with the bishop’s consent, to whichever priest he wishes for the sacred office of that diocese, provided that the priest is not unsuitable. [Note: *is*: Abbo.]

### Chapter XXXIV. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Gregory, book VII, indiction 1, to Secundinus, Bishop of Tauromenium.

[Note: Epistle 31, written A.D. 598, book 8, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 5, chapter 8; Polycarpus, book 3, title 12.]

The order of reason does not permit anyone to claim a monastery, contrary to the founders’ will, from their control [Note: “or administration”: added in the Basel edition.] for his own arbitrary disposal.

[Note: In Anselm and Polycarpus this passage occurs in the same form. In the epistle itself the sentence depends on what precedes and reads: “Because the order of reason does not permit that the monastery itself, especially contrary to the founders’ will, should be withdrawn from their control for the arbitrary disposal of any person—particularly a lay person—or that anyone should claim any right in it for himself.” When it says “from their control,” it means the monks, of whom it had spoken above.]

Gratian. Nevertheless, founders ought to honour churches under the oversight and admonition of the bishop.

Therefore Gregory [Note: In the Capitularies, Lombard laws, Burchard, and Ivo—who likewise cite Gregory’s decrees—the text reads: “Concerning churches divided among co-heirs, it must be considered how,” etc. Since these words make the meaning clearer, they seemed worth adding, but in another order so that the familiar beginning of the chapter would not be altered. Formerly it read: “It must be considered how,” etc.] [Note: Rather, from the Capitularies of the Frankish Kings, book 5, chapter 99; Lombard Laws, book 3, title 1, chapter 44; Regino, book 1, chapter 242; Burchard, book 3, chapter 41; Anselm, book 5, page 79; Ivo, Decree, part 3, chapter 45.]

### Chapter XXXV. Churches are to be honoured by their founders under the oversight of bishops.

It must be considered concerning churches divided among co-heirs whether, if the co-heirs wish to retain them under the oversight and admonition of the bishop, they also carry out acts of honour toward them. [Note: *honour*: in the common Lombard editions, “perform honours.”] But if they oppose this, it remains in the bishop’s power whether he wishes to permit them to continue, or to remove the relics from them.

### Chapter XXXVI. Relics are to be removed from churches if several heirs dispute over them. Likewise from the Council of Tribur, chapter 32.

[Note: Chapter 32 of the Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895, abbreviated. — Regino, same place; Burchard, book 3, chapter 40; Ivo, Decree, same place.]

If several heirs dispute over a common church, [Note: *dispute*: Basel edition. — *as to*: Argentoratum edition.] the bishop shall order the holy relics to be removed and the church closed, until by common consent and with the bishop’s counsel they establish there a priest and the means by which he may live.

### Part IV

Gratian. Therefore, as is gathered from these authorities, churches are not to be received from the hand of laymen except with the consent of bishops, according to that decree of the First Council of Mainz under Charles, chapter 29. [Note: Held in A.D. 813. — Regino, book 1, chapter 241, from the Capitularies of the Frankish Kings, book 5, chapter 87; Burchard, book 3, chapter 111; Ivo, Decree, part 3, chapter 87.]

### Chapter XXXVII. Laymen may not expel priests from a church.

Laymen shall not expel priests from churches, nor install them in those churches without the consent of their bishops. [Note: “in those churches”: absent from the cited Capitularies and Collection. — *their own bishop*: Basel edition.]

### Chapter XXXVIII. Without bishops’ consent, laymen may not expel priests from churches. Likewise from the Second Council of Chalon, chapter 42.

[Note: Held in A.D. 813. — Burchard, book 3, chapter 112; Ivo, Panormia, book 2, chapter 46; Decree, part 3, chapter 88. — The Argentoratum edition attributes it to Chalcedon.]

It has been found that many persons, through the rashness of their own will and, what is more serious, led by greed, give churches to or take them away from priests without the consent of the bishops. [Note: “laymen”: added in the Basel and Lyons editions. — “led”: added in Basel. — “their own”: added in the collected editions; Ivo.] Therefore it is necessary, with the canonical rule observed, that no one give a church to any priest without the consent of his own bishop. If he has lawfully acquired it, he is not to lose it except because of a grave fault of his own, and by canonical severity before the bishop.

Gratian. Therefore, just as by Jerome’s authority [Note: Cause 16, question 1, final chapter.] monks may, with the bishop’s consent, receive from laymen improperly possessed tithes and retain them with perpetual security, so also monks may, with bishops’ consent, receive churches improperly held by laymen for ecclesiastical ordering, and provide for them permanently.

Therefore Pope Urban II [Note: This chapter may perhaps be referred to chapters 5 and 6 of the Council of Melfi, held A.D. 1089.]:

### Chapter XXXIX. Without the bishops’ will monks may not accept tithes or churches from laymen.

Monks shall not accept tithes or churches from laymen without the consent and will of the bishops. [Note: “possessed”: added in the Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] If this is presumed otherwise, they shall be subject to canonical punishment.

[Col. 1057A]

### Chapter XL. No one may convert a monastery to his own use; nevertheless, he may transfer it to another for ecclesiastical ordering. Likewise from the decree of Pope Sylvester.

[Note: In the Capitularies the text reads: “No king or any person may hand over, exchange, or sell a monastery by any transaction whatever.”] [Note: Rather, from the Capitularies of the Frankish Kings, book 5, chapter 386; Burchard, book 3, chapter 23; Ivo, Decree, part 3, chapter 27; Polycarpus, book 3, title 12.]

No king or any person may hand over a monastery into his own possession, [Note: “No king or any person”: absent in Ivo. — “into his own possession”: absent in the original, Burchard, and Ivo.] except to another monastery; nor exchange it except with another monastery; nor sell it by any transaction whatever. [Note: “or convert”: added in the collected editions except Argentoratum, Nuremberg, and Venice I. — *contrivance*: original and Burchard; *advantage*: Ivo. — In the cited sources the following occurs: “Divine, apostolic, and canonical authority has also established this under penalty of anathema.”] If this has been done, it shall not be valid; rather, the monastery itself shall be restored to its former condition.

### Chapter XLI. No one is to be prevented from placing a monastery elsewhere for improvement, with the bishop’s and brethren’s advice. Likewise from the decree of Boniface.

[Note: The Nuremberg and Venice I–II editions cite the same authority, that is Sylvester; the Argentoratum edition cites Mainz. It should, however, be referred to Theodore’s Penitential, chapter 6. — Burchard, book 3, chapter 26; Ivo, Decree, part 3, chapter 31.]

### Part V

If anyone wishes to place his monastery elsewhere for improvement, it shall be done with the advice of the bishop and his brethren, and he shall leave a priest in the former place for the ministries of the church. [Note: “in another place … it shall be done”: Basel edition. — *council*: Venice I and Lyons I editions. — “some priest”: added in Basel.]

### Chapter XLII. Those who presume, by deceiving others, to shave them are to be subjected to public penance. Likewise from the Council of Mainz.

[Note: This chapter is also cited by Burchard and Ivo as from Mainz, and much more fully, in precisely the form now found in the Second Council of Chalon, chapter 7.] [Note: Rather, from the Council of Chalon, held A.D. 813, chapter 7; Burchard, book 8, chapter 93; Ivo, Decree, part 7, chapter 111. Compare Cause 20, question 3, chapter 5.]

### Part VI

This holy assembly has indeed decreed that bishops or abbots who, seeking not the profit of souls but greed and shameful gain, deceive and shave any persons, and by such persuasion steal their property, shall be subject to canonical penance as pursuers of shameful gain. [Note: *has decreed*: absent from Basel. — *profit*: collected editions.] Those, however, who were enticed into laying aside their hair shall be compelled to persevere in what they began; [Note: *received*: Basel; *began*: remaining editions except Lyons II–III.] but their property shall be restored to their heirs.

### Chapter XLIII. Without the brethren’s consent an abbot cannot appoint one of his own relatives as successor. Likewise from the Council of Toledo.

[Note: Burchard, book 8, chapter 86, and Ivo, Decree, part 7, chapter 104, cite this from the Council of Mainz. Basel: from the same authority, which is the same thing. It is found in Theodore’s Penitential, chapter 6.]

The community ought to elect an abbot for itself after its abbot’s death, or while he is living if he departs or sins. For the bishop ought not forcibly to keep an abbot in his position. [Note: *his position*: Basel edition.] But he himself cannot appoint any of his relatives or friends without the brethren’s consent.

## Cause XVII

[Col. 1057]

[Col. 1057B]

### GRATIAN

A certain priest, burdened by illness, said that he wished to become a monk; he renounced his church and benefice into the hand of the advocate. After recovering, he immediately denied that he would become a monk and demands back the church and benefice. (Question I.) First it is asked whether, as one bound by a vow, he is obligated, or whether he may depart from his heart’s intention. (Question II.) Second, whether the church and benefice which he had previously freely rejected ought to be restored to him. (Question III.) Third, if it had happened that he had handed himself and his possessions over to a monastery, whether, with the abbot’s permission, he might return to his own affairs. (Question IV.) Fourth, if he went back without the abbot’s permission, whether his possessions ought to be restored to him by the abbot.

## Question I

[Col. 1058B]

### GRATIAN

### Part I

That one may not depart from a vow is proved by many authorities. For the Prophet says: “Make vows and fulfil them to the Lord your God.” [Note: Psalm 75:12.]

### Chapter I. What is vowed to God must necessarily be fulfilled. Likewise Augustine.

[Note: The exact words of this chapter have not been found in Blessed Augustine, but nearly the same words occur in Cassiodorus on Psalm 75, at “Make vows,” whom the ordinary gloss cites at that passage.] [Note: Rather, Cassiodorus on the cited Psalm.]

There are some things which we owe even without making a vow; there are also some which we do not owe unless we have vowed them. But once we promise them to God, we are necessarily bound to fulfil them.

### Chapter II. On the same matter. Likewise Jerome.

[Note: Compare distinction 27, chapter 4.]

For those who vow virginity, not only marriage but even the wish to marry is blameworthy. [Note: “to God”: absent in the Argentoratum, Nuremberg, Venice I–II editions; added in the remaining editions.]

[Col. 1059A]

### Chapter III. A person who withdraws himself from God by breaking a vow deserves punishment. Likewise Gregory, *Register*, book I, epistle 33, to Venantius.

[Note: Epistle 34, written A.D. 591, book 1, Maurist edition; Collection in three parts, part 1, title 55, chapter 21.]

Ananias had vowed money to God, but afterward, overcome by the devil’s persuasion, he withheld it. [Note: *the devil’s*: collected editions.] But you know by what death he was punished. Therefore, if he was worthy of the danger of death who took from God the coins he had given, consider how great a danger you will deserve at the divine judgment—you who have withdrawn, not coins, but yourself from almighty God, to whom you had dedicated yourself under the monastic habit. [Note: *monastic*: original; Argentoratum and Basel editions.]

### Chapter IV. They fall before God’s eyes who refuse to perform the good they intend. The same, on Ezekiel, book I, homily 3.

[Note: Sense rendered in summary.]

Those who do good, if they resolve to do better things and, after resolving upon them, do not do them, though they persist in their earlier good works, have nevertheless fallen in God’s sight through their resolution. Likewise, a little earlier:

§ 1. There are people who resolve to leave everything, submit themselves to God’s service, and restrain themselves by the bridle of chastity; but, when they see others fall after chastity, they draw back and lose their merit.

Gratian. Therefore, if everyone is necessarily compelled after a vow to fulfil what he vowed, and if for those who vow it is blameworthy not only to marry but even to wish to marry, it is clear that this priest must be compelled to carry out his vow, and that for him not only not becoming, but even wishing not to become, a monk is blameworthy.

§ 1. That he must be counted among those who have vowed is clear from Augustine’s words, [Note: Compare De penitentia, distinction 1, chapter 5.] saying: “I said, I will confess,” and so forth. Great is God’s mercy, that at a mere promise he forgives sins. For the person has not yet spoken with his mouth, yet God already hears in his heart; for a vow is reckoned as a deed. Therefore, just as the Prophet is counted among those who vow because he said, “I will confess,” so this man must be counted among them because he said, “I will become a monk.”

The answer is as follows: it is one thing to conceive a purpose in one’s heart and even announce it orally; it is another to make oneself liable to a vow by a subsequent obligation.

§ 2. Therefore, because he simply announced with his mouth his heart’s purpose, but did not hand himself over to a monastery or abbot and did not write a promise, he is by no means considered liable to a vow.

[Note: “Therefore”: in most old copies this begins Question II; in the Basel edition, the end of the question is in the following chapter, *Gonsaldus*.]

## Question II

[Col. 1060A]

### GRATIAN

Therefore Pope Alexander II says [Note: Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chapter 428: Alexander II to Udo of Trier and Theodoric, Bishop of Verdun; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 183. The Louvain edition: Calixtus III to Hugh of Trier and Theodoric, etc.; the Basel edition: Calixtus III to Hugh of Trier and Theodoric, Bishop of Virilinum. — Epistle of uncertain date.]:

### Chapter I. No one is compelled to remain in a monastery unless he has made profession into the abbot’s hand.

The priest Consaldus, formerly while oppressed by the fervour of illness, promised to become a monk; yet he did not hand himself over to a monastery or abbot, nor did he write a promise, but renounced the benefice of his church into the hand of the advocate. But once he recovered, he immediately denied that he would become a monk. Therefore, because both the Rule of Blessed Benedict and especially the canonical ordinance of our father and predecessor Saint Gregory the Pope forbid one to become a monk before a probation of one year, we judge and by apostolic authority command that the aforesaid priest receive, possess, and peacefully retain his benefices and altars.

[Note: *Benefices*: in old copies and in Ivo, where this chapter occurs more fully, the singular *benefice* is read; but it was not altered because of the gloss.]

### Chapter II. A wife taken after a purpose of continence ought not to be dismissed. Likewise Augustine to Count Boniface, Epistle LXX.

[Note: This chapter was composed from words of Blessed Augustine in Epistle 70, but reduced to an epitome; Ivo reports it in full.] [Note: Epistle 220, written A.D. 427, Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decree*, part 7, chapters 9–10, part 8, chapter 16.]

We know, we are witnesses, that you wished to leave all the public business with which you were occupied, retire into holy leisure, and live the life lived by the monks, servants of God. When we rejoiced that you had this purpose, you sailed away and took a wife. If you did not have a wife, I would tell you what we told Tubunis: that you should live in the holiness of continence. [Note: *Tubanis*: collected editions. — *chastely in continence*: same editions.] But your wife is an impediment to my exhorting you to that life, since you may not live continently without her consent. For although you ought not to have taken a wife after those words of yours at Tubunis, [Note: *Tubunensian*: same editions. — *ought*: same editions.] she, knowing none of those things, innocently and simply married you.

Gratian. See: he conceived in his heart that he would become a monk and declared orally that he wished to withdraw into holy leisure; yet afterward he was not compelled to undertake what he had conceived in his heart and declared orally. That authority of Alexander, following the ordinance of Blessed Gregory and Blessed Benedict, allows one year for testing those who are known, but grants three years to those who are unknown.

Therefore, from the decree of Boniface [Note: This chapter is also cited in the *Panormia* from Boniface. Burchard, Ivo, and most old copies of Gratian attribute it to the Council of Toledo; in the Basel edition likewise. But it has not been found in any printed or manuscript collection of that council. Nearly the same provisions occur in the Capitularies and in Julian the Antecessor, Novel 123, chapter 52.] [Note: Rather, chapter 55 of Novel 115 in Julian; Burchard, book 8, chapter 20; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 184; *Decree*, part 7, chapter 41. Compare Capitularies of the Frankish Kings, book 5, chapter 380.]:

### Chapter III. No one is to be admitted to a monastery before a three-year probation.

If an unknown person wishes to enter a monastery, the monastic habit is not to be conferred on him before three years. [Note: *within*: collected editions except Lyons II–III.] If, within three years, a slave, freedman, or dependent tenant is claimed by his master, he shall be restored to him with everything he brought, provided assurance of immunity from punishment is given. [Note: *Freedman*: corrected from several manuscripts and the indicated sources; the author of the gloss also had this reading. Formerly the text read “free man”; Basel and Lyons II–III: “free man or”; remaining editions: “free man or freedman”; Capitularies and cited collections: “freedman or.”] But if he has not been claimed within three years, he cannot afterward be claimed, unless he is so far away that he cannot be found. But the slave’s master may take only those things which he brought into the monastery. [Note: These words were added from the indicated sources.]

## Question III

[Col. 1061B]

### GRATIAN

As to the question whether, after his surrender, it is lawful for him, with the abbot’s permission, to return to his own property, it is easily shown that this cannot be done. For returning itself is criminal. Whoever fails to oppose a manifest wrongdoing when he can do so consents to it. Here the abbot not only does not oppose it but, by permitting it, even becomes an abettor. Therefore an abbot may not give anyone permission to go back, nor may that person go back, because from the moment he has once subjected himself to the abbot, he can do nothing without his permission.

## Question IV

### GRATIAN

### Part I

But if he has left the monastery without the abbot’s permission, it is asked whether his property ought to be restored to him or not. Yet neither an abbot nor anyone else may alienate possessions and property given to the church in any manner whatsoever.

Therefore Pope Symmachus: “The possessions which each person,” etc. [Note: Above, Cause 16, question 1, chapter 61.] And again, in the Third Roman Synod, chapter 6 [Note: Held A.D. 502. — Anselm, book 4, chapter 30; Polycarpus, book 6, title 15.]:

### Chapter I. He who presumes to alienate anything belonging to the church is to be deprived of his office.

Any bishop, priest, or deacon who, forgetful of God and unmindful of this decree, commits an offense against this present ordinance and attempts to alienate an estate, great or small, of the church, or anything belonging to the church, whether as donor, alienator, or seller, shall be punished by loss of his office.

[Note: *Unmindful*: in the council itself there follows: “by which we wish the priests of the city of Rome to be bound with religious bonds.” For, as was said above, Cause 12, question 2, chapter *Non liceat*, Symmachus prescribed this law in that Roman synod only for the Roman church. — *present*: this passage, omitting the words of chapter 6, substitutes material from the headings of the same council; the compiler adapted the whole chapter in his own manner from that synod’s words.]

### Chapter II. PALEA. [Likewise Gregory to Anthimius, subdeacon, book XI, epistle 31.]

[Note: Epistle 51, written A.D. 599, book 9, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 5, chapter 38; Polycarpus, book 3, title 12. Compare Compilatio I and X, *De praebendis*, chapter 3. The word *Palea* is absent from the Argentoratum and Basel editions.]

“No reason permits that what is known to have been given for the common benefit should be applied to anyone’s private use.”

### Chapter III. He who thinks that what he contributed to the church should be recalled incurs the crime of sacrilege. Likewise Ambrose, book II, *On Penance*, chapter 9.
