There are those who, after contributing their wealth to the church through an impulsive movement of mind rather than by settled judgment, later think that it ought to be recalled. [Note: *have contributed*: collected editions except Basel.] For them neither the first reward is valid, nor the second, because the first lacked judgment and the second involves sacrilege. There are those who have regretted distributing their wealth to the poor. Such persons who do penance ought to fear only this: that they do not repent of their penance itself.

[Note: “Thus them”: the original reads: “But those who do penance ought not to repent of this alone, lest of penance itself,” etc.; it was not corrected because of the gloss. — *secure*: Venice II; *pleasing*: remaining editions. — *have regretted*: Basel; *regret*: remaining editions.]

### Chapter IV. He who seeks to retain what has been left to sacred places commits sacrilege. Likewise Gregory to Sabinus, subdeacon, book VIII, epistle 6.

[Note: Epistle 5, written A.D. 600, book 10, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 5, chapter 39; Polycarpus, book 3, title 12.]

It is sacrilege and contrary to the laws if anyone attempts, through the designs of a perverse will, to retain for his own profit what has been left to venerable places.

### Chapter V. Those who alienate the resources of the church are judged sacrilegious. Likewise Lucius, bishop, to the bishops of Gaul and Spain, Epistle I, chapter 6.

[Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter. — Regino, book 2, chapter 284; Anselm, book 12, chapter 4 (5); Burchard, book 11, chapter 19; Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 140, part 14, chapter 89.]

By apostolic authority we anathematize, expel, and condemn all plunderers of churches and alienators of their resources from the thresholds of holy Mother Church, and judge them to be sacrilegious; and not only them, but all who consent to them, because not only those who commit the act are judged guilty, but also those who consent to the perpetrators. For an equal punishment encompasses both those acting and those consenting.

[Note: *of that same*: collected editions. — *anathematized*: original, Anselm, Ivo, part 3; *anathematizing*: Regino, Burchard, Ivo, part 14. — “and”: absent from Basel. — *perpetrating*: Basel.]

[Col. 1063A]

### Chapter VI. He who attempts to violate the boundaries of a church is to be excommunicated. Likewise Pope Nicholas to all bishops.

[Note: *we decree*: Argentoratum, Nuremberg, and Venice I editions.]

### Part II

As was ordained long ago by the holy Fathers, we decree that a major church shall have forty paces of surrounding ground, [Note: *sixty*: Ivo.] and chapels or smaller churches thirty. § 1. But whoever attempts to violate their boundaries, or removes from there a person or that person’s goods, unless he is a public robber, shall be excommunicated until he makes reparation and restores what he has taken.

[Note: *boundary*: Ivo; Argentoratum, Nuremberg, Venice I–II, Paris editions. — *their*: same editions and Lyons I, Paris editions; Ivo, *Decree*; absent in the *Panormia*. — *is*: collected editions.]

### Chapter VII. What is paid in compensation for violation of a church’s immunity is to be paid to the altar. Likewise from the Council of Tribur.

[Note: Extracted from chapters 4 and 6 of the Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895. — Regino, book 2, chapter 37; Burchard, book 3, chapter 196; Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 113.]

If anyone commits a fight or homicide in a churchyard, whatever must be paid in compensation for the violated immunity shall be paid to the altar of that church, whoever owns it.

[Note: *commits*: collected editions. — *Immunity*: Burchard likewise has this reading. Ivo reads “for violated immunity.” In some old copies of Gratian one reads “for the violated immunity of the church.” The substance of this chapter occurs in the surviving Council of Tribur, chapters 4 and 6.]

### Chapter VIII. No one may remove a person from a church. Likewise Augustine to Boniface, Epistle CLXXXVII.

[Note: A spurious epistle. — Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 122.]

I marvel that the enemy’s ram has so suddenly breached the wall of faith. For I know with what devotion you have always revered the Church of God. By whose instigation did you dare commit this deed? Did you seize a man from the church? If a fugitive belonging to your friend had perhaps presumed such a thing against you, he could undoubtedly obtain pardon through an intercessor’s intervention. Therefore, if a friend is considered, why is God offended? [Note: “Is considered” (*intenditur*): the Basel edition reads *attenditur*, “is regarded.”] But if this is presumed on the strength of power [Note: “But if”: the collected editions read *et si*, “and if.”], consider King Nebuchadnezzar, who, because of pride, was changed from a man into an ox. [Note: “By what instigating crime did you dare [to do this] to a man,” etc.: Ivo. “By what instigating fury [did you dare],” etc.: the original.] [Note: “Changed”: at this point the following had been inserted: “and, fleeing from his kingdom as an exile, he did not regain his kingdom until, having been converted, he proclaimed God” [thus the collected editions, the earlier Argentinensis and Basel editions]. These words are absent from many ancient copies, from the original, and from Ivo. They occur, however, among Gratian’s words below, *On Penance*, distinction 1, chapter *Voluissent*.]

I write this not to shame you, but admonish you as a most beloved son. [Note: “Son”: Bohm adds “my” (*meum*).] Therefore restore unharmed to the church the man whom you seized as one most irreligious. [Note: “As” (*ut*): omitted in the collected editions.] [Note: “Most irreligious”: the same editions and the earlier Argentinensis edition read *irreligiosissime*, “most irreligiously.”] I have ordered that the clergy not receive an offering from your household, [Note: “I have forbidden”: Ivo and the collected editions read *interdixi*.] and I forbid you communion until, after you have completed the penance prescribed by me for your audacity or error, and at the appointed time [Note: “Appointed”: Ivo reads *condonato*, “forgiven” or “remitted.”], you offer God for this deed a worthy sacrifice with a contrite and humbled heart. [Note: “Heart”: the Argentinensis edition reads *cum corde*, “with the heart.”]

## C. IX. No one may dare drag away a person fleeing to a church

Likewise from Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 90. [Note: Chapter 39, Council of Mainz, held A.D. 813. *Capitularies*, book 5, chapter 155. Burchard, book 3, chapter 194. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 75; *Decree*, part 3, chapter 123.]

No one may dare drag away a defendant fleeing to a church, [Note: “Fleeing”: Ivo reads *fugientem*, “one fleeing.”] nor hand him over from there to punishment or death, so that the honour of God and his saints may be preserved. Rather, the rulers of churches should endeavour to secure his peace, life, and limbs; nevertheless, he must lawfully make amends for what he unlawfully did. [Note: “Hand over” (*donare*): thus corrected—for the text formerly read *damnare*, “condemn” [thus only in Lyons I]—from Charlemagne’s Capitularies, the Council of Mainz, most ancient copies of Gratian, and the other collectors. Yet in Burchard, from the council at Théodonville, and in the *Panormia*, from the Book of Capitularies, this chapter is reported much more fully.] [Note: “Honour of the church may be preserved”: Basel; “honour of churches may be preserved”: the remaining collected editions and Ivo.]

## C. X. One who has violently seized someone from a church is barred from entering a church

Likewise Gelasius, to Bishops Victor, Constantine, Martyrius, Felicissimus, Serenus, and Timothy. [Note: Letter of uncertain date. Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 120; *Polycarpus*, book 7, title 1.] [Note: “Martyrius”: the collected editions read “Martinus.”]

[Col. 1064B] Our brother and fellow bishop Epiphanius reported to us that Benenatus and Maurus, citizens of the city of Benevento, had rushed forth in an affront to religion of excessive bitterness and punishable obstinacy. They did not allow their municipal official, fleeing to the precincts of a church, even there to be safe or secure from their attack; [Note: “Nor”: the same editions and Bohm read *nec*, “nor.”] and, in a rash eruption of mind, dared to perpetrate what even authorities or princes have never been allowed to perpetrate: taking advantage of the priest’s absence, they violently dragged away a man standing in the sanctuary, although he resisted and cried out. [Note: “Allowed”: Argentinensis reads *sinuerunt*, “permitted”; the remaining editions, *dimiserunt*, “let go” or “left.”] [Note: “Eruption”: the collected editions, except the earlier Basel and Lyons II–III editions, read *irreptione*, “intrusion.”]

So far as his report revealed to us, he rightly judged them unworthy of sacred communion. And if it is indeed established that so grave a crime was committed, our authority likewise concurs in this matter. For one who did not hesitate to commit sacrilege ought not rightly be admitted to supplication. [Note: “Who”: Basel reads *ubi*, “where.”] Let no one suppose that, within thresholds assigned to such great veneration, both things are permitted him at his own discretion: that he may claim both humility and rage for himself. [Note: “Humility”: the collected editions, except the earlier Basel edition, read *humanitatem*, “humanity.”] Therefore, dearest brothers, if a manifest complaint proves the guilt of the aforesaid persons, bar them by the authority of our command from all churches in your dioceses, [Note: “In”: the Lyons editions read *ad*, “to.”] so that not only those proved to have rushed into injury against holy places may deservedly receive punishment proportionate to their deed, [Note: “Are proved”: Ivo reads *probabuntur*, “will be proved.”] but that others also may be recalled from such presumption through fear of this punishment.

## C. XI. One who violates churches is unworthy to enter them

The same, to Bishop Epiphanius. [Note: Chapter of uncertain origin. Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 119.]

We have sent instructions to the other bishops that they are to judge persons reported to have violated churches unworthy of access to them.

## C. XII. One who devastates the Church of God and persecutes its priest is judged sacrilegious

Likewise Pope Pius, Letter II, to the Italians. [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter. Burchard, book 11, chapter 29. Anselm, book 5, chapter 30 (29). Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, chapter 243; part 13, chapter 39. *Polycarpus*, book 6, title 15.] [Note: “Strips” (*exspoliat*): the collected editions read *spoliat*, “despoils.”]

Just as one who devastates the Church of God and strips, plunders, and invades its estates and gifts becomes sacrilegious, so also one who persecutes its priests is guilty of sacrilege and is judged sacrilegious. And below, §1: Therefore fornication is not a graver sin than sacrilege. And just as a sin committed against God is greater than one committed against a human being, so it is more serious to commit sacrilege than to fornicate. [Note: “Against God”: the collected editions read *Deo* rather than *Deum*.] [Note: “Against a human being”: they read *homine* rather than *hominem*.]

## C. XIII. The penalty inflicted upon one who attempts to harass estates dedicated to the uses of the church

Likewise Urban, in a letter to all bishops, chapter 2. [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare the *Theodosian Code*, book 16, title 2, chapter 40; *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, book 5, chapter 339.]

All must take care lest estates dedicated to the uses of the heavenly mysteries be harassed by persons making incursions. If anyone does this, after the severity of due punishment—which ought rightly to be exacted from sacrilegious persons—he shall be condemned to perpetual infamy and handed over to prison, or be consigned to exile by perpetual deportation. [Note: The collected editions read *servetur*, “be preserved,” for *uratur*, “be burned” or “consigned.”]

## C. XIV. PALEA

Likewise Pope Hyginus. [Note: This *Palea* occurs in only one Vatican manuscript, in which, as in the printed editions and the *Panormia*, it is cited from Hyginus. Burchard and Ivo, however, cite it from the decrees of Julius.] [Note: It is read in the same way in the Roman Penitential edited by Antonio Agustín, volume 4, chapter 17. Burchard, book 3, chapter 204. Anselm, book 5, chapter 18 (19). Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 70; *Decree*, part 3, chapter 127. *Polycarpus*, book 6, title 15.]

> “If anyone burns a church with fire, [Note: “Burns”: Anselm, Burchard, and Ivo read *comburit*, “burns.”] let him do penance for fifteen years, [Note: “Fifteen”: Basel reads twenty-five.] diligently restore it, and distribute his own payment to the poor.” [Note: “His own payment”: in Burchard, book 19, in the chapter on sacrilege, the text reads: “Have you burned a church, or consented to it? If you did it, restore the church, and distribute your own payment—that is, your *wergeld*—to the poor; and do penance for fifteen years on the lawful fast-days.”] [Note: “Distribute”: the collected editions read *restituat*, “restore.”]

## C. XV. One who steals the ornaments of a church is shown to be like Judas

Likewise Clement, Letter II, to James. [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Clement I, §1, in Mansi. Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, chapter 88.]

If any priest or deacon should sell a linen cloth or veil removed from the sacristy, he shall be considered like Judas Iscariot. [Note: “Removed”: the original reads *subtracta*; Ivo reads *subtractum*.] [Note: “Considered”: Basel reads *existimabitur*.] Whoever does this deed out of greed should know that he will receive the punishment of the aforesaid Judas.

## C. XVI. On the same matter. PALEA

Likewise from Theodore’s Penitential. [Note: Chapter 73 among the capitularies edited by D’Achery, volume 1, and chapter 2 in Bede, *On Remedies for Sins*. Regino, book 2, chapter 266, “from Roman law”; Anselm, book 11, chapter 114.]

> “Church money stolen or taken by force shall be restored fourfold; but the people’s property shall be doubled. [Note: D’Achery reads *popularia*, “the people’s property”; Regino also reads *popularia*.] [Note: “Shall be doubled”: Regino reads *duplicatur*, “is doubled”; the collected editions, except the earlier Basel and Lyons II–III editions, read *duplum*, “double.”] If anyone has stolen anything from the ministry of holy Church, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water.”

## C. XVII. On the same matter. PALEA

Likewise from the Roman Penitential. [Note: Similar provisions occur in Burchard, book 11, chapter 58, and Ivo, *Decree*, part 13, chapter 44.] [Note: Compare Theodore’s Penitential, edited by Petit, p. 56, and the purported Roman Penitential of Halitgar, volume 4. Regino, book 2, chapter 268. Burchard, book 11, chapter 58. Anselm, book 11, chapter 116. Ivo, *Decree*, part 13, chapter 44.]

> “If any cleric commits a major theft—that is, steals a four-footed animal, breaks into a house, or steals any thing of greater value [Note: “Of greater support or value” (*praesidii vel pretii*): the collected editions.]—let him do penance for seven years; a layman for five. But if anyone commits a lesser theft once or twice, let him make restitution to his neighbour and do penance for one year on bread and water; and if he cannot make restitution, let him do penance for three years.”

## C. XVIII. One who steals the Church’s money commits sacrilege

Likewise Anacletus, Letter I, chapter 2. [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Boniface, Letter 72, edited by Wurdtwein. *Three-Part Collection*, part 1, title 2, chapter 5.]

One who steals a neighbour’s money commits iniquity; but one who takes money or property belonging to the church commits sacrilege.

## C. XIX. A cleric who presumes to beat his slave or pupil fleeing to a church is to be separated from the church

Likewise from the Council of Lleida, chapter 8. [Note: Held A.D. 546. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 76; *Decree*, part 3, chapter 117.]

No cleric may dare drag away, or presume to flog, his slave or pupil fleeing to a church. If he does this, until he has made worthy penance, he shall be separated from the place to which he did not give honour.

§1. [Note: Chapter 11 there.] If any clerics burst forth into mutual violence, the bishop shall punish them more severely in proportion as the dignity of their offices has suffered dishonour through such an offence. [Note: The collected editions and the earlier Argentinensis, Basel, and Nuremberg editions read the plural *vindicentur*, “shall be punished”; Bohm retains the singular *vindicetur*.]

## C. XX. One who drags a fugitive from the church courtyard or porticoes is excommunicated

Likewise from the Council of Tribur, chapter 20. [Note: Rather, from the *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, book 5, chapter 337.]

If anyone, being obstinate or proud, has no fear of God or reverence for holy churches, and forcibly drags away from the courtyard of a church [Note: “Courtyard”: two ancient Gratian manuscripts read *de altario*, “from the altar” [thus Argentinensis]; the Capitularies read *de ecclesia*, “from the church.”] or from porticoes in any manner attached to a church, his own fleeing slave or one whom he has himself pursued, he shall pay the bishop nine hundred solidi for the immunity, [Note: Burchard, book 3, chapter 197, and Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 114, from the Council of Metz, chapter 2, likewise read “to the bishop.”] and he himself shall be punished by public penance according to the bishop’s just judgment. [Note: The same source, Burchard, and Ivo read *juxta judicium*, “according to judgment.”]

Gratian. Therefore sacrilege exists whenever anyone violates what is sacred: whether by taking something sacred from a sacred place, something sacred from a non-sacred place, or something non-sacred from a sacred place.

§1. One is also said to commit sacrilege who lays violent and impious hands upon a cleric.

§2. Sacrilege itself entails a twofold penalty: a monetary penalty and excommunication. The monetary penalty must be paid to those to whom the complaint concerning sacrilege belongs.

Accordingly Pope John VIII writes to all bishops. [Note: In a manuscript letter of John VIII, written to bishops and abbots established in the provinces of Narbonne and Spain, observance is commanded of the law against sacrilegious persons issued in the Council of Troyes before Emperor Louis and fifty-three bishops. The wording of that letter differs from that recited by Gratian and the other collectors, but the sense is the same.] [Note: The first part of this chapter through §1 should be referred to the letter of John VIII found among the acts of the Council of Troyes, held A.D. 878; compare Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 80; *Decree*, part 3, chapter 98. No author has been found for what follows through §3, which Ivo, *Panormia*, chapter 79, presents from the book of Gothic law. §3, in Anselm, book 5, chapter 50, is taken from the Council of Ravenna, held A.D. 877.]

## C. XXI. On the various kinds of sacrilege and their punishment

Whoever is found guilty of sacrilege shall pay thirty pounds of assayed, purest silver to the bishops, abbots, or persons to whom the complaint concerning sacrilege rightly belongs. [Note: Basel adds *et purissimi*, “and purest.”]

§1. Sacrilege is committed if anyone breaks into a church, or the thirty ecclesiastical paces which surround a church, [Note: “If anyone”: Lyons II reads *si quis*.] or houses situated within the said paces, by plundering [Note: “Plundering”: Argentinensis reads *rapiendo*, “taking by force.”] or taking anything from there; or if anyone inflicts injury [Note: Basel adds *facit*, “does.”] upon, or takes property from, unarmed clerics, monks, persons devoted to God, and all ecclesiastical persons. [Note: “Which were”: Basel omits *fuerint*; the remaining editions read *sunt*, “are.”] [Note: “All ecclesiastical persons”: Ivo reads “devout persons, ecclesiastical persons.” It then adds: “For chapels situated inside the circuit of castle walls are not included or placed within this observance.” The other collectors say little differently.] Chapels within the circuit of the walls of fortified places are not included in this thirty-pace observance. [Note: “Within”: the collected editions, except the earlier Lyons II–III editions, read *infra*, “inside.”]

§2. Likewise sacrilege is committed by taking something sacred from a sacred place, something non-sacred from a sacred place, or something sacred from a non-sacred place.

The same: §3. If anyone violates the house of God and, without the permission of the person known to have charge of it, takes anything from it, or injures ecclesiastical persons, let him know that he is deprived of communion until, lawfully admonished in an assembly, he makes satisfaction. But if, after the second and third summons before the bishop, he refuses to make satisfaction, let him be held liable to the peril of sacrilege by all, so that, according to the Apostle, [Note: 1 Corinthians 5.] he may associate with none of the faithful.

The same: §4. [Note: Regino, book 2, chapter 288, correctly cites this from the Council of Meaux, held A.D. 845. Burchard, book 11, chapter 22. Anselm, book 5, chapter 47 (40). Ivo, *Decree*, part 14, chapter 92. They attribute it to John.] If any persons break into monasteries, places dedicated to God, or churches, and take deposits or any other things from them, [Note: “Take”: Basel reads *abstraxerint*, “have taken away.”] they shall make ninefold compensation for the damage and threefold payment for the immunity; and, as sacrilegious persons, they shall be subjected to canonical sentence. [Note: “These persons”: Basel and Venice II read *hi* rather than *si*.]

## C. XXII. A layman who seizes a bishop not canonically judged is excommunicated

Likewise Pope Alexander II. [Note: This appears referable to chapter 3 of the Eighth Synod held under Photius. *Three-Part Collection*, part 2, title 50, chapter 20.]

If henceforth any layman, whether of the rank of prior or of any dignity [Note: “Any”: Basel reads *cujuslibet*, “of any one.”] or order whatever, seizes a bishop, strikes him, or expels him by force from his own see—unless the bishop has first been canonically judged—the authors and accomplices of so great a crime shall be anathematized, and their goods shall be handed over in perpetuity to the right of that church.

§1. But if he presumes these same acts against a priest or any cleric of lower rank, he shall be subject to canonical penance and deposition. If he is obstinate, he shall be excommunicated.

## C. XXIII. Those who flog priests are to be excommunicated if, after the third admonition, they do not repent

Likewise Pope Nicholas, to Thado, Archbishop of Milan. [Note: Chapter of uncertain date. Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, chapter 20.]

Concerning those who flog, kill, or rob priests—that is, persons not restrained by the secular arm—it has seemed good, according to the Lord’s command, [Note: “Has seemed good”: Basel reads *placuit*, “seemed good.”] that they should be approached in brotherly love a second and a third time. If they do not listen to you, after the church has been assembled, we grant leave to deprive them of sacred communion and, should they perhaps persist in their obstinacy and despise priestly admonitions, to cut them off from the body of the church under the prohibition of anathema. [Note: “Who, if”: Argentinensis reads *qui et si te*, “who, even if [they do not hear] you”; the remaining editions read *qui requisiti si*, “who, if summoned.”] [Note: “To deprive”: the collected editions, except the earlier Lyons II–III editions, read *privari*, “to be deprived.”] [Note: “Persisting”: Ivo reads *parvipendentes permanserint*, “having treated [them] as of little account, they persist.”] [Note: “To cut off”: Basel reads *resecari*, “to be cut off.”]

§1. You should know that they may also, after at last repenting and first making worthy satisfaction, be restored to the bosom [Note: “Bosom”: the collected editions, except the earlier Lyons II–III editions, read *gremio* rather than *gremium*.] of holy mother Church. [Note: The words “of holy mother Church” are absent in Ivo.] [Note: “To restore”: Basel reads *revocare*, rather than *revocari*, “to be restored.”]

## C. XXIV. PALEA

[Likewise from the Council of Mainz under Rabanus, chapter 24. [Note: This *Palea* occurs in only one Vatican manuscript of Gratian.] [Note: Held A.D. 847. Regino, book 2, chapter 43. Burchard, book 6, chapter 7. Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, chapter 136. Compare *Compilatio I*, *On Purgation*, chapter 2; *X*, *On Penance and Remission*, chapter 2. The entire chapter is omitted in the Basel edition.]]

> “Upon one who kills a priest, penance of twelve years shall be imposed according to the canons; [Note: “Twelve”: thus in the Vatican manuscript and the other places cited. In the printed Gratian copies the reading was “a penalty of twenty years.”] or, if he denies it and is free, let him clear himself with seventy-two oaths; [Note: “With seventy-two”: the council itself reads “with twelve”; Burchard, Ivo, and the Vatican manuscript nevertheless agree with the printed reading.] but if he is a slave, let him clear himself by twelve glowing ploughshares. But, convicted of the offence, [Note: “Offence”: the collected editions read *noxa*, “harm” or “wrong.”] let him be deprived of the belt of military service until the end of his life, and remain without hope of marriage.” [Note: “Belt of military service”: the Decretals, Burchard, and Ivo have the same wording. The council reads, “let him lay aside his belt and lose his wife.”]

## C. XXV. PALEA

[Likewise from the Council of Tribur. [Note: This is not extant in the Council of Tribur, although Regino, book 1, chapter 133, Burchard, book 6, chapter 10, and Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, chapter 139, cite it as coming from that council.]]

> “Priests are not to travel unless clothed in a stole or *orarium*. If while travelling they are robbed, wounded, or killed while not wearing a stole, they shall make simple compensation; but if they wear a stole, threefold compensation.” [Note: Basel reads *spolientur, vulnerentur, occidantur*, “are robbed, wounded, or killed.”] [Note: “They shall make compensation” (*solvantur*): Venice I–II read *absolventur*, “shall be acquitted”; the remaining editions, except the earlier Basel edition, read *absolvantur*, “shall be absolved.”]

## C. XXVI. PALEA

[Likewise from the same source, chapter 5. [Note: This *Palea* also occurs in only one Vatican manuscript. It is, however, in the Capitularies, whence it is cited in the *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 15, and in the Decretals, title *On Penalties*, chapter *Presbyteri*. Something similar is also found in the extant Council of Tribur, chapter 4.] [Note: Rather, from the *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, book 5, chapter 186. Regino, book 2, chapter 41. Burchard, book 6, chapter 11. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 6; *Decree*, part 10, chapter 140. Omitted in the Basel edition. Compare *Compilatio I* and *X*, *On Penalties*.]]

> “All priest-killers (*presbyteri interfectores*; an incongruous reading retained by the source) shall pay compensation to the bishop in whose diocese they belong, [Note: “Priest-killers”: the *Panormia* likewise reads *interfectores*. The Vatican manuscript reads *interfecti*, “priests killed,” as do all the cited collections and the Argentinensis, Nuremberg, and Venice I–II editions. The Capitular reads: “For priests killed, payment shall be made to the bishop to whose diocese they belong, according to the capitulary of our glorious father Charles, namely, etc.” In the Decretals, Burchard, and Ivo it reads: “The compensation for priests killed shall be paid to the bishop in whose diocese he belonged, namely, etc.” Since this is the opening of the chapter, however, no change was thought proper here; the remainder was corrected from the cited places.] namely, that the bishop shall assign one half of his *wergeld* [Note: “Wergeld” (*Wirigeldi*): the text formerly read “Renaldus.” The editions read either “one half shall be assigned to Bishop Renald and to the benefit of the church over which he presided” (*medietas Renaldi episcopi eius et utilitati ecclesiae, cui praefuerit, tribuatur*), or “Bishop Renald shall assign one half to him and to the benefit of the church over which he presided” (*medietatem Renaldus episcopus ei et utilitati ecclesiae, cui praefuerit, tribuat*). The text was corrected from the other cited places, except the Decretals, where both words are absent, although the word occurs in the first collection.] to the benefit of the church over which he presided, and shall justly distribute the other half in alms for him, [Note: “For him”: the cited collections read *eius*, “for him” or “for that one,” rather than *illius*.] because no heir of his seems nearer to us than the one who joined him to the Lord.” [Note: “Shall distribute”: the collected editions read *dispertiatur*, “shall be distributed.”]

## C. XXVII. Those who kill clerics are to be fined according to the diversity of their ranks

Likewise from Book III of the Capitularies, chapter 25. [Note: Also book 5, chapter 261, Capitular II, A.D. 803; compare Ripuarian Law, title 36. Burchard, book 6, chapter 5. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 7; *Decree*, part 10, chapter 9.]

One who kills a subdeacon shall pay 300 solidi; one who kills a deacon, 400; one who kills a priest, 600; one who kills a bishop, 900; one who kills a monk, 400.

## C. XXVIII. On the same matter

Likewise from Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 90. [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 8; *Decree*, part 10, chapter 10.]

One who kills a monk or cleric shall lay aside arms and serve God in a monastery all the days of his life, never to return to the secular world; and he shall perform public penance for seven years. [Note: Basel reads *per septem annos*, “for seven years”; Ivo’s *Decree* and the original read *agat*, “perform,” rather than *gerat*, “undergo.”]

## C. XXIX. One who strikes a cleric is excommunicated and may be absolved only by the Roman Pontiff

Likewise Pope Innocent II, in the Lateran Council, chapter 15. [Note: Held A.D. 1139. The entire council is appended at the end of the *Panormia*. The same provisions had already been issued in the Council of Reims, held A.D. 1131.]

If anyone, at the devil’s prompting, incurs the guilt of this sacrilege by laying violent hands upon a cleric or monk, he shall be bound by the bond of anathema. No bishop may presume to absolve him, except in pressing danger of death, until he is presented before the apostolic presence and receives its command. [Note: “Guilt” (*reatum*): corrected from manuscript copies of the council and the Council of Eugenius III, chapter 16, in which the same provision is repeated. The former reading was *vitium vel crimen*, “vice or crime.” Basel reads *crimen*, “crime”; Argentinensis, *vitium*, “vice”; the remaining editions, *vitium vel crimen*.]

## III Part

Gratian. But one who forcibly removes someone from a church, or inflicts any injury in the church itself, or upon its place, worship, priests, or ministers, shall be accused as for a public crime and treason against majesty; and, if convicted or confessing, shall be struck with capital sentence by the provincial governors, as is read in Book I of the Code, title *On Bishops and Clerics*, law *If Anyone Has Rushed into This Kind of Sacrilege*, and in the Digest, title *On the Julian Law concerning Extortion*, final law. [Note: “On the Julian Law concerning Embezzlement” (*peculatus*), rather than “Extortion” (*repetundarum*), is the correct reading.]

§1. They likewise commit sacrilege who, contrary to the sanctity of divine law, commit offences through ignorance, or violate and offend it through negligence; or who dispute a prince’s judgment, doubting whether the person chosen by the prince is worthy; or who seek, in a province in which provincials and citizens are established, the office of administering or assuming administration, as in Code, Book 9, title *On the Crime of Sacrilege*.

§2. Likewise, no one is permitted to dispute the judgment of the supreme Pontiff.

Accordingly Pope Nicholas writes to all bishops. [Note: The letter from which this chapter was taken is not extant; something similar, however, is found in Letter 1 to Emperor Michael.] [Note: Written A.D. 867. Anselm, book 1, chapter 21 (22). Ivo, *Panormia*, book 4, chapter 10.]

## C. XXX. No one is permitted to judge what the Pope has decreed or reconsider his judgment

No one is permitted to judge the judgment of the Apostolic See or reconsider its sentence, namely because of the primacy of the Roman Church divinely bestowed, through Christ’s gift, upon the blessed Apostle Peter.

Gratian. One also incurs the guilt of sacrilege who entrusts public offices to Jews.

Accordingly, in the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 64, it is read: [Note: Held A.D. 633. Ivo, *Decree*, part 13, chapter 97.]

## C. XXXI. Those who entrust public offices to Jews commit sacrilege

The holy council decreed that Jews, or persons descended from Jews, are in no way to seek public offices, because under this pretext they injure Christians. Therefore provincial judges, together with their priests, shall suspend fraudulently procured intrusions [Note: “Procured” (*elicitas*): corrected from the royal Lucca manuscript, although other manuscripts of the councils and Gratian read *relictas*, “left behind.”] and shall not permit them to exercise public offices. But if any judge permits this, excommunication shall be pronounced against him as against a sacrilegious person; [Note: “As against a sacrilegious person”: Basel reads *velut in sacrilegium*, “as against sacrilege.”] and the person who has intruded himself shall be assigned to public floggings. [Note: “Floggings”: Ivo reads *codicibus*, “documents,” for *caedibus*.]

## IV Part

Gratian. Yet lest reverence for religion should defraud masters of their right, if slaves fleeing to church precincts could not be dragged away from there, the sacred canons established that, after the master has sworn an oath of immunity, they must also be restored to him against their will.

Accordingly Pope Gelasius writes to Bishop Boniface. [Note: Ivo, *Decree*, part 16, chapter 68, attributes this to Gregory; part 3, chapter 115, to Gelasius. The *Panormia* cites the same authority, giving part of the chapter, book 3, chapter 74.]

## C. XXXII. After security has been given, slaves who flee to a church are to be restored

Slaves fearing their masters, if they flee to church precincts, ought to seek intercession, not hiding places, lest this very presumption of delay increase the rashness of resistance. For our son, the distinguished man Peter, complains that his slave has remained too long in the church of Saint Clement. [Note: “Has remained”: Argentinensis reads *commoratum*, “having remained.”] Since he had arranged that assurances be given, the slave refused for no reason to come out.

Therefore, once the aforesaid man has been sent at once with the person whom you choose to dispatch, when he has furnished assurances concerning the slave’s immunity, cause the slave immediately to return to his master by every means. Or, if he perhaps persists in this obstinacy, after assurances have been furnished to him, let him be returned against his will. [Note: Ivo reads “let the aforesaid men be sent.”] [Note: Ivo reads “of the aforesaid man”; Argentinensis reads simply “of the aforesaid.”] [Note: Ivo reads “they have furnished.”] [Note: Ivo reads “will cause [him to return]”; Basel omits this verb.] [Note: Lyons II–III read *quod*, “that,” instead of *aut*, “or.”] [Note: “Obstinacy”: Ivo reads *pervicacia*, “stubbornness.”] [Note: The collected editions read *exstiterit*, “has stood fast,” rather than *perstiterit*, “has persisted.”]

## C. XXXIII. Once security has been received, fugitives are to be compelled to return from church to render accounts

The same, to John, Bishop of Vienne. [Note: Ivo, part 16, chapter 77, attributes this to Gelasius writing to John, Bishop of Viviers. Chapter of uncertain origin.]

The wife and daughters of Felix arrived at Rome, as was necessary. Indeed, concerning this same man, who first conveyed himself to the basilica of the barbarians [Note: “Conveyed himself”: Basel reads *transferentem*, “transferring himself.”] and boasted that he had good grounds, we ordered him to come out on this condition: if he faithfully and reasonably stated his case, we would allow nothing whatever harsh or severe to be done to him. Otherwise, if he were proved to have acted contrary to faith and his master’s interest, he would impute it to himself [Note: “Would impute”: Ivo reads *imputet*, “let him impute.”] and be subject to his master’s appropriate disposition. [Note: “And his master’s”: omitted in Ivo.] [Note: “Would be subject”: the collected editions, except the earlier Argentinensis edition, read *subjaceat*, “let him be subject.”]

When our son, the distinguished man Orthasius, arrived, he was so convicted on every point that he could not open his mouth, [Note: “Could”: Basel reads *possit*, “can.”] and admitted in his own voice that the allegations against him were true. [Note: “Admitted”: Basel reads *fatetur*, “admits.”] Therefore he is committed to custody. [Note: “Committed to custody” (*custodiae mancipatus*): Argentinensis reads *custodia*; the remaining editions read *in custodia*, “in custody.”] [Note: “Is committed”: Basel and Lyons II–III read *teneatur*, “let him be held.”]

## C. XXXIV. A Christian slave on whom a Jew has imposed the mark of circumcision is to be rescued into freedom; otherwise he is to be restored against his will from the church to his master

The same, to the Bishops of Syracuse, Constantine, and Laurence. [Note: Chapter of uncertain origin. Ivo, *Decree*, part 13, chapter 113.] [Note: “Syracuse”: Ivo reads *Siracusio*.]

Judas, who professes Judaism, has reported that a slave belonging to him by legal title, whom he says he bought a few years ago, has now fled to the church of Venafrum, as the text of the attached petition shows, because the slave says that, although a Christian from infancy, the aforesaid master lately imposed on him the mark of circumcision. Therefore let your attentive and solicitous care diligently examine the truth of the matter between the two, so that neither religion may seem rashly violated nor the slave, lying in this accusation, seek to evade the rights of his lawful master. [Note: “By”: Lyons II–III read *ab*, “from.”]

## C. XXXV. A fugitive is not to be dragged away from the church courtyard enclosed by thirty paces until security has first been given

Likewise from the Twelfth Council of Toledo, chapter 10. [Note: Held A.D. 681. *Three-Part Collection*, part 2, title 43, chapter 3. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 78; *Decree*, part 3, chapter 121.]

The holy council decreed that no one may dare drag away those fleeing to, or residing in, a church, nor inflict upon persons residing in the holy place any harm, loss, or plundering whatsoever. [Note: “Whatsoever” (*quodcunque*, neuter singular): Argentinensis reads *quaecunque*, feminine plural; Basel reads *quascunque nocibilitates damni*, “whatever harmful losses.”] Rather, it shall be fully lawful for those who seek churches to proceed thirty paces from the church doors, [Note: “In”: Ivo’s *Panormia* reads *intra*, “within.”] within which thirty paces the reverence due to each church is protected around its whole circuit. [Note: “Paces”: the Hispanic Collection reads *passibus*, ablative plural, rather than *passus*.] [Note: “Is protected”: the Hispanic Collection reads *defendetur*, “will be protected”; Ivo, *defendantur*, “let them be protected.”]

Nevertheless, those who flee there must in no way withdraw into houses foreign to, or far separated from, the church; [Note: “Withdraw” (*abscedant*): the Hispanic Collection reads *obcelentur*, “may conceal themselves.”] instead, within the reckoning of these thirty paces, without the shelter of foreign houses, [Note: “Shelter” (*receptaculo*, singular): the Hispanic Collection reads *receptaculis*, plural.] they shall have leave to proceed, [Note: “To proceed” (*progrediendi*): Ivo and the collected editions read *progredientes*, “proceeding.”] so that [Note: “So that” (*qualiter*): Ivo reads *ut*.] they may go out to fitting places for the necessary uses of nature, [Note: The word *ad* before *requisitae* is absent in the *Panormia*; the Hispanic Collection reads *et* in its place.] and may not be constrained by any emergency of necessity, since they have entrusted themselves to the Lord’s enclosures for protection. [Note: “Required” (*requisitae*): Ivo’s *Panormia* reads *acquis*; the *Decree* reads *requis*.] [Note: “May go out” (*exeant*): the Hispanic Collection reads *expleant*, “may perform” or “fulfil.”] [Note: “Have entrusted themselves” (*commiserint*): the Hispanic Collection and Ivo read *commiserunt*, “have entrusted themselves.”]

§1. If anyone attempts to violate this decree, he shall be subject to ecclesiastical excommunication and struck by the sentence of royal severity. [Note: “Shall be struck”: the Hispanic Collection reads *ferietur*.]

§2. But if, in accordance with the ordinances of the ancient canons, those who demand them provide assurances, and the priest of that church does not drag from the church doors those who have taken refuge there, then the flight of such persons, should it occur, must be sought by the priest, or a sentence of damages is to be imposed upon such priests according to the ruler’s decision. [Note: “Those themselves” (*ipsos autem*): the Hispanic Collection and Ivo read *tamen*, “nevertheless.”] [Note: “Have taken refuge” (*fecerunt*): the Hispanic Collection reads *fecerint*, “have made”; Argentinensis and Basel read *confugiunt*, “flee.”] [Note: “Those who demand them” (*qui eos repetunt*): the Hispanic Collection reads *competunt*, “seek” or “claim.”] [Note: “Does not drag away” (*non abstraxerit*): Argentinensis reads *ab ecclesiae*, “from the church,” rather than *ab ecclesiae foribus*, “from the church doors”.] [Note: “The flight of such persons” (*aut fuga talium*): Ivo reads *cum fuga talium*, “with the flight of such persons.”] [Note: “Should it occur” (*si evenerit*): Ivo and the Hispanic Collection read *venerit*, “comes” or “happens.”] [Note: “Is to be imposed”: the collected editions, except the earlier Argentinensis edition, add *est*.]

## C. XXXVI. Before security has been received, a fugitive is not to be compelled to leave the church courtyard

Likewise from the First Council of Orléans, chapters 3 and 5. [Note: Held A.D. 511. Rabanus, *Penitential*, chapter 22. Burchard, book 3, chapters 190 and 192. Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapters 107 and 109.]

We decree that what the ecclesiastical canons have ordained and Roman law has established shall be observed: namely, that it is altogether unlawful to remove accused persons from the precincts of a church or from the bishop’s house, or even to hand them over to another, unless oaths have been given upon the Gospels securing them against death, mutilation, and every kind of punishment, so that satisfaction may be arranged with the person against whom the accused has committed a crime.

[Note: [Col. 1073C] *Accused persons* (*reos*): Thus corrected from the original, Rabanus, Burchard, and Ivo, whereas even Gratian manuscripts read *eos*, “them” [Col. 1073D]. [Col. 1073] Burchard and Ivo read *eos*, as do the collected editions.]

But if anyone is convicted of having violated his oath, as guilty of perjury he shall be separated not only from communion with the Church or with all clerics, but also from fellowship at the table of Catholics.

[Note: [Col. 1073] *Consignari*, “to be handed over”: Hispanic Collection.—Burchard.]

[Note: [Col. 1073] *Qui si*, “who if”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1073] Omitted in the collected editions, the Hispanic Collection, and Burchard.]

[Note: [Col. 1073] *Et*, “and”: omitted by Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 1073] *A*, “from”: omitted in the Argentinensis, Basiliensis, Venetian I, and Noric editions.]

And if the person to whom the accused is liable refuses a settlement proposed to him, and the accused himself, driven from the church, departs through fear, he is not to be sought by the clerics of the church.

[Note: [Col. 1073] Omitted in the Hispanic Collection and in Burchard.]

[Note: [Col. 1073] Added: “for guilt,” Argentinensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1073D] *Noluerit sibi*, “refuses for himself”: Formerly the text read *voluerit*, “wishes” [Col. 1073]. It was changed from conciliar exemplars, including manuscripts [Col. 1074C], and from some copies of Gratian himself and other compilers, although the word *sibi* is absent from the more recent Cologne edition [Col. 1074D].]

[Col. 1074B]

[Note: [Col. 1073] *Requiratur*, “be sought”: Ivo.—Burchard.]

§ 1. A slave also who has fled to a church because of any fault, if his master has given an oath concerning the fault committed, shall immediately be compelled to return to his master’s service. And, after he has been handed over to his master upon the giving of that oath, if it is proved that he has suffered any punishment for the same fault for which he is excused, he shall be held, because of contempt for the Church and breach of faith, as excluded from communion and the table-fellowship of Catholics. But if a slave, defended by the Church for his fault, has received from the clerics, at their demand, an oath from his master concerning impunity, his master may seize him if he refuses to leave.

[Note: [Col. 1073] Panormia, book 2, chapter 73.]

[Note: [Col. 1073] *Etiam*, “also”: omitted in the Hispanic Collection and the cited collections; *autem*, “however”: Basiliensis and Lyons II–III editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1073] Omitted in the Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: [Col. 1073] *Admissam*, “committed”: *commissam*: Hispanic Collection and cited collections.]

[Note: [Col. 1073] *Postquam*, “after”: *sed posteaquam*, “but after”: Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: [Col. 1073] *Fuerit*, “has been”: *fuit*, “was”: Basiliensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1073] *Qua*, “for which”: *qui*: Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 1074D] *Excusatur*, “is excused”: Thus in all printed and manuscript copies of Gratian and the councils. In the other compilers it is *accusatur*, “is accused.”]

[Note: [Col. 1073] *Sacramenta*, “oaths”: *sacramentum*, singular: same source.]

[Note: [Col. 1073] Added: “his”: same source.]

[Col. 1074C] Fifth Part. Gratian. For a slave must not, under the pretext of religion, despise his master and abandon his service.

Accordingly, in the Council of Gangra, chapter 3, one reads:

[Note: [Col. 1073] Held c. A.D. 355.]

C. XXXVII. Under the pretext of religion, a slave must not dare to despise his master.

If anyone teaches another person’s slave, under the pretext of religion, [Col. 1075A] to despise his master and abandon his service, instead of teaching him to serve his master in good faith and with every mark of honour, let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 1075] *Eum*, “him”: *illum*, “that man”: Basiliensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1075] *Suo domino*, “his master”: *dominum suum*, “his master” in a different construction: same edition.]

C. XXXVIII. Let one who, on account of religion, teaches a slave to despise his master be rebuked most severely in every respect. From the Council of Pope Martin, chapter 47.

[Note: [Col. 1075] The same chapter of Gangra, from the translation of Martin of Braga.—Burchard, book 8, chapter 25.]

If anyone teaches another person’s slave, on account of religion, to despise his master and withdraw from his service, let him be most severely reproved before all.

C. XXXIX. The necessity which compels the alienation of Church property is to be reported to the primate. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 26.

[Note: [Col. 1075C] This is chapter 26 of the single Council of Carthage incorporated into the code of canons, and likewise into the Greek collection; it was taken from chapter 4 of the Fifth Council of Carthage. Yet neither contains all these words, “let no one alienate property of the Church,” but rather: “It was resolved that no one sell Church property,” as also in Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 1075] Held A.D. 409.—Anselm, book 5, chapter 45 (49). Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 153.]

Let no one alienate the property of the Church. But if it produces no revenue and some overwhelming necessity compels this, [Col. 1075B] we judge that the matter should be reported to the primate of that province, so that, with a prescribed number of bishops, he may decide whether it ought to be done. But if the Church’s need is so urgent that it cannot consult the primate beforehand, let it at least summon neighbouring bishops as witnesses, taking care to refer to a council every necessity of the Church. If it does not do this, the seller shall be held guilty before God and the holy council, having lost his office.

[Note: [Col. 1075C] *Quod si reditus*, “But if it has no revenues”: the Greek is: “ὅπερ πρᾶγμα ἐὰν προσόδους μὴ ἔχῃ,” that is, “But if that property has no revenues.”]

[Note: [Col. 1075] *Et*, “and”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1075] Omitted in the original and in Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 1075D] *Vicinos testes*, “neighbouring bishops as witnesses”: Thus in the code of canons, almost in the Greek canon, and in the margins of the more recent Cologne editions. In their text, however, and in the older editions, two Vatican manuscripts, and Ivo, one reads: “Let him at least, after the fact, make inquiry, and report this beforehand to the neighbouring bishops and to the council,” etc. But the royal Soria manuscript reads: “Let him take care to do this immediately, or [report] to neighbouring [bishops],” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 1075] *Consilium*, “counsel”: Argentinensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1076C] *Honore amisso*, “having lost office”: These words occur in the council incorporated into the code of canons, in the royal Soria manuscript, and in the Greek canon; but they are absent from every edition of the Fifth Council of Carthage, from the two Vatican copies, and from Ivo.]

C. XL. Whatever an abbot sells without the bishop’s permission is to be annulled. From the Council of Agde, chapter 56.

[Note: [Col. 1075] Held A.D. 506.—Regino, book 1, chapter 355. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 163.—Compare Gratian after chapter 22, Distinction 54.]

In sales which abbots presume to make, this procedure shall be observed: whatever has been sold without the bishop’s permission shall be restored to the bishop’s control.

[Note: [Col. 1076C] *Licentia*, “permission”: so added in the margin of the more recent Cologne editions; but the older editions, manuscript copies, and Ivo read *notitia*, “knowledge” [Col. 1075], as does the Hispanic Collection.]

[Col. 1075C] § 1. Slaves given to monks may not be manumitted by the abbot. For we think it unjust that, while monks perform their daily rural work, their slaves should enjoy the leisure of freedom.

[Note: [Col. 1075] *Abbate*, “by the abbot”: *abbatibus*, “by abbots”: same source.]

[Note: [Col. 1075] *Non liceat*, “it is not lawful”: *licet*, “it is lawful”: collected editions.]

[Col. 1076A]

[Note: [Col. 1075] *Potientur*, “should enjoy”: *ponantur*, “should be placed”: Argentinensis edition.]

Sixth Part. Gratian. Even if an abbot, with the bishop’s consent, has granted a monastery’s possession, the grant shall have no force—unless perhaps the grant was made for erecting the fabric of a church. In that case alone he may give as much as is enclosed by the church walls.

Accordingly Gregory writes in book VII, indiction 1, letter 33, to John, Bishop of Squillace:

[Note: [Col. 1075] Letter 34, written A.D. 598, Maurist edition.—Reduced to an epitome, it is read in Abbo of Fleury, chapter 25, in Mabillon, *Vetera Analecta*.]

C. XLI. Under no title may property of a monastery be separated from its right.

The monks of the aforesaid monastery have complained to us that their abbot granted your Fraternity, under the title of a donation for building [Col. 1076B] a church, land within the fortress of Squillace, extending six hundred feet. Therefore we wish that as much as the walls of the church built can enclose shall be claimed for the right of the church. But whatever may lie outside the walls of that church shall, without any difficulty, return to the rights of the monastery, because the enactments neither of secular laws nor of sacred canons permit monastery property to be separated from its right under any title whatsoever. Therefore restore without delay the donation of that land, which was made contrary to reason.

[Note: [Col. 1076D] *Intra Scyllacaenum castrum*, “within the fortress of Squillace”: Thus corrected from many manuscripts of the letters; some copies of Gratian differed little from this reading. The common text read *in Tranquillitanum* [Col. 1075]: *Transquillitanum*, Venetian editions I–II; *Quillitanum*, Basiliensis; *Squillitanum*, Noric; *Scillatinum*, Argentinensis; *Scillitanum*, original.]

[Note: [Col. 1075] *Et*, “and”: omitted in the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1075] *Vendicari*, “be claimed”: *vendicare*, “claim”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1075] *Ad jura*, “to the rights”: *in jure*, “in the right”: same editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1075] *Revertatur*, “shall return”: *reportatur*, “is carried back”: Basiliensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1075] *De*, “from”: *ab*, “from”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1075] *Ejus*, “its”: *ejusdem*, “of the same”: same editions; Argentinensis and Basiliensis first editions.]

C. XLII. PALEA.

[Note: [Col. 1076D] This *Palea* is absent from the old copies, with one exception, and was rashly transferred here, since it occurs below at 18, question 2, chapter *Quam sit*, § “Hanc ergo,” where some points will be noted.]

[Note: [Col. 1075] Compare note to chapter 5, Cause 18, question 2.—Not found in the Basiliensis edition.]

“Therefore we decree that this document of our writings shall, throughout all time to come, be kept firm and inviolate by you and by all bishops: so that, with the Lord’s help, they may be content solely with the right of their own church, [Col. 1077A] and monasteries may in no way be subject to ecclesiastical impositions, forced public services (*angariae*), or any secular obligations; may render service to no canonical jurisdictions; but, freed from vexations, may accomplish the divine work with the utmost devotion.”

[Note: [Col. 1075] *Scriptorum nostrorum*, “of our writings”: *scripturarum nostrarum*, “of our documents”: collected editions.]

Seventh Part. Gratian. But it must be observed that one thing is to divert Church property to one’s own use or that of relatives—a ruinous covetousness which the sacred canons everywhere forbid and condemn—and another is what, by the dispensation of humane charity, provides for human weakness, namely, that property may sometimes be returned to one who scorns to remain in a sacred undertaking. We read that certain saints did this, not so much by the law of the forum as by the law of heaven. For blessed John the Evangelist returned gold and gems to two young men who repented of having [Col. 1077B] left all their possessions for Christ and distributed them to the poor, so that they might buy back everything they had sold.

But the objection is made: Blessed John did not return offerings that had already been distributed to the poor, but compensated them with other things which had never been counted among the resources of the poor or of churches. Likewise, if an abbot or bishop has possessions that have not yet been numbered among ecclesiastical resources, let him, following blessed John’s example, give those to the person withdrawing; but let him retain the things offered to the Church.

§ 2. There will therefore follow another example showing that the very things which have been offered may laudably be returned.

[Note: [Col. 1077] *Sequetur*, “will follow”: *sequitur*, “follows”: Böhm.]

[Col. 1077C]

For Augustine says in Sermon II, *On the Life of Clerics*:

[Note: [Col. 1077] Sermon 355, Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 177.]

C. XLIII. The Church ought not to accept things offered to it by a person who disinherits his son.

Whoever wishes to make the Church his heir by disinheriting his son, let him find someone else [Col. 1078A] to accept it, not Augustine; indeed, God being gracious, he will find no one. How praiseworthy was the deed of the holy and venerable Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage! How did he fill the mouths of all who know of it with praises of God! For a certain man, having no children and expecting none, gave all his possessions to the Church, retaining the usufruct for himself. Children were later born to him, and the bishop returned to the man—who did not even expect it—what he had given. The bishop had the power not to return it, but this was so by the law of the forum, not by the law of heaven.

[Note: [Col. 1077] *Alterum*, “another”: *alium*, “another [person]”: Basiliensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1077] *Nullum*, “no one”: *neminem*, “no one”: Ivo; collected editions; Böhm.]

[Note: [Col. 1077] *Inveniet*, “will find”: *inveniat*, “may find”: Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 1077] Omitted in the collected editions and the first Basiliensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1077] *Quae*, “what”: *ea quae*, “those things which”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1077] *Habebat*, “had”: *habet*, “has”: Argentinensis, Noric, and Venetian I editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1077] *Poli*, “of heaven”: *coeli*, “of heaven”: original.]

Gratian. Behold: things offered are sometimes returned lawfully and laudably. Nevertheless, this example does not show that a person departing from the religious life ought to receive back what is his. For it is one thing to persevere in one’s profession of life, another to depart from the purpose of one’s order. If Saint Aurelius returned offered goods to one living in lay dress because children had been born to him after the offering, it does not follow that their property should be returned to those entering apostasy. It would be more useful to deprive them of necessities, so that constraint might bring them back to the order from which they had withdrawn. Yet, just as we are commanded to supply necessities to enemies and persecutors, and as the Apostle exhorts us to redeem the time so that we may devote ourselves more freely to prayer: so, lest the Church suffer scandal, lest the departing person plunge into worse evils, lest, because of his possessions, he burn with rage to the destruction of monks or the burning of the monastery, it is more commendable—not, I say, that his property be returned to him, but—that he be permitted to take it away, rather than that these evils be inflicted by him.

# CAUSE XVIII

[Col. 1077]

[Col. 1077C] GRATIAN.

A certain abbot, consecrated bishop, first bestowed much upon his monastery and later acquired more in his episcopate. When the brothers sought a successor for him, [Col. 1077D] the bishop of the place wished to insert himself into the election, so that through him an abbot might be ordained in the monastery; the brothers resist. (Question I.) The first question is whether the monastery may claim what was acquired by the bishop, and whether the episcopal church may claim for itself what [Col. 1078C] was conveyed to the monastery. (Question II.) Secondly, whether the abbot is to be elected and ordained through the bishop, or appointed only by his own brethren.

## QUESTION I

[Col. 1078D]

GRATIAN.

The first question is decided by the Council held at Altheum, in which the following decree is read:

[Note: [Col. 1077D] Burchard, book I, chapter 230, cites a council at Alth., held in the presence of King Conrad; Ivo likewise, part 5, chapter 343, but expressly calls it Altheim. In part 14, chapter 116, Ivo reports more from this council in these words: “In the fifth year of the reign of Conrad, the most pious and most Christian king, a holy general synod was assembled at Altheum (otherwise Altheim), in the district of Rhaetia [Col. 1078D], in the presence, namely, of the lord John, the pope’s *apocrisiarius* [envoy], and of the venerable Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Ostia.” [Col. 1077] Read: “Rhaetia.”]

[Note: [Col. 1077] Perhaps from the Council at Altheim, held A.D. 916.—In the Basiliensis edition it is cited as from the Council at Altheum, otherwise Lateran.—Burchard, book I, chapter 231. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 343.]

[Col. 1079A]

C. I. A monk made bishop shall leave to the monastery what he possessed before consecration; what he acquired after consecration he shall leave to his own church.

It was decreed and reasonably confirmed by the synod according to the holy Fathers that a monk whom canonical election releases from the yoke of the monastic rule and profession, and whom sacred ordination makes a bishop from a monk, may thereafter, as a lawful heir, have the right to claim his paternal inheritance; but whatever he had acquired, or appeared to have possessed, he shall leave to the monastery and to the discretion of the abbot whom he formerly had according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. For after he is ordained bishop, he shall assign to the altar to which he is consecrated and entitled whatever he may acquire according to the sacred [Col. 1079B] canons.

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Regulae*, “of the rule”: *regulari*, “regular”: Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Visus fuerat*, “appeared to have”: *jussus*, “was commanded”: same source.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Titulatur*, “is entitled”: *intitulatur*, “is entitled”: collected editions.]

## QUESTION II

GRATIAN.

First Part. The second question, however, is decided by the authority of the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 50, which says:

[Note: [Col. 1079] Held A.D. 633.—Abbo of Fleury, in Mabillon, *Vetera Analecta*, chapter 23.]

C. I. Abbots and other offices ought to be appointed by bishops.

Let priests claim for themselves in a monastery only what the canons prescribe: namely, to admonish monks toward holy conduct, appoint abbots and other officers, and correct acts done outside the rule. But if they presume to do anything forbidden to monks by the canons, or attempt to usurp anything from the monastery’s property, they shall not lack a sentence of excommunication.

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Monasterio*, “in a monastery”: *monasteriis*, “in monasteries”: Hispanic Collection; Abbo; collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Facta*, “acts”: *acta*, “acts”: Hispanic Collection and collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Quippiam*, “anything”: *quicquam*, “anything”: collected editions.]

[Col. 1079C]

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Illis*, “them”: *eis*, “them”: same editions.]

Second Part. Gratian. Conversely Gregory writes to Castorius, Bishop of Rimini:

[Note: [Col. 1079C] This chapter has the same sense as the following one, which contains the very words of blessed Gregory. Hence this appears to be a summary of the following chapter, and for that reason they are not distinguished in some old copies.]

C. II. The monastic community, not the bishop or any outsider, shall appoint the abbot.

An abbot shall not be ordained in a monastery by a bishop or [Col. 1080A] by any outsider, nor shall Mass be celebrated there by a bishop, so that it may be subject to no church.

C. III. On the same matter. The same [Gregory] to the same Castorius, Bishop, book IV, letter 43.

[Note: [Col. 1079] Letter 41, written A.D. 592, book 2, Maurist edition.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 174 (192). Polycarpus, book 3, title 15; book 4, title 33.]

We wish that no one be ordained abbot in any monastery except the person whom the whole community, by common consent, has requested as worthy in character and deeds of monastic discipline. We absolutely forbid public Masses to be celebrated in a monastery by a bishop or clerics.

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Cuilibet*, “any”: *eidem*, “the same”: original.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Tota*, “whole”: omitted in the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Ordinari volumus*, “we wish [him] to be ordained”: *te volumus ordinare*, “we wish you to ordain”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] Added: *illic*, “there”: original.]

[Note: [Col. 1079D] *Vel clericos*, “or clerics”: These words are not found in Gregory [Col. 1079], though they occur in Anselm; indeed, some passages seem deliberately altered by the compiler.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Monasterio*, “in a monastery”: *monasteriis*, “in monasteries”: collected editions and first Lyons edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Omnimodo*, “absolutely”: *omnino celebrari*, “to be celebrated at all”: collected editions.]

[Col. 1080B]

C. IV. The man whom his community and the owner of the property request to be ordained should be appointed abbot. Pope Pelagius to Mellitus the subdeacon.

[Note: [Col. 1079] An uncertain chapter.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 195. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 24.]

We wish that the person be ordained abbot in a monastery whom both the election of the monks from their own community and the owner of the property, and, what must be observed above all, the manner of life and merit, have requested to be ordained.

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Mellito*: *Milleo*, Anselm; *Melleo*, Ivo.]

C. V. On the liberty of monks. Gregory to all bishops.

[Note: [Col. 1079D] This chapter occurs in the decree of the Lateran Council issued by blessed Gregory for the peace and liberty of monks [Col. 1080C]; it is found in the second volume of the councils among Gregory I’s decrees, and Gregory himself reports the greater part of it in book 7 of the register, first indiction, letter 18, to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] Held A.D. 601.—Nearly the same words occur in letter 15, book 8, to Marinianus, reported by Abbo of Fleury in Mabillon, chapter 15.—Anselm, book 5, chapter 58 (64). Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 11. Polycarpus, book 3, chapter 15.]

How necessary it is to provide for the peace of monks, etc. And below:

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Monachorum*, “of monks”: *monasteriorum*, “of monasteries”: original and collected editions.]

§ 1. Therefore, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we forbid—whose office we exercise in this Roman Church—that no bishop or secular person shall hereafter presume in any way, on account of the revenues, property, or charters of monasteries, or of their cells or hamlets, to diminish them, or to commit any frauds, intrusions, or acts of violence against them.

[Note: [Col. 1079] Added: “our”: original; Ivo; collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Prohibemus*, “we forbid”: omitted in the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] Added: “holy”: Basiliensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1080D] *Aut saecularium*, “or secular persons”: absent from some editions of the councils and Gratian manuscripts [Col. 1079], though not from Anselm and Ivo.]

[Col. 1080C]

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Vel rebus*, “or property”: omitted in the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1080D] *Chartis*, “charters”: the council reads *curtis*, “estates,” but the letter and Ivo read *chartis*, “charters” [Col. 1079], as does the Maurist edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] *De*, “of”: omitted in the collected editions, first Argentinensis and Basiliensis editions, and Lyons II–III.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Cellulis*, “cells”: *cellis*, “cells”: original, cited collections, and Argentinensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] *De villulis*, “of hamlets”: *villis*, “estates”: original, cited collections, and collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] Added: “that is, new legal actions”: Argentinensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Aut violentias*, “or acts of violence”: omitted in the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] Added: “against themselves”: Basiliensis and Lyons II–III editions.]

And below:

[Note: [Col. 1079] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 181. Polycarpus, book 4, title 33.]

§ 2. When the abbot of any community has died, no outsider shall be chosen, but one from that same community whom the united brotherhood has freely chosen; and the person elected shall be ordained without fraud or any venal payment. If they cannot find among themselves a suitable person, they shall diligently choose someone from other monasteries, likewise to be ordained.

[Note: [Col. 1079] *Cujusquam*, “of any”: *cujuscunque*, “of whatsoever”; *cujusque*, “of each”: collected editions, Ivo *Panormia*, original, and Ivo *Decretum*.]

[Note: [Col. 1079] “No outsider shall be chosen”: omitted by Ivo.]

[Col. 1081A]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Quem*, “whom”: *et quem*, “and whom”: Basiliensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Et qui electus fuerit sine dolo vel venalitate aliqua ordinetur*, “and the person elected shall be ordained without fraud or any venal payment”: omitted in the collected editions.]

And below:

§ 3. It must equally be observed that monks ought not to be taken from a monastery, against the abbot’s will, in order to govern other monasteries or to receive sacred orders or a clerical office.

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Ad ordinandum*, “to govern”: *ordinanda*, “to be governed”: original and Ivo *Panormia*.]

And below:

§ 4. No monk may hold any position in a church or be promoted to any office without the testimony and permission of his abbot.

[Note: [Col. 1081C] From this point to the end, these provisions are not found in the letter, but in the council.]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Nullus monachus*, “no monk”: *monachum*, “a monk”: original, Anselm, and collected editions, first Argentinensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *In ecclesia aliquem locum teneat*, “hold any position in a church”: original, Anselm, and collected editions read *ecclesia aliqua teneatur*, “be held in any church.”]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Teneat*, “may hold”: *teneatur*, “may be held”: Argentinensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Promoveatur*, “be promoted”: *promoveat*, “promote”: collected editions and first Argentinensis edition.]

§ 5. Therefore we decree that this document of our writings shall throughout all time to come be kept firm and inviolate by all bishops, so that, with the Lord’s help, they may be content solely with the right of their own churches; and that monasteries may in no way be subject to ecclesiastical impositions, forced services, or any secular obligations, may render service to no canonical jurisdictions, but, with vexations and every burden removed, may fulfil the divine work with the highest devotion of mind.

[Note: [Col. 1081] Compare Cause 17, question 4, chapter 42.]

[Note: [Col. 1081C] *Ut et suae ecclesiae*: The council reads: “And let the holy Church, with the Lord’s help, be content with its own boundary or right,” etc. But letter 43, book 4—where almost the same thing is written to Castorius, bishop of Rimini—reads: “So that your church, with the Lord’s help, may be content solely with its own right, and that monastery,” etc. [Col. 1081D]]

[Col. 1081B]

[Note: [Col. 1081D] *Juribus*, “jurisdictions”: the council reads *curis*, “cares”; the letter reads *canonicaeve jurisdictioni*, “canonical jurisdiction.”]

C. VI. Bishops are not to celebrate public Masses in a monastery, lest they impose any burden on it. The same [Gregory] to Castorius, Bishop of Rimini.

[Note: [Col. 1082C] In book four of the register these are letters 41, to Abbot Luminosus, and 43, to Castorius, Bishop of Rimini [Col. 1081]: Letter 41, written A.D. 592, book 2, Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapters 12–13. They contain the passages relevant to this chapter. Yet the precise words down to “Masses” occur not in those letters but in the council discussed in the immediately preceding chapter [Col. 1082D], except for the opening words, “At the report of Abbot Luminosus”; certain matters have been corrected and added from it.]

At the report of Abbot Luminosus, we have learned that in many monasteries monks have endured many wrongs and burdens from bishops. Your Fraternity’s care must therefore make a salutary provision for their future peace, so that those living in them may, with God’s grace supporting them, persevere in His service with free minds. We absolutely forbid public Masses to be celebrated in monasteries, lest an occasion for any popular assembly be afforded in the retreats and dwellings of God’s servants, or women be admitted there; for this is not beneficial to their souls. Nor may a bishop dare to establish his chair there or exercise any power of command, or carry out any ordination, however slight, unless invited by the abbot of the place, so that monks may always remain under the authority of their abbots and, all vexations and burdens removed, may accomplish the divine work with the utmost devotion of mind.

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Ipsius*, “of Him”: *illis*, “them”: collected editions.]

[Col. 1081C]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *In coenobiis*, “in monasteries”: original reads *ab eo in coenobio*, “by him in the monastery.”]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *In*, “in”: omitted in the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Vel mulierum fiat illis introitus*, “or women be admitted there”: original reads *novus*, “new”; Böhm reads *illic*, “there.”]

[Note: [Col. 1082D] *Episcopus*, “bishop”: the council continues: “or anyone endowed with any other dignity or power, or [exercise] any authority of command,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 1081] Omitted in the original.]

[Col. 1082A]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Exercere*, “exercise”: *habere*, “have”: original.]

[Note: [Col. 1081] Compare above, chapter 5.]

C. VII. A baptistery may not be established in a monastery. Pope Gregory, book II, indiction 11, letter 56, to Bishop Secundinus.

[Note: [Col. 1081] Letter 59, written A.D. 593, book 3, Maurist edition.—Formerly cited as Gelasius.—Polycarpus, book 4, title 34.]

We previously ordered that the baptistery be removed from the monastery of Saint Andrew, which is above Mascalas, on account of the disturbance it caused the monks, and that an altar be established in the place where the fonts are. Completion of this matter has so far been delayed. Therefore we admonish your Fraternity that, once you have received this present letter of ours, you ought to permit no further delay; but, after the place of the fonts has been filled in, let an altar for celebrating the sacred mysteries be established there without any delay, so that the aforesaid monks may more securely celebrate the work of God, and our mind may not be provoked against your Fraternity because of your negligence.

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Mascalas*: *Maschalas*, Basiliensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Molestias*, “disturbances”: *insolentias*, “insolences”: original.]

[Col. 1082B]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Ut*: omitted in the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Inserere*, “to introduce”: *inferre*, “to bring in”: Argentinensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Deb(e)as*, “you ought”: omitted in the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Ad sacra celebranda mysteria*, “for celebrating the sacred mysteries”: omitted in the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Secur(i)us*, “more securely”: *secure*, “securely”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1081] “Your”: omitted in the Basiliensis edition; the other editions read *tua*, “your.”]

C. VIII. With the bishop’s permission an abbot may leave his place. From the Council of Mainz.

[Note: [Col. 1081] Something similar occurs in the Council of Mainz, held A.D. 847. The same words occur in Theodore’s Penitential, chapter 6.—Burchard, book 8, chapter 86. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 104.]

An abbot, for the sake of humility and with the bishop’s permission, may leave his place; nevertheless the brothers shall choose an abbot from among themselves, if they have one; otherwise, from outsiders.

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Pro*, “for”: *propter humiliationem*, “for the sake of humility”: Basiliensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1081] *Relinquere*, “leave”: *deserere*, “abandon”: Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 1081] Added: “if they have [one]”: Burchard; “if they have”: original in Theodore, collected editions, and Böhm.]

[Col. 1082C]

Third Part. Gratian. Behold, in the Council of Toledo it is said that priests ought to appoint abbots and other officers. Blessed Gregory and Pelagius prohibit this, saying that an abbot is to be elected and ordained by the brothers of his own community. How, then, can so great a divergence be brought into harmony? But it must be understood that some monks are stiff-necked and of unbridled [Col. 1083A] pride. When abbots attempt to compel them toward religious discipline, they conspire to depose them and strive to place over themselves another suited to their own character—such as those who are recorded to have conspired to kill blessed Benedict. It was for persons of this kind that it was decreed that abbots and other officers should be appointed by priests.

Accordingly Pope Pelagius writes to Opilio the *defensor*:

[Note: [Col. 1083] An uncertain chapter.—Collection in three parts, part I, title 54, chapter 17.—Anselm, book 7, chapter 185 (194).]

C. IX. Monks may not at their own discretion expel abbots or appoint others.

Henceforth we leave monks no power and no permission, at their own discretion, either to expel abbots or appoint others for themselves—since no authority will remain to an abbot if he begins [Col. 1083B] to be subject to the power of monks—so that henceforth the abbot’s diligence, to whom all authority ought properly to belong, may faithfully and diligently perform everything pertaining either to the reverence of divine worship or to the benefit of that monastery.

Fourth Part. Gratian. Hence also it was decreed that the clerics of individual monasteries should be under the power of bishops, and that no one may build monasteries without their knowledge.

Accordingly, in the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 4, one reads:

[Note: [Col. 1083C] Since the translation of this chapter up to § 1, “First, clerics,” differs from those current in the codices of the councils, although Ivo and the *Panormia* convey nearly the same sense, it seemed appropriate to give the Greek words and a new translation:

“Οἱ ἀληθῶς καὶ εἰλικρινῶς τὸν μονήρη μετιόντες βίον, τῆς προσηκούσης ἀξιούσθωσαν τιμῆς. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ τινες τῷ μοναχικῷ κεχρημένοι προσχήματι, τάς τε ἐκκλησίας καὶ τὰ πολιτικὰ διαταράσσουσι πράγματα, περιόντες ἀδιαφόρως ἐν ταῖς πόλεσιν, οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ μοναστήρια ἑαυτοῖς συνιστᾶν ἐπιτηδεύοντες, ἔδοξεν μηδένα μὲν μηδαμοῦ οἰκοδομεῖν, μηδὲ συνιστᾶν μοναστήριον ἢ εὐκτήριον [Col. 1083D] οἶκον παρὰ γνώμην τοῦ τῆς πόλεως ἐπισκόπου.”

That is: “Let those who truly and sincerely pursue the solitary life be accorded the honour due to them. But since some, using the appearance of monasticism, disturb both churches and civil affairs, wandering indiscriminately in the cities and, moreover, undertaking to establish monasteries for themselves, it has seemed good that no one anywhere should build or establish a monastery [Col. 1084C] or house of prayer without the approval of the bishop of the city.”]

[Note: [Col. 1083] The author of the translation supplied in the proem to the canon has not been discovered. §§ 1 and 2 are taken from the Isidorian version; § 3 from the ancient translation.]

C. X. No one shall build a monastery without the bishop’s knowledge.
