Some wearing the habit of monks roam indiscriminately through cities and even commend monasteries and themselves by their own presumption. It was therefore resolved that no one should build or establish monasteries or a house of prayer without the knowledge of the bishop of that city.

[Note: [Col. 1083] Added: “through”: Basiliensis and Lyons I editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1083] *Monasteria*, “monasteries”: *monasterium*, “a monastery”: Argentinensis, Noric, and Venetian I editions.]

[Col. 1083C]

From the same chapter 8:

§ 1. Clerics established in poorhouses (*ptochia*), [Col. 1084A] monasteries, or martyr-shrines shall be under the authority of the bishop of the city in which they are, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, and shall not presumptuously withdraw from their bishop. § 2. Those who dare in any way to abolish such an institution, or who refuse to be subject to their own bishop, shall, if they are clerics, be subject to the penalties of the canons according to the rank of their persons; but if laypersons or monks, they shall be deprived of communion.

[Note: [Col. 1083] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 358.]

[Note: [Col. 1084C] *Ptochiis*: Thus in some old Gratian manuscripts, in the Vatican council manuscript, and in the ancient translation—from which this little passage seems to derive—and it is the word used by the Greek canon. But the common Gratian editions and some council books read *parochiis*, “parishes” [Col. 1083], as does Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 1083] *Et in*, “and in”: *monasterii*, “of a monastery”: Argentinensis edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1083] *Eos*, “those”: *si*, “if”: Hispanic Collection.]

[Note: [Col. 1083] *Institutionem*, “institution”: *ordinationem*, “ordination”: same source.]

[Note: [Col. 1084C] *Pro personarum ordinatione*, “according to the rank of their persons”: thus in the same ancient translation [Col. 1083]; collected editions read *secundum personarum ordinationem*, with the same sense; the Hispanic Collection reads *paternorum ordinationem*, “according to paternal ordinances.” But in the Greek canon and Dionysius Exiguus’s translation there is nothing corresponding to these words.]

[Note: [Col. 1083] “Of the canons”: omitted there.]

[Note: [Col. 1083] *Communione priventur*, “be deprived of communion”: *excommunicentur*, “be excommunicated”: same source.]

From the same source:

[Note: [Col. 1083] Ivo, same place, chapter 359.]

§ 3. Clerics who preside over the administration of the poor, monasteries, or martyr-shrines shall remain under the authority of the bishops of their respective cities according to the tradition of the canons, and shall not, through their own rashness, decline the governance of their bishop. But those who dare in any way to subvert such administration and do not obey their bishop shall, if they are clerics, be subject to canonical condemnation; but if they are monks or laypersons, they shall be suspended from communion.

[Note: [Col. 1084C] “Again, clerics”: This is the same as the paragraph immediately above, but from another translation, which does not occur in the volumes of councils; this same repetition may also be observed in Ivo, part 6, chapters 358 and 359 [Col. 1084D].]

[Note: [Col. 1083] *Dispositioni*, “administration”: *dispensationi*, “stewardship”: original in Ballerini.]

[Note: [Col. 1083] Added: “holy”: same source and Ivo.]

[Col. 1084B]

C. XI. A person to be placed over religious women shall be examined by the bishop. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 97.

[Note: [Col. 1083] Chapter 39 of the *Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua*.—Compare note to chapter 9, Distinction 18.—Burchard, book 8, chapter 76. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 94.]

The man who is to be placed over religious women shall be approved by the bishop of the place.

[Note: [Col. 1083] *Qui*, “who”: original reads *vir, qui*, “the man who.”]

[Note: [Col. 1083] *Est*, “is”: *sit*, “shall be”: Burchard and Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 1083] *Episcopo*, “bishop”: *episcopis*, “bishops”: collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1083] *Loci*, “of the place”: omitted in the cited collections.]

[Note: [Col. 1083] *Comprobetur*, “shall be approved”: *probetur*, “shall be approved”: cited collections and the original.]

Gratian. Likewise, no one may begin or found a monastery without the bishop’s permission.

Accordingly, in the Council of Agde, chapter 27, one reads:

[Note: [Col. 1083] Held A.D. 506.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 157.]

C. XII. Without the bishop’s permission no one shall presume to begin or found a monastery.

No one among monks shall presume to begin or found a new monastery unless the bishop permits or approves it.

[Col. 1084C]

[Note: [Col. 1084D] *De monachis*, “Concerning monks”: these words are absent from the more recent editions of the councils [Col. 1083] and the Hispanic Collection, but not from the older editions, manuscript copies, or Ivo.]

C. XIII. On the same matter. From the same source, chapter 58.

[Note: [Col. 1085] Rather, from the Council of Epaone, chapter 10.—Compare note to chapter 30, Distinction 23.—Burchard, book 8, chapter 74. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, chapter 165; part 7, chapter 92.]

We forbid new cells or small monastic communities to be established without the bishop’s knowledge.

[Col. 1085A]

[Note: [Col. 1085C] *Congregatiunculas*, “small communities”: formerly the text read *congregantium*, “of those assembling” [Col. 1085]; the Basiliensis edition reads *congregationum*, “of congregations.” It was corrected from most manuscripts and the passages cited.]

C. XIV. No monk shall presume to build a cell without the consent of bishop or abbot. From the First Council of Orléans, chapter 24.

[Note: [Col. 1085] Held A.D. 511.—Compare Capitularies, book 6, chapter 140.]

No monk, having abandoned the community of his monastery, may presume, under the impulse of ambition and vanity [variant: “variation,” editions collectively], to build a cell [variant: “cells,” Basel edition; addition: “for himself,” Hispana Collection] without the bishop’s permission or his own abbot’s consent.

**Part V. Gratian.** There are also others who, for the prosecution of various affairs, admit indiscriminately persons who dissolve their discipline and disturb the peace of religious life.

[Col. 1085B] Concerning these it is read in the Council of Tribur [Note: Something similar is read in the Rule of Benedict, ch. 60, above Distinction 61, ch. 14; Burchard, bk. 8, ch. 96; Ivo, *Decrees*, part 7, ch. 114]:

**Chapter XV. An abbot who is not prudent in government is to be deprived of his office by his own bishop and neighboring abbots.**

If any abbot is not prudent in government, humble, chaste, merciful, discerning, and sober, and does not show forth the divine commandments by word and example, he is to be deprived of his office by the bishop in whose territory he resides, by neighboring abbots, and by the other God-fearing; even if the whole community, consenting to his vices, should wish to retain him as abbot.

**Chapter XVI. Abbots are subject to the authority of bishops.** Likewise from the First Council of Orléans, ch. 21 [Note: held A.D. 511; Burchard, bk. 8, ch. 67; Ivo, *Decrees*, part 7, ch. 85; cf. *Capitularies*, bk. 6, ch. 139].

**Part VI.** Abbots, for the sake of the humility [variant: “usefulness,” Hispana Collection; yet “humility” is found in the variant readings] of religious life, are to remain under the authority of bishops; and, if they do anything contrary to the rule, they are to be corrected by the bishops. Once [Note: This is likewise read in the printed and manuscript councils and in the *Capitularies*. But in Burchard and Ivo, after “are to be corrected,” ch. “Not once,” below in the same distinction, has been inserted] a year, when summoned, they are to assemble at the place chosen by the bishop.

§ 1. Monks, moreover, are to be subject to their abbots with every obedience and devotion. If anyone proves disobedient through contumacy, or [variant: “and,” Hispana Collection; Burchard; Ivo] presumes to wander about from place to place, or [variant: “and,” Hispana Collection; Burchard; Ivo] to possess anything as his private property, everything he has acquired is to be taken away by the abbots, according to the Rule, for the benefit of the monastery [variant: “which is to benefit,” ibid.]. Those who have wandered about are, wherever they are found, to be brought back under guard as fugitives with the assistance of the bishop [addition: “and restrained,” Burchard; Ivo].

§ 2. Let that abbot recognize that he will be guilty who does not punish such persons [variant: “such persons,” dative, editions collectively except the first Lyons editions] according to the Rule [variant: “subjects them to regular discipline,” Hispana Collection], or who receives another abbot’s monk.

**Chapter XVII. On the same matter.** Likewise from the Council of Arles [Note: ch. 2, Fifth Council of Arles, held A.D. 554].

Monasteries and the discipline of monks belong to the bishop in whose territory they are established.

**Chapter XVIII. No bishop is to administer episcopal functions to abbots unwilling to be subject to any bishop.** Pope Paschal II [Note: A chapter of uncertain source].

No bishop whatsoever is to administer any episcopal functions to abbots who are subject neither to a bishop, nor to a metropolitan, nor to a primate, nor to a patriarch. For since they profess themselves absolutely subject to no bishop, it follows [Col. 1086B] that no bishop should bestow upon them, as outsiders, those things which are his own.

**Gratian.** For this reason it has been established that the affairs and interests of monasteries are to be administered through bishops.

Accordingly Gregory writes to Vitalis, Defender of Sardinia, book VII, epistle 65 [Note: Epistle 64, written A.D. 599, bk. 9, Maurist edition; Anselm, bk. 7, ch. 184 (202)]:

**Chapter XIX. The interests of a monastery must be administered by its own bishop.**

We have learned that each person, at his own pleasure and in pursuit of various affairs, disturbs monasteries of God’s servants, whether men or women [variant: “they disturb,” original; Anselm; Argentinensis edition; “may disturb,” remaining editions]. We do not accept this at all favorably; and we admonish your experience on this point that, having received our authority, you must not again permit anyone to usurp this practice [variant: “be usurped,” Lyons editions II and III]. Rather, the bishop of the place, under whose governance they live, is to have the care of administering their affairs and interests [omitted in Argentinensis, Basel, and Nuremberg editions]. For it is very unfitting [variant: “indecent,” editions collectively] that, passing him over, any other person should interfere in their affairs; rather, he who is compelled to render account to God [addition: “to God,” Basel and Lyons editions II and III] for the souls entrusted to him ought to order their life by fitting and regular governance.

**Part VII. Gratian.** For this reason also St Gregory forbids women indiscriminately to approach a monastery and to make themselves the monks’ *commatres*—spiritual co-mothers—writing to Valentinus, abbot, book III, epistle 40 [Note: Epistle 42, written A.D. 594, bk. 4, Maurist edition; Anselm, same book, ch. 183 (201)]:

[Col. 1087A] **Chapter XX. Monks may neither make women their *commatres* nor approach women.**

It has come to us that women freely enter [variant: “approach,” Lyons and Paris editions] your monastery and, what is still more serious, make your monks their *commatres*, and thereby have an imprudent familiarity with them. Therefore, lest on this occasion the enemy of the human race deceive them—God forbid—by his cunning, we admonish you in this tenor of command: henceforth, you are to permit no women, on any pretext, to enter [variant: “approach,” same editions] your monastery; nor are you to permit your monks to make women their *commatres*. For if this should in any way again come to our ears, know that you will be subjected to so very severe a punishment [variant: “to the most severe punishment,” original; Lyons editions II and III; Böhm] that others will unquestionably be corrected by the character of your punishment.

[Col. 1087B] **Part VIII. Gratian.** Not only is imprudent familiarity with other women forbidden to them, but they are also prohibited from dwelling with nuns.

Accordingly it is read in the Seventh Synod, ch. 20 [Note: held A.D. 787; Ivo, *Decrees*, part 7, ch. 25]:

**Chapter XXI. Monks may not live with nuns.**

We determine that a double monastery is by no means to be established, since it becomes a scandal and stumbling-block to many. If any persons, together with relatives, should wish to renounce the world and pursue the monastic life, men should indeed enter a community of men and women a monastery of women. For in this [variant: “thence,” Argentinensis edition; “therefore,” Basel edition] God is pleased.

§ 1. But those which until now have been [variants: “are,” Ivo and Argentinensis edition; “have been,” Basel edition] double are to be organized in accordance with the Rule of our holy father Basil and his command. Monks and nuns are not [variant: “so that monks and nuns may not,” ibid.] to live in one monastery. For adultery interrupts cohabitation [Note: This has been emended from most manuscripts of Gratian—thus also in the Basel edition and Ivo—and from two manuscripts of Anastasius’s translation, though this is not wholly that translation. Formerly it read “cohabitation”; the Greek is: *μοιχεῖα γὰρ μεσολαβεῖ τὴν συνδιαίτησιν*, “for adultery comes between cohabitation”], if a monk has [variant: “has access,” Basel edition; original: “does not have access”] access to a nun, or a nun to a monk, for a private individual conversation.

§ 2. A monk is not to sleep in a women’s monastery, nor dine alone with a nun. When the necessities of life are brought from the men’s side to the religious women [variants: “to the nuns,” Ivo; Basel and Lyons editions; “to the holy women,” Argentinensis edition], the abbess of the women’s monastery is to receive them outside the gate, together with some elderly nun [variant: “a certain elderly nun,” Ivo; editions collectively].

§ 3. Moreover, if it should happen that a monk wishes to see some female relative, he is to speak with her in the presence of the abbess, using few and brief words, and depart from her quickly [Note: “And quickly” is not in the standard printed edition of the Greek canons, but occurs in Balsamon].

**Chapter XXII. Monks and nuns may not dwell together in any place.** Likewise in Gregory’s *Register* [Note: Burchard and Ivo also cite Gregory, in whom there is some relevant material: *Register*, bk. 1, ep. 48, and bk. 7, indiction 2, ep. 39. The actual words, however, are found in Julian the Antecessor, Novella 123, ch. 54.] [Note: Rather, Julian, *Epitome* of Novella 115, ch. 57; Anselm’s collection, bk. 6, ch. 119; Burchard, bk. 8, ch. 65; Ivo, *Decrees*, part 7, ch. 83; Polycarpus, bk. 4, title 34].

We permit monks and nuns to inhabit no single monastery [variants: “into one,” editions collectively except Argentinensis, which reads “in one”], nor even those which are called [variant: “are called,” editions collectively] double monasteries [addition: “monasteries,” editions collectively except Argentinensis and Basel]. If there is any such establishment, a conscientious bishop is to take care that the women remain in their own place and compel the monks to build another monastery for themselves [addition: “for themselves,” original]. But if there are many such monasteries [variant: “more,” ibid.], nuns are to be separated into different monasteries and monks into others; and the property which they hold in common is to be distributed to them according to the rights belonging to them.

**Chapter XXIII. Monasteries of girls are to be built at a greater distance from monasteries of monks.** Likewise from the Council of Agde, ch. 28 [Note: held A.D. 506; Ivo, *Decrees*, part 3, ch. 158].

Monasteries of girls are to be situated farther away [variant: “far,” Basel edition] from monasteries [variants: “a monastery,” Ivo and editions collectively] of monks, whether because of the snares of the devil or because of human reproaches [variant: singular “reproach,” same editions].

**Chapter XXIV. Monasteries of girls are to be governed under the protection and ministry of monks.** Likewise from the Second Council of Seville, ch. 11 [Note: held A.D. 619; *Collectio tripartita*, part 2, title 49, ch. 6].

In the tenth session [variant: “eleventh,” Hispana Collection] we have decreed by common consent that monasteries of virgins founded in the province of Baetica [variants: “Bethelica,” Nuremberg and Venice editions; “Bethilica,” remaining editions except Basel and Lyons I; addition: “founded,” Hispana Collection] are to be governed by the administration and protection of monks. For then we provide wholesome support [variants: “we provide,” Hispana Collection; “we approve,” editions collectively except Basel and Lyons I] for virgins dedicated to Christ when we choose [variant: “have chosen,” Hispana Collection] spiritual fathers for them, by whose guidance they may not only be protected but also built up by their teaching. Yet this precaution concerning the monks must be observed: removed from familiarity [variant: “private property,” Hispana Collection] with the women, they are not even to have habitual permission to approach as far as the vestibule. Nor is it permissible for the abbot, or the person who presides, to say anything to the virgins of Christ outside the presence of the woman who presides over them, which pertains to their instruction [Note: The old manuscripts of Gratian read “which pertains to their instruction”; editions collectively except Basel read “instruction or administration,” while the more recent Cologne editions read “which does not pertain to moral instruction”]. Nor should they speak frequently even with that woman alone [omitted in the Hispana Collection], but only in the presence of two or three sisters, so that visits may be infrequent and conversation altogether brief.

**Part IX. Gratian.** Nuns are also forbidden to possess private quarters.

Accordingly Innocent II, in the Council held at Rome, chs. 26 and 27 [Note: Second Lateran Council, held A.D. 1139], says:

**Chapter XXV. Nuns may not possess private rooms or dwellings.**

We decree that the pernicious and detestable custom of certain women be abolished—women who, although they live neither according to the Rule of St Benedict, nor that of Basil or Augustine, nevertheless wish commonly to be considered nuns. For while, according to the Rule [Note: The standard printed texts added “of St Benedict” here; yet other rules were mentioned immediately above. Those words have therefore been removed on the authority of old manuscripts and of the council itself, from which some other passages have likewise been corrected], dwelling in communities, they ought to be together both in church and in refectory and dormitory, they build private rooms and separate dwellings for themselves. There, under the pretext of hospitality, they are not ashamed to receive indiscriminately guests, including less religious persons [omitted in Lyons editions II and III], contrary to the sacred canons [omitted in editions collectively except Lyons II and III] and good morals. Since, therefore, everyone who does evil hates the light, and they accordingly think that, concealed in the dwelling-place of the righteous, they can hide from the eyes of the Judge who sees all things [variant: “beholds,” editions collectively], we altogether forbid, and prohibit under pain of anathema, this so shameful and detestable crime [addition: “unjust,” Basel edition] from continuing.

§ 1. In the same way we forbid nuns to meet together with canons or monks in one choir in church for psalmody.

[Col. 1089C] **Part X. Gratian.** There are others also who, burdening them, neglect the salvation of their souls and seek upon any pretext to alienate the goods of monasteries. Such were certain clerics of the church of Ravenna, who, under a feigned religious profession, wished to be set over monasteries without adopting monastic dress or renouncing ecclesiastical service.

Concerning them Gregory writes to John, Bishop of Ravenna, book IV, epistle 1 [Note: Epistle 1, written A.D. 595, bk. 5, Maurist edition; Anselm, bk. 5, ch. 61 (65); Ivo, *Decrees*, part 3, ch. 18; Polycarpus, bk. 3, ch. 15]:

**Chapter XXVI. Monasteries ought not to become residences of clerics or laypersons.**

[Col. 1090A] It has come to me that in the churches [variant: “church,” editions collectively; Ivo] of your brotherhood certain places, formerly [omitted in Gregory and Ivo] consecrated as monasteries, have now become dwellings either of clerics or even of laypersons. Those who are in the churches pretend to live religiously, seek to be set over monasteries, and through their manner of life monasteries are destroyed. For no one can [perform] ecclesiastical offices [Note: *Causa* 16, question 1, ch. 2] etc. And below:

§ 1. Therefore let your brotherhood hasten to correct this, wherever it has occurred [variant: “if this … has occurred,” editions collectively], because I by no means permit [variant: “will permit,” original and editions collectively] sacred places to be destroyed by clerical ambition.

[Col. 1090B] **Chapter XXVII. Those constituted in sacred orders are to have no authority in monasteries.** The same to Marinianus, Bishop of Ravenna, book VI, epistle 40 [Note: Epistle 43, written A.D. 597, bk. 7, Maurist edition; Anselm, bk. 5, ch. 65 (66); Polycarpus, same place].

Long ago reports from many persons reached us that monasteries established in the region of Ravenna [variants: “Ravennatine,” original, Anselm, and Argentinensis edition; “of Ravenna,” Lyons I and Paris editions; “of the people of Ravenna,” remaining editions] were altogether oppressed by the domination of your clerics. Under the pretext of, as it were, governing them, they possess those monasteries [addition: “indeed,” editions collectively]—a grievous thing to say—as their own property. Greatly grieving for them, we sent letters to your predecessor [variant: “to your predecessor … letters,” same editions], requiring him to correct this in every respect. But since he was overtaken too soon by the end of life, lest this burden should remain [variant: “remain,” same editions] upon the monasteries, we recall that we have written these same things to your brotherhood [variant: “now,” Argentinensis edition]. Since, as we have learned, correction of this matter has so far been neglected, we have thought fit to send these letters to you once more [addition: “having heard this,” Anselm and editions collectively].

We therefore exhort you, putting aside every delay [Col. 1090C] and every excuse, to endeavor to relieve the monasteries themselves from this burden, so that henceforth neither clerics nor those constituted in sacred orders [the words “nor those who are” are omitted in the Basel edition] may have permission to enter them for any purpose other than solely for exhortation [Note: The printed and manuscript original, and Anselm, read “for prayer.” It has not been altered because of the gloss and because the word “exhorting” occurs in the following chapter; other matters, however, have been corrected], unless perhaps they are invited to celebrate the sacred mysteries of the Mass [variant: “ministries,” Basel edition]. But, lest [there be interference] for the advancement of any monk or abbot, etc. [Note: *Causa* 16, question 1, ch. 37]. And below:

§ 1. Nor are they thereafter to have any authority there [variant: “have,” Basel edition], lest monasteries, under cover of this pretext, be compelled to bear the burdens which we forbid [Note: Standard printed editions continued: “together with canons and monks in church”; these words have been removed on the authority of the original and two copies of Gratian]. Therefore, let your holiness, now admonished for the second time, not delay to correct all these matters with watchful care [variant: “zeal,” Basel edition], lest, if after this we find you negligent—which we do not believe—we be compelled to make other provision for the peace of the monasteries. For let it be known to you that we do not permit the community of servants of God to remain subject any longer [variant: “will not permit,” editions collectively; Böhm] to so great a necessity.

**Chapter XXVIII. A bishop may visit a monastery for purposes of visitation and exhortation.** Likewise to the same person, book VII, indiction 1, epistle 18 [Note: Epistle 16, written A.D. 598, bk. 8, Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decrees*, part 7, ch. 14].

**Part XI.** For the purpose of visitation and exhortation, the bishop of the city may visit a monastery whenever he sees fit; but the bishop must carry out there the office of charity in such a way that the monastery incurs no burden.

**Chapter XXIX. Bishops are to visit monasteries frequently and correct what needs correction.** Likewise from the Council of Orléans [Note: This chapter is inserted in Burchard and Ivo under the chapter “Abbots,” above in the same distinction, as noted there; something similar occurs in Panormia from the Council of Rouen, bk. 3, ch. 215] [Note: ch. 10, Council of Rouen, held A.D. 650, reduced to an epitome; Burchard, bk. 8, ch. 67; Ivo, *Decrees*, part 7, ch. 85].

Not once, but more often in the year, bishops are to visit monasteries of monks; and, if anything requires correction, it is to be corrected.

**Part XII. Gratian.** On account of persons who, though they have no care of souls, nevertheless wished to divert the goods of monasteries to their own uses, it was established that monasteries with their property should be wholly free from the power and domination of bishops. Yet the statement that monasteries are subject to no canonical laws is not to be understood as excluding an offering to the bishop, under the name of a *eulogia*—a blessing-gift—either on the day of dedication or on the feast day of the saints in whose name the monastery itself is dedicated.

Accordingly Pope Pelagius [Note: Formerly this read “Gelasius.” It has been changed on the authority of Polycarpus, because another part of this same letter above, Distinction 91, ch. “Eleutherius,” is cited from Pelagius, and because Anselm, who brings both chapters together, attributes them to Pelagius] says [Note: A chapter of uncertain date; Anselm, bk. 7, ch. 145 (169); Polycarpus, bk. 4, title 27]:

**Chapter XXX. A bishop must not demand anything from a monastery beyond the terms established at its dedication.**

Our brother and fellow bishop Eleutherius complains that his mother built and dedicated an oratory on an estate called Castellum, and established monks in the same place, one of whom is a priest. At the time of its dedication, he asserts, it was agreed between Bishop Cardellus, whose diocese it is, and his mother that whatever came in through the offerings of the faithful on the day of dedication or the feast day of the martyrs whose relics are in that monastery, one half should belong to the monastery itself and the other half be offered to the bishop. Contrary to this agreement, the priest Marius [variants: “Marius the priest,” Basel edition; “Marianus the priest,” Argentinensis edition; the name Marius is omitted in the Nuremberg edition] is said, whether with the bishop’s knowledge or without it, to have done violence to the monks themselves or to the priest who is one of them, and to cause frequent troubles; so much so that he nearly struck the said priest and in no way permits him to celebrate Mass, saying that he ought to establish some payment as though it were a rent.

We therefore command you carefully to investigate all these matters; and if it is established before you by clear [variant: “clearly established,” Argentinensis edition] evidence [variant: “truth,” Anselm] that, at the time when that monastery was dedicated, the conditions stated above were agreed upon, we command by our authority that they be observed and that nothing further be demanded from it by anyone [variants: “nor,” Basel edition; “otherwise,” Lyons I edition; “attempted to be demanded,” Anselm]. But if nothing of the kind is established [addition: “between them,” Venice II, Paris, and Lyons editions], we wish that through your mediation it be decided between the monks and the priest what ought to be offered to that bishop as a *eulogia*. Yet it remains secure that the priest Gaudentius, who is also a monk, must no longer be forbidden by anyone to celebrate Mass in his own monastery as he has been accustomed to do.

**Chapter XXXI. Monasteries are to render to bishops their customary services.** Likewise Urban II [Note: Rather, ch. 19 of the First Lateran Council, held A.D. 1123].

[Col. 1092C] We also grant the service which monasteries or their churches have rendered from the time of Gregory VII until this time.

**Gratian.** The canonical laws to which monasteries are not subject, therefore, mean synodal exactions. For an abbot is not to be compelled—as is established in the Council of Tours—to attend a synod unless some reasonable cause exists. There are also certain servile obligations, such as compulsory labor-services, frequent billeting, annual exactions, and fines imposed upon offenders; from all of these monasteries are free.

# CAUSE XIX

[Col. 1093]

[Col. 1093A] **GRATIAN**

Two clerics wished to enter a monastery. Each sought leave from his bishop: one abandoned his own church against the bishop’s will; the other left a house of regular canons and went to a monastic community. The question is now raised: (Question I) must the bishop permit a cleric to enter a monastery after leaving his own church? (Question II) if the bishop refuses to grant permission, may he enter a monastery against the bishop’s will? (Question III) if it should happen that they were themselves regular canons, should admission into a monastery be granted them?

## QUESTION I

**GRATIAN**

[Col. 1093B] That a bishop ought to grant clerics permission to enter a monastery is commanded in the Fourth Council of Toledo, in which the following ordinance is read in ch. 49 [Note: held A.D. 633; Burchard, bk. 8, ch. 21; Anselm, bk. 7, ch. 197; Ivo, *Decrees*, part 6, ch. 371; Abbo of Fleury in Mabillon, *Vetera Analecta*, ch. 23; Polycarpus, bk. 3, title 15, bk. 4, title 34]:

**Chapter I. Entry must not be denied to clerics who seek the monastic vocation.**

Clerics who seek the monastic vocation—because they desire to follow a better life—ought to be granted free entry into monasteries by bishops [variant: singular “bishop,” Hispana Collection; Ivo; Anselm; Abbo], and their purpose must not be prohibited [Note: These words through the end are absent from the manuscripts, though they occur in the council; omitted in the Argentinensis, Basel, and Nuremberg editions], since they strive to pass over to the desire of contemplation.

## QUESTION II

**GRATIAN**

But Leo the Bishop testifies that no one is to receive a cleric against the will of his bishop, writing to Anastasius, Bishop of Thessalonica, epistle LXXXII, otherwise LXXXIV, [Col. 1093C] ch. 9 [Note: Epistle 14, written A.D. 446, Ballerini edition; formerly cited from the letter to Rusticus of Narbonne; Anselm, bk. 7, ch. 161 (175); Ivo, *Decrees*, part 6, ch. 60]:

**Chapter I. No one is to receive a cleric against the will of his bishop.**

Let no one receive another bishop’s cleric against that bishop’s will.

**Gratian.** But the following must be understood: unless he wishes to pass over to the purpose of a better life. For in that case he is free to enter a monastery, even if the bishop objects.

Accordingly Pope Urban II, in the chapter of Saint-Ruf [Note: A chapter of uncertain source, and one which you would scarcely judge appropriate to Urban; Anselm, at the end of bk. 7: “Lord Pope Urban says, etc.”], says:

**Chapter II. Whoever seeks the monastic vocation is to be received even against the will of his bishop.**

“There are,” he says, “two laws: one public, the other private. [Col. 1094A] The public law is that which has been confirmed in writing by the holy Fathers, such as the law of the canons, which was given indeed because of transgressions. For example, it has been decreed in the canons that a cleric must not transfer from his own bishopric to another without letters of recommendation from his bishop. This was established because of offenders, lest persons of bad repute be received by another bishop. For they used to celebrate their offices in another bishopric when they could not do so in their own; this practice has rightly been condemned by precepts and written enactments.

§ 1. “The private law, however, is that which is written in the heart by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says of certain persons [Note: Romans 2:15]: ‘They have the law of God written in their hearts’; and elsewhere [Note: Romans 2:14]: ‘When Gentiles who do not have the law do by nature the things of the law, [Col. 1094B] they are a law to themselves.’ If one of these remains in his own church under a bishop, overseeing a people [variant: “his own people,” corrected from Polycarpus], and lives secularly, but, inspired by the Holy Spirit, wishes to save himself in a monastery or a house of regular canons [variant: “regular canonical house,” editions collectively except Lyons II and III], then, because he is guided by private law [variants: “for he who is,” Basel and Lyons editions; “from public law,” Lyons II and III], no reason requires him to be bound by public law. For private law is more worthy than public law. The Spirit of God is indeed law, and those who are moved by the Spirit of God [omitted in the Basel edition] are guided by the law of God; and who can worthily resist the Holy Spirit? Whoever, therefore, is led by this Spirit is, by our authority, to go free even though his bishop objects. For the law is not laid down for the righteous; but where the Spirit of God is, there is freedom [Note: 2 Corinthians 3:17], and if you are led by the Spirit of God, you are not under the law.”

## QUESTION III

[Col. 1094C]

**GRATIAN**

**Part I.** Regular canons, however, are forbidden by many authorities to transfer to a monastery.

Accordingly, in the Council of Autun, assembled under Gregory VII, it is read [Note: Something similar occurs in ch. 10 of the Council of Autun, held A.D. 670, under Leodegar]:

**Chapter I. Regular canons must not become monks.**

No abbot or monk may dare to draw regular canons away from the undertaking of their canonical profession, and receive them by drawing them into monastic dress [addition: “of profession,” Basel edition], so that they become monks, as long as they can find a church of their order [Col. 1095A] in which, living canonically, they may serve God and save their souls. If they attempt this by rash presumption, they are to be bound by the bond of anathema.

**Chapter II. On the same matter.** Likewise Pope Urban II [Note: The source has been found to be Anselm of Havelberg, in the book *On the Order of Regular Canons*, ch. 5, published in Pez’s *Thesaurus*, vol. 4; Anselm, end of bk. 7; Polycarpus, bk. 4, title 31]:

We command and universally forbid that any canon regularly professed [variant: “regular canon,” Basel edition] become a monk unless—God forbid—he has publicly fallen. If anyone, presuming to act contrary to our decree, attempts to do this, we command that he return to the canonical order; thereafter he is to wear the commemorative cowl [variant: “the cowl commemorating his presumption,” original; corrected from Polycarpus] and remain last in choir.

**Gratian.** Yet it must be understood that this applies unless he has adopted the religious vocation with his superior’s permission. Accordingly Pope Urban II writes to the abbot of Saint-Ruf [Note: Ivo, *Decrees*, part 6, ch. 411, and Anselm at the end of bk. 7: “Urban II to the Abbot of St Ruf.” The entire letter was published by Petit, vol. 2, *Penitential of Theodore*, p. 614]:

[Col. 1095B] **Chapter III. Regular canons may become monks with their superior’s permission.**

We establish that no person belonging to the canonical profession, after he has placed a man over his head in God’s stead, may dare, prompted by frivolity or under pretext of a stricter religious life, to withdraw from that cloister without the permission of his superior [Note: Three old manuscripts read “of the superior and of the whole community”; Ivo reads “without the permission of the abbot and of the whole community”; Anselm likewise] and of the whole community. No abbot, bishop, or monk is to receive one who departs without a common written guarantee.

**Part II. Gratian.** The question is asked whether monasteries once dedicated may become residences of clerics or secular persons. This is forbidden in every way by the Council of Chalcedon, ch. 24 [Note: This translation differs somewhat from the Dionysian translation cited by Burchard and Ivo, ch. 22] [Note: held A.D. 451; Dionysian translation; Burchard, bk. 3, ch. 19; Anselm, bk. 5, ch. 60 (62); Ivo, *Decrees*, part 3, ch. 17; Polycarpus, bk. 3, ch. 15]:

[Col. 1095C] **Chapter IV. What has once been dedicated as a monastery must remain a monastery forever.**

Monasteries once dedicated, with the counsel [omitted in the original, Burchard and Ivo, and editions collectively except Basel] of bishops [variant: “council,” Argentinensis, Nuremberg, and Venice I editions; addition: “who hold the cities,” Burchard and Ivo], are to remain monasteries forever; and the property belonging to them must be kept for the monasteries [variant: “ought to be kept,” same authors], nor may they thereafter become secular dwellings. Those who permit this to happen are subject to [Col. 1096A] the condemnations established by the canons.

**Chapter V. A cleric who makes sacred places into common lodging-houses is to be deposed; a layperson is to be excommunicated.** Likewise in the Seventh Synod, ch. 13 [Note: The beginning of this canon in Anastasius’s translation of the Seventh Synod reads: “Because, owing to the calamity which has occurred in the Church because of our sins, certain venerable houses—namely, etc.—have been seized by certain men.” Several details in this chapter have been corrected from two manuscript copies of that translation] [Note: held A.D. 787; Anastasius’s translation; Anselm, bk. 7, ch. 190; in the Argentinensis, Nuremberg, and Venice I editions it is attributed to the Eighth Synod].

Since certain venerable houses, both bishoprics [variant: “episcopal properties,” Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I, and Lyons II–III editions] and monasteries, have been seized by certain men and made into common lodging-houses: if those who retain them [variant: “this one,” Basel edition] wish to restore them so that they may be restored to their ancient state, this is good and excellent. Otherwise, if they belong to the sacred order [variant: “sacred,” Anselm], we command that they be deposed; but if they are monks or laypersons, that they be excommunicated. It is clear that these persons are condemned by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and assigned [variant: “will be assigned,” editions collectively] to the place where their worm does not die [variant: “will not die,” same editions; Anselm; cf. Mark 9:16] and the fire is not extinguished [variant: “will not be extinguished,” same editions; Anselm], because they oppose the voice of the Lord [variant: “are opposed to God,” same editions], who says [Note: John 2:16], “Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.”

**Part III. Gratian.** The question is asked concerning those who come for conversion: at what time should they be tonsured? Gregory writes concerning them to Fortunatus, Bishop of Naples, book VIII, epistle 23 [Note: Epistle 24, written A.D. 600, bk. 10, Maurist edition; Anselm, bk. 7, ch. 197 (199)]:

**Chapter VI. No one is to be tonsured before completing two years in conversion.**
Monasteries of every kind must be most strictly forbidden by your brotherhood to dare in any way to tonsure those whom they have received for conversion [*convertendum*, “to be converted”: original; *conversationem*, “monastic life”: editions of Nuremberg and Venice, first] before they have completed two years in the monastic life [*conversione compleverint*, “have completed in conversion”: collected editions]. Rather, during this period let their life and conduct be carefully tested, lest any of them either be dissatisfied with what he desired [phrase lacking in the original and Basel edition], or fail to ratify what he has chosen. For while [*cum*, “since”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions; Böhm] it is serious to associate untried persons with human services, who can say how much [*quanto*: original, Anselm, collected editions] more serious it is to apply unapproved persons to God’s service [“To apply unapproved persons”: formerly read, “to apply wicked persons” (*improbos applicare*), as in Anselm and the collected editions. Corrected from the printed and manuscript original]? But if a soldier wishes to convert, no one may presume, before notice has been given to us [*denuncietur*: Basel edition], to receive him for any reason whatever without our consent [“Without our consent”: Blessed Gregory ordered this at that time so that he might not seem wholly to disregard the law enacted by Emperor Maurice, forbidding soldiers to be received into monasteries before completing their term of military service. Gregory himself vigorously criticized this law in Book XI, indiction XI, epistle 61, writing to Maurice—a point the author of the gloss does not seem to have noticed], by whatsoever ground [*qualibet*: collected editions].

[Col. 1097A] **Part IV. Gratian.** It is asked whether those entering a monastery are thereafter left free to make a will. Gregory forbids this, writing as follows to Januarius, Bishop of Caralis, Book VII, indiction 2, epistle 7 [Epistle 7, written A.D. 599, line 9, Maurist edition; Anselm, Book VII, chapter 182 (200)]:

### Chapter VII. After entering a monastery, no one is left free to make a will.

Since those entering a monastery for the sake of conversion have no further freedom to make a will, but [added *ut*, “that”: collected editions] their property becomes [*sint*, “may be”: same editions] the legal right of that monastery, this has been decreed by an explicit provision of the law [*definitum*, “defined”: Basel edition].

### Chapter VIII. After entering a monastery, everything must be conferred upon that same monastery.

Likewise Pope Gregory to Cyprian the Deacon, Book III, epistle 6 [Epistle 6, written A.D. 594, line 4, Maurist edition; cf. chapter 2, X, *de test.*]:

It has been reported to us that a woman named Petronilla, born in the province of [Col. 1097B] Lucania, was converted through the exhortation of Bishop Agnellus, and that she bestowed upon the monastery which she entered—even under the specific title of donation—all her property which she could possess, although it might legally have belonged to her; nevertheless [*non*, “not”: Basel edition] she bestowed that same property [*eidem*, “upon the same [monastery]”: original; *eos eidem*: Argentinian, Basel, and Nuremberg editions] upon the monastery which [*in quod*, “into which”: collected editions] she entered.

**Gratian.** On the other hand, Paul the first hermit left in his will [“In his will”: Blessed Jerome says something quite different in the *Life of Paul*: he writes that Blessed Antony wrapped Paul’s body in the cloak Athanasius had given him, and adds: “Lest a devout heir should possess nothing from the goods of an intestate person, he claimed for himself Paul’s tunic, which Paul had woven for himself from palm leaves in the manner of baskets”] his sleeveless tunic to Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, and his other tunic to Blessed Antony. But the case is different for those who, having entered a monastery, have handed over themselves and their goods, and for those who, living a solitary life, have handed themselves over to no church [*tradiderunt*, “have handed over”: corrected from most manuscripts; formerly read, “are able to hand over”]. The former, once they have transferred these things, cannot transfer them to anyone else; the latter, having offered them to no one, may freely make a will.

### Chapter IX. Likewise in the *Authentics*, constitution 9.

[Novella 123, chapter 38; *Auth. Si qua mul.*, Code *de SS. EE.*]

[Col. 1097C] If any woman or man chooses the monastic life [Col. 1098A] and enters a monastery, leaving no children, we command that his or her property belong to the monastery entered. §1. But if a person who has children enters a monastery before disposing of his or her property among them, that person may afterward divide it among them, without diminishing their lawful share [the *Authentics* reads *legitima nulli*, “without diminishing anyone’s lawful share”; added: “by a third or a half”: collected editions and first Basel edition]; and what he or she does not give [*dederit*, “has given”: *Authentics*, collected editions, and Böhm] to them shall belong to the monastery. §2. But if the person wishes to divide the entire estate among the children, he or she shall count himself or herself among the children and retain a share which ought to belong to the monastery [*debeat*: collected editions]. §3. But if the person dies after entering, before dividing it among them, the children shall receive their lawful [added: “share”: same editions] portion [*percipient*: *Authentics*], and the remainder of the estate shall belong to the monastery.

In the *Authentics* [*Auth. Nunc autem*, Code *de episcopis et clericis*; Novella 5, chapter 5], concerning monks, constitution 5, in Collation 1, §4: “Now, however, when a person has become a monk [*esset*: collected editions and first Argentinian edition], by that very fact he is deemed to have offered his property [added: “all”: *Authentics* and collected editions], if he has not previously made a will; and thereafter, his own discretion ceasing, the law provides that, if he has children upon whom he has conferred, under any title of gift, either nothing or less than the lawful portion, so much shall be deducted from the property assigned to the monastery that nothing inequitable may befall the children.”

### Chapter X. Likewise from Novella CXXIII.

[This chapter is expressly found in Julian the Antecessor, Novella 123, chapter 59. Some criticized Gratian for this, although they could by no means have seen Julian’s epitome.] [Julian’s Epitome, Novella 115, chapters 62–63; Anselm’s Collection, Book VI, chapters 125–126.]

Parents may not exclude children who have become monks from their inheritance, nor children exclude parents who have become monks, even if, while they were laypersons, they had incurred an action for ingratitude. §1. Likewise, parents may not remove from monasteries [*monasterio*, singular: collected editions] their children who are entering the solitary life.

# CAUSE XX

[Col. 1097]

[Col. 1097C] **GRATIAN.**

Two boys, both in their childhood years, were given to a monastery by their parents. One unwillingly and the other willingly put on the cowl. Upon reaching the years of puberty, the unwilling one returned to secular military service; the willing one seeks a stricter monastery (Question I). The first question now is whether those given over in childhood are compelled to maintain their religious purpose [Col. 1098C] (Question II). Secondly, if someone in childhood receives tonsure or the religious habit against the wishes of his parents, can it be taken off him or her, or not? (Question III). Thirdly, is one who put on the cowl against his own will compelled to retain it, or not? (Question IV). Fourthly, may a person transfer from one monastery to another that is more strict?

# QUESTION I

[Col. 1099A]

**GRATIAN.**

**Part I.** That those given over during childhood have, when grown up, free choice to remain or depart is proved by the authority of the ninth [“Ninth”: some old copies read “eighth.” But this is not found in the eighth synod held under Hadrian II; rather, it occurs in Blessed Basil’s book *On the Institutions of Monks*, chapter 8, translated by Rufinus. Similar material is also found in Basil’s *Longer Rules*, chapter 15] Synod [rather, from Basil’s Rule, chapter 8. In the collected editions and first Basel edition it is cited from the Ninth Synod; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 2, title 14, chapter 17].

### Chapter I. At what time the profession of virginity begins to be binding.

The profession of virginity will be binding when adult age has already begun, and when she has reached the age usually regarded as fit for marriage and as complete [“And as complete”: these words are not found in that passage of Basil].

**Gratian.** Therefore, if the profession of virginity begins to be binding when a person has begun to be of adult age, the profession of religion likewise ought only then to become binding when adulthood has been attained. But the subject here is that [Col. 1099B] profession which a person in childhood offers to God by his or her own decision, and which parental consent does not confirm. Yet a profession offered to God by parents must be kept inviolate.

Accordingly Gregory writes to Augustine, bishop of the English [this is also cited by Ivo. It occurs in epistle 4 of Gregory III to Boniface, legate of Germany, and similar matter is found in the Council of Worms, chapter 22] [rather, Gregory II, in the chapters addressed to Boniface, A.D. 726; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 15]:

### Chapter II. A person whom father or mother has caused to be enrolled in a monastery during infancy may not leave the monastery.

You have further asked whether, if a father or mother has entrusted a son or daughter within the walls of a monastery to regular discipline during the years of infancy, they may leave after reaching [*pervenerint*: Argentinian edition; *inolveerint* [uncertain OCR]: remaining editions and Ivo] puberty and enter marriage. We wholly forbid this, because it is wicked that the reins of pleasure should be loosened for children offered to God by their parents [*voluntatis*, “of the will”: Lyons editions].

[Col. 1099C] ### Chapter III. Either personal profession or parental devotion makes a monk.

Likewise from the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 48 [held A.D. 633; Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 6; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 30; *Polycarpus*, Book IV, title 54]:

A monk is made either by parental devotion or by personal profession. Whichever of these has occurred shall hold him bound [*allegatum*, “bound/attached”: two Vatican conciliar manuscripts and the Lucchese royal manuscript]. Accordingly, we bar such persons from returning to the world [*reverti*: Burchard; Basel edition] and forbid every return to secular life [“every return”: Hispanic Collection].

[Col. 1100A] ### Chapter IV. Those given over by their parents are to remain in the monastery permanently.

Likewise Isidore [This is not found in the books of Blessed Isidore; Smaragdus, however, in his exposition of the Rule of Blessed Benedict, chapter 59, reports the same thing from Isidore] [chapter uncertain; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 2, title 50, chapter 1]:

Whoever has been committed to a monastery by his own parents must know that he is to remain there permanently [*mansurum*: collected editions]. For Anna devoutly offered to God her son Samuel, a child who had been weaned; he remained in the service of the temple to which his mother had assigned him, and served where he had been placed.

### Chapter V. On the same matter. [PALEA.]

Likewise from Gregory’s *Register*, Book I, epistle 48, to Anthemius [Epistle 50, written A.D. 591, line 1, Maurist edition; cf. chapter 1, Compilation II, and chapter 6, X, *de regularibus*; the name *Palea* is found in the collected editions and first Argentinian and Basel editions]:

> “Since the gathering of monks on the islands is difficult, we also prohibit boys from being received into the same monasteries before the age of eighteen [twenty-eight: Basel edition]; and if any are there now, let your prudent oversight [*experientia*, “experience”: original and Basel edition] remove them and send them to the city of Rome. We wish you to observe this in every respect in Palmaria and the other islands as well.”

### Chapter VI. One given to a monastery by forebears may not leave it.

Likewise from the Council of Tribur [chapter 27, Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895, abridged; Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 97; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 115]:

A person whom his forebears have given to a monastery, and who has begun to sing and read in church, may neither take a wife nor abandon the monastery. If he departs, he shall be brought back; if he abandons the tonsure, he shall be tonsured again; if he has taken a wife, he shall be compelled to dismiss her.

[Col. 1100C] ### Chapter VII. PALEA.

[Likewise from Theodore’s *Penitential* [Almost the same words are found in Theodore’s chapters, chapter 37, in d’Achery, volume 1].]

> “A child may be given in a monastery in exchange for a child, although the other has been vowed [printed *vocatus*, “called”; apparently it should read *votus*, “vowed”]. Yet it is better to fulfill the vow. Likewise livestock are to be redeemed at an equal price, if necessary.”

**Part II. Gratian.** From these authorities it is inferred that a parental profession holds children bound, and that they may not depart from the undertaking which they embraced in childhood through parental devotion. But the following statement of Pope Leo is objected, epistle XC—otherwise XCII—to Bishop Rusticus, chapters 13 and 14 [Epistle 167, written A.D. 458 or 459, Ballerini edition; Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 2; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 20; *Polycarpus*, Book IV, title 35]:

### Chapter VIII. Girls who have voluntarily undertaken the purpose of virginity may not choose marriage.

Girls who have undertaken the purpose and habit of virginity not under compulsion from parental command but by spontaneous [*ex spontaneo*: Hispanic Collection] judgment, if afterward they choose [*elegerint*: collected editions] marriage, commit a breach of faith, even though [added: “the grace of consecration has not yet come to them”: Hispanic Collection, Burchard, Ivo, collected editions] consecration has not been conferred upon them—a gift of which they certainly would not be deprived if they remained in their purpose. [The words that follow are absent from Dionysius, Pseudo-Isidore of Merlin, the Ballerini original, Burchard, and Ivo, but occur in the Hispanic Collection.] Nor can there be doubt that a grave offense is committed where both [*et*, “and,” lacking in the collected editions and first Basel edition] the undertaking is abandoned and consecration is violated. For if human agreements [*facta*, “deeds”: Nuremberg, Venice I–II, and Paris editions] cannot be trampled underfoot with impunity, what awaits those [*eas*, “them [feminine]”: Hispanic Collection; *de his*, “those persons”: Argentinian and Nuremberg editions; *de eis*: remaining editions] who have violated the covenants of a divine sacrament?

**Gratian.** Since, then, the beginning of this chapter says, “Girls who have not been compelled by the command of their parents,” it is understood that if they received the habit of virginity under compulsion, they may abandon it without breach of faith. But the girl meant here is marriageable; as is shown below, after her twelfth year she has free choice, and in choosing her undertaking she is not compelled to follow parental command.

The same sense must be given to what was enacted in the synod held under Pope Eugenius II, chapter 32 [held A.D. 826]:

### Chapter IX. Those shut up in monasteries against their own will are not to be held there.

Just as those who have chosen monasteries are not permitted to leave monasteries, so persons who have been brought in unwillingly, without a just ground of offense, are not to be held unless they are willing; for they do not observe what they do not seek. Therefore such persons should be considered more disposed to commit sins than to bewail them [*maxime*, “especially”: original], as is most clearly contained in the decree of the most holy Pope Leo [added: Book VII: Basel and Lyons II–III editions; Book VI: remaining editions]. [The words from “as” through the end of the sentence are absent from the Argentinian edition.]

[Thus Pope Marcellus [This is marked as *Palea* also by the author of the gloss, but it occurs in nearly all old copies without the name *Palea*] [chapter uncertain; something similar is found in chapter 23 of the Council of Mainz, held A.D. 813]:]

### Chapter X. PALEA.

> “We judge that the following should be enacted: if children have been offered to a monastery while under age and have received the sacred tonsure or veils, we have deemed it proper that, in their fifteenth year, they should be admonished by their superiors [*censuimus*, “we have judged”: Basel edition; *monitis et verbis*, “by admonitions and words”: same; *moniti verbis*, “admonished by words”: remaining editions] and asked whether they desire to remain in that habit or not. If they profess that they wish to remain, they can by no means thereafter take up an opportunity to repent. But if they wish to return to secular dress, permission to return must in no way be denied them, because it is quite useless for compulsory service to be rendered to the Lord [*Deo*, “God”: Argentinian edition].”

**Part III. Gratian.** A veil, however, may not be imposed upon virgins except on specified days.

Accordingly Pope Gelasius, to the bishops throughout Lucania, chapters 14 and 15 [written A.D. 494; Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 15; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book III, chapter 189; *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 36; *Polycarpus*, Book IV, title 35]:

### Chapter XI. The veil is to be imposed upon virgins only on specified days.

Let the sacred veil not be imposed upon virgins devoted to God [*quoque*, “also”: Hispanic Collection, Burchard, Ivo], except either on the day of Epiphany [*in epiphania*, “at Epiphany”: Burchard and Ivo; *in epiphaniae die*: Hispanic Collection and collected editions], in the octave of Easter, or on the anniversaries of the apostles [Col. 1102B] [*natalitiis*, “birthdays”: same editions], unless perhaps, as has been said concerning baptism, it is requested by persons seized with serious illness, lest they depart this world without this gift; in that case it must not be denied. §1. Let no bishop presume to veil widows.

**Part IV. Gratian.** The time of their consecration is likewise observed.

Accordingly Gregory in the *Register*, Book III, epistle 11 [Epistle 11, written A.D. 594, line 4, Maurist edition; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 1, title 55, chapter 91; *Polycarpus*, Book IV, title 35]:

### Chapter XII. Virgins are not to be consecrated before their sixtieth year.

We most emphatically forbid young women to be made abbesses. Therefore let your brotherhood permit no virgin to be veiled unless she is sixty years old, and unless her life [*aetas*, “age”: original] and character require this.

[Col. 1102C] ### Chapter XIII. Likewise from the Third Council of Carthage.

[It is cited thus in all the old copies, but it has been found in no Council of Carthage. The same text, with some additions, occurs in the Council of Agde, chapter 19.] [Rather, chapter 19 of the Council of Agde, held A.D. 506.]

Consecrated women are not to be veiled before their fortieth year.

### Chapter XIV. Virgins are not to be consecrated before their twenty-fifth year.

Likewise from the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 4 [Formerly cited from the Fourth African Council; but above, Distinction 77, chapter *Placuit*, it is cited from the Third Council of Carthage, where it occurs] [held A.D. 397; Burchard, Book II, chapter 11; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book III, chapter 30; *Polycarpus*, Book II, title 27]:

It has been decided that neither deacons may be ordained nor virgins consecrated before the age of twenty-five, and that readers [“reader … greet”: Burchard and Ivo] may not greet the people.

[Col. 1103A] ### Chapter XV. PALEA.

Likewise Pope Pius [This chapter has not been found among Pius’s decrees and is absent from three old copies of Gratian. The grounds upon which virgins can be veiled before age twenty-five are considered in the Council of Milevis, chapter 26, and the African Council, chapter 93; from the latter it is reported in the *Capitularies*, Book I, chapter 46.] [This chapter is composed from chapter 93 of the African Council, in the Hadrian manuscript, and from Gelasius’s decree cited above in chapter 11, as Regino expressly observed, Book II, chapter 177; Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 18; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book III, chapter 190; *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 39; *Polycarpus*, Book IV, title 35]:

Virgins are not to be veiled before the age of twenty-five, unless perhaps necessity arises from endangered virginal chastity; and they are not to be consecrated [*offerendae*, “offered”: Basel edition] except on Epiphany, on the Saturday [“Saturday”: one old copy reads “in the octave,” and the other collectors read “in the octave of Easter”] of Easter, or on the feasts of the apostles, unless death is imminent.

**Part V. Gratian.** Although widows are forbidden to be veiled, they must nevertheless make their profession of widowhood in writing. They must also be given a garment suitable to their profession, which they are to wear everywhere.

Accordingly, in the Tenth Council of Toledo, chapter 4 [held A.D. 656; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 2, title 41, chapter 2]:

### Chapter XVI. Those who propose to preserve chastity shall make a profession of widowhood and take the religious habit.

[Col. 1103B] A widow who wishes to undertake the purpose of holy religion shall make to the priest or minister, either the one to whom she comes or the one who happens to come to her, a written profession marked by herself either with a sign or a signature, declaring [*continere*, “to declare”: Basel edition] that she wishes both to undertake the religious purpose and to preserve it perpetually and inviolate. Then, having received from the priest or minister clothing appropriate to the profession [*usui*, “use”: Hispanic Collection; *et professionis*, “and of profession”: Basel edition] of religion, whether resting in bed or standing in any place whatever, she shall wear it steadily [*incunctanter*, “without hesitation”: Hispanic Collection]. That garment must not be conspicuous through a different color or a different cut, but must be religious and not open to suspicion.

# QUESTION II

[Col. 1103C] **GRATIAN.**

**Part I.** Concerning those who have received tonsure or religious clothing contrary to their parents’ wishes, the Tenth Council of Toledo, chapter 6, makes the following determination [held A.D. 656; Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 1; Anselm, Book XI, chapter 176; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 2, title 41, chapter 3; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book III, chapter 186; *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 27]:

### Chapter I. Tonsure or religious clothing received while under age can be nullified by the parents.

If, while their children of either sex are under age, either one or both parents have perhaps [“Have perhaps given”: conciliar manuscripts also read “have certainly given” [so in the Hispanic Collection and in Burchard and Ivo’s *Decretum*]; in the *Panormia*: “have given, or certainly to unwilling persons,” etc.] given them clothing due to religion or religious tonsure, either to unwilling children or to children unaware of what is being done [words lacking in the Hispanic Collection and Anselm], and have not disavowed what they saw to have been received by their children immediately, but have permitted those children, either before themselves or before the church [“bishop”: Ivo’s *Panormia* and collected editions], openly and in a public assembly, to possess such things, it will thereafter be wholly unlawful for those children to return to secular dress. Rather, once they are proved to have had tonsure or religious dress at some time, they shall immediately be recalled to the worship and habit of religion and compelled, under strict [*aeterna*, “eternal”: Hispanic Collection] discipline [*observatione*, “observance”: same] to serve in this observance.

§1. Parents may have authority to commit their children to religion only up to the fourteenth [“Fourteenth”: the *Panormia* likewise reads this; but one old Gratian manuscript and conciliar manuscripts read “up to the tenth” [as in the Hispanic Collection and Anselm]; other collectors read “up to twelve”] year of their age. Afterward, whether the solitary vow is made with parental consent or by their own [*si suae*: collected editions] devotion, the children may adopt the practice of religion.

[Col. 1104B] §2. Whoever is discovered to have committed this transgression by removing the tonsure or putting on secular clothing shall receive the sentence of excommunication and remain attached to religion forever.

### Chapter II. Until twelve years of age, a girl is subject to her father’s will.

Likewise from the Council of Tribur, chapter 24 [Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895, chapter 24, abridged; Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 98; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 116]:

If, before twelve years of age, a girl has of her own accord taken the sacred veil, her parents or guardians may immediately nullify that act if they wish. But if, by overlooking it, they consent for a year and a day, neither they nor she can thereafter change this [added: “will”: Lyons II–III editions]. §1. But if, at a more mature age, a young woman or young man chooses to serve God, the parents have no power to forbid it.

**Part II. Gratian.** No abbess or other consecrated woman may impose the veil upon anyone.

Accordingly Pope Eutychian says [rather, chapter 47, Book I of the Sixth Council of Paris, held A.D. 829; Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 17; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book III, chapter 194; *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 38]:

### Chapter III. An abbess who presumes to veil a virgin or widow is to be excommunicated.

We decree that if, after this ruling, an abbess or any consecrated woman should proceed to such boldness as to presume to veil either a widow or a virgin girl, she shall be subjected to canonical judgment until she has made satisfaction.

**Part III. Gratian.** The authority just cited and parental profession teach that any person is bound in childhood, and that one who has embraced the undertaking apart from their will is said to be bound—unless the parents immediately disavow the tonsure or religious dress once they see it. But when little children are offered, they must be received only with many witnesses.

Accordingly, in the ninth Synod one reads [It occurs in the same little book of Blessed Basil and in the same chapter as chapter *Firma* above in this same Question I, and follows it continuously] [rather, from Basil’s Rule; in the Basel edition it is cited from the Seventh Synod; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 2, title 14, chapter 17]:

### Chapter IV. Children offered by their parents are to be received under the testimony of very many persons.

Children must be received, with the will and consent of their parents—indeed, offered by the parents themselves—under the testimony of very many persons [Col. 1105B], so that every occasion for malicious reproach may be excluded from the worst of men [“Worst”: that little book reads “very many”].

# QUESTION III

**GRATIAN.**

**Part I.** Pope Leo also testifies, in epistle XC—or rather XCII—to Bishop Rusticus, chapter 12, that a person who has accepted a religious undertaking unwillingly is not to be compelled to observe an unwilling undertaking [Epistle 167, Ballerini edition, written A.D. 458 or 459; Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 8; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book III, chapter 182; *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 19; *Polycarpus*, Book IV, title 34]:

### Chapter I. A monastic undertaking voluntarily assumed cannot be abandoned.

A monk’s undertaking, assumed by his own judgment and will, cannot be abandoned without sin. For what a person [added *quis*, “a person”: original, cited collections, collected editions] vows [*vovet*, “vows”: collected editions] to God, he must also perform. Therefore, one who abandons [Col. 1105C] the profession of the solitary life for military service or marriage must be purified by the satisfaction of public penance; for although military service may be innocent and marriage honorable, nevertheless it is a transgression to have abandoned the choice of better things [*meliorem*, singular: Burchard and Böhm].

### Chapter II. A person wishing to abandon a religious habit voluntarily assumed must be compelled to return to it.

Likewise from the Sixth Council of Toledo, chapter 6 [held A.D. 638; Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 14; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 35]:

The path to pleasure is downhill, and nature imitates vices. Therefore any man or woman who has once voluntarily put on the religious habit—or, if a man, has been assigned to the church choir, or, if a woman, has been or was assigned [*aut fuit*, “or was,” lacking in Böhm; *deligata*, “bound”: Hispanic Collection] to a monastery of girls [Col. 1106A]—must, in either sex, be compelled against his or her will, if an apostate, to return to the undertaking: the man is to be tonsured, and the girl to return to the monastery [“enter the monastery”: Burchard and Ivo; “be restored to the monastery”: Hispanic Collection]. If, however, deserters wish to remain so through any patronage, they are to be held by priestly sentence as excluded from the company of Christians, so that they have no place at all in communion [Lucchese royal manuscript: “so that no conversation at all may be held in common with them”; the other manuscripts agree with Gratian. Ivo reads: “so that they have no place at all in common”]. §1. Widows likewise—as the universal synod [Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 55] has long since decreed—who abandon their profession or habit shall be condemned by the foregoing sentence.

### Chapter III. Those once enrolled among the clergy or assigned to monasteries are not to return to military service.

Likewise from the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 7 [held A.D. 451; Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 4; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 28; both from Dionysius]:

We have decreed that those once enrolled among the clergy or assigned to a monastery [*monasteriis*, plural: Hispanic Collection, Basel edition, Böhm] shall not enter either military service [Col. 1106B] or secular offices. Those who dare to do this, and do not choose to repent in order to return to that very state which they had formerly undertaken for themselves under the pretext [or “on account”] of God [*proposuerant*: Hispanic Collection; *proposuerint*: Basel edition], ought to be anathematized [*anathema esse*, “be anathema,” omitting “it is fitting”: Hispanic Collection].

**Part II. Gratian.** When it is said, “a monk’s undertaking assumed by his own judgment and will,” it is understood that if it has not been assumed by his own will, he is not compelled to observe it.

Accordingly Pope Nicholas writes to all bishops in the kingdom of Louis [chapter uncertain; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 356]:

### Chapter IV. No one is to be subjected unwillingly to monastic disciplines.

The present cleric, named Lambert, together with his father, named Attho—formerly a count, but now a cleric—hastening to the thresholds of the apostles, came before us. He asserted that his father, while still in the lay estate [Note: [Col. 1105] “dress”: Ivo.], had built two monasteries on his own lands, intending that, after his death [Note: [Col. 1105] “departure”: ibid.], his present son Lambert should succeed him in his place [Note: [Col. 1105] “him”: ibid.]. When Lambert was still of tender age, between his eighth and tenth [Note: [Col. 1105] “eleventh”: Ivo.] year, the aforesaid father, of his own decision and without regular institution, against all Lambert’s own will, clothed him in the cowl [Note: [Col. 1105] “with a cowl”: ed. Arg.].

Accordingly, after some time had passed, Salomon the bishop, as Lambert says, together with certain others, without an offering from his father or a blessing received from an abbot [Note: [Col. 1105] “received”: ed. Bas.], caused this Lambert—unwilling, as they report [Note: [Col. 1107] “it is reported”: ibid.; Ivo.]—to put on the monastic habit [Note: [Col. 1107] “with the monastic habit”: ibid.]. Under this pretext, he says, his brothers deprived him of his paternal or maternal inheritance; and, against his entire will, as stated, they wish him to remain as though he were a regular monk [Note: [Col. 1107] “wished”: ibid.; Ivo.].

Investigating this matter with diligent care, we questioned his father under oath as to whether he spoke the truth. But Attho replied that he had had, and still had, such an intention that [Note: [Col. 1107] “that also”: ed. Bas.] his son should become [Note: [Col. 1107] “had become”: Ivo.] a true monk and succeed him in his place [Note: [Col. 1107] “and had succeeded”: ibid.]. Yet he affirmed under sworn testimony [Note: [Col. 1107] omitted in ed. Bas.] that, when he first put the cowl upon him, Lambert always resisted and never consented to become a monk. At length, however, those pursuing the matter forcibly clothed him in the monastic habit [Note: [Col. 1107] “monkish”: Ivo; eds. Arg. and Bas.], while he maintained that he had never promised any rule [Note: [Col. 1107] “at any time”: ibid.]; nor, said Attho, had he, Lambert’s father, offered him clothed in the altar-cloth [Note: [Col. 1107] “veil”: Ivo; “wrapped”: ed. Arg.], nor had Lambert, after receiving the blessing of any priest or abbot—as custom requires [Note: [Col. 1107] “demands”: Ivo.]—ever promised that he would be subject to the rule of monks [Note: [Col. 1107] “that he had ever been made subject as a monk”: ibid.].

On all these matters the aforesaid cleric Attho further testified that, had he then understood the monastic rule to be of such severe observance [Note: [Col. 1107] “monkish”: ed. Bas.], he would never have compelled his son [Note: [Col. 1107] “his”: ed. Bas.; Ivo.], Lambert, to wear the cowl.

§ 1. Therefore, recalling prudently the words of the psalmist [Note: [Col. 1107] Ps. 53, 108, 118.], by which he declares that he will sacrifice to God willingly and prays that the voluntary offerings of his mouth may be pleasing in God’s sight, we judged that the present cleric Lambert, as stated [Col. 1107C], ought by no means to be made a monk under such compulsion. For what a person neither chooses nor desires, he surely does not love; and what he does not love, he readily despises. Indeed, no good exists unless it is voluntary. Therefore the Lord commanded that no rod be carried on the road by which violence might be inflicted upon anyone. It will consequently be wiser if, by preaching contempt for the world and love of God through pious persuasion, you kindle them to that heavenly love, rather than by inflicting violence.

We have therefore decreed to send this letter of our apostolic authority to the charity of you all, admonishing and commanding that, if matters are indeed as these persons state, no bishop, abbot, or community of the remaining monks may compel Lambert against his will to be subject to monastic rules [Col. 1107D]; nor may his brothers, on this pretext, have any license whatever [Col. 1108A] to deprive him of paternal or maternal inheritance [Note: [Col. 1107] “which may it not be”: Ivo.]. Rather, until, pierced by divine inspiration, he voluntarily submits himself to a rule [Note: [Col. 1107] “rules”: ibid.], he may live the canonical life among religious and ecclesiastical men, removed from worldly and lay wanderings or business. For we do not think—far be it from us—that religious canons are separated from the life and fellowship of holy monks, since, according to the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1107] 1 Cor. 3:8.], each shall receive his own reward according to his labour.

### Part III. Gratian

But if some have received tonsure or the religious habit because they were enticed by the promises of a bishop or abbot, they themselves should remain in what they have undertaken, while their property is to be restored to their heirs.

[Col. 1108B] Hence one reads in the Council of Mainz [Note: [Col. 1107] This citation was discussed above, 16, q. 7, penultimate chapter.] [Note: [Col. 1107] Cf. on c. 42, C. 16, q. 7.]:

### Chapter V. The property of those who were deceived by bishops or abbots into laying aside their hair is to be restored to their heirs.

This holy assembly has decreed that bishops or abbots who, not seeking the profit of souls but coveting greed and shameful gain, have tonsured persons by deceiving them and have seized their property through such persuasion, are to be subject to canonical penance as pursuers of shameful gain. Those, however, who were enticed into laying aside their hair are to be compelled to persevere in what they have begun [Note: [Col. 1107] “had undertaken”: the collected editions and first Basle edition.], while their property is to be returned to their heirs.

## QUESTION IV

[Col. 1108C]

### GRATIAN

### Part I

That monks are free to transfer from one monastery to another of stricter observance is established from the Council of Tribur, where the following was decreed [Note: [Col. 1107] c. 26, Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895, abridged.—Regino, bk. 1, c. 180; Burchard, bk. 8, c. 22; Ivo, Decree, pt. 7, c. 42.]:

### Chapter I. Consecrated virgins who wish to enter another monastery for the sake of religion are not to be forbidden.

If consecrated virgins, for the benefit of their souls and on account of a stricter life, resolve to go to another monastery and to remain there, the synod permits it. But if they seek another place in flight from discipline, they are to be compelled to return.

Gratian. What this chapter decrees concerning consecrated virgins is correspondingly understood also concerning monks [Col. 1108D], and indeed concerning every cleric.

[Col. 1109A]

### Part II, § 1

But the following saying of Basil is objected [Note: [Col. 1109C] The sense of this chapter can in some measure be drawn from Sermon 2, *On the Institution of Monks*, and chapter 28 of St Basil’s *Monastic Constitutions*.] [Note: [Col. 1109] Rather, from Theodore’s Penitential, c. 6.—Burchard, bk. 8, c. 9; Ivo, Decree, pt. 7, c. 32; Polycarpus, I.4, title 34.]:

### Chapter II. A monk’s vows are void without his abbot’s consent.

A monk [Note: [Col. 1109] “monks”: ed. Bas.] may not make a vow without the consent of his abbot; but if he does make one [Note: [Col. 1109] “they make”: eds. Bas. and Venice II.], it must be broken.

Likewise, that of the Council of Agde, chapter 27 [Note: [Col. 1109] Held A.D. 506.—§ 1 is cited by Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 3, c. 157.]:

### Chapter III. No one may receive or ordain a monk without his abbot’s permission.

No abbot may presume to receive or retain a monk who moves to another monastery without either his abbot’s permission or his consent; wherever he may be, he is to be recalled to his own abbot by the authority [Note: [Col. 1109] “under the authority”: ed.
