Bas.] of the canons [Note: [Col. 1109] “recalled”: Coll. Hisp.]. § 1. Likewise, clerics may not wander about without letters of recommendation [Note: [Col. 1109] “or letters”: ed. Bas.] and the permission of their own bishop [Note: [Col. 1109] “or bishop”: ed. Lugd. II.]. The same form of judgment is also to be observed in the case of monks [Col. 1109B]; if verbal rebuke does not correct them, we decree that they are to be restrained even by beatings [Note: [Col. 1109] “them also and”: ed. Bas.; “is to be done”: Coll. Hisp., eds. Bas., Nor., Venice I, Böhm.].

§ 2. It must likewise be observed concerning monks that they may not leave the community for solitary cells [Col. 1110A], unless perhaps, after their labours have been proved and completed, or because the need of illness requires it, a stricter rule is relaxed with the abbot’s permission [Note: [Col. 1109C] “Permission”: this word is absent from the older editions of the councils, two Vatican manuscripts, and two manuscripts of Gratian. In more recent Cologne editions the reading is: “let a stricter rule be permitted by the abbots” [Col. 1110C] [as in Coll. Hisp.]. But in Julian the Praetorian, Novella 123, no. 53, where there is a similar provision, the abbot’s permission is required.]. This is to be done only on condition that, while remaining within the same monastery’s enclosure and nevertheless under the abbot’s authority, they may be permitted to have separate cells.

An abbot likewise [Note: [Col. 1110C] “An abbot likewise”: so in some editions of the councils. In others, especially the four-volume Cologne edition: “individual abbots also [may have] separate cells” [Col. 1110D] [as in Coll. Hisp.].] [Note: [Col. 1109] “indeed”: ed. Bas.] may not have individual separate [Note: [Col. 1109] “and separate”: eds. Bas., Lyons, Paris.] cells or more than one monastery, except only to establish refuges within the walls on account of hostile incursions [Note: [Col. 1109] “hospitality”: Coll. Hisp.].

Gratian. But this must be understood of monks who live religiously: they may not, without their abbot’s consent, make vows of special abstinence or of any strict practice beyond the general custom of their brethren, lest the brethren take offence at them. This was also established for those who, evading regular discipline, take upon themselves vows of pilgrimage. This is lawful neither for a monk nor for any cleric, lest under that pretext he return to secular life.

## CAUSE XXI

[Col. 1109]

[Col. 1109B] ### GRATIAN

The archpriest of a certain church has received the provostship of another, yet does not wish to leave the former. He also becomes the manager of secular affairs; adorning himself with brilliant and splendid garments, he is rebuked by his bishop; abandoning his office, he has recourse to a secular judge [Col. 1109C]. (Question I.) First, it is asked whether a cleric may be enrolled in two churches. (Question II.) Secondly, if he wishes to leave one, may he transfer to another? (Question III.) Thirdly, may clerics undertake the management of secular affairs? (Question IV.) Fourthly, is it fitting for them to adorn themselves with brilliant and splendid garments? (Question V.) Fifthly, when rebuked by their bishop, may they abandon their office and have recourse to a secular judge?

## QUESTION I

[Col. 1110B]

### GRATIAN

That no one may be enrolled in two churches is prohibited by the Seventh Synod, which says in chapter 15 [Note: [Col. 1109] Held A.D. 787.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 98 (110); Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 6, c. 311.]:

### Chapter I. A cleric must in no way be enrolled in two churches.

[Col. 1110C] From the present time, a cleric is not to be enrolled in two churches. For this is characteristic of trading and shameful gain [Note: [Col. 1109] “profit”: Ivo; “gain”: ed. Bas.; “personal gain”: the remaining editions; the Greek has αἰσχροκερδείας, “shameful gain.”], and wholly alien to ecclesiastical custom. For we have heard from the Lord’s own utterance [Note: [Col. 1109] Matt. 6:24.] that no one can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will bear with the one and despise the other. Each person, according to the apostolic saying [Note: [Col. 1109] Cf. 1 Cor. 7.], ought to remain in the state in which he was called and be assigned to one church.

Things done in ecclesiastical affairs for shameful gain [Col. 1111A] are alien from God; but for the necessities of this life there are various occupations. From these, therefore, whoever wishes may acquire what is necessary for the body [Note: [Col. 1111] “for the body”: the collected editions.]. For the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1111] Acts 20:34.], “These hands have supplied what was needed by me and by those who were with me.” This is to be observed in this God-protected city [Note: [Col. 1111C] Earlier the text read, “to be observed in this city.” It has been corrected from manuscripts of Anastasius; for the Greek is ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ θεοφυλάκτῳ πόλει, “in this God-protected city.” In Ivo: “in this protected city” [as in ed. Arg.; ed. Bas. incorrectly: “these things … are to be observed.”].]. But in the country districts [Note: [Col. 1111C] Greek χωρίοις, which has a broader scope and often means “regions.”] outside it, an allowance is to be made because of the scarcity of people.

Gratian. But the two churches meant are churches of two cities, in which no one ought to be enrolled.

Hence the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 10, decreed [Note: [Col. 1111] Held A.D. 451; Dionysius’s translation, with some alterations.—Burchard, bk. 2, c. 96; Anselm, bk. 7, c. 108; Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 7, c. 173.]:

### Chapter II. On the same matter.

A cleric ought not to be enrolled in churches of two cities *at the same time* [Col. 1111B] [Note: [Col. 1111] “at the same time” is absent in the original and Coll. citt.] [Note: [Col. 1111] “be permitted”: ibid.].

Gratian. Yet, on the other hand, a bishop of one city sometimes becomes archbishop of another city without abandoning his former church. The earlier church is left, as it were, in commendam; the second is held as a title.

Hence Leo IV writes [Note: [Col. 1111] Chapter of uncertain source.—Collection in three parts, pt. 1, title 60, c. 6.]:

### Chapter III. One who is titled in one church may hold another in commendam.

One who holds several churches ought to hold one as a title and another in commendam [Note: [Col. 1111] “hold”: the collected editions.].

The following provision of the Council of Agde, chapter 57, is to be understood in the same way [Note: [Col. 1111] Held A.D. 506.—Cf. on c. 30, Dist. 23; cf. Council of Epaone, c. 9.—Burchard, bk. 8, c. 81, from the Council of Orange; Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 3, c. 164, pt. 7, c. 99.]:

### Chapter IV. One abbot cannot preside over two monasteries.

[Col. 1111C] We forbid one abbot to preside over two monasteries.

Gratian. He may also preside over each as though it were titular, but by a special law rather than the common law.

Hence Gregory, book II, letter 13, to Bishop Agnellus [Note: [Col. 1111C] The meaning of St Gregory differs from what Gratian appears to suppose. Agnellus, formerly bishop of Fundi, was made cardinal priest of Terracina because that city had been devastated by the enemy, as appears in the following chapter. This matter was noted above, Dist. 71, chapter *Fraternitatem*.] [Note: [Col. 1111] Letter 13, written A.D. 593, bk. 3, Maurist ed.—Anselm, bk. 5, c. 28 (27); Polycarpus, bk. 1, title 8.]:

### Chapter V. One bishop is placed over two churches.

The report of the clergy and people living at Terracina [Note: [Col. 1112C] “Terracina”: corrected from old copies, whereas the vulgate read “of the Tarraconensian people.” The original reads “living at Terracina” [and so Anselm; “Terraconensian”: Lyons editions].] greatly rejoices us, because it gives good testimony concerning your brotherhood. Since, after the death of their bishop Peter, they ask that you be appointed their cardinal priest, we have judged that their wishes [Note: [Col. 1111] “desires”: Anselm and the collected editions.] must necessarily be granted.

And below:

§ 1. Therefore hasten with the whole purpose of your mind to make gain of souls for our God [Note: [Col. 1111] “the Lord”: original and collected editions.], so that a worthy reward may find you before his presence on the day of recompense. Whatever you shall carefully and canonically provide to ordain or do concerning the affairs or patrimony of the aforesaid church, the ordering or promotion of its clergy, and all things generally pertaining to it, you shall have full authority in every respect, as its proper priest.

### Chapter VI

[Note: [Col. 1112C] In old manuscripts this is joined to the preceding chapter, as in the letter itself and in Anselm.] [Note: [Col. 1111] Anselm, ibid.]

[Col. 1112B] Your brotherhood must also know that we have appointed you cardinal priest of the aforesaid church of Terracina in such a way that you do not cease to be bishop of the church of Fundi, nor neglect its care and government. For we command your brotherhood to preside over the often-mentioned church of Terracina [Note: [Col. 1111] “we impose upon your brotherhood the care of the church of Terracina”: the collected editions.], *as we have said*, in such a way that we by no means withdraw from you the rights or authority of the aforementioned church of Fundi.

Gratian. For he cannot preside over both as titular churches; rather, he is to preside over one as held in commendam and the other as titular.

## QUESTION II

### GRATIAN

[Col. 1112C] ### Part I

One who wishes to leave his own church and transfer to another is by no means to be received without letters dimissory from his bishop.

Hence one reads in the Sixth Synod, chapter 17 [Note: [Col. 1111] Rather, from the Synod in Trullo, held A.D. 692.—Collection in three parts, pt. 2, title 11, c. 7.—In the collected editions and first Basle edition it is cited from the Seventh Synod.]:

### Chapter I. A cleric is not to be ordained in a foreign church without letters dimissory.

Since clerics of various churches leave the churches in which they were ordained, hasten to other bishops, and, without the knowledge [Note: [Col. 1112C] Greek: Γνώμης δίχα τοῦ οἰκείου ἐπισκόπου, that is, “without the judgment/approval of their own bishop.”] of their own bishop, are established in foreign churches [Col. 1113A], where it happens [Note: [Col. 1113C] Greek: Ἐκ τούτου τε συνέβη ἀνυποτάκτους αὐτοὺς καταστῆναι, “and from this it has resulted that they become unsubordinate.”] that they remain without examination by their own bishop, we command henceforth that no cleric whatsoever, of whatever rank, may have leave to be established in another church without letters dimissory from his own bishop. But whoever henceforth fails to observe this [Note: [Col. 1113] “observed”: ed. Bas.] is to be deposed, to the disgrace of the one [Note: [Col. 1113C] Greek: Ἐπεὶ ὁ μὴ τοῦτο ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν παραφυλαττόμενος, ἀλλὰ καταισχύνων, τό γε ἐπ’ αὐτῷ, τὸν τὴν χειροτονίαν αὐτῷ ἐπιτεθηκότα καθαιρείσθω; that is, “For he who from the present time does not observe this, but, so far as lies in him, disgraces the one who imposed ordination upon him, is to be deposed,” etc.] who ordained him, as is the person who received him without due cause.

### Chapter II. A cleric may not transfer to another church if his own has been left without its proper ministers. From the Second Council of Seville, chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 1113] Held A.D. 619.—Collection in three parts, pt. 2, title 49, c. 2.]

It was decreed that, if any cleric, after his own church has been left without ministers [Note: [Col. 1113] “ministers”: eds. Arg., Nor., Venice I.], transfers to another, he is to be sent back to the church in which he formerly served, at the compulsion of the priest to whom he fled [Col. 1113B] [Note: [Col. 1113] “had fled”: the collected editions.]. The person who receives him but does not immediately choose to send him back to his own church without any resistance is to recognize that he is deprived of communion until he restores him [Note: [Col. 1113] “recognize”: the same editions.]. It is fitting that the deserting cleric, stripped for a time of the insignia of his rank and order, be confined in a monastery [Note: [Col. 1113] “bound”: Coll. Hisp.; “relegated”: ed. Bas.], and afterward recalled to the ministry [Note: [Col. 1113] “monastery”: ed. Venice II; “ministry”: remaining editions.] of ecclesiastical order. For the license of wandering [Note: [Col. 1113D] In editions of the councils and Vatican manuscripts, the readings are partly *propagationibus*, partly *pervagationis*; in the royal Lucca manuscript, *praevaricationis* (“transgression”) [“wanderings”: Coll. Hisp.].] cannot be removed in such persons unless correction follows discipline for their rebuke [Note: [Col. 1113] “through”: collected editions; “correction”: the same editions and Coll. Hisp.].

Gratian. But the following canon of the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 10, is objected [Note: [Col. 1113] Held A.D. 451.]:

### Chapter III. One transferred from one church to another is to have nothing in common with the former church.

### Part II

If anyone has already been transferred [Note: [Col. 1113] “however”: ed. Arg.] from one [Note: [Col. 1113] “another”: collected editions.] church to another, he is to have nothing in common with the former *church* [Note: [Col. 1113] “has”: Lyons II and III.], whether with martyr-shrines established under *that* church [Note: [Col. 1113] “mother churches”: ed. Bas.; “martyrs”: remaining editions.], with parishes [Note: [Col. 1113] “poorhouses”: Coll. Hisp.], with guesthouses, or with their business affairs. Those who, after the ordination of this great and ecumenical synod [Col. 1114A], dare to do what is prohibited, the holy synod decrees are to fall from [Note: [Col. 1113] “from his”: eds. Bas., Lyons II and III.] their own rank.

Gratian. But it is one thing to be transferred, another to transfer by one’s own rashness. The former may occur by apostolic authority; the latter is prohibited in every way.

### Part III, § 1

Moreover, just as one person ought not to be placed over two churches, so one church cannot be divided among several persons.

Hence one reads in the Council of Rheims [Note: [Col. 1113] Chapter of uncertain source.—Regino, bk. 1, c. 243; Burchard, bk. 3, c. 45; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 44; *Decree*, pt. 3, c. 49.]:

### Chapter IV. One church cannot be divided between two priests.

Just as there ought to be one presbyter in each church, so the church itself, which is called his bride or wife, cannot be divided among several presbyters. It is to have only one priest, who governs it chastely and [Col. 1114B] sincerely. We therefore forbid anyone to presume to divide a church between two or more persons, because Christ’s church ought to be a wife and bride, not a prostitute, as Pope Callixtus testifies [Note: [Col. 1113] Cf. C. 7, q. 1, c. 39.].

### Part IV. Gratian

A church must not be entrusted to hired priests.

Hence Innocent II, in the Roman Synod, chapter 10 [Note: [Col. 1114C] Eugenius III repeats this chapter in the same words at a Lateran council whose text is in the Vatican Library.] [Note: [Col. 1113] Second Lateran Council, held A.D. 1139.]:

### Chapter V. A church is not to be entrusted to hired priests.

We also command that churches are not to be entrusted to hired priests, and that every church which has sufficient means is to have its own priest.

## QUESTION III

### GRATIAN

[Col. 1114C] That clerics may not be managers of secular affairs is proved by the authority of the First Council of Carthage [Note: [Col. 1113] Held A.D. 348 or 349.—Burchard, bk. 2, c. 150.—Cf. Dist. 54, c. 3.], at which Nicasius, bishop of Culusita, is recorded as having spoken in chapter 6 [Note: [Col. 1114C] “Nicasius”: this heading has been corrected from the council itself and old manuscripts of Gratian, where previously it was wrongly read “Pope Nicholas to the bishops of Castile” [“Custilian”: ed. Bas.; “Tulistan”: eds. Arg., Nor., Venice I.]. This heading belongs to the chapter *Credo*, immediately following the interpolated *Palea*.]:

### Chapter I. PALEA

[Note: [Col. 1114D] This same canon, chapter 3 of the Council of Chalcedon, is cited above, Dist. 86, final chapter, from another translation. This *Palea* is absent from the collated copies except two.] [Note: [Col. 1113] Council of Chalcedon, c. 3, held A.D. 451; above, Dist. 86, final chapter, cited from the same Spanish translation, where variants are recorded.—Burchard, bk. 2, c. 145; Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 6, c. 214, from Dionysius.—Absent from ed. Bas.]

“It has come to the holy synod’s attention that certain persons enrolled among the clergy, for the sake of shameful gain [Col. 1115A], undertake leases of other persons’ estates [Note: [Col. 1115] “of greater persons”: collected editions.] and secular lawsuits [Note: [Col. 1115] “undertake; separate; resort; undertake”: collected editions.]. Through negligence they separate themselves from holy ministries and flock to the houses of secular persons, undertaking administration of their property for the sake of greed.

“The holy and great synod has therefore decreed that henceforth none of these—that is, no bishop, cleric, or monk—may lease estates or involve himself in secular management, except perhaps those whom the laws unavoidably draw into guardianships or curatorships for minors, or one to whom the bishop of the city itself has entrusted the administration of ecclesiastical affairs, or of orphans, unprotected widows, or persons who especially need ecclesiastical assistance because of the fear of God [Col. 1115B]. But if anyone transgresses these decrees, he is to be subject to ecclesiastical correction.”

### Chapter II. Those attached to the clergy are not to become managers of secular estates.

I believe that my proposal is pleasing to your holiness, and that it displeases you that those who serve God and are attached [Note: [Col. 1115] “have been attached”: ed. Bas.] to the clergy should engage in legal business, administration, or management of houses [Note: [Col. 1115] “secular”: added in the collected editions.]. Bishop Gratus said: “The ordinances of the Apostles also say [Note: [Col. 1115] 2 Tim. 2:4.], ‘No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs.’ Therefore, let clerics be free from the management of houses, or managers be without clerical office.” All said: “Let us observe this.”

### Chapter III. On the same matter. Likewise, from the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 15.

[Note: [Col. 1115] Held A.D. 397.—Burchard, bk. 2, c. 151; Anselm, bk. 7, c. 151 (161); Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 6, c. 142.]

[Col. 1115C] It was decreed that bishops, presbyters, deacons, and clerics are not to be lessees or [Note: [Col. 1115] “or”: Coll. Hisp., Burchard, Ivo.] managers [Note: [Col. 1115] “of private persons”: added in Coll. Hisp., Burchard, and Ivo.], nor seek their livelihood through any shameful [Note: [Col. 1115] “gain”: added in ed. Bas.] or dishonourable business, because they ought to remember what is written [Note: [Col. 1115] 2 Tim. 2:4.]: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs.”

### Chapter IV. Clerics are not to undertake management of secular affairs. Likewise, from Cyprian’s letter to the presbyters, deacons, and people of Furni, book I, letter 9.

[Note: [Col. 1115] Written c. A.D. 249.—Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 6, c. 393.] [Note: [Col. 1115] “of Furna”: collected editions.]

Cyprian, to the presbyters, deacons, and people dwelling at Furni [Col. 1116A] [Note: [Col. 1115] “of Furna”: the same editions.], greetings. Long ago it was decreed in a council of bishops that no one should appoint in his will any cleric or minister of God as guardian or [Note: [Col. 1115] “and”: ed. Bas.; “or”: remaining editions.] curator [Note: [Col. 1115] “name”: Ivo and collected editions.], since all who have been honoured with the divine priesthood and placed in clerical [Note: [Col. 1115] “of clerics”: collected editions.] ministry ought to serve only the altar and sacrifices and devote themselves to petitions and prayers [Note: [Col. 1115] “ought”: ed. Bas.]. For it is written [Note: [Col. 1115] 2 Tim. 2:4.]: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, in order that he may please the one who approved him” [Note: [Col. 1115] “to whom”: collected editions.].

And below:

§ 1. Our bishops and predecessors, considering this religiously and providing beneficially, decreed that no departing brother [Note: [Col. 1115] “departing”: collected editions.] should name a cleric to a guardianship or curatorship. If anyone did so, no offering was to be made for him, nor was sacrifice to be celebrated for his repose. For the person who wished to call priests and ministers away from the altar does not deserve to be named [Col. 1116B] [Note: [Col. 1115] “deserve”: the same editions.] in the prayer of priests before God’s altar [Note: [Col. 1115] “before”: collected editions; “wish”: the same editions; “summon”: ed. Arg.].

### Chapter V. Clerics may not be bound by burdens and secular affairs. Likewise, from the same source.

[Note: [Col. 1115] Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 6, c. 394.]

Those occupied with divine and spiritual things ought not to be bound by burdens [Latin printed: *mollitiis*; the true reading is *molestiis*, “burdens”] [Note: [Col. 1115C] The true reading is *molestiis*. But because it begins the chapter, it has not been altered; some other readings in this and the preceding chapter have been corrected.] [Note: [Col. 1115] “soft things”: ed. Arg.] and snares of secular affairs [Note: [Col. 1115] “by secular affairs and snares”: Ivo and collected editions.], nor can they leave the church [Note: [Col. 1115] “bind themselves”: collected editions; “are”: added in the same editions and Ivo.] and devote themselves to earthly and secular activities [Note: [Col. 1115] “nor to”: the same editions and Ivo; the words enclosed in asterisks are likewise absent from Ivo.].

### Chapter VI. Clerics are not to be bound to secular affairs. Likewise, from the same source.

[Note: [Col. 1115] Ivo, ibid., c. 395.]

Those who are promoted in the Lord’s Church to clerical ordination [Note: [Col. 1115C] “Clerical”: the genuine reading of Cyprian has been restored, preserved by the oldest manuscripts [Col. 1115D] [“clerical”: Ivo; “of clerics”: collected editions]. In all manuscripts of Cyprian, *clerical ordination* and *clerical letters* occur twice in bk. 2, letter 5, and near the end of bk. 3, letter 21.] are in no respect to be called away from divine administration [Note: [Col. 1115] “called to”: eds. Arg. and Bas.], nor bound [Note: [Col. 1115] “lest”: Ivo.] by burdens and secular affairs [Note: [Col. 1116C] This passage has been corrected and amplified from the printed original and a manuscript.]. Rather, receiving, as tithes from produce, the honoraria of contributing brethren [Col. 1116C], they are not to withdraw from the altar [Note: [Col. 1115] The words from “rather” to “receiving” are absent from Ivo.] [Note: [Col. 1115] “nor from”: Ivo and collected editions; “altars”: Ivo.], but are to serve heavenly and spiritual things day and night.

### Chapter VII. On the same matter. Likewise, as above, Cyprian in the same place.

[Note: [Col. 1115] Ivo, ibid., c. 396.]

Let the religious and necessary decree concerning the priesthood [Note: [Col. 1115] “of priests”: original and Ivo.] be observed by us, and let an example be given also to the other brethren [Note: [Col. 1115] “together with the brethren, as to the others”: ed. Bas.; “together with the brethren”: eds. Arg., Nor., Venice I.] [Note: [Col. 1115] “a good [example]”: added in ed. Bas.], so that no one may call priests and ministers of God, occupied with his altar and church, away to secular [Col. 1117A] burdens. Hereafter it will be possible to ensure that this is no longer done with respect to clerics [Note: [Col. 1117] “and concerning”: ed. Arg.; “that anyone do this”: Ivo and collected editions.], if what has now been done is punished [Note: [Col. 1117] “if”: ed. Arg.; “now”: retained by the printed text; “has been”: collected editions, first Basle edition, Lyons II and III.].

## QUESTION IV

### GRATIAN

That they may not adorn themselves in splendid and brilliant garments is commanded in the Seventh Synod, where chapter 16 decrees as follows [Note: [Col. 1117] Held A.D. 787.—Anastasius’s translation.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 195 (192); Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 5, c. 377.]:

### Chapter I. Clerics who indulge themselves with ointments and brilliant, splendid garments are to be rebuked.

Every ostentation [variant: *jactura*, “loss”: Venice I–II, Lyons I–II, Paris] and bodily adornment is foreign to the sacred order [variant: *sacro*, “sacred”: Ivo; *sit*, “is to be”: Argentinensis edition]. Therefore bishops or clerics who adorn themselves with glittering and splendid garments ought to be corrected. [Col. 1117B] If they persist in this, they are to be subjected to penance [variant: *contradantur*, “let them be handed over”: collected editions]. Likewise those who anoint themselves with perfumes.

§ 1. Since, indeed, the heresy [earlier reading: *haereticorum*, “of heretics,” in the collected older editions; corrected from Anastasius and Ivo to accord with the Greek αἵρεσις, “heresy”; several other readings were likewise restored from them] of those who slander Christians [omitted in the Argentinensis edition] has arisen as a root of bitterness and has brought defilement into the Catholic Church, and those who have accepted it have not only abhorred painted images [variant: *scripturas*, “writings”: collected older editions], but have also rejected every reverence, giving offence to those who live religiously and piously, and thus there is fulfilled in them what is written [Ecclus. 1:26]: “The worship of God is an abomination to a sinner”; therefore, if they are found ridiculing those clothed in humble and religious garments, they are to be corrected by penance [variant: *corriguntur*, “are corrected”: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I–II].

§ 2. For [the passage from *a* through *usque* is omitted in Ivo] from ancient [variant: *sanctus*, “holy,” for *sacratus*, “consecrated”: Argentinensis] times every consecrated man lived in a modest and humble garment [variant: *aut*, “or,” for *et*, “and”: collected older editions, first Argentinensis and Basel editions]. For everything received not for one’s necessity but [Col. 1117C] for elegance bears the reproach of pride, as the great Basil says [Shorter Rules, c. 49]. Nor did anyone put on a garment variegated with silken fabrics, nor place ornaments of various colours upon the upper edges [variant: *summitatibus*, “upper parts”: original and Ivo] of clothing. For they heard from the divine tongue that [Matt. 11:8] “those who wear soft clothing are in the houses of kings.”

[Col. 1118A] **C. II. Clerics, whether travelling or residing elsewhere, are to use clothing suitable to them. Likewise from the Sixth Synod, c. 27.**

[Note: Rather, from the Quinisext Council, held A.D. 692.—*Coll. tr.*, pt. 2, tit. 11, c. 12.]

None of those numbered among the clergy is to have unbecoming clothing, whether residing in a city or travelling, but is to use the stoles granted to clerics. If anyone does such a thing, he is to be suspended for one week.

[Note: The Greek has ἀφοριζέσθω, that is, “let him be separated.”]

**C. III. Clerics are to use not secular clothing, but clothing suitable to their order. Likewise Pope Zachary, in the Roman Synod, c. 3.**

[Note: This synod held by Pope Zachary is found in the Vatican and Royal libraries.]

[Note: Held A.D. 743.—Anselm, bk. 8, c. 41.]

Bishops, priests, and deacons are not to use secular garments, except, as is fitting, the priestly tunic. Nor, when they walk in the city, on the road, or in the streets, are they to presume to walk without a covering [Col. 1118B] except [variant: *praeterquam*, “except”: collected older editions] when they have travelled on a long journey [variant addition: *tempore*, “for a time”: the same editions, first Argentinensis]. For [variant: *sicut enim*, “for just as”: Basel] just as a woman praying in church [variant: *ecclesiis*, “churches”: collected older editions] with her head uncovered dishonours her head, according to the Apostle’s saying [variant: *apostolicam*, “apostolic”: the same editions; cf. 1 Cor. 11:4], so a priest without a covering dishonours his priesthood. If he rashly presumes to act contrary to these enactments, he is to be deprived of communion until he hastens to fulfil what has been established.

**C. IV. Priests are not to appear outside their homes without their proper dress. Likewise Pope Leo IV, in the Roman Synod, c. 12.**

[Note: Rather, from the synod of Eugenius II, held A.D. 826.—Anselm, bk. 7, c. 162 (116).]

It is not fitting for priests to appear outside their homes without priestly dress [variant: *nullo modo*, “in no manner”: collected older editions], lest they suffer insults like some layman [variant: *aliqui*, “some laymen”: Basel]; but they are to observe only those things which appear to have been established by the Fathers [this clause is absent in Anselm]. Whoever is found contrary to this must either desist [variant addition: *deinceps*, “thereafter”: original] or be subject to canonical discipline [Col. 1118C].

**C. V. Those who disdain correction by bishops are to be deprived of ecclesiastical benefices. Likewise Pope Innocent II, in the Lateran Council, c. 4.**

[Note: This chapter was issued by Innocent II at the Lateran Council and was subsequently renewed by Eugenius III in the Roman council.]

[Note: Held A.D. 1139.—Ivo, *Panormia*, at the end of bk. 8, c. 140.]

We command that bishops as well as clerics should strive to please God and men in disposition of mind and bodily attire, and that by excess, slashing [*scissura*: this word does not occur in Innocent’s council; in Eugenius’ synod the French manuscript reads *fissura*. The Vatican manuscript has *scissurae*, and some old manuscripts of Gratian have *fissurae*; the Argentinensis and Basel editions have *fissurae*, the remaining editions *scissurae*, and Ivo *scissura*], or colour [Col. 1119A] of their clothing, or by their tonsure, they should not offend the sight of those who look upon them—for they ought to be an example and pattern—but should rather display before themselves what befits their holiness [variant: *quae eos deceat*, “what befits them”: original; *decet*, “befits”: Basel]. If, after being warned by bishops, they refuse to amend, they are to be deprived of ecclesiastical benefices.

## QUESTION V

**GRATIAN.**

No one may abandon his own bishop, withdraw from his office, and have recourse to a secular judge.

Accordingly, one reads in the Council of Agde, c. 8 [held A.D. 506.—*Coll. tr.*, pt. 2, tit. 28, c. 7]:

**C. I. A cleric who has recourse to a secular judge is to be expelled from communion with the Church.**

It has pleased us that if a cleric, abandoning his office because of disciplinary severity, perhaps has recourse to a secular judge [the word *judicem*, “judge,” appears in more recent Cologne editions of the councils, but is absent from older editions, Vatican manuscripts, and the *Capitulare*, bk. 6, c. 143], and the person to whom he appeals affords him the assistance of defence [omitted in the Spanish Collection], he is to be expelled from the Church’s communion together with that person.

**C. II. A priest or deacon deposed by his bishop is not to approach the emperor. Likewise from the Council of Antioch, c. 12.**

[Note: Held A.D. 332.—Burchard, bk. 2, c. 180; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 225, from Dionysius.]

If a priest [variant: *vel presbyter*, “or a priest”: Spanish Collection] or deacon is deposed by his own bishop, or if any bishop is deprived of office by a synod, he is not to presume to bring his grievance before imperial ears. Rather, he is to turn to a larger synod of bishops, state before their council the grounds which he believes he has in justice, and await from them the judgment that shall be pronounced concerning him. If, weakened by faint-heartedness, he refuses to do this, but importunes the emperor, such a person is to receive no pardon [variants: *habet*, “has”: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I; *habere*, “to have”: remaining editions], have no opportunity of asserting his cause, nor any hope of recovering his rank in the future.

**C. III. One condemned by the judgment of bishops is not to be defended by anyone. Likewise from the Fifth Council of Carthage, c. 2.**

[Note: Held A.D. 401.—*Coll. tr.*, pt. 2, tit. 19, c. 2; Deusdedit, pt. 4.]

If a cleric of any rank has been condemned by the judgment of bishops [Col. 1120A] for any crime whatever [omitted in the Spanish Collection], it is not lawful for him to be defended either by the churches over which he presided or by any person, under penalty of loss of money and rank; and we decree that neither age nor sex excuses anyone from that penalty [variants: *a quo*, “from whom”: same source; *qua*, “from which”: Basel].

**C. IV. He who presumes to shelter one fleeing the rule of ecclesiastical discipline is to be deprived of communion. Likewise from the Council of Arles, c. 4.**

[Note: Third Council of Arles, held A.D. 524.]

If any cleric [variant: *quis*, “anyone”: Basel], evading the rule of ecclesiastical discipline, has wandered away, whoever receives him and not only fails to reconcile him to his bishop, but even presumes to defend him, is to be deprived of the Church’s communion.

**C. V. One condemned by bishops who appeals to the emperor is to lack hope of reconciliation. Likewise from the Council of Pope Martin, c. 35.**

[Note: c. 12 of the Council of Antioch, from the translation of Martin of Braga.]

[Col. 1120B] If any bishop, priest, or deacon, having been excommunicated in a council, complains that he has been unjustly condemned, let him return to a greater synod of bishops [variant: *concilium*, “council”: Spanish Collection] and, awaiting their inquiry and judgment [variant: *ut*, “that”: collected older editions], set before them whatever just grounds he thinks he has [omitted in the Spanish Collection]. But if he scorns this and, importunately [variant: *importunans*, “importuning”: Spanish Collection] presenting himself at court, wishes to trouble the ears of princes, he can obtain no pardon and shall have no hope of future reconciliation [variant: *habere*, “to have”: Basel].

[Note: “Greater”: formerly read “council of the greater bishops” [variant: *consilium*, “counsel”: Argentinensis]. It has been corrected from the Royal Lucchese manuscript, because it agrees with the canon of Antioch above, “If anyone by his own …,” whence it seems to have been taken.]

**C. VI. The cases of bishops ought not to be examined before princes. Likewise Gregory to the Empress Constantina, bk. IV, ep. 34.**

[Note: In the common editions and most manuscripts the addressee reads “Constantine Augustus.” It has been corrected from one old manuscript of Gratian and another of the letters of Blessed Gregory, although editions of those letters read “Constantia Augusta.” Zonaras, Nicephorus, Cedrenus, Anastasius the Librarian, and John the Deacon, in his *Life of Blessed Gregory*, bk. 3, no. 51, attest that the wife of Emperor Maurice, to whom Gregory wrote, was named Constantina. John the Deacon, recounting the letter from which this chapter is taken, says that it was addressed to the Empress Constantina.]

[Note: Ep. 21, written A.D. 595, bk. 5, Maurist edition.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 196.]

If the cases of bishops entrusted to me are managed before our most pious sovereigns through the patronage [variant singular: *patrocinio*, “patronage”: collected older editions] of others, [Col. 1120C] what am I, unhappy man, doing in this Church? Yet if my bishops [omitted in Basel] despise me and seek refuge against me with secular judges, I give thanks to almighty God and attribute it to my sins. Nevertheless, I state this briefly: I shall wait a little; and if they delay *long* in coming to me [variant: *distulerit*, “he delays”: original], I shall by no means cease to exercise canonical severity against them [variant: *eo*, “him”: same source].

# CAUSE XXII

[Col. 1121]

[Col. 1121A] **GRATIAN.**

A certain bishop swore falsely what he believed to be true. When this became known, his archdeacon swore that he would never render him obedience. The archdeacon is compelled by the bishop to show him the customary reverence. The bishop is accused of a double perjury: both because he swore what was false and because he compels the archdeacon to commit perjury. (Question I.) First it is asked whether an oath ought to be taken or not. (Question II.) Second, whether one who swears falsely what he believed true is perjured. (Question III.) Third, whether the archdeacon was permitted to refuse the bishop his customary obedience. (Question IV.) Fourth, if what the archdeacon swore is found unlawful, whether it must be kept. (Question V.) Fifth, if it is found that it must be kept, whether the bishop [Col. 1121B] is guilty of perjury in compelling his archdeacon to act against the oath.

## QUESTION I

**GRATIAN.**

**Part I.** That an oath ought not to be taken is proved by the authority of canonical Scripture. For Christ says to his disciples in the Gospel [Matt. 5:37]: “Let your speech be: Yes, yes; no, no; and what is more than this is from evil.” Likewise James says in his epistle [Jas. 5:12]: “Before all things, my brethren, do not swear at all.” By both authorities the taking of oaths is prohibited. But it is one thing to resort voluntarily to an oath, another to offer an oath either to establish one’s innocence, to confirm compacts of peace, or to persuade hearers, when they are slow to believe what is useful for them. The first is forbidden; the second is permitted. For swearing altogether is not a sin.

Accordingly, one reads in the Eighth Council of Toledo, c. 2 [held A.D. 653.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 83; *Decretum*, pt. 62, c. 2]:

**C. I. An oath is to be made for a pact of peace.**

Everything which enters into pacts of peace [variant: *foedere*, singular, “a pact”: Spanish Collection] then stands more firmly [Col. 1122A] when the addition of an oath strengthens it [variant: *substat*, “stands”: Spanish Collection]. And everything which reconciles the minds of friends then lasts more faithfully [variant: *fixius*, “more fixedly”: Spanish Collection] when the bonds of a sacred oath bind them. Everything also [variant: *enim*, “indeed”: Ivo and collected older editions] which is supported by witnesses [variants: *testis*, singular, “a witness”: Ivo and Spanish Collection; *adstipulat*, singular, “supports”: Spanish Collection] is then established more truly when the addition of swearing [variant: *adjurationis*, “adjuration”: Basel] confirms it. And even if a witness is lacking, the mere imposition of an oath reveals the trustworthiness of the innocent.

[Note: Older editions of the councils, two Vatican manuscripts, and one manuscript of the Dominican monastery read: “But even if the record is lacking, the faith of the guilty,” etc. More recent Cologne editions and the Royal Lucchese manuscript agree with Gratian, Ivo, and the *Panormia*.]

**C. II. Swearing is not to be forbidden, nor sought as though it were a good. Likewise Augustine, on the Epistle to the Galatians, c. 1, at the end.**

[Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 84; *Decretum*, pt. 12, c. 3; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, bk. 3, c. 39; Polycarp, bk. 5, tit. 11.]

An oath which comes from evil is not contrary to God’s command; the evil is not that of the person swearing, but of the unbelief [variant: *increduli*, “of the unbeliever”: collected older editions] of the person to whom [variant: *a quo*, “by whom”: same editions and Ivo] he is compelled to swear. For this [omitted in Basel; variants: *hinc*, “from this”: Ivo’s *Decretum*, Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I; *hic*, “here”: remaining editions and Ivo’s *Panormia*] makes it understood that the Lord so forbade swearing [variant: *jurejurando*, “oath-taking”: collected older editions] that, so far as lies within a person’s power, no one should swear—a practice contrary to that of many who have an oath constantly in their mouths as though it were something great or pleasant [variant: *et*, “and”: same editions and Ivo’s *Decretum*]. For the Apostle surely knew [variant: *novit*, “knows”: collected older editions] the Lord’s command, and yet he swore. Those who suppose that these are not oaths are not to be listened to. What, indeed, will they make [variants: *faciant*, “might make”: Ivo’s *Panormia*; *faciunt*, “make”: Basel] of this oath [addition *juratione*, “oath”: collected older editions, first Argentinensis and Nuremberg]: [1 Cor. 15:31] “I die daily, by your glory, brethren, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord”? The Greek copies prove beyond doubt that this is an oath [variant: *ostendunt*, “show”: collected older editions].

[Note: In Blessed Augustine and the other collectors, this passage reads: “Therefore, so far as lies within his power, the Apostle does not swear; for he does not seek an oath from desire or delight in swearing. For it is more than ‘yes, yes; no, no,’ and therefore it is from evil—but from weakness,” etc.]

Therefore we are forbidden to swear from desire or delight [variant: *dilectione*, “love”: collected older editions and Ivo’s *Panormia*] in swearing. Although an oath is more than “yes, yes; no, no” [variant: *vel non non*, “or no, no”: same editions], and is therefore from evil, it is nevertheless not from your evil but from the weakness or unbelief [addition: *a malo*, “from evil”: Argentinensis, Basel, Lyons II–III] of those who are not otherwise moved [Col. 1122C] to faith.

**C. III. It is perjury, not swearing, that is sin. Likewise Augustine, in Epistle CLIV to Publicola.**

[Note: Ep. 43, Maurist edition, written A.D. 398.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 85; *Decretum*, pt. 12, c. 4.]

It is said in the New Testament [Matt. 5:35] that we should not swear at all. This seems to me to have been said not because swearing *truthfully* is a sin, [Col. 1123A] but because perjury is an enormous sin. He wished us to remain far from it when he admonished us not to swear at all [variants: *commovit*, “moved”: Basel; *commonuit*, “admonished”: remaining editions and Ivo].

**C. IV. In necessary cases, swearing truthfully is not a sin. The same author, Sermon XXX, on the Words of the Apostle.**

[Note: Sermon 180, Maurist edition.—Polycarp, bk. 6, tit. 11.]

So that you may know that swearing truthfully is not a sin, we find that the Apostle Paul also swore [1 Cor. 15:31]: “I die daily, by your glory, brethren, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord.” “By your glory” is an oath. For he did not say, “By your glory I die” [addition: *ego*, “I”: Argentinensis and Basel], as though your glory made me die [variants: *faciat*, “may make”: Lyons III; *fecit*, “made”: remaining editions except Lyons II], in the way that, if one said “he died by poison,” “he died by the sword,” “he died by a beast,” or “he died by an enemy,” it would be understood that he died through the agency of the enemy, the sword, or the poison [Col. 1123B].

[Note: In Blessed Augustine and Bede this reads: “as if he said, ‘He died by poison, he died by the sword, he died by a beast, he died by an enemy,’ that is, through the enemy’s action, the sword’s action, poison’s action, and the like. He did not say this of ‘your glory.’”]

**C. V. An oath is not to be sought as a good, nor avoided as an evil. The same author, *On the Lord’s Sermon*, bk. I, c. 30.**

[Note: Anselm, bk. 11, c. 76.]

The Lord is therefore understood to have commanded that no oath be sworn [variant: *juraretur*, “be sworn”: collected older editions], lest anyone seek an oath as though it were a good, and by the habit of swearing fall through custom into perjury. Accordingly, whoever understands that an oath is to be used not among good things but among necessities should restrain himself [variant: *refrenat*, “restrains”: same editions] as far as possible, and not use it unless necessity [variant: *necessitate quum videt*, “when he sees necessity”: original] compels him—namely, when [variant: *ut*, “that”: Basel] he sees people slow to believe what it is useful for them to believe unless it is confirmed by an oath [variant: *firmentur*, plural, “they are confirmed”: same source]. Thus [variant: *utique*, “certainly”: collected older editions] the saying [Matt. 5:37] applies: “Let your speech be: Yes, yes; [Col. 1123C] no, no.” This is good and is to be sought. But what is more is from evil—that is, if you are compelled to swear, know that it arises from the necessity caused by the weakness [addition: *utique eorum*, “certainly of those”: Basel] of those to whom you are commending something [variant: *suadeas*, “you commend”: same source]. That weakness is certainly an evil, from which we pray daily to be delivered when we say [Matt. 6:14], “Deliver us from evil.” Therefore he did not say [omitted in Basel], “What is more is evil.” For you do not do evil when you use an oath rightly [omitted in Basel].

[Col. 1124A] **C. VI. Swearing is not a sin. The same author, immediately following.**

[Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 86; *Decretum*, pt. 12, c. 5.]

You do not do evil when you use an oath rightly. Although it is not good, it is nevertheless necessary in order to persuade another of that which you usefully commend to him [variants: *suades*, “you commend”: original, Ivo, Argentinensis, Basel]. But it is from the evil of the person through whose weakness you are compelled to swear.

[Note: In Augustine, after the final words of the preceding chapter, “when you use an oath rightly,” there follows immediately: “although it is not good,” etc.; likewise in one very old manuscript of Gratian, in which these two chapters are not divided.]

**C. VII. Swearing by God is permitted, lest one swear by idols. Likewise Jerome, on Jeremiah, at c. 4.**

[Note: Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, bk. 3, dist. 39.—Cf. Jer. 4:2.]

“And they shall swear, ‘As the Lord lives,’ in truth, in judgment, and in righteousness; and the nations shall bless him [addition *omnes*, “all”: Basel and Lyons II–III] and praise him.” How, then, does the Gospel prohibit us from swearing? Here [variant: *hoc*, “this”: Argentinensis], “you shall swear” [variant: *juramentum*, “oath”: collected older editions] is said concerning confession and for the condemnation [Col. 1124B] of idols, by which Israel used to swear. Thus stumbling-blocks are removed, and one swears [variant: *jurat*, “swears”: original] by the Lord [addition: *Deum*, “God”: collected older editions, first Argentinensis]. The phrase “As the Lord lives” is, in the Old Testament, an oath for [variant addition: *et*, “and”: Argentinensis and Basel] the condemnation of the dead beings by whom every idolater swears.

[Note: In Jeremiah c. 4 the text reads *jurabis*, “you shall swear”; but because this is the beginning of the chapter it was not altered, and a little later *jurabis* was restored where *juramentum*, “oath,” had previously been read.]

**C. VIII. Swearing is permitted to the weak. Likewise Jerome, on Matthew, bk. I, at c. 5.**

[Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 87; *Decretum*, pt. 12, c. 6; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, bk. 3, dist. 39.]

Observe that *here* [omitted in Ivo] the Saviour did not prohibit swearing by God [variant: *Dominum*, “the Lord”: Argentinensis], but prohibited swearing [variant: *prohibuit*, “prohibited”: collected older editions] by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, and your own head. This was granted by the Law, as it were, to little children: just as they offered sacrifices to God lest they offer them to idols, so they were permitted to swear in [variant: *per*, “by”: same editions, first Argentinensis] God. This was not because they did right in doing so, but because it was better [variant: *est*, “is”: collected older editions] to render this to God than to demons [variant: *daemoniis*, “demonic beings”: same editions and Ivo] [Col. 1124C].

**C. IX. A cleric who obstinately swears by created things is to be excommunicated. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Carthage, cc. 61 and 62.**

[Note: cc. 74–75, *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*.—Cf. on c. 9, Distinction 18.—Regino, bk. 1, cc. 130, 155; Burchard, bk. 2, cc. 170, 175; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, cc. 266, 261.]

A cleric who swears by created things is to be rebuked most sharply; if he persists in the vice, he is to be excommunicated. We also decree that one who sings during meals is to be restrained by the severity of the aforesaid judgment.

[Col. 1125A] **C. X. A cleric swearing by God’s hair or head is to be deposed; a layman is to be anathematized. Likewise Pope Pius.**

[Note: Similar provisions occur in Novella 77 of Julian the Antecessor, but not exactly the same. Hence Ivo cites the passage from the *Novellae*, pt. 12, c. 32; but this chapter is cited, c. 27, from the Decrees of Pius, as also by Burchard.]

[Note: Cf. Roman Penitential, tit. 2, c. 10.—Burchard, bk. 12, c. 15; Anselm, bk. 11, c. 72 (71); Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 12, c. 72.]

If anyone swears by God’s hair or head, or uses blasphemy against God in any other way, if he belongs to ecclesiastical order [variant: *ex*, “from”: cited collections], he is to be deposed; if he is a layman, he is to be anathematized. If anyone swears by a creature [variant plural: *creaturas*, “creatures”: collected older editions], he is to be punished most severely and to do penance according to the synod’s judgment.

§ 1. If anyone does not report such a person, there is no doubt that he too is restrained by divine condemnation.

§ 2. But if [variant: *et si*, “and if”: Argentinensis and Basel] a bishop neglects to correct these matters, he is to be rebuked most sharply [addition: *a synodo*, “by the synod”: Burchard].

**Part II. Gratian.** It is asked who is more strictly bound: one who swears by God, or one who swears upon the sacred [Col. 1125B] Gospels. John Chrysostom answers this question, saying:

**C. XI. Swearing by the Gospel is not greater than swearing by God.**

[Note: Rather, the author of the *Opus imperfectum*, Homily 44 on Matthew 23.—Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, bk. 3, dist. 39; Polycarp, bk. 6, tit. 11.]

If some matter arises, the person who swears by God appears to do something minor, whereas the person who *swears* by the Gospel seems to do something greater. To such people one must *likewise* say [variant: *est ita, o stulti*, “It must be said thus, O fools”: Basel]: “Fools: the Holy Scriptures [*sanctae*, “holy,” corrected from several old manuscripts, the original, and Polycarp; earlier reading *factae*, “made”: Basel and Lyons II–III] exist for God’s sake, not God for the Scriptures’ sake.”

**C. XII. Perjury must be avoided not only at the altar or upon relics, but also in ordinary speech. Likewise Jerome.**

[Note: Burchard and Ivo cite this from Jerome’s sayings, where it has not been found, but it occurs in the Capitularies, bk. 1, c. 63.]

[Note: Rather, from the Capitularies of the Frankish Kings, bk. 1, c. 61.—Regino, bk. 2, c. 311; Burchard, bk. 12, c. 2; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 12, c. 59.]

We have it written in the Law of God [Lev. 19:12]: “You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of your God in vain.” Therefore all are to be admonished carefully [Col. 1125C] to avoid perjury, not only at the altar or upon the relics of saints, but also in ordinary speech.

**C. XIII. God does not prohibit swearing, but perjury. Likewise Isidore, *Sentences*, bk. II, c. 31.**

[Note: Burchard, bk. 12, c. 10; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 88; *Decretum*, pt. 12, c. 7; Polycarp, bk. 6, tit. 12.]

Swearing is not contrary to God’s command; but while we make use of swearing, we incur the guilt of perjury.

**C. XIV. Swearing is not a sin. Likewise Augustine, on the Words of the Apostle, Sermon 28, otherwise 30.**

[Note: Sermon 180, Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 89; *Decretum*, pt. 12, c. 8; Polycarp, bk. 6, tit. 11.]

If swearing were a sin, neither would it be said in the old Law [reference as printed: Lev. 10:12]: “You shall not swear falsely; but you shall render [variants: *reddes*, “you shall render”: Ivo and collected older editions, first Paris and Lyons I; *autem*, “but”: omitted in collected older editions, first Lyons II–III] your oaths to the Lord.” A sin would not be commanded to us.

Likewise below, § 4: We do not tell you that we do not swear. If we said this, we would lie. So far as concerns me, I swear [variant: *non juro*, “I do not swear”: collected older editions], but, as it seems to me, only when compelled by great necessity: when I see [variant: *video*, “I see”: same editions and Ivo’s *Panormia*] that I am not believed [variant: *quod creditur*, “that what is believed”: Basel] unless I do so, and that it is not expedient for the person who does not believe me that he should not believe. Having weighed this reasoning and balanced it with careful consideration, I say with great fear: “Before God,” or “God is witness” [variant: *est mihi Deus*, “God is my witness”: Ivo’s *Panormia* and collected older editions], or “Christ knows” that this is so in my mind [variant: *quod sic est*, “that it is so”: collected older editions and Ivo’s *Decretum*]. And I see that it is something more—that is, more than “yes, yes; no, no.” But what is more [variant: *hoc quod*, “this which is more”: collected older editions] is from evil [variant: “what is more is from the evil not of the one swearing but of the one who does not believe”: same editions], though it is not from the evil of the person swearing, but from the evil of the person who does not believe [Col. 1126A].

**Part III. Gratian.** From the foregoing it is gathered that swearing is not a sin; yet it is not to be sought as a good, lest through the habit of swearing we fall into perjury. But since it is said to proceed from the evil of the unbeliever, it appears that, although swearing is not a sin, receiving an oath is nevertheless evil. But by the name “evil” is understood not wickedness, but the punishment of sin. For that unbelief by which we are compelled to swear proceeds from penal weakness. Yet just as swearing itself is not a sin, so receiving an oath from another is not evil.

Accordingly Augustine writes to Publicola in Epistle CLIV:

[Note: Ep. 43, Maurist edition, written A.D. 398.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 12, c. 4.]

**C. XV. We are not forbidden to receive an oath.**

Although it has been said that we should not swear, I do not recall ever having read [variant: *legi meminerim*, “I may remember having read”: original] anywhere in the Holy Scriptures that we should not receive an oath from someone [variants: *alio*, “another”: original and Ivo’s *Decretum*; *recipiamus*, “receive”: collected older editions].

[Col. 1126C] **Part IV. Gratian.** But it is asked whether one ought to rely upon the good faith of a person who swears by demons. Augustine writes as follows on this subject in the same Epistle CLIV to Publicola:

[Note: Anselm, bk. 11, c. 75 (74); Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 117; *Decretum*, pt. 12, c. 35; Polycarp, bk. 6, tit. 11; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, bk. 3, dist. 39.]

**C. XVI. It is lawful to rely upon the good faith of one who swears by demons in order to keep it.**

You ask whether one should rely on the good faith of a person who has sworn by demons in order to keep it. Here I want you first to consider whether, if someone has sworn by false gods that he will keep faith and then has not kept it, he does not seem to you [variant: *videtur*, “seems”: collected older editions, first Lyons II–III] to have sinned twice. If he had kept [variant: *custodiret*, “guarded”: original] the faith promised by such an oath, he would have been judged to have sinned only [variant: *tamen*, “nevertheless”: collected older editions] because he swore by such gods [variants: *de deos falsos juraverit*, “swore by false gods”: same editions; addition: *se fidem servaturum*, “that he would keep faith”: same editions, first Argentinensis, Basel, Nuremberg]. But no one would blame him for keeping faith [variant: *reprehendet*, “will blame”: Ivo’s *Decretum*; addition *recte*, “rightly”: Böhm]. Now, however, because he both swore by those by whom he ought not to have sworn and acted contrary to the faith he had promised, which he ought not to have done, he certainly sinned twice. Consequently, the person who relies on the good faith of someone known to have sworn by false gods, and relies on it not for an evil purpose but for one lawful and good [variant: *non ad malum, sed ad licitum et bonum*, “not for an evil matter but for one lawful and good”: original, Anselm, Ivo, and collected older editions], does not associate himself with that person’s sin [variant: *illius*, “that person’s”: Ivo and collected older editions] by which [variant: *qui*, “who”: same editions] he swore by demons, but with the good compact by which he kept faith.

Nor do I mean here the faith by which those baptized in Christ are called believers. That faith is far different and clearly distinct from the fidelity involved in human agreements and compacts. Nevertheless, without any doubt, it is a lesser evil to swear truthfully by false gods than to swear falsely by the true God. [Col. 1127B] For the holier [variant: *id per*, “that by”: Lyons editions] that by which one swears, the more punishable is perjury.

§ 1. There is, therefore, another question: whether the person who causes someone to swear to him by false gods does not sin, since the person who swears to him swears by false gods which he worships.

[Note: In printed letters of Blessed Augustine it reads: “than he who swears to him worships false gods”; in a Vatican manuscript of the same letters: “when he who swears to him worships false gods”; in the Froben edition and Ivo: “because he who swears to him worships false gods.”]

In support of this question may be adduced the testimonies which you yourself mentioned concerning Laban and Abimelech [Gen. 21 and 31], if indeed he swore by his own gods, as Laban swore by the God of Nahor.

[Note: *Nachor* is corrected from Genesis itself, Ivo, and one old manuscript of Gratian; the common editions had *per Deum Sochot*, “by the god Sochot” [Basel, Lyons II–III], or *Socoth* [remaining editions]. Augustine reads “by the God of Jacob.”]

**Gratian.** Likewise, when the Romans are read in the book of Maccabees to have confirmed peace with the Jews, they must be understood to have sworn by false gods, just as the Jews swore by the true God. The same must be understood concerning an oath made by created things: swearing itself by created things is evil, because it is prohibited by God; but keeping what is sworn is good, so that the sin of lying and deceit may be avoided.

§ 1. But it is objected that Joseph, a holy man, swore by a creature when he said to his brothers [Gen. 42:15], “By the life of Pharaoh, you shall not leave here.”

§ 2. But it must be understood that the saints swore not so much by creatures as by the Creator of creatures, and in creatures venerated nothing other than their Creator. Thus Joseph, in swearing by Pharaoh, venerated in him the fact that, by God’s judgment, he had been placed in a lowly position. Hence the Apostle [Col. 1128A] says [Rom. 13:1], “All authority is from God.” Likewise Christ says to Pilate [John 19:11], “You would have no authority over me unless it had been given you from above.” But God prohibited swearing by creatures, lest either, after the manner of the gentiles, some divine power should be believed to dwell in creatures, or lest, regarding creatures as contemptible, we should count promises made by them as nothing.

§ 3. But it is asked which is graver: to swear falsely by creatures or by the Creator. The person who swears falsely by creatures is guilty in two ways: he swears contrary to the prohibition by that by which it is not lawful for him to swear—an offence from which the person who swears only by the Creator is free—and he deceives his neighbour, as does one who swears falsely by the Creator. But if perjury is more punishable in proportion as that by which one swears is holier, it is apparent [Col. 1128B] that, although one who swears falsely by creatures sins in two ways, one who swears falsely by the Creator nevertheless subjects himself to a graver punishment.

V. Part. § 4. The penalty for perjury is most severe; if anyone, through fear of it, refuses to come to confession, he is to be excluded from the fellowship of the faithful.

Hence Pope Eutychianus [Note: [Col. 1128C] Burchard, Polycarp, and Ivo also cite this from Eutychianus. It is, however, found among certain chapters written by Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, to his priests, ch. 26, preserved in an ancient manuscript at Rome.] [Note: [Col. 1127] Rather, ch. 26, Chapters of Theodulf of Orléans.—Burchard, bk. 12, ch. 14. Anselm, bk. 11, ch. 71 (70). Ivo, Decree, pt. 12, ch. 71.]:

C. XVII. Let him who refuses to do penance for perjury be deprived of the fellowship of the faithful.

It must also be preached that the faithful should beware of perjury and abstain from it with the utmost care, knowing it to be a great crime, prohibited in the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel. For we have heard [Note: [Col. 1127] “however”: Ivo.—Old collected editions.] that some make light of this crime and impose upon perjurers a penance that is, in some sense, slight; [Col. 1128C] such persons [Note: [Col. 1127] addition: “also”: ibid.] ought to know that a penance for perjury should be imposed such as is imposed for adultery, fornication, voluntary homicide, and the other criminal vices. § 1. But if anyone, having committed perjury or any other criminal sin, refuses through fear of a long penance [Note: [Col. 1127] “the long affliction of penance”: original.] to come to confession, he is to be expelled from the Church, that is, from communion and the fellowship of the faithful, so that no one may eat or drink with him, *or pray* [Note: [Col. 1128D] “Or pray”: this has been added from Theodulf, Burchard, and Ivo.], or receive him into his house.

## QUESTION II

[Col. 1129A]

## GRATIAN

I. Part. That perjury consists in swearing falsely is easily proved. For Augustine says in his exposition of the Psalms, on “The earth is the Lord’s” [Note: [Col. 1129D] What is cited here from Blessed Augustine in the interlinear gloss on Psalm 23, at the verse “nor sworn deceitfully,” is derived from Cassiodorus.]:

C. I. He commits perjury who will act otherwise than he promises.

He swears deceitfully who will act otherwise than he promises, since perjury is wickedly to deceive one who trusts [Note: [Col. 1129] “those who trust”: Basel edition.].

C. II. What companions an oath ought to have. Likewise Jerome on Jeremiah, book I, on chapter 4 [Note: [Col. 1129] Ivo, Panormia, bk. 8, ch. 123; Decree, pt. 12, ch. 22; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, bk. 3, distinction 39.].

It must be observed that an oath should have these companions: truth, judgment, and justice. If these are absent, it will by no means be an oath, but perjury.

[Col. 1129B] Gratian. Likewise, he who swears falsely lies. But to swear while lying is nothing other than to commit perjury. § 1. Therefore, since all who speak falsehood are to perish, according to the Psalmist’s words [Note: [Col. 1129] Psalm 5:7.], “You will destroy all who speak falsehood,” much more condemnable are those convicted of committing perjury by lying, because they take the name of their God in vain. § 2. But swearing falsely is one thing; swearing deceitfully is another. Not everyone who will act otherwise than he promises swears deceitfully. For although the Apostle would act otherwise than he promised the Corinthians in the First Epistle, when he said [Note: [Col. 1129] 1 Corinthians 16:5.], “I shall come to you,” he nevertheless did not swear deceitfully or promise falsely. For the man who swears deceitfully or promises falsely has it in his mind that he will not act as [Col. 1129C] he promises; but he who promises a falsehood which he believes to be true neither swears deceitfully nor promises falsely.

Hence Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*, sermon XXVIII, alternatively XXX [Note: [Col. 1129] Sermon 180, Maurist edition.—Ivo, Panormia, bk. 8, ch. 111; Decree, pt. 12, ch. 39; Peter Lombard, ibid.]:

C. III. Concerning one who swears falsely what he believes to be true.

People swear falsely either when they deceive or when they are deceived. For either [Note: [Col. 1129] omitted in the old collected editions, first Lyons II and III.] a person thinks true what is false and swears rashly; or he knows or thinks it false, yet swears that it is true, and nonetheless swears wickedly. These two kinds of perjury which I have mentioned differ. Suppose [Note: [Col. 1129] “he makes”: ibid.] a man [Note: [Col. 1129D] “Suppose a man”: likewise in Ivo, in one Vatican manuscript of Augustine’s sermons, and in the Antwerp edition. Other witnesses read, “he swears more easily.”] swears to what he thinks true; he thinks it true, yet it is false. He does not commit perjury deliberately [Note: [Col. 1129] “commits perjury”: original; Ivo; old collected editions; first Paris and Lyons.], but is mistaken: he takes as true what is false, and does not knowingly introduce an oath concerning a false matter. [Col. 1130A] Give me another man who knows something to be false, says that it is true, and swears as though what he knows to be false were true. Do you see what a detestable monster this is, to be banished from human affairs? Who would wish [Note: [Col. 1129] omitted in Ivo, *Panormia*, and in the old collected editions, first Paris and Lyons.] this to happen [Note: [Col. 1129] “wished”: Ivo, *Panormia*]? Everyone detests such things. Suppose another man *who* [Note: [Col. 1129] omitted in Ivo and Venice I.] thinks something false and swears as if it were true, though perhaps it is true. For example, so that you may understand [Note: [Col. 1129] “you may understand”: old collected editions, first Basel and Lyons II.], it is raining in that place. You ask a man, and he thinks [Note: [Col. 1129] “and says that it rained”: old collected editions.] that it has not rained; yet his business requires him to say, “It rained,” though he thinks it did not rain. *He is asked, “Did it really rain?” “It really did,” and he swears* [Note: [Col. 1130D] “And he swears”: these words have been supplied from the original and Ivo in order to make the passage complete. An oath must precede if a man is to be called perjured, yet in Gratian’s manuscripts there was no mention of the oath. Some other matters also have been corrected.]; and yet it did rain there, but he does not know it and thinks that it did not rain: *he is perjured*. It matters how the word proceeds from the mind. The tongue is not guilty unless the mind is guilty.

[Col. 1130B] Gratian. Therefore, since this man’s mind was not guilty—for he did not know that what he swore to be true was false—and since he seemed to himself to have discovered, not rashly or negligently but with great diligence, that as true which he swore, though it was false, he is by no means to be judged guilty of perjury. Likewise, the statement “he who swears falsely lies” must not be understood universally. For not everyone who says what is false lies, just as not everyone who lies says what is false.

Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 22 [Note: [Col. 1129] Peter Lombard, bk. 3, distinction 38.]:

C. IV. To say as false what one believes true is not to lie.

But the person [Note: [Col. 1129] “Everyone”: original.] who lies [Note: [Col. 1129] “who lies lies”: Basel, Lyons II and III editions.] speaks, with the intention of deceiving, contrary to what he feels in his mind. § 1. Certainly, words were instituted not [Note: [Col. 1129] “not so that people might deceive one another by them, but so that by them”: old collected editions.] so that people might deceive one another by them, but so that each might convey [Col. 1130C] his thoughts to another’s knowledge by them [Note: [Col. 1129] “carry over”: original.]. Therefore, to use words for deception rather than for the purpose for which they were instituted is a sin. § 2. Nor should any lie be thought not to be a sin because by lying we may sometimes benefit someone. For we can also benefit someone by stealing, if the poor person to whom something is openly given feels the advantage, while the rich person from whom it is secretly taken feels no loss; yet no one would say [Note: [Col. 1129] “said”: old collected editions.] that such theft is not a sin. And above, ch. 18 [Note: [Col. 1129] Peter Lombard, ibid.; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, ch. 133; Decree, pt. 12, ch. 51.]:

§ 3. No one is to be judged a liar who says [Note: [Col. 1129] “said”: Basel edition.] what is false but believes it true, because, so far as he is concerned, he does not deceive but is deceived. Thus the person who carelessly [Col. 1131A] [Note: [Col. 1131] “incautiously”: Basel, Paris, Lyons II and III editions; “more incautiously”: Ivo; “more incautiously believes things credited as true”: original.] believes false things and regards them as true should be accused not of lying but sometimes of rashness. Conversely, so far as he is concerned, the person lies who says as true [Note: [Col. 1131] “as though true”: old collected editions, first Argentinensis.] what he thinks false. For, so far as his mind is concerned, because he does not say what he thinks, he does not speak truth, even though what he says is found to be true. Nor is one who unknowingly speaks truth with his mouth in any way free from lying, if he knowingly lies in intention [Note: [Col. 1131] “intention”: Basel edition.]. Therefore, considering not the things themselves of which something is said, but the speaker’s intention alone, better is the person who unknowingly says what is false because he believes it true, than the person who knowingly harbours an intention to lie, while not knowing that what he says is true.

C. V. He does not lie who has no intention to deceive. Likewise Pope Gelasius [Note: [Col. 1131] In Anselm, bk. 13, ch. 22, this chapter—whose author has not been discovered at all—is given at much greater length.].

The blessed Apostle Paul is not, God forbid, to be thought to have deceived or to have proved inconsistent with himself because, although he had promised to go to Spain [Note: [Col. 1131] “Spain”: Basel edition.], he was occupied, by divine ordering, with more important causes and could not fulfil what he had promised. For, as far as his own will was concerned, he declared what he truly wished to accomplish. But, as to the hidden counsels of the divine plan [Note: [Col. 1131] “council”: Argentinensis, Basel, and Venice II editions.]—which, though full of God’s Spirit, he could not as a man know in every respect—he was prevented by a higher disposition and left his purpose unfulfilled. § 1. Nor is the blessed Apostle Peter, God forbid, to be regarded as having deceived or as having failed to abide by his own resolve because, out of devotion to divine reverence, he answered the Lord himself [Note: [Col. 1131] John 13:8.], “You shall never wash my feet,” but immediately yielded [Note: [Col. 1131] “yielded”: Basel edition.] to that same divine will and, constrained by the causes of human salvation, willingly allowed to be done what he had said [Col. 1131C] he would not do [Note: [Col. 1131] “constrained”: ibid.].

II. Part. Gratian. Therefore, the person who lies by swearing falsely is he who knows that what he swears is false. For a lie is, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1131] In the book addressed to Consentius, *On Lying*, ch. 12.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, ch. 125; Decree, pt. 12, ch. 45.], a false signification by speech [Note: [Col. 1131] omitted in the original and in Ivo’s *Decree*.] with the intention of deceiving. § 1. But since deceiving always belongs to the will, whereas being deceived arises either from weakness or rashness, and since what proceeds from the will is more serious than what proceeds from rashness or weakness, it sometimes happens that being deceived is either no sin or a very small one; sometimes, from the varying nature of the matters considered, it is less bad to deceive than to be deceived.

[Col. 1132A] Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 21 [Note: [Col. 1131] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, ch. 132; Decree, pt. 12, ch. 45; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, bk. 3, distinction 39.]:

C. VI. In matters not pertaining to faith, to be deceived is either a small sin or no sin.

In matters [Note: [Col. 1131] “certain matters”: original.] in which it makes no difference for attaining God’s kingdom whether they are believed or not, and whether they are true, whether in fact or merely thought to be so, or false, to err in them, that is [Note: [Col. 1131] “and”: old collected editions, first Basel.], to think one thing is another, is not to be judged a sin; or, if it is a sin, it is most slight and trivial.

C. VII. In matters pertaining to faith, it is more serious to be deceived than to deceive others. The same, *Enchiridion*, ch. 18 [Note: [Col. 1131D] In Blessed Augustine, and not much differently in Ivo, the reading is [Col. 1131] substantially the same in the *Panormia*: “In the consideration of the things themselves which are spoken of, it makes such a difference in what matter each person is deceived or lies that, although, as regards a person’s will, to be deceived is a lesser evil than to lie, nevertheless in these matters it is far more tolerable,” etc. But because of the gloss on the phrase *utcumque* [alternatively *ubicumque*, “wherever”], it was not altered.] [Note: [Col. 1131] Ivo, *Panormia*, ibid., ch. 133; Decree, ibid., pt. 51.].

In considering the matters themselves [Note: [Col. 1131] addition: “also”: Basel edition.] which are spoken of, there is such a difference that, whether someone is deceived or lies, although in any case being deceived is a lesser evil than lying, [Col. 1132B] as regards human will, nevertheless [Note: [Col. 1131] “and nevertheless”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.] it is far more tolerable to lie in matters separated from religion [Note: [Col. 1131] “region”: Basel edition; addition: “of faith”: Basel and Lyons editions.] than to be deceived in matters without faith or knowledge of which God cannot be worshipped [Note: [Col. 1131] “heaven”: Basel edition; “to be compelled”: Venice II and Paris editions.] [Note: [Col. 1131] “nor be deceived”: Lyons I and Paris editions; omitted in the Argentinensis edition.].

III. Part. Gratian. Likewise, the statement, “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” [Note: [Col. 1131] Psalm 5:7.], must not be understood of every lie. For there are certain lies in which, though there is some fault, they are not damnable—indeed, they ought to be regarded as though they were not lies. There are other lies of graver fault, and it is of these that the words are understood: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood.” § 1. In order that it may be clear which lies are venial and which damnable, we must distinguish how many kinds of lies there are.

[Col. 1132C] Of these Augustine writes in *On Lying*, ch. 14 [Note: [Col. 1131] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, ch. 124; Decree, pt. 12, ch. 1; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, ibid., distinction 38.]:

C. VIII. How many kinds of lying are there?

The first [Note: [Col. 1131] “The first is the lie to be avoided, a capital…”: original.] is the capital lie, and one to be avoided far above all others: that which is made in religious teaching. No one ought, under any condition, to be induced to this lie. The second is a lie intended unjustly to injure someone, which *also* [Note: [Col. 1131] absent from the original and Ivo; “nor” in Böhm.] is such that [Note: [Col. 1131] “which”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.] it *both* benefits no one and harms someone. The third benefits one person while harming another, although it does not harm that person by bodily impurity. The fourth, *which is committed* from a mere appetite for lying and deceiving, is a sheer [Note: [Col. 1131] “mere”: original; Ivo, *Decree*.] lie. The fifth [Col. 1133A] is done from a desire to please by agreeable speech [Note: [Col. 1133] “pleasant eloquence”: Ivo, *Panormia*, and old collected editions.]. When all these have been entirely avoided and rejected, there follows the sixth kind: that which *both* harms no one and benefits someone, as when a person, knowing where another’s money is, lies that he does not know, when it is about to be unjustly [Note: [Col. 1133C] “Unjustly”: this word is absent from the original; in two manuscripts of Gratian, “justly” is read in its place.] taken away, *whoever may ask him* [Note: [Col. 1133C] “Whoever may ask”: these words have been added from the original.]. The seventh [Note: [Col. 1133] addition: “kind of lying”: old collected editions, first Argentinensis.] is that which harms no one and benefits someone, as when a person lies because he does not wish to betray someone sought for death [Note: [Col. 1133] “being unwilling”: original, Ivo, and old collected editions; Böhm.]. And later in the same place: The eighth kind of lying harms no one and benefits someone by protecting that person from bodily impurity. And later, ch. 21:

§ 1. Therefore one must not lie in the teaching of piety; for it is a great [Note: [Col. 1133] “which”: Argentinensis edition; “because”: the remaining editions, except Basel, which omits it; Ivo.] crime and the first kind of detestable lie. One must not lie in the second kind, because no injury is to be done to anyone. One must not lie in the third [Col. 1133B] kind, because no one should be helped at another’s injury. One must not lie in the fourth kind, on account of the appetite for lying, which is vicious in itself. One must not lie in the fifth kind, because even truth itself should not be uttered merely for the sake of pleasing people [Note: [Col. 1133] “cause”: old collected editions; “desire”: Ivo, *Panormia*.]; how much less a lie, which, precisely because it is a lie, is certainly shameful in itself? One must not lie in the sixth kind, for not even the truth of testimony may rightly be corrupted for anyone’s temporal advantage or safety [Note: [Col. 1133] “any person’s”: Ivo, *Panormia*; “anyone whatsoever’s”: Ivo, *Decree*, and old collected editions.]; and no one is to be led to eternal salvation with a lie’s assistance. And later: One must not lie in the seventh kind either, for no one’s temporal advantage or safety is to be preferred to the fulfilment of faith; nor should anyone suppose that he is so badly affected by our right actions as to become even worse in mind and farther removed from piety [Note: [Col. 1133C] “Let no one [suppose]: But if anyone is so badly affected by our right actions as to become worse in mind and much farther removed from piety, right actions are not therefore to be abandoned.” This is the reading in Blessed Augustine and Ivo. But because of the gloss on the words “right actions,” it was not altered.].

And later: One must not lie in the eighth kind either, because among good things chastity of the mind takes precedence over bodily chastity [Note: [Col. 1133D] “bodily chastity; and among evils, what we ourselves do is worse than what we allow to be done.” This is the reading in the same sources.
