But the same reason prevented alteration.], and among evils, *that* which we ourselves do is more blameworthy for us than what we allow to be done. § 2. In these [Note: [Col. 1133] “therefore”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.] eight kinds, one sins less in lying the farther [Col. 1134A] [Note: [Col. 1134C] “The farther”: the original reads, “the nearer he rises to the eighth, the less; the nearer he descends to the first, the more.” But there was a gloss on the word “withdraws.”] one withdraws from the first. But whoever thinks there is any kind of lie that is not a sin shamefully deceives himself, when he supposes [Note: [Col. 1133] “supposes”: old collected editions.] himself to be an honourable deceiver of others.

C. IX. It is not permitted to lie for humility’s sake. Likewise Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*, sermon XXXI, alternatively XXIX [Note: [Col. 1133] Sermon 181, Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, ch. 128; Decree, pt. 12, ch. 42.].

When you lie for humility’s sake, if [Note: [Col. 1133] omitted in the Argentinensis and Basel editions.] you were not a sinner before you lied [Note: [Col. 1133] “had lied”: Argentinensis and Basel editions; “will lie”: Nuremberg and Venice I–II editions.], by lying you become what you had avoided. Truth is not in you unless you call yourself a sinner in such a way that you recognize yourself to be one. Truth itself is that you say what you are [Note: [Col. 1133] “is”: Ivo, *Panormia*, and old collected editions.]. For how can there be humility where falsehood reigns?

C. X. On the same matter. Likewise Gregory [Note: [Col. 1133] “Augustine, alternatively Gregory”: Argentinensis edition.], *Morals*, book XXVI, ch. 2.

[Col. 1134B] Carelessly [Note: [Col. 1133] “careless”: old collected editions.] humble [Note: [Col. 1134C] “They are carelessly humble”: so in most manuscripts. The vulgate reading was, “People are unwisely humble.” The complete passage of Blessed Gregory runs: “They are unwisely humble who ensnare themselves by lying while they avoid arrogance; indeed, by lying they are proud, because they raise themselves against truth, which they abandon.”] are [Note: [Col. 1133] “people”: Venice II, Lyons, and Paris editions.] those who ensnare themselves by lying.

C. XI. It is not permitted to lie in order to avoid arrogance. Likewise Augustine on John, tractate XLIII.

Arrogance should not be avoided in such a way that truth is abandoned.

C. XII. Not every lie is equally sinful. The same, *Enchiridion*, ch. 18 [Note: [Col. 1134D] Some matters in this chapter have been inserted and others corrected from Blessed Augustine and Ivo.] [Note: [Col. 1133] Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 12, ch. 51.].

It seems to me [Note: [Col. 1133] “does not seem unreasonable”: old collected editions.] that every lie is indeed a sin, but it makes a great difference with what intention and about what matters each person lies. For the person who lies with an intention to help does not sin in the same way as the person who lies with an intention to harm; nor [Note: [Col. 1133] “or indeed”: original; Ivo.] does the one who sends a traveller by lying onto the wrong [Note: [Col. 1133] “different”: original; Ivo.] road do as much harm as the one who corrupts the way of life by deceptive lying.

[Col. 1134C] C. XIII. No one at all ought to be deceived. Likewise Augustine, *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, ch. 19 [Note: [Col. 1133] Collected works, third part, vol. 22, ch. 26; Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 12, ch. 44.].

One ought to deceive no one, either by artful lying or by simple speech, because however [Note: [Col. 1134D] “However”: the little book itself reads, “Whatever artifice a person may use in lying, the mouth that lies kills the soul.” But Ivo agrees with Gratian.] anyone lies, he kills his soul.

[Col. 1135A] C. XIV. A perfect person ought not to lie for someone’s temporal life. Likewise Augustine on Psalm 5, at the verse “You will destroy all who speak” [Note: [Col. 1135] Anselm, bk. 11, ch. 79 (78); Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, ch. 130; Decree, pt. 12, ch. 46.].

Let no one suppose that a perfect and spiritual person ought to lie for this temporal life, in [Note: [Col. 1135] “by whose death either his own or another’s soul is killed”: old collected editions.] whose death neither his own soul nor another’s is killed; for lying is one thing and concealing truth another. To speak falsehood is one thing and to keep truth silent another. Thus, if someone perhaps *does not wish* [Note: [Col. 1135] “wishes”: old collected editions.] to betray a person to this visible death, he ought to be prepared to conceal the truth, not to speak falsehood, so that he neither betrays nor lies, lest he kill his own soul for another’s body. And later:

§ 1. There are altogether two kinds of lies in which the fault is not great, yet which are not without fault: when we joke, or [Note: [Col. 1135] “or lie to our neighbour”: Ivo, *Panormia*; “or lie for our neighbour”: Ivo, *Decree*; “or lie in helping our neighbour”: old collected editions.] lie in order to benefit our neighbours. The first kind, joking, is not most destructive [Note: [Col. 1135] “destructive”: old collected editions and Ivo.] because it does not deceive: the person to whom it is said knows that it was spoken in jest [Note: [Col. 1135] “for joking … it was”: old collected editions.]. The second is milder [Note: [Col. 1135] “milder”: original; Argentinensis edition.] because it retains some benevolence.

§ 2. But that which does not have a double heart is not even to be called a lie. For example, if a sword is entrusted to someone, and he promises to return it when the one who entrusted it asks; if the owner who entrusted it [Note: [Col. 1135] “has entrusted it”: old collected editions.] should demand his sword back while insane, it is clear that it *must then not be returned* [Note: [Col. 1135] “believed”: Basel edition.], lest he kill either himself or others [Note: [Col. 1135] “another”: old collected editions.], until his sanity is restored. This person does not have a double heart because, when he promised to return the sword to the person who asked, the person to whom the sword had been entrusted did not think that the owner might demand it while insane. And later:

§ 3. It is clear [Note: [Col. 1135C] In Blessed Augustine these precede: “But the Lord also concealed truth when he said to disciples not yet able to receive it: ‘I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now’ [John 16:12]; and the Apostle Paul when he said, ‘I could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal’ [1 Corinthians 3:1]. [Col. 1136C] Hence it is clear,” etc.] that sometimes concealing truth is not blameworthy, but speaking falsehood is not found to have been permitted *to perfect persons* [Note: [Col. 1135] “to holy persons”: old collected editions and Ivo.].

C. XV. We ought not to provide for another’s safety by our own sin. The same, *Against Lying*, ch. 17 [Note: [Col. 1135] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, ch. 125; Decree, pt. 12, ch. 48.].

Let a person do what he can for the temporal safety [Note: [Col. 1135] “temporal life or safety”: Basel edition; “temporal life and safety”: Argentinensis edition.] of human beings. But when he reaches [Col. 1136A] the point [Note: [Col. 1135] “when it comes to this point”: old collected editions and Ivo, *Panormia*.] at which he cannot provide for such safety except by sinning, he should then judge that he has nothing left to do, when he sees that the only thing remaining is what he should rightly [Note: [Col. 1136C] “Rightly”: the original reads “not rightly,” but this was not corrected because of a case.] do [Note: [Col. 1135] The Roman edition reads “not rightly,” but it was altered together with the very notation in the errata index, a fact overlooked by all subsequent editors.—“will do”: old collected editions, first Lyons II and III.].

C. XVI. On the same matter. Likewise Isidore, *Synonyma*, ch. 10 [Note: [Col. 1135] Book 2, ch. 10.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, ch. 126; Decree, pt. 12, ch. 49.].

Flee every kind of lie most carefully. Speak no falsehood either accidentally or deliberately. Do not seek to lie even in order to do a service, and do not defend anyone’s life by any deception whatever. Beware of lying in [Note: [Col. 1135] “with”: Basel edition.] all matters.

C. XVII. On the same matter. [PALEA.] Likewise Augustine, *On Lying*, ch. 6 [Note: [Col. 1136C] This chapter is absent from most ancient manuscripts; in two it appears under the name *Palea*.] [Note: [Col. 1135] Augustine’s own words are not quoted.].

“If anyone should flee to you [Note: [Col. 1135] “has fled to you, who by”: old collected editions.] and could be freed from death by your lie, you are not to lie. For the mouth that [Col. 1136B] lies kills the soul [Note: [Col. 1135] “Every … who”: Argentinensis and Basel editions; cf. Wisdom 1:11.].” And later: § 1. “Therefore, since eternal life is lost by lying, one must never lie for anyone’s temporal life [Note: [Col. 1135] omitted in the Argentinensis edition.].”

C. XVIII. Statements of things that are not so, when made in jest, are not reckoned lies. Likewise Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 44, question 145 [Note: [Col. 1135] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, ch. 129; Decree, pt. 12, ch. 43.].

Joseph’s words to his brothers, “Did you not know that a man such as I divines by divination?” [Note: [Col. 1135] “that a man such as I does not divine by divination”: old collected editions; cf. Genesis 44:15.]—and the fact that he also ordered his *own man* [Note: [Col. 1135] “his own”: recovered reading.] to mention this divination to them—occasion the question of what he meant by it: because it was not said seriously but [Note: [Col. 1135] Ivo, *Panormia*, and old collected editions, first Lyons and Paris.] in jest, as the outcome showed, is it not to be regarded as a lie? For lies are seriously performed by liars, not in jest. But when things that are not are said as though [Note: [Col. 1135] addition: “they are”: old collected editions, first Argentinensis.] in jest, they are not [Col. 1136C] reckoned [Note: [Col. 1135] “reckoned”: old collected editions.] lies.

Gratian. But many things were permitted in the Old Testament whose examples may not lawfully be used today.

Hence Gregory, *Morals*, book XVIII, ch. 3:

C. XIX. It is not permitted to lie on the example of the ancients.

If someone wishes to defend his own lie by the Old Testament because it perhaps harmed certain persons less there, he must say that the seizure of others’ property [Col. 1137A] *and* [Note: [Col. 1137] “let him speak of retribution”: Basel edition.] repayment of injury, which were there granted to the weak, cannot harm him. It is clear to everyone with what severity truth now pursues all these things [Note: [Col. 1137] “may pursue”: same edition.], now that, having set aside the shadow of their signification, it is manifested to us in true flesh.

C. XX. The midwives were rewarded for piety and punished for lying. The same, in the same book, ch. 2 [Note: [Col. 1137] The first part of the chapter is found in Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 12, ch. 41.].

If any fault is customarily cleansed by the pious action which follows it, how much more easily is that fault wiped away which piety itself, the mother of good action, accompanies? Yet some try to maintain, from [Note: [Col. 1137] “from”: Lyons II and III editions; omitted in the rest.] the midwives’ deception, that this kind of lie is not a sin, especially because it is written concerning them while they lied [Note: [Col. 1137] Exodus 1:21.], “The Lord built houses for them” [Note: [Col. 1137] “a house”: Venice I and Nuremberg editions.]. In this very recompense [Col. 1137B] it is more clearly recognized what the fault of lying deserves. For the reward of their kindness, which could have been repaid them in eternal life, was, because the fault of lying had preceded it [Note: [Col. 1137] “admitted,” alternatively “mixed in”: original.], diverted to an earthly [Note: [Col. 1137] “to earthly recompense”: old collected editions, first Lyons II and III.] recompense.

Gratian. Abraham too, speaking to his servants, said [Note: [Col. 1137] Genesis 22:5.], “Stay here with the ass; the boy and I will go on as far as that place, and, when we have worshipped, we shall return to you.” Although he had resolved to do otherwise, he is nevertheless excused from lying. Hence Ambrose, *On the Patriarchs* [Note: [Col. 1137] Book 1, *On the Patriarchs*, ch. 8.]: Abraham prophesied [Note: [Col. 1137] omitted in the Argentinensis, Basel, and Nuremberg editions.] what he did not know. He alone intended to return after sacrificing his son. But the Lord spoke through his mouth what He was preparing to do. He spoke guardedly to the servants, lest, once the matter was known, someone should hinder him [Note: [Col. 1137] addition: “him”: old collected editions.] or interrupt with lamentation or weeping.

[Col. 1137C] V. Part. § 1. Sometimes, by commanding something, we signify that we wish it to be done, although we do not wish it to be done; rather, we seek a trial of obedience. Thus Abraham is recorded as having been tested by God [Note: [Col. 1137] Genesis 22.] when he was commanded to sacrifice the son whom the Lord did not wish him to kill. Hence, in the same book, Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1137] Same, ch. 8.]:

For God did not wish the father to sacrifice his son [Note: [Col. 1137] addition: “his”: old collected editions, first Argentinensis, Nuremberg, and Venice I.], nor did He wish this offering to be completed—He who supplied a sheep to be sacrificed in place of the son—but He tested the father’s affection, to see whether he would prefer God’s commands to his son. And later: “Do not lay your hand upon the boy, nor do anything to him.” [Note: [Col. 1137] “to him”: old collected editions.] And later: “I sought your affection, not demanded your deed; I tested your mind, whether you would spare not even your most beloved son for my sake. I do not take away what I myself gave, [Col. 1137D] nor do I begrudge the heir whom I granted to one who had none.”

[Col. 1138A] C. XXI. Simulation is useful and may be adopted at the proper time. Likewise Jerome, on Galatians, ch. 2.

Let the example of Jehu, king of Israel, teach us that useful simulation may be adopted at the proper time. Since he could not put the priests of Baal to death unless he pretended [Note: [Col. 1137] “pretended”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions omit *nisi*, “unless.”] that he wished to worship the idol, he said [Note: [Col. 1137] “saying”: old collected editions; cf. 4 Kings [2 Kings] 10:18–19.], “Gather to me all the priests of Baal. *For if* King Ahab served Baal [Note: [Col. 1137] “him”: old collected editions.] in a few things, I shall serve him [Note: [Col. 1137] “himself”: same editions, first Lyons II and III.] in many.” And David too, when he changed his appearance before Abimelech, who dismissed him, and he departed [Note: [Col. 1137] 1 Kings [1 Samuel] 21.]. Nor is it surprising that even righteous persons should simulate certain things temporarily for their own safety and that of others, when our Lord himself [Note: [Col. 1137] addition: “Jesus Christ”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.], having no sin and no flesh of sin, assumed the semblance of sinful flesh [Col. 1138B] [Note: [Col. 1137] “assumed”: old collected editions, first Lyons II–III.] so that, condemning sin in the flesh, he might make us the righteousness of God in himself.

Gratian. Behold which lies are venial and which damnable. § 1. But the question is raised why Augustine says that one must not lie for someone’s temporal life, when Abraham, descending into Egypt, asked Sarah to say falsely that she was his sister, saying [Note: [Col. 1137] Genesis 12:11 ff.], “I know that you are a beautiful woman, and that when the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘She is his wife,’ and they will kill me but preserve you. Say, I beg you, that you are my sister, so that it may go well with me because of you and my life may be preserved for your sake.” But Abraham wished not that a lie be spoken, but that the truth be concealed.

[Col. 1138C] Hence Augustine himself says in *Questions on Genesis*, question 26 [Note: [Col. 1137D] Not all the words of this chapter occur in question 26 itself; it has also been compiled from book 22 *Against Faustus*, *Against Secundinus*, and other passages.] [Note: [Col. 1137] Augustine’s words in this chapter have been altered here and there. Similar passages occur in book 22 *Against Faustus*, chs. 33 and 34.]:

C. XXII. How Abraham is excused from lying when he called Sarah his sister.

The question is raised why the patriarch wished to lie by calling Sarah his sister, rather than entrusting the matter to God, who, if He wished, could preserve her chastity with Pharaoh. But he wished truth to be concealed, not a lie to be spoken. For she was called his sister because she was the daughter of his brother. This shows that no one ought to test his God while he has something that he can do by reasonable counsel. Abraham did what he could; what he could not do he entrusted to God, in whom he hoped, and neither faith nor hope deceived him. But if, when questioned, he had identified that *woman* [Note: [Col. 1137] “judged”: Argentinensis and Basel editions; “identified”: the remaining editions.] as his wife, he would have entrusted two things to God’s protection: both his own life and his wife’s chastity.

[Col. 1138D] Gratian. It is further objected that Jacob [Note: [Col. 1137] Genesis, chapter 22], by lying, [Col. 1139A] both benefited himself and harmed another, yet is not reproached but commended. But Jacob, when he said that he was Esau the firstborn, did not lie. For he did not say that he was firstborn by birth, but that, since Esau had sold it, he was rightly assuming the right of the firstborn. Thus Christ also said that John [Note: [Col. 1139] Matthew, chapter 11] was Elijah—not in person, but by imitation of virtue. Jacob therefore was Esau, not by birth, as we have said, but by purchase of the birthright, passing from non-firstborn to firstborn; just as Esau himself, by selling the birthright, deserved to become non-firstborn from being firstborn. So also the Jews, although according to the flesh they were children of Abraham, because they were not his children by imitation are not counted among Abraham’s children, but are called children of the devil, whose children they are not by birth but by imitation. Hence they deserved to hear from the Lord [Note: [Col. 1139] John 8:39]: “If you are Abraham’s children, [Col. 1139B] do the works of Abraham; but now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you. Abraham did not do this. You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father.”

§ 1. Conversely, although the Gentiles were alien to Abraham according to the origin of the flesh, they nevertheless succeeded to the status of Abraham’s children through imitation of faith and righteousness. Hence the Apostle says to them [Note: [Col. 1139] Galatians 3:29]: “But if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring.” For this reason the same Apostle, writing to the Romans, says [Note: [Col. 1139] Romans 2:25–26]: “O Jew, if you are circumcised but do not observe the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision; just as uncircumcision, if it keeps the righteous requirements of the law, is reckoned as circumcision.” Therefore, as follows from what has been said, imitation in conduct is preferred to origin in the flesh.

[Col. 1139C] Jacob therefore truly, not falsely, said that he was Esau; and he benefited himself not by lying but by speaking the truth, while he did no harm to the other, because he received the blessing owed to him and did not steal what belonged to another.

§ 2. This bishop, however, whose case is at issue, even if he swore falsely, is nevertheless not held guilty of perjury, because, as stated above [Note: [Col. 1139] above, the same chapter, section 3], it is only a guilty mind that makes the tongue guilty. This is also proved by the example of Saul. When he was about to fight against the Philistines, he swore that he would kill whoever ate before sunset. But Jonathan [Note: [Col. 1139] 1 Kings 21], his son, not having heard the king’s oath, after inflicting a great slaughter on the enemy in battle and bringing deliverance to Israel, was suffering from hunger. He saw a honeycomb, took it with the royal staff that he held in his hands, and ate; immediately his eyes, which hunger had almost [Col. 1139D] closed, were opened, and his face brightened. When Saul learned this, he wished to put him to death; but, appeased by the prayers and devout entreaty of the people, he revoked the sentence of death, so that he should not kill the man through whom deliverance [Col. 1140A] had been given to Israel, and by whose fighting that people had been freed from the hands of its enemies. Behold, Saul swore falsely, because, recalled by the prayers of the people, he did not do what he had decreed by oath that he would do. Yet he is not accused as guilty of perjury, because, insofar as it lay within him, he fulfilled what he had sworn when he passed sentence of death upon his son—a sentence that he revoked not out of carnal affection but at the people’s entreaty.

## QUESTION III

## GRATIAN

Since, therefore, as has been demonstrated by reasoning and example, the bishop was not guilty of perjury, the archdeacon ought not to have withheld his customary obedience from him. For, [Col. 1140B] even if it had been established that he was criminal, nevertheless, before a definitive sentence, as has been shown above, none of his clerics was permitted to withdraw from him. It is therefore clear that what the archdeacon confirmed by oath was unlawful. Hence it is rightly asked whether it ought to be observed or not.

## QUESTION IV

## GRATIAN

### Part I

That unlawful oaths ought not to be observed is read in the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 2, where it was decreed as follows [Note: [Col. 1139] Found in A.D. 653; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 90; *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 9]:

**Chapter I. It is better not to fulfill the vows of a foolish promise than to commit a crime.**

[Col. 1140C] If, in public sacramental proceedings—may God avert it—anyone had put forward an unlawful or improper condition [Note: [Col. 1139] “bound”: the Hispanic Collection; Ivo; the second and third Lyon editions], one that would compel him either to kill the soul of a father or to commit the rape of a most sacred virgin, would it not be more tolerable to reject the vows of a foolish promise than, by keeping useless promises, to complete the dreadful measure of crimes?

**Chapter II. Sometimes it is not expedient to keep a promised oath. Likewise Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I, chapter 50.** [Note: [Col. 1139] Compare the Eighth Council of Toledo, in the same place; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 91; *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 10; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book 3, distinction 39.]

It is also sometimes contrary to duty to fulfill a promised oath—to keep it [Note: [Col. 1139] “To keep”: this word has been added from the original and from the Council of Toledo, where it is cited]—as in the case of Herod, who swore that he would give Herodias’s daughter whatever she requested [Note: [Col. 1139] “was requested”: Ivo, *Decretum*; “was going to request”: *Panormia*; the collected editions; compare Matthew 14], *and* procured the death of John, lest [Col. 1140D] he deny his promise.

Gratian. Likewise, in the sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, on the beheading of Saint John the Baptist, which begins, “When the holy Gospel was being read” [Note: [Col. 1139] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 92; *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 11; Peter Lombard, in the same place]:

[Col. 1141A] **Chapter III. It was an act of piety that David did not kill Nabal as he had sworn.**

That David did not fulfill his oath by shedding blood was the greater piety. I see [Note: [Col. 1141C] “I see”: these are the words of Blessed Augustine in that sermon. The preceding words seem to be a kind of summary and are not found in Ivo or in the *Panormia*] David, a pious and holy man, fall into a rash oath and prefer not to do what he had sworn rather than fulfill his oath by shedding a man’s blood [Note: [Col. 1141] “Fulfill”: the collected editions].

**Chapter IV. On the same matter. The same author, in the same place** [Note: [Col. 1141] Ivo, *Decretum*; Peter Lombard, in the same place; *Panormia*, in the same place, chapter 96].

David swore rashly, but through greater piety he did not fulfill his oath. And below:

§ 1. Behold, St David did not indeed shed a man’s blood in anger; but who can deny that he swore falsely? [Variant: “though bound by an oath”: Ivo, *Panormia*, and the collected editions; “could”: Argentinensis edition.] Of two sins he chose the lesser [Variant: “the least”: Ivo and the collected editions]; but it was lesser in comparison with the greater [Variants: “former”: Ivo and *Panormia*; “worse”: the collected editions]. For, weighed in itself, [Col. 1141B] false swearing [Variants: “a false oath”; “to swear falsely”: the same editions] is a great evil.

**Chapter V. Shameful vows must not be observed. Likewise Isidore, *Synonyma*, book II** [Note: [Col. 1141C] “Book II”: Saint Braulio likewise records two books of the *Synonyma* in his life of Isidore. In the *Synonyma*, recently printed at Paris with Isidore’s other works, a division into two books would readily fit. For from the latter part there seems to have been taken the little book *On the Rule of Life*, which is found in the same Paris manuscript [Col. 1141D]. Another little book, *On Contempt of the World*, which was printed both there and earlier at Antwerp and formerly at Venice under the title *Isidore: On Man and Reason Lamenting, and on Man and Reason Consoling*, seems to be a kind of epitome of the *Synonyma*.] [Note: [Col. 1141] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 12; compare the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 2, and the Council of Tribur, chapter 21.]

Break faith in evil promises. Change your resolution in a shameful vow. Do not do what you rashly vowed (ne facias; variant non facias [Note: [Col. 1141] “not”: the original; Ivo; the Argentinensis and Basel editions]). For a promise fulfilled through wickedness is impious.

**Chapter VI. An oath by which evil is rashly promised must not be observed. Likewise Bede, Homily XLIV, on the feast of the beheading of Saint John** [Note: [Col. 1141] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 94; *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 13; compare below, chapter 16.]

If it should happen that we have sworn something rather incautiously [Note: [Col. 1141] “To swear”: the collected editions], and its observance would lead to a worse outcome, let us know that it must freely be changed by sounder counsel, and that, under pressing necessity, we should rather commit perjury than [Col. 1141C] turn aside, in avoiding perjury, into another and graver crime. Thus David swore [Note: [Col. 1141] 1 Kings 25] by the Lord [Note: [Col. 1141] “By God”: the collected editions] to kill Nabal, a foolish and impious man, and to destroy everything that belonged to him [Note: [Col. 1141] “Belonged to him”: the same editions]. But at the first intercession of Abigail, a prudent woman, he immediately withdrew his threats, returned the sword to its sheath, and did not grieve that he had incurred any guilt through such [Note: [Col. 1141] “Through such”: the same editions] perjury.

[Col. 1142A] **Chapter VII. Of two evils the lesser must be chosen. The same author, in the same place** [Note: [Col. 1141] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 95; *Decretum*, in the same place.]

Not only in swearing [Note: [Col. 1141] “In”: absent in the Argentinensis and Basel editions], but in everything that we do [Note: [Col. 1141] “Everything”: Ivo, *Panormia*; the collected editions, first Lyon editions], this moderation must be observed with the greatest care [Note: [Col. 1141] “More anxiously”: the collected editions], so that, if we should happen to fall through the snares of the crafty enemy into such a predicament that we cannot rise from it without some contagion of sin [Note: [Col. 1141] “Can”: the same editions; Ivo, *Panormia*], we should seek the avenue of escape in which we see that we shall suffer the lesser danger.

**Chapter VIII. It is more tolerable not to fulfill an oath than to do what is shameful. Likewise Ambrose, *On Duties*, book III, chapter 12** [Note: [Col. 1141] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 17; compare the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 2.]

Let each person speak simply [Note: [Col. 1141] Addition: “his own”: the Argentinensis, Basel, and second and third Lyon editions]; let him possess his vessel in sanctification, and let him not ensnare his brother by deception in words. Let him promise nothing dishonorable; or, if he has promised it, it is more tolerable not to do what was promised than to do what is shameful. Often many bind themselves by the sacrament of an oath, and, when they themselves recognize that they ought not to have made the promise, nevertheless, out of regard for the oath, they do what they pledged, as we wrote above concerning Herod [Note: [Col. 1141] Matthew 14], who shamefully promised a reward [Note: [Col. 1141] Addition: “which”: the collected editions] to the dancing girl and cruelly paid it. It is shameful [Note: [Col. 1141] Addition: “it is”: the same editions] that a kingdom should be promised for a dance; it is cruel [Note: [Col. 1141] Addition: “it is”: the same editions] that the death of a prophet should be given for the sake of religious scruple concerning an oath [Note: [Col. 1141] “Given”: the same editions; Ivo, *Panormia*]. How much more tolerable would perjury have been in such an oath [Note: [Col. 1141] “Homicide”: Ivo, *Decretum*. It is not, however, read this way in all Ambrose’s manuscripts: the Maurist editions of Ambrose’s works attest that some read *dejeratus*, others *ejuratus* (as in the *Panormia*), and others *iratus*]? If indeed it can be called perjury when a drunken man swore amid wine, when, emasculated [Col. 1142C] amid the choruses of dancers, he had made a promise [Note: [Col. 1142C] “Evirated”: corrected from Saint Ambrose [Col. 1142D] and Ivo. Previously it read: “and having sworn”]. The prophet’s head is brought in on a platter [Col. 1142C], and what was madness was judged to be fidelity [Note: [Col. 1141] “Friendship”: Ivo and the collected editions, first and second Lyon editions].

And shortly afterward, discussing Jephthah [Note: [Col. 1141] Judges 11]:

§ 1. “Miserable,” he says, “is the necessity that is discharged by parricide. It is better not to vow than to vow what the person to whom it is promised would not wish to have paid” [Note: [Col. 1141] “Than to vow”: absent from the Argentinensis and Basel editions].

And shortly afterward:

§ 2. Therefore not all promises must always be fulfilled [Note: [Col. 1141] “Fulfilled”: Basel edition]. For the Lord himself often changes his sentence, as Scripture indicates [Note: [Col. 1141] Compare below, chapter 12].

[Col. 1143A] **Chapter IX. The unchangeable God sometimes changes his own ordinances. Likewise, from the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 2** [Note: [Col. 1143C] The beginning of this chapter has been corrected from the Cologne editions of the councils and the royal Lucchese manuscript. In the older editions, however, and in two Vatican manuscripts and two manuscripts of the Dominican monastery, after the verse “To be bound,” which in the council itself precedes this chapter, the following words continue without interruption: “For although the statements of the unchangeable deity are most firm, nevertheless frequently …,” with the intervening material omitted.] [Note: [Col. 1143] Found in A.D. 653.]

The unchangeable [Note: [Col. 1143] “The unchangeable and ever-existing God, ever the same, and the supreme nature of God”: the Argentinensis and Basel editions. “The unchangeable God, ever the same and ever-existing, and the supreme nature of God”: the remaining editions] and ever-existing nature of God, ever the same [Note: [Col. 1143] “Ever the same”: the Hispanic Collection], is often read in the sacred writings to have changed its promises, *sparing* [Note: [Col. 1143] “Surpassing”: the Hispanic Collection] and tempering its sentence out of mercy. Therefore, although it is impassible and unchangeable [Note: [Col. 1143] “Inchangeable”: the same editions], and although the utterances of that same divinity are most firm [Note: [Col. 1143] “Although the same divinity is indeed of the firmest”: the Hispanic Collection], nevertheless both its oaths and its repentance are frequently recorded, veiled in the sacred mysteries [Note: [Col. 1143] “Is veiled”: Basel edition]. For God’s swearing is his in no way overturning what he himself has ordained; but his repenting is his changing those same ordinances when he wills. Thus through Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 1143] Jeremiah 18:7] he says: “Suddenly I will speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to root it up, destroy it, and annihilate it [Note: [Col. 1143] “And scatter it”: Basel edition]. If that nation repents [Col. 1143B] of its evil [Note: [Col. 1143] “From”: the Hispanic Collection], “concerning which I have spoken against it,” I too will repent of the evil that I have thought to do to it [Note: [Col. 1143] “To them”: the same editions].

**Chapter X. It is the mark of a wise person to retract what he has said wrongly. Likewise Augustine** [Note: [Col. 1143] The chapter is of uncertain attribution.]

It is a mark of great wisdom for a person to retract what he has spoken wrongly.

**Chapter XI. What punishment is inflicted upon one who makes an unlawful oath. Likewise, from the Council of Lleida, chapter 8** [Note: [Col. 1143] Found in A.D. 546; Regino, book 2, chapter 321; Burchard, book 12, chapter 17; the *Collectio trichuriana*, part 2, title 34, chapter 6; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 74.]

Whoever binds himself by an oath never to return to peace with anyone with whom he is in dispute shall, on account of one perjury, be separated for one year [Note: [Col. 1143] “From”: absent in the Basel edition] from communion in the body and blood of the Lord, and shall absolve his guilt by alms, tears, [Col. 1143C] and as much fasting as he is able. But let him hasten swiftly to charity, which covers a multitude of sins [Note: [Col. 1143] Compare 1 Peter 4:8].

[Col. 1144A] **Chapter XII. Not all promises must be fulfilled. Likewise Ambrose, *On Duties*, book III, chapter 12** [Note: [Col. 1143] Compare above, chapter 8.]

Not all promises must always be fulfilled [Note: [Col. 1143] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 102: “From the Council of Lleida”]. For the Lord himself often changes his sentence [Note: [Col. 1143] Absent in the Argentinensis and Basel editions], as Scripture indicates.

**Chapter XIII. On the same matter. Likewise Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, chapter 31** [Note: [Col. 1143] Burchard, book 12, chapter 10; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 112; *Decretum*, part 12, chapters 36 and 67; Polycarp, book 6, title 12; compare the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 2.]

An oath [Note: [Col. 1143] “Must be preserved”: the original, Burchard, and Ivo, chapter 67] by which evil is rashly promised [Note: [Col. 1143] “Sacrament”: the original, Burchard, Ivo, and the collected editions] must not be observed, as when someone promises an adulteress perpetual fidelity in remaining with her. For it is more tolerable not to fulfill the oath than to remain in the disgrace of fornication.

**Chapter XIV. One who swears wrongly should do penance. Likewise, from the Council of Toledo, chapter 2** [Note: [Col. 1143C] The actual words of this chapter and the following one are not in canon 2 of the Eighth Council of Toledo, although Rabanus, in book 21 of his *Book on Penance*, and Burchard, book 12, chapter 29, cite them from it. They give this material together with what is found in that second canon. The same Burchard, chapter 7, cites it from Toledo, chapter 9; Ivo cites it simply as from Toledo. These two chapters are joined in their works, as also in several old copies of Gratian, without the word “Likewise.”] [Note: [Col. 1143] In the Eighth Council of Toledo only the passages from Exodus 20:7 and Leviticus 19:12, which appear in this and the following chapter, are found. Compare the corrections; Burchard, book 12, chapters 7 and 29; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 64.]

It is necessary that one who swears wrongly perform worthy penance, because he has taken the name of the Lord in vain against his commandment. For it is written in Exodus: “The Lord will not hold guiltless the one who takes [Note: [Col. 1143] “Has taken”: the collected editions] the name of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1143] Absent in the Basel edition] his God in vain.”

**Chapter XV. [Likewise] And in Leviticus** [Note: [Col. 1143] Leviticus 19:12]:

“You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of your God: I am the Lord.” Yet [Note: [Col. 1143] “For”: the Basel and first Lyon editions] he must by no means do the evil which he has devoted himself by oath to do [Note: [Col. 1143] “Had devoted”: the collected editions], because foolish vows must be broken.

**Chapter XVI. An oath by which evil is rashly promised must not be observed. Likewise, from the Decree of Pope Soter, chapter 3** [Note: [Col. 1144C] The other collectors likewise give it this way. Above, in the same section, chapter 6, the passage beginning “If it should happen” is given in the same words from Bede, as indicated there.] [Note: [Col. 1143] Compare above, chapter 6; Regino, book 2, chapter 323; Burchard, book 12, chapter 18; Anselm, book 11, chapter 73 (75); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 118; *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 75; Polycarp, book 6, title 11.]

If it should happen that we have sworn something rather incautiously, and its observance would lead to a worse outcome, let us know that it must be changed by sounder counsel, and that, under pressing necessity, we should rather commit perjury [Note: [Col. 1143] “Commit perjury”: the collected editions, especially the Lyon editions; Regino; Ivo] than, for the sake of an oath already made [Note: [Col. 1144C] “On account of the deed”: Ivo and the *Panormia* read “for the sake of avoiding perjury,” as above in chapter 6 [ [Col. 1143] “Perfectly”: Regino and Burchard]. Polycarp has “indeed into another.” Anselm agrees with Gratian], turn aside into another and graver crime.

[Col. 1145A] **Chapter XVII. Rashness is corrected when an incautious determination is set aside. Likewise, from the Council of Elvira, chapter 1** [Note: [Col. 1145C] Ivo cites it as Gratian does. Burchard, however, cites it from the Council of Ireland, and that is how it appears in a manuscript collection of canons by an uncertain author.] [Note: [Col. 1145] It is found in book 34 of the collection of Irish canons published by d’Achery in volume I of the *Spicilegium*; Burchard, book 12, chapter 25; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 80.]

An incautious determination should commendably be set aside; this is not prevarication but correction of rashness.

**Chapter XVIII. An unlawful oath must not be observed. Likewise** [Note: [Col. 1145] Found in A.D. 787; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapters 98–100; *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 15; Peter Lombard, book 3, distinction 39.]

In the fourth session of the Seventh Synod [Note: [Col. 1145C] “In the fourth session of the Seventh Synod”: in one old manuscript of Gratian these words are a title, as also in Ivo; the actual beginning of the chapter is “John,” etc., and this is not the translation of Anastasius Bibliothecarius], John, envoy (*apocrisiarius*) of the eastern sees, said: “The saying of our father Sophronius signifies that it is better for one who has sworn to commit perjury [Note: [Col. 1145] “To commit perjury”: Ivo and the collected editions, especially the Lyon editions] than to keep an oath involving the breaking of sacred images. We say this because some excuse themselves by an oath.”

Patriarch Tarasius said: “Because Father Sophronius knew the goodness of God, he therefore wished to transgress an impious oath.” [Note: [Col. 1145D] “Because Father”: the synod has the passage differently. There, from the *Limonarion*, or *Spiritual Meadow*, whose author is Sophronius, the counsel of Abbot Theodore Aeliotes is reported as having been given to a confined man: that he should by no means keep an oath given to the devil not to venerate an image of the Virgin Mary carrying the infant Jesus.]

Likewise, a little later:

§ 1. Patriarch Tarasius [Col. 1145B] said: “Herod kept his oath and perished; but Peter denied with an oath, then was converted, wept, and was saved” [Note: [Col. 1145] “Was”: the Argentinensis and Basel editions]. “For the good God forgives every sin if someone repents with his whole heart.”

The holy synod said: “Thus holy Scripture teaches [Note: [Col. 1145] “May it teach”: Basel edition] us.”

Likewise Leontius [Note: [Col. 1145] “Leontinus”: the Lyon editions], bishop of Phocaea (Latin *Phoceae*; variant *Phocae*) [Note: [Col. 1145] “Phocae”: the Paris edition; “Phoceae”: the remaining editions and Ivo], said: “It is written [Note: [Col. 1145] Zechariah 8:17]: ‘Do not love a false oath.’ For this reason let our false oath be dissolved, as though it possessed no force.”

**Chapter XIX. Oaths contrary to the divine commandments must not be observed. Likewise Isidore** [Note: [Col. 1146C] In Saint Basil’s *Book on the Institutes of Monks*, translated by Rufinus, the following is found: “If anyone has been led into determining to do something that does not please God.” The response then adds: “He must do penance,” and afterward: “Whatever is established presumptuously against the commandment of God ought to be recalled as invalid.”] [Note: [Col. 1145] The first part of the chapter is found in Basil, *Shorter Rules*, question 184; the second in the *Roman Penitential*, edited by Antonio Agustinus, volume 2, chapter 15; *Collectio trichuriana*, part 2, title 14, chapter 16.]

If anyone has been led into determining to do something that does not please God, let him do penance, and let what has been established contrary to the Lord’s command be revoked as invalid.

Likewise Jerome, in the book *On Nature* [Note: [Col. 1145] No book by Jerome entitled *On Nature* survives]:

§ 1. Oaths entered into are to be dissolved in three ways. First, when someone swears wrongly. Second, when someone swears incautiously, not thinking that this is a sin. Third, if boys or girls in their parents’ household have bound themselves by an oath and, after hearing of it, their fathers object.

[Col. 1146A] ### Part II

Gratian. Behold, unlawful oaths are commendably dissolved and damnably kept. This is to be understood when an unlawful oath is abandoned in order to return to what is good.

§ 1. But if it is abandoned for the purpose of passing into another evil, the unlawful oath is damnably kept, but its contempt is still more damnable.

Hence Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 4 [Note: [Col. 1145] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 86; *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 14]:

**Chapter XX. A pledge used for committing sin should not be called faith.**

If a pledge is given for committing sin [Note: [Col. 1145] “But when it is given for admitting sin”: the original], it is surprising if it ought to be called faith [Note: [Col. 1145] “Is called”: Ivo; “may be called”: the collected editions]. Yet, whatever its character, if it is also violated, the result is worse [Note: [Col. 1145] “Is”: the same editions], except when it is abandoned in order to return to true and lawful faith—that is, in order that sin may be corrected [Col. 1146B] by reforming the depravity of the will. For example, if someone, unable by himself to strip a man of his possessions [Note: [Col. 1145] “Could”: the Argentinensis and Basel editions], finds a companion in wickedness and makes an agreement with him that they will do it together and divide the spoil, but, after committing the crime, takes the whole thing away by himself, the other indeed grieves and complains that faith has not been kept with him. Yet in his very complaint he ought to consider that he should rather have kept faith with human society itself by living uprightly, so that unjust spoil should not be made from a human being, if he perceives how unjustly faith was not kept with him in their partnership in sin [Note: [Col. 1145] “Observed”: the same editions]. That man is certainly to be judged more criminally faithless in both respects.

**Chapter XXI. If a pledge is not kept in order that one may return to the good, it is not thereby called violated. The same author, in the same place** [Note: [Col. 1145] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 97; *Decretum*, in the same place.]

[Col. 1146C] If a woman, having violated marital fidelity, keeps faith with an adulterer, she is certainly wicked; but if she does not keep faith even with the adulterer, she is worse [Note: [Col. 1145] Absent in the Argentinensis and Basel editions]. But if she repents of her disgrace and, returning to marital chastity, annuls the adulterous compacts and agreements, I wonder whether even the adulterer will regard her as a violator of faith.

Gratian. From these matters it therefore appears that if anyone, as we have said, does not keep an unlawful oath in order to turn aside into another destructive evil, he sins all the more gravely, because sins are accumulated upon sins all the more damnably. But if it is abandoned in order to return to the good, no guilt is incurred through such perjury; rather, one should lament if it has happened that, on some occasion arising from that oath, we have committed sin.

Hence Augustine writes to Severus, bishop of Milevis, who had consulted him concerning a certain Hubald, who had been compelled by the kinsmen of a concubine to swear that he would take her as his wife and thereafter provide no necessities to his mother or brothers. Blessed Augustine therefore replies, as we have said, to Severus, bishop of Milevis, as follows [Note: [Col. 1147] We judge that this canon has nothing in common with Augustine]:

[Col. 1147B] **Chapter XXII. Concerning a certain Hubald, who swore that he would not provide necessities for his mother and brothers.**

Among other matters, as you had requested, I asked our father Ambrose what you, dearest one [Note: [Col. 1147] Absent in the Argentinensis and Basel editions], ought to do concerning Hubald, your parishioner, who, having been seized and driven by fear of death [Note: [Col. 1147] “Compelled”: the same editions], confirmed by oath to his concubine that he would take her as his wife, expel his own mother together with his brothers from the house, and never provide them with any sustenance. But because it is not a sin to take in marriage the woman whom he had previously had as a concubine [Note: [Col. 1147] Absent in the collected editions, especially the Basel and second Lyon editions], let the marriage be firm and stable in God.

§ 1. An oath, however, was not instituted in order that it might be a bond of wickedness, matricide, fratricide, or any crime whatever. Nor do I think that a sacrament should be made for this purpose: that an unjust oath should become an unjust stripping of their goods for those who swear unjustly [Col. 1147C] and eternal damnation for the recipient [Note: [Col. 1147] Addition: “also be”: the Basel and second and third Lyon editions]. For the punishment of perjury strikes, and at the final judgment the one through whom the most holy Gospel is brought forward as testimony for what is unjust, unlawful, and by no means pleasing to God—as though it were testimony to a just and human petition—will be struck down like a murderer by the righteous judge.

§ 2. Therefore let Hubald support his mother and brothers, and let him grieve if anything was lacking to his mother because of the compulsion and fear of the oath. But those who compelled him to swear what he ought not to have sworn are to be held bound by the guilt of perjury. For an injury unjustly inflicted is the disgrace of the one who commits it. What an unlawful condition of necessity has extorted is in no way imputed as a reproach to a coerced will.

### Part III

Gratian. But although all these authorities prove that unlawful [Col. 1147D] oaths must not be observed, it is objected that Joshua did not destroy the Gibeonites contrary to the Lord’s command because the elders of Israel had confirmed peace with them by oath. But it must be observed that, although the elders of Israel knew that the Lord had commanded them to destroy the nations of the promised land, they were deceived by the Gibeonites and did not know that these were inhabitants of the promised land. For they came, as the history relates, with worn-out shoes [Col. 1148A] and dry loaves, saying: “We are peaceful men; we have come from a distant land. Our shoes are worn out on our feet; the bread has failed in our provision-bags. We have heard that the Lord is with you, and we have come to make peace.” This proposal pleased the elders of Israel, and they made peace with them. But on the third day, when the children of Israel drew near to the Gibeonites, those to whom the elders of Israel had sworn came out to meet them. Seeing that they had been deceived, they wished to destroy them; but Joshua spared them because of the oath of the elders of Israel.

Hence Ambrose, *On Duties*, book III, chapter 10:

**Chapter XXIII. Some things, although forbidden by God, are nevertheless not to be avoided when confirmed by oath** [Note: [Col. 1147] “Observed”: the Venetian editions I and II, and the Lyon and Paris editions.]

“The innocent person believes every word” [Note: [Col. 1147] Proverbs 14:15]. Such readiness to believe is not blameworthy [Col. 1148B], but goodness is praiseworthy. To be innocent is to be ignorant of what harms; and, if one is deceived by someone, nevertheless to judge well of all people, because one believes that fidelity exists in everyone. Therefore Joshua, inclined by this devotion of mind [Note: [Col. 1147] “Devoutly”: the first Lyon edition; “by a gift”: the remaining editions] to believe the Gibeonites, established a covenant [Note: [Col. 1147] “A witness of God”: the Basel edition; “God’s covenant”: the Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venetian I, and second and third Lyon editions], granted peace, and confirmed an alliance. But when they came into their lands, the fraud was discovered: although they were neighbors, they had pretended to be strangers [Note: [Col. 1147] “Had pretended to be strangers”: the Argentinensis and Brescia editions]. The people of the fathers began to be indignant that they had been deceived. Yet Joshua [Note: [Col. 1147] “Jesus”: the collected editions] did not judge that the peace he had granted should be revoked, because it had been confirmed by the religious obligation of an oath, lest, while reproving another’s faithlessness, he should dissolve his own fidelity. Nevertheless he punished them with the service of a more lowly ministry [Note: [Col. 1147] “He punished them, however, with the better service of ministry”: the same editions]. A more merciful sentence, but a more lasting one.

Gratian. Therefore an unlawful oath which is forbidden to be kept must be understood as one known to be unlawful when it is sworn. But if its unlawfulness is unknown, ignorance itself excuses, provided it is thought lawful—not through ignorance of the law, but of the fact. For it is one thing if a particular union is believed lawful because the woman is not known to be a blood-relative, or because she is believed to be a widow; it is another if it is thought lawful because the union of blood-relatives or marriage with women left by others is believed to be prohibited by no law. In the latter case there is ignorance of law, which excuses no one except a person permitted not to know the law; in the former, ignorance of fact, by which a person is truly excused. The elders of Israel, however, did not fail to know that the nations of the land of promise were, by the Lord’s command, to be destroyed [Col. 1148D]; but they did not know that the Gibeonites were inhabitants of the land of promise. They were ignorant, indeed, of the fact, but not of the law governing the fact; and therefore, although what they swore was unlawful, nevertheless what they confirmed by oath had to be maintained.

§ 1. But the statement that an unlawful oath is forbidden to be kept is not to be understood universally. For an oath, as Jerome testifies on Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 1147] above, question 2, chapter 2], must have three companions: truth, judgment, and justice. Where these are lacking, there is not an oath but perjury. Hence it is understood that an oath lacking any one of these is unlawful; yet, whenever one of them happens to be lacking, the oath is not in every case forbidden to be kept.

§ 2. For sometimes justice is lacking in an oath—for example, when someone, after a vow of chastity, takes a wife and confirms by oath that he will never leave her. Although this is unlawful, because justice is shown to be absent from it, nevertheless, by Augustine’s authority, it is commanded to be maintained. But if anyone contends that this is maintained by the prerogative of marriage rather than on account of the sanctity of the oath, let him observe that the Gibeonites were spared, contrary to the Lord’s command, solely on account of that sacred obligation. Since every command of the Lord is just, it is clear that justice is absent from what is found contrary to his command [Col. 1149B].

§ 3. Judgment too is sometimes evidently lacking in an oath, as when a person, led by his own rashness, swears that he will eat and drink. Although this is shown unlawful through undiscerning frivolity, it is nevertheless not thereby commanded to be violated.

§ 4. An oath, then, is understood to be unlawful in several ways. It is sometimes unlawful because of what is sworn, sometimes because of an externally arising cause, and sometimes because of the manner of swearing. An oath is unlawful because of what is sworn when the thing sworn is evil by its own nature or takes away life, such as adultery, homicide, and similar acts; or when it prevents restoration—for example, not returning to peace with an enemy or not mercifully helping one in need. Since these things contain manifest injustice in themselves, even if confirmed by oath [Col. 1149C], they must not be kept. The rulings above concerning unlawful oaths that are not to be observed are certainly to be understood of such oaths. Therefore whoever has bound himself by oath to do something by which bodily or spiritual salvation is taken away, or without which neither salvation can be restored or confirmed, is forbidden to keep the faith he promised. The preceding authorities furnish examples: they do not permit one who has promised under oath to commit homicide, to withhold sustenance from his mother and brothers, to persist in adultery, or not to return to peace with his adversary, to observe such unlawful vows under the more salutary counsel.

§ 5. What is sworn is also sometimes evil, not in its own nature, but because of external circumstances [Col. 1149D]; for example, when someone, after a vow of chastity, swears that he will take a certain woman as his wife. To have a wife is not in itself evil; yet for this person it is harmful because of his vow. Although this oath is unlawful, it is not forbidden to be kept [Col. 1150A]; rather, penance is to be imposed upon him for violating the vow.

§ 6. An oath is unlawful because of the manner of swearing when something is sworn carelessly and without forethought, by which neither bodily nor spiritual salvation is taken away, and without which both kinds of salvation can be restored and life preserved. For example, a person compelled by his parents to receive clerical tonsure or the religious habit may bind himself by oath never to do either. Although this seems blameworthy to some, because he has promised by oath not to perform a work of charity, nevertheless no authority forbids its observance. For even if he never receives clerical tonsure or the religious habit, he may not therefore be less able to attain salvation, since some are found most holy and beloved of God in lay dress. From this example [Col. 1150B] it is clearly understood that whenever someone swears not to do something which would prepare for him a more direct path to blessedness, provided that he can find salvation without it, he is not forbidden to keep that oath. Thus, when we swear that we will not give someone something without which both forms of his salvation may remain unimpaired, even though it would afford him some advantage, we are forbidden by no authority to keep the oath, provided another means is available to us for relieving his necessities.

## QUESTION V

## GRATIAN

### Part I

The fifth question asks whether, if what the archdeacon had sworn was lawful [Col. 1150C], the bishop who compelled the archdeacon to commit perjury was guilty of perjury. This can readily be decided. For if one who consents is to be punished with the same penalty as the doer, much more is he who compels another proved guilty of the crime committed. Hence Pope Pius says [Note: [Col. 1149] Anselm cites this from Theodore’s Penitential, as do Burchard and Ivo in the following chapter.] [Note: [Col. 1149] from Theodore’s Penitential: Anselm, book 11, chapter 63 (62), cites the first part simply as “from the Penitential.” Regino, book 2, chapter 330.—“from Pius,” Burchard, book 12, chapter 4; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 61.—Cf. Roman Penitential, ancient, Augustine, vol. 2, chapter 1.—The first part is also in Egbert, *On the Remedies of Sins* (Mansi, vol. 12).]:

### C. I. Both he who compels perjury and he who is compelled are proved perjurers.

One compelled by his lord knowingly commits perjury [Note: [Col. 1149] “knowingly commits perjury”: Burchard, Ivo.—“commits perjury, if knowingly”: Regino]; both lord and servant are perjurers: the lord because he commanded it; the servant because he loved his lord more than his soul. If he is free, let him do penance for forty days on bread and water, and for the following seven years; but if he is that lord’s slave [Note: [Col. 1149] “but if”: editions of Arg., Bas.], let him do penance for three Lents and the prescribed fast-days.

[Col. 1150D]

### C. II. The penance of one who has committed perjury upon a bishop’s hand or upon a consecrated cross. Likewise.

[Note: [Col. 1149] Nearly the same words are found in Egbert, book 1, chapter 9; thence Rabanus cites them in his letter to Heribald, chapter 18.—Regino, book 2, chapters 331–332; Burchard, book 12, chapter 5; Anselm, book 11, chapter 64 (63); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 62; Polycarpus, book 6, title 11.]

One who commits perjury [Note: [Col. 1149] “commits perjury”: Regino, Ivo; editions generally, first Lugdunensis I–II and Paris] upon a bishop’s hand or upon a consecrated cross [Col. 1151A] shall do penance for three years. But if it is upon an unconsecrated cross, let him do penance for one year. Whoever has been compelled and, unknowingly, committed perjury [Note: [Col. 1151] “has committed perjury”: editions generally, first Lugdunensis; Ivo.—“swore”: Regino], and afterwards learns it, shall do penance for three Lents.

### C. III. What punishment should be inflicted upon one who, compelled by necessity, commits perjury. Likewise, from Theodore’s Penitential.

[Note: [Col. 1151] It is found in the same chapter in Egbert.—Regino, book 2, chapter 332; Burchard, book 12, chapter 6, and Ivo, *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 63, cite it from the Roman Penitential; Anselm, book 11, chapter 64, from Theodore.—Polycarpus, book 6, title 11.]

If anyone, compelled to ransom his life, or for any cause or necessity, commits perjury [Note: [Col. 1151] “commits perjury”: Burchard.—“perjures himself”: Ivo], because he loved his body more than his soul, let him do penance for three Lents. Others, however, judge that he should do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water.

### C. IV. What punishment should be inflicted upon one who commits perjury and makes others commit perjury. Likewise, Pope Gelasius.

[Note: [Col. 1151C] Polycarpus attributes this to Pius; the other named collectors attribute it to Pelagius.] [Note: [Col. 1151] Something similar is read in the penitential book produced by Regino, book 1, chapter 300; the same appears in the ancient Roman Penitential, Augustine, vol. 2, chapter 5.—Burchard, book 12, chapter 9; Anselm, book 11, chapter 67 (65); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 12, rubric 66; Polycarpus, ibid.]

[Col. 1151B] If anyone has committed perjury [Note: [Col. 1151] “has perjured himself”: Anselm, Burchard; editions Arg. and Bas.—“has perjured himself”: Ivo; “has committed perjury”: editions Nor. and Ven. I–II] and knowingly led others into perjury [Note: [Col. 1151] “has led”: editions Arg., Bas., Lugdunensis II–III], let him do penance for forty days on bread and water, and for the following seven years, and never be without penance. The others too, if they were aware, are to do penance similarly.

### C. V. He who knowingly compels a person to perjury is worse than a murderer. Likewise, Augustine, in the sermon on the beheading of St John, that is, Sermon XI *On the Saints*.

[Note: [Col. 1151] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 108; *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 28; Peter Lombard, book 3, distinction 39.]

The man [Note: [Col. 1151] “The man who incites another”: Ivo] who incites someone to swear, knowing that he will swear falsely [Note: [Col. 1151] “to swear”: Ivo, *Panormia*], is worse than a murderer. For the murderer will kill a body; that man kills a soul—indeed, two souls: both that of the person whom he incited to swear and his own. You know that what you say is true, and that what he says is false [Col. 1151C], and you compel him to swear? Behold [Note: [Col. 1151] added: “what he” in editions generally], he swears; behold, he commits perjury [Note: [Col. 1151] “commits perjury”: Ivo; editions generally, first Paris and Lugdunensis]; behold, he perishes. What have you gained? Indeed, you too have perished, for you wished to satisfy yourself upon his death.

### C. VI. One does not sin by requiring an oath from one whom one does not know will swear falsely. The same, in the sermon on perjuries, that is, in the sermon *On the Words of the Apostle*, XXX, otherwise XXVIII.

[Note: [Col. 1151] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 110; *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 30; Peter Lombard, ibid.]

There is a great difference, when one requires an oath, between not knowing and knowing that the other will swear falsely. For if one does not know and says for that reason, “Swear to me, so that confidence may be established for him” [Note: [Col. 1151] “may be”: Ivo; editions generally], it is not a sin [Note: [Col. 1151C] “It is not a sin”: in the original the words are: “I do not dare say that it is not a sin.” But it has not been altered because of this discrepancy.]—yet it is a human temptation. But if he knows that the man has done it—knows that he has done it, sees that he has done it—and compels him to swear [Col. 1152A], he is a murderer. For the other kills himself by his perjury [Note: [Col. 1151] “destroys”: editions Arg. and Bas.; Ivo, *Panormia*; “destroys”: remaining editions; Ivo, *Decretum*], but this man both placed and pressed the hand of the killer upon him [Note: [Col. 1151] “expressed”: original].

### C. VII. One who draws others into perjury is not to receive communion until the end of life. Likewise, from the First Council of Mâcon, chapter 17.

[Note: [Col. 1151] Held in A.D. 581.—Burchard, book 16, chapter 8; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 26.]

If anyone is convicted of having drawn others into false [Note: [Col. 1152C] “False”: In the Council of Mâcon itself—where the citation has been restored from manuscripts, since it had formerly been cited as Mainz—the reading is: “false testimony or perjury” [Note: [Col. 1151] thus editions generally]; thus Burchard.] testimony or perjury, or of having solicited them by any corruption, he himself shall not receive communion until the end of his life. Those, however, who are proved to have consented with him in perjury are thereafter to be excluded from all testimony [Note: [Col. 1151] “forbidden”: original] and, according to the law, marked with infamy [Col. 1152B].

### Part II

Gratian. Likewise, one who hears someone swear falsely and remains silent sins.

Accordingly Augustine says in *Questions on Leviticus*, question 1, on chapter 5: “The soul that hears the voice of one swearing falsely,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1151] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 109; *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 29.]

### C. VIII. When what is sworn by someone is to be judged false.

This seems to say that a person sins when someone swears falsely in his hearing, and he knows that the person is swearing falsely, and remains silent. But he knows it when he was a witness of the matter concerning which the oath is made, or saw it [Note: [Col. 1151] “seeing”: editions generally; Ivo], or was privy to it [Note: [Col. 1151] “was”: editions generally]—that is, learned of it in some manner, either saw it with his own eyes, or the very person who swears informed him [Note: [Col. 1151] “that very person”: editions generally; Ivo]. For in this way he could have been privy to it.

§ 1. But between fear of this sin and [Col. 1152C] fear of betraying people there is often no small temptation. We can call back someone prepared for perjury from so grave a sin by warning or forbidding him. But if he does not listen, and in our presence swears falsely concerning a matter we know, whether he ought to be denounced, if, when denounced, he may even incur the danger of death, is a most difficult question. But since Augustine did not state to whom this should be reported—whether to the person to whom the oath is sworn, or to some priest [Note: [Col. 1151] “or to anyone”: original; Ivo] [Note: [Col. 1153] thus in editions generally] [Col. 1153A], who not only cannot persecute him by inflicting punishment, but can also pray for him—it seems to me that a person frees himself from the bond of sin if he reports it to such persons, who are more able to benefit than harm the perjurer, whether to correct him or to propitiate God for him, provided he himself also applies the discipline of confession [Note: [Col. 1153] “remedy”: original; Ivo; editions generally; Bohm].

Gratian. Therefore, if, as stated above, one who hears a false oath and remains silent sins, much more guilty is one who compels another to commit perjury.

### Part III

§ 1. The question is raised concerning one who believes that by verbal cunning he deceives the person to whom he offers an oath: is he guilty of perjury unless he performs what he is believed to have sworn?

[Col. 1153B] Isidore writes as follows on this in *Sentences*, book II, chapter 31 [Note: [Col. 1153] Burchard, book 12, chapter 10; Anselm, book 11, chapter 76 (75); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 112; *Decretum*, part 12, chapters 36 and 67; Peter Lombard, book 3, distinction 39.]:

### C. IX. On one who swears by verbal cunning.

By whatever artifice of words anyone swears [Note: [Col. 1153] “anyone”: editions generally], nevertheless God, who is witness of the conscience, receives it as the person to whom the oath is sworn understands it. Such a person becomes guilty in two ways: because he takes God’s name in vain and ensnares his neighbour by deceit.

### C. X. One who swears falsely upon a stone is a perjurer. Likewise, from St Augustine’s thirtieth sermon *On the Words of the Apostle*.

[Note: [Col. 1153] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 116; *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 34.]

Behold, I say to your charity: he too who swears falsely upon a stone is a perjurer [Note: [Col. 1153] “who”: editions Paris and Lugdunensis II–III; “upon”: original; Ivo]. Why do I say this? Because many are deceived in this [Note: [Col. 1153] absent from Basle; “deceive”: Lugdunensis II–III] and think that, because the thing by which they swear is nothing, they are not bound by the guilt of perjury. You are absolutely a perjurer, because you swear falsely by that which [Col. 1153C] you do not think holy [Note: [Col. 1153C] “You do not think”: likewise Ivo. In the original it stands without negation, and perhaps the reading should be *putat*, “he thinks.”]. If you do not think it holy, regard as holy the person to whom you swear [Note: [Col. 1153D] “If you do not think it holy”:  in the printed Augustine manuscripts and one Vatican manuscript: “but I do not think him holy.” In another Vatican manuscript, and in Ivo: “but I do not think it holy.”] [Note: [Col. 1153D] “let [him] think it”: thus in the printed manuscripts of St Augustine; but in one Vatican manuscript, and in Ivo, the *Panormia*, and several old Gratian manuscripts: *putat*, “he thinks” [Note: [Col. 1153] thus editions generally, first Lugdunensis II–III].]. For when you swear, you do not swear to yourself or swear to the stone, but swear to your neighbour [Note: [Col. 1153] added: “your” in editions generally]. You swear to a human being before a stone, but are you not also before God? The stone does not hear you speaking, but God punishes you for deceiving.

But Gregory’s statement is objected, from book XXVI of the *Moralia*, chapter 7:

### C. XI. Before God our words proceed not from the mouth but from the heart.

Human ears judge our words according to the sound they make outwardly [Col. 1154A]. Divine judgments, however, hear them according to how they are brought forth from within [Note: [Col. 1153] “outwardly”: editions generally].

§ 1. Certainly [Note: [Col. 1153] The author of what follows has not been discovered.] let him know, whoever explains another’s intention and will by various words, that one ought not to consider the words but the will and intention; for intention ought not to serve words, but words intention.

Gratian. Therefore, if divine judgments hear our words outwardly as they are brought forth from within, and if intention ought not to serve words but words intention, it is plain that God does not receive an oath as the person to whom it is sworn understands it, but rather as the swearer understands it, since the oath-recipient hears our words not from what lies within but from what is uttered outwardly.

§ 1. Again, the case is objected of one who swears upon a stone, believing that he swears upon the most holy Gospels: he is held just as if he had sworn upon the Gospels [Col. 1154B], although the person to whom he swears caused him to swear upon that stone so that, if he does not perform what he promises, he may be bound by the guilt of perjury.

§ 2. Again, the case is objected of citizens who believe they are swearing to obey their consuls in all things commanded them for the honour of their city. But lest, by refusing obedience, they be entangled in the guilt of perjury, a written slip is placed before those about to swear, containing something other than what they think they will swear—namely, that they will not turn the Po into the Nile or do anything of that sort. If, then, contrary to what they believed they had sworn, they denied obedience to their consuls, would God receive that oath according to the intention of the recipient or rather according to the intention of the swearer?

§ 3. Again, if an innocent person accused of adultery or [Col. 1154C] theft wished to assert his innocence, but swore that he was as free from the charges as the written slip he believed he had written with his own hands contained, while it actually contained that he was guilty of those charges—would he be judged a perjurer by the Lord? Or could he be accused of having sworn that he had incurred guilt of adultery or theft? No.

Chromatius also says on Matthew 5 [Note: [Col. 1154D] Chromatius: formerly Chrysostom, sermon 33, was cited, an error occasioned by the similarity of the initial letters.]:

### C. XII. There ought to be no difference between an oath and the speech of believers.

This is the purpose of an oath [Note: [Col. 1153] “of this”: editions Arg. and Bas.; “of this sort”: remaining editions] is that everyone who swears swears in order to speak what is true [Note: [Col. 1153] “speak”: editions generally]. Therefore the Lord wills there to be no distance between an oath and our speech, because, as there ought to be no faithlessness in an oath, so too there ought to be no lie in our words [Col. 1155A]. For both perjury and lying are condemned by the punishment of divine judgment, as Scripture says [Note: [Col. 1155] Wisdom 1:11]: “A mouth that lies kills the soul.” Whoever therefore speaks truth swears, because it is written [Note: [Col. 1155] Proverbs 14:5]: “A faithful witness does not lie.”

### C. XIII. Before one swears, one commits perjury if prepared to swear against conscience. The same.

[Note: [Col. 1155] This is not found in Chromatius and seems excerpted from Homily 12 on Matthew 5 in the *Opus imperfectum*.]

One prepared to commit perjury [Note: [Col. 1155] “to commit perjury”: editions Arg., Nor., Ven. I–II] seems already to be a perjurer before he swears [Note: [Col. 1155] “before he committed perjury”: Lugdunensis I; Paris: “commits perjury”; editions Arg., Nor., Ven. I–II], because God judges not from deeds alone [Note: [Col. 1155] added: “alone” in Basle and Lugdunensis II–III], but from thoughts and from the heart [Col. 1155B].

Gratian. From all these matters it is gathered that God judges oaths according to the intention of the one making them, not of the one receiving them. How then, according to Isidore, does God receive an oath sworn by whatever verbal artifice as the person to whom it is sworn understands it? But just as swearing by a cunning artifice of words differs from simply declaring one’s intention by oath, so receiving an oath made with a simple intention differs from employing cunning in receiving it. For just as no one can injure another before God, so neither can anyone aid another contrary to that person’s intention. God, who abhors duplicity, considers the simple intention of both parties, and rejects and hates verbal artifice both on the part of the recipient [Col. 1155C] and on the part of the maker.

### Part IV

§ 1. A question is raised concerning the age of those who swear: at what age ought a person be compelled to swear? The following is found determined in chapter 63 of the first book of the *Capitularies* [Note: [Col. 1155] Aachen capitulary of Charlemagne, A.D. 789, chapter 62.—Regino, book 2, chapter 313; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 103; *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 23.]:

### C. XIV. No one should be compelled to swear before the age of reason.

Little children who have not reached the age of reason are not to be compelled [Col. 1156A] to swear, as the Gunebodigni do [Note: [Col. 1155C] “as the Gunebodigni do”: these words are added from the original. Pithou maintains that the oldest manuscripts of the Lombard laws, in which this chapter is inserted in book 2, title 55, chapter 22, read: “as those living under Gundebad’s law.”]. And whoever has once committed perjury is thereafter neither to be a witness nor approach the sacrament, nor act as an oath-taker in his own cause or that of another.

### C. XV. No one should be compelled to swear before fourteen years. Likewise, from the Council of Elvira.

[Note: [Col. 1155C] Burchard cites this from the Irish council, as he does other material attributed to the Council of Elvira.] [Note: [Col. 1155] It should be read “Irish,” with Burchard, book 12, chapter 26; for something similar is read in the collection of Irish canons published in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapters 104–105; *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 81.]

Children under fourteen years are not to be compelled to swear. Likewise, if a girl, while still under age and living in her father’s house, binds herself by oath without his knowledge, and her father, upon hearing of it, immediately objects, her vows and oaths shall be void, and she shall be more easily corrected.

### C. XVI. On the same matter, and that oaths should be rendered while fasting. Likewise, Pope Cornelius.

[Note: [Col. 1155C] The other collectors also cite this from the decrees of Pope Cornelius. But it appears in book 1 of the *Capitularies*, chapter 63, with some additional words. From there Ivo reports the first part of this chapter in chapter 33.] [Note: [Col. 1155] Cf. chapter 14 above.—Regino, book 2, chapter 312; Burchard, book 12, chapter 12; Anselm, book 11, chapter 69; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 120; *Decretum*, part 12, chapters 69 and 33.]

[Col. 1156B] It also seems fitting that one who ventures [Note: [Col. 1155] “has”: Ivo, *Panormia* and *Decretum*, part 33] to swear upon holy things should do so fasting, with all propriety and fear of God; and that children under fourteen years should not be compelled to swear [Note: [Col. 1155] “and”: absent in editions Arg., Nor., Ven. I; “that”: absent in Basle].

Gratian. Moreover, there are certain times during which we are forbidden to swear.

Accordingly, in the council held at Saint-Médard [Note: [Col. 1155] Something similar occurs in a capitulary of Charles the Bald confirming the council at Saint-Médard; in Regino, book 2, chapter 319; and Burchard seems to have composed his chapter from it, book 12, chapter 20.]:

### C. XVII. During what times we are forbidden to swear.

The holy synod decreed that from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter, and from Advent until the octave of Epiphany; likewise during the fasts of the four seasons, the greater litanies, Sundays, and Rogation days—except for reconciliation and peacemaking—no one shall presume to swear upon the holy Gospels [Col. 1156C].

### Part V

Gratian. Concerning the form of fealty, and what each person owes his lord, or conversely, the following is found in the letter of Bishop Fulbert [Note: [Col. 1156C] This letter of Fulbert, sent from Gaul and copied from an ancient manuscript of the Church of Beauvais, has this heading: “Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, offers the aid of his prayers to W., glorious duke of the Aquitanians.”] [Note: [Col. 1155] Fulbert of Chartres, letter to William, duke of Aquitaine, printed among his other letters in vol. 18 of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 122; *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 76.—Cf. *Feuds*, book 2, title 6.]:

### C. XVIII. What must be observed in fealty.

Having been asked to write something on the form of fealty, I have briefly noted for you, on the authority of books, the following. One who swears fealty to his lord must always keep six things in mind: safety, security, honour, advantage, ease, possibility.

Safety: namely, that he should not harm his lord in his person [Col. 1157A].

Security: that he should not harm him in respect of his secrets or the fortifications by which he can be secure.

Honour: that he should not harm him in respect of his justice or other matters that seem to belong to his honour.

Advantage: that he should not harm him in respect of his possessions.

Ease or possibility: that he should not make difficult for his lord a good thing which the lord could readily do, nor render impossible what was possible.
