That a faithful man should avoid these harms [Note: [Col. 1157] “these instructions”: Basle; “these instructions”: remaining editions] is just [Note: [Col. 1157] “just and good”: Basle, Lugdunensis I and III; “good”: remaining editions].

§ 1. But because it is not sufficient [Note: [Col. 1157C] In the letter itself: “But he does not thereby deserve the fief; it is not sufficient for him.” In Ivo: “But he does not thereby deserve the fief. For it is not sufficient,” etc.] to abstain from evil unless what is good is done, it remains that, in those same six matters, he should faithfully render counsel and aid to his lord [Note: [Col. 1157] “faithfully”: Ven. II, Paris, Lugdunensis; “as a faithful man”: remaining editions], if he wishes to seem worthy of a benefice and [Col. 1157B] secure in the fealty that he swore.

§ 2. The lord, too, ought to render the corresponding return to his faithful man in all these matters. If he does not, he will rightly be deemed faithless [Note: [Col. 1157] “maleficent”: Basle], just as one who is discovered treacherous and perjured by committing or consenting to violation of these obligations [Note: [Col. 1157D] “Who in their”: in the letter: “if immediately by violation”; in Ivo: “if in their violation.” In the *Panormia*, however, as in Gratian.].

### C. XIX. On the same matter. [PALEA.] Augustine.

[Note: [Col. 1157] The author of this canon seems briefly to have treated matters discussed more fully in the Tenth Council of Toledo, chapter 2, and Sixteenth Council, chapter 8.—Burchard, book 12, chapter 21; Anselm, book 11, chapter 74 (73); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 78; Polycarpus, book 6, title 11.—It is also included in the ancient Roman Penitential, Augustine, vol. 2, chapter 7.] [Note: [Col. 1157D] This chapter is absent from the better Gratian manuscripts. Burchard and Ivo cite it from Augustine’s sayings. Something similar occurs in the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, chapter 8, sent from Spain.]

“If any layman, by violating the oath which he swears to his king and lord, profanes it, and afterwards treacherously and deceitfully attacks his kingdom and plots by some device against his life, because he commits sacrilege by laying his hand upon the Christ of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1157] “of God”: Basle, Lugdunensis II–III; “the Lord”: remaining editions], let him be anathema unless he makes amendment through worthy satisfaction of penance [Col. 1157C], as established by the holy synod: that is, let him leave the secular life, lay down arms, enter a monastery, and do penance all the days of his life. Nevertheless, at the end of his life let him receive communion with the Eucharist [Note: [Col. 1157] “receive”: Burchard, Ivo; editions generally].

§ 1. But a bishop, priest, or deacon who commits this crime shall be deposed.”

### Part VI

Gratian. Thus, as appears from what precedes, a lie ought neither to be uttered in simple speech nor confirmed by oath [Col. 1158A]. But a lie is proved to exist not only in words but also in feigned deeds.

Accordingly Ambrose says in a sermon preached on the Sunday concerning Abraham [Note: [Col. 1158C] The sermon begins: “Know, brothers.”] [Note: [Col. 1157] It does not appear to be Ambrose’s.]:

### C. XX. One lies who does not show his profession in deeds.

Beware of falsehood, brothers [Note: [Col. 1157] added: “dearest” in editions Arg. and Bas.], because all who love falsehood are children of the devil [Note: [Col. 1158C] “Devil”: in the Vatican manuscript containing this sermon there follows: “for he is not only a liar, but also the father and inventor of lying itself. For all pretence and all duplicity is falsehood. Therefore not only,” etc.].

And below:

§ 1. Falsehood exists not only in false words, but also in feigned deeds. For it is falsehood to call oneself a Christian and not do Christ’s works. It is falsehood to profess oneself bishop, priest, or cleric, and to act contrary to that order.

[Col. 1158B]

### C. XXI. Whenever evil speech proceeds from our mouth. Likewise, Jerome, on Ephesians 4.

[Note: [Col. 1157] “not at a fitting time, or not in a fitting place”: editions generally.]

Whenever we speak, whether not at the proper time, or in an unsuitable place, or not as befits the hearers, evil speech proceeds from our mouth to the destruction of those who hear. Therefore let us consider what we say, because we must render account on the day of judgment for every idle word.

### Part VII

Gratian. A cleric, however, ought not give an oath to a layperson.

Thus the following is read in the Council of Reims [Note: [Col. 1157] It is not found in the councils of Reims. Something similar is in the extracts called Egbert’s, chapter 19 (Mansi, vol. 12), the capitulary of Charlemagne, A.D. 801, chapter 20, and chapter 38 of the Council of Meaux.—Burchard, book 2, chapter 188; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 11; *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 233.]:

### C. XXII. No cleric may presume to swear anything to any layperson.

No one of the ecclesiastical order may presume to swear anything to any layperson upon the most holy Gospels [Col. 1158C] [Note: [Col. 1157] “upon”: editions generally; “upon the holy and sacred Gospels”: Burchard; Ivo, *Panormia*], but let him simply say, with truth and purity: “Yes, yes; no, no.” But if anything is alleged against him [Note: [Col. 1158D] In Burchard and Ivo there follows: “let it be referred to the bishop in whose territory he is, and according to what those of the same order judge, let him either be corrected or cleared.”], according to the judgment of those of the same order, let him either be corrected or cleared.

[PALEA.]

“A cleric likewise ought not give an oath to a bishop, unless perhaps to one who entrusts him with the administration of a church.”

[Note: [Col. 1159] Matthew 5:39.] [Note: [Col. 1159] Deuteronomy 32:35.]

[Col. 1159A] Accordingly Urban II says [Note: [Col. 1159D] In several old copies the end of this cause is at the words “let him be cleared.” These words and the following chapter, “No one,” are absent. But one copy contains not only these, but also chapter 1 on the oath of calumny and Henry’s new constitution.] [Note: [Col. 1159] It is not found in Urban II’s letters.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 172.—Cf. chapter 1, *Compilatio I*, and chapter 5, *X*, *On Oaths*.]:

### C. XXIII. On the same matter.

“No bishop shall compel his clerics to swear to him, except perhaps those to whom [Col. 1160A] the administration of ecclesiastical property has been entrusted.”

## CAUSE XXIII

[Col. 1159]

[Col. 1159A] **GRATIAN**
Certain bishops, together with the people entrusted to them, fell into heresy. They began to compel the Catholics living around them to embrace heresy by threats and tortures. When this became known, the Apostolic See ordered the Catholic bishops of the surrounding regions, who had received civil jurisdiction from the emperor, to defend the Catholics against the heretics and, by whatever means they could, to compel them to return to the truth of the faith. The bishops, receiving these commands of the Apostolic See, summoned soldiers and began to fight against the heretics openly and by ambushes. At length, after some of them had been put to death, others stripped of their own or ecclesiastical property, and others confined in prison and the workhouse, they were compelled to return to the unity of the Catholic faith.

(Question I.) Here it is first asked whether military service is sinful. (Question II.) Second, what war is just, and how just wars were waged by the children of Israel. (Question III.) Third, whether an injury done to allies should be repelled by arms. (Question IV.) Fourth, whether vengeance should be inflicted. (Question V.) Fifth, whether it is sinful for a judge or official to kill the guilty. (Question VI.) Sixth, whether the wicked are to be compelled to what is good. (Question VII.) Seventh, whether heretics should be stripped of their own and the Church’s property, and whether one who possesses things taken from heretics is said to possess another’s property. (Question VIII.) Eighth, whether bishops or any clerics may take up arms on their own authority, or by command of the Apostolic See or the emperor. [Note: The reading *sine* (“without”) is absent from the Venice I, Nuremberg, Lyons II–III, and Paris editions; the Argentinian, Venice II, and Lyons I editions read *sive* (“or”).]

[Col. 1159B]

## QUESTION I

### GRATIAN

That military service seems foreign to evangelical discipline can apparently be proved from this: every form of military service has been instituted either to repel injury or to inflict vengeance; but injury is repelled either from one’s own person or from an ally, and both are forbidden by evangelical law. For when it is said, “If anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also” [Col. 1160A], and again, “Whoever compels you to go a thousand paces, go with him two thousand”; likewise, when the Apostle says [Rom. 12:19], “Beloved, do not defend yourselves, but give place to wrath”—what else are we forbidden except to repel injury done to our own person?

§ 1. Likewise, when Christ said to Peter, who was defending his master with a sword, “Put your sword back into its sheath; do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” [Matt. 26:52]; finally, as is read concerning blessed Andrew, when crowds of people gathered in order to rescue him from the hands of an unjust judge and defend him from the injury of death, he, on the contrary, teaching patience by example and word, begged them not to hinder his martyrdom—what else are we admonished except that, as we patiently bear injuries done to ourselves, so also those done to our allies; that we should not resort to arms, but prepare our minds by their example to endure similar things?

§ 2. Likewise, when it is said in Proverbs [Note: This saying is indeed commonly used in the manner of a proverb, but it is not found in the Book of Proverbs. It is cited by blessed Paul in Romans 12, together with another saying from Proverbs 25, and in Hebrews 10; in the Song of Deuteronomy 32 it is written: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.”], “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord”; likewise, when it is said in the Gospel [Matt. 7:1], “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged”; likewise, when the householder says to servants wishing to gather the tares [Matt. 13:30], “Let both grow until the harvest; then I shall say to the reapers, Gather the tares and bind them in bundles to be burned” [Col. 1160C];

§ 3. Likewise, when that king who made a wedding for his son is said to have sent his armies—that is, angels—to destroy the murderers of the prophets and apostles, who, because they did not believe, scorned to come when called to the wedding; likewise, when the Apostle Paul says in the Epistle to the Romans [Rom. 14:4], “Do not judge one another”; and again, “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls to his own master. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s. For Christ died and rose again for this purpose, that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead”—in all these passages what else is commanded than that vengeance upon offenders be reserved for the divine judgment? Since, therefore, as stated above, military service seems instituted either to repel injury [Col. 1161A] or to inflict vengeance, and both are forbidden by evangelical law, it appears that military service is sinful.

Gregory also says [Note: Rather, Origen, Homily 15 on the Book of Joshua]:

### Chapter I. Carnal wars prefigure spiritual wars

Unless these carnal wars prefigured spiritual wars, I think that the books of Jewish history would never have been handed down by the Apostles, to be read in the churches by the disciples of Christ, who came to teach peace. For how would this description of wars benefit those to whom Jesus says [John 14:27], “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you”—where “my peace I leave you” is absent in the Basel edition—and to whom the Apostle commands and says [1 Cor. 6:6], “Do not avenge yourselves, but rather accept injury, and rather [Col. 1161B] suffer fraud”? Thus, knowing that no carnal wars are any longer to be waged by us, but that the soul’s contests against spiritual adversaries must be labored through, the Apostle, like a commander of Christ’s army, gives orders to Christ’s soldiers, saying [Eph. 6:11], “Put on the armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil” [the Basel edition, with the Vulgate, reads “ambushes” instead of “wiles”].

Gratian. The following is the answer: the commands of patience are to be maintained not so much by an outward display of the body as by the preparation of the heart.

Accordingly Augustine says in his sermon on the centurion’s servant [Note: Anselm likewise cites it [in the cited Anselm manuscript it is cited from Augustine’s letter to Marcellinus]. Polycarpus gives no author. It is found, however, in Augustine’s Letter 5 to Marcellus.] [Col. 1161C] [Letter 138, Maurist edition, written A.D. 412; Anselm, book 13, chapter 3; Polycarpus, book 7, title 7]:

### Chapter II. The commands of patience must be observed by strength of mind, not by outward display of the body

A just and devout person should be prepared patiently to endure the malice of those whom he seeks to make good, so that the number of the good may rather increase, and he may not add himself also to the number of the wicked by equal malice [the other editions read *quis*, “someone,” for *se quoque*, “himself also”]. Finally, these commands belong more—indeed, the other editions and Anselm read *magis sunt*, “belong more”—to the preparation of the heart, which is within [Note: The words *quae intus est* (“which is within”) are absent from Anselm.], than to the action performed openly: patience with benevolence must be preserved in the inward disposition, while outwardly that should be done which seems capable of benefiting those toward whom we ought to be well disposed.

§ 1. Hence it is clearly shown that the Lord Jesus himself, the unique example of patience, when struck on the face [the Basel, Venice I and II, and Nuremberg editions read “on the face” rather than “on the cheek”], answered [John 18:23], “If I have spoken wrongly [the other editions read “If I have spoken”], testify concerning the wrong; but if rightly, why [the Basel edition reads “why” rather than “for what reason”] do you strike me?” Thus, if we look at the words, he did not at all fulfill his own command. For he did not offer the striker the other side [Col. 1162A], but rather forbade the one who had done the injury to increase it [the Basel edition reads “lest he do and increase the injury”; the other editions read “lest he do and increase the injury” with a different manuscript form]. Yet he had come prepared [the other editions read “had come”] not only to be struck on the face, but also to be crucified and killed for those from whom he suffered these things [the Basel edition omits “from whom”; the other editions have “for this”]; for them he said while hanging upon the cross [Luke 23:34], “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

§ 2. Nor does the Apostle Paul seem to have fulfilled the command of his Lord and master when he himself was struck on the face [the Nuremberg and Venice editions read “on the face”] and said to the high priest, “God will strike you, whitewashed wall! You sit to judge me according to the law, and contrary to the law you order me to be struck” [cf. Acts 23:3; other editions read “May God strike you”]. And when those standing by said, “Do you insult the high priest?” he, mockingly [the original reads “mockingly”], wished to remind them of what he had said, so that those with understanding might perceive that the whitewashed wall—that is, the hypocrisy of the Jewish priesthood—was now to be destroyed by Christ’s advent. For he said, “I did not know, brothers, that he is a ruler. For it is written [Exod. 22:28], ‘You shall not curse the ruler of your people.’” Yet surely one who had grown up among that people and had been instructed in the law, and who could not have failed to know the high priest, could not deceive in any way those to whom that ruler was so well known by claiming not to know him. The original reads “there,” rather than “in the same place,” and Anselm likewise has “there.”

Therefore these commands of patience must always be preserved in the preparation of the heart, and this same benevolence—that evil not be returned for evil—must always be fulfilled in the will [Anselm reads “this benevolence also”; the other editions have “this same benevolence”].

§ 3. Yet many things must be done, even to unwilling persons, by a certain kindly severity in punishing them; for their benefit is to be considered rather than their wishes. And below: For in correcting a son [the other editions read “a child”], however severely, paternal love is certainly never lost. What he does not wish is nevertheless done, and one who seems to need healing through pain even against his will suffers pain [the other editions read “may suffer pain”].

§ 4. Consequently, if this earthly commonwealth keeps Christian commands, even its wars will not be waged without benevolence, so that provision may more readily be made for the defeated toward a peaceful fellowship of piety and justice [the other editions read “but so that,” and add “rather”]. For one from whom the freedom to commit iniquity is taken is beneficially conquered [the other editions read “more beneficially”], since nothing is more miserable than the prosperity of sinners, by which punitive impunity is nourished and an evil will, like an inner enemy, is strengthened.

And a little later:

§ 5. For if Christian discipline condemned all wars, the Gospel would rather have told soldiers seeking counsel for salvation to throw away their arms and withdraw altogether from military service. But they were told, “Extort from no one; bring no false accusation against anyone; let your wages suffice you” [Luke 3:14]. The complete Gospel passage is restored here, as it stands in the letter itself [and in Anselm; cf. Luke 3:14] and in Book 22 against Faustus, chapter 74. Previously the text read, “Be content with your wages,” as in the other editions. In commanding those for whom their own wages ought to suffice, he certainly did not forbid military service.

### Chapter III. Soldiers may please God while bearing arms

Likewise, from the same author, to Boniface, Letter CCVIII [Letter 189, Maurist edition, written A.D. 417; Anselm, book 13, chapter 4; Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, chapter 126; Polycarpus, book 7, title 13]:

Do not suppose that no one can please God while serving in arms [the other editions read “serving” rather than “serving in arms”; Anselm likewise]. Among such persons was holy David, to whom the Lord gave so great a testimony. Among them were also very many righteous people of that time. Among them was also that holy centurion [the other editions read “that centurion”] who said to the Lord [Matt. 8:8], “I am not worthy that you should enter beneath my roof.”

And below:

§ 1. First consider this, therefore, when you arm yourself for battle [the Basel edition reads *pugnandum*, “for fighting”]: that even your bodily strength [Col. 1163B] is God’s gift. Thus you will reflect that one must not act against God by means of God’s gift. The earlier text read: “Thus [the other editions: *si*, ‘if’] you will reflect [the Basel and Lyons II–III editions add *hoc*, ‘this’] concerning God’s gift, you will not act [Basel: *facias*, ‘you should act’] against the Lord.” Anselm has the reading indicated by the corrector. This passage and many others were emended from the original [Col. 1164D].

For faith, once pledged, must be kept even to an enemy against whom war is waged—how much more to a friend for whom one fights? The will ought to have peace; necessity ought to have war, so that God may deliver us from necessity and preserve us in peace. Anselm has: “Peace belongs to the will, war to necessity.” Another reading is: “Peace belongs to the will, war, however, ought to be,” and so forth. Peace is not sought in order to stir up war [the other editions read “to carry on war,” rather than “to stir up war”], but war is waged in order to obtain peace. Therefore be peaceful even while fighting, so that by conquering you may lead those whom you overcome to the benefit of peace [the Basel and Lyon II and III editions read “to unity”]. “Blessed are the peacemakers,” says the Lord [Matt. 5:9], “for they shall be called children of God.” If human peace is so sweet for the temporal safety of mortals, how much sweeter is divine peace for the eternal salvation of angels? Let necessity, therefore, kill the enemy who fights, not the will [Anselm reads “let necessity overcome”; the other editions read “let necessity overcome”]. [Col. 1163C] As violence is returned to one who rebels and resists [the other editions read “to one who fights”], so mercy is now owed to one conquered or captured. The editions vary between “to one captured by victories,” “to one captured by the victor,” and “to one captured by the victor,” especially where no disturbance of peace is feared.

Likewise, from the same author against the Manichaeans—that is, Book XXII against Faustus, chapters 74 and 75 [Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 45]:

### Chapter IV. What is rightly blamed in war

What is blamed in war? Is it that persons who will someday die are killed, so that those who conquer may rule in peace? To condemn this belongs to the timid, not to the religious [the Basel edition reads “the arrogant,” rather than “the timid”]. The desire to harm, the cruelty of revenge, an unappeased and implacable spirit, savage rebellion, the lust to dominate, and whatever things are similar—these are what are rightly blamed in wars. It is often so that these may also be justly punished that wars themselves are undertaken by good people against the violence of those who resist, whether by God’s command or by the command of some lawful authority, when they find themselves in that ordering of human affairs in which the order itself binds them either justly to command such things or justly to obey in such matters.

Therefore John does not command soldiers to leave military service [Luke 3], and Christ tells men to render tribute to Caesar [Matt. 22], because soldiers’ pay is necessarily provided on account of wars [the Basel edition reads “so that pay may be provided”]. [Note: From “Therefore John” through “order,” Gratian has summarized Augustine’s teaching, which Ivo gives in full and Augustine expounds more fully and clearly; the same is true from “But if war is waged from human greed” through “For there is no authority except from God.”] Yet that natural order, fitted to the peace of mortals, requires that the authority and decision to undertake war belong to rulers [the other editions read “be in the power of rulers”].

And below:

§ 1. But if war is waged from human greed, it does not harm the saints, over whom no one has authority unless it has been given from above [John 19]. For there is no authority except from God, whether he commands or permits [Rom. 13]. Therefore, if a just man serves even under a king who is himself a sacrilegious man, he may rightly wage war at that king’s command, provided that, maintaining the order of civil peace, it is certain that what is commanded of him is not contrary to God’s command, or it is not certain whether it is contrary. Thus perhaps the injustice of commanding makes the king guilty, whereas the order of obedience shows the soldier innocent.

[Col. 1164C]

### Chapter V. Military service is not sinful

Likewise, from the same author, in the book *On the Words of the Lord*, tractate or sermon XIX [Note: This is not Augustine’s, according to the judgment of the Maurists. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 60; *Decree*, part 10, chapter 125]:

Military service is not an offense; but to serve as a soldier for plunder is sinful. Nor is administering the commonwealth criminal; but to administer the commonwealth in order rather to increase one’s household wealth seems condemnable. For this reason pay has been established by a certain providence for soldiers, lest, while expenses are being sought, the plunderer range abroad [the original and Ivo read *praeda*, “plunder,” in place of *praedo*, “plunderer”].

And below:

§ 1. The Lord himself says [Matt. 22:21], “Render to God the things that are God’s, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s.” Therefore what Caesar commands must be borne [the Venice I and II and Nuremberg editions read “has commanded”]; what the emperor imposes must be endured [the same editions read “commands”]. But it becomes unbearable when tax-collectors heap up exactions as plunder [the original reads “when the collectors accumulate that plunder of exaction”].

And below:

§ 2. Soldiers asked John, saying [Luke 3:14], “What shall we also do?” He said to them, “Extort from no one, bring no false accusation against anyone, but be content with your wages.” Here every person who serves must now understand himself [Ivo and the other editions read “Thus every person should understand himself”]. For Scripture speaks not only of those soldiers who are engaged in armed service: whoever bears the belt of his office is enrolled as a soldier of his rank, and therefore this saying may be addressed, for example, to soldiers, protectors, and all governors. Whoever receives publicly assigned pay, if he seeks more, is condemned by John’s saying as a false accuser and extortioner.

### Chapter VI. Wars are peaceful when they are waged to restrain the wicked and assist the good

Likewise, from the same author, *On Various Observances of the Church* [Note: Ivo also cites it in this manner, although it has not been found in blessed Augustine, even though Augustine’s letter to Januarius has almost such a title. A similar passage is found above under the same heading, “Do Not Suppose,” in the section beginning “Therefore,” and in *The City of God*, book 19, chapter 12.] [Note: No book of Augustine entitled *On Various Ecclesiastical Observances* exists. Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, chapter 105]:

Among true worshippers of God, even wars themselves are peaceful when they are waged not from greed or cruelty but from the pursuit of peace, in order that the wicked may be restrained and the good assisted [the Basel edition has the corrupt reading *peccuta*, materially uncertain].

[Col. 1165C]

### Chapter VII. The highest praise of military service is to render obedience for the welfare of the commonwealth

Likewise, Gregory to all soldiers at Naples, Book XII, Letter 24 [Letter 31, written A.D. 592, book 2, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 13, chapter 9]:

Among other good services, this is the highest praise of military service: to render obedience for the welfare of the commonwealth [the original reads *sanctae reipublicae*, “of the holy commonwealth”], and to obey whatever is usefully commanded [the text has *quodque*, “and that which”; the other editions read *quicquid*, “whatever”]. We have learned that your devotion has now done this: you obeyed our letters, by which we appointed the distinguished man Constantius [the other editions, especially Arg., read “Constantinus”] as tribune to preside over the guard of the city, and displayed the fitting obedience of military devotion. Therefore by this present writing we have taken care to admonish you that you must render to the aforesaid distinguished tribune, as you have done, every obedience necessary for the interests of our most serene lords and for preserving the city, so that by the vigilance and diligence of the present time you may increase whatever good conduct has hitherto been recognized in you [the Basel edition reads “is shown and recognized”; the Arg. edition reads “is recognized”]. The other editions have “through the present” rather than “of the present time.”

Gratian. From all these passages it is gathered that military service is not sinful, and that the commands of patience are to be observed in the preparation of the heart, not in an outward display of the body.

## QUESTION II

### GRATIAN

As to the question what a just war is, Isidore says in *Etymologies*, book XVIII, chapter 1 [Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 54; *Decree*, part 10, chapter 116]:

### Chapter I. What a just war is

A just war is one waged by public decree to recover things, or for the sake of repelling enemies [the original reads *repetitis*, “recovered,” for *repetendis*, “to be recovered”; the other editions read *hominum*, “men,” for *hostium*, “enemies”]. [Note: In Isidore’s manuscripts, including manuscript copies, the reading is also *ex praedicto* (“from a prior declaration”). He is citing Cicero’s books *On the Commonwealth*, where Cicero denies that a war is just unless it has been announced, declared, and undertaken for recovery of property.]

And in chapter 15:

§ 1. A judge is so called as one who declares law to the people, or because he adjudicates according to law [the Venice II edition reads “because he declares the law”; the other editions read “because he dictates the law”; Ivo has another form]. To adjudicate according to law is to judge justly. But there is no judge unless justice is in him [the other editions read “For there is no judge unless justice is in him”].

### Chapter II. It makes no difference to justice whether one fights openly or by ambush

Likewise Augustine, in Book VI of *Questions*, question 10:

Our Lord Jesus Christ commanded Joshua son of Nun to set ambushes behind him—that is, soldiers lying in wait to ambush the enemy [the note in the original observes that God, speaking to Joshua in Joshua 8, commanded him to arrange ambushes]. From this we are admonished that it is not unjust for those who wage a just war to do this [the phrase “to do this” is absent from the original]; and that in such matters a just person ought chiefly to consider nothing except that he undertake a just war, if it is lawful for him to wage war. For it is not lawful for everyone. But once he has undertaken a just war, it makes no difference to justice whether he fights in open battle or wins by ambush [the editions vary between “whether he fights openly or by ambush”].

Wars are usually defined as just when they avenge injuries: if some nation or state which must be attacked by war has either neglected to punish an evil deed committed by its own members or to restore what has been taken by injury [the editions vary between “if some nation or state is to be attacked” and “which is to be attacked”]. But without doubt that kind of war is also just which God commands—he in whom there is no injustice and who knows what ought to happen to each person [the other editions read “who knows what ought to be done to each person”]. In such a war the commander of the army, or the people themselves, are to be judged not so much the authors of the war as ministers.

Gratian. Since, therefore, a just war is one waged by public decree or one by which injuries are avenged, it is asked how just wars were waged by the children of Israel.

Augustine writes thus concerning this in *Questions on Numbers*, question 44, on chapter 20 [Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 57; *Decree*, the other editions, part 10, chapter 119]:

### Chapter III. Harmless passage was denied to the children of Israel; therefore they waged just wars

It should certainly be noted how just wars were waged by the children of Israel against the Amorites. For harmless passage was refused them, though by the most equitable law of human society it ought to have been allowed [the words “against the Amorites” are absent from the original but occur in Ivo].

## QUESTION III

### GRATIAN

That an injury done to allies ought not to be repelled by arms is proved by examples and authorities. For when the Lord was sought by Herod in order to kill him [Matt. 2], he did not seek the protection of arms, although by a hidden prompting he could have turned the hands of the Jews against him; instead, fleeing into Egypt, he lay hidden there for seven years. Likewise, when the Jews sought to stone him [Matt. 21], he hid himself and went out of the temple. Likewise, when he was led to the cross, he was unwilling to stir up against the elders of the Jews the crowd which had recently gone out to meet him and had received him with palms and praises. Likewise, when Pilate asked him whether he was a king, he said [John 18:36], “My kingdom is not of this world. For if it were of this world, my servants would certainly fight, so that I might not be handed over to the Jews,” thereby indicating that those belong to the kingdom of this world who strive to protect themselves from impending injury by the aid of human strength, not by divine protection.

Likewise, when he says to his disciples [Matt. 10:23], “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another,” he taught that flight, not arms against arms, should be opposed to persecutors.

§ 1. Likewise, as is read in Isaiah, Egypt was devastated by Nebuchadnezzar because it promised the children of Israel help of protection and defense against the Assyrians and Chaldeans. Therefore it was said [Isa. 36:6], “The king of Egypt is a staff of reed: if anyone leans upon it, it will break and pierce the hand of the one leaning upon it.” The Jews themselves were also carried away captive because they placed the hope of their liberation not in God alone but in man. Thus also it is read of the first believers [Acts 5] that they received the plundering of their goods with joy, seeking no other persons’ protection, but rejoicing because they were found worthy to suffer insult for Jesus’ name. Thus the Apostle urges the Corinthians in the first epistle [1 Cor. 6:7] patiently to bear injury and fraud rather than scandalize their brothers by seeking redress. Thus he judges that one ought rather to abstain from food offered to idols and from every sort of food than eat it to the scandal of brethren. Thus he also abstains from expenses, lest he provide any offense to the Gospel of Christ.

Since, therefore, the person who is warded off from injury by arms is scandalized no less than the person from whom property taken away is claimed in court, it is evident that the assistance of arms must not be sought for repelling injury. But what ought not to be sought ought not rightly to be provided.

§ 2. But, conversely, many things are rightly provided that are nevertheless not rightly sought. A good person, for example, does not rightly seek vengeance for an injury, because he would return evil for evil; yet a judge would rightly inflict it, and would return nothing but good for evil.

Accordingly Augustine says in his exposition of Psalm 108 [Note: Blessed Augustine most aptly explains these six distinctions in his exposition of Psalm 108. The author of the Ordinary Gloss briefly reported his teaching at the same place, and this chapter seems to have been taken from that gloss.]:

### Chapter I. What the distinctions among requitals are

There are six distinctions: to return good for evil; not to return evil for evil. These two belong to the good, and the former is better [the Basel and Lyons II–III editions read *sed*, “but,” for *et*, “and”]. Not to return good for good; to return evil for good. These two belong to the wicked, and the latter is worse [the other editions likewise read *sed* for *et*]. To return good for good; evil for evil. These two belong to those in the middle: the former is nearer to the good and also befits the wicked—Christ does not rebuke it, but says that more is required, because even the Gentiles do this; the latter is nearer to the wicked, though it nevertheless also befits the good. [Note: “It also befits the wicked” is absent from most old manuscripts, the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice I–II editions, and the Gloss, although it does not depart far from Augustine’s words; *et* before “the Gentiles” is absent from the Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]

Thus the law establishes a measure of vengeance [Exod. 21:24]: “An eye for an eye.” This is, if one may say so, the justice of the unjust—not because the vengeance established by the law is unjust, but because the desire for vengeance is vicious. It belongs more to a judge to determine this among people than to a good person to demand it for himself. For the latter would return evil for evil; but the judge punishes, not from delight in another’s misery, which is evil for evil, but from love of justice, returning what is just for what is unjust, which is good for evil. God the judge does this also.

Gratian. Likewise, one may unjustly demand a captive’s possessions from him, yet they may rightly be offered to ransom his life. Likewise, sacred vessels may be unjustly demanded from a barbarian, but they may rightly be given for the redemption of captives. So too the repelling of injury, although it may be unjustly requested, is nevertheless rightly provided—although even that request is not proved altogether unjust. [In the preceding example, sacred vessels are unjustly demanded by a barbarian, not from one.]

§ 1. For it is one thing to repel injury in order that one may be free to live pleasurably; another, in order that one may freely attend to the benefit of others. Thus it is one thing to seek assistance from a human being as a minister of justice, so that the evil will of adversaries may be deprived, through his office, of its effect, and the good will [Col. 1169B] may obtain effect through his assistance; another thing to transfer one’s hope from God to man, so that adversities inflicted by God for the correction of life may be driven away by human help without any prior correction. This was the case with the Israelites, who thought that through Egyptian assistance they could escape the captivity threatening them without repentance for their former life, not recalling: “Give us help in tribulation, for vain is the salvation of man” [Ps. 59:13]; and likewise, “These trust in chariots and those in horses, but we shall call upon the name of our God” [Ps. 19:8].

Therefore, to seek or provide help in tribulation so that someone may live pleasurably in sin is damnable. But to seek or provide aid so that the wicked may be deprived of the opportunity to sin, so that the Church may obtain peace, or so that someone may be preserved for the benefit of many, is useful and honorable; to disregard it is most blameworthy. Thus it is read of Paul [Acts 23] that when certain Jews had sworn not to eat bread unless they killed him, he requested soldiers from the prefect, by whose protection he might be kept unharmed from the injury of the Jews—not to live for his own pleasure, but for the benefit of all. Thus in the Gospel [John 10] the hired man is called one who sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees.

§ 2. Thus the Church too is taught to seek aid from the emperor for its defense.

Accordingly Augustine says to Boniface, Letter L [written A.D. 417; Letter 185, Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, chapter 59; Polycarpus, book 1, final title]:

### Chapter II. The Church ought to request help from the emperor

Maximianus, bishop of Vaga, sought help [Col. 1170A] from the Christian emperor against enemies of the Church [the words “against the enemies of the Church” are absent from the original but occur in Ivo], not so much in order to avenge himself as to protect the Church entrusted to him [the Basel edition reads “handed over to him”]. Had he neglected this, his patience would not have been praiseworthy; rather, his negligence would deservedly have been blamed. Nor was the Apostle Paul providing for his own transitory life [the other editions and Ivo read “provided”] when he brought it about that the plot of those conspiring to kill him should be disclosed to the tribune [cf. Acts 23]. As a result, an armed soldier escorted him to the place to which he was to be brought, lest he suffer their ambushes [the other editions read “lest he suffer their ambush”].

### Chapter III. Catholics may request defense from established authorities against heretics

Likewise Augustine to Emeritus, Letter CLXIV [Letter 87, Maurist edition, written A.D. 405; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 26; *Decree*, part 10, chapter 80].

Our people seek from the constituted authorities protection against the unlawful and private acts of violence of your people [Col. 1170B] (acts at which you yourselves there—who do *not* commit such things—grieve and lament [Note: [Col. 1169D] *Do not commit*: the negation has been supplied from the original and from Ivo [it is absent from the Panormia]; other corrections have also been made. Blessed Augustine there reports what had been decreed in the holy Council of Carthage [Col. 1170D], and is repeated in canon 60 of the African Council; it is cited below in the same question, chapter *Ab imperatoribus*]), not in order that the authorities may persecute you, but that they may defend themselves [Note: [Col. 1169] *protection*: *vengeance*, Ivo, *Panormia*—the collected editions. — “that”: Basel edition; “because”: the remaining editions—Ivo. — “you”: “these persons,” collected editions—Ivo. — “that”: “because,” the same editions—“this.”].

### Chapter IV. How great the difference is between the persecution of Catholics and that of heretics

Likewise, the same author, *Against the Letters of Petilian*, book II, chapter 88 [Note: [Col. 1169] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, chapter 75].

All who rage against you and resist you for the members of Christ are still of *weak faith* in the Catholic Church, and have the disposition Peter then had when he drew the sword in Christ’s name [Note: [Col. 1169] “church”: collected editions. — “weak … faith”: absent in Ivo. — John 18]. But there is a great difference between your persecution and theirs. You are like the servant of the Jewish high priest [Note: [Col. 1169] “Jewish” is absent in Ivo], because, serving your leaders, you arm yourselves against the Catholic Church—that is, against Christ’s body [Col. 1170C]. But these persons are such as Peter then was, who even fought physically for Christ’s body—that is, for the Church [Note: [Col. 1169] absent in the Basel edition].

### Chapter V. A person who defends his country from barbarians in war is full of justice

Likewise, Ambrose, book I of *On Duties*, chapter 27 [Note: [Col. 1169] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 34; *Decretum*, part 10, chapter 97].

Courage, which either in war defends one’s country from barbarians, or at home protects the weak, or protects one’s companions from robbers, is full of justice [Note: [Col. 1169] “justice”: collected editions = Chapter VI].

### Chapter VI. He benefits a robber or pirate who disables his limbs

Likewise, Jerome on Zephaniah, chapter 1 [Note: [Col. 1169] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 50; *Decretum*, part 10, chapter 113].

If anyone weakens the strength of a robber, pirate, or thief, and renders them weak, their weakness benefits them. For their disabled limbs, which they had previously used badly, will cease from evil work [Note: [Col. 1169] “and”: “or,” collected editions. — “and thief”: absent in Ivo. — “weakens”: “plunders,” original—Ivo. — “them”: absent in Ivo. — *reddat* (“may render”): *reddit* (“renders”), collected editions. — “also benefits,” Argentinensis edition]. [Col. 1171A]

### Chapter VII. One who does not repel an injury done to an associate is like one who commits it

Likewise, Ambrose, book I of *On Duties*, chapter 36.

The law of virtue concerns not inflicting injury, but repelling it. For one who, if able, does not repel injury from an associate is as much at fault as the one who commits it. Hence Saint Moses first began to give proofs of martial courage. For when he saw a Hebrew suffering injury from an Egyptian, he defended him by striking down the Egyptian and hiding him in the sand. Solomon likewise says: “Rescue him who is being led to death” [Note: [Col. 1171] “Do not inflict”: Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, Venice I and II; “not in bearing”: remaining editions. — “repels”: Basel edition. — “martial”: thus corrected from the original, although Gratian manuscripts also read *imbellis* (“unwarlike”); “feeble,” collected editions. — “suffering”: Basel edition; cf. Exodus 2. — Proverbs 24:11].

[Col. 1171B]

### Chapter VIII. Whoever ceases to oppose evildoers abets their impiety

Likewise, Pope Anastasius and Damasus [Note: [Col. 1171] Found in the letter of Damasus to Stephen in Pseudo-Isidore.—Anselm, book 13, chapter 19; Polycarpus, book 7, title 11; cf. canon 3, Distinction 83; canon 3, Distinction 86].

One who can oppose and thwart the perverse, but does not do so, does nothing other than favor their impiety. Nor is one free from the guilt of secret complicity who ceases to oppose an open crime.

### Chapter IX. Those who despise divine commands are to be restrained by severe punishments

Likewise, Calixtus, Letter II, to the bishops of Gaul [Note: [Col. 1171] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Gregory the Great, letter 41, book 9, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 13, chapter 13; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 346; Polycarpus, same place].

It is just that those who despise divine commands and prove disobedient to the injunctions of the Fathers should be corrected by more severe punishments, so that others may fear to commit such acts, all may rejoice in fraternal harmony, and everyone may take an example of severity and goodness. For if—God forbid—we neglect ecclesiastical concern and vigor, negligence destroys discipline, and the souls of the faithful will certainly be harmed [Note: [Col. 1171] “fatherly,” collected editions. — “honesty,” Basel edition]. [Col. 1171C]

### Chapter X. Emperors, with the bishops’ provision, ought to undertake the Church’s defense against the power of the wealthy

Likewise, from the Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 9 [Note: [Col. 1171] Held A.D. 401.—Collection of Three Parts, part 2, title 19, chapter 9].

It has been considered necessary to petition all emperors, on account of the oppression of the poor, by whose troubles the Church is wearied without interruption, that defenders be assigned to them, with the bishops’ provision, against the power of the wealthy [Note: [Col. 1171] “the emperor,” Hispanic Collection. — “It has been considered”: thus corrected from printed and manuscript codices of the council. Formerly it read, “It is just to request assistance,” as in the collected editions. — “selected,” Hispanic Collection]. [Col. 1172A]

Gratian. See: sometimes the perverse must be opposed, and the injuries done to associates must be repelled by arms, so that both the removal from evildoers of the opportunity to sin may benefit them, and the desired opportunity freely to provide for the Church may be furnished to the good. Whoever does not do this gives consent.

Hence Augustine says on Psalm 81:

### Chapter XI. Those who do not free people whom they can free from the deed are not exempt from guilt

The Prophet shows that those also were not exempt from guilt who allowed Christ to be killed by rulers, although the rulers were feared because of the crowd, and although they could have freed both the rulers from the deed and themselves from consent. Whoever ceases to oppose when able, consents [Note: [Col. 1171] “to crucify and kill,” Basel and Lyons II–III editions. — These words, “Whoever ceases,” are reported in the same gloss from Cassiodorus, whose words are: “For when you can oppose the perverse, if you cease to resist, it is consent to error.” [Col. 1172B–C] — “Whoever ceases to oppose the perverse … and does not do so appears to consent,” Basel edition; Lyons II–III similarly, except that the end reads “consents.”].

## QUESTION IV

### GRATIAN

**Part I.** That vengeance ought not to be inflicted is proved in many ways. For evildoers are to be tolerated, not cast out; struck by rebuke, not physically expelled.

Hence Augustine says in the eighteenth sermon *On the Words of the Lord* [Note: [Col. 1172C] This chapter occurs in the Ordinary Gloss on 2 Corinthians 6, at the words “Go out from their midst.” The sense, however, is taken from Augustine’s eighteenth sermon *On the Words of the Lord*, from which below, in the same question, chapters *Ecce* and *Recedite*, dealing with the same matter, are cited.] [Note: [Col. 1171] Sermon 88, Maurist edition]:

### Chapter I. How evildoers are to be tolerated, and how one ought to withdraw from them

Evildoers must indeed be tolerated for the sake of peace, and one must not physically withdraw from them; but to go out spiritually is to do, so far as is permitted by each person’s rank and while preserving peace, what belongs to correcting evildoers. To disapprove is not to touch. For the prophets who said these things did not abandon their people; rather, they lived among those whom they rebuked, entered the one temple with them, and celebrated the same sacraments. This is to go out: not to spare with one’s mouth. This is not to touch what is unclean: not to consent in one’s will [Note: [Col. 1172D] “Spiritually”: the two words *spiritualiter autem* (“but spiritually”) formerly inserted here have been deleted, since they are absent both from most ancient witnesses and from the Ordinary Gloss. — “this,” collected editions]. [Col. 1172C]

[Col. 1173A]

### Chapter II. That evildoers are to be tolerated by the good

The same author [Note: [Col. 1173C] The beginning of this chapter is in Tractate 50 on John. The remainder seems taken from the Ordinary Gloss on Psalm 9 at the words “For he said in his heart,” and from Blessed Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 10, whose actual words are cited above, Question 1, chapter 1, *Christus*. The same point is expounded at length by him in Letter 162.] [Note: [Col. 1173] Cf. Gratian, §3 after chapter 48, Cause 7, Question 1].

You who are good, tolerate the evil. For Christ too, although he knew Judas to be a thief, tolerated him, sent him out to preach, and gave him the Eucharist with the others.

### Chapter III. Evildoers are to be tolerated for the peace of the Church

The same author, on John, Tractate 50, on chapter 12 [Note: [Col. 1173D] Many things in this chapter have been corrected from Blessed Augustine.] [Note: [Col. 1173] Polycarpus, book 7, title 7].

What then, my brothers, did our Lord Jesus Christ wish to impress upon his Church when he wished to have one lost man among the twelve, except that we should tolerate evildoers lest we divide Christ’s body? See, Judas is among the saints; see, Judas is a thief—and, lest you despise him, a sacrilegious thief; not an ordinary thief, but a thief of money-boxes, and indeed of the Lord’s money-boxes: money-boxes, yet sacred ones. If crimes are distinguished in court between ordinary theft and embezzlement—for embezzlement means theft from the public treasury, and theft of private property is not judged as theft of public property—how much more severely should a sacrilegious thief be judged, one who has dared not to steal from just anywhere, but to steal from the Church [Note: [Col. 1173] *Si* (“if”): *sic* (“thus”), collected editions, including the early Basel edition. — *foro* (“court”): the editions give expanded and differing readings contrasting a thief, ordinary theft, and embezzlement]. Whoever steals something from the Church is compared to Judas the lost one [Note: [Col. 1173] “contend”: collected editions. — “is a thief and sacrilegious”: Basel, Nuremberg, Lyons editions; “thief and sacrilegious,” remaining editions. — Variant expanded readings: “a thief, but a thief of the Lord’s money-boxes and sacrilegious”; etc. — “to steal”: “that is, commit sacrilege … but from the Church,” collected editions. — “betrayer,” Basel and remaining editions; Böhm]. [Col. 1173B]

### Chapter IV. On the same matter

The same author, Sermon XVIII, *On the Words of the Lord* [Note: [Col. 1173] Sermon 88, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 12, chapter 65 (64); Polycarpus, same place].

“See,” they say, “the Prophet says: ‘Depart, go out from there, and do not touch what is unclean.’ How then shall we tolerate evildoers for peace, when we are commanded to go out and depart from them, lest we touch what is unclean?” We understand this departure spiritually; they understand it physically. For I too cry out with the Prophet; and whatever kind of vessels we are, God employs us in dispensing to you. We too cry out and say to you: “Depart, go out from there, and do not touch what is unclean”—but by the touch of the heart, not of the body. For what is it to touch what is unclean except to consent to sins? And what is it to go out from there except to do, as far as can be done while preserving peace, what belongs to correcting evildoers, in accordance with each person’s rank and office?

And a little later:

§1. Therefore, my brothers, all among you who are still weighed down by love of the world—greedy persons, perjurers, adulterers, spectators of trifles, consultees of astrologers, devotees of frenzied cults, augurs, diviners, drunkards, the licentious, and whatever evils you know to exist among you—disapprove of them as far as you can, so that you may withdraw in heart; rebuke them, so that you may go out from there; and do not consent, so that you may not touch what is unclean [Note: [Col. 1173] Isaiah 52:11. — absent in Basel edition. — “cry out”: “will cry out,” same edition. — “And whatever”: thus corrected from Augustine and Bede; formerly *aequalia* (“equal”), in the collected editions and Anselm. — “our,” Basel edition. — *contactu* (“by contact”): *tactu* (“by touch”), Basel edition. — “and”: absent in the collected editions and in Lyons II–III. — “spectators”: Argentinensis and Basel; “inspectors,” other editions. — “consultees”: “consultators,” collected editions. — “devotees of frenzied cults”: absent in Argentinensis and Nuremberg editions. — “so that … not”: collected editions, though Basel reads “lest.”]. [Col. 1173C–1174A]

### Chapter V. Peaceful is the person who corrects what he can, or excludes from himself what he cannot

The same author, book II *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, chapter 1.

Whoever either corrects by rebuke what he can, or excludes—without breaking the bond of peace—what he cannot correct, or disapproves in fairness what he cannot exclude without breaking the bond of peace, and bears it with firmness, is peaceful; and he is altogether free, completely safe, and utterly removed from that curse of which Scripture says: “Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil,” and so forth.

And below:

§1. “How,” says Parmenian, “will you be able to remain uncorrupted if you associate with the corrupt?” [Note: [Col. 1174C–D] In Blessed Augustine, Parmenian’s question is followed immediately by the answer printed in the next chapter, “Yes indeed.” The question and Augustine’s response would certainly be more suitably contained in a single chapter.]

### Chapter VI. What it is to associate with evildoers

The same author, continuously in the same chapter [Note: [Col. 1173] Polycarpus, same place].

Yes indeed: a person associates with evildoers if he commits something evil with them or favors those who commit it. But if he does neither, he does not associate with them at all. Further, if he adds a third point—not to be sluggish in punishment, but either to rebuke and reprove in mercy, as is just, or, if he occupies the appropriate office and the preservation of peace permits it, to rebuke sinners before all, so that the rest may fear; even to remove them either from some rank of honor or from communion in the sacraments themselves—and does all this in love for their correction, not in hatred of persecuting them, he has fulfilled the fullest duty not only of most chaste innocence, but also of most diligent severity. But where the other measures are prevented, those two always retained preserve one uncorrupted and chaste: neither to do evil nor to approve what has been done [Note: [Col. 1173] *mali* (“evil”): absent in Basel. — “adds”: “adds [again] or a third [point],” Argentinensis. — “judging,” Basel. — “and before,” collected editions. — “let them be removed,” Paris; “let him be removed,” other editions. — “let him do,” collected editions. — “also,” Basel]. [Col. 1174C–1175A]

### Chapter VII. Another person’s sins in the Church do not prejudice anyone

The same author, Letter 152, against the Donatists [Note: [Col. 1175] Letter 141, Maurist edition, written A.D. 412; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 101].

If anyone has been separated from the Catholic Church, however praiseworthy he may think his life to be, by this crime alone—that he has been severed from Christ’s unity—he will not have life, but God’s wrath remains upon him. But anyone who lives well in this Church is not prejudiced by the sins of others; for in it each person shall bear his own burden, as the Apostle says.

And below:

§1. Therefore communion with evildoers does not stain anyone through participation in the sacraments, but through consent to their deeds. For if a person does not consent to them in their evil deeds, the evildoer bears his own cause and his own person, and does not prejudice another whom he does not have as a partner in the crime through consent to the evil act [Note: [Col. 1175] “Christendom”: formerly read here, as in Ivo and the collected editions; restored from the original and Bede, together with certain other readings. — “holy,” collected editions. — “says”: same editions—Ivo; cf. Galatians 6:5. — “anyone”: Basel; “any person,” Lyons II–III. — *consensione* (“consent”): *concessione* (“permission”), Basel].

### Chapter VIII. An evildoer does not stain you if you do not consent to him but rebuke him

The same author, Sermon XVIII, *On the Words of the Lord* [Note: [Col. 1175] Sermon 88, Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 102].

Always be separated from evildoers in heart; cautiously joined to them in body for a time.

And below:

§1. An evildoer does not stain you in two ways: if you do not consent to him, and if you rebuke him. This is not to communicate: not to consent. For communication occurs when one joins to his deed a partnership of will or approval.

And below:

§2. Therefore do not consent to evildoers, so as to approve them; do not be negligent, so as not to rebuke them; nor be proud, so as to rebuke them insultingly [Note: [Col. 1175] absent in Basel. — “insulting”: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I; “arrogantly,” Ivo—Böhm]. [Col. 1175C]

### Chapter IX. To touch what is unclean is to consent to sins

The same author, from the same work [Note: [Col. 1175] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 103; cf. above, chapter IV].

“Depart, go out from there, and do not touch what is unclean.” But this means by the touch of the heart, not of the body. For what is it to touch what is unclean except to consent to sins? And what is it to go out from there except to do, as far as can be done while preserving peace, what belongs to correcting evildoers, according to each person’s rank and office? Has what someone has done in sin displeased you? You have not touched what is unclean. Have you rebuked, reproved, warned, and—if the matter requires it—employed appropriate discipline that does not violate unity? You have gone out from there.

And below:

§1. Moses proclaimed these things; Isaiah proclaimed them; Jeremiah proclaimed them; Ezekiel proclaimed them. Let us see whether they abandoned the people of God and transferred themselves to other nations. How many things, and how vehemently, Jeremiah rebuked in the sinners and criminals of his own people! Yet he remained among them, entered the one temple with them, celebrated the same sacraments, and lived in the same assembly of criminal persons; but by crying out he went out from there. This is to go out from there: this is not to touch what is unclean—not to consent in will and not to spare with one’s mouth [Note: [Col. 1175] Isaiah 52:11. — “and go out”: collected editions. — “therefrom,” Basel. — “with touching,” Ivo. — “but”: absent in Ivo. — “go out”: “go out [plural],” Argentinensis. — “anyone”: Lyons II–III—Ivo. — “has sinned”: “will have sinned,” Ivo—collected editions. — *unitatem* (“unity”): *unitatis* (“of unity”), Lyons I and Paris. — “violates”: collected editions. — Numbers 16; Isaiah 52; Lamentations 4; Ezekiel 14. — absent in Basel and Lyons II–III. — “of God”: the same editions; absent in the others. — “to the will,” Basel]. [Col. 1176A]

[Col. 1176B]

### Chapter X. The deeds of wrongdoers do not stain the innocent when they cannot be proved to or believed by them

The same author, Letter XLVIII, to Vincentius [Note: [Col. 1175] Letter 93, written A.D. 408, Maurist edition].

How great a crime it is to separate oneself from the communion of these innocent persons! For the deeds of wrongdoers which cannot be shown to innocent persons, or believed by innocent persons, stain no one, even if, once known, they are endured for the fellowship of the innocent. For the good must not be abandoned because of the wicked; rather, the wicked must be tolerated because of the good. Thus the prophets tolerated those against whom they spoke such great things, without leaving the communion of that people’s sacraments; thus the Lord himself tolerated guilty Judas until his deserved end, and permitted him to share in sacred things with the innocent; and thus the Apostles tolerated those who proclaimed Christ from envy—which is the devil’s own vice [Note: [Col. 1175] Cf. below, chapter 37. — “even for the fellowship of the innocent,” collected editions. — “them,” same editions. — Cf. Philippians 1]. [Col. 1176C]

### Chapter XI. Evildoers whom the Church receives and does not expel must be tolerated, not judged, by the good

The same author, Sermon XXIV, *On the Words of the Apostle* [Note: [Col. 1176D] It was formerly cited from book I *On the One Baptism*, where it is not found.] [Note: [Col. 1175] Sermon 164, Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 94].

Perhaps next to you in God’s people stands someone greedy, rapacious, coveting another’s possessions, whom you know to be such; and he is a believer—or rather, he is called a believer. You cannot drive him from the Church; you have no means to correct him by chastisement and rebuke. He will approach the altar with you. Do not fear: each person shall bear his own burden.

Likewise below:

§1. “How,” you say, “can I endure someone whom I know to be evil?” Would you not better endure him than carry yourself outside? Here is how you will bear him: heed the Apostle saying, “Each person shall bear his own burden.” Let this saying set you free. For you would not share his greed; you would share Christ’s table with him. And what harm would it do you to share Christ’s table with him? The Apostle says: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself”—to himself, not to you. Certainly, if you are a judge, if you have received the power of judging, then according to ecclesiastical rule, if he is accused before you and convicted by true evidence and witnesses, restrain him, rebuke him, excommunicate him, depose him [Note: [Col. 1175] “him,” collected editions. — Galatians 6:3. — “his own,” collected editions. — “bring yourself outside,” Lyons II. — “will bear”: original—Ivo—Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I–II; “would bear,” the printed text. — “heed”: original “if you had heeded”; Ivo “you would heed”; Argentinensis “heeding.” — Galatians 6:5. — “his own,” collected editions. — “greed, but if”: Basel. — 1 Corinthians 11:29]. [Col. 1177A]

Gratian. There is also another distinction between those who are to be tolerated and those who are to be avoided, which may be gathered from Augustine’s words in Sermon XLIX, *On the Words of the Lord* [Note: [Col. 1177] Sermon 137, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 6, chapter 148 (145)]:

[Col. 1177B]

### Chapter XII. The shepherd is to be loved, the hired hand tolerated, and the robber avoided

The Lord spoke in the Gospel of three persons—and we ought to seek them out—the shepherd, the hired hand, and the thief. And a little later: he said that the shepherd lays down his life for his sheep and enters by the door. He said that the thief and robber climbs in another way. He said that the hired hand, if he sees a wolf or even a thief, flees, because he does not care about the sheep: he is a hired hand, not a shepherd. The one enters through the door because he is a shepherd; the other climbs in another way because he is a thief; the one who sees those wishing to carry off the sheep fears and flees because he is a hired hand, because he does not care about the sheep—he is indeed a hired hand [Note: [Col. 1177] “because he does not care”: “nor does he care,” collected editions]. If we discover these three persons, your holiness will discover whom you should love, whom you should tolerate, and whom you should avoid. The shepherd is to be loved, the hired hand tolerated, the robber avoided [Note: [Col. 1177] “and hired hand,” Basel. — John 10. — “and robber”: these two words are absent from the original; Anselm nevertheless has them. — “also,” collected editions. — “but,” the same editions, Lyons II–III. — “and not,” collected editions. — “who,” the same editions]. [Col. 1177C–D]

Gratian. See, then, that evildoers are to be tolerated, and punished not by bodily but by spiritual vengeance. Hence, when the disciples, not having been received by the Samaritans, wished to call down fire from heaven upon them, saying to their Master, “Do you wish us to say, ‘Let fire descend from heaven and consume them’?” they heard: “You do not know whose spirit you are.” Likewise: “Everyone who takes up the sword shall perish by the sword” [Note: [Col. 1177] Luke 9:54; Matthew 26:52].

### Chapter XIII. The spiritual person never persecutes the carnal person; rather, the reverse

Jerome likewise says in his commentary on Galatians, chapter 4:

“He who was born according to the flesh persecuted the spiritual.” For the spiritual person never persecutes the carnal, but forgives him as a rustic brother. He knows that he can advance in time; and if he sees the son of the Egyptian woman becoming angry, he remembers the one Father, who created oxen and gnats, and who willed that in a great house there should be not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay [Note: [Col. 1177] Galatians 4:29. — “persecutes”: Basel. — “indeed,” collected editions. — “rustic”: the same editions, Basel. — “will remember,” collected editions. — *Oxen*: in printed codices of Jerome it reads *qui lucem boves*, but in the Vatican codex of these commentaries, *qui lucam bovem*. It signifies an elephant. — 2 Timothy 2:20. — “he willed,” collected editions]. [Col. 1178A, D]

### Chapter XIV. In this life the good can never be completely separated from the evil

Likewise, Augustine, book IV of *On Baptism*, chapter 12 [Note: [Col. 1178D] These are Cyprian’s words in book 4, letter 2 to Antonianus—rather, to Maximus and the others, Letter 54, Oxford edition—cited by Augustine in book 4, chapter 12, *On Baptism against the Donatists*].

How great the swelling of arrogance, how great the forgetfulness of humility and gentleness, how great the boasting of arrogance, that anyone should dare—or believe himself able—to do what the Lord did not grant even to the Apostles: namely, to think that he can distinguish tares from wheat [Note: [Col. 1177] “and arrogance,” collected editions. — “either dare, or”: absent in Ivo. — Matthew 13. — “namely,” Basel and Lyons II–III. — “tares”: collected editions, Basel].

[Col. 1178B]

### Chapter XV. The present Church receives good and evil alike

Likewise, Gregory, Homily XXXVIII on the Gospels.

This life, situated between heaven and hell, stands as it were in the middle and receives in common the citizens of each side; yet the holy Church receives them now without distinction, and will distinguish them afterward at their departure. Therefore, if you are good, so long as you remain in this life you ought to bear evildoers patiently. For whoever does not tolerate evildoers bears witness against himself, through his own intolerance, that he is not good. For he refuses to be Abel whom Cain’s wickedness does not test [Note: [Col. 1177] absent in Basel. — “now”: “received,” Argentinensis. — “tolerate,” collected editions. — “ought”: the printed text. — “his own”: the printed text].

**Part II. Gratian.** From all these things it is gathered that vengeance upon evildoers must be reserved to God, and that they must not be punished bodily, but invited to correction by frequent admonition and the benefit of charity. Hence Christ says in the Gospel [Matthew 5:38]: “You have heard that it was said in the law”—which established this measure of retaliation—“An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth” [Exodus 21:24]. But I, removing this reciprocity and inviting you to gentleness and the perfection of charity, say to you: “Do not resist evil, but love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, that you may be children of your Father, who makes his sun rise upon good and evil, and rains upon just and unjust” [Matthew 5:39].

Paul likewise says [Romans 12:20]: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink” [Proverbs 25:21]. For every unjust person is an enemy of the good; and every friend of this world is also an enemy of God [James 4:4]. But an enemy of God is an enemy of goodness and justice, and therefore cannot love one who loves justice and goodness. Therefore, when we are commanded to love enemies, to do them good, and to supply them food and drink, we are forbidden to persecute and punish enemies.

§1. In the law of the Old Testament bodily punishment was established; but in the law of the Gospel forgiveness through repentance is promised to every sinner. Hence the former began with terror, saying [Exodus 20:5]: “I am the Lord, a jealous God, visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation.” The latter begins from the mildness of gentleness and mercy, saying [Matthew 5:3]: “Blessed are the poor in spirit; blessed are the meek; blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” In the former it was said [cf. Exodus 19]: “Whoever does this or that shall surely die.” In the latter [Luke 15:7]: “I rejoice over one sinner repenting more than over ninety-nine just persons who have no need of repentance.” Likewise [Matthew 9:13]: “I came not to call the just, but sinners to repentance.” “Be merciful, as your Father also is merciful” [Luke 6:36].

Moreover, the beginning of the preaching of our Savior and of his herald invited sinners to repentance. For each began thus, saying [Matthew 3:2]: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” Thus, in the Acts of the Apostles, when the Jews, pierced with remorse over the crime of Christ’s death, said to Peter, “What shall we do, brothers?” Peter is recorded as answering [Acts 2:38]: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized.” And, to put it universally: under the law that unformed people were compelled by servile fear of punishments; hence they received the law as a pedagogue [cf. Exodus 1; Galatians 5]. But in the Gospel, the people of grace, free and mature, are invited by filial love and by the certainty of inheritance to the worship of divine service. Therefore, when some preached that the law, as though coercive, ought to be kept together with grace, the Apostle said [Romans 8:15]: “For you have not received again a spirit of slavery in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry: ‘Abba, Father.’”

§2. Gregory likewise says in his exposition of the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven was made like a king who made a wedding feast for his son.”

### Chapter XVI. Under the law everyone was permitted to love a friend and hate an enemy

Since it is written in the law, “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy,” the righteous then had received permission to restrain, with all the strength they could, God’s enemies and their own adversaries, and to strike them with the edge of the sword. This is undoubtedly restrained in the New Testament, when Truth himself preaches, saying: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you.” What, then, is signified by the bulls but the fathers of the Old Testament? For, since by the permission of the law they had received authority to strike their adversaries with retaliatory hatred, they were, so to speak, bulls striking their enemies with the horn of bodily strength. But what is signified by fatted cattle but the fathers of the New Testament? Since they receive the grace of inward richness, relying on eternal desires, they are raised aloft by the wings of their contemplation [Note: [Col. 1179] Homily 38, on Matthew 22. — Leviticus 19:18. — “enemies of God”: absent in the original. — “by the sword”: the original and four very old Gratian manuscripts read “by right of the sword”; collected editions, Paris and Lyons. — Luke 6:27. — “What”: collected editions. — “are signified”: original. — “bodily”: Basel. — “from earthly desires,” Basel—the original. — The collected editions read: “they raise themselves to the heights as if on the wing of contemplation.”]. [Col. 1179D–1180A]

Gratian. The answer to these points is as follows. Some matters are to be reproved only by salutary admonition, not punished with bodily lashes; but their punishment must be reserved solely for divine judgment—namely, when we cannot exercise discipline upon offenders, either because they are not subject to our jurisdiction, or because their crimes, though known to us, cannot be proved by manifest judicial evidence.

§1. Of those who are not under our jurisdiction, the Apostle says in the First Letter to the Corinthians: “What concern is it of mine to judge those who are outside? For the Lord will judge them.”

Explaining this, Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1179D–1180D] The sense of this chapter occurs in Blessed Augustine, *On the Remedy of Repentance*, chapter 3; almost all its words are in the Ordinary Gloss on 1 Corinthians 5, at the verse “Otherwise,” and in the interlinear gloss at the verse “Within.” — Cf. above, Cause 2, Question 1, chapter 18]:

### Chapter XVII. Conversations and meals with unbelievers are not to be avoided

We cannot win unbelievers to Christ if we avoid conversation and meals with them. Thus the Lord too ate and drank with tax collectors and sinners. But among those who are within—that is, unbelievers—the rot must be cut away [Col. 1180C].

Gratian. Hence also, when the Prophet says [Note: [Col. 1179] Ps. 145:7], “The Lord executes judgment for all who suffer wrong,” Augustine adds in exposition: “from those who are not their own masters,” against whom discipline cannot be exercised. § 1. Likewise, when a multitude is involved in wickedness and the wicked cannot be punished while the Church’s peace is preserved, they should rather be tolerated than punished with the Church’s peace violated.

Accordingly Augustine says in the book *On Faith and Works*, chapters 4 and 5 [Note: [Col. 1179] Anselm, book 12, ch. 63; Polycarpus, book 7, title 7]:

### C. XVIII. Some evils must be punished, and some tolerated.

But some, *indeed … go astray* [Note: [Col. 1179] The words *vero—periclitantes* (“indeed … go astray”) are absent from Anselm], on the contrary, when they have perceived that the mingling of good and evil in the Church has been demonstrated or foretold, and have learned the precepts of patience—which make us so steadfast that, even if weeds seem to be [Note: [Col. 1179] *videantur*, “seem to be”: Basel edition; *videatur*, singular, “seems to be”: the remaining printed editions except Argentinian] in the Church, neither our faith nor our charity is hindered, and [Note: [Col. 1181] “and”: the collected editions and the original] because we see weeds in the Church, we do not ourselves withdraw from the Church [Note: [Col. 1181] “we ourselves do not therefore withdraw”: the collected editions and original; *zizaniam*, singular, “a weed”: Lyons II and III]—think that ecclesiastical discipline ought to be abandoned [Note: [Col. 1181D] *Destituendam*, “to be abandoned”: in St Augustine the reading is *instituendam putant ecclesiam et disciplinam*, “they think that the Church and discipline ought to be established”; the other collectors agree with Gratian. Many other readings from those sources and from the original have likewise been restored throughout this chapter], granting those set over the Church a thoroughly perverse security: that it pertains to them only to say what should be avoided and what should be done, while they need not care what anyone does.

But we judge that sound doctrine requires us to regulate, from both classes of testimonies, a secure judgment [Note: [Col. 1181] *sacram*, “sacred,” for *sanam*, “sound”: Argentinian edition; Anselm and the collected editions and original read *vitam sententiamque*, “life and judgment,” in place of *ex utrisque testimoniis tutam sententiam*, “a secure judgment from both testimonies”; *moderare*, imperative, “regulate”: Basel edition]: that we tolerate dogs in the Church for the peace of the Church, but do not give what is holy to dogs where the Church’s peace is safe.

Therefore, whether through the negligence of those set over it [Note: [Col. 1181] *praelatorum*, “prelates”: Argentinian edition], through some other excusable necessity [Note: [Col. 1181] *aliam*, “other”: Venetian I and II, Paris, and Lyons editions], or through secret infiltrations [Note: [Col. 1181] *surreptiones*, “secret intrusions”: the collected editions and original], we find in the Church evil persons whom we cannot correct or restrain by ecclesiastical discipline, then let no impious and pernicious presumption rise in our hearts, by which we suppose [Note: [Col. 1181] *aestimemus*, “judge”: the same editions, before Basel, and Lyons II and III] that we must separate ourselves from them lest we be defiled by their sins, and then attempt to draw others after us as though they were pure and holy disciples, severed from the bond of unity as though from association [Note: [Col. 1181] *conjunctione*, “connection”: the collected editions and original] with the wicked [Note: [Col. 1181] *separatos*, “separated”: Argentinian and Basel; *segregandos*, “to be separated”: the remaining editions].

Instead, let those comparisons from Scripture, divine utterances, and most certain examples come to mind, by which it has been demonstrated and foretold [Note: [Col. 1181] *pronunciatum*, “declared”: the collected editions and original] that the wicked will be mingled with the good in the Church until the end of the age and the time of judgment, and that they will do no harm to the good, in the unity and participation of the sacraments, if those good persons have not consented to their deeds [Note: [Col. 1181] *futuri tolerandos*, “destined to be tolerated”: the same editions; *ab futuros*, an apparent erroneous separation: Lyons II and III].

§ 1.
