But when those through whom the Church is governed have [Note: [Col. 1181] *abest*, “lacks”: the same editions] the power, with peace preserved, to exercise discipline against depraved or criminal persons [Note: [Col. 1181] *exercenda*, singular: Basel], then, again, lest we sleep in heedlessness and sloth [Note: [Col. 1181] The collected editions and original have *neque socordia neque segnitia, sed aculeis*, “not by heedlessness or sloth, but by goads”], we must be stirred by *other* goads of the precepts [Note: [Col. 1181] *aliis*, “other,” is absent from Anselm] which concern the severity of coercion [Note: [Col. 1181] *correptionis*, “rebuke”: Basel], so that, guided and aided by Him [Note: [Col. 1181] *actore adiutore*, “acting and helping”: the same edition], we may direct our steps in the way [Note: [Col. 1181] *vias*, “ways”: the same edition] of the Lord according to both testimonies, neither becoming torpid under the name of patience nor becoming cruel under the pretext of diligence.

### C. XIX. Secret offenses are to be punished more lightly, but manifest offenses more severely, by the Church.

The same, *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, book III, chapter 2 [Note: [Col. 1181] Ivo, Prologue and *Decree*, part 2, ch. 97; Polycarpus, book 7, title 7].

Whenever any brother—that is [Note: [Col. 1181] “and”: the collected editions and original; Ivo, Prologue] any Christian established within the fellowship of the Church—is detected in a sin of such a kind that he is judged worthy of anathema, let this be done where there is no danger of schism.

And below:

§ 1. When the crime of any person is so known to *all* [Note: [Col. 1181] *ita*, “so,” is absent from Ivo’s Prologue; *omnibus*, “all,” is wanting there] and appears detestable to all [Note: [Col. 1181] *appareat*, subjunctive, “may appear”: collected editions, Argentinian before Norimberg and Venetian I; Ivo, Prologue], that he has either no defenders at all or none of such a kind as can cause a schism, the severity of discipline must not sleep.

### III. Part. Gratian.

There is another reason why correction by blows or words seems useless or superfluous. Those predestined to life are changed without correction, as Peter was [Note: [Col. 1181] Luke 22 = C. XX], whom the Lord, looking upon him while no one rebuked him, moved to tears. Those foreknown for death become worse amid punishments, as Pharaoh did. Thus correction is found superfluous for the good and useless for those to be condemned. The answer to this is supplied by the authority of Gregory and Augustine.

For Augustine says in the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 5:

### C. XX. As one must not cease from prayer, so neither from correction.

Just as one must not cease praying for those whom we wish to be corrected, although the Lord looked upon Peter when no human being prayed for him and caused him to weep for his sin, so correction [Note: [Col. 1181] *correctio*, “correction”: collected editions and original] must not be neglected, although God may make those whom He wishes corrected even without correction [Note: [Col. 1181] *correctos*, “corrected,” in place of *correptos*, “rebuked”: the same editions]. But a person benefits from correction [Note: [Col. 1181] *ex correctione*, “from correction”: the same editions] when He who acts has mercy and helps, and makes those whom He wishes progress even without correction [Note: [Col. 1181] *correctione*, “correction”: the same editions].

[Col. 1182C] But Gregory says in the *Dialogues*, book I, chapter 8 [Note: [Col. 1181] Burchard, book 20, ch. 19; Ivo, *Decree*, part 17, ch. 31]:

### C. XXI. Only the predestined are saved, who have merited through their labor in petitioning.

Things which were not predestined cannot in any way be obtained [Note: [Col. 1181] *fuerint*, future perfect, “have been”: original, cited collections, and collected editions]. But the things holy men bring about by prayer are predestined in such a way that they are obtained by prayers. For even the predestination of the everlasting kingdom itself has been so disposed by almighty God that the elect arrive there through labor, so that by asking they may merit to receive what almighty God ordained before the ages to give them.

### C. XXII. By God’s hidden judgment the wicked are hardened by punishments, while the good are corrected.

Likewise Augustine, in the book *On Predestination and Grace*, chapter 15 [Note: [Col. 1181] Learned authorities agree that this book is not Augustine’s].

[Col. 1182D] Nebuchadnezzar [Note: [Col. 1181] John 4] attained fruitful repentance. Did he not, after countless impieties, repent when scourged, and receive again the kingdom which he had lost? But Pharaoh [Note: [Col. 1183] Exodus 5 and following] was made worse by the very scourges and perished. Let him who judges divine counsel with an excessively lofty [Note: [Col. 1183] *alte*, “loftily”: collected editions; the original has *altum sapienti corde*, “with a lofty wise heart”] and wise heart give me the reason why a remedy prepared by the hand of one physician proved for one person unto destruction and for another unto salvation, unless it is because the good fragrance of Christ [Note: [Col. 1183] 2 Cor. 2:15–16] is to some a fragrance of life unto life, and to others a fragrance of death unto death.

With respect to nature, both were human beings. With respect to rank [Note: [Col. 1183] *dignitates*, plural, “ranks”: Basel], both were kings. With respect to their circumstance, both held God’s captive people. With respect to punishment, both were gently admonished by scourges. What, then, made their ends different, except that one, feeling the hand of God, groaned in remembrance of his own iniquity, while the other fought by free choice against God’s most merciful truth?

### C. XXIII. The same.

[Note: [Col. 1183D] In most ancient copies this chapter is joined to the preceding one, and the title is “Likewise” [as in the Argentinian and Basel editions], not “The same.” The beginning of the chapter occurs in Fulgentius’s book *To Monymus* and is cited as Augustine in Burchard, book 20, ch. 35, and Ivo, *Decree*, part 17, ch. 46. The chapter is composed from the indicated passages of Fulgentius, Prosper, and St Augustine.]

God would never repay destruction to vessels of wrath if a human being were not found to possess sin voluntarily; for neither would God justly inflict wrath upon a sinful human being if that human being had fallen into fault by God’s predestination.

The same [Note: [Col. 1183] From Prosper’s *Against the Chapters of the Gauls*, ch. 6]:

§ 1. It is most ineptly said that God’s predestination operates in human beings either for good or for evil [Note: [Col. 1183] *omnibus*, “all human beings”: collected editions and original], as though some necessity impelled human beings to either; whereas in the good the will must be understood as not without grace, but in the wicked the will must be understood [Note: [Col. 1183] “is”: added by the same editions, before Basel] as without grace.

§ 2. [Note: [Col. 1183] From the same book, ch. 11.] When, however, we read that some have been given over by God to their desires, hardened, or abandoned, we profess that they have deserved this by their very great [Note: [Col. 1183] *magis*, “more”: collected editions, before Basel] sins [Note: [Col. 1183] *in peccatis*, “in sins”: Lyons II and III], because such crimes preceded on their part that they themselves ought to incur penalties [Note: [Col. 1183] The original reads more fully: *ipsi sibi poena fieri debuerint*, “they themselves ought to have become a punishment to themselves”] which would turn even their punishment into guilt [Note: [Col. 1183] *poenam*, singular, “punishment”: collected editions and original; the alternate reading *qua … verteretur* makes the relative singular]. Thus we neither complain of God’s judgment, by which He abandons those deserving abandonment, nor fail to give thanks for His mercy, by which He delivers those undeserving of deliverance.

§ 3. [Note: [Col. 1183] Chapter 12 of the same work.] Therefore He did not withdraw from anyone the powers of obedience because He had not predestined him; but for that reason He did not predestine him, because He foresaw that he would depart from that obedience [Note: [Col. 1183] The words *ideo—praedestinavit*, “therefore … predestined,” are absent from the original].

§ 4. [Note: [Col. 1183] Chapter 15 of the same work.] Therefore God’s predestination is always directed toward good [Note: [Col. 1183] *quoque*, “also,” for *igitur*, “therefore”: collected editions], which [Note: [Col. 1183] *qui*, masculine: Basel] knows that sin, committed solely by human will, is either to be forgiven to the praise of mercy or punished to the praise of justice [Note: [Col. 1183] The Roman edition wrongly prints *emittendum*, “to be sent out,” in place of *remittendum*, “to be forgiven”]. In our evil works, however, God’s foreknowledge alone must be understood [Note: [Col. 1183] These are the closing words of Prosper’s whole treatise], because, just as He foreknew and predestined what He Himself did and gave us to do, so He only foreknew, and did not predestine, what He neither did Himself nor required us to do.

§ 5. [Note: [Col. 1183] This occurs in chapter 12 of the *Answer to the Vincentian Objections for Augustine*, commonly attributed to Prosper.] But these [Note: [Col. 1183] “are”: added by Basel], of whom it is said [Note: [Col. 1183] “here”: added by Lyons II and III; John 2:19], “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us,” went out by their own will and fell by their own will. Because they were foreknown to be about to fall, they were not predestined; but they would have been predestined had they been destined to return and to remain in holiness and truth. Accordingly, God’s predestination is for many a cause of standing firm; for no one is it a cause of falling.

Gratian. Therefore divine predestination or foreknowledge does not produce a necessity either of correction or of hardening: the good are corrected through grace, while the wicked perish by free choice. For things predestined or foreknown do not occur necessarily merely because God’s predestination or foreknowledge cannot be mistaken, just as future things are not necessarily predestined or foreknown. Rather, good cannot occur without His grace, nor evil apart from His knowledge.

§ 1. Although it may fittingly be said, “If these things are predestined or foreknown, they will necessarily happen,” it is not therefore unqualifiedly true that things predestined or foreknown will necessarily happen. For in the former statement necessity refers to the occurrence of things, in the latter to the sight of divine foreknowledge. Thus Augustine says [Col. 1184C; Note: [Col. 1183] From the book *On Predestination*; cf. C. XXII; Burchard, book 20, ch. 21; Ivo, *Decree*, part 17, ch. 32. [Col. 1184D] Burchard and Ivo cite “There are two necessities” as Augustine, *On Predestination*. The thought is set forth at length in the treatise *On the Predestination of God* among Augustine’s works, volume 7]:

“There are two necessities. One is simple, as when all human beings must be mortal; the other is conditional: if someone knows that a person is walking, that person must be walking. For what anyone knows to be cannot be otherwise than [Note: [Col. 1183] *ac*, “than”: Burchard, Ivo, and Basel] it is known to be. But this latter necessity does not at all bring the former with it; for it is not nature itself [Note: [Col. 1183] *ipsa*, “itself”: Basel] that produces this necessity, but the addition of a condition. No necessity compels one who walks by choice to walk, although, while he is walking [Note: [Col. 1183] *radiatur*, “is shaved,” an erroneous reading: collected editions], it is necessary that he walk.

“In the same way, whatever present providence sees must be, although it has no necessity of nature. Yet [Note: [Col. 1185] *At quidem*, “but indeed”: the same editions] God beholds as present [Note: [Col. 1185] *praescientia*, “foreknowledge”: the same editions] those future things which arise from freedom of choice. These therefore become necessary in relation to the divine gaze, through the disposition of divine knowledge; but, considered in themselves, they do not lose the absolute freedom of their own nature [Note: [Col. 1185D] Burchard and Ivo read: *ab absoluta libertate non desinunt*, “they do not cease to possess absolute freedom”]. Hence all things which God foreknows will be future will doubtless come to pass; but some of them arise from free choice, and although they occur [Note: [Col. 1185] *veniant*, “come”: Basel; *eveniunt*, present “occur”: Lyons II and III], they nevertheless do not lose, by existing, the nature by which, before they came to pass, they could also not have come to pass.”

§ 2. By all this our evils are attributed to free choice, although elsewhere they are attributed to divine indignation. Thus Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1185] *Morals*, book 9, ch. 12]:

“When heavenly indignation, so to speak, is stirred from its depths, human opinion or opposition [Note: [Col. 1185] *vel oppositio*, “or opposition,” is omitted in the Argentinian and Basel editions] does not remove it, nor does anyone’s prayer [Note: [Col. 1185] *cujuslibet*, “of anyone”: collected editions and original] usefully set itself against it, when God has once, in anger, determined something from His inmost being. Thus Moses [Note: [Col. 1185] Exodus 32], who wiped away before the Lord [Note: [Col. 1185] “God”: Basel] the guilt of the entire people by his prayers and, offering himself as a barrier, appeased the force of divine wrath, nevertheless, on coming to the rock of Horeb and losing faith concerning the provision of water, could not enter the promised land while the Lord was angry.”

§ 3. Likewise Augustine:

“What else can we say concerning the Tyrians [Note: [Col. 1185D] Very similar words occur in Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, ch. 14; nearly the same words occur in Prosper, *To the Excerpts of the Genoese*, answer to doubt 8 or 9] and Sidonians except that it was not given them from above [Note: [Col. 1185] *desuper*, “from above”: added by collected editions and original, before Argentinian; cf. Matt. 11:21] to believe, although Truth itself says [Note: [Col. 1185] *docet*, “teaches”: collected editions and original] that they would have believed if they had seen signs of powers such as were performed among those who did not believe? Let those who cavil say, if they can, why this was denied them, and show why the Lord performed miracles among those for whom they would not have been beneficial, yet did not perform them among those for whom they would have been beneficial.

“But even if we cannot penetrate the rationale [Note: [Col. 1185] *ratione*, ablative, “by reason”: the same editions] of this deed *and* the depth of His judgment, we know most certainly both that what He said is true and that what He did is just; and that not only Tyre and Sidon, but also Chorazin and Bethsaida, could have been converted and believers made from unbelievers, if the Lord had willed to work this in them. For no one can regard as false what Truth says [Note: [Col. 1185] John 6:44]: ‘No one can come to me unless it has been given him by my Father.’

“Likewise, through the Prophet He promised the Jewish people [Note: [Col. 1185] Hos. 2:6]: ‘Behold, I shall hedge up your ways with thorns and fortify them with squared stones,’ that is, ‘I shall take away from you the power to sin.’ Likewise He said through the Psalmist concerning those to be condemned [Note: [Col. 1185] Ps. 34:6]: ‘Let their ways be darkness and slipperiness, and let the angel of the Lord pursue them.’

“But in all these things our vices are attributed to the choice of the human mind. Divine mercy mercifully turns that choice toward good in the elect, but justly leaves it toward evil in those condemned. Therefore, just as, although we know with complete certainty that no one will live beyond the limit appointed for him by God, we nevertheless appropriately treat every sick person, so, although no one is saved unless predestined to life, correction must nevertheless be applied to every offender, and the discipline of the wicked must not be neglected.”

[Col. 1186B] Hence the same Augustine says in Letter L to Boniface [Note: [Col. 1185] Ep. 185, Maurist edition, written A.D. 417; Anselm, book 12, ch. 61 (60); Polycarpus, book 7, title 5]:

### C. XXIV. Vengeance must not always be exercised against those who sin.

Piety itself, truth, and charity do not permit us to accept against Caecilian the testimony of persons whom we do not see in the Church to which God [Note: [Col. 1185] “the Lord”: collected editions and original] bears witness. For those who do not follow divine testimonies have lost the weight of human testimony.

Likewise below:

§ 1. The physician is troublesome to the raging madman, and the father to the undisciplined son: the former by binding, the latter [Note: [Col. 1185] “the former”: collected editions and original, before Lyons II and III] by beating; but both by loving. If, however, they neglect them and permit them to perish, this false gentleness is rather cruelty.

Likewise below:

§ 2. If, by the authority [Note: [Col. 1185] *potestate*, “by authority”: original and Anselm; cf. below, question 6, chapter 1] which the Church received by divine gift, through the religion and faith of *kings* [Note: [Col. 1185] *propter*, “because of,” for *per*, “through”: collected editions and original], at the time when it ought to have received it, those found in the roads and *hedges* [Note: [Col. 1186C] The marked phrase is *in … sepibus*, “in … hedges”]—that is, in heresies and schisms—are compelled to enter, they should not criticize because they are compelled, but consider why [Note: [Col. 1185] *quo*, “whither,” for *quare*, “why”: original, Argentinian, Norimberg, Venetian I] they are compelled [Note: [Col. 1185] *coguntur*, present “are compelled”: collected editions and original]. The Lord’s banquet is the unity of Christ’s body, not only in the sacrament of the altar but also in the bond of peace.

In the same letter below:

§ 3. The emperor Theodosius [Note: [Col. 1185D] Anselm has Gratian’s wording; but Augustine’s own words, where he discusses restraining the madness of the Donatists, are: “We think this might in some degree be done if they were to confirm more expressly against the Donatists—who denied that they were heretics—the law of pious memory of Theodosius, which he promulgated generally against all heretics, providing that any of their bishops or clerics found anywhere should be fined ten pounds of gold,” followed by the remainder] promulgated a law generally against all heretics, providing that any of their bishops or clerics found anywhere should be fined ten pounds of gold [Note: [Col. 1185] Cf. *Theodosian Code*, book 16, title 5, ch. 21].

Likewise below:

§ 4. If two persons lived together [Note: [Col. 1185] “together”: added by the collected editions and original] in one house which we knew with complete certainty was about to collapse, and, despite our warning, refused to believe us and persisted in remaining in it [Note: [Col. 1187] *eadem*, “the same house”: the same editions, before Basel], then, if we could pull them out even against their will and afterwards show them that impending collapse [Note: [Col. 1187] *postea*, “afterwards,” is absent from Anselm; *praemonstravimus*, “we showed beforehand”: Basel; *praedemonstravimus*, “we previously showed”: the remaining editions and Anselm], so that they would not dare return into its danger [Note: [Col. 1187] *periculo*, ablative, “in danger”: Basel], I think that, if we did not do this, we would rightly be judged cruel.

But if one of them said to us, “When you enter to rescue us, I shall immediately kill myself” [Note: [Col. 1187] *cruciabo*, “I shall torture myself”: Norimberg and Venetian I], while the other neither wished to leave nor allowed himself to be rescued, yet did not dare kill himself, what should we choose: to leave both to be crushed by the collapse, or, after freeing at least one through our work of *mercy* [Note: [Col. 1187] *nostra opera*, “through our work”: Argentinian], to permit the other to perish, not through our fault but rather through his own [Note: [Col. 1187] “we would permit”: added by collected editions and original, before Argentinian]? No one [Note: [Col. 1187] “for”: added by Basel] is so unfortunate that he cannot readily judge what ought to be done in such circumstances.

A little later:

§ 5. But if very many were in the collapsing house and at least one could be freed, while, as we attempted this, the others killed themselves by throwing themselves down, our grief for the others would be consoled by the salvation of at least one [Note: [Col. 1187] The collected editions and original read: *doleremus de ceteris, verum*, “we should grieve for the others, but”]. Yet we would not allow all to perish with no one rescued merely because others might destroy themselves. What, then, should be judged concerning the work of mercy which we owe to people for attaining eternal life and avoiding eternal punishment, if true and kindly reason compels us to help people in rescuing them for this salvation—not merely temporal, but brief, for this very small span of time [Note: [Col. 1187] *ad id*, “for that purpose”: Argentinian; *ed ad*, a corrupt form: remaining editions]?

Likewise below:

§ 6. “If,” say the Donatists [Note: [Col. 1187] The whole of § 6 is cited by Ivo in the Prologue], “we must repent of having been outside and opposed to the Church in order to be saved, how can we remain clerics or even bishops among you after such repentance?”

This would not be done, because indeed [Note: [Col. 1187] Basel reads: *revera faciendum, quod fieri non debet*, “in truth, what ought not to be done must be done”]—as must be admitted—it ought not to be done, unless they were healed by compensation for peace itself [Note: [Col. 1187] *pauci ipsa*, a corrupt reading, for *pacis ipsius*, “of peace itself”: collected editions and original]. But let those say this to themselves, and grieve with the deepest humility, who lie [Note: [Col. 1187] *jacent*, “lie”: original, Ivo, and collected editions] in the great death of separation, so that they may be restored to life by this certain wound of mother [Note: [Col. 1187] “the Catholic Church”: added by collected editions and original] Catholic Church.

For when a severed branch is grafted in, another wound is made in the tree to receive it, so that it may live which was perishing without the life of the root. But when the graft received has united with that which receives it, then vigor and fruit follow [Note: [Col. 1187] *consequitur*, singular, “follows”: original, Ivo, and collected editions]. If it has not united, it certainly withers [Note: [Col. 1187] *arescet*, future, “will wither”: collected editions and original], but the life of the tree remains.

There is also a kind of grafting in which, without any branch within being cut off, that which is outside is grafted in; not, however, with no wound at all to the tree, but with a very slight wound [Note: [Col. 1187] *vel*, “or even,” is absent from the same edition].

Thus, when these persons come to the Catholic root, even though, after repentance for their error [Note: [Col. 1187] The collected editions read: “although after they have scarcely repented of their error”; Basel: *poenitent*, “they repent”], the honor of cleric or bishop is not taken from them, something is indeed done, as it were, upon the bark of the mother tree, contrary to the integrity of strictness [Note: [Col. 1187] *si quidem fit aliquid*, “if indeed something is done”: the same editions]. Yet because neither the planter nor the waterer is anything [Note: [Col. 1187] 1 Cor. 3:7], when prayers are poured out to God’s mercy and the grafted branches are united in peace [Note: [Col. 1187] *suorum*, “their own”: collected editions and original], charity covers a multitude of sins [Note: [Col. 1187] 1 Pet. 4:8].

And a little later:

§ 7. But in causes of this kind, where because of serious divisions arising from dissensions the danger concerns not this or that individual but the destruction of many peoples [Note: [Col. 1187] *plurimorum*, “very many”: collected editions and original, before Argentinian] lies before us [Note: [Col. 1187] *jacet*, singular, “lies”: collected editions, before Argentinian, Norimberg, and Venetian I], something must be remitted from strictness so that sincere charity may bring aid to the healing of greater evils.

Let *these persons* [Col. 1188B] have bitter sorrow for their past detestable error, as Peter had for the fear of falsehood [Note: [Col. 1187] *mendaci*, “falsehood”: original] and let them come to the true Church of Christ, that is, mother Catholic Church. Let them be [Note: [Col. 1187] *sunt*, indicative “they are”: Argentinian, Norimberg, Venetian I] clerics there; let them be [Note: [Col. 1187] *sunt*, indicative: the same editions] usefully bishops there, though they were formerly hostile against [Note: [Col. 1187] *in*, “against”: Argentinian] her [Note: [Col. 1187] *eam*, “it”: collected editions and original].

We do not begrudge this; indeed, we welcome it, desire it, urge it. Those whom we find in the roads [Note: [Col. 1187] *in inviis*, “in trackless places”: Basel] and [Note: [Col. 1187] *aut in*, “or in”: collected editions and original; Bohmer: *aut*, “or”] hedges we compel to enter; and do we fail even now to persuade some of them [Note: [Col. 1187] *etsi*, “although”: original] because we seek not their possessions but themselves?

### C. XXV. By medicinal severity the wicked are to be compelled toward good.

The same, to Festus, Letter CLXVII [Note: [Col. 1187] Ep. 89, Maurist edition, written A.D. 408; in the collected editions it is addressed to Faustus; Anselm, book 9, chs. 56–57; Polycarpus, book 7, title 5].

What [Note: [Col. 1187] The original reads: “What, then, is the Church’s medicine to do here?”] is the Church’s medicine to do here, seeking everyone’s salvation with motherly charity, as though distressed between madmen and lethargic patients? Must it, or can it, despise them or desist? It must necessarily be troublesome [Col. 1188C; Note: [Col. 1187] *si nec. est*, an incomplete or corrupt reading: collected editions and original; *molesta est*, “is troublesome”: Basel and Lyons II–III; *ut sit molesta*, “that it may be troublesome”: the remaining editions] to both, because [Note: [Col. 1187] *quae*, “which”: collected editions and original] it is hostile to neither [Note: [Col. 1187] *ventris*, “of the belly,” an erroneous reading: Argentinian].

For madmen do not wish to be bound, and lethargic persons do not wish to be roused; but the diligence of charity persists in chastising [Note: [Col. 1187] *ligare*, “binding”: collected editions and original] the madman, stimulating the lethargic person, and loving both. Both are offended, but both are loved. While sick, both resent being troubled [Note: [Col. 1187] *molestari*, infinitive, “to be troubled”: the same editions]; when healed, both rejoice [Note: [Col. 1187] *sanari*, infinitive, “to be healed”: Basel].

And below in the same letter:

§ 1. They do not begin to be Catholics unless they cease to be heretics. Their sacraments are not hostile to us, since they are shared by them and us [Note: [Col. 1187] *in illis*, “in them”: collected editions and original; “also”: added by Basel]; for they are not human but divine. Their own error must first [Note: [Col. 1187] *prius*, “first,” for *proprius*, “their own”: collected editions and original] be removed, which they have wrongly imbibed [Col. 1189A; Note: [Col. 1189] *inierunt*, “entered into”: the same editions], not the sacraments which they have received in the same manner. They bear and possess these sacraments to their own punishment; the more unworthily [Note: [Col. 1189] *quamvis indigne*, “although unworthily”: the same editions, before Argentinian] they possess them [Note: [Col. 1189] The phrase “they possess them” is absent from Norimberg and Venetian I], yet they do possess them.

### IV. Part. Gratian.

Behold: crimes must be punished when they can be struck without violation of the Church’s peace; but discernment must nevertheless be employed. Sometimes a multitude of offenders must long be awaited in patience for repentance; sometimes punishment must be imposed on a few, so that the rest may be frightened by their example and called to repentance. Thus, when the disciples wished to consume the Samaritans with heavenly fire [Note: [Col. 1189] Cf. Luke 9:54], they were forbidden, and the Samaritans were awaited for repentance, so that they might be converted to faith when Christ preached.

[Col. 1189B] Accordingly Ambrose says in book VII of his commentary on Luke, chapter 9, verse 54 [Note: [Col. 1189] This passage is not found in Ambrose]:

### C. XXVI. Vengeance must not always be exercised against those who sin.

Christ’s rebuke of the disciples [Note: [Col. 1189] “his”: added by the collected editions and original] because they desired [Note: [Col. 1189] *gestiebant*, “eagerly desired”: original and collected editions] fire to come down from heaven [Note: [Col. 1189] “from heaven”: added by the same editions, before Argentinian and Basel] upon those who had not received Him [Note: [Col. 1189] *Christum*, “Christ”: original] shows us that vengeance must not always be taken upon those who have sinned [Note: [Col. 1189] *peccant*, present, “sin”: collected editions and original], because sometimes mercy is more beneficial: to you, toward patience [Note: [Col. 1189] *poenitentiam*, “repentance”: the same editions]; to one who has fallen, toward correction [Note: [Col. 1189] *quam lapso*, “than to one fallen”: the same editions; Bohmer likewise].

Indeed, the Samaritans more quickly believed, though fire was withheld from them in this passage. Nor did the disciples sin in following the law. For they knew that Phinehas [Note: [Col. 1189] Num. 25] had it reckoned to him as righteousness because he killed sacrilegious persons, and that fire descended from heaven at Elijah’s prayer [Note: [Col. 1189] 4 Kings 1], *so that the Prophet’s injury might be avenged* [Note: [Col. 1189] These words are added because Gratian himself cites them below in the same chapter, *Si illic*].

[Col. 1189C] Gratian. The following may be understood in this prohibition of the Apostles. The Apostles wished to consume the Samaritans with fire not from zeal for justice but from bitter hatred, to avenge the wrong done in their expulsion. But the Lord, wishing them to bear with patience and joy an injury to His own person, while not leaving unavenged an injury to God’s service, said [Note: [Col. 1189] Luke 9:55], “You do not know of what spirit you are.”

Thus Peter also, who had heard with the others, “Blessed are you when people curse you, persecute you, and speak every evil against you; rejoice and exult on that day, because your reward is abundant in heaven” [Note: [Col. 1189] Matt. 5:11], received with joy the insults done to himself; but he punished most sharply sins committed against God. Thus he struck Ananias and Sapphira [Note: [Col. 1189] Acts 5], who lied to the Holy Spirit, with sentence of death.

Likewise Paul, while recalling the Corinthians from contempt for himself by pious admonition and manifold commendation of himself, struck with blindness the magician Elymas [Note: [Col. 1189] Acts 13], who was turning those about to believe away from the faith, so that the others, terrified, would not hinder his preaching but, believing in Christ, would escape the blindness of their souls. And he handed over that Corinthian fornicator [Note: [Col. 1189] 1 Cor. 13] to Satan for affliction, because he had sinned against God.

Gregory likewise writes to Bishop Januarius, rebuking him because he had excommunicated someone over an injury to his own person. He says, book II, indiction 10, Letter 34 [Note: [Col. 1189] Ep. 49, written A.D. 592, book 2, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 12, ch. 23; Polycarpus, book 7, title 1]:

### C. XXVII. A bishop may not excommunicate anyone for a personal injury.

Among many complaints, the most illustrious man Isidore [Col. 1190B] has complained that your brotherhood excommunicated and anathematized him without cause. When we wished to learn from your cleric, who was present, why this had been done, it became known that it was done for no other reason than that he had injured you. This matter grieves us deeply [Note: [Col. 1189] *afflixit*, past tense, “grieved”: collected editions and original], because [Note: [Col. 1189] *quia*, “because”: original], if it is so, you show that you think nothing of heavenly things, but indicate that your manner of life is earthly, since, for vengeance over a personal injury—a thing forbidden by the sacred rules—you have inflicted the curse of anathema.

Therefore, henceforth be altogether watchful and careful, and do not again presume to inflict such things upon anyone in defense of your own [Note: [Col. 1189] “own”: absent from the original] injury. For if you do anything of this kind, know that it is thereafter to be punished in you [Col. 1190C; Note: [Col. 1189] *esse vindicandum*, “is to be punished”: collected editions and original; these words constitute C. XXVIII].

Gratian. Hence the same author says in his homilies, showing that sins committed against God or one’s neighbor must be punished by us, whereas offenses committed against ourselves are to be borne patiently or, rather, passed over:

### C. XXVIII. He gravely offends who remits the Lord’s debts with impunity.

[Note: [Col. 1189] This saying is not found in Gregory.]

If a superior remits without punishment the faults of a debtor to the Lord, he certainly offends seriously: by his own presumption he cancels the debts of the heavenly King and Lord. Those things committed against us [Note: [Col. 1189] *quos*, “whom”: Lyons II; *nos*, “us”: Lyons III; *nobis*, “to us”: the remaining editions] we can easily forgive; but things committed against God we must remit with great discernment and not without repentance [Note: [Col. 1189] *nec tamen*, “and yet not”: Argentinian, Basel, Norimberg; *nec non*, “and also not”: Venetian I and II; *possumus*, “can”: collected editions and original].

[Col. 1191A] ### V. Part. Gratian.

Once a fault has been forgiven, it must not be recalled to mind again with renewed grief.

From Gelasius to the bishops Geruntius, John, Germanus, and Peter. [Note: [Col. 1191] Chapter of uncertain date.—Collection in three parts, part 1, tome 46, chapter 55.—cf. below, Distinction 4, on penance, chapter 24.]

### C. XXIX. An injury, once forgiven, ought not to be recalled again.

If, in the place where these things were done, it shall be established in the presence of both parties both that Stephen made satisfaction and that the person who was badly treated, having received his supplication, forgave him, a punishment remitted once in an act of abolition [Note: [Col. 1191] “abolition”: Edd. coll. o.] ought not to be repeated through renewed grief, in imitation, of course, of the divine clemency, which does not allow forgiven sins to return for vengeance. [Note: [Col. 1191] “according to imitation”: Edd. Arg., Bas., Nor., Ven. I, II.] [Note: [Col. 1191] “allows”: Ed. Bas.] But if nothing is proved either concerning satisfaction or concerning forgiveness, let it be shown by the statement of your charity what has taken place, so that, whether suitable satisfaction may at least now be forthcoming, that course may rather be pursued by which it can heal the mind of the injured person; [Col. 1191B] or, if bitterness persists without forgiveness, vengeance may nevertheless be exacted there, where the punishable presumption arose. [Note: [Col. 1191] “it seems it ought to be read”: *redivivo*, “renewed.”] [Note: [Col. 1191] “preserve”: ibid.] [Note: [Col. 1191] “But if”: Edd. coll. o., except Nor. and Ven. I.] [Note: [Col. 1191] “unforgivable”: Edd. coll. o.] [Note: [Col. 1191] “persists”: same editions, except Par. and Lugdd.]

### VI. Part. Gratian.

But that saying of Ambrose is objected: “At Elijah’s prayers fire came down from heaven, so that the Prophet’s injury might be avenged.” [Note: [Col. 1191] cf. above, chapter 26.] This is understood to have occurred when Ahab [Note: [Col. 1191] Rather, Ahaziah.—cf. 4 Kings, chapter 1.] king of Israel, after that barrenness of three years and six months which came about when heaven was shut at Elijah’s prayers for three years and six months, sent two captains of fifty to Elijah, to say to him: [Note: [Col. 1191] 4 Kings 1:9–10.] “Man of God, the king of Israel summons you”; and he said: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down [Col. 1191C] from heaven and consume you.” And immediately fire came down from heaven and consumed them. By this act he wished to show, not what his own merit before God was, but that the God whom he worshipped was the true God, not the one to whose worship Jezebel was urging some by the prostitution of their own bodies; this he took care to demonstrate by the clearest proofs. Therefore the Prophet’s injury is understood as none other than the injury of the Lord himself, which is to be avenged upon a few so that the rest may be afraid.

Likewise, that statement of Pope Silverius to Bishop Amator is objected. [Note: [Col. 1191] Apocryphal letter.—Anselm, book 12, chapters 8, 9; Polycarpus, book 1, title 7.]

### C. XXX. The Apostolic See anathematized those who seized him, or who thereafter should seize any bishop.

Our patrician Guilisarius [Note: [Col. 1191D] “Guilisarius”: In three ancient copies from which this chapter was restored to Silverius—it had previously been attributed to Silvester—the reading is “Bellisarius”; but because it stands at the beginning of the chapter, it has not been changed.] ordered me to come peaceably to him [Col. 1192A] in the imperial palace concerning certain ecclesiastical arrangements. At the first and second curtain he detained all the clergy and people who were coming with me, and permitted no one to enter except myself alone and our deacon Vigilius. But after I had been forcibly detained and brought before the aforesaid patrician woman, [Note: [Col. 1192D] “The aforesaid patrician woman”: Thus corrected from the letter itself and the Life of Silverius, where this patrician woman is called Antonina. It was formerly read, “the aforesaid patrician.” [Col. 1191] Thus in Edd. coll. o.; in Anselm the reading is as restored.] they sent me into exile, where I am now sustained on the bread of tribulation and the water of distress. Yet for that reason I did not relinquish, nor do I relinquish, my office; but with the bishops whom I was able to assemble, I anathematized those who did such things against me, and together with them, by apostolic *and synodal* authority, decreed that no one should ever be deceived in this manner as I was deceived; and if anyone thereafter should ever deceive any bishop in this manner, he should become *anathema maranatha* in the sight of God and the holy angels. [Col. 1192B]

The same to Vigilius. [Note: [Col. 1191] A letter equally apocryphal.]

§ 1. Therefore hold, together with those who agree with you, the sentence of full condemnation; and recognize that the name and office of priestly ministry have been taken from you, condemned by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by apostolic authority exercised by us.

Gratian. But here too he avenged not his own injury, but that of the Church. That the sin of a people ought to be punished in a few persons Moses taught by his own example: [Note: [Col. 1191] Exodus, chapter 32.] he punished the sin of idolatry in a few worshippers of the calf, expiating the sins of many by the death of a few, frightening men in the present and establishing discipline for the future. Thus he himself also punished the sins of the whole people by the death of a few, when, because of the fornication of the whole people, twenty-four thousand perished in one day. [Note: [Col. 1191] Numbers, chapter 25.] Thus too, because of the sin of murmuring [Col. 1192C] or of testing God, some were punished, so that the rest might be compelled to repentance by their example. [Note: [Col. 1191] Numbers, chapter 11.] Thus God daily punishes some, so that it may be known that divine providence watches even over human affairs; and he also waits for some through long periods for repentance, so that he may show us the patience of his kindness. Thus Elijah also punished the worship of Baal by killing its priests and prophets, expiating by the death of the instigators the sins of peoples who imitated them. [Note: [Col. 1191] 3 Kings, chapter 18.]

§ 1. But that sins which are abandoned by public indications ought not to be punished is proved by the example in which Christ—who alone knew Judas to be a thief—is said not to have reproached him, but to have borne him patiently. [Note: [Col. 1191] John, chapter 12.]

[Col. 1193A] Therefore Ambrose, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 5, says: [Note: [Col. 1193] It is not by Ambrose.—cf. Cause 2, question 1, chapter 17.]

### C. XXXI. It is not the judge’s role to condemn without an accuser.

If someone lacks the power to reject a person whom he knows to be guilty, or cannot prove him guilty, he is free from blame; and it is not the judge’s role to condemn without an accuser. For even the Lord did not at all reject Judas when he was a thief, since he was not accused. [Note: [Col. 1193D] “When he was a thief”: Certain words from the original have been added here. It was formerly read: “just as Christ did not reject Judas.”]

Gratian. Similarly, sentence should not be pronounced when a multitude is involved in the case, or when the sinner has a multitude as accomplices.

[Col. 1193B] Therefore Augustine, in book III, chapter 2, *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, says: [Note: [Col. 1193] Ivo, in the prologue.]

### C. XXXII. What is sinned by a multitude, or by one who has a multitude as accomplices, is not punished by the Church, but mourned.

Correction by many cannot be salutary unless the person corrected does not have a multitude as accomplices. But when the same disease has seized very many, nothing remains for the good except sorrow and groaning, so that by that sign which is revealed to the holy Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 1193] Ezekiel, chapter 9.] they may deserve to escape unharmed from their devastation. [Note: [Col. 1193] “may escape”: Ed. Arg.] [Note: [Col. 1193] “their”: Edd. coll. o.]

And below:

§ 1. Truly, if the contagion of sinning has invaded a multitude, the severe mercy of divine discipline is necessary. For counsels of separation are both vain and harmful and sacrilegious, because they are impious and proud; [Note: [Col. 1193] “become”: Ivo.] and they disturb weak good people more than they correct resolute bad people.

And below:

§ 2. But a crowd of the wicked, when there is opportunity among the peoples to win acceptance for speech, [Col. 1193C] must be struck by a general rebuke, especially if some scourge from the Lord above has furnished an occasion and opportunity, by which it appears that they are being beaten according to their deserts. [Note: [Col. 1193] “advance”: Böhm.]

Gratian. The Gospel commands [Note: [Col. 1193] Luke 6:27.] concerning love of enemies and mercy to be bestowed on neighbours, and the Apostle’s exhortations [Note: [Col. 1193] Romans 12:20.] concerning feeding or giving drink to enemies, are not to be understood so as to relax the impunity of sinning, but so that correction may be administered to the offender and aid to his nature, until, by the sentence of a judge and with hope of correction removed, the practice of evils may be taken away. Therefore we are commanded in this respect to love enemies [Col. 1194A] and to show them mercy: that we may grieve over their destruction, desire their salvation, labour and pray daily for their correction, and provide consolations to those repenting, bearing one another’s burdens; [Note: [Col. 1193] Galatians 6:5.] not that we should grant impunity to those who are obstinate and persevere in evil.

For just as we are warned to be not severe but merciful toward penitents, according to the saying, [Note: [Col. 1193] Ecclesiastes 7:17.] “Do not be excessively righteous,” because “there is a righteous person who perishes in his righteousness”; [Note: [Col. 1193D] “Do not be”: Gratian does not quote the exact words of Ecclesiastes. They are: [Col. 1194D] “I have also seen this in the days of my vanity: a righteous man perishes in his righteousness, and a wicked man lives long in his wickedness. Do not be excessively righteous, nor be wiser than necessary, lest you become astonished.”] and again: “Judgment without mercy shall be for him who has not shown mercy”; [Note: [Col. 1193] James 2:13.] and also that saying of the Apostle in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: [Note: [Col. 1193] 2 Corinthians 2:10.] “To whom you have forgiven anything, I also forgive. For if I have forgiven anything, I forgave it for your sake, as though Christ himself had forgiven, that we may not be outwitted by Satan. For we are not ignorant of his devices”—who makes those whom he cannot deceive by agreement [Col. 1194B] excessively harsh—so, I say, we are forbidden to show mercy to penitents and to those obstinate in evil.

Therefore Ambrose, in Sermon VIII on Psalm 118, verse 2, says: [Note: [Col. 1193] It was formerly cited from Ambrose’s book *On Duties*.—Polycarpus, book 6, title 21.]

### C. XXXIII. On just and unjust mercy.

There is an unjust mercy. Indeed, it is written in the Law concerning a certain person: [Note: [Col. 1193] Deuteronomy 19:13.] “You shall not spare him”; and in the books of Kings [Note: [Col. 1193] “book”: Edd. coll. o., except Bas.] you read [Note: [Col. 1193] “kings”: Edd. coll. o.—cf. 1 Kings, chapter 15.] [Note: [Col. 1193] “is read”: same editions.] that Saul *afterward* incurred God’s displeasure because he spared Agag, king of the enemies, whom the divine sentence had forbidden to be spared. [Note: [Col. 1193] “God”: Edd. Bas., Lugdd. II, III.]

Accordingly, [Note: [Col. 1193] “Thus”: Ed. Arg.—But the original reads: “But if anyone, moved by the pleading of a robber’s children …”] if someone, moved by the pleas of a robber’s children and swayed by his wife’s tears, thinks that a robber should be absolved while he still aspires to robbery, does he not hand over the innocent to destruction when he frees one who is plotting the destruction of many? [Note: [Col. 1193] “thinks”: Edd. coll. o.] [Note: [Col. 1193] “will hand over”: same editions.] Certainly, if he restrains the sword and looses the chains, why does he release him to destruction? [Note: [Col. 1193] The editions read “releases exile”; it appears, with the Ambrosian manuscripts, that the reading should be *exitio*, “to destruction.”] Why does he not take away by the gentler available route the opportunity for robbery, when he has been unable to extort the will to rob?

Then, between two persons—that is, accuser and defendant—contending at equal risk of life, [Note: [Col. 1193] “contesting”: Edd. coll. o.] the one being at risk if he has not proved the case, the other if he has been convicted by the accuser, let the judge not follow what justice requires: [Note: [Col. 1193] “if not”: same editions.] [Note: [Col. 1193] “carry out”: same editions.] but, while he has mercy on the defendant, let him condemn the accuser who proves the charge; [Note: [Col. 1193] “of the other”: same editions.] [Note: [Col. 1193] “or will condemn the one proving it”: same editions.] or, while he favours an accuser who cannot prove the charge, let him adjudge the innocent person guilty. [Note: [Col. 1193] “which”: same editions.] [Note: [Col. 1193] “to be proved”: Edd. Arg., Ven. I.] [Note: [Col. 1193] “could”: Edd. Bas., Ven. I, Par., Lugd. I.] [Note: [Col. 1193] “condemns”: Ed. Lugd. I; “will condemn”: Edd. Par., Lugdd. II, III; “will add”: remaining editions.] Therefore this cannot be called just mercy.

In the Church itself, where one ought most of all to show mercy, the rule of justice ought especially to be maintained, lest anyone excluded [Col. 1195A] from fellowship in communion [Note: [Col. 1195C] “Excluded”: It was formerly read “removed from the fellowship of communion or accusation.” This and many other passages have been corrected from the original. [Col. 1195] “or accusation”: not read in Ed. Arg.; “communion, accusation”: Ed. Bas.] should, by a brief tear readily supplied for the moment, or even by more abundant weeping, extort from a priest’s leniency the communion which he ought to seek over a very long time. [Note: [Col. 1195] “in abundance”: ibid.] [Note: [Col. 1195] “from”: Ed. Arg.] Does not one who indulges a single unworthy person provoke very many to the contagion of falling away? [Note: [Col. 1195] “also”: Edd. coll. o.] [Note: [Col. 1195] The editions read: “calls all universally to the contagion of falling away” (*prolapsionis*; Ed. Arg., Nor., Ven. I read *prolationis*).] For ease in granting pardon provides an incentive to wrongdoing.

### C. XXXIV. We ought not to spare a poor person in a bad cause.

Likewise Augustine in the book of Psalms, Psalm 32. [Note: [Col. 1195D] Almost the same material occurs in the Ordinary Gloss on Psalm 32, at the verse “He loves mercy,” in a sentence collected from Blessed Augustine.] [Note: [Col. 1195] Ordinary Gloss on Psalm 32, from Augustine.]

Do not, with judgment lost, be merciful to a poor person in a bad cause. If you spare his purse, you strike his heart [Note: [Col. 1195] “his”: Edd. Bas., Lugdd. II, III.] and make him so much the worse, inasmuch as he sees justice favouring him.

[Col. 1195B]

### C. XXXV. One must show mercy to the man and be angry with the sinner.

The same. [Note: [Col. 1195D] The beginning of this chapter occurs in Sermons 94 and 109 *On Time*, and Homily 6 in the book of fifty homilies. But the complete text is in Bede’s commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 6.] [Note: [Col. 1195] Rather, Bede on Galatians 6, using words collected here and there from Augustine.—Anselm, book 13, chapter 21; Polycarpus, book 6, chapter 21.]

When we say these two names, “man” and “sinner,” they are certainly not said without purpose. Because he is a sinner, rebuke him; because he *is* a man, show mercy to him. You will never wholly free the man unless you persecute the sinner. Let discipline be diligent in this duty of the name, as is fitting and appropriate to every ruler: not only to a bishop governing his people, but also to a poor man governing his household, a rich man governing his servants, a husband governing his wife, a father governing his offspring, a judge governing his province, and a king governing his people. [Note: [Col. 1195] “and because”: Edd. Bas., Lugdd. II, III.] [Note: [Col. 1195] “every”: the true reading.—Anselm.]

And a little later:

§ 1. Thus mercy must not be closed to any human being; but impunity must not be granted to any sinner. [Note: [Col. 1195] “just as to no”: Edd. coll. o., except Arg., Nor., Ven. I.] [Note: [Col. 1195] “sin”: Anselm.] Hence it must especially [Col. 1195C] be understood that almsgiving, bestowed upon all poor persons by right of humanity, is not to be despised; since the Lord will relieve the need of the poor even from those money-bags which he filled *from* the wealth of others. [Note: [Col. 1195] “that”: Edd. coll. o.] [Note: [Col. 1195] “never”: Ed. Bas.] [Note: [Col. 1195] “will relieve”: Edd. coll. o.] [Note: [Col. 1195] “works”: same editions, except Arg.]

And a little later:

§ 2. Therefore let us not receive sinners because they are sinners; [Note: [Col. 1195] “For which reason”: Edd. Arg., Nor., Ven. I; “because of this, that”: the remaining editions.] but nevertheless, because they too are human beings, let us treat them with human consideration. Let us pursue in them their particular iniquity; let us pity their common condition. [Col. 1196A] [Note: [Col. 1195] “nature”: Edd. coll. o.]

Gratian. Likewise, Augustine explains that Gospel saying which had been objected—“Whoever uses the sword shall fall by the sword”—in book 22 *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, chapter 70, as follows: [Note: [Col. 1195] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 44; *Decretum*, part 10, chapter 110.]

### C. XXXVI. Who is said to take up the sword.

He takes up the sword who arms himself to shed someone’s blood with no higher and lawful authority either commanding or permitting it. [Note: [Col. 1195] “blood”: Ed. Bas.]

### VII. Part. Gratian.

Further, Jerome’s statement [Note: [Col. 1195] above, chapter 13.] that the Church persecutes no one must not be understood to mean that the Church persecutes absolutely no one, but that she persecutes no one unjustly. For not every persecution is blameworthy; rather, we reasonably persecute [Col. 1196B] heretics, just as Christ bodily persecuted those whom he drove from the Temple.

Therefore Augustine says to Vincentius, Letter XLVIII: [Note: [Col. 1195] Letter 93, Maurist edition; written A.D. 408.—Anselm, book 12, chapter 55.]

### C. XXXVII. The disorderly are beneficially corrected by the office of authority.

The *Donatists* are exceedingly disorderly, [Note: [Col. 1196C] “Donatists”: In Anselm the title is “Augustine to Vincentius.” But the chapter begins “The Donatists exceedingly,” and in Blessed Augustine “But the Donatists exceedingly.” Therefore the word *Donatists* has been restored here and removed from the title; for the former reading in the title was “Augustine says to Vincentius the Donatist.” [Col. 1195] Thus in Edd. coll. o.] and I do not think it useless that they be restrained and corrected through the authorities ordained by God. [Note: [Col. 1196D] “Authorities”: The printed editions continued “secular”; this word is absent from most ancient copies, Anselm, and the original. Many other matters, especially from the original itself, have been corrected.] For we already rejoice at the correction of many.

Likewise below:

§ 1. If anyone saw his enemy, made frenzied by dangerous fevers, running toward a precipice, [Note: [Col. 1195] “headlong”: original; Ed. Arg.] would he not then rather repay evil with evil if he allowed him to run in that manner, than if he took care that he should be seized and bound? [Note: [Col. 1195] “go”: Edd. coll. o.] [Note: [Col. 1195] “should be corrected, treated, and bound”: same editions.] Yet he would seem most troublesome [Col. 1196C] and hostile to him then, when he had proved most useful and merciful. But once health was restored, he would give him thanks all the more abundantly, in proportion as he realized that the other had spared him less.

And after a few words:

§ 2. But indeed these measures do not benefit some persons. Is medicine therefore to be neglected because the disease of some is incurable?

Likewise, after some material:

§ 3. Not everyone who spares is a friend, nor everyone who strikes is an enemy. [Note: [Col. 1195] above, Cause 5, question 5, chapter 2.] The wounds of a friend are better than the flattering [Note: [Col. 1197] absent from Ed. Arg.; “voluntary”: original.] kisses of an enemy. [Note: [Col. 1197] Proverbs 27:6.] It is better to love with severity than to deceive with gentleness. Bread is more beneficially taken away from a hungry person if, secure in food, he neglected justice, [Note: [Col. 1197] “neglects”: original; Edd. coll. o.] than bread is broken for the hungry person so that, seduced by injustice, he may acquiesce in it.

Likewise, after a few words:

§ 4. Do you think that no one ought to be compelled to justice, when you read that the master of the household said to his servants, [Note: [Col. 1197] Luke 14:23.] “Compel whomever you find to enter”; and when you read [Note: [Col. 1197] Acts, chapter 9.] that Saul himself, later Paul, was compelled by the great violence of Christ compelling him to know and hold the truth?

Likewise, after a few words:

§ 5. You know that a thief sometimes scatters fodder to draw cattle away, and that a shepherd sometimes recalls straying cattle *to the flock* with a whip. [Note: [Col. 1197] “And you know”: Edd. Arg., Nor., Ven. I; “and when you know”: the remaining editions.]

Likewise below:

§ 6. If it were always blameworthy [Col. 1197B] to carry out persecution, it would not be written in the holy books: [Note: [Col. 1197] Psalm 100:5.] “The one secretly slandering his neighbour, him I persecuted.” Therefore sometimes the person who undergoes persecution is unjust, and the person who inflicts it is just. But certainly evil persons have always persecuted good persons, and good persons *have persecuted* evil persons: the former by doing harm through injustice, the latter by providing care through discipline; the former cruelly, the latter with restraint; the former serving cupidity, [Note: [Col. 1197] “raging with cupidity”: Edd. coll. o., except Bas., Lugdd. II, III.] the latter charity. For one who kills does not consider how he tears apart; [Note: [Col. 1197] Ed. Bas. reads: “how he should cut; but one wishing to heal considers …”] but one who heals considers how he cuts. The former persecutes health; the latter [Note: [Col. 1197] “the former”: Ed. Bas.; original.] corruption.

The ungodly killed the Prophets; the Prophets also killed the ungodly. The Jews scourged Christ; Christ also scourged the Jews. The Apostles were handed over by men [Col. 1197C] to human authority; the Apostles *also* handed over men to the power of Satan. In all these cases, what is considered except which acted for truth, which for wickedness, which for the purpose of harming, and which for the purpose of correction?

And a little later:

§ 7. The Emperor Constantine *first* decreed that the property of those convicted and obstinately resisting unity should be claimed by the fisc.

And after a few words:

§ 8. Certainly, another’s crime does not stain one who does not know of it. [Note: [Col. 1197] cf. Cause 1, question 4, chapter 1.]

Likewise below:

§ 9. The deeds of wrongdoers [Note: [Col. 1197] “wrongdoer”: Ed. Bas.] which cannot be shown to innocent persons or believed by them do not defile anyone, if even known deeds are endured for the sake of fellowship with the innocent. [Note: [Col. 1197] “defile”: Edd. coll. o., except Arg.] For good persons are not to be abandoned because of the bad; rather, bad persons are to be tolerated because of the good, [Col. 1198A] as the Prophets tolerated those against whom they spoke such severe words and yet did not leave the communion of that people’s sacraments. [Note: [Col. 1197] absent from the original and Ed. Arg.] [Note: [Col. 1197] “sacred things”: Edd. Lugdd. II, III.]

### C. XXXVIII. Heretics are to be drawn to salvation even against their will.

Likewise, to the presbyter Donatus, Letter CCIV. [Note: [Col. 1197] Letter 173, Maurist edition; written A.D. 416.—Anselm, book 12, chapter 57 (56); Deusdedit, part 2.]

Does it displease you that you are being drawn to salvation, when you have drawn so many of ours to destruction? [Note: [Col. 1197] “nevertheless”: Edd. coll. o; “you”: added by Ed. Bas.] What do we want, [Note: [Col. 1197] “wanted”: original.] except that you be seized, brought forward, and saved, lest you perish? As for the injury to your body, you inflicted it upon yourself, since you refused to use the animal immediately brought to you and violently threw yourself to the ground. For another man brought along with you, your colleague, arrived unharmed; [Note: [Col. 1197] “and unharmed”: Edd. Bas., Lugdd. II, III.] he did not do such things to himself. Yet you do not think even this ought to have been done to you, [Note: [Col. 1197] “these things”: Ed. Bas.] [Col. 1198B] because you think that no one ought to be compelled *to* the good. [Note: [Col. 1197] “who”: Edd. coll. o.]

Consider what the Apostle said: [Note: [Col. 1197] cf. 1 Timothy 3:1.] “Whoever desires the episcopate desires a good work.” And yet so many are held, led, shut in, and *kept* against their will in order that they may undertake the episcopate; they suffer [Note: [Col. 1197] The original adds “such great”; Ed. Bas. “evils”; remaining editions, “evils unwillingly.”] what they do not wish until the will to undertake the good work comes to them. How much more ought you to be drawn and led from the ruinous error in which you are enemies to yourselves, to a truth that you must either know or choose—not merely in order that you may beneficially possess honour, but also that you may not perish most miserably? [Note: [Col. 1197] “led forth”: Ed. Bas.; “led”: original.]

§ 1. You say that God gave free choice, and therefore a human being ought not to be compelled *even* to the good. Why, then, are those whom I mentioned above compelled to the good? [Note: [Col. 1197] “mentioned”: Edd. coll. o.] Consider, then, [Col. 1198C] what you refuse to consider. [Note: [Col. 1197C] “Consider, then”: This passage, like many other passages in this chapter, has been corrected from Blessed Augustine. It formerly read: “Consider, then, and consider that a good will is not mercifully bestowed in order that a person’s evil will may be loved.” [Col. 1197] Thus in Edd. coll. o.] A good will is mercifully bestowed so that a person’s evil will may be directed. [Note: [Col. 1197] “loved”: same editions.] For who does not know that a person is condemned only through the merit of an evil will, and is freed only if he has a good will? Yet those who are loved ought not therefore to be cruelly and with impunity abandoned to their evil will; rather, where authority is granted, they ought both to be restrained from evil and compelled to good. [Note: [Col. 1197] “are”: added by Edd. coll. o.]

For if an evil will must always be left to its own freedom, why were the Israelites, when they refused and murmured, restrained from evil by such harsh punishments and compelled toward the land of promise? If an evil will [Note: [Col. 1197] “indeed”: added by same editions, except Arg., Nor., Ven. I.] must always [Note: [Col. 1197] absent from Edd. Arg., Nor., Ven. I.] be left to its own freedom, why was Paul not permitted to employ the very evil will by which he persecuted the Church? Instead, he was thrown down so that he might be blinded; [Col. 1199A] blinded so that he might be changed; [Note: [Col. 1199] “made blind”: Edd. coll. o.] changed so that he might be sent; [Note: [Col. 1199] “was changed … was sent”: same editions.] sent so that he might suffer for the truth such things as he had done in error. [Note: [Col. 1199] “may have done”: same editions, except Bas., Lugdd. II, III.]

If an evil will must always be left to its own freedom, why is a father instructed in the holy Scriptures [Note: [Col. 1199] cf. Ecclesiasticus chapter 30, verse 12.] not only to correct a harsh son by words but also to strike his sides, so that, compelled and tamed, he may be directed to good discipline? Hence the same author [Note: [Col. 1199] absent from Ed. Arg.; “Solomon”: added by Edd. coll. o.—cf. Proverbs 23:14.] says: “You strike him with the rod, but you free his soul from death.” If an evil will must always be left to its own freedom, why are negligent shepherds rebuked and told: [Note: [Col. 1199] Ezekiel 34:4.] “You did not bring back the straying *sheep*; you did not seek the lost.” [Note: [Col. 1199] “corrected”: Ed. Bas.] [Note: [Col. 1199] “lost one”: Edd. coll. o.; “indeed”: added by Edd. Lugdd. II, III.] [Col. 1199B] [Note: [Col. 1199] “sought again”: original; Ed. Bas.]

And you are Christ’s sheep. You bear [Note: [Col. 1199] “indeed”: added by Ed. Arg.] the Lord’s mark in the sacrament which you received; [Note: [Col. 1199] “bore”: Ed. Bas.] but you stray and perish. Do not for that reason be displeased with us because we call back those who stray and seek those who are lost. For we fulfil better the will of the Lord, who commands that [Note: [Col. 1199] “if”: Edd. Bas., Lugdd. II, III.] we compel you to return to his sheepfold, than if we consented [Note: [Col. 1199] “consent”: Böhm.] to the will of the straying *sheep* and permitted you to perish.

§ 2. Therefore do not now say what I constantly hear you saying: [Note: [Col. 1199] “said”: Edd. coll. o., except Arg.] “Thus I wish to err; thus I wish to perish.” For we altogether do not permit this, so far as we are able. [Note: [Col. 1199] “For we”: “here”: Ed. Bas.] [Note: [Col. 1199] “to perish”: added by Edd. coll. o., except Bas.]

Now, you cast yourself into a well in order that you might die; [Note: [Col. 1199] “in which”: Edd. coll. o.] [Note: [Col. 1199] “you die”: Ed. Bas., Ven. I–II, Nor., Par.; “you will die”: Ed. Lugd. I.] certainly, you did so by free choice. But how cruel would God’s servants be if they left you to this evil will of yours [Col. 1199C] and did not free you from that death? Who would not deservedly blame them? Who would not rightly judge them impious? Yet you willingly cast yourself into water so that you might die; they lifted you unwilling from the water so that you might not die. You acted according to your will, but for your own destruction; they acted against your will, but for your salvation. [Note: [Col. 1199] “and they”: Edd. coll. o., except Arg., Bas.] [Note: [Col. 1199] “against your death”: Edd. coll. o.]

Therefore, if this bodily life must be guarded so carefully that it is preserved even in unwilling persons by those who love them, how much more must that spiritual life be guarded, in the forsaking of which eternal death is feared? Yet even in this death which you wished to inflict upon yourself, you would die not only for a time but also eternally. For [Col. 1199D] [Col. 1200A] even if you were compelled, not to salvation, not to the peace of the Church, not to the unity of Christ’s body, not to holy and indivisible charity, but to some evil, you still ought not to inflict death on yourself. [Note: [Col. 1199] “nor”: Edd. Bas., Lugdd. II, III.]

Examine the divine Scriptures, consider as much as you can, and see whether any of the righteous and faithful ever did this when they endured such great evils from persons who were driving them toward *eternal* destruction, not toward the *eternal* life to which *you* are being compelled. [Note: [Col. 1199] “here”: Ed. Bas.]

And after a few words:

§ 3. You repeat, as I hear, that the seventy [Note: [Col. 1199] Some editions add “seventy-two”: Edd. Ven. I–II, Lugd. I, Par.—cf. John 6:68.] disciples withdrew from the Lord, as it is written in the Gospel, and were allowed the choice of their wicked and impious departure; and that the remaining twelve were answered: “Do you also wish to go away?” [Note: [Col. 1199] “depart”: Edd. coll. o.] You fail to consider that at that time the Church was first budding forth in new growth, [Col. 1200B] and that the prophecy had not yet been fulfilled in her: [Note: [Col. 1199] “not yet”: Ed. Bas., Lugdd.] “All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him.” [Note: [Col. 1199] Psalm 71:11.] [Note: [Col. 1199] “him”: Edd. coll. o.]

The more this is fulfilled, the greater authority the Church employs, so that she not only invites but also compels to the good. *Then* the Lord meant to signify this: although he possessed great authority, he nevertheless first chose to commend humility. [Note: [Col. 1199] “here”: Ed. Bas.; “however”: added by Ed. Arg.] He also showed this quite clearly in the parable of the banquet, [Note: [Col. 1199] “is shown”: Edd. coll. o., except Bas.] where he sent to those invited and they refused to come; and he said to the servant: [Note: [Col. 1199] Luke 14:21.] “Go out into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor, the infirm, the blind, and the lame.” [Note: [Col. 1199] “Into the streets”: Corrected from Luke’s Gospel by deleting two words. It was formerly read: “Go out quickly into the roads and streets.” [Col. 1199] Thus in Edd. coll. o., except Arg., Bas.] And the servant said to the Lord: “It has been done as you commanded, and there is still room.” And the Lord said [Col. 1200C] to the servant: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled.”

See now how, concerning those who came first, [Note: [Col. 1199] “had come first”: Ed. Bas.; “came first”: remaining editions.] it was said, “Bring them in”; but now it is said, “Compel them.” Thus the beginnings of the Church, still growing, were signified, so that it would have strength also to compel. [Note: [Col. 1199] “by strength”: Edd. Lugdd., Par.; Böhm.]

### C. XXXIX. Heretics beneficially suffer what Catholics beneficially inflict.

The same, on John, Tractate XI, on chapter 3. [Note: [Col. 1199] Anselm, book 12, chapter 54; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, chapter 99; Polycarpus, book 7, title 6.]

When God wills to stir up the authorities against heretics, against schismatics, against those who scatter the Church, against those who spurn Christ, [Col. 1200D] against blasphemers of baptism, let them not be surprised. [Col. 1201A] For God stirs up [Note: “calls”: ed. Arg.; “repeatedly calls”: ed. Bas.] Sarah to chastise Hagar, so that Hagar may recognize her position and bow her neck; for, when she departed humbled from her mistress, the angel met her and said [Note: Gen. 21:17]: “What is the matter, Hagar, servant of Sarah?” When she had complained of her mistress, what did she hear from the angel? “Return to your mistress.” She is therefore afflicted for this purpose: that she may return; and would that she might return, since her offspring, like the sons of Jacob, will possess an inheritance with their brothers. Yet they are astonished because Christian authorities are moved against the detestable scatterers of the Church. But if they were not moved, how would they render an account of their rule to God? Let your charity attend to what I say: it pertains to Christian kings of this world that, in their own times, they should wish their mother, the Church, from whom they were spiritually born, to be at peace.

And a little later:

§ 1. King Nebuchadnezzar issued a decree, saying [Note: Dan. 3:96]: “Whoever speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be destroyed, and their house given over to destruction.” See how the foreign king rages lest the God of Israel, who was able to deliver three boys from the fire, should be blasphemed. And yet they do not wish Christian kings to act vigorously because Christ is spurned—Christ by whom not three boys but the whole world, together with the kings themselves, is delivered from the fire of hell.

And below:

§ 2. How, then, should these kings not be moved, when they consider not merely three boys delivered from a flame, but themselves delivered from hell, when they see Christ, by whom they were delivered, spurned [Col. 1201C] among Christians? When they hear a Christian told: “Say that you are not a Christian”? They wish to do such things, yet are unwilling even to suffer such things. For consider what they do and what they suffer: they kill souls; they are afflicted in body. They inflict eternal deaths, and complain that they suffer temporal ones.

[Note: “against blasphemers and spurners of Christ’s baptism, they do not merit …” [the reading is defective]: ed. Bas.; “against those who spurn and blaspheme Christ, let them not be surprised”: eds. Lugdd. II–III; other editions vary in the placement of “and.”]

[Note: “put on her own [neck]”: ed. Bas.; “submit”: the other editions except Arg.]  
[Note: “which”: older collected editions.]  
[Note: “what is the matter with you?”: older collected editions.]  
[Note: “having complained”: same editions; Böhm.]  
[Note: “these things”: ed. Bas.]  
[Note: “and would that she return”: omitted there.]  
[Note: “offspring”: other editions; the preceding words omitted in Bas.]  
[Note: “shepherds of the Christian faith”: Ivo.]  
[Note: “against”: older collected editions.]  
[Note: “but if”: eds. Arg., Bas., Lugdd. II–III.]  
[Note: “were stirred”: older collected editions except Arg.]  
[Note: “namely”: same editions.]  
[Note: “to destruction”: older collected editions except Bas.]  
[Note: “dispersion”: Bas.; “in dispersion”: the remaining editions.]

[Note: “from the fiery furnace”: Bas., Lugdd. II–III.]  
[Note: “and yet”: same editions.]

[Note: “the flame of hell”: same editions.]

### C. XL. The Church persecutes heretics by reason

The same, *Against the Letters of Petilian*, book II, ch. 79. [Note: Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, ch. 75.]

One who sins does not sin by the authority of the law, but against the authority of the law. But since you ask me what is the rationale of persecution, I in turn ask you whose voice it is in the Psalm that says [Note: Ps. 100:5]: “Him who secretly slanders his neighbor, I persecuted.” Why then do you ask about either the cause or the manner of persecution? And do not, in such great ignorance, condemn persecutions of the wicked in general.

And below, ch. 82: “For we do not persecute you except as truth persecutes falsehood.”

Likewise above, ch. 10:

§ 2. Petilian said: “Did the Apostles persecute anyone, or did Christ hand anyone over?” Augustine replied: I could indeed say that Satan himself is worse than all wicked men, yet the Apostle handed a man over to him for the destruction of the flesh, that his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus [Note: “of our Lord Jesus Christ”: older collected editions except Arg.; cf. 1 Cor. 5:5]; and likewise others, of whom he says [Note: 1 Tim. 1:20], “Whom I handed over to Satan, that they might learn not to blaspheme.” And Christ the Lord drove the wicked merchants out of the temple after scourging them [Note: John 2], where there is also joined the testimony of Scripture saying [Note: Ps. 68:10], “Zeal for your house has consumed me.” Behold, we find an Apostle who hands over, and Christ who persecutes.

And below, [Col. 1202B] ch. 19:

§ 3. Finally, why are you wickedly aggressive, even unprovoked, against Catholic churches through most violent mobs, wherever you can? The matter itself shows this by innumerable examples. But you say that you defend your own places, and you resist with clubs and beatings, as far as you are able. Why did you not hear there the voice of the Lord saying [Note: Matt. 5:39], “But I say to you, do not resist evil”? Or, if it is possible that violent persons may sometimes rightly be resisted by bodily force, and that the command we heard from the Lord—“But I say to you, do not resist evil”—is not thereby violated, why can it not also happen that, through regular and lawful authorities, the godly man expels the ungodly, and the just man the unjust, from seats which are unlawfully usurped or retained to God’s injury? For the false prophets did not suffer persecution from Elijah in the same manner in which Elijah himself suffered it from the most wicked king; nor, because the Lord was scourged by persecutors, are those whom he himself drove scourged from the temple therefore to be compared with his sufferings.

§ 4. It remains, therefore, that you must admit that nothing else is to be investigated except whether you have separated yourselves justly or wickedly from communion with the whole world. For if it is found that you did so wickedly, do not be surprised if God has ministers by whom you are scourged, because you suffer persecution not from us but, as it is written, from your own deeds.

And in the book *On the Unity of the Church*, ch. 17:

§ 5. Your complaint concerning persecution will be calmed if you first consider and understand that not every persecution is blameworthy. Otherwise it would not be said commendably [Note: Ps. 100:5], “Him who secretly slanders his neighbor, I persecuted.” For every day we see a son complain of his father as his persecutor, a wife of her husband, a slave of his master, a tenant farmer of his proprietor, a defendant of the judge, and a soldier or provincial of a commander or king—when those persons often, by a most orderly exercise of authority, restrain and check those subject to them from graver evils by the fear of lighter punishments; but often also deter them from good living and good actions by threats and violence. But when they prohibit evil and unlawful conduct, they are correctors and advisers; when they prohibit good and lawful conduct, they are persecutors and oppressors. Even those who prohibit evil are blameworthy if the degree of coercion exceeds the degree of the offense.

Bas. reads “to resist”; Arg. reads “and you beat whomever”; the other editions have variants of “as far as you are able.” The command “do not resist evil” is “do not resist” (*nolite*) in Par. and Lugd. on both occurrences. Bas. has “bodily”; Arg. (and Böhm) has “acts of violence”; Ivo and the older collected editions have “orderly.” Bas. reads “the same”; cf. 3 Kings 18–19.
