Bas. reads “to be left” for “to be investigated.” “They prohibit” is “they may prohibit” in the older collected editions.]

### C. XLI. The Church may seek help from the kings of the earth against her enemies

The same, in Letter XLVIII to Vincentius. [Note: Ep. 93, Maurist edition; written A.D. 408. *Collectio trium partium*, part 2, title 50, ch. 30.]

“No example is found in evangelical and apostolic writings of anything being requested from the kings of the earth for the Church and against the Church’s enemies.” Who denies that no such example is found? But the prophecy had not yet been fulfilled [Note: Ps. 2:10]: “And now, understand, O kings; be instructed, you who judge the earth; serve the Lord in fear.” For that was still being fulfilled which is said a little earlier in the same Psalm: “Why have the nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together [Note: “etc.”: eds. Arg., Bas., Lugdd. II–III] against the Lord and [Col. 1203C] against his Christ.”

Nevertheless, if past events in the prophetic books were figures of things to come, then both periods were prefigured in that king who was called Nebuchadnezzar: both the period which the Church had under the Apostles and that which it now has. Thus, in the times of the Apostles and martyrs, what was prefigured was fulfilled when that king compelled the pious and just to worship an image and cast those who refused into the flames. But now is fulfilled what was a little later prefigured in the same king, when, converted to honor the true God, he decreed in his kingdom that whoever blasphemed the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego should be subject to the penalties due.

Therefore the earlier period of that king signified the earlier times of unbelieving kings, whom Christians suffered on behalf of the ungodly; but the later period of the same king signified the times of later kings, now faithful, whom the ungodly suffer on behalf of Christians. But certainly, in the case of those who, under Christ’s name, have been led astray by the perverse—lest perhaps they are wandering sheep of Christ, and must be recalled to the flock by some other means—moderated severity and still greater gentleness are to be maintained, so that, by the coercion of exile and the affliction of losses, they may be admonished to consider what they suffer and why, and may learn to prefer the Scriptures which they read to the rumors and calumnies of men.

For which of us, which of you, does not praise the laws issued by emperors against pagan sacrifices? And yet a far more severe penalty was established there: capital punishment was ordained for that impiety. But in correcting and coercing you, account has been taken so that you might rather be admonished to depart from error than be punished for crime.

[Note: “all”: Bas.]  
[Note: “not”: same edition.]  
[Note: “is read”: older collected editions.]

### C. XLII. The Church justly persecutes the wicked

Likewise, the same author to Count Boniface, Letter L. [Note: Ep. 185, Maurist edition; written A.D. 417. Anselm, book 13, ch. 14; Polycarpus, book 7, title 11.]

If the true Church is the one which suffers persecution, not the one which inflicts it, let them ask the Apostle which Church Sarah signified when she persecuted the slave-woman. For he says that our free mother, the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, the true Church of God—was prefigured in the woman who afflicted the slave-woman. But if we examine more closely, Hagar persecuted Sarah more by her pride than Sarah persecuted her by coercion. For Hagar did wrong to her mistress; Sarah imposed discipline upon pride.

Then I ask: if good and holy persons persecute no one but only suffer persecution, whose voice do they suppose occurs in the Psalm where it is read [Note: Ps. 17:38], “I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I shall not turn back until they fail”? Therefore, if we wish to speak or acknowledge the truth, there is an unjust persecution which the ungodly inflict upon Christ’s Church, and there is a just persecution which Christ’s churches inflict upon the ungodly. The former Church, accordingly, is blessed because it suffers persecution for righteousness; but those others are miserable because they suffer persecution for unrighteousness. Therefore, the former persecutes by loving, the latter by raging; the former in order to correct, the latter in order to overthrow; the former in order to call back from error, the latter in order to cast headlong into error.

And below:

§ 1. Those who do not wish just laws to be enacted against their impieties say that the Apostles did not request such things from the kings of the earth; but they do not consider that the time was then different and that all things are done in their proper times. For what emperor had then believed in Christ, so that he might serve him by enacting laws for piety against impiety, when that prophetic saying was still being fulfilled: “Why have the nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.” But what is said a little later in the same Psalm was not yet being enacted: “And now, understand, O kings; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear and exult before him with trembling.”

How, then, do kings serve the Lord in fear, unless by religious severity prohibiting and punishing what is done contrary to the Lord’s commands? For he serves in one way because he is a human being, and in another because he is also a king. Because he is a human being, he serves God by living faithfully; but because he is also a king, he serves by establishing with fitting vigor laws which command what is just and prohibit what is contrary.

[Note: “is”: older collected editions except Arg.]  
[Note: “and not”: Bas., Lugdd. II–III.]  
[Note: “did”: older collected editions except Par., Lugdd. II–III.]  
[Note: “let it be asked”: older collected editions.]  
[Note: “signifies”: Arg.]  
[Note: “true”: older collected editions.]  
[Note: “men”: older collected editions.]  
[Note: “knowing”: Bas.]  
[Note: The words “and there is a just persecution … Christ’s churches [inflict] upon the ungodly” through “the latter by raging” were added from the original; they are absent from Anselm.]  
[Note: “for”: original.]  
[Note: “fitting”: older collected editions.]  
[Note: “Who indeed”: same editions.]  
[Note: “raged”: same editions.]  
[Note: “then indeed”: same editions.]  
[Note: “was not fulfilled”: Nor.]  
[Note: “peoples”: Bas.]  
[Note: “indeed”: older collected editions.]  
[Note: “God”: Arg.]  
[Note: “have been done”: older collected editions.]  
[Note: “also” is absent from Arg., Bas., Lugdd. II–III.]  
[Note: “keeps”: Arg., Bas., Ven. I, Nor.]
[Note: “Her” is absent from Bas. The original’s editorial note states that the words from “And there is a just persecution” through “Accordingly, this [Church]” (*Ista itaque*), together with many other readings, were corrected from the original; they are absent from Anselm.]

[Col. 1205C]

### C. XLIII. By Christ’s example, the wicked are to be compelled toward the good

The same, in the same letter. [Note: Anselm, book 13, ch. 16; Polycarpus, same place.]

Who can love us more than Christ, who laid down his soul for his sheep? And yet, when he had called Peter and the other Apostles by word alone [Note: “recalled”: Nor., Ven. I; “called forth”: the remaining editions except Arg.; cf. Acts 9], Paul—first Saul, later a great builder of his Church, but formerly a terrible devastator—not only restrained by a word, but also struck down by power; and while raging in the darkness of unbelief, he first struck him with bodily blindness, so that he might rise to desire the light of the heart. If that punishment had not existed, he would not afterwards have been healed from it; and when, with his eyes opened, he saw nothing, if he had had them sound, Scripture would not relate that, at Ananias’s laying on of hands, something like scales, by which his sight had been shut up, fell from them.

Where is what these men habitually cry out: “It is free to believe or not to believe; on whom did Christ use force? Whom did he compel?” Behold, they have the Apostle Paul. Let them recognize in him Christ first compelling and afterwards teaching, first striking and afterwards consoling. It is remarkable how he who entered the Gospel compelled by bodily punishment labored in the Gospel more than all those who had been called by word alone; and how the greater fear which compelled him to love was cast out by his perfect love. Why, then, should the Church not compel lost sons to return, if lost sons have compelled others to perish?

[Note: The following words through the end, beginning “if lost sons,” were added from the original and are absent from Anselm.]  
[Note: “afterwards”: Bas.]  
[Note: “sound”: Bas.]  
[Note: “casts out”: older collected editions; cf. 1 John 4:8.]  
[Note: “for”: Arg., Nor., Ven. I.]  
[Note: The words beginning “and while raging” are absent from Arg., Nor., Ven. I, and Böhm.]  
[Note: Bas. reads, uncertainly: “to rage [or, raging] into the darkness.”]
[Note: “Indeed” (*enim*): Arg., Nor., and Ven. I. Cf. below, question 6, chapter 1.]

### C. XLIV. Moses scourged the people, not out of cruelty but out of love

The same, *Against Faustus*, book XXII, ch. 79. [Note: Anselm, book 13, ch. 1; Polycarpus, same place.]

What cruel thing did Moses either command or do, when, zealously caring for the people entrusted to him and desiring that they be subject to the one true God, he learned that they had fallen away to make and worship an idol and had prostituted their impure mind to demons? In avenging himself by the sword upon a few of them—whom God himself, whom they had offended, had willed, by a lofty and hidden judgment, to be struck down immediately—he both wholesomely terrified them in the present and established discipline for the future. For who does not recognize from his words, as he prayed [Col. 1206C] for their sin and said [Note: Exod. 32:31–32], that he did what he did with no cruelty but with great love: “If you forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me out from your book”?

And below:

§ 1. In precisely the same way, the Apostle handed a man over to Satan, not cruelly but lovingly, for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus [Note: “of our Lord Jesus Christ”: older collected editions except Arg., Bas.]; and he handed over others [Note: 1 Tim. 1:20], that they might learn not to blaspheme.

[Note: “or”: original reading; “and”: older collected editions.]  
[Note: “living and”: older collected editions.]  
[Note: “only”: same editions except Arg., Bas.]  
[Note: “unique”: same editions except Arg.]  
[Note: “cast down”: Arg.]  
[Note: “sins”: older collected editions.]  
[Note: Böhm adds “not.”]  
[Note: “of life”: older collected editions except Arg.]
[Note: “His spirit” is absent from Arg. and Bas.]

### C. XLV. No guilt is imputed to believers who, in the course of their office, employ torture or pronounce a capital sentence

Likewise Pope Innocent, Letter III to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse, ch. 3. [Note: Written A.D. 405; Burchard, book 6, ch. 44; Anselm, book 13, ch. 32; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, ch. 94.]

A question was also asked concerning those who, after baptism, have held public office and have either administered tortures alone or even pronounced a capital sentence. We read that the ancients defined nothing regarding these persons. For they remembered that these powers had been granted by God [Note: Rom. 13:4], that the sword had been permitted for the punishment of wrongdoers, and that a minister of God had been appointed as an avenger in such matters. How, then, could they condemn an act which they saw to have been permitted by God’s authority? Therefore, concerning such persons, let us maintain the rule observed up to this point, lest we seem either to overthrow discipline or to act contrary to the Lord’s authority. But in rendering their account, all their deeds will be reserved for them.

[Note: The text has been corrected from the original and Ivo: “and that a minister of God had been appointed as an avenger in such matters.” Earlier it read: “and that it had been granted from God’s ministry to such avengers.” The gloss also suitably applies to the term “avenger.”]  
[Note: “savage”: Bas., Lugdd.; omitted in Arg.]  
[Note: “turn away”: Ivo and older collected editions except Bas., Lugdd.]  
[Note: “may seem”: Böhm.]  
[Note: “will be kept in reserve”: Bas.]
[Note: “And” after “have held public office” is absent from the older collected editions except Arg. “Tortures alone” is absent from Arg.; Bas. and Lugd. read “cruel” (*saeva*). “Punishments” (*vindictas*): Bas.]

### C. XLVI. A petitioner is free from guilt when the authority of the laws is exercised against the wicked

The same, in the same letter, ch. 5. [Note: “The same, to the bishop of Toledo”: Ven. II, Lugdd., Par.; “the same, to the bishop of Toulouse”: the remaining editions.]

You also wished to inquire whether, after the regeneration of baptism, those who dictate petitions are freely permitted to request from rulers the death or blood of someone on a criminal charge. Rulers never grant this without examination, but always refer the matters or crimes themselves to judges, so that, once the case is heard, they may be punished. When such matters have been delegated to an investigator, either acquittal or condemnation is pronounced according to the nature of the case. And while the authority of the laws is exercised against the wicked, the petitioner will be free from guilt.

[Note: “the case itself”: older collected editions except Bas.]  
[Note: “They may be punished”: corrected from the original. Earlier it read: “they punish, who, when the delegated matters have been investigated, etc.” Older collected editions read this earlier form, except that Bas. has “they judge.”]  
[Note: Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, ch. 94.]

### C. XLVII. Almighty God is appeased by the correction of the wicked

Likewise Gregory to Brunhild, Queen of the Franks, book VII, indiction I, letter 5. [Note: Ep. 11, written A.D. 599, book 9 of the Maurist edition; Anselm, book 13, ch. 24.]

If, therefore, you know any persons to be violent, adulterers, thieves, or devoted to other depraved acts, hasten to appease God by their correction, so that through you the scourge of faithless nations—which, insofar as we see, has been stirred up for the punishment of many peoples—may not be brought upon you; lest, if—what we do not believe—the wrath of divine vengeance has been provoked by the deeds of criminals, the plague of war destroy those whom the commandments of God do not recall from sin to the way of uprightness.

[Note: “By their correction”: restored from variant manuscripts of Gregory’s letters. Earlier editions read “of the gods.”]  
[Note: The original reads “upon you”; “through you” is retained because of the gloss on *scourge*. Anselm has “through you.”]

[Col. 1208A]

### C. XLVIII. Enemies of the Church’s religion are to be restrained even by wars

The same, to Gennadius, patrician and exarch of Africa, book I, letter 72. [Note: Ep. 74, written A.D. 591, book I of the Maurist edition; Anselm, book 13, ch. 29.]

As the Lord has caused your Excellency to shine in this life with the splendor of victories in hostile wars, so it is fitting also that you oppose the enemies of his Church with every vigor of mind and body, in order that the renown of his twofold triumph may shine ever more brightly: both because you vigorously resist in secular wars the opponents of the Catholic Church on behalf of the Christian people, and because you fight ecclesiastical battles bravely as soldiers of the Lord.

For it is known that adherents of heretical religion, if—far be it from us—they are given an opportunity to do harm, rise up fiercely against the Catholic faith so as to pour out the poisons of their heresy, if they can, to corrupt the members of Christ’s body. We have learned that they raise their necks against the Catholic Church, although the Lord opposes them, and seek to bend the faith of the Christian name. But let your Eminence restrain their efforts and press their proud necks under the yoke of uprightness.

Moreover, order the council of Catholic bishops to be admonished that it should not make a primate on the basis of rank of place, while disregarding merits of life, since with God it is not a more distinguished rank but the conduct of a better life that is approved. Let the primate himself reside, not indiscriminately through the villages, as is customary, but in one city chosen near them according to their election, so that the opportunity afforded by his acquired dignity may be directed, with sounder judgment, toward resisting the Donatists.

If any from the council of Numidia desire to come to the Apostolic See, permit them; and if any person wishes to obstruct their journey, oppose him. Indeed, the glory of your Excellency before the Creator grows greatly if, through it, the fellowship of scattered churches can be restored. For when he sees the gifts he has bestowed being employed for the glory of his name, he grants still more generously, in proportion as he sees the dignity of his religion enlarged through him.

Furthermore, returning the affection of paternal charity, we pray the Lord that he may make your arm strong for crushing enemies and sharpen your mind with zeal for the faith, like the point of a flashing sword.

[Note: “even in hostile wars”: Bas.; “from hostile wars”: Nor., Ven. I–II, Par.; “enemies”: Arg.]  
[Note: “subdue”: Ven. II, Par., Lugd. I.]  
[Note: “desires”: Lugd. II; “desire”: other editions.]  
[Note: “arrive; permit”: Arg.]  
[Note: “thinks”: Arg., Anselm; other witnesses vary between singular and plural forms of “wish” and “think.”]  
[Note: “great”: Anselm; “therefore”: Bas.; “accordingly”: remaining editions; original: “with great profit.”]  
[Note: “your Excellency”: older collected editions except Bas., Lugdd. II–III.]  
[Note: The original reads “through it”; the older editions read “through him,” while Bas. has “through her.”]  
[Note: “who”: original; Arg., Bas., Nor., Ven. I–II.]  
[Note: “his”: older collected editions.]  
[Note: “sword-point”: original.]

### C. XLIX. Victory in war is obtained through the merit of faith

The same, to the same person, book I, letter 73. [Note: Ep. 75, written A.D. 591, book I of the Maurist edition; Burchard, book 15, ch. 18; Anselm, book 13, ch. 30; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 16, ch. 19.]

If such success in military undertakings did not come to your Excellency through the merit of faith and the grace of Christian religion, it would not be especially remarkable, since we know that this has also been granted to ancient leaders in war. But since, with God granting them, you anticipate future victories not by carnal prudence but rather by prayers, it comes as a wonder that your glory descends not from earthly counsel but from God’s bestowal from above.

Where does the eloquent report of your merits not spread abroad? It declares that you frequently undertake wars not from a desire to shed blood, but for the purpose of extending the commonwealth in which we see God worshipped, so that Christ’s name may range everywhere among subject peoples through the preaching of faith. For just as outward works of virtue make you eminent in this life, so also inward ornaments of character, proceeding from a pure heart, glorify you in the life to come by participation in heavenly joys.

For we have learned that your Excellency has rendered very many services for feeding the sheep of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, so that you have restored—not inconsiderable places of his patrimony, stripped of their own cultivators—by granting them the dwellings of the Dacians [*Dacorum*; the reading is uncertain]. Whatever, therefore, you confer there upon those people with a most Christian mind, you await the recompense for these things in hope at the future judgment.

[Note: Original: “had been”; Burchard and Ivo: “had been.”]  
[Note: “here”: Bas.]  
[Note: “counsel”: Bas., Lugd. I.]  
[Note: “departs”: Burchard.]  
[Note: “only”: older collected editions; Böhm.]  
[Note: “for the purpose of extending”: Arg.]  
[Note: “might range”: older collected editions; Burchard.]  
[Note: Two manuscript letter-books read “in participation in the joys to come”; one reads “in participation in the joys of heaven in the life to come.” Burchard and Ivo: “in the life to come.” The Vatican manuscript reads as in Gratian.]  
[Note: “may glorify”: Arg.; “will glorify”: Bas.]  
[Note: Original and older collected editions add “services.”]  
[Note: Printed letter-books and two manuscripts read *Daditiorum*; Anselm has the same. Arg. offers “of the ancients,” “of others,” or “of those given”; the Maurists, following Clüver, judge that *Daratitiis* ought to be read. Some old copies of Gratian read *Dacorum*, “of the Dacians,” or “of others.”]  
[Note: “inhabitants”: original, Anselm, older collected editions, and Böhm.]  
[Note: Original and older collected editions: “had restored.”]  
[Note: “here” is absent from the original; Arg.: “here upon those”; remaining editions: “there.”]  
[Note: Original: “Christian.”]

### Part VIII. Gratian

It has been briefly shown that good persons laudably persecute the wicked, and wicked persons damnably persecute the good. But the Apostle’s saying [Note: Rom. 14:4], “Who are you to judge another’s servant?” must be understood concerning the hidden things of another person’s heart. It has been shown that vengeance may be inflicted. It remains now to show that it ought to be inflicted, and that those who are punished are loved more than those who are left unpunished; both propositions are established by the authority of many.

For Augustine says [Note: rather, Gregory to Marinianus and Benenatus, book 3, letter 27, written A.D. 593, Maurist edition]:

### C. L. God is provoked to anger when the punishment of evils is delayed

If we delay to pursue or avenge the things by which God is gravely offended, we certainly provoke divine patience to anger. Did not Achor [Note: Achan in the Vulgate], the son of Zerah, transgress the Lord’s command, and did not his wrath rest upon the whole people of Israel? Yet he was one man; and would that he alone had perished in his crime.

[Note: The words from “If we delay” through “we provoke” occur in the register of blessed Gregory, book 2, indiction 11, letter 27, written to Abbot Martin and the notary Benenatus. What follows is not found there, but consists of the words of Holy Scripture, Joshua ch. 22.]  
[Note: Josh. 22:20.]

### C. LI. Vengeance which serves correction is not to be prohibited

Likewise Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, book I, chs. 37–38. [Note: Anselm, book 13, ch. 2; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, ch. 60.]

That vengeance which serves correction is not forbidden; it also belongs to mercy and does not hinder that purpose by which each person is prepared to endure more from the one whom he wishes to see corrected.

[Note: [Col. 1210D] “That vengeance”: In Blessed Augustine and Anselm this is read: “Nor is that vengeance forbidden here which is also effective for correction. For it itself belongs to mercy and does not impede,” etc.]

But no one is fit to inflict this vengeance unless he has overcome, by the greatness of love, the hatred with which those who desire to avenge themselves customarily burn.

[Note: [Col. 1209] *referendae* (“to be returned/repaid”): the editions compared read *inferendae* (“to be inflicted”).]

[Note: “Hatred”: the Basel and Lyon editions add *homines* (“people”): “with which people who desire to avenge themselves customarily burn.” The editions compared and Ivo read *mansuetudine* (“by gentleness”) instead of *dilectionis magnitudine* (“by the greatness of love”).]

For there is no fear that parents will seem to hate their little son when he is beaten by them [Col. 1210C] for sinning, so that he may not sin further.

[Note: [Col. 1209] *vapulet* (“may be beaten”): Basel.]

Certainly, the perfection of love itself is proposed to us for imitation in God the Father, when it is said below [Matt. 5:44]: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you.”

[Note: [Col. 1209] “Certainly”: one edition reads *recte* (“rightly”).]

[Note: “For imitation”: the editions compared read *imitanda* (“to be imitated”).]

Yet it is said of God himself through the prophet [Prov. 3:12]: “For the Lord reproves the one whom he loves [Col. 1211A], and he scourges every son whom he accepts.”

[Note: [Col. 1211] *autem* (“however”): Böhm.]

The Lord also says [Luke 12:47–48]:

[Note: [Col. 1211C] “The servant”: This entire passage has been restored from the Gospel and from Blessed Augustine, and many other matters corrected.]

“The servant who does not know the will of his lord and does things deserving blows shall be beaten with few blows; but the servant who knows the will of his lord and does things deserving blows shall be beaten with many blows.”

[Note: [Col. 1211] The editions compared read *non digna plagis vap.*: “does things not deserving blows, shall be beaten.”]

Therefore, the sole *question asked* is *that he too* should avenge—the one to whom authority has been given by the order of things—and that he should avenge with the disposition with which a father scourges a little son, whom, because of his age, he is not yet able to hate.

[Note: [Col. 1211] Böhm lacks *non est* (“is not”) after “the question is.” The editions compared read *ipse* (“he himself”) for *ille* (“he”).]

[Note: [Col. 1211C] “With the disposition with which a father”: the original reads, “with the disposition with which a father [acts] toward a little son whom …”]

[Note: [Col. 1211] Basel adds *suum* (“his”) after “little son”; the editions compared add *tamen* (“nevertheless”) after “whom”; and they read *non* (“not”) rather than *nondum* (“not yet”).]

Thus an especially fitting example is supplied, by which it sufficiently appears that sin can be avenged out of love rather than left unpunished, so that he whom one punishes may be wished to become blessed, not through punishment miserable, but through correction; while nevertheless being ready, if need be, to endure with an even temper more things inflicted by the one whom he wishes to be corrected [Col. 1211B], whether he has authority to restrain him or not.

[Note: [Col. 1211] The Lyon editions read *hic* (“here”) for *hinc* (“thus/from this”); Lyon II–III read *autem* (“but”) for *enim* (“for”).]

[Note: “Especially fitting”: Ivo and the editions compared read *apertissimum* (“most evident”).]

[Note: “Is supplied”: the original reads *ducitur* (“is drawn”); the Argentinensis and Venetian II editions read *dicitur* (“is said”).]

[Note: “He whom”: Ivo and the editions compared read *quem* (“whom”) for *illum, in quem* (“him, upon whom”).]

[Note: “Become”: the editions compared add *esse* (“to be”).]

[Note: “Being ready”: the editions compared add *sit* (“he should be”).]

[Note: “If need be”: the Norcia, Venetian I–II, Paris, and Lyon I editions read *fiat* (“if it is done”).]

[Note: “Inflicted”: Ivo and the editions compared read *illicita* (“unlawful”) for *illata* (“inflicted”).]

[Note: “Over him”: the Basel edition reads *in eo* (“in/on him”) instead of *in eum* (“over/against him”); the sense is whether he has power to restrain that person.]

§ 1. Although great and holy men knew very well that this death, which separates the soul from the body, was not to be feared, nevertheless, taking account of the minds of those who feared it, they punished certain sins by death, so that a useful fear might be instilled in the living and so that, for those punished by death, it might not be death itself that caused harm, but rather that the sin—which could have increased if they lived—might be diminished.

[Note: [Col. 1211] The original, Anselm, and Ivo read *qui jam* (“who already”) for *quanquam* (“although”). Basel reads *utilibus* (“useful [persons]”) for *utilis* (“useful”). The final clause concerning sin being diminished is absent from the original, Anselm, and Ivo.]

They did not judge rashly, those to whom God had granted such judgment.

[Note: [Col. 1211] Basel and Lyon II–III read *vindicabant* (“punished” or “avenged”) for *judicabant* (“judged”); Basel reads *paraverat* (“had prepared”) for *donaverat* (“had granted”).]

Hence Elijah put many to death both with his own hand *and* [*et*] by fire obtained from God [3 Kings 18], while many other great men, in the same spirit, deliberating for human affairs, did not act rashly.

[Note: [Col. 1211] The editions compared, Anselm, and Ivo read *quod … fecerunt* (“that … did”) for *quum … fecerint* (“while … did”); Basel adds “great and divine” to “many other great men”; the original reads *consulendi* rather than *consulendo*.]

When the disciples had offered the Lord [*Domino*] the example of Elijah [Luke 9], recalling what had been done by him, so that he might also give them power to ask fire from heaven to consume those who had not offered them hospitality, the Lord rebuked in them not the example of the holy prophet but their ignorance concerning vengeance, which was still present in the unformed. He perceived that they desired vengeance not out of love but out of hatred [Col. 1212A].

[Note: [Col. 1211] Ivo and the editions compared read *consumendum* (“to consume”) for *consumendos* (“to consume them”). The original, Anselm, and Ivo read *praeberent* (“were offering”) for *praebuerant* (“had offered”). Ivo reads *amare* (“to love”) for *amore* (“out of love”).]

Accordingly, after he had taught them what it means to love one’s neighbor as oneself, and after the Holy Spirit had also been poured out—the Spirit whom, ten days after his ascension had been completed, he sent from above as he had promised—such acts of vengeance did not cease, although they occurred much more rarely than in the Old Testament. For there, for the most part, people serving under fear were oppressed; here, free people were nourished with the greatest love.

[Note: [Col. 1211] Ivo, the editions compared, and Böhm read *posteaquam* for *postquam* (“after”). The original, Ivo, and the editions compared read *maxime* (“most greatly”) for *maxima* (“with the greatest”).]

Thus, at the words of the apostle Peter, Ananias and his wife fell dead, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles [Acts 5]; they were not restored to life but were buried.

[Note: [Col. 1211] The Argentinensis, Norcia, Venetian I, and Böhm editions add *sunt* (“were”) after “buried.”]

[Col. 1212B] C. LII. Christians ought to pursue what is contrary to truth. Likewise Augustine, *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, book III, chapter 51.

[Note: [Col. 1211] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 15; *Decretum*, part 10, chapter 61.]

“You say: ‘Whoever persecutes a Christian is an enemy of Christ.’ You speak truly, if he persecutes in that Christian what is hostile to Christ. For a master in his servant, a father in his son, and a husband in his wife, when both are Christians, ought to pursue vices contrary to Christian truth. Or, if they do not pursue them, will they not deservedly be held guilty of negligence?”

[Note: [Col. 1211C–D] “A Christian”: Previously it was read: “Whoever, being a Christian, does not persecute the unjust …” Basel reads *qui iniquus* (“who is unjust”); Ivo’s *Panormia* has the same preceding wording, while the *Decretum* reads: “An unjust man persecutes a Christian.” The passage has been corrected from the original. These are Cresconius’s words, as the author of the gloss also observed.]

[Note: [Col. 1211] Argentinensis reads *deberet* (“ought”) for *debent* (“ought [plural]”); Basel reads *persequentur* (“will pursue”) for *persequantur* (“should pursue”).]

C. LIII. How a person ought to love his neighbor as himself. Likewise Augustine, to Macedonius, letter LII.

[Note: [Col. 1211] Letter 155, Maurist edition, written A.D. 414; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 16; *Decretum*, part 10, chapter 62.]

A person ought to love his neighbor as himself, so that he may lead any person whom he can—*whether* by the consolation of beneficence, by instruction in doctrine, or by the restraint of discipline—to worship God.

[Note: [Col. 1211] The Paris and Lyon editions read *beneficentia* (“by beneficence”) for *beneficentiae consolatione* (“by the consolation of beneficence”); Lyon II–III read *consultatione* (“by counsel/consultation”).]

C. LIV. On the same subject. Likewise Augustine, to Donatus the presbyter, letter CCIV.

[Note: [Col. 1212C–D] Augustine discusses this matter at length above, in the chapter beginning “It displeases,” on the same subject. Here the substance of that discussion has been gathered in a few words. Compare above, chapter 38.]

The wicked must be prevented from evil and compelled toward good.

[Col. 1213A] Gratian. From all these passages it is gathered that vengeance must be inflicted not out of love for vengeance itself but from zeal for justice; not so that hatred may be exercised but so that depravity may be corrected. But since vengeance is sometimes inflicted through damage to property, sometimes through scourging, and sometimes even through death, the question arises whether it is a sin for a judge or public official to hand the guilty over to death.

## QUESTION V

## GRATIAN

Part I. That no one is permitted to kill anyone is proved by the command in which the Lord prohibited homicide in the Law, saying [Exod. 20:13]: “You shall not kill.” Likewise in the Gospel [Matt. 26:52]: “Everyone who takes up the sword shall perish by the sword.”

[Col. 1213B] C. I. The wicked are not to be killed but corrected by scourges. Likewise Augustine, to Count Marcellinus, concerning captured Donatists, letter CLIX.

[Note: [Col. 1213] Letter 133, Maurist edition, written A.D. 412; Anselm, book 13, chapter 10; *Polycarpus*, book 7, title 11.]

I have learned from your nobility that the Circumcellions and clergy of the Donatist party, whom concern for public discipline had brought from the city of Hippo to trial for their deeds, have been heard; and that many of them confessed to the murder they committed against Restitutus, a Catholic presbyter, and to the killing of Innocentius, another Catholic presbyter, as well as to gouging out his eye and cutting off his finger.

[Note: [Col. 1213] “From the city of Hippo” is absent from the original. The editions compared read *causa* (“cause”) for *cura* (“concern”); Basel reads *voluntate* (“will”) for *nobilitate* (“nobility”).]

Therefore I have been seized by the greatest anxiety, lest perhaps your highness should judge that they must be punished with such severity of the laws that they suffer the same things as they inflicted. Accordingly, in this letter I implore your faith, which you have in Christ, by the mercy of our Lord himself, that you neither do this nor permit it to be done at all.

[Note: [Col. 1213] The editions compared read *non* (“not”) for *nec* (“nor”); Böhm reads *ne* (“lest”).]

For although we could overlook their death, since they seem to have been brought before the court not by our accusers but by their own notaries, whose duty it was, through vigilance, to safeguard the public peace, nevertheless we do not wish the sufferings of the servants of God to be avenged by equal punishments, as though by retaliation against the opposing party.

[Note: [Col. 1213] Basel reads *interitum* (“destruction”) for *interitu* (“death”); the editions compared read *quia* (“because”) for *qui* (“who”).]

[Note: [Col. 1213C–1214C] *Notariis* (“notaries”): In printed books of Blessed Augustine the reading is partly *notaria* and partly *notoria*; Anselm likewise has *notariis*. In the Vatican manuscript of Augustine’s letters, *notaria* is read throughout; and in letter 160, which concerns the same matter, *notaria* is found in printed and manuscript codices, likewise once in the *Breviculus* in the conference of the first day and twice in that of the second. *Notoria* is mentioned in the Digest, “On Accusations,” law *Ab accusatione*, § *Nunciatores*, concerning the senatorial decree on the Turpillian law, and in the Code, “On Accusations,” law *Ea quidem*. Apuleius also has *notoriam* in book 7 of *The Golden Ass*, and the glossary reads: *notoria*, ἀναφορά, “report” or “reference.”]

[Note: [Col. 1213] Anselm and the editions compared read “as though in punishment of the opposing party.”]

This is not because we wish to prevent criminal people from being deprived of the freedom to commit crimes; rather, we wish it to suffice that they remain alive and, without any part of their bodies being mutilated [Col. 1214A], be either directed by the restraint of the laws from insane unrest toward the tranquility of soundness, or assigned from wicked works to some useful labor.

[Note: [Col. 1213] Basel adds *sui* (“their own”) after “body.”]

This too is indeed called condemnation; but who does not understand that it ought rather to be called a benefit than a punishment, where neither the boldness to act savagely is released nor the healing remedy of repentance withdrawn?

[Note: [Col. 1213] The editions compared add *salutaris* (“salutary”) after “remedy.”]

Christian judge, fulfill the office of a devoted father. Be angry with iniquity in such a way that you remember to care for humanity; and in the atrocities of sinners do not exercise a desire for vengeance, but apply to the wounds of sinners the will to heal.

[Note: [Col. 1214C] “Be angry”: This has been corrected, with several additions, from the original, Anselm, and *Polycarpus*. Previously it read: “Remember so to be angry with iniquity that …” Basel reads *dilectionem vel diligentiam* (“love or diligence”).]

Do not lose the fatherly care that you preserved in the very investigation, when you extracted the confession of such great crimes not by stretching them on the rack, not by claws tearing furrows, not by burning flames, but by beatings with rods [Col. 1214B]—a mode of coercion used both by teachers of the liberal arts and by parents themselves, and often even employed by bishops in judicial proceedings.

[Note: [Col. 1213] Anselm has the same reading, “which you preserved.” Argentinensis reads *extendendo* (“by extending”), while the remaining editions read *extento* (“with the rack extended”), for *non extendente* (“not extending”). The editions compared, apart from the first Argentinensis and Basel editions, read *aculeo* (“spike” or “thorn”) for *equuleo* (“rack”).]

[Note: “Used by parents”: the editions compared add *adhibetur* (“is employed”); they also read *ut* for *et*, and Venetian II reads *ipse* for *saepe*.]

Therefore do not avenge more harshly what you *discovered* more gently; the need to investigate is greater than the need to punish. For this reason even the gentlest people carefully and persistently examine a hidden crime, so that they may find people whom they can spare.

[Note: “Hidden crime”: the editions compared read *admissum* (“committed crime”); they read *examinare debent* (“ought to investigate”) for *examinant* (“investigate”).]

C. II. The guilty must be punished otherwise than by the penalty of death. The same author, to Marcellinus, letter CLVIII.

[Note: [Col. 1213] Letter 139, Maurist edition, written A.D. 412; Anselm, book 13, chapter 11; *Polycarpus*, book 7, title 12.]

I ask you that the punishment of those who have confessed such great crimes be something other than the penalty of death, both for the sake of our conscience and in order to commend Catholic gentleness. For the very fruit of their confession reaches us, because the Catholic Church has found an occasion to preserve and display her gentleness even toward the most atrocious enemies. In such great cruelty, whatever vengeance proceeds short of their bloodshed will appear great gentleness.

[Note: [Col. 1213] Basel reads *eorum* (“of them”) for *illorum* (“of those persons”); it adds *eorum* (“of them”) after “bloodshed.”]

Although this may now seem unworthy to some of our people, who have been disturbed by that atrocity, and almost like laxity and negligence, nevertheless, once the agitations of impious minds have passed—agitations which recent events customarily stir more turbulently—an outstanding and splendid goodness will appear.

[Note: [Col. 1213] Basel reads *ex nostris* (“from our people”) for *quibusdam nostris* (“some of our people”); the remaining editions read *vestris* (“your people”). Basel adds *impiorum* (“of the impious”) after “minds.”]

[Col. 1215A] C. III. The wicked must be prevented from evil and compelled toward good. The same author, to Donatus, letter CXXVII.

[Note: [Col. 1215] Letter 100, Maurist edition, written A.D. 408; Anselm, book 13, chapter 12; *Polycarpus*, in the same place.]

There is only one thing that we fear in your justice: perhaps, because whatever evil impious and ungrateful people commit against the Christian community is undoubtedly more serious and atrocious than if *such things* were committed against others, you too may judge that it should be restrained according to the enormity of the crimes, rather than with consideration for Christian gentleness.

[Note: [Col. 1215] *Quoniam* (“because”) is absent from the Basel edition. The editions compared read *committatur* (“is committed”) for *committantur* (“are committed”).]

We implore you through Jesus Christ not to do so.

And a little later:

§ 1. Taking occasion from the terrible judgments and laws, we wish them to be corrected, lest they undergo the punishments of eternal judgment, not killed. We neither wish discipline concerning them to be neglected nor that they be restrained by the punishments which they deserve [Col. 1215B]. Thus restrain their sins, so that there may be people who repent of having sinned.

[Note: [Col. 1215] The original reads *incidant* (“lest they fall into”) for *luant* (“lest they undergo/pay”). The source reads *exerceri* (“to be exercised”) for *coerceri* (“to be restrained”).]

And a little later:

§ 2. Therefore, if you judge that men guilty of these crimes should be put to death, you will deter us from allowing anything indeed of this kind to reach your tribunal through our agency. Once this becomes known, *those people* will attack us with more unrestrained boldness, since necessity will have been imposed and enjoined upon us, so that we would choose rather to be killed by them than to bring them before your courts to be put to death.

[Note: [Col. 1215] “In these crimes” is absent from the editions compared except Basel. The editions compared read *viros putatis* (“you judge men”) for *homines putaveritis* (“you will judge people”); they add *quidem* (“indeed”). The original and Basel read *impacta et indicta* (“imposed and enjoined”) for *impacta* (“imposed”). The editions compared read *inferamus* (“bring before”) for *ingeramus* (“bring in/present”).]

C. IV. The peace of the Church is aided by the severity of rulers. The same author, to Macedonius, letter LIV.

[Note: [Col. 1215] Letter 153, Maurist edition, written A.D. 414; *Polycarpus*, book 1, final title.]

Your severity is *also* beneficial, through whose ministry our peace too is assisted. Our intercession is *also* beneficial, through whose ministry your severity too is tempered [Col. 1215C]. Do not be displeased that you are entreated by good people, because good people are not displeased that they are feared by the wicked.

§ 1. For the apostle Paul terrified human iniquity not only *by* the future judgment but also by your present secular authorities, asserting that they too belong to the administration of divine providence. “Let every soul,” he says, “be subject to the higher authorities,” and so forth [Rom. 13:1].

[Note: [Col. 1215C–D] “Present secular authorities”: In older editions of Blessed Augustine’s letters the margin reads, “by your present axes.” In the Antwerp edition this same reading appears in the text, but without the word “present.”]

These words of the apostle show the usefulness of your severity. Therefore, just as those who fear are commanded to owe love to those who cause fear, so those who cause fear are commanded to owe love to those who fear them.

Let nothing be done out of a desire to harm, but let everything be done out of the charity that seeks another’s good; let nothing be done cruelly, nothing inhumanely. Thus let the punishment imposed by the investigating judge be feared [Col. 1216A], yet let the religious plea of the intercessor not be despised, because both in punishing and in pardoning the only good purpose is the correction of human life.

But if perversity and impiety are so great that neither discipline nor pardon can avail for correcting it, nevertheless, in every intention and conscience that God sees, whether through severity or gentleness, let nothing except the duty of love be fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 1215D–1216C] “For correcting it”: This has been corrected from the original. Previously it read: “so that neither the remedies of discipline nor pardon may avail for correcting the guilty.”]

[Note: [Col. 1215] The editions compared read *ab omni* (“from every”) for *a bonis* (“by good persons”).]

C. V. PALEA

[Note: [Col. 1216D] This *Palea* is absent from the old copies that were collated, except one, in which it is joined to the preceding chapter.]

[Note: [Col. 1215] These are Gratian’s own words, transferred here from the dictum that follows, chapter 43 of Distinction 3, concerning penance. They are omitted in the Basel edition; in the Argentinensis edition they are attached to the preceding chapter.]

“This, however, must be understood of those whom present punishments change for the better, not of those who are obstinate in evil. If they were always to live, they would always sin; their punishment begins here and will endure eternally.”

[Col. 1216B] C. VI. Some are punished in the present life lest they be scourged eternally. Likewise Jerome, *On the Prophet Nahum*, on chapter 1.

[Note: [Col. 1215] *Polycarpus*, book 6, title 12.]

“What then,” he says, “do you devise against the Lord? He is [*ipse est*; the editions compared, except Basel and Lyon II–III, add *est*] the one who created the world and will bring about its consummation. But if he seems to you cruel, harsh, and bloody because in the Flood he destroyed the human race, rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah [cf. Gen. 7 and 19], drowned the Egyptians in the waves, and struck down the corpses of the Israelites in the wilderness, know that he inflicted punishments in the present for this reason: that he might not punish eternally.

[Note: [Col. 1215] Basel reads *creaverat* (“had created”) for *creavit* (“created”), and adds *Deus* (“God”) after “bloody.” The editions compared read *in fluctibus* (“in the waves”), while Lyon II–III read *in fluctu* (“in the wave”). Compare Exodus 15.]

“Certainly, either what the prophets say is true or it is false. If what they seem to say about his severity is true, they themselves said [Nah. 1:9, according to the Septuagint]: ‘The Lord will not take vengeance twice for the same thing in affliction.’ But if they are false, then false too is what is said [the same passage, according to the Vulgate]: ‘Double affliction shall not arise.’ Therefore the cruelty described in the Law is also false.

[Note: [Col. 1215] The editions compared read *scripta* (“written”) for *descripta* (“described”).]

“But if it is true—as they cannot deny—when the prophet says, ‘The Lord will not take vengeance twice for the same thing in affliction,’ then those who have been punished will not afterwards be punished. But if *they* will afterwards be punished, Scripture lies, which it is impious to say. Therefore those who perished in the Flood, the Sodomites, the Egyptians, and the Israelites in the wilderness received their evils during their lifetime.

[Note: [Col. 1215] The editions compared read *judicabit Deus* (“God will judge”) for *vindicabit Dominus* (“the Lord will take vengeance”).]

§ 1. Someone may ask here: if a believer caught in adultery is beheaded, what happens to him afterward? Either he will be punished, and this saying is false: ‘The Lord will not take vengeance twice for the same thing in affliction’; or he will not be punished, and adulterers ought to desire to escape eternal torments by being tortured in the present by a brief and swift punishment.

[Note: [Col. 1215] The editions compared again read *judicabit Deus* (“God will judge”) for “the Lord will take vengeance”; they add *ergo* (“therefore”). Compare chapter 44 of Distinction 3, concerning penance.]

“To this we shall answer that God, just as he knows the measures of all things, *also* knows the measures of punishments [Col. 1217A]; that he is not forestalled by the sentence of a judge; that the power to inflict punishment on the sinner afterward is not taken away from him; and that a great sin is expiated by great and lasting torments.

[Note: [Col. 1217] The editions compared read *mensuram* (“the measure”) for *mensuras* (“the measures”).]

“But if someone has been punished as was the man in the Law who cursed the Israelites [Lev. 24], or the one who gathered wood on the Sabbath [Num. 15], such persons are not afterwards punished, because a slight fault has been compensated by the present punishment.”

[Note: [Col. 1217] Basel adds *et brevis* (“and brief”) after “slight”; Argentinensis adds *ejus* (“of it”). The editions compared add *severitatis* (“of severity”) after “present punishment.”]

[Col. 1217B] C. VII. Those guilty of blood must be defended by the Church. Likewise Pope Gregory.

[Note: [Col. 1217] This is a summary of what is cited above from Gregory at C. 14, question 6, chapter 3. See Burchard, book 19, chapter 109; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, chapter 121.]

Let the Church defend those guilty of blood, lest it become a participant in the shedding of blood.

[Note: [Col. 1217C] In Burchard and Ivo, who cite this from sayings of Augustine, the reading is *non defendat* (“let it not defend”). Ivo reads *effusionis sanguinis* (“of the shedding of blood”) for *effusione sanguinis* (“in the shedding of blood”).]

Part II. Gratian. From this it is apparent that the wicked are to be restrained by scourges, not punished by mutilation of limbs or temporal death.

§ 1. But the saying that the Lord spoke to Moses is brought forward [Exod. 22:18]: “You shall not permit sorcerers to live.” Likewise [Lev. 20:15]: “Whoever lies with an animal shall surely be put to death.” A person marked by the crime of adultery or blasphemy is likewise ordered to be stoned without mercy.

Moses too, who had received the Law, punished idol-worshipers by death. Samuel also cut Agag, a very fat king, into pieces. Phinehas likewise pierced with a sword the Jew who was lying with a Midianite woman, and this was reckoned to him as righteousness. Similarly, some people are found in the Old Testament to have slain the wicked, yet they are called not transgressors of the Law but its defenders.

§ 1. Therefore, by that command each person is forbidden to arm himself on his own authority for someone else’s death; but the command of the Law does not forbid handing the guilty over to death. For one who, exercising public authority, kills the wicked by the command of the Law itself is considered neither a transgressor of that command nor excluded from the heavenly homeland.

Hence Augustine, to Publicola, letter CLIV.

[Note: [Col. 1217] Letter 47, Maurist edition, written A.D. 398; Anselm, book 13, chapter 18; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 1; *Decretum*, part 10, chapter 1; *Polycarpus*, book 7, title 11.]

C. VIII. To kill a person in the exercise of an office is not a sin.

[Col. 1218A] Concerning killing people so that no one may be killed by them, I do not approve the plan unless perhaps the person is a soldier or is bound by a public office, so that he does this not for himself but for others or for the state, in which he himself is included, having received lawful authority, if this is appropriate to his position.

[Note: [Col. 1217] The original and Ivo’s *Decretum* read *quisque* (“each person”) for *quisquam* (“anyone”).]

Those who are restrained by some fear from doing wrong perhaps receive some benefit even through this.

[Note: [Col. 1217] The editions compared read *mala* (“evil things”) for *male* (“wrongly”); Basel and Lyon II–III read *praestetur* (“may be bestowed”) for *praestatur* (“is bestowed”).]

Hence it was said [Matt. 5:39]: “Let us not resist evil,” lest perhaps vengeance delight us—the kind of vengeance that feeds the mind on another’s harm—not because we should neglect the correction of people.

[Note: [Col. 1217] Basel adds *forte* (“perhaps”); the Lyon II–III editions read *vos* (“you”) for *nos* (“us”).]

Thus neither is a person guilty of another’s death who, after enclosing his property with a wall made of stones, has someone struck and killed through the use of those stones [Col. 1218B].

[Note: [Col. 1217D–1218D] “From stones”: This has been corrected from the Vatican manuscript of Augustine’s letters. The printed editions omit these words. Gratian previously read: “when he has led a circuit of walls around his property.” Ivo’s *Panormia* has nearly the same wording; the *Decretum* reads, “when he has surrounded his property with walls”; Anselm reads, “when he has surrounded his property with a wall.”]

[Note: [Col. 1217] The original reads *ex ipsius ruinis* (“by its ruins”), and Böhm *ex ipsorum lapsu* (“by their fall”), for *ex ipsorum usu* (“through their use”). The editions compared read *interiit* (“died”) for *intereat* (“may die”).]

Nor is a Christian guilty if his ox kills someone by goring him, or his horse by kicking him, or for that reason ought Christian oxen not to have horns, horses hooves, or dogs teeth.

[Note: [Col. 1217] The editions compared and Ivo read *canes* (“dogs”) for *canis* (“dog”).]

Or, since the apostle Paul took sufficient steps to have it reported to the tribune that certain desperate men were preparing an ambush for him, and for that reason received armed escorts [Acts 23], if the wicked had fallen upon those *arms*, would Paul acknowledge himself guilty of their bloodshed?

[Note: [Col. 1217] Anselm and Argentinensis read *at* (“but”); the original reads *aut* (“or”); Ivo and the remaining editions read *aut vero* (“or indeed”). The editions compared read *perferret* (“report”) for *perferretur* (“be reported”), and *praeparatus* (“prepared”) for *praeparari* (“to be prepared”). The critical sign applies precisely to *arma* (“arms”).]

Far be it that things which we do or possess for a good and lawful purpose should be imputed to us if, through them and against our will, any harm happens to anyone.

[Note: [Col. 1217] Basel reads *propter* (“because of”) for *per* (“through”); the editions compared, except Basel and Lyon II–III, read *hoc* (“this”) for *haec* (“these”); Basel reads *quicquam* (“anything”) for *cuiquam* (“to anyone”).]

Otherwise household and agricultural tools ought not to be kept, lest someone kill himself or another with them; nor should a tree or a rope be kept, lest someone hang himself from it; nor should a window be made, lest someone throw himself down through it.

[Note: [Col. 1217] The Paris and Lyon I editions read *aliquando* (“at some time”) for *alioqui* (“otherwise”); the editions compared read *aut* (“or”) for *et* (“and”), and *ex eis* (“from/by them”) for *eis* (“with them”).]

[Note: The editions compared add “nor should trees be planted”; Ivo’s *Panormia* omits the words “nor a tree … throw himself down.” The critical sign applies to *aut restis* (“or a rope”), and to *est* (“is/should be”) in “nor should a window be made.” Böhm reads *quispiam* (“some person”) for *quisquam* (“anyone”).]

Why say more, when by listing such things I could not finish? For what is there in good and lawful human use from which harm could not also be inflicted?

[Note: [Col. 1217] The editions compared add *et* (“and”) before “what”; the critical signs apply precisely to *enim* (“for”) and *etiam* (“also”).]

[Col. 1219A] Part III. Gratian. No one is permitted by any authority of law even to kill himself.

Hence Augustine, book I of *The City of God*, chapters 17 and 18.

[Note: [Col. 1219] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, chapter 4. In the *Panormia* the beginning of the chapter through § 2, and §§ 3–5, are found.]

C. IX. Those who waged wars by God’s authority did not in any way transgress the commandment not to kill.

If it is not lawful for anyone, by private authority, to kill a human being—whether guilty or innocent—whose killing no law permits, then certainly one who kills himself is a murderer; and he becomes so much more guilty when he has killed himself, the more innocent he was in the matter for which he judged himself deserving of death. For if we rightly detest Judas’s deed, and truth judges that, when he hanged himself, he increased rather than expiated the crime of that wicked betrayal, because, by despairing of God’s mercy and repenting unto destruction, he left himself no place for wholesome repentance [Col. 1219B], how much more ought one who has nothing in himself to punish by such a penalty to refrain from killing himself? For Judas, when he killed himself, killed a wicked man; yet he ended this life guilty not only of Christ’s death but also of his own, because, although he was killed on account of his own crime, he was nevertheless killed by another crime of his own.

§ 1. But why should a man who has done no evil do evil to himself, and by killing himself kill an innocent human being, lest he suffer at another’s hands a guilty one, and commit in himself his own sin lest another’s be committed in him?

Likewise, chapter 20:

§ 2. “And it is not without reason” that nowhere in the holy and canonical books can we find anything divinely commanded or permitted to us to inflict death upon ourselves, whether for attaining immortality itself or for remedying and avoiding any evil [Col. 1219C]. For we must understand that we are forbidden where the Law says: “You shall not kill,” especially because it did not add “your neighbour,” as it did when forbidding false witness: “You shall not,” it says, “bear false witness against your neighbour.” Yet no one who bears false witness against himself should therefore suppose himself free from this crime, since the lover of his neighbour has received from himself the rule for loving his neighbour, for it is written: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” [Col. 1220A].

Moreover, if one who confesses a falsehood concerning himself is no less guilty of false witness than if he did this against his neighbour—although, in the commandment prohibiting false witness, it is prohibited against one’s neighbour, and the undiscerning may therefore think it is not forbidden for anyone to become a false witness against himself—how much more must it be understood that a man may not kill himself, when in the words, “You shall not kill,” with nothing further added, no one is excepted, certainly not the very person to whom the command is given?

Likewise, later in the same chapter:

§ 3. “You shall not kill”—not another; therefore, not yourself. For one who kills himself kills nothing other than a human being.

§ 4. The same divine authority did indeed make certain exceptions, so that it may be lawful for a human being to be killed; but these are excepted: those whom God commands to be killed, either by a law given generally, or by an express command addressed to a particular person for a particular time. Yet the person who performs the service owed to one giving the command does not himself kill, just as a sword is an instrument to its user. Therefore those who have waged wars with God as their author, or who, bearing the office of public authority, have punished criminals with death according to His laws—that is, according to the command of the most just reason—have by no means acted against the commandment, “You shall not kill.”

And Abraham was not only not accused of the crime of cruelty, but was even praised for piety, because he was willing to kill his son, not wickedly, but obediently [Col. 1220C]. And it is rightly asked whether what Jephthah did—killing the daughter who met her father—should be regarded as done by God’s command, since he had vowed to sacrifice to God whatever should first meet him as he returned victorious from battle. Nor is Samson otherwise excused for crushing himself along with his enemies in the collapse of the house, except because the Holy Spirit, who performed miracles through him, had secretly commanded this. Therefore, apart from those whom either a just law generally, or God Himself, the fountain of justice, specially commands to be killed, whoever kills a human being—whether himself or anyone else—is bound by the crime of homicide.

Likewise, chapter 26:

§ 5. We say this, we affirm it, and we approve it in every possible way: that no one ought voluntarily to inflict death upon himself, as though fleeing temporal troubles lest he fall into everlasting ones; no one on account of another’s sins, lest he thereby begin to have as his own a most grievous sin that another’s sin had not stained; no one on account of his past sins, for which he has all the more need of this life, so that they may be healed through repentance; no one as though from desire for a better life hoped for after death, because a better life after death does not receive those guilty of their own death.

[Col. 1221B] **C. X. No one may lay violent hands upon himself.** The same, *Against the Letters of Petilian*, book II, chapter 49. [Note: Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, c. 99; part 10, c. 7.]

You said: “The traitor perished by a noose; he left the noose to such people.” This has absolutely nothing to do with us. For we do not venerate as martyrs those who tied a noose about their own necks.

**C. XI. On the same matter.** Likewise Jerome, *On the Prophet Jonah*, on chapter 1, near the end. [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, c. 3.]

It is not ours to seize death, but willingly to receive it when inflicted by others. Hence even in persecutions it is not lawful for me to perish by my own hand—except where chastity is endangered—but one must submit one’s neck to the striker.

[Col. 1221C] **C. XII. No prayer is to be made for those who kill themselves.** Likewise, from the First Council of Braga, c. 34. [Note: Held A.D. 561.—*Regino*, book 2, c. 92; Burchard, book 19, c. 130; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, c. 188, part 15, c. 140.]

It was resolved that, for those who voluntarily inflict violent death upon themselves—whether by sword, poison, a precipice, hanging, or any other means—absolutely no commemoration be made for them in the offering, nor their bodies be escorted to burial with psalms. For many arrogate this practice to themselves through ignorance. It was similarly resolved concerning those who are punished for their crimes.

Gratian. Understand: those who are unrepentant. Likewise Augustine, in the same first book of *The City of God*, chapter 26. [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, c. 35; *Decretum*, part 10, c. 98.]

[Col. 1222A] **C. XIII. A soldier who kills a man in obedience to authority is not guilty of homicide.**

**IV. Part.** When a soldier, obeying the authority under which he has been lawfully placed, kills a man, he is guilty of homicide under no law of his state; indeed, unless he does so, he is guilty of deserting and despising command. But if he had acted on his own initiative and authority, he would have incurred the crime of shedding human blood. Thus, for the very act for which he is punished if he does it without command, he will be punished if he does not do it when commanded.

**C. XIV. A person is a murderer who, on his own initiative, kills those whom a judge commands to be killed.** Likewise, *Questions on Exodus*, question XXXIX, on chapter 11. [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, c. 39; *Decretum*, part 10, c. 103.]

When an officer of a judge kills someone whom the judge [Col. 1222B] ordered to be killed, certainly, if he does so on his own initiative, he is a murderer, even if he kills someone whom he knows ought to have been put to death by the judge.

**C. XV. As obedience is deservedly praised, so one who usurps what has not been granted to him is blamed.** The same, *Against Faustus*, book XXII, chapter 73.

The eternal law has placed certain matters, as it were, in an intermediate position for human beings, so that boldness is deservedly blamed in usurping them, whereas obedience is justly praised in carrying them out. Abraham, if his impulse in killing his son had been spontaneous, would have been deemed abominable; but he performed obedient service to God’s command.

[Note: This chapter has been compiled from the words of Blessed Augustine, but altered at the compiler’s discretion. Augustine’s text continues: “Therefore, if a spontaneous impulse in killing his son is detestable, while service obedient to God’s command is found not merely blameless but even praiseworthy, why, Faustus, do you reproach Moses because he despoiled the Egyptians,” etc.]

**C. XVI. Duties of punishment may be discharged in a good spirit.** The same, *Questions on the Gospels*, book I, question 10. [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, c. 40; *Decretum*, part 10, c. 106.]

[Col. 1222C] Duties of punishment may be discharged in a good spirit, as may the law and the judge.

**C. XVII. One who prosecutes a crime in order to free the person is not unjust but humane.** The same, *To Macedonius*, letter LIV. [Note: Letter 153, Maurist edition; written A.D. 414.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, c. 107.]

He is bound by a fellowship not of injustice but rather of humanity who prosecutes a crime precisely in order that he may be a liberator of the human being.

**C. XVIII. Why royal authority and legal punishments were instituted.** The same, in the same letter. [Note: Ivo, ibid., c. 108.]

The authority of the king, the legal right of the examiner, the executioner’s claws, the soldier’s arms, the discipline of the ruler [Col. 1223A], and even the severity of a good father were not instituted without purpose. All these have their proper limits, causes, reasons, and uses. When they are feared, the wicked are restrained, and the good live more peacefully among the wicked.

**C. XIX. Sometimes the person who occasions a death sins more than the one who kills.** The same, ibid. [Note: Ivo, ibid.]

When one human being is killed by another, it makes a great difference whether it occurs from a desire to harm or to take something unjustly—as happens at the hands of an enemy or a robber—or in the ordered course of vengeance or obedience—as by a judge or an executioner—or from necessity of escape or rescue, as when a robber is killed by a traveller or an enemy by a soldier.

§ 1. And sometimes the person who caused the death is more at fault than the one who killed: for example, if someone deceives his surety and that surety undergoes legal punishment on his behalf. Yet not everyone who causes another’s death is guilty. For what if someone solicits illicit sex and kills himself if he does not obtain it? What if a son, fearing his father’s loving blows, dies by throwing himself from a height? What if one person, because another has been set free—or lest another be set free—inflicts death on himself? Are we, on account of these causes of other persons’ deaths, either to consent to crime, or to abolish punishment for sin—which is undertaken not from a desire to harm but from zeal for correction—even paternal blows, or to restrain works of mercy? When such things happen, we ought to feel human sorrow for them, but not on that account to repress our willingness to do what is right, lest such things happen.

[Col. 1223C] **C. XX. What priests cannot accomplish through teaching, authority should compel through the fear of discipline.** Likewise Isidore, *Sentences*, book III, *On the Supreme Good*, chapter 55. [Note: Burchard, book 15, c. 43; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 16, c. 44; *Polycraticus*, book 6, title 1.]

Secular rulers sometimes hold the heights of authority within the Church in order that, through that same authority, they may safeguard ecclesiastical discipline. Otherwise, powers within the Church would not be necessary, except so that what priests cannot accomplish through the word of teaching [Col. 1224A], authority may accomplish through the fear of discipline. Often the heavenly kingdom advances through the earthly kingdom, so that those within the Church who act against the faith and discipline of the Church may be crushed by the rigour of princes, and sovereign authority may impose upon the necks of the proud that discipline which the Church’s humility is unable to exercise; and, in order that it may deserve reverence, it may impart the force of authority.

[Note: “Reverence”: in various editions of this book the reading is: “and in order that it may deserve reverence, it may impart by the strength of authority.” In the Council of Paris under Louis and Lothair, book 2, chapter 2, where this passage is cited, the reading is: “and, in order that it may deserve reverence, authority may impart strength.” But in Ivo—for Burchard’s manuscript plainly contains an error—the reading is: “and thus it deserves reverence, so that it may impart the strength of authority.”]

Let secular princes know that they must render an account to God on behalf of the Church which they undertake to defend for Christ. For whether the Church’s peace and discipline are increased through faithful princes or dissolved, He who entrusted His Church to their authority will demand an account from them.

[Col. 1224B] **C. XXI. Both royal power and priestly authority should defend matters pertaining to the divine confession.** Likewise Pope Leo, letter XXIX, to the Empress Pulcheria. [Note: Letter 60, written A.D. 460, Ballerini edition; *Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 43, c. 3; Anselm, book 1, c. 74; *Polycraticus*, book 1, title 27.]

Human affairs cannot otherwise be secure unless matters pertaining to the divine confession are defended by both royal and priestly authority.

**C. XXII. Those whom priestly admonition cannot correct, secular power should correct.** Likewise, from the Third Council of Tours, c. 41. [Note: Held A.D. 813.—Burchard, book 7, c. 29; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 9, c. 65; cf. *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, book 2, c. 43.]

Among us are found many incestuous persons, parricides, and murderers; but some of them refuse to heed priests’ admonitions, wishing to persist in their former crimes. Such persons ought to be restrained from so depraved a custom by the discipline of secular power [Col. 1224C], since they were unwilling to be converted by the saving admonitions of priests.

**C. XXIII. It is the office of kings to restrain the wicked and support the good.** Likewise Jerome, *On Jeremiah*, on chapter 22.

The proper office of kings is to execute judgment and justice; to rescue from the hand of those who oppress by accusation the person crushed by force; and to give aid to the stranger, the orphan, and the widow, who are more easily oppressed by authorities [Col. 1225A]. And in order to lay upon them a greater concern for God’s commandments, the Prophet added: “Do not afflict,” so that you should not merely fail to rescue them, but should not even allow them, through your connivance, to be afflicted by others; “and do not shed innocent blood in this place.” That is, murderers, sacrilegious persons, and so forth. [Note: Cf. below, c. 31.] And a little later: “If,” he says, “you do these things, O kings of Judah, you will retain your former power.”

**V. Part. Gratian.** Yet faith and reverence ought to be maintained toward princes and authorities themselves; anyone who does not show these cannot obtain rewards from God.

[Col. 1225B] Therefore the same Jerome, in his letter on Titus, chapter 2, at the verse “Servants toward masters”:

**C. XXIV. One who disdains to maintain faith and reverence toward authorities is deprived of eternal reward.**

If servants are faithful in the least things toward earthly masters, greater rewards will begin to be entrusted to them by God. He adorns the teaching of the Lord who does what is appropriate to his condition; conversely, he disgraces it who is not subject in all things, whose condition displeases him, and who, being contentious and fraudulent, shows good faith in nothing. For how can one be faithful with God’s substance who was unable to show faithfulness to an earthly master?

**C. XXV. Military discipline preserves everything for the king.** Likewise Ambrose, book I, *On the Patriarchs*, that is, *On Abraham*, chapter 3.

[Col. 1225C] Someone may say: “Since Abraham himself was victorious, how does he say to the king of Sodom, ‘I will take nothing from you,’ when the spoil was surely within the victor’s power?” He teaches military discipline: that everything be preserved for the king. Yet he maintains that a share of the gain should be granted as payment for labour to those who had perhaps joined him as allies for assistance. And therefore, because he did not seek reward from a human being, he received it from God, as we read written: “After these things the word of the Lord came to Abraham in a vision, saying: ‘Do not fear, Abraham; I will protect you; your reward shall be exceedingly great.’”

**VI. Part. Gratian.** Moreover, just as we are obliged to show faith and reverence to princes and authorities, so the administrators of secular dignities bear the obligation of defending churches [Col. 1225D]. If they disdain to do this, they are to be excluded from communion.

[Col. 1226A] Therefore John VIII:

**C. XXVI. Those who hold public dignities ought to hear the complaints of churches attentively.**

Administrators of secular dignities, who undoubtedly ought to be appointed for the protection of churches, the defence of orphans and widows, and the restraint of the rapacious, should, whenever they are approached by bishops and ecclesiastical persons, listen attentively to their complaints; and, as necessity requires, examine them without negligence and correct them with diligent care. But if, not keeping the fear of God before their eyes, they are found to neglect these matters after a second and third admonition, let them know that they are deprived of all communion until they make fitting satisfaction.

[Col. 1226B] **C. XXVII. Not only human beings, but also hostile powers, are agents of God’s wrath.** Likewise Jerome, *On Joel*, on chapter 2. [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, c. 48; *Decretum*, part 10, c. 111.]

**VII. Part.** Not only human beings are ministers and avengers of God’s wrath against those who do evil—hence they do not bear the sword without reason—but also hostile powers, which are called the fury and wrath of God.

**C. XXVIII. One who slays cruel people is not such as he appears to those who suffer.** The same, *On Isaiah*, on chapter 13. [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, c. 49; *Decretum*, part 10, c. 112.]

One who slays cruel people is not cruel; but he is called cruel because he appears cruel to those who suffer [Col. 1226C]. For a robber hanging from the gallows also considers the judge cruel.

**C. XXIX. One who strikes the wicked insofar as they are wicked is God’s minister.** The same, *On Ezekiel*, book III, on chapter 9. [Note: Burchard, book 6, c. 43; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, c. 51; *Decretum*, part 10, c. 114; cf. below, question 8, c. 33.]

One who strikes the wicked insofar as they are wicked, and has instruments of killing in order to kill the most wicked, is the Lord’s minister.

**C. XXX. A judge does not commit a crime by overcoming wicked people.** The same, *On the Epistle to the Galatians*, book II, on chapter 3. [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, c. 52; *Decretum*, part 10, c. 115.]

A judge is not the author of wrongdoing by overcoming wicked people.

[Col. 1226D] **C. XXXI. One who punishes murderers, sacrilegious persons, and poisoners does not shed blood.** The same, *On Jeremiah*, book IV, on chapter 22.

To punish murderers, sacrilegious persons, and usurers [Col. 1227A] is not the shedding of blood, but the administration of the laws.

**C. XXXII. Secular princes ought not spare the most wicked.** Likewise Cyprian, *On the Exhortation to Martyrdom*, chapter 5.

“If you hear in one of the cities which the Lord your God will give you to dwell there, people saying: ‘Let us go and serve other gods, foreign gods, whom you have not known,’ you shall kill and slay all who are in the city with the sword; and you shall burn the city with fire, and it shall remain uninhabited forever; it shall not be rebuilt again, so that the Lord God may turn away from the indignation of His wrath. And He shall give you mercy and have mercy on you and multiply you, if you obey the voice of the Lord your God and keep His commandments.”

Mindful of this commandment and its force, Mattathias [Col. 1227B] killed the man who had approached the altar to sacrifice. If these commandments were observed before Christ’s coming with respect to worshipping God and despising idols, how much more ought they to be observed after Christ’s coming, when He came not merely to exhort us in words, but also in deeds?

**C. XXXIII. Faithlessness is sometimes chastised by the scourges of tribulation.** Likewise Augustine, *Against the Letters of Petilian*, book II, chapter 83. [Note: Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, c. 75.]

No one is to be compelled unwillingly to the faith; but faithlessness is accustomed to be chastised by the scourges of tribulations through the severity—indeed also through the mercy—of God. Because excellent morals are chosen by freedom of will, does it follow that the worst morals are not punished by the integrity of the law? Yet the punitive discipline directed against evil living is misplaced unless the prior care of instruction in good living is set forth.

Therefore, whatever laws have been enacted against you, you are not compelled by them to do good, but are forbidden to do evil. For no one can do good unless he chooses and loves it, which lies within free will.

And below, chapter 84:

§ 1. When kings enact something against you, believe that you are being admonished to consider why you suffer these things. If it is for justice’s sake, then truly they are your persecutors, while you are blessed, who, having suffered persecution for justice’s sake, shall possess the kingdom of heaven. But if it is because of the wickedness of your schism [Col. 1228A], what are they but your correctors? You, however, like the guilty perpetrators of other crimes who pay penalties under the laws, are surely unhappy both in this world and in the world to come.

**C. XXXIV. Injury done to Christ’s sacraments ought to be punished by kings.** The same, in the same book, chapter 92. [Note: Ivo, ibid.]

If King Nebuchadnezzar was not a persecutor because he most justly punished the crime committed against holy Daniel, how ought kings punish the fact that Christ’s sacraments are scornfully rejected, if the Prophet’s limbs deserved to be avenged because they had been exposed to danger?

[Col. 1228B] **C. XXXV. The most diligent rulers are those who persecute the wicked so that they may flee from wickedness.** The same, *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 17. [Note: Ivo, ibid.]
