If holy and canonical Scripture proves that you have erected an altar against Christ’s Church, that you have separated yourselves from Christian unity, which is spread throughout the whole world, by sacrilegious schism, and that you oppose the body of Christ—which is the Church spread throughout the whole world—by rebaptizing, blaspheming, and attacking it as far as you can, then you are impious and sacrilegious. But those who decree that you should be deterred and restrained for so great a crime by the very mild warnings of losses—of places, honours, or money—so that, considering why you suffer these things, you may recognize and flee your sacrilege and be freed from eternal condemnation, are counted both most diligent rulers [Col. 1228C] and most merciful counsellors.

**C. XXXVI. A servant or son is not loved when he is not corrected.** The same, *Homilies on the First Epistle of John*, tractate VII. [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, c. 22; *Decretum*, part 10, c. 76.]

Do not suppose that you love your servant when you do not beat him, or that you love your son when you do not discipline him, or that you love your neighbour when you do not correct him. This is not charity but weakness. Let charity be fervent in correcting and reforming. If conduct is good, let it be approved; if it is bad, let it be amended.

[Col. 1229A] **C. XXXVII. It is the duty of an innocent person both to harm no one and to punish the sinner.** The same, *The City of God*, book XIX, chapter 16. [Note: Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, c. 77.]

[Note: The complete passage in Blessed Augustine reads: “For just as it is not beneficence, by giving help, to bring it about that a greater good is lost, so neither is it …” The printed reading *plectitur* (“is punished”) has been restored from the original; formerly the text read *prius odio habetur* (“is first held in hatred”), while Ivo reads *oditur* (“is hated”).]

It is not innocence to spare someone and allow him to fall into a graver evil. Therefore it pertains to the duty of an innocent person not only to inflict evil on no one, but also to restrain from sin or to punish sin, so that either the person punished may be corrected by experience, or others may be frightened by the example.

**C. XXXVIII. One who spares vices so that they may be nourished is not merciful.** The same, *To Lotharius*. [Note: Letter 104, Maurist edition, written to Nectarius A.D. 405; Ivo’s *Decretum* calls him “Laetarius,” part 10, c. 79; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, c. 25.]

One who spares and cherishes vices so that he may not grieve the wills of sinners is no more merciful than one who does not wish to take a knife from a child lest he hear him crying, and does not fear that the child may suffer pain when wounded or be destroyed.

**C. XXXIX. Enormous crimes should be punished through secular judges.** Likewise Haymo, *On the Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 13. [Note: In printed editions this was cited from Augustine, but in old copies it is attributed to Haymo, in whom it is found.]

[Note: It seems rather to be the work of Remigius of Auxerre. In the Basel and Lyons II–III editions it is attributed to Ambrose; in the remaining editions and in Ivo’s *Panormia* (book 8, c. 5), to Augustine. Ivo’s *Decretum*, part 10, c. 11, is cited.]

There are certain enormous crimes which are punished rather by the judges of the world than by bishops and rulers of churches: for example, when someone kills the Apostolic Pontiff, a bishop, a presbyter, or a deacon. Kings and princes of the world condemn persons guilty of such acts. Therefore they do not bear the sword without reason [Col. 1229C], those who judge such crimes. For they are especially established for robbers, murderers, and plunderers, both to condemn them and to restrain others through fear of them.

## Textual apparatus

[Col. 1219] *innocentem* (“innocent”): Edd. coll. o.—Ivo, *Panormia*. *fuerit* (“he was”): Argentinensis and Basel editions. *desperandum* (“one must despair”): Basel edition. *sui caede* (“from his own killing”): Lyons II–III; *sua caede* (“from his killing”): remaining editions—Ivo, *Decretum*. “also of his own [death]” is omitted in Edd. coll. o., Basel I, and Lyons II–III. *suo* (“by his own [crime]”) is absent in Basel and Lyons II–III.

[Col. 1219] In §2, the words from *Neque* (“and not”) through *frustra* (“without reason”) are absent from Ivo’s *Decretum*. *ipsius* (“itself”): Edd. coll. o. *carendi* (“lacking”) is the original reading—Ivo, *Decretum*; *curandi* means “remedying.” *criminis* (“of crime”): Basel edition. *necesse* (“necessity”): same edition. Exodus 20:3 is cited for “You shall not kill”; Exodus 20:16 for the false-witness quotation. *apud* (“with”): Argentinensis edition. *Non* (“not”): Argentinensis and Basel editions. “Yet” is absent in Basel; “anyone” is missing there. *dilector* (“lover”) is not found in Ivo. *quoniam quidem* (“since indeed”): Edd. coll. o. Matthew 22:39 is cited for “You shall love your neighbour.” *testimonio* (“by false witness”): Basel. *fateatur* (“confesses”): same. *assistat* (“stand by”) is the original reading—Ivo and Basel; the printed text’s *exsistat* means “become” or “appear.” *nihil* (“nothing”): Ivo and Edd. coll. o. *intelligatur* (“is understood”): Ivo and the same editions.

[Col. 1219] In §3, Ivo and the same editions read: “not yourself, nor another.”

[Col. 1219] In §4, *tamen* (“however”): Argentinensis and Nuremberg editions; *vero inde* (“indeed thence”): Basel and Lyons II–III. *faciat* (“may make”): Venice II, Lyons I, and Paris; *facit* (“makes”): Nuremberg and Venice I. The words from *ut* (“so that”) through *occidi* (“to be killed”) are omitted in the *Panormia*, Ivo’s *Decretum*, and Edd. coll. o. except Lyons II–III, but occur in Augustine. *sive* (“or”): absent in Ivo and the *Panormia*. Ivo’s *Panormia* reads “or indeed he who kills”; Edd. coll. o. have the same sense but omit *autem* (“however”).

[Col. 1219D–1220D] “Yet he does not himself kill”: corrected from the original, especially the Antwerp copy. Previously this whole passage stood very differently; many other restorations have also been made.

[Col. 1219] *praebet* (“renders” or “provides”): Lyons II–III. *jus legis* (“the law’s right”): Edd. coll. o. Genesis 22 is cited for Abraham. Judges 11 for Jephthah. “He had” is absent in Edd. coll. o., Basel I, and Lyons II–III. *advovisset* (“had additionally vowed”): Ivo, *Decretum*. *victuro* (“about to conquer”): Basel. Judges 16 is cited for Samson. *sanctus* (“Holy”) is added in Basel and Lyons editions. *ista* (“that”): Basel.

[Col. 1221] In §5, Edd. coll. o. except Argentinensis, Nuremberg, and Venice I add *peccatum* (“sin”). Basel and Lyons II–III read: “lest another’s [sin] be committed in him”; Ivo and the remaining editions omit the words altogether. *in hac* (“in this”): Edd. coll. o. *possit* (“it may be possible”): Basel. *reus* (“a guilty person”): Argentinensis; *reum* (“the guilty”) in the remaining editions. Argentinensis reads *meliorem vitam* (“a better life”) for *melior ... vita* (“a better ... life”).

[Col. 1221] C. X: *perit* (“perishes”): Basel; *hic* (“this”): same.

[Col. 1221] C. XI: *accipere* (“receive”): Edd. coll. o. *perfectionibus* (“perfections”): Venice I. Edd. coll. o. except Basel I add *mihi* (“for me”).

[Col. 1221] C. XII: Edd. Lyons II–III add *iis* (“for those”); the remaining editions, the Spanish Collection, Burchard, and Ivo read *hi* (“these”). *voluntarie* (“voluntarily”) is absent from the Spanish Collection and Regino. “Absolutely” is absent from the same Collection, Regino, Burchard, and Ivo. “For” is missing in the Spanish Collection; *eis* (“them”): Basel. *usurparunt* (“have arrogated”): Spanish Collection, Regino, Burchard, and Ivo. *moriuntur* (“die”): Edd. coll. o.

[Col. 1221] C. XIII: *si non* (“if not”): Edd. coll. o.

[Col. 1221–1222] C. XV: the compiler altered Augustine’s words. Augustine’s text continues: “Therefore, if a spontaneous impulse in killing his son is detestable, while service obedient to God’s command is found not merely blameless but even praiseworthy, why, Faustus, do you reproach Moses because he despoiled the Egyptians, etc.”

[Col. 1221] C. XVI: the original, Ivo, and Edd. coll. o. except Basel and Venice I read *implere boni* (“good people may discharge”); Basel and Venice I read *impleri boni* (“to be discharged by good people”).

[Col. 1221] C. XVII: *devictus* (“conquered”): Edd. coll. o. and Ivo; the printed *devinctus* means “bound.”

[Col. 1221–1223] C. XVIII: the original adds *gladii* (“of the sword”) after “the examiner’s right.” *quieti* (“the good, at peace”): Ivo and Edd. o.

[Col. 1223] C. XIX: *aut* (“or”): Basel; *vel* (“or”): Edd. o. Basel and Lyons II–III add *quando* (“when”). Ivo and Edd. o. read *velut si* (“as if” or “for example if”). *quisquis* (“whoever”): Basel; *quispiam* (“someone”): the remaining editions except Argentinensis. Edd. coll. o. except Basel read *Aut etiam* (“or even”). They add *verbera* (“blows”) after “paternal”; they read *toleranda* (“to be endured”) for *tollenda* (“to be abolished”). *occidant* (“kill”) is Basel’s reading for *accidant* (“happen”). *reprimimus* (“we repress”): Ivo; *reprimamus* (“let us repress”): Edd. coll. o. Argentinensis reads *veritatem vel voluntatem* (“truth or willingness”) for *voluntatem*.

[Col. 1223–1224] C. XX: Edd. coll. o. read *praevalent sacerdotes* (“priests prevail”) for *praevalet sacerdos* (“the priest prevails”). *impetret* (“obtain”): Venice I–II and Paris; *imperet* (“command”): remaining editions, original, Burchard, and Ivo. *utilitas* (“usefulness”): Burchard and Edd. coll. o. *prius* (“previously”): Basel. *impertiatur* (“may impart”): Lyons II–III; *impartiatur* (“may bestow”): remaining editions. *reddituros esse* (“will have to render”): Edd. coll. o. The phrase “from” is absent in those editions except Lyons II–III. *exigit* (“demands”): Burchard and Edd. coll. o. *tradidit* (“handed over”): those editions except Basel; Basel and Lyons II–III add *committendam* (“to be entrusted”).

[Col. 1223] C. XXI: *Res autem* (“but affairs”) is absent from Leo, Anselm, and the Argentinensis, Nuremberg, and Venice I editions. *omnes* (“all”): Edd. coll. o. and Anselm.

[Col. 1223–1224] C. XXII: the original, the Capitularies, and the cited Collections add *proh dolor* (“alas”). *potentiam disciplinae* (“the power of discipline”): Basel. *converti* (“be converted”): Argentinensis; *reverti* (“return”): remaining editions.

[Col. 1223–1225] C. XXIII: the original adds *autem* (“however”); Basel reads *enim* (“for”). *officium* (“office”) is absent from Jerome. *calumniantium* (“of those oppressing by accusation”): Edd. coll. o. *quae* (“who,” feminine): Basel. *potestatibus* (“authorities”): same. Burchard, Ivo’s *Panormia*, and *Decretum* are cited at this point. Basel and Lyons II–III add *Propheta* (“the Prophet”). Jeremiah 7:6 is cited. *contristari* (“to be afflicted”): Edd. coll. o. Those editions expand the phrase: “that, through your connivance, they should come to be afflicted by others.” *hoc* (“this”): Edd. coll. o.

[Col. 1225] C. XXIV: *minimis* (“the least things”): those editions. They add *praemia* (“rewards”). *ut* (“so that”): Argentinensis, Basel, and Nuremberg. *confundat* (“may disgrace”): Argentinensis and Basel.

[Col. 1225] C. XXV: *Ducet* (“will lead”): original. *dixit* (“said”): Edd. coll. o. except Argentinensis; Genesis 14:23 is cited. *decet* (“is fitting”): original and Edd. coll. o. except Basel and Lyons II–III. *visione* (“vision”): Argentinensis; Genesis 15:1 is cited. *magna* (“great”): Edd. coll. o.

[Col. 1225] C. XXVI is, rather, chapter 13 of the Council of Ravenna, held A.D. 877; Anselm, book 3, c. 107 (110), is cited.

[Col. 1225] C. XXVII: *in* (“against” or “in”): absent from Ivo. *et* (“and”): original, Ivo, and *Decretum*.

[Col. 1225–1226] C. XXVIII: the words *crudelis ideo vocatur* (“he is therefore called cruel”) are absent from the original, Ivo, and the Argentinensis edition. *videatur* (“may appear”): original and Ivo’s *Decretum*. *et* (“also”): absent from Ivo.

[Col. 1225] C. XXIX: *causam* (“cause”) is Burchard’s reading for *vasa* (“instruments”); *Dei* (“God’s”): Burchard and Edd. coll. o.

[Col. 1225] C. XXX: *hominem* (“a wicked person”): Argentinensis. *interimendo* (“killing”): Basel.

[Col. 1225] C. XXXI: *fenerarios* (“usurers”): Argentinensis and Basel; the printed *venenarios* means “poisoners.”

[Col. 1227] C. XXXII: Deuteronomy 13:12 ff. is cited. *te* (“there”) is absent from Argentinensis. *alienis* (“foreign”): Edd. coll. o. They add *Deos* (“gods”). *noscis* (“you know”): Argentinensis; *novistis* (“you have known,” plural): Basel. *interficies necabisque* (“you shall kill and slay”): Argentinensis and Basel. *Deus* (“God”): Edd. coll. o. 1 Maccabees 2 is cited for Mattathias. Basel and Lyons II–III add “with respect to worshipping God.” *adhortatus* (“exhorted”): Basel; *sit* (“may be”): Edd. coll. o.

[Col. 1227–1228] C. XXXIII: “as you say” is absent from Ivo; Edd. coll. o. read “as you say” in connection with the opening clause. *praeposita* (“set before”) is Basel’s reading for *praepostera* (“misplaced”). In Augustine and Ivo the text reads: “unless, when the preceding teaching of right living is despised”; it was not changed because of the gloss on *cura* (“care”). *Sic* (“thus”): Edd. coll. o. *aliqui* (“some persons”): Basel. *leges* (“laws”): Edd. coll. o. Basel and Lyons II–III add *estis* (“you are”); Edd. coll. o. except Argentinensis add the same after “having suffered persecution.” *quia possidebitis* (“because you shall possess”): those editions. Ivo and Edd. coll. o. read *illi quidem* (“those indeed”). Edd. coll. o. except Argentinensis and Basel read *pendent* (“pay”) for *pendunt* (“pay”). Edd. coll. o. except Argentinensis, Nuremberg, and Venice I add *eritis* (“you will be”).

[Col. 1227] C. XXXIV: *fuerit* (“has been”): Basel. Edd. coll. o. except Argentinensis add *rex* (“king”); Daniel 3 is cited.

[Col. 1227–1228] C. XXXV: *altaria* (“altars”): Ivo and Edd. coll. o. *corpore* (“body,” ablative): Nuremberg and Venice I. *expugnando* (“destroying” or “assailing”): Edd. coll. o. except Basel and Lyons II–III. *adversarios* (“adversaries”): Edd. coll. o. *sepultura* (“burial”): Nuremberg and Venice I. Edd. coll. o. add *estis* (“you are”). *bonorum* (“property”): those editions except Argentinensis, Nuremberg, and Venice I.

[Col. 1227] C. XXXVI: *te* (“you”) is absent from Ivo in each of the two marked occurrences. *corrigis* (“correct”): Edd. coll. o. and Ivo. *sint* (“may be”): Argentinensis, and also Basel and Lyons II–III in the second instance; it is absent from the remaining editions. *delectentur* (“may they delight”): Nuremberg and Venice I. Edd. coll. o. except Argentinensis add *autem* (“however”).

[Col. 1229–1230] C. XXXVII: Augustine’s complete passage begins: “For just as it is not beneficence, by giving help, to bring it about that a greater good is lost, so neither is it ...” The printed *plectitur* (“is punished”) has been restored from the original; formerly the text read *prius odio habetur* (“is first held in hatred”), while Ivo reads *oditur* (“is hated”).

[Col. 1229] C. XXXVIII: *fovet* (“cherishes”) is the original and Ivo’s *Decretum*; *voluntates* (“wills”): Basel.

[Col. 1229] C. XXXIX: This chapter is found under Haymo’s name in old copies, but seems rather to be by Remigius of Auxerre; Basel and Lyons II–III attribute it to Ambrose, while the remaining editions and Ivo’s *Panormia* attribute it to Augustine. Ivo’s *Decretum*, part 10, c. 11, is cited. Ivo’s *Decretum* and Edd. coll. o. add *est* (“is”); Ivo’s *Panormia* reads *enim* (“for”). The original and Ivo read *portat ... dijudicat* (“bears ... judges”); Basel reads *vindicant* (“punish” or “avenge”) for *dijudicant* (“judge”). *latrones* (“robbers”) is absent from Ivo. Ivo and the original read *compescere faciant* (“cause [others] to be restrained”) for *compescant* (“restrain”).

### C. XL. The king must restrain thefts and crimes. Likewise Cyprian, in the ninth kind of abuse

[Note: This little work, *On the Twelve Degrees of Abuse*, was printed in the ninth volume of the works of Blessed Augustine; but it is also found in one Vatican manuscript of the works of Blessed Cyprian, and in the Council of Paris, book 2, chapter 1, this same ninth kind of abuse is reported from Cyprian, as also in Ivo and the Panormia.]

[Note: It is neither Cyprian’s nor Augustine’s, to whom some have attributed it.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, ch. 33; *Decretum*, part 10, ch. 96.]

A king ought to restrain thefts, punish adulteries, remove the impious from the land, not allow parricides and perjurers [variant: “perjured persons”: collected older editions; “those committing perjury”: Ivo] to live, and not allow his own sons to act impiously.

### C. XLI. One who kills a guilty person in the discharge of office does not sin. Likewise Augustine, *On Free Choice of the Will*, book I, chapter 4

[Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, ch. 38; *Decretum*, part 10, ch. 101.]

If homicide is the killing of a human being, nevertheless one may sometimes kill without sin. For neither the soldier who kills an enemy, nor a judge or his officer who kills a guilty person, nor one from whose hand a weapon happens to fly without his willing it or knowing it, seem to me to sin when they kill a human being.

[Note: Variant: “from his hand”: editions of Basel, Paris, and Lyons.]

[Note: Variant: “strikes”: Ivo, *Decretum*; “shall fly”: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected older editions and first Argentinensis edition.]

Evodius: “I agree.”

[Note: “Evodius: I agree”: these words have been added from the original and Ivo. The work is written as a dialogue. In the *Panormia* it reads: “Nor do I agree.”]

But such persons are not usually called murderers.

[Note: Variant: “nor even”: collected older editions.]

The same author, in *Questions on Leviticus*, question 68, on chapter 19, §1: “When a man is justly killed, the law kills him, not you.”

[Col. 1230B]

### C. XLII. It is not the person who compels toward good, but the person who compels toward evil, who persecutes. Likewise Pope Pelagius

[Note: These words are also found in the second letter of Pelagius I to Narses, and in his letter to Valerian, published among the documents by Holstenius.—Anselm, book 12, ch. 47 (45); Deusdedit, part 1; Polycarpus, book 7, title 6.—Part of this chapter is also found in Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, ch. 95.]

Let not the empty talk of people who say that the Church persecutes, when it either restrains the acts being committed or seeks the salvation of souls, delay you. Such fabricators of this report are mistaken. No one persecutes except one who compels toward evil. But one who either punishes evil already done or prevents it from being done does not persecute: he loves. For if, as they suppose, no one is to be restrained from evil or drawn back from evil to good, then human and divine laws must necessarily be rendered void—laws which, at justice’s prompting, establish punishments for the wicked and rewards for the good.

[Note: Variant: “rebuked”: collected older editions.]

Now that schism is evil, and that persons of this sort ought to be suppressed even by external authorities, is taught us both by the authority of canonical Scripture and by the truth of the fathers’ rules. Therefore, whoever is separated from the apostolic sees is undoubtedly in schism and attempts to set up an altar against the universal Church.

§1. But let Your Glory consider what canon, inserted in the Council of Chalcedon, decrees concerning such persons. After other matters it says as follows:

[Note: “Inserted in Chalcedon”: In Session 4 of the Council of Chalcedon, in the letter of the archimandrites to that council for the restoration of Dioscorus, canon 5 of the Council of Antioch is cited; and the passage occurs there in nearly the same form as it is reported here. It nevertheless agrees closely with neither ancient translation of that council.]

> Whoever separates himself from communion, holds an assembly, sets up an altar, and refuses to agree with the bishop who summons him, or to submit to and obey him when he summons him the first and second time, is to be condemned altogether; nor is he ever to obtain restoration [Greek: *therapeias*, “treatment/restoration”], nor can he receive honor. But if he persists in creating disturbances and seditions in the Church, he is to be suppressed as seditious by external authority.

[Note: “Or restoration”: In both councils—that is, Antioch in the ancient translation and Chalcedon—the reading is “restoration.” The Greek is *καὶ μηκέτι θεραπείας τυγχάνειν*, “and no longer to obtain restoration.”]

§2. And Blessed Augustine says concerning such persons:

> Much must also be done, with a certain kindly severity in punishing even those who are unwilling, since their welfare must be considered rather than their wish. For in correcting a son, however sternly, paternal love is never lost; yet what he would not wish is done, so that one who appears to need healing through pain may be healed even against his will.

See how, by the testimony of so great a father, the Church does not persecute such persons by restraining them, but always loves them by correcting them. Therefore do you also do what we frequently urge you to do, knowing the purpose of your Christianity; make every effort that such acts may no longer be allowed, and also—something which I do not doubt is very easy for you—that those who have ventured upon such acts be sent under suitable guard to the most pious emperor.

§3. For Your Highness ought to recall what God accomplished through you at the time when Totila the tyrant possessed Istria and Venetia, while the Franks too were laying everything waste. You nevertheless did not permit the case of the bishop of Milan to be acted upon until you had referred it to the most merciful emperor and had again learned from his written instructions what should be done. And, amid enemies raging everywhere, both the man who was to be ordained and the man who was to ordain him were brought safely to Ravenna through the foresight of your high office.

### C. XLIII. Secular authorities should restrain schismatics and heretics. The same author, to Narses, Patrician and Duke in Italy

[Note: Anselm, book 6, ch. 196 (198); Polycarpus, book 7, title 5.]

What shall I say of the Ligurian, Venetian, and Istrian bishops? Your Excellence is fully able to restrain them both by reason and by authority; yet you allow them, in contempt of the apostolic sees, to boast of their own rusticity. If anything in the judgment of the universal synod held at Constantinople during the first recently elapsed indiction troubled them, they ought—as has always been done—to have sent representatives chosen from among themselves to the apostolic see, representatives capable of giving and receiving an account; they ought not, with their eyes shut, to tear apart the body of Christ our God, that is, the holy Church.

[Note: Variant: “whatever persons”: Basel edition.]

Therefore do not hesitate to suppress persons of this sort by princely or judicial authority. For the rules of the Fathers have specifically established that if any person in ecclesiastical office resists the one to whom he is subject, holds separate assemblies, erects another altar, or causes schism, he is to be excommunicated and condemned. If he should also despise this and persist in making divisions and schism, he is to be suppressed by public authorities.

[Note: Variant: “schisms”: Basel edition and Anselm.]

See, my lord, lest your mind perhaps be timid through fear of seeming to persecute: I have taken care briefly to set these matters before you on the authority of the Fathers, although there are a thousand other examples and enactments by which it is clearly recognized that those who make ruptures in the holy Church ought to be restrained by public authorities not only through exile, but also through confiscation of property and harsh detention.

### C. XLIV. Those separated from the unity of the Church should be restrained by secular authorities. Likewise Pelagius

[Note: To Narses, letter 1.—Anselm, book 12, ch. 46; Polycarpus, book 7, title 5.]

We believe that we have knowledge, not only of your own, but of many—indeed nearly all—of the zealous efforts of Your Glory; and therefore, concerning matters which we are astonished are being done there in your presence, we have considered it right to lodge a confident complaint before Your Glory.

For Thracius [variant: Arsacius: Anselm; Tertius: Argentinensis edition] and Maximilianus, who possess only the names of bishops, are said both to disturb ecclesiastical unity there and to appropriate all church property for their own uses. Indeed, against one of them, Maximilianus, certain persons, compelled by necessity, came to us tirelessly over so long a journey to present petitions. For this reason we have decided to send to those places Peter, a presbyter of our see, and also Projectus, a notary, so that they may either restrain with due punishment the acts which they discover to have been committed by the aforesaid pseudo-bishops contrary to canonical enactments, or bring those persons all the way to us.

And therefore, greeting Your Glory with paternal affection, we ask that you afford every assistance in all things to those aforesaid persons sent by our see; and do not think it any sin if persons of this kind are suppressed. For both divine and human laws have established that those divided from the unity of the Church, and most wickedly disturbing its peace, are to be restrained even by secular authorities. Nor is there anything greater by which you can offer sacrifice to God than if you arrange for those who rage to their own and others’ ruin to be restrained with suitable force.

[Col. 1233B]

### C. XLV. The wickedness of evil persons, even though it benefits the good, must nevertheless be punished. Likewise Pope Pelagius to John, patrician

[Note: Nearly the same words occur in Pelagius’ third letter to Narses.—Anselm, book 12, ch. 47; Polycarpus, same place.]

On rereading Your Excellence’s letter, we were deeply grieved by the injury which the presumption of wicked people inflicted upon you. But because we know that, by God’s hidden judgment, your soul was preserved from the contamination of schism, although through the wickedness and pride of others, we gave thanks to almighty God, who is accustomed to work good even from the evil acts of human beings.

For it must not be believed that it occurred without His providence that foolish and perverse people should go so far as, thinking their own division to be the Catholic Church, to exclude you from their pollution. Thus, through God’s mercy, it came about even without their knowing it that, rescued from the faction of schismatics, you were preserved for the Catholic Church which you love.

[Note: Variant: “communion”: collected older editions.]

Although, therefore, benefit accrued to you through their crime, do not allow the unpunished presumption of wicked persons to go unchecked. For unless what they ventured against Your Glory is suppressed by punishment, there can no longer be any doubt what force they may have in lesser persons if they cannot be punished.

[Note: In some old copies and in Anselm: “what they may be able to do in lesser persons can no longer be doubted,” etc.]

Exercise, therefore, the authority due in such matters; and, lest their boldness to commit such acts increase further, let them be restrained by your coercive measures. For by God’s will they ventured such acts even against you so that, by your correcting such acts, you might, with God’s favor, fortify others against the same crime.

What sort of persons those are who flee the Church is clearly shown to you by the crimes of Eufrasius, crimes which God no longer wished to remain hidden. In murder he considered neither human kinship, nor brotherly love, nor reverence for the priesthood. By incestuous adultery he also deprived vengeance itself of any measure: for if you punish the adultery, nothing remains upon which the incest can be avenged; if you impose a penalty for the incestuous act, the crime of adultery will remain unavenged.

See from what company those are who, so far as their own pride was concerned, attempted to inflict injury upon you, and who, so far as God’s providence was concerned, preserved you undefiled for the Church. Remove such persons from that province. Use the opportunity God has afforded you to suppress the faithless. This can be done more fully if the authors of the crimes are sent to the most merciful emperor—especially the invader of the Church of Aquileia, who, both in schism and accursed in it, can retain neither the honor nor the merit of a bishop.

[Note: Anselm reads: “and cursed by a schismatic.”]

### C. XLVI. Whoever dies in the conflict waged against unbelievers merits the heavenly kingdom. Likewise Nicholas to the army of the Franks

[Note: Ivo, part 10, ch. 87, under the words “We wish all of your charity,” cites this same passage from a letter of Leo IV to the Frankish army. There he also gives the passage reported below in the same question, chapter “With All Fear,” from the same Leo.]

[Note: A chapter of uncertain origin, attributed by Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, ch. 30, to Alexander II, and in the *Decretum*, part 10, ch. 87, to Leo IV.]

We wish all of your charity to know that whoever—though we say this without wishing it—dies faithfully in this conflict of war, the heavenly kingdoms will by no means be denied to him.

[Col. 1234C]

### C. XLVII. Those who take arms against the excommunicated out of zeal for mother Church are not murderers. Likewise Urban II to Godfrey, bishop of Lucca

[Note: A chapter of uncertain date.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, ch. 54.]

Impose upon those who kill excommunicated persons, according to what you have learned in the order of the Roman Church, a fitting measure of satisfaction in accordance with their intention.

[Note: Ivo reads: “as you know the custom of the Roman Church.”]

For we do not judge those to be murderers who, burning with zeal for their Catholic mother, may happen to have slain some persons among the excommunicated. Yet, lest the discipline of that same mother Church be abandoned, impose upon them a suitable penance, in the manner we have stated, so that they may be able to appease against themselves the eyes of divine simplicity, should they perhaps have incurred any duplicity through human frailty in that offence.

[Note: Variant: “contracted”: Ivo; “incurred”: Argentinensis edition.]

### C. XLVIII. The peace of the Church consoles the sorrow caused by those who are lost. Likewise Augustine, letter L to Boniface, on restraining heretics

[Note: Letter 185, Maurist edition, written A.D. 417.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, ch. 59.]

For which of us would wish any one of those persons not merely to perish, but even to lose anything? But if the house of David could not otherwise obtain peace unless Absalom, his son, were killed in the war he waged against his father—although David had earnestly commanded his men to preserve him alive and unharmed as far as possible, so that there might be one to whom a father’s affection could grant forgiveness when penitent—what prevented him except to mourn the lost one and, having acquired peace for his kingdom, to console his own sorrow?

[Note: The reading “which of us” has been corrected from Blessed Augustine, from whom Ivo differs little. Gratian formerly read: “Which of you would wish any of your enemies not merely,” etc.]

Gratian. Therefore, if holy men and public authorities waging wars were not transgressors of the commandment “You shall not kill,” though they put criminal persons to a deserved death; if a soldier obeying his authority is not guilty of homicide if, at its command, he kills any criminal person; if punishing murderers and poisoners is not the shedding of blood but the service of the laws; if the peace of the Church consoles the sorrow caused by those who are lost; if those who, inflamed by zeal for their Catholic mother, kill excommunicated persons are not judged murderers: it is clear that evil persons may lawfully be not only scourged but also killed.

§1. But it is asked: if it happens that certain evil persons are punished by persons who do not have lawful authority, are those through whom they are punished guilty of shedding blood?

Ambrose writes as follows concerning these matters, in book II of *Cain and Abel*, chapter 4.

[Note: There are some who deny that this work is Ambrose’s.]

### C. XLIX. Sins are sometimes punished through peoples stirred up by divine command

Sins are forgiven through the word of God, of which a Levite is the interpreter and in some sense the executor. They are forgiven also through the office of a priest and sacred ministry. Sins are likewise punished through human beings, such as judges, who exercise authority for a time.

And below:

§1. Sins are also punished through peoples, as we read that the Jewish people was often subdued by foreigners, stirred up at God’s command because of the offence against the divine majesty.

Gratian. From this it should be noted that God sometimes punishes sins through persons who do not know, and sometimes through persons who do know. He punishes sins through those who do not know, as through Sennacherib, Nebuchadnezzar, Antiochus, Roman princes, and certain kings of the Gentiles: at times He afflicted the sinful people of Israel, at times He carried them into captivity.

§1. Hence the Lord Himself says through the prophet: “Assyria is the rod of my fury; but he did not know it.” Assyria was the rod of the Lord’s fury because through him divine justice had determined to scourge countless nations. But he himself did not know it, because, lifted up in pride, he attributed the victory he had achieved not to divine power but to his own strength. Therefore the Lord speaks against his pride, saying: “Shall the saw boast against him who cuts with it? Or shall the axe exalt itself against him who chops with it?”

By these comparisons it is shown quite clearly that, just as a saw and an axe cannot cut or chop wood unless directed by another, and therefore ought not to be proud against those directing them, so those through whom God punishes can accomplish nothing apart from the prompting of divine providence and therefore are not permitted to be proud against Him who directs them.

§2. Such persons are said to serve God in punishing; but insofar as, not knowing themselves to be ministers of God’s wrath, they are proudly exalted in impious vanity, they find from God no reward for their service except a temporal one, and they do not escape the punishment for their pride. Thus, when the Lord said to the prophet concerning Nebuchadnezzar, “What shall I give him for the labor by which he served me at Tyre?” He immediately added: “Give”—that is, pronounce Egypt and Ethiopia as granted to him. But when he later said in his proud heart, “Is this not Babylon, which I built by the strength of my kingdom?” and so forth, God immediately changed his rational mind and clothed him with the brutishness of a wild beast, so that, fleeing from people, he lived among the beasts.

§3. Likewise through Antiochus, when the Lord punished the idolatry of the Jewish people and turned to their destruction the peace which, having rejected God’s law and adopted the sacred rites of nations, they sought, Antiochus, being ignorant of God’s disposition, attributed the devastation of that people to his own power. Therefore the prophet invokes a curse against him, saying: “Pour out your wrath upon the nations that have not known you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name, lest they say among the nations: ‘Where is their God?’”

§4. Similarly, when God had decreed to punish through the Romans the sin of Christ’s death, they began to ascribe the destruction of the city and the wretched captivity of the Jewish people to their own strength. Therefore the prophet invokes a curse against them, saying: “Lift up your hands against the pride of those who hate you, and of those who have done much evil and set up monuments of their victory in the midst of your court.”

§5. Sins are punished through those who know, as God wished through the children of Israel to punish the sins of the Amorites, Canaanites, and other nations whose land He gave the Israelites to possess; and He commanded them to spare none of those peoples but to hand them all over to death. That this befell them because of their sins is apparent from the Lord’s words. When He said to Abraham, “To your seed I will give this land,” Abraham might, as it were, ask why He did not give it immediately; he heard: “For the sins of the Amorites are not yet complete.” Those sins are understood to have become complete when the people delivered from Egyptian bondage received their land as an inheritance, as had been promised to Abraham.

§6. Therefore, when people are stirred up by divine command to punish sins in this manner—as the Jewish people was stirred up to occupy the land of promise and destroy sinful nations—guilty blood is shed without fault, and possessions wrongly held by those people lawfully pass into the right and dominion of the good.

§7. But when some are moved by hidden prompting to persecute the wicked, as Sennacherib and the others who persecuted the sinful people were, although they are stirred to persecution by a hidden prompting working through the people’s deserts, they are nevertheless not free from guilt. For, because of a depraved intention, they seek not to punish the sins of offenders but to seize their goods or bring them under their own dominion.

It should also be noted concerning them that they are sometimes stirred up to punish the sins of the good, so that eventually, after the good have been corrected, they too may be punished. Thus in the book of Judges we read of Jabin, king of the Canaanites, and of the Midianites: because of the people’s idolatry, God raised them up to afflict Israel and occupy its land. But when the people of God, long afflicted under their hands, acknowledged their sin and made God propitious to themselves through repentance, Barak, accompanied by Deborah the prophetess, wife of Lapidoth, by God’s command crushed Jabin, king of the Canaanites, and Sisera, commander of his army; and Gideon put to death Zebee and Salmana, kings of the Midianites, and Oreb and Zeeb, their commanders.

§8. It is clear, therefore, that evil people are sometimes not only scourged but lawfully destroyed for their sins, sometimes through those exercising lawful authority and sometimes through peoples stirred up by divine command. Nor is Augustine’s statement contrary to this, when, interceding with Marcellinus on behalf of the Circumcellions, he asked that they be restrained by beatings rather than destroyed by death. For although in his intercession he requested that time for life be preserved for them, he did not teach that the severity of the laws by which such persons are punished by death was not to be observed.

## QUESTION VI

### GRATIAN

As to the question whether evil persons are to be compelled toward good, the answer is easy to see. That ancient people was compelled by fear of punishments to observe the law. In the Gospel also the Lord says to his disciples: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him”—that is, serve Him in fear—“who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.” Paul too, when he was persecuting the Church of God, was compelled to turn to God when he was struck blind on the road. Therefore he testified that he was like one untimely born, saying: “Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me.”

Hence Augustine writes in letter L to Boniface:

[Note: The beginning of this chapter, where Blessed Augustine deals with the Donatists, reads as follows: “Where is what these men are accustomed to cry out: ‘It is free to believe; whom did Christ compel by force?’” etc., as above, question 4, chapter “Who compelled us?”]

### C. I. The Church ought to compel evil persons toward good, as Christ compelled Paul

Schismatics say: “On whom did Christ inflict force? Whom did he compel?” They have before them the apostle Paul. Let them recognize in him Christ first compelling and afterwards teaching; first striking and afterwards consoling. It is remarkable, however, how the one who entered the Gospel compelled by bodily punishment labored in the Gospel more than all those who were called by word alone; and the one whom greater fear compelled toward love had his perfect love cast out fear.

Why then should the Church not compel lost children to return, if lost children compelled others to perish? And even those whom they did not compel but only seduced, if they are recalled to her bosom through terrible but salutary laws, the pious mother embraces more tenderly and rejoices much more over them than over those whom she had never lost.

§1. Does it not belong to pastoral diligence also, when those sheep which have wandered from the flock not through violent seizure but by gentle and mild seduction have begun to be possessed by strangers, to bring them back, once found, to the Lord’s sheepfold by the fear or even the pains of scourges, if they resist?

And below:

§2. We have shown that Paul was compelled by Christ. The Church therefore imitates her Lord in compelling these persons. At first, in order to compel no one, she waited until the prophetic prediction concerning the faith of kings and nations should be fulfilled.

§3. From this also the apostolic saying can not improperly be understood, where Blessed Paul said: “Ready to punish every disobedience, when your former obedience has been fulfilled.”

§4. Accordingly, the Lord Himself first commands guests to be brought to his great supper and afterwards to be compelled. For when his servants answered him, “Lord, what you commanded has been done, and there is still room,” he said: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel whomever you find to enter.” Thus, in those who were first brought in gently, the prior obedience was fulfilled; but in those who are compelled, disobedience is restrained.

And below:

§5. If, through the authority which the Church received by God’s gift, through the religion and faith of kings, at the time when she ought to have received it, those found in the roads and hedges—that is, in heresies and schisms—are compelled to enter, let them not find fault because they are compelled, but consider the end toward which they are compelled.

### C. II. God corrects those who err in various ways. The same author, to the Donatists, letter CLXVI

[Note: Letter 105, Maurist edition, written A.D. 409.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, ch. 64.]

“The thing which had strayed,” says the Lord, “you did not call back; and the thing which had perished you did not seek.” God Himself does this for you through us: whether by entreating, threatening, correcting, losses, hardships, His hidden admonitions or visitations, or the laws of temporal authorities.

### C. III. What must be considered is not that someone is compelled, but the nature of that toward which he is compelled. The same author, letter XLVIII, to Vincentius

[Note: Letter 93, Maurist edition, written A.D. 408.—Collection of Tracts, part 2, tome 50, ch. 34.]

You see, I think, that what must be considered is not that a person is compelled, but the nature of that toward which he is compelled—whether it is good or evil. This does not mean that anyone can be good unwillingly; rather, through fearing what he does not wish to suffer, he either abandons a hindering obstinacy or is compelled to recognize an unknown truth, so that through fear he either rejects the falsehood he had defended or seeks the truth he did not know, and then willingly holds what he had not wished to hold.

And below:

§1. My initial opinion was that no one ought to be compelled to the unity of Christ; that one ought to act by word, contend by discussion, and prevail by reason, lest we have false Catholics whom we had known to be open heretics. But this opinion of mine was overcome not merely by the words of opponents but by demonstrative examples. My own city was first set against me: though wholly on the side of Donatus, it was converted to Catholic unity through fear of the imperial laws. Now we see it so detesting the ruinous effect of this obstinacy of yours that it is believed never to have been subject to it. So too many other cities, named to me individually, enabled me to recognize from the facts themselves that even in this matter what is written may rightly be understood: “Give an opportunity to a wise person, and he will become wiser.”

[Col. 1240B]

### C. IV. A peasant is to be compelled to turn to the Lord by the burden of a tax. Likewise Gregory, to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, book III, letter 26

[Note: Letter 26, written A.D. 594, book 4 of the Maurist edition.—Collection of Tracts, part 1, tome 55, ch. 90.]

But if a peasant is found to be of such great faithlessness and obstinacy that he refuses altogether to come to God, he is to be burdened with such a weight of tax that the punishment of the exaction itself compels him to hasten toward rectitude.

[Additional editorial apparatus and references]

C. XLI: After “nevertheless,” the reading *non est* (“is absent”) occurs in Augustine, Ivo, and the Argentinensis edition; Basel and Lyons II–III add *alius alium* (“one person [kills] another”). The source reads *de manu* (“from [his] hand”); the Basel, Paris, and Lyons editions do likewise. Ivo’s *Decretum* reads *figit* (“strikes”); Ivo’s *Panormia* reads *fugerit* (“shall fly”); the collected older editions and the first Argentinensis edition have the printed reading. 

C. XLII: In “either restrains,” *vel* (“either”) is absent from the Basel edition; Basel reads *erroris* (“of this error”) for *rumoris* (“of this report”). The collected older editions read *reprehendendus* (“rebuked”) for *reprimendus* (“restrained”); they omit *a malo* (“from evil”), and the Argentinensis edition reads: “nor is anyone to be compelled toward good.” The collected older editions read *in Chalc[edonensi]* (“in Chalcedon”) for “inserted in the Council of Chalcedon”; Basel has *statuit* (“has decreed”), and the other editions *constituat* (“may decree”). The Correctors rightly observe that this canon is neither the Hispanic nor the Dionysian translation, nor does it agree with the ancient translation. The Argentinensis and Basel editions read *noluit* (“refused”) for each occurrence of *noluerit* (“shall refuse”); Argentinensis reads *prius* (“earlier”), and the other editions, except Lyons II–III, *et prius* (“and earlier”), for *primo* (“the first time”). Basel reads *extraneam* (“foreign”) for *exteram* (“external”). Augustine is introduced with *ait* (“says”) in Basel; compare Distinction 45, canon 11. In §3 Basel adds *etiam* (“also”).

C. XLIII: Anselm reads *excellentiae vestrae* (“your Excellence’s”) for *excellentia vestra*; the same witness reads *sicut* (“as”) for *si quid* (“if anything”), while the Basel edition reads *quibuslibet* (“any persons whatsoever”) for *aliquibus* (“some”). Argentinensis reads *et* (“and”) for *vel* (“or”) in “princely or judicial”; compare canon 5 of Antioch and the preceding chapter. Basel reads *hic* (“here”) for *hoc* (“this”), omits *iste* (“he”), and again reads *hic* for *hoc*; it and Anselm have *schismata* (“schisms”) for *schisma* (“schism”). The collected older editions read *Ecce de quo animo* (“See with what disposition”) for the printed opening; Argentinensis and Basel read *nobis* (“us”) for *vobis* (“you”), and Basel again reads *hic* for *haec* (“these matters”). Basel, Norimberga, and Venice I read *sunt* (“are”) for *sint* (“there are”); Argentinensis, Basel, and Lyons II–III read *ostenditur et agnoscitur* (“is shown and recognized”) for *agnoscitur* (“is recognized”).

C. XLIV: Basel adds *etiam* (“also”) in “both divine and human laws.”

C. XLV: The collected older editions read *perversissimi* (“most perverse”) for *perversi* (“perverse”); Basel omits *hoc* (“this”) in “even without their knowing it.” The collected older editions read *communione* (“communion”) for *factione* (“faction”). Some old copies and Anselm read, “what they can do in lesser persons can no longer be doubted”; Basel reads *in minoribus valeat puniri* (“may be able to be punished in lesser persons”), while Venice I–II, Norimberga, Paris, and Lyons I add *omnibus* (“all”). The collected older editions read *spes* (“hope”) for *spiritus* (“spirit/boldness”); Argentinensis and Basel read *eorum* (“their”) for *eodem* (“the same”), and the collected older editions *possetis* (“you might”) for *possitis* (“you may”). Those same editions read *sunt* (“are”) for *sint* (“may be”); Basel reads *in adulterio* (“in adultery”), Argentinensis, Norimberga, and Venice I omit *etiam* (“also”), and the collected older editions and Lyons II–III read *ipsi* (“to it”) for *ipsius* (“of it”).

C. XLVII: Argentinensis and Norimberga read *didicisti* (“you have learned,” singular) for *didicistis* (“you have learned,” plural). Ivo and the Panormia have *intentionem ipsorum* (“their intention”), but *ipsorum* is not added because of the gloss. The collected older editions and the first Argentinensis edition add *ecclesiae* (“Church”) after “Catholic mother.” Ivo reads *desaeviat* (“become violently cruel”) for *deseratur* (“be abandoned”). Ivo omits *eo* (“in that”); Basel reads *secundum tenorem* (“according to the tenor”), Argentinensis *tenorem, secundum quem* (“the tenor according to which”), and the other editions *eo tenore, secundum quem* (“in that tenor according to which”). Ivo reads *pervaleant* (“may fully be able”) for *valeant* (“may be able”).

C. XLVIII: The corrected reading is *nostrum* (“of us”); Argentinensis and Norimberga likewise have *nostrum*, while Basel adds *non* (“not”). Ivo and the collected older editions read *inimicorum* (“enemies”) for *illorum* (“those [persons]”); the latter, except Argentinensis and Basel, add *suorum* (“their own”). The collected older editions and Lyons II–III read *et* (“and”) for *ut* (“so that”).

C. XLIX: The attribution to Ambrose is disputed by some. The collected older editions and first Basel and Lyons II–III editions read *quidem* (“indeed/in some sense”) for *quidam* (“a certain [executor]”); they add *peccata* (“sins”) after “are also punished.” References in this section are: 4 Kings 25 (Sennacherib); 2 Maccabees 5 (Antiochus); Isaiah 10:5 and 10:15; Ezekiel 29:18–19; Daniel 4:27; 1 Maccabees 1; Psalms 78:6, 10 and 73:3; Joshua 5–6; Deuteronomy 7:2; Genesis 15:18; Judges 4 and 8. Compare above, question IV, chapter 1, concerning Augustine’s petition for the Circumcellions.

Question VI: References are Matthew 10:28; Acts 9; and 1 Corinthians 15:8. Augustine’s original Donatist passage begins: “Where is what these people are accustomed to cry: ‘It is free to believe; whom did Christ compel by force?’” Compare above, question IV, chapter “Who compelled us?” The source cites Letter 185, Maurist edition, written A.D. 417; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, chapter 59; and above, question IV, chapter 43.

C. I: References are 1 Corinthians 15:10, 1 John 4:18, 2 Corinthians 10:6, Luke 14:23, and compare above, question IV, chapter 24. The collected older editions read *mittit* (“casts out”) for *misit* (“cast out”); Argentinensis reads *perfidi* (“faithless”) for *perditi* (“lost”), and Basel *cogerent* (“were compelling”) for *coegerunt* (“compelled”). The collected older editions read *et* (“and”) for *sed* (“but”); they and Lyons II–III read *gremio* (“bosom,” ablative) for *gremium* (“bosom,” accusative), as does Ivo. They read *hoc pertinet* (“does this belong”) for *an non pertinet* (“does it not belong”), *aberraverant* (“had wandered”) for *aberraverint* (“have wandered”), and *coeperant* (“had begun”) for *coeperint* (“have begun”). In §2 they read *qui* (“which,” masculine) for *quae* (“which,” feminine); Basel adds *et* (“and”) and reads *gentilium* (“of the Gentiles”) for *gentium* (“of nations”); the original, Ivo, Basel, and Lyons read *praedicatio* (“preaching”) for *praedictio* (“prediction”). In §3 the original, Ivo, and Argentinensis read *Parati* (“ready,” plural), while the other editions read *Paratus sum* (“I am ready”). In §4 the collected older editions and first Argentinensis add *et* (“and afterwards”); Basel adds *adventu* (“at [the first] coming”), and Venice II reads *leviter* (“lightly”) for *leniter* (“gently”). In §5 Ivo reads *potestate* (“through authority”) for *potestatem*; Basel has *cogantur* (“may be compelled”), while the collected older editions read *coguntur* (“are compelled”) for *cogantur* in the final clause.

C. II: Reference: Ezekiel 34:4. The collected older editions insert *ipse* (“himself”) after both *sive* (“whether”).

C. III: The Basel edition omits *illud* (“that thing”); Lyons reads *ad quod* (“to which”) for *quo* (“by which”); the original reads *quo* for *quod*; Basel and Lyons II–III add *quandoque* (“sometimes”). In §1 the original reads: “My initial opinion was that no one [was to be compelled]”; Argentinensis, Norimberga, Basel, Venice I, and the source’s ecclesiastical edition read *veritatem* (“truth”) for *unitatem* (“unity”); Basel and Lyons add *et ecclesiae* (“and of the Church”); Basel reads *sed verbo* (“but by word”), Venice I–II, Paris, and Lyons *verum verbo* (“but indeed by word”); Argentinensis, Norimberga, and Venice I read *etiam* (“also”); the collected older editions and first Basel read *repugnandum* (“arguments must be opposed”) for *pugnandum* (“one must contend”); they read *haberem—noveram* (“I might have—I had known”) for *haberemus—noveramus* (“we might have—we had known”). They add *tantum* (“merely”); read *partes* (“parties”) or, in the original, *parte* (“party”) for *partem* (“side”); Basel reads *vidimus* (“we saw”) for *videmus* (“we see”); Norimberga and Venice I read *nostrae* (“our”) for *vestrae* (“your”); and the collected older editions add *Item et* (“Likewise also”) for *Ita* (“So”).

C. IV: The cited letter is Letter 26, written A.D. 594, book IV in the Maurist edition; compare *Collection of Tracts*, part I, tome 55, chapter 90. Argentinensis reads *Dominum* (“the Lord”), while the other editions and the original read *Dom[inum] Deum* (“the Lord God”), for *Deum* (“God”).

Gratian. From all these authorities it is inferred [Note: [Col. 1239] understood: Bohm.], that the wicked are to be compelled toward the good. § 1. But it is objected that no one should be compelled to that to which he is compelled without benefit. Yet each person is compelled toward the good without benefit, since God rejects forced services. Hence the Apostle, when exhorting the Corinthians concerning almsgiving, says [Note: [Col. 1239] 2 Cor. 9:7]: [Col. 1240C] “Each one, as he has determined in his heart, not out of sorrow or necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver.” From this it is understood that one who gives unwillingly because of immediate shame loses both the thing and the merit. Likewise, when he gave the reason why he abstained from receiving support, he said [Note: [Col. 1239] 1 Cor. 9:16]: “If I preach the gospel out of necessity, there will be no glory for me.” § 2. Likewise: “If I preach unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me. But if I do this willingly, I have a reward with God.” Likewise, when writing to the Galatians that legal observances are not to be maintained, he says [Note: [Col. 1239] Gal. 5:18]: “If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.” From this it is evident that he who is under the law—that is [Note: [Col. 1239] “that is” is absent in Bohm.], he who serves through fear of punishment rather than love of justice—is not led by the Holy Spirit. But if he is not led by the Holy Spirit, he is wholly unable to please God. § 3. Likewise [Note: [Col. 1239] Rom. 8:15]: “You have not received [Col. 1240D] again the spirit of slavery in fear, but [Col. 1241A] you have received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry: Abba, Father.” From these words it is understood that, although in the Old Testament people were compelled toward the good through fear of punishment, yet in the New Testament they are to be invited to faith by liberty alone and love of justice. Hence those are called servants and sons of the slave woman, belonging to Ishmael [Note: [Col. 1241] Gal. 4:22 ff.]; whereas these are called free and sons of the free woman, belonging to Isaac. § 4. Likewise John says in his epistle [Note: [Col. 1241] 1 John 4:18]: “Fear is not in charity, but perfect charity casts fear out.” But one who is compelled is led by that fear which is not in charity: it restrains the hands, not changes the mind; punishment is feared, not the good loved. Yet without love of the good no one can please God or be counted among the good. Hence, when the Prophet [Col. 1241B] said [Note: [Col. 1241] Ps. 67:11]: “Your animals shall dwell in it”—namely, in the inheritance—showing how they attain that dwelling [Note: [Col. 1241] “attains”: Bohm.], he adds: “In your sweetness, which you, O God, have prepared for the poor,” calling “sweetness” the delightfulness of a good work, by which good is done not through fear of punishment but through delight [Note: [Col. 1241] “love”: ibid.] in justice. Therefore, since without this sweetness animals do not dwell in the inheritance, it is clear that no one is compelled toward the good except without benefit by fear alone. For whoever is compelled toward the good by fear alone is not led by love. Therefore the wicked are not to be compelled toward the good. § 5. The reply is as follows: If the good toward which the wicked are compelled were always borne unwillingly, and they never served voluntarily, they would be compelled toward it without benefit. But because it belongs to human nature both to shrink from things which are brought into disuse and to cherish accustomed things with great care, the wicked are to be restrained from evil by the lashes of tribulations and prompted toward the good, so that, while evil is brought into disuse through fear of punishment, it may become abhorrent, and good, through habit, may become sweet. Hence Augustine, on Psalm 127: “When by fear [Note: [Col. 1241C] This passage agrees more closely with the Ordinary Gloss on the same Psalm; nevertheless, there are here some things from Blessed Augustine which are not in the Gloss.] of hell a person restrains himself from sin, a habit of justice arises, and what was hard begins to be loved; fear begins to be excluded by charity, and there succeeds the chaste fear of which it is said here, [Col. 1242A] by which we fear lest the bridegroom delay, lest he depart, lest we be deprived of him. That fear is useful, but it does not remain eternally as this one does.”

## QUESTION VII

### GRATIAN

The question now is whether heretics are to be stripped of their own and of the Church’s property; and whether those who possess things taken from heretics are said to possess another’s property.

Augustine writes thus on these matters to Vincentius, Epistle XLVIII [Note: [Col. 1241] Ep. 93, Maurist edition; written A.D. 408. — Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, c. 179; Polycarpus, bk. 7, tit. 5.]:

### C. I. Earthly goods are held only by divine or human right.

Whoever persecutes you on the occasion of this imperial law, not from the love of correcting you but from hatred in enmity, displeases us. And although no earthly thing whatever [Note: [Col. 1241] “whatever”: Ivo; collected editions.] can rightly be possessed by anyone except either by divine right, by which all things belong to the just, or by human right, which lies in the power of the kings of the earth (and therefore you falsely call your property things which you do not possess justly [Note: [Col. 1241] “just”: original text]), and although you have been ordered to lose them according to the laws of earthly kings, and although you have said in vain, “We laboured to assemble them” [Note: [Col. 1241] “in them”: collected editions. — “we labour”: the same, first Lyons edition II and III.], when you read that it is written [Note: [Col. 1241] Prov. 13:22], “The labours of the ungodly [Note: [Col. 1241C] Similar to this statement is what is written in Prov. 13: *θησαυρίζεται δὲ δικαίοις πλοῦτος*, “wealth is stored up for the righteous”; as below in the same chapter, *Quemadmodum*: “But the riches of the ungodly are stored up for the just.” Where the Vulgate has: “the substance of the sinner is kept for the just.” Likewise Isaiah 61 says: *καὶ δώσω τὸν μόχθον αὐτῶν δικαίοις*, “and I will give their toil to the righteous,” after first saying: *ἰσχὺν ἐθνῶν κατέδεσθαι*, “to consume the strength of nations.” Wisdom 10 reads: “Therefore the just took the spoils of the ungodly,” below in the same chapter, *Quemadmodum*.] shall be eaten [Note: [Col. 1241] “shall eat”: original text; Ivo.] by the just”—nevertheless, whoever, on the occasion of this law [Note: [Col. 1241D] In the Theodosian Code, bk. 16, tit. [Col. 1242C] 5, are laws 43, 52, and 54 of Honorius and Theodosius, commanding that buildings, estates, and places previously belonging to the meeting-houses of Donatists or other heretics be claimed by, or united to, Catholic churches. Blessed Augustine seems to refer to these laws both here and in Tractate 6 on John, as noted above, Distinction 8, *Quo jure*, and in *Against Petilian’s Letters*, as in the immediately following chapter, and elsewhere.] which the kings of the earth, serving Christ, promulgated for the correction of your impiety, greedily covets your own property, displeases us. Likewise, whoever holds, not through justice but through greed, the property itself of the poor or the basilicas of congregations which you held under the name of the Church—things which are owed altogether only to that Church which is the true Church of Christ—displeases us. Whoever [Note: [Col. 1241] Cf. C. 24, q. 1, c. 38.] receives one expelled by you for some disgraceful deed or crime [Note: [Col. 1242D] “By you”: so corrected from old manuscripts and the original, whereas the printed texts here and below, at 24, q. 1, *Quisquis*, read “by us” [ [Col. 1241] so in the Basel, Lyons I, and Paris editions, and in Ivo.]. “But you”: “expelled” has not been altered on account of the gloss. For the old copies here and below in the cited chapter, Ivo, and the original, read *projectum*, “cast out.”] as persons are received who, except for the error by which they separate themselves from us, lived without crime among you, displeases us. But [Note: [Col. 1241] added “nevertheless”: Basel edition.] you do not readily prove such cases; and if you prove them [Note: [Col. 1241] “and—prove” absent from the collected editions and first Lyons II and III editions, which nevertheless, like the original in Ivo and Bohm., read “you prove.”], we tolerate some whom we cannot correct or punish. We do not abandon the Lord’s threshing-floor because of the chaff [Col. 1243A], nor tear the Lord’s nets because of bad fish, nor [Note: [Col. 1243] added “indeed”: Basel edition.] desert [Note: [Col. 1243] “gathering”: same edition. — “we deserted”: Venice I.] the Lord’s flock because of the goats to be separated at the end, nor migrate from the Lord’s house because of vessels made for dishonour.

### C. II. Catholics do not possess another’s goods merely because they hold things taken from heretics.

The same, *Against the Letters of Petilian*, book II, chapter 43 [Note: [Col. 1243] Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, c. 75.].

If you complain concerning ecclesiastical property or places which you *held, and* do not hold, the Jews too [Note: [Col. 1243] “may be seen”: Basel edition.] may call themselves just and charge us with injustice, because Christians now possess the place in which they once ruled impiously [Note: [Col. 1243] “impious”: Ivo; collected editions.]. What then is improper if Catholics hold, according to the corresponding will of the Lord, those things which heretics held? For that utterance of the Lord applies to all *such persons—that is, to all* ungodly and unjust persons [Note: [Col. 1243] Matt. 21:43]: [Col. 1243B] “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation doing justice.” Or is it written in vain [Note: [Col. 1243] Prov. 13:22]: “The labours of the ungodly [Note: [Col. 1243] “unjust”: collected editions except the Argentinian and Basel editions.] shall be eaten by the just [Note: [Col. 1243] “the devout”: same editions except Basel.]”? Therefore you ought rather to wonder that you still hold anything than that you have lost something. Likewise, chapter 59: § 1. If, now cut off [Note: [Col. 1243] “cut to pieces”: Ivo; original text.], you have begun to possess any things because the Lord [Note: [Col. 1243] “by you”: Basel edition. — “God”: same edition; “the Lord God”: other editions.] gave us what was taken from you, we do not therefore covet another’s goods, because by the command of Him to whom all things belong they have become ours, and are justly ours. For you used *these things* for severance; we [Note: [Col. 1243] “not”: Bohm.] use them for unity. Otherwise, those who were expelled by divine power from before the face of the first people of God, because [Note: [Col. 1243] “who”: collected editions.] they used that land badly, could accuse them of coveting another’s property; and the Jews themselves, from whom the kingdom was taken according to the word [Note: [Col. 1243] “words”: same editions except the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice I editions; cf. Ps. 134.] of the Lord and given to a nation doing justice, can accuse the Church of Christ of coveting another’s property because it possesses the places where the persecutors of Christ formerly ruled [Note: [Col. 1243] added “formerly”: collected editions except Argentinian and Basel.].

### C. III. Ecclesiastical goods are unjustly possessed by heretics.

The same, Epistle L to Boniface [Note: [Col. 1243] Ep. 185, Maurist edition; written A.D. 417. — Anselm, bk. 12, c. 59 (57); Polycarpus, bk. 7, tit. 5.].

As to their charge against us that we covet and take away their property [Note: [Col. 1243] added: “they do not charge this rightly”: collected editions except Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice I.], would that they became Catholics and possessed, in peace and charity with us, not only what they call theirs but ours as well. Yet they are so blinded by their eagerness to slander that they do not observe how contradictory their own statements are. They themselves certainly say, and seem to complain most resentfully, [Col. 1244A] that we coerce them into our communion [Note: [Col. 1243] “our communion”: collected editions except Lyons II and III.] by the violent force of laws. We certainly would not do this at all [Note: [Col. 1243] “therefore”: collected editions.] if we wished to possess their property. For what [Note: [Col. 1243] added “indeed”: same editions except Argentinian.] miser seeks a co-possessor? Who, inflamed [Note: [Col. 1243] “puffed up”: Basel edition.] with the desire to rule, or exalted by the arrogance of domination, wishes to have a partner? Let them look at those who were formerly theirs and are now [Note: [Col. 1243] “now also”: collected editions.] our companions, joined to us in brotherly love, and see how they possess not only what they had, but also what was ours and they had not possessed; yet, if we are fellow-poor with the poor [Note: [Col. 1243] “equals”: collected editions.], those things are both ours and theirs. But if we privately possess things sufficient for us, they are not ours but the poor’s, whose administration we in some manner carry out; we do not claim ownership for ourselves by a condemnable usurpation [Col. 1244B]. Therefore whatever the Donatist party possessed in the name of churches [Note: [Col. 1243] “party”: original text; Bohm. — “the parties of the Donatists possessed”: collected editions.] Christian emperors commanded, by religious laws, to pass with the churches themselves to the Catholic [Note: [Col. 1243] added “unity”: Basel edition. — “unity of the Church”: Lyons II and III. — “Church”: other editions.] Church [Note: [Col. 1243] “to be transferred”: Lyons II and III. — “to transfer”: other editions.]. Since, therefore, the congregations of those same churches are with us [Note: [Col. 1243] “are”: collected editions except Lyons II and III], and with us [Note: [Col. 1243] added “are”: Lyons II and III; “are”: other editions except Argentinian.] are the poor fed from those same small estates, let those who remain outside rather cease to covet another’s goods and enter *into* the fellowship of unity, so that together we may administer not only those things which they call theirs, but also those called [Note: [Col. 1243] “which they call”: collected editions.] ours. For it is written [Note: [Col. 1243] 1 Cor. 3:22–23]: “All things are yours; but you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.”

### C. IV. One cut off from Christ’s body cannot retain the spirit of justice.

The same, in the same Epistle L [Note: [Col. 1243] It was formerly cited as from the letter to Vincentius, in which it is not found.] [Note: [Col. 1243] *Collectio trium partium*, part 2, tit. 50, c. 36.].

[Col. 1244C] Just as a member, if it is cut off from the living body of a human being, cannot retain the spirit of life, so a person cut off from the body of Christ the Just cannot in any way retain the spirit of justice, even though he retains the appearance of the member which he received in the body. Let them therefore enter into this fabric of the body, and possess their labours not from a desire to rule but in the piety of using them well. But we clear our intention, as has already been said, from the filth of this desire, with any enemy judging [Note: [Col. 1243] “of enemies”: same editions except Argentinian and Basel.], when, to the extent that we can, we seek those very persons whose labours they are said to be, so that with us they may use both those goods and ours in Catholic fellowship. § 1. “But,” they say, [Col. 1245A] “this is what troubles us: if we are unjust, why do you seek us?” We reply: We seek you as unjust persons, lest you remain unjust; we seek you as lost persons, that we may rejoice over you when found, saying [Note: [Col. 1245] Luke 15:32]: “My brother [Note: [Col. 1245] added “our”: Basel and Lyons editions.] was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.” “Why then,” he says, “do you not baptize me, so that you may wash me from sins?” I answer: Because I do no injury to the emperor’s mark when I correct the error of a deserter. “Why,” he says, “do I not even [Note: [Col. 1245] absent in Basel edition.] do penance with you?” Rather, unless you do penance, you cannot be saved. For how indeed [Note: [Col. 1245] “therefore”: ibid.] will you rejoice that you have been corrected unless you grieve that you were perverse? “What then,” they say, “do we receive among you when we come over to you?” I answer: You do not indeed [Note: [Col. 1245] “do you not”: ibid. — “not indeed”: other editions.] receive baptism, which could be present in you outside the fabric of Christ’s body but [Col. 1245B] could not benefit you; rather, you receive the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace—without which no one can see God—and charity, which, as it is written, covers [Note: [Col. 1245] “covers”: collected editions; 1 Pet. 4:8.] a multitude of sins.

And above: § 2. But if we consider what is written in the Book of Wisdom [Note: [Col. 1245] Wis. 10:19], “Therefore the just took the spoils of the ungodly”; and likewise what is read in Proverbs [Note: [Col. 1245] Prov. 13:22], “But the riches of the ungodly are stored up for the just,” then we shall see that the question is not who has the property of heretics, but who are [Note: [Col. 1245] “are”: Basel edition.] in the fellowship of the just. Likewise, after some intervening material: § 3. If Christ’s body takes the spoils of the ungodly, and the riches of the ungodly are stored up [Note: [Col. 1245] “may store up”: Basel edition. — “may be stored up”: other editions except Lyons II and III.] for Christ’s body, the ungodly ought not to remain outside [Note: [Col. 1245] “outside”: collected editions.] in order to slander, but rather enter in, that they may [Note: [Col. 1245] added “within”: Basel edition.] be justified. [Col. 1245C] Likewise, after some intervening material: § 4. Let them therefore enter into the fabric of Christ’s body and possess their labours not from a desire to rule but in the piety of using them well [Note: [Col. 1245] “living well”: Basel and Lyons I editions.]. But we clear, as has already been said, our intention from the filth of this desire, with any enemy judging [Note: [Col. 1245] “we cleared”: collected editions.], when, to the extent that we can, we seek those very persons whose labours they are said to be, so that with us they may use both those goods and ours in Catholic fellowship.

Gratian. These authorities therefore plainly show that goods unjustly possessed by heretics are justly taken from them by Catholics, and that Catholics are not thereby said to possess another’s goods.

## QUESTION VIII

[Col. 1246A]

### GRATIAN

**Part I.** As to bishops or any clerics, it is easily proved that they may not take up arms either on their own authority or by the authority of the Roman Pontiff. For when Peter, the first of the apostles chosen by the Lord, wielded the material sword in order to defend his master against the outrage of the Jews, he heard [Note: [Col. 1245] Matt. 26:52]: “Put your sword back into its sheath, for everyone who takes up the sword shall perish by the sword.” As though he were plainly told: Until now it was permitted to you and your predecessors to pursue the enemies of God by the bodily sword; henceforth, as an example of patience, put your sword—that is, what has until now been permitted you—back into its sheath, and wield only the spiritual sword, which is the word of God, in [Col. 1246B] slaying the old life. For everyone other than one who uses legitimate authority, or acts by his authority—that authority of him who, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1245] Rom. 13:4], “does not bear the sword without cause,” and to whom every soul is bound to be subject—everyone, I say, who takes up the sword apart from such authority shall perish by the sword. § 1. Likewise Ambrose [Note: [Col. 1245] Cf. c. 3]: “The weapons of a bishop are tears and prayers.” Likewise, the Apostle’s saying [Note: [Col. 1245] Rom. 12:19], “Do not defend yourselves, beloved,” though addressed generally to all, is nevertheless to be understood as addressed particularly to prelates.

Hence Pope John VIII, justifying Bishop John’s removal from military service, says to the Empress Engelberga [Note: [Col. 1245D] The name *Palea* is not prefixed in the printed editions to this chapter or the next. Nevertheless, both together with the following *Palea* are absent from most old copies.] [Note: [Col. 1245] It is not found among the letters of John VIII.]:

### C. I. On the same matter. [PALEA.]

[Col. 1246C] “He certainly greatly fears, and rightly dreads, to perform secular military service contrary to the profession of his order. To defend territory, to deliberate on battles and arms, belongs to earthly power.”

### C. II. On the same matter. [PALEA.]

Likewise Pope Innocent [Note: [Col. 1245] This chapter is entirely uncertain.].

“When,” he says, “the Lord was being seized by the Jews and Peter cut off the ear of a certain disobedient man, he forbade striking; and, as the pattern for all priests—of whom Peter was the chief—he prohibited even the taking of carnal arms for his own sake.”

### C. III. On the same matter. PALEA.

Likewise Ambrose [Note: [Col. 1245D] The opening of this chapter, which evidently consists of two iambic dimeters, has not been found. The remainder occurs in book 5 of the letters, in the address against Auxentius, although some words are altered here. For Blessed Ambrose has the wording given below, in the same chapter, *Convenior*, § *Quid ergo turbamini*.] [Note: [Col. 1245] Polycarpus, bk. 4, tit. 15.].

“Christ’s soldiers seek neither iron missiles nor weapons. I do not know how to resist when compelled; but sorrow, weeping, [Col. 1246D] prayers, and tears have been my weapons against soldiers. [Col. 1247A] Such are the defences of a priest. I neither ought nor can resist otherwise; but I am not accustomed [Note: [Col. 1247] “am able”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] to flee and abandon the church. The servant [Note: [Col. 1247] “The servant of Christ is accustomed to be protected not by temporal guard but by the Lord’s providence”: collected editions.] of Christ is accustomed to be defended not by bodily protection but by the Lord’s providence.”

Gratian. Accordingly, the Council of Tribur made the following ruling concerning those who die in war or a brawl [Note: [Col. 1247] It is not in the Council of Tribur. Similar provisions occur in Herard of Tours, cc. 50, 113, 134; Burchard, bk. 2, c. 233; Ivo, *Decree*, part 6, c. 308.]:

### C. IV. For a cleric who dies in war or a brawl, no prayer or offering is to be made.

Any cleric who dies in war, in a brawl, or in [Note: [Col. 1247] Absent from Burchard, Ivo, and the collected editions except Lyons II–III.] pagan games is to be prayed for neither in an offering nor in prayer, but is to fall into the hands of the Judge; nevertheless, he is not to be deprived of burial.

[Col. 1247B]

### C. V. Clerics who voluntarily take up arms are to be deprived of rank and consigned to a monastery.

Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 44, concerning clerics bearing arms [Note: [Col. 1247] Held A.D. 633. — Regino, bk. 1, c. 167.].

Clerics who are found willingly to have taken up, or took up, arms in any sedition [Note: [Col. 1247] “faction”: collected editions.] are, after losing their clerical rank, to be consigned to a monastery [Note: [Col. 1247] “to the monastery permanently”: same editions.] for penance [Note: [Col. 1247C] “For penance”: thus read in Anselm [ [Col. 1247] cited by Corr., bk. 7, c. 187, though it does not occur at that place in the collated codex.], and in printed and manuscript council codices, although in later Cologne editions *perenniter*, “permanently,” is written in the margin, as Gratian had formerly read.] [Note: [Col. 1247] “be handed over”: Hispanic Collection.].

### C. VI. Clerics bearing military arms are to be punished by loss of their own rank.

Likewise, from the Council of Meaux, chapter 37 [Note: [Col. 1247] Held A.D. 845. — Regino, bk. 1, c. 175; Burchard, bk. 2, c. 211; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, c. 168; *Decree*, part 6, c. 128.].

Any who appear to belong to the clergy must not take up military arms or go about armed, but must display the title of their profession by religious conduct and religious dress. If they despise this, then, as despisers of the sacred canons and profaners of ecclesiastical holiness [Col. 1247C] [Note: [Col. 1247] “authority”: collected editions.], they are to be punished by [Col. 1248A] loss of their own rank, because they cannot serve God and the world at the same time.
