**Part II. Gratian.** The reply to these authorities is this: Priests ought not to take up arms with their own hands; but they may exhort others to take them up for the defence of the oppressed and for the assault upon God’s enemies.

Hence Leo IV writes to the Emperor Louis [Note: [Col. 1247C] The letters of Leo IV from which this and the following two chapters are taken do not survive. In old *Pontificals*, however, material relevant to these chapters is read: when it was announced that a large fleet of Agarenes had set sail from Africa to ravage Rome, Neapolitans, Amalfitans, and Gaetans came in ships to Ostia to fight the Agarenes in defence of St Peter and the Roman city. Pope Leo summoned their leaders to him and discussed many things with them. The very words relevant to this chapter are as follows: “Receiving them kindly in the Lateran palace, he asked the reason for their coming. They testified that they had come for no other reason than that written above. The pious Apostolic, trusting their words, immediately hastened with a great army and martial array to the city of Ostia, and received them all joyfully. On seeing the supreme Pontiff, they all began to kiss his feet. The chief prelate celebrated Mass in the church of Blessed Aurea, gave the Lord’s body to all, and bestowed upon them, after they had received the body, this prayer: ‘O God, whose right hand raised blessed Peter as he walked upon the waves, lest he sink, and freed his fellow apostle Paul, shipwrecked for the third time, from the depths of the sea: graciously hear us, and grant that, through the merits of both, the arms of these your faithful servants fighting against the enemies of your holy Church may be strengthened and made powerful by your almighty right hand, so that, through their achieved triumph, your holy name may appear glorious among all nations.’ On the following day, after the aforesaid Pontiff had returned from the aforesaid city, those accomplices or partners in wickedness—namely, the Agarenes—appeared off the coast of Ostia with many ships. The aforesaid men attacked them and overcame them all through the prayers of the Apostles and of the holy prelate.”] [Note: [Col. 1247] This chapter and those following are not found among Leo IV’s letters. — Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 27; *Decree*, part 10, c. 83.]:

### C. VII. Against the Saracens the Pope orders the people to assemble and meet them at the seashore.

Therefore, since adverse reports often arrive from the regions of the Saracens, some said that Saracens would come secretly and furtively into the Roman harbour. For this reason we have ordered our people to assemble, have resolved to go down to the seacoast, and have departed from Rome [Note: [Col. 1247] “to Rome”: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions.].

[Col. 1248B]

### C. VIII. The Pope ought to be the avenger and chief helper of his flock.

Likewise Leo [Note: [Col. 1247] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 28; *Decree*, part 10, c. 84.].

You ought to know that we never permit our people to be oppressed by anyone; but if any necessity [Note: [Col. 1247] “their”: Ivo, *Decree*. — “that”: Basel edition.] arises, we avenge them in person, because in all things we ought to be the avengers and chief helpers of our flock.

### C. IX. One who dies in defence of Christians obtains the heavenly kingdom from God.

The same, to the army of the Franks [Note: [Col. 1247] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 30.].

Putting aside every fear and terror, strive to act manfully against the enemies of the holy faith and adversaries of all religion. For the Almighty [Note: [Col. 1247] added “God”: Basel edition.] knows that, if any one of you dies, he has died for the truth of the faith, [Col. 1248C] the salvation of his country, and the defence of Christians, [Col. 1249A] and will therefore receive from Him a heavenly reward [Note: [Col. 1249] “predestined”: Ivo B.] [Note: [Col. 1249] “receives”: Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I–II editions.].

### C. X. At Pope Hadrian’s entreaty Charles undertook war against the Lombards.

Likewise Alcuin [Note: [Col. 1249C] What is reported here from Alcuin occurs in the life and deeds of Charlemagne written by Einhard. In that book, and in Ivo, the word *rogatu*, “at the request,” appears instead of *hortatu*, “at the urging.”] [Note: [Col. 1249] Ivo, *Decree*, part 10, c. 91; *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 32: from the deeds of Charlemagne according to Alcuin. — Deusdedit, part 5. — It is read in Einhard, *Life of Charlemagne*, c. 7, Pertz edition.].

At the urging and prayers of Hadrian, bishop of the Roman city, King Charles, being persuaded, undertook war against the Lombards; this war had previously, at the pleading of Pope Stephen, been undertaken by his father Pippin [Note: [Col. 1249] Not in Einhard.] with great difficulty.

### C. XI. We ought not to persecute Jews, but Saracens.

Likewise Pope Alexander II, to all the bishops of Spain [Note: [Col. 1249] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 29; *Decree*, part 13, c. 114. — In the margin of the *Decree*, this letter is said to be directed to the bishops of Gaul, which seems preferable.].

The cases of Jews and Saracens are plainly different. For war is justly made upon those who persecute Christians [Col. 1249B] and drive them from their cities and their own homes; but these [Note: [Col. 1249] Absent from Ivo and the Argentinian, Basel, and Nuremberg editions.] are everywhere ready to serve.

### C. XII. Whoever does not correct crimes which he can amend commits them himself.

Likewise John VIII [Note: [Col. 1249] Fragment of a lost letter.], to the glorious Duke Demago [Note: [Col. 1249] Domagol: Ivo, *Decree*. — Domago: *Panormia*.].

Moreover, we exhort the zeal of your devotion to be stirred all the more vehemently against the sea-robbers who, under the pretext of your name, rage against Christians, as you know that the reputation of your name has been obscured by their wickedness. For although it may be believed that they lie in wait for sailors against your will, nevertheless [Note: [Col. 1249] Absent from Ivo, *Panormia*, and the Basel edition.], because they are said to be capable of being restrained by you, unless you restrain them [Note: [Col. 1249] “have restrained”: Ivo, *Decree*.], you will not be held innocent. For it is written: “He who does not correct crimes which [Note: [Col. 1249] “what”: collected editions.] he can [Note: [Col. 1249] “will be able to”: same editions except Basel, Lyons II and III.] amend commits them himself.”

[Col. 1249C]

### C. XIII. To punish crime for God is not cruelty, but piety.

Likewise Jerome to Riparius against Vigilantius [Note: [Col. 1249] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 21; *Decree*, part 10, c. 72.].

I have read of Phinehas’s *syromasten* (“dagger” or “spear”) [Note: [Col. 1249C] *Syromasten*: Blessed Jerome, at Num. 25 and Malachi 2, interprets Greek *σειρομάστην* as “dagger”; but at 3 Kings 18 and 4 Kings 11 as “spear,” as does Hesychius, who says that *σειρομάστην* is a *εἶδος λόγχης*, “a kind of lance.”] [Note: [Col. 1249] Num. 25], the severity [Note: [Col. 1249] “authority”: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions; cf. 4 Kings 1.] of Elijah, the zeal of Simon [Note: [Col. 1249] Matt. 10] the Canaanite, the severity of Peter in slaying Ananias and Sapphira [Note: [Col. 1249] “slaying”: collected editions; Ivo; cf. Acts 5], and Paul’s [Col. 1250A] constancy, by which he condemned Elymas the magician, resisting the ways of the Lord, to perpetual blindness [Note: [Col. 1249] “severity”: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions; cf. Acts 13]. To punish crimes for God is not cruelty but piety [Note: [Col. 1250C] The Roman edition reads: “Piety for God is not cruelty.” The Lyons edition: “It is not credulity for God, but piety.” Gratian’s reading, however, does not seem to be rejected.]. Hence it is also said in the Law [Note: [Col. 1249] Deut. 13:6 ff.]: “If your brother, your friend [Note: [Col. 1249] added “your”: Basel edition.], or your wife who is [Note: [Col. 1249] “sleeps”: collected editions; Ivo, *Panormia*.] in your bosom should wish to lead you astray [Note: [Col. 1249] “to corrupt you from the truth”: collected editions except Lyons II and III; Ivo, *Panormia*.] from the truth [Note: [Col. 1249] “should wish”: Lyons I edition.], let your hand be upon them and shed their blood [Note: [Col. 1249] “their own”: Ivo; collected editions.].

### C. XIV. Some things permitted in the Old Testament are forbidden in the New.

Likewise John Chrysostom, on Matthew, Homily XVII, on chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 1249] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 18; *Decree*, part 10, c. 65.].

Phinehas killed a man [Note: [Col. 1249] Cf. Num. 25], and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. But Abraham [Note: [Col. 1249] Absent from the Argentinian edition; cf. Gen. 22], becoming not only a murderer but even a parricide [Note: [Col. 1249] “indeed”: Basel edition. — “a killer of his son”: Argentinian edition.]—which is certainly more serious—was more pleasing, *and all the more pleasing*, to God [Note: [Col. 1249] “pleased”: Ivo; collected editions.]. Peter [Col. 1250B] [Note: [Col. 1249] “But Peter also”: Ivo. — “Peter likewise”: Basel. — “Peter nevertheless”: other editions.] committed a double homicide; nevertheless, what was done was a spiritual work. Therefore let us not look only at actions [Note: [Col. 1249] “only”: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions. — “to actions”: ibid.], but also [Note: [Col. 1249] added “also”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] examine with the utmost care the time [Note: [Col. 1249] “as to time—as to cause”: collected editions.], the cause, the intention [Note: [Col. 1249] “as to intention”: same editions except Nuremberg and Venice I.], the difference between persons [Note: [Col. 1249] “persons also”: collected editions.], and whatever other circumstances attach to the acts themselves [Note: [Col. 1249] “attached”: same editions; Ivo, *Panormia*.] [Note: [Col. 1249] “investigate”: Basel edition.]. For we cannot otherwise arrive at the truth.

### C. XV. When necessity presses, it is permissible to wage war even during the days of Lent.

Likewise Pope Nicholas, in response to the Bulgarians’ inquiries, chapter 46 [Note: [Col. 1249] Written A.D. 866. — Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 37; *Decree*, part 10, c. 93.].

If no necessity presses, one must abstain from battles not only *during* Lent but [Note: [Col. 1249] “but also at every time”: collected editions.] at all times. But if unavoidable urgency presses [Note: [Col. 1249] “opportunity”: original text; Ivo. — “necessity or urgency”: Basel edition.], preparation for war must undoubtedly not be neglected, even in Lent, for the defence [Col. 1250C] both [Note: [Col. 1249] “not so much”: ibid.] of oneself and of one’s country or ancestral laws, lest a person appear to tempt God when he has something he can do and does not take care to provide for his own safety and that of others or prevent injuries to holy religion.

[Col. 1251A]

### C. XVI. Peter delivered Ananias and Sapphira to death by rebuking them.

Likewise Gregory, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 30 [Note: [Col. 1251] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 19; *Decree*, part 10, c. 65. — Cf. Acts 9 and 5.].

Peter, who raised the dead Tabitha by praying, delivered Ananias and Sapphira, when they lied, to death by rebuking them. For it is not recorded that he prayed at their destruction, but only that he rebuked the fault they had committed [Note: [Col. 1251] *patraverant*, “they had perpetrated”: Basel edition]. It is therefore clear that such things [Note: [Col. 1251] *talia*, “such things”: Ivo; collected editions] are sometimes performed by authority, but sometimes indeed [Note: [Col. 1251] *vero* is absent in Ivo] by petition [Note: [Col. 1251] *exhibentur*, “are performed”: the original reads *exhibent*]: for he took life from these persons by rebuking them and restored it to her by praying.

## C. XVII. Blessed Gregory urges certain persons to assemble soldiers and courageously prepare arms against the enemy

The same, to Velox, Master of the Soldiers, Book XII, Epistle 21 [Note: [Col. 1251] Epistle 3, written A.D. 592, Book 2, Maurist edition; Anselm, Book 13, ch. 6, with the added note: dated on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, indiction 10; Ivo, *Decree*, Part 10, ch. 90, quotes a portion; Polycarpus, Book 7, title 13].

As we formerly informed Your Glory [Note: [Col. 1251] *Et*, “and”: original; Anselm; Norberg edition; *notificavimus*, “we notified”: collected editions], soldiers were ready to go there; but since your letter had indicated that the assembled enemies were also ranging hither [Col. 1251B], this reason kept them here. Now, however, it has seemed useful that some soldiers be sent there [Note: [Col. 1251] *et*, “and”: Basel edition; *aut*, “or”: Venice II edition], and Your Glory should take care to admonish [Note: [Col. 1251] *et admonere*, “and admonish”: Basel edition] and exhort them to be ready for service [Note: [Col. 1251] “for justice and for service”: collected editions]. When an opportunity is found, speak with our glorious sons Mauritius [Note: [Col. 1251] “Marcus”: Has edition] and Vitalian [Note: [Col. 1251] “Vitalis”: Arg., Nor., and Venice I editions], and do whatever, with God’s help, they determine [Note: [Col. 1251] *persuaserint*, “they persuade”: collected editions, including the second and third Lyon editions] to be beneficial to the commonwealth [Note: [Col. 1251] *vobis*—“for you”—is absent from the principal collected editions, Basel, and the second and third Lyon editions]. If you learn that Ariulf [Note: [Col. 1251] “Arnulf”: the same editions] is making an incursion either here or into the territory of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 1251] “at Ravenna”: collected editions]—a man who should not even be named—work upon his rear [Note: [Col. 1251] *ita*, “thus,” is absent in the same edition; *occurrere*, “to meet”: Basel edition] as befits brave men [Note: [Col. 1251] *condecet*, “befits”: collected editions], so that, by God’s assistance, your reputation may advance still further in the commonwealth through the quality of your exertions.

Above all, however, we admonish you to release without any delay or excuse the household of Maloin [Col. 1251C] [Note: [Col. 1251C] *Maloin*: These names have been restored as they occur in the printed and manuscript codices of the letters. Ancient copies of Gratian differ greatly at this point both from the received texts and from one another [Col. 1251]: *Alioni, Hoym, Lugidifrisim*: Arg. edition; *Alioin, Adhonaim, Lugidifrisim*: Nor. and Venice I editions; *Aloym, Adoym, Lugidifrusym*: Basel edition; *Alioim, Adhoniaim, Lugidifrusim*: Venice II edition; *Alioym, Adhoniaym, Lugidifrosim*: first Lyon edition; *Alioyn, Adhoniaym, Lugidifrusim*: Paris and second and third Lyon editions; *Aloin, Adobin atque Ingildi, Gnisgini*: Anselm], and of Adobin, Vigildi, and Grussingi, who are known to be with the glorious Master of the Soldiers Mauritius [Col. 1252A], so that, when these aforementioned men come there [Note: [Col. 1251] “and the aforementioned”: Böhm edition], they may proceed with them without any impediment.

## C. XVIII. Likewise, the same author to Mauritius and Vitalian, Book XII, Epistle 23

[Note: [Col. 1251] Epistle 30, written A.D. 592, Book 2, Maurist edition; Anselm, Book 13, ch. 8; Polycarpus, same place.]

We have humbly given instructions to Your Glory, both orally and in writing, through our son Vitalian, with whom you should confer [Note: [Col. 1251] *ut*, “that”: original; *tractaretis*, “you might confer”: original, Anselm, and the second and third Lyon editions; *tractaveritis*, “you will have conferred”: the remaining editions]. On the eleventh day of June, Ariulf [Note: [Col. 1251] Here and below the collected editions read “Arnulf”] forwarded this letter which we directed to you. Therefore reread it and see whether the Suanenses have remained faithful to the allegiance which they promised the commonwealth [Note: [Col. 1251] this phrase is absent from the collected editions, Basel, and the second and third Lyon editions]; and receive from them suitable hostages in whom you can have confidence [Note: [Col. 1251] *accipite*, “receive”: collected editions, principally Arg., rather than *percipite*, “take or receive”]. Bind them once more by oaths [Note: [Col. 1251C] “Once more”: This word is absent from the printed and manuscript letter codices, but occurs in old copies of Gratian and in Anselm], restoring to them what you took in place of a pledge [Col. 1252B] [Note: [Col. 1251] *quae*, “which”: Basel edition; *quos vel quod*, “whom or what”: Arg. edition] and reassuring them by your words [Note: [Col. 1251] *et*, “and”: absent from the Böhm edition].

But if you learn most clearly that they have spoken with Ariulf concerning their submission [Note: [Col. 1251] original: *subditione*, “subjection”], or have indeed given him hostages—as Ariulf’s letter, which we sent you, has made us doubtful [Note: [Col. 1251] *abest ab Ed. Bas.*, “absent from the Basel edition”—the words “them” and “with Ariulf” are absent there]—then, after considering the matter with sound counsel, do whatever you judge useful to the commonwealth, lest either your soul or ours be burdened in any respect concerning the oaths [Note: [Col. 1251C] “Your or”: These two words are absent from the letter codices, though present in the Maurist edition and in Anselm]. But let Your Glory act in such a way that there is neither anything for which we may be reproached by our adversaries nor anything in which the good of the commonwealth may be neglected—may the Lord avert it [Note: [Col. 1251] “our commonwealth”: collected editions; original: “the commonwealth”; the original also reads *exigit*, “requires,” rather than “in which … may be neglected”].

Furthermore, glorious sons, be watchful; for, as I have learned, the enemy has a multitude assembled [Note: [Col. 1251C] In the letters of Blessed Gregory one finds partly *hostem collectum habet*, “he has the enemy assembled,” and partly *hostis collectam habet*, “the enemy has an assembly.” Anselm has *hostem collectam habet*, “he has the enemy’s assembly”] and is said to be stationed in Marchia [Note: [Col. 1252C] The printed letters read *Narinas*; one manuscript reads *Narnia*, and so does Anselm; the Arg. edition has *Mardias*, and the Basel edition *in ardius*]. If, with God angered against him, he should wish to direct his course here [Col. 1252C], plunder his places as far as the Lord assists you, or at least let the *sculpas* [Note: [Col. 1252C] *Sculpas*: Most old copies, as also the printed and manuscript codices of Gregory, read *scultas*. Arg. reads “*culpas* or *scultas*”; the remaining editions, apart from Basel, Paris, and the second and third Lyon editions, read *scultas*. The reading should be *sculcas*, since Greek *σπούλκα* (*spoulka*) among writers of late Greek denotes watches or patrols. The word also means “scouts” in Paul the Deacon and other writers, as the author of the gloss recognized] whom you send [Col. 1253A] search diligently, lest, distressed, he rush upon us [Note: [Col. 1253] *milites*, “soldiers”: Arg., Nor., and Venice I editions; *mittetis*, “you will send”: the remaining editions, principally Basel; *vos*, “you”: Anselm, Basel, and Venice II editions].

Gratian. It is also read in the register that Blessed Gregory ordered the citizens of Tuscia to prepare arms against the Lombards and assigned pay to those serving as soldiers. From this example and the foregoing authorities, therefore, it is clear that priests, although they ought not themselves to take up arms, may nevertheless, by their authority, either persuade those to whom such duties have been entrusted or command any persons to take them up.

## Part III, § 1

But that statement of Nicholas to Kings Louis and Charles is objected to [Note: [Col. 1253D] The letter from which this chapter is taken exists at Rome in the monastery of the Dominicans. It was written to Kings Louis and Charles and begins, “We believe from God’s gift.” In it the pontiff, turning his discourse directly to Charles, complains of certain excuses, especially the excuse contained in this chapter: that no bishops had been sent to Rome for the synod which he wished to hold. For this reason the title, formerly “To Emperor Charles,” was changed] [Note: [Col. 1253] written A.D. 863; Ivo, *Decree*, Part 5, ch. 334]:

## C. XIX. Bishops ought not to be occupied with military affairs

It is plainly very blameworthy what you have added [Col. 1253B], namely, that the greater part of all the bishops keep watch day and night with your other faithful subjects against sea pirates, and that for this reason the bishops are prevented from coming [Note: [Col. 1253] *militibus*, “soldiers”: Ivo]. For soldiers of Christ ought to serve Christ, and soldiers of the world the world [Note: [Col. 1253] *militibus*, “soldiers”: Ivo; “but let soldiers serve the secular world”: collected editions], according to what is written [Note: [Col. 1253] 2 Timothy 2:4]: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs.” But if soldiers of the world devote themselves to secular military service [Note: [Col. 1253] *saeculari*, “secular”: absent from Ivo], what concern have bishops and soldiers of Christ except to be free for prayers [Note: [Col. 1253] original: singular “prayer”]?

## C. XX. Bishops should fear to involve themselves in the death of any human being

Likewise, Pope Gregory, Book VII, Epistle 1, to Sabinianus [Note: [Col. 1253] Epistle 47, written A.D. 594, Book 4, Maurist edition].

If I had wished to involve myself in the death of the Lombards [Note: [Col. 1253] *mortem*, “death”: Basel and the second and third Lyon editions], the Lombard people [Col. 1253C] would today have neither king nor dukes nor counts [Note: [Col. 1253] Basel reads “peoples … would have”], and would be divided in utter confusion. But because I fear God, I am afraid to involve myself in the death of any human being.

Gratian. Behold, Pope Nicholas forbids bishops to be occupied in secular military service; nor does he permit them to go to battle even against sea pirates. How then does Pope Leo go out from the city against the Saracens, summon people from every quarter in order to drive them away from the shore, personally avenge the injuries done to his people, and, together with Gregory, invite soldiers to arms?

But it must be observed that some bishops are content solely with the Levitical portion [Col. 1254A]. As they are numbered only in God’s lot, so they receive God alone as their inheritance, saying [Note: [Col. 1253] Psalm 15:5]: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.” Such persons have nothing in common with the rulers of the world, because they wholly reject temporal things, lest they be held liable to the laws of emperors on their account. No occasion for secular military service remains to such persons; for, since they live on tithes and first-fruits, they are, as sons of the highest King, free in every kingdom from earthly imposts, so that they may say [Note: [Col. 1253] John 14:30]: “The ruler of this world comes, and he has nothing in us.”

Others, however, are not content with tithes and first-fruits, but possess estates, villages, castles, and cities, from which they owe tribute to Caesar, unless they have obtained immunity from such obligations through imperial favor [Col. 1254B]. To them the Lord says [Note: [Col. 1253] Matthew 22:21]: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” The same Apostle says to them [Note: [Col. 1253] Romans 13:7]: “Render to all what is due: tribute to whom tribute is due; tax to whom tax is due.”

Therefore Ambrose, in Epistle XXXIII to his sister Marcellina [Note: [Col. 1254D] This chapter has been compiled from various places in the letter to Marcellina and the oration *Against Auxentius* on not surrendering the basilicas, as noted in their proper places. The earlier citations beginning “And below” have been inserted, and much has been corrected from the same passages] [Note: [Col. 1253] written A.D. 386; Epistle 20, Maurist edition], says:

## C. XXI. Churches are not subject to emperors

I myself was approached by counts and tribunes [Note: [Col. 1253] collected editions add “through me”], demanding that the basilica be surrendered at once, saying that the emperor was exercising his right [Note: [Col. 1253] “had ordered that it must be surrendered, since everything was in his power”: collected editions], because all things were in his power. I answered that, if he asked for what was mine—that is, my estate, my silver, or any such property belonging to me [Note: [Col. 1253] collected editions, principally Arg. and Basel, read “and any such property”; the original reads “whatever such property”]—I would not resist, although everything that was mine belonged to the poor [Note: [Col. 1253] the Arg. edition omits “mine”]. But things divine are not subject to imperial authority [Note: [Col. 1253] “are not subject”: collected editions, principally Basel]. If my property is demanded [Note: [Col. 1253] “if he demands my property”: collected editions], seize it; if my body, I shall come forward. Do you wish to drag me into chains? Do you wish me dead? It is a pleasure to me [Note: [Col. 1253] Arg. reads “to my will”; Basel, “my will”]. Therefore I shall not barricade myself behind crowds of people, nor cling to the altars begging for life; rather, I shall more gladly be sacrificed for the altars [Note: [Col. 1253] collected editions read *gratis*, “gratuitously,” rather than *gratius*, “more gladly”].

For I was horrified in spirit when I learned that armed men had been sent to occupy the basilica of the church, lest, while the people claimed the basilica [Note: [Col. 1253] collected editions read “while the people claimed it”], some slaughter should occur that would result in the ruin of the whole city [Note: [Col. 1253] collected editions read “would come” rather than “would result”]. I prayed that I might not outlive the funeral pyre of so great a city—or rather, of all Italy.

And below:

### § 1

The command is given [Col. 1255A] [Note: [Col. 1255] “You perceive what is commanded when the order is given”: original]: “Surrender the basilica”; that is: “Speak some word against God, and die” [Note: [Col. 1255] Job 2:9]. And not only speak against God, but also act against God. The command is given: “Surrender God’s altars.” We are therefore pressed by royal commands; but we are strengthened by the words of Scripture, which replied: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks” [Note: [Col. 1255] Job 2:10].

And in the oration *Against Auxentius*:

### § 2

Why then are you troubled? I will never voluntarily abandon the right [Note: [Col. 1255] Polycarpus, Book 4, title 15]; compelled, I do not know how to resist [Note: [Col. 1255] collected editions read “I do not know how to abandon you”]. I can grieve, I can weep, I can groan; against arms [Note: [Col. 1255] compare above, ch. 3], even against Gothic soldiers, my tears are my weapons. Such are a priest’s defenses. Otherwise I neither ought nor am able to resist.

And a little below:

### § 3

Would that I were certain that the Church would not be handed over to heretics: I would gladly go to the emperor’s palace, if it were fitting to a priest’s office that I should contend more in the palace than in the church [Col. 1255B]. But in the imperial council Christ is not ordinarily the accused, but the judge. Who would deny that a cause of faith must be heard in the church? If anyone is confident, let him come here.

And in the same letter to Marcellina:

### § 4

It is alleged that the emperor may do everything and that all things are his. I answer: Do not burden yourself, Emperor, by imagining that you have any imperial right in matters divine. Do not exalt yourself; rather, if you wish to reign longer, be subject to God [Note: [Col. 1255] “subject”: collected editions]. For it is written [Note: [Col. 1255] editions add “for”]: “The things of God to God; the things of Caesar to Caesar” [Note: [Col. 1255] “Render the things that are God’s”: collected editions; Basel adds “that are”; compare Matthew 22:21]. Palaces belong to the emperor; churches to the priest. The right over public walls has been entrusted to you, not over sacred things.

Again it is said [Note: [Col. 1255] editions add “to me”]: “The emperor has commanded; I too ought to have one basilica.” I answered [Col. 1255C] [Note: [Col. 1255] collected editions, principally Basel and the second and third Lyon editions, read “I answer”]: “You are not permitted to have it” [Note: [Col. 1255] “any”: collected editions, principally Arg., Nor., and Venice I]. What have you to do with an adulteress? For she is an adulteress who is not joined in lawful marriage to Christ [Note: [Col. 1255] this phrase is absent from the Basel edition].

And in the same oration *Against Auxentius*:

### § 5

We know that Naboth, a holy man and owner of his vineyard, was pressed by a royal request to give up his vineyard, where the king, after cutting down the vines, might plant a worthless vegetable garden; and he answered: “Far be it from me that I should surrender the inheritance of my fathers” [Note: [Col. 1255] 3 Kings 21:3]. The king was grieved because, by a just answer, he had been denied a right that was another’s; but, deceived by a woman’s counsel [Note: [Col. 1255] *concilio*, “counsel”: Basel edition], he came to the field through Naboth’s death [Col. 1255D]. [Note: [Col. 1255D] In the original, immediately after this word, come the words “Naboth his vines.”] For holy Naboth defended his vines even with his own blood [Col. 1256A].

If he did not surrender his vineyard, shall we surrender Christ’s Church? What answer, then, was made by me in defiance? I said, when summoned: “Far be it from me that I should surrender Christ’s inheritance. If he did not surrender the inheritance of his fathers, shall I surrender Christ’s inheritance?” [Note: [Col. 1255] This entire sentence is absent from the Arg. edition; the remaining editions have: “Naboth did not surrender his own, and shall I …?”] But I added this also [Note: [Col. 1255] Arg. reads “still”]: “Far be it from me that I should surrender the inheritance of the Fathers—that is, the inheritance of Dionysius, who died in exile for the faith [Note: [Col. 1255] editions add “who was placed in exile”]; the inheritance of Eustorgius the confessor; the inheritance of Myrocles [Note: [Col. 1255] “Mirocletus”: collected editions]; and the inheritance of all faithful bishops of former times.”

I answered what belongs to a priest [Note: [Col. 1255] collected editions add “I will do”]; let the emperor do what belongs to an emperor. Let him take my life before he takes my faith.

And below:

### § 6

Caesar’s tribute is not denied. It is God’s Church. It certainly ought not to be added to Caesar [Note: [Col. 1255] “is owed”: collected editions], because the temple of God cannot be Caesar’s right [Col. 1256B]. No one can deny that this is said with honor toward the emperor. For what is more honorable than that the emperor be called a son of the Church? When he is so called [Note: [Col. 1255] editions add “a son”], it is said without sin [Note: [Col. 1255] Arg. reads “with glory”; Basel, “with grace”], with grace [Note: [Col. 1255] this phrase is absent from the Arg. and Basel editions]. For a good emperor is within the Church, not above the Church. A good emperor seeks the Church’s aid; he does not reject it.

And above in the same oration:

### § 7

If something of my own were asked of me—a farm, house [Note: [Col. 1255] editions add “or a field,” principally Nor., Venice I and II, Paris], gold, or silver, anything within my legal right [Note: [Col. 1255] editions read “and silver” rather than “or silver”]—I answered that I would gladly offer it [Note: [Col. 1255] collected editions read “I would offer it”; original]. But I cannot take anything away from, nor hand over, God’s temple; I received it to guard, not to surrender [Note: [Col. 1255] collected editions expand: “I can take nothing away from it, nor can I hand it over, since I received it to guard, not to surrender”]. I must also have regard for the emperor’s safety [Note: [Col. 1255] “myself”: Basel edition], because it would benefit neither me to surrender it nor him to receive it [Col. 1256C]. Let him accept the voice of a free priest: if he wishes his own welfare to be considered [Note: [Col. 1255] editions add “it is necessary”], let him withdraw from an injury to Christ. These words are full of humility and, as I think, full of the affection which a priest owes the emperor.

## C. XXII. Churches pay taxes from their external possessions

Likewise Pope Urban [Note: [Col. 1255] This is not found among the letters of Urban II].

The tribute was found in the fish’s mouth when Peter fished [Note: [Col. 1255] compare Matthew 17], because the Church pays tribute from its external possessions, which are openly visible to all. Yet Peter was not commanded to give the whole fish, but only the stater found in its mouth [Col. 1256D], because the Church is not to be given to the emperor, nor can the pontifical dignity, which stands preeminent in the mouth of the head of the Church, be subjected to kings. But certainly, as we have said, what is found in the fish’s mouth is commanded to be given for Peter and the Lord, because from the Church’s external possessions that which has been established from ancient times must be paid to emperors for the peace and tranquillity by which they ought to protect and defend us.

## Part IV

Gratian. Yet persons of this kind do not seem to be subject to imperial exactions. For when, in a time of famine, Pharaoh bought for himself the land of all the Egyptians and subjected everything to his own servitude under that same famine, he supplied the priests with necessities in such a way that they were deprived neither of possessions nor of freedom, the Lord then declaring that priests ought to be free among every people [Note: [Col. 1257] Genesis 47].

[Col. 1257B] Thus Constantius and Constans [Note: [Col. 1257] Rather, Constantius alone; Theodosian Code, Book 16, title 2, ch. 16, written A.D. 361; Anselm, Book 4, ch. 14. In the Arg., Venice II, Paris, and Lyon editions, “Constantine” appears in place of “Constantius”; Arg. nevertheless adds “or Constantius”] granted this immunity to the Church, saying:

## C. XXIII

In whatever city, town, village [Note: [Col. 1257] “or village, or castle”: collected editions], castle, or municipality [Note: [Col. 1257] “and municipality”: Arg. and Basel; “or municipality”: the remaining editions], whoever by a vow of Christian religion [Note: [Col. 1257] original: “of the law of Christian religion”] has made known to all the merit of outstanding and singular virtue shall enjoy perpetual security [Note: [Col. 1257] Basel reads “shall suffer”]. For we wish him always to rejoice and glory in faith [Note: [Col. 1257] editions add “him”], knowing that our commonwealth is sustained more by religions than by offices, bodily labor, or sweat [Note: [Col. 1257] Basel reads “labors”]. Gratian [Note: [Col. 1257] The collected editions attribute this also to Emperors Valentinian and Valens; Anselm, Book 4, ch. 15; compare Theodosian Code, same title, ch. 26], Valentinian, and Theodosius likewise decreed:

### § 1

We decree that all those known to be guardians of churches [Note: [Col. 1257] Basel and the second and third Lyon editions read “guardians of souls or churches”] or holy places, and to serve in religious duties [Note: [Col. 1257] *et*, “and”: collected editions], are to endure no burden of any compulsory public service [Col. 1257C] [Note: [Col. 1257] *nullam*, “no”: collected editions, principally Arg. and Basel; these read “not to endure”].

Emperor Justinian [Note: [Col. 1257] Code of Justinian, *On Holy Churches*, ch. 22; Anselm, Book 4, ch. 22]:

### § 2

We ordain that property passing to venerable churches, or hospices (*xenones*), monasteries, houses for the poor (*ptochotrophia*), foundling hospitals (*brephotrophia*), orphanages (*orphanotrophia*), homes for the aged (*gerontocomia*), or, finally, any other such institution [Note: [Col. 1257] “or any other such association”: Basel, Paris, and the second and third Lyon editions; “if there is any other such association”: Arg., Nor., Venice I and II; the first Lyon edition adds “which exists”], through any generosity of a municipal councillor [Note: [Col. 1257] *curiali*, “municipal councillor”: collected editions read *curialis*], whether among the living, by reason of death, or contained in last wills, shall be free and exempt from the registrations of acquisitions [Col. 1258A] [Note: [Col. 1257] “from the registrations of acquisitions” is absent from the first and third Lyon editions]. The law established concerning such registrations shall retain its force with respect to other persons, but shall temper its force, out of regard for piety, in respect of the ecclesiastical portion or of other establishments assigned to such pious institutions [Note: [Col. 1257] “these”: collected editions, principally Arg., Basel, and the second and third Lyon editions].

Likewise it is read in the Council of Paris [Note: [Col. 1257C] Burchard and Ivo, Part 3, ch. 56, cite something similar from the Council of Meaux, ch. 8. But Ivo, in the same part, ch. 175, gives this same passage from the Council of Paris, in which what is now found in the Council of Meaux, ch. 63, appears to have been renewed] [Note: [Col. 1257] Rather, ch. 63 of the Council of Meaux, held A.D. 845; Burchard, Book 3, ch. 53; Ivo, *Decree*, Part 3, chs. 56 and 175]:

## C. XXIV. A priest is not to be compelled to pay a tax from church land

According to canonical authority and the constitution of Lord Emperor Louis, concerning church land, a holding, and serfs—which he established in his capitularies [Note: [Col. 1257C] “Capitularies”: This seems to refer to the chapter immediately following, namely Book 1 of the Capitularies, ch. 91—or if anyone has bestowed anything on a church for the place of burial, no one is to compel any priest to pay any tax from tithes [Note: [Col. 1257D] “From tithes”: In the said ch. 63 of the Council of Meaux and in Ivo, ch. 175, the reading is: “nor is anyone to impose upon any priest any tax from the tithes and offerings of the faithful,” etc. Ivo, ch. 56, however, has Gratian’s reading] and offerings of the faithful [Col. 1258B]. Nor may anyone of whatever rank or dignity take anything from these, or exact any temporal payment whatsoever [Note: [Col. 1257] Basel reads “any repayment or temporal payment”]. If anyone does so, let him be deprived of communion until satisfaction has been made, and be compelled by royal power to make payment [Note: [Col. 1258C] “Be compelled to make payment”: the council reads, “be compelled by law to correct this.” Ivo, however, agrees with Gratian; Burchard has only as far as “let him be deprived”].

## C. XXV. [PALEA.] Likewise, from the Council of Worms, ch. 50

[Note: [Col. 1258D] This chapter is absent from most ancient copies, but is found in the places indicated] [Note: [Col. 1257] ch. 10, Capitularies of Louis the Pious, A.D. 816; Capitularies, Book 1, ch. 85; compare Council of Worms, held A.D. 858, ch. 50; Regino, Book 1, ch. 24; Burchard, Book 3, ch. 52; Ivo, *Decree*, Part 3, ch. 55 and Part 16, ch. 262; the entire chapter is absent from the Arg. edition].

“It has been decreed that one whole holding, free from every service, shall be assigned to each church; and that priests established in them shall perform no service other than ecclesiastical service from tithes, offerings of the faithful, houses, courts, gardens situated next to the church, or the prescribed holding [Note: [Col. 1257] “nor from houses, nor … situated”: absent from the Council of Worms, though found in the Capitularies of Louis]. If they possess anything more, they shall render the service due from it to their superiors [Col. 1258C] [Note: [Col. 1257] the original reads “to their elders” rather than “to their superiors”].”

Gratian. From this it is understood that the Church, with respect to those things it possesses by imperial grant or from persons bestowing them for the benefit of burial, is bound to no one’s jurisdiction except that of the bishop. But with respect to those things which it has bought from anyone or received by gifts of living persons, it owes the customary services to rulers: it must both pay them annual tribute [Col. 1259A] and, when the army is called out, proceed with them to the camp. Yet even this itself ought not to be done without the consent of the Roman Pontiff.

Therefore Pope Gelasius, to Bishop Elpidius [Note: [Col. 1259] “To Elpidius of Volaterrae”: Ballerini, from comparison with Deusdedit, Part 1, ch. 139; Anselm, Book 6, chs. 118 and 120; Polycarpus, Book 1, title 17]:

## C. XXVI. Bishops are not to venture to go to the imperial court without the authority of the Roman Pontiff

With what audacity, with what rashness, do you write that you are preparing to go to Ravenna [Note: [Col. 1259] “to Ravenna”: collected editions], when the canons plainly command that no bishop at all should make for the imperial court unless he has first appeared before us and consulted us [Note: [Col. 1259C] *contendere*, “to make for”: Polycarpus continues: “Although the long-established bishops of Pistoia, Lucca, and Fiesole are shown recently to have done this by reason either of age or office, how, you who seem to have held the priesthood only a few days, etc.”]? How do you think yourself permitted to do what is not permitted, except because you are hastening to lose that office, of which you show yourself unworthy by such transgressions?

[Col. 1259B]

## C. XXVII. Bishops are not to go to the emperor without the counsel of the metropolitan or of the provincial bishops

Likewise, from the Council of Antioch, ch. 11 [Note: [Col. 1259] held A.D. 332; Anselm, Book 6, ch. 124 (121); Burchard, Book 2, ch. 77; Ivo, *Decree*, Part 6, ch. 268, all from Dionysius].

If any bishop, priest, or indeed anyone at all established under ecclesiastical rule goes to the emperor apart from the counsel [Note: [Col. 1259] “council”: first Lyon edition] or letters of the bishops within the province, and especially apart from the counsel of the metropolitan [Note: [Col. 1259] Basel adds “with counsel”; the first Lyon edition reads “without a council”; the remaining editions read “without counsel”], we decree that he must not only be deposed and expelled from communion, but also deprived of his own rank [Note: [Col. 1259] the Hispanic Collection omits this], as troublesome and unwelcome to imperial ears in contravention of ecclesiastical ordinances [Note: [Col. 1259] collected editions, principally the second and third Lyon editions, read “we decreed”].

Gratian. The Gallican bishops, therefore, are rebuked by Nicholas [Note: [Col. 1259] Above, ch. 19], because, despising apostolic authority, they chose rather to follow arms than to present themselves before the Apostolic See. Yet their going to the court can be understood not as accompanying the emperor in order to assist him by arms, but in order to commend him and his army to God in daily prayers [Col. 1259C]. This seems to be the case addressed by the authority of the Council of Sardica, in whose eighth chapter Bishop Hosius is recorded as having said [Note: [Col. 1259D] This chapter occurs in almost the same words in Isidore’s collection and the Code of Canons, and does not differ greatly from the sense of the Greek canon] [Note: [Col. 1259] held A.D. 347; Anselm, Book 16, ch. 120 (117), through “were”; Polycarpus, Book 4, title 17]:

## C. XXVIII. Bishops who have not been invited or summoned by devout emperors are not to go to the imperial court

If it pleases you, dearest brethren, decree that bishops should not go to the imperial court, except perhaps those who have been invited or summoned by devout emperors [Note: [Col. 1260C] “By devout emperors”: In place of these words, Isidore’s collection and the Code of Canons read “by the letters of our most devout emperor”; likewise in Greek: *Παρεκτὸς τούτων, οὓς ἄν ὁ εὐλαβέστατος βασιλεὺς ἡμῶν τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ γράμμασιν μεταβαλλοῖτο*—“Except those whom our most pious emperor may summon by his own letters”]. But since it often happens that those suffering injury take refuge in the Church’s mercy, and that sinners are condemned to exile or islands, or receive any other sentence [Note: [Col. 1259] the Hispanic Collection reads “whoever … receive it,” rather than “whoever receives any sentence”], they must be aided; and pardon must without doubt be sought for them through the Church [Note: [Col. 1259] “therefore”: the same edition; collected editions].

Gratian. Church prelates may therefore, following the example of Blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 1259] Above, ch. 17], ask emperors or any commanders for defense on behalf of the faithful. They may also, with Blessed Leo [Note: [Col. 1259] Above, ch. 7], courageously exhort anyone to defend himself against adversaries of the holy faith and stir all persons to repel far off the violence of unbelievers. But no bishop may order the shedding of blood by his own authority or that of emperors [Col. 1260B].

Therefore it is read in the Fourth Council of Toledo, ch. 30 [Note: [Col. 1259] held A.D. 633; Burchard, Book 2, ch. 149; Ivo, *Decree*, Part 6, ch. 222]:

## C. XXIX. Priests are to consent to act as judges where remission is promised under oath

Rulers often entrust their affairs to priests against persons liable for offences against majesty. But since priests have been chosen by Christ for the ministry of salvation, they should consent to act as judges for kings where remission of punishment is promised under oath [Note: [Col. 1259] collected editions read “punishments,” principally Arg., Lugden. II and III], not where a sentence involving danger is being prepared. Therefore, if any priest, contrary to this common determination, serves as an examiner [Note: [Col. 1259] collected editions, principally Basel and the second and third Lyon editions, read “one who proceeds”] in cases involving others’ peril, he shall be guilty before Christ of blood shed and shall lose his own rank in the Church.

## C. XXX. Those who administer the Lord’s sacraments ought not to conduct a trial involving blood

[Col. 1260C] Likewise, from the Eleventh Council of Toledo, ch. 6 [Note: [Col. 1259] held A.D. 675; Regino, Book 2, ch. 55, from the Council of Mainz, ch. 5; *Collection in Three Parts*, Part 2, title 42, ch. 6; Burchard, Book 1, ch. 201; Ivo, *Decree*, Part 5, ch. 315].

Those who are to administer the sacraments of the Lord may not exercise judgment involving blood. Therefore such excesses must be strictly prohibited, lest, driven by impulses of indiscriminate presumption, they presume either to judge by their own sentence what ought to be punished by death, or themselves inflict mutilations on any persons, or order them to be inflicted.

[Note: [Col. 1259] “Is absent from the Spanish Collection.”]

[Note: [Col. 1259] “Of such persons”: the same collection.—“Such an excess must be prohibited”: Burchard; Ivo.]

[Note: [Col. 1259] “Mutilation of limbs”: the editions in the other collections, except Basel.]

[Note: [Col. 1259] “Whatever persons”: the Spanish Collection.—“Or through”: the same collection; Burchard; Ivo; Basel edition.]

But if anyone, forgetful of these commands, has done anything of this sort either to the servants of his own church or to any persons whatever, let him be deprived of the honour of the rank conferred upon him and of his office.

[Note: [Col. 1261] “Servants”: the editions in the other collections.]

[Note: [Col. 1261] “And of the conferred”: the Spanish Collection.—“Deprived”: the same collection.]

[Note: [Col. 1261] “Is absent from the same collection.”]

[Note: [Col. 1261] “Is absent from Burchard and Ivo.”]

Let him also be confined in a prison of perpetual condemnation.

[Note: [Col. 1261] “From”: Basel edition.—“Banished”: the editions in the other collections, except Argentinensis.—“Let him be banished”: Burchard; Ivo.]

Nevertheless, communion is not to be denied him when he departs from this life, because of the mercy of the Lord, who “does not will the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live” [Ezek. 33:11].

Gratian. Others also are forbidden, without judicial authority, to carry out mutilations of limbs and burnings of houses.

Hence in the Decrees of Pope Eutychian:

[Note: [Col. 1261] Rather, chapter 7 of the Council of Ravenna, held A.D. 877.—Burchard, bk. 11, ch. 30; Anselm, bk. 11, ch. 60; Ivo, *Decrees*, pt. 13, ch. 40; *Polycarpus*, bk. 6, tit. 15.]

### C. XXXI. Whoever mutilates limbs or burns houses without judicial authority is to be excommunicated.

If anyone performs mutilations of limbs or burnings of houses, or orders them to be done, or consents to one doing them, let him acknowledge himself deprived of the Church until he has made amends for each of these matters lawfully and amicably before the bishop of the city and the other citizens. But if, after a second and third summons, he has not made amends for all the matters of which he is accused, let him be separated from the entire fellowship of Christians as a heathen and a tax collector.

### Part VI. Gratian.

Concerning arsonists also, Innocent II, in chapter 18 of a general council, made the following general enactment [Note: [Col. 1261] Held A.D. 1139.—Ivo, *Panormia*, at the end.]:

### C. XXXII. Whoever burns houses out of favour or hatred for someone is to be excommunicated.

We utterly condemn and prohibit, by the authority of God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, the utterly wicked, destructive, and dreadful malice of arsonists.

And below: § 1. Therefore, if anyone after the promulgation of this our prohibition maliciously sets fire, whether from hatred or revenge, or causes it to be set, or knowingly gives counsel or help to those who set it, let him be excommunicated. If the arsonist dies, let him be deprived of Christian burial; nor is he to be absolved unless he first makes restitution, according to his means, for the damage he inflicted, and swears that he will not set fire again.

[Note: [Col. 1261] “He inflicted”: Basel edition.—“Having made restitution”: the editions in the other collections; the original.—“And swears”: the editions in the other collections, except Lyon II and III.]

Let this penance be imposed upon him: that he remain for one full year at Jerusalem or in Spain in the service of God. But if any archbishop or bishop relaxes this provision [ch. 19 of the same council], let him restore the damage and abstain from episcopal office for a year. Indeed [ch. 20, ibid.], we do not deny to kings and princes the power to administer justice after consultation with bishops and archbishops.

### C. XXXIII. A person who, without holding public office, kills or maims someone is a murderer. Likewise Augustine, in *The City of God*.

[Note: [Col. 1261C] The first part of this chapter, down to the words “But whoever,” is cited above, in the same question 5, *Qui malos*, from the commentaries of St Jerome on Ezekiel, where it is also found.]

[Note: [Col. 1261] In the collections cited at chapter 29. In C. 3, q. 5, where the earlier words of the chapter are quoted, the material printed here from “But whoever” onward is absent, and indeed appears to be by a much later author, perhaps Gratian himself.]

Whoever strikes evil persons precisely insofar as they are evil, and has cause for killing, is a minister of God.

[Note: [Col. 1261D] “And has cause for killing”: above, in the same question 5, *Qui malos*, and in St Jerome, the ordinary gloss, *Panormia*, and Ivo, pt. 10, ch. 114, the reading is *habet vasa*, “has instruments.” The words of Ezekiel being explained are: “Each has an instrument of killing.” But in Burchard and Ivo, the same part, ch. 171, the reading is as in Gratian.]

But whoever, without any public administration, kills an evildoer, thief, sacrilegious person, adulterer, perjurer, or any criminal whatever, or mutilates or maims him in his limbs, shall be judged as a murderer—and all the more severely because he did not fear abusively to usurp a power not granted to him by God.

[Note: [Col. 1261] “And”: absent from the Venice II edition.—“And”: the Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, and Venice I editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1261] “Maims”: the editions in the other collections.—“Kills”: the same editions.]

### Part VII. Gratian.

But concerning those who wound a man together, the question arises: if he dies, which of them incurs the guilt of homicide?

The following was enacted concerning them in the Council at Vermeria:

[Note: [Col. 1261] This is not found in the Council of Vermeria.—Regino, bk. 2, ch. 97, cites the preceding words, down to “shall be judged,” from the Council of Mainz, where they likewise do not occur. We trace the origin to the laws of Rothari, ch. 12.—Lombard Laws, bk. 1, tit. 9, ch. 1.—Burchard, bk. 6, ch. 42; Ivo, *Decrees*, pt. 10, ch. 170.]

### C. XXXIV. If several persons fight against one, by what punishment each is to be punished.

If four or five men, or even more, have fought against one man, and he has died after being wounded by them, whoever inflicted a blow upon him shall be judged a murderer according to the statutes of the canons. The rest, however, who attacked him intending to kill him, shall likewise do penance. But those who neither attacked nor wounded him, and were cooperators neither by counsel nor assistance, but were merely present, are to be free from blame.

# CAUSE XXIV

[Col. 1263]

[Col. 1263A] **GRATIAN**

A certain bishop, having lapsed into heresy, deprived some of his priests of office and marked them with a sentence of excommunication. After his death he was accused of heresy and condemned, together with his followers and his entire household. (Question I.) Here it is first asked whether one who has lapsed into heresy can deprive anyone of office or mark anyone with a sentence. (Question II.) Secondly, whether anyone can be excommunicated after death. (Question III.) Thirdly, whether an entire household is to be excommunicated for the sin of one person.

## QUESTION I

**GRATIAN**

That no one can be deposed or excommunicated by a heretic is easily proved. For every heretic either follows a heresy already condemned or invents a new one. But whoever follows a heresy already condemned makes himself a participant in its condemnation.

Thus, when Acacius complained that he had been condemned by the Apostolic See without synodal authority, Gelasius writes in reply [Note: [Col. 1263C] The sense of this chapter is the same as that of the chapter shortly following, namely, “Acacius,” although the wording differs.] [Note: [Col. 1263] In the *Commonitorium* to Faustus, written A.D. 493; with wording altered here and there.]:

### C. I. Whoever falls into a heresy already condemned makes himself a participant in its condemnation.

Acacius did not become the inventor of a new error, but the imitator of an old one; and therefore it was unnecessary for a new sentence to be issued against him, but only for the old one to be renewed. Thus I became the executor of an old ordinance, not the promulgator of a new one. For whoever falls into a heresy once condemned involves himself in its condemnation.

[Note: [Col. 1263] “New enactments should be issued”: Basel edition.]

### C. II. What a synod has once decreed against any heresy is not to be reopened. Likewise Gelasius, in a letter to the bishops of Dardania.

[Note: [Col. 1263] Written A.D. 495.—Collection in three parts, pt. 1, tit. 46, ch. 3; Anselm, bk. 12, ch. 68; *Polycarpus*, bk. 7, tit. 7.]

Our predecessors, perceiving by divine inspiration what was necessary, wisely provided that what a synod, once assembled against any heresy, had promulgated for the communion of faith and for Catholic and apostolic truth should not thereafter be impaired by new reconsiderations, lest an opportunity be afforded to the wicked for assailing what had been medicinally decreed.

[Note: [Col. 1263] “Necessary”: Basel edition.—“After this”: the same edition.] Rather, when the author of any insanity and the error itself had alike been condemned, they judged it sufficient that anyone who at any time should prove to be a sharer in that error should be bound by the original sentence of its condemnation.

And below: § 1. Thus a synod condemned Sabellius; and it was unnecessary that individual synods should afterward be held to condemn his followers one by one. Rather, according to the tenor of the ancient constitution, the universal Church judged that all who had been participants either in that depravity or in its communion were to be rejected.

[Note: [Col. 1263] “Should have been”: the editions in the other collections.] Thus, by a synod once held condemning Arius, Eunomius [Note: [Col. 1263] “And Eunomius also”: the Basel, Venice II, Paris, and Lyon editions.], Macedonius, and Nestorius, it did not allow a resort thereafter to new councils [Note: [Col. 1263] “Allows”: the editions in the other collections.].

### C. III. One who relapses into a condemned heresy ought not to be proceeded against further. Likewise Pope Felix.

[Note: [Col. 1263C] Polycarpus, bk. 1, tit. 16, cites this from Gelasius, in whose *Commonitorium* to Faustus it occurs.]

[Note: [Col. 1263] Compare chapter 1.—*Polycarpus*, bk. 1, tit. 16.]

Acacius was not an inventor of a new or personal error, so that new enactments should be issued against him; but by his communion he joined himself to another’s crime.

[Note: [Col. 1263] “Should proceed”: Argentinensis edition.] It is therefore necessary that, by a just balance, he should fall under that sentence which the author of the error had incurred together with his successors through synodal agreement.

[Note: [Col. 1263D] *Convenientiam*, “agreement”: this is the reading in old copies of Gratian and in more recent editions of the councils. In older editions of the councils and of papal letters the reading is *conniventiam*, “connivance” [*continentiam*, Basel edition; *conviventiam*, the other editions].]

Gratian. Therefore, if that bishop lapsed into a heresy already condemned, being condemned by the old excommunication he could not condemn others. For one who is excommunicated cannot excommunicate others.

Hence Alexander II writes to Valerian, bishop of Martyr:

[Note: [Col. 1264C] “Martyr”: in Ivo the recipient is “William of Marcion.” In old copies of Gratian, “Martyr” or “Martur” is read, apparently intended to identify the church of which he was bishop; in certain copies there is simply “to Valerian, bishop.”]

[Note: [Col. 1263] In Ivo, *Decrees*, pt. 14, ch. 57, the reading is “to William of Marcion”; in the Victorine manuscript of the *Panormia*, bk. 5, ch. 133, as Baluze observes, “Willermus Martinioni” (in the Basel edition, as in Gratian). In the acts of the Council of Beauvais, in D’Achery, vol. 1, p. 635: “William Marchion.”]

### C. IV. One who is excommunicated cannot excommunicate another.

We have heard that Henry, called archbishop of Ravenna, has attempted to excommunicate you. But because one who is excommunicated could not excommunicate you, we command, by apostolic authority, in absolving you and yours, that you never concern yourselves with this matter.

[Note: [Col. 1263] “Heretical”: the editions in the other collections.—“Having attempted”: Ivo; Council of Beauvais, bk. 1; the editions in the other collections.]

Gratian. But if, from his own heart, he has fabricated a new heresy, from the time he began preaching such things he could condemn no one, because one already cast down cannot cast down another.

[Note: [Col. 1265D] “But if”: some have believed these words also to be Alexander’s. But they are absent from Ivo and the *Panormia*, and old manuscripts of Gratian here bear the mark customarily attached to Gratian’s words. They are the second member of the division proposed by Gratian at the beginning of the question itself; both the style and the arguments offered in confirmation concur.] For the power of binding and loosing was entrusted by the Lord to true, not false, priests. For when He was about to say to the Apostles, “Whose sins you forgive,” etc., He first said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” [John 20:22–23], so as plainly to show all that one who does not have the Holy Spirit cannot retain or forgive sins. Moreover, no one receives the Holy Spirit except within the Church, because by grace He also brings about unity itself.

§ 1. Hence “Receive the Holy Spirit” was said only when they had been gathered together as one; nor did the Holy Spirit descend on the day of Pentecost except upon those gathered together as one [Acts 2]. But just as He is not received outside the Church, so outside it He accomplishes nothing. Therefore, since, as the Apostle says, the Spirit intercedes [Rom. 8:26]—that is, the Spirit obtains—

[Note: [Col. 1266D] “The Spirit intercedes”: these are the Apostle’s very words: “Likewise the Spirit helps our weakness. For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings.” The interlinear gloss on that passage reads: “The Spirit obtains.”]

outside the Church He neither causes persons to intercede nor obtains for them.

Hence, when the Lord was about to say, “Whatever you ask,” etc., He first said: “If two of you agree on earth concerning anything,” etc. And again: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst” [Matt. 18:19–20]—plainly showing all that He does not dwell in the hearts of those who, following the isolating principle of pride, tear themselves away from the coherence of Christ’s body. But where Christ does not dwell, the Holy Spirit, fleeing the divisions of minds, has no place.

Therefore, since forgiving or retaining sins, excommunicating or reconciling, is the work of the Holy Spirit and the power of Christ, it is apparent that those outside the Church can neither bind nor loose; neither restore anyone to ecclesiastical communion by reconciliation, nor deprive anyone of its fellowship by excommunication—a fellowship from which they themselves are plainly wholly excluded, being defiled by heresy or schism or marked by sentence.

Hence, when the Lord gave all the disciples equal power of binding and loosing, He promised Peter, on behalf of all and before all, that He would give him the keys of the kingdom of heaven, saying: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” [Matt. 16:19]. Whoever, therefore, is alienated from the unity of the Church—which is understood through Peter—may curse, but cannot consecrate; he has no power of excommunication or reconciliation.

[Note: [Col. 1265] “May not curse”: Bohm edition.]

Hence, when the Apostle wrote that the Corinthian fornicator must be excommunicated, he said: “Although absent in body, yet present in spirit, I have already judged, as though present, the one who has done this thing: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are assembled and my spirit is with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, to hand such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh” [1 Cor. 5:3–5]. In this, showing the form of excommunication, he taught that only a believer can be marked by a believer. For only a believer can do anything in the name of the Lord and with His power cooperating, since no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except in the Holy Spirit [1 Cor. 12:3].

Likewise, since the Lord forbids the lamb to be eaten outside the Catholic Church, those who are alienated from it by their profession of faith are not expelled from a participation which they abandoned by their own choice, but are permitted to depart. Thus those who heard, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood,” etc. [John 6:54], said: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” and so went back—not driven away, but allowed to depart. Thus also, when the Apostle dealt with those to be excommunicated, he first said, “If anyone is called a brother,” etc.; but concerning unbelievers he added: “God will judge those who are outside. But he entrusted judgment concerning those who are inside to us” [1 Cor. 5:13].

Just as it is apparent from the Apostle’s saying “brother,” and from what he added about believers and unbelievers, that only a believer is to be excommunicated, so also, because this is written only to believers—or rather, because, just as the one who blesses is greater than the one blessed, so the one who curses by virtue of office is greater than the one cursed—it is plainly established that one who departs from the integrity of the Catholic faith has absolutely no power either to curse or to bless. He cannot curse a Catholic, since the latter is his superior; nor can he pass sentence upon one alienated from the faith, as being his equal.

These statements concerning heretics, schismatics, and excommunicated persons—namely, that they possess no power of binding or loosing—are proved by many authorities.

For Pope Leo says, in Sermon III on the anniversary of his accession and Sermon II on the feast of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 1265] Sermon 4, Ballerini edition.—*Polycarpus*, bk. 7, tit. 2.]:

### C. V. Nothing is loosed or bound except what the authority of blessed Peter has loosed or bound.

Peter’s privilege therefore remains wherever judgment is rendered according to his equity; and neither severity [Note: [Col. 1265] Absent from the Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, and Venice I editions.] nor leniency [Note: [Col. 1265] Absent from the Basel, Paris, and Lyon editions.] is excessive where nothing will be bound and nothing loosed except what blessed Peter has either loosed or bound.

### C. VI. In the person of Peter the Church received the power of binding and loosing. Likewise Augustine, *On John*, tractate L, on chapter 12.

[Note: [Col. 1267] Anselm, bk. 12, ch. 7; *Polycarpus*, bk. 7, tit. 2.]

“Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” [Matt. 16:19]. If this was said only to Peter, the Church does not do this. But if, as indeed is the case, it happens in the Church that what is bound on earth is bound in heaven, and what is loosed on earth is loosed in heaven—because, when the Church excommunicates, the excommunicated person is bound in heaven, and when the Church reconciles, the reconciled person is loosed in heaven—then, when Peter received the keys, he signified the holy Church. If in Peter’s person the good within the Church were signified, in Judas’s person the evil within the Church were signified.

[Note: [Col. 1267] “In the heavens”: the editions in the other collections.—*Uti quae*, “as indeed, which”: the same editions; *utique qui*, “as indeed, who”: Bohm.—“And on earth”: Argentinensis edition.—“And in”: the editions in the other collections.—“Are bound”: Basel edition; absent from the remaining editions.—“Are loosed and in”: the editions in the other collections.—“On earth and”: Basel edition; “on earth”: the remaining editions, except Argentinensis.—“Already remains loosed”: Basel edition; “and is loosed in heaven”: the remaining editions.]

### C. VII. One secure by his own merits is sometimes disturbed by those of another. Likewise Ambrose on Luke, chapter 5.

[Note: [Col. 1267] In most old copies there is simply: “Likewise Ambrose.” In the printed editions, “on Mark” was added.—Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 37 (38); *Polycarpus*, bk. 7, tit. 3.]

The ship that has Peter is not disturbed; the one that has Judas is disturbed. Although many merits of the disciples sailed in it, it was still agitated by the treachery of the traitor. Peter was in both; but the one firm through his own merits is disturbed by those of another. Therefore let us beware the faithless man, beware the traitor, lest through one man we, many though we are, be tossed about.

Therefore this ship, in which prudence sails, in which treachery is absent and faith breathes favourably, is not disturbed.

[Note: [Col. 1267] “Many are tossed by a single wave”: Basel edition.]

For how could that vessel be disturbed over which presided the one in whom is the Church’s foundation?

[Note: [Col. 1267] “How”: Basel edition.]

Disturbance, therefore, is there where faith is slight; security is here where love is perfect.

[Note: [Col. 1267] “Is”: the same edition.—“Where”: Venice II edition; “there”: the remaining editions.]

Finally, although the others are commanded to let down their nets [Note: [Col. 1267] “For a catch”: the Basel and Lyon II and III editions.], only Peter is told [Note: [Col. 1267] Luke 5:4]: “Put out into the deep,” that is, into the depth of disputations. For what is so lofty as to see the height of riches, to know the Son of God, and to take up the confession of the divine generation? Though the human mind cannot fully comprehend this by rational inquiry, nevertheless the fullness of faith embraces it.

[Note: [Col. 1267] That is, “to know”: the editions in the other collections.—“Full”: Lyon II and III editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1267] “Providence”: the same collection.—“Faith surpasses”: the same collection.]

### C. VIII. Peter alone received the command to catch a fish with a hook. The same author, a little further below.

[Note: [Col. 1267] *Polycarpus*, ibid.]

There is another apostolic manner of fishing, by which the Lord commands Peter alone to fish, saying [Matt. 17:26]: “Cast the hook, and take the first fish that comes up.”

[Note: [Col. 1267] “And another”: the original.]

[Note: [Col. 1267] “First”: the editions in the other collections.]

### C. IX. Let no disturbance draw one away from the path of the apostolic see, which has always destroyed every heresy. Likewise Pope Lucius to the bishops of Gaul and Spain.

[Note: [Col. 1267] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Compare Agatho’s letter to Constantine Pogonatus.—Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 35 (36); *Polycarpus*, bk. 1, tit. 3.]

Therefore do not depart from the right faith and apostolic path because of any persecution [Note: [Col. 1267] “Disturbance”: the editions in the other collections.—Anselm.], knowing that according to the judgment of the Saviour, blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake [Matt. 5:10].

This is the living [Note: [Col. 1267] “Eternal”: the Basel and Lyon II and III editions.—“True”: Basel edition.] tradition of the Apostles; this is the true charity which must be preached and especially loved and fostered, and confidently maintained by all. This is the holy and apostolic Church of Christ, mother of all churches, which by the grace of almighty God is proved never to have erred from the path of apostolic tradition, nor to have succumbed, corrupted by heretical innovations [Note: [Col. 1267] “To be corrupted”: Anselm; the editions in the other collections.], but, as it received at its beginning the rule of Christian faith from its founders, the chief Apostles of Christ, it remains uncorrupted to the end.

[Note: [Col. 1267] *Fide tenus*, “as far as faith”: the same editions; Pithou edition.]

### C. X. The faith of the Roman Church destroys every heresy and cherishes none. Likewise Pope Sixtus II, to Bishop Gratus, letter I.

[Note: [Col. 1267] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 36 (37); *Polycarpus*, bk. 1, tit. 3.]

I remember that I preside in the name of that Church whose confession was glorified by the Lord Jesus Christ, and whose faith has never cherished any heresy, but indeed destroys every heresy.

[Note: [Col. 1267] The other editions and collections read “whose faith,” with *et*; the original has “to whom faith belongs. Faith never deceives anyone, but …”]

I understand that I am permitted to act in no other way than to devote all my efforts to that cause in which the salvation of the universal Church is endangered.

### C. XI. The Roman Church has succumbed to no heresies. Likewise Pope Eusebius to the bishops of Tuscany, letter III.

[Note: [Col. 1267] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.]

In the Apostolic See the Catholic religion has always been preserved free from stain.

### C. XII. Matters of faith are to be referred to the Roman Church whenever they are discussed. Likewise Pope Innocent to the bishops of the Council of Milevis, letter XXVI.

[Note: [Col. 1269] Written A.D. 417.—Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 27 (28), bk. 2, ch. 54 (53).]

Whenever a question of faith is debated, I think that all our brothers and fellow bishops ought to refer only to Peter—that is, to the author of his name and honour—as your charity has now referred it, so that it may be of common benefit to all churches throughout the whole world.

[Note: [Col. 1269] “Authority”: the editions in the other collections.]

### C. XIII. The Roman Church has possessed zeal for Christian religion above the others. Likewise Pope Julius to the Eastern bishops, letter I.

[Note: [Col. 1269] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 38 (41), cites it from Siricius, whose words in the prologue to his letter to Himerius were adopted by whoever was the author of the Pseudo-Isidorian decretals.—*Polycarpus*, bk. 1, tit. 3.]

In consideration of our office, we are not at liberty to dissemble or remain silent, upon whom the zeal for Christian religion rests more than upon all others.

[Note: [Col. 1269] “Rests”: Merlin reads “succumbs.”]

### C. XIV. The faith commended by the Roman Church fears no one’s denunciation. Likewise Jerome to Damasus, in an exposition of the Creed.

[Note: [Col. 1269] This is not by Jerome.—*Polycarpus*, ibid.]

Most blessed Pope, this is the faith which we have learned in the Catholic Church, and which we have always held and do hold. If perhaps anything has been set down in it with insufficient skill or caution, we wish it to be corrected by you, who hold both Peter’s faith and his see. But if this confession of ours is approved by the judgment of your apostolate, whoever wishes to blame me will prove himself ignorant, ill-disposed, or even non-Catholic—not me a heretic.

[Note: [Col. 1269] “And [your] apostolate”: Basel edition.—“Stain”: the original.—“But”: the editions in the other collections.]

Likewise: § 1. The holy Roman Church, which has always remained unstained [Note: [Col. 1269] “Has remained”: the editions in the other collections.], and will remain in the future through the Lord’s providence and the help afforded by blessed Peter the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1269] “In the age to come”: the Basel and Lyon II and III editions.], shall stand firm and immovable for all time [Note: [Col. 1269] “And firm”: the editions in the other collections.], without any assault of heretics.

[Note: [Col. 1269C] These words seem to be taken from Pope Mark’s letter to Athanasius, but adapted differently. For after certain other words it reads there: “Not that we suppose any evil on your part, but we should wish that we and you, and they, might all think one thing in the future without any wavering, and that the holy Roman Church, which has always remained unstained, might remain in the future, by the Lord’s providence and the assistance of blessed Peter the Apostle, firm and immovable at all times, without any assault of heretics.”]

### C. XV. It is permitted neither to think nor teach otherwise than the Roman Church. Likewise Pope Marcellus to all bishops established throughout Antioch, letter I.

[Note: [Col. 1270C] In this chapter some matters have been added and restored to their proper place from the original. The gloss on the word “ought” can easily be transposed.]

[Note: [Col. 1269] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Compare the preface to the Council of Nicaea found in the Quesnel manuscript (in Ballerini, *Works of Leo the Great*, vol. 3); Innocent I, letter 2; and Gregory the Great, letter 59, bk. 9, Maurist edition.—Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 15 (16); *Polycarpus*, bk. 1, ch. 15.]

We ask you, brothers [Note: [Col. 1269] “Most beloved”: the editions in the other collections.], not to teach or think otherwise than what you have received from blessed Peter the Apostle, the other Apostles, and the Fathers. *For you were first instructed by him. Therefore you ought not to abandon your own father and follow others.*

[Note: [Col. 1269] The words enclosed in asterisks are absent from Anselm.]

For he is head of the whole Church, to whom the Lord said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church,” etc. His see was first among you, but afterward, by the Lord’s command, was transferred to Rome, over which, with divine grace aiding us, we preside on this day. Nor ought you to depart from its ordering, to which, by divine dispensation, all greater ecclesiastical affairs were commanded to be referred, so that they might be regularly disposed of by that see from which they took their beginning. But if your Antiochene see, which was formerly first, yielded to the Roman see, there is none that is not subject to its jurisdiction.

[Note: [Col. 1269] The whole sentence beginning “Nor ought” and ending “first principles” is placed at the end of the chapter in the editions of the other collections.]

### C. XVI. The Alexandrian Church may not dissent from the Roman Church. Likewise Pope Leo to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, letter LXXIX, otherwise LXXXI.

[Note: [Col. 1269] Letter 9 in the Ballerini edition, written A.D. 445.—Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 30 (31).]

Since the most blessed Peter received apostolic primacy from the Lord, and the Roman Church abides in his institutions, it is impious to believe that his holy disciple Mark, who first governed the Alexandrian Church, established the decrees of his traditions by other rules, when without doubt there was one Spirit of grace in disciple and master alike, so that the ordained man could not hand down anything other than what he received from the one who ordained him.

[Note: [Col. 1270C] “Traditions”: this has been corrected from two old manuscripts of Gratian, Anselm, and the original itself. Formerly the text read “by other rules [“churches”: Venice I edition] and traditions he established his decrees.”]

[Note: [Col. 1269] “Apostle”: Anselm.—“His own”: the Spanish Collection; Anselm; Basel edition.—“That one”: the other editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1269] “Were”: Basel edition.—“More orderly”: Lyon I edition.—“Was able”: the editions in the other collections.]

### C. XVII. By its profession of faith the Roman Church cut off the ear of error. Likewise Ambrose, in his commentary on Luke, chapter 22, book X, chapter 12.

[Note: [Col. 1271C] It was formerly cited from Gregory, in whom it has not been found.]

[Note: [Col. 1271] Compare John, chapter 18.]

If Peter struck off the ear intentionally, he taught that they ought not to have an ear in outward appearance which they did not have in ministry. But the good Lord restored hearing even to him, showing according to the prophetic sayings [Isa. 35] that those wounded in the Lord’s Passion can also be healed if they are converted, because every sin is washed away by the mysteries of faith.

[Note: [Col. 1271] “In hope”: the editions in the other collections.—“Ought”: Argentinensis edition.—“In mystery”: the original; “in monastery”: Venice II edition.—“Had”: the editions in the other collections.—“Of Christ”: the same editions.—“By the ministry of faith”: the same editions.]

Therefore Peter removes the ear. Why Peter? Because he is the one who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven. For he condemns who also absolves, because he has received the same power of binding and loosing.
