He removes the ear of one who hears wrongly; with the spiritual sword he removes the inward ear of one who understands wrongly.

[Note: [Col. 1271] “The ear”: Bohm edition.—“But the ear”: the editions in the other collections.]

Let us beware lest anyone’s little ear be cut off while the Passion of the Lord is being read.

[Note: [Col. 1271] This sentence is absent from the original.]

If we refer the weakness of the bodily Passion to His divinity, the little ear is cut off—and cut off by Peter, who did not permit Christ to be regarded as a prophet, but taught that He was to be marked out as the Son of God by faithful confession.

### C. XVIII. The Holy Spirit is not received outside the unity of the holy Church. Likewise Cyprian, in the treatise *On the Unity of the Church*.

[The supplied source ends here.]

The Lord speaks to Peter [Note: [Col. 1271] Matt. 16:18]: “I say to you,” he says, “that you are Peter, and upon this [Note: [Col. 1271] *hanc*, ‘this’: Edd. coll. o.] rock I will build my Church.” He builds the Church upon one [Col. 1271C]; and although after his resurrection he grants equal authority to all the Apostles and says [Note: [Col. 1271] John 20:21], “As the Father sent me, I also send you. Receive the Holy Spirit,” nevertheless, in order to make unity manifest, by his authority he arranged that the origin of that same unity should begin from one.

Certainly the other Apostles were also what Peter was, endowed with an equal share both of honour and authority. But the beginning proceeds from unity, so that the Church [Note: [Col. 1271] *of Christ* added: Anselm; Edd. coll. o.] may be shown to be one. The Holy Spirit, speaking in the person of the Lord, also designates this one Church in the Song of Songs [Note: [Col. 1271] Song 6:8] [Col. 1272A], and says: “My dove is one, my perfect one; she is one [Note: [Col. 1271] *and one*: Edd. coll. o., early Basle and Lyons II–III editions.] to her mother [Note: [Col. 1271] *matris*, “of her mother”: Edd. coll. o.], the chosen one of her mother [Note: [Col. 1271] *genetricis*, “of her mother/begetter”: same editions].”

[Note: [Col. 1271D] *Unity*: What follows, through the word “When” at [Col. 1272C], was added from the original [it is not in Anselm]; from that original other matter was likewise added and corrected.]

Who believes that he holds the faith if he does not hold this unity of the Church? Who is confident that he is in the Church when he opposes and resists the Church? When the blessed Apostle Paul teaches [Note: [Col. 1271] *teaches*: Anselm; Edd. coll. o.] this same thing and displays the sacrament of unity, saying [Note: [Col. 1271] Eph. 4:4–5]: “One body and one Spirit; one hope of your calling” [Note: [Col. 1271] *our*: Edd. coll. o., early Basle edition], “one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God,” we must firmly maintain and uphold this unity, especially we bishops [Note: [Col. 1271] *we bishops*: Edd. coll. o.] who preside in the Church [Note: [Col. 1271] *of God* added: same editions], in order to show that the episcopate itself is one and undivided. Let no one deceive the brotherhood by falsehood; let no one corrupt the truth of faith by faithless treachery.

§ 1. [Col. 1272B] The episcopate is one, of which each holds a share in its entirety [Note: [Col. 1271] *cuius singularis*, “of which an individual [holds a share]”: Edd. coll. o.; original]. The Church [Note: [Col. 1271] *and the Church*: same editions; *the Church also*: original] is one, which spreads more widely into a multitude through the increase of its fruitfulness: as there are many rays of the sun [Note: [Col. 1271] *there are* added: Edd. coll. o.], but one light; and many branches of a tree [Note: [Col. 1271] *there are* added: same editions], but one strength founded upon a tenacious root; and when [Note: [Col. 1271] *as*: same editions; Anselm, book 5, line 5.] many streams flow from one spring, though their number appears dispersed through the abundance of overflowing plenty, unity is nevertheless preserved in the source [Note: [Col. 1271] *and their number*: Edd. coll. o.; *entire* added: same editions].

Separate a ray from the body of the sun: its unity does not admit a division of light. Break off a branch from a tree: it cannot put forth fruit [Note: [Col. 1271] *fractus*, “broken”: original]. Cut off a stream from its spring: once cut off, it will dry up [Note: [Col. 1271] *dries up*: Edd. coll. o.]. So too the Church of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1271] *of God*: Basle edition], flooded with light, extends its rays throughout the whole world; yet it is one light [Note: [Col. 1271] absent in Anselm, book 5] that is diffused everywhere, and the unity of the body is not divided.

It stretches its branches [Col. 1272C] over [Note: [Col. 1271] *through*: Edd. coll. o.] the whole earth in rich abundance [Note: [Col. 1271] *displays*: Arg., Nor., Venice I–II editions]; it spreads broad its copiously flowing streams [Note: [Col. 1271] *bestows streams, branches*: Edd. coll. o., early Basle; *expands*: original and same editions]. Yet there is one head, one source, and one mother [Note: [Col. 1271] *and one* is absent from the Nor. and Venice I–II editions], rich in the successive increase of fruitfulness [Note: [Col. 1271] *of rich abundance*: Edd. coll. o., early Basle]. “We are born from her offspring, nourished by her milk, and animated by her Spirit.” The bride of Christ cannot be adulterated: she is incorrupt and chaste. She knows one house; in chaste modesty [Note: [Col. 1271] *in chaste modesty*: Edd. coll. o., early Basle] she guards the holiness of one chamber [Note: [Col. 1271] *bedchamber*: Basle edition].

[Col. 1273A] C. XIX. Whoever abandons the unity of the universal Church does not have God as Father. The same author, in the same place, a little further on [Note: [Col. 1273] Anselm, book 5, ch. 2 (3); Polycarpus, same place].

He is an outsider, profane, an enemy: he can no longer have God as Father who does not have the Church as mother [Note: [Col. 1273] “who does not hold the unity of the universal Church”: Anselm; Edd. coll. o.].

Again, below:

§ 1. For when the Lord urged unanimity and peace upon his disciples [Note: [Col. 1273] *said to them, in order that*: Edd. coll. o., early Basle], he said [Note: [Col. 1273] Matt. 18:19–20]: “I say to you that if two [Note: [Col. 1273D] *If two*: this reading occurs in eight ancient manuscripts of St Cyprian, both here and elsewhere where this Gospel saying is cited. In the commonly printed texts, however—as formerly in Gratian—the reading is, *If two of you agree* [Col. 1274D] [thus in Edd. coll. o.].] of you agree on earth concerning anything whatever [Note: [Col. 1273] *whatever … shall come to pass*: same editions] that you ask, it shall be granted to you by my Father who is in heaven. For wherever two or three are gathered in my name, I am with them” [Note: [Col. 1273] *them*: same editions, early Arg. and Basle editions].

Thus showing [Note: [Col. 1273] *shows*: Edd. coll. o.] that the greatest weight is given, not to the number of those praying, but to their unanimity. “If two of you,” he says, “agree on earth”: he first set forth unanimity; he first sent before it the concord of peace; he taught that we must agree faithfully and firmly. But how can he agree with anyone [Note: [Col. 1273] *with himself*: same editions; *another*: Basle edition] when he is not in agreement with the body of the Church itself and with the entire brotherhood? How can two or three be gathered in Christ’s name when it is clear that they [Note: [Col. 1273] *who*: Edd. coll. o.; *whom*: the base text] have separated themselves from Christ and from his Gospel?

C. XX. Whoever does not possess the unity of Catholic peace has no power to bind and loose. Augustine, *On Baptism*, book VII, ch. 51 [Note: [Col. 1274D] This chapter and the following one were formerly attributed to Jerome, as also in Anselm and Polycarpus [thus in Edd. coll. o.; Anselm, book 5, ch. 3 (4); Polycarpus, book 7, title 3].]

Having considered everything, I think that I may say without rashness that some persons are in the house of God in such a way that they themselves are also that same house of God—the house said to be built upon the rock [Note: [Col. 1273] Matt. 16:18], called the one dove [Note: [Col. 1273] Song 6:8], the beautiful bride without spot or wrinkle [Note: [Col. 1273] Eph. 5:24], the enclosed garden [Col. 1273C], sealed spring, well [Note: [Col. 1273] *and well … and paradise*: Edd. coll. o.] of living water, paradise with the fruit of trees. This house also received the keys and the authority of loosing and binding. If anyone despises this house when it rebukes and corrects him, let him be to you [Note: [Col. 1273] Matt. 18:17] as a heathen and a tax collector.

Of this house it is said [Note: [Col. 1273] Ps. 25:8]: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells”; and: “Who makes those of one mind dwell in a house” [Note: [Col. 1273] Ps. 67:7]; and: “I rejoiced [Note: [Col. 1273] *was glad*: Edd. coll. o.; cf. Ps. 121:1] in the things said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord’”; and [Note: [Col. 1273] Ps. 83:5]: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; for ages upon ages they shall praise you.”

[Col. 1274A] C. XXI. Different crimes must be punished by different penalties. The same author, book II, ch. 6.

Let us not produce false balances [Note: [Col. 1273] Cf. Prov. 11:1], in which we weigh whatever we wish and however we wish according to our own judgment, saying, “This is serious; this is slight.” Rather, let us bring forth the divine balance from the Holy Scriptures, as from the Lord’s treasures, and weigh in it what is more serious—or rather, let us not weigh it, but recognize what has been weighed by the Lord.

At the time when the Lord showed that earlier offences were to be guarded against by fresh examples of punishment [Note: [Col. 1273] Cf. Exod. 32; Num. 16; Jer. 36; C. XXII], an idol was made and worshipped; a prophetic book was burned in contempt by an angry king; and schism was attempted. Idolatry was punished by the sword, the burning of the book by slaughter in war and foreign captivity, and schism by the earth’s opening its mouth: its leaders were buried alive, and the rest consumed by heavenly fire [Col. 1274B]. Who, then, could doubt that a more heinous offence was committed where a heavier punishment was inflicted?

C. XXII. The Lord receives sacrifice only from the Church. Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXXV, ch. 6 [Note: [Col. 1273] Anselm, book 1, ch. 56 (57); Polycarpus, book 7, title 3].

Because truth is perceived only from within the Catholic Church, the Lord declares that he has a place from which he may be seen [Note: [Col. 1273] *forbids*: Basle edition]. Moses is placed upon a rock so that he may behold the appearance of God [Note: [Col. 1273] *face*: Anselm; Edd. coll. o.; cf. Exod. 33], because unless a person holds firmly to the solidity of faith, he does not know [Note: [Col. 1273] *acknowledge*: same source; cf. Matt. 16:18] the divine presence. Of this solidity the Lord says: “Upon this rock I will build,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1273] “my Church”: Edd. coll. o.]

And above:

§ 1. For it alone is the Church through which the Lord willingly receives sacrifice; it alone intercedes confidently for those who err [Note: [Col. 1273] *will intercede*: Basle edition]. Hence, concerning the victim of the lamb, the Lord commanded, saying [Note: [Col. 1273] Exod. 12:46]: “It shall be eaten in one house [Note: [Col. 1273] *you shall eat*: Nor. and Venice I editions; *you shall eat*: other editions; *the lamb* added: Basle, Lyons II–III editions], and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside” [Note: [Col. 1273] *do not carry out*, or *may it not be carried out*: Anselm; *you shall bring*: Venice II, Paris, Lyons I editions; *outside the doors*: Edd. coll. o.].

For the lamb is eaten in one house [Note: [Col. 1273] *lamb* absent in Anselm], because the true sacrifice of the Redeemer is offered in the one Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 1273] *for the Redeemer*: same source]. The divine law forbids its flesh to be taken outside, because it forbids what is holy to be given to dogs [Note: [Col. 1273] Matt. 7:6]. It alone is the Church in which a good work is fruitfully carried out [Note: [Col. 1273] This whole sentence is absent from Anselm; *a good work*: original]; hence only those who had laboured within the vineyard received the reward of the denarius [Note: [Col. 1273] Matt. 20:9]. It alone [Col. 1275A] preserves those placed within it by the strong bond of charity. Hence also the waters of the flood [Note: [Col. 1275] Gen. 7] lifted the ark to higher places, but destroyed all whom they found outside the ark [Note: [Col. 1275] *killed*: Anselm].

C. XXIII. Whoever tears apart Christ’s body does not show faith toward Christ. Ambrose, in the funeral oration *On the Death of His Brother* [Note: [Col. 1275] Anselm, book 12, ch. 48; Polycarpus, book 7, title 4].

Cyprian summoned Bishop Satyrus to himself [Note: [Col. 1275C] In St Ambrose and Anselm the text reads: “Satyrus summoned the bishop to himself.” Ambrose relates that his brother Satyrus, when he had arrived in Sardinia, summoned a Sardinian bishop to himself in order to learn whether he was a Luciferian or a Catholic. But the text has not been altered because of the gloss and the person who wrote the case.], and regarded no grace as true except the grace of the true faith. He asked him [Note: [Col. 1275] *from the same person*: Edd. coll. o.] whether [Note: [Col. 1275] *whether*: Basle edition] he belonged to the Catholic bishops—that is, whether he was in communion with the Roman Church. Perhaps at that time the Church of that region was in schism. For Lucifer had then separated himself from our communion; and although he had been exiled for the faith and had left heirs of his faith, Satyrus nevertheless did not consider faith to exist in schism. For even if they maintained faith toward God, they did not maintain it toward God’s Church, whose limbs, as it were, they allowed to be divided and whose members to be torn apart.

For since Christ suffered for the Church, and the Church is Christ’s body, faith is not seen to be shown to Christ by those through whom his passion is rendered void and his body divided [Note: [Col. 1275] *and*: Edd. coll. o.]. Therefore, although he possessed the interest (*foenus*) of grace [Note: [Col. 1275D] *Interest*: formerly the reading was *foedus*, “covenant.” *Foenus* has been restored from several ancient copies, the original text, and the other collectors.], and feared to sail as a debtor to so great a name, he nevertheless preferred to cross to the place where he could safely [Note: [Col. 1275] *safely*: same editions] discharge his debt [Note: [Col. 1275] *may be able*: Basle edition; *remove*: Arg. edition]. For he judged that the grace of divine payment [Note: [Col. 1276D] In several manuscripts, in St Ambrose, and in the other collectors, the reading is: “the payment of divine grace.” But it has not been corrected because of the gloss; it will nevertheless be worthwhile to read the whole passage in Ambrose.] consisted in affection and faith; and, because [Note: [Col. 1275] *indeed*: original; Edd. coll. o., early Lyons II–III] he did not delay to fulfil it as soon as [Note: [Col. 1275] *when*: Edd. coll. o., early Basle] the Church first had freer opportunity, he both received the grace he had desired [Col. 1275C] and preserved the grace he had received.

C. XXIV. One must withdraw even bodily from one who does not have the faith of Christ. Bede, on the Second Epistle of John, sole chapter.

“Everyone [Note: [Col. 1275] Coll. tr., part 2, title 50, chs. 13–14; 2 John 9–11] who departs and does not remain in the teaching [Note: [Col. 1275] *of Jesus*: Basle edition] of Christ does not have God. Whoever remains in the teaching [Note: [Col. 1275] *of Jesus*: Basle edition] of Christ has both the Father and the Son. If anyone comes [Note: [Col. 1275] *shall come*: Edd. coll. o.] to you and does not bring this teaching [Note: [Col. 1275] *shall bring*: Arg., Nor., and Venice I–II editions] [Col. 1276A], do not receive him into your house, nor say ‘Greetings’ to him. For whoever says ‘Greetings’ to him shares in his evil [Note: [Col. 1275] *wicked*: Edd. coll. o.] works.”

John taught these things in words concerning schismatics or heretics who must be detested [Note: [Col. 1275] *avoided*: Edd. coll. o.], and also demonstrated them in deeds [Note: [Col. 1275] *for* added: same editions, early Lyons II–III]. § 1. For Polycarp, his hearer [Note: [Col. 1275] *his*: same editions], the most holy man [Note: [Col. 1275] *man* added: same editions] and most courageous martyr, bishop of the Smyrnaeans, relates concerning him that [Note: [Col. 1275] *because*: same editions] once, when he had entered baths at Ephesus for washing and saw Cerinthus there, he immediately sprang out [Note: [Col. 1275] *went out*: Basle edition; *to go out*: other editions] and [Note: [Col. 1275] *and* absent from Edd. coll. o., except the early Basle edition] departed [Note: [Col. 1275] *departed*: Edd. coll. o.] without washing, saying: “Let us flee from here, lest [Note: [Col. 1275] absent from the Basle edition] the baths themselves also collapse [Note: [Col. 1275] *corrupt us*: Edd. coll. o., early Basle edition], in which Cerinthus, the enemy of truth, is washing” [Note: [Col. 1275] *are being washed in*: Edd. coll. o.].

The same Polycarp, when he once met Marcion, who said to him, “Do you recognize us?” [Note: [Col. 1275] *recognize*: same editions], replied: “I recognize the firstborn [Col. 1276B] of Satan.”

C. XXV. Whoever attempts to eat the lamb outside the Church of St Peter is profane. Jerome to Damasus [Note: [Col. 1275] A letter of uncertain date, but apparently genuine; Anselm, book 1, ch. 64 (65); Polycarpus, book 9, title 4].

Because [Note: [Col. 1276C] *Vetusto* (“long ago”): formerly the reading was *vetus* (“old”) [so also Anselm]. It was corrected from the original, since the gloss nevertheless agrees.] the East, long ago shattered by the rage of peoples against one another, tears into pieces [Note: [Col. 1275] *piecemeal, into fragments*: Anselm; Edd. coll. o.] the Lord’s seamless [Note: [Col. 1275] *unquestioned*: Arg. edition; cf. John 19:23] tunic, woven from above [Note: [Col. 1275] *woven together*: Basle, Nor., Paris, Lyons editions], and because foxes ravage Christ’s vineyard, so that amid broken cisterns which have no water it is difficult [Note: [Col. 1275] *and difficult*: Edd. coll. o.] to understand where the sealed spring and enclosed garden may be, I judged that I ought to consult the chair of Peter and the faith praised by the apostolic mouth [Note: [Col. 1275] Cf. Rom. 1], now asking from it nourishment for my soul, as I once received Christ’s garments from it.

Neither [Note: [Col. 1275] *for*: Basle and Lyons II–III editions] the great [Note: [Col. 1275] *so great*: Edd. coll. o.] expanse [Note: [Col. 1275] absent in Anselm] of the liquid element [Col. 1276C] nor the intervening length [Note: [Col. 1275] *breadth*: Edd. coll. o.] of lands could prevent me from seeking the precious pearl. “Wherever the body is, there [Note: [Col. 1275] *there*: Vulgate and Edd. coll. o.] the eagles [Note: [Col. 1275] *and eagles*: Vulgate and Edd. coll. o.] shall gather” [Note: [Col. 1275] Matt. 16:28; *shall be gathered*: same source and Anselm]. The inheritance of the fathers remains wholly uncorrupted among you alone [Note: [Col. 1275] *wholly*: Edd. coll. o.; *authority*: same editions and Anselm], the patrimony having been squandered by an evil offspring. There, in the fertile soil [Note: [Col. 1275] *fertile*: Basle edition; cf. Matt. 13], the purity of the Lord’s seed yields a hundredfold fruit; here, grain buried in furrows degenerates into tares and wild oats [Note: [Col. 1275] *ruptured*: Venice I–II editions; *in* absent in Anselm and Arg./Basle editions].

[Col. 1277A] Now in the West the Sun of righteousness rises; but in the East that Lucifer who fell has set his throne above the stars. “You are the light of the world; you are the salt of the earth; you are vessels of gold and silver” [Note: [Col. 1277] Matt. 5:14]. Here there are earthen [Note: [Col. 1277] *of clay*: Edd. coll. o.; cf. 2 Tim. 2:20] or wooden vessels, destined for an iron rod [Note: [Col. 1277D] In St Jerome the reading is: “They are destined for an iron rod and eternal fire.” [And in Anselm.] But it has not been corrected because of the gloss; this was also the reason why at several other places it seemed sufficient to indicate the original reading in the margin.] and eternal fire [Note: [Col. 1277] *eternal … fire*: Edd. coll. o., early Basle, Paris, Lyons editions].

Although your greatness terrifies me, your humanity [Note: [Col. 1277] *humility*: Edd. coll. o.] nevertheless invites me. From the priest I, a victim by his gift, ask salvation [Note: [Col. 1277] *the victim of salvation*: original and Anselm]; from the shepherd I ask protection as a sheep. Let envy of the Roman height cease; let ambition withdraw. I speak with the successor of the fisherman and disciple [Note: [Col. 1277] *disciples*: Anselm; *disciple*: Basle; *the disciple*: Arg.; *disciple*: remaining editions] of the cross [Note: [Col. 1277] *of Christ*: Anselm and Edd. coll. o.]. Seeking no reward [Note: [Col. 1277] *first*: original and Anselm] except Christ, I am joined in communion with your Blessedness—that is, with the chair of Peter [Note: [Col. 1277] *of Blessed Peter*: Arg. and Basle editions; *of Saint Peter*: remaining editions]. I know that the Church has been built upon that rock [Note: [Col. 1277] Matt. 16:18]. Whoever eats the lamb outside this house is profane [Note: [Col. 1277] Exod. 12:46]. If anyone is not in Noah’s ark [Note: [Col. 1277] Gen. 7], he will perish when the flood reigns.

And because, on account of my sins, I have moved to that wilderness which Syria bounds where it meets the frontier of barbarian territory [Note: [Col. 1277] *joined*: Edd. coll. o.], and cannot continually seek the holy thing of the Lord from your Holiness across so many intervening distances, therefore [Note: [Col. 1277] *and therefore*: same editions; the following *here* is absent in Anselm] here I follow your Egyptian fellow-confessors [Note: [Col. 1277] *martyrs and confessors*: Edd. coll. o.], and hide in a little boat beneath cargo [Note: [Col. 1277] *honorary*: Basle; *hourly*: Arg.; *ships* absent in Anselm] ships. I do not know Vitalis; I reject Meletius [Note: [Col. 1277] *Miletus*: Edd. coll. o.]; I am unfamiliar with Paulinus. Whoever does not gather with you scatters [Note: [Col. 1277] Matt. 12:30]; that is, whoever is not Christ’s is Antichrist’s.

C. XXVI. Catholics must flee the associations of heretics. Ambrose, in his commentary on Luke, chapter 9 [Note: [Col. 1277] Anselm, book 5, ch. 25 (22); Polycarpus, book 3, final title].

[Col. 1277C] What house is worthier of the entrance of apostolic preaching than the holy Church? Or who appears more worthy to be preferred above all than Christ [Note: [Col. 1277] *is* added: Edd. coll. o., early Lyons I; cf. John 13], who is accustomed to wash the feet of his guests and does not allow [Note: [Col. 1277] *may not allow*: Anselm; Edd. coll. o., early Lyons II] those whom he has received into his house to remain with polluted footsteps, but deigns [Note: [Col. 1277] *may deign*: Arg., Basle, Lyons II] to cleanse [Note: [Col. 1277] *change*: original] their subsequent steps, though they are stained by their former life?

He alone, therefore, is the one whom no one ought to desert or exchange, to whom it is rightly said [Note: [Col. 1277] John 6:69]: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we have believed.” [Col. 1278A] You see one who fulfilled the heavenly commands, who, because he did not change his lodging, earned the fellowship of the heavenly dwelling [Note: [Col. 1277] *heavenly*: Edd. coll. o.; *consecration*: Anselm].

Therefore faith must first be sought in the Church, in which, if Christ is its inhabitant, it must without doubt be read [Note: [Col. 1277] *read*: Edd. coll. o.; the wording is uncertain]. But if a faithless people or a heretical teacher disfigures the dwelling [Note: [Col. 1277] *of the Church* added: same editions, early Arg.] of the Church, communion with heretics must be avoided, the synagogue must be fled, and the dust must be shaken from one’s feet, lest the trace of your mind be polluted, as upon dry and sandy ground, by the crumbling droughts of barren unbelief [Note: [Col. 1277] *ground*: Böhm; *dry and sandy*: Edd. coll. o., early Basle; Anselm reads *moist and sandy*, omitting *ground*].

For just as the preacher of the Gospel ought to take upon himself the bodily infirmities of the faithful people, and, as it were by his own footsteps, lighten and abolish vain deeds comparable to dust, according to what is written: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” [Note: [Col. 1277] 2 Cor. 11:29], so, if there is any church that rejects the faith and does not possess the foundations of apostolic preaching, it must be abandoned, lest it be able to scatter any stain of unbelief upon one. The Apostle also plainly affirmed this, saying [Note: [Col. 1277] Titus 3:10]: “Avoid a heretical person after a first [Note: [Col. 1277] *first*: Anselm; Edd. coll. o., early Basle] and second [Note: [Col. 1277] *and another*: Basle; absent in other editions, which have *namely the first*] admonition” [Note: [Col. 1277] *correction*: Edd. coll. o., early Arg.].

C. XXVII. Whoever is separated from the unity of the Church can neither be released from sins nor enter the heavenly kingdom. Bede, on Matthew, in the homily for the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, on Matthew 16 [Note: [Col. 1277] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, ch. 25].

Whoever in any manner separates themselves [Note: [Col. 1277] *shall have separated themselves*: Edd. coll. o.] from the unity of faith or the fellowship of the Apostle Peter can neither be released from the bonds of sins nor enter the gate [Col. 1278C] of the heavenly kingdom.

C. XXVIII. The sacrifices of those whose faith and life are rejected are not accepted. Jerome on the Prophet Amos, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 1277] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, ch. 108].

“I hate [Note: [Col. 1277] Amos 5:21–22] and reject your feasts, and I will not take in the odour of your assemblies. And if you bring me your burnt offerings and your gifts, I will not accept them, and I will not look upon the vows of your fat ones” [Note: [Col. 1277] *I will reject*: Edd. coll. o.].

§ 1. God hates, moreover, and not only hates but also rejects [Note: [Col. 1277] omitted in the same editions, early Lyons II–III] the festivals of those who do not celebrate God’s festivals [Col. 1279A], but their own. [Note: [Col. 1278D] In the commentaries of St Jerome, here—as also in other places in this chapter—several words are inserted. But Ivo has the text here as Gratian does.]

And a little later:

§ 2. To hate [Note: [Col. 1279D] Before these words, Jerome and Ivo have the chapter *God hates*, above, 1, question 1.], reject, and refuse to smell are expressions spoken by analogy with human beings, so that we may know God’s disposition through our own language [Note: [Col. 1279] *we know*: Edd. coll. o.; Ivo]. And if they offer burnt offerings, in order to appear to fast, give alms, or promise chastity—things which are true burnt offerings—the Lord does not accept them, nor does he deign to look upon their fattest victims [Note: [Col. 1279] “nor … their”: not found in Ivo]. For [Note: [Col. 1279] absent from Ivo; *For indeed*: Edd. coll. o.] he judges not the magnitude of the sacrifices but the merits and motives of those making the offering.

§ 3. Hence the widow who in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1279] Cf. Mark 12] had put two small coins into the treasury is preferred by the Saviour to all others, because the Lord regards not the things offered but the will of those who offer them.

[Col. 1279B] C. XXIX. Where charity is absent, faith or righteousness has no place. Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, book I, ch. 9.

Where sound faith is absent, righteousness cannot exist, because “the righteous lives by faith” [Note: [Col. 1279] Rom. 1:17]. Nor should schismatics promise themselves anything from this reward, because likewise righteousness cannot exist where charity is absent. For love of neighbour does no evil [Note: [Col. 1279] Rom. 13:10]; if they had it [Note: [Col. 1279] *heretics* added: Edd. coll. o.], they would not tear apart the body of Christ, which is the Church [Note: [Col. 1279] *Catholic* added: same editions, early Lyons I].

C. XXX. The person who departs from the faith loses the perfection of the Spirit. Pope Innocent to Alexander, epistle XVIII [Note: [Col. 1279] Written A.D. 415; Anselm, book 12, ch. 52; Polycarpus, book 7, title 5; cf. C. 1, question 1, ch. 75].

Heretics, when they departed from the Catholic faith [Note: [Col. 1279] *were withdrawing*: Anselm; *departed*: Basle; *shall have ceased*: remaining editions], lost the perfection of the Spirit which they had received [Col. 1279C].

C. XXXI. Heretics are entirely without the power of sacred office [Note: [Col. 1279] *Office*: thus corrected from most ancient copies. Formerly the reading was *sacrifice* [thus Edd. coll. o.].]. Cyprian, greeting his son Magnus, book I, letter 6 [Note: [Col. 1279] Written A.D. 255; Anselm, book 12, ch. 41; Polycarpus, book 7, title 5].

We have learned [Note: [Col. 1279] *We say*: original; Arg. edition] that all heretics and schismatics absolutely have no power or right. Therefore Novatian neither ought nor can be exempted from being counted among adversaries and antichrists, since he too stands outside the Church and acts against Christ’s peace and love.

And a little later:

§ 1. The Church is one; it cannot be one and at the same time both within and without. For if it is with Novatian, it was not with Cornelius [Col. 1280A]. But if it was with Cornelius, who succeeded Bishop Fabian by lawful ordination and whom, beyond the honour of priesthood, the Lord also glorified by martyrdom, Novatian is not in the Church and cannot be counted as a bishop [Note: [Col. 1279] *so that he cannot be counted as a bishop*: same editions]. He arose from himself, succeeding no one, after scorning Gospel and apostolic tradition. For one who has not been ordained in the Church can in no way possess or hold the Church.

And a little later:

§ 2. The fact that they are said to know the same God the Father as we do, the same Christ the Son, and the same Holy Spirit, cannot help such persons [Note: [Col. 1279] Cf. C. 7, question 1, ch. 9].

And below:

§ 3. We find [Note: [Col. 1279] Cf. C. 1, question 1, ch. 70.] that in such a crime not only leaders and originators but also participants are assigned to punishments unless they separate themselves from communion with the wicked. For the Lord commanded through Moses, saying [Note: [Col. 1279] Num. 16:26]: “Separate yourselves from the tents of these most hardened men, and touch nothing belonging to them [Note: [Col. 1279] *from*: Edd. coll. o.; *their*: same editions], lest you perish with them in their sins.”

What the Lord had threatened through Moses he fulfilled: whoever [Note: [Col. 1279] *whoever who*: same editions] did not separate himself from Korah, Dathan, and Abiram paid the penalty at once for impious fellowship [Note: [Col. 1279] *pious fellowship*: Basle edition]. By this example it is shown and proved that all will be liable both to guilt and punishment who recklessly and irreligiously associate themselves with schismatics against bishops and priests. As the Holy Spirit also testifies and says through the prophet Hosea [Note: [Col. 1279] Hos. 9:4]: “Their sacrifices shall be like bread of mourning; all [Note: [Col. 1279] *and all*: Edd. coll. o.] who eat them shall be defiled,” thus teaching and showing that absolutely all who have been defiled by their sin [Note: [Col. 1279] *sins*: Edd. coll. o.] shall be joined in punishment with their authors [Note: [Col. 1279] *their* added: Edd. coll. o.; *of marriage*: Nor. and Venice I–II editions] [Col. 1280C]. What merit before God, then, can belong to those upon whom punishments are divinely imposed?

And below:

§ 4. But if all heretics and schismatics outside the Church do not have the Holy Spirit, and therefore hands are laid upon them among us [Note: [Col. 1279] *among us* absent from the original] so that they may receive here what can neither exist nor be given there [Note: [Col. 1279] *does not exist*: Edd. coll. o.], it is manifest that remission of sins cannot be given through those whom it is certain do not possess the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1279] *is not*: Edd. coll. o.].

C. XXXII. Those who strive against the Church’s peace must be stripped of their own rank. Pope Liberius, in a letter to Athanasius [Note: [Col. 1279] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Lateran Council under Martin, ch. 4; Anselm, book 5, ch. 65 (69)].

Those who act against the peace of the Church, if they possess rank [Col. 1281A] or a military belt [Note: [Col. 1281] *or military service*: original], are to be stripped of them. If they are private persons and of noble rank [Note: [Col. 1281] *are*: same editions], they are to suffer confiscation of their property; if they are of low birth, they are not only to be flogged bodily but punished with perpetual exile.

C. XXXIII. A bishop who exists in schism neither consecrates nor is consecrated. Pope Pelagius [Note: [Col. 1281] To John the Patrician, of uncertain date; Anselm, book 12, ch. 42; Polycarpus, book 7, title 5].

The plunder in the division is shameful, so to speak: he is not a consecrated bishop but an execrated one. For if we examine the very name of consecration with rational and living understanding, one who refuses to be consecrated together with the universal Church can by no reasoning be called or be consecrated. For to consecrate is to make sacred together. But one divided from the bosom of the Church and separated from the apostolic [Col. 1281B] sees rather performs an execration himself, and does not consecrate. He may therefore rightly be called only execrated, not consecrated, whom the Church does not recognize as making sacred together in unity with the joined members.

Let us nevertheless see whether they have observed even the custom of the parties themselves in his ordination. [Note: The Basel edition reads “in his disordination” (*exordinatione*); the collected editions and Lyons II read “he has observed” (*conservaverit*).] Certainly the ancient custom was that, since it had been burdensome for them to be ordained by the Apostolic See because of distance or the difficulty of travel, the bishops of Milan and Aquileia were to ordain one another; provided, however, that the bishop of the other city should come to the city in which the bishop was to be ordained, so that *also* the election of the ordinand might be better and more easily recognized by the ordainer present, with the consent of the whole Church over which he was to preside, and that he who was to be promoted to the episcopate—though not to be subject to his ordainer—might be ordained in his own [Col. 1281C] church. [Note: Some editions read “so that he might be ordained” (*ut ord.*); others, including the Norican and Venetian editions, read “of the Church” (*ecclesiae*) rather than “in his own Church” (*ecclesia*).]

For since, as we have said, the Church is one, to which it is said in the Song of Songs [6:8], “My dove is one,” it is evident that no other Church exists except that founded upon the apostolic root, from which it cannot be doubted that the faith itself has been propagated *in* the whole world. [Note: The editions variously read “this” (*his*) or “here” (*hic*) for “is”; add “to be” (*esse*) after “propagated”; and read “world” in the dative (*orbi*) rather than the ablative (*orbe*). The subsequent text reads “to us” (*nobis*), or “that we,” in place of “to you” (*vobis*).]

Although this is altogether well known to you, let us nevertheless establish it by the testimony of blessed Augustine. Hear what that most illustrious doctor says to the Church in one of his works. For he says [Note: A similar passage occurs in Distinction 11, chapter 9]:

> “But if a Church in which there is schism cannot rightly be called a Church in any way, it follows that, since there cannot be no Church, it is that Church which is established in the root of the Apostolic See through the successions of bishops, and which the malice of persons cannot in any way extinguish, even if it cannot be excluded [the printed reading *nota* is uncertain], but is judged to be tolerated according to the circumstances of the time.”

[Note: The Basel edition reads “is absent from” (*abest ab*) for “in”; the collected editions and Basel’s earlier printing add “evil” (*malorum*) to “persons”; and Basel reads “by no means” (*nullo*) for “in any way” (*ullo*).]

### C. XXXIV. One who agrees with schismatics does not communicate with unity.

The same [to Viator and Pancratius, as Holstenius published it in the Roman collection from the collection of Deusdedit; Anselm, book 12, chapter 44; Polycarpus, book 7, title 5].

Schism itself, indeed, is a Greek word meaning “a tearing apart.” But there can be no tearing apart in unity. Therefore those who communicate with schismatics do not communicate with unity. [Note: The printed editions variously read *communicant* (“they communicate”) and *communicat* (“he communicates”); the meaning is otherwise unchanged.] They have made parties for themselves; and, separating themselves from that which is one, to use now the Apostle Jude’s words [Jude 19], they do not have the Spirit. From all this it follows that, because they are not one in unity, because they wished to be in a party, because they do not have the Spirit, they cannot possess the sacrifice of Christ’s [Col. 1282B] body. [Note: The editions preserve the grammatical variant *parte* (“in a part”) rather than *partem* (“a part”); the distinction is one of case and construction, not of English meaning.]

§ 1. Our present question, however, is not whether we ought to tolerate the wicked, but whether we ought to associate with schismatics. For if they themselves, although abounding in their own opinion, had nevertheless sought truth while remaining within their mother’s bosom, they were not to be repelled by us until, under the guidance of reason, the truth of the matter had become clear to them. But because they separated themselves from the universal Church, as blessed Augustine says above in the same chapter 33, every Catholic securely detests that party which he knows does not communicate with the universal Church, strengthened by the apostolic sees.

§ 2. Nor does it lessen their crime—rather, it increases it—that you have said they resisted for so long lest those communicating with the apostolic sees should be received into their communion. For although those [Col. 1282C] who wished to communicate with such persons are blameworthy in this matter, much more must those be execrated who despised communion with the apostolic sees not only in priests but even in laypeople. [Note: One edition reads *noluerint* (“who did not wish”) rather than *voluerint* (“who wished”); the Basel edition and the other editions read *voluerint*.] Nor does it avail them that, in those same letters, you report that they suspended themselves from communion with us through ignorance of reason or simplicity of understanding. For that itself is the greater reason why they are schismatics: they were divided not by a judgment arising from divergent belief, but by a most pernicious opinion—fearing something reported among themselves but unknown to them, and rashly believing it against the Apostolic See. [Note: The printed text has *majus* (“greater”) in one place rather than *magis* (“more”); the sense is unchanged.]

§ 3. Blessed Augustine declares that this is specifically schism, saying of such persons [cf. Distinction 19, chapter 6]:

> “By rashly believing against the authority of those churches which deserved to receive letters from the Apostolic [Col. 1283A] See, he will be unable to avert from himself the most monstrous crime of schism.”

[Note: Anselm and Polycarpus read: “which deserved to receive apostolic sees and letters”; this agrees with Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book II, chapter 8, as noted above at Distinction 19, in the canon law.]

In short, either you believe that they are the Church—and, since there cannot be two Churches, you will judge us, God forbid, to be schismatics—or, if it is evident that the true Church is in the apostolic sees, recognize both that they have been divided from unity and that the question of communion has been removed; for true communion is manifestly unable to exist except in unity. [Note: Some editions read *possunt* (“cannot”) rather than *possint* (“may be unable”); the construction remains substantially the same.]

§ 4. Therefore do not wish, as though there were no difference between schismatics and the Church, to associate indiscriminately with the sacrifices of both. What a schismatic consecrates is not Christ’s body, if we are directed by truth. No one can imagine Christ to be divided without incurring the Apostle’s condemnation [cf. 1 Cor. 1]. As has often been said, it is certain that the Church which is Christ’s [Col. 1283B] body is one, and cannot be divided into two or more. For as soon as anyone departs from it, it ceases to be the Church.

### C. XXXV. From the time a bishop teaches what is contrary to the faith, he cannot excommunicate another.

[Note: The rubric has been corrected from most of the old editions. The Venetian I and II, Paris, and Lyons I editions read, elliptically: “From the time a bishop teaches the Church’s faith, even an excommunicated [person] can…”]

Likewise Pope Nicholas writes to the Emperor Michael, Letter VII [written A.D. 865; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 134; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 58].

Pope Celestine says, writing to the eastern bishops:

> “If anyone has been excommunicated or stripped of the rank either of bishop or cleric by Bishop Nestorius or by others who follow him, from the time when they began to preach such things, it is evident that he has *also* remained and remains in our communion; nor do we judge him to have been removed, because the sentence of one who had already made himself liable to removal could remove no one.” [Col. 1283C]

[Note: Nicholas here cites a letter of Pope Celestine written to John, Juvenal, and the other bishops throughout the East, as found in the Council of Ephesus in the Vatican Library and in the Paris edition. The source explicitly introduces the passage as Celestine’s words; it should not be confused with Nicholas’s surrounding commentary.]

### C. XXXVI. Those excommunicated by heretics are not regarded as excommunicated.

Likewise, to the clergy of Constantinople.

[Note: Here Nicholas likewise cites another letter of the same Celestine, which is among the acts of the Council of Ephesus.]

[Note: This is taken from the same letter of Nicholas to Michael. The heading of the chapter should be referred to the letter of Celestine identified by the correctors, of which Nicholas quotes a portion. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 135; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 59.]

He says:

> “The authority of our See has expressly decreed that no bishop, cleric, or Christian of any profession who has been deposed from his office or communion by Nestorius or persons like him, from the time when they began preaching such things, is to be considered deposed or excommunicated. Rather, all these persons *both were and* continue until now in our communion, because one who wavered while preaching such things [in the faith] could *either* depose or remove no one.” [Note: The Basel, Lyons II, and Lyons III editions add “in the faith” (*in fide*); the Basel edition reads *titubat* (“wavers”) rather than *titubabat* (“was wavering”).]

“Have you understood,” [Note: Here Nicholas’s own words begin.] “Emperor, from the persons mentioned above [Col. 1284A] that those who had formerly been removed *themselves* could not remove—not to call him their superior, but even any person whatsoever—nor depose anyone *who had been* already cast down?” [Note: One witness reads *imperatorem* (“the emperor”) rather than the vocative *imperator* (“Emperor”); another reads *supra* (“above”) rather than *ex superius* (“from the persons mentioned above”). The editions also vary over whether *ipsi* (“themselves”) and *qui fuerant* (“who had been”) are present.]

### C. XXXVII. Excommunicated persons are not to be admitted to judge.

Likewise Pope Nicholas, in the same place a little below [*Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 62, chapter 67].

> “We wonder how excommunicated persons have been admitted to judge, since according to the apostolic canons they are forbidden to be received even into communion alone without letters of recommendation. For it is absurd that one who is not permitted even to communicate with the least persons according to the sacred rules should be permitted among you to judge even concerning greater matters.” [Note: The editions vary between *sint* (“have been”) and *sunt* (“are”); one also reads “even to judge concerning his own matters” rather than “concerning greater matters.”]

Gratian. By these authorities it is clearly shown [Col. 1284B] that, from the time someone begins to teach anything against the faith, he can neither depose nor condemn anyone.

§ 1. Yet the statement of Augustine is objected to [Causa 1, question 1, chapter 97]: “Those who depart from the faith lose neither baptism nor the power to baptize.” Therefore, since both powers, namely that of baptizing and that of excommunicating, accompany priestly anointing, those who depart from the faith will either retain both or lack both. But the power of an office is one thing, its exercise another. Often the power of office is either received—as by monks in priestly anointing—or, once received, retained without its exercise—as by suspended persons, from whom administration is forbidden but the power is not removed. Thus power is not taken away from those departing from the faith, just as it is not restored to those returning, lest an injury seem to be done not to a human being but to the sacrament.

Accordingly, when those baptized or ordained by heretics return to the unity of the Catholic faith, if they are received in their orders for the sake of ecclesiastical peace, the sacrament shown to have been administered in the Church’s form is not repeated; rather, by the laying on of hands there is conferred the efficacy of the sacrament, which is taught to have been conferred on no one outside the Church. Since, therefore, both powers remain in heretics, if a heretic excommunicates a Catholic or another heretic in order to draw him into the communion of his own heresy, the sentence, being unjust, has no weight.

§ 2. But if he passes sentence against a Catholic living wickedly, or against a heretic given over to disgraceful deeds or crimes, in order that each may otherwise return to the standard of right living, it seems proper to ask whether both, or the heretic alone, are bound by his [Col. 1285A] sentence. It may be said that a Catholic is in no way bound by a heretic’s sentence. For he cannot strike with the sword of his mouth one whom he is unable to accuse or against whom he is unable to testify. If those whom divine testimonies do not support, because they are outside the Church, have lost the weight of human testimony against those who appear to be in the Church, neither can those proved to have departed from its faith—and therefore condemned by the Church—have the weight of ecclesiastical authority against those same persons. But a heretic seems to have authority over a heretic, just as the devil has authority over the wicked, as over his own flock.

[Col. 1285B] Hence Augustine writes to Vincentius the Donatist and Rogatist, Letter XLVIII [cf. above, Causa 23, question 7]:

### C. XXXVIII. One excommunicated by heretics for a crime is not to be received by Catholics.

> “Whoever receives a person cast out by you for some disgraceful act or crime in the same way as persons are received who, apart from the error by which you separate yourselves from us, have lived among you without crime, displeases us. But you do not easily demonstrate such cases; and if you do demonstrate them, we tolerate some persons whom we cannot correct or punish. We do not abandon the Lord’s threshing floor because of the chaff, nor desert the Lord’s flock because of the goats to be separated at the end, nor depart from the Lord’s house because of vessels made for dishonour.” [Note: The editions vary between *vixerunt* (“they have lived”) and *vixerint* (“they may have lived”).]

### C. XXXIX. Whoever is excommunicated by heretics on disciplinary grounds is not to be received by Catholics.

The same, to Eusebius, Letter CLXIX [Letter 35 in the Maurist edition, written A.D. 396; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 390 and following].

A certain subdeacon of the Spanish (*Spaniensis*) Church [Basel: *Hispalensis*, “of Seville”; the other editions: *Hispan.*], named Primus, was forbidden improper access to consecrated women; and when he despised orderly and wholesome commands, he was removed from the clergy. And below:

§ 1. “If it pleases the Lord, I follow this practice: whoever has been degraded among them on disciplinary grounds and wishes to come over to the Catholic [Col. 1285C] Church is received in the humiliation of penance—something they themselves perhaps would have required of him had he wished to remain among them.”

Gratian. But Augustine’s statement above, in chapters 38 and 39, is to be understood as spoken not because of the force of the sentence—which has no power outside the Church—but in detestation of crimes, which are to be punished equally among heretics as among Catholics. Augustine’s statement [cf. Causa 1, question 1, chapter 97] may nevertheless be understood of the power of baptizing, not of binding or loosing, nor of administering the other [Col. 1286A] sacraments. For baptism, whether administered by a heretic or a layperson, provided it is received in the unity of the Catholic faith, will not lack effect. But the other sacraments—such as that of the sacred body and blood of the Lord, excommunication, or reconciliation—if administered by a heretic or by a Catholic who is not a priest, will have either no effect or a deadly effect. Therefore they are in no way to be received by any of the faithful.

Accordingly Augustine writes in book 1 of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 2 [Anselm, book 9, chapter 49 (51); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 1, chapter 170; Polycarpus, book 7, title 2]:

### C. XL. A person at the point of death may receive penance even from a heretic.

> “If perhaps extreme necessity compels someone, when he cannot find a Catholic from whom to receive it, and, while preserving Catholic peace in his heart, receives through someone situated outside Catholic unity what he would have received in that Catholic unity [Anselm reads: “while preserving Catholic peace” (*pacem cath. custodiens*)]: if he immediately departs even from this life, we regard him as nothing other than Catholic. But if he is delivered from bodily death, when he restores himself in bodily presence to the Catholic congregation from which he had never departed in heart, we not only do not disapprove of what he did but praise it most confidently and most truly. For he believed God to be present to his heart, where he preserved unity, and he did not wish to depart from this life without the sacrament of holy baptism—which, wherever he found it, he knew to be God’s, not human beings.”

> “But if someone, though able to receive it in the *Catholic* Church itself, chooses through some perversity of mind to be baptized in schism, even if afterwards he comes to the Catholic Church, it is certain that there the sacrament is beneficial which may *indeed* be received elsewhere; he is perverse and wicked, and the more harmful because the more knowingly so.”

[Note: The original reads: “even if afterwards he intends to come to the Catholic Church, because he is certain that the sacrament is beneficial there—which may indeed be received elsewhere, but cannot be beneficial elsewhere—he is perverse,” etc. The text was not corrected because of the gloss.]

### C. XLI. Let one who unknowingly receives forbidden communion from a heretic do penance for a year.

Likewise Pope Julius [Note: The Argentinian edition attributes this to Pope Lucian, which is senseless. Burchard, book 19, chapter 105; Anselm, book 11, chapter 135; and Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, chapter 117, attribute it to Pope Eutychian. It is found in the penitential book commonly attributed to Jerome.]

If anyone gives or receives communion from the hand of a heretic and does not know that the Catholic Church forbids it, once he understands, let him do penance for a full year. But if he knows and disregards this, and afterwards does penance, let him do penance for ten years. Others judge seven years, and some more leniently, that he should do penance for five years. [Note: Anselm omits the phrase from “Others” through “let him do penance.”]

§ 1. If anyone permits a heretic to celebrate his Mass in a Catholic church and does not know the prohibition, let him do penance for forty days. If he does so out of reverence for [Col. 1287A] the heretic, let him do penance for a full year. If he does so in condemnation of the Catholic Church and Roman custom, let him be cast out of the Church as a heretic unless he undertakes penance; if he does, let him do penance for ten years. If he leaves the Catholic Church for the congregation of heretics, persuades others, and afterwards does penance, let him do penance for twelve years: three outside the Church, seven among the hearers, and two still outside communion. [Note: Burchard and Ivo read: “four years outside the Church, six among the hearers,” etc.; this passage is nevertheless absent from Anselm. Other copies read “outside communion without offering,” omitting the rest.]

Of such persons the canon says that in the twelfth year they receive communion without the offering. [Note: Burchard and Ivo read “in the tenth year”; other editions read *annis* (“for years”) rather than *anno* (“in the year”).]

### C. XLII. It is preferable to embrace death rather than receive communion from the hand of a heretic.

Likewise Pope Gregory, *Dialogues*, book 3, chapter 31 [Polycarpus, book 7, title 6; cf. Causa 1, question 1, chapter 72].

[Col. 1287B] The young King Ermenegild began to despise his earthly kingdom, and, seeking the heavenly one with strong desire, lay bound in haircloth, pouring out prayers to almighty God for strength. The more he recognized that what could be taken away was nothing, the more sublimely he despised the glory of the passing world. [Note: The editions read *despiciens* (“despising”) rather than *despicere* (“to despise”), *sed* (“but”) rather than *et* (“and”), and *jacere* (“to lie”) rather than *jacens* (“lying”). They also vary between “to almighty God” and “and therefore to almighty God,” between “for strengthening” and “for comforting,” and between *potuerit* (“could have been taken away”) and *poterat* (“could be taken away”).]

When the feast of Easter came, his faithless father sent an Arian bishop to him in the silence of the dead of night, so that he might receive from his hand communion of sacrilegious consecration and thereby deserve to return to his father’s favour. But the man devoted to God rebuked the visiting Arian bishop as he ought, and repelled his perfidy from himself with fitting censures. For although he lay outwardly bound, within himself he stood secure upon a lofty summit of mind. The bishop returned to the father; the father raged, and immediately sent his officers to kill the most steadfast confessor of God where he lay. [Note: Some editions read *occiderunt* (“they killed”) rather than *occiderent* (“to kill”).] *And this was done.*

## QUESTION II

## GRATIAN

### Part I

That no one can be excommunicated or absolved after death is shown by the words of the Gospel, which say [Matt. 16:19]: “Whatever you bind on earth,” etc. “On earth,” he says, not under the earth; showing that we may loose or bind the living according to the diversity of their merits, but cannot pronounce sentence concerning the dead.

Hence Pope Leo, writing to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, Letter XC, chapter 7, alternatively Letter XCII, chapter 6 [Letter 167, Ballerini edition, written A.D. 458 or 459; Regino, book 1, chapter 115; Burchard, book 11, chapter 52; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 115; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 60]:

### C. I. Those who did not wish to be absolved by the Church in this life cannot be absolved after death.

“Concerning persons deprived of communion and so deceased.” [Note: These words are the heading of the twentieth decree of Leo I in the code of canons, and Burchard does not contain them. The rest are Leo’s own words.]

> “The case of these persons must be reserved to God’s judgment, in whose hand it was that their death should not be delayed until the remedy of communion. But we cannot communicate with the dead when we did not communicate with them while living.” [Col. 1288B]

### C. II. The Church can bind or loose the living, not the dead.

Likewise Pope Gelasius, in an instruction to Faustus, master serving as legate at Constantinople. [Note: The instruction from which this chapter is taken first relates that the senators of Constantinople asked Gelasius to permit them to communicate with Acacius, who had been excommunicated by the Apostolic See, and requested that this pardon be granted them. Rejecting their absurd request, Gelasius set forth in this instruction to Faustus, whom he was sending to Constantinople, the matters contained in this chapter.]

[Written A.D. 493; *Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 46, chapter 2, and partly Anselm, book 11, chapter 7.]

> “Let it be read, from the beginning of the Christian religion; or at least let an example be given in the Church of God that any pontiffs, the Apostles themselves, or finally the Saviour himself ever granted pardon except to those who corrected themselves. For under this heaven it is neither read nor at all said that they utter the words: ‘Grant us pardon, while nevertheless we persist in error.’ Let those also who endeavour to oppose canons to us show alike in what [Col. 1288C] canons, what rules, what reading, or what authority—whether from our elders, from the Apostles themselves, who are undoubtedly to be ranked above all others, or from the Lord and Saviour himself, who is believed to judge the living and the dead—this has ever been done, or is commanded to be done.

> “We read that Christ raised the dead; we do not read that he absolved those dead in error. And he who alone certainly had the power to do this chiefly commanded the blessed Apostle Peter [cf. Matt. 16:19]: ‘What you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and what you loose on earth [Col. 1289A] shall be loosed in heaven.’ ‘On earth,’ he says. For nowhere did he say that one who died while under *this* bond is to be absolved.”

[Note: The collected editions vary between “it has been heard” (*auditum*) and “it has been heard” in the feminine form (*auditam*), and between *autem* (“but”) and *enim* (“for”); they also read *non* (“not”) rather than *nec* (“nor”), and “from whose voice” rather than “which is uttered by their voice.” The cited Gospel wording is variously expanded to: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven, and whatever you bind on earth, etc.” The editions also read *nunquam* (“never”) rather than *nusquam* (“nowhere”), and “is to be absolved” rather than “he said that he was absolved.”]

### C. III. We need not abstain after their death from the alms of persons with whom we did not cease to communicate during life.

Likewise Urban II, to Bishop Guilmund. [Note: The name appears variously as Guimund of Aversa, Julimund, Guilmund, and Guilimund in Ivo and the editions.]

“Certainly, we praise what your fraternity is known to have done concerning Richard, son of Borrell, out of zeal for God and love of souls. But you should not be so afraid, nor should you so greatly abstain from his alms. For among the other Fathers of our faith, blessed Pope Leo, that outstanding teacher, says [cf. above, chapter 1]: ‘We ought not to communicate with the dead with whom we did not communicate while they were alive.’ It follows, therefore, that with those with whom we communicated while living—to speak conversely—we may also communicate when they are dead.

“We, plainly, are placed between two hostile groups, namely the impious and the schismatics. We cannot in any way communicate with schismatics—or, as the printed text has it, ‘or it is permitted’ (*aut licet*), an evidently difficult reading; but we communicate provisionally with sinners and robbers because they have supported the Church until now and promise to remain faithful in the future. [Note: Ivo’s *Decretum* reads “for the time being” (*pro tempore*) for “provisionally.”] Otherwise we would have to depart from the regions of this world. Under this same pledge we recently granted them absolution at the feast of blessed Peter’s nativity. Therefore, because the aforesaid man neither was excommunicated by name nor *exiit* (“departed,” here apparently died) while communicating with those excommunicated by name—but remained in faith and service to his Lord—we may provisionally—that is, so long as we tolerate them—share in his alms [Col. 1289C] and assist the soul of the deceased by every means of Christian religion.” [Note: Ivo’s *Decretum* reads *obiit* (“died”), while the *Panormia* reads *exigit* (“demands”), for *exiit*. The editions also vary between *religionis* (“of religion”) and *religioni* (“to religion”), between *modis* (“by means”) and *moribus* (“by customs”), and between *adjuvare* (“to assist”) and *adunare* (“to unite”).]

### C. IV. On the same matter.

Likewise Pope Gelasius, to all bishops established throughout Dardania or Illyricum.

[Note: The letter from which this chapter is taken survives among other writings of Gelasius in an old Vatican manuscript, which also contains many letters of other pontiffs.]

[Written A.D. 494; Anselm, book 12, chapter 30; Polycarpus, book 7, title 1.]

> “Let no one at all persuade you that Acacius’s crime of prevarication was remitted. For after returning to the fellowship of wickedness, he rightly deserved to be excluded from apostolic communion [Col. 1290A], and he died while persisting in this same condemnation. *Now* dead, he cannot obtain an absolution which, while alive, he neither sought nor deserved. For it was entrusted to Christ’s Apostles by his own voice: ‘What you bind on earth,’ etc. But concerning one now placed under divine judgment, it is not lawful for us to determine anything other than that in which the final day found him. Therefore, unless his name has been repudiated, together with those of the other associates in this error, you must share the purity of the Lord’s table with absolutely none of them—a purity which our predecessors always took great care to preserve distinct from heretical defilement.”

### C. V. A sentence of condemnation against one who remains incorrigible cannot be relaxed.

Likewise Pope Leo, Letter XIII to the Empress Pulcheria. [Note: Leo’s words concerning Eutyches are: “When he saw that the meaning of his folly displeased Catholic ears, he ought to have withdrawn from his opinion and not so disturbed the Church’s bishops as to deserve a sentence of condemnation—a sentence which, if he wishes to persist in his opinion, no one will be able to relax.”] [Letter 31, Ballerini edition, written A.D. 449.]

> “Whoever deserves to receive a sentence of condemnation, if he wishes to persist in his own opinion, no one will be able to relax it.”

### Part II. Gratian

These authorities prove that we can loose or bind the living, not the dead. Yet this must not be understood of every crime. For there are certain crimes for which anyone can be accused or condemned even after death, such as heresy.

Hence, in the first session of the Fifth Synod we read [held A.D. 553; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 115 and following; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 62 and following]:

[Note: This chapter is taken from various passages of the Fifth Synod, approximately as it appears in the four-volume Cologne edition.]

### C. VI. Heretics are to be excommunicated even after death.

[Col. 1290C] Certainly [Note: [Col. 1290C] *Certainly:* In the letter of the emperor Justinian, reported in the first session or conference of that Fifth Synod, this passage reads as follows: “We urge that this also be discussed, which is variously advanced by those who say [Col. 1290D] that heretics ought not,” etc. But the sense is not very different.] [Note: [Col. 1289] *vainly:* original.] some maintain that heretics ought to be anathematized after death, and that in this they follow the teaching of the holy Fathers, who condemned not only living heretics but also *after death, those who had died in their impiety*; just as they restored after death those who had been unjustly condemned, and enrolled them in the sacred diptychs [Note: [Col. 1290C] *Diptychs:* This was corrected from the council itself, since it had previously been read as *dicticis*. Diptychs were two tablets: one contained the names of the living, the other those of the dead, whose names were recited at Mass. The term was transferred from the diptych of oysters, mentioned by St Ambrose, *Hexameron*, book 5, chapter 8. Such ecclesiastical diptychs—of the living, of the dead, or of both—are mentioned in the letter of Innocent I to Decentius, chapter 2; in letter 137 of St Augustine to the clergy and people of the church of Hippo, above, 2, question 1, chapter *Nomen*, and 11, question 3, chapter *Quid obest*; in the letter of Gelasius to the emperor Anastasius; in the letter of the bishops of the Egyptian diocese to Anatolius, found after the Council of Chalcedon; and frequently elsewhere.] [Note: [Col. 1289] *tipicis:* there.—*scripturis* (“writings”): Argentinian edition.—*dicticis* (which the gloss thinks derives from *dico*, “I say”): the remaining early Basle editions.] wrote them down. This was done *also* [Note: [Col. 1289] Absent from Ivo.] in the cases of John and Flavian, bishops of Constantinople of revered memory. Likewise, in Session V, §1: *Augustine says* [Note: [Col. 1291] Chapter 3, *On the Unity of the Church*]: “If [Note: [Col. 1291] “And if”: collected editions and early Basle edition.] perhaps these books identify their betrayer as the Lord identified Judas, let Caecilian by name and expressly, or the ordainers [Note: [Col. 1291] Added: “of”: Ivo; collected editions.] of those books, be read in them as betrayers; and unless [Note: [Col. 1291] “If not”: Panormia; the same editions.] I anathematize them, may I myself be judged to have betrayed along with [Note: [Col. 1291] Absent from the original.] them.”

(And later in the same session:) §2. What has just been recited is what Augustine of holy memory [Note: [Col. 1291] “by Gelasius of holy memory” (with the following words omitted): Ivo, *Decretum*.] taught, and it agrees [Note: [Col. 1291C] *And agrees:* This has been corrected from the synod itself; [Col. 1291D] it was formerly read, “and he established that it be maintained” [ [Col. 1291] thus Basle and Lyons II–III editions; “he established that it be decided and maintained”: remaining editions; “he fittingly established that it be maintained”: Ivo, *Panormia*.]] with what has been established and maintained from the beginning in the Church. But an impious [Note: [Col. 1291] Absent from Ivo, *Decretum*—“for”: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions.] doctrine has already been strongly censured [Note: [Col. 1292C] *Strongly censured:* The interlinear gloss in two old manuscripts of Gratian reads: “that is, very strongly censured.”] and condemned; and the Church’s tradition requires that those subject to such a doctrine be anathematized, even if they have died. Therefore Augustine of holy memory says: “*That* [Note: [Col. 1291] Absent from Ivo.] if Caecilian should now be convicted of the charges [Col. 1291B] brought [Note: [Col. 1291] Added: “now”: Basle edition.] against him, I anathematize him even after his death [Note: [Col. 1291] Added: “his”: collected editions.]” [Note: [Col. 1291] “that man”: the same editions; Ivo.]

(Likewise above in the same session:) §3. Many bishops assembled [Note: [Col. 1291] Added: “are”: the same editions; Panormia; cf. African Council, chapter 84, in Dionysius.] and, making certain arrangements concerning various matters pertaining to ecclesiastical order, decreed concerning deceased bishops [Note: [Col. 1291] “the bishops themselves”: there.] who left their property to heretics [Note: [Col. 1291] “leave”: original; Ivo; Argentinian and Basle editions.] that they too should be subjected to anathema after death. There are also letters of Augustine of holy memory saying that, if any persons did not think rightly during their lives, although they had not yet been condemned while living, nevertheless, once their sin has been shown, they too are to be subjected to anathema after death.

Likewise below: §4. “If the things objected *by them* to Caecilian were true, and could at some time be shown [Note: [Col. 1291] “can”: there; Böhm.] to us, we would anathematize him, though he is *already* dead” [Note: [Col. 1291] “let us anathematize”: Argentinian edition.] [Note: [Col. 1291] Augustine, to Boniface, letter 185.].

(Likewise below:) §5. “You say [Note: [Col. 1291] Book 3, *Against Cresconius*, chapter 39.] that it is permitted [Col. 1291C] to me to pass judgment even *today* upon the dead, because judgment can be rendered not only concerning the living but also concerning [Note: [Col. 1291] Absent from the collected editions, early Venetian II, Paris, and Lyons editions.] the dead” [Note: [Col. 1291] “is customarily rendered”: collected editions.].

(And later: §6. Rambulas [Note: [Col. 1291] “Rabanus”: Basle, Paris, and Lyons editions—“Rabula”: remaining editions; Ivo, *Decretum*.] of holy [Col. 1292A] memory, made bishop of the city of Edessa, who shone among the priests [Note: [Col. 1291] “shone brightly”: original; Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions and early Basle edition, in which it reads, “is said to have shone brightly.”], anathematized this Theodore *of Mopsuestia* [Note: [Col. 1291] “this” absent from Ivo—“the same man”: Böhm.] even after his death [Note: [Col. 1291] Added: “his”: collected editions.] in the Church.” [Note: [Col. 1291] “Mosophenus”: Basle, Paris, and Lyons editions—“Mosothemus”: Argentinian and Venetian I–II editions—“Mosothenus”: Norimberg edition, which adds the word *venustum* (“beautiful”); Ivo, *Panormia*.]

Likewise below: §7. “The Church of Rome also, some years ago, anathematized Dioscorus [Note: [Col. 1292C] *Dioscorus:* In the ancient *Pontificals*, in the Life of Boniface II, the following is found: “He, namely Boniface, was ordained amid contention along with Dioscorus; Dioscorus in the Constantinian basilica, but Boniface in the basilica of Julius. There was therefore dissension among clergy, people, and senate for twenty-eight days, until Dioscorus died on the fifth day before the Ides of October. In those days Boniface, moved by zeal and in great bitterness, convoked a synod and, by a written declaration under bond of anathema, condemned Dioscorus; he reconciled the clergy and deposited that declaration [Col. 1292D] in the Church archive.”], who had been pope of that same Church, after his death [Note: [Col. 1291] “excommunicated”: Ivo, *Panormia*.], although he had not sinned against the faith. All [Note: [Col. 1291] Added: “men”: the same source; collected editions.] who live at Rome [Note: [Col. 1291] “the Romans here”: Ivo—“here at Rome”: collected editions.] know this, especially those holding dignities, who also remained in communion with that Dioscorus until his death.”

Likewise below: §8. “*If anyone has recourse to the times of Theophilus of holy memory or earlier, he will find Origen too [Note: [Col. 1291] “found”: Argentinian, Basle, and Lyons I editions.] anathematized after death. Your Holiness has also done this *now* [Note: [Col. 1291] Absent from Ivo, *Decretum*.] in this [Note: [Col. 1291] “that very case”: original.] matter, as has Vigilius [Note: [Col. 1291] “Julius”: Venetian I–II editions.] the most reverend pope of elder [Col. 1292B] Rome.*”

Likewise below: §9. The holy synod said: “What has been said and produced is indeed [Note: [Col. 1291] Absent from Ivo, *Panormia*.] sufficient to show the ecclesiastical tradition: heretics ought to be anathematized even after death.”

Likewise, in Conference VIII [Note: [Col. 1291] Ivo and the collected editions cite this from Session IV.], §10. The holy synod said: “Various letters of Augustine of holy memory, who shone among the African bishops, have been read, indicating that heretics ought to be anathematized even after death. Other most reverend African bishops also observed this ecclesiastical tradition; and the holy Roman Church anathematized certain bishops even after death, although they had not been accused during their lives on account of the faith. The records held by us attest both points.”

## QUESTION III

[Col. 1292C]

## GRATIAN

### Part I

That an entire household ought to be excommunicated for the sin of one person is proved by many examples. For the sin of the Sodomites [Note: [Col. 1293] Genesis, chapter 19.], their little children, who through the privilege of age did not know their fathers’ crimes, were consumed by heavenly fire.

§1. Likewise, for the sin of the Amalekites [Note: [Col. 1293] 1 Samuel, chapter 15.], not only their children but even their beasts, down to everyone urinating against a wall, were commanded by the Lord to be destroyed.

§2. Likewise, Dathan and Abiram [Note: [Col. 1293] Numbers, chapter 16.] were authors of schism against Moses and Aaron; and not they alone, but all their possessions with them, went down into the depths.

§3. Even in the New Testament, severe pestilence is sometimes recorded as raging when sins required it; it involved even those who had no awareness of sin. Therefore, if little children are found to have been punished so severely for their parents’ sins, there can be no doubt that for the sins [Col. 1293B] of those same parents they can likewise be struck by a sentence of excommunication.

§4. The reply to this is as follows. That little children are corporally chastised for their parents’ sins appears from the words of the Gospel, where the disciples are said to have asked Christ concerning the man blind from birth [Note: [Col. 1293] John, chapter 9, verse 2.]: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” In them is also fulfilled what the Lord said to Moses [Note: [Col. 1293] Exodus, chapter 20, verse 5.]: “I am a jealous God, visiting the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation.” Yet little children are not spiritually liable for their parents’ sins once they have been cleansed from original sin through the sacrament of regeneration. Hence the Lord says through Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 1293] Ezekiel, chapter 18, verse 20.]: “The soul that sins shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity [Col. 1293C] of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.” Whatever sins their parents committed, once a child has been personally separated from them, are not imputed to that child for punishment. Therefore all descendants are said to be bound by Adam’s sin because no one had yet been materially propagated from him. But since God considers not priests’ sentence but their lives, it is clear that one whom the stain of sin does not infect ought not to be marked by a sentence.

Thus Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: “If anyone called a brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or serving idols, with such a person you ought not even to take food.” From these words it is understood [Col. 1294A] that unless someone has first been publicly named [Note: [Col. 1293D] *Named:* This explanation of St Paul’s passage to the Corinthians, here and above at 11, question 3, *Ad mensam*, § *Evidenter*, seems derived from St Augustine’s *Fifty Homilies*, final homily, chapter 12, above at 2, question 1, chapter *Multi*.] in connection with a crime—that is, either accused and convicted before a judge, or personally confessed in court—he is neither to be struck by a sentence nor avoided in communion. Therefore an entire household is not to be excommunicated for the sin of one person.

[Note: [Col. 1293] 1 Corinthians, chapter 5, verse 11.] [Note: [Col. 1293] Thus, in substance, Anselm.]

Hence Augustine writes to Bishop Auxilius in Letter LXXV [Note: [Col. 1293] Letter of uncertain date, 250 in the Maurist edition—Anselm, book 12, chapter 67; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 126; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 44.]:

### Chapter I. A son is not to be anathematized for his father’s sins

If you have an established judgment on this matter, based on certain reasons or testimonies of Scripture, be so good as to teach us *also* [Note: [Col. 1293] Absent from Ivo.] how a son may rightly be anathematized for his father’s sin; or a wife for her husband’s [Note: [Col. 1293] Added: “sin”: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions.]; or a slave for his master’s [Note: [Col. 1293] “master”: collected editions, early Basle, Venetian I, and Norimberg editions.]; or even anyone [Col. 1294B] not yet born in the household [Note: [Col. 1293] Added: “for anyone’s sins”: Basle edition.], if born at the time when the whole household is bound by anathema and cannot be helped by the washing of regeneration because of danger of death. For this was [Note: [Col. 1293D] *For this was:* Thus also in Ivo and the *Panormia*; but the letter itself reads, “For neither is this a bodily punishment, by which we read that certain despisers of God were killed together with all their people who were not participants in the same [Col. 1294D] impiety.” Yet, because of the gloss and the doctors’ statements, nothing has been changed.] [Note: [Col. 1293] “is”: Ivo.] a bodily punishment, by which we read that certain despisers of God, along with all their people who were participants in the same impiety, were killed together. At that time, indeed [Note: [Col. 1293] “to be sure”: the same source; Anselm; collected editions.], mortal bodies—destined in any event [Note: [Col. 1293] “also”: there.] to die—were put to death in order to frighten the living. But the spiritual punishment, by which what is written is brought about [Note: [Col. 1293] Matthew, chapter 16, verse 19.], “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven,” binds souls, concerning which it is said: “The soul [Note: [Col. 1293] “As the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son, is mine”: collected editions; Vulgate; Ezekiel, chapter 18, verse 5.] of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins shall die.”

§1.
