You have perhaps heard [Note: [Col. 1293] “You heard”: Ivo, *Panormia*—“You heard [plural]”: *Decretum*; collected editions.] that certain priests of great renown anathematized some sinners along with their households. But perhaps, if they were questioned, they would be found capable of giving an account of it. Yet I, because [Note: [Col. 1293] Absent from Ivo.] if anyone should ask [Note: [Col. 1293] “from”: Ivo—“shall ask”: Ivo; collected editions.] me whether [Note: [Col. 1293] Added: “this”: collected editions.] this is rightly done, cannot find what answer to give, have never dared to do it in response to certain crimes [Col. 1294C] committed unanimously against the Church, unless I was very gravely provoked. [Note: [Col. 1294D] *Of certain:* The same gloss prevented this from being changed, and it also agrees with Ivo and the *Panormia*. But the original reads: “when I was very gravely moved by certain crimes monstrously committed against the Church.”] But [Note: [Col. 1293] “But … learn” is lacking in Ivo.] if the Lord has revealed to you that [Note: [Col. 1293] “because”: original—added “this”: collected editions.] it is justly done, I do not despise your youthful age and the first stages of ecclesiastical rank. *Behold, I am here:* [Note: [Col. 1293] “Behold, I am present”: absent from Anselm.] an old man, I am ready to learn from a young fellow bishop, and a bishop of so many years from a colleague not yet one year old, how we can render [Col. 1295A] a just account to God and men if we punish innocent souls for another’s crime—which they do not derive [Note: [Col. 1295] “which”: Anselm; collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 1295] “contract”: Venetian I–II, Norimberg, Paris, and Lyons I editions.], *as* [Note: [Col. 1295] “as” absent from Anselm.] they derive *original sin* from Adam, in whom all sinned—with a spiritual penalty.

For the son of Classicianus [Note: [Col. 1295] “Classianus”: Lyons II–III editions.], although he inherited from his father [Note: [Col. 1295] “parent”: collected editions.] the guilt [Note: [Col. 1295] “offense”: the same editions; Anselm.] of the first man, to be cleansed away by the sacred font of baptism, nevertheless whatever sin his father committed after [Note: [Col. 1295] “afterward”: collected editions.] begetting him, he did not participate in it; who doubts that it does not [Note: [Col. 1295] Absent from Anselm and Basle, Venetian I–II, and Paris editions.] concern him? What shall I say of the wife [Note: [Col. 1295D] *What shall I say of the wife?* These words are absent from the other editions of the letters, except the Antwerp edition. They occur, however, in their Vatican manuscript and in Ivo and the *Panormia*.]? What of so many souls in the entire household [Note: [Col. 1295] “of the whole household”: Anselm; collected editions.]? Hence, if [Note: [Col. 1295] “and if”: collected editions.] one soul should perish through this severe discipline [Note: [Col. 1295] Added: “discipline”: Venetian I–II editions—“of discipline”: the remaining editions.] by which the whole household has been anathematized, dying without baptism, then the death of innumerable bodies would not be comparable to this loss, even if innocent people were violently dragged from the Church and [Col. 1295B] killed. Therefore, if you can give an account of this matter, please provide it to us in writing as well, so that we too may be able to do so. But if you cannot, why does an unconsidered agitation of mind lead you to do something for which, if questioned, you cannot find a sound answer [Note: [Col. 1295] “cannot give an answer”: original; collected editions.]?

I have said this even if our son Classicianus [Note: [Col. 1295] “Classianus”: Lyons II–III editions.] committed something which seemed to you most justly punishable by anathema.

### Part II. Gratian

Therefore, as this authority shows most plainly, a person is unlawfully excommunicated for another’s sin; nor do those have any valid reasoning who pronounce a sentence of excommunication upon an entire household for one person’s sin. But an unlawful excommunication [Col. 1295C] harms not the person marked, but the excommunicator.

Hence Gregory writes to Magnus, bishop of Milan, book II, letter 26 [Note: [Col. 1295] Letter 26, written in 593; book 3 in the Maurist edition—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 129; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 17; *Polycarpus*, book 1, title 22.]:

### Chapter II. Whoever unlawfully excommunicates someone condemns himself, not that person

We have learned that Laurence, formerly our brother and fellow bishop, deprived you of communion although no fault on your part required it [Note: [Col. 1295] “being present”: original; Ivo; Basle edition.]. Therefore, fortified by the authority of this our order, carry out your office without anxiety and receive communion without any fear.

### Chapter III. Those who curse not in their hearts but with their mouths incur uncleanness of the lips

Likewise, Jerome on Leviticus [Note: [Col. 1295] This and the following chapter belong to Origen’s Homily 14 on Leviticus, chapter 24.].

Those who neglect to cut off the habit of a cursing mouth [Note: [Col. 1295] “accursed”: collected editions, early Lyons II–III editions.], even if they do not curse *from* the heart, *even if they do not utter curses with a wicked intention and purpose*, nevertheless incur uncleanness of the lips and defilement of the mouth, according to Isaiah’s word [Note: [Col. 1295] Isaiah, chapter 6, verse 5.].

### Chapter IV. Life, not a sentence, binds or looses anyone

Likewise, Jerome in the same place [Note: [Col. 1295] Cf. below, chapter 7.].

If someone is driven away and cast outside by the unsound judgment of those who preside [Col. 1296B] over the Church, and if that person has not already gone out—that is, if he has not acted so as to deserve to go out—he suffers no harm from seeming to have been expelled by human beings through an unsound judgment. Thus it happens that sometimes one who is cast out is within, and one who seems to be retained within is outside.

### Chapter V. On the same point

Likewise, Rabanus, *On Ecclesiastical Pressures*, book I [Note: [Col. 1295] Rather, Atto of Vercelli, whose work this is—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 132; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 20.].

We are not condemned forever when we are unjustly accused, as the Psalm says [Note: [Col. 1295] “the Psalmist”: original; Ivo; collected editions.]: “Nor will he condemn him [Note: [Col. 1295] “him”: original.] when judgment is rendered against him.” Many priests profess that they are pursuing guilt out of zeal for God; but when this is done [Note: [Col. 1295] “here”: Basle edition.] indiscreetly [Note: [Col. 1295] “do”: original; Ivo.], they incur the crime of sacrilege, and while they rush headlong as though to correct others [Note: [Col. 1295] “come”: Basle edition.], they themselves fall much more grievously.

[Col. 1296C]

### Chapter VI. What penalty strikes one who unlawfully excommunicates another

Likewise, from the Council of Paris in the time of Louis [Note: [Col. 1295] The author or compiler of this chapter has been identified as Hincmar of Reims in work 55, *Chapter against Hincmar of Laon*, chapters 70 and 28, and in the pamphlet of remonstrance against him, chapters 5 and 35—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 124; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 21.].

Concerning unlawful excommunication, the law of Justinian, the Catholic emperor, which the Catholic Church approves and observes, decreed in Constitution CXXIII [Note: [Col. 1295] Julian’s *Epitome* of Novel 115, chapter 15; cf. C. 2, question 1, chapter 12.] [Note: [Col. 1295D] This is the reading in Justinian’s Novels, in the *Epitome* of Julian the antecessor, and in several manuscripts of Gratian, though others read CXXVIII [ [Col. 1295] thus in the collected editions and in the *Panormia* and Ivo.]. The chapter-number [ [Col. 1295] CCCLII: Basle edition—chapter XXX, book I: Argentinian edition—chapter CCC, book I: Venetian I and Lyons I editions—chapter CCC, book I: Norimberg, Lyons II–III, and Paris editions; Ivo, *Panormia*—in Hincmar himself it is correctly CCCCXLI—in Ivo’s *Decretum*, CCCCLI.] has been corrected from old copies. Formerly the Novels were cited by chapters, not by books.] chapter CCCLI: *no bishop* and no presbyter may excommunicate [Col. 1297A] anyone before the cause for which ecclesiastical canons direct this to be done has been proved. But if anyone excommunicates someone contrary to it [Note: [Col. 1297] “that”: Hincmar; Ivo.], the excommunicated person shall be restored to the grace of holy communion by the authority of the higher priest; while the person who did not excommunicate lawfully shall abstain from holy communion for as long as seems fit to the higher priest, so that he may justly suffer what he unjustly did [Note: [Col. 1297] “did”: Argentinian and Basle editions.].

And thus St Gregory, writing among other things to Bishop John, who had excommunicated unjustly, says [Note: [Col. 1297] Book 3, letter 6, Maurist edition.]:

“After first annulling and reducing to nothing the decrees of your aforesaid sentence, we decree [Note: [Col. 1297] “decreed”: Basle edition.] by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that for thirty days you be deprived of holy communion and beseech almighty God *our* [Note: [Col. 1297B] God.] for pardon for so great an offense with the utmost penitence and tears. But if we learn that you have carried out this sentence of ours too leniently [Note: [Col. 1297] “have not carried out”: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions, early Lyons I edition.], know that, with the Lord’s help [Note: [Col. 1297] “helping”: Hincmar; Ivo; collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 1297] “God”: collected editions.], not only your injustice but also the contumacy of your brotherhood will be punished more severely; for no one is to be judged precipitately or out of order, that is, without having been admonished and summoned [Note: [Col. 1297] “convicted”: the same editions; Ivo, *Panormia*.].”

§1. Concerning the summons of such a perpetrator [Note: [Col. 1297] “of this emperor”: collected editions.] of manifest crimes, the law says [Note: [Col. 1297] Interpretation on Paul’s *Sentences*, book 5, title 5, A, §7.]: “Anyone who has been summoned three times by judicial authority, or called to court by three edicts, or summoned by one peremptory notice in place of all three—that is, one which extinguishes the action [Note: [Col. 1297] “called”: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions.]—and has refused to appear before the judge by whom notice was given, may be judged as contumacious. Indeed, cases cannot be reopened by appeal whenever judgment has been rendered against a contumacious party.”

Pope Celestine, writing to Nestorius, and the Ephesian Synod deciding concerning him, establish this rule of three judicial summonses from evangelical authority [Note: [Col. 1297C] *Celestine:* In the Vatican copy of the Council of Ephesus and the Paris printed copy, the following relevant words occur in Celestine’s letter to Nestorius: “I want you to know that, after his first and second correction—that is, Cyril’s—and this correction of ours, which is evidently now the third, you are wholly separated from the body of the college and from the assembly of Christians unless the things wrongly said are at once corrected.” In the same council, recently printed at Ingolstadt, this letter appears in volume 4, chapter 16.] [Note: [Col. 1297D] *Ephesian:* In the same Vatican and Paris copies of the Ephesian Council, the synod’s letter to Nestorius reads: “Behold, with the holy synod gathered in great Rome and with our most holy and reverend brother and fellow minister, Bishop Celestine, presiding, we now make this third written summons to you,” etc. In the sentence deposing [Col. 1298C] Nestorius himself, after mention of two summonses, there is added: “Since the canons direct that a disobedient person be summoned a third time, we again sent other most holy bishops to him and found him contumacious and resisting,” etc. In the Ingolstadt printed council, volume 2, chapter 2, the three citations of Nestorius are set out explicitly.], and St Gregory, writing to John, confirms it [Note: [Col. 1297] “confirmed”: the same editions—“confirms”: Ivo, *Panormia*.].

§2. The African Council [Note: [Col. 1297] Chapter 44.] demonstrates the rule concerning a peremptory [Note: [Col. 1297] “however” absent from Ivo, *Panormia*.] notice in the case of Cresconius: if, after being summoned, he refuses to reform, then by his own contempt and [Note: [Col. 1297] “also”: collected editions, early Lyons II–III editions.] his [Note: [Col. 1297] Absent from Ivo.] contumacy he is to be excluded forthwith by judicial authority [Note: [Col. 1297] “at once”: collected editions.].

Likewise, St Gregory, writing concerning a judgment against a contumacious person to Maximus, the usurping bishop of Salona, says [Note: [Col. 1297] Book 6, letter 3.]:

“We urge you to hasten to come to us, setting aside every excuse, so that, justice being observed and Christ revealing it, we may both investigate and decide, according to the canonical ordinances, the charges brought against you [Note: [Col. 1297] “may”: Basle edition.]. Take care that you do not now create further delays in coming, lest your very absence make you more liable to the allegations, and lest the matter compel us to render [Col. 1298B] a rather severe conciliar judgment against you as a contumacious person, not only on account of the charges [Note: [Col. 1297] “aforesaid”: collected editions.] which you evade clearing, but also on account of the fault of disobedience.” [Note: [Col. 1297] “council”: Argentinian, Norimberg, Venetian I–II editions.]

### Chapter VII. Life, not a sentence, expels someone from the Church or restores that person to it

Likewise, Origen on Leviticus, Homily XIV, on chapter 24 [Note: [Col. 1298D] In Origen, after the chapter *Those who neglect*, cited above in the same place, follows: “Yet this man, though born of an Israelite mother, was nevertheless begotten by an Egyptian father; he went out, and in naming the Name he cursed. I think that, unless he had gone out, he would neither have quarrelled against the true Israelite nor cursed in naming the Name. For he went out from truth, from the fear of God, from faith and charity, as we explained above how through these things a person goes out from the camp of the Church,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 1297] Cf. above, chapter 4; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 18.].

When someone departs [Note: [Col. 1297] “departed”: Argentinian, Norimberg, Venetian I–II editions.] from truth, fear of God, faith, and charity, that person departs [Note: [Col. 1297] “departed”: the same editions.] from the camp of the Church, even though he is not at all cast out by a bishop’s voice. Conversely, when [Note: [Col. 1297] Absent from the collected editions, early Lyons II–III editions.] someone is cast out by an unsound judgment—that is [Note: [Col. 1297] “but”: there.], if he has not already departed, if he has not acted so as to deserve to depart—he suffers no harm [Note: [Col. 1297] “not”: Argentinian edition.]. For sometimes one cast outside is inside, and one who is outside [Col. 1298C] seems to be retained within.

### Chapter VIII. Those who are not joined to the faithful through open sacrilege or a depraved life are shown not to belong to the Church

Likewise, Augustine, Sermon XI on the Words of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1298D] In the indicated sermon, St Augustine, treating of those who have wholly separated themselves from the Church, says that their schism is very different from the dissension of certain persons remaining in the Church’s unity, as the Corinthians did. Paul, writing to them in First Corinthians, calls them carnal because they said, “I belong to Paul,” “I belong to Apollos.” Therefore, concerning those who are plainly separated from the Church, St Augustine says, the Apostle’s words in 1 Corinthians 2, “not receiving the things of the Spirit,” are not to be understood; rather, what Jude says in his letter: “Those who separate themselves, animal persons, not having the Spirit.”] [Note: [Col. 1297] Sermon 71, Maurist edition.]:

Of those who are separated from the Church, he does not say [Col. 1299A] [Note: [Col. 1299] 1 Corinthians, chapter 2, verse 14.] “not receiving the things of the Spirit,” lest this be referred to their apprehension of knowledge [Note: [Col. 1299] “will be referred”: Argentinian and Basle editions—“may be referred”: remaining editions.]; rather, it is said [Note: [Col. 1299] Jude, verse 19.], “not having the Spirit.”

(And later:) §1. This indeed [Note: [Col. 1299] “But this”: Basle edition.] could in no way be said [Note: [Col. 1299D] *This indeed:* What precedes in St Augustine concerning little children and carnal persons who nevertheless remain within the Church’s unity must be repeated. “Finally,” he says, “that we may know most certainly that little children in Christ, although they do not receive the things of God’s Spirit, nevertheless have God’s Spirit, let us shortly afterward consider how, rebuking these same persons, he says: ‘Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?’ This he would indeed in no way say to persons separated from the Church,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 1299] “would be said, unless of persons separated from the Church”: collected editions.] to those separated from the Church, who are said not to have the Spirit. Nor should one be said to be in the Church and to belong to this fellowship of the Spirit who mingles with Christ’s sheep with a feigned heart. For the Holy Spirit of discipline [Note: [Col. 1299] Wisdom, chapter 1, verse 5.] will flee [Note: [Col. 1299] “will escape”: collected editions.] the deceitful person. For not only [Note: [Col. 1300D] *For not only:* From here to the end these words have not been found. Yet relevant to this proposition is what is written in book 3, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 17.] [Note: [Col. 1299] Added: “those”: Basle and Lyons II–III editions.] do those shown manifest by the open sacrilege of separation fail to belong to the Church; those who are bodily mingled in its unity but separated by a most wicked life also fail to belong to it.

### Chapter IX. We separate from God those whom we show to be impious

Likewise, from the Fifth Synod, Conference 5 [Note: [Col. 1299] Held in 553—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 89; *Decretum*, part 14, chapter 49.]:

[Col. 1299B] It is certain that one shown to be impious [Note: [Col. 1299] Absent from the Basle edition.] is altogether separated from God, just as one anathematized as impious is separated. For anathema means nothing other than separation from God [Note: [Col. 1299] “separation”: Ivo, *Decretum*.].

### Part III. Gratian

Thus, as appears from the foregoing, an unlawful excommunication harms not the person marked but the person who marks him. Consequently, innocent persons cannot be condemned for another’s crime, as the households of powerful persons are customarily marked by imprudent people for their masters’ sins. But an objection still remains: not only innocent persons, but even guilty persons, ought not to be struck by a sentence of cursing. For Christ says in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1299] Matthew, chapter 5, verse 44.]: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you; do good to those who hate you.” The Apostle likewise says [Col. 1299C] [Note: [Col. 1299] Romans, chapter 12, verse 14.]: “Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse.” Likewise [Note: [Col. 1299] Galatians, chapter 5, verse 9.]: “Those who curse will not possess the kingdom of God.”

### Chapter X. The faithful ought to be free from every curse

Likewise, Jerome on the Epistle to Titus, at the beginning of chapter 3.

If, then, Michael did not dare to pronounce a judgment of blasphemy against the devil—though the devil was certainly most worthy of a curse [Note: [Col. 1299] “of cursing”: collected editions, early Lyons I edition.]—how much more ought we to be free from every curse? The devil deserved a curse, but blasphemy ought not to have issued through an archangel’s mouth. Read again the ancient books [Note: [Col. 1299] Deuteronomy, chapter 27.] and see which tribes were stationed on Mount Gerizim to bless the people, and which on the other mountain to curse. Reuben, who had defiled his father’s bed; Zebulun, Leah’s youngest son; and the children of the maidservants, are placed on Mount Heliel [Note: [Col. 1299] “Ebal”: original.] to curse those worthy of cursing.

### Chapter XI. Whom those chosen from the children of Israel for blessing, and those for cursing, signify

Likewise, in the Book of Joshua [Note: [Col. 1299] “Judges”: collected editions, early Lyons I edition—the ninth homily of Origen on Joshua, chapter 8.].

When, therefore, such a variety of purpose exists among the faithful individually, it seems to me that this is signified in this passage [Col. 1300B]: that those halves who proceed beside Mount Gerizim (the mountain chosen for blessings [Note: [Col. 1299] “blessing”: the editions compared with the other sources, and the Lyons first edition.]) figuratively indicate those who come to salvation not through fear of punishment but through desire for blessings and promises; whereas those other halves who proceed beside Mount Gebal [Note: [Col. 1299] “Ebal”: ibid.], on which curses were pronounced, indicate [Note: [Col. 1299] “indicate”: the editions compared with the other sources.] those who, through fear of evils and dread of punishments, fulfil what is written in the Law and attain salvation.

Gratian. Yet he who commanded prayer for persecutors struck our first parents with the curse of death for transgressing the commandment. Cain also [Note: [Col. 1299] Genesis, chapter 4.], because he added fratricide to the first transgression, received from the Lord a sentence of cursing. The Lord also said to Abraham [Col. 1300C] [Note: [Col. 1299] Genesis 12:3.]: “I will curse those who curse you, and I will bless those who bless you.” In the Gospel also [Note: [Col. 1299] Matthew, chapter 21.], when he came hungry to the fig tree and found no fruit on it, he condemned it by his curse to perpetual barrenness.

§ 1. Likewise, when Noah learned that his nakedness had been mocked by Ham, he cursed his son Canaan, saying [Note: [Col. 1299] Genesis 9:26.]: “Cursed be Canaan; let him be the servant of his brothers.” Likewise Isaac, when blessing his son Jacob [Col. 1301A], said [Note: [Col. 1301] Ibid., 27:29.]: “Let him who curses you be cursed, and let him who blesses you be filled with blessings.”

§ 2. Likewise, as is read in the book of Deuteronomy [Note: [Col. 1301] Deuteronomy, chapter 27.], Moses, by God’s command, divided the twelve tribes of the children of Israel into two parts. He ordered six tribes, proceeding beside Mount Gebal [Note: [Col. 1301] “Ebal”: the correct reading.], to proclaim aloud the curse of those who transgress the Law; but he commanded the others, proceeding beside the other mountain, to cry aloud the blessings of those who observe it.

§ 3. In the New Testament also, the apostle Peter is read to have cursed Simon when he said [Note: [Col. 1301] Acts 8:20.]: “May your money be with you unto perdition.” Paul likewise, who had said [Note: [Col. 1301] Romans 12:14.], “Bless, and do not curse,” ordered the Corinthian fornicator [Note: [Col. 1301] 1 Corinthians 6:18.] to be excommunicated. Likewise, in the same epistle [Note: [Col. 1301C] “In the same”: it was formerly read, as also in the manuscripts, “in another.” Gratian reports the sense of this and the following passage, but not precisely the Apostle’s own words.], he says [Col. 1301B] [Note: [Col. 1301] Chapter 16:22.]: “If anyone has not followed the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema, maranatha”—that is, accursed; “the Lord has come.” Likewise to the Galatians [Note: [Col. 1301] Galatians 1:8.]: “If an angel coming from heaven should preach to you another gospel, let him be anathema.”

§ 4. A distinction must therefore be made between the curse which is forbidden and the curse which is reasonably pronounced by the Lord and by most holy men. The forbidden curse is that which proceeds from a desire for revenge and hatred of the persecutor, not from love of justice. But the curse by which the saints curse proceeds from love of justice, not from the rancour of vengeance.

Therefore Gregory says in the *Morals*, book IV, chapter 6 [Note: [Col. 1301] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 82; *Decretum*, part 14, chapters 4–5.]:

### C. XII. Holy men curse certain persons not from a desire for revenge, but from love of justice.

When holy men pronounce a sentence of cursing, they do not break forth into this from a desire for revenge, but from an examination of justice [Col. 1301C]. For inwardly they behold the subtle judgment, and know that evils arising outwardly ought to be struck with a curse; and *in that* curse they do not sin, *in which* they do not disagree with the inward judgment.

[Note: [Col. 1301] Ivo’s *Panormia* and the original read “into this [curse]” (*in hanc*) rather than “into it”; “from” is absent in the Basel edition; the original and Ivo’s *Decretum* read “judgment of God”; the compared editions read “regard” rather than “behold”; they and Ivo’s *Panormia* read “arising” rather than “emerging”; they and Ivo read “by what curse” rather than “because”; *eo*, “in that [curse],” is absent from Ivo; “in which” is absent from Ivo and the Basel edition; the compared editions, especially Basel, read “eternal” rather than “inward”; Ivo and the compared editions read “judge” rather than “judgment.”]

The same author, above, chapter 5:

§ 1. Sacred Scripture speaks of a curse in two ways: one which it approves, another which it condemns. A curse is pronounced in one way by the judgment of justice [Note: [Col. 1301D] In what follows Gratian does not reproduce entirely the actual words of blessed Gregory, nor those of the other compilers, although he approaches them more closely; the meaning nevertheless remains the same.], as was pronounced upon the first sinner himself [Col. 1302A], when he heard [Note: [Col. 1301] Genesis 3:17.]: “Cursed is the earth in your work,” etc.; and as it is said to Abraham [Note: [Col. 1301] Ibid., 12:3.]: “I will curse those who curse you.” But a curse is pronounced in another way when it is uttered not by the judgment of justice but by the rancour of vengeance. We are warned by the voice of the preaching Apostle to refrain from this, when he says [Note: [Col. 1301] Romans 12:14.]: “Bless, and do not curse.”

[Note: [Col. 1301] Argentinensis reads “is destroyed” (*perimitur*), and the other editions, especially Basel, and Ivo’s *Panormia* read “is punished” (*punitur*), in place of “is uttered” (*promitur*); Basel reads “from which” rather than “from this.”]

### C. XIII. Those who err and those who lead others into error are to be excommunicated. Pelagius, Pope, to Bishop Anglius.

[Note: [Col. 1301] The chapter is wholly uncertain. Argentinensis and Basel read “Angelio.”]

By the example of apostolic authority we have learned that the spirits of those who err and of those who lead others into error are to be handed over to Satan, so that they may unlearn blasphemy.

[Col. 1302B]

### C. XIV. Offenders are to be corrected by priests; if found incorrigible, they are to be excommunicated. Anacletus, Pope, Epistle III.

[Note: [Col. 1301] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore; Burchard, book 1, chapter 136; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, chapter 250.]

Both priests and all the remaining faithful ought to take the greatest care for those who perish, so that by rebuking them they may either be corrected from their sins or, if they prove incorrigible, be separated from the Church.

### C. XV. After a second or third admonition, a sentence of excommunication is to proceed. Gregory, Pope, book II, epistle 37, to Natalis, Bishop.

[Note: [Col. 1301] Epistle 53, written in A.D. 592, book 2 of the Maurist edition; *Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 55, chapter 63.]

Your Blessedness complains without cause concerning the matter of excommunication—which has, as I may say, now been appended of necessity, with the condition of a second or third stage having been interposed—whereas the Apostle Paul says [Note: [Col. 1301] 2 Corinthians 10:6.]: “Being ready to avenge every disobedience.”

[Note: [Col. 1302C] “Stage”: in three ancient copies of blessed Gregory’s letters and in one copy of Gratian, the reading is “in the second stage,” etc. [Col. 1302D] This is not in the Maurist edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1301] “Subjected” rather than “appended”: Basel editions.]

### C. XVI. The wicked are to be removed from the Church. Jerome, in his Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 5.

[Note: [Col. 1302D] In Jerome: “Putrid flesh must be cut away, and a scabby animal driven from the sheepfolds.”]

Putrid flesh must be cut away, and a scabby sheep driven from the sheepfolds, lest the whole house, lump, body, and flock burn, be corrupted, rot, and perish. Arius was one spark in Alexandria; but because it was not immediately suppressed [Note: [Col. 1301] The compared editions read the masculine “suppressed” (*oppressus*) rather than the feminine *oppressa* printed here.], his flame ravaged the whole world.

[Col. 1303A]

### C. XVII. According to the diversity of faults, subjects are to be rebuked by their superiors. Augustine, *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 15.

Therefore subordinate brethren are to be rebuked by their superiors with rebukes arising from charity, differing according to the diversity of their offences, whether lighter or more serious. For even that which is called condemnation, administered by episcopal judgment—than which there is no greater punishment in the Church—may, if God wills, turn out and prove to be a most salutary correction [Note: [Col. 1303] “Rebuke” (*correptionem*) rather than “correction” (*correctionem*): the compared editions, especially Paris and Lyons.]. For we do not know what may happen on the following day. Is anyone to be despaired of before the end of this life? [Note: [Col. 1303] Basel reads “Is there no hope?” (*haud*); the other editions read “or” (*aut*).] Or [Note: [Col. 1303] Basel reads “not” (*haud*) rather than “or” (*aut*).] can God be prevented from looking upon such a person [Note: [Col. 1303] “Such” is added in the compared editions.] and granting repentance, and, when the sacrifice of a troubled spirit and contrite heart has been received [Col. 1303B], absolving him from the guilt even of a just condemnation [Note: [Col. 1303] “Absolves” rather than “absolve”: ibid.], and himself not condemning one already condemned? [Note: [Col. 1303C] “And the condemned person”: corrected from the original; the gloss was not thought to prevent this correction. Formerly the text read, “the condemned person, whom he himself does not condemn,” as in the compared editions.]

Yet pastoral necessity requires that, lest dreadful contagions spread among many, the diseased sheep be separated from the healthy sheep [Note: [Col. 1303] Basel reads “from all” rather than “from healthy [sheep].”]—perhaps to be healed by that very separation by Him to whom nothing is impossible. For, not knowing who belongs to the number of the predestined and who does not, we must be so affected by charity that we desire all to be saved.

### C. XVIII. Those unwilling to be corrected must be cut off by the sword of excommunication. Prosper, *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 7.

[Note: [Col. 1303] Rather, Julianus Pomerius.]

But if the crimes of any persons become known from whatever source, even though the criminals themselves are unwilling to confess them [Note: [Col. 1303] Basel reads “even if” (*et si*) rather than “if” (*si*).], whatever has not been healed by the mild remedy of patience [Note: [Col. 1303] “Light” rather than “mild”: the compared editions, especially Lyons II and III.] must be burned and treated, as it were, by the fire of devout rebuke [Col. 1303C]. [Note: [Col. 1303] Argentinensis reads “have cried out” rather than “have become known.”] But if the remedy of one who bears patiently and rebukes devoutly has not succeeded even thus [Note: [Col. 1303] The compared editions read “nor”; the original, “has profited.”] among those who, though long borne with and salutarily admonished, have refused to be corrected [Note: [Col. 1303] Basel reads “so that” rather than “among.”], they must be cut off like putrid parts of a body by the sword of excommunication [Note: [Col. 1303] The original and the compared editions read feminine “putrid” (*putridae*) rather than masculine *putres*.], lest, just as flesh dead from disease, if it is not cut off, corrupts the health of the remaining flesh by the contagion of its rot [Col. 1304A], so these persons, if they disdain amendment and persist in their disease, and remain in the fellowship of the saints with depraved habits, infect others by the example of their own ruin [Note: [Col. 1303] The original reads “perversion” (*perversionis*) rather than “ruin” (*perditionis*).] [Note: [Col. 1303D] In Prosper, the chapter beginning “Moreover” follows immediately; see below, *On Penance*, distinction 1.] [Note: [Col. 1303] “Infect”: the compared editions.]

### C. XIX. A person who presumes to have two wives at once is to be excommunicated. Nicholas, Pope, to King Lothair.

[Note: [Col. 1303] This letter of Nicholas does not survive; closely similar material occurs in his letter to the Bulgarians, chapter 51; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 227.]

Are you not to be struck by stern punishment, you who are known, in having two wives, to have imitated Lamech’s adultery and disgrace? The Lord did not erase this except by his saving advent after seventy-seven generations, whereas Cain’s fratricide had been washed away by the waters of the Flood in the seventh generation [Note: [Col. 1303] The compared editions, especially Basel, add “that is, the deluge”; compare Genesis, chapter 4.].

[Col. 1304B]

### C. XX. False witnesses and murderers are to be deprived of communion. From the Council of Agde, chapter 37.

[Note: [Col. 1303] Held in A.D. 506; Burchard, book 6, chapter 29; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, chapters 38 and 158.]

Therefore we have decreed that murderers and false witnesses are to be excluded from ecclesiastical communion, unless they wash away the crimes they have committed by the satisfaction of penance.

[Note: [Col. 1303] “And false witnesses” is absent from Burchard and Ivo, chapter 158; the compared editions read “are to be excluded” rather than “to be removed.”]

### C. XXI. A powerful person who presumes to despoil a poor cleric or religious person is to be excommunicated. From the First Council of Toledo, chapter 11.

[Note: [Col. 1303] Held in A.D. 400; Regino, book 2, chapter 38; Anselm, book 7, chapter 173 (178).]

If any powerful person despoils a cleric, any poor person [Note: [Col. 1303D] Most ancient copies, Anselm, and the printed and manuscript copies of the council read “a poorer person” [Col. 1304C]; so also the Hispanic Collection.], or a religious person, and the bishop orders him to come before himself [Note: [Col. 1303] The Hispanic Collection reads “and orders him to come to the bishop.”] so that he may be heard [Note: [Col. 1303] The Hispanic Collection reads “so that he may hear, and he.”], but he scorns the order, letters are immediately to circulate among all the bishops of the province and all whom they can reach, so that he is held excommunicate [Note: [Col. 1303] Absent from the same collection.] until he obeys [Note: [Col. 1303] Regino reads “until he is heard.”] and restores what belongs to another.

[Col. 1304C]

### C. XXII. On the same matter. [PALEA]. From sayings of Pope Gregory.

[Note: [Col. 1304C] This chapter is absent from most manuscripts. Burchard and Ivo, however, cite it from the Council of Gangra.]

[Note: [Col. 1303] Burchard, book 10, chapter 65, and Ivo, *Decretum*, part 12, chapter 79, and part 13, chapter 65, report it from the Council of Tongeren. Berardus reports it from the Council of Trosly, held in A.D. 909, chapter 5, from which it seems to have been excerpted. Nevertheless, we suspect with no less right that Burchard drew it from a chapter of Charlemagne—*Capitularies* II, of uncertain year, edited by Baluze, chapters 8–12. The whole chapter is absent from the Argentinensis edition.]

“Whoever by deceit lays his hand upon the Christ of the Lord—that is, upon a bishop [Note: [Col. 1303] “Upon a bishop”: Böhm.] or priest—commits grave sacrilege. And if anyone devastates [Note: [Col. 1303] Basel reads “devastates the Church”; the compared editions, especially Norbertine, omit the words.] the Church of God, attacks it, or burns it, this too is a most grave sacrilege. The holy synod has decreed that first all his goods are to be confiscated by public proscription; then, confined in one place, that is [Col. 1305A], in a monastery, he is to do penance for all the days of his life.”

[Note: [Col. 1304D] In Burchard and Ivo, the text reads “so that in one place,” without the words inserted here.]

### C. XXIII. A person who presumes to molest pilgrims to Rome, other pilgrims, or merchants is to be deprived of communion. Calixtus, Pope.

[Note: [Col. 1305] At the First Lateran Council, held in A.D. 1123.]

If anyone attempts to seize pilgrims to Rome, pilgrims, visitors to the thresholds of the Apostles and the shrines of other saints, or to despoil them of the goods they carry, or to harass merchants [Note: [Col. 1305] “And merchants” is absent from the original.] with new exactions of tolls and passage-dues [Note: [Col. 1305] “Pedaticorum,” passage-dues: Argentinensis, Norbertine, and Venetian editions I and II.], let him lack Christian communion until he makes satisfaction.

### C. XXIV. Those who presume to attack persons who pray, churches, their goods, or persons serving there are to be excommunicated. Urban, Pope.

[Note: [Col. 1305] Rather, the same Calixtus, chapter 20 of the same council.]

[Note: [Col. 1305] The word “likewise” (*pariter*) is absent, also in Anselm.]

Instructed by the examples of paternal traditions, and discharging the duty of our pastoral office, we decree that churches with their goods—both persons and possessions [Note: [Col. 1305] “Their” is added in Basel and Lyons II and III.], namely clerics and monks, together with their converts [Note: [Col. 1305C] In printed copies there followed “or those entrusted,” which has been deleted because it is absent from most manuscript copies of Gratian [Col. 1305D] and from a certain old codex, in which this and three other canons are copied at the end as a fragment of some council.]—and also those who pray [Note: [Col. 1305] The original reads “those who plough” (*aratores*).], together with the goods they carry, are to be secure and free from molestation. If anyone presumes to act against this decree, and after recognizing his crime does not suitably make amends within [Note: [Col. 1305] The original reads “below”; the compared editions, especially Lyons II and III, read “within.”] thirty days, he is to be excluded from the thresholds of the Church and struck with the sword of anathema.

### C. XXV. Those who meet with evil intent persons who pray, poor persons not bearing arms, are to be excommunicated. Nicholas, Pope, to all bishops.

[Note: [Col. 1305] Nicholas II, at the Roman Council held in A.D. 1059. Nicholas himself cites the first part of the chapter in his letter to the bishops of Gaul and others; the second was published from an ancient canonical collection by Mansi, volume 19; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 5, chapter 115.]

Those who have plundered pilgrims or persons praying at the shrine of any saint, whether clerics, monks [Col. 1305C], women, or unarmed poor persons, or have seized their goods, or have met them with evil intent [Note: [Col. 1305] Basel reads “him” rather than “them.”], are to be struck with the bond of anathema unless they make worthy amendment.

§ 1. Moreover, that peace which we call the Truce [Note: [Col. 1305] “Of God” is added in the compared editions and in the original printed by Mansi.] is to be observed as it has been established by the archbishops and bishops [Note: [Col. 1305] “By” is absent from the compared editions, especially Basel and Lyons II and III; “and bishops” is absent from Ivo.] of each province. Whoever violates it is to be subjected to excommunication.

[Col. 1306A]

## Part IV. Gratian

Since the discussion concerns heretics, it must be considered what difference there is between schism and heresy, who heretics are, and how many sects of heretics there are.

Jerome, in his Epistle to Titus, chapter 3, sets forth the distinction between schism and heresy, saying [Note: [Col. 1305] Anselm, book 12, chapter 49; Polycarp, book 7, title 3.]:

### C. XXVI. The difference between schism and heresy.

They consider this to be the difference between heresy and schism: heresy possesses a perverse doctrine, whereas schism likewise separates from the Church because of dissension concerning a bishop [Note: [Col. 1305] The compared editions read “after” rather than “because of”; Basel reads “separation,” and the other editions “departure,” rather than “dissension.”]. This can in some measure be understood at the beginning [Note: [Col. 1306D] The word “different” formerly followed; it is absent from the cited editions, the Vatican copies, and Anselm.]; nevertheless, no schism fails to devise for itself some heresy, so that it may appear to have rightly withdrawn from the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1305] The compared editions read “to be” rather than “to exist.”]

[Note: [Col. 1305D] In printed copies of these commentaries from Germany, France, and Ferrara, and in two Vatican manuscripts, the reading is “is separated from the Church.”]

[Note: [Col. 1305] “Is separated”: Venetian editions I and II, and Paris; “may separate”: Lyons II and III.]

[Col. 1306B]

Jerome defines in his Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 5, why it is called heresy, saying [Note: [Col. 1305] Anselm, book 12, chapter 50; Polycarp, same place.]:

### C. XXVII. Why it is called heresy.

In Greek, *heresy* is so called from “choice,” because each person chooses for himself the discipline which he thinks better. Therefore whoever understands Scripture otherwise than the sense required by the Holy Spirit, in accordance with which it was written, may be called a heretic even if he has not withdrawn from the Church; and he belongs to the works of the flesh, choosing what is worse.

[Note: [Col. 1305] Argentinensis reads “according to” (*secundum*) in place of “because, that is” (*quod scilicet*); the compared editions read “from the Church” rather than “of the Church”; and they read “by whom” rather than “from whom.”]

## Part V. Gratian

Augustine, in *On the Usefulness of Believing*, chapter 1, explains who are properly called heretics, saying:

### C. XXVIII. Who are properly called heretics.

[Note: [Col. 1305] Anselm, book 12, chapter 53; Deusdedit, part 2; Polycarp, same place.]

A heretic is one who, for the sake of some temporal advantage [Col. 1306C], and especially for the sake of glory and his own preeminence, either originates or follows false and novel opinions. But one who believes such people is a person deceived by some imagined appearance of truth and piety.

### C. XXIX. Those who are led astray into error not by their own audacity but by that of others are not heretics. The same author, to Glorius, Eleusius, and others, Epistle CLXII.

[Note: [Col. 1305] Epistle 43 in the Maurist edition, written in A.D. 397; Anselm, book 12, chapter 6; Polycarp, same place.]

The Apostle said [Note: [Col. 1305] Titus 3:10.]: “Avoid a heretical person after a first and second rebuke [Note: [Col. 1305] “Correction”: the compared editions.], *knowing* [Col. 1307A] that such a person is perverted and sins, *and is* self-condemned.” But those who defend their opinion, however false and perverse it may be, without obstinate animosity—especially an opinion which they did not produce by the audacity of their own presumption [Note: [Col. 1307] “May have produced”: the compared editions, especially Argentinensis and Basel.], but received from parents who had themselves been deceived and fallen into error—if they seek the truth with cautious concern and are ready to be corrected when they find it, are by no means to be counted among heretics.

[Note: [Col. 1307] The compared editions read “in himself” rather than “by himself.”]

### C. XXX. Those who despise the discipline of truth become teachers of error. Leo, Pope, Epistle X, to Flavian.

[Note: [Col. 1307] Epistle 28 in Ballerini’s edition, written in A.D. 449.]

What could be more unjust than to entertain impious views and refuse to believe persons wiser and more learned [Note: [Col. 1307] Lyons I and Paris read “teachers” rather than “more learned.”]? Yet those fall into this folly who, when [Note: [Col. 1307] The compared editions, especially Argentinensis, read “whoever.”] hindered by some obscure impediment [Col. 1307B] [Note: [Col. 1307] The Hispanic Collection reads “obstacle.”] from recognizing the truth, have recourse not to prophetic utterances, not to apostolic writings, nor to evangelical authorities, but to themselves [Note: [Col. 1307] The compared editions, especially Lyons and Paris, omit “to,” both here and in what follows.]. Thus they become teachers of error because they were not disciples of truth.

### C. XXXI. Heretics are those who obstinately defend what they perversely think. Augustine, against the Manichees.

[Note: [Col. 1307] From book 18 of *The City of God*, chapter 51; Anselm, book 12, chapter 57; Polycarp, same place; Deusdedit, part 2.]

Those who in Christ’s Church think something diseased and perverse [Note: [Col. 1307] “Something” is added in the compared editions.], if, when corrected [Note: [Col. 1307] “Corrected” rather than “rebuked”: ibid.] so that they may think soundly and rightly, they resist obstinately and refuse to amend their pestilential and deadly doctrines, but persist in defending them, become heretics.

### C. XXXII. One who defends another’s error is more blameworthy than the erring person. Urban, Pope.

[Note: [Col. 1307] The chapter is uncertain.]

One who defends another’s error is far more blameworthy than those who err, because he not only errs [Note: [Col. 1307] The compared editions read “he” rather than “one.”], but also prepares and confirms stumbling-blocks of error for others. Therefore, because he is a teacher of error, he must be called not merely a heretic but also a heresiarch.

[Col. 1307C]

### C. XXXIII. Those who alter truth by falsehood are proved to move the boundaries fixed by the Fathers. Jerome, book II of the Commentary on Hosea, chapter 5.

The princes of Judah [Note: [Col. 1307] Absent from Lyons II and III; the other editions, especially Norbertine, read “from there.”] move the boundaries which their fathers set [Col. 1308A], when they change truth into falsehood [Note: [Col. 1307] Basel reads “may change”; Argentinensis, “in falsehood”; Basel, “into falsehood.”] and preach something other than what they received from the Apostles.

Likewise below, in the same chapter:

§ 1. The meaning concerning heretics is plain: by their sophistries and dialectical art they often overwhelm churchmen [Note: [Col. 1307] Paris and Lyons read “overwhelm.”].

Likewise on chapter 9:

§ 2. Searching ancient histories, I cannot find that anyone tore apart the Church and led peoples away from the house of the Lord except those who had been priests and prophets appointed by God—that is, watchmen. These, therefore, are turned into a twisted snare, setting stumbling-blocks in every place.

### C. XXXIV. Those who join in the perversity of opponents are to be cast out. Leo, Pope, Epistle LXXIV, to Anatolius.

[Note: [Col. 1307] Epistle 115 in Ballerini’s edition, written in A.D. 457; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 339.]

I make known that this particularly displeases me: that among the clerics of Your Belovedness [Note: [Col. 1307D] Corrected from the letter itself. The common and most ancient copies of Gratian read “that the clerics of your jurisdiction”; Norbertine, Venetian I and II, Paris, and Lyons have that reading. Two copies, as also Ivo, read “among the clerics subject to your authority.” [Col. 1308D]] there are said to be some [Col. 1308B] who join in the perversity of the opponents [Note: [Col. 1307] The original reads “connive.”], and that vessels of wrath [Note: [Col. 1308D] Corrected from the original, alluding to Romans 9. Gratian and Ivo read “vessels of madness”; the original printed by Ballerini reads “vessels of wrath mixed with vessels of mercy.”] are mixed with vessels of mercy. Your diligence ought to insist vigilantly on investigating them and restraining them with suitable severity, so that cutting off does not spare those whom correction cannot benefit [Note: [Col. 1307] “Could benefit”: the compared editions.] [Note: [Col. 1307] “Correction” rather than “rebuke”: the same editions, the original, Ivo, and Böhm.]. For we must remember the evangelical command, by which [Note: [Col. 1307] “Which”: the compared editions.] Truth itself orders that, if an eye, a foot, or a right hand causes us to stumble, it is to be removed from the union of the body; for it is better to be without such members in the Church [Note: [Col. 1307] The compared editions read “in the age” rather than “in the Church.”] than to go with them into eternal punishments. For we resist those set outside the Church in vain if we are wounded, through those who are within, in the persons whom they deceive. This pestilential forbearance must utterly be rejected from priestly firmness; by sparing the sins of others, it does not spare itself [Col. 1308C].

### C. XXXV. Clerics must avoid both the associations and the banquets of heretics. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapters 70, 71, and 72.

[Note: [Col. 1307] Chapters 80–82 in the *Statuta ecclesiae antiqua*; compare distinction 18, chapter 9.]

A cleric is to avoid equally [Note: [Col. 1307] The original printed by Ballerini reads “especially.”] the banquets and associations of heretics and [Note: [Col. 1307] “Or”: the compared editions.] schismatics. Their gatherings are to be called not churches but conventicles [Note: [Col. 1307] The original reads “councils of devils.”]. One must neither pray nor sing psalms with them.

[Col. 1309A]

### C. XXXVI. Observers of the canons must enter into no contest with heretics. Gelasius, Pope, in an epistle to the bishops of Dardania.

[Note: [Col. 1309] Written in A.D. 495; Anselm, book 12, chapter 68.]

With whom was a synod to be held? Catholic pontiffs had already been driven out from every side, and only associates of the faithless remained [Note: [Col. 1309] “They alone”: the compared editions.]. With these it was no longer lawful even to have a meeting [Note: [Col. 1309] Basel reads “a council and a meeting.”], as the Psalm says [Note: [Col. 1309] Psalm 25:4.]: “I have not sat in the council [Note: [Col. 1309] The Vulgate and the compared editions read “with”; the compared editions, especially Basel and Lyons, read “counsel.”] of vanity, and I will not enter in with those who practise iniquity.” Nor is it ecclesiastical custom to mix a council [Note: [Col. 1309] Venetian I and II, Norbertine, Paris, and Lyons I read “to mingle”; Argentinensis, Norbertine, and Venetian I and II read “counsel.”] with persons whose communion is polluted and mingled with the faithless. Therefore such prevarication was rightly repelled by the decree of the Synod of Chalcedon rather than summoned to a council [Note: [Col. 1309D] The original reads “rather than through a council”; the printed text reads “rather than summoned to a council,” as does Anselm.], which was neither necessary after the first synod [Col. 1309B] nor lawful to hold with such persons.

The same author in a memorandum to Faustus [Note: [Col. 1309] Written in A.D. 493.]:

§ 1. “For us, masters and guardians of the canons, it is not lawful to enter into any contest with persons alien to communion.”

[Note: [Col. 1309D] Gelasius, rebuking in this memorandum those Greeks who most seriously violated the canons while pretending to be their observers, bursts out in these words: “O masters and guardians of the canons! For us it is not lawful …” [Col. 1310D]]

### C. XXXVII. One who excommunicates evil persons does not contradict but rather obeys the Gospel. From an epistle of Pope Urban.

[Note: [Col. 1309] The chapter is uncertain.]

It should be noted that some say that we act contrary to the evangelical parable in which the Lord commanded that tares not be uprooted [Note: [Col. 1309] Matthew 13:29.], when we subject to excommunication persons worthy of excommunication. They also say that Saint Augustine contradicts this in the passage where he says: “Since unity is not to be cut off, evil persons must be borne with, not cast out.”

The first answer to them is this [Note: [Col. 1309] The compared editions read “here.”]: if heretics and evil persons are not to be excommunicated [Col. 1309C], why did Augustine himself [Note: [Col. 1309] The compared editions, especially Lyons II and III, read “and Augustine himself.”], together with the legates of the holy Roman Church and his holy fellow bishops, excommunicate Pelagius and Coelestius [Note: [Col. 1309] “Coelestinus”: the compared editions.], who were introducing a new heresy into God’s holy Church, and separate them from the Church of God? Why did both he and the whole Church of God hold the Donatists—against whom he speaks these things and many similar things—as excommunicated, and refuse them communion unless they had first repented and been reconciled by the laying on of hands?

The same Lord who narrates [Note: [Col. 1309] The compared editions read “explains.”] this here in a parable openly commands excommunication elsewhere, saying [Col. 1310A] [Note: [Col. 1309] Matthew 18:17.]: “The brother who is rebuked by the Church and does not obey, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector.” It is therefore plainly evident that excommunication is one thing, and uprooting another [Note: [Col. 1309] The Argentinensis, Basel, and Lyons II and III editions add “and another.”]. For one who is excommunicated is excommunicated, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1309] 1 Corinthians 5:5.], in order that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord. Excommunication is discipline, not uprooting.

Gratian. Unless, perhaps, it results from the contempt and pride of the person excommunicated.

[Note: [Col. 1309] The compared editions print this as belonging to the preceding chapter.]

Therefore Origen, in Homily XV on chapter 23 of the book of Numbers [Note: [Col. 1310D] “Origen” has been restored; formerly the text read “Augustine.” The ordinary gloss cites most of this chapter at the same place from Origen, and some readings have consequently been corrected.]:

### C. XXXVIII. A divine curse indicates the merit of the person cursed.

When God curses [Note: [Col. 1309] Norbertine and Venetian read “those whom” (*quibus*) rather than “when” (*quando*).], he indicates the merit of the one cursed [Col. 1310B], and pronounces a sentence [Note: [Col. 1309] The compared editions, especially Argentinensis, add “true.”], since neither the nature of the sin nor the disposition of the sinner deceives him. But a human being, because he cannot know these things [Note: [Col. 1309] The compared editions read “this.”]—for one person cannot see or know another’s purpose and mind [Note: [Col. 1309] Basel reads “recognize.”]—even if he utters a curse with the intention of pronouncing judgment or sentence, cannot have a *just* ground for cursing where the sinner’s disposition is unknown, especially since human vice [Note: [Col. 1309] The compared editions and Böhm read “human judgment.”] knows [Note: [Col. 1309] Basel reads “knows” rather than “know.”] how to utter curses when perhaps it is provoked by insults or injuries [Note: [Col. 1309] Lyons III reads “and” rather than “or.”]. Desiring to cut off this vice, lest we provoke curses by curses and insults by insults [Note: [Col. 1309] Basel reads “are provoked.”], the Apostle lays down the necessary command that we should bless, *and not curse* [Note: [Col. 1309] Romans 12:14.], in order that the vice of reviling may be removed, not that the truth of judging—which is hidden from human beings—and the authority of pronouncing judgment may be abolished [Col. 1310C].

Gratian. Isidore, in book VIII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 5, defines how many sects of heretics there are and whence they have received their names, saying [Note: [Col. 1309] Anselm, book 13, final chapter. The corrector cites Ivo’s *Panormia*, book 5, chapters 3–5; the passage is nevertheless absent from Brandt’s edition.]:

### C. XXXIX. How many sects of heretics there are.

### C. XXXIX. How many sects of heretics there are.

Some heretics who have departed from the Church are named after their authors; others, however, after the causes which, by choosing them, they established.

§ 1. The Simonists are called after Simon, skilled in the art of magic [Note: [Col. 1309] “discipline”: original—Anselm—editions compared with the original.], whom Peter cursed in the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 1309] cf. ch. 8.] because he had wished to buy with money from the Apostles the grace of the Holy Spirit. They say that creation was made not by God, but by some higher power.

§ 2. The Menandrists are named after Menander the magician, Simon’s disciple, who maintained that the world was made not by God but by angels.

§ 3. The Basilidians are called after Basilides, who, among his other blasphemies, denied that Jesus suffered.

§ 4. The Nicolaitans are called after Nicholas, a deacon of the Church of Jerusalem, who was appointed by Peter along with Stephen and the others. Because of her beauty he had left his wife, saying [Note: [Col. 1311] “said”: editions compared with the original—absent from the original.] that whoever wished might use her. This custom turned into sexual immorality, so that they exchanged spouses with one another. John condemns them in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 1311] ch. 2, v. 6.], saying: “But this you have, that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans” [Note: [Col. 1311] Added: “which I also hate”: editions compared with the original, first Argentinensis and Basiliensis editions.].

§ 5. The Gnostics [Col. 1311B] wished to call themselves so because of the excellence of their knowledge. They say that the soul is of God’s nature; in their doctrines they invent a good God and an evil God [Note: [Col. 1311] “Lord”: Basiliensis edition.].

§ 6. The Carpocratians are called after a certain Carpocrates, who said that Christ was merely a man and was begotten by both sexes.

§ 7. The Cerinthians are named after a certain Cerinthus. Among other things, they observe circumcision and proclaim that after the resurrection there will be a thousand years of fleshly pleasure. Thus they are called in Greek *Chiliasts* (Χιλιάσται), and in Latin *Millenarians* [Note: [Col. 1311] “Miliastae”: Anselm—Basiliensis edition—“Miciliastae”: the remaining editions, first Lugdinensis II and III.].

§ 8. The Nazarenes are so called. Although they confess Christ—who was called Nazarene after the village—to be the Son of God [Note: [Col. 1311] “although they confess”: editions compared with the original.], nevertheless they observe everything of the old Law.

§ 9. The Ophites are named after the serpent; for serpent is called *ophis* (ὄφις) in Greek. They worship the serpent, saying that it brought knowledge of virtue into Paradise [Note: [Col. 1311] “in Paradise”: same editions.] [Col. 1311C].

§ 10. The Valentinians are called after a certain Valentinus, a follower of Plato [Note: [Col. 1311] “of Platonic [teaching]”: original.]. He introduced certain *aeons* (αἰῶνας), that is, ages [Note: [Col. 1311] “crimes”: editions compared with the original, first Lugdunensis I.], into the origin of God the Creator; and he maintained that Christ assumed nothing bodily from the Virgin, but passed through her as if through a pipe [Note: [Col. 1311] “to pass”: Basiliensis edition.].

§ 11. The Appellites, whose founder [Note: [Col. 1311] “leader”: original—“leader”: ancient Apostolic source—editions compared with the original—Anselm.] was Apelles, made the Creator some glorious angel of the higher God, asserted that he was that fiery God of the Law of Israel [Note: [Col. 1311] Added: “and”: original.], and said [Note: [Col. 1311] “who said”: editions compared with the original.] that Christ appeared not truly as God but as a man in appearance [Col. 1312A].

§ 12. The Archontiacs are called after the rulers [Note: [Col. 1311] “Archontius”: Basiliensis edition.], because [Note: [Col. 1311] “who”: editions compared with the original.] they maintain that the universe which God created is the work of archangels [Note: [Col. 1311] “angels”: Anselm.].

§ 13. The Adamites are so called [Note: [Col. 1311] “are called because”: editions compared with the original.] because they imitate Adam’s nakedness. Hence they pray naked, and naked men and women meet together among themselves.

§ 14. The Cainites [Note: [Col. 1311D] “Cainani”: In St. Augustine’s book *On Heresies*—from which Isidore took a large part of this chapter—and in several old copies of Gratian, the reading is *Cayani*. In one copy of Gratian it is *Cayni* [ [Col. 1311] “Gajani”: Anselm—Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venetian I and II editions.]. Tertullian writes thus concerning these heretics in his book *On Prescription against Heretics*: “There are even now other Nicolaitans; their heresy is called Cainian.” And a little further below: “Likewise another heresy also arises, which is called that of the Cainites. For they too exalt Cain, as though conceived from some powerful force which worked in him.”] are so named because they worship Cain.

§ 15. The Sethians [Note: [Col. 1311] “Sethiani”: original—editions compared with the original, first Argentinensis and Venetian I and II, in which it is “Sechiani.”] take their name from Adam’s son, who was called Seth [Note: [Col. 1311] “Sech”: Venetian I and II editions.], saying that he [Note: [Col. 1311] “him”: editions compared with the original.] is Christ.

§ 16. The Melchizedekians are so called because they consider Melchizedek, the priest of God [Note: [Col. 1311] “Lord”: same editions.], not to have been a man but to have been God’s power.

§ 17. The Angelics are so called because they worship angels.

§ 18. The Apostolics [Note: [Col. 1311] Added: “are called”: Basiliensis edition.] took this name for themselves [Note: [Col. 1311] “presumptuously took”: original—Anselm.] because, possessing nothing of their own, they by no means receive those [Note: [Col. 1311] “them”: editions compared with the original.] who use anything [Note: [Col. 1311] “something”: original.] in this world [Col. 1312B].

§ 19. The Cerdonians are named after a certain Cerdon [Note: [Col. 1311] “called”: editions compared with the original.], who maintained two opposed principles.

§ 20. The Marcionites are called after Marcion, a Stoic philosopher, who followed Cerdon’s doctrine and maintained one God to be good, the other just [Note: [Col. 1311] “Lord”: Basiliensis edition.], as though there were two principles, of creation [Note: [Col. 1311] “Creator”: Anselm.] and of goodness.

§ 21. The Artotyrites [Note: [Col. 1311] “Artateritae”: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venetian I and II, and Aarhus edition—“Artoteritae”: Basiliensis edition—“Artatyrites”: Lugdunensis II and III editions.] are named from their offering. For they offer bread and cheese, saying that the offering was celebrated by the first human beings from the fruits of the earth and the fruits of sheep.

§ 22. The Aquarians are called because they offer water alone in the chalice of the sacrament.

§ 23. The Severians arose from Severus. They do not drink wine; they reject the Old Testament and the resurrection.

§ 24. The Tatianists are called after a certain Tatian, and are also called Encratites [Note: [Col. 1311] “Encratics”: editions compared with the original, first Lugdunensis.], because they abhor meat.

§ 25. The Alogians [Col. 1312C] are called as though “without the Word”; for *logos* (λόγος) is called “Word” in Greek. They do not believe in God the Word, rejecting John’s Gospel and the Apocalypse.

§ 26. The Cataphrygians received their name from the province of Phrygia because they arose there. Their founders were Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla [Note: [Col. 1311] Absent from the original.]. They assert that the coming of the Holy Spirit was delivered not to the Apostles [Note: [Col. 1311] “in the Apostles”: original—Basiliensis edition.] but to themselves.

§ 27. The Cathari [Note: [Col. 1311] “Marthoree”: Venetian I and II editions—“Cathoree”: Argentinensis edition.] named themselves thus because of purity. Boasting of their own merits, they deny forgiveness of sins to penitents; if widows remarry, they condemn them as adulteresses [Col. 1313A]; they proclaim themselves purer than all others [Note: [Col. 1313] “than all”: Basiliensis edition.]. If they wished to recognize their own name, they would call themselves worldly rather than pure.

§ 28. The Paulianists arose from Paul of Samosata, who said that Christ had not always existed, but took his beginning from Mary.

§ 29. The Hermogenians are called after a certain Hermogenes, who introduced uncreated matter [Note: [Col. 1313] “Mary”: Anselm.], compared it to the unbegotten God, and asserted it to be the mother and goddess of the elements [Note: [Col. 1313C] “Uncreated”: This passage has been corrected from most old copies and from Isidore. It formerly read: “Introducing not nature, he compared it to God, not to nature” [ [Col. 1313] thus the editions compared with the original.].] [Note: [Col. 1313] “and idea”: Basiliensis edition—“idea”: the remaining editions.], whom the Apostle condemns as serving the elements.

§ 30. The Manichaeans arose from a certain Persian called Manes. He introduced two natures and [Note: [Col. 1313] Added: “two”: editions compared with the original.] two substances, namely good and evil, and maintained that souls flow out from God as from a sort of fountain. He rejects [Note: [Col. 1313] “they reject”: original—Anselm—editions compared with the original, first Venetian I and II.] the Old Testament and accepts [Note: [Col. 1313] “they accept”: original—Anselm—editions compared with the original—“he accepted”: Böhm.] the New in part.

§ 31. The Anthropomorphites [Note: [Col. 1313D] “Anthropomorphites”: In the common editions of Isidore’s manuscripts, and in several manuscripts, the following precedes: “The Anomoeans are called in Latin ‘without law’;” but these words are absent from a very ancient and carefully corrected Isidore manuscript in the monastery of St. Augustine at Carbonara, Naples.] are so called [Col. 1313B] because, in rustic simplicity, they suppose that God has human limbs, as these are written in the divine books. For *anthrōpos* (ἄνθρωπος) is interpreted in Latin as “man.” They do not understand the Lord’s saying [Note: [Col. 1313] John ch. 4, v. 24.], “God is spirit.” For he is incorporeal, and is neither distinguished by limbs [Note: [Col. 1313] “for he is not”: editions compared with the original.] nor measured by bodily mass.

§ 32. The Hierachites [Note: [Col. 1314C] “Hierachites”: Thus altered from St. Augustine’s treatise, although in some editions of it the reading is “Hierarchites.” The heretic Hierachas is mentioned by St. Hilary, *On the Trinity*, books 4 and 6. It formerly read: “Heraclites, after Heraclius” [Col. 1314D [Col. 1313] thus the same editions.].] arose from Hierachas, their founder. They admit only monks, reject marriages, and do not believe that little children possess the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 1313] “say”: Basiliensis edition.].

§ 33. The Novatians arose from Novatian [Note: [Col. 1313] “Novatus”: editions compared with the original.], a presbyter of the city of Rome. Attempting to seize the episcopal chair against Cornelius, he established a heresy, refusing [Note: [Col. 1313] “refused”: Basiliensis and Lugdunensis I editions—“wished”: the remaining editions.] to receive apostates [Note: [Col. 1313] “accept”: Paris and Lugdunensis editions.] and rebaptizing those already baptized.

§ 34. The heretics called Montanians [Note: [Col. 1314D] “Montanians”: St. Augustine makes no mention of these, but of the Montenses, a name by which, he reports, the Donatists were customarily called at Rome.] were so named because they hid in the mountains during [Note: [Col. 1313] “at the time of”: editions compared with the original, first Lugdunensis II and III.] persecution; on that occasion they separated themselves from the body of the Catholic Church [Col. 1313C].

§ 35. The Ebionites are called after Ebion, or after poverty. For they think that Christ became a righteous man solely through advancement [Note: [Col. 1313] “progress”: editions compared with the original.]. Thus they are aptly called Hebionites, for poverty of understanding [Note: [Col. 1313] “summoned”: original.]. For they are [Note: [Col. 1313] Absent from the original and Anselm.] half-Jews [Note: [Col. 1313] “Jews”: editions compared with the original.], and so hold the Gospel that they observe the Law carnally; against them the Apostle writes vehemently to the Galatians [Note: [Col. 1313] Galatians ch. 5.] [Col. 1314A].

§ 36. The Photinians are named after Photinus, bishop of Sirmium in Gallic Greece, who revived the Ebionite heresy and asserted that Christ was conceived from Mary through Joseph in marital intercourse.

§ 37. The Aerians [Note: [Col. 1313] “Sirmiae”: original—Argentinensis edition—“Syriniae”: Venetian I, II, and Nuremberg editions—“Smyrnae”: the remaining editions.] [Note: [Col. 1313] “Herians—after Herius”: Basiliensis edition.] are named after a certain Aerius. They [Note: [Col. 1313] “Like these, they”: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venetian I and II editions.] despise offering [Note: [Col. 1313] “being offered”: editions compared with the original.] sacrifice for the dead.

§ 38. The Aetians [Note: [Col. 1313] “Boetians—after Boetius”: Basiliensis edition.] are named after Aetius; they are also Eunomians, after a certain Eunomius, a dialectician and disciple of Aetius, by whose name they became better known. They maintain that the Son is unlike the Father, and the Holy Spirit unlike the Son. They also say that no sin is imputed to those who remain in the faith [Note: [Col. 1313] “to none”: Basiliensis and Lugdunensis I editions.].

§ 39. The Origenians arose from Origen, their author, saying that the Son cannot see the Father [Col. 1314B], nor the Holy Spirit the Son. They also say that souls sinned at the beginning of the world and, according to the diversity of their sins, deserved different bodies, as though chains, from heaven down to earth; and that this was the cause for which the world came to be [Note: [Col. 1313] “had come to be”: original.].

§ 40. The Noetians [Note: [Col. 1313] “Noeticians”: Venetian I, II, Nuremberg, Paris, and Lugdunensis I editions.] are named after a certain Noetus. They said that Christ [Note: [Col. 1313] “bishop”: Basiliensis edition.] is the same as both Father and Holy Spirit, and understand the Trinity itself as existing in names of offices, not in persons. Hence they are also called Patripassians, because [Note: [Col. 1313] “who”: editions compared with the original, first Lugdunensis II and III.] they say that the Father suffered.

§ 41. The Sabellians are said to have sprung from the same Noetus, whose disciple Sabellius is reported to have been. They became especially known through Sabellius’s name, and hence are called Sabellians. They maintain one person of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1313] “assert”: Anselm.].

§ 42. The Arians arose from Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 1313] “arose”: editions compared with the original.] [Col. 1314C]. Refusing to acknowledge the Son as coeternal with the Father, he maintained different substances in the Trinity, contrary to what the Lord says [Note: [Col. 1313] John ch. 10, v. 30.]: “I and the Father are one.”

§ 43. The Macedonians are named after Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople; they deny that the Holy Spirit is God.

§ 44. The Apollinarists [Col. 1315A] are called after Apollinaris, saying that Christ assumed only a body without a soul [Note: [Col. 1315] “assumed”: editions compared with the original.].

§ 45. The Antidicomarites [Note: [Col. 1315] “Antidicomarianites”: Lugdunensis I edition—“Anticomarites”: Venetian I, II, and Paris editions.] are so called because they contradict Mary’s virginity, maintaining that after Christ’s birth she had intercourse with her husband.

§ 46. The Metangismonites [Note: [Col. 1315C] “Metangismonites”: Thus corrected from Isidore and St. Augustine, whereas it formerly read, “The Metangi are so called” [ [Col. 1315] “The Getangi are so called”: Venetian I and II editions.].] [Note: [Col. 1315] “gangios”: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venetian I and II editions.] received this name because *angos* (ἄγγος) means “vessel” in Greek. For they maintain that the Son is in the Father as a smaller vessel within [Note: [Col. 1315] “below”: same editions and Paris—“between”: Basiliensis edition.] a larger vessel.

§ 47. The Patricians [Note: [Col. 1315] “Atrians”: Venetian II edition—“Patrians”: Venetian I edition.] are named after a certain Patricius, who say that the substance of human flesh was made by the devil.

§ 48. The Coluthians [Note: [Col. 1315] “Collicians—after Collicius”: editions compared with the original.] are named after a certain Coluthus, who say that God does not make [Note: [Col. 1315] “created”: Basiliensis edition.] evils, contrary to what is written [Note: [Col. 1315] Isaiah ch. 45, v. 7.]: “I am the Lord, creating evils.”

§ 49. The Florians are named after Florianus [Note: [Col. 1315] “Florinus”: original—Anselm.], who, on the contrary, say that God created [Col. 1315B] evils, contrary to what is written [Note: [Col. 1315] Genesis ch. 1, v. 31.]: “God made all things good.”

§ 50. The Donatists are named after a certain Donatus, an African [Note: [Col. 1315] Added: “are”: editions compared with the original.]. Coming from Numidia, he deceived almost all Africa by his persuasion, maintaining that the Son is less than the Father and the Holy Spirit less than the Son, and rebaptizing Catholics.

§ 51. The Bonosians [Note: [Col. 1315] “Bonosiacs”: original.] are reported to have arisen from a certain bishop Bonosus, who maintain that Christ, the Son of God, is adopted rather than proper.

§ 52. The Circumcellions are so called because they are rustic people; they are called Scotopics [Note: [Col. 1315D] “Scotopics”: In Isidore, the *Panormia*, and several Gratian manuscripts, the reading is “Cotopites” [ [Col. 1315] thus Isidore and Anselm—“Scotopias”: Basiliensis edition—“Scotopics”: the remaining editions, first Lugdunensis II and III.]. But the statement, “having the doctrine of the aforementioned heresy,” [Col. 1316C] must be referred to the Donatists, not to the Bonosians.] and have the doctrine of the aforementioned heresy. Out of desire for martyrdom they kill themselves, so that by departing violently from this life they may be called martyrs.

§ 53. The Priscillianists are called after Priscillian, who in Spain composed a mixed doctrine from the error of the Gnostics and the Manichaeans [Col. 1315C].

§ 54. The Luciferians arose from Lucifer, bishop of Sardinia [Note: [Col. 1315] “of Sirmium”: Anselm—“of Smyrna”: editions compared with the original.]. They condemned Catholic bishops who, during Constantius’s persecution, had been assenting to the unfaithfulness of the Arians [Note: [Col. 1315] “during the persecution”: same editions.], but afterwards, having been corrected, chose to return to the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 1315] “to the see”: same editions.], whether for what they had previously believed [Note: [Col. 1315] Absent from the same editions except Lugdunensis II and III.] [Note: [Col. 1315] Added: “previously”: editions compared with the original.] [Note: [Col. 1315] “believed—pretended”: same editions, first Lugdunensis II and III.] or for what they had pretended to believe. The Catholic Church received them into her maternal bosom, as Peter after the tears of his denial. But those men, arrogantly receiving this maternal charity and unwilling to receive them [Note: [Col. 1315] “them”: editions compared with the original.], withdrew from communion with the Church; and with Lucifer himself, their founder, who rose in the morning, they deserved to fall [Col. 1316A].

§ 55. The Jovinianists are named after a certain monk Jovinian, maintaining that there is no difference between married women and virgins, nor any distinction between those who abstain and those who simply feast.

§ 56. The Helvidians are named after Helvidius [Note: [Col. 1315] Added: “or are named”: same editions.], who say that after Christ’s birth Mary bore other children to her husband Joseph [Note: [Col. 1315] Absent from Böhm.] [Note: [Col. 1315] “her”: absent from the original, Anselm, and editions compared with the original, first Lugdunensis II and III.].

§ 57. The Paternianists [Note: [Col. 1315] Added: “therefore”: editions compared with the original, first Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venetian I and II.] arose from a certain Paternus and suppose that the lower parts [Note: [Col. 1315] “who [suppose] the lower”: editions compared with the original—“of the lower”: Basiliensis and Venetian I and II editions.] of the body were made by the devil.

§ 58. The Arabics are so called because they arose in Arabia, saying that the soul dies with the body and that both rise again at the end.

§ 59. The Tertullianists are named after Tertullian, a presbyter of Carthage, a city in the African province. They proclaim [Note: [Col. 1315] “who say [that] the soul”: editions compared with the original.] that the soul is immortal, but bodily [Col. 1316B], and think that after death the souls of sinful human beings are turned into demons.

§ 60. The Tessarescaedecatites [Note: [Col. 1315] “Tesseresedecadae”: Basiliensis edition—“Tessaresedecatae”: Lugdunensis I edition—“Tesseresedecatae”: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venetian I and II editions—“Tesserasedecatae”: Paris edition—“Tesserescedatistae”: Lugdunensis II and III editions.] are so called because they maintain that Passover must be observed with the Jews on the fourteenth moon [i.e. the fourteenth day of the lunar month] [Note: [Col. 1315] “to observe”: editions compared with the original.]. For *tessares* (τέσσαρες) signifies “four,” and *deka* (δέκα), “ten.”

§ 61. The Nyctages [Note: [Col. 1315] “Ictages”: Venetian I and II editions—“Victages”: Nuremberg edition.] are named after sleep because they reject night vigils, saying that it is superstition for the divine laws to be violated by him who assigned the night for rest [Note: [Col. 1315] “to violate”: Anselm.].

§ 62. The Pelagians arose from Pelagius the monk. They place free will before divine grace, saying that the will suffices for fulfilling the divine commands.

§ 63.
