The Nestorians are named after Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who maintained that the Blessed Virgin Mary was mother not of God but only of a human being [Note: [Col. 1315] “bearer”: original—Anselm—Basiliensis edition.], in order to make one person of the flesh and another of the Godhead. Nor did he believe in one Christ in the Word of God and flesh [Col. 1316C], but preached separately and distinctly one Son of God and another son of man [Note: [Col. 1315] “separate and disjoined”: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venetian I and II editions.] [Note: [Col. 1316C] In the same ancient Neapolitan manuscript of Isidore, this is the end of the chapter, and a new chapter begins: “On the philosophers of the gentiles.”].

§ 64. The Eutychians are called after Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople. After the assumption of humanity, he denied that Christ exists in [Note: [Col. 1315] “from”: original—Anselm—editions compared with the original.] two natures, but maintained that in him there is only the divine nature.

§ 65. The Acephali [Note: [Col. 1315] “Acephalites”: editions compared with the original.] are so called, that is, “without a head.” For no founder from whom they arose is found among them [Note: [Col. 1315] “from whom they arose”: same editions.]. These opponents of the Three Chapters of Chalcedon [Note: [Col. 1316D] “Of Chalcedon”: The Three Chapters were debated and defined at the Fifth Synod under Justinian, as noted above, distinction 15, *Sicut sancti*. But those who departed from the Church on account of these Three Chapters attacked not the Council of Chalcedon, but the Fifth Synod.] deny the property of two substances in Christ [Col. 1317A] and proclaim one nature in his person.

§ 66. The Theodosians [Note: [Col. 1317D] “Theodosians”: They are mentioned by Liberatus in the *Breviary*, Nicephorus, book 18, chapters 45, 49, and 50, and George Cedrenus in the fourteenth year of Emperor Justinian. St. Augustine mentions the Theodotians, after Theodotion; but he seems to be the same as Theodotus, of whom Epiphanius, book 2, tome 1, heresy 54, says: “The Theodotians [are named] after Theodotus,” as also Philastrius and Damascene.] and Gaianites are named after Theodosius and Gaianus. In the time of Emperor Justinian, they were ordained bishops at Alexandria on one day by the election [Note: [Col. 1317] Added: “province”: Basiliensis and Lugdunensis II and III editions.] [Note: [Col. 1317] “election”: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venetian I and II editions—“by election of the perverse people”: the remaining editions.] of a perverse people. Following the errors of Eutyches and Dioscorus, they reject the Council of Chalcedon and maintain one nature in Christ from two natures. The Theodosians contend that it is corruptible; the Gaianites, incorruptible.

§ 67. The Agnoites and Tritheites [Note: [Col. 1318D] “Agnoites and Tritheites”: Thus restored, although Isidore’s and Gratian’s manuscripts read “Gnoites” [ [Col. 1317] thus Anselm—“Tritonites”: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venetian II editions.] and “Thritheites.” Nicephorus mentions them in the places just indicated and writes that they sprang from the Theodosians. St. Gregory says much about the Agnoites in book 8, letters 35 and 42, to Eulogius.] arose from the Theodosians. The Agnoites are called after ignorance because, in addition to the perversity [Note: [Col. 1317] “to perversity”: original—Anselm.] from which they sprang, they add this: that Christ’s divinity does not know future things, which are written concerning the last day and hour. They do not recall the person of Christ speaking in Isaiah [Note: [Col. 1317] “speaking”: Lugdunensis II and III editions—“I do not know how to speak”: the remaining editions, first Basiliensis.]:  “The day [Col. 1317B] of judgment is in my heart” [Note: [Col. 1317] Isaiah ch. 63, v. 4.].

§ 68. The Tritheites are so called because, just as they maintain three persons in the Trinity, so they also maintain that there are three Gods—contrary to what is written [Note: [Col. 1317] Deuteronomy ch. 6, v. 4.]: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God.”

§ 69. There are [Note: [Col. 1317] Added: “however”: Venetian II, Paris, and Lugdunensis editions.] other heresies also, without founder and without names. Of these, some believe God to be three-formed [Note: [Col. 1317] “threefold”: editions compared with the original, first Lugdunensis II and III.]; others also [Note: [Col. 1317] Added: “also”: editions compared with the original.] call Christ’s divinity capable of suffering; others assign a beginning in time to Christ’s birth from the Father [Note: [Col. 1317] “birth”: Nuremberg edition—“of [his] birth”: the remaining editions, first Paris and Lugdunensis—Added: “in time”: editions compared with the original, first Lugdunensis II and III.]; others do not believe that the liberation of human beings in hell was effected by Christ’s descent [Note: [Col. 1317] “descent”: Argentinensis and Basiliensis editions.]; others deny that the soul is the image of God; others think that souls are changed into demons and into every kind of animal [Col. 1318A] [Note: [Col. 1317] “think”: same editions.]; others disagree concerning the state of the world; others imagine innumerable worlds; others make water coeternal with God; others walk barefoot; others do not eat with people. These are heresies that have arisen against the Catholic faith and have been condemned beforehand by the Apostles, holy Fathers, or councils [Note: [Col. 1317] “in”: Basiliensis edition.]. Though divided among themselves by many errors and disagreeing with one another [Note: [Col. 1317] “may disagree”: same edition.], they nevertheless conspire under one common name against the Church of God.

§ 70. Moreover [Note: [Col. 1317] Absent from the same edition—cf. above, ch. 26.], whoever understands Holy Scripture [Note: [Col. 1317] “most holy”: editions compared with the original.] otherwise than the sense of the Holy Spirit, by whom it was written, may nevertheless be called a heretic, even if he has not departed from the Church.

[Col. 1318B]

### C. XL. Why divine providence permits many to err.

Likewise Augustine, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book I, chapter 1 [Note: [Col. 1317] “Pope Augustine”: Lugdunensis II and III editions.].

**Part VI.** Divine providence permits many heretics of diverse error to exist, so that, when they assail us and question us about matters we do not know, we may thus shake off laziness [Note: [Col. 1317] “examine”: editions compared with the original.] and desire to know the divine Scriptures. Therefore the Apostle also says [Note: [Col. 1317] 1 Corinthians ch. 11, v. 19.]: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” [Note: [Col. 1317] “There must be”: absent from editions compared with the original, first Lugdunensis II and III.]. Those, however [Note: [Col. 1317] “For those”: original.], are approved by God [Note: [Col. 1317] “from God”: editions compared with the original.] who can teach well; but they cannot be made manifest to human beings unless they teach [Note: [Col. 1318D] “But [they] cannot be manifest”: These words have been added from the original, as have several others, and corrections.].

## CAUSE XXV

[Col. 1317]

[Col. 1317C] **GRATIAN**

The Holy Roman Church endowed a certain baptismal church with its privileges, assigning to it in full the tithes of its diocese. It likewise endowed a certain monastery with special privileges, decreeing that it should pay tithes to no one from its own estates. It therefore happened that, within the diocese of the privileged baptismal church, the aforesaid monastery acquired estates for itself, some by purchase and others by donation. A dispute therefore arose between the monks and the clerics concerning tithes.

[Col. 1318C] (Question I.) The first question here is whether, by authority of this privilege, the clerics of the baptismal church may claim for themselves in full the tithes of their diocese. (Question II.) The second is whether the later privilege of the monks derogates from the more ancient privileges of baptismal churches.

## QUESTION I

**GRATIAN**

**Part I.** That the clerics cannot claim for themselves in full the tithes by authority of that privilege is proved from this: according to the decrees of the holy Fathers, tithes are divided into four parts—one part assigned to bishops, the second to clerics, the third to restoration of church buildings, and the fourth to the poor. Now none is more obliged to observe the decrees of the holy canons than the Apostolic See.

Hence Pope Gelasius says in a letter to the bishops of Dardania [Note: [Col. 1319] Written A.D. 495—Anselm, book 1, ch. 48 (50)—Polycarpus, book 1, title 14.]:

### C. I. The Roman See must observe a decree of a synod approved by the assent of the universal Church.

We are confident that no true Christian is now ignorant that, among all sees, none ought more to carry out the decree of every synod which the assent of the universal Church has approved than the first see [Col. 1319B], which both confirms every synod by its authority [Note: [Col. 1319] “confirmed”: Basiliensis edition—“formed”: the remaining editions.] and preserves it by continuous [Note: [Col. 1319] “constant”: Basiliensis edition.] governance.

### C. II. Whoever negligently feeds the Lord’s flock committed to him is shown not to love the chief Shepherd.

Likewise Pope Leo, letter IV, to the bishops of Sicily [Note: [Col. 1319] Letter 16, Ballerini edition; written A.D. 447—Anselm, book 1, ch. 43 (44).].

We are urged by divine commands and apostolic admonitions to watch with untiring concern over the state of all churches, and, if anything anywhere is found liable to censure [Note: [Col. 1319] “ever”: *Collectio Hispana*—but not Ballerini—editions compared with the original.] [Note: [Col. 1319] “is found”: *Collectio Hispana*—same editions.], to recall it with swift solicitude [Note: [Col. 1319] “with swift solicitude”: absent from Basiliensis edition.] either from the incompetence of ignorance or from the usurpation of presumption. For, by the injunction of the Lord’s voice [Note: [Col. 1319] “divine”: same editions.], Peter the most blessed Apostle is instructed by a threefold admonition [Note: [Col. 1319D] “Admonition”: In the original and in Anselm, the reading is “by a threefold repetition of a mystical ordinance.” Several other passages have been corrected from the letter itself.] [Note: [Col. 1319] “repetition”: *Collectio Hispana* and Ballerini—Basiliensis edition.] through mystical ordinances, so that the one who loves Christ may feed Christ’s sheep [Col. 1319C]. Reverence for the very See over which we preside through the abundance of divine grace constrains us [Note: [Col. 1319] “instead of reverence”: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venetian I and II editions.] [Note: [Col. 1319] “urges us”: *Collectio Hispana*.] to avoid, as far as we can, the danger of negligence, lest the profession of the chief Apostle, by which he testified that he was a lover of the Lord, be found vain in us [Note: [Col. 1319] “not”: same source—Ballerini—editions compared with the original.]; because, whenever anyone negligently feeds the Lord’s flock entrusted to him, he is thereby shown not to love the chief Shepherd [Note: [Col. 1319] “because whenever anyone negligently feeds the Lord’s flock entrusted to him, he is thereby shown,” etc.: editions compared with the original, first Argentinensis.] [Note: [Col. 1319] Absent from *Collectio Hispana* and Ballerini.] [Col. 1320A].

### C. III. Provisions ordained for perpetual peace must by no means be changed.

The same, to Bishop Anatolius, letter LI [Note: [Col. 1319] Letter 106, Ballerini edition; written A.D. 452—Anselm, book 6, ch. 121 (127)—Ivo, *Decree*, part 16, ch. 317—Capitularies of the Frankish Kings, book 6, ch. 328; book 7, ch. 227.].

Things established generally for perpetual benefit [Note: [Col. 1319] “ordained”: editions compared with the original.] are not to be altered by any change, nor are provisions laid down for the common good to be drawn toward private advantage. Rather, while the boundaries established by the Fathers remain, let no one unjustly [Note: [Col. 1319D] “Unjustly”: St. Leo reads, “let no one lay claim to another’s right.” Ivo and the *Capitularies* read, “let no one condemn another’s [right]”; Anselm reads, “let no one condemn unjust things.”] usurp another’s property; but within his own proper and lawful bounds, let each exercise himself in the breadth of charity, as he is able [Note: [Col. 1319] “each”: editions compared with the original—Ivo.] [Note: [Col. 1319] “is willing”: Ivo.].

### C. IV. No one may rashly violate divine constitutions or decrees of the Apostolic See.

Likewise Pope Hilary in the Roman Synod, chapter 1 [Note: [Col. 1319] I. 6, A.D. 465—Anselm, book 1, chs. 46, 64—Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 37—Polycarpus, book 1, title 7.].

[Col. 1320B] Let it be lawful for no one, without danger to his own standing, rashly to violate either divine constitutions or decrees of the Apostolic See. For we, who administer the offices of the most mighty priest [Note: [Col. 1320D] “Most mighty”: This is the reading in Anselm and in all the other old copies of Gratian except one, which has the reading of the council itself: “most excellent.”], shall bear the blame for such transgressions [Note: [Col. 1319] Absent from Basiliensis edition—“such”: the remaining editions.] [Note: [Col. 1319] “transgression”: Basiliensis edition.] if we are found negligent in the causes of God [Note: [Col. 1319] Added: “of God”: editions compared with the original.], because [Note: [Col. 1319] “who”: Basiliensis edition.] we remember how God threatens the negligence of priests [Note: [Col. 1319] Ezekiel chs. 3 and 34.]. Indeed, one who enjoys greater honor sins with greater guilt [Note: [Col. 1319] “enjoys”: editions compared with the original.], and the exalted standing of sinners makes their sins more grievous [Note: [Col. 1319] “judgments”: Basiliensis edition.] [Note: [Col. 1319] “dignities”: original—Anselm.].

### C. V. Those who violate the sacred canons blaspheme against the Holy Spirit.

Likewise Pope Damasus [Note: [Col. 1319] To Aurelius: Carthage; Pseudo-Isidorian Capitularies—Anselm, book 3, ch. 116 (112)—Polycarpus, book 4, final title—Deusdedit, part 4.].

Those who willfully violate the canons [Note: [Col. 1319] “willfully”: original—editions compared with the original.] are severely judged by the holy [Col. 1320C] Fathers and condemned by the Holy Spirit, by whose inspiration and gift the canons were dictated [Note: [Col. 1319] “dedicated”: editions compared with the original, first Basiliensis.]. For those who, not compelled by necessity but willingly—as has been stated—either act or presume to speak anything insolently against these same sacred canons, or freely consent to others wishing to act, seem not inappropriately to blaspheme the Holy Spirit. Such presumption [Col. 1321A] is plainly one kind of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, because, as has already been said, it acts against him by whose will [Note: [Col. 1321] “impulse”: original—“effort”: Anselm—“command”: Basiliensis edition.] and grace the holy canons were promulgated.

### C. VI. In what matters the Roman Pontiff may enact new laws.

Likewise Pope Urban [Note: [Col. 1321] This is found among the letters neither of Urban I nor of Urban II.].

There are some who say that the Roman Pontiff has always had the right to enact new laws. This we not only do not deny, but strongly affirm. Yet it must especially be understood that he can enact new laws only where the Evangelists and Prophets have said nothing. [Note: “And the Prophets”: these words are absent from many manuscripts and from the Basel edition.] But where the Lord, or his Apostles, and the holy Fathers who followed them, have expressly defined something, there the Roman Pontiff ought not to introduce a new law, but rather confirm, even unto death, what has been proclaimed. For if he should strive to destroy what the Apostles and Prophets taught—which God forbid—he would be proved not to render a judgment, but rather to err. But let this be far from those who have always guarded the Lord’s Church [variant: “Churches”] most excellently against the snares of wolves.

### C. VII. The authority of the Apostolic See has no power to enact anything contrary to the statutes of the saints. Pope Zosimus.

[Note: The letter from which this chapter was taken has not been found. Ivo, however, in the indicated place and in his letter to Hugh, Archbishop of Lyons, attributes this passage to a letter of Zosimus to the bishops of the province of Narbonne; Zosimus himself, in his first letter to Hesychius, relates that he wrote to the bishops of Gaul and Spain.] [Note: From a letter to the bishops of the Viennese and Narbonensian provinces, published after Baronius by Constantius; written A.D. 417. Ivo, *Decree*, part 4, ch. 226.]

Not even the authority of this See may enact or alter anything contrary to the statutes of the Fathers. For among us antiquity lives with its roots unshaken [variant: “may live”], to which the decrees of the Fathers have accorded reverence.

### C. VIII. What has been done contrary to evangelical or prophetic teaching or ordinance cannot stand. Pope Marcellinus, letter II.

[Note: “Marcellinus” has been restored from old copies. For the common editions had “Marcellus.”] [Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Council of Nicaea, ch. 9; C. 11, question 3, ch. 89; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 1, title 28, ch. 2; Anselm, bk. 1, ch. 39, and bk. 3, ch. 87; Ivo, *Decree*, part 16, ch. 9.]

Everything irreproachable the Catholic Church defends. And below, § 1: An unjust judgment and an unjust decision, established by judges through royal [variant: “religious”] fear or command, is invalid. Nor shall anything whatever [Note: This passage has been corrected from Marcellinus’s letter itself.] which has been done contrary to the ordinance of evangelical, prophetic, or apostolic teaching, or of their successors, or of the holy Fathers, stand; and whatever has been done by unbelievers or heretics shall be wholly annulled.

[Note: The common editions read: “Nothing whatever contrary to the evangelical, prophetic, or apostolic teaching or ordinance of them …”]

### C. IX. Not to depart from the statutes of the Fathers and to keep the rule of faith is the first salvation. Pope Hormisdas to the bishops of Spain.

[Note: Rather, from the formulary, or rule of faith, which Hormisdas sent to John, Bishop of Nicopolis, in A.D. 516. The reason for this heading is that Hormisdas sent the same formulary to the bishops of Spain. *Collection in Three Parts*, part 1, title 49, ch. 2.]

The first salvation is to preserve the rule of right faith and in no way to depart from the ordinances of the Fathers.

### C. X. Pope Pelagius professes that he observes in every respect the tome of his predecessor. Pope Pelagius to King Childebert.

[Note: Letter of Pelagius I, of uncertain date. Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 358.]

Care must be taken that, in order to remove the scandal of suspicion, we render the service of our confession to the laws [variant: “kings”] to which Holy Scripture commands that we too are subject. For Rufinus, a man of high rank and ambassador of Your Excellence, came and confidently requested of us, as was fitting, either that we should inform you that the tome of Pope Leo of blessed memory is in every respect preserved by us, or that we should send a confession of our faith in our own words.

We immediately fulfilled the first part of his request, since it was easier; and by this profession we signify to you that, God being gracious, we preserve in all things the tome of the Pontiff, written for the defense of the Catholic faith. [Variants: *meque*: “and me”; *neque*: “nor”; *significare*: “to signify”; *significari*: “to be signified”; *signavimus*: “we signed”; *significavimus*: “we have signified.”]

But lest thereafter any occasion for suspicion should remain—which God forbid—I hastened to do also the other thing of which the aforementioned illustrious man reminded me: that is, I set forth in my own words the confession of faith which we hold. [Variant: “setting it forth.”] [Note: The phrase “I hastened” is absent from Ivo; Ivo reads “setting it forth.”]

### C. XI. Let him be under anathema before God who violates the authoritative decrees of the Roman Pontiffs. Pope Hadrian, in the *Capitularies*, final chapter.

[Note: Anselm, bk. 3, ch. 82 (92), bk. 12, ch. 2 (3); Polycarpus, bk. 4, final title; cf. *Capitularies of the Kings of the Franks*, bk. 6, ch. 322.]

By a general decree we establish [variant: “we judge and establish”] that whoever hereafter, whether king, bishop [Note: These words do not occur in the chapter itself or in the *Capitulary*, but are found in Anselm, bk. 12—though not in its third chapter—and in Polycarpus.], or powerful person, has believed or permitted the authoritative force of the decrees of the Roman Pontiffs to be violated in any respect, shall be subject to an accursed anathema [variants: “an accursed person”; “let it be”] and shall always stand guilty before God as a transgressor of the Catholic faith.

[Note: “Roman”: the chapter reads, “the authoritative force of the canons hereafter,” and the *Capitulary* is not substantially different. Yet Anselm and Polycarpus have the reading printed by Gratian.]

### C. XII. No bishop may do anything contrary to the decrees of the Roman Pontiffs. Pope Damasus, letter IV, to Bishop Prosper.

[Note: The common editions read “Stephen.” This is taken from the Pseudo-Isidorian letter of Damasus concerning chorepiscopi, and is repeated from Leo the Great’s letter to the bishops of Campania, letter 4 in the Ballerini edition. Anselm, bk. 4, ch. 47 (50); Polycarpus, bk. 3, title 22.]

We command that all decretals and enactments of all our predecessors [variant: “predecessors” in the narrower sense], promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and canonical disciplines, be observed by you [variant: “by you and”] and by all bishops, and generally by all priests [variant: “in all things by all”], in such a way that anyone who violates them shall know that pardon [addition in some editions: “of office”] is henceforth denied him. [Other textual forms read: “if anyone commits anything in them, they shall know …”; the differing forms are *quid*, “anything,” *commiserint*, “they shall have committed,” and *noverint*, “they shall know.”]

### C. XIII. He who does not know how to obey the sacred canons must not communicate at the sacred altars. Gregory, book II, letter 7, to Bishop John.

[Note: Letter 7, written A.D. 593, book 3 in the Maurist edition; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 1, title 55, ch. 34; Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 130; Polycarpus, bk. 4, final title.]

By this [variant: “these”] decision consonant with the holy Fathers we decree that one who does not know how to obey the sacred canons is worthy neither to minister at the sacred altars [variant: “to minister at the altars”] nor to receive communion at them. [Note: The clause “nor to receive communion” is absent from the cited editions.]

### C. XIV. The rules enacted by the holy Fathers in synod must be observed. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 1.

[Note: Held A.D. 451; Dionysius’s translation.]

We decree that the rules set forth by the holy Fathers in every synod up to the present shall be kept. [Variant: “that [they] keep.”]

### C. XV. Those who wish their own enactments to be observed should keep the will and statutes of their predecessors. Gregory to Montanus and Thomas, book V, letter 12.

[Note: Letter 12, written A.D. 596, book 6 in the Maurist edition; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 1, title 55, ch. 104.]

The order of justice and reason counsels that one who desires his own commands to be observed by successors should without doubt preserve the will and statutes of his predecessor. [Variant: plural, “those who desire … should preserve.”]

### C. XVI. Whoever does not preserve intact the statutes of the holy Fathers acts against them. Pope Leo IV.

[Note: Ivo, *Decree*, part 4, ch. 186: Leo IV to Archbishop Colorodo and Bertusus. Chapter of uncertain date.]

By the Lord’s permission we have been made shepherds of men so that we may in no way exceed what our Fathers established, whether in sacred canons or in secular laws. For we act contrary to their most salutary ordinances if we do not preserve intact what they themselves established by divine counsel. [Variant: “the things which … by counsel, intact.”]

## Part II. Gratian

If, therefore, the first see ought before all others to observe the statutes of councils; if it must watch with tireless concern for the condition of all churches; if what Roman Pontiffs have decreed ought to be observed by all; if those who do not know how to obey sacred canons ought not to minister at the altars—it is clear that privileges by which the condition of churches is confused or disturbed ought not to be granted by the Apostolic See contrary to the statutes of the holy canons.

§ 1. The answer to this is as follows: The most holy Roman Church imparts law and authority to the sacred canons, but is not bound by them. For it possesses the right of making canons, being the head and hinge of all churches, from whose rule no one may dissent. Thus it confers authority upon the canons without subjecting itself to them.

But just as Christ, who fulfilled the law according to the flesh—being circumcised on the eighth day [Note: Luke 2] and presented with offerings in the Temple on the fortieth day, in order to sanctify it in himself—afterwards, in order to show himself Lord of the law, cleansed a leper by touching him contrary to the letter of the law [Note: Matthew 8], and also excused the Apostles, who contrary to the letter of the Sabbath passed through grainfields, plucking ears of grain and rubbing them in their hands, by the approved example of David, circumcision, and the Temple [Note: Matthew 12:3 ff.; cf. 1 Samuel 21]. He said: “Have you not read what Abimelech did when David came to him, and he gave them the loaves of presentation, of which none but priests were permitted to eat, and he himself ate, and his servants?”

Again: “On the eighth day a boy is circumcised according to the law, and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath.” [Note: Leviticus 12.]

Again, since the perpetual burnt offering is offered by law, and since a male, on the fortieth day, but a female on the eightieth day after birth, was presented in the Temple with offerings according to the command of the law—whereby priests offering sacrifices in the Temple break the letter of the Sabbath and are guiltless—the Son of Man has still greater power to loose the letter of the law, for he is also Lord of the Sabbath.

Hence it is also said of him: “Jesus was teaching as one having authority” [Note: Matthew 7:29]; that is, as Lord of the law, adding to moral precepts what was lacking for perfection, changing the shadow of figurative things into the light of spiritual understanding, unlike their scribes, who, bound by the letter of the law, did not dare to add or alter anything.

So too the Pontiffs of the highest See show reverence to canons made by themselves or by others under their authority; and by humbling themselves before them, they themselves keep them so as to set them before others for observance. Yet sometimes, whether by commanding, defining, or acting otherwise, they show themselves to be lords and makers of decrees. In the preceding chapters, therefore, necessity of obedience is imposed upon others; but the supreme Pontiffs are shown to possess authority to observe, so that, by observing what they themselves have handed down, they show others that it ought not to be despised. This follows Christ’s example: he first received in himself the sacraments which he commanded the Church to observe, in order to sanctify them in himself.

Therefore the first See, as we have said, ought to observe what it has commanded by decree, not by necessity of obedience, but by authority of imparting it. It may consequently grant itself special privileges contrary to general decrees, and by special benefit concede what is prohibited by a general decree.

§ 2. Nevertheless, if we carefully consider the intention of the decrees, it will be found that nothing is granted contrary to the authority of the holy canons. For the sacred canons establish matters in such a way as to reserve interpretive authority to the holy Roman Church. Only those who have the right to make canons have authority to interpret them. Thus in certain chapters of councils, when something is decreed to be observed, it is immediately added: “Unless the authority of the Roman Church commands otherwise”; or, “saving, however, in all matters the right of the holy Roman Church”; or, “saving, however, in all matters Apostolic authority.”

Whatever is defined by sacred canons concerning tithes or any ecclesiastical matters must therefore be understood as necessarily to be observed, unless the authority of the Roman Church commands or permits otherwise. When, therefore, certain privileges are granted by the Apostolic See, even though they seem to say something contrary to the general law, they are nevertheless not understood to grant anything contrary to that law itself, since by the authority of that law privileges for particular persons are reserved to the mother of all churches. Indeed, privileges would not be granted to anyone if nothing special were granted to anyone outside the general law. Privileges are so called as though they were *private laws* (*privata legia*), because they create a private law for individuals.

Gregory, indicating this definition, says: “If you claim this neither by general custom nor by privilege, it remains that you have usurped what you did.” [Note: D. 100, ch. 8.]

§ 3. Likewise Jerome, in his exposition of Jonah, chapter 1: “The privileges of individuals cannot make a common law.”

§ 4. Therefore, as is gathered from the foregoing, the holy Roman Church has power to fortify anyone by its privileges and, outside general decrees, to grant certain things by special favor—yet with due regard to the equity of reason, so that she who is mother of justice may in no respect be found to dissent from it. Thus privileges granted for the sake of religion, necessity, or service rendered must not so enrich someone by relieving him that, through failure to consider the losses of many, they cast others into the misery of poverty. Let them recall what the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says: “We do not wish relief for others and distress for you.” [Note: 2 Corinthians 8:13.]

The sacred law of the emperors agrees: “We order all judges to reject rescripts procured contrary to law, unless perhaps there is something which does not harm another, benefits the petitioner, or pardons a crime for suppliants.” [Note: Cf. below, question 2, ch. 15.]

§ 5. Likewise, the emperor’s constitution addressed to the people: “Nothing detrimental to the treasury or contrary to law ought to be requested.” [Note: There, ch. 14.]

§ 6. Therefore the clerics of this baptismal church, fortified by the authority of this privilege, may claim in full the tithes of their diocese for themselves—unless perhaps the bishops are compelled by extreme necessity to receive their fourth share, and those clerics are shown to have an excess.

# QUESTION II

## GRATIAN

### Part I

That subsequent privileges cannot derogate from earlier ones is proved by the authority of Anacletus, who, writing to all bishops and the remaining priests of Christ, says in Letter I, chapter 3:

[Note: A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Boniface of Mainz, letter 72, Wurdtwein edition; Anselm, bk. 4, ch. 1.]

### C. I. The privileges of churches must be preserved inviolate in every age.

We decree that the privileges of churches and priests [Note: The original reads: “The holy Apostles, by command of the Savior, decreed that the privileges of priests should remain uncorrupted and inviolate at all times,” etc.] shall remain uncorrupted and inviolate for all times. [Variants: “all”; “we have decreed.”] We confirm the laws of the Church by Apostolic authority and remove foreign judgments.

### C. II. The privileges of churches must neither be altered by novelty nor overthrown by wickedness. Pope Leo to Emperor Marcian, letter LII, alternatively LIV.

[Note: Letter 104 in the Ballerini edition, written A.D. 452; Anselm, bk. 4, ch. 2; cf. below, ch. 17.]

The privileges of churches and monasteries [Note: “And monasteries” is absent from the letter and from the repeated passage below. It has not been removed because the passage below—“If, therefore, privileges”—refers to it, and Anselm has it in bk. 4, ch. 2. But because this chapter was deliberately reduced to a summary by the compiler and altered in several places, Leo’s actual words should be set out, as they occur also in the Hispanic Collection:

“Indeed, the privileges of churches, established by the canons of the holy Fathers and fixed by decrees of the venerable Synod of Nicaea, can be overthrown by no wickedness and altered by no novelty. In faithfully carrying out this work, with Christ’s help, it is necessary that I display persevering service; for a stewardship has been entrusted to me, and it tends to my guilt if, with my connivance—which God forbid—the rules of paternal enactments made in the Synod of Nicaea, under the instruction of God’s Spirit, for the governance of the whole Church, are violated, and if the will of one brother has greater weight with me than the common benefit of the whole house of God.”]

The privileges of churches and monasteries, established by the authority of the holy Fathers, can be overthrown by no wickedness and altered by no novelty. In faithfully carrying out this work, with Christ’s help, the Pontiffs of this holy See must display persevering service. For the stewardship has been entrusted to us, and it tends to our guilt if, with our consent or through our negligence, the rules of paternal enactments are violated.

### C. III. No one ought to strip a church of the privilege of its rank. Gregory to Augustine, Bishop of the English, response 9.

[Note: Letter 64, written A.D. 601, book 11 in the Maurist edition; cf. on ch. 1, D. 5; Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 97 (94).]

We grant you no authority over the bishops of Gaul [variant: “the bishops”], because from ancient times of my predecessors [variant: “our predecessors”] the bishop of Arles has received the pallium, and we must by no means deprive him of the authority he has received. Therefore, if your brotherhood should happen to travel to the provinces of Gaul and something must be done by authority, let it be done with the aforesaid bishop of Arles [variant: “the bishops of Arles”], lest what the ancient institution of the Fathers has found [variant: *invenerit*, “has found”] be passed over [variant: “nor may this be omitted”].

But we commit all bishops of the Britons to your brotherhood, so that the unlearned [variant: “the inducted”] may be taught, the weak [some editions add: “and the weak”] strengthened by persuasion, and the perverse corrected by authority. [Note: “The perverse … corrected” is added from the original and is absent from Anselm.]

### C. IV. An Apostolic bishop ought not to destroy the enactments of his Apostolic predecessors. The same, to Bishop Felix, book XII, letter 31.

[Note: There are those who say that this letter is spurious, and we too consider that their view ought to be accepted. In the Maurist edition it is letter 17, book 14, A.D. 604; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 1, title 55, ch. 7.]

If I destroyed what our predecessors established, I should justly be proved not a builder [variant: “destroyer”], but an overthrower, as the voice of Truth testifies when it says: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall not stand, and every knowledge and law divided against itself shall be destroyed.” [Note: Luke 11:17; the Vulgate reads, “divided against itself shall be laid waste.”]

### C. V. Let a metropolitan retain inviolate the right of the dignity anciently entrusted to him. Pope Leo, letter LXXXII, alternatively LXXXIV, to Anastasius, chapter 2.

[Note: Letter 14 in the Ballerini edition, written A.D. 446; Ivo, *Decree*, part 5, ch. 346.]

Accordingly, in conformity with the canons of the holy Fathers, made by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we have decreed that the metropolitan bishops of the individual provinces, to whom, by our delegation, the care of your brotherhood extends [variants: “is extended”; “is entrusted”], shall retain inviolate the right of the dignity anciently entrusted to them [variant: “we decree”]; so that they do not depart from the established rules [variant: “rules conferred”] through negligence or presumption.

### C. VI. The privileges of metropolitans must be preserved unshaken. Pope Hormisdas, in a letter to Bishop John.

[Note: Written A.D. 517; *Collection in Three Parts*, part 1, title 49, ch. 1.]

While preserving the privileges of metropolitans, we delegate to you the functions of the Apostolic See *to this extent*, so that, upon examination, those things which concern the canons [variants in the Hispanic Collection: “be watchful and …”; “which concern the canons and [have been commanded] by us”], or which have recently been commanded by us, may be observed; and that matters concerning ecclesiastical cases which come to your attention [variants: “if anything”; “which are worthy of report”; singular “comes”] may be disclosed to us in your report [some editions add: “be reported”]. It will be a matter of your diligence and care to show yourself in these entrusted duties such that you imitate the faith and integrity of him whose care you undertake.

### C. VII. Apostolic decrees must be violated by no presumption. Gregory to Boniface, first Defender, book VII, letter 17.

[Note: Letter 14, written A.D. 598, book 8 in the Maurist edition; Anselm, bk. 4, ch. 5; Polycarpus, bk. 3, title 15.]

We establish that the decrees of our ordinance [variant: “constitution”], which have been arranged concerning the privileges and appointment of defenders, shall be preserved with perpetual stability and without any opposition—whether we have decreed them in writing or they appear to have been arranged in our presence [variant: “may appear.”] We decree that they may not be overthrown or altered [variants: “changed”; “we have decreed”], wholly or in part, by any pontiff on any pretext.

For it is exceedingly harsh, and especially hostile to the good morals of priests, for anyone to endeavor, under whatever [variant: “however great”] excuse of reason, to rescind arrangements that have been well made, and by his own example to teach others that they may at some time dissolve their own enactments after them [variants: “can”; “be dissolved.”]

### C. VIII. The Apostolic bishop ought to preserve unimpaired the privileges of churches. The same, to Dominic, Bishop of Carthage, book II, indiction 10, letter 39.

[Note: Letter 47, written A.D. 592, book 2 in the Maurist edition; Anselm, bk. 5, ch. 6; Polycarpus, same place.]

Concerning ecclesiastical privileges, let your brotherhood hold this without doubt: just as we defend our own rights, so we preserve to every individual church its rights. Nor do I confer on anyone, through favor, more than he deserves [one edition adds: “for”]; nor, prompted by self-seeking, will I take from anyone what belongs to his own right. Rather, I desire in every way to honor my brethren and strive to advance each one in honor, provided that there is nothing which one may lawfully set against another.

### C. IX. What has been reasonably defined must in no respect be violated. The same, to Virgilius, Bishop of Arles, book VII, letter 117.

[Note: Letter 111, written A.D. 599, book 9 in the Maurist edition; Anselm, bk. 4, ch. 7; Polycarpus, same place.]

Since the desire of pious will and the purpose of praiseworthy devotion [variant: “decision”] must always be aided by priestly efforts, care must be applied with diligence so that matters ordained for the peace of monks [Note: Omitted by Anselm.] and religious life [variant: *religiosae* for *religiosaeque*; *conversationi*, “religious life” in the dative, for *conversationis*] may be neglected neither through disregard nor disturbed by any presumption [variants: *fuerint*, “have been,” / *sunt*, “are”; some editions add “or disposed”]. But just as what the reason of expediency required [variant: “what was expedient”] had to be defined [variant: “prevailed”], so what has been defined ought not to be violated—unless perhaps where there is greater authority.

[Note: “Unless perhaps”: this exception is absent from most ancient manuscripts, the Argentinian and Basel editions, Anselm, and printed and manuscript copies of Gregory. In one copy of Gratian it was inserted as a gloss, and occurs above, 6, question 4.]

### C. X. Whoever disturbs the rights of his brethren does injury to himself. The same, to Bishop Natalis, book II, letter 37.

[Note: Letter 52, written A.D. 592, book 2 in the Maurist edition.]

As to what you say [variant: “you say”]—that in our time those things ought to be preserved which were handed down and kept by my predecessors [variant: “predecessors” in the narrower sense] also—far be it from me [some editions add: “this”] to violate in any church the enactments of my elder fellow-priests [variant: “with my fellow-priests”], because I do injury to myself if I disturb the rights of my brethren.

### C. XI. What was instituted by the Apostles and their successors must be violated by no presumption. Pope Julius, letter I, to the Easterners, chapter 4.

[Note: Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 127 (132); Polycarpus, same place.]

When every excess of usurpation has been cut off, no one ought to presume [variant: “no one may presume”] upon things which do not appear to have been granted to him. And below, § 1: Those things instituted by the Apostles and their successors must not be neglected through any carelessness, violated through any dissension, or disturbed through any contention.

### C. XII. Things reasonably ordered must be disturbed by no opposition. Pope Gregory, book VII, indiction 2, letter 60, to the illustrious Praerectus.

[Note: Letter 57, written A.D. 599, to the illustrious Praejecta, book 9 in the Maurist edition; Anselm, bk. 4, ch. 9; cf. C. 35, question 9, ch. 1.]

It is wholly fitting to ecclesiastical moderation that what has been ordered, or reasonably decided, should not thereafter be disturbed by any opposition.

[Note: “Reasonably” is absent from most manuscripts, the Argentinian and Basel editions, and copies of St. Gregory; nor is it found below at 35, question 9, *By every means*. It has not been removed because all copies of Gratian have this word, including in the heading.]

### C. XIII. Things done contrary to laws are treated as though they had not been done. In the Register, book VII, indiction 2, letter 7, to Januarius of Cagliari.

[Note: Letter 7, written A.D. 599, book 9 in the Maurist edition; Deusdedit, parts 1 and 3.]

It is expressly enacted by imperial constitution [variant: “it has been constituted by imperial sanction”] that things done contrary to laws are to be regarded not only as useless, but as though they had not been done. [Variant: “are to be regarded.”]

### C. XIV. Code, book I, title “On petitions to be offered to the emperor”: Emperor Constantine.

[Note: Issued A.D. 354; *Code of Justinian*, bk. 1, title 19, ch. 3.]

Nothing detrimental to the treasury or contrary to law ought to be requested.

### C. XV. Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian.

[Note: Issued A.D. 426; *Code*, same title, ch. 7.]

We order all judges to reject rescripts obtained contrary to law, unless perhaps there is something which [variant: “is”] does not harm another, benefits the petitioner, or pardons a crime for suppliants [variant: singular, “the suppliant”].

### C. XVI. A rescript deserves effect when it accords with the reason of right and laws. Pope Pelagius to Count John.

[Note: Ivo, *Decree*, part 4, ch. 191; letter of uncertain date.]

To one who said that he had sacred commands in hand, we replied that he ought to know that the most merciful emperor himself had established by general laws that sacred grants made in response to an individual suppliant’s request prevail and take effect only when they agree with the reason of right and laws [variants: “has established”; “take effect”]. But those obtained perhaps by concealment or false petitions bring no remedy to suppliants.

Gratian. Rescripts, whether annotations or pragmatic sanctions, ought expressly to contain the condition: “If the petitions rest upon truth.” For a lying petitioner must be deprived of what he has obtained; and those to whom the writings are directed must be punished if they have forbidden the falsehood of petitions to be challenged.

Thus the Emperors Diocletian, Maximian, and Constantius, Code book I, title “If [a rescript is] contrary to law or public utility”:

§ 1. When the defense of falsehood is raised, whether a falsehood is found in the statement of law, in that of fact, or in deceitful concealment, the judge appointed must investigate according to the tenor of truth, not according to the petitioner’s assertion, and accordingly render judgment in the case.

Likewise Emperor Constantine:

§ 2. We order judges who forbid the falsehood of petitions to be challenged to be punished by a fine of ten pounds of gold. [Variant: “we ought to order”; “who forbade.”]

Likewise Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian:

§ 3. Even if a lying petitioner produces a sacred pronouncement consistent with the laws, let the petitioner be wholly deprived of what he has obtained; and if the excessive wickedness of the liar is found [variant: “is found to be”], let him also be subject to the severity of the judge.

Likewise Emperor Constantine:

§ 4. Even where not inquiry but execution is commanded, the truth of the petitions must be investigated, so that, if fraud intervenes [variant: “has intervened”], the entire matter may be examined. [One edition omits “the entire.”]

Likewise Emperor Anastasius:

§ 5. We admonish all judges, of whatever greater or lesser administration, throughout our whole commonwealth, not to allow any rescript, pragmatic sanction, or sacred annotation which appears [variant: “appear”] contrary to general law or public utility to be produced in the litigation [variant: “in litigation”] of any suit; rather, let them not hesitate in any way to observe the general sacred constitutions.

Code, title “On diverse rescripts.” Emperors Diocletian and Maximian:

§ 6. We enact that the authentic rescripts themselves and the originals subscribed also by our own hand—not copies of them—shall be presented. [Variants: “and”; “from” in place of “of.”]

Emperor Constantine:

§ 7. If any personal grants are found without date and consul, they shall lack authority.

Emperor Zeno:

§ 8. We order that all rescripts, whether issued to the persons petitioning or to any judge, whether called an annotation or any pragmatic sanction [some editions omit “any”], shall be produced subject to this condition: “If the petitions rest upon truth” [variant: “rest upon”]. A petitioner shall receive no benefit from a pronouncement obtained, even if in court he asserts [variant: “affirms”] the truth, unless the question of the truthfulness of the petitions is shown to have been inserted in the imperial grant.

For the illustrious quaestor and the distinguished masters of the records, who dictate any imperial response without the aforesaid addition, and the judges who receive it, shall incur censure; and the record clerks, *pragmaticarii*, or assistants of the chief clerks of whatever bureau who dare to write unlawful dictations shall be punished by loss of their belt of office. [Variant: “shall be struck” with loss of the belt.]

[Col. 1331C] C. XVII. The privileges of churches must not be overturned by any wrongdoing. Likewise Pope Leo, Epistle LII, alternatively LIV, to the Emperor Marcian. [Note: [Col. 1331] Compare above at c. 2.—Anselm, bk. 4, c. 10.]

The privileges of churches, established by the canons of the holy Fathers and fixed by the decrees of the venerable Synod of Nicaea, can be overthrown by no wrongdoing and altered by no innovation. [Note: [Col. 1331] “or”: editions collectively.]

[Col. 1332A] Likewise Pope Nicholas, presiding over a universal synod, said in the Roman Council, final chapter. [Note: [Col. 1331C] This chapter occurs in the Council of Rome at which Pope Nicholas I deposed the bishops Theutgaud and Gunther. That council was printed at Rome after his letters.] [Note: [Col. 1331] Held in A.D. 863.—Anselm, bk. 4, c. 26; bk. 12, c. 3 (4). Deusdedit, pt. 4. Ivo, Decree, pt. 5, c. 35. Polycarpus, bk. 1, tit. 17.]

C. XVIII. Let him be anathema who has scorned to observe the commands or decrees of the Roman Pontiffs.

If anyone scorns the doctrines, commands, prohibitions, enactments, or decrees beneficially promulgated by the prelate of the Apostolic See for the discipline of the Catholic faith, [Note: [Col. 1331] “for the Catholic faith or ecclesiastical discipline”: editions collectively; Anselm.] for the correction [Note: [Col. 1331] “rebuke”: Anselm.—The following words, marked by asterisks, are not in Anselm, bk. 4.] *of the faithful, for the amendment of the wicked, or for the prohibition* of imminent or future evils, let him be anathema.

Likewise Gelasius, to Cresconius and John, bishops of Messala, among other matters. [Note: [Col. 1331] Berardus judged Callistus II to be the author of this chapter, since the same words occur in his Epistle (14), to Anseric. In this he erred remarkably; for the chapter is found also in the collection of Deusdedit, bk. 2, c. 92 (compare Ballerini, *Works of Leo the Great*, vol. 3, p. CCCIV), and in Anselm’s treatise against Wibert (in Canisius, vol. 3). In both it reads: “Cresconius, John, and the bishops of Messala.”]

C. XIX. Successors ought to observe the enactments of their predecessors.

Just as it is fitting that a successor preserve his predecessors’ enactments when lawful and just, so also he ought to correct those that were wrongly made.

[Col. 1332B] Hence Arcadius and Honorius also declare: [Note: [Col. 1331] Theodosian Code, bk. 16, tit. 2, c. 29, dated A.D. 395.—Anselm, bk. 4, c. 16.]

C. XX.

Whatever has been enacted at various times by our forefathers concerning the most holy churches, we command to remain inviolate and uncorrupted. Therefore let nothing be altered in their privileges, and let protection be extended to all who serve the churches; for in our times [Note: [Col. 1331] Adds “also”: editions collectively.] we wish rather to add to their reverence [Note: [Col. 1331] “reverence” in the accusative: same editions.] than to alter anything among those things granted long ago. The same emperors, law 30. [Note: [Col. 1331] Theodosian Code, same title.—Anselm, same place, c. 17.]

§ 1. By this present enactment we do not so much prescribe anything new as confirm those things which seem to have been granted long ago. Therefore we forbid, even under threat of punishment, that the privileges [Note: [Col. 1331] “to itself”: Basel edition.] which the reverence of religion [Note: [Col. 1331] “of religion and order”: Nuremberg and Venice I editions.—“of religion or order”: other editions except Argentinensis and Basel.] formerly obtained be impaired, [Note: [Col. 1331] “to impair”: editions collectively, except Lyons II and III.] so that those also [Col. 1332C] who obey the Church may enjoy her benefits. [Note: [Col. 1331] “those to whom the Church grants benefits”: original.] The same emperors, law 34. [Note: [Col. 1331] Theodosian Code, same title.—Justinian Code, bk. 1, tit. 3, c. 13.—Anselm, bk. 4, c. 18.]

§ 2. If the privileges of a venerable church have been violated by anyone’s rashness [Note: [Col. 1331] “of anyone”: original; Anselm.] or neglected through dissimulation, the offender shall be punished by a condemnation of twelve [Note: [Col. 1331D] “Twelve”: in the law itself, both in the Theodosian and Justinian Codes, the reading is “five pounds of gold.”] pounds of gold, as was also previously established. [Note: [Col. 1331] “shall be condemned”: edition of the Theodosian Code; edition of Gothofredus.] Nevertheless, those privileges [Note: [Col. 1332C] “And those privileges”: these words through the end are not in that law; instead, the Theodosian Code reads: “Therefore, if anything contrary to the laws has been obtained against churches or clerics through surreptitious petition, or by heretics, or by persons of this sort, we annul it by the authority of this enactment.”] [Col. 1333A] shall retain their fullest force in every respect.

Likewise Pelagius, to Armentarius, Master of Soldiers, among other matters. [Note: [Col. 1333] Chapter of uncertain date.—Deusdedit, pt. 1. Anselm against Wibert, in Canisius, vol. 3.]

C. XXI. A pontiff may not depart from the Church’s right, when it is confirmed by the authority of documents.

After the rights of the Church have been confirmed by the authority also of intervening documents, a pontiff must by no means be permitted to have freedom to depart from them, even if he wishes it. [Note: [Col. 1333] “wishes”: Anselm.]

Gratian. Therefore, if the privileges of monasteries or of any churches whatsoever are kept inviolate by the authority of Leo, Gregory, Gelasius, and certain other pontiffs of the holy Roman Church; if things done contrary to the laws are to be regarded as undone; if a pontiff [Col. 1333B] has no permission to depart from the documents by which the Church’s rights are confirmed: it is clear that later privileges cannot derogate from earlier ones, nor can any exception be raised against them on their authority, since, even if acts were specifically done contrary to those privileges, they would have to be regarded as undone.

Part II. § 1. The reply to this is as follows: the holy Roman Church, assembled by its own authority, has power to separate what has been joined and to join what has been separated, provided that the equity of reason is considered. Accordingly, out of regard either for piety or necessity, it can alter, wholly or partly, what it has once granted. For the necessity of correcting vices causes the privileges of many churches to be reduced or entirely altered, whether individually or generally.

§ 2. Individually, according to this passage: [Note: [Col. 1333] Compare C. 11, q. 1, c. 63.]

A person entirely deserves to lose a privilege who abuses the authority allowed him.

C. XXII. Let him lose what he has who usurps what he has not received. Likewise Pope Silverius, to Bishop Vigilius, Epistle II. [Note: [Col. 1333] Apocryphal chapter.—Anselm, bk. 6, c. 155 (1[.....]0). Ivo, Decree, pt. 6, c. 73.]

Thus it is fitting that the faith of the holy Fathers be preserved in the Catholic Church: that he who has arrogated to himself, through reprehensible rashness, what he did not receive, should lose what he possessed.

C. XXIII. He loses a privilege who does not lawfully use his authority. Likewise Pope Simplicius, Epistle II, to John, bishop of Ravenna, after some words in which he forbade him an unlawful ordination. [Note: [Col. 1333] Compare above, Distinction 74, c. 7.—Collection in three parts, pt. 1, tit. 45, c. 2.]

We announce, however, that if hereafter [Note: [Col. 1333] “after such a thing here”: Basel edition.—“after this such a thing”: other editions.] you presume anything [Col. 1334A] of this kind, and believe that you may perhaps make any bishop, priest, or deacon against his will, know that your authority to ordain for the churches of Ravenna and Emilia will be taken away.

C. XXIV. Those who consecrate an unworthy person lose the right of ordination. Likewise Pope Leo, Epistle LXXXV, alternatively LXXXVII, to the African bishops. [Note: [Col. 1333] Compare at c. 43, C. 1, q. 1.]

If any bishops consecrate as a priest someone who ought not to be such, even if in some way they escape loss of their own rank, they will nevertheless no longer possess the right of ordination; nor will they ever participate in that sacrament which, disregarding divine judgment, they conferred upon one unworthy.

Gratian. Generally, for example, when episcopal dignity is perpetually withdrawn from a city [Col. 1334B] accustomed to murder its own bishops.

Thus Pope Gelasius writes: [Note: [Col. 1333] In Polycarpus, and in Anselm and Ivo, the chapter *Comperimus* immediately follows. Below, concerning consecration, Distinction 2.] [Note: [Col. 1333] To Majoricus and John, bishops.—Deusdedit, pt. 2, c. 92 (compare Ballerini, *Works of Leo the Great*, vol. 3, p. CCCIV). Anselm, bk. 6, c. 148 (144). Ivo, Decree, pt. 10, c. 18. Polycarpus, bk. 3, tit. 30.]

C. XXV. Episcopal dignity is withdrawn from a city which has murdered its own bishops.

The repeated slaughter of the bishops of Scyllacium [Note: [Col. 1333] “of Squillace”: Ballerini from Deusdedit.—“indeed of the Latins”: Ivo.—“of Sillanum”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.—“of Syllanum”: other editions.] has appalled us by the atrocity of so horrible a crime, [Note: [Col. 1333] “appals”: Argentinensis, Basel, and Nuremberg editions.] so that the decision of our deliberation long hesitated, while we both abhorred appointing anyone [Note: [Col. 1333] “anyone whatsoever”: Ivo.] as bishop amid examples of parricide, [Note: [Col. 1333] “we abhor”: Basel edition.] and did not judge that a church, though deprived, ought for that reason to be left altogether abandoned. [Note: [Col. 1333] “and—from ‘left’ onward”: not in Ivo.] Therefore, now shunning, as it were, the practice and custom of sacrilege, we judged it necessary to make this provision for religion: that it be governed as a parish by priests situated outside it, [Note: [Col. 1333] “in place of the parish”: Ivo.—“of yours”: editions collectively.] since those dwelling there [Col. 1334C] have learned by the sword to kill their pastors; [Note: [Col. 1333] “have learned”: Ivo.] and, by an unheard-of crime—one which nowhere at all is recorded to have occurred even in provinces afflicted by continual and various incursions of wars—[Note: [Col. 1333] “has occurred at all”: Ivo; Anselm.] this city [Note: [Col. 1333] “some city”: editions collectively.] has been found to strike down its bishops, who minister to it the sacraments of the Christian faith, [Note: [Col. 1333] “ministering the faith of Christ”: Ivo.—“of administering”: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I and II, Paris editions.] without a persecutor. [Note: [Col. 1333] Omitted in the same editions and in Basel and Lyons I.] Therefore care must be taken that *there* this deadly ruin may be healed by the cessation of its own bishops, and that thus at least the occasion for so great a frenzy may be removed: if [Note: [Col. 1333] “if—from ‘if’ to the end”: omitted by Ivo.] no person remains there against whom [Note: [Col. 1333] “in which”: editions collectively except Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I.—“whom”: Böhm.] this bitterness can be perpetrated, and so that city itself, [Note: [Col. 1333] Omitted by Ivo.] having no one upon whom to vent its savagery, may desist from such rashness, [Col. 1335A] or may not provide others with a dreadful contagion [Note: [Col. 1335] “those imitating”: Ivo.] of imitation. [Note: [Col. 1335] “may not furnish an example”: editions collectively.] Let it therefore lack episcopal assistance, supplied to it from elsewhere, [Note: [Col. 1335] “expended”: Anselm and Ivo.—“weighed out”: Basel edition.] since it cruelly stains with shed blood the sacred dignity placed in its own bosom; for it must be punished by this retribution in either case, whether it commits this *crime* by domestic instigation or stirred by external furies. [Note: [Col. 1335] “externally”: same editions.—Ivo, with whom the chapter ends here.]

Therefore let your charity provide the ministry of visitation to the church placed in this condition; and, whether by coming together or in turns, as the character of circumstances and the matter requires, let it present the divine ministries [Note: [Col. 1335] “mysteries”: Argentinensis, Basel, Venice I editions.] to those who are ungrateful, lest, while avoiding tares, [Note: [Col. 1335] “the tare”: editions collectively except Basel and Paris III.] we seem to pass over the Lord’s wheat.

Part III. Gratian. Episcopal sees are also transferred because of the necessity of hostility or poverty, or [Col. 1335B] two are reduced into one, as blessed Gregory is recorded to have done above, under the title concerning the transfer of bishops. [Note: [Col. 1335] Compare C. 7, q. 1, cc. 42, 44; C. 16, q. 1, c. 48.] Therefore church privileges are not deemed to remain so inviolable that, when certain reasons intervene, they cannot be derogated from by apostolic authority; otherwise the multitude of churches would be reduced to a small number, since countless churches are frequently found established within the dioceses of others.

Let the privileges of churches therefore be preserved unshaken through all times, so that no one may lawfully act against them apart from the authority of him by whom they were granted.

§ 1. But there is objected that statement of Pope Symmachus: “The possessions which each person leaves to a church at his own discretion,” etc., [Note: [Col. 1335] Compare C. 16, q. 1, c. 61.] which is set down above under the title [Col. 1336A] concerning the alienation of ecclesiastical property. From this it is understood that things conferred from the right of an individual church, whether out of necessity—as for pilgrims—or from regard for piety—as for religious houses—are to be possessed not perpetually but temporarily by those to whom they are conferred.

Yet that statement of Symmachus may refer to a consideration of necessity, not to a prospect of piety: namely, that those things which necessity has prompted to be bestowed on pilgrims or captives, not those granted to religious houses for the tranquillity of religious life, are forbidden to be possessed perpetually. Or, rather, it is to be understood of both: that just as persons suffering necessity, when the necessity has ceased, are compelled to renounce the benefits which the consideration of mercy granted them, so persons living religiously, when they have ceased from religion, [Col. 1336B] are stripped of the privileges which their religious way of life merited.

Thus privileges granted to religious houses must either be understood in the case in which provision is made for them without derogating from anyone’s rights—for example, that by authority of privileges they are not compelled to pay tithes from newly cultivated lands, whose tithes had been assigned to no one—or, if provision cannot be made for them because of an urgent temporal necessity unless others are derogated from, [Note: [Col. 1335] “unless others were derogated from”: Böhm.] the authority of privileges must be deemed preserved in such a way that their poverty is relieved, not so that, through increase of their riches and a substantial extension of their possessions, baptismal or parish churches are utterly destroyed.

# CAUSE XXVI

[Col. 1335]

[Col. 1335C] GRATIAN.

A certain priest is convicted before a bishop of being a caster of lots and diviner; corrected by the bishop, he refused to desist; he is excommunicated; finally, when at the point of death, he is reconciled by a certain priest without consulting the bishop; a penance is imposed upon him according to the length of time fixed by the canons. (Question I.) The first question here is: who are casters of lots? (Question II.) Second, is it a sin to be a caster of lots? (Question III.) Third, from whom did the practice of divination take its origin? (Question IV.) Fourth, how many kinds of divination are there? (Question V.) Fifth, are casters of lots or diviners to be excommunicated if they refuse to desist? (Question VI.) Sixth, can one excommunicated by a bishop be reconciled by a priest without consulting that bishop? [Col. 1335D] (Question VII.) Seventh, must a penance of a specified duration be imposed on those who are dying?

# QUESTION I

[Col. 1336C]

GRATIAN

Isidore defines who casters of lots are, in Book VIII, chapter 9, of the *Etymologies*, saying as follows. [Note: [Col. 1335] Ivo, Decree, pt. 11, c. 22.]

C. I. Who are casters of lots?

Casters of lots are those who, under the name of a feigned religion, profess knowledge of divination through certain lots which they call the lots of saints [Note: [Col. 1335] Adds: “or apostles”: editions collectively.] or promise future events by examining any writings whatsoever.

# QUESTION II

GRATIAN

Part I. That it is not sinful to seek lots is proved both by examples and by authorities. For when [Col. 1336D] Achan [Note: [Col. 1335] “Achan”: Vulgate.] had secretly stolen something devoted to destruction, and because of his sin the people had been slaughtered at Ai [Note: [Col. 1335] “Nay”: Roman edition, through a printer’s error.—Compare Joshua, c. 7.] and had turned their backs to their enemies, the Lord commanded Joshua to discover by lots through whose sin [Col. 1337A] the people had deserved to fall into the hands of their enemies. Receiving the command, Joshua cast lots first upon the tribes, then upon the families, and finally upon the persons; and thus the lot fell upon Achan.

Saul also, [Note: [Col. 1337] 1 Samuel, c. 14.] when fighting against the Philistines, had sworn that he would kill anyone among the people who ate before sunset. By lot he discovered that his son Jonathan had eaten honey which he had taken with his staff; and when Saul wished to deliver him to death, he withdrew the sentence at the people’s entreaty.

Jonah likewise, [Note: [Col. 1337] Jonah, c. 1.] when fleeing from the face of the Lord, was discovered by lot by the sailors, cast into the sea, and swallowed by a great fish. It is also written of Zechariah [Note: [Col. 1337] Luke, c. 1.] that he went out by lot to offer incense. But Matthias [Note: [Col. 1337] Acts, c. 1.] was chosen by lot by blessed Peter for the apostleship and as Judas’s successor. Therefore, what is confirmed by the examples of so many persons [Col. 1337B] is plainly not evil.

Hence Augustine also says in the book on the Psalms, on Psalm XXX, sermon 2, at the verse, “In your hands are my lots.” [Note: [Col. 1337] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 77.]

C. I.

A lot is not something evil, but a thing which, in human uncertainty, judges the divine will.

Part II. Gratian. The reply to this is as follows: before the Gospel became clear, many things were permitted which were utterly eliminated in the time of more perfect discipline. For marriage between priestly persons or blood relatives is forbidden neither by legal, evangelical, nor apostolic authority; yet it is wholly prohibited by ecclesiastical law. So too it is shown that there is nothing evil in lots; nevertheless, they are forbidden to the faithful, lest under this guise [Col. 1337C] of divination they return to the ancient cults of idolatry.

Hence the Apostle says to certain persons who observe constellations and signs of future events: [Note: [Col. 1337] Galatians, c. 4, v. 10.] “You observe days, and months, and seasons, and years. I fear for you, lest perhaps I have laboured among you in vain.” Thus astronomy, or astrology, too, has fallen into disuse among Catholics, because, while they were excessively intent upon these matters from their own curiosity, they had less leisure for matters suited to the salvation of souls.

That one ought not to put trust in lots is attested by Jerome, writing on Jonah, c. 1. [Note: [Col. 1337] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 73; *Decree*, pt. 11, c. 21.]

C. II. The examples of Jonah and Matthias do not warrant belief in lots.

We ought not immediately, under the example of Jonah, to put faith in lots, nor join to this testimony that passage from the Acts [Note: [Col. 1337] Acts, c. 1.] of the Apostles [Col. 1337D] in which Matthias is chosen by lot for the apostleship, *since the privileges [Note: [Col. 1337D] “Since the privileges”: these words through the end were added from blessed Jerome. They are cited by Bede from the same source below, in the same question, c. “Not by the example.”] of individuals cannot make a common law*.

[Col. 1338A] C. III. Divine oracles must not be turned to secular affairs. Likewise Augustine, to Januarius’s inquiries, Epistle CXIX. [Note: [Col. 1337] Epistle 55, written A.D. 400, Maurist edition.]

Those [Note: [Col. 1337] “If”: Lyons II and III editions.—“Those”: Nuremberg edition.—Ivo, *Panormia*.] who read lots from the pages [Note: [Col. 1337] “pagans”: Venice I and II editions.] of the Gospels—although it is preferable that they do this rather than run to consult demons—nevertheless, this custom too displeases me: wishing to turn divine oracles, *which speak [Note: [Col. 1337] The words marked with an asterisk are not in Ivo.] of another life*, to secular business and the vanity [Note: [Col. 1337] “necessity”: Basel edition.] of this life.

C. IV. The examples of Matthias and Jonah do not warrant indiscriminate belief in lots. Likewise Bede, on the Acts of the Apostles, at c. 1. [Note: [Col. 1337] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 78.—Compare above, c. 2.]

One must not indiscriminately believe in lots because of the example of Matthias, or because the prophet Jonah was discovered by lot, since the privileges of individuals, as Jerome says, cannot at all make a common law. [Note: [Col. 1337] “cannot”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.] And below:

§ 1. Yet if, compelled by some necessity, persons think that God must be consulted by lots after the example of the Apostles, let them observe that the Apostles themselves did this only after an assembly [Note: [Col. 1337] “at an assembly of the brethren with weeping”: Ivo, *Panormia*.] of the brethren had been gathered and prayers poured out to God.

But Augustine writes concerning diviners in Book V on Deuteronomy, c. 19, saying as follows. [Note: [Col. 1337] Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 11, c. 10.]

C. V. Things commanded by diviners are not to be observed, even though what they predict comes to pass.

The Lord intended it to be understood that even those things which are spoken by diviners not according to God, if what they say comes to pass, are not to be received in such a way that the things they command [Col. 1338C] are done or the things they worship are worshipped.

C. VI. Which human institutions are superstitious and which are not. The same author, Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapters 19, 20, and 21. [Note: [Col. 1337] Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 11, c. 13.]

That which rests upon human institutions is partly superstitious and partly not superstitious. Superstitious is everything instituted by human beings that pertains to making and worshipping idols, or to worshipping as God [Note: [Col. 1337] “the Lord”: Basel edition.] a creature or any part of a creature, or to consultations and certain agreed and covenanted compacts of signs with demons—such as the contrivances [Note: [Col. 1337] “volumes”: editions collectively except Basel.] of magical [Col. 1338D] arts, which poets are accustomed rather to mention than to teach. [Note: [Col. 1337] “certain persons”: same editions except Basel and Lyons II–III.—“are accustomed”: same editions except Lyons II–III; Ivo.] Of this kind, though with a somewhat more licentious vanity, are the books of haruspices and [Col. 1339A] augurs.

§ 1. To this class also belong all charms and remedies which even medical science condemns: whether in incantations, in certain signs called *characters*, in certain objects hung up and tied on, or even in things somehow danced, not for the regulating [Note: [Col. 1339] “repairing”: Basel edition.] of bodies but for certain hidden or even [Note: [Col. 1339] Omitted in Ivo and in the editions collectively except Lyons II–III.] manifest significations. These are called *physical* by a more imposing [Note: [Col. 1339] “milder”: original.] name, so that they may seem not to involve superstition [Note: [Col. 1339] “superstitiously”: Ivo.] but to benefit nature, [Note: [Col. 1339] “nature”: Ivo.] as, for example, earrings at the upper part of each ear, or rings made from ostrich [Note: [Col. 1339] “destructions”: Basel and Venice I–II editions.] bones upon the fingers; or when a person hiccoughing is told to hold his left thumb with his right hand. To these are added thousands of utterly vain [Note: [Col. 1339] “monstrous”: same editions.] observances: if some limb twitches; if, while friends walk together, a stone, *a dog*, or a boy passes between them. [Note: [Col. 1339] “separately”: Basel, Venice I–II, and Paris editions.—“separately”: Argentinensis edition.—“if joined”: Nuremberg edition.]

And below:

§ 2. Of this kind also are such practices as treading on a threshold while passing before one’s own house; returning to bed if one sneezes while putting on shoes; returning home [Note: [Col. 1339] “to the house”: editions collectively.] if one stumbles when setting out; [Note: [Col. 1339] “falls down”: same editions except Basel.] when [Note: [Col. 1339] “or if”: editions collectively.] a garment is gnawed by mice, [Note: [Col. 1339] “is being gnawed”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] *fearing the suspicion of a future evil more than grieving over the present loss*.

§ 3. Nor are those to be separated [Note: [Col. 1339] Omitted in the editions collectively except Lyons II–III.] from this kind of pernicious superstition who were once called genethliacs because of their consideration of days of birth, [Note: [Col. 1339] “natural”: editions collectively except Basel and Lyons II–III.] but are now commonly called mathematicians. [Note: [Col. 1339] Omitted in the same editions except Lyons II–III.] For although they follow, [Note: [Col. 1339] “attain and investigate thoroughly”: editions collectively except Lyons.] and sometimes even accurately investigate, the true positions of the stars at a person’s birth, they grievously err when they attempt from this to predict either our actions or the outcomes of actions, [Note: [Col. 1339] “outcome”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.—“outcomes”: other editions.] [Col. 1339C] and *sell to unlearned people a pitiable slavery*. [Note: [Col. 1339] “to produce”: editions collectively except Lyons II–III.]

And below, c. 23:

§ 4. Divine Scripture has not kept silent concerning this kind of fornication of the soul, [Note: [Col. 1339] “authority”: editions collectively.] nor has it deterred the soul from it merely by saying that such things should not be followed because their professors speak falsehood; [Note: [Col. 1339] “him”: Basel edition.] rather, [Note: [Col. 1339] “even by”: same edition.—“and by”: other editions.—“if even”: Basel edition.] “even if they tell you,” it says, “and it comes to pass, do not believe them.” [Note: [Col. 1339] Deuteronomy, c. 13, v. 8.] For the fact that the image of the dead Samuel [Note: [Col. 1339] 1 Samuel, c. 28.] truthfully foretold events to Saul the *king* [Note: [Col. 1339] Omitted in Ivo.] does not make those sacrileges by which that image was presented less detestable. Nor does the fact that, in the Acts of the Apostles, [Note: [Col. 1339] Acts, c. 16.] a ventriloquist woman bore true [Col. 1340A] testimony to the Apostles of the Lord mean that the Apostle Paul spared that spirit; rather, he cleansed the woman by rebuking [Note: [Col. 1339] “correction”: editions collectively except Lyons I.] and expelling that demon.

§ 5. Therefore every art of this kind, whether of frivolous or harmful superstition, established from a certain pestilential association of human beings and demons, as though by the pacts of a faithless and deceitful friendship, must be wholly rejected [Note: [Col. 1339] “must be rejected and fled”: editions collectively.] and fled by a Christian.

C. VII. An inquiry or cure sought from diviners or magical practitioners is not life but death. The same author, in the book *On the City of God*. [Note: [Col. 1339] Rather, Rabanus, *On the Deceptions of Magicians*.—Collection in three parts, pt. 3, tit. 21, c. 13. Burchard, bk. 10, c. 41. Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 11, c. 66.]

He who wishes to have salvation without the Saviour, and thinks that he can become wise without true wisdom, will labour not in health but in sickness, not wisely but foolishly, in continual infirmity; and in harmful blindness he will remain [Col. 1340B] foolish and mad. Accordingly, every inquiry and every cure sought from diviners and magicians, [Note: [Col. 1339] “magical”: editions collectively; Böhm.—Adds “arts”: editions collectively.] or from demons themselves in the worship of idols, must be called death rather than life; and those who pursue them [Note: [Col. 1339] “pursue”: Basel edition.], unless they correct themselves, tend toward eternal destruction. For the Psalmist says: [Note: [Col. 1339] Psalm 95, v. 5.] “All the gods of the nations are demons,” who daily strive, through deceived persons, to deceive others, in order to make them participants in their own destruction.

Thus this vanity of magical arts has prevailed throughout the whole world for many centuries through a tradition of evil angels, through a certain knowledge of future and infernal things; and through their inventions [Note: [Col. 1339] “evocations”: Isidore.] were invented haruspicy, augury, what are called oracles, and necromancy.

[Col. 1340C] C. VIII. Christian and true piety rejects and condemns astrologers. The same author, Book IV of the *Confessions*, c. 3. [Note: [Col. 1339] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 79; *Decree*, pt. 11, c. 20.]

I did not cease to consult those astrologers, [Note: [Col. 1339] With Augustine one should read *planos* [“impostors”], since they used to call flatterers *plani*.] whom they call mathematicians, because apparently there was no sacrifice [Note: [Col. 1339] “was for them”: Ivo, *Decree*.—“by them”: Lyons II–III.—“for them”: other editions; Ivo, *Panormia*.] and no prayers directed to any spirit for divination. Yet Christian and true piety consistently rejects [Note: [Col. 1339] “expels”: Ivo; editions collectively.] and condemns this.

C. IX. To observe auguries and inquire into the courses of the stars is a form of idolatrous worship. Likewise Jerome. [Note: [Col. 1339] Rather, Origen, Homily 5 on Joshua, c. 5.]

But add this as well: that he who commits fornication sins against [Col. 1341A] his own body—not merely that body [Note: [Col. 1341] “that”: Basel edition.] which has become the temple of God, but also that of which it is said that the whole Church is the body of Christ. And he who defiles his own body [Note: [Col. 1341] “pollutes”: editions collectively.] seems to sin against the whole Church, because through one member defilement is spread over the whole body.

§ 1. There is also that reproach of Egypt which, if you neglect it, is suggested even after crossing the Jordan and after the second circumcision of baptism, by the ingrained mark of an old custom: observing auguries, investigating the courses of stars and seeking out from them the outcome of future events, *observing dreams*, and becoming entangled in other superstitions of this kind. [Note: [Col. 1341] “becoming entangled”: Nuremberg and Venice II editions.] For Egypt is the mother of idolatry, from which such reproaches are certainly known to spring.
