If, after you have *already* crossed the Jordan, you take them up [Col. 1341B] and bind yourself again in these snares, [Note: [Col. 1341] “tie yourself”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.] you undoubtedly carry with you the reproaches of Egypt.

Part III. Gratian. Yet these practices of casting lots are not to be detested to such an extent that, if anything from a threshing floor or winepress has been offered to demons, what remains should therefore be believed unclean; or that, if it happens that we unknowingly consume what was offered, we should therefore believe that we have sinned.

Hence Augustine, to Publicola, Epistle CLIV. [Note: [Col. 1341] Epistle 47, Maurist edition, written A.D. 397.—Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 11, c. 98.]

C. X. What remains is not unclean merely because something is taken from a threshing floor or winepress for sacrifices to demons.

If something is taken from a threshing floor or winepress [Note: [Col. 1341] “is taken”: Ivo; editions collectively.] for sacrifices to demons, a Christian who knows of it sins because [Note: [Col. 1341] Omitted in the original.] he permits it to be done, [Note: [Col. 1341] “if”: original; Ivo.] where he has the power to prevent it. [Col. 1341C] But if he does not discover that it has been done, [Note: [Col. 1341] “does not discover”: Basel edition.] or has no power to prevent it, [Note: [Col. 1341] “has had”: same edition.—“has”: other editions.] he uses the remaining fruits, which are clean, from which those things were taken.

C. XI. One who buys, without knowing it was offered to idols, is free from guilt. Likewise Ambrose, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, at c. 10. [Note: [Col. 1341] Ivo, *Decree*, pt. 11, c. 96.]

Although something is polluted incidentally, [Note: [Col. 1341] “by incidental things”: editions collectively.] that is, by an offering to an idol, nevertheless, when the buyer does not know *this*, he suffers no scruple and is guiltless before God.

# QUESTIONS III AND IV

[Col. 1342A]

GRATIAN.

But from whom the practice of divination took its origin, and how many kinds of it there are, Augustine [Note: [Col. 1341] Rather, Rabanus, *On the Deceptions of Magicians*, who in almost every respect followed in the footsteps of Isidore, *Etymologies*, bk. 8, c. 9.—Burchard, bk. 10, c. 43. Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, c. 66; *Decree*, pt. 11, c. 68.] explains in the book *On the Nature of Demons*, saying as follows:

C. I. On the manifold kinds of divination.

Thus the kind of divination is said to have been brought from the Persians. [Note: [Col. 1341C] *Persians*: Augustine, in Book VI, chapter 35, of *The City of God*, speaking of hydromancy, writes thus: “Varro says that this kind of divination [Col. 1341D] was brought from the Persians.” The remainder of this [Col. 1342C] chapter occurs in Rabanus’s little book *On the Deceptions of Magicians*, which he himself [Col. 1342D] compiled from various passages of Augustine and Isidore, and which Gratian often cites under Augustine’s name.] [Note: [Col. 1341] “to have been invented or brought”: Basel edition.—“to have been brought”: the remaining editions.]

§ 1. Varro, however, says that there are four kinds of divination: earth, water, air, and fire; hence he judges that they are called geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy, and pyromancy. [Note: [Col. 1341] “divinations”: collected editions.—“called”: Lyons III edition.—“called,” singular: original.—Burchard, Ivo, and collected editions preceding Lyons II and Paris.—“they judge”: collected editions and Ivo Panormia.]

§ 2. *Divini* [diviners] are so called as though filled with a god. For they pretend to be full of divinity, and by a certain crafty fraud predict future things to people. [Note: [Col. 1341] “by craftiness—and fraud”: Ivo Panormia and Basel edition.—“crafty—fraud”: collected editions.—Burchard and Ivo.] There are, moreover, two kinds of divination: art and frenzy. Incantators are so called because they perform their art by words. [Note: [Col. 1341] “said”: original, cited collections, and collected editions.]

§ 3. *Arioli* are so called because they utter wicked prayers around the altars of idols, offer deadly sacrifices, and receive the demons’ responses at these observances. [Note: [Col. 1341] “on account of”: original and Ivo.—Absent from the Basel edition.]

§ 4. *Haruspices* are named as though “inspectors of hours”; for they watch days and hours in undertaking business and works, and attend to what a person ought to observe at each particular time. [Note: [Col. 1341] “what people ought”: Basel edition.] They also inspect the entrails of cattle and foretell future events from them.

§ 5. Augurs are those who attend to the flights and cries of birds, and report other signs of things or unexpected observations that meet people. They are also auspices; for auspices are the signs observed by persons setting out on a journey. [Note: [Col. 1341] “There are also”: original.—“Likewise”: Ivo Panormia.—“The same also”: Burchard.—Collected editions before Lyons II, III, and Paris.—The added “and”: Burchard and collected editions.] *Auspicia* are so called as though *avium spicia*, “the observing of birds”; and *auguria* as though *avium garria*, that is, the cries and tongues of birds. [Note: [Col. 1341] “aspicia”: original, Burchard, Ivo Decretum.—The words “auguries—augur” are absent from the Argentinian edition.—The phrase *id est avium* (“that is, of birds”) is absent from the Basel edition.] Again, *augurium* is as though *avigerium*, “that which birds bear.” There are two kinds of auspices: one pertaining to the eyes, the other to the ears—flight, namely, to the eyes, and the cry of birds to the ears.

§ 6. *Pythons* [pythonesses] are so called from Pythian Apollo, because he was the originator of divination. [Note: [Col. 1341] “Pythonesses”: Burchard, Ivo, Lyons II and III editions.—Other editions have either *Phitonissae/Phitonio* or *Phytonissae/Phytonio*; *Phiton* in the Argentinian edition.—“are”: collected editions.] Astrologers are so called because they augur from the stars. *Genethliaci* are named from their consideration of birthday days. For they describe people’s births through the twelve signs of heaven, [Col. 1343A] and by the course of the stars attempt to predict the character, actions, and events of those being born: that is, under what sign a person was born, or what condition of life the person being born will have. [Note: [Col. 1343] “course”: Burchard, Ivo, and collected editions before Lyons II and III.—“at such a time”: Ivo Panormia.—“they interpret”: Burchard, Ivo, and collected editions.] These are those popularly called mathematicians [astrologers], whose superstitious practice the Latins call *constellationes*, that is, notations of the stars—how they stand when anyone is born. [Note: [Col. 1343] “in Latin”: Basel edition.]

§ 7. At first, however, these same interpreters of the stars were called magi, as is read of those in the Gospel who announced Christ’s birth. [Note: [Col. 1343] “that is”: Ivo and collected editions.—Matthew 2.] Afterwards only mathematicians [astrologers] were called by this name. Knowledge of this art was permitted until the Gospel, so that, once Christ had appeared, no one thereafter might interpret anyone’s nativity from heaven. [Note: [Col. 1343] “Christ”: collected editions.—“may interpret”: those editions and cited collections.] Horoscopists are so called because they observe the hours of human births, with their unlike and diverse fate. [Note: [Col. 1343] “Horospici”: Basel edition.] Sortilegists are those who, under the name, etc. [Note: [Col. 1343] Above, Question I, sole chapter.] As above:

§ 8. *Salitores* are so called because, whenever any parts of their limbs twitch, they predict that something prosperous or sad is thereby signified to them. [Note: [Col. 1343] *Salisatores*: original, Isidore, and cited collections.—“who”: collected editions.]

## Part II. Gratian

The question is raised concerning the nature of demons: of what nature they are, whether they can know future things beforehand, and in how many ways they foreknow them.

Augustine writes concerning these matters as follows in the same book *On the Divination of Demons*, chapter 3. [Note: [Col. 1343] Rather, Rabanus, Book I, who made his own what Augustine wrote in the book *On the Divination of Demons*.—Burchard, Book X, chapters 45–46; Ivo Panormia, Book VIII, chapter 68, through § 1; Decretum, Part XI, chapters 70–71.]

### C. II. In how many ways demons foreknow future events

It must be understood that the nature of demons is such that, through the perception of their airy body, they easily surpass the perception of earthly bodies; and that, through speed, because of the higher mobility of that same airy body, [Col. 1343C] they incomparably exceed not only the running of any people or beasts, but even the flight of birds. [Note: [Col. 1343] “of things”: Ivo Panormia and collected editions.] Furnished with these two things, so far as an airy body is concerned—namely, keenness of perception and swiftness of movement—they announce beforehand things known much earlier, or report things at which people marvel because of the slowness of earthly perception. [Note: [Col. 1343] “acuteness”: there.—“things thought”: collected editions before Lyons II and III.—“things known and announced beforehand, which”: Nuremberg and Venice I–II editions.—“things announced beforehand, which”: the remaining editions except Argentinian.]

The demons have also acquired, through the very long period to which their life extends, a far greater experience of things than can come to human beings because of the brevity of life. By these capacities which the nature of an airy body has received, demons not only predict many future things, [Note: [Col. 1343] “to people”: Basel edition.] but also perform many remarkable things. Since people cannot say and do such things, some judge demons worthy of being served and of receiving divine honors, [Col. 1344A] especially at the prompting of the vice of curiosity, out of love for false and earthly happiness and temporal eminence. [Note: [Col. 1343] “investigating”: Basel edition.]

And below, chapter 5:

§ 1. Now therefore, since the question concerns the divination of demons, it must first be understood that they most often predict things which they themselves will do. [Note: [Col. 1343] “very often”: Argentinian edition.] For they frequently receive power both to inflict diseases and, by corrupting the very air, to make it unhealthy; and to urge evil deeds upon perverse persons and lovers of earthly advantages, whose dispositions they know, knowing that they will consent to such suggestions. They suggest these things by wondrous and invisible means, penetrating the bodies of people who do not perceive it through the subtlety of their bodies, and mingling themselves with their thoughts [Col. 1344B] through certain imaginary visions, whether of persons awake or asleep. [Note: [Col. 1343] The words “and” are absent from the Basel edition.—“For they suggest”: remaining editions and Ivo.—“to them”: collected editions before Argentinian and Basel.]

§ 2. Sometimes, however, they predict beforehand not things which they themselves do, but things which they foreknow will occur through natural signs—signs which cannot come within human perception. For a physician is not to be regarded as divine merely because he foresees what one ignorant of his art does not foresee. [Note: [Col. 1343] “does not know how to foresee”: original, Burchard, Ivo, and collected editions.—“his”: original, cited collections, and collected editions before Lyons II and III.—“nevertheless”: those editions.]

What wonder, then, if, as the physician foresees future health or illness from the disturbed or modified constitution of the human body, so a demon foresees future storms from a condition of the air known to it but unknown to us? [Note: [Col. 1343] “or disturbed”: original, cited collections, Basel, Lyons II and III.—“mortified”: collected editions.—“or”: Nuremberg and Venice I–II editions.—The collected editions read: “demons foresee future storms from conditions of the air known to them, unknown to us.”]

Sometimes they also learn, with complete ease, human dispositions not only uttered in speech but conceived in thought, when certain signs from the mind are expressed in the body; and from this they likewise announce many future things beforehand—marvelous, of course, to others who do not know these dispositions. [Col. 1344C]

And below, chapter 6:

§ 3. They deceive both from a zeal for deceiving and from an envious will, by which they delight in human error. [Note: [Col. 1343] “envy”: Basel edition.] But lest they lose the weight of their authority among their worshippers, they arrange that blame should be assigned to their interpreters and conjecturers of their signs whenever these have either been deceived or have lied. [Note: [Col. 1343] “they themselves wicked”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.—“they themselves”: remaining editions.]

§ 4. At times the malignant spirits themselves—the deceivers of human beings and assailants of their salvation—are accustomed to predict the decline of their worship and the ruin of idols, so that they may seem to know beforehand what will happen in particular kingdoms or places and what adversity may befall their faction. [Note: [Col. 1343] “observers”: original and cited collections.] Those who read the histories of the Gentiles are not ignorant of this either. What wonder, therefore, if, when the overthrow of temples and images was already imminent—a thing which the prophets of the most high God had predicted so long beforehand—the demon Serapis disclosed this shortly beforehand to one of his worshippers, that in departing or fleeing he might commend his supposed divinity? [Col. 1345A] [Note: [Col. 1345] “divination”: collected editions.]

## Part III. Gratian

That the devil apprehends human dispositions conceived in thought through outward signs does not seem to be established by firm reasoning.

[Col. 1345B] Therefore the same Augustine says in Book II of the *Retractations*, chapter 30: [Note: [Col. 1345] Compare the chapter immediately above.]

### C. III. That the devil’s apprehension of the inward thoughts of the mind from bodily movements is a most hidden matter

In one place I said that demons sometimes learn, with complete ease, human dispositions not only uttered in speech but conceived in thought, when certain signs from the mind are expressed in the body. I spoke of a most hidden matter with a bolder assertion than I ought. [Note: [Col. 1345] “assertion”: collected editions.] For it has been discovered from certain experiences that such matters come to the demons’ knowledge. But whether certain signs are given from the bodies of thinkers, perceptible to demons but hidden from us, or whether they know these things by another force, and a spiritual one, is either most difficult for human beings to discover or cannot be discovered at all. [Note: [Col. 1345] “special”: Argentinian edition.]

# QUESTION V

[Col. 1345C]

## GRATIAN

### Part I

By reason and authority it is proved that sortilegists and diviners, if they refuse to cease, must be excommunicated. For there is a certain kind of idolatrous worship: predicting future things by consulting demons. Just as the avaricious person, because he bestows upon money the worship due to God, is called by the Apostle an idolater, [Note: [Col. 1345] Ephesians 5.] so those who labor to discover future things—which are sometimes found revealed by God’s oracle—whether by consulting demons or by any deceptions whatever, attribute the prerogatives of divinity to creatures. [Note: [Col. 1345] Colossians 3.] For foreknowing future things belongs to God alone, who also enables angels to foreknow them in the contemplation of himself. Thus Isaiah says: “Declare to me the former things and the last things, and I shall say that you are gods.” [Col. 1346A] [Note: [Col. 1345] Isaiah 45:21.]

§ 1. Worshippers of idols, moreover, are to be separated from the communion of the faithful. Thus the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “If anyone called a brother is a fornicator, or avaricious, or serving idols, do not even take food with such a person.” [Note: [Col. 1345] 1 Corinthians 5:11.] Hence one also reads in the decrees of Gregory the Younger, presiding at the Roman Council, chapter 12: [Note: [Col. 1345] Held in 721.—Regino, Book II, chapter 349; Burchard, Book X, chapter 23; Anselm, Book X, chapter 50; Ivo Panormia, Book VIII, chapter 61; Decretum, Part XI, chapter 1; Polycarpus, Book VI, title 12.]

### C. I. Let one who observes diviners or incantators be anathema

If anyone observes diviners, haruspices, or incantators, or uses their phylacteries, let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 1345] “their”: collected editions before Argentinian.]

[Col. 1346B]

### C. II. Let one who seeks divinations do penance for five years

Likewise, from the Council of Ancyra, chapter 23, or 24. [Note: [Col. 1345] Held in 314.—Dionysian translation.—Regino, Book II, chapter 347; Burchard, Book X, chapter 3; Ivo Panormia, Book VIII, chapter 62; Decretum, Part XI, chapter 2; Polycarpus, same place.]

Those who seek divinations and follow the custom of the Gentiles, [Note: [Col. 1345C] *Gentiles*: The printed Greek has χρόνων, “times,” but the old Vatican manuscript and Balsamon have ἐθνῶν, “nations/Gentiles.”] or introduce persons of this kind into their homes in order to discover something by an evil art, or for the sake of expiation, shall lie under the rule of five years, according to the defined stages of penance, etc. [Note: [Col. 1345] “nations”: Basel edition.—[Col. 1346C] *Exquirendi*: The Greek is ἐπὶ ἀνευρέσει φαρμακειῶν, that is, “for finding medicines.”—“magical”: collected editions and Ivo.]

### C. III. Christians may not worship the elements or observe the courses of the moon or stars in their activities

Likewise, from the Council of Pope Martin—that is, from the Capitula of Martin of Braga—chapter 72. [Note: [Col. 1345] Chapters 72, 74, 71, and 75, *Capitula Martini Bracarensis*; Regino, Book II, chapters 348 and 366–68; Burchard, Book X, chapters 13, 20, 6, and 19; Ivo Decretum, Part XI, chapters 40, 47, 34, and 46, and Part VIII, chapter 330.]

Christians must not retain the traditions of the Gentiles or observe or worship the elements, or the courses of the moon or stars, or the empty deception of signs for building a house, sowing crops, planting trees, or contracting marriages. [Note: [Col. 1345] “course”: Spanish Collection and cited collections.] For it is written: “Whatever you do, in word or deed, do all in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God.” [Col. 1346C] [Note: [Col. 1345] Colossians 3:17.]

§ 1. In gathering medicinal herbs, no observances or incantations may be heeded, except only the divine Creed or the Lord’s Prayer, so that God alone, Creator and Lord of all, may be honored. [Note: [Col. 1345] “gathering”: Spanish Collection and cited collections.—“medicinal”: cited collections.—“and”: those editions.]

§ 2. But if anyone, following pagan custom, introduces diviners or sortilegists into his house, as though to drive evil out, discover magical practices, or perform pagan lustrations, let them do penance for five years. [Note: [Col. 1345] Absent from those editions and the Spanish Collection.—“his house”: Spanish Collection.—“do penance”: Burchard and Ivo.—“let him”: Spanish Collection.]

§ 3. Christian women likewise may not observe vanity in their wool-working; rather, they should invoke God as their helper, who gave them the wisdom of weaving. [Col. 1347A] [Note: [Col. 1345] Absent from the same source.—“stretching out”: Nuremberg and Venice I–II editions.—“has given the wisdom of weaving”: collected editions before Basel.]

### C. IV. Persons devoted to sacred offices must not become magicians or incantators

Likewise, from the Council of Laodicea, chapter 36. [Note: [Col. 1347] Held between 347 and 381.—Dionysian translation.—Ivo Panormia, Book VIII, chapter 63; Decretum, Part XI, chapter 3.]

Those devoted to sacred offices, or clerics, ought not to be magicians or incantators, or to make phylacteries, which are proved to be bonds upon their souls. [Note: [Col. 1347] “or”: absent from Basel and Lyons II–III editions.—“are proved”: collected editions before Basel.] And we have ordered that those who use such things be cast out of the Church. [Note: [Col. 1347] “These”: collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 1347C] The preceding material in this chapter is from Dionysius’s translation; what follows is from the ancient translation, which is in Isidore’s collection [and is not in Ivo].]

### C. V. Let the bishop or presbyter who consults magicians or haruspices be deprived of honor

Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 28. [Note: [Col. 1347] Held in 633.—Burchard, Book X, chapter 48; Anselm, Book XI, chapter 130; Ivo Panormia, Book III, chapter 169, and Book VIII, chapter 64; Decretum, Part XI, chapters 5 and 73; Polycarpus, Book VI, title 12.]

If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone from the clerical order is found to have consulted magicians, haruspices, incantators, *arioli*, augurs, sortilegists, persons professing the magical art, or any persons practicing similar things, he shall be suspended from the honor of his dignity, undertake the care of a monastery, and there, devoted to perpetual penance, expiate the crime of sacrilege he has committed. [Note: [Col. 1347] “from the orders”: collected editions.—The words “magicians or” are absent from Ivo and Burchard.—“or incantators, or—augurs,” and the following “or—magicians,” are absent from Anselm.] [Note: [Col. 1347C] *Magical*: In older editions of the councils, in two Vatican manuscripts, in the royal Lucchese manuscript, and in Polycarpus, the reading is “some art.”] [Note: [Col. 1347] “to consult”: Spanish Collection.] [Note: [Col. 1347C] *Suspended*: All editions of the councils, the collated manuscripts, and Polycarpus read “deposed” [as do the same source, Burchard, Ivo Decretum, and Anselm; Panormia, Book III, reads “expelled”]. But it has not been changed because of the gloss.] [Note: [Col. 1347C–D] *Care*: Thus in the older editions of the councils and two Vatican manuscripts; but the later Cologne editions read “penalty,” while the royal manuscript reads “punishment” [as does the Spanish Collection; “penalty” in Ivo, chapter 75; Anselm and Burchard have “having entered a monastery, and there,” etc.].] [Note: [Col. 1347] “undertake”: Spanish Collection; Ivo Panormia, Book VIII; Decretum.—“of the sacrilege committed”: Anselm, Ivo Panormia, Book VIII, and Decretum.—“suffer”: Spanish Collection; Burchard, Anselm, Ivo Decretum, chapter 73.]

### C. VI. Concerning those who pursue auguries and divinations

Likewise, from the Council of Agde, chapter 42. [Note: [Col. 1347] Held in 506.—Burchard, Book X, chapter 27; Ivo Panormia, Book VIII, chapter 69; Decretum, Part XI, chapter 4.]

Some clerics and laypersons pursue auguries and, under the name of a fictitious religion, profess knowledge of divination through what they call “the lots of the saints,” or promise future events by inspecting writings of whatever kind. [Note: [Col. 1347] “fathers”: Ivo Panormia and collected editions.] Any cleric or layperson found either to consult or to teach such things shall be regarded as alien to the Church. [Note: [Col. 1347] “this”: Ivo.—“here”: Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice I–II editions.]

[Col. 1348A]

### C. VII. A lot is decreed to be nothing other than divination and evil magic

Likewise, Leo IV to the bishops of Britain, chapter 4. [Note: [Col. 1348C] In the letter of Leo IV, part of which survives in an old manuscript, chapter 4 reads: “Concerning the seeking of divinations or evil magical acts, we indeed have written in the sacred canons that we should set down the canon itself thus: ‘Those who seek divinations,’ etc., above in the same matter from the Council of Ancyra. Therefore, after the analogy of those things, we decree that the lots by which you decide everything in your disputed judgments are nothing other than the divinations and evil magic condemned by those Fathers,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 1347] Written in 850.—Ivo Panormia, Book VIII, chapter 70; Decretum, Part XI, chapter 8.]

We decree that the lots by which you decide all things in your disputed judgments—something condemned by the Fathers—are nothing other than divinations and evil magical practices. [Note: [Col. 1347] “provinces”: collected editions and Ivo.] Therefore we wish them to be entirely condemned; we no longer wish them to be named among Christians; and, under prohibition of anathema, we forbid their practice. [Note: [Col. 1347] “that they be cut off”: original, Ivo Decretum.—“that it be cut off”: Panormia.—“we command”: original.]

### C. VIII. Incantators and sortilegists must be pursued as enemies of Christ

Likewise, Gregory to Hadrian the Notary, Book IX, letter 47. [Note: [Col. 1347] Letter 53, written in 601, Book XI of the Maurist edition.—Collection of Three Parts, Part I, title 55, chapter 84; Burchard, Book X, chapter 4; Ivo Decretum, Part XI, chapter 33.]

It has come to us that you have pursued certain incantators and [Col. 1348B] sortilegists; know that your concern and zeal have been wholly pleasing to us. [Note: [Col. 1347] “have been”: Basel edition.] And below: “And therefore let it be your concern diligently to seek out, and, whenever you find any enemies of Christ of this sort, correct them with severe punishment.” [Note: [Col. 1347] “for”: collected editions.]

### C. IX. Let a cleric, monk, or layperson who follows divinations, auguries, or lots be excommunicated

Likewise, from the First Council of Orléans, chapter 32. [Note: [Col. 1347] Held in 511.]

If any cleric, monk, or secular person believes that divination or auguries are to be observed, or communicates to anyone whatever lots which they falsely claim are those of the saints, let him, together with those who have believed them, be expelled from the communion of the Church. [Note: [Col. 1347] “or monk”: Basel edition.—“regular”: Argentinian edition.—Absent from the Spanish Collection.—“with them”: Paris and Lyons editions.]

[Col. 1348C]

### C. X. Let pastoral vigilance keep watch against sortilegists and idolaters

Likewise, Gregory, Book VII, letter 66, to Januarius, bishop. [Note: [Col. 1348C–D] This chapter has been enlarged from Gregory’s letter by comparison with old exemplars.] [Note: [Col. 1347] Letter 65, written in 599, Book IX of the Maurist edition.—Burchard, Book X, chapter 13; Anselm, Book XI, chapter 132, where nearly everything appears as in Gratian before correction; Ivo Decretum, Part XI, chapters 32 and 85.]

We exhort your fraternity to keep far more vigilant pastoral watch against worshippers of idols, haruspices, and [Col. 1349A] sortilegists; publicly address the people against persons of this kind, and by persuasive exhortation call them back from the stain of so great a sacrilege, from the threat of divine judgment, and from the danger of the present life. [Note: [Col. 1347] “haruspices and sortilegists”: Burchard and Ivo, chapter 32.—“your”: Burchard, Ivo, and collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 1349] “threat”: Maurist edition.]

If, nevertheless, you find that they are unwilling to amend and correct themselves from such practices, we wish you to apprehend them with fervent zeal. If they are slaves, punish them with beatings and tortures by which they may be able to attain amendment; but if they are free, they are to be subjected to a fitting and severe confinement in penance, so that those who despise to hear words bringing salvation and recalling them from the danger of death may at least be restored by bodily torture to the desired health of mind. [Note: [Col. 1349] “we wish them to be punished”: Anselm and collected editions.—“worthy”: there.—“severe punishment”: collected editions.—“severe penance”: Anselm.—“in penance”: Ivo, chapter 32; Burchard and Ivo, chapter 95.—“to direct”: original, Anselm, Burchard, and collected editions.—“to constrain”: Ivo, chapter 32.—“to bind”: the same, chapter 95.]

[Col. 1349B]

### C. XI. Let one devoted to auguries and incantations be separated from the Church

Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 89. [Note: [Col. 1349] Chapter 83, *Ancient Ecclesiastical Statutes*; compare chapter 9, Distinction 18.—Burchard, Book X, chapter 7; Ivo Panormia, Book VIII, chapter 72; Decretum, Part XI, chapter 35.]

We command that one devoted to auguries or incantations, and likewise one adhering to Jewish superstitions or festivals, be separated from the assembly of the Church. [Note: [Col. 1349] “devoted”: Basel edition.—“we command” is absent from the original and Burchard.—“we decree”: Ivo Decretum.]

### C. XII. Let bishops strive by every means to eliminate sortilegious and magical art

Likewise, from the Council of Anquira, chapter 1. [Note: [Col. 1349C] *Anquira*: Thus also in the old copies. Burchard and Ivo have “Ancyran.” Nevertheless, it is not found in the Greek or Latin Council of Ancyra, whether printed or manuscript, though the editors of the council volumes assert that it occurs in a certain old manuscript of sixteen partial books.] [Note: [Col. 1349] It seems to have been taken from an unpublished capitulary of the Frankish kings.—It is brought forward by Regino, Book II, chapter 364, under the heading “from above”; deceived by this, Burchard, Book X, chapter 1; Ivo Decretum, Part XI, chapter 30; and Panormia, Book VIII, chapter 75, thought the Council of Ancyra—the chapter of which precedes it in Regino—to be its source.]

Let bishops and their ministers strive by every means to root utterly out of their parishes the pernicious sortilegious and magical art invented by the devil; and if they find any man or woman practicing such wickedness, let them shamefully dishonor the person and expel him or her from their parishes. [Note: [Col. 1349] “with all their strength”: cited collections and collected editions.—“Zabulus”: Ivo Panormia and collected editions.—“evil magical”: cited collections.—“erase”: Regino.—“find”: collected editions.]

For the Apostle says: “Avoid a heretical person after a first and second correction, knowing that one who is such has been subverted.” [Note: [Col. 1349] Titus 3:10.—“one”: Regino, Burchard, Ivo Decretum.—“admonition”: the same sources.—“correction”: Ivo Panormia and collected editions.] Those who, abandoning their Creator, seek the devil’s assistance are subverted and held captive by the devil; therefore the holy Church must be cleansed of such a plague. [Col. 1350A]

§ 1. Nor should this be omitted: certain wicked women, turned back after Satan and deceived by demonic illusions and phantasms, believe and profess that in the hours of night they ride upon certain beasts with Diana, goddess of the pagans, or with Herodias, and an innumerable multitude of women; that in the silence of the dead of night they traverse great expanses of lands; that they obey her commands as those of a mistress; and that on fixed nights they are summoned to her service. [Note: [Col. 1349D] *Wicked*: Almost the same words occur in the work attributed to Blessed Augustine, *On Spirit and Soul*, chapter 28, and in the Life of Pope Damasus I, preserved at Rome in a very ancient manuscript of lives of saints belonging to St Mary Major. After certain matters are reported from the Roman synod in which Damasus condemned Macedonius and Apollinaris, it is added that persons devoted to evil magical practices, superstitions, and incantations were anathematized in that synod. These women are also mentioned, who supposed that in the silence of the night they rode upon beasts with [Col. 1350C–D] Herodias and an innumerable multitude of women, traversing many stretches of land.]

But would that these alone had perished in their perfidy and had not dragged many with them into the destruction of unbelief. For an innumerable multitude, deceived by this false opinion, believe these things to be true; and by believing they stray from the right faith and are entangled in pagan error, since they suppose that there is some divinity or divine power besides the one God. [Note: [Col. 1349] “and innumerable”: collected editions.]

Therefore priests ought, throughout the churches committed to them, to preach to the people of God with every urgency that they may know these things to be wholly false, and that such phantasms are inflicted upon the minds of the faithful not by a divine but by a malignant spirit. [Col. 1350B] [Note: [Col. 1349] “in every way”: Regino, Burchard, Ivo Decretum.—“unfaithful”: Regino, Burchard, Ivo Panormia.—“upon unbelievers”: Argentinian edition.—“they may suppose”: Nuremberg and Lyons II–III editions.—“we suppose”: remaining editions.]

§ 2. For Satan himself, who transforms himself into an angel of light, when he has seized the mind of any little woman and brought her into subjection to himself through unbelief, immediately transforms himself into the forms and likenesses of diverse persons. Deluding the mind that he holds captive in dreams, he shows it now joyful things, now sad things, now persons known, now unknown; he leads it through every byway; and, although the spirit alone undergoes this, [Col. 1350C] the unbelieving mind supposes that it occurs not in the mind but in the body. [Note: [Col. 1349] “woman”: collected editions.—“dreams”: Böhm.]

For who is not carried outside himself in dreams and nocturnal visions, and while asleep sees many things he had never seen while awake? [Note: [Col. 1349] “outside himself”: cited collections and collected editions.—“led out”: Venice I–II, Paris, and Lyons editions.] But who could be so foolish and dull as to suppose that all these things, [Col. 1351A] which occur in the spirit alone, happen also in the body? Ezekiel the prophet saw the visions of the Lord in the spirit, not in the body; and John the apostle saw and heard the mystery of the Apocalypse in the spirit, not in the body, as he himself says: “Immediately,” he says, “I was in the spirit.” [Note: [Col. 1351] Revelation 4:2.] And Paul does not dare to say that he was caught up in the body. [Note: [Col. 1351] 2 Corinthians 12.]

Therefore it must be publicly proclaimed to all that whoever believes such things and things like them has lost the faith; [Note: [Col. 1351] “loses”: Burchard, Ivo, and collected editions.] and whoever does not have the right faith in the Lord belongs not to him, but to the one in whom he believes, namely the devil. For it is written of our Lord: “All things were made through him,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1351] John 1:3.] Whoever, therefore, believes that anything can be done, or that any creature can be changed for better or worse, or transformed into another form or likeness, [Col. 1351B] except by the Creator himself, who made all things and through whom all things were made, is without doubt an unbeliever and worse than a pagan. [Note: [Col. 1351] “or into”: collected editions.—The words “and worse than a pagan” are absent from Regino.]

## Part II. Gratian

Some persons are found who, moved by inward malice to destroy their enemies, strip altars of their sacred vestments, clothe them with mourning garments, withdraw from the churches of God the customary services of lights, or celebrate for living persons the Mass appointed for the repose of the dead.

The Thirteenth Council of Toledo condemns all such most wicked magical practices, saying in chapter 7: [Note: [Col. 1351D] The beginning of this chapter through the word *Plerique* (“Very many”) is from the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, chapter 7. The rest is from the Seventeenth Council of Toledo, chapter 5. Two copies of these councils were obtained from Spain, and certain things were corrected and added here from them.] [Note: [Col. 1351] Held in 683.]

### C. XIII. Let the priest who has applied himself to practices of this kind be cast out

Any priest or minister who henceforth, moved by any grief or bitterness, [Col. 1351C] presumes either to strip the divine altar of its sacred vestments, clothe it with any other mourning garment, withdraw the customary service of sacred lights from the temple of God, or order them extinguished, shall know that, unless satisfaction through true repentance before the metropolitan has previously purified him, he is subjected to perpetual ignominy and deprived of the dignity and honor of his office in accordance with the preceding sentence of the lord. [Note: [Col. 1351] “consecrated”: Spanish Collection.—Absent from Böhm.—“or”: Spanish Collection; Basel edition.—“has purified”: Basel edition.—“and office”: Spanish Collection.]

Those persons, however, are plainly excepted from this sentence of punishments who have happened to do such things through fear of defilement of sacred orders, overthrow of the holy faith, hostile attack or siege, or the sentence of divine judgments; for in their act humility, by which God is appeased, is shown more than the guile of inward malice. [Col. 1352A] [Note: [Col. 1351] “these”: Lyons II–III editions; absent from the rest.—“may be appeased”: Spanish Collection.—“toil”: the same.]

§ 1. Very many priests also, wounded by the treachery of enmity, endeavor through a deceitful vow to celebrate for living persons the Mass appointed for the repose of the dead, for no other reason than that the person for whom that sacrifice is offered might, through the intervention of that most holy oblation, incur the danger of death and perdition. [Note: [Col. 1351] Chapter 5 of the Seventeenth Council of Toledo, reduced to a compendium.—“the very thing”: Spanish Collection.—“and perdition”: the same.]

Accordingly, the assembly of our unanimity has decided that, if any priest henceforth is discovered to have perpetrated such acts, he shall be deposed from the rank of his own order; and both that priest and the person found to have incited him to carry out such acts shall be confined in the prison of perpetual exile. [Note: [Col. 1351] “Accordingly”: Spanish Collection.—“priest”: the same.—“confined”: the same.—“shall be banished”: collected editions.]

[Col. 1352B] **Part III. Gratian.** From the foregoing authorities it is inferred that diviners, haruspices, enchanters, and casters of lots, together with other followers of this kind, are to be expelled from the Church and, unless they repent, perpetually excommunicated. § 1. But whereas in the final chapter of the Council of Ancyra [Note: [Col. 1351] cf. above, c. 12.] things done through enchanters are said to be done not in the body but in the spirit, Augustine seems to maintain in his book *On the City of God* that they are thus done, saying as follows [Note: [Col. 1352D] This whole chapter is contained in Rabanus’s little book *On the Deceptions of Magicians*, which he himself compiled, as was stated above, from various passages of Augustine and Isidore. Burchard cites it from the sayings of Augustine.] [Note: [Col. 1351] Rather, Rabanus, book *On the Deceptions of Magicians*.—Burchard, bk. 10, cc. 42, 44. Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 8, cc. 65, 67. *Decretum*, part 11, cc. 67, 69.]:

### C. XIV. Things done by the deceptions of magicians are shown not to be real, but phantasmal.

Nor is it surprising concerning the deceptions of magicians, whose arts of wickedness have advanced so far that they even opposed Moses with signs very like his own [Note: [Col. 1351] “among them”: Ivo.—editions collectively], turning rods into [Col. 1352C] dragons and [Note: [Col. 1351] absent from the original, the cited collections, and the earlier collective editions, Lyons II and III.] water [Note: [Col. 1351] “waters”: editions collectively] into blood [Note: [Col. 1351] added: “are said”: the same editions, except Basel, Lyons II and III.]. It is also reported [Note: [Col. 1351] “Since it is reported”: Burchard.—“It is read”: editions collectively, except Basel.] in pagan books that a certain exceedingly famous sorceress, Circe, changed Ulysses’ companions into beasts. We also read concerning the sacrifice [Note: [Col. 1351] “sacrifices”: Basel edition] which the Arcadians offered to their god Lycaeus [Note: [Col. 1351] “Lieus”: Ivo, *Panormia*—Argentine, Nuremberg, Venice I and II editions.—“Lego”: Basel edition], that whoever partook of it was changed into the forms of beasts [Note: [Col. 1351] “would be changed”: cited collections and editions collectively]. But all these things were feigned by magical deceptions rather than accomplished in the truth of things.

Therefore, in order that these errors may become evident to those who are ignorant, we judge it fitting first to speak, according to the tradition of the elders, of their character and inventors.

§ 1. Magicians are those who are commonly called *malefici* (“evil-doers”) because of the magnitude of their crimes. These [Note: [Col. 1351] “Those are they who”: Lyons II and III.—“These are they who”: the remaining editions], by God’s permission, shake the elements, disturb the minds of persons less trusting in God, and, without any drinking of poison, kill by the force of a spell alone [Col. 1353A] [Note: [Col. 1353] added: “men”: Basel edition]. Hence Lucan [Note: [Col. 1353] “and Lucan”: ibid.—original and cited collections]:

> “The mind, polluted by no corruption of drunk poison, perishes when enchanted.”  
> [Note: [Col. 1353] “perishes when disenchanted”: cf. Lucan, *Pharsalia*, bk. 6, vv. 457–458.]

For, having summoned demons, they dare to exert themselves so that each may destroy [Note: [Col. 1353] “may destroy”: original—Ivo, *Decretum*; “whoever”: Burchard; “all whom”: Basel; “whomever”: remaining editions—Ivo, *Panormia*.] his enemies by evil arts. They also use blood and victims, and often touch the bodies of the dead.

§ 2. Necromancers are those through whose incantations the dead appear to be raised, to foretell the future, and to answer questions. For νεκρός (*nekros*) in Greek is called “dead” [Note: [Col. 1353] “nigro”: Ivo, *Panormia*—Argentine and Basel editions; “nigron”: remaining editions, except Lyons II and III.], and μαντεία (*manteia*) “divination” [Note: [Col. 1353] “mantio”: Argentine, Basel, Nuremberg, and Venice I editions; “mansio”: Venice II edition]. In raising such persons, blood is added to the corpse. For demons are said to love blood; and therefore, whenever necromancy is performed, gore is mixed with water so that they may be more easily summoned by the color of blood [Col. 1353B] [Note: [Col. 1353] “and … are summoned”: original—Burchard—Basel edition].

§ 3. Hydromancers are so called from water. Hydromancy consists in calling forth the shadows of demons by looking into water [Note: [Col. 1353] “waters”: Ivo, *Panormia*—editions collectively], seeing their illusory images [Note: [Col. 1353] “images of deception”: cited collections—Basel edition; “deceiving images”: original], and hearing something there from them; and by the use of blood they are said even to raise the dead below. [Note: [Col. 1353D] “Raise”: In Rabanus, the chapter “It Is Read,” above, the same question, cc. 3 and 4, is inserted here.]

And below:

§ 4. To all these aforesaid practices belong bindings used as accursed remedies, which the art of physicians condemns [Note: [Col. 1353] “commends”: Ivo, *Decretum*; “does not commend”: Burchard, Ivo, *Panormia*, and editions collectively], whether in incantations or in characters, or in suspending and binding any objects whatsoever [Note: [Col. 1353] “whatever objects”: Böhm], in all of which is the art of demons, arising from a certain pestilential association of human beings and evil angels [Note: [Col. 1353] “arisen”: Argentine edition]. Accordingly, all these things [Note: [Col. 1353] added: “and”: Ivo, *Panormia*—Basel edition; “these”: remaining editions] must be avoided by the Christian, and altogether rejected and condemned with every execration.

§ 5. The Phrygians first invented auguries from birds [Col. 1353C] [Note: [Col. 1353] “But auguries are from birds. These, however, …”: cited collections and editions collectively; absent from Basel edition.].

§ 6. Mercury is said to have first invented prestidigitation [Note: [Col. 1353] “earlier”: Basel edition; “first”: Venice I and II editions]. It is called *praestigium* because it binds or dazzles the sight of the eyes.

§ 7. A certain Tages is said to have first handed down the art of haruspicy [Note: [Col. 1353] “of haruspicy”: Ivo, *Panormia*; “haruspicy”: original—Ivo, *Decretum*—editions collectively] to the Etruscans. He dictated haruspicy from the hours [Note: [Col. 1353] “lifeless”: Ivo, *Panormia*—editions collectively, except Lyons II and III], and afterward appeared no more. For it is fabulously said that, while a certain countryman was ploughing, he suddenly sprang out of the clods of earth and dictated haruspicy; and on that very day he died. The Romans translated these books from the Etruscan language into their own.

§ 8. By such prodigies human curiosity is mocked through the deceit of demons [Col. 1354A], when people shamelessly seek to know [Note: [Col. 1353] “seeks”: Basel edition] what it is in no way fitting for them to investigate. This power is given to unclean spirits so that, through vessels suited to themselves—that is, wicked persons—they may seduce those [Note: [Col. 1353] “that through the perverse they may ensnare for themselves”: Ivo, *Panormia*; variant defective readings in Basel and other editions.] [Note: [Col. 1353] added: “namely”: editions collectively, except Basel] who despise truth and believe a lie; and who, according to Paul’s statement, will not endure sound teaching [Note: [Col. 1353] “will bear”: editions collectively, except Lyons II and III; cf. 2 Tim. 4:3–4; 2:7], but according to their own desires will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears; they will turn their hearing indeed away from truth and turn aside to fables; laden with sins, they will be led away by various desires, always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of truth [Note: [Col. 1353] “the truth of knowledge”: editions collectively].

But as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth: people corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning [Col. 1354B] the faith. Yet they shall not advance farther, for their folly will be manifest to all, as theirs also was.

§ 9. Nor should anyone therefore believe that any persons can accomplish anything through magical arts without God’s permission—for he either does by just judgment all things that are done, or permits them to be done thus by his permission—because the aforesaid magicians are read to have done things resembling those of Moses, who threw down his rod and it was changed into a dragon; and they themselves [Note: [Col. 1353] absent from Ivo, *Panormia*.] threw down their several [Note: [Col. 1353] “each”: original—cited collections—editions collectively; cf. Exod. 7.] rods, which were changed into dragons, but Aaron’s rod devoured their rods [Note: [Col. 1353] “Moses’”: Basel edition].

For neither the magicians nor the evil angels, by whose agency they performed those things, were creators of serpents. There are in bodily things, throughout all the elements of the world, certain hidden seminal principles; when a temporal and causal opportunity has been given to these [Col. 1354C], they emerge into their due forms according to their own modes and limits. Yet the angels who do this are not called creators of animals, any more than farmers ought to be called creators of crops or trees, or of anything whatever growing in the earth, although they know how to provide certain visible opportunities and causes for such things to come into being. What these persons do visibly, those others do invisibly. But God alone is the one Creator, who implanted in things the causes themselves and the seminal principles.

§ 10. Furthermore [Col. 1355A], some think the question ought to be asked how Scripture relates [Note: [Col. 1355] “relates”: Böhm] that the Pythoness [Note: [Col. 1355] In the *Panormia* and the Argentine, Nuremberg, Basel, Paris, and Lyons I editions, both here and below, it is “Phitoness”; in Venice I and II, “Phytoness.”] raised up Samuel the prophet for a conversation with Saul, that most impious king, if Pythonic divination is to be reckoned among the errors of magical art.

The following reply may be given to those who ask this: it would be an utterly unworthy deed if assent were granted according to the words of the narrative [Note: [Col. 1355] “commended”: Ivo, *Panormia*.]. For how could it happen that a man holy by birth [Note: [Col. 1355] “from birth”: editions collectively] and righteous in the works of his life should be drawn by magical art—or, if he was not drawn, should consent [Note: [Col. 1355] “grant”: Argentine and Venice I–II editions]? Either belief is contrary to what is to be believed of a righteous man.

For if he was brought forth unwillingly, righteousness has no efficacy; but if voluntarily, he lost the spiritual merit which, while placed in the flesh, he had sought. This is wholly absurd, since one who departs from here righteous remains righteous. [Note: [Col. 1355] Added “for”: editions collectively; the words from “For if” through “But this” do not occur in Burchard or Ivo, *Panormia*.] But this [Col. 1355B] is Satan’s deception [Note: [Col. 1355] “defense”: Argentine edition], by which, in order to deceive very many, he feigns that even good persons are in his power. The Apostle shows this among other things, saying [Note: [Col. 1355] 2 Cor. 11:14.]: “Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light.”

Thus, in order to produce an error in which he might glory [Note: [Col. 1355] “might boast”: original—Burchard—Ivo, *Decretum*; “might glory” is absent in the Argentine edition], he clothed himself in the appearance and name of a righteous man, so as falsely to declare that the hope preached by the worshippers of God accomplished nothing [Note: [Col. 1355] “to worshippers”: original—cited collections—Basel, Lyons II and III editions], when he pretended that the righteous who depart from here were in his power.

But some are deceived by the fact that he did not lie concerning the death of Saul and his son, as though it were some great thing for the devil [Note: [Col. 1355] “Satan”: Basel edition] to foresee bodily death before its occurrence, when certain signs customarily appear in those who are about to die, especially in persons from whom God’s protection seems to have been withdrawn. How much more might this be possible to the devil [Note: [Col. 1355] “the devil”: original; “of the devil”: Argentine edition; “by the devil”: remaining editions, except Lyons II and III], whom prophetic oracles testify to have been exalted in angelic power, concerning whose greatness the Apostle says [Col. 1355C] [Note: [Col. 1355] Rev. 2:24.]: “Do you not know the depths of Satan?”

What wonder, then, if he could foresee imminent death close at hand, since this is one of the means by which he deceives and wishes to be worshipped as though he were in God’s power? For Saul had become mad with such dullness that he resorted to the Pythoness. Corrupted by reason of sin, he turned to things [Note: [Col. 1355] “this”: editions collectively] which [Note: [Col. 1355] “which”: the same editions, except Argentine] he had condemned.

But if anyone, on account of the narrative and the things expressed in its words, thinks these matters should not be passed over lest the sense of the history be empty, he will indeed do rightly [Note: [Col. 1355] “let him do”: Burchard; “does”: editions collectively], provided that he does not at all draw this matter into the account of truth [Note: [Col. 1355] “return”: Basel edition], but into Saul’s sight [Note: [Col. 1355] “use”: ibid.] and understanding. For, having become reprobate, he could not have good understanding.

The historian, therefore, described Saul’s mind and Samuel’s appearance [Col. 1356A] [Note: [Col. 1355] “condition”: editions collectively], recounting what was said [Note: [Col. 1355] “foretold”: Basel edition] and seen, while passing over whether it was true or false [Note: [Col. 1355] “whether true”: Lyons II and III editions]. For what [Note: [Col. 1355] “who”: editions collectively; cf. 1 Sam. 28:14.] does he say? “On hearing in what appearance he had been raised, he understood,” he says, “that this was Samuel.” He reported what Saul understood; and because Saul did not understand correctly, he worshipped someone other than God, contrary to Scripture, and, thinking that he worshipped Samuel, he worshipped the devil, so that Satan might obtain the fruit of his deception.

For this is what he strives after [Note: [Col. 1355] “lies”: Argentine edition; “relies upon”: Venice II, Lyons I, and Paris editions]: to be worshipped as God. For if Samuel had truly appeared to him, that righteous man would certainly not have permitted himself to be worshipped [Note: [Col. 1355] “worship”: Basel edition], since he had preached that God alone must be worshipped. And how could a man of God, who was with Abraham in refreshment, say [Note: [Col. 1355] “say”: editions collectively] to a man of pestilence, worthy [Note: [Col. 1355] “and worthy”: Basel, Lyons II and III editions] of the fire of Gehenna: “Tomorrow you shall be with me” [Col. 1356B]?

By these two marks the unwary Satan disclosed the subtlety of his deception [Note: [Col. 1355] “discloses”: Basel edition]: first, because, under the appearance and name of Samuel, he allowed himself to be worshipped contrary to the law; secondly, because he falsely said that a man burdened with sins would be with the most righteous Samuel, although there is a great separation between sinners and the righteous. Yet, if the name of Samuel is left unmentioned, it may appear true that Saul was to be with the devil; for he passed over to the one whom he worshipped.

The devil, therefore, always betrays himself while lying hidden beneath a veil, whenever he invents things that are abhorrent [Note: [Col. 1355] “shrink from”: Ivo, *Panormia*; “adhere”: editions collectively] to the persons [Note: [Col. 1355] “person”: original] through whom he seeks to deceive.

§ 11. But if anyone [Note: [Col. 1355] “anyone whatever”: Burchard, Ivo, *Decretum*, and editions collectively; “by any persons”: Ivo, *Panormia*.] objects to me and asks, “How do those things happen which these diviners foretell will occur? Or how can they provide remedies to the sick, or inflict sickness on the healthy, if they possess no power and ability of their own [Col. 1356C] [Note: [Col. 1355] “possess”: editions collectively]?” let him receive from me [Note: [Col. 1355] “from us”: the same editions—cited collections] this answer [Note: [Col. 1355] “let them receive”: Basel, Lyons II and III editions]: no one ought to believe them merely because what they predict sometimes happens, or because they appear to cure the infirm or harm the healthy. For this occurs by God’s permission, in order that those [Note: [Col. 1355] “these”: Basel edition] who hear or see these things [Note: [Col. 1355] “this”: editions collectively, except Lyons II and III] may be tested, and it may become apparent [Note: [Col. 1355] “may become apparent [plural]”: editions collectively] with what faith or devotion [Note: [Col. 1355] “what kind of”: cited collections—Argentine, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice I and II editions] they are toward God.

As is read in Deuteronomy, Moses, by the word [Note: [Col. 1355] “from the word of God”: editions collectively] of the Lord, commanded God’s people [Note: [Col. 1355] “of the Lord”: Basel edition], saying thus [Note: [Col. 1355] Deut. 13:1–4.]:

> “If a prophet arises in your midst, or one who says that he has seen a dream, and predicts a sign or [Note: [Col. 1355] “and”: Basel edition] portent, and what he has spoken comes to pass, and he says to you, ‘Let us go and follow foreign gods, whom you do not know, and [Col. 1357A] let us serve them,’ you shall not hear the words of that prophet or dreamer, because the Lord your God is testing you, that it may become manifest whether you love him or not. Follow the Lord your God with all your heart [Note: [Col. 1357] added: “your”: Basel, Lyons II and III editions] and with all your soul; fear him, keep his commandments, hear his voice, serve him, and cling to him,” and so forth.

Here he plainly intended it to be understood [Note: [Col. 1357] cf. above, question 2, c. 5.] that even things said by diviners otherwise than according to God, if what is said happens [Note: [Col. 1357D] “If what is said happens”: This passage has been corrected from St Augustine, as it occurs above in the same question, c. “To Be Understood.” In Rabanus, however, it reads: “if the things which [Col. 1358D] are said happen, they are not to be received; or even if things commanded by them are done, or things are worshipped,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1357] substantially thus Burchard and Ivo, *Panormia*.]], are not to be received in such a way that what they command is done, or what they worship is worshipped [Note: [Col. 1357] “are not”: editions collectively, except Basel; “nor”: Venice II, Paris, Lyons editions].

Nor does God show that the occurrence of these things lies beyond his power; rather, as though it were asked why he permits them, he explained the reason as testing: namely, to make known their love, whether [Col. 1357B] they have it toward their God—made known, however, more to themselves than to him who knows all things before they happen.

## QUESTION VI

## GRATIAN

That one excommunicated by a bishop cannot be reconciled by another bishop without consulting him, unless perhaps through his metropolitan or through the supreme pontiff, is proved by reason and authority. For presbyters receive the power of excommunicating or reconciling from bishops, not bishops from presbyters. Therefore bishops can reconcile those excommunicated by presbyters, but presbyters cannot reconcile those excommunicated by bishops [Col. 1357C]. For the reconciliation of penitents belongs to the episcopal office, not to the priestly office.

Hence in the Second Council of Carthage, [Note: [Col. 1357] held A.D. 390.—Collections, third part, part 2, tome 16, c. 2.], c. 3, Bishop Fortunatus [Note: [Col. 1357] Numidius of Maxula: Spanish Collection.] said:

### C. I. The reconciliation of penitents, the making of chrism, and the consecration of virgins are not to be performed by presbyters.

If your holiness commands, I shall make a proposal. For I remember that at the preceding council [Note: [Col. 1357] “at the preceding councils”: ibid.] it was decreed that chrism, the reconciliation of penitents, and likewise the consecration of virgins, should not be performed by presbyters [Note: [Col. 1357] “be performed”: Basel edition]. But if anyone [Note: [Col. 1357] absent from the same source] should arise [Note: [Col. 1357] “should issue forth”: Lyons I edition] doing [Note: [Col. 1357] “to do”: Spanish Collection] this, what ought to be decreed concerning him?

Bishop Aurelius [Note: [Col. 1357] Geneclius: ibid.] said: “Your dignity has heard the proposal of our brother and fellow bishop Fortunatus [Note: [Col. 1357] Numidius: ibid.]. What do you say to these matters?” All the bishops said: “The making of chrism and the consecration of virgins [Col. 1358A] are not to be performed by presbyters; nor is it lawful for a presbyter to reconcile anyone in the public Mass” [Note: [Col. 1357] “may be lawful”: editions collectively]. This pleases everyone.

**Gratian.** Yet the consecration of virgins may be performed by a presbyter after consultation with the bishop.

Hence in the Third Council of Carthage, c. 36 [Note: [Col. 1357] held A.D. 397.]:

### C. II. A presbyter may consecrate virgins with the bishop’s permission.

A presbyter shall not consecrate virgins without consulting the bishop; but he shall never make chrism.

### C. III. It is not lawful for a presbyter either to perform the ministry proper to a deacon or to bless a penitent in church. Likewise from the Council of Agde, cc. 43 and 44 [Note: [Col. 1357] held A.D. 506.—Collections, third part, part 2, tome 28, cc. 41, 42.].

A deacon shall not presume to perform the ministry, nor a presbyter to consecrate an altar. § 1. Nor shall it be lawful at all for a presbyter to pronounce a blessing [Col. 1358B] upon the people in church, or to bless a penitent in church.

**Gratian.** Behold, then, that one excommunicated by a bishop cannot be reconciled through a priest. But it should be noted that one kind of reconciliation is public, another private. Public reconciliation occurs when penitents are publicly presented before the entrance of the church and are publicly reconciled to the Church through the imposition of the bishop’s hand. This appears to be forbidden to priests. Hence, near the end of that chapter, penitents are not simply forbidden to be reconciled, but forbidden to be reconciled in the public Mass.

Private reconciliation, however, occurs when penitents for hidden sins, or persons at the point of death, receive the grace of reconciliation. This reconciliation can [Col. 1358C] be performed by a priest.

Hence Pope Evaristus says [Note: [Col. 1357] Rather, Herard of Tours, in the *Capitularies*, c. 59.—Burchard, bk. 18, c. 16. Anselm, bk. 11, c. 10. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, c. 38.—cf. *Capitularies of the Kings of France*, bk. 6, c. 206.]:

### C. IV. By order of the bishop, presbyters are to reconcile penitents for hidden sins.

By order of the bishop, presbyters shall reconcile penitents for hidden sins and, as we have stated above, absolve and communicate the sick.

### C. V. If the bishop is absent, a person in danger is to be reconciled through a presbyter. Likewise from the Second Council of Carthage, c. 4 [Note: [Col. 1357] held A.D. 390.—Regino, bk. 1, c. 109. Burchard, bk. 18, c. 73. Anselm, bk. 11, c. 12. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, c. 2.].

Bishop Aurelius [Note: [Col. 1357] Geneclius: Spanish Collection.] said: “If anyone is placed in danger and asks to be reconciled to the divine altars, if the bishop is absent, the presbyter must certainly consult the bishop, and then, at his command, reconcile the person in danger. This [Col. 1359A] matter we ought to strengthen by a salutary resolution.”

All the bishops [Note: [Col. 1359] “all”: editions collectively] said: “We approve what your holiness has deigned necessarily to instruct us concerning.”

### C. VI. A person reconciled for fear of death, if restored to health, shall complete the appointed time without receiving penitential communion. Likewise from the Council of Martin of Braga, c. 82 [Note: [Col. 1359] c. 12 of the Council of Nicaea, in Martin of Braga’s translation.—“from the Council of Pope Martin”: editions collectively].

If anyone departing from the body requests the final and necessary viaticum of communion, it shall not be denied him. But if, after receiving communion while in despair, he is restored to health, he shall share only in prayer [Note: [Col. 1359] “in prayer”: the same editions, except Basel—Böhm; “of prayer”: Spanish Collection], and shall not receive the sacrament [Note: [Col. 1359] “but he shall not receive the sacrament”: Spanish Collection] until he has completed the appointed [Note: [Col. 1359] “established”: editions collectively] time of penance. Therefore those who are at the point of death and desire to receive the sacrament ought to receive it with the bishop’s consideration and examination.

[Col. 1359B]

### C. VII. Penitents departing from the body are to be reconciled without imposition of hands. Likewise from the Council of Orange, c. 3 [Note: [Col. 1359] held A.D. 441.—Burchard, bk. 18, c. 17. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, c. 39.].

It has been decreed that those who depart from the body after receiving penance be communicated without the imposition of the reconciling hand [Note: [Col. 1359] “to them”: Spanish Collection—Burchard—Ivo—editions collectively; “be communicated”: Spanish Collection], which suffices for the reconciliation [Note: [Col. 1359C] “For reconciliation”: In the printed and manuscript original, and in Burchard and Ivo, the reading is “for consolation” [Note: [Col. 1359] thus the same source], or: “with consolation.”] of one dying, according to the determinations of the Fathers, who suitably called such communion a viaticum [Note: [Col. 1359] “suitably”: ibid.—Ivo; “suitable”: Burchard].

But if they survive, they shall remain in the order of penitents, so that, after displaying the necessary fruits of penance, they may receive lawful communion with the imposition of the reconciling hand. § 1. Penance is likewise not to be denied to clergy who desire it [Note: [Col. 1359] “therefore, considering”: Basel edition]. § 2. Likewise, one suddenly rendered speechless may, as has been decreed, be baptized or receive penance [Col. 1359C], if he has testimony of his earlier will in the statements of others [Note: [Col. 1359] “or of his earlier [will]”: ibid.] or of his present will in his own gesture [Note: [Col. 1359] “may have”: ibid.]. § 3. Even to persons of unsound mind, all things pertaining to mercy are to be given [Note: [Col. 1359] “reconciled or given”: Basel edition].

### C. VIII. A dying person is to be reconciled on the testimony of others if he has become speechless or delirious. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 76 [Note: [Col. 1359] cc. 20, 21, *Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua*—cf. on c. 9, Distinction 18.—Burchard, bk. 18, cc. 10, 23. Anselm, bk. 11, c. 18. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, cc. 8, 10. Polycarpus, bk. 8, title 1.].

One who asks for penance in illness, if by chance, while the summoned priest is coming to him, he is overcome by illness and becomes speechless [Col. 1360A] or delirious [Note: [Col. 1359] “changed”: editions collectively; the words “or … becomes” are absent from Burchard and Anselm], let those who heard him give testimony, and let him receive penance. And if he is believed to be dying immediately, let him be reconciled through the imposition of hands, and let the Eucharist be poured into his mouth. If he survives, let him be admonished by the aforesaid witnesses that his request has been granted [Note: [Col. 1359] “that he will satisfy [his petition] and submit himself”: Burchard, Anselm], and let him be subject to the established laws of penance for as long as the priest who gave [Note: [Col. 1359] “will have given”: editions collectively] the penance judges proper.

Likewise, c. 78:

§ 1. Penitents who have received the viaticum of the Eucharist in illness [Note: [Col. 1359] “receive”: the same editions, except Basel] are not to consider themselves absolved without imposition of hands, if they survive.

[Col. 1360B]

### C. IX. The dying are to be reconciled with the bishop’s care and examination. Likewise from the Council of Nicaea, c. 12 [Note: [Col. 1359D] This canon is from the ancient translation found in Isidore’s collection, where it is numbered 12; in Greek, however, and in Dionysius, it is 13.] [Note: [Col. 1359] held A.D. 325.—Regino, bk. 1, c. 107. Burchard, bk. 18, c. 6. Anselm, bk. 11, c. 23. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, cc. 31, all from Dionysius.].

Concerning those who depart from the body, the rule of the ancient law shall still be observed: if anyone should perhaps depart [Note: [Col. 1359] absent from Spanish Collection; “departs”: editions collectively] from [Note: [Col. 1359] “from”: Basel edition] the body, he shall not be deprived of the necessary viaticum for his life. But if someone thought beyond hope survives after receiving communion, he shall be among those who communicate only in prayer. For in the case of all those who depart from the body, in giving [Note: [Col. 1359] “in giving … communion”: the same source] them communion, the bishop’s care and examination shall be present.

### C. X. Reconciliation is not to be denied to those who implore it at a time of necessity. Likewise Leo, bishop, to Theodore, Epistle LXXXIX, otherwise XCI [Note: [Col. 1359] Epistle 108, written A.D. 452, Ballerini edition.—Regino, bk. 1, c. 108. Burchard, bk. 18, c. 4. Anselm, bk. 11, c. 13. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, c. 29, all through § 1.—Collections, third part, part 2, tome 48, cc. 38, 39.—cf. Distinction 4, *On Penance*, c. 49.].

Those who, at a time of necessity and under the pressure of imminent danger, seek the aid of penance and then [Col. 1360C] [Note: [Col. 1359] “measure”: Argentine, Nuremberg, Venice I, II, and Paris editions; “gift”: remaining editions] reconciliation are neither to be forbidden satisfaction nor denied reconciliation. For we can neither set limits nor define times for God’s mercy; with him conversion suffers no delays in forgiveness [Note: [Col. 1360C] “Forgiveness”: Thus in editions of the councils, in Ivo, and below, *On Penance*, Distinction 1, c. “Manifold.” But in the printed codex of letters with other works of St Leo, in Burchard, and in most ancient copies of Gratian, it reads: *venire moras* (“delays in coming”) [Note: [Col. 1359] thus Regino and Argentine, Basel, and Venice I editions.]], as the Spirit of God says through the prophet [Note: [Col. 1359] “through Ezekiel the prophet”: editions collectively, except Argentine, Basel, and Nuremberg; cf. Ezek. 30:15 according to the Septuagint]: “When, having turned, you groan, then you shall be saved.”

And below:

§ 1. But if they have been so burdened by some illness that they are unable to signify, in the presence [Col. 1361A] [Note: [Col. 1361C] “They sought”: What follows has been corrected from certain manuscripts of Gratian and from the original itself, since the common editions had it somewhat differently.] [Note: [Col. 1361] “in the present … testimony”: editions collectively] of the priest, what they sought a little earlier, the testimony of faithful persons and [Note: [Col. 1361] absent from the original in Ballerini, the Spanish Collection, and the Basel edition] bystanders ought to avail for them [Note: [Col. 1361] “their testimony ought to avail”: editions collectively, except Basel], so that they may obtain both the benefit of penance and of reconciliation [Note: [Col. 1361] added: “nevertheless”: Spanish Collection—editions collectively; the following “and” is absent from editions collectively, except Basel], while nonetheless preserving the rule of the canons of the fathers [Note: [Col. 1361] “holy canons”: editions collectively, except Argentine] concerning those persons who have sinned by departing from the faith in God [Note: [Col. 1361] “the Lord”: the same source; “in the Lord’s”: Basel; “from the Lord’s”: Lyons II and III; “from the Lord”: remaining editions].

### C. XI. The offering of one who, hastening to penance, could not find a priest is not to be rejected. Likewise from the Council of Epaone [Note: [Col. 1361] Rather, from the Roman penitential found in Halitgar, bk. 6, c. 10.—Regino, bk. 2, c. 436. Burchard, bk. 11, c. 51. Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 5, c. 120; *Decretum*, part 14, c. 114.—In the Basel edition, cited as from the Council of Seville.—In *Panormia*, I. v., as from the Council of Narbonne.].

If someone excommunicated [Note: [Col. 1361D] “Excommunicated”: This word has been added from the other compilers.] has died, having already confessed and possessing good testimony, but could not come to a priest because death overtook him at home or on the road, let his relatives make [Col. 1361B] an offering [Note: [Col. 1361] “offerings”: Basel edition] for him at the altar and give a redemption-payment for captives.

**Gratian.** Thus it is clear that, at the bishop’s command, penitents for hidden sins, or persons placed in danger, can be reconciled through a presbyter. § 1. But if a sinner is pressed by the necessity of death and the bishop is so far away that the presbyter cannot consult him, is penance to be denied to the dying person? Is the benefit of reconciliation not to be granted to the penitent, whom God receives, once converted, unto forgiveness, according to the saying [Note: [Col. 1361] Ezek. 18:27.], “In whatever hour the sinner is converted,” etc., and likewise [Note: [Col. 1361] Mal. 3:7.], “Turn to me, and I will turn to you”? Will the Church neglect to reconcile to herself one whom God has inwardly raised up? Will the Church disdain outwardly to absolve one whom God has enlightened by the grace of his presence [Col. 1361C] through the laver of regeneration?

Even the dying are assisted by laypersons if presbyters are lacking. Why, therefore, can he not be assisted by the benefit of reconciliation through a presbyter if it happens that the bishop is absent? If, according to Augustine, one at the point of death who confesses [Col. 1362A] to a companion the shamefulness of his crime becomes worthy of pardon through his desire for a priest, why should one who does not withhold from the priest the stain of his guilt not likewise be worthy of reconciliation through his desire for a bishop? Moreover, presbyters ought not to deny penance to the dying.

Hence Pope Julius says [Note: [Col. 1361] This is a crude summary of the matters found in Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul; cf. the following chapter.—It is found in the penitential published by Canisius as the sixth book of Halitgar in *Antiquae Lectiones*, tome 2.—Burchard, bk. 18, c. 21. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, c. 43. Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, bk. 4, distinction 20.]:

### C. XII. A presbyter who refuses penance to the dying is guilty of souls.

If a presbyter refuses penance to the dying, he shall be guilty of souls, because the Lord says [Note: [Col. 1361] Ezek. 18:27.]: “On whatever day the sinner is converted, he shall live and shall not die.” For true confession [Note: [Col. 1361] “conversion”: the cited penitential—Burchard—Ivo] can occur at the final time, because the Lord is the examiner not only of time but also of the heart; just as the thief, by the penance of a single moment, deserved to be in paradise [Col. 1362B] in the final hour of confession [Note: [Col. 1361] Luke 23.—C. XIII.].

Likewise Pope Celestine says in his second letter to the Bishops of Gaul [Note: [Col. 1361] written A.D. 428.—Rabanus, *On Penance*, c. 38. Anselm, bk. 11, c. 20, omitting the passages “We shudder … to liberate” and “True … to be revealed.” Burchard, bk. 18, cc. 22 and 1. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, cc. 44 and 26.]:

### C. XIII. Penance is not to be denied to the dying.

We have learned [Note: [Col. 1361] *Cognovimus* (“We have learned”): Basel Edition] that penance is denied to the dying, and that the requests of those who, at the time of death, desire this remedy for the aid of their souls are not granted. We shudder—I confess—that anyone should be found [Note: [Col. 1361] *reperiri* (“be found”): Hispanic Collection; Burchard IV; Basel Edition] capable of such great impiety as to despair of God’s goodness [Note: [Col. 1361] *pietate* (“mercy”): Hispanic Collection; Burchard IV], as though he could not come to the aid, at whatever time, of one who hastens to him and redeem a man endangered beneath the burden of sins [Note: [Col. 1361D–1362D] *Redimere* (“redeem”) is likewise the reading in the manuscripts and older editions of the councils. But the printed *Code of Canons* and one manuscript among Celestine’s decrees, no. 15, read *perdere* (“destroy”). The more recent Cologne edition of the councils, and likewise Burchard and Ivo, read *pondere* (“from the burden”); the Hispanic Collection reads: *quo se ille expediri desiderat, liberare*, “to free him from that burden from which he desires to be released”], from which he desires to be released and set free [Note: [Col. 1361] *se velle* (“that he wishes himself”): the collected editions].

What, therefore [Note: [Col. 1361] *ergo* (“therefore”): Basel Edition], I ask, is this but to add death to one who is dying, and by one’s cruelty to kill his soul, so that it cannot be absolved? Since God [Note: [Col. 1361] *Dominus* (“the Lord”): the collected editions] is most ready to help [Col. 1362C] [Note: [Col. 1361] *ut parati simus* (“that we may be ready”): Basel Edition], inviting [Note: [Col. 1361] *invitet* (“may invite”): same edition; *invitat* (“invites”): the remaining editions] the sinner to repentance, thus promises [Note: [Col. 1361] *promittit* (“promises”): Basel Edition; *promittens* (“promising”): the remaining editions; *proclamat* (“proclaims”): Burchard] the sinner [Note: [Col. 1361] Hispanic Collection: *Peccator, inquit* (“The sinner, he says”); compare Ezekiel 33:15], saying: “On whatever day [Note: [Col. 1361] *hora* (“hour”): the collected editions] he has turned, his sins shall not be reckoned against him”; and again [Note: [Col. 1361] Ezekiel 18:23]: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but only [Note: [Col. 1361] *ut* (“that”): Hispanic Collection, Burchard, Ivo, Böhm; *ut magis* (“but rather that”): the collected editions] that he turn and live.”

Whoever, therefore, denies a man salvation [Note: [Col. 1361] *hominum* (“of men”): the first Basel edition] by denying him at the time of death the *hoped-for* [Note: [Col. 1363] Absent from the Hispanic Collection and Burchard and Ivo] penance [Note: [Col. 1363] *sibi* (“for himself”): the collected editions] [Note: [Col. 1363] *denegat* (“denies”): the same editions and the first Basel edition], and despairs [Note: [Col. 1363] *desperavit* (“despaired”): Hispanic Collection; *desperaverit* (“will have despaired”): Burchard, Ivo, Basel Edition; *desperet* (“may despair”): the remaining editions] of the mercy [Note: [Col. 1363] *clementia* (“clemency”): Hispanic Collection, Burchard, Ivo] of God, does not believe [Note: [Col. 1363] *credidit* (“believed”): Burchard and Ivo; *crediderit* (“will have believed”): Basel Edition] that he can suffice to aid a dying person even in a moment.

The thief hanging on the cross at Christ’s right hand would certainly have lost his reward [Note: [Col. 1363] *utique* (“certainly”): the collected editions and the first Argentan edition; compare Luke 23] if the repentance of one hour had not helped him. Though under punishment, he repented, and by the confession of a single saying [Note: [Col. 1363] *pro* in place of *per* (“by”): the collected editions] earned, God promising it [Note: [Col. 1363] *eo* (“by him”): the same editions], a dwelling-place in paradise.

True conversion to God in those at the end of life must therefore be judged by the disposition of the mind rather than by time [Note: [Col. 1363] *non* (“not”): Hispanic Collection], as the prophet declares in these words [Note: [Col. 1363] Ezekiel 18:33]: “When, having turned, you groan, then you shall be saved.” Since, therefore, the Lord examines the heart, repentance must not at any time be denied to one who asks for it, since he [Note: [Col. 1363] *illi* (“to him”): Hispanic Collection, Burchard, Argentan and Basel editions] binds himself to the judge to whom he knows [Note: [Col. 1363] *noluerit* (“will not have wished”): Basel Edition] that all hidden things will be revealed [Col. 1363B].

**Gratian.** Reconciliation must likewise not be denied to one to whom repentance is not refused. Therefore, a priest ought not to reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, unless final necessity compels him.

Thus, in the Third Council of Carthage, canon 32, we read [Note: [Col. 1363] Held A.D. 397; Burchard XIX.40; Anselm XI.21; Ivo, *Decretum* XV.4; Peter Lombard, same place]:

### Canon XIV. A priest must not reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, unless final necessity compels him.
