A priest shall not reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, unless final necessity compels him while the bishop is absent [Note: [Col. 1363] *ultima* (“final”) is absent from the Hispanic Collection and Burchard, Anselm, and Ivo] [Note: [Col. 1363] *necessitate cogente* (“necessity compelling”): same sources]. But if the crime of any penitent is public and very widely known, such that it has stirred the whole Church [Note: [Col. 1363C] The text formerly read *urbem* (“the city”). It has been corrected to *ecclesiam* (“the Church”) from most editions of the councils, two Vatican manuscripts, the royal manuscript of Soria, Burchard, and Ivo. The more recent Cologne edition reads: *quod universa ecclesia noverit*, “which the whole Church knows”], hands shall be laid upon him before the apse [Note: [Col. 1363] The collected editions add *ecclesiae* (“of the church”); they gloss *ante absidam* as “in the atrium,” while Basel reads *ante atrium*, “before the atrium”] [Col. 1363C].

## QUESTION VII

### GRATIAN

**Part I.** Concerning the time of satisfaction—whether it ought to be imposed upon the dying—Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury, lays down the following in his *Penitential* [Note: [Col. 1363] This is not among Theodore’s fragments in Petit and D’Achery; Burchard XVIII.14; Ivo, *Decretum* XV.36; Peter Lombard IV, distinction 20]:

[Col. 1364A]

### Canon I. For persons placed in danger, the amount of penance is not to be imposed but made known.

From sick persons placed in danger of death, priests must seek a sincere confession of sins. Yet the amount of penance is not to be imposed upon them, but made known; and the burden of penance is to be lightened by the prayers of friends and the practice of almsgiving, *and*, should they perhaps depart this life, they are not to become bound and estranged from communion and the fellowship of pardon. If someone, rescued by God from that danger, recovers, he shall diligently observe the measure of penance imposed upon him by his priest [Note: [Col. 1363] *suo confessore* (“his confessor”): Burchard and Ivo]. Therefore, according to canonical authority, lest the door of mercy seem closed to them, they are to be strengthened with ecclesiastical prayers and consolations, with the sacred anointing of consecrated oil [Note: [Col. 1363] *animati* (“encouraged”): same sources], and, according to the statutes [Note: [Col. 1363] *canonica statuta* (“canonical statutes”): Basel Edition] of the holy Fathers, with communion as viaticum [Col. 1364B].

**Part II. Gratian.** But for others, periods of penance must be fixed according to the character of the sin and the judgment of those who preside.

Thus Pope Leo, Epistle LXXVII, alternatively LXXIX, to Bishop Nicetas, chapter 6 [Note: [Col. 1363D] In the epistle, and in Burchard and Ivo, the following precedes: “But concerning those about whom your devotion thought fit to consult us—those who were either compelled by fear or led astray by error to repeat baptism, and now acknowledge that they acted against the sacrament of the Catholic faith—such moderation must be observed that they receive unity of communion into our fellowship only through the remedy of penance and the laying-on of the bishop’s hand, the period of penitence being moderated at your discretion, according to …”] [Note: [Col. 1363] Epistle 159, written A.D. 458, Ballerini edition; Burchard IV.48; *Collection of Three Parts*, I.43.32; Ivo, *Decretum* I.242; *Polycarpus* III.10]:

### Canon II. Periods of penitence are to be fixed at the discretion of those presiding.

The periods of penitence are to be established with moderation at your judgment, according as you see the minds of the converted to be devout, likewise taking account of old age and considering the necessities of every danger or illness [Note: [Col. 1363] *habentes* (“having”): Burchard, Ivo, and the collected editions; *aegritudinum* (“of illnesses”): Hispanic Collection—though not Ballerini—Burchard, Ivo, and the collected editions; *respicientes* (“considering”): Burchard and the collected editions; *dispicientur* (“will be considered”): Ivo]. If anyone is so grievously pressed that, while he is still repenting, there is despair of his salvation, the grace of communion must be brought to his aid through priestly care [Col. 1364C] [Note: [Col. 1363] *sollicitudinem* (“solicitude”): Hispanic Collection and Ballerini, Burchard, Ivo, and the collected editions].

### Canon III. In imposing satisfaction, the priest must consider both the character of the crime and the contrition of penitents. Likewise Pope Nicholas.

[Note: [Col. 1363] From the letter to Rodulfus of Bourges, written A.D. 864; *Collection of Three Parts* I.62.52.]

Concerning those who have done penance for crimes [Note: [Col. 1363] *gerunt* (“are doing penance”): original and Basel Edition] and return to the military belt, it is clear [Col. 1365A] that they act contrary to the sacred rules. But because crimes are unequal, and because you report that some of them have fallen into despair through excessive dullness, while others have fled to pagans for this reason, we entrust the decision to you, since, being present, you can examine the places and times of that religious observance [Note: [Col. 1365] *regionis* (“region”): same source and Böhm], the degree of the fault, as well as the penance and groans of persons coming to confession.

### Canon IV. On the same subject. Likewise from the Council of Laodicea, canon 2.

[Note: [Col. 1365] Held between A.D. 347 and 381; Burchard XIX.41; Ivo, *Decretum* XV.56, from Dionysius.]

For those who fall into various sins and demonstrate a complete conversion from their evils by prayer [Note: [Col. 1365C] Greek: *Καὶ προσκαρτεροῦντας τῇ προσευχῇ τῆς ἐξομολογήσεως καὶ μετανοίας*, “and persevering in the prayer of confession and repentance,” which Dionysius translates: *et perseverantes in oratione confessionis et poenitentiae*, “and persevering in the prayer of confession and penance.” The Hispanic Collection reads: *orationi instant, confessioni et poenitentiae—demonstrantes*, “persisting in prayer, confession, and repentance—demonstrating.” Dionysius’s version, in this and the other portions of this chapter, approaches the Greek words more closely than the old translation, although the sense is maintained here] confession, and repentance, a time of penance is to be allotted according to the character of the sin [Note: [Col. 1365] *conversationem* (“conduct of life”) for *conversionem* (“conversion”): the collected editions] [Col. 1365B], because of God’s mercy and goodness. Persons of this kind are therefore to be recalled and admitted to communion.

### Canon V. At the bishop’s judgment, periods of penance are to be allotted according to the character of sins. Likewise from the Third Council of Carthage, canon 31.

[Note: [Col. 1365] Held A.D. 397; Regino I.301; Burchard XIX.40; *Collection of Three Parts* II.17.21; Anselm XI.21, from the Roman penitential; Ivo, *Decretum* XV.3.]

For penitents, periods of penance shall be fixed [Note: [Col. 1365] *decernentur* (“shall be fixed”): Basel Edition] at the bishop’s judgment according to the differences among sins.

### Canon VI. Penance is to be granted, without respect of persons, to one who asks for it. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 74 [75, 80, 82, 81, 64, 79].

[Note: [Col. 1365] In the *Ancient Ecclesiastical Statutes*: chapters 18, 19, 65, 67, 66, 77, and 22; compare Distinction 18, canon 9; Regino I.302, 308; Burchard XIX.35, 38, both as far as *reconc.*; Ivo, *Decretum* XV.6, 7, 12, 13, 11, omitting the clauses from *Omni* (“At every”) to *catholicus* (“Catholic”).]

[Col. 1365C] A priest shall impose penance upon one who asks for it, without respect of persons [Note: [Col. 1365] *personae* (“of a person”): original, cited collections, Argentan and Basel editions; *acceptione* (“acceptance”) for *acceptione personarum* (“respect of persons”): original, cited collections, collected editions, and Böhm], according to the laws [Note: [Col. 1365] *poenitentiae leges* (“the laws of penance”): original and cited collections]. More negligent penitents are to be reconciled more slowly [Note: [Col. 1365] *recipiantur* (“received”): original]. At every time of fasting [Note: [Col. 1365] *Omni* (“every”) is absent from the same source; *etiam* (“also”): the collected editions], priests shall lay hands upon penitents. On days of remission, penitents shall bend their knees [Note: [Col. 1365] *reflectant* (“bend back”): Böhm], and shall bring the dead into the church [Note: [Col. 1365C] The more recent Cologne edition reads *ecclesiae afferant*, “bring [them] to the church.” In the older editions and two Vatican manuscripts, the complete passage is: *mortuos ecclesiae poenitentes efferant et sepeliant*, “penitents shall carry the dead out of the church and bury them” [Note: [Col. 1365] Thus the original in Ballerini, the Hispanic Collection, and Ivo; *ecclesia efferat*, “the church shall carry [them] out”: Basel Edition]] and bury them [Note: [Col. 1365] *auferant* (“carry away”): Nuremberg Edition]. On Sunday [Note: [Col. 1365C] In place of the following words through *catholicus*, canon 64 reads: *Qui dominico die studiose jejunat non credatur catholicus*, “One who deliberately fasts on Sunday is not to be considered Catholic” [Note: [Col. 1365] Thus the original in Ballerini and the Hispanic Collection]] they shall not fast; for one who deliberately fasts on Sunday is not believed to be Catholic.

Penitents who diligently observe the laws of penance, if by chance they die on a journey or at sea, where help cannot be given them [Note: [Col. 1365] *potuit* (“could be given”): same source; *possit* (“may be given”): Ivo and Basel Edition; the words from *ubi* to *potest* are absent from the Argentan Edition], shall have their memory commended by offerings and prayers.

Thus, in the Eighth Synod, we read [Note: [Col. 1365D–1366C] This appears to have been taken from Basil’s *Shorter Rules*, chapter 106; elsewhere it has been noted that this occurs in chapters attributed to the Eighth Synod] [Note: [Col. 1365] Rather, it is from Basil, to whom the following chapters, through chapter 11, are also ascribed; compare the correction; *Collection of Three Parts* II.14.9]:

### Canon VII. A period of penance is to be spent according to the character of the sin.

[Col. 1366B] A period of penance is to be spent according to the character of the offense.

### Canon VIII. The time and manner of penitence for offenders are to be imposed at the judgment of those presiding. Likewise:

[Note: [Col. 1366C] This chapter is found in Basil’s booklet *On the Institutes of Monks*, translated by Rufinus, chapter 90. There the final question is: “What corrections ought to be employed among the brothers for the amendment of those who offend?” The answer: “Let this be left to the judgment of those who preside, whether for how long …” Thus this chapter, like the two following, was made from the question and answer found in the same Rufinus.]  
[Note: [Col. 1365] *Collection of Three Parts*, book and chapter 10.]

This must be left to the judgment of those who preside: both how long and in what way offenders ought to do penance, because age and education [Note: [Col. 1365] *ad eruditionem* (“for instruction”): the collected editions] produce a great difference in punishment.

**Part III. Gratian.** With what affection we must receive a penitent and reject an unrepentant person is clearly shown by the same Synod, when it says [Note: [Col. 1366C–1366D] Burchard and Ivo cite this from the sayings of Bishop Basil. The statement occurs in Basil’s *Shorter Rules*, no. 8, but appears to have been drawn from chapter 24 of the same booklet *On the Institutes of Monks*. There the second question is: “Father, how ought those who repent from the heart to be received?” The answer: “As the Lord shows when he says, ‘He who summoned …’”] [Note: [Col. 1365] *Collection of Three Parts*, same book, chapter 11; Regino I.321; Burchard XIX.39; Ivo, *Decretum* XV.55]:

### Canon IX. We must receive a penitent with the deepest affection of charity.

[Col. 1366C] A penitent ought to be received from the heart, as the Lord shows when he says that he summoned [Note: [Col. 1365] *convocavi … meos* (“I summoned … my”): the collected editions; Luke 15:6] [Col. 1367A] his friends and neighbours, saying: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that I had lost.”

### Canon X. Let penitents love God’s law and hate iniquity. Likewise:

[Note: [Col. 1367C] The statement of this chapter is in the *Shorter Rules*, no. 5. It seems, however, to have been drawn from chapter 19 of the same booklet, in which the question is: “How should a person repent for each offense?” The answer: “By taking into himself that disposition which was possessed by him who said: ‘I hated iniquity …’”]  
[Note: [Col. 1367] *Collection of Three Parts*, same book, chapter 12.]

Let the penitent take into himself the disposition possessed by him who said [Note: [Col. 1367] *dicebat* (“was saying”): the collected editions; compare Psalm 118:163]: “I hated iniquity and abhorred it”; and likewise what is written in the sixth Psalm and in very many others [Note: [Col. 1367] *secundum ea* (“according to those things”): same editions; *vel secundum ea* (“or according to those things”): Lugdunensis II and III; *vel ea* (“or those things”): the remaining editions]; and likewise what the Apostle said to those who had been made sorrowful according to God [Note: [Col. 1367] 2 Corinthians 7:11]: “How much [Note: [Col. 1367] *quantum* (“how much”): Argentan, Basel, Venice I–II, and Paris editions],” he says [Note: [Col. 1367] *inquit* (“he says”) is absent from the Argentan and Basel editions], “has this very thing produced [Note: [Col. 1367] *operatus* (“having produced”): Argentan, Basel, Venice I–II, and Paris editions] in you [Note: [Col. 1367] *hoc ipsi* (“this to them”) is absent from the collected editions before Lugdunensis II–III; *nobis* (“in us”): Basel, Venice I–II, Paris, and Lugdunensis I], concern, yes, defence, yes, indignation, yes, zeal, yes, vindication. In everything you have shown yourselves pure [Note: [Col. 1367C] *castos* (“pure”): formerly *cautos* (“careful”) was read. Corrected from Rufinus’s booklet; the Vulgate has *incontaminatos* (“undefiled”), Greek *ἁγνούς*, “pure”] in the matter.” And, in those very things [Note: [Col. 1367] *et* (“and”) is absent from the collected editions; *in* (“in”) is absent from Basel Edition] in which he sinned, he should do many contrary things, as Zacchaeus did.

### Canon XI. The unrepentant are to be treated as pagans. Likewise:

[Note: [Col. 1367C–1368C] This too occurs in the *Shorter Rules*, no. 9. In chapter 24 of the same booklet the last question is: “Father, how ought we to deal with one who does not repent for sin?” The answer: “As the Lord commanded, saying, ‘Let him be to you …’” Burchard and Ivo, who cite this from Augustine’s sayings, begin: *Erga eum, qui pro peccato commisso non poenitet, tales …*, “Toward one who does not repent for a sin committed, [we should be] such …,” which accords better with the preceding question than Gratian’s wording.]  
[Note: [Col. 1367] *Collection of Three Parts*, same book, chapter 13; Regino I.324; Burchard XIX.64; Ivo, *Decretum* XV.78.]

Toward one who does not punish his sins, we ought to act as the Lord commanded, saying [Note: [Col. 1367] Matthew 18:17]: “Let him be to you as a heathen [Note: [Col. 1367] *gentilis* (“Gentile”): Basel Edition] and a tax collector”; and as the Apostle taught, saying [Note: [Col. 1367] 2 Thessalonians 3:6]: “Withdraw from every brother walking disorderly and not according to the tradition which we handed down to you.”

### Canon XII. It is better to err through the mercy of forgiving than through the severity of punishing. Likewise John Chrysostom.

[That is, the author of the *Imperfect Work*, Homily 43 on Matthew 23.]

[Col. 1367C] “For [Note: [Col. 1367] *enim* (“for”): Basel Edition] they bind heavy and unbearable burdens,” and so forth. Such even now are the priests who enjoin all righteousness upon the people, while they themselves observe not even a little [Col. 1368A] [Note: [Col. 1367] *modicam* (“a little”): the collected editions], namely, not in order that they may be righteous by doing [Note: [Col. 1367] *faciendo* (“by doing”): same editions] but that they may appear righteous by saying [Note: [Col. 1367] *dicendo* (“by saying”): same editions; *docentes* (“by teaching”): original].

Such also are [Note: [Col. 1367] *quia* (“because”): the collected editions] those who lay a heavy burden upon persons coming to repentance: they speak and do not act; and so, while the punishment of present penance is avoided, the future punishment of sin is despised. For just as, if you place a bundle on the shoulders of a youth who cannot carry it, he must either cast off the bundle or be crushed beneath its weight, so also a man [Note: [Col. 1367] *homo* (“a man”): the collected editions] on whom you impose [Note: [Col. 1367] *imposueris* (“you have imposed”): Basel Edition] a heavy burden of penance must either reject your penance [Note: [Col. 1367] *rejiciet* (“will reject”): the collected editions], or, accepting it, sin still more through being scandalized, because he cannot endure it [Note: [Col. 1367] *sufficere* (“suffice”): Argentan Edition; *peccat* (“sins”): the collected editions and first Argentan edition].

Furthermore, if we err in imposing a light penance, is it not better to render an account for mercy [Col. 1368B] [Note: [Col. 1367] *dare* (“give [an account]”): original, Argentan and Basel editions] than for cruelty [Note: [Col. 1367] *credulitatem* (“credulity”): Lugdunensis II]? For where the master of the house is generous, the steward ought not to be miserly. If God is kind, why should his priest be harsh? Do you wish to appear [Note: [Col. 1368C] This passage has been enlarged from the cited homily, since it formerly read: “Why does his priest wish to appear harsh?”] holy? Be strict toward your own life, kindly toward that of another.

### Canon XIII. The observances of the calends must not be performed. Likewise Martin of Braga, chapter 74.

[Note: [Col. 1367] *M. Papa* (“Pope Martin”): the collected editions; compare Laodicea, canon 39; Tours II, canon 22; Burchard X.15; Ivo, *Decretum* XI.42; *Polycarpus* VI.12.]

**Part IV.** It is not lawful [Note: [Col. 1367] *liceat* (“may be lawful”): Hispanic Collection] to perform the wicked observances of the calends, or to devote oneself to pagan [Note: [Col. 1367] *otiosis* (“idle”): Argentan Edition; *gentilibus* (“pagan”) is absent from Ivo and Burchard] idleness; nor to encircle houses with laurel or the greenery of trees. For every such observance belongs to paganism [Note: [Col. 1367] *paganorum* (“of pagans”): Burchard, Ivo, and the collected editions].

Thus Pope Zachary, in the Roman Council, canon 9 [Note: [Col. 1368C–1369C] This is canon 9 of the council held at Rome by Zachary, preserved in the Vatican Library, from which some readings have been corrected and added. On this superstition Boniface, legate to Germany, writes at length to Zachary in Epistle 2 in the volumes of councils. Zachary, replying in his final letter, appears to refer to this council: “And because, through the instigation of the devil, these things were again sprouting, from the day divine mercy commanded us—though we are unworthy—to act in the Apostle’s place, we immediately cut them all off.” The same is forbidden at greater length in the canons ascribed to the Sixth Synod, canon 62. Tertullian writes much on this superstition in *On Idolatry*, as do other serious authors] [Note: [Col. 1367] Held A.D. 743; Burchard X.16; Ivo, *Decretum* XI.43; *Polycarpus*, same place]:

### Canon XIV. Let one who observes the pagan rite and the calends be anathema.

If anyone presumes to observe the calends of January [Note: [Col. 1367] *Januarii* (“of January”): Ivo and the collected editions] and the winter solstice [Note: [Col. 1367] *et brumam* (“and the winter solstice”) is absent from Burchard and Ivo] according to the pagan rite [Col. 1369A], or to do anything additionally new because of the new year [Note: [Col. 1369C] The words *vel aliquid plus novi facere propter novum annum* are absent from the Vatican manuscript of this council], or to prepare tables in houses with dishes [Note: [Col. 1367] *lapidibus* (“stones”): Burchard; *lampadibus* (“lamps”): Ivo and the collected editions] or feasts, and to lead songs [Note: [Col. 1369] *cantores* (“singers”): Ivo, Burchard, and the collected editions] and dances through lanes and streets—*which is a great wickedness before God*—let him be anathema.

### Canon XV. Incantations furnish no remedy for human infirmities. Likewise Augustine.

[Note: [Col. 1369C–1369D] Burchard and Ivo cite this chapter from Augustine’s sayings, where similar matters occur in passages cited above in this same Question, canon 5. Yet the identical words, except for the last clause, occur in Tours III, canon 42, and in the appended Capitularies, canon 94.]  
[Note: [Col. 1369] Tours III, canon 42, held A.D. 813; *Capitularies, Appendix III*, chapter 93; Burchard X.40; Ivo, *Decretum* XI.65; *Polycarpus*, same place.]

Let priests warn the faithful people [Note: [Col. 1369] *populum* (“people”): Basel Edition; *suos* (“their”): the remaining editions except the first Argentan] that they should know that magical arts and incantations can give no remedy for any human infirmities, can cure nothing in animals that are sick, lame, or even dying, and that bindings [Note: [Col. 1369D] From here through *prodesse* (“avail”) the words are added from the council and the Capitularies] of bones or herbs applied to any mortal avail nothing [Col. 1369B]. Rather, these things [Note: [Col. 1369] *hoc* (“this”): Basel Edition] are the snares and traps of the ancient enemy, by which that treacherous one seeks to deceive humankind. And [Note: [Col. 1369] *Et* (“And”) is absent from the same edition] if anyone practises these things [Note: [Col. 1369D–1370C] This entire final clause is absent from the council and Capitularies, but occurs in Burchard and Ivo] [Note: [Col. 1369] *hoc* (“this”): the collected editions], let the cleric be deposed and the layperson anathematized.

### Canon XVI. Egyptian days and the calends of January are not to be observed. Likewise Augustine.

[Note: [Col. 1370C] In most old copies there is only *Item* (“Likewise”), and *Polycarpus* also gives it without an author’s name.]  
[Note: [Col. 1369] It is certain that this is not Augustine’s. In large part it is compiled from Martin of Braga, chapters 71, 73, and 75; *Polycarpus* VI.12.]

Do not observe days called Egyptian, or the calends of January, on which certain songs, feasts, and mutual gifts [Note: [Col. 1369] *donaria* (“presents”): Basel Edition] are given, as though under an omen of good fortune at the beginning of the year; nor months [Note: [Col. 1369] *aliquot* (“several”): the collected editions except Lugdunensis II and III], seasons, days, years, or the course of moon and sun [Note: [Col. 1369] *aut* (“or”): Böhm; *et mensis* (“and [of] the month”): Basel Edition]. For one who observes these things [Note: [Col. 1369] *eas* (“them”): Argentan Edition; *et has* (“and these”): the remaining editions except Lugdunensis II and III], or any divinations, fates, or omens, or attends to them or assents to those observing them, proceeds uselessly and without cause more [Note: [Col. 1369] *et magis* (“and more”): Basel Edition] toward his own condemnation than toward salvation.

So too those who, through certain numerical combinations of letters and of the moon, and through Pythagorean necromancy, inquire into the life or death of sick people or future prosperity [Col. 1370A] or adversity; those who heed dream writings and writings falsely [Note: [Col. 1369] *falsa* (“false,” feminine): Nuremberg, Venice I–II, and Paris editions] entitled with Daniel’s name [Note: [Col. 1369] *in Dan.* (“in Daniel”): Basel Edition]; those who heed lots called those of the holy Apostles, auguries of birds, or utter charms in building houses, arranging marriages, or gathering herbs; and those who place written *pyctaciola* [Note: [Col. 1369] *pictaciolas … scriptas* (“written little placards/amulets”): the collected editions except Basel I and Lugdunensis II–III. The printed *pyctaciola* is uncertain, perhaps *pittaciola*] upon persons or animals for any illness, apart from the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer; or who believe magical falsehoods in hail-producing storms [Note: [Col. 1369] *et tempestatibus* (“and storms”): the collected editions except Basel I and the Lugdunensian editions].

Those who believe such things, or go to their homes, or bring them into their own homes in order to consult them [Note: [Col. 1369] *et* (“and”): the collected editions] [Note: [Col. 1369] *interrogant* (“they consult”): the same editions apart from Basel], should know that they have violated the Christian faith and baptism and, as pagans and apostates—that is, persons who turn back and enemies of God—have gravely incurred God’s wrath for eternity [Col. 1370B], unless, corrected by ecclesiastical penance, they are reconciled to God. For the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1369] 1 Corinthians 10:31]: “Whether you eat or drink, or do anything else, do all in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom we live and move and are.”

Augustine also writes concerning the observance of times in the *Enchiridion* [Note: [Col. 1370C] The words formerly following *Enchiridio*, “that is, manual book,” have been deleted, since they are absent from the older copies], chapter 79 [Note: [Col. 1369] Ivo, *Panormia* VIII.80; *Decretum* XI.19]:

### Canon XVII. It is a grave sin to observe days, months, and years.

Who would suppose [Note: [Col. 1369] *existimaret* (“would suppose”): the collected editions] how great a sin it is to observe days, months, years, and seasons—as do those who on fixed days, months, or years wish or refuse to begin something, because, according to the vain teachings of men, they judge times fortunate or unfortunate [Note: [Col. 1369] *existimant* (“judge”): Basel Edition]—unless we considered the greatness of this evil from the Apostle’s fear, when he says to such persons [Note: [Col. 1369] Galatians 4:11]: “I fear lest perhaps I have laboured among you in vain.”

Likewise, in his exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 4 [Note: [Col. 1369] Ivo, *Decretum* XI.15]:

§ 1. Let the reader understand that superstitious observances of times involve such danger to the soul that the Apostle added at this point [Note: [Col. 1370C–1370D] Augustine, explaining the Apostle’s words in Galatians 4, “You observe days, months, seasons, and years,” shows that these may refer both to Gentiles and Jews; he then adds: “Let the reader choose whichever interpretation he wishes, provided he understands that …”] [Col. 1371A]: “I fear for you [Note: [Col. 1371] *vos* (“you”) is absent from the Paris and Lugdunensian editions and Böhm], lest perhaps I have laboured among you in vain.” Although this is read with such solemnity and authority throughout the churches of the world, our assemblies are nonetheless full of persons who receive from mathematicians the times for conducting [Note: [Col. 1371] *augendarum* (“for increasing”): same source] their affairs. Moreover, they often do not hesitate to warn us not to commence buildings or any similar works on days they call Egyptian [Col. 1372A].

### Canon XVIII. It is lawful to possess herbs or stones without incantation. Likewise Jerome.

[Note: [Col. 1371C] Burchard and Ivo also cite this from Jerome’s sayings, but *Polycarpus* does not name the author.]  
[Note: [Col. 1371] Chapter uncertain; Burchard X.50; Anselm XI.131; Ivo, *Decretum* XI.75; *Polycarpus* VI.12.]

A person afflicted by a demon may possess stones or herbs without incantation.

# CAUSE XXVII

[Col. 1371]

[Col. 1371B]

### GRATIAN

A certain man, having a vow of chastity, betrothed a wife to himself. She, renouncing her former condition, gave herself to another and married him. The man to whom she had first been betrothed demands her back. (Question I.) First, it is asked whether marriage can exist between persons under vows. (Question II.) Second, whether it is lawful for a betrothed woman to leave her betrothed and marry another.

## QUESTION I

### GRATIAN

**Part I.** That persons under vows cannot contract marriages is proved by many authorities.

For in the Fourth Council of Carthage, in its final canon, a statute is found concerning widows who violated their professed continence [Note: [Col. 1371] This is not among the ecclesiastical statutes in Ballerini, although it circulates in the commonly printed editions of the so-called Fourth Council of Carthage; Burchard VIII.39; Ivo, *Decretum* VII.58, and in part VII.147]:

### Canon I. Let widows who have cast off the religious habit and chosen marriage be excommunicated.

Just as the reward of chastity is good, so it must be guarded with greater observance and injunction, so that if any widows, however young in years and left by their husbands at an immature age, have devoted themselves to the Lord, and, laying aside secular dress, have appeared in a religious habit under the testimony of the bishop and the Church, but afterward have passed over to secular marriage, they shall, according to the Apostle, incur condemnation, because they have dared to make void the pledge of chastity which they vowed to the Lord. Such persons, therefore, are to be separated from the communion of Christians, nor are they to share a meal with Christians.

[Note: “Is absent”: absent from the collected editions and the first editions of Basel and Lyons.]

[Note: “Is to be established”: the Spanish Collection reads *constituendum*, “is to be established.”]

[Note: “Although still in younger years”: *quamlibet*, “however much,” is read in the Spanish Collection, by Burchard, Ivo, and the Basel edition; other editions have *quamvis*, “although.” Burchard also reads “and mature,” whereas the other editions have “and not yet mature.”]

[Note: “Immature”: in various editions of the councils, in two Vatican manuscripts, and in the royal manuscript of Soria, the reading is *matura*, “mature.” Ivo has *in matura*, “at a mature [age].”]

[Note: “Devoted themselves”: the Basel edition reads *devoverunt*, “they devoted themselves.”]

[Note: “To the Lord”: the Spanish Collection, Burchard, Ivo, and the collected editions read “to God.”]

[Note: “Secular dress”: the Argentinian edition reads *laica*, “secular.”]

[Note: “Passed over”: the Spanish Collection and the Argentinian, Basel, Nuremberg, and first Venetian editions read *transierint*, “shall have passed over.”]

[Note: “According to the Apostle”: 1 Timothy 5:12.]

[Note: “Dared”: other collected editions read *visae*, “were seen.”]

[Note: “Are to be separated”: the Spanish Collection reads, “let them be excluded, who also are not even …”]

[Note: “Communion”: the collected editions and the first editions of Basel and Nuremberg read “communion or fellowship.”]

[Note: “Nor share a meal”: thus emended from manuscript copies of Gratian, with the words “until they return to the good which they had begun” deleted; those words seem to have been transferred here from the following chapter. In printed and manuscript copies of the councils the reading is: “Such persons are to remain without Christian communion, nor are they even to share a meal with Christians.”]

For if adulterous wives are liable to their husbands under the charge of adultery, how much more shall widows who have changed their religious commitment be marked by the crime of adultery, if they corrupt by lustful pleasure the devotion which they freely, and not under compulsion, offered to God, and make the transition to second marriages? Even if they have been violated by someone through an act of violence, yet afterward consent to remain in marriage to their abductor or violent husband for the pleasure of lust, they are to be held liable to the condemnation set forth above. Of such women the Apostle says: “When they have become wanton, they wish to marry, having condemnation, because they have made void their first pledge.”

[Note: “Adulterous wives”: thus emended from the aforementioned copies of the councils. Previously it read: “For if wives are guilty of adultery, if they have not been subject to their husbands, how much more,” etc. Burchard, Ivo, and the collected editions have this reading, though Burchard and Ivo omit *non*, “not.”]

[Note: “Religious commitment”: the same editions read “the religious commitment of God.”]

[Note: “Have changed”: the Spanish Collection reads “had vowed”; the Basel edition, “shall have changed.”]

[Note: “Freely”: the Spanish Collection reads *spontanee*, “spontaneously.”]

[Note: “Corrupt”: the Basel edition reads *corripuerint*, “shall have rebuked.”]

[Note: “Pleasure”: Burchard and Ivo read *voluntate*, “by will.”]

[Note: “Violated”: the Spanish Collection reads *praereptae*, “snatched away.”]

[Note: “Of such women”: the same editions add “for thus.” Compare 1 Timothy 5:11.]

[Note: “When”: Burchard, Ivo, and the collected editions add *enim*, “for.”]

[Note: “Wish to marry”: the same witnesses add “in Christ.”]

## Chapter II. Concerning widows and virgins who depart from their religious profession

Likewise, from a letter of Gregory sent to Boniface.

[Note: The other collectors likewise cite it thus; it also occurs, somewhat more fully, in the appended *Capitularies*, chapter 215.]

[Note: This appears to be a letter of Gregory III to Boniface of Mainz.—Burchard, book 8, chapter 45; Anselm, book 11, chapter 177; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 204; *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 63.]

Concerning widows departing from their resolution of widowhood, about whom your affection, dearest brother, wished to consult us: I believe you know from St. Paul and from many holy Fathers that, unless they are converted, they have long been condemned. We too judge that they are to be condemned by apostolic authority and excluded from the communion of the faithful and from the thresholds of the Church, until they obey their bishops and return, whether unwillingly or willingly, to the good which they had begun.

§ 1. But concerning virgins who are not veiled, if they go astray, we have this decree of our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Innocent: “Those women who, though not yet covered by the sacred veil, have nevertheless always professed that they would remain in a virginal purpose—although they have not been veiled—if they marry, must perform penance for some period, because their pledge was held by the Lord. For if contracts made in good faith between human beings are customarily dissolved for no reason, how much more can that promise which she made in covenant with God not be dissolved without punishment,” etc.

§ 2. If unmarried virgins not yet veiled are punished with such public penance and excluded from the assembly of the faithful until satisfaction is made, how much more must widows—who are of more mature age and wiser judgment and counsel, have often experienced the company of men, assumed the religious habit, and finally apostatized and returned to their former vomit—be excluded by us and all the faithful from the thresholds of the Church and from the assembly of the faithful until satisfaction, and committed to prisons, so that, in accordance with the Apostle Paul, “delivering such a person to Satan,” their spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.

For concerning such persons the Lord also speaks through Moses, saying: “Remove evil from your midst.” Concerning them He also says through the Prophet: “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance; he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner.” For of such persons, their like, and those who consent to them it is said: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are guilty.”

[Note: “Wished to consult”: the Basel edition reads *voluerit*, “shall have wished.”]

[Note: “The good which they had begun”: Lyons editions II and III read “had begun.”]

[Note: “We have this decree”: compare below, chapter IX.]

[Note: “Have professed”: another reading also has “have professed.”]

[Note: “Although they have not been veiled”: the Basel edition reads “are not.”]

[Note: “Finally”: the Basel edition reads “then.”]

[Note: “Apostatized”: the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venetian editions I–II read “shall have apostatized.”]

[Note: 1 Corinthians 5:5.]

[Note: Basel and Lyons editions II–III add from the Vulgate: “for the destruction of the flesh.”]

[Note: “Day of the Lord”: the Basel edition reads “day of judgment.”]

[Note: Deuteronomy 13:5.]

[Note: Psalm 57:11. The collected editions and Ivo’s *Panormia* add “of the wicked.”]

[Note: “Sinner”: the collected editions read “sinners.”]

[Note: “Their”: the Basel edition reads “these.”]

[Note: Romans 1:32. The collected editions, the first Basel edition, and Ivo’s *Decretum* read “are to be judged.”]

## Chapter III. Widows and virgins may not pass over to marriage after a religious profession

Likewise, from the decree of Pope Gelasius sent to the bishops of Sicily, chapter 9.

[Note: Rather, this is from Symmachus to Caesarius, written A.D. 502.—Burchard, book 8, chapter 46; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 203; *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 64, and, under the heading “Pope Gelasius to Caesarius,” chapter 144; Polycarp, book 4, title 35.]

We do not permit widows to pass over to marriage who have remained for a long observance in a religious profession. Likewise, we forbid virgins to marry who have spent many years of their lives in monasteries.

## Chapter IV. A woman may be corrupted through any bodily sense

Likewise, Cyprian to Pomponius, concerning virgins.

[Note: Written A.D. 249.]

Nor should anyone think herself able to be defended by this excuse, that it can be inspected and tested whether she is a virgin, since both the hands of midwives and their eyes are often deceived; and even if a virgin is found uncorrupted in that part by which a woman may be so examined, she may nevertheless have sinned through another part of the body, which can be corrupted but cannot be inspected. Surely intercourse itself, embraces themselves, conversation itself, kissing, and the shameful and foul sleeping together of two persons—how much disgrace and crime do they confess! If a husband coming upon his bride sees her lying with another, does he not grow indignant and rage, and perhaps, in the pain of jealousy, take a sword in his hand? What then does Christ our Lord and Judge do when He sees His virgin, dedicated to Him and destined for His holiness, lying with another? How indignant and angry He is with her; and what punishments He threatens for unions of this kind, incestuous as they are! In order that each brother may escape His spiritual sword and the coming day of judgment, we must make provision and labor with every care.

[Note: “Eyes”: the original has the singular *oculus*, “eye”; the collected editions and the first Lyons editions II–III likewise.]

[Note: “Are often deceived”: the original reads “is often deceived”; the Basel edition, “may be deceived”; other editions, “are deceived.”]

[Note: “May have sinned”: the collected editions and Lyons II–III read “will be able to have sinned.”]

[Note: “Confess”: the original reads “confesses”; the collected editions and Böhm, “confess.”]

[Note: “Sees”: the Basel edition reads “has seen.”]

[Note: “Through the pain”: the Basel edition reads “before grief.”]

[Note: “Jealousy”: the original reads “envy.”]

[Note: “Take a sword in his hand”: the collected editions and Lyons II–III read “in grief he bears a sword in his hand.”]

[Note: “What then”: the Basel edition reads “And indeed, if”; Lyons II–III, “And what, thus?”]

[Note: “Dedicated”: the Basel edition reads “consecrated.”]

[Note: “With another”: the Basel edition reads “with an adulterer”; the Argentinian edition, “with another or with an adulterer.”]

[Note: “With her”: the collected editions and the first Basel edition add “with her.”]

[Note: “Incestuous”: the Basel edition reads “criminal”; other editions, “in criminal [unions].”]

[Note: “Such”: the collected editions and Lyons II–III read “this kind.”]

[Note: “Labor”: the collected editions read “work diligently.”]

## Chapter V. On the same matter

The same author in the same letter.

But if they have performed penance for this unlawful cohabitation and have separated from one another, let the virgins be examined again with care by midwives; and if they are found to be virgins, let them be admitted to the Church after receiving communion. This warning, however, must be given: if afterward they return to the same men, or live with them in one house and under the same roof, they are to be expelled under a more severe censure and not afterward easily received into the Church. But if any of them are found to have been corrupted and detected, let them perform full penance, because she who committed this crime is the adulteress not of a husband but of Christ; and therefore, after a just period has been assessed, let her return to the Church after making *exomologesis*—that is, confession or penance. But if they persist obstinately and do not separate from one another, let them know that in this shameless obstinacy of theirs they can never be admitted by us into the Church, lest by their sins they begin to furnish others an example leading to ruin. Nor should they think that they can give account for their life or salvation if they refuse to obey bishops and priests.

[Note: “Have performed”: the Basel edition reads “performed … separated.”]

[Note: “Again”: in printed editions of Cyprian and in eight manuscripts collated at Rome for the correction of his works, the reading is *interim*, “meanwhile”; this variation is also noted in the gloss.]

[Note: “And”: the Basel edition reads “because.”]

[Note: “The same roof”: the collected editions, the first Basel edition, and Lyons II–III read “one and the same.”]

[Note: “Are to be expelled”: the Basel edition reads “rejected.”]

[Note: “Into the Church”: the collected editions and Lyons II–III read “in the Church.”]

[Note: “If any of them”: those editions read, “if any corrupted woman among them has been detected, let her perform [penance].”]

[Note: “Because”: absent from those editions.]

[Note: “She who committed”: those editions read, “she who is not now …”]

[Note: The Argentinian edition reads the corrupt form *exanieloyson sui*; the Basel edition, *exhomoloyso sui*; the other editions except Lyons II–III, *exameloyson sui*, adding “that is, by confession or penance.”]

## Chapter VI. Let a cleric be deposed and a layman excommunicated who has committed adultery with a consecrated woman

Likewise, from the Sixth Synod in Trullo, chapter 4.

[Note: Held A.D. 692.—Trullan Collection, part 2, tome 30, chapter 5.]

If any bishop, priest, deacon, subdeacon, reader, psalmist, or doorkeeper commits adultery with a woman consecrated to God, let him be deposed, because he has corrupted the bride of Christ; but if he is a layman, let him be excommunicated.

## Chapter VII. Widows and girls who marry after assuming the religious habit are to be suspended from communion

Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 8.

[Note: It has not been found in the councils of Toledo. It is, however, in book 7 of the *Capitularies*, chapter 338.]

[Note: Rather, this is from the Council of Paris, held A.D. 615, chapter 13.—Burchard, book 8, chapter 48; Anselm, book 11, chapter 96; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 66.]

Concerning widows and girls who have changed the religious habit in their own homes, whether through their parents or by themselves: if afterward, contrary to the institutions of the Fathers or the precepts of the canons, they think marriages ought to be contracted, both are to be kept suspended from communion until they amend what they have unlawfully perpetrated. If they neglect to amend it, they are to be permanently excluded from communion and from every meal shared by Christians.

[Note: “Have changed”: the Basel edition reads “shall have changed.”]

[Note: “Think”: the collected editions, the first Basel edition, and Lyons II–III read “thought.”]

[Note: “Both”: the original, Burchard, Ivo, and the Basel edition have *utrique*, “both parties”; they also read “suspended … excluded.”]

## Chapter VIII. On the same matter

Likewise, from the Council of Pope Martin. [PALEA.]

[Note: This chapter is absent from some copies of Gratian. Burchard and Ivo, though not Ivo’s *Panormia*, cite it from the Council of Mainz, chapter 6. It occurs in the Council of Tribur, chapter 25. In this chapter and the two following, decrees of Gelasius are cited as they stand in the *Code of Canons*, that is, in Dionysius.]

[Note: Rather, this is from the Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895.—Burchard, book 8, chapter 36; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 197; *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 55.]

“No bishop shall presume to veil widows, as is established in chapter XIII of the decrees of Pope Gelasius: neither divine authority nor the form of the canons has prescribed this. But if she has professed continence by her own will, chapter XXI of the same Gelasius states that her intention must answer for itself before God; for, just as according to the Apostle she was in no way forbidden to marry if she could not remain continent, so, once she has deliberated with herself, she ought to preserve for God the pledged faith of chastity. But we, supported by the authority of the Fathers, decree and freely judge in this holy council that, if she has voluntarily put upon herself a veil, even though unconsecrated, and in church has offered the oblation among the veiled women of God, whether willing or unwilling she must thereafter retain the habit of consecrated life, although she may wish to establish by an oath that she put the veil upon herself with this condition and understanding, that she could put it off again.”

[Note: “Chapter XIII”: thus in the *Code of Canons*; but in the first letter of Gelasius to the bishops through Lucania it is chapter 15, just as the passage called a chapter here is chapter 23 in that letter.]

[Note: “Has prescribed”: the cited collections and the collected editions read “has established.”]

[Note: “But we”: the Council of Tribur reads: “Supported by the authority of the paternal sentence, in this sacred assembly we decree,” etc. These same provisions concerning the widow who voluntarily put upon herself an unconsecrated veil occur in the *Decretals*, chapter *Viduas*, title “On Religious Houses”; printed codices cite it from the Council of Arles, but the first collection and ancient codices cite it from Orléans.]

[Note: “Holy council”: the original and cited collections read “sacred assembly”; the Basel edition, “sacred common council.”]

## Chapter IX. Concerning those who, having vowed virginity, marry although not yet covered by the sacred veil

Likewise, from the decrees of Pope Innocent, chapter 20 in the *Code of Canons*, and letter 2 to Victricius, chapter 13.

[Note: Written A.D. 404. Compare above, chapter II.—Burchard, book 8, chapter 12; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 18; Polycarp, book 4, title 35.]

Those women who, though not yet covered by the sacred veil, have nevertheless professed that they would always remain in a virginal purpose—although they have not been veiled—if they should happen to marry, must perform penance for some period, because their pledge was held by the Lord. For if a contract of good faith is customarily dissolved among human beings for no reason, how much more should that promise which she made in covenant with God not be dissolved without punishment? For if the Apostle said that those who had departed from the purpose of widowhood “have condemnation, because they have made void their first pledge,” how much more [is this true of] virgins who have not at all kept faith with their agreement?

[Note: “Not yet”: the collected editions read “not yet … are covered.”]

[Note: “Covered by the sacred veil”: the Spanish Collection reads “are consecrated.”]

[Note: “Always”: absent from the Spanish Collection and the original cited by Coustant.]

[Note: “Have professed”: the Basel edition reads “shall have professed”; the Spanish Collection and the cited original, “had promised.”]

[Note: “Although they have not been veiled”: the cited original and the Basel edition read “are not”; other editions, “are.”]

[Note: “Must perform”: thus emended from the *Code of Canons*, the letter, and the Council of Tours; the same reading occurs above in the chapter *Viduas*. Here even the manuscripts had: “it is permitted to undertake penance for some period.” The Spanish Collection and the collected editions read this; Burchard reads: “they must be recalled, and they must perform penance.”]

[Note: “The Lord”: the cited original and the collected editions except Basel read “God.”]

[Note: “If”: the Spanish Collection and the collected editions read “For if”; the whole sentence is absent from Burchard.]

[Note: “Is customary”: the Basel edition reads “are customary.”]

[Note: “That”: the Spanish Collection reads “this.”]

[Note: “Made in covenant”: the Spanish Collection and Dionysius read “made”; Ivo likewise.]

[Note: “Should not be”: Dionysius and Ivo read “cannot be”; in Ivo this is the end of the chapter.]

[Note: “The Apostle”: the cited original and the Spanish Collection read “Paul.” Compare 1 Timothy 5:12.]

[Note: “Departed”: the Spanish Collection reads “shall have departed”; the cited originals and collected editions, “departed.”]

[Note: “Said”: the Spanish Collection and Dionysius read “directed”; Burchard and the Basel edition, “had said”; the cited originals, Dionysius, and the collected editions except Basel add “them.”]

[Note: “Condemnation”: the cited original, Dionysius, Burchard, and the Basel edition read “damnation.”]

[Note: “Faith with their agreement”: the cited original reads “shall break faith with the prior promise”; Dionysius and Burchard, “have attempted to break faith with the prior promise”; the Basel edition, “are attempting to break faith with their agreement.”]

## Chapter X. Consecrated virgins are not to be admitted to penance if they marry publicly afterward

Likewise, from the decree of the same pope, chapter 19 in the *Code of Canons*; in the letter to Victricius, chapter 12.

[Note: Burchard, book 8, chapter 13; Anselm, book 11, chapter 94; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 17; Polycarp, there and book 6, title 20.]

Those who marry Christ spiritually and are veiled by a priest, if they subsequently marry publicly, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the men to whom they joined themselves have departed from the world. For if this rule is observed concerning human beings, that any woman who marries while her husband is alive is considered an adulteress and is not granted leave to perform penance unless one of them has died, how much more must it be observed concerning her who had first joined herself to an immortal bridegroom and afterward passed over to human marriage?

[Note: “Marry”: in the old edition of the councils and letters and in the printed *Code of Canons*, the reading is *nupserint*, “have married”; the original in Coustant, Dionysius, and the Spanish Collection have *nupserunt*, “married.” But two manuscripts have *nubunt*, “marry,” after which all copies continue, “and are veiled by a priest”; this has therefore been supplied.]

[Note: “And”: absent from the collected editions except the first Basel edition.]

[Note: “Are veiled”: the cited original and the Spanish Collection read “feared to be veiled.”]

[Note: “If they subsequently marry publicly”: older Cologne and Paris editions read: “if afterward they marry, or are corrupted either publicly or secretly.” The two- and three-volume Cologne edition reads: “if afterward they either marry publicly or are corrupted secretly.” The final four-volume edition reads: “if afterward they either marry publicly or corrupt themselves secretly.” The Spanish Collection, Anselm, and Ivo have the second wording; Dionysius, the cited original, Burchard, and Regino have the third.]

[Note: The Basel and Lyons II–III editions add: “so that they may be restored to their former rank.”]

[Note: “Unless the men”: Dionysius, the cited original, Regino, and Burchard IV have the singular “unless the man.”]

[Note: “From the world”: the cited original reads “from secular life”; Dionysius and Burchard, “from the world”; the Spanish Collection, “from this life”; Ivo, “has departed.”]

[Note: “Human beings”: the cited original and Anselm read “all”; the Spanish Collection, “lay human beings.”]

[Note: “Is not granted”: the collected editions and Lyons II–III read “is not granted.”]

[Note: “One of them”: the cited original, the Spanish Collection, Regino, Burchard, and Ivo read “one out of them.”]

[Note: “Passed over”: the Basel edition reads “shall have passed over”; Ivo and Anselm, “chose to pass over.”]

## Chapter XI. Shameful persons among monks or nuns are to be expelled from the Church and confined in prisons

Likewise, from the Council of Tribur, chapter 6.

[Note: This chapter occurs in letter 1 of Siricius, and in the *Code of Canons* is chapter 15 among his decrees; Burchard and Anselm also cite it; Corr. book 7, chapter 188, cites it as well, though it does not occur in the collected Code. Part of this chapter occurs below under “If anyone sacred,” in the same Question; this portion is found in the Council of Tribur, which survives.]

[Note: These are excerpts from Siricius’s letter to Himerius, written A.D. 385, and are partly repeated in chapters 23 and 26 of the Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895.—Regino, book 2, chapter 164; Burchard, book 8, chapter 29; Polycarp, book 4, title 34.]

We command that shameful and detestable persons among monks—namely, monks and nuns—who, casting aside their purpose of holiness, have mingled themselves in unlawful and sacrilegious defilement, and, brought by despair of conscience to a precipitous state, have freely begotten children from illicit embraces, be expelled from the assembly of monasteries and gatherings of churches; so that, confined in their own prisons and mourning such a great crime with continual lamentation, they may be purified by the cleansing fire of repentance, and so that aid may be given them, even at death, through the grace of communion, solely in view of mercy.

[Note: “Monks”: some witnesses add “namely.”]

[Note: “To a precipitous state”: thus emended from many editions of Siricius’s letters and from the *Code of Canons*. Previously it read: “to the judgment of their own conscience”; the Basel edition omits the phrase.]

[Note: “Confined”: the same edition reads “shut up.”]

[Note: “Mourning”: the same edition reads “weeping.”]

## Chapter XII. If a monk or a virgin consecrated to the Lord marries, let them be excommunicated

Likewise, from the same source.

[Note: This is chapter 16 of the Council of Chalcedon in Dionysius’s translation; part of it is cited below under “If anyone sacred.”]

[Note: Chapter 16, Council of Chalcedon, held A.D. 451, translated by Dionysius.—Burchard, book 8, chapter 36; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 49; Polycarp, there.]

We decree that a virgin who has consecrated herself to God, and likewise a monk, may not contract the rights of marriage. If they are found to have done this, let them be excommunicated. But we decree that the bishop of the place has authority to grant mercy and humane treatment to those who confess.

[Note: The Basel and Lyons II–III editions add: “after reaching adult age.”]

[Note: “This”: the Argentinian edition omits it; the Basel edition reads “this [woman]”; other editions, “these [persons].”]

[Note: “We decree”: Burchard, Ivo, the Basel and Lyons I editions, and the Paris edition read “we have decreed.”]

## Chapter XIII. While they live, those who knowingly unite themselves to consecrated women are to afflict themselves with the lamentations of penance

Likewise, from the same source.

[Note: Burchard and Ivo attribute this chapter to Paschal.]

[Note: Uncertain chapter.—Burchard, book 8, chapter 31; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 50.]

Therefore those who knowingly join themselves in marriage to consecrated women, to the injury of Christ, are to be separated according to the censure of Christian zeal. They must never be permitted to be bound or joined in a marital bond, but, while they live, must grievously afflict themselves with the lamentations of penance.

[Note: “Therefore”: absent from Ivo and the Argentinian and Basel editions.]

[Note: “Consecrated women”: Burchard and Ivo add *feminis*, “women.”]

[Note: “Knowingly”: the Basel and Lyons II–III editions read “with knowledge.”]

[Note: “In marriage”: Burchard, Ivo, and the collected editions read “in matrimony.”]

[Note: The Basel edition adds “or joined.”]

## Chapter XIV. Those who join themselves to sacred virgins are to be deprived of holy communion

Likewise, from the same source.

[Note: This chapter is number 12 in Gelasius’s first letter, and chapter 20 among his decrees in the *Code of Canons*. It is also reported in book 1, chapter 106 of the *Capitularies*, and in Polycarp under Gelasius’s name.]

[Note: From Gelasius’s letter to the bishops of Lucania, written A.D. 494.—Regino, book 2, chapter 166; Burchard, book 8, chapter 32; Anselm, book 11, chapter 95; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 51.]

We have learned that some persons rashly join themselves to sacred virgins and, after a purpose has been dedicated to God, enter into incestuous and sacrilegious unions. It is right that they be immediately thrust out from holy communion and not received at all except through public and approved penance. Yet viaticum is not to be denied to them when they depart this world, if they have repented worthily.

[Note: The Spanish Collection and Anselm read: “And certainly to these persons.”]

[Note: “Yet”: the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venetian editions I–II read “only.”]

[Note: “If they have repented worthily”: the Spanish Collection, Regino, and Anselm read “nevertheless.”]

## Chapter XV. She who refuses to depart from fornication is to be recalled and confined in a monastery

Likewise, Gregory.

[Note: A letter on this same matter seems to have been written to Bishop Marinianus, *Register*, book 8, letter 9. This chapter, however, was either taken from another letter or has been substantially altered.]

[Note: These words appear to have been excerpted by Regino, book 2, chapter 165, from Gregory the Great’s letter to Marinianus of Ravenna, letter 42, book 7, written A.D. 597.—Trullan Collection, part 1, tome 55, chapter 84.]

It has come to us that a certain utterly wicked man, by diabolical instigation, persuaded a certain woman consecrated to God to leave her monastery; that she was recalled by a certain man from whom she had gone out; and that this utterly wicked man, again driving the woman from the monastery by evil persuasion, is keeping her with himself shamelessly. We desire, therefore, that by the authority of your episcopate she be recalled and confined in the monastery.

[Note: “Persuaded”: the collected editions, the first Basel edition, and Lyons II–III read “had persuaded.”]

[Note: “And that”: Böhm reads “but that.”]

[Note: “From a man”: the Basel and Lyons editions read “from a good man.”]

[Note: “The woman”: absent from Regino and the Basel edition.]

[Note: Regino adds “until now.”]

[Note: “Therefore”: the Basel edition reads “indeed.”]

[Note: “Confined”: Regino reads “thrust in.”]

## Chapter XVI. Widows may not lawfully depart from their sacred purpose after receiving the veil

Likewise, from the Council of Orléans, chapter 3.

[Note: It appears that Regino, book 2, chapter 179, and chapter 25 of the Council of Tribur intended to render this passage.—Burchard, book 8, chapter 35; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 3, chapter 198; *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 54.]

The holy synod decreed that widows who, by their voluntary will, receive the sacred veil from the altar of conversion must remain in the same purpose. For we decree that, after they have once consecrated themselves to the Lord under the veil, and have made offerings among the veiled women, it is not lawful for them again to be permitted to lie to the Holy Spirit.

[Note: “Receive”: the Basel edition reads “accept.”]

[Note: Regino, Burchard, and Ivo’s *Decretum* add “them.”]

[Note: The cited collections add: “and have made offerings among the veiled women.”]

## Chapter XVII. Let one who takes in marriage a woman covered by the sacred veil be anathema

Likewise, from the same source.

[Note: Burchard and Ivo also cite this from the Council of Orléans. It occurs, however, in the Council of Tribur, chapter 23.]

[Note: Chapter 23, Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895.—Burchard, book 8, chapter 38; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 57.]

If anyone takes in marriage a woman consecrated by the sacred veil and, after a purpose has been dedicated to God, enters into incestuous and sacrilegious unions, then, as is read in chapter XX of the enactments of Pope Gelasius, it is right that they immediately be thrust out from holy communion and not received at all except through public and approved penance. Yet, if they repent, viaticum is not to be denied them when they depart this world.

§ 1. In chapter XVI of the Council of Chalcedon: “Let those who commit this be excommunicated; but mercy is to be granted to those who confess, by the authority of the bishop.”

§ 2. Likewise, in chapter 6 of the letter of Pope Siricius: “If veiled women consecrated to God, casting aside their purpose of holiness, secretly mingle themselves in sacrilegious defilement and publicly and freely bear children from unlawful embraces, it has been ordained that these shameful and detestable persons be expelled from the company of monasteries and assemblies of churches, so that, confined in prisons, they may mourn so great a crime with continual lamentation.” Therefore, by the word of the Lord and canonical authority, we command in this holy synod that they be entirely separated and bound by oath that they shall henceforth live together beneath one roof.

[Note: “They”: absent from the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venetian editions I–II.]

[Note: “Yet”: the Basel edition reads “these.”]

[Note: “Chapter XX”: that is, in the Dionysio-Hadrian *Code of Canons*.]

[Note: Chapter XVI of Chalcedon: the Basel edition reads, “These … are excommunicated.”]

[Note: Compare chapter XI.]

[Note: “These shameful and detestable persons”: Burchard and Ivo read “these detestable marriages”; the collected editions read “these detestable and shameful persons.”]

[Note: “Confined”: Burchard, Ivo, and the collected editions read “thrust down.”]

[Note: “Therefore”: absent from the original and cited collections; the Argentinian and Basel editions read “in.”]

## Chapter XVIII. She who has cast off her religious dress is to be compelled to return to the habit and be confined in a monastery

Likewise, Gregory to Vitalian, bishop of Siponto, book VII, indiction 1, letter 9.

[Note: Letter 8, written A.D. 598, book 8 of the Maurist edition.—Burchard, book 8, chapter 49; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 67.]

[Note: Burchard and Ivo also cite this from the Council of Orléans. It occurs, however, in the Council of Tribur, chapter 23.]

If you had been the guardian of the religious habit, or knew that you were a bishop, then, while you were stationed there, the daughter of Tullianus, of glorious memory, master of the soldiers, could neither have returned to secular dress after casting off her religious garments, nor have been able to send us her perverse letter. But because you are oppressed by excessive negligence and torpor, an unlawful act has at present been committed with impunity, to your disgrace. For if, as we have said, you had been diligent, the punishment of the most wicked woman ought to have reached us before her offence. Therefore, because you are so dull and so negligent that, unless you experience canonical coercion in your own case, you do not know how to maintain strictness and discipline in others, we shall show you at a suitable time, if it please the Lord, how diligent you ought to be.

§ 1. Therefore, upon receiving this letter, keep watch; and, now at least awakened, carry out what, oppressed by sloth, you have until now delayed. Accordingly, by your diligence apprehend the aforesaid woman together with Sergius our defender; immediately recall her, without any excuse, to the habit which she has wickedly despised; and also thrust her into a monastery, where she may be kept under the strictest guard. Show such complete concern concerning her that through your severity she may recognize how wicked is what she has committed.

§ 2. If in this matter any layperson—or cleric, according to another reading—something we do not believe, should attempt by any contrivance to oppose you, hasten to suspend him from participation in the most sacred communion and report to us, so that, since he has failed to perceive by his own reflection how abominable is what he has presumed, he may recognize it through the manner of his correction.

§ 3. In all these matters strive to show yourself careful and watchful, so that negligence may not double your fault, but your diligence may to some extent lessen it.

[Note: “Guardian of the religious habit”: Burchard and Ivo add “had been”; the Basel, Lyons, and Paris editions read “were.”]

[Note: “Knew”: the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venetian editions I–II read “know.”]

[Note: “Tullianus”: the Basel edition reads “Julianus.”]

[Note: “Could”: the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venetian editions I–II read “could have.”]

[Note: “For if”: the original, Burchard, Ivo, and the collected editions read “just as … if only.”]

[Note: “Strictness”: Ivo reads “a stricter discipline.”]

[Note: “The Lord”: the collected editions and the first Basel edition read “God.”]

[Note: “Negligence”: the collected editions read “by negligence … may.”]

[Note: Burchard and Ivo read “and diligence.”]

## Chapter XIX. One who has returned from a religious profession to secular dress is to be committed to strict custody

The same author to Sergius the Defender, book VII, indiction 2, letter 10.

[Note: Letter 9, written A.D. 598, book 8 of the Maurist edition.]

If you had been a man, or had possessed any discernment [Note: [Col. 1381] *strictness* (*districtionem*): original], you ought to have shown yourself so vigilant a guardian of regular discipline that you would have corrected by punishment [Col. 1381B] [Note: [Col. 1381] “would have corrected by punishment”: Paris edition.—“would have corrected by punishment”: Arg., Nor., Ven. I–II.—“would have corrected by punishment”: remaining editions] what was unlawfully done there before news of it reached us. But since excessive folly makes you negligent [Note: [Col. 1381] “may make”: Basel edition], we are offended not only by those persons, but are also moved to punish your own sloth. Therefore, setting aside every delay and every excuse, hasten, together with our brother and fellow bishop Vitalian, to apprehend the daughter of Tullian [Note: [Col. 1381] Julian: same edition], of glorious memory, master of the soldiery. Having cast off the religious garments which she had voluntarily assumed [Note: [Col. 1381] “assumed”: same edition], she has disfigured herself in secular dress. Recall her once more to the religious habit and send her into a monastery [Note: [Col. 1381] “in a monastery”: Arg. and Basel editions], where she may be kept under the strictest guard. Do not allow her custody to be relaxed in any respect until you receive further written instructions from us. For if you prove negligent or slow in this matter in any way, know that punishment will be inflicted upon you with the utmost severity [Col. 1381C], so that, through the penalty’s disclosure [Note: [Col. 1381] “cutting off” (*resecante*): original, collected editions, and first Lyons edition], you may come to know what you do not know from yourself: namely, that if, as we have said, you had possessed human understanding, we ought to have learned from you beforehand—even with punishment—that the things which you are now commanded to do had been done [Note: [Col. 1381] “you ought previously”: collected editions] by you [Note: [Col. 1381] “by you”: same editions].

### C. XX. Permission to marry is not granted to those who have resolved to preserve continence.

Likewise Augustine, *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, ch. 24. [Note: [Col. 1381] Not Augustine.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 6, ch. 4; *Decretum*, pt. 8, ch. 72.]

Permission to marry is granted to some: namely, to those [Col. 1382A] who have in no way professed virginal or [Note: [Col. 1381] “and”: Böhm] widowed chastity [Note: [Col. 1381] “chastity”: collected editions]. But it is not granted [Note: [Col. 1381] “conceded”: Basel edition] to others: namely, to those who have resolved to be virgins or continent persons. Fornication, however, is permitted to no one with impunity.

### C. XXI. Women who violate a resolve of continence are worse than adulteresses.

Likewise, in the book *On the Good of Marriage*. [Note: [Col. 1381D] Augustine’s actual words from *On the Good of Widowhood* occur below in this same causa, ch. “Nuptiarum,” at the words “Quapropter non possum.” In Bede’s commentary on 1 Corinthians 7, however, Augustine’s passage is reported somewhat differently.] [Note: [Col. 1381] cf. below, ch. 41.]

It is plain that women who have fallen away from a better resolve, if they marry, are worse than adulteresses by reason of the holier chastity that has been vowed to God.

### C. XXII. A monk and a virgin who dedicate themselves to God cannot be joined in marriage.

Likewise, from the Council of Chalcedon, ch. 16. [Note: [Col. 1382D] This is the same canon cited above in this same causa, ch. “Virginem.” That was Dionysius’s translation; this is the ancient translation, from which the next two chapters also derive.] [Note: [Col. 1381] Held A.D. 451.—Above, ch. 12, the same is reported from Dionysius.]

If any virgin dedicates herself to God, and likewise any monk [Col. 1382B] [Note: [Col. 1381] “and a monk”: Spanish Collection], they are not permitted [Note: [Col. 1381] “to be permitted”: same source] to be joined in marriage [Note: [Col. 1381] “be joined”: Basel edition]. If they are found doing this, let them remain excommunicated. We decree, however, that clemency may be shown them if the bishop of the place judges it appropriate [Note: [Col. 1381] “that clemency may be shown in their case”: Spanish Collection].

### C. XXIII. A deaconess who marries after ordination is to be anathematized.

Likewise, from the same council, ch. 15. [Note: [Col. 1381] Polycarp, bk. 4, tit. 36.]

We decree that a deaconess ought not to be ordained before the age of forty [Note: [Col. 1381] absent from the Spanish Collection], and then only after careful examination [Note: [Col. 1381] “this woman”: Basel edition]. But if she has received ordination, has observed the ministry for however long a time [Note: [Col. 1381] “in the ministry”: Spanish Collection], and afterward gives herself in marriage, thereby insulting the grace of God, let this woman be anathematized [Note: [Col. 1381] “this man”: Basel edition; “this thing”: Arg., Nor., and Ven. I–II editions], together with the man who entered into her marriage [Note: [Col. 1381] “and with”: collected editions except Basel and Lyons II–III].

[Col. 1382C]

### C. XXIV. Those who break a promise of virginity are to be reckoned among the twice-married.

Likewise, from the Synod of Ancyra, ch. 18. [Note: [Col. 1381] Held A.D. 314.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, ch. 351, from Dionysius.]

All who, having promised virginity [Note: [Col. 1381] “having promised”: Spanish Collection], have broken that profession in contempt of it [Note: [Col. 1381] masculine: “having broken”: same collection; Basel edition], must be counted among the twice-married—that is, among those who have proceeded to a second marriage.

### C. XXV. Virgins dedicated to God are not to be given communion even at the end, if they have served lust.

Likewise, from the Council of Elvira, ch. 13. [Note: [Col. 1381] Held no later than A.D. 310.]

Virgins who have dedicated themselves to God [Note: [Col. 1381] “have dedicated”: Spanish Collection; “shall have dedicated”: Nor. and Ven. I–II editions], if they have broken [Col. 1383A] the covenant of virginity [Note: [Col. 1383C] “They have broken”: thus in all printed and manuscript codices of this council that were collated; but in the Third Council of Mainz, under Arnulf, ch. 26, where this is quoted, it reads: “have betrayed.”] and have served that same lust, not understanding what they have lost [Note: [Col. 1383] “have committed”: Arg. edition], it has been decided that communion is not to be given them even at the end [Note: [Col. 1383] “the end”: Spanish Collection]. But if they have persuaded themselves [Note: [Col. 1383C] “Themselves”: in two Vatican codices of the councils it reads, “But if, once persuaded …” In the Council of Mainz: “But if, once persuaded, they have fallen into the defects of a weak body.” In the royal Lucca codex: “But if, once persuaded or corrupted by a lapse of a weak body”; as in the margin of the Council of Mainz. In three Cologne editions of the councils and two Paris editions it reads: “But if they themselves repent because of weakness,” etc.] that they fell through bodily weakness, and have done penance throughout [Note: [Col. 1383C] “Throughout”: this word is absent from several old copies of Gratian, the old Cologne edition of the councils, two Paris editions, and two Vatican codices; [Note: [Col. 1383] “all”: Spanish Collection]] their whole life [Note: [Col. 1383] added: “such women”: Spanish Collection], and have abstained from intercourse [Note: [Col. 1383] the words “and … abstained” are absent from the Basel edition; Spanish Collection: “that they abstain from intercourse”] [Note: [Col. 1383C] “Have abstained”: all editions of the councils, two Vatican codices, and the royal Lucca codex continue with these words: “because they appear rather to have fallen”; these words are absent from the Council of Mainz], it has been decided that they ought to receive communion at the end [Note: [Col. 1383] “the end”: Spanish Collection].

### C. XXVI. A cleric’s daughter is to be compelled to do penance if, though devoted, she takes a husband.

Likewise, from the Council of Martin of Braga, ch. 30. [Note: [Col. 1383] In the collected editions, “of the Pope”; cf. First Council of Toledo, ch. 19. “Concerning … deacon”: these words are a chapter heading in Martin.]

Concerning the daughter of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon: if she is devoted and takes a husband, and if her father or mother receives her affectionately [Note: [Col. 1383] singular: “receives her”: collected editions], they are to be excluded from communion. Let the father know that he will have to answer for the case before the council [Col. 1383B]. The woman is not to be admitted to communion unless, after her husband has died, she has done penance. But if, while he is living, she withdraws from him and does penance [Note: [Col. 1383] “does penance”: Spanish Collection and Basel edition], or seeks communion, she shall receive it at the very end [Note: [Col. 1383] absent from the Spanish Collection] of her life [Note: [Col. 1383] added: “her”: collected editions] when dying [Note: [Col. 1383] “communion”: Spanish Collection].

### C. XXVII. A devoted woman is not to be received into the Church unless she ceases to sin.

Likewise, from the First Council of Toledo, ch. 16. [Note: [Col. 1383] Held A.D. 400.—Anselm, bk. 11, ch. 100.]

We decree [Note: [Col. 1383] absent from the Spanish Collection] that a devoted woman who sins is not to be received [Note: [Col. 1383] added: “to be”: collected editions] in the Church [Note: [Col. 1383] “into the Church”: Spanish Collection], unless she ceases to sin; and, if she ceases and performs suitable penance for ten years [Note: [Col. 1383] i.e. let her do penance for ten years: collected editions except Basel], let her receive communion. Before she is received into the Church [Note: [Col. 1383] “to the Church”: Anselm] for prayer, she is not to attend the meal of any Christian woman. If she is admitted, the woman who received her is likewise to be held excluded [Note: [Col. 1384C] “Excluded”: corrected from more recent editions of the councils, the royal Lucca codex, and Martin of Braga, ch. 31, which repeats this chapter; although the old one-volume Cologne edition, two Paris editions, and two Vatican codices read “in absence,” [Note: [Col. 1383] thus collected editions], as also in manuscript copies of Gratian]. An equal penalty shall bind her seducer [Col. 1384A]. But the woman who has taken a husband is not to be admitted to penance unless either, while her husband is still living, she begins to live chastely, or after he has died.

### C. XXVIII. Concerning a nun led into the fall of adultery.

Likewise Gregory to Januarius, Bishop of Cagliari, book III, letter 9. [Note: [Col. 1383] Letter 9, written A.D. 594, bk. 4 of the Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 123.]

If any nun, whether through earlier [Note: [Col. 1383] “more ancient”: collected editions] license or through the evil custom of impunity, has been led into the fall of adultery, or has been drawn into the abyss of sexual violation [Note: [Col. 1383] “future”: original], after the fitting severity of punishment we desire her to be placed for penance in another, stricter monastery of virgins, so that there she may devote herself to prayers and fasts [Note: [Col. 1384C] “Fasts”: most editions of the letters read, “and by fasting may make progress in penance for herself,” etc.; the old Vatican manuscript of the letters and Ivo read as Gratian does], and thus make progress in repentance [Col. 1384B], while furnishing the others a fear-inspiring example of stricter discipline. The man found with such women in any wickedness is to be deprived of communion [Note: [Col. 1383] “of all communion”: collected editions], if he is a layman; if he is a cleric [Note: [Col. 1383] added: “he be”: original and Ivo], he is also to be removed from his office and at once confined in a monastery, to bewail his transgressions [Note: [Col. 1383] “confined again”: Basel edition].

### C. XXIX. After worthy penance, those who violate religious women are to receive communion.

Likewise Gregory to Januarius, Bishop, book III, letter 24. [Note: [Col. 1383] Letter 27, written A.D. 594, bk. 4 of the Maurist edition.]

But those who violated the aforesaid [Note: [Col. 1383] “religious”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions; absent from the rest] women who left their monasteries, and who are now said to be suspended from communion [Note: [Col. 1384C] “Suspended from communion”: corrected from most old copies of Gratian and the original itself; formerly it read, “to be suspended from communion,” [Note: [Col. 1383] thus collected editions except the first Arg. and Basel editions]], if your Fraternity finds that they have worthily repented of such an offense, we wish you to restore them to sacred communion.

[Col. 1385A]

### C. XXX. Concerning the laws of the emperors.
