Likewise, from the Novels of Emperor Justinian. [Note: [Col. 1385] Julian, *Epitome of the Novels*, 115, ch. 67.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 143; Polycarp, bk. 4, tit. 38.]

If anyone abducts, solicits, or corrupts an *ascetria*—that is, a female ascetic [Note: [Col. 1385C] “Assisteriam”: it should unquestionably be read *ascetriam*, from the Greek and Latin Novels, Julian the Antecessor, and Polycarp; but it has not been changed because of the gloss; [Note: [Col. 1385] “assistriam”: Arg. and Basel editions; “matricuriam”: Ivo]]—or a deaconess, nun [Note: [Col. 1385] “monasterial woman”: Ivo; added: “or monastria”: Basel edition], or any other woman having religious life or habit, his property, and that of those contaminated by participation in such a crime, is to be claimed by the religious institution in which such a woman lived [Note: [Col. 1385] “lives”: Böhm], through religious bishops, stewards, provincial governors, and their officials; but the offenders themselves are subject to capital punishment. The woman is to be sought everywhere and, with her possessions, committed to a safer monastery [Note: [Col. 1385] “into a monastery”: Basel edition; “to the protection of the monastery”: Ivo]. But if she is a deaconess having legitimate children, the lawful portion is to be given to her legitimate children.

[Col. 1385B]

### C. XXXI. Women who are veiled under the pretext of religion must chastely observe the religious habit.

Likewise, from the decree of Pope Eugenius II, in the Roman Council, ch. 29. [Note: [Col. 1385C] In the council preserved in the Vatican Library these are the actual words of the decree: [Note: [Col. 1385] Burchard followed Anselm’s dedicated collection, which also reports this chapter, bk. 6, ch. 41, and other chapters of Eugenius’s council in abridged form:] “Women who have assumed a religious habit or veil under the pretext of religious life, while they were of marriageable age, are thereafter not to be permitted to unite themselves to a man; but, choosing monasteries, they are to live under rule, or in their homes are to observe chastely the habit they have assumed.”] [Note: [Col. 1385] Held A.D. 826.—Burchard, bk. 8, ch. 54; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 72; Polycarp, bk. 4, tit. 34.]

Women veiled under the pretext of religion are either to live under rule in a monastery or to observe chastely in their own homes the habit they have assumed.

### C. XXXII. A monk who takes a wife is never to obtain the office of a sacred rank.

Likewise, from the First Council of Orléans, chs. 22 and 23. [Note: [Col. 1385] Held A.D. 511.]

A monk [Note: [Col. 1385] accusative: “a monk”: Spanish Collection] may not have a stole in the monastery or *zancas* [Note: [Col. 1385] Read with the Spanish Collection: *zancas*, a kind of footwear] [Col. 1385C]. And if afterward he is joined to a wife [Note: [Col. 1385D] “Afterward”: thus in the old Cologne edition of the councils, two Paris editions, and two Vatican codices. In later Cologne editions: “And if afterward [he is joined] to a concubine or wife”], being guilty of so great a violation, he is never to obtain the office of an ecclesiastical rank.

[Col. 1386A]

### C. XXXIII. Widows who wish to marry should do so before professing continence.

Likewise Augustine, *On the Good of Widowhood*, ch. 8. [Note: [Col. 1385] cf. at ch. 2, p. 27.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 200; *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 146.]

Widows who do not keep continence should marry before they profess [Note: [Col. 1385D] “Having professed”: thus also in Ivo and the *Panormia*. But Augustine reads: “before they profess continence, before they vow to God”] continence and vow it to God. If they do not fulfill it, they are justly condemned [Note: [Col. 1385] “are to be condemned”: Ivo, *Panormia*].

### C. XXXIV. A widow is not to be permitted to abandon her vow after professing continence.

Likewise Nicholas to Charles, Archbishop, and his suffragans. [Note: [Col. 1385] Rather, ch. 21 of the Council of Worms, held A.D. 868.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 199; *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 145.]

A widow [Note: [Col. 1385] absent from the Basel edition] who has placed the sacred veil upon her head [Note: [Col. 1385] “has placed”: same edition, original, and Ivo], has prayed in church among the other veiled women, and has offered offerings with them [Note: [Col. 1386C] “Offerings”: the Council of Worms, Ivo, and the *Panormia* read the singular “offering”; but the gloss agrees more nearly with “offerings”], if she has professed that she will remain in that habit, promising never to lay aside the veil of religion, must not presume to depart from the observance of religion.

### C. XXXV. No one is permitted to violate a profession of widowhood made before a bishop after the habit has been assumed.

Likewise, from the Council of Orange, ch. 27. [Note: [Col. 1385] Held A.D. 441.—Collection in three parts, pt. 2, tit. 26, ch. 11; Burchard, bk. 8, ch. 43; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 201; *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 61.]

We decree that a profession to preserve widowhood, made before the bishop in the sacristy, after the widow’s garment has been imposed before the bishop [Note: [Col. 1386C] “Before the bishop”: thus also in the other collectors. But all editions of the councils and manuscript codices read “by a presbyter”; [Note: [Col. 1385] “by a bishop”: Spanish Collection], is not to be violated. We decree that a woman who abandons such a profession is deservedly to be condemned [Note: [Col. 1386C] “Her”: the old Cologne edition of the councils, two Paris editions, and two Vatican codices read: “her repudiator, or herself”; and the Cologne editions in two and three volumes have the same reading in the text, with “the abductor of such women, or herself” in the margin [Note: [Col. 1385] “her abductor or herself”: Spanish Collection]. This latter reading appears in the text of the last four-volume edition. The other collectors read as Gratian does.] [Note: [Col. 1385] absent from the Spanish Collection; “we have decreed”: Ivo, *Panormia*, and collected editions except Basel and Lyons II–III].

[Col. 1386C]

### C. XXXVI. The manner and solemnity for making a profession are to be observed in this order.

Likewise, from the Tenth Council of Toledo, ch. 5. [Note: [Col. 1386D] In canon 5 of the Tenth Council of Toledo it is first decreed that women previously clothed in religious dress are to be admonished and, if unwilling to obey, compelled even by force to persevere in religious life. It then adds: “All these women, whether coming to religion for the first time or, after transgression, undertaking a renewed conversion, are, as stated above, to cover their heads with a mantle and make a written and ratified profession, by which they are thereafter not permitted to relapse into the boldness of transgression.” The *Panormia* has the remainder as Gratian, only adding “and the document” after “make.”] [Note: [Col. 1385] Held A.D. 656.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 202.]

All women coming to sacred [Note: [Col. 1385] “first”: Spanish Collection] religion are to cover their heads with a mantle, and make a written [Note: [Col. 1385] “written”: Lyons II–III editions; “and written”: the remaining editions except Lyons I; Spanish Collection and *Panormia*] and ratified profession [Col. 1387A], after which written document they are not to be permitted to relapse into the boldness of transgression. § 1. But any of them found to have given their mind [Note: [Col. 1387] “a ring” (*annulum*): Basel edition] or garment in transgression [Note: [Col. 1387] “in transgression”: Spanish Collection] are to incur a sentence of excommunication [Note: [Col. 1387] “and excommunication”: Spanish Collection], and, their habit changed again, are to remain confined [Note: [Col. 1387] “remain permanently”: *Panormia* and collected editions] in monasteries under the hardships of severe penance until they close their final day.

### C. XXXVII. Those who violate the bodies of women consecrated to God are sons of perdition.

Likewise, from the Council of Arles. [Note: [Col. 1387] Rather, from the Capitularies of the Kings of the Franks, bk. 6, ch. 414.—Burchard, bk. 8, ch. 51; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 3, ch. 207; *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 69.]

All should know that the bodies of women consecrated to God, by the vow of their own promise and by the words of the priest, are proved by scriptural testimonies to be temples consecrated to God; and therefore their violators are known to be sacrilegious persons and, according to the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1387] 2 Thess. 2:3], sons of perdition [Col. 1387B].

### C. XXXVIII. On the same subject. *Palea.*

[Likewise [Note: [Col. 1387] Rather, from the Third Council of Toledo.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 8, chs. 18–19.—cf. C. 32, q. 2, ch. 16.]]

> “If widows choose to marry before they profess continence [Note: [Col. 1387] “profess”: collected editions], let them marry those whom they shall have chosen [Note: [Col. 1387] “have chosen”: the same editions, except Lyons II–III and Ivo] as husbands by their own choice [Note: [Col. 1387] “wish,” or “may wish”: editions as specified]. The same rule [Note: [Col. 1387] “Likewise this”: collected editions] is to be applied [Note: [Col. 1387] “is applied”: editions except Basel] to virgins also: they are not to be compelled to take husbands [Note: [Col. 1387] singular: “a husband”: collected editions] against the will either of their parents or of themselves.”

### C. XXXIX. Monks joined to wives are to be confined in monasteries.

Likewise Gregory to Anthimus, subdeacon, in letter 40, book I. [Note: [Col. 1387] Letter 42, written A.D. 591, bk. 1 of the Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 122.]

[Col. 1387C] And because we have learned that certain monks have gone so far into wickedness as publicly to take wives, we command that you seek them out with every vigilance [Note: [Col. 1387] “we command that under”: collected editions], and, once found, send them back under fitting coercion [Note: [Col. 1387] “due”: Ivo; “customary”: collected editions] to the monasteries of which they had been monks [Note: [Col. 1387] “to which”: the same editions; “were”: original], or cause them to be sent back [Note: [Col. 1387] collected editions].

### C. XL. Whoever takes a wife after professing continence is to be separated from her.

Likewise Pope Innocent II, in the Roman Council, ch. 7, § “Ut lex.” [Note: [Col. 1387] Held A.D. 1139.—Ivo, *Panormia*, at the end of bk. 8.]

In order that the law of continence and purity pleasing to God may be extended among ecclesiastical persons and sacred orders [Col. 1388A], we decree that bishops, presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, regular canons, monks, and professed converts who, transgressing their holy [Note: [Col. 1387] “sacred”: collected editions] resolution, have presumed to take wives are to be separated. For we judge that such a union, which is clearly contracted against the ecclesiastical rule, is not a marriage. Once separated from one another, they are to do fitting penance for such offenses. We likewise decree that the same is to be observed concerning religious women if, God forbid, they should attempt to marry.

Gratian. By all these authorities, persons who have made vows are forbidden to contract marriages, and some of them, if they do contract them, are ordered to be separated.

[Col. 1388B]

## Part II

Augustine maintains, on the contrary, that it is sinful to separate such persons, saying as follows in *On the Good of Widowhood*, ch. 8. [Note: [Col. 1387] cf. at D. 27, ch. 2.—Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, bk. 4, dist. 38.]

### C. XLI. The marriages of those who have made vows are not to be dissolved.

The good of marriage is always indeed a good; but among the people of God it was once an observance of the law, while now it is a remedy for weakness and, for some, a consolation of human nature. The desire to devote oneself to the procreation of children—not in canine fashion through promiscuous intercourse with women, but in the honorable order of marriage—is not to be condemned in a human being; yet a Christian mind that contemplates heavenly things more laudably transcends and overcomes it. But because, as the Lord says [Note: [Col. 1387] Matt. 19:11], not all receive this saying, let her who can receive it receive it; let her who does not contain herself marry; let her who has not begun deliberate; let her who has undertaken it persevere. Let no opportunity be given to the adversary; let no offering be withdrawn from Christ.

§ 1. In the marital bond, indeed, if chastity is not preserved [Note: [Col. 1387] “preserved”: Basel edition; “observed”: remaining editions], condemnation is not feared. But in virginal and widowed continence there is sought the excellence of a greater gift; once sought, chosen, and offered in payment of a vow, not only entering marriage but even wishing to marry, though one does not marry, is blameworthy. For, to show this, the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1389] cf. 1 Tim. 5:11–12] did not say, “When they have lived luxuriously, they marry in Christ,” [Note: [Col. 1389D] “They marry”: in several old copies and in the original, “they do not marry”; [Note: [Col. 1389] thus Arg. edition.] Both readings appear sustainable. Many other passages have been corrected from Augustine himself.] but, “They wish to marry, having condemnation, because they have made void their first faith”—even if not by marrying, still by willing it. This is not because marriage itself, or the marriages of such persons, should be judged condemnable; rather, the fraud of their resolve is condemned, the faith of a broken vow is condemned, and not the assumption of a lesser good but the fall from a higher good is condemned. Finally, such women are condemned not because they later entered marital fidelity, but because they made void their first pledge of continence. To indicate this briefly, the Apostle did not wish to say that those who marry after a resolve of greater holiness have condemnation—not because they are not condemned [Note: [Col. 1389] “are condemned”: collected editions], but lest marriage itself be thought condemned in them. Rather, after saying, “They wish to marry,” he immediately added, “having condemnation,” and explained why: “because they have made void their first faith.” Thus it is clear that the will which has fallen away from the resolve is condemned, whether marriage follows or not.

§ 2. Therefore those who say that such marriages are not marriages but rather adulteries do not seem to me to consider sufficiently acutely and carefully what they are saying. They are deceived by a likeness to the truth. Because women who marry in Christian holiness are said to choose Christ’s marriage [Note: [Col. 1389D] “They marry”: several old copies and the original read “they do not marry”; both readings appear sustainable], some argue as follows: “If a woman whose husband is alive marries another man, she is an adulteress, as the Lord himself declares in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1389] Mark 10:11; Rom. 6:9]; therefore, since Christ is alive, over whom death has no further dominion, a woman who has chosen his marriage, if she marries a man, is an adulteress.”

§ 3. Those who say this are indeed moved by a subtle point, but pay little attention to the great absurdities that follow from this argument. For when, even while her husband is alive and with his consent, a woman commendably vows continence to Christ, according to their reasoning no woman ought to do this, lest she make Christ himself—an impious thought—an adulterer, by marrying him while her husband lives. Further, since first marriages are of greater merit than second marriages, far be it that holy widows should think of Christ as though he were a second husband. For they had him even before [Note: [Col. 1389] “before”: Böhm], when they faithfully served in submission to their husbands, as a husband not carnally but spiritually. The Church herself, whose members they are, is his spouse; and she is wholly a virgin in the integrity of faith, hope, and love, not only in sacred virgins but also in faithful widows and married women. For the Apostle says to the whole Church, of which those women are members: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” [Note: [Col. 1389] cf. 2 Cor. 11:2]. He knows how a virgin-spouse may bear offspring without corruption, since in his own flesh his mother was able to bear him without corruption.

§ 4. But this insufficiently considered opinion—that the unions of women who have fallen from their holy resolve are not marriages if they marry—produces no small evil: wives are separated from their husbands as if they were adulteresses and not wives; and, when men wish to restore those separated women to continence, they make their husbands genuine adulterers [Col. 1390B], when those husbands take other wives while their own wives are alive.

§ 5. Therefore I cannot say that the unions of women who have fallen from a better resolve, if they marry, are adulteries and not marriages. But I would certainly not hesitate to say that falls and collapses from the holier chastity vowed to God are worse than adulteries. For if, as cannot in any way be doubted, it pertains to an offense against Christ when one of his members does not keep faith with her husband, how much more grievously is he offended when faith is not kept with Christ himself in a matter where he requires what has been offered, though he did not require it to be offered? For when anyone fails to render what he vowed—not compelled by command but prompted by counsel—the injustice of a fraudulent vow is increased in proportion as the necessity of making the vow was less [Col. 1390C].

### C. XLII. Concerning widows who have made void their first faith.

Likewise Gelasius, in a letter to the bishops of Lucania and Bruttium, ch. 23. [Note: [Col. 1389] Written A.D. 494.—Burchard, bk. 8, ch. 34; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 7, ch. 53; Polycarp, bk. 4, tit. 34.—In the Arg., Nor., Ven. I–II, Paris, and Lyons I editions it is attributed to Pelagius.]

Above we have discussed at length and sufficiently widows who are not to be veiled under any blessing. If by their own will and an inconstant mind they trample upon the chastity of their former marriage which they have professed [Note: [Col. 1389] “have trampled”: Basel edition], it concerns their own peril by what satisfaction they ought to appease God, because, according to the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1389] 1 Tim. 5:12], they have made void their first faith. For just as, if perhaps they could not contain themselves, they were by no means forbidden to marry according to the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1389] 1 Cor. 7:9], so, after deliberating with themselves, they must preserve the pledged faith of chastity promised to God [Col. 1391A]. But we ought to lay no snare upon such women; rather, we should set before them only exhortations concerning eternal reward and the punishments of divine judgment, so that our conscience may be clear and their intention may render to God an account for itself. For we must beware of what the blessed Apostle Paul testifies concerning their character and conduct [Note: [Col. 1391] 1 Tim. 5:12]. We refrain from explaining this more fully, lest the unstable [Note: [Col. 1391] “frail and unstable”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions] sex seem not so much restrained [Note: [Col. 1391] “frightened”: Spanish Collection, Burchard, Ivo, and collected editions] as admonished.

### C. XLIII. On the same subject.

Likewise Theodorus. [Note: [Col. 1391] cf. D. 27, ch. 4.]

If anyone has a vow of virginity, etc.

[Supplementary apparatus omitted above: In C. XXV, the Lucca reading in the note on “themselves” omits *fuerint* (“they have been”); in C. XXXVI, “their heads” is absent from the Spanish Collection, *fuerint* (“were”) replaces “are found,” and *permanere* means “to remain permanently.” In C. XL, *observare* (“to observe”) replaces “to be observed” in the specified editions, and *decrevimus* means “we have decreed.”

In C. XLI: the opening variants read “which is a good,” “but otherwise,” “now … commendable,” “who” for “which,” and “having left it” for “having undertaken it.” The variant *mulieris* means “woman” for “gift.” The Apostle-note reads, “the Apostle says, not ‘when’”; *degerent* and *degerint* mean “were living” and “have lived” for “have lived luxuriously.” Other variants are “or because,” masculine “broken,” “from” for “out of,” “they said,” omission of “from,” and “to be condemned.” In §2, “sufficiently” is absent in Basel; *diffinivit* means “declared,” “Christ indeed lives” replaces “while Christ lives,” *dominabitur* means “will have dominion,” and the variants read “therefore,” “had chosen” or “chose,” respectively. In §3, the variants read “by this argument,” omission of “now,” “ought” or “ought to have,” “Christ himself,” “assent” for “think,” “adultery” for “adulterer,” “before,” “not only in,” omission of “widows also,” “all those women,” and “I have desired” for “I have fitted/betrothed.”]

Gratian. That those who make vows are, by the foregoing authorities, commanded to separate from one another, whereas the marriages of others are not to be dissolved on the authority of Augustine and Theodore [Note: cf. the cited chapter 4, Distinction 27], is clearly shown in the chapter on the ordination of clerics [Col. 1391B]. § 1. That statement of Innocent [Note: above, in the same place, chapter 10], by which consecrated virgins who publicly marry, while he to whom they had joined themselves is alive, are forbidden to be admitted to penance, must not be understood as though those who are willing worthily to perform penance are excluded from penance for any period; rather, those who are unwilling to depart from an incestuous union are forbidden admission to penance. For after adopting the purpose of sacred religion, she cannot be reconciled to God through penance if she has neglected to return to the habit of her profession. For then he to whom she had joined herself will be dead to her, when she has wholly withdrawn from his unlawful embraces. Thus the sense of the chapter is this: those who are spiritually married to Christ, if afterward they marry publicly, are judged not to be admitted to penance unless those to whom they had joined themselves [Col. 1391C] have departed from the world—namely, while those women are married to them. For then husbands depart from the world; then they die, when the women themselves wholly remove themselves from their desire, just as the world is said to be dead to a person whom it does not bind by its allurements, and a person is declared dead to the world who desires nothing worldly in the world.

That this is to be understood in this way Innocent himself shows by the following example, saying [Note: cf. cited chapter 10]: “Any woman who, while her husband lives, marries another is to be deemed an adulteress, nor is a place for doing penance to be granted her unless one of these has died.” This is to be understood of a deserted wife: if, while her husband lives, she marries another, she is an adulteress and is not admitted to penance unless either the first returns to the dust from which he was taken [Col. 1391D], or the second dies to her by ceasing sexual union with her, as was said above. Therefore, since Christ, to whom they are spiritually married, no longer dies—death [Note: Rom. 6:9] shall no longer have dominion over him [Col. 1392A]—it remains that he whom they marry secondly must die to her. In either case, unless this were so understood, the passage would be contrary to the Lord speaking through the Prophet [Note: Ezek. 33:12]: “In whatever hour the sinner is converted,” etc.; and it would be found opposed to all interpreters of the divine law. The same point is proved by the authority of that chapter [Note: cf. above, chapter 27] in which a vowed woman who has taken a husband is forbidden to be admitted to penance unless either both have professed continence, or he to whom she had joined herself has departed from this world.

## QUESTION II

## GRATIAN

### Part I

The second question follows: whether girls betrothed to another may renounce their former [Col. 1392B] commitment and transfer their vows to someone else. (Question I.) Here it must first be considered whether there is marriage between them. (Question II.) Second, whether they may separate from one another. § 1. That they are spouses is readily proved both from the definition of marriage and from the authority of many writers. For nuptials or marriage are the union of a man and a woman, retaining an indivisible partnership of life [Note: chapter 81, Book I, On paternal power (1.9); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 1; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 1]. Between these persons there was a union which required an indivisible partnership of life. For between them there was consent, which is the efficient cause of marriage, according to Isidore’s saying [Note: cf. below, chapter 6]: “Consent makes marriage.” Likewise John Chrysostom [that is, the author of the *Opus imperfectum*, Homily XXXII on Matthew]:

### C. I

[Note: Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 233; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 27.]

[Col. 1392C] Marriage is not made by intercourse but by will; and therefore it is not dissolved by bodily separation but by *separation* of will. Hence one who dismisses his wife and does not take another is still a husband. For although he is now separated in body, he is still joined in will. But when he has taken another, then he fully dismisses her [Note: add “her”: the collected editions, first Basel edition—Böhmer]. Therefore, it is not the man who dismisses his wife who commits adultery, but the man who takes another.

### C. II. Likewise Pope Nicholas, in his replies to the Bulgarians, chapter 3

[Note: This chapter has been corrected from Nicholas’s own responses.]  
[Note: written A.D. 866; Anselm, book 10, chapter 30; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 107; Peter Lombard, same place.]

Let the consent alone of those whose unions are at issue suffice according to the laws [Note: add “or of the women”: collected editions]. If this *consent* alone should perhaps be lacking *at the wedding*, all the *other things*, even if celebrated together with intercourse itself, are void.

[Note: “by consent and union”: same editions, first Basel edition.]

[Col. 1392D] Gratian. Therefore, since consent intervened between these persons, and consent alone makes marriage, it is clear that they were spouses. But the question is asked: what consent makes [Col. 1393A] marriage? Is it consent to cohabitation, consent to sexual union, or both? If consent to cohabitation makes marriage, then a brother can contract marriage with a sister; if consent to sexual union does, there was no marriage between Mary and Joseph. For Mary had vowed to remain a virgin. Hence she said to the angel [Note: Luke 1:34]: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” That is, “I have resolved that I shall not know one.” For it was not necessary to ask how she could have a son merely because she did not then know a man; rather, she asked because she had resolved never to know one. § 1. Therefore, if afterward, contrary to her purpose, she consented to sexual union, she became guilty in mind of violating a virginal vow, even if not in deed. It is impious to think this of her. Rather, as Augustine says [Note: This chapter is joined to the preceding one in old copies [Col. 1393D], and appears to have been compiled by the collector from various places in St. Augustine, especially from the treatise *On Virginity*]:

[Col. 1393B]

### C. III

Blessed Mary [Note: Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 30] resolved in her heart to keep the vow of virginity [Note: “to preserve”: Argentinian and Basel editions], but did not express that vow of virginity with her lips. She submitted herself to the divine ordering when she resolved to remain a virgin unless God revealed otherwise to her. Entrusting her virginity, therefore, to the divine ordering, she consented to sexual union—not desiring it, but obeying divine inspiration in both matters. Afterward she bore a son; and what she had conceived in her heart she expressed with her lips together with her husband, and both remained in virginity. § 1. Therefore, consent to live together and to retain an indivisible partnership of life, intervening between them, made them spouses. An indivisible partnership of life means that she presents herself to her husband in all things as she is to herself, and conversely [Col. 1393C]. Thus, belonging to this indivisible partnership is that, without her lawful husband’s consent, she cannot even sometimes devote herself to prayer [Note: add “also”: collected editions, first Basel edition], nor profess continence. Therefore, since this consent existed between them [Note: “these persons”: Basel edition], it is clear that they were spouses.

### C. IV. PALEA. John Chrysostom

[That is, the author of the *Opus imperfectum*, Homily XXXII on Matthew. Note: This *Palea* occurs in many old codices. But its opening through the words “Marriage is” is the first rule among the rules of law contained in the Decretals. The words of Homily 32 are these: “Everything is dissolved through the same causes through which it comes into being. Marriage,” etc.]  
[Note: cf. on chapter 1.]

> “Everything is dissolved through whatever causes it comes into being [Col. 1394A]. For marriage is not made by intercourse but by will; and therefore it is not dissolved by bodily separation but by *separation* of will. Hence one who dismisses his wife and does not take another is still a husband. For although he is now separated in body, he is still joined in will. But when he has taken another, then he plainly dismisses her [Note: “fully”: original—Ivo—the collected editions, which add “her”]. Therefore, it is not the man who dismisses his wife who commits adultery, but the man who takes another.”

Gratian. Likewise, they are proved to be spouses by authority. For Ambrose says in the book *On the Institution of a Virgin*, chapter 6 [Note: Anselm, book 10, chapter 1; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 14; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 2; Peter Lombard, same place, distinction 27]:

### C. V. The marital agreement, not the deflowering of virginity, makes marriage

When marriage is begun, *then* the name of marriage is assumed [Note: “is received”: Ivo—“is obtained”: Paris and Lyons editions]. For it is not [Note: absent in Basel edition—“For—not”: remaining editions] the deflowering of virginity that makes [Col. 1394B] marriage, but the marital agreement. Finally, when a girl is joined [Note: “is joined together”: Anselm, Ivo, collected editions] to a man [Note: “woman”: collected editions and first Basel edition; add “to a man”: collected editions], there is marriage—not when she is known by sexual union with a man.

### C. VI. From the first pledge of betrothal they are more truly called spouses. Likewise Isidore, *Etymologies*, book IX, chapter 7

[Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 15; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 3; Peter Lombard, same place.]

They are more truly called spouses from the first pledge of betrothal, although marital intercourse is not yet known between them.

### C. VII. PALEA

[Note: This *Palea* is absent from all the collated copies [and from the Basel edition—this is the rubric of the following chapter], except two; in one, the more correct copy, it is placed [Col. 1394C] as though it were a summary of the following chapter. In neither, however, were the words “Likewise from the African council” found at the end of the preceding chapter, and therefore they have been removed.]

> “That an imposed condition is invalid is proved from the African council.”

### C. VIII. On the same subject. PALEA

[Note: This *Palea* is also appended in the Decretals, title *On Conditions Appended*, chapter *Quicunque* [and in Compilation I, same title, chapter 1], and in the collection divided into fifty parts (which is printed in the volumes of councils after the decrees of Alexander III), part 6, chapter 5; it is cited as from the African council. But it is not found in the surviving text of that council.]

> “Whoever has betrothed a woman under the name of a condition and afterward wishes to leave her: we declare that the condition is broken, and that the betrothal is to remain irrevocably binding.”

### C. IX. On the same subject. Likewise Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book I, chapter 11

[Note: Thus restored from Ivo, whereas it was previously cited as the book *On the Good of Marriage*.]  
[Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 16; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 14; Peter Lombard, same place.]

A woman is called a spouse from the first pledge of betrothal, whom Joseph had not known by intercourse [Note: “acknowledged”: collected editions], nor was going to know [Note: “Joseph” absent from the original—it is repeated from the preceding passages—also absent from Ivo and the Argentinian, Basel, and Nuremberg editions]; and the designation “spouse” had neither failed nor remained false where there neither had been nor would be any [Col. 1395A] union of flesh [Note: “carnal”: collected editions]. And below: § 1. For this reason both deserved to be called the parents of Christ through a faithful marriage—not only she, his mother, but also he, his father, as the spouse [Note: “and continuing”: same editions] of his mother [Note: add “was”: same editions, first Argentinian, Basel, and Nuremberg editions]: both in mind, not in flesh [Note: “both”: Basel edition].

### C. X. The threefold good of marriage was present in Christ’s parents. Likewise in the same book and chapter

[Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 30; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 15; Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 30.]

Therefore every good of marriage was fulfilled in those parents of Christ: offspring, fidelity, sacrament. We recognize the offspring as the Lord himself [Note: “God”: Basel edition], *Jesus* [Note: absent from Ivo]; fidelity, because there was no adultery; sacrament, because there was no divorce. Only marital intercourse was absent there, because in the flesh of sin it could not occur without that shameful desire of the flesh [Note: “conscience”: Basel edition] which [Col. 1395B] arises from sin, and without which he who was to be without sin chose to be conceived.

Gratian. Likewise, in Deuteronomy the Lord commanded Moses, saying [Note: Deut. 22:25]: “If anyone violates another man’s betrothed woman in a field, he shall surely die, because he has violated another’s wife.” § 1. Likewise, in the laws of princes a betrothed woman is commanded to mourn her fiancé’s death as that of her husband.

Likewise, it is found in the Canons [Note: This is an abridgment of chapter 41 of the Council of Tribur; cf. below, chapter 15]:

### C. XI. A brother may not marry his brother’s betrothed after his death

If anyone has betrothed a woman to himself and, death intervening, has been unable to know her sexually, his brother may not take her as [Note: absent from Basel edition] a wife.

[Col. 1395C]

### C. XII. Likewise Gregory to the Emperor Maurice, concerning a certain count who married the betrothed of his deceased nephew

[Note: In Anselm, before this chapter, this heading is written in red letters: “Chapters of the blessed doctor Gregory [Col. 1395D] concerning the line of consanguinity.” Afterward another heading is written in black letters: “To Emperor Maurice concerning a report about a certain count who married as his wife the betrothed virgin of his deceased nephew.” Then follows: “He who has taken a betrothed woman,” etc.]  
[Note: There are certain similar passages in the Council of Gregory II, held A.D. 721, chapters 10–11—Anselm, book 11, chapter 93 (92); Polycarp, book 6, title 4; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 27.]

He who takes in marriage the betrothed girl of his neighbor is to be anathema, he and all who consent to it, because according to the law of God he is decreed to die. § 1. For it is the custom of divine law to call betrothed women spouses, as the Gospel says [Note: add “it is said”: collected editions; cf. Matt. 2:13], “Take Mary your spouse,” and as it says in Deuteronomy [Note: Deut. 22:25]: “If anyone [Col. 1396A] violates a betrothed girl of any man in a field or in any place” [Note: “finds or violates”: Anselm], “or carries her into his own house” [Note: add “with marital effect, as the Lord commanded through Moses”: same source], “let him die” [Note: “let him surely die”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions], “because he has violated his neighbor’s wife”—not one who was already his wife, but one who was to become his wife by her parents’ arrangement. And below: § 2. As [Note: cf. Cause 35, question 2, chapter 7] no Christian may take in marriage a woman from his own consanguinity, or one whom his kinsman has had [Note: “has had” absent from Basel edition; “will have”: same edition], so neither may he take one from the consanguinity of his wife.

### C. XIII. When a wife has died, a man may take another, but not one repudiated or betrothed. Likewise Jerome

[Note: Before this chapter Ivo cites chapter “Tria” [Col. 1396C], below, Cause 36, question 2. Neither passage, however, has been found in St. Jerome.]  
[Note: An uncertain chapter—Register, book 2, chapter 107; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 34; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 41.]

A fourth lawful marriage is added. When any man’s wife has died, he may take another, but not a woman repudiated or [Note: “or”: Basel edition] betrothed to a husband, but a free woman; and the woman likewise ought to do so. Hence [Col. 1396B] Paul also says [Note: Rom. 7:2]: “A woman who is under a husband is bound by the law of her husband as long as her husband lives. Therefore, while her husband lives, she is called an adulteress if she is joined to another [Note: “another”: Basel edition] man. But if her husband has died, she is freed from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is joined [Note: absent from Ivo—“is joined to another”: Basel edition] to another man.”

### C. XIV. After anyone’s death, none of his kindred may take his betrothed. Likewise Gregory

[Note: In both this and the following chapter, the Collectors seem to have intended to give a summary of chapter 41 of the Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895—Peter Lombard, same place.]

If anyone has betrothed a wife or given her an earnest, even though afterward, because her day of death intervened, he was unable [Note: absent from Basel edition] to take her as his wife, nevertheless no one from his kindred may take her in marriage [Note: “as a spouse”: same editions]. If this is found to have been done, they are to be separated altogether.

[Col. 1396C]

### C. XV. On the same subject. Likewise Pope Julius

[Note: Thus corrected from manuscripts and the Master. In the printed editions it was “Julianus” [as in the Venice II, Paris, and Lyons editions]. In Polycarp it is cited as: “from the Council of Tribur, confirmed by Pope Julius.” There is some error underlying this heading.]  
[Note: cf. chapter 14—Polycarp, book 6, title 4; Peter Lombard, same place.]

If anyone has betrothed a wife or given her an earnest, and [Note: “if death intervenes”: Basel edition] either because the day of death intervenes, or because certain other causes arise [Note: “his own”: Basel edition], has not known her sexually, neither his surviving brother nor any one of his kindred may ever take that same woman as his wife at any time [Note: “in time”: same edition].

[Col. 1397A]

### Part II. Gratian

By all these authorities, these persons are proved to be spouses. But Augustine testifies to the contrary, saying [Note: This chapter has not been found in St. Augustine and appears to be a summary of the following chapter] [Note: This is a summary of the following chapter—Peter Lombard, same place]:

### C. XVI. There is no marriage between persons whom sexual union does not join

There is no doubt that a woman does not belong to a marriage with whom sexual union is not shown to have occurred.

### C. XVII. A woman with whom the nuptial rite is not performed does not belong to marriage. Likewise Pope Leo

[Note: In the printed and manuscript codices of Leo’s letters, in epistle 90 or 92, to Rusticus, chapter 4, and likewise in Burchard and Ivo, this passage reads very differently. “Since,” he says, “the partnership of marriage was so constituted from the beginning that, besides the union of the sexes, it contained within itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to a marriage in which the nuptial mystery is not shown to have existed.” Yet, in order to answer Gratian’s words, who plainly uses this corrupted passage, as do the Master, the gloss, and later doctors, nothing has been changed in the text.]  
[Note: In Leo’s epistle to Rusticus (Epistle 107, written A.D. 458 or 459, Ballerini edition), these words certainly occur very differently, and are cited thus by Burchard, book 9, chapter 1; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapters 74 and 139. In contrast, in the *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 23, they appear as in Gratian—cf. Cap. book 7, chapters 59 and 105.]

Since the partnership of marriage was established from the beginning in such a way that, apart from the union of the sexes, nuptials do not have within themselves the sacrament of the union of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to marriage with whom the nuptial rite is shown not [Col. 1397B] to have occurred.

### C. XVIII. PALEA

[Benedict, servant of the servants of God, to the Patriarch of Grado, greeting, etc. Note: This *Palea* occurs in most manuscripts. It is also in Bernard of Pavia’s first collection of Decretals and in the other collection divided into fifty parts (which is inserted in the volumes of councils after the decrees of Alexander III), part 6, chapter 27.]  
[Note: It is apocryphal—cf. Compilation I, book 4, title 2, chapter 1.]

> “The law of divine institution has made the apostolic see the teacher of the whole world [Note: “magistracy”: Basel edition], so that wherever anything is in doubt, the explanation of it may be sought from that see. Now a certain John, in your name, addressed the occupant of that same see by letter and asked concerning the marriage of his surviving daughter. Her deceased sister had been betrothed in simple words to a young man named Stephen, and had died before reaching the wedding: whether the surviving daughter could celebrate marriage with the same young man or not. [Col. 1397C] For he testified that the resolution of this matter was regarded among you as uncertain. Taught by God, we give the following entirely certain answer [Note: “will give”: Basel and Lyons I editions].
>
> “That first-created man, our root and origin, seeing a rib taken from himself formed into a woman [Note: “woman”: Basel edition], uttered among other things by the prophetic Spirit [Note: Gen. 2:24]: ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and [Col. 1398A] mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.’ By these words it was made known that a man and woman cannot become one flesh otherwise than by cleaving to one another through bodily union. Therefore, how one who has not at all been united in the nuptial bond with a woman previously unrelated to him can become one flesh merely through bare words of betrothal, we are wholly unable to see. For blood relationship is spoken of in words [Note: “is said in words”: absent from the Basel edition], not produced by words. Nor does a kiss produce relationship, because [Note: “because”: same edition] it produces no mingling of blood.
>
> “But since John’s case is precisely such that he wishes, as it were, to unite a second daughter [Note: absent from the Argentinian edition] *to that man* in marriage, to whom he had already decreed that his first should be betrothed, we command, by the judgment of apostolic [Note: “of the Apostle”: in the volumes of councils: ‘by apostolic judgment’; in the first collection of Decretals: ‘by the judgment of apostolic teaching’] authority, that this can be done without the taint of any crime [Note: “any one”: Basel edition], if it accords with the will of both parties [Note: “has yielded itself”: Venice II edition; ‘if it accords with the will of both parties’: these words are absent from the collection inserted in the councils]. For why should that be forbidden which Holy Scripture never declares ought to be forbidden? Nor do secular laws, when they enumerate the persons who [Note: “to whom”: collected editions, first Lyons II–III editions] do not contract marriage with one another [Note: “do not contract”: in certain old copies and in the first collection of Decretals, ‘contract marriage’; the other collection reads: ‘who are not permitted to contract marriage with one another’], say anything concerning such a matter [Note: “concerning this matter”: Basel edition]. Therefore do not deny what you teach by no reasoning ought to be denied [Note: “we decree”: Lyons II–III editions—“we have decreed”: the remaining editions, except the first Basel edition].”

Gratian. Likewise, the Apostle [Note: 1 Cor. 7:3] commanded that a wife render the marital due to her husband and a husband to his wife, except perhaps by consent for a time, that they may more freely devote themselves to prayer. Hence it is understood that without the other’s consent it is not lawful for either to devote himself or herself to prayer. § 1. Likewise, a husband cannot adopt the purpose of a better life without his wife’s consent, and conversely.

Accordingly Gregory writes to Theoctista the Patrician, book IX, epistle 39 [Note: Epistle 45, written A.D. 601, book 11, Maurist edition—Anselm, book 10, chapter 18 (20); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 78; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 129; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 27]:

### C. XIX. Marriages must not be dissolved for the sake of religion

[Col. 1398C] There are [Note: “If they say—one must know”: original—Ivo] those who say that marriages ought to be dissolved for religion’s sake. But it must be understood that, *although* [Note: “if”: collected editions, first Basel and Lyons II–III editions] human law has permitted this, divine law nevertheless forbids it. For Truth himself says [Note: Matt. 19:6, 9]: “What God has joined together, let no man separate.” He also says: “It is not lawful to dismiss one’s wife, except for the cause of fornication.” Who [Note: “Who—one”: absent in Ivo] [Col. 1399A] then can contradict this *heavenly* lawgiver? We know that it is written [Note: Gen. 2:24]: “The two shall be one flesh.” Therefore, if husband and wife are one flesh [Note: add “and one body”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions], and for religion’s sake a husband dismisses [Note: “dismiss”: Basel edition] his wife, or a woman dismisses her husband, who remains in the world or perhaps even goes over to unlawful vows [Note: absent from the original and Ivo], what kind of conversion is this [Note: “this migration or conversion”: in the original, though not in the Maurist edition], in which one and the same flesh passes partly to continence and remains partly in defilement? But if both agree to lead a continent life, who would dare [Note: “dares”: Basel edition] to condemn this? For [Note: “when”: collected editions—“For—Therefore”: absent in Ivo—the same words, “Therefore—lawful,” are omitted by Anselm] it is certain that almighty God, who granted lesser things, did not forbid greater. Indeed [Note: These words have been restored to their proper place; formerly they had been transposed between “lawful” and [Col. 1400D] “But if” [as in the collected editions, which read “For thus” instead of “Indeed”]], we know that many saints led a continent life first with their wives and afterward passed to the government of holy Church. For holy men customarily abstain even from [Col. 1399B] lawful things [Note: “from what is lawful”: Böhmer] in two ways: sometimes that they may increase their merits before almighty God; sometimes that they may cleanse away the faults of their former life. And below: § 1. Therefore, when good spouses desire either to increase merit or to erase the faults of their former life, it is lawful for them to bind themselves *to continence* and seek a better life. But if the wife does not follow the continence sought by the husband, or the husband rejects that sought by the wife, the marriage cannot be divided [Note: “it is lawful”: Ivo], because it is written [Note: 1 Cor. 7:4]: “The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”

[Col. 1399C]

### C. XX. A woman placed in a monastery without her husband’s consent is not forbidden to return to union with him. The same, to Leo, Bishop of Catania, book III, epistle 34

[Note: Epistle 46, written A.D. 594, book 4, Maurist edition—Anselm, book 7, chapter 148; Polycarp, book 4, title 31; cf. Distinction 32, chapter 2.]

We have learned from the report of many that there was formerly among you this custom [Note: “was”: collected editions]: that subdeacons lawfully had intercourse with their wives. In order that no one might presume this again, Servodei, deacon of our see, by the authority of our predecessor [Note: “forefather”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions], forbade it in this way: that at the same time those already joined to wives should choose one of two alternatives, namely either not presume to minister on any account, or abstain from their wives. And, as is said, [Col. 1400A] the subdeacon Speciosus then suspended himself from the office of administration on account of this matter; until the time of his death [Note: “times”: Argentinian, Basel, and Nuremberg editions] he performed the office of notary and abstained from the ministry which it had been his duty to render as a subdeacon. After his death, because his widow Honorata had joined herself to a husband, we have learned that *she* was assigned by your brotherhood to a monastery [Note: “appointed”: original—Basel edition]. Therefore, if, as is reported, her husband suspended himself from administration [Note: “has suspended himself”: Basel edition], it ought not to count against the aforesaid woman that she entered upon a second [Note: “second—vows”: collected editions] marital union [Note: “has entered”: Basel edition], especially if she was not joined to the subdeacon with the intention of abstaining from the pleasures of the flesh. If, therefore, you know that the truth is as we have been informed, it is altogether fitting that you release the aforesaid woman from the monastery, so that she may return to her [Col. 1400B] husband without any fear.

### C. XXI. He who has assumed the religious habit without his wife’s consent is to be compelled to return to his wife. The same, to Hadrian, notary of Palermo, book IX, epistle 44

[Note: Epistle 50, written A.D. 601, book 11, Maurist edition—Burchard, book 9, chapter 48; Anselm, book 10, chapter 19 (21); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 84; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 186; Polycarp, book 6, title 5; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 27.]

Agathosa, bearer of the present letter, has complained that her husband [Note: “man”: collected editions] entered the monastery of Abbot Urbicus against her will. Since this is undoubtedly relevant to the blame and disrepute of that abbot, we command your experience to investigate the matter diligently, in case he perhaps entered religious life *with* her consent, or she herself promised to change her life. If you find this to be so, ensure that he remains in the monastery [Note: “continues”: collected editions—original—Burchard, Anselm, Ivo], and compel her to change her life as she promised. But if none of this is the case, and if you find that the aforesaid woman did not commit any [Note: “a certain”: original—Burchard—Ivo] [Col. 1400C] crime of fornication—on account of which it is lawful for a *husband* [Note: absent from Anselm] even [Note: add “also”: Basel edition] to dismiss [Note: “leave”: original—Burchard—Ivo, *Decretum*] his wife [Note: “wives”: Lyons II–III editions]—then, lest his conversion should become an occasion of ruin to the wife left in the world, we wish you to restore her husband to her, even if he has already been tonsured [Note: “is”: Basel edition], all excuse [Note: “every pretext whatsoever”: same edition] ceasing. For although secular [Note: The secular law is found in Novel 123, chapter 58, as divided by Julian] law commands [Note: “commanded”: Basel edition] that marriage may be dissolved for the sake of conversion even if one party is unwilling, divine law does not permit this [Note: “permitted”: same edition]. For except [Note: “unless”: collected editions] for the cause of fornication, a husband [Note: “a husband”: collected editions, first Lyons I edition—Burchard, Ivo, *Decretum*; “to a husband”: Ivo, *Panormia*] is granted no [Col. 1401A] [Note: “some”: Venice I–II editions] ground [Note: “ground”: Basel edition] for dismissing [Note: “grants”: Argentinian and Basel editions] his wife. For after husband and wife are made one body by marital union, one part cannot enter religious life while the other remains in the world [Note: “remain”: collected editions].

### C. XXII. A husband cannot adopt a religious purpose without his wife’s consent. Likewise from the Eighth Synod

[Note: Rather, Basil; cf. the Corrections—Burchard, book 9, chapter 45; Anselm, book 10, chapter 20 (22); Collection in Three Parts, part 2, title 14, chapter 22; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 183; Peter Lombard and Polycarp, same place.]

If a married man [Note: “If a married man”: these words through “For if, while he lives” are found in St. Basil, *Longer Rules*, chapter 12. Burchard, Polycarp, and Ivo, part 8, chapter 183, cite this whole chapter from Basil’s sayings. But Ivo, chapter 220, and the author of the [Col. 1401D] *Panormia* [book 6, chapter 85] cite an epistle of Alexander II written to Landulf, in which the same passage is quoted from St. Basil. The earlier part of that epistle occurs below, Cause 33, question 5, “Notificasti.”] wishes to enter a monastery, he is not to be received unless he has first been released by his wife professing chastity. For if, while he lives, she marries another through incontinence, she will undoubtedly be an adulteress. Nor is the conversion of that husband accepted by God when the prostitution of the marital bond follows from it. Therefore such persons follow Christ without fault, leaving [Note: “having left”: collected editions] the world, when they have a mutual consent to chastity [Col. 1401B] from equal willingness.

### C. XXIII. Husband and wife may not separate for religion’s sake without the bishop’s knowledge. Likewise from the Synod of Pope Eugenius II, Roman Synod, chapter 36

[Note: held A.D. 826—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 76; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 127; Peter Lombard, same place.]

If husband and wife agree with one another to separate solely for the religious life, this must by no means occur without the bishop’s knowledge, so that he may provide a separate place for them. For if the wife is unwilling [Note: “willing”: Ivo, *Panormia*—Basel and Lyons II–III editions], or either one of them is unwilling, the marriage is not dissolved even for such a reason.

### C. XXIV. A husband may not practise continence without his wife’s consent. Likewise John Chrysostom, Homily I on Psalm 50

[Note: It was previously cited as Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*; in that work, book 8, chapter 4, the thought but not the words occurs, and therefore the heading has been restored from Ivo.]  
[Note: It is regarded as apocryphal—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 79, under Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 130; Peter Lombard, same place.]

If you abstain without your wife’s consent, you grant her permission [Col. 1401C] to commit fornication, and her sin will be imputed to your abstinence.

### C. XXV. A man is not to be admitted into a monastery unless his wife converts. Likewise, Gregory to Abbot Urbicus, Book V, Epistle 49.

[Note: [Col. 1401] Epistle 48 (written A.D. 596), line 6. Maurist edition.]

Because Agatho, bearer of this letter, wishes to convert in the monastery of your charity, we exhort you to receive him with all gentleness and charity [Note: [Col. 1401] “and devotion”: Basel edition.]. And below:

§1. Yet understand that he is to be received only if [Note: [Col. 1401] Omitted in the Venetian II, Paris, and Lyons I editions.] his wife likewise [Note: [Col. 1401] “with him” added: Basel and Lyons II and III editions.] wishes to convert. For, since the two have been made one body by the union of marriage, it is incongruous for one part to convert while the other remains in the world.

### C. XXVI. A wife may not undertake vows of continence unless her husband has chosen the same life. Likewise, Pope Nicholas to King Charles.

[Note: [Col. 1401] Written A.D. 867.—Regino, Book 2, ch. 113; Burchard, Book 9, chs. 49, 53; Anselm, Book 10, ch. 21 (23); Ivo, *Panormia*, Part 6, chs. 77, 83; *Decretum*, Part 8, chs. 128, 188; Peter Lombard, ibid.]

Queen Thietberga [Note: Theberga: Basel, Paris, and Lyons I editions; Theoberga: the remaining editions and Ivo’s *Panormia*; Theiberga: Ivo’s *Decretum*.] wrote [Note: [Col. 1402C] From “wrote” through “chose,” this is from Nicholas I’s letter to King Charles, beginning “Never sorrow,” and extant in the manuscript of the Dominican monastery.] to us that she wished to be stripped of royal dignity and the marital bond, and desired to be content with a private life alone. We replied to her that this could not be done otherwise than if her husband Lothair chose the same life. [Note: “We replied”: Basel edition.]

*And in another letter* [Note: Written in the same year.] *to King Lothair*:

§1. For although it is written, “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” [Note: Matthew 19:6.], nevertheless God, and not a human being, separates when, for the sake of divine love and with the consent of both spouses, marriages are dissolved. But we forbid mutual separation to be made in any other way.

**Gratian.** Here it is shown that married persons cannot profess continence without the consent of one another. Betrothed persons, however, are shown by examples and authorities to be able to preserve continence even without consulting those to whom they have been betrothed. For, as Blessed Jerome relates, Macarius, preeminent among Christ’s hermits, after the wedding feast had been celebrated, when he was about to enter the bridal chamber in the evening, left the city, sought lands beyond the sea, and chose for himself the solitude of the desert.

§1. Likewise, Blessed Alexius, son of the famous Euphemianus, similarly called by divine grace from his wedding, left his betrothed and began to serve Christ naked. From their example it is clear that betrothed men can profess continence without having sought the consent of their betrothed women [Col. 1402C].

The same is proved by the authority of Pope Eusebius, who says [Note: [Col. 1401] Found in the penitential book of Theodore of Canterbury, as edited by Petit, ch. 11.—Burchard, Book 8, ch. 19; Ivo, *Decretum*, Part 7, ch. 40; Peter Lombard, ibid.]:

### C. XXVII. A betrothed girl is not forbidden to choose a monastery.

Parents may not give a betrothed girl to another man; nevertheless, she may choose a monastery for herself.

### C. XXVIII. A betrothed woman may choose a monastery without penalty. Likewise, Gregory in the *Register*, Book VI, Epistle 20, to Fortunatus.

[Note: [Col. 1403] Epistle 23 (written A.D. 597), line 7. Maurist edition.—Anselm, Book 10, ch. 8; Peter Lombard, ibid.]

The legal decrees have judged that a betrothed woman, if she wishes to convert, is to be punished by no penalty whatever.

**Gratian.** Therefore, since the continence of married persons cannot be offered to God except with the consent of both; since a husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does [Note: 1 Corinthians 7:4.]; yet betrothed women may choose a monastery and betrothed men may undertake a purpose of the better life without seeking the consent of their betrothed women: it is evident that there is no marriage between a betrothed man and a betrothed woman.

§1. Likewise, since according to Augustine [Note: [Col. 1403C] Here Gratian repeats, in a very corrupt form, matters cited above in the chapters *There is no doubt* and *When there is a partnership*, from Augustine and Leo, as noted there.] that a woman does not belong to marriage with whom it is taught that there has been no sexual intercourse [Col. 1403B]; and likewise, since according to Leo [Note: Cf. above, ch. 17.] she does not belong to marriage with whom it is not shown that there has been a nuptial ministry: it appears that there is no marriage between a betrothed man and a betrothed woman.

§2. Likewise Pope Nicholas [Note: Cf. Cause 32, question 7, ch. 25.] commanded concerning those who have been blinded and mutilated by enemies that, on account of this infirmity, the marriages of such persons were not to be dissolved.

§3. But concerning those who, because of frigidity, cannot render the marital debt to their wives, Pope Gregory [Note: Cf. Cause 33, question 1, ch. 2.] decreed that each of them, with the seventh hand of relatives touching the most holy relics, should swear that they had never been joined through the mingling of flesh and made one flesh. Then the woman may contract a second marriage; but the man, being of a frigid nature, is to remain without hope of marriage. Each is to make this oath with seven relatives, touching the most holy relics.

[Col. 1403C] Therefore the same writer [Note: [Col. 1403D] This same chapter is cited below, Cause 33, question 1, from Gregory to John, bishop of Ravenna; likewise by Burchard and Ivo, Part 8, ch. 178. In the *Panormia* it is expressly attributed to “Gregory the Younger.” In the Brandt edition it is simply cited from Gregory to John of Ravenna. The ruling itself is reported from Gregory in the *Decretals*, title *On Frigidity and Sorcery*, ch. *Laudabilem*, and by Ivo in the same part, ch. 80, from the *Capitularies*, where it appears in Book 6, ch. 55.] writes to Venerius, bishop of Cagliari, as follows [Note: [Col. 1403] Rather, this is from Rabanus, letter to Heribald, ch. 29 (written A.D. 853).—Regino, Book 2, ch. 242; Burchard, Book 9, ch. 40; Anselm, Book 10, ch. 26; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 6, ch. 115; *Decretum*, Part 8, ch. 178; *Polycarpus*, Book 6, title 4; Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 34.—Cf. below, Cause 33, question 1, ch. 1.]:

### C. XXIX. If a woman proves that she has never been known by her husband, she is to be separated.

What you asked me [Note: “me” added: collected old editions.] concerning those joined in marriage [Note: “in marriage”: Basel edition; “joined together”: the collected old editions and first Basel edition.] who cannot marry [Note: “but,” rather than “and”: Basel edition.]—whether he may take another woman, or she another man—concerning such persons [Note: “concerning” is omitted in Ivo and Burchard; “such” (*quibus*) is read by the collected old editions, Regino, Ivo, and Burchard.] it is written thus [Note: “thus” is omitted in those same witnesses and in the Basel edition.] [Col. 1404A] as follows [Note: [Col. 1403D] The gloss’s author says here, “in the Lombard law”; and below, in Cause 33, question 1, says at this same point, “in the first book of Charlemagne’s capitulary,” namely, in the Lombard law. It is now found in the *Capitularies*, Book 6, ch. 55, with these words added at the end: “because, according to the Apostle, he was unable to render her her due.”]:

If a man and a woman have joined themselves together, and afterwards the woman says of the man that he cannot have intercourse with her [Note: “with her”: the same edition; “with him”: Böhm.], if she can prove by a true judgment [Note: The words “by a true judgment” are absent from the *Capitularies* and Ivo, ch. 80, but occur in Rabanus, Regino, Burchard, Anselm, and Ivo II and III. Those witnesses nevertheless read *justum* (“just”) instead of *verum* (“true”).] that this is true, let her take another man.

**Gratian.** See: inability to have intercourse, if discovered in either person after carnal union, does not dissolve the marriage. But if it is found before carnal union, it makes the woman free to take another husband. Hence it appears that they were not spouses; otherwise, they could not lawfully depart from one another except for the cause of fornication, and those departing in that manner must remain unmarried or be reconciled to one another.

§1. Likewise, if a betrothed woman were a wife, upon the death of her betrothed she would remain a widow. But if she were a widow, her husband could not ascend to holy orders [Col. 1404B]. For the husband of a widow, just as much as a man twice married, is forbidden to become a priest. Yet no one is prohibited from holy orders by this union. For, as Pope Pelagius says [Note: Cf. Distinction 34, final chapter.], “There is nothing, so far as this point is concerned, that opposes him under the canonical institutions.” It is therefore evident that these were not spouses.

§2. Likewise, if they were spouses, their departure from one another would be divorce. But Ambrose denies that their separation is divorce, saying of Blessed Mary, whom Joseph had betrothed to himself and taken into his home:

“Joseph never knew her. For if a just man had known her, he would never have allowed her to depart from him; nor would the Lord—who commanded that a wife was not to depart from her husband except for the cause of fornication—by entrusting her to the disciple, have been the author of a divorce.”

[Note: [Col. 1404D] The words of Blessed Ambrose, Book 1 of his commentary on Luke 1, which come closer to this passage than those found in Book 10 on chapter 23, are: “Certainly, had they come together, she would never have left her own husband, nor would her just husband have allowed her to depart from him. How, moreover, could the Lord have commanded a divorce, when it is his own judgment that no one ought to dismiss his wife except for the cause of fornication?”]

See: Mary’s entrusting to John [Col. 1404C] and her removal from Joseph are denied to have been a divorce because Joseph had not known her. It follows that they were not spouses. If, however, Blessed Mary, whom Joseph had betrothed to himself and taken into his home, is denied to have been a wife, then much less should this woman, who was merely betrothed, be called a wife.

### C. XXX. One who defiles his wife’s sister can have neither of them. Likewise, from the Council of Orléans.

[Note: [Col. 1405D] This same text below, Cause 32, question 7, *Whoever has slept*, appears to be cited from the Council of Mainz. But it has been found in neither an Orléans nor a Mainz council, just as the following texts have not been found in the Council of Tribur.]

[Note: [Col. 1405] Rather, from Verneuil, held A.D. 752.—Regino, Book 2, ch. 115; Burchard, Book 17, ch. 3; Ivo, *Decretum*, Part 9, ch. 69.]

Whoever sleeps with two sisters, one of whom had formerly been his wife [Note: *Had been*: collected old editions; *was*: Burchard.], is to have neither of them; nor are those adulterers ever to be joined in marriage [Note: *The adulterer*: collected old editions; *is to be joined*: Paris and Lyons editions.].

**Gratian.** That is: he may not render the marital debt even to his own wife, whom he has made unlawful to himself by knowing her sister. Nor, even after the death of his wife, may he be joined in marriage either to her or to any adulteress [Note: “Adulteress”: Böhm.].

But concerning a betrothed woman the contrary is read in the Council of Tribur [Note: [Col. 1405] Burchard, Book 17, ch. 49, and Ivo, *Decretum*, Part 9, ch. 100, seem to have wished briefly to report what Regino had already done before them in his customary fashion, Book 2, ch. 245.]:

### C. XXXI. Concerning one who slept with his brother’s betrothed.

A certain man betrothed and endowed a woman, but could not have intercourse with her; his brother secretly violated her and made her pregnant. It was decreed that, although she could not have been married to her lawful husband [Note: *Could not have*: collected old editions, especially Basel.], nevertheless the brother could not have the woman betrothed to his brother; but the adulterer and adulteress should indeed undergo the punishment for fornication, while lawful marriages are not to be denied them.

### C. XXXII. If anyone violates his son’s betrothed, he, together with her, is to remain without hope of marriage. Likewise, from the same source.

[Note: [Col. 1405] Rather, from Compiègne, ch. 10, held A.D. 756.—Regino, Book 2, ch. 217; Burchard, Book 17, ch. 18; Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 27.]

If anyone violates his son’s betrothed, and afterwards his son takes her, the father is thereafter to have no wife, nor the woman a husband. The son, who did not know of his father’s crime [Col. 1405C] [Note: *Had not known*: Basel and Lyons II and III editions.], is to take another woman.

**Gratian.** If the woman whom a man has known as his brother’s wife is prohibited from marriage forever, but this man who violated his brother’s betrothed is permitted to contract marriage after performing penance, it is evident that she was not his brother’s wife.

§1. Likewise, a woman dismissed by her husband on account of fornication is either to be reconciled to him or, while he lives, remain unmarried. But concerning a betrothed woman the contrary is found in Book I of the *Capitularies*, ch. 105 [Note: [Col. 1405] Ch. 24 of the Capitularies of Aachen, dated A.D. 816.—*Capitularies*, Book 1, ch. 99, Baluz edition; Ivo, *Decretum*, Part 8, ch. 26.], and Book VII, ch. 183, where the following is read:

### C. XXXIII. If a betrothed man is unwilling to receive back a woman who has been abducted, she may marry another.

The abductor is to be punished by public penance. But if the betrothed man is unwilling to receive the abducted woman, and she did not consent to the same crime, she is not to be denied permission to marry another.

### C. XXXIV. On the same matter. Likewise, from the Council of Toledo.

[Note: [Col. 1405D] It has been found in no Council of Toledo. But nearly the same provisions are read in the Council of Rheims at Trosly, in Book 1 of the *Capitularies*, ch. 105, and Book 7, ch. 183, and in the Lombard laws, Book 1, title *On the Abduction of Women*, law 12.]

[Note: [Col. 1405] This is ch. 24 of the Capitularies of Aachen, A.D. 816, reported in Book 1, ch. 99 of the *Capitularies*, and repeated at Trosly, ch. 8.—Burchard, Book 9, ch. 37; Anselm, Book 11, ch. 98; Ivo, *Decretum*, Part 8, ch. 175; Peter Lombard, ibid.]

It was decreed by the holy assembly that, if anyone abducts another’s betrothed, he is to be punished by public penance and remain without hope of marriage. And if she did not consent to the same crime [Col. 1406B], she is not to be denied permission to marry another. But if after this they themselves presume to join together [Note: “themselves” is added in the *Capitularies* and Council of Trosly; *presume*: those sources; *presumes*: Basel and Venetian I editions.], both are to be anathematized [Note: The collected old editions read, “each is to be anathematized.”] until satisfaction has been made [Note: [Col. 1406D] The words “until satisfaction” are not in the Council of Trosly or the *Capitularies*, but occur in Burchard and Ivo, who also cite Toledo [and Anselm].].

**Part III. Gratian.** It is therefore apparent that she was not a wife, since, while her betrothed is alive, she is not denied permission to marry another. How then, according to Ambrose and the other Fathers, are betrothed women called wives, while by all these arguments they are proved not to be wives? We must understand that marriage is begun by betrothal and completed by sexual union. Hence, between a betrothed man and a betrothed woman there is marriage, but marriage begun; between persons joined in intercourse there is ratified marriage.

Accordingly Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1406D] The complete text is given below under the same heading, *When marriage is begun.] [Note: Cf. above, ch. 5.]:

### C. XXXV. Marriage is begun in betrothal.

When marriage is begun, the name of marriage is assumed [Note: “Unless then, when”: Basel edition.]; it is not assumed when the girl is known by union with the man [Note: “By intercourse”: same edition.].

**Gratian.** See: marriage is begun in betrothal, not completed.

### C. XXXVI. The bodily union of persons joined completes marriage. Likewise, Ambrose, Book I, *On the Patriarchs*.

[Note: [Col. 1407D] This chapter has not been found in Ambrose, nor the following one in Jerome.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] Chapter of uncertain source.—Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 30.]

In every marriage a spiritual union is understood, which the bodily mingling of those joined together confirms and completes.

### C. XXXVII. Marriage is begun by the agreement of betrothal and completed by sexual union. Likewise, Jerome on the prophet Obadiah.

[Note: Chapter of uncertain source.]

“For this reason your daughters will commit fornication, and your brides will be adulteresses” [Note: Hosea 4:13.]. It should be noted that he says fornication will occur among daughters, and adultery among wives [Note: “Marriages”: Basel edition.], which are begun by the agreement of betrothal [Note: “By conjunction”: collected old editions.] and completed by bodily intercourse.

### C. XXXVIII. When a betrothed woman has been handed over and brought into use, she is rightly called a wife. Likewise, Ambrose to Paternus, Epistle LXVI.

[Note: Written about A.D. 390.—Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 6, ch. 17; *Decretum*, Part 8, ch. 101.]

If anyone has intercourse with a woman betrothed and handed over to him, it is rightly called marriage [Note: [Col. 1407D] In Blessed Ambrose the text reads, “If anyone has intercourse with her, he calls it marriage.” The same appears in Ivo. What precedes and follows shows that Ambrose’s meaning differed from what Gratian and the author of the *Panormia* supposed.].

**Gratian.** Augustine shows in Book VIII of the *Confessions*, ch. 3, why betrothed women are not handed over immediately after the marriage contract, saying [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 6, ch. 10; *Decretum*, Part 8, ch. 33; Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 27.]:

### C. XXXIX. Why betrothed women are not handed over immediately after the contract.

It was instituted that brides already pledged should not immediately be handed over, lest a husband hold cheaply a woman bestowed on him whom, as bridegroom, he had not longed for while she was delayed [Note: The *non* (“not”) is absent from Ivo; “whom he had sighed for while the bridegroom delayed her”: Ivo’s *Decretum*; “whom he sighed for”: Basel edition.].

**Gratian.** In accordance with this distinction, Augustine’s authority [Note: Cf. above, ch. 16.] must be understood: “There is no doubt that that woman does not belong to marriage with whom there is shown to have been no sexual intercourse” [Col. 1407C]. Perfected marriage must be understood: namely, such marriage as has in itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church. Pope Leo’s statement [Note: Cf. above, ch. 17.] must likewise be understood.

§1. But Augustine’s statement is objected [Note: Cf. above, ch. 3.]: “Between Mary and Joseph there was a perfect marriage.” Yet “perfect” is understood not from the marital act, but from the things accompanying the marital act: namely fidelity, offspring, and sacrament. Augustine’s authority proves that all these existed between Christ’s parents. Therefore all the authorities introduced concerning the indissolubility of marriage concern perfected marriage: marriage begun by the agreement of betrothal and consummated by the act of bodily union. But those authorities by which separable marriage is shown concern marriage begun, which has not yet been completed by its proper act [Col. 1408A].

§2. A different distinction may also be made. Betrothed women are called wives in the usage of Scripture because of the hope of future events, not because of a present reality. Thus Ambrose, when he said [Note: Cf. above, ch. 5.], “When marriage is begun,” did not add, “then its reality or effect begins,” but “then the name of marriage is assumed,” showing that such persons have the name of marriage, not its reality or effect. Likewise Augustine, speaking of the Lord’s parents, says [Note: Cf. above, ch. 9.]: “They were spouses in mind, not in flesh, and likewise parents.” From this it is understood that Joseph was called the Lord’s father not by the fact of begetting, but by the office and care of providing; so too he is called the husband of Christ’s mother not by the effect of marriage, but by supplying necessities and by the affection of an undivided mind.

Thus Augustine says [Note: Cf. the same chapter.]: “Do not fear to take Mary your wife; he called her wife because she was going to be a wife.” So too Bede on Leviticus: “If anyone violates another’s betrothed,” etc.; he calls the betrothed woman a wife, not because she then was a wife, but because she was going to be a wife. So too Jerome on Matthew’s Gospel [Note: On Matthew 1:18: “When she had been betrothed.”]:

### C. XL. In Scriptural usage, betrothed women are called wives and betrothed men husbands.

“He begot Joseph, the husband of Mary” [Note: Matthew 1:16.]. When you hear “husband,” do not let a suspicion of marriage come upon you, but recall the usage of Scripture: betrothed men are called husbands, and betrothed women wives.

And below:

§1. She was found by no one other than Joseph, who, through something close to the licence of marriage, knew everything concerning his future wife [Col. 1408C].

And below:

§2. “Joseph, son [Note: “sons”: Böhm.] of David,” etc. [Note: Matthew 1:20.]. Now [Note: “Now indeed, just as”: Basel edition.] and [Note: “that”: the collected old editions and first Basel edition.] as we have already said, brides are called wives [Note: “It is established that”: those editions.], as the book *Against Helvidius* teaches more fully.

### C. XLI. On the same matter. The same author on Genesis.

[Note: [Col. 1407D] In this chapter Gratian cited words from the ordinary gloss on Genesis 19, drawn from Jerome.]

“So Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, who were going to take his daughters” [Note: Genesis 19:14.]. Later Lot’s daughters are said to have been virgins [Note: “To have been”: collected old editions, especially Argenteus.]. And he himself said to the Sodomites: “Behold my two daughters, who have not known a man.” Yet he is now said to have had sons-in-law. Some [Note: “But some”: collected old editions.] suppose that those who had husbands perished in Sodom, while those who were virgins went out with their father.

But the Hebrew text has: “Lot went out and spoke to his betrothed sons-in-law,” who were going to take his daughters [Col. 1409A]. [Note: [Col. 1408D] The words following “his betrothed sons-in-law,” namely “who were going to take his daughters,” are expunged, since they occur neither in Jerome nor in the ordinary gloss.
