From the same sources the words from “Therefore” to the end were added, because Gratian’s intended point is inferred from them.] *Therefore his virgin daughters had not yet been joined in marriage.*

**Gratian.** Hence it is understood that Scripture calls betrothed men sons-in-law.

### C. XLII. Mary is called a wife by Scriptural usage, although she was merely betrothed. Likewise, John Chrysostom, Homily IV on Matthew 1.

“Before they came together” [Note: Matthew 1:18.]. He did not say, “Before she was brought into the bridegroom’s house.” For antiquity observed the custom that brides should reside in the homes of their bridegrooms [Note: “For”: collected old editions.]. *We sometimes see this done even now.* For just as Lot’s sons-in-law are read to have lived [Note: “to live”: the collected old editions.] with their father-in-law while still betrothed and not yet joined to their brides by the law of marriage, so Mary too lived with her betrothed.

And below:

§1. He did not wish to drive her out of the house, but to dismiss her [Note: Matthew 1:19.].

And below:

§2. “Do not fear to take Mary your wife” [Note: Matthew 1:20.]. By these words he likewise indicated her simply [Note: “Simply”: Basel edition.] as a betrothed woman, just as Scripture customarily calls even those who are still betrothed “sons-in-law.” For what does “take Mary your wife” mean [Note: “What, moreover, does it mean to take Mary your wife?”: the same edition.]? Surely, to keep her in the house. For he had already dismissed her in his mind [Col. 1409B].

And below:

§3. Just as Christ himself later entrusted her to the disciple [Note: “Entrusts”: the same edition.], so now the angel joins her to her betrothed—not in the solemn covenant of marriage, but in the fellowship of a shared dwelling.

### C. XLIII. The Lord would not have entrusted his mother to the disciple if Joseph had known her. The same author, Homily V on Matthew 1.

[Col. 1409C] For if he had known her and regarded her as occupying a wife’s place, how could the Lord have entrusted her to the disciple as though she lacked support and had absolutely nothing, commanding him to receive her into his own home [Note: “Receive”: Basel edition.]?

### C. XLIV. Mary is called Joseph’s wife because he thought that she would become so. Likewise, Origen on the same passage, Homily I on the Gospel.

[Note: This is not by Origen.]

“She was found to be with child” [Note: Matthew 1:19.]. A. B. Joseph, although he did not touch her, nevertheless knew everything concerning his future wife, as was supposed [Note: “Future,” rather than “future wife”: Basel edition; some editions read “had vowed” instead of “knew.”].

And below:

§1. If she is called your wife, if she is said to be betrothed to you [Note: [Col. 1409D] Thus corrected from the homily itself. Formerly it read: “and if in betrothal she is said to be your wife.” Several other passages were also corrected and added.], she is not nevertheless your wife, but the chosen mother of God’s only-begotten Son [Note: “Of the eternal one”: Basel edition; “eternal”: the remaining editions.].

And below:

§2. I call her wife in order to conceal her virginity from the devil [Note: “To conceal”: Basel edition.], *and to exclude and overthrow the perversity of the Jews, and* not to destroy the ordinances of the law. In what follows I shall show that neither is this woman considered your wife according to the custom of marriage [Col. 1410A], nor is he who is begotten believed to be your son [Note: “Also” added: the same editions and the first Basel edition.].

### C. XLV. Joseph did not proceed to marriage with Mary. Likewise, Gregory in his exposition of the Gospels, Homily XVI.

Thus the Lord permitted the disciple to doubt after his resurrection [Note: Cf. John 20.], yet did not abandon him in doubt; just as before his birth he willed Mary to have a betrothed, who nevertheless did not proceed to her marriage. For the doubting and touching disciple became a witness of the true resurrection, just as her betrothed became the guardian of the mother’s wholly intact virginity [Note: “The betrothed had been the guardian of the mother’s virginity”: collected old editions, especially Basel.].

**Gratian.** From all these authorities it is clear that betrothed women are called wives because of the expectation of future events, not by present reality. How then are they said to be wives from the first pledge of betrothal, if this woman who is asserted to be a betrothed woman is denied to be a wife? She is said to be called a wife from the first pledge of betrothal, not because she becomes a wife in the betrothal itself, but because, by the faith which they owe one another from the betrothal, they afterwards become spouses. Just so, sins are said to be forgiven through faith—not because they are forgiven through faith before baptism, but because faith is the reason why we are cleansed from sins in baptism.

§1. John Chrysostom’s statement [Note: Cf. above, ch. 1.], “Intercourse does not make marriage, but will,” and Ambrose’s statement [Note: Cf. above, ch. 5.], “Not the defloration of virginity, but the marital agreement makes marriage,” must be understood as follows: intercourse without the will to contract marriage, and defloration of virginity without a marital agreement, do not make marriage. Rather, the preceding will to contract marriage [Col. 1410C], and the marital agreement, make it the case that, in the defloration of her virginity or in intercourse, a woman is said to marry a man or celebrate nuptials.

§2. Likewise Pope Siricius [Note: Cf. below, ch. 50.] calls the departure of a betrothed woman from her betrothed a marital separation. But such a departure is called the violation not of a union already existing, but of a future union hoped for from the betrothal itself. Thus the devil is said to have fallen from blessedness—not only the blessedness he then had, but also that blessedness for which he had been created. Thus a person chosen for priest or bishop because of the merit of his life or learning, if in the meantime he deserves to have his election annulled through his own fault, is said to lose the priestly or episcopal anointing, not one he had already received, but one to receive which he had been chosen. Therefore a betrothed woman cannot be proved to be a wife from that authority.

§3. But even if it is granted that a betrothed woman is not a wife, the question remains whether she may renounce the earlier engagement.

[Col. 1411A] This, however, is forbidden by the authority of the Council of Ancyra, ch. 11, in which the following ruling is read [Note: Held A.D. 314.—Dionysius’s translation.—Regino, Book 2, ch. 155; Burchard, Book 9, ch. 38; Anselm, Book 10, ch. 8 (10); Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 6, ch. 19; *Decretum*, Part 8, ch. 170.]:

### C. XLVI. Betrothed girls must be restored to their former betrothed men if they have been abducted.

It has pleased the council that betrothed girls, even after being abducted by others, should be recovered and returned to those to whom they had formerly been betrothed, even if it is established that violence has been inflicted upon them by their abductors [Note: “By” is omitted in the collected old editions, first Basel, Paris, and Lyons editions; “has been”: Basel edition.].

### C. XLVII. A betrothed woman is to be deprived of communion unless she is willing to leave her abductor and return to her betrothed. Likewise, John VIII to Archbishop Rostanus.

[Note: [Col. 1411D] “Eighth” is restored from most ancient copies and from Ivo. In the printed editions it was “Chrysostom.”]

[Note: A letter of uncertain date, written to Rostanus, bishop of Arles.—Ivo, *Decretum*, Part 14, ch. 64.]

Atho [Note: Otto: Basel edition.], bearer of this letter, while faithfully attending to our service, complains that a certain man abducted a woman betrothed to him. Therefore, strengthened by our authority, your brotherhood is to summon its suffragan bishops in person; and, by their unanimous judgment, if the abductor does not restore the betrothed woman to this man, both he and the abducted woman—if she is unwilling to return to her former betrothed—are to be deprived of all communion [Col. 1411B] [Note: “Are unwilling”: Basel edition, an openly erroneous plural reading; “is to be deprived”: Basel edition.].

**Part IV. Gratian.** But it is one thing to renounce an earlier engagement and to make marriage with another; it is another thing to be abducted—that is, unlawfully violated.

Thus Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book V, ch. 26, says [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 6, ch. 53; *Decretum*, Part 8, ch. 26.—Cf. Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.217; cf. Cause 36, question 1, ch. 1 and its correction.]:

### C. XLVIII. What is abduction?

Abduction (*raptus*) is unlawful intercourse, so called from corruption; hence one who possesses an abducted woman enjoys her by violation.

**Gratian.** But this woman is shown not to have been abducted from another, but betrothed to another. Pope Gelasius forbids such a woman to be called abducted, saying [Note: Chapter of uncertain source.—Anselm, Book 10, ch. 11 (12).—Cf. Cause 36, question 1, ch. 2, and *Decretals*, title *On Abduction*, ch. 6.]:

### C. XLIX. Abduction occurs where a girl is taken away concerning whose earlier marriage no arrangement is proved to have been made.

That law of the former rulers declared that abduction had been committed where a girl concerning whose marriage no prior arrangement had been made [Note: “Had been”: collected old editions.] appears to have been taken away [Note: “Is seen”: Basel edition; “was seen”: the remaining editions. “By force” is added in the Basel edition.].

**Part V. Gratian.** The added words at the end of the chapter [Note: Cf. above, ch. 46.], “even if it is established that violence has been inflicted upon them by their abductors,” were included because some abducted women expose themselves to be abducted, while others are carried away by force. Therefore, however they may be abducted, they must be restored to their prior betrothed men. But this woman, as stated above, is counted not among abducted women but among other betrothed women [Col. 1412A]; therefore she is not to be taken from this man and restored to the former one.

§1. Other authorities follow which forbid this woman to marry a second man and command her to return to her former vows.

For Pope Siricius says to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, Epistle I, ch. 4 [Note: Written A.D. 385.—Regino, Book 2, ch. 154; Burchard, Book 9, ch. 31; Anselm, Book 10, ch. 9; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 6, ch. 18; *Decretum*, Part 8, ch. 169.]:

### C. L. One man cannot take in marriage a girl betrothed to another.

Asked concerning the violation [Note: *Veiling*: the Hispanic Collection.] of marriage, whether one man may take in marriage a girl betrothed to another: we anathematize such a union and forbid it by every means [Note: “We interdict it”: Basel edition.], because the blessing which the priest lays upon a bride is, among the faithful, like a certain sacrilege if it is violated by any transgression.

[Note: [Col. 1411D] In manuscripts of Siricius’s letters, in the *Code of Canons*, and among the other collectors—except the *Panormia*—as well as in the Basel-printed *Capitularies* of Charlemagne, Book 1, final chapter, the reading is: “We forbid by every means that this be done.” But, since the case mentions an anathema, the wording was not changed.]

**Gratian.** But by this authority of Siricius, she is forbidden to proceed to second vows [Col. 1412B] only when she has been taken into her own home and has been veiled and blessed with her betrothed. By the departure of such women the blessing which a priest imposes upon brides is violated. But this woman had not yet been taken by her betrothed into his home, nor had she received the blessing with him. Therefore a union of this kind is not forbidden by this authority.

§1. Likewise Pope Eusebius’s statement [Note: Cf. above, ch. 27.], “Parents may not give a betrothed girl to another man,” is understood similarly of a betrothed woman who has been veiled and blessed with her betrothed.

§2. Likewise, Gregory’s statement is objected [Note: Cf. below, Cause 33, question 1, ch. 2.]: “A woman who has been separated from her husband because of frigidity and married to another, if her husband has known another woman, is to be taken from the second and restored to the first.” But it is resolved in the same way [Col. 1412C], because that woman had received the blessing with him.

### C. LI. If anyone has pledged the faith of consent to a woman, he may not take another. PALEA.

[Augustine, *On the Faith of Pledge and Consent*.]

[Note: [Col. 1412D] It is also cited in the *Decretals*, title *On the Betrothed of Two Men*, ch. 1, as from Augustine, in whom it has not been found.]

[Note: Chapter of uncertain source.—Cf. ch. 1, *On the Betrothed of Two Men*, First Compilation, and *Decretals*, same title, ch. 1.]

“Faith is spoken of in two ways: that of agreement and that of consent. If someone has pledged faith of agreement to a woman, he ought not to marry another. If he marries another, he ought to do penance for having broken his pledged faith; nevertheless, he should remain with the woman whom he married, for such a sacrament ought not to be dissolved. But if he has pledged faith of consent, he may not marry another. If, however, he has married another, he shall put her away and adhere to the former [wife].

[Note: Col. 1411: Immediately, *if*: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 1411: *do penance*: the other collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1411: “and nevertheless remain with”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.]

[Note: Col. 1413: *let him put away*: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 1413: “to the former wife”: same edition; “to the first wife”: the remaining editions.]

But faith of agreement exists when someone promises a woman that he will marry her if she permits him to have intercourse with her, or even in return for consent. Faith of consent exists when, even though he does not join hands, he nevertheless consents in heart and speech to marry her; and they mutually give themselves to one another and mutually receive one another.”

[Note: Col. 1413: This passage too is presented in the first compilation of the Decretals as part of the chapter *Duobus*.]

## CAUSE XXVIII

[Col. 1413]

[Col. 1413A] GRATIAN.

A certain unbeliever, being in a marriage, converted to the faith; but his wife departed from him out of hatred for the Christian faith. He took a certain believing woman as his wife; when she died, he became a cleric. At length, on account of the merit of his life and learning, he is elected bishop.

(Question I.) Here it is first asked whether marriage exists among unbelievers. (Question II.) Second, whether this man may marry another while the former wife is alive. (Question III.) Third, whether a man is to be considered a bigamist who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism.

## QUESTION I

GRATIAN.

### Part I

That there is no marriage among unbelievers is proved by many authorities. For Paul says:

> “Everything that is not from faith is sin.”

[Note: Col. 1413: Romans 14:23.]

But the union of unbelievers is not from faith, and is therefore sin. Therefore it is not marriage, because no marriage is sin.

Likewise Augustine:

> “The chastity of an unbelieving man with his wife is not true chastity.”

[Note: Col. 1413D: Augustine: The very words of blessed Augustine are cited below in the same cause, under *Sic enim*, at the words *Nec vera*.]

But where true chastity cannot exist, neither can true marriage exist.

Likewise Ambrose:

> “Ezra commanded foreign wives to be put away, through whom men went after foreign gods. For that which is contracted outside God’s ordinance must not be thought a marriage. But when it is recognized, it must be corrected.”

[Note: Col. 1413D: Ambrose: These words are rather taken from the ordinary gloss on the passage indicated, at 1 Corinthians 7.]

Likewise Augustine:

> “A marriage which is without God is not valid.”

[Note: Col. 1413D: Augustine: This is not found in blessed Augustine. But in blessed Ambrose, on the same seventh chapter of First Corinthians, these words are read: “For a marriage which is without devotion to God is not valid”; and similar words occur in the ordinary gloss there, drawn from blessed Ambrose.]

From all these authorities it is proved that marriage does not exist among unbelievers.

§ 1. But, on the contrary, other authorities are found by which it is proved that marriage does exist among unbelievers. The first of these is that Gospel passage in which Christ says:

> “There shall be five in one house: two shall be divided against three, and three against two.”

[Note: Col. 1413: Luke 12:52.]

Then, after enumerating those persons, he said that wife would be divided against husband, and conversely.

Likewise:

> “Whoever does not hate father, or mother, or wife, or sister for my sake is not worthy of me.”

[Note: Col. 1413: Luke 14:26.]

He said that an unbelieving wife, not a believing one, is to be hated.

Likewise:

> “Everyone who has left house, or father, or sister, or wife for my sake, shall receive a hundredfold,” etc.

[Note: Col. 1413: Matthew 19:29.]

In this place “wife” signifies an unbelieving wife, who is put away for Christ’s sake when Christ’s faith is not abandoned in preference to her.

Likewise the Apostle:

> “If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not put her away; and if any woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not put away her husband. For the unbelieving husband has been sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife has been sanctified through the believing husband.”

[Note: Col. 1413: 1 Corinthians 7:12 ff.]

Likewise, to Titus:

> “Exhort young women to love their husbands.”

[Note: Col. 1413: Titus 2:4.]

This must be understood of unbelievers as well as believers. For women ought to be more devotedly obedient to unbelieving husbands for God’s sake, so that in this way they may be able to win their husbands for Christ. This is read to have happened remarkably in the Passion of blessed Clement, in the case of Theodora and Sisinnius.

### Chapter I. Those who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism are shown to be bigamists.

Likewise Pope Innocent, in Epistle XXII, chapter 2, to Rufus and Eusebius, bishops of Macedonia.

[Note: Col. 1413: Written A.D. 414.—Burchard, book 4, chapter 98. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 96. *Decretum*, part 1, chapter 292; part 8, chapter 303.—Compare above, Distinction 26, chapter 3.]

Will not those born of the woman who was a wife before baptism be admitted to share in the inheritance? Or are they to be called either natural children or bastards, because, as it seems to you, no marriage is lawful except that which is contracted after baptism?

[Note: Col. 1413: *was*: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 1413: “either” and “or bastards” are spurious; they are absent from Ivo’s *Panormia* and from part 8 of the *Decretum*.]

[Note: Col. 1413: *to us*: Paris and Lyons editions; Ivo’s *Panormia*.]

The Lord himself, when he was asked by the Jews whether it was lawful to put away a wife, and explained that this ought not to be done, added:

> “What God has joined together, let no human being separate.”

[Note: Col. 1413: Matthew 19:6.]

[Note: Col. 1413: *Those whom*: the other collected editions.]

And lest he be thought to have spoken of those who acquire wives after baptism, let them remember both that he was questioned by Jews and that his answer was given to Jews.

[Note: Col. 1413: *be believed*: the Hispanic collection and the cited collections.]

[Note: Col. 1413: Compare the correction to chapter 3, Distinction 26, note f.]

I ask—and I ask anxiously—whether the wife is one and the same in the case of a man who was first a catechumen and afterward becomes a believer, and who had children by her while he was a catechumen and then other children when he was a believer. Are they to be called brothers, or, when their father has died, are they not to share with the others in the division of the family inheritance, because spiritual regeneration is believed to have deprived them of the name of sons?

[Note: Col. 1415: Add “was”: Basel edition; “was”: the remaining editions.]

[Note: Col. 1415: Add “of the family”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]

[Note: Col. 1415: *is said*: Ivo’s *Panormia* and part 8 of the *Decretum*; the other collected editions.]

Since it is absurd to hold and judge in this way, what reason is there for defending this evil and vaunting it on an empty opinion rather than confirming it by any authority, when that which the law commanded and God joined together cannot be counted among sins?

[Note: Col. 1415: The other collected editions, the Hispanic collection, and Ivo read: “What reason is there for defending this evil?”]

[Note: Col. 1415: *proved*: Hispanic collection.]

[Note: Col. 1415: *joined together*: the other collected editions, Ivo part 1, *Panormia*, and Burchard; *joins*: Ivo part 8; *enjoined*: Böhm.]

[Col. 1415B] ### Chapter II. After baptism, it is in the believer’s power to take back a wife whom he had previously put away.

Likewise, from the Decree of Pope Eutychian.

[Note: Col. 1415: It is read in Theodore of Canterbury, edition of Petit, chapter 11.—Burchard, book 9, chapter 59. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 97. *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 195.]

### Part II

If a pagan puts away his pagan wife before baptism, after baptism it shall be in his power either to have her or not to have her.

### Chapter III. A believer is not compelled to follow an unbeliever who departs.

The same authority.

[Note: Col. 1415: Read in Theodore, book 1.—Burchard, book 9, chapter 60. Ivo, same place. *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 196.]

Similarly, if one of the spouses has been baptized and the other is a pagan and does not wish to follow, as the Apostle says, “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart.”

[Note: Col. 1415: “and the other pagan does not wish to follow him”: Basel edition; “and the other is a pagan and does not wish to follow”: the remaining editions.]

[Note: Col. 1415: Absent from the Basel edition; compare 1 Corinthians 7:15.]

[Note: Col. 1415: *has departed*: Basel edition.]

### Chapter IV. A wife who does not wish to live with a believer is left without blame.

Likewise Augustine, *On Faith and Works*, chapter 16.

[Note: Col. 1415: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, chapter 32. *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 251.]

A wife joined in lawful union is left without any blame if she does not wish to remain with her Christian husband.

[Note: Col. 1415D: *Wife*: Augustine’s passage reads thus: “For this reason, too, they do not attend to the following, which they say in an attempt, as it were, to prove how much faith alone avails: where the Apostle says, ‘But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart; for brother or sister is not subject to bondage in such cases’—that is, that even a wife joined in lawful union is left without any blame if she is unwilling to remain with her Christian husband because he is a Christian—do not attend to the manner,” etc. But because of the glosses, especially at the words *Non attenditur*, and because Ivo and the *Panormia* agree with Gratian, nothing has been altered.]

It is not considered that she is most rightly put away in the same way if she says to her husband: “I will not be your wife unless you heap up riches for me by your robbery, or unless, though you are now a Christian, you continue the customary procuring from which you formerly maintained our household; or unless you do some other criminal or shameful thing in which she knew her husband to engage, and by which she either found pleasure and satisfied her lust, or had an easy livelihood, or even went about more splendidly adorned.”

[Note: Col. 1415: *her*: the other collected editions; Ivo.]

[Note: Col. 1415: Add “your”: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 1415: *supply*: Ivo and the *Panormia*; *amass*: the other collected editions.]

Then the husband to whom this wife says such things, if, when he came to baptism, he truly did penance for dead works and has as his foundation the faith which works through love, will doubtless be held more strongly by love of divine grace than by the lust of the flesh, and will courageously cut off the member which causes him to stumble.

[Note: Col. 1415: *said*: Ivo and the *Panormia*; the other collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1415: *has done*: the other collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1415: Galatians 5:6.]

[Note: Col. 1415: *lust*: the other collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1415: *caused him to stumble*: same editions.]

### Chapter V. A wife who seeks to compel her husband to evil is lawfully put away.

The same author, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, book I, chapters 27 and 28.

Idolatry, which unbelievers follow, and every harmful superstition, is fornication. But the Lord permitted a wife to be put away on account of fornication. Yet, because he permitted it and did not command it, he gave the Apostle occasion to advise that whoever wishes may not put away his unbelieving wife, so that perhaps through this means she may become a believer.

[Note: Col. 1415: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, chapters 29–30. *Decretum*, part 8, chapters 248–250.]

[Note: Col. 1415: 1 Corinthians 7:15.]

[Note: Col. 1415: “and did not”: the other collected editions; Böhm.]

[Note: Col. 1415: “does not wish to put away”: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 1415: *with whom*: the other collected editions except the first Argentinensis and Basel editions.]

Likewise, chapter 28:

§ 1. If unbelief is fornication, and idolatry unbelief, and avarice idolatry, then there can be no doubt that avarice too is fornication. Who, then, can rightly separate any unlawful desire from the category of fornication, if avarice is fornication? From this it is understood that on account of unlawful desires—not only those committed in acts of debauchery with other men or women, but absolutely every desire which makes the soul, while misusing the body, depart from God’s law and corrupts it ruinously and shamefully—a husband may without fault put away his wife, and a wife her husband. For the Lord makes an exception for the cause of fornication, which fornication, as was mentioned above, we are compelled to understand in a general and universal sense.

[Note: Col. 1415: The other collected editions read “on account of which”; Basel and Lyons II–III add “desires.”]

[Note: Col. 1415: Add “his”: the other collected editions.]

But when he says, “Except for the cause of fornication,” he did not say whose fornication it was, whether the man’s or the woman’s. For permission is given not merely to put away a wife who commits fornication; whoever also puts away that wife by whom he himself is compelled to commit fornication puts her away, certainly, on account of fornication. For example, if a wife compels someone to sacrifice to idols, he who puts away such a wife puts her away on account of fornication—not only hers, because she commits fornication, but his own as well, lest he commit fornication.

[Note: Col. 1415: Absent from the Basel edition; the remaining editions read *says*.]

[Note: Col. 1415: *or*: the other collected editions.]

[Col. 1417A] ### Chapter VI. A woman who makes an image and does not repent is to be put away by her husband.

The same author, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book II.

[Note: Col. 1417C: It does not occur in that book, but in Hermas, *The Shepherd*, Mandate 4, from which Ivo cites this passage together with the Palea, “I said,” below, Cause 34, question 1 and 2; and because that mandate treats both husband and wife, there is some variation in wording, though the sense is the same.]

[Note: Col. 1417: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, chapter 34. *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 243.]

Not only does she commit adultery who defiles her flesh, but she also commits adultery who makes an image. If she persists in these acts and does not repent, depart from her and do not live with her. Otherwise you too will be a partner in her sin.

[Note: Col. 1417: *who*: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 1417: *has repented*: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]

[Note: Col. 1417: *the same*: Basel edition.]

### Chapter VII. One must not abandon the faith out of love for anyone.

Likewise Ambrose, to Hilary.

[Note: Col. 1417D: So also Ivo; but it is found in blessed Augustine, Epistle 89. Bede, on 1 Corinthians 7, cites it from Augustine’s reply to Hilary’s questions.]

[Note: Col. 1417: From Augustine’s letter to Hilary, Epistle 157 in the Maurist edition, written A.D. 414.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, chapter 33. *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 253.]

“If the unbeliever departs,” says the Apostle, “let him depart; for brother or sister is not subject to bondage in such cases.” That is: if the unbeliever is unwilling to remain with his believing spouse, let the believer recognize his freedom, lest he consider himself so subject to bondage that he abandons the faith in order not to lose an unbelieving spouse.

[Note: Col. 1417: Absent from the Venice II, Paris, and Lyons I editions; compare 1 Corinthians 7:15.]

[Note: Col. 1417: Add “his/her own”: the other collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1417: *recognize*: same editions.]

[Note: Col. 1417: *think*: same editions.]

This is to be understood also concerning children and parents, and concerning brothers and sisters: all are to be left for Christ’s sake when this condition is proposed, that one must abandon Christ in order to retain them.

[Note: Col. 1417: *believing children*: Ivo and the *Panormia*; *daughters*: Basel edition; *sons and daughters*: Argentinensis edition; *unbelieving sons and daughters*: the remaining editions.]

[Note: Col. 1417: Add “also”: the other collected editions; Ivo.]

[Note: Col. 1418C: *Christ*: Earlier the reading was, “that he abandon [them] for Christ’s sake, if he desires to have him with him,” as in the other collected editions except Basel, from which the word *for* is absent. It has been corrected from the epistle of blessed Augustine. The remainder is partly from it and partly from old manuscripts of Gratian.]

[Note: Col. 1417: *him*: Ivo and the other collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1417: *desires*: Böhm.]

Accordingly, the same must be understood here concerning house and lands, and concerning those things which are possessed by monetary right.

[Note: Col. 1417: Ivo reads “that is, concerning these things”; the other collected editions read “and concerning the rest.”]

[Note: Col. 1417: “in this place” is absent in Ivo.]

[Note: Col. 1417: *understood*: the other collected editions and Ivo’s *Panormia*; absent from the *Decretum*.]

### Chapter VIII. Even unbelievers are spouses, and a believer may put away an unbeliever.

Likewise Augustine, to Pollentius, book I of *On Adulterous Marriages*, chapters 13 and 14.

[Note: Col. 1417: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 100.]

### Part III

Let us now consider what the Apostle says:

> “But to the rest I speak, not the Lord”—

[Note: Col. 1417: *we see*: Lyons II–III editions.]

[Note: Col. 1417: 1 Corinthians 7:12.]

—when he is speaking, that is, of unequal marriages, where both parties were not Christians. It seems to me that he said this as advice. For because a believing spouse could lawfully leave an unbelieving spouse, the Apostle, not the Lord, forbids this to be done. What the Lord forbids may absolutely not be done.

[Note: Col. 1417: *namely*: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 1417: *can*: Ivo and the other collected editions.]

Therefore the Apostle advises, so that there may be an opportunity to win many persons, that believing spouses should not use the permission granted them to leave unbelievers. But it seems to you that unbelievers may not be put away by believers either, because the Apostle forbids it; whereas I say that it is lawful, because the Lord does not forbid it—yet it is not expedient, because the Apostle advises that it not be done. He also gives the reason why it is not expedient, although it is lawful.

[Note: Col. 1417: Basel reads: “that this is lawful, which [the Apostle] does not…”]

[Note: Col. 1417: Ivo and the other collected editions read, “I say that it is expedient.”]

[Note: Col. 1417: The other collected editions except the first Basel and Lyons II–III editions read, “that these things may not be done.”]

For how do you know, he says, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife? For he had also said above:

> “For the unbelieving husband has been sanctified in the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife has been sanctified in the brother”—that is, in the Christian. “Otherwise,” he says, “your children would be unclean; but now they are holy.”

[Note: Col. 1417: Ivo reads *What?*; compare 1 Corinthians 7:16.]

[Note: Col. 1417: Add “he says”: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 1417: Lyons II–III add “believing.”]

Thus, to win spouses and children for Christ, he seems to have exhorted them even by examples which had already occurred. Why, then, it is not expedient for believing persons to put away unbelieving spouses is plainly expressed: the Apostle forbids departure from unbelieving spouses not because a marital bond with such persons must be preserved, but in order that they may be won for Christ.

[Note: Col. 1417: Absent from the other collected editions except the first Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]

[Note: Col. 1417: Add “the Apostle”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]

[Note: Col. 1417: *even unbelieving*: Ivo and the other collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1417: *marital pact*: Ivo and the other collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1417: “that they may be sought in Christ”: Ivo and the other collected editions.]

For many things are to be done not because the law commands them, but from free love; and those things are more pleasing in the performance of our duties which, though we were permitted not to render them, we nevertheless render out of love. Hence the Lord himself first, although he had shown that he did not owe the tribute, nevertheless paid it, lest he cause offense to those for whose eternal salvation he was accommodating himself while bearing human nature.

[Note: Col. 1417: Add “to pay”: Ivo and the other collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1417: *custom*: Ivo and the other collected editions.]

Moreover, the Apostle’s own words show how he commends these things, where he says:

> “For though I am free from all, I made myself the servant of all, that I might gain the more”—

[Note: Col. 1417: *may testify*: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 1417: 1 Corinthians 9:19 and 5–7.]

—after having said a little earlier:

> “Do we not have the right to eat and drink? Do we not have the permission to take about with us a woman who is a sister, as do the other Apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? Or do only I and Barnabas lack the power to do this work? Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who feeds a flock and does not eat of the milk of the flock?”

[Note: Col. 1417: Here and below, the other collected editions except Basel read *we had*.]

[Note: Col. 1417: *brother*: Ivo and the other collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1419: *this*: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 1419: *of the flock*: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]

And a little later:

> “If others share in your right, why not we still more? But we have not made use of this right; rather, we endure all things, lest we give any hindrance to the Gospel of Christ.”

[Note: Col. 1419: *our*: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I–II, Paris, and Lyons II–III editions; Basel and Venice II add “by right”; the remaining editions read *rights*; Böhm.]

[Note: Col. 1419: The other collected editions read, “why not we still more?”; absent from the Basel edition.]

### Chapter IX. It is lawful to depart from unbelieving spouses, but it is not expedient.

The same author, in the same work, chapter 18 and those following.

[Note: Col. 1419: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 101.]

Thus faithful men or women are not forbidden by the Lord to depart from unbelieving wives or husbands, so as not to be commanded to do so. [Col. 1419: “nor depart”: editions collated, with *o*; “nor” absent in the Basel and Lyons I editions; “they are commanded”: Basel, Paris, and Lyons editions; Venetian I–II read *subeantur*, “they are undertaken/submitted to,” an uncertain or corrupt reading.] For if they were commanded to dismiss such spouses, there would be no place for the Apostle’s counsel advising that this not be done. For in no way would a good servant forbid what the Lord commands to be done. [Col. 1419: “forbids”: editions collated, with *o*.]

Likewise, a little later: “When, therefore, the Gospel had begun to be preached to the Gentiles” [Col. 1419: “had begun”: with *etiam*, “also,” added in the Basel and Lyons II–III editions; “Gentiles” is *gentilibus*, “gentile peoples,” in the Lyons editions; Ivo and the editions collated, except the first Basel edition, read *praedicare*, “to preach”], “he found Gentile spouses already joined to Gentiles.” [Col. 1419: “joined”: editions collated, with *o*; “had found”: Basel and Lyons II–III; “spouses” is *conjugibus*, “with spouses,” in Ivo and the editions collated.] “If both did not believe, but one unbelieving man or woman consented to live with the believer” [Col. 1419: “and an unbeliever”: the same editions], “the believer ought neither to have been forbidden by the Lord to dismiss the unbeliever, nor commanded to do so. They were not forbidden, namely, because justice permits one to depart from an adulterer, and the fornication of an unbelieving person is greater in the heart; nor can that person’s chastity with a spouse be called true” [Col. 1419: “indeed” added in the same editions], “because everything that is not from faith is sin, although the believer has true chastity even with an unbelieving spouse, who does not have true chastity. But believers ought not to have been commanded to separate from unbelievers, because both Gentiles had been joined together not contrary to the Lord’s command.” [Col. 1419: “were,” rather than “had been,” in the same editions.]

§ 1. Therefore, since the Lord neither forbids nor commands a believer to depart from an unbeliever [Col. 1419: “does not forbid”: the same editions; Ivo reads “not”], the Apostle says, so that the believer may not depart, “I say, not the Lord” [1 Cor. 7:12], certainly possessing the Holy Spirit, in whom he can give useful and faithful counsel. Hence, when he had said concerning the woman whose husband had died [Col. 1419: “had been dead”: editions collated, with *o*; cf. 1 Cor. 7:40], “But she will be happier if she remains thus, according to my counsel,” lest anyone think that this counsel, as human rather than divine, ought to be despised, he added: “But I think that I too have the Spirit of God.”

Accordingly, we must understand that even those things which are not commanded by the Lord but are usefully advised by his holy servant are advised by the inspiration of the same Lord. Far be it from any Catholic to say that what the Holy Spirit advises is not advised by the Lord, since he himself is Lord and the works of the Trinity are inseparable.

Yet the Apostle says [Col. 1419: “for”: the same editions and the first Basel edition; “the Apostle” added by Ivo and the editions collated; cf. 1 Cor. 7:25]: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord; but I give counsel”—not that we should regard this counsel as foreign to the Lord, since he immediately continues and says: “as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful.” Therefore he gives faithful counsel according to God in that Spirit [Col. 1419: “in the same Spirit”: editions collated, with *o*] concerning whom he says: “But I think that I too have the Spirit of God.”

§ 2. Nevertheless, the command of the Lord who commands is one thing, and the faithful counsel of a fellow servant [Col. 1419: “servant”: editions collated, with *o*; “indeed” added in the same editions and the first Basel edition], given according to the mercy of charity which has been inspired and bestowed upon him by the Lord, is another. For in the former case it is not permitted to do otherwise [Col. 1419: “would be permitted”: Noric and Venetian I–II editions]; in the latter it is permitted, yet in such a way that what is permitted is at one time advantageous and at another not advantageous.

It is advantageous when it is not only permitted through justice [Col. 1419: “because of”: Ivo and the editions collated, except Lyons II–III] which is before the Lord [Col. 1419: “before God”: Ivo and the editions collated], but also brings no impediment to human salvation. Thus, when the Apostle gives virgins counsel not to marry—whence he testifies that he does not have a command of the Lord—it is permitted to do otherwise, that is, to marry, and to retain the good of marriage, less than continence but nevertheless a good. [Col. 1419: “to retain the good in marriages,” omitting “than” and “nevertheless”: Ivo and the same editions.]

What is permitted is itself advantageous, because it receives the weakness of the flesh, otherwise about to rush into forbidden and unlawful acts, through the honourableness of marrying. [Col. 1419: “received”: the same editions and Lyons II–III; “honourableness”: Lyons II–III; “honourableness,” in the accusative construction, Basel, Paris, and Lyons editions.] Thus it impedes no one’s salvation, although it would be more advantageous and more honourable if the virgin embraced the counsel to which no command compels her.

But what is permitted is not advantageous when it is indeed allowed, yet the exercise of that power brings others an impediment to salvation. Such is—as we have long been discussing—the departure of a believing spouse from an unbelieving spouse. The Lord does not forbid it by a command of law, because it is not unjust before him; but the Apostle forbids it by the counsel of charity, because it brings an impediment to the salvation of unbelievers: not only because they are most perniciously scandalized when offended, but also because, when they enter other marriages while those by whom they were dismissed are living, they are bound in adulterous ties and are released only with the greatest difficulty. [Col. 1419: “with difficulty”: Ivo and the same editions.]

§ 3. Therefore, here, where what is permitted is not advantageous, one cannot say: “If he dismisses the unbeliever, he will do well; if he does not dismiss him, he does better” [Col. 1419: “does well”: Ivo and the same editions], as it was said: “He who gives in marriage does well, and he who does not give in marriage does better” [1 Cor. 7:38]. [Col. 1419: Here and below, the editions collated and Ivo read *nuptui*, “for marriage,” rather than *nuptum*, “in marriage.”]

For there both alternatives are not merely equally permitted [Col. 1419: “but so that”: the same editions and Ivo]—so that no one is compelled to either by the Lord’s command—but both are also advantageous, one less and the other more. Therefore whoever can receive it is urged, by the Apostle’s counsel [Col. 1421: “to use” added in the Basel edition; cf. Matt. 19:12], toward what is more advantageous.

But here, where the question concerns dismissing or not dismissing an unbelieving spouse [Col. 1421: “a spouse with an unbeliever”: one edition; “with a believer”: the remaining editions and Ivo], both alternatives are indeed equally permitted through justice before the Lord, and therefore the Lord forbids neither. But both are not advantageous because of human weaknesses [Col. 1421: “weakness”: editions collated, with *o*]. Therefore the Apostle forbids what is not advantageous, the Lord granting him free scope to forbid it, because the Lord neither forbids what the Apostle advises nor commands what the Apostle forbids. If this were not so, the Apostle would neither advise anything contrary to the Lord’s prohibition nor forbid anything contrary to his command.

§ 4. Accordingly, in these two cases—one concerning marrying or not marrying, the other concerning dismissing or not dismissing an unbelieving spouse [Col. 1421: here and below, the editions collated read “an unbelieving wife to be dismissed”—something similar and something dissimilar is found in the Apostle’s words. They are similar in this [Col. 1421: “that point”: editions collated and Ivo]: there he says [Col. 1421: “and there”: Ivo; “there”: Basel; “to you”: Argentinian, Noric, and Venetian I–II], “I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel” [cf. 1 Cor. 7:25], and here he says, “I say, not the Lord.”

For “I have no command of the Lord” is equivalent to “the Lord does not say it,” and “I give counsel” [Col. 1421: “but” added in the editions collated, except Argentinian] is equivalent to “I say.” But they differ in this: concerning marrying and not marrying, it can be said that one course is done well and the other better, because both are advantageous, one less and the other more. Concerning dismissing or not dismissing an unbelieving spouse, however, since one alternative is not advantageous and the other is advantageous, it ought not to be said, “He who dismisses does well, and he who does not dismiss does better”; rather, it ought to be said, “Let him not dismiss,” because, although it is permitted [Col. 1421: “if it is permitted, nevertheless not”: Basel; “namely”: the remaining editions except Lyons II–III and Ivo], it is not advantageous.

Thus we can say that it is better not to dismiss an unbelieving spouse, although it is permitted to dismiss one, just as we rightly say that what is both permitted and advantageous is better than what is permitted but not advantageous. [Col. 1421: “and” absent in Ivo and the editions collated, except Lyons II–III.]

§ 5. For these reasons it happened that [Col. 1421: “where”: Basel; “that I”: the remaining editions and Ivo], when I was expounding the Lord’s discourse, which he delivered at length on the mountain, and had reached the question of dismissing or not dismissing spouses, I said, adducing apostolic testimonies, that it was the Apostle’s counsel, not the Lord’s command, where he says: “But to the rest I say, not the Lord,” advising those who had [Col. 1421: “have”: editions collated, except Lyons II–III] unbelieving spouses not to dismiss them if they consented to live with them. [Col. 1421: Ivo and the editions collated expand the note as: “I had applied the counsel spoken by the Apostle, not the Lord’s command”; cf. 1 Cor. 7:12.]

This had to be advised, not commanded, because people are not to be restrained from doing permitted things, although they are not advantageous, with as great a weight as unlawful things are to be prohibited. [Col. 1421: “are prohibited”: editions collated.] If the Apostle has somewhere also deigned to advise things which must be commanded [Col. 1421: “deigns”: the same editions and Ivo], he did this by sparing weakness, not by prejudicing the command.

Hence he himself said [Col. 1421: “thus says”: the same editions; “thus said”: Ivo; cf. 1 Cor. 4:14]: “I write these things not to shame you, but to admonish you as my most beloved children.” What question, then, is there where he says, “I say, not the Lord,” as compared with where he says [Gal. 5:2], “Behold, I Paul say to you that, if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing”? Did he also say here, “I say, not the Lord”? [Col. 1421: “Behold, I say”: Ivo and the editions collated.]

These statements, therefore, are not alike, because it is neither unworthy nor contrary for the Apostle also to advise things which the Lord commands. [Col. 1421: “and the Apostle”: Basel.] For we advise those whom we hold dear [Col. 1421: “them” added in Ivo and the editions collated] to do the Lord’s precepts or commands.

But when he says, “I say, not the Lord,” he sufficiently shows that the Lord does not forbid what he himself forbade. [Col. 1421: “may forbid”: Venetian II and Paris; “had forbidden”: Basel and Lyons I.] The Lord would have forbidden it if it were unlawful. Therefore, according to what we have said and discussed at length above, it was permitted through justice; but even what was permitted was not to be done because of free benevolence. [Col. 1421: “if permitted”: Basel.]

§ 6. But you, who hold that what the Lord does not forbid but the Apostle forbids is unlawful in the same way as what the Lord forbids—when you wished to explain what was meant by “I say, not the Lord,” spoken to believers whose spouses were unbelievers—you said that the Lord had commanded that marriages between persons of different religions should not be joined. You adduced the Lord’s testimony [Deut. 7:3]: “You shall not take a wife for your son from the daughters of foreigners, lest she lead him after her gods and his soul perish.”

You also added the Apostle’s words [1 Cor. 7:39]: “A woman is bound as long as her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is free: let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.” You explained this by adding [Col. 1421: “join” rather than “add”: editions collated, except the first Basel and Lyons II–III; “in the Lord” added in Basel]: “that is, to a Christian.”

Then you continued and added: “This, therefore, is the Lord’s command in both the Old and the New Testament, that marriages remain joined only between persons of one religion and faith.” [Col. 1421: The words marked by asterisks are absent in Ivo.] If this, then, is the Lord’s command in both the Old and New Testament, and if the Lord commands and the Apostle teaches that marriages should remain joined only between persons of one religion and faith [Col. 1421: “the same”: Ivo and the editions collated], why does the Apostle command, contrary to this command of the Lord [Col. 1421: absent in Ivo and the editions collated, except Lyons II–III], contrary to his own teaching [Col. 1421: “holy teaching”: Ivo and the editions collated], and contrary to the precept of the Old and New Testament, that marriages between persons of different faith remain joined?

[Col. 1423D: From “Does the Apostle command” through “now in marriage,” and again from “See, lest perhaps” to the end, the following material was added from Blessed Augustine, as also at the end, in order to make the sentence complete. Many readings were corrected from the same original, with manuscript copies and Bede also collated.]

“Because,” you say [Col. 1423: “he says”: Ivo and the editions collated], “Paul, preacher and apostle of the Gentiles, commands those already in marriage—not only advises them—that if one husband or wife had believed [Col. 1423: “the other”: Ivo and the editions collated], the other, unbelieving but consenting to live with the believer, should not dismiss him or her.” By these words of yours you show clearly enough [Col. 1423: “indeed” added in Ivo and the editions collated, except Argentinian, Basel, and Lyons II–III] that this matter is one thing and that matter another.

The former concerns marriages which are initially joined: that a woman should not marry a man not of her religion [Col. 1423: “unless”: editions collated], or that a man should not take such a woman as wife. This, as you say, the Lord commands, the Apostle teaches, and both Testaments prescribe. But who would deny that the latter is different, where [Col. 1423: “there”: the same editions, except Lyons II–III; “therefore” added in Basel] the matter concerns not persons to be joined but persons already joined?

For both were of one and the same unbelief when they were joined. [Col. 1423: “and of the same”: Böhm; “and of that same”: Ivo and the editions collated.] But when the Gospel came, one believed without the other, either the husband without the wife or the wife [Col. 1423: “another without the other”: Basel] without the husband.

If, then, this is different—as plainly appears without any scruple of doubt—why should not the Lord, just as the Apostle commands, command a believing husband to remain in marriage with an unbelieving wife? [Col. 1423: “a believing man with an unbelieving spouse”: Ivo and the editions collated, except Basel; “it is not permitted” added in Ivo and Argentinian, Noric, Venetian I–II, Paris, and Lyons I; “not,” with *and*, absent in the same editions except Lyons II–III.] Unless perhaps in this passage that statement which the Apostle himself [Col. 1423: “himself” absent in the same editions, except Lyons II–III; “the Apostle” absent in Argentinian] makes so confidently [Col. 1423: “faithfully”: Ivo and the editions collated, except Argentinian and Lyons II–III] has no force: “Do you wish to receive proof of Christ who speaks in me?” [2 Cor. 13:3.] And Christ is certainly the Lord.

§ 7. Do you understand what I mean? Or shall I linger somewhat more carefully in explaining it? Attend, so that we may set the matter itself before our eyes for consideration in clearer speech. [Col. 1423: “to be explained” added in Ivo and the editions collated; “to be declared”: Ivo and the same editions, except Lyons II–III.]

Behold: two spouses were of one unbelief when they were joined. [Col. 1423: “were thus”: Ivo, Basel, and Lyons I.] There is no question concerning them that pertains to that command of the Lord, apostolic teaching, and precept of the Old and New Testament by which a believer is prohibited from joining in marriage with an unbeliever. They are already spouses, and both are still unbelievers; they are still such as they were before they were joined [Col. 1423: “were joined together”: Ivo and the editions collated], and such as they were when they were joined.

A preacher of the Gospel arrives [Col. 1423: “and arrives”: the same editions, except Lyons II–III]. One of them, husband or wife, believes [Col. 1423: “believes”: editions collated, except Argentinian and Basel; “or one”: Ivo and the editions collated], but in such a way that the unbeliever consents to live with the believer. Does the Lord command the believer not to dismiss the unbeliever [Col. 1423: “that he not”: Basel; “that”: the remaining editions, except Lyons II–III], or does he not command it? [Col. 1423: “or”: Basel.]

If you say that he commands it, the Apostle objects: “I say, not the Lord.” If you say that he does not command it, I ask the reason. You will not answer me with the reason which you inserted in your letter: namely, that the Lord forbids believers to be joined to unbelievers. [Col. 1423: “namely” added in the editions collated.] Here that is in no way the reason; for we are speaking of those already joined [Col. 1423: “because of those already joined”: Noric, Venetian I–II, Paris, and Lyons editions; “joined together”: Ivo and Lyons II–III], not of those who are to be joined. [Col. 1423: “joined together”: Ivo and the editions collated.]

If, then, you have not found your reason [Col. 1423: “your”: Ivo and the editions collated, except Lyons II–III] why the Lord does not forbid what the Apostle forbids—you see now, I think [Col. 1423: “I judge”: Ivo and the editions collated, except Basel and Lyons II–III], that it is not that very reason [Col. 1423: “reason” added in Ivo and the editions collated] which you had thought—see whether perhaps it is the reason which seemed to me both then to be advanced and now to be defended: namely, that we should understand the Lord to say that which involves justice that cannot in any way be transgressed before him; that is, what he commands or forbids in such a way that it is wholly impermissible to do otherwise.

## Part IV. Gratian

The contrary is found in the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 62 [held A.D. 633].

### Chapter X. Unless a Jew comes to the faith, he is to be separated from his believing wife.

Jews who have Christian women as wives are to be admonished by the bishop of that city [Col. 1423: “that one”: editions collated, with *o*] that, if they wish to remain with them, they should become Christians. If, after being admonished, they refuse, they are to be separated, because an unbeliever cannot remain in the union of one who has now been transferred to the Christian faith. But the children who are born of such unions [Col. 1423: “are”: the same editions] are to follow the faith and condition of their mother. Likewise, those [Col. 1423: “those persons”: the same editions] begotten of unbelieving women and believing men are to follow the Christian religion, not Jewish superstition.

Gratian. But this was decreed so that, while the believer seeks the salvation of the unbeliever, he might instead find with her the destruction of unbelief. Therefore, in the same Council, chapter 59, it was decreed concerning both the children of Jews and others coming to the faith that they should avoid the association of unbelievers [Burchard, book 4, chapter 83; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 73; *Decretum*, part 1, chapter 277]:

### Chapter XI. Believing children are to be separated from association with unbelieving parents, lest they be entangled in their errors.

We decree [Col. 1425: “we decreed”: Basel] that the sons and daughters of Jews be separated from their parents’ association, lest they be further entangled in their errors; they are to be assigned [Col. 1425: “to be assigned”: editions collated, except Basel; “and handed over”: Ivo] either to monasteries, or to Christian men, or to God-fearing women, so that under their manner of life they may learn the worship of faith and, being better instructed in [Col. 1425: “in” absent in Basel] morals as well as faith, may advance.

### Chapter XII. Jews coming to the faith are to have no fellowship with unbelievers. Likewise in the same Council, chapter 61.

[E.g. Burchard, book 4, chapter 84; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 74; *Decretum*, part 1, chapter 278.]

Evil associations often corrupt even the good; how much more those who are inclined toward vices? Therefore let there be no further fellowship of Jews transferred to the Christian faith with those who still remain in the old rite, lest they perhaps be overthrown through participation with them. [Col. 1425: “through participation”: Spanish Collection.] Therefore, whoever among those who have been baptized henceforth does not avoid the association of unbelievers is to be assigned to public beatings unless entrusted to Christians. [Col. 1425: “these”: Basel.]

### Chapter XIII. One must neither eat nor live with Jews, nor receive medicine from them. Likewise from the Sixth Synod, chapter 11.

[In fact, from the Trullan Synod, held A.D. 692; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, chapter 116.]

No one in holy orders [Col. 1425: “constituted” added in Basel and Lyons II–III], nor any layperson, shall eat the unleavened bread of the Jews [Col. 1425: “their”: editions collated, with *o*], live with them [Col. 1425: “associate with them”: Basel], summon any of them in illness, receive medicine from them, or bathe with them in a bathhouse. If anyone does this, if he is a cleric, let him be deposed; if a layperson [Col. 1425: “if, however, a layperson”: the same edition and Ivo], let him be excommunicated.

### Chapter XIV. Clerics and laypeople are to avoid Jewish banquets and are not to receive Jews into their own company. Likewise from the Council of Agde, chapter 40.

[Held A.D. 506; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 13, chapter 117.]

Henceforth all clerics and laypeople are to avoid Jewish banquets [Col. 1425: “shun”: editions collated, with *o*], and no one is to receive them at a banquet. [Col. 1425: “whoever”: Spanish Collection; “welcome”: Spanish Collection and Basel.] For since they do not use common foods among Christians, it is unworthy and sacrilegious for Christians to consume their foods, when they judge unclean the things which we consume with the Apostle’s permission [cf. 1 Tim. 4]. Thus Christians would begin to be inferior to Jews if we used what they set before us while they despised what was offered to them by us.

## Part V. Gratian

From these things it is therefore clearly concluded that marriage exists among unbelievers. But the Apostle’s statement, “Everything that is not from faith is sin” [Rom. 14:23], is not to be understood as though whatever is done by unbelievers must be believed to be sin. Rather, everything done contrary to conscience builds toward Gehenna.

Hence Ambrose [Col. 1425D: These words are reported from the Ordinary Gloss on this Pauline passage. Ambrose’s actual words on the same passage are: “He rightly calls sin that which is done otherwise than it has been approved.”]: “Sin is what is done otherwise than it has been approved.”

§ 1. Likewise Augustine, on the same passage [Col. 1425D: These words are not found in Blessed Augustine; from “Not everything” through “harms” they come from the same Ordinary Gloss on that passage]: “Everything done otherwise than it has been approved is sin; nevertheless, not everything done with faith is good. For ignorance arising from fault is harmful.” Hence the Apostle also says [Rom. 14:22]: “Blessed is he who does not judge himself in what he approves,” that is, who does not make himself liable to condemnation [Col. 1425D: The Interlinear Gloss reads: “who does not make himself liable to condemnation by harming others through his good”] by acting otherwise than he approves ought to be done.

Or, everything not from faith is called sin because whatever is not done with the faith by which it may avail for eternal salvation is reckoned useless before the Lord. Hence Augustine says: “The whole life of unbelievers is sin, nor can what is done without God be good.” [Col. 1426D: Blessed Augustine and the Ordinary Gloss read: “and nothing is good without the highest good”; the remainder is as in Gratian.] For where knowledge of eternal and unchangeable truth is lacking, there is false virtue even in the best moral conduct.

§ 2. Likewise, when it is said, “The chastity of an unbelieving person with his or her spouse is not true,” chastity is denied to be true with respect to its effect, namely, the reward of eternal salvation. For just as among heretics sacraments are denied to be true, not with respect to their form but with respect to their efficacy, so virtues among unbelievers are denied to be true, not because genuine virtues are not present in them, according to the saying attributed to Jerome, “By virtues the Romans earned the empire,” but because they lack the effect of eternal salvation. [Col. 1426D: This sentence was not found in Blessed Jerome; the thought may be derived from Blessed Augustine, *City of God*, book 5, chapters 12–15.]

§ 3. Likewise, Ambrose’s statement cited above [Col. 1425: “above, at the beginning of this same section”], “A marriage made outside God’s decree is not to be considered a marriage; but when it is recognized, it must be corrected,” does not show that marriage does not exist among unbelievers. For no command of the Lord prohibits Gentiles from joining with Gentiles. Their marriage, therefore, is not made outside God’s decree.

By that authority, then, those who have been joined to one another contrary to the decree of God or of the Church are commanded to be separated: namely, unbelievers with believers, blood-relatives with blood-relatives, or relatives by marriage with relatives by marriage. All these, if they have been joined to one another, must be separated.

Hence the same Ambrose, in Book I of *On the Patriarchs*, concerning Abraham, chapter 9 [Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 39]:

### Chapter XV. Believers are not to be joined in marriage with unbelievers.

Beware, Christian, of giving your daughter to a Gentile or a Jew. Beware, I say [Col. 1427: “he says”: editions collated, with *o*], of taking for yourself a Gentile woman, a Jewish woman, or a foreign woman—that is, a heretical woman—and every wife alien to your faith. [Col. 1427: “do not take”: Argentinian and Basel; “to take”: the remaining editions.] The first fidelity of marriage is for the sake of chastity.

And below:

§ 1. If she is Christian, that is not enough unless both of you have been initiated by the sacrament of baptism. You must rise together at night for prayer, and God must be entreated by your united prayers. [Col. 1427: “adored”: Basel; “observed”: Argentinian.]

### Chapter XVI. Catholics are not to intermarry with heretics. Likewise from the Council of Agde, chapter 67.

[Held A.D. 506; cf. distinction 23, chapter 30. Nearly the same provisions occur in the Council of Laodicea, chapter 31; Burchard, book 9, chapter 78; and Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 204.]

It is not proper to intermingle marriages with heretical persons, or to give sons or daughters to them, but rather to receive them, provided that they profess themselves willing to become Christians and Catholics. [Col. 1427: “or and—and”: editions collated, except Basel and Lyons II–III; “profess”: editions collated, except Paris and Lyons; “and” absent in the Spanish Collection.]

### Chapter XVII. Whoever joins himself in the bond of marriage to Jewish perversity is to be deprived of Christian communion. Likewise from the Council of Auvergne.

[Col. 1427C: The same judgment, with certain words changed, occurs in the Council of Auvergne, chapter 6; similar provisions occur in the Second Council of Orléans, chapter 19. Chapter 4; Council of Auvergne, held A.D. 535; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 39.]

If anyone is joined in marital union to Jewish perversity [Col. 1427: Spanish Collection: “is joined in a marital bond”], whether a Christian woman is carnally joined to a Jew, or a Jewish woman to a Christian man [Col. 1427: Spanish Collection: “that is, if a Christian woman or a Jewish woman”], whoever is known to have committed so great a crime [Col. 1427: “are known”: Spanish Collection] is immediately to be separated from the Christian assembly and table-fellowship, and from the communion of the Church. [Col. 1427: “they are to be separated”: Spanish Collection; “let him be separated”: Basel.]

Gratian. Likewise, Augustine’s statement cited above [Col. 1427: “above, at the beginning of this same section”], “A marriage without God is not valid,” does not deny that marriage exists among unbelievers. For one marriage is lawful and not valid; another is valid and not lawful; another is both lawful and valid.

A lawful marriage is one contracted according to legal institution or the customs of a province. This is not valid among unbelievers, because their marriage is not firm and inviolable. [Col. 1427C: “Inviolable”: thus in all the old copies that were collated. The printed editions read, “and therefore violable.”] For, once a bill of repudiation has been given, they may withdraw from one another and join themselves to others by the law of the forum, not by the law of heaven, which they do not follow.

Among believers, however, marriage is valid, because marriages once contracted between them cannot thereafter be dissolved. Some of these are lawful, as when a wife is given by her parents, endowed by the bridegroom, and blessed by a priest. Such marriages are called lawful and valid. But the marriages of those who, having despised all those solemnities, join a woman to themselves as wife solely by affection are believed to be not lawful but valid only.

## Question II

### Gratian

That a man cannot take another wife while his wife is living [Col. 1427D: The printed editions add, “who dismissed an unbelieving woman”; these words are absent from manuscript copies] is testified by Scripture. [Col. 1427D: These are not the actual words of Scripture. The Ordinary Gloss, derived from Ambrose, on 1 Cor. 7, “otherwise your children,” and so forth, reads: “If you dismiss one another, though unwilling to live together, and join yourselves to others, you are adulterers, and your children are illegitimate and therefore unclean.”] It says: “Otherwise, if you separate from one another, and dismiss those willing to live together, and join yourselves to others, you will be adulterers, and your children born afterward will be unclean,” that is, illegitimate.

### Chapter I. No one may take another wife after baptism while she whom he had joined to himself as a virgin before baptism is living.

Likewise from the Council of Meaux, chapter 1. [Similar provisions occur in the Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895, chapter 39; Burchard, book 9, chapter 61; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 98; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 197.]

If anyone had a virgin wife before baptism, he cannot have another after baptism while she is alive. For sins are forgiven in baptism, not marriages.

Gregory, however, testifies to the contrary, saying [Col. 1428C: These words were not found in Blessed Gregory, but nearly the same matter is found more fully and suitably explained in Blessed Ambrose on 1 Corinthians 7; Col. 1427: from the Commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Corinthians, commonly attributed to Ambrose; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 39]:

### Chapter II. A believer may take another wife when an unbelieving woman dismisses him out of hatred for the Christian faith.

[Col. 1428D: The reading is *quam*, “whom,” feminine, also in the old copies; *quem*, “whom,” masculine, would seem to fit the wording of the heading better.]

“If an unbeliever departs because of hatred for the Christian faith, let her depart. For a believing brother or sister is not subject to servitude in such a case.” [1 Cor. 7:15; Col. 1427: “if she departs”: Basel; “believing” added in Basel and Lyons II–III.]

For it is not a sin for the person dismissed on account of God to join himself or herself to another. Contempt for the Creator dissolves the right of marriage with respect to the person who is left behind. The unbeliever who departs sins both against God and against marriage, nor must marital fidelity be preserved with one who departs for the very reason that he or she would not hear that Christ is God of Christian marriages. [Col. 1429D: In the cited passage the reading is: “lest he should hear that God is the author of Christian marriages.”]

Gratian. Here a distinction must be made: dismissing one who is willing to live together is one thing, and not following one who is departing is another. One may indeed dismiss a spouse who is willing to cohabit, but may not take another while that spouse is living. One ought not to follow a departing spouse, however, and may take another while the first is living.

Yet this must be understood only of those who were joined in unbelief. But if both were converted to the faith, or if both were believers when joined in marriage and later one of them abandoned the faith and left the spouse out of hatred for the faith, the abandoned person is not to accompany the one who departed; nevertheless, while that spouse is living, the abandoned person cannot take another, because their marriage had been valid and can in no way be dissolved.

## Question III

### Gratian

Whether a person who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism must be considered a bigamist is clear from the authority of Jerome. For he says on Paul’s Epistle to Timothy [Col. 1429D: The substance of this chapter occurs above, distinction 26, chapter “Of One,” from the Ordinary Gloss on 1 Timothy 3. Blessed Jerome also touched on the matter in his letter on Titus, chapter 1, and treated it extensively in his letter to Oceanus; cf. distinction 26, chapter 1]:

### Chapter I. A person who had one wife before baptism and another afterward is not a bigamist.

“A bishop must be the husband of one wife.” But this applies after baptism. If, however, he had one wife before baptism and had another after baptism [Col. 1429: “had”: Lyons II–III], he is not to be regarded as a bigamist [Col. 1429: “another” in the editions collated, with *o*], since, being wholly renewed through baptism, all old things have been put away.

But Augustine testifies to the contrary, as does Innocent. For Augustine says on Paul’s Epistle to Titus [Note: [Col. 1430D] The substance of this chapter is found in Bede’s collections and in the ordinary gloss on ch. 1 of the Epistle to Titus, as above, Distinction 26, ch. *Acutius*.] [Note: [Col. 1429] cf. ch. 2, Distinction 26.]:

### Chapter II. A man who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism ought not to be made bishop.

They take the matter more strictly who judge that even he who had [Note: [Col. 1429] “had”: Basel edition.] one wife before baptism and another after baptism ought not to be ordained. For in baptism sins are abolished [Note: [Col. 1429] “are absolved”: same edition.], but the marital bond is not dissolved. Just as a woman who was violated while a catechumen cannot be consecrated among the virgins of God, so one who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism can only be reckoned a bigamist. For he has lost something pertaining not to the merit of his life, but to the sacrament of the sign.

Gratian. Likewise Innocent [Note: [Col. 1429] cf. Distinction 26, ch. 3, and above, Question 1, ch. 1.] proves to Rufus and Eusebius, bishops of Macedonia, by many arguments that such a man is to be reckoned a bigamist. Therefore, since the man whose case is now being considered had one wife before baptism and another after baptism, he is judged a bigamist; and although he is distinguished by merit of life, diligence, and learning, he nevertheless cannot be ordained bishop.

## CAUSE XXIX

[Col. 1429]

[Col. 1429C] GRATIAN.

A certain noblewoman was informed that the son of a certain nobleman sought her in marriage, and she gave her consent. But another man, of low and servile status, presented himself in that man’s name and took her as his wife. The man who had first pleased her at length arrived and sought her in marriage. She complains that she was deceived and aspires to union with the former man.

(Question I.) The first question is whether a marriage exists between them. (Question II.) Second, if she first believed this man to be free and later discovered him to be a slave, may she immediately leave him?

### QUESTION I

[Col. 1430C] GRATIAN.

That there is a marriage between them is proved as follows. Marriage or matrimony [Note: [Col. 1429] cf. ch. 1, law concerning paternal power.] is the union of a man and a woman, retaining an indivisible partnership of life. Likewise, the consent of both makes a marriage. Therefore, because these persons were joined so as to preserve an indivisible partnership of life, and because each consented to the other, they should be called spouses.

§ 1. The reply is this: Consent [Note: [Col. 1429] cf. Digest, fragment 1, *On Agreements*.] is the agreement of perception of two or more persons concerning one thing. But one who errs does not perceive; therefore he does not consent—that is, he does not think together with others. This woman, however, erred; therefore she did not consent. Accordingly she is not to be called a wife [Col. 1431A], because there was not the consent of both, without which no marriage can exist. For just as one who is ordained by a person whom he thinks to be a bishop, but who is still a layman, is mistaken and is not called ordained—indeed, he must still be ordained by a bishop—so this woman, being deceived, is joined in marriage to no one; indeed, she must still be joined in marriage.

§ 2. Further, not every error nullifies consent. One who takes as wife a defiled woman whom he believes to be a virgin, or one who takes a prostitute whom he believes to be chaste, each errs: the former believes a defiled woman to be a virgin, the latter judges a prostitute to be chaste. Are they therefore to be said not to have consented to them? Or shall each be granted the liberty of dismissing her and taking another? It is true that not every error excludes consent. But one error concerns the person, another fortune, [Col. 1431B] another status, another quality.

Error concerning the person occurs when someone is thought to be Virgil but is actually Plato. Error concerning fortune occurs when a man who is poor is thought to be rich, or conversely. Error concerning status occurs when one thought free is a slave. Error concerning quality occurs when one thought good is bad. Error concerning fortune and quality does not exclude matrimonial consent. But error concerning person and status does not admit matrimonial consent.

For if someone agreed to sell a field to Marcellus, and afterwards Paul came, saying that he was Marcellus, and bought the field from him, did that man agree with Paul about the price, or should he be said to have sold him the field? Again, if someone promised to sell me gold, and offered me [Col. 1431C] brass instead of gold and so deceived me, would I be said to have consented to brass? I never wished to buy brass, and therefore never consented to it, since consent is nothing but an act of will. Therefore, just as error concerning the material excludes consent in this case, so error concerning the person does in marriage. For she consented not to this man, but to the man whom she believed him to be.

§ 3. But an objection is raised [Note: [Col. 1431D] cf. Genesis ch. 29.]: Jacob had not consented to Leah, but to Rachel; for he had served seven years for Rachel. Therefore, when Leah was substituted for him without his knowing it, there was no marriage between them, if error concerning the person excludes consent; for, as was said, he had consented not to her but to Rachel.

The answer is this: one consent precedes, another follows. Consent precedes when both, before carnal union, consent to an indivisible partnership of life; it follows when, after concubinal or fornicated intercourse, they agree upon the same thing. Therefore Jacob and Leah were not made spouses by preceding consent, but by subsequent consent. Yet they are not judged guilty of fornication from the first intercourse, since he knew her with marital affection and she rendered him the marital due with wifely affection, believing herself lawfully joined to him by the law of primogeniture and by her father’s commands.

§ 4. That error concerning the person excuses some persons is proved by the authority according to which a wife’s sister is reported to have entered her bed, with both sister and husband unaware, and to have been known by her sister’s husband. Although she is judged to remain perpetually without hope of marriage, the man who knew her through ignorance is nevertheless excused.

This is proved in another way as well. The devil sometimes transforms himself into an angel of light; nor is the error dangerous if he is then believed good when he pretends to be good. Therefore, if he should then ask some simple person whether he wished to be a participant in his blessedness, and that person replied that he wished to enter into his fellowship, should he be said to have consented to partnership in diabolical damnation, or rather to participation in eternal brightness?

Likewise, if one of the heretics, under the name of Augustine, Ambrose, or Jerome, presented himself to some Catholic and invited him to imitate his faith, and the latter consented, to whose doctrinal faith would he be said [Col. 1432B] to have consented? Not to the sect of the heretics, but to the integrity of the Catholic faith, which that heretic falsely claimed to possess. Therefore, because this woman, deceived by error concerning the person, consented not to this man but to him whom this man falsely claimed to be, it is clear that she was not his wife.

§ 5. Error concerning fortune and quality does not exclude consent.
