For example, if someone consented to the prelacy of a church which he believed rich, and it proved less well endowed, although he was deceived by an error concerning fortune, he could not resign the prelacy he had accepted. Similarly, a woman who marries a poor man believing him rich cannot renounce her former status, although she has erred. Error concerning quality likewise does not exclude consent. Thus, if someone bought a field or vineyard which he believed extremely fertile, although he erred concerning the quality of the property by buying something less fertile, he nevertheless cannot rescind the sale. Similarly, one who marries a prostitute or a defiled woman whom he believes chaste or virgin cannot dismiss her and take another.

### QUESTION II

GRATIAN.

**Part I.** The second question concerns status: may a woman dismiss a man whom she believed free if she later discovers him to be a slave? That a woman may not leave a slave appears capable of proof by many reasons. For in Christ Jesus there is neither [Col. 1432D] Jew nor Greek, slave nor free; therefore neither is there such a distinction in the marriage of Christians. For each is governed by the same law in faith in Christ. The Apostle says without distinction to all [Note: [Col. 1431D] 1 Corinthians ch. 7, v. 39.], “Whoever wishes to marry, let him marry in the Lord.” And again: “Let a woman marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.” It is not commanded that a freeborn woman marry a freeborn man or a slave-woman a slave; rather, any one of them may marry whom she wishes, provided it is in the Lord.

### Chapter I. Slaves may contract marriages.

Likewise Pope Julius, chapter 4 [Note: [Col. 1433C] This chapter in Burchard and Ivo follows the final words of the chapter “If anyone,” *a slave-woman*, below in the same section.] [Note: [Col. 1433] Chapter of uncertain origin.—Burchard, book 9, ch. 18. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, ch. 38. *Decretum*, part 8, 156.]:

All of us have one Father in heaven, and every person—rich and poor, free and slave—will equally render an account for himself and for their souls [Note: [Col. 1433] “give”: the cited collections.]. Therefore we do not doubt that all persons, of whatever status, have one law insofar [Note: [Col. 1433] Added: “concerned”: Ivo, *Panormia*; “concerns”: the collected editions except Basel.] as concerns God [Note: [Col. 1433] “the Lord”: Basel edition.]. But if all have one law [Note: [Col. 1433C] “But if all have one law”: these words to the end occur indeed in the *Panormia*, but not in Burchard or Ivo, and appear to be the compiler’s own.], then, just as a freeborn person cannot be dismissed, so neither can a slave, once joined in marriage, thereafter be dismissed.

### Chapter II. A slave-woman taken in marriage may not be dismissed by either spouse.

Likewise Pope Zacharias [Note: [Col. 1433] It is read in the chapters of Theodore of Canterbury in Petit, ch. 12, and in the excerpts called Egbert’s, ch. 124.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 53. Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 36.—cf. *Capitularies*, book 6, ch. 95.]:

If a free man has taken a slave-woman in marriage, [Col. 1433B] he has no permission to dismiss her if they are joined by the consent of both, except [Note: [Col. 1433C] “Except”: from here to the end these words are not in the *Capitularies*, nor in Ivo, who cites them [Note: [Col. 1433] nor in the cited penitential.]. The Master of the Sentences, however, has: “unless on account of fornication.”] for the cause of fornication; but henceforth there shall in every respect be one law for man and woman [Note: [Col. 1433] “henceforth” absent from the Basel edition.].

### Chapter III. A marriage between a patron and his freedwoman is acknowledged to be lawful.

Likewise Pope Julius [Note: [Col. 1433] This is Constitution 26 of the Code of Justinian, *On Marriages*, with some alterations.—Burchard, book 9, ch. 18. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, ch. 37; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 156. *Polycarpus*, book 6, title 4.—In the Basel edition it is ascribed to Pope Pius.]:

If anyone grants his slave-woman freedom [Note: [Col. 1433] “to freedom”: Basel edition; “into freedom”: the other editions except Lyons II and III.] and joins her to himself in marriage, some have doubted [Note: [Col. 1433] “it was doubted”: Burchard; Ivo, *Decretum*.] whether marriages of this kind are to be regarded as lawful or not. We, therefore, settling this ancient doubt, judge such unions lawful. For if all marriages are made from affection, and nothing impious or contrary to the laws can occur in such a union, why should we judge [Col. 1433C] the aforesaid marriages to be prohibited [Note: [Col. 1433] “not prohibited”: Basel edition.]? [Note: [Col. 1433] “we judged”: same edition; “we shall judge”: the other editions except Lyons II and III; Burchard; Ivo.]

**Part II.** Gratian. The response is this: it is not denied that a freeborn woman can marry a slave; but it is said that, if she does not know him to be of servile status, she may freely dismiss him [Col. 1434A] when his slavery has been discovered. The statements of the Apostle and Pope Julius must be understood concerning persons whose status is known to both. But this man’s status was unknown to the woman; therefore she is not compelled by the foregoing authorities to remain with him, but is shown to be free either to remain or to depart.

Accordingly, at the Council of Vermeria, attended by King Pippin, it was decreed in chapter 6 [Note: [Col. 1433D] The entire University of Louvain wrote to His Holiness Pope Gregory XIII that a manuscript book survives in the library of St Trudo, under the title *Excerpts of Decrees*, in which, among other chapters of this Council of Vermeria, this and the following chapter are found.] [Note: [Col. 1433] Held A.D. 752.—Regino, book 2, ch. 119. Burchard, book 9, ch. 26. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chs. 41, 111; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 164. Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 36.]:

### Chapter IV. Concerning one who took as wife a slave-woman whom he believed free.

If a freeborn man takes as wife another’s slave-woman and believes her to be freeborn, and that woman is afterwards discovered to be in slavery [Note: [Col. 1434C] “Discovered”: in the Master it is read, “reduced into slavery”; but in Burchard, *inservita* (“enslaved”) [Note: [Col. 1433] thus in the Council of Vermeria and in Regino.], a word occurring in this same sense in book 3 of the *Capitularies*, ch. 28.], he should redeem her from slavery if he can; if he cannot, he may take another wife if he wishes. But if he knew that she was a slave-woman [Col. 1434B] and approved of it, he should hold her as his lawful wife [Note: [Col. 1434C] “As”: in several old manuscripts there is “after as,” likewise “afterwards as” [Note: [Col. 1433] “afterwards as”: Basel edition; “after as”: Burchard, Ivo, *Decretum*, and *Panormia*, ch. 41.], as also in Burchard and Ivo.]. A freeborn woman must do likewise concerning another’s slave.

### Chapter V. A woman who knowingly took a slave as husband may not dismiss him.

Likewise from the same source, chapter 8 [Note: [Col. 1433] Ch. 5, Council of Compiègne, held A.D. 757.—Burchard, book 9, ch. 27. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, ch. 42; *Decretum*, part 8, chs. 52 and 165. Peter Lombard, same place.—*Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, book 5, ch. 20.]:

If a freeborn woman takes a slave, knowing that he is a slave, she must keep him, because we all have one Father in heaven [Note: [Col. 1434D] “Because we all have one Father in heaven”: these words are not in the *Capitularies*, nor in Ivo, part 8, ch. 52, where he himself cites the capitularies. They are, however, in the same author, ch. 165, where he reports it from the Council of Vermeria, as Gratian now does.]. There shall be one law for man and woman.

### Chapter VI. A woman who establishes her freedom after a dispute over status cannot be dismissed on the ground of slavery.

Likewise Gregory, book VI, letter 1, to Fortunatus, bishop [Note: [Col. 1433] Letter 1, written A.D. 597, book 7, Maurist edition.]:

When the bearer of this letter came here last year with her mother, compelled by the circumstances of the matter, your Fraternity knows more carefully that her husband, your cleric, is known to have removed her from his companionship because she had been accused of servile status; [Col. 1435A] and they state that you, being there, promised that, if with God’s help she could prove herself free, you would restore her to her husband in marriage. Therefore let your Fraternity know that, God—the author of freedom—having revealed it, she has been proved free, and no stain of slavery has been found in her. Knowing these things, we wish her to be restored without any delay to her husband *through you*, and that the same man should not hereafter seek pretexts to enable him to cast her off. For if this is not fulfilled by you—which we do not believe—and he should perhaps delay in receiving her, know that we [Note: [Col. 1435] “you”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] shall correct that with severe punishment [Note: [Col. 1435] “to correct”: collected editions.].

Gratian. When it says [Note: [Col. 1435] cf. above, ch. 5.], “knowing him to be a slave,” it gives us to understand that, if she did not know him to be a slave, she need not remain with him. Therefore, because this woman has suffered deception both as to person [Col. 1435B] and status, she is not compelled to adhere to him by whose fraud she was deceived. But if she took him as free, and he made himself another’s slave in order to create a cause of separation, neither may he dismiss his wife nor may she, by reason of the marital bond, be reduced to slavery.

Accordingly, at the Council of Tribur [Note: [Col. 1435] It is not found in the printed Council of Tribur.—Regino, book 2, ch. 203. Burchard, book 9, ch. 75. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, ch. 99; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 212. Peter Lombard, same place.]:

### Chapter VII. A husband may not leave a woman whom he took while she was free, on the pretext that her status has been fraudulently changed.

It was reported to the holy synod that a certain freeborn man took a freeborn woman as wife [Note: [Col. 1435] “has taken”: Burchard and Ivo.], and, after the begetting of children, made himself a slave [Col. 1436A] on some pretext for divorce [Note: [Col. 1435] “has made”: same authors; Basel edition.]. The question was asked whether he must necessarily keep the woman and, if he keeps her, whether she too ought under secular law to be subjected to slavery [Note: [Col. 1435] “subjects”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1435D] “The question was asked”: these two words are absent from the other collectors except the Master. The secular law mentioned here is among the laws of the Lombards, as the gloss states.]. It was judged that the wife must by no means be dismissed; nevertheless, by Christ’s law the woman is not to be reduced to slavery, since he made himself a slave without his wife’s consent [Note: [Col. 1435] “made”: Burchard, Ivo, *Panormia*.], although she had taken him as a free man for her husband [Note: [Col. 1435] “took”: Burchard and Ivo, *Decretum*; “shall have taken”: Ivo, *Panormia*.].

Gratian. It is also asked whether, if the slave of one person takes the slave-woman of another, there is a marriage between them.

Concerning them it was decreed at the Second Council of Chalon, chapter 30 [Note: [Col. 1435] Held A.D. 813.—Burchard, book 9, ch. 29. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, ch. 40; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 167, part 16, ch. 335. Peter Lombard, same place.—cf. *Additional Capitularies* III, ch. 54.]:

### Chapter VIII. Masters are not to dissolve lawful marriages of slaves by their own authority.

[Col. 1436B] It has been reported to us that certain persons, by a kind of arbitrary presumption, dissolve lawful marriages of slaves [Note: [Col. 1435] “matrimonies”: original; Burchard; Ivo; *Capitularies*; Basel edition.], without attending to the Gospel saying [Note: [Col. 1435] Matthew ch. 19, v. 6.], “What [Note: [Col. 1435] “Whom”: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions.] God has joined, let no human being separate.” Therefore it has seemed good to us that marriages of slaves are not to be dissolved even if they have different masters, but that, remaining in one marriage, they should serve their masters. This is to be observed where there has been a lawful union and it occurred through [Note: [Col. 1435] “by the will of”: Ivo, *Panormia*.] the consent of the masters.

## CAUSE XXX

[Col. 1435]

[Col. 1435C] GRATIAN.

A certain man, hindered by a crowd of people, received his own son from baptism, believing that he was receiving another’s child. But his wife, wishing craftily to receive her own child, received another’s, whom her husband adopted as his son. A daughter was born to him by his wife, and while both were in their cradles he gave that daughter to his adopted son—his wife’s spiritual son—in marriage. After three years his wife died, and the man secretly betrothed to himself the widow of his wife’s *compater*; some time passed, and another man publicly took her as wife.

(Question I.) The first question is [Col. 1435D] whether one who received his own son from sacred baptism may render the marital due to his wife. (Question II.) Second, whether betrothals can be contracted between infants. (Question III.) Third, whether spiritual or adopted children may be joined to natural children [Col. 1436C] in marriage. (Question IV.) Fourth, whether anyone may take as wife the wife of his wife’s *compater*. (Question V.) Fifth, whether a clandestine betrothal prejudices a public one.

### QUESTION I

GRATIAN.

**Part I.** That one who transfers his own son into a spiritual relationship with himself cannot render the marital due to his wife is proved by reason and authority. For no authority permits anyone to have carnal intercourse with his *commater*—that is, the woman with whom he shares a spiritual child. But this man has made his own wife his *commater*; therefore he can no longer have carnal intercourse with her.

[Col. 1437A] Accordingly Deusdedit, bishop of the Holy Roman Church, writes to Gordian, bishop of the church of Hispalis [Note: [Col. 1437C] “Of Hispalis”: in the fragment of this letter found in the volumes of councils it is read “of the Spains”; in Anselm and Burchard, “Hispaniensis.”], and beloved brother [Note: [Col. 1437] Apocryphal letter.—Burchard, book 17, ch. 41. Anselm, book 10, ch. 29 (36). Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, ch. 127; *Decretum*, part 1, ch. 305. *Polycarpus*, book 6, title 4. Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 42.]:

### Chapter I. Men who, by some accident, hold their own newborn children before a bishop are to be separated from their wives.

Your deacon [Note: [Col. 1437] absent from Ivo.], bearing the letter of your Holiness, came to us and reported that some men and women, on the past Saturday of Easter, through the great press of people, unknowingly received their own children from the holy washing. You therefore wish to know whether, because of such an occurrence, men and women ought to return to their own spouses or not. Saddened by this matter [Note: [Col. 1437] “in”: same editions.] [Note: [Col. 1437] “sorrow”: Burchard.], we inquired into the pronouncements of our forefathers [Note: [Col. 1437] “our fathers”: absent in Ivo; “fathers”: absent in Burchard.]. We found, moreover, in the archives of this Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 1437] “of this apostolic see”: absent from the Basel edition.] that such cases had already occurred in the churches of Isauria, Ephesus, and Jerusalem together, and of other cities [Col. 1437B] [Note: [Col. 1437C] “Cities”: this passage is read variously in old manuscripts and among the collectors; it has been adapted chiefly from Anselm [Note: [Col. 1437] “other churches of the bishops, and their cities”: Burchard, Anselm, Ivo; in the collected editions “churches” stands for “cities”.].].

When the bishops of those cities likewise wished to know from this Apostolic See whether men and women should return to their own marriage-bed, the most holy Fathers of blessed memory—Julius, Innocent, and Celestine—acting with the consent [Note: [Col. 1437] “assembly”: Burchard.] of very many bishops and priests in the church of the Prince of the Apostles, wrote prohibiting [Note: [Col. 1437] “wrote in reply”: Basel edition; “prescribed”: Böhm.] and confirmed that men and women who, for any reason, had received [Note: [Col. 1437] “who for whatever reason”: Burchard; “who for whatever reason”: Ivo, *Panormia*.] their own newborn children [Note: [Col. 1437] “their own”: absent in Burchard, Basel edition, and Ivo, *Decretum*.] should by no means return to one another in marriage, but should separate, lest such a vice grow through the devil’s prompting.

You know that, just as there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, so there are seven gifts of baptism, from the first nourishment of consecrated salt and entrance into the church up to the confirmation of the Holy Spirit by chrism. From this first [Note: [Col. 1437] “from the first, therefore”: Ivo, *Decretum*; collected editions.] gift of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1437C] to the seventh [Note: [Col. 1437] “seven”: collected editions except Basel, Paris, and Lyons.] no Christian should take his *commater* in marriage [Note: [Col. 1437] “receive”: Burchard; “take”: Basel edition.]. Whoever presumes to do so is to be bound by the bond of anathema until he has performed worthy penance [Note: [Col. 1437] “exacted”: same edition.].

### Chapter II. He who held his stepchild before a bishop is to be separated from his wife.

Likewise from the Council of Vermeria, chapter 3 [Note: [Col. 1438C] Burchard and Ivo, book 9, ch. 80, cite this from the Council of Vermeria; and the University of Louvain reported that in the *Excerpts of Decrees* in the library of St Trudo it is cited from the same council. But the same Ivo, part 1, ch. 302, and the Master of the Sentences cite it from the *Capitularies*, where it occurs at book 5, ch. 5.] [Note: [Col. 1437] Ch. 12, Council of Compiègne, held A.D. 757.—Regino, book 2, ch. 218. Burchard, book 17, ch. 22. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, ch. 125; *Decretum*, part 1, ch. 302, part 9, ch. 80. Peter Lombard, same place.—cf. *Capitularies*, book 5, ch. 7.]:

If anyone has held his own stepson [Note: [Col. 1437] Added: “his own”: Basel, Paris, and Lyons editions.] or stepdaughter before a bishop for confirmation, he shall be separated from his wife and shall never take another wife [Note: [Col. 1437] Added: “and likewise the woman”: *Capitularies*; Burchard; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 9; collected editions.].

**Part II.** Gratian. On the contrary, Nicholas writes to the bishop of Salona, saying [Note: [Col. 1437] It is not found among the published letters of Nicholas.—In Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, ch. 124, it is said to have been written to the bishop of “Salomonita”; in the *Decretum*, part 1, ch. 136, to “Bishop Salemonius”.]:

### Chapter III. A woman who raised her stepson from the sacred font is not to be separated from her husband.

You wish to know whether a woman who has raised from the sacred font the son of her husband, born from another woman, may afterwards be joined to that same husband. We decree that they can be joined [Note: [Col. 1437] “be joined together”: collected editions.], because according to the sacred canons a spouse ought not to leave a spouse under the pretext of any religious observance unless by the consent of both. [Col. 1438B] It is, moreover, conducive to the wife’s great ruin when, hating her husband or taking no account of his weakness, she performs an impious act under the semblance of piety—especially since the Apostle commands [Note: [Col. 1437] 1 Corinthians ch. 7, v. 5.], “Do not defraud one another, except by consent for a time, that you may [Note: [Col. 1437] Added: “more freely”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same thing, lest Satan tempt you because of [Note: [Col. 1437] “but I say this because of”: Basel edition.] your lack of self-control.”

Therefore, if it is proved that this was not done by the consent of both spouses, they are not to defraud one another but are to return again to the same thing, especially since the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1437] 1 Corinthians ch. 7, v. 4.], “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; and likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”

### Chapter IV. A woman who fraudulently held her own son before a bishop is not to be separated from her husband, but is to do penance.

Likewise from the Second Council of Chalon, chapter 31 [Note: [Col. 1437] Held A.D. 813.—Burchard, book 17, ch. 23. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, ch. 65; *Decretum*, part 9, ch. 81. Peter Lombard, same place.]:

It has been reported to us that some women, carelessly, and others fraudulently, in order to separate themselves from their husbands, have held their own children before bishops [Note: [Col. 1437] “before a bishop”: Basel edition.] for confirmation. [Col. 1439A] Therefore we have judged it fitting that, if any woman has through carelessness or fraud held her own son before a bishop for confirmation, she should do penance for her deceit or fraud as long as she lives [Note: [Col. 1439] “lives”: same edition; “may live”: Argentinensis edition; Burchard and Ivo.]; yet she is not to be separated from her husband [Note: [Col. 1439] absent from the Norimberga, Venice I–II, Paris, and Lyons I editions.] [Note: [Col. 1439] “depart”: Basel edition.].

### Chapter V. Those who take their goddaughter or spiritual mother as wife are to be separated and punished with severe penance.

Likewise from the Council of Mainz, chapter 10, held in the cloister of Alban [Note: [Col. 1439] Rather, from Rabanus’s letter to Heribald, written A.D. 853, with some alterations; cf. Regino, book 2, 196. Burchard, book 17, ch. 24. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, ch. 66; *Decretum*, part 9, ch. 82. Peter Lombard, same place.]:

Concerning what you asked—whether one who has taken his goddaughter as wife [Note: [Col. 1439] “has taken”: collected editions except Paris and Lyons.], one who has had intercourse with his spiritual *commater* [Note: [Col. 1439] “mother”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.], and one who has baptized his own son while his wife [Note: [Col. 1439] “and whose”: Burchard and Ivo; Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] received him from the font, did so in order that [Col. 1439B] a dissolution [Note: [Col. 1439] “discidium”: Burchard, Ivo, *Panormia*, and collected editions except Lyons II–III.] of the marriage might occur—may remain afterwards in such a union: concerning such people the answer must be no.

If anyone has taken his goddaughter or *commater* in marriage [Note: [Col. 1439] “in marriage”: Ivo; Basel edition.], we judge that they must be separated and punished with severe penance. But if lawful spouses, one or both, have deliberately arranged to receive their own child from the font [Note: [Col. 1439] Added: “so that a dissolution may occur”: Burchard and Ivo.], it is good if they wish to remain unmarried; but if not, severe penance is to be imposed upon the plotter, and they are to remain together. If the violator of marriage outlives the other, he is to be punished with the most severe penance and remain without hope of marriage.

### Chapter VI. Those who hold their stepchildren before bishops are not to be separated from their wives.

Likewise Pope Nicholas to Rodulph, bishop of Bourges [Note: [Col. 1439] Written A.D. 864.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, ch. 126; *Decretum*, part 1, ch. 304. Peter Lombard, same place.]:

Concerning those who hold their stepchildren for confirmation before [Col. 1439C] bishops—that is, those who support over themselves the children of their wives by a previous husband while they are anointed with chrism by bishops—if this is done through ignorance, as you assert [Note: [Col. 1439] “as is asserted”: Ivo, *Decretum*.], although it is a sin, it is nevertheless not to be punished by separation of the marriage [Note: [Col. 1439] “they are not to be punished”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]. Yet they should grieve and, cleansing [Note: [Col. 1439] “atone for”: Basel edition.] this by worthy penance, say to the Lord [Note: [Col. 1439] Psalm 24, v. 7.]: “Do not remember the sins of our ignorance.”

### Chapter VII. One who baptized his own son out of necessity is not to be separated from his wife.

Likewise Pope John VIII [Note: [Col. 1439] Letter 188 in Mansi, dated the seventh day of June, indiction XII, i.e. A.D. 879.—Anselm, book 10, ch. 30 (37). Ivo, *Decretum*, part 1, ch. 306. *Polycarpus*, book 6, title 4. Peter Lombard, same place.] to Anselm, bishop of the church of Limoges [Note: [Col. 1439] “Lemozinae”: Anselm and Ivo; “Lemosinae”: collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 1439C] The letter of John VIII from which this chapter is taken is in the Vatican Library, written to Anselm, bishop of the church of Limoges; and in the subscriptions to the Council of Pavia, held in the time of the same John with his legates and a great part of the bishops of Italy and Gaul, it reads: “Anselm, bishop of the church of Limoges.” It has therefore been corrected to “Lemovicinae,” whereas it was previously read “Lemosinae.”]:

This man, Stephen by name, having come here in person to the thresholds of the blessed [Note: [Col. 1439] “of the blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles”: collected editions.] princes of the apostles Peter and Paul for prayer, made known to our episcopal office that his son was at the point of death and had not yet been washed in the water of baptism. Since priests were absent and extreme necessity compelled him, he had baptized the child [Note: [Col. 1439] “baptized”: same editions.] and, holding him in his own hands, had received him [Note: [Col. 1439] “received”: same editions.]. Because this matter was brought to your notice, your Reverence, as though zealous for rectitude, judged [Note: [Col. 1439] “judged”: same editions.] that the aforesaid man must be separated from his wife.

This must by no means be done, [Col. 1440B] since Scripture says [Note: [Col. 1439] cf. Proverbs ch. 19, v. 14, according to the Septuagint.] that a wife is joined to her husband by the Lord, and: “What [Note: [Col. 1439] “Whom”: collected editions; cf. Matthew ch. 19, v. 6.] God has joined, let no human being separate.” Therefore the Lord also plainly commands in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1439] Ivo: “in the Gospel says that no one can dismiss…”] that a man cannot dismiss his wife except for the cause of fornication.

Accordingly, relying especially on the command of so great an authority [Note: [Col. 1439] “principal”: collected editions.], we say that what necessity has brought about must be disregarded [Note: [Col. 1440C] “Must be disregarded”: thus corrected from several old copies, the letter itself, and Ivo. Below also, Cause 34, Questions 1 and 2, ch. 1, Leo uses the same words: *omittendum est* (“it must be disregarded”) and “must be judged blameless,” whom John seems to have wished to imitate. The vulgate editions read: “is not to be dismissed” [Note: [Col. 1439] “must be dismissed”: Anselm; Argentinensis, Norimberga, Venice I–II, Paris editions; “not to be dismissed”: Basel and Lyons I; “a woman is not to be dismissed”: Lyons II–III.].] and judged blameless. For the work of baptism may freely be performed by faithful laypersons, if necessary, according to canonical authority [Note: [Col. 1439] “ordinance”: original; Ivo.].

Thus, if the aforesaid father, seeing his son dying bodily, washed him in the sacred water of baptism lest he allow the child’s soul to perish in eternal death, so that he might rescue him from the power of the author of death and darkness and send him without doubt into Christ’s kingdom, now to reign [Col. 1440C] [Note: [Col. 1439] “reborn”: original; Ivo.], he is praised for having acted well. For that reason, we judge that he is to remain lawfully joined to his wife, already lawfully united to him, without penalty as long as he lives, and that he ought in no respect to be separated from her on this ground contrary to the aforesaid divine authorities [Note: [Col. 1439] “ought to have been”: Ivo.].

**Part III.** Gratian. A spiritual daughter is called such not only in relation to the person who receives her, but also in relation to the person who immerses her in sacred baptism with the formula of the threefold immersion. A woman who confesses her sins to a priest is also called that priest’s [Col. 1441A] spiritual daughter. A shameful union with any of these women is to be punished with the same penalty.

[Note: [Col. 1441] Thus the collected editions except Basel.]

Accordingly Pope Symmachus says [Note: [Col. 1441] Chapter of uncertain source.—In the Basel edition it is attributed to Pope Nicholas.—Peter Lombard, ibid.—cf. Roman Penitential, ancient Augustinian, vol. 8, ch. 3.]:

**C. VIII. An equal penance is imposed upon one who is shown to have violated his spiritual daughter and his penitent.**

All whom we receive into penance are our spiritual children, just as are those whom the water of sacred baptism has regenerated, whether we received them ourselves or immersed them with the formula of the threefold immersion. Silvester also, teaching, warns every priest [Note: [Col. 1441] *priests*: editions compared, first Paris, Lyons I.], that no one should approach his own penitent on account of fornication, because it is written: “All whom we receive into penance [Note: [Col. 1441] *receive*: Basel edition.], are as much our children as those received in baptism.” Therefore, if anyone has committed this crime, [Col. 1441B] let him lose not only the honor of his rank, but let him submit himself [Note: [Col. 1441] *be subjected*: Basel edition.] to continual penance until the end of his life [Note: [Col. 1441] *of his life*: absent from the Argentinian edition; *his* absent from the Basel edition.].

**C. IX. On the same matter. Likewise Coelestine** [Note: [Col. 1441] Chapter of uncertain source.—Anselm, book 11, ch. 30, though omitting the heading and changing words here and there.—Polycarp, book 4, title 39.—Roman Penitential, ibid., ch. 4.]

If any priest has fornicated with his spiritual daughter [Note: [Col. 1441] add: *his own*: Basel edition.], let him know that he has committed a grave adultery. Therefore, if the woman is a laywoman, let her leave everything and give her possessions to the poor [Note: [Col. 1441] *bestow*: same edition.]; and, converted, let her serve God in a monastery until death [Note: [Col. 1441] add: *in continual penance*: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]. But the priest, who has given people an evil example, is to be deposed from every office and do penance for twelve years as a pilgrim [Note: [Col. 1441] fifteen years: Roman Penitential; ten years: Basel edition.]; afterward he is to go to a monastery, and there serve God throughout all the days of his life.

**C. X. On the same matter. Likewise** [Note: [Col. 1441] Chapter equally of uncertain source.—Polycarp, ibid.]

A bishop or presbyter ought not to have intercourse [Col. 1441C] with women who have confessed their sins to him. If, by chance—which God forbid—this should happen [Note: [Col. 1441] *occur*: Basel edition.], he is to do penance as for a spiritual daughter: a bishop for fifteen years [Note: [Col. 1441] *years*: same edition.], a presbyter for twelve; and he is to be deposed, if [Note: [Col. 1441] *if—becomes public*: absent from the Argentinian edition.] the matter has nevertheless become known to the people.

Gratian. Thus it appears from these authorities that, whether a woman has received from the sacred font her own son or merely the son of her husband, she is not for that reason to be separated from her husband. The same is likewise to be understood concerning the husband.

## QUESTION II

[Col. 1442A]

## GRATIAN

Betrothals cannot be contracted before the age of seven. For they are contracted by consent alone, and consent cannot intervene unless what is being done between them is understood by both parties [Note: [Col. 1441C] *Both*: thus corrected from most ancient copies; formerly it read: *either one*, whereas the consent of each is necessary.]. Therefore it is proved that betrothals cannot be contracted between children, whose weakness of age does not admit consent. Pope Nicholas testifies to the same effect, saying [Note: [Col. 1441D] In the Decretals, title *On the Betrothal of the Impubescent*, ch. 2, the beginning of this chapter is found, and other material from that rescript of Nicholas is added [Col. 1442C].] [Note: [Col. 1441] Chapter of uncertain date.—cf. Compilation I, *On the Betrothal of the Impubescent*, ch. 4, and ch. 2, X, at this title.—Ivo, Panormia, title 6, ch. 122.]:

**SOLE CHAPTER. Marriage cannot be contracted before the time for consenting.**

Where there is not the consent of both, there is no marriage [Note: [Col. 1441] *there is not*: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]. Therefore, those who give girls to boys in the cradle, and conversely, do nothing unless each of the children, after reaching the years of discretion, [Col. 1442B] consents [Note: [Col. 1442C] *Consents*: in the vulgate codices there follows [Note: [Col. 1441] thus editions compared and Ivo.]: “and there is no marriage unless there is the consent of both”; these words are absent from most manuscripts.], even if father and mother have willed and done this.

## QUESTION III

## GRATIAN

**Part I.** That spiritual or adoptive children cannot be joined to natural children, Pope Nicholas, answering the inquiries of the Bulgarians, chapter 2, testifies in these words [Note: [Col. 1441] written A.D. 866.—Anselm, book 10, ch. 29; Ivo, Panormia, book 6, ch. 123; Decretum, part 1, ch. 135, part 9, ch. 34; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 42.]:

**C. I. One received from the sacred font is the child of the person by whom he is received.**

A man ought to love him who receives him [Note: [Col. 1441] *himself*: editions compared, first Argentinian and Basel.] [Note: [Col. 1441] *will have received*: Norwegian edition; *received*: remaining editions; Ivo, Decretum, part 1.] from [Note: [Col. 1441] *out of*: original and Ivo, Decretum; *from*: Panormia.] the sacred font as a father. Likewise:

§ 1. Between spiritual brothers and children there is a gratuitous and holy fellowship, which is not to be called blood-relationship, but [Col. 1442C] rather is to be regarded as spiritual kinship. Therefore we do not think [Note: [Col. 1441] *I do not think*: editions compared.] that any lawful marriage can take place between them, since the venerable Roman laws do not permit marriages to be contracted either between those who are children by nature or between those who are children by adoption.

Likewise:

§ 2. If, therefore, marriage is not contracted between those whom adoption joins [Note: [Col. 1441] *unites*: Basel edition.], how much more ought those whom regeneration by the heavenly sacrament of the Holy Spirit binds [Note: [Col. 1441] *has joined*: Ivo, Decretum; *binds*: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] to refrain from carnal cohabitation with one another? Much more fittingly, therefore [Note: [Col. 1441] add: *he says*: Ivo, Panormia; editions compared.], is he called the son of my father or my brother whom divine grace, rather than human choice, selected to be my father’s son or my brother; and more wisely are we kept apart from reciprocal bodily intercourse.

**C. II. A spiritual daughter can in no way marry a natural son. Likewise Zacharias, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend Theodore, bishop of the church of Ticinum** [Note: [Col. 1443] written about A.D. 745.—Anselm, book 10, ch. 27 (31); Ivo, Panormia, book 6, ch. 128; Decretum, part 1, ch. 307.]

Your venerable brotherhood [Note: [Col. 1443] *charity*: Basel edition.] presented us with a little written petition [Note: [Col. 1443] “the document which was presented to us … we received”: Ivo, Panormia and editions compared.], by which you sought to inquire [Note: [Col. 1443] *wished*: Ivo, Panormia and editions compared.] whether it is lawful for a son whose father has received another’s daughter from sacred baptism [Note: [Col. 1443] *font*: Ivo, Decretum.]—the received girl, that is, the spiritual daughter of his father—to take her in marriage [Note: [Col. 1443] *receive*: editions compared.], a thing which, you assert, has happened monstrously among you. [Col. 1443B]

§ 1. But your holy brotherhood well knows that the Lord commanded [Note: [Col. 1443] *commanded Moses*: same editions; cf. Lev. 18:8.] through Moses, saying: “You shall not uncover the nakedness [Note: [Col. 1443C] *Nakedness*: in the decrees of Zacharias, found in an old codex, and in Anselm and Ivo, all this occurs as in Leviticus 18.] of your father, or mother, or sister; for it is your own nakedness.” Since, therefore, we are commanded to abstain from our own blood-relationship [Note: [Col. 1443C] *Since, therefore*: in the same decrees it reads: “One is said not to uncover nakedness when we are commanded to abstain from one’s own blood-relationship. Much more,” etc.], much more, setting aside every excuse or pretext, ought we under the strictest obligation to beware of the spiritual daughter of our father, lest anyone who, having involved himself [Note: [Col. 1443] *intermingled*: Basel edition.] in such a deed, has not restrained the reins of lust should incur the wrath of the divine judgment [Note: [Col. 1443] *of the divine examination*: editions compared; Ivo, Panormia.].

Therefore all must absolutely guard themselves against such criminal intercourse [Note: [Col. 1443D] In Anselm: “Therefore every instance of intercourse in such a crime must be absolutely avoided.”] [Note: [Col. 1443] *deed*: same edition.], lest they perish for ever [Note: [Col. 1443] *eternally*: original in Anselm; Anselm and Ivo.]. But your brotherhood should by every means strive to separate and subject to fitting penance this man, the author of this ruinous presumption [Note: [Col. 1443] *author* is absent from the original in Mans., Ivo, and the Argentinian and Basel editions.], who, despising the salvation of his soul, has entered into a most impious marriage [Note: [Col. 1443] *impious*: editions compared and Ivo, Panormia.] [Note: [Col. 1443] *has entered*: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.], so that you may win his soul, rescued from eternal condemnation [Note: [Col. 1443] “the souls of them, rescued from condemnation”: original; Anselm; “rescue … their souls”: Ivo, Decretum; “free … their souls”: Panormia.].

**C. III. No one should dare give to his son the daughter whom he received from the sacred font. Likewise Zacharias and Deusdedit** [Note: [Col. 1443] Chapter of uncertain source.—Anselm, book 10, ch. 28 (33); Polycarp, ibid.]

No one ought ever to give in marriage to his son the daughter [Note: [Col. 1443] add: *his own*: editions compared.] whom he has received from the sacred font, [Col. 1444A] because in the divine judgment they are found to be siblings. If anyone involved in such a deed has not restrained the reins of lust, he shall be abhorred by the catholic Church. But if he has converted, after the separation he is to do penance for seven years. The same condition applies to those who knew of it together with the perpetrator: that is, together with the collaborators and consenting persons, let them do penance [Note: [Col. 1443] *let them do penance*: Basel edition.].

**Part II. Gratian.** Children, whether born before or after spiritual co-parenthood, may lawfully be joined in marriage.

Accordingly Urban writes to Vitalis, presbyter of Brescia, saying [Note: [Col. 1443] Chapter of uncertain date.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 50, ch. 23.—Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 42.—Baluze testifies that in ancient codices this Vitalis is incorrectly called *of Brives*.]:

**C. IV. Sons or daughters born before or after spiritual co-parenthood may be lawfully joined.**

Concerning the matters on which your affection consults [Note: [Col. 1443] *has consulted*: editions compared.] us, it seems to us that this answer should be given: that baptism is valid [Note: [Col. 1443] *and* is absent from Böhm.] if, under pressing necessity, a woman baptizes a child in the name of the Trinity; and that sons or daughters of spiritual parents, born before or after the spiritual co-parenthood [Note: [Col. 1443] *born* [feminine]: same editions.], may lawfully be joined, except the person through whom they became co-parents.

But Paschal II, prohibiting the union of persons born after spiritual co-parenthood, writes to Bishop Regino [Note: [Col. 1444C] Anselm, book 10, ch. 34, reports almost the whole of this letter; likewise Polycarp, whose beginning occurs in the chapter *After the Wife’s Death*, below, this same question, question 4; directly after it follows this chapter, and then the chapter *Moreover, of Two*, below, Causa 32, questions 2 and 3. They too identify the author of the letter as Paschal II.] [Note: [Col. 1443] Baluze testifies that it is absent from the most ancient Anselm codex of Saint-Germain-des-Prés monastery. Yet it occurs in the collated codex, book 10, ch. 35, added with other material after Anselm’s death, under this heading: “From a letter of Pope Paschal II, sent to Regino the good elder,” with the added subscription: “Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Kalends of May.”—Polycarp, book 6, title 6; Peter Lombard, ibid.]:

**C. V. Those born from a co-father or co-mother after children have been received from the font cannot be joined.**

After a spiritual son or daughter has been received from the font [Note: [Col. 1443] *the sacred font*: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.], persons born from a co-father or co-mother cannot be joined in marriage, because secular laws forbid unemancipated persons to be joined with adoptive kin. [Col. 1444C]

**C. VI. PALEA** [Note: [Col. 1444D] This Palea occurs in some old copies from which it is usually absent elsewhere, and it is not separated from the preceding chapter.]

The same is inferred from book XXIII of the *Digest*, title *On the Rite of Marriage*, where it reads as follows [Note: [Col. 1443] title 2, fragment 17.]:

> “Brotherhood acquired through adoption impedes marriage so long as the adoption remains. Therefore I may marry as wife the woman whom my father adopted and emancipated. Likewise [Note: [Col. 1445] *Likewise* is absent from the editions compared, except Lyons II–III.], if, after I have been emancipated, he retains her under his authority, we may be joined in marriage. Thus one who wishes to adopt a son-in-law is advised to emancipate his daughter. Similarly, one who wishes to adopt a daughter-in-law is advised to emancipate his son.”

**Part III. Gratian.** But if someone, by some accidental circumstance, has taken as wife the daughter of his own co-mother, he is not compelled to put her away.

Accordingly, in the Council of Tribur, ch. 48, one reads [Note: [Col. 1445] held A.D. 895.—Burchard, book 17, ch. 46; Ivo, Decretum, part 9, ch. 97; Peter Lombard, ibid.]:

**C. VII. No one is compelled to put away the daughter of his own co-mother whom he has taken in marriage.**

We neither define this by canonical enactment nor reject it by any prohibition; but because some think differently about it, we mention something here on account of them. [Col. 1445B] If anyone has taken in marriage the daughter of his own spiritual co-mother through an accidental and so occurring turn of events, let him, after taking more mature counsel [Note: [Col. 1445] *greater*: Basel edition.], keep her [Note: [Col. 1445] *her* absent from Ivo and Burchard.] and faithfully fulfill the duties of lawful marriage.

## QUESTION IV

## GRATIAN

**Part I.** No one may take as wife the widow of his wife’s co-father.

Accordingly Pope Nicholas writes to Solomon, bishop of Constance [Note: [Col. 1445] Chapter of uncertain date.—Ivo, Panormia, book 7, 63; Decretum, part 1, ch. 137, part 9, ch. 35; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 42.]:

**C. I. It is not lawful for anyone to have two co-mothers.**

Your holiness asks us whether a man [Col. 1445C] may have two co-mothers, one after the other. In this matter he should remember that it is written [Note: [Col. 1445] Gen. 2:24.]: “The two shall be one flesh.” Therefore, since it is evident [Note: [Col. 1445] *is evident*: Norwegian, Venetian I–II, Paris, Lyons II–III editions.] that man and woman become one flesh through marriage, it necessarily follows that the man is made co-father to that woman of whom the wife taken in marriage appeared to be co-mother. It is therefore clear that the man cannot be joined [Note: [Col. 1445] *be joined*: editions compared.] in intercourse [Note: [Col. 1445] *into intercourse*: Venetian I–II, Paris, Lyons II–III editions.] with that woman who was his co-mother, with whom he had become one flesh.

[Col. 1446A]

**C. II. Let one who has intercourse with two co-mothers do penance for eight years. Likewise from the Council of Chalcedon** [Note: [Col. 1445D] Nothing of this sort is found discussed or determined in the Council of Chalcedon. Yet it is also reported under that authority in a penitential fragment of uncertain authorship, and is cited in the same manner below in the chapter *After the Wife’s Death*.] [Note: [Col. 1445] At the end of Anselm, book 11, there is a booklet by an unknown author on various kinds of incest, alleged to derive from the Council of Chalcedon; Gratian made this chapter from it.]

If a father and son, or two brothers, have had intercourse with one woman; or if anyone has had intercourse with a mother and daughter, or with two sisters, or with two co-mothers, let him, according to the ancient and milder ruling, do penance for eight years.

**C. III. No one is to have intercourse with two co-mothers. Likewise Innocent to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse** [Note: [Col. 1445] In the ancient Hérivaux collection, partly published by Petit, it is produced after a canon borrowed from Innocent (p. 233), whence it came about that this too was thought to be Innocent’s, as happened in Anselm, book 9, ch. 23.—Polycarp, book 6, title 6.]

If one spouse [Note: [Col. 1446D] *If one*: in most ancient copies and in the same collection of decrees by an unknown author: “If one person from a marriage …” [Note: [Col. 1445] thus editions compared, first Lyons II–III; in the Argentinian edition, however: *spouses*.—“If one person from a marriage”: Hérivaux Collection.] This is not found in Innocent’s letter written to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse.] receives the son or daughter of another from the sacred font, or holds the child at chrism, or performs the ministry [Note: [Col. 1445] *mystery*: same editions; Argentinian, Norwegian, Venetian I–II editions.] of Christian initiation, both husband and wife are co-parents to the child’s parents, because man and woman have become one flesh. [Col. 1446B]

**Part II. Gratian.** Conversely, the Council of Tribur, ch. 47, contains the following [Note: [Col. 1445] held A.D. 895.—Burchard, book 17, ch. 45; Ivo, Panormia, book 7, ch. 67; Decretum, part 9, ch. 96; Polycarp, book 6, title 6; Peter Lombard, book 6, title 42.]:

**C. IV. He may marry the wife of his co-father, if she herself was not his co-mother.**

If a man has a spiritual co-father, whose son he has received from the washing of the sacred font, and that man’s wife is not his co-mother, then, after his co-father has died, he may take the widow as his wife, provided that he has no blood-relationship to her. For why not? Can persons be joined whom no carnal kinship or spiritual descent separates [Note: [Col. 1445] *kinship*: editions compared.]?

**C. V. On the same matter. Likewise in the letter of Pope Paschal II to Bishop Regino** [Note: [Col. 1445] cf. on ch. 5, question 3, the same causa.—Anselm, book 10, ch. 34 (35); Polycarp; Peter Lombard, ibid.]

[Col. 1446C] After the wife’s death, no authority or reason appears to forbid the surviving husband from being joined in marriage to his wife’s co-mother. For spiritual kinship is not comparable to kinship of the flesh, nor does union of the flesh pass over into union of the spirit.

**Part III. Gratian.** It must be noted, however, that it is one thing to know a person’s co-mother carnally, and another to become the co-mother of someone abandoned by another. The authority of Pope Nicholas and of the Chalcedonian synod prohibits [Col. 1447A] the man who rendered the marital debt to his wife after she had become another woman’s co-mother from being joined in marriage to his wife’s co-mother. But the authority of the Council of Tribur permits those to be joined in marriage whose wife becomes his co-mother only after she has been abandoned by her husband, and is not known carnally by her husband after the spiritual co-parenthood. It is asked, however, whether a wife ought to receive a child in baptism together with her husband.

Urban II writes on this matter to Vitalis, presbyter [Note: [Col. 1447C] *presbyter*: previously read *bishop*. Corrected from all collated ancient copies. The same citation occurs above in this same causa, question 3, *Concerning the matters*.] of Brescia [Note: [Col. 1447] cf. on ch. 4, question 3, the same causa.—Collection in three parts, part 2, title 50, ch. 24; Peter Lombard, ibid.]:

**C. VI. A wife should not receive someone’s child in baptism together with her husband.**

No authority is found to forbid a wife from receiving a child in baptism together with her husband. But, in order that the purity of spiritual [Col. 1447B] fatherhood may remain free from every stain and reproach, we decree [Note: [Col. 1447] *decreed*: Basel edition.] that neither of them [Note: [Col. 1447] *each of them*: Basel edition.] should presume to aspire to this together [Note: [Col. 1447] *breathe*: Argentinian, Norwegian, Venetian I–II editions.]. Since one who married two co-mothers as though they were two sisters committed an expiatory crime, a great penance proportionate to the offense ought to be imposed upon him.

Gratian. The ruling of the Council of Tribur, “If a man has a spiritual co-father,” etc., is to be understood as having been made before this prohibition; or “co-mother wife” is to be understood as deriving not from the same child as the husband’s, but from another.

## QUESTION V

## GRATIAN

**Part I.** Pope Evaristus, writing in his first letter to the bishops of Africa, testifies that clandestine marriages ought not to be made [Note: [Col. 1447] Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—cf. Second Council of Tours, ch. 20, and *Ancient Ecclesiastical Statutes*, ch. 101 (ch. 5 below).—Anselm, book 10, ch. 2; Ivo, Panormia, book 6, ch. 31; Decretum, part 8, ch. 4; Polycarp, book 6, title 4; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 28.—cf. Capitularies, book 7, ch. 463.]:

**C. I. Clandestine marriages ought not to be made.**

A marriage is not otherwise lawful [Note: [Col. 1447D] *Lawful*: in the letter itself these words are inserted: “as we have received from the fathers and find handed down by the holy apostles and their successors.”] unless the woman is sought from those who appear to exercise authority over her and by whom she is guarded as a wife; unless she is betrothed by parents and [Note: [Col. 1447] absent from Ivo and Basel edition.] nearer relatives, endowed according to law, and at the proper time blessed sacerdotally, as custom requires, by a priest with prayers and offerings; and unless, guarded and joined [Note: [Col. 1447] *joined together*: original and editions compared; “and joined” absent from Panormia.] by the bridal attendants as custom teaches, she is sought from her relatives at a fitting time, is given according to law [Note: [Col. 1447D] *is given*: formerly it read “is endowed according to law,” which had already been said above. Corrected from old editions of the councils, the Capitularies, Anselm, and Ivo.], and is solemnly received. Then for two or three days they are to devote themselves to prayer and preserve chastity.

Likewise:

§ 1. Know that marriages carried out in this manner are lawful unions. But do not doubt that unions undertaken otherwise are not marriages but rather adulteries, concubinages, seductions, or fornications, than lawful marriages [Note: [Col. 1447] *it is doubted*: Ivo, Panormia and editions compared.], unless their own will gives support and lawful vows come to their aid.

**C. II. It is not lawful to celebrate secret weddings. Likewise from the Decrees of Pope Hormisdas, ch. 6** [Note: [Col. 1448C] Burchard, Ivo, Polycarp, and the collection found in volume 3 of the councils after the decrees of Alexander III, part 49, ch. 10, similarly cite this from the decrees of Hormisdas. Yet the second collection of Decretals, title *On Clandestine Betrothals*, cites it from Alexander III, who cannot be the first author of this chapter, since he was later than Gratian.] [Note: [Col. 1447] It appears to have been intended to reproduce Burchard, book 9, ch. 3; Herard of Tours, ch. 130.—Ivo, Panormia, book 6, ch. 5; Decretum, part 8, ch. 141; Polycarp, ibid.]

No believer, whatever his condition, is to make a marriage secretly; rather, having received the priest’s blessing, let him marry publicly in the Lord.

[Col. 1448B]

**C. III. Marriages must be celebrated publicly. Likewise Nicholas, in answer to the inquiries of the Bulgarians, ch. 3** [Note: [Col. 1447] written A.D. 866.—Ivo, Panormia, book 6, ch. 9; Decretum, part 8, ch. 6.]

Our people, both men and women, when they contract marital bonds, do not wear upon their heads a band of gold or silver, or one made of any metal whatever. But after betrothal [Note: [Col. 1447] add: *bonds*: editions compared.], which is a promise of the future marriage [Note: [Col. 1447] *promise*: same editions and Ivo, Panormia; *promised bonds, which*: original and Ivo, Decretum.], the marriage contract is also celebrated with the consent of those who enter into it and of those under whose authority they are. After the bridegroom has betrothed the bride by earnest-money, with a ring placed upon the finger of faith [Note: [Col. 1447] *placed upon her*: Ivo and editions compared.], and has given her, before persons invited by both parties, the dowry agreed upon by both, together with a written instrument containing this agreement—either at once or at a suitable time, so that they may not presume [Note: [Col. 1447] *presume to do such a thing*: Ivo and same editions.] to do this before the time fixed by law—they are both brought to the marriage rites. [Col. 1448C] First indeed, they are established in the church of the Lord with offerings which they ought to offer to God through the priest’s hand; and only then do they receive the blessing and the heavenly veil.

Likewise:

§ 1. These are [Note: [Col. 1447] The editions compared, except Basel, read: “Besides these there are other matters …”], besides other matters which do not occur to memory, the solemn covenants of marriage [Note: [Col. 1447] *of married persons*: Basel edition.]. We do not say that it is a sin if all these things do not occur in the marriage covenant, as you say that the Greeks maintain.

[Col. 1449A]

**C. IV. These things must be observed in contracting marriage. Likewise Pope Leo** [Note: [Col. 1449C] Burchard, Anselm, Ivo, and Panormia also cite this from Leo. But substantially the same passage is reported from St Augustine in the Council of Trosly, ch. 8, and in book 7 of the Capitularies, ch. 179; and below, Causa 36, question 2, chapter *Three Things*—which is cited from St Jerome—the words “and the rest which follow in the foregoing” appear to indicate the matters contained in this chapter.] [Note: [Col. 1449] cf. Correction.—Burchard, book 9, ch. 2; Anselm, book 10, ch. 3; Ivo, Panormia, book 6, ch. 36; Decretum, part 8, ch. 140; Polycarp, book 6, title 4.]

What sort of wife [Note: [Col. 1449] *spouse*: Basel edition.] ought she be who is to be taken according to the law? A chaste virgin, betrothed while a virgin, lawfully endowed, handed over by her parents [Note: [Col. 1449] *handed over to the bridegroom*: Anselm.], to be received by the bridegroom and bridal attendants, and thus openly taken in marriage according to law and Gospel by public nuptials; never to be separated for the sake of any man throughout all the days of life, unless by mutual consent and for the purpose of devotion to God. If she has committed fornication [Note: [Col. 1449D] *has committed*: in the Council of Trosly and the Capitularies follows: “and if her husband wishes.”], she is to be put away; but while she lives, another woman is not to be taken [Note: [Col. 1449] absent from the Basel edition.], because adulterers shall not possess the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 1449] 1 Cor. 6:9.], and her penance is to be received in writing [Note: [Col. 1449D] *her*: in the same sources: “and penance is to be received for her.”].

[Col. 1449B]

**C. V. How bridegroom and bride are to approach the blessing. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 13** [Note: [Col. 1449] cf. on Distinction 23, final chapter.]

When bridegroom and bride are to be blessed by the priest, let them be presented by their parents or by their bridal attendants [Note: [Col. 1449D] *Let them be presented*: the words “in the church to the priest” followed [Col. 1450C] [Note: [Col. 1449] thus editions compared.], but are absent from editions of the councils and manuscript codices, from Burchard and Ivo, and from Distinction 23, final chapter above, where the same passage is cited.]. Having received the blessing, let them remain virgins that same night out of reverence for the blessing itself.

**C. VI. No one is to take a wife without public nuptials. Likewise from the Council of Arles, ch. 6** [Note: [Col. 1449] Rather from the Capitularies of the Frankish Kings, book 6, ch. 133.—Burchard, book 9, ch. 6; Ivo, Panormia, book 6, ch. 6; Decretum, part 8, ch. 144.]

Let no marriage take place without a dowry; the dowry is to be provided according to means; and no one is to presume to marry or take a wife without public nuptials.

Gratian. By all these authorities clandestine weddings are prohibited; therefore, since they are marriages contrary to authority, they ought to be regarded as not having been made.

[Col. 1449C]

**Part II, § 1.** But it is asked what the ceremonies of the veil and ring, observed in marriages, signify.

Isidore writes concerning these matters in book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, ch. 19 [Note: [Col. 1449] Ivo, Panormia, book 6, ch. 8; Decretum, part 8, chs. 7–8.]:

**C. VII. Why women are veiled when they marry.**

Women are veiled when they marry so that they may know themselves always subject [Note: [Col. 1449] *subjected*: original and Ivo.] and humble toward their husbands [Note: [Col. 1449] *men*: original, Ivo, and Basel edition.].

§ 1. Likewise, the fact that newly married persons are joined to one another after the blessing by a fillet (*vitta*) [Note: [Col. 1450C] *Veil*: in the Cologne edition of Isidore it reads: “the veils are joined to one another by a single bond, namely, lest they break the compact …” [Note: [Col. 1449] thus Ivo, Decretum.] etc. But in the Vatican codex: “after the blessing, by the Levite, to one another,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 1449] *life*: Argentinian edition, with addition “that is,” Norwegian and Lyons II editions.], as though by one bond [Note: [Col. 1449] absent from the original, Ivo, Decretum, and Argentinian and Basel editions.], is done so that they may not break the bond of conjugal unity.

§ 2. Moreover, because that same fillet is intermingled with white and purple coloring, the white belongs to purity of life [Note: [Col. 1449] The variant reads: “white is purity of life” or “white is for purity.”] and the purple to the offspring of blood, so that by this sign they may be admonished that the law of continence is to be observed by both for a time [Note: [Col. 1450D] *The law of continence*: thus corrected from the printed and manuscript original. Previously it read: “so that by this sign both continence and the law of abstinence may be maintained for a time” [Note: [Col. 1449] thus editions compared.].], and thereafter the marital due ought not to be denied [Note: [Col. 1449] *the rendering*: Basel edition.].

§ 3. Likewise, the fact that in the first transactions a ring is given by the bridegroom to the bride occurs either as a sign of mutual faithfulness [Note: [Col. 1449] *love*: Ivo and editions compared.] or, more especially, so that their hearts may be joined by this pledge. The same ring is put on the fourth finger because [Note: [Col. 1449] “that is, because”: Ivo, Decretum; “therefore, because”: Panormia and editions compared.] a certain vein in it, as is said, reaches as far as the heart.

[Col. 1450B]

**C. VIII. Nuptials are called from veiling, because brides customarily veil their heads. Likewise Ambrose, in the book *On the Patriarchs*** [Note: [Col. 1449] that is, book 1, *On Abraham*, ch. 9.]

**Part III.** Nor is it without significance [Note: [Col. 1449] add: *is*: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] that, when Rebecca came, she saw Isaac walking [Note: [Col. 1449] *walking about*: editions compared.]; and when she had asked who he was, and learned [Note: [Col. 1449] add: *indeed*: Basel edition.] that he was the one whose wife she was to be, she descended and began to veil her head, teaching that modesty ought to precede marriage. Hence too they are called *nuptials*, because girls veil themselves for the sake of modesty [Note: [Col. 1449] absent from the same edition.].

**Part IV. Gratian.** But an objection is made to the foregoing: many things are prohibited which, if done, become valid after the fact. Those under vows are forbidden to contract marriages; yet, if they contract them, they ought to remain inviolate. So too clandestine marriages are indeed made contrary to the laws, yet, once contracted, they cannot be dissolved, because they are made firm by a subsequent lawful vow. Hence Evaristus, after saying [Note: [Col. 1449] above, same question, ch. 1.] that unions undertaken otherwise are not marriages but adulteries, added: “unless their own will gives support and lawful vows come to their aid.”

[Col. 1451A]

Likewise, in the *Novels* [Note: [Col. 1451] Julian, Epitome of Novels 67, ch. 4.—Ivo, Panormia, book 6, ch. 7; Decretum, part 8, ch. 44, part 16, ch. 142; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 28.]:

**C. IX.**

If anyone, having touched the divine Scriptures, swears to a woman that he will have her as his lawful wife, or gives such an oath in an oratory, she shall be his lawful wife [Note: [Col. 1451] *lawful wife*: absent from the Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1451D] *Wife*: in Julian the Antecessor, from whom this chapter seems to have been taken, there follows: “provided that she has been joined to him.”], although no dowry or other written instrument has intervened.

Gratian. The answer to this is as follows: marriages contracted secretly are not denied to be marriages, nor are they ordered to be dissolved if they can be proved by the confession of both parties. Nevertheless, they are prohibited, because if one of them changes his mind, proof cannot be made to the judge by the confession of the other. Thus, publicly, when one party’s vows have passed to the other side, no judgment can be rendered on behalf of the former marriage, which is uncertain to the judge. [Col. 1451B] For, as Pope Sixtus writes to bishops established throughout Spain [Note: [Col. 1451] Letter 2.], no bishop should presume to judge uncertain matters; and although they are true, they are not to be believed unless established by certain indications, unless proved by manifest judgment, unless published according to judicial procedure. Pope Victor likewise writes to Bishop Theophilus [Note: [Col. 1451] Letter 1.]: “Let us judge nothing uncertain, dearest brother, until the Lord comes, who will bring hidden things into the light, illuminate the secrets of darkness, and reveal the counsels of hearts.” For although matters may be true, they are not to be believed unless established by manifest indications, unless proved by manifest judgment, unless published according to judicial procedure.

[Col. 1451C]

**C. X. No one is to be judged or condemned before just proof. Likewise Pope Evaristus, letter II, to all bishops** [Note: [Col. 1451] Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—cf. Causa 2, question 1, ch. 20.]

We ought not to judge or condemn anyone before true and just proof, as the Apostle testifies when he says [Note: [Col. 1451] Rom. 14:4.]: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own Lord he stands or falls.” Therefore, let evil reports move no one, nor should anyone ever believe indiscriminate allegations without certain proof; but before accepting reports, let him investigate carefully, lest anyone act precipitately [Note: [Col. 1451] *nor*: editions compared, first Lyons II.] [Note: [Col. 1451] *anything*: Argentinian, Norwegian, Venetian I–II editions; *another person*: Basel edition.].

**C. XI. Nothing is to be judged before it is demonstrated by certain indications. Likewise Pope Eleutherius, in a letter to the provinces of Gaul** [Note: [Col. 1451] Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—cf. Breviary of Alaric, book 2, title 18, ch. 1, with interpretation; Anselm, at the end of book 3, among the chapters of Hadrian, where it appears as ch. 26; Ivo, Panormia, book 4, chs. 119, 120, 104; Decretum, part 6, chs. 316–317; Polycarp, book 5, title 1.]

A judge ought to investigate everything and examine the sequence of events by a full inquiry [Note: “plain”: Basel ed.; “run through”: ibid.], allowing patience for questioning, answering, and raising objections, so that there the case of both parties may be fully illuminated [Note: In the cited sources it reads “limited” [*limitata*]; Ivo, *Decretum*: “limited”; in the *Panormia* it is as in Gratian. In many old manuscripts of Gratian: “illuminated” (*luminata*)], and so that the judge may not wish to anticipate the litigants by his own judgment until, all proceedings having been completed, they themselves have nothing remaining to advance in the dispute [Col. 1452B], and the case has been debated until the truth of the matter is reached. It is necessary to question repeatedly [Note: also added in the Basel ed.; “to be questioned”: the other collected editions and Ivo, *Panormia*], lest perhaps something be left out which ought to be added.

Gratian. From the foregoing it is manifestly inferred that one must not depart from what is certain because of what is uncertain, nor render a definite judgment in a doubtful matter. But since proof of a doubtful matter cannot be made to a judge except by the confirmation of witnesses or a lawful confession, and since, by the authority of Pope Calixtus [Note: cf. Causa 3, question 9, c. 15], witnesses cannot give testimony concerning causes or transactions other than those which they know to have occurred in their presence: it is apparent that clandestine marriages are prohibited for this reason: when one party wishes to deny having had marital affection for the other, he or she cannot be convicted by lawful proofs [Col. 1452C]. When such proofs are lacking, both, having been duly acquitted by the judge’s sentence, incur the guilt of adultery if, while both are alive, they join themselves to others.

# CAUSA XXXI

[Col. 1451]

[Col. 1451C] GRATIAN.

One man seduced another’s wife; after the husband’s death, the adulterer took the adulteress as his wife; he swore that he would give the daughter born of her in marriage to a certain man [Col. 1451D]; she did not give her consent; afterward the father gave her to another [Col. 1452C]; she is claimed back by the first man. (Question I.) It is asked whether a woman previously defiled by adultery may be taken in marriage. (Question II.) Secondly, whether a daughter may be given to anyone against her will. (Question III.) Thirdly, whether, after her father’s betrothal-promise [Col. 1452D], she may marry another.

# QUESTION I

[Col. 1453A]

GRATIAN.

Part I. A woman defiled by adultery is forbidden to be taken in marriage on the authority of Pope Leo, who says [Note: Rather from the Council of Tribur, c. 51; cf. below, c. 3; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 35]:

## C. I. A woman defiled by adultery is not to be married by the same man.

No one shall take in marriage a woman whom he previously defiled by adultery.

But Augustine testifies to the contrary, writing to Valerius, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book I, chapter 10 [Note: Peter Lombard, ibid.]:

## C. II. A man may lawfully take in marriage a woman whom he previously defiled by adultery.

Finally, after the death [Note: “of him”: the other collected editions] of the man with whom there was a true marriage, marriage may be contracted [Note: “A true marriage cannot be contracted”: in editions of the works of Blessed Augustine, one Vatican manuscript, and one manuscript of Gratian. In two more recent Vatican manuscripts of the same work, the negation is absent.] with the woman [Note: “with whom”: the same editions] with whom adultery had previously occurred. Likewise, in *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 14 [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, c. 45; *Decretum*, part 8, c. 10]:

[Col. 1453B] § 1. That marriages may indeed arise from persons unlawfully joined [Note: “lawful marriages”: the other collected editions; “illicitly”: ibid.], when an honourable agreement subsequently follows [Note: “follows after”: ibid.], is manifest.

Gratian. This latter authority of Augustine speaks of concubines, declaring that concubines can pass to the honourable agreement of marriage. Augustine’s first authority speaks of a repudiated woman: whoever takes her in marriage while her husband is alive commits adultery; yet he has some pardon for this adultery, because their union is believed to be lawful. § 1. But Pope Leo’s statement must be understood of a woman who had not been repudiated by her husband, whose husband was alive and rendering her the marital due.

[Col. 1453C] Hence it was enacted in the council held at Althaeum, in the presence of King Conrad, chapter 6 [Note: Rather from the Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895, c. 51; Burchard, book 9, c. 74; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, c. 10; *Decretum*, part 8, c. 211. In the Basel edition it is cited from a council at Alphenum; in the others, with the *Panormia*, from a council at Alphesum]:

## C. III. No one shall take in marriage a woman whom he previously defiled through adultery.

By common decree, according to the institutions of the canons, we define and determine beforehand that, if anyone has committed fornication with another man’s wife while her husband was alive, then, after the husband’s death, unlawful access to her shall be closed to him by synodal judgment [Col. 1454A], lest he be joined to her further in marriage [Note: “nor”: Ivo, *Panormia*, and the other collected editions; “in marriage”: Basel ed.], whom he previously defiled by adultery. For we do not wish it, nor is it compatible with the Christian religion, that anyone should take in marriage a woman whom he previously defiled through [Note: “by adultery”: the other collected editions except Basel] adultery.

Gratian. Here one must understand: unless penance has first been completed, and provided that he plotted nothing against the husband’s life, or did not, while the husband was alive, pledge faith to the adulteress that he would take her as wife if he survived her husband.

Hence, in the Council of Tribur one reads [Note: The substance of this chapter occurs in c. 40 of the extant Council of Tribur. But because Burchard cites it from c. 3, it appears to belong to another, missing chapter.] [Note: c. 40, Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895, abridged; Burchard, book 9, c. 66; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, c. 9; *Decretum*, part 8, c. 202; Peter Lombard, ibid.]:

## C. IV. After the husband’s death, a man who while the husband was alive pledged an oath of future marriage may not take the adulteress in marriage.

It has been reported to the ears of the holy priests that a certain man violated another’s wife by sexual defilement and, furthermore [Col. 1454B], while her husband was alive, gave the adulteress an oath that, after the death of her lawful husband, if he survived [Note: “should survive”: Basel ed.], he would take her [Note: “her in”: the other collected editions] as wife; and this was done. Therefore we prohibit and anathematize such a union.

## C. V. After completing penance, he may take in marriage the widow whom he defiled by adultery while her husband was alive. Likewise in the same source

[Note: Burchard and Ivo cite the Council of Meaux, c. 69, where this occurs. But in the *Decretals*, title “On one who takes as wife a woman whom he defiled by adultery,” c. *Cum haberet*, Clement III cites this very passage from the Council of Tribur, as do Gratian and the *Panormia*.]  
[Note: Rather from the Council of Meaux, held A.D. 845, c. 69; Burchard, book 9, c. 65; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, c. 12; *Decretum*, part 8, c. 201.]

If [Note: “He who”: original; cited collections] anyone is accused of having committed adultery with another man’s wife while her husband was alive, and, when he has died shortly afterward, is known to have taken that same woman, he shall in every way be subjected [Note: “compelled”: original; cited collections] to public penance. After the aforesaid penance, the rule concerning him shall be observed if expedient [Note: In the Council of Meaux it reads “the aforesaid,” as indicating the rule already set out there in c. 65, and cited below, Causa 36, question 2, “But if”]—unless perhaps the man [Note: “the same”: original and Ivo; “that is”: Burchard; “the same man”: editions of Argentinensis, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice I, Lyons II–III], or the woman, is found to have killed the husband who had died, or unless kinship or any other criminal act [Col. 1454C] prevents it [Note: absent from Ivo, *Panormia*]. But if this has been proved, they shall remain forever in penance, without any hope of marriage.

## C. VI. PALEA. [Likewise, from the Council at Vermerias

[Note: This *Palea* occurs in many old manuscripts in which *Paleae* are not ordinarily found. It is also cited as from the Council at Vermerias in excerpts of the decrees of the monastery of St Trudo, and by Burchard and Ivo, although in printed manuscripts of the *Decretals*, title “On Divorce,” c. 1, it is corruptly given as “From the Council at Worms.” Earlier, the heading of this *Palea* read: “From the Council of Elvira at Vermerias.” The word “of Elvira” was inserted, but belongs to the following chapter. For the insertion of *Paleae* has very often occasioned errors of this kind in headings.]  
[Note: held A.D. 752; Regino, book 2, c. 118; Burchard, book 6, c. 41; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, c. 169.]]

If any woman has plotted [Note: absent from the original, cited collections, and Basel ed.] with others for the death of her husband [Col. 1455A], and that husband, defending himself, has killed one of them, then, if the husband can prove that she is guilty of the plot, he may, as seems to us, dismiss his wife and, if he wishes, take another [Note: “take”: Burchard; “let him take”: original and Regino]. [Note: The words “and if he wishes take another” are absent from Ivo and the Argentinensis edition, though they occur in the original, Burchard, and Regino. In the *Decretals*, however, it reads: “after his wife’s death, he himself may, if he wishes, take another.”] But the plotting woman herself shall remain subject to penance, without hope of marriage.

## C. VII. After penance, the widow who has taken her adulterer as husband is to be reconciled to communion. Likewise from the Council of Elvira, c. 72.

[Note: Held no later than A.D. 310; Collection of the Three Parts, part 2, title 30, c. 13.]

If a widow has committed adultery and afterward has had that same man as husband, it has pleased us that, after a period of five years and lawful penance performed [Note: “completed”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions], she be reconciled to communion [Note: In various printed and manuscript copies of this council, it reads “by communion” or “to communion”: Hispana Collection].

Part II. Gratian. But an objection is made: David committed adultery with Bathsheba and plotted Uriah’s death [Col. 1455B], and nevertheless afterward took Bathsheba as wife. But in the Old Testament many things were permitted because of weakness which have been eliminated in the perfection of the Gospel. Thus anyone was permitted to give a bill of divorce, lest innocent blood be shed through hatred. But afterward the Lord prohibited this in the Gospel, saying that a wife is not to be dismissed by her husband except for fornication. Certain things were permitted because of weakness and as sacraments of things to come: thus [Note: cf. Leviticus 9] the Lord permitted the children of Israel to offer him in sacrifice animals which they had been accustomed in Egypt to sacrifice to demons, preferring that they be offered to him rather than to idols, and that they might be sacraments of future things. Thus Bathsheba also was permitted to be taken as wife, not so much because of David’s weakness as for the signification of future things.

§ 1. But there is another reason why the wife of a deceased man cannot marry this man. For men and women are generally forbidden to contract marriages repeatedly [Col. 1456A]. Hence priests ought not to be present at the banquet of second marriages, as is read in the Council of Neocaesarea, chapters 3 and 7 [Note: held A.D. 314; Burchard, book 9, c. 22; Anselm, book 10, c. 69; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, cc. 160, citing Dionysius; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 42]:

## C. VIII. Faith and conduct shorten the penance of those who marry repeatedly.

Concerning those who marry wives repeatedly, and those who marry more than once [Note: “who”: Hispana Collection], the appointed period of penance is certainly plainly fixed for them [Note: “the prescribed period is plainly observed”: Hispana Collection; “of penance” absent from Basel ed.], but their conduct and faith shorten the time. § 1. A presbyter, however [Note: Burchard, book 2, c. 133; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, c. 67; *Decretum*, part 8, c. 48, likewise from Dionysius], ought not to be present at the banquet [Note: Printed editions had “marriage”; corrected from old copies and the original itself. The Greek is: *mē estiasthai*, “not to attend a banquet.”] of second marriages; especially since [Note: The Greek here reads: *Epei metanoian aitountos tou digamou, tis estai ho presbyteros ho dia tēs estiasēos synkatatithemenos tois gamois*—“For when a twice-married man seeks penance, what presbyter will there be who, by attending the banquet itself, consents to the marriage?”] penance is prescribed [Note: “sought”: Hispana Collection] for second marriages: what presbyter, then [Note: “is therefore”: ibid.], would consent to those marriages because of the banquet?

[Col. 1456B]

## C. IX. By the standard of truth, one who takes a second wife is convicted of fornication. Likewise John Chrysostom—that is, the author of the imperfect work on Matthew [Note: An apocryphal work], Homily XXXII.

For this reason the Apostles also commanded people to enter into second marriages because of human lack of continence.
