To take a second wife is indeed lawful according to the Apostle’s precept [Note: “is lawful”: the other collected editions], but according to the standard of truth it is truly fornication [Note: The genuine John Chrysostom speaks far more cautiously, both elsewhere and especially in the letter *To a Younger Widow on Not Marrying Again*, recently printed at Rome; he explicitly denies that a second marriage is fornication]. Yet, when it is publicly and lawfully committed with God’s permission, it becomes honourable fornication. Therefore he rightly said [Note: “God”: Basel ed.; “Christ in the Gospel”: the remaining editions; cf. Deuteronomy 24:1; Matthew 19:8] that Moses permitted this; he did not command it. For to command is one thing, to permit another. For what we permit, we command unwillingly [Note: In the ordinary gloss on Matthew 5, at “bill of divorce,” it reads thus. But in the cited homily: “What we command always pleases us; but what we permit, we command unwillingly.”], because we cannot wholly forbid human beings’ evil wills [Col. 1456C].

[Col. 1457A]

## C. X. To avoid the danger of fornication, second marriages are allowed. Likewise Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book I.

[Note: “Jerome, On Virgins against Jovinian”: Lyons II–III editions; “Jerome, On Virgins”: the remaining editions except Lyons I.]

Just as, because of the danger of fornication, he permits marriage to virgins [Note: “because of danger of fornication”: Basel ed.] and makes excusable what is not desirable in itself, so, in order to avoid the same fornication [Note: “because of the same danger of fornication”: Lyons II–III; “by the same danger”: the other editions], he permits widows to contract second marriages [Note: “to contract”: the other collected editions except Basel and Lyons II–III]. For it is better, even if it be a second or third husband, to know one man than many; that is, it is more tolerable to be prostituted to one person [Note: “man”: Basel ed.] than to many. Indeed, the Samaritan woman in John’s Gospel [Note: John 4], saying that she had a sixth husband, is reproved by the Lord because he was not her husband; for where there is a number of husbands, there the husband—who is properly one—has ceased to be [Note: “ceases”: the other collected editions except Lyons II–III]. One rib at the beginning was made into one wife [Col. 1457B]. “And they shall be,” he says [Note: Genesis 2:24], “two into one flesh” [Note: “one flesh”: Vulgate and other collected editions], not three or four; otherwise they are no longer two, but many. Lamech, the first bloodthirsty murderer, divided one flesh into two wives; the same punishment of the flood destroyed both fratricide and bigamy: for the one it was avenged sevenfold, for the other seventy-sevenfold. As great as the difference in number, so great also the difference in crime.

§ 1. How holy second marriage is is also shown by this [Note: “also”: Basel II–III editions]: a twice-married man cannot be chosen for the clergy [Note: “to”: the other collected editions except Lyons II–III]; and thus the Apostle says to Timothy [Note: cf. 1 Timothy 5:9]: “Let a widow be chosen not less than sixty years old, who has been the wife of one husband.” This entire precept concerns widows supported by the Church’s alms, and therefore an age is stipulated, so that only those women may receive [Col. 1457C] the food of the poor who can no longer work. Consider also that a woman who has had two husbands, even if she is old, decrepit, and needy, does not deserve to receive the Church’s alms; but if the bread of alms is taken away from her, how much more that bread [Note: “that bread” is absent from the other collected editions except Lyons II–III] which came down from heaven, of which whoever eats unworthily shall be guilty of profaning the body and blood of Christ [Note: “of the Lord”: ibid.; Vulgate; cf. 1 Corinthians 11:27]? Yet some interpret the testimonies I have set above, in which widows are permitted to marry again if they wish, as speaking of those widows whom the faith of Christ found thus after they had lost their husbands [Note: “had found”: ibid.].

Part III. Gratian. But we think that he said this as an exhortation to widowed continence, not as a condemnation of second and subsequent marriages, which, as is clear from many authorities, are lawful—as can be understood from his own words. For he says to Pammachius in the *Apology against Jovinian* [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, c. 62; *Decretum*, part 8, c. 270; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 42]:

## C. XI. Neither second, nor third, nor subsequent marriages are to be condemned.

Let my detractors [Note: “our”: Basel ed.] open their ears, I pray, and see that I have allowed second and third marriages in the Lord. Could I condemn first marriage when I did not condemn second and third? Likewise there:

[Col. 1458B] § 1. I do not condemn twice-married persons—indeed, not even thrice-married persons, or, if the word can be used, persons married eight times.

Likewise there:

§ 2. Even now I proclaim in a free voice that second marriage is not condemned in the Church, nor indeed third marriage; and that it is as lawful to marry a fifth, sixth, or further husband as a second husband [Note: “rightly to marry”: Basel, Paris, Lyons editions; “not to marry”: Nuremberg and Venice I–II editions; Ivo, *Panormia*].

## C. XII. Second marriages, like first marriages, are shown to be lawful. Likewise Augustine, book II, *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, chapter 11.

[Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, cc. 22 and 61; *Decretum*, part 8, c. 269; Peter Lombard, ibid.]

God joined male and female in marital chastity for the propagation of the human race, and showed that second marriages, which are permitted in both [Note: The original reads “in each new [testament]”; Ivo’s *Decretum* and *Panormia*, c. 61, have this, and traces of the true reading occur in several manuscripts of Gratian, which read “in each one.” Certainly there was no doubt concerning the Old Testament [Col. 1457D]. But it was not altered because the author of the gloss appears to have read “in both.”] testaments, are lawful [Col. 1458C].

## C. XIII. On the same subject. The same author on the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

[Note: Gratian took the words of the ordinary gloss on 1 Corinthians 7 from Augustine, *On the Good of Widowhood*, c. 12.]  
[Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, cc. 59 and 61; *Decretum*, part 8, c. 268, give Augustine’s words themselves; Polycarpus, book 6, title 4; Peter Lombard, ibid.]

“But if her husband has fallen asleep” [Note: 1 Corinthians 7:39]. He does not say “the first,” “the second,” or “which number” [Note: “third”: Basel ed.; “fourth”: the remaining editions]; nor should we define what the Apostle has not defined. Therefore I ought neither to condemn any marriages nor to take from them the shame of multiplicity [Note: Earlier it read “impose”; corrected from the gloss and Blessed Augustine, whose words the other compilers report]. But the Lord [Note: cf. Matthew 22:28 ff.] did not condemn the woman who had had seven husbands [Col. 1459A], nor does he say that she cannot exist in the resurrection, but only: “They neither marry nor are given in marriage.” Therefore I do not dare, contrary to the sense of human modesty, to say that they may marry as often as they wish [Note: “whenever”: Basel ed.], nor from my own heart to condemn marriages of any number. What is said concerning a widow of one husband is said also of every widow [Note: “also” absent from the same edition; 1 Corinthians 7:39]: “But she will be happier if she remains thus.”

# QUESTION II

GRATIAN.

That no woman is to be compelled to marry anyone, Ambrose testifies in his commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “‘Let her marry whom she wishes [Note: 1 Corinthians 7:39], only in the Lord’: that is, let her marry the man she judges suitable for herself, because marriages entered unwillingly usually have bad outcomes. But ‘only [Col. 1459B] in the Lord’ means this: let her marry without suspicion of disgrace, and marry a man of her own religion.”

## C. I. A girl is not compelled to marry the man to whom her father has bound her by oath, when she has never given consent. Likewise, a judgment of Pope Urban.

[Note: It does not occur among the printed letters of Urban; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, c. 108; *Decretum*, part 8, c. 23; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 29.]

If what the envoys of Prince Jordan have reported to us is established as true—namely, that he himself, compelled and grieving, betrothed his infant daughter to the son of Rainald Rodeli [Note: “Ridelli”: Ivo, *Decretum*; “Rigelli”: *Panormia*; “Radelli”: Basel ed.; “Rodelli”: remaining editions except Paris and Lyons], though she was unwilling, weeping, and resisting with all her power, and though her mother and kindred did not consent but grieved deeply—then, since the authority of canons [Note: “and canons”: Basel ed.] and laws does not approve such betrothals, as is shown below, we temper our judgment lest what we say appear too harsh to those ignorant of laws and canons. Thus, if the prince wishes to complete what was begun with the consent of his daughter [Col. 1459C], mother, and kindred, we grant this. But if not, let our legate hear both parties; and, if there is nothing further on the part of the aforesaid Rainald which prevents it, let him receive from Jordan himself an oath that these facts stand as they have been stated. Then, following the enactments of canons and laws, we henceforth do not forbid the aforesaid daughter to marry another man, if she wishes—only in the Lord.

[Col. 1460A]

## C. II. PALEA. [Conversely, Pope Hormisdas writes to Bishop Eusebius

[Note: This *Palea* appears in the *Decretals*, c. 1, title “On the Betrothal of the Underage”; in printed copies it is cited from Honorius, but in the first collection of *Decretals* from Hormisdas, as here.]  
[Note: Uncertain chapter; cf. c. 1, X, *de desponsatione impuberum*, and c. 2, First Compilation, same title.]]

“Your holiness has asked us [Note: “asked of us”: First Compilation], venerable brother, concerning an adult son whom his father wishes to have enter into marriage: whether he can do so without the adult son’s will. To this we say that, if the son does not consent in any way, it cannot be done. But regarding a son not yet adult, whose will cannot yet be discerned, the father may give him to whom he wishes in marriage [Note: “in matrimony”: Basel ed.; “join in matrimony”: First Compilation]; and afterward, when the son has reached full age, he must observe and fulfill it completely. This [Note: “We decree all these things to be observed by you as adherents of the orthodox faith”: First Compilation] we decree to be observed by all adherents of the orthodox faith, and command you to observe [Note: “and by us”: Nuremberg and Venice I–II; “and by you”: Argentinensis; “by you”: Basel and Lyons I and III].”

[Col. 1460B]

## C. III. Those whose body is to be one ought also to have one mind; and therefore no woman is to be joined to anyone against her will. Likewise Urban II, Decree, to the King of Aragon.

[Note: “Decree”: corrected from old manuscripts, the *Panormia*, and histories of the kings of Aragon. Earlier it read “Sacratio”; Argentinensis ed.: “Likewise to the same person”; remaining editions except Basel: “Sacratio.”]  
[Note: That this letter is Urban II’s is attested by Hildebert of Le Mans, Urban’s contemporary, Letter 42; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, c. 109; *Decretum*, part 8, c. 24.]

Concerning the marriage of your niece, whom, under pressure of a critical necessity, you confirmed by a pledge of faith that you would give to a certain knight, we decree, as equity dictates, that if she wholly refuses that man, as is said, and persists firmly in that resolution of will, so as utterly to refuse marriage to him [Note: “would refuse”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions], you shall by no means compel her, unwilling and resisting, to be joined in marriage with that man. For those whose body is one ought also to have one mind, lest perhaps the maiden, when joined to someone against her will, incur, contrary to the command of the Lord and the Apostle, either the guilt of discord or the crime of fornication [Col. 1460C]. And it is clear that the evil of this sin falls back upon the man who joined her against her will. [Note: This final clause is absent from the original in Mansi, from the Victorine manuscript of the *Panormia* used by Bérard, and from Hildebert.] The same must likewise be understood concerning a man [Note: “known”: the other collected editions except Basel and Lyons II–III].

## C. IV. A man may not abandon the woman whom he took as wife after a dowry was first given and public attestation made. Likewise Nicholas, to Radoald, bishop of Porto, and John, bishop of Ficolensis.

[Note: written A.D. 863; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, c. 334. “Rodoald”: Böhm; “Siculensis”: Basel ed.; “Sicoliensis”: remaining editions.]

King Lothar (in the memorandum [Note: These words, “in the memorandum,” seem to be taken as a heading and separated from what follows, to indicate that this chapter was drawn from the memorandum which Nicholas gave to his legates, Rodoald bishop of Porto and John bishop of Ficolensis. For the entire chapter consists of Nicholas’s own words, instructing his legates how they should conduct themselves in this matter. Nicholas testifies, in his letter to the bishops assembled at Convicinum, in the appendix to the Library of the Holy Fathers, that he gave this memorandum to these legates, in these words: “Furthermore, what we have judged concerning Lothar’s wives—for you wrote also about this to our episcopal office—you may discover in copies of our letters which we sent into Gaul through our brothers and fellow bishops Rodoald and John. We transmitted those copies, together with the memorandum which we gave to these same brothers of ours, sent to King Lothar concerning this same matter, through our brother and fellow bishop Odo to your holiness.”]) declares [Col. 1461A] that he received Waldrada from her father after a dowry had first been promised [Note: “with promised dowries”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions], and afterward admitted the sister of Hubert [Note: “Hucbert”: original in Mansi]. First inquire through diligent investigation. If you find that this glorious king received the aforesaid Waldrada, after a dowry had first been given, before witnesses, according to the law and the rite by which marriages are customarily celebrated, and that the said Waldrada was admitted into his marriage by public manifestation, it remains for you to investigate why she was repudiated or Boso’s daughter admitted. But because this same glorious king says that he admitted Theutberga [Note: “Teberga”: the other collected editions; “Thietberga”: original; Böhm] through fear, so great a king ought not, through fear of one man, to plunge himself into a monstrous abyss against the divine command [Note: “ought”: Basel ed.; “immerse”: ibid.]. In this he certainly [Note: “therefore”: ibid.] shows himself the more blameworthy, because he preferred love of the world to the love of God, since not even murderers of the body are to be feared when they drive a person against justice [Col. 1461B]. [Note: “Since not even”: These words are not here in Ivo, but somewhat earlier, after “he says that he admitted,” where many passages are inserted, including these words, though in another order. They were not altered because of the gloss.]

Therefore we command you to do nothing else, once the king himself has been convicted by his own declaration, except to decide his case in our stead, relying on canonical authority. But if it is by no means proved that Waldrada was his lawful wife, or that she was joined to our son Lothar through marriages celebrated according to custom [Note: “rite”: the other collected editions], namely with a priest’s blessing, advise him not to take it ill that his lawful wife be reconciled to him, if she is found innocent. And below:

§ 1. Moreover, I wish you to know that the aforesaid Theutberga appealed twice and three times to the apostolic see, and complained that she had been unjustly cast down by the aforesaid glorious king [Note: “made complaint”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions], and compelled by force to devise a false crime against herself. For at that time she sent to the apostolic see a written appeal in which she made known that, though she had not yet confessed, she was being compelled to state a false accusation against herself, adding further [Col. 1462A]: “If I am compelled any further, know that I shall say what they wish [Note: “he wishes”: the other collected editions], not because it is true, but out of fear of death and from the desire to escape—for I cannot otherwise. Yet remember me, who am informing you of these things.”

Therefore we command you that, when this same Theutberga comes to the appointed synod, as we have decreed, you shall handle her cause by careful examination. If it is alleged against her that she confessed to having committed some crime [Note: “perpetrated”: Basel ed.], and she in turn declares that she suffered violence, or if she testifies that those judges were her enemies, then renew that judgment according to the standard of equity, so that she may not be crushed under the weight of injustice.

Gratian. These authorities plainly show that no woman is to be joined to anyone unless by free will.

# QUESTION III

[Col. 1462B]

GRATIAN.

But that after a parental betrothal-promise they cannot marry others is shown by the authority of the Council of Elvira, chapter 54, which says [Note: held no later than A.D. 310; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, c. 46]:

## C. UN. Concerning parents who break the pledged faith of betrothals.

If any parents break the pledged faith of betrothals, they shall keep themselves from communion for three years [Note: “be kept”: Hispana Collection, omitting what follows: “from communion”]. Yet if the same bridegroom or bride has not been discovered in that grave crime [Note: The original reads without the negation, as does Ivo; it moreover lacks the word “that,” and thus reads: “have been discovered in a grave crime”: Hispana Collection], the parents shall be excused. But if there is vice in them and they defile themselves by consenting [Col. 1462C] [Note: “if there is vice in the same persons”: ibid.; “If—let [the ruling] be observed”: absent from Ivo; “by consenting” absent from the Hispana Collection], the preceding sentence shall be observed.

Gratian. See: parents are not permitted to break their children’s betrothals. But this must be understood of those contracted with the children’s consent.

# CAUSA XXXII

[Col. 1461]

[Col. 1461C] GRATIAN.

A certain man, who had no wife, joined to himself in marriage a certain prostitute who was barren [Col. 1462C], the granddaughter of a freeborn man and daughter of a *originarius* (a person bound by birth to an estate). When her father wished to give her to another, her grandfather joined her to this man, solely because of his lack of continence. Then this man, moved to penance, began to seek children for himself from his own slave woman [Col. 1463A]. Later, convicted and punished for adultery, he asked a certain man forcibly to violate his wife, so that he might thereby dismiss her. This being done, he joined to himself a certain unbelieving woman, but on the condition that she should convert to the Christian religion. (Question I.) First it is asked whether a prostitute may lawfully be taken as wife. (Question II.) Secondly, whether a woman taken because of lack of continence should be called a wife. (Question III.) Thirdly, whose decision she should follow: that of her freeborn grandfather or of her *originarius* father. (Question IV.) Fourthly, whether a man may seek children from a slave woman while his wife is alive. (Question V.) Fifthly, whether a woman who suffers violence is proved to lose her chastity. (Question VI.) Sixthly, whether an adulterer may dismiss an adulteress. (Question VII.) Seventhly, whether, while the dismissed woman is alive, he may take another. (Question VIII.) [Col. 1463B] Eighthly, whether a member of the faithful may take an unbelieving woman as wife under the foregoing condition.

# QUESTION I

GRATIAN.

Part I. That a prostitute ought not to be taken as wife is proved by many authorities and arguments. For a woman convicted as guilty of adultery ought not to be retained in the fellowship of marriage unless after penance has been completed.

Hence John Chrysostom—that is, the author of the imperfect work, Homily XXXII—says on Matthew 19 [Note: Apocryphal work; Anselm, book 10, c. 31; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, c. 8; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 35]:

## C. I. The man who refuses to dismiss his adulterous wife is a patron of immorality.

[Col. 1463C] Just as he is cruel and wicked who dismisses a chaste woman, so he is foolish and unjust [Note: [Col. 1463] *wicked*: Basel edition.] who keeps a prostitute. For he is the protector of her shamefulness who conceals his wife’s crime.

C. II. A husband may dismiss his wife on account of fornication, but may not take another. Likewise Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 19. [Note: [Col. 1463] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, chapter 7; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 43; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 35.]

The Lord said in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1463] Matthew 19:9.]: “Whoever dismisses his wife [Note: [Col. 1463] Addition: *his*: Basel edition.], except on account of [Note: [Col. 1463] *except for the cause of fornication*: same edition.] fornication, and takes another, commits adultery; and he who takes the dismissed woman commits adultery.” Fornication alone overcomes the wife’s affection [Note: [Col. 1463] *overcomes*: Ivo; collected editions; Böhm.]; indeed, since she has divided one flesh into another [Note: [Col. 1463] *two*: Basel edition.] and separated herself from her husband by fornication, she ought not to be retained, lest she bring her husband also under a curse. For Scripture says [Col. 1463D] [Note: [Col. 1463] Proverbs 18:22.]: “He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious.” Therefore, wherever there is fornication or a suspicion of fornication, a wife may freely be dismissed. And because it could happen that someone might bring a false accusation against an innocent woman and impute a crime to his former wife for the sake of a second marital union [Note: [Col. 1463] *a marital union with the former union*: collected editions.], he is commanded to dismiss his first wife in such a way that he does not have a second while the first is alive.

C. III. The husband’s fornication alone defiles the wife. The same, on Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 6, in the ordinary gloss. [Note: [Col. 1463] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 42.]

Whatever sins a person in marriage commits do not darken his own spouse; but fornication [Note: [Col. 1463] Addition: *also*: same edition.] defiles the wife, so that she is no longer lawful to her husband, but is, as it were, an adulteress.

[Col. 1464B] C. IV. He who refuses to dismiss his adulterous wife shall do penance for two years if he renders her the marital debt. Likewise John Chrysostom. [Note: [Col. 1463D] This chapter has not been found in the works of St John Chrysostom. It seems to be a canon of some council or penitential book; something similar occurs in the Council of Nantes, chapter 12.] [Note: [Col. 1463] There are indeed similar provisions in the Council of Nantes, cited by the Correctors (cf. *Reg.* book 2, chapter 131), but the precise words have nowhere been found.]

If anyone finds his wife adulterous and thereafter chooses to keep her in marriage, let him do penance for two years, because he has had intercourse with an adulteress [Note: [Col. 1463] *had intercourse*: collected editions; first Basel edition.] who has not yet been purged of her crime; or let him abstain from marriage with her until the satisfaction for her sin by penance is completed, because after satisfaction by penance she no longer deserves to be called an adulteress. Likewise, if a wife finds her husband adulterous, the judgment is not different.

II. Part. Gratian. This is to be understood as applying unless the woman is unwilling to withdraw from adultery; in that case the husband may receive his wife back without incurring any danger.

[Col. 1464C] Hence Pope Pelagius, to the subdeacon Melleus [Note: [Col. 1463] A chapter of uncertain date.—Anselm, book 11, chapter 94 [93], addressed to “Melitus the Subdeacon.”]:

C. V. After penance for adultery, a husband may receive his wife back.

Concerning Benedict also, whom you reported [Note: [Col. 1463] *judged*: collected editions; first Basel edition.] to have violently taken another man’s wife with criminal intent and up to now presumptuously kept her in his household: if this is the truth of the matter, we command your experience not to delay sternly punishing him together with that adulteress, shaving them and separating them from one another, and sending him without delay to Lucius the defender, on the estate in the province of Apulia; but her, if her husband perhaps wishes to receive [Note: [Col. 1463] *receive back*: Argentinensis and Basel editions.] her without any deceit, let him receive under precautions arranged by you, with no danger being brought upon him, provided only that henceforth he commits nothing similar. But if he altogether refuses to receive her, place her, through prudent [Col. 1464D] administration [Note: [Col. 1463] *arrangement*: Anselm; Argentinensis edition.], in some other location where she cannot live wickedly.

[Col. 1465A] C. VI. He who renders the marital debt to an adulteress shall do penance for three years. From the Penitential of Theodore. [Note: [Col. 1465] This is not extant among Theodore’s fragments edited by Petitus and D’Achery.—Anselm, book 11, chapter 83 [99].]

If anyone knows that his wife is adulterous and does not wish to dismiss her but to keep her in marriage, let him do penance for three years [Note: [Col. 1465] *three years*: Basel edition.], and, for as long as he does penance [Note: [Col. 1465D] “And for as long as he does penance”: in most old copies, “and for as long as she does penance” [so Anselm and the Basel edition].], let him abstain from her.

C. VII. Once adultery has been purged by penance, reconciliation of the marriage may take place. Likewise Augustine, to Pollentius, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book 2, chapter 6. [Note: [Col. 1465] Anselm, book 10, chapter 60; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, chapter 35; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 242; Polycarpus, book 6, title 4; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 35.]

What seems harsh to you—that after adultery a spouse should be reconciled to a spouse [Note: [Col. 1465] Absent from the *Panormia*.]—will not be harsh if faith is present. For why do we still count as adulterers those whom we believe have been cleansed either by baptism or by penance? In the old law of God these crimes were cleansed by no sacrifices; but in the law [Col. 1465B] of the New Testament they are cleansed without legal purification [Note: [Col. 1465D] In Augustine the text reads: “which are undoubtedly cleansed in the blood of Christ of the New Testament” [Ivo’s *Decretum*, with the Maurist edition of Augustine: “which are undoubtedly cleansed by the blood of the New Testament”; *Panormia*: “which in the law of the New Testament, by blood,” etc.]. It has not been corrected because of the gloss.]. Therefore then it was altogether forbidden to receive back a wife defiled by another man [Note: [Col. 1465] *someone*: same editions; first Argentinensis edition.], although David, as a prefigurer of the New Testament, without hesitation received Saul’s daughter, whom the father of that woman had separated from him and given to another [Note: [Col. 1465] 1 Samuel 18; *contamination*: original and Ivo.]. But now, after Christ said to the adulteress [Note: [Col. 1465] John 8:11, misprinted as “1 John.”], “Neither do I condemn you; go, sin no more,” who does not understand that the husband ought to forgive what he sees the Lord of both of them has forgiven [Note: [Col. 1465] *God*: collected editions.]? Nor ought he any longer call her an adulteress when he believes that, by divine mercy, the sin of the penitent woman has been erased [Note: [Col. 1465] “her crime has been erased by God”: collected editions.].

[Col. 1465C] C. VIII. On the same matter. The same author, in the same book, chapter 9. [Note: [Col. 1465] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, chapter 37; *Decretum*, same place; Peter Lombard, same place. In the Argentinensis and Norimbergensis editions this chapter is marked with the name *Palea*.]

Reconciliation of spouses will be neither shameful nor difficult, even after adultery has been committed [Note: [Col. 1465] *prepared*: Venetian editions I and II; *committed*: the remaining editions; Ivo.] and purged, where forgiveness of sins through the keys of the kingdom of heaven is not doubted; not so that an adulteress may be recalled after divorce by her husband, but so that she may not be called an adulteress after union with Christ.

C. IX. When the vice of fornication is excluded, the virtue of chastity is admitted. Likewise Ambrose, *On Cain and Abel*, book 2, chapter 4.

When wickedness is renounced, virtue is immediately admitted. The departure of evil brings about the entrance of virtue, and by the same effort [Note: [Col. 1465] *by that effort also*: Basel edition.] by which crime is excluded, innocence is joined [Col. 1466A].

C. X. Before God, one who returns to truth by penance is not counted deceitful. Likewise Gregory, Homily 19 on the Gospels.

For with the merciful Judge, even one who returns to truth after having lied is not counted deceitful, because almighty God, while gladly receiving our penance, by his own judgment conceals the error we have committed.

Gratian. But if she chooses to persist in adultery, the husband will be regarded as a protector of disgrace and guilty of procuring prostitution, unless he is willing to accuse her as guilty of adultery. Thus, in book 9 of the Code, *On Adultery and Seduction*, Emperors Severus and Antoninus state [Note: [Col. 1465] Chapter 2, book 9, title 9.]:

Those who retain [Col. 1466B] in marriage a wife caught in adultery incur the crime of pandering [Note: [Col. 1465] *detained*: collected editions.], not those who have merely had her under suspicion of adultery [Note: [Col. 1465] *had*: same editions.].

§ 1. This does not apply to women. They are not permitted to prosecute their husbands for adultery. Hence, in the same book and title, the same Emperors state [Note: [Col. 1465] There, chapter 1.]:

The Julian Law declares that women do not have the right of a public accusation of adultery [Note: [Col. 1465] *have*: collected editions; first Basel and Lyon editions II and III.], even if they wish to complain that their own marriage has been violated; for although it granted men, by the right of husbandhood, the power to accuse, it did not grant women the same privilege.

§ 2. Therefore, if, as is gathered from these authorities, no one is permitted to retain an adulteress, much less may anyone marry a woman of whose chastity there is no hope. For fidelity and sacrament must be preserved between spouses; when these are absent, they are called not spouses but adulterers.

[Col. 1466C] Hence Augustine writes against Julian, book 1 [Note: [Col. 1466D] It is cited in the same way in the *Panormia*, and also in Ivo, except that the latter says book 2. The thought frequently occurs in Augustine; in *Against Julian*, while defining marriage as the union of bodies, he discusses it especially in book 5, final chapter.] [Note: [Col. 1465] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 29; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 77.]:

C. XI. The reality of marriage does not consist in the union of male and female.

For the reality of marriage does not lie solely, as you absurdly claim, in the union of male and female, though without that union married persons cannot beget children. There are other things properly belonging to marriage, by which marriages are distinguished from adulteries [Note: [Col. 1465] *determined*: Ivo.]: namely, fidelity to the marriage-bed, the care of begetting children in an orderly manner, and—what is the greatest difference—the good use of an evil thing, that is, the good use of fleshly concupiscence, which adulterers use badly [Note: [Col. 1465] *evil*: Ivo’s *Decretum*.].

[Col. 1467A] Gratian. These are the goods by which marriages are commended and distinguished from unlawful use.

III. Part. On the other hand, Ambrose [Note: [Col. 1467] “Ambrose”: so also in the manuscripts, but the passage has not been found in his works. It occurs in St Jerome, book 1, *Against Jovinianus*.] seems to disapprove marriage, saying:

C. XII. By this authority, first or second marriages appear to be disapproved.

Marriages fill [Note: [Col. 1467] *fill*: collected editions; first Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, and Venetian editions I and II.] the earth; virginity fills paradise. But one must also observe, strictly according to the Hebrew truth, that when Scripture, after the works of each individual day had been completed on the first, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth days [Note: [Col. 1467] “of the individual days, said”: collected editions; cf. Genesis 1:10.], said, “And God saw that it was good,” on the second day [Note: [Col. 1467] Addition: *indeed*: Basel and Lyon editions II and III.] it entirely omitted this, leaving us to understand that the number two, which divides from unity and prefigures the bonds of marriage, is not good. Hence in Noah’s ark [Note: [Col. 1467] Absent from the Basel edition; cf. Genesis 7.] [Col. 1467B] all animals which enter two by two are unclean. The odd number is clean, although another sacramental meaning is shown [Note: [Col. 1467] *understood*: collected editions.] in the even number as well: that even among beasts and unclean birds second marriage was not approved. For the unclean enter two by two [Note: [Col. 1467] *for two by two and two by two*: same editions.], while the clean enter seven by seven [Note: [Col. 1467] Addition: *and seven by seven*: Basel edition.], so that after the flood Noah might have something from the odd number to offer immediately to God [Note: [Col. 1467] *from*: printed text; apparently anomalous.].

Gratian. But this relates to exhortation, not to an obligation to preserve virginity. Hence Ambrose says in his book of exhortation to virgins [Note: [Col. 1467] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, chapter 120.]:

C. XIII. Virginity is commended by counsel, not commanded by decree.

Bodily integrity is to be sought by you [Note: [Col. 1467] *by us*: Ivo; collected editions.]; I commend it as counsel, not prescribe it as command. [Col. 1467C] Virginity alone can be recommended; it cannot be commanded. It is a matter of vow rather than precept [Note: [Col. 1467] Addition: *is*: Basel edition; additions: *is*: remaining editions; Böhm.].

IV. Part. Gratian. Therefore, since in a prostitute, as we have said, there is no hope of fidelity and no certainty of chastity, it is clear that she is not to be taken in marriage. § 1. But an objection is made: Rahab of Jericho [Note: [Col. 1467] Joshua 2 and 6.], though a prostitute, was nevertheless joined in marriage to a prince of the tribe of Judah, and Christ afterwards deigned to be born from her. Hosea also [Note: [Col. 1467] Hosea 1 and 3.], the first of the twelve prophets, by the Lord’s command bought a prostitute for a *cor* of barley and joined her to himself in marriage. But it is one thing to marry a prostitute or retain an adulteress so that you may adorn her by your customary life, chastity, and purity; it is another to keep one of those women whom you can in no way recall from the indulgence of her flesh [Col. 1467D]. The latter is altogether forbidden; the former is recorded as having been laudably done.

[Col. 1468A] Hence Jerome, on Hosea, book 1, on chapter 1 [Note: [Col. 1467] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 57; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 38.]:

C. XIV. It is not a sin to take a prostitute as wife.

The prophet Hosea is not to be blamed—if for the moment we follow the historical account—for turning the prostitute whom he married to chastity [Note: [Col. 1467] *turned*: collected editions.]. Rather, he is to be praised for making a good woman out of a bad one [Note: [Col. 1467] *made*: same editions.]. For one who remains good is not himself defiled if joined to an evil person; but one who is evil is turned to good [Note: [Col. 1467] *is converted*: same editions; Ivo, *Panormia*.] if he follows the examples of the good. From this we understand that the prophet, joined to a prostitute, did not lose chastity; rather, the prostitute acquired [Note: [Col. 1467] *took*: collected editions; first Basel edition.] the chastity which she previously lacked.

## QUESTION II

[Col. 1468B] GRATIAN

I. Part. That a woman taken solely for the sake of incontinence is not a wife seems capable of proof from this: marriage was instituted by God for propagation, not for satisfying lust. For this was the blessing of marriage: “Increase and multiply.”

Hence Ambrose, on Luke, book 1, on chapter 1 [Note: [Col. 1467] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapters 24–25; *Decretum*, part 8, chapters 75–76.]:

C. I. Bearing children is women’s sole reason for marrying.

It is a shame for women not to possess the rewards of marriage, since this is their sole reason for marrying. The same author, book 2, at the beginning:

§ 1. When [Note: [Col. 1467] *When*: original; Ivo, *Panormia*.] childbearing is the reward of marriage and the grace of wedlock for women, there is also no slight reason why Mary’s virginity should deceive the prince of this world.

Gratian. Therefore those who join one another not for begetting offspring [Col. 1468C], but for satisfying lust, appear to be not so much spouses as fornicators.

Jerome also, on chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Ephesians [Note: [Col. 1467] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 277.]:

C. II. Those not joined according to Christ’s precepts are called not spouses but adulterers.

Just as not every assembly of heretics can be called Christ’s Church, nor is Christ their head [Note: [Col. 1467] Addition: *is*: Ivo; collected editions.], so not every marriage in which a wife is joined not to her own husband [Note: [Col. 1467] Absent from Ivo.] according to Christ’s precepts can rightly be called marriage; it is rather adultery.

II. Part. Gratian. The first institution of marriage was made in paradise, so that the marriage-bed might be undefiled and marriage honorable, and so that they might conceive without passion and give birth without pain. The second was made outside paradise [Col. 1468D] [Col. 1469A] to eliminate an unlawful manner [Note: [Col. 1469] Cf. Genesis 2.], so that human weakness, prone to fall into shamefulness, might be sustained by the honorableness of marriage. Therefore the Apostle writes to the Corinthians [Note: [Col. 1469] 1 Corinthians 7:2.]: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband.” From this cause it follows that married people owe themselves to one another and cannot deny themselves to one another. Hence the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1469] Ibid., verse 5.]: “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by agreement and for a time, so that you may more freely devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same thing, lest Satan perhaps tempt you. But I say this because of your incontinence.” Therefore those who are urged, because of incontinence, to return to natural intercourse are plainly commanded to unite not only for the begetting of children.

§ 1. Yet marriage is not on that account judged evil. What is done apart from the intention of begetting [Col. 1469B] is not an evil of marriage, but is venial because of marriage’s good, which is threefold: fidelity, offspring, and sacrament.

Hence Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 6 [Note: [Col. 1469] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 234.]:

C. III. The immoderate use of married persons is not an evil of marriage, but is venial because of marriage’s good.

Whatever married persons do between themselves that is immodest, shameless, or filthy is a defect of human beings, not a fault of marriage. Even in the more immoderate [Note: [Col. 1469] *immoderate*: Ivo; collected editions.] demanding of the carnal debt, which the Apostle prescribes to them not as a command [Note: [Col. 1469] *the command of marriage*: Basel and Lyon editions II and III.] but by way of concession [Note: [Col. 1469] *the Apostle permits*: Ivo; same editions; cf. 1 Corinthians 7.]—so that they may have intercourse even apart from the reason of procreation—although corrupt habits impel them to such intercourse, marriage nevertheless protects them from adultery [Col. 1469C] or fornication. For this is not permitted because of marriage, but is forgiven because of marriage. Married persons therefore owe each other not only the fidelity of sexual intercourse itself for the sake of begetting children—which is the primary association of the human race in this mortal condition—but also a kind of mutual servitude for supporting each other’s weakness and avoiding unlawful intercourse, so that, even if perpetual continence pleases one of them [Note: [Col. 1469] *conscience*: Basel edition.], he or she cannot undertake it without the other’s consent [Note: [Col. 1469] “cannot be done”: collected editions; Böhm.].

III. Part. Gratian. The presence of the Holy Spirit is not granted at the time when marital acts take place.

Hence Jerome, on Matthew [Note: [Col. 1469] This chapter occurs in Origen, Homily 6 on Numbers, and from him is cited in the ordinary gloss on Numbers 11.] [Note: [Col. 1469] Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 32.]:

C. IV. The presence of the Holy Spirit is not granted at the time when marital acts take place.

[Col. 1469D] Lawful marriages are indeed free from sin; nevertheless, at the time when marital acts take place, the presence of the Holy Spirit is not granted [Col. 1470A], even if the person fulfilling the office of generation appears to be a prophet. There are many other matters in which human power alone suffices, and in which neither is the thing in need of, nor is it fitting for, the presence of the Holy Spirit to be there.

Gratian. Therefore, just as such intercourse is not fornication but lawful because of the good of marriage, so also the union under discussion is not fornication but lawful because of the good of marriage.

Likewise, as Augustine says in *On Marriage*, chapter 14 [Note: [Col. 1469] Anselm, book 10, chapter 13; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 45; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 10; Polycarpus, book 6, title 4.]:

C. V. Concubines taken temporarily do not make their concubinage just, even if they have intercourse for the sake of children.

[Col. 1470B] IV. Part. Gratian. Conversely, this must be understood of those who are joined to each other with marital affection: even if they come together not for begetting children but for satisfying lust, they are for that reason called not fornicators but spouses.

This same point is proved by Augustine’s authority in *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 1469] Anselm, book 10, chapter 12; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapters 27 and 44; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 65; Polycarpus, same place.]:

C. VI. Those who join themselves to each other solely because of incontinence are spouses.

It is customary to ask whether, when a man and woman—neither he the husband of another nor she the wife of another—join themselves to each other not for the begetting of children but because of incontinence [Note: [Col. 1469] *because of incontinence*: original; *incontinence*: Basel edition; *of incontinence*: remaining editions, except Lyon II and III.], for the sake only of intercourse, on the mutual pledge that neither he [Col. 1470C] will do this with another woman nor she with another man, they should be called married. Perhaps this may not unreasonably be called marriage if it pleases them to remain so until one of them dies, and if, though they did not join for the purpose of producing offspring, they have nevertheless not avoided procreation by either refusing to have children born to them [Note: [Col. 1469] *refused*: Basel edition.] or even doing some evil deed to prevent their birth. But if either both or one of these conditions is absent, I do not see how we can call these persons married [Note: [Col. 1469] *can*: Basel and Lyon editions II and III.]. For if a man takes a woman to himself temporarily until he finds another worthy of his rank or property, whom he may take as an equal [Note: [Col. 1469] *in marriage*: Ivo, *Panormia*, chapter 27; collected editions.], he is an adulterer in his very intention—not with the woman he hopes to find, but with this one with whom he lies [Col. 1470D] in such a way that he does not have a marital partnership with her.

[Col. 1471A] C. VII. Those who procure drugs of sterility are fornicators, not spouses. The same author, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, chapter 15. [Note: [Col. 1471] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, chapter 55; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 31.]

Sometimes this lustful cruelty, or cruel lust, goes so far as to procure drugs of sterility and, if they achieve nothing, somehow to extinguish and discharge [Note: [Col. 1471] *extinguish—discharge*: Argentinensis edition.] the conceived fetuses within the womb [Note: [Col. 1471] *or*: collected editions.], wishing their offspring to perish before living; or, if it was already alive in the womb, to be killed before it is born [Note: [Col. 1471] *to be born*: original; Ivo; collected editions.]. If both are such, they are not spouses; and if they were such from the beginning, they came together not by marriage but rather by debauchery. But if they are not both such, I dare say that either she is in some sense a prostitute or he an adulterer against his wife.

[Col. 1471B] V. Part. Gratian. Concerning those who procure abortion, the question is asked whether they are judged murderers or not.

Augustine, in his book *Questions on Exodus*, question 80, says [Note: [Col. 1471] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 12; *Decretum*, part 10, chapter 56; Peter Lombard, same place.]:

C. VIII. One who procures an abortion before a soul has been infused into the body is not a murderer.

That the law did not wish an unformed fetus [Note: [Col. 1471C] *Fetus*: the printed editions continued, “Moses, or the law,” [so Ivo, *Panormia*, and the collected editions except the first Basel edition], but these words are absent from most old copies and the original. Several other items have likewise been corrected from these.] to count as homicide proves that it did not count what is carried in the womb in such a state as a human being [Note: [Col. 1471] *would have counted*: Basel edition.]. Here there is customarily debate about the soul: whether what has not been formed can even be understood to be ensouled, and whether therefore it is not homicide because it cannot be called deprived of soul if it did not yet have a soul [Note: [Col. 1471] Absent from the collected editions except Lyon II and III.].

Likewise:

§ 1. If then that unformed fetus had indeed come to exist [Note: [Col. 1471] *had existed*: Ivo; collected editions.] but was still in some way ensouled without form [Col. 1471C]—because no judgment should be rashly hurried forward, without examination, in so great a question about the soul [Note: [Col. 1471] Addition: *there is*: Ivo, *Panormia*; same editions; *judgment*: collected editions except Norimbergensis and Venetian I–II.]—the law therefore did not wish it to count as homicide, because a living soul cannot yet be said to be in that body which lacks sensation.

C. IX. On the same matter. The same author, in *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, chapter 23. [Note: [Col. 1471] This work is not Augustine’s.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 13; *Decretum*, part 10, chapter 57; Peter Lombard, same place.]

Moses transmitted [Note: [Col. 1471] Exodus 21:22.]: “If anyone strikes a pregnant woman and causes an abortion [Note: [Col. 1471] *causes a miscarriage*: Vulgate; Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions.], if it is formed, [Col. 1472A] let him give life for life; but if it is unformed, let him be fined money,” so as to demonstrate that there is no soul before form [Note: [Col. 1471] *formed*: Ivo, *Panormia*; *formed*: Basel and Lyon I editions; Böhm.]. Thus, if it is given to an already formed body [Note: [Col. 1471] *let it be given to the body*: Basel edition.], the soul is not born with the bodily conception, derived from the seed [Note: [Col. 1471] *the soul derived*: same editions.]. For if the soul existed from a soul together with the seed [Note: [Col. 1471] *from*: Basel edition.], many souls would perish every day when seed, by a certain discharge [Note: [Col. 1471] *from discharge*: collected editions; *in some manner*: Norimbergensis and Venetian I–II editions.], does not advance to birth. But if we look more closely [Note: [Col. 1471] *earlier*: Ivo; collected editions except first Basel and Lyon I editions.], we shall see what we ought to follow. Let us consider the making of Adam. For in Adam an example was given, so that we may understand [Note: [Col. 1471] *understand*: collected editions.] that a body already formed receives a soul [Note: [Col. 1471] *received*: same editions; original; Ivo.]. For God could have mixed the soul into the clay of the earth and thus formed the body [Note: [Col. 1471] *could*: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions except first Basel edition; Addition: *God*: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions.]. But this was refuted by reason [Note: [Col. 1471] *was informed*: original.], because the house first had to be put together and then its inhabitant introduced. The soul [Col. 1472B], certainly, because it is spirit, cannot dwell in what is dry; therefore it is said to dwell in blood [Note: [Col. 1471] Absent from the original and Ivo’s *Decretum*.]. Therefore, when the outlines of the body have not been put together, where will the soul be [Note: [Col. 1471] *of the body*: absent from Ivo and the collected editions except Lyon II and III.]?

C. X. On the same matter. Likewise Jerome, to Algasia, question 4. [Note: [Col. 1471] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 8, chapter 14; *Decretum*, part 10, chapter 58; Peter Lombard, same place.]

Just as seeds are gradually formed in the womb and a human being is not reckoned to exist [Note: [Col. 1471] *homicide*: Ivo; collected editions.] until the elements, having been completed [Note: [Col. 1471] *confused*: original.], receive their forms and limbs, so a thought conceived by reason, unless it bursts forth into action, is still held in the womb and quickly perishes through the enemy [Note: [Col. 1471D] “Through the enemy”: the original and Ivo [but not the *Panormia*] read, “and the abortion quickly perishes.” Jerome elsewhere, and in the same question, uses the word *abortion*: “the attack of the adversary,” he says, “causes the things conceived to perish by abortion”; but it has not been changed because of the gloss.].

VI. Part. Gratian. Therefore, since one who takes a woman to himself temporarily is said to be an adulterer with her, he does not sin by leaving her or by giving his daughter to him.

[Col. 1472C] Hence Pope Leo, to Rusticus, Bishop of Narbonne, Epistle 90, alternatively 92, chapters 5 and 6 [Note: [Col. 1471] Epistle 167, written A.D. 458 or 459, Ballerini edition; cf. Decree 7, *On Penance*, chapter 1.]:

C. XI. It is an advance in honorableness to cast aside a prostitute and take a lawful wife.

To cast aside a slave-woman from one’s bed and take a wife of established free birth is not a doubling of marriage, but an advance in honorableness.

§ 1. The negligence of such persons is indeed to be blamed [Note: [Col. 1471] *is*: collected editions.], but they are not utterly to be despaired of; rather, by repeated exhortations, they should be encouraged faithfully to carry out what they sought out of necessity [Note: [Col. 1471] *sought necessarily*: same editions.]. For no one is to be despaired of while he remains in this body [Note: [Col. 1473D] After the word *given* two old manuscripts cite from Justinian’s Code, book 5, title *On Marriage*, law 12, *Nec filium*, and law 20, *In conjunctione*; from the Digest, title *On the Marriage Rite*, law 2, *Nuptiae consistere*; and from the Institutes, title *On Marriage*, from the beginning through the words *praecedere debeat*.] [Col. 1473A] [Note: [Col. 1473] *remains*: same editions; original.], because what is delayed by distrust in youth is sometimes accomplished by more mature judgment.

C. XII. A woman given to a man who has a concubine is joined to him in lawful marriage. The same author, in the same place, chapter 4. [Note: [Col. 1473] Burchard, book 9, chapter 1; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 35; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 139; Polycarpus, book 6, title 4.]

Not every woman joined [Note: [Col. 1473] *joined*: collected editions.] to a man is that man’s wife, just as not every son is his father’s heir. But the bonds of marriage are lawful among persons of free birth and among equals [Note: [Col. 1473] *equal*: Hispanic Collection; cited collections.], God having established this very thing long before Roman law began [Note: [Col. 1473] *began*: collected editions.]. Therefore a wife is one thing, a concubine another; a slave-woman is one thing [Note: [Col. 1473] “is a slave-woman, and”: same editions.], a free woman another.

§ 1. Therefore, to make the distinction between these persons plain, the Apostle adduces testimony [Note: [Col. 1473] Galatians 4:30; *to make plain*: collected editions except first Argentinensis edition; *adduced*: same editions; cf. Genesis 21:10.] from Genesis, where Abraham is told: “Cast out the slave-woman and her son; for the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with my son [Col. 1473B] Isaac” [Note: [Col. 1473] “with the son of the free woman”: Hispanic Collection; editions of Leo before Quesnel; Basel edition.].

(And below:)

§ 2. If a cleric of any locality [Note: [Col. 1473C] “A cleric of any locality”: so in editions of the letters; but Canon 18 of the Code of Canons and the cited collectors read, “a layman of any locality.” In the Council of Tribur, where this is cited, the text is “If anyone gives his daughter,” etc.] gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine, this must not be understood as though he gave her to a married man, unless perhaps that woman appears to have been made free, lawfully endowed, and honored with public marriage rites.

§ 4. Women joined to men by paternal decision [Note: [Col. 1473] Addition: *for*: Basel and Lyon editions II–III; Addition: *women*: collected editions; *enjoined*: Hispanic Collection; *joined*: Burchard and Ivo.] are free of blame if the women whom the men had kept were not wives in marriage [Note: [Col. 1473] *were*: Ivo’s *Decretum*; collected editions.], because a wife is one thing [Note: [Col. 1473] *a bride*: Burchard and Ivo.], a concubine another.

VII. Part. Gratian. Therefore, when it is said, “joined to men by paternal decision,” it is understood that paternal consent is required in marriage and that marriages without it are not lawful, according to the statement of Pope Evaristus [Note: [Col. 1473] Cf. above, Cause 3, question 5, chapter 1.]: “A lawful marriage is not otherwise made, unless she is given by her parents.”

[Col. 1473C] C. XIII. Likewise Ambrose, in the book *On the Patriarchs*—that is, book 1 *On Abraham*, final chapter:

Rebecca’s parents are honored with gifts. The young woman is consulted not about the betrothal—for in this matter she awaits the judgment of her parents; it is not modest for a virgin [Col. 1474A] to choose a husband—but, once already betrothed to the man, she is consulted about the day of departure. Nor was it without reason that she did not cause delay: she rightly ought to hasten to her husband.

Hence it is clear from where that saying of Euripides [Note: [Col. 1473] *Andromache*, verse 987.], which many wonder was borrowed, has been taken. For he says in the person of a woman who nevertheless wished to leave her husband and was being sought for another marriage:

> *Νυμφευμάτων μὲν τῶν ἐμῶν πατὴρ ἐμὸς  
> Μέριμναν ἕξει, κοὐκ ἐμὸν κρίνειν τάδε.*

That is: “My father shall take responsibility for my marriage arrangements; this is not my concern to decide.” [Note: [Col. 1473] Addition: *for himself*: collected editions except first Basel and Lyon II–III; *undertakes*: Norimbergensis edition; *undertook*: collected editions except first Argentinensis and Lyon II–III.]

Therefore, preserve, virgins, what even the philosophers themselves admired [Note: [Col. 1473] *preserved*: Lyon editions II–III.]. Even if a woman, soon widowed while still young [Note: [Col. 1473] *and young*: Norimbergensis and Venetian I–II; Paris and Lyon I editions.], fears falling into the snare [Note: [Col. 1473] *into the snare*: Basel and Lyon I editions.] of her weakness, if she wishes to marry [Note: [Col. 1473] Addition: *to marry*: collected editions.], let her marry, but only in the Lord; let her defer the choice of a husband to her parents, lest she be thought [Col. 1474B] [Note: [Col. 1473] *is absent*: Lyon II–III.] to be the author of an over-bold desire [Note: [Col. 1473] *is judged*: Lyon II–III.] if she claims for herself the choice in her own marriage. For she ought rather to seem sought by a man than herself to have sought a man. Let her put modesty first before she marries, so that modesty may commend the marriage itself still more.

### C. XIV. Likewise in the Book of Numbers, chapter XXX [vv. 4 ff.]

If a woman has made any vow and bound herself by an oath, while she is in her father’s house and still of maidenly age, if her father learns of the vow which she has promised and of the oath by which she has bound her soul, and remains silent, she shall not be held liable [Note: “She shall not be held liable”: In the original it reads: “she shall be liable for the vow, whatever she has promised,” etc. But it has not been corrected because of the gloss.]; but [Note: “if”: edition of Bas.] whatever she has promised and sworn she shall fulfil in deed [Note: “shall fulfil”: “has fulfilled”: editions of Arg., Bas.]. But if, as soon as he hears of it, her father objects [Col. 1474C] [Note: “objected”: editions of Arg., Bas., Nor.], both her vows and her oaths shall be void, and she shall not be held bound by the promise, because her father objected.

### C. XV. Augustine, Question LVII on Numbers

[Note: Formerly it read: “Likewise Augustine.” The word “Likewise” has been removed, since it is absent from most ancient copies. For the words of Blessed Augustine, or of the ordinary gloss, cited here are an explanation of the previously quoted passage from Numbers. In the same ancient copies all these chapters to which no heading is attached are included under one chapter.]

Here there is good reason to inquire also concerning a vow of virginity. For women, even virgins, are customarily called “women” in Scripture [Col. 1475A]; and the Apostle too seems to speak of a father when he says [Note: 1 Cor. 7:37–38]: “Let him keep his virgin”; and: “Let him give his virgin in marriage.”

Conversely, in the Third Council of Toledo, canon 10 [Note: held A.D. 589.—Burchard, book 8, c. 44. Ivo, Decree, part 7, c. 62; part 8, cc. 18, 19]:

### C. XVI. Widows and virgins are to choose husbands for themselves by their own will

This holy council declares [Note: “confirms”: Ivo.—The older collected editions read: “that widows who wish to preserve chastity are not to be compelled by any force to remarry”: Spanish Collection; Burchard; Ivo.] that widows, if it please them, may preserve chastity [Note: “Chastity”: In the older editions of the councils and in two Vatican manuscripts, the remainder reads as in Gratian; but after this word are added: “and no widow shall be compelled by force to remarry. But if,” etc. In more recent editions and among the other collectors the arrangement of the words varies somewhat, but the meaning is the same.]. But if, before professing continence, they choose to marry, let them marry those whom by their own will they wish to have as husbands. Let the same rule apply to virgins; nor are they to be compelled, against either their parents’ will or their own, to take husbands. But if anyone hinders the resolution of chastity of a widow or virgin, let him be excluded from holy communion and from the thresholds of the church.

[Col. 1475B] Gratian. From the authorities set forth above it is plainly maintained that, although some persons unite not for the procreation of children but because of incontinence, they are nevertheless called spouses.

## QUESTION III

### GRATIAN

Concerning the third question, Pelagius gives a decision in writing to Potentius the Defender [Note: Letter of uncertain date.—Ivo, Decree, part 8, c. 27]:

### C. UN. In marriage, a girl ought to follow the decision of her freeborn grandfather, not of her unfreeborn father

It is established that the father of the girl, a servant of our church [Note: “your church”: edition of Bas.], was born of servile status, but that her grandfather was born free; and therefore [Col. 1475C] we decree that the choice of the grandfather concerning the union of his granddaughter is to be regarded more than that of her father [Note: absent in the same source], whose decision can in no way be free.

Gratian. Since, therefore, it is proved that this woman married him by her grandfather’s choice, it is established that she has been lawfully joined to him.

## QUESTION IV

### GRATIAN

That it is permissible for someone to seek children from a female slave because of his wife’s barrenness is proved by the example of Abraham [Note: Gen. 16], who, because of the barrenness of his wife Sarah, went in to Hagar the Egyptian in order to receive children from her. Likewise Jacob [Note: ibid., Gen. 30], when he could not have children by Rachel, raised up children for himself by her handmaid; and it is recorded that he went in to Leah’s handmaid and begot children by her not only because of barrenness, but even because fertility had ceased. From all these things it is inferred that, because of a wife’s barrenness, children may lawfully be sought either from a female slave or from any other woman; otherwise Abraham and Jacob will be marked with the stain of adultery. But just as, after Sarah’s death [Note: ibid., Gen. 25], Abraham took Keturah as wife, lest, according to Augustine, Christians [Note: “Christians”: In the following chapter Augustine says: “lest heretics should think.”] should think it sinful to take another wife after the death of one’s wife, so he seems to have received children from a female slave while his wife was alive, lest anyone should count this as a crime.

This is said by Augustine against the adversary of the Law and the Prophets, book II, chapter 9:

[Col. 1476B]

### C. I. How Abraham is excused from the charge of fornication

This man [Note: Ivo, Panormia, book 6, c. 60; Decree, part 8, c. 269.] charges Abraham even into decrepit old age [Note: “old age”: “the age of old age”: collected editions.] with the crime of fornication, surely because after Sarah’s death he took another wife. Even if no sacrament of a hidden matter were understood here, Abraham ought to have done this for this reason alone: lest heretics, contrary to the Apostle [Note: “the people of God”: Ivo, Panormia; collected editions; cf. 1 Cor. 7]—among whom Tertullian also appears as a supporter [Note: “is present”: Ivo; collected editions.]—should think it a crime to take a wife after the death of one’s wife.

Gratian. The sacramental meaning of this matter is that by good persons both evil and good persons were to be generated in faith, and by evil persons both good and evil persons were to come to faith.

[Col. 1476C] Therefore Augustine says on John, Tractate XI [Note: This chapter has been composed partly from Tractate 11 on John and partly from book I, On Baptism against the Donatists, cc. 16–17; certain things have been added from there and many things corrected.] [Note: “our”: collected editions]:

### C. II. As good and evil are generated in faith through the ministry of the good, so also through the ministry of the evil

Let your mind now return to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. In these three we find free women giving birth, and also slave women giving birth. There we find the offspring of free women, and also the offspring of slave women. The slave woman signifies nothing good. “Cast out the slave woman,” he says, “and her son” [Note: Gen. 21:10.—In Augustine this is cited more fully.]. And below:

§ 1. In these generations of free women and slave women we find a remarkable thing: namely, four classes of human beings, in whom is fulfilled the figure of the entire future Christian people. Thus it is no wonder that of those three it was said: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” [Note: Exod. 3:6; “and”: absent from the collected editions except Bas.]. For among all Christians [Note: “consider”: collected editions]—brothers, pay attention—either good persons are born through evil persons, or evil persons through good persons, or good through good, or evil through evil. Beyond these four classes you cannot find any others [Note: “cannot be found”: same editions].

And below:

§ 2. There you find good sons of Jacob born of slave women, and good sons of Jacob born of free women. Their birth from the wombs of slave women did them no harm, once they recognized their seed in their father; and accordingly they held the kingdom with their brothers. Therefore, just as in Jacob’s sons those who were born of slave women were not hindered from holding the kingdom and receiving the land of promise [Note: “the promise which they received with their brothers”: same editions] equally with their brothers—not their slave-woman birth, but their father’s seed prevailed—so all who are baptized through evil ministers seem to be born of slave women. Yet, because they are born from the seed [Col. 1477B] of the word of God [Note: added: “they are born”: collected editions], which is figured in Jacob, let them not be distressed: they shall possess the inheritance together with their brothers.

Let him therefore be secure who is born of good seed; only let him not imitate the slave woman. If he is born of a slave woman [Note: “you are born—you imitate”: same editions], let him not imitate the evil, proud slave woman. Why indeed did Jacob’s sons born of slave women possess the land of promise with their brothers, while Ishmael, born of a slave woman [Note: “of Hagar the slave woman”: same editions], was cast out from the inheritance? Why, except because he was proud and they humble? He raised his neck and wished to deceive his brother, playing with him. There is a great sacramental meaning there. Ishmael and Isaac were playing together; Sarah saw them playing, and said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” [Note: Gen. 21:10]. And when Abraham was distressed, the angel confirmed to him, from the Lord, the saying of his wife.

§ 3. [Note: “But she who”: In Blessed Augustine these words follow after the verse “All shall be written,” in the chapter “Just as in the sacraments,” *De consecratione*, distinction 4.] [Note: Augustine, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, book I, chapter 17.] But she who bore Abel and Enoch and Noah and Abraham, she also bore Moses [Note: “and Moses”: collected editions; Böhm.] and the Prophets later in time before the Lord’s coming; and she who bore these, also bore the Apostles, our martyrs, and all good Christians. For all appeared as born at different times, yet they are contained in the fellowship of one people; and, as citizens of the same city, they have experienced the toils of this pilgrimage—some now experience them, and the rest will experience them until the end.

Likewise, she who bore Cain, Ham, Ishmael, and Esau, that same one bore Dathan and others like him in the same people; and she who bore these also bore Judas the false apostle, Simon Magus, and false Christians down to the present time, obstinately hardened in carnal disposition, whether they are mixed within the unity or dissent through open separation.

§ 4. But when such people are evangelized and instructed in the sacraments by spiritual persons, Rebecca herself, as it were, gives birth to them, as she did Esau [Note: Gen. 23, evidently an erroneous citation]; but when such people are generated in God’s people through those who do not chastely proclaim the Gospel, Sarah indeed gives birth, but through Hagar. Likewise, when good spiritual persons are generated through carnal evangelists [Note: “When … evangelists”: thus corrected from most ancient copies and the original, in Eugyppius, vol. 2, p. 216. Formerly it read: “when they are evangelized and are generated through carnal sacraments or baptisms.” The collected editions except Bas. read: “they are evangelized, or are generated by carnal baptizers.”] or baptizers, Leah or Rachel gives birth to them by right of marriage, but through the womb of slave women.

§ 5. But when good believers are generated through spiritual persons in the Gospel—those who either attain to a spiritual disposition of piety, or do not cease to strive toward it [Note: Augustine and Eugyppius read: “either attain to the disposition of spiritual maturity.”], or fail to do so because they cannot—then, like Isaac from Sarah’s womb or Jacob from Rebekah’s [Note: Gen. 17], they are born into the new life and the New Testament. Thus, whether they appear to dwell within or are openly outside, what is flesh is flesh; whether in the threshing-floor it persists in its barrenness [Note: “persist”: collected editions], or on occasion of temptation is carried outside as though by wind [Note: “are carried away”: same editions], what is chaff is chaff. And he who is mingled with the congregation of the saints in carnal hardening is always divided from the unity of that Church which is without spot or wrinkle [Note: Eph. 5:27]. Yet no one is to be despaired of, whether he appears such within [Note: “appear”: collected editions] or more manifestly opposes from outside [Note: “oppose”: same editions].

## Part II

Gratian. The answer to these matters is this: according to the diversity of times, a varying dispensation of the Creator is found. It was promised to Abraham [Note: Gen. 12] that all nations would be blessed in his seed [Col. 1478C]; and God had also promised to give his seed the land of his sojourning [Note: ibid., Gen. 14]. Therefore, when the Lord had chosen Abraham and his sons as a people peculiarly his own, leaving all others in idolatry, the multiplication of God’s people was rightly sought through the fruitfulness of many women, because succession in faith lay in succession of blood. Hence it was said in the law: “Cursed is the barren woman who has left no seed upon the earth” [Note: These words are not found in Sacred Scripture, although they are cited from it by many holy and ancient teachers. Deuteronomy 7 has: “There shall not be among you either sex barren, among human beings or among your flocks.”].

For this reason marriage was prescribed even for priests, because succession to the office was secured through succession in the family. But because through Christ’s incarnation the grace of faith has spread everywhere, it is no longer said, “Speak to the house of Judah and to the house of Israel”; rather: “Go and teach all nations” [Note: Matt. 28:19], and: “In every nation, whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” [Note: Acts 10:35]. The choice for office is not sought in succession of lineage, but in perfection of life and purity of knowledge; virginity is preferred to fruitfulness, and the chastity of continence is commanded to priests.

Therefore Abraham and Jacob did not sin because, besides a wife, they sought children from a female slave; nor is anyone allowed, by their example, to seek fertility in any woman beyond the marital obligation. For their marriages are equal to, or preferred over, the virginity of our own people; while the immoderate use of marriage in our own time almost imitates the shamefulness of fornication in that time.

[Col. 1479B] Accordingly Ambrose writes in the book *On the Patriarchs*, book I, *On Abraham*, chapter 4 [Note: Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 33]:

### C. III. Abraham is not guilty of adultery, though he received children from a slave woman while his wife was alive

Sarah said to Abraham [Note: Gen. 16:2]: “Behold, the Lord has shut me up so that I may not bear; go in therefore to my slave woman, that you may make a son from her.” And so it was done. But let us consider first that Abraham lived before the Law of Moses and before the Gospel; adultery did not yet seem to have been forbidden [Note: added: “therefore”: same editions.—“Therefore not”: Böhm.]. The penalty for a crime dates from the time of the Law, which prohibited the crime; and before the Law there is no condemnation of an act, except from the Law. Abraham therefore did not offend against the Law, but preceded the Law. God had praised marriage in Paradise, but had not condemned adultery [Note: the original reads: “although he had praised marriage.”].

And below:

§ 1. You have the first defence of Abraham. The second is that he did not set aside the marital bed for cohabitation with a slave woman through the heat of some wandering lust, nor because he had been captivated by the beauty of a wanton form, but out of zeal for seeking descendants and propagating offspring. Even after the flood there was still a scarcity of the human race; there was also a concern for religion, lest anyone seem not to have rendered nature its due. Indeed Lot and his daughters also had this reason for seeking descendants, lest the human race fail; and therefore, for the sake of a public duty, he covered a private fault.

### C. IV. What is committed apart from a lawful wife is condemned as the crime of adultery

The same author, in the same book and chapter [Note: Polycarpus, book 6, title 8].

Let no one flatter himself by appealing to human laws. Every sexual defilement is adultery, and what is not permitted to a woman is not permitted to a man. The same chastity is owed by a husband as by a wife. Whatever is committed with a woman who is not a lawful wife [Col. 1479D] is condemned as the crime of adultery [Note: the original reads “her” rather than “a woman”].

And in the same book, chapter 7:

§ 1. No one is permitted to know a woman other than his wife; for this reason the right of marriage has been given to you, lest you fall into the snare [Note: added: “of the devil”: editions of Bas., Lugd.] and sin with another woman.

And a little later:

§ 2. A fault concealed is more tolerable than authority claimed for a fault. Nor is adultery only sinning with another man’s wife, but everything which lacks the authority of marriage. Yet this passage teaches that the crime is more serious where the rights of a contracted marriage are violated and a wife’s modesty is undone. Therefore, when Abimelech pleaded that he did not know the woman to be another man’s wife, since the man himself had called her his sister [Note: “said”: edition O; “had said”: Böhm.], the Lord answered him [Note: Gen. 20:7]: “And I knew that you did this with a pure heart, and I spared you so that you should not sin against me; for this reason I did not allow you to touch her.”

We recognize God as the overseer and guardian [Col. 1480B] of marriage: he does not permit another man’s marriage-bed to be polluted; and if anyone does so, he sins against God, whose law he violates and whose grace he nullifies. And therefore, because he sins against God, he loses fellowship in the heavenly sacrament.

### C. V. Nothing is fouler than to love one’s wife as though she were an adulteress

Likewise Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book I [Note: Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 31].

## Part III

The origin of love was indeed honorable, but its excess was shameful.

§ 1. It makes no difference from what honorable cause a person becomes mad. Hence Xystus [Note: “Sextus”: same editions, especially Lugdd. II–III; added: “the Pythagorean”: collected editions except Bas.; and “says”: collected editions.] says in his *Sentences*: “A husband too ardent a lover of his own wife is an adulterer.” For every love for another man’s wife is disgraceful, but excessive love for one’s own wife is disgraceful as well [Note: “lover”: same editions, especially Lugdd. II–III.]. A wise man ought to love his wife with judgment, not passion. Let him govern the impulses of pleasure and not rush headlong into intercourse [Note: The collected editions read: “Let not the impulse of pleasure rule in him, nor let him be carried precipitously into intercourse.”]. Nothing is fouler than to love one’s wife as though she were an adulteress.

§ 2. Certainly, those who say that they marry wives for the sake of the commonwealth and the human race, and procreate children, should at least imitate cattle: after their wives’ wombs have swelled, they should not destroy their children, nor present themselves to their wives as lovers [Note: “offer themselves”: collected editions], but as husbands.

### C. VI. Virginal chastity is not preferred to Abraham’s marriage

The same author, book II [Note: Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 33].

Who does not know [Note: “does not know”: collected editions] that, under another dispensation of God, all the saints of old were of the same merit as Christians are now? As Abraham formerly pleased God in marriage, so virgins now please him in perpetual chastity. He served the law and the time proper to him [Col. 1480D]; let us also serve the Gospel [Note: “the law”: collected editions] and the time proper to us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come [Note: “have arrived”: same editions].

[Col. 1481A]

### C. VII. The patriarchs had several wives not to satisfy lustful desire, but for the sake of numerous offspring

Likewise Augustine [Note: “Augustine”: restored from all ancient copies, whereas the common editions read “Ambrose.”], book XXII *Against Faustus*, chapters 47 and 48 [Note: Peter Lombard, ibid.].

Jacob’s four wives are objected to him; but when it was the custom, it was not a crime. As the patriarchs had intercourse with their wives who received their seed, not through desire for obtaining pleasure [Note: “accomplishing”: collected editions], but through care for propagating a line of succession, so the Apostles delighted in hearers who admired their teaching, not through eagerness to gain praise, but through love for sowing truth.

[Note: In Blessed Augustine the order of the words differs: “Just as the Apostles,” he says, “delighted in hearers admiring their teaching, not through eagerness to gain praise, but through love for sowing truth; so the patriarchs,” etc.]

### C. VIII. It is better to die childless than seek offspring by illicit intercourse

Likewise Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 16 [Note: Peter Lombard, ibid., at the end; cf. Distinction 56, c. 3].

[Col. 1481B] ## Part IV
