Just as it is better [Note: “holier”: editions of Bas., Lugd. I.] to die of hunger than to eat food sacrificed to idols, so it is better [Note: “holier”: editions of Bas., Par., Lugdd.] to die without children than to seek offspring by illicit intercourse [Note: “cohabitation”: collected editions]. But wherever human beings are born, if they do not follow their parents’ faults and rightly worship God, they shall be honorable and saved. For human seed, from whatever human being it may come [Note: added: “it may be”: collected editions except Arg., Bas.], is God’s creation; it will be evil to those who use it evilly, but it itself will never be evil.

### C. IX. Children are not to be sought from a slave woman

Likewise Ambrose, in the sermon on St. John which begins, “We said last Sunday,” no. LXV [Note: It is not by Ambrose.—Ivo, Decree, part 8, c. 30.].

Someone may say: “I do not have a wife; therefore I have joined a slave woman to myself.” Hear what Scripture says to Abraham [Note: Gen. 21:10]: “Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman.” If, therefore, the son of the slave woman is not an heir, neither is he a son. Why then is such a marriage sought, from which the son received can be neither heir of the succession nor heir of the bloodline? For he cannot share in the inheritance who does not have the privilege of origin. Why, I ask, is such cohabitation sought, from which those born are not sons of marriage but witnesses of adultery? Why are such adulterine offspring received, who bring shame to their father rather than honor? Scripture says [Note: Wis. 3:16]: “The children of adulterers shall come to their consummation, and seed from an unlawful bed shall be exterminated” [Note: The remaining words of Scripture have been restored from Blessed Ambrose; ancient copies have “etc.,” while common editions have “are an abomination to God” [“is”: editions of Arg., Nor., Ven. I–II].].

Therefore, if your woman is endowed with such character as to deserve partnership, let her deserve also the name of wife. Grant your concubine [Col. 1482A] freedom and the name of wife, lest you yourself be an adulterer rather than a husband [Note: added: “more truly”: edition of Ven. I; “true”: the remaining editions except Bas.].

### C. X. Adulteries must not be committed even with the intention of generating children

Likewise Augustine to Claudius, *Against Julian*, chapter 8 [Note: In Augustine, book I, c. 16, certain similar but not identical statements are found.—Ivo, Panormia, book 7, c. 20; Decree, part 8, c. 105.].

Thus adulteries must not be committed even with the intention of generating children who are to be regenerated [Note: “children”: Ivo, Panormia; collected editions], just as thefts must not be committed even with the intention of feeding holy poor people. This must instead be done not by perpetrating thefts, but by making good use of the mammon of unrighteousness.

## Part V

Gratian. Behold: it is in no way lawful for anyone, while his wife lives, to seek children either from a female slave or from any other woman; and even children thus received are judged unworthy of the name of children. Simple fornication also is forbidden in Sacred Scripture.

Accordingly Augustine, in the *Questions on Deuteronomy*, Question XXXVII, on chapter 23 [Note: Ivo, Decree, part 8, cc. 311, 279], says:

### C. XI. Illicit intercourse and every non-lawful use of those organs are understood under the name of adultery

The Lord forbids women to be prostitutes and men to go to prostitutes, whose shamefulness is publicly for sale. But in the Decalogue he does not seem openly to have forbidden this under the name of adultery, because *moechia* ordinarily means only adultery.

The same author, *On Exodus*, Question 71:

§ 1. Every adultery is also called fornication in the Scriptures. But whether every fornication can also be called adultery, I do not at present find an example of this usage in those Scriptures. Yet if every fornication cannot also be called adultery, I do not know whether it can be discovered where the Decalogue [Col. 1482C] forbids that fornication which unmarried men commit with women who have no husbands [Note: “men”: Ivo; collected editions]. But if under the name of theft every unlawful appropriation of another’s property is rightly understood—for he who forbade theft did not permit robbery, but plainly intended that the whole be understood from a part, whatever is unlawfully taken from a neighbor’s possessions [Note: “to understand”: collected editions; “would have intended”: editions of Arg., Bas.]—then certainly under the name of adultery every illicit intercourse and every non-lawful use of those organs must be understood as forbidden.

### C. XII. Unusual pleasure and immodest acts of marriage are called lust and uncleanness

Likewise Jerome, on chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Galatians, on the verse “But the works are manifest.”

In this respect the fornicator is guilty of a greater crime, because he takes away Christ’s members and makes them members of a prostitute; for “the two shall be one flesh” [Note: 1 Cor. 6:16]. The unbeliever, who neither trusts nor believes in Christ, makes his own members members of a prostitute; one who believes and commits fornication makes Christ’s members members of a prostitute [Note: the words “The unbeliever … prostitute” are absent from the collected editions except Lugdd. II–III.]. Conversely, whether an unbeliever in his fornication violates or builds up a temple for an idol, I do not know. For by the vices of lust [Note: “lust”: this word is absent from most ancient copies and the original; it occurs only in the editions of Bas., Par., Lugdd.] demons are worshipped especially [Note: absent from editions of Par., Lugdd.]. This one thing I know: one who commits fornication after coming to faith in Christ violates God’s temple.

The second work of the flesh is called uncleanness, and lust follows as its companion. For just as, in the old Law, Scripture included generally the unspeakable crimes which are done in secret and which it is most shameful even to name—lest both the mouth of the speaker and the ears of the hearers be defiled—saying [Note: Lev. 15:31], “Make the children of Israel modest or reverent [*verecundos vel reverentes*] from every uncleanness” [Note: “fearing”: collected editions except Lugdd. II–III], so in this place it called all other unusual pleasures—including the acts of marriage themselves, if they are not performed modestly [Col. 1483B] and honorably, as though under God’s eyes, so that they serve only the begetting of children—“uncleanness” and “lust” [Note: editions vary: “with modesty and honor”; “modestly and with honor”; “modestly and honorably.”].

### C. XIII. Solomon was drawn into idolatry by immoderate use of women

Likewise Gregory, *Morals*, book XII, chapter 12.

Solomon, indeed, was brought so far by the immoderate use of and constant association with women that he built a temple for idols. He who had formerly constructed a temple for God did not fear, through habitual lust, to be subjected even to unbelief and to construct temples for idols [Note: collected editions read: “and, deprived of perfection, subjected to unbelief.”].

[Col. 1483C]

### C. XIV. The procreation of children is praised in marriage; harlot-like pleasure is condemned even with one’s wife

Likewise Jerome, on chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Ephesians, on the verse “Husbands, love.”

Therefore, as we have said, marital acts for the procreation of children are permitted; but pleasures taken from the embraces of prostitutes are condemned even with one’s wife [Note: added: “are”: same editions].

## Part VI

Gratian. But why such persons are not called sons, or which parent they follow when they are born of a free man and a slave woman, Isidore determines in the *Etymologies*, book IX, chapter 5 [Note: Ivo, Decree, part 8, c. 71]:

### C. XV. Who are freeborn, and what condition they follow

Those are called freeborn [Note: added: “are”: collected editions; Ivo.] who are born from a free marriage. For children born of a free person and a slave woman are of servile condition [Col. 1484A]. For one who is born always takes the inferior part [Note: In Isidore’s manuscripts also, the reading is: “takes the inferior status of the parent.”]. But the children of freeborn concubines are called natural children: nature alone, not the honorability of marriage, generated them. And below:

§ 1. Those who are not from a lawful marriage follow their mother rather than their father.

## QUESTION V

### GRATIAN

## Part I

That chastity cannot be taken away by force is proved by many authorities. For it is a virtue of the mind which does not experience violence. Force is inflicted upon the body, not upon the mind. Therefore, although the body is corrupted by force, if chastity of mind remains unharmed, chastity is nevertheless doubled. Thus Blessed Lucy is reported to have said to Paschasius [Note: In the martyrdom of Blessed Lucy]: “If you cause me to be violated against my will, my chastity will be doubled for my crown.” For the body is not defiled except by the consent of the mind. “If you place incense in my hand and use my hand to offer sacrifices, God sees these things and laughs at them [Note: “does not see, he who also”: collected editions except Bas.]. For God judges from intentions [*sensibus*] and wills” [Note: “consents”: same editions, especially Ven. I–II. In the edition of Arg. the words “For the body … laughs at them” are omitted.].

Accordingly Ambrose writes in book II, *On Virgins* [Note: Ivo, Decree, part 7, c. 137; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 33]:

### C. I. Virginity of mind is better than virginity of flesh

It is more tolerable to have a virgin mind than virgin flesh [Note: edition of Bas. reads: “a virgin mind … virgin flesh.”]. Both are good, if possible; if not possible, let us at least be chaste not for human beings but for God [Note: “chaste”: formerly “chaste [masculine],” as in the collected editions and Ivo; but Blessed Ambrose there introduces Theodora as speaking.].

And below:

§ 1. A virgin can be prostituted, but cannot be made an adulteress [Col. 1484C]. Wherever God’s virgin is, there is God’s temple; brothels do not disgrace chastity, but chastity even removes the disgrace of a place.

### C. II. When the mind is uncorrupted, the flesh is not corrupted

The same author, *To a Fallen Virgin*, chapter 4 [Note: Learned critics deny that this book is by Ambrose.—Ivo, Decree, part 7, c. 138; Peter Lombard, ibid.].

Truly, the flesh cannot be corrupted unless the mind has first been corrupted.

### C. III. Another’s lust defiles no one

Likewise Augustine, *City of God*, book I, chapter 18 [Note: Ivo, Decree, part 7, c. 139].

Is it feared, then, that another’s lust might defile someone? It does not defile [Note: “will defile”: Ivo; collected editions], if it belongs to another; but if it does defile, it will not belong to another. But since chastity is a virtue of the mind, and has courage as its companion—a courage by which it resolves rather to endure any evils than to consent to evil—and since no high-minded and chaste person has in his power [Note: “has”: same editions] what is done to his body, but only what he assents to or refuses in his mind: who, then, in a sound mind would suppose that chastity is lost if another’s lust is exercised and satisfied upon his or her body when seized and overpowered by force? [Col. 1485A]

### C. IV. On the same subject

The same author, in the same place [Note: Ivo, ibid.].

With the resolve of the mind remaining, by which the body too deserved to be sanctified, violence arising from another’s lust does not take holiness away even from the body itself [Note: [Col. 1485] “Even from the body itself it does not take away”: Ivo.—The editions compared with the original.], a holiness preserved by the perseverance of its own continence. But if some woman, corrupt in mind and having violated the resolve which she had vowed to God, proceeds to be defiled by her seducer, shall we still call her holy as she proceeds—holy even in body—although that holiness of mind, through which the body was being sanctified [Note: [Col. 1485] “Is being sanctified”: the same editions.], has been lost and destroyed? Far be this error! Rather, let us be warned by this: bodily holiness is not lost while holiness of mind remains, even when the body is oppressed [Note: [Col. 1485] “Untouched”: the same editions and Ivo; the words marked with asterisks are likewise absent from Ivo.], just as bodily holiness is lost when holiness of mind is violated [Note: [Col. 1485D] “Thus bodily holiness is not lost while holiness of mind remains”: this passage has been enlarged from the original, where it was also somewhat briefer in Ivo.].

The same, ch. 19, §1: They certainly extol Lucretia [Note: [Col. 1485] “Certainly” is absent from Ivo.], a noble matron of ancient Rome, with great praises for chastity. When the son of King Tarquin had violently [Note: [Col. 1485] “Violent”: the editions compared with the original and Ivo.] possessed her body in lust [Note: [Col. 1485] Absent from Ivo.], she disclosed the crime of that most wicked young man to her husband Collatinus and to her kinsman Brutus, men most distinguished and courageous, and bound them to vengeance. Then, distressed and impatient at the foul deed committed against her [Note: [Col. 1485] The editions compared with the original add “of the crime.”], she killed herself. What shall we say [Note: [Col. 1485] “What do we say”: the same editions.]? Is she to be judged an adulteress or chaste [Note: [Col. 1485] “To be called”: the same editions and Ivo.]? Who would think that a judge must labour over this controversy [Note: [Col. 1485] Absent from Ivo and the Basel edition; “will labour”: Ivo and the editions compared with the original.]? Someone has admirably [Note: [Col. 1485] “Indeed”: the same editions, first Paris and Lyons I.] and truthfully declaimed on this matter: “Wonderful to say: there were two, and one committed adultery” [Note: [Col. 1485] “Committed”: Ivo and the editions compared with the original.]. Splendidly [Note: [Col. 1485] “Most splendidly”: the same editions.] and most truthfully said. For, observing in the union of two bodies the utterly polluted desire of one and the most chaste will of the other [Note: [Col. 1485] “Of one”: the same editions.], and attending not to what was done by the joining of limbs [Note: [Col. 1485] “Bodies”: Ivo and the same editions.], but to what was done by the difference of minds [Col. 1486A], he said: “There were two, and one committed adultery” [Note: [Col. 1485] “Committed”: the same editions.].

## Chapter V. The same, in the same book, chapter 27

Let not your life, O faithful of Christ, be burdensome to you because your chastity was made a mockery by enemies [Note: [Col. 1485D] The original reads: “Therefore, not to you, O faithful of Christ”; because it stood at the beginning of the chapter, it has not been changed. The remainder has been restored and enlarged.]. You have [Note: [Col. 1485] “Having”: the editions compared with the original.] great and true consolation if you retain the faithful conscience that you did not consent to the sins of those who were permitted to sin against you [Note: [Col. 1485] “And if it was made a mockery”: the Basel edition; “but if it was made a mockery”: the remaining editions.].

The same, *On Two Souls*, ch. 10, §1: No one sins except by the will.

## Chapter VI. On the same subject. The same, *On Free Choice*, book I, ch. 5

Who would doubt [Note: [Col. 1485] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, ch. 140.] [Note: [Col. 1485] “Would doubt”: the Basel edition; “doubted”: the remaining editions.] that chastity is established in the mind, since it is a virtue? Therefore it cannot itself be taken away even by a violent ravisher.

Likewise Jerome on the Epistle to the Romans, book I, §1 [Note: [Col. 1485D] Nothing of this sort is found in St Jerome. But in Origen, book II on ch. 2 of the Epistle to the Romans, these words are found: “For it cannot happen that, unless someone has first committed adultery in the heart, he can commit adultery in the body.”] [Note: [Col. 1485] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, ch. 141.]: It cannot happen that anyone can commit adultery in body unless he has first committed adultery in heart [Note: [Col. 1485] “That he can commit adultery”: the editions compared with the original, first Lyons editions.].

The same on Luke, book II, §2 [Note: [Col. 1486D] These words occur in St Jerome’s commentaries on Matthew, book II, ch. 11, and have been corrected from there. Nothing by St Jerome on Luke survives.] [Note: [Col. 1485] Compare the final chapter of Chapter XV, Question 1.]: Suppose that during a persecution some virgin is prostituted [Note: [Col. 1485] “Suppose that someone has known a virgin prostituted in some persecution”: the editions compared with the original.]. In the Gospel she is received as a virgin, because she does not sin in will [Note: [Col. 1485] “Has not sinned”: the same editions.]; in the Law she is rejected as though defiled.

The same, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, on ch. 12, §3: Violence does not stain a woman’s body, but will does.

Likewise Augustine, *On Holy Virginity*, ch. 8, §4 [Note: [Col. 1485] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 11.]: Just as no one uses the body immodestly unless wickedness has first been conceived in the spirit, so no one preserves chastity in the body unless chastity has first been implanted in the spirit.

[Col. 1486C]

## Chapter VII. Chastity cannot be violated in the body if the mind is kept inviolate. The same to Victorianus, Epistle CXXII [Note: [Col. 1485] Epistle 111, written A.D. 409, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 10, ch. 52 (59).]

He who is accustomed to be present with his own will certainly be present with those of his who groan to God, and he will either permit nothing to be perpetrated by hostile lust upon their most chaste members [Note: [Col. 1485] “Permits”: the editions compared with the original.], or, if he permits it, since their mind is stained by no disgraceful consent [Note: [Col. 1485] “Stained”: the same editions.], he defends even their flesh from guilt [Note: [Col. 1485] “They defend”: the Argentan and Basel editions.]. Whatever lust does in it, when the sufferer’s will neither commits nor permits it, will be the fault of the doer alone; and all that violence will be reckoned not as the disgrace of corruption [Col. 1487A] but as the wound of suffering. For such is the power of the integrity of chastity in the mind that, if it remains inviolate, chastity cannot be violated even in the body whose members may have been overcome [Note: [Col. 1487] “Were able to be overcome”: the editions compared with the original.].

## Chapter VIII. The flesh does not sin if the soul has been clean from defilement. Likewise Isidore, *Synonyms*, book II, ch. 1 [Note: [Col. 1487] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 7, ch. 142; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 33.]

The body cannot be corrupted unless the mind has first been corrupted. When the soul is clean from defilement [Note: [Col. 1487] The original reads: “Therefore cleanse the mind from thought.”], the flesh does not sin [Note: [Col. 1487] The editions compared with the original add *namque*, “for.”].

## Chapter IX. Chastity of the flesh is not taken away if it is preserved in the mind. Likewise Augustine to Bishop Honoratus, Epistle CLXXX [Note: [Col. 1487] Epistle 228, written A.D. 429, Maurist edition; Anselm, book 10, ch. 51 (58); Polycarp, book 4, title 35.]

Let us fear more that, when the inward sense is corrupted, the chastity of faith may perish than that women may be forcibly violated in the flesh. For chastity is not violated by violence [Col. 1487B] if it is preserved in the mind; indeed, it is not violated even in the flesh when the sufferer’s own will does not disgracefully use the flesh, but endures without consent [Note: [Col. 1487] “Is endured”: the same editions, first Argentan edition.] what another does [Note: [Col. 1487] “Nor is anyone violated in the flesh”: the editions compared with the original.].

## Chapter X. Neither sin nor righteousness is accomplished by an act without will. Likewise John Chrysostom [that is, the author of the *Imperfect Work*, an apocryphal work] on Matthew, Homily XXXII, on ch. 19 [Note: [Col. 1487] “Apocryphal work.”]

For just as sin does not make an act without will, so righteousness is not brought to completion by an act unless will too is present. Many indeed pursue chastity in body, yet commit adultery in will [Note: [Col. 1487] “Yet”: Lyons II and III; “indeed”: the remaining editions.]. For unless fornication were completed by will alone, the Lord would never say [Note: [Col. 1487] Matthew, ch. 5, v. 28.] [Col. 1487C]: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” [Note: [Col. 1487] The editions compared with the original add: “when the Lord says.”]. Therefore the will frequently sins without the act. That [Note: [Col. 1487] The editions compared with the original add “therefore.”] is glorious continence: not that which the necessity of an enfeebled body cannot transgress [Note: [Col. 1487] “Of weakness”: the original.], but that which the will of a holy purpose embraces.

## Chapter XI. Virginity of the flesh is not preserved when the mind is corrupt. Likewise Jerome, in the letter to Eustochium, *On the Guardianship of Virginity* [Note: [Col. 1487] This chapter has in many places been restored from old copies and the original.]

### Part II

If Paul the Apostle, a vessel of election [Note: [Col. 1487] Compare Acts, ch. 9.], and set apart [Note: [Col. 1487] “Prepared”: the editions compared with the original.] for the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1487] “In the Gospel”: the same editions, first Lyons II and III.] of Christ, because of the stings of the flesh and incentives to vices, restrains his body and makes it subject to servitude [Note: [Col. 1487] 1 Corinthians, ch. 9, v. 19.], lest, after preaching to others, he himself be found reprobate, and nevertheless sees [Note: [Col. 1487] “Saw”: the editions compared with the original.] another law in his members [Note: [Col. 1487] Romans, ch. 7, v. 23.], resisting the law of his mind and is *led captive* into the law of sin [Note: [Col. 1487] “Captivating”: the Vulgate at the cited place and the editions compared with the original; the marked word is *duci*, “to be led.”]; if, after nakedness, fasts, hunger [Note: [Col. 1487] “Hungers”: the editions compared with the original, first Lyons II and III.], prisons, scourgings, and punishments, returning into *himself* [Note: [Col. 1487] The marked word is *ipsum*, “himself.”], he cries [Note: [Col. 1487] 2 Corinthians, ch. 11, v. 27; Romans, ch. 7, v. 24.]: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from this body of death?”—do you think that you ought to be secure [Note: [Col. 1487] “Secure,” masculine: the editions compared with the original, first Lyons I.]? Take care, I beg you, lest God should ever say *of you* [Note: [Col. 1487] “And concerning you”: the editions compared with the original.] [Note: [Col. 1487] Amos, ch. 5, v. 2.]: “The virgin Israel has fallen, and there is no one to raise her up” [Note: [Col. 1487] Absent from Böhm.].

I shall speak boldly [Note: [Col. 1487] “Boldly”: the editions compared with the original, first Lyons II and III; “I shall say”: the editions compared with the original.]: although God can do all things, he cannot raise up a virgin after her fall. He is indeed able to free her from punishment, but he does not wish [Note: [Col. 1487] “He is able”: the same editions.] to crown her once corrupted.

§1. Let us fear that prophecy, lest it too be fulfilled in us [Col. 1488B; Note: [Col. 1487] Amos, ch. 8, v. 13.]: “Good virgins shall fail” [Note: [Col. 1487] “And good virgins”: the editions compared with the original.]. Observe what it says: “Good virgins shall fail” [Note: [Col. 1487] “And good virgins”: the same editions; the words are absent from the same editions, first Basel.], because there are also bad virgins. “Whoever,” he says [Note: [Col. 1487] Matthew, ch. 5, v. 28.], “looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” Therefore virginity also perishes in the mind. These are bad virgins: virgins in flesh, not in spirit; foolish virgins [Note: [Col. 1487] Compare Matthew, ch. 25.], who, having no oil, are shut out by the bridegroom.

But if even those who are virgins are not saved by bodily virginity because of other faults, what will become of those who have prostituted Christ’s members and turned the temple of the Holy Spirit into a brothel? Immediately she shall hear [Note: [Col. 1487] “Hear also”: the first Lyons editions; “shall hear”: the remaining editions; Böhm adds, “Say to her, the prophet”; Isaiah, ch. 47, vv. 1 ff.]: “Come down; sit on the ground, virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground. There is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans [Note: [Col. 1487] “Seat”: the Vulgate.]. You shall no longer be called soft and delicate. Take a millstone and grind flour [Note: [Col. 1487] “And grind”: the same edition.], uncover your veil, bare your legs [Note: [Col. 1487] The editions compared with the original add “your”], cross the rivers. Your shame shall be revealed; your reproaches shall appear.”

And this after the bridal chambers [Note: [Col. 1487] “Bridal chambers”: the same editions.] of the Son of God, after the kisses of a brother and a bridegroom; she of whom prophetic speech once sang [Note: [Col. 1487] Psalm 44, v. 10.]: “The queen stood at your right hand in a golden garment, surrounded with variety.” She shall be stripped, and her hind parts [Note: [Col. 1487] “Her back”: the editions compared with the original.] shall be set before her face [Note: [Col. 1487] “Before her face”: the Basel edition; “in her face”: the remaining editions; “hers”: the editions compared with the original.]. She shall sit by the waters of desolation and, placing a vessel, shall spread her legs for every passer-by [Note: [Col. 1487] Ezekiel, ch. 16, v. 15.], and shall be defiled even to the crown of her head.

It would indeed have been better [Note: [Col. 1487] The editions compared with the original add “indeed.”] to undergo the marriage of human beings and to walk on level ground [Col. 1489A; Note: [Col. 1489] The same editions add “and to walk.”] than, striving toward higher things, to fall into the depth of hell. Let not [Note: [Col. 1489] “Not”: the same editions.] faithful Zion become a harlot-city [Note: [Col. 1489] “Daughter”: the editions compared with the original; Isaiah, ch. 1, v. 21.]; let not demons dance there after the lodging-place of the Trinity, nor sirens [Note: [Col. 1489] *Sirenae*, “sirens”: goddesses.] nest there, nor hedgehogs [Note: [Col. 1489] Isaiah, ch. 34, v. 11.].

## Chapter XII. Chastity is sometimes lost while the body remains untouched. Likewise Augustine, Sermon III on the Common Life of Clerics, and Epistle CIX to Nuns [Note: [Col. 1489] Epistle 111, written A.D. 423, Maurist edition.]

### Part III

A woman is desired, and desires, not only by touch [Note: [Col. 1489] “By affection and touch, but also by sight”: the editions compared with the original.] but also by affection and sight [Note: [Col. 1489] “The lust of women”: the same editions.]. Do not say that you have chaste minds if you have unchaste eyes, because an unchaste eye is the messenger of an unchaste heart. When unchaste hearts announce themselves to one another by their mutual gaze, even while the tongue is silent, and delight in one another’s ardour according to the lust of the flesh, chastity itself flees from their conduct, although their bodies remain untouched by impure violation.

## Chapter XIII. Adultery is committed when even an unmarried woman is shamefully desired. Likewise Gregory, *Morals*, book XXI, ch. 9

“Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” [Note: [Col. 1489] Matthew, ch. 5, v. 28.]. Since *moechus* is the Greek term for “adulterer,” and since the prohibition concerns seeing not another’s wife but a woman, Truth plainly shows that adultery is committed even by sight alone when even an unmarried woman is shamefully desired. Yet the degree of the guilt of lust is often distinguished by the position [Note: [Col. 1489] The editions compared with the original add “and time.”] or rank [Note: [Col. 1489] “Or from”: the editions compared with the original.] of those who desire: that is, *scilicet*, “namely,” diligent lust pollutes this man in sacred orders, just as [Note: [Col. 1489] “As”: the same editions, for *scilicet*.] the guilt of adultery pollutes that man; though in persons not dissimilar, the same liability of lust is distinguished [Note: [Col. 1489] “Thus”: the same editions, for “just as.”].

### Part IV. Gratian

Although women forcibly overpowered have not lost chastity, they nevertheless ought not to dare compare themselves with uncontaminated virgins.

Therefore Pope Leo, Epistle LXXXV, alternatively LXXXVII, to the Bishops of Africa, ch. 5 [Note: [Col. 1489] Epistle 12, written A.D. 446, Ballerini edition; Polycarp, book 4, title 34.]

## Chapter XIV. Those who are violated ought not dare compare themselves with uncontaminated virgins

Those handmaids of God who lost the integrity of their modesty through barbarian violence will be more praiseworthy in their humility and modesty [Note: [Col. 1489] “Their”: absent from the Spanish Collection.] if they do not dare compare themselves with uncontaminated virgins. Although every sin arises from will, and the mind, unwilling, may remain unstained by corruption of the flesh, it will nevertheless be less harmful to them [Note: [Col. 1489] “This will harm them”: Ballerini; “this will harm those women”: the editions compared with the Spanish Collection.] if they grieve that they have lost even in body what they could not lose in mind.

Gratian. Since, therefore, it cannot be proved that she who has suffered violence lost chastity, she is in no way convicted of having incurred the crime of fornication or adultery. For, as Augustine says in *On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 4 [Note: [Col. 1489] The original reads: “The violation of this fidelity is called adultery when …”; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, ch. 22; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 102.]: Adultery is committed when, either at the prompting of one’s own lust or with another’s consent, one lies with another man or woman contrary to the marriage covenant; and thus faith is broken—a great good of the mind even in bodily and lowly matters—and therefore it is certain that it ought to be set before bodily safety, in which this life itself is contained [Note: [Col. 1489D] In St Augustine the text reads: “and therefore it is certain that it ought to be set before bodily safety also, in which this life is contained.” Ivo reads the same in the *Decretum* and *Panormia*, except that in this passage the reading is “it ought not to be set before” [*non debet praeponi*]. But, because of the gloss, and because the sense is the same, nothing has been changed.].

## Chapter XV. He commits adultery who has intercourse with someone outside the marriage covenant. Likewise Isidore on Exodus, ch. 29 [Note: [Col. 1489] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, ch. 23; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 107; compare Exodus, ch. 20, v. 14.]

“You shall not commit adultery”: that is, no one is to join himself to other women outside the covenant of his own marriage [Note: [Col. 1489] “Nor”: the Argentan and Basel editions; “his own”: absent from the original and Ivo.] in order to satisfy lust [Note: [Col. 1489] “Be joined”: the editions compared with the original.]. For *specifically* [Note: [Col. 1489] Ivo, *Panormia*, reads “spiritually.”], he commits adultery who goes to another woman besides his own.

## Chapter XVI. He who knows another woman while his own wife lives commits adultery. Likewise Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book II, ch. 13 [Note: [Col. 1489] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 242.]

I think that no Christian disputes that the man [Note: [Col. 1489] Absent from Ivo and the Argentan and Basel editions.] is an adulterer who, while his own wife is either long ill, long absent, or desirous of living continently [Note: [Col. 1489] “With his wife left behind”: the same editions.], has intercourse with another woman.

### Part V. Gratian

Since none of these circumstances is found in her—for she neither joined another at the prompting of her own lust, nor with another’s consent, nor while her husband was ill, absent, or desirous of living continently, but, overpowered by another’s lust, endured force—it is clear that she can be called neither adulteress nor fornicator. Therefore she cannot validly be dismissed on any pretext.

For when the Jews asked Christ [Note: [Col. 1489] Matthew, ch. 19, vv. 2 ff.] whether it was lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any cause whatever, he answered them: “Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female? Therefore what God has joined, let no human being separate.” He then concluded his discourse by saying that no one could dismiss his wife except for the cause of fornication. Hence the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Corinthians [Note: [Col. 1491] 1 Corinthians, ch. 7, v. 10.]: “To those joined in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife not depart from her husband.” From this it is understood that, whatever sort of persons husband and wife may be, once they have joined themselves to one another in marital affection, they cannot thereafter depart from each other.

Therefore Ambrose writes in the *Hexaemeron*, under the heading of the fourth day [Note: [Col. 1491] Book 5, ch. 7; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, ch. 103; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 232.]:

## Chapter XVII. Whatever sort of husband he may be, once he has pleased her, he is not to be dismissed

A husband is dreadful and uncultivated [Note: [Col. 1491D] In St Ambrose the text reads: “But he is rough and uncultivated; he has pleased you once,” etc. Before this chapter is the chapter “Adam through Eve,” below, 33, Question 5.] [Note: [Col. 1491] “A husband who”: Ivo, *Panormia*, and the editions compared with the original.]: he has pleased you once. Is a husband to be chosen repeatedly [Note: [Col. 1491] “Another”: Ivo and the same editions.]? An ox seeks its mate, and a horse loves its mate [Note: [Col. 1491] Ivo, *Panormia*: “Its mate an ox”; *Decretum*: “Its mate, both ox and horse.”]; if another is substituted, the mate does not know how to draw the yoke with another’s mate and does not think itself whole. Do you repudiate your yokefellow [Note: [Col. 1491] “Your spouse”: Ivo, *Panormia*, and the editions compared with the original.] and think that he must often be changed [Note: [Col. 1491] The Basel edition adds “and you change”; the remaining editions, with Ivo, *Panormia*, read “change” as an imperative.]? If he fails for one day, you bring in a rival [Note: [Col. 1491] “Bring in”: the editions compared with the original and Ivo, *Panormia*.], and immediately, without knowing the cause, you avenge, as though known [Note: [Col. 1491] “Known”: Ivo, *Decretum*.], an injury to modesty [Note: [Col. 1491] “May avenge”: Lyons II and III.]?

## Chapter XVIII. The same is to be understood concerning the wife. Likewise Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, book I, ch. 32 [Note: [Col. 1491] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, ch. 104; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 238; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 34.]

If someone has a wife [Note: [Col. 1491] “Everyone has [a wife], whether barren, whether …”: the original.] who is barren, deformed in body, weak in limbs, blind, deaf, lame, or afflicted by any other condition—whether worn away by illnesses, pains [Note: [Col. 1491] “Labours and pains”: the editions compared with the original; “pains and labours”: Ivo.], and infirmities—or by anything else that can be imagined as exceedingly horrible, he should endure it, except in the case of fornication [Note: [Col. 1491] “For the cause of fornication”: Ivo, *Panormia*, and the editions compared with the original.], for the sake of faithfulness and fellowship [Col. 1491C].

## Chapter XIX. A husband may not dismiss his wife except for the cause of fornication. Likewise Jerome to Oceanus, on the death of Fabiola [Note: [Col. 1491] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, ch. 3; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 240; Peter Lombard, same distinction, 35.]

The Lord commanded [Note: [Col. 1491] “Commands”: Lyons II.] that a wife ought not to be dismissed except for the cause of fornication and that, if she has been dismissed, she must remain unmarried. Whatever is commanded to men [Note: [Col. 1491] “Prescribed”: the editions compared with the original and Ivo.] applies correspondingly [Note: [Col. 1491] “To”: the editions compared with the original.] to women. For an adulterous wife is not to be dismissed while an adulterous husband is retained [Note: [Col. 1491] “Held”: the original and Ivo; the editions compared with the original add “is.”].

[Col. 1492A]

## Chapter XX. On the same subject. The same, in the same place [Note: [Col. 1491] Ivo, same place.]

Among us, what is not lawful for women is equally not lawful for men, and the same bondage is assessed under equal conditions.

## Chapter XXI. He who dismisses his wife outside the cause of fornication is to be deprived of communion. Likewise from the Twelfth Council of Toledo, ch. 8 [Note: [Col. 1491] Held A.D. 681; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, ch. 1; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 329.]

### Part VI

It is the Lord’s command that a husband must not dismiss his wife except for the cause of fornication. Therefore, whoever dismisses his wife for any reason apart from the guilt of the aforesaid crime [Note: [Col. 1491] “Outside”: Ivo, *Panormia*, and the editions compared with the original, first Argentan edition.], because he has resolved to separate what God has joined [Note: [Col. 1491] “The human being”: the Argentan and Basel editions; compare Matthew, ch. 19, v. 6.], shall be deprived of ecclesiastical communion and remain excluded from the assembly of all Christians until he sincerely embraces and cherishes the fellowship of his abandoned wife [Note: [Col. 1491] The Spanish Collection expands: “and returns to the fellowship of the abandoned wife and receives again as a lawful wife the part of his body.”].

Therefore [Note: [Col. 1491] “Thus”: Ivo; “yet they”: the Spanish Collection.] those who, after being admonished once, twice, and three times by the priest to amend themselves [Note: [Col. 1491] “May be corrected”: the editions compared with the original.], refuse to return to the marital bed [Note: [Col. 1491] “Fellowship”: the same editions; Ivo reads “to the fellowship of the bed of their own wives, to which they are unwilling to return”; the Spanish Collection, “to the fellowship of their own wives, to which they are unwilling to return.”] of their wives shall, by their own deserts, separate themselves also from the office of palatine rank; furthermore, they shall lose the testimony of noble rank for as long as they remain guilty, because they have delivered their own flesh to the knife of discord.

## Chapter XXII. On the same subject. Pope Nicholas, *Responses to the Questions of the Bulgarians*, ch. 96 [Note: [Col. 1491] Written A.D. 866; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 228.]

Whatever your wife may think *or do* against you, or even if she accuses you, she is not—except for the cause of fornication—to be rejected or held in utter hatred; she is to be loved as the Church is to be loved by Christ, as the Apostle commands [Note: [Col. 1492D] The words “which is … to be loved” through the end were added from the Responses themselves.] [Note: [Col. 1491] Ephesians, ch. 5, v. 25.].

### Part VII. Gratian

But the question is asked: since the condition of both is equal, why are husbands who communicate with adulterous wives not admitted [Col. 1492C], whereas, conversely, wives seem to remain in the company of adulterous husbands?

Pope Innocent writes as follows on these matters, Epistle III to Bishop Exsuperius, ch. 4 [Note: [Col. 1491] Written A.D. 405; *Register*, book 2, ch. 139; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 214; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 35.]:

## Chapter XXIII. Adultery is punished on an equal principle in both sexes

The Christian religion condemns adultery on an equal principle in both sexes. But women do not easily accuse their husbands of adultery, and hidden sins have no punishment. Men, however, have been accustomed more freely to report adulterous wives to priests; and therefore communion is denied to women when their crime is exposed. But when men’s offence remains hidden, scarcely anyone is excluded merely on suspicions [Note: [Col. 1493] “He refrains”: the editions compared with the original.]; though he too will certainly be removed if his disgrace is discovered. Therefore, although the case is equal, sometimes, when proof is lacking, the ground for punishment is at rest [Note: [Col. 1493] “For”: the same editions.].

# QUESTION VI

## GRATIAN

Behold: this woman cannot be dismissed, since she is found innocent of fornication. But suppose that she is an adulteress. The question is whether an adulterer may dismiss her for the cause of fornication. For it does not seem that one infected with an equal crime can punish another for the same crime. Thus, when the Jews accused the adulteress, they received from the Lord a judgment of equity [Note: [Col. 1493] John, ch. 8, v. 7.]: “Whoever among you is without sin, let him first cast a stone at her.” Hence too the Gospel commands [Note: [Col. 1493] Luke, ch. 6, v. 42.]: “Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will draw the speck out of your brother’s eye.”

Augustine likewise writes in book I of *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, ch. 28 [Note: [Col. 1493] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, ch. 31; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 250; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 35.]:

## Chapter I. One who fornicates cannot dismiss his wife for the cause of fornication

Nothing is more unjust [Note: [Col. 1493] “It is”: the editions compared with the original.] than to dismiss one’s wife for the cause of fornication if one is oneself convicted of fornicating. For this saying applies [Note: [Col. 1493] Romans, ch. 2, v. 1.]: “In judging another, you condemn yourself; for you do the same things that you judge” [Note: [Col. 1493] The editions compared with the original add “you.”]. Therefore, whoever wishes to cast off his wife for the cause of fornication [Note: [Col. 1493] The editions compared with the original add “his own wife.”] ought first to have been cleansed from fornication [Note: [Col. 1493] The editions compared with the original and Ivo, *Panormia*, add “and free from it.”]. The same, I would say, applies likewise to a woman [Note: [Col. 1493] “Is”: the Argentan edition; absent from the Argentan, Nuremberg, Venetian I and II, and Paris editions.].

## Chapter II. Each person should keep himself for his wife as he wishes to find her for himself. The same, *On the Words of the Lord*, tract or sermon XLVI [Note: [Col. 1493] Sermon 132, Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 45.]

If you are going to take wives, keep yourselves for your wives. As you wish to find them, so they themselves ought to find you [Note: [Col. 1493] The original and Ivo read: “As you wish them to come to you, so they themselves ought to find you.”]. What young man [Note: [Col. 1493] “Living”: the editions compared with the original.] does not wish to marry a chaste wife? If he is going to receive a virgin, who does not desire her untouched? You seek one untouched? Be untouched yourself; you seek one pure? Do not be impure [Note: [Col. 1493] “Be pure”: the same editions.]. She cannot be so if you cannot be so.

[Col. 1494A]

## Chapter III. One who refuses to be judged should not seek judgment upon another. The same, in the letter to Pascentius, an Arian count, Epistle CLXXIV [Note: [Col. 1493] An epistle of uncertain date, Epistle 238 in the Maurist edition; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, ch. 392.]

It is unjust that anyone [Note: [Col. 1493] “Anyone”: Lyons II and III.] should wish to judge another and refuse to be judged concerning himself.

## Chapter IV. Husbands ought to be punished more severely for adultery than women. The same, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book II, ch. 8 [Note: [Col. 1493] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, ch. 36; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 242; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 35.]

Husbands are indignant if they hear that adulterous men suffer punishments like those of adulterous women, although men ought to be punished so much more severely as it belongs more to them both to conquer by virtue and to govern women by example.

[Col. 1494B]

## Chapter V. Just as a husband is the head of a wife, so by committing adultery he sins more gravely than the wife. The same, *On the Ten Strings*, ch. 3 [Note: [Col. 1493] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 263.]

“You shall not commit adultery” [Note: [Col. 1493] Exodus, ch. 20, v. 14.]: that is, you shall not go to any other woman besides your wife. Yet do you demand this of your wife and refuse to give it to your wife? And when you ought to lead your wife in virtue—because chastity is a virtue—do you fall under one onset of lust? Do you want your wife to be victorious while you lie defeated [Note: [Col. 1493] “And you defeated”: Ivo and the editions compared with the original.]? And though you are the head of your wife [Note: [Col. 1493] “Your”: the editions compared with the original.], shall she whose head you are go before you to God [Note: [Col. 1493] “Goes before”: Ivo and the same editions.]? Do you wish your household to hang head downward? For the husband is the head of the wife. But where a wife lives better than her husband, the household hangs head downward. If the husband is the head, the husband ought to live better than the wife [Note: [Col. 1493] The editions compared with the original add “than the wife.”] and precede his wife in all good works, so that she may imitate her husband and follow her head [Note: [Col. 1493] These words are absent from Ivo.].

Gratian. These authorities show that an adulterer cannot dismiss an adulteress.

# QUESTION VII

## GRATIAN

### Part I

The question now is whether a man who has dismissed his wife for the cause of fornication may, while she is alive, take another. Augustine testifies that this cannot be done in *On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 7, saying [Note: [Col. 1493] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, ch. 6; *Decretum*, part 8, chs. 9 and 235.]:

## Chapter I. The bond of marriage cannot be dissolved by fornication

When divorce intervenes, that marital covenant is not abolished [Note: [Col. 1493] “That”: absent from Ivo.], so that the spouses remain married to one another even when, after their repudiation, they commit adultery with those to whom they have been joined [Col. 1495A; Note: [Col. 1495] “Even”: the editions compared with the original; “adultery is committed”: the same editions and Ivo, *Panormia*.].

## Chapter II. A marriage once shown to have been contracted is dissolved on no ground. The same, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book II, chs. 4–5 [Note: [Col. 1495] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, ch. 5; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 235.]

A spouse may lawfully be dismissed for the cause of fornication [Note: [Col. 1495] “Wife”: the editions compared with the original and Ivo, *Panormia*.], but the prior bond remains. Therefore anyone [Note: [Col. 1495] “Whoever”: the editions compared with the original.] who marries a dismissed woman, even for the cause of fornication, becomes guilty of adultery. For just as [Note: [Col. 1495] “However”: the editions compared with the original and Ivo, *Panormia*.] a person excommunicated because guilty of a crime does not lack the sacrament of regeneration, even if never reconciled to God, so a wife may be dismissed for the cause of fornication while the bond of the marital covenant remains in her, nor will she lack that bond even if she is never reconciled to her husband [Col. 1495B; Note: [Col. 1495] Ivo reads: “while the bond remains, she does not lack the sacrament of marriage, even if …”]. But she will lack it if her husband has died.

[Note: [Col. 1495C] This whole passage has been restored from the original: “Every person excommunicated is guilty of a crime; thus a woman separated from her husband will never lack the sacrament of marriage, even if she is not reconciled to her husband. But she will lack it if he has died,” etc. Many other passages have likewise been corrected from the original and old copies.]

An excommunicated person guilty of a crime [Note: [Col. 1495] “A person is excommunicated who is guilty”: Ivo; Panormia adds “is”; “excommunicated persons”: the Nuremberg and Venetian I editions; “of excommunication”: the remaining editions.] will never lack the sacrament of regeneration, even unreconciled [Note: [Col. 1495] The editions compared with the original read “even if he has not been reconciled.”], because God never dies [Note: [Col. 1495] The Argentan and Basel editions and Ivo, *Panormia*, add: “to whom he is joined in baptism.”].

## Chapter III. Whether husband departs from wife or wife from husband for the cause of fornication, each is forbidden to have another. The same, on Paul’s Epistle to the Corinthians [Note: [Col. 1495D] This occurs in Bede on 1 Corinthians 7, from book I, ch. 26, of St Augustine’s *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*. The *Register*, book 2, ch. 105; Burchard, book 9, ch. 71; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, ch. 2; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 208—all from Augustine’s sayings. The *Register* adds “from *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*”; the *Panormia* reads “on Paul’s Epistle to the Corinthians.” Polycarp, book 6, title 4; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 35.]

The Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1495] 1 Cor. ch. 7, v. 10.]: [Note: [Col. 1495D] *The Apostle says:* In Blessed Augustine, Book I of *On the Sermon on the Mount*, ch. 26, one reads [Col. 1496C]: “But let us consult the Apostle, lest we say anything rashly. ‘To those who are in marriage,’ he says, ‘I command,’ etc.” But in Bede, on 1 Corinthians 7: “To those who are in marriage [Col. 1496D] the Lord commanded through the Apostle: ‘Let the wife,’ etc.” Moreover, many readings in this and the following chapters—“It can happen,” “and the Lord,” and others—have been corrected from the cited passages of the same Blessed Augustine and Bede.] “To those who are in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife not separate from her husband [Note: [Col. 1495] add: *her own*: the collected editions.]; but if she does separate, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband.” For it may happen that she separates for the cause which [Note: [Col. 1495] *which*: editions of Arg. and Bas.] the Lord permitted. Or [Note: [Col. 1495] *and*: Arg. ed.—*but*: the remaining editions—Ivo, *Panormia*], if it is lawful for a woman to dismiss her husband *even* apart from [Note: [Col. 1495] *on account of*: Burchard, Ivo, *Decretum*—the collected editions—*the cause of fornication*: Ivo, *Panormia*] the cause [Col. 1495C] of fornication, *and it is not lawful for a man*, [Note: [Col. 1495] *and … man* are absent from the cited collections.] what shall we answer concerning what he said later: “And let not a husband dismiss his wife” [Note: [Col. 1495] add: *his own*: the collected editions.]? Why does he not add [Note: [Col. 1495] *added*: Lugd. editions II and III—the cited collections.], “except for the cause [Col. 1496A] of fornication,” which the Lord permits? Unless it is because he wishes the same pattern to be understood: that, if he dismisses her—which is permitted on account of fornication—he should remain without a wife, or be reconciled to his wife? And a little later:

§ 1. The Lord permitted a wife to be dismissed on account of fornication [Note: [Col. 1495] *to dismiss*: the collected editions.]. But because he permitted it, he did not command it.

### C. IV. The same, *On the Sermon on the Mount*, Book I, ch. 25. [Note: [Col. 1495] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 237.]

It can happen [Note: [Col. 1495] *could happen … dismissed*: Bas. ed.] that a husband dismisses his wife for the cause of fornication, which the Lord wished to be excepted. But if she is not permitted to marry another man while the husband [Note: [Col. 1495] add: *her own*: the collected editions.] from whom she departed is alive, nor is he permitted to take another wife while the wife [Note: [Col. 1495] add: *his own*: same editions.] whom he dismissed is alive, then still less is it lawful for them to commit unlawful fornications with anyone whatsoever.

[Col. 1496B] ### C. V. A man dismissed by his wife, or a woman dismissed by her husband, is to be brought to penance unless they choose either to live continently or to be reconciled to one another. The same, from the Council of Milevis, ch. 17. [Note: [Col. 1495] Rather, from the Council of Carthage held in A.D. 407 (Dionysian Code, ch. 102).—Regino, Book 2, ch. 104; Burchard, Book 9, ch. 64; Anselm, Book 10, ch. 15 (17); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 200; *Polycarpus*, Book 6, title 4.]

It was decreed that, according to evangelical and apostolic discipline, neither a man dismissed by his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband should be joined to another; rather, they should remain thus or be reconciled to one another. If they scorn this, they are to be brought to penance.

### C. VI. He who presumes to marry a woman dismissed by her husband commits adultery. The same, Augustine, Book I, *On the Sermon on the Mount*, ch. 25. [Note: [Col. 1495] Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 7, ch. 4; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 237; Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 35.]

In order to reinforce the point that a wife should not readily be dismissed, the Lord excepted only the cause of fornication; all other [Note: [Col. 1495] *universal*: Ivo, *Decretum*—*innumerable*: *Panormia*—*universal and innumerable*: collected editions, first Bas. ed.] troubles, should any [Col. 1496C] perhaps [Note: [Col. 1495] absent from Ivo.] arise, he commands to be borne bravely for the fidelity of marriage and for [Note: [Col. 1495] *and for*: Ivo, *Decretum*—the collected editions.] chastity. And he called adulterous even the man who marries her who has been released by her husband.

[Col. 1497A] ### C. VII. A woman who marries another while her husband is alive is proved to be an adulteress. The same, Jerome to the presbyter Amandus. [Note: [Col. 1497] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 239, down to “is not lawful”; *Polycarpus*, Book 6, title 4.] [Note: [Col. 1497C] *Amandus:* Thus in most old copies. For the common editions read *Damasus* [Note: [Col. 1497] thus Nor. and Lugd. editions—*Damasium*: Bas. ed.—*Damascus*: remaining editions.]. But some things in this chapter have been corrected from the original itself, where the gloss did not obstruct this [Col. 1497D] correction.]

The Apostle, cutting off every pretext [Note: [Col. 1497] *accusations*: Arg. ed.], has most plainly determined that a woman is an adulteress if, while her husband is alive, she marries another. Do not bring before me the violence of an abductor, a mother’s solicitation [Note: [Col. 1497] *persuasion*: original text.], a father’s authority, a crowd of relatives, the snares of slaves [Note: [Col. 1497] add: *and injuries from parents*: Nor. and Par. editions—*the snares, injuries from parents*: Arg., Ven. I and II—*the snares, affronts and injuries from parents*: Lugd. I—*the snares, affronts from parents, injuries*: Bas., Lugd. II and III.], contempt, or losses to the household estate. So long as her husband lives, even if he is an adulterer, even if a sodomite, even if covered with every disgrace, and though his wife has left him because of these crimes, he is accounted her husband [Note: [Col. 1497] *was accounted*: Ivo—*yet he is to be accounted her husband, namely of her to whom*: collected editions.], and she is not permitted to take another husband. Nor does the Apostle decree these things on his own authority [Note: [Col. 1497] *decreed*: Arg. and Bas. editions.], but, with Christ speaking in him, he followed Christ’s words [Col. 1497B], who says in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1497] cf. Matt. ch. 19, v. 9.]: “Whoever dismisses [Note: [Col. 1497] *dismisses*: collected editions.] his wife, except for the cause of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever receives the dismissed woman is an adulterer.” Hence the Apostles too, understanding the heavy burden of marriage [Note: [Col. 1497] ibid., vv. 10, 12.], say: “If it is so, it is not expedient for a man to take a wife.” To them [Note: [Col. 1497] *that*: collected editions.] the Lord says: “He who is able,” [Note: [Col. 1497] absent from the collected editions, first Bas., Lugd. II and III.] “to receive this, let him receive it” [Note: [Col. 1497] *to receive this*: same editions.]; and immediately, by the example of the three kinds of eunuchs, he adds the blessedness of virginity, which is held by no law of the flesh [Note: [Col. 1497D] After these words Jerome continues with ch. *Non satis*, 34, question 1 and 2.] [Note: [Col. 1497] *restrained*: collected editions.].

### C. VIII. A faithful woman who dismisses an adulterous husband may not marry another. The same, from the Council of Elvira, ch. 9. [Note: [Col. 1497] Held no later than A.D. 310.—Regino, Book 2, ch. 103; Burchard, Book 9, ch. 63; Anselm, Book 11, ch. 97; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 199.]

A believing woman who has left her adulterous but believing husband and has taken another [Note: [Col. 1497] add: *husband*: Par. and Lugd. editions—*adulterous [husband]*: cited collections.] husband [Note: [Col. 1497] *takes*: same editions—Bas. ed.—Spanish collection.] is to be forbidden to take one. But if [Note: [Col. 1497] absent from the Spanish collection.] she has taken one, she is not to receive communion until [Col. 1497C] the man whom she left [Note: [Col. 1497] *has left*: collected editions.] has departed this world, unless [Note: [Col. 1497] add: *perhaps*: Spanish collection—*by chance*: cited collections—the collected editions.] the necessity of illness compels it to be given.

[Col. 1498A] ### C. IX. One joined in many marriages is to be compelled to penance. The same, from the Council of Pope Martin—that is, from Martin of Braga, ch. 80. [Note: [Col. 1497] Ch. 3, Council of Neocaesarea, in Martin of Braga’s translation.—Burchard, Book 9, ch. 20; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chs. 158 and 332.]

If anyone has been joined in many marriages, let him do penance. But the conduct and faith of the penitent [Note: [Col. 1497] *of the one doing penance*: Ivo, ch. 332.] should shorten the time [Note: [Col. 1497D] *Should shorten the time:* In the original and in Ivo it reads: *shortens the time* [Note: [Col. 1497] thus the Spanish collection.]. In Burchard, corruptly: *compendit*. And in the Council of Neocaesarea, [Col. 1498C] ch. 3, above, 31, question 1, from which this was taken, it reads: *abbreviates*. But it has not been changed because of the gloss.].

### C. X. One who dismisses his wife because of fornication and marries another is shown to commit adultery. The same, Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, Book I, ch. 9. [Note: [Col. 1497] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 255.]

Just as it cannot rightly be said, “Therefore, if a man does not know [Note: [Col. 1497] *may not know*: Bas. ed.], he does not sin”—for there are sins even of those who are ignorant, though less grave than those of persons who know—so neither can it rightly be said: “Therefore, if a husband dismisses his wife because of fornication [Col. 1498B] and marries another, he does not commit adultery.” For even those commit adultery who marry other women after leaving their former wives because of fornication; but theirs is certainly a lesser adultery than that of those who dismiss their wives not because of fornication *and marry other women*.

## Part II. Gratian

There are degrees in fornication. Thus, just as an adulterer sins more gravely than a fornicator, so one who, without dismissing his own wife, marries another sins more gravely than one who, dismissing his own wife, has intercourse with another woman. Likewise, one who has a wife and approaches his neighbour’s wife sins more gravely than one who has no wife and violates another’s bed, or than a married man who approaches an unmarried woman. But incestuous persons surpass all these; and those who sin against nature surpass them.

[Col. 1498C] Hence Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages* [Note: [Col. 1498D] In many old copies this chapter is joined to the preceding one, and it contains words of Blessed Augustine gathered from various places, principally from *On the Good of Marriage*, chs. 8, 9, and 11; Ivo and the Master also cite that book.] [Note: [Col. 1497] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 9, ch. 110, comes closer to Augustine’s actual words; Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 38.]:

### C. XI. The evil of adultery surpasses fornication, but is surpassed by incest.

It is worse to lie with one’s mother than with another man’s wife. But worst of all these is what is done against nature: for example, if a man wishes [Note: [Col. 1497] *wishes*: Bas. ed.] to use a woman’s member, not granted for this purpose. For natural intercourse, if it exceeds measure, is [Col. 1499A] a venial sin [Note: [Col. 1499] add: *sin*: collected editions.] indeed with a wife, but damnable with a prostitute. But the act [Note: [Col. 1499] *that which*: same editions.] against nature is performed abominably with a prostitute, but more abominably with a wife. So much force belongs to the ordering of the Creator and the order of creation that, in matters granted for use, even when the proper measure is exceeded, the excess is far more tolerable than even one or a rare excess in matters not granted.

### C. XII. Intercourse according to nature is a lesser evil than sinning against nature. The same, Ambrose, *On the Patriarchs*, Book I, *On Abraham*, ch. 6. [Note: [Col. 1499] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 9, ch. 115, down to the word “sinning.”]

Holy Lot offered the chastity of his daughters [Note: [Col. 1499] cf. Gen. ch. 19.]. For although that too was shameful impurity, yet intercourse according to nature was a lesser evil than sinning against [Col. 1499B] nature. He preferred the claims of hospitality, inviolable even among barbarian peoples, to the honour of his household.

### C. XIII. Shameful acts proven to be against nature are more grievous. The same, Augustine, *Confessions*, Book III, ch. 8. [Note: [Col. 1499] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 9, ch. 105.]

Shameful acts that are against nature must everywhere and always be detested [Note: [Col. 1499] *rejected*: Ivo; the collected editions.] and punished, such as were those of the Sodomites. If all nations committed them, they would be held guilty by the same charge under the divine law, which did not make human beings so that they might use one another in that way [Note: [Col. 1499] *might use*: same source and the collected editions.]. For the very fellowship that ought to exist between us and God is violated when that same nature, of which he is the author, is defiled by the perversity of lust.

[Col. 1499C] ### C. XIV. Use against nature is more shameful and disgraceful than fornication or adultery. The same, *Against Jovinian*, Book I. [Note: [Col. 1499D] This chapter has not been found either in *On the Good of Marriage*—a work which Blessed Augustine says, in *Retractions*, Book 2, ch. 22, that he wrote against Jovinian—or in the books *Against Julian*, whose fifth book Ivo cites. Yet these acts are treated in *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 2, chs. 19 and 20.] [Note: [Col. 1499] Chapter of uncertain authorship.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 9, ch. 115.]

Natural use is lawful in [Note: [Col. 1499] *as in marriage; unlawful, as in adultery*: collected editions.] marriage, just as it is unlawful in adultery. But use against nature is always unlawful and, beyond doubt, more disgraceful and shameful; the holy Apostle [Note: [Col. 1499] Rom. ch. 1, v. 26.] reproved it among both women and men, wishing it to be understood as more condemnable than if they sinned in natural intercourse, whether by adultery or fornication.

[Col. 1500A] ### C. XV. Every unclean defilement is fornication, although the sins of fornication vary. The same, Isidore, Book II, *On the Highest Good*, ch. 39.

## Part III

Sin reigns in a person not only when fornication has been committed, but also, without doubt, if that person still takes delight in it [Note: [Col. 1499] *takes delight*: collected editions, first Par. and Lugd.] and holds it in the mind. Fornication of the flesh is adultery [Note: [Col. 1499] add: *is*: collected editions—the original]; fornication of the soul is slavery to idols. There is also spiritual fornication, concerning which [Note: [Col. 1499] *according to which*: original.] the Lord says [Note: [Col. 1499] Matt. ch. 5, v. 28.]: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” Every unclean defilement is called fornication, although each person prostitutes himself to a different pleasure of shamefulness [Note: [Col. 1499] *will*: collected editions.]. For from the delight of fornicating arise various disgraceful acts, by which both the kingdom of God is shut [Note: [Col. 1499] *so that … is separated*: same editions.] and a human being is separated from God.

[Col. 1500B] § 1. Among the other seven vices, the vice [Note: [Col. 1499] *fornication is a crime of the greatest wickedness*: original.] of fornication is a crime of the greatest wickedness, because through uncleanness of the flesh it violates the temple of God [Note: [Col. 1499] *is violated*: collected editions.] *and, taking a member of Christ, makes it a member of a prostitute.* But there are [Note: [Col. 1499D] *But there are:* These words are not found in Isidore, but in Origen, Homily 3 on Genesis ch. 19 [Col. 1500D], and similar words in Blessed Jerome on Ephesians ch. 5.] certain women [Note: [Col. 1499] add: *namely, women*: Arg., Bas., Lugd. II and III editions.] who, like animals, serve lust continually and without any discrimination; I would not compare them even with dumb cattle. For once cattle have conceived, they no longer permit males access to themselves.

### C. XVI. Adultery occupies second place among punishments. The same, from Clement’s First Epistle to James. [Note: [Col. 1500D] Nicholas I cites this passage from Clement’s epistle in his letter to all the archbishops and bishops in the kingdom of Lothair, beginning *Optaremus*; it survives in Rome in the library of the Dominican monastery.] [Note: [Col. 1499] From the earlier part of Clement’s first epistle, published by Rufinus.—Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 7, ch. 21; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 99; Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 28.]

What sin is more grievous than adultery? For it occupies second place among punishments, since [Note: [Col. 1499] *whom*: Ivo, *Panormia*—the collected editions.] the first place is held by those who stray from [Col. 1500C] God, even if they have lived soberly.

Gratian. These authorities show with the greatest clarity that whoever dismisses his wife because of fornication cannot marry another while she lives; and if he does marry one, he is guilty of adultery.

## Part IV

§ 1. The reply is as follows. These authorities speak either of those whose continence is not hindered by bodily weakness, or of those who, having furnished the cause of the separation, have made themselves unworthy of union with others [Note: [Col. 1499] *made*: Böhm.].

[Col. 1501A] Hence Ambrose, on Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, ch. 7 [Note: [Col. 1501D] In this passage attributed to Ambrose the matter is set out at greater length; but Blessed Ambrose maintains the contrary opinion in *On Abraham*, Book 1, chs. 4 and 7, reported above in the same question, ch. 4, *Nemo*; and in his commentary on Luke ch. 16, through ch. 1 of Book 8, part of which is reported below, 33, question 2, ch. *An quod*.] [Note: [Col. 1501] It is not by Ambrose.—Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 35.]:

### C. XVII.

“A wife [Note: [Col. 1501] 1 Cor. ch. 7, vv. 10–11.] must not separate from her husband, except for the cause of fornication; but if she separates, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband; and likewise a husband must not dismiss his wife.” He does not add concerning the husband what he stated concerning the wife, because it is lawful for a husband to take another wife.

### C. XVIII. It is lawful for a husband, whose wife cannot render the marital debt because of bodily illness, to take another wife. The same, Gregory III, to Bishop Boniface, Epistle IV. [Note: [Col. 1501D] The epistle from which this chapter is taken survives in print in volume 3 of the *Councils* and in manuscript in the library of the Dominican monastery [Col. 1502D]; it is cited below, 33, question 1. What follows, and the next chapter, appear to belong to this Gregory III.] [Note: [Col. 1501] Rather, Gregory II, A.D. 726, whom Anselm in the extract, Book 7, Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 6, ch. 112, and *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 78, correctly name as the author.]

You asked what a husband should do if a woman, stricken with illness [Note: [Col. 1501] *corrupted*: Arg. and Bas. editions.], cannot render the marital debt to him. It would be good if he remained thus, that he might devote himself to [Col. 1501B] abstinence. But because this belongs to the strong, one unable to contain himself should rather marry; yet he must not withdraw supporting help *from her* [Note: [Col. 1501] *from her*: omitted by Ivo, *Panormia*.] whom illness hinders, rather than detestable fault excludes [Note: [Col. 1501] *when not*: Ivo, *Decretum*—*but not*: *Panormia*—the collected editions.].

## Part V. Gratian

But the statement attributed to Ambrose is said to have been inserted by falsifiers. Gregory’s statement is found wholly contrary to the sacred canons—indeed, to evangelical and apostolic doctrine. Some, however, wishing to preserve Ambrose’s opinion, think that it is not to be understood of every kind of fornication: not that, because of any fornication whatever, a husband may lawfully dismiss his wife and marry another while the dismissed wife lives; but that it is to be understood only of incestuous fornication, when, namely, a man’s wife has publicly given herself to be violated by his father, son, brother, or [Col. 1501C] paternal uncle, or someone similar. Since by such an act she has made herself permanently unlawful to her husband—because affinity, through union with a blood-relative, has passed into the first, second, or third degree—she may lawfully be dismissed, and another woman may be brought in while she is alive.

If anyone contends here that this is no more lawful for a husband than for a wife, if a man commits fornication in the same manner, let him know that Ambrose called the husband “man” not with reference to sex, but to strength of mind; and let him understand that he called the wife “woman” not with reference to bodily sex [Col. 1502A], but to softness of mind. But since no authority permits another wife to be brought in while the first wife lives, Ambrose’s statement is understood of the aforesaid kind of fornication—not, however, to mean that the innocent party can marry another while the dismissed person lives, but that after the death of the fornicator, male or female (both of whom, as said above, are called “woman” on account of the corruption of lust), the person free from fornication, man or woman, may be joined to another. But adulterers, if they survive, may in no way be joined to others.

Thus is understood also what is read in a chapter of a certain council [Note: [Col. 1502D] Something similar is read in Book 5 of the *Capitularies*, ch. 19.] [Note: [Col. 1501] Something similar occurs in the Council of Compiègne, held A.D. 756, and in the Capitularies of the Frankish Kings, at the place cited by Corr.]:

### C. XIX. Lawful marriage is not to be denied to the man whose wife has slept with his brother.

A certain woman slept with her husband’s brother. It was decreed that adulterers should never be joined in marriage [Note: [Col. 1501] *in marriage*: Bas. ed.]; but lawful marriages are not to be denied to the man whose wife has been violated.

Thus is understood also the decree of the Council of Mainz [Note: [Col. 1502D] The sense of this chapter is found in the First Council of Mainz, ch. 56; the Second Council under Hrabanus, ch. 29; and Book 5 of the *Capitularies*, ch. 101, where most of the same words also occur.] [Note: [Col. 1501] Nearly the same words occur in ch. 56 of the Council of Mainz, held A.D. 813; in the other Council of Mainz, held A.D. 847, ch. 19; in *Capitularies*, Book 5, ch. 101; and in Hrabanus’s letter to Heribald, ch. 20, whence Regino, Book 2, ch. 197, reports them—Burchard, Book 17, ch. 9; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 6, ch. 121; *Decretum*, part 9, chs. 71 and 77.]:

### C. XX. Those who have committed any of the following acts are to be separated and never joined in marriage.

If anyone has married a widow [Note: [Col. 1501] *marries*: Par. and Lugd. I editions—*married*: the remaining editions, first Lugd. II and III.] and afterward has committed fornication with his stepdaughter; or with two sisters [Note: [Col. 1501] add: *while one remains his wife*: collected editions, first Arg. and Nor.]; or if a woman has done so with two brothers, or with father and son; if anyone has defiled his brother’s widow, his niece, his stepmother, his daughter-in-law, his female cousin, his maternal uncle’s daughter, or her widow, or his stepdaughter: we command that they be separated and never thereafter joined in marriage.

[Col. 1502C] ### C. XXI. One who defiles his wife’s sister cannot retain either woman. The same. [Note: [Col. 1501] Rather, the Council of Vermerie, held A.D. 752.—Cf. ch. 30, Cause 27, question 2.]

Whoever has slept with two sisters, one of whom was formerly his wife, is to have neither of them; nor are those adulterers ever to be joined in marriage.

### C. XXII. One who leaves his wife because of adultery must observe continence. The same statement of Gregory. [Note: [Col. 1501] Something similar is read in Book 1 of the *Capitularies*, ch. 43; *Polycarpus*, Book 6, title 4; Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 34.]

Those who find their wives in adultery [Note: [Col. 1501] *if*: Nor. ed.] may not, whether man or woman, take another wife or another husband so long as both are alive. But if the adulteress dies, her husband may, if he wishes, marry—only in the Lord. The adulteress, however, may never marry, even if her husband has died. Throughout all the days of her life, nevertheless, she must render the lamentations of the most severe penance.

### C. XXIII. One who defiles his wife’s sister is to have neither woman. The same, from the decree of Pope Zachary. [Note: [Col. 1503] Rather, from the penitential book inserted in Book 19, ch. 5, of Burchard’s collection.—Peter Lombard, ibid.]

Have you lain with your wife’s sister? If you have, have neither woman. And if she who was your wife was unaware of the crime [Note: [Col. 1503] *was*: collected editions, first Par. and Lugd.], and does not wish to remain continent [Note: [Col. 1503] absent from Arg. and Bas. editions], she may marry in the Lord whom she wishes. But you and the adulteress must remain without hope of marriage, and for as long as you live, perform penance according to the priest’s command.

### C. XXIV. One who has slept with his stepmother, stepdaughter, or wife’s sister cannot enter marriage; yet lawful marriages are not denied to their husbands. The same, from the Council of Tribur. [Note: [Col. 1503] Rather, from Vermerie, held A.D. 752, ch. 10.—Regino, Book 2, ch. 214; Burchard, Book 17, ch. 11.]

If anyone sleeps with his stepmother, neither can enter marriage [Note: [Col. 1503] *in no way*: Regino.]; but her husband may, if he wishes, take another wife, if he cannot remain continent. § 1. The same rule is to be observed if anyone [Note: [Col. 1503] *if anyone*: cited collections—the collected editions, first Par. and Lugd.] sleeps with his stepdaughter or his wife’s sister [Note: [Col. 1503] *may stand*: Council of Vermerie—the cited collections.].

[Col. 1503C] Gratian. Although some understand the provision placed at the end of the Council of Mainz to concern not persons lawfully married but fornicators—namely, that fornicators should separate from each other and remain without hope of marriage—the statement of Gregory to Boniface was permitted temporarily for the English [Note: [Col. 1503D] *For the English:* Here the author of the gloss correctly observes that Gratian has applied what Gregory III wrote to Boniface, legate in Germany, concerning German affairs, to matters that Blessed Gregory I had written much earlier to Augustine, bishop of the English [Col. 1504D], granting dispensations to the English recently converted to the faith concerning degrees of consanguinity and affinity. It occurs below, 35, questions 2 and 3, ch. *Quaedam lex*, and question 5, ch. *Ad sedem*.], to whom Blessed Gregory permitted marriages to be contracted in the fourth and fifth generation. Otherwise the statement would be meaningless, since Augustine says in *On the Sermon on the Mount* [Note: [Col. 1503] Above, same question 5, ch. 18.]: “If someone has a barren wife,” etc.

[Col. 1504A] ### C. XXV. Marriages may not be dissolved because of illness or bodily loss. The same, Nicholas to Charles, Bishop of Mainz. [Note: [Col. 1503] Rather, from the interpretation of Paul’s *Sentences*, Book 2, title 19, § 7.—Regino, Book 2, ch. 130 (from Roman law); Burchard, Book 9, ch. 28; Anselm, Book 10, ch. 27; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 6, ch. 93; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 166; *Polycarpus*, Book 6, title 4; Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 34.]

## Part VI

Those [Note: [Col. 1503] *If any*: Regino, Burchard, Ivo, *Decretum*.] who contracted marriage in health [Note: [Col. 1503] *contracted*: collected editions.] and then one of the two suffers madness [Note: [Col. 1503] *insanity*: Ven. I and II, Par., Lugd. I editions.], frenzy, or some illness, cannot have their marriages dissolved on account of that illness [Note: [Col. 1503] add: *and cause*: collected editions, first Lugd. II and III.]. The same judgment must be made [Note: [Col. 1503] *it must be known*: Ivo, *Panormia*—the collected editions.] concerning those who are blinded by enemies, deprived of limbs [Note: [Col. 1503] *mutilated*: Regino, Burchard, Anselm, Ivo.], or [Note: [Col. 1503] *or … have been*: absent from the same sources.] castrated by barbarians.

### C. XXVI. A madman or madwoman cannot contract marriage. The same, Pope Fabian. [Note: [Col. 1503] Rather, Paul’s *Sentences*, Book 2, title 19, § 7.—Regino, Book 2, ch. 129, from Roman law; Burchard, Book 9, ch. 30; Anselm, Book 10, ch. 28; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 6, ch. 92; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 168; *Polycarpus*; Peter Lombard, ibid.]

Neither a madman nor a madwoman can contract [Col. 1504B] marriage; but if it has been contracted, they are not to be separated [Note: [Col. 1503] *is not to be separated*: Regino, Burchard, Ivo, *Panormia*.].

## Part VII. Gratian
