Therefore, as is gathered from the foregoing, it is not lawful for this man, after dismissing his wife, to marry another. For a certain marital bond remains between them, which is not dissolved even by their separation.

Hence Augustine says in *On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 7 [Note: [Col. 1503] Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 6, chs. 28 and 105; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 254.]:

### C. XXVII. No one may dismiss a barren wife and marry another for the sake of offspring.

So powerful is that social bond *of spouses* [Note: [Col. 1503] The words *that* and *of spouses* are absent from Ivo.] that, although it is contracted for the purpose of begetting children [Note: [Col. 1503] *is contracted*: collected editions—Ivo, *Panormia*.], not even that purpose of begetting is dissolved [Note: [Col. 1503] *is dissolved*: collected editions, first Bas. ed.]. A man could indeed dismiss a barren wife and marry another by whom he might have children [Note: [Col. 1503] *might have*: collected editions.], yet this is not lawful.

[Col. 1504C] Likewise, ch. 15:

§ 1. The bond of marriage remains, even if offspring, for whose sake it was entered upon, does not follow because of manifest barrenness; so that, although the spouses know that they will have no children, they may not separate, even for the sake of children, and join themselves to others. If they do so, they commit adultery with those to whom they join themselves; yet they themselves remain spouses [Note: [Col. 1503] *while that spouse remains*: Ivo, *Decretum*—*while their own marriage remains*: *Panormia*—*while their own marriage remains*: collected editions.]. Clearly, among the ancient fathers it was lawful, with the wife’s consent, to introduce another woman so that common children might be born: by the union and seed of one, but by the legal right and authority of the other. Whether this too is lawful now, I would not rashly say.

### C. XXVIII. On the same matter. The same, Book I, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. 10. [Note: [Col. 1505] Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 6, ch. 74; *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 12; Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 31.]

The rights of marriage once entered into remain so strongly between living persons [Note: [Col. 1505] *may remain*: collected editions, first Lugd. II and III.] that those who have separated from one another are spouses to each other rather than to those others [Note: [Col. 1505] *are spouses to one another even when separated*: Ivo—the collected editions.] to whom they have attached themselves. And a little later [Note: [Col. 1505D] In Augustine’s text, ch. *Denique*, above, 31, question 1, is inserted here. Some things have also been added and corrected in this chapter from the original itself, as in the preceding chapter.]:

§ 1. Among living persons there remains a certain marital bond [Note: [Col. 1505] *a certain marital something*: original.] which neither separation nor union with another [Note: [Col. 1505] *adulterer*: Ivo, *Decretum*—add: *man*: collected editions.] can remove; *it remains, however, for the guilt of the crime, not for the bond of the covenant.* [Note: [Col. 1505] The words *it remains … covenant* do not occur in Ivo.] This is like an apostate soul, withdrawing as though from marriage with Christ: even after faith is lost, it does not lose the sacrament of faith which it received in the washing [Note: [Col. 1505] *in the washing*: collected editions.] of regeneration. For it would undoubtedly be restored to the returning person if it had been lost upon departure. But the person who has departed possesses it for an increase of punishment, not for the merit of reward.

[Col. 1505B] ## QUESTION VIII

## GRATIAN

Since, therefore, it has been proved that this man cannot dismiss his wife and marry another, the question is asked whether he may sin on this condition: that he brings an unbelieving woman to the faith. Augustine affirms that this cannot be done, [Col. 1506A] saying as follows in *On Adulterous Marriages*, Book I, ch. 24 [Note: [Col. 1505] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, ch. 73.]:

### C. UN. No one ought to withdraw from a vow of continence even if an unbelieving woman promises to become a Christian.

Not only must adultery not be committed—which is committed not by some particular person, but by everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another, even if he marries her for the purpose [Note: [Col. 1505] add: *her*: collected editions.] of making her a Christian—but also whoever, not bound to a wife, has vowed continence to God [Note: [Col. 1505] *vowed*: same editions.] must by no means sin on this pretext, so as to believe that he ought to marry a wife because the woman seeking marriage with him has promised that she will become a Christian. For what was lawful to someone before he made the vow becomes unlawful when he has vowed never to do it—provided, however, that he has vowed what ought to have been vowed [Note: [Col. 1505] *is*: same editions.], [Col. 1506B] such as perpetual virginity; or widowed chastity after marriages have been experienced and the marital bond has been dissolved [Note: [Col. 1506D] *Or after:* In the common manuscripts of Blessed Augustine and also in Ivo, this passage, down to the words “Therefore these,” differs somewhat.]; or unbroken continence for faithful and chaste spouses who vow it by mutual consent and mutually release each other from carnal obligations—which neither may lawfully vow without the other. [Note: [Col. 1505] *unbroken continence* is absent from Ivo.] Therefore these, and whatever other things are most rightly vowed, once people have vowed them, must not be broken under any condition, since they were vowed without any condition.

# CAUSE XXXIII

[Col. 1505]

[Col. 1505C] ## GRATIAN

A certain man, hindered by spells, could not render the marital debt to his wife. Meanwhile another secretly seduced her; separated from her husband, she publicly married her seducer. She confessed the crime she had committed to God only in her heart. The former husband regained the ability to have intercourse with her and reclaimed his wife. After receiving her back, in order that he might devote himself more freely to prayer and approach the flesh of the Lamb more purely, he promised to observe continence; but his wife did not give her consent.

(Question I.) The first question is whether, because of inability to have intercourse, a woman should be separated from her husband.

(Question II.) Second, after the separation, whether she may marry the man with whom she had previously committed fornication.

(Question III.) Third, whether a crime can be erased by confession of the heart alone.

(Question IV.) Fourth, whether during a time of prayer [Col. 1505D] a person may render the marital debt.

(Question V.) Fifth, whether a husband can vow continence without his wife’s consent, or whether he may extort from her, by threats or terrors, permission to make the vow.

[Col. 1506C] ## QUESTION I

## GRATIAN
# I. Part

That a woman cannot be separated from her husband because she is unable to render the marital due is proved by evangelical and apostolic authority. For Christ says in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1505] Matthew, chapter 19, verse 9.]: “No one may dismiss his wife except on account of fornication”—either because one of them has committed fornication, as Augustine explains, or because one wishes to draw the other into fornication. Likewise the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1505] Romans, chapter 7, verses 1–2.]: “A woman, for as long as her husband lives, is bound by his law”—not by a law requiring her to render the marital due to him, but by one forbidding her to transfer herself to another. Likewise [Note: [Col. 1505] 1 Corinthians, chapter 7, verse 10.]: “To those joined in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife not depart from her husband, except on account of fornication.” Therefore evangelical and apostolic authority forbids a woman to depart from her husband except for that cause known to all, in the presence of which, if she departs, she must remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. Hence it is understood that inability to render the marital due does not dissolve the marriage bond.

§ 1. The answer is as follows: marriage is confirmed by consummation, as was proved above [Note: [Col. 1507] “As above”: this seems to refer to *Non dubium* and *Quum societas*, above, Causa 27, question 1; the matter was noted there.]. But once it has been confirmed by consummation, a husband may not dismiss his wife, nor may a wife depart from her husband, except on account of fornication. Before it is confirmed, however, inability to perform the marital act dissolves the marriage bond.

Accordingly Gregory [Note: [Col. 1507] More properly, Rabanus to Heribald; compare Causa 27, question 2, chapter 29, and the collection there.] writes to John [Note: [Col. 1507] “To John”: the material noted above under Causa 27, question 2, should be repeated here.], bishop of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 1507] “Archbishop”: the collected editions and the Argentinian edition read “archbishop.”]:

## C. I. A woman may marry another man if, because of impotence, her husband cannot have intercourse with her.

What you asked concerning those who are joined in marriage but cannot have intercourse—whether he may take another woman or she another man—is answered as follows. It is written: If a man and woman have joined themselves together, and afterwards the woman says of the man that he cannot have intercourse with her, then, if she can prove by a just judgment that this is true, she may take another man. But if he has taken another woman, they are to be separated.

## C. II. Likewise, from an epistle of the same author [Note: [Col. 1507] The chapter’s origin is uncertain. Burchard, book 9, chapter 44; Anselm, book 10, chapter 25; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 116 (examples of Gregory II to John, archbishop of Ravenna); *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 182; *Polycarpus*, book 6, title 4; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 34.].

You asked [Note: [Col. 1507] “You asked”: Burchard and Ivo, *Panormia*, read “you asked.”] concerning those who, because of a cold nature, say that they cannot unite with one another by rendering the service of the flesh [Note: [Col. 1507] “Of the flesh”: Burchard, Anselm, and Ivo read “of the flesh.”]. If the man cannot use her as a wife, let him have her as a sister. But if they wish to sever the marital bond, let both remain unmarried. For if he could not naturally suit this woman, how will he suit another [Note: [Col. 1507] “Will suit”: Ivo, *Panormia*, reads “may suit”? The Basel edition has “may suit.”]? If, therefore, the man wishes to take another wife, the reason is plainly evident [Note: [Col. 1507] “The reason”: Ivo, *Panormia*, reads “the reason is evident.”]: prompted by the devil [Note: [Col. 1507] “Prompted”: Burchard, Anselm, Ivo, and the *Decretum* read “following.”], he has conceived a seed of hatred [Note: [Col. 1507] “A seed”: Ivo, *Panormia*, reads “a seed of hatred.” The collected editions read “with a seed of hatred.”] and has come to hate her, and therefore attempts to dismiss her through the falsehood of a lie.

But if the woman pleads and says, “I wish to be a mother and bear children,” and [Note: [Col. 1507] The word “and” is absent from Burchard, Anselm, and Ivo.] both of them, with seven relatives touching the most holy relics, swear under oath that they had never been joined through intercourse of the flesh so as to become one flesh, then the woman seems able to contract a second marriage. I speak in human terms because of the weakness of their flesh [Note: [Col. 1507] Romans, chapter 6, verse 19.]. But the man who is of a cold nature is to remain without a wife. If he too takes another union [Note: [Col. 1507] This phrase is absent from the Basel edition.], then those who swore are to be held guilty of perjury, and, after completing penance, are to be compelled to resume their former marriages.

# II. Part

Gratian. This is prescribed where both parties make the same confession. But if the husband asserts that he has rendered the marital due to his wife, while she denies it, it is rightly asked to whom credit should rather be given.

The following was decreed concerning this at the council held at Compiègne [Note: [Col. 1507] Held in A.D. 756. Regino, book 2, chapter 244; Burchard, book 9, chapter 42; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 119; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 180; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 34.]:

## C. III. If the woman denies that she has been known by him, the husband’s statement is to stand.

If anyone has taken a wife and has had her for some time, and the woman says that he has never had intercourse with her, while the man says that he did, the husband’s statement is to stand, because the man is the head of the woman.

# III. Part

Gratian. Here, then, inability to render the marital due dissolves the marriage bond. But this was decreed concerning natural incapacity. In the present case, however, she has been separated from her husband because the marital due was prevented by the impediment of sorcery, not by natural frigidity. Hence it is asked whether, even in this case, she may leave her husband and join herself to another.

Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, writes as follows concerning this to Rodulph and Frotarius [Note: [Col. 1507] To Rodulph and Frotarius, A.D. 860. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 117; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 194; Peter Lombard, there.]:

## C. IV. Concerning those who, hindered by spells, cannot have intercourse.

If, through sorcerous and harmful practices [Note: [Col. 1508] “Harmful practices”: the common editions continued with “arts”; that word is absent from most ancient manuscripts and from the other collectors.], secretly—but never without God’s just judgment permitting it [Note: [Col. 1507] “Never” or “nowhere”: the original reading.], and the devil preparing it—intercourse does not take place, those to whom this happens should be exhorted to make a pure confession of all their sins, with contrite heart and humble spirit, to God and to a priest; and, with abundant tears, more generous almsgiving, prayers, and fasts, to make satisfaction to the Lord. Through exorcisms and the other ministries of the Church’s healing, ministers of the Church should endeavor, insofar as the Lord grants, to heal such persons—the Lord who healed Abimelech and his household through Abraham’s prayers [Note: [Col. 1507] Compare Genesis, chapter 20.].

But if perhaps they cannot be healed [Note: [Col. 1507] The common collected editions read “cannot heal them.”], they may separate. Yet after they seek other marriages, while those to whom they had been joined remain alive [Note: [Col. 1507] The original reads “had been joined”; the common editions read “have been joined.”], they will not be able to be reconciled to their former spouses whom they left, even if the ability to have intercourse is restored to them [Note: [Col. 1507] The original reads “has been restored”; the editions of Norimberga and Venice I and II read “will have been restored.”].

[Col. 1509A] Gratian. But this appears contrary to the preceding chapter of Gregory. There, once ability has been restored, the person is commanded to separate from the one whom he or she married second and return to the first. Here, however, while the person to whom she had been joined second is alive, she cannot be reconciled to the first.

# QUESTION II

## GRATIAN

# I. Part

That after separation she may marry the man with whom she had previously committed fornication has been proved above. For her husband is dead to her. Once, by the judgments of the Church, she has been separated from him, she is released from his law. Therefore, according to the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1509] 1 Corinthians, chapter 7, verse 39. C. I.], “let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.”

§ 1. But it is asked whether, if he had departed from her without ecclesiastical judgment and without any reasonable ground of separation having been proved, he should be compelled to return to her. The following was decreed concerning this at the Council of Carthage, attended by Augustine, chapter 30 [Note: [Col. 1509] This passage is also cited in manuscripts and by Ivo, part 8, chapter 328, as from the Council of Carthage, although it has been found in no such council. Rather, it is from the Council of Agde, chapter 25, from which Ivo cites it in the same part, chapter 231, and from the *Capitularies*, book 7, chapter 305.] [Note: [Col. 1509] More properly, from the Council of Agde, held in A.D. 506. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 106; *Decretum*, part 8, chapters 231 and 328.]:

## C. I. No one may dismiss a wife unless the ground of separation has first been proved before the Church.

Laymen who dismiss, or have dismissed, their marital union without any grave fault [Note: [Col. 1509] “Without any”: in more recent editions of the councils, the Council of Agde reads “without a more serious fault”; the *Capitularies* read “without a graver fault”; in ancient Paris editions of the councils and in two Vatican manuscripts: “a marital union because of a graver fault.” The Spanish Collection has the same reading.], and who, without setting forth any plausible grounds of separation, abandon their marriages in order to presume upon either unlawful unions or unions belonging to another [Note: [Col. 1509] Some manuscripts and editions read: “in order either to approach that woman or another,” or “in order to approach either her or another.”], if, before presenting their grounds of separation before the bishops of their province and before being condemned in judgment, they cast aside their wives [Note: [Col. 1509] This phrase is absent from the Spanish Collection.], are to be excluded from communion with the holy [Note: [Col. 1509] This phrase is absent from the common collected editions, especially the second and third Lyon editions.] Church and from the assembly of the holy [Note: [Col. 1509] The common editions read “of the holy people”; others read “of the saint,” or “of the holy.” The Spanish Collection omits this phrase.] people, because they defile faith and marriage.

## C. II. The divine law forbids a man to dismiss his wife except on account of fornication. Likewise Ambrose on Luke, chapter 16.

“Is what is wicked against those subject to one lawful against an equal? You dismiss your wife as though by right [Note: [Col. 1509] “As though by right”: this is also found in the common manuscripts of Ambrose. Three of Gratian’s manuscripts read: “although you know that she lives without fault.”], though she is without fault, and think that this is permitted you because human law does not forbid it? But divine law forbids it [Note: [Col. 1509] “Divine law”: the same editions read “divine law”; compare Matthew, chapter 19, verse 6.]. You who obey human beings, fear God; hear the law of the Lord, whom even those who make laws obey: ‘What God has joined together, let no human being separate.’”

## C. III. A woman dismissed by her husband without examination of the case is to be restored in all respects. Likewise Pope Nicholas to King Charles [Note: [Col. 1509] The heading is possibly transferred from the following chapter. This woman is mentioned by Justin in the first *Apology for the Christians* and by Eusebius in *Ecclesiastical History*, book 4, chapter 16. The words of this chapter have not been found in Nicholas’s printed or manuscript letters, but nearly the same words occur in Isidore’s preface to his collection of canons. It is nevertheless preferable to consult Justin and Eusebius.].

The ecclesiastical history composed by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, says concerning a certain woman who was accused by her husband because of her chastity [Note: [Col. 1509] The editions read “concerning chastity” rather than “because of chastity.”]: “By an imperial law it was commanded [Note: [Col. 1509] The original adds “and it was forbidden.”] that she should first be allowed sufficient freedom to arrange her household affairs; then only should she answer the accusations brought against her.” This is prescribed by all laws, ecclesiastical as well as common and public.

§ 1. But if these provisions have been made for women and laymen [Note: [Col. 1509] Other manuscripts read “lay people.”], they are granted all the more to ecclesiastical persons [Note: [Col. 1509] Other manuscripts read “ecclesiastical men.”] and priests.

## C. IV. Unless after restoration, no judgment concerning either the marriage bond or the charge of adultery is to be undertaken between husband and wife. Likewise Pope Nicholas in an epistle to King Charles [Note: [Col. 1510] The epistle from which this chapter was taken is preserved at Rome in a manuscript of the Dominican monastery; from it some material has been added and corrected.] [Note: [Col. 1509] Written in A.D. 867. Regino, book 2, chapter 116; Burchard, book 9, chapter 52; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 116; *Polycarpus*, book 6, title 4.].

# II. Part

Whether judgment is to be undertaken concerning the marriage bond or concerning a charge of adultery, no reason permits Thietberga [Note: [Col. 1509] The editions of the collected authorities read “Tebergam.”] to enter even the slightest contest [Note: [Col. 1509] The original reads “to enter a lawful contest”; Regino, Burchard, and Ivo read “to undergo a lawful contest.”] of litigation with Lothar, unless she has first for a time been restored to her own control and freely reunited with her own relatives. A place must also be provided among them [Note: [Col. 1509] The original reads “among whom”; another reading has “among those same.”] where no violence from a crowd is to be feared [Note: [Col. 1509] The collected editions read “where no violence from a crowd may be feared.”] and where it is not difficult to produce witnesses or the other persons whom both the holy canons and the venerable Roman laws require in controversies of this kind [Note: [Col. 1509] Some editions read “nor be difficult”; others “nor be impossible.”].

# III. Part

Gratian. Although this chapter seems to state the reason why no one may dismiss his wife on his own authority, so that, when that reason ceases, the prohibition itself also seems to cease, nevertheless, because separation itself is a penalty, and no penalty is to be imposed on anyone except by a judge, this must be understood generally: whether for the aforesaid cause or when no cause exists, no one may dismiss his wife on his own authority. The same must be understood concerning the penalty for homicide or any other offense.

Accordingly Pope Nicholas writes to Rodulph, archbishop of Bourges [Note: [Col. 1511] Written in A.D. 864. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, chapter 15; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 125; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 38.]:

## C. V. Marriage is altogether forbidden to those who kill their wives.

Since you do not add that they are adulteresses or anything of that kind, what else are those who kill their wives without judgment to be considered but murderers, and therefore persons to be reduced to penance? Marriage is altogether denied to them, except for young persons, concerning whom the twenty-fifth decretal rule of the blessed Pope Leo—or rather the indulgence—is to be observed [Note: [Col. 1511] “Twenty-fifth”: the same number is found in the *Code of Canons* among the decrees or rules of Leo, that is, in Dionysius. Compare below, chapter 14.].

Gratian. In this chapter Nicholas appears to permit husbands to kill their wives for adultery or another crime of that sort. But ecclesiastical discipline commands that criminals be struck with the spiritual sword, not a material one: namely, the sword with which Peter is commanded to kill and eat [Note: [Col. 1511] Compare Acts, chapter 10.]. Christ also says in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1511] Matthew, chapter 10, verse 34.]: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword.”

Hence the same Nicholas writes to Archbishop Albinus [Note: [Col. 1511] This occurs in an epistle said to have been sent by Nicholas to the bishops of Germany, Charles of Mainz and others, and appended by Mansi to the Council of Mainz, held in A.D. 857. Berardus rightly has serious doubts about its authenticity, since it appears to have been composed from various German conciliar canons in a crude and inelegant style. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, chapter 145; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 124 (Nicholas to Charles, archbishop, and his suffragans), and chapter 333; *Polycarpus*, book 6, title 10; Peter Lombard, there.]:

## C. VI. No one may kill his adulterous wife.

Among these matters, your holiness has taken care to add whether, if someone’s wife has committed adultery, her husband may lawfully kill her according to secular law [Note: [Col. 1511] The common collected editions, except the Argentinian edition, read “so that if.”]. But the holy Church of God is never bound by secular laws; it has no sword except a spiritual one [Note: [Col. 1511] Ivo, *Panormia*, and the collected editions omit “it has no sword.”]; it does not kill, but gives life.

## C. VII. The penance of one who kills his own wife without cause. Likewise Pope Pius [Note: [Col. 1511] Compare the Capitularies of Louis, A.D. 829, book 3, chapter 3; the Capitularies of the Frankish kings, book 5, chapter 300, and Regino, book 2, chapter 76; Burchard, book 6, chapter 37; Anselm, book 10, chapter 56 (57); Ivo, *Decretum*, part 10, chapter 166; Peter Lombard, there.].

Whoever kills his own wife without legal authority, or without cause and certain proof [Note: [Col. 1511] The collected editions read “and without cause.”], and takes another wife, must lay aside his arms and perform public penance. If he is obstinate and proves disobedient to his bishop, he is to be anathematized until he consents. The same law shall apply to one who kills his lord.

## C. VIII. The penance of Hastulph, who killed his wife. Likewise Pope Stephen V to Hastulph [Note: [Col. 1511] More properly, Paulinus of Cividale to Heistulph, A.D. 794, as Burchard, book 6, chapter 40, correctly entitles it. Its text otherwise differs greatly from Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, chapter 16; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 126; and Gratian, who followed those versions. “Astulph” is read by Ivo and by the collected editions.].

We strive to admonish you with tears and much groaning of heart [Note: [Col. 1511] Burchard reads “with groaning of heart.”], son Hastulph; but you ought not to be called a son, since, wretched man, you have committed so cruel a murder. For you killed your wife, a part of your own body, joined to you in lawful marriage, without any cause of death. She was not resisting you, nor plotting against your life in any way [Note: [Col. 1511] Ivo reads “in any manner”; the collected editions read “in any manner whatsoever.”]. You did not find her committing an abominable act with another man. But stirred by the devil and inflamed with impious fury [Note: [Col. 1511] The collected editions and Ivo read “and impious fury.”], more cruel than every beast, you slaughtered her more savagely with your sword, after the manner of robbers [Note: [Col. 1511] Burchard reads “in the manner of robbery.”].

And now, after her death, you add iniquity to iniquity, wicked plunderer of your own children. You spared not their mother and made your children orphans; after her death you wish to fabricate against her a cause of death, and by means of one murderer and reprobate witness [Note: [Col. 1511] The collected editions read “one man who is a murderer.”] you wish to accuse the dead woman. Since neither the Gospel nor any divine or human law condemns or acquits anyone on the testimony of one witness, however suitable he may be [Note: [Col. 1511] Burchard notes: “Neither the Gospel nor any law permits this.”], how much less ought she to have been condemned while living through this utterly shameful and criminal man, or accused by you after her death [Note: [Col. 1511] Burchard and Ivo read: “nor, nevertheless, will you be able to excuse yourself after her death.”]?

First [Note: [Col. 1511] The collected editions add “therefore.”], the cause of the alleged crime ought to have been carefully investigated; then, if it had been found true, she should have received the punishment of vengeance according to the course of law [Note: [Col. 1511] Burchard and Ivo, *Decretum*, read “receive the punishment.”]. For if what that adulterer lied were true—which God forbid—after seven years’ penance had been performed, you could have dismissed her for an approved cause, if you wished; yet you ought by no means to have killed her. For God does not will the death of the sinner [Note: [Col. 1511] Ezekiel, chapter 33, verse 11.], but that he be converted to penance and live.

Therefore let our counsel please you, and do this which may seem better and lighter to you [Note: [Col. 1511] The editions read “may be better.”]: have mercy on your soul, lest you become your own murderer [Note: [Col. 1511] The Basel edition reads “your own murderer”; the Paris and second and third Lyon editions omit “your own.”]. Leave, therefore, we beg you, this evil [Note: [Col. 1511] Burchard reads “malignant.”] world which drew you into so monstrous a crime of sin [Note: [Col. 1513] The Bohm edition omits “so monstrous.”]. Enter a monastery; humble yourself beneath the hand of an abbot; aided by the prayers of many brothers, observe with a simple heart everything commanded to you [Note: [Col. 1513] Ivo reads “with a submissive heart.”], so that perhaps the infinite goodness of God may forgive your sins and refresh your soul before you are tormented in everlasting flames. Know with certainty that this is lighter and better for you.

But if you wish to perform public penance while remaining in your own house or in this world—which you should not doubt is worse, harsher, and more burdensome for you—we exhort you to do as follows [Note: [Col. 1513] The original reads “as you ought”; the collected editions read “as you should.”]. On every day on which you must do penance [Note: [Col. 1513] The collected editions read “on every day so that you must do penance.”], do not drink wine or strong drink [Note: [Col. 1513] Ivo reads “all strong drink”; the editions of Nuremberg, Venice I and II, Paris, and Lyon I read “all strong drink.”]. Never eat flesh at any time [Note: [Col. 1513] Ivo reads “never, at any time”; the collected editions read “never, at any time.”] except at Easter and on the day of the Lord’s Nativity. Do penance with bread, water, and salt; persevere always in fasts, vigils, prayers, and almsgiving. Never gird yourself with weapons, nor presume to engage in litigation in any place. Never take a wife, keep no concubine [Note: [Col. 1513] The same editions read “never have a concubine.”], and dare not commit adultery. Never wash in a bath; never mix yourself with the gatherings of those who rejoice. In church, set yourself humbly apart from other Christians behind the door and doorposts [Note: [Col. 1513] The Basel edition reads “behind the doorposts.”]; humbly commend yourself to the prayers of those entering and leaving [Note: [Col. 1513] The same edition reads “to commend yourself.”]. Consider yourself unworthy of communion in the body and blood of the Lord for every day of your life. Yet on the final day of your life, if you are worthy and someone is present to give it to you [Note: [Col. 1513] The collected editions, especially Argentinensis and Norimbergensis, add “to you.”], we permit you only in the way of pardon to receive it as viaticum.

There are many other things, wretched man, which, in proportion to the great weight of your sin, ought to be imposed upon you still more harshly and severely. But if, with a perfect heart and the Lord’s help, you do and observe all these things mercifully stated above, we trust in the boundless mercy of God that you will obtain forgiveness of your sins, and that, according to the judgment [Note: [Col. 1513] Burchard reads “command.”] of the just and good Shepherd, the holy Church will loose you from this bond of sin on earth, so that through the grace of him who acquired her with his own blood you may be loosed in heaven.

But if you act otherwise and despise this saving admonition of the holy Mother Church, be your own judge [Note: [Col. 1513] The Basel edition reads “be your own judge”; the Paris and second and third Lyon editions omit “your own.”]. You will remain in the devil’s snare in which you are entangled, and your blood shall be upon your own head. As for us, separated from communion with you for the salvation of God’s other children [Note: [Col. 1513] The collected editions read “for the salvation of the faithful and other children of God.”], with God’s help we labor with every care for their salvation and implore the Lord’s mercy more earnestly each day.

## C. IX. Rather let a man take another wife while his wife lives than shed human blood. Likewise Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book 2, chapter 15 [Note: [Col. 1513] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, chapter 17; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 242.].

If—as is more truly said—it is not lawful for a Christian man to kill an adulterous wife, but only to dismiss her, who is so mad as to tell him: “Do what is unlawful, so that you may be allowed to do what is unlawful”? Since under Christ’s law both acts are unlawful—both killing an adulterous wife and taking another while she lives—one must abstain from both, and an unlawful deed must not be committed in exchange for another unlawful deed. If he is going to do what is unlawful, let him commit adultery and not homicide: let him take another woman while his wife lives, rather than shed human blood. But if both are wicked [Note: [Col. 1513] This sentence is absent from Ivo, *Decretum*.], he ought not to commit one in place of the other [Note: [Col. 1513] Ivo, *Panormia*, and the collected editions read “through one in place of the other.”], but avoid both.

# IV. Part

Gratian. In the foregoing authorities, all are forbidden to kill their adulterous wives; but after seven years of penance they are permitted to dismiss them. If, however, they kill them, they are ordered to remain forever without hope of marriage, unless perhaps mercy is extended to them for contracting marriages because of a lapse caused by youthful incontinence. Clerics, however, are permitted, if their wives sin, to keep them in custody without the severity of death and compel them to fast, though not to afflict them to the point of death.

Accordingly, in the First Council of Toledo, chapter 7 [Note: [Col. 1513] Held in A.D. 400. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 283.], we read:

## C. X. If clerics’ wives sin, the clerics are to keep them at home, short of death, and compel them to salutary fasts.

It pleased the council that, if the wives of any clerics sin [Note: [Col. 1513] Ivo reads “have sinned”; the collected editions, especially the second and third Lyon editions, read “had sinned.”], lest they have greater freedom to sin, their husbands may have the power to keep and bind them in their own houses, short of death [Note: [Col. 1513] The Spanish Collection omits “and to bind.”], compelling them to salutary, not deadly, fasts [Note: [Col. 1513] The Spanish Collection omits “compelling them to fasts.”]. Poor clerics are to give one another assistance if they happen not to have servants [Note: [Col. 1513] The word “perhaps” is absent from Ivo.]. But they are not to take meals with those wives who have sinned [Note: [Col. 1513] The collected editions read “who had sinned”; Ivo reads “nor eat.”], unless perhaps, moved by fear of God, they return through penance [Note: [Col. 1513] The Spanish Collection reads “unless they return through penance.”].

# V. Part

Gratian. It is now asked why the sacred canons have established that penitents be restored to their former condition after seven years. Isidore writes as follows to Bishop Masson in the preface to the book *On the Supreme Good* [Note: [Col. 1513] Compare Distinction 50, chapter 28; Anselm, book 8, chapter 37; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 398; *Polycarpus*, book 4, title 39.]:

## C. XI. Why penitents are established to return to their former condition after seven years.

This very provision—that the discipline of the canons commands a penitent to return after seven years to his former condition, and so forth, as in the treatise on the ordination of the fallen [Note: [Col. 1515] This phrase is absent from most ancient manuscripts, but it has not been deleted because Gratian commonly cites in this manner, as is indicated in *Presbyter*, above, Distinction 82.]—was ordained by the holy Fathers not by the choice of their own judgment [Note: [Col. 1515] The Bohm edition omits “by.”], but rather by the sentence of divine judgment. For it is read that Miriam [Note: [Col. 1515] Compare Numbers, chapter 12.], Aaron’s sister and a prophetess, when she incurred the offense of speaking against Moses [Note: [Col. 1515] The original reads “detraction”; the other reading is “backbiting.”], was immediately struck with the mark of leprosy [Note: [Col. 1515] Ivo and the collected editions read “struck” rather than “covered.”]. When Moses asked that she be cleansed, God commanded her to go outside the camp for seven days and, after cleansing, to be admitted again into the camp [Note: [Col. 1515] Ivo reads “within the camp.”].

Miriam, Aaron’s sister, is understood to signify the flesh of the priest. When, given over to pride, it is stained by the foul contagions of thoughts [Note: [Col. 1515] The original reads “corruptions”; Ivo reads “enticements.”], it is cast outside the camp for seven days—that is, outside the fellowship of the holy Church for seven years [Note: [Col. 1515] The collected editions, especially the second and third Lyon editions, omit “of the holy Church.”]—so that, after amendment of its vices [Note: [Col. 1515] The collected editions read “after cleansing.”], it may recover the merit of its place or former dignity. And a little later:

§ 1. At the end of the letter I thought it should be added that whenever a disagreement of judgment is found in the records of councils, the opinion should rather be followed whose authority is older or prior [Note: [Col. 1515] The collected editions read “and prior”; Ivo reads “or prior.”] [Note: [Col. 1516] From “At the end” to the conclusion, this material is absent from one ancient copy of Gratian.].

Gratian. Although this seems to have been said particularly concerning priests, it must nevertheless be understood generally of all penitents. For in imitation of that divine judgment, David [Note: [Col. 1515] Compare 2 Samuel, chapter 12.], reproved for adultery and homicide, is read to have offered to God a fast of one week in satisfaction for the crime he committed. Hence ecclesiastical custom has also adopted the practice that penance for graver crimes should be concluded within a period of seven years, unless either the eminence of office or the magnitude of crimes exceeding ordinary custom requires the aforesaid period to be extended—for example, when we shamefully join ourselves against the nature of human society to parents, children, or other persons of that kind; when, abandoning natural use, we commit fornication against nature in the Sodomitic manner; or when we descend even to intercourse with brute animals.

# VI. Part

§ 1. It is also asked concerning penitents whether, after their penance has been completed, marriage is generally permitted to them. For, by canonical authority, penitents are generally forbidden to return to secular military service or to contract marriages.

Accordingly Pope Siricius, in his first letter to Bishop Himerius, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 1515] Written in A.D. 385. Burchard, book 19, chapter 57; Anselm, book 11, chapter 150; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, chapter 71.], writes:

## C. XII. Penitents are forbidden to contract marriages.

Your belovedness rightly thought that the Apostolic See should be consulted concerning those who, after completing penance, return like dogs and swine to their former vomit and wallowing, and again seek the military belt, theatrical pleasures, new marriages, and forbidden intercourse, while children born after absolution have exposed their professed continence [Note: [Col. 1515] Burchard reads “after completing penance”; the collected editions read “unprofessed” instead of “professed.”]. Since they no longer have the refuge [Note: [Col. 1515] The Spanish Collection reads “support.”] of penance, we have decreed that they should be joined with the faithful only in prayer outside the church [Note: [Col. 1515] The Spanish Collection and the collected editions read “within” rather than “outside.”]; that they should be present, although they do not deserve it, at the sacred celebrations of the mysteries [Note: [Col. 1515] Burchard and Ivo read “at the celebration”; the original as preserved by Coustant reads “at the solemnities”; the editions of Argentan, Basel, Nuremberg, and Venice read “at the solemnities.”]; but that they should be excluded from the banquet of the Lord’s table. Thus, at least corrected by this severity [Note: [Col. 1515] Burchard and Ivo read “corrected”; the collected editions read “corrected” or “punished.”], they may themselves chastise their errors within themselves and furnish an example to others, so that they may be drawn back from shameful desires [Note: [Col. 1515] The Spanish Collection reads “so that they may be drawn out.”].

Yet since they have fallen through fleshly weakness, we wish that, when they begin their departure to the Lord, help be given them by the grace of communion as viaticum [Note: [Col. 1515] The same source reads “that they be raised up.”]. We judge that the same rule is to be observed also concerning women who, after penance, have bound themselves to such defilements [Note: [Col. 1515] The original as preserved by Coustant reads “women who have bound themselves”; the Spanish Collection reads “whom.”].

Gratian. But because some delay approaching penance through fear of dissolving their marriages, or neglect to receive the remedy of penance because they fear a lapse of youth, canonical authority permits them either to retain marriages already contracted or to contract others.

Accordingly Pope Leo writes to Galerius, bishop of Tripoli [Note: [Col. 1515] The chapter is wholly uncertain in origin. Compare the collected tracts, part 1, title 60, chapters 11–12.]:

## C. XIII. By indulgence, lawful marriages are not to be denied after penance.

We have heard from some persons that in your dioceses and territories communities of Christians withdraw themselves from the yoke of penance on a slight pretext, saying: “If we do penance, we must abandon the union of marriage.” In this they err and depart from the path of truth, because every worshipper of Christ’s name ought most earnestly to undergo and perform penance for all unlawful deeds, as the Lord says [Note: [Col. 1515] Matthew, chapter 3, verse 2.]: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near.” But no orthodox believer undergoing penance may dissolve a lawful marriage. And below:

§ 1. It is fitting that you instruct them with sacred words [Note: [Col. 1517] The editions of Argentan and Basel read “with sacred addresses” rather than “with sacred words.”], so that they may be delivered from the darkness of error and, joined in lawful unions, may strive to perform penance for all unlawful acts [Note: [Col. 1517] The editions of Argentan, Basel, and Nuremberg read “may take care”; Venice I and II read “may strive.”].

## C. XIV. Lawful marriages are not to be denied to penitents because of a lapse of youthful incontinence. Likewise Pope Leo to Rusticus, epistle 90, alternatively 92, chapter 11 [Note: [Col. 1517] Epistle 167 in the Ballerini edition, written in A.D. 458 or 459. Anselm, book 11, chapter 106. In the older collected editions it is ascribed to Leo IV.].

If, while still young, a man performed penance under pressure of fear of death or danger of captivity [Note: [Col. 1517] The collected editions read “if he has performed penance” and “has chosen.”], and afterwards, fearing a lapse of youthful incontinence, chose union with a wife so as not to incur the crime of fornication, he seems to have done something pardonable, provided that he has known no woman whatsoever apart from his wife. Yet in this we establish not a rule, but judge what is more tolerable.

C. XV. This penance is to be imposed upon one who has killed his mother. Likewise Pope Nicholas to Rhatold, Bishop of the holy Church of Strasbourg. [Note: [Col. 1517C] The penance for parricides prescribed here is found in the Council of Worms, c. 30.] [Note: [Col. 1517] In Ivo, *Decrees*, part 10, c. 173, and in the older collected editions it is wrongly said to have been addressed to Radulphus (Rhotald: Böhm); for it is certain that Rhadold, rightly named by Burchard, bk. 6, c. 46, and Anselm, bk. 11, c. 52 (51), governed the Church of Strasbourg (the Church of *Argenteae Retensi*: the cited collections—the older collected editions) in Nicholas’s time.—Polycarpus, bk. 6, tit. 10.]

**Seventh Part.** We have learned that the bearer of this letter is a matricide. We command him to remain under the yoke of penance as follows: for a whole year he is not to enter the church, but is to persevere before the doors of the basilica, praying [Note: [Col. 1517] standing and praying: the older collected editions] and entreating God that he may be delivered from so great a crime. When the cycle of the year has been completed, he may be permitted to enter the church; nevertheless, let him stand among the hearers, but not yet communicate. [Col. 1517C] When the course of three years has been completed, let the grace of Holy Communion be granted him; but he is not to make offerings until the courses of another seven years have first been completed.

§ 1. Throughout all these years and periods, he is not to eat flesh or presume to drink wine, except on feast days, Sundays, and from Easter until Pentecost. Wherever he wishes to go, he is not to be conveyed in any vehicle, but is to travel on foot; he is not to bear arms except against pagans; and he is to fast three [Note: [Col. 1517] three days: Burchard, Ivo] days each week [Col. 1518A] until evening. He is not to separate from his own lawful wife, lest he fall into the abyss of fornication—a thing which we hope may not happen. But if the end of his life should draw near before the completion of the three-year course, let him partake of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; otherwise, let what we have prescribed above be done. Yet if, in every flourishing action and best work, you see his conversion [Note: [Col. 1517] manner of life: Burchard, Ivo] and fountain of tears springing up, let *your* watchful concern appear more humane toward him and show itself gentle in all things [Note: [Col. 1517] in all: the older collected editions].

C. XVI. After worthy penance, lawful marriages are permitted to young persons. Likewise. [Note: [Col. 1517D] Ivo cites this, as also the following passage, as from Nicholas to Archbishop Charles and his suffragans. The same passage occurs in the Council of Worms, c. 33, except that, in place of the words, “having fallen, that she may not be led into the abyss of fornication,” it reads: “having fallen into fornication, let it be permitted” [Col. 1518C] [Note: [Col. 1517] In the original in Harzheim it reads as in Gratian, except that after the word *chaos* it adds: “let it be accomplished.”].] [Note: [Col. 1517] c. 33, Council of Worms, held A.D. 868.—Collected Treatises, part 1, tome 62, c. 22.]

[Col. 1518B] **Eighth Part.** If anyone has fornicated with two sisters, or with those persons concerning whom Holy Scripture gives a prohibition, and has performed worthy penance but has not been able to endure the continence of chastity, let him be permitted to take a lawful wife in marriage. The same applies to a woman [Note: [Col. 1517] woman: original—the older collected editions, except Lyons II and III] who has fallen into such a crime, so that she may not be led into the abyss of fornication. But we establish this only concerning lay men and women.

C. XVII. Let one who commits these crimes be punished, yet not put away his lawful wife. Likewise. [Note: [Col. 1517] Ibid., c. 34.—Regino, bk. 2, c. 228. Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 7, c. 64; *Decrees*, part 1, c. 138, part 9, c. 36, cite it from the letter of Nicholas to Archbishop Charles.—Collected Treatises, same part, c. 23.]

If anyone has fornicated with a spiritual mother [Note: [Col. 1518C] “With a mother.” Thus in the *Panormia* and in Ivo, part 9, c. 36; but in his part 1, [Col. 1518D] c. 138, it reads: “if anyone with a co-mother,” as also in the Council of Worms.], he is struck by the blows of anathema, as you know. Likewise we decree that he be struck who has committed the crime of fornication with her whom he received from the sacred font of baptism, or [Col. 1518C] with her whom he held before the bishop when she was anointed with holy chrism; nevertheless, let him not put away [Note: [Col. 1517] be compelled to put away: Ivo, *Decrees*, part 9, and *Panormia*—puts away: part 1] the lawful wife, if he has one [Note: [Col. 1517] has had: original—Ivo].

**Ninth Part.** § 1. For those whom God has joined together, no human judge ought to separate by his own authority. [Note: [Col. 1518D] “For those whom”: These words are not in the Council of Worms or Ivo, but almost the same words occur in the *Panormia*.] [Note: [Col. 1517] “A human being ought not to separate”: Ivo, *Panormia*.]

Although Isidore [Note: [Col. 1517] Cf. Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, bk. 2, c. 19.] understands this differently, saying:

C. XVIII. A human being does not separate those whom punishment condemns.

“What God has joined together, let no human being separate.” [Note: [Col. 1517] Matt. 19:6.] You ask [Col. 1519A] how? Supply: violently, unlawfully, without reason. Those whom God has joined together, let no human being separate. For a human being does not separate those whom punishment condemns, whom guilt accuses, whom wrongdoing restrains.

Gratian. But this must be understood as said of those whom secular judges strike for their crimes with the severity of the laws, whom they either punish by death or order deported.

C. XIX. On the same matter. Likewise from the Sixth Council of Toledo, c. 8. [Note: [Col. 1519] Held A.D. 638.—Collected Treatises, part 2, tome 38, c. 3.]

**Tenth Part.** It is the judgment of the ancient and most holy father, Pope Leo [Note: [Col. 1519] “This is”: Venice I and II, Paris, Lyons], that he who, while in the age of youth, fearing the possibility of death, has come [Note: [Col. 1519] if he has come: the older collected editions] to the remedy of penance, if perhaps he has been married and is incontinent, should return to his former marriage, lest he afterward incur a fall into adultery, until through maturity of age he may attain the state of continence. [Col. 1520A] We judge the same concerning women as concerning men. [Note: [Col. 1519] “As”: same editions.—“And so”: original—Paris and Lyons—“and thus”: the remaining editions.] This, indeed, is not prescribed generally and canonically [Note: [Col. 1519] “Lawfully” precedes: same edition], but is plainly an indulgence granted *by us* [Note: [Col. 1519] by you: the older collected editions except Strasbourg] on account of human frailty, and for this reason only: if the one who is not bound by the laws of penance should die before one of them has, by mutual consent [Note: [Col. 1519] common consent: Basel and Lyons], returned to continence, the survivor may not pass again to the embraces of a wife. [Note: [Col. 1519C] “One of them”: In the old editions of the councils the reading is “of them,” whence; in one Vatican manuscript, “the other of the same persons”; in the royal Lucchese manuscript, “has gone to their continence” [Note: [Col. 1519] thus the Hispanic Collection]; but in the later Cologne editions, “let the other go to continence, from which he has returned.” Accordingly, amid such great variation, Gratian’s received reading has been retained, since it is also found in the manuscript copies of his work.]

But if the life of the one who has not received [Note: [Col. 1519] has received: the older collected editions] absolution [Note: [Col. 1519] blessing: Hispanic Collection] as a penitent survives, let that person marry, if unable to remain continent, and enjoy the companionship of another wife. That this has been decreed by us concerning both sexes in the same manner [Note: [Col. 1519] “In”: the older collected editions.—“In the same manner”: same editions—Hispanic Collection.—“We … decreed”: Hispanic Collection] is plainly evident: namely, that in all these matters [Note: [Col. 1519] “In all these”: same edition—the older collected editions except Paris and Lyons] the decision of the priest should be awaited, so that, according as he sees a suitable age [Note: [Col. 1519] completed age: Hispanic Collection] or foresees it [Note: [Col. 1519] foresees: same collection—Basel edition], he may prescribe the rule of penitential absolution [Note: [Col. 1519] continence, with “absolution” omitted: Hispanic Collection], *or strictness*.

# TREATISE ON PENANCE

[Note: [Col. 1519C] Gratian brought forward much material to explain this third question. Those who followed him divided this very long treatise into seven distinctions. In the older copies there is no division into distinctions; [Col. 1520C] in some, however, the margin merely reads: “First Distinction,” “Second,” and so forth.] [Note: [Col. 1519] Rubric: “Treatise on Penance”: absent from the older collected editions except Paris and Lyons.]

## QUESTION III

[Col. 1519]

[Col. 1519B] **GRATIAN**

Having briefly run through these matters, in which we have wandered somewhat beyond the end of the business, let us return to the treatment of the third question of the proposed case, in which it is asked:

## DISTINCTION I

**GRATIAN**

**First Part.** Whether anyone can make satisfaction to God by contrition of heart alone [Note: [Col. 1520C] “Whether by contrition alone”: These words must be joined with what precedes, as they are joined in the very ancient copies; for they depend upon it.] and secret satisfaction, without oral confession, let us return to this. For there are those who say that anyone may obtain pardon for a crime without making confession to the Church [Col. 1520B] and without priestly judgment, according to that statement of Ambrose on Luke, at chapter 22.

C. I. [Note: [Col. 1519] Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 17.—Cf. Luke 22.]

Peter grieved and wept because, being human, he had erred. I do not find what he said; I find [Note: [Col. 1519] I know that he wept: the older collected editions] that he wept. I read of his tears; I do not read of his satisfaction.

C. II. Likewise. [Note: [Col. 1520C] The following was added: John Chrysostom [Note: [Col. 1519] thus the older collected editions—Peter Lombard, same place], though these very words are not found anywhere in his writings. But in St Ambrose, after the final words of the preceding chapter, follows: “But what cannot be defended can be washed away. Let tears wash away the sin,” etc. Nor is the sense much different in sermon 46, *On Peter’s Penance*; and the Master of the Sentences cites Ambrose.]

Let tears wash away [Note: [Col. 1519] wash: the older collected editions] the sin which shame prevents one from confessing *aloud*.

C. III. Likewise the Prophet. [Note: [Col. 1519] Ps. 50:19.]

A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.

[Col. 1521A] C. IV. Likewise. [Note: [Col. 1521] Ps. 31:5.]

I said, “I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,” and you forgave the impiety of my sin.

Explaining this, Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1521D] The beginning through the words “Not yet” is Cassiodorus’s, whom the Ordinary Gloss and the Master cite. [Col. 1522D] What follows is for the most part from St Augustine.] [Note: [Col. 1521] Ordinary Gloss on Ps. 31:5.—Peter Lombard, same place.—Cf. C. 17, q. 1, c. 4.]

C. V. God’s mercy is great [Note: [Col. 1521] the Lord’s: Basel edition], in that he forgave sins upon the promise alone.

§ 1. He has not yet uttered it with his mouth, and yet God already hears in his heart, because the very saying of it is, as it were, a kind of utterance. For a vow [Note: [Col. 1521] however: Strasbourg edition] is reckoned as a deed.

C. VI. Code, book I, *On Bishops and Clerics*: Emperor Jovian. [Note: [Col. 1521] Constitution 5, Code bk. 1, tit. 3, issued A.D. 364.—Jovinian: Böhm.—Justinian: the older collected editions.—Cf. C. 36, q. 2, c. 3.—Polycarpus, bk. 4, tit. 35.]

**Second Part.** If anyone should dare, not merely to carry off, but even to make an attempt against most sacred virgins for the purpose of contracting marriage, let him be punished by the capital penalty. [Col. 1521B] [Note: [Col. 1521] shall be punished: the older collected editions except Lyons.]

C. VII. Likewise, book II, title *On Petitioning*: Emperors Leo and Anthemius to Nicostratus, Praetorian Prefect. [Note: [Col. 1521] Final constitution, Code bk. 2, tit. 6, issued A.D. 468.]

No one may enter, whether before the tribunal of Your Magnificence, a provincial court, or any judge, into the association of advocates unless he has been instructed in the sacred mysteries of the Catholic religion. But if [Note: [Col. 1521] adds “anything else”: Basel edition—“of such persons”: the remaining editions] anything is done or attempted in any way or through some contrivance, the office of Your Sublimity shall bear, by way of condemnation, the loss of one hundred pounds of gold.

C. VIII. The same emperors. [Note: [Col. 1521] The same Augustine: the older collected editions.] Immediately afterward in the same place.

Whoever dares, contrary to the provident decree of Our Serenity, to seize the office of advocacy by surreptitious means [Note: [Col. 1521] snatch away: Basel edition], and exercises prohibited advocacy, shall be removed from the office of advocate and shall especially undergo the punishment of proscription and perpetual exile. Provincial governors are also to know that anyone under whose administration anything of this sort has been attempted shall undergo proscription of half his property and the penalty of exile for five years.

C. IX. Likewise, book IX of the Code, title *On the Julian Law of Treason*, law 5. [Note: [Col. 1521] Constitution 5, Code bk. 9, tit. 8, issued A.D. 397.—Cf. C. 6, q. 1, c. 21.]

Whoever [Note: [Col. 1521] If anyone: Strasbourg edition] has plotted with soldiers, etc. [Note: [Col. 1521] absent from the older collected editions except Paris and Lyons]—for the laws have willed that criminal intent be punished with the same severity as the completed act—*that person himself, etc.*

[Col. 1522A] Gratian. Likewise, under the Cornelian law concerning assassins: [Note: [Col. 1521] Constitution 7, Code bk. 9, tit. 16: “If anyone,” etc.] If anyone carries a weapon for the purpose of killing a human being, just as one who has killed a person, or by whose malicious fraud the act has been committed [Note: [Col. 1521] has been committed: the older collected editions], is punished under the penalty of the Cornelian law concerning assassins. [Note: [Col. 1521] may be punished: same editions.]

C. X. Emperors Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian. [Note: [Col. 1521] Constitution 8, Code, same title, issued A.D. 374.—In the older collected editions the heading both of this and of the following chapter is mutilated and corrupt.]

If anyone has undertaken, whether male or female, the crime of killing an infant [Note: [Col. 1521] has undertaken: same editions], let that person know that he or she is to be punished by capital punishment.

C. XI. Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius. [Note: [Col. 1521] Rather, the Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, constitution 9, Code, same title, issued A.D. 385.]

If a woman should be found to have laid traps for her husband’s death, or to have had the intention of killing by any other means, or if a husband should in the same way persecute [Note: [Col. 1521] in that: the older collected editions] [Col. 1522B] [Note: [Col. 1521] pursues: same editions except Lyons II and III] his wife, inquiry in the same case must be made of the entire household, not only of the husband but also of his wife—provided that she was then at home—without anyone’s defence.

C. XII. Likewise, Digest, title *On Insults*, law “But It Is a Question.” [Note: [Col. 1521] Law 47, Digest tit. 10, fragments 9 §4, 10, 11.]

If anyone attempts to make either a woman or a man, whether freeborn or freed, sexually dishonorable, he shall be liable for insult. § 1. But if the chastity of a slave has been assaulted [Note: [Col. 1521] is, an injury: the older collected editions], an action for insult is available. § 2. Chastity is said to be assaulted when something is done so that a chaste person may become unchaste. § 3. Not only the person who committed the injury—that is, who struck another—is liable for insult; included also is [Note: [Col. 1521] absent from the Strasbourg edition—liable: the remaining editions] the person who acted fraudulently or arranged for [Note: [Col. 1521] “for a jaw”: the older collected editions except Lyons II and III; evidently corrupt] another to be struck with his fist on the cheek.

[Col. 1522C] C. XIII. Likewise, in the law “With Labeo.” [Note: [Col. 1521] Same title, fragment 15.]

If a person has indeed not been struck, but hands have been raised against him [Note: [Col. 1521] adds “have been”: the older collected editions except Strasbourg, in which it reads: “If anyone who has not been struck has dared to raise hands against him”] and he has repeatedly been frightened *as though he were about to be beaten*, yet has not struck [Note: [Col. 1521] struck: the older collected editions], the offender is liable under the *useful* action for insult.

**Third Part.** On the other hand, under the title *On Punishments*: [Note: [Col. 1521] Law 48, Digest tit. 19, fragment 18.]

CAP. XIV.

No one suffers punishment for thought. [Note: [Col. 1521] may suffer: the older collected editions.]

C. XV. Likewise, under the title *On Extraordinary Crimes*. [Note: [Col. 1521] Law 47, Digest tit. 11, fragment 1.]

Solicitors of another’s marriage, and likewise disturbers of marriages, even though they cannot attain the accomplishment of their crime, are punished extra ordinem because of their intention of pernicious [Col. 1523A] lust. And below:

§ 1. Anyone who persuades a boy to sexual violation—after his companion has been taken away from him or corrupted—or solicits a woman or girl, or does anything for the sake of unchastity, provides a house [Note: [Col. 1523D] “A house.” So also in Paul’s *Sentences*, bk. 5, tit. 4, passage “Anyone who [does this] to a boy”; but the Florentine Pandects read: “a house.”] or gives a payment by which he may persuade him, is punished by death if the disgraceful act has been completed; if incomplete, he is deported to an island. Corrupted [Note: [Col. 1523] adds “however”: Basel edition] companions are subjected to the highest penalty.

C. XVI. Likewise, under the title *On Thefts*. [Note: [Col. 1523] Law 47, Digest tit. 2, fragment 21.]

The common question is whether one who takes a modius from a heap of grain commits theft of the entire thing, or only of what he took. Ofilius thinks that he is a thief of the entire heap. For one who touches another person’s ear also seems to have touched the whole person, says Trebatius. Thus one who opens a cask and takes from it a little wine [Col. 1523B] seems to have committed theft, not only of what he took but of the entire thing. [Note: [Col. 1523] seems to be a thief: original.] But the truth is that they are liable in an action for theft only to the extent of what they took. [Note: [Col. 1523] him: the older collected editions—took: Basel edition—the remaining editions.]

For if anyone opens [Note: [Col. 1523] opened: the older collected editions except Basel] a chest which he could not carry away, handles all the things in it, and then departs, later returns and takes one of them, and is caught before he carries it off to where he intended, he will be both a manifest and a non-manifest thief of the same thing. Likewise, if someone before daylight [Note: [Col. 1523D] “Before daylight”: The Florentine Pandects [Col. 1524D] read: “but one who cuts grain by daylight.”] cuts and handles a crop, he is a manifest and a non-manifest thief of that which he cuts. [Note: [Col. 1523] “Of the same thing which”: Strasbourg edition—“of that which”: Paris and Lyons.—“A manifest thief, not a non-manifest [thief]”: Basel—“is a manifest thief and will be a non-manifest thief”: Strasbourg—“is a manifest thief and will be non-manifest”: Nuremberg, Venice I and II—“is a manifest thief, and not non-manifest”: Paris and Lyons.]

C. XVII. Likewise, book II, title *Whatsoever Anyone*, law 1. [Note: [Col. 1523] Law 2, Digest tit. 2, fragment 1.]

We understand these words—“What [Note: [Col. 1523] “What [he] immediately”: Nuremberg and Basel—“He who decreed”: Paris, Venice I and II—“What those who preside over jurisdictions have decreed”: Strasbourg edition] one who presides over a jurisdiction has decreed”—as requiring effect, not merely the words. Therefore, if, when he wished to decree, he was prevented and the decree had no effect [Note: [Col. 1523] has had: Basel and Lyons], the edict fails. For the word *has decreed* signifies a thing completed and an injury consummated, not one merely begun.

C. XVIII.

Punishments—as is read in the Digest, title *On Punishments*—[Note: [Col. 1523] Law 48, Digest tit. 19, fragment 42] ought rather to be softened by interpretation of the laws than made harsher. [Note: [Col. 1523] made excessively harsher: the older collected editions.]

Gratian. Therefore they do not exceed their particular case. [Col. 1524A] But the rules that have been stated concerning the abduction of virgins, advocates, the crime of treason, or assassins were introduced in favor of religion and faith, and because of the sovereign’s hatred of assassins. In cases of insult, however, a person can become guilty in many ways according to their variety. Thus variety in crimes produces variety in punishments.

Therefore, in the Digest, title *On Punishments*: [Note: [Col. 1523] Fragment 16, same title.]

C. XIX.

**Fourth Part.** Either acts are punished, such as thefts and killings; or words, such as insults and unfaithful [Note: [Col. 1523] treacherous: Basel edition] advocacy; or writings, such as false [Note: [Col. 1523] adds “document”: the older collected editions except Basel] instruments and defamatory libels; or counsels, such as conspiracies and complicity with robbers, and those who have aided others by persuasion [Note: [Col. 1523] hinted: Paris and Lyons I—advised: the remaining editions except Lyons II and III] are treated as criminals.

§ 1. But these four kinds must be considered in seven ways: cause, person, place, time, quality, [Col. 1524B] quantity, and outcome.

§ 2. Cause: as in beatings, which are unpunished when inflicted by a teacher or parent, because they appear to have been applied for correction [Note: [Col. 1523] adds “with the intention”: the older collected editions], not for injury. But they are punished [Note: [Col. 1523] adds “however”: Basel and Lyons II] when someone is struck in anger by a stranger. [Note: [Col. 1523] is struck: the older editions except Lyons III.]

§ 3. Person is considered in two ways: that of the doer and that of the sufferer. Slaves are punished differently than free persons for the same offences; and a person who has dared something against a master or parent differently than one who has acted against a stranger, a magistrate [Note: [Col. 1523] “and against a magistrate than against”: the older editions], or a private person. In such consideration account should also be taken of age. [Note: [Col. 1523] is taken: Basel and Lyons II–III.]

§ 4. Place makes the same offense either theft or sacrilege, and makes it punishable by death or by a lesser penalty.

§ 5. Time distinguishes an absentee from a fugitive [Note: [Col. 1524D] “Furtive”: In several old manuscripts and in the original it is “fugitive.” But it has not been corrected because of the gloss.], and a breaker-in or daytime thief from a nighttime thief. [Note: [Col. 1523] and nighttime: Basel edition.]

§ 6. Quality, when [Note: [Col. 1523] absent from the older editions except Nuremberg] the act is more grievous or lighter: for example, manifest thefts are customarily distinguished from non-manifest thefts, brawls from highway assaults, plundering from theft, and wanton outrage from violence. Concerning this, Demosthenes, the greatest of Greek orators, says in his speech against Meidias: [Note: [Col. 1523] In the speech against Meidias.—The Greek words themselves with the translation—which is plainly different from that circulating in the Digest—are absent here and below from editions published before Contius.]

> For it was not the blow that provoked anger, but the dishonor itself; nor is it so terrible for free persons to be beaten—though it is terrible—as to be beaten with insult. For the man striking another, Athenians, may do many things, some of which the sufferer could not even report to another: by his posture, his look, [Col. 1525A] his voice—now behaving as an insulter, now as an enemy, now striking with his fists, now upon the cheek. These things stir and unnerve people unaccustomed to being subjected to shameful abuse.

§ 7. Quantity distinguishes a thief from a cattle-rustler. For one who steals a single pig is punished as a thief; one who steals a herd, as a cattle-rustler.

§ 8. The outcome is considered: thus deeds done by the gentlest person [Note: [Col. 1525C] “By the gentlest”: This has been corrected from the Florentine Pandects, whereas it formerly read “by the most insane” [Note: [Col. 1523] thus the older collected editions]. In the *Basilica*, bk. 60, tit. 52, law 16, this is explained thus: “A merciful and non-seditious man who takes up arms, as though for the purpose of killing, is not punished as a murderer unless the outcome also follows. But among seditious persons, even without an outcome, the intention of the mind is punished, solely because they have gone forth armed.” Thus law 1, under the Cornelian law [Col. 1526C] concerning assassins.]—although the law punishes no less one who has carried a weapon with intent to kill a person [Note: [Col. 1525] adds “been found”: same editions] than one who has killed—are considered. Therefore among the Greeks accidental cases were expiated by voluntary exile, as is written in the foremost of poets: [Note: [Col. 1525] adds “Greek”: Basel and Lyons II.—Cf. Homer, *Iliad* 23.85–88.]

> At the time when Menoetius led me, while I was still a little boy,  
> From Opus to your house, because of grievous manslaughter—  
> On the day when I killed the son of Amphidamas,  
> Foolishly and unwillingly, angered over knucklebones.

That is:

> At the time when my father led me as a boy to your house  
> From Opus, because of the dreadful killing I had done:  
> Angered over knucklebones, I killed the son of Amphidamas,  
> Unaware and at the same time unwilling.

[Col. 1525C] C. XX. [Note: [Col. 1526C] To this passage, which in the printed editions is divided as a chapter, in most old copies is attached the mark indicating that these are Gratian’s words [Note: [Col. 1525] and therefore they are printed in a different typeface].]

**Fifth Part.** Thought does not deserve punishment under civil law when it remains within its own bounds. Yet those matters which require completion by law are distinguished from wrongdoing. For in these matters the judgment of intention alone is considered.

Therefore, in the Digest, title *On Divorce*: [Note: [Col. 1525] Law 24, Digest tit. 2, fragment 3.]

C. XXI.

A divorce is not valid unless it is made with the intention of establishing a permanent [Col. 1526A] separation. [Note: [Col. 1525] dissension: original.] Therefore whatever is done or said in the heat of anger is not valid [Note: [Col. 1525] otherwise: the older collected editions] until persistence has appeared [Note: [Col. 1525] has approved: Strasbourg—has appeared: the remaining editions—Böhm] to show that it was a judgment of the mind. Consequently, if a wife returns soon after a repudiation was sent in the heat of anger, she is not considered to have been divorced. [Note: [Col. 1525] adds “by her”: the older collected editions.—“Soon”: “within a short time”: same editions.]

Hence also in the Canons: [Note: [Col. 1525] Cf. C. 2, q. 3, c. 5.]

C. XXII.

If anyone in anger charges someone with a crime, etc.

**Sixth Part.** Gratian. Augustine proves that someone may be held liable for counsel as for an act, [Note: [Col. 1525] Regino, bk. 2, c. 49 [from statements of the deacon Ferrandus]; Burchard, bk. 6, c. 31; Anselm, bk. 11, c. 45; Ivo, *Decrees*, part 10, c. 160; Polycarpus, bk. 6, tit. 10.] saying thus: [Note: [Col. 1526D] This chapter has been compiled from various passages of St Augustine: namely, bk. 3, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, c. 13; exposition of Psalms 56 and 63; and Tractates 114 and 115 on John.]

C. XXIII. Not only those who kill with their hands, but also those through whose counsel and deceit others are killed, are shown to be murderers.

[Col. 1526B] They deceive themselves perniciously [Note: [Col. 1525] dangerously: Regino, Burchard, Anselm, Ivo—the older collected editions] [Note: [Col. 1525] are deceived: the older collected editions except Basel] who think that only those are murderers who kill a person with their hands, rather than also those through whose counsel, deceit, and exhortation people are destroyed. For the Jews did not kill the Lord with their own hands, as it is written: [Note: [Col. 1525] “For it is written”: Basel edition—Cf. John 18:31.] “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone.” Yet the Lord’s death is imputed to them, because they killed him with their tongues, saying, “Crucify him, crucify him.” Therefore one Evangelist says that the Lord was crucified at the third hour, [Note: [Col. 1525] Mark 15:25] another at the sixth, [Note: [Col. 1525] Luke 23:44] because the Jews crucified him at the third hour with their tongues, and the soldiers at the sixth with their hands. Thus the one who handed a man over [Note: [Col. 1525] has handed over: Basel—hands over: Lyons II and III—Regino, Burchard, Anselm, Ivo] killed him, as the Lord says: [Note: [Col. 1525] John 19:11.] “He who handed me over to you has the greater sin.” Hence Psalm 56: “The children of men: their teeth are weapons and [Col. 1526C] arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.” [Note: [Col. 1525] Ps. 56:5.] Therefore let those by whose counsel blood is shed submit themselves to penance, if they wish to obtain pardon. [Note: [Col. 1525] wish: the older collected editions except Basel—Regino.]

C. XXIV. Killers of their brothers, their detractors, and those who hate them are accounted murderers. Likewise from the letter of Clement I to James. [Note: [Col. 1525] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter.—Burchard, bk. 6, c. 28; Anselm, bk. 11, c. 43 (42); Ivo, *Decrees*, part 10, c. 157; Polycarpus, same place.]

St Peter said that there are three kinds of murderers [Note: [Col. 1525] murderers: Burchard, Ivo] and that their punishment would be equal. [Note: [Col. 1525] perhaps: Nuremberg, Venice I and II.] For just as he declared that those who kill their brothers are murderers, so also [Col. 1527A] their detractors [Note: [Col. 1527] adds “also”: the older collected editions except Strasbourg and Basel] and those who hate them are murderers. [Note: [Col. 1527] absent from the Strasbourg edition.] For both the one who kills his brother, the one who hates him, and the one who detracts from him are equally shown to be murderers. [Note: [Col. 1527] “Has killed”: Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Venice I and II.—“Murderer … is shown”: Burchard and Ivo—“murderer … is demonstrated”: the older collected editions except Basel.]

C. XXV. In wrongful acts, intention is reckoned as the deed. Likewise Jerome on Isaiah, c. 33.

Every iniquity, oppression, and injustice is a judgment of blood; and although one does not kill with the sword, one nevertheless kills by intention. [Note: [Col. 1527] “You do not kill … you kill”: the older collected editions except Basel.]

C. XXVI. On the same matter. Likewise Cyprian, tract IV, *On Mortality*.

Did Cain, when he offered a gift to God, already kill his brother? [Note: [Col. 1527] Gen. 4.] Yet God, who foresees all things, condemned beforehand the parricide [Note: [Col. 1527] fratricide: the older collected editions] conceived in his mind. As there evil thought and pernicious conception were foreseen by God’s providence, [Col. 1527B] so also among God’s servants, in whom *confession* is contemplated and martyrdom conceived in the mind, the soul devoted to good is crowned by God the judge. For it is one thing for the mind to fail martyrdom; another for martyrdom to fail the mind. As the Lord finds you when he calls, so likewise he judges you, when he himself testifies and says: [Note: [Col. 1527] testifies and says: same editions—Cf. Rev. 2:23.] “And all the churches shall know that I am the searcher of kidneys [Note: [Col. 1527] kidneys: the older collected editions] and heart.”

C. XXVII. A murderer is one who persuades his brother to evil. Likewise Augustine, tractate XLII on John, c. 8.

Do not think that you are not a murderer when you persuade your brother to evil. If you persuade your brother to evil, you kill him. And that you may know that you kill [Note: [Col. 1527] may kill: Basel edition], hear the Psalm: [Note: [Col. 1527] Ps. 56:5.] [Col. 1527C] “The children of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp machaera [sword].” [Note: [Col. 1527] sharp sword: Vulgate—sharp sword or sharp machaera: Basel edition.]

C. XXVIII. One kills who is moved to harm. The same author, book XIX, *Against Faustus*, c. 23. [Note: [Col. 1527D] These are St Augustine’s own words: “Because they understood homicide only as the destruction of a human body, by which life was taken away, the Lord made clear,” etc.]

Homicide forbidden by the law was thought [Note: [Col. 1527] will be thought: Böhm] to be nothing other than the destruction of the body. Therefore the Lord made clear that every unjust movement to harm one’s brother is reckoned among homicide. [Note: [Col. 1527] reckoned: Strasbourg edition.]

C. XXIX. Those who do not steal solely out of fear are guilty of theft. Likewise Augustine, book L of *Homilies*, homily 28.

If you do not commit theft because you fear being seen [Col. 1528A] [Note: [Col. 1527] judged: the older collected editions except Basel], you have *committed it* inwardly; you have committed it in your heart. You are guilty of theft [Note: [Col. 1527] thief: original], though you have taken nothing.

C. XXX. The one who lacks only the opportunity does not therefore sin less. The same author, *On Free Will*, bk. I, c. 3. [Note: [Col. 1527] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 7, c. 19; *Decrees*, part 8, c. 104.]
