Even if someone has no opportunity to lie with *this* [Note: [Col. 1527] absent from Böhm] other man’s wife, yet it is in some way plain that he desires *it* and, if power were given him, would do it, he is no less guilty than if he were caught in the act itself. Likewise, as authority testifies:

§ 1. Intention [Note: [Col. 1527D] “Intention”: From this point to the end is taken from homily 26 of the *Imperfect Work on Matthew*.] is rewarded, not the deed. Intention is in contrition of heart, but the deed is in oral confession.

Gratian. It is clearer than daylight that sins are forgiven by contrition of heart, not by oral confession.

[Col. 1528B] C. XXXI. Likewise Prosper, book II, *On the Contemplative Life*, c. 7. [Note: [Col. 1527] Rather Julianus Pomerius, whose this book is.—Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 17.]

Moreover, those whose sins are hidden from human knowledge, neither confessed by themselves nor made public by others, if they refuse to confess or amend them, will have God, whom they have as witness, as their avenger also. What does it profit them to escape human judgment, when, if they remain in their evil, they are going [Note: [Col. 1527] are: the older collected editions—Böhm] to eternal punishment, God repaying them? But if they make themselves [Note: [Col. 1527] absent from Böhm—“judges of themselves”: Paris and Lyons—“they themselves judges”: the remaining editions] their own judges and, as avengers of their own iniquity, here impose voluntarily upon themselves the punishment of most severe correction, they will exchange eternal punishments for temporal ones, and with tears flowing from true compunction of heart will quench [Note: [Col. 1527] restrain: Basel—cool: Strasbourg—extinguish: Nuremberg, Paris, Lyons] the fires of eternal flame.

[Col. 1528C] C. XXXII. And below in the same place. [Note: [Col. 1528D] In most ancient copies this chapter is joined to the preceding one; in some, moreover, what follows as far as the chapter “Medicine” is also joined.] [Note: [Col. 1527] Peter Lombard, same place.]

They will more readily make God propitious to themselves who, not convicted by human judgment but voluntarily acknowledging their crime [Note: [Col. 1527] “but”: editions Basel, Lyons II and III.], either disclose it by their own confessions, or, while others remain unaware (as such persons are hidden [Note: [Col. 1527] add: “themselves”: Basel edition]), themselves pronounce upon themselves the sentence of voluntary excommunication; and, separated from the altar at which they ministered, not in disposition but in office, mourn their life as though dead—certain that, once God has been reconciled to them through the fruits of efficacious repentance [Note: [Col. 1527] “having been reconciled”: collected editions; “by God”: the same editions], they will not only recover what they lost, but, made citizens of the heavenly city, attain eternal joys.

[Col. 1529A] **Seventh Part.** Gratian. The same point is proved by that prophetic authority [Note: [Col. 1529] Ezekiel 33:12.]: “At whatever hour the sinner turns and groans,” etc. For it is not said, “when he has confessed with his mouth,” but only, “when he has turned and groaned, he shall live and shall not die.” Hence the Prophet also says [Note: [Col. 1529] Joel 2:13.]:

**C. XXXIII.**

“Rend your hearts, and not your garments” [Note: [Col. 1529] add: “your”: Vulgate; editions Basel, Lyons II and III.].

Gratian. He shows that sins are forgiven in contrition of heart, understood in the rending of the heart, and not in confession of the mouth, which is a part of outward satisfaction and which he designated by the rending of garments—understanding the whole from a part.

Hence also the Lord says through the same Prophet [Note: [Col. 1529D] This sentence has been compiled from the words of Joel, chapter 2, and Zechariah, chapter 1.] [Note: [Col. 1529] Joel, ibid., verse 12; Zechariah 1:3.]:

**C. XXXIV.**

[Col. 1529B] “Turn to me with your whole heart, and I will turn to you.”

Gratian. Conversion is so called as though it were a turning of the heart in every direction. If our heart is turned wholly away from evil toward God, it immediately earns the fruit of its conversion: God, turning from wrath to mercy, grants pardon for the sin for which He had first been preparing vengeance. Hence it is understood that, even while the mouth is silent, we can obtain pardon.

Thus also those lepers [Note: [Col. 1529] Compare Luke 17.] whom the Lord commanded to show themselves to the priests were cleansed on the way, before they came to the priests. From this event it is certainly understood that, before we show our mouths to the priests—that is, before we confess our sins—we are cleansed from the leprosy of sin.

So too Lazarus [Note: [Col. 1529] John 11.] came forth alive [Col. 1529C] from the tomb. He was not first brought out of the tomb and then raised by the Lord; rather, after the stone closing the tomb had been removed, he revived in the sepulchre and came forth alive.

§ 1. Again, in order that the Lord might show that the sinner is cleansed not by priestly judgment but by the generosity of divine grace, He cleansed the leper by touching him [Note: [Col. 1529] Matthew 8.] and afterwards commanded him to offer the sacrifice prescribed by the law to the priest. For the leper is touched when the sinner’s mind, illuminated by the regard of divine mercy, is pierced with compunction.

Thus, after his threefold denial, Peter [Note: [Col. 1529] Luke 22.], when the Lord looked upon him, shed bitter tears by which he washed away the guilt of his denial. The leper presents himself to the priest when the penitent confesses his sin to the priest. He offers the sacrifice prescribed by the law when he performs in deeds the satisfaction imposed upon him by the judgment of the Church. But before he comes to the priest, he is cleansed, when forgiveness of sin is granted through contrition of heart before confession with the mouth.

Again, physicians are said not to raise anyone so that, once raised, he may confess, since it is said through the Prophet [Note: [Col. 1529] Psalm 87:11.]: “Will physicians raise the dead, and will they confess to you?” Likewise [Note: [Col. 1529] Ecclesiasticus 17:26.]: “From the dead, as the authority says, confession perishes, as from one who is not.”

Therefore that penitent man, terrified by fear of the eighth day, had cried out [Note: [Col. 1529] Psalm 6:2, 5–6.]: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger”; later, in supplication, he said: “Save me for the sake of your mercy, for in death there is none who remembers you; but in hell none shall confess to you.”

If, therefore, none shall confess unless he has been raised, while no one who is a child of eternal [Col. 1530B] Gehenna and deserving of perpetual damnation lives, it is clear that before anyone confesses sin, he is absolved, through the grace of inward compunction, from the guilt of his transgression, for which eternal punishments were due to him.

§ 2. Again: if, before anyone confesses, he is raised by the Lord, then either, once raised, he lives while he confesses, or after being raised he is dead again and confesses. But just as, while dead before he was raised, he could not confess, so, once dead after resurrection, he cannot confess. It remains, therefore, that when raised he lives while he confesses sin [Note: [Col. 1529D] “Confesses”: here the printed editions inserted: “Therefore contrition alone, in which resurrection takes place, removes sin” [thus in the collected editions except Basel]; these words are absent from most and from the better manuscripts of Gratian.]. Thus he has his raiser present with him and dwelling within him.

Therefore Augustine says on Psalm 70 [Note: [Col. 1529D] In the Ordinary Gloss on Psalm 70, at “You have taught me, O God,” and “Wonders,” these words are cited from Augustine: “What is more wonderful than to raise the dead? A body once raised lives even when its raiser is absent; not so a soul raised without God.” This thought is more fully expounded by St Augustine in his second sermon on the same Psalm.]:

**C. XXXV.**

[Col. 1530C] “A body once raised lives when its raiser is absent. But a soul raised does not live in the same way.”

Gratian. Since God is the life of the soul and the soul the life of the body, just as the body cannot live when the soul is absent, so the soul can live only when God is present. The soul therefore has God present to it through grace; living by that grace, it confesses its sin, and the Life which is God dwells in it and, by dwelling there, makes it live.

But if He dwells in it, it has become a temple of the Holy Spirit; therefore it is enlightened; therefore it is cleansed from the darkness of sins; therefore it has ceased to be a temple of the devil, since it has come to the light, whose presence drives away darkness. For there is no, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1529] 2 Corinthians 6:15.], fellowship of Christ with Belial, no participation of light with darkness, no communion of righteousness and iniquity, [Col. 1531A] no agreement of the temple of God with idols.

Likewise, as Christ says [Note: [Col. 1531] John 3:20.], “Everyone who hates evil acts in the light.” But whoever acts in the light, as Augustine says, works in Christ. Whoever works in Christ is proved to be His son. For each person is said to be the son of the one whose works he does.

Hence the Lord says to some [Note: [Col. 1531] John 8:39 and following.], “If you are children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham.” Again: “You are of your father the devil, because you wish to do the works of your father.” No one, however, can be the son of God and of the devil at the same time. For no one, as He himself says [Note: [Col. 1531] Matthew 6:24.], can serve two masters.

Likewise, as John says in his First Epistle, chapter 3:

**C. XXXVI.**

“Whoever has been born of God does not sin” [Note: [Col. 1531] 1 John 3:9.].

Gratian. Therefore he is not a son of the devil either. For we are children of the devil through sin alone. Therefore we have been transferred from his kingdom into the kingdom of the charity of the Son of God, and we have been delivered [Note: [Col. 1531] Colossians 1:13.] from the power of darkness and made children of light.

Since, then, as has been proved, before confession we have been raised through grace and made children of light, it is most evident that sin is forgiven through contrition of heart alone, without confession of the mouth.

**C. XXXVII.** Likewise John, in the same place [Note: [Col. 1531] 1 John 3:14.]:

“Everyone who does not love” [Note: [Col. 1531] add: “God”: editions Basel, Paris, and Lyons.] “remains in death.”

Gratian. If, then, he lives, he loves; if he loves, love is in his heart; but love is not in evil. For it is the proper fountain of good things, in which what is alien has no share.

Therefore this man has been made good through grace before confession of sin; hence he is not evil, for no one can be both good and evil at the same time. But if [Col. 1531C] he is not evil, he is shown not to be a member of the devil; therefore he is not worthy of Gehenna, which is owed only to the devil and his members, just as eternal blessedness is prepared only for Christ. Thus sin is not forgiven in confession, since it is proved already to have been forgiven. Confession therefore takes place for the manifestation of repentance, not for the obtaining of pardon; and just as circumcision was given to Abraham [Note: [Col. 1531] Compare Genesis 17.] as a sign of righteousness, not as the cause of justification, so confession is offered to the priest as a sign of pardon received, not as the cause of pardon still to be received.

**Second Part.** § 1. Others, on the contrary, testify that without confession of the mouth and satisfaction in deed no one can be cleansed from sin, if he has had time to make satisfaction. [Col. 1531D] Hence the Lord says through the Prophet [Note: [Col. 1531] Isaiah 43:26.], “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified.”

[Col. 1532A] **C. XXXVIII.** Likewise Ambrose, *On Paradise*, chapter 14 [Note: [Col. 1531] Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 17.]:

“No one can be justified from sin unless he has first confessed his sin.”

**C. XXXIX.** The same, in the First Sermon for Lent [Note: [Col. 1531] The learned editors reject this sermon as not by Ambrose—Peter Lombard, ibid.]:

“Behold, now is the acceptable time, in which confession frees the soul from death, confession opens paradise, confession gives hope of salvation. Hence Scripture says [Note: [Col. 1531] Isaiah 43:26.], ‘Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified.’

“These words show that one who does not wish to confess sins during life [Note: [Col. 1531] “has not wished”: Basel; “did not wish”: the other editions] does not deserve to be justified. Therefore that confession [Note: [Col. 1531] omitted in the Basel edition] frees us [Note: [Col. 1531] “you”: the same edition; “not”: the original] which is made with repentance.

“§ 1. True repentance [Note: [Col. 1531] Compare D. 3, *On Penance*, c. 1.] is sorrow of heart and bitterness of soul for the evils [Note: [Col. 1531] “through evils”: Basel] that each person has committed [Note: [Col. 1531] add: “or”: Basel; add: “or consented to”: collected editions.]. Repentance is also [Note: [Col. 1531] *et* (“and”) is absent from Böhm.] to mourn past evils and not to commit again what must be mourned.”

**C. XL.** Likewise John Chrysostom, in the homily *On Repentance* beginning “With provident mind” [Note: [Col. 1531] Omitted as spurious in the Maurist edition—Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 17; compare D. 3, *On Penance*, c. 8.]:

“Perfect repentance compels the sinner willingly to endure all things. And below: § 1. In his heart, contrition; in his mouth, confession; in his work, complete humility [Note: [Col. 1531] “complete”: *toto*, Böhm]: this is fruitful repentance.”

**C. XLI.** The same [Note: [Col. 1531] Rather, Chromatius; compare c. 4, distinction 4, *On Consecration*.]:

“No one can receive the grace of the heavenly gift of God [Note: [Col. 1531] “God”: collected editions.] unless he has first [Note: [Col. 1531] omitted in the editions Arg., Basel, and Nor.] been cleansed from every stain of sin through penitential confession, through the gift of saving baptism.”

**C. XLII.** Likewise Augustine, *On Continence*, chapter 6 [Note: [Col. 1531] Anselm, book 11, c. 142; Polycarpus, book 6, title 20; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 17.]:

[Col. 1532C] “No one receives pardon for a deservedly heavier punishment unless he has paid some punishment, even though it be far less than he ought. For God’s abundance of mercy is granted in such a way that the justice of discipline is not abandoned *either*.”

**C. XLIII.** The same to Vincentius, Epistle XLVIII [Note: [Col. 1531] Epistle 93, Maurist edition, written A.D. 408; Anselm, book 11, c. 168; Polycarpus, ibid.; in Venetian editions I and II attributed to Innocent.]:

“Do not suppose that anyone [Note: [Col. 1531] “nor anyone”: the original.] can pass from error to truth, or [Note: [Col. 1531] “and”: collected editions] from any sin, whether great or small, to correction [Note: [Col. 1531] “corruption”: Venice II; “reproof”: the other editions except Paris and Lyons], without repentance.”

**C. XLIV.** The same, in the book of Fifty Homilies, Homily 49, *On Repentance* [Note: [Col. 1531] Compare D. 34, c. 6; Polycarpus, ibid.; Peter Lombard, ibid.]:

“Do the repentance that is done in the Church, so that the Church may pray for you. Let no one say to himself: ‘I do it secretly; I do it before God; God knows, who forgives me [Col. 1532D] [Note: [Col. 1531] “may forgive”: editions Venice II, Paris, and Lyons], because [Note: [Col. 1531] “which”: collected editions] I do it in my heart.’

“Then it was said in vain [Note: [Col. 1531] Matthew 16:19.], ‘What you loose on earth shall be loosed also in [Col. 1533A] heaven.’ Then the keys were given to the Church of God in vain; we make void the Gospel of God [Note: [Col. 1533] “word”: collected editions except Arg.], we make void Christ’s words; we promise you [Note: [Col. 1533] “if we promise”: Basel and Lyons] by words [Note: [Col. 1533] “to you”: Basel and Lyons II] what He denies. Do we not deceive you?

“Job says [Note: [Col. 1533] Job 31:33.], ‘If I was ashamed to confess my sins before the people.’ And therefore [Note: [Col. 1533D] These two words, “And therefore,” were added by the compiler because he changed the order of Augustine’s words. In Augustine, what follows here precedes what was set above.], if you could not preserve, or did not wish to preserve [Note: [Col. 1533] “you wished”: Arg.], marital chastity or continence, and have strayed from your purpose—whether from the marriage bond or from a commitment to continence—let there be in you the sorrow and humility of repentance.

“I speak more plainly: let no one say, ‘I did not understand.’ You [Note: [Col. 1533] “because”: collected editions] who have defiled yourselves after your wives by unlawful intercourse—if you have lain with any woman besides your wives—do repentance, etc.”

**C. XLV.** Likewise Jerome on Exodus [Note: [Col. 1533D] Here too, as has often elsewhere been observed, Origen’s eleventh homily on Exodus 18 is cited under the name of St Jerome.] [Note: [Col. 1533] Rather, Origen, Homily 11 on Exodus.]:

**Second Part.** “And Aaron,” he says [Note: [Col. 1533] Exodus 18:12.], “came, and all the elders [Col. 1533B] of Israel, to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law in the presence of God” [Note: [Col. 1533] “the Lord”: Basel.].

Therefore all that the saints do, they do in the presence of God [Note: [Col. 1533] “the Lord”: ibid.]; but sinners [Note: [Col. 1533] singular, “the sinner”—the original] flee from the presence of God. Indeed, it is written that Adam, after he sinned, fled from God’s presence and, when questioned, replied [Note: [Col. 1533] Genesis 3:10.], “I heard [Note: [Col. 1533] add: “he said”: collected editions] your voice [Note: [Col. 1533] add: “and your”: Arg.] and hid myself, because I was naked.”

Cain also, *after* he had *been* condemned by God for parricide [Note: [Col. 1533] “fratricide”: the original and collected editions], “went out” [Note: [Col. 1533] Genesis 4:16.] [Note: [Col. 1533] “went out”: the original and collected editions except Arg., Paris, and Lyons II–III], it says, “from the face of God and dwelt in the land of Noim.” Therefore one who is unworthy of God’s [Note: [Col. 1533] “his”: collected editions] sight departs from the face of God. But the saints eat and drink in God’s presence, and do all that they do in His [Note: [Col. 1533] “God’s”: the same editions] presence.

Examining this passage more deeply, I see that those who receive fuller knowledge of God and are more fully [Col. 1533C] instructed in divine teaching, even if they do evil, do it before God [Note: [Col. 1533] “the Lord”: Basel] and in His presence, like the one who said [Note: [Col. 1533] “says”: Böhm; compare Psalm 50:6.], “Against you alone have I sinned, and done evil before you.”

What [Note: [Col. 1533] The words “What” through “this” are absent from the Basel edition], then, does one who does evil before God have in addition? Certainly this [Note: [Col. 1533] “This” through “this” are omitted in the collected editions except Lyons]: he repents at once and says, “I have sinned.” But one who departs from God’s presence does not know how to turn back and purge his sin by repentance [Note: [Col. 1533] “be purified”: Basel]. This, therefore, is the difference between doing evil before God [Note: [Col. 1533] “the Lord”: the same edition] and sinning after departing from God’s [Note: [Col. 1533] “his”: the same edition] presence.

[Col. 1534A] **C. XLVI.** Likewise Ambrose, *On Repentance*, book II, chapter 4 [Note: [Col. 1534D] This chapter was formerly cited as Augustine’s [thus the collected editions]; it has been restored from Ambrose, and the Scriptural passage has been corrected from him, for it follows the Septuagint reading.]:

“But immediately He who had said [Note: [Col. 1533] Hosea 11:8, according to the Septuagint.], ‘I shall make you like Adama and like Seboim’—two cities which, through their proximity to Sodom, shared the same destruction—said: ‘My heart has been turned’ [Note: [Col. 1533] “My heart has turned within me; my repentance has been troubled”: collected editions]; in that very thing my repentance has been troubled; ‘I will not act according to the anger of my wrath.’

“Does it not therefore appear [Note: [Col. 1533] add: “therefore”: the same editions] that the Lord Jesus is angry with us when we sin so that He may turn us by the terror of His anger? His anger, then, is not the execution of vengeance but rather the working of absolution.”

**C. XLVII.** The same Ambrose, *On Paradise*, chapter 14 [Note: [Col. 1533] Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 17.]:

“The serpent [Note: [Col. 1533] Genesis 3:13.] deceived me, and I ate.” It is a pardonable fault when confession of the offence follows. Therefore [Col. 1534B] the woman was not despaired of, because she did not keep silence before God but rather confessed her sin; and a medicinal [Note: [Col. 1533] “curable”: collected editions except Paris and Lyons] sentence followed. It is good to be condemned in sin and scourged in wrongdoing, so that we may be scourged with human beings.

Thus Cain [Note: [Col. 1533] Genesis 4.], because he wished to deny his crime [Note: [Col. 1533] “who”: collected editions], was judged unworthy to be punished in his sin, but was dismissed without a prescribed punishment [Note: [Col. 1533] “prescription”: the original]—perhaps not so much guilty [Note: [Col. 1533] omitted in the original and Basel] of the greater crime of parricide (for he committed [Note: [Col. 1533] “committed”: Basel] this against his brother) as of sacrilege, because he believed that God [Note: [Col. 1533] “who [said] to the Lord”: Basel] must be lied to, saying [Note: [Col. 1533] Genesis 4:9.], “I do not know; am I my brother’s keeper?”

Therefore his accusation was reserved for the devil, his accuser, so that he may be scourged with the devil and his angels [Note: [Col. 1533] “with him and his”: collected editions except Arg.], since he did not wish to be scourged with human beings.

And in *On Repentance*, book I, chapter 1:

§ 1. For that evangelical shepherd [Note: [Col. 1533] Luke 15.] is read to have carried the fallen sheep [Col. 1534C] and not cast it away; and Solomon says [Note: [Col. 1533] Ecclesiastes 7:17.], “Do not be excessively [Note: [Col. 1533] “too”: collected editions] righteous.” Moderation must temper righteousness. For how can one offer himself to you to be cured [Note: [Col. 1533] “present himself to be cured”: the same editions] if you regard him with disgust [Note: [Col. 1533] “have him in contempt”: the same editions]? He will think that he is to be an object of contempt, not of compassion, to his physician.

**C. XLVIII.** Likewise Ambrose, in the same book I, *On Repentance*, chapter 11:

“I gladly forgive; I readily pardon; I prefer mercy [Note: [Col. 1533] Hosea 6:6.] to sacrifice, because by [Note: [Col. 1533] “on account of”: Basel] sacrifice the righteous person is commended, but by mercy the sinner is redeemed. ‘I came not’ [Note: [Col. 1533] Matthew 9:13.] ‘to call the righteous, but sinners.’ In the law there is sacrifice; in the Gospel, mercy. The law [Note: [Col. 1535] John 1:17.] was given through Moses; grace through me.”

**C. XLIX.** Likewise Leo, bishop, to Theodore, bishop of Forum Julii, Epistle LXXXIX, alternatively XCI [Note: [Col. 1535D] This chapter, as it appears in Gratian, agrees more closely with the printed original among the works of St Leo than with the version in the volumes of councils.] [Note: [Col. 1535] Epistle 108, Ballerini edition, written A.D. 452; Anselm, book 11, c. 13; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 17.]:

God’s manifold mercy so assists human falls that the hope of eternal life is restored not only through the grace of baptism but also [Note: [Col. 1535] omitted in Lyons II and III] through the remedy of repentance. Those who have violated the gift of regeneration [Note: [Col. 1535] “gifts”: Ballerini, the Hispanic Collection, and the collected editions], condemning themselves by their own judgment, may attain remission of their crimes; yet the aids of divine goodness [Note: [Col. 1535] “will”: collected editions] have been so ordained that God’s pardon [Note: [Col. 1535] “pardon ... may obtain”: collected editions] cannot be obtained except through the prayers of priests.

For Christ Jesus, the human mediator between God and human beings [Note: [Col. 1535] add: “the Lord”: the same editions; Hispanic Collection], handed over this power to the rulers of the Church: [Col. 1535B] both to impose penitential satisfaction [Note: [Col. 1535] “action”: Ballerini; “sanction”: Hispanic Collection] upon those who confess and to admit to communion of the sacraments, through the gate of reconciliation, those cleansed by that saving satisfaction.

And shortly afterward:

§ 1. “But if anyone for whom we pray to the Lord, intercepted by any obstacle whatever, departs from the benefit of present pardon [Note: [Col. 1535] “falls away”: the same editions] and ends temporal life in the human condition before reaching the appointed remedies [Note: [Col. 1535] “might reach”: Hispanic Collection], he cannot obtain when stripped of flesh [Note: [Col. 1535] “from the flesh”: Arg.] what, while remaining in the body, he did not receive [Note: [Col. 1535] “received”: the same collection, Ballerini, and editions Arg. and Basel].”

And shortly afterward:

§ 2. “Those, however, who in a time of necessity and under the urgent pressure of danger seek the aid of repentance and immediately reconciliation must be denied neither satisfaction nor reconciliation, because we can impose neither measures [Col. 1535C] [Note: [Col. 1535] “a measure”: collected editions except Basel] nor time-limits upon God’s mercy [Note: [Col. 1535] “impose”: editions Arg., Noricum, Venice I and II, and Paris]; conversion suffers no delay with Him in whose presence it occurs.”

### C. LVII. Likewise Cyprian, Bishop, Book IV, Letter 2, to Antonianus

[Note: [Col. 1539] Written A.D. 252.]

I am astonished that some are so obstinate as to think that repentance should not be granted to the fallen, or that forgiveness should be denied to those who repent, although it is written: “Remember from where you have fallen; repent, and do the former works.” This is plainly said to one known to have fallen, and whom the Lord urges to rise again through works, because it is written: “Almsgiving delivers from death”—not, of course, from that death which Christ’s blood once extinguished, and from which the grace of saving baptism and of our Redeemer has delivered us, but from that death which afterwards creeps in through sins.

### C. LVIII. Likewise Jerome to Damasus

[Note: [Col. 1539] A letter of uncertain date.]

The importunate woman in the Gospel at last deserved to be heard; and, though the door was shut with bolts, a friend received bread from his friend even at midnight. God himself, who cannot be overcome by any forces opposed to him, is conquered by the prayers of the tax collector. The city of Nineveh, which had perished through sin, stood firm through tears. Why have these things been repeated in such a lengthy preface? Clearly, that you who are great may look upon the little one, and that you, a wealthy shepherd, may not despise the sick sheep. Christ brought the robber from the cross into paradise; and, lest anyone should regard a late conversion as too late, he made the penalty of murder into martyrdom. Christ, I say, joyfully embraces the returning prodigal son; and, leaving ninety-nine sheep, he carries on the good shepherd’s shoulders the one little sheep which had remained behind.

### III. Part. Gratian

But it seems false that, on Ambrose’s authority, forgiveness is promised to everyone who sins. For forgiveness is denied to some, either on account of the magnitude of the sin or on account of their rank of office. Thus John says in his letter: “There is a sin unto death. Who shall pray for it?” Elsewhere it is also read: “Who will heal an enchanter wounded by a serpent?”

[Note: [Col. 1539] 1 John 5:16.]

[Note: [Col. 1539] “I do not say that anyone should pray for that person”: Vulgate.]

[Note: [Col. 1539] Ecclesiasticus 12:13.]

### C. LIX. Likewise

[Note: [Col. 1540C] In the First Book of Kingdoms, chapter 2 [v. 25], it is read: “If a man sins against a man, God can be appeased for him; but if he sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?” Thus it is cited by St Ambrose, *On Repentance*, Book 1, chapter 8, and by other Fathers. Yet St Gregory, on chapter 2 of First Kings, chapter 3, draws from this very Vulgate reading the proposition which Gratian now advances, as was noted above, Distinction 50, chapter *Alienum*.]

If a priest sins, who will pray for him?

### Gratian

But questions of this kind do not always imply a negation; rather, they indicate difficulty or rarity, as in the Gospel saying: “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent servant?” Hence Ambrose also says: “O God, who is like you?” Certainly not “no one,” because the Son is the image of the Father. Thus the saying, “Who will pray for him?” should be understood similarly: that is, someone of exceptional life must pray for the person who has sinned against the Lord. And below:

For how could John say that one should not pray for the graver offence, when he had read that Moses prayed and obtained his request where there was deliberate transgression, and when he knew that Jeremiah too had prayed?

§ 1. John’s statement may also be understood differently, according to Augustine, “There is a sin unto death,” and so there is no contradiction between it and the foregoing. For he says: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for that person.” Since the nature of this sin is not specified, many different opinions may be held. But I say that it is the sin of abandoning, until death, the faith which works through love. This is also blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which the Lord declared in the Gospel shall be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come. Whether a person perseveres in sin until death through delight in sin or through despair of forgiveness, it is just that one who has sinned without end should be punished without end.

[Note: [Col. 1541] Matthew 24:45.]

[Note: [Col. 1541] Ambrose, *On Repentance*, Book 1, chapter 8.]

[Note: [Col. 1541] Psalm 82:1.]

[Note: [Col. 1541] Ambrose, ibid., chapter 9.]

[Note: [Col. 1541] Augustine, *On Correction and Grace*, chapter 12.]

[Note: [Col. 1541] 1 John 5:16.]

[Note: [Col. 1541] Matthew 12:32.]

### C. LX. Hence Pope Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 43

[Note: [Col. 1541] Anselm, Book 11, chapter 153.]

The wicked would, if they could, live without end so that they could sin without end. For they show that they always desire to live in sin, since they never cease sinning while they live. Therefore it belongs to the great justice of the Judge that those who in this life never wished to be without sin should never be without punishment.

[Note: [Col. 1541] *utique* (“certainly”): original.]

[Note: [Col. 1541] *desistunt*: Basel edition.]

### IV. Part. Gratian

From these passages, therefore, it appears that sin is not forgiven without confession by the mouth and satisfaction through works. For if it is necessary that we declare our iniquities so that we may afterwards be justified; if no one can be justified from sin unless he has first confessed his sin; if confession opens paradise and obtains forgiveness; if only that confession is useful which is made with repentance—where it is noted that confession is one thing and repentance another, whether repentance be understood as inward or outward; if the person who promises forgiveness to one repenting secretly before God but not before the Church makes the Gospel and the keys given to the Church void, and also promises what God denies to the offender; if no one can obtain forgiveness unless he has paid some penalty for sin, however small and even if less than he ought; if the power of binding and loosing has been entrusted by God to priests alone; if no one receives forgiveness unless he strives to obtain it through the Church’s prayers: it follows that no one abolishes the guilt of sin before oral confession and satisfaction through works.

§ 1. Finally, that it may be clearly apparent that no one is cleansed from sin without confession, let us begin at the very origin of the human race. The first parents, corrupted by the sin of transgression, were questioned by the Lord concerning their fault, so that they might erase by confession the sin they had committed by transgressing. But the serpent was not questioned concerning fault, because he was not recalled to life through confession. Likewise Cain, after adding fratricide to the first transgression, was questioned by the Lord concerning his fault, when he was told: “Where is Abel your brother?” But because in his pride he refused to confess his sin and instead attempted to deceive God by lying denial, saying, “Am I my brother’s keeper?”, he was judged unworthy of forgiveness. Hence he was plunged into the depths of despair when he said: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for.” He went forth a wanderer and fugitive from the Lord’s presence, signifying that those who conceal their sins rather than confessing them are held unworthy of the regard of divine mercy.

The kings also who, led by ignorance, had sinned against Abraham deserved to be healed only when he prayed. This signifies that afflictions of character are not healed except by the Church’s prayers. The Lord also commanded Moses that, should leprosy appear in skin, house, garment, or hair, it should be shown to the priest and, according to his judgment, be set apart and declared either unclean or clean. Likewise Saul, when he was tormented by an evil spirit, could not return to the function of a sound mind unless David first took up the psaltery and sang before him; then the devil ceased from tormenting him. This mystically shows that anyone enslaved to the devil because of sins cannot be rescued from his dominion unless David—that is, the Church—takes up the psaltery and sings before him; that is, makes him a participant in spiritual grace and, through salutary admonition, devout prayer for him, and the presentation of examples of good works, restrains the devil from his invisible tormenting of that person.

David also, after committing adultery and murder, did not hear the Prophet say, “The Lord has taken away your sin from you,” until he had confessed the sin itself. For he first confessed to the Prophet rebuking his sin, and afterwards heard: “The Lord has taken away your sin from you.” Ahab likewise, when he heard God’s threatening sentence concerning the shedding of innocent blood, clothed himself in sackcloth, making satisfaction to God through repentance. Therefore the Lord said to Elijah: “Because Ahab has reverenced my face, I shall not bring evil in his days.” The Ninevites, when they heard, “Yet forty days and Nineveh shall be overthrown,” repented at the decree of the king and princes, saying: “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him?” By this humble satisfaction they deserved to escape the impending overthrow. Their examples clearly show that no one obtains forgiveness from God unless he first makes satisfaction through repentance.

Nebuchadnezzar also, because of his pride, was changed from a rational mind into a beastlike disposition and fled, banished from his kingdom; he did not recover the kingdom until, having turned, he proclaimed God. Finally, the people of Israel, handed over to captivity because of the fault of their transgression, did not deserve liberation until, confessing their sins, they received forgiveness through the prayers of Daniel and the other saints.

§ 2. In the Gospel too, those coming to John to be baptized by him with the baptism of repentance first confessed their sins, showing that everyone must confess the sins which are to be condemned and promise renewal of a better life, if he desires to receive the grace of regeneration. Christ is also recorded to have raised some from the dead, cleansed others from leprosy, given sight to others, and restored limbs disabled by paralysis; yet in every case a request made by the person’s own voice or by friends is recorded as having preceded the healing. For, as Luke relates, he was first asked on behalf of Peter’s mother-in-law before he restored her to health. But the leper whom the Lord, coming down from the mountain, cleansed, first cried to him: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me”; and the Lord afterwards cleansed him by touching him. Likewise, when the blind man cried to him, “Have mercy on me, Son of David,” Jesus asked him: “What do you want me to do for you?” He said: “Rabboni, that I may see the light.” He also heard of three dead persons whom he restored to life at the prayers of others. He heard of a fourth from a disciple; but because the living who might pray for him were absent, he did not deserve to be raised.

§ 3. These examples most plainly make it understood that one whom the stain of a more grievous fault defiles cannot be healed unless by confession from his own mouth or by the Church’s intercession supporting him. Hence that penitent, who had first deserved to have his sins scourged because he kept silent, afterwards, once rebuked, said: “Because I kept silent, my bones grew old while I cried out all day.” Hence Christ, speaking in the person of his members, says: “Let not the deep swallow me, nor let the pit press its mouth over me.” Augustine explains this, saying: “The pit is the depth of human iniquity. If you fall into it, it will not close its mouth over you if you do not close your own mouth. Therefore confess and say, ‘Out of the depths I have cried to you, Lord,’ and you will escape. The Lord closes it over the person who despises while in the depths; from one who is dead—as though he were not—confession perishes.” Hence the same Prophet says: “Enter his gates with confession,” showing that no one can reach the gates of mercy except through confession of sin.

§ 4. Hence also blessed John the Baptist and our Savior began their preaching with repentance, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near,” showing that no one can reach the kingdom of heaven unless he has first endeavored to make satisfaction to God through repentance. Hence it is also read in the Acts of the Apostles that believers came to the Apostles, declaring their deeds.

§ 5. From all these things it is readily shown that no one can merit forgiveness without confession.

[Note: [Col. 1541] Matthew 16:19.]

[Note: [Col. 1541] Compare Genesis 3.]

[Note: [Col. 1541] Compare Genesis 12 and 26.]

[Note: [Col. 1541] Compare Leviticus 13–14.]

[Note: [Col. 1541] Compare 1 Kings 16.]

[Note: [Col. 1541] 2 Samuel 12:13.]

It is not enough to change one’s conduct for the better and withdraw from past evils, unless one also makes satisfaction to God for what has been done through the sorrow of repentance, through the groaning of humility, through the sacrifice of a contrite heart, with almsgiving and fasting cooperating.

It is one thing justly to demand what is owed; another, out of love for perfection, to disregard what is one’s own. ### C. LXVI. Likewise Jerome, on Joel, chapter 1

Whoever is a holy priest and eats at the Lord’s Passover should gird himself with the belt of chastity and hear with the Apostles: “Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands.” But whoever is a sinner and is reproved by his own conscience should gird himself with sackcloth, mourn either his own offences or those of the people, enter the church from which he had departed because of sins, and lie or sleep in sackcloth, so that through severity of life he may compensate for the past pleasures by which he had offended God.

### C. LXVIII. The same, on Daniel, chapter 4

“Therefore, O king, let my counsel please you: redeem your sins by almsgiving, and your iniquities by mercies to the poor; perhaps God will forgive your offences.” If he announced a sentence of God which cannot be changed, how does he urge almsgiving and mercies to the poor in order that God’s sentence may be changed? This is easily resolved by the example of King Hezekiah, whom Isaiah had said would die, and of the Ninevites, to whom it was said: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.” Yet at the prayers of Hezekiah and Nineveh God’s sentence was changed—not through fickleness of judgment, but through the conversion of those who deserved forgiveness. Otherwise, in Jeremiah God says that he threatens evils against a nation and, if it does good, changes his threats by clemency. Again, he asserts that he promises good things to one who acts rightly; and, if that person acts wrongly, he says that he changes his own sentence—not concerning people, but concerning works that have changed. For God is angry not with people but with vices; and when these are absent from a person, he by no means punishes what has changed.

Let us put it differently. Nebuchadnezzar indeed acted mercifully toward the poor in accordance with Daniel’s counsel, and for that reason the sentence against him was delayed until the twelfth month. But because later, walking in the palace of Babylon, he boasts and says, “Is this not great Babylon, which I have built as the house of a kingdom, by the strength of my power and for the glory of my name?” he lost the good of mercy through the evil of pride. “Perhaps God will forgive your offences.” Since blessed Daniel, foreknowing the future, doubts concerning God’s sentence, those who boldly promise forgiveness to sinners act rashly. Yet it should be known that, if forgiveness is promised to Nebuchadnezzar when he does good works, it is promised much more to others who have committed lighter sins.

[Note: [Col. 1545] Daniel 4:24.]

[Note: [Col. 1545] “in mercies”: the collected editions, first Lyons II, III.]

### C. LXIX. The same

[Note: [Col. 1545] Ordinary Gloss from Origen, Homily 3 on Judges, chapter 3.]

See the kindly Lord, mingling mercy with severity and weighing the measure of punishment itself by a just and merciful balance. He did not hand sinners over to punishment for everlasting destruction; rather, “for as long,” he says, “as they served the Baals, so long let them serve Chusarsaton”—that is, eight years. Learn this also, O hearer, whoever you are who know yourself guilty of some error: for as long as you know that you have erred, for as long as you have sinned, for that same time nonetheless humble yourself before God and make satisfaction to him in the confession of repentance. Do not wait until Chusarsaton humbles you and necessity wrings repentance from you against your will. Rather, forestall the harshness of this torturer; for if you correct yourself, if you amend yourself, God is pious and merciful, and tempers vengeance away from the one who forestalls it by repentance. But let us consider this: as long as those who had been handed over for their sins served Chusarsaton and did not cry to the Lord, no one was raised up who could save them. But when they cried to the Lord, then the Lord raised up a savior for Israel and saved them.

[Note: [Col. 1546C] *libratione* (“by a balance”): formerly the reading was *deliberatione* (“by deliberation”); the collected editions, first Basel, read *moderatione* (“by moderation”). Yet *libratione* is the reading. It was corrected from Origen’s homily, as were several other passages.]

### C. LXX. The same Jerome, on Ephesians, chapter 5

The Church of Christ is glorious, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of that kind. Therefore one who is a sinner and stained with some defilement cannot be called a member of Christ’s Church, nor be said to be subject to Christ. Yet it is possible that, just as the Church, which formerly had wrinkle and stain, was afterwards restored to youth and purity, so too the sinner may run to the physician; because the healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are ill, so that their wounds may be healed and they may become members of the Church, which is Christ’s body.

[Note: [Col. 1547] *habuerat*: original.]

### C. LXXI. The same, on Amos, chapter 1

“For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn her back.” We can say this in the tropological sense. The first sin is to think evil things. The second is to consent to perverse thoughts. The third is to carry out in deed what one has resolved in the mind. The fourth is not to repent after sin, but to take pleasure in one’s own offence.

[Note: [Col. 1547] Amos 1:3.]

[Note: [Col. 1547] *eum* (“him”): Vulgate and collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1547] Hosea 12:9.]

### C. LXXV. The same, on Daniel, chapter 9

Jeremiah had foretold seventy years of the desolation of the Temple, after which the people would again come into Judea and the Temple and Jerusalem would be built. This did not make Daniel negligent; rather, it urged him all the more to pray that what God had promised through his own mercy might be fulfilled through their prayers, lest negligence produce pride and pride produce offence.

§ 1. Finally, in Genesis we read that one hundred and twenty years of repentance were appointed before the flood. Because they refused to repent during so long a time—that is, one hundred years—God did not wait for the other twenty years also to be completed, but brought upon them before its time what he had afterwards threatened. Hence, because of the hardness of the heart of the Jewish people, Jeremiah is told: “Do not pray for this people, for I will not hear you.” And Samuel is told: “How long will you mourn for Saul? I have rejected him.” Thus, in ashes and sackcloth, Daniel asks that God’s promise be fulfilled, not because he disbelieved the future, but lest security produce negligence and negligence produce offence.

[Note: [Col. 1547] Compare Jeremiah 29 and 52.]

[Note: [Col. 1547] *venirent populi* (“the peoples would come”): Basel.]

[Note: [Col. 1547] *aedificarent*: that edition; *reaedificaretur*: Argentinian edition; *reaedificarent*: the remaining editions. Addition: *ibi* (“there”): Argentinian and Basel; *ibidem* (“in that same place”): the remaining editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1547] *in*: the collected editions, first Argentinian and Basel.]

[Note: [Col. 1547] *pariat*: the same editions, first Basel; Böhm.]

[Note: [Col. 1547] *voluerunt*: Venice I, II.]

[Note: [Col. 1547] *Hieremiae*: the same editions; compare Jeremiah 7:16.]

### C. LXXVI. We do not purchase God with works of mercy, but redeem ourselves. Likewise Ambrose, in the sermon for the Sunday concerning Abraham

[Note: [Col. 1549C] This chapter occurs in the book *On Elijah and Fasting*, and the following words precede it there: “Although we have sinned grievously, we have found a great physician; we have received the great medicine of his grace. For medicine removes great sins.” But the word “of mercy” is absent both there and from the passage in Ecclesiasticus, chapter 10.]

The medicine of mercy [Note: [Col. 1549] Ecclesiasticus, chapter 10, verse 4, according to the Septuagint.] takes away great sins. We *also* have [Note: [Col. 1549] Böhm reads *enim*, “for.”] further means by which to redeem our sins [Note: [Col. 1549] “We redeem”: the editions consulted.]: you have money—redeem your sin. The Lord is not for sale; rather, you yourself are for sale. You have been sold under your sins; redeem yourself by your works, redeem yourself with your money. Money [Note: [Col. 1549] “Nothing is cheaper than money”: Argentinian edition.—“Money is cheap”: the remaining editions.—Addition: “your”: Basel edition.] is cheap, but mercy is precious.

§ 1. “Almsgiving,” he says, “delivers from sin.” [Note: [Col. 1549] Tobit, chapter 12, verse 9.] Therefore crimes are redeemed by alms. [Col. 1549B] [Note: [Col. 1549] These final words are not Ambrose’s, but Gratian’s.]

C. LXXVII. Likewise John Chrysostom, Homily IX, on chapter 6 of the Epistle to the Hebrews. [Note: [Col. 1549D] The Greek reads as follows: Τὸ γὰρ μάλιστα ἰσχυρὸν ἐργαζόμενον τὸ φάρμακον τῆς μετανοίας τοῦτο ἐστὶ. Καὶ καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῶν ἰατρικῶν βοηθημάτων ἐστὶ φάρμακον, πολλὰς μὲν λαμβάνον βοτάνας, μίαν δὲ τὴ κυριωτάτην, οὕτω καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς μετανοίας αὕτη ἡ βοτάνη κυριωτέρα, καὶ τὸ πᾶν αὕτη γένοιτο ἄν. That is: “For this is what makes the medicine of repentance especially powerful. And just as among medical remedies there is a medicine that takes many herbs but one chief herb, so also in repentance this herb is more chief, and it alone could accomplish everything.” Listen, etc.]

The stronger medicine, which works most powerfully in repentance, is this. [Note: [Col. 1549] Addition: “almsgiving”: Basel and the second and third Lyon editions.] Just as in medical prescriptions a medicine receives many herbs, but one that is especially dominant, so also in repentance this herb is more dominant and more powerful, and it accomplishes everything. For hear what divine Scripture says [Note: [Col. 1549] Luke, chapter 11, verse 41.]: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.” [Note: [Col. 1549] Absent from nearly all the editions consulted, especially Basel and the second and third Lyon editions.]

C. LXXVIII. Likewise Ambrose, Book I, *On Repentance*, chapter 2.

God makes no distinction [Note: [Col. 1549] Original: “distinction.”], since he promised his mercy to all and granted his priests [Col. 1549C] the authority to release sins without any exception. But let the person who has aggravated the fault aggravate the repentance also. [Note: [Col. 1549] “He will have aggravated”: the editions consulted.] For greater crimes are washed away by greater tears.

C. LXXIX. The same, Book II, *On Repentance*, chapter 10.

Let mother Church weep for you and wash your fault with tears. Let Christ see you grieving, so that he may say [Note: [Col. 1549] Matthew, chapter 5, verse 5.]: “Blessed are the sorrowful, for you shall rejoice.” He loves many to pray for one person. Finally, in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1549] Compare Luke, chapter 7.], moved by the widow’s tears, because very many were weeping for her, he raised her son.

C. LXXX. The same, in the same Book II, chapter 11.

Immediately after Adam’s fault God drove him out of paradise. He did not delay; rather, he immediately separated him from its delights, so that he might do penance. At once he clothed him in a garment of skin, not of silk. [Note: [Col. 1549] “A garment of skin”: he clothed him in a skin garment, not a silk one: all the editions consulted.]

C. LXXXI. Likewise Augustine, Book L of the *Homilies*, the final homily, chapter 3. [Note: [Col. 1550C] This chapter has been compiled from the words of Blessed Augustine in Book 50 of the *Homilies*, the final homily—words that also occur, almost identically, in the book *On the Medicine of Repentance*, chapter 2—and in Epistle 108, to Seleuciana.] [Note: [Col. 1549] Sermon 351, Maurist edition.—Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 16.]

V. Part. There are three practices of repentance, which your learning recognizes with me. [Note: [Col. 1549] Addition: “however”: the editions consulted.] “For they are customary in the Church and known to those who attend carefully.” [Col. 1550B]

One is that which gives birth to the new person until, through saving baptism, the washing away of all past sins takes place. [Note: [Col. 1550D] “Saving baptism”: the homily reads “through saving baptism”; but the book *On the Medicine of Repentance* reads: “which gives birth to the new person through baptism, until the saving washing away of all past sins takes place.”]

And a little later: “For everyone who has now been established as master of his own will, when he approaches the sacraments of the faithful, cannot begin a new life unless he repents of his former life.” [Note: [Col. 1549] Compare Distinction 4, *On Consecration*, canon 96.] “From this repentance, when they are baptized, only little children are exempt. For they cannot yet use free choice. Nevertheless, for their consecration and the remission of original sin, the faith of those by whom they are presented benefits them.” [Note: [Col. 1549] “Only”: the same edition.]

And below, chapter 4, § 1: “The second repentance, however, is that whose practice must be undertaken throughout this entire life, in which we live in mortal flesh, with continual humility of supplication. First, because no one desires eternal, incorruptible, and immortal life unless he is dissatisfied with this temporal, corruptible, and mortal life. For no one is born into new life through the sanctification of baptism in such a way that, as he lays aside there all past sins, he also immediately lays aside mortality itself of the flesh and its corruption.” [Note: [Col. 1549] “No one”: the editions consulted.] [Note: [Col. 1550C] “And its corruption”: addition, “of life,” in the editions consulted, especially the Argentinian edition.] [Note: [Col. 1549] Absent from the Basel edition.]

And below, chapter 9, § 2: “The third [Note: [Col. 1549] Addition: “however”: Basel and the second and third Lyon editions.] practice of repentance is that which must be undertaken for those sins contained in the Decalogue of the Law, concerning which the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1551] Galatians, chapter 5, verse 21.]: ‘For those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God.’ In this repentance each person ought to exercise greater severity upon himself, so that, judged by himself, he may not be judged by God, as the same Apostle says” [Note: [Col. 1551] 1 Corinthians, chapter 11, verse 31.]: “For if we judged ourselves, we certainly would not be judged by the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 1551] Absent from the Argentinian edition.]

And below [Note: [Col. 1551C] “And below”: the following words are found in full in the Epistle to Seleuciana; nevertheless, the sentence and certain words also occur in the same homily, chapter 8, and in the book *On the Medicine of Repentance*, chapter 2, where the second practice of repentance is discussed. They are referred to the words that now follow.] § 3: “There is also the daily penitential punishment of good and humble believers, in which we beat our breasts, saying [Note: [Col. 1551] Matthew, chapter 6, verse 12.]: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.’ For we do not wish those things to be forgiven us which we do not doubt were forgiven in baptism, but rather those which, though small, nevertheless frequently creep in through human frailty; if they are gathered against us, they will burden and overwhelm us just as some one great sin would. For what difference does it make to a shipwreck whether a ship is covered and overwhelmed by one great wave, or whether water, gradually creeping into the bilge and left there through negligence and contempt, fills the ship and sinks it? For these things fasts, alms, and prayers keep watch; and when in them we say, ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive,’ we show that we have something to be forgiven, and by humbling our souls in these words we do not cease, in a certain sense, to perform daily repentance.”

C. LXXXII. Likewise Gregory. [Note: [Col. 1551D] This chapter is found in its entirety in the commentaries published under the name of Eucherius, on 2 Kings, Book II, chapter 8, but a large part is also found in Blessed Gregory, *Morals*, Book IX, chapter 27.] [Note: [Col. 1551] In Anselm it is cited from Augustine.—“Likewise Augustine, alternatively Gregory”: Argentinian edition.—Anselm, Book XI, chapter 157.]

[Col. 1551C] VI. Part. If the Lord transferred David’s sin, so detestable as it was, what does it mean that, after all that the Lord had said to him through the Prophet concerning that sin, he afterward endured such great sufferings? But undoubtedly the Lord does not leave wrongdoing without punishment. Either the man himself punishes it in himself as he repents, or God strikes him, avenging it together with the man. [Note: [Col. 1551] Addition: “the man”: Anselm; the editions consulted, especially Paris and Lyon.] [Note: [Col. 1551] “Utterly”: the editions consulted.] Therefore sin is by no means spared, because it is in no way released without vengeance.

Thus David deserved to hear after his confession [Note: [Col. 1551] 2 Kings, chapter 12, verse 13.]: “The Lord has transferred your sin,” and yet afterward, afflicted by many torments and fleeing, he paid the penalty for the guilt he had committed. [Note: [Col. 1551] “And fleeing”: Basel edition.] [Col. 1552A] Thus we too are absolved from the guilt of the first man by the wave of salvation. Yet, while washing away the guilt of that same fault, although absolved we still die bodily, because he cuts away our offenses either through us or through himself, even when he releases them. [Note: [Col. 1551] “We also”: the same edition.] [Note: [Col. 1551] “We die and pay the penalty”: Argentinian edition, from a gloss.] For he strives to cleanse from his elect, through temporal affliction, the stains of iniquities that he does not wish to see in them forever. [Col. 1552D] [Note: [Col. 1552D] “We die”: In Blessed Gregory there follows: “Therefore it is rightly said, ‘knowing that you would not spare the offender,’” etc.; for he repeats the words of Job that he had set before himself for interpretation. Eucherius, however, has the text as Gratian does.]

C. LXXXIII. Likewise Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, Book II, chapter 34. [Note: [Col. 1551] Anselm, Book XI, chapter 158.]

Just as the first human beings, by afterward living rightly, are rightly believed to have been freed from the final judgment through the Lord’s blood, yet did not deserve in that life to be restored to paradise, so also the flesh of sin, even if a person lives rightly in it after sins have been forgiven, does not thereby immediately deserve not to suffer the death which it drew from the propagation of sin. [Note: [Col. 1551] “Contracted”: the editions consulted, especially the Argentinian and Basel editions.]

Something of this kind is intimated to us concerning the patriarch David in the Book of Kings [Note: [Col. 1551] Compare 2 Kings, chapter 12.]. When the Prophet had been sent to him and threatened him, on account of the sin he had committed, with evils that would come from God’s anger, he obtained pardon by confessing his sin. The Prophet replied that the offense and wicked deed had been forgiven; yet what God had threatened followed, so that he might thus be humbled by his son.

Why, then, is it now said that, if God had threatened that on account of the sin, he fulfilled what he had threatened after the sin had been forgiven? Unless, if it is expressed in this way, the entirely correct answer is that the sin was forgiven so that the man might not be prevented from receiving eternal life; but the effect of the threat followed so that the man’s piety might be exercised and tested in that humility. [Note: [Col. 1551] “What had been threatened to him”: the editions consulted.] [Note: [Col. 1552D] “Why, then, is it now said”: The original reads, “Why is it not also said here?” But it has not been changed because of the gloss. Many other passages from the same source have likewise been corrected.] Thus God inflicted bodily death on human beings because of this sin, and after the remission of sins did not remove it, in order that righteousness might be exercised. [Note: [Col. 1551] “Also in”: the same editions.] [Col. 1552C] [Note: [Col. 1551] “That threat”: the same editions.]

C. LXXXXIV. The measure of sorrow rather than of time must be considered in the practice of repentance. The same, in a homily on repentance. [Note: [Col. 1551] From the *Enchiridion*, chapter 65. Ivo, *Decree*, part XI, chapter 23. *Polycarpus*, Book VI, title 20. Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 20.]

VII. Part. In the practice of repentance, when such a crime has been committed that the person who committed it is separated even from the body of Christ [Note: [Col. 1553] “Would be separated”: Basel edition.], the measure of time must be considered less than that of sorrow [Note: [Col. 1553] Psalm 50, verse 19.]: “For God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart.” But because the sorrow of one heart is often hidden from another and does not come to the knowledge of others except through words [Col. 1553C] or whatever other signs, although it is before him to whom it is said [Note: [Col. 1553] Psalm 37, verse 10.], “My groaning is not hidden from you,” periods of repentance are rightly established by those who preside over the Church, so that satisfaction may also be made to the Church, in which those sins themselves are forgiven. For outside it they are not forgiven. [Note: [Col. 1553] “In the churches”: Ivo; Basel edition. “In churches”: Argentinian edition.]

Therefore, when the wound and force of the disease of sin are so great that the remedies of the body and blood of the Lord must be deferred, each person ought, by the authority of the bishop, to be removed from the altar in order to perform repentance, and by the same authority to be reconciled. [Note: [Col. 1553C] “Therefore”: These words are not in the *Enchiridion*, but in Epistle 118, to Januarius, spoken under another person’s name. Thus he says: “Another objects: Rather,” he says, “if the wound of sin is so great,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 1553] From the letter to Januarius, Epistle 54.] [Note: [Col. 1553] Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 17.] [Note: [Col. 1553] “Each person ought to remove himself from the altar”: Ivo; the editions consulted.]

C. LXXXV. The same, in the same homily L, chapter 11. [Note: [Col. 1553] Sermon 351, Maurist edition.—Ivo, *Decree*, part XV, chapter 24. Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 17.]

Let a person judge himself in these matters willingly while he can, and change his conduct for the better, lest, when he can no longer do so, he be judged by the Lord even against his will. And when he has pronounced upon himself the sentence of the most severe medicine [Note: [Col. 1553] Original: “medicine, but nevertheless a medicine.” The editions consulted: “medicine, but nevertheless the most useful.”], let him come to the bishops, through whom the keys are administered in the Church; and, as a good son now beginning to be such, preserving the order of the mother’s members, let him receive from the overseers of sacred things [Note: [Col. 1553] “Of the sacraments”: the same editions; the original; Ivo.] the measure of his satisfaction. Thus, devout and suppliant, in offering the sacrifice of a contrite heart, let him do what benefits not only himself toward receiving salvation but also the others as an example, so that, if his sin lies not only in his own grave evil but also in such great scandal to others, and if this seems expedient to the bishop for the Church’s welfare, he should not refuse to perform repentance in the knowledge of many, or even before the whole multitude of the people [Note: [Col. 1553] “Or before the multitude of the entire people”: the editions consulted.], nor resist, nor add swelling through shame to a deadly and fatal wound. [Note: [Col. 1553] “Nor”: the same editions. “Lest”: Basel edition; “nor”: the remaining editions.]

And below [Note: [Col. 1553] Compare chapter 18, Causa 2, question 1.], § 1: “For many are corrected, as Peter was; many are tolerated, as Judas was,” etc.

[Col. 1554A] C. LXXXVI. The mortification of vices, rather than abstinence from food, is more necessary for the penitent. Likewise Jerome. [Note: [Col. 1553D] This chapter, which Burchard and Ivo also cite from the sayings of Blessed Jerome, is one that Beatus Rhenanus testifies in his annotations on Tertullian to have read in an ancient penitential. Some passages have been corrected from it and from the other compilers, and the final clause has also been enlarged. The thought is also found in the Seventh Council, canon 21; in Basil’s letter to Amphilochius, chapter 2; and in the Council of Metz of the year 859, chapter 10.] [Note: [Col. 1553] This chapter was taken from the preface placed before a penitential book, printed in d’Achery, volume I.—Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 31; Anselm, Book XI, chapter 145; Ivo, *Decree*, part XV, chapter 49; *Polycarpus*, Book VI, title 20; Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 20.]

The canons do not set out sufficiently explicitly the measure of time for performing repentance for each crime, so as to say of individual crimes how each must be corrected. Rather, they decree that the matter should be left to the judgment of an understanding priest, because before God the measure of time is not as valuable as sorrow, nor abstinence from food as much as the mortification of vices. For this reason they direct that the periods of repentance themselves be shortened in accordance with the faith and conduct of penitents, and lengthened in accordance with negligence. [Note: [Col. 1553] Addition: “they judge”: Burchard, Anselm, Ivo; Basel and the second and third Lyon editions. “They estimate”: the remaining editions.]

Nevertheless, modes of repentance imposed for certain faults remain, [Note: [Col. 1553] “Nevertheless—modes are imposed”: Burchard, Anselm, Ivo; the editions consulted.] according to which other faults must be weighed, since by these same modes it is easy to estimate the penalty and censure of the canons. [Note: [Col. 1553] The words “according to which” through “they estimate” are absent from Anselm.]

C. LXXXVII. Likewise John Chrysostom [that is, the author of the *Imperfect Work on Matthew*, Homily 40]. [Note: [Col. 1553] An apocryphal work.]

Who has ever seen a cleric quickly performing penance? [Note: [Col. 1553] “Who sees”: the editions consulted, especially Basel.] But even if, when caught, he humbles himself, he does not grieve because he has sinned; rather, he is ashamed because he has lost his glory.

VIII. Part. Gratian. By these authorities it is maintained that no one can be cleansed from sins without repentance and confession in his own voice. Therefore the preceding authorities, by which it seemed to be proved that forgiveness is granted by contrition of heart alone, must be interpreted otherwise than they are expounded by those who cite them.

For Peter’s denial was followed by the satisfaction of tears and by the threefold confession of love for the Lord, by which he utterly erased the sin of his threefold denial. Therefore a definite satisfaction for his sin was not necessary for him, since the whole course of his life was devoted to obedience to his Creator. For he imitated that prophetic saying [Note: [Col. 1553] Psalm 36, verse 27.]: “Turn away from evil and do good”; and that saying of Isaiah [Note: [Col. 1553] Isaiah, chapter 55, verse 7.]: “Let the wicked abandon his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts,” etc. Nothing further than this is required of the sinner.

Therefore that authority of Pope Leo does not deny that penitential satisfaction is necessary for every offender, but only for one who, imitating Blessed Peter, entirely renounces this world and utterly mortifies within himself the tinder of every vice.

§ 1. Likewise, that saying of John Chrysostom [Note: [Col. 1555D] “Of John Chrysostom”: Above, the same chapter. It has been noted under “Tears” that these are the words of Blessed Ambrose, whom the Master of the Sentences cites.]: “Let tears wash away the offense which shame prevents one from confessing aloud”; and that other saying written in the Epistle to the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 1555] Chrysostom, Homily 31 on the Epistle to the Hebrews.]: “I do not tell you to expose yourself publicly, nor to accuse yourself before others; but I want you to obey the Prophet who says [Note: [Col. 1555] Psalm 36, verse 5.]: ‘Reveal your way to the Lord.’ Therefore confess your sins before God; before the true Judge, declare your offenses with prayer, not with your tongue [Note: [Col. 1555D] “Not with your tongue”: The Greek is: Εὐχόμενος, εἰ καὶ μή τῇ γλώττῃ, ἀλλὰ τῇ μνήμῃ, that is: “offering prayers, if not with the tongue, at least with the memory.”], but in the memory of your conscience; and then at last hope that you can obtain mercy, if you continually keep your sins in mind. You will never retain evil in your heart against your neighbor.”

This must not be understood to mean that sins are said to be forgiven without confession of the mouth, but without public satisfaction. For secret sins are cleansed by secret confession and hidden satisfaction, nor is it necessary that what we have once confessed to a priest should be confessed again; but with the tongue of the heart, not of the flesh, we must continually confess them before the true Judge.

Hence the same John Chrysostom says [Note: [Col. 1555] In the same Homily 31.]: “Now, if you remember your sins and frequently [Note: [Col. 1555D] ‘And frequently’: Συνεχῶς αὐτὰς προσφέρης τῷ Θεῷ, και ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν δέῃ, that is: ‘you continually offer them to God and pray for them.’] declare them in the sight of God and entreat his mercy for them, you will erase them more quickly. But if you now forget your sins, then you will remember them, even unwillingly, when they are made public throughout the whole world and brought forth in the sight of all, both your friends and your enemies, and the holy angels and heavenly powers. For he did not say only to David [Note: [Col. 1555] 2 Kings, chapter 12, verse 12.]: ‘What you did in secret I shall reveal to all’; this is said also to all of us.”

§ 2. Likewise that saying of Prosper is understood [Note: [Col. 1555] Above, chapter 32.]: “Those who voluntarily acknowledge their crime and either disclose it by their own confessions, or, when others do not know it, being such as are hidden, etc.” “When others do not know,” that is, those who confess their sin to these others by hidden confession, without making it public.

Likewise the saying of the Prophet [Note: [Col. 1555] Psalm 31, verse 5.]: “I said: I will confess, and you forgave”—that is, you judged forgivable—the impiety of my sin. So also Augustine’s saying is understood [Note: [Col. 1555] Above, chapter 5.]: “Great is the mercy of God, that at a mere promise he forgave sins”—that is, judged them forgivable.

Likewise there: “A vow is reckoned as a deed when the capacity to perform the deed is lacking.” Hence the vow of confession is reckoned in place of the deed of speech when the capacity for confession is lacking.

Likewise [Note: [Col. 1555] Above, chapter 30.]: “The will is rewarded, not the work,” is understood thus: the will makes a work rewardable; the work does not make the will so.

Likewise that saying [Note: [Col. 1555] Above, chapter 32.]: “At whatever hour the sinner has turned,” etc. A person is said to turn who turns wholly; and one turns wholly whose deed, speech, and thought labor at the mortification of sin as earnestly as they formerly served iniquity. Thus also that saying is understood [Note: [Col. 1555] Above, chapters 34 and 33.]: “Turn to me,” etc.

Likewise: “Tear your hearts, and not your garments,” is addressed to those who, without any preceding inward satisfaction, trust that they can please God by outward means alone.

Likewise, all the things brought forward concerning lepers cleansed or Lazarus raised are to be referred to contrition of heart, not to the forgiveness of remission. For obstinacy of mind and contempt for confession are a kind of death of impiety and leprosy of pride, from which each person comes back to life when, by grace, sorrow for sin and the vow of confession are inspired in him.

§ 3. Those statements also belong to this point which are made concerning persons who live, walk in the light, possess the love of God, or have been made dwelling places of the Holy Spirit: namely, that each person is said to have attained all these things through the contrition of heart which he possesses, not through the full remission of sin, which he has not yet found. For just as sin is forgiven in baptism and yet its penalty is reserved, so by contrition of heart each person is said to be raised up by God, although he is still held by the guilt of sin. Therefore, by the foregoing authorities or arguments, no one is proved to be cleansed from sin without confession of the mouth and satisfaction in deed.

II. Part. § 4. Conversely, that authority of John Chrysostom [Note: [Col. 1555] Compare § 1 of this saying.] and of Prosper [Note: [Col. 1555] Compare above, chapter 32.] seems to have been wrested from the author’s meaning. For it does not say, “I do not tell you to accuse yourself publicly,” but, “I do not tell you to accuse yourself before others.” Likewise Prosper does not say, “before all,” but simply, “when others do not know.” Therefore it is understood most clearly [Note: [Col. 1555D] “Therefore it is understood most clearly”: He speaks in the person of one defending the opposing side. In truth, this conclusion is not drawn from those authorities. One who confesses to a priest as to God is by no means said to accuse himself before others; rather, while others remain ignorant, he punishes himself. And Chrysostom plainly says what is now denied: “I do not tell you,” he says, “to make yourself public, nor to accuse yourself before others.” This second clause has the same force as the first: to accuse oneself before others is the same as to make oneself public. Therefore, a little later, Gratian himself refutes the things now adduced: “Conversely, the things stated in support,” etc.] that sins can be erased without confession of the mouth.

But the things said to exhort repentance and confession do not seem contrary to this opinion. For they are either words of exhortation, not command, as the saying [Note: [Col. 1557] James, chapter 5, verse 16.]: “Confess your sins to one another,” etc.; or, if some things are spoken as commands, they are to be referred not to confession of the mouth but of the heart, and not to outward satisfaction but inward satisfaction.

§ 5. For there is one repentance that is inward and another that is outward. Inward repentance is that of which Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1557] Above, chapter 31, at the beginning.]: “Everyone who has been established as master of his own will cannot begin a new life unless he repents of his former life.” Likewise Peter is read to have said concerning the same repentance in the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 1557] Acts, chapter 2, verse 38.]: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized.” This is understood to have been said of inward repentance, not outward repentance.

Of outward repentance Ambrose says, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans [Note: [Col. 1557] Compare chapter 99, Distinction 4, *On Consecration*]: “The grace of God in baptism does not require groaning or lamentation, nor any work, but only contrition of heart, and freely pardons all things.” Therefore everything said by way of command concerning repentance is to be referred, as we have said, not to outward but to inward repentance, without which no one can ever be reconciled to God.

§ 6. Augustine’s statement [Note: [Col. 1557] Compare above, chapter 42.], by which each person is said unable to obtain forgiveness unless he has first paid some penalty, however small, for sin, is not found to oppose this opinion. For no one is asserted to be cleansed from sin unless he has undergone the penalty of sin. But it is one thing to confess sin to a priest and make satisfaction for it according to his judgment; it is another to confess to God in the heart and punish sin in oneself by hidden satisfaction.

For repentance is, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1557] Compare below, Distinction 3, *On Repentance*, chapter 4.], sorrow of heart by which each person punishes in himself what he has done wrong. Concerning this satisfaction the same author says again, explaining Psalm 50: “For I acknowledge [Note: [Col. 1557D] “For I acknowledge my iniquity”: Here and in the two following passages the words are not reproduced exactly from Blessed Augustine, but the meaning is.] my iniquity. Do not punish me, because I punish myself; forgive me, because I acknowledge it.” [Note: [Col. 1557] Bohm adds: “and do not dissemble.”]

And below: “Thus God gives mercy so as to preserve truth, so that the sins of the person whom he forgives are not unpunished. For he forgives the one who punishes himself. It is mercy that the person is freed; it is truth that the sin is punished.”

The same author, on Psalm 84: “Truth has sprung up from the earth”—that is, confession from a human being, so that he may accuse himself—and thus righteousness looked down from heaven, so that the tax collector [Note: [Col. 1557] Compare Luke, chapter 18.] returned justified as he confessed. Righteousness looked down from heaven, as though God were saying: “Let us spare this person, because he does not spare himself; let us forgive, because he acknowledges.” And below: “Therefore righteousness looked down from heaven”—that is, justification was given by God to the one confessing.

§ 7. This hidden satisfaction, therefore, is to be offered to God for slight or secret crimes, and those things that are believed to be expiated in this way are shown not to be released without punishment. But what is said concerning public satisfaction or confession of the mouth is to be understood of public and manifest crimes. For the sins of Nebuchadnezzar [Note: [Col. 1557] Compare Daniel, chapter 4, and Jonah, chapter 3.], which the Prophet urged him to redeem by works of mercy and alms, and the sins of the Ninevites, which were expiated by public satisfaction, were known to all. And a public offense, as Augustine testifies [Note: [Col. 1557] Gloss of the ordinary commentary on chapter 5 of Mark.], requires a public remedy.

§ 8. Therefore, by the foregoing authorities, public satisfaction and confession of the mouth are shown to be required for manifest crimes. But hidden sins are not shown necessarily to be confessed to a priest and expiated according to his judgment.

III. Part. § 9. Conversely, the things stated in support of this opinion rest partly on truth and partly lack weight. For it is firmly established and supported by the strongest reasoning that no sin can be forgiven without contrition of heart, and that hidden sins ought to be expiated by hidden satisfaction, while public sins ought to be expiated by manifest repentance. But that a grave offense can be expiated without confession of the mouth, if the opportunity for confessing has not been lacking, is shown to be wholly contrary to authority.

For how, according to the authority of Pope Leo [Note: [Col. 1557] Above, chapter 49.], can pardon be obtained without the supplications of priests, if we can be cleansed from sin without confession of the mouth? For who will pray for a sin that he does not know?

§ 10. Likewise, how, according to Augustine [Note: [Col. 1557] Above, chapter 44.], does a person frustrate the keys of the Church by performing repentance without the judgment of a priest, if he obtains forgiveness for a crime without confession of the mouth? [Col. 1558C]

§ 11.
