Likewise, how, according to Ambrose [Note: [Col. 1557] Above, chapter 51.], is the power of binding and loosing entrusted by the Lord to priests alone, if each person binds himself by sinning according to his own judgment, or, by hidden repentance according to Prosper, pronounces upon himself a sentence of excommunication, and after satisfaction reconciles himself to God or to his altar without priestly judgment?

§ 12. These things do not accord with the foregoing authorities; rather, many examples prove the contrary. For the Lord raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue [Note: [Col. 1557] Matthew, chapter 9.] after the crowds had been sent away. Yet she was restored to life only in the presence of the girl’s father and mother, and of Peter, James, and John. In this we are morally instructed that secret sins, which are signified by the girl’s death, are considered forgiven by the Lord only through the prayers of the Church, signified by the girl’s father and mother, and through the ministry of priests, signified by Peter and the others.

§ 13. Likewise in Leviticus [Note: [Col. 1558D] “In Leviticus”: Here too the sense of Leviticus is cited in chapter 27, not its exact words; the same occurs shortly afterward concerning Hesychius.]: “Whoever vows or consecrates his house or field to the Lord [Note: [Col. 1557] Leviticus, chapter 27, verse 18.] cannot redeem it except with the sanctuary shekel, with the priest—not the person himself—calculating the number of years up to the jubilee.” [Col. 1559A]

Here likewise we are taught that whoever wishes through repentance to offer to the Lord the house of conscience or the field of conduct, and by the price of good works to redeem himself from the vain conduct of his life, cannot do so except with the sanctuary shekel—that is, by the works of repentance prescribed in sacred Scripture.

Therefore Blessed John, when the crowds came to him, did not say simply [Note: [Col. 1559] Luke, chapter 3, verse 8.], “Perform repentance,” or, “The fruits of repentance,” but added, “worthy,” so that works of a quality corresponding to the character of the sins might be offered. For the fruit of a good work ought not to be equal for one who has sinned not at all or little and for one who has committed great offenses. The former, conscious of no crime, permits himself the use of lawful things; the latter, burdened by many sins, ought to abstain even from lawful things.

At the jubilee full remission was granted [Note: [Col. 1559] Leviticus, chapter 25, verse 10.]; hence perfect remission of sin is signified by it. Therefore the priest calculates the number of years up to the jubilee when the periods of repentance are determined according to his judgment, through which each person may find full remission of sin. For, as Hesychius says concerning the same passage [Note: [Col. 1559] Compare the ordinary gloss on the cited passage of Leviticus.], no one is fully cleansed from sin immediately after the prescribed repentance.

§ 14. Therefore, since, as is gathered from the foregoing, the periods of repentance are determined according to the priest’s judgment, it is perfectly clear that sins are not forgiven without confession in one’s own voice. For who will prescribe periods of repentance for someone unless that person first takes care to disclose his sins to him?

§ 15. Likewise: Silence about sin arises from pride of heart. For each person desires to conceal his sin lest his iniquity become known to others, lest he be thought outwardly by people to be such as he has long since shown himself to be in the sight of God. No one can doubt that this arises from the source of pride. For it is a form of pride to wish to appear righteous while being a sinner; and a person is convicted as a hypocrite if, in imitation of the first parents, he tries by evasive speech to diminish his sins, or, like Cain [Note: [Col. 1559] Genesis, chapter 4.], seeks utterly to suppress his sin by keeping silent about it.

Where pride or hypocrisy reigns, humility cannot have a place. Without humility, however, no one may hope for forgiveness. Therefore, where there is silence in confession, forgiveness of the crime is not to be hoped for. This same point is proved by the authority of Augustine, who says in chapter 10 of the book *On True and False Repentance* [Note: [Col. 1559] This book is not by Augustine.—Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 17.]:

C. LXXXVIII.

Whoever repents must repent utterly and show his sorrow with tears; let him present his life to God through the priest and forestall God’s judgment through confession. For the Lord commanded those being cleansed to show themselves to the priests, teaching that sins must be confessed in bodily presence, not disclosed through a messenger or in writing. For he said, “Show your faces,” and “All of you,” not one person for everyone; do not appoint another messenger to offer on your behalf the offering established by Moses, but let those who sinned through themselves be ashamed through themselves. For shame itself has a share in remission.

[Note: At [Col. 1559], *sacerdotes* (“priests”): the editions compared, except the Basel edition. Luke 17:14; Leviticus 9:7.]

For the Lord commanded this out of mercy, so that no one would repent secretly. For when a person himself tells the priest and conquers his shame through fear of having offended, forgiveness of the crime is granted. Through confession, what was criminal in its execution becomes pardonable; and, even if it is not immediately cleansed, what he had committed mortally nevertheless becomes life-giving.

[Note: “Life-giving”: the original reads “pardonable,” but a gloss was present.]

For he has offered much satisfaction who, mastering his shame, has withheld from God’s messenger none of the things he committed. For God is merciful and just: just as he preserves mercy in justice, so also he preserves justice in mercy. To forgive sins to the sinner is an act of mercy; but the just person must show mercy justly. He must consider not only what the person grieves over but also in what manner he grieves, if he is worthy—not, I say, of justice but of mercy. For justice alone condemns; but worthy of mercy is the person who seeks grace through spiritual labor. The mind labors by undergoing shame; and, since shame is a great punishment, whoever is ashamed for Christ becomes worthy of mercy. Hence it is clear that the more widely he confesses the disgrace of his crime in hope of pardon, the more readily he will obtain the mercy of forgiveness.

[Note: At “God is merciful”: *qui mis.* (“who is merciful”): the editions compared, except the original. At “seeks grace”: *quaerit* (“seeks”): the Basel edition. At “the more”: *quantum* (“how much”): Venice I–II and Paris; *quando* (“when”): the Lyons edition; the remainder is lacunose. At “he confesses”: *confitetur* (“he confesses”): Basel and Lyons editions. At “will obtain”: *consequitur* (“he obtains”): the editions compared and Böhm.]

The priests themselves can then make greater progress and spare those who confess more. For those whom they forgive, the Lord forgives. The Lord presented Lazarus, already raised from the tomb, to the disciples to be unbound, thereby showing that the power of loosing had been granted to priests.

[Note: *sacerdoti* (“to a priest,” singular): the Argentinian and Basel editions.]

For he said: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven”; that is: I, God, and all the ranks of the heavenly host, and all the saints in my glory praise with you and confirm those whom you bind and loose.

[Note: At “shall be loosed”: the Vulgate and the Basel edition read *solutum erit* (“shall have been loosed”).]

He did not say, “Those whom you think you bind or loose,” but “those upon whom you exercise the work of justice or mercy.”

[Note: *exercueritis* (“you shall have exercised”): the editions compared, except the original and the Basel edition.]

I recognize no other works of yours upon sinners.

[Note: *cognosco* (“I know”): the editions compared.]

§ 1. Therefore, whoever wishes to confess his sins in order to find grace should seek a priest who knows how to bind and loose, lest, when he has proved negligent concerning himself, he be neglected by the one who mercifully admonishes him and seeks him, lest both fall into the pit which the foolish man refused to avoid.

[Note: Compare Distinction 6, *On Penance*, chapter 1.]

§ 2. Such, then, is the power of confession that, if a priest is lacking, one should confess to one’s neighbor. For it often happens that a penitent cannot confess before the priest whom he desires, because neither place nor time is available to him. And if the one to whom he confesses does not have the power of loosing, he nevertheless becomes worthy of pardon because of his desire for a priest, since he confesses the disgrace of his crime to his companion. For the lepers were cleansed while they were going to show themselves to the priests, before they reached them. Hence it is clear that the Lord looks to the heart when necessity prevents them from reaching the priests.

[Note: *penitus* (“utterly”): the Basel edition. *verecundari* (“to be ashamed”): the editions compared. *habeat* (“has”): the same editions. *ibant* (“were going”): the same editions. *se ostendere sacerdotibus* (“to show themselves to the priests”): the Basel and Lyons II–III editions. *Deum* (“God”): the editions compared.]

Often, indeed, they seek them while healthy and cheerful; but, while they seek them, before they reach them, they die.

[Note: The words *dum quaerunt* (“while they seek”) are absent from the Argentinian edition. *Ad eos* (“to them”) is not read in the Basel edition. *Pervenirent* (“they reached”): the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice I–II editions.]

But the mercy of God is everywhere. He knows how to spare even the righteous, although not as quickly as if they had been loosed by a priest.

[Note: The transmitted reading is *et justis* (“and the righteous”). Considering the entire course of the tradition, *et istis* (“and these persons”) seems preferable; nevertheless, all collated manuscripts agree with Gratian’s reading. *Sic et si* (“thus, even if”): the same editions. *Sicut solvuntur* (“as they are loosed”): the Basel edition.]

§ 3. Therefore whoever confesses should confess to as good a priest as he can; and, if the sin is secret, it is enough to bring it to the priest’s knowledge, so that the offering of the gift may be acceptable.

[Note: *et sacerdoti* (“and to a priest”): the editions compared.]

For at the resurrection of the ruler’s daughter only a few were present to see it. She had not yet been buried, had not yet been carried outside the gate of the city, and had not yet been carried outside the house into public knowledge.

[Note: *resurrectione* (“resurrection”): the editions compared; compare Luke chapter 18. The second *nondum* (“not yet”) is deleted and absent from the Basel edition. *Portata* (“carried”): the editions compared.]

He raised within the house the one whom he found within, leaving only Peter, John, and James, and the girl’s father and mother, in whom the priests of the Church are figuratively represented.

[Note: Luke 7.]

But concerning those whom he found outside, it must be observed how he raised them. The crowd was weeping after the widow’s son. Martha and Mary wept, making supplication for their brother. The crowd that had followed Mary also wept, stirred by Mary’s tears.

[Note: John 11. At “making supplication,” the original has the singular *supplicans* (“making supplication”).]

In this we are taught that for those who sin publicly, not their own merit but the merit of the Church is sufficient.

## C. LXXXIX. The confession first offered to God and then to the priest is sufficient.

Likewise Pope Leo, Letter LXXVIII, alternatively LXXX.

[Note: Letter 168 in the Ballerini edition, written to the bishops of Campania in A.D. 459; *Collectio trium partium*, part 1, tome 43, chapter 42; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, chapter 167; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 17.]

### Part IX

Although fullness of faith may seem praiseworthy—faith which, because of fear of God, does not hesitate to be ashamed before human beings—nevertheless, since not everyone’s sins are of such a kind that those seeking penance need not fear making them public, let so improper a custom be removed, lest many be kept from the remedies of penance while they are either ashamed or afraid to disclose their deeds to their enemies, for which deeds they may be punished under the provisions of the law.

[Note: In “sins which,” *quae* (“which”): the Spanish Collection and Ballerini. *Tam* (“so”) is absent from the Spanish Collection and Ivo. *Timent* (“fear”): the editions compared. *Reserari* (“to be disclosed”): the Spanish Collection, Ballerini, and Ivo. *Pro* (“for”) is absent from those sources, from Ivo, and from the editions compared, except the Lyons II–III editions. *Possit* (“may be able”): the Spanish Collection; *possint* (“may be able”): Ballerini, Ivo, and the Basel edition. Compare above, chapter 61.]

For that confession is sufficient which is first offered to God and then also to the priest, who approaches as an intercessor for the sins of penitents. Only then will more people be able to be called to penance, if the conscience of the one confessing is not made public to the ears of the people.

[Note: *Demum* (“only then”) is absent from the Spanish Collection and Ivo.]

**Gratian.** By what authorities, or by what supports of reasoning, each of the two opinions concerning satisfaction and confession is sustained, we have briefly set forth for consideration. Which of these should rather be followed is left to the reader’s judgment. For each has wise and religious men as its supporters.

[Note: “To the reader’s judgment”: it is entirely certain, and must be regarded as entirely certain, that sacramental confession is necessary for mortal sin, administered in the manner and at the time established, after other councils, by the Council of Trent.]

Accordingly, Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury, says in his *Penitential*:

[Note: Burchard and Ivo also cite this chapter from Theodore’s *Penitential*. In the appended *Capitularies*, chapter 58, the following is read: “Some say that sins ought to be confessed to God alone; others judge that they should be confessed to priests. Both are done within the holy Church not without great benefit, provided that we confess our sins both to God, from whom comes the forgiveness of sins, and say with David: ‘I made my offense known to you, and I did not hide my injustice. I said: I will confess my injustices against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my sin’; and, according to the Apostle’s teaching, that we confess our sins to one another and pray for one another, that we may be saved. Thus confession made to God cleanses sins; but that made to a priest teaches how those sins are cleansed. For God is the author and giver of salvation and health, often through the work of physicians.” In the Second Council of Chalon, chapter 33, nearly the same words occur, with *because* added at the beginning and with certain words added in the final clause; these will be noted.]

[Note: This passage is not found among Theodore’s chapters as printed by d’Achery and Petit. It is nevertheless read in the Second Council of Chalon, held in 813, chapter 33, and in the *Capitularies* of Theodulf—who probably supplied the name—chapter 30; Burchard, book 19, chapter 145; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, chapter 155.]

## C. XC

Some say that sins ought to be confessed to God alone, as do the Greeks.

[Note: The words “as do the Greeks,” together with “as does almost the entire holy Church,” “and this belongs to the perfect,” and “which belongs to the righteous,” are absent both from the *Capitulary* and from the council.]

Others judge that they should be confessed to priests, as does almost the entire holy Church. Both are done within the holy Church not without great benefit, provided that we confess our sins to God, who is the forgiver of sins; and this belongs to the perfect, so that with David we may say: “I made my offense known to you, and I did not hide my injustice. I said: I will confess my injustices against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my sin.”

[Note: At “so that with David,” *et* (“and”): the Council of Chalon, Burchard, Ivo, and the editions compared, except the Basel edition. Psalm 31:5 and following.]

Yet the Apostle’s instruction must be followed by us, so that we confess our sins to one another and pray for one another, that we may be saved.

[Note: In the *Capitulary* and the council, the sentence still depends upon the earlier clause, “provided that we confess to God,” and so forth; its second member is supplied by the words “and according to the Apostle’s instruction,” and so forth.]

Thus confession made to God alone, which belongs to the righteous, cleanses sins. But confession made to the priest teaches how those sins are to be cleansed. For God, the author and giver of salvation and holiness, often provides this medicine of his penance through invisible administration, and often through the work of physicians.

[Note: The council, Burchard, and Ivo read *suae potentiae* (“of his power”) instead of “of his penance.” In the *Capitulary*, as its text shows, this entire first member of the period is absent.]

# DISTINCTION II

# GRATIAN

### Part I

Since discussion of penance has once begun, it seems necessary to return to the matter at somewhat greater length, setting forth for consideration the opinions of different people, supported by definite authorities. Some say that penance is useful only once. For it is single and cannot be repeated. But if it is repeated, the preceding penance was not genuine. And although, according to the judgment of the judge, sins seem to have been forgiven on account of its merit, nevertheless, in the presence of him to whom all future things are present, they are never regarded as forgiven, because the sentence of the true priest was not observed: “Go, and sin no more.” Likewise: “See, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.”

[Note: John 8:11; John 5:14.]

Likewise from the Eighth Synod:

[Note: Rather, Basil. The passage occurs in the book *On the Institutes of Monks*, translated by Rufinus, chapter 22, from Basil’s *Shorter Rules*, no. 289; *Collectio trium partium*, part 2, tome 14, chapter 14.]

## C. I. Whoever later falls back into a vice has not wholly extinguished its first cause.

If anyone has once been marked by the vice of envy or contention and has again fallen into that same fault, let him know that he has hidden in the inner marrow the first cause, of which we spoke above, from which envy or contention arises. Therefore he must be healed through contrary and adverse means, that is, through the exercise of humility.

[Note: *evitari vel curari* (“avoided or healed”): the editions compared, except the original and the Basel edition.]

The exercises of humility are these: that he submit himself to humbler duties and give himself over to more lowly services. Thus the vice of arrogance and human glory can be healed, so that, through the habit of humility, the disposition may no longer fall into the sin of arrogance and empty glory.

[Note: *in consuetudine* (“in the habit”): the editions compared.]

And in each individual vice of this kind a similar remedy should be applied.

[Note: *Sed* (“but”): the same editions. *Adhibetur* (“is applied”): the Argentinian and Basel editions.]

**Gratian.** Likewise, without charity no adult person’s sin is forgiven. But one who will at some time sin mortally does not possess charity.

Accordingly Augustine says to Count Julian:

[Note: In ancient editions of the letters of Blessed Augustine, this was Letter 111 to Julian, in which this chapter appeared. It is now in tome 4 under the title *On Saving Instructions to a Certain Count*, chapter 7. In Jerome’s letter to Rufinus, however, something similar is read: “Friendship,” he says, “which can cease was never true.”]

[Note: The passage is not Augustine’s but Paulinus of Aquileia’s. Peter Lombard, book 3, distinction 31.]

## C. II. Charity which can be abandoned was never true.

## C. III. The same, on the First Epistle of John, tractate 8.

[Note: Peter Lombard, same place.]

Has charity taken root? Be secure: nothing evil can proceed from it.

## C. IV. Likewise Gregory, book X of the *Moralia*, chapter 22.

[Note: Peter Lombard, same place.]

“Love is strong as death.” For love is compared to the power of death, because it utterly kills, as it were, the mind which it has once begun to remove from delight in the world.

[Note: Canticles 8:6. The original has *ceperit* (“has begun”); *dilectione* (“love”) is also the original reading.]

## C. V. Likewise Prosper, in book III of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 13.

[Note: This chapter was compiled from words of Prosper gathered here and there; the first part is also found in the treatise *On the Praises of Charity*, among the works of Blessed Augustine, tome IX, in nearly the same form as in Gratian. Some passages have been corrected, and some have also been added from Prosper himself. It will nevertheless be worthwhile to read the complete passage in its original author, for it is explained there fully and most elegantly.]

[Note: Rather, this is Julianus Pomerius, whose book it is.]

Charity is, as it seems to me, a right will, entirely turned away from all earthly and present things, inseparably joined and united to God, kindled by a certain fire of the Holy Spirit, from whom it comes and to whom it is directed; foreign to every defilement, ignorant of corruption, subject to no vice of changeability, exalted above all things loved carnally, the most powerful of all affections, eager for divine contemplation, always unconquered in all things, the sum of good actions, the health of morals, the end of heavenly commandments, the death of crimes, the life of virtues, the strength of those who fight, the palm of victors, the soul of holy minds, the cause of good merits, and the reward of the perfect. Without it no one has pleased God; with it no one could or can sin. It is fruitful in penitents, joyful in those who advance, glorious in those who persevere, victorious in martyrs, and active in all the faithful without exception; from it everything that is a good work lives.

[Note: At “joined to God,” *vero Deo* (“indeed to God”): the editions compared, except the Argentinian edition. At “kindled,” *ignita* (“kindled”): the Basel, Paris, and Lyons editions; at “fire,” *igni* (“fire”): the Nuremberg and Venice I–II editions. At “to be corrupted,” *corrumpi* (“to be corrupted”): the original. At “weapons,” *arma* (“weapons”): the Basel and Lyons II–III editions; the Argentinian edition has *arma vel anima* (“weapons or soul”). At “lives,” *viret vel vivet* (“flourishes or will live”): one edition; *vivet* (“will live”): the remaining editions.]

Likewise below:

§ 1. This is true, genuine, perfect charity, which the holy Apostle calls “a more excellent way”; and it truly is the way which leads those walking by it to their homeland. For just as no one reaches the place toward which he is going without a road, so without charity, which has been called the way, people cannot walk but wander.

[Note: 1 Corinthians 13:10. The marked clause “and it truly is the way which leads those walking by it to their homeland” is printed as such. At “for just as,” *sicut enim* (“for just as”): the editions compared.]

Likewise, in the same place, chapter 15:

§ 2. Therefore, if we offer charity to God and to our neighbor from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith, we easily resist sin, abound in every good work, despise the enticements of the world, and accomplish with delight everything difficult or even harsh to human frailty—provided that we love God with perfect charity, which comes from him, with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength.

[Note: At “good works,” *operibus* (“works”): the Argentinian edition. At “love,” *dilectione* (“love”): the editions compared. At “from him,” *ab illo* (“from him”): the same editions.]

For a person sins in that part by which he loves God less. If we love him with all our heart, there will be nothing in us through which we may serve sinful desires.

And what is it to love God except to cleave to him in mind, to conceive an affection for enjoying his vision, to hate sin, to despise the world, and also to love one’s neighbor, whom he judged should be loved in himself, preserving in that love the lawful measure and not perverting the established order of love?

[Note: The original reads *occupare animum* (“to occupy the mind”); the Basel edition reads *eum occupare animo* (“to occupy him in the mind”).]

Those pervert the order of love and do not keep the proper measure of loving who either love the world, which ought to be despised; or love their bodies, which ought to be loved less, more than they should; or do not love their neighbors as themselves; or perhaps do not love God more than themselves.

Likewise below:

§ 3. Because our body is part of ourselves, it must be loved by us for this purpose: that we naturally provide and act for its health and frailty, so that, being subject in due order to the spirit, it may attain eternal salvation after receiving immortality and incorruption.

[Note: *a nobis* (“by us”): the Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]

Likewise below:

§ 4. We love our neighbors as ourselves when we love them not for any advantage of our own, not for benefits hoped for or received, not for kinship or blood relationship, but solely because they share in our nature.

[Note: *speranda* (“benefits to be hoped for”): the editions compared.]

Likewise below:

§ 5. Not only those joined to us by degrees of blood are to be regarded as our neighbors; rather, all human beings who share in our nature, as I have said, are to be regarded as our neighbors.

Likewise below:

§ 6. Accordingly, we love all our neighbors when, in order that they may attain good conduct and eternal life, we provide for their salvation as for our own; when we reflect upon ourselves in their sins and dangers; and, as we desire aid for ourselves, so we aid them according to our ability—or, if the means are lacking, retain the will to aid them.

[Note: At “according to,” *secundum* (“according to”): the Argentinian edition. At “our,” *nostros* (“our own”): the editions compared, except the Argentinian edition. At “we should desire,” *optaremus* (“we should desire”): the editions compared. At “we may aid,” *subveniamus* (“we may aid”): the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice I–II editions.]

Therefore this is the complete love of neighbor: that you should will for your neighbor the good that you wish to be given to yourself, and should not will for your neighbor the evil that you do not wish to happen to yourself.

[Note: “This is the complete love of neighbor”: this reading occurs not only in the original but also in the older manuscripts of Gratian. The common editions read: “Therefore, dearest one, strive with all love that good …” At “given,” *fieri* (“done”): the Basel and Lyons editions; the words are absent from the remaining editions. The marked maxim is: “and the evil which you would not wish to happen to yourself, do not wish for your neighbor.”]

But those love God more than themselves who, for love of him, do not spare their own temporal well-being, give themselves over to tribulations and dangers, are ready to be stripped of their possessions, become exiles from their homeland, renounce their parents, wives, and children, and, to say everything in one word, not only do not flee bodily death itself but also willingly receive it, desiring more to depart from the life of their body than from God, who is the life of their life.

[Note: At “their own children,” *suis* (“their own”) is marked. *Et ipsam* (“and bodily death itself”): the Basel edition. *Qui est vita* (“who is life”): the Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]

## C. VI. Likewise Bede on John, chapter 1.

It must meanwhile be asked how it was a special sign for recognizing the Son of God that the Spirit descended and remained upon him.

[Note: *Praetereundum non est* (“it must not be passed over”): the Argentinian edition. *Filii* (“of the Son”): the editions compared. “Holy” is added after “Spirit” by the same editions; compare John 1:33.]

And below:

§ 1. What great thing is it for the Son of God that the Spirit is said to remain in him? It must therefore be noted that the Holy Spirit always remained in the Lord; but in holy human beings, as long as they bear a mortal body, he partly remains forever and partly departs in order to return.

[Note: “It must therefore be noted” is absent from the Argentinian edition. Variants are: *Notandum itaque est* (“therefore it must be noted”), Lyons II–III; *Notandum quoque est* (“also it must be noted”), Basel; and *Notandumque est* (“and it must be noted”), the remaining editions. *Omnibus* (“all”): Basel. *Gestaverit* (“has borne”): Basel; *gestaverunt* (“have borne”): the remaining editions.]

He remains with them so that they may persist in good deeds, love voluntary poverty, pursue meekness, mourn from desire for eternal things, hunger and thirst for righteousness, and embrace mercy, purity of heart, and the tranquillity of peace; and so that they may not fear to suffer persecution for keeping righteousness, but may desire to devote themselves to almsgiving, prayers, fasts, and the other fruits of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: *Manat—secedit* (“flows forth—withdraws”): the Basel, Paris, and Lyons editions. *Consequantur* (“attain”): the editions compared. *Aeterno* (“eternal,” singular): the same editions. *Revereantur* (“fear”): the Basel edition. “Holy” is added after “Spirit” by the Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]

But he withdraws for a time, so that they may not always have the power to heal the weak, raise the dead, cast out demons, or even prophesy. He always remains so that they may possess virtues and themselves live wondrously. He comes for a time so that, through signs of miracles, they may also shine forth to others as the kind of persons they are within.

[Note: The original instead reads *possint habere virtutem* (“may be able to have power”). The words from *ut* through *et* are absent from the original.]

## C. VII. Likewise the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 13.

“Charity never fails.”

[Note: 1 Corinthians 13:4; Peter Lombard, same place.]

## C. VIII. Likewise Augustine on the First Epistle of John, tractate 3.

The invisible anointing is the Holy Spirit; the invisible anointing is charity, which, in whomever it is, will be like a root for him; although the sun burns fiercely, it cannot wither; nourished by the sun’s heat, it does not wither.

[Note: “The invisible anointing is charity”: from this point to the end, the text is the same in the Master and in Gratian. But Blessed Augustine has it differently: “The invisible anointing,” he says, “is that charity which, in whomever it is, will be like a root for him; although the sun burns fiercely, it cannot wither. Everything that is rooted is nourished by the sun’s heat and does not wither.” Thus he does not deny that charity can wither, but says this of what is rooted in charity. The repeated *quae* (“which”) is absent from the Argentinian and Basel editions.]

## C. IX. Likewise Gregory on Ezekiel, tome III.

The winged living creatures—that is, the holy preachers—when they proceed, do not turn back at all, because they so pass from earthly actions to spiritual things that they never afterward turn themselves back to what they have left.

[Note: The editions compared summarize the passage: “The winged creatures do not turn back when they proceed, because the holy preachers, and so forth.” *Transeunt* (“pass”): the same editions. *Reliquerant* (“had left”): the same editions.]

And a little later: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” For to put one’s hand to the plow is, as it were, to open the soil of one’s heart by a plowshare of compunction so that it may yield fruits. But one looks back behind the plow who, after beginning a good work, returns to the evils he left. Since this never happens to God’s elect, the Prophet rightly says here: “They did not turn back when they went.”

[Note: Luke 9:62. “His” is added after “hand” by the editions compared. Ezekiel 1:17; the Vulgate reads *ambularent* (“they walked”).]

And a little later: Hence Paul says: “Forgetting the things that are behind and stretching myself toward those that are before, I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling.” For, stretching toward what lay before, he had forgotten what lay behind, because, despising temporal things, he sought only those which are eternal.

[Note: Philippians 3:13. The Basel edition has the expanded reading “but, forgetting what is behind.” The Vulgate and the editions compared, together with the Basel edition, read *obliviscens* (“forgetting”).]

## C. X. The same, on the same book, Homily V.

“They did not turn back when they went,” because every one of the elect so tends toward good things that he does not return to commit evil.

[Note: Ezekiel 1:17; the original reads *ambularent* (“they walked”). *Bonum* (“good,” singular): the Basel edition.]

For “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.” And, as Solomon says: “The path of the righteous is like a shining light: it advances and increases unto the perfect day.”

[Note: Matthew 10:22; Proverbs 4:18. The Basel edition has “shining and increasing.”]

In their minds, indeed, good desire and understanding of inward light are already a portion of the day; but because they advance in virtue to the end of life, they reach the perfect day when, led into the heavenly kingdoms, they will no longer lack anything of the light they desire.

[Note: *Animo* (“mind,” singular): the editions compared. *Perveniunt* (“arrive”): the Basel and Lyons II–III editions.]

## C. XI. The same, in the same place.

The movement and mobility of the Spirit may be understood in this way. In the hearts of the saints he always remains with respect to certain virtues; but with respect to others he comes intending to depart, and departs intending to come.

[Note: The original reads *requisitione alterius considerationis* (“by the inquiry of another consideration”). *Maneat* (“may remain”): the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice I–II editions; *manet* (“remains”): the remaining editions.]

For in faith, hope, charity, and other good things without which one cannot reach the heavenly homeland—such as humility, chastity, justice, and mercy—he does not leave the fruitful hearts of the perfect.

[Note: *Foecunda perfectorum* (“fruitful [hearts] of the perfect”): the editions compared.]

But in the power of prophecy, the eloquence of teaching, and the performance of miracles, he is sometimes present to his own elect and sometimes withdraws himself.

[Note: At “his own,” *suis* (“his own”) belongs to “elect.” *Doctrina foecunda* (“fruitful teaching”): the editions compared before Lyons II–III.]

And a little later:

§ 1. Therefore, in those virtues without which one cannot at all attain life, the Holy Spirit remains in the hearts of his elect; hence he is rightly called stable.

[Note: “Hence he is rightly called stable” was transferred here by the compiler, in different language, from a somewhat earlier discussion of Blessed Gregory.]

But in those things through which the power of holiness is displayed, he is sometimes mercifully present and sometimes mercifully withdraws.

[Note: *Misericorditer* (“mercifully”) is absent from the Basel edition.]

Accordingly Ambrose, on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 6:

## C. XII. Charity is feigned when it abandons someone in adversity.

[Note: The words cited are from the ordinary gloss; Blessed Ambrose’s words are: “Feigned charity is in those who abandon their brethren in need.”]

### Part II

**Gratian.** From what has been set out, then, it appears that charity, once possessed, is not afterward lost. For whoever has once possessed charity cannot afterward sin mortally, so that the impossibility is referred to grace, not to nature. That one who possesses charity cannot sin mortally is attested by Augustine in book L of the *Homilies*, Homily 8, where he says:

[Note: This is not Augustine’s. Peter Lombard, book 3, distinction 31.]

## C. XIII.

Because covetousness is the root of all evils and charity is the root of all good things, and both cannot exist together, unless one has been entirely uprooted the other cannot be planted. In vain does anyone attempt to cut off the branches if he does not strive to pull out the root.

[Note: 1 Timothy 6:10. At “wholly,” *radicitus* (“from the root”): the original and the Basel edition. At “can,” *potest* (“can”): the editions compared.]

**Gratian.** Therefore, since one who sins mortally is shown never to have possessed charity, it evidently follows that a person who sins mortally at any time does not perform penance.

Accordingly Augustine says:

[Note: This statement is not found in Blessed Augustine, although in Psalm 103, at the verse “You who roof with waters,” he takes the waters to signify charity, as do Prosper and the ordinary and interlinear glosses on the same passage.]

## C. XIV.

Charity is the water of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst forever.”

[Note: John 4:13.]

**Gratian.** Therefore, when the reprobate is consigned to eternal fires and thirsts forever, how will he drink living water, or how will he drink water springing up into eternal life, he who, like lead sunk into the depths, pays the penalties of eternal damnation? Likewise, without charity, how can anyone have true contrition of heart? How, then, can he have forgiveness of sins? If these have not been forgiven, how are not all things without exception to be exacted in punishment?

Likewise the Lord says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me has eternal life.” [Note: John 6:47.] Therefore whoever does not have eternal life does not believe in Christ. But one believes in Christ who has charity. For to believe in Christ is to tend toward him by loving him. This is the faith which, as the Apostle defines it, works through love; forgiveness of sins is promised to this alone. But if charity cannot be separated from the Christian faith, to which alone forgiveness is promised, how could one who did not possess charity have the Christian faith—that is, have believed in Christ? How, then, did he receive forgiveness of sins? If he did not receive it, how are not all his works without exception to be punished with eternal penalties?

Likewise the Lord says: “I am the living bread who came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever.” [Note: John 6:51.] Therefore one who does not live forever has not eaten the living bread; but one who has not eaten it has not believed. For eating the living bread means believing in Christ, that is, tending toward him in love. Therefore, since the reprobate did not believe in him whom he did not eat, and thus did not have the Christian faith—by which alone sins are forgiven—how, if the Lord lives, to whom the Father has given all judgment, will he escape the judgment of perpetual damnation for all sins, not only actual but also original?

### Part III

§ 1. These statements about charity may be understood of perfect charity, which, once possessed, is never lost. But the beginnings of charity are nourished so that they may grow, and trampled down so that they may fail. For no one suddenly becomes supreme; rather, in good conduct—which does not exist without charity—each person begins with the least things in order to reach great things. Therefore there are degrees not only between one virtue and another but also within the same virtue.

Accordingly Gregory writes in Homily XV on Ezekiel:

## C. XV.

[The supplied source ends here.]

When [Note: [Col. 1569] *Dum* (“when”): Basel, Paris, and Lyon I editions.] the Lord receives the holy Church [Note: [Col. 1569] *suscepit* (“received”): Basel, Venice I–II, Paris, Lyon I editions.], he is recognized in her stages, because her glory is made manifest through her increase. For as much as the holy Church advances by ascending [Note: [Col. 1569] *profecerit* (“will have advanced”): original reading.], so much does God become known to human beings through her virtues [Note: [Col. 1569] *virtute* (“virtue,” singular): editions collated, except the original.]. Blessed Job also speaks of these stages, saying [Note: [Col. 1569] Job 31:37.]: “At each of my steps I shall proclaim him.” For he proclaims the almighty Lord [Note: [Col. 1569] “God”: Basel edition.] at each of his steps who, through the increases of the virtues that he has begun [Note: [Col. 1569] *accepit* (“received”): same edition; *accipit* (“receives”): remaining editions.], continually renders to him praise for his loving-kindness. If there were indeed [Note: [Col. 1569] *quidem* (“indeed”): collated editions, except the original and Argentinian edition.] no stages in the ascent of the heart, the Psalmist would not say [Note: [Col. 1569] Psalm 83:8.]: “They went from strength to strength.” Nor is it surprising that there are stages from one virtue to another, when each virtue itself is exercised [Note: [Col. 1569] *augetur* (“is increased”): same editions.] as it were by certain stages, and is thus led through the increase of merits to the highest point. [Note: [Col. 1569] The words “from one virtue to another” are absent from the Venice II edition; *si* (“if”) is absent from the Basel edition.]

§ 1. The beginnings of virtue are one thing, its progress another, its perfection another [Note: [Col. 1569] Some editions add “of virtue” after “another”; *profectus* (“progress”) is read as *provectus* (“advancement”) in the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice I–II editions.]. For if faith itself were not led to its perfection by certain stages [Note: [Col. 1569] This clause is absent from the original; compare Peter Lombard, book 1, distinction 31.], the holy Apostles would never have said [Note: [Col. 1569] Luke 17:5.]: “Increase [Note: [Col. 1569] *auge* (“increase”): collated editions.] our faith” [Note: [Col. 1569] “in us”: Basel edition.]. And a certain man came to Jesus [Note: [Col. 1569] “God”: same edition; “Lord”: remaining editions.], wishing his son to be healed; but when asked whether he believed, he answered [Note: [Col. 1569] Mark 9:23.]: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.” Consider, I pray you, what is said. If he believed, why did he speak of unbelief? But if he knew that he possessed unbelief, how did he believe? Yet because faith grows by the hidden inspiration of grace through the stages of its merits, at one and the same time the person who had not yet believed perfectly both believed and was unbelieving [Note: [Col. 1569] *is* (“the person”): absent from the Basel edition.].

§ 2. The Lord plainly describes these stages under the name of harvest, saying [Note: [Col. 1569] Mark 4:26.]: “The kingdom of God is as though a man should cast [Note: [Col. 1569] *jactet* (“should toss”): collated editions.] seed upon the ground, and should sleep and rise by night and by day, and the seed should sprout and grow while he does not know it. For the earth brings forth fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear; and when it has brought forth the fruit, immediately he sends in the sickle, because the time of harvest is at hand.” [Note: [Col. 1569] The words “when it has brought forth fruit” are absent from the Vulgate; “when it brings forth” is the reading of the original.]

A man casts seed upon the ground when he implants a good intention in his heart; and after casting the seed, he sleeps, because he now rests in hope of a good work [Note: [Col. 1571] “now”: absent from the original and the Basel edition.]. He rises by night and by day [Note: [Col. 1571] “rises”: collated editions.], because he advances amid adversities and prosperities; and the seed sprouts and grows while he does not know it [Note: [Col. 1571] These words are absent from the Basel edition.], because, while [Note: [Col. 1571] “and when”: original; “when”: collated editions.] he is still unable to measure his own increase, the virtue once conceived is led onward to perfection [Note: [Col. 1571] “advancement”: original reading.]. And the earth brings forth fruit of itself, because, grace going before it, the human mind spontaneously [Note: [Col. 1571] “spontaneously” as a feminine adjective: collated editions.] rises to the progress [Note: [Col. 1571] “fruit”: original reading.] of a good work [Note: [Col. 1571] “rises”: collated editions, except the original and Basel edition.].

But this same earth first produces the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear [Note: [Col. 1571] “the ear”: Basel edition.]. To produce the blade is still to possess the tender freshness of a good beginning [Note: [Col. 1571] “the tenderness of the good for this purpose”: same edition.]. The blade reaches the ear [Note: [Col. 1571] “comes”: collated editions.] when the virtue conceived in the mind draws itself onward to the progress [Note: [Col. 1571] “advancement”: Argentinian and Nuremberg editions.] of good work [Note: [Col. 1571] “draws itself forth”: Lyon II–III editions.]. But full grain bears fruit in the ear when virtue has now advanced so far that it can be a strong and perfect work. But when it has brought forth fruit [Note: [Col. 1571] “But when it has produced fruit”: original reading.], immediately he sends in the sickle, because the time of harvest is at hand. For almighty God, when fruit has been produced, sends in the sickle and cuts down his harvest [Note: [Col. 1571] This phrase is absent from the Basel edition]: when he has brought each person to perfect works, he cuts short that person’s temporal life by the sentence he issues, in order to bring his grain into the heavenly barns.

Therefore, when we conceive good desires, we cast seed into the ground. When we begin to do what is right, we are the blade. When we grow toward the progress [Note: [Col. 1571] “advancement”: Argentinian and Basel editions.] of good work, we come to the ear [Note: [Col. 1571D] This sentence—“When we grow toward the progress of good work, we come to the ear”—is absent from the original.]; and when we are made firm in the perfection of that same work [Note: [Col. 1571] “of good work”: original reading.], we produce full grain in the ear.

§ 3. Peter was indeed a blade when, at the time of the Passion, following the Lord out of love, he was afraid to confess him before a maidservant’s voice. There was already greenness in his mind, because he believed in the Lord, the Redeemer of all [Note: [Col. 1571] “the Redeemer”: Basel edition; “the Lord of all”: remaining editions, except the Argentinian edition.]; but it was still very pliant and was trodden down by fear. He had already risen into an ear when, after being afraid to confess him as one who would die, he saw him alive in Galilee at the angel’s announcement. But he had attained full grain in the ear [Note: [Col. 1571] “then”: original; “in the ear”: Basel edition.] when the Spirit came down from above [Note: [Col. 1571] “the Holy Spirit”: Basel and Lyon II–III editions.] and strengthened his mind in the Lord’s love, so that, made firm, he despised the violence of his persecutors when beaten and freely preached his Redeemer amid scourges.

§ 4. Therefore let no one be despised who is seen still to be in the tender state of mind’s good purpose, because God’s wheat begins as a blade in order to become grain. Thus the man *clothed in linen* comes [Note: [Col. 1571] “may come”: Lyon II–III editions.] to the gate, because our Lord and Redeemer brings his members, as they enter, to himself [Note: [Col. 1571D] Most old copies, and Blessed Gregory, read “is brought”; it has not been emended because of the gloss.]; and he ascends by its stages, because as we advance he is more highly exalted for us [Note: [Col. 1571] These words are absent from the Argentinian and Basel editions.], in proportion [Note: [Col. 1571] “as”: original and collated editions.] as he is known to be lofty [Note: [Col. 1571] “loftier”: Basel and Lyon editions.] and incomprehensible [Note: [Col. 1571] “more incomprehensible”: Lyon editions.]. He is said to ascend in the virtue of our *minds* [Note: [Col. 1571] “of virtues”: collated editions, except the original and Venice II; “of our minds” is absent from the original, while the editions add “by stages”; compare Bohm.], because he is shown to us to be so much more sublime [Note: [Col. 1571] These words are absent from the Basel edition.] as our mind is separated from lowly or infirm things [Note: [Col. 1571] “infirm or lowly”: Argentinian edition.].

[Col. 1572B] Likewise Augustine says in the book *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 17:

### Chapter XVI

Whoever wishes to perform God’s commandments [Note: [Col. 1571] *mandatum* (“commandment”): original reading.] and cannot already has a good will indeed, but one still small and weak. Yet he will be able when he has made it great and strong. For when the martyrs performed those great commandments, they performed them surely with a great will—that is, with great love—of which love the Lord himself says: “No one has greater love than this” [Note: [Col. 1571] Some collated editions add “has”; compare John 15:13.], etc.

(And a little later [Note: [Col. 1571] Peter Lombard, book 3, distinction 29.]:)

§ 1. The Apostle Peter did not yet possess that very love [Note: [Col. 1571] “had”: collated editions.] when he denied the Lord three times through fear. “For fear is not in love,” as John the Evangelist says in his Epistle [Note: [Col. 1571] 1 John 4:18.], “but perfect love casts fear out.” Yet love, though small and imperfect, was not absent from him [Note: [Col. 1571] “love was not lacking in him”: collated editions.] when he said: “Lord, I will lay down my life for you” [Note: [Col. 1571] “I lay down”: collated editions, except the Basel and Lyon II–III editions.].

(The same author, in his fifth tractate on the First Epistle of John: § 2. If anyone has such great love that he is ready even [Note: [Col. 1571] “even”: absent from the Basel edition.] to die for his brethren, love is perfect in that person. But is it wholly perfect as soon as it is born? It is born in order to be perfected; once born, it is nourished; once nourished, it is strengthened; once strengthened, it is perfected. When it has reached perfection, what does it say [Note: [Col. 1571] “what do you say”: collated editions; compare Philippians 1:21.]? “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. I desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ, which is far better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake.” He wished to live for those for whom he was prepared to die.)

*From “I desired to be dissolved” to the end, the words are added from Blessed Augustine because they contribute to the completeness of the argument.*

### Chapter XVII

The same author, in the ninth tractate on the same Epistle [Note: [Col. 1573] Peter Lombard, book 3, distinction 34.].

Just as a needle introduces linen [Note: [Col. 1573] “thread”: collated editions, except the Basel edition.], so fear introduces love [Note: [Col. 1573] These words are absent from the Basel edition.]; love grows, fear diminishes, and conversely.

[Note: [Col. 1573] Augustine’s actual words are: “Just as we see flax introduced by a needle when something is sewn—the needle enters first, but unless it comes out, the thread does not follow—so fear first occupies the mind. But fear does not remain there, because it entered in order to introduce love.” And a little above: “The greater the love, the less the fear; the less the love, the greater the fear.” This chapter has been compiled from these words.]

### Chapter XVIII

Likewise, tractate 5 on the same Epistle [Note: [Col. 1573] The words have been transposed.].

Perhaps love has been born in you, but is not yet perfect; do not despair. Nourish it, lest it be choked [Note: [Col. 1573] “lest it perhaps be suffocated”: collated editions.].

### Chapter XIX

The same author, to Jerome, Epistle 29 [Note: [Col. 1574] This chapter is a kind of summary of Augustine’s words at the indicated place.], [Note: [Col. 1573] Epistle 167 in the Maurist edition, written A.D. 415; Peter Lombard, book 3, distinction 36.]

Love in some people is perfect [Note: [Col. 1573] These words are absent from the collated editions, except the original, Basel, and Lyon II–III editions.], in others it is imperfect; but the most perfect love cannot be possessed in this life.

### Chapter XX

The same author, in the book of Fifty Homilies, Homily 9 [Note: [Col. 1573] Sermon 178 in the Maurist edition; in the collated editions it is ascribed to Gregory; Peter Lombard, same place.].

If my discourse finds in your hearts some spark of God’s gratuitous love, nourish it [Note: [Col. 1573] “to nourish it”: Nuremberg and Venice I–II editions.]; devote yourselves to increasing it [Note: [Col. 1573] “devote yourselves to it”: Lyon II–III editions; the remaining collated editions read “strive to increase it,” or a similar form.]. And a little later: Weep [Note: [Col. 1574C] “Weep” has not been emended because of the gloss. Many old manuscripts read *flate* (“blow”), as do the Argentinian, Basel, Nuremberg, and Venice I–II editions; the original reads: “Nourish within yourselves this spark of good love, of which the Lord says: ‘I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it should burn?’ Blow upon it; nourish it within yourselves,” etc.], nourish it within yourselves. When it has grown and produced a most worthy flame, it will consume the wood of *fleshly* desires [Note: [Col. 1573] The wording concerning its growth and the consumption of the fuel is connected differently in the collated editions; the original reads “the hay.”].

Gratian. Conversely, stages in virtue are also proved by the fact that the stages of sin itself are plainly evident. For just as no one becomes supremely good suddenly, so no one becomes utterly vile suddenly.

Hence Augustine also says in book I of *The Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 23 [Note: [Col. 1573] Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 16.]:

### Chapter XXI

Just as one arrives at sin through three stages—suggestion, delight, consent [Note: [Col. 1573] “consensus”: Basel and Lyon II–III editions.]—so there are three distinctions of sin itself: in the heart, in deed, and in habit [Note: [Col. 1573] The collated editions read “in the heart, in deed, and in consent.”], as though three deaths. One is as though in the house: that is, when the heart consents to lust. Another is as though already carried outside the gate: when assent proceeds to action. The third is when the mind, oppressed by the force of evil habit as by an earthly mass, lies already rotting, as though in the tomb. Whoever reads the Gospel recognizes that the Lord raised these three kinds of dead persons [Note: [Col. 1573] “whoever will have read”: Basel and Lyon II–III editions; compare Matthew 9 and Luke 7.].

### Chapter XXII

Likewise Gregory, book XXV of the *Moralia*, chapter 16.

It must be known that sin is committed [Note: [Col. 1573] “admitted”: collated editions.] in three ways: by ignorance, by weakness, or deliberately. Sin committed through weakness is indeed graver than that committed through ignorance; but sin committed deliberately is much graver [Note: [Col. 1573] “stronger”: Basel edition.] than that committed through weakness.

### Chapter XXIII

The same author, book XXI of the *Moralia*, chapter 3.

Meanwhile it must be understood that what the mind suffers from the temptation of the flesh is one thing, but what happens when it is bound by consent to delight [Note: [Col. 1573] “delights”: Argentinian and Basel editions.] is another. For it is often struck by an evil thought, yet resists [Note: [Col. 1573] “is weakened”: same editions, chiefly Argentinian and Nuremberg.]. But often, when it conceives something perverse [Note: [Col. 1573] “what is conceived”: Argentinian and Basel editions; one edition reads “what it conceives.”], it also inwardly wills *it* [Note: [Col. 1573] Some editions add “already.”] through desire. And surely an unclean thought [Note: [Col. 1573] “malignant thought”: Basel edition.] does not defile the mind when it assaults it, but when it subjugates the mind to itself through delight. Hence the outstanding preacher *says* [Note: [Col. 1573] 1 Corinthians 10:13.]: “Let no temptation seize you except a human one.” For a human temptation is that by which we are commonly touched in thought even against our will, since it belongs to us, from the burden of corruptible humanity itself, that at times *even* unlawful things should come to the mind [Note: [Col. 1573] “come”: collated editions, except the original and Lyon II–III editions.]. But temptation is now demonic and not human when the mind binds itself by consent to what the corruptibility of the flesh suggests.

### Chapter XXIV

Likewise Jerome on Amos, chapter 1.

“On account of three crimes of Damascus,” etc., as above [Note: [Col. 1573] Chapter 71, Distinction 1, *On Penance*.].

Gratian. It is no wonder that stages are said to exist in virtue, since the stages of sin are displayed with equal clarity.

§ 1. Therefore this love, which was a blade in Peter before his denial and which arises in each person before it is strengthened, is lost before it reaches its perfection and is restored. Hence Augustine says in the book *On Correction and Grace*, chapter 7:

All those who have been separated from that original condemnation by the bounty of this divine grace are, without doubt, provided with an opportunity to hear the Gospel; and when they hear, they believe; and in the faith which works through love they persevere to the end. And if at any time they stray, they are corrected and amended; and some of them, even if they are not corrected by human beings, return to the way which they had left.

[Col. 1575A] ### Chapter XXV

The same author, in the same place.

“The firm foundation of God stands, immovable [Note: [Col. 1575D] “Immovable” is absent from the original but has not been deleted because of the gloss.], bearing this seal: ‘The Lord knows [Note: [Col. 1575] “knew”: Vulgate; “has known”: Augustine; “God”: Basel edition.] those who are his.’” [2 Timothy 2:19.] Their faith, which works through love, certainly either does not fail at all, or, if there are any whose faith does fail, it is restored [Note: [Col. 1575] “they are restored”: collated editions.] before this life ends; and, when the intervening wrongdoing has been erased, perseverance is reckoned to them unto the end [Note: [Col. 1575] “they are reckoned to perseverance unto the end”: same editions.].

### Chapter XXVI

The same author, in the same book, chapter 9 [Note: [Col. 1575] Compare below, Distinction 4, chapter 8.].

No one of them, changed from good to evil [Note: [Col. 1575] “changed” rather than “transformed”: collated editions.], ends this life.

### Chapter XXVII

The same author, in the same place.

“For those who love *him*, all things work together for good,” [Note: [Col. 1575] Basel adds “it is said”; the collated editions read “God” for “those who”; “cooperate”: collated editions.]—indeed, all things so completely that even if some of them wander and stray, he makes even that itself work to their good [Note: [Col. 1575] “will make”: collated editions.].

### Chapter XXVIII

Likewise the Apostle, to the Galatians, chapter 5, verse 6.

“Circumcision is nothing, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love.” And this was formerly so among you [Note: [Col. 1575] These words seem to be either a gloss or the words of Gratian.], because you were running well through the works of faith from [Note: [Col. 1575] “and from”: collated editions, chiefly Lyon.] love.

### Chapter XXIX

The same author, to the Hebrews, chapter 6, verse 10.

“God is not so unjust as to forget your work,” etc.

Gratian. The work by which they had made all their possessions common, and this out of love, and this for the glory of God. Behold a threefold good, as if he said: formerly you performed many deeds, on account of which, if you repent of evil deeds, God will do good to you. Furthermore, when the Apostle rebukes the Romans and the Galatians, he proves that by the merit of faith they had obtained remission of sins, sanctification in the Holy Spirit, and the righteousness of good works. All these either were never truly present in them without love, or else those who afterwards fell away—the persons who boasted of works of the law—had possessed true love, from which they later fell.

Likewise Augustine says of every adult [Note: [Col. 1575] This sentence is read in tractate 6 on the First Epistle of John, at 1 John 3:6.]:

### Chapter XXX

Take away love: hatred takes possession. Likewise:

§ 1. Everyone who does not love hates.

Likewise in the Gospel:

§ 2. “No one can serve two masters; for he will either hate the one and love the other, or endure the one and despise the other.” [Matthew 6:24.]

Gratian. Now Adam, since he was created by the Lord in mature adulthood, before he was tempted by the devil—while a wife was formed from his side, while he was caught up in ecstasy and was present among the angelic court, while upon awakening he prophesied the future mysteries of Christ and the Church—had either love or hatred. But if he had hatred, the devil was not the author of our sin. Again, if he was created by God without love, he did not receive God’s likeness in his creation. Again, if he was created without love, he was not made righteous and innocent by God; for a creature capable of reason and free choice cannot share in righteousness and innocence without love. It follows, therefore, that Adam possessed love before he sinned, without which he could not have been righteous and innocent.

[Col. 1576B] Hence Augustine, in *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book VI, chapter 24 [Note: [Col. 1575D] In this and the following chapter, some material has been added from the original, in which these propositions are nevertheless expounded much more fully and clearly.]:

### Chapter XXXI

How are we said to be renewed if we do not receive *this* [Note: [Col. 1575] “receive”: original; “we receive”: collated editions.] which the first man lost, “in whom all die”? We plainly receive this: namely, the righteousness from which he fell into sin [Note: [Col. 1575] “through which”: original; “from which”: Basel edition.].

And a little later, chapter 7 [Note: [Col. 1575] Colossians 3:9–10.]:

§ 1. “Putting *yourselves* off from the old man *with his deeds*, put on the new man, who is renewed in the knowledge [Note: [Col. 1575] “in knowledge”: Basel edition; “in cognition”: remaining editions.] of God [Note: [Col. 1575] “of faith”: collated editions; absent from the Vulgate.] according to the image of him who created him.” Adam lost this image, impressed upon the spirit of death (*mortis*) [Note: [Col. 1575] “mind” (*mentis*): original and collated editions.], through sin.

And after a few words:

§ 2. “That first robe” [Note: [Col. 1575] Luke 15:22.] is the righteousness itself [Note: [Col. 1575] “that very righteousness”: original; collated editions.] from which Adam fell.

### Chapter XXXII

The same author, in Homily 11 [Note: [Col. 1575] This is compiled from scattered words of the sermon to catechumens on the Creed against the Jews, which the Maurists rejected as apocryphal.].

The prince of all vices, when he saw Adam made from the clay of the earth in God’s image, adorned with chastity, ordered by temperance, surrounded by love [Note: [Col. 1575] “splendid”: collated editions.], stripped our first parents of those gifts and great goods, and moreover destroyed them [Note: [Col. 1575] “and likewise”: Basel edition; “and equally”: remaining editions.]. For when he had taken chastity, self-control, *love, and immortality* from humankind, he subjected humankind to his own dominion [Note: [Col. 1575] “subjugated”: collated editions.].

And a little later:

§ 1. Adam, having lost temperance, became intemperate [Note: [Col. 1575] “became”: collated editions.]; having lost love, he was found evil.

### Chapter XXXIII

Likewise Ambrose, book VI, Epistle 41, to Sabinus [Note: [Col. 1575] Epistle 39 in the Maurist edition.].

When Adam was alone, he did not transgress, because his mind adhered to God.

[Col. 1577A] ### Chapter XXXIV

Likewise, to the same person, in the same book, Epistle 42 [Note: [Col. 1577] Epistle 45, same edition.].

The first man was a fresh work of God, a continual companion in conversation, a citizen [Note: [Col. 1577] “who had been planted together with the virtues of the holy angels”: absent from the Basel edition; collated editions.] of the saints, planted together [Note: [Col. 1577D] In the common editions: “planted together with angels.” This word is absent from many manuscripts and from the original.] with the virtues.

### Chapter XXXV

The same author, *Hexaemeron*, book VI, chapter 7.

That soul is painted by God which has within itself the resistant grace of virtues and the brightness of piety [Note: [Col. 1577] “is joined together”: collated editions.]. That soul is well painted in which the image of divine operation shines forth. That soul is well painted in which are the splendor of glory and the image of the Father’s substance. According to this shining image, the painting is precious. According to this image Adam was painted before sin [Note: [Col. 1577] “was painted”: absent from the original.]; but when he fell, he laid aside *the image of the heavenly one and assumed an earthly likeness*.

### Chapter XXXVI

The same author, *On Flight from the World*, chapter 4.

To be like God is to possess righteousness, *to possess* wisdom, and to be perfect in virtue [Note: [Col. 1577] “of God”: collated editions, chiefly the Basel edition.].

### Chapter XXXVII

The same author, book II, *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*, chapter 5.

The wise person is never empty, but always has within himself the garment of prudence, and can say [Note: [Col. 1577] Job 29:14.]: “I put on righteousness, *and* I clothed myself in judgment, *as Job said*.” For these are the inner coverings of the mind, which no one else can take away except when someone is stripped by his own fault. Thus Adam, stripped in this way [Note: [Col. 1577] “stripped”: collated editions.], was found naked.

### Chapter XXXVIII

The same author, in the book *On Isaac and the Soul*, chapter 5.

Nor was the first Adam [Note: [Col. 1577D] The original reads “at first.” Because of the gloss, the wording was not changed. The word “man,” which follows in the common editions, is likewise absent from many manuscripts.] naked when innocence clothed him [Note: [Col. 1577] “when it clothed him”: collated editions.].

### Chapter XXXIX

The same author, in the book *On Paradise*, chapter 13.

“When they knew that they were naked” [Note: [Col. 1577] “And”: original; compare Genesis 3:7.]. They had indeed been naked before, but not without the coverings [Note: [Col. 1577] “covering”: collated editions.] of virtues.

Gratian. There is also the objection, loudly proclaimed by every authority: if Adam had remained as he was before sin, he would have been translated into the glory which the saints will possess; but no adult enters without love. Therefore he had love.

§ 1. An objection is likewise drawn from Moses, whose faith the Apostle commends in his Epistle to the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 1577] Compare Hebrews 11.] and whose merits he proclaims with worthy praises: when he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter [Note: [Col. 1577] Exodus 2.]; when he chose affliction with his brethren rather than enjoyment of a temporal palace; when, out of compassion for his brother, he buried the Egyptian in the sand; when, fearing the Egyptian king’s anger, he left Egypt; when, fortified by divine assistance, he despised the king’s fury and led the people out of Egypt by the power of signs. With what praises can all this be extolled if love was not then in him, when the branch of a good work has no greenness in itself unless it proceeds from the root of love?

And how did he not possess love, to whom the Lord spoke face to face [Note: [Col. 1577] Exodus 33.], as one is accustomed to speak with a friend? How did he not possess love, when praying for the people he said [Note: [Col. 1577] Exodus 32:31 ff.]: “Either forgive them this sin, or blot me out of your book”? Did he not love his neighbor, who offered himself for the people and delivered them from destruction [Note: [Col. 1577] Numbers 16.]? Did he not love God, when, raging for his sake against the worshippers of the calf, he crushed the calf’s head into powder, mixed it with water, and gave it to the Israelites to drink, ordering some of its worshippers struck with the sword, so as to reconcile to God the people whose destruction would otherwise have been greater [Note: [Col. 1577] Exodus 33.]?

Did he not possess love, from whose spirit the Lord took and placed it upon the seventy elders of Israel [Note: [Col. 1577] Numbers 11.]? Yet at the waters of contradiction, doubting God’s power or his kindness, although he had promised with otherwise certain faith that he would bring water from the rock, he cried out distrustfully, saying [Note: [Col. 1577] Numbers 20:10.]: “Can I bring water out of this rock for you?” Let no one regard this as slight, since, as punishment for his sin, the Lord said to him and Aaron [Note: [Col. 1577] “Because you did not heed my voice, so as to glorify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring this people into the land which I gave them” (Numbers 12).]:

§ 2. Did Aaron not possess love when he was given to his brother as a helper, to be his mouth to the people, and so that signs might be performed through him in Egypt [Note: [Col. 1577] Exodus 4.]? Yet afterwards, in the worship of the calf [Note: [Col. 1577] Exodus 32.], he gave his consent to the people. Did he not possess love when, out of the entire multitude of Israel’s children, he alone was chosen by the Lord [Note: [Col. 1577] Leviticus 8.] to exercise the high priesthood before him? If he did not possess love, he was not good; but if he was not good, why was he chosen by the Lord as high priest above the rest? Did he not possess love when he stood against the plague for the people with a censer and appeased God’s wrath? Yet, as stated above, at the waters of contradiction he later provoked the Lord’s wrath against himself.

§ 3. Did David also not possess love, upon whom the Spirit of the Lord came directly from the day of his anointing [Note: [Col. 1577] 1 Samuel 16.]? Or will it perhaps be said that it came upon him merely so that from then on he might have the grace of prophecy, not so that he might receive the grace of divine love? It seems entirely absurd to hold this concerning one of whom the Lord said [Note: [Col. 1579] Acts 13:22.]: “I have found a man according to my heart.”

How did he not possess love when he spared the man seeking his life, cut off the hem of his cloak, and afterwards was grievously stricken in heart, crying [Note: [Col. 1579] 1 Samuel 24:15.]: “Whom are you pursuing, king of Israel? A dead dog and a single flea.” How did he not possess love when he grieved so deeply over the death of his enemy [Note: [Col. 1579] 2 Samuel 1.]? How did he not possess love when he did not drink the water from the cistern of Bethlehem, brought to him at the peril of his men, but poured it out before the Lord [Note: [Col. 1579] 2 Samuel 23.]? How did he not possess love when Michal, Saul’s daughter, mocked him because he had danced before the ark of the Lord, striking the harp and psaltery, and he said [Note: [Col. 1579] 2 Samuel 6:22.]: “I will play and become yet more lowly in my own eyes”?

If he did not possess love, with what conscience did he confidently call down this prayer upon himself, saying [Note: [Col. 1579] Psalm 7:5.]: “If I have repaid evil to those repaying me, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies”? If he did not possess love, with what rashness did he ask to be judged justly, saying [Note: [Col. 1579] Psalm 25, heading]: “Judge me, O God, according to my righteousness and according to my innocence which is upon me”? Likewise: “Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence.”

Yet after these and countless other evidences of divine and heavenly love, no one who has heard of Bathsheba’s adultery and Uriah’s murder is ignorant how grievously he sinned [Note: [Col. 1579] 2 Samuel 11.]. If he offered his repentance to the Lord without love, he did not possess true contrition of heart. How then did he dare promise the Lord the sacrifice of a contrite heart and afflicted spirit, saying [Note: [Col. 1579] Psalm 50:18 ff.]: “If you had desired sacrifice, I would surely have given it; you will not delight in burnt offerings. The sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit,” etc.?

Finally, since no remission is promised by God for false repentance, how did he deserve to hear from the Prophet [Note: [Col. 1579] 2 Samuel 12:13.], “Your sin has been forgiven,” if he did not possess true contrition of heart? It is therefore plain that he possessed love at that time and, out of love, offered to the Lord the sacrifice of a contrite heart and afflicted spirit. Otherwise, he would rashly have asked [Note: [Col. 1579] Psalm 50:11.]: “Turn your face away from my sins,” and the other things contained in the same Psalm, unless hatred of evil and love of good had moved him to the humility of repentance.

Concerning him Saint Ambrose also writes in the book *On Isaac and the Soul*, chapter 3 [Note: [Col. 1579] The wording has been changed, but the meaning remains intact.]: “Holy David fled the hatreds [Note: [Col. 1579] “hatred”: Bohm.] of King Saul, not by leaving the lands but by avoiding the contagion of an unmerciful and proud king, because his mind adhered to God”—to whom no adult can adhere without love. Yet how grievously he later sinned in numbering the people is shown by the punishment of that sin [Note: [Col. 1579] 1 Chronicles 21.].

§ 4. Likewise, on this view, anyone who has committed a grave sin has not obtained true remission of sins in baptism, whether that person approached baptism in infancy or as an adult, because he did not possess God’s love, without which no one has ever found grace. Thus, according to the heresy of Jovinian, if anyone has truly been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot afterwards commit grave sin; or, if he does commit grave sin, he is shown to have been reborn only from water, not from the Spirit.

The following saying from John’s Epistle seems to agree with this position [Note: [Col. 1579] 1 John 3:9.]: “Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he is born of God. In this the children of God and the children of the devil are manifest.” And at the end of the Epistle [Note: [Col. 1579] 1 John 5:18.]: “Everyone who is born of God does not sin, but God’s begetting preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him.”

But how far this apostolic authority favors that position, and how much that sect’s error opposes the truth, Jerome shows by writing against Jovinian, book II, at the beginning:

### Chapter XL

[Note: [Col. 1579D] To understand better the matters pertaining to the beginning of this long chapter, it is necessary to read the preceding material in Blessed Jerome, where the objection derived from Saint John’s words is set out. Indeed, throughout this chapter one must often return to the original, although much has been corrected from it and some things that appeared more necessary have been added.]

For if, he says, everyone who is born of God does not sin and cannot be tempted by the devil, how does he command them to beware lest they be tempted, saying [Note: [Col. 1579] 1 John 5, final verse]: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” [Note: [Col. 1579] “commanded”: editions compared with the original Paris and Argentinian editions]? And again in the same Epistle: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and [Note: [Col. 1579] added: “God”: editions compared with the original Basle edition] just, to forgive us our sins and cleanse [Note: [Col. 1579] “will cleanse”: Basle edition; “will wash”: Lyons editions II and III; “may cleanse”: remaining Vulgate editions] us from all iniquity. If [Note: [Col. 1579] added: “however”: editions compared with the original Basle edition] we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us” [Note: [Col. 1579] 1 John 1:8] [Col. 1580C]. I think [Note: [Col. 1579] “I judge”: editions compared with the original Lyons editions II and III] that John [Note: [Col. 1579] “the blessed John”: editions compared with the original editions] wrote as one baptized to the baptized, and that every sin is from [Note: [Col. 1579] “out of”: same editions] the devil. He confesses himself a sinner and hopes for forgiveness of sins after baptism. Yet my Jovinian says: “Do not touch me, for I am clean.” What then? Does the Apostle contradict himself? By no means. For in the same place he immediately explains why [Note: [Col. 1579] “when he had said”: Basle edition] he said this [Note: [Col. 1579] “declared”: editions compared with the original Lyons editions]: “My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin. But [Note: [Col. 1579] “and if”: Basle edition; “but if”: remaining editions] if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins, not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world. And by this we know that we have known him, if we keep his commandments” [Note: [Col. 1579] 1 John 2:1 ff.; “if we have kept”: editions compared with the original Basle edition] [Col. 1581A]. “Whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him. But whoever keeps his word, truly in him the love of God is perfected. By this we know that we are in him. Whoever says that he remains in him ought also to walk as he [Note: [Col. 1581] “himself”: editions compared with the original editions] walked.”

Therefore, he says, I write to you, my little children, “everyone who is born of God does not sin,” so that [Note: [Col. 1581] “and therefore I say to you that”: editions compared with the original editions] you may not sin, and that you may know that you remain in the begetting of the Lord as long as you have not sinned; indeed, those who persevere in the Lord’s begetting cannot sin. For what fellowship has light [Note: [Col. 1581] “of light” (“to light”: Basle edition) with darkness, Christ (“to Christ”: Basle edition) with Belial: editions compared with the original editions] with darkness, or Christ with Belial? As day and night do not seek [Note: [Col. 1581] “cannot”: same editions; “are not able”: Böhm] to be mixed [Col. 1581B], so *neither* can righteousness and iniquity, sin and good works, Christ and antichrist.
