If we receive Christ as a guest in the lodging of our breast, we immediately drive out [Note: [Col. 1581] “let us flee”: Basle edition] the devil. If we sin, and the devil enters through the door of sin, Christ at once withdraws. Hence David too says after sin: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” [Note: [Col. 1581] Psalm 50:14]—namely, the joy which he had lost by sinning.

“Whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him” [Note: [Col. 1581] 1 John 2:4]. Christ is called truth [Note: [Col. 1581] added: “indeed, is”: editions compared with the original editions]: “I,” he says, “am the way, the truth, and [Note: [Col. 1581] “and life”: absent from Jerome] the life” [Note: [Col. 1581] John 14:6]. We applaud ourselves in vain for belonging to him [Note: [Col. 1581] “applaud”: editions compared with the original editions] whose commandments we do not perform. “For one who knows [Note: [Col. 1581] James 4:17] the good [Note: [Col. 1581] added from the Vulgate: “to do”: Basle and Lyons II–III editions] and does not do it, it is sin.” As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead [Col. 1581C]. Nor should we think it a great thing to know one God, since even demons believe and tremble [Note: [Col. 1581] James 2:19]. “Whoever says that he remains in him ought also to walk as he [Note: [Col. 1581] “and he himself”: editions compared with the original editions] walked” [Note: [Col. 1581] 1 John 2:6].

## IV. Part. § 1

Let the opponent choose which of two alternatives he wishes—for we give him the choice: does he remain in Christ, or does he not remain? If he remains, then let him walk as Christ did. But if it is presumptuous to promise likeness to the Lord’s virtues, he does not remain in Christ, because he does not walk as Christ did. He “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth”; when reviled, he did not revile in return, and, like a lamb before its shearer [Note: [Col. 1581] added: “itself”: editions compared with the original editions], so he did not open his mouth [Note: [Col. 1581] 1 Peter 2:22]. The ruler of this world came to him and found nothing in him [Note: [Col. 1581] John 14:30]. Though he had committed no sin, God made him to be sin for us [Note: [Col. 1581] “was made sin”: Basle edition; “God made himself sin,” i.e. he bore the punishment of sin: remaining editions; cf. 2 Corinthians 5:21] [Col. 1582A].

But we, according to the Epistle of James, all commit many sins, and no one is clean from sins—not even an infant whose life is only one day old [Note: [Col. 1581] James 5:16; this is absent from the original]. For who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will trust that he is clean from sins? And we are held guilty in the likeness of Adam’s transgression [Note: [Col. 1581] Proverbs 20:9; Romans 9:14]. Hence David also says: “Behold [Note: [Col. 1581] added: “for”: Basle and Lyons editions],” he says [Note: [Col. 1581] absent from Basle and Lyons I editions], “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived [Note: [Col. 1581] “gave birth to”: editions compared with the original Basle edition] me” [Note: [Col. 1581] Psalm 50:7]. And blessed Job says: “If I am righteous, my mouth will speak impiously; and if blameless, I shall be found perverse; and if purified with snow and washed with clean hands, you have sufficiently stained me with filth, and my garment has become abhorrent to me” [Note: [Col. 1581] Job 9:20–21 according to the Septuagint].

But [Note: [Col. 1581] “nevertheless”: editions compared with the original Argentinian edition], lest we despair entirely, supposing that after the sins committed following baptism we cannot be saved [Col. 1582B], he immediately moderates this very statement: “And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins—not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world” [Note: [Col. 1581] 1 John 2:1]. He speaks this to believers after baptism and promises the Lord as advocate for their sins. Nor does he say, “If you have sinned in any respect [Note: [Col. 1581] absent from editions compared with the original Basle edition], you have Christ [Note: [Col. 1581] “Jesus Christ”: editions compared with the original editions; added: “the righteous”: Paris and Lyons editions] as an advocate with the Father, and he is the propitiation for your sins” [Note: [Col. 1581] “our”: Basle and Lyons II–III editions], lest you should say that they had received baptism without full faith. Instead, he says, “We have Jesus [Note: [Col. 1581] “Jesus Christ”: absent from Argentinian and Nuremberg editions; “our Lord Jesus Christ”: remaining editions compared with Basle] Christ as an advocate with the Father, and he is the propitiation for our sins”—and not only for John’s [Note: [Col. 1581] “our sins and those of others”: editions compared with the original editions] and their sins, but also for those of the whole world. Now the Apostles and all believers are included in the whole world [Col. 1582C]. From this it is plainly proved that one may sin after baptism [Note: [Col. 1581] “to prove”: Venetian editions I–II; “to sin”: remaining editions compared with Lyons II–III]. For we have Jesus Christ as advocate [Note: [Col. 1581] added: “with the Father”: editions compared with the original editions] in vain if sin is impossible.

The apostle Peter, to whom it had been said, “He who has washed does not need to wash again,” and, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” [Note: [Col. 1581] John 13:10; Matthew 16:18], denies him when frightened by a maidservant. And the Lord himself says: “Simon [Note: [Col. 1581] “To Simon”: Basle edition; absent from the others], Simon, behold, Satan has demanded [Note: [Col. 1581] “sought”: Vulgate and Basle edition] you, that he might sift you as wheat; but I prayed for you, that your faith might not fail” [Note: [Col. 1581] Luke 22:31; “may not fail”: Basle edition]. And below:

### § 2

If we do not sin [Note: [Col. 1581] “have not sinned”: same edition] after baptism, why do we ask for the forgiveness of sins which have already been forgiven us in baptism? *Why do we pray that we may not enter into temptation and that we may be delivered from evil [Note: [Col. 1581] Matthew 6:13], if the devil cannot tempt those already baptized [Col. 1583A]?* The alternative is that this prayer applies to catechumens [Note: [Col. 1583] after “applies,” the editions compared with the original insert Matthew 6:12], and does not suit the faithful and Christians. Paul, the vessel of election, disciplines his body and brings it into slavery, lest after preaching to others he himself should be found reprobate [Note: [Col. 1583] 1 Corinthians 9:27]. And below:

### § 3

Writing also to the Hebrews, he says: “For it is impossible to renew again to repentance those who have once been enlightened and have tasted the heavenly gift, and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit, and likewise have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt” [Note: [Col. 1583] Hebrews 6:4 ff.]. Certainly, we cannot deny that those who have been enlightened, have tasted the heavenly gift of *God*, have become partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good word of God [Col. 1583B] have been baptized. But if the baptized cannot sin, how does the Apostle now say, “and have fallen away”?

But lest Montanus and Novatus here [Note: [Col. 1583] “thence”: editions compared with the original editions] laugh, who maintain that those who have crucified for themselves [Note: [Col. 1583] added: “themselves”: editions compared with the original editions] the Son of God and exposed him to contempt cannot be renewed through repentance, he consequently resolves this error and says: “But we are persuaded concerning you, beloved, of better things and things nearer to salvation [Note: [Col. 1583] “to salvation”: Vulgate, editions compared with the original editions, and Böhm], though we thus speak. For God [Note: [Col. 1583] “the Lord”: editions compared with the original editions] is not unjust so as to forget your work and the love which you showed in his name, in that you have ministered to his saints [Note: [Col. 1583] absent from Basle edition], and do minister” [Note: [Col. 1583] Hebrews 6:9–10]. Indeed, it would be great injustice in God if he punished sins alone and did not receive good works. “I have spoken thus,” says the Apostle, “so that I might withdraw you from sins and make you more cautious through fear of despair” [Col. 1583C]. “But I am confident of better things concerning you, beloved, and things nearer to salvation.” For it is not consonant with God’s justice to forget the good works and ministry which you have rendered and render to the saints for his name’s sake, while remembering sins alone. And shortly afterward:

### § 4

God created us with free will; we are drawn neither to virtues [Note: [Col. 1583] “virtue”: editions compared with the original Lyons editions] nor to vices by necessity. Otherwise, where necessity exists, there is neither condemnation [Note: [Col. 1583] “nor condemnation”: absent from editions compared with the original Lyons II–III editions] nor crown. As God is the perfecter [Note: [Col. 1583] “more perfect”: editions compared with the original editions] in good works—“for it is not of one who wills, nor of one who runs, but of God who has mercy and helps, that we may be able to reach the finish” [Note: [Col. 1583] Romans 9:16]—so in evils and sins the seeds and incitements are ours, while the devil supplies their completion. When he sees us building hay [Col. 1584A], wood, and stubble upon Christ’s foundation, he then applies fire [Note: [Col. 1583] 1 Corinthians 3:12]. Let us therefore build [Note: [Col. 1583] absent from editions compared with the original Lyons editions] gold, silver, and precious stones, and he will not dare to tempt us. Yet [Note: [Col. 1583] “anyone”: Argentinian, Paris, and Lyons editions] even in this there is no secure and certain possession. For the lion sits in ambush and in secret places, to kill the innocent [Note: [Col. 1583] absent from Basle and Lyons II–III editions; cf. Psalm 9:8]; and the furnace tests the potter’s vessels, but the trial of tribulation tests righteous people [Note: [Col. 1583] Ecclesiasticus 27:6]. Elsewhere it is written: “My son, when approaching [Note: [Col. 1583] “approach”: Argentinian and Basle editions] the service of God, prepare yourself for temptation” [Note: [Col. 1583] “in”: Basle edition; Ecclesiasticus 2:1].

Again the same James says [Note: [Col. 1583] “says”: editions compared with the original editions; cf. James 1:22]: “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only. If anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks at the face of his birth in a mirror: he looked at it and immediately, on departing, forgot what he was like” [Note: [Col. 1583] “will have been”: Vulgate, Basle, and Lyons II–III editions; “was”: remaining editions]. He admonished them in vain to join works to faith if they could not sin after baptism [Col. 1584B]. “Whoever,” he says, “keeps the whole law and sins in one point has become guilty of all” [Note: [Col. 1583] James 2:10]. Which of us [Note: [Col. 1583] “of you”: editions compared with the original editions; cf. John 8:7] is without sin [Note: [Col. 1583] added: “is”: editions compared with the original editions]? God “has shut up all under sin, that he may have mercy on all” [Note: [Col. 1583] Romans 11:32]. Peter likewise says: “The Lord [Note: [Col. 1583] “God”: editions compared with the original editions] knows how to rescue [Note: [Col. 1583] “deliver”: same editions and Vulgate] the godly from temptation” [Note: [Col. 1583] 2 Peter 2:9]. And concerning false teachers: “These are springs without water and mists driven by whirlwinds, for whom the gloom of darkness is reserved. For speaking arrogant [Note: [Col. 1583] “arrogant”: Vulgate] emptiness, they entice [Note: [Col. 1583] “entice”: same edition, editions compared with the original editions, and Böhm] through fleshly desires and licentiousness those who had scarcely escaped and have returned [Note: [Col. 1583] “turned”: Basle edition] to error” [Note: [Col. 1583] 2 Peter 2:17].

Does the apostolic discourse not seem to you to have portrayed a new sect of ignorance? They open up as though they were springs of knowledge, although they have no water of doctrines [Note: [Col. 1583] “have”: editions compared with the original Lyons II–III editions]; they promise rain as though they were prophetic clouds, to which the truth of God may come [Col. 1584C], but they are driven about by whirlwinds of demons and vices. They utter great things, and all their speech is pride—for everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God—so that those who had somewhat withdrawn from sins may return to their own error; and they recommend the delights of food and flesh in licentious indulgence [Note: [Col. 1583] “delights”: editions compared with the original editions]. For who would not gladly hear, “Let us eat and drink, and we shall reign for ever” [Note: [Col. 1583] Isaiah 22:13; 1 Corinthians 15:32]? They call wise and prudent persons perverse, while they listen all the more to those who are sweet in speech.

John the Apostle—or rather, the Savior writing through John—says to the angel of the church of Ephesus: “I know your works, your labor, and your patience,” etc., “and because you have endured for my name’s sake and have not grown weary; but I have against you [Note: [Col. 1583] added: “a few things”: editions compared with the original editions] that you have abandoned your first love. Remember [Col. 1585A] from where you have fallen, repent, and do the first works. But if not, I shall come [Note: [Col. 1585] “I come”: same editions and Vulgate] to you and remove your lampstand from its place [Note: [Col. 1585] added: “its”: same editions], unless you repent” [Note: [Col. 1583] Revelation 2:2 ff.]. Likewise he summons the other churches—Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea—to repentance, and threatens them if they do not return to their former works. In Sardis, he says that he has a few who have not defiled their garments and will walk with him in white, because they are worthy.

Now to whom does he say [Note: [Col. 1585] “write”: same editions], “Remember [Note: [Col. 1585] Revelation 2:5] from where you have fallen”; “Behold [Note: [Col. 1585] ibid. 2:10], the devil is about to cast some of you into prison, that you may be tested”; “I know [Note: [Col. 1585] ibid. 2:13] where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is”; “Keep in mind [Note: [Col. 1585] ibid. 3:3] how you received and heard”; “Keep it, and repent”; and the remaining words [Note: [Col. 1585] “and do the first works”: Basle edition]? Surely he says this to one who has believed [Note: [Col. 1585] “has believed and been baptized”: editions compared with the original editions] and been baptized [Col. 1585B], and who, once standing, fell through transgression.

### § 5

I had postponed examples from the Old Testament for a little while, because, wherever it tells against them [Note: [Col. 1585] “tell”: same editions compared with the original Argentinian edition], they are accustomed to say: “The Law and the Prophets were until John” [Note: [Col. 1585] Matthew 11:13]. Yet who does not know [Note: [Col. 1585] “does not know,” in the second reading: Argentinian and Basle editions; cf. C. 32, question 4, chapter 6] that, under another dispensation of God, all his former saints were of the same merit as Christians now are? As before Abraham pleased God in marriage, so now virgins please him in perpetual chastity. He served the law and his own time; let us also serve the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1585] “the law”: editions compared with the original Lyons editions] and our own time, upon whom the ends of the ages have come [Note: [Col. 1585] “have arrived”: editions compared with the original editions; cf. 1 Corinthians 10:11].

David, chosen according to the Lord’s heart, who had done all his will, and who had said in one Psalm, “Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence, and [Note: [Col. 1585] the words “and … my” are omitted in the Basle edition] trusting in the Lord, I shall not be weakened. Test me, O Lord, and try [Col. 1585C] me; burn my reins and my heart” [Note: [Col. 1585] Psalm 25:50], was afterward tempted by the devil and after sin, repentant, said: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” [Note: [Col. 1585] Psalm 50:1]. He wishes a great sin to be wiped away by great mercy.

Solomon, beloved of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1585] “by the Lord”: editions compared with the original editions; cf. 2 Kings 12; added: “of Babylon”: editions compared with the original Basle and Lyons editions; cf. 2 Chronicles 33], to whom God had twice appeared, departed from God’s love because he was a lover of women. The book of Chronicles relates that Manasseh, a most impious king, was restored to his former dignity after Babylonian captivity. And Josiah, a holy man, was pierced by the Egyptian king in the plain of Megiddo.

Jesus son of Jozadak, the high priest, although he prefigured the Savior, who bore our sins and joined to himself the Church, a foreign woman from among the nations, nevertheless is presented, in the literal sense, as defiled after his priesthood [Note: [Col. 1585] Zechariah 3:3]; the devil stands at his right hand [Note: [Col. 1585] Psalm 108:6]; and white garments are afterward restored to him [Col. 1585D] [Col. 1586A].

It is superfluous to write about Moses and Aaron, that they offended God at the waters of contradiction and did not enter the promised land [Note: [Col. 1585] “who … offended” (“had offended”: Basle edition) … “entered”: editions compared with the original editions; cf. Numbers 20], since blessed Job also says that even angels and every creature can sin [Note: [Col. 1585] “had mentioned”: Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venetian I–II editions; “mentions”: remaining editions], saying: “What then? Is any human being clean before God? Or is a man without blemish in [Note: [Col. 1585] absent from Argentinian edition; “from works”: remaining editions] his works [Note: [Col. 1585] “does a man live”: Lyons II–III; “lives”: remaining editions compared with Lyons I]? If he does not trust his servants, and finds something perverse in his angels, how much more those who dwell in houses of clay, of which [Note: [Col. 1585] “for”: editions compared with the original editions] we too are made from the same clay?” [Note: [Col. 1585] Job 15:14; 4:17]. “The life of man upon the earth is a trial” [Note: [Col. 1585] Job 7:1; “warfare”: Vulgate].

And Lucifer fell, who sent [Note: [Col. 1585] “was sent”: editions compared with the original Argentinian and Lyons II editions] forth to all nations [Note: [Col. 1585] “also from heaven”: editions compared with the original Argentinian and Basle editions; cf. Isaiah 14:12]; and he who was nourished in the paradise of delights among the twelve stones was wounded by the Lord’s death and descended into hell. Hence the Savior says in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” [Note: [Col. 1585] Luke 10:18] [Col. 1586B]. If that loftiest exaltation fell, who cannot fall? If there are falls in heaven, how much more on earth?

Yet though Lucifer fell—indeed, after his fall, the ancient serpent—his strength is in his loins and his power over the navel of his belly [Note: [Col. 1585] Job 40:11; added: “his”: Vulgate and editions compared with the original Argentinian]. Great trees are shaded beneath him, and he sleeps beside reed, rush, and sedge. He is king of all things that are in the waters: that is, where there are pleasure, luxury, propagation, and the irrigating [Note: [Col. 1585] “incitement”: Paris and Lyons editions] of marriages. And below, at the end of Book II:

### § 6

We have passed [Note: [Col. 1585] “we pass”: Basle edition] to the second division [Note: [Col. 1585] “participation”: Argentinian edition], in which he denies that those who have received baptism with whole faith can afterward sin. We have shown that, except for God, every creature is subject to fault—not because all have sinned, but because they can sin [Col. 1586C], and because the fall of those like them is a cause of fear to those who stand.

**Gratian.** It is therefore evident from what has preceded that some possess charity, which they later lose by sinning grievously. But if anyone contends that this must be understood not of the virtue itself but of its exercise, let him consider what answer he will give concerning Adam’s innocence, the righteousness of Moses, David, and the others. For those who approach baptism with full faith, although they are afterward to fall, nevertheless taste the heavenly gifts and become partakers of the Holy Spirit; so that they are found to be born again of water and the Holy Spirit not only before human beings, but even before God’s eyes. If they did not possess the love of God, they would be regenerated by water alone, not by the Spirit. For works, or participation in sacraments, unless they proceed from charity, produce before God neither righteousness nor innocence. For, says the Apostle: “If I have all faith, so that I remove mountains [Col. 1587A], and if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I burn, but have not charity, it profits me nothing” [Note: [Col. 1585] 1 Corinthians 13:2–3].

### § 1

But because some concede concerning those predestined to life that they lose charity and recover what they have lost, we must also consider concerning the reprobate whether they have charity, which, when lost, results later in their condemnation.

Augustine writes thus concerning them in *On Correction and Grace*, chapter 9. Chapter XLI.

The Apostle, knowing that some love God but do not remain to the end in that good [Note: [Col. 1587] “way”: editions compared with the original editions]—that is, do not persevere [Note: [Col. 1587] “persevere”: same editions]—immediately added: “those who are called according to the purpose [Note: [Col. 1587] added from the Vulgate: “saints”: editions compared with the original editions],” etc. [Note: [Col. 1587] Romans 8:28].

The same author, in the same book, chapter 6, § 1. Can this man, still [Col. 1587B] unwilling to be corrected [Note: [Col. 1587] “and”: absent from the same editions compared with the original Basle edition], say: “What have I done, which [Note: [Col. 1587] “that which”: editions compared with the original editions] I have not received?” [Note: [Col. 1587D] “Which I have not received”: this passage has here been restored from the original, for previously it was badly corrupt. Yet because these passages are quoted in a very mutilated form, it will be worthwhile to go to the source.] It is certain that he received it and, through his own fault, lost what he had received. “I can,” he says, “I certainly can, when you rebuke me [Note: [Col. 1587] “rebukes”: original] because by my own will I have fallen back from a good life into an evil one, still say: ‘What have I done, which [Note: [Col. 1587] “that which”: editions compared with the original editions] I have not received?’ For I received faith, which works through love; but I did not receive in it perseverance to the end.”

In the same work, chapter 9, § 2. “Without doubt he wished them to remain in the good [Note: [Col. 1587] ‘I wished … to remain’: editions compared with the original editions]; they certainly [Note: [Col. 1587] added: “those persons”: Basle edition] were in the good, but did not remain in it.” In the same work, chapter 13, § 3. “For the usefulness of this secret, it must be believed that some of the children of perdition, not having received the gift of persevering to the end, begin to live in the faith which works through love [Col. 1587C], and *live faithfully and justly for some time*, and afterward fall,” etc.

**Gratian.** There are many similar passages concerning the reprobate, also in the Gospel: “He who perseveres to the end,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1587] Matthew 10:22]. In the same: “Again this man begins,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1587] Not found.]

## Chapter XLII

The same Augustine, in the same book, *On Correction and Grace*, chapter 8 [Note: [Col. 1587] The sense is collected in summary form].

It is remarkable why God gives to certain children of perdition faith working through love, but does not give them perseverance in it.

**Gratian.** Likewise, that saying of the Gospel: “Not he who begins, but he who perseveres to the end, shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 1587] Matthew 10:22].

## Chapter XLIII

Likewise Gregory, Book VIII of the *Moralia*, chapter 35 [Note: [Col. 1587] Rather, the Ordinary Gloss on 2 Chronicles 9, at the end].

Many begin well who end their lives in evil.

[Col. 1588A] **Gratian.** But no one begins well who never acts from charity. If, however, he does something from charity at some time, charity must at some time be in him.

## V. Part. § 1

But Gregory’s statement [Note: [Col. 1587] in the following chapter], “Those who may at some time be seduced and will not return,” etc., must be understood not of reprobates generally, but specifically of hypocrites. This is made evident by his own words. For when he had raised the question why the merciful God permits these things to happen—namely, that Leviathan [Note: [Col. 1587] Job 41:21], either now by crafty suggestions or then through that damned man whom he fills, may subject to himself either rays of the sun, that is, learned and wise men, or gold, that is, men radiant with the brightness of holiness, and as it were securely lay them beneath himself by defiling them with vices—he immediately added the following in answering this question [Col. 1588B], saying [Note: [Col. 1587] *Moralia*, Book 34, chapter 13, on Job 41]:

## Chapter XLIV

We answer this more readily: the gold which can be laid down like mud beneath his wicked persuasions was never gold in God’s sight. For those who can at some time be seduced so as not to return seem to lose a holiness once possessed before human eyes, but they never possessed it before God’s eyes. For a person is often secretly entangled in many sins and appears great in some single virtue. That virtue itself also fails and becomes empty, because when it becomes known to people it is undoubtedly praised, and its praise is greedily sought. Thus it comes about that even the virtue itself is not virtue before God’s eyes, since [Col. 1588C] it conceals what displeases him and displays what pleases him. What merits, then, can there be before God when evils are secret and goods public [Note: [Col. 1587] “published”: Paris and Lyons I editions]?

For often, as we have said, pride lies hidden while chastity becomes known. Therefore the charity [Note: [Col. 1587] “chastity”: Basle edition; absent from Argentinian and Nuremberg editions] displayed for a long time is lost near the end of life, because the concealed pride remains uncorrected [Note: [Col. 1587] “unrebuked”: Basle edition] until [Note: [Col. 1587] “in”: editions compared with the original editions] the end. Another devotes himself to almsgiving and distributes his possessions, yet serves many injustices, or perhaps exercises his tongue in detractions. It often comes about that one who had been merciful burns with the impulses of rapacity and cruelty near the end of his life. This is done by a most just judgment [Note: [Col. 1587] added: “of God”: Basle and Lyons editions], so that he may lose before human beings even that by which he pleased human beings, since he never took care to correct that by which he displeased God. Another cultivates patience; but *while* he fails to guard against envying others and retaining malice in his heart, he sometimes becomes impatient, because the grief which had long lain hidden [Note: [Col. 1589] “who”: original] emerges.

Thus they are gold in one respect and mud in another. And this gold is laid down like mud when, because hidden sins demand it, even the virtue which had publicly shone is destroyed. § 1. But we believe it worthwhile to consider more carefully, in these cases, the power of the heavenly ordering. For almighty God often long tolerates the hidden evils of certain persons [Note: [Col. 1589] “of them”: editions compared with the original Lyons II–III editions], in order that he may arrange [Note: [Col. 1589] “and … arrange”: editions compared with the original Lyons II–III editions] their visible goods for the benefit of his elect. For some people, not abandoning the world utterly, take up the narrow path without intending to persevere, yet by their example inflame those who will persevere to seek the narrow way. Hence it often happens that the very fact that they appear to live well means that they live not for themselves but rather for the elect alone, since those who will not persevere, by their examples, spur others who will persevere to devote themselves to living well [Col. 1589B].

For we often see some people set out upon a road and hasten toward their intended destination. Others, seeing them go, follow and seek the same destination with them. But it often happens that, when some entangling difficulty arises, those who were leading turn back, while those who followed arrive at the destination. Such, indeed, are those [Note: [Col. 1589] added: “they”: editions compared with the original Basle edition] who take up the way of holiness without intending to persevere [Note: [Col. 1589] “who do not persevere, and”: editions compared with the original editions]. They begin the path of virtue which they will not complete in order that they may show those who will arrive the path [Note: [Col. 1589] “persevere”: same editions compared with the original Argentinian edition; “road”: Lyons II; absent from the original and Lyons III] upon which they are to walk [Note: [Col. 1589] “walk”: editions compared with the original Basle and Lyons II–III editions]. Even their fall serves the progress of the elect with no small benefit: when the elect observe their fall [Col. 1589C], they tremble for their own standing, and the ruin that damns the former humbles the latter. For they learn to trust in the protection of heavenly help [Note: [Col. 1589] “help”: original and editions compared with the original editions], when they see many who presumed upon their own powers [Note: [Col. 1589] “virtues”: editions compared with the original Basle edition] fall [Note: [Col. 1589] absent from Argentinian, Basle, and Nuremberg editions]. Therefore, when the reprobate appear to act well, they show a level road to the elect who follow; but when they fall into wickedness, they show the elect advancing behind them, as it were, a pit of pride to be avoided.

Gratian. That the reprobate are said not to eat the bread that came down from heaven or to drink living water [Note: [Col. 1589] cf. above, ch. 14] is not to be understood as though they were wholly alien from charity, but as meaning that they are not understood to put down roots in charity. For drinking or eating is one thing, and tasting another. Hence it is read in the Gospel concerning Christ [Note: [Col. 1589] Matt. 27:34]: “And when he had tasted, he would not drink.” Therefore, he drinks living water and eats the bread that came down from heaven who puts down roots in charity; he tastes who shares in it to some extent but afterward departs from it by sinning. Of such persons the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1589] Heb. 6:4]: “It is impossible for those who were once enlightened, who tasted the heavenly gift, and who afterward fell away, to be renewed again to repentance.”

§ 1. Hence the devil likewise is denied to have stood in the truth, not to have been created in it [Note: [Col. 1589] John 8:41]. For he was created in truth; but, when he presumptuously relied upon himself in pride, he became alien from it. But how is he said to have been created in truth if he is proved to have been created without love for his Creator? Or how is he maintained to have been created good by God if he received no divine love in his creation? How did he exist without fault before the impulse of pride, if he did not love his Creator at all? Or how is he said to have been created equal or superior to the others if, while some of them were created in the love of God, he was made empty of that love? From what, then, did this difference between good and evil angels proceed?

If from the Creator, God appears unjust: either because he inflicts punishment before sin, or because he punishes what he himself infused in creating. But if not from the Creator, and since it did not proceed by propagation, it remains that the vice of pride entered angelic nature through the choice of its own freedom. Therefore that nature was created good, though through its own vice it was changed from good into evil. But how could it have been good if it wholly lacked love? For the angel was not made like us, whom weakness burdens up to a certain age, so that neither virtue nor any vice has a place in us. Therefore he received love in his creation, as did the others, of whom it is said [Note: [Col. 1589] Ordinary Gloss on Gen. 1:6]: “The angelic powers which remained steadfast in the love of God.” It does not say, “which began to love God,” but, “which remained steadfast in his love”: they had begun to love from their creation, so that the beginning of divine love is to be believed common to all. Perseverance, however, is understood to belong only to those who deserved to receive, in recompense, that they might be confirmed and thereafter unable to fall, and might know this concerning themselves with the greatest certainty.

Hence Moses aptly says that heaven was made first and the firmament afterward: angelic nature was first created equally subtle in the heights, and afterward those who persisted in the love of their Creator were wonderfully confirmed.

§ 2. Hence Gregory also, in the *Morals*, rehearsing much concerning the perfection of angelic creation, denies that he was filled with charity, but does not assert that he was wholly without it; for, if he had wholly lacked it, what is said concerning his excellence could never suitably be understood of him.

[Col. 1590D] C. XLV. Blessed Gregory, *Morals*, Book XXXII, ch. 24, otherwise 18.

“For Behemoth,” says Blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 1589] The words “says Blessed Gregory” are omitted by Bohmer; cf. Job 40:14], “is called the beginning of the ways of God because, when he was making all things, he created this one first and made him more eminent than the remaining angels. The Prophet beholds the eminence of his primacy when he says: ‘The cedars were not higher in the paradise of God; the fir trees did not equal his height; the plane trees were not equal to his foliage; no tree of the paradise of God was likened to him and to his beauty, because he made him beautiful with many dense branches’ [Note: [Col. 1589] Isa. 2:13; Ezek. 31:8].

[Note: [Col. 1591] The Vulgate and the original read *aequae*, “equal,” rather than *aequales*, “equal.” The collected editions add *pretiosum*, “precious,” after “tree.” The collected editions read *condensis*, “dense.”]

“For what [the collected editions read *Quid*, “what,” rather than *Quae*, “which”] can be understood by cedars, fir trees, and plane trees, except those ranks of heavenly powers, lofty in their height, planted in the verdure of eternal joy? [Note: [Col. 1591] The Basel edition reads *celsitudinis*, “of height.”] Although they were created lofty, they were nevertheless neither preferred to nor made equal to this one, who is said to have been made beautiful with many dense branches, because the beauty by which he was set above the other legions made him more splendid in proportion as the multitude of angels placed beneath him adorned him. [Note: [Col. 1591] The collected editions and the original read *et*, “and,” rather than *ei*, “to him.”] This tree in the paradise of God had, as it were, as many dense branches as it beheld legions of heavenly spirits placed beneath it. [Note: [Col. 1591] The collected editions and the original read *et idcirco*, “and for this reason,” rather than *idcirco*, “for this reason.”] He was condemned without pardon when he sinned because he had been created great beyond comparison.

“Again, through the same Prophet it is said to him [Note: [Col. 1591] Ezek. 28:12]: ‘You are the seal of the likeness of *God*, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God.’ For, intending to speak much concerning his greatness, he comprehended everything in the first word. What good did he not possess who was the seal of God’s likeness? [Note: [Col. 1591] The original reads *si*, “if,” in place of *qui*, “who.”] For from the impression of a ring’s seal such a likeness is pictorially expressed as is held essentially in that seal itself. Although man was created in God’s likeness, he attributes something greater, as it were, to the angel: he does not say that the angel was created in the likeness of God, but that he himself was the seal of God’s likeness, so that, the subtler he is in nature, the more fully the likeness of God is believed to be expressed in him. [Note: [Col. 1591] The collected editions read *illum*, “him,” rather than *illo*, “him/in him.”]

§ 1. “Hence, still indicating the power of his primacy, the same Prophet adds [Note: [Col. 1591] Ezek. 28:13]: ‘Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald.’ He named nine kinds of stones because there are nine orders of angels. For, when angels, archangels, thrones, dominations, virtues, principalities, powers, Cherubim, and Seraphim are expressly mentioned in the sacred utterances *themselves*, the number of distinctions among the heavenly citizens is shown. This Behemoth, however, is described as having been covered by them because he had them as a garment for his adornment [Note: [Col. 1591] The original reads *ornatum*, “adornment,” rather than *ornamentum*, “ornament”]; and, because he surpassed their brightness, he was brighter by comparison with them.

§ 2. “Still describing him *there*, the Prophet adds [Note: [Col. 1591] Ezekiel, in the same place]: ‘Gold was the work of your beauty, and your openings were prepared on the day when you were created.’ Gold was the work of his beauty because he shone with the brightness of wisdom, which he received when he was created good. Openings are made in stones so that, when bound with gold, they may be joined in the construction of an ornament and may not at all be separated from one another; the gold poured between them binds them by filling their openings.

“Thus the openings of this stone were prepared on the day of its creation because it was created capable of charity; and, if it had wished to be filled with charity, it could have clung to the steadfast angels, as stones placed in the king’s ornament. For if it had made itself penetrable by the gold of charity, joined to the holy angels in the royal ornament, it would, as we have said, have remained a fixed stone. This stone therefore had openings; but through the vice of pride [Note: [Col. 1591] The original reads *per superbiae vitium*, “through the vice of pride”] they were not filled with the gold of charity. For, since stones are bound with gold so that they do not fall, this one fell because, though perforated by the craftsman’s hand, it scorned to be bound by the bonds of love. [Note: [Col. 1591] The collected editions read *Namque*, “for indeed,” rather than *Nam*, “for.”] But now the other stones, which had likewise been perforated, have been bound to one another by penetrating charity [Note: [Col. 1591] The collected editions read *penetrantes*, “penetrating,” rather than *penetranti*, “by penetrating”]; and when this one fell, they deserved this gift: that they should never thereafter be released from the royal ornament by falling. [Note: [Col. 1591] The collected editions read *hic*, “this one,” rather than *huic*, “to this one.”]

§ 3. “Still beholding the height of this primacy, the same Prophet adds [Note: [Col. 1591] Ezek. 28:14]: ‘You are the outspread [*extensus*] and protecting Cherub upon the holy mountain of God, and you walked perfect in the midst of fiery stones.’ [Note: [Col. 1591] The reading printed here is *extensus*, “outspread”; the Vulgate, original, and collected editions read *extentus*, “outspread.” The Paris edition omits *extenti* (“by being extended”), while the Basel and Lyons editions read *extente*, “outspreadly,” and the remaining editions *extentum*, “outspread.”] Cherub is interpreted as ‘fullness of knowledge’; and therefore this one is called Cherub because there is no doubt that he surpassed all in knowledge. He walked perfect in the midst of fiery stones because, among hearts of angels kindled by the fire of charity, he shone in the glory of his created condition. He aptly calls him outspread and protecting. For whatever we protect by being spread over it, we overshadow; and *because* he is believed to have overshadowed the brightness of the others by comparison with his own brightness, he is found to have been outspread and protecting. [Note: [Col. 1591] The original reads *perhibetur*, “is said,” rather than *reperitur*, “is found.”] He covered the others as though by overshadowing them, because he surpassed their greatness by a greater excellence.

§ 4. “Therefore, what is there called beautiful with many branches, the seal of likeness, Cherub, and protecting, is here called by the Lord’s voice Behemoth, this beginning of the ways of God. He thus sets forth such wondrous things as he possessed and lost in order to show *terrified* man what he himself will suffer through the fault of his pride if he becomes proud: God did not spare in striking him whom, in creating, he had raised to the glory of such great brightness. Let man therefore consider what he deserves when proud upon earth, if *even* an angel set above angels is cast down from heaven to earth. [Note: [Col. 1591] The Basel edition reads *praelatus angelus*, “an angel set above”; the remaining editions read *praelatus angelis angelus*, “an angel set above angels.” The words *de coelo in terram*, “from heaven to earth,” are absent from the original and the collected editions except Basel and Lyons.]”

[Col. 1592D] VI. Part. Gratian. Charity that is abandoned in adversity is said to be feigned—that is, clay-like and fragile—just as faith, from which charity proceeds, is said by the Apostle not to be feigned, that is, fragile. Likewise, charity that can be abandoned in adversity is said never to have been true. For, as Jerome writes against Jovinian [Note: [Col. 1593] “is”: Basel edition], “Every creature is under fault,” not because every creature has sinned, but because none exists which cannot sin. But the ability to sin, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1593] Book XV, *On the Trinity*, ch. 15], is not an ability to do something; indeed, it is an inability. Hence he alone is called omnipotent who cannot do this, because he can do all things which are an ability to do something.

Therefore, just as in comparison with him who knows no change every creature is called faulty because it is capable of change, according to the saying [Note: [Col. 1593] Ps. 142:2], “No living person shall be justified in your sight,” and [Note: [Col. 1593] Job 15:15], “The stars are not clean in his sight,” so in comparison with that creature which does not receive change, every creature which changes is shown to be not true but vain. Hence [Note: [Col. 1593] Pss. 115:11 and 143:4] every human being is called a liar and is said to have become like vanity.

§ 1. Hence Ecclesiastes also says [Note: [Col. 1593] Eccl. 1:2]: “All things under the sun”—that is, all things which undergo the vicissitude of times—are said to be not merely vanity, which belongs to every creature by reason of mutability, but “vanity of vanities,” because of the variety of change which they undergo. Thus, in comparison with divine charity, no virtue is proved true; or, in comparison with charity which is not abandoned, that which is lost is denied to be true. Yet, as every creature is called good and true in its own way, so charity which is abandoned is shown to be good and true in its own way; otherwise no one would abandon it if it existed in no way. For what in no way truly exists can in no way be abandoned. But if it is truly abandoned in some way, it must also truly exist in some way.

## DISTINCTION III

## GRATIAN

### I. Part

We have written these brief remarks on charity on account of those who deny that repentance can be repeated. They maintain that, just as charity once possessed is never lost, so repentance once truly performed is stained by no subsequent fault; but if a grave fault ever follows it, the repentance was not true and never obtained forgiveness from the Lord. They undertake to prove this from the definition of repentance itself and from the authorities of many writers.

For, as Ambrose says in a certain sermon for Lent [Note: [Col. 1593] Sermon 9, *On Lent*; Ivo, *Decree*, part 15, ch. 1; Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 14; cf. below, ch. 6]:

[Col. 1594A] C. I.

Repentance is both to lament past evils and not again to commit what must be lamented.

C. II. The same, Book II, *On the One Repentance*, ch. 10 [Note: [Col. 1593] cf. D. 50, after ch. 61; Peter Lombard, ibid.]:

There are found [Note: [Col. 1593D] The original reads: “Those are rightly reproved who think repentance should be undertaken repeatedly, because they indulge their lusts,” etc., as above, Distinction 50, “If anyone afterward …”] persons who think repentance should be performed often, who indulge their lusts in Christ. For if they truly performed repentance, they would not think it must afterward be repeated; because, just as there is one baptism, so also *one* repentance.

[Note: [Col. 1593D–1594D] The phrase “so also one repentance,” a passage not emended because of intervening glosses, reads thus in Blessed Ambrose: “So also there is one repentance, which nevertheless is performed publicly. For we ought to repent daily of sin; but this concerns lighter offenses, whereas that concerns graver ones. Yet I have more easily found …”]

Nevertheless, we ought always to repent of past sin; but this concerns lighter offenses. [Note: [Col. 1593] The edition reads *hic*, “this,” rather than *hoc*, “this.”] Yet I have more easily found those who have preserved innocence [Note: [Col. 1593] The collected editions correctly read *servaverit*, “has preserved,” rather than *servaverint*, “have preserved”] than those who have suitably performed repentance. [Note: [Col. 1593] The Argentan edition reads *ageret*, “performed,” while the remaining editions read *egerit*, “has performed.”]

C. III. The same, Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Doctrines*, ch. 54 [Note: [Col. 1593] This is not Augustine’s]:

The satisfaction of repentance is to cut off the causes of sins and not to grant their suggestions an entrance.

C. IV. The same, in the book *On True and False Repentance*, ch. 8 [Note: [Col. 1593] This is not Augustine’s; Peter Lombard, ibid.]:

Repentance is a kind of vengeance in one who grieves, punishing in oneself what one grieves to have committed. And below, ch. 19:

§ 1. One must grieve continually for sin; the force of the word itself makes this clear. [Note: [Col. 1593] The Basel edition reads *dilectionis*, “of love,” rather than *dictionis*, “of the word.”] For *to repent* (*poenitere*) is *to hold punishment* (*poenam tenere*), so that one always punishes in oneself, by taking vengeance, what one committed by sinning. [Note: [Col. 1593] The Basel edition reads *poenitentiae*, “of repentance,” rather than *poenitere*, “to repent.”] Punishment properly means an injury which punishes and avenges what each person has committed. *Therefore* he holds punishment [Note: [Col. 1593] The original and collected editions read *vindicat*, “avenges,” rather than *igitur poenam tenet*, “therefore holds punishment”] who always punishes what he grieves to have committed. [Note: [Col. 1593] The original reads *ipse*, “he himself,” after “committed.”]

Gratian. Repentance, therefore, is vengeance always punishing in oneself what one grieves to have committed.

C. V. In the same book, ch. 13:

If the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1593] Rom. 6:3] continually laments even sins remitted through baptism, what remains for us, placed upon the foundation of the apostles, except to lament? [Note: [Col. 1593] The Basel edition omits *etiam*, “also.”] What remains except always to grieve in this life? For where grief ends, repentance also fails. But if repentance ends, what remains of forgiveness? Let one rejoice and hope in grace only as long as one is sustained by repentance. For the Lord said [Note: [Col. 1593] The collected editions read *Dicit*, “says,” rather than *Dixit*, “said”; cf. John 8:11], “Go, and henceforth [*jam*] do not sin.” He did not say, “Do not sin,” but, “Let not even the will to sin arise in you.” [Note: [Col. 1593] The collected editions read *ne*, “lest,” rather than *non*, “not.”] How can this be observed unless grief is continually guarded in repentance? Hence let him always grieve, rejoice in his grief, and, if it should happen, always grieve over the repentance of grief; and let it not be enough that he grieves, but let him grieve from faith, and not grieve that he has not always grieved.

C. VI. Likewise Gregory, for the summer season, that is, Homily XXXIV on the Gospels [Note: [Col. 1595] The earlier part of this chapter occurs in Anselm, Book XI, ch. 4]:

We cannot perform repentance worthily unless we also know the measure of that repentance. [Note: [Col. 1595] The collected editions add *quippe*, “indeed”; the Basel edition omits *quoque*, “also.”] For to perform repentance is both to lament evils committed and not to commit what must be lamented [Note: [Col. 1595] cf. above, ch. 1]. For whoever so laments some sins that he nevertheless commits others [Note: [Col. 1595] The collected editions, except Argentan, read *iterum*, “again,” after *tamen*, “nevertheless”] either pretends to perform repentance or does not understand it. What good does it do if someone weeps for sins of lust but still pants with the heats of avarice?

Likewise, Book IX, Letter 39 to Theoctista [Note: [Col. 1595] Letter 45, written A.D. 601, Book XI, Maurist edition]:

§ 1. There are [Note: [Col. 1595] The original reads, “But if they say …”] persons who say that a short time of repentance ought to suffice against sin [Note: [Col. 1595] The Basel edition correctly reads *sufficere*, “to suffice”], so that it is afterward permissible to return to sin. The judgment of the first Shepherd rightly strikes them when he says [Note: [Col. 1595] 2 Pet. 2:22]: “The event has happened to them which is described by the true proverb: the dog has returned to its own vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mire.” Great indeed is repentance’s power against sin, but only if one perseveres in that repentance.

And below:

§ 2. To perform repentance truly is to lament what has been committed and to avoid again committing what must be lamented. [Note: [Col. 1595] The original reads *sed*, “but,” rather than *et*, “and”; the Argentan edition reads, “but again not to commit what must be lamented.”]

C. VII. Likewise Augustine, Tractate CXXIV on John 21:

Punishment lasts longer than guilt, lest guilt be thought slight if punishment ended with it. Accordingly, whether to display the misery due, to correct a life prone to fall, or to exercise necessary patience, punishment holds a person temporarily even when guilt no longer holds him liable to eternal condemnation. [Note: [Col. 1595] The collected editions and Lyons II–III read *retinet*, “holds back,” rather than *detinet*, “holds.”]

And shortly afterward:

§ 1. God’s wrath is not like a human being’s—that is, a disturbance of an agitated mind—but the tranquil establishment of a just punishment.

C. VIII. Likewise John Chrysostom, in a homily on repentance [Note: [Col. 1595] cf. above, Distinction I, ch. 40]:

Perfect repentance compels the sinner willingly to endure everything. And below: In his heart there is contrition, in his mouth confession, and in his deed complete humility. This is *perfect and* fruitful repentance.

C. IX. Likewise Smaragdus, in his exposition of the Rule of St Benedict, ch. 4 [Note: [Col. 1595] cf. Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, Book II, ch. 13]:

That person performs repentance worthily who so laments the past evils *which he committed* [Note: [Col. 1595] The words *quae commisit*, “which he committed,” are absent from Isidore] that he does not commit them again in the future. For one who laments sin [Note: [Col. 1595] The Basel and Lyons II–III editions add *suum*, “his own”] and commits sin again is as though someone [Latin *si*, “if”] washed an unbaked brick: for the more he washes it, the more mud he makes. [Note: [Col. 1595] The collected editions read *quem … abluit*, “which he washes,” rather than *si … laverit*, “if he should wash.”]

C. X. Likewise Augustine, Homily XLI [Note: [Col. 1595] It does not appear to be Augustine’s; Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 15]:

You who are repenting—if indeed you are penitents and not mockers—change your life; be reconciled to God, and you will feed yourselves with a chain. You ask, “With what chain?” With that of which it is said [Note: [Col. 1595] Matt. 16:19], “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven.” You hear of binding, and do you think you can impose upon God? Do you perform repentance, kneel, laugh, and mock God’s patience? If you perform repentance, you repent; if you do not repent, you are not repentant. [Note: [Col. 1595] The collected editions read: “If you perform repentance, you repent; if you do not repent, you are not repentant”; the Basel edition reads *patientiam*, “patience,” for *poenitentiam*, “repentance,” and *poenitet te*, “you regret,” for *poenites*, “you repent.”] Therefore, if you repent, why do you do what you did wrongly? If you repent of having done it, do not do it; if you still do it, certainly you are not repentant. [Note: [Col. 1595] The collected editions read *poenites*, “you repent,” rather than *poenitet*, “you regret”; the Argentan edition reads *poenites*, while the remaining editions except Basel read *poeniteas*, “may you repent.”]

C. XI. Likewise Isidore, Book II, *On the Highest Good*, ch. 16 [Note: [Col. 1595] Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 14]:

He is a mocker, not a penitent, who still does what he regrets; he does not appear to beseech God as one subject to him, but to mock him in pride. A penitent returning to sin is a dog returning to its vomit. For many continually shed tears and do not cease from sinning. It is evident that some receive tears for repentance but do not possess the disposition of repentance [Note: [Col. 1595] The collected editions read *cerno*, “I discern,” rather than *constat*, “it is evident”], because through inconstancy of mind they now shed tears at the recollection of sin, but when the habit revives they again commit what they had wept over. [Note: [Col. 1595] The collected editions except Basel read *non*, “not,” rather than *nunc*, “now”; the collected editions read *fleverunt*, “they wept,” rather than *fleverant*, “they had wept.”]

Isaiah says to sinners [Note: [Col. 1595] The collected editions read *de peccatoribus*, “concerning sinners”; cf. Isa. 1:16], “Wash yourselves; be clean.” *Therefore* he is washed and clean who both laments the past and does not again commit what must be lamented. [Note: [Col. 1595] The collected editions and the original read *admittit*, “admits,” rather than *committit*, “commits.”] *He is washed* and not clean who laments what he has done but does not abandon it *nevertheless*, but after tears repeats what he had wept over. [Note: [Col. 1595] The original omits *tamen*, “nevertheless”; it reads *et*, “and,” while the collected editions read *sed*, “but.”]

C. XII. Likewise Augustine, in the book *Soliloquies* [Note: [Col. 1595D–1596D] This chapter has not been found in Blessed Augustine; nearly the same material is, however, found in Isidore—whom the Master cites—in the *Dialogue*, or *Synonyms*, not far before the chapter on chastity] [Note: [Col. 1595] Rather, Isidore, at the end of *Synonyms*, Book I; Peter Lombard, ibid.]:

Repentance is empty when subsequent guilt defiles it. A repeated wound is healed more slowly; one who sins and mourns frequently scarcely merits pardon. [Note: [Col. 1595] The original reads *frequens*, “frequent,” rather than *frequenter*, “frequently.”] Laments are of no use if sins are repeated. It is of no avail to seek pardon from evils and repeat evils anew. Therefore persist in confession; be firmly established in repentance; do not cease to maintain the good life which you have received [Note: [Col. 1595] The source cited as Isidore, and the Basel edition, read *coepisti*, “you have begun,” rather than *accepisti*, “you have received”]; preserve continually the resolve of a good life.

[Col. 1597A] C. XIII. Likewise Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, Admonition 31 [Note: [Col. 1597] Anselm, Book XI, ch. 143; Peter Lombard, ibid.]:

Those who lament sins committed but nevertheless do not abandon them should carefully understand that they cleanse themselves vainly by weeping while they wickedly defile themselves by living, since they wash themselves with tears in order to return clean to filth.

C. XIV. The same, in the same place:

He who laments sins committed but does not abandon them subjects himself to a guilt almost more grievous [Note: [Col. 1597] The original reads *tanto*, “by so much,” rather than *pene*, “almost”; the collected editions read *poenae*, “of punishment,” rather than *culpae*, “of guilt”], because he despises the very pardon which he could have obtained by weeping. [Note: [Col. 1597] The original reads *contempsit*, “despised,” rather than *contemnit*, “despises.”]

C. XV. The same, in the same place:

“Wash yourselves; be clean” [Note: [Col. 1597] Isa. 1:16]. For after washing, whoever does not preserve innocence of life after tears neglects to remain clean. Therefore those who do not cease to weep for what they have committed but again commit what must be wept over are washed and by no means clean. [Note: [Col. 1597] The collected editions read *nec mundi*, “nor clean”; the collected editions except Lyons III read *flendo*, “by weeping,” rather than *flenda*, “things to be wept over.”]

C. XVI. The same, in the same place:

He who is cleansed from sin by tears is indeed baptized by one dead. [Note: [Col. 1597] The collected editions read the plural: “They are baptized … cleanse themselves.”] But after baptism he touches a dead person who repeats his guilt after tears. [Note: [Col. 1597] The Basel edition reads the plural, “they touch … repeat”; the collected editions read *culpas*, “guilts,” rather than *culpam*, “guilt.”]

C. XVII. The same, in the *Morals*, Book I, final chapter:

Good is done in vain if it is abandoned before the end of life, for one runs swiftly to no purpose who fails before reaching the goal.

### II. Part. Gratian

But the words of the definition refer not to different times but to the same time: namely, that at the time when one laments the evils which one committed, one should not commit what one would still have to lament. This is made clear by the following words of the same authority, where it says [Note: [Col. 1597] above, the same ch. 6], “For whoever so laments some sins that he nevertheless commits others either pretends to perform repentance or does not understand it.”

Hence Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*, ch. 70 [Note: [Col. 1597] Anselm, Book XI, ch. 32; Ivo, *Decree*, part 17, ch. 121; Peter Lombard, ibid.]:

C. XVIII.

Certainly, one must take care lest anyone suppose that those unspeakable and wicked crimes [Note: [Col. 1597] The Basel edition reads *et nefanda*, “and wicked,” while the remaining editions except Argentan read *nefanda*, “wicked,” in place of *infanda*, “unspeakable”], such that those who commit them will not possess the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 1597] 1 Cor. 6:9], are to be committed daily and redeemed daily by almsgiving. Rather, one’s life must be changed for the better, and God must be made propitious through almsgiving for past sins—not, as it were, bought off so that one may always commit them with impunity. For he has given no one license to sin, although in mercy he wipes away sins already committed, provided that fitting satisfaction is not neglected.

[Col. 1598A] C. XIX. The same, in the same place, ch. 76 [Note: [Col. 1597] Ivo, *Decree*, part 17, ch. 129]:

Whoever wishes to give alms in an orderly manner must begin with himself and first give them to himself. For almsgiving is a work of mercy, and it has most truly been said [Note: [Col. 1597] The Basel edition reads *verisimile*, “very probable,” and the remaining editions read *verissimae*, “most true,” rather than *verissime*, “most truly”; cf. Ecclus. 30:24/34], “Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God.” For this reason we are reborn: that we may please God.

C. XX. The same, in the same place, ch. 71 [Note: [Col. 1597] This chapter was formerly cited from John Chrysostom. It has been restored from Blessed Augustine, whom the Master, Ivo, and the Fourth Council of Toledo, ch. 9, cite] [Note: [Col. 1597] Ivo, *Decree*, part 17, ch. 122; Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 16]:

For daily, brief, and light sins, without which this life is not lived [Note: [Col. 1597] Ivo and the collected editions read *brevibus*, “brief,” rather than *brevioribus*, “briefer”], the daily prayer of the faithful makes satisfaction. For it belongs to those who say [Note: [Col. 1597] Matt. 6:9], “Our Father, who are in heaven,” who have already been regenerated as children of such a Father through water and the Holy Spirit. This prayer completely removes these least and daily sins; it also removes those from which the life of the faithful, though formerly lived wickedly, departs after being changed for the better through repentance. [Note: [Col. 1597] The collected editions except Basel read *commutata*, “changed,” rather than *mutata*, “changed for the better.”]

Provided that, just as it is truthfully said [Note: [Col. 1597] Matt. 6:12], “Forgive us our debts,” since there are things to be forgiven, so it is truthfully said, “As we forgive our debtors”: that is, if [Note: [Col. 1597] Ivo omits *si*, “if”] what is said is done, because it is itself an almsgiving to forgive the person seeking pardon. [Note: [Col. 1597] The Argentan edition reads *poscentibus*, “those seeking,” and the remaining editions except Basel read *poenitentibus*, “penitents,” rather than *petenti homini*, “the person seeking.” The collected editions read *omnino*, “altogether,” after *homini*, “person.”]

C. XXI. Likewise Pope Pius, Letter I [Note: [Col. 1597] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Caesarius, or Eucherius, Homily 23; Anselm, Book XI, ch. 8; *Polycarpus*, Book III, title 25; Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 14; cf. ch. 23, D. 5, *On Consecration*]:

It profits a person nothing to fast, pray, and perform other good works of religion [Note: [Col. 1597] The collected editions read *opera*, “works,” rather than *bona*, “good things”] unless the mind is recalled from iniquity.

### III. Part. Gratian

The saying of Smaragdus, “That person performs repentance worthily,” and so forth, is also understood as spoken from the standpoint of such a penitent [Note: [Col. 1597] cf. above, chs. 9, 10, 11, 15, 12, 13, 14, and 2]; likewise Augustine’s “You who are repenting,” Isidore’s “He is a mocker, not a penitent,” Isaiah’s “Wash yourselves and be clean,” and the saying of the *Soliloquies*, “Repentance is empty,” and so forth. Likewise Gregory’s “Those who lament sins committed,” and “He is baptized by one dead.” But Ambrose’s statement, “There are found,” and so forth, is to be understood not according to the general but according to the special custom of the Church concerning solemn repentance, which among some, once performed, is not repeated.

Hence Augustine writes to Macedonius, Letter LIV [Note: [Col. 1597] cf. above, ch. 62, D. 50]:

C. XXII.

Although it has wisely and salutarily been provided that the place of that most humble repentance be granted once in the Church, lest a remedy made cheap become less useful to the sick—which is more health-giving in proportion as it is less contemptible—yet who would dare say to God: “Why do you still spare this man, who, after his first repentance, again binds himself with the snares of iniquity?” [Note: [Col. 1599] The collected editions except Basel and Lyons II–III read *adstringit*, “binds,” rather than *obstringit*, “binds fast.”]

### IV. Part. Gratian

By this authority Ambrose’s statement is also determined, and forgiveness is shown to be granted again to the sinner through the first repentance; otherwise God would by no means spare again one whom he had not yet spared [Note: [Col. 1599] cf. above, ch. 3]. The satisfaction of repentance, and the saying [Note: [Col. 1599] cf. Book I, ch. 5], “Go, and henceforth do not sin,” have the same meaning as the definition. But what is said in the book [Note: [Col. 1599] ibid., ch. 4] *On Repentance* must be understood of perfect repentance. For just as charity is one thing in beginners, another in those advancing, and another in the perfect, so repentance is one thing in beginners, another in those advancing, and another in the perfect.

Just as forgiveness of sins is granted in baptism to charity not yet perfect—so that, although someone may afterward sin gravely, he is nevertheless understood at that time to have been reborn not by water alone, as Jovinian taught, but by water and Spirit, as Jerome writes against him—so forgiveness is not denied to the repentance of beginners. It can in one respect be called perfect because it groans and grieves with the whole heart, though in another respect it can be called imperfect because it will not endure to the end.

§ 1. According to the first manner of perfection, the saying of John Chrysostom is understood [Note: [Col. 1599] ibid., ch. 8], “Perfect repentance,” and so forth. According to the second manner of perfection, Augustine’s statement is understood [Note: [Col. 1599] ibid., ch. 4], “Repentance is vengeance always punishing in oneself what one grieves to have committed.” But the saying [Note: [Col. 1599] ibid., ch. 5], “If repentance ends, nothing remains of forgiveness,” can be understood in two ways.

For if, according to the opinion of some, remitted sins return, it is easy to understand that nothing remains of forgiveness because the sins which had previously been remitted are repeated. For, just as one manumitted from rightful servitude into freedom is truly free again, although afterward, because of ingratitude, he may be recalled into servitude, so sins are truly remitted to the penitent, though afterward, because of ingratitude for forgiveness, he may be entangled in those same sins.

But if remitted sins do not return, it is said that nothing remains of forgiveness because nothing remains to him of the purity of life and hope of eternal blessedness which he obtained with forgiveness. For, just as perfectly purified silver retains none of its beauty if it is defiled by subsequent verdigris, though it is stained not by the former but by the later impurity, so nothing of forgiveness is said to remain in one purified through repentance, although he is now defiled not by sins already erased but by sins still needing purification.

### V. Part

§ 2. That sins are remitted through repentance not only once but very often is proved by the authority of many writers.

For Jerome says in his letter to Rusticus concerning repentance:

[Col. 1600A] C. XXIII.

“The righteous person falls seven times and rises again” [Note: [Col. 1599] Prov. 24:16; the Vulgate reads *cadet … resurget*, “will fall … will rise,” rather than *cadit … resurgit*, “falls … rises”]. If he falls, how is he righteous? If he is righteous, how does he fall? Yet he does not lose the title of righteous who always rises again through repentance. And not only seven times [Note: [Col. 1599] Matt. 18:22], but seventy times seven, sins are forgiven to one who sins if he turns to repentance. “He to whom more is forgiven loves more” [Note: [Col. 1599] Luke 7:47; the collected editions read *donatur*, “is given,” rather than *dimittitur*, “is forgiven”].

Gratian. David also obtained through repentance forgiveness for adultery and homicide together.

[Col. 1600B] Concerning his repentance Jerome says in the same book [Note: [Col. 1599] Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 14]:

C. XXIV.

The fiftieth Psalm displays the whole repentance of the sinner, when David went in to *Bathsheba*, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and, rebuked by the prophesying Nathan [Note: [Col. 1599] *Prophet*: the collated editions.], answered, saying [Note: [Col. 1599] Absent from the original—cf. 2 Kings 12:13.], “I have sinned,” and immediately deserved to hear: “And the Lord has taken away your sin.” For he had joined murder to adultery; yet, turning to tears, he says [Note: [Col. 1599] *says*: Basel edition—cf. Psalm 50:1 ff.], “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy, *and according to the multitude of your compassions blot out my iniquity*.” For a great sin needed [Note: [Col. 1599] *needs*: the collated editions.] great mercy. Hence he adds [Note: [Col. 1599] *subjoins*: the same editions.] and says: “Wash me greatly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin; for I acknowledge [Note: [Col. 1599] *know*: the same editions—the Vulgate.] my iniquity, and my offence is always before me [Col. 1600C].” “Against you alone have I sinned” (for he was king [Note: [Col. 1599] The original has: “I was … I feared”; addition: “he had no one above himself”: the collated editions and first Basel edition.], and feared no other), “and have done evil before you, that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.” For God has shut up all things under sin [Note: [Col. 1599] Romans 11:32.], that he may have mercy upon all. And he advanced so far [Note: [Col. 1599] *advances*: Nuremberg, Venice I and II, Paris editions.] that, once a sinner and penitent, he passed into the role of teacher and said [Note: [Col. 1599] “And says” is absent from the Argentinian and Basel editions; Venice I and II have “he says”; the remaining editions have “for he says”—cf. Psalm 50:15.], “I will teach the lawless your ways, and the ungodly shall turn to you.” For confession and beauty are before him, so that he who [Note: [Col. 1599] *because*: Bohmer.] has confessed his sins and has said [Note: [Col. 1599] Psalm 37:6.], “My scars have putrefied [Note: [Col. 1599] *Have thoroughly putrefied*: the collated editions.] and become corrupt because of my foolishness,” may change the foulness of wounds into the beauty of health.

### C. XXV. Likewise Ambrose, *Apology of David*, chapter 2

That great and powerful king did not allow the consciousness of his offence to remain with him even for the briefest moment [Col. 1600D], but by prompt confession and boundless grief restored his sin to the Lord. And below, § 1: Finally, the pain of his inmost feeling moved [Note: [Col. 1599] *moves—and where*: Basel edition.] the Lord, so that Nathan said [Col. 1601A; Note: [Col. 1601] 2 Kings 12:13.]: “Because you have repented, the Lord has taken away your sin.” Thus the promptness of the pardon made clear how profound was the king’s repentance [Note: [Col. 1601] *in the king*: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.], which removed the offence of so great an error [Note: [Col. 1601] *removed*: Basel edition.].

And below, § 2: The saints who strive to complete the devout contest and to run the course of salvation, if perhaps they fall as human beings, through the frailty of nature rather than through a desire to sin, rise again more vigorously to run, repairing their contests with greater efforts under the spur of shame, so that their falls may be thought not merely to have brought no impediment, but even to have added incentives to swiftness. Therefore, if the course of runners is not interrupted when some have perhaps fallen [Note: [Col. 1601] *fell*: the original and collated editions.], nor the contest of wrestlers, but their struggles remain unimpeded—and indeed many have conquered with greater grace after one or two falls [Col. 1601B]—how much more should those who have entered the contest of godliness not be judged by the setback of a single lapse, when blessed is the person who has been able [Note: [Col. 1601] *was able*: Basel edition; *is able*: the remaining editions.] to restore himself after a fall?

And below, chapter 4, § 3: That he sinned belongs to his condition [Note: [Col. 1601] *the condition of corruption*: Basel edition.]; that he prayed belongs to correction [Note: [Col. 1601] *correction*: the collated editions.]. The fall is common, but confession is particular. Thus, to incur guilt belongs to nature; to erase it [Note: [Col. 1601] *to wash it away*: the same editions—the original.] belongs to virtue.

And below, chapter 13, § 4: Sin is either forgiven, or blotted out, or covered. It is forgiven through grace, blotted out through the blood of the cross, and covered through love. Likewise iniquity, which [Note: [Col. 1601] Absent from Venice I–II, Paris, and Lyons editions.] is reckoned a disposition of an unjust mind—although John in his Epistle has said that the one who commits [Note: [Col. 1601] *committed*: Basel edition.] sin has also [Note: [Col. 1601] Absent from Paris and Lyons editions.] committed iniquity—*as we have it written* [Note: [Col. 1601] 1 John 5:17.]: “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity [Col. 1601C]. Sin is iniquity, because iniquity is in sin itself.” Nevertheless, as it seems to us, sin is [Note: [Col. 1601D] *Sin is*: in the common printed original one reads: “Every sin is iniquity; but iniquity is the producer of fault or offence. Therefore it is more …”; Gratian’s reading was judged better.] the work of iniquity, whereas iniquity is the producer of fault or [Note: [Col. 1601] *and*: the collated editions.] offence. Therefore iniquity itself must first be blotted out: the root and seedbed of sins must be cut away; *the evil root must be removed lest it bear evil fruit; every attachment to error must be abolished; every kind of iniquity must be removed*. Thus, just as instruction, entering into the soul of the wise, removes imprudence, and knowledge removes ignorance, so perfect virtue removes iniquity, and the remission of sins blots out every sin.

### C. XXVI. The same, in the same book, chapter 7 [Note: [Col. 1601] Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 14.]

How marvellous indeed [Note: [Col. 1601] The original: “But how admirable also is that”; *admirable*: the collated editions.] is this: David offered himself to the angel striking the people [Note: [Col. 1601] Absent from the Basel edition.], saying [Note: [Col. 1601] 1 Chronicles 21:17.]: “What has this flock done? Let your hand be upon me [Col. 1602A] and upon the house of my father.” By this deed he was immediately declared worthy of sacrifice, though he had been thought [Note: [Col. 1601] *was thought*: the collated editions and Lyons II–III editions.] unworthy of absolution. Nor is it surprising that, by such an offering of himself for the people, he obtained pardon for his sin, since Moses [Note: [Col. 1601] Cf. Exodus 32.], by offering himself to the Lord for the people’s error, *also the people’s* [Note: [Col. 1601] “Also the people’s” is absent from the original.] sins blotted out [Note: [Col. 1601] *washed away*: the collated editions and Lyons II–III editions.].

Did he therefore cover his sins, or not? Yet who could deny it, when this very Prophet taught [Note: [Col. 1601] Psalm 31:1.] that iniquities are forgiven [Note: [Col. 1601] *iniquity is forgiven*: Basel edition.], sins covered, and sin not imputed by the Lord? He taught that his sin had been forgiven, as it is written [Note: [Col. 1601] Psalm 31:5.]: “I acknowledge [Note: [Col. 1601] Addition: *I*: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] my offence [Note: [Col. 1601] *know*: Basel edition.], and I did not cover my injustice. I said, ‘I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety [Note: [Col. 1601] *iniquity*: the same edition.] of my heart [Note: [Col. 1601] *sin*: Vulgate—the collated editions.]” [Note: [Col. 1601] The collated editions read: “If he said.”]. He said, “I will declare,” [Col. 1602B] and deserved pardon before he declared it. How much more, once he declared it concerning himself, saying, “I acknowledge my iniquity” [Note: [Col. 1601] Absent from Bohmer; *I acknowledge*: Basel edition; the collated editions add from Psalm 50:5: “and my sin is always before me.”], was every sin forgiven him? Although Nathan the prophet specifically also answered concerning this [Note: [Col. 1601] 2 Kings 12:13.]: “And the Lord has taken away your sin.”

Therefore he obtained remission of iniquity; he covered and concealed his sins by love, and covered them by good works. Nor was sin to be imputed to him [Note: [Col. 1601] *imputed*: the same editions and Lyons edition.], because there was in him not the guile of malice but a lapse of error; then [Note: [Col. 1601] The original and collated editions: “Finally, not …”], because there was not the heat of wickedness but the shadow of a mystery. Yet he confessed his offence, acknowledged his iniquity, saw the washing and both saw and believed; he loved much, so that by exceeding love he might cover every error.

### VI. Part. Gratian

Behold, the repentance here commended, and to which pardon is shown to have been given through the Prophet [Col. 1602C], demonstrates how grievously afterward the multitude of the people, once brought low, sinned. Ahab also—so Jerome writes against Jovinian—the most impious king, obtained by fasting and sackcloth that he might evade God’s sentence and that the destruction of his house might be deferred to his descendants.

Concerning him the same Jerome writes to Rusticus, saying:

### C. XXVII

Ahab, the most impious king, gained possession of Naboth’s vineyard by bloodshed; and when Jezebel, joined to him not so much by marriage as by cruelty, is rebuked by Elijah’s reproof, the Lord says [Note: [Col. 1601] *this*: Basel edition; *to him, this*: the remaining editions—cf. 3 Kings 21:19 ff.]: “You have killed and taken possession”; and again: “In the place where the dogs licked [Col. 1603A] Naboth’s blood, there they shall lick your blood. And dogs shall eat Jezebel before the walls of Jezreel.” When Ahab heard this, he tore his garments, put sackcloth upon his flesh, fasted, and slept in haircloth. And the word of the Lord came to Elijah, saying: “Because Ahab has reverenced my face, I will not bring evil in his days.” The crime of Ahab and Jezebel was one and the same; yet, when Ahab turned [Note: [Col. 1603] *and so … having turned*: Basel edition; *but so … having turned*: the remaining editions; the original has *having turned*.] to repentance, the penalty is deferred to his descendants, while Jezebel, persisting in her crime, is condemned by present judgment.
