### C. XXVIII. Likewise John Chrysostom, *On the Restoration of the Fallen* (Letter V to Theodore Who Had Fallen) [Note: [Col. 1603D] This translation, though it differs somewhat from the version circulated among the Latin works of John Chrysostom, nevertheless does not depart far from the Greek wording. This small work survives in manuscript in the Vatican Library.]

Believe me: such, yes such, is God’s mercy toward human beings. He never despises repentance if it is offered to him sincerely and [Col. 1603B] simply. Even should someone reach the summit of evils, if he nevertheless wishes thence to return to the path of virtue, God receives him and gladly embraces him. He does all that he can to recall him to his former state; and what is still more excellent and lofty, even if a person cannot [Note: [Col. 1603] *can*: Basel edition.] complete the entire course of satisfaction, he does not reject whatever repentance has been performed, however small it may be and however brief the time in which it was undertaken. He receives even that and does not allow the reward of even the slightest conversion to be lost.

Isaiah indicates this to me when he says something of this kind concerning the Jewish people [Note: [Col. 1603] Isaiah 57:17, according to the Septuagint.]: “Because of sin I troubled him a little, struck him, and turned my face away from him; he was grieved and walked sorrowfully, and I healed him and comforted him.” Yet that impious king [Col. 1603C; Note: [Col. 1603] *most impious*: Basel edition.] provides us with even clearer testimony. Through his wife’s wickedness he sought the prey of his own desire; but, troubled by the enormity of that crime, he repented, clothed himself in haircloth, wept for his deed, and thus stirred the Lord’s mercy toward him, so that God absolved him from all his sins. For God says to Elijah [Note: [Col. 1603] 3 Kings 21, final verse.]: “Have you seen how Ahab has been pierced with compunction before me? Because [Note: [Col. 1603] *and because*: Basel edition.] he wept in my sight, I will not bring evils in his days.”

### C. XXIX. Likewise Gregory, Homily X on Ezekiel, at the end

Just as [Note: [Col. 1603] *Thus*: the original.] Ahab, the wicked king, rebuked by the Prophet, when he heard the divine sentence against himself, was terrified and overwhelmed by great [Note: [Col. 1603] *in great*: the collated editions.] sorrow [Note: [Col. 1603] *cast down*: the original.], so that the Lord said to his Prophet [Note: [Col. 1603] 3 Kings 21, final verse.], “Have you not seen [Col. 1603D] Ahab humbled before me? Since therefore he has humbled himself on my account, I shall not bring evil in his days.” In these words of the Lord we must consider how the sorrow of bitterness is pleasing to him [Col. 1604A; Note: [Col. 1603] *is well-pleasing*: Basel edition.] in his elect, who fear to lose God, if repentance was thus pleasing to him even in a reprobate [Note: [Col. 1603] The original and collated editions: *in the reprobate*.] who feared to lose the present world; or how voluntary affliction for faults is acceptable to him in those who please him, if it was acceptable for a time even [Note: [Col. 1603] “And in him who displeased”: the same source and editions.] in those who displeased him.

Gratian. The Ninevites also [Note: [Col. 1603] Jonah 3.], whom the Lord commends in the Gospel, did penance at Jonah’s preaching; and, obtaining pardon through the Lord’s mercy, deserved to escape the destruction of overthrow. But the text of the Book of Kings shows how Ahab lived after receiving pardon. Ambrose likewise writes concerning this in his book *On Naboth* [Note: [Col. 1603] In the book *On Naboth*.], that Jezebel his wife, by whose will he was inflamed, turned his heart, made him detestable by excessive sacrileges, and recalled him from this disposition of repentance [Col. 1604B].

But Jerome writes concerning the Ninevites in the prologue to Jonah [Note: [Col. 1603] The sense, not Jerome’s actual words.]:

### C. XXX

As Herodotus says, Nineveh was overthrown by the king of the Medes, when Josiah was reigning among the Hebrews. Hence it is evident that, through repentance at Jonah’s preaching, it deserved pardon; but because afterward [Note: [Col. 1603] *after*: Argentinian and Basel editions.] it returned to its vomit, it was overthrown by God’s wrath.

### C. XXXI. The same, in the prologue to Nahum [Note: [Col. 1603] Nor are Jerome’s actual words given here.]

Hebrew tradition confirms that the prophet Nahum lived before the coming of the king of Assyria, who had carried the people of Israel captive into his own [Note: [Col. 1603] *his own regions*: the collated editions.] land. For at the end of this passage the same Prophet is shown to announce the coming of the aforesaid king [Col. 1604C]. But when the inhabitants of Nineveh, at Jonah’s preaching of the city’s destruction, had repented of their sins and impiety lest they suffer the destruction proclaimed by divine wrath, they received God’s mercy, but then entangled themselves in graver crimes. For this reason the aforementioned Prophet, full of the Holy Spirit, announcing God’s judgment, spoke thus [Note: [Col. 1603] Nahum 1:2.]: “The Lord God *is* jealous and avenging.”

### VII. Part. Gratian

Likewise, that pardon is frequently granted to the penitent is attested by Augustine in the book *On Repentance* [Note: [Col. 1603] Chapter 5 of *On True and False Repentance*, wrongly attributed to Augustine—Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 14.], writing against certain heretics who said that repentance was useful only once for those sinning after baptism.

### C. XXXII

The faithless still insist, who [Col. 1604D; Note: [Col. 1603] *because*: the collated editions.] are wise beyond what is fitting—not sober, but exceeding measure. They say: although repentance is effective once for those who sin after baptism [Col. 1605A], yet repeated repentance will not profit those who sin often; otherwise pardon would be an encouragement to sin. For they say: “Who would not always sin, if one could always return?” They make the Lord [Note: [Col. 1605] *God*: the same editions.] an encourager of evil if he should always assist the penitent [Note: [Col. 1605] *assists*: the same editions and first Lyons edition.], and assert that sins please him if grace is always ready for them.

But they are mistaken; indeed, it is clear that sins greatly displease him who is always ready to destroy them. For if he loved them, he would not always destroy them, but preserve [Note: [Col. 1605] *save*: Basel edition.] them and cherish them as his gifts. He always destroys the sins he finds, lest what he created be dissolved and what he loved be corrupted.

These hypocrites draw an argument from the Lord’s deeds. Whom did he make blind [Note: [Col. 1605] Absent from the collated editions and first Lyons edition.] see twice? Whom did he cleanse twice from leprosy? Whom did he raise from the dead twice [Col. 1605B]? Not Lazarus, whom he loved; not the widow’s son [Note: [Col. 1605] Cf. Luke 7.], whom in pity he restored to his mother; he is not recorded as having received twice the prodigal son [Note: [Col. 1605] Luke 15.]; nor as having twice delivered the daughter [Note: [Col. 1605] Cf. Matthew 15.] of Abraham from a demon. In no individual did he repeat the deed, thereby teaching, as they say, that remedy is not often effected by the Lord. He said to the woman [Note: [Col. 1605] John 8:11.], “Go, and sin no more, lest something worse happen to you,” promising punishment, not further pardon.

§ 1. But the fact that he made many blind persons see at different [Note: [Col. 1605] *in different*: the collated editions.] times [Note: [Col. 1605] *made see; strengthened*: Basel edition.], and strengthened many weak persons, shows that the same sins are often forgiven in different people: so that he may at another time make the person whom he first healed as a leper see as a blind man [Note: [Col. 1605] The original has *made see*; Basel has *may make see*.]. Thus he healed [Note: [Col. 1605] The original: *saved*; the following “feverish, so many sick, so many” are absent from the Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I–II, and Paris editions.] so many fevered persons, so many sick, so many lame, blind, and withered persons, lest the sinner despair [Note: [Col. 1605] *might despair*: the original.]; and thus no one is recorded [Col. 1605C; Note: [Col. 1605] *is described*: Basel edition.] as healed except once [Note: [Col. 1605] The collated editions: *anyone … healed*.], so that each person may fear to be submerged [Note: [Col. 1605] *joined*: the same editions and first Lyons II–III editions—the original.] in sin.

We still see daily in the Church persons frequently fevered, frequently sick, frequently seized by sufferings, frequently delivered, so that it may appear that the merciful work is performed as often as the penitent’s confession is made. For how could he often heal the body—which is more worthless and less like himself—and not as often free the soul, which is worthier and redeemed? He calls himself a physician [Note: [Col. 1605] Mark 2:17.], fitting not for the healthy but for the sick. But what sort of physician would this be, who could not cure a repeated evil [Col. 1606A]? It belongs to physicians to *visit a sick person a hundred times, to cure him a hundred times*. He would be inferior to other physicians if he did not know what is possible to others. He is mindful of himself, who says [Note: [Col. 1605] The collated editions: *promised*—the original—cf. Ezekiel 33:11.], “I do not will the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live.” What sinner has he excluded [Note: [Col. 1605] *excludes*: Basel edition.]? And that he promised pardon to all, he also makes clear by other promises.

“Whoever confesses me before human beings” [Note: [Col. 1605] Matthew 10:32.]—that is, every sinner, however great and however often he has sinned, of whatever rank, even if he is a priest—“I too will confess him before my Father” [Note: [Col. 1605] “Before my Father” is not read in the Argentinian and Nuremberg editions.]. For “whoever calls upon the name of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 1605] *whoever*: the collated editions—cf. Joel 2, final verse.]—that is, according to what the Lord’s name signifies; that is, whoever calls upon [Note: [Col. 1605] *calls*: Basel edition.] him by serving him, not [Note: [Col. 1605] *and not*: the collated editions.] by opposing him, as perhaps he has often done—every person, that is, whatever sinner he may be [Col. 1606B], shall be saved. For this promiser has filled every soul with good things, even those sitting [Note: [Col. 1605] *sitting*: the original—cf. Luke 1:79.] in darkness and the shadow of death, excluding no soul.

§ 2. That disciple understood [Note: [Col. 1605] *understood*: the collated editions—cf. 1 Corinthians 13.] this master who wished to correct the Corinthians through his letters, and, as he himself testifies, corrected them three times in *his letters*. For as often as he saw [Note: [Col. 1605] *saw*: the same editions.] them fall, so often he ought to help them rise [Note: [Col. 1605] *help them to rise*: Basel edition.]. For he remembered the one who had said [Note: [Col. 1605] John 20:23.], “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them.” We know also [Note: [Col. 1605] *indeed*: Basel edition.] that the first Fathers, and the Church of God in every age, always, up to seventy times seven—that is, always—forgive [Note: [Col. 1605] *remit*: the collated editions.] sins. These men endeavour to take this authority away from the Church *of God*. For the Church must so believe [Note: [Col. 1605] Addition: *of God*: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.], which [Col. 1606C; Note: [Col. 1605] The collated editions and first Basel and Lyons II–III editions: *who confess*.] confesses that it often sins [Note: [Col. 1605] Absent from the same editions and first Lyons edition.].

Those who dare to boast that they are without sin, being deceived, deny the truth [Note: [Col. 1605] *Deceived*: the original reads “to be in themselves,” and 1 John 1:1 seems to be indicated; but it was not altered because of the gloss.]. For “we all offend in many things” [Note: [Col. 1605] James 3:2.], and not even an infant of one day can be without sin upon the earth [Note: [Col. 1605] Job 14:1.]. Therefore this error must be eliminated from the Church, which ever [Note: [Col. 1605] *never*: Basel edition.] denies pardon to the penitent.

For it does not ask what the Apostle meant when he said [Note: [Col. 1605] 1 Corinthians 4:4.], “I am conscious of nothing, but I am not thereby justified.” For knowing [Note: [Col. 1605] Argentinian: *but perceiving*; Nuremberg, Venice I–II, Paris: *also perceiving*; Lyons: *also knowing*; Basel: *for knowing he is justified*.] that sins regularly befall even the righteous [Note: [Col. 1605] *the unrighteous*: Argentinian edition.], he did not assert that he was without sin—he who knew [Note: [Col. 1605] *recognized*: the collated editions.] himself joined to Christ by the indissoluble bond [Col. 1607A] of love [Note: [Col. 1607] *joined*: the same editions and first Basel edition.]. For unless he knew that the righteous often come for pardon, how could he doubt that he sinned, though he knew that he possessed God’s Spirit and served him with the purest intention?

Why would the Lord have washed Peter’s feet [Note: [Col. 1607] Cf. John 13.] and taught the Church to do the same, unless because offence is daily and remission ought therefore to be daily? Why would he teach those praying to say [Note: [Col. 1607] Matthew 6:12.], “Forgive us our debts,” unless he himself, being merciful, continued [Note: [Col. 1607] *persuaded*: Nuremberg, Venice I–II, Paris editions; *continued for us*: Basel edition.]—he who does not wish us to fail in this petition?

### C. XXXIII. Likewise Augustine to Macedonius, Letter LIV [Note: [Col. 1607D] This chapter has been enlarged in two places from the original.] [Note: [Col. 1607] Written A.D. 414—Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 14.]

Human iniquity sometimes advances so far that, even after repentance has been performed and reconciliation with the altar, people commit like or graver offences. Yet God makes his sun rise even upon such persons [Col. 1607B; Note: [Col. 1607] Absent from the Basel edition.], and grants them no fewer than the exceedingly abundant gifts of life and salvation which he granted before. And although in the Church the place of the humblest [Note: [Col. 1607] *that*: the original.] repentance is not granted to them, God nevertheless does not forget his patience toward them.

If someone from their number should say to us [Note: [Col. 1607] Absent from the Basel edition; *to you*: Argentinian and Nuremberg editions.]: “*Either grant me once more the same opportunity to repent, or allow me, as one without hope, to do whatever I please, insofar as my means support me and human laws do not prohibit me: among prostitutes and in every luxury—indeed condemnable before the Lord, but even praiseworthy among most people; or, if you call me back from this wickedness*—tell me whether it will profit me at all for the life to come if, in this life, I despise the allurements of most enticing pleasure [Col. 1607C], *restrain the provocations of lust, deprive myself of many things even lawful and permitted in order to discipline my body*, torment myself in repentance more vehemently than before, groan more miserably, weep more abundantly, live better, support the poor more generously, and burn more ardently with the love that covers a multitude of sins”: which of us is so foolish as to say to this person, “These things will do you no good hereafter; go, at least enjoy [Note: [Col. 1607] *use/enjoy*: the collated editions.] the pleasantness of this life”? May God avert such monstrous [Note: [Col. 1607] *vain*: the same editions and Lyons II–III editions.] sacrilegious [Note: [Col. 1607] *and sacrilegious*: the collated editions.] madness [Note: [Col. 1607D] In blessed Augustine the chapter *Although* follows, above at the same distinction.] [Note: [Col. 1607] *judgment*: Basel edition.]!

### VIII. Part. Gratian

Whether someone says that only the first repentance after baptism is useful, and not a later one, or contends that pardon is granted only to the last repentance and not to an earlier one, he is always opposed to authority [Col. 1608A], which very often promises pardon to the penitent. What true repentance is, to which pardon is never denied, and what false repentance is, to which pardon is never promised, Adamantius and Hesychius testify in their commentaries on Leviticus.

### C. XXXIV [Note: [Col. 1608D] In this and the following chapter the very words of the *ordinary gloss* are adduced, although much is taken from Origen Adamantius and Hesychius.]

“Meanwhile, the goat which had been offered, burnt, etc.” [Note: [Col. 1607] Leviticus 10:16.] Not to sin belongs to God alone; to correct oneself belongs to the wise. But you will rarely find [Note: [Col. 1607] *find*: Basel edition.] anyone who corrects himself. Confession of sin is rare; repentance is rare. Nature and shame resist it, because every flesh is subject to guilt, and everyone is ashamed to confess sin, thinking more of present things than future ones.

Moses wishes to find the soul free from sin, so that it may put off the spoils of error [Col. 1608B] and depart naked of fault, without shame at its own condition [Note: [Col. 1607] *fault*: Basel edition.]. But irrational impulse comes first, and the flame of a most swift movement devours [Note: [Col. 1607] *burns and devours*: the collated editions and first Basel edition.] the soul and *burns up* its innocence. Present things outweigh future things, pleasant things serious ones, joyful things sorrowful ones, and hasty things slower ones [Note: [Col. 1607] *hurried*: the same editions and first Basel edition.]. For iniquity is swift: it presents an opportunity to harm. Virtue is slow and deliberative; before beginning [Note: [Col. 1607] *begins*: the same editions and first Argentinian edition.], it judges what is becoming and honourable. Iniquity rushes everything headlong.

But repentance is sluggish and ashamed, because it is weighed down by shame at present things [Note: [Col. 1607] *therefore*: the collated editions.]. It attends only to future things [Note: [Col. 1607] *only*: the same edition.], whose hope is delayed and whose fruit slow [Note: [Col. 1607] *slower*: the collated editions.]. Meanwhile shamelessness runs ahead [Note: [Col. 1607] *unchastity*: Argentinian edition.]; through hope of present things repentance is excluded, and its disposition is burned away and abolished. The Law seeks it and does not find it: it has been burned [Note: [Col. 1608C; Note: [Col. 1607] *consumed*: the collated editions.] by the heat [Note: [Col. 1607] *in the heat*: the same editions and first Basel edition.] and smoke of iniquity. Therefore it is angry and says that repentance ought to have been consumed in the holy of holies [Note: [Col. 1607] *holy things*: Basel edition.]; it rebukes the priests as though negligent.

§ 1. Aaron answers that priestly judgment ought to be prudent, and that this office should not lightly be entrusted to an apparently sound conscience, lest the *last* error be worse [Note: [Col. 1607] *more serious*: the collated editions.] than the former. For either oil or wine easily spoils in a foul vessel. But how, where there was strange fire, could sin be burned up in [Note: [Col. 1607] *and in*: the same editions.] the sight of the Lord, before whom all things [Note: [Col. 1607] *everything*: the same editions and first Basel edition.] are open? It is as though he said: God is not pleased with one who keeps injustice enclosed in his heart [Note: [Col. 1607] *in the heart*: Basel edition.] and claims [Note: [Col. 1607] *shut up*: the same edition.] to do repentance. Strange fire is lust, avarice, and every perverse desire. This fire burns up; it does not cleanse. Those in whom it is found, if they make an offering before the Lord, are consumed by heavenly fire [Col. 1609A], like Nadab [Note: [Col. 1609] Leviticus 10.] and Abihu together with the things that had been offered for sin.

§ 2. Therefore let the one who wishes to be cleansed remove strange fire and offer himself to that fire which burns up guilt, not the human being. This fire [Note: [Col. 1609] Mark 5.] dried up the flowing blood of the woman with a haemorrhage; this fire [Note: [Col. 1609] Addition: *by miracles*: Basel edition—cf. Luke 23.] dried up the robber’s guilt. For it is a consuming fire [Note: [Col. 1609] Addition: *which*: the collated editions and first Argentinian and Basel editions.]; it heals [Note: [Col. 1609] *which heals*: Basel edition.] those who confess simply and purely. Judas says [Note: [Col. 1609] Matthew 27:4.], “I have sinned, betraying innocent blood”; but he held strange fire in his breast, and, inflamed by it, ran to the noose. He was unworthy of remedy because he did not repent with a pure mind.

Moreover, the priests do not take away his guilt, because he offers deceitfully [Note: [Col. 1609] *offers himself*: the same editions.]; nor can they feast upon him, for their food is the forgiveness of sins. Hence the true priest says [Note: [Col. 1609] John 4:34.], “My food is to do [Col. 1609B] the will of the Father [Note: [Col. 1609] *my Father*: the collated editions; addition: “who is in heaven”: the same editions and first Argentinian, Basel, and Nuremberg editions.],” that is, that sinners, converted and penitent, may be saved. For no sacrifice is acceptable to God unless it is true and sincere.

### C. XXXV. Likewise Hesychius, book II, on Leviticus chapter 10 [Note: [Col. 1609] Cf. the ordinary gloss on Leviticus 10:16.]

“Meanwhile, the goat which had been offered,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1609] *this*: Basel edition; *is offered*: the collated editions and first Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] Since every sin is blotted out through repentance, and those who committed the aforementioned sin of strange doctrine and blasphemy were not saved, the Lawgiver explains the cause of their death: “Meanwhile, the goat which had been offered,” etc. That is, because Aaron’s sons did not eat what was for sin in the holy place: they did not cause repentance for the sin committed to be performed in the Church. This command was given to those whom Christ established in the Church as his vicars [Col. 1609C; Note: [Col. 1609] Addition: *his*: the collated editions.].

For he himself [Note: [Col. 1609] *however*: the collated editions.] offered in the holy place—that is, in heaven, in the Father’s sight [Note: [Col. 1609] Addition: *his*: Lyons II–III editions.]—the blood of his offering, which was offered for our blood. But this sacrifice must be eaten [Note: [Col. 1609] Addition: “or received”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] in a holy place, namely in the Church, for the propitiation of sins. Hence he adds: “as it was commanded to me,” *that is, as* I commanded [Note: [Col. 1609] *thus I commanded*: the collated editions; the words “and commanded” occur only in Lyons II–III editions.] and ordained. For Moses bears the person of Christ.

He found it burned because they had sinned against the Holy Spirit: the offering for repentance was taken away by the intelligible [Col. 1610A] fire [Note: [Col. 1609] Addition: *namely*: Lyons II–III editions.] of the Holy Spirit. For to those who sin willingly no sacrifice for sin remains [Note: [Col. 1609] Absent from the collated editions and first Lyons II–III editions—cf. Hebrews 10:26.]. For just as true repentance gains pardon, so feigned repentance provokes God, because [Note: [Col. 1609] Wisdom 1:5.] “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit.” The holy Fathers called this [Note: [Col. 1609] *this*: Basel edition.] the unforgivable sin and blasphemy against the Holy Spirit: to persevere in crimes to the end of life [Note: [Col. 1609] *and in*: the collated editions and first Basel edition; *in*: Basel edition.], to despair of one’s own salvation [Note: [Col. 1609] *his*: the same edition; the words “to despair of one’s own salvation” are omitted in the Argentinian and Nuremberg editions and, in the rest except Basel, moved to the end of the chapter.], and to distrust the power and mercy of the Redeemer [Note: [Col. 1609] *of God and the Redeemer*: Argentinian, Nuremberg, Basel, Venice I; *of God the Redeemer*: the remaining editions.].

### C. XXXVI. Likewise John Chrysostom, Homily XXXI on chapter 12 of the Epistle to the Hebrews
Source preparation: Embedded foreign-language text recovered from the supplied local archive and translated with its supplied apparatus retained.

Judas [Note: [Col. 1609] Matt. ch. 27] repented, but badly; for he hanged himself with a noose. Esau too [Note: [Col. 1609] Gen. ch. 27] repented, but badly; but this man did not even repent. For those tears [Col. 1610B] were not of repentance, but of a violent spirit [Note: [Col. 1609D] “Of a violent spirit”: the Greek is *ἀλλὰ ἐπηρείας καὶ θυμοῦ μᾶλλον, καὶ δείκνυσι τὰ ἑξῆς*, that is, “but rather of an insolent impulse and anger, as the following things show.” An old codex reads *πικρίας καὶ θυμοῦ*, “bitterness and anger”; these two terms are also joined by Blessed Paul in his Epistle to the Ephesians, ch. 4. Certain passages in this chapter have been corrected partly from Gratian’s manuscript codices and partly from the original itself.], and of inward indignation [Note: [Col. 1609] Added: alternatively, “infernal”: Ed. Arg.]. This is made evident by his deeds. And below:

§ 1. Therefore, I beseech you, let us not deny our sins, nor let shamelessness make us hard. Let us punish our sins voluntarily, lest we suffer punishments unwillingly. Cain heard God say [Note: [Col. 1609] Gen. ch. 4, v. 9]: “Where is Abel your brother?” And he said: “I do not know. Am I indeed my brother’s keeper?” Do you see how by this he made his sin more grievous? [Note: [Col. 1609] Variant: “Did he not act more grievously through sin? Was not his father also similar? For Adam himself too, when he heard, etc.” The words “and himself” are absent from Ed. Bas.: collected editions; cf. Gen. ch. 3, v. 9.] But his father, when he heard, “Adam, where are you?” did not respond in that way. He said: “I heard your voice, Lord, and I was afraid, because I am naked, and I hid myself.” It is a great good for a person to acknowledge his sins and to keep their memory continually. No remedy for sins is found comparable to their unceasing remembrance.

[Col. 1610C] **C. XXXVII. Likewise Ambrose, Book II of *On Repentance*, ch. 11.**

“Upon the willows,” he says, “in its midst we hung our instruments. How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?” [Note: [Col. 1609] Ps. 136, vv. 1 and 4.] For if the flesh resists the mind and is not subject to the governance of the soul and the command of the mind, it is a foreign land, not subdued by the cultivation of its tiller [Note: [Col. 1609] “And this”: absent from the collected editions and the earlier Lyons editions II and III]; and therefore it cannot bear the fruits of charity, repentance, and peace [Note: [Col. 1609] Added: “indeed”: Ed. Bas.] [Note: [Col. 1610D] “Repentance of peace”: many old copies read “of repentance and peace” [ [Col. 1609] thus the collected editions]; the printed original reads “patience of peace.”].

It is better, then, to remain quiet when you cannot perform works [Note: [Col. 1609] “When [you can] perform”: absent from Lyons II and III; “than to perform”: the remaining editions] [Note: [Col. 1609] “You do not seek”: the collected editions] [Col. 1611A] of repentance, lest in repentance itself there occur something which afterwards needs repentance. For if repentance has once been undertaken and not lawfully performed, it neither obtains the fruit of the former nor leaves the use of a later one. Indeed, even when the flesh resists, the mind ought to be intent upon the Lord [Note: [Col. 1611] “God”: the same editions]; and, if works do not follow, faith must not be abandoned [Note: [Col. 1611C] “Faith must not be abandoned”: some manuscripts read “faith must not abandon”; older editions of Blessed Ambrose’s works read “faith must desire”; the more recent Paris edition reads “faith must serve.”]. If either fleshly allurements or adverse powers attack, let the mind remain devoted to God.

For then we are most strongly pressed [Note: [Col. 1611C] “We are pressed”: some old copies read “is pressed, when the flesh does not yield” [ [Col. 1611] “Yields”: the same editions and the earlier Lyons editions II and III].] when the flesh yields, and there are those who press hard upon the wretched soul, seeking to remove every defence. Hence that saying [Note: [Col. 1611] Ps. 136, vv. 7 ff.]: “Lay bare, lay bare” [Note: [Col. 1611] Absent from Eds. Bas., Ven. I and II.] “even to its foundation.” David, pitying her, says: “Wretched daughter of Babylon, wretched” [Note: [Col. 1611] The words “wretched,” “and,” and “because” are absent from the collected editions and the earlier Lyons editions II and III.], surely wretched because she is Babylon’s daughter [Note: [Col. 1611] Added: “the soul”: the same editions and the earlier editions of Bas. and Lyons II and III], having ceased to be God’s daughter. Yet he summons a physician for her, saying: [Col. 1611B] “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones” [Note: [Col. 1611] “Your”: Vulgate; Ed. Lyons III.] “against the rock”; that is, who dashes weak and slippery thoughts [Note: [Col. 1611] “Dashes”: Ed. Bas.; “crushes”: the remaining editions.] against Christ [Note: [Col. 1611] “Against the rock, that is, against Christ”: Eds. Bas., Lyons II and III], who crushes all his irrational impulses by reverent examination and discernment [Note: [Col. 1611] “Description”: Ed. Par.; “discernment”: the remaining editions.].

**C. XXXVIII. Likewise Jerome on Matthew, at ch. 27 [Note: [Col. 1611] Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 15.].**

It did Judas no good to have performed repentance [Note: [Col. 1611D] “To have performed repentance”: this is the reading in the gloss, from which this chapter seems to have been taken; but Blessed Jerome and the Master read “late repentance.” A little later, however, the Master has the corrupt reading, “cannot amend.”], through which he could not correct his crime. If [Note: [Col. 1611] “But”: Ed. Bas.] a brother sins against a brother in such a way that he can amend what he has done, it can be forgiven him [Note: [Col. 1611] Added: “divinely”: the collected editions]; but if the deeds remain, repentance is vainly taken up in words. This is what is said *in the Psalm* concerning that [Note: [Col. 1611] “Him”: the same editions] *most unhappy Judas* [Note: [Col. 1611] Ps. 108, v. 7]: “Let his prayer become sin,” so that he could not only fail to amend the wickedness of betrayal, but also add the crime of his own murder.

[Col. 1611C] **C. XXXIX. Likewise Pope Leo, in the sermon beginning “Among all things,” that is, the third on the Passion of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1611] Sermon 54, Ballerini edition.].**

More wicked and more unhappy than all others you proved to be, O Judas: repentance did not call you back to the Lord, but despair dragged you to the noose. You should have awaited the completion of your crime; and, until Christ’s blood had been shed for *all* sinners, you should have delayed the shameful hanging of death.

[Col. 1612A] **Part IX. Gratian.**

By these authorities it is shown what repentance is true and what false; and it is proved that no forgiveness is granted to false repentance. In this the opinion of those is destroyed who maintain that one entangled in several sins obtains from the Lord, by repentance for one offence, forgiveness of that offence without repentance for another crime. They also endeavour to prove this by many authorities. The first is that of the prophet Nahum [Note: [Col. 1611] Nahum, ch. 1, v. 9, according to the Septuagint]: “God will not judge twice in the same matter.” But whom the priest judges, God judges, whose person the priest bears in the Church. Therefore one punished once by a priest for sin will not again be judged by the Lord for the same sin.

**C. XL. Likewise Gregory on Ezekiel, Homily X [Note: [Col. 1611D] A similar summary of Blessed Gregory’s words occurs in the ordinary gloss on Amos 4, but is not wholly the same [Col. 1612C].] [Note: [Col. 1611] The sense, but not the actual words.—Peter Lombard, ibid.].**

“The Lord rained upon one city, and upon another he did not rain; and he rained upon the same city in part and left it dry in part” [Note: [Col. 1611] Amos, ch. 4, v. 7; “left”: the collected editions and the earlier Lyons editions II and III.]. When one who hates his neighbour corrects himself of other vices, one and the same city is rained upon in part and remains dry in part, because there are some who, while cutting away certain vices, persist grievously in others.

**C. XLI. Likewise Ambrose, in the eighteenth octonary of Psalm 118 [Note: [Col. 1611] Cf. the ordinary gloss on Psalm 118, *Sade* (vv. 137 ff.).].**

The first consolation is that God does not forget to show mercy; the second comes through punishment [Note: [Col. 1612C] “Punishment”: formerly “compunction” was read [ [Col. 1611] the collected editions read “punishment”]. It has been corrected from the ordinary gloss, of which this chapter is a kind of summary, and agrees better with Blessed Ambrose’s sense; nevertheless, his complete passage should be read carefully.], where, even if faith [Note: [Col. 1612D] “Faith”: the gloss adds, “that is, consciousness of guilt,” and Gratian explains it thus below in the chapter *Quaerat*.] is lacking, punishment [Note: [Col. 1611] “Repentance or punishment”: the collected editions and the earlier editions of Bas. and Lyons II and III.] makes satisfaction and brings relief.

**Gratian.** Jerome is also objected, since he appears, on Nahum, to think that, if a believer [Note: [Col. 1612D] “Believer”: so corrected from certain old copies, Blessed Jerome, and the Master. Earlier the text read “unbeliever” [ [Col. 1611] thus the collected editions], as also below in the same chapter *Quaerat* and in the chapter *Ignis*.] were killed in adultery, he would not thereafter be punished by God for adultery. Again, if the satisfaction which, while living in adultery, he offered for homicide was not satisfaction, then, when he has repented of adultery, repentance for both must be imposed upon him. But this is shown to be contrary to reason by ecclesiastical custom, which imposes repentance twice upon no one for the same sin, unless it has been repeated.

§ 1. But that forgiveness for one sin is not granted to a man who reserves another crime to himself is proved not only by the authorities previously cited from Hesychius, Adamantius, Gregory, Augustine, Smaragdus, [Col. 1613A] and Isidore, but also by another authority of the same Augustine in the book *On Repentance* [Note: [Col. 1613] Not Augustine’s.—Peter Lombard, ibid.—The following words, “For he says,” are omitted by Böhm.]. For he says:

**C. XLII.**

There are many who repent of having sinned, but not wholly, reserving to themselves certain things in which they delight; they do not observe [Note: [Col. 1613] “Observe”: Ed. Bas.] that the Lord at the same time freed from the demon one who was deaf and mute, thereby teaching us that we are never healed except of everything. For if he had wished sins to be retained in part, one who had seven demons, one remaining, could have made progress after six had been expelled [Note: [Col. 1613] “Having”: Ed. Bas.; “could”: the collected editions]. But he expelled all seven, to teach that all crimes must be cast out together. And when he cast the legion out of another, he left none from among them [Note: [Col. 1613] “Of”: the same editions; cf. Mark, ch. 5.] to possess the person who had been freed, showing that, even if sins are a thousand, one must repent of them all.

[Col. 1613B] For the Lord was praised [Note: [Col. 1613] “To be praised”: Eds. Bas., Lyons II and III; cf. Matt. ch. 9.] when, after the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke [Note: [Col. 1613] “When”: Ed. Bas.; “because”: the remaining editions.]. He never healed anyone whom he did not wholly set free [Note: [Col. 1613] Absent from Ed. Bas.]. He healed the whole person on the Sabbath, because he freed both the body from infirmity and the soul from every contagion, showing that the penitent [Note: [Col. 1613] “Penitents”: the collected editions and the earlier edition of Bas.] ought at once to grieve over every crime arising in soul and [Note: [Col. 1613] “And in”: the same editions.] body.

For I know God [Note: [Col. 1613] “The Lord”: Ed. Bas.] to be the enemy of every criminal person. How, then, will one who reserves a crime receive forgiveness for another? He would obtain forgiveness without love of God, without which no one has ever found grace. For he is God’s enemy while he persists in offending him. It is a kind of impious unbelief to hope for half a pardon from him who is righteous and righteousness itself. For this would be to find grace without repentance [Col. 1613C] [Note: [Col. 1613] Variant: “For how would he find grace without true repentance?” “Finds, and”: Lyons II and III; collected editions.]. True repentance seeks to bring the confessor to baptismal purity. A person truly repenting ought rightly to wash away whatever defilement he has contracted after purification, at least by tears of the mind [Note: [Col. 1613] “In tears”: the collected editions and the earlier edition of Bas.]. But he is very hard whose bodily eyes cannot reveal the pain of his mind. Yet let him know that he is culpably hard who weeps for temporal losses or the death of a friend, but does not show the pain of sin in tears. No one, then, may excuse himself for lacking a fountain of tears if he sometimes shows by tears grief over temporal things [Note: [Col. 1613] “Through love of temporal things”: the collected editions.]. Therefore, let him who repents repent wholly, etc. [Note: [Col. 1613] Above, ch. 88, Distinction 1.]

**Part X. Gratian.** That authority of the prophet Nahum [Note: [Col. 1613] Ch. 1, v. 9, according to the Septuagint], “God will not judge twice,” etc., does not indiscriminately show that everything punished temporally [Col. 1613D] is not to be punished further by God. Although Jerome says, on the same passage, that the Sodomites, Egyptians, and Israelites in the wilderness were punished temporally by God so that they should not be punished eternally, this is nevertheless not to be understood generally of all. Otherwise every wicked person ought to desire that, struck by a heavenly thunderbolt, drowned in waters, or wounded by serpents, he might perish by divine action for his sins, so that a short and momentary penalty might bring eternal torments to an end.

That saying of the Apostle would also be false: writing in the Epistle to the Hebrews concerning those who fell in the wilderness, he says [Note: [Col. 1613] Heb. ch. 3, v. 19], “Because of their unbelief they did not enter the land of promise.” Here it is proved that, just as through the merit of their unbelief they lost that rest, so through the same unbelief they did not at all enter the true rest of eternal blessedness.

§ 1. Jerome’s statement, therefore, is understood only of those who repented amid the very punishments; God does not reject that repentance, though brief and momentary [Col. 1614B]. Likewise, the prophet’s saying [Note: [Col. 1613] Nahum, ch. 1, v. 9, according to the Septuagint], “God will not judge twice in the same matter,” must be understood only of those whom present punishments change for the better, against whom a double affliction shall not arise. But those who become harder and worse amid chastisements, like Pharaoh, who was made harder when scourged by the Lord, join eternal punishments to present ones, so that temporal punishment becomes for them the beginning of eternal condemnation.

Hence Augustine, in the Song of Deuteronomy [Note: [Col. 1613] The thought occurs in Gregory, *Morals*, Book 18, ch. 12.]:

**C. XLIII.**

“A fire has been kindled,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1613] Cf. the ordinary gloss on Deut. ch. 32, v. 22.] This means: vengeance begins here [Note: [Col. 1613] “Begins”: Eds. Bas., Par.] and will burn until final condemnation.

**Gratian.** This is to be noted against those who say [Col. 1614C] that “God will not judge twice in the same matter” [Note: [Col. 1613] Nahum, ch. 1, v. 9, according to the Septuagint] applies to every chastisement, because some are corrected by chastisements here, while others are punished both here and eternally, as Antiochus and Herod.

§ 1. But that Jerome appears to think otherwise concerning the believing adulterer is proved false from his own words. For, by the examples of the man who cursed the Israelites and of the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath, he shows that small sins are purged by short and temporal punishments, while great sins are reserved for long and eternal punishments.

For he says on the first chapter of Nahum [Note: [Col. 1613] Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 15; cf. C. 23, question 5, ch. 6]:

**C. XLIV.**

Someone may ask here: if a believer [Note: [Col. 1613] “Unbeliever”: the collected editions.] caught in adultery is beheaded, what becomes of him afterwards [Note: [Col. 1613] “Becomes”: Ed. Bas.]? Either he will be punished, and this saying is false [Note: [Col. 1613] “God will judge”: the collected editions; cf. Nahum, ch. 1, v. 9, according to the Septuagint]: [Col. 1614D] “The Lord will not take vengeance twice in the same matter in affliction”; or he will not be punished, and adulterers ought to desire that they escape [Col. 1615A] eternal torments at present by a brief *and swift* punishment [Note: [Col. 1613] Variant: “that they be punished by a brief punishment”: the collected editions.].

To this we shall answer [Note: [Col. 1615] “We answer”: the same editions] that God, as he knows the measures of all things, knows also the measures of punishments; that the sentence of the Judge cannot be forestalled; that his power thereafter to inflict punishment on the sinner cannot be taken away; and that great sin is expiated by great and long-lasting torments [Note: [Col. 1615] “Washed away”: the original.]. But if anyone has been punished, as the man in the Law who cursed the Israelite [Note: [Col. 1615] “The Israelites”: the collected editions; cf. Num. ch. 15.] and the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath, such persons are not punished afterwards, because a slight [Note: [Col. 1615] “Mild”: Ed. Bas.] fault has been compensated by present punishment.

**Gratian.** Gregory’s saying [Note: [Col. 1615] Cf. above, ch. 40], “The Lord rained upon one city,” etc., is to be referred not to forgiveness of the crime but to detestation of it: part of the city is said to be rained upon because it begins to detest the crime which it loved, not because it receives forgiveness for it. The detestation of sin is called rain because it is instilled into our heart from the fountain of divine grace, so that a person may thus either come to true repentance or be punished less by God, in proportion as more prolonged delight in sin had accumulated a greater punishment for him.

But if the rain is referred to forgiveness of sin, it will seem to conflict with the evangelical teaching. For if, because of hatred of a brother, even sins which have been forgiven are recalled for punishment, much more is it proved that sins not forgiven are reserved for vengeance.

§ 1. Again, if, according to Augustine [Note: [Col. 1615] Cf. above, Distinction 1, ch. 81], one who is master of his own will cannot begin a new life unless he repents of his old life, how will he who has not laid aside the oldness of hatred attain the newness of forgiveness? Therefore that rain belongs, as has been said, to detestation of sin, not to its forgiveness.

§ 2. Again, Ambrose’s statement [Note: [Col. 1615] Cf. above, ch. 41], “Even if faith is lacking, punishment makes satisfaction,” is not to be understood of the faith of which it is said [Note: [Col. 1615] Jas. ch. 2, v. 17], “Faith without works is dead,” but of that of which the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1615] Rom. ch. 14, v. 23], “Everything which is not from faith,” that is, everything done against conscience, “is sin.” Faith is therefore lacking when consciousness of sin is absent. But because no one understands every offence [Note: [Col. 1615] Ps. 18, v. 13], there is sometimes sin in a person of which he has no consciousness. Hence the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1615] 1 Cor. ch. 4, v. 4], “I am conscious of nothing, but I am not thereby justified.” Therefore, if patiently borne, the punishment for a sin of which consciousness is lacking makes satisfaction and relieves the burdened person.

But the argument raised at the end [Note: [Col. 1615] Above, ch. 41], “If that was satisfaction, it obtained forgiveness; but if it did not obtain forgiveness, it was not satisfaction; and if it was not satisfaction, punishment must still be imposed,” does not follow. Satisfaction exists when the cause of the sin itself is cut off and access is not granted to its suggestions; yet its fruit is not received, being hindered by a sin which is not abandoned. It will, however, be received when repentance for that sin follows. Thus one approaching the laver deceitfully receives the sacrament of regeneration, yet is not born again in Christ; but he will be born again by the power of the sacrament which he received, when that deceit has departed from his heart through genuine repentance.

Likewise Augustine writes in the book *On Repentance* [Note: [Col. 1615] The original reads somewhat differently, but the Master has nearly Gratian’s wording.] [Note: [Col. 1615] Not Augustine’s.—Peter Lombard, ibid.; cf. below, Distinction 5, ch. 1]:

**C. XLV.**

It is pious to believe, and our faith requires this [Note: [Col. 1615] “This our faith requires”: the collected editions], that when Christ’s grace has destroyed a person’s former evils [Col. 1616B], it also rewards good things; and, when it has destroyed what it did not find to be its own, it loves [Note: [Col. 1615] “Loves and cherishes”: the same editions] and cherishes the good which it planted *even* in the sinner.

In this sense also Jerome’s saying on Haggai, ch. 1, appears to be intended [Note: [Col. 1615] Peter Lombard, ibid.]:

**C. XLVI.**

Whenever you see someone amid many evil works of sinners [Note: [Col. 1615] “Amid many evil works”: absent from the original and Ed. Bas.; “a sinner”: the collected editions and the earlier edition of Bas.] doing certain things [Note: [Col. 1615] “Some”: absent from Ed. Arg.; “some things”: the remaining editions] which are just, God is not so unjust that, because of many evils, he forgets a few good things.

**Part XI. Gratian.** Although remembrance of good works may be referred to present recompense, as Gregory writes in his homily on the rich man and Lazarus [Note: [Col. 1615] The saying occurs in Gregory, Homily 40, on Luke 16]:

**C. XLVII.**

We must beware lest, if perhaps we do some good [Note: [Col. 1615] “Some good thing”: Ed. Bas.], we receive its recompense in the present world [Note: [Col. 1615] “Do not receive”: Eds. Bas., Lyons II and III], lest perhaps it be said of us [Note: [Col. 1615] “To us”: Ed. Bas.], “They have received their reward” [Note: [Col. 1615] Matt. ch. 6, v. 5]. For unless this rich man had done some good, for which he received recompense in the present world, Abraham would never have said to him [Note: [Col. 1615] Luke, ch. 16, v. 25], “You received good things in your lifetime.”

**C. XLVIII. Likewise John Chrysostom, Homily LXVII to the people of Antioch [Note: [Col. 1615] It must be denied to Chrysostom, according to the judgement of the Maurists.].**

Why then are we troubled? Let no one be troubled on seeing wicked people enjoy prosperity. Here there is no recompense either of wickedness or of virtue; and, even if it sometimes happens that there is some recompense of wickedness or of virtue [Note: [Col. 1615] “Happens in some way”: Ed. Bas.], it is not according to what is deserved, but simply as a kind of foretaste of judgement [Note: [Col. 1615] Added: “or justice” [“or”: Ed. Bas.]: the collected editions and the earlier editions of Arg. and Nor.], so that those who do not believe in the resurrection may be taught by such things.

When [Note: [Col. 1617] “When”: the collected editions and the earlier Paris and Lyons editions.] therefore we see a wicked person grow rich, let us not be cast down; and when we see a good person suffer evils, let us not be troubled. There is the crown; there are the punishments. There is also another reason: an evil person cannot be evil in every respect, but has some good things; nor can a good person be good in every respect, but has some sins. When a wicked person [Note: [Col. 1617] “A wicked person”: Ed. Bas.] therefore enjoys prosperity, it is to the harm of his own head. For when [Note: [Col. 1617] “Therefore”: the same edition] he receives here recompense for those few good things, he will there be punished more fully.

**Gratian.** Remembrance of good works may also be referred to the obtaining of a milder punishment: good things done amid evils do not avail to obtain a reward in this life or the next, but to undergo more tolerably the punishment of the last judgement. Augustine writes this concerning faith and other things possessed without charity, in the book *On Patience* [Note: [Col. 1617] “On Repentance”: the collected editions], ch. 26:

**C. XLIX.**

But if someone, lacking the charity which belongs to the unity of the Spirit and the bond of peace by which the Catholic Church, gathered together, is joined [Note: [Col. 1617] “Is converted”: Ed. Bas.], being established in some schism, endures tribulations, distresses, hunger, thirst [Note: [Col. 1617] “Thirst”: absent from the original and Eds. Arg. and Nor.], nakedness, persecution, dangers, prisons, chains, torments, sword, flames, beasts, or even the cross itself, through fear of Gehenna [Note: [Col. 1617] “Of Gehennas”: the original; Ed. Bas.] and eternal fire, these things are in no way to be blamed. Indeed, such patience is to be praised. For we cannot say that it would have been better for him [Note: [Col. 1617] “Have been”: the collected editions] to deny Christ and suffer none of those things which he suffered by confessing Christ; rather, we must judge that perhaps his judgement will be more tolerable than if, by denying Christ, he had avoided all [Note: [Col. 1617] “None of the things he suffered”: the same editions] those things.

Hence also the Apostle’s saying [Note: [Col. 1617] 1 Cor. ch. 13, v. 3], “If I give my body [Note: [Col. 1617] Added: “thus”: Vulgate; the collected editions] to be burned, but have not charity” [Note: [Col. 1617] “Have”: Ed. Bas.], “it profits me nothing,” is understood to mean that it profits nothing toward obtaining the kingdom of heaven, not that it profits nothing toward undergoing more tolerably the punishment of the last judgement. And above, ch. 23:

§ 1. Let these things be said concerning charity, without which true repentance [Note: [Col. 1617] “Patience”: the original.] cannot exist in us, because in good people there is the charity of God, which endures all things.

**Part XII. Gratian.** Repentance, therefore, as appears from what has preceded, is of no use to anyone persevering in sin; nevertheless, it is not to be denied to anyone, because he will experience its fruit when he has performed repentance for the other crime. Thus the definition of repentance and the other authorities agreeing with it deny that one persevering in sin performs repentance useful and fruitful to himself.

§ 1. Ambrose’s saying [Note: [Col. 1617] Above, in the same Distinction, ch. 37], “Repentance once undertaken and not truly performed both takes away the fruit of the former and loses the use of the later,” is to be understood of solemn repentance. When this has not been truly performed, it loses both the fruit of the former—that is, its own fruit, which was to follow the preceding act—because it despised the forgiveness which it could have obtained; and it removes the use of a subsequent repentance, according to the custom of certain churches in which solemn repentance is not repeated. The same repentance is also meant by the saying [Note: [Col. 1617] Cf. above, after ch. 61, Distinction 50]: “There is no second place for repentance.”

# DISTINCTION IV

## GRATIAN

**Part I.** Since it has been shown above by many authorities that repentance is truly performed and sins are truly forgiven for one who will at some time fall back into sin, the question is asked whether forgiven sins return. On this question different persons hold differing opinions: some maintain, while others deny, that sins once forgiven are subsequently recalled for punishment.

§ 1. That sins once forgiven return is proved by many authorities. The first is that of the prophet: “Let the iniquity of his fathers return into remembrance” [Note: [Col. 1617] Ps. 118, v. 14]; the second that of the Gospel: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all the debt” [Note: [Col. 1617] Matt. ch. 18, v. 32].

Then Augustine says in the book of Psalms, on Psalm 108:

**C. I.**

If Judas had retained [Note: [Col. 1617] “Had retained”: the collected editions] that to which he was called, neither his own past sins nor his parents’ iniquity would in any way have concerned him [Note: [Col. 1617] “Reached him”: the same editions and the earlier edition of Arg.]. But because he did not retain adoption in the household of God, but chose instead the iniquity of the ancient race, the iniquity of his fathers returned [Note: [Col. 1617] “And returned”: Eds. Arg., Nor., Ven. I and II.] before the Lord, that it too might be punished in him, *and the sin of his mother might not be blotted out* [Note: [Col. 1617] “Himself”: the original.].

Likewise Rabanus [Note: [Col. 1617] These are not Rabanus’s own words.—Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 22]:

§ 1. “He delivered him to the torturers,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1617] Matt. ch. 18, v. 34.] It should be noted that he says “the whole debt,” because not only the sins which a person committed after baptism will be imputed to him for punishment, but also original sins, forgiven him in baptism.

**C. II. Likewise Gregory, Book IV of the *Dialogues*, ch. 60 [Note: [Col. 1617] Peter Lombard, ibid.].**

It is clear *from the words of the Gospel* that, if we do not forgive from the heart *that* which is committed against us [Note: [Col. 1617] “What”: Ed. Lyons II], then that too is again exacted which we rejoiced had already been forgiven us through repentance.

**C. III. Likewise Augustine, Homily XV on the Words of the Lord.**

[Col. 1618D] The Lord says [Note: [Col. 1617] “Says”: the collected editions, the earlier Paris and Lyons editions, and the original; cf. Luke, ch. 6, v. 37], “Forgive, and they are forgiven [Note: [Col. 1617] “It is forgiven”: Ed. Bas.; “it will be forgiven”: the remaining editions and the original; “you will be forgiven”: Vulgate] you.” If I forgave first [Note: [Col. 1617] “Previously”: the collected editions], forgive even afterwards. For if [Note: [Col. 1617] “Even if”: the same editions and the earlier Bas. edition] you do not forgive, I shall call you back and charge back to you whatever *I had forgiven you*.

[Note: [Col. 1619] Peter Lombard, ibid.]

[Col. 1619A] **C. IV. Likewise in the same place [Note: [Col. 1619] These words are not found in Augustine.—Peter Lombard, ibid.].**

One who, forgetful of divine kindness, wishes to avenge his own injuries will not only fail to merit forgiveness for future sins, but even past sins, which he believed had already been forgiven him, will be charged back to him for vengeance.

**C. V. Likewise Bede on Luke, Book IV, ch. 48 [Note: [Col. 1619] Peter Lombard, ibid.].**

“I will return into my house, from which [Note: [Col. 1619] “From which I came out”: absent from Ed. Bas.] I came out” [Note: [Col. 1619] Matt. ch. 11, v. 44]. This little verse must be feared, not expounded, lest the fault which we believed extinguished in us, through negligence while we are unoccupied, overwhelm us.

**C. VI. The same, in the same place *.**

For anyone whom either heretical depravity or worldly covetousness seizes after baptism, it will immediately cast him down into the depths of every vice [Note: [Col. 1619] The printed reading is *quaecunque*; the original and Eds. Arg. and Bas. read “whomever” (*quemcunque*).].

**C. VII. Likewise Augustine, in the Book of Questions on Deuteronomy, Question XLII.**

[Col. 1619B] The sin contracted from Adam [Note: [Col. 1619] “Drawn”: Ed. Bas.] is repaid temporally, because all die because of it; but it is not repaid eternally by those who have been [Note: [Col. 1619] “Were”: the collected editions and the earlier Bas. edition] spiritually regenerated [Note: [Col. 1619] “Reborn”: Ed. Arg.] through grace, and remain in it [Note: [Col. 1619] “If they remain in it”: the collected editions] to the end.

**Part II. Gratian.** Of those who follow this opinion, some say that sins which will return are forgiven according to justice, but not according to foreknowledge; just as the names of disciples who went back were written in the book of life according to the justice which they served, but not according to foreknowledge, which did not contain them in the number of the saved. Thus a thousand are said to fall at God’s side and ten thousand at his right hand [Note: [Col. 1619] Ps. 90, v. 7], although divine foreknowledge had never [Col. 1619C] numbered them among its own. Hence the Lord says to Moses [Note: [Col. 1619] Exod. ch. 32, v. 32], “Whoever has sinned before me, I shall blot him out of the book of life” [Note: [Col. 1619] “Your [book]”: Vulgate], so that, according to the justice of the Judge, one is said to be blotted out by sinning who, according to foreknowledge, had never been enrolled.

§ 1. Hence Augustine, in the Epistle to the Corinthians [Note: [Col. 1619D] “In the Epistle to the Corinthians”: this is found in Bede’s commentary on 1 Corinthians, ch. 10, drawn from Blessed Augustine on Psalm 77, where it is explained more fully.] [Note: [Col. 1619] 1 Cor. ch. 10, v. 5]:

> “Yet God was not pleased with many of them, though with some he was. All the sacraments are common to all, but grace is not common; so baptism too is now common, but the power of baptism is not.”

**Part III.**

§ 2. But this is understood of those who approach deceitfully, or of those baptized outside the Church: they indeed receive the integrity of the sacrament, but do not attain its power. But to infants, or adults approaching in full faith, all sins are forgiven, even if they are at some time to depart from good into evil and end their lives in that state.

[Col. 1620A] Hence Augustine, in the book *On Correction and Grace*, chs. 8 and 9:

**C. VIII.**
If [Col. 1619: the original reads: “For we are discussing those who do not have perseverance in goodness, but fall away from good,” etc.] those who fall away from good into evil [the collected editions: *deficientes*, “falling away”] die with a good will, let them answer, if they can [*possint*: Argenteus edition], why God did not then, while they were living faithfully and devoutly, snatch them from the dangers of this life, lest wickedness should change their understanding [Basel edition: *illorum*, “of them”; cf. Wisdom 4:11], or [the collected editions: *et*, “and”] lest deceit should beguile their souls. Was this beyond his power [Basel edition: *habuerit*, “has had”], or did he not know their future evils? Surely neither of these things can be said except most perversely and madly. Why, then, did he not do it? Let those who mock us answer when, in such matters, we exclaim [Romans 11:33]: “How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!”

For God does not fail to grant this to whom he wills; nor indeed [Argenteus omits *aut vero*, “or indeed”; Venice I–II, Lyon I, and Paris read *vera*, “true”] does that Scripture lie which, concerning the seemingly premature death of a righteous person, says [Wisdom 4:11]: “He was taken away lest wickedness should change his understanding, or [the collected editions: *et*, “and”] lest deceit should beguile his soul.” Why, then, does God give this very great benefit to some and not to others—God with whom there is no injustice or respect of persons, and in whose power lies the length of each person’s remaining in this life, which has been called a trial upon earth?

Therefore, just as they are compelled to admit that it is God’s gift that a person should finish [Argenteus, Nuremberg, Venice I–II, Lyon I, and Paris add *Dei*, “of God”] this life before being changed from good into evil, yet do not know [the earlier Lyon II–III editions: *ignoratur*, “it is unknown”] why this is granted to some and not to others, so [Basel: *id autem*, “but this”; the remaining earlier editions except Argenteus: *id tamen*, “yet this”] let them admit with us, according to the Scriptures—of which I have already adduced many testimonies—that perseverance in goodness is God’s gift; and let them deign, without murmuring against God, to be ignorant with us why it is given to some and not to others.

§ 1. Nor should it disturb us that God does not give this perseverance to certain of his children. Far be it [Basel adds *hoc*, “this”] that it should be so [the collected editions: *sit*, “should be”], if they belonged to those predestined and called according to the purpose [the same editions add *sanctis*, “saints”], who are truly children of promise.

For such persons, while they live devoutly, are called children of God; but because they will live wickedly and die in that same wickedness, God’s foreknowledge does not call them children of God [Argenteus omits *Dei*, “of God”; the collected editions except Argenteus read: “For God’s foreknowledge [Venice I–II and Lyon II–III: *praesentia*, ‘presence’] are children of God”; Basel and Lyon II–III omit *Dei* in that alternative wording]. For there are children of God who are not yet such for us, but already are such for God; concerning them the evangelist John says [John 11:51–52]: “Jesus was going to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also that he might gather into one the scattered children of God.” They were, of course, to become such through faith by the preaching of the Gospel; nevertheless, before this had happened, they were already inscribed in the unshaken permanence of their Father’s memorial record [the earlier Lyon II–III editions read: “in the memorial record of their Father … are inscribed”] as children of God [the collected editions and the earlier Lyon II–III editions read *qui*, “who,” for *quod*, “which”].

Conversely, there are certain persons whom we call children of God because of grace received, though only temporarily, but who nevertheless are not such before God [the collected editions: “children of God”]. Of them the same John says [1 John 1:19]: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” [the collected editions and the earlier Lyon editions: *mansissent*, “would have remained”].

He does not say: “They went out not from us, but, because they did not remain with us, they are no longer of us” [Basel: “not of us”]; rather, he says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.” That is: even when they appeared to be from us [Basel: *in*, “in”]—the collected editions and the earlier Basel and Lyon II–III editions add *nomine*, “in name”—they were not from us. And as if someone were to ask him, “How do you show this?” he says: “For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.”

This is the voice of the children of God: John speaks as one occupying a pre-eminent place among the children of God. Therefore, when the children of God say [the collected editions: *dicuntur*, “are said”] of those who did not possess perseverance, “They went out from us, but they were not of us,” and add [Basel: *addit*, “adds”], “For [Argenteus omits *quod*, “for”; the remaining editions read *quoniam*, “because”] if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us,” what else do they say [Basel: *dicit*, “does he say”] except that they were not children even when they bore the profession and name of children? This was not because they feigned righteousness, but because they did not remain in it.

For he does not say: “If they had been of us, they would certainly have held true rather than feigned righteousness with us”; rather: “If they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.” Without doubt he meant that they should remain in the good. Accordingly, they were in the good; but because they did not remain in it—that is, did not persevere to the end—he says that they were not of us even when they were with us. That is, they were not of the number of the children even while they were in the faith of children, because those who are truly children [Argenteus omits this; the remaining earlier editions add *Dei*, “of God”] are foreknown and predestined [Col. 1621C] to be conformed to the image of his Son [the collected editions add *Dei*, “of God”], and are called according to the purpose [the same editions add *sancti*, “saints”], that they may be elect.

For a child of promise does not perish, but a child of perdition does. These persons, therefore, belonged to the multitude of those called, but did not belong to the small number of the elect. God, then, did not withhold perseverance from his predestined children. For they would have had it if they had belonged to that number of children; and what would they have had which they had not received, according to the Apostle’s true saying [1 Corinthians 4:7]?

Thus such children would have been given to Christ the Son, as he himself says to the Father [John 6:39]: “That everything which you have given me may not perish, but may have eternal life.” Those, therefore, are understood to be given to Christ [Basel: *in Christo*, “in Christ”] who are appointed to eternal life. They are those predestined and called according to the purpose [the collected editions: “called saints”], none of whom perishes [cf. above, Distinction 2, chapter 26]. Consequently, none of them ends this life changed from good into evil, since he is so appointed, and therefore given to Christ, that he may not perish but have eternal life.

Again, those whom we call his enemies, or the infant children of his enemies—whichever among them he will regenerate [the same edition: *regnaturus*, “will reign”] so that they finish this life in the faith which works through love—are already, even before this happens, his children in that predestination, and have been given to Christ his Son, so that they may not perish but have eternal life.

§ 2. Finally, the Savior himself says [the collected editions add *ait*, “says”; cf. John 8:31]: “If you remain,” he says [omitted in the collected editions, except the earlier Basel], “in my word, you are truly my disciples” [the Vulgate, Basel, and Lyon II–III: *eritis*, “you will be”]. Is Judas, who did not remain in his word, to be numbered among them? Are those to be numbered among them of whom the Gospel speaks as follows?

When the Lord had commended the eating of his flesh and drinking of his blood, the Evangelist says [John 6:60 ff.]: “He said these things [the collected editions and the earlier Basel: *hoc*, “this”] while teaching in the synagogue [Basel: *synagogis*, “synagogues”] at Capernaum. Therefore many of his disciples, hearing, said: ‘This saying is hard; who can hear it?’ But Jesus, knowing within himself that his disciples were murmuring about this, said to them: ‘Does this offend you? What, then, if you see [the collected editions and the earlier Basel and Lyon II–III: *videbitis*, “you will see”] the Son of Man ascending where he was before? It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life. But there are some among you who do not believe.’ For Jesus knew from the beginning who were believers and who would betray him. And he said: ‘Therefore I said to you that no one comes to me unless it has been given him by my Father.’ From this time many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him.”

Were not these too called disciples, as the Gospel speaks? Yet they were not true disciples, because they did not remain [the same editions, especially Basel: *remanserunt*, “remained”] in his word, in accordance with what he said [John 8:31]: “If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples” [the collected editions and the earlier Lyon I: *eritis*, “you will be”]. Therefore, because they [Basel and Lyon editions add *non manserunt*, “did not remain”] did not possess perseverance, they were neither truly disciples of Christ nor truly children of God, even while they seemed and were called such.

We therefore call those whom we see regenerated and living devoutly [the collected editions and the earlier Basel and Lyon II–III: *et pie*, “and devoutly”; Basel: *decernimus*, “judge”] both Christ’s elect disciples [Basel: “Christ’s disciples”] and children of God, because they ought thus to be called [Basel omits *sic*, “thus”; Argenteus, Nuremberg, Venice I–II, and Paris: *et*, “and”]. But they are truly what they are called only if they remain in that on account of which they are so called. If, however [Basel: *sed quum*, “but when”], they do not possess perseverance—that is, do not remain in what they began to be—they are not truly called what they are called [the collected editions except Lyon I: *propter quod*, “on account of which”], and are not such. For before him [the same editions and the earlier Basel: *Deum*, “God”] who knows what they will become—that is, evil out of good—they are not such.

[Col. 1622D] **Part IV. Gratian.** The conclusion of this authority agrees with the opinion of those who say that sins are forgiven according to justice and not according to foreknowledge. Others, however, although they admit that sins return, nevertheless maintain that sins are completely forgiven, whether through baptism or through penance; and that one who approaches the laver with full faith is reborn not by water only but also by the Holy Spirit. If he is afterwards to sin, they affirm that when he finally repents—even if he is someday to fall again—he is so perfectly cleansed at the time of his repentance that, if he died then, he would find eternal salvation. The beginning of the same authority supports their view.

For when it asks why God did not then remove from the dangers of this life those foreknown for death, while they were living faithfully and devoutly, lest wickedness should change their understanding or deceit beguile their souls—whereas Scripture says of the premature death of one predestined [Wisdom 4:11], “He was taken away lest wickedness should change his understanding, or lest deceit beguile his soul”—it plainly shows that these persons were such that, if they had been withdrawn from the dangers of this life by the necessity of death, they would certainly have attained eternal life.

Therefore, in order that the end may agree with the beginning and it may not seem to contradict itself, it must be determined what it means to be written in the book of life and to be erased from it according to justice, and what it means according to foreknowledge. To be written according to foreknowledge is to be preordained to life; and this was done from eternity.

Thus the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter 1 [Ephesians 1:3 ff.]:

### Chapter IX

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and spotless [Col. 1623C] before him in love; who predestined us to the adoption of sons through Jesus Christ *unto himself*.”

**Gratian.** Similarly, to be erased according to foreknowledge is to be foreknown for death rather than life; and this too was done from eternity. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel [John 3:18]: “He who believes in me has eternal life; but he who does not believe has already been judged.”

Hence Augustine also says [Col. 1623D: This statement occurs in Blessed Augustine, *Tractate 12 on John* and *City of God* 20.7; Bede cites it on 2 Timothy 2. The wording is nearly identical in the Ordinary Gloss on the same Pauline passage]:

### Chapter X

“The Lord knows [2 Timothy 2:19; Vulgate: *cognovit*, “has known”] those who are his. None of these is led astray. The judgment has not yet appeared, but it has already been made.”

**Gratian.** Furthermore, to be written according to justice is, with God as author, to perform such deeds as make one worthy of eternal salvation. The Lord set forth this twofold manner of writing in the Gospel, saying to his disciples [John 14:2 ff.]:

“In my Father’s house are many dwelling places; if it were otherwise, I would have told you, because I go to prepare a place for you; and if I go and prepare [Vulgate: *praeparavero*, “shall have prepared”] a place for you, I come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, you also may be.”

In saying, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places; if it were otherwise, I would have told you, because I go to prepare a place for you,” he shows that those to whom he was speaking were written in the book of life by predestination. By adding, “If I go and prepare a place for you,” and so forth, he shows that they still had to be written by their works.

Hence Augustine says in explaining the same passage [Col. 1623D: The sense of this chapter is in *Tractate 68 on John*, but the words themselves are in the Ordinary Gloss on John 14; some have been corrected from that Gloss]:

### Chapter XI

[Col. 1624B] “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” [John 14:2]. The house of God, the temple of God, the kingdom of God, and the kingdom of heaven are righteous persons, among whom are many differences *among themselves*; these are the dwelling places of that house. These have already been prepared in predestination, as the Apostle says [Ephesians 1:4]: “He chose us” [the collected editions: “you”] before the foundation of the world, by predestining; but they are prepared in action [Argenteus and Basel: *parandae*, “to be prepared”].

Hence [Romans 8:30]: “Those whom he predestined, he also called, *and justified, and glorified.*” And in this sense [Basel: *quod*, “which”; the remaining editions: *hoc quod*, “that which”] it is said [cf. Isaiah 43:19]: “God made the things that are to be,” that is, the things which he will make [the collected editions: *erat*, “was going to make”].

And below:

§ 1. “If it were otherwise” [John 14:2] confirms that they exist; for if they did not exist, he would have said: “I will go and prepare,” that is, “I will predestine.” But because they are *already* there, there is no need to prepare anything. Yet because they do not yet [Col. 1624C] exist in action, he adds: “And if I go and prepare” [Vulgate and the collected editions: *praeparavero*; Vulgate and Basel add *vobis*, “for you”]. By going away, but not leaving them [Basel: *delinquens*, “sinning”], he prepares them, because he withdraws himself and remains hidden, so that there may be faith, which is not of a thing seen; and from this comes the merit of faith.

§ 2. The righteous person lives by this, and, while he is a pilgrim, his heart is cleansed through it, and by it he desires what he does not yet possess. *And* this is the preparation of the dwelling place [the collected editions and the earlier Basel add *ejus*, “of it”], for thus he prepares us for himself and himself for us, that he may remain in us and we in him, according as each will share in him more [Basel: *vel plus*, “or more”] or less according to the diversity of merits. And this is the multitude of dwelling places [Col. 1624D: In the collected editions there followed “Likewise,” as if another passage from Augustine or the Gloss were cited. It is absent from most manuscripts; what follows seems to be Gratian’s].

**Gratian.** According to justice, one is erased when, grace having been withdrawn, he is permitted to perform deeds by which he deserves eternal condemnation. Hence the Prophet, speaking in the person of Christ, says [Psalm 68:29]: “Let them be erased from the book of the living.” That is: let grace be withdrawn from them; once it is withdrawn, let them be cast headlong into the abyss of vices and thereafter into eternal condemnation, and let them not be written with the righteous—that is, let grace not be bestowed upon them, through which they may be made worthy of eternal salvation.

Thus sins are forgiven according to foreknowledge when grace is prepared from eternity, by which one who is called may be justified and one who has been justified may finally be glorified eternally. But sins are forgiven according to justice when either baptism is received with full faith or penance is performed with the whole heart; and this remission itself may not improperly be said to occur according to foreknowledge.

§ 1. For, as may be understood from the authority of the Apostle set forth above, there are two preordinations: one by which each person is preordained here to receive righteousness and forgiveness of sins; the other by which someone is predestined [Col. 1625B] to obtain eternal life in the future. Their effects are present justification and future glorification; and all these are suitably distinguished in the authority quoted above.

The first predestination, by which persons are preordained to present righteousness, is indicated when it is said [Ephesians 1:4]: “Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world,” etc.; its effect is then set down below [ibid., verse 6]: “in which he made us gracious in his beloved Son,” etc. The second preordination is shown there [ibid., verse 8]: “who predestined us to the adoption of sons,” etc. Its effect is stated beforehand in the words [ibid., verse 3]: “who has blessed us with every blessing,” etc.

§ 2. These two preordinations and their effects stand in such a relation that the first and its effect precede by nature and follow by the law of consequence. For if someone is preordained to life, it consequently follows that he is predestined to righteousness; and if he obtains eternal life, it follows that he has obtained righteousness. But the converse does not hold. Hence many share in the first preordination and its effect, while the second, or its effect, is shown not to concern them at all.

§ 3. According to this distinction, that statement of John must be understood [1 John 2:19]: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.” “They went out from us,” he says—that is, they withdrew from our fellowship, in which they had shared with us in the first preordination and its effect. “But they were not of us”—that is, they had not entered with us into fellowship in the second preordination and its effect.
