This may be seen from the fact that, if they had been of us—that is, if they had shared with us in that preordination—they would certainly have remained with us; that is, they would not have withdrawn [Col. 1626A] from fellowship in the effect of that preordination which they had contracted with us.

For if both clauses were referred to the second preordination, it would not suitably follow, “They would have remained”; rather, “They would certainly have begun to be with us.” But if both were referred to the first, the proposition, “If they had been of us,” and so forth, would be false. For many become participants in present righteousness and holiness, yet do not persevere therein. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel [Matthew 10:22]: “Not he who has begun, but he who has persevered unto the end, shall be saved.”

### Chapter XII

[Col. 1625D: In ancient codices this chapter is joined to the preceding one. These are Gratian’s words, citing several passages in his customary manner.]

[Note: These are Gratian’s words.]

If anyone says that this fellowship is contracted by the condemned merely in name and profession, and not in the reality of the matter, he is refuted by the testimony of the same authority. For concerning those who share in the first, but not the second, preordination, it says [Basel and Lyon II–III: “Augustine says”; cf. above, chapter 8]: “Nor should it disturb us that God does not give this perseverance to certain of his children. Far be it that it should be so [the collected editions: *sit*, “should be”], if they belonged to *those* predestined [Argenteus and Basel: *praedestinati*, “predestined”],” and the rest contained above in the same authority.

For the sheep of whom the Lord says in the Gospel [John 10:16], “I have other sheep which are not of this fold,” and the children of whom John says [ibid. 11:52], “that he might gather into one the scattered children of God,” were sheep and children by foreknowledge in such a way that, with respect to their present quality—not merely in appearance [Col. 1626D: *specie*, “in appearance”: corrected from a very ancient manuscript. Previously *spe*, “in hope,” was read; that word greatly disturbed the sense]—but even before God’s eyes, they were children of wrath and of eternal perdition.

Hence the Apostle does not say, “We seemed to be,” but: “We too were by nature children of wrath” [Ephesians 2:3]. Nor does he say, “You will be reckoned by human beings,” but [ibid. 5:8]: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord.” Likewise, writing of himself to Timothy, he does not say, “I seemed to be,” but [1 Timothy 1:13]: “I was a persecutor, a blasphemer, and an insolent man; but now I have obtained mercy.”

All [the collected editions and the earlier Basel: “All, whoever are in Christ”] who are reborn in Christ and redeemed from the devil by his blood are first born sinners from Adam and subject to the devil’s bondage. Therefore, just as these, though they are to become children of God, are nevertheless first children of the devil, so those of whom the discussion is concerned, though by falling away from righteousness they will become children of eternal perdition, nevertheless, while they live devoutly and faithfully, are truly children of God, righteous, and worthy of eternal blessedness.

Hence the authority does not say, “while they seemed to live devoutly and faithfully” [after *viverent*, “they lived,” Basel repeats the immediately preceding words, “are truly … worthy”], but “while they lived devoutly and faithfully.” Nor could those who were never truly good be truly changed from good into evil. Likewise, the Lord does not say through Ezekiel [Ezekiel 18:24]: “If the righteous person turns away [Col. 1627A] from the righteousness which he seemed to possess,” but “from his righteousness,” namely, that which he truly possesses [Basel: *habebat*, “possessed”].

§ 1. But what follows in the same authority—“They were not in the number of the children when they were in the profession of children”—must be understood thus: Children of God are called such in two ways [Col. 1627D: The printed editions added: “They are called in one way in the future, in another in the present, which is threefold.” These words are absent from all manuscripts and even from the older editions].

They are called children of God by participation in the eternal inheritance, as John says in the Gospel [John 1:12]: “To as many as believed in him, he gave power to become children of God.” And the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Romans [Romans 8:19, 21, 23]: “The expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the children of God.” And below: “Creation itself shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.” And again: “We ourselves groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption of the children of God.”

Hence Augustine, explaining the same words of the Apostle, says [Col. 1627D: In *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 67, after other matter occur these words: “And creation itself—that is, that which has not yet been called the perfected form of children, but is called merely creation—will be delivered,” etc.; Bede cites them in his commentary on Romans 8. The Gloss there has the same words as Gratian]: “At present creation is only creation” [Basel and Lyon: “creation exists, not yet …”], “since it has not yet attained the perfect form of children.” In this sense, therefore, none are children of God except participants in eternal blessedness.

§ 2. In the present they are also called children in three ways: either by predestination alone, as those of whom John says [John 11:52], “that he might gather into one the children of God who were scattered”; or by predestination and hope of eternal blessedness, as those to whom the Lord says [ibid. 13:33], “Little children, yet a little while I am with you”; or by the merit of faith and present righteousness [the collected editions; Böhm: *praesentis*, “present”], but not by predestination to eternal glory, as those of whom the Lord says [Psalm 88:31]: “If his children forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments,” and so forth.

Those, then, of whom the present discussion is concerned are children by the merit of faith and present righteousness, but are not children of eternal adoption. Therefore, those who confess that forgiven sins return must also confess that sins are forgiven according to justice and not according to foreknowledge. Just as sins are imputed according to justice, not according to foreknowledge, unto eternal condemnation in those who are to be saved, so every individual sin will be brought forward again for punishment against those who fall from good into evil, whereas none will be imputed for eternal punishment against those who persevere in the good unto the end [Argenteus and Nuremberg omit the final clause].

**Part V. Gratian.** Those, however, who say that forgiven sins do not return attempt to confirm their opinion by the authority of Gregory and Prosper.

[Col. 1628A] For Gregory says in the *Morals*, book XV, chapter 22 [Col. 1628D: The very words of this chapter occur in the Ordinary Gloss on Exodus 34, from Gregory at the place indicated; some readings here have been corrected from that Gloss]:

### Chapter XIII

What does this mean which is said [cf. Exodus 10:5; Job 21:19]: “Who repays [Argenteus: *reddit*, “repays”] the iniquity of the *fathers* upon the children and grandchildren”? We draw original sin from our fathers, and unless we are saved through the grace of baptism, we also bear our parents’ guilt, because we are *still* one with them. He repays [the collected editions and the earlier Lyon II–III: *reddet*, “will repay”] the iniquity of the fathers upon the children [Argenteus, Nuremberg, Venice I–II: *in filiis*, “in the children”], when, on account of a parent’s guilt, the offspring’s soul is stained by original sin. Yet again he does not repay [Basel: *reddet*, “will repay”] iniquity upon the children [Argenteus, Nuremberg, Venice I–II: *in filiis*, “in the children”], because when we are freed from original guilt through baptism, we no longer bear our parents’ sins, but those which we ourselves commit.

[Col. 1628B] Likewise, in Prosper’s replies to the second objection of the Gauls:

### Chapter XIV

He who departs from Christ and ends this life estranged from grace—into what does he fall [the collected editions: *vadit*, “goes”] except perdition? Yet he does not relapse into what has been forgiven, nor will he be condemned in original sin. Nevertheless, *because of his latter crimes* [Col. 1628D: These words are added from the original, by which the sense is greatly clarified], he will suffer [the collected editions: *afficitur*, “is afflicted”] the death which was due to him on account of *those sins which* have been forgiven [the original: *remissa*, “forgiven”; the collected editions except the earlier Argenteus add *peccata*, “sins”].

**Gratian.** The conclusion of this authority seems contrary to its beginning. For forgiven sins returning, or being condemned in original sin, is nothing other than suffering, after remission, the punishment due to sin. But the advocates of this opinion resolve the apparently contrary authorities thus: forgiven sins are said to return because whoever, after receiving remission of sins, returns to his vomit will be punished all the more severely in proportion as he has proved ungrateful for the remission received for each sin by abusing God’s kindness.

**Part VI.** § 1. But the other opinion seems more favourable, because it is strengthened by more authorities and confirmed by clearer reasoning. For, as the Lord says through Ezekiel, chapter 18 [Ezekiel 18:24; Peter Lombard, book IV, distinction 15]:

### Chapter XV

“If the righteous person turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity according to all the abominations which the wicked person is accustomed to do, shall he live? None of his acts of righteousness which he had done shall be remembered; in his sin [Col. 1629A] he shall die, and his acts of righteousness which he did shall not be remembered” [Basel omits the final clause; Argenteus: *fecerat*, “had done”; the remaining editions except Basel: *fecerit*, “shall have done”].

### Chapter XVI. Likewise Gregory, explaining the same passage

This must above all be considered: when we commit evils, we recall our former good deeds *to mind* without cause, because in the commission of evils no confidence ought to be placed in past goods.

### Chapter XVII. The same, in Homily IV on Ezekiel, chapter 1

For from a pierced sack what is put in at one place comes out at another [the collected editions and the earlier Lyon II–III: *mittitur*, “is put in”], because undiscerning minds do not consider how the reward acquired from a good work is lost through an evil work [Basel: “how they lose it through an evil work”].

### Chapter XVIII. Likewise Peter, in the Second Epistle, chapter 2

[Col. 1629B] “If, after escaping the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and [the collected editions and the earlier Basel omit *et*, “and”] Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, their latter state has become worse than their former. For it would have been better for them not to know the way of righteousness than, after recognition [the collected editions: *cognitionem*, “knowledge”], to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them” [2 Peter 2:20; Basel omits *in*, “in”].

Likewise Paul, writing to the Hebrews, says in chapter 6 [Hebrews 6:1]:

### Chapter XIX

“Leaving the elementary teaching of Christ, let us be carried on to perfection [Vulgate: *perfectiora*, “more perfect things”; the collected editions add *ejus*, “of it”], not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works.”

**Gratian.** By calling the former good deeds “dead works,” the Apostle signifies that they had become dead through subsequent sin, because by sinning these persons had rendered their earlier good works void. Just as these are rendered void through sin, so through penance they revive; and each of them, including those found mixed with sins, begins to avail toward the merit of eternal blessedness. Hence Augustine: “It is pious to believe,” etc.; and Jerome: “God is not unjust,” etc. [cf. above, Distinction 3, chapters 45–46].

The Apostle also, writing to the Hebrews, after briefly mentioning their faith, love, and good works, shows that after penance they will receive from the Lord the reward for all these things which they had lost through sin. Moreover, he who said through the Prophet [Ezekiel 18:24, 21–22], “If the righteous person turns away from his righteousness,” himself promised through the same Prophet: “If the wicked person repents of all his sins which he has committed, and keeps all my commandments and performs judgment [Col. 1629D] and righteousness, he shall live and not die. I will not remember any of his iniquities which he has committed; in the righteousness which he has performed he shall live.”

Likewise, when the children of Israel were to be carried captive by the Assyrians, the Lord reproaches them through Hosea for the sin of their ancient idolatry, and shows that the sin which had been forgiven their fathers at Moses’ intercession had revived in the children, saying:

### Chapter XX

“Woe to them, for they have departed from me; they shall be laid waste, because they have transgressed against me. And [the collected editions: “Yet I”] I redeemed them, but they have spoken lies against me. They did not cry to me in their heart [Basel: “with their whole heart”], but howled upon their beds; they ruminated over grain and wine, and departed from me. I instructed them and strengthened their arms, but they devised evil against me. They turned back so that they might be without a yoke; they became like a deceitful bow. Their princes shall fall by the sword because of the fury of their tongue” [Hosea 7:13 ff.].

[Col. 1630B] **Part VII. Gratian.** The divine word reproaches the children with the ancient sins of their fathers and therefore predicts that their princes will fall by the sword. But through the same Prophet the Lord shows that he acts otherwise, saying:

### Chapter XXI

“Lest perhaps they say in their hearts, ‘I have remembered all their wickedness’: now their devices have surrounded them; they have been done before my face” [Hosea 7:2].

### C. XXII. Likewise Jerome on Hosea, chapter 7

[Note: [Col. 1629D] The meaning of this chapter is indeed found in Blessed Jerome’s commentary on Hosea 7, but its actual words occur in the interlinear gloss there, [Col. 1630D] on the words: “Lest perhaps they say in their hearts.”]

When they are punished in this way, let them not think that I punish them for the old sins of their fathers; for now, that is, at the present time, they are surrounded by punishment for their own wicked deeds, which I have found. Their evils, as they suppose, [Col. 1630C] cannot be hidden from me; rather, their very devices lie open before my face, which sees all things clearly.

### C. XXIII. The same, in the same place

[Note: [Col. 1630D] This chapter too occurs in the Ordinary Gloss on the same place, drawn from Blessed Jerome.]

Heretics cannot allege old sins against God [Note: [Col. 1629] “the Lord” (*Domino*): Basel edition.], since they add new impiety to their former deeds and are bound by their own sins. When they think [Note: [Col. 1629] “they think” (*putent*): editions compared with the original before Basel.] that they conceal themselves from God, they cannot escape his eyes, because “the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” [Note: [Col. 1629] Psalm 33:17.].

### C. XXIV. Likewise Pope Gelasius

[Note: [Col. 1629] Compare Causa 23, question 4, canon 29.]

Divine clemency does not allow sins which have been forgiven to return thereafter for punishment.

Gratian. But by these authorities we are taught that children cleansed from original sin are not punished because their fathers [Col. 1630D] sinned, but that their fathers’ sins return upon them because they follow their fathers’ guilt. Thus also good deeds which die through sin do not avail for reward merely because [Col. 1631A] they were done, but because they return to life through repentance. Such is also Augustine’s statement in the book on the Psalms [Note: [Col. 1631] Compare above, canon 1.]: “If Judas had retained adoption,” etc. Gregory’s statement in the *Morals* is likewise to be understood in this way [Note: [Col. 1631] Compare there, canon 13.]: “What is meant by the saying, ‘You repay the iniquity of the fathers upon the children,’ etc.?” For the iniquity of parents is repaid to those who are punished because they drew the bitterness of sin from the root. But it is not repaid to those in whom the parents’ sins do not revive through the merit of their own iniquity.

Therefore, just as good deeds which die through sin return to life for reward through repentance, so evils which are erased through repentance return to life for punishment. Hence the Prophet laments in the person of one repenting, saying [Note: [Col. 1631] Psalm 37:6.]: “My scars have become putrid and corrupt because of my foolishness”—that is, wounds healed through baptism. [Col. 1631B] Thus the same Prophet, although he knew that he had been cleansed from original sin through faith and the sacrament of circumcision, nevertheless understood that it had revived through the adultery and homicide which he committed; and so, not without reason, among other things he confesses that very sin and says [Note: [Col. 1631] Psalm 51:7.]: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities,” etc.

## DISTINCTION V

### GRATIAN

#### Part I

What a sinner ought to consider in repentance is taught by Augustine in the book *On Repentance*, where he says [Note: [Col. 1631] Falsely attributed to Augustine.—Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 16.]:

### C. I

[Col. 1631C]

Let him consider [Note: [Col. 1631] “He considers” (*considerat*): first and second Venetian editions.] the character of the crime: its place, time, persistence, the variety of persons, the temptation under which he committed it, and the repeated execution of the vice itself in many ways. For one who has committed fornication must repent according to the eminence of his rank or office, and [Note: [Col. 1631] “or” (*aut*): editions compared with the original.] according to the status of the prostitute, and according to the manner [Note: [Col. 1631] “according to the manner” (*secundum modum*): original.] of his act, and according to how he carried out his shamefulness [Note: [Col. 1631] “he performed” (*egerit*): Basel edition; “he has carried out” (*peregerit*): the remaining editions.]: whether in a sacred place [Note: [Col. 1631] “consecrated” (*sacrato*): editions compared with the original before Basel.], or in a place toward which he owed the special regard due to faith [Note: [Col. 1631] “he will have owed” (*debuerit*): Basel edition.], such as the homes of lords and many others; or at a time appointed for prayer, or [Note: [Col. 1631] Added: “such as feasts of saints” (absent from the Argentinensis edition) “and times of fasting”: editions compared with the original.] on a feast of saints and during a fast.

Let him consider how long he persisted, and mourn that he sinned persistently [Col. 1632A] [Note: [Col. 1631] “he sinned” (*peccavit*): the same editions.], and how great his strength was in the struggle. [Note: [Col. 1631C] The words “and how great his strength was” (*et quanta virtus*) occur in the original as: “and by how great an assault he was overcome” (*et quanta victus fuerit impugnatione*) [Col. 1631D] [Note: [Col. 1631] Thus the Argentinensis and Basel editions.]. The text was not altered because of the gloss. Many other corrections of great importance were made, wherever possible, both from the original itself and from ancient Gratian manuscripts.]

For there are some who are not merely not overcome, but voluntarily offer themselves to sin. They do not await temptation, but anticipate pleasure, and deliberate with themselves in how many kinds of vicious action they may delightfully sin [Note: [Col. 1631] “he deliberates” (*pertractat*): Argentinensis edition; “he sinned” (*peccavit*): the same edition; “they sinned” (*peccaverunt*): Basel edition; “they may sin” (*peccaverint*): the remaining editions.]. All this variety must be confessed and bewailed [Note: [Col. 1631] Added: “must be disclosed and” (*ostendenda et*): Basel edition.], so that, when he has recognized [Note: [Col. 1631] “has acknowledged” (*agnovit*): editions compared with the original before Basel.] that the sin is great, he may quickly find God merciful [Note: [Col. 1631] “will find” (*inveniet*): Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, and first and second Venetian editions.].

§ 1. In recognizing the increase of sin, let him consider what age he was, what wisdom and rank he possessed, and every condition of another who did not sin. Let him dwell upon each of these points and perceive the measure of the crime, cleansing every feature of the vice with tears.

§ 2. Let him mourn the virtue of which he was meanwhile deprived. For one must grieve, and be cleansed by grief, not only because one sinned, but also because one deprived oneself of virtue. [Col. 1632B] For although one hopes to obtain pardon, one can nevertheless grieve because one did not merit that from which one confidently hopes for reward.

§ 3. Let him be distressed and grieve that, while escaping punishment for past acts, he, wretched man [Note: [Col. 1631] Added: “nevertheless” (*tamen*): editions compared with the original.], should not thereby expect glory [Note: [Col. 1631] “grace” (*gratiam*): original.], for the attainment of which he ought to have striven throughout all his time [Note: [Col. 1631] “his work and time” (*opus et tempus*): Argentinensis and Basel editions.], since it is very short.

§ 4. Let him also mourn because, by offending in one matter, he has become guilty of all through ingratitude. For he was ungrateful who, though full of virtues, did not fear God at all. In this respect each sinner becomes more culpable insofar as he is more acceptable to God. Adam therefore sinned more because he abounded in every good.

In another way too, one who offends in one matter is guilty of all, because every virtue suffers injury [Note: [Col. 1631] “all virtues suffer” (*omnes virtutes patiuntur*): editions compared with the original before Basel.] from one vice [Col. 1632C] [Note: [Col. 1631] “from a single vice” (*unico vitio*): Basel edition.]. For if someone falls into avarice, he destroys generosity and also diminishes chastity. Love of money would either violate chastity or at least love it less. For if he still has such chastity for God’s sake that he does not wish to lose it [Note: [Col. 1631] “lose it at last” (*eam tandem*): Argentinensis edition; “lose the same” (*eandem*): the remaining editions.], he nevertheless guards it with less joy and less affection [Note: [Col. 1631] “affection” (*affectione*): editions compared with the original.] where he sees financial loss arising from it [Note: [Col. 1631] “where he would see loss arising” (*ubi videret ... procedere*): Basel edition, with the continuation marked for deletion.]. So also in other virtues: even if they are not expelled, they are nevertheless diminished greatly or slightly through the conception of one vice [Note: [Col. 1631] “perception” (*perceptione*): editions compared with the original.], or made worse in intention [Note: [Col. 1631] The original reads “in intensity” (*intensione*).]. Therefore every virtue must be mourned in connection with any sin [Note: [Col. 1631] Added: “omitted” (*omissa*): editions compared with the original, Argentinensis, Basel, and Norimbergensis.; “through a crime of whatever kind” (*cujuscunque criminis*): Basel edition.], and pardon sought for all things.

§ 5. One must also notice, and in noticing mourn, the soul of one’s neighbour, which the fornicator has snatched from God, or, having snatched it away, confirmed in evil. He must also mourn that he has been an example of evil in performing his crime, though it would have profited him more to have been a cause of conversion for others. Let him therefore groan over another’s life corrupted in himself, or not preserved uncorrupted, and over the benefit to his neighbour which he would have bestowed by an example of good. Let him grieve over the sadness which he inflicted on the good by sinning, and over the joy which he did not give them. Let him consider not only what and how he has done [Note: [Col. 1633] “did” (*fecit*): Argentinensis edition.], but how unjustly, as we have said, he offended God by sinning.

Let him fear that saying of Truth [Note: [Col. 1633] Matthew 6:24.]: “You cannot serve two masters.” Let him therefore fear lest, while persisting in one sin, he has lost through the contamination of evil [Note: [Col. 1633] “through evil excommunication” (*excommunicatione mala*): editions compared with the original.] every good thing which he did, so that he who served the devil through crime has lost the service of God which he offered [Col. 1633B] [Note: [Col. 1633] The editions read: “has lost the virtues which he offered to God” (*Deo quas obtulerit amiserit virtutes*); “he offered” (*obtulit*): Basel edition.].

Yet it is devout to believe that, when God’s grace has been received—which destroys the former evils in him [Note: [Col. 1633] “destroyed” (*destruxit*): Basel edition; “all former evils” (*omnia mala priora*): editions compared with the original, Argentinensis, and Basel.]—it also [Note: [Col. 1633] Omitted in the Argentinensis and Norimbergensis editions and in the first and second Venetian editions.] rewards good deeds, so that, after it has destroyed what it did not find to be its own [Note: [Col. 1633] “found” (*invenerit*): editions compared with the original before Basel.], it may love and cherish the good which it planted even [Note: [Col. 1633] Omitted in Basel.] in the sinner.

§ 6. In all these matters, grieving, let him either leave the world [Note: [Col. 1633] “let him leave” (*relinquat*): editions compared with the original.] or at least those occupations which are not administered without an admixture of evil: trade, military service, and other things harmful to those who practise them, such as offices administering secular powers, unless he uses them by permission of obedience. Let him put himself wholly under the power of the judge and the judgment of the priest, reserving nothing of himself, so that at the priest’s command he is ready to do, for the restoration [Note: [Col. 1633] “recovery” (*recuperanda*): Basel edition; “receiving” (*recipienda*): the remaining editions.] of the soul’s life, whatever he would do to avoid bodily [Col. 1633C] death; and let him do this with desire, since he recovers endless life, like God. For one who will become immortal ought joyfully to do what, while mortal, he would do to postpone death.

Let him always pray to God, being certain of pardon, who would plead with earthly power in every way and without any weariness [Note: [Col. 1633] Added: “all” (*omni*): editions compared with the original before Basel.], though uncertain. Let one who has committed unlawful acts through freedom of choice abstain from many lawful things [Note: [Col. 1633] “in liberty” (*in libertate*): editions compared with the original.]. Let him always offer God his mind and contrition of heart, and then what he can from his possessions; then let him securely offer what he offers [Note: [Col. 1633] “let him offer to God” (*offerat Deo*): the same editions before Basel.]. For “the Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts” [Note: [Col. 1633] Genesis 4:4.]. But he first looked upon Abel before his gifts [Note: [Col. 1633] “said” (*dixit*): Basel edition; “says” (*dicit*): the remaining editions and the original.]. Receiving the mind which he knew to be humble and pure, [Col. 1634A] he rewarded the gifts of his generosity. But he did not look upon Cain or his gifts. Since he did not recognize his mind, he did not receive his gifts [Note: [Col. 1633] The original adds “humble” (*humilem*).].

For in judging the heart, one must consider the almsgiving of the giver; one must no longer ask how much he gives, but with what mind and affection he gives what he can. The widow, generous with the two small coins which she had [Note: [Col. 1633] Compare Matthew 12; “having bestowed” (*largita*): Basel edition.], gave more than all. Whoever therefore wishes to redeem his sins by a temporal offering must take care first to offer his mind [Note: [Col. 1633] “must lack” (*careat*): Basel edition.].

§ 7. Let the penitent be cautious [Note: [Col. 1633] Added: “penitent” (*poenitens*): editions compared with the original.] lest, led by shame, he divide confession within himself and wish to disclose different matters to different priests. Some conceal from one what they reserve to disclose to another [Note: [Col. 1633] “preserve” (*conservant*): original and Basel edition.]. This is to praise oneself, tend toward hypocrisy, and always lack the pardon which one thinks to attain whole by fragments.

§ 8. Let one whom true repentance delights beware of past sins [Note: [Col. 1633] “besides” (*praeterea*): editions compared with the original.]; let him not approach the Lord’s body until a good conscience strengthens him [Note: [Col. 1633] “strengthens him” (*confortet illum*): editions compared with the original.]. But in this separation let him consider God’s dreadful judgment, where a greater [Note: [Col. 1633] Omitted in the Argentinensis, Basel, and Norimbergensis editions.] and more terrible sentence will separate the unrepentant into fire [Note: [Col. 1633] The original reads: “where a more terrible sentence will separate sinners into fire.”]. Let him groan that he does not yet dare [Note: [Col. 1633] “may dare” (*audeat*): the same editions before Basel.] to receive the saving food [Note: [Col. 1633] “the Saviour” (*salvatorem*): Basel edition.] which he greatly desires. These are the worthy fruits of repentance, freeing the captive soul from snares and preserving it in liberty.

§ 9. Moreover, one who wishes to attain the perfect grace of remission must restrain himself from games and worldly spectacles. For Dinah [Note: [Col. 1633] Added: “daughter of Jacob”: editions compared with the original before Argentinensis and Norimbergensis; compare Genesis 34.], if she had restrained herself and remained among her own [Note: [Col. 1633] “and even if” (*et si*): Norimbergensis and first and second Venetian editions.], would not have been corrupted by a foreign ravisher [Note: [Col. 1633] “would not be” (*esset*): editions compared with the original.]. Therefore the soul which has often, or even once, been corrupted and ravished should all the more guard and restrain itself. Taught now by experience, let it fear what the virgin did not know [Note: [Col. 1633] “did not know” (*ignoraverit*): Argentinensis, Norimbergensis, and first Venetian editions.]; let it choose whom to imitate, and not follow one whom its own mind condemns. For one judges oneself who does not remove from oneself a person lacking the fruits of repentance.

Let him praise and love those whom he knows to bear worthy fruit [Note: [Col. 1633] “what” (*quod*): Basel edition.]; let him seek worthy fruits, even if they are not fruits worthy of repentance. For there are worthy fruits, the fruits of virtues, which do not suffice for penitents. Repentance demands weightier fruits, so that the Church may thus be appeased [Note: [Col. 1633] “may be made pleasing” (*placetur*): the same edition.], and, appeased [Note: [Col. 1633] “made pleasing” (*placata*): the same edition; “sins” (*peccata*): second and third Lyon editions.] by grief and groans, may obtain pardon for the dead [Note: [Col. 1633] “life” (*vitam*): original and editions compared with the original.].

[Col. 1635A]

### C. II. Penitents should renounce the profits of trade

Likewise Pope Leo, Letter 90, alternatively 92, to Bishop Rusticus, chapter 9.

[Note: [Col. 1635] Letter 167 in Ballerini’s edition, written in A.D. 458 or 459.—Regino, book 1, chapter 313; Burchard, book 2, chapter 128, book 19, chapter 95; Anselm, book 11, chapter 139; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 6, chapter 202, part 13, chapter 25, part 15, chapter 107; *Polycarpus*, book 4, title 31.]

#### Part II

The character of gain either excuses [Note: [Col. 1635C] “Excuses” (*excusat*): thus the original, *Polycarpus*, Ivo, Burchard, and Anselm; Gratian’s manuscripts read “accuses” (*accusat*).] or condemns the trader, because gain may be honourable or shameful. Nevertheless, it is more beneficial for a penitent even to suffer losses than to be bound [Note: [Col. 1635] “to be bound” (*adstringi*): the same editions; Regino, book 2, and Ivo, part 6.] by the dangers of trade, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene between buyer and seller.

### C. III. After repentance it is not lawful to return to secular military service

The same, in the same place, chapter 10.

[Note: [Col. 1635] Regino, book 2, chapter 314; Burchard, book 19, chapter 66; Anselm, book 11, chapter 147; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, chapter 80.]

It is altogether contrary [Note: [Col. 1635] Added: “indeed” (*vero*): editions compared with the original before Basel.] to ecclesiastical rules to return to secular military service after undertaking repentance, since the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1635] 2 Timothy 2:4.]: “No one serving as a soldier for God [Col. 1635B] entangles himself in secular affairs.” Therefore one who wishes to entangle himself in worldly military service [Note: [Col. 1635] “worldly military service” (*militia mundana*): Hispanic Collection; Ballerini.] is not free from the snares of the devil [Note: [Col. 1635] “to be entangled” (*implicari*): Hispanic Collection.].

### C. IV. Those returning to secular military service after repentance shall do penance for ten years

Likewise from the Council of Nicaea, chapter 11.

[Note: [Col. 1635C] This chapter is the latter portion of chapter 11 in the ancient—that is, Hispanic—translation. That translation was omitted in the latest Cologne edition of the councils in four volumes, and four translations were put in its place; from these, passages which are sometimes obscure and mutilated here can easily be corrected. For the sense of the canon, see what Zonaras and Balsamon adduce in its exposition; Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 10, chapter 6; and the Cardinal of Warmia, *Against Brenz*, book 3. [Col. 1636C] It concerns those soldiers whom the impious Licinius forbade to retain the military belt if they wished to keep faith pledged to Christ. They preferred to lay it aside rather than break faith; yet later, conquered by earthly desire, they tried to recover it, thereby showing that they were falling away from the faith. [Col. 1636D] In the Code of Canons the heading of this chapter is: “Concerning those who renounced and again returned to the world.”]

[Note: [Col. 1635] Held in A.D. 325.—Anselm, book 11, chapter 148, from Dionysius.]

But if any, called by God’s [Note: [Col. 1635] “faith’s” (*fidei*): Hispanic Collection.] grace, first showed their faith by laying aside the military belt, but afterwards [Note: [Col. 1635] “after this” (*post hoc*): Basel edition.] returned to their own vomit, so as both to give money and seek again to return to military service, they shall be among the penitents for ten years after the first three years during which they were among the hearers. Above all, however, let their disposition and the fruits of repentance be observed [Col. 1635C] [Note: [Col. 1635] “let it be observed, or let it chiefly be considered”: Basel edition.].

For whoever, with all fear, persevering tears, and good works, demonstrates his conversion [Note: [Col. 1635] “conduct” (*conversationem*): Hispanic Collection and editions compared with the original.] not by words alone but in deed and truth, may, once he has completed even the period prescribed for them and has begun to share in the prayers, receive from the bishop a more merciful consideration. But those who regard their fall indifferently [Note: [Col. 1635] “indifferent” (*indifferentem*): Basel edition.] and suppose it enough that they have entered within [Note: [Col. 1635] Omitted in the Hispanic Collection.] the Church [Col. 1636A] [Note: [Col. 1635] “their own” (*suum*): Hispanic Collection.] shall in every case complete the prescribed periods.

### C. V. Those returning to secular pursuits after repentance shall be suspended from communion

Likewise from the First Council of Orléans, chapter 13.

[Note: [Col. 1635] Held in A.D. 511.]

Concerning those who, having undertaken repentance, forget the religious character of their profession and relapse into secular affairs, it has been decided that they be suspended from communion and separated from the meals [Note: [Col. 1635] “meal” (*convivio*): Hispanic Collection.] of all Catholics. If, after the prohibition, anyone presumes to eat with them [Note: [Col. 1635] “with him, whoever” (*eo quisquis*): the same collection.], he too shall be deprived of communion.

### C. VI. What false repentance is

Likewise Gregory VII, in the Roman Synod held in 1078, chapter 6.

[Note: [Col. 1635] Held in A.D. 1078.—*Polycarpus*, book 6, title 20; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 16.]

#### Part III

We call false those repentances which are not imposed according to the authority of the holy Fathers in proportion to the character of the crimes [Col. 1636B] [Note: [Col. 1635] “of the crime” (*criminis*): Basel edition.]. Therefore any soldier, or [Note: [Col. 1635] “and” (*et*): editions compared with the original before Basel.] trader, or person devoted to an office which cannot be exercised without sin, if entangled in serious faults comes [Note: [Col. 1635] “came” (*venit*): Basel edition.] to repentance; or anyone who unjustly retains another’s goods; or anyone who harbours hatred in his heart [Note: [Col. 1635] “has harboured” (*egerit*): Norimbergensis and first and second Venetian editions.]—must recognize that he cannot perform true repentance through which he may attain eternal life, unless he abandons his occupation [Note: [Col. 1635] “leaves” (*relinquat*): editions compared with the original.], forsakes his office, dismisses hatred from his heart, restores the goods [Note: [Col. 1635] Added: “indeed” (*quidem*): the same editions.] which he has unjustly taken, lays down arms [Note: [Col. 1636D] The entire clause concerning arms occurs in the original and in *Polycarpus* before the words “unless he abandons his occupation”; the order was not restored because of the gloss.], and bears them no longer except upon the advice of religious bishops for the defence of justice.

Yet [Note: [Col. 1635] “Nor” (*nec*): Basel edition.] let him not despair. Meanwhile we urge him to do whatever good [Note: [Col. 1635] Added: “he does or” (*fecerit vel*): the same edition.] he can do, so that almighty God may enlighten his heart [Col. 1636C] toward repentance.

### C. VII. After conversion it is not lawful to return to an occupation which cannot be conducted without sin

Likewise Gregory, Homily 24 on the Gospels.

[Note: [Col. 1635] Anselm, book 11, chapter 140.]

It was not blameworthy, after conversion, to resume an occupation which before conversion existed without sin. And below: There are many occupations which can scarcely, or not at all, be carried on without sins [Col. 1637A]. The mind must therefore not return after conversion to things which entail sin.

### C. VIII. On the same matter

Likewise Pope Innocent II, at the Roman Council, chapter 22.

[Note: [Col. 1637] Second Lateran Council, held in A.D. 1139.—Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 15.]

#### Part IV

We admonish our brother bishops and priests not to permit the souls of laypeople to be deceived by false repentances and dragged to hell. Repentance is clearly false when, though many sins are neglected, repentance is performed for one alone; or when it is performed for one in such a way that one does not depart from another. Hence it is written [Note: [Col. 1637] James 2:10.]: “Whoever keeps the whole law, but offends [Note: [Col. 1637] “will offend” (*offendet*): Argentinensis and Norimbergensis editions; “offends” (*offendit*): first and second Venetian, first Lyon, and Paris editions; “and offends” (*et offendat*): Basel edition.] in one point, becomes guilty of all”—that is, with respect to eternal life. For just as if he were entangled in all sins, so too, if only one remains, he will not enter the gate of eternal life.

Repentance also becomes false [Note: [Col. 1637] Added: “indeed” (*enim*): editions compared with the original before Basel.; “is” (*est*), rather than “becomes” (*fit*): editions compared with the original.] when the penitent does not withdraw from an official, courtly, or commercial occupation [Note: [Col. 1637] “or a courtly occupation” (*vel curiali negotio*): the same editions before Basel.] which can in no way be conducted without sin [Note: [Col. 1637] “without sins—at all” (*peccatis ... nullatenus*): editions compared with the original.]; or when hatred is harboured in the heart [Note: [Col. 1637] “has harboured” (*gesserit*): editions compared with the original.]; or when one does not make satisfaction to anyone offended [Note: [Col. 1637] “has made satisfaction” (*satisfecerit*): Basel edition; “should make satisfaction” (*satisfaciat*): the remaining editions.]; or when the offended person does not forgive the offender; or when someone bears arms against justice [Note: [Col. 1637] “an instrument” (*instrumentum*): Basel edition; “carries” (*ferat*): editions compared with the original before Basel.].

## DISTINCTION VI

### GRATIAN

#### Part I

To whom confession ought to be made, and what sort of person he ought to be who judges the crimes of others, is taught in the same book *On Repentance*, chapter 10 [Note: [Col. 1637] Falsely attributed to Augustine.—Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 17.—Compare above, Distinction 1, canon 88.], where it says:

### C. I

[Col. 1637C]

Whoever wishes to confess his sins [Note: [Col. 1637] Added: “his own” (*sua*): editions compared with the original.] in order to find grace [Note: [Col. 1637] “repentance” (*poenitentiam*): Argentinensis edition.] should seek a priest who knows how to bind and loose, lest, when he has been negligent concerning himself, he be neglected by the one who mercifully warns and petitions him, and both fall into the pit which the fool refused to avoid.

So great is the power of confession that, if a priest is lacking, one should confess to one’s neighbour. For it often happens that a penitent cannot confess [Note: [Col. 1637] “be ashamed” (*verecundari*): editions compared with the original.] before a priest, because neither place nor time is afforded to one who desires it; and if the person to whom he confesses has no power to loose, he nevertheless becomes worthy of pardon through his desire for a priest when he confesses the shamefulness [Col. 1638A] of his crime to a companion. For the lepers were cleansed while they went [Note: [Col. 1637] “were going, showing themselves” (*ibant ostendentes se*): the same editions; compare Luke 17.] to show their faces to the priests, before they reached them. It is thus clear that God [Note: [Col. 1637] “the Lord” (*Dominum*): Basel edition.] looks upon the heart when necessity prevents one from reaching priests [Note: [Col. 1637] “prevents them” (*prohibentur*): editions compared with the original.].

Indeed, they often seek priests while healthy [Note: [Col. 1637] “but healthy and cheerful, while” (*sed sani et laeti, dum*): the same editions.] and cheerful; but, while seeking, before they reach them [Note: [Col. 1637] “them” (*eos*): omitted in editions compared with the original before Basel and in the second and third Lyon editions.], they die. But God’s mercy is everywhere, and he knows how to spare them too [Note: [Col. 1637] The printed *et justis* appears to require *et istis*, “these persons.”], though not as quickly as if they were loosed by a priest. Whoever therefore confesses at all [Note: [Col. 1637] “confesses, let him confess altogether” (*confitetur, omnino confiteatur*): editions compared with the original.] should confess to the best priest he can find [Note: [Col. 1637] “and if to a priest” (*et si sacerdoti*): first and second Venetian editions and Paris edition; “and to a priest” (*et sacerdoti*): the remaining editions.], and if the sin is secret, it is enough to report it to the priest’s knowledge [Note: [Col. 1637] “to confess by mouth” (*ore confiteri*): Argentinensis edition.], so that the offering of the gift may be acceptable.

And below, chapter 12:

§ 1. Let the penitent labour to be in the Church and tend toward the unity of the Church. Unless the unity of the Church comes to help, unless it supplies by its operation [Col. 1638B] [Note: [Col. 1637] “assistance” (*opitulatio*): original.] what the sinner lacks, the soul of the dead man will not be snatched from the enemy’s hands. For it must be believed—and the piety of faith demands that it be believed—that all the alms of the whole Church, its prayers, works [Note: [Col. 1637] “activity” (*operatio*): Basel and second and third Lyon editions.] of justice, and acts of mercy assist one who recognizes his death toward his conversion. Therefore no one can repent worthily unless the unity of the Church sustains him; and therefore he should not seek priests separated from the unity of the Church by any fault.

For Judas, repenting [Note: [Col. 1637] “who repented” (*qui poenitens*): editions compared with the original.], went to the Pharisees and left the Apostles. He found no help, but [Note: [Col. 1637] “except” (*nisi*): the same editions.] an increase of despair. For they said [Note: [Col. 1637] Matthew 27:4.]: “What is that to us? See to it yourself. If you sinned, let it concern you; we do not help you; we do not charitably take up your sins, nor promise to bear them with you; nor do we teach you how [Col. 1638C] to lay down the burden [Note: [Col. 1637] “us” (*nos*): second and third Lyon editions.]. For what have we to do with mercy, when we do not follow works of justice?”

He ought to have gone to the brethren, to those who had prayed for Peter’s fever-stricken mother-in-law [Note: [Col. 1637] Luke 4.], who had offered mercy to the importunate Canaanite woman [Note: [Col. 1637] Matthew 15.]. He ought to have sought Peter shedding tears for himself; he ought not to have fled Mary and Martha, who had obtained life for Lazarus [Note: [Col. 1637] John 11.], nor the weeping crowd which had restored an only son to the widow [Note: [Col. 1637] Luke 7.]. He went to those who were divided, and, divided, he perished.

And below, chapter 20:

§ 2. The priest, therefore, to whom every sinner is presented [Note: [Col. 1637] “is brought forward” (*profertur*): original.], before whom every infirmity is set, must not be liable to judgment in any of those matters in which he is ready to judge another [Note: [Col. 1637] “to be judged” (*dijudicandus*): Basel edition.]. For one who judges another while he himself is liable to judgment condemns himself. Let him therefore know himself and purge in himself what he sees others lay before him.

Let him beware [Col. 1639A] that he has cast away [Note: [Col. 1639] “has thrown out” (*projecerit*): Basel edition; “let him throw out” (*projiciat*): the remaining editions.] from himself whatever [Note: [Col. 1639] “that which” (*quod*): Böhm.] he finds harmful in another. Let him heed the saying [Note: [Col. 1639] John 8:7.]: “Let him who is without sin [Note: [Col. 1639] Added: “among you” (*vestrum*): Vulgate, Basel, and Lyon editions.] be first to cast a stone at her” [Note: [Col. 1639] “that woman” (*illam*): Vulgate and editions compared with the original.]. He freed the sinful woman because there was no one who could justly cast a stone. How could one stone her when he knew himself to deserve stoning? No one was without sin; by this it is understood that all were guilty of grave sin [Note: [Col. 1639] “of grave sin” (*crimine*): omitted in editions compared with the original before the second and third Lyon editions.]. For venial offences [Note: [Col. 1639] Added: “all” (*omnia*): Basel edition; “sins” (*peccata*): second and third Lyon editions.] were always remitted through ceremonies. Whatever sin, therefore, was in them was a grave sin.

In this respect priests who do not first build themselves up are worse than those who watched the Lord with snares. The crime of priests who do not first judge themselves and then bind others is therefore most manifest [Note: [Col. 1639] “most powerful” (*potentissimum*): Basel and second and third Lyon editions.] and beyond measure detestable. For they ought to fear in themselves the crime which they feared in others [Col. 1639B] and considered detestable [Note: [Col. 1639] Added: “which they guarded against and” (*caverunt et*): second and third Lyon editions; “judged” (*judicaverunt*): the remaining editions; “considered” (*censuerunt*): Basel and second and third Lyon editions.]. Those men [Note: [Col. 1639] “These who” (*hi, qui*): editions compared with the original before the second and third Lyon editions.] were indeed so blind that they hoped to ensnare highest Wisdom by their snares. What was evident to them, what each then avoided, let the priest avoid; in this error [Note: [Col. 1639] Omitted in Basel.] he would be worse than those Jews [Note: [Col. 1639] “was” (*exstitit*): editions compared with the original before Basel and the second and third Lyon editions.].

§ 3. Let the spiritual judge beware that, just as he has not committed the crime of wickedness, so he does not lack the gift of knowledge [Note: [Col. 1639] “and” (*et*): Basel edition; omitted in the remaining editions before the second and third Lyon editions.]. For he must know how to discern whatever he has to judge. Judicial power requires that he distinguish what he must judge. Let him therefore be a diligent inquirer and subtle investigator, questioning the sinner wisely and, as it were, shrewdly about what he perhaps does not know [Note: [Col. 1639] “may not know” (*ignoret*): Argentinensis and Basel editions.] or wishes to conceal from shame.

Once the crime is known, he should not hesitate to investigate its variations, its place and time, and the other things stated above in setting forth [Col. 1639C] their qualities [Note: [Col. 1639] “which are to be set forth concerning their character” (*exponenda ... qualitate*): editions compared with the original.]. Having learned these, let him be kindly disposed, ready to impose a burden and carry it with him. Let him have sweetness in affection, compassion for another’s crime, and discernment amid its varieties. Let him help the confessor by praying, giving alms [Note: [Col. 1639] “doing” (*faciendo*): Argentinensis and Basel editions; omitted in the remaining editions.], and doing other good works [Note: [Col. 1639] “good works” (*bona opera*): Basel and second and third Lyon editions.] for him. Let him always help by mitigating, consoling, promising hope, and, when necessary, rebuking.

Let him teach by speaking [Note: [Col. 1639] “Let him teach” (*doceat*): the correct reading; the printed text has “Let him grieve” (*doleat*).], instruct by acting, and share the labour if he wishes to share the joy. Let him teach perseverance, and beware lest he fall and justly lose judicial authority. Although [Note: [Col. 1639] “Even if” (*etsi*): Basel edition; “and if he truly repents, or if” (*et si vere poenitet, vel si*): the remaining editions before the second and third Lyon editions.] repentance can obtain grace for him, it does not immediately restore [Note: [Col. 1639] “restore” (*restituat*): Basel edition.] him to his former authority. Although Peter was restored after his fall, and the authority of rank was often restored to fallen priests, it is nevertheless not necessary that this be granted to all as if by authority [Col. 1639D] [Col. 1640A] [Note: [Col. 1639] “by this authority” (*ex hac auctoritate*): Basel edition.].

There is also authority which permits and, as it were, commands; another which by no means permits but forbids. These do not conflict with Scripture, but agree if place, time, and the manner of repentance bring reconciliation. For since so many fall that they defend their former rank by authority and make for themselves, as it were, a licence [Note: [Col. 1639] “use” (*usum*): editions compared with the original.] for sinning, this hope must be cut off. But if there is a situation in which these conditions do not occur, those who sin may be restored. Therefore a just and discerning bishop is not compelled always to depose his priests, nor immediately to restore them, unless this has been decreed by the Roman Pontiff.

#### Part II

Gratian. Let the priest beware lest he reveal penitents’ sins to others. If he does so, he shall be deposed.

[Col. 1640B]

Hence Gregory [Note: [Col. 1639] The chapter is of uncertain origin.—*Polycarpus*, book 6, title 20; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 2.]:

### C. II. A priest who presumes to publish a penitent’s sins shall be deposed

Above all, a priest must beware lest he recount to anyone the sins of those who confess their sins [Note: [Col. 1639] Added: “their own” (*sua*): editions compared with the original; added: “that he has confessed them” (*quod ea confessus est*): the same editions.] to him—not to relatives [Note: [Col. 1639] Added: “not to friends”: Basel and second and third Lyon editions.], not to strangers, nor, God forbid, for the sake of any scandal. For if he does this, he shall be deposed and shall proceed in disgrace as a pilgrim for all the days of his life.

III. Gratian’s Part. But the statement that a penitent should choose a priest who knows how to bind and loose appears contrary to what is found in the canons: namely, that no one should presume to judge another’s parishioner. Yet it is one thing to despise one’s own priest out of favour or hatred, which the sacred canons forbid; it is another to avoid a blind man, which everyone is here warned by this authority to do, lest, if a blind man offers guidance to a blind man, both fall into the pit. [Col. 1640C]

Therefore Pope Urban II. [Note: [Col. 1639] cf. C. 9, question 2, chapter 2.]

C. III. Let no priest receive for penance a person entrusted to another priest, except because of that priest’s ignorance.

It has been decided that henceforth no priest may receive for penance any person entrusted to another priest without the consent of the one to whom he had previously entrusted himself, except because of the ignorance of the one to whom the penitent first confessed. But whoever attempts to act contrary to these enactments shall be liable to forfeiture of his rank.

## DISTINCTION VII

### GRATIAN

I. Part. The time for penance extends to the very last article of life. [Col. 1640D]

[Col. 1641A] Therefore Pope Leo, Letter 90, or 92, to Rusticus, chapter 5. [Note: cf. C. 32, question 2, chapter 11.]

C. I. On the same subject.

No one is to be despaired of while he remains in this body, because what is deferred through the lack of confidence belonging to age is sometimes accomplished through maturer judgment.

II. Gratian’s Part. Although Augustine writes concerning those who defer penance, in Book 50 of the *Homilies*, Homily 41: [Note: These and the following two chapters are taken from Homily 41 of Blessed Augustine; but this first one appears in a different order and with many words altered. Thus Burchard and Ivo cite not Augustine but “sayings of Augustine.” Therefore nothing has been changed; it is altogether preferable to read the homily itself. In the *Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum*, vol. 7, the same material is attributed to Blessed Caesarius, bishop of Arles.] [Note: It does not appear to be Augustine’s. — Burchard, book 18, chapter 12; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 15, chapter 22; Polycarp, book 8, title 1; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 2.]

C. II.

If anyone, placed in the final necessity of his illness, wishes to receive penance, receives it, and is immediately reconciled [Note: “will be reconciled”: the collected editions, except the first Lyons editions II and III], he departs from here. I confess to you: we do not deny him what he asks; but neither do we presume that he will depart well from here [Note: “departs”: editions of Basel and Lyons II–III]. If he departs safely from here, I do not know. We can give penance, but we cannot give assurance. Do I say, “He will be condemned”? No. But neither [Note: “nor”: Basel edition; Burchard and Ivo] do I say, “He will be delivered.” Do you wish, therefore [Note: absent from the editions of Argentinensis and Basel], to be freed from doubt? Do you wish to escape what is uncertain? Do penance while you are well. If you do this, I tell you that you are safe, because you performed penance at a time when you were still able to sin. But if you wish to perform penance when you are no longer able to sin, your sins have left you, not you them [Note: “sins”: Basel edition; Burchard and Ivo].

C. III. The same author, in the same homily, a little earlier.

Whoever has truly performed penance, has been released from the bond by which he was bound [Note: “obligated”: Basel edition], and has been separated from the body of Christ, and has lived well after penance, as he ought to have lived before penance [Note: “ought”: same edition], whenever he dies after reconciliation goes to God, goes to rest, will not be deprived of the kingdom of God, [Col. 1641C] and will be separated from the people of the devil.

C. IV. The same, in the same place.

“But if anyone,” etc. [Note: In Blessed Augustine the words quoted a little earlier in the chapter “If anyone, placed …” follow here, as far as “will depart well from here.”] And below: “One baptized at the hour departs safely from here; a believer living well departs safely from here; one doing penance and reconciled while well, and afterwards living well, departs safely from here. One doing penance at the last moment and reconciled: if he departs safely from here, I am not safe. Where I am safe, I speak and give assurance; where I am not safe, I can give penance, but I cannot give assurance.” [Col. 1642A] And a little later:

§ 1. “But how do you know,” you ask [Note: “he asks”: collected editions], “whether perhaps God will forgive me?” You speak truly. How do I know? I do not know; I know that statement, but I do not know this. For that reason I give you penance: because I do not know. If I knew that it would do you no good, I would not give it to you. Likewise, if I knew that it would benefit you, I would not admonish you or frighten you. There are two possibilities: either you are forgiven or you are not forgiven. Which of these will happen to you, I do not know. Therefore hold fast to what is certain; leave what is uncertain.” [Note: “and leave”: collected editions.]

Gratian. Cyprian shows why Augustine said this, saying in Book IV, Letter 2, to Antonianus [Note: written A.D. 251]:

C. V.

For this reason, dearest brother [Note: “dearest brothers”: collected editions], we have judged that those who do not do penance, nor attest with their whole heart and with an open profession of mourning the sorrow [Note: “in the sorrow … an open profession of their lamentation”: same editions] for their offences, ought altogether to be barred from hope of communion [Note: “communication”: same editions] and peace, if, in illness and danger, they begin [Note: “began”: collected editions, except Basel and Lyons II–III] to entreat it. For it is not repentance for sin but the warning of imminent death that compels them to ask; and one who has not reflected that he is to die is not worthy to receive consolation in death.

C. VI. Likewise Augustine, in the book *On Penance*, chapters 17 and 18. [Note: It is not Augustine’s. — Peter Lombard, in the same place.]

Let no one wait until he is no longer [Note: absent from collected editions except Lyons II–III] able [Note: “is able”: same editions] to sin. Let him seek freedom of choice [Note: “seeks”: Argentinensis edition], so that he may grieve [Note: “erase”: collected editions] over deeds committed, rather than necessity. He who is first abandoned by sins before he abandons them [Note: “abandons”: Basel edition] condemns them not freely but, as it were, from necessity. [Col. 1642C] Although the thief obtained pardon at the end for all his crime [Note: “even for all his crime”: same edition; cf. Luke 23], he did not thereby give the baptized authorization to sin and persevere in sin. For he was baptized [Note: added: “in faith”: editions of Basel and Lyons II–III] when [Note: “because”: Basel edition] he first confessed Christ upon the cross.

For if penance comes at the final gasp of life, it heals and frees through the washing [Note: “abolition”: same edition] of baptism, so that those baptized at the end do not experience purgatory; rather [Note: added: “rather”: editions of Basel and Lyons II–III], enriched by the goods of holy mother Church, they are to receive manifold good in true [Note: “eternal”: Basel edition] blessedness. But those who, while they could, never wished to be converted, confessing when they can no longer sin, do not [Note: “nor”: collected editions except Lyons] so easily obtain [Note: “is obtained”: editions of Argentinensis, Nuremberg, and Venice I–II] what they desire. For penance must bear fruit in such a way as to obtain life for one who is dying. For it is written [Note: 1 Corinthians 13:3] that no one is saved without charity.

Thus a human being does not live by fear alone. Therefore one who repents late must not merely fear God as judge, but also [Note: omitted in the collected editions except Lyons II–III] love him as just; [Col. 1643A] he must not fear punishment, but love glory. [Note: Other editions read: “he must not merely fear punishment, but be anxious.”] He ought to grieve for his sin and for every previously stated form of it. Since this is scarcely possible, Augustine could doubt concerning his salvation. [Note: “Since this is scarcely possible”: thus corrected from the Plantin edition. Previously it read: “Although it is possible concerning his salvation, Augustine,” etc. The author here plainly wished not to accuse Augustine but to interpret him, doubtless as his follower. Many other passages in this chapter have been corrected, partly from old manuscripts of Gratian and partly from the original source.]

§ 1. I do indeed believe him who said [Note: Ezekiel 33:12], “At whatever hour the sinner groans and is converted, he shall live” [Note: added: “and shall not die”: collected editions]. He said that the converted person, not merely the one turned about, lives. [Note: “shall live” omitted in editions of Basel, Nuremberg, Venice I–II; “he shall live” omitted in Argentinensis.] I consider turned about the person who grieves for his sin; converted, the person who grieves for every form of it that we have described. One turns from sin who now wishes to abandon sin; one is converted who is now wholly and altogether turned, who no longer [Note: absent from the same editions except Lyons II–III] merely does not [Note: “not merely” absent from editions of Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I–II, Paris] fear punishments, but hastens to strive for the good of the Lord [Note: “God”: Basel edition]. If such conversion happens to someone even at the end, his forgiveness is not to be despaired of. But because so just a conversion is scarcely or rarely found, the late penitent is to be feared for.

For one pressed by sickness and frightened by punishment will scarcely attain [Note: “will attain”: Basel; “comes”: other editions except Lyons I] true satisfaction, especially when children whom he loved unlawfully [Note: “loved”: collected editions except Basel], [Col. 1643C] his wife, and the world are present and call him back. Late penance [Note: “many” is absent from the same editions] often deceives many. But because God is always powerful, he can always [Note: “is able”: collected editions] help in death those whom he pleases. Since fruitful penance is the work not of man but of God, his mercy can inspire it whenever he wills and can reward in mercy those whom he can condemn [Note: “condemn”: Basel edition] in justice.

But since many things hinder and draw back even the sick person, [Col. 1644A] it is most dangerous and close to destruction to defer the remedy of penance until death. Yet great is the person in whom God then inspires true penance [Note: added: “true penance”: editions of Basel and Lyons II–III]. Therefore, if anyone seeks true penance then, let him await God’s mercy, sensing God’s goodness to be greater than his own wickedness. [Note: The words “if anyone … penance” are absent from Basel. Other editions variously read: “For if there is anyone who awaits true penance, experiencing God’s mercy …,” etc.]

§ 2. But even if one thus converted escapes, lives [Note: “life”: Böhm] and does not die [Note: “shall live and shall not die”: collected editions], we nevertheless do not promise that he escapes every punishment. For one who postponed the fruit of conversion to another age must first be purified by the fire of purification. This fire, although not eternal, is nevertheless marvellously severe. For it surpasses every punishment anyone has ever suffered in this life. Never has so great a punishment been found in the flesh, [Col. 1644B] although martyrs endured extraordinary torments and many wicked wrongdoers [Note: “unwillingly”: Nuremberg edition] endured such [Note: “as great”: collected editions] punishments, often [Note: “often endured”: same editions except Basel]. Therefore each person [Note: “each person”: collected editions] should strive to correct offences in such a way that after death he need not endure such punishment. [Note: Basel reads “him”; the other editions, except Lyons II–III, omit “such.”]

§ 3. For some sins [Note: added: “indeed”: Argentinensis edition], which are mortal—“which are” [Note: other editions read “which in”]—become life-giving in penance [Note: “in his penance”: Argentinensis, Basel, Venice I–II, and Paris; “venial”: original], but are not immediately healed [Note: “are healed”: collected editions except Argentinensis]. Indeed, sick persons would often die unless they were treated [Note: Other editions variously read: “there are those who would die,” “were treated,” and “is healed”]; yet they are not immediately healed: the one who will live languishes, though he had been about to die. But one who dies impenitent dies altogether and shall be tormented eternally [Note: “is tormented”: collected editions]. For one who ends impenitent would always sin if he lived forever. Yet it belongs to the merciful God that he brings an end to the sinner [Note: “sin”: Argentinensis; “sinning”: the remaining editions]; for this reason he will be tormented without end, [Col. 1644C] because he will never be enriched [Note: “is enriched”: same edition] with virtue. Ever full of wickedness, ever without charity, he shall be tormented [Note: “is tormented”: same edition] without end.

## QUESTION IV

### GRATIAN

I. Part. That during a time of prayer one may not engage in the marital act, Blessed Jerome writes in a certain sermon [Note: Sermon *On Eating the Lamb*, falsely attributed to Jerome. — Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 87; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 32], saying as follows: [Note: The earlier part of this chapter, through the word “Likewise,” appears deliberately collected into a summary; the remainder has been corrected and enlarged from the original.]

C. I. During the time when the marital due is rendered, one must abstain from the flesh of the lamb.

Know, dearest brothers, that whoever renders the marital due to his wife cannot devote himself to prayer and ought not eat the flesh of the lamb. Likewise, a little later:

§ 1. If the loaves of the offering [Note: cf. 1 Samuel 21] could not be eaten by those who had touched their wives, how much more may that bread which came down from heaven not be violated and touched by those who shortly before clung in marital embraces? Not because [Note: “because”: Ivo] we condemn marriage—for we do not say this—but because, at the time when we are about to eat the flesh of the lamb, we ought not to devote ourselves to works of the flesh. [Note: “from carnal works”: collected editions; “from works of the flesh”: Ivo.]

[Col. 1645B] C. II. Marital intercourse must be abstained from on holy festivals. Likewise Augustine, Sermon II *On the Time*, that is, on the Second Sunday of Advent. [Note: It is not Augustine’s. — Peter Lombard, in the same place.]

Whenever either the birthday of the Lord or the other festivals arrive [Note: “arrive”: collected editions], as I have often advised, several days beforehand, abstain not only from the company of unbelieving [Note: “unhappy”: original] concubines, but also from your own wives.

C. III. One must abstain from one’s own wives on days of fasting. Likewise Ambrose, in his sermon *On the Advent of the Lord*. [Note: Falsely attributed to Ambrose.]

Brothers, not only ought you to abstain from every uncleanness, but you should also most diligently refrain from your own wives. Let no one at all join himself to his own wife [Note: Basel reads “let his own wife join herself”] on fast days. [Note: In this sermon, preserved in manuscript in the Vatican Library, the words from here to the end are not found. But another manuscript sermon on Lent reads: “Let no one whatsoever join himself to his own wife before the octave of Easter.” In most old manuscripts of Gratian the words “on fast days,” concerning which Blessed Ambrose was nevertheless speaking and which therefore also occur in the rubric, are absent.]

C. IV. The same author, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 7. [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 21; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 84; Peter Lombard, in the same place.]

If a wife is taken for the purpose of begetting children, not much time seems permitted for the act itself, because feast days, days of processions, and the very condition of conception and childbirth according to the law show that the use of the flesh ought to cease at such times.

[Col. 1646A] C. V. The use of one’s wife is ordered to cease on certain days. Likewise Augustine, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, Question 127. [Note: Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 89; Peter Lombard, in the same place.]

For a Christian it is sometimes permitted to have intercourse with his wife, and sometimes it is not permitted. On account of days of processions [Note: added: “and fasts”: collected editions], it is sometimes not permitted to have intercourse, because one must abstain even from lawful things, in order that what is sought may be obtained more readily. Hence the Apostle says [Note: 1 Corinthians 7:5] that by mutual consent one ought to abstain for a time, in order to devote oneself [Note: “that you may devote yourselves”: Ivo, Vulgate; “that you may devote yourselves more freely”: collected editions] to prayer. For according to the law, on a fast one may not strike or quarrel; afterwards, however, it is permitted, because greater reverence is owed to the things of God. [Note: The clause “because … things of God” is absent from Ivo.]

C. VI. He does not truly perform penance who does not preserve continence. Likewise John Chrysostom. [Note: This chapter has not been found in Blessed John Chrysostom, from whom it is cited. But almost the same things are found in Blessed Jerome’s commentaries on Joel 2, and expounded more fully.]

[Col. 1646B] Whoever says that he performs penance through mortification in food vainly promises this in speech unless he leaves his chamber [Note: Joel 2:16] and adds continence to fasting.

C. VII. A man sleeping with his own wife ought to refrain from entering church. Likewise Gregory, in answer 10 to Augustine’s questions. [Note: Letter of doubtful authenticity, Letter 64, book 11, written A.D. 601; Maurist edition. — Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 88; Polycarp, book 6, title 7; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 31.]

II. Gratian’s Part. A man sleeping with his own wife ought not enter church unless washed with water; but even when washed, he ought not enter immediately. And below:

§ 1. Although different nations of men hold different opinions in this matter and appear to observe different practices, the custom of the Romans, handed down from their forebears, has always been to seek cleansing by washing after intercourse with one’s own wife, [Col. 1646C] and reverently to abstain for a little while from entering church. [Note: “refrain”: collected editions.] In saying this, we do not judge marriage to be blameworthy [Note: the editions read “this” for “these things,” “think” for “judge,” and “blameworthy” for “blame”]; but because even lawful intercourse between spouses [Note: “with one’s wife”: the collected editions] cannot occur without pleasure of the flesh, one must abstain from entering a holy place [Note: the collected editions add “therefore”], because pleasure itself can by no means exist without fault.

For it was not of adultery or fornication, but of lawful marriage, that the man was conceived who said: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities” [Note: Psalm 50:7; added: “etc.”: collected editions], “and in sins my mother bore me.” And below:

§ 2. Therefore a lawful union of the flesh ought to be for the sake of offspring, not pleasure [Note: The reading “a lawful union of the flesh ought to be” was corrected from various manuscripts of Gregory; the former reading was “therefore lawful bodily intercourse ought to be.” Many other readings were also corrected]; and bodily intercourse should be for the begetting [Note: “procreation”: Basel and Lyons II–III] of children, not the satisfaction of vices. If, then [Note: Basel reads “for”; the other editions read “indeed,” “truly,” or omit the word], someone uses his wife not because he is seized by the desire for pleasure but solely for the sake of begetting children, he should certainly be left to his own judgment concerning entry into church or receiving the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood [Note: “ministry”: Basel edition], since we ought not forbid reception to one who, though placed in the fire, does not know how to burn. But when desire, rather than love for begetting offspring, rules in the act of intercourse, spouses have something in their own intercourse to lament.

[Col. 1647B] And a little later:

§ 3. A man who, after intercourse with his wife, has washed with water may receive the mystery of holy communion when, in accordance with the judgment already stated, he has also been permitted to enter church.

III. Gratian’s Part. Accordingly, marriages are also forbidden to be celebrated on days of abstinence.

Therefore it is read in the Council of Laodicea, chapter 52 [Note: held between A.D. 347 and 381; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 49]:

C. VIII. It is not permitted to celebrate marriages in the days of Lent.

One ought not celebrate either marriages or any birthday festivals during Lent.

C. IX. On the same subject. Likewise from the Council of Martin of Braga, chapter 48. [Note: “Pope Martin”: collected editions; chapters 51–52 of the Council of Laodicea, through the interpretation of Martin of Braga; cf. Burchard, book 15, chapter 10; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, chapter 43.]

[Col. 1647C] It is not permitted [Note: “is permitted”: *Collectio Hispana*] to celebrate the birthday commemorations [Note: “anniversaries”: the same collection and the collected editions] of martyrs during Lent, but only on Saturday [Note: “on the Sabbath”: collected editions] and Sunday [Note: “on the Lord’s day”: *Collectio Hispana*] may offerings be made in commemoration of them. [Note: The collected editions read “through commemoration” and “to offer.”] But neither birthday celebrations nor marriages may be celebrated [Note: *Collectio Hispana* reads “be celebrated”] during Lent.

C. X. On the same subject. Likewise from the Council of Lleida. [Note: Similar in the Council of Seligenstadt, held A.D. 1022, chapter 3. — Burchard, book 9, chapter 4 and at the end of book 20; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 2; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 142; Polycarp, book 6, title 5; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 32.]

One ought not celebrate marriages from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter, during the three weeks before the feast [Col. 1648A] of Saint John the Baptist [Note: omitted in Basel], or from the Advent of the Lord until after Epiphany. If this has been done, they are to be separated.

C. XI. On the same subject. Likewise Pope Nicholas, in his responses to the Bulgarians, chapter 48. [Note: written A.D. 866; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 3; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 47; Peter Lombard, in the same place.]

We judge [Note: the collected editions read “I judge in no manner,” with Argentinensis variously “in no” or “in no way”] that it is in no way fitting to take a wife or hold banquets during the Lenten season.

IV. Gratian’s Part. These provisions must be observed if the wife is willing to give her consent; otherwise, without her consent, continence must not be observed even for the sake of prayer.

Therefore Augustine, in Book I *On Adulterous Marriages*, chapter 2. [Note: Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 133; Peter Lombard, in the same place.]

[Col. 1648B] C. XII. Spouses cannot devote themselves to prayer except by common consent.

The Apostle did not wish spouses to defraud one another of the marital due, even temporarily in order to devote themselves to prayer [Note: Basel reads “to devote oneself”; the remaining editions read “that they may devote themselves”], except by consent.

Likewise it is read in the Second Council of Arles, chapter 22 [Note: held no later than A.D. 460; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 280; part 15, chapters 14 and 123]:

C. XIII. Penance is not to be given to married persons except by common consent.

We command that penance be given to married persons only by consent. [Note: The collected editions add: “we decree that this is to be done.”]

## QUESTION V

### GRATIAN

I. Part. That a husband cannot vow continence without his wife’s consent is proved by many authorities. For Augustine says at the end of his exposition of Psalm 149: [Note: Ivo, *Decretum*, part 9, chapter 127; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 32.]

C. I. A husband cannot preserve continence unless he has his wife’s consent.

If the husband says, “I now wish to be continent; but I do not wish to have a wife,” he cannot do so. [Note: Augustine and Ivo read: “I now wish to be continent; I no longer wish a wife.”] For what you wish, she does not wish. Should you make her an adulteress by your continence? [Note: Ivo and the collected editions read “should she be made an adulteress.”] If she marries another while you are alive, she will be an adulteress. God does not wish to compensate such loss with such gain. Render the marital due; and if you do not demand it, render it.
