God will count it to you as perfect satisfaction [Note: In several manuscripts, and in Augustine, the Master, and Ivo, “sanctification” occurs; it has not been changed because of the gloss], if you do not demand what is due to you, but render what is due to your wife.

C. II. A woman’s consent to the continence vowed to God must not be extorted. Likewise Pope Alexander II, to Landulf in Corsica. [Note: written about A.D. 1065; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 85; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 220.]

You reported that, having been ill unto death and greatly frightened by the remembrance and terror of your sins, you anxiously sought to become a monk; that you extorted permission for this from your wife by threats and terrors of killing her; that you then put on the monastic [Note: “monk’s”: Ivo’s *Panormia*; “monastic”: *Decretum* and Argentinensis edition] habit without an abbot and sought a monastery; but that afterwards, when you had recovered, overcome by your wife’s protests, cries [Note: “howls”: same edition; “and her howls”: other editions], and lamentations, and by the dispersal of your household, you returned home as one who had repented. [Note: Ivo reads: “overcome as one repenting”; the *Panormia*: “utterly overcome, he returned home.”] After many days, on the advice [Note: Basel reads “by the advice”] of certain wise men, you returned to the bed of the woman already mentioned. You now ask our advice whether it is lawful for you to have intercourse with your wife.

If the matter is indeed as your messenger relates, it does not seem to us that this was done reasonably or soundly. For, whereas every person tending toward monastic life ought lawfully, holily, and justly to carry it out, you, acting contrary to the laws, followed a wrong path: exhausted partly by terror of death and partly by the pains of your illness, you threatened and violently departed from your wife without any permission, as they say, and sought a monastery. [Note: “examined”: Ivo, the *Decretum*, original, *Panormia*, and Basel; “exhausted or examined”: Argentinensis.] For this must be done not by force but by equal will and consent, as the holy Fathers say; nor should a husband choose a monastery or, having professed continence, change his habit hastily. [Note: Ivo and the *Panormia* read: “Nor is a husband to be received into a monastery unless his wife has chosen a nunnery or, having professed continence, has promptly changed her habit.” It has not been changed, because the gloss appears to agree better with Gratian’s reading.]

C. III. A husband may reject vows of continence which his wife has offered to God without his consent. Likewise from the Council at Compiègne. [Note: held A.D. 756; *Regino*, book 2, chapter 126; Burchard, book 9, chapter 47; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 185 and part 9, chapter 124; cf. *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, book 5, chapter 16.]

If a woman, without the permission [Note: “leave”: *Capitularies*; “authorization”: Ivo, part 9] of her husband, places a veil upon her head, [Col. 1650A] he may receive her again into marriage if it pleases him.

C. IV. A husband cannot annul vows of continence which a woman made to God with his consent. Likewise Augustine, to Ecdicia, Letter 199. [Note: Letter 262 in the Maurist edition; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 6, chapter 80; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 136.]

What both of you had vowed to God by mutual consent, both of you [Note: omitted in Ivo] ought to have rendered steadfastly to the end. If he has fallen away from that purpose, you at least persevere most earnestly. [Note: The original and Ivo read “most steadfastly.”] I would not exhort you to this unless he himself had consented to it. [Note: “consented”: editions of Basel and Lyons II–III; “will have consented”: the remaining editions.] For if you had never had his consent, no number of years would protect you.

And a little later:

§ 1. Your husband did not cease to be your husband because you both abstained from bodily intercourse; on the contrary, you remained spouses between yourselves all the more holy because you kept more holy agreements in concord. [Note: The editions read “and in concord,” except Basel and Lyons II–III.] [Col. 1650B] Therefore you ought not, without his decision, to do anything concerning your clothing, your gold [Note: Basel reads “or anything concerning your silver”], silver, money, or any of your earthly possessions. [Note: Basel and Paris–Lyons read “or concerning”; Paris and Lyons I omit “possessions,” Lyons II–III read “those,” and the remaining editions read “none.”]

And below:

§ 2. There is a certain matronly dress, appropriate to one’s station, distinct from widow’s apparel, which can suit married believers without compromising religious observance. If your husband did not wish you to lay this aside, lest you should vaunt yourself as a widow while he lived, I think that he ought not to have been brought in this matter as far as the scandal of disagreement: the evil of disobedience weighs more than the good of such abstinence. [Note: “anyone’s”: original and Ivo’s *Decretum*.]

For what is more absurd than for a woman to be proud of a humble garment against her husband, whom it would suit her better to obey in bright morals than to oppose in dark clothing? Even if the garment of a nun pleased you, it could be assumed more acceptably with your husband duly regarded and persuaded than rashly adopted without consulting him and while disregarding him. But if he would not permit it at all, what would be lost from your purpose? Far be it that you should displease God because, while your husband was not yet dead, you were not clothed as Anna, but as Susanna. [Note: Variants read “were widowed” or “were clothed”; cf. Luke 2; Daniel 13.]

[Col. 1651A] C. V. He who is compelled to render the marital due because of his wife’s incontinence possesses the merit of continence. The same author in the same letter. [Note: This chapter, also found in the same form in Polycarp, has been compiled from two indicated passages of Blessed Augustine, with certain words partly omitted and partly altered, while retaining the sense.] [Note: Polycarp, book 6, title 4; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 32.]

In accordance with the words of the Apostle, even if the husband had wished to restrain *himself*, and you had not wished to do so, he would have been compelled to render you the marital due; and God would have counted it to him as continence if he yielded not to his own weakness but to yours, lest you fall into adultery. [Col. 1651: *si*, “if”: Argentinian edition; *voluisses*, “you had wished”: Nuremberg and Venice I–II; *abest ab orig.*, “absent from the original”; *et si*, “even if”: Basel edition.]

§ 1. Therefore, whoever, compassionating his wife’s weakness, renders the marital due [*reddidit*, “rendered”: the other editions, including the first Basel and Paris editions], rather than demands it [*exegit*, “demanded”: the same editions]; or, if because of his own weakness he takes a wife [*duxit*, “took”: Lyons II–III], lamenting rather that he could not remain without a wife than rejoicing that he married [*conduxit*, “contracted marriage”: Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I–II]; whoever sells what he knows to be useful [*utile novit*, “knows to be useful”: the other editions, including the first Basel and Lyons II–III], because, even if it remained, it would not make him blessed; whoever knows that what he buys will pass away [*transit*, “passes away”: the same editions, first Argentinian and Basel], does not presume upon these things, and from what he has shows mercy to those who do not have [*fecit*, “did”: the other editions]—such a person securely awaits the last day. [Col. 1651B.]

## C. VI. Vows of continence cannot be discharged without the wife’s consent

The same, to Armentarius, Riparius, and Paulina, Letter XLV. [Col. 1651: Letter 127 in the Maurist edition, written A.D. 411, to Armentarius and Paulina. The name Riparius was transferred into the heading by Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 134, from the beginning of the letter itself, where Ruferius is mentioned.—Peter Lombard, same place.]

There could be only one reason why we should not merely refrain from exhorting you to fulfil what you vowed, but should even forbid you to fulfil it: namely, if perhaps your wife, because of weakness of mind or body, refused to undertake this with you. For married people ought not to make vows of this sort except by common consent and will; and, if it has been done too hastily [*propere*, “hastily”: the other editions, including the first Argentinian, Basel, and Nuremberg editions], rashness ought rather to be corrected than the promise discharged. For God does not require someone to vow something out of another person’s property; rather, he forbids the usurpation of what belongs to another. [Col. 1651C.]

## C. VII. Neither virginity alone saves without other works, nor do other works profit without virginity

Likewise Jerome, Book I, *Against Jovinianus*.

**Part II.** Then a woman will be saved if she has borne those children who will remain virgins; if she recovers in her children what she herself lost, and compensates by flower and fruit for the loss of the root and its decay. [Col. 1651: Basel reads *carnem*, “flesh,” for *cariem*, “decay”; Basel and Lyons II–III read *in flore*, “in flower,” for “by flower.”]

## C. VIII. The same, in the same place

This alone I now say [Böhm reads “not”]: just as virginity alone does not save without other works, so all works without virginity [Basel: *virginitatis*, “of virginity”], purity, continence, and chastity are imperfect. [Col. 1651–52A.]

## C. IX. The same, in the same place

“Let him who thirsts come and drink; let him who is able to receive it receive it.” [Col. 1651: John 7:37; Matthew 19:12.] He does not say, “Whether you wish it or not, you must drink and run”; rather, “Whoever wishes, whoever can run and drink, that person will conquer” [*vincit*, “conquers”: the other editions, including Lyons II–III], “that person will be satisfied” [Basel adds *ab eo*, “by him”].

Therefore Christ loves virgins more, because they freely give what had not been commanded them; and it is a greater grace to offer what one does not owe than to render what is demanded of one [*exigeris*, “you are required”: the other editions].

The Apostles, considering the burdens of a wife [Col. 1651: the other editions read, “For the Apostles, considering the burden of a wife”; Venice I–II and Paris read *honore*, “honour,” for *onere*, “burden”; compare Matthew 19:10], say: “If such is the case of a man with a wife, it is not expedient to marry.” Approving their judgment, the Lord says: “You rightly perceive that it is not expedient for a man striving toward the heavenly kingdoms [the same editions: “the kingdom of heaven”] to take a wife; but the matter is difficult, and not all receive this saying, but those to whom it has been given. Nature makes some eunuchs, and human force others [Basel adds *homines*, “human beings”; the remaining editions read *hominum*, “of men”]. Those eunuchs please me whom not necessity but will has castrated; I gladly receive into my embrace [the other editions: “into my bosom”] those who have castrated themselves [Basel omits *se*, “themselves”; the remaining editions read *se ipsos*, “themselves”] for the kingdoms [the other editions: “kingdom”] of heaven, and who, for my worship [the same editions: “for my sake”], did not wish to remain what they were born.

“At the same time this saying must be considered” [Basel and Lyons add *haec*, “this”; the other editions: *est sententia*, “the saying is”; compare Matthew 19:12]: “Those who have castrated themselves for the kingdoms [the other editions: “kingdom”] of heaven.” If those castrated have the reward of the kingdom [Basel: “kingdoms”] of heaven, then those who have not castrated themselves cannot receive the place of those who have.”

**Gratian.** The end of this authority and the two preceding authorities are understood of the disposition toward virginity, which exists not merely in will but in necessity; its beginning, however, is understood of its effect, which exists not in necessity and before a vow, but in will, and is not required unless it has been promised. [Col. 1652B–C.]

## C. X. A man who has allowed his wife to be veiled may not take another wife

Likewise, from the Council of Rheims. [Col. 1651: chapter 21 of the Council of Vermeries, held A.D. 752.—Regino, Book 2, chapter 125; Burchard, Book 9, chapter 46; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 6, chapter 82; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 184; Peter Lombard, same place.]

**Part III.** Whoever has allowed his wife to be veiled [Ivo, *Panormia*: *velari*, “to be veiled”] shall not take another, but shall likewise be converted. [The words “but shall likewise be converted” are absent from the original and Regino.]

## C. XI. Vows of abstinence which a woman has promised with her husband’s permission: when he forbids her, she is not compelled to keep them

Likewise Augustine, *Questions on Numbers*, question LIX. [Col. 1653: Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 7, chapter 48; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 98; Peter Lombard, same place.]

**Part IV.** It is evident that the Law intended a woman to be subject to her husband in such a way that none of her vows which she has made for the sake of abstinence may be discharged by her unless her husband has authorized it by permitting it [Basel omits *vir*, “husband”]. For since the Law intended it to count as the sin of that same husband [the other editions and Ivo’s *Panormia* add *lex*, “the Law”], if he first permitted and afterward forbade, even here [Basel: *hoc*, “this”; the remaining editions and Ivo: *et hoc*, “and this”] it nevertheless did not say that the woman should do what she had vowed because she had previously been permitted by her husband.

It said that it was the husband’s sin because he withdrew what he had formerly granted; yet it did not even thereby give the woman *permission* [the other editions: *jussum*, “a command”] that, although her husband had previously granted it to her [Ivo, *Decretum*, and Basel: *quum*, “when”; Venice II, Paris, and Lyons: *concesserat*, “had granted”; the printed text has the same form], he may be disregarded if he afterward forbade it [the printed text: *contemnatur*, “he is disregarded”; the original: *condemnetur*, “he is condemned”; Argentinian: *contemnat*, “she should disregard him”]. [Col. 1653A–B.]

**Gratian.** From the foregoing authorities it appears that neither a woman can offer vows of continence to God without her husband’s consent, nor a husband without his wife’s consent. But if one of them has made a promise with the consent of the other, and the one who permitted it afterward wishes to render it void, that person cannot do so; for in the marital due the woman has power equally with the man, just as the man has with the woman. Therefore, if either releases the other from that person’s right, he cannot recall that person to the former servitude.

But because in other matters the man is the head of the woman and the woman the body of the man, a woman may promise vows of abstinence with her husband’s permission, yet, if he subsequently forbids it, she cannot fulfil what she has promised. This, as we have said, is because of the condition of servitude by which she ought in all things to be subject to her husband. [Col. 1653B–C.]

Therefore Augustine, in the book *Questions on Genesis*, question CLIII, says: [Col. 1653: Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 7, chapter 43; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 94.]

## C. XII. Women ought to be subject to their husbands

There is a natural order among human beings: women should serve men, and children [Ivo and the other editions: “and children”] their parents, because there is no justice in the greater serving the lesser.

[Col. 1653–54A: In the *Panormia* the remainder appears as in Gratian, except that it corruptly reads, “the lesser should serve the greater.” In the original, from which Ivo does not depart far, the reading is: “because there too this justice exists, that weaker reason should serve stronger reason.” The text was not emended because of the gloss. The other editions read: “because this justice exists among them, that the lesser should serve the greater”; Ivo’s *Panormia*: “because among them this justice exists, that the inferior serves the superior”; Ivo’s *Decretum*: “because among them this justice exists, that the inferior serves the superior.”]

## C. XIII. The man is the head of the woman

The same, in *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, mixed from both, chapter 106. [Col. 1653: This work is not Augustine’s.—Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 7, chapter 44; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 95.]

This is the image of God in man: that one man was made [Basel adds *facta*, “made”], as a lord, from whom the rest might arise, possessing God’s authority as his vicar; for every king bears the image of God.

[Col. 1653C–D: What follows has been corrected partly from old witnesses, partly from the original itself, and partly from Ivo. For in the later printed editions of Gratian it was read: “man was made, from whom the rest arise, possessing God’s authority as God’s vicar, because the man bears the image of the one God.”]

Therefore woman was not made in the image of God. Thus Scripture says [Basel and Lyons II–III add *scriptura*, “Scripture”; compare Genesis 1:27; Wisdom 2:23]: “And God made man; in the image of God he made him.” Hence [Ivo’s *Panormia*, the other editions, and Böhm: “Hence also the Apostle”] the Apostle says: “A man indeed ought not to cover his head, because he is the image and glory of God; but the woman should cover herself” [Ivo and Basel: “covers herself”], “because she is not the glory or image of God.”

[Col. 1654C: After “image” followed “and likeness” in the other editions, including the first Argentinian and Nuremberg editions. These words have been deleted because they occur neither in Augustine, nor in the standard Greek text, nor in the older Latin text, nor among the other compilers. Basil discusses this question well in his exposition of this passage in Genesis, and Origen in *Periarchon*, Book 3, chapter 6.]

## C. XIV. The same, Book V of *Questions on Deuteronomy*, question XXXIII

[Col. 1653: Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 7, chapter 45; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 96.]

From this it sufficiently appears how the Law intended women to be subject to men, and wives almost to be female servants: namely, when it decreed that, if a husband bore testimony against his wife whereby she might be stoned, and the charge proved true, he himself would nevertheless not in turn be stoned if it proved false. He is merely chastised and fined, and is ordered to remain attached to her forever, though he had wished to be rid of her.

In other cases, however, it commands that one who has injured anyone by false testimony—if, were the accusation proved, the law would have ordered that person to be killed [Ivo, *Decretum*, and Basel and Lyons I: *jussit*, “ordered”]—be punished by the same penalty [Ivo: *jubet*, “orders”; the printed reading: *plecti jubetur*, “is ordered to be punished”; *fuerat*, “had been,” in Ivo] by which that man [the editions: *ipse*, “he himself”; the corrected *iste*, “that man,” is supported by several manuscripts, the original, and Ivo] would have been punished had the charge been true.

[Col. 1654C–D: The passage is almost identical in Ivo and the *Panormia*. In the original, however, it reads *eademque poena plecti jubet*, “it orders him to be punished by that same penalty.”]

## C. XV. Likewise Jerome, on the Epistle to Titus, chapter 2

[Col. 1653: Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 7, chapter 46; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 97.]

Since the man is the head of the woman, and Christ the head of the man, any wife who is not subject to her husband—that is, to her head—is guilty of the same offence as is the man if he is not subject to Christ, his head. [The Argentinian, Basel, and Nuremberg editions omit “his head”; the remaining editions read, “to her head, that is, to Christ.”]

The word of the Lord is blasphemed either while [Ivo, *Decretum*, Basel, and Lyons: *quum*, “when”; the remaining editions and Ivo’s *Panormia* omit it] God’s first sentence is despised and treated as nothing, or when Christ’s Gospel is dishonoured: when, contrary to the law and faith of nature, a woman who is Christian and subject to a man by God’s law desires to rule her husband, although even Gentile women serve their husbands under the common law of nature. [Col. 1654C–55A.]

## C. XVI. A woman ought to follow her husband’s judgment in all things

Likewise Augustine, *Questions on Numbers*, question LIX. [Col. 1655: Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 7, chapter 47; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 98.]

The Law therefore did not wish a woman to vow anything to God against herself in such a way that, in abstinence from certain lawful and permitted things, female authority might prevail in those same vows, but rather male authority.

[Col. 1655D: In the *Panormia* it reads, “so that in abstinence from certain things”; in Ivo, “so that in abstinence from certain things”; in the ordinary gloss, “that is, in things.” But the whole passage is much better in the original: “The Law intended a woman, before marriage, to be under her father and, after marriage, under her husband, to vow something to God against herself—that is, in abstinence from certain lawful and permitted things—in such a way that female authority should not prevail in those vows, but male authority.”]

Thus, even if her father had already granted an unmarried woman permission to discharge it [Böhm omits *et*, “and”; Ivo and the other editions read *ut*, “that”], if she marries before discharging it and her husband learns of it and does not approve, she shall not discharge it [Col. 1655B] and shall be wholly without sin, because God has cleansed her [Ivo and the same editions: “God has cleansed”], that is, judged her clean, as the Law says [Ivo, *Decretum*, Basel, and Lyons add “the Law”]. Nor should this be thought to be done against God, since God himself commanded it and willed it.

## C. XVII. A woman has no authority, but is subject in all things to her husband’s dominion

Likewise in the book *Questions on the Old Testament*, question XLV. [Col. 1655D–56D: This chapter has been restored to blessed Augustine, and some material added from him. Formerly it was cited from blessed Ambrose.—Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 7, chapter 49; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 85.]

It is established that a woman is subject to the dominion of her husband [Basel adds *sui*, “her own”] and possesses no authority; for she cannot teach, bear witness, give testimony [the original and Ivo read *dicere*, “speak”], or judge—how much less can she rule?

## C. XVIII. Likewise Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, in the treatment of the fourth day

[Col. 1655: Book 5, on Genesis, chapter 7.—Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 7, chapter 50; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 91.]

Adam was deceived through Eve, not Eve through Adam. It is just that she should take as her governor the man whom the woman summoned into fault, lest he again fall through feminine weakness.

[Col. 1656D: It formerly read, “that he should take her into governance”; Ivo’s *Decretum* reads “governance,” the *Panormia* “in governance,” and the other editions, including the first Basel and Lyons II–III, “in governance.” It has been corrected from blessed Ambrose to *gubernatorem*, “governor,” because the gloss fits that word very well.]

## C. XIX. Likewise, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 2

[Col. 1655: Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 7, chapter 51; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 92.]

A woman ought to cover her head because she is not the image of God. But, in order that she may be shown to be subject [the other editions add “to the husband”], and because transgression began through her, she ought to have this sign [the same editions and Böhm: *signum*, “sign”]: that [Ivo omits *ut*, “that”] in church, because of reverence for the bishop, she should not have her head uncovered but covered with a veil; nor [Ivo’s *Panormia* and the other editions: “not”] should she have authority to speak, because the bishop bears the person of Christ.

Thus, as before a judge [Ivo’s *Panormia*, the other editions, the original, and Böhm add “Christ”], so before the bishop [the other editions: “thus before the bishop”], because he is the Lord’s vicar [Basel: “God’s”], she ought to appear subject on account of original sin.

[Col. 1656D: In blessed Ambrose and Ivo the reading is “on account of the origin of guilt”; in the *Panormia*, “on account of original guilt.” The text was not altered because of the gloss; the remainder has been corrected.]

## C. XX. The same, in the book *On Paradise*, chapter 10

**Part V.** Nor is it without significance [the other editions add “is”] that woman was made not from the same earth from which Adam was formed, but from Adam’s own rib, so that we might know that man and woman have one bodily nature and one source of the human race. Therefore two—a man and a woman—were not made in the beginning [Basel and Lyons II–III add *sunt*, “are”]; nor two men, nor two women; but first man, then woman from him.

For God, wishing to establish one nature of humankind, beginning this creature from one origin [the other editions: *hoc*, “this”], removed the possibility of many and unlike natures. [Col. 1656B.]

**Gratian.** Therefore it is most evident that the man is so the head of the woman that she may offer no vows of abstinence or religious life to God without his permission. Even if she has made the promise with her husband’s permission, she may not fulfil the vow in deed when her husband wishes to withdraw what was permitted. Vows of continence, however, are validly offered by one spouse with the other’s permission in such a way that, after permission, they cannot be rendered void. [Col. 1656C.]

# CAUSE XXXIV

[Col. 1655.]

## GRATIAN

A certain man was taken into captivity. Later his wife, hearing that he was dead, married another. At last he returned from captivity and demanded back his wife; but she, captivated by love for the latter husband, rejected the bed of her former husband. (Question I.) The first question is whether she is guilty of adultery, having married another while her husband was alive. (Question II.) Secondly, when the first husband returns, must she be compelled to leave the second and return to the first? [Col. 1655C–56C.]

# QUESTIONS I AND II

## GRATIAN

**Part I.** Both questions are settled by the authority of Pope Leo, who, writing to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, in Letter LXXVII, chapter 1 and following, says: [Col. 1657: Letter 159 in the Ballerini edition, written A.D. 458.—Anselm, Book 1, title 10, chapter 22 (24); Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 6, chapters 87–88; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 244, through the words “are deprived”; *Polycarp*, Book 6, title 4; Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 38.]

## C. I. A woman who married another, thinking her husband dead, is compelled, upon his return, to return to the former husband

You say that through the devastation of war and the most grievous assaults of hostility certain marriages have been so divided that, when husbands were carried off into captivity, their abandoned wives believed that their own husbands had either been killed [the original: *putarent*, “were thinking”; Ivo and the other editions: the same imperfect] or would never be freed from unjust domination [the other editions and Ivo’s *Panormia*: *ab iniqua dominatione*, “from unjust domination”; Lyons I: *damnatione*, “condemnation”]; and, compelled by anxiety [the original: *solitudine*, “solitude”], passed into marriage with others [the other editions and Ivo’s *Panormia*: *et in*, “and into”; the other editions: *transierunt*, “passed”].

And now [the words from *nunc*, “now,” through *separet*, “separate,” are absent from Anselm], with the state of affairs, by the Lord’s help, turned for the better, some of those thought to have perished have returned [the other editions: *remearunt*, “returned”]. Your charity therefore seems rightly uncertain what ought to be decreed by us concerning the women who have joined themselves to other husbands.

But because we know it is written [the other editions, including the first Basel, and Ivo’s *Panormia*: *praeceptum*, “commanded”] that a woman is joined by God to her husband [the other editions add *suo*, “her own”], and again know the command that what [the same editions: *quos … conjunxit*, “those whom God joined”] God has joined no human being should separate, it is necessary that we hold the bonds of lawful marriages must be restored. Once the evils [Ivo and the other editions: *his*, “these”] which hostility brought have been removed, what each one lawfully possessed must be restored to each one [the other editions and Ivo: *id, quod lex intulit*, “that which the law brought”], and every effort must be made that each receive what is his or her own. [“And therefore every effort must be made” is Basel; the words from *omnique* through *proprium est* are absent from Anselm.]

§ 1. Yet the person who has assumed the position of the husband who was believed no longer to exist [the Hispanic collection and the other editions, including the first Lyons II–III: *aestimabatur*, “was thought”] ought not to be judged guilty, nor regarded as an invader of another’s right [Argentinian: *non*, “not”; Basel: *et non*, “and not”; Burchard, Ivo, the other editions, and Ballerini add *habeatur*, “be regarded”; the words from “and” through “belonged” are absent from Ivo, chapter 244].

For many things that belonged to those taken into captivity could pass into another’s legal possession, and yet it is wholly just [Argentinian: *plane*, “plainly”; the remaining editions: *lanae*, apparently an OCR-corrupt reading] that, when they return, their own possessions be restored to them. If this is properly observed [Ivo’s *Decretum*, chapter 244, the *Panormia*, and the other editions: *recte*, “rightly”] in slaves [the other editions, including the first Basel, add *mansis*, “dwellings/holdings”], fields, even houses and possessions, how much more ought it be done in the restoration of marriages [the Hispanic collection: *redintegrationem*, “restoration”; Argentinian: *integritate*, “integrity”], so that what was disturbed by war’s necessity [the same editions, Ivo’s *Decretum*, chapter 244, and the *Panormia*: *clade*, “calamity”] may be restored [Nuremberg and Venice I–II: *formetur*, “be formed”] by the remedy of peace? [The word *sic*, “thus,” is absent from Ballerini, Burchard, Ivo, Basel, and Lyons II–III; the remaining editions read *si quid*, “if anything.”]

And therefore [Burchard, Book 9, chapter 58; Ivo, part 8, chapter 193], if husbands returning after a long captivity persist in affection for their wives, desiring them to return to their fellowship, what necessity brought about must be passed over and judged blameless, and what fidelity requires must be restored. [Col. 1657C–58A.]

And below, chapter 4. [Col. 1657: Burchard, same place, chapter 57; Ivo, same place, chapter 192.]

§ 2. But if certain women are so captivated by love for their latter husbands that they prefer [Ivo’s *Panormia* and the other editions: *maluerint*, “have preferred”] to remain attached to them rather than return to lawful fellowship [Basel: “to pass into lawful unions”], they rightly deserve censure, so that they are even deprived of ecclesiastical communion [*etiam*, “even,” absent from Burchard and Ivo; the remainder through the end is absent from Anselm and Ivo, chapter 244]. They chose the defilement of crime out of a matter that could be excused [Lyons II–III: *quod*, “which”; the Hispanic collection: “because they have inexcusably chosen the contamination of crime”], showing that, because of their own incontinence, they approved what just remission could have expiated [Lyons I: *elegerent*, “were choosing”; Lyons II–III: *eligerint*, “have chosen”; Basel: *potuit*, “could,” for *poterat*, “could have”].

Let marriages therefore return to their former state by voluntary restoration, and let what the condition of necessity extorted in no way be turned into a reproach of evil will. For just as those women who refuse to return to their husbands [Basel: *noluerunt*, “refused”; the remaining editions and Burchard and Ivo: *noluerint*, “will refuse”] are to be regarded as impious, so those who return to the affection established by God are deservedly to be praised in judgment [*judicio*, “in judgment,” absent from the original, Burchard, and Ivo]. [Col. 1658A–B.]

## C. II. When a husband or wife returns from captivity, their original marriages are restored

Likewise Pope Innocent, to Probus, in Letter IX. [Col. 1657: A letter of Innocent I, of uncertain date.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 245.—Ivo’s *Panormia*, Basel, Nuremberg, Paris, and Lyons add “bishop.”]

While the woman Ursa was held in captivity, we learned that Fontanus had contracted another marriage with Restituta [the original: *Fortunius iniisse cognoscitur*, “Fortunius is known to have entered into it”; Ivo’s *Decretum*: “we know Fortunius to have entered into it”; Ivo’s *Panormia*: “we know Fontanus to have entered into it”].

But Ursa, restored by the Lord’s favour, came to us and, with no one disputing it, proved that she was the wife of the aforesaid man. Therefore, most illustrious lord son [Ivo’s *Panormia* omits this; the other editions: “most dear son”], supported by the Catholic faith, we decree that the marriage first founded by divine grace is the valid marriage, and that the union with the second woman, while the first survives and has not been dismissed by divorce [Basel: *divortia*, “divorces”; Lyons II: *ejecto*, masculine “dismissed”], can by no means be lawful. [Col. 1658B–C.]

## C. III. A woman who has left her first husband and attached herself to a second cannot be reconciled to the first unless she leaves the second

Likewise Jerome, to the presbyter Amandus. [Col. 1657D–58D: The words of this chapter in Jerome’s letter and in *Polycarp* immediately follow those cited above at Cause 32, question 7, chapter “All Excuses.” Therefore their opening reads: “Nor was I sufficiently able to discern.”] [Col. 1657: *Polycarp*, Book 6, title 4; Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 35.]

I have not sufficiently been able to discern what your letter [Basel and Lyons I add “your letter”; the remaining editions, through Paris: “your letter,” plural] intended by saying: “having accepted another man by force.” What is “having accepted by force”? Presumably, having gathered a crowd, he carried her off against her will. Why then did the woman who had been carried off not afterward leave her ravisher? Let her read [Basel: *legas*, “you should read”] the books of Moses, and she will find [Basel: *invenies*, “you will find”; the remaining editions, including Lyons II–III: *inveniat*, “let her find”] that a woman betrothed to a man, if violated in a city and not crying out, is punished as an adulteress; but if violated in a field [the other editions: *vi*, “by force”; the other editions: *oppressam*, “violated,” accusative], is innocent of the crime, and the violent man is subject to the laws.

Therefore this sister [Argentinian omits “therefore”; the other editions, including the first Basel and Lyons II–III, add “of yours”], who, as she says [the same editions: “as she said”], suffered violence so as to be joined to another [the other editions: “to an adulterer”], if she wishes to receive the body of Christ and not be accounted an adulteress, must do penance, provided only that from the time of her penance she does not unite herself with the second man, who is called not a husband but an adulterer.

But if this seems harsh to her and she cannot leave one she has once loved, or prefer the Lord to pleasure, let her hear the Apostle crying aloud [the other editions: *clamantem*, “crying”; compare 1 Corinthians 10:20]: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.” And elsewhere [the other editions: “in another place”; compare 2 Corinthians 6:14]: “What fellowship has light with darkness?” [the same editions and the Vulgate and Böhm: “light with darkness”] “What agreement has Christ with Belial?” [the same editions and Ivo: “agreement of Christ with”; Ivo’s *Decretum*: “agreement with Christ and Belial.”]

I say something new—or rather, not new but old, established [Basel and Lyons II–III: “confirmed”] by the authority of the Old Testament. If she leaves the second husband and wishes to be reconciled to the first, she cannot be. For it is written in Deuteronomy [Deuteronomy 24 and following]:

“If a man takes a wife and has her, and she does not find favour in his sight because of some indecency, he shall write [the other editions, including Lyons II–III: “let him write to her”] a bill of divorce, give it into her hand [the other editions: “give it to her”], and dismiss [Argentinian: “dismisses”; Nuremberg, Venice I–II, and Paris: “let him dismiss”] her from his house. When she has gone out, an adulteress, and has taken a husband [the printed source: *adultera*, “an adulteress”; the original reads *alterum*, “another”], and that husband also hates her, gives her a bill of divorce, and dismisses her from his house, or certainly has died, her former husband cannot take her again as his wife, because she has been defiled and made abominable before the Lord, lest you cause your land to sin, which the Lord your God has given you to possess.” [Col. 1659A–C.]

**Part III. Gratian.** But if, compelled by unavoidable necessity, a husband flees into another district or province and his wife refuses to follow him, she must remain unmarried while he lives.

Therefore, at the Council of Vermeries: [Col. 1659: held A.D. 752, chapter 9.—Regino, Book 2, chapter 124; Burchard, Book 9, chapter 54; Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 6, chapter 91; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 189.]

## C. IV. A woman who refuses to follow a husband carried into captivity must remain unmarried as long as he lives

If anyone, compelled by unavoidable necessity, flees into another duchy or province, and his wife, though able and capable, refuses to follow him because of love for her relatives and [the original, the cited collections, and Basel: *aut*, “or”] possessions, she shall remain unmarried for the entire time that her husband, whom she did not follow [the other editions: *insecuta*, “pursue/follow after”], lives [the other editions, including the first Argentinian: *fuerit*, “will live”]. [Col. 1659–60A.]

**Part IV. Gratian.** What Pope Leo says by authority concerning married women must also be understood concerning virgins: if, without knowing it, they marry another’s husband, they are not bound as adulteresses.

Therefore Augustine, in the book *On Faith and Works*, chapter 7, says: [Col. 1659: Anselm, Book 10, chapter 63.]

## C. V. A virgin who unknowingly marries another’s husband is not an adulteress

If a virgin unknowingly marries another’s husband, then, if she remains always unaware, she will never thereby be an adulteress. But if she learns it, she will begin [Böhm omits *ex hoc*, “thereby”; the other editions: *incipit*, “begins”] to be so from the time when she knowingly lies with another husband [Basel omits *viro*, “husband”], just as, in the law concerning estates, someone is most rightly called a possessor in good faith for as long as he does not know that he possesses another’s property. But when he knows and does not withdraw from another’s possession, then he is described as a possessor in bad faith; then he is rightly called an unjust [the other editions, including the first Argentinian, Basel, and Nuremberg, and Böhm add “possessor”] possessor. [Col. 1660B.]

**Part V. Gratian.** Hence ignorance also excuses one who unknowingly slept with his wife’s sister.

Therefore, at the Council of Tribur: [Col. 1659: chapter 43 of the Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895; abridged in Regino, Book 2, chapter 286; Burchard, Book 17, chapter 4.—Compare the ancient Roman and Anglo-Saxon penitentials, Book 3, chapter 5.]

## C. VI. One who unknowingly slept with his wife’s sister must not be compelled to dismiss his lawful wife

While the wife was absent, the wife’s sister went into her husband’s bed; believing that she was his own wife, he slept with her. It has been decided concerning this that, if he proves with true assurance that he committed this offence unknowingly, he shall indeed perform whatever penance is imposed [Regino, Burchard, and Basel: *indicata*, “prescribed”] upon him, but he shall be permitted to retain his lawful marriage. The woman, however, shall be afflicted with punishment worthy of vengeance and deprived of marriage forever. [Regino and Burchard preserve “she shall be afflicted … and deprived.”] [Col. 1660C.]

## C. VII. PALEA

[Likewise Hermes, in the book *The Shepherd*, Mandate IV. Col. 1659: In this chapter some material has been corrected and added from the original and the other compilers.—Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 7, chapter 38; *Decretum*, part 8, chapter 243; Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 35.—Compare chapter 3 of the First Compilation and Book X of the *Decretals*, “On adultery.”—This *Palea* is not printed in the Argentinian edition.]

“I said to the shepherd: ‘Lord, if a man has a wife [Ivo’s *Panormia* and the other editions: *mulierem*, “a woman”] faithful in the Lord and finds [Basel: “will find”] her in adultery, does the man sin if he lies with her [the other editions: “with her”]?’ And he said to me: ‘So long as he does not know her sin, the man living with her is without guilt [Ivo’s *Panormia*: “he is without guilt with her”; Basel and Lyons: “he lives with her”; the whole sentence is absent from the remaining editions].

‘But if the man knows that his own wife has sinned, and the woman does not do penance but remains in her fornication, and the man lies with her [the original and Ivo’s *Decretum*: *convivit*, “lives with her”], he will be guilty of her sin and a participant in her adultery [the other editions: “fornication”].’

‘And I said to him [Ivo, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice I–II: “he said”]: “What then [the other editions: “what, however”], if the woman remains [the same editions and Ivo: “remains,” present tense] in her vice?” And he said: “Let the man dismiss her, and let the man remain by himself. But if he dismisses his wife and takes another, he too commits adultery.”

‘And I said to him: “If the woman who has been dismissed does penance and wishes to return to her husband, will she not [Ivo, Nuremberg, Venice I–II, and Paris omit *nonne*, “will she not”; Basel and Lyons: *numquid*, “will she perhaps”] be received by her husband?” And he said to me [the other editions, including the first Basel: “he receives”]: “Indeed, if her husband does not receive her, he sins and commits a great sin against himself; rather, he ought to receive the sinner who has done penance. Therefore, after dismissing his wife [Ivo and the other editions: *uxore*, “wife,” for *conjuge*, “spouse”], a man ought not to take another. This practice is alike in man and woman.”’” [Col. 1661A–B.]

**Part VI. Gratian.** The same principle must be applied to those simply guilty of fornication, or with two sisters, or with mother and daughter, or with father and son: marriages must not be denied to those who acted in ignorance, but must be forbidden forever to those who acted knowingly.

[Col. 1662A] Hence, in the same Council of Tribur one reads [Note: [Col. 1661D] Burchard also cites from the Council of Tribur, c. 9. Something similar is found in the printed Triburian council, c. 45, as also in the Council of Worms, c. 33.] [Note: [Col. 1661] c. 45 of the Council of Tribur (held A.D. 895), abridged. Regino, bk. 2, c. 208. Burchard, bk. 17, c. 5.]:

### C. VIII. Marriage is not forbidden to those whose incest is excused by ignorance.

If anyone has committed fornication with two sisters, and one sister did not know that the other had previously been violated by the same man; or if he himself [Note: [Col. 1661D] “Or if he himself”: thus restored from Burchard. Previously it read: “or himself the sister” [ [Col. 1661] thus the collected editions].] did not recognize the sister whom he had previously violated as her sister [Note: [Col. 1661] “recognized”: the same editions, first Paris and Lyons editions], if they have done worthy penance and cannot remain continent, marriage is not to be denied them after seven years. But if they were not ignorant [Note: [Col. 1661] “were not ignorant”: Regino, Burchard], they are to abstain from marriage until death.

### C. IX. On the same subject. Likewise from the same source.

[Note: [Col. 1662D] Gratian cites this same chapter, which he here attributes to the Council of Tribur, below, Causa 35, question 2, from the council at Verberie; Burchard and Ivo do likewise. Its ruling occurs in the Council of Worms, c. 63.] [Note: [Col. 1661] c. 14 of the Council of Compiègne, held A.D. 756. Regino, bk. 2, c. 219. Burchard, bk. 17, c. 12. Ivo, Decretum, pt. 9, c. 72.]

If anyone has committed fornication with a mother and her daughter [Note: [Col. 1661] “has”: the collected editions], the mother being ignorant concerning the daughter and the daughter concerning the mother, he [Note: [Col. 1661] added: “the man”: Basel edition; Lyons editions II and III] shall never take a wife; but the women, if they wish, may take [Col. 1662B] husbands. But if the women themselves knew this, they are to remain forever without husbands [Note: [Col. 1661] “in perpetuity”: Burchard; “in perpetual [state]”: Regino, Ivo].

### C. X. On the same subject. Likewise in the same source.

[Note: [Col. 1661] Ruling c. 43 of the Council of Tribur (held A.D. 895), briefly transcribed. Regino, bk. 2, c. 207. Burchard, bk. 17, c. 16. Ivo, Decretum, pt. 9, c. 76.]

A certain man committed fornication with a certain woman; afterward [Note: [Col. 1661] “and afterward”: the collected editions] his son, unaware of his father’s deed, violated the same woman. When the father learned this [Note: [Col. 1661] “had learned”: Regino; “was learning”: Burchard, Ivo; “did not know”: Lyons edition I; “knew the matter”: the remaining editions, first Paris and Lyons editions II and III], he confessed regarding himself and his son. They decreed that it was better for such persons, after worthy penance, to be allowed lawful marriages than that they might perhaps commit worse offenses. But the fornicatress [Note: [Col. 1661] “but more severe measures are to be taken with that fornicatress”: Regino] is to remain without hope of marriage.

# CAUSA XXXV

[Col. 1661]

[Col. 1661C] **GRATIAN**

A certain man, after his wife had died, joined another woman to himself in marriage. She was related in the fourth degree to his deceased wife, but was connected to the man himself in the sixth line. After three years, children having been born from her, he is accused before the Church; he pleads ignorance.

(Question I.) Here it is first asked whether it is lawful to take as wife a woman from one’s own kinship.

(Question II.) Secondly, whether a woman from the blood-relationship of one’s wife may be taken in marriage.

(Question III.) Thirdly, to what degree everyone ought to abstain both from his own blood relatives and from those of his wife.

(Question IV.) Fourthly, why blood relationship is reckoned to the sixth degree, so that it is neither extended beyond that nor stops short of it.

(Question V.) Fifthly, how degrees of blood relationship are to be calculated.

[Col. 1662C] (Question VI.) Sixthly, who ought to establish kinship by oath.

(Question VII.) Seventhly, whether those born of incestuous persons are to be regarded as children.

(Question VIII.) Eighthly, if a woman has unknowingly been taken as wife despite some blood relationship or affinity, whether by dispensation she may remain united to her husband.

(Question IX.) Ninthly, if it happens that the Church is deceived and separates a woman from her husband on account of blood relationship, but after four years—marriages having been celebrated on both sides—it is discovered that she was not related to her former husband, whether the second marriages are to be dissolved and the former ones restored.

(Question X.) Tenthly, if the widow of someone’s own kinship has entered a second marriage, whether offspring born from that union may attain fellowship with any member of the first husband’s kindred.

# QUESTION I

[Col. 1663A]

**GRATIAN**

That it is lawful for us to take in marriage women related either to ourselves or to our wives is proved by examples and authorities. For Abraham [Note: [Col. 1663] Genesis, c. 11.] took Sarai, the daughter of his brother—that is, the sister of Lot—as his wife. Isaac [Note: [Col. 1663] ibid., c. 24.] took Rebecca as his wife; she was the daughter of his mother’s first cousin. Jacob [Note: [Col. 1663] ibid., c. 29.] joined to himself in marriage two sisters, Leah and Rachel, daughters of his maternal uncle Laban.

§ 1. In the Law also [Note: [Col. 1663] Numbers, c. 36, v. 6.] the Lord commanded Moses that no one should take a wife except from his own tribe and family. Likewise [Note: [Col. 1663] Deuteronomy, c. 25, v. 5.], if anyone should die without children, the Lord commanded that his brother should take the deceased man’s wife for himself and raise up offspring for his brother. Moreover, all those to whom that Law itself has come [Col. 1663B] are shown to be bound by its commands, except such commands as are shown to have been nullified either by Gospel precepts or apostolic ordinances. But no Gospel precept or apostolic ordinance is found forbidding unions of blood relatives. Hence, as they were lawful at the beginning, so they are shown to be lawful now.

§ 2. The response to these arguments is as follows. Unions of blood relatives are found to have been permitted at times for necessity’s sake, and at times commanded for the sake of a just reason. For when, at the beginning, one man and one woman from his side were formed by God, sisters necessarily were joined to brothers. But what is done under compulsion of necessity ought likewise to cease when the necessity ceases. Thus the union of blood relatives is now assumed all the more damnably inasmuch as it is shown to be less necessary.

[Col. 1663C] Hence such a union is found later to have been forbidden by law, the Lord saying through Moses [Note: [Col. 1663] Leviticus, c. 18, v. 9.]: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister.”

Augustine says accordingly in *The City of God*, book XV, c. 16 [Note: [Col. 1663] Ivo, Panormia, bk. 7, c. 32; Decretum, pt. 8, c. 39.]:

### CHAPTER ONE. Why it was established that we should not take blood relatives as wives.

Since, then, the human race after the first union of the man made from dust and his spouse made from the man’s side required the union of males and females in order to multiply by begetting, and since there were no human beings except those born from those two, [Col. 1664A] men took their sisters as wives. Certainly, the more ancient this was under the compulsion of necessity, the more damnable it became when later performed in defiance of religious prohibition.

For the most sound [Note: [Col. 1663] “most certain”: the collected editions] principle of charity was adopted, that human beings, for whom harmonious union was useful and most honorable [Note: [Col. 1663] “honorable”: the original; Ivo], should be bound together by ties of diverse relationships; and that one person should not possess many relationships in a single person [Note: [Col. 1663] “in one”: the collected editions], but that individual relationships should be distributed among individual persons, so that, for the more diligent binding together of social life [Note: [Col. 1663] absent from the same editions, first Lyons editions II and III], many people might hold many people.

“Father” and “father-in-law,” indeed, are names of two relationships. Therefore, while someone has one man as father and another as father-in-law [Note: [Col. 1663D] “Therefore, while someone has”: in printed manuscripts of St Augustine, and in Ivo and Panormia, it reads: “Therefore, that each person may have another as father.” But Gratian’s reading was judged preferable.], charity extends itself more widely [Note: [Col. 1663] “may extend”: Ivo]. Yet Adam was compelled to be both father and father-in-law to his sons and daughters, when brothers and sisters were united in marriage [Note: [Col. 1663] “marriage”: Ivo; the collected editions] [Note: [Col. 1663] “were united”: Basel edition]. Likewise Eve [Col. 1664B] his wife was both mother and mother-in-law to children of each sex; if there had been two women, one mother *and* the other mother-in-law, social affection would have bound itself together more abundantly.

And below:

§ 1. But there was then no source from which this could happen, when there were no human beings except brothers and sisters descended from those first two. It therefore had to happen when [Note: [Col. 1663] “which”: the collected editions] it could happen: when an abundance existed from which [Note: [Col. 1663] “where”: the same editions; Ivo, Panormia] wives might be taken who were no longer sisters; *and* not only would there be no necessity for this to happen [Note: [Col. 1663] “and that would not happen where”: the same editions], but, if it did happen, it would be a crime.

And below:

§ 2. As the human race increased *and multiplied* [Note: [Col. 1663] “and multiplied”: absent from Ivo], we see this observed even among impious worshipers of many false gods: even though fraternal marriages are permitted by perverse laws [Note: [Col. 1663] “were permitted”: Basel edition], nevertheless [Col. 1664C] a better custom prefers to shrink in horror from that very permission, *and [Note: [Col. 1663] “and—from ‘permission’”: absent from Ivo], although it was altogether lawful to take sisters in marriage in the earliest times of the human race*, it abhors the practice [Note: [Col. 1663] “and abhors”: the same source; the collected editions] [Note: [Col. 1663] “opposes”: the same editions; Ivo, Panormia] as though it could never have been lawful.

And below:

§ 3. The union of male and female, insofar as concerns the mortal race [Note: [Col. 1663] “human”: the same editions], is a certain nursery-ground [Note: [Col. 1663D] “Nursery-ground”: Ivo and Panormia have the remainder as Gratian does, but in place of “of charity” have “of the city.” The complete passage in St Augustine is: “The union, therefore, of male and female, insofar as concerns the mortal race, is a certain nursery-ground of the city. But the earthly city needs generation only; the heavenly city also needs regeneration, in order to escape the guilt of generation.” Yet because of the gloss on the phrase “city,” nothing has been changed. Many other matters, however, have been corrected chiefly from the original itself.] of charity; but the heavenly city has need, in order to escape the guilt of generation.

**Gratian.** Thus Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the others who took wives from their own [Col. 1665A] kindred are excused by this custom, which had its origin in the very beginning of the propagation of humankind and which no law commanding the contrary had nullified. Yet another very sound reason why this was done may also be understood.

All others having been defiled by idolatry, the family of Heber alone [Note: [Col. 1665] Genesis, c. 11.] remained in the worship of the one God. Hence Abraham was thrown by the Chaldeans together with his brother Aram into the fire which he refused to worship, so that by being burned he might experience the power of the divinity whom he had disdained to honor by worship. Therefore, lest believers should fall into idolatry through union with unbelievers and thus offend God—as formerly before the Flood [Note: [Col. 1665] ibid., c. 6.] the sons of God, mingled with the daughters of men, had provoked him to anger—it was most rightly provided that the most holy patriarchs should take wives only from their own kinship, that is, from the family of believers.

Thus also, when the children of Israel, about to enter the land of promise, heard from the Lord that they should neither take daughters of the Canaanites [Col. 1665B] as wives nor give their own daughters to them in marriage, the Lord immediately added [Note: [Col. 1665] Deuteronomy, c. 7, v. 4.]: “Lest they cause you to depart from your God and commit fornication with foreign gods.” Thus Ezra also [Note: [Col. 1665] cf. Ezra, c. 10.] commanded that Idumean women and women of other nations, through whom the children of Israel were going after foreign gods, be separated from them.

§ 1. There is also another reason why unions of blood relatives were at first permitted—or rather commanded—among the people of God. For God so ordered the salvation of humankind from the beginning that he established the primitive Church in the people who were near to him by blood relationship of the flesh. Accordingly, he first chose apostles from the Jewish people and established them as, so to speak, the foundation of the Church; through their preaching many from that same people were converted to God and in themselves furnished the origin of the Church.

[Col. 1665C] Then, after the Jewish people had been abandoned in the blindness of its unbelief, Gospel preaching was transferred to the Gentiles, who were alien from Christ both in faith and in kinship of the flesh. And Christ, as though rejecting union with a blood relative, chose a wife for himself from an alien kindred, fulfilling what he had promised through the Prophet [Note: [Col. 1665] Isaiah, c. 50, v. 1.]: “Because of your sins I dismissed your mother as an adulteress and a repudiated woman.” And again through another Prophet [Note: [Col. 1665] Hosea, c. 2, final verse.]: “I shall call ‘my people’ those who were not my people.”

Therefore, as a sacrament of this matter, unions of blood relatives were initially allowed among the people of God, but are now forbidden. And because the people of the faithful are found not in one family alone but among every multitude of nations, everyone is permitted to take a wife not from his own kindred but from any other.

§ 2. Now the assertion that precepts [Col. 1666A] of the Law are to be observed unless they are shown to have been nullified by Gospel or apostolic institutions is true. But since the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1665] Romans, c. 8, v. 2.] proves that all figurative ordinances were given for a time, and therefore declares that, truth having come, they are no longer to be observed; and since this ordinance, as has been shown above, is proved to have been instituted by God for the sake of a sacrament: it is most certain that this too was nullified together with the other figurative ordinances.

Nevertheless, just as the Apostle added certain things by way of counsel [Note: [Col. 1665] cf. Galatians, c. 5.] which were not found defined in Gospel precepts, and yet were not therefore rejected by the other Apostles as rash or superfluous, so also, after the apostolic age, the Church added certain counsels of perfection—for example, concerning the continence of ministers, the confecting of the mysteries, and the celebration of offices—which are by no means [Col. 1666B] to be rejected, but to be received with diligent reverence. Therefore unions of blood relatives, although they are not found forbidden by Gospel and apostolic precepts, must nevertheless be avoided because they are restricted by ecclesiastical institutions.

# QUESTIONS II AND III

**GRATIAN**

Since, therefore, it is necessary to abstain from unions of blood relatives, as has been proved, it must be considered to what degree one ought to abstain from one’s own blood relatives, and whether it is lawful to take as wife a woman from one’s own wife’s kindred.

[Col. 1666C] Pope Gregory writes as follows concerning these matters in the Council of Meaux [Note: [Col. 1665D] “Council of Meaux”: Burchard, Ivo, and the author of the Panormia cite merely “from the Council of Meaux”; the Master says “Gregory.” Polycarp [Col. 1666D] has: “Gregory in the decrees.” It may easily have happened that Gregory’s decree was reported in some council of Meaux, giving rise to Gratian’s citation.] [Note: [Col. 1665] It is absolutely certain that these are neither Gregory I’s nor the Council of Meaux’s. The author of this chapter seems to have looked to the first letter of Gregory III to Boniface. Burchard, bk. 7, c. 16. Ivo, Panormia, bk. 7, c. 81; Decretum, pt. 9, c. 51; Polycarp, bk. 6, tit. 4; Peter Lombard, bk. 4, distinction 41.]:

### C. I. No one shall take a wife from his own kinship unto the seventh generation.

Concerning affinity arising from blood relationship, it has been resolved that the degrees of kinship be observed unto the seventh generation [Note: [Col. 1665] “be observed”: Basel edition]. For the inheritance of property too, sanctioned by the legal determinations of written instruments, extends the succession of heirs to the seventh degree. For they would not succeed [Note: [Col. 1665] added: “to them”: Argentinian, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice I editions] unless it were owed them by descent from their kindred.

### C. II. Those who take blood relatives as wives are to be marked with infamy. Likewise Pope Callixtus, Letter II to the Bishops of Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 1665] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Council of Orléans III. Burchard, bk. 7, c. 1; Anselm, bk. 11, c. 90 (to the words “repel”); Ivo, Decretum, pt. 9, c. 22.]

Forbid unions of blood relatives to be made [Note: [Col. 1665] “are forbidden”: the original; Ivo, Decretum; the collected editions; added: “wherefore”: the same editions], since both divine laws and [Note: [Col. 1665] absent from Nuremberg and Venice I–II editions; “and of the secular world”: the remaining editions] secular laws forbid them. Divine laws, therefore, in dealing with this matter, not only cast out those who issue from such unions, [Col. 1667A] but also call them accursed. Secular laws [Note: [Col. 1667] “also”: Argentinian edition; “therefore”: the remaining editions] call such persons infamous and exclude them from inheritance. But we, following our fathers *and [Note: [Col. 1667] “and—adhering”: absent from Burchard and Ivo] adhering to their footsteps,* mark them with infamy and judge them to be infamous, because they are stained with the marks of infamy; nor ought we to accept either them as men or their accusations, whom [Note: [Col. 1667] “which”: the collected editions] secular laws reject.

And below:

§ 1. We call those persons blood relatives whom divine law and the laws of emperors, Romans, and Greeks call blood relatives, and whom they admit to inheritance and cannot exclude.

[Col. 1667B]

### C. III. Affines may be joined in the fifth generation; in the fourth, if they are found so joined, they are not to be separated. Likewise Pope Fabian.

[Note: [Col. 1667] Rather, from Theodore’s *Penitential*, c. 11, in Petitus. Peter Lombard, ibid.; cf. below, c. 13.]

Concerning relatives who become connected by affinity through husband and wife: when the wife or husband has died, they may be joined in the fifth generation; in the fourth, if they are found so joined, they are not to be separated. But in the third degree [Note: [Col. 1667] “nevertheless”: the collected editions, first Argentinian edition] of kinship it is not lawful to take the other’s wife [Note: [Col. 1667] “to marry”: Basel edition] after that person’s death. A man is to be joined in marriage on equal terms to women who are his own blood relatives and to the blood relatives of his wife after his wife’s death.

### C. IV. The same authority.

[Note: [Col. 1667] A chapter of uncertain origin.]

Those who take as wives women close in blood and are separated shall not be permitted to join other wives to themselves in marriage so long as both are alive [unless [Note: [Col. 1667] “unless—excused”: apparently Gratian’s words] ignorance excuses them].

[Col. 1667C] Hence, in the Council at Verberie [Note: [Col. 1667C] This chapter has been discussed above, Causa 34, questions 1 and 2.] [Note: [Col. 1667] cf. above, Causa 34, questions 1 and 2, c. 9.]:

### C. V. He who unknowingly commits incest is not forbidden to take a wife.

If anyone has committed fornication with a mother and her daughter [Note: [Col. 1667] “has”: the collected editions], the mother being ignorant concerning [Col. 1668A] the daughter and the daughter concerning the mother, he shall never take a wife; but the women, if they wish, may take husbands. But if the women themselves knew this, they are to remain forever without husbands.

### C. VI. Likewise from the same source.

[Note: [Col. 1667C] Burchard and Ivo also cite from the Council at Verberie, c. 5; the ruling, however, occurs in the Council of Tribur, c. 44.] [Note: [Col. 1667] The ruling is reported as c. 24 of the Council of Tribur, held A.D. 895. Regino, bk. 2, c. 210; Burchard, bk. 17, c. 13; Ivo, Decretum, pt. 9, c. 73.]

If [Note: [Col. 1667] added: “however”: Argentinian edition; “indeed”: Basel edition] a man has committed fornication with a woman and his brother, unaware of it, has taken the same woman as wife, the brother who committed fornication, because he concealed the offense from his brother, shall do penance for seven years [Note: [Col. 1667C] “Seven years”: these two words are absent from Burchard and Ivo [ [Col. 1667] and Regino]. Yet in Burchard, bk. 19, c. 5, where a priest questions a penitent concerning this sin and gives counsel, these words are found: “If you have done this, because you concealed the offense from your brother, do penance for seven years during the lawful fast-days.” But in the Council of Tribur: “Let him be restrained by a very severe penance and suitable chastisement.”], and after penance shall marry. But the woman shall do penance until death and [Note: [Col. 1667] “and—remain”: absent from Regino] remain without hope of marriage.

**Gratian.** The other authorities are to be understood concerning those who are joined unknowingly.

[Col. 1668B] Hence Pope Julius [Note: [Col. 1667D] This chapter as far as the word “Furthermore” is cited by Burchard, Ivo, and Panormia—though the Master has it as Gratian does—from the Council of Orléans, c. 10; many matters relevant to this question occur there. The remaining part of this [Col. 1668] chapter occurs in the Panormia—since the other collectors do not have it—as from the same council; but Gratian, below, Causa 27, question 2, c. *Qui desponsatam*, attributes it to Gregory.] [Note: [Col. 1667] c. 10 of the Third Council of Orléans, held A.D. 538, abridged. Burchard, bk. 7, c. 14; Ivo, Panormia, bk. 7, c. 79; Decretum, pt. 9, c. 49; Peter Lombard, bk. 4, distinction 41.]:

### C. VII. No one shall take a wife from blood relationship of his own or of his wife unto the seventh degree.

We permit no person of either sex to take a wife from the kinship of his own blood or of his wife unto the [Note: [Col. 1667] “in”: Burchard, Ivo; the collected editions] seventh degree of descent [Note: [Col. 1667] “generation”: Basel edition], or to be united with the stain of incest [Note: [Col. 1667] “be stained”: cited collections]. Furthermore, we have added this: just as it is not [Note: [Col. 1667] cf. Causa 27, question 2, c. 12.] lawful for any [Note: [Col. 1667] “some”: Basel edition] Christian to take a spouse from his own blood relationship, so it is not lawful to take one from the blood relationship of his wife, because of the unity of the flesh.

### C. VIII. Incestuous persons are worthy of no name of marriage. Likewise from the Council of Agde, c. 61.

[Note: [Col. 1667] Held A.D. 506; cf., however, Causa 30, distinction 23, c. 30; cf. Council of Orléans III, c. 2; Epaone, c. 30; Tours II, c. 22; *Collectio tripartita*, pt. 2, tit. 28, c. 59; Ivo, Decretum, pt. 9, c. 25. The first portion is reported by Burchard, bk. 7, c. 4; Anselm, bk. 11, c. 88; Ivo, Decretum, ibid., c. 40.]

For incestuous [Note: [Col. 1667] “incest”: Argentinian edition] unions we reserve absolutely no pardon, unless they heal adultery by separation. Incestuous persons [Note: [Col. 1667] “incestuous [persons]”: Hispanic Collection; Ivo; Basel edition] are not to be assigned any name of marriage, whom it is even disastrous to specify.

[Col. 1668C] § 1. For we judge these persons to be incestuous: anyone who defiles by carnal union his brother’s widow—who [Note: [Col. 1667] “who—from ‘had been’”: absent from Ivo] had previously almost been his sister; anyone who takes his full sister as wife [Note: [Col. 1667] “takes”: the same source]; anyone who marries his stepmother; [Col. 1669A] anyone who joins himself to his first cousin [Note: [Col. 1669] “or cousin”: the same source; “and cousin”: the collected editions]; anyone who has intercourse with the widow or daughter of his maternal uncle, or with the daughter of his paternal uncle [Note: [Col. 1669] “father”: the same source], or with his stepdaughter; or anyone who defiles in intercourse or takes as wife a woman from his own blood relationship, or one whom his blood relative has had [Note: [Col. 1669] “has had”: the collected editions].

All these persons, both formerly and now, we do not doubt to be incestuous under this constitution [Note: [Col. 1669] “institution”: the collected editions, first Basel and Lyons editions II–III], and we command them to remain among the catechumens and pray until lawful satisfaction has been made. We so forbid this at the present time that we do not dissolve things which have thus far been established.

§ 2. Certainly, those to whom unlawful union is forbidden shall have [Note: [Col. 1669C] “Shall have”: this is the reading in the Council of Agde and in Ivo. In the Council of Epaone it reads: “shall not have.” But in the Council of Tours, which cites Epaone, it reads: “shall have.” The same occurs below, question 8, c. *Haec salubriter*, from Gregory. In the indicated Capitularies this ruling is more fully explained: “But those to whom unlawful union is forbidden—unless they are persons whom decrees of the holy Fathers prohibit from being joined in marriage—shall have freedom to enter a better marriage.”] freedom to enter a better marriage.

[Col. 1669B]

### C. IX. Incestuous persons are to be excommunicated until satisfaction. Likewise from the Council of Lleida, c. 4.

[Note: [Col. 1669] Held A.D. 546. Burchard, bk. 7, c. 3; Ivo, Decretum, pt. 8, c. 29.]

Concerning those who stain themselves with incestuous [Note: [Col. 1669] “incest”: Burchard, Ivo] defilement [Note: [Col. 1669] “pollute”: the same sources; Hispanic Collection; Basel edition], it has been resolved that, as long as they persist in that detestable and unlawful cohabitation of the flesh, they are to be admitted into church only as far as the Mass of the Catechumens. No Christian may even take food with them, as the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1669] “says the Apostle,” or “commanded”: Hispanic Collection] commanded [Note: [Col. 1669] “ought”: the same source, Burchard, Ivo; cf. 1 Corinthians, c. 5, v. 11.].

### C. X. No one shall take as wife a woman carnally known by a blood relative or defiled by any pollution. Likewise Pope Gregory to Felix, Bishop of the city of Messina, book XII, letter 31.

[Note: [Col. 1669] A spurious letter. Anselm, bk. 10, c. 41; Ivo, Decretum, pt. 9, c. 26.]

No Christian is certainly permitted, nor shall be permitted, to take in marriage a woman whom someone of his own blood relationship had as wife [Note: [Col. 1669] “has had—or has defiled”: Basel edition] or defiled by any unlawful pollution, because such intercourse is incestuous [Col. 1669C] and abominable to God and to all human beings. We read that the holy Fathers long ago ordained that incestuous persons are to be assigned no designation of marriage [Note: [Col. 1669] “under no”: Basel edition; cf. above, c. 8.].

[Col. 1670A] **Gratian.** That is, in the natural order; but if it occurs extraordinarily, it is not so.

For Pope Urban II says to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble [Note: [Col. 1669D] “Of Grenoble”: previously it read: “Urban II, to Gratian, Bishop of Naples” [ [Col. 1669] thus the collected editions]. It was corrected from Polycarp; this Hugh is mentioned by Sigebert under the year 1084 and by Trithemius [Col. 1670] under Guy, Abbot of La Grande Chartreuse.] [Note: [Col. 1669] Letter of uncertain date; cf. Ivo, letter 232 to Hildebert; Polycarp, bk. 6, tit. 1.]:

### C. XI. Extraordinary pollution in the natural organs does not impede marriage.

Extraordinary pollution, unless [Note: [Col. 1670C] “Unless”: Polycarp reads: “unless committed in the natural organs.”] committed in the natural organs, or repeatedly perpetrated without marital intention [Note: [Col. 1670C] “Intention”: the same source reads “effect”], if it has been established by sacramental proofs to be so, as was reported to us in your letter [Note: [Col. 1669] “indicated”: Argentinian and Basel editions], does not seem to impede marriage, although it is itself criminal and condemnable.

### C. XII. No one shall take in marriage the widow of his wife’s blood relatives unto the third generation. Likewise Pope Julius.

[Note: [Col. 1670C] “Of his wife”: thus corrected from ancient copies. In the common editions it read “of his own [relatives]” [ [Col. 1669] thus the collected editions, first Argentinian and Basel editions].] [Note: [Col. 1669] Rather, from Theodore’s *Penitential*, c. 11, in Petitus. Peter Lombard, bk. 4, distinction 41.]

[Col. 1670B] It has likewise been decreed that no one shall take in marriage the widow of his wife’s father, the widow of his wife’s brother, or the widow of his wife’s son; no one shall take as wife the widow of his wife’s blood relatives unto the third generation [Note: [Col. 1669] added: “for himself”: Basel and Lyons editions II–III]; but in the fourth [Note: [Col. 1669] “fourth—and fifth”: the collected editions; Böhm] and fifth generations, if they are found so joined, they are not to be separated.

### C. XIII. Everyone must equally abstain from his own blood relatives and those of his wife. The same authority.

[Note: [Col. 1669] Cf. above, c. 3. Burchard, bk. 7, c. 6; Ivo, Decretum, pt. 9, c. 43; Polycarp, bk. 6, tit. 4; Peter Lombard, ibid.—all from Julius.]

A man is to be joined equally to his own blood relatives and to the blood relatives of his wife.

### C. XIV. The same degree of blood relationship is to be observed in one’s own kindred and that of one’s spouse. Likewise Isidore from the Council of Mâcon.

[Note: [Col. 1669] Cf. the Second Council of Chalon, held A.D. 813, c. 29, and the Council of Worms, held A.D. 868, c. 78. Burchard, bk. 7, c. 8; Ivo, Panormia, bk. 7, c. 69; Decretum, pt. 9, c. 44; Peter Lombard, ibid.; cf. Hugh of St Victor, *On the Sacraments*, bk. 2, pt. 11, c. 15.] [Note: [Col. 1670C] In the Panormia this is cited as here. Hugh, however, has “from the Council of Mâcon”; Burchard, “of Mâcon”; Ivo, “of Mantica,” with no mention of Isidore. [Col. 1670D] In Polycarp it is placed together with c. *Conjunctiones*, above in this same question, which is in fact Callixtus’s. It occurs in the Second Council of Chalon, c. 29, and in the Council of Worms it is the second part of canon 78.] [Note: [Col. 1669] “Of Mâcon”: Basel edition.]

[Col. 1670C] Certainly, the degree of blood relationship which must be observed [Note: [Col. 1669] “preserved”: the same source; “observed”: the remaining editions] in respect of the husband himself must likewise be maintained by the law of marriage in the kindred of his wife. For since it is established that the two are [Note: [Col. 1669] “were”: Burchard, Ivo; the collected editions] one flesh, their kindred on either side [Col. 1671A] [Note: [Col. 1671] “on both sides”: Council of Worms] must be reckoned common to them [Note: [Col. 1671] “believed”: the same source; Burchard, Ivo; Argentinian and Basel editions; “yielded”: Nuremberg and Venice I–II editions], as it is written [Note: [Col. 1671] Genesis, c. 2, v. 24.]: “The two shall be one flesh.”

### C. XV. A daughter-in-law is to be regarded no differently than a daughter. Likewise Augustine, book XXII against Faustus, c. 61.

If husband and wife are no longer two but one flesh, a daughter-in-law is to be regarded no differently than a daughter.

### C. XVI. Everyone must keep track of his own lineage unto the seventh generation. Likewise Pope Gregory to the Bishops of Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 1671C] Burchard both cites and reports this as Gratian does; Hugh, the author of Polycarp, and the Master cite Gregory without qualification. Anselm and Ivo cite it from St Gregory’s letter to Felix. In the Panormia both headings are joined thus: “From Gregory’s letter sent to the bishops of Gaul, letter 31, book 12.” The chapter occurs in the Capitularies, bk. 6, c. 80; and in the additions is the first part of c. 200, which the index attributes to Pope Gregory from letters sent to St Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz. Indeed, the first part, as far as the word “generation,” is found in the final letter of Gregory II inserted in the volumes of councils.] [Note: [Col. 1671] The first part of the chapter is in Letter 1 of Gregory III, written A.D. 731, to Boniface, c. 5; the second in the thirteenth letter of Gregory II, written A.D. 726, to the same person, c. 1. Cf., however, the apocryphal letter of Gregory to Felix of Messina. Burchard, bk. 7, c. 11; Anselm, bk. 10, c. 40 (41); Ivo, Panormia, bk. 7, c. 76; Decretum, pt. 9, c. 26; Hugh, ibid.; Peter Lombard, bk. 4, distinction 40; Polycarp, bk. 6, tit. 4.]

We decree that everyone must keep track of his own lineage unto the seventh generation [Note: [Col. 1671C] “Everyone”: in St Gregory, Anselm, and Ivo the following words are inserted here [ [Col. 1671] read in the apocryphal letter to Felix]: “concerning those who have been faithfully instructed and now stand firmly planted with an immovable root.”] [Note: [Col. 1671] “preserve”: Basel edition], and, so long as they recognize themselves as near in affinity, we deny them access to marital union. If they do so, they are to be separated [Note: [Col. 1671C] “If they do so, they are to be separated”: these words occur only in Burchard [ [Col. 1671] and Ivo, Panormia, and Hugh]. In St Gregory, Anselm, and Ivo, the words of the chapter *Nec eam*, above in this same question, immediately follow those above.].

[Col. 1671B]

### C. XVII. On the same subject. Likewise Pope Nicholas II to the Suffragans of the Church of Amalfi.

[Note: [Col. 1671] It is read in the Roman Council held A.D. 1059, cc. 11–12, and in the letter of Nicholas II to the suffragan bishops of the Church of Amalfi, written in the same year. Peter Lombard, ibid.]

No one shall take a wife from his own blood relationship until after the seventh generation [Note: [Col. 1671] “unto”: Roman Council], or so long as the kindred can be known.

§ 1. A layman who has at the same time a wife and a concubine shall not receive communion in the Church.

### C. XVIII. So long as descent between any persons is recollected or retained in memory, they shall not be joined to one another. Likewise from the Council of Worms, c. 32.

[Note: [Col. 1671] Held A.D. 868. Regino, bk. 2, c. 262; Burchard, bk. 7, c. 2; Ivo, Decretum, pt. 9, c. 39.]
