[Col. 1672A] In the union of the faithful we do not define a numerical limit of generations, but establish *this*: that no Christian may take a wife from his own blood relationship or kindred, for so long as the descent is recollected, known [Note: [Col. 1671] “or known”: the collected editions], or retained in memory [Note: [Col. 1671] “in memory”: the same editions; Böhm].

C. XIX. No one shall take a wife from among those related by his own blood up to the seventh degree. Likewise from the Council of Lyons. [Note: [Col. 1671D] The other collectors also cite this as from the Council of Lyons. In some manuscripts of Gratian it reads: “from the Council of Lugdunum.” [Col. 1672C] Blessed Boniface, in a letter to Pope Zacharias, mentions a synod of London, held by disciples of Blessed Gregory, at which incestuous unions had been treated. Something similar occurs in *Capitularies*, book 6, ch. 128. Moreover, in chapter 8 of the Council of Trosly at Rheims, among many other matters, these words are read: “And elsewhere in the canons it is commanded that no one contract marriages within the line of affinity or the nearness of his own blood; nor should anyone presume to marry virgins without a priest’s blessing.”] [Note: [Col. 1671] Cf. *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, book 6, ch. 130.—Burchard, book 7, ch. 13. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, ch. 78; *Decree*, part 9, ch. 48. Peter Lombard, ibid.]

No one shall take wives from among those related by his own blood up to the seventh degree, nor without a priest’s blessing. Those who are about to marry, having been blessed by a priest, may dare to marry, and must not presume otherwise. [Note: [Col. 1671] “who had previously been unmarried”: Burchard, Ivo, *Decree*—“had been married”: *Panormia*.]

Gratian. By the authorities set forth above, everyone is forbidden union with blood relatives up to the seventh generation. But the following is objected: that statement of Gregory to Augustine, bishop of the English, ch. 6. [Note: [Col. 1672C] The words of this chapter down to “But the same” occur in Blessed Gregory. Yet both these and what follows occur in John the Deacon’s *Life of Blessed Gregory*, book 2, ch. 38, from ch. 37. Hugh, Burchard, Ivo, and the *Panormia* cite it as from a letter of John, bishop of Constantinople, to Felix, bishop of Sicily. These same words of Blessed Gregory are also repeated in two letters of Alexander II: one reported by Ivo, part 9, ch. 6, and in the *Panormia*, book 7, [Col. 1672D] chs. 55–56; the other reported below, question 5, ch. “To the See.” Much in this chapter has been restored from Blessed Gregory and John the Deacon.] [Note: [Col. 1671] This chapter is taken from John the Deacon, book 2, ch. 38.—Cf. letter to Augustine, letter 64 (written A.D. 601), book 11, Maurist edition; and the spurious letter to Felix, bishop of Messina.—Burchard, book 7, chs. 19–20. Anselm, book 10, ch. 13 (38, 39). Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, chs. 71–72; *Decree*, part 9, chs. 55–56. Polycarpus, book 6, title 4.—Hugh of St Victor, book 2, part 11, ch. 16. Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 40.]

C. XX. The English are permitted to unite in the fourth or fifth generation.

A certain *earthly law in* the Roman commonwealth permits the son and daughter either of a brother and sister, or of two full brothers, or of two sisters, to unite. [Note: [Col. 1671] “a law in the Roman republic”: Burchard, Ivo, *Decree*, Hugh.] [Note: [Col. 1671] “that the son either of a brother or of a sister”: original—“that either brother and sister”: Burchard, Ivo, *Decree*, Hugh—“that the son either of a brother or of a sister”: editions collated by the editors, first Basel edition.] But experience has taught us that offspring cannot thrive from such a marriage, *and sacred law forbids the uncovering of the shame of kinship*. [Note: [Col. 1671] “and”: revised text—absent from the cited collections.] [Col. 1673A] Hence it is necessary that the faithful may lawfully be joined to one another in the fourth or fifth generation. [Note: [Col. 1673] “already”: same editions—absent from the Argentinensis and Basel editions.] [Note: [Col. 1673C] In Blessed Gregory the reading is “in the fourth”; and, not much differently, [Col. 1673D] in John the Deacon: “it is necessary that already in the third or fourth generation the faithful may lawfully be joined to one another. For the second, of which we have spoken, must entirely abstain from one another.” Thus it is quoted in Alexander’s letter below, question 5, ch. “To the See,” § “This computation.” In the other letter of the same Alexander, indicated in the preceding note, however, the reading is: “already in the fourth or fifth.” He who placed the case here followed this reading.] [Note: [Col. 1673] “generation”: original—Burchard, Anselm, Ivo, *Decree*—Argentinensis, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice, first edition.] [Note: [Col. 1673] “the faithful”: Hugh.] [Note: [Col. 1673] “be joined”: the cited collections.]

§ 1. But the same most humble Father Gregory, when after a long time he was asked by Felix, bishop of the Sicilian city of Messina, whether he had written to Augustine that marriages contracted among the English in the fourth generation should by no means be dissolved, gave, among other things, this answer: “What I wrote to Augustine, bishop of the English people—your foster-son, as you remember—concerning union of blood, I wrote specifically for him and for the English people, who had recently come to the faith, *and not generally* for *others*, lest they should withdraw through fear of stricter measures from the good which they had begun.” [Note: [Col. 1673] “reason”: same editions—Argentinensis, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice, first edition.] [Note: [Col. 1673] absent from the Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1673] “consanguinity”: original—the cited collections.] [Note: [Col. 1673] “had received”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.] [Note: [Col. 1673] absent from Ivo, *Panormia*.] [Note: [Col. 1673] “others”: absent from the cited collections.] [Note: [Col. 1673] “certainly”: absent from the original.] You should know that I wrote this with complete certainty. Therefore the whole city of Rome bears witness for me. Nor did I prescribe these commands to them in writing with the intention that, after they had been established with a firm root in the faith, if they should be found within their own blood relationship, they should not be separated, or that they should unite within the line of affinity—that is, up to the seventh generation. [Note: [Col. 1673] “I wrote these commands to him/them”: editions collated by the editors—cited collections.] [Note: [Col. 1673] “be joined”: Basel edition.]

Rather, while they are still neophytes, it is necessary very often first to teach them about unlawful things, to instruct them by words and examples, and *reasonably and faithfully to prohibit what they may thereafter do in such matters*. [Note: [Col. 1673] The editions collated by the editors and the cited collections read: “But because, while those neophytes still existed there, it was first permissible to allow them unlawful things, and …”; the words marked with asterisks are likewise absent from them.] [Note: [Col. 1673] “to teach them to avoid”: original.] For, according to the Apostle, who says, “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food,” [Note: [Col. 1673] 1 Corinthians 3:2.] we allowed them *these things* for the time being—not for their successors, as has been stated—lest the good which had been planted with a *still* weak root be uprooted, but rather be strengthened somewhat and preserved unto perfection. [Note: [Col. 1673] “be burned up”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1673] “begun”: original.]

[Col. 1673C] C. XXI. No one henceforth shall be joined in marriage in the fifth or sixth generation. Likewise, the following from the Council of Chalon is objected. [Note: [Col. 1674D] The other collectors and Hugh likewise cite it from the Council of Chalon. It appears in book 5 of the *Capitularies*, ch. 99. Except for the words “or in the fifth and sixth,” the remainder is read almost identically in the Council of Mainz under Charles, ch. 54; in another Council of Mainz under Rabanus, ch. 30; and in the Council of Worms, in the first part of canon 78. For the latter part is the chapter “Certainly, consanguinity,” cited above.] [Note: [Col. 1673] Rather, it is from Mainz, held A.D. 813, ch. 54, as Regino correctly cites it, book 2, ch. 226.—Burchard, book 6, ch. 18. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, ch. 70; *Decree*, part 9, ch. 54. Hugh, ibid.]

We forbid anyone henceforth to be joined in marriage in the fourth, fifth, or sixth generation. [Note: [Col. 1673] “or fifth, or sixth”: Basel edition—“or seventh”: absent from Regino and the original.] Where such a union is found after the prohibition has been made, it shall be separated. [Note: [Col. 1673] “has been made, they shall be separated”: Regino.]

Gratian. Since marriage is prohibited in the sixth generation by this authority, it seems to be permitted in the seventh. But degrees of kinship are variously reckoned by some. [Col. 1674A] Some place the father in the first degree and the children in the second. Others call the children the first degree, denying that there is a degree of kinship between father and son, since father and son are shown to be one flesh. Therefore the authorities which forbid union of consanguinity up to the seventh degree place the father in the first degree; whereas those which forbid it up to the sixth degree call the children the first degree. Thus the same persons are found, according to this difference, in the sixth or seventh degree.

§ 1. Again, that statement of Fabian, by which relatives by affinity are ordered to unite in the fifth generation, seems contrary to that decree of Pope Julius [Note: [Col. 1673] Ibid., ch. 7.]: “As it is not lawful for any Christian to take a wife from his own consanguinity, so neither is it lawful to take a spouse from the consanguinity of his wife, because of the unity of the flesh.” [Col. 1674B] Likewise it is found contrary to that chapter of Gregory [Note: [Col. 1673] Ibid., ch. 10.]: “Nor [may he take] her whom he had as wife from his own consanguinity,” etc. But Fabian’s statement must be understood of two sisters, or of persons joined to one another by affinity, such as the wives of two brothers. If it happens that one of them is joined to someone in marriage, after her death the man cannot take the surviving affine as wife unless they are found in the fifth degree of affinity. Hence, one who has taken someone’s stepmother as wife cannot, after her death, take the stepson’s wife. Therefore Pope Julius himself says elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1673] Ibid., ch. 12.]: “No one shall take as wife, up to the fourth generation, the widow of the blood relatives of his wife.” He does not say “a female blood relative of his wife,” but “the widow of the blood relatives of his wife.” [Col. 1674C] Pope Paschal II, however, writing to Bishop Regino, assigns a third kind of affinity, whose union is found forbidden no further than the second degree. For he says: [Note: [Col. 1673] Cf. Causa 30, question 3, ch. 5.—Anselm, book 10, ch. 34 (35). Polycarpus, book 6, title 4.]

C. XXII. The wives of two first cousins cannot marry one and the same man.

Moreover, the wives of two first cousins cannot marry one and the same man, one after the other upon the death of the other, even at different times; this is opposed by the justice of public decency itself, apart from canonical authority. [Col. 1675A] And your prudence knows that one must abstain from the blood relatives of a wife just as from those of a husband.

Gratian. But the statement of Gregory and Pope Julius is to be understood concerning the consanguinity of the husband or wife: after the death of either of them, the survivor is not to be joined in marriage to anyone from the kindred of the deceased. It has been shown up to what degree each person ought to abstain from his own consanguinity or from the kindred of his wife.

## QUESTION IV

### GRATIAN

The question now is why marriage is forbidden up to the sixth degree of consanguinity. Isidore writes thus concerning this in *Etymologies*, book 9, ch. 6. [Note: [Col. 1675C] This chapter has been corrected from Augustine, *City of God*, book 15, ch. 16, from which it appears at first to have been taken.] [Note: [Col. 1675] Cf. Augustine, *City of God*, book 15, ch. 16.—Burchard, book 7, ch. 10. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, ch. 75; *Decree*, part 9, ch. 46. Hugh of St Victor, book 2, part 11, ch. 14. Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 40.]

[Col. 1675B] ONLY CHAPTER. Why consanguinity is observed up to the sixth degree.

When consanguinity, gradually dividing itself through the ranks of its offshoots, has withdrawn to the final degree and has ceased to be proximity, the law of marriage again pursues it with the bond of marriage and, in some manner, calls back the fleeing consanguinity. [Note: [Col. 1675] “often”: Argentinensis, Basel, Nuremberg editions.] [Note: [Col. 1675] “offspring”: same editions.] [Note: [Col. 1675] “has withdrawn itself”: editions collated by the editors.] [Note: [Col. 1675] The same editions read: “then for the first time the law receives it into the bond of marriage and calls it back.”] [Note: [Col. 1675] Addition: “consanguinity”: Basel edition.] Consanguinity has been fixed up to the sixth degree of generation because, just as the generation and state of humankind end with the six ages of the world, so the nearness of kinship might be bounded by the same number of degrees. [Note: [Col. 1675] “kind”: Isidore—Burchard, Ivo, *Decree*, Hugh—Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1675] “established”: editions collated by the editors.] [Note: [Col. 1675] Addition: “is remembered”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1675] “may be bounded”: cited collections—editions collated by the editors.]

## QUESTION V

### GRATIAN

Concerning the degrees of consanguinity and how they are to be reckoned, [Col. 1675C] Isidore speaks as follows. [Note: [Col. 1675D] Burchard, Ivo, and the *Panormia*, who cite partly Isidore and partly material from Isidore’s statements, make one chapter from this and from the chapter “Consanguinity” above in question 4; they read: “The series of consanguinity is divided into seven degrees,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 1675] These words are not in Isidore.—Cf. the cited collections on the sole chapter, Causa 35, question 4.]

C. I. How degrees of consanguinity are divided.

The series of consanguinity is divided in this manner into six degrees: let the son and daughter—that is, brother and sister—be the trunk itself. When they have been separately divided, these little branches issue from the root of that trunk: grandson and granddaughter, first; great-grandson and great-granddaughter, second; great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter, third; third great-grandson and third great-granddaughter, fourth; fourth great-grandson and fourth great-granddaughter, [Col. 1676A] fifth; the son of a fourth great-grandson and the daughter of a fourth great-grandson, sixth. [Note: [Col. 1675] “grandson”: cited collections.] [Note: [Col. 1675] “third great-granddaughter, sixth”: Ivo, *Decree*.] [Note: [Col. 1675] “granddaughter”: Burchard, Ivo, *Panormia*, Hugh—Basel edition.]

C. II. How degrees of consanguinity are to be reckoned. Likewise Pope Alexander II, to all bishops and clerics, and likewise judges established throughout Italy. [Note: [Col. 1675] Written A.D. 1065.—Anselm, book 11, ch. 92 (91). Polycarpus, book 6, title 4.—A part is reported by Hugh of St Victor, book 1.] [Note: [Col. 1675D] Thus corrected from Hugh, Anselm, and Polycarpus, who reproduce this same letter. [Col. 1676C] But Ivo and the *Panormia* report two chapters of another letter of the same Alexander, written on the same subject to the clergy of Naples, or, [Col. 1676D] as in the *Panormia*, to the metropolitans. In Gratian, both inscriptions had been joined in this manner: “To the clergy of Naples, and to all bishops and judges established throughout Italy.” Much in this entire chapter has been corrected from the same Hugh, Anselm, and Polycarpus.] [Note: [Col. 1675] “Alexander II writes to the clergy of Naples and to all bishops and judges established throughout Italy concerning these matters as follows”: editions collated by the editors.]

A question recently arisen concerning degrees of consanguinity has been brought to the Apostolic See. Certain persons, ignorant of laws and canons, have stirred it up and are attempting, contrary to the sacred canons and ecclesiastical custom, to count the same degrees of kinship. They affirm in a novel and unheard-of error that full brothers or sisters are in the second generation with respect to one another, their sons or daughters in the fourth, and their grandsons or granddaughters [Col. 1676B] in the sixth. [Note: [Col. 1675] “and”: same editions.] Counting descent in this fashion and ending it at this sixth degree, they say that thereafter men and women may contract the rights of marriage with one another. To confirm this profane error, they invoke as evidence the secular laws promulgated by Emperor Justinian concerning the succession of blood relatives. [Note: [Col. 1675] *Institutes*, book 3, titles 5 and 6.] Relying on these, they strive to show that brothers are counted in the second degree, their sons in the fourth, and their grandsons in the sixth. [Note: [Col. 1675] “to be counted”: Basel and second and third Lyons editions.] [Note: [Col. 1675] Addition: “and granddaughters”: editions collated by the editors.] By thus terminating the line of genealogy, they attempt with a kind of perverse cunning to disturb the enumeration of the holy Fathers and the ancient computation of the Church handed down to our time. But, God granting it, we took care to examine this question in a synod held in the Lateran consistory, summoning [Col. 1676C] for this work bishops, clerics, and judges from diverse provinces.

§ 1. Finally, after laws and sacred canons had been long debated, we found clearly that one computation is made in the laws and another in the canons for different reasons. For in the laws, degrees are mentioned for no other purpose than that an inheritance or succession may pass among blood relatives from one person to another. In [Col. 1677A] the canons, however, descent is reckoned in order that it may be plainly shown up to what generation one must abstain from marriages with blood relatives. There it is prescribed that inheritance be conferred lawfully upon relatives; here, that marriages among the faithful be celebrated rightly and canonically. In the laws, degrees are not separately counted beyond the sixth; [Note: [Col. 1677] “sixth”: second and third Lyons editions—addition: “degree”: Basel edition.] in the canons, however, they are distinguished up to the seventh generation. [Note: [Col. 1677] “is distinguished”: editions collated by the editors, first Basel edition.] Therefore, because inheritances cannot be transferred except from one person to another, the secular emperor took care to assign one degree to each individual person. [Note: [Col. 1677] “themselves”: same editions.] [Note: [Col. 1677] “assign”: Basel edition—“complete”: the remaining editions.] But because marriages cannot take place without two persons, sacred canons therefore place two persons in one degree. [Note: [Col. 1677] “cannot”: Basel edition.]

§ 2. Yet if both computations are viewed attentively [Col. 1677B] and carefully, it will be entirely manifest that they have the same meaning and arrive at the same limit. [Note: [Col. 1677] “have the same judgment in them”: Anselm, Hugh.] For Justinian did not define in his laws up to what degree consanguinity itself endures. The canons, however, count no generation beyond the seventh. [Note: [Col. 1677] “count”: Anselm—the editions collated by the editors.] When the sixth degree had been set out, the emperor added in the laws themselves: [Note: [Col. 1677] Title 6, law 3.] “Let it suffice to have shown thus far how degrees of kinship are counted. For from these things it is plainly evident how we ought to count further degrees *also*. For each person born *always* adds a degree.” [Note: [Col. 1677] “consanguinity”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1677] “will be”: same edition.] [Note: [Col. 1677] “also”: absent from Anselm and Hugh.] [Note: [Col. 1677] “always”: absent from Anselm and Hugh.] In these *brief* words it is plainly shown that such degrees as these persons reckon are to be counted not only [Col. 1677C] to the sixth but beyond it as well, since he decrees that further degrees beyond the sixth are to be counted. For where he names further degrees, he plainly indicates that there are not merely six degrees, but that after six are completed still others are to be counted. Nor is this surprising, since in the preceding passage the emperor himself affirmed that blood relatives may succeed one another even in the tenth degree. [Note: [Col. 1677] The editions collated by the editors read: “the tenth degree also, saying that it is not …”] By naming the tenth, he confesses more clearly than light that there are not merely six.

§ 3. Therefore let those whom this sort of error has hitherto struck awake and apply the sharpness of their minds, if they can. [Note: [Col. 1677] “endured”: Argentinensis, Basel, Paris, first Lyons edition.] For where, according to the laws, succession passes between agnates or cognates, there is no doubt that they are blood relatives. For they would not succeed one another *unless they were held together by the bond of kinship. [Col. 1677D] Now, according to Justinian’s testimony, they succeed one another* in the tenth degree; therefore those who succeed one another are blood relatives to one another. [Note: [Col. 1677] Addition: “are related to one another”: editions collated by the editors.] [Note: [Col. 1677] “thus to one another”: same editions.] If they are blood relatives to one another in the tenth degree, consanguinity has not ended, as these people admit, in the sixth degree alone. [Col. 1678A] What, then, will they say? Once degrees are counted as they count them, consanguinity either ends in the sixth degree or it does not. [Note: [Col. 1677] “would say”: same editions, first Basel edition.] If it ends, the laws on which they rely will be false, since they command blood relatives to succeed one another in the tenth degree. But if consanguinity does not end in that sixth degree, then these people will be speaking falsely when they refuse to count consanguinity beyond that sixth degree. Therefore either the laws will be false or those who thus terminate the generations.

§ 4. But in order that the laws may be true and the canons truthful, let us say what truth holds: namely, that consanguinity does not end in that sixth degree, but ends according to the canons in the seventh. [Note: [Col. 1677] “this”: same editions.] For, as we said above, both computations are enclosed within one limit. [Col. 1678B] For two legal degrees constitute one canonical degree. [Note: [Col. 1677] Absent from the same editions, first Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1677] “make”: Basel edition.] Thus brothers, who according to secular laws are said to be in the second degree, are counted in the first according to the canons. Sons of brothers, who are counted there in the fourth, are counted here in the second; grandsons, who are in the sixth there, are counted here in the third. Thus subsequently, those written *in* the laws in the eighth and tenth are defined in the canons in the fourth and fifth. [Note: [Col. 1677] “are inscribed”: editions collated by the editors, first Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1677] “understood”: Basel edition.] The rest must be understood in the same way: those said to be in the sixth or seventh according to the canons are taken in the twelfth or fourteenth according to the laws. [Note: [Col. 1677] “are taken”: editions collated by the editors, first Basel edition.]

§ 5. Understanding this computation, the most prudent Pope Gregory, when asked in what generation the faithful ought to unite, [Col. 1678C] brought forward the secular laws themselves as testimony and wrote thus to Augustine, bishop of the English: [Note: [Col. 1677] “testament”: same edition.] [Note: [Col. 1677] Cf. above, questions 2 and 3, ch. 20.] “A certain earthly law in the Roman commonwealth permits the son and daughter either of a brother and sister, or of two full brothers, or of two sisters, to unite. But experience has taught us that offspring cannot thrive from such a marriage. Hence it is necessary that already in the third or fourth generation union of the faithful may lawfully take place. For they must altogether abstain from the second generation of which we have spoken.” [Note: [Col. 1677] Gregory reads: “For the second, of which we have spoken, must entirely abstain from one another.”] [Note: [Col. 1677] “entirely”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1677] “one must abstain”: Anselm.] Here it is plainly shown that the sons and daughters of brothers are counted in the second generation. And if brothers’ sons and daughters are counted in the second, it cannot be that the brothers themselves are not in the first. If brothers are counted in the first and their sons in the second, [Col. 1678D] there is no doubt that their grandsons are in the third, their great-grandsons in the fourth, and so on through the seventh. [Note: [Col. 1677] “seventh degree”: same edition.]

§ 6. But there are some who, from these words of Gregory—when he says that the faithful may unite in the third or fourth generation—take an occasion [Col. 1679A] for contracting unlawful marriages, saying that they may justly do what that most prudent teacher defined by his judgment. [Note: [Col. 1679] “so prudently”: Anselm—the editions collated by the editors.] Let those, therefore, who attempt to defend themselves under this covering observe in the statements of the same Father that he prescribed this not generally to all, but specifically to the English people. For afterwards, questioned by Felix, bishop of the Sicilian city of Messina, [Note: [Col. 1679] Addition: “city”: Basel and second and third Lyons editions—cf. above, ch. 20, questions 2 and 3.] whether what he had ordered Augustine was to be observed generally by the whole Church, he very plainly affirmed that he had ordered this not for others but for that people, lest they should abandon through fear of harsher things the good which they had begun. [Note: [Col. 1679] “if”: Anselm—Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1679] “showed”: editions collated by the editors.] [Note: [Col. 1679] “had begun”: Basel edition.] But he judged that, once they had been strengthened in the faith with a firm root, and always for the universal Church, this must be observed: no one may dare to join to himself in marriage anyone from his own consanguinity or affinity within the seventh generation.

§ 7. [Col. 1679B] Behold, it has been plainly shown both from the words of the law itself and from the authority of the most prudent Pope Gregory what we ought to think concerning the counting of degrees of consanguinity. Although another argument also refutes these adversaries in the same way. [Note: [Col. 1679] “defeats”: Basel and second and third Lyons editions.] For if, as they admit, consanguinity ended in that sixth degree, all the little branches of persons which are contained beyond that degree in the diagram of the tree would have to be cut away as superfluous. But since all who are numbered in the depiction of the aforesaid tree belong to one kinship, they can never be separated from one another without detriment to consanguinity, just as hands, arms, and feet cannot be cut from one’s own body without injury to the person. [Note: [Col. 1679] “are contained”: editions collated by the editors.]

§ 8. That precept of the sacred canons also, which commands abstention from one’s own consanguinity so long as the generation is remembered or retained in memory, [Col. 1679C] does not differ from the aforesaid calculation of kinship. [Note: [Col. 1679] “holy”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1679] “to abstain”: editions collated by the editors, first Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1679] “or in”: Basel edition.] For if they are reckoned canonically and in customary fashion, all names of relationship are *contained* within seven degrees. [Note: [Col. 1679] “in these”: Basel and second and third Lyons editions—“thus in”: Böhm.] [Note: [Col. 1679] “are reckoned”: editions collated by the editors, first Basel, second and third Lyons editions, omitting what follows: “all names …”] Beyond these neither consanguinity is found, nor are names of degrees discovered, nor can succession be further extended, nor can a generation be remembered by anyone.

§ 9. But lest any ambiguity should thereafter remain in this reckoning of consanguinity, we have judged that another enumeration, which some employ, should also be concluded in this discussion. [Note: [Col. 1679] Addition: “other”: editions collated by the editors, first Argentinensis edition.] [Note: [Col. 1679] “computation”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1679] “examined”: editions collated by the editors.] There are some who begin to count genealogy not from brothers but from their children—that is, from paternal cousins or first cousins—[Col. 1680A] saying that the sons of brothers ought to be counted in the first generation, because brothers are like a trunk from which the remaining little branches arise. [Note: [Col. 1679] “arise”: Basel edition.] But this computation of degrees, if rightly understood, cannot differ in meaning from that which we have explained above. For those who begin counting from the sons of brothers do not proceed beyond the sixth generation; rather, just as there are six ages of the whole world and likewise six stages of human life, so they maintain that only six generations are to be counted in consanguinity. When these are ended, they say that a new union can begin, so that they may, as it were, call back fleeing consanguinity.

§ 10. Therefore this computation, which begins with the sons of brothers [Col. 1680B] and counts to the sixth *generation*, has the same force as that which begins with brothers and counts to the seventh. [Note: [Col. 1679] “is counted”: editions collated by the editors.] There is no difference in meaning, though there appears to be variation in the number of degrees. [Note: [Col. 1679] “consists”: same editions.] For the final generation, if counting begins from brothers, is found to be the seventh; if from sons of brothers, it is found to be the sixth. [Note: [Col. 1679] “is found”: Basel edition.] Thus, the degrees of consanguinity having been determined, we warn you by apostolic authority, brothers and sons, that you are to make known to everyone that the line of genealogy must be counted in the manner decreed by the holy Fathers and shown by the ancient custom of the holy and universal Church to have been calculated long ago for many ages. [Note: [Col. 1679] “admonish”: editions collated by the editors.] For if anyone, in a perverse and obstinate mind, should wish to depart from the straight path of the Apostolic See [Col. 1680C] and should insist upon counting degrees of kinship in the celebration of marriages otherwise than we do, let him know that first he shall be punished by heavenly penalty for his rashness, and afterwards struck down by the sword of perpetual anathema. Given at Rome, etc.

C. III. Why the wife’s consanguinity is said to pertain to the husband, and how affinity is to be counted. Likewise Pope Gregory. [Note: [Col. 1679D] In Polycarpus this chapter and the following one are likewise cited as from Zacharias. Indeed Gratian, in the final words of the following chapter, indicates that this chapter too was by Zacharias.] [Note: [Col. 1679] This and the following chapter are taken from a letter falsely attributed to Gregory I as writing to Venerius of Cagliari. Mansi, vol. 12, p. 256, attributes it to Zacharias.—Polycarpus, book 6, title 4. Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 41.]

Concerning affinity, which you say is a kinship that pertains to a husband on the wife’s side, or to a wife on the husband’s side, the reason is perfectly clear. For if, according to the divine declaration, my wife and I are one flesh, then surely for me and for her the nearness of my kinship and hers becomes one. Therefore [Col. 1681A] my wife’s sister and I shall be in one and the first degree; her son shall be in the second degree from me; and her granddaughter in the third. [Note: [Col. 1679] Addition: “but”: original in Mansi—Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1679] “you say”: second and third Lyons editions.] [Note: [Col. 1681] “shall be from me”: absent from Mansi.] [Note: [Col. 1681] “in the third degree”: Basel edition.] And the same must be done reciprocally in the remaining lines of descent. [Note: [Col. 1679] “and in that manner”: Mansi.]

§ 1. As for the wife of *my* relative, of whatever degree he may be, I must regard her in the same way as I would some woman of my own kinship in the corresponding degree. This, of course, must likewise be observed by my wife concerning the kinship of her husband in all degrees of relationship. [Note: [Col. 1681] Addition: “my”: Mansi—the editions collated by the editors.] [Note: [Col. 1681] Mansi reads: “and … observe”; the remaining editions read “and observe.”] But those who think otherwise are Antichrists, against whom you must guard all the more carefully because you see more openly that they oppose the divine laws. [Note: [Col. 1681] “from whom, etc.” is absent from Mansi, vol. 12.] [Note: [Col. 1681] “more diligently”: editions collated by the editors, first Lyons edition.] [Note: [Col. 1681] “attack”: editions collated by the editors.]

C. IV. How degrees of kinship are counted. Likewise Pope Zacharias. [Note: [Col. 1681] Polycarpus, ibid. Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 40.]

We reckon degrees of kinship in this way: [Note: [Col. 1681] “are reckoned by us”: Mansi, vol. 12.] I and my brother are one generation and constitute the first degree, and we are separated by no degree. Again, my son and my brother’s son are the second generation and make the second degree, nor are they separated from one another by any degree. And the remaining lines of descent are to be counted in this manner. [Note: [Col. 1681] “are to be counted”: absent from the Argentinensis and Nuremberg editions—“the lines of descent are”: Basel edition—“the lines of descent are to be held”: the remaining editions.] Concerning affinity, which you call kinship, etc., as in the preceding chapter of Gregory.

C. V. It is an equivocal usage when a wife’s sister is called a kinswoman. Likewise Pope Alexander II. [Note: [Col. 1681D] It is likewise reported in Polycarpus immediately after ch. “To the See,” so that it appears to belong to the same Alexander. From the word “wife” to the end it occurs in Isidore, book 9, final chapter.] [Note: [Col. 1681] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 9, final chapter.—Cf. the *Correctores*.—Polycarpus, ibid. Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 41.]

That the brother or sister of your wife is called your kinsman or kinswoman happens by the logic of equivocation and by the necessity of popular usage rather than for any reason of blood relationship. [Col. 1681C] For the wife of a brother is more properly called a sister-in-law (*fratrissa*) than a kinswoman. A husband’s brother is called a *levir* (“brother-in-law”). The wives of two brothers are called *janitrices*, as though wearing away the same doorway or entering through the same doorway. [Note: [Col. 1681D] *Janitrices*: this reading also stood in the law *Non facile*, Digest, “On Degrees,” before Alciato restored the passage, book 2, *Disputations*, ch. 23. There is therefore nothing surprising if Isidore, or someone else, devised the etymology given here. But the law now reads εἰνατέρες, “sisters-in-law.”] [Note: [Col. 1681] “holding”: editions collated by the editors.] A husband’s sister is called *glos* (“sister-in-law”). A sister’s husband has no special name, nor does a wife’s brother.

C. VI. The names of degrees ascending, descending, and collateral. Likewise Isidore. [Note: [Col. 1682D] This chapter, also reported by Hugh and the collectors, occurs in the *Sentences* of Paul, with words of the interpreter Anianus added in more than one place. Much of it is nevertheless also found in Isidore, book 9, ch. 5.] [Note: [Col. 1681] Rather, Paul, *Sentences*, recension, book 4, title 11, together with the interpretation, which we have placed in parentheses and printed in a typeface different from the rest.—Burchard, book 7, ch. 28; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 7, ch. 89; *Decree*, part 9, ch. 64. Hugh of St Victor, book 2, part 11, ch. 14.]

In the first ascending degree are contained father [Col. 1682A] and mother; in the descending degree, son and daughter; no other persons are joined to these.

§ 1. In the second degree are contained, in the ascending line, grandfather and grandmother; in the descending line, grandson and granddaughter; in the collateral line [Note: [Col. 1681] *in trans.*: the collected editions—Burchard, Ivo’s *Decretum*—*interversa*: Ivo’s *Panormia*—*in transverso*: Hugh.], brother and sister. These persons are doubled. For grandfather [Note: [Col. 1681] absent from the Basel edition.] and grandmother are understood both through the father and through the mother. These persons likewise, in all subsequent [Note: [Col. 1681] “whatever”: original.] degrees, are doubled in the same order according to their respective substance [Note: [Col. 1681] “their”: collected editions—Ivo’s *Panormia*], in [Note: [Col. 1681] “which in each”: original—“which in which”: cited collections—Basel edition.] whichever degree they stand.

(These persons are called double in the second [Note: [Col. 1681] “in the second”: cited collections—the collected editions.] degree because there are two grandfathers, paternal [Note: [Col. 1681] “and paternal”: same editions.] and maternal. Likewise, there are two kinds of grandchildren: those begotten through a son and those through a daughter. Brother and sister come from the opposite, that is, collateral, direction [Note: [Col. 1681] “collateral”: same editions—original.], namely, either the brother [Note: [Col. 1682D] “Namely, either the brother”: This passage through the words “who themselves” is not found in the indicated place [ [Col. 1681] though it is found in the interpretation.], but only among the collectors.] of the father, or the brother of the mother, who is called either paternal uncle (*patruus*) or maternal uncle (*avunculus*); and these themselves are likewise doubled in this order.)

§ 2. In the third degree come above [Col. 1682B] great-grandfather and great-grandmother; below, great-grandson and great-granddaughter. Collaterally: the son and daughter of a brother or sister; paternal uncle and paternal aunt—that is, the brother and sister of the father; maternal uncle and maternal aunt—that is, the brother and sister of the mother.

§ 3. In the fourth degree come above great-great-grandfather and great-great-grandmother; below, great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter. Collaterally: the grandson and granddaughter of a brother or sister; paternal cousin and paternal female cousin, that is, the son and daughter of a paternal uncle; *consobrinus* and *consobrina*, that is, the son and daughter of a maternal uncle and maternal aunt; *amitinus* and *amitina*, that is, the son and daughter of a paternal aunt; likewise *consobrini*, who are born of two sisters. To these are added [Note: [Col. 1681] “was added”: Ivo’s *Decretum.] great paternal uncle and great paternal aunt, that is, the brother and sister of the paternal grandfather; great maternal uncle and great maternal aunt, that is, the brother and sister of both the paternal and maternal grandmother.

§ [Col. 1682C] 4. In the fifth degree come, above, *atavus* and *atavia*; below, *atnepos* [Note: [Col. 1681] “great-great-grandson, great-great-granddaughter”: Basel edition.] and *atneptis*. Collaterally: the great-grandson and great-granddaughter of a brother or sister; the son and daughter of a paternal cousin, a paternal female cousin, an *amitinus*, an *amitina*, a *consobrinus*, and a *consobrina*; the nearer male cousin [Note: [Col. 1681] *proconsobrinus*, *proconsobrina*: Hugh—“own”: Burchard.] (*propior consobrinus*) [Note: [Col. 1681] “cousin”: original, Basel edition.], and nearer female cousin [Note: [Col. 1681] absent from the cited collections.] (*propior consobrina*) [Note: [Col. 1681] “female cousin”: original—Basel edition.], that is, the son and daughter of a great paternal uncle, great paternal aunt, great maternal uncle, or great maternal aunt. To these [Note: [Col. 1681] “to which is added”: Ivo’s *Panormia*—“to which are added”: the remaining cited collections—the collected editions.] are added a great-great-paternal-uncle (*propatruus*) and a great-great-paternal-aunt (*proamita*). These are the brother and sister of the paternal great-grandfather; a great-great-maternal-uncle (*proavunculus*) and a great-great-maternal-aunt (*promatertera*). These are the brother and sister of the paternal and maternal great-grandmother, and of the maternal great-grandfather [Col. 1683A].

(This category can be explained neither in degrees other than those written nor by other terms.)

§ 5. In the sixth degree come above *tritavus* and *tritavia*; below, *trinepos* and *trineptis*. Collaterally: the great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter of a brother and sister; the grandson [Note: [Col. 1683] “grandson, granddaughter”: absent from the cited collections.] and granddaughter of paternal cousins, paternal female cousins, *amitini*, *amitinae*, *consobrini*, and *consobrinae*; the grandson and granddaughter of great paternal uncles, great paternal aunts, great maternal uncles, and great maternal aunts—that is, the son and daughter of a nearer cousin [Note: [Col. 1683] “*consobrinus*”: same editions—the collected editions.], who are called *consobrini*. To these are added laterally the son and daughter of great-great-paternal-uncles, great-great-paternal-aunts, great-great-maternal-uncles, and great-great-maternal-aunts; a great-great-great-paternal-uncle (*abpatruus*) and great-great-great-paternal-aunt (*abamita*). These are the brother and sister of the great-great-grandfather; a great-great-great-maternal-uncle (*abavunculus*) and great-great-great-maternal-aunt (*abmatertera*). These are the brother and sister of the paternal and maternal great-great-grandmother, and of the maternal great-great-grandfather.

(This too [Note: [Col. 1683] “These”: the collected editions, first Basel edition.] cannot be explained [Col. 1683B] further [Note: [Col. 1683] “cannot”: same editions—the cited collections.] than as the author himself sets it forth.)

§ 6. In the seventh degree, relatives in the direct ascending and descending line are not designated by their own specific names; but in the collateral line are included the great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter of a brother or sister, and the sons and daughters of *consobrini*.

§ 7. Seven [Note: [Col. 1683] “six”: the collected editions.] degrees of succession have therefore been established, because beyond them, by the nature of things, neither can names be found nor can life be extended to successors [Note: [Col. 1683] “succession beyond”: same editions—Ivo’s *Panormia*.] or propagated [Note: [Col. 1683] “propagated”: the same editions.].

(In these [Note: [Col. 1683] adds “indeed”: Paris and Lyons editions.] seven [Note: [Col. 1683] “six”: the collected editions.] degrees are contained all [Note: [Col. 1683] “all the names of all relationships”: same editions.] names of kinship, beyond which neither affinity can be found nor [Note: [Col. 1683] adds “beyond”: Basel edition.] succession [Note: [Col. 1683] adds “of blood-relationship”: the collected editions, first Basel edition.] can be propagated further [Note: [Col. 1683] “extended”: the collected editions, Ivo’s *Decretum*.].)

Gratian. It has been sufficiently shown, on the authority of Isidore, Gregory, and Alexander, how many degrees of consanguinity or affinity there are, how they are to be computed, and by what names they are called [Col. 1683C]. [Note: [Col. 1683] A tree of consanguinity and affinity, together with John Andreae’s commentary upon it, will be supplied at the end of our edition, so that it need not be repeated in each collection of the Decretals—as was done in the Roman edition.]

## QUESTION VI

## GRATIAN

### Part I

The question now is: by whose accusations or testimony is a union of blood-relatives to be dissolved?

[Col. 1684A] Pope Fabian thus decreed concerning these matters [Note: [Col. 1683] Cf. Theodosian Code, bk. 2, tit. 7, ch. 9, with the interpretation—Burchard, bk. 7, ch. 21; Anselm, bk. 10, ch. 60 (67); Ivo’s *Panormia*, bk. 7, ch. 84; *Decretum*, part 9, ch. 57; Polycarpus, bk. 6, tit. 4; Peter Lombard, bk. 4, distinction 41.]:

### C. I. Only blood-relatives, or, if the line of descendants has failed, old and truthful persons, are to compute the relationship in synod.

Let no one accuse blood-relatives of outsiders, or compute their consanguinity in synod; rather, let the relatives to whose knowledge it pertains do so: namely, father, mother, brother, sister, paternal uncle, maternal uncle, paternal aunt, maternal aunt, and their descendants. But if the entire line of descendants has failed, the bishop shall canonically investigate the matter through older and more truthful persons [Note: [Col. 1683] “more venerable persons”: Ivo’s *Panormia*, Basel edition.] to whom the same relationship is known; and, if the relationship is found, they shall be separated.

### C. II. PALEA. A Decree of Pope Celestine sent to the Church of Florence [Note: [Col. 1683D] This Palea is absent from most ancient copies. It occurs in *Extra*, “Who may accuse a marriage,” ch. 3, under Clement III, alternatively Celestine, addressed to the bishop of Florence, alternatively to the Church of Florence. It has therefore been corrected from some manuscripts, with several words added and removed.] [Note: [Col. 1683] Decree of Celestine II; cf. ch. 1, “On marriage contrary to the ecclesiastical prohibition,” in *Compilatio I*, and ch. 3, *X*, “Who may accuse a marriage.”]

[Col. 1684B] “It seems to us that the second woman, whom he took in violation of the Church’s prohibition, is not his wife, even if he had not betrothed the first. For the authority of both divine and human law declares that what has been done contrary to the Church’s prohibition and order is not to be held valid as something disordered. Therefore, because the woman whom he unlawfully took in addition is not his wife, the prohibition standing in the way, he must be compelled to take back the woman to whom he swore and whom he betrothed, and by whom he has begotten offspring. Thus the sacred obligation of the oath may not be despised, the mutual pledge of faith may be preserved, the offspring may be nurtured and educated in the worship of God, and others may be unable thereby to take an opportunity for perjury [Note: [Col. 1683] “sinning”: the collected editions.] and for deceiving others.

§ 1. That parents, brothers, and relatives of either [Col. 1684C] sex are admitted to give testimony concerning their own kin, for contracting or dissolving a marriage, is approved both by ancient custom [Note: [Col. 1683] “both by ancient custom approved by laws and by divine and human laws” (or “is approved”: Basel, Venice I and II). “In dissolving a marriage, parents are especially received; or, if parents are lacking, the nearest relatives are admitted”: the collected editions.] and by laws. Parents are especially admitted for this reason; and, if parents are lacking, the nearest relatives, because everyone takes pains to know his own genealogy both by witnesses and documents and also [Note: [Col. 1683] “parents are received; or, if”: *Compilatio I.*] from the recitation [Note: [Col. 1683] “exercise”: *Compilatio I*—“by exercise and recitation”: the collected editions, Basel edition.] of his ancestors. For who ought better to be admitted than those who [Col. 1685A] know better, and whose interest is involved, so that, if they have not been present and have not given consent, according to the laws no marriage takes place? [Note: [Col. 1683] “Therefore, because they know better than others, they are especially admitted. Likewise they are received in testimony for contracting a marriage”: the collected editions.]

§ 2. But what is read—‘A father is not to be received in his son’s case, nor a son in his father’s case’ [Note: [Col. 1685] Cf. Digest, “On witnesses,” fragment 2 (22.5).]—is true in criminal cases and contracts. But in contracting [Note: [Col. 1685] “contracting”: the collected editions.] and dissolving a marriage, by reason of the prerogative of marriage itself, and because it is a favored matter, they are rightly admitted.”

### C. III. Who ought to establish a relationship by oath. Pope Urban likewise to Richard [Note: [Col. 1685] With Ivo’s *Decretum*, part 9, ch. 33, one should read “Cyriacus,” who became bishop of Genoa around A.D. 1090—Ivo’s *Panormia*, bk. 7, ch. 85.] Bishop of Genoa.

We notify you that after three or two of the nearer relatives of the already deceased wife of the man accused—or of his living wife [Note: [Col. 1685] “or of his living wife, of the man who accuses”: the collected editions.]—have established this relationship by oath [Col. 1685B], or after three or two of the older Genoese [Note: [Col. 1685] “Genoese”: the collected editions, Argentinensis edition.] to whom this relationship is known [Note: [Col. 1685] “is”: the collected editions.], and who are of good repute and give truthful testimony, have established consanguinity in the aforesaid manner, free from affection, fear, payment, and every evil motive, the marriages shall be dissolved without any delay. But if relatives or outsiders merely testify verbally to the relationship and are unwilling or unable to prove it by oath, the marriage is by no means to be dissolved; rather, a fitting penance shall be imposed on them because of the reproach or stain of sin, if perhaps they have incurred any in this matter [Note: [Col. 1685] “in this”: the collected editions.].

### C. IV. Those whose incest no one affirms on oath are left to their own confession. Likewise, from a council of Pope Urban held in Apulia [Note: [Col. 1685] Council of Troia, about A.D. 1093—Ivo’s *Decretum*, part 9, ch. 53; Peter Lombard, same place.]

[Col. 1685C] If two or three men establish consanguinity by oath, or if the persons themselves [Note: [Col. 1685] “they themselves”: the collected editions.] perhaps confess it, the marriages shall be dissolved. But if neither occurs, bishops shall adjure them by baptism [Note: [Col. 1685] “by the faith of baptism”: Basel edition.], by faith, and by the judgment of Christ, under true obedience, publicly to declare whether they acknowledge themselves to be blood-relatives, as common report has it. If they deny it, they are to be left to themselves; yet they should know that, if they harbor something different in conscience [Note: [Col. 1685] “anything”: Basel edition.], they are separated from the thresholds of the Church, from the body [Col. 1686A] and blood of the Lord, and from communion with the faithful, and have become infamous, until they desist from the deed of incest. If they separate themselves by the judgment of bishops, then, if [Note: [Col. 1685] “who”: the collected editions.] they are young, they are not to be prohibited from contracting other marriages.

### Part II

Gratian. Here are those by whose accusations or testimony unions of blood-relatives are to be dissolved. But the sort of oath to be required from an accuser is found in the Roman Order [Note: [Col. 1685C] The other collectors [ [Col. 1685] though not Burchard and Ivo’s *Decretum*, which have no heading at all.] cite this not from the Order but from a Roman council under Gregory III. From these collectors and from ancient copies of Gratian, several readings have been corrected in this and the following [Col. 1686C] [Col. 1686D] chapters.] [Col. 1685D]. It is as follows [Note: [Col. 1685] It is not in the book of the Roman Order, and seems, like the following passages, to be attributable to Regino (bk. 2, chs. 231–233)—Burchard, bk. 7, ch. 25; Ivo’s *Panormia*, bk. 7, ch. 87; *Decretum*, part 9, ch. 61; Polycarpus, bk. 6, tit. 4.]:

### C. V. The accuser’s oath

Concerning that kinship which they say exists between N. [Note: [Col. 1685] The letters “N. and N.” are omitted by Regino, Ivo’s *Panormia*, and the collected editions, first Basel edition. The words “him” and “this woman” are absent from the Basel edition. “Between this man and this woman”: the remaining editions—Ivo’s *Panormia*.] and this wife of his, N., whatever you know about it and [Note: [Col. 1685] “or”: Regino—“or”: Burchard and Ivo—the collected editions.] have heard from your neighbors or your older relatives: swear that you will conceal none of it from your bishop [Note: [Col. 1685] “your bishop or his delegate”: the collected editions—Regino.] or from his delegate, whom he has ordered to investigate this, whenever he questions you concerning it—neither by any contrivance [Col. 1686B], nor because of fear, affection, reward, or blood-relationship. So may God help you, and these relics of the saints [Note: [Col. 1685] “these of the saints”: the collected editions—“and … or”: absent from Regino.].

### C. VI. The oath of witnesses [Note: [Col. 1685] Cf. ch. 5—Regino, bk. 2, ch. 232; Burchard, bk. 7, ch. 26; Ivo’s *Panormia*, bk. 7, ch. 87; *Decretum*, part 9, ch. 62.]

That oath which this man swore concerning that kinship computed between N. and his wife N.—you shall observe it insofar as you know or have heard. So may God help you.

### Part III

Gratian. This oath is not one of separation but a synodal oath, established by Pope Eutychian. For he says [Note: [Col. 1685] Cf. ch. 5—Regino, bk. 2, chs. 2 ff.; Burchard, bk. 1, chs. 91–93; Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 152 (157).]:

### C. VII. The synodal oath

[Col. 1686C] A bishop presiding in synod, after a suitable address, ought to summon into the midst seven men from the people of that parish, or more if he sees fit: men mature, honorable, and truthful. Having brought forth the holy pledges, he shall bind each of them by this oath:

“From this time [Note: [Col. 1685] “that from this time”: the collected editions.] onward, whatever you know or have heard, or shall afterward investigate, which has been done or will be done contrary to God’s will and right Christianity in this parish [Col. 1687A], if it happens in your lifetime [Note: [Col. 1687] “happens”: the collected editions, first Basel edition.], provided only that it comes to your knowledge in any manner: if you know, or it has been indicated to you, that it is a synodal cause and pertains to the bishop’s office, you shall in no way conceal it from the bishop [Note: [Col. 1687] “the bishop of Trier or his delegate”: Regino—“the bishop [adds ‘your’: Basel, Lyons II and III] or his delegate”: the collected editions.] or his delegate, whom he has ordered to investigate it, whenever he questions you concerning it—neither because of affection, fear, payment, nor kinship. So may God help you, and these relics of the saints.”

“The oath” [Note: [Col. 1687D] Burchard reads “this oath” [ [Col. 1687] as do Regino and Anselm.] and before these words places this heading: “The oath of the rest” [ [Col. 1687] “Let the rest swear thus”: Regino.].] which this man has sworn [Note: [Col. 1687] “swore”: Regino, Burchard—the collected editions, first Lyons edition.] concerning a synodal cause, you shall yourself observe insofar as you know, have heard, or shall afterward investigate from this day onward. So may God help you, etc.”

### Part IV

Gratian. This oath [Col. 1687B] was taken from that one, with its beginning somewhat altered. But Pope Innocent II writes concerning the oath of separation to Otto, Bishop of Lucca, as follows [Note: [Col. 1687] Written about A.D. 1142.]:

### C. VIII. The oath of those who prove consanguinity

Concerning the kinship about which you wished to consult us, and concerning which an appeal has also been made to our hearing, we received writings from other brethren, who related the case itself in a different manner. At first, they are said to have disagreed both in the degrees and in the names of the persons; but afterwards, in one of them, the reckoners of this same kinship are said to have agreed. In cases of this kind, however, the character of the persons who [Col. 1687C] wish to establish anything against anyone must be most carefully considered. They also ought to take an oath that they say this against the persons concerned neither from favor, payment, fear, nor hatred of anyone, but rather because they believe [Note: [Col. 1687] “believe”: Basel edition.] it to be true and have thus heard it from their ancestors. In all these things no variation or contradiction ought to be found.

### Part V

Gratian. But those who are separated from one another shall take the following oath [Note: [Col. 1687] The author is Regino himself, bk. 2, ch. 233—Burchard, bk. 7, ch. 27; Ivo’s *Panormia*, bk. 7, ch. 88; *Decretum*, part 9, ch. 63; Polycarpus, bk. 6, tit. 4.]:

### C. IX. The oath of separation

From this day onward, you shall by no contrivance associate yourself [Note: [Col. 1687] “join yourself”: Basel edition.] with this female blood-relative of yours [Note: [Col. 1687D] “Female blood-relative”: The following words through “you committed” are added from Burchard and Ivo, along with several other passages.] N., with whom, contrary to law and right Christianity, you have committed adultery and incest; nor shall you join her to yourself either in marriage [Col. 1688A] or in adultery; nor shall you eat and [Note: [Col. 1687] “or”: Basel, Lyons II and III.] drink with her at one table, or live under one roof, except perhaps [Note: [Col. 1687] “in one”: the collected editions, first Basel edition.] in church or in another public place where no evil suspicion can arise, and where, before suitable witnesses, you may speak together on account of a definite necessity. Nor shall you take another wife, unless perhaps, after completion of penance, permission has been granted you by your bishop or his delegate. So may God help you and these relics of the saints.

### Part VI

Gratian. No one may dismiss his wife on the pretext of consanguinity and take another, unless the cause has first been proved.

[Col. 1688B] Therefore Pope Alexander II [Note: [Col. 1687] Letter of uncertain date.] to William of Monstrolio [Note: [Col. 1687] *Monasteriolo*: Ivo’s *Decretum*—*Monstreolo*: Basel edition—*Monsterolo*: Argentinensis edition—*Monstrolico*: remaining editions—Ivo’s *Panormia*.]:

### C. X. A man may not dismiss his wife unless consanguinity has been proved before the Church

We have learned from the report of many persons that you wish to cast off your own wife and cleave to another, alleging the pretext of consanguinity. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we command you under prohibition that you presume in no way to dismiss the wife whom you now have or to take another, until a council [Note: [Col. 1687] “council”: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I and II.] of devout bishops examines this cause [Note: [Col. 1687] “examines the just cause”: the collected editions—Ivo’s *Panormia*.].

### Part VII

Gratian. But the man who is to take back the woman whom he unjustly dismissed shall swear as follows:

### C. XI. The oath of reconciliation [Note: [Col. 1687] Rather, Regino himself, bk. 2, ch. 240—Burchard, bk. 9, ch. 81; Ivo’s *Panormia*, bk. 7, ch. 217; Polycarpus, same place.]

From this day onward you shall keep this wife of yours, N., [Col. 1688C] whom you unjustly dismissed, as a husband ought rightly [Note: [Col. 1687] “rightly”: absent from Ivo’s *Panormia*.] to have his wife: in love and due discipline. You shall not separate her from yourself by any evil contrivance, nor, while she lives, take another. So may God help you, etc.

Gratian. But that marriages are dissolved among some persons on the testimony of one witness has no validity whatever. For since the Lord has said [Note: [Col. 1687] Deuteronomy 19:15.], “Every word shall stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses”; and likewise, since the Council of Lleida, ch. 20, says [Note: [Col. 1687] A.D. 546—Burchard, bk. 7, ch. 17; Ivo’s *Panormia*, bk. 7, ch. 83; *Decretum*, part 9, ch. 52.] that every controversy concerning ecclesiastical matters is to be settled under two or three witnesses according to divine law, the Lord saying [Note: [Col. 1687] Deuteronomy 19:15; Matthew 18:16.], “Let not one person stand against another [Note: [Col. 1688D] “Against another”: In Deuteronomy these words are added: “whatever sin or crime it may be.” In the Gospel, only the following words occur: “that by the mouth of two,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 1687] “anyone”: Vulgate.], but let every word stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses” [Col. 1689A]; and likewise, since elsewhere it is said, “Let no matter be believed on the testimony of one person [Note: [Col. 1689C] “Of one person”: In the Theodosian Code, bk. 11, tit. 14, these words are read: “and now we plainly decree that the statement of only one witness is not to be heard, even if he is distinguished by the illustrious honor of the curia.” Similar words are cited by Ivo, part 16, ch. 204. Gratian, above, Cause 6, question 2, at the beginning, has cited almost the same proposition.] however practiced”—it is most plainly evident that marriages are not to be dissolved upon the assertion of one person.

## QUESTION VII

## GRATIAN

But regarding the question whether those born from incestuous unions are to be reckoned children, Augustine determines it in the book of *Questions on Leviticus*, chapter or question 76, saying:

### Sole Chapter. Those born from incestuous unions are not called children

What does this mean [Note: [Col. 1689] Leviticus 20:21.]—“Whoever sleeps with his female blood-relative [Note: [Col. 1689D] “Whoever sleeps with his female blood-relative”: These words are not found here in St Augustine, but at the beginning of his question 76.], shall die childless”—when children have both previously been born [Col. 1689B] from such unions [Note: [Col. 1689] “are”: the collected editions, first Lyons II and III.] and are born even today? Is this to be understood as established by the law of God: that whoever are born from them are not reckoned children, that is, have no right at all [Note: [Col. 1689] “and no”: the collected editions.] of succession from their parents?

## QUESTION VIII

## GRATIAN

But concerning those who have been joined unknowingly, in what degree of consanguinity or affinity they may remain by the Church’s dispensation, Gregory determines in the *Register*, saying [Note: [Col. 1689D] In Polycarpus it is cited from Gregory’s *Decrees*.] [Note: [Col. 1689] This chapter is uncertain and plainly alien to the time of Gregory the Great—Polycarpus, bk. 6, tit. 4.]:

### C. I. Those who are unknowingly joined within the seventh generation are not to be separated

Concerning degrees of kinship: those found in marriage within the seventh generation, if they have done so unknowingly [Note: [Col. 1689] “unknowingly”: the collected editions.] and many courses of years [Col. 1689C] have already passed [Note: [Col. 1689] “have”: same editions.], so that they have children—those found in the sixth degree, or perhaps in the fifth—are not to be separated until, the Lord permitting, we speak face to face. But I say this by way of indulgence, not command. Those who appear to have contracted new marriages in these two degrees, that is, [Col. 1690A] within the year’s term, are to be separated in every way. Henceforth, however, general statutes extending throughout the whole province are to be firmly established so that no one may thereafter dare to commit such a crime; and those who do so are to be separated and punished by harsher [Note: [Col. 1689] “more harshly”: the collected editions, first Argentinensis and Lyons II and III.] penalties without the mercy of revocation. But those who have taken in marriage blood-relatives of their wives, as we wrote to you previously, if they are found in the same degree, are to be separated, or their case is to be suspended until, with the Lord’s aid, we meet together.

The same:

§ 1. Concerning those who, after [Note: [Col. 1689] “after the death of their wives”: the collected editions.] their wives have died, wish to contract second marriages [Note: [Col. 1689] “wish”: Basel edition.], we have justly, honorably, and reasonably provided that they abstain from their wives’ blood-relatives through the fourth degree of genealogy [Note: [Col. 1689] “abstain”: the collected editions.]. This [Note: [Col. 1689] “these things”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.] we have set forth more mildly according to the indulgence of holy mother Church [Col. 1690B]. But according to the judgment of secular laws [Note: [Col. 1690C] On punishment of incestuous persons, see Justinian, Novella 12; *Capitularies*, bk. 7, chs. 432 and 435; and the additions, chs. 124 and 127.] all these evils and unlawful acts must in every way be cut off by worthy restraints and severe measures of discipline [Note: [Col. 1689] “attacks”: Argentinensis, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice I.], so that in time to come all things may be at rest.

### C. II. Those found joined in the fourth and fifth degrees are to be separated. The same to Felix, Bishop of the city of Messana [Note: [Col. 1690D] The whole chapter “We decree these prudent measures,” as it stands in Gratian, is also cited by Anselm from Gregory. In Polycarpus it follows the chapter *Pyctacium*, above, Cause 30, question 3, attributed to Zachary. In the Second Council of Toledo, ch. 5, cited by Burchard and Ivo, the remaining words of this chapter occur, except those which will be indicated.] [Note: [Col. 1689] It is not found in Gregory; nevertheless it occurs in part in the Second Council of Toledo, held A.D. 531, from which Burchard, bk. 7, ch. 6, and Ivo’s *Decretum*, part 9, ch. 42, cite it—Anselm, bk. 10, ch. 39 (40); Polycarpus, bk. 6, tit. 4.]

We decree that these matters be prudently guarded against: that no member of the faithful should desire to join in marriage a blood-relative [Note: [Col. 1689] “to a blood-relative”: Basel, Lyons II and III.] of his own, so long as the lines of affinity are discerned through the succession of generations [Note: [Col. 1689] “are discerned, in”: the Spanish collection—Burchard and Ivo.]; but, as [Note: [Col. 1690D] “But, as”: These words through “they shall be separated” are absent from the council, Burchard, and Ivo.] our elders have determined, it must in every way be observed, because we grant no one permission to contract a union within the seventh degree of kinship [Col. 1690C], namely, those who descend from father and mother in a relationship of blood. But any man [Note: [Col. 1689] “also”: the collected editions, first Basel.] or woman found joined in the fourth or fifth degree [Note: [Col. 1689] “found”: absent from the Basel editions.] shall be separated, because it is written [Note: [Col. 1689] Leviticus 18:6.], “No man shall approach a blood-relative [Note: [Col. 1689] “shall approach”: the Spanish collection—Burchard, Ivo, and the collected editions.] of his to uncover her nakedness”; and again [Note: [Col. 1691] Leviticus 18:29.], “The soul that does any of these things [Col. 1691A] [Note: [Col. 1691] “of the abominations”: Spanish collection—the Vulgate.] shall perish from the midst of its people.” Certainly, those to whom an unlawful union is forbidden [Note: [Col. 1691C] “Certainly, those”: These words are absent from the printed council, although they are joined with the preceding words in Burchard and Ivo. They are found, however, in the Councils of Agde, Epaone, and Tours III, and in the added Capitularies, though with some variation, as noted above in the same Question 2 and 3, “On incestuous persons.”] shall have freedom to enter a better marriage.

Unless they persist obstinately in the same [Note: [Col. 1691C] “Unless in the same”: These words are found nowhere and appear to be Gratian’s, as that manner of speaking indicates: “Therefore, in the Council of Orléans.”] crime until the death of one of them.

Therefore, in the Council of Orléans [Note: [Col. 1691D] Burchard and Anselm also cite this from the Council of Orléans, and something pertinent occurs in the Third Council of Orléans, ch. 10, as also in the Council of Agde, ch. 61, from which Ivo seems to cite it. But ch. 4 of the Council of Lleida, reported above in the same Questions 2 and 3, “On those who are incestuous,” agrees much more closely with this chapter. Precisely the same words occur in *Capitularies*, bk. 7, ch. 433, and in the additions, ch. 125, except for the passages that will be indicated.] [Note: [Col. 1691] Rather, *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, bk. 7, ch. 433—Burchard, bk. 7, ch. 5; Anselm, bk. 11, ch. 89; Ivo’s *Decretum*, part 9, ch. 41.]:

### C. III. Those who have persisted in incest until the death of one party may not take wives

Incestuous persons [Note: [Col. 1691] “Incestuous”: *Capitularies*.], while they remain in that detestable and abominable crime, are not to be counted among Christian faithful but among gentiles or catechumens. That is, they shall neither take food nor drink with Christians, but shall do this alone; they shall neither kiss nor receive greeting from them. And if they prove disobedient to their priests and refuse to separate themselves [Col. 1691B] from so abominable a crime [Note: [Col. 1691] “to be separated”: the collected editions.] and return to public penance, they are to be counted among those endangered by an unclean spirit, or even among those of whom Truth himself says [Note: [Col. 1691] Matthew 18:17.], “If he will not hear you, let him be to you as a gentile and a publican.” And if one of them [Note: [Col. 1691D] “And if one of them”: These words are absent from the cited *Capitularies*, but in their place occur these: “For they ought not pray with the faithful or enter church, but keep watch at the church door; and, as persons enter [Col. 1692C] and depart, lie prostrate with face to the ground, ask pardon, and not disdain to beg that prayer be made for them. With abundant tears, contrite countenance, and humbled spirit they must always appear before all until satisfaction has been rendered to the Church and they await canonical reconciliation by their own bishop; they must never return to the former incest, exercise no secular business, nor take part in pleas, accusations, or testimony. Rather, by the frequent prayers of priests, laying-on of the hands of their own bishop, giving of alms, and performance [ [Col. 1691] read: “works.”] of other good works, they ought to be cleansed and healed.”] is overtaken by death, the other, so long as he or she lives, shall do severe penance and remain without hope of marriage.

Gratian. By this authority, those found joined in the fourth or fifth degree of consanguinity are commanded to be separated by the Church.

## QUESTION IX

## GRATIAN

### Part I

[Col. 1691C] The question therefore is whether, if the Church, deceived by the fraud or ignorance of witnesses, has separated persons who afterward contracted other marriages, and if the witnesses’ cunning or false opinion is afterward discovered, the earlier marriages ought to be restored. That this cannot be done is proved by arguments and authorities. For a judgment, unless it has been challenged by appeal within the term established by law, obtains irreversible force [Col. 1692A]. Hence Blessed Gregory also writes, saying [Note: [Col. 1692D] In the published copies of Gratian this was attributed to Blessed Augustine. It was restored to Blessed Gregory from several ancient copies and Anselm. Above, Cause 25, question 2, ch. *Ecclesiasticae*, it is cited from Gregory; it is found in almost the same words in bk. 7, indiction 2, letter 60.] [Note: [Col. 1691] Cf. ch. 12, Cause 25, question 2.]:

### C. I. It is not expedient that matters reasonably decided be changed

In every respect it accords with ecclesiastical discipline and moderation that what has been reasonably ordered or decided ought not thereafter to be disturbed by any opposition.

### C. II. What has been beneficially decided should be strengthened by successors; what has been rashly undertaken should be cut off. Likewise Pope Stephen V to Paul, Bishop of Piacenza [Note: [Col. 1692D] The substance of this chapter, and many of its words, are taken from Blessed Gregory, bk. 7, indiction 1, letters 13 and 28.] [Note: [Col. 1691] Cf. Gregory the Great’s letter to Candidus, bk. 8, letter 11, and to John of Syracuse, same book, letter 27 (Maurist edition)—Collection of three parts, bk. 1, tit. 64, ch. 1.]

The consideration of our passage admonishes us, on the authority of reason, to uphold what our predecessors have usefully decided [Col. 1692B], and nevertheless promptly to punish what rash persons have presumed. For let him know that he stands guilty before the sight of the divine Judge who strives to undo things beneficially concluded and to violate what has been confirmed by any audacity whatsoever. The order of ecclesiastical strength is indeed thrown into confusion if unlawful things are rashly presumed, or things not permitted are attempted with impunity. Therefore, if we negligently overlook what is wrongly usurped, we undoubtedly open a way for excesses by others.

**Gratian.** Therefore, since this judgment was reasonably given and was not challenged by appeal within the appointed period, it appears that the earlier marriages must by no means be restored. The answer to this is: it is one thing to set aside a judgment and disturb what has reasonably been decided, and [Col. 1692C] another to correct matters obtained by fraud when they are discovered. For each person is permitted to correct his own error; and therefore what is unlawfully done by anyone, or is found to have been allowed by predecessors, ought to be recalled to a better state. Now a wife was unlawfully separated from her husband and joined to another while he was alive, since the Lord [Note: [Col. 1693] written A.D. 414.—Polyc. there.] [Col. 1693A] commands that a wife be separated from her husband only on the ground of fornication. Thus, if a woman whose husband was thought dead were joined to another man, and on the intervention of any circumstance left his companionship, although by judgment of the Church she were compelled to return to the man whom she had left, nevertheless, if after three years the husband thought dead happened to return, the earlier marriage would be restored. So too, when persons separated from one another on the ground of consanguinity are discovered not to have been related by blood, the bonds of their former union must be repaired.

**Part II, § 1.** That things unlawfully admitted, or found to have been admitted, ought to be corrected, and that even a judgment of the Roman see may be altered for the better, is shown by the authority of Popes Hilary and Nicholas.

[Col. 1693B] For Hilary, bishop of the city of Rome, presiding over a synod, says, chapter 4 [Note: [Col. 1693] held A.D. 465.—Collection in three parts, part 1, title 44, sole chapter.—Anselm, book 6, chapter 157 (154). Deusdedit, part 1; Polycarpus, book 4, title 20.]:

### C. III. What is unlawfully admitted, or found to have been admitted by predecessors, must be corrected.

What anyone has unlawfully committed, or finds to have been admitted by his predecessors, he shall condemn if he wishes to avoid danger to himself. For we wish to exercise severity of punishment in no matter; but whoever, in matters of God, sins either through stubbornness or through some excess, or refuses himself to abolish what [Note: [Col. 1693] “what—does”: collected editions.] he has wrongly done, will find in himself whatever he has failed to cut away in another. Therefore, so that this may henceforth be observed more steadfastly, if it please you, produce all your judgments [Note: [Col. 1693] “all judgments”: the same editions.], causes, and subscriptions, so that by synodal judgment access may be closed to unlawful persons [Col. 1693C] [Note: [Col. 1693] “unlawful”: the same editions.].

### C. IV. An apostolic judgment may be altered according to the tenor of its condition. Likewise Gregory [Note: [Col. 1693D] In Anselm and Polycarpus it is cited from an epistle of Pope Nicholas I to King Charles. It occurs in the often-mentioned manuscript of the Dominican monastery, in an epistle of Nicholas entitled “To King Louis,” and in another by him to all the bishops in Louis’s kingdom, beginning: “We rejoice.”] [Note: [Col. 1693] Rather, Nicholas I, epistle 58, in Mansi, written A.D. 866.—Anselm, book 2, chapter 69. Deusdedit, same place; Polycarpus, book 5, title 6.]

The judgment of the Apostolic See is always conceived with such moderation of counsel, tempered by such bold patience, and pronounced with such gravity of deliberation, that it *does not require reconsideration*, nor deems alteration necessary—unless perhaps it has been issued in such a manner [Note: [Col. 1693] “in such a manner”: Böhm.] that it can be reconsidered, or is to be altered [Note: [Col. 1693] “or altered”: thus in the collected editions and first Basel edition.] according to the tenor of the condition set forth above.

### C. V. The Apostolic Church restores to their former state persons condemned by predecessors, at the supplication of others. Likewise Pope Innocent, Epistle XXII, to the Bishops of Macedonia.

[Col. 1694A] I now come to Maximus [Note: [Col. 1694D] “I now come to Maximus”: the reading at Lérins is: “I now come to Photinus, as to a kind of great theme” [thus Collection Hispana—Basel edition]. But nothing has been altered because of the gloss.] Photinus, as to a certain theme, and—what is anxious and most difficult for me—I shall review the judgments of my predecessors. Something rather severe had in some fashion been decreed concerning him, as you yourselves also remember [Note: [Col. 1693] “remember”: Collection Hispana.]. But since you show that this was foisted upon this See through a false report, as you assert [Note: [Col. 1693] “which through”: collected editions and first Basel edition.], and obtained by intrigues [Note: [Col. 1693] “is shown”: collected editions.], because the matter has returned to a salutary state, we, following apostolic custom, grant this pardon after condemnation in response to your earnest efforts [Note: [Col. 1693] “and pardon”: Coustant.—“and admits pardon to you only, not to us”: Basel edition; “admits pardon to you alone (to us: Argentinensis edition) from this point”: remaining editions.]; and we judge it harsher than all harsh things not to give assent to assertions so strong [Col. 1694B] on your part, and to persons so good and so dear as yourselves [Note: [Col. 1693] “ourselves”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.]. Therefore, brethren most beloved, by reason of your approval, judgment, and petition, have Photinus as bishop [Note: [Col. 1693] “it is permissible to have it thus established”: Coustant.]; for it is permissible to establish it as you request.
