And receive our judgment, turned to a better result and attained through your labor or testimony, as making you sharers in your wish [Note: [Col. 1694D] “making you sharers in your wish”: the same reason caused the reading not to be changed. It should be read: “making you sharers in your wish” [thus Collection Hispana—Coustant.].] . But do not expect Eustathius [Note: [Col. 1693] “Eustasius”: Basel edition.—“Eustacius”: Argentinensis edition.—“Eustachius”: remaining editions.—“And Eustathius”: Coustant.—“Eustathius likewise”: Collection Hispana.], whom I have approved very often, to be stripped of the rank [Note: [Col. 1693] “diaconate”: Coustant; collected editions and first Argentinensis and second Venice editions.] of deacon [Note: [Col. 1693] “by favor”: Coustant.]. For I gladly hear that you are concerned for salvation; I do not gladly permit action against the head,* even if it must be done [Note: [Col. 1693] “is”: collected editions.]. To whomever you extend your hand, I extend mine with you; to whomever I extend mine, extend yours with me.

### C. VI. It is permissible to alter a judgment of the Roman See for the better. Likewise Pope Nicholas to Emperor Michael, in Epistle VII. [Note: [Col. 1693] Epistle 8, in Mansi, written A.D. 862.—Anselm, book 1, chapter 75. Ivo, Decretum, part 5, chapter 19.]

[Col. 1694C] We do not deny that a judgment of the Roman See may be altered for the better, when something has either been fraudulently imposed upon *it*, or when it itself, in consideration of ages, times, or grave necessities, has determined to arrange something by dispensation [Note: [Col. 1693] “some arrangement by dispensation”: collected editions and first Basel edition.]—for we read that the outstanding Apostle Paul also did certain things by dispensation which he is known later to have disapproved [Col. 1695A] [Note: [Col. 1695] “we read”: Ivo and the collected editions.]—but only when that Church, namely the Roman Church, has chosen this to be done with most discerning consideration, not whenever it wishes to reconsider what has been decided [Note: [Col. 1695] “when, however, this must be observed, when that is, namely, the Roman Church, with most eloquent consideration, chooses this to be done, etc.”: collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 1695] “almost”: original in Mansi.] [Note: [Col. 1695D] “wishes”: so also in the printed original; but Anselm and Ivo have “refuses.”].

### C. VII. The authority of the Apostolic See can reconsider anyone’s judgment. Innocent to the bishops established throughout Macedonia, Epistle VII. [Note: [Col. 1695] written about A.D. 415.—Anselm, book 2, chapter 28 (29). Polycarpus, book 5, title 4.]

It ought not to seem burdensome [Note: [Col. 1695] “ought”: collected editions and first Basel edition.] to your most devout minds that anyone’s judgment should be reconsidered [Note: [Col. 1695] “to reconsider”: the same editions and second and third Lyons editions.], because truth, when more often examined, shines more brightly into the light [Note: [Col. 1695] “light”: collected editions.], and destruction, recalled to judgment, is condemned more severely and without repentance [Note: [Col. 1695] “judgment”: Basel edition.]. For it is a divine fruit that justice should be reviewed often [Note: [Col. 1695] “and fruit”: same edition.].

### C. VIII. Those deposed by predecessors are restored by successors. Likewise from the *Liber Pontificalis*. [Note: [Col. 1695D] The same material, only in a different order, occurs above, Distinction 50, chapter “John Chrysostom,” § “Bishop Misenus” [Col. 1696D]. In most old copies of Gratian this chapter is placed before chapter “Grave,” without the name of Palea [thus Basel edition; the name Palea is appended in the collected editions and first Argentinensis and Basel editions].] [Note: [Col. 1695] cf. Distinction 50, chapter 13.]

[Col. 1695B] Gregory IV consecrated as bishop of the Church of Segni Theodosius, whom his predecessor Eugenius had deprived of the honor of the priesthood [Note: [Col. 1695] “Senguinae”: Argentinensis edition.—“sanguine”: Nuremberg and first and second Venice editions.—“Seguinae”: remaining editions.]. Leontius was deposed while he was a priest, but [Note: [Col. 1695] “and”: collected editions.] afterward became patriarch in Antioch. Gelasius, successor of Pope Felix, both restored Bishop Misenus, whom Felix had condemned, to communion and restored him to his own church.

### C. IX.

Therefore, just as the judgment of the Roman See may be altered for the better, so the judgment of any church, when it is known to have been issued through fraud, may reasonably be revoked [Note: [Col. 1695] These are Gratian’s words.].

## QUESTION X

[Col. 1695C]

**GRATIAN.**

Concerning a woman who enters a second marriage, however, it is reasonably asked whether she remains in the same affinity with the blood relatives of her former husband, or whether offspring born of the second marriage may be joined to the blood relatives of the former husband.

Pope Gregory writes thus on these matters to Venerius, Bishop of Cagliari [Note: [Col. 1695] A spurious epistle.—Anselm, book 10, chapter 53 (54). Ivo, Panormia, book 7, chapter 68; Decretum, part 9, chapter 38. Hugh of St Victor, book 2, part 11, chapter 15.]:

### C. I. Affinity is not erased in the surviving spouse.

[Col. 1696A] To the diligent acumen of your brotherhood [Note: [Col. 1695] “your”: Ivo, Decretum; Basel and first Lyons editions.], beloved brother, I return the thanks which I owe. Since you have asked what you ought to ask, you have made me glad. I therefore answer your questions kindly. You have resolved to consult the Apostolic See whether a woman joined in marital union to a man outside her family belongs to his kindred; whether, if he dies, the relationship remains [Note: [Col. 1695] “continues”: collected editions.]; whether, under another husband [Note: [Col. 1695] “another”: Ivo.], the names of relationship are dissolved; or whether offspring born to her may lawfully pass into union with the kindred of the former husband.

For the word of the Lord is mighty *and* strong; it is [Note: [Col. 1695] “and—and—and”: collected editions; absent from Hugh.] enduring, unchangeable, permanent—not momentary, not passing. For Truth itself, who is God and the Word of God [Note: [Col. 1695] add “is”: Ivo, Panormia, and collected editions.—cf. Luke 21:33.], says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.” Before God appeared [Col. 1696B] in the flesh among humankind, Adam, inspired by him, said [Note: [Col. 1695] Genesis 2:24]: “Therefore a man shall leave his father [Note: [Col. 1695] absent from Ivo.] and mother [Note: [Col. 1695] add “his”: same source; Hugh; Basel edition.], and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh”; *and the Lord did not contradict this.* Then, when Truth rose from the earth upon earth and appeared visibly in humanity, he was asked whether it was lawful for a man to leave his wife. Prohibiting this *to be done*, he forbade it, unless fornication might exclude the marital union. He therefore immediately brought forward that same judgment which, existing with the Father before the ages, he the Word had inspired in Adam; himself [Note: [Col. 1695] add “the same”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.] confirming [Note: [Col. 1695] “strengthening”: Argentinensis edition.] what the first man himself [Note: [Col. 1695] “time”: same edition.] had uttered [Note: [Col. 1695] “immediately”: Ivo, Decretum; absent from Hugh.] [Note: [Col. 1695] Matthew 19:5]: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother [Note: [Col. 1695] add “his”: Basel edition.], and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.”

If they become [Col. 1696C] one flesh [Note: [Col. 1695] “becomes”: collected editions.], how can a relative of either one belong to the one without belonging to the other? It must be believed that this cannot happen. Moreover, when one dies, affinity is not erased in the survivor; nor can another marital union dissolve [Note: [Col. 1695] “absolve”: Argentinensis edition.] the affinity of the former union [Note: [Col. 1695] “is able”: collected editions.]. Nor does it seem right that the offspring of another union should pass into the fellowship of affinity with the former husband, because the word of the Lord is mighty and strong, and because, as the Prophet says [Note: [Col. 1695] absent from the collected editions and first Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1695] “says”: Basel edition.—cf. Isaiah 40:8.—“word”; “prophet”: absent from Ivo, Panormia, and Hugh.], “The word of the Lord remains [Note: [Col. 1695] “stands”: collected editions.] forever.” And another Prophet [Note: [Col. 1695] Psalm 148:5 ff.] says [Note: [Col. 1697] “says”: same editions.—cf. John 17:20.]:

[Col. 1697A] “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. He established them for ever and ever; he gave a commandment, and it shall not pass away.”

For God can through *his* word and command make [Note: [Col. 1697] “made”: same editions and Ivo.] two persons one flesh—namely male and female—though he has not ceased to make with himself one innumerable multitude of both sexes [Note: [Col. 1697] “also innumerable”: Basel edition.], as Truth himself said: “I pray not for these only, but also for those who shall believe in me through their word, that they all may be one [Note: [Col. 1697] absent from Ivo and Hugh.], as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us.”

Therefore, if anyone with rash and sacrilegious audacity seeks to extinguish kinship in one who has died, or to dissipate it under the name of another affinity, or believes that offspring born of another union [Note: [Col. 1697] “offspring born”: Basel edition.] can lawfully be joined to the kinship of the former union, that person denies [Col. 1697B] that God’s word is mighty and strong; and whoever seeks so readily and so swiftly to dissolve it does not believe that the word of God remains forever.

Take earth from four places widely distant from each other, and, having formed it, imagine it fashioned and joined together [Note: [Col. 1697] “formed and joined together”: collected editions and first Basel edition.] into a body of whatever shape or vastness you wish. Would there be any human ingenuity able to separate those four parts from one another, so that each could be recognized by itself? So two persons are made one from four grandparents, and from two comes one creation. You may draw this comparison from the four elements from which the human being was made, if you assign each sort of them—which is distributed in many divisions—by parts distinct from one another [Note: [Col. 1697] “marked out”: Basel edition.]. The same occurs in metals; also in liquids. The painter proves it [Note: [Col. 1697] “It is proved. In colors, the painter continues the colors by art, etc.”: collected editions.] even in colors, following *nature* by art and mixing colors [Note: [Col. 1697D] “Mixing”: In Polycarpus and Anselm, from whom the preceding words have been restored, this place reads thus: “mixing colors with dyes, fashioning bodies from invisible things.” But “lest the Lord’s ordinance …,” for much follows in those sources.], fashioning bodies from visible dyes [Note: [Col. 1697] “fixing”: first and second Venice editions.].

### C. II. Offspring from second marriages ought not be joined to the blood relatives of the former husband. Likewise Pope Innocent. [Note: [Col. 1697] Chapter of uncertain source.]

If a man’s paternal uncle or maternal uncle dies while married, and that woman afterward takes another husband and bears sons or daughters by him, we prohibit all relations with these persons in every way, because husband and wife are one flesh [Note: [Col. 1697] “are”: Basel edition.].

### C. III. On the same matter. Likewise from a Roman Synod. [Note: [Col. 1697] Chapter of uncertain source.—The name Palea is attached in the Argentinensis edition both to this and to the following chapters.]

If any woman enters a second marriage and bears offspring from it, that offspring can in no way attain fellowship [Col. 1698B] with the kindred of the former husband.

### C. IV. On the same matter. [PALEA.] Likewise Pope Hyginus. [Note: [Col. 1697] Chapter of uncertain source.—Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 41.]

“If any woman enters a second marriage and has offspring from it, that offspring cannot be joined to the kindred of the former husband up to the fourth generation.”

Hence Pope Innocent [Note: [Col. 1697] Chapter of uncertain source.—Anselm, book 10, chapter 67 (68).]:

### C. V. On the same matter. [PALEA.]

“If any woman enters a second marriage and bears sons and [Note: [Col. 1697] “or”: collected editions and first Lyons edition.] daughters to the second husband, the holy Roman Synod has utterly forbidden them to be joined [Note: [Col. 1697] “ought not”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.] to the grandchildren of the former husband.”

## CAUSE XXXVI

[Col. 1697]

[Col. 1697C] **GRATIAN.**

A certain man enticed someone’s daughter, without her father’s knowledge, by gifts and invited her to a banquet. When the banquet was over, the young man violated the maiden. When this became known, the girl was handed over to the young man by her parents; he endowed her in the manner of those marrying, and publicly took her as his wife. (Question I.) First, it is asked whether he committed abduction. (Question II.) Second, whether the abducted woman may marry her abductor if her father gives consent.

## QUESTION I

[Col. 1698C]

**GRATIAN.**

That he did commit abduction is proved by the authority of many writers.

For Isidore says in *Etymologies*, book V, chapter 26 [Note: [Col. 1697D] Ivo has almost exactly what Gratian has here and above, Cause 27, question 2, chapter “Raptus”; nor does the Panormia differ greatly. In the printed Isidore manuscript it reads: “*Stuprum* is properly illicit intercourse, called *raptus* from corruption. Hence Virgil: *rapto potimur*, that is, ‘he enjoys sexual violation.’”] [Note: [Col. 1697] cf. Cause 27, question 2, chapter 48.—Ivo, Panormia, book 6, chapter 53; Decretum, part 8, chapter 26.]:

### C. I. What abduction is.

*Raptus* (“abduction”) is likewise named from corruption as illicit intercourse; hence one who obtains by *raptus* enjoys *stuprum* (sexual defilement).

[Note: [Col. 1699] 2. cf. Cause 27, question 2, chapter 49.]

[Col. 1699A] Hence Pope Gelasius [Note: [Col. 1699] “girls or women”: collected editions.]:

### C. II. Where abduction occurs.

That law of the former emperors declared abduction to have been committed where a girl, concerning whose marriage nothing had previously been arranged [Note: [Col. 1699] “had been”: Argentinensis, Nuremberg, and first and second Venice editions.], appears [Note: [Col. 1699] “appeared”: Paris and Lyons editions.—“appears”: Böhm.] to have been carried away.

**Gratian.** Therefore, since this woman was defiled by illicit intercourse, and was carried away in this manner—that is, taken from her father’s house—when nothing had been previously arranged concerning her marriage, it cannot be denied that she must be called abducted. Yet not every illicit intercourse, nor every unlawful deflowering of a woman, is called *raptus*. For fornication is one thing, *stuprum* another, adultery another, incest another, and *raptus* another.

§ 1. Fornication, although it seems to be the general category of every illicit intercourse occurring outside lawful marriage, is nevertheless understood specifically of intercourse with widows, prostitutes, or concubines.

§ 2. *Stuprum*, properly speaking, is the unlawful deflowering of virgins: namely, when a virgin is violated by a man with the consent of both parties, without a preceding marital agreement, and her father does not, immediately upon learning of it, take the injury to heart.

§ 3. Adultery is the violation of another’s bed. Hence *adulterium* is so called as though it were an approach to another’s bed.

§ 4. Incest is sexual misuse of blood relatives or relatives by marriage. Hence persons are called incestuous who misuse blood relatives or affines.

§ 5. *Raptus* is committed when a girl is violently carried away from her father’s house in order that, after being defiled, she may be kept as a wife, whether force is shown to have been inflicted on the girl alone, on the parents alone, or on both; this is punished by death. But if he flees to a church with the abducted woman, he obtains immunity from capital punishment by the privilege of the Church.

Accordingly, in the First Council of Orléans, chapter 4, we read [Note: [Col. 1699] held A.D. 511.—Burchard, book 3, chapter 191; Anselm, book 10, chapter 57 (64); Ivo, Panormia, book 2, chapter 72; Decretum, part 3, chapter 108.]:

### C. III. What should be done if an abductor flees to a church with the abducted woman?

[Col. 1699C] Concerning abductors, we have judged that the following should be ordained: if an abductor flees to a church with the abducted woman [Note: [Col. 1699] “comes together”: Collection Hispana.], and it is established that the woman herself suffered violence, she shall immediately be freed from the power of the abductor [Note: [Col. 1699] add: “and restored to her parents”: Burchard and Ivo; Basel and Lyons editions.]; and the abductor, having been granted immunity from death or punishments [Note: [Col. 1699] “immunity”: Böhm.], shall either be subjected to servitude or have free power to ransom himself [Note: [Col. 1699] “having been granted, shall have free power to depart”: Burchard and Ivo, who also depart completely from the council in what follows.—The council: “to the condition of servitude,” etc.: Collection Hispana.]. But if the girl who is abducted is established to have a father, and the girl consents to the abductor, she shall be restored without blame to the father’s authority, and the abductor shall be bound to make satisfaction to the father according to a higher social rank [Note: [Col. 1699] “by the father”: same source.].

[Col. 1699D] **Gratian.** From this authority it is clear that force is sometimes inflicted on parents and not on the girl, when it says: “if the girl consents to the abductor.” Sometimes both suffer violence, when it says beforehand: “if the abductor flees with the abducted woman, and it is established that the woman herself suffered violence.” But force is inflicted on the girl and not on the parents when, contrary to the father’s will, the girl is violently carried off in order that she may suffer intercourse with one to whose union she never gave consent. Yet this man seems to have inflicted force neither on the parents nor on the girl, since she was not carried off by force either while they forbade it or while she resisted. For it is one thing to seduce someone by promises, another to inflict force upon her. Therefore, because force is proved to have been inflicted on neither, he should not be called an abductor under this law.

But robbery is said to occur in two ways. Sometimes the thing itself is stolen; sometimes only the use of the thing is violently taken away. The thing itself is stolen when it is violently taken from its owner in order to be held forever; but sometimes the thing itself is not sought, while its use is violently usurped against the owner’s will [Col. 1700B]. Therefore this man committed *raptus*, because he violently took away the flower of virginity from the resisting girl.

## QUESTION II

**GRATIAN.**

**Part I.** It is now asked whether, once the fault of abduction has been purged, the abductor may take the abducted woman as his wife. Their union is altogether prohibited by the authority of the holy canons.

For in the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 27, we read [Note: [Col. 1699] held A.D. 451.—Dionysius’s translation.—Burchard, book 9, chapter 35; Anselm, book 10, chapter 49 (56); Ivo, Decretum, part 8, chapter 173; Polycarpus, book 6, title 4.]:

### C. I. Abductors of girls and those consenting to them are to be excommunicated.

Those who carry off women under the pretext of living together [Col. 1700C] [Note: [Col. 1699] “cohabiting”: same editions and first Basel edition.], *or* assist abductors or connive at them—the holy synod decreed that, if they are clerics, they shall be deprived of their proper rank [Note: [Col. 1699] “from their proper rank”: Burchard and Ivo.—“from proper rank”: collected editions.]; but if laymen, they shall be anathematized.

### C. II. Because of the enormity of the crime, abductors of widows or virgins are to be expelled. Likewise Pope Symmachus, Epistle to Caesarius, chapter 3. [Note: [Col. 1699] written A.D. 502.—Regino, book 2, chapter 162; Collection in three parts, part 1, title 48, chapter 2; Anselm, book 10, chapter 58 (65); Polycarpus, book 6, title 8.]

We therefore detest abductors of widows or virgins because of the enormity of so great a crime, pursuing even more severely those who attempt to join sacred virgins, whether willing or unwilling, in marriage [Note: [Col. 1699] “in marriage”: collected editions and first Basel edition.—add “their own”: collected editions.]. Because of the atrocity of such a most wicked crime, we command that they be suspended from communion.

### C. III. On the same matter. Likewise from Book I of the Code, title “On Bishops and Clerics.” [Note: [Col. 1699] cf. above, Distinction 1, on Penance, chapter 6.] Emperor Jovian [Note: [Col. 1699] “Justinian”: collected editions.]

[Col. 1700D] If anyone should dare, I will not say to abduct, but even merely to attempt, for the purpose of contracting marriage with most sacred virgins, he shall be struck with capital punishment.

### C. IV. On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Chalon. [Note: [Col. 1701] Rather, from the Capitularies of Louis, A.D. 816.—cf. Capitularies, book 1, chapter 104; book 7, chapter 183; and Council of Worms, held A.D. 868, chapter 77.—Regino, book 2, chapter 158; Burchard, book 9, chapter 36; Ivo, Panormia, book 6, chapter 55; Decretum, part 8, chapter 174.]

[Col. 1701A] Concerning girls abducted but not yet betrothed [Note: [Col. 1701] “nor”: Argentinensis edition.—“and not”: Ivo, Panormia.], it was decreed in the Council of Chalcedon [Note: [Col. 1701] cf. above, chapter 1.] that those who carry off girls under the pretext of living together [Note: [Col. 1701] “cohabiting”: Ivo, Panormia.], those assisting abductors and those conniving at them, should, as the holy synod decreed, if they are clerics, be deprived of their proper rank [Note: [Col. 1701] “from their proper rank”: Regino and collected editions.—“of proper rank”: Burchard and Ivo.], but if laymen, be anathematized [Note: [Col. 1701] “excommunicated”: collected editions.]. These words make clear how the authors of this evil ought to be condemned [Note: [Col. 1701] “are”: Regino, Burchard, Ivo, Panormia, collected editions, and Böhm.], when participants in the plan and those who connive are struck with so great an anathema that [Note: [Col. 1701] “and”: Regino, Burchard, and Basel edition.] according to canonical authority they can by no means lawfully claim the abducted women for themselves in lawful marriages [Note: [Col. 1701] “can”: Regino, Burchard, Ivo, and Basel and first and second Venice, Paris, and first Lyons editions.].

### C. V. Abductors of a widow or virgin, with those favoring them, are to be excommunicated. Likewise Pope Gregory II, in a Roman Synod. [Note: [Col. 1701C] This chapter was made from chapters 10 and 11 of the decree of Gregory II, which in the Code of Canons is called “Junior.”] [Note: [Col. 1701] held A.D. 721.—Burchard, book 9, chapters 11–12; Anselm, book 10, chapter 49 (51); Ivo, Panormia, book 6, chapter 54; Decretum, part 8, chapters 149–150.]

[Col. 1701B] If anyone, unless he has betrothed her, abducts or steals a virgin or widow to make her his wife, he and those favoring him shall be anathema.

### C. VI. Let him be excommunicated who abducts another’s widow or daughter outside the will of her parents, or seeks her through royal favor. Likewise from the First Council of Paris, chapter 6. [Note: [Col. 1701] Third Council in the conciliar collection, held A.D. 557.—Ivo, Decretum, part 8, chapter 25.]

No one shall dare either to abduct another’s widow or daughter outside her parents’ will, or to consider that she should be sought through royal favor [Note: [Col. 1701] “either—or”: Ivo and the collected editions.]. If he does so, let him be removed from communion with the Church and struck by the sword of anathema [Note: [Col. 1701] “be punished with condemnation”: original.].

**Part II. Gratian.** These authorities clearly indicate that an abductor cannot take the abducted woman as his wife [Col. 1701C]. But “abductor” and “abducted woman” are names of vices, not of persons. When vices have been purged by penance, however, their names are abolished.

Thus Gregory says in a homily [Note: [Col. 1701] The very words of Gregory occur above, Cause 32, question 2, chapter 10.]:

### C. VII.

For in the sight of almighty God [Note: [Col. 1701] “Lord”: Basel edition.], that person is not accounted deceitful who blots out the guilt of lying through repentance [Note: [Col. 1701] “ought”: same edition.].

**Gratian.** Therefore, by the authorities cited above, the abducted woman is prohibited from being joined to the abductor until the fault of abduction has been abolished—so long as he is lawfully called an abductor and she an abducted woman [Col. 1702A]. But when she has been restored to her father’s authority, and the abductor has performed penance for his abduction, and the will of the parents of both has come together in agreement, they are not prohibited from being joined to each other.

Accordingly Jerome says [Note: [Col. 1702C] After this chapter, Ivo and the Panormia have the chapter “Another is added,” cited above from Jerome also, Cause 27, question 2.] [Note: [Col. 1701] Chapter of uncertain source.—Regino, book 2, chapter 107; Ivo, Panormia, book 6, chapter 33; Decretum, part 8, chapter 40.—cf. Cause 27, question 2, chapter 13.]:

### C. VIII. How many lawful marriages there are, and that an abducted woman may marry her abductor with her father’s consent.

Three lawful marriages are read of in Scripture. The first lawful *marriage* [Note: [Col. 1701] absent from Ivo, Panormia.] is when a chaste virgin is lawfully given to a man in her virginity, and [Note: [Col. 1701] “and—the preceding words”: not found in Regino.] the rest that follows in what has been said above. The second is when a virgin [Note: [Col. 1701] add “chaste”: Basel and second and third Lyons editions.—cf. Deuteronomy 22.] is discovered in a city by a man and joined to him by force. If her father wishes it, this man shall endow her in whatever amount her father determines, and shall give the price for her chastity [Note: [Col. 1701] “his”: Basel edition.]. The third is the daughter described above who has been found out. If it is not her father’s will, he shall take her away [Note: [Col. 1701] “remove”: Basel edition.—“withdraw”: second and third Lyons editions.] from the said man, give her to another, endow her, and she shall be his lawful wife. But the first is preferred to these two.

### C. IX. It is permitted to have abducted women in marriage with their parents’ consent. Likewise Ambrose, *Apology of David*, chapter 8. [Note: [Col. 1701] cf. Deuteronomy 22:29.]

[Col. 1702B] Finally, the father of a girl who, unbetrothed to any man, has suffered the violence of intercourse [Note: [Col. 1701] “suffered”: collected editions.] shall receive fifty silver drachmas; but she herself shall remain in marriage.

### C. X. After penance, marriages are lawfully permitted to the abductor or the abducted woman. Likewise from the Council of Meaux, chapter 65. [Note: [Col. 1701] held A.D. 845. Regino, book 2, chapter 159; Burchard, book 9, chapter 39; Ivo, Panormia, book 6, chapter 56; Decretum, part 9, chapter 177.]

But if they have not yet taken in marriage those whom they abducted, with their parents’ consent, under the name of betrothal [Col. 1702C] [Note: [Col. 1701] “betrothal”: Ivo, Panormia; collected editions and Böhm.] or dower [Note: [Col. 1701] “shall have taken”: Basel edition.—“have taken”: cited collections.], when this decree has been promulgated to everyone’s hearing [Note: [Col. 1701] “when these things”: Argentinensis edition.—“when these things have [been promulgated] to everyone”: Basel edition.—“when these things [have been promulgated] to all”: remaining editions.], they shall be separated from their union and subjected to public penance [Note: [Col. 1701] “subjected”: Basel edition.]; but the abducted women [Note: [Col. 1701] “and the abducted women”: collected editions and first Basel edition.] shall be lawfully restored to their parents.

Once public penance has been completed, if age and incontinence require it [Note: [Col. 1701] “incontinence”: Ivo, Panormia, and collected editions.], let them be joined in a lawful marriage agreed upon by both parties [Note: [Col. 1701] “of each”: collected editions and first Argentinensis and Basel editions.] [Note: [Col. 1701] “approved marriages”: Argentinensis edition.]. For we do not establish a rule in these cases [Note: [Col. 1701] “Therefore not in these cases”: collected editions.], but, to use the words of the great Leo, judge what is more tolerable [Col. 1703A]. If one of the married persons dies, and the one who performed public penance survives [Note: [Col. 1703] “performed”: same editions and Böhm.], that person shall not presume to marry again, unless perhaps the bishop sees fit [Note: [Col. 1703] “grants”: collected editions.] to grant some indulgence, in order that he may remove a graver offense.

**Gratian.** By this authority of the Council of Meaux, an abductor is not permitted to be joined to the abducted woman after penance; rather, each of them is permitted after penance to be joined in lawful marriage. Thus the abducted woman is to marry not her abductor but another man after penance; likewise, after penance, the abductor is permitted to have not the woman he abducted but another as wife. For when the abductor and the abducted woman are commanded to undergo penance, if that authority permitted their union with one another, it would say vainly near the end of the chapter: “If one of the married persons dies, and the one who performed public penance survives, that person shall not presume to marry again.” For whenever either of those who performed penance dies, the other remains alive. Therefore, this authority does not prove that an abductor can take the abducted woman in marriage.

Rather, it is found in a council at Aachen [Note: [Col. 1703] Rather, in the Capitularies of the Frankish Kings, book 7, chapter 395.—Burchard, book 9, chapter 33; Ivo, Decretum, part 8, chapter 171.] that they cannot be joined to each other even with their parents’ consent. For the following is read in the aforesaid council [Note: [Col. 1703] Burchard and Ivo also cite this chapter from Aachen, chapter 3. It occurs in book 7 of the Capitularies, chapter 395, and from there is reported in the Council of Trosly at Reims, chapter 8.]:

### C. XI. Abductors cannot have abducted women as wives even with a parent’s consent.

[Col. 1703B] It has pleased us that those who abduct women, steal them, or seduce them [Note: [Col. 1703] “that [they may] seduce them”: original.] shall by no means have them as wives, even though they subsequently come to an agreement with them [Note: [Col. 1703] “come to an agreement”: collected editions.], or have endowed them, [Col. 1704A] or have nevertheless taken them in marriage [Note: [Col. 1703] add “nevertheless”: Argentinensis and Basel editions.] with the consent of their parents [Note: [Col. 1703] “received”: same editions.].

Gratian. This authority does not prejudice the authority of Jerome, especially since the latter rests upon the testimony of divine law. Therefore, after penance has been completed, the abductor may lawfully unite himself to the woman whom he abducted, unless the girl’s father should wish to take her away from the abductor. [Note: [Col. 1703] What follows is absent from the Basel edition.]

[PALEA.]

“Likewise, Code, book 5, title *On Marriages* [Note: [Col. 1703] *Code of Justinian*, book 5, title 4, chapter 12]: The discipline of the laws does not permit even a son under paternal authority to be compelled against his will to take a wife. Therefore, as you desire, provided the precepts of law are observed, you are not prevented from joining in marriage whomever you wish; yet in contracting the marriage your father’s consent must be given. Likewise, in the same work [Col. 1704B], law 20: In the marriage of daughters dedicated to sacred service, the father’s decision is to be awaited. [Note: [Col. 1703] *expetitur*, ‘is sought’: editions commonly collated.] Likewise, *Digest*, *On the Rite of Marriage*, law 2 [Note: [Col. 1703] *Digest* 23.2, fragment 2]: Marriages cannot exist unless all consent: that is, those who are joined together and those under whose authority they are. Likewise, *Institutes*, book 1, title *On Marriages* [Note: [Col. 1703] title 10, opening]: Roman citizens contract lawful marriages with one another when they unite according to the precepts of the laws: males when pubescent, females when capable of marriage [Note: [Col. 1703] Omitted by Bohm.], whether they are heads of households or children under paternal authority, provided that children under paternal authority have the consent of the parents under whose authority they are. For both civil and natural reason persuade that this ought to be done—so strongly that a parent’s command must come first.” [Note: [Col. 1703] *ordo*, ‘order’: editions commonly collated, first Lugdanum edition.]

## Third Part of the Decree: On Consecration

[Note: [Col. 1703] “On the consecration of churches, and that Masses are to be celebrated elsewhere than in places consecrated to God”: Argentinian edition.—“On the consecration of churches, and that Masses must be celebrated only in places consecrated to God”: Basel edition.—“On the consecration of churches and the celebration of Masses”: Nuremberg edition.]

[Col. 1703]

## Distinction I

[Col. 1703C] **Chapter I.** [Note: [Col. 1703C] The words of the following chapter are not separated from those above in old copies of Gratian, just as they are not separated in the letter of Felix IV itself or in other collectors. They have not been altered because of citations by the Doctors. Some matters, however, have been corrected.] [Note: [Col. 1703] From Pseudo-Felix, letter 1, chapter 1; compare the Council of Paris, A.D. 829, book 1, chapter 47.—Burchard, book 3, chapters 57 following; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 33; *Decree*, part 3, chapter 60.]

It is clear to all who know the precepts of the Old and New Testaments that the consecration of churches and the celebration of Masses ought not, except under grave necessity, to take place elsewhere than in places consecrated to the Lord. [Note: [Col. 1703] “On the consecration of churches and celebrations of Mass”: original; cited collections; editions commonly collated, first Paris and Lyons editions.]

[Col. 1705A] **Chapter II.** [Note: [Col. 1705] Burchard, book 3, chapters 57–58; Ivo, *Panormia*, same place, down to “we know”; *Decree*, part 3, chapters 60–61.]

For [Note: [Col. 1705] “indeed”: original, Burchard, and Ivo.] we read that Moses, at the Lord’s command, made and consecrated the tabernacle, together with its table and altar, its bronze vessels [Note: [Col. 1705] “other”: original; “are”: Burchard and Ivo; editions commonly collated.] and implements for carrying out divine worship. And we know that he consecrated them not only by divine prayers, but also, at the Lord’s command, anointed them with holy oil. How these things were done, and how [Note: [Col. 1705] “so that”: Paris and Lyons editions.] those sacred things [Note: [Col. 1705] “sacraments”: editions commonly collated.] were handled, carried, erected, and taken down only by priests [Note: [Col. 1705] “they themselves” added: the same editions.] anointed with sacred unction and consecrated to the Lord in holy vestments, and by Levites, is found in the ordinances [Note: [Col. 1705] “constitutions”: Basel edition; compare Exodus 31 and Numbers 7.] written by Moses at the Lord’s command in the Law of the Lord.

We likewise read in the Book of Kings how David, the most devout of kings, enlarged [Note: [Col. 1705] “expanded”: Basel edition; compare 2 Samuel 7.] God’s worship and wished to build a temple for the Lord [Note: [Col. 1705] “of the Lord”: original, Burchard, Ivo, editions commonly collated.] [Note: [Col. 1705] “wished”: original, Burchard, and Ivo.], but was forbidden because of the much blood he had shed; and he himself gathered the resources. [Note: [Col. 1705] 1 Chronicles 22.] Solomon his son, with God commanding and assisting, accomplished the very thing which David had wished to do, and consecrated the temple with its altar and the other things required for carrying out divine worship.

And below:

§ 1. Then Solomon [Note: [Col. 1705C] “Then Solomon”: Before these words the letter of Felix itself inserts everything preceding this in chapter 8 of the Third Book of Kingdoms. Burchard and Ivo also omit these matters and conclude the chapter with the verse “He consecrated.”] [Note: [Col. 1705] “also”: Basel edition.] celebrated at that time a solemn feast, and all Israel with him, a great multitude from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of Egypt, before the Lord our God, for seven days and seven days—that is, fourteen days—and on the eighth day he dismissed the people.

§ 2. Therefore the Jews regarded the places in which they sacrificed to the Lord as consecrated by divine supplications, and offered gifts to the Lord in no places other than those dedicated to God. [Note: [Col. 1705] “in God”: same edition; “dedicated”: editions commonly collated, first Basel edition; “to God”: editions commonly collated.] For if the Jews, who served the shadow of the Law [Note: [Col. 1705] “of God” added: Basel and Lyons II–III editions.], did this, how much more ought we, to whom truth has been revealed and grace has been given through Jesus Christ, [Note: [Col. 1705] John 1:17.] to build temples for the Lord; to adorn them as best we can; devoutly and solemnly consecrate them by divine prayers and holy anointings, together with their altars, vessels, vestments, and other implements necessary for divine worship; and to celebrate Masses and offer sacrifices to the Lord not in other places but in places consecrated in the Lord by bishops—and not by chorepiscopi, who have often been forbidden to do this except, as said above, where supreme necessity requires it.

And if [Note: [Col. 1705C] Burchard reads *nisi summa*, “unless [there is] supreme necessity,” rather than *si summa*, “if [there is] supreme necessity.”] supreme necessity compels this [Note: [Col. 1705] “these things”: editions commonly collated.], it must be done not in houses [Note: [Col. 1705C] “Not in houses”: This passage through “be done” has been corrected and augmented from the original, Burchard, and Ivo. Previously it read: “it was forbidden that offerings be made in houses,” far from the canon’s meaning.] (“because in the sacred canons sacrifices are forbidden to be offered in houses”), but in tents dedicated by bishops through divine prayers, and on tables consecrated to the Lord and anointed with sacred unction by bishops. This is to be done because of supreme necessity, as has been prescribed, and not at anyone’s whim or through laziness.

And below [Note: [Col. 1705D] “And below”: The things inserted here in the letter occur below in this same chapter, “Just as”]:

§ 3. But if, as is read in the Council of Laodicea, chapter 26 [Note: [Col. 1705] Dionysius’s translation.] [Note: [Col. 1705] Chapter 37: Basel edition; 27: the remaining editions.], those not ordained by bishops cannot perform exorcisms either in churches or in houses, much less may ministries of a higher rank be performed, or sacrifices offered, except by those consecrated to the ranks whose offices they are to exercise. [Note: [Col. 1706C] “It is not lawful that sacrifices be offered”: The original has “it is lawful that sacrifices be offered.” But in the same text, a little above, where the text has “much more,” the margin reads: “alternatively, much less.” Burchard and Ivo indeed read as Gratian does.]

Moreover, as was touched on a little above, that offerings ought not to be made in houses is prohibited in the same council, chapter 58 [Note: [Col. 1705] Dionysius’s translation.] [Note: [Col. 1705] Chapter 59: editions commonly collated, first Basel edition.], as follows: “Offerings ought not to be celebrated in houses by bishops and presbyters.” [Note: [Col. 1705] “or”: Council of Laodicea; editions commonly collated.] [Note: [Col. 1706C] “And presbyters”: In the original and in Burchard, the words of the chapter “Solemnities of dedications,” below in the same distinction, are joined with these.]

**Chapter III. The consecration of churches must not take place without Mass. Likewise Pope Hyginus, chapter 5.** [Note: [Col. 1706D] This chapter through “consecrated” is cited by most collectors from Evaristus, or from Evaristus’s decretals. The remaining words, reported by them under another chapter, are attributed to Hyginus.] [Note: [Col. 1705] Rather, from the Capitularies of Louis, A.D. 829, title 1, chapter 3; compare *Capitularies*, book 5, chapter 275; *Regino*, book 2, chapter 39; Burchard, book 3, chapters 27 and 21; Anselm, book 5, chapter 83; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 13, through “consecrated”; *Decree*, part 3, chapters 32 and 26; Polycarpus, book 3, title 3.]

**Part II.** All basilicas must always be consecrated with Mass.

§ 1. So that, with respect to churches which have been destroyed, where either there are more than are needed or they are too large to be restored from the resources belonging to them, a means may be found through the bishop’s provision by which they may continue to exist. [Note: [Col. 1705] “and”: editions commonly collated; “however”: same; “them”: same; “may”: same, first Paris and Lyons II–III editions.]

**Chapter IV. A new church is not to be dedicated without the command of the Apostolic See. Likewise Pope Gelasius to the bishops throughout Lucania, chapter 27.** [Note: [Col. 1705] Written A.D. 494; Anselm, book 5, chapter 80.]

**Part III.** Although we have treated briefly above of the consecration of holy places [Note: [Col. 1707] “more strictly”: Basel edition; “or in writings” added: Argentinian edition.] it has also been brought to us [Note: [Col. 1707] “to me”: editions commonly collated.] that some persons presume, without an order of the Apostolic See, to make churches or oratories that have been built. [Note: [Col. 1707] “to consecrate”: same editions; Anselm; Hispanic Collection.]

**Chapter V. A new church is not to be dedicated without the authority of the supreme pontiff. The same author.** [Note: [Col. 1707] Chapter of uncertain origin.—Anselm, book 5, chapter 5 (7); Polycarpus, book 1, title 12.]

The synodal commands sent a few months ago from our see to the province agree with the ancient canons [Note: [Col. 1707D] “Ancient canons”: Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 2, chapters 8 and 17, reports as a most ancient canon that no church can be dedicated without the authority of the Roman bishop. [Col. 1707] This is utterly false and especially alien to the discipline of the ancient Church; Socrates says only this in the cited passages: that churches can decide nothing apart from the judgment of the Roman pontiff.], and we have added what seemed insufficiently provided for. Both parts establish that a newly founded church cannot be dedicated without the authority of the supreme pontiff. We therefore consider it fitting that you have suspended Masses in that basilica which had thus been brought into use for a procession.

But because a devout place ought not long to remain without the grace of ministries, most beloved brother, you shall consecrate it, on receiving the written authorization of our authority, in the names of the martyrs contained in the report; so that the gathering of the people, whom you have commanded eagerly to assemble there, may, with ecclesiastical rules and canons observed, possess an unharmed assembly, its religion having been established. [Note: [Col. 1707] “divine” added: editions commonly collated.]

**Chapter VI. Basilicas built apart from the authority of the Apostolic See are not to be dedicated. The same author to the bishops throughout Lucania, chapter 6.** [Note: [Col. 1707D] The words of this chapter through “another’s” also occur in the *Worms Collection*, chapter 48.] [Note: [Col. 1707] Written A.D. 494; Anselm, book 5, chapter 4 (6); Polycarpus, book 3, title 3.]

Let them not dare to dedicate newly established basilicas without first requesting the customary orders; nor may bishops seek to claim for themselves clerics who are under another’s jurisdiction. [Note: [Col. 1707] “no one shall hear”: Hispanic Collection; editions commonly collated.]

And chapter 11:

§ 1. Since we too earnestly endeavor to preserve the decrees of venerable enactments, and believe that even those matters which perhaps seem to require relaxation for some expedient benefit should be relaxed without detriment to them; since we desire that nothing be rashly permitted to us contrary to the reverence due to salutary rules; and since the Apostolic See, superior to all these, by the Lord’s favor strives with pious and devoted purpose to observe those things laid down by the canons of the Fathers: it is quite unworthy that any bishop or subordinate order should reject this observance, which it sees that the See of blessed Peter both follows and teaches. And it is entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree in this observance, which it sees to flourish there where the Lord placed the primacy of the whole Church. [Note: [Col. 1707] “yield”: Anselm; “establish”: Basel edition; “we”: editions commonly collated; “say”: same; “above”: Hispanic Collection; “is”: same.]

**Chapter VII. Public processions are not to take place in oratories consecrated apart from the authority of the Apostolic See. The same author to John, bishop of Sora.** [Note: [Col. 1707] Anselm, book 5, chapter 8, with added subscription: “Given on the Ides of April.” The Ballerini also published it from Deusdedit, book 2, chapter 93, in *Works of Leo the Great*, vol. 3, p. CCCIV.]

It is certainly established both by our orders that no one should suppose that a public procession may be conducted in a church or oratory which is not recorded as dedicated by permission of our see, lest founders should advance by furtive subterfuges against the statutes of the rules.

But because Megetia, a woman of rank, represented to us through a petitionary offering that she had laid the bodies of her own people upon her own estates, beloved brother, out of regard for humanity—and provided that the earlier statutes are not compromised by funerals and tombs—you shall understand that ministries may be furnished only at the places specified in the petition for the sake of the solemnity, so that divine offices alone may be celebrated in the name of the dead, with public attendance and procession discontinued. [Note: [Col. 1707] “Megentia”: editions commonly collated, first Basel edition; “petitions”: Basel edition; “petitionary”: remaining editions; “may compromise”: the true reading.]

**Chapter VIII. A church ought not to be founded without the assent of the Apostolic See. Likewise Pope Nicholas to the bishop-elect and clergy of the Church of Nona.** [Note: [Col. 1707] Chapter of uncertain date.—Anselm, book 5, chapter 42 (44).—Pope Nicholas to the clergy and people of the Church of Vienne: “Venensis,” Argentinian edition; “Novensis,” Basel edition; editions commonly collated.]

How can the Church—that is, the assembly of Catholics—be founded without the assent of the Apostolic See, when, according to the sacred decrees, not even a newly built basilica itself ought to be constructed without the Pope’s command, though it is known to embrace the very multitude of Catholics within itself? [Note: [Col. 1707] Omitted in the Nuremberg and Venice I–II editions.] [Note: [Col. 1707] “itself” added: Basel edition and Bohm.]

[Col. 1708C] **Chapter IX. A new church is not to be dedicated without the authority of the bishop of the place. Likewise from the Council of Orléans.** [Note: [Col. 1707] Rather, Julian, *Novellae*, constitution 61, chapter 1; compare *Capitularies*, book 5, chapter 382; Burchard, book 3, chapter 6; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 6; *Decree*, part 3, chapter 8; Polycarpus, book 3, title 2.]

**Part IV.** No one shall build a church before the bishop of the city comes and there sets up a cross, publicly marks out the precinct, and first determines, for the person wishing to build, what will suffice for lights, for protection, and for the stipends of the guardians. Once the donation has been displayed, he may then build the church; and after it has been consecrated, he shall sprinkle the precinct of the same church with holy water. [Note: [Col. 1707] “define”: Basel edition; “and—for safeguarding”: absent from Basel edition; “and—to ‘sprinkle’”: absent from Julian and the *Capitularies*.] [Note: [Col. 1708D] “And after it has been consecrated”: More fully and suitably in the Roman Order: “Therefore, after the bishop has set a cross in the place where the altar is to be constructed, he shall sprinkle the place with blessed water, singing this antiphon,” etc.]

[Col. 1709A] **Chapter X. A church built for the profit of greed is not to be consecrated. Likewise from the Second Council of Braga, chapter 6.** [Note: [Col. 1709] Held A.D. 572; Tripartite Collection, part 2, title 46, chapter 6.]

If anyone builds a basilica not from devotion of faith but for the profit of greed, so that he may divide with the clerics half of whatever is collected there from the people’s offerings, because he founded the basilica on his own land for gain [Note: [Col. 1709] “He himself founded it on his own land”: Hispanic Collection; “had founded”: Basel edition; “founded”: remaining editions.]—something which is said to be done in some places even now—then this is henceforth to be observed: no bishop shall consent to so abominable a purpose, nor dare to consecrate a basilica founded not for the patronage of saints but rather under a tributary condition. [Note: [Col. 1709] “It was decided that if”: Hispanic Collection; “there” omitted by the same; “therefore” added by the Hispanic Collection; “for” omitted by Basel.]

[Col. 1709B] **Chapter XI. Sacrifices are to be offered only upon an altar and in places consecrated to God. Likewise Bishop Felix to all the orthodox, letter I.** [Note: [Col. 1709C] This chapter occurs in Polycarpus and Anselm in the same form as in Gratian, compiled here and there from words of that first letter of Felix IV—part of which was reported above in this same distinction, “Consecration,” and in “Tabernacle”—arranged very differently but with the sense intact.] [Note: [Col. 1709] Compare above, chapter 2, and the collections cited there; Anselm, book 7, chapter 134 (138); Polycarpus, book 3, title 16.]

**Part V.** Just as no one except priests consecrated to the Lord ought to sing Masses or offer sacrifices upon an altar, so likewise it is not permitted to sing Masses or offer sacrifices except in places consecrated to the Lord—that is, in tents anointed by bishops through divine prayers—unless supreme necessity compels it. [Note: [Col. 1709] “to God”: editions commonly collated; “celebrate”: same; “consecrated”: same.] [Note: [Col. 1709C] “That is, in tents”: In the letter and in Ivo these words do not occur here but a little above; nor in precisely this form, but as they have been restored above in the chapter “Tabernacle.”] [Note: [Col. 1709] Anselm: “dedicated by bishops through divine prayers, and on tables consecrated to the Lord and anointed with sacred unction by bishops.”]

It is therefore better [Note: [Col. 1709] Ivo, *Decree*, part 2, chapter 76; “more holy”: Basel edition.] not to sing or hear Mass than to do so in places where it ought not be done, unless supreme necessity arises, because necessity has no law. Hence it is written: “Take care not to offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see, but in the place which the Lord your God shall choose.” [Note: [Col. 1709] Deuteronomy 12:13; “chose”: Basel edition.] Yet it is by no means lawful for bishops or presbyters to celebrate offerings in houses. [Note: [Col. 1709] “therefore” omitted by the Argentinian edition; “those”: editions commonly collated.]

**Chapter XII. The solemnities of Mass are to be celebrated only in sacred places. Likewise from the Council of Tribur.** [Note: [Col. 1709D] In the Council of Mainz under Arnulf, chapter 9, the words of this chapter and of the chapter “We permit,” below in the same distinction, occur together. Burchard and Ivo, who likewise place both together, cite, as Gratian does, the Council of Tribur, chapter 4.] [Note: [Col. 1709] Rather, from the Council of Mainz, held A.D. 888; Burchard, book 3, chapter 56; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 30; *Decree*, part 3, chapter 59.]

We decree that the solemnities of Mass are to be celebrated not everywhere but in places consecrated by the bishop, or where he himself has permitted. [Note: [Col. 1709] “wherever”: Ivo and Basel edition.]

**Chapter XIII. Churches are to be consecrated by divine prayers. Likewise Clement, letter II, to James.** [Note: [Col. 1709] Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Polycarpus, book 3, title 4; compare Cause 16, question 7, chapter 28.]

Build churches in suitable and useful places, which ought to be consecrated by divine prayers; and priests dedicated to God by divine prayers ought to be established in each of them, whom all ought to venerate and no one burden. [Note: [Col. 1709] “divine” added: Basel edition; “consecrated”: editions commonly collated.] [Note: [Col. 1710C] “And in each”: These words through “ought” have been added from the original and Polycarpus.]

**Chapter XIV. It is not lawful to sacrifice or celebrate Masses except in places consecrated to God. Likewise Clement, letter III.** [Note: [Col. 1709] Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Tripartite Collection, part 1, title 1, chapter 22; Burchard, book 3, chapter 59; Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 62; Polycarpus, book 3, title 16.]

Therefore, while we are placed here—that is, in the present life—we must recognize the will of God, where there is a place both for acting and for sacrificing. For it is not lawful to sacrifice or celebrate Masses in other places except those in which the proper bishop has ordered it, or which have been consecrated by a canonically ordained bishop holding the city. Otherwise these things are not to be done or rightly celebrated. [Note: [Col. 1709] “that is” absent from the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice I editions; “that is” reads “this is” in the original, Burchard, and Ivo; “and” absent from Ivo and editions commonly collated except Argentinian and Basel; “to sacrifice—and to celebrate”: editions commonly collated; “have been consecrated”: original, Burchard, and Ivo.]

Likewise Pope Sylvester, sitting in a general synod, said: [Note: [Col. 1709] Apocryphal chapter; Anselm, book 7, chapter 133 (137); Polycarpus, book 3, title 4.]

**Chapter XV. Priests who presume to celebrate Masses in unconsecrated places are to be removed.**

No presbyter who wishes henceforth to remain a participant in the priesthood may presume to celebrate Masses except in places consecrated by the bishop.

[Col. 1710C] **Chapter XVI. The solemnities of dedications are to be celebrated annually, and a church whose consecration is uncertain is also to be consecrated. Likewise Pope Felix to all the orthodox, letter I, chapters 1 and 2.** [Note: [Col. 1710C] This chapter has been compiled from words of the same letter of Felix, chapters 1 and 2, omitting certain portions which are placed in the following chapter by Gratian.] [Note: [Col. 1709] Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare Pseudo-Gregory’s letter to Felix; Burchard, book 3, chapter 58; Anselm, book 5, chapter 24 (25); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 11; *Decree*, part 3, chapter 24.]

**Part VI.** The solemnities of the dedications of churches, bishops, and priests are to be celebrated solemnly every year. [Note: [Col. 1710D] “Bishops”: This word is absent from the original, Burchard, Ivo, Anselm, the Nuremberg and Venice I–II editions, the Paris and Lyons I editions, and most old copies of Gratian; but it has not been removed because of the gloss.]

§ 1. Whenever there is doubt concerning a church’s consecration, and there is neither a reliable written record nor reliable witnesses by whom the consecration may be known, know without any doubt that it is to be consecrated. Such anxiety does not constitute repetition, because what is not known to have been done is not shown to have been repeated. [Note: [Col. 1711] “dedication”: Ivo, *Panormia*; “consecrations”: editions commonly collated; “where”: Basel and Lyons I editions; “so that”: remaining editions; “may exist”: editions commonly collated.] [Note: [Col. 1711C] “Such anxiety does not constitute repetition”: Ivo and the *Panormia* read nearly as Gratian: “nor does such anxiety incur repetition”; the gloss’s interpretation agrees with this reading. But the original, Burchard, and Anselm read: “lest such anxiety cause deterioration.” The words of blessed Gregory, book 12, letter 31, to Felix, speaking of this same matter, correspond to this reading: “lest such doubt,” he says, “become the ruin of the faithful.” A similar sense is expressed below, Distinction 4, chapter “It was decided,” in these words: “lest this anxiety cause them to be deprived of the purgation of the sacraments.” It is found in the Fifth Council of Carthage.]

**Chapter XVII. On the same matter, and that the solemnity of a dedication is to be celebrated for eight days. Likewise Pope Gregory.** [Note: [Col. 1711C] In this chapter the earlier part of the preceding chapter through “to be celebrated” is repeated; then those words from Felix’s letter which were omitted there are added. Gregory, however, whom Gratian cites here, has in book 12, letter 31, certain matters concerning church dedications. But they seem to accord more closely with the preceding chapter, at “Concerning the consecration of churches.”] [Note: [Col. 1711] Rather, Pseudo-Felix; compare the corrections.—Burchard, same place; Anselm, same place; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 10; *Decree*, same place.]

The solemnities of the dedications of churches and priests are to be celebrated solemnly every year, the Lord himself giving an example. For he came to celebrate the same feast of dedication with the rest of the people, giving all a pattern for doing this, as it is written: “The Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem, and it was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s portico.” [Note: [Col. 1712C] “And priests”: These two words are absent from some old copies and from the Argentinian and Basel editions.] [Note: [Col. 1711] “doing”: original; “to be done”: Burchard, Ivo, and the *Decree*; compare John 10:22 following.]

That the dedication festival is to be celebrated for eight days you will find in the Book of Kings, when you have read the account of the temple’s dedication. [Note: [Col. 1711] Compare 1 Kings 8 and 2 Chronicles 7; “completed”: original, Burchard, Ivo, and the *Decree*; “perfected”: *Panormia*; “you will find”: editions commonly collated.]

**Chapter XVIII. Churches whose consecration is doubtful are to be consecrated. Likewise from the Council of Meaux, chapter 8.** [Note: [Col. 1711] Rather, Capitularies of the Kings of the Franks, book 1, chapters 144–145; Regino, book 1, chapter 30; Burchard, book 3, chapter 10; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 18; *Decree*, part 3, chapter 11, “from the Council of Orléans, chapter 45”; Polycarpus, book 3, title 16.]

**Part VII.** Churches or altars whose consecration is uncertain are to be consecrated, and superfluous altars are to be destroyed.

**Chapter XIX. When a church is to be consecrated again, and when it is to be exorcised only with salt. Likewise Pope Hyginus.** [Note: [Col. 1711] Chapter of uncertain origin.—In the excerpts called Egbert’s, in Mansi, vol. 12, chapter 139, it is adduced under the name of Vigilius.—Burchard, book 3, chapters 11–12; Anselm, book 5, chapters 13–14; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapters 20–21; *Decree*, part 3, chapters 13–14; Polycarpus, book 3, chapter 5.]

If the altar has been moved, the church is to be consecrated anew; if the walls are changed but not the altar, it is to be exorcised only with salt.

§ 1. If a church has been violated by homicide or adultery, it is to be purified most diligently and consecrated anew.

[Col. 1712A] **Chapter XX. When a church once consecrated to God is to be consecrated again. Likewise from the Council of Nicaea.** [Note: [Col. 1711] Compare Distinction 68, chapter 3.]

Churches once consecrated to God ought not to be consecrated again, unless they have been burned by fire, polluted by the shedding of blood, or polluted by the semen of anyone. For just as an infant, once baptized by any priest in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, ought not to be baptized again, so neither should a place dedicated to God be consecrated again except for the causes named above—provided that those who consecrated it held the faith of the Holy Trinity. [Note: [Col. 1711] “dedicated”: Argentinian and Basel editions; “have consecrated”: Argentinian, Basel, Nuremberg, Venice I–II editions.]

**Chapter XXI. On the same matter. Likewise Pope John to the bishops of Italy.** [Note: [Col. 1711] Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Burchard, book 3, chapter 32; Anselm, book 5, chapter 22 (23); Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 37; Polycarpus, book 3, title 4.]

Wherever you find Arian churches, consecrate them without any delay as Catholic churches by divine prayers and works. For when we were in Constantinople, both on account of Catholic religion and on business in the cause of King Theodoric, while the most devout and most Christian orthodox emperor Justin was urging and exhorting us and rooting out the Arians, we consecrated as Catholic to the Lord, with the Lord’s help, whatever churches of theirs we were able to find in those regions. [Note: [Col. 1711] In editions commonly collated and Anselm, the chapter ends here: “as we also did when we had been at Constantinople on King Theodoric’s business.”] [Note: [Col. 1712C] “On account of Catholic religion”: This passage has been expanded from the letter itself, Burchard, and Ivo.]

**Chapter XXII. On the same matter. Likewise in Gregory’s *Dialogues*, book III, chapter 30.** [Note: [Col. 1711] Anselm, book 5, chapter 24; Polycarpus, same place.]

An Arian church in that district of the city called the Suburra, after remaining closed until two years before, was ordered to be dedicated in the Catholic faith—with the relics of blessed Sebastian and of Saint Agatha, virgin and martyr, brought into it—and this was done. [Note: [Col. 1711] “of this city”: editions commonly collated; “Suburban”: Basel edition; “to”: editions commonly collated.] [Note: [Col. 1712C] “Virgin and”: These two words are absent from most manuscripts and Polycarpus. The *Dialogues* itself reads “blessed Stephen and Saint Martha, martyrs.” But in book 3 of the *Register*, letter 19, this church is called the Church of Saint Agatha. John the Deacon, book 2, chapter 31, reads: “Saint Sebastian and Saint Agnes, martyrs.”]

[Col. 1713A] **Chapter XXIII. Likewise.** [Note: [Col. 1713C] “Likewise”: Formerly “Pope Agapetus” followed; those words had rashly entered the heading from the chapter itself and are absent from some manuscripts. This chapter occurs at the end of an old codex of Gregory I’s register, in a writing “On the character, life, and death of Pope Agapetus I,” in the Vatican Library.] [Note: [Col. 1713] Chapter of doubtful authenticity.]

Pope Agapetus, a Catholic vessel, trumpet of the Gospel, and herald of justice, cleansed by his Catholic prayers the coverings of the sacred altar and see which had been defiled by the sacrilegious fables of Anthimus. [Note: [Col. 1713] “Arian”: Argentinian edition; “Anthemius”: Basel, Paris, and Lyons editions; “washed”: Maurists, appendix to vol. 2 of the *Works of Gregory*.]

**Chapter XXIV. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Vigilius to Eutherius, letter I, chapter 4.** [Note: [Col. 1713D] It was attributed to Julian, but has been restored from old copies to Vigilius, in whose work it occurs and from whom Burchard and Ivo also cite it.] [Note: [Col. 1713] Attributed to Julian in the Paris and Lyons editions, to Julius in the rest and in Ivo’s *Panormia*; it is in Vigilius’s letter to Profuturus, written A.D. 538; Burchard, book 3, chapter 62; Anselm, book 5, chapter 81 (82); Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 14; *Decree*, part 3, chapter 25; Polycarpus, book 3, title 6.]

Regarding the rebuilding of any church which has been destroyed, and whether the solemnity of consecration should be repeated in a place where no holy relics (*sanctuaria*) had been placed, we judge that nothing prevents it if exorcised water is not sprinkled through it, because we know that the consecration of any church in which the pledge of the Holy Spirit is not placed consists only in the celebration of Masses. [Note: [Col. 1713] “ruptured”: Burchard, Ivo, and *Panormia*; “blessed”: original; “in the consecration”: editions commonly collated; *ara*, “altar”: original, Burchard, Anselm, Ivo, and Basel edition.]

Therefore, if any basilica of the saints has even been rebuilt from its foundations without moving the altar, then, without any doubt, once the solemnity of Masses has been celebrated in it, the sanctification of the whole consecration will be completed. [Note: [Col. 1714C] “Without moving the altar”: These words are absent from the original, Burchard, Ivo, and Anselm, but are explained in the gloss. Some other matters have also been corrected.] [Note: [Col. 1713] “consecration of sanctification”: editions commonly collated.]

But if the holy relics (*sanctuaria*) which it possessed have been removed, it will receive again the reverence of sanctification through their replacement and the solemnity of Masses. [Note: [Col. 1713] “laying down”: same editions and Anselm; “arrangement”: Ivo’s *Panormia*.]

**Chapter XXV. No altar is to be raised in a consecrated church without the bishop’s permission. Likewise from the Decrees of Pope Hormisdas, chapter 10.** [Note: [Col. 1713] Rather, Capitularies of the Kings of the Franks, book 6, chapter 202; Burchard, book 3, chapter 17; Ivo, *Decree*, part 3, chapter 20; Polycarpus, book 4, title 31.]

**Part VIII.** No presbyter shall erect another altar in a consecrated church except one consecrated or permitted by the bishop of the place, so that there may be a distinction between what is sacred and what is not sacred; nor shall he feign a dedication where none exists. If he does so, if he is a cleric, let him be degraded; but if a layman, let him be anathematized. [Note: [Col. 1714C] Ivo reads: “consecrated by the bishop of the place or his delegate, so that there may be a distinction,” etc. Polycarpus and Burchard: “consecrated by the bishop of the place or with his permission, so that there may be,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 1713] “has been”: editions commonly collated.]

**Chapter XXVI. Altars raised without relics of saints are to be destroyed. Likewise from the African Council, chapter 50.** [Note: [Col. 1713] Chapter 83 in Dionysius and 49 in the Hadrianic codex; chapter 14 of the Fifth Council of Carthage, held A.D. 401; Burchard, book 3, chapter 54; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, chapter 28; *Decree*, part 3, chapter 57; compare Anselm, book 5, chapter 14.]

It was decided that altars which are built here and there in fields and villages [Col. 1714A] [variant: “roads”: original; Burchard, Ivo, *Decretum*], as though they were memorials of martyrs, but in which no body or relics of martyrs [variant: “of a martyr”: Ivo; editions collated with the original, first Basel edition] are proved to have been deposited, should, if possible, be demolished by the bishops who preside over those same places. But if this is not allowed because of popular disturbances [variant: “through”: original; Burchard, Ivo], the people should nevertheless be warned not to frequent those places, so that those who think rightly may not be held captive there by any superstition. And in general no memorial of martyrs should be accepted as authentic [variant: “should be accepted, unless either where”: Burchard, Ivo; editions collated with the original], except where a body or certain relics exist, or where the origin of some dwelling, possession, or suffering is handed down on wholly trustworthy authority [variant: “be handed down”: Basel edition]. For altars established anywhere through dreams and the empty, so-called revelations of any persons whatsoever must be rejected altogether [variant: “are rejected”: Paris and Lyons editions].

[Col. 1714B] C. XXVII. A church in which a pagan is found to have been buried is not to be consecrated. Likewise from the Council of Orléans, c. 3.

[Note: [Col. 1713] It is read in the Penitential of Theodore, in Petitus, c. 1.—Burchard, book 3, c. 13. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 13; *Decretum*, part 3, c. 43.]

It is not permitted to consecrate a church in which [variant: “where”: Basel edition] a pagan has been buried [variant: “to be consecrated”: editions collated with the original, Lyons II–III; Ivo], nor to celebrate Masses in it [variant: “for Masses to be celebrated”: Ivo, *Decretum*]; but he must be cast out [variant: “to cast out”: Ivo, *Panormia*; editions collated with the original] and it must be cleansed [variant: “to cleanse”: Lyons II–III editions].

C. XXVIII. Concerning a church in which the bodies of faithful or unbelieving persons are buried. Likewise from the Council of Cologne.

[Note: [Col. 1713] Rather, from the same Theodore in the cited place.—Burchard, book 3, c. 38. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, cc. 13 and 8; *Decretum*, part 3, c. 43.]

It is not lawful to consecrate a church in which the corpses of dead unbelievers [variant: “of believers or unbelievers”: editions collated with the original, first Nuremberg and Venice I–II editions] are buried. But if it appears suitable for consecration, after the bodies have been removed and the walls or beams of that place scraped away [variant: “or after the timbers have been washed”: Burchard; Theodore, cited place], it should be rebuilt. But if it had previously [variant: “earlier”: Burchard, Ivo; Theodore; Basel edition] been consecrated, it is permitted to celebrate Masses in it, provided that those buried in it were [variant: “are”: editions collated with the original, first Basel edition] faithful.

[Col. 1714C] C. XXIX. The mysteries are not to be distributed over tombs in the open country. Likewise from the Council of Pope Martin [of Braga, cc. 68 and 69 of the Greek synods].

[Note: [Col. 1713] Burchard, book 10, c. 38, and Ivo, *Decretum*, part 11, c. 63, report the final portion.]

Ignorant and presumptuous clerics [variant: “presumptuous”: editions collated with the original, first Argentinian, Basel, and Nuremberg editions] ought not to carry ministries [Col. 1715A] [variant: “mysteries”: Nuremberg, Venice I–II, Paris, Lyons I editions; added: “or altars”: editions collated with the original, first Basel edition] out over tombs in the field [variant: “in the field”: Hispana collection], or distribute the sacraments. Rather, offerings for the dead should be offered in a church or basilica where martyrs’ relics have been deposited, where [variant: the words “where … are customarily offered” are absent from the editions collated with the original] offerings [variant: “to offer an offering”: Hispana collection] are offered. § 1. Nor [variant: “not”: the same source] may Christians bring meals to the tombs of the dead and sacrifice to the dead [variant: “and render sacrifices of the dead to God”: the same source; C. XXX].

C. XXX. How Mass may be celebrated in a burned church. Likewise from the Council of Tribur.

[Note: [Col. 1715C] On this chapter, see the note above at the chapter “The solemnities of Mass.”]

[Note: [Col. 1715] Rather, from the Council of Mainz, held A.D. 888.—Burchard, book 3, c. 56. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 33; *Decretum*, part 3, c. 59.]

We also permit that, wherever—something which, through our sins [variant: “faults”: original], has happened very often—churches have been set on fire and burned by Normans, Slavs, Hungarians [variant: “Bulgarians”: Ivo; Basel edition], evil Christians, or in any other [variant: “some other”: editions collated with the original] manner, Masses may meanwhile be celebrated in chapels with a consecrated altar-table [Col. 1715B], until the churches themselves can be restored. For those travelling, however, if a church is lacking, we permit the solemnities of Mass to be celebrated in the open air or in tents, if [variant: “likewise if”: Burchard, Ivo; Basel and Lyons II–III editions] a consecrated altar-table and the other sacred implements pertaining to that office are present [variant: “are present”: original]. *In every other case we forbid it altogether* [variant: “we oppose it”: Ivo, *Panormia*; “otherwise … forbid”: absent from the original].

C. XXXI. Altars are not to be anointed with chrism unless they are of stone. Likewise from the Council of Epaone, cc. 26 and 27.

[Note: [Col. 1715C] Ivo cites this, like the common printed copies of Gratian, as from the Council of Hippo [thus the editions collated with the original]. But it has been restored from Burchard and old manuscripts of Gratian as “Epaone,” [Col. 1716C] from whose chapters 26 and 27 it was compiled.]

[Note: [Col. 1715] Held A.D. 517.—Burchard, book 3, c. 25. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 32; *Decretum*, part 3, c. 30.]

If altars are not [variant: “are not”: Burchard; “may not be”: Ivo] of stone, they are not to be consecrated by the anointing of chrism [variant: “by the unguent of chrism”: Burchard, Ivo]. But, in celebrating the divine offices, provincial bishops must observe [variant: “preserve”: Argentinian edition] the order which the metropolitans maintain [variant: “provincial”: same source; added: “their”: same source and editions collated with the original].

[Col. 1715C] C. XXXII. Altars are to be consecrated by anointing with chrism and priestly blessing. Likewise from the Council of Agde, c. 14.

[Note: [Col. 1715] Held A.D. 506.—Tripartite Collection, part 2, title 18, c. 12. Polycarpus, book 3, title 4.]

It was decided that altars [variant: added “indeed”: Hispana collection] should be consecrated not only by the anointing of chrism but also by priestly blessing.

[Col. 1716A] C. XXXIII. It is permitted to pray in private oratories, but not to celebrate Mass. Likewise from the Council of Orléans, c. 3.

[Note: [Col. 1716C] Burchard and Ivo likewise cite the Council of Orléans. The very ruling is found in the *Capitularies*, book 5, c. 230, book 6, c. 101, and Novel 58 in Julian the Antecessor, at the end.]

[Note: [Col. 1715] Rather, from a capitulary of Louis, A.D. 824.—Compare *Capitularies*, book 5, c. 383; book 6, c. 102.—Burchard, book 3, c. 86. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 39; *Decretum*, part 3, c. 76.]

Each of the faithful may have an oratory in his own house and pray there; but it is not permitted to celebrate Masses there.

C. XXXIV. In private oratories no one may presume to minister without the bishop’s consent. Likewise from the Sixth Synod, c. 31.

[Note: [Col. 1715] Rather, from the Council in Trullo, held A.D. 692.—Tripartite Collection, part 2, title 11, c. 14.]

We decree that clerics who minister *or baptize* in oratories within houses are to do this with the consent of the bishop [variant: added “of that”: Argentinian, Basel, Nuremberg, Lyons II–III editions] of the place. But if anyone does not observe this, let him be deposed.

C. XXXV. Those who have oratories outside parishes are to be compelled on these days to return to the parish churches. Likewise from the Council of Agde, c. 21.

[Note: [Col. 1715] Held A.D. 506.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, c. 9.]

[Col. 1716B] If anyone wishes to have an oratory *in the countryside* outside parishes in which there is a lawful and customary assembly, we permit him, on the remaining feasts [variant: “on the other feasts”: Basel edition], to hear Mass there [variant: “hold [Mass]”: Ivo], by proper arrangement [variants: “according to order”: same sources; “in due order”: editions collated with the original] because of the fatigue of his household. But at Easter, the Nativity [variants: “natale”: Hispana collection and Argentinian edition; “the Nativity” accusative: Ivo] of the Lord, the Epiphany [variants: accusative: Hispana collection and Ivo] *of the Lord* [absent from the Hispana collection], the Ascension [variants: accusative: Hispana collection, Ivo, Argentinian edition] of the Lord [absent from Ivo], Pentecost [variants: accusative: Hispana collection, Ivo, Argentinian edition], the Nativity [variants: “natale”: Hispana collection and Argentinian edition; “the birth”: Ivo] of St. John the Baptist, and any other principal feast days, they are to hear Mass only in cities or parish churches [variant: “hold [Mass]”: same source; Ivo]. But clerics who, on the feasts [variant: absent from editions collated with the original, first Argentinian and Basel editions] mentioned above [variants: “on these feasts”: Hispana collection, Ivo, editions collated with the original; added: “in oratories”: Ivo and Basel edition; “in these oratories”: Hispana collection], wish to celebrate Masses [variant: “Masses there”: editions collated with the original] without the bishop’s command or [variant: “and”: Böhm] permission [variants: “perform or hold [them]”: Hispana collection, Ivo], are to be deprived of communion [variants: “be expelled from communion”: Hispana collection, Ivo, Basel edition; “be deprived of communion”: remaining editions].

[Col. 1716C] C. XXXVI. For what reasons places of saints ought to be moved. Likewise Augustine.

[Note: [Col. 1715] An uncertain chapter.—“Augustine, to Ignarus”: editions collated with the original.—Burchard, book 3, c. 90. Anselm, book 5, c. 16 (17). Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 38; *Decretum*, part 3, c. 80.]

IX. Part. Places of saints should be moved for three reasons [variant: “from”: Ivo, *Panormia*]. First, when the necessity caused by persecutors [Col. 1717A] has oppressed their places. Second, when the places are difficult of access. Third, when they are burdened by association with wicked people.

C. XXXVII. When no one may transfer the bodies of saints from place to place. Likewise from the First Council of Mainz, c. 51.

[Note: [Col. 1717] Held A.D. 813.—Burchard, book 3, c. 232. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 36; *Decretum*, part 3, c. 273.]

No one may presume to transfer the bodies of saints from place to place without the counsel [variant: “council”: Lyons II–III editions] of the prince, or without permission from the bishops and the holy [variant: “and the holy synodical”: editions collated with the original] synod.
