C. XXXVIII. Timber from a dedicated church may not be converted to lay use. Likewise Pope Hyginus.

[Note: [Col. 1717] This occurs in the capitulary of Theodore, published by D’Achery, folio 1.—Burchard, book 3, c. 39. Anselm, book 5, c. 17 (18). Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 7; *Decretum*, book 3, c. 44. Polycarpus, book 3, title 16.]

X. Part. Timber from a dedicated church [Note: [Col. 1717C] “Dedicated”: formerly “dedicated” was read here and in the heading [thus editions collated with the original, first Argentinian and Basel editions]; this has been corrected, as have certain other readings, from old copies, Burchard, and Ivo, who also cite this chapter from the decrees of Hyginus] must not be used for another work, except for another church; or it must be burned, or used for the benefit of brothers in a monastery [Col. 1717B] [variant: “monastery”: Ivo]. It must not, however, be admitted to lay use [variants: “lay” absent from Burchard, Anselm, and editions collated with the original, first Basel and Lyons II–III editions; “works”: Burchard, Anselm, Ivo, *Decretum*, editions collated with the original].

C. XXXIX. Sacred vestments and vessels worn out by age are to be burned, and their ashes cast into hidden places. Likewise Pope Clement to James, bishop of Jerusalem, Letter II.

[Note: [Col. 1717] Read in that portion of Pseudo-Clement’s Letter II, composed long before Pseudo-Isidore, issued under the title *Instructions of St. Peter on Preserving the Sacraments*, published by the Ballerini in *Works of Leo the Great*, vol. 3, p. 674.—Compare c. 4, D. 23.—Burchard, book 3, c. 216. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 266, and, down to “are given,” part 2, c. 66.]

An altar-cloth, chair [variant: “chalice”: Ballerini], candlestick, and veil, if worn out by age, are to be given to the fire; for things that have been in the sacristy [variant: “sanctuary”: same source] may not be improperly handled, but all are to be committed to the fire. Their ashes also are to be taken into the baptistery [variant: “in the baptistery”: same source and editions collated with the original], where no one has passage [variant: “where there is no passage”: Burchard, Ivo], or cast into a wall or beneath the paving, lest they be defiled by the feet of those entering [variant: “polluted”: editions collated with the original].

[Col. 1717C] C. XL. Dead persons are not to be wrapped in altar vestments. The same source, in the same place.

No cleric through ignorance [variant: absent from the Argentinian edition; added: “altar-cloth”: Ballerini] is to think that a dead person ought to be wrapped [variant: “wrapped around”: editions collated with the original, first Lyons II–III editions], nor may a deacon wish to cover the dead person’s shoulders with an altar-cloth that was [variant: “has been”: editions collated with the original, first Basel edition] upon the altar, or indeed with that which was given to the deacon [Col. 1718A] [variant: absent from Ballerini] at the Lord’s table [variant: “table”: editions collated with the original]. Whoever does this, or treats *the divine mysteries* as something trivial, as though they were nothing, and negligently [variant: “has sacred vessels”: Ballerini], shall be excluded from the Lord’s altar for three years and six months [variant: “removed”: editions collated with the original], struck with a severe anathema. But if a priest does not warn [variant: “admonish”: Ballerini] the cleric, he is to be excommunicated for ten years and six [variant: “five”: same source] months, because he has not removed from the Lord’s sacraments the ministries entrusted to him [variant: “has admonished”: same source and editions collated with the original, first Paris and Lyons editions]; afterward, with great [variant: “grave”: Ballerini] humility, he is to be reconciled to mother Church.

§ 1. But altar-cloths [Note: [Col. 1717] Burchard, book 3, c. 216. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 226, down to § 2.] and sanctuary veils, if they have been soiled in ministry [variants: “which have been soiled in the ministry of the sanctuary”: Ballerini; Burchard; “which have been soiled in the sanctuary”: Ivo, Basel edition; “those in the sanctuary, if they are dirty”: remaining editions; added “and implements”: editions collated with the original], are to be washed within the sanctuary by deacons with humble assistants, not thrown outside from the sacristy [variant: “sanctuary or sacristy”: Basel edition]. They are to wash the coverings of the Lord’s table, lest perhaps dust from the Lord’s body fall improperly [Note: [Col. 1718C] “Fall”: the original reads, “fall from a linen cloth washed outside” [“from a linen cloth carried outside”: Burchard, Ivo]. But the gloss prevented alteration. Many other readings of no small importance have, however, been corrected from the original itself.]. They are not to wash the linen cloth [Col. 1718B] outside; doing so will be sin for the person who does it [variants: “this”: same source; Böhm: “this is not”; editions collated with the original: “this is not”]. Therefore we command the ministers carefully to preserve *these holy things* within the sacristy [the words “these holy things” are absent from Burchard and Ivo]. Let a new basin be procured, and let it touch nothing else besides this. Nor is that basin itself [variant: added “outside”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions] to be used for washing veils except those pertaining to the service of the Lord’s altar. The altar-cloths alone are to be washed in it, and the door-veils in another basin.

§ 2. *Concerning the door-veils* [the words “Concerning … door-veils” are absent from Ballerini], let the doorkeepers also take care [variants: “let there also be care”: Ballerini; “let there be care also”: editions collated with the original], as instructed by their elders [variant: “elder”: same editions], that no careless or ignorant person wipe his hands unawares [variant: “indiscreetly”: Ballerini; “unawares”: Böhm] on the veil of the doorway of the house of the Lord. Rather, every person must at once be restrained and taught that the veil of the court of the Lord’s house is *holy*.

[Col. 1718C] C. XLI. Sacred vessels are to be handled only by consecrated persons. Likewise Pope Sixtus, Letter II.

[Note: [Col. 1717] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore.—Burchard, book 3, c. 214. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, c. 70, down to “his own,” and part 3, c. 264. Polycarpus, book 3, title 9.]

It has been decreed in *this* holy apostolic see that sacred vessels are to be handled by none other than persons consecrated and dedicated to the Lord [Col. 1719A]. *For it is wholly unworthy that the Lord’s sacred vessels, whatever they may be, should serve human uses or be handled by men other than those who serve the Lord and are dedicated to him* [Note: [Col. 1719] “For it is wholly unworthy”: these words as far as “men,” and several others, have been added from the original, Burchard, and Ivo.], lest the Lord, angered by such presumptions, inflict plagues upon his people, and even those who have not sinned [variant: “sinned”: Burchard, Ivo, editions collated with the original] *suffer evils or* perish; for the righteous often perish because of the wicked.

C. XLII. Consecrated vestments are to be kept only by consecrated persons. Likewise Bishop Stephen to his familiar friend Hilary, Letter I, c. 3.

[Note: [Col. 1719] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore, compiled from the *Book of the Popes*.—Anselm, book 5, c. 29 (30). Ivo, *Decretum*, part 5, c. 72. Polycarpus, book 3, title 16.]

Ecclesiastical vestments [variant: “vestments of the church”: editions collated with the original], by which service is rendered to the Lord, must be both consecrated and honorable. They must not be used for any purposes other than *in* ecclesiastical [Col. 1719B] offices worthy of God; nor may they be touched or carried [variant: “offered”: same editions] by anyone except consecrated persons, lest the vengeance which struck King Belshazzar [absent from Anselm and Ivo; compare Daniel 5] come upon those who transgress in this matter [variant: “upon those who transgress in this and presume such things”: Anselm] *and presume such things*, and cause them to fall to the depths.

C. XLIII. Sacred implements are not to be provided for wedding adornments. Likewise from the Council of Orléans.

[Note: [Col. 1719] Rather, from the First Council of Clermont, held A.D. 535.—Burchard, book 3, c. 108. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, final chapter; *Decretum*, part 2, c. 143. Polycarpus, book 3, title 24.]

Sacred implements are not to be provided for wedding adornment [variants: “let them not be provided”: Hispana collection; Burchard; “nor let them be provided”: Ivo, *Decretum*], lest, while they are polluted by the touch [variant: “touch or”: Hispana collection; Burchard, Ivo, editions collated with the original] of wicked persons and by the pomp of worldly luxury [variant: “are polluted”: Burchard, Basel edition], they appear unworthy for the offices of the sacred mystery [variant: “ministry”: Hispana collection, Ivo, *Decretum*, editions collated with the original, first Basel edition].

C. XLIV. The sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood are not to be celebrated in wooden vessels. Likewise from the Council of Tribur, c. 18.

[Note: [Col. 1719] Held A.D. 895.—Burchard, book 3, c. 223. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 282.]

[Col. 1719C] XI. Part. The vessels in which [variant: absent from the original, Burchard, Ivo, and Argentinian and Basel editions] the most holy mysteries are performed are chalices [variant: absent from editions collated with the original, first Argentinian edition] and patens. Concerning them, Boniface, martyr and bishop, when asked whether it was lawful to perform the sacraments in wooden vessels, replied: “Formerly golden priests used wooden chalices [variant: “vessels and chalices”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions], but *now, conversely, wooden priests use golden chalices*.” Zephyrinus, the sixteenth bishop of Rome, decreed that Masses be celebrated [Col. 1720A] [variant: “to celebrate”: editions collated with the original; compare the *Book of the Popes*] with glass patens. *Then* Pope Urban [variant: added “the eighteenth”: original, Burchard, Ivo; “seventeenth”: Basel edition; “tenth”: remaining editions] made all sacred implements of silver. For in this, as in the remaining observances, the splendor of churches increased more and more with the passage of time. Therefore, in our own [variant: “also”: Basel edition] days, since we are servants of the master of the household, lest the splendor of mother Church be diminished [variant: “lessened”: editions collated with the original], but rather accumulated and increased, we decree that henceforth no priest may in any manner presume to perform the sacred mystery of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ in wooden vessels, lest God be angered by the very thing through which he ought to be appeased.

C. XLV. Of what material a chalice with paten ought to be made. Likewise from the Council of Rheims, c. 6.

[Note: [Col. 1719] An uncertain chapter.—*Regino*, book 1, c. 67. Burchard, book 3, c. 96. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, c. 161; *Decretum*, book 2, c. 131.]

[Col. 1720B] The Lord’s chalice with paten [words absent from the Argentinian edition], if it is not of gold [variant: added “is”: Basel and Lyons I editions], should nevertheless [variants: “altogether nevertheless”: same editions; “in every way”: Ivo, *Panormia*; “by all means”: Regino, Burchard] be made of silver. And below:

§ 1. But if anyone is so poor [variant: “very poor”: Regino], he should at least have a pewter chalice.

§ 2. A chalice is not to be made of bronze [variant: added “but”: editions collated with the original, first Lyons II–III editions; Regino, Burchard] or orichalcum [variant: “or of”: same sources and editions collated with the original], because the power of wine produces verdigris [variant: “produces and at the same time”: editions collated with the original; “and at the same time”: Ivo], which provokes vomiting.

§ 3. No one may presume to sing Mass in a wooden or glass chalice.

C. XLVI. The altar sacrifice is to be consecrated not upon a silk cloth, but upon pure linen. Likewise from the letter of Popes Eusebius and Sylvester.

[Note: [Col. 1719] From the Acts of Sylvester, inserted in the *Pontifical*.—Burchard, book 3, c. 99. Anselm, book 9, c. 2. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, c. 162; *Decretum*, part 2, c. 134.]

By the deliberation [variant: “deliberation”: Burchard; Basel edition] of all, we decree that no one may presume to celebrate the altar sacrifice upon a silk or dyed [variant: “immersed”: Ivo and editions collated with the original] cloth [variant: added “Mass”: same editions], but upon pure linen [variants: “flaxen”: Burchard, Ivo, *Panormia*; “flaxen or linen”: editions collated with the original, first Basel edition] consecrated by a bishop, namely linen produced from the earth’s flax [Col. 1720C] and woven; just as the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was buried in a clean linen shroud.

C. XLVII. By whom the celebration of Mass was handed down. Likewise from the Sixth Synod, c. 32.

[Note: [Col. 1719] Rather, from the Quinisext Council, held A.D. 692.—Tripartite Collection, part 2, title 11, c. 15.]

XII. Part. James, the brother of the Lord according to the flesh, to whom the church of Jerusalem was first entrusted, and Basil, bishop of Caesarea, whose renown shone throughout the whole world [Col. 1721A] [variant: “glowed”: editions collated with the original], handed down to us in writings the celebration of Mass.

[Note: [Col. 1721C] “Handed down to us in writings”: the Greek is: **ἐγγράφως τὴν μυστικὴν ἡμῖν ἱερουργίαν παραδεδωκότες, οὕτω τελειοῦν ἐν τῇ θείᾳ λειτουργίᾳ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ οἴνου τὸ ἱερὸν ποτήριον ἐκδεδώκασιν**, that is: “having handed down to us in writing the mystical sacrifice, they set forth that in the divine liturgy the sacred cup is to be prepared in this manner, from water and wine.” Yet nothing has been changed, both because of the gloss [Col. 1721D] and because the compiler seems deliberately to have reported it summarily. This chapter is absent from certain old manuscripts [Col. 1722C].]

C. XLVIII. At what hour the solemnities of Mass are to be celebrated. Likewise Pope Telesphorus VII, successor of Peter, in the letter to all, c. 2.

[Note: [Col. 1721] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore, compiled according to the *Book of the Popes*.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, c. 71. Polycarpus, book 3, title 25.]

XIII. Part. On the holy night of the Nativity of the Lord and Savior, priests are to celebrate Masses and solemnly sing the angelic hymn in them, because on that same night he was announced by an angel to the shepherds. And below:

§ 1. “And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest [variant: “the most high”: original, Ivo, and the Vulgate, Luke 2:14], and on earth peace to people of good will.”

At other times, however, celebrations of Mass are by no means to take place before the third hour of the day [Col. 1721B], because at that hour the Lord was crucified and the Holy Spirit is read to have descended upon the Apostles.

[Note: [Col. 1721] Burchard, book 3, c. 63. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 40; *Decretum*, part 3, c. 65.]

C. XLIX. The sacraments of the altar are to be celebrated only by fasting persons. Likewise from the Council of Africa, c. 8.

[Note: [Col. 1721] “From the Third Council of Carthage, c. 8”: Basel edition; “from the Council of Carthage, c. 8”: remaining editions.—C. 8 in the Hadrian collection and c. 41 in Dionysius; c. 29 of the Third Council of Carthage, held A.D. 397.—Regino, book 1, c. 188. Anselm, book 9, c. 3.]

XIV. Part. The sacraments of the altar are to be celebrated only by fasting persons, except on the one annual day on which the Lord’s Supper is celebrated. For if a commendation of any dead persons, whether bishops or others, must be made in the afternoon, it is to be made by prayers alone if those who perform it are already found to have eaten [variants: “perform”: editions collated with the original, first Basel edition; “are found”: Lyons II–III editions and original].

[Col. 1721C] C. L. During Lent it is not permitted to eat before the solemnities of Mass, sung about the ninth hour. Likewise from the Council of Chalon.

[Note: [Col. 1722C] Ivo and the *Panormia* cite it thus also. Burchard, however, cites the decrees of Pope Silverius; Polycarpus, Eusebius. It occurs in the capitularies of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, c. 39.]

[Note: [Col. 1721] Rather, Theodulf of Orléans, c. 38, in Mansi, vol. 13.—Burchard, book 13, c. 12. Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, c. 184; *Decretum*, part 4, c. 45. Polycarpus, same place.]

XV. Part. Many people who suppose that they are fasting in Lent customarily eat as soon as they hear the signal for the ninth hour [variant: “hear [the signal] at the ninth hour”: original] . Such people are not to be considered fasting at all if they eat before the evening office is celebrated. For they must hasten to Mass, and, after hearing the solemnities of Mass and the evening offices and giving alms, they are to proceed to food [Col. 1722A]. But if someone is constrained by necessity and cannot come to Mass, then, when he has reckoned the evening hour and completed his prayer, he is to break [variant: “complete”: Burchard; “ought to break”: original] his fast.

XVI. Part. Gratian. On the fasts of the four seasons likewise, the solemnities of Mass are to be celebrated about the evening hours; on Holy Saturday, however, about the beginning of night. Hence Bishop Leo: “What [was established] by our fathers.” Likewise Gelasius: “The ordinations of priests.” Likewise Pelagius: “The replies to your charity.” Seek these in the treatise on ordinations. It is also not inappropriate to celebrate the solemnities of Mass in the first part of the day.

Hence Pope Leo, to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, Letter LXXIX, alternatively LXXXI, c. 2:

[Note: [Col. 1721] Letter 9, Ballerini edition, written A.D. 445.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, c. 87.—The preceding part, down to “assemble,” is quoted by Burchard, book 3, c. 228, and Ivo, *Decretum*, part 3, c. 268.]

C. LI. It is also permitted to celebrate Masses in the first part of the day.

[Col. 1722B] But it is necessary that some part of the people be deprived of its devotion if, by preserving the practice of only one Mass, they cannot offer the sacrifice unless *those who* assemble in the first part of the day [variant: singular, “unless he assembles”: Venice II, Paris, Lyons editions]. Therefore we admonish your charity earnestly *and* affectionately [variant: “brotherhood”: Ivo and editions collated with the original] that your care likewise not neglect what has become established in our custom through the pattern of paternal tradition [variant: “has become established”: Basel edition], so that in all things we may agree with us in faith *and* deeds. For this reason we gave this letter to be conveyed to your brotherhood [variant: “charity”: same sources and editions] by our returning son, the priest Possidonius, who often took part in our processions and actions [variant: “ordinations”: Ballerini and Hispana collection], and, having been sent to us so often, learned what authority of the apostolic see maintained in all things.

[Note: [Col. 1722C] “Authority of the apostolic see”: the letter itself reads, “what we maintained in all things by apostolic authority” [thus the same sources]. Yet all manuscripts of Gratian and Ivo agree.]

[Col. 1722C] C. LII. Private Masses are not to be sung publicly. Likewise Augustine.

[Note: [Col. 1721] Burchard, book 2, c. 54, and Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, c. 119, cite this as “from the sayings of Augustine.” It is among the chapters of Theodulf of Orléans, in Mansi, vol. 13, titles 45–46.—Polycarpus, book 3, title 16.]

This too must be observed: private Masses which are performed by priests on solemn days must not be celebrated so publicly that, because of them [variant: “through”: original], the people are drawn away from the public solemnities of Mass, which are canonically celebrated at the third hour. And below:

§ 1. Rather, the priests who are around the city or in the city itself, and the people, are to assemble together [Col. 1723A] for the public celebration of Mass—*except consecrated women of God, who customarily do not go out in public but remain confined within the enclosure of the monastery*.

[Note: [Col. 1723D] “Except”: the words from here to the end have been added from Theodulf, Burchard, and Ivo, in whom other matter omitted by Gratian after the word “drawn away” may also be read.]

C. LIII. How many Masses a priest may celebrate in one day. Likewise Alexander II.

[Note: [Col. 1723] An uncertain chapter.—Somewhat similar material occurs in the *Excerpts* attributed to Egbert, c. 54.—Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, c. 81.]

XVII. Part. It is sufficient for a priest to celebrate one Mass on one day, because Christ suffered once [variants: “suffered also”: absent from Argentinian edition; “suffered, who”: Basel edition] and redeemed the whole world. It is no small matter to perform one Mass, and blessed indeed is he who can celebrate one worthily. Yet some celebrate one for the dead and another of the day, if necessary [variant: “if it is”: Basel edition]. But those who presume to celebrate several Masses in one day for money or the flattery of secular persons, I do not think [Col. 1723B] [variant: “I judge”: Ivo and editions collated with the original, first Argentinian, Paris, Lyons I editions] can escape condemnation.

C. LIV. We are taught by the example of the Savior and the Apostles to sing hymns. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Toledo, c. 12.

[Note: [Col. 1723] Held A.D. 633.—Tripartite Collection, part 2, title 37, c. 1. Polycarpus, book 3, title 22.]

### XVIII. On Singing Hymns: We Have the Example of Both the Saviour and the Apostles

For we are told that the Lord himself sang a hymn, as the Evangelist Matthew attests: “And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.” [Note: [Col. 1723] *testante*: “attesting”: editions cited above; cf. Matt. 26:30. *Oliveti*, “of Olivet”: *Olivarum*, “of Olives,” in the editions cited above.]

And the Apostle Paul, writing to the Ephesians, says: “Be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs.” [Note: [Col. 1723] Eph. 5:18–19. *Implemini*, “be filled”: *Impleamini*, “be ye filled,” editions cited above. “Holy” is absent from the Hispanic Collection. *vobismetipsis*, “to yourselves”: *vos*, “you,” in the same.]

Since certain hymns are known to have been composed by human skill in praise of God and in celebration of the triumphs of the Apostles and martyrs—such as those published by the most blessed doctors Hilary and Ambrose [Col. 1723C]—yet some people especially reject these because they do not derive from the writings of the holy canons or from apostolic tradition, let them then reject also that hymn composed by men which we say every day, in public and private office, at the end of all the psalms: “Glory and honour to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, unto ages of ages. Amen.” [Note: [Col. 1723] “only” is added in the Basel edition.]

For that hymn which the angels sang when Christ was born in the flesh—“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will,” and the rest that follows there—was composed by ecclesiastical doctors. [Col. 1724A] [Note: [Col. 1723] Luke 2:14. *in excelsis*, “in the highest”: *altissimis*, “in the loftiest places,” Vulgate.] Are they therefore not to be sung in churches because they are not found in the books of Holy Scripture?

Masses, prayers, orations, commendations, and impositions of hands are composed; if none of these are sung in church, all ecclesiastical offices stand vacant. [Note: [Col. 1723] “Thus hymns are composed, just as…” in the Hispanic Collection. *decantentur*, “are sung”: *decantantur*, editions of Paris and Lyons II–III; *decantetur*, Basel and Lyons I; *dicantur*, “are said,” Hispanic Collection. “In church” is absent from the Argentinensis edition.]

The Apostle instructs and urges Timothy that these things be done, saying: “I urge, therefore, first that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and for all who are in high station.” [Note: [Col. 1723] 1 Tim. 2:1–2. “Of all” is added from the Vulgate in the Basel and Lyons editions.]

Therefore, just as prayers, so too hymns composed in praise of God: let none of us henceforth disapprove of them; but let them be celebrated in the same manner in Gaul and Spain. Those who dare to reject a hymn are to be punished with excommunication. [Note: [Col. 1723] “And hymns” is absent from the editions cited above. *nostrum*, “of us”: *vestrum*, “of you,” Argentinensis, Basel, and Lyons II–III. “But likewise in” is absent from the Hispanic Collection. *Gallicia*, “Gaul”: *Gallia*, same collection and Böhm. *hymnum*, “a hymn”: *hymnos*, “hymns,” same collection.]

### C. LV. Which Hymns Are Found in the New Testament to Have Been Sung by Angels

Leo IX. [Note: [Col. 1723] Rather, Humbert, *Against the Greeks*, in Canisius, vol. 6.]

Only these two hymns are found in the New Testament to have been sung by angels: “Alleluia,” and “Glory to God in the highest.” [Note: [Col. 1723] Rev. 19:3; Luke 2:14.]

We omit both together during Septuagesima, because, through the sin of the old man, expelled from the assembly of angelic rejoicing into the Babylon of this wretched life, we sit beside its rivers and weep while we remember that Zion, in which “praise is fitting for God.” [Note: [Col. 1723] “For the sin” in the Basel and Lyons II–III editions. Cf. Ps. 136. *recordamur*, “we remember”: *recordaremur*, “we might remember,” editions cited above. Ps. 64:1.]

Since we omit Alleluia for nine weeks, we appropriately understand the nine weeks as the nine orders of angels. Their tenth order, falling through pride, [Col. 1724C] diminished the angelic number and disturbed its blessedness. [Note: [Col. 1723] Cf. Rev. 12.] Grieving for their own diminution and fearing a similar ruin for themselves, they were hindered from the perfect praise of the Creator. [Note: [Col. 1723] *suae*, “their own”: *sui*, Basel edition. *diminutionis*, “of diminution”: *deminutioni*, “at the diminution,” editions cited above. *praepediti*, “hindered”: *impediti*, Basel; “deprived or hindered,” Argentinensis.]

Providing for their restoration and consolation, almighty God the Creator first formed man from the clay of the earth, so that by the multiplication of his race he might repair the losses of the heavenly homeland and supply the angels’ joys. [Note: [Col. 1723] *recuperationi*, “recovery,” editions cited above. “And consolation” is absent from the Argentinensis edition. “Creator” is absent from the Basel edition.] At this hope the angelic choir rejoiced greatly. [Note: [Col. 1723] “Rejoiced exceedingly,” same editions.]

Nor is it surprising that it was disturbed by the fall of man himself. [Note: [Col. 1723] *fuit*, “was”: *fuerat*, “had been,” editions cited above. *perturbatus*, “disturbed”: *conturbatus*, “troubled,” Basel.] Thus the harmony of the nine orders remained [Col. 1725A] imperfect in the praise of God the Creator until that fallen first-created man rose again in the rising of Christ. [Note: [Col. 1725] *in laudem*, “for the praise”: *laude*, “in praise,” Argentinensis, Nuremberg, Venice I–II. “God” is absent from Basel. *permansit*, “remained”: *remansit*, “remained behind,” Basel. *lapsus*, “fallen”: *prolapsus*, “cast down,” editions cited above.]

There, rejoicing at the increase of its fellowship and in better hope, the whole angelic host rose up anew into Alleluia and remains devoted in it. We too, imitating this according to our measure, omit Alleluia for nine weeks from Septuagesima, when the fall of the first-created man is read in church, namely until Easter; there Christ, rising from the dead, turns our sorrow into joy and restores Alleluia to us. [Note: [Col. 1725] *reddit*, “restores”: *reddidit*, “restored,” Basel.]

### C. LVI. On the Lord’s Supper, “Glory to God in the Highest” Is to Be Sung

Likewise, Pope Nicholas to Rodolph, Archbishop of Bourges. [Note: [Col. 1725] Written A.D. 867; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 5, c. 20.]

Moreover, “Glory to God in the highest” is to be said by bishops, according to our custom, amid the solemnities of Mass on the Lord’s Supper. [Col. 1725B] On that same day, those alone to whom the Apostolic See has granted permission may use the apostolic pallium. [Note: [Col. 1725D] “Apostolic” is absent from certain Vatican manuscripts, though Ivo has it. “Alone” is added in the original.]

### C. LVII. A Cleric Is Not to Enter to Celebrate the Solemnities of Mass with a Staff or with His Head Covered

Likewise, Pope Zacharias, in the Roman Synod, chapters 13 and 14. [Note: [Col. 1725D] Earlier the reading was “Macarius” [Col. 1726D], as in the editions cited above except the Argentinensis; it was corrected from certain ancient manuscripts and the other compilers. The chapter itself is found in a manuscript council of Zacharias. Held A.D. 743; Burchard, bk. 3, c. 230 ff.; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, c. 271; Polycarpus, bk. 3, tit. 16.]

### XIX. Part

No bishop, presbyter, or deacon is to presume, when celebrating the solemnities of Mass, to enter carrying a staff or to stand at God’s altar with his head covered, since the Apostle also forbids men to pray in church with their heads covered. Whoever rashly presumes to do so is to be deprived of communion. [Note: [Col. 1725] “Or presbyter,” editions cited above. *celebrandum*, singular, original, Burchard, Argentinensis, Basel, Nuremberg. 1 Cor. 11:4. *qui*, “who”: *si*, “if,” original, Burchard, Ivo, and editions cited above. Plural “presume … be deprived,” same editions except Argentinensis and Basel.]

When a bishop or presbyter has entered to celebrate the solemnities of Mass, unless some emergency arises, he must in no way dare to depart after the prayer has been given, so that the solemnities of Mass may be completed by another bishop or presbyter. Rather, the person who begins must complete it to the end, “because it is written: ‘Whoever perseveres to the end, that person shall be saved.’” Whoever presumes to act otherwise than we have laid down is suspended from the sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. [Note: [Col. 1725] *aliquo*, “some other”: *alio*, editions cited above. Matt. 10:22. *posuimus*, “laid down”: *exposuimus*, “explained,” original; *disposuimus*, “ordained,” Basel and Lyons II–III.]

[Col. 1726A]

### C. LVIII. PALEA

[Likewise from the Decrees of Pope Soter. [Note: [Col. 1725] Rather, from the Eleventh Council of Toledo; cf. C. 7, q. 1, c. 15, and the collections cited there. Absent from the Argentinensis edition.]]

“To ensure that each person guards against that saying of the divine oracle in which it is written, ‘Woe to one alone, because when he falls, he has no one to lift him up,’ we must most earnestly fear and take care lest, at those hours and times when psalms are sung or sacrifice is offered to God, some destructive illness or bodily infirmity should come upon anyone individually engaged in the divine offices, one which either suddenly brings down the body or throws the mind into confusion through distraction or terror. [Note: [Col. 1725] *Et*, “and”: Nuremberg and Venice I–II. Eccl. 4:10. “Their” is added in Basel.]

“Therefore, making provision for cases of this kind, we have judged it necessary to establish that, where the abundance of time, place, or clergy permits, everyone singing to God and offering sacrifice is to have behind him the help of a neighbouring assistant, so that, if [Col. 1726B] the person who comes forward to perform the offices is disturbed by some mishap or struck to the ground, he may always have behind him one who fearlessly performs his part and completes the office begun.” [Note: [Col. 1725] *casibus*, “cases”: *ausibus*, “attempts,” Basel. “Each person … and complete” is absent from the Hispanic Collection.]

### C. LIX. How Many Witnesses a Bishop Offering Sacrifice Must Have with Him

Likewise, Anacletus, servant of Jesus Christ, to all bishops, Letter I. [Note: [Col. 1725] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Anselm, bk. 6, c. 138 [137]; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 2, c. 67; Polycarpus, bk. 4, tit. 12.]

### XX. Part

A bishop offering sacrifice to God is to have witnesses with him, and more than another priest; for as he enjoys a higher rank of honour, so he needs a greater reinforcement of testimony. On more solemn days he is to have with him either seven, five, or three deacons, who are called his eyes, and subdeacons and the remaining [Col. 1726C] ministers. Clothed in sacred vestments, they are to stand before and behind him; and the presbyters, opposite him on right and left, are to stand with contrite heart, humbled spirit, and lowered countenance, guarding him against malicious people and giving their assent to the sacrifice. After the consecration has been completed, all who do not wish to be excluded from the thresholds of the church are to communicate. [Note: [Col. 1725] *incrementatione*, “increase,” Ivo and Anselm. *solennibus*, “solemn,” Basel. “In” rather than “from” in the editions cited above. *e*, “from”: *a*, Basel and Lyons II–III. *malevolis*, “malicious”: *malifluis*, “evil-flowing,” Nuremberg. *praebeant*, “give”: *praebentes*, “giving,” editions cited above. *Peracta*, “completed”: *Peractaque*, “and when completed,” Basel.]

[Col. 1727A]

### C. LX. Bishops Are Not to Consecrate the Lord’s Sacraments without Religious Witnesses

Likewise, Pope Lucius to the bishops of Gaul and Spain, chapter 1. [Note: [Col. 1727] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Anselm, bk. 6, c. 140 [138]; Polycarpus, bk. 4, tit. 13.]

By apostolic authority we command that you always have priests and Levites as witnesses with you. [Note: [Col. 1727C] In the letter itself it reads: “For such reasons, brothers, we urge you, as we have established in this holy church, that you always…” *diaconos*, “deacons,” original.] And although one’s own conscience may suffice, nevertheless, because of malicious persons, according to the Apostle, you must also have a good testimony from those outside; for in this holy see we have established that two presbyters and three deacons are not to leave a bishop in any place, for the sake of ecclesiastical testimony. [Note: [Col. 1727] 1 Tim. 3:7. *vos*, “you”: *nos*, “we,” editions cited above except Basel. “For … that” is absent from Anselm. “Therefore, two” in Anselm and the editions cited above.]

[Col. 1727B]

### C. LXI. A Presbyter Is Not to Presume to Celebrate Mass Unless Two Are Present

Likewise, Pope Soter. [Note: [Col. 1727C] Burchard and Ivo also cite this from the decrees of Pope Soter. In the *Micrologus*, c. 7, it is said to have been established by Anacletus and Soter. Burchard, bk. 3, c. 68, reports a similar ruling from the Council of Nantes, c. 30. Almost the same is found in the First Council of Mainz, c. 43. Regino, bk. 1, c. 191, gives something similar from the Council of Nantes, which Burchard, bk. 3, c. 74, seems to have followed; cf. *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, bk. 5, c. 159; Anselm, appendix, bk. 7; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, c. 159; *Decretum*, pt. 2, c. 127; Polycarpus, bk. 4, tit. 31.]

This too has been decreed: no presbyter is to presume to celebrate the solemnities of Mass unless two are present and respond to him, so that he himself may be counted as the third. For, when he says in the plural, “The Lord be with you,” and says in the secret prayers, “Pray for me,” it is altogether fitting that a response be made to his greeting. [Note: [Col. 1727] “And he himself,” editions cited above. *ipsius*, “to him”: *et ipsi*, “and to him,” Burchard and Ivo.]

### C. LXII. Those Who Have Not Heard the Solemnities of Mass to the End Are to Be Deprived of Communion

Likewise, from Canon 10 of the Apostles. [Note: [Col. 1727] Cf. Council of Antioch, c. 2; Regino, bk. 1, c. 193; Burchard, bk. 2, c. 67; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 163; Polycarpus, bk. 3, tit. 16.]

### XXI. Part

All the faithful who assemble at church for the sacred solemnities are to hear the writings of the Apostles and the Gospel. [Note: [Col. 1727] Original: “those who enter church and hear the Scriptures, but do not persevere in prayer, nor receive the holy…” *solennibus*, “solemn occasions,” Burchard. [Col. 1728C] “At sacred solemnities”: in the council volumes these same words appear in the margin of the ancient translation, as here in Gratian, Burchard, Ivo, and Polycarpus. The Greek is simply: **τοὺς εἰσιόντας**, “those entering”; this is likewise found in the *Codex Canonum*, evidently from Dionysius’s translation.]

But those who do not remain in prayer until the Mass is completed, and do not receive holy communion, are to be deprived of communion as persons stirring up disturbances in the church. [Note: [Col. 1728C–D] “Hear. But those…” is likewise in that margin and in Polycarpus. But Burchard and Ivo are closer to the Greek: “they hear, but do not remain…”]

[Col. 1728A]

### C. LXIII. On the Same Matter

Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 24. [Note: [Col. 1727] c. 31 of the *Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua*; cf. on c. 9, Distinction 18; Regino, bk. 1, c. 197; Burchard, bk. 2, c. 66; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 162.]

Anyone who leaves the assembly while the priest is speaking the word in church is to be excommunicated. [Note: [Col. 1727] Burchard and Ivo add: “without grave necessity.”]

### C. LXIV. On Sunday Laypersons Must Hear the Entire Mass

Likewise, from the Council of Agde, c. 47. [Note: [Col. 1727] Held A.D. 506; cf., however, on c. 30, Distinction 23; *Collection in Three Parts*, pt. 2, tit. 28, c. 45.]

By a special ordinance we command that laypersons hear the whole Mass on the Lord’s Day, so that the people do not presume to leave before the priest’s blessing. If they do so, they are to be publicly rebuked by the bishop. [Note: [Col. 1727] *audire*, “hear”: *tenere*, “observe/attend,” with a special ordination, Hispanic Collection.]

### C. LXV. The People Must Not Depart before the Mass Has Been Fully Celebrated

Likewise, from the First Council of Orléans, c. 28. [Note: [Col. 1727] Held A.D. 511; Regino, bk. 1, c. 196; Burchard, bk. 3, c. 29; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 8, c. 34.]

[Col. 1728B] When the people gather in God’s name to celebrate Masses, they are not to depart before the solemnity of Mass is completed; and where no bishop is present, they are to receive the priest’s blessing. [Note: [Col. 1727] *convenitur*, “they gather”: *convenit*, “there gathers,” Burchard and Ivo; *convenerit*, “shall have gathered,” Basel. *non fuerit*, “is not present”: *defuerit*, “is absent,” Hispanic Collection, Burchard, and Ivo; *fuerit*, “is present,” Ivo. *sacerdotis*, “of the priest”: *a sacerdote*, “from the priest,” editions cited above.]

### C. LXVI. Anyone Who, Neglecting the Church Assembly, Goes to Spectacles Is to Be Excommunicated

Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 88. [Note: [Col. 1727] c. 33 of the *Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua*; cf. on c. 9, Distinction 18; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 8.]

Anyone who, on a feast day, neglects the solemn assembly of the church and goes to spectacles is to be excommunicated. [Note: [Col. 1727] The second *solenni*, “solemn,” is absent from the Hispanic Collection, Ballerini, and Ivo.]

### C. LXVII. No One Is to Be Forbidden to Enter Church Until the Mass of the Catechumens

Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 84. [Note: [Col. 1727] c. 17 there; Burchard, bk. 3, c. 28; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 41; *Decretum*, pt. 3, c. 33.]

### XXII. Part

A bishop is to forbid no one to enter [Col. 1728C] church and hear the word of God—whether a pagan, a heretic, or a Jew—until the Mass of the catechumens. [Note: [Col. 1727] “And” is absent from Ballerini.]

[Col. 1729A]

### C. LXVIII. We Must Hear the Gospels Standing, Not Sitting

Likewise, Anastasius, Bishop, to the Bishops of Germany and Burgundy, Letter I, c. 1. [Note: [Col. 1729] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Burchard, bk. 3, c. 103; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 2, c. 138 and pt. 6, c. 93.]

### XXIII. Part

By apostolic authority we command that, when the holy Gospels are recited in church, priests and all others present, not sitting but standing reverently bowed in the presence of the Gospel, listen attentively to the words of the Lord and faithfully adore them. [Note: [Col. 1729] *recitantur*, “are recited”: *leguntur*, “are read,” editions cited above. “Present” is absent from Burchard and Ivo. [Col. 1729C] *curvi*, “bowed”: so in the original and Ivo, pt. 6, c. 93; but this word is absent from Ivo, pt. 2, c. 138, Burchard, the Argentinensis edition, and other editions.]

### C. LXIX. Something Must Always Be Offered at the Solemnities of Mass

Likewise, Gregory VII, in the Roman Synod held in the year of the Lord 1078, c. 13. [Note: [Col. 1729] Anselm, bk. 3, c. 40 [41]; Polycarpus, bk. 3, tit. 16.]

### XXIV. Part

Every Christian should take care to offer something to God at the solemnities of Mass [Col. 1729B] and call to mind what God said through Moses: “You shall not appear before me empty-handed.” [Note: [Col. 1729] *ducere*, “to bring”: *ducat*, “let him bring,” original; *reducere*, “to bring back,” Basel. Exod. 23:15.]

For it is plainly evident in the collections of the holy Fathers that, according to the practice of the holy Fathers, all Christians ought to offer something to God. One must first flee to him who can heal the sufferings of our soul. But people, in perverse order, first seek aid for themselves from other people. When human help has failed, then they think that the grace of divine favour must be sought. [Note: [Col. 1729C–D] From “One must first…” to the end of the chapter is not found there in Gregory, Anselm, or Polycarpus, and appears to be Gratian’s own.]

### C. LXX. Why “Lift Up Your Hearts” Is Said in the Preface

Likewise, Cyprian, Sermon VI on the Lord’s Prayer. [Note: [Col. 1729] “Pope Cyprian,” editions cited above.]

### XXV. Part

But when we stand for prayer, beloved brothers, we must be watchful and devote ourselves to prayers with our whole heart. Every carnal and worldly thought must depart, and at that time the mind must think of nothing but that alone for which it prays. [Note: [Col. 1729] *vigilare*, “be watchful”: *invigilare*, “keep watch,” same editions. *cogitatio omnis*, “every thought”: *hominis*, “of a person,” same editions. “Other” is added in the same editions.]

Therefore, before the prayer, after the preface has been spoken, the priest prepares the minds of the brethren by saying, “Lift up your hearts,” so that, when the people answer, “We have them toward the Lord,” they may be reminded that they ought to think of nothing but the Lord. [Note: [Col. 1729] *et*, “also”: *autem*, “but,” Basel.]

Let the breast be closed against the adversary and open only to God, and let it not allow the enemy of God to approach it at the time of prayer. [Col. 1730A] [Note: [Col. 1729] *omni*, “every,” same edition; *adire*, “approach”: *venire*, “come,” editions cited above.]

### C. LXXI. Which Prefaces Are to Be Sung at Mass

Pelagius II, Bishop of the Roman Church and Apostolic See, to all the bishops of Germany and Gaul. [Note: [Col. 1729] An apocryphal chapter. In editions cited above, except Basel, it is attributed to Gelasius. Burchard, bk. 3, c. 69; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, c. 158; *Decretum*, pt. 2, c. 77; Polycarpus, bk. 3, tit. 20.]

### XXVI. Part

We find that only these nine prefaces are to be received in the sacred catalogue, which long-standing antiquity has hitherto observed in the Roman Church: one for the Paschal white garments; another for the Ascension of the Lord; a third for Pentecost; a fourth for the Nativity of the Lord; a fifth for the Manifestation of the Lord; a sixth for the Apostles; a seventh for the Holy Trinity; an eighth for the Cross; and a ninth, to be said only for the fast in Lent. [Note: [Col. 1729] *recipiendas*, “to be received”: *receptus*, “received,” Ivo. “Of the Ascension” / “on the day of the Ascension,” various editions. “Day of Pentecost,” editions cited above. “Day of the Nativity,” Basel. “Of the Manifestation” is absent from Argentinensis. “Only to be said” is absent from the same.]

[Col. 1730B] The Holy Roman Church maintains and guards these prefaces; we command you to maintain them.

### C. LXXII. At Every Solemnity of Mass Prayer Is to Be Made for the Dead

Likewise, from the Second Council of Chalon, c. 39. [Note: [Col. 1729] Held A.D. 813; Burchard, bk. 3, c. 64; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, c. 66.]

### XXVII. Part

Moreover, it has seemed good to us that, at all solemnities of Mass, the Lord be entreated at the appropriate place for the souls of the departed. For just as no day is excepted on which the Lord is not entreated for the living and for whatever needs may arise, so likewise no day should be excepted on which prayers are not poured out to the Lord, in the solemnities of Mass, for the souls of the faithful. [Note: [Col. 1729] “The church entreat the Lord,” Basel; “in church, to the Lord,” other editions. *Dominus*, “the Lord”: *Dominum*, “the Lord” as object, editions cited above; absent from Ivo.]

Accordingly, the holy Church has from ancient times maintained this custom: that in the solemnities of Mass and in other prayers it commends to the Lord the souls of those at rest. Blessed Augustine says: “Supplications for the spirits of the departed must not be omitted; we approve that they be made for all in Christian and Catholic fellowship.” [Col. 1730C] [Note: [Col. 1729] *tenet*, “maintains”: *tenebat*, “maintained,” Basel. Variants concerning “in the solemnities of Mass … commends.” Augustine, *On Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, c. 4. *defunctorum*, “of the departed”: *mortuorum*, “of the dead,” original, Burchard, Ivo, and editions cited above.]

Even when the names of the departed are unspoken—those whom the Church has received under a general commemoration—this is done so that those lacking parents, children, relatives, or friends to do these things for them may receive them from the one common pious mother. [Note: [Col. 1729D–1730D] The compilers contain several variants. Augustine, with little variation in the council and Amalarius, bk. 4, c. 42, reads: “For all the dead in Christian and Catholic fellowship, even though the names of any persons are unspoken, whom the Church has received under a general commemoration.” The gloss caused the text not to be altered. *istam*, “this [thing],” Basel. *exhibeantur*, “may be supplied”: *exhibeatur*, singular, editions cited above.]

[Col. 1731A]

### C. LXXIII. Names Are Not to Be Recited by the Priest before the Prayers

Likewise, Innocent, Bishop of the City of Rome, to Decentius of Gubbio, Letter I, c. 2. [Note: [Col. 1731] Written A.D. 416.]

As for reciting names before the priest makes the prayers and commends by his prayer the offerings of those whose names are to be recited, you yourself, in your prudence, recognize how superfluous it is: that you should announce someone’s name before offering that person’s sacrifice to God, although nothing is unknown to him. [Col. 1732A] [Note: [Col. 1731] *preces*, “prayers”: *precem*, “prayer,” Hispanic Collection and Coustant. “And” is absent from Basel and Lyons II–III. *recognoscis*, “you recognize”: *recognosces*, “you will recognize,” Hispanic Collection and Coustant; *recognoscas*, “you may recognize,” editions cited above except Lyons II–III. *illi*, “to him”: *ei*, editions cited above.]

## DISTINCTION II

[Col. 1731]

[Col. 1731A]

### GRATIAN. C. I. Bread, Wine, and Water Are to Be Offered in the Sacraments

Likewise, Alexander, Bishop of the City of Rome, to all the orthodox, Letter I, c. 4. [Note: [Col. 1731C] This chapter was enlarged from the original and the other compilers, except Anselm, which contains the text as Gratian formerly had it. [Col. 1731] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; compare the second book of the *Liber Pontificalis*; Burchard, bk. 5, c. 5; Anselm, bk. 9, c. 1; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 2, c. 15; Polycarpus, bk. 3, tit. 9.]

### I. Part

In the sacramental offerings that are offered to the Lord during the solemnities of Mass, the passion of the Lord is to be mingled in, so that the passion of him whose body and blood are consecrated may be celebrated; and, rejecting superstitious opinions, only bread and wine mixed with water are to be offered in sacrifice. [Col. 1731B] For, as we have received from the Fathers and as reason itself teaches, neither wine alone nor water alone ought to be offered in the Lord’s chalice, but both mixed together, because both are read to have flowed from his side in his passion. [Note: [Col. 1731] “Passion [is] superfluous” is absent from Anselm. *quamvis*, “although,” Venice I–II. “Only” is absent from the editions cited above except Basel. *sacrificio*, “in sacrifice,” original, Burchard, and Ivo. “As … teaches” is absent from Anselm.]

### C. II. It Is Not Permitted to Offer Wine without Water, or Conversely, in the Sacraments

Likewise, Cyprian, book II, letter 2: “Greeting to brother Caecilius.” [Note: [Col. 1731] Written A.D. 234. “Pope Cyprian,” editions cited above; Anselm, bk. 9, c. 4.]

Thus, in consecrating the Lord’s chalice, water alone cannot be offered, just as wine alone cannot be offered. For if anyone offers wine only, the blood of Christ begins to be without Christ. [Note: [Col. 1731] *Sic*, “thus”: *Sicut*, “just as,” editions cited above. *calice*, “chalice”: *calicem*, “chalice” accusative, same editions. [Col. 1731C–1732C] At Cyprian the text reads: “The blood of Christ begins to be without us; but if the water is alone, the people begin to be without Christ.” These words are also quoted below in the chapter “When every…,” but the text was not changed because of the gloss. Many other passages, where that obstacle did not occur, have been corrected from the letter itself, as also in the following chapter.]

But when both are mixed and, by a united blending, are joined to one another, then the spiritual and heavenly sacrament is accomplished. Thus the Lord’s chalice is neither water alone nor wine alone, unless both are mixed with one another; just as the Lord’s body cannot be flour alone or water alone, unless both have been united and joined, and made solid in the compactness of one bread. [Note: [Col. 1731] *enim*, “indeed”: *autem*, “but,” same editions. *commiscetur*, “is mixed together,” Basel. *copulatur*, singular: *copulantur*, plural, editions cited above. “And spiritual … is accomplished,” same editions. *Si*, “if,” Basel, Venice II, Paris, Lyons I. *nec*, “nor,” Argentinensis. *aut*, “or”: *et*, “and,” editions cited above. *Christi*, “of Christ,” Basel.]

[Col. 1732A]

### C. III. The Same, in the Same Letter

Scripture says: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.” Therefore, whenever we offer the cup in commemoration of the Lord and of his passion, let us do what the Lord is known to have done. [Note: [Col. 1731] 1 Cor. 11:26. *Quotiescunque*, “as often as”: *ut quotiescunque*, “that as often as,” editions cited above. *commemorationem*, “commemoration”: *commemoratione*, “in commemoration,” Basel. “And the Lord,” Argentinensis.]

But consider, dearest brother, whether, if any of our predecessors through ignorance or simplicity did not observe and retain what the Lord taught us to do by his own example and instruction, pardon may be granted to that person’s simplicity through the Lord’s mercy. Yet we cannot be forgiven, since we are now warned and instructed by the Lord to offer the Lord’s chalice mixed with wine, according to what the Lord offered. [Col. 1732B] [Note: [Col. 1731] *vide*, “consider”: *viderit*, “let him consider,” original. *servavit*, “observed”: *observavit*, Basel; future-perfect forms in Argentinensis and Lyons II–III. “And retained” has future-perfect in Lyons II–III. “And” is absent from editions cited above except Lyons II–III. *ejus*, “his”: *ejusdem*, “of that same person,” same editions except Basel. *poterit*, “will be able”: *potest*, “is able,” editions cited above. *admoniti*, “warned”: *moniti*, “advised,” Basel.]

### C. IV. Nothing besides Bread, Wine, and Water Must Be Offered in the Sacrament

Likewise, from the Council of Martin of Braga, c. 55. [Note: [Col. 1731] “Pope Martin,” editions cited above; cf. following chapter.]

Nothing else ought to be offered in the sacrament besides bread, wine, and water, which are blessed as a type of Christ; for while he hung on the cross, blood and water flowed from his body. These three are one in Christ Jesus; this is the victim and offering of God, a sweet-smelling savour. [Note: [Col. 1731] *sanctuario*, “sanctuary,” Hispanic Collection; *sacrario*, “sacristy/sanctuary,” Basel. “Son” is added in the same.]

### C. V. On the Same Matter

Likewise, from the Third Council of Carthage, c. 24. [Note: [Col. 1731] Held A.D. 397; Burchard, bk. 5, c. 3; Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 2, c. 13.]

In the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord, nothing further is to be offered than what the Lord himself handed down: that is, bread and wine mixed with water. And below, §1: Nothing more is to be offered in sacrifices than what comes from grapes and grain. [Col. 1732C] [Note: [Col. 1731] *sacramento*, singular: *sacramentis*, plural, Hispanic Collection, Burchard, Ivo. “That” is added in Burchard, Ivo, and editions cited above. *aquae*, “of water”: *aqua*, “with water,” same witnesses. *sacrificiis*, “sacrifices”: *primitiis*, “firstfruits,” same witnesses and Hispanic Collection.]

[Col. 1733A]

### C. VI. No One Is to Add Grapes to the Sacrifice of the Offering

Likewise, from the Sixth Synod, c. 28. [Note: [Col. 1733C] This is a kind of summary of the canon cited. It contains rather more words, but almost the same meaning. [Col. 1733] Rather, from the Trullan Synod, held A.D. 692; *Collection in Three Parts*, pt. 2, tit. 11, c. 13.]

We have learned that in certain churches priests add grapes to the sacrifice of the offering, grapes which are customarily offered at the altar, and thus distribute both together to the people. We therefore command that no priest do this any longer; rather, he is to distribute to the people the offering alone for the remission of sins. The people, however, are to receive separately blessed grapes if they request them, and give thanks to the giver of fruits. [Note: [Col. 1733C] “And give thanks to the giver of fruits”: Greek, **πρὸς τὴν τοῦ δωτῆρος τῶν καρπῶν εὐχαριστίαν**, “for giving thanks to the giver of fruits.”]

### C. VII. On Those Who Erred in Various Ways While Offering Sacrifice

Likewise, Pope Julius to the bishops throughout Egypt. [Note: [Col. 1733D] “Throughout Egypt”: the other compilers read “to those sent through Egypt”; but the *Micrologus*, c. 19, cites the same Julius as addressing the bishops of Egypt. Nearly the same material is now found in the Third Council of Braga, c. 1, and the ruling is summarized in the *Worms Collection*, c. 4. [Col. 1733] Rather, from the Third Council of Braga, held A.D. 675; Burchard, bk. 5, c. 1; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, c. 147; *Decretum*, pt. 2, cc. 11 and 85; Polycarpus, bk. 3, tit. 9.]

Since every crime and sin is wiped away by sacrifices offered to God, what henceforth shall be given to the Lord for the expiation of offences, when error is committed in the very offering of the sacrifice? [Col. 1733B] For we have heard that certain persons, held by schismatic ambition, contrary to divine ordinances and apostolic institutions, consecrate milk instead of wine in the divine sacrifices; that others give the people a dipped Eucharist as the completion of communion; that some also offer pressed wine in the sacrament of the Lord’s cup; and that others keep throughout the year a linen cloth dipped in must and, at the time of sacrifice, wash part of it in water and so offer it.

[Note: “But”: Argentinian edition.]  
[Note: “Pressed wine.” Thus in Ivo, in the *Panormia*, and in the Council of Braga. In several old copies, however, it reads “a pressed cluster” [so the Basel edition], as somewhat below in this same chapter. But Burchard has “unpressed wine.”]

How contrary this is to evangelical and apostolic teaching, and how opposed to ecclesiastical custom, will not be difficult to prove from the very source of truth, from which the ordered mysteries of the sacraments themselves proceeded. [Note: “Is proved”: Argentinian and Basel editions.] For when the Teacher of truth commended the true sacrifice of our salvation to his disciples, we know that he gave them not milk, but only bread and a cup under this sacrament. [Note: “No one [received] milk”: Ivo; the other editions compared.] [Note: “We know”: Burchard and Ivo read “we know.”] For it is written in the truth of the Gospel [Note: Matthew 26:26]: “Jesus took bread and the cup, and, blessing them, gave them to his disciples.” Let milk, therefore, cease to be offered in sacrifice, since the clear and evident example of evangelical truth has shone forth: apart from bread and wine, it is not lawful to offer anything else. [Note: “In sacrifice”: the other editions compared.] [Note: “To offer”: Argentinian and Basel editions.] [Note: “May be lawful”: Burchard and Ivo.]

§ 1. As for their giving the people a dipped Eucharist as the completion of communion, neither does the testimony drawn from the Gospel admit this, where he entrusted his body and blood to the Apostles. [Note: “Receive”: the other editions compared.] [Note: “Have received”: the same editions.] The handing over of the bread is mentioned separately, and that of the cup separately. For we do not read that Christ gave dipped bread to others, except only to that disciple whom the dipped morsel of the Teacher showed to be the betrayer, not a morsel signifying the institution of this sacrament. [Note: “Teacher”: Basel edition.]

As for the people’s communicating from a pressed cluster—that is, from grape-berries—this is altogether very confused. But if necessity requires it, the cluster should be pressed into the cup and water mixed with it, because the Lord’s cup, in accordance with the prescriptions of the canons, ought to be offered mixed with wine and water. [Note: In the Braga text: “according to what a certain teacher explains.” The reference is to blessed Cyprian, cited above in the same distinction, “In sanctifying.”] For we see that the people are understood in the water, while the blood of Christ is shown in the wine. Therefore, when water is mixed with wine in the cup, the people are united with Christ, and the body of believers is joined and bound to him in whom it believes. This joining and union of water and wine is so mixed in the Lord’s cup that the mixture cannot be separated. [Note: “Mixture”: Burchard; Basel edition.] For if anyone offers wine alone, the blood of Christ begins to be [present] without us. [Note: The word *sibi* (“with the other”) is absent from Burchard and Ivo.] But if the water is alone, the people begin to be [present] without Christ. Therefore, when the cluster alone is offered, in which only the efficacy of wine is signified, the sacrament of our salvation, signified through water, is neglected. For the Lord’s cup cannot be water alone or wine alone, unless each is mixed with the other.

§ 2. And therefore, since from this matter there has already flowed forth the abundant and manifold judgment of the fathers, [Note: “Judgment.” In the Braga text there follows: “whose religious devotion toward God both discussed abundantly the effects of these sacraments and most truly explained their institutions.”] every such error and presumption must henceforth cease, lest the disorderly combination of perverse persons weaken the standing of truth. [Note: “And in”: Ivo and the *Panormia*; the other editions compared.] Therefore henceforth it shall be lawful for no one to offer anything in the divine sacrifices except, according to the judgment of the ancient councils, bread alone and a cup mixed with wine and water. [Note: “And thus”: Basel edition.] Whoever hereafter acts otherwise than has been prescribed shall cease from offering sacrifice until, corrected by lawful penitential satisfaction, he returns to the function of his rank, which he has lost. [Note: “Corrected”: Burchard and Ivo.] [Note: “Of his office”: Basel edition.]

### C. VIII. No offering can be compared with the body and blood of Christ.

Likewise, Pope Alexander, fifth from Peter, Letter I.  
[Note: A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore.—Burchard, book 5, chapter 5; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapters 15 and 68.]

Part II. Nothing in sacrifices can be greater than the body and blood of Christ, nor is any offering superior to this; rather, this surpasses all others. It must be offered to the Lord with a pure conscience, received with a pure mind, and venerated by all. [Note: “Completed”: Burchard and Ivo, chapter 15.] And as it is superior to the rest, so it ought especially to be honoured and revered.

[Col. 1735B]

### C. IX. We ought not offer the peace before the mysteries have been completed.

Likewise, Pope Innocent, greeting Decentius, bishop of Eugubium, Letter I, chapter 1.  
[Note: Written A.D. 416.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 1, title 38, chapter 1.]

Part III. You assert, therefore, that some distribute the peace to the people, or exchange it among themselves as priests, before the mysteries have been completed; whereas, after all things—which I ought not disclose—the peace must necessarily be proclaimed, by which it is made clear that the people have given their assent to all that is done in the mysteries and celebrated in the Church, and that these things are shown to have been concluded by the seal of the peace that brings them to a close. [Note: “Ministries”: Basel edition, both for “mysteries” before “completed” and, in the latter occurrence, in the Argentinian and Basel editions.] [Note: “To command”: the Hispanic Collection and Coustant; Basel edition.] [Note: “Necessary”: Hispanic Collection.] [Note: The word “in” before “the mysteries” is absent from the other editions compared.]

### C. X. A minister who scorns to communicate after the consecration is to be deprived of access to the thresholds of the church.

Likewise, Pope Anacletus, Letter I.  
[Note: This was attributed to Calixtus in the other editions. It has been restored to Anacletus from several old copies and from Burchard, to whom it is attributed to Anacletus also above, *On Consecration*, distinction 1, “The Bishop.”]  
[Note: A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore, compiled from Apostolic Canon 10.—Cf. above, Distinction 1, chapter 62.—Burchard, book 3, chapter 77; Anselm, book 6, chapter 137.]

When the consecration has been performed, all who do not wish to be excluded from the thresholds of the church shall communicate. For thus the Apostles also decreed, and the holy Roman Church maintains it.

### C. XI. Every priest, as often as he celebrates Mass, shall receive holy communion as often.

Likewise, from the Twelfth Council of Toledo, chapter 5.  
[Note: Held A.D. 681. Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 114.]

Part IV. It has been reported to us that some priests do not receive the grace of holy communion as many times as they appear to offer sacrifices in one day; rather, if they offer several sacrifices by themselves on one day, they refrain from communion in all the offerings and receive the grace of holy communion only at the final offering of the sacrifice—as though one were not to partake of that true and singular sacrifice as often as the immolation of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is known to have occurred. [Note: The words “in one day” are absent from the Basel edition.] [Note: The addition “by themselves”: “to God,” in the Hispanic Collection, Ivo, and the other editions.] [Note: “They offer”: the same editions.] [Note: “By communicating”: Hispanic Collection.] [Note: “They suspend themselves”: Ivo and the other editions.] [Note: “Of the final sacrifice”: Hispanic Collection, Ivo, and Basel edition.] [Note: “They receive”: Ivo and the other editions.] [Note: Basel edition has “the final.”] [Note: “It will have ceased to be that true and singular sacrifice of his as often as he is a participant in the body of Christ”: Hispanic Collection.]

For behold, the Apostle says [Note: 1 Corinthians 10:18]: “Are not those who eat the sacrifices partakers of the altar?” [Note: “If, therefore, those who eat the sacrifices are partakers of the altar, it is certain, and so forth”: Hispanic Collection.] It is certain, then, that those who, while offering sacrifice, do not eat are guilty with respect to the Lord’s sacrament. [Note: “Those who sacrifice, if”: Basel edition.] Therefore, any priest who henceforth approaches the divine altar to offer sacrifice and refrains from communion shall know that he is excluded for one year from that grace of communion of which he has improperly deprived himself. [Note: “Has deprived himself”: Ivo; “will deprive himself”: the other editions, especially Paris and Lyon.]

[Col. 1736B] For what kind of sacrifice will that be in which even the one offering it is not known to be a participant? [Note: “Of which”: Ivo and Basel edition.] [Note: “To have participated”: Hispanic Collection.] [Note: “Is discerned”: the other editions.] Thus it must by every means be maintained that, as often as a celebrant immolates on the altar the body and blood of Jesus Christ our Lord, so often he makes himself a participant in receiving the body and blood of Christ. [Note: “For participation”: Hispanic Collection.] [Note: “Of the body and blood of Christ our Lord Jesus Christ”: absent from the Norwegian edition; present in the other editions.]

### C. XII. A priest must not receive Christ’s body without his blood.

Likewise, Pope Gelasius to Bishops Majoricus and John.  
[Note: It has been noted concerning this chapter above, Cause 25, question 2, final chapter, that in Anselm and in Polycarp, title 30—for in title 9 it is a separate chapter—it is part of the letter cited there.]  
[Note: Cf. Cause 25, question 2, final chapter; Anselm, book 6, chapter 147; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 89; Polycarp, book 3, titles 9 and 30.]

We have learned that certain persons, having received only a portion of the sacred body, abstain from the cup of the sacred blood. Such persons, beyond doubt—since I do not know by what superstition they are taught to be bound—must either receive the sacraments in their entirety or be barred from them entirely, because the division of one and the same mystery cannot occur without grave sacrilege. [Note: “Consecrated”: the other editions.] [Note: “Bound fast”: Basel edition; “to be bound”: the remaining editions.]

[Col. 1737A]

### C. XIII. One who receives Eucharistic communion daily is neither censured nor praised.

Likewise, Augustine, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 53.  
[Note: This chapter has been compiled from two passages of blessed Augustine and reduced to a summary; from the same passages, where it seemed necessary, it has also been corrected and enlarged. Alger, in *On the Truth of the Lord’s Body and Blood*, book 1, chapter 22, and Walafrid Strabo, in *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 12, cite it down to the word “The same,” from Gennadius, presbyter of Marseilles, whom blessed Thomas also, *Quodlibet* 12, article 10, makes the author of the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*. Platina, in the Life of Symmachus, and the Master of the Sentences, book 2, distinction 8, do likewise.]  
[Note: It is not Augustine’s.—Regino, book 1, chapter 194; Burchard, book 5, chapter 15; Anselm, book 9, chapter 9; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 150; *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 25.—Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 12.]

Part V. I neither praise nor condemn receiving Eucharistic communion every day; yet I urge and exhort [everyone] to communicate on every Lord’s Day, provided that the mind is without an affection for sin. [Note: “Eucharist”: Argentinian and Basel editions.] [Note: “To receive”: Ivo and the other editions compared.] [Note: “I urge and exhort” is absent from Regino, Anselm, Burchard, and Ivo.] [Note: “But if the mind”—Burchard reads “fear” for “mind”—“is in an affection for sin, I say that it is weighed down more”: Regino, Burchard, Anselm, and Ivo, *Decretum*; the original, Ivo’s *Panormia*, and the other editions read, “provided that the mind is not in an affection for sin.”]

Likewise, Letter 118, chapter 3.  
[Note: Regino, same place; Burchard, book 5, chapter 16; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 26.—Letter 54 in the Maurist edition, written A.D. 400.]

§ 1. Let one person say that the Eucharist should not be received daily; let another maintain that it should be received daily. [Note: “If someone says”: the other editions.] [Note: “Maintains”: the other editions.] Let each do what, according to his faith, he devoutly believes ought to be done. For neither of them dishonours the body and blood of the Lord, if they strive, as if in rivalry, to honour the most health-giving sacrament. [Note: The words between asterisks are absent from Regino, Burchard, and Ivo.]

For Zacchaeus [Note: Cf. Luke 19.] and that centurion did not quarrel with one another, nor did either set himself above the other: one joyfully received the Lord into his house, [Note: “In his own house”: the other editions, Regino, Burchard, and Ivo.] while the other said [Note: Matthew 8:8]: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” [Note: “Lord, I am not”: Regino, Burchard, Ivo, and Basel, Lyon II and III editions. “O Lord, I am not”: the remaining editions.] Both honoured the Saviour in a different and seemingly contrary way, [Note: “Although not in the same way”: Regino, Burchard, and Ivo.] both were wretched through sins, and both obtained mercy. [Note: Basel edition adds “they are.”] This is the point of the fact that manna tasted in each person’s mouth according to that person’s own desire. [Note: “This is the point”: the complete passage should be read in the original.]

### C. XIV. One who always sins should always receive the medicine of the heavenly sacrament.

Likewise, Ambrose, book IV, *On the Sacraments*, final chapter.  
[Note: It is not Ambrose’s.—Burchard, book 5, chapter 18; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 28; Polycarp, book 3, title 16; Peter Lombard, same place.]

As often as Christ’s blood is shed, it is shed for the remission of sins; therefore I ought always to receive it, so that my sins may always be forgiven. [Note: “It”: absent from Burchard and Ivo; the other editions read “rightly.”] I who always sin ought always to have the medicine. [Note: “To experience”: Ivo and the other editions.]

### C. XV. Let no one abstain from the Lord’s body except one who deserves excommunication.

Likewise, Bishop Hilary.  
[Note: The other collectors and Alger, *On the Truth of the Lord’s Body and Blood*, book 1, chapter 22, likewise cite this from Hilary. In Augustine, Letter 118, there occurs: “If the sins are not so great that a person should be judged worthy of excommunication, he ought not separate himself from the medicine of the Lord’s body”; and something not very different is found in Bede on 1 Corinthians 11.]  
[Note: Rather, Augustine, from the letter cited above in chapter 13, section 99.—Burchard, Ivo, and Polycarp, same place.]

If a person’s sins are not so great that he is excommunicated, he ought not separate himself from the medicine of the Lord’s body and blood.

Likewise Pope Fabian says:  
[Note: It is cited in the same manner by those same collectors. Yet, apart from the final words, “namely at Easter,” and so forth, it occurs in the Third Council of Tours, chapter 50, and in the *Capitularies*, book 2, chapter 45.]  
[Note: Rather, from the Third Council of Tours, held A.D. 813, chapter 50.—The words “at Easter,” and so forth, seem to have been taken from the Council of Agde, chapter 18; cf. below, chapter 19.—Regino, book 2, chapter 45; Burchard, book 5, chapter 17; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 151; *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 27; Polycarp and Peter Lombard, same place.]

### C. XVI. Each of the faithful shall communicate three times a year.

Even if not more frequently, lay persons shall communicate at least three times a year, unless perhaps someone is prevented by certain graver crimes: namely, at Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord. [Note: “If”: Regino, Burchard, Ivo, and *Decretum*.]

Likewise Pope Soter says:  
[Note: From chapter 47 of the Second Council of Chalon, held A.D. 813.—Burchard, book 5, chapter 20; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 30; Polycarp, same place.]

### C. XVII. We ought also receive holy communion at the Lord’s Supper.

On the Lord’s Supper, reception of the Eucharist is neglected by some. Since it ought on that day to be received by all the faithful—except those to whom it has been forbidden because of grave crimes—ecclesiastical usage shows this, since even penitents on that day are reconciled for receiving the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood.

[Col. 1739A]

### C. XVIII. One who turns away from sacramental communion because of his own lust is to be cast out of the Church.

Likewise, from the Council of Martin of Braga, chapter 83.  
[Note: Chapter 2 of the Council of Antioch, in Martin of Braga’s translation; the other editions add “Pope.”]

If anyone enters the Church of God and hears the sacred Scriptures, but because of his own lust turns himself away from sacramental communion and, in observing the mysteries, departs from the established rule of discipline, we decree that such a person is to be cast out of the catholic Church until he performs penance and shows the fruit of his penance, so that, having received communion, he may be able to obtain forgiveness. [Note: “Within the church”: Hispanic Collection.] [Note: “Does not listen while chattering”: the Hispanic Collection.] [Note: “This one”: the other editions; the Hispanic Collection.] [Note: “In the ministries”: the other editions, especially Basel.] [Note: “May obtain forgiveness after receiving communion.” In more recent editions of the councils the reading is: “so that, having received communion, they may merit forgiveness.” But the ancient editions and Vatican manuscripts have the reading found in Gratian. The words of chapter 2 of the Council of Antioch—from which this seems to have been taken—are: καὶ παρακαλέσαντες τυχεῖν δυνήθωσι συγγνώμης, that is, “and, having pleaded, may be able to obtain pardon.”]

### C. XIX. Those who cease communicating at these three times are not to be considered catholic.

Likewise, from the Council of Agde, chapter 18.  
[Note: Held A.D. 506.—Regino, book 2, chapter 387; Burchard, book 5, chapter 23; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 33.]

Secular persons who have not communicated at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost are not to be believed catholic or counted among Catholics. [Note: “In the Church of the Lord”: Argentinian edition.] [Note: “And”: the same edition; “and at the Nativity of the Lord.”]

### C. XX. Those who scorn to communicate in church are to be corrected.

At the First Council of Toledo, chapter 13.  
[Note: Held A.D. 400.]

Those who enter the church and are found never to communicate are to be admonished. [Note: “Concerning these”: Hispanic Collection.] [Note: “Church of God”: the other editions, especially Argentinian and Basel.] If they do not communicate, they are to undertake penance. [Note: “But if they do not communicate”: Hispanic Collection.] If they do communicate, they must not always abstain; if they fail to do so, they are to be excluded. [Note: In the original the reading is “let them be excluded,” as also at the end of the chapter in the old copies of Gratian. But here the interpretation of the gloss better suits the verb “let them abstain.”] [Note: “Let him abstain”: the same edition; the other editions compared.]

### C. XXI. Before holy communion each person shall abstain from his own wife.

Likewise, from the Council of Elvira.  
[Note: Something similar occurs in Theodore, Petit’s edition, chapter 11.—Regino, book 1, chapter 331, after a canon cited from the Council of Hibernia, which gave Burchard occasion for error; Burchard, book 5, chapter 22; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 151; *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 32.]

Every man ought, before holy communion, to abstain from his own wife for three, or four, or eight days. [Note: Regino has “seven, or five, or three days”; Burchard, “three, or five, or seven days”; Ivo, “three, or four, or seven days”; Basel edition, “three, four, five, six, or seven days.”] Nor shall he be counted among Catholics if, at these times—namely Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord—he has not communicated. [Note: The words from “nor shall he” to the end are absent from Burchard and Ivo, though not from the *Panormia*; they constitute a summary of the chapter “Secular persons” above in the same distinction.] [Note: “Be numbered”: Argentinian edition.]

[Col. 1740A]

Likewise Pope Sergius says:  
[Note: Nearly the same occurs in Amalarius, *On the Divine Offices*, book 3, chapter 35, and the very bad attribution seems to have been derived from this source, because in the preceding material Amalarius relates certain matters concerning Sergius drawn from the *Liber Pontificalis*.—Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 141.]

### C. XXII. Why three parts are made from Christ’s body.

Part VI. The Lord’s body is threefold. The portion of the offering placed in the cup signifies Christ’s body, which has now risen. [Note: “Of the offering”: formerly it read “the offering”; this and other readings have been corrected from old manuscripts, the ordinary gloss, and the other writers cited.] [Note: “Demonstrates”: Basel edition.] The portion eaten signifies [his body] still walking upon the earth. [Note: “Walking”: Basel and Lyon II and III editions.] The portion remaining on the altar until the end of Mass signifies the body lying in the tomb, because until the end of the age the bodies of the saints will be in tombs. [Note: “Lying”: the word is absent from Burchard and Ivo.]

Likewise Pope Clement says in Letter II: [Note: Cf. Distinction 1, *On Consecration*, chapter 39; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 34; Polycarp, book 3, title 16.]

### C. XXIII. By whom the Lord’s sacraments are to be handled.

Part VII. The sacraments of the divine mysteries are entrusted to three ranks: the presbyter, the deacon, and the minister; with fear and trembling they must preserve the remaining fragments of the Lord’s body. [Note: “Of the Lord”: Ivo, the other editions, and the Bohemian witness.]

Likewise, in the same place:

§ 1. Let as many offerings be made at the altar as ought to suffice for the people. If any remain, they are not to be kept for the next day but consumed, with fear and trembling, by the careful attention of the clergy. [Note: “And diligently”: the other editions.] Those, moreover, who consume what remains of the Lord’s body left in the sacristy must not immediately proceed to receive ordinary food, lest they seem to mingle food with the holy portion, food which, digested through the belly, is discharged into the privy.
