[Note: “To be mingled”: the original; “to mingle”: Regino, Burchard, and Ivo.] [Note: “Through passages”: Regino.] [Note: “Is discharged”: Regino, Burchard, and Ivo; “is diffused”: the other editions.] Therefore, if the Lord’s portion is eaten in the morning, the ministers who consumed it shall fast until the sixth hour; and if they receive it at the third or fourth hour, they shall fast until evening. [Note: “Until evening”: Basel edition; the other editions have “until vespers.”] Thus the sacraments are to be guarded in enduring hallowed secrecy.

And below:

§ 2. We also command that no part of the fragments of Christ’s offerings ever be set upon the table for a foreign cleric of the Church or for a lay person. [Note: “Lest anything be given to a cleric or lay person”: Argentinian edition.] [Note: The original reads “to an excommunicated cleric of the Church or lay person.”] How do you know—you who indiscriminately dispense the breads of the sanctuary to the unworthy—how do you know whether those to whom you dispense them are clean from women? [Note: The words between asterisks are absent from Ivo.] Thus David too, when he was questioned by Abimelech the priest and asked him for bread to eat, ate the bread of the Presence after he had been asked whether he was clean from a woman and had declared himself clean for the preceding three days. [Note: “Breads”: Ivo and the other editions.] [Note: “For himself”: absent from those editions.]

### C. XXIV. Wicked persons who do not cease communicating are defiled, not cleansed.

Likewise, Isidore, book I, *On the Highest Good*, chapter 24.  
[Note: Cf. below, Distinction 4, chapter 115.]

Part VIII. Those who live wickedly in the Church and do not cease communicating, believing that they are cleansed by such communion, should learn that it profits them nothing for cleansing, as the Prophet says [Note: Jeremiah 11:15]: “What is it that my beloved has done in my house—many wicked deeds? Will holy flesh take away your evils from you?” And the Apostle says [Note: 1 Corinthians 11:28]: “Let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup.” [Note: “For correction”: Basel edition.]

Likewise, from the Eighth Synod, Bishop Basil said:  
[Note: This chapter of Basil is from Rufinus’s translation, chapter 70, though with some omissions. From this citation now given by Gratian and from other places in him, as has been stated elsewhere, it seems possible to infer that those rules of blessed Basil had been placed after the Eighth Synod in the codex used by Gratian—in the collection often cited, following Theiner, under the name *Collection of Three Parts*.]  
[Note: Rather, Basil; cf. the *Corrections*.—*Collectio trium partium*, part 2, title 14, chapter 8.]

### C. XXV. Those who unworthily communicate in Christ’s sacraments acquire condemnation, not salvation.

The Apostle teaches us fear, saying [Note: 1 Corinthians 11:27]: “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself.” [Note: “Indeed”: Basel edition.] But the Lord’s word teaches us faith, saying [Note: Luke 22:19]: “This is my body, which shall be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” [Note: “Given for many”: the other editions.] [Note: “Lord”: Basel, Lyon II and III editions.]

And below:

§ 1. The Apostle also says of the only-begotten Son of God [Note: Philippians 2:8]: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross.” Therefore, when the soul has faith in these words, considers the magnificence of his glory, and marvels at the excess of humility—how one so great and such as he was obedient to the Father unto death for our life [Note: Basel edition adds “even death on a cross”]—I think that it can be moved to affection [Note: The other editions have “unto”] and love for him and for God the Father, who [Note: Romans 8:32] “did not spare his only Son but delivered him up for us all.”

And below:

§ 2. A person who receives the Lord’s bread and cup ought to prepare in his mind such affection and faith. [Note: “Or”: Basel edition.]

### C. XXVI. The question is not by whom, but before whom, an offering is made.

Likewise, Augustine, *Questions on Numbers*, question XXX.

“And the Lord said to Moses and to Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest [Note: Numbers 16:37 and following]: ‘Take the bronze censers from the midst of the burnt men, and scatter this alien fire there, because these sinners sanctified the censers in their souls; and make them hammered plates, a covering for the altar, because they were offered before the Lord and were sanctified, and became a sign to the children of Israel.’” [Note: “Bronze”: Lyon editions; “golden”: the other principal editions.] [Note: “Scatter”: the original has “scatter it.”] [Note: “Make”: Basel edition has “you shall make”; the other editions have “you will make.”] [Note: “A covering”: the other editions compared.] [Note: “Altar”: the Argentinian, Norwegian, and Venetian editions have “altars.”] [Note: “You shall make”: the other editions.] [Note: “A covering”: Argentinian edition; “coverings”: the other principal editions.] [Note: Augustine reads “in their hands”; but in the Septuagint, which he usually follows, it is ἐν ταῖς ψυχαῖς αὐτῶν, *en tais psychais autōn*, “in their souls.”]

But it should be observed that their punishment is, in a new manner of speaking, called sanctified—the punishment of those by whom this sin had been committed—because through them an example was given to the rest, that they might fear. Why he wished a covering for the altar to be made from them, he added, saying: “because they were offered before the Lord and were sanctified and became a sign to the children of Israel.” [Note: This clause is absent from the other editions.] Therefore he did not wish what had been offered by such persons to be rejected in them; rather, he wished this to be considered and attended to: before whom they had been offered, that is, before the Lord—so that in them the name of the Lord, before whom they were offered, might have more force [Note: “May have”: Basel edition] than the utterly evil merit of those by whom they were offered.

### C. XXVII. The penance of one through whose negligence something of Christ’s blood drips.

Likewise, from the Decree of Pope Pius.  
[Note: Rather, from Theodore’s *Penitential*, Petit’s edition, chapter 51.—Burchard, book 5, chapter 47; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 159; *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 56; Polycarp, book 3, title 16.]

Part IX. If, through negligence, anything of the Lord’s blood drips upon the ground, it shall be licked up with the tongue and the board scraped. [Note: “From the cup”: the original; Burchard and Ivo.] [Note: “Of the Lord”: absent from the original.] [Note: “The tongue shall be licked”: absent from Theodore; Burchard has “it shall be licked with the tongue.”] If there is no board, the place shall be scraped so that it is not trodden underfoot, and it shall be consumed by fire; the ashes shall be placed within the altar, and the priest shall do penance for forty days. [Note: “Shall be scraped”: Paris edition; “shall nevertheless be scraped”: the other principal editions.] [Note: “Shall be placed”: Ivo’s *Decretum* and the other editions.]

If the cup drips upon the altar, the minister shall swallow the drop and do penance for three days. If it drips upon the altar-cloth and the drop reaches another [cloth], he shall do penance for four days. If it reaches as far as the third, he shall do penance for nine days. [Note: Argentinian edition has “three.”] [Note: This sentence is absent from the original, Burchard, and Basel edition.] If as far as the fourth, he shall do penance for twenty days. [Note: This sentence is absent from the original and Burchard; it is omitted in Ivo’s *Panormia*.] The cloths touched by the drop shall be washed three times by the minister, with a cup placed beneath; the water from the washing shall be consumed and placed near the altar. [Note: “Had touched”: Basel edition.] [Note: “Have touched the drop”: Argentinian edition; the original and Burchard have “touched the drop.”]

### C. XXVIII. What penance is to be imposed on one who vomits the sacrament.

Likewise, from the *Penitential* of Bede the Presbyter, chapter “On Drunkenness.”  
[Note: In Bede and the collectors there is some variation, especially in the number of days; Bede’s account is altogether more distinct.]  
[Note: Regino, book 1, chapter 149; Burchard, book 5, chapter 43; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 153; *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 55.]

If someone vomits the Eucharist through drunkenness or gluttony, if he is a layman he shall do penance for forty days; clerics, monks, or deacons, and priests, shall do penance for seventy days; bishops, for ninety. [Note: The original, Regino, Burchard, and Ivo distinguish the penalties: “Deacons shall do penance for forty days; priests, for seventy days.”] If they vomit because of illness, they shall do penance for seven days. [Note: Regino and Burchard have the singular “if he vomits … let him do penance.”]

[Col. 1743B]

### C. XXIX. Priests shall administer the divine sacraments only in person.

Likewise, from the Council of Reims, chapter 2.  
[Note: Nearly the same provisions occur in the Council of Rouen, held A.D. 650.—Regino, book 1, chapter 120; Burchard, book 5, chapter 30; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 154; *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 39.]

Part X. It has come to our attention that certain presbyters so disparage the divine mysteries that they give the sacred body of the Lord to a lay person or a woman to carry to the sick; and those who are forbidden to enter the sacristy or approach the altar are entrusted with the holy of holies. [Note: “They entrust”: Basel edition.] The judgment of all devout persons recognizes how horrible and detestable this is. Therefore the synod utterly forbids such rash presumption to occur hereafter; rather, the presbyter himself in every case shall communicate the sick person. [Note: “In every manner”: Regino; “in every way”: Ivo’s *Panormia* and the other editions.] [Col. 1743C] If he acts otherwise, he shall be subject to peril of his rank.

[Col. 1744A]

### C. XXX. When Mass is celebrated, a layperson shall not presume to enter the presbytery.

Likewise, Pope Clement.  
[Note: This chapter appears in the synod of Eugenius II—from which Anselm also cites it—as well as in the synod of Leo IV, chapter 33, and in book 7 of the *Capitularies*, chapter 278.]  
[Note: From the Roman Synod of Eugenius II, held A.D. 826.—Anselm, book 5, chapter 78.]

Part XI. It is fitting that the ranks of priests and other clerics serving churches be visibly distinguished from the place of lay persons. [Note: The phrase “from the place of lay persons” is absent from the original, Anselm, and Basel edition.] [Note: “Are fitting”: Argentinian, Norwegian, Venetian I and II editions.] Therefore no lay person may stand, while Mass is being celebrated, in that place where priests and the other clerics stand—which is called the presbytery—so that they may freely and honourably perform the sacred offices. [Note: “Celebrate”: Argentinian edition; “be celebrated”: Basel edition.]

### C. XXXI. As in the metropolitan church, so everywhere the solemnities of the Mass are to be celebrated. Likewise from the Council of Gerona, ch. 1.  
[Note: [Col. 1743] held A.D. 517. Burchard, bk. 3, ch. 36. Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 3, ch. 68.]

**Part XII.** The ordering [Note: [Col. 1743] “Concerning the ordering of Masses, as to how”: *Collectio Hispana*.] of Masses, as it is performed [Note: [Col. 1743] “are performed”: same source; Burchard; Ivo.] in the metropolitan church, is in God’s name to be observed likewise in all [Col. 1744B] provinces [Note: [Col. 1743C] “In all provinces”: the council itself reads, “in the province of Tarragona” [Col. 1743: “in the whole Tarraconensian province”: *Collectio Hispana*]; but Burchard and Ivo read, “in all the fellow-provincial churches.”], both the order of the Mass itself and the custom of chanting and ministering.

### C. XXXII. What sacrifice is, and what sacrament is. Likewise Augustine, *City of God*, bk. 10, ch. 5.  
[Note: [Col. 1743] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, ch. 130; *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 8.]

**Part XIII.** A visible sacrifice [Note: [Col. 1743C] “Sacrifice”: in the original, and in Lanfranc and Ivo, the text is: “A visible sacrifice, therefore, is the sacrament of an invisible sacrifice, that is, a sacred sign”; but it has not been changed because of the gloss.] is a sacrament, that is, a sacred sign. Likewise elsewhere: §1. A sacrament [Note: [Col. 1743C] “Sacrament”: in *On Instructing Beginners*, ch. 26, these words occur: “Concerning the sacrament which he has received, when it has been suitably commended to him, [he is to understand] that visible things are signs of divine realities, but that the invisible realities themselves are honoured in them.” In Epistle 166: “But if he is wicked, God works through him the visible form of the sacrament; but God himself bestows invisible grace.” From these passages the familiar definition of a sacrament seems to have been derived.] is the visible form of invisible grace.

### C. XXXIII. What a sign is. The same author, *On Christian Doctrine*, bk. 2, ch. 1.  
[Note: [Col. 1743] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 131; *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 8.]

A sign is a thing which, beyond the appearance it presents to the senses, causes something else to come into knowledge *through itself* [Note: [Col. 1743] The words “through itself” are absent from Böhm and seem altogether superfluous.] [Note: [Col. 1743] “thought”: original.].

[Col. 1744C] Likewise Pope Gregory says in his Easter homily [Note: [Col. 1744C] Ivo cites this from Lanfranc, in whom the material immediately following the words of Gregory taken from the Easter homily is found continuously. So too many other following passages, which Gratian cites from other authors, occur in the same Lanfranc and in Alger [Col. 1743: i.e. in the book *On the Truth of the Lord’s Body and Blood*; yet Gratian seems to have used neither Lanfranc nor Alger themselves], sometimes more fully than in Ivo and Gratian.] [Note: [Col. 1743] Rather, Lanfranc, *Against Berengar*.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 132; *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 9.]:

### C. XXXIV. After consecration, not the substance but the appearance remains.

“Appearance” and “likeness” are terms for those things which existed before, namely bread and wine. Hence at the end of a certain Mass this prayer is said: “May thy sacraments accomplish in us, we beseech thee, O Lord, what they contain, so that what [Note: [Col. 1745] “which”: original; Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions.] we now bear under appearance we may receive in the reality of things.” For the priest asks that Christ’s body, which is now borne under the appearance of bread and wine, may at some time be received in manifest vision as it truly is. Of this vision the Lord says in the Gospel according to John [Note: [Col. 1745] Absent from Ivo, *Panormia*, and the Basel edition.—The original reads, “he says to the disciples”; cf. John 14:21.]: “He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him.” Although some explain, not implausibly, [Note: [Col. 1745] “explain”: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions except Lyons II and III.] in this passage the truth of flesh and blood as their efficacy itself, that is, the remission of sins.

[Col. 1745B]

### C. XXXV. Visible creatures are invisibly converted into Christ’s body and blood. Likewise Eusebius of Emesa.  
[Note: [Col. 1745] It is not by Eusebius; some attribute it to Eucherius of Lyons, others to Hilary or Caesarius of Arles, and still others to Rabanus or Bede. Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 4; Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 8.]

**Part XIV.** Because he was about to remove the body which he had assumed from *our* eyes [Note: [Col. 1745] Absent from Ivo.—The Basel edition adds, “of men.”] and carry it into the stars, it was necessary that, on the day of the Supper, he should consecrate for us the sacrament of his body and blood, *his own* [Note: [Col. 1745] Absent from Ivo.], so that what was offered once as the price might continually be worshipped through mystery; so that, because the daily and unwearied redemption for the salvation of humankind [Note: [Col. 1745] “of all”: collected editions.] was proceeding, there might also be a perpetual offering of redemption, and that victim might live everlastingly in memory and be always present in grace: the truly [Note: [Col. 1745] “true”: Paris and Lyons editions.] unique and perfect offering, to be appraised by faith, not by appearance nor judged by outward sight, but by inward devotion. Hence, *rightly* [Note: [Col. 1745] Absent from Ivo.] heavenly authority confirms: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” [Note: [Col. 1745] John 6:56.].

§1. Therefore let every uncertainty of unbelief depart, since [Note: [Col. 1745] “because what”: collected editions.] he who is the author of the gift is himself also [Note: [Col. 1745] Absent from the Basel edition.] the witness of its truth. For the invisible [Note: [Col. 1745] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 129; Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 19.] priest converts visible creatures, by his word and secret power, into the substance of his body and blood, saying: “Take and eat: this is *indeed* [Note: [Col. 1745] Absent from Ivo and the Vulgate.] my body”; and, after repeating the sanctification, [Note: [Col. 1745] The Basel edition adds “he says”; the other editions add after “drink,” “he says.”] “Take and drink: this is my blood.” Therefore, just as at the command of the Lord who gave the order, the heights of heaven, the depths of the waves, and the vastnesses of earth suddenly came into being from nothing, so by equal power in the spiritual sacraments, where [Note: [Col. 1745] “as”: Basel edition.] power gives the command, [Note: [Col. 1745C] “Where power gives the command”: so in Ivo and the *Panormia*. In Paschasius it reads: “where power commands, the effect serves the thing”; and perhaps “of the word” should be read in place of “where.” In an older edition of the homily: “power is furnished by the words, and the effect serves the thing”; in a more recent edition: “power is furnished by the word, and the effect serves the thing.” Many passages elsewhere have been corrected partly from the original and partly from Ivo.] the effect serves.

§2. Consider, therefore, how great and how worthy of celebration are the benefits wrought by the power of divine blessing, *and attend* [Note: [Col. 1745] Absent from Ivo.]; and, lest it seem to you [Note: [Col. 1745] “and how”: Ivo; Argentinian, Basel, Nuremberg editions; “how”: the remaining editions.] new and impossible that earthly and mortal things are converted into Christ’s substance, question yourself, who have now been reborn in Christ. Formerly, alien from life, estranged from mercy, inwardly dead and exiled from the way of salvation, you were initiated into Christ’s laws and renewed by saving mysteries; you passed into the body of the Church not by sight but by faith, and, from being a child of perdition, by hidden purification you merited to become God’s adopted child. Remaining in visible measure, you were invisibly made greater than yourself without any increase in quantity; though you remained the same person, you became greatly other [Note: [Col. 1745] “otherwise”: Ivo; Argentinian edition.] through the advances of faith. Nothing was added outwardly, and everything was changed inwardly; and thus the human being became Christ’s child, and Christ was formed in the human mind.

Therefore, just as, without bodily perception, you put off your former vileness and suddenly put on a new dignity; and just as that which God healed in you when wounded, cleansed when infected, and wiped clean when stained [Note: [Col. 1745] “stained”: original; Ivo.], was not entrusted to your eyes or [Note: [Col. 1745] “but”: same source; collected editions.] senses, so also [Note: [Col. 1745] “and when”: Ivo; “and when”: collected editions.], when you ascend to the venerable [Note: [Col. 1745] “to the venerable”: Basel, Lyons II and III editions.] altar to be satisfied with heavenly food, look upon, honour, and marvel at the sacred body and blood of your God with faith; touch it with the mind, receive it with the hand of the heart, and above all take it in by the inward draught [Note: [Col. 1745] “wholly by the draught of the inward man”: collected editions; Ivo.].

[Col. 1746C]

### C. XXXVI. Why Christ ministered his sacrament to us under the appearance of bread and wine. Likewise Augustine.  
[Note: [Col. 1746C] Bede, on 1 Corinthians 10, cites this from the sermon *On the Sacraments of the Faithful, Monday of Easter*, and Ivo does so with little variation.]  
[Note: [Col. 1745] It is not found in Augustine, and perhaps was compiled by Bede himself, on 1 Corinthians 10, from Augustine’s Tractates 26 and 27 on John.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 1, from the sermon *On the Sacraments*; cf. below, this same distinction, ch. 62.]

Because the Lord suffered for us, he commended to us in this sacrament his body and blood, and he also made us ourselves [his body]. [Note: [Col. 1745] “ourselves”: Ivo; collected editions.] For we too have been made his body, and by his mercy we are what we receive [Note: [Col. 1745] “received”: same source; same editions except Lyons II.]. Remember: you also once were not, and you were created; you were carried to the Lord’s threshing floor; by the labours of oxen—that is, of those proclaiming the Gospel—you were threshed. While you were being held back as catechumens [Note: [Col. 1747] “being brought”: same editions; Ivo.], you were kept in the granary; you gave your names; you began to be ground by fasts *and* exorcisms; afterwards you came to the water, were sprinkled, and were made the Lord’s bread. Behold what you have received. As you see that what has been made is one, so be one yourselves: love one another [Note: [Col. 1747] “loving”: same editions; same source.], hold one faith, one hope, indivisible charity.

When heretics receive this [Note: [Col. 1747] The Basel and Lyons II–III editions add “sacrament.”], they receive testimony against themselves, because they seek division, whereas this bread signifies unity. So too wine was in many clusters, but now it is one; it is one [Note: [Col. 1747C] “It is one”: this has been corrected from Bede, as have many other things. A trace of this reading was in the manuscripts and in Ivo. The printed editions read: “wine in its natural state, then the cup,” etc. [Col. 1747: “one in its natural state”: Ivo; Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I–II editions; “wine is in its natural state, the cup is,” etc.: Basel edition.]] in the sweetness of the cup after the pressing of the winepress. [Col. 1747B] And you, after those fasts, labours, humility, and contrition *of heart* [Note: [Col. 1747] Absent from Ivo.], have now been brought in Christ’s name, as it were, to the Lord’s cup [Note: [Col. 1747] Absent from the same source and from the Basel edition.—The remaining editions read “Christ’s.”]; and there you are on the table, and *there you are* [Note: [Col. 1747] “there you are” is absent from Ivo.] in the cup; you are with us. For we take this together and drink together, because we live together.

Likewise in the sermon *On Infants*: §1. Thus the Lord [Note: [Col. 1747] The same source and collected editions add “our.”] Jesus Christ has signified us and wished us to belong to him; he consecrated the mystery of our peace and unity on *his* table. Whoever [Note: [Col. 1747] Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 8.] receives [Note: [Col. 1747] “approaches”: Basel edition.] the mystery of unity and does not maintain the bond of peace does not receive the mystery for his benefit, but a testimony against himself. No one is [Note: [Col. 1747C] “No one is”: this material to the end is found below, dist. 4, “No one,” and is cited in Polycarpus from Innocent.] [Note: [Col. 1747] Cf. Dist. 4, *De consecratione*, ch. 131; Polycarpus, bk. 3, tit. 10; Peter Lombard, same place.] in any respect to doubt that each believer becomes a participant in the Lord’s body and blood when, in baptism, he is made a member of Christ; nor is he excluded from fellowship in that bread and cup, even if, before he eats that bread and drinks that cup, he departs from this world while established in the unity of Christ’s body [Note: [Col. 1747] “has departed”: collected editions; Ivo.]. For he is not deprived [Note: [Col. 1747] “will be deprived”: collected editions.] of participation in and benefit from that sacrament when he finds in himself that which the sacrament signifies [Note: [Col. 1747] “will have found”: Basel edition; “is found”: remaining editions; Ivo.].

### C. XXXVII. While the offering is broken, Christ’s passion is recalled to mind. Likewise in Prosper’s book of sentences.  
[Note: [Col. 1747C] In Lanfranc, in whom nearly all that Gratian cites from Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*, or from Augustine in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*, is found, these words precede: “For sacraments always bear a likeness to those realities of which they are sacraments; as in the sacrament about which this question is being discussed, when the offering is broken,” etc.]  
[Note: [Col. 1747] Rather, Lanfranc, *Against Berengar*.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 140; *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 9.]

When [Note: [Col. 1747] “While”: original; Ivo, *Decretum*; Basel edition.] the offering is broken, and when blood from the cup is poured into the mouths of the faithful, what else is signified except the immolation of the Lord’s body on the cross and the pouring out of his blood from his side?

[Col. 1748B] Likewise Bishop Leo and the holy synod which met in the city of Rome write thus to the clergy, dignitaries, and people established at Constantinople [Note: [Col. 1747] Through the word “we pass on,” this is taken from Epistle 59 of Leo the Great, written A.D. 459 (Ballerini ed.); Anselm, bk. 9, ch. 6. The remainder is Ambrose’s, beginning at “concerning,” from his commentary on Luke 17 (bk. 8, ch. 7) and Luke 22 (bk. 10, ch. 9); Anselm, bk. 6, ch. 7.]:

### C. XXXVIII. It is not permissible to doubt the truth of Christ’s body and blood.

**Part XV.** In what darkness of ignorance, in what torpor of negligence, have these people lain until now, that they have neither learned by hearing nor known by reading what is so unanimously confessed in every mouth in the Church of God that the truth of Christ’s body and blood is not silent even on the tongues of infants amid the common sacraments [Note: [Col. 1747] The Basel edition omits “in.” The original reads, “is not silent amid the sacraments of communion”; the collected editions, “is taught amid the sacraments of communion.”] *of faith*: namely, that in that mystical distribution of spiritual nourishment this is imparted, this is received, so that, receiving the power of heavenly food, we may pass into the flesh of him who became our flesh?

The same is [Note: [Col. 1747] Absent from the Argentinian edition.] food [Note: [Col. 1748C] “The same is food”: in several old manuscripts, “The same Pope Leo. It is food,” etc.; Anselm likewise cites Leo. Yet these words have not been found in Leo the Blessed, but in Ambrose the Blessed, and the following material also is his, collected from various places.] of refreshment; it is [Note: [Col. 1747] “and”: collected editions except the Argentinian and Basel editions; Böhm.] food of blood. For as the Lord’s flesh [Note: [Col. 1747] “Christ’s”: Basel edition.] is truly food, so his blood [Note: [Col. 1747] “and blood”: Lyons I; the Basel and Lyons II–III editions add “his.”] is truly *our* drink.

The same: §1. There is *also* a body of which it is said [Note: [Col. 1747] “whence”: Paris and Lyons I editions.] [Note: [Col. 1747] John 6:56.], “My flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink.” Around this body are the eagles which circle with spiritual wings.

The same: §2. Therefore [Note: [Col. 1747] “Therefore, and the same”: collected editions.] we eat Christ’s body, so that we may be able to participate in eternal life.

The same: §3. Why do we employ arguments concerning this? [Note: [Col. 1748C] Gratian below, ch. “Indeed,” reports this from Ambrose thus: “But why do we employ arguments? Let us use his own examples, of the incarnation,” etc.; Alger does likewise. Ivo gives the remainder in the same way, differing only in reading “by the novelty of the incarnation.” Gratian’s reading has been retained, both because of the gloss and because Lanfranc largely agrees with Gratian where he confirms the Catholic truth he has expounded with the words of Ambrose the Blessed.] [Col. 1749A] [Note: [Col. 1749] Cf. below, ch. 69.] Let us use his own examples, and establish the truth of the mystery by the example of the incarnation [Note: [Col. 1749] “also by the incarnation”: collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 1749] “destroy”: Lyons II–III editions; “we are established”: Venice I–II editions.]. And below: §4. Why [Note: [Col. 1749] Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 10.] do you seek here [Note: [Col. 1749] “therefore”: Basel edition.] the order of nature in Christ’s body, when the *Lord Jesus* Christ himself was born from a Virgin beyond nature?

### C. XXXIX. Christ’s body and blood are made for us not by nature but by consecration. Likewise Ambrose, *On Instructing Beginners*.  
[Note: [Col. 1749C] Ivo cites Augustine, *On Instructing Beginners*. Bede on 1 Corinthians 10 and Alger cite Augustine, *Against Faustus*, where it occurs in bk. 20, ch. 13. Yet Alger [Col. 1749: *On the Truth of the Lord’s Body and Blood*, bk. 1, ch. 6] and Ivo reduce it to a summary, while in Gratian it is elsewhere additionally corrupted, which corruptions have not been corrected because of the gloss. Augustine’s words are: “But our bread and cup are not just any bread and cup, as though Christ were bound in ears of grain and vine-shoots, as those foolish persons suppose; but they are made mystical for us by a definite consecration, not by being born. Accordingly, what is not so made, although it is bread and cup, is food for refreshment, not a sacrament of religion—except that we bless it and give thanks to the Lord for every gift of his, not only spiritual but also bodily.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1749] Rather, Augustine; cf. the correction.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 123; *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 1.]

Bread and cup are made mystical for us not by any arbitrary means but by a definite consecration; they are not born. Accordingly, what is so made for us, although it is bread and cup, is food [Note: [Col. 1749] Absent from the Argentinian edition.] of resurrection, not a sacrament of religion; not [Note: [Col. 1749] “except”: Ivo.] that which we bless and for which we give thanks to the Lord in every gift of his, not only spiritual but also bodily.

[Col. 1749B]

### C. XL. What is bread and wine before the blessing is Christ’s body and blood after the blessing. The same Ambrose, *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*, ch. 9.  
[Note: [Col. 1749] Cf. below, ch. 69; Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 124; *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 7; Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 10.]

Before the blessing *of the heavenly words* [Note: [Col. 1749] “of heavenly words” is absent from Ivo.] another appearance is named; after the blessing Christ’s body is signified [Note: [Col. 1749] The Basel and Lyons editions add “Christ’s”; “is marked”: Argentinian edition.]. Likewise in the same place: §1. Christ is in that sacrament. Likewise, bk. 4, *On the Sacraments*, ch. 5: §2. Whoever eats this body will receive forgiveness of sins.

### C. XLI. Under the appearance of bread and wine we honour Christ’s invisible flesh and blood. Likewise Augustine, in Prosper’s book of sentences.  
[Note: [Col. 1749] Rather, Lanfranc, *Against Berengar*.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 125; *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 9; Peter Lombard, same place.]

But under the appearance of bread and wine which we see, we honour invisible realities, namely the flesh and blood *of Christ*; nor do we comprehend [Note: [Col. 1749] “weigh”: Ivo; original.] [Col. 1749C] these two appearances, *from which the Lord’s body is consecrated* [Note: [Col. 1749] The words “from which … body” are absent from Ivo.], in the same way as we comprehended them before consecration [Note: [Col. 1749] “weighed”: Ivo; original.], since we faithfully confess that before [Col. 1750A] consecration they are bread and wine [Note: [Col. 1750C] And wine: in Lanfranc, while he interprets words from Augustine’s *On Instructing Beginners* which an adversary had objected against him, the passage reads thus: “to be bread and wine, that is, those things which nature formed; but during consecration to be converted into Christ’s flesh and blood, both of which realities blessing consecrated.” Ivo, however, has nearly the same text as Gratian.], formed by nature; but after consecration, Christ’s flesh and blood [Note: [Col. 1749] “truly”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1749] Ivo and the Basel and Lyons II–III editions add “to be.”], consecrated by blessing.

### C. XLII. Berengar’s confession.  
[Note: [Col. 1750C] In the register of Gregory VII, bks. 3 and 6, another abjuration by the same Berengar is found at the synod of A.D. 1079. What occasioned that repetition is explained in the scholia on the councils printed at Cologne in four volumes.]  
[Note: [Col. 1749] From the Roman council held A.D. 1059.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 126; *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 10; Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 12.]

**Part XVI.** I, Berengar [Note: [Col. 1749] “Berlengar”: Venice I–II editions.], unworthy deacon of the church of St Maurice at Angers [Note: [Col. 1749] The collected editions add “church.”], acknowledging the true Catholic and apostolic faith, anathematize every heresy, especially that on account of which I have hitherto been defamed, which attempts to maintain that the bread and wine placed upon the altar after consecration are merely a sacrament and not the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that they cannot be sensibly handled by priests’ hands, broken, or ground by the teeth of the faithful, except in the sacrament [Note: [Col. 1749] “not”: Ivo, *Panormia*; Venice I–II and Nuremberg editions.].

But I agree with the holy [Col. 1750B] Roman [Note: [Col. 1749] The collected editions add “church.”] and apostolic see, and profess with mouth and heart [Note: [Col. 1749] “confess”: Argentinian, Basel, Lyons II–III editions.] that I hold concerning the sacraments [Note: [Col. 1749] “sacrament”: Basel edition.] of the Lord’s table the same faith which the lord and venerable Pope Nicholas and this holy synod, by evangelical and apostolic authority, have handed down as to be held and have confirmed to me [Note: [Col. 1749] “have strengthened”: Ivo, *Panormia*; Argentinian and Basel editions.]: namely, that the bread and wine placed upon the altar after consecration are not merely a sacrament but also the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and are sensibly handled by priests’ hands, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful not only sacramentally [Note: [Col. 1749] “in the sacrament”: Ivo, *Panormia*; “sacrament”: collected editions.] but in truth. I swear this by the holy and *homoousion* Trinity—“of the same substance”—and by these most sacred Gospels of Christ.

I declare that those *indeed* [Note: [Col. 1749] Absent from Ivo, *Panormia*.] who oppose this faith, together with their doctrines and followers [Note: [Col. 1749] “fellow-followers”: Basel edition; “consecrations”: Argentinian edition; “consecrators”: remaining editions except Lyons II–III.], are worthy of eternal anathema. But if I myself should ever presume to think or preach anything against these things [Note: [Col. 1749] “this”: Ivo, *Decretum*; collected editions.], may I be subject to the severity of the canons. Having read and reread it, I freely subscribed.  

§1. Pope Nicholas sent this confession of faith [Note: [Col. 1751] From the codex of Lanfranc.] [Note: [Col. 1751] “his faith”: Ivo; collected editions.] concerning the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, made by Berengar at Rome before 113 bishops, through the cities of Italy, Germany, and Gaul, and to all places to which the report of his depravity had earlier been able to reach, so that the churches which had formerly grieved over one hostile and perverse [Note: [Col. 1751C] “Perverse”: Ivo likewise. Lanfranc has “hostile” [Col. 1751: “hostile and perverse”: Ivo, *Decretum*; “hostile and diverse”: Basel edition.], might afterwards rejoice over one returned and converted [Note: [Col. 1751] “may rejoice”: collected editions.].

### C. XLIII. Why the appearances of the elements are retained although it is truly Christ’s body and blood. Likewise Ambrose, *On Duties*.  
[Note: [Col. 1751] Rather, from the books *On the Sacraments* (bk. 6, ch. 2), falsely attributed to Ambrose.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 127; *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 7.]

Perhaps you say: “How is it true flesh? How is it true blood? I see the likeness of flesh; I do not see the truth of blood” [Note: [Col. 1751C] “I do not see”: it is nearly the same in Ivo. In the original, however, and with little difference in Lanfranc, this passage reads: “Perhaps you say: How is it true? I see the likeness; I do not see the truth of flesh; I do not see the truth of blood.”]. First of all, I told you concerning Christ’s word, which works so as to be able to alter [Col. 1751B] and transform the kinds and ordinances of nature. Then, when his disciples could not bear Christ’s saying, but withdrew on hearing that he would give them his flesh to eat [Note: [Col. 1751] “for eating, for drinking”: Ivo; collected editions.] and his blood to drink, Peter alone said [Note: [Col. 1751] “then”: Ivo, *Decretum*; “only”: *Panormia*; “nevertheless”: collected editions.]: “You have the words of eternal life; and where should I go from you?” [Note: [Col. 1751] John 6:69.] Therefore, lest more should say this, and lest there should be, as it were, a certain horror at bloodshed, while the grace of the Redeemer remained [Note: [Col. 1751] “of redemption”: Lanfranc; Ivo; Argentinian, Basel, and Nuremberg editions.], you receive the sacrament indeed under a likeness, but attain the grace and power of the true nature. “I am,” he says, “the living bread that came down from heaven” [Note: [Col. 1751] John 6:41.].

### C. XLIV. We must receive Christ’s body and blood not carnally but spiritually. Likewise Augustine, in his exposition of Psalm 54.  
[Note: [Col. 1751] Compiled from various Augustinian passages: the exposition of Psalms 54 and 98, and Tractates 28, 27, and 30 on John.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 133; *Decretum*, bk. 2, ch. 8; Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 10.]

“Indeed, the first heresy,” he says, [Note: [Col. 1751] Absent from Ivo and the Argentinian and Basel editions.] “arose among Christ’s disciples, as it were, from the harshness of his saying. For when he said, ‘Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he shall not have eternal life’ [Note: [Col. 1751] John 6:54.], they, not understanding, said to one another: ‘This saying is hard; who can hear it?’” [Note: [Col. 1751] The collected editions add “but”; cf. John 6:61. “eat”: same editions.] [Col. 1752A] Saying that this saying was hard, they separated themselves from him; he remained [Note: [Col. 1751] “and remained”: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions.] with the twelve [Note: [Col. 1751] “two”: Venice I–II editions; the collected editions add “disciples.”]. When they had departed, he instructed those who remained: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life.”

Have you understood spiritually? They are spirit and life. Have you understood carnally? Even [Note: [Col. 1751] “even if”: Böhm.] thus they are spirit and life, but they are not spirit and life to you who do not understand spiritually. Understand spiritually what I have said. You will not eat this body which you see, nor drink that blood which those who crucify me are going to pour out [Note: [Col. 1751] “will pour out”: Ivo, *Panormia*; collected editions.]. I have commended a certain sacrament to you; understood spiritually, it will give you life; but the flesh profits nothing.

But how did they understand it? They understood flesh as it is sold in a corpse [Note: [Col. 1751D] “Sold in a corpse”: Alger likewise [Col. 1751: *On the Truth of the Lord’s Body and Blood*, bk. 1, ch. 11] and Ivo, in whom this entire chapter occurs in the same form as in Gratian: assembled from here and there, with words sometimes transposed, condensed, and altered. But Augustine the Blessed and Lanfranc have here: “as it is torn apart in a corpse, or sold in a butcher’s shop, not as it is enlivened by the Spirit.”], or torn apart in a butcher’s shop. But Jesus, knowing this, said [Note: [Col. 1751] John 6:62.]: “Does this offend you because I said, ‘I give you my flesh to eat and my blood to drink’? If therefore you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?” What is this? Here [Note: [Col. 1751] “here”: collected editions except the Argentinian and Basel editions.] he resolves what had troubled them; here [Note: [Col. 1751] “here”: same editions except the Argentinian, Basel, and Nuremberg editions.] he opens up the matter over which they had been offended; here [Note: [Col. 1751] “here”: same editions except the Argentinian and Basel editions; absent from Ivo, *Panormia*.] plainly, if they understood. For they thought [Note: [Col. 1751] “but”: Ivo; collected editions.] that he was going to distribute his body [Note: [Col. 1751] Absent from the same source and editions except the Argentinian and Basel editions.]. But he said that he would ascend into heaven, certainly whole. “When you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before,” surely then you will see that he does not distribute his body in the manner you suppose, or then you will understand that his grace is not consumed by bites [Note: [Col. 1751] “is sick”: Argentinian edition.].

Likewise, in Tractate 30 on John: §1. Until the age [Col. 1752C] comes to an end, the Lord is above; yet the Lord, who is Truth, is also here with us. For the body *of the Lord* [Note: [Col. 1751] Absent from Ivo.], in which he rose again, must be in one place; but his truth is spread everywhere.

[Col. 1753A]

### C. XLV. How Christ’s body, which hung upon the cross, is received—and how it is not. Likewise Augustine, in the letter to Irenaeus.  
[Note: [Col. 1753C] Alger cites and nearly reproduces this in the same way twice [Col. 1753: bk. 1, chs. 9 and 11], namely as from Augustine to Irenaeus. Ivo, pt. 2, ch. 9, reproduces it in the same way but cites it from the homily on Psalm 98—thus correcting an error from ch. 8—from which Bede also gives the proper words on 1 Corinthians 11. Since Berengar objected to these words against Catholics, Lanfranc explains them more fully than is done in this chapter, especially where he begins to expound the faith of the holy Church. Nearly the same material occurs in the letter of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, to Haymeric, interpreting the same words of Augustine the Blessed on Psalm 95; the letter is printed by Jean Garet and elsewhere.]  
[Note: [Col. 1753] From Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 98.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 9, “from the homily on Psalm 28”; *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 134; Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 10; cf. above, ch. 44.]

“You will not eat this body which you see, nor drink that blood which those who crucify me will pour out [Note: [Col. 1753] “will pour out”: collected editions.]; it is indeed the same, and not the same: the same invisibly, and not the same visibly.” Hence it is added: “*And* [Note: [Col. 1753] Absent from the *Panormia*.] if it must be celebrated visibly, it must nevertheless [Note: [Col. 1753] Absent from the collected editions except the Argentinian and Basel editions.] be understood invisibly” [Note: [Col. 1753] “it”: absent from Ivo and the Basel edition.].

### C. XLVI. What it is to eat Christ’s body and drink his blood. Likewise Augustine, in the sermon on the words of the Gospel.  
[Note: [Col. 1753] Similar passages occur in Tractate 26 on John.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 135; *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 8, “in the sermon on the words of the Gospel; Tractate 26 on John.”]

What is it to eat Christ? It is not only to receive his body in the sacrament [Note: [Col. 1753] “sacraments”: Basel edition.]. For many receive unworthily, of whom the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1753] 1 Corinthians 11:29.]: “He who eats *the bread* [Note: [Col. 1753] Absent from Ivo.] and drinks the Lord’s cup [Note: [Col. 1753] “the blood, or the cup”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1753] Absent from the collected editions except the Basel and Lyons editions.] unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” But how must Christ be eaten? As he himself says [Note: [Col. 1753] “said: For he who”: collected editions; cf. John 8:57.]: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood [Note: [Col. 1753] The Basel and Lyons II editions add “worthily.”] remains in me, and I in him.” *Therefore, if he remains in me and I in him, then he eats and then he drinks; but whoever does not remain in me, nor I in him,* [Note: [Col. 1753C] “Therefore, if…”: this passage has been enlarged from Bede [Col. 1753: on 1 Corinthians 11], the Master, and Ivo.] even if he receives the sacrament [Note: [Col. 1753] The collected editions add “unworthily.”], acquires great torment.

### C. XLVII. To believe in Christ is to eat and drink Christ. Likewise Augustine.  
[Note: [Col. 1754C] It was cited from the book *On the Remedy of Penance*, and in Alger [Col. 1753: bk. 1, ch. 8] from the second book *On Penance*. It seems, however, to have been compiled from two passages of Augustine the Blessed, in Tractates 25 and 26 on John. Ivo cites from that exposition, but joins it with what he had brought from the book *On the Remedy of Penance*.]  
[Note: [Col. 1753] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 137; *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 4; cf. below, ch. 59.]

Why do you prepare [Note: [Col. 1753] added: “he says,” in blessed Augustine’s exposition of the Evangelist: IV,] teeth [Note: [Col. 1753] “tooth”: the editors, compared with O.] and stomach? Believe, and you have eaten. For to believe in him is to eat the living bread [Col. 1753C] [Note: [Col. 1754C] “The living bread”: In the printed editions it read “bread and wine” [ [Col. 1753] thus Ivo, *Panormia*, and the editors compared with O. and the first Basle edition]. The reading has been restored from most old copies, the original, and Ivo, as also below in the same chapter: “To believe.” Some further material has also been added here which is likewise found in Ivo.]. Whoever believes in him eats him [Col. 1754A]; *he is invisibly nourished [Note: [Col. 1753] “invisibly … reborn”: absent from Ivo, *Panormia*.], because he is also invisibly reborn.*

### Chapter XLVIII. The sacrament and the reality of the sacrament constitute the Church’s sacrifice. Likewise Augustine in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*

[Note: [Col. 1754C] The same material is found in Lanfranc (from whom Ivo cites it) and in Algerus [ [Col. 1753] bk. 1, chs. 5 and 11]—who, like Gratian, likewise draws from Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*—though it is not arranged in the same order. Some readings have indeed been corrected from these authorities [Col. 1754D].]

[Note: [Col. 1753] Rather, Lanfranc, *Against Berengar*.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 138 (Augustine in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*). *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 9. Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 10.]

This is what we say; this [Note: [Col. 1753] “that”: Ivo.—The editors, compared with O.] is what we strive by every means to establish: *namely,* that the Church’s sacrifice [Note: [Col. 1753] “namely”: absent from Ivo.] is made up in two ways [Note: [Col. 1753] “in two ways”: added by *Panormia*.—The editors, compared with O.] and consists of two things: the visible appearance of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; of the sacrament [Note: [Col. 1753] “and the sacrament”: the editors, compared with O.] and the reality of the sacrament, that is, the body of Christ. Thus Christ’s person consists and is made up from God [Note: [Col. 1753] “from God”: the same editions.—Ivo, *Panormia*.] and man, since Christ himself is true God and true man; for every thing contains in itself the nature and reality of those things from which it is constituted.

The Church’s sacrifice, then, is constituted by the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, the body of Christ [Note: [Col. 1753] “by two things”: the same editions.—Ivo.]. Therefore there is the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, namely the body of Christ.

Likewise, §1. His flesh is that which we receive in the sacrament veiled under the form of bread; and his blood, that which we drink under the appearance and taste of wine. The flesh is the sacrament of flesh, and the blood the sacrament of blood; by flesh and blood—both invisible, intelligible, and spiritual—is signified [Note: [Col. 1753] “is marked”: the same first Basle edition.] the visible, tangible [Note: [Col. 1753] “and tangible”: the collected editions.] body of our Lord Jesus Christ, full of the grace of every virtue and of divine majesty.

Likewise, §2. Therefore, just as the heavenly bread, which truly is Christ’s flesh, is in its own manner called Christ’s body, although in reality it is the sacrament of Christ’s body—namely, that body which was visible, tangible [Note: [Col. 1753] “which was tangible”: the same editions.], and mortal [Note: [Col. 1753] “is”: added by the Argenteuil, Nuremberg, and Venice editions, parts I and II.] and was hung upon the cross [Note: [Col. 1753] “placed”: Ivo.—The editors, compared with O.]—so too the very offering of the flesh, performed by the hands of the priest [Col. 1755A], is called Christ’s passion, death, and crucifixion—not in the reality of the thing, but by the signifying mystery [Note: [Col. 1755] “of the signified thing”: the Argenteuil and Basle editions]. Thus the sacrament of faith, which is understood as baptism, is faith.

### Chapter XLIX. In how many ways Christ’s flesh is understood. Jerome, in the Epistle to the Ephesians, on chapter 1

[Note: [Col. 1755] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 139. *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 3. Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 8.]

Christ’s flesh and blood are understood in two ways [Note: [Col. 1755] “in many ways”: Ivo, *Panormia*.—The Nuremberg and Venice editions, parts I and II.—“he says”: added by Ivo.—The Basle edition.]: either as that spiritual and divine flesh, concerning which he himself says [Note: [Col. 1755] John, ch. 6, v. 56.], “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink,” and, “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have eternal life” [Note: [Col. 1755] the same chapter, v. 54]; or as my flesh [Note: [Col. 1755] “my”: added by Ivo, *Panormia*.—The collected editions.], which was crucified, and the blood which was poured out by the soldier’s spear.

### Chapter L. On the same subject. Likewise Ambrose, on chapter 11 of First Corinthians

[Note: [Col. 1755C] It was cited from Augustine’s *On the Trinity to the Corinthians* [ [Col. 1755] thus the collected editions]. Algerus [ [Col. 1755] Algerus, same work, bk. 1, ch. 19] likewise cites Augustine’s *On the Trinity*. But several old copies of Gratian have “Ambrose,” which is indeed correct; Ivo likewise cites it, although immediately after citing the book *On the Trinity*.]

[Note: [Col. 1755] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 142. *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 7.]

Because we have been delivered by the Lord’s death, being mindful of this fact, we signify, in eating and drinking, the flesh and blood [Note: [Col. 1755] “of him”: added by the Basle, Lyons II and III editions.] which were offered for us [Note: [Col. 1755] “or sanctify”: added by Ivo, *Panormia*.].

### Chapter LI. How Christ was sacrificed once, and how he is sacrificed daily. Likewise Augustine on Psalm XXI

[Note: [Col. 1755] Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 143. *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 8. Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 12.]

**Part XVII.** Christ died once [Note: [Col. 1755] 1 Peter, ch. 3, v. 18], the righteous for the unrighteous; and we know, hold as certain, and retain with unshaken hope, that Christ, risen from the dead, dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him [Note: [Col. 1755] “and”: absent from Ivo.].

These are the Apostle’s words [Note: [Col. 1755] Romans, ch. 6, v. 9]. Yet, lest you forget [Note: [Col. 1755] “lest we forget”: the original; Ivo, *Decretum*; the Basle and Lyons II and III editions.—“they do not forget”: Ivo, *Panormia*.], what was done once is enacted in our remembrance every year [Note: [Col. 1755] “may be enacted”: the collected editions, compared with the first Basle edition]. Whenever Easter is celebrated, does Christ die as often [Note: [Col. 1755] “is killed”: Ivo and the collected editions]? No [Note: [Col. 1755] “No, but”: the same editions, including the first Argenteuil and Basle editions]; yet the yearly recollection as it were represents what was formerly done, and so moves us [Note: [Col. 1755] “instructs us”: the same editions, including the first Basle edition] as though we saw the Lord hanging [Note: [Col. 1755] “present”: Ivo and the collected editions] on the cross—*not mocking him, however, but believing* [Note: [Col. 1755] “not … believing”: absent from Ivo.].

### Chapter LII. Likewise, in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*

[Note: [Col. 1755C] Ivo also cites this from Lanfranc, both reporting and explaining it as words of blessed Augustine; Algerus does likewise, bk. 1, chs. 16 and 18. The words of blessed Augustine, in the Epistle to Boniface, which Algerus also cites, are these: “Was Christ not sacrificed once in himself? Yet in the sacrament he is sacrificed for the peoples not only at every Easter solemnity but every day.”]

[Note: [Col. 1755] Rather, Lanfranc, *Against Berengar*.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 144. *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 9.]

Christ was sacrificed once in himself, yet is sacrificed daily in the sacrament. This must be understood thus: in the manifestation of his body, in the distinction [Note: [Col. 1755] “indistinctly”: the Basle edition.—“into distinction”: Ivo, *Panormia*.] of all his members [Note: [Col. 1755] “his”: added by Ivo.—The collected editions], as true God and true man, he hung upon the cross only once, offering himself to the Father as a living, passible, mortal victim, powerful unto the redemption of the living and the dead—namely, those whom the depth of divine counsel judged, foreknew, predestined, and called to be redeemed, in the manners and times in which this was fitting.

[Note: [Col. 1755C] “Was fitting”: In Lanfranc the following words occur, corresponding to the second member of blessed Augustine’s proposition: [Col. 1755D] “Yet in the sacrament, which the Church repeatedly celebrates in remembrance of this event, the Lord’s flesh is daily sacrificed, divided, eaten, and his blood is drunk from the chalice by the mouths of the faithful” [Col. 1756C].]

### Chapter LIII. The victim offered once is offered daily in remembrance of his death. Likewise Ambrose, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 10

[Note: [Col. 1755] It is not by Ambrose.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 145. *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 6.]

In Christ the victim was offered once, powerful unto eternal salvation. What, then, of us? Do we not offer every day? We do *indeed* offer [Note: [Col. 1755] “offer”: absent from Ivo, *Panormia*, and the collected editions, compared with the first Argenteuil edition], but in remembrance of his death [Note: [Col. 1755] “indeed”: absent from Ivo.], and there is one victim, not many. How is it one and not many? Because Christ was offered once. This sacrifice, moreover, is the representation [Note: [Col. 1755] “model”: the original] of that sacrifice; it is the same thing [Note: [Col. 1755] “but it is the same”: Ivo, *Panormia*.] and always [Note: [Col. 1756C] “And always”: In the works printed under the names of blessed Ambrose and blessed John Chrysostom, these words are added: “We offer—not one lamb now and another tomorrow, but always the very same one.” In the best manuscript this is Greek (for it is lacking in the Verona copy): “οὐ νῦν μὲν ἕτερον πρόβατον, αὔριον δὲ ἕτερον, ἀλλ᾽ ἀεὶ τὸ αὐτό”—“not one sheep now and another tomorrow, but always the same one.”] the same thing.

Therefore this sacrifice is one [Note: [Col. 1755] “the same”: the collected editions.—Absent from Ivo, *Panormia*.] sacrifice [Note: [Col. 1755] “alone”: added by the Basle edition]; otherwise [Note: [Col. 1755] “it will be said”: added by the collected editions], because it is offered in many places, are there many Christs? By no means. Rather, Christ is one everywhere, whole here and whole there.

For just as that which is offered everywhere is one body and not many bodies, so too there is one sacrifice. That high priest is the one who offered the victim that cleanses us. We now also offer *the same* victim that was then offered, which cannot be consumed [Note: [Col. 1757] “is”: added by the collected editions]. What we do is done in commemoration of what was done: for he says, “Do this in remembrance of me” [Note: [Col. 1755] “he says”: absent from the Argenteuil and Basle editions; compare Luke, ch. 22, v. 19.].

[Note: [Col. 1756C] “For just as”: In commentaries printed under Ambrose’s name the reading is, “just as the one who is offered everywhere.” Algerus’s [ [Col. 1755] same work, bk. 1, ch. 15], Ivo’s, and Gratian’s reading has not been altered. The Greek reads: “ὥσπερ οὖν πολλαχοῦ προσφερόμενος ἓν σῶμά ἐστι”—“for, being offered in many places, he is one body.” Some other readings have been corrected [Col. 1756D].]

### Chapter LIV. We ought to receive the sacrament of Christ’s body only while fasting. Likewise Augustine, in the Book of Responses to Januarius, chapter 6

[Note: [Col. 1757] Epistle 54, Maurist edition, manuscript A, ca. 400.—Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 1, ch. 146. *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 112.]

**Part XVIII.** It is quite clear that, when the disciples first received the Lord’s body and blood, they did not receive them fasting. But should the whole Church therefore be censured because it is always received by persons fasting? For the Holy Spirit was pleased that, in honor of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s body should enter the mouth of the Christian before other foods. This custom is therefore observed throughout the world.

For the fact that the Lord gave it after food does not mean that brethren who have eaten or supped ought to assemble to receive that sacrament, or that they ought to mix it with their meals, as did those whom the Apostle rebukes [Note: [Col. 1757] “corrects”: the collected editions] and corrects [Note: [Col. 1757] compare 1 Corinthians, ch. 11, vv. 20 ff.]. For the Savior, in order to commend the depth of that mystery more forcefully, intended to impress it last upon the hearts and memories of the disciples from whom he was about to depart for his passion; and therefore he did not prescribe in what order it should thereafter be received, but reserved this matter for the Apostles, through whom he was to order the churches. For had he instructed that it must always be received after other foods [Note: [Col. 1757] “received again”: the collected editions], I think no one would have changed that custom [Note: [Col. 1757] “altered”: the original and Ivo, *Decretum*.].

But when the Apostle, speaking of this sacrament, says [Note: [Col. 1757] 1 Corinthians, ch. 11, vv. 33–34], “Therefore, brothers, when you assemble to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you may not assemble for judgment,” he immediately adds: “The rest I shall arrange when I come.” [Note: [Col. 1757C] “He immediately added”: In the printed editions there followed [ [Col. 1757] thus the collected editions and the first Basle edition]: “the matters which pertain to the order of this same sacrament, namely, how [it is received] fasting, etc.” These words are absent from most manuscripts, the original, and the other collectors.] From this it may be understood [Note: [Col. 1757] “where”: the collected editions—meaning, “where it is understood”: Ivo, *Panormia*.] that it was too extensive a matter for him to set out in a letter the whole order of proceeding [Note: [Col. 1757] “to them”: Ivo.—The collected editions] which the Church throughout the world observes, having been instituted by him, and which is varied by no diversity of regions [Note: [Col. 1757] “hours”: Ivo; the Argenteuil edition.—“customs”: the original] [Col. 1758A].

### Chapter LV. Before consecration it is bread, but by Christ’s words it is changed into his body. Likewise Ambrose, Book IV of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 4

[Note: [Col. 1757] It is not by Ambrose. Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 10.]

**Part XIX.** The bread on the altar is ordinary bread before the sacramental words; when consecration has been added, bread becomes Christ’s flesh. Let us therefore establish this [Note: [Col. 1757] “Let us establish this”: absent from the Basle edition]. How [Note: [Col. 1757] “however”: added by the collected editions] can that which is bread be Christ’s body? *By consecration.* But by what words, and whose speech, is consecration effected? By the words of the Lord Jesus.

For throughout all the rest which is said [Note: [Col. 1757] “in the preceding parts by the priest”: added by the collected editions and the first Basle edition], praise is offered [Note: [Col. 1757] “is offered”: the Basle edition.—“is reported”: the Paris and Lyons editions] to God; prayer is made for the people, for kings, and for the others. But when the point is reached at which the venerable sacrament is to be performed [Note: [Col. 1757] “But when the sacrifice is constituted”: the collected editions], the priest no longer uses his own words but uses Christ’s words. Therefore Christ’s word effects this sacrament.

What is Christ’s word? Surely, that word [Note: [Col. 1757] absent from the first Argenteuil, Basle, and Lyons II and III editions] by which all things were made. The Lord commanded, and heaven was made; *the Lord commanded, and earth was made; the Lord commanded,* and the *seas were made*; the Lord commanded [Note: [Col. 1757] “the Lord commanded … was made”: absent from the same editions], and every creature came into being [Note: [Col. 1757] “was created”: the Argenteuil editions].

You see, therefore, how efficacious [Note: [Col. 1757] “of the operator”: the second Lyons edition] Christ’s word is. If there is such power in the word of the Lord Jesus that things which did not exist began to exist [Note: [Col. 1757] “that what did not exist should begin to exist”: the collected editions], how much more efficacious is it that things which existed [Col. 1757C] should be changed into something else [Note: [Col. 1757] “should be changed”: the Basle edition]?

[Note: [Col. 1757C] “That things which existed”: These words of blessed Ambrose, which Berengar alleged against Catholics, are carefully explained by Guitmund, bk. 3, and Algerus, bk. 1, ch. 7. Lanfranc not only interprets them very well but adds that some manuscripts read: “If, therefore, there is such power in the word of the Lord Jesus that things which did not exist began to exist, how much more efficacious is it that things which existed should be changed into something else?” [Col. 1758C].]

Thus what was bread before consecration is now Christ’s body after consecration, because Christ’s word changes creatures [Note: [Col. 1757] “creatures”: the same edition]; and so bread becomes Christ’s body, and wine mixed with water in the chalice [Note: [Col. 1757] “the chalice”: the Lyons II and III editions] becomes blood by the consecration of the heavenly word [Note: [Col. 1757] “mixed”: the collected editions.—Böhm].

§1. But perhaps you say, “I do not see the appearance of blood.” Yet it has a likeness. For just as you received the likeness of death, so you also drink the likeness of the *precious* blood [Note: [Col. 1757] “of Christ”: added by the Basle edition], so that there may be no horror of gore, while nevertheless it accomplishes the price of redemption. You have learned, *therefore,* that *what* you receive *is* Christ’s body.

And chapter 5, §2. Do you wish to know that it is consecrated by heavenly words? Receive the words that are spoken. The priest says: “Make for us,” he says, “this offering recorded, reasonable, *acceptable [Note: [Col. 1759D] ‘Acceptable’: Gratian’s manuscripts read only ‘reasonable, etc.’ All the words through ‘See’ have been added, whereas previously the text began ‘From that point’ [ [Col. 1759] thus the collected editions]. They seem highly important for understanding what follows], which is the figure of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; who, on the day before he suffered, took bread into his holy hands, looked up to heaven—to you, holy Father, almighty and eternal God—gave thanks, blessed it, broke it, and gave it, when broken, to his Apostles and disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat of this, all of you; for this is my body, which shall be broken for many.’ Likewise, after supper, on the day before he suffered, he took the chalice, looked up to heaven—to you, holy Father, almighty and eternal God—gave thanks, blessed it, and gave it to his Apostles and disciples, saying: ‘Take and drink from it, all of you; for this is my blood.*’”

See: all those words down to “Take,” whether concerning the body or the blood, are the Evangelist’s words. From that point the words are Christ’s: “Take, drink from it [Note: [Col. 1759] “and drink from this”: the collected editions], all of you; for this is my blood” [Note: [Col. 1759] absent from the same editions except the Basle edition]. Examine each point. “On the day before he suffered,” he says, “he took bread into his holy hands.” Before it is consecrated [Note: [Col. 1759] “was consecrated”: the collected editions], it is bread; but when Christ’s words have been added [Note: [Col. 1759] “have been added”: the same editions], it is Christ’s body. Finally, hear him saying: “Take and eat of it [Note: [Col. 1759] “of this”: the same editions], all of you; for this is my body.” And before Christ’s words the chalice is full of wine [Note: [Col. 1759] “of wine and water”: the Basle edition] and water. When Christ’s words have worked [Col. 1759C] [Note: [Col. 1759] “have worked”: the collected editions and the first Basle edition], there blood is effected, which redeemed the people.

§3. See, then, in how many ways [Note: [Col. 1759] “how powerful”: the collected editions] Christ’s word is powerful to change all things. Then the Lord Jesus himself [Note: [Col. 1759] “Christ”: the same first Basle edition] testifies to us [Note: [Col. 1759] “to whose faith and testimony we ought not to be doubtful”: the collected editions] that we receive his body and his blood. Must we doubt his trustworthiness and testimony?

### Chapter LVI. The bread of eternal life sustains not the body but the substance of the soul. The same Ambrose, Book V of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 4

[Note: [Col. 1759] It is not by Ambrose.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 7. Peter Lombard, in the same place.]

This is not the bread that passes into the body, but that bread of eternal life which sustains the substance of our soul [Note: [Col. 1759] “sustained”: the Lyons editions].

And shortly afterward, §1. This is daily bread [Col. 1760A]; receive daily what benefits you daily. Live in such a way that you may deserve to receive daily.

### Chapter LVII. Christ is living bread also according to the flesh. Likewise Augustine, in the Epistle to Irenaeus

[Note: [Col. 1759] It appears to be drawn from Augustine, Tractate 26 on John, chapter 6; compare the Ordinary Gloss there.]

Christ is the bread of which whoever eats lives eternally, concerning which he himself says [Note: [Col. 1759] “said”: the collected editions; compare John, ch. 6, v. 52], “And the bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world,” etc. He determines how he is bread: not only according to the Word by which all things live, but *also* according to the flesh assumed for the life of the world. For human flesh, which was *liable to sin and therefore* dead, united and incorporated with his *own* pure flesh and made one with him [Note: [Col. 1759] “with it”: the collected editions, except the first Argenteuil edition], lives [Note: [Col. 1759] “live”: the Nuremberg, Venice I and II, Paris, and Lyons I editions] by his Spirit, just as a body lives by its own spirit [Note: [Col. 1759] “by his spirit”: the Argenteuil edition]. But whoever is not of Christ’s body does not live by Christ’s Spirit.

### Chapter LVIII. How Christ is visibly received in the sacraments and spiritually eaten and drunk. Likewise Augustine, Sermon II on the Words of the Apostle

[Note: [Col. 1759D] The teaching in the first part of this chapter is found, more fully explained, in blessed Augustine, Sermon 2 on the Words of the Apostle. The rest, from “Christ is eaten” to the end, is found in Bede on 1 Corinthians 10 [Col. 1760D]; part is also quoted below in the chapter “He invites” [Col. 1759].]

[Note: [Col. 1759] Compare chapters 70 and 75 below.]

Those who eat and drink Christ eat and drink life. To eat him is to be refreshed; to drink him is to live. What is visibly received in the sacrament is spiritually eaten and drunk in the reality itself. Let Christ be eaten [Note: [Col. 1759] “Christ is eaten”: the collected editions.—Böhm]; when eaten, he lives, because, though slain, he rose again [Note: [Col. 1759] “rose”: the Argenteuil and Basle editions]. Nor, when we eat him, do we divide him into parts.

Indeed, in the sacrament this is so, and the faithful know how to eat Christ’s flesh: each receives his own portion, which is why the graces themselves are called “parts” [Note: [Col. 1759] “and”: absent from the collected editions except the first Lyons edition]. He is eaten in portions and *yet remains whole entire [Col. 1760C]; he is eaten in portions in the sacrament and remains whole entire in heaven*; he remains whole entire in your heart. He was whole with the Father when he came into the Virgin; he filled her and did not depart from him [Note: [Col. 1759] “Christ”: added by the Basle edition].

And below, §1. What is seen is bread and a chalice, as the eyes report. But what faith, which must be instructed, requires is this: the bread is Christ’s body, the chalice [Note: [Col. 1759] “and the chalice is his blood”: added by the Basle edition] is his blood.

And below, §2. These are called sacraments because in them one thing is seen and another understood [Note: [Col. 1759] “and another”: the collected editions]. What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has a spiritual fruit.

And below [Note: [Col. 1759] compare above, chapter 36], §3. Whoever receives the mystery of unity and does not maintain the bond of peace receives the mystery not for himself, but as testimony against himself.

### Chapter LIX. How Christ’s body is to be received spiritually. Likewise Augustine on John, chapter 6, Tractates XXVI and XXVII

[Note: [Col. 1761C] This chapter is compiled from sayings of blessed Augustine in Tractates 26 and 27 on John, Psalm 42, and Prosper, as indicated in their respective places.]

[Note: [Col. 1761] Compare above, the same chapter 47.]

To believe in Jesus Christ is to eat the living bread. Whoever believes *in him* eats [Note: [Col. 1761] “in him”: the Basle, Paris, and Lyons I editions]. He is invisibly nourished because he is *also* invisibly reborn [Note: [Col. 1761] “and invisibly”: the Basle, Paris, and Lyons I editions]. “And whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood [Note: [Col. 1761] John, ch. 6, v. 55] has eternal life.”

For by participation in the Son [Note: [Col. 1761] “of God”: added in the Basle edition]—that is, through unity in Christ’s body [Note: [Col. 1761] “his”: the same edition] and blood—the person who eats lives, not merely by receiving in the sacrament, which evil persons also do, but by participating even in the Spirit: so that he may remain in the Lord’s body as a member and be given life by his Spirit, which is so when he keeps his commandments [Note: [Col. 1761] “they are kept”: the same edition].

§1. He comes to the invisible altar of God—to which no unrighteous person approaches—who comes to this present altar justified [Note: [Col. 1761] In Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*, ch. 189, and Augustine on Psalm 42]. There he will find his life [Note: [Col. 1761] “also there”: the Basle edition], who here discerns his own cause.

### Chapter LX. The Holy Spirit invisibly sanctifies Christ’s body and blood. The same, Book III of *On the Trinity*, chapter 4

[Note: [Col. 1761C] In blessed Augustine the following precedes this: “For we do not call Christ’s body and blood either his tongue [he is speaking of Paul], or parchments, or ink, or meaningful sounds uttered by the tongue, or written letters marked upon skins; but only that which is taken from the fruits of the earth, etc.” It is altogether worthwhile to read that passage complete [Col. 1761D].]

We call Christ’s body and blood that which, taken from the fruits of the earth and consecrated by mystical prayer, we duly [Note: [Col. 1761] “rightly”: the collected editions] receive for spiritual salvation in remembrance of *the Lord’s passion for us.* Although it is brought by human hands [Note: [Col. 1761] “by the hand of a human being”: the same editions] to that visible appearance [Note: [Col. 1761] “is brought”: the same editions], it is not sanctified so as to become so great [Col. 1761C] a sacrament [Note: [Col. 1761] “worthy”: the Argenteuil edition] except through the invisible working of the Spirit of God, while God performs all those things which are done in that work through bodily motions.

### Chapter LXI. By blessing, bread becomes Christ’s body. Likewise

[Note: [Col. 1761] Compare Bede on 1 Corinthians 10:16.]

Not every bread, *but* bread receiving Christ’s blessing, becomes Christ’s body.

### Chapter LXII. Christ’s body is understood in two ways. The same

[Note: [Col. 1761] Compare above, chapter 36, at the end.]

For Christ commended to us [Note: [Col. 1761] “for he”: the collected editions] in this sacrament [Note: [Col. 1761] “this”: the same editions] his body and blood [Note: [Col. 1761] absent from the Argenteuil edition], which also made us ourselves; for we too have become his body.

### Chapter LXIII. The sacrifice of the altar is the sacrament of unity. The same, Tractate XXVI on John, chapter 6

[Note: [Col. 1761D] Compare Bede on 1 Corinthians 10:16.]

This is the sacrament of devotion [Note: [Col. 1761D] In the original: “O sacrament of devotion, O sign of unity, O bond of charity.” From that original the remainder has been corrected and enlarged [Col. 1762C].], the sign of unity, the bond of charity. Whoever wishes to live has where he may live and whence he may live: let him approach, believe, be incorporated [Note: [Col. 1761] “and let him incorporate this food”: Böhm.—“let him incorporate it”: the collected editions], so that he may be given life.

And below, §1. By this food and drink, therefore, he wishes the fellowship of his body and members to be understood—that is, the Church [Note: [Col. 1761] “of the Church”: the same first Argenteuil and Lyons II and III editions] in the predestined.

### Chapter LXIV. We ought to receive Christ’s body more spiritually than bodily. The same, in the same place

[Note: [Col. 1761] Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 4.]

**Part XX.** To eat the heavenly bread [Note: [Col. 1762C] “Eat the heavenly bread”: The original reads [ [Col. 1761] thus Ivo]: “Eat the heavenly bread spiritually; bring innocence to the altar”; likewise among the cited collectors [Col. 1762D]. Yet account was taken of the author who wrote the case-form, and blessed Thomas also followed Gratian’s reading in his *Catena* on that passage of John. The remainder has been corrected and enlarged.] spiritually [Note: [Col. 1761] “at the altar”: the collected editions] is to bring innocence to the altar [Note: [Col. 1761] “to carry”: the same editions]. Even if sins are daily [Note: [Col. 1761] “may be”: the same editions], or [Note: [Col. 1761] “or”: absent from Ivo.] let them not be deadly [Note: [Col. 1761] “are”: Böhm]. Before you approach the *altar,* *consider what* you say [Note: [Col. 1761] “what”: Ivo]: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.” If you forgive, you will be forgiven; approach securely: it is bread, not poison [Note: [Col. 1761] “and not”: the same editions except the Basle edition]. But see whether you forgive. For if you do not forgive, you lie—and you lie to one whom you do not deceive. You can lie to God; you cannot deceive God [Col. 1762C]. [Note: [Col. 1761] At this point the Argenteuil and Basle editions read: *non mentiaris Deo* (“do not lie to God”); the remaining editions read: *ne mentiaris Deo* (“do not lie to God”).]

### Chapter LXV. Whoever is at discord with Christ receives the sacrament, not the reality, of Christ’s body. The same, Book of Sentences, chapter 139

[Note: [Col. 1761] Attributed to Prosper.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 8.]

Whoever is at discord with Christ neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, even if he daily receives without distinction [Note: [Col. 1761] “receives”: the collected editions] the sacrament of so great a thing, unto the judgment due to his presumption.

### Chapter LXVI. Holy things harm the evil, and evil things benefit the good. The same, Tractates VI and LXII on John

[Note: [Col. 1763] What is explained much more fully in blessed Augustine, Tractates 6 and 62 on John, is here gathered into a kind of summary.]

[Note: [Col. 1763] Compare Bede on 1 Corinthians 11.]

Holy things can harm the evil; for the good they are unto salvation, for the evil unto judgment. Hence the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1763] 1 Corinthians, ch. 11, v. 27]: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself,” not because that thing is evil, but because an evil person receives badly what is good. For the morsel which the Lord gave Judas [Note: [Col. 1763] “gave”: the collected editions; compare John, ch. 13] was not evil. The physician gave salvation; but because the recipient was unworthy, he received it to his own destruction [Note: [Col. 1763] The Basle edition reads: “but because he gave it worthily, the one who was unworthy received it to his destruction, etc.”]. Evil things also benefit the good, just as Satan’s angel benefited Paul. For good results from evil when evil is received well.

### Chapter LXVII. Evil persons are not forbidden to eat from the Lord’s table. The same

[Note: [Col. 1763] From the Ordinary Gloss on Psalm 22, v. 30.]

Let not the steward forbid the rich of the earth to eat at the Lord’s table [Note: [Col. 1763] absent from the Basle edition], but let him warn the collector to fear.

### Chapter LXVIII. Even one who receives unworthily receives Christ’s body. The same, Book V of *On Baptism*, chapter 8

[Note: [Col. 1763] Anselm, bk. 9, ch. 11. Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 9.]
