Just as Judas, to whom the Lord gave the morsel [Note: [Col. 1763] “when”: the Basle edition] [Note: [Col. 1763] “by giving”: the Venice I and II editions, omitting the following words through “but”], did not receive something evil but, by receiving badly [Note: [Col. 1763] added: “the good”: the collected editions], made room for the devil *within himself* [Note: [Col. 1763] “within himself”: the Venice I and II editions, omitting the following words through “but”], so anyone who receives the Lord’s sacrament [Note: [Col. 1763] “Christ’s body”: the collected editions] unworthily [Note: [Col. 1763] “understand”: the Venice I and II editions] does not cause it, because *he himself* is evil, to be evil; nor does he cause himself to have received nothing because he receives it not unto salvation [Note: [Col. 1763] “may receive”: the Lyons II and III editions.—“receives”: the remaining editions]. For the *Lord’s* body [Note: [Col. 1763] absent from the Argenteuil edition] and blood were nevertheless [Col. 1763C] *also* [Note: [Col. 1763] “also”: the collected editions] present in those [Note: [Col. 1763] “in those”: the same editions] to whom the Apostle said [Note: [Col. 1763] 1 Corinthians, ch. 11, v. 27]: “Whoever eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.”

### Chapter LXIX. By what examples it is proved that, beyond nature, the substance of bread and wine is converted into Christ’s body and blood. Likewise Ambrose, in the book *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapters 8 and 9

[Note: [Col. 1763] Previously cited from Ambrose’s *On the Sacraments*.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 2, ch. 7.]

XXI. Part. Truly it is wonderful that God rained manna upon the fathers and that they were fed with daily nourishment from heaven. Hence it was said [Note: Col. 1763, Ps. 77:25]: “Man ate the bread of angels.” Yet all who ate that bread died in the wilderness. But this food which you receive [Note: Col. 1763: “you receive”: collected editions], this living bread which came down from heaven, supplies the substance of eternal life; and whoever eats this bread shall not die forever, because it is the body of Christ. Consider now whether the bread of angels is more excellent, or the flesh of Christ, which is indeed the body of life. That manna was from heaven; this is above heaven. That was of heaven; this belongs to the Lord of heaven. That was liable to corruption if it were kept until the next day; this is removed from every corruption: *whoever* reverently tastes it cannot experience corruption. Water flowed for them from the rock; for you, blood flows from Christ. Water satisfied them for an hour; the blood washes you for eternity. The Jew drinks and thirsts; when you have drunk, you cannot thirst; *and* that was in shadow, this in truth. If what you marvel at is a shadow, how great is that whose *and* shadow you marvel at? Hear that what occurred among the fathers [Note: Col. 1763: “the brothers”: Basel edition; “the ancients”: Ivo] is a shadow: “They drank,” he says [Note: Col. 1763, 1 Cor. 10:4], “from the rock following them” [Note: Col. 1763: “from the spiritual”: Vulgate and collected editions]; “and the rock was Christ. But God was not well pleased with many of them, for they were overthrown in the wilderness. Now these things were done as a figure of us” [Note: Col. 1763: “figure”: the same edition; the same editions; Ivo]. You have recognized the greater things [Note: Col. 1763: “You have recognized”: Böhm]: for light is greater than shadow, truth than figure, and the body of the author [Note: Col. 1763: “creator”: collected editions] than manna from heaven.

[Note: Col. 1763: After “this food,” Basel adds “is”; “you receive” is plural in the collected editions; “supplies” is “ministers” in the same editions; Ivo reads “and” for “because”; “above” is “above” (*supra*) in the same source; the words “how great is that” are absent from the collected editions except the first Basel edition. Böhm reads “You have recognized” in the plural; the collected editions read “more powerful things” (*potiora*); Ivo, the Basel, Paris, and Lyons editions read “light is” rather than “light.”]

§ 1. Perhaps you say [Note: Col. 1763: “you say”: Basel and Lyons I editions]: “I see something else; how do you maintain to me that I receive Christ’s body?” And this still remains for us to prove. By how many examples, then, do we proceed to prove [Note: Col. 1763: “examples? Let us prove”: original] that this is not what nature formed, but what blessing consecrated; and that blessing has greater power than nature, because by blessing even nature itself is changed? Moses held a rod [Note: Col. 1763, Exod. 7]; he threw it down, and it became a serpent. Again he seized the serpent’s tail, and it returned to the nature of a rod. You see, therefore [Note: Col. 1763: “also” is absent from Ivo; “also” appears in the Argentinian and Basel editions], that by prophetic grace the nature both of serpent and rod was changed twice. The rivers of Egypt ran in their pure watery course [Note: Col. 1763, Exod. 7]; suddenly blood began to burst forth from the veins of the springs. There was no drink in the rivers. Again, at the prophet’s prayers, the gore ceased in the streams and the nature of water returned.

The Hebrew people was enclosed on every side [Note: Col. 1765, Exod. 14]: hemmed in by Egyptians on one side, shut in by the sea on the other [Note: Col. 1765: “shut in”: Ivo; Basel edition]. Moses raised the rod; the water divided [Note: Col. 1765: “and the water”: Böhm] and froze into the likeness of walls [Note: Col. 1765: “likeness”: Ivo; Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice I and II editions], and a footpath appeared amid the waves. The Jordan, turning backward contrary to nature, returned to the beginning of its own source [Note: Col. 1765, Josh. 4]. Is it not clear that the nature either of the sea-waves or of the river-current was changed? The people of the fathers thirsted [Note: Col. 1765, Num. 20]; Moses touched the rock, and water flowed from the rock. Did not grace work contrary to nature, so that the rock might pour forth water which nature did not possess? The river Marah was exceedingly bitter [Note: Col. 1765, Exod. 15], so that the thirsty people could not drink. Moses cast wood into the water, and the nature of the water cast off its bitterness, which an infused grace suddenly tempered. Under Elisha the prophet [Note: Col. 1765, 4 Kings 6], iron slipped from an axe belonging to one of the sons of the prophets [Note: Col. 1765: “from”: collected editions] and immediately sank. The man who had lost the iron asked Elisha; Elisha too cast wood into the water, and the iron floated [Note: Col. 1765: “swam”: the same editions; Ivo]. Certainly we recognize [Note: Col. 1765: “recognize”: Ivo; “we have recognized”: collected editions] that this also happened contrary to nature; for the substance of iron is heavier than the fluid of water.

§ 2. Therefore we observe that the grace of God is of greater power than nature [Note: Col. 1765: “God’s grace is greater”: Ivo; “of God” is absent from Ivo and from the Argentinian, Basel, and Nuremberg editions], and yet we are still reckoning the grace of prophetic blessing [Note: Col. 1765: “before prophetic”: collected editions except Basel and Lyons]. But if human blessing had such power as to change nature, what shall we say of the divine consecration itself [Note: Col. 1765: Ivo reads “consideration”], where the very words [Note: Col. 1765: “very”: absent from the Argentinian and Basel editions] of the Lord and Saviour work? For this sacrament which you receive is effected by Christ’s word. If Elijah’s word had such power as to bring down fire from heaven [Note: Col. 1765, 4 Kings 1; “draw down”: Ivo], shall not Christ’s word have power to change the appearances of the elements? You have read concerning the works of the whole world [Note: Col. 1765, Ps. 148:5]: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.” Therefore the word of Christ, which could make from nothing what did not exist, cannot [Note: Col. 1765: Basel reads “could”] change things which exist into what they were not [Note: Col. 1765: “was”: Basel and Lyons editions]? For it is no less to give new natures to things than to change natures.

[Note: Col. 1765C: Formerly this was read—so the collected editions and Ivo—“For it is no less to give than to change new natures to things.” It has been corrected from the original. In Guitmund, *Against Berengar*, book 3; Lanfranc, *Against Berengar*; Alger, book 1, chapter 9; and Ivo, one reads: “to give new things, than to change natures.”]

§ 3. But why do we use arguments? Let us use his own examples, and establish the truth of the mystery by the *example* of the incarnation [Note: Col. 1765: “incarnation” is *incarnationis* in the Nuremberg, Venice I–II, Paris, and Lyons I editions; Ivo reads “novelty” rather than “example”]. Did the ordinary course of nature precede [Note: Col. 1765: “preceded or was present”: Argentinian edition; “perceived beforehand”: the remaining editions] when the Lord Jesus was born from Mary? If we seek the normal order, a woman joined with a man has been accustomed to bear children. It is therefore evident that the Virgin bore contrary to the order of nature. And this which we effect is the body from the Virgin. Why do you seek the order of nature here in Christ’s body, when the Lord Jesus himself was born from the Virgin contrary to nature? Certainly [Note: Col. 1765: “For true”: Basel edition; “truly”: the remaining editions except Nuremberg] Christ’s flesh [Note: Col. 1765: “is”: Basel edition] which was crucified and buried is true flesh. Therefore this is truly the sacrament of that flesh. The Lord Jesus himself cries out [Note: Col. 1765: “our”: Basel edition; compare Luke 22:19]: “This is my body.” Before the blessing of the heavenly words another kind is named; after consecration, the body of Christ is signified [Note: Col. 1765: “is truly said”: Lyons II and III editions; “is marked”: the remaining editions except Basel; compare above, chapter 40]. He himself calls it his blood. Before consecration it is called something else; after consecration it is called blood [Note: Col. 1765: “Christ”: Basel and Lyons II and III editions]; and you say, “Amen,” that is, “It is true.” Let the inward mind confess what the mouth speaks; let the heart feel what the word sounds.

[Note: Col. 1765: The words “What … confess” are absent from the Nuremberg and Venice I and II editions.]

[Note: Col. 1765: The words “mind … confess” are omitted in the Paris and Lyons I editions.]

[Note: Col. 1765: “attentive”: Argentinian, Basel, Lyons II and III editions.]

[Note: Col. 1765: “confesses”: Argentinian edition.]

### LXX. How Christ is eaten in portions and yet remains whole. Likewise Augustine, in a certain sermon on the words of the Gospel.

[Note: Col. 1765: Compare above, chapter 58, and below, chapter 75. Ivo, *Decree*, part 2, chapter 8; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 12.]

The Lord invites his servants and has prepared himself as food for them [Note: Col. 1765: “that he may prepare”: collected editions; “and” and “for them” are absent from Ivo]. Who would dare to eat his Lord? And yet he says [Note: Col. 1765, John 6:58]: “Whoever eats me lives because of me.” When Christ is eaten, life is eaten; nor is he killed in order to be eaten, but he gives life to the dead. When he is eaten, he refreshes, but is not diminished [Note: Col. 1765: these words are absent from Ivo]. *Therefore, brothers, let us not fear to eat this bread, lest perhaps we consume him and afterwards find nothing to eat.* Christ is eaten; when eaten he lives, because, having been killed, he rose again [Note: Col. 1765: “rose again”: Ivo; Paris and Lyons editions]; nor, when we eat, do we make parts of him [Note: Col. 1765: “parts” is absent from Ivo]. And indeed this is so in the sacrament; and the faithful know how they eat Christ’s flesh [Note: Col. 1765: “body”: Basel edition]. Each receives his own portion—*hence the very gifts are called “portions.”* He is eaten in portions and remains wholly entire; he is eaten in portions in the sacrament and remains wholly entire in heaven; he remains wholly entire in your heart.

[Note: Col. 1765: “and” and “for them” are absent from Ivo.]

[Note: Col. 1765: “rose again”: Ivo; Paris and Lyons editions.]

[Note: Col. 1765: “and” is absent from Ivo.]

[Note: Col. 1765: “body”: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 1765: The words “whence … called” are absent from Ivo.]

### LXXI. The daily sacrifice is not a repetition of Christ’s passion, but a commemoration. Likewise Paschasius, in the book *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, chapter 9.

[Note: Col. 1767: And Rabanus, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, chapter 22; compare the following chapter, § 1.]

XXII. Part. This offering is repeated daily, although Christ, having suffered once in the flesh, saved the world by one and the same passion of death [Note: Col. 1767: “saved”: Argentinian and Basel editions]. Rising from that death to life, death shall no longer have dominion over him [Note: Col. 1767: “to him”: collected editions], for the wisdom of God the Father has certainly foreseen this as necessary for many reasons. First, because we sin daily, at least in those sins without which mortal frailty cannot live. For although all sins have been forgiven in baptism, the weakness of sin still remains in the flesh [Note: Col. 1767: “remains”: collected editions]. Hence the Psalmist says [Note: Col. 1767: “Hence the Psalmist”: These words of the prophet, and certain others which are found neither in Paschasius nor in Blessed Thomas, who cites him in the treatise *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, are nevertheless found in the same book issued under Rabanus’s name] [Note: Col. 1767, Ps. 102:1]: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your infirmities.” And therefore, because we stumble daily, Christ is mystically sacrificed for us daily, and Christ’s passion is handed down in the mystery [Note: Col. 1767: “ministry”: Böhm], so that he who once conquered death by dying may daily remit the recurrent sins of transgressions through these sacraments of body and blood. Hence we pray [Note: Col. 1767, Matt. 6:12]: “Forgive us our debts” [Note: Col. 1767: “etc.”: collected editions]; because, if we say that we have no sin [Note: Col. 1767, 1 John 1:6], we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us.

Likewise, below in the same chapter:

§ 1. This mystery is repeated for the commemoration of Christ’s passion, as he himself says [Note: Col. 1767, 1 Cor. 11:25]: “As often as you do this, do it in remembrance of me.” Therefore, as often as you receive this bread and drink this cup [Note: Col. 1767: “blood”: collected editions except Basel], you shall proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. Certainly this is not to be understood as though until Christ’s death should come [Note: Col. 1767: “therefore”: original], since he no longer dies; rather, until the Lord himself comes for judgment [Note: Col. 1767: “will come”: collected editions except Lyons II and III]. Meanwhile [Note: Col. 1767: “Meanwhile”: the true reading; Basel edition], Christ’s death must always be proclaimed to posterity for the life of the world [Note: Col. 1767: “through the life of the age”: collected editions], so that they may learn with what love he loved his own, he who deigned to die for them; and all of us owe him a return of love, because he loved us first [Note: Col. 1767: “God”: original] when we were children of Gehenna, in order that, now freed from death, we might love him.

[Note: Col. 1767: “and this for”: collected editions; “and for”: original.]

[Note: Col. 1767: “by proclaiming”: Lyons II edition; “to be proclaimed”: the remaining editions.]

### LXXII. The sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood is celebrated not only under a figure but also in truth. Likewise Augustine.

[Note: Col. 1767: Rather, Paschasius in the same book.]

[Note: Col. 1767D: In Paschasius, from whose passages this chapter seems to have been compiled, the opening words are the title of chapter 4: “Whether, under a figure or in truth, this mystery becomes the true flesh and true blood of Christ.” The chapter begins: “That body and blood are made in truth by the consecration of the mystery, no one who believes the divine words doubts. Hence Truth says,” etc. Alger, who has nearly the same material in chapter 16, also cites Augustine from the book *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, and begins thus: “Truth says,” etc.]

Whether, under a figure or in truth, this mystical sacrament of the cup comes to be [Note: Col. 1767: “under”: collected editions]. Truth says [Note: Col. 1767, John 6:56]: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” Otherwise, how will this be a great thing [Note: Col. 1767: “true”: original; compare John 6:52]: “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world,” unless it is true flesh? But because it is not lawful that Christ be devoured with teeth, the Lord willed [Note: Col. 1767: absent from the original and Basel edition] that this bread and wine should truly be created, by the consecration of the Holy Spirit, as his flesh and blood in the mystery and in power [Note: Col. 1767: absent from the same and from the Argentinian and Basel editions], and that they should be mystically sacrificed daily for the life of the world; so that, just as true flesh is created from the Virgin by the Holy Spirit without intercourse, so by that same Spirit Christ’s same body may be mystically consecrated from the substance of bread and wine. Christ’s body is both truth and figure: truth, when Christ’s body and blood are made from the substance of bread and wine by the power of the Holy Spirit, by his own power [Note: Col. 1767: the original reads “word”]; but figure is that which is outwardly perceived [Note: Col. 1767: absent from the Basel edition].

§ 1. This offering is repeated daily, although Christ suffered once, because we sin daily—*at least* with sins without which mortal frailty cannot live. And therefore, because we stumble daily, Christ *too* is mystically sacrificed for us.

[Note: Col. 1767: Compare above, chapter 71.]

§ 2. Within the holy catholic Church [Note: Col. 1767: “holy”: collected editions; compare Distinction 1, Question 1, chapter 77; *Polycarpus*, book 3, title 9] nothing greater is accomplished by a good priest, nor anything less by an evil priest, in the mystery of Christ’s body; for it is accomplished not by the merit of the consecrator but by the word of the Creator and by the power of the Holy Spirit. For if it depended on the priest’s merit, it would in no way belong to Christ. But now, just as Christ himself is the one who baptizes [Note: Col. 1767: “Christ”: Basel edition], so he himself is the one who by the Holy Spirit makes this his flesh and changes wine into blood. Hence the priest also says: “Command these things to be borne by the hands of your holy angel to your high altar in the sight of your divine majesty.” Why does he ask that they be carried into the light, unless it may be understood that these things are done in *his* priesthood? Therefore, may he deem this offering blessed, through which *we* are blessed; enrolled, through which all of us are enrolled in heaven; ratified, through which we are reckoned to be within Christ’s bowels; rational, through which we are stripped of brutish understanding; and acceptable, so that we who have displeased ourselves may through this become acceptable in his only Son.

[Note: Col. 1768D: Paschasius and Polycarpus, following Paschasius addressed to Placidus, read “pours forth blood” instead of “changes wine into blood”; the reading has not been altered because of the gloss.]

[Note: Col. 1767: “absent from the Argentinian edition”: the words concerning wine.]

[Note: Col. 1767: “absent from the Basel edition”: the words concerning the priest’s statement.]

[Note: Col. 1767: “this”: collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1767: “to be made or borne”: Argentinian edition.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “carried down”: collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1769C: In Paschasius and Rabanus—for the work issued under the one name and the other is nearly the same—the prayer is complete: “But imploring the Father through the Son, through whom we have access to him: ‘We ask,’ he says, ‘that this offering be blessed, through which we are blessed; enrolled, through which we may all be enrolled in heaven; ratified, through which we may be reckoned within Christ’s bowels; rational, through which we may be stripped of brutish understanding; and that he may deign to make it acceptable, so that we too, through that whereby we displeased ourselves, may be acceptable in his only Son.’”]

[Note: Col. 1769: “we are blessed”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “men”: Argentinian and Basel editions.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “are enrolled”: Argentinian edition; “we are enrolled”: the remaining editions.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “from”: Basel and Lyons editions; absent from the others.]

[Note: Col. 1769: absent from the Argentinian, Nuremberg, and Venice I and II editions.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “that is, through”: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “delivered”: Argentinian edition; “we are delivered”: Lyons II and III editions.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “displease”: collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “flesh and blood”: Basel and Lyons II and III editions; “and blood”: the remaining editions.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “by the pagans”: collected editions.]

Nothing is more reasonable: because we have already received the likeness of his death in baptism, let us also receive the likeness of *his* flesh, *and drink the likeness of his precious blood,* in such a way that truth may not be absent from the sacrament, and that it may not become an object of ridicule to pagans that we drink the blood of a slain man. For if the disciples could not patiently bear what the Lord said—“Whoever does not eat my flesh,” etc.—but said [Note: Col. 1769, John 6:61], “This saying is hard,” how could unbelievers bear these things? It must be believed that the sacraments are effected by Christ’s words [Note: Col. 1769: “of the Lord or of Christ”: Basel edition]. For by the power of him by whom they are first created [Note: Col. 1769: absent from the Argentinian edition], they are certainly brought forth anew by his word to something better [Note: Col. 1769: “are recreated”: original].

§ 3. Everything else which the priest says, or the choir of clergy sings [Note: Col. 1769: “choir” is absent from the same source; “sings” appears in the same source and in the collected editions], is nothing but praise and thanksgiving, or certainly prayers and petitions of the faithful. Hence the priest also first says, taking up the words of the Evangelists [Note: Col. 1769: “Gospels”: Argentinian edition]: “Who, on the day before he suffered” [Note: Col. 1769, 1 Cor. 11:23 ff.], etc. *But thereafter they are the words of God, full of power and every efficacy: “Take and eat; this is my body.”* In this, then, that body is created.

[Note: Col. 1770C: The words “But thereafter” were added from Paschasius, chapter 15, through “In this, then,” so that the sense itself might be understood.]

### LXXIII. In the blood of Christ the Lamb, the blood which is truly now received was formerly prefigured. Likewise Pope Gregory, in the Paschal homily, that is, Homily XXII on the Gospels.

[Note: Col. 1769: Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 11.]

You have learned what the blood of the Lamb is, not merely by hearing but by drinking. That blood is placed upon both doorposts [Note: Col. 1769, compare Exod. 12:7] when it is drawn not only with the mouth of the body but also with the mouth of the heart.

Likewise, *Dialogues*, book 4, chapter 58:

§ 1. This saving victim restores to us in mystery that death of the only-begotten Son, who, although risen from the dead and now dying no more, *and* though death shall no longer have dominion over him, nevertheless, living in himself immortally and incorruptibly, dies again *for us* in this mystery. There indeed his body is received; his flesh suffers for the salvation of the people [Note: Col. 1769: the original reads “is distributed”]; his blood is poured out, no longer into the hands of unbelievers but into the mouths of the faithful. Let us therefore consider what kind of sacrifice this is *for us*: it always imitates, for our absolution, the passion of the only-begotten Son. For what faithful person could doubt that, at the very hour of immolation, at the priest’s voice, the heavens are opened; that the choirs of angels are present in that mystery of Jesus Christ; that the highest things are joined to the lowest, *earthly things joined with heavenly,* and one thing made from the invisible and visible?

[Note: Col. 1769: “singularly”: original.]

[Note: Col. 1769, Rom. 6:9.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “to him”: collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1770C: The original reads, “is sacrificed in the sacred offering.” It has not been changed because of the gloss.]

[Note: Col. 1769: Ivo, *Decree*, part 2, chapter 8.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “indeed everywhere”: collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “is distributed”: original.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “mouth”: Paris and Lyons I editions.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “is poured forth”: collected editions.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “sacrament”: the same editions.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “could”: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “ministry”: collected editions except Paris and Lyons.]

[Note: Col. 1769: “the highest with the lowest”: original.]

§ 2. “At one and the same time and moment,” he says, “it is borne up to heaven by the ministry of angels to be joined to Christ’s body, and is seen before the priest’s eyes upon the altar” [Note: Col. 1769: the collected editions read “to be joined” in the masculine, *sociandus*].

[Note: Col. 1770C: This passage occurs in Alcuin’s *On the Divine Offices*, in the chapter on the celebration of Mass, which cites Gregory.]

And below:

§ 3. So great is the Church’s unity in Christ that everywhere there is one bread of Christ’s body and one cup of his blood. For the cup which a catholic priest offers is no other than that which the Lord handed to the Apostles [Note: Col. 1769: “sanctifies”: Argentinian and Basel editions]; because, just as the divinity of God’s Word is one [Note: Col. 1769: “life”: collected editions] and fills the whole world, so, although that body is consecrated [Note: Col. 1769: Basel reads “is consecrated”] in many places [Note: Col. 1769: “in many”: the same editions except Paris and Lyons] and on innumerable days, there are nevertheless not many bodies of Christ nor many cups, but one body of Christ and one blood with that body which he took in the Virgin’s womb and gave to the Apostles. For the divinity of the Word fills that which is everywhere, joins it, and makes it so that, just as it is one, it is *joined* to Christ’s body and is one body of him in truth [Note: Col. 1769: “voice”: Venice I and II editions; “and body”: the same editions; “Christ’s body” is absent from the collected editions except Argentinian and Venice I and II]. Hence it must be observed that whether anyone receives more or less of it, all equally receive Christ’s body wholly entire—everyone generally and each person individually.

§ 4. It is called the mystery of faith because you must believe that our salvation rests there [Note: Col. 1771: “and”: Argentinian edition; “may rest”: Basel edition]. For the Lord, providing for us, gave this sacrament of salvation so that, because we sin daily and he can no longer die, we may obtain forgiveness of sins through this sacrament of his body. For he himself is eaten and drunk daily in truth, yet remains whole, living, and undefiled. Therefore it is a great and awe-inspiring mystery, because one thing is seen and another understood. But since it is a mystery, how is it called body and blood? By the Lord’s action it has the appearance of bread and wine, because we are not accustomed to eat raw flesh and drink blood.

[Note: Col. 1771C: What follows “remains” in Alcuin reads: “A mystery is that in which one thing is seen and another understood. What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has a spiritual fruit. But since it is a mystery, how is it called Christ’s body and blood? Almighty God, taking thought for our weakness—for we are not accustomed to eat raw flesh and drink blood—causes those two gifts to remain in their former appearance, and yet they are truly Christ’s body and blood, as he himself says.”]

### LXXIV. After consecration, although *here* the appearance of bread and wine remains, there is nevertheless nothing there except Christ’s body and blood. Likewise Ambrose.

[Note: Col. 1771: Similar material occurs in book 4, *On the Sacraments*, a book commonly attributed to Ambrose; compare Paschasius, *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, chapter 1.]

“Whatever the Lord willed, he made in heaven and on earth” [Note: Col. 1771, Ps. 134:6]. And because he willed it [Note: Col. 1771: the Argentinian and Basel editions read, “he willed it, and so it was done”; the remaining editions, “he willed it; thus it was done”], although here the appearance of bread and wine remains [Note: Col. 1771: the collected editions read, “although the appearance of bread and wine seems to be here, nevertheless nothing else”], it must be believed that after consecration there is absolutely nothing else than Christ’s flesh and blood [Note: Col. 1771: the collected editions read the singular, “it must be believed”]. Hence Truth himself says to the disciples [Note: Col. 1771, John 6:52]: “This is my flesh for the life of the world.” And, to speak more wonderfully, it is plainly none other than that which was born of Mary, suffered on the cross, and rose from the tomb: it is this very flesh, I say. And therefore Christ’s flesh is what is still offered today for the life of the world, and, when it is received worthily [Note: Col. 1771: “is received”: collected editions], certainly works eternal life in us.

The bread, indeed, which we receive in the mystery, I understand to be that bread which was formed by the hand of the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb and baked by the fire of passion upon the altar of the cross. For the bread of angels became the food of human beings [Note: Col. 1771, Ps. 77:25]; hence he himself says [Note: Col. 1771, John 6:51–52]: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” [Note: Col. 1771: “of life”: Basel edition; “came down”: Basel, Nuremberg, and Venice I and II editions], and again [Note: Col. 1771: “again”: Basel edition]: “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.” From these two statements it is plainly given to understand that this bread and that bread are not two breads, but one bread and one flesh, undoubtedly constituting one body: truly and certainly that body which was taken from the Virgin, which suffered and was buried, which rose [Note: Col. 1771: “and which”: Basel edition; “rose again”: collected editions except Paris and Lyons], ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father, and will come to judge the living and the dead.

[Note: Col. 1771D: These words to the end, also reported by the Master, are not read in this place in Paschasius or Rabanus. But something similar occurs in Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 67.]

### LXXV. Although Christ is eaten daily, he nevertheless remains whole and living. Likewise Augustine, from a sermon on the words of the Lord.

[Note: Col. 1772C: Nearly the same material occurs above in the chapter “Whoever eats,” and the chapter “He invites.”]

[Note: Col. 1771: Compare above, chapters 58 and 70.]

“Whoever eats me lives because of me” [Note: Col. 1771, John 6:58]. *Therefore, brothers, let us not fear to eat this bread, lest perhaps we consume him and afterwards find nothing to eat.* [Note: Col. 1771: “lest perhaps” is absent from the collected editions except the Argentinian and Basel editions.] Let Christ be eaten: when eaten he lives, because he rose when slain; nor, when we eat, do we make parts of him. Indeed this is so in the sacrament, and the faithful know how they eat Christ’s flesh [Note: Col. 1771: “flesh or body”: Basel and Lyons II and III editions]. Each receives his own portion, whence the very gifts are called portions in the sacrament [Note: Col. 1771: “in the sacrament”: the same editions]. He is eaten in portions and remains wholly entire; he is eaten in portions in the sacrament and remains wholly entire in heaven; he remains wholly entire in your heart. For he was wholly with the Father when he came into the Virgin; he filled her and did not depart from him. He came into flesh [Note: Col. 1771: “in flesh”: collected editions] so that human beings might eat him [Note: Col. 1771: “eat or consume”: Argentinian edition], and remained whole with the Father so that he might feed the angels.

### LXXVI. No one may eat Christ’s body and blood according to itself. Likewise Jerome on Leviticus.

[Note: Col. 1771: This is not in Jerome. A similar passage occurs in Origen, Homily 7 on Leviticus 10.]

Of this victim, indeed, which is wonderfully made in commemoration of Christ, it is lawful to eat; but of that which Christ offered upon the altar of the cross, no one may eat according to itself.

### LXXVII. In individual portions, individual persons receive Christ wholly. Likewise, in the sermon for the fifth Sunday after Epiphany.

[Note: Col. 1771: Ivo, *Decree*, part 2, chapter 7.]

[Note: Col. 1772D: It occurs in the Ambrosian Missal in the preface for the fifth Sunday after Epiphany, and also in ancient prefaces for the same Sunday. Alger and Ivo cite it from Ambrose, although the Master cites Jerome. Guitmund says that it is from a preface sung throughout the Latin world.]

[Note: Col. 1771: “Theophany”: Ivo.]

Each receives Christ the Lord, and in every portion he is whole; nor is he diminished by individual persons, but offers himself entire in each.

### LXXVIII. On the same subject. Likewise Hilary.

[Note: Col. 1773: “Pope Hilary”: collected editions. It is in the fifth homily after Easter, attributed to Eusebius, Eucherius, or Hilary.]

Where there is a part of the body, there is also the whole. The same principle applies to the Lord’s body as to manna, which preceded in its figure and concerning which it is said [Note: Col. 1773, Exod. 16:18]: “He who had gathered more had no surplus, nor did he who had prepared less find less” [Note: Col. 1773: “had”: collected editions]. In this mystery, visible quantity is not to be assessed at all [Note: Col. 1773: “for” is added in the same editions except Basel]; rather, what is to be assessed is the spiritual power of the sacrament [Note: Col. 1773: “is” is absent from those editions except Basel, Paris, and Lyons].

### LXXIX. Christ’s body which is received is figure in appearance and truth in substance. The same author.

[Note: Col. 1773C: Ivo also cites this from Hilary and, below, in the same chapter “In Christ,” at the end, it is reported together with Hilary’s words, although it has not been found in Hilary. Alger cites Augustine, *On the Sacrament of the Altar*. Nearly the same material occurs in Paschasius, chapter 4, and in others who treat this same question.]

[Note: Col. 1773: Ivo, *Decree*, part 2, chapter 7; compare below, chapter 82.]

Christ’s body, which is received from the altar, is a figure while bread and wine are outwardly seen; but it is truth while Christ’s body and blood are believed inwardly in truth.

### LXXX. We receive at the altar life-giving flesh, made the very flesh of the Word. Likewise from the Ephesian Creed.

[Note: Col. 1773C: This chapter, compressed into almost excessive brevity, has been restored to its full integrity, chiefly from the original.]

[Note: Col. 1773: Rather, from the letter of Cyril and the Synod of Alexandria to Nestorius, first translated into Latin by Dionysius Exiguus; Ivo, *Decree*, part 2, chapter 4.]

Therefore we necessarily add this also. “*For, proclaiming according to the flesh the death of the only-begotten Son of God, that is, Jesus Christ, and likewise confessing his resurrection and ascension into heaven,*” we celebrate in the churches the bloodless service of sacrifice. “*Thus we also approach the mystical blessings*” and are sanctified, made participants in the “*holy*” body and precious blood of Christ, “*the redeemer of us all,*” not receiving common flesh—“*(far be it)*”—nor as of a man sanctified and joined to the Word according to a unity of dignity, “*or as one possessing a divine indwelling,*” but as flesh truly life-giving and made the very own flesh of the Word.

[Note: Col. 1773: “ecclesiastical sacrifices”: Basel edition.]

[Note: Col. 1773: “life-giving”: collected editions except Basel.]

### LXXXI. How manna and water from the rock were the same as our food and drink. Likewise Augustine, Tractate XXVI on John chapter 6.

[Note: Col. 1774C: This matter is explained more fully by Blessed Augustine. But Ivo has it almost as Gratian does.]

[Note: Col. 1773: Ivo, *Decree*, part 2, chapter 4.]

The Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1773] 1 Corinthians, ch. 10, v. 3]: “All ate the same spiritual food” [Col. 1774A]. “Spiritual,” certainly, the same; for bodily food was different [Note: [Col. 1773] “bodily food was different” is absent from the Argentinian edition], because they had manna [Note: [Col. 1773] added: “they ate”: editions compared with the original], whereas we had something else. And he adds [Note: [Col. 1773] 1 Cor., same place, v. 4]: “And all drank the same spiritual drink.” One thing for them, another for us—but in visible appearance. Yet it is the same [Note: [Col. 1773] “in”: Böhm] in spiritual efficacy.

### C. LXXXII. That we receive the reality of the Lord’s body and blood. Likewise, Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book VIII [Note: [Col. 1773] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, ch. 4.]

**Part XXIII.** The Father in Christ and Christ in us make us one in these things. Therefore, if Christ truly [Note: [Col. 1773] “truly” is absent from the editions compared with the original, except Lyons II and III] assumed the flesh of our body, and if that man who was born of Mary truly is Christ [Note: [Col. 1773] “is”: Lyons II and III; the words “who—was” are absent from the remaining editions], and if we truly receive, under the mystery, the flesh of his body [Note: [Col. 1773] absent from Ivo; “his own”: editions compared with the original] [Col. 1774B], then through this we shall be one, because the Father is in him and he in us. How, then, can a unity of will be asserted, when natural property through the sacrament is the sacrament of perfect unity [Note: [Col. 1773] “perfect”: editions compared with the original]?

We must not speak of the things of God according to human or worldly understanding [Note: [Col. 1773] “of these things”: editions compared with the original], nor is the perversity of an alien and impious interpretation to be wrested from the soundness of heavenly sayings by violence [Note: [Col. 1773] “violence”: the same editions, except Lyons II and III; Ivo] and shameless proclamation [Note: [Col. 1773] “preacher”: Argentinian edition]. “Let us read what has been written, understand what we have read, and then perform the office of perfect faith.” [Note: [Col. 1774C] These words through “concerning the natural …” were added from the original, along with certain other passages that seemed to contribute to the integrity of the sense.] For what we say concerning the natural reality of Christ in us—unless we learn it from him [Note: [Col. 1773] Basel: “unless we have said it and learned it from him”; Ivo and editions compared with the original: “unless we have learned it”]—we say foolishly and impiously [Note: [Col. 1773] Ivo and editions compared with the original, except Lyons II and III: “we shall say”].

For he himself says [Note: [Col. 1773] John, ch. 6, v. 56]: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, [Col. 1774C] and I in him.” No room for doubt has been left concerning the reality of the flesh and blood. For now, both by the Lord’s own declaration and by our faith, it is truly flesh and truly blood; and, received and drunk, these bring it about that we are in Christ and Christ is in us. Is this not reality? [Note: [Col. 1773] The words “Is this not reality?” and what follows through “we are in him” are absent from the editions compared with the original, except Lyons II and III.] Let it indeed fail to be true for those who deny that Christ Jesus is true God. Therefore he himself is in us through the flesh, and [Col. 1775A] we are in him, while, according to that which we are, he is in God [Note: [Col. 1775] Original: “with himself”]. [Note: [Col. 1775] §§ 1 and 2 are omitted by Ivo.]

§ 1. Moreover, that we are in him through the sacrament of the flesh and blood which we share, he himself testifies, saying [Note: [Col. 1775] John, ch. 14, v. 19]: “And now the world does not see me; but you will see me, because I live and you shall live, because I am in my Father [Note: [Col. 1775] Editions compared with the original: “I abide”], and you in me, and I in you.” [Note: [Col. 1775] The words “And now—the world sees” are absent from the editions compared with the original, except Lyons II and III.] If he had meant only a unity of will, why did he set forth a certain rank and order by which unity is consummated? Was it not so that, since he was in the Father by the nature of divinity [Note: [Col. 1775] The words “since he was” are absent from the same editions, except Lyons II and III], we, conversely, might be believed to be in him through his bodily birth, and he again in us through the mystery of the sacraments’ indwelling [Note: [Col. 1775] Basel: “may be believed”], and so perfect unity through the mediator might be taught? Thus, while we abide in him, he abides in the Father; and, abiding in the Father, he himself [Note: [Col. 1775] absent from editions compared with the original, except Lyons II and III] abides [Col. 1775B] in us; and thus we advance [Note: [Col. 1775] absent from the same editions; editions compared with the original: “we might advance”] to the unity of the Father, since we too are naturally in him who is naturally present according to his birth [Note: [Col. 1775] Basel adds: “eternal”], he himself naturally remaining in us.

§ 2. But that this unity is natural in us [Note: [Col. 1775] Editions compared with the original, except Lyons II and III: “naturally”], he testified thus [Note: [Col. 1775] John, ch. 6, v. 57]: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.” For no one [Note: [Col. 1775] absent from editions compared with the original, except Lyons II and III] will be in him unless Christ himself is in him, having taken into himself only [Note: [Col. 1775] Editions compared with the original: “nevertheless”] the flesh of him who has assumed his own flesh [Note: [Col. 1775] Editions compared with the original, except Lyons II and III: “had assumed”].

“But he had already taught above the sacrament of this perfect unity, saying: ‘As the living Father sent me, and I live through [Note: [Col. 1775] Vulgate and editions compared with the original, except Basel: “because of”] the Father, so whoever eats my flesh shall himself live through [Note: [Col. 1775] Same edition group: “because of”] me.’ Therefore he lives through the Father, and in the same way as he lives through the Father, we shall live through his flesh [Col. 1775C] [Note: [Col. 1775] Original and Basel: “we live”]. For every comparison is adopted as a pattern for understanding, so that we may grasp the matter at issue in accordance with the proposed example.”

§ 3. This, then, is the cause of our life: that we, being fleshly [Note: [Col. 1775] absent from editions compared with the original, except Lyons II and III], have Christ abiding in us through the flesh [Note: [Col. 1775] Argentinian edition: “that God may abide in you”; Basel: “God abiding”; Nuremberg, Venice I and II, and Paris: “that God abide”], and that we who are to live [Note: [Col. 1775] Editions compared with the original: “about to live”] live through him under the same condition in which he lives through the Father. [Note: [Col. 1775] The words “If therefore—we live through the Father” are absent from the Argentinian edition.] Therefore, if we naturally live through him according to the flesh—that is, if we have received the nature of his flesh—how can he not naturally have the Father in himself according to the Spirit, when he himself lives through the Father?

Likewise below [Col. 1776A] [Note: [Col. 1775] The following material through the end is not found in Ivo]:

§ 4. These things have been recalled by us because heretics, falsely asserting that there is only a unity of will between Father and Son, employed our unity with God [Note: [Col. 1775] Editions compared with the original, except Basel and Lyons II and III: “the Lord”] as an example, as though we were united to the Son, and through the Son to the Father, only by religious obedience and will, and as though no proper natural communion of flesh and blood were granted through the sacrament [Note: [Col. 1775] Editions compared with the original: “or”]. Yet, through the honour given to us by the Son of God [Note: [Col. 1775] Argentinian edition: “the Son gives”; remaining editions, except Lyons II and III: “the Son gives the honour”], through the Son abiding bodily in us [Note: [Col. 1775] absent from editions compared with the original, except Lyons II and III], and through our bodily and inseparable union in him [Note: [Col. 1775] Editions compared with the original: “and we”], the mystery of true and natural unity must be proclaimed.

Likewise [Note: [Col. 1775C] Formerly it read “that is” [thus Argentinian and Basel editions]. It has been corrected from ancient manuscripts. On this passage see above, the same chapter, “Body.”] [Note: [Col. 1775] Compare above, ch. 79]:

§ 1. The body of Christ received from the altar is a figure, insofar as bread and wine are outwardly seen; but it is reality insofar as the body and blood of Christ are inwardly believed in truth.

[Col. 1776B]

### C. LXXXIII. Why water is mixed with wine in the sacrifice. Likewise, Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book V, ch. 1 [Note: [Col. 1776C] This chapter, compiled and reduced to a summary from the indicated passages of St Ambrose, has been corrected from the original and enlarged in several places.] [Note: [Col. 1775] It is not by Ambrose.]

**Part XXIV.** Wine is put into the cup [Note: [Col. 1775] Editions compared with the original, except Lyons II and III: “into the cup”]—and what else? Water. But you say to me [Note: [Col. 1775] Editions compared with the original, especially Basel: “you will say”]: How, then, did Melchizedek [Note: [Col. 1775] Compare Gen. ch. 14, v. 18] offer bread and wine? What is the meaning of the admixture of water? “Hear the explanation. And after a few intervening words: God commanded Moses to touch the rock, and the rock poured out a great stream of water, as the Apostle says” [Note: [Col. 1775] 1 Cor. ch. 10, v. 10]: “They drank from the rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.” It was not an immovable rock, since it followed the people. You too, drink, that Christ may follow you. See the mystery. Moses—that is, the prophet; the rod—that is, the word of God. The priest touches the rock with the word of God; water flows, and God’s people drink.

“The priest therefore touches [Col. 1776C] the cup”; water overflows in the cup, springs up into eternal life, “and the people of God drink, having obtained grace. Have you learned this? Receive [Note: [Col. 1775] Editions compared with the original, except Basel and Paris: “Receive”; Basel adds: “and see”] another point” [Note: [Col. 1775] Editions compared with the original: “that point”].

And after a few intervening words:

§ 2. From his side [Note: [Col. 1775] Compare John, ch. 19, v. 34] flowed water [Note: [Col. 1775] Editions compared with the original: “flowed out”] and blood [Note: [Col. 1775] “and blood, water” is absent from Venice II and Paris]. Why water? Why blood? Water, that it might cleanse; blood, that it might redeem. Why from the side? Because grace came from the same source as guilt: guilt through a woman, grace through the Lord Jesus Christ.

Likewise, ch. 3:

§ 3. Hear the Psalm. See how suited it is to the heavenly sacraments [Note: [Col. 1775] Ps. 22, vv. 1, 4]: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing,” etc. “Your rod and your staff [Note: [Col. 1777] Editions compared with the original add: “etc.”], they have comforted me.” The rod is authority [Note: [Col. 1777] Basel, Paris, and Lyons editions: “is the authority of divinity”]—that is, Christ’s eternal divinity [Note: [Col. 1777] Editions compared with the original: “Deity”]; the staff is his bodily passion. The former created; the latter redeemed [Note: [Col. 1777] Ps., same place, v. 5]. “You have prepared before me a table,” etc., and “your intoxicating cup—how excellent it is” [Note: [Col. 1777] Argentinian edition, following the Vulgate: “the cup that intoxicates me, how excellent it is”; Basel: “my” for “your”].

(And below:)

§ 4. Whenever you drink, you receive forgiveness of sins and are intoxicated “in” the Spirit [Note: [Col. 1777] Basel and Lyons II and III add: “Holy”]. Hence the Apostle “says” [Note: [Col. 1777] Eph. ch. 5, v. 18]: “Do not become intoxicated with wine, but be filled [Note: [Col. 1777] Vulgate and editions compared with the original, except Basel, Paris, and Lyons II and III: “be filled”] with the Holy Spirit.” For one intoxicated with wine wavers and staggers; one intoxicated with the Spirit is rooted in Christ. Therefore it is “a splendid [Note: [Col. 1777] “Splendid—mind” is absent from the Argentinian edition] intoxication” [Note: [Col. 1777] Editions compared with the original, except Basel: “is an intoxication”], which produces sobriety [Note: [Col. 1777] Basel: “through sobriety”] of mind.

Likewise, ch. 4:

§ 5. “May your will be done, as in heaven also upon earth. Give us this day our daily bread,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1777] Matt. ch. 6, v. 10.] By Christ’s blood all things have been reconciled [Col. 1777B] [Note: [Col. 1777] Lyons II and III: “all things in heaven and earth”; remaining editions: “all things either in heaven or on earth”], whether in heaven or on earth. Heaven was sanctified; the devil was cast down, where [Note: [Col. 1777] Original: “there, where both the enemy and man dwell”] man dwells—the man whom he deceived.

And shortly afterward:

§ 6. I told you that before Christ’s words are spoken, what is offered is called bread [Note: [Col. 1777] Basel and Paris: “is called”]. Once Christ’s words have been brought forth, it is no longer called bread, but is called body. Why, then, in the Lord’s Prayer, “which follows afterward,” does he say [Note: [Col. 1777] Matt. ch. 6, v. 11], “Our bread”? He did indeed say “bread” [Note: [Col. 1777] Editions compared with the original: “for”], but he said ἐπιούσιον (*epiousion*), that is, “supersubstantial.”

### C. LXXXIV. We eat the true flesh of Christ and drink his true blood. The same author, book VI of *On the Sacraments*, ch. 1.

[Col. 1777C]

**Part XXV.** Just as our Lord Jesus Christ is the true Son of God—not as human beings are sons through grace, but as Son from the substance of the Father—so the flesh which we receive is true flesh of Christ [Note: [Col. 1777] Editions compared with the original: “Christ’s flesh is true”; compare John 6:56], as he himself said, and his blood is true drink [Note: [Col. 1777] “It is drink.” After these words, the original continues with the chapter “Perhaps,” above in the same place].

Likewise shortly afterward:

§ 1. “I,” he says [Note: [Col. 1777] John, same place, v. 51], “am the living bread which came down from heaven.” But the flesh did not come down from [Note: [Col. 1777] Editions compared with the original: “from”] heaven—“that is, he assumed flesh on earth from the Virgin.” How, then, did “the bread” come down from [Note: [Col. 1777] Same editions: “from”] heaven, “and” how is it living bread? Because the same “our” Lord Jesus “Christ shares both” in divinity and body. And you, because [Note: [Col. 1777] Editions compared with the original: “who”] you receive the bread, [Col. 1778A] participate in his divine substance in that food [Note: [Col. 1777] Same editions: “you participate”].

### C. LXXXV. In the sacrifice we receive not bodily but spiritual food. Likewise, in the book *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*, ch. 9.

In that sacrament Christ is present, because it is Christ’s body. Therefore it is not bodily food, but spiritual food. Hence the Apostle says of its type [Note: [Col. 1777] 1 Cor. ch. 10, v. 3] that our fathers ate spiritual food [Note: [Col. 1777] Editions compared with the original, following the Vulgate: “the same spiritual food”] and “drank spiritual drink.” For God’s body is a spiritual body; Christ’s body is the body of the divine Spirit.

[Col. 1778B]

### C. LXXXVI. We offer the flesh assumed by Christ and the body transfigured on the altar. Likewise, in the sermon on Abel and Cain, that is, in the book *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation*, ch. 4.

If you believe [Note: [Col. 1777] Editions compared with the original: “you believe”] that flesh was assumed by Christ, and offer a body to be transfigured [Note: [Col. 1777] Same editions: “a transfigured body on the altar”] on the altars, yet fail to distinguish [Note: [Col. 1777] Same editions: “you do not distinguish”] the nature of the Word and of the body [Note: [Col. 1777] Same editions, except the Argentinian: “the body of Christ”], then it is said to you [Note: [Col. 1777] Gen. ch. 4, v. 7, according to the Septuagint]: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.”

### C. LXXXVII. At the supper Christ was both guest and banquet. Likewise, Jerome to Hedibia, question II [Note: [Col. 1777] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, ch. 5.]

Moses did not give us [Note: [Col. 1777] Editions compared with the original: “you”] true bread [Note: [Col. 1777] Basel: “living”], but the Lord Jesus [Note: [Col. 1777] Basel adds: “Christ”] himself was both guest [Note: [Col. 1777] Argentinian and Basel: “is a guest”] and banquet: himself eating, and himself being eaten.

[Col. 1778C]

### C. LXXXVIII. In the reality of his body and blood, Christ presented to his disciples what Melchizedek sacramentally offered. Likewise, Jerome on Matthew, book IV, on ch. 26.

“Take [Note: [Col. 1777] Matt. ch. 26, v. 26] and eat: this is my body.” After the typical Passover had been completed [Note: [Col. 1777] Editions compared with the original: “was completed”], and he had eaten the flesh of the lamb with the Apostles, he takes [Note: [Col. 1777] Same editions, except Argentinian: “he took”] bread, which strengthens [Note: [Col. 1777] Same editions, except Basel: “is the strengthener of”] the human heart [Note: [Col. 1777] Ps. 103, v. 15], and passes to the true sacrament of the Passover [Note: [Col. 1777] Lyons II and III: “passed”; remaining editions: “passes”]. Thus, just as Melchizedek, “priest of the Most High God” [Note: [Col. 1777] Gen. ch. 14, v. 18], had acted in its prefiguration by offering bread and wine, Christ himself might also present it in the reality of his body and blood [Note: [Col. 1777] Original: “in the reality of his body”].

[Col. 1779A]

### C. LXXXIX. Christ is both priest and sacrifice. The same author, in the book *On the Members of the Lord*, otherwise entitled *On Things Attributed to God in Scripture* [Note: [Col. 1779] It is not by Jerome.]

The Son of God is called [Note: [Col. 1779] Editions compared with the original: “is called”] priest of God the Father [Note: [Col. 1779] absent from the Argentinian edition], not according to his divinity but according to his humanity. In that humanity he offered himself to God the Father for us, through his passion and death, as an acceptable sacrifice, so that he himself might be [Note: [Col. 1779] Editions compared with the original: “may be”] both priest [Note: [Col. 1779] Same editions: “and is”] and sacrifice.

### C. XC. The Jews who believed drank the blood which they shed on the cross. Likewise, Augustine, book L of Homilies, sermon 27, *On the Benefit of Doing Penance* [Note: [Col. 1779] Sermon 352, Maurist edition.]

Then Peter announced to them [Note: [Col. 1779] Acts, ch. 2, v. 38] that they ought to worship him whom they had crucified, so that by believing they might drink his blood—the blood which they had shed [Note: [Col. 1779] Lyons II and III: “had shed”; remaining editions: “shed”] while thirsting [Note: [Col. 1779] Original and editions compared with it: “while raging”].

[Col. 1779B]

### C. XCI. The body taken from the Virgin is received by the faithful. Likewise, Ambrose, Letter LXII, otherwise book VIII, letter 1, to Irenaeus [Note: [Col. 1779] Written about A.D. 380; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, ch. 9.]

That bodily manna is now such a great miracle, because what is perfect has come; and the perfect bread from heaven is the body from the Virgin, concerning which the Gospel teaches you sufficiently. [Note: [Col. 1779D] “Is now”: In St Ambrose it reads: “And that bodily manna is indeed still found in many places today; but now the miracle is not so great, because there has come,” etc. Yet it has not been corrected because of the gloss.] [Note: [Col. 1779] Argentinian: “is from”; Basel and Nuremberg: “is from”; remaining editions: “is the body born of the Virgin.”]

### C. XCII. We daily eat Christ’s true body and drink his true blood. Likewise, Augustine on Psalm XXXIII [Note: [Col. 1779] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2, ch. 9.]

The Jews came to Jesus in order to crucify him; let us come to him in order to receive his body and blood. [Note: [Col. 1779] Sermon 2 on Psalm 33.]

Likewise below:

§ 1. Truly great is the Lord [Col. 1779C] [Note: [Col. 1779] Ivo and editions compared with the original: “God”], and truly great is his mercy, who gave us his body to eat, in which he suffered such great things, and his blood [Note: [Col. 1779] Ivo and same editions add: “his”] to drink.

Likewise, on Psalm 45, addressed to the Jews:

§ 2. Now drink securely the blood which you shed. [Note: [Col. 1779] This passage through “they shed” is absent from Ivo, as is the material following § 3.]

Likewise, on Psalm 65:

§ 3. The blood which they shed through madness, they drank through grace.

Likewise, on Psalm 98:

§ 4. From Mary’s flesh he took flesh. “And because he walked here in that flesh,” [Col. 1780A] he gave that same flesh “to us” to eat for salvation [Note: [Col. 1779] Editions compared with the original: “for eating”]. But no one eats that flesh unless he has first adored it.

Likewise, on Psalm 33 [Note: [Col. 1779] Sermon 1 on Psalm 33]:

§ 5. David [Note: [Col. 1779] 1 Sam. ch. 21, v. 13] “was carried” [Note: [Col. 1779D] In the common Greek text it is παρεφέρετο (*parephereto*), that is, “he was staggering”] in his own hands. No one is carried in his own hands. How this is to be understood of David himself, we do not find according to the letter; but we do find it in Christ. For Christ was carried in his own hands when, commending his own body, he said [Note: [Col. 1779] Matt. ch. 26, v. 26]: “This is my body.” That body was carried in his own hands [Note: [Col. 1779] Original: “he carried”].

The same author, *Tractates on John*, tractate 21:

§ 6. Until they drank [Note: [Col. 1779] Basel: “had drunk”] the blood which they had shed [Note: [Col. 1779] Editions compared with the original: “shed”], they despaired of their salvation.

Likewise, on Psalm 54 [Note: [Col. 1779] This seems rather to refer to Augustine on Psalm 100]:

§ 7. The Jews fed, as it were, upon the Lord’s punishment. “For” we too feed upon the Lord’s cross, because we eat his body. And below: Therefore the impious have their feasts [Col. 1780B], and the pious also have theirs. “Hear the feast of the pious”: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” [Note: [Col. 1779] Matt. ch. 5, v. 6].

### C. XCIII. A presbyter should always have the eucharist prepared for the sick. Likewise, from the Council of Worms [Note: [Col. 1779] Rather from the Frankish Royal Capitularies, book 1, ch. 155; Regino, book 1, ch. 69 (“from synodal capitularies”; compare Walter of Orléans, *Capitula*, ch. 7); Burchard, book 5, ch. 10; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, ch. 145; *Decretum*, part 2, ch. 20.]

**Part XXVI.** A presbyter should always have the eucharist prepared, so that, when [Note: [Col. 1779] Argentinian: “when”; Basel: “whenever”] anyone becomes ill [Note: [Col. 1780D] In Burchard and Ivo, which likewise cite the Council of Worms, ch. 5, and in the *Capitularies*, book 1, ch. 161, these words are inserted after this point: “or when a little child is ill”] [Note: [Col. 1779] *Capitularies* and Regino: “becomes sick”], he may immediately communicate that person, lest the person die without communion.

### C. XCIV. The penance of one who does not keep the sacrament properly. Likewise, from the Council of Arles [Note: [Col. 1779] Found among Theodore’s chapters in Petit, ch. 55; Burchard, book 5, ch. 51; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, ch. 157; *Decretum*, part 2, ch. 60. Burchard, Ivo’s *Panormia*, and the Argentinian, Basel, Nuremberg, Lyons II and III editions attribute it to Orléans.]

**Part XXVII.** Whoever does not guard the sacrament properly, and a mouse or some other animal eats it, shall do penance for forty days [Note: [Col. 1779] Theodore: “days”; Burchard and Ivo: “day”]. But whoever loses it [Col. 1780C] in church, or if part of it falls and is not found, shall do penance for thirty [Note: [Col. 1779] Theodore and Burchard: “twenty”] days [Note: [Col. 1779] Basel: “for thirty day”].

### C. XCV. Sacred mysteries are not to be entrusted to actors. Cyprian greets his brother Eucratius, book I, letter 10 [Note: [Col. 1779] Written about A.D. 256; Burchard, book 5, ch. 21; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, ch. 153; *Decretum*, part 2, ch. 31 and part 11, ch. 83.]

**Part XXVIII.** Because of your affection [Note: [Col. 1779] Original: “your mutual affection and true regard”; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2: “your affection and true mutual regard”; *Panormia*: “your affection and regard”; Burchard: “your affection and regard, so that”] and mutual regard, dearest brother [Col. 1781A], you considered that I should be consulted on what seems right to me concerning a certain actor [Note: [Col. 1781] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 2: “that actor”; Burchard, Ivo’s *Panormia*, and editions compared with the original: “that actor and magician”], who lives among you and still persists in the disgrace [Note: [Col. 1781] Venice I and II: “decoration”] of that same profession [Note: [Col. 1781] Same witnesses: “still in the disgrace of his profession”]. He is both master and teacher, not of boys to be instructed but of boys to be ruined; and what he learned wickedly [Note: [Col. 1781] Lyons II: “learns”; Basel and Venice II: “says”], he also instils in others [Note: [Col. 1781] absent from Ivo’s *Decretum* and *Panormia*; Argentinian: “in all others”]. Should such a person communicate with us? [Note: [Col. 1781] Burchard, Ivo’s *Decretum* and *Panormia*, and editions compared with the original: “whether such a person ought to be given sacred communion with the other Christians, or ought to communicate with you”; Ivo’s *Decretum* and *Panormia* omit “or”; Burchard: “with us”; Basel: “with us”; Burchard and *Panormia* omit “ought to.”] “For I” [Note: [Col. 1781] “For I” is absent from Burchard, Ivo’s *Panormia*, and *Decretum*, part 2] do not think [Note: [Col. 1781] “I think” is absent from Burchard and *Panormia*] that it accords either with the divine majesty or with evangelical discipline for the modesty and honour of the Church to be defiled by so shameful and infamous a contagion.

### C. XCVI. After conversion, the grace of communion is not to be denied. Likewise, from the Third Council of Carthage, ch. 35 [Note: [Col. 1781] Held A.D. 397; Collection in Three Parts, part 2, title 17, ch. 25; compare Burchard, book 4, ch. 36; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 1, ch. 230.]

Actors, performers, and other persons of that sort [Col. 1782A], as well as apostates who have converted or [Note: [Col. 1781] “or return” is absent from Basel] returned to the Lord [Note: [Col. 1781] Basel and the Hispanic Collection: “to God”], are not to be denied grace or reconciliation.

### C. XCVII. A presbyter is not to celebrate Mass at an altar where a bishop has celebrated on the same day. Likewise, from the Council of Urbicus [Note: [Col. 1781] The ruling occurs in ch. 10 of the Council of Auxerre, held A.D. 578; Burchard, book 3, ch. 226; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 2, ch. 35; *Decretum*, part 3, ch. 270.]

At an altar where a bishop has sung Mass, a presbyter must not presume to celebrate another on the same day.

## DISTINCTIO III

[Col. 1781]

[Col. 1781B] **GRATIAN.**

### C. I. The times for refraining from work are to be announced to the laity during Mass. Likewise, from the Council of Lyons [Note: [Col. 1781] Found in the chapters of Haito of Basel, ch. 8 (Harzheim, vol. 2); Burchard, book 2, ch. 77; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, ch. 14; compare the *Capitularies*, book 1, ch. 164, book 2, ch. 35, and the Council of Mainz, A.D. 813, ch. 36.]

**Part I.** The laity are to be informed [Note: [Col. 1781C] “Laity” is absent from the Vatican copies, Burchard, and Ivo; Basel, Paris, and Lyons I: “It is to be announced that the laity”; Lyons II and III: “It is to be announced to the laity”] so that they may know the times for refraining from work throughout the year: namely, every Sunday from evening to evening, lest they be ensnared by Judaism [Note: [Col. 1781] Burchard: “in Judaizing”; editions compared with the original, except Lyons II and III: “from Judaizing”].

The days of rest during the year are these: the Nativity of the Lord; St Stephen; St John the Evangelist; the Holy Innocents; St Silvester; the Octaves [Note: [Col. 1781] Original and editions compared with it: “octave”; Burchard: “octave of the Nativity of the Lord”] of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1781C] “Octaves of the Lord”: this reading occurs in most ancient copies, in the *Capitularies*, in Ivo, and in nearly all other ancient writers, except Burchard. Nevertheless, the eighth day of the Nativity itself is meant. Why the plural number was used is explained by Alcuin in the chapter *On the Octave of the Lord*], and the Theophany [Note: [Col. 1781] Original: “Theophany”; Burchard and Ivo: “Theophania”]; the Purification of St Mary; holy Easter with the whole week; the Rogation Days for three days; the Ascension [Note: [Col. 1781] Argentinian and Basel: “of the Ascension”] of the Lord; the holy days of Pentecost; St John the Baptist; the twelve Apostles, but especially [Note: [Col. 1781] Lyons II and III: “and especially”] Saints Peter and Paul, [Col. 1781C] who enlightened the world [Note: [Col. 1781] Original: “Europe”] by their preaching; St Lawrence; the Assumption of St Mary; the Nativity [Note: [Col. 1781] Nuremberg, Venice I and II, and Paris: “of the Nativity”; “Nativity—Mary” is absent from the original; Ivo: “of the same”] of St Mary [Note: [Col. 1781] Burchard and Basel add: “Virgin”]; the dedication of a church [Note: [Col. 1781] Original, Burchard, and Ivo: “basilica”; Basel omits it]; St Michael the Archangel; the dedication of any oratory; All Saints; St Martin; and those feasts which individual bishops approve with the people in their own dioceses [Note: [Col. 1781] Burchard: “bishoprics”; in Haito this is reported more briefly]. These are to be announced only to those dwelling nearby, not generally to all [Col. 1782B].

For the remaining feasts of the year [Note: [Col. 1781] Original, Burchard, and Ivo: “remaining”; Basel: “remaining”], people are not to be compelled to refrain from work [Note: [Col. 1781] Original, Burchard, Ivo, and Basel: feminine “to be compelled”], nor are they to be forbidden [Note: [Col. 1781] Burchard, Ivo, and Basel: feminine “to be forbidden”; original: singular “to forbid”]. But whenever an appointed fast has been proclaimed [Note: [Col. 1781] Original adds: “by the palace or by the household”], it is to be observed by all.

### C. II. On saints’ solemnities the people should devote themselves to divine offices, not to dancing or songs. Likewise, from the Third Council of Toledo, ch. 23 [Note: [Col. 1781] Held A.D. 589; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, ch. 12.]

It is an irreligious custom which the common people habitually practise on saints’ solemnities. People who ought to attend to divine offices give their attention to dancing “and” indecent songs [Note: [Col. 1781] Ivo and editions compared with the original: “they give attention to dancing and indecent songs, singing not only bad songs but also …”], harming not only themselves, [Col. 1782C] but also creating a noisy disturbance during the offices of the religious [Note: [Col. 1781] Editions compared with the original: “they create a disturbance”]. That this may be banished from every province [Note: [Col. 1781] Hispanic Collection: “from all Spain”; Ivo: “from all provinces”], the holy council entrusts its care to priests and judges [Note: [Col. 1781] Argentinian and Venice I and II: “counsel”; Argentinian: “court”].

[Col. 1783A]

### C. III. Litanies are to be celebrated for three days before the Lord’s Ascension. Likewise, from the First Council of Orléans, ch. 29 [Note: [Col. 1783] Held A.D. 511; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, ch. 11.]

It has been decided that Rogation Days, that is, litanies, are to be celebrated before the Lord’s Ascension, so that the preceding three-day fast shall be ended [Note: [Col. 1783] Ivo: “after Mass”] on the solemnity of the Lord’s Ascension [Note: [Col. 1783] Hispanic Collection: “after the fast preceding the solemnity”]. During these three days male and female servants are to be released from work [Note: [Col. 1783] Hispanic Collection adds: “all”], so that the whole people may gather more fully. During those three days all are to abstain and also [Note: [Col. 1783] Editions compared with the original add: “also”] use Lenten foods.

### C. IV. A bishop must not be absent from church on Sunday. Likewise, from the same council, ch. 33.

Unless prevented by illness, a bishop must not be absent on Sunday from the church nearest to him.

[Col. 1783B]

### C. V. Townspeople may not celebrate these days in the countryside. Likewise, from the same council, ch. 27 [Note: [Col. 1783] Burchard, book 2, ch. 75; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, ch. 12.]

No townsman [Note: [Col. 1783] Editions compared with the original add: “ever”] may celebrate in a country estate the solemnity of Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, and [Note: [Col. 1783] Basel: “or”] Lent [Col. 1783D] [Note: [Col. 1783] The printed original also reads “and Lent.” But Ivo has “or Quinquagesima” [thus the Hispanic Collection]. Burchard has “or Pentecost,” as do the Council of Agde, ch. 63, and the Council of Clermont, ch. 14], unless illness is proved to have confined him there [Note: [Col. 1783] Editions compared with the original: “is permitted”].

### C. VI. Lent is to be observed before the solemnity of Easter. Likewise, from the same Council of Orléans, ch. 26.

It is decreed for all priests that before the solemnity of Easter, not Quinquagesima but Lent is to be observed.

### C. VII. It is not permitted to end the fast on Thursday of the final week of Lent. Likewise, from the Council of Pope Martin of Braga, ch. 50 [Note: [Col. 1783] Ch. 50 of the Council of Laodicea, in Martin of Braga’s translation.]

It is not permitted on Thursday [Note: [Col. 1783] Editions compared with the original add: “brothers”] of the final week [Col. 1783C] to end the fast and dishonour all Lent [Note: [Col. 1783] Venice I and II: “adorn”]; rather, by sincerely abstaining [Note: [Col. 1783] Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I and II: “and”], they are to complete the whole of Lent [Note: [Col. 1783] Editions compared with the original and the Hispanic Collection: “pass through”; the Hispanic Collection adds: “using drier foods”].

### C. VIII. On the same matter. Likewise, from the Council of Laodicea, ch. 50 [Note: [Col. 1783] Held between A.D. 347 and 381; Burchard, book 13, ch. 8; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, ch. 41; they attribute it to Dionysius.]

It is not proper [Note: [Col. 1783] Hispanic Collection: “It is not proper in Lent”] in Lent to break the fast on Thursday of the final week [Note: [Col. 1783] “fast” is absent from the same source] and dishonour all Lent. Rather, during all “these” days [Note: [Col. 1783] Basel and Lyons II and III add: “of Lent”], they are to fast and use foods suitable to abstinence, that is, drier foods.

[Col. 1784A]

### C. IX. Except on Sundays, the fast is not to be broken in Lent. Likewise, from the Council of Agde, ch. 12 [Note: [Col. 1783] Held A.D. 506.]

It has been decided that all children [Note: [Col. 1783] Argentinian and Basel: “the faithful”; absent from the Hispanic Collection] of the Church, except on Sundays, shall fast in Lent even on Saturday, after priestly prayer [Note: [Col. 1784D] The council reads: “ordination, and under threat of strict discipline shall fast” [thus the Hispanic Collection]; it has not been altered because of the gloss] has been completed [Note: [Col. 1783] Argentinian adds: “completed”] and after receiving the communion of discernment [Note: [Col. 1783] Argentinian adds: “received”].

### C. X. Neither on Sunday nor during the days of Pentecost are knees to be bent in prayer. Likewise, from the Council of Nicaea, ch. 20 [Note: [Col. 1783] Held A.D. 325; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 4, ch. 18; Burchard, book 2, ch. 88, attributes it to Dionysius.]

Because there are some who bend their knees in prayer on Sunday and during the days of Pentecost, the holy synod has decreed [Note: [Col. 1783] Ivo and Basel: “therefore it has decreed”; remaining editions: “therefore it decrees”]—because a harmonious and fitting practice should be observed in all churches—that we should render our vows to the Lord while standing [Col. 1784B].

### C. XI. At what time abstinence from eating meat is required. Likewise, Pope Leo IV [Note: [Col. 1783] A chapter of uncertain date; Collection in Three Parts, part 1, title 60, ch. 7.]

**Part II.** Among you [Note: [Col. 1783] Editions compared with the original: “among us”], the most ancient and unobjectionable tradition concerning eating meat must always be maintained: from the end of supper, which is held at the beginning of the night preceding Wednesday, until the dawn of Thursday; and likewise from the supper of the night preceding Friday until the light of Saturday. Fasting is appropriately to be prolonged until daylight on Saturday, for whatever portion of the day each person may wish or ought to fast.

[Col. 1784C] C. XII. The Sabbath day is not to be kept as a holiday, nor is bathing on the Lord’s Day to be forbidden. Likewise, Gregory, to his most beloved fellow-citizens of Rome, Book XI, Epistle 3. [Note: [Col. 1783] Epistle 1 (written A.D. 603), Book 13, Maurist edition.—Ivo, Decrees, part 2, c. 4; and down to “Sabbath,” Panormia, Book 2, c. 169.]

Part III. It has come to my attention that certain men of perverse spirit have sown among you some wrong teachings contrary to the holy faith, so as to forbid any work from being done on the Sabbath day. What else can I call them but preachers of Antichrist? [Note: [Col. 1783] “Can we call”: Ivo.—Collected editions.] For when he comes, he will cause both the Sabbath day and the Lord’s Day to be observed as days free from all work. For, because he feigns that he has died and risen again, he wishes the Lord’s Day to be held in veneration; and because he will compel the people to Judaize [Note: [Col. 1783] “Compels”: Ivo, Decrees.—Basel edition.], so as to restore the outward rite of the Law and subject them to the unbelief of the Jews, [Col. 1785A] he wishes the Sabbath to be observed.

And a little later:

§ 1. Another matter has also been reported to me: that perverse men have preached to you that no one ought to bathe on the Lord’s Day. Certainly, if anyone wishes to bathe for luxury [Note: [Col. 1785] “For indulgence of mind”: original.—Ivo, Decrees.] and pleasure, we do not permit this even on any other day. But if it is for bodily necessity, we do not forbid it even on the Lord’s Day. [Note: [Col. 1785] “On Lord’s Days”: original.]

C. XIII. Out of reverence for the Lord’s burial, we ought to fast on Saturday. Likewise, Pope Innocent, Epistle I to Decentius, c. 4. [Note: [Col. 1785] Written A.D. 416.—Ivo, Panormia, Book 2, c. 177; Decrees, part 4, c. 28; Polycarpus, Book 3, title 25.]

Part IV. The clearest reasoning demonstrates that Saturday ought to be a fast. For if we celebrate the Lord’s Day not only at Easter because of the venerable resurrection of our Lord [Col. 1785B] Jesus Christ, but also repeatedly observe, through each weekly cycle, the representation of that day itself [Note: [Col. 1785] “Through each week”: collected editions.], and if, as [Note: [Col. 1785] “But as”: Lyons edition III.—“And as”: remaining editions.—“As if”: Hispanic Collection.] we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s Passion, we ought not to omit Saturday, because [Note: [Col. 1785] “That”: Hispanic Collection.—Coustant.] it appears enclosed between the sorrow and the joy of that time. [Note: [Col. 1785] “Time”: Hispanic Collection.—“To be”: added by Basel edition.] For it is certainly established that the Apostles, during these two days, were in mourning and hid themselves because of fear of the Jews. [Note: [Col. 1785] “Had hidden themselves”: collected editions.] And it is beyond doubt that they fasted so strictly during the two days mentioned that the Church’s tradition provides that the sacraments are not celebrated at all on those two days. [Note: [Col. 1785] “Sacrament”: Basel edition.]

This pattern, indeed, [Note: [Col. 1785] “Also”: added by collected editions.] must be observed every week, because the commemoration of that day is always to be celebrated. But if they think one must fast only once, on one Saturday, then [Col. 1785C] the Lord’s Day and Friday likewise would have to be celebrated only once, at Easter.

C. XIV. A fast is not to be observed on the Lord’s Day or on Thursday. Likewise, Pope Melchiades to the bishops of Spain, c. 3. [Note: [Col. 1785] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore, compiled from the Liber Pontificalis.—Ivo, Panormia, Book 2, c. 176; Decrees, part 4, c. 27; Polycarpus, ibid.]

Part V. No one ought to observe a fast on the Lord’s Day or Thursday, in order that a true and not false distinction may be maintained between the fast of Christians and that of Gentiles, true believers and unbelievers [Col. 1786A] and heretics. [Note: [Col. 1785] “And true”: Ivo, Decrees.—Basel edition.—“Or true”: Lyons editions II and III.—“And not true believers and heretics”: Ivo, Panormia.]

C. XV. On the same matter. Likewise, from the Council of Saragossa, c. 2. [Note: [Col. 1785] Held A.D. 380.—Collection of Three Parts, part 3, title 33, c. 1.]

Let no one fast on the Lord’s Day on account of fear [Note: [Col. 1785D] “Fear”: This is explained in the gloss. But the council reads: “on account of the time,” that is, because it is the Lord’s Day. On this matter see above, Distinction 30, chapter *Si quis tanquam*, and the final chapter.
