It is also read in the Pontifical of Damasus that Miltiades decreed that no one should fast on the Lord’s Day or Thursday, because pagans observed those days as a kind of sacred fast. In Burchard, Book 19, a penance is imposed upon one who fasts on the Lord’s Day from abstinence and religious motive.], or persuasion, or superstition; nor, during the days of Lent, let the faithful be absent from the churches, [Note: [Col. 1785] “Day”: same source.—“From”: absent in the same source.] nor let those who persist in suspicions dwell in the hiding-places of bedrooms and mountains; but let them observe the example and command of the priests, and not assemble at outlying estates for the purpose of holding meetings. It was said by all the bishops: Let him who has done these things be anathema. [Note: [Col. 1785] “This”: Hispanic Collection.—Collected editions.]

[Col. 1786B] C. XVI. The fasts of Wednesday and Friday are to be observed. Likewise, from the sayings of St. Apollonius. [Note: [Col. 1786D] This chapter is found in Palladius, in the Life of Abbot Apollonius.] [Note: [Col. 1785] Rather, from Book 2 of the *Lives of the Holy Fathers*, translated by Rufinus, c. 7.—Ivo, Panormia, Book 2, c. 179; Decrees, part 4, c. 32.—The words “But on the Lord’s Day,” etc., are taken from Smaragdus’s exposition of the Rule of St. Benedict, and are cited by Ivo, Decrees, ibid., c. 13, as from the statutes of the Fathers.]

The lawful fasts, namely Wednesday and Friday, are not to be relaxed unless there is some grave necessity, because on Wednesday Judas planned the betrayal [Note: [Col. 1785] “The betrayal”: collected editions.] of the Lord, [Note: [Col. 1785] “Learned”: Venice editions I and II.—“Had planned”: Ivo, Panormia.] and on Friday the Savior was crucified. Therefore, one who without any necessity relaxes the appointed fasts on these days will appear either to betray the Savior with him who betrayed him, or to crucify him with those who crucified him.

But on the Lord’s Day nothing else is to be done except to devote oneself to God. No work is to be performed on that holy day; rather, that day is to be spent only in hymns, psalms, and spiritual songs.

C. XVII. On Thursday of the last week of Lent penitents are to receive remission. Likewise, Pope Innocent, Epistle I to Decentius, c. 7. [Note: [Col. 1785] Written A.D. 416.—Burchard, Book 18, c. 18; Anselm, Book 11, c. 27; Ivo, Decrees, part 15, c. 40.]

[Col. 1786C] Part VII. As for penitents—whether they are doing penance for graver offenses or for lighter ones—unless illness intervenes, the custom of the Roman Church shows that they are to be reconciled on the Thursday before Easter. [Note: [Col. 1785] “To be”: added by collected editions.]

§ 1. But it belongs to the priest to judge the gravity of offenses, so that he may consider the penitent’s confession and the tears and weeping of the person being corrected, *and then order him to be released when he sees fitting satisfaction*.

§ 2. Certainly, [Col. 1787A] if anyone falls ill [Note: [Col. 1787] “Into illness”: Burchard, Ivo, and collected editions.—Böhm.] [Note: [Col. 1787] “Has fallen”: collected editions.—“Has incurred”: Coustant.] and reaches the point of despair, he is to be released before Easter, lest he depart this world without communion. [Note: [Col. 1787] “Of life”: added by Basel and Lyons editions.—“Die”: collected editions.]

C. XVIII. Every year, on Thursday of the last week of Quinquagesima, new chrism is to be prepared. Likewise, Pope Fabian, Epistle II to the eastern bishops. [Note: [Col. 1787] In the original the matter is explained more fully than either Gratian or Ivo gives.] [Note: [Col. 1787] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore.—Ivo, Decrees, part 2, c. 73; Polycarpus, Book 3, title 16.]

Part VIII. Among other matters inserted in your letters, we find that certain bishops of your region [Note: [Col. 1787] “Religion”: collected editions, first Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1787] “Our”: Argentinian and Basel editions.] depart from the practice of your order and ours, [Note: [Col. 1787] “From our order”: Argentinian edition.] and do not prepare chrism every year at the Lord’s Supper. And below: But those who devise such things are in error, and, thinking with a deranged rather than a sound mind, dare these things. [Note: [Col. 1787] “Dare to do this”: collected editions.] And below:

§ 1. For just as the solemnity of that day must be celebrated every year, [Col. 1787B] so the preparation of that holy chrism must be performed every year, renewed from year to year, [Note: [Col. 1787] “Renewed”: Argentinian edition.] and delivered [Note: [Col. 1787] “Is”: added by collected editions.] to the faithful, [Note: [Col. 1787] “Delivered”: Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I and II.] because it is a new sacrament to be renewed each year on the day already mentioned; and the old chrism is to be burned in the holy churches. We have received these practices from the holy Apostles and their successors, and we command you to observe them.

C. XIX. The feast of the finding of the Lord’s Cross is to be observed by all. Likewise, Pope Eusebius, Epistle III. [Note: [Col. 1787] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore, compiled from the Liber Pontificalis.—Ivo, Decrees, part 4, c. 5.]

Part IX. We command you solemnly to celebrate the feast of the finding of the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, which was recently found, while we held the governance of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Nones of May, on the aforesaid calendar day of its finding. [Col. 1787C]

C. XX. Why it was established that water sprinkled with salt should be sanctified. Likewise, Pope Alexander V, from Peter, Epistle I, c. 5. [Note: [Col. 1787] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore, compiled from the Liber Pontificalis.—Regino, Book 1, c. 210; Burchard, Book 2, c. 53; Ivo, Decrees, part 2, c. 68.]

Part X. We bless water sprinkled with salt for the people, so that all who are sprinkled with it may be sanctified and purified. And we command that all priests do this. For if the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled with blood, sanctified and cleansed the people, [Note: [Col. 1787] Hebrews 9:13–14.] how much more does water sprinkled with salt and consecrated by divine prayers sanctify and cleanse the people? And if, by salt scattered through the prophet Elisha, the barrenness [Note: [Col. 1787] Cf. 4 Kings, c. 2.] [Col. 1788A] of water was healed, how much more does salt consecrated by divine prayers [Note: [Col. 1787] “Consecrated water”: Regino, Burchard.] remove the barrenness of human things, sanctify and cleanse those who are defiled, purify them, multiply other good things, turn aside the devil’s snares, and defend people from the wiles of apparitions? [Note: [Col. 1787] “Of an apparition”: original—Ivo—collected editions.]

C. XXI. Holy Easter is to be celebrated only on the Lord’s Day. Likewise, Pope Pius IX, from the Apostle Peter, in the first book of his decretals. [Note: [Col. 1787] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore, compiled from the Liber Pontificalis; the passage is cited in Ivo, Decrees, part 4, c. 145. The chapter itself is found in the same author, ibid., c. 3.]

We wish you to know that the Lord’s Easter [Note: [Col. 1787] “Only”: added by Basel and Lyons editions II and III.] is to be celebrated on the Lord’s Day in the annual seasons [Note: [Col. 1787] “Solemnities”: original.]. In these times Hermes, teacher of faith and of Scripture, [Note: [Col. 1787] “Of Scripture”: Ivo and collected editions.] shone among us. And although we celebrate this Easter on the aforesaid day, [Note: [Col. 1787] “Celebrated”: same source and collected editions.] because [Note: [Col. 1787] “And because certain persons doubted it, nevertheless”: same source.] nevertheless [Col. 1788B] certain persons doubted this, [Note: [Col. 1787] Absent from Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1787] “Doubt”: Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I and II, Paris editions.] an angel of the Lord appeared to Hermes himself in the guise of a shepherd, in order to strengthen their souls, and commanded him that the Lord’s Easter be celebrated by all on the Lord’s Day. Therefore, by apostolic authority we instruct you also [Note: [Col. 1787] “And we ... establish”: collected editions.] that all ought to observe the same, because we also observe it; nor ought you in any way to depart from the head. [Note: [Col. 1787] “Depart”: collected editions.]

C. XXII. Holy Easter is to be celebrated only on the Lord’s Day. Likewise, Pope Victor XIII, from Peter, in his first decretal. [Note: [Col. 1787] A chapter of Pseudo-Isidore, taken from the Liber Pontificalis.—Collection of Three Parts, part 1, title 12, c. 1; Anselm, Book 9, c. 18, through “be found”; Ivo, Decrees, part 4, c. 4, through “conduct themselves.”]

Our predecessors have already decreed that the celebration of holy Easter must take place on the Lord’s Day, [Note: [Col. 1787] “Only on the Lord’s Day”: Basel and Lyons editions II and III.] and we command you solemnly to celebrate it [Note: [Col. 1787] “You”: Ivo.] on that same day, [Note: [Col. 1787] “Celebrate”: collected editions, first Paris and Lyons editions—Ivo.] because it is not fitting that the members should differ from the head [Col. 1788C] or act contrary to it. [Note: [Col. 1787] “Or act otherwise”: collected editions.] This feast is to be celebrated from the fourteenth moon of the first month until the twenty-first day of that same month.

§ 1. At that same time [Note: [Col. 1787] Burchard, Book 4, c. 3; Ivo, Decrees, part 1, c. 198.] [Note: [Col. 1787] “Also”: collected editions.] Catholic baptism is to be celebrated. Yet if necessity demands it or danger of death threatens, Gentiles coming to the faith are to be baptized wherever and whenever this occurs—whether in a river, sea, or spring—provided only that the Christian confession of faith has been made clear. [Note: [Col. 1787] “Enlightened”: collected editions.] They themselves must also carefully heed what they promised in baptism, lest they be found unbelievers rather than believers. But those who are marked by the stain of unbelief become infamous and are not at all counted among the faithful. [Col. 1789A] [Note: [Col. 1789] “Be counted”: collected editions, first Paris and Lyons editions.]

§ 2. These decrees [Note: [Col. 1789] § 2 is absent from Burchard and Ivo.] must not be overturned by any wickedness or altered by any novelty, because the rationale of secular matters is one thing, that of divine matters another.

C. XXIII. On the same matter. Likewise, from the Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 65. [Note: [Col. 1789] Statutes of the Ancient Church, c. 65.—Cf. Distinction 18, c. 9.]

The solemnity of Easter is to be celebrated on one day and at one time.

C. XXIV. The day of Easter is to be announced to all by the subscription of the council’s formal letters. Likewise, from the Fifth Council of Carthage, c. 7. [Note: [Col. 1789C] “Of the council”: In certain old copies there is “and of the council.” In the printed original, the heading of this chapter is: “On the Easter season, or the council.” In the *Codex canonum*, in the index to chapter 40 of the African Council: “The day of Easter and the day of the council are to be announced.” In Greek, c. 64: περὶ τοῦ τὴν ἡμέραν τοῦ Πάσχα ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῆς συνόδου ἀγγέλλεσθαι, that is: “That the day of Easter be announced on the day [Col. 1789D] of the synod.”] [Note: [Col. 1789] Held A.D. 401.]

It was resolved that the day of venerable Easter be announced to all by the subscription of the formal letters; [Note: [Col. 1789] “Of the lands”: added by Basel edition.] but the day of the council [Note: [Col. 1789] “Of counsel”: Argentinian edition.] is to be kept on the eleventh day before the Kalends [Note: [Col. 1789D] “Eleventh day before the Kalends”: Thus in the Fifth Council of Carthage. But in the African Council, also in the *Codex canonum*, and in the Greek Council of Carthage, it is: “the tenth day before the Kalends of September.” [Note: [Col. 1789] Thus Hispanic Collection.]] of November. [Note: [Col. 1789] Absent from the collected editions except the first Basel and Lyons editions II and III.] Letters must also be written [Note: [Col. 1789] “And write to”: Hispanic Collection.] to the primates of every province whatever, so that whenever they assemble a council [Col. 1789B] among themselves, [Note: [Col. 1789] “Whenever”: same source.] [Note: [Col. 1789] “Councils”: Argentinian edition and remaining editions.] they do not obstruct that day.

C. XXV. When all matters have been decreed in the council, the coming Easter is to be announced. Likewise, from the Second Council of Braga, c. 9. [Note: [Col. 1789] Held A.D. 572.—Collection of Three Parts, part 2, title 46, c. 9.]

It was resolved that, after all matters have been arranged in the council of priests, [Note: [Col. 1789] “Counsel”: Argentinian edition.] this must in every respect be observed: the metropolitan bishop is to announce on what day of the Kalends or on what lunar day the coming Easter of that year ought to be observed. [Note: [Col. 1789] “Observed”: collected editions.—“Coming”: same sources except Basel.] [Note: [Col. 1789] “On what”: collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 1789] “Announced”: Hispanic Collection.] The other bishops and remaining clergy are to make a brief written note of this; and each is to announce it in his own church on the approaching feast of the Lord’s Nativity, with the people present, after the Gospel reading. [Note: [Col. 1789] “Present”: Hispanic Collection.] [Note: [Col. 1789] “Announce”: same source.]

[Col. 1789C] C. XXVI. Easter is to be celebrated throughout the whole world on one day and at one time. Likewise, from the First Council of Arles, confirmed by Pope Sylvester, c. 1. [Note: [Col. 1789] Held A.D. 314.—Ivo, Decrees, part 4, c. 19.]

Concerning the observance of the Lord’s Easter, [Note: [Col. 1789] “The Lord’s Day”: Hispanic Collection.—“Of the Lord’s Day”: Argentinian and Basel editions.] we decree that it be observed throughout the whole world on one day and [Note: [Col. 1789] “One”: added by Hispanic Collection.] at one time, and that, according to custom, letters be sent to all. [Note: [Col. 1789] “You are to send letters to all,” i.e. Sylvester: same source—Ivo.]

[Col. 1790A] C. XXVII. Concerning the images of saints: they are not to be violated. Likewise, Gregory to Serenus, Bishop of Marseilles, Book IX, Epistle 9. [Note: [Col. 1789] Epistle 13, written A.D. 601, Book 1, Maurist edition.—It is correctly addressed in the collected editions to Serenus.—The latter part, from the words “It is one thing,” is cited as Gregory to Secundinus by Burchard, Book 3, c. 36; Ivo, Panormia, Book 2, c. 56; Decrees, part 3, c. 41.]

Part XII. It had been reported to us that, inflamed by an unconsidered zeal, you had broken images of the saints under the pretext, as it were, that they ought not to be adored. We indeed wholly praised you because you had forbidden their adoration, [Note: [Col. 1789] Absent from Lyons editions II and III.] [Note: [Col. 1789] “Forbid”: Argentinian edition.—“To have forbidden”: remaining editions.] but we reproved you for breaking them. Tell me, brother: from what priest have you ever heard that what you did was done? *If nothing else, at least this ought to have restrained you: that, scorning your other brothers, you might not believe yourself alone to be holy and wise.* [Note: [Col. 1790C] From “If nothing else” through the word “thing” are added from the original.]

For it is one thing to adore a picture, another to learn from the pictured narrative what ought to be adored. For what Scripture provides to those who read, a picture provides to the unlearned who look upon it: for in it even the ignorant see what they ought to follow; in it those who do not know letters read. Therefore a picture is especially a means of reading for the Gentiles. [Note: [Col. 1789] “And the unlearned”: collected editions.] [Col. 1790B]

C. XXVIII. Images of saints are a memorial and recollection of things past. Likewise, in the Seventh Synod, Session VI. [Note: [Col. 1789] Second Council of Nicaea, held A.D. 787.—In the collected editions it is cited as from the Sixth Synod.]

Christians do not call venerable images gods; nor do they serve them as gods; nor do they place their hope of salvation in them; nor do they expect the future judgment from them. Rather, they venerate and adore them as a memorial and recollection of things of old; yet they do not render them divine worship, nor do they render it to any creature.

[Col. 1790C] C. XXIX. Christ is to be represented not in the form of a lamb but of a human being. Likewise, Pope Hadrian to the Patriarch Tarasius, in Session II of the same Seventh Synod. [Note: [Col. 1790C] Concerning the Sixth Synod and its canons, see the note above, chapter “The Sixth Synod.”] [Note: [Col. 1789] Cf. on c. 5, Distinction 16.—Ivo, Decrees, part 4, c. 122.]

Part XIII. I receive the holy Sixth Synod with all its canons, in which it is said: In certain representations [Note: [Col. 1789] “In which”: Ivo.] [Note: [Col. 1789] “Writings”: collected editions.] of holy images, the lamb is depicted as being pointed out by the finger of the Forerunner; the lamb, which passes into a figure of grace [Note: [Col. 1790C] “Passes into a figure of grace”: Both in Hadrian’s letter and in Ivo, part 4, c. 122, the reading is *in typum gratiae assumtus est*, “was received as a type of grace.” In Ivo, c. 126, from Hadrian to Charles: *in signum relictus est gratiae*, “was left as a sign of grace.” In the Greek canon of the Sixth Synod: ὃς εἰς τύπον παρελήφθη τῆς χάριτος, that is, “who was received as a type of grace.” But it has not been changed because of the gloss.], but showing us through the Law of Moses [Col. 1791A] the Lamb, Jesus Christ our Lord.

Therefore, bidding farewell to the ancient figures and shadows handed down to the holy Church as a prefiguration of the truth, [Note: [Col. 1791] “And to”: same editions.] [Note: [Col. 1791D] “Bidding farewell”: Thus Ivo. Hadrian’s letter reads “embracing”; Greek: κατασπαζόμενοι, “greeting/embracing.”] we prefer grace and truth, and thus receive the fullness of the Law. We therefore command that from now on our Lord Jesus Christ, the true Lamb, be depicted in images also in his human form, in place of the former lamb. [Note: [Col. 1791] “Who depicts the Lord ... in a human image”: Ivo.] [Note: [Col. 1791] “Also”: absent there.] [Note: [Col. 1791] “And in”: absent from Argentinian edition.—“And in images”: omitted in Basel edition.]

C. XXX. Concerning the faith of the Trinity and Unity, which is to be maintained inviolate. Likewise, Augustine, Book I, *On the Trinity*, c. 4. [Note: [Col. 1791] Ivo, Panormia, Book 1, c. 7; Decrees, part 1, c. 2.]

All the Catholic interpreters of the divine books, old and new, whom I have been able to read and who wrote before me concerning the Trinity which is God, have aimed to teach according to the Scriptures that the Father, [Col. 1791B] the Son, and the Holy Spirit declare one divine unity, with an inseparable equality of one and the same substance; [Note: [Col. 1791] “Declare”: collected editions.] and therefore [Note: [Col. 1791] “Thus”: Argentinian and Basel editions.] they are not [Note: [Col. 1791] “Are”: Ivo and collected editions—Böhm.] three Gods but one God.

Yet the Father has begotten the Son, and therefore the Son is not the one who is the Father; and the Son has been begotten by the Father, and therefore the Father is not the one who is the Son. And the Holy Spirit [Col. 1792A] is neither Father nor Son, but only the Spirit of the Father and the Son; [Note: [Col. 1791] “Only”: same source and editions.] he too is coequal with the Father [Note: [Col. 1791] “And with the Father”: same source and editions.] and the Son, and belongs to the unity of the Trinity.

Nevertheless, it was not that same Trinity which was born of the Virgin Mary, crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate, rose on the third day, [Note: [Col. 1791] “And on the third”: same source and Basel edition.] and ascended into heaven, but the Son alone. Nor was it that same Trinity which descended in the form of a dove upon Jesus when he was baptized, [Note: [Col. 1791] Cf. Mark c. 1.] or which, on the day of Pentecost after the Lord’s ascension, came with a sound from heaven as though a violent wind were being borne along, and with divided tongues, as of fire, *resting upon each one of them*; [Note: [Col. 1791] Cf. Acts c. 2.] [Note: [Col. 1791] “From ‘but’ through ‘them’”: absent from Ivo, Panormia.] but the Holy Spirit alone.

Nor was it that same Trinity which said from heaven, [Note: [Col. 1791] Mark 1:11.] “You are my Son,” whether when he was baptized by John [Note: [Col. 1791] “Was baptized”: collected editions except the first Argentinian and Lyons editions II and III.] or on the mountain, [Col. 1792B] when the three disciples were with him, or when the voice sounded, saying, [Note: [Col. 1791] John 12:28.] “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again”; but it was the voice of the Father alone addressed to the Son of God. [Note: [Col. 1791] “Of God”: added by Basel edition.] Yet the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, just as they are inseparable, work inseparably.

DISTINCTION IV.

[Col. 1791]

[Col. 1791B] GRATIAN. C. I. Without the visible sacrament and invisible faith, no one is saved. The same author, on John. [Note: [Col. 1791] From the ordinary gloss on John 3:5.]

[Col. 1791C] Part I. The visible sacrament of water is necessary for the cleansing of the visible body, just as the invisible teaching of faith is necessary for the sanctification of the invisible soul. The same author:

§ 1. A human being is reborn from water, the visible sacrament, and spirit, the invisible understanding, [Note: [Col. 1791] “Namely”: added by collected editions.] so that he may visibly receive the symbol of baptism. [Note: [Col. 1791] “Receive”: same editions.] Or, he is reborn from visible water and the Holy Spirit.

C. II. In baptism concupiscence is extinguished, not so that it does not exist, but so that it does no harm. The same author, Book I, *On the Merits and Remission of Sins, or On the Baptism of Infants*, c. 39. [Note: [Col. 1791D] This chapter has been restored to its integrity [Col. 1792D] so that the teaching of Blessed Augustine may be understood better. The gloss did not stand in the way.]

Through Christ’s baptism, the flesh of sin is made void. It is made void, [Note: [Col. 1791] “But it is not made void in such a way”: same editions.] not so that, in the living flesh itself, concupiscence, diffused and inborn, is suddenly consumed and ceases to exist; but so that it does no harm to one who has died, [Col. 1792B] though it harmed him when he was born. [Note: [Col. 1791] “Was present”: original.]

For if, after baptism, he lives and can reach an age capable of receiving a command, [Note: [Col. 1791] “Reach the natural age”: collected editions.] he then has that with which to fight; and, with God’s help, he overcomes it, if he has not received his grace [Col. 1792C] in vain, *if he does not wish to be rejected*. [Note: [Col. 1791] “They have ... fight ... overcome ... have received”: collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 1791] “And it”: Rome edition, erroneously.]

For not even adults [Note: [Col. 1791] “Adults”: collected editions.] are granted this in baptism, except perhaps by an ineffable miracle of the omnipotent Creator, [Note: [Col. 1791] “God”: same editions.] namely, that the law of sin which is in the members, resisting the law of the mind, should be utterly extinguished and cease to exist. Rather, whatever evil a person has done, said, or thought [Note: [Col. 1791] “And thought”: Basel, Paris, and Lyons editions.] while his mind served subject to that same concupiscence, is wholly abolished and regarded as though it had not been done. [Note: [Col. 1791] “As if”: same editions.] [Note: [Col. 1791] “Is”: same editions.]

C. III. Whoever is conceived from a man and a woman is born with original sin and is not saved without baptism. The same author, to Deacon Peter, c. 26. [Note: [Col. 1791] Rather, Fulgentius of Ruspe, in the book *On the Faith to Peter*.—Ivo, Panormia, Book 1, c. 8; Decrees, part 1, c. 26.]

Hold most firmly and do not doubt in any way that every human being conceived through the intercourse of a man and a woman is born [Col. 1793A] with original sin, subject to ungodliness and enslaved to death, and for that reason is by nature [Note: [Col. 1793] “Naturally”: collected editions.] born a child of wrath, concerning which the Apostle says: [Note: [Col. 1793] Ephesians 2:3.] “For we too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest.” [Note: [Col. 1793] “We too”: absent from Ivo, Panormia.] No one is delivered from that wrath [Note: [Col. 1793] “Will be delivered”: collected editions.] except through faith in the mediator of God and men, the man Jesus Christ.

Likewise, c. 27:

§ 1. Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in any way, that not only persons already exercising reason, but also infants—whether they begin to live in their mothers’ wombs and die there, or, when [Note: [Col. 1793] “Already”: Ivo and collected editions.] born from their mothers, they depart this world without the sacrament of holy baptism, given in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are to be punished with everlasting fire; [Note: [Col. 1793] “The everlasting punishment of eternal fire”: original—Ivo.] for although they have committed no sin by their own act, [Note: [Col. 1793] “Have”: Basel edition.—“Have”: remaining editions.] they have nevertheless incurred the condemnation of original sin through fleshly conception and birth. [Col. 1793B] [Note: [Col. 1793] “From”: collected editions; “and birth” absent from Panormia.] [Note: [Col. 1793] “Contracted”: Lyons editions II and III.]

C. IV. On the same matter. Likewise, John Chrysostom. [Note: [Col. 1793] Cf. above, On Penance, Distinction 1, c. 41.]

No one can receive the grace of heavenly life unless he has first been cleansed from every stain of sin through the confession of repentance, through the gift of the saving baptism of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ages of ages.

C. V. Just as sins are now remitted in baptism, so formerly they were remitted in circumcision. Likewise, Gregory, *Morals*, Book IV, c. 2. [Note: [Col. 1793] Ivo, Panormia, Book 1, c. 10; Decrees, part 1, c. 49.]

What the water of baptism accomplishes among us was accomplished among the ancients either, in the case of little children, by faith alone; or, in the case of older persons, by the efficacy of sacrifice; or, in the case of those who sprang [Col. 1793C] from Abraham’s stock, [Note: [Col. 1793] “Had sprung”: Ivo.] by the mystery of circumcision.

C. VI. Original sin is now remitted in baptism, but formerly in circumcision. Likewise, Augustine to Valerius against Julian, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book II, c. 11. [Note: [Col. 1793] Ivo, Panormia, Book 1, c. 11; Decrees, part 1, c. 50.]

From the time circumcision was instituted among the people of God—it was then a seal of the righteousness of faith [Note: [Col. 1793] “Which”: Basel edition.] [Note: [Col. 1793] “Of the righteousness of God’s faith”: Ivo, Panormia and collected editions.]—it had efficacy for signifying [Note: [Col. 1793] “Sanctification”: same editions.] the cleansing even of little children [Col. 1794A] from original and old sin, just as baptism began, from the time it was instituted, [Note: [Col. 1793] “From that time”: added by Basel and Lyons editions II and III.] to have efficacy for the renewal of the human being. [Note: [Col. 1793] “Established”: collected editions.]

C. VII. In baptism, the faith of those presenting infants benefits them. The same author, *On Free Choice*, Book III, c. 23. [Note: [Col. 1793] Ivo, Panormia, Book 1, c. 12; Decrees, part 1, c. 120.]

People commonly inquire what the sacrament of Christ’s baptism benefits infants, since after receiving it they often die before they can know anything from it. [Note: [Col. 1793] “Themselves”: Ivo, Panormia and collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 1793] “Could have come to know”: same editions—Ivo.] In this matter it is quite rightly and devoutly believed that the faith of those by whom the infant is offered for consecration benefits the infant. And the Church commends this by her most salutary authority, so that each person may thereby understand how his own faith benefits him: when, for the benefit of others [Note: [Col. 1793C] “Benefit”: The same reading occurs in Ivo’s *Panormia* and in the original margin. But the text reads “benefit,” which, for those who do not yet have their own, can be supplied from another.], who do not yet have their own [Note: [Col. 1793] “Has”: Rome edition, erroneously.] [Col. 1794B] capacity, another’s faith can be of service.

C. VIII. Through faith and baptism we are justified from sins. The same author, *On the Baptism of Infants*, Book I, cc. 32 and 33. [Note: [Col. 1793C] This chapter is a summary of Blessed Augustine’s words in the passages indicated.]

The Son of God assumed flesh of sin [Note: [Col. 1793D] “Flesh of sin”: In Blessed Augustine the passage is much fuller and more accurate: “But the Lord did not transfer sin into his flesh as the poison of a serpent; he transferred death alone, so that in the likeness of sinful flesh there might be punishment without guilt, by which both guilt and punishment might be dissolved in sinful flesh.” There is therefore a great difference between sinful flesh and the likeness of sinful flesh. Explaining this, Blessed Augustine, often elsewhere but especially in Sermon 48, *On the Words of the Lord*, added: “If, therefore, it was the likeness of sinful flesh, not sinful flesh, how could it be said that sin was condemned in the flesh because of sin? A likeness can take the name of that thing of which it is the likeness.”], and punishment without guilt, so that in sinful flesh both guilt and punishment might be dissolved. Therefore through faith and his baptism a human being is freed from sin by justification, and from death by resurrection.

§ 1. Baptized infants too are counted among believers through the power of the sacrament and the response of those presenting them. But those who are not baptized are judged among unbelievers according to the Gospel of John: [Note: [Col. 1793] John 3:5.] “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”

[Col. 1794C] C. IX. Through the water of baptism a human being becomes heavenly from earthly. Likewise, Ambrose, Book I, *On the Sacraments*, cc. 4 and 5.

By the water [Note: [Col. 1793] “who passes through this fountain, passes from earthly things”: original] of baptism there is a passage from [Note: [Col. 1793] “from”: the collected editions, with comparison of other editions] earthly things to heavenly things. For this [Note: [Col. 1793] “Therefore Passover is called a passage; this passage is from sin, etc.”: the same editions] is Passover, that is, his passage: a passage from sin to life, from [Note: [Col. 1793] “from guilt … from defilement”: the same editions] guilt to grace, from defilement to sanctification. Whoever passes through this [Note: [Col. 1793] “this water”: the collected editions] fountain does not die, but rises again.

§ 1. Not every water heals, but that water [Note: [Col. 1793] “that”: the same editions] heals which has the grace of Christ [Note: [Col. 1793] “God”: the Argentinensis edition]. One thing is the element, another consecration; one thing is the work, another the operation. Water is the work; the operation is the Holy Spirit. Water does not heal unless the Holy Spirit descends [Note: [Col. 1795] “descends”: the collected editions; “descend”: the same editions] and consecrates that water [Note: [Col. 1795] “consecrate”: the collected editions], [Note: [Col. 1795] “into it”: the Basel and Lyons II–III editions] just as you have read that, when our Lord Jesus Christ was giving the form of baptism, he came to John, and John said to him [Note: [Col. 1795] Matthew 3:14]: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” Christ [Note: [Col. 1795] “Jesus”: the collected editions] answered him: “Allow it now,” for [Note: [Col. 1795] “thus”: the same editions] thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness. See [Note: [Col. 1795] “See what all righteousness is”: the same editions] that all righteousness is established in baptism.

Therefore why [Note: [Col. 1795D] From “Therefore why” through “For no,” these words have been corrected from Saint Ambrose. Previously the text read: “Christ descended to baptism, not that the flesh might be cleansed, which he assumed from our condition.” In many other places in this chapter the true reading has likewise been restored.] did Christ descend, unless that flesh might be cleansed—the flesh which he assumed from our condition? For no washing away of his own [Note: [Col. 1795] “of sin”: the same editions] sins was necessary [Note: [Col. 1795] “was”: the same editions] for Christ, who committed no sin; but it was necessary for us, who remain [Note: [Col. 1795] “remained”: the same editions] subject to sin.

[Col. 1795B] And a little later:

§ 2. Christ descended; the Holy Spirit also descended. Why [Note: [Col. 1795] “however”: the same editions] did Christ descend first, and the Spirit [Note: [Col. 1795] “the Holy Spirit”: the same editions] afterward, when the form and practice of baptism require that the font first be consecrated and then the one [Note: [Col. 1795] “who”: the same editions] to be baptized descend?

And after a few intervening words:

§ 3. But Christ descended first, and the Spirit followed [Note: [Col. 1795] so the same editions]. For what reason? So that the Lord Jesus himself might never appear to require the mystery of sanctification, but [Note: [Col. 1795] “but rather that”: the collected editions] that he himself might sanctify, and that the Spirit [Note: [Col. 1795] addition: “the Holy Spirit”: the same editions] might sanctify also.

## C. X. The water of baptism would not cleanse sins unless it had been sanctified by contact with the Lord’s body. Likewise Chromatius, *On Matthew*, chapter 6.

[Note: [Col. 1795D] “Chromatius”: Chrysostom was formerly cited here [Col. 1796D] [so the same editions], but the passage has not been found in him; it is in fragments of Chromatius. — Peter Lombard, book IV, distinction 3.]

The waters of baptism could never have cleansed the sins of believers unless they had been sanctified by contact with the Lord’s body.

## C. XI. General baptism is to be celebrated only on Holy Saturday of Easter and at Pentecost. Likewise Pope Siricius to Himerius of Tarragona, Letter I.

[Note: [Col. 1795] Written A.D. 385. — Burchard, book IV, chapter 5; Ivo, *Panormia*, book I, chapter 16; *Decretum*, part I, chapters 58 and 200; Peter Lombard, ibid.]

Part II. It is presumed, not on the basis of any authority, but through sheer rashness, that everywhere and freely, at the Nativity [Note: [Col. 1795] “at the Nativity”: the collected editions; “on the birthday”: Ivo’s *Panormia* and *Decretum*, chapter 58] of Christ, or at the Epiphany [Note: [Col. 1795] “of the Epiphany”: original], and likewise [Note: [Col. 1795] “and”: absent from Ivo] at the feasts of apostles or martyrs, countless congregations, *as you assert*, receive the mystery of baptism [Note: [Col. 1795] “are baptized”: the Argentinensis edition; “are to be baptized”: the remaining editions], although the Lord’s Passover, together with its [Note: [Col. 1795] “its”: Burchard; Ivo’s *Decretum*, chapter 58; “Holy”: the Lyons II–III editions; “holy”: the remaining editions and Ivo’s *Panormia*] Pentecost, specially claims this privilege for itself both among us and among all churches.

## C. XII. On the same matter. Likewise Pope Leo to all bishops established throughout Sicily, Letter IV, chapter 5.

[Note: [Col. 1796D] The first part of this chapter, down to “Therefore, because,” is not found in precisely these words in the letter. But in the *Codex canonum* it stands as a rubric in place of this chapter, and it is cited in the First Council of Mainz, chapter 4.]

[Note: [Col. 1795] Letter 16 in the Ballerini edition; written A.D. 447. The earlier words of the chapter are the chapter-rubric in the Spanish Collection and in Dionysius, and are cited by Anselm, book IX, chapter 13; the remainder occurs in Regino, book I, chapter 264; Burchard, book IV, chapter 2; and Ivo, *Decretum*, part I, chapter 197. — *Collectio tripartita*, part I, title 43, chapter 4.]

Two times, namely Easter and Pentecost, have lawfully been fixed by the Roman Pontiff for baptism. Therefore, since it is most plainly evident [Note: [Col. 1795] “appears”: the Argentinensis and Basel editions] that these two times [Note: [Col. 1795] addition: “that is, Easter and Pentecost”: Regino, Burchard, and Ivo] of which we have spoken are the lawful times for the chosen persons to be baptized in the Church, we admonish your charity not to mingle any other days with this observance.

[Col. 1796B] ## C. XIII. Why baptism is celebrated at the aforesaid times. The same, in the same letter, chapter 3.

Properly speaking, in the death of the Crucified One and in the resurrection from the dead, the power of baptism made a new creature out of the old [Note: [Col. 1795] “makes”: the Spanish Collection, Ballerini, and Ivo], so that in those being reborn both the death of Christ and his life may operate. As the blessed Apostle Paul [Note: [Col. 1795] “the words ‘blessed’ and ‘Apostle’ are absent from Ivo”] says [Note: [Col. 1795] compare Romans 6:4 ff.]:

“Do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death [Note: [Col. 1795] “in death”: the collected editions, except Lyons II–III], so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life. For if we have been made united to the likeness of his death, we shall likewise be united to his resurrection,”

and the other things which the teacher of the Gentiles discussed at greater length in commending [Col. 1796C] the sacrament of baptism. Thus it might appear, from the spirit of this teaching, that for the sons of humankind being regenerated and adopted as children of God, that day and that time [Note: [Col. 1795] “is”: absent from the Spanish Collection] were chosen in which, through the likeness and form of the mystery, the things done in the members corresponded to those done in Christ himself [Note: [Col. 1795] “in Christ”: the Argentinensis and Basel editions], the head [Note: [Col. 1795] “correspond”: the collected editions]. For in the rule of baptism death intervenes through the slaying [Note: [Col. 1795] “slaying”: the Argentinensis and Basel editions; “slaying of”: the same editions] of sin, the threefold immersion imitates the three-day burial, and the lifting from the waters is like one rising from the tomb. Therefore the very nature of the rite teaches that the lawful day for the general celebration of grace is that on which both the power of the gift and the form of the action arose [Note: [Col. 1797] “is to be celebrated”: the Basel edition; “arose”: the Spanish Collection].

§ 1. For confirmation of this, it is of great weight that the Lord Jesus Christ himself, after he had risen from the dead, gave his disciples—in whom all the rulers of the churches were instructed—both the form and the power of baptizing, saying [Note: [Col. 1797] Matthew 28:19]:

“Go therefore now [Note: [Col. 1797] “therefore now”: absent from Ivo] and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

Certainly he could have instructed them about this before his passion [Note: [Col. 1797] “and before”: Ivo and the collected editions], unless he had wished it to be understood in particular that the grace of regeneration began from his [Note: [Col. 1797] absent from Bohm] resurrection.

§ 2. Moreover, to this observance is added the sacred [Note: [Col. 1797] “consecrated”: the Spanish Collection, Ballerini, and Ivo] solemnity of Pentecost, consecrated by the coming of the Holy Spirit. It depends upon the point of the Paschal feast; and whereas different feasts belong to other days, this [Note: [Col. 1797] “this one”: the Basel edition] always occurs on that [Note: [Col. 1797] “the same”: the Spanish Collection] day which is distinguished by the Lord’s resurrection. It stretches out, as it were, the hand of assisting grace, and invites [Note: [Col. 1797] “inviting”: Ivo; but the original reads “it has shut out the unwilling, or those hindered by whatever necessities”: the Spanish Collection; “and those hindered by whatever necessities”: the same source] those whom illness, the length of a journey, or the difficulty of a voyage has prevented from attending on Easter Day, so that, hindered by whatever necessities, they may obtain the fulfillment of their desire through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

And below, chapter 4:

§ 3. We prove by a sufficiently apt example that we defend this not from our own persuasion, but observe it on apostolic authority, following the blessed Apostle [Col. 1797C] Peter. On the day when the promised coming of the Holy Spirit filled the whole [Note: [Col. 1797] “the entire”: the same editions and the Spanish Collection] multitude of believers, Peter consecrated in the washing of baptism a people of three thousand converted by his preaching. Holy Scripture, which contains the Acts of the Apostles, teaches this in its trustworthy narrative, saying [Note: [Col. 1797] Acts 2:37 ff.]:

“On hearing this, they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and *to* the rest of the apostles [Note: [Col. 1797] “to the disciples and apostles”: the Argentinensis and Basel editions], ‘What shall we do, brothers?’ But Peter said to them, ‘Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus [Col. 1798A] Christ for the forgiveness of sins [Note: [Col. 1797] addition: “of all your sins”: the collected editions; “of your sins”: Ballerini and the Vulgate], and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.’”

## C. XIV. On the same matter. Likewise in the same letter, chapter 6 [Note: [Col. 1797] Ivo, *Panormia*, book I, chapter 18; *Decretum*, part I, chapter 47.].

If anyone thinks that the feast of Epiphany—which in its own order is to be venerated with due honor—has the privilege of baptism [Note: [Col. 1797] “considers”: Ballerini, Ivo’s *Panormia*, and the Argentinensis and Basel editions] because some suppose that on that day the Lord came to the baptism of holy [Note: [Col. 1797] absent from the same editions] John, let him know that that baptism had a different grace and a different rationale, and did not belong to the same efficacy by which those are reborn through the Holy Spirit of whom it is said [Note: [Col. 1797] John 1:13]:

“Who were born not of bloods [Note: [Col. 1797] “blood”: the Spanish Collection and Ballerini], nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God.”

For the Lord, needing no remission of sin [Col. 1798B] and seeking no remedy of rebirth, wished to be baptized just as he wished [Note: [Col. 1797] “and wished”: the Spanish Collection, Ballerini, Ivo, and the Basel edition] to be circumcised and to have an offering of purification offered for himself [Note: [Col. 1797] “through cleansing”: the collected editions]. Thus he who had been made of a woman, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1797] Galatians 4:4], was also made under the law, which he had come not to abolish but to fulfill and, by fulfilling it, to bring it to an end, as the blessed Apostle proclaims, saying [Note: [Col. 1797] Romans 10:4]: “For Christ is the end of the law [Note: [Col. 1797] addition: “is”: the collected editions] for righteousness to everyone who believes.”

But he established in himself the sacrament of his baptism, because, holding primacy in all things, he taught himself to be the beginning; and he ordained the power of regeneration when blood of redemption and water of baptism flowed from his side [Note: [Col. 1797] “his”: the Argentinensis and Basel editions].

[Col. 1798C] ## C. XV. Catechumens are to be baptized at the Easter and Pentecost solemnities. Likewise from the Council of Gerona, chapter 4.

[Note: [Col. 1797] The restored chapter is taken from its original.]

[Note: [Col. 1797] Held A.D. 517. — Ivo, *Panormia*, book I, chapter 20; *Decretum*, part I, chapter 60.]

With regard to catechumens to be baptized, it has been decreed [Note: [Col. 1797] “established”: Ivo and the collected editions] that [Note: [Col. 1797] addition: “because”: the Spanish Collection], at the solemnity of Easter [Note: [Col. 1797] “at the Paschal solemnity”: the collected editions] or Pentecost [Note: [Col. 1797] “the Nativity of the Lord”: the Spanish Collection], the greater the celebration’s solemnity, the more they should come for baptism [Note: [Col. 1797] The words “the greater … come for baptism” are absent from Ivo; the Spanish Collection reads: “when the greater solemnity of the greater celebration is held, fewer come for baptism”]; at other solemnities only the sick [Note: [Col. 1797] “only”: Ivo’s *Panormia*; “only such”: the collected editions] ought to be baptized, to whom [Note: [Col. 1797] “to whom … baptism not be denied”: absent from Ivo] baptism ought not to be denied at any time.

[Col. 1799A] ## C. XVI. When necessity compels, baptism may be administered at any time. Likewise Pope Leo, Letter IV, chapter 6.

[Note: [Col. 1799C] In Pope Leo, the sense of this chapter occurs after the chapter “Two Times” and before the chapter “But if Anyone,” above.]

[Note: [Col. 1799] This is the rubric of chapter 5 of the letter itself; cf. above, chapter 12. It occurs in Dionysius, Anselm, book IX, chapter 13; and Ivo, *Panormia*, book I, chapter 19.]

Those who are pressed by the necessity of death, illness, siege, persecution, or shipwreck [Note: [Col. 1799] “These”: the Argentinensis and Basel editions] ought to be baptized at every time.

## C. XVII. Unless necessity compels, no one is to presume to baptize except between Easter and Pentecost. Likewise Pope Gelasius to the clergy and people of Taranto.

[Note: [Col. 1799C] In the letter of Gregory II to the clergy and people of Thuringia, from which Ivo cites it—although it may also be Gelasius’s—and in the Council of Worms, from which Burchard cites it [and Regino, book II, chapter 269], the reading is “of most holy baptism”; likewise in Ivo, chapter 202. But in chapter 63 it reads “general,” and in the margin “venerable.”]

[Note: [Col. 1799] It is not established whether this is Gelasius’s. It is read in the *Liber diurnus of the Roman Pontiffs*, in a capitulary issued by Gregory II to Martinianus and Georgius, and in a letter of the same pope cited by Corr. (Mansi, vol. 12). — Burchard, book IV, chapter 7; Anselm, book VI, chapter 47; Ivo, *Panormia*, book I, chapter 21; *Decretum*, part I, chapter 63.]

A bishop should not presume to administer the venerable [Note: [Col. 1799] “general”: Ivo’s *Decretum*] sacrament of baptism except at the Easter and Pentecost feasts, excepting those for whom, because the danger of death is pressing, it is necessary to provide such remedies lest they perish eternally.

[Col. 1799B] ## C. XVIII. On the same matter. The same Gelasius, Letter to the Bishops of Lucania, chapter 12.

[Note: [Col. 1799] Written A.D. 494. — Burchard, book IV, chapter 4; Anselm, book IX, chapter 12; Ivo, *Decretum*, part I, chapter 199.]

Let no one suppose that baptism may be administered freely and indiscriminately at any time, except at the Paschal feast and the venerable sacrament of Pentecost—except only in the onset of very grave illness, in which there is reason to fear that, as the danger of the disease increases, the sick person may perhaps depart, overtaken by death, without the remedy of salvation.

## C. XIX. No one but a priest is to presume to baptize. Likewise Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 24.

[Note: [Col. 1799] Ivo, *Panormia*, book I, chapter 23; *Decretum*, part I, chapter 67; Peter Lombard, book IV, distinction 6.]

It is established that baptism is to be administered by priests alone [Note: [Col. 1799] “entrusted”: original, Ivo, and the Basel edition], and that it is not lawful even for deacons to perform its mystery without a bishop or priest, unless, when these are far away, the final necessity of illness compels it. This is also often permitted to faithful laypersons, lest anyone be called from this world without the remedy of salvation [Note: [Col. 1799] “nor be summoned”: absent from Ivo’s *Panormia*].

Likewise Pope Gelasius [Note: [Col. 1799] Compare Distinction 93, chapter 13]:

§ 1. “Deacons likewise [must observe] their proper …,” etc., as above in the treatise on those to be ordained, where the reverence of deacons toward priests is discussed.

[Col. 1800A] ## C. XX. A woman is not to presume to baptize. Likewise from the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapters 99 and 100.

[Note: [Col. 1799] This is compiled from chapter 37—cf. chapter 29, Distinction 23, and the collections cited there—and chapter 41 of the *Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua*. Cf. chapter 9, Distinction 18; Ivo, *Panormia*, book I, chapter 25; *Decretum*, part I, chapter 65.]

Part III. A woman, however learned and holy, is not to presume to teach men in an assembly or to baptize anyone [Note: [Col. 1799] “shall presume”: the Argentinensis and Basel editions].

Gratian: Unless necessity [Note: [Col. 1799] addition: “of death”: the Basel and Lyons II–III editions] compels.

[Note: [Col. 1799] Compare Cause 30, question 3, chapter 4.] Hence Pope Urban II: “On the matters about which he consulted,” etc., as above in the treatise on marriage, where spiritual kinship is discussed.

## C. XXI. Laypersons also may baptize when necessity compels. Likewise Augustine to Fortunatus.

[Note: [Col. 1799] This passage itself is not in Augustine; there are, however, certain similar passages in the letter to Fortunatus (Letter 228 in the Maurist edition). — Ivo, *Panormia*, book I, chapter 26; *Decretum*, part I, chapter 191 (“from the book to Fortunatus”).]

In necessity, when bishops, presbyters, or any ministers cannot be found, and danger presses upon the person who requests it [Note: [Col. 1799] “perishes”: Bohm], lest he end this life without this sacrament, we commonly hear that laypersons too administer the sacrament which they have received.

## C. XXII. On the same matter. [PALEA.] Likewise from the Decree of Pope Martin III.

[Note: [Col. 1799] In the Argentinensis edition it is ascribed simply to Pope Martin; in another Argentinensis edition, to Fabian. It is not found in Martin III, nor in the *Capitularies* of Martin of Braga; nevertheless it is similar to Theodulf of Orléans, chapter 27 (Mansi, vol. 13). — Burchard, book IV, chapter 47; Anselm, book IX, chapter 54; Ivo, *Decretum*, part I, chapter 241; *Polycarpus*, book III, title 10.]

“Any presbyter who, in his own province or another, or wherever he may be found, refuses to baptize a sick person entrusted to him—whether on account of an intended journey or any other excuse—and the person thus dies without baptism, shall be deposed.”

## C. XXIII. Baptism administered by a pagan is not repeated. Likewise Isidore.

[Note: [Col. 1800C] This chapter was discussed above, chapter 1, question 1, “If anyone through ignorance.”]

[Note: [Col. 1799] Compare chapter 59, Cause 1, question 1.]

The Roman Pontiff judges not the person who baptizes, but that the Spirit of God supplies the grace of baptism, even though the one baptizing is a pagan.

[Col. 1800C] ## C. XXIV. On the same matter. Likewise Nicholas, in response to the inquiries of the Bulgarians, chapter 104.

[Note: [Col. 1799] Written A.D. 865. — Ivo, *Panormia*, book I, chapter 29.]

You state that many in your country have been baptized by a certain Jew, though you do not know whether he was a Christian or a pagan, and you ask what should be done concerning them. If indeed they were baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, or even only in the name of Christ, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 1801] “is read”: the same editions; compare Acts 2 and 19]—for these are one and the same, as Saint Ambrose explains [Note: [Col. 1801] *On the Holy Spirit*, book I, chapter 3]—it is established [Note: [Col. 1801] “because it is not theirs but his, they ought not to be rebaptized”: the collected editions; Ivo’s *Panormia* omits the words “rebaptized …”] that they are not to be baptized again.

[Note: [Col. 1800C] “By a Jew”: In Alger, *On the Truth of the Body and Blood of the Lord*, book III, chapter 6, it reads “as I hear.” But in the original the following words come after this chapter: “but first it must be investigated whether this Jew himself was a Christian or a pagan, or whether he subsequently became a Christian.”]

## C. XXV. Baptism is administered equally through a good and through an evil minister. Likewise Augustine, *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, book III, chapter 6.

[Note: [Col. 1801] Ivo, *Panormia*, book I, chapter 30; *Decretum*, part I, chapter 160.]

If among good ministers, although one is better than another, the baptism administered through the better is not better [Note: [Col. 1801] “when the same baptism is given”: the collected editions, especially Basel], then the baptism administered even through an evil minister is in no way evil, since [Note: [Col. 1801] “because”: the Basel edition] the same baptism is administered. Therefore, through unequal ministers God’s gift is equal, because it is not theirs but his.

[Col. 1801B] ## C. XXVI. In baptism it is not the merits of ministers but Christ’s power that operates. The same, *On John*, part I, tractate V, on chapter 1.

[Note: [Col. 1801] Ivo, *Panormia*, book I, chapter 31; *Decretum*, part I, chapters 156–159; Peter Lombard, book IV, distinction 5.]

Baptism is such as he is in whose power it is given, not such as he is through whose ministry it is given.

Likewise in the same place:

§ 1. What did John the Baptist know? Our Lord [Note: [Col. 1801] addition: “our”: the collected editions]. What did he not know? That the power of the Lord’s baptism would pass from the Lord to no human being, though its ministry plainly would pass on: the power would not pass from the Lord to any minister [Note: [Col. 1801] addition: “would come”: the Basel edition; “would pass”: the remaining editions], but the ministry [Note: [Col. 1801] “but the ministry”: the collected editions] would pass [Note: [Col. 1801] “and”: absent from the same editions, especially Lyons II–III] both to good persons and to evil. Let not the dove be horrified by the ministry of the evil; let it look to the Lord’s power [Note: [Col. 1801] “but let it receive”: the Argentinensis edition; “but let it look”: the remaining editions]. What can an evil minister do to you where the Lord is good? What does a malicious herald hinder where the judge is benevolent [Note: [Col. 1801] “good”: the Argentinensis edition]?

Likewise below:

§ 2. “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” [Note: [Col. 1801] 1 Corinthians 3:7].

Likewise in the same place:

§ 3. I say [Note: [Col. 1801C] “I say”: Ivo also has this, but the original reads: “And I, and all of us, say that ministers of so great a judge ought to be just. Let the ministers be just, if they wish. But if they do not wish …” The portions of this chapter have been collected from various places in the same fifth tractate], and we all say that all through whom baptism is administered ought to be just [Note: [Col. 1801] “all ought to be just”: absent from the Basel edition and Ivo; “all … ought to be”: absent from Bohm], the ministers of so great a judge ought to be just, if they wish to minister justly [Note: [Col. 1801] Ivo has “let the ministers be just, if they wish”]. But if those who sit in Moses’ seat are unwilling to be just, my teacher makes me secure [Note: [Col. 1801] “made me secure”: the collected editions; Ivo], of whom his Spirit said [Note: [Col. 1801] “says”: the same editions and Ivo]: “This is he who baptizes” [Note: [Col. 1801] John 1:33].

Likewise below:

§ 4. I do not fear an adulterer, *not* a drunkard, nor a murderer, because I attend to the dove, through whom it is said to me: “This is he who baptizes.”

## C. XXVII. On the same matter. The same, tractate VI on John, chapter 1.

When an evil person baptizes through some ignorance [Note: [Col. 1801] “or through”: the Basel, Paris, and Lyons I editions] or tolerance of the Church [Note: [Col. 1801] absent from the Lyons II–III editions]—for evil persons are either unknown [Note: [Col. 1801] “evil things”: the Basel edition] or tolerated as chaff [Note: [Col. 1801] “the chaff”: Ivo; “the chaffs”: the collected editions] until the threshing-floor is winnowed at the end—that which is given is one; it is not unequal because the ministers are unequal, but alike and equal because of him [Note: [Col. 1801] “because of this”: the Argentinensis edition; “because of this one who”: the remaining editions and Ivo] of whom it is said: “This is he who baptizes.”

## C. XXVIII. Baptism administered in the name of the Holy Trinity is not repeated. The same, *On Ecclesiastical Rules*, chapter 52.

[Note: [Col. 1801] Ivo, *Decretum*, part I, chapter 160; likewise there, chapter 233; and Burchard, book IV, chapter 39, from the Rouen collection.]

[Col. 1802B] If those who have been baptized among heretics who baptize with confession of the Holy Trinity [Note: [Col. 1801] addition: “who are”: the Argentinensis and Venetian I–II editions; Ivo has “are baptized”] come to us [Note: [Col. 1801] “to the Catholic Church”: Ivo; “to the Catholic faith”: the collected editions], they are indeed to be received as baptized [Note: [Col. 1801] “some”: the Lyons II edition], lest the invocation or confession of the Holy Trinity be nullified. But they are to be fully taught and instructed in the sense in which the mystery of the Holy Trinity is held [Note: [Col. 1801] “they hold”: the collected editions] in the Church; and, if they agree to believe or consent to confess it, once cleansed *already* [Note: [Col. 1801] absent from Ivo] by the soundness of faith, they are to be confirmed [Note: [Col. 1801] “strengthened”: Ivo; the collected editions] by the laying on of hands. But if they are children or mentally incapable persons [Note: [Col. 1801] “and”: Ivo and the collected editions; the Argentinensis edition omits “and mentally incapable”] who cannot grasp instruction, those who present them are to answer for them according to the custom of baptizing; and thus, having been anointed with chrism through the laying on of hands, they are to be admitted to the mysteries of the Eucharist [Note: [Col. 1802C] The original reads: “And thus, fortified by the laying on of hands and chrism, they are admitted to the Eucharist,” etc. But it has not been altered because of the gloss. The collected editions read “with the Eucharist.”]

## C. XXIX. On the same matter. The same, to Orosius, in the *Dialogue of Sixty-Five Questions*, question 59.

[Note: [Col. 1801] This does not appear to be Augustine’s. — Ivo, *Panormia*, book I, chapter 28 (down to “denying”); *Decretum*, part I, chapter 165.]

Although there is one baptism—that of heretics, namely those who are baptized [Note: [Col. 1801] “baptize”: original, Ivo, and the collected editions] in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and that of the Catholic Church—nevertheless, because they are baptized outside *and beyond* [Note: [Col. 1801] these words are absent from Ivo] the Church, they receive baptism not unto salvation [Note: [Col. 1801] addition: “saving and”: the Argentinensis edition] but unto destruction, having the form of the sacrament [Note: [Col. 1802C] “The form of the sacrament”: the same wording occurs in Ivo. The original reads: “having indeed an appearance of godliness, but denying its power.” And again: “sensual persons, I mean, not having the Spirit.” Therefore the Church, etc. The passage uses the words of Saint Paul, 2 Timothy 3, and Jude 1], while denying its power. Therefore the Church does not baptize them again, because they have been baptized in the name of the Trinity. This indeed is the form of the sacrament. Therefore, when they have returned, they receive the power of the Holy Spirit, which those baptized outside the Church do not yet possess [Note: [Col. 1803] “which those who are baptized outside the Church do not yet have”: Ivo; “which they do not have if outside the Church”: the collected editions].

## C. XXX. Those proved to have been baptized only in the name of the Lord are baptized. Likewise Pope Pelagius to Bishop Gaudentius.

[Note: [Col. 1803] This appears to be Pelagius II, written to Gaudentius of Nola. — *Collectio tripartita*, part I, title 54, chapter 3; Ivo, *Panormia*, book I, chapter 62, down to “you will baptize”; *Decretum*, part I, chapter 161.]

If those heretics who are said to live in places neighboring to your beloved charge [Note: [Col. 1803] Ivo’s *Decretum* reads “assigned neighboring places”] perhaps confess that they have been baptized only in the name of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1803] absent from the collected editions, especially Paris and Lyons], you shall baptize them without any ambiguity of doubt when they come to the Catholic faith, in the name of the Holy Trinity. But if, in the clear confession of those who wish to be converted, it becomes evident to you that they were baptized in the name of the Trinity, you should hasten to unite them with the Catholic faith by the grace of reconciliation alone, so that, this dispensation being observed, nothing may appear to have been done through a spirit of rashness otherwise than evangelical authority commands.

## C. XXXI. Whether baptism administered by one who has not been baptized is to be approved. Likewise Augustine, *On the One Baptism*, book VII, chapter 53.

[Note: [Col. 1803] Ivo, *Decretum*, part I, chapter 162; Peter Lombard, book IV, distinction 6.]

Part IV. It is also commonly asked whether baptism received from one who has not received it should be approved, if perhaps he has learned through some curiosity how it ought to be given [Note: [Col. 1803] “how”: the collected editions], and whether it makes any difference with what intention the recipient receives it, whether with pretense or without pretense; and, if with pretense, whether he is deceiving, as in the Church or in what is thought to be the Church, or whether he is jesting, as in a mime [Note: [Col. 1803C] Here in Saint Augustine and Ivo much is inserted which it is worthwhile to read for understanding what follows].

And below:

§ 1. Nevertheless, if someone were to press me, placed in a council where such a question was under discussion and without the prior merits [Note: [Col. 1803C] The original and Ivo read “such persons” (*talibus*). It has not been altered because of the gloss.] of those whose judgment I should prefer to follow, to state what I myself thought—if I were then disposed as I was when I dictated these things—I would not at all doubt that those possess baptism who, wherever and from whomever they received it [Note: [Col. 1803] “quocunque” (probably “from anyone”): the collected editions, except Basel], received it consecrated with evangelical words without pretense on their own part [Note: [Col. 1803] “of their own”: absent from the same editions, especially Basel and Lyons II–III] and with some faith, although it would not benefit them for spiritual salvation if [Note: [Col. 1803] namely, “if”: the same editions, especially Basel] they lacked the charity by which they are incorporated [Note: [Col. 1803] “are incorporated”: the collected editions] into the Catholic Church.

For, he says [Note: [Col. 1804C] “If I have faith”: True faith can exist without charity, but not the true power of faith. True faith is one thing; true power is another, as Saint Thomas taught, *Second Part of the Second Part*, question 4, article 5. The author of the gloss does not seem adequately to have perceived this] [Note: [Col. 1803] 1 Corinthians 13:2], “If I have faith so as to move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing.”

Likewise, in accordance with the already established decrees of the elders, I do not doubt [Note: [Col. 1803] “do not doubt”: the collected editions, especially Basel; “you do not doubt”: the same editions] that even those possess baptism who, although they receive it deceitfully, receive it in the Church, or in what is thought to be the Church by those in whose communion they receive it [Note: [Col. 1803] “by them”: absent from the same editions, especially Basel and Lyons II–III]—those of whom it has been said [Note: [Col. 1803] 1 John 2:19]: “They went out from us.”

But where there were neither any fellowship of persons believing in this way, nor did the recipient himself believe in this way [Note: [Col. 1803] “was believed”: the collected editions], but everything was done theatrically, mimically, and in jest, I would judge that the question whether baptism so given should be approved must be sought from the divine judgment by an oracle of some revelation, through united prayer and [Note: [Col. 1803] “with the expenditure of suppliant devotion”: the same editions, especially Basel] earnest entreaty with devout groans. Yet I would humbly await those who would state opinions after me, should they bring forward anything already investigated and known [Note: [Col. 1803] “thought through or recognized”: the Argentinensis edition; “asserted”: the Basel edition; “investigate”: the Lyons II–III editions; “investigated”: the remaining editions].

## C. XXXII. Baptism administered by heretics in faith in the Holy Trinity is not repeated. Likewise book I, *Against the Donatists*, chapter 1.

### Part V

It is shown that those act impiously who attempt to rebaptize the unity of the world, and that we act rightly who do not dare to invalidate God’s sacraments even in schism. [Note: “[they] show [us] to be Catholics” (*ostendunt catholicos*) added: Basel; Lyons II, III.] For in that in which they agree with us, [Col. 1804C] in that they are also with us. [Note: “in that” (*in eo*): absent from the collected editions, except the same.] But they have departed from us in that in which they disagree with us. [Note: “indeed” (*enim*): the same editions, except the same.]

Likewise, a little earlier. [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 87.]

§1. The sacrament of baptism is what the baptized person possesses, [Note: “that person” (*ille*) added: collected editions.] and the sacrament of conferring baptism is what the ordained person possesses. [Note: “baptism” (*baptismum*): the same editions except Basel; “receives” (*suscipit*): Basel.] For just as one who has been baptized does not lose the sacrament of baptism if he departs from unity, [Note: “indeed” (*enim*): collected editions; Ivo.] so likewise one who has been ordained does not lose the sacrament of conferring baptism if he departs from unity. No sacrament, indeed, is to be wronged. [Col. 1805A] If he departs from evils, both depart; if he remains in evils, both remain.

Therefore, just as baptism is accepted which the person departing from unity could not lose, [Note: “has departed” (*discesserit*): Arg.; Nor.; Venice I, II; Paris.] so baptism must also be accepted which was conferred by one who, when departing, had not lost the sacrament of conferring it.

Likewise, in the same book, chapter 12:

§2. If someone approached baptism falsely, [Note: “approaches” (*accedit*): collected editions.] were his sins forgiven him, or were they not forgiven? [Note: “to him” (*ei*) added: the same editions.] Let them choose what they wish: whichever they choose [Note: “whatever” (*quodcunque*): the same editions.] will suffice for us. [Note: “suffices” (*sufficit*): the same editions.] If they say that they were forgiven, how then will the Holy Spirit of discipline flee from the false person, if he has wrought remission of sins in this false person? [Note: Wisdom 1:5.] If they say that they were not forgiven, I ask whether, if afterward he confessed his falseness with a contrite heart [Note: “converted” (*converso*): collected editions.] and true sorrow, [Note: “they might confess” (*faterentur*): Basel; “he may confess” (*fateatur*): the remaining editions.] he would be judged to require baptism again. [Col. 1805B]

But if it is utterly foolish to say this, let them admit that a man can be baptized with Christ’s true baptism and yet, while his heart persists in wickedness or sacrilege, not permit the abolition of sins [Note: “absolution” (*absolutionem*): Ivo; Basel, Paris, Lyons.] to occur. Let them thus understand that persons can be baptized in communions separated from the Church, [Note: “communications” (*communicationibus*): collected editions.] where Christ’s baptism is given and received with the same celebration of the sacrament, but that it then profits toward remission of sins when someone, reconciled to unity, is stripped of the sacrilege of dissension, [Note: “separation” (*discessionis*): Basel.] by which his sins were held bound and were not permitted to be forgiven. [Note: “and were not permitted to be forgiven”: absent from Arg.]

[Col. 1805C]

### Chapter XXXIII. Baptism avails for salvation even if infants are not offered with that faith.

The same, in Letter XXIII to Boniface. [Note: Letter 98, written A.D. 408, Maurist edition; cf. below, chapter 129; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 95; *Decretum*, part 1, chapter 171; *Polycarpus*, book 3, title 10; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 6.]

### Part VI

[Note: “Not” (*Non*): the original reads “Nor” (*Nec*).]

Do not let this disturb you: some bring infants for receiving baptism not with the faith that they may be regenerated by spiritual grace [Note: “special” (*speciali*): Arg.] unto eternal life, but because they think that by this remedy they retain or recover temporal health. Yet they are not, for that reason, not regenerated, because they are not offered by these persons with that intention. [Note: “are offered” (*offerantur*): Arg.]

### Chapter XXXIV. The shedding of blood takes the place of baptism.

Likewise, *On the One Baptism against the Donatists*, book IV, chapter 22. [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 109; *Decretum*, part 1, chapter 177; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 4.]

### Part VII

That suffering sometimes fulfills the role of baptism is shown by the case of that thief, to whom, though unbaptized, it was said: “Today you shall be with me in Paradise.” [Note: Luke 23:43.] Blessed Cyprian adduces this as no slight proof. [Note: “adduced” (*assumsit*): collected editions except Basel; cf. Cyprian, *To Jubaianus*.] [Col. 1806A]

Considering this repeatedly, I find that not only suffering for Christ’s name can supply what was lacking from baptism, but also faith and conversion of heart, [Note: “way of life” (*conversationemque*): Ivo, *Panormia*; “confession” (*confessionemque*): Basel.] if, in the straits of time, help cannot be obtained for celebrating the mystery of baptism.

For that thief was not crucified for Christ’s name, but for the deserts of his crimes; nor did he suffer because he believed, but, while suffering, he believed. [Note: “while he was suffering” (*pateretur*): collected editions except Arg.] How greatly that saying of the Apostle avails even without the visible sacrament of baptism—“With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” [Note: Romans 10:10]—has been made plain in that thief.

But it is invisibly fulfilled when the mystery of baptism is excluded not by contempt for religion but by a circumstance of necessity. [Col. 1806B]

And below, chapter 24:

§1. And just as, in that thief, the goodness of the Almighty supplied what was lacking from the sacrament of baptism, [Note: “from” (*de*): Ivo, *Decretum* and collected editions; Ivo, *Panormia*: “what baptismal sacrament was lacking.”] because it was lacking through necessity, not through pride or contempt, [Note: “not”: omitted by the collected editions.] so in infants who die baptized [Note: “who do not die without baptism”: Arg.] the same grace of the Almighty must be believed to supply what they lack, because it is lacking not through an impious will, but through the incapacity of age: they cannot either believe with the heart unto righteousness or confess with the mouth unto salvation. [Note: “complete” (*explere*): collected editions and Ivo.]

Therefore, when others answer for them, [Note: “prayer is offered for them”: Ivo, *Decretum*; in the *Panormia*, everything from “unto salvation” through “And baptism outside” is omitted.] so that the celebration of the sacrament may be fulfilled for them, this certainly avails for their consecration, [Note: “celebration” (*celebrationem*): Ivo and collected editions.] because they themselves cannot answer.

Likewise, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book 6, chapter 4:

§2. It is indeed another’s act when one believes through another, [Note: “or knows” (*vel scit*) added: Basel; Lyons II, III.] just as it was another’s act when he sinned in another. [Note: “another” (*alterum*): collected editions.]

Likewise, in the same fourth book *Against the Donatists*, chapter 23:

§3. Just as in the thief, because baptism was bodily lacking through necessity, salvation was complete because it was spiritually present through piety, [Note: “specially” (*specialiter*): Basel.] so too, when baptism itself is available, if through necessity what the thief possessed is lacking, [Note: “was not lacking” (*non defuit*): collected editions.] salvation is completed.

This is the tradition maintained by the universal Church when infant children are baptized. Certainly [Note: “certainly” (*certe*): absent from the same editions except the first Basel edition.] they cannot yet believe with the heart unto righteousness [Note: “with the heart” (*corde*): absent from Ivo and Basel.] or confess with the mouth unto salvation, as the thief could; indeed, while the mystery is celebrated in them, they interrupt its very mystical words by crying and wailing, [Note: “they themselves” (*ipsi*): the same editions except the first Basel edition.] and yet no Christian would say that they are baptized in vain. [Note: “when” (*quando*): collected editions, for *quin* (“indeed”).]

Likewise, chapter 25:

§4. By all these considerations [Note: In Blessed Augustine, these words are preceded by those printed below under the same heading, “When others answer for infants.”] [Col. 1807A] it is shown that the sacrament of baptism is one thing and conversion of heart another, but that human salvation is completed by both. Nor, if one of them is lacking, ought we therefore to suppose that the other is also lacking, because the one can exist without the other in an infant, [Note: “could” (*potuit*): Basel and Lyons.] and the other could exist without the one in the thief, [Note: “so that in” (*ut in*): collected editions; the same, except Arg.] God supplying in either the thing which was lacking, provided that it was not lacking through will. [Note: “from” (*ex*): absent from Ivo.] But when one of these is lacking through will, a person is entangled in guilt. [Note: “indeed” (*enim*): collected editions except the first Basel, Nor.]

Baptism can indeed be present where conversion of heart is lacking. [Note: “confession” (*confessio*): collected editions.] But conversion of heart can be present where baptism has not been received; it cannot be present where baptism has been despised. [Note: “despised baptism”: absent from the collected editions except the first Basel.] For conversion of heart to God [Note: “the Lord” (*Dominum*): collected editions except the first Basel.] can by no means be affirmed when God’s sacrament is despised. [Note: “for” (*enim*): absent from Ivo.]

[Col. 1807B]

### Chapter XXXV. Not everything in a person is baptized.

The same, *Against Julian*, book IV, chapter 6. [Note: Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 112; *Decretum*, part 1, chapter 184.]

If you think that whatever is in a person, when he is baptized [Note: “and sanctified” added: collected editions.] must be considered baptized and sanctified, [Note: “with the person” added: the same editions except the first Basel; “believed” (*credendum*): collected editions.] you will say that the things in him which are in the intestines and bladder, and which are to be digested through the body’s digestion, are themselves baptized and sanctified. [Note: “by digestion of the body”: Ivo omits *per digestionem corporis*; “digestive processes” (*digestiones*): original and Arg., Basel; “are carried on” (*geruntur*): Arg.; “are digested” (*digeruntur*): remaining editions and Ivo; “to be expelled” (*egerenda*): original.]

You will say that a person situated in his mother’s womb is baptized and sanctified if necessity compels a pregnant woman to receive this sacrament, and that therefore the child who is born ought no longer to be baptized. [Note: “formed in the womb”: Arg.] Finally, you will say that fevers themselves are baptized and sanctified when the sick are baptized. [Col. 1807C]

### Chapter XXXVI. Baptism is valid even if it is administered by laypersons.

Likewise, to Fortunatus. [Note: Not extant in Augustine; cf. chapter 21.]

Baptism is holy in itself when it is given in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that in the same sacrament there is also the authority of transmission from our Lord to the Apostles, and through them to bishops and other priests, [Note: “and through them, or through the bishops”: Basel; “into”: Ivo; “and”: collected editions.] or even to Christian laypersons proceeding from the same origin and stock. [Note: “and” (*et*): collected editions.]

And below: [Note: Here Ivo inserts the words of the chapter *In necessitate*, cited above under the same heading.]

§1. For whenever that story is told, all who hear it are moved almost to tears. [Note: “are moved” (*moventur*): the same editions.] When shipwreck began to threaten on a certain ship, [Note: “and shipwreck immediately began to threaten”: collected editions except Lyons II, III.] there was no believer there except one penitent.

There was a certain man, not unmindful of his salvation and an exceedingly urgent petitioner for the sacrament, [Note: “a most honourable man in regard to the sacrament of his salvation”: Arg.] and there was no one who could give it except that penitent. For he had received it, but by the sin for which he was doing penance he had lost holiness, though he had not lost the sacrament. For if sinners lose this, why are they not baptized again when they are reconciled after penance?

He therefore gave what he had received; and, lest he end his life dangerously unreconciled, he asked the very person whom he had baptized [Note: “from him” (*ab eo*): absent from Ivo and the editions of Arg. and Lyons II–III.] [Col. 1808B] to reconcile him, and it was done: they escaped shipwreck. [Note: “and thus they escaped shipwreck”: collected editions except the first Basel; “and they escaped shipwreck”: Bohm.]

You know what they did. There was none among those of so devout a disposition who did not believe that the Lord had been present to their counsels in that danger. For a religious and suppliant mind demanded the sacrament from a human being, but itself obtained holiness from God.
