**Part XIX.** In catechism [Note: [Col. 1831] “catechumenate”: Burchard, Anselm, Ivo’s *Panormia*], baptism, and confirmation, one godparent [Note: [Col. 1831] “father”: Burchard and Anselm] may serve if [Col. 1832B] necessity compels. This is not, however, the Roman custom; rather, individual persons receive individual candidates [Note: [Col. 1831] “let them receive”: the other collected editions].

**C. CI. Not more than one, but one person, should receive an infant at baptism.** Likewise, from a decree of Pope Leo [Note: [Col. 1831C] The other collectors cite decrees of Pope Leo to St. Medard [Col. 1832C].] [Note: [Col. 1831] It does not occur in the Council of Soissons at Medard, which the heading of Burchard, Book 4, chapter 23, seems to suggest; nor in Anselm, Book 9, chapter 19 (24), Ivo’s *Panormia*, Book 1, chapter 78, or *Decretum*, Part 1, chapter 219, as indicated by the Correctors.]

No more than one person, whether man or woman, shall come forward to receive an infant from baptism. The same shall also be done in confirmation.

**C. CII. One who has not been baptized or confirmed ought not to hold another in chrism or baptism.** Likewise, from the Council of Mainz [Note: [Col. 1831] It seems to have been taken from chapter 4 of Theodore in Petit.—Burchard, Book 4, chapter 26. Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 1, chapter 79. *Decretum*, Part 1, chapter 220.]

A person who has not himself been baptized or confirmed cannot receive another as a godchild in baptism or chrism [Note: [Col. 1831] “as a son”: Burchard].

[Col. 1832C] **C. CIII. It is not permitted for an abbot or monk to have comothers.** Likewise, from the Council of Auxerre, chapter 25 [Note: [Col. 1831] Held A.D. 578.—Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 1, chapter 80. *Decretum*, Part 1, chapter 132.]

An abbot or monk may not receive children from baptism, nor have comothers [Note: [Col. 1831] “nor monks”: Ivo’s *Decretum*; “or monks”: *Panormia*].

**C. CIV. On the same matter.** Likewise, from the book of Capitularies [Note: [Col. 1832C] In the index of the seventh book of the *Capitularies*, number 494—for chapters 478 through 558 are missing from the volume received from Gaul—the following is read: “Let monks not make for themselves compadres and commadres.” These chapters are now usually listed under the name “First Addition”; Baluze deliberately omitted them because he had already published the Aachen Capitular separately.] [Note: [Col. 1831] Capitular of Aachen, A.D. 817, chapter 16.—Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 1, chapter 81; *Decretum*, Part 1, chapter 133.]

Monks shall not make for themselves compadres or commadres, nor shall they kiss women.

[Col. 1833A] **C. CV. Those who receive little children at baptism stand surety for them before God.** Likewise, from the sermon of St. Augustine after Easter, which begins, “This present day” [Note: [Col. 1833C] Ivo likewise cites it from the first Sunday after Easter. In Sermon 163, *On Time*, attributed to St. Augustine, these words occur: “Whatever men, whatever women have spiritually received children from the sacred font, let them know that they have stood surety for them before God, and therefore should always bestow upon them the care of true charity.” Similar statements occur in Sermon 215, the second sermon for the tenth Sunday after the feast of the Trinity.] [Note: [Col. 1833] It is by Caesarius, from the sayings of Maurus.—Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 1, chapter 81. *Decretum*, Part 1, chapter 134; Part 11, chapter 17.]

I exhort you above all, both women and men, who have received children at baptism, to recognize that you have stood surety before God for those whom you seemed to receive from the sacred font. Therefore always admonish them to preserve chastity, love justice, and hold fast to charity. And a little later: § 1. Above all, keep the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer yourselves, and show them to those whom you received [Note: [Col. 1833] “excepted”: Ivo’s *Decretum* and Argentinensis; “received”: *Panormia* and the remaining editions except Lyons] from the sacred font.

**C. CVI. A priest ought to have vessels of his own for the office of baptism and for washing altar-cloths.** Likewise, from the Council of Herdensis [Note: [Col. 1833C] Similar provisions occur in the Roman Order concerning divine offices, p. 156.] [Note: [Col. 1833] Burchard, Book 4, chapter 13; Ivo’s *Decretum*, Part 1, chapter 208, attribute it to the Council of Meaux; it is, however, among the chapters of Hincmar of Rheims, chapter 3, in Mansi, vol. 15.—Regino, Book 1, chapter 79.]

[Col. 1833B] **Part XX.** Every priest who cannot have a stone font shall have a suitable vessel exclusively [Note: [Col. 1833] “only for”: the other collected editions] for the office of baptism, which is not to be carried outside the church. Likewise, vessels of their own shall be kept for washing the corporal and altar-coverings, and nothing else shall be done in them.

**C. CVII. Neither rebaptisms nor reordinations may be performed.** Likewise, from the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 38 [Note: [Col. 1833] Held A.D. 397.—Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 1, chapter 83. *Decretum*, Part 1, chapter 152.]

**Part XXI.** It is not permitted to perform rebaptisms, and [Note: [Col. 1833] “and” is omitted by Ivo] reordinations [Note: [Col. 1833] “reordinations”: Venetian II], or translations of bishops [Note: [Col. 1833] “retranslations”: Argentinensis, Basiliensis, and Lyons II–III].

**C. CVIII. On the same matter.** Likewise, from Augustine’s Epistle CCIII, to Maximinus [Note: [Col. 1833] Epistle 23, Maurist edition, written A.D. 392.—Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 1, chapter 84. *Decretum*, Part 1, chapter 172. Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 6.]

To rebaptize a heretical person who has received these signs of holiness [Col. 1833C] [Note: [Col. 1833] “of the Holy Trinity”: the other collected editions] which Christian discipline has handed down [Note: [Col. 1833] “hands down”: Böhm] is altogether a sin; but to rebaptize a Catholic is a most heinous crime.

[Col. 1834A] **C. CIX. Concerning Arians: when they are to be baptized and when they are not.** Likewise, from the First Council of Arles, chapter 8 [Note: [Col. 1833] Held A.D. 314.—Tripartite Collection, Part 2, title 23, chapter 3.]

Concerning Arians, who follow their own law [Note: [Col. 1833D] In the printed council the words follow: “that they be rebaptized” [as also in the Hispanic Collection]. St. Augustine relates in chapter 49 of *On Heresies* that Catholics, and perhaps non-Catholics too, were customarily rebaptized by Arians. In some very ancient manuscripts of this council, however, the text reads: “Concerning Africans, because they follow their own law in order to rebaptize: it was decided,” etc. Concerning Africans, see above, Distinction 98, chapter *Afros*, which is by Gregory I and is repeated in the letter of Gregory II to all the clergy and people of Thuringia, and likewise in the synod of Felix III.], it was decided that, if any from this heresy come to the Church, the priests of our faith should question them on the Creed; and if they ascertain that they were baptized in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, hands alone are to be laid upon them [Note: [Col. 1833] “let them lay hands”: the other collected editions], that they may receive the Holy Spirit. But if, when questioned, they do not answer concerning this Trinity, they are to be baptized [Note: [Col. 1833] “rebaptized”: Argentinensis, Basiliensis, and Lyons II–III].

**C. CX. Those concerning whom it is unknown whether they have been baptized are to be baptized.** Likewise, Gregory III to Boniface, Epistle IV [Note: [Col. 1833] Rather, Gregory II, written A.D. 726. Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 1, chapter 92. *Decretum*, Part 1, chapter 146.]

[Col. 1834B] Little children who have been taken away from their parents [Note: [Col. 1833] “from” is absent from Basiliensis], and whose baptism is unknown [Note: [Col. 1833] “whether or not they were baptized”: Ivo’s *Decretum* and the other collected editions], ought, as reason requires according to the tradition of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 1833] “traditions”: the other collected editions], to be baptized if there is no one who can testify [Note: [Col. 1833] “it is unknown”: the other collected editions; Ivo].

**C. CXI. On the same matter.** Likewise, from the Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 1833] Held A.D. 401.—Tripartite Collection, Part 2, title 19, chapter 6. Burchard, Book 4, chapter 45. Anselm, Book 9, chapter 56 (15). Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 1, chapter 93. *Decretum*, Part 1, chapters 147 and 239.—Compare the Council of Worms, held A.D. 868, chapter 70, and canon 85 of the Sixth Synod.]

It was decided concerning infants that, whenever the most reliable witnesses who can testify without doubt that they have been baptized are not found, and the infants themselves are not old enough to answer concerning the sacraments administered to them, they are to be baptized without any scruple, lest this hesitation deprive them of the cleansing of the sacraments. Hence also the envoys of the Moors [Note: [Col. 1833] “your envoys”: Ivo’s *Decretum*, chapter 239], our brothers [Note: [Col. 1833] “dearest”: Basiliensis, Paris, and Lyons], consulted us, because they redeem many such persons from barbarians [Col. 1834C] [Note: [Col. 1833] “return”: Argentinensis; “have redeemed”: the other collected editions except Basiliensis]. Likewise [Note: [Col. 1834C] From “Likewise” to the end these words are absent from the royal manuscript of this council, from Greek canon 72 of Carthage, from Worms, and from Burchard, as well as from the Hispanic Collection, Anselm, and Ivo’s *Decretum*, chapter 239. In the canon of the Sixth Synod, the preceding words—“Hence also,” etc.—are likewise absent.] and [Note: [Col. 1833] “and” is absent from the Paris and Lyons editions] concerning churches, whenever there is doubt about their consecration, action must be taken so that they are consecrated without any hesitation.

[Col. 1835A] **C. CXII. On the same matter.** Likewise, Pope Leo [Note: [Col. 1835] Epistle 166, written A.D. 458, Ballerini edition.—Ivo’s *Decretum*, Part 1, chapter 48] to Leo [Note: [Col. 1835] “Neon”: Ballerini], Bishop of Ravenna, Epistle XXXV, chapter 1.

Therefore, since the one who desires regeneration remembers nothing of his baptism, nor can another testify concerning him who knows him to have been consecrated, nor [can] the one who is consecrated. We indeed know [Note: [Col. 1835D] “Remembers nothing”: Ivo likewise has this wording, though the rest more fully than Gratian. The complete passage is: “Therefore, when neither the one who desires regeneration remembers that he has been baptized, nor can another testify concerning one whom he does not know to have been consecrated, there is nothing into which sin can creep, since in this matter of his conscience neither the one who is consecrated nor the one who consecrates is guilty. We indeed know,” etc. But, because of the gloss at the words “nor the one,” the text has not been corrected.]. We indeed know that it is an inexpiable crime whenever anyone is compelled, according to the condemned doctrines of heretics and contrary to the ordinances of the holy Fathers, to undergo twice the washing that has been granted once for regeneration, in opposition to the apostolic declaration [Note: [Col. 1835] “teaching”: the Hispanic Collection; Ballerini; compare Ephesians 4:5], which proclaims to us one Godhead in the Trinity, one confession in faith, one sacrament in baptism. But in this case nothing similar is feared, since what is wholly unknown to have occurred [Col. 1835B] cannot incur the charge of repetition. Therefore, whenever such a person is encountered, first investigate by careful examination, and over a long period—unless perhaps death is imminent [Note: [Col. 1835] “is imminent”: the Hispanic Collection]—inquire whether there is absolutely no one who can by testimony assist the ignorance of the person who does not know [Note: [Col. 1835] Omitted by Basiliensis]. And when it has been established that one who needs the sacrament of baptism is vainly kept from it by suspicion alone, let him approach without fear to receive the grace of which he knows no trace in himself; nor should we fear to open to him the gate of salvation, which he is not shown ever to have entered before.

**C. CXIII. On the same matter.** The same, Epistle XC, alternatively XCII, to Rusticus, chapter 16 [Note: [Col. 1835] Epistle 167, Ballerini edition, written A.D. 458 or 459.—Burchard, Book 4, chapter 44. Anselm, Book 9, chapter 15 (14). Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 1, chapter 94. *Decretum*, Part 1, chapter 238. *Polycarpus*, Book 3, title 10.]

If there are no indications among relatives or household members [Note: [Col. 1835] “and”: Ivo’s *Decretum* and the other collected editions], none among clergy or neighbors, by which those under inquiry can be shown to have been baptized, action must be taken that they be born again, lest they manifestly perish; for in their case reason does not [Note: [Col. 1835] “no reason”: the other collected editions] permit what is not shown to have been done to appear repeated [Note: [Col. 1835] “so that it may appear repeated”: apparently absent from Ivo’s *Decretum*]. But those who can remember coming to church with their parents can recall whether they received what was being given to their parents. Yet if even this is absent from their memory, what is unknown to have been conferred seems to be conferred upon them, because no rash presumption intervenes where there is the diligence of piety.

**C. CXIV. Whatever is in a mother’s body is not baptized with her.** Likewise, Augustine, *Against Julian*, Book VI, chapter [Note: [Col. 1835] Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 1, chapter 111. *Decretum*, Part 1, chapter 184.]

**Part XXII.** If what is conceived in a mother belonged to her body in such a way as to be reckoned her part [Note: [Col. 1835] “belongs”: the other collected editions], an infant whose mother had been baptized in some pressing danger of death while she carried him in the womb would not be baptized. But now, since he too is baptized [Note: [Col. 1835] “would be baptized”: Ivo’s *Decretum*, Venetian I–II, and Paris; “let him be baptized”: the remaining editions; Ivo’s *Panormia*], he certainly is not regarded as having been baptized twice [Note: [Col. 1835] “is regarded”: the other collected editions]. Therefore, while in the womb he did not belong to the mother’s body [Note: [Col. 1835] “not, therefore, did he belong”: the same editions; Ivo].

[Col. 1836B] **C. CXV. Why one in a mother’s womb is not baptized with the mother.** Likewise, Isidore, Book I of *Sentences, On the Supreme Good*, chapter 24 [Note: [Col. 1835] Ivo, *Panormia*, Book 1, chapter 112. *Decretum*, Part 1, chapter 185. Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 6.]

Those who are in their mothers’ wombs cannot for that reason be baptized together with their mother, because one who has not yet been born according to Adam cannot be reborn [Note: [Col. 1835] “rebaptized”: Ivo, *Pan.*—“regenerated”: the collected editions.] according to Christ. For regeneration cannot be spoken of in [Note: [Col. 1835] “in him”: the same editions—Ivo.] one whom generation has not preceded. And below: §1. Let those who live wickedly in the Church and do not cease to communicate, supposing that they are cleansed by such communion, learn that it profits them nothing toward cleansing.

### C. CXVI. On the same subject. Likewise, from the Council of Martin of Braga, c. 54 [Note: [Col. 1835] c. 6, Council of Neocaesarea, in Martin of Braga’s translation (“Pope”: collected editions).]

If any pregnant woman should desire [Note: [Col. 1835] “desired”: Basel edition—Bohmer—“should designate”: Nuremberg, Venice I–II, Paris, Lyons I editions.] to receive the grace of baptism, she may have authority to do so whenever she wishes. For in this matter the mother shares nothing with the child who is born, because each person’s [Note: [Col. 1835] “for each”: Spanish Collection—the collected editions.] own [Note: [Col. 1835] adds: “power”: Spanish Collection.] will is manifested in confession [Note: [Col. 1835] “may be manifested”: the same collection.].

### C. CXVII. On those who are unknowingly baptized twice. Likewise, from Theodore’s Penitential [Note: [Col. 1835] Read among Theodore’s Chapters in D’Achery, c. 9—Burchard, bk. 4, c. 51; Ivo, *Pan.* bk. 1, c. 122; *Decr.* pt. 1, c. 245.]

**Part XXIII.** Those who have unknowingly been baptized twice need not do penance for this, except that, according to the canons, they cannot be ordained unless some grave necessity compels it. But those who, not unknowingly, have been baptized again, as though [Note: [Col. 1837] “because as though”: collected editions, first Argentinian and Nuremberg editions.] they had crucified Christ anew, shall do penance for seven years on the fourth and sixth days of the week, and shall fast for three [Note: [Col. 1837] “four”: Ivo, *Pan.*.] Lents [Note: [Col. 1837] “shall do penance”: Burchard, Ivo, *Decr.*—“shall abstain”: *Pan.*]. If they did it because of some vice [Note: [Col. 1837] “it was done”: Burchard, Ivo.], likewise. But if [Note: [Col. 1837] “But if”: Argentinian and Basel editions.] they thought it was for purification, they shall do similar penance for three [Note: [Col. 1837] “three times in the year”: Basel edition.] years.

### C. CXVIII. On those who are deliberately baptized twice. Pope Felix III, Epistle I, c. 2 and following [Note: [Col. 1837] Written A.D. 488—Burchard, bk. 4, c. 99; Ivo, *Decr.* pt. 1, c. 293.]

Those who are known to have been bishops, presbyters, or deacons, and who—whether perhaps willingly [Note: [Col. 1837] “resisting”: Argentinian edition.] or under compulsion—are known to have cast away that one and *saving* laver [Note: [Col. 1837] “Casting-away”: After these words the original, Burchard, and Ivo insert many passages which must certainly be read.], must lie in penance until the day of their death, if they repent [Note: [Col. 1837] “if they reject”: Basel edition.]; nor may they in any way attend even the prayers of catechumens, much less those of the faithful. Only lay communion is to be restored to them at death.

§1. Concerning clerics, monks, consecrated virgins, or laypersons [Note: [Col. 1837] “and”: the collected editions—Ivo.], we decree that the rule [Note: [Col. 1837] “and this rule”: collected editions, first Argentinian and Basel editions.] be observed which the Nicene Synod decreed should be observed concerning those who have fallen or may fall [Note: [Col. 1837] “among”: the collected editions; “are”: Basel edition.]: namely, that those who, under no necessity, fear of anything, or danger [Note: [Col. 1837] “and”: Burchard, Ivo—the collected editions.], wickedly delivered themselves to heretics in order to be rebaptized [Note: [Col. 1837] “might be rebaptized”: Burchard, Argentinian and Basel editions.], if they nevertheless repent from the heart, shall be among the hearers for three years; for seven years they shall remain among penitents under the hands of priests; and for two [Note: [Col. 1837] absent from Ivo—“also for two”: Burchard.] years they shall also [Note: [Col. 1837] absent from the original.] not in any way be permitted to offer oblations [Note: [Col. 1837] “to oblations”: Burchard, with the following word “offer” omitted.], but shall be joined only with laypeople [Note: [Col. 1837] “the people”: Burchard, Ivo—the collected editions.] in prayer. Let not one who did not fear to deny God be ashamed to bow the neck before him [Note: [Col. 1837] plural: “they did not fear”: the same editions.].

§2. But to children—whether clerics or laypersons—and to similarly situated girls, for whom [Note: [Col. 1837] “who”: the same editions.] the ignorance of age pleads, and who are called “prepubescent” because they are still without puberty [Note: [Col. 1837] “unclothed”: Burchard—“in clothing”: Ivo—“beardless”: Argentinian edition; “purity”: Burchard, Ivo.], communion is to be restored after they have for some time been kept under laying-on of hands. Nor is the penance to be awaited of those whom ecclesiastical discipline exempts [Note: [Col. 1837] “receives”: Basel editions—“exempted”: Nuremberg, Venice I–II, Paris, Lyons I; “for coercion”: collected editions.] from correction.

### C. CXIX. Presbyters may anoint those baptized with chrism. Pope Innocent, to Bishop Decentius, Epistle I, c. 3 [Note: [Col. 1837] Written A.D. 416—Burchard, bk. 4, c. 69; Anselm, bk. 9, c. 32; Ivo, *Pan.* bk. 1, c. 116; *Decr.* pt. 1, c. 263; Polycarp, bk. 3, title 10; Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 7.]

**Part XXIV.** Presbyters, whether they baptize apart from the bishop or in his presence [Note: [Col. 1837] “when they baptize”: Spanish Collection—Constantinus = Burchard, Anselm, Ivo.], may anoint the baptized with chrism [Note: [Col. 1837] absent from the Argentinian and Nuremberg editions.] [Note: [Col. 1837] “may not”: Ivo, *Pan.*—“may”: *Decr.* and the collected editions.], provided that it has been consecrated by the bishop. Yet they may not mark the forehead with this oil, for this belongs solely to bishops when they impart the *Paraclete Spirit* [Note: [Col. 1837] absent from Burchard, Anselm, and Ivo.].

### C. CXX. Presbyters may not anoint the foreheads of the baptized. From Gregory’s Register, to Januarius, Bishop of Cagliari, bk. III, epistle 9 [Note: [Col. 1837] Epistle 9, written A.D. 594, bk. 4, Maurist edition—Burchard, bk. 4, c. 70; Ivo, *Pan.* bk. 1, c. 117; *Decr.* pt. 1, c. 264; Peter Lombard, ibid.]

Presbyters must not presume to mark baptized infants on their foreheads with sacred chrism [Note: [Col. 1837] “rebaptized”: Basel edition.]. Rather, presbyters should anoint the baptized upon the breast, so that bishops may afterward anoint [Note: [Col. 1837] “confirm”: Burchard, Ivo—the collected editions.] them on the forehead.

### C. CXXI. A chrism-cloth may be anointed a second time and placed over another baptized person. From a Council at Beauvais [Note: [Col. 1837] Rather, from Theodore’s Penitential in Petit, c. 4—Burchard, bk. 4, c. 94; Ivo, *Pan.* bk. 1, c. 99; *Decr.* pt. 1, c. 288.]

If anyone wishes to anoint a cloth with chrism [Note: [Col. 1837] “of chrism”: Burchard, Ivo.] again and place it over another baptized person, it is not improper.

### C. CXXII. Baptism may not be consecrated with old chrism. From a Council of Lyons [Note: [Col. 1837] An uncertain chapter; compare, however, *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, Additions III, c. 7.]

If anyone attempts to baptize with any chrism other than the new chrism which he has received by the gift or permission of his own bishop [Note: [Col. 1837] “his own”: Basel edition—“for”: the other editions; “received”: Burchard, Ivo.], except where death is imminent, he clearly pronounces upon himself the sentence of his own condemnation for the rashness of his deed.

### C. CXXIII. Presbyters are to receive chrism only from their own bishops. From a Council at Valencia [Note: [Col. 1837] Rather, from the Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 36, or the *Statuta Ecclesiae Antiqua*, c. 87; compare c. 9, D. 18. The heading derives from Burchard, bk. 4, c. 76, and Ivo, *Decr.* pt. 1, c. 270; *Pan.* bk. 1, c. 101, from Anselm’s collection, bk. 4, c. 115.]

Presbyters who govern diocesan churches [Note: [Col. 1837] “through dioceses”: Ballerini.] shall seek chrism before the solemnity of Easter not from just any bishops but from their own bishop, and not through an inferior [Note: [Col. 1837] “younger”: Ballerini—Burchard, Ivo, Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] cleric, but personally, or through one [Note: [Col. 1839] “another”: Basel edition.] who is of the same order [Note: [Col. 1839] “who keeps the sacristy”: Ballerini.].

### C. CXXIV. A bishop may make chrism and send it through his dioceses at any time. From the Council of Martin of Braga, c. 51 and following [Note: [Col. 1839] Compiled by Martin of Braga (“Pope”: collected editions) from c. 20 of the First Council of Toledo and c. 56 of the Council of Laodicea; compare D. 95, c. 11.]

A bishop [Note: [Col. 1839] “bishops”: Spanish Collection.] may [Note: [Col. 1839] “may”: collected editions, first Basel edition.] at any time make chrism and send it through his dioceses [Note: [Col. 1839] “direct it”: Spanish Collection.], provided that, before Easter Day, a deacon or subdeacon is sent from each church to the bishop to receive chrism.

§1. A presbyter [Note: [Col. 1839] adds: “indeed”: collected editions.] shall not sign infants in the bishop’s presence, unless perhaps the bishop has directed him to do so.

§2. A presbyter [Note: [Col. 1839] “nor”: the same editions.] may not enter the baptistery before the bishop, but with the bishop, unless perhaps the bishop is absent or ill.

### C. CXXV. He who undertakes the office of baptizing must not proceed without chrism. From the Council of Orange, c. 1 [Note: [Col. 1839] Held A.D. 441—Regino, bk. 1, c. 78; tripartite collection, pt. 2, title 21, c. 1; Burchard, bk. 4, c. 73; Ivo, *Decr.* pt. 1, c. 267.]

No minister who undertakes the office of baptizing may go anywhere without chrism, because we have decided that chrism is to be applied once in baptism [Note: [Col. 1839] “in baptism” absent from the Spanish Collection.]. But as for one who, through whatever necessity, has not been anointed with chrism in baptism, the priest shall be reminded at confirmation [Note: [Col. 1839C] “The priest shall be reminded”: In Burchard and Ivo, who here end the chapter, which they cite from Vaison, c. 5, prompted by Regino’s collection, in which c. 3 of the Council of Vaison was prefixed, it reads: “it shall be completed in the confirmation of the priest,” or, in Ivo: “let it be completed.”] [Note: [Col. 1839] “shall be moved”: Basel editions.]. For among us there is but one blessing of chrism itself. We say this not as prejudging anyone, but so that chrismation may be regarded as necessary [Note: [Col. 1839D] “That it may be regarded as necessary”: There is a notable variation in the Cologne edition in three volumes. There it is also read thus: “let repeated chrismation not be regarded as necessary”; “let repeated chrismation not be regarded as necessary”; and “let repeated chrismation be regarded as necessary” [Note: [Col. 1839] “not as prejudging anything, but that repeated chrismation not be regarded as necessary”: Spanish Collection.]. This last reading alone was retained in the four-volume edition.].

### C. CXXVI. Before chrism is poured in, water may be taken from the font for sprinkling. *Capitulary*, bk. VI, c. 77 [Note: [Col. 1839] Ivo, *Pan.* bk. 1, c. 103; *Decr.* pt. 1, c. 112.]

On the holy Saturday of Easter or Pentecost, if anyone wishes to receive consecrated water for sprinkling in his home, he shall receive it before the infusion of chrism [Note: [Col. 1839] “they shall receive”: the original—“he shall receive”: Ivo, *Decr.*].

### C. CXXVII. The source from which the sanctification by sprinkling took its beginning. Cyprian, bk. IV, epistle 7, to Magnus [Note: [Col. 1839] “Pope Cyprian”: collected editions—written about A.D. 256.]

Nor should anyone be disturbed because the sick are commanded to be sprinkled or poured upon when they receive the Lord’s grace, since Holy Scripture speaks and says through Ezekiel the prophet: “And I will sprinkle [Note: [Col. 1839] “may he sprinkle upon us”: Argentinian edition.] clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your uncleannesses [Note: [Col. 1839] “sins”: Basel edition.] and from all your idols [Note: [Col. 1839] “defilements”: the same edition.]; and I will cleanse you, and give you a new heart, and give a new spirit within [Note: [Col. 1839] absent from the same edition.] you.”

Likewise, in Numbers [Note: [Col. 1839] Num. 19:11.]:

§1. “Whoever touches the corpse [Note: [Col. 1840C] From “Whoever touches” to the verse “And he spoke,” these matters are expounded by Blessed Cyprian in other words; on that basis many things in the remaining parts of this chapter have been corrected.] of a human being and is thereby unclean for seven days, shall be sprinkled with this water on the third and seventh days, and thus shall be cleansed.” [Note: [Col. 1839] “from”: Vulgate—Argentinian and Basel editions.]

Likewise:

§2. “If he has not been cleansed by faith in the Trinity, he shall be unclean at the resurrection among the company of the saints [Note: [Col. 1840D] “At the resurrection”: Some traces of this proposition occur in the interlinear gloss on this passage of Numbers.]. If he has not been sprinkled on the third day, he cannot be cleansed on the seventh. Everyone who touches a human corpse and has not been sprinkled with this mixture will defile the tabernacle of the Lord and will perish from Israel; because whoever has not been sprinkled with the water of expiation shall be unclean, and his filth shall remain [Note: [Col. 1839] “remains”: Basel edition.] upon him.”

And again [Note: [Col. 1839] Num. 8:6.]: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take the Levites from the midst of the children of Israel, and you shall purify them. And you shall do thus for their purification: you shall sprinkle them all around with water of purification.” And again: “The water of sprinkling is purification.”

Hence it is evident that sprinkling with water also possesses the effect of the saving laver; and when these things are performed in the Church [Note: [Col. 1839] “are performed, it is most truly known through the faith of the recipient and giver, etc.”: collected editions.], where there is faith both in the recipient and in the giver, all things stand whole and can be completed and perfected by the Lord’s majesty and the truth of faith [Note: [Col. 1839] adds: “or confirmed”: Argentinian edition.].

And below:

§3. The Holy Spirit is not given by measure [Note: [Col. 1841] “is given by measure”: original.], but is wholly poured upon the believer [Note: [Col. 1841] “believers”: collected editions.]. For if the day dawns equally for all, and if the sun spreads its equal and impartial light over all [Note: [Col. 1841] “equally”: Basel edition—“spreads equally over all”: Argentinian edition.], how much more does Christ [Note: [Col. 1841] absent from the same edition.], the true sun and day, bestow in his Church the light of eternal life with equal impartiality?

We see the sacrament of this equality celebrated in Exodus, when manna fell from heaven and, as a foreshadowing of things to come, displayed the nourishment of heavenly bread and the food of the coming Christ. There, without distinction [Note: [Col. 1841] “discrimination”: the same edition.] of sex or age, an omer was gathered equally by each person [Note: [Col. 1841] “each gathered equally”: collected editions; “each woman”: Lyons I.]. From this it appeared that Christ’s mercy and heavenly grace, which were to follow, would be divided equally among all: without distinction of sex, without discrimination [Note: [Col. 1841] “discrimination”: Argentinian edition.] of years, without respect [Note: [Col. 1841] “exception”: Basel editions.] of persons; the gift of spiritual grace [Note: [Col. 1841] adds: “of God”: collected editions, first Argentinian edition.] would be poured out upon all the people of God.

Certainly, the same spiritual grace which believers receive equally in baptism is afterward either diminished or increased in our manner of life and conduct. Thus in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1841] Matt. 13:8.] the Lord’s seed is sown equally; but according to the diversity of the soil, one portion is consumed [Note: [Col. 1841] absent from the collected editions except the first Basel edition; also absent from the Argentinian edition through “into manifold abundance”; “is taken up”: collected editions.], while another is heaped up in manifold abundance by its fruit, increasing thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or a hundredfold [Note: [Col. 1841] absent from the Argentinian edition; “increasing”: Argentinian and Basel editions—“are increased”: the other editions.].

And a little later:

§4. But if anyone is troubled because some of [Note: [Col. 1841] “from”: Argentinian and Basel editions.] those who are being baptized while sick are still held by unclean spirits [Note: [Col. 1841C] “Are held”: The printed original has *tentantur*, “are tempted,” but five manuscripts have *tentabantur*, “were being tempted.” This is what Blessed Cyprian means: while the rites preceding baptism are administered, people may still be tempted by unclean spirits; but the temptation ceases in the absolution of baptism, that is, in the saving water. For Cyprian here uses *baptizantur* (“are baptized”) as philosophers often use *generari* (“to be generated”), namely for the alteration preceding the bringing forth and emergence of a form.], let him know that the devil’s stubborn wickedness has power up to the saving water, but in baptism loses all the poison of its wickedness [Note: [Col. 1841] “all”: Basel edition—“every”: original; “powers”: Bohmer—the collected editions.].

We see this example in King Pharaoh [Note: [Col. 1841] absent from the same editions except the first Basel edition; compare Exod. 14.], who, having long struggled and persisted in his treachery [Note: [Col. 1841] “by force”: collected editions except the first Basel and Lyons editions; “pride”: Basel edition.], was able to resist and prevail only until he came to the water. When he came to it, he was conquered and destroyed.

But Blessed Paul the Apostle declares that sea to have been a sacrament of baptism, saying [Note: [Col. 1841] 1 Cor. 10:1; the printed citation “1 Cor. 30:1” is evidently erroneous.]: “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers [Note: [Col. 1841] “your”: collected editions except the first Basel, Nuremberg, and Lyons II–III editions.] were all under the cloud, and all passed through [Note: [Col. 1841] absent from the Vulgate and the Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in [Note: [Col. 1841] “and in”: collected editions except the first Basel edition.] the cloud and in the sea.” And he added, saying: “Now all these things happened as figures [Note: [Col. 1841] “as a figure of us”: the same editions.] of us.”

What was formerly enacted through Pharaoh is also performed today: through exorcists, by a human voice and divine power, the devil is scourged [Note: [Col. 1841] “is scourged, burned, tortured”: Basel edition.], burned, and tortured. Although he often says that he is going out and abandoning the people of God, yet in what he says [Note: [Col. 1841] “had said”: collected editions.] he deceives [Note: [Col. 1841] “is deceitful”: the same editions except Lyons II–III.], and exercises the same obstinacy and fraud. Nevertheless, when one comes to God’s saving water and to the sanctification of baptism, we must know and trust [Note: [Col. 1841] “have confidence”: collected editions.] that there the devil is crushed, and the person consecrated to God is freed by divine mercy.

### C. CXXVIII. On those who defer receiving baptism until the end of life. John Chrysostom, *Homilies on the Epistle to the Hebrews*, Homily XIII, on c. 7

**Part XXV.** When someone sins for the very reason that he may receive holy baptism at his last breath, perhaps he will not obtain it. Believe me: I do not say what I am about to say to frighten you. I have known many who suffered this: in hope of baptism they committed many sins, but departed empty at the day of death [Note: [Col. 1841] “withdrew”: Argentinian and Basel editions.]. For God gives baptism in order to forgive sins, not to add to them [Note: [Col. 1842C] “Not to add”: The Verona edition mistakenly has ἵνα αὐξήσῃ, “that he may increase”; it should be corrected from the manuscripts to οὐχ ἵνα αὐξήσῃ, “not that he may increase.”]. But if someone uses baptism for this purpose, that he may sin more greatly, baptism itself becomes a cause of negligence.

### C. CXXIX. The unbelief of parents does not harm baptized infants. Augustine to Boniface, Epistle XXIII [Note: [Col. 1841] Epistle 98, Maurist edition; written A.D. 408—Anselm, bk. 9, c. 41 (53); Polycarp, bk. 3, title 10.]

**Part XXVI.** You ask me whether unbelieving parents [Note: [Col. 1841] adds: “unbelieving”: Argentinian, Basel, and Lyons II–III editions.] harm their baptized infants when they try to cure them by sacrifices to demons; *and, if they do not harm them,* how the faith of parents benefits them when they are baptized, if the parents’ unbelief cannot harm them.

I answer that the power of that sacrament, namely saving baptism, is so great within the holy structure of Christ’s body that one who has once been regenerated [Note: [Col. 1842C] “Once regenerated”: More fully in Blessed Augustine [thus Anselm]: “that one who has once been generated through carnal pleasure, when he has once been regenerated through the spiritual will of others,” etc. Many things in this chapter were corrected where the gloss permitted. The propositions themselves have been transposed by the compiler at his discretion.] through the will of others can no longer be bound by the chain of another’s iniquity, to which he has given no consent by any will of his own [Note: [Col. 1843] “gives consent”: original—the collected editions except Lyons II–III.].

For, he says [Note: [Col. 1843] absent from Bohmer.], [Note: [Col. 1843] Ezek. 18:4.] “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine”; and again: “The soul which sins shall itself die.” But [Note: [Col. 1843] “for”: the collected editions.] the infant does not himself sin when his parents, or anyone else, apply to him, without his knowing it, the sacrileges of demons [Note: [Col. 1843] “his”: the same editions—adds: “at all”: the same editions except the Argentinian edition; absent from the Argentinian edition.]. Rather [Note: [Col. 1843] “But altogether”: Argentinian, Basel, and Lyons II–III editions—“But if indeed”: the other editions.], he derived sin from Adam so that it might be loosed by the grace of that sacrament, because the soul was not yet living separately—that is, another soul of which it could be said: “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine.”

He therefore says [Note: [Col. 1843] The original and Anselm read, “Now likewise, when a human being”; so also C. 1, question 4, c. 8. “When” is absent from the Basel edition; “and from” occurs in the Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] that, when a human being is in himself made distinct from the one who begot him, he is not held liable for another’s sin without his own awareness [Note: [Col. 1843] “consent”: original—Basel edition.]. And below:

§1. How then [Note: [Col. 1843] “therefore”: Basel edition—“but when”: the original.] do adults sin against an infant by presenting him and trying to bind him in the sacrilegious chains of demons? Their souls are not one shared soul, so that they can also have a shared guilt. Guilt is not shared through the will of another in the way that grace is shared through the unity of the Holy Spirit.

Likewise, a little earlier: The regenerating Spirit [Note: [Col. 1843] adds: “Holy”: collected editions.] is shared by the adults presenting the child and by the infant who is presented and reborn. Therefore, through this fellowship of one and the same Spirit, the will of those who present the child benefits the infant presented [Note: [Col. 1843] “Likewise”: Basel and Lyons editions—“The same”: the other editions.].

And below: In this person and that person there can be one Holy Spirit, even if they do not know one another, through whom grace is shared by both [Note: [Col. 1843] “becomes”: Argentinian edition; “to both”: Basel edition.]. But there cannot be one spirit shared by this human being and that human being, through which, although one sins and the other does not sin, guilt is nevertheless common [Note: [Col. 1843] “the other sins, so that”: collected editions.].

Accordingly, an infant once generated from his parents’ flesh can be regenerated by God’s Spirit, so that the obligation contracted from them may be loosed. But one who has once been regenerated by God’s Spirit cannot be regenerated from his parents’ flesh, so that an obligation which has been loosed may be contracted again. Therefore an infant does not lose the grace of Christ once received, except through his own impiety.

And a little later:

§2. Nevertheless, parents, or any adults whatsoever, who try to bind baptized children or any infants in the sacrileges of demons are rightly called spiritual [Note: [Col. 1843] “specially”: Basel editions.] murderers. They do not indeed bring about their death, but, so far as lies in them, they become killers. It is therefore rightly [Note: [Col. 1843] “rightly”: the original—“rightly therefore”: the collected editions.] said to them when they are forbidden this crime: “Do not kill your little children.”

For the Apostle also says: “Do not quench the Spirit [Note: [Col. 1843] adds: “Holy”: collected editions except the first Basel edition; compare 1 Thess. 5:19.],” not because he can be quenched, but because those who act as if they wished him to be quenched are rightly called, so far as lies in them, his extinguishers [Note: [Col. 1843] “to be quenched”: Basel edition.].

§3. “Nor should that trouble you,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1843] Compare above, c. 33.] And below: “For the necessary ministries are celebrated through them” [Note: [Col. 1843] “mysteries”: Argentinian and Basel editions.].

And below: Infants are offered to receive spiritual [Note: [Col. 1843] “special”: Basel edition.] grace not so much by those in whose hands they are carried [Note: [Col. 1843] “in whose hands”: Argentinian, Nuremberg, Venice I–II, and Paris editions.]—although they too offer them, if they themselves are good believers [Note: [Col. 1843] “are”: Basel editions.]—as by the whole fellowship of saints and believers. For they are rightly understood to be offered by all those to whom their offering is pleasing and who, by their holy and undivided love, assist them toward communion [Note: [Col. 1843] “communication”: collected editions.] in the Holy Spirit.

Therefore the whole mother Church, which exists in her saints [Note: [Col. 1843] adds: “her own”: the same editions.], does this, because she as a whole gives birth to all, and as a whole gives birth to each individual.

Likewise below:

§4. You seem, indeed, to have proposed a most difficult question at the end of your inquiry, with that intention by which you are accustomed earnestly to avoid falsehood. “If,” you say, “I place before you an infant and ask whether, when he grows up [Note: [Col. 1843] “comes to adult age”: the same editions.], he will be chaste, or a thief, or will not be a thief, you will doubtless answer: ‘I do not know.’ And if I ask whether, while established in that same infant age, he thinks anything good or bad, you will say: ‘I do not know.’”

If, therefore, you dare promise nothing definite about his future conduct [Note: [Col. 1843] “definitely”: Bohmer.] or his present thought [Note: [Col. 1843] “knowledge and thought”: Argentinian edition.], what else is it than that, when infants are offered for baptism, parents answer for them as guarantors [*fidei auctores*] of faith [Note: [Col. 1843] “agents”: Argentinian edition—*fidedictores*, “speakers of faith”: original.] and say that they do what that age cannot think, or, if it can think it, what is hidden?

For we ask those by whom they are offered and say: “Does he believe in God?” concerning an age which does not know whether God exists. They answer: “He believes.” And each of the other questions is answered in the same way [Note: [Col. 1843] “to each question, thus is the answer”: collected editions.].

Therefore I wonder that parents answer so confidently on behalf of an infant in these matters, saying that he does such great goods as the baptizer asks at the hour when he is baptized, yet, if at that same hour I ask whether the one being baptized will be chaste, or [Note: [Col. 1843] “or a thief, or will not be”: the same editions.] will not be a thief, I do not know whether anyone would dare say that he will or will not be any of these things, just as he answers me without doubt that he believes [Note: [Col. 1843] “believes”: the same editions.] in God and turns himself to God [Note: [Col. 1843] “the Lord”: collected editions except the first Basel edition.].

And below:

§5. See: I do what I can. May the Lord help me to do what you ask. Certainly we often speak thus: as Easter approaches [Note: [Col. 1845] “draws near”: collected editions except the first Basel edition.], we say that the Lord’s Passion is tomorrow, or the day after tomorrow, or three days hence, or four days hence [Note: [Col. 1845] original: “is tomorrow or the day after tomorrow.”], although he suffered so many years ago and that Passion occurred only once. Likewise, on Sunday itself we say: “Today the Lord rose,” although so many years have passed since he rose.

Why does no one so foolish accuse us of lying when we speak this way? Is it not because we name these days according to their likeness to the days on which these things occurred, so that the day which is not that very day, but is like it through the recurrence of time, is called that day; and what did not happen on that day but long ago is said to happen on that day because of the celebration of the sacrament [Note: [Col. 1845] “which is not the same by the recurrence of time, but by its likeness”: collected editions; “in that day”: Argentinian, Basel, and Lyons II–III editions; adds: “at another time”: collected editions except the first Argentinian edition.]?

And below [Note: [Col. 1845] Compare above, c. 76.]:

§6. “Thus the infant,” etc.

And below:

§7. But when a human being begins to have understanding, he does not repeat that sacrament, but understands it and will conform himself also by a will consonant with its truth [Note: [Col. 1845] “will constrain himself”: Venice I–II and Paris editions.]. So long as he cannot do this [Note: [Col. 1845] “But this, as long as the child can understand”: Basel and Lyons editions.], the sacrament will avail for his protection against adverse powers; and it will avail so much that, if he leaves this life before the use of reason [Note: [Col. 1845] “before a more mature age”: collected editions.] [Note: [Col. 1845] absent from the Argentinian edition.], he may, through that sacrament and through the Church’s commending love, be freed by Christian aid from that condemnation which entered the world through one human being [Note: [Col. 1845] “commended”: collected editions.].

Whoever does not believe this and judges it impossible is certainly an unbeliever, even if he possesses the sacrament of faith. Far better is that infant who, even if he does not yet possess faith in thought [Note: [Col. 1845] “knowledge”: collected editions.], nevertheless does not oppose to it the obstacle of an adverse thought [Note: [Col. 1845] “thought”: Basel and Lyons I editions.], and therefore receives its sacrament beneficially.

### C. CXXX. The faith of others saves infants in baptism. Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians, to Boniface, bk. I, c. 22 [Note: [Col. 1845] Written about A.D. 420—Anselm, bk. 9, c. 43 (55).]

In the Church of the Savior, infants believe through others, just as they contracted from others the sins which are remitted to them in baptism [Note: [Col. 1845] “and”: Lyons II–III editions.]. Nor should you think [Note: [Col. 1845C] “Should you think”: It was not altered because of the gloss. But the old codices and the original have *cogitatis*, “you think,” and all these words depend upon what precedes; hence the entire passage must be read.] that those who lack the body and blood of Christ can have life, since he himself says [Note: [Col. 1845] “the Lord himself”: Basel and Lyons II–III editions; compare John 6:54.]: “Unless you eat my flesh,” etc.

### C. CXXXI. He who is made Christ’s member through baptism partakes of Christ’s body and blood. The same author [Note: [Col. 1845] Compare c. 36, D. 2, *de consecratione*, where the same passage is reported—Anselm, bk. 9, c. 23 (35); Ivo, *Decr.* pt. 2, c. 1; Polycarp, bk. 3, title 10; Peter Lombard, bk. 4, dist. 9.]

There can be no doubt whatever that each of the faithful [Note: [Col. 1845] “believer”: collected editions except the first Basel and Lyons II–III editions.] becomes a participant in the Lord’s body and blood [Note: [Col. 1845] “of the Lord”: collected editions.] when, in baptism, he is made a member of Christ [Note: [Col. 1845] “of the body”: Argentinian edition—“of Christ’s body”: the other editions and Anselm.]. Nor is he excluded from participation in that bread and cup, even if, before eating that bread and drinking that cup, he departs from this world while established in the unity of Christ’s body.

For he is not deprived of participation in and benefit from that sacrament when he himself finds what that sacrament is [Note: [Col. 1845] “itself”: Anselm—“when he himself finds in himself that which is the sacrament itself”: collected editions; compare D. 2, c. 36, end.] [Note: [Col. 1845C] “Is the sacrament”: In Bede—for the original has not been found—it reads “signifies the sacrament,” as above, Distinction 2, “Because he suffered,” at “No one”; and the author of the gloss here interprets the word *is* in that way.].

### C. CXXXII. Why one born of a baptized person must be baptized. The same author, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins and on the Baptism of Infants*, bk. II, cc. 25–26 [Note: [Col. 1846C] This chapter too has been compiled from the words of Blessed Augustine, but at the compiler’s discretion: altered, transposed, and reduced to a summary. The same occurs in many following chapters, so that it is altogether necessary to consult the author himself. Therefore only a few things have been corrected—mostly from old copies of Gratian—which greatly obscured the sense and were not protected by the gloss.]

**Part XXVII.** If Christ’s flesh, which was without sin, was baptized for the example of imitation, how much more must mortal flesh be baptized in order to avoid the judgment of condemnation? And just as, in the time of circumcision, one born of a circumcised person had to be circumcised, so now one born of a baptized person must be baptized.

§ 1. For the sacrament of baptism is the sacrament of regeneration. Therefore, [Col. 1846C] just as one who has not lived cannot die, so one who has not been born cannot be reborn. From this it follows [Note: [Col. 1845] “is seen”: the collected editions.], that no one could be reborn in his parent while not yet born [Note: [Col. 1845] “since he is not yet born”: the same editions.]. And although a parent’s own sins do not harm that parent after conversion [Note: [Col. 1845] “harm”: editions of Arg. and Bas.], they nevertheless harm those generated from him. They do not harm the parent [Note: [Col. 1845] “Parent”: the same editions.] on this account, because he has been reborn; but they harm those born of him unless they too are reborn in the same way. The things contracted from the parent [Col. 1847A] [Note: [Col. 1847] “drawn”: edition of Arg.] harm them, because even a renewed [Note: [Col. 1847] Addition: “is”: the collected editions.] father begets carnally, not from the newness but from the remnants of oldness; and children, propagated in the flesh of sin from the remaining oldness of their parents [Note: [Col. 1847] “oldness, propagated wholly in old flesh, [for] the condemnation of sin”: edition of Bas.—“oldness, propagated fleshly, [for] the condemnation of sin”: the remaining editions.], escape condemnation through the sacrament of regeneration.

### C. CXXXIII. In baptism all sins die.

Likewise, in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 52.

In order to show that we are dead to sin, the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1847] Rom. 6:3.]: “Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death?” If, therefore, we are shown to be dead to sin because we have been baptized into Christ’s death, then surely infants also, who are baptized into Christ, die to sin because they are baptized into his death. [Col. 1847B] For, with no exception, it was said: “All of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” [Note: [Col. 1847] “and into”: edition of Bas.]; and it was said for the purpose of proving [Note: [Col. 1847] “might prove”: the collected editions.] that we are dead to sin. [Note: [Col. 1847] “But infants, by being reborn, die to that sin which they contracted by being born”: the collected editions; “to that sin”: the Venice I–II and first Paris and Lyons I editions.] But to what sin do infants die by being reborn, except that which they contracted by being born? And consequently what follows also applies to them [Note: [Col. 1847] Rom. 6:4.]: “For we have been buried with him through baptism into death” [Note: [Col. 1847] “death”: the collected editions.]. And below:

§ 1. Therefore, speaking to those baptized into Christ’s death—in which not adults alone but infants too are baptized—he says [Note: [Col. 1847] Rom. 6:11.]: “So reckon yourselves indeed dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus.”

### C. CXXXIV. Just as baptism is denied to no one, so there is no one who does not die to sin.

Likewise, in the same work, chapter 43 [Note: [Col. 1847] Ivo, *Decretum*, part 17, chapter 4; Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 4.].

[Col. 1847C] From a newly born [Note: [Col. 1847] “recently”: the collected editions.] infant [Note: [Col. 1847] “infant”: the collected editions and the first Paris and Lyons II–III editions.—Addition: “for”: edition of Bas.] to a decrepit old man, just as no one is to be barred from baptism [Note: [Col. 1847] Omitted in the same editions, first Paris and Lyons.], so there is no one who does not die to sin in baptism. But infants die only to original sin, whereas adults also die to all [Note: [Col. 1847] Omitted in the edition of Arg.] those sins which they added by living wickedly [Note: [Col. 1847] Addition: “to original [sin]”: collected editions, except the remaining editions.] to that which they contracted by being born.

### C. CXXXV. In John’s baptism there was no remission of sin.

Likewise, in the same work, chapter 49.

Those [Note: [Col. 1847] “who also” and “were baptized”: omitted in the edition of Arg.] baptized with John’s baptism were not regenerated [Note: [Col. 1847] “were reborn”: the original.—“were regenerated or reborn”: collected editions and first Arg.] [Note: [Col. 1847] Addition: “by whom he himself was also baptized”: the original.]. But, by the ministry of that forerunner who said [Note: [Col. 1847] Mark 1:3.], “Prepare the way of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 1847] Addition: “Christ Jesus”: edition of Bas.—“Christ”: the remaining editions except Arg.], they were being prepared for this one alone, in whom alone they could be reborn [Note: [Col. 1847] “who were being prepared”: the collected editions.]. For his baptism is not in water only, as John’s was [Note: [Col. 1847] “as”: the same editions.], but also in the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1847] “Holy Spirit”: edition of Bas.], so that whoever believes in Christ may be regenerated from that Spirit, from whom Christ was regenerated, though he had no need of regeneration [Note: [Col. 1847] “generated, [and] had no need of regeneration”: the original.].

[Note: [Col. 1847C] “So that he may be regenerated from that Spirit”: this passage has been restored from St Augustine, where the gloss did not impede it. Previously it read: “So that whoever believes in Christ may be regenerated from him” [thus the collected editions, first Arg. and Bas.], “from whom Christ is regenerated” [“Christ”: edition of Arg.; “is generated”: edition of Bas.], “who knew regeneration,” etc.]

And a little below:

§ 1. He was willing to be baptized in water [Note: [Col. 1847] Addition: “therefore”: editions of Arg. and Bas.] by John, not in order that any iniquity of his might be washed away, but in order that his great humanity might be commended [Note: [Col. 1847] “humility”: the original.]. Thus indeed [Col. 1848B] [Note: [Col. 1847] “Thus”: the collected editions.] baptism had nothing in him to wash away [Note: [Col. 1847] “be washed away”: editions of Arg., Nor., Venice I–II, and Paris.], just as death found nothing in him to punish.

### C. CXXXVI. Not only original but also actual sins are remitted in baptism.

The same author, *On the Baptism of Infants, or On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, book I, chapters 15 and 16.

When the flesh generates, only original sin is contracted [Note: [Col. 1847] “drawn”: editions of Arg. and Bas.]; but when the Spirit regenerates [Note: [Col. 1847] Omitted in the edition of Bas.] [Note: [Col. 1847] Addition: “Holy”: the collected editions and first Bas.], remission is made not only of original sins but also of voluntary sins.

[Note: [Col. 1847C] “When the flesh generates, only original sin is contracted; but when the Spirit regenerates, remission is made not only of original sins but also of voluntary sins”: St Augustine, explaining why the Apostle said, “Thus grace also may reign through righteousness unto eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord,” advanced these words.]

Therefore it can rightly be said that infants departing from the body without baptism [Note: [Col. 1847] “dying”: the collected editions.] will undergo the mildest condemnation of all [Note: [Col. 1847] “the mildest punishment of all”: the collected editions; “the most un-mild”: edition of Bas.]. But [Note: [Col. 1847] “He deceives”: edition of Bas.—“For he deceives”: the remaining editions.] he greatly deceives and is deceived who declares that they will not be under condemnation [Note: [Col. 1847] “into condemnation”: edition of Bas.], since the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1847] Rom. 5:18.], “Through one trespass came condemnation upon all human beings” [Note: [Col. 1847] “into condemnation”: Vulgate and edition of Bas.—“in condemnation”: the remaining editions.], etc.

### C. CXXXVII. Whoever is born from concupiscence is regenerated through baptism.

The same author in the same work, chapter 16 [Note: [Col. 1847] The sense rather than the words.].

Whoever is carnally generated from the concupiscence of the flesh and from the law of sin and death needs to be spiritually regenerated, so that he may not only be brought to the kingdom of God but also [Col. 1849A] be freed from the condemnation of sin [Note: [Col. 1849] Thus the collected editions and first Arg.]. For just as they are born in sin and death through the first human being [Note: [Col. 1849] Addition: “also”: the collected editions and first Lyons II–III editions.], so also they are reborn in baptism through Christ in righteousness and eternal life [Note: [Col. 1849] Omitted in the edition of Bas.].

### C. CXXXVIII. The faith of those presenting them makes infants believers.

The same author in the same book, chapter 19 [Note: [Col. 1849] A summary of Augustine’s words reported in the following chapter.].

Infants are rightly called believers because [Note: [Col. 1849] “who”: the collected editions.], through the words of those who carry them, they in some fashion profess the faith [Note: [Col. 1849] “confess”: the same editions.], and through those persons’ words renounce the devil and the world. This happens through the power of the sacrament and of the divine grace which the Lord [Note: [Col. 1849] “God has given”: the same editions.] bestowed upon the Church. But if an infant who is baptized, upon reaching the age of reason, does not believe or does not abstain from unlawful things, what he received as an infant profits him nothing.

### C. CXXXIX. On the same subject.

Likewise Augustine, in the same book I, *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, chapters 25 and 19.

Mother Church supplies a maternal mouth to infants [Note: [Col. 1849] “provides”: the collected editions.], so that they may be imbued with the sacred mysteries, because they are not yet able to believe with their own heart unto righteousness [Note: [Col. 1849] Cf. Rom. 10:10.] or to confess with their own mouth unto salvation. Yet no believer hesitates to call them believers [Note: [Col. 1849] “can call them unbelievers”: the collected editions.], because [Note: [Col. 1849] “for the reason that”: the same editions and first Bas.] their name is certainly derived from believing, although it is not they themselves but others who answer for them during the sacraments. But if they are rightly called believers because through the words of those who carry them they in some fashion profess faith, why should they not first also be regarded as penitents, since through the words of those same carriers they are shown to renounce the devil and this world [Note: [Col. 1849] Addition: “by faith”: edition of Bas.—“faith”: first Lyons edition.]?

### C. CXL. The charity of the Church remits or retains sins.

The same author, Tractate 121 on John, chapter 20 [Note: [Col. 1849] Peter Lombard, book 4, distinction 18.].

The charity of the Church, which is poured out through the Holy Spirit into the hearts of those who share in it [Note: [Col. 1849] Addition: “in it”: the collected editions.], remits sins; it retains the sins of those who do not share in it.

### C. CXLI. Christ alone remits sins.

The same author, *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, book I, chapter 23.

No one [Note: [Col. 1849] Cf. John 1:36 and the ordinary gloss there.] takes away sins except Christ alone, who is the Lamb taking away the sins of the world. And below: He takes them away both by forgiving what has been done—where [Note: [Col. 1849] “and”: omitted in the edition of Bas. and Bohm.] original sin too is included [Note: [Col. 1849] Addition: “sin”: edition of Bas.]—by helping that they may not be done, and by leading to the life in which they cannot be done at all [Note: [Col. 1849] “can”: the same edition.].

### C. CXLII. Apart from Christ’s baptism, no salvation is promised to infants.

The same author, in the same place and chapter 25 [Note: [Col. 1849] A summary of Augustine’s words.—Peter Lombard, in the same place.].

No salvation apart from Christ’s baptism is promised to infants, because infants, unless through the sacrament divinely instituted for this purpose they pass into the number of believers [Note: [Col. 1849] “pass”: the collected editions and first Bas.], certainly remain in darkness.

### C. CXLIII. Those baptized are incorporated into Christ and become his members.

The same author, in the same place, chapter 26 [Note: [Col. 1849] A summary of Augustine’s words.].

The efficacy of baptism is that the baptized are incorporated into Christ [Col. 1850B] and [Note: [Col. 1849] “that”: the collected editions and first Paris and Lyons.] are accounted his members [Note: [Col. 1849] “become”: edition of Bas.]; they are buried with him, and, offered through the sacrament and the charity of believers, are reconciled to God, so that in him they may become living, safe, freed, redeemed, and enlightened [Note: [Col. 1849] “in him”: the collected editions.].

### C. CXLIV. The same author, in the same place, chapter 27.

Who does not know that for infants to believe is to be baptized, while not to believe is not to be baptized?

### C. CXLV. Grace not only remits sins but also causes the law to be fulfilled.

The same author, *On Grace and Free Will*, addressed to Valentinus, chapter 14 [Note: [Col. 1849] A summary of Augustine’s words.].

Grace, which is given through Christ, not only brings remission of sins, but also causes the law to be fulfilled and nature to be liberated, so that sin may not rule [Note: [Col. 1849] “nor”: the collected editions and first Arg. and Bas.]. The Spirit of grace also gives faith, which is granted by God even when not requested, so that other things may be granted to the person who asks. For faith is not merely a matter of free choice, but a gift of God [Note: [Col. 1849] Eph. 2:8.].

### C. CXLVI. The old infirmity is not wholly consumed in baptism, but loses its strength.

The same author, *On the Baptism of Infants, or On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, book II, chapter 7.

[Note: [Col. 1849D] It has already been indicated concerning many chapters that they are composed from passages of St Augustine, but differently arranged and gathered into a summary. This is especially evident in this chapter, in which, however, not a few things have both been corrected and added.]

**Part XXVIII.** From the moment a person is baptized, not every old infirmity in him is consumed; rather, renewal begins with the remission [Note: [Col. 1850D] “With remission”: previously it read “remission,” etc. It was corrected from most old copies and from the original.] of all sins and with spiritual understanding and action. The remaining things have been accomplished in hope, until they are accomplished also in reality [Note: [Col. 1849] “is accomplished”: edition of Bas.]; this will be at the resurrection. For in baptism, although complete remission of sins is made, there is not yet complete newness and perfect transformation, because corruption still remains not only in the body but also in the soul, which is the inward human being. If in it newness were perfect, the Apostle would not say that it is renewed [Note: [Col. 1851] “are renewed”: edition of Arg.; cf. 2 Cor. 4:16.] day by day.

Likewise, in the same book, chapter 27:

§ 1. We must remember that complete and perfect remission of all sins is made only in baptism [Note: [Col. 1851] “in baptism”: the collected editions.], while the whole person is not immediately transformed. Rather, in those who make good progress, as newness grows day by day, what is old and carnal is transformed, until it is renewed [Note: [Col. 1851] “removed”: Venice I–II.] so that the animal weakness of the body may attain spiritual and incorruptible strength.

And chapter 28:

§ 2. But this law of sin, concerning which the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1851] Rom. 6:12.], “Let not sin reign in your mortal body,” does not remain [Note: [Col. 1851] “remains permanently”: the Paris and Lyons editions.—“may remain permanently”: the remaining editions.] in the members of those who have been reborn as though its remission had not been made [Note: [Col. 1851] “full remission”: the collected editions and first Arg.] for them [Note: [Col. 1851] “for them”: the collected editions.], where there is altogether full and perfect remission of all sins [Note: [Col. 1851] “of all our sins”: the collected editions.], all enemies by whom we were separated from God having been killed. Rather, it remains in the oldness of the flesh as something conquered [Note: [Col. 1851] “separated”: edition of Bas.] and slain, unless by unlawful acts of consent [Note: [Col. 1851] “by unlawful sentiment”: edition of Arg.—“by unlawful consent”: the remaining editions.] it somehow comes to life again [Note: [Col. 1851] “revives”: edition of Arg.] and is recalled to its own kingdom and dominion.

Yet the life of the Spirit is so distinguished from this oldness of the flesh [Note: [Col. 1851] “of flesh and of sin, which has now been remitted”: the collected editions.]—in which is this law of sin, or sin already remitted—that those baptized are reborn in its newness through God’s grace, and are called even [Note: [Col. 1851] Omitted in the editions of Arg. and Bas.] in the present not only not [Note: [Col. 1851] Omitted in the collected editions except Bas. and Lyons II–III.] to be in sin, but not even to be in the flesh [Col. 1851C] whose desires they do not follow, but to be in the Spirit [Note: [Col. 1851] “but are in the Spirit”: editions of Bas. and Lyons II–III.].

But one uses corruptible flesh well when one turns its members to good works, not living according to the desires of the flesh through the law of sin which, though already remitted, nevertheless remains in the oldness of the flesh. Married believers use it well: from their existence in Christ’s newness, they do not allow lust to rule them; but from their still carrying Adam’s oldness [Note: [Col. 1851] “are drawn toward oldness”: edition of Bas.—“draw toward oldness”: the remaining editions.], they generate mortal children who are to be regenerated immortally, with that offspring of sin by which those who have been reborn are not held liable and from which those who are born are freed by being reborn [Note: [Col. 1851] “are reborn”: edition of Bas.].

Likewise, a little lower:

§ 3. Just as wicked deeds, words, and thoughts belong to soul and body and, in respect of their motions, have already passed away and are no longer [Note: [Col. 1851D] “Of soul and body”: the original reads: “Insofar as the movements of soul and body themselves are concerned, they have already passed away and are no more; nevertheless, although they have passed and no longer exist, their guilt remains,” etc. But this was not corrected because of the gloss.] [Note: [Col. 1851] “are in them”: the same edition.], their guilt nevertheless remains after they have passed unless sin is loosed through remission [Note: [Col. 1851] “through remission of sin”: editions of Arg. and Bas.]; so, on the contrary, in the law of concupiscence which has not already passed away but still remains, its guilt is loosed and will not remain when full remission of sins is made in baptism [Note: [Col. 1851] “of sin”: the collected editions and first Arg. and Bas.].

### C. CXLVII. Christ’s disciples are believed to have been washed by his baptism.

The same author, Epistle 108, to Seleuciana [Note: [Col. 1851] Epistle 265 in the Maurist edition, date uncertain; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 104; *Decretum*, part 1, chapter 309; cf. John 3.].

**Part XXIX.** When Jesus left Jerusalem with his disciples for the land of Judaea, and remained there [Note: [Col. 1851] “there”: Ivo and the collected editions.] with them, he baptized, not personally [Col. 1852B] but through his disciples. We understand these disciples already to have been baptized, either with John’s baptism, as some suppose, or, more credibly, with Christ’s baptism.

Likewise, in the same place:

§ 1. The Lord answered Peter [Note: [Col. 1851] John 13:10.], “One who has bathed needs only to wash his feet, but is wholly clean.” From this it is understood that Peter had already been baptized [Note: [Col. 1851] “had been”: Ivo.].

### C. CXLVIII. All the Apostles are believed to have been baptized with Christ’s baptism.

Likewise, to Vincentius and Victor, book III, *On the Soul and Its Origin*, chapter 9 [Note: [Col. 1851] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 105; *Decretum*, part 1, chapter 310.].

If we maintain that those concerning whom it is not written [Note: [Col. 1851] “it is doubtful”: edition of Arg.] whether they were baptized [Note: [Col. 1851] Addition: “or not”: Ivo, *Panormia*, and the collected editions.] departed this life without baptism, we cast an accusation upon the Apostles themselves. Apart from the Apostle Paul, we do not know when they were baptized [Col. 1852C]. But we may know that they were baptized from the Lord’s words to the blessed Apostle Peter [Note: [Col. 1851] John 13:10.]: “One who has bathed needs only to wash his feet.”

### C. CXLIX. A Catholic catechumen is preferred to a baptized heretic.

The same author, book IV, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 21.

**Part XXX.** I do not doubt that a Catholic catechumen burning with divine charity is to be preferred to a baptized heretic; indeed, within the Catholic Church itself [Note: [Col. 1851] Addition: “Church”: the collected editions.], we prefer a good catechumen to an evil [Note: [Col. 1851] “badly”: edition of Bas.] baptized person. Yet we do not thereby wrong the sacrament of baptism with which the latter has already been imbued and the former has not.

And a little later:

§ 1. The centurion Cornelius, not yet baptized, was better than baptized Simon [Note: [Col. 1853] “Cornelius, not yet baptized, is preferred to baptized Simon”: the collected editions; cf. Acts 10.]. For Cornelius was filled with the Holy Spirit even before baptism [Note: [Col. 1853] Addition: “having received”: the same editions—“received” before: edition of Bas.]; Simon was puffed up with an unclean spirit even after baptism. Yet if Cornelius, even after already receiving the Holy Spirit, had refused baptism, he would have become guilty by contempt [Note: [Col. 1853] “through contempt”: the collected editions.] for so great a sacrament.

And below:

§ 2. Just as baptism is lacking to a good catechumen for attaining the kingdom of heaven, so true conversion is lacking to an evil baptized person [Note: [Col. 1853] “confession or conversion”: edition of Arg.; “confession”: the remaining editions.]. For he who said [Note: [Col. 1853] John 3:3.], “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven,” also said [Note: [Col. 1853] Matt. 5:20.], “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

### C. CL. Baptism consists not so much in washing of the body as in faith of the heart.

Likewise, in the book of Sentences of Prosper [Note: [Col. 1853] Lanfranc, *On the Sacraments against Berengar*; similar in Augustine, Tractate 80 on John 13; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 110; *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 9.].

True baptism consists not so much in washing [Note: [Col. 1853] “abolition”: edition of Bas.] of the body as in faith of the heart, as [Note: [Col. 1853] “just as”: the collected editions.] apostolic teaching has handed down, saying [Note: [Col. 1853] Acts 15:9.], “Cleansing their hearts by faith”; and elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1853] 1 Pet. 3:21.], “Baptism saves, not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience to God.”

### C. CLI. As some in the Old Testament were spiritual, so some in the New are found to be carnal.

Likewise Augustine, book I, *On Baptism*, chapter 15.

Just as in the sacraments of the Old Testament certain spiritual persons lived [Col. 1853C], secretly belonging to the New Testament which was then hidden [Note: [Col. 1853] “was hidden”: the collected editions.], so now in the sacraments of the New Testament, which has now been revealed [Note: [Col. 1853] “reported”: edition of Bas.—“lifted up”: edition of Arg.], many live as animal persons [Note: [Col. 1853] “certain”: the collected editions.]. who, if they are unwilling to advance [Note: [Col. 1853] Omitted in editions of Arg. and Bas.—“for themselves”: the remaining editions.] to apprehend the things of the Spirit of God, to which the apostolic word exhorts them [Note: [Col. 1853] “which”: editions of Arg. and Bas.—“to which”: the remaining editions; 1 Cor. 2:14.], will belong [Note: [Col. 1853] “and will belong”: the collected editions and first Arg. and Bas.—“belonged”: editions of Nor., Venice I–II, Paris, and Lyons I.] to the Old Testament. But if they advance, then even before they receive baptism [Note: [Col. 1853] Omitted in the original.], by that very advancement and approach they belong to the New Testament; and if, before becoming spiritual [Note: [Col. 1853] “become”: edition of Arg.], they are snatched away from this life [Note: [Col. 1853] “are snatched away”: the collected editions.], safeguarded by the holiness of the sacrament they are counted in the land of the living, where our hope is and the Lord is our portion.

Nor do I find what more truly may be understood [Col. 1854A] in that which is written [Note: [Col. 1853] “may be found”: the same editions.], “Your eyes saw my imperfect state” [Note: [Col. 1853] Ps. 138:16.], since there follows: “And in your book all shall be written.”

Likewise, book III, chapter 14:

§ 1. When the integrity and holiness of the sacrament are under discussion, it makes no difference what a person believes and with what kind of faith the recipient of the sacrament has been imbued [Note: [Col. 1853] “or”: the collected editions.—“received”: edition of Bas.]. It makes very great difference indeed for the way of salvation, but it makes no difference for the question of the sacrament.

And below:

§ 2. It is clear that, even where faith is not whole, the sacrament of baptism may remain whole in someone.

Likewise, chapter 15:

§ 3. If [Note: [Col. 1853] “If it were possible that each person could be carefully questioned”: the collected editions.—“is possible”: edition of Bas.] each person could be carefully questioned, perhaps as many varieties of opinion would be found as there are persons counted [Note: [Col. 1853] Addition: “would be found”: the same editions.]. For the animal person does not receive the things that are of God’s Spirit [Note: [Col. 1853] 1 Cor. 2:14.]. But do they therefore receive a defective sacrament [Col. 1854B]? Or if they make progress and correct the vanity of their carnal opinions, must what they received be repeated? Each receives according to his faith, but only to the extent that he is capable, under the governance of that mercy of God concerning which the same Apostle, trusting in it, says: “If you think differently about anything, God will reveal this also to you.”

### C. CLII. Adam was to die not by a necessity of nature but by the demerit of sin.

Likewise, from the Council of Milevis [Note: [Col. 1853] Rather, the Council of Carthage held in A.D. 418; *Collectio tripartita*, part 2, title 22, chapter 1.], at which Augustine and Anselm [Note: [Col. 1853] It should read: Asellus.] the legate of the Roman Church were present, against the Pelagians, chapter 1.

**Part XXXI.** It has therefore pleased all the bishops who were in this holy synod to establish the matters determined in the present council: that whoever says that Adam, the first human being, was made mortal in such a way that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would die in the body—that is, depart from the body—not as the due of sin but by the necessity of nature, let him be anathema.

### C. CLIII. Infants derive from their parents not punishment only but guilt as well.

Likewise, of the same Council, chapter 2 [Note: [Col. 1853] *Collectio tripartita*, same part and place, chapter 2; Burchard, book 4, chapter 34; Ivo, *Decretum*, part 1, chapter 128.].

It has pleased the council that whoever denies that infants fresh from their mothers’ wombs are to be baptized, or says [Note: [Col. 1853] “says”: Bohm.] that they are indeed baptized for the remission [Note: [Col. 1853] “in remission”: edition of Bas.] of sins but derive no original sin from Adam that must be expiated by the washing of regeneration—whereupon it follows [Col. 1855A] that the formula of baptism “for the remission [Note: [Col. 1855] Addition: “indeed”: *Collectio Hispanica.] of sins” must be understood in their case not truly but falsely—let him be anathema.

[Note: [Col. 1853C] “That they are baptized”: this has been corrected from certain old copies and the originals themselves. Previously it read “that they are not baptized” [thus Burchard, Ivo, and editions of Bas. and Lyons II–III].]

For the Apostle’s saying [Note: [Col. 1855] Rom. 5:12.], “Through one human being sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and thus it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned,” is to be understood only as the Catholic Church, spread everywhere, has always understood it. For the sake of this rule of faith, even infants, who have not yet been able to commit any sins in themselves, are truly baptized for the remission of sins, so that by regeneration there may be cleansed in them what they derived by generation.
