### C. CLIV. Grace remits sins and helps prevent their repetition.

Likewise, of the same Council, chapter 3 [Note: [Col. 1855] *Collectio tripartita*, same place, chapter 3; Burchard, book 20, chapter 18, and Ivo, *Decretum*, part 17, chapter 30, attribute it to Gregory’s *Moralia*.].

It has pleased the council that whoever says that the grace of God by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord [Note: [Col. 1855] “our Lord”: omitted in the edition of Bas.] is effective only for the remission of sins already committed, and not also as aid so that they may not be committed, let him be anathema.

### C. CLV. Grace teaches what sin is and enables what it makes known.

Likewise, of the same Council, chapter 4 [Note: [Col. 1855] *Collectio tripartita*, same place, chapter 4; Burchard and Ivo, in the same place.].

Whoever says that the same grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord helps us not to sin only because through it the understanding of the commandments is disclosed and opened to us, so that we may know what we ought to seek and what to avoid, but that through it we are not enabled both to love and to accomplish what we have learned must be done [Note: [Col. 1855] “what we ought to do”: *Collectio Hispanica.—“or must”: the collected editions.], let him be anathema.

### C. CLVI. Without divine grace the commandments cannot be fulfilled.

Likewise, of the same Council, chapter 5 [Note: [Col. 1855] *Collectio tripartita*, same place; Burchard and Ivo, in the same place.].

**Part XXXII.** It has pleased the council that whoever says that grace of justification is given to us so that, through grace, we may more easily fulfill what we are commanded to do by free choice—as if, even if grace were not given, we could still fulfill the divine commandments without it, though not easily [Note: [Col. 1855] “we can”: *Collectio Hispanica.]—let him be anathema.

## DISTINCTION V

[Col. 1855]

### GRATIAN. C. I. After baptism the sacrament of confirmation is to be conferred.

Likewise Pope Urban, to all Christians, Epistle I, chapter 7 [Note: [Col. 1855] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*, chapter 4; *Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 15, chapter 5; Anselm, book 9, chapter 23 (30); Burchard, book 4, chapter 66; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 113; *Decretum*, part 1, chapters 260 and 296.].

[Col. 1855C] **Part I.** All believers ought, after baptism, to receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of bishops’ hands [Note: [Col. 1855] “layings-on”: the collected editions and first Paris and Lyons.], in order that they may be found to be complete Christians; for when the Holy Spirit is infused, the faithful heart is enlarged toward prudence and conscience.

### C. II. What the Holy Spirit confers in baptism and what in confirmation.

Likewise Pope Melchiades, in an epistle to the bishops of Spain, chapter 2 [Note: [Col. 1855] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Eusebius—or Eucherius—homily on the day of Pentecost; *Collectio tripartita*, part 1, title 31, chapter 2; Anselm, book 9, chapter 31; *Polycarpus*, book 3, title 10.].

The Holy Spirit, who descends upon the waters of baptism in a saving descent [Note: [Col. 1855] “descent”: the collected editions.], grants fullness at the font for innocence and gives an increase toward grace in confirmation. Since persons who are to live their whole lifetime in this world must walk amid invisible enemies and dangers [Col. 1856B], we are regenerated in baptism for life and confirmed after baptism for battle; we are washed in baptism and strengthened after baptism. And [Note: [Col. 1855] “And thus”: Anselm.] although the benefits of regeneration suffice for those who are about to pass on at once, the aids of confirmation are necessary for those who are to live.

Regeneration by itself saves those immediately to be received into the peace of the blessed age [Note: [Col. 1855] “Peace of the blessed age”: thus corrected from manuscripts, the original, and *Polycarpus*. Previously it read “the peace of baptism or of the age” [thus the collected editions and first Bas.].]; confirmation arms and equips those reserved for the contests and battles of this world. But one who, after baptism, reaches death unstained, with acquired innocence, is confirmed by death, because after death he cannot sin [Note: [Col. 1855] “they reach … are confirmed”: the same editions.].

### C. III. The sacrament of laying on hands is more worthy than the sacrament of baptism.

The same author, in the same place [Note: [Col. 1855] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; Burchard, book 4, chapter 61; Anselm, book 9, chapter 33; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 114; *Polycarpus*, same place.].

Concerning the matters about which you asked to be instructed [Note: [Col. 1855] “you repeatedly asked”: the original; “you ask”: Burchard; “you ask”: Ivo’s *Decretum.]—namely, whether the greater sacrament is the laying on [Note: [Col. 1855] “laying on”: the collected editions; Burchard and Ivo.] of bishops’ hands or baptism [Note: [Col. 1855] “is”: *Panormia*—“may be”: the collected editions—Ivo’s *Decretum.]—know that both are great sacraments. And just as one is performed by greater persons, that is, by the supreme pontiffs [Note: [Col. 1857] “by greater persons, that is, by the supreme pontiffs, has been supplied”: the collected editions and Ivo’s *Panormia*.], and cannot be performed by lesser persons [Note: [Col. 1857] “except by greater persons”: the collected editions.—“completed”: the same editions, the original, Burchard, and Ivo.], so it is to be revered and held in greater veneration [Col. 1857A]. Yet these two sacraments are so joined that, unless death intervenes, they can by no means be separated from each other [Note: [Col. 1857] “can”: editions of Arg., Bas., and Nor.], nor can one be duly completed without the other [Note: [Col. 1857] Omitted in editions of Arg. and Bas.].

### C. IV. The sacrament of laying on hands can be administered by none but bishops.

Likewise Pope Eusebius, Epistle III, to the bishops of Tuscany and Campania [Note: [Col. 1857] A Pseudo-Isidorian chapter; cf. Innocent’s letter to Decentius of Gubbio; Burchard, book 4, chapter 63; Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 115; *Decretum*, part 1, chapters 257 and 297.].

The sacrament of laying on hands too is to be held in great veneration. It cannot be administered by anyone except the high priests; nor is it read or known to have been performed in the time of the Apostles by anyone other than the Apostles themselves [Col. 1857B], nor may it ever be administered or performed by anyone other than those who hold their place [Note: [Col. 1857] “through them”: editions of Bas. and Lyons II–III; “by those themselves”: Ivo’s *Decretum*, chapter 297; omitted in the same chapter of the *Panormia* and the collected editions]. For if it is presumed otherwise, it is to be regarded as void and empty, and shall never be reckoned among the ecclesiastical sacraments [Note: [Col. 1857] “nor ever”: the original, Burchard, and Ivo’s *Decretum*; editions of Arg. and Bas.].

### C. V. Why the sacrament of confirmation is conferred upon the baptized.

Likewise Rabanus, *On the Institution of Clerics*, book I, chapter 20 [Note: [Col. 1857] Ivo, *Panormia*, book 1, chapter 118.].

[The supplied source ends here, before the text of C. V.]

### C. XV. On the same matter.

From the day of the Resurrection until the Saturday in albis, and from the day of Pentecost until the Saturday of the same week, we sing and read, according to the ancient custom, only three psalms at nocturns and three lessons. On all other days throughout the year, if it is a feast day, we say nine psalms and nine lessons. On other days, however, we recite twelve psalms and three lessons. On Sundays we say eighteen psalms—except on Easter and Pentecost—and nine lessons. But those who wish on ordinary days to celebrate only three psalms and three lessons are shown to do this not from the rule of the holy Fathers, but from distaste and negligence. The Romans, however, began to act differently, especially from the time when governance of our Church was granted to the Germans. But we, investigating the Roman order and imitating the ancient custom of our Church, following the ancient Fathers, decree that it be done as we have set down above.

### C. XVI. On the observance of Lent. Likewise, from a homily of Pope Gregory.

[Note: [Col. 1859D] As reported by the compilers, this chapter appears in part to have been taken from Homily 16 of St. Gregory. But many things occur here that are not read there, and conversely many things occur there that are absent here.]

[Note: [Col. 1859] An uncertain chapter; cf. Corrections.—Burchard, bk. 13, c. 1. Ivo, *Panormia*, bk. 2, c. 182; *Decretum*, pt. 4, c. 34. *Polycarpus*, bk. 3, tit. 25.]

**Part V.** Lent is to be observed with the utmost strictness, so that the fast in it—apart from Sundays, which are exempted from abstinence—may in no way be broken, unless illness prevents someone from observing it; for these days are the tithe of the year. From the first Sunday of Lent until the Lord’s Easter six weeks are counted, which make forty-two days. Since six Sundays are subtracted from abstinence, no more than thirty-six days remain for abstinence. For example, if the year runs through 365 days and we afflict ourselves for thirty-six days, we give God, as it were, the tithe of the year. But in order that the sacred number of forty days, which our Savior consecrated by his holy fast, may be completed, the four days of the preceding week are taken to make up the forty days: namely, Wednesday, which is marked as the beginning of the fast, the following Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. For unless we add these four days to the preceding thirty-six, we do not have forty days of abstinence. We are also commanded by almighty God to give tithes of all our goods, etc.

### C. XXII. In how many ways the vice of gluttony tempts us. Likewise, Gregory, in his exposition of blessed Job, bk. 30, c. 27.

The vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways. Sometimes it anticipates the time of need; sometimes, however, it does not anticipate the time but seeks more luxurious foods; sometimes it demands that whatever is to be eaten be prepared with greater care; sometimes it is suited both to the quality of foods and to the time, yet in the very quantity consumed it exceeds the measure of moderate refreshment. At times, moreover, what it desires is cheap, yet it sins more grievously through the very heat of its boundless desire.

### C. XXIV. A lesser good is not to be preferred to a greater. Likewise, Jerome.

[Note: [Col. 1861] In the Rule of Monks compiled from Jerome.—*Polycarpus*, bk. 3, tit. 25.]

Those err no little who prefer a lesser good to a great one. Does not a rational person lose his dignity if he prefers fasting to charity, or vigils to soundness of mind, so that through immoderate abstinence and indiscriminate chanting of psalms or offices he incurs the reproach either of madness or of sadness? Can God, like a human being, be bent by a multitude of words? For God is to be prayed to not by words alone but by the heart. Better is the chanting of five psalms with purity, serenity, and spiritual cheerfulness of heart than the chanting of the whole Psalter with anxiety and sadness of heart. Therefore, when a psalm or a mass is said for all souls, no less is received than if it had been said for any one of them. Let those, then, who withhold from the body things necessary to it, hear what the Lord says through the Prophet [Isa. 61:8]: “I, the Lord, hate robbery in a burnt offering.” He offers a burnt offering from robbery who afflicts his body immoderately either by excessive deprivation of food or by lack of sleep. Let him therefore consider what the Apostle says [Rom. 13, end]: “Make no provision for the flesh in its lusts,” etc.

### C. XXV. To abstain not from foods but from wickedness is the great and general fast. Likewise, Augustine, on John, Tractate XVII.

But the great and general fast is abstinence from wickedness and unlawful pleasures of the world; this is the perfect fast. And below, §1: Therefore, in this world we celebrate, as it were, a Lent of abstinence when we live well, when we abstain from wickedness and unlawful pleasures. But because this abstinence will not be without reward, we await that blessed hope and the revelation of the glory of the great God and Savior Jesus Christ. In that hope, when the hoped-for thing has become reality, we shall receive the reward, the denarius. And below, §2: The denarius, therefore, which takes its name from the number ten, is returned, and joined to forty becomes fifty. Hence we celebrate Lent before Easter with labor, but the Fifty Days after Easter with joy, as though the reward had been received. For to this health-giving labor of good work, which belongs to the number forty, is added the denarius of rest and happiness, so that it becomes fifty. The Lord Jesus himself signified this much more clearly when, after the resurrection, he remained on earth with his disciples for forty days; but on the fortieth day, when he had ascended into heaven, after ten days had elapsed he sent the reward of the Holy Spirit.

### C. XXVIII. Moderation in food produces health; abundance produces the opposite. Likewise, John Chrysostom, Homily XXIX on Hebrews, c. 12.

For nothing is so pleasant as food well digested and cooked. Nothing so produces health, nothing so sharpens the senses, nothing so drives away illness, as moderate refreshment; for sufficiency together with nourishment produces both health and pleasure, whereas abundance causes disease, brings discomforts, and generates illnesses. What hunger does, fullness of food does also—but more so and with much worse effects. Hunger indeed removes a person in a few days and releases him from this penal life; but excess of food consumes and putrefies the human body, wastes it with prolonged illness, and then destroys it by a cruel death.

### C. XXIX. Delicacies of food, if they abound, are harmful. Likewise, Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, bk. II.

Let us not take such foods as we either digest with difficulty or, once consumed, regret having prepared at great cost and wasted with much labor. Vegetables, fruits, and legumes are easier to prepare, need neither the skill nor the expense of cooks, sustain the human body without care, and, when moderately eaten—for one does not greedily devour what has no incentives to gluttony—are digested more easily. For no one is burdened to the point of distention of the stomach by one or two such cheap foods; that distention arises from the variety of meats and pleasure in flavors. When dishes steam with varied odors, they draw one to eat them as captives, even after hunger has been satisfied. Hence diseases too are stirred up by excessive fullness; and many remedy gluttonous impatience by vomiting, and more shamefully expel what they shamefully took in. Hippocrates teaches in the *Aphorisms* that thick and obese bodies which have completed their measure of growth, unless they are promptly reduced by bloodletting, fall into paralysis and the worst kinds of diseases; and that therefore bloodletting is necessary, so that they may again have room in which to grow. For the nature of bodies cannot remain in one state, but must always either grow or decrease; nor can a living creature live unless it is capable of growth. Hence Galen, a most learned man and interpreter of Hippocrates, says in his *Exhortation to Medicine* that athletes, whose life and profession are fattening, can neither live long nor be healthy; their souls, wrapped as though in mud by excessive blood and fat, think of nothing fine or heavenly, but always of meats, belching, and the gluttony of the belly.

### C. XXX. Fasts heal many infirmities. The same author, somewhat further below.

We read that some who suffered from joint disease and the humors of gout recovered after confiscation of their property reduced them to a simple table and poor food. For they had lacked the concern of administering a household and the lavishness of feasting, which break both body and soul. Horace ridicules the appetite for foods which, once consumed, leave repentance.

[Note: [Col. 1865] *Corruerant*, “they had fallen”: Ed. Bas.]

[Note: [Col. 1865] *puellarum*, “of girls”: the collected editions before Lugdd. II–III.]

[Note: [Col. 1865] Horace, *Epistles*, bk. 1, ep. 2, v. 55.]

### C. XXXI. We ought to abstain from meat on Saturdays. Likewise, Gregory VII, in a synod held at Rome in the sixth year of his pontificate, c. 8.

[Note: [Col. 1865] Held A.D. 1078.—Anselm, in the extracts, bk. 7. *Polycarpus*, bk. 3, tit. 25.]

**Part VII.** Because Saturday has been held in abstinence by our holy Fathers as a notable day, following their authority we beneficially admonish that whoever desires to be a participant in the Christian religion should abstain from eating meat on that day, unless a greater feast intervenes or illness prevents it.

### C. XXXII. A monk is not permitted to taste meat. Likewise, Bishop Fructuosus.

[Note: [Col. 1865] This is read in c. 5 of Fructuosus’s earlier Rule, published by Holstenius.]

**Part VIII.** No monk is granted permission either to take or to taste flesh, not because we judge God’s creature unworthy, but because abstinence from flesh is considered useful and fitting for monks, while preserving nevertheless the moderation of compassion toward the sick. And below, §1: If any monk violates this and presumes, contrary to the sanction of the Rule and the usage of the ancients, to eat flesh, he shall be subject to seclusion and penance for a period of six months.

[Note: [Col. 1865] *veterem*, “ancient”: the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1865] “seven”: Ed. Arg.]

### C. XXXIII. On the daily occupations of monks. Likewise, Jerome to the monk Rusticus, *On the Manner of Living*.

[Note: [Col. 1865] Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 7, c. 5.]

Let a book never leave your hand and eyes; let the Psalter be recited word for word, prayer without ceasing. Let your mind be watchful and not open to wandering thoughts; let body and soul alike be directed toward the Lord. Overcome anger by patience. Love knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh. Do not let your mind be idle amid varied disturbances: if they settle in the breast, they will rule you and lead you into the greatest sin. Do some work, so that the devil may always find you occupied. If the Apostles, though they had authority to live from the Gospel, labored with their own hands so as not to burden anyone, and gave assistance to others from whom they ought to reap material things in return for spiritual ones, why do you not prepare things that will serve your own needs? Either weave a small basket of reeds or plait a basket from pliant twigs; let the ground be hoed, and let garden-beds be divided by an even boundary. When seeds of vegetables have been cast in them, or plants set out in rows, let channels of water be led for irrigation, so that you may stand as a spectator of these most beautiful lines:

> Behold, from the brow of a sloping path he draws forth water;
> it falls, raises a hoarse murmur over smooth stones,
> and tempers the thirsty fields with its streams.

§1. Let unfruitful trees be grafted either with buds or shoots, so that after a little time you may pluck the sweet fruits of your labor. Make hives for bees, to which Solomon’s Proverbs send you [Prov. 6:6]; and in these small creatures learn the order of monasteries and royal discipline. Let nets also be woven for catching fish. Let books be written, so that the hand may procure food by work and the mind be satisfied by reading. Every idle person is in desires. The monasteries of Egypt observe this custom: they admit no one without the labor of work, not so much for the necessity of sustenance as for the soul’s salvation, lest the mind wander among destructive thoughts and, like adulterous Jerusalem [Ezek. 16:25], spread its legs to every passerby. And in what follows, §2: “What then? Will all who live in cities perish? Look: they enjoy their possessions, minister to churches, go to baths, do not reject ointments, and move amid every kind of abundance.” To this I have already replied, and now reply briefly: in the present little work I am not disputing about clerics, but instructing a monk.

[Note: [Col. 1865] “or eyes”: Ed. Bas.; “or eyes”: the remaining editions.]

### C. XXXIV. Canons may do nothing without permission of their superior. Likewise, in Book V of the *Capitularies*, c. 115.

[Note: [Col. 1865] From the Council of Mainz, held A.D. 813, c. 9.—*Capitularies*, bk. 5, c. 185.—Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 402.]

**Part IX.** Therefore in all things, insofar as human frailty permits, we decree that canonical clerics should live canonically, observing the teaching of Holy Scripture and the instructions of the holy Fathers; and that they should presume to do nothing disorderly without permission of their own bishop or their master. In every bishopric they are to eat and sleep together, where they have the means to do so; or those who receive stipends from ecclesiastical property are to remain in their cloister. Every day, early in the morning, they are to come for reading and hear what is commanded them. Likewise at table they are to hear a reading and render obedience, according to the canons, to their ministers.

[Note: [Col. 1867] *decernimus*, “we decree”: the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1867] “or clerics”: Ed. Bas. and Lugdd.]

### C. XXXV. Priests who assemble together are especially to avoid drunkenness and feasting. Likewise, from the Council of Nantes, c. 10.

[Note: [Col. 1867] Cf. at c. 7, Distinction 44.]

**Part X.** No priest, whenever he has assembled with other priests for the anniversary, thirtieth, seventh, or third day of any deceased person, or for any gathering by invitation, is ever to presume to get drunk; nor, when invited to drink in honor of saints or of some soul, to drink or compel others to drink, or to gorge himself in response to another’s invitation. Nor is he to presume there to recite or sing improper applause, unrestrained laughter, or empty tales; nor is he to allow obscene games, a bear, or female acrobats to perform before him; nor is he to consent to demonic masks being carried before him, for this is diabolical and forbidden by the sacred canons.

[Note: [Col. 1867] *convenerint*, “have assembled,” with the plural used thereafter: the collected editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1867] *nullatenus*, “in no way”: the same editions.]

### C. XXXVI. A cleric or layperson is not to travel without the bishop’s authorization. Likewise, from the Council of Laodicea, cc. 41 and 42.

[Note: [Col. 1867] Held between A.D. 347 and 381.—Burchard, bk. 2, c. 45. Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 6, c. 146, from Dionysius.]

**Part XI.** Ministers of the altar, or any clerics, ought not to set out on a journey without the bishop’s authorization. §1. A layperson likewise ought not to go anywhere without canonical letters, that is, letters of commendation.

[Note: [Col. 1867] “a minister of the altar or any cleric”: Spanish Collection.]

[Note: [Col. 1867] *peregrina*, “traveling”: the same source.]

### C. XXXVII. At what spectacles a cleric ought not to be present. Likewise, from the same source, c. 54.

[Note: [Col. 1868C] This chapter is not in the Greek collection of canons printed at Paris in 1540 [though it is found in later editions]. It is nevertheless found in Balsamon and seems to be indicated by c. 42 of the Sixth Synod. Gratian, however, cites it from the ancient version.]

[Note: [Col. 1867] Ivo, *Decretum*, pt. 11, c. 78.]

C. XXXVIII. Women ought not to use cosmetic paints. Likewise Augustine to Possidius and the brethren with him, Epistle LXXIII.  
[Note: [Col. 1867] Ep. 245 (of uncertain date), Maurist edition.—Collection of three parts, part 2, tome 50, ch. 39.]

Twelfth Part. To paint oneself with pigments [Note: [Col. 1867] “To paint oneself”: the original reads *fucari*.], so as to appear either redder or whiter [Note: [Col. 1867] added: “or more modest”: editions compared with the original.] is adulterous deception [Col. 1868B], by which I do not doubt even husbands themselves [Note: [Col. 1867] absent from the Basel edition.] are unwilling to be deceived; women should be permitted to adorn themselves for them alone by indulgence, not by command. For true adornment, especially for Christian men and women, is not merely the absence of every deceitful cosmetic; it is not even the splendor of gold and clothing, but good character. [Note: [Col. 1867] “not so much any false cosmetic”: Argentinian edition; “not only is there no false cosmetic”: remaining editions; added: “an artificial contrivance”: Basel edition.]

§ 1. The detestable superstition of amulets, which are even hung from the upper parts of men’s ears on one side, is employed not to please human beings but to serve demons.  
[Note: [Col. 1867] “is superstition”: Basel and second and third Lyons editions. “Joints”: Argentinian edition; “at the joints”: Norwegian edition. “Are worn”: original and editions compared with it. “Because they are not”: Basel and second and third Lyons editions. “Are displayed”: Argentinian edition; “are employed”: remaining editions.]

C. XXXIX. That the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Likewise from the Creed of the Ephesian Council of Two Hundred Bishops, held against Nestorius.  
[Note: [Col. 1867] Rather, from the letter of Cyril and the Alexandrian synod to Nestorius.—Collection of three parts, part 2, tome 9, unique chapter. Ivo, *Decree*, part 1, ch. 3.]

[Col. 1868C] Thirteenth Part. Concerning the Spirit, the Lord says in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1867] John 16:14]: “He will glorify me.” [Note: [Col. 1867] “When he also speaks concerning the Spirit”: Hispanic Collection; Ivo. “Glorify”: Hispanic Collection.] Understanding this most correctly, we confess one Christ, Lord and Son, not as though he needed another’s glory, to have received glory from the Holy Spirit; because his Spirit [Col. 1869A] is neither better nor greater than he himself, but because, while performing wondrous works to demonstrate his divinity, he employed the power of his own Spirit, he is said to be glorified by him, just as his own power or any sort of discipline glorifies each person. [Note: [Col. 1867] “Lord” absent from Ivo and the Hispanic Collection. “To need”: Argentinian edition. “Human”: Ivo and editions compared with the original. “To be glorified”: Ivo and Hispanic Collection; “having been glorified”: editions compared with the original. “Since”: same editions; “glorifies”: same and first Basel edition.]

Although his Spirit is in his own substance, and personal distinctiveness is understood insofar as he is Spirit and not Son, nevertheless he is not alien from him. For he is called the Spirit of truth [Note: [Col. 1869] John 16:13], and Christ is the truth. Therefore he proceeds from Christ in the same manner as from God the Father. Finally, this same Spirit, performing glorious miracles through the hands of the holy apostles, glorified the Lord Jesus Christ after he ascended into heaven. For Christ was believed to be God by nature, working mighty deeds through his Spirit; and therefore he said [Note: [Col. 1869] John 16:14]: “He shall receive of mine, and shall declare it unto you.”  
[Note: [Col. 1869] “And his Spirit is understood”: Hispanic Collection. “Hence”: editions compared with the original, except the Argentinian, Basel, and Norwegian editions. “To”: Basel edition. “Is believed”: editions compared with the original. “Existing”: Hispanic Collection and Ivo.]

C. XL. On the same subject. Likewise Didymus, Book II *On the Holy Spirit*, against the errors of the Greeks.  
[Note: [Col. 1869] Collection of three parts, part 2, tome 14, ch. 31.]

The Savior, who is also the truth, says [Note: [Col. 1869] John 16:13]: “For he shall not speak of himself”; that is, not without me and without the will of myself and the Father, because he is inseparable from my will and the Father’s. [Note: [Col. 1869] In the original these words precede: “Then, in what follows, concerning the Spirit of truth, who is sent by the Father and is the Paraclete, the Savior,” etc. Added “is”: editions compared with the original. “Speaks”: Basel, Norwegian, first and second Venetian, and Paris editions. Added “without”: Basel edition.]

And further:

§ 1. Because he is not from himself, but is from the Father and from me. For the very fact that he subsists and speaks is from the Father [Col. 1870A] and me. “I speak the truth,” that is, I inspire the things which he speaks, since he is the Spirit of truth. [Note: [Col. 1869] “From” (*a*): Norwegian edition. “*a me ille est*” (“he is from me”): Basel edition; “*ex me ille est*” (“he is from me”): second and third Lyons editions; “*a me est*” (“is from me”): remaining editions. “That he is, subsists, and speaks”: editions compared with the original. “*a me illi est*” (“it is from me to him”): Argentinian, Paris, and second and third Lyons editions; “*a me ille est*” (“he is from me”): remaining editions. John 16:7.]

But “to say” and “to speak” in the Trinity must not be understood according to our ordinary usage, by which we converse and speak with one another, but according to the manner of incorporeal natures, and especially of the Trinity, which inserts its will into the heart of believers and of those worthy to hear it: this is what “to say” and “to speak” mean. [Note: [Col. 1869] “For”: editions compared with the original, except the Basel edition. “According to customary usage” absent from the Argentinian edition. “And we”: Argentinian, Norwegian, first and second Venetian, and first Lyons editions. “With one another” absent from editions compared with the original, except the second and third Lyons editions. Added “is”: editions compared with the original. Added “or natural”: same editions, except the second and third Lyons editions. “Puts into hearts”: same editions. “And puts it into their hearts”: second and third Lyons editions; “puts it into their hearts”: remaining editions. “It is therefore clear that the Father speaks and the Son hears”: editions compared with the original.]

And below:

§ 2. Therefore, the Father’s speaking and the Son’s hearing—or conversely, the Father’s hearing while the Son speaks—is a sign that Father and Son are of the same nature and that there is agreement in Father and Son. The Holy Spirit also, who is the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of wisdom, cannot, when the Son speaks, hear things unknown to him, since [Col. 1870B] that which is uttered by the Son is itself the Spirit proceeding from the Truth, the Comforter flowing from the Comforter, God from God, the Spirit of truth proceeding. [Note: [Col. 1869] “The Son speaking and the Father hearing, [is a sign] that Father and Son are of the same nature, and of the agreement—and connection and communion—of the Holy Spirit, who is,” etc.: editions compared with the original. “The Son speaking”: same editions, except second and third Lyons. “That is, God proceeding from God, the Spirit of truth proceeding from Truth,” etc.: editions compared with the original. Added “God”: same, except the Argentinian and Basel editions.]

Finally, lest anyone separate him from the will and fellowship of the Father and Son, it is written [Note: [Col. 1869] John 16:13]: “For he shall not speak of himself, but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak.” [Note: [Col. 1869] “Speaks”; “hears and speaks”: editions compared with the original, except the second and third Lyons editions.] The Savior likewise says something similar concerning himself [Note: [Col. 1869] “Speaks”: Argentinian and Basel editions; compare John 5:30]: “As I hear, I judge”; and elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1869] John 19]: “The Son can do nothing, except what he sees the Father doing.” [Note: [Col. 1869] Added “of himself”: Vulgate and editions compared with the original.]

[Col. 1871]

# I. MORE ACCURATE INDEX OF THE CANONS OF THE DECREE

[Note: [Col. 1871] Canons omitted by previous editors have been restored, and the immense mass of errors with which this index of chapters formerly teemed has been removed. In chapters beginning with the same word, several words from each have been added so that they may be more readily distinguished from one another. Finally, the *paleae* are printed in what is called italic type, with an asterisk added to those chapters which, only in this edition and following III Bickell, are designated by the name *Paleae*. Rejected, however, because they seemed to have no use, are the slight and not infrequently erroneous summaries of Gratian’s opinions and the inscriptions customarily repeated since the time of the Correctors.]
